In Double-A, Hence sat 92-96 mph with a fastball that can get great ride up in the zone. He has a history of touching 99 in the pros, so there could be more in the tank. His mid-80s changeup had his best whiff rate, getting 32 misses on 51 swings (63 percent) in the Texas League, and the pitch made some hitters look foolish as it dove arm side. Notably, it also helped him post reverse splits and keep lefties in check. A mid-80s slider gives another above-average look with two-plane break, but he could hang it in the zone, leading Double-A batters to slug .613 off it. He pocketed a curveball that had flashed plus earlier in his career. The 6-foot-1 hurler has still yet to crack 100 innings in a season, and he's been in and out of the Double-A rotation this summer due to various injuries. The stuff is there for him to be a mid-rotation starter, but he needs to prove durability or else it might be worth a look at turning him into a split-resistant reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals made Hence the highest Arkansas prep player selected since 2005 (Travis Wood, 60th overall) when they selected him 63rd in the shortened 2020 Draft. The organization has been cautious with the 6-foot-1 right-hander ever since. First, it limited him to only eight Florida Complex League appearances while they kept him heavily monitored in 2021. Then last season, St. Louis moved Hence to Single-A Palm Beach and originally kept him to a three-inning/50-pitch limit that expanded ever so slightly as the year went on. When Hence did pitch, he was downright dominant with a 1.38 ERA and 41.5 percent K rate in 16 starts (52 1/3 frames), earning him a limited run in the Arizona Fall League. On a pitch-by-pitch basis, Hence looked like one of the most promising arms in the Minor Leagues in 2022. His mid-90s fastball, which touched 99 last year, explodes up in the zone and often leaves batters hacking and swinging below the pitch. As if that wasn’t enough, he’ll drop in an upper-70s curve with bite that gives him another whiff-heavy option below the knees. His mid-80s fading changeup and mid-80s slider give him two more above-average offerings and round out one of the best pitch mixes in the Minors. Hence walked only 7.7 percent of his batters faced in the Florida State League, but the consistency of his command still needs work. That -- and Hence’s limited workload -- are the only knocks against him at this stage. The stuff needs to hold up into the fifth and sixth innings -- and over 100-plus frames overall -- before Hence could be considered a potential ace, but the individual pieces are there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals selected Hence with the 63rd overall pick in 2020, making him the highest Arkansas high-schooler selected since Travis Wood (60th overall) in 2005. He signed for just north of slot at $1,115,000 after showing special velocity in tournaments during the previous fall. Don’t be alarmed just yet by his baseball-card statistics in the pros. Hence pitched only eight games in the Florida Complex League in 2021 as St. Louis wanted to keep him heavily monitored in West Palm Beach. Hence has been incredibly effective in short starts at Single-A Palm Beach this season with a strikeout rate comfortably above 40 percent. Hence has always been pegged for a velocity jump, and that has come in the abbreviated outings this season to the point where he’ll sit 95-97 and has touched as high as 99 per Statcast. He showed a plus slider in high school, but has scrapped it since in deference to a 79-81 mph curveball with good spin and bite. He’s grown more and more confident in a mid-80s changeup with armside fade as 2022 has rolled along, and that pitch too gets a healthy whiff rate. The right-hander isn’t huge at 6-foot-1, but he uses every bit of his athleticism to showcase his electric arm. While he isn’t expected to get taller, he could fill out a little more as he matures, securing his velo gains in longer outings. The building blocks are there for Hence to see a Major League rotation someday, and after a breakout 2022, he could become one of the game’s best young pitchers when his workload increases again next summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest Arkansas prep pitcher taken since Travis Wood went 60th in 2005, the Cardinals selected Hence 63rd overall in 2020 and signed the supplemental second rounder for $1,115,000. The right-hander’s stock rose in the fall when his fastball was clocked at 94 mph during the Future Stars Series in September and followed that up with a 96 mph heater a month later at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship. He made his professional debut in 2021 in the Florida Complex League, where the Cardinals are keeping a close eye on him and building up his arm. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 175 pounds, Hence has a small frame, but makes up for it with a quick arm and natural athleticism. In addition to the mid-90s fastball, he’s armed with a plus slider that reaches the low 80s and has shown a feel for a developing changeup. Yes, he has a small frame, but Hence has a bunch of potential upside and the athleticism needed to remain a starter. Consistently around the strike-zone, Hence has shown the ability to locate his pitches with a smooth, repeatable delivery. If he’s ultimately moved to the bullpen, Hence’s fastball/slider combination may play up a bit and permit him to take on a high leverage role in the back-end of a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adams was signed away from a Michigan State commitment with a $282,500 (sixth-round money) as a 12th-rounder out of the Illinois high-school ranks in 2022. He’s been a steady climber ever since on the strength of his career .423 on-base percentage entering 2026. He was limited to only 64 games with Double-A Biloxi by a left shoulder contusion suffered in June but still managed a 159 wRC+ in the Southern League. Adams made up for the lost time in the Arizona Fall League and thrived in the hitting-rich environment with a .333/.471/.569 line in 16 games. Adams’ proclivity toward hit-by-pitches has become legendary in the Minor Leagues. He’s been plunked 85 times in 272 games since the start of the 2023 season (second-most in MiLB) because of a combination of his large frame at 6-foot-4 and unwillingness to get out of the way. Adams’ OBP has also been fueled by another unwillingness -- one to expand the zone, or in some cases swing at all. The Brewers have tried to work with Adams to get more aggressive on drivable pitches early in counts to increase his overall damage; right now, his power is closer to average, though it’s possible the shoulder affected him in ’25. That’s an issue because Adams has moved across the diamond from third to first on a full-time basis. He’s a better fit there as a big target for his fellow infielders and less of a worry having to snare hard-hit grounders at the hot corner, especially with his below-average speed. Right-right first basemen have a high offensive bar to clear, and it’ll be on Adams to show that he can be more than just an on-base machine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adams was just a 12th-round pick out of Hinsdale (Ill.) Central High School in 2022 but signed for sixth-round money at $282,500. He put himself on the map with a strong first full season for Single-A Carolina, winning Carolina League All-Star honors with a .233/.400/.401 line, 11 homers and 30 steals in 99 games. Playing in his age-20 season last year, Adams put up remarkably similar numbers (.227/.443/.397, 11 HR, 28 SB) in 101 games with High-A Wisconsin and helped push the Timber Rattlers to an appearance in the Midwest League Championship Series. Standing at 6-foot-4, the right-handed slugger makes for a sight in the box with high hands and an interesting leg kick that leads into an extended front side. There is good raw power in Adams’ frame, but he doesn’t play as well into it yet because of high groundball and infield popup rates. The Brewers hope to add more verticality to his swing to get the elevation needed for better pop. But for now, Adams can still scare pitchers away from pitching in the zone (or in some cases into him with an astounding 40 hit-by-pitches in ’24), and while he can be too passive early in counts, that approach has worked to his benefit to this point. Adams has been willing to push the envelope on the basepaths but will likely settle into below-average speed as he matures. He can make it work at third base despite rough actions at times, but he's made the move to first base in 2025. The power and aggression will have to come around more, even as he comfortably clears the offensive standard for every league he's played in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adams was one of the Brewers’ biggest popup prospects in 2023. Drafted out of Hinsdale (Ill.) Central High School in 2022, the infielder signed for the equivalent of sixth-round money with a $282,500 bonus and proved why he was worth it at Single-A Carolina in his first full season. Adams produced a 135 wRC+ over 99 games with the Mudcats -- third-best in the Milwaukee system among Minor Leaguers with at least 400 plate appearances -- while slashing .233/.400/.401 with 11 homers and 30 stolen bases. The right-handed slugger’s at-bats can be a sideshow before he even takes a swing. Standing in at 6-foot-4, he lifts his left leg high during the delivery and extends the foot out straight before stomping down, generating the kinetic energy needed to play into his plus raw power. All the movement also helps with elevation on contact; many of his batted balls (42.2 percent) were fly balls in the Carolina League. Despite all the movement, he’s kept the strikeouts relatively in check in pro ball, and his walk rate continues to pop off the page at every stop he's made, the result of an approach that continues to impress Brewers officials. A below-average runner, Adams was still super aggressive on the basepaths in his first full season and registered a 75 percent success rate. He might continue to slow down as he matures, and while he can make some plays at third base, his lack of range might fit better at first or in left field, where he got some looks in 2023. Tapping into the power will remain the key to Adams’ success in 2024 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: TJ Pre-Season 2026
mlb_pipeline.text: Caceres has done nothing but hit since signing with the Guardians for $300,000 out of Venezuela in 2024, and he's quickly become their best prospect from that international signing class. After slashing .340/.425/.504 in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with more walks than strikeouts in his debut season, he continued to thrive in 2025 as the second-youngest hitter in both the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League (.289/.419/.469) and Single-A Carolina League (.250/.331/.345). Swinging from the left side, Caceres displays a leg kick before unleashing a quick, short swing. He controls the zone well, swinging often but rarely missing, especially against fastballs, thanks to great hand-eye coordination. Caceres posts impressive exit velocities and could add more strength to his 5-foot-10 frame, although he hasn't been able to translate that into over-the-fence power because he puts the ball on the ground too much. The Guardians have played Caceres at all three outfield positions, often bumping him off of center field in deference to better fielders. He has roughly average foot speed and makes quality reads, although he could slow down as he matures. Being able to stick in center would put less pressure on him to hit for power, but his promising hit tool should still play well in a corner, and Cleveland has shown with Steven Kwan that it doesn't want hitters to lose who they are to fit a typical profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Caceres' $300,000 bonus was just the eighth-highest in the Guardians' 2024 international class, he might be the best player in the crop. He exceeded expectations in his first taste of pro ball, slashing .340/.425/.504 and leading the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League's 16-year-olds in on-base percentage and strikeout rate (11 percent). He may be the youngest player in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League when he makes his U.S. debut this year. Caceres takes aggressive uphill swings from the left side of the plate yet has a knack for putting the barrel on the ball. Though he didn't homer in his debut, he did drill 17 extra-base hits in 40 games while producing high-end exit velocities for his age. He uses the entire field well and has no trouble driving the ball in the air, so he could hit for a solid average with 20-homer power once he adds strength and is fully developed. Caceres possesses just fringy to average speed yet will steal and take extra bases when given the opportunity. He has good outfield instincts as well, though he projects to lose a step as his 5-foot-10 frame gets thicker. He divided his time among all three outfield spots in 2024 but fits best on the corners and has average arm strength.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 5’10″, 170 | Bat/Throw: L/L | IFA: $300,000, 2024 (CLE) | ETA: 2028

A left-handed hitter with the potential for above-average hit and power, Caceras was one of the best hitters in the DSL in 2024 before showcasing more of the same in the ACL, earning a promotion to Low-A prior to his 18th birthday. Caceres possesses standout bat speed for his age and good hand-eye; it’s just a matter of converting it at the higher levels.

A somewhat noisy operation, Caceres will start with the bat on his shoulder before getting into a sizable leg kick as he pushes his hands upwards. Caceras gets by on hand-eye coordination and plus bat speed, but if he is able to smooth out his mechanics as he matures, there could be even more in the tank.

His hands can get somewhat wrapped behind him, likely causing his lower half to feel like it needs to leak out early, evident by the toes of his front foot facing the pitcher when he lands from his stride. That can cause him to pull off of stuff away and lose some power, and even then, Caceres ran a 90th percentile exit velocity of 105 MPH with a max of 111.4 MPH in his age 17 season.

With more power and refined mechanics, there could be a lethal combination of hit and power, but if he cannot clean up the mechanics, there could be some challenges against more difficult competition. There’s clearly a great feel for the barrel regardless, running a contact rate of 85% in 2025.

The bat is ahead of the glove or Caceres, who will almost surely land in an outfield corner. He is an average runner with at least an average arm, but showcases enough speed to cover ample ground in a corner as his first step and routes improve.

It’s a projection game with Caceres, but he is easy to dream on between his plus bat speed and natural feel for the barrel. If he can refine his mechanics, there will be even more in the tank, exit velocities-wise–in addition to simply maturing–and he will likely have much more success getting the ball in the air.

With gains in those two departments, plus power is not out of the question down the line.

Even if he does not reach that ceiling, it’s easy to envision at least average hit and game power for Caceres, with his raw pop aiding both departments. There’s plenty of time for the teenager to push towards the loftier outcome as he gets his second taste of Low-A in his age-18 season in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has never been a hitter who was drafted out of the Canadian province of Alberta and made it to the big leagues, though three have been selected in the past two years. The Blue Jays took Tim Piasentin in the fifth round last year, while two went in 2024: catcher Nathan Flewelling to the Rays in the third round and Hartman, the Braves’ final selection of the Draft in Round 20. Atlanta went over slot to sign him for around $340,000 and he provided some solid early returns with Single-A Augusta during his first full season while dealing with some hamstring issues. Right now, Hartman’s calling card is his speed. He is one of the fastest players in the system, recording 30 ft/sec sprint speeds, which helped him steal 48 bases in 54 attempts in 2025. At the plate, Hartman is a left-handed hitter who has displayed solid contact skills overall. He limits chases out of the zone and draws walks, with an understanding that his job is to get on base, but he’s going to have to do a better job against spin as he advances. At the outset, Hartman saw time in left field and at second base as the Braves tried to assess where he might fit best, but he was seeing all of his time in center field by the end of the year, with an arm that still needs work. If he can show he can do a little damage, tighten up some holes in his swing and stick in center, he could be a table-setting type of catalyst if everything clicks.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 6’1″, 185 | Bat/Throw: L/L | 20th Round (611), 2024 (ATL) | ETA: 2029

A blazing runner who made as significant of a power leap as any prospect in Minor League Baseball heading into 2026, Hartman was a diamond in the rough find by the Braves in the 20th round out of the Canada prep ranks in 2024. Now getting more runway in centerfield as well, Hartman has a sky-high ceiling.

After previously featuring more of a slash and dash operation in the box, Hartman improved his mechanics to more effectively engage his back side while loading his hands into a far more powerful position. The improved mechanics paired with added strength helped Hartman tap into what is now plus raw power.

The shift in batted ball data is eye-popping. Within his first 40 games of 2026, Hartman exceeded his 2025 max exit velocity of 108.5 MPH eight times, with a new max of 113.5 MPH. Harman’s 90th percentile exit velocity jumped by more than four MPH. The improved mechanics also helped Hartman slash his ground ball rate by 10%.

Unsurprisingly, the sum of those aforementioned parts is a power breakout in his what is largely his age 19 season at a new level. The swing can be a little bit rigid as he is very geared for pull, leaving him susceptible to swinging over softer stuff down. Hartman also has a good feel for laying down bunts and will steal hits that way as well given his blazing speed.

The hit tool likely lands closer to fringy, but Hartman’s newfound plus raw power and batted ball angles geared for him to be able to get into it makes it reasonable to dream on 30 homer upside. The important variable will be his swing decisions, especially given his intent at the plate. Hartman has a solid feel for the strike zone, but is still learning how to be a bit more selective against spin.

An absolute burner of a runner, Hartman was simply too fast to be splitting time between left field and second base, which the Braves acknowledged by shifting his focus entirely to the outfield and predominantly in centerfield in 2026. Hartman is still getting acclimated to the different reads in centerfield with some inconsistent jumps, but the closing speed is elite, which paired with a plus arm, should give him the chance to be an above average defender up the middle with more reps. At worst, he’ll land as an above average corner outfielder whose speed can allow him to plug in at center.

He already has a good feel for where he’s at on the field and flashes the standout athleticism to complete highlight reel plays. Truly one of the fastest runners in the Minor Leagues, Hartman swiped 48 bags on 54 tries in 2025 and has continued his high volume, high efficiency efforts on the base paths in 2026.

Hartman’s ridiculous leap in his second pro season not only has him set as the top prospect in the Braves system, but also as one of the higher ceiling outfield prospects in the Minor Leagues. There’s checkpoints Hartman still needs to hit, but based on the skill set, there’s 30/30 upside with a chance to stick in centerfield. Suffices to say, if Hartman continues on that trajectory, he will become one of the best outfield prospects in baseball by the end of 2026.

If he doesn’t get there, it’s likely a result of too much swing and miss against secondaries and maybe the reads in centerfield not improving as expected. Even in that scenario, Hartman would have the fall back of a toolsy, but volatile corner outfield option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers used their top pick (36th overall) in the 2023 Draft on the fastest player in the class, signing George for a below-slot $1,847,500. After an inconsistent first full pro season, he earned Midwest League All-Star honors in 2025 after leading the High-A circuit in on-base percentage (.409), runs (93), walks (84) and steals (100). He swiped 42 bases in his final 39 games to become the fourth Minor Leaguer to reach triple digits in the last two decades. If the scouting scale ranged wider than from 20-80, George might earn 100 grades for his speed. He went from the left side of the plate to first base in 3.4 seconds on a bunt in a PDP League game in 2022, and he routinely gets there in less than four seconds on normal balls in play, allowing him to register 40 hits on grounders to the left side of the infield last year. He creates havoc on the bases and covers a lot of ground in center field, though he still has room to improve his reads and jumps in both areas. His arm is below average but playable in center. Los Angeles unsuccessfully tried to help George add a bit of pop in 2024, leading to a 28 percent swing-and-miss rate, but he cut that to 19 percent last season by playing to his strengths. He focuses on getting on base by using a discerning eye and slashing at balls, posting the lowest pull rate (23 percent) and the 10th-highest groundball/flyball ratio (2.93) in the Minors in 2025. That approach yields almost no power and all three of his homers last year occurred from April 13-18, though one came off a 94 mph Chase Burns fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: George created havoc for Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in September 2022, reaching base 10 times in 18 plate appearances and stealing five bases. The fastest player in the 2023 Draft, the Texas high schooler went 36th overall to the Dodgers and signed for a below-slot $1,847,500. He continues to dazzle with his speed and stole 36 bases in 84 Single-A games last year, but there are questions about his bat and impact after he struck out at a 21 percent clip and slugged just .328. Some scouts have joked that George possesses 90 speed on the 20-80 scale, and he got from the left side of the plate to first base in 3.4 seconds on a bunt in a PDP League game in 2022. His quickness enables him to run wild on the bases and cover wide swaths of ground in center field, though he needs to refine his reads and jumps so he could become dominant in both regards. He's a potential big league basestealing champ and Gold Glover, though he comes with a below-average arm. George understands his strengths and weaknesses at the plate, recognizing that he lacks the physicality to be a slugger and should focus on getting on base. Los Angeles has helped him incorporate his legs more in his left-handed stroke and to learn how to pull and lift balls more frequently so pitchers will have to respect him, changes that have produced higher exit velocities but also more swing and miss. He still doesn't drive balls particularly hard and produces a lot of grounders to the left side of the infield, but he can turn those into infield hits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As fast as any player in last year's Draft, George starred for Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in September 2022, reaching base 10 times in 18 plate appearances and stealing five bases. The Dodgers selected him with their top pick (supplemental first round) out of a Texas high school last July and signed him for a below-slot $1,847,500. More advanced as a hitter than expected, he batted .362 in Rookie ball and .381 in Single-A during his pro debut. George raced from the left side of the plate to first base in 3.4 seconds on a bunt in a PDP League game in 2022 and regularly covers that distance in less than four on a normal swing, prompting some evaluators to joke that he's a 90 runner on the 20-80 scale. His raw speed alone allows him to wreak havoc on the bases and cover tremendous ground in center field. The next step will be to hone his reads and jumps so he can become a dominant basestealer and potential Gold Glove defender (albeit with a below-average arm). George repeats his compact left-handed stroke easily and makes consistent contact. He's not very physical and understands his strengths and weaknesses, focusing on making contact and getting on base rather than worrying about power. While he won't ever be a slugger, he did add 10 pounds as a high school senior and Los Angeles thinks he can unlock a bit more pop if he does a better job of incorporating his legs in his swing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former walk-on, Kepley topped Conference USA with 53 walks and 25 steals at Liberty in 2024 and earned all-star honors in the Cape Cod League that summer before transferring to North Carolina. Overcoming a slow start attributed to Tar Heels coaches spreading him out and taking away his leg kick, he led the Atlantic Coast Conference in strikeout rate (7 percent) and finished fourth in NCAA Division I with 45 swipes. Signed for an under-slot $1.4 million in the second round, he broke into pro ball by slashing .299/.488/.433 with 16 steals in 28 games at Single-A. An on-base machine, Kepley repeatedly makes quality swing decisions and almost never swings and misses, especially against strikes and fastballs. He has a relatively flat left-handed swing geared for contact and hits balls where they're pitched, using the entire field. Though he has some sneaky bat speed and strength, he won't offer much power because he produces pedestrian exit velocities and has yet to make much impact with wood bats. Kepley not only has plus speed but also a fine understanding of basestealing that enabled him to pilfer 134 bases in 146 attempts (92 percent) during 240 games in college and summer leagues. His quickness, instinct and energy also translate into quality range in center fieler. Though his arm is below average, it's playable in center and he gets to balls quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario reclassified to the 2020 Draft and was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 71 prospect in the class but went undrafted, in part because of his strong commitment to Miami. He never popped with the Hurricanes as expected, and the Rangers took him in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft as a build-back project. The right-hander took off in pro ball, posting a 2.24 ERA with 129 strikeouts and only 13 walks in 88 1/3 innings at Single-A and High-A; his 33.1 K-BB percentage was the best among Minor Leaguers with at least 80 frames in that 2024 season. Rosario injured his elbow getting ready for Spring Training in 2025, and Tommy John surgery was delayed until 2026. Before he officially underwent the procedure, the Nationals acquired him in January as part of the prospect return in the MacKenzie Gore deal. Rosario and the Nationals now must target a 2027 return to the mound, making him one of the biggest dart throws in prospectdom. He showed a 94-98 mph fastball that touched 100, and his move away from sinking movement and more toward riding action fueled his breakout. An 88-92 mph splitter became his best secondary pitch with tumble that A-ball hitters couldn’t handle. He also discarded a curveball and cutter from his Miami days and focused more on an 83-85 mph slider that flashed plus. The Rangers moved Rosario to the third-base side of the rubber and had him more focused on deception with a more closed delivery, and the improvements in control were astounding on the pro side. But by 2027 (his age-25 season), his early success will be a distant memory, and he’ll need to show his stuff and strike-throwing can return after a lengthy two-year layoff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario rated as a top-three-rounds talent after reclassifying into the 2020 Draft as a Florida high schooler, yet went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Miami. He got pounded for a 6.47 ERA in three years with the Hurricanes before the Rangers took him in 2023's fifth round and gave his mechanics and pitch mix a makeover. The results were dramatic during his pro debut last year as he posted a 2.24 ERA between two Class A stops while ranking first in the Minors in K-BB percentage (33.1 percent) and second in strikeout percentage (36.9 percent) and K/BB ratio (9.9) among pitchers with at least as many as his 88 1/3 innings. But then he injured his elbow getting ready for Spring Training in February and after other health issues, he still couldn't get his needed elbow surgery until 2026. Despite those, the Nationals acquired him as part of the mega-prospect return in January’s MacKenzie Gore trade. Rosario operated at 94-98 mph and reached 100 with his fastball in 2024, and he found more success blasting it by hitters at the letters in pro ball than he did sinking it down in the zone in college. His 88-92 mph splitter was a swing-and-miss pitch with devastating tumble and run at its best last year. He has scrapped the curveball and cutter he toyed with at Miami to focus on an 83-85 mph slider that shows flashes of giving him a third plus offering. After Rosario turned pro, the Rangers moved him to the third-base side of the rubber and had him keep his delivery closed longer to hide the ball better from hitters. He also creates some deception with his flat approach angle and his new mechanics have allowed him to pound the strike zone after he battled his control and command with the Hurricanes. Before he got hurt, he once again looked like the pitcher who intrigued scouts in high school and has the upside of a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seattle’s recent track record on the international market -- from Julio Rodríguez to Noelvi Marte, Lazaro Montes and Felnin Celesten -- has earned the organization the benefit of the doubt when it invests heavily in young talent. And Bautista may be next in line. The Venezuelan outfielder, ranked No. 6 on the 2025 Top 50 International Prospects list, signed for $2.1 million and arrives with some of the loudest tools in the class. Nicknamed “La Bestia,” Bautista is a left-handed hitter and thrower whose raw power immediately stands out. His setup is unconventional -- he rests the bat on his back shoulder before striding -- but the results speak loudly. Evaluators consistently note the elite bat speed and double-plus raw pop. In batting practice and cage work, the ball carries farther and faster than most of his peers, and it showed up in games during his debut, with seven homers in the Dominican Summer League. Beyond the tools, it’s Bautista’s presence that resonates. In the Dominican Republic, he carried himself with a polish uncommon for his age -- mature in his routine, professional in his work habits and advanced in the way he controls the barrel. Defensively, his arm strength rivals his power, giving him a chance to profile in right field long term. But with plus speed and athleticism, he’ll get an opportunity to develop in center field. He’s young and still evolving, yet the combination of physicality, makeup and explosive tools makes him one of the most exciting recent additions to Seattle’s system, and he’s expected to play in the United States for the first time in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners are no strangers to landing big-time players on the international market, from Julio Rodríguez in 2017 to Noelvi Marte the year after that, not to mention Top 100 prospects Lazaro Montes (2022) and Felnin Celesten (2023). The Mariners are trying not to be too excited about Bautista, the No. 6 prospect on the 2025 Top 50 International Prospects list, the Venezuelan outfielder they signed for $2.1 million. Nicknamed \"La Bestia\" (The Beast), he has as loud of tools as just about anyone in the class. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Bautista utilizes an unusual swing and set up, resting his bat on his back shoulder until he strides forward. It's worked for him so far, with elite bat speed and double-plus raw power that he'll be able to continue to get to consistently as he gets more reps. Bautista's arm strength matches his power as one of the strongest in the class. He has the chance to be a plus defender, and he should get the chance to play center field with his plus speed as he gets his pro career underway this summer. He could end up in right field -- his arm and power bat certainly fit there, eventually, but they also said the same thing once about Rodríguez.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: By the time Castillo blossomed physically as a Venezuelan amateur, teams had committed most of their bonus pool money, allowing the Rangers to sign him for the relative bargain price of $647,500 in 2024. He slashed .377/.481/.415 in his pro debut between two Rookie levels and then held his own as an 18-year-old in Single-A at the end of 2025. He has one of the highest floors among the system's position players as well as a high ceiling, especially if his power develops. Even against significantly older competition, Castillo continued to display impressive bat-to-ball skills and an advanced approach. The right-handed hitter has begun to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame, which along with increased bat speed allows him to flash high-end exit velocities. Though he only went deep once in his first 123 pro games, his hitting ability and projectability portend at least future 15-homer power if not more. Castillos' solid speed, quick first step and instincts helped him steal 29 bases in 31 attempts (94 percent) during 88 games last season. His smooth actions, range to both sides, quick hands and solid arm strength leave no doubt that he'll stick at shortstop, and he also looked good at third base last summer. His high baseball IQ and strong work ethic allow him to get the most out of his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A late bloomer physically as a Venezuelan amateur, Castillo signed for $647,500 in January 2024. He would have commanded a higher bonus had teams not previously committed most of their bonus pool money, and he definitely would now after one of the best debuts in the 2024 international class. He batted .377/.481/.415 with nearly twice as many walks (27) as strikeouts (15) in 35 games between two Rookie leagues, hitting his way to the United States after just a month in the Dominican Summer League. With a contact-oriented right-handed stroke and a very mature approach for a teenager, Castillo has some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. Though he had just five extra-base hits (all doubles) in his introduction to pro ball, he has plenty of room to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame and could grow into 15-homer power once he does. His bat speed has increased as he has begun to mature physically and should continue to do so. Castillo has solid speed with a quick first step that should help him steal a few bases. He's a no-doubt shortstop with smooth actions, range to both sides, quick hands and solid arm strength. The Rangers love his makeup and high baseball IQ as much as they appreciate his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After logging an 0.89 ERA, .095 opponent average and 47/7 K/BB ratio as a Tennessee freshman reliever in 2023, Russell came down with shoulder soreness and forearm pain when he tried to start as a sophomore. He had internal brace surgery in June 2024 and was inconsistent in just 25 1/3 innings of work after returning last spring, but his unicorn fastball still intrigued scouts. The Rangers drafted him in the second round and signed him for an over-slot $2.6 million. Russell's heater parks at 93-96 mph and tops out at 98 with an unhittable combination of an exceptionally low release point, wide angle, significant armside run and carry. Hitters repeatedly chase his fastball out of the zone, miss it in the zone and rarely do damage when they do make contact. His low-80s slider features plenty of sweep and grades as a plus pitch when it's on, though it wasn't as reliable in 2025 as it had been previously. Despite using it only sparingly last spring, Russell made some progress with a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink, giving him a viable third pitch. His control hasn't been as sharp since his spectacular freshman year, but he throws enough strikes to succeed in the rotation. He has a ceiling of frontline starter but will have to prove he can hold up and maintain his stuff in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cannarella entered 2025 as a potential top-10 pick, having won Atlantic Coast Conference freshman of the year honors in 2023 and increasing his homer output as a sophomore despite dealing with a shoulder injury. However, his offensive game didn't take another step after offseason labrum surgery and he fell to the end of the supplemental first round, where the Marlins signed him for an over-slot $2,227,425 bonus. The Clemson product made a 22-game cameo at High-A to end the year and posted a slash line of .284/.337/.375. Batting from the left side, Cannarella stands out for his bat-to-ball skills as he stings line drives to all fields. He currently doesn't hit for much power between a lack of physicality and a knack for hitting the ball on the ground, but there's reason to be optimistic that he has more pop in the tank. He has a patient approach and is chasing less than he once did, though further improvements there should enable him to see more balls he can drive. Additionally, the further he is from labrum surgery, the more he'll be able to train properly and add strength. Cannarella's biggest selling point, however, remains his defense in center field. He's a true burner who runs efficient routes and can make highlight plays. Cannarella has long had a below-average throwing arm which seemed even less efficient after the shoulder surgery. The Marlins will thusly be tasked with helping him regain strength and maximizing his speed on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his three years at San Diego State, Carrigg showed off electric tools while touching every position on the diamond at least once between his time with the Aztecs and playing in summer leagues. After the Rockies took him No. 65 overall in the 2023 Draft, he began seeing time behind the plate, at shortstop and in center field while flashing a power-speed combination at the plate. He had a solid first full season with High-A Spokane, but things unraveled a bit with a move to Double-A, even as he still occasionally showed off his pop and wheels. The conundrum with Carrigg has been how to allow him to keep the fire/aggression he plays with while helping learn to turn down the temperature just a little bit. A passive Carrigg won’t be successful, but high miss and chase rates led to a 27-percent strikeout rate in 2025 (vs. a just 8.4 percent walk rate). The switch-hitter has a flatter path and decent attack angle with his right-handed swing, but he doesn’t get that many at-bats from that side. He tends to tinker a lot with his left-handed swing and takes big hacks all the time. With an up-tempo style of play, the Rockies have worked with him on sticking with an approach and staying present pitch-to pitch. Carrigg’s speed certainly plays, with 99 steals over the last two years, and his defensive assignments have been simplified by having him play the outfield exclusively in 2025, while still having him work out on the dirt not in games, and his double-plus arm racked up 18 assists last year. He’s an above-average defender in center, at least, one who has big league regular tools if he can find a little balance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes you can have a Swiss Army knife and realize you don’t necessarily need to use every single thing it can do. That’s what the Rockies are learning about Carrigg after taking him in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2023 Draft. He had spent three years at San Diego State doing just about everything but selling hot dogs, showing flashes of all five tools while playing all over the diamond. He followed up a solid pro debut after signing by leading the High-A Northwest League in home runs (16) and finishing second in stolen bases (51) while whittling down his defensive homes. A super high-energy player who gets some “hair on fire” evaluations, Carrigg is a switch-hitter who makes a ton of contact from both sides of the plate. There was some concern about his aggressive nature and hit tool and how it would translate to this level, but the transition has gone well so far as Carrigg doesn’t strike out much and even drew a decent amount of walks. There’s more pop than many expected, with most of it coming from the left side of the plate to his pull side. He also can turn singles into extra-base hits and doubles into triples -- he led the league in three-baggers, too -- with his plus speed clearly an asset and giving him at least 20-30 potential. With one of the best arms in baseball, there were some who wanted to see if catching would work at this level, but that’s been shelved. He’ll keep getting some reps on the dirt at shortstop to maintain some versatility, but it should surprise no one if he shows up to Coors Field as an every day center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his three years at San Diego State, Carrigg did everything but play first base (including some relief appearances on the mound). His flashes of incredible tools excited scouts even more than his versatility, really jumping on the Draft prospect map when he hit .329 with 15 stolen bases in the Cape Cod League in 2022. That put him on the precipice of first-round conversations, but while he wasn’t bad during his junior year, he wasn’t quite as dynamic and ended up going to the Rockies in Competitive Balance Round B. He signed for $1.3 million and then opened some eyes with a .350/.408/.600 debut between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Fresno. A switch-hitter who can make a ton of contact from both sides of the plate, Carrigg can be a little overly aggressive at times. There were some questions about how his bat would transfer to the pro game, but so far they’ve been unfounded, as he’s been athletic in the box and shown good bat speed with the ability to drive the ball. He’s a plus runner who should continue to be a threat on the basepaths. Defensively, Carrigg has seen most of his time up the middle: at short, in center field and behind the plate. His double-plus arm is an asset in all three spots, as is his athleticism. His best position is center, with the Rockies cognizant that a plus arm is needed there in the vast expanse of Coors Field. He’s constantly on the attack on ground balls at short, and there’s confidence that would play if he got more reps there. He loves to catch, but it’s seen as the third-best option and the Rockies may not want to take his speed away by having him there full-time. Wherever he is, his hair-on-fire style of play should help him maximize his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hagaman redshirted his freshman year at West Virginia and pitched out of the bullpen the next two years before undergoing internal brace surgery late in May 2024. The Rangers took him in the fourth round two months later and signed him for $515,000. Hagaman made his Minor League debut in the Arizona Complex League as a starter in June 2025, got five Single-A starts after that and was traded to the D-backs as part of the Merrill Kelly deal at the Deadline. He rose to High-A after joining Arizona and ended his adventurous year with 12 more innings in the Arizona Fall League. Standing 6-foot-4, Hagaman generates elite extension down the mound and repeatedly exceeded the seven-foot mark in the AFL. That would help his 93-95 mph fastball play up as is, but he also gets really good induced vertical break on the heater, ranging from 16-20 inches. The D-backs believe there might be another tick or two of velo to be found the further he gets from elbow surgery and rehab too. Hagaman increased the use of his 82-85 mph curveball after the trade, and it flashed strong depth and sweep. There’s a tighter, slightly harder gyro slider too, and his 86-89 mph changeup flashes average with good drop compared to the four-seamer. Hagaman walked only 6.1 percent of his Minor League batters faced in his first pro season, though that climbed to 13.5 percent in the desert. He relied on a lot of low-level batters chasing his stuff outside the zone to get there, and it’s a safe bet that’ll happen less against more disciplined hitters. Hagaman still needs to take on longer workloads, both in games and over the course of a season, and how everything holds up will determine his future place in an MLB rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Hagaman redshirted in his first season at West Virginia and compiled 73 1/3 innings over the next two years, mostly as a reliever, before injuring his elbow last April. Though he had internal brace surgery a month later, the Rangers still selected him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft. They used him as a starter when he debuted in the Minors in June and traded him to the D-backs as part of the Merrill Kelly deal at this year’s Deadline. Hagaman’s promising three-pitch mix begins with a 92-94 mph fastball that climbs as high as 98 with plenty of carry and armside run. His best strikeout pitch with the Mountaineers was a tight mid-80s slider that he threw nearly as often as his heater. Considering his relief background and inexperience, he shows surprising aptitude for throwing a mid-80s changeup with fade. An athletic mover with a 6-foot-4 frame and loose arm, Hagaman gets down the mound well and creates plenty of extension. To make it as a starter, he’ll have to improve his control after battling the strike zone in college and in summer ball. He’ll also have to prove that he can hold up and maintain his stuff while handling a rotation workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles used their first two picks on catchers in the 2025 Draft, taking Ike Irish from Auburn 19th overall before selecting Bodine from Coastal Carolina 11 picks later. Bodine proved himself as a hitter throughout his collegiate career, batting .367 as a freshman then hitting .384 in the Cape Cod League, .328 as a sophomore and .318 in his final season, when he led the Chanticleers to a runner-up finish in the Men’s College World Series. Bodine received a full-slot bonus of $3.11 million, played 11 games for Single-A Delmarva then went to the Rays as part of the prospect-laden Shane Baz deal. Bodine is a polished player in every aspect of the game. He’s a switch-hitter who’s an equally capable contact hitter from both sides of the plate. Evaluators rave about his feel for the barrel, praising his consistent ability to square up the ball with both swings. He pairs that with a good feel for the strike zone and a simple approach in which he doesn’t try to sell out for power, instead focusing on gap-to-gap line drives. That obviously limits his power potential, and he’s shown little pop throughout his career, but there’s a chance he could tweak his swing to lift a few more homers. Defensively, Bodine has quick hands and moves his glove extremely well, which made him one of the best pitch-framers in college baseball. That trait should serve him well behind the plate, and he’s earned early praise for controlling the strike zone and handling pitchers. He’s not the best athlete behind the plate, but he has quick feet and good instincts. His arm strength is good enough when paired with his quick release, and he was an effective thrower in his junior season. Between Nathan Flewelling, Bodine and Dominic Keegan, there’s some hope that the Rays will find an internal solution to their long-running issues developing a homegrown catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown homered 13 times in 26 games as a fifth-year senior at NCAA Division II Florida Southern in 2021, then signed for $7,500 as a money-saving 10th-rounder. He crushed Rookie-level pitching in his pro debut, a prelude to a spectacular first full season in 2022 during which he led the Minors in hitting (.346) and OPS (1.060), ranked second in slugging (.623) and sixth in OBP (.437) and totaled 23 homers and 44 steals in 103 games. A right knee injury limited him to two Double-A at-bats, required cleanup surgery that kept him out of the Arizona Fall League and the subsequent rehab cost him the first month of last season. He also battled hamstring injuries and played in just 59 games, slashing .221/.284/.421 in Double-A. Brown offers a stunning combination of physicality and tools, but he also enters 2024 at age 25 with precious few at-bats against advanced pitching. His massive strength and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke creates well above-average power, combining with his plus-plus speed and basestealing acumen (72-for-79 as a pro) to give him 30-30 upside. He has solid range in center field and is a plus defender on the corner, and his average arm plays fine at all three positions. Injuries cost Brown 500 at-bats in the upper Minors and the AFL in 2022-23, and he still has yet to prove he can handle high fastballs and stop chasing breaking balls against age-appropriate pitchers. Those issues and his pull-happy mentality resulted in 37.5 percent strikeout and 43 percent swing-and-miss rates in Double-A last year. He worked on reducing his leg kick and head movement last year and will have to make further adjustments to approach his lofty ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pandemic protocols limited NCAA Division II Florida Southern to 26 games in 2021 and cut down on Brown's exposure, but he homered 13 times as a fifth-year senior and Giants area scout Jim Gabella spearheaded the decision to take him in the 10th round. Signed for a mere $7,500, Brown tore up Rookie ball in '21 before leading the Minors in hitting (.346) and OPS (1.060) while ranking third in slugging (.623) and sixth in OBP (.437) during his first full pro season in 2022. He added 23 homers and 44 steals in 103 games while rising from Single-A to Double-A, though right knee discomfort limited his Double-A stint to two at-bats and led to cleanup surgery that kept him from playing in the Arizona Fall League. Brown will be 25 this season and has dominated significantly younger competition, but he's as physical as any player in the Minors and his tools are real. His massive bat speed and quick right-handed swing create well-above-average raw power and his plus-plus speed and base-stealing savvy contribute to his 30-30 potential. His quickness also translates to the outfield, where he's a plus defender on the corners and solid up the middle, and he possesses average arm strength. Despite his runaway success in his first two years as a pro, Brown will have to prove he can repeat it against more advanced and age-appropriate pitching. He struck out at 26 percent rate in 2022 and can get overly pull-conscious, though he did a better job of using the opposite field in High-A. He does have some holes in his swing, and some scouts wonder whether he can catch up to high fastballs and lay off breaking balls that veer out of the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lightly regarded as a physically underdeveloped California prepster, Forcucci became UC San Diego's top starter by the end of his freshman season in 2022 and looked like a first-round pick when he dominated in early 2024. He blew out his elbow that March and had Tommy John surgery a month before the Draft, but that didn't stop the Astros from making him the highest-drafted pitcher in Tritons history and paying him an over-slot $997,500 bonus in the third round. His recovery has gone slower than expected, so he won't make his pro debut until 2026. Before his elbow gave out, Forcucci dealt with a fastball that parked at 92-95 mph and hit 97 with a nice combination of low release height, carry and armside run. His mid-80s slider with tight spin and good depth graded as a plus offering at its best and was tough on right-handers. He also showed a fading upper-80s changeup that was too firm and a fringy upper-70s curveball. Forcucci has a simple three-quarters delivery that he repeats well, which allowed him to provide consistent strikes throughout his college career. Houston has been patient during his rehab, and he could move quickly once he regains his stuff and feel for pitching. He has the highest ceiling among the system's pitching prospects but also much to prove.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Forcucci flew under the radar as a southern California prepster but emerged as UC San Diego's Friday-night starter by the end of his freshman season. He continued to improve and generated first-round buzz when he dominated in his first five starts last spring, only to blow out his elbow in March and have Tommy John surgery three months later. The Astros still made him the highest-drafted pitcher in Triton history and paid him an over-slot $997,500 in the third round. Forcucci's fastball sits as 92-95 mph and touches 97 with a nasty combination of low-release height, carry and armside run. His mid-80s slider also grades as a plus pitch at times with tight spin and nice depth. He also mixes in a fading upper-80s changeup that's too firm and a fringy upper-70s curveball. With a simple delivery that he repeats well, Forcucci provided strikes throughout his college career and posted a 37/6 K/BB ratio in 25 innings before he got hurt as a junior. He probably won't make his pro debut until late in the 2025 season, but once he regains his stuff and feel, he could move quickly. He's a potential mid-rotation starter with a strong mound presence and a higher floor than most of Houston's mound prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The system that brought you Chandler Simpson has another elite speedster to watch. Bush might not steal 100 bases like Simpson, but he might give him a tough time in a foot race. The son of the seven-year Major Leaguer and 1998 World Series champion by the same name, Bush broke out at Grand Canyon University in 2023 and went to the Padres in the fourth round of that year’s Draft. After a brief stint in Double-A for a postseason push, he returned to High-A for his first full season and got dealt from San Diego to Tampa Bay at the Trade Deadline as part of the Rays’ three-player return for reliever Jason Adam. Bush is big and physical, a pure athlete with natural raw power and top-of-the-scale speed. He has leaned into his wheels and dislike for strikeouts by choking up on the bat, spreading out in the box, putting the ball in play and legging out singles. The Rays encouraged him last year to tap into his explosive athleticism by standing more upright and using a bigger leg kick, but the results were largely the same, as he hit .301 with zero homers and only 20 extra-base hits in 121 games for Double-A Montgomery. They’re still hoping to see him create more elevation with his swing, leading to more extra-base power, but his floor is clearly that of a high-average hitter with patience and sub-20 percent strikeout rates. Bush’s speed plays everywhere, whether it’s at the plate, on the bases or in center field. He stole 57 bases in 114 games in 2024 and 57 more in 121 games last year, not quite Simpson’s numbers but still a huge asset. His wheels also give him a ton of range as a true center fielder, with instincts, jumps and reads to go along with it. His footwork continues to improve, which will be key as he works to get better on balls hit behind him. If nothing else, Bush’s bat and speed give him the floor of a fourth outfielder who can make an impact on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of seven-year Major Leaguer and 1998 World Series champion Homer Bush broke out in a big way as a junior at Grand Canyon University in 2023, batting .370 with a .978 OPS, 25 steals and more walks (38) than strikeouts (27) in 58 games. The Padres selected him in the fourth round of that year’s Draft, gave him a slot-value bonus of $511,600 and pushed him to Double-A for San Antonio’s postseason push. He returned to High-A for his first full season, only to be dealt from San Diego to Tampa Bay at the Trade Deadline as part of a three-player deal for reliever Jason Adam. Bush is built like a young defensive end; a physical specimen with natural raw power and elite speed -- a tick below Chandler Simpson, who practically breaks the scale with his wheels. He preferred to keep his strikeouts down and emphasize his bat-to-ball skills by choking up on the bat and spreading out in the box, crouched over and closed off. That approach worked, as he put balls in play and let his speed work. But the Rays wanted to tap into his size and explosiveness, so they worked last fall to get him more upright in the box, with more of a hand load and a leg kick to unleash his bat speed and turn his strength into game power. Regardless, Bush offers value with his speed on the bases -- he stole 57 bases in 114 games last year -- and his excellent defense in center field. He has a ton of range, and his instincts, jumps and reads have continued to improve. The Rays view him as their best defensive outfielder, and they’re known for having a high bar for center-field defense, having leaned in recent years on speedsters like Kevin Kiermaier and Jose Siri. If his significant swing change takes hold and works as planned, Bush could support his speed-and-defense profile with much more upside offensively than he’s shown so far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the seven-year Major Leaguer and 1998 World Series champ of the same name, Bush was a two-time solid summer performer in the Appalachian and Cape Cod Leagues, but he really made a name for himself as a junior at Grand Canyon, slashing .370/.478/.500 with 38 walks, 27 strikeouts and 25 steals in 58 games. The Padres took Bush in the fourth round, signed him for slot money at $511,600 and then gave him 44 games in the Minors, including eight for Double-A San Antonio during a Texas League postseason push. He spent the start of his first full season with High-A Fort Wayne and was traded to the Rays at the Trade Deadline as part of a three-player return for reliever Jason Adam. Batting from the right side, Bush can get aggressive in the box as he lets his bat-to-ball skills do the work to keep strikeouts down. In college and his first taste of the pros, that approach came at the detriment of his power, and the Padres have worked with Bush on swing changes, beginning with standing up a little taller in the box to let his natural raw power -- which shows up in batting practice -- play in games. Even when he does hit dribblers, his plus-plus speed tests defenses, and he got even more aggressive with his wheels in the Minors, stealing 22 bags in 44 games. That quickness gives Bush ample range in center field, and his instincts out there improved over time in school. It was notable that the former Antelope rotated to the corners in deference to Samuel Zavala and fellow 2023 pick Dillon Head during his time at Single-A, but he was back to the middle of the grass before the trade. He gives Tampa Bay another absolute speedster alongside Chandler Simpson.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: How’s this for symmetry? Needing a reliable reliever in July 2025, the Rays traded the 37th overall pick in the Draft (a Competitive Balance Round A selection) to the Orioles for right-hander Bryan Baker. About five months later, the Orioles traded a haul of young talent -- including de Brun, who they took with that selection -- to get starter Shane Baz from … the Rays. Drawing comparisons to D-backs star Corbin Carroll, another undersized outfielder from the Pacific Northwest, the 5-foot-10 de Brun received an over-slot bonus of $4 million from Baltimore and didn’t play a professional game before he was dealt to Tampa Bay. Don’t let de Brun’s height fool you: He’s still a physical player. He earned attention with his performance on the summer showcase circuit in 2024, then showed up ahead of the Draft with more strength and an improved ability to drive the ball with his left-handed swing. But power isn’t necessarily going to be the key for de Brun. He has a pretty simple approach and stays behind the ball well, allowing him to put the ball in play and get on base, then use his plus speed to wreak havoc on the bases. He’s built well for that, as he has above-average bat-to-ball skills and an advanced eye at the plate for his age. de Brun’s speed also helps him in the outfield, where he has plus range and enough arm to let the rest of his skills carry him as a no-doubt center fielder. He has a big personality -- and a side gig as a musician/producer going by the name of “Lil Slayyy” -- and is highly regarded for his energetic attitude and work ethic. He’ll have to show what he can do on the field as he begins his pro career, but he has the makings of a table-setting offensive player and an impactful defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Baseball Hall of Fame Class of 2026 member Andruw Jones looked like a potential star as an amateur, picking up Gatorade High School Player of the Year honors in Georgia and showing off multiple tools in showcase events. The D-backs took him second overall in 2022 and signed him to a $8,189,400 bonus that remains the club’s highest for a Draft pick. He dealt with shoulder, quad and hamstring injuries early in his career, repeated Single-A in 2024 and headed to High-A Hillsboro for his age-21 season in 2025. He hit .255/.335/.360 with five homers, 28 steals and a 92 wRC+ in 123 games with the Hops. Three full seasons into his career, Jones hasn’t blossomed into the offensive player many hoped he would. He’s been a constant work in progress with the mechanics of his swing, often yanking out early leading to a lot of ground-ball and opposite-field contact. He appeared to adjust to stand more over the plate in the second half of the season, and all five of his homers came after July 1. But of those five, none were true pull shots, and two were inside-the-park jobs. There is still intriguing raw power, but it’s still dulled by the directionality and angles off the bat. To his credit, Jones, like his father, is a stellar defender in center field. With plus-plus speed, he can chase down balls gap to gap, and he’ll pop up in plenty of highlights for his five-star thefts. His plus arm strength gives him another defensive asset, and it’s likely his wheels and glove get him to the Majors in some capacity, likely as a fourth or fifth option on the grass.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Braves star Andruw Jones was more than just a name as an amateur. He looked like a potential star in summer showcases, became Gatorade’s Georgia High School Player of the Year in 2022 and helped Wesleyan (Norcross) win the Georgia Class A private school state title. The D-backs selected him second overall that July and signed him to a franchise-record $8,189,400 bonus. His first tastes of the pros were marred by shoulder, quad and hamstring injuries, and he returned to Single-A Visalia for 2024, slashing .275/.409/.405 with six homers and 21 steals in 109 games. It's been a process getting Jones going offensively. He didn’t chase as much in his second bite at the California League apple, but he also didn’t swing much either -- only Juan Soto (36.9 percent) had a lower swing rate in the Majors than Jones’ at Single-A (38.0). When he did decide to hack, it was too often on the ground and to the opposite field, dulling the above-average raw power he exhibited as an amateur. D-backs coaches are working with Jones on improving the directionality of his swing while not sacrificing contact after he still whiffed on his share of sliders. Entering his age-21 season, Jones remains a special defender in center field, one who can track balls down with plus-plus speed and make tremendous snags when needed. His plus arm strength is another weapon. The typical caution about all development not being linear applies, but Jones will need to start showing more growth at the plate to come close to his cathedral-high ceiling. After a bumpy start to 2025, he started to show mid-season adjustments -- namely calming some of his preswing movements -- that have allowed his natural power to play a little better with High-A Hillsboro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the son of former Braves star Andruw Jones, the younger Jones became one of the most closely followed talents in the 2022 Draft, and he impressed at nearly every stop with his multitool potential before going second overall to the Diamondbacks, who signed him to a franchise-record $8,189,400 bonus. Shortly after, Jones sustained a left shoulder injury during batting practice before he could debut in the Minors, and then he battled quad and hamstring injuries during his first full season last year. When he did get on the field, he slashed .252/.366/.351 with two homers in 29 games at Single-A Visalia. Starting with the positives, which remain numerous, Jones is an easy plus-plus runner who tracks down balls with ease in center field, much like his father did on his way to winning 10 Gold Gloves. The teenager made that defense stand out in his first pro game when he made a Willie Mays-style over-the-shoulder grab in the deepest part of the ballpark. His arm strength will also give plenty for opposing runners to chew on, and if he only had the wheels and glove, he’d still be a solid prospect. Listed at 6-foot-4 and 180 pounds, Jones has ample bat speed and generates solid exit velocities relative to his age and experience. The ingredients are there for at least above-average power. But his bat left something to be desired in the California League as he pushed the ball 48.1 percent of the time to the opposite field while also hitting it into the ground a rough 61.3 percent. Cleaning up the mechanics of his swing (e.g. keeping his front end from leaking out) as he gets farther from the health issues would help in his pursuit of reaching his immense ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of 10-time Gold Glover Andruw Jones, the younger Jones was always going to be a close follow for scouts out of Georgia leading up to the 2022 Draft. The 6-foot-4 outfielder was a consistent showcase standout and then took his game to another level with more consistent at-bats back home. He picked up team (state title) and individual (Gatorade Player of the Year honors) in the Peach State and was considered MLB Pipeline’s No. 1 Draft prospect heading into July. The D-backs selected him second overall and signed him to the third-highest bonus in Draft history at $8,189,400. Before Jones could step on the field in the Minors, he suffered a left shoulder injury in batting practice, and he's battled quad and hamstring issues throughout his first full season in 2023. When healthy, Jones has the potential to be one of the toolsiest players in the Minors. He showed plenty of bat speed from the right side before the shoulder injury, though it's becoming clear the bat will need longer to develop than the other aspects of his game. He had little issue putting the ball in the gaps in high-school showcases, and given his current size, he projects for potential plus power at his peak once he reins in his early whiff issues. He certainly follows in his father’s footsteps on the defensive side. Jones’ plus-plus speed is an obvious asset in center, and he has the instincts to track down balls most would miss. His well-above-average arm strength gives him another weapon from the grass and may aid his own future Gold Glove pursuits. He’s in a system with two other stellar outfield defenders in Alek Thomas and Corbin Carroll, though it’ll likely be years before the trio joins forces depending on how Jones’ bat takes to the pro game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The switch-hitting Perez made big strides in 2021 to earn a promotion from the Arizona Complex League to Low-A Modesto for the final two weeks of the season, hitting a combined .308/.455/.378 (.832 OPS). This followed a strong impression he made in his age-17 season during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019. The Nicaragua native joined the Mariners’ organization the year prior for $175,000. Perez’s on-base numbers are among the best in Seattle’s system, thanks to an incredibly relaxed and confident approach at the plate and solid barrel control. His flatter-than-usual swing path leads to more quiet contact, which is why his power numbers aren’t off the charts, yet he makes up for it with his high average. For that reason, and given how young he is, the Mariners might opt to let that approach be for the time being. While his hitting profile doesn’t exactly stand out for a third baseman, he does have the chance to play there defensively with a huge arm and decent actions. Though some are worried about his range long-term, the Mariners are bullish on his potential to add more strength, grow into more power and fit the corner infield profile long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The switch-hitting Perez impressed in his professional debut during the Dominican Summer League in 2019, slashing .274/.381/.388 with four homers as a 17-year-old. Though he is so young, there is still plenty of room to grow athletically. He projects more as a third baseman, but he’ll need to show more pop at the plate to wind up there long term. His arm strength could even allow the Mariners to move him to the outfield if needed. Though he’s been more effective from the left side, the uber-confident Perez has shown elite bat-to-ball skills that have led to high line-drive and fly-ball rates, thanks to some quality bat speed. His power could be the determining factor in whether or not he remains at third, though the Mariners are bullish on his potential to rake, particularly after getting more looks at him at the fall developmental league in Arizona in 2020 -- his first reps stateside. Entering 2021, the “next step” phase for Perez will be simply playing. He was one of the many victims of the cancellation of the Minor League season, and the Mariners are excited about getting a clearer scope of how he projects by referring to a more tangible representation of his profile that can only be accumulated with playing time in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he had some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the 2022 prep class, Kilen slid to the Red Sox in the 13th round because of a strong commitment to Louisville. After two years with the Cardinals, he transferred to Tennessee and slashed .357/.441/.671 with an 11 percent strikeout rate last spring. A consensus first-team All-American at second base, he signed for $5,247,500 as the 13th overall pick and played in 10 Single-A games before a bruised hip ended his pro debut. Kilen's hand-eye coordination, quick left-handed stroke and feel for the barrel allow him to make contact with ease. His home run output increased from zero to nine to 15 over three college seasons, and while he may not have more than average raw power, his hitting ability enables him to get most of it. He doesn't have any obvious holes in his swing or weaknesses against any particular pitches, and his only real weakness at the plate may be that his penchant for contact cuts into his walk totals. More skilled than tooled up, Kilen has average speed and arm strength. While those traits seem better suited for second base, he spent more time at shortstop in college and the Giants believe he can handle the more demanding position. He does have good actions and instincts, though more scouts outside the organization see him as an offensive second baseman along the lines of fellow Wisconsin high school product Gavin Lux.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a 2023 Draft loaded with high school hitters (outfielders, in particular), Head stood out for his burner speed and contact ability and went 25th overall to the Padres, who signed below slot for $2.8 million. It's been a rocky couple of years since as three separate injuries have limited him to 151 games, including a season-ending hip injury in 2024 shortly after the Marlins acquired Head as part of the return for Luis Arraez. The Chicago native showed off his wheels in his repeat of Single-A with nine triples and 36 steals but slashed just .223/.334/.318. Head's swift legs remain his carrying tool as he'll crack sub-4-second home-to-first times and 31 ft/sec sprint speeds. He's been working on making his speed more functional on the bases too, cutting down on caught stealings and understanding more of the nuances of baserunning. Likewise, he has the potential to be a dynamic center-field defender with elite range, although his pre-pitch hop and technique in the outfield have made him as an average defender. His arm is just middling, but he's working to compensate for it by getting the ball out quicker. Although Head still makes plenty of contact with a sweet left-handed swing and a good approach against secondary pitches, his lack of impact makes his hit tool round down and is a concern against more advanced pitching. Head hasn't been able to consistently get to his top exit velocities (110 mph). His speed and defensive potential give him a high floor as a bench player, and this will be a key season to prove he can hit enough to be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few high school players in the 2023 Draft could match Head's combination of hitting ability and pure speed, which enticed the Padres to draft him 25th overall and sign him for a below-slot $2.8 million. They traded him just 10 months later, sending him to the Marlins as the headliner in a four-prospect package for Luis Arraez. He played in just five games with his new organization before injuring his left hip and requiring season-ending surgery, though he's fully healthy again for 2025. Head possesses at least plus-plus speed and gets top-of-the-scale grades from some evaluators. He uses his quickness to beat out infield hits and should be a terror on the bases once he learns the nuances of basestealing. He chases balls down from gap to gap and enhances his average-to-solid arm strength by getting to balls quickly. After making consistent contact to all fields in his pro debut, Head was much more aggressive and pull-happy before he got hurt last year. A left-handed hitter, he's at his best when he tries to hit balls from gap to gap and focuses on getting base. He's not very physical and won't be a slugger, but he has enough bat speed and strength to hit 12-15 homers per year and be more than just a slap hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An Illlinois high school product, Head exhibited one of the most exciting combos of speed and pure hitting ability in the 2023 prep class. Typical of their willingness to bet on loud tools at premium positions, the Padres took the Clemson commit with the 25th overall pick and signed him for a below-slot $2.8 million. And typical of their willingness to trade almost any prospect at any time, they shipped him to the Marlins 10 months later as the headliner in the Luis Arraez deal. He injured his left hip in June and required season-ending surgery. The 6-foot outfielder instantly became one of the fastest runners in the Minors with elite speed he's able to use all over the diamond. Those wheels make him an impressive defender in center with gap-to-gap coverage, and he's able to gather good momentum to generate above-average arm strength when he needs a cannon. Head should be a stolen-base threat too, and he can also turn infield grounders into base knocks with the way he fires out of the left-handed batter's box. That's good news because Head's power remains the biggest question about his game. While he looked stronger at the dish in front of scouts in his Draft spring, he put the ball on the ground at a 56 percent clip in his brief pro debut. Entering his age-19 season, he has plenty of time to develop more in-game pop and could get to 12-15 homers per season while he lets the rest of his game provide plenty of flash.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending his first two college seasons at East Carolina, Root transferred to Arkansas and became the ace of a team that finished third at the 2025 College World Series. He finished fifth in NCAA Division I with 126 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and offered one of the highest floors among college starters. The Dodgers chose him with their first pick at No. 40 overall and immediately followed with Razorbacks teammate Charles Davalan at No. 41. Root used a low-90s sinker to generate groundball contact in college, but Los Angeles is having him focus on a four-seamer with nasty ride up in the zone that topped out in the upper 90s during offseason workouts. His best weapon is a fading 83-85 mph changeup, though his low-80s curveball is close behind and he topped D-I with 51 strikeouts via his bender last spring. He also employs a mid-80s cutter/slider and mixes his pitches very well. Root creates a lot of deception with an unusual delivery that features a high leg kick and a deep arm swing leading up to a three-quarters arm slot that enables him to stay on top of his offerings. His mechanics don't hamper his strike-throwing ability, though he's not overpowering and sometimes catches too much of the plate.
