Signed for $2,197,500, he'll make his pro debut in 2026 and is a reasonable bet to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jorge stands with Leo Balcazar as two of the more successful prospects to date from the 2021 international signing class. Signed for $495,000 that January, Jorge hit the ground running by posting an OPS over 1.000 in his Dominican Summer League debut and backed it up with two solid seasons in the United States. He hit his first stumbling block in 2024, hitting just .220 with a .685 OPS for High-A Dayton before rediscovering some of his approach, albeit without much impact, in his return to the level in 2025. What kind of player Jorge ultimately becomes is linked to him buying into an approach that works for him. The undersized left-handed hitter is at his best when he focuses on smaller ball: contact, getting on base, bunting, stealing bases. He’s capable of using the middle of the field well with a line-drive approach and got back to some of that in 2025, but as he did the previous season, his ability to get to some power at times can also lead to his downfall in the form of being too aggressive, not taking walks and increasing his swing-and-miss. Initially signed as a shortstop, Jorge first moved to second base as the Reds hoped to keep him on the dirt. He was introduced to center field in 2023 and has grown there so much that he’s no longer going to play the infield and is considered one of the best defensive outfielders in the system. Jorge wasn’t put on the 40-man last offseason but wasn’t taken in the Rule 5 because he’s still a few years away. He still has the chance to be a table-setting type if he can commit to that profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over the early stages of his pro career since signing in January 2021 for $495,000, Jorge had produced at pretty much every stop, from the Dominican Summer League after signing to the Arizona Complex League in 2022 and then in a strong full-season debut that got him to High-A Dayton in 2023. The progress halted a bit in 2024 as he struggled for the first time back with Dayton. He finished with a .686 OPS, though the Reds think there were some signs of positive development at the end of the season before a sprained left thumb ended his year in August. When he's swinging the bat well, Jorge uses his left-handed swing to send line drives to all fields. He'd added strength to his 5-foot-10 frame to provide a little more extra-base thump. But he lost his approach for much of the 2024 season, and while he showed he was capable of reaching the seats to his pull side, he got too pull happy, leading to more strikeouts and fewer walks. He was seeing the ball a bit better in the second half and embracing using the middle of the field more prior to his injury. Jorge has used his plus speed well on the basepaths, with 114 steals over four summers. It also serves him well as he continues to get used to the outfield, something the Reds introduced to Jorge, who initially signed as a shortstop, in 2023. He'll keep getting some ground balls at second base, but look for him more often in center field, where the Reds think he's superior defensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds handed out two seven-figure bonuses to outfielders Malvin Valdez and Ariel Almonte when the 2020-21 international signing period finally opened in January 2021. They doled out a half-dozen other six-figure bonuses that January, and it's been Jorge -- signed for $495,000 -- who has been the best performer to date. He showed off his offensive potential right out of the gate with an OPS north of 1.000 in the Dominican Summer League after signing, performed well in the Arizona Complex League in 2022 and then hit his way from Single-A to High-A in 2023. A left-handed hitter who has added a good amount of strength to his 5-foot-10 frame, Jorge has exhibited a solid overall line-drive approach at every stop since signing. He uses the whole field and can drive the ball to the gaps with some extra-base authority. He has plus speed and he's stolen at least 27 bases in each of his three summers of pro ball heading into 2024. While he was originally signed as a shortstop, Jorge's only chance to stay on the dirt defensively is at second base. He has decent enough hands and instincts to stay there, but the Reds started having him dabble in center field last year. He'll split time between second and center in 2024, with the new spot helping his athleticism play at the upper levels while perhaps providing some positional versatility to get his bat to Cincinnati faster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds signed Jorge out of the Dominican Republic for $495,000 right when the delayed 2020-21 international signing period opened in January 2021. He wasted no time making a strong first impression, finishing with a 1.015 OPS in the Dominican Summer League and landing among the league leaders in a host of offensive categories. He made a fairly strong transition to the United States and the Arizona Complex League in 2022. Small with a compact build, Jorge looks like he might be an impactful offensive player. He's an excellent athlete who plays with a lot of energy. A left-handed hitter with a line-drive stroke, Jorge uses the entire field and can shoot the ball to the gaps, with the chance to develop into an average hitter or better with better strike zone awareness. He's added a lot of strength to his smaller frame, and while he likely won't have a ton of home run thump, there is extra-base power in there. At least an above-average runner, he's aggressive and has good instincts on the basepaths, making him a threat to run. Initially signed as a shortstop, Jorge has shifted over to second base and possesses the hands and instincts to stay on the dirt, though some feel he could end up at third or perhaps the outfield in the future. The Reds think he could be a big league regular at second, one with four solid tools, though it might take a while for him to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Asigen turned 16 years old in August 2025, making him one of the youngest players in this year’s international class, but he also entered the pro side with ample international experience, including a turn with the Dominican Republic’s squad at the 2024 WBSC U-15 Baseball World Cup in Colombia. (He walked 12 times in eight games in that tournament.) After being considered arguably the most advanced offensive player in this year’s international group, he signed with the Mets for $3.9 million at the opening of the window on Jan. 15. A left-handed hitter, Asigen already shows inspiring traits in the box. Despite his age, he’s already posted exit velocities above 110 mph, and using his quick hands, he shows an advanced feel for finding the barrel. He can create loft with his swing that could also help his loud contact translate nicely to the pro side. That said, Asigen did struggle to make contact on elevated fastballs on the outer third of the zone during his World Cup run a year ago, and his overall contact rate will deserve monitoring in the Dominican Summer League and beyond. A plus runner who can flash above that, Asigen has the quick-twitch movements that have enticed international scouts and made many believe he could stick at shortstop long-term. Those wheels could help elsewhere on the dirt if he were to ever move to second or third, but Asigen’s athleticism looks like it will be enough to hold off those chats for at least a few years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torin joined the D-backs organization with a $240,000 signing bonus out of his native Venezuela in January 2022 and has hit his way quickly through the system with a career .281 average and .391 on-base percentage entering 2026, his age-21 season. He slashed .287/.381/.385 with six homers over 122 games for High-A Hillsboro last season and ranked third among all batters at the level with 134 hits. Torin was promoted to Double-A Amarillo for the club’s postseason push in the Texas League, and he’ll head back to the upper Minors ahead of his upcoming Rule 5 eligibility after the ’26 campaign. If you just looked at Torin’s bat-to-ball skills, you’d think he’d be a future plus hitter. He stays straight to the ball with a slightly closed-off stance, unexaggerated load and quick hands from the right side of the box, and the data backs up the mechanics. He made contact on 86 percent of his swings with Hillsboro and sported a 91 percent in-zone contact rate, which would have ranked in the Top 25 among MLB qualifiers. The ball doesn’t come off the bat loud though; Torin set a career high with six homers but doesn’t project for the pop that would get him even double that total in the Majors. A below-average runner, Torin has the right actions and hands to be a defensive asset at shortstop, and his throws are strong on a line across the diamond. If he must move to second base permanently because of a more well-rounded player at the six, he could be a plus defender there. Torin’s lack of impact will be his biggest separator between being a regular on the dirt and a contact-heavy middle-infield option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the D-backs for $240,000 out of Venezuela in January 2022, Torin has continued to move through the ranks of the Arizona system with a strong hit tool and approach. That was first evident in the Dominican Summer League, where he batted .333 with a .465 OBP over 50 games in '22, and he pushed through the Arizona Complex League after hitting .320 with a 9/21 K/BB ratio across 26 games a year later. After a dip with Single-A Visalia in the second half of ’23, Torin returned to the California League for all of last season and finished with a .255/.381/.344 line with four homers, 15 steals and almost as many walks (81) as strikeouts (84) across 108 games. There were 46 players aged 19 or younger to reach the qualifying standard at Single-A in 2024, and Torin ranked among the top six in on-base percentage, walk rate (15.8 percent), strikeout rate (16.4), hits (107) and total walks. As expected for those numbers, the right-handed hitter doesn’t expand the zone much and rarely misses when he does swing, staying straight to the ball. That approach has come with limited in-game impact to this point. Torin does lift and pull the ball but prioritizes contact at the detriment of power. Swinging with more intent could help that improve moving forward. D-backs officials note that Torin looked leaner entering ’25. He was just an average runner at best, but his actions and movements -- as well as his quick throws -- on the dirt portend a possible above-average shortstop. He’ll need to improve his consistency, though, as he can occasionally mishandle playable balls. The D-backs have gotten him some time at second base at each stop, but so much depends on Torin’s impact at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torin joined the Arizona organization in January 2022 and has moved fairly quickly on the strength of some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the entire system. After posting a .465 OBP and 1.85 BB/K ratio over 50 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first taste of the Minors, the infielder shot out of the gate with a .320/.437/.427 line, 21 walks and only nine strikeouts over 26 games in the Arizona Complex League last season, earning a mid-July callup to Single-A Visalia. Results were rougher in the California League, but it was notable that Torin was one of only 16 players to get more than 150 plate appearances at Single-A during their age-18-or-younger season in 2023, joining Top 100 prospects Ethan Salas and Samuel Basallo on that list. Regardless of level, Torin led all Minor Leaguers in that age bracket (min. 250 PA) with his 13.8 percent strikeout rate, and his 8.8 percent swinging-strike rate at Single-A ranked fourth among players 18 or younger at that level (min. 150 PA). That barrel control has been more about protecting the plate than driving balls in the early going, but there’s hope that the right-handed hitter could get to at least below-average power as he adds more oomph behind his hacks. The 5-foot-10 infielder has already shown some signs of physical maturation, and he’s trending toward being more of an average runner. He still shows great actions at shortstop, and while he has more than enough arm for the six, he’s gotten some looks at second base, too, because of Arizona’s deep group of middle infielders at the lower levels. Torin profiles as a potential high-contact, high-OBP option at a premium position, and power will be the biggest decider in his future role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2022 international signing window, eight players got higher bonuses from the D-backs than Torin’s $240,000, but in just one short year, the Venezuela native already looks like the most prominent player of the bunch. The right-handed-hitting middle infielder astoundingly walked 37 times and struck out on only 20 occasions in 50 games in the Dominican Summer League. That not only helped him bat .333 with a .465 OBP, but his 1.85 BB/K ratio ranked fourth among the 1,581 Minor Leaguers with at least 200 plate appearances in 2022. Arizona officials were instantly taken aback by how well Torin controls the strike zone and showed a mature approach by staying in the zone. He tended to make contact when he swung too, which helped keep the strikeouts low and the average high. While it may be notable that Torin didn’t homer in the DSL, the 5-foot-10 slugger can square balls up, and the D-backs believe at least some pop will come as he adds strength beyond his teen years. His decisions to swing only at balls he can drive certainly helps that case. One thing evaluators don't have to worry about is his ability to stick at shortstop, even though he got some looks at second. Torin does a good job of getting to balls all over the dirt, and plus arm strength means he can make throws from deep in the hole too. What’s more, Torin was aggressive on the basepaths (21 successful steals in 27 attempts), and with the new rules, he could continue to push the envelope on that side. His advanced approach and strong defensive acumen have already helped push him from the Arizona Complex League to Single-A Visalia in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top hitters on the international market in 2021, Morrobel landed the highest bonus ($1.8 million) in the Rangers' class. The Dominican ranked in the top eight in all three slash categories (.329/.405/.487) in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in his U.S. debut in 2022, then recovered from a slow start in Single-A last year to slash .342/.402/.405 in May and early June. But he also swung so hard that he injured his right shoulder and required surgery that ended his season after just 37 games. With a quick left-handed stroke and better skills to recognize pitches and manage the strike zone, Morrobel makes repeated contact to all fields. He hits the ball hard but had trouble turning on and lifting pitches in 2023, muting his power. The Rangers hope that increased strength and adjustments to his swing path will allow him to tap into at least average pop. Morrobel has average speed and can steal an occasional base. He spent his first pro season exclusively in center field but has played more on the corners the last two years and fits best in right. He has solid arm strength and registered six assists in 34 games in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better hitters in the 2021 international class, Morrobel signed for $1.8 million out of the Dominican Republic. He made his U.S. debut last summer, finishing in the top eight in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in all three slash categories at .329/.405/.487. He earned a late promotion to Single-A at age 18 and returned to that level this year before shoulder surgery ended his 2023 season after two months. Morrobel has advanced bat-to-ball skills, making consistent contact to all fields with his quick left-handed swing. He recognizes pitches and controls the strike zone better than most players his age. He gained strength and worked on adding lift to his stroke during the offseason, moves that could help him gain 20-homer power as he further develops. After playing exclusively in center field during his pro debut, Morrobel divided his time nearly equally among all three outfield positions last year. With average speed and solid arm strength, he fits best in right field. He'll need to realize his power potential to profile as a regular in right, or else he could be more of a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top player in the Rangers' 2020-21 international class, Morrobel signed for $1.8 million out of the Dominican Republic. Like Evan Carter, the club's surprise second-rounder in the 2020 Draft, Morrobel could develop solid tools across the board after going relatively unhyped as an amateur. He made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, batting .270/.395/.411 with 18 extra-base hits and eight steals in 51 games. Morrobel has a quick left-handed stroke and advanced approach that allow him to make repeated contact. He has uncanny bat-to-ball skills for such a young player and shows the ability to make adjustments at the plate. He walked more than he whiffed in his debut and already shows a knack for launching balls in the air to his pull side, which could translate into 20 or more homers per season once he adds some needed strength. Morrobel has solid speed but probably will become more of an average runner once he matures physically. He broke into pro ball as a center fielder and will have to maintain most of his quickness and hone his instincts in order to remain there. His plus arm and offensive ability easily would fit the right-field profile should he have to shift to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The jewel of the Rangers' 2020 international class, Morrobel signed for $1.8 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021. He's somewhat similar to Evan Carter, their surprise second-round pick in the 2020 Draft, in that it's possible he could develop solid tools across the board but didn't receive a lot of hype before turning pro. He made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League this summer. Morrobel has a track record of producing in game situations with a quick left-handed swing and a mature approach. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate and makes consistent hard contact. He also has the bat speed and projectable strength to provide 20 or more homers on an annual basis. Presently a solid to plus runner, Morrobel figures to have more average speed once he fills out. He'll begin his pro career in center field and will have to maintain most of his present quickness and improve his reads and routes to stay there. If he has to move to a corner, his plus arm and his offensive upside make him a natural fit in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain $10,000 signing from the Dominican Republic in 2019, Santos made some mechanical adjustments after getting rocked in High-A in 2023. He took off the following year, leading the system in wins (11) and strikeouts (138 in 110 1/3), appearing in the Futures Game, reaching Double-A and grabbing a spot on the Rangers' 40-man roster. He made just two starts in Double-A in 2025 before a stress reaction in his back sidelined him for four months, though he returned for the end of the season and the Arizona Fall League. Santos maintained a quality fastball during his rough 2025, sitting at 95-97 and touching 100 with impressive carry and armside run, though his secondary pitches regressed a bit. His tight mid-80s slider was merely an average offering rather than the plus weapon it was the season before. His slightly harder changeup tumbled at times but lacked consistency. Santos isn't very physical and has never pitched more than 110 1/3 innings in a season, so he still needs to prove he can hold up as a starter. His athleticism helps his cause, as does his ability to provide reliable strikes from a low release height. If he can refine his fastball command and hone his slider and changeup, he could be a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, Santos had his pro debut delayed until 2021 by the pandemic but progressed nicely until getting tuned up for a 6.29 ERA at High-A in 2023. He made some mechanical adjustments at the end of that season that paid off with a breakout last year between that level and Double-A. He led the system in wins (11) and strikeouts (138 in 110 1/3 innings), pitched in the Futures Game and claimed a spot on the the Rangers' 40-man roster. Santos' fastball added a couple of ticks of velocity in 2024, sitting at 94-96 mph and maxing out at 98 with natural cut and ride. He also tightened his mid-80s slider into a legitimate plus offering that he can throw by hitters in the zone or get them to chase. His mid-80s changeup isn't as reliable as his other two pitches, but it plummets at the plate when it's working right. Santos is just 6 feet tall and lacks physicality, but he's athletic and provides plenty of strikes from a flat approach angle. He surrendered eight homers in 10 Double-A starts, mostly on heaters that he didn't locate high enough in the zone. Once he refines his fastball command and changeup consistency, he could be a mid-rotation starter. After making just two starts for Double-A Frisco this season, Santos landed on the IL in June due to a stress reaction in his back and is expected to be out indefinitely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lalane received the highest bonus of any pitcher in the Yankees' 2020-21 international class, signing for $350,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He spent his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before making his U.S. debut in 2023, when he was as impressive as any mound prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He struck out 34 and walked just four in 21 2/3 innings. Lalane has the potential for three plus pitches, beginning with a fastball that parks at 93-95 mph and touches 97 with running action and good carry up in the strike zone. He has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades at the plate. His change is more consistent than his slider, though the latter still misses bats and sits around 80 mph. Despite being young and 6-foot-7, Lalane does a nice job of keeping his long limbs in sync and repeating his delivery to throw strikes. He shows the makings of solid command and features a low release point that belies his height and adds to his deception. While he'll need time to reach his ceiling, he has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the former St. Francis and European pro basketball forward of the same name, Lalane was born in the Bronx, moved back to his dad's native Dominican Republic as a youngster and played the outfield before taking up pitching at age 14. He signed for the largest bonus ($350,000) the Yankees gave to a pitcher in their 2020-21 international class, then opened eyes in his U.S. debut in 2023, when he was the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He looked great in two shutout innings against the Blue Jays during Spring Breakout last March, but shoulder issues restricted him to just 12 1/3 frames during the regular season. When healthy, Lalane demonstrates the potential for three plus pitches with possibly control to match. His fastball can sit at 93 mph and touch 97, though it could use more armside run and carry to keep it off barrels against more advanced hitters. He has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks, while he's still learning to harness a sweeping 78-82 mph slider. The 6-foot-7 Lalane inherited size and athleticism from his father, and he does a fine job of keeping his long limbs in sync to repeat this delivery and pound the strike zone. His big frame offers some natural extension, and his low release height provides extra deception. While he has a huge ceiling, he also worked just 123 2/3 innings -- and just six above Rookie ball -- in his first four years as a pro and will be Rule 5 Draft-eligible after this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in the Bronx, Lalane is the son of former St. Francis and European professional basketball forward of the same name. He moved back to his dad's native Dominican Republic as a youth and played the outfield before moving to the mound at age 14. The recipient of the largest bonus ($350,000) of any pitcher in the Yankees' 2020-21 international class, he made his U.S. debut last year and stood out as the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He missed the first half of the 2024 season with shoulder issues. Lalane could have three plus pitches when he's a finished product, starting with a fastball that sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 with plus arm-side run and carry up in the zone. He already demonstrates advanced feel for a fading mid-80s changeup that's his more reliable secondary offering at this point. His 78-82 mph slider has a lot of lateral action, but he doesn't command it as well as his other two pitches. The 6-foot-7 Lalane has inherited his father's height and athleticism, and he has the body control to keep his long limbs in sync and repeat his delivery. He pounds the strike zone, shows the makings of solid command and works from a low release height that creates deception. He'll need time to develop but has a huge ceiling as a potential frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Houston was Wake Forest’s starting shortstop for three years straight, earning the job as a freshman because of his glove in 2023, then slowly developing his offensive game to turn into a legitimate Draft prospect in 2025. A swing overhaul allowed him to get to more impact as a junior and his 15 homers with a 1.055 OPS enabled him to land in the middle of the first round with the Twins, who signed him for $4.5 million. He got his professional feet wet with 24 games split between Single-A Fort Myers and High-A Cedar Rapids. A 6-foot-3 right-handed hitter, Houston has continued to work on his swing path since joining the Twins. He’s always controlled the zone well, with nearly as many walks as strikeouts with the Demon Deacons, and he has long had a contact-over-damage approach. That started to change in his last college season and he’s worked with the Twins to find better line drive angles and barrel the ball more without selling out for power. Adding strength and muscle this offseason could help answer questions about future impact. If Houston can be an average hitter with fringy pop, he has the chance to play in the big leagues for a long time. He’s at least a plus defender at shortstop, with impressive actions and plenty of range to both sides. He has more than enough arm for the premium position as well, giving him a very high floor with a chance to move quickly through the Twins system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers grabbed the top Venezuelan prospect in three straight international classes: Diego Cartaya in 2018, Luis Rodriguez in 2019 and Diaz in 2020-21. Diaz commanded a $2,697,500 bonus with his potential for solid or better tools across the board. Beset by nagging injuries in his 2021 pro debut, he batted just .232/.308/.354 in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, and he has had swing-and-miss issues in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League this year. Scouts who saw Diaz as an amateur thought he had the upside of a .280 hitter with 20 homers per season. He has a quick right-handed stroke and some aptitude for driving the balls in the air, but he tries to launch nearly every pitch he sees and chases way too many of them out of the strike zone. He'll need to tone down his swing and improve his plate discipline and may have to repeat the ACL in 2023. Diaz has plus speed that presently translates more into range at shortstop than stolen bases. He's a gifted defender at short with smooth actions and plenty of range and arm strength. He'll need time to develop but still has one of the higher ceilings among Los Angeles' position prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers landed the top Venezuelan prospect in each of the last three international classes, including signing Diaz for $2,697,500 in January. He comes from the same training program (Alexis Quiroz's AQ Sport Agency) that also spawned Dodgers catching prospects Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. He had one of the more advanced bats in the 2020 international crop and has the potential to develop solid or better tools across the board. With a quality right-handed swing and an advanced ability to recognize pitches, Diaz makes hard contact to all fields. He also has plenty of bat speed and loft in his stroke, and he could become a 20-homer threat as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. His speed enhances his offensive profile, as he has been clocked at 6.4 seconds in the 60-yard dash and shows promise as a basestealer. Diaz has the athleticism, quickness and arm to play several positions, though there's no reason he should have to move off shortstop. He has smooth actions and covers plenty of ground, projecting as a possible plus defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As they’ve reemerged into the international market in recent years, the Orioles have proven more prone to sign position players to large bonuses than pitchers. As such, the $150,000 they used to sign Mejia out of the Dominican Republic in 2024 represents one of the biggest bonuses the current front office has bestowed upon a hurler. He racked up 97 strikeouts across his first 68 professional innings in the Dominican and Florida Complex Leagues in 2024 and '25, then flashed triple-digit radar readings in three starts with Single-A Delmarva. It might not be long until Mejia proves more than worthy of that initial investment. The 6-foot-3 righty features electric stuff, easily overpowering lower-level hitters with a fastball that cranks up to 102 mph with arm-side run. His best secondary offering is a hard, gyro-like slider he can snap in the low 90s, and he also throws a firm, developing changeup in the low 90s that is still a work in progress despite good action. Mejia throws from a low, three-quarters slot and is getting better at repeating his delivery, which should lead to improved command as he gains experience. Bettering that command could be critical -- he’s walked more than five per nine in his brief career -- in determining how high Mejia’s ceiling actually is. Just 19 for all of the 2026 season, he still offers plenty of projection, both in terms of size, strength and ability. But there is a ton to dream on here, given his tantalizing combination of age and eye-popping raw stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mayer earned all-conference recognition in both of his seasons at St. Charles (Mo.) CC and Appalachian League Pitcher of the Year honors in the summer of 2021 in between, but he lost all off of 2023 recovering from Tommy John surgery after transferring to Missouri. While he posted a 6.58 ERA in his return to the mound, his pitch data enticed the Astros to take him in the 16th round in 2024 and give him every penny they could ($175,812) without exceeding their bonus pool by more than 5 percent, which would have cost them a future first-rounder. Houston named him its 2025 Minor League Pitcher of the Year after he reached Double-A in his first pro season while logging a 4.11 ERA and 112/27 K/BB ratio in 87 2/3 innings between three stops. Mayer went from averaging 91 mph with his fastball as a redshirt junior to dealing at 91-94 and touching 96 a year later, missing bats with explosive carry coming out of a low release height. He shapes a pair of solid breaking balls as well: an upper-70s curveball with downer break that works against both lefties and righties, and a sweeping low-80s slider. His mid-80s changeup lags well behind his other offerings but features some nice sink at its best. The best pitching prospect in the system, Mayer has done a better job of throwing strikes and getting empty swings with his secondary pitches than he did at Missouri. He works from a three-quarters slot with good extension and average control and command. No one finds bargain pitchers better than the Astros, who may have unearthed a mid-rotation starter with the 493rd overall pick in the 2024 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mayer sandwiched all-conference honors in both of his seasons at St. Charles (Mo.) CC around Appalachian League pitcher of the year accolades in the summer of 2021, but he missed all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery after he transferred to Missouri. Though he posted a 6.58 ERA in his return to the mound last spring, the Astros liked his pitch data enough to take him in the 16th round and give him every dollar they could ($175,812) without forfeiting a future first-rounder for exceeding their bonus pool by more than 5 percent. His name began getting mentioned in trade requests after he made three Single-A appearances in his pro debut. After averaging 91 mph with his fastball during the spring, Mayer worked at 94-96 mph with explosive carry coming out of a low-release height during his brief introduction to pro ball. He creates good shapes on his secondary pitches as well, highlighted by an upper-70s curveball with downer break. He also has a sweeping 82-85 mph slider and a changeup with similar velocity and some fade and depth when it's on. Excited about the potential to improve the quality and usage of Mayer's arsenal, Houston plans to develop Mayer as a starter. To make it in the rotation, he'll have to do a better job of landing his secondary pitches in the zone and missing bats when he does than he did at Missouri. He has a strong 6-foot-3 frame that should lend itself to durability and works from a three-quarters arm slot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It would have been fair to look at Nichols’ numbers at Arizona and wonder what the Rays saw in the 6-foot-5 right-hander. He bounced between roles as a freshman, made 16 starts with a 5.50 ERA as a sophomore then put together an unsightly 8.27 ERA and 1.60 WHIP in his Draft year. Nevertheless, Tampa Bay selected him in the sixth round in 2023, gave him a roughly slot bonus of $304,800, believing his stuff was better than his results. He pitched well in his full-season debut for Single-A Charleston in 2024 then broke out as their Minor League Pitcher of the Year last season, going from High-A Bowling Green to Double-A Montgomery while posting a 2.90 ERA with 156 strikeouts in 133 2/3 innings. Nichols throws hard, sitting between 95-97 mph and touching 99 with his fastball, but the pitch was hit hard when he threw it down in the zone (as he often did in college) because it doesn’t have any particularly special movement. It improved when he learned to harness it at the top of the zone and became a big two-strike offering for him, generating a 25 percent whiff rate in the Minors last year. He complements his heater with two secondary pitches -- a mid-80s slider and a mid-80s changeup -- and both improved as putaway offerings last year. The slider produced a 35 percent whiff rate with two strikes, and his changeup checked in at 38 percent in those situations. The slider breaks well on both planes, and the changeup is mostly effective due to the roughly 10 mph velocity gap with his fastball. The challenge for Nichols will be keeping his fastball at the peak performance level he reached last year, because he’s run into issues leaving pitches in the heart of the zone. But what he did last season should provide an enormous boost of confidence in his ability to stick as a starter. He cut down on his walk rate, issuing free passes to only 30 of the 524 batters he faced, and he continued to fill up the zone with all three of his offerings. Another season that goes anything like last year could accelerate his path to Tampa Bay’s big league staff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Once viewed as a potential top-five pick out of high school, Watson fell to the No. 16 pick in 2021 -- and was traded to the Guardians two years later -- in part due to makeup concerns. He's had a winding path through the Minors but has shown flashes of the talent that earned him a $4,540,790 bonus. Watson reached Triple-A for the first time at age 22 and put together his best campaign yet, with a .250/.346/.467 slash line, 16 homers and 17 steals. The North Carolina native is a dynamo athlete at 5-foot-9 and displays plus raw power from the left side with a quick, lofted swing that's geared for extra bases. That power comes with plenty of whiffs, though, especially against secondary pitches, and the team is working to improve his approach, especially as he gains more access to information on how teams attack him. He did make notable strides in being more selective and making better contact upon his promotion to Triple-A. Watson has also struggled against southpaws, which could point to a platoon role if his bat-to-ball skills don't continue to develop as hoped. After coming up as a shortstop and moving around the infield, Watson spent an entire season in the outfield for the first time in 2025 and looked like a viable center fielder. He made dramatic progress throughout the season and displayed great reads for someone with little experience. He has enough arm to play anywhere in the outfield, and his plus straight-line speed is an asset there -- he's also working to utilize his speed better on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A candidate to go No. 1 overall to the Pirates on a below-slot deal in the 2021 Draft, Watson instead dropped to the Marlins at No. 16 amid signability and makeup worries and landed an over-slot $4,540,790 bonus. His first full pro season was a struggle, as he hit .232/.296/.395 with a 35 percent strikeout rate and got demoted for a month after making a threatening gesture toward an umpire. He posted similar numbers in 2023, when the Guardians bought low on him in an August trade that sent Josh Bell to Miami. Watson still has the physical tools and the upside of a 25-25 shortstop that made him a first-round pick. He has a smooth left-handed swing, some of the best bat speed in the system and plus raw power. He also can flash well-above-average speed and show off plus arm strength at his best. The question is whether Watson can translate those tools into skills and approach his ceiling. He made some progress with his discipline in 2023 but still gets out of control at the plate, chasing pitches and not keeping his upper and lower halves in sync. He covers ground at shortstop but is erratic there, looks much more comfortable at second base and probably will get some time in center field this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A candidate to go No. 1 overall in the 2021 Draft on a below-slot deal to the Pirates, Watson instead slipped all the way to the Marlins at No. 16 amid signability and makeup concerns. Signed for $4,540,790, he batted .232/.296/.395 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in Single-A during his first full pro season and was demoted for a month after making a threatening gesture toward an umpire in July. He was posting similar numbers in High-A this year before Miami shipped him and Jean Segura to the Guardians for Josh Bell at the Trade Deadline. Watson still possesses the physical ability that enchanted the Marlins. He has a smooth left-handed swing, plenty of bat speed and sneaky strength that lead to at least solid raw power and well-above-average speed. But he won't come close to realizing his potential if he can't learn to make better swing decisions and stop getting himself out at the plate, and he also needs to do a better job of controlling his emotions. An explosive athlete, Watson has the quickness to be a dynamic basestealer and cover plenty of ground at shortstop. He has nice infield actions and plus arm strength but needs to develop more consistency after making 14 errors in 51 games at short last season. He was more reliable at second base and that also has been the case in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson was a candidate to go No. 1 overall to the Pirates on a below-slot bonus as well as a consensus top-10-pick talent last July, but he dropped all the way to the Marlins at No. 16 when his signability became a factor due to the slide. Miami signed him for $4,540,790, the largest bonus it has ever given a high-school position player, but his first full pro season has gone poorly after a strong April. He has struck out in nearly 40 percent of his plate appearances, and the Marlins sat him down for three weeks for gesturing at an umpire. Listed at just 5-foot-9 and 178 pounds, Watson plays much bigger than that at the plate thanks to an abundance of bat speed and a take-no-prisoners left-handed stroke. But after he had a history of making consistent hard contact as an amateur despite his aggressive mentality, his approach has been exploited by Single-A pitchers and he has yet to show he can make adjustments. He has plus raw power that could produce 20 or more homers per season if he can improve his hittability and turn on more pitches. Watson is an explosive athlete who can use his well-above-average speed to wreak havoc on the bases. He has all the attributes needed to play a solid shortstop, including smooth actions, range to both sides, arm strength and keen instincts, and he just needs to develop consistency that should come with experience. He has the athleticism to play almost anywhere on the diamond and also has seen action at second base this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals were down $500,000 in their international spending pool for 2024 after signing Willson Contreras the previous offseason, but they still managed to bring in a pair of interesting talents that year in Top 100 prospect Rainiel Rodriguez and Padilla, who signed for $760,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He and Rodriguez were both Dominican Summer League midseason All-Stars that year with Padilla posting a .287 average and a .795 OPS in 35 games. He headed stateside for 2025 and slashed .283/.396/.367 with seven extra-base hits, 24 steals and a 21/18 K/BB ratio across 38 games. A switch-hitter, Padilla has spent significantly more time as a lefty hitter at this early stage in his career, and the experience shows in the results with better impact coming from the left side. His overall contact rate took a nice jump with his move to the Florida Complex League, but coincided with less swinging overall, including on drivable pitches over the plate. Balancing out those decisions should be a priority higher up the chain. Padilla will flash good exit velocities for his age, including a 102.1 90th-percentile EV in the FCL, but he needs to improve his angles by cutting down on ground balls and easy-out infield popups. With plus wheels, Padilla is always a threat to steal bases and his athleticism, which includes a plus arm, has kept him locked in at shortstop to this point. He still requires development to remain at the six, but if he fills out with more strength, he could slide over to third where he’d handle the throws well. Everything hasn’t quite clicked into gear for Padilla yet, and there’s a chance some of his skills could backslide in full-season ball. But he still has everyday upside at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals weren’t massive spenders at the opening of the January 2024 international window -- they were down $500,000 in pool money due to Willson Contreras’ signing the previous offseason -- but they still might have managed to sign a potential star in Padilla for $760,000 out of the Dominican Republic. The shortstop slashed .287/.391/.404 with one homer, four triples, five doubles and 22 steals in 35 games. He was named a Dominican Summer League midseason All-Star alongside fellow Top 30 talent Rainiel Rodriguez. A switch-hitter, Padilla saw a lot more time from the left side than the right, where he only got 24 plate appearances and went 2-for-18 (.111) with five walks. That’s a sample-size issue but something worth monitoring as he heads stateside. His overall contact rate was solid, and he’s already shown a willingness to take his walks against wild DSL arms. His power was limited to the gaps in ’24. Optimistic evaluators expect he’ll get to at least average in-game pop as he fills out his frame, while others are concerned he’s behind the curve when it comes to current raw power. Padilla can fly, though, and he can turn those balls to the gaps into doubles and triples with ease. He’s also a constant stolen-base threat, and he uses those wheels well with his promising range at shortstop. His plus arm strength gives him another defensive weapon, and while there’s always a chance he could slide to third, those concerns are quieter now than when he signed. The best farm systems are built around high-quality shortstops, and after graduating Masyn Winn in 2024, the Cardinals could have their next one at the six in Padilla.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After growing up in Iowa, Gamble attended IMG Academy tennis and baseball camps in Florida during the summer. But his baseball talent stood out, and he was invited to come year-round for high school. Gamble evolved into a Draft prospect at IMG and played against premium competition before the Royals took him No. 23 overall in the 2025 Draft, signing him away from a Vanderbilt commitment with a $3,997,500 signing bonus. Gamble made his unofficial pro debut in 2025 playing in Bridge League games and then the instructional league at the club's complex in Arizona. The Royals drafted Gamble as an athletic, toolsy hitter, but he showed up in the spring already taller, leaner and with more strength than what he had in the fall. His left-handed swing is smooth and direct, with good bat speed and a knack for finding the barrel. He’s finding more and more power as he gains strength, and he has a good understanding of the strike zone. Gamble is a plus runner with the instincts to be a basestealing threat, and that speed will help him in center field. He’s probably more natural in the outfield, but he’ll likely get reps in the infield this season too. Gamble has an above-average arm that helps him wherever he plays. Evaluators rave about Gamble’s makeup as a competitor and leader. He should be headed for a full-season debut in 2026 at Single-A Columbia, and the Royals will take their time with his development. But they feel Gamble, as well as fellow top 2025 draftee Josh Hammond, are major reasons why the farm system has become more athletic recently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tiger played three seasons at Butler County (Kan.) CC sandwiched around a one-year sabbatical, setting school records for career wins (21) and strikeouts (243) as well as single-season whiffs (121). The highest pick in Grizzlies history as a seventh-rounder in 2023, he starred in Spring Breakout the following March, missed the first two months of the season with elbow inflammation and then returned to pitch well and reach High-A before his elbow gave out in August. Internal brace surgery a month later cost him all of him 2025 but he's fully healthy for this season. Before he got hurt, Tiger's fastball sat at 94-97 mph and touched 100 with good carry but just modest life, and he held his velocity deep into games. He also could overpower hitters with an upper-80s slider that climbed to 92 mph and featured two-plane depth, though it was more of a chase pitch than something he could trust to land for strikes. The Rangers had him scrap his mid-80s changeup after he turned pro, replacing it with a promising upper-80s splitter. Tiger's athleticism and clean delivery translate into decent control, though his lack of fastball movement and overall deception means he can get hit hard when his command is off. Texas has discussed giving him a curveball to use as a non-power offering, but his elbow issues put that plan on hold. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but is also 25 years old with just 50 innings of pro experience, so the Rangers could be tempted to expedite him as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 60 | Splitter: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Tiger spent the shortened 2020 season at Butler County (Kan.) CC, left school in 2021, then returned for the next two years. He set Grizzlies records for single-season (121) and career (243) strikeouts, as well as career wins (21) in 2023 and became the highest pick (seventh round) in school history. He dazzled during Spring Breakout last March, missed the first two months of the season with elbow inflammation, then compiled a 2.93 ERA with 59 strikeouts in 46 innings at three stops. But his elbow gave out in August, requiring internal brace surgery in September that will sideline him for all of 2025. A healthy Tiger can blow hitters away with a four-seam fastball that sits at 94-97 mph and tops out at 100 with quality carry but modest life, and he holds his velocity deep into games. His upper-80s slider hits 92 mph and misses bats with its two-plane depth, though it’s more of a chase pitch than one he can land regularly for strikes. After he turned pro, Texas had him dump a traditional mid-80s changeup and add a promising upper-80s splitter. Tiger’s athleticism and clean delivery give him decent control, though his lack of fastball life and overall deception means his stuff can get hit harder than it should if his location is off. The Rangers considered having him try a curveball to give him a non-power pitch, but his elbow issues scrapped that plan, at least for 2024. He has the upside of a No. 3 starter but he’ll also be 25 with just 50 innings of pro experience when he returns next year, so he could get expedited as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tiger began his junior college career at Butler County (Kan.) CC during the shortened 2020 season, was out of school in 2021 and then returned for the next two years. He set school records for single-season (121) and career (243) strikeouts as well as career wins (21) in 2023 and became a rare 22-year-old juco draftee when the Rangers made him the highest pick (seventh round) in Grizzlies history. He impressed in a brief pro debut that included six strikeouts in three hitless innings in the Single-A Carolina League playoffs. Tiger's four-seam fastball parks at 94-97 mph and tops out at 100 with carry but only modest life, and he maintains his velocity deep into games. His upper-80s slider touches 92 mph with two-plane depth, inducing a lot of empty swings, though he'll have to prove he can land it for strikes when hitters don't chase it. Texas had him scrap a traditional mid-80s changeup and install an upper-80s splitter with promising tumble. A quality athlete with a clean delivery, Tiger provides a decent amount of strikes. He does lack fastball movement and overall deception, so his stuff gets hit harder than it should at times. The Rangers will work with him to improve his pitch shapes and perhaps add a curveball to give him a softer option, seeing a potential No. 3 starter who also offers some intrigue as a relief option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas all-state wide receiver in high school, Cauley signed for an over-slot $1 million as a 2021 third-rounder. No one in the system offers a better combination of speed and defensive versatility, but his offensive game is still a work in progress entering his sixth pro season. His .253/.325/.448 batting line and 25 percent strikeout rate in Double-A last year represented the best numbers of his career. Cauley's small stature, big personality and ability to barrel balls with a high-effort right-handed stroke drew Dustin Pedroia comparisons in high school. His aggressiveness hasn't worked as well in pro ball, where he chases too many pitches and has some in-zone contact issues, even against fastballs. He does produce high exit velocities and elevates balls to his pull side, so he could provide 15-20 homers per season. Cauley uses his plus-plus speed well on the bases, where he's a prolific basestealer with a career 87 percent success rate. His quickness gives him good range at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength but has had some issues with inconsistent accuracy with his throws. He played center field for the first time in 2025 and looked natural there, and he's also a quality defender at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high schooler who signed for an over-slot $1 million as a 2021 third-rounder, Cauley drew some comps to a speedier Dustin Pedroia because he was a small middle infielder with a big personality and impressive hitting ability. While Cauley’s bat-to-ball skills haven’t translated to pro ball, he has shown promise in other phases of the game and with his nonstop energy. He slashed .235/.297/.411 with 35 extra-base hits and 27 steals in 93 games at High-A in 2024, missing a month early in the season with turf toe. After displaying a smooth right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed and good feel for the barrel in high school, Cauley has had in-zone swing-and-miss issues as a pro. He gets overly pull-conscious and swings with so much effort, resulting in a 29 percent strikeout rate last year. He does hit the ball hard when he makes contact and could deliver 15-20 homers per season, but he may never provide much in the way of batting average or on-base percentage. A Texas all-state wide receiver in high school, Cauley has plus-plus speed and uses it aggressively on the bases, stealing 111 bags at an 89 percent success rate in 297 games during his first four seasons. His quickness also allows him to cover plenty of ground at shortstop, where he has solid arm strength but doesn’t always make accurate throws. He’s much more reliable at second base and has the tools to become a dynamic center fielder, though he hasn’t played there as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high school product, Cauley reminded some area scouts of Dustin Pedroia as a small infielder with hitting ability and a ton of swagger. Since signing for an over-slot $1 million as a 2021 third-rounder, he hasn't displayed the same bat-to-ball skills he showed as an amateur but has delighted the Rangers with the rest of his game and constant energy. He slashed .245/.333/.411 with 12 homers, 36 steals and a 31.6 percent strikeout rate between two Class A stops last year, then had more issues making contact in the Arizona Fall League. Cauley showed a smooth right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed and good feel for the barrel in high school, but he has gotten too aggressive as a pro. He swings with so much effort and gets overly pull-happy at times, throwing off his timing at the plate, though he hits the ball hard when he connects. He may never hit for a high average but he could provide 20 homers per season with plenty of walks. A former Texas all-state wide receiver, Cauley can create havoc with plus-plus speed that translated into 84 steals in 95 attempts (88.4 percent) in 201 games during his first three seasons. His quickness also gives him plus range at shortstop, where he has solid arm strength and some issues with throwing accuracy. He's a dynamic and more reliable defender at second base, and has similar upside in center field, where he has yet to play as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An all-state wide receiver before he gave up football as a Barbers Hill (Mont Belvieu) senior, Cauley led the Eagles to their first Texas 5-A state championship last spring. With his hitting ability and swagger packed in a frame generously listed at 5-foot-10, he reminded some area scouts of Dustin Pedroia. After signing for an over-slot $1 million in the third round last July, he batted .255 with 10 steals in 24 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Though Cauley's hand-eye coordination and smooth right-handed stroke should allow him to make consistent contact, he struck out at a 30 percent clip in his pro debut. It might simply have been a case of trying to do too much, as he got too pull-happy at times. He has enough bat speed and sneaky strength to produce 12-15 homers per season, though he'll need to launch balls more regularly to get there. A sparkplug built for the top of a batting order, Cauley has well-above-average speed and uses it to wreak havoc on the bases. He has the quickness, actions and instincts to remain at shortstop unless his merely average arm forces a move. He'd profile well athletically and offensively at second base or center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey missed most of the prime events on the 2023 high school showcase circuit because of a leg injury and football, but his stock shot up the following spring. He drew repeated Trea Turner comparisons while establishing himself as the fastest player in the 2024 Draft, where he went 23rd overall and signed for $3,297,500. He played just 32 games in his pro debut last year, with an impingement in his right (throwing) shoulder landing him on the injured list in mid-May and back issues shutting him down after he made four rehab appearances in July. Lindsey batted .280 in Single-A but also struck out at a 32 percent clip, taking too many early-count pitches and then coming up empty when he turned his right-handed stroke loose. The Dodgers believe it's more an approach issue than a swing issue, and his .431 average on balls in play alludes to the pressure his speed puts on a defense. He won't be a huge home run threat but is hitting the ball harder than he did as an amateur and could go deep 12-15 times per season. With his top-of-the-scale speed, Lindsey can get from home to first in 3.5 seconds on a bunt, beat out routine grounders for hits and contend for big league stolen base titles. There were questions about whether his average arm would allow him to remain at shortstop even before his injury, though he certainly has the actions and quickness to do so. If he has to move, he has the tools to become a quality defender in center field or at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey wasn't highly touted entering 2024 after missing much of the summer showcase circuit with a leg injury, then skipping the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October because he was busy playing quarterback for Hardee HS (Wauchula, Fla.). But his stock rose quickly during the spring, when he gave off Trea Turner vibes as one of the fastest players and best shortstop prospects in the prep class. The Dodgers signed him for $3,297,500 as the 23rd overall pick, their biggest Draft bonus since 2010 and earliest selection since 2017. Lindsey clocked sub-6.3-second times in the 60-yard dash and has the top-of-the-scale speed to be a devastating basestealer and to cover plenty of ground in the field. Los Angeles had him focus on adding strength and tightening his right-handed swing rather than making his pro debut after he signed. While he won't be a slugger, he's barreling balls more consistently and hitting them harder, which could result in 12-15 home run pop. Turner had similar power projections at the same stage of his career, and like Lindsey, came with questions about whether his average arm would allow him to remain at shortstop. Lindsey has the actions, range and quick hands to play there, and the Dodgers believe they can help him improve his arm strength and release. If not, he has the tools to become a plus defender in center field or at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herring was a key part of Louisiana State’s bullpen for two years, helping the Tigers win the 2023 national championship and continued to dominate as a Draft-eligible sophomore reliever in 2024. The Yankees went well over slot to sign him in the sixth round of that year’s Draft, then sent him out as a starter in 2025. He threw very well across two levels of A ball before being sent to the Rockies in the Ryan McMahon Trade Deadline deal. He finished off with seven strong starts in High-A with his new organization, finishing second among all Minor Leaguers with his 1.89 combined ERA. One conversation with Herring would leave you thinking he was an analyst and not a pitcher, and his ability to integrate data into what he does on the mound should serve him well, especially with the Rockies’ new pitching group. There’s hope there might be a bit more in the tank with his fastball which currently sits around 90 mph but plays above that because of movement and command of the pitch. He throws his slider a lot, a sweeping mid-80s breaker that misses a ton of bats. His changeup took a very nice step forward during his first full season as a pro, and the Rockies think the mid-80s cambio could be a third at least above-average offering in time. Herring’s feel to pitch is a huge asset and while he has a longer arm action and not the smoothest delivery, he throws enough strikes, while showing he can find success down in the zone as well as up, keeping hitters off-balance by mixing his offerings well and pitching backwards. He has the ingredients to stay in a rotation, especially if he can find just a few more ticks on the fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the unsung heroes in Louisiana State's 2023 national championship run, Herring worked 4 2/3 innings of scoreless relief to beat Wake Forest in an elimination game at the Men's College World Series. The Tigers' best bullpen option as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2024, he logged a 1.79 ERA with a 67/13 K/BB ratio in 50 1/3 innings while scouts lamented that he was too valuable in that role to get an opportunity to start. The Yankees gave him that chance when he made his pro debut this year after signing for a well-over-slot $797,500 in the sixth round and he was running with it, pitching well across two levels of A-ball when he was dealt with Josh Grosz to the Rockies for Ryan McMahon near the Trade Deadline. Herring's best pitch is a sweeping mid-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action that confounds both lefties and righties. He can't overpower hitters with his fastball, which operates in the low 90s and tops out at 94 with some armside run, and he'll need to find more velocity or life against better competition. He threw only 11 changeups at LSU but emphasized the pitch more during three Cape Cod League starts last summer, showing some decent if firm mid-80s cambios with depth. Herring has a long arm action and a less-than-smooth delivery, though it throws batters' timing off and didn't stop him from pounding the strike zone as a sophomore. To succeed as a pro starter, he'll need to add more strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and improve his fastball and changeup. If he can't, he still could become a high-leverage reliever thanks to his slider and mound presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the most physical shortstops in the 2026 international class, Fermin has a projectable 6-foot-3 frame reminiscent of fellow Samana, D.R., product Hanley Ramirez at the same stage of their careers. He received the highest bonus in Houston's crop this year, signing for $2,147,500. Besides his tools, scouts also like his makeup and how he plays the game with swagger. A switch-hitter who's more advanced from the left side because he has gotten more at-bats there, Fermin has advanced feel for contact. He already shows some ability to recognize pitches and control the strike zone, and he hits the ball harder than most 17-year-olds. Once he fills out and learns to elevate balls, he could develop plus raw power and provide 20 or more homers per season. Fermin's potential offensive impact overshadows his athleticism. He'll flash plus speed but likely will settle in as a solid runner once he's physically mature, and he has a strong arm that definitely works on the left side of the infield. His quick first step enhances his chances of remaining at shortstop, though it's possible that he outgrows the position and winds up at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays spent years scouting Valdez, who comes from the Dominican city of Baní, and their belief in him was evident in the $3.5 million signing bonus they awarded him in January 2026. It was the third-largest sum the Rays have given an international amateur, trailing only the bonuses given to Wander Franco ($3.85 million) and Brailer Guerrero ($3.7 million). It’s a big bet on a young player with a long way to go and extraordinary upside. Valdez has the traits of a middle-of-the-order hitter. He sprays line drives to all fields with a simple right-handed swing and a mature approach for his age. He has a good feel for the strike zone and doesn’t chase too much. He’s already producing 100-104 mph exit velocities in games, which speaks to his physicality and strength, and he has shown the ability to use his hips to pull the ball with authority. A move to third base seemed inevitable for Valdez at one point, and that would be a fine outcome given his offensive profile and his cannon of an arm that fires 92-94 mph throws across the infield. But the Rays are going to give him a shot to stick at shortstop, believing he showed enough leading up to his signing that he has earned the opportunity. He showed improvement in his first step, smooth actions and above-average body control. Wherever he lands in the infield, his bat gives him a chance to be special.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aponte was one of the best shortstops in the 2025 international class and the Reds had circled his name, signing the Venezuelan infielder -- he hails from Miranda, home of big leaguers like Miguel Rojas and Oswaldo Cabrera -- for $1.9 million. Known primarily for his defensive work, Aponte showed some unexpected life at the plate during his debut in the Dominican Summer League, leading his team with seven home runs. Conversation about Aponte, who will play all of the 2026 season at age 18, still starts with his glove. One of the best defenders in his class, he’s going to play shortstop for a long time, with plus agility, actions and the ability to make highlight-reel type plays. Like with a lot of young middle infielders, he can still improve on making the routine play, and while he has enough for the premium position, he should able to improve his arm strength as well. It surprised some that Aponte found as much power as he did right out of the gate because he has more of a handsy, “hitterish” approach at the plate. He makes a lot of contact and can use the whole field. The Reds want him to keep staying up the middle and making good swing decisions and not chase power. And even with the home run total, he needs to add strength before he’s ready to come stateside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aponte hails from Miranda, Venezuela, home to big leaguers like Miguel Rojas and Oswaldo Cabrera. He hopes to be the next to represent his hometown after the Reds made him their primary target at the start of the 2025 international signing period, bringing him into the organization for $1.9 million. Aponte leads with his glove, but added strength helped improve his stock, landing him at No. 18 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list at the start of the signing period. At the plate, Aponte has good contact skills from the right side of the plate, using a simple toe tap to time up pitchers. He’s content to use the middle of the field to spray line drives. He’s likely never going to be a huge power guy, but is good with bat control and the ability to bunt and move runners over while not striking out much. As intriguing as his bat might end up being, Aponte’s glove is what got him paid. He’s possibly the best defender in his signing class, with evaluators saying things like he has “magic in his hands.” He makes tough plays look easy with plenty of flash along the way. He’s a no-doubt shortstop with plenty of arm, range and actions, even if he has to learn some consistency on the mundane plays to be as well-rounded of a defender as he can be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eagen really struggled in his first two years at Presbyterian and dealt with elbow and shoulder issues in his sophomore year in 2023. He found regained health and success that summer in the Appalachian League and returned to the Blue Hose to win the 2024 Big South Pitcher of the Year with a school record 122 strikeouts in 77 2/3 innings. He became the first Presbyterian player drafted in 11 years when the D-backs selected him in the third round in ’24, and he added to his award closet as the 2025 Northwest League Pitcher of the Year after posting a 2.49 ERA with 132 strikeouts in 97 2/3 innings. After adding four Double-A starts, Eagen led all Arizona farmhands with 153 total K’s. Solidly built at 6-foot-4, Eagen added velocity late in his collegiate career and continued to run his four-seam fastball into the mid 90s during his first full pro season. His high arm slot helps him generate really good carry out of the hand with induced vertical break up to 20 inches. His 81-83 mph curveball complements that nicely with its sharp downward action that makes it effective against batters from both sides, and a mid-80s gyro slider can be equally good as a weapon versus righties. Eagen has folded in an 85-88 mph splitter too, and it shows flashes of being a future average MLB offering. Eagen doesn’t have the most effortful delivery with that high release, but he can finish with a flourish moving toward the first-base side. He relies on batters biting on the breaking stuff moving out of the zone, and when more disciplined hitters lay off those, he could settle into slightly below-average control if trends continue. He would still have enough of a mix to work as a backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Presbyterian last had a Major Leaguer in World War II hero Lou Brissie, who retired in 1953, but Eagen has a great shot at being the next. The right-hander struggled in his first two seasons with the Blue Hose and missed most of 2023 with elbow and shoulder concerns before making up for the lost time in the Appalachian League. He was rejuvenated upon his 2024 return, winning Big South Pitcher of the Year honors while setting a school record with 122 strikeouts in 77 2/3 innings. The D-backs took him in the third round and signed him for $650,000, ending an 11-year drought for Presbyterian Draft picks. The 6-foot-4 hurler's fastball velocity jumped roughly 5 mph in his final season on campus. It sat 93-94 mph and touched 96 with good carry out of his high arm slot. He played off it well with an 80-82 mph downer curveball that contrasted nicely with the high heat and sported a 53 percent whiff rate in his junior year. His mid-80s slider was a distinct third option (and rarely used against lefties) but got plenty of swing-and-miss. He didn’t use much of a changeup in school and will focus on developing one as a pro. Eagen’s velocity trajectory proved promising, especially since he didn’t add effort to his delivery to get there. Bolstering the mix with an armside offspeed pitch could be key to his starting chances in pro ball, even if he continues to pound the strike zone, but the fastball-curveball combo would at least get him MLB looks as a reliever if its quality is maintained.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Luis signed for $525,000 with the D-backs in January 2022 and has been a little ahead of the curve ever since. He spent his age-20 season with High-A Hillsboro and ranked third in the Northwest League with a .304 average while finishing with five homers, 22 steals and a 106 WRC+ across 102 games. After missing some time with a shoulder injury, he got extra at-bats in the Arizona Fall League and finished with a .213/.311/.247 line in 25 games. A switch-hitter, Luis still comes with a ton of projection in his 6-foot frame. Despite the impressive batting average, he posted a 34 percent chase rate with Hillsboro, and unless he reels in that aggression, upper-level pitchers will be able to take advantage of his lack of discipline. Good bat-to-ball skills, especially on fastballs, should help though. Now as he works deeper into his 20s, it will be time to start showing more impact alongside the physical maturity; the fact that 50.7 percent of his AFL batted balls were with 95-plus mph exit velocities could be a preview of at least average pop to come. Luis can get going down the line with plus speed, and he should be a constant threat to steal 20-plus bags over full seasons. He got the bulk of his work at second base with Hillsboro but moved over to third base in the AFL with the D-backs wanting to keep that avenue open considering the crush of options they have at the keystone. His athleticism and arm strength would play better up the middle if he could hold off Demetrio Crisantes and JD Dix, but he’ll have to stay fresh at the hot corner, where the pressure for his power to come through is greater.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Luis signed with the D-backs for $525,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2022 and has already become a better prospect than many who signed for at least twice that bonus. He was a standout at the Dominican and Arizona complexes in '22 and 2023 respectively, and jumped to Single-A Visalia for the first time at just 18 years old during the latter season. He returned to the California League for ’24 and slashed .265/.337/.414 with seven homers and 20 steals in 109 games. He was one of only of five players aged 19 or younger to get at least 500 plate appearances in Single-A last season. It's still very much a projection game with Luis. The switch-hitter evened out his splits in '24 after looking better from the left side earlier in his career, and at a listed 6 feet, 170 pounds, there’s still the expectation that he’ll grow into average power, even if it didn’t quite show up in the hitter-friendly Cal League. His chase rate also drastically improved between his two trips to Single-A, but it still remained relatively high against all pitch types in ’24 and particularly on changeups. Luis is an above-average runner who will press for 20+ steals, even if he slows down a little with extra bulk. The D-backs rotated him between shortstop, third base and second base because of their low-level infield depth, but the lion’s share of his looks came at the six. His average arm strength might still make him a better fit at the keystone long term, but he could be valuable there as a split-resistant hitter with some pop, even if the OBPs never truly stand out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 The D-backs signed Luis for $525,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2022, and despite being the club’s fifth-most expensive signing of the period, he’s already developed into the most notable member of the class. After hitting .345 with a 125 wRC+ over 47 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first taste of pro ball, the middle infielder slashed .297/.381/.496 with three homers in 25 games in the Arizona Complex League and was promoted to Single-A Visalia in July of his age-18 season. He held his own in the California League at a young age and is headed toward a truer full season away from the complex in 2024. A switch-hitter, Luis has proven more adept from the left side, where he has more experience given the propensity of right-handers in the lower Minors. He has a quick, whippy swing from both sides that helped drive those early solid averages and contact rates, although he got more aggressive with his hacks at Single-A and his K and BB percentages suffered. He could reel that back in with more experience. Luis already has wiry strength and finished with seven homers in 62 games last season. More power should come as his body continues to mature, and he has the lift in his swing to get to at least above-average pop at peak. Luis split his time between shortstop and second base in both of his first two seasons, and he has the quickness to stick up the middle. Standing at 6-foot, he has just enough arm for short but might be an even better long-term fit at the keystone with above-average upside there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres made the big splash of the 2024 international class when they signed Leodalis De Vries for $4.2 million. That didn’t give them much to work with in their pool, so they traded 2023 12th-rounder Blake Dickerson to the Tigers for more international signing money and signed Cruz for $750,000 days later. A standout at the U18 World Cup for Mexico, Cruz stayed on the domestic side and made two abbreviated starts in the Arizona Complex League after signing. There’s a ton to dream on with the 6-foot-1 right-hander. He previously sat in the upper 80s during his international experience but was averaging around 94 mph with his fastball and touching 97 after joining the San Diego ranks. The pitch came with good armside run too, and Padres officials believed it could be a ground-ball machine when hitters make contact. His low-80s changeup fades well off that fastball, generating good chase and keeping left-handed hitters at bay. Cruz’s gyro slider has also improved, moving into the low 80s with decent spin.
