The floor is still awfully attractive, though. You’ll hear “machine” and “robot” thrown around, which are high compliments. Kasevich is a natural leader by example, a young player who even more veteran Minor Leaguers have followed. He fits the Blue Jays’ idea of a model teammate, fully and completely. Defensively, the Blue Jays are much higher on Kasevich than many are externally, and it’s easy to see where their confidence comes from. He’s not flashy, but he won’t give you a reason to pick apart his defense, either. He’s steady and reliable with a chance to play games at shortstop in the big leagues, while also mixing in some second and third. If Kasevich can drive the ball harder and get it off the ground more consistently, he profiles as a big leaguer based on the all-around package he presents.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming off a successful NCAA career at Oregon and a good stint in the Northwoods League, the Blue Jays selected Kasevich in the second round of the 2022 Draft and signed him to a $1 million bonus. Along with third-rounder Alan Roden, that’s got a chance to be a fine Draft class for Toronto. Kasevich got his feet wet at Single-A that season, then jumped to High-A in ‘23 where he posted a .284/.363/.365 line. In ‘24, he opened at Double-A and eventually jumped to Triple-A with a combined line of .296/.348/.385. Kasevich is an organizational favorite, from coaches to the development staff. You’ll hear the word “machine” a lot, and some coaches have even noticed older players gravitating towards Kasevich, given how he handles his business. Prospects younger than Kasevich have tried to emulate him, too, which is one of the highest forms of praise. Another extremely intelligent young prospect, Kasevich is also one of the strongest defensive shortstops in the organization with tremendous body control while fielding. He’ll still see the odd game at third base, but the Blue Jays fully believe in Kasevich as a shortstop long-term, betting heavily on both his mental and physical games. At the dish, contact is Kasevich’s identity. His 10 home runs in 247 career Minor League games don’t paint much of a power hitter, but that’s not his game. If Kasevich can drive the ball more consistently, sneaking a few more balls through the infield while turning some singles into doubles, that should be enough to make his bat play at the MLB level. If that happens, Kasevich’s defense will help his case, and his intangibles could take him over the top. A stress reaction in his lower back has kept Kasevich from pushing through the Minors' top level in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Kasevich in the second round of the 2022 Draft, fresh off a successful career at Oregon and a good run in the Northwoods League, and signed him to a $1 million bonus. His brief introduction to pro ball was a learning experience, batting .262 with little power (.336 slugging percentage) over 25 games with Single-A Dunedin, but strong internal reviews earned him a trip to High-A Vancouver in ‘23 and Kasevich did not disappoint. There, Kasevich hit .284 with a .728 OPS over 94 games, and while his four home runs don’t point to much power, there’s belief he could grow into 10-15 homers annually. Few players in this organization receive stronger reviews than Kasevich for his work ethic and approach to the game. He’s been lauded as a teammate for making those around him better and is one of the best defensive shortstops in the organization. Internally, the Blue Jays are very high on his defensive profile. Kasevich may not be the flashiest athlete at shortstop but is solid fundamentally and makes nearly every play he gets to. He’ll still see plenty of time at third base, but make no mistake, Kasevich will keep shortstop on his résumé right through to the higher levels. At the plate, Kasevich’s identity will need to be that of a contact hitter and he shines in that role. Strikeouts should never be an issue, and in an organization preaching “competitive at-bats,” Kasevich fits the bill, though he could be particularly prone to BABIP-related fluctuations if he doesn’t begin driving the ball more. If that suddenly happens, then Kasevich climbs to another tier, but his ability to put the ball in play and defend at short -- plus the intangibles -- will keep him ranked highly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kasevich showed some impressive contact skills over his final two seasons with the University of Oregon, hitting .324 and .310 respectively, and he carried that success into the Northwoods League, where he batted .374 over 40 games in 2021. The Blue Jays picked him up in the second round of the 2022 Draft and signed Kasevich for a $1 million bonus. Kasevich got a taste of pro ball in ’22, hitting .262 with a .681 OPS over 25 games for Single-A Dunedin. There, he walked 11 times while striking out only nine, showing the same plate discipline the Blue Jays liked in the Draft. Kasevich has a strong contact profile that he should show more of in the coming years, but power will be a separating factor for him. He’s worked to add more, focusing on keeping his bat path in the zone a bit longer. The Blue Jays believe Kasevich has the tools to stick long term at shortstop, where he’s fundamentally sound and moves well enough for the position. He’ll continue to see some time at third base too, and that positional versatility should only help as he climbs the ladder. At 22 with his NCAA experience, Kasevich could be a quick mover once he gets rolling through a full season, depending on how well the slugging ability translates to the pro game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kent starred in both baseball and football as an Illinois high schooler before heading to the University of Arizona. He went from a redshirt freshman in 2022 to the Wildcats’ Friday night starter in '24, and that ascent, along with an impressive Cape Cod League run, pushed him to the Nationals in the fourth round. He posted a 4.61 ERA with 132 strikeouts over 123 innings between High-A and Double-A in his first full season, and his 18.5 K-BB percentage was best in the Washington system. The 6-foot-3 left-hander generates huge extension, allowing him to lower his release height and create a difficult angle for opposing batters. His fastball only sat 91-93 mph (touching 95) in 2025, but the ride on the pitch showed more promise than that. Early spring reports indicate that Kent could be set to add a little extra velo in his second full season. Maybe the best thing his current heater does, however, is set up his plus changeup, an 80-83 mph armside offering with just the right amount of velo separation and movement to keep righties swinging over it time and again. (The pitch had a 51 percent whiff rate in 2025.) Kent can also spin a mid-80s slider against lefties and flips in an upper-70s curveball, though the command of the latter can be all over. There is some effort in Kent’s delivery to get to his extension, and his walk rate did jump from 6.5 percent at High-A to 10.7 in a limited Double-A sample. But the southpaw commands the fastball well enough to deliver strikes, while setting up the changeup for chase. If the velo bump holds, he could be a backend rotation candidate in the Majors by the end of his age-23 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 After starring in both baseball and football back home in Illinois, Kent headed to the University of Arizona, where he redshirted in 2022 and worked as a reliever in 2023. He headed to the Cape Cod League that summer and put himself squarely on the radar with a 2.52 ERA and 27 strikeouts in six starts (25 innings). The Wildcats made Kent their Friday night starter, and he handled himself well with the elevated role, posting a 4.08 ERA with 89 strikeouts in 86 frames. The Nationals selected him in the fourth round and signed him to a $625,000 bonus. The 6-foot-3 southpaw has a full bevy of pitches that can leave hitters guessing. He bumped up his fastball velocity ahead of the Draft to sit 90-93 mph, and he touched as high as 96. The pitch can play better than the velo too with a flat approach from a lower angle in his delivery. Kent’s 82-84 mph changeup is his most effective offering – one that works well down and armside leading to whiffs and groundballs. He has two different breaking pitches in a low-80s slider and mid-70s curve. The former was slightly more effective at missing bats in school, but the latter can drop in for an easy strike too. Kent had some control issues on the Cape but was much better at sticking to the zone with the Wildcats in the spring. With only one year as a starter against quality competition under his belt, Kent could keep building on his 2024 gains, but even if he’s capped at being a hurler with a deep arsenal but no true plus pitch, that could still work in the back of future MLB rotations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the same Whitefish Bay HS program that produced Craig Counsell, Dix was an increasingly common Wisconsin prep standout, and after working around a right labrum surgery before his senior season, he went to the D-backs with the 35th overall pick in 2024. He signed for $2.15 million, making him the third-highest high school signing from the Badger State behind only Jarred Kelenic and Gavin Lux. Dix split his first full season between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia, hitting .297/.404/.406 with two homers and 28 steals in 89 games. A switch-hitter, Dix was more swing-happy from right side during his time in the California League, and as such, more susceptible to breaking stuff. But he was on fastballs well from both sides and really good at keeping his swings inside the zone from the left, giving him at least an average hit tool projection. His power will be based on how much strength he can add to his 6-foot-2 frame moving forward. There’s enough size for him to get to 15-20 homers eventually as he matures physically. Dix is a true burner on the basepaths and was willing to test opposing batteries consistently during his first taste of the Minors. The shoulder surgery made his arm strength a major question mark, and he was limited to second-base duties by the D-backs because of his throwing issues. The organization put him on a throwing program in the offseason and believes he’ll show renewed oomph with the arm in ’26, enough that he could push for opportunities on the left side of the infield down the line. For now, he’s a cold-weather talent with a well-rounded skill set and room to grow in his second full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wisconsin is garnering a reputation for developing notable high school hitters over the past decade or so, and you can add Dix -- who hails from the same Whitefish Bay HS program that claims Craig Counsell as an alum -- to the growing list. Ahead of his senior year, the switch-hitting shortstop was slowed in summer showcases by a right shoulder injury and underwent labrum surgery that fall. He showed enough in his senior spring to go to the D-backs at the 35th overall pick and signed for $2.15 million. Only Jarred Kelenic ($4.5 million) and Gavin Lux ($2,314,500) have signed for more as Wisconsin high schoolers. Dix shows a simple stroke from both sides of the plate, though he tends to look a little better from the left. He has been willing to spread the ball all around the field to pick up his hits, impressing scouts with his potential for an above-average hit tool. The shoulder issues brought some questions about Dix’s power, both before and after the Draft. There is projectable strength in his 6-foot-2 frame, and he could threaten for 15-20 homers by the time everything comes together. The former Wake Forest commit played all four infield spots at the Area Code Games in an attempt to leave an impression on evaluators, and many believed he has the range and hands to stick at shortstop. He showed good arm strength before the injury, but that skill hadn’t come back in the spring. As a result, the D-backs have found him to be a better fit at second base in his first taste of the pros.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dreiling served in a platoon role as a Tennessee freshman before starring for the 2024 national champions, earning most outstanding player honors at the College World Series after homering in all three games in the finals. One of the top sophomore-eligible prospects in the 2024 Draft, he signed for $1,287,600 in the second round. The Rangers sent him straight to High-A for his pro debut and back there for his first full season, and he slashed a combined .221/.323/.354 with 13 homers and 20 steals in 134 games. Those numbers belie Dreiling's offensive ability, because he's a left-handed hitter with a sound approach, bat-to-ball skills and plus raw power. He has made good swing decisions and consistent contact against all types of pitches in High-A without the production to show for it. He has shown the ability to work counts to draw walks as well as to elevate balls to his pull side when given the opportunity. An average runner who will flash a bit more speed once he gets going, Dreiling can steal a few bases but more with savvy than quickness. Primarily a left fielder at Tennessee, he has spent much of his pro career in center but lacks the range to play there long term. His below-average arm strength will relegate him to left field, where he's a decent defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Dreiling stood out with his hitting ability and athleticism as a Kansas high schooler, he injured his hamstring in the second game of his 2022 senior season and went undrafted. He played well in a platoon role as a Tennessee freshman and starred as an everyday player for the 2024 national champions, earning Most Outstanding Player accolades at the Men's College World Series after homering in all three games in the final round. Signed for $1,287,600 as a sophomore in the second round, he started his pro career at High-A. The lefty-hitting Dreiling stands out most with his plus raw power, the product of bat speed, strength and an aptitude for driving balls in the air to his pull side. He's also a fairly well-rounded hitter who makes hard contact to all fields while managing the strike zone well and drawing walks. After going 0-for-16 against southpaws as a freshman, he made adjustments and slashed .398/.491/.739 against them as a sophomore. While Dreiling has solid-to-plus speed once underway, he doesn't have great instincts on the bases or in the outfield. He was rough defensively when he got to Tennessee and spent most of his freshman year at DH. He improved in 2024 and can become an average left fielder with a below-average arm, but there's little chance he'll stay in center after spending his pro debut there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fien was a showcase standout heading into his senior year of high school as the 2024 MLB High School All-American Game MVP and a Team USA star. He didn’t quite hold that same offensive consistency as a senior at Great Oak HS in California, but his stock didn’t tumble completely. The Rangers selected him 12th overall in July and signed him for below slot at $4.8 million. After getting his feet wet at Single-A to round out 2025, Fien was traded to the Nationals in the offseason as the best prospect in the return for left-handed starter MacKenzie Gore. Starting from a slightly closed off stance, Fien begins his work in the box with hands held higher than most batters, and that unorthodoxy brings some pause in how it will translate to the pro side. He has done plenty of damage with it in the past by showing an ability to lift the ball consistently, and with a 6-foot-3 frame already, he could pack on enough muscle to get to plus power down the line. In his brief foray in the Minors, he did swing over a lot of sliders and changeups, and he’ll need to find the barrel more often to get the most of his pop. Fien got quicker over his high school career and could be an average runner, though there’s the possibility he slows down a tad as he matures. He has a plus arm that should work from the left side of the infield, but where exactly will deserve watching. He’s now in the same organization as No. 1 overall pick Eli Willits, a potential plus shortstop. The Nats plan to rotate Fien, who underwent offseason surgery to address a bone spur in his right hand, between short, third base and even second while hoping his bat does much of the talking in Year 1.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendez showed he had an idea of what he was doing at the plate almost immediately after signing with the Brewers in January 2021 for $800,000, hitting (.316 combined average) his way from the Dominican Summer League to the United States and the Arizona Complex League during his debut summer after signing. He played at age 19 in High-A ball in 2023, then was sent to the Phillies that offseason in a deal for Oliver Dunn. He hit well in 2024 and 2025, without much thump, before he finished with a flourish (.911 OPS) in Double-A with the Twins after coming over in the Harrison Bader Trade Deadline deal. At every level, Mendez has shown a strong propensity for making contact. He has an incredible feel for the strike zone and is coming off of a year where he walked more than he struck out, pretty much in line with his career 12.8 percent walk rate and 13.9 percent strikeout rate entering 2026. He’s always hit the ball hard, but typically on the ground too much. He’s continuing to work on finding ways to create a little loft, and to pull the ball a bit more, without giving up his natural feel to hit. Some small adjustments did lead to more impact last year and he did set a career low in groundball rate. Mendez’s ultimate value lies in his bat. He’s yet to find a true defensive home, with an outfield corner – left makes the most sense – the best bet, and the Twins have worked with him on route efficiency. He took some reps at first base last spring and did it again this year with his new organization in the hopes to find somewhere he can get to average defensively so that his bat can get in the lineup regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Brewers in January 2021 for $800,000, Mendez made a very strong first impression, hitting his way from the Dominican Summer League to the United States and the Arizona Complex League during his summer debut. After holding his own as one of the younger regulars in Single-A and High-A in 2022 and 2023 -- missing time with leg issues in ‘23 -- he was sent to the Phillies for Oliver Dunn during that offseason. Returning to the High-A level with his new organization, he put up solid numbers, albeit without a ton of impact, in 2024. It was more of the same during his first taste of Double-A in 2025, and he was sent to the Twins at the Trade Deadline in the Harrison Bader deal. A 6-foot-3 left-handed hitter, Mendez has some traits in the box that are easy to like. His batted ball profile is good, limiting swing-and-miss and chase and registering a solid hard-hit rate (43.1 percent). The one thing he needs to do is learn how to get the ball in the air more, after registering a ground ball rate over 60 percent in '24, and 52.7 percent in 2025 at the time of the trade, so he can get to some of his raw power. An average runner at best, Mendez is a fringy outfield defender who is serviceable in a corner. He’s played more right field than anything but left might be the best spot for him when all is said and done. He’s just 21 for the 2025 season so there is hopefully time for him to take his approach and contact skills to the next level to give him the chance to grow into an offensive profile of an every day corner outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendez began his pro career with the Brewers in 2021 after he signed that January for $800,000 and wasted no time making a strong first impression. He quickly hit his way from the Dominican Summer League to the Arizona Complex League that first summer, finishing with a combined .879 OPS. He held his own at age 18 in full-season ball in 2022, but he didn’t swing the bat as well with a push up to High-A in 2023, as leg issues forced him to miss a chunk of the season. He made up for some lost at-bats in the Arizona Fall League and then came to the Phillies with Robert Moore in a trade for Oliver Dunn. The left-handed-hitting Mendez’s best trait continues to be his knack for contact. He carries a 14.3 percent strikeout rate with him into his first season with the Phillies, and he’s walked nearly as much (11.9 percent). What he hasn’t done is make consistent quality contact. There is some raw power and bat speed in there, and strength to come as he matures. He’s going to have to learn not to pound the ball into the ground (61.5 percent combined ground-ball rate in 2022 and '23). While Mendez is a solid athlete for his size, he’s likely going to slow down as he matures. He’s already moved to a corner, playing more right field than left to date. Still only 20 for the 2024 season, he’s going to have to learn how to add some loft to his swing to fit the corner outfield profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Having signed with the Brewers for $800,000 on Jan. 15, 2021, Mendez shot out of the gate in the Dominican Summer League that subsequent season, most notably hitting .296 while striking out in only two of his 64 DSL plate appearances. Milwaukee pushed the then-17-year-old stateside, where he was again an impressive performer with a .333 average and .885 OPS over 19 games in Arizona – earning himself an honor as the 2021 Brewers Complex Player of the Year. Having been 18 for the entire season, he was the youngest player to meet the qualifying standard at Single-A in 2022 and held his own with a .244/.357/.318 line and 98 wRC+ in 105 games with Carolina. He missed time in 2023 with leg issues and didn’t swing the bat as well as a teenager in High-A. He was one of the youngest participants in the Arizona Fall League and then was sent with Robert Moore to the Phillies in return for Oliver Dunn. Mendez’s ability to make contact still drives his offensive profile. His 15.7 percent K rate was sixth-lowest among the 109 Single-A qualifiers in 2022, while his 6.1 swinging-strike rate (whiffs per pitches faced) was second-lowest. It isn’t exactly loud contact, however, because the current angle of his swing tends to drive the ball directly into the ground. His 62.5 percent ground-ball rate was second-highest among the 609 Minor Leaguers from all levels with at least 400 plate appearances. And while there is some physical strength likely coming, it’ll take a swing change to incorporate into game pop. An average runner with just an average arm, he’s already been forced to the corner outfield in his early pro days, and while he was the primary right fielder for Carolina last year, he might be best served in left. Mendez will still only be 20 years old for all of the 2024 season, so there’s time for him to better round out his profile in his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shortly after shooting up to 6-foot-2 in stature, Mendez signed with the Brewers on Jan. 15, 2021, at the start of the international window, and the Dominican Republic native instantly took to pro ball because of an incredible ability to make contact. He struck out just twice in 138 plate appearances in the Dominican Summer League while hitting .296 in the same span, prompting an early stateside move at just 17 years old. He more than held his own in the Arizona Complex League with a .333/.425/.460 and 10/10 K/BB ratio in 19 games, and the Brewers rewarded him with their 2021 Complex Player of the Year award. The left-handed slugger mixes up how he faces pitchers, using a toe tap against right-handers and a leg kick against fellow southpaws. The strategy seems to work based on his bat-to-ball skills and ability to spray the ball all over the diamond this early in his career. He didn’t show a ton of power in the early Minor League looks (one homer in 37 hits), in part because of some severe groundball rates. Experience and some approach tweaks geared toward lifting the ball could get him to average pop. He was primarily a corner outfielder in Arizona, and while he moves decently well now, he’ll likely slow down enough in time to stay away from center. Mendez certainly put his name on the map in 2021. He remains a far-away lottery ticket, but one that seems much closer to hitting based on his elite contact rates. Anything approaching decent power would go a long way toward making him into an impact corner outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A .333 hitter with more walks than strikeouts in his final season on campus, Brown became the highest Draft pick in Coastal Carolina program history when he went 27th overall to the Brewers in 2022. His first full season was marred by injuries -- hip, head on a hit-by-pitch, right thumb and fractured left scapula -- and those limited him to 63 games with High-A Wisconsin. He slashed .265/.362/.348 with four homers and 37 steals in that span, got a cameo with Double-A Biloxi and then finished the season with even stronger numbers (.297/.391/.462) over 25 games in the Arizona Fall League. Brown has a noticeably unorthodox stance with his hands up near his head, his feet far back in the box, his back almost arched backward and a decent leg kick. He’s reeled some of that in since his college days, and he spoke during the Fall League about a desire to get more into his legs instead of letting his hands do so much of the work. He possesses impressive hand-eye coordination that keeps strikeouts in check, and some of the alterations did allow the power to play better in the Fall League. But given how much he prioritized contact in Wisconsin (only 12 extra-base hits), it’ll take a longer record of performance to project closer to average power. The former Chanticleer has speed to burn and is willing to get aggressive on the basepaths with 47 total steals across all stops in 2023. He has the range, actions and internal clock to remain at shortstop, but with his arm strength, he might be a better fit at second base, where he got 10 starts in the AFL. A high-contact quality defender up the middle can be valuable, and 2024 could be go time for Brown with improved health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 After an All-Star turn in the Cape Cod League in 2021 and a 2022 spring campaign in which he slashed .330/.460/.544 with more walks (39) than strikeouts (28), Brown became the highest Draft pick in Coastal Carolina history when he went 27th overall to the Brewers in July. He dipped his toe into full-season ball for 23 games with Single-A Carolina, slashing .262/.370/.441 with three homers while showing more aggression on the basepaths (15-of-17 in steal attempts). Brown’s setup at the plate is one all his own and could be mimicked across Wisconsin backyards if and when he takes it to Milwaukee. He begins with his elbow near his head, drops it as the pitcher's delivery gets underway, directs the head of the bat toward the mound, starts his load with a leg kick and then syncs everything in time to make contact. His hand-eye coordination helps him find the barrel -- despite all the noise -- but his power hasn't yet much shown up in pro ball. An above-average runner, Brown’s skills play above his pure speed because of his aggression on the basepaths and his instincts on the defensive end. He has the hands, feet and internal clock for shortstop, though questions about his arm strength could make him a better fit at second in the end. At the least, he’s a quality up-the-middle talent who will draw interest and study wherever he goes because of his unorthodox swing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendez signed with the Padres for only $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2021 when he was 18 years old and couldn’t break past Single-A through his first four pro seasons. In 2025, he became San Diego’s breakout star. With Rule 5 eligibility looming for the first time in his career, Mendez surged up three levels from Lake Elsinore to Double-A San Antonio and finished with a 3.22 ERA and 118 strikeouts over a career high 95 innings. He was an easy addition to the Padres’ 40-man roster in the offseason. Standing 6-foot-2, Mendez can look lithe on the mound, but his increased heat fueled his climb up the chain last season. His four-seamer sits 95-98 mph, occasionally tickling triple-digits, and comes with explosive, carrying life that helps keep it above bats in the upper portion of the zone. His mid-80s slider was a similarly dynamite weapon that played off that fastball, often forcing righties to lunge late. His upper-80s changeup has enough velocity separation off the fastball to get whiffs but wasn’t often used; it was even his third option against lefties, who had a .756 OPS against Mendez in ’25. Mendez cut his walk rate from 14.9 percent in 2024 to 11.2 last season, and that improved control strengthened his 40-man case and potential to remain a starter moving forward. There were some hiccups at Double-A, and he’ll need to turn to the third pitch more often if he’s going to repeat his success in the upper Minors and force his way to the Majors. The Padres have already said Mendez is now part of the big club’s pitching depth, and even if he needs to be eased in as a reliever, the fastball-slider combo could make him special in a shorter role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2017-18 international signing class, García got $2.5 million to sign with the Phillies and almost immediately set out to prove he was worth it, making his pro debut stateside and winning the Gulf Coast League batting title in 2018. His move to full-season ball in 2019 was a disaster offensively and then he missed out on a year of at-bats due to the shutdown. He did use 2020 to add strength and that started showing when he repeated Low-A, putting up better numbers all around and earning a late bump up to High-A and a 40-man roster addition in the offseason. His offensive struggles returned in 2022, however, and the Tigers claimed him on waivers from the Phils in September. A switch-hitting shortstop, García really started to find his swing in 2021, especially in the power department, more than doubling his career total with 13 homers for the season. That added strength has led to better bat speed and increased exit velocities from both sides and his improved approach -- his walk rate increased significantly and his strikeout rate dropped compared to 2019 -- allowed him to get to his raw power more consistently. Even with the increased physicality, García still looks every bit like an everyday shortstop defensively. He’ll need to continue to watch his conditioning, but he has excellent actions and a plus arm from the premium position. He’s continued to get reps at second and with there being enough confidence in his future as a middle infielder, he still has time to turn himself into a bench option in the Detroit system. García only turns 22 in October.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia was one of the top prospects in the 2017-18 international amateur class, coming in at No. 8 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list. The Phillies signed the middle infielder for $2.5 million, the fifth highest bonus in a class headlined by Shohei Ohtani and current No. 1 overall prospect Wander Franco. Garcia immediately started making good on the investment by making his pro debut in the United States in 2018 and winning the Gulf Coast League batting title. The Phillies pushed Garcia aggressively to full-season ball in 2019, a move that did not pay off as he finished with a .516 OPS. It might be OK to give the teenager a mulligan for last season as he still has the raw tools that made him such a premium talent on the international market and plenty of time to figure it out. The switch-hitter didn’t produce much at the plate in 2019, though he was better from the right side, mostly because of his inability to recognize breaking stuff. In the Gulf Coast League, pitchers were largely working on fastball command and Garcia can punish a fastball. But there are a lot more breaking balls in the South Atlantic League, something Garcia hadn’t seen, and he struggled to adjust. He does have plenty of bat speed and the Phillies are still confident he’ll be able to hit and even grow into some power. Garcia runs well and while he saw a lot of time at second base to improve his versatility, he definitely can play shortstop, with more than enough range and arm to play the position long-term. His first taste of full-season ball was full of growing pains. Now it’s time to see how he uses those lessons to take the next step in his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes it takes a young prospect to get his professional legs under him, especially if it's a young player just signed out of the Dominican Republic. Then there are prospects like Garcia, who signed with the Phillies for $2.5 million in July 2017 and hit the ground running, making his professional debut in the United States and winning the Gulf Coast League batting title in 2018. It's hard not to get excited about Garcia's tools, though it should be tempered with the fact that much of it is projection and the teenager has a long way to go. He's still not very big, with strength gains to come, but he showed a solid approach from both sides of the plate during his debut, making consistent contact and drawing some walks. There's raw power to tap into there and it should come as he matures. His defensive acumen might outstrip his bat, at least for now. He has a strong and accurate arm that flashes better than plus, a quick first step, quick hands and outstanding athleticism. It's easy to see Garcia becoming the best prospect in the system in the future and eventually be thought of as one of the top shortstop prospects in the game. He could battle the \"other\" Luis Garcia, the Nats' prospect on the Top 100, for NL East shortstop supremacy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 7 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list, Garcia's defensive acumen and offensive upside excited enough for the Phillies to spend $2.5 million to bring him into the fold. While data in games won't show up until this summer, Garcia did make a strong first impression in the Dominican Republic and at instructs with his feel for the game at such a young age. One of the bigger things that stood out was Garcia's glove at shortstop. He has plus range, excellent hands and good footwork, with a plus arm that really stands out. Given that he's just 17 for all of the 2018 season, there are obvious strength gains that will need to occur, but there's confidence that will come as he starts to mature. There are some ingredients at the plate the Phillies already like, including a solid approach at the plate that doesn't feature too much free or wild swinging. He exhibits some balance from both sides of the plate with barrel control. This isn't the kind of investment that brings a quick return. The Phillies knew they were in it for the long game when they signed Garcia. Now it's time for him to start his long path up the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tigers fans of a certain age can be forgiven for looking at the lefty Jacobs and his specs and thinking back to former Detroit starter Nate Robertson. Even the arsenals have some similarities. But Jacobs was very much a West Coast pitcher, from his prep days in Huntington Beach to his first college stop at UCLA. After five innings for the Bruins as a freshman, Jacobs transferred to Arizona State and blossomed into the Sun Devils’ Friday night starter. He entered his Draft season with first-round potential but fell to the third, where the Tigers made him part of their search for young pitching and signed him for $722,500. Jacobs doesn’t have a dominant pitch that he leans on so much as he succeeds with a good mix and a feel for hitters, from a 92-94 mph fastball that can touch 96 to a traditional low-80s slider and a changeup with good fade. While his strikeout rates were impressive at ASU, he has to show in the pros that he can get outs in the strike zone and put hitters in situations where they’re apt to chase. He repeats his delivery well, which should bode well for progress in strike throwing. Jacobs has a chance to advance quickly in the system, starting with full-season ball, if he can demonstrate an ability to get outs in the zone. He has the profile of a backend starter if he makes the adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid Georgia high school prospect, Simmons struggled at the plate a bit during his senior year in 2018 to hurt his Draft stock. The Phillies liked the power potential and overall athlete enough to take him in the sixth round that June and go over-slot to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment for $750,000. It’s been a slow development process since, though he did lead the New York-Penn League in slugging percentage in 2019. He did show some glimpses of his offensive upside in his full-season debut in 2021, but injury, a pitch to the helmet and COVID-related shutdowns limited him to just 46 total games. Simmons has always had considerable raw power from the right side of the plate; the question since his high school days was if he’d hit enough to tap into it. He’s had flashes of bringing a solid approach to the plate, with a willingness to draw walks, but he does strike out a fair amount. When he does make contact, it’s loud with good exit velocity and the ability to hit the ball over the fence, especially to the pull side. The Phillies believe his bat is trending in the right direction. The high school shortstop has played three infield positions professionally, but as his body continues to get bigger and stronger, it doesn’t look like he’ll be able to play short long-term. He’s probably best suited for third, where his strong arm plays well, but will continue to get plenty of time at second base as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Simmons entered his senior year of high school in Georgia as an intriguing shortstop prospect with a ton of raw power. He struggled making contact during the spring leading up to the Draft, causing his stock to drop, but the Phillies thought the strength and athleticism were worth taking a chance on in the sixth round and they gave him an over-slot bonus of $750,000 to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment. Simmons struggled in his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League and got off to a slow start in the short-season New York-Penn League in 2019, but he found his power stroke and finished as the league-leader in slugging percentage. The Phillies are thrilled with the growth Simmons has shown since starting his pro career. The ball jumps off his bat with solid exit velocity. He’s shown the ability to stay inside the baseball well and nearly all of his home run pop has come to his pull side so far. There are still some swing-and-miss issues, but he offsets them somewhat with a solid walk rate. Simmons is an average runner, but he isn't going to be basestealing threat. Drafted as a shortstop, there are those who think he’d be able to play the premium position long-term, especially because of his strong arm. But the Phillies started having him play second and third in 2019, and he’ll likely continue to move around the infield as his power bat carries him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the premier power hitters on the 2026 international market, Rosario signed for $2.5 million, the largest bonus in the Rangers' class. He hails from East Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic, which also has produced big league outfielders Bryan de la Cruz and Victor Robles. Rosario grew up playing shortstop but transitioned to the outfield as he got more physical. Already 6-foot-2 and 195 pounds at age 17, Rosario is built to hit for power. He has present and projectable strength, along with a quick right-handed stroke with loft, enabling him to generate impressive exit velocities and launch balls out of the park to all fields. He aggressively looks to do damage, so he does come with some swing-and-miss concerns. Rosario has average speed but could lose a step as he continues to mature physically. Though he has outgrown shortstop, some scouts believe he still moves well enough to play third base. His solid arm strength would work at the hot corner or in right field, his likely destination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 6-foot-5 and 200 pounds at 16, Solarte is a rare physical specimen and one of the best athletes his age. Ranked as the No. 16 overall prospect in the 2026 international class, he signed with the Marlins for $1 million and will head to the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League to begin his pro career. The Venezuela native immediately stands out for his physical strength with near-top-of-the-line exit velocities from the left side of the plate. The question as he matures, of course, is how much he'll be able to tap into it. Solarte is quite coordinated for his size, although his longer limbs will challenge his ability to make consistent contact. Still, he has plenty of bat speed from his closed-off stance and displays strong pitch recognition. Solarte is currently an above-average runner but figures to slow down as he adds weight. He uses his athleticism well on defense with clean actions and a strong arm. There are few big league shortstops his size, but he'll be given every chance to stick there, even if the Marlins may give him playing time at second and third, as they do with most infield prospects. He will have as much upside as anyone in the Marlins' system if he can tap into his tremendous tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilken set the ACC career record with 71 homers over his three years at Wake Forest, prompting the Brewers to take him with the 18th overall pick in 2023. It hasn’t been an ideal start to his career from a health standpoint. Wilken was hit in the face in his fifth game of in his first full season, and while he returned to Double-A Biloxi a month later and got some time in the Arizona Fall League, he admitted later he needed eye therapy to work on his depth perception the following offseason. He returned to the Southern League for 2025 and had a .392 OBP, .550 SLG and 18 homers in 65 games before suffering a dislocated left kneecap during a first-round division title celebration. He tried to return in August, but issues still lingered and he underwent knee surgery early in the offseason. The Demon Deacons legend would have broken through to Triple-A at last in the second half if not for the most recent injury, and the IL time has very much clouded his standing. From the positive side, he did an even better job of honing in on pitches in the zone at Double-A in ’25, and his ability to lift and pull the ball allowed him to post big slugging numbers when healthy. Among the negatives, his stiffness at the plate still makes him highly vulnerable to sliders down and away, and upper-level arms will pick up on that. With well-below-average speed, Wilken was never a stolen-base threat, and while he has the arm for the hot corner, his lack of quickness will hinder him from being an asset there. He’s yet to play first base in the pros entering 2026. Health will be paramount in his push to bring his pop to Milwaukee before becoming Rule 5-eligible next offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilken was a slugging force during his days at Wake Forest, winning the 2021 Cape Cod League MVP and setting the ACC career record with 71 homers (31 of which came in his junior year). Milwaukee selected the hulking infielder 18th overall in 2023, signed him for $3.15 million and got aggressive with him in his first full season with an opening assignment to Double-A Biloxi. He was hit in the face by a fastball on April 11 in just his fifth game of 2024, missed roughly a month and never quite recovered in terms of results, finishing with a .199/.312/.363 line and 17 homers in 108 games with the Shuckers. A move to the Arizona Fall League, where he batted .155 with 32 strikeouts in 100 plate appearances, didn’t do much to end the year on a high note. It's tough to balance the impact of the early-season HBP, as well as the move to the pitcher-friendly Southern League. Batting hunched over from the right side with a toe tap, the Demon Deacons legend is built to rip hard-hit balls in the air to the pullside, and he still has ample strength. His 17 homers were fourth-most in the SL, but he’s also proved to be extremely vulnerable to soft stuff low and away, and pitchers took advantage. To his credit, he'd done an impressive job of cutting down on his chase rate in a return to Biloxi in 2025 and looked to be pushing for a move to Triple-A before suffering a dislocated patella in his left knee. A well-below-average runner, Wilken has been third-base-only in pro ball, and while he has ample arm strength for the hot corner, he still might be a better fit at first base long-term, given his range and 6-foot-4 frame. His early 2025 trajectory provided hope that he could still be valuable at either corner-infield spot when healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cape Cod League MVP in 2021, Wilken set multiple home run records at Wake Forest and finished as both the Demon Deacons’ and ACC’s all-time leader with 71 long balls over his three years on campus. Thirty-one of those came in his junior campaign, placing him second in Division I. That helped push him into the first round to the Brewers with the 18th overall pick and he signed for $3.15 million. Wilken reached Double-A Biloxi in his first taste of the pros and finished with a .285/.414/.473 line with five homers over 47 games across three levels. The right-handed slugger relies on the strength in his upper half to generate bat speed and loft that helps him send balls over fences in bunches. He can look almost hunched over the plate before ripping at the ball with a slight step as a lower load. Wilken’s swing decisions improved over his time at Wake, and while he’ll take his walks, the early strikeout concerns that emerged in college could return against more advanced pro arms, as they did in his small Double-A sample. Standing 6-foot-4, Wilken clocks in as a well-below-average runner. He can move around capably at the hot corner and has more than enough arm for the position, but his defense doesn’t figure to add much value to his overall profile. Given his size and speed, he might have to move across the diamond to first, where his power would still more than fit the bill.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frey won Louisiana 2-A state titles in his final two seasons at Rosepine HS in 2021 and '22, then two College World Series championships at Louisiana State in 2023 and '25. He got just 76 at-bats in his first two years with the Tigers, in part because of a torn labrum in his right shoulder that required surgery in the summer of 2024. He didn't become a full-time starter until midway through last spring yet finished with the best batting line (.331/.420/.641) in LSU's lineup and provided several clutch hits during the postseason. After signing for $997,500 as a third-rounder, he slashed .330/.434/.470 during a month in Single-A. Physically imposing at 6-foot-6 and 225 pounds, Frey generated the highest measured bat speed in the 2025 Draft as well as some of the best exit velocities. He's a disciplined hitter who waits for pitches he can drive, and he has shown the ability to handle lefties and righties and all types of pitches. The Astros hope he can create a steeper bat path so he can elevate the ball more consistently and realize his 30-homer potential. While he spent most of his college career as a DH, Frey is an underrated athlete who was a catcher and dual-threat quarterback in high school. A solid runner who's quicker once he gets going, he'll get the opportunity to play center field in pro ball. At worst, he projects as a right fielder with solid arm strength and perhaps more if he can lengthen his arm action.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes in the 2022 prep class, Jordan went undrafted because he was a three-star wide receiver set on playing two sports at Mississippi State. He never stepped on the gridiron for the Bulldogs but performed well for two seasons before signing for a well-above-slot $1,997,500 in 2024's fourth round. He led the Single-A California League with 14 homers in his first full pro season despite missing the final month with an oblique strain, and he fell just one hit and one RBI short of the triple crown. Jordan has the quickest swing and the best all-around tools in the system. His right-handed stroke generates huge exit velocities and at least double-plus raw power that plays to any part of any ballpark. Though he still needs to tame a tendency to swing through in-zone fastballs and chase breaking balls, he did cut his strikeout rate from 27 percent with the Bulldogs to 23 percent last year. Jordan can get from home to first base in less than four seconds on a grounder, and he started translating that plus-plus speed into stolen-base and center-field prowess in 2025. He swiped 27 bags in 31 attempts (87 percent) after stealing just seven in two college seasons, and he looked very comfortable in center after playing only 13 games there at Mississippi State. He still needs to hone his defensive instincts but his 30/30 upside will work anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Jordan was one of the best high school athletes in the 2022 class, he went undrafted because he planned on playing baseball and football at Mississippi State. A three-star wide receiver recruit, he never took the gridiron for the Bulldogs but batted .336 with 30 homers in two seasons. After forfeiting their 2024 second- and third-rounders to sign free agents Matt Chapman and Blake Snell, the Giants were thrilled to find Jordan available in the fourth round and paid him a well over-slot $1,997,500. Jordan may have had the quickest swing in the 2024 Draft, and his bat speed and strength produce high-end exit velocities and plus-plus raw power to all fields. He'll need to tame his right-handed swing and approach to make the most of his pop, because he swings through fastballs in the zone and chases breaking balls off the plate. While he did improve his pitch recognition and plate discipline during two seasons in college, he still struck out at a 27 percent clip. Jordan has at least plus baseball speed and may have double-plus straight-line quickness, but he's still figuring out how to use it. He's not aggressive on the bases -- he swiped just seven bags in two years at Mississippi State -- and has shaky instincts in the outfield. He spent most of his time with the Bulldogs on the outfield corners while improving his arm strength from fringy to average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $2.3 million at the start of the 2024 international signing period, Lugo provided some intriguing early returns with a strong debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he showed off his potential power-speed combination. His first time in the United States wasn’t a failure, but lacked the same kind of impact, with the organization erring on the side of caution by shutting him down after just 35 games because of a back strain. The Angels are looking forward to seeing what a fully healthy Lugo can do at age 19 this season. The right-handed hitter has as much raw power as anyone in the system, it’s just a question of him learning to get to it more consistently. He can hit the ball hard to all fields, with most of that pop showing up to his pull side. Adding more loft so that he’s not hitting the ball hard on the ground should help. He was more patient during his time in the Arizona Complex League, though the strikeout rate remained high, and he needs to work to cut down his tendency to chase. Lugo has only played shortstop thus far in his brief career, and there’s no reason to move him from the premium position yet. He’s agile enough with plenty of arm to stick there, at least for the time being. There is a chance that the strong 6-foot-3 infielder will slow down as he continues to fill out his frame, which could necessitate a move over to third in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as one of the better infielders in the 2024 international class, Lugo received a $2.3 million bonus to sign with the Angels. The younger brother of former big leaguer Dawel Lugo, Joswa made a strong first impression during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, slashing .301/.370/.466 with five homers and 18 steals, raising the excitement bar for his arrival stateside in 2025. A right-handed hitter with easy raw power, Lugo can make hard contact with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, even if most of his thump is showing up to his pull side thus far. The strikeout rate was a little higher than expected, just over 23 percent, coming mostly from his tendency to chase. He can get to a lot of pitches that he shouldn’t be swinging at, and that will be an area of focus in his development. He has as much offensive upside as any hitter in the system. An average runner right now, Lugo will play shortstop -- where he played exclusively in the DSL -- for as long as he can. While he has a strong arm and good hands, there’s a chance he outgrows the premium position and has to slide over to third base. The good news is he has the instincts to be really strong at the hot corner and could very well have the hitting profile to match.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dawel Lugo went to the Futures Game and spent parts of three seasons in the big leagues with the Tigers. Now it’s his younger brother Joswa’s turn after he signed with the Angels at the start of the 2024 international signing period for $2.3 million. The No. 37 prospect on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International prospects list for this year’s class, he brings a lot of offensive potential in a bigger infielder’s frame to the organization. Lugo’s tools have reminded some scouts of those of Reds infielder Noelvi Marte when he first entered pro ball. Lugo flashes easy raw power, but not at the expense of contact. There isn’t a ton of swing-and-miss in his game so far, showing an ability to make consistent hard contact with confidence that gap power will reach the seats as he matures. How much he physically matures will determine if he can stick at shortstop. The Angels will send him out at the premium position for the time being, and he has good hands and footwork to go along with enough arm to play there. It’s possible that as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame, he’ll lose a tick from his average speed, in which case moving to third (much like Marte has done for the Reds) might make sense. The good news is he might have the run-producing power profile teams like at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $2.5 million out of the Bahamas in July 2017, Robinson vaulted to as high as No. 43 on MLB Pipeline's preseason Top 100 in the spring of 2020. That April, he was arrested and charged with assaulting a police officer after he was seen walking on a Phoenix-area highway. He later said the incident was the result of mental health struggles, but legal issues -- including those surrounding his visa -- kept him from playing in official Minor League games until the 2023 season. Robinson slashed .283/.382/.532 with 14 homers and 23 steals in 65 games across three levels following his return, reaching as high as Double-A. Added to the 40-man roster in 2021, he was designated for assignment last August but remained in the organization. Allowed to work out at the D-backs' facility and participate in extended spring training games during his absence, Robinson still had plenty of rust in his bat upon his return, as expected for someone with that much missed time. He struck out 31.6 percent of the time in 2023, a stat that increased with every stop. At Double-A in particular, Robinson often whiffed against quality softer stuff. That aside, he did show some pop out of a relaxed batting stance when he did make contact, and the hope for eventual plus all-fields power remains entering his age-23 season. Robinson moves well in his 6-foot-3 frame, and as he showed in 2023, he isn't afraid of pushing the envelope on the basepaths. He did move primarily from center field to the corners last season, and he could be an above-average defender in either spot with enough arm for right. Robinson will work back toward the 40-man with more at-bats in '24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs tapped into the same Bahamian talent pipeline from which they signed Jazz Chisholm ($200,000) in 2015 to get Robinson, signing the toolsy outfielder for $2.5 million in July 2017. He made a strong impression on club officials in his pro debut the following year, finishing the season in the Rookie Pioneer League at age 17. Robinson garnered midseason All-Star honors in the Class A Short Season Northwest League in 2019 to earn a full-season promotion up to Class A Kane County, where he was more than three years younger than the Midwest League's average player. Robinson spent time at the D-backs' alternate training site and fall instructional program in 2020 and sat out all of 2021 as he worked his way through a legal issue, though he did get in some work at the D-backs' facility in the Dominican Republic. With Robinson's special combination of size and athleticism, it should come as no surprise that the young outfielder also possesses multiple impact tools. None is louder than the massive right-handed raw power that could one day make Robinson one of the sport's premier sluggers. He gets to it often, generating effortless pull-side power, as well as opposite-field pop that was much improved in 2020 after Robinson improved his diet and added nearly 25 pounds of muscle. Scouts who wonder whether he will ever hit enough to reach his power ceiling cite his swing-and-miss issues and ground-ball tendencies as reasons for concern. Others are more optimistic about Robinson's bat, viewing him as a natural hitter whose offensive development has been slowed by a lack of reps. Robinson's plus speed and long strides give him enough range to play center field for the time being, though it's widely expected he will outgrow the position and move to an outfield corner -- most likely right field, where his plus arm strength fits well. Robinson has been away from game action for two years, so it remains to be seen how much -- if anything -- has changed. While the two lost years hurt, Robinson is still young and will play the entire 2022 season as a 21-year-old. If he's able to get back into form quickly, he has the tools to be a quick riser through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs tapped into the same Bahamian talent pipeline from which they signed Jazz Chisholm in 2015 ($200,000) to get Robinson, signing the toolsy outfielder for $2.5 million in July 2017. He made a strong impression on club officials in his pro debut the following year, finishing the season in the Rookie Pioneer League at age 17. Robinson garnered midseason All-Star honors in the Class A Short Season Northwest League in 2019 to earn a full-season promotion up to Class A Kane County, where he was more than three years younger than the Midwest League's average player. Robinson spent time at the D-backs' alternate training site and fall instructional program in 2020. While Robinson has not played in any games in 2021 as he works through a pending legal issue, he has gotten in some work at the D-backs' facility in the Dominican Republic. With Robinson's special combination of size and athleticism, it should come as no surprise that the young outfielder also possesses multiple impact tools. None is louder than the massive right-handed raw power that could one day make Robinson one of the sport's premier sluggers. He gets to it often, generating effortless pull-side power, as well as opposite-field pop that was much improved in 2020 after Robinson improved his diet and added nearly 25 pounds of muscle. Scouts who wonder if Robinson will ever hit enough to reach his power ceiling cite his swing-and-miss issues and ground-ball tendencies as reasons for concern. Others are more optimistic about Robinson's bat, viewing him as a natural hitter whose offensive development has been slowed by a lack of reps. Robinson's plus speed and long strides give him enough range to play center field for the time being, though it's widely expected he will outgrow the position and move to an outfield corner -- most likely right field, where his plus arm strength fits well. Such a move down the defensive spectrum should have little impact on Robinson's development, and there are some who think it could even lead to his expedited arrival in Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arizona landed a potential impact international prospect when they signed Bahamian shortstop Jazz Chisholm for $200,000 in 2015, then tapped into that same youth pipeline again two years later to get Robinson, who signed for $2.5 million. It hasn't taken long for the power-hitting teenager to reward the D-backs for their investment. After an impressive pro debut that saw him reach the Rookie Pioneer League at age 17, Robinson continued to fare well against older competition in 2019, earning midseason All-Star honors in the Class A Short Season Northwest League before advancing to the Class A Midwest League, where he was more than three years younger than the circuit's average player. Robinson is both a physical specimen -- listed at 6-foot-3, 190 pounds -- and an impressive athlete who shows the makings of having average or better tools across the board. He has the type of prodigious right-handed power that could one day make him one of the game's more revered sluggers, and he already applies it during games from line-to-line. Robinson also shows feel to hit, with plate discipline and contact skills that stand out for his age and experience. That hitting ability is the reason why scouts are so bullish about Robinson's power potential, and he stands to make a major jump in that department as he learns to consistently hit the ball in the air. While Robinson has the speed, range and instincts to handle center field for the time being, he's likely to lose a step and ultimately outgrow the position as he adds strength to his ultra-projectable frame. He profiles better at a corner-outfield spot long term -- likely right field, where his strong arm is a clean fit. Luckily, a move down the defensive spectrum should have little impact on Robinson's overall ceiling, which is the highest in Arizona's system and one of the highest among all teenage prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two years removed from their signing of shortstop Jazz Chisholm for $200,000, the D-backs tapped into the Bahamian baseball pipeline again in 2017. This time, however, they shelled out big money to land Robinson, signing MLB Pipeline's No. 15 international prospect for more than $2.5 million. He already looks to be a worthy investment for the club after an impressive pro debut at age 17 that he followed with a red-hot start in the Class A Short Season Northwest League in 2019. Robinson is a physical specimen who generates massive raw power to all fields and already has shown that he can apply it during games. His understanding of the strike zone and plate discipline stands out given his age and lack of experience. Those qualities, along with his explosive swing, give Robinson a chance to be at least an average hitter. He has the speed, range and instincts for center field, though, with so much physical projection remaining, there is a chance he'll outgrow the spot, in which he'll fit nicely at either outfield corner. Robinson has the highest ceiling of any player in Arizona's system as a slugger who also has feel to hit and the potential to stick in center field. While the early returns have been impressive, the D-backs continue to preach patience with regards to Robinson's development, as they note that coming from the Bahamas isn't the same as coming from a place like the Dominican Republic in terms of experience. At the same time, it's hard not to get excited about a player that oozes as much potential as Robinson.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most people think of the Bahamas as a vacation destination. The scouting industry, more and more of late, is seeing it as a place to mine for baseball talent. The D-backs have been particularly busy, signing Jazz Chisholm for $200,000 in 2015 and going all in on Robinson's tools for more than $2.5 million. Robinson was No. 15 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list heading into the July signing period in 2017 because of his raw tools, athleticism and tremendous ceiling. The D-backs love his physicality and potential to tap into his considerable raw power. He showed a pretty good understanding of the strike zone with some plate discipline already, especially given his age and lack of experience, and the D-backs know there will be a learning curve in terms of recognizing breaking and offspeed stuff. Robinson has enough speed to stay in center, but there's the chance he'll outgrow the spot, in which case he'll fit nicely in a corner. The D-backs are preaching patience and caution when talking about Robinson, noting that coming from the Bahamas isn't the same as coming from a place like the Dominican Republic in terms of experience. They see Red Sox shortstop Xander Bogaerts as a potential model, one who played in the Dominican Summer League for his first summer of pro ball, while Robinson was able to make his debut in the United States, playing in the rookie-level Arizona Leaegue in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With an uptick in velocity and stuff during his senior season, Slawinski displayed an exciting combination of projectability and polish to become the best pitching prospect in Texas (and one of the best prep lefties in the 2025 class). He was projected to go in the top two rounds, but landed in Round 3 to the Angels, who went way over slot with a $2.5 million bonus -- around Competitive Balance Round A money -- to sign him away from his Texas A&M commitment. From the scouting department to player development, there is universal excitement about Slawinski’s upside and how he carries himself. The 6-foot-3 lefty finished his senior season with a fastball that sat in the 90-93 mph range and touched 95, and it plays up because of its ride and the extension in his delivery. He has two breaking pitches, with an upper-70s slider that has two-plane depth ahead of his mid-70s curve, which isn’t as consistent. He already has very good feel for his fading low-80s changeup. As a four-sport standout in high school, Slawinski uses his athleticism on the mound to his advantage. He gets down the mound with ease and has a very good feel to pitch, with the ability to land all his offerings for strikes. Continued added strength will only help his stuff tick up, and going from a tiny school to pro instruction could help him eventually develop three plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McKenzie was a Top 100 prospect as the 2025 Draft approached, one who reminded some of fellow North Carolina high school product MacKenzie Gore, especially in terms of his ability to spin a breaking ball. He didn’t have the same velocity jump as Gore did in his senior year, but some scouts did think McKenzie flashed first-round potential as the Draft approached. His commitment to LSU stood in the way, but the Braves took him in the fourth round, giving him a first-round caliber bonus of $3 million to walk away from the Tigers. The Braves have never shied away from a high school pitching prospect, and McKenzie is very much a ball of clay ready to be molded. His feel for spin is unquestionable, with a hammer 75-78 mph curveball that is already a plus pitch; it will only get better as he adds strength and power. He showed glimpses of excellent velocity (90-95 mph) out of the gate last spring, but isn’t yet able to maintain it deep into his starts. There’s some fade and sink in his low-80s changeup, something he’ll have to commit to throwing more as a pro to allow it to develop. McKenzie has shown an ability to throw strikes overall, but that also can improve if he can tighten up his delivery and long arm action. There’s room to add to his 6-foot-2 frame, though he has a narrow build. There’s a great variance in what he can become, but there are those who thought had he gone on to LSU, he might have emerged as the next Kade Anderson, who went No. 3 overall in the 2025 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the 2018-19 international signing period opened on July 2, 2018, the Angels had to wait until the end of August to sign Ramirez when he turned 16, getting the outfielder for $1 million. He immediately showed off his power, and the holes in his swing, during his Dominican Summer League debut in 2019. It was more of the same during his United States debut in 2021, though he did enough in the Arizona Complex League to get a late promotion to full-season Lake Elsinore shortly before he turned 19. Ramirez’s potential is tied to his raw power from the right side of the plate. He has as much raw pop as anyone in the organization, with high exit velocities and the ability to drive the ball to all fields. His swing gets long and he’s super-aggressive, a combination that has led to a 34.7 percent strikeout rate heading into 2022, leading some to wonder if he’s going to make enough contact to be productive. He does draw some walks, but needs to be better at recognizing and not chasing spin out of the zone. A solid athlete, Ramirez runs well enough to keep getting reps in center field, where he’s largely played since signing. As he physically matures, right field seems like a better long-term home, with the hope that more reps will help him refine his approach and provide the kind of run-producing bat the Angels need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez was one of the youngest players in the 2018-19 international amateur class, one who couldn’t sign until the end of August, when he turned 16. The Angels were more than willing to wait, inking the outfielder for $1 million on his birthday. He showed off his raw power with 17 extra-base hits in 39 games during his 2019 debut in the Dominican Summer League, but also struck out in more than 33 percent of his plate appearances, trends that continued during his United States debut in 2021. It is the 6-foot-2 Ramirez’s offensive profile that made him such an attractive prospect in the first place. His calling card is certainly his easily plus raw power from the right side of the plate. He drives the ball to all fields and had very high exit velocities during his brief professional career thanks to outstanding bat speed. There is some length to his swing which, in combination with an aggressive approach, has contributed to that high strikeout rate. More reps will help his pitch recognition, and there’s confidence in time he’ll refine his gameplan at the plate. With a big, strong and athletic frame, Ramirez showed he could handle playing center field during his debut with a tick-above-average speed. He’s likely destined to a corner, with an arm that should be strong enough for right field in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top outfielders in the 2018-19 international signing class, Ramirez landed on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list because of his athleticism and raw power. It’s what the Angels saw when they gave him $1 million to sign in August 2018 and much of it was on display during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, along with signs that he has a long path ahead of him. There is no question about Ramirez’s raw power. He can drive the ball to all fields with elite bat speed and absolutely vicious swings. He produced an average exit velocity of 95 mph in the DSL last summer, sky high for that level. With that came a whole lot of swing and miss, but the Angels aren’t overly concerned about his high strikeout rate given his age and experience level, believing he’ll start making more contact as he refines his approach. Ramirez is a big and powerful athlete, one who belongs in the conversation of the top tier of athletes in a system full of them. He runs well for his size, and while he likely won’t have the range to stay there long-term, he’s shown he can currently play a solid center field. The Angels will likely let him keep playing there for a while, knowing he could eventually develop into a run-producing right fielder type in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just because the Reds were limited in their international spending during the 2017-18 signing period does not mean they didn’t find any good players. Case in point is Cerda, a toolsy outfielder who signed for $100,000 in July 2017. After a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2018, Cerda struggled when he first came stateside, though he still hit for power in the rookie-level Appalachian League. He tapped into it with more consistency in his full-season debut in 2021, earning a late promotion up to High-A and getting added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. Though he’s still far away from the big leagues, the Reds thought Cerda’s tools were loud enough to warrant protection on the roster. He has tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate, but has yet to maximize it in games due to inconsistency in his approach. There’s plenty of bat speed, but he chases too much, leading to high strikeout rates, though he is willing to draw walks to help offset that a bit. While Cerda has above-average speed, he hasn’t been much of a basestealing threat. And while he’s largely been a center fielder in the early stages of his career, most think he’ll be best suited for right field, where he played after his promotion to High-A. He could be a more controlled version of former Reds outfield prospect Jose Siri at the plate, one who fits the corner outfield power profile well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds weren’t allowed to spend over $300,000 on any player on the international market during the 2017-18 signing period. They think they may have found a steal in Cerda, who signed for $100,000 at the start of the signing period and then posted a very respectable .841 OPS during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. Aggressively jumped to the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, he couldn’t replicate that success, though his power was still on display. Big, athletic and projectable, Cerda’s raw power is his calling card on the offensive side. The raw pop is plus from the right side of the plate, but there are questions about his ability to make enough contact to get to it. He uses a narrow stance with a high leg lift and hasn’t always been on time, contributing to a 26.6 percent strikeout rate in his brief career. He does offset the swing-and-miss somewhat with a willingness to draw walks (11.9 BB rate). Cerda might have a tick above-average speed and combines that with good instincts to give him every chance to play center field for a long time. He’ll flash an above-average arm that might be plus in time, so he could profile as a power-hitting right fielder should he have to shift over to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have assembled a line of shortstop prospects in their system, but Montilla might be the least publicized of the bunch. Signed out of Venezuela for a $500,000 bonus in the 2022 international class, the speedy switch-hitter has been on a slow but steady climb up the organizational ladder. It’s not an indictment on his ability as much as a history of mastering a level with time. He was on his way to a strong campaign with the Flying Tigers and a potential summer promotion when a torn ACL ended his season in July. Montilla brings a lot of tools to his game, from athleticism and speed on the bases to a slashing bat, though he’s more effective hitting from the left side. He handles velocity well and produces strong hard-hit rates for a young player who has yet to hit for power at any level. More of his exit velocity comes from line drives than fly balls, and he showed an ability to use all fields well before his injury. His strikeout rate is a little high for someone with a reasonable swing rate, but he needs to make more consistent contact, particularly from the right side. He has the athleticism and skills to stick at shortstop with a little more consistency. The Tigers could find themselves with options at shortstop in a few years with any luck. Montilla could break out as a shortstop prospect and still find himself in competition with Bryce Rainer, who’s returning from injury as well. How Montilla matures at the plate could determine whether he’s a full-time player or more of a utility infield option. He’ll need some patience first as he adjusts back to the daily grind once he returns from his knee surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
