He hit .249/.355/.399 with 13 homers and 64 steals in 114 games at High-A and Double-A in his first full season before being traded to the Rays in the offseason as part of the Shane Baz deal. Overn’s carrying tool is that speed, which some scouts hung an 80 grade on coming out of the Draft. Those wheels make him a legitimately disruptive threat on the bases and a double-plus defender in center field, where he uses good reads, instincts and body awareness to run down balls other defenders can’t. Overn’s athleticism allows him to make such an impact with his glove and feet it’ll likely keep him in center long-term despite what might be a tick-below-average arm. Overn’s potential impact at the plate is more of an open question. He’s a left-handed slasher type in the classic table-setter mold who needs to focus on putting the ball in play, getting on-base and making things happen. Though he can occasionally drop the barrel, his slug should come from turning singles into doubles and doubles into triples rather than trying to hit homers. His glove-first speedster profile is not unlike his former organizationmate Enrique Bradfield Jr.. Now with Tampa Bay -- an organization that values speed and defense highly -- the progress Overn makes offensively will determine whether he develops into a high-floor regular or more of a bench player in the Reggie Willits mold.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked in the top 20 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the 2021 signing period opened, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million. After an impressive debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing, his first taste of life in the United States and the Arizona Complex League did not go as well. He was middling along with a .707 OPS when he was sent to the Reds at the 2022 Trade Deadline for Brandon Drury. While the numbers in his first full season with his new organization weren’t eye-popping, he more consistently showed off his solid tools with the move to the Florida State League. A switch-hitter, Acosta has shown the ability to swing the bat well from both sides of the plate with quick hands and bat speed, though he was a bit better from the left side with Daytona last year. While he keeps the strikeouts relatively in check and draws walks, he can get overly aggressive at times because he has such strong contact skills. He’s never going to be a huge power guy, but there were some good exit velocities coming off his bat in 2023, and he has the chance to find his way to some extra-base thump in the gaps. The hope is that Acosta, who is an above-average runner, will be able to stick at shortstop, and the Reds will likely keep giving him reps there for as long as possible. He has a decent arm and actions, but some see a move to second base eventually becoming necessary. How far his offense advances will determine if he can profile as an everyday guy at one spot in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acosta was thought to be one of the better prospects available on the international amateur market when the 2021 signing period opened, with the Padres swooping in and signing him for $1.8 million on the opening day (Jan. 15). He made a strong first impression that summer with an OPS over .900, but he was having less success in his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League when he was sent to the Reds in the Brandon Drury Trade Deadline deal in 2022. In the early stages of his pro career, Acosta has shown some acumen for getting on base and making contact from both sides of the plate. He has quick hands and an aggressive approach, but he’s shown a willingness to see pitches and draw walks. There hasn’t been much power to speak of, and he needs to add strength to his frame, which could help him translate his contact skills into more extra-base authority. Acosta is a good athlete who runs well and possesses all of the defensive tools -- range, arm, footwork and instincts -- to stick at shortstop. He’ll keep getting reps on both sides of second base to potentially provide defensive versatility down the line and also to make sure he gets the at-bats he needs to reach his offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 19 prospect in the 2020-21 international class, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million on Jan. 15, 2021. The early returns were promising as the Dominican Republic native flashes five-tool potential and hit .285/.431/.484 over 56 games in his Dominican Summer League debut, though he was having less impact offensively during his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League when he was sent to the Reds in return for Brandon Drury at the Trade Deadline. A switch-hitter, Acosta boasts an impressive set of tools. The teenager has quick hands and is an aggressive hitter with a swing-first mentality. As a result of the aggression, he handles fastballs better than off-speed pitches, though that’s not all that uncommon in young hitters. He doesn’t hit for a ton of power yet, but still has time to grow into his 5-foot-11, 170-pound frame and there’s hope he’ll tack on a bit more power as he develops. A projectable athlete, Acosta has the athleticism to stick at short, but could also wind up at second base. Above-average speed, which helped him steal 26 bases in 56 games last season, gives Acosta the range to make all the necessary plays up the middle, though the accuracy on his throws isn’t always consistent. He does, however, have plenty of arm strength and could develop into a middle of the diamond star if everything goes well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arguably the prize of their 2020-21 international haul, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million out of the Dominican Republic. He’s clearly worth dreaming on. Acosta boasts five-tool potential and is a twitchy athlete with lots of projection. A switch-hitter, Acosta has extremely quick hands, which should make his swing play from both sides of the plate. As he grows into his frame and perhaps adds an inch or two – at 16, he stands 5-foot-11, 170 pounds – the Padres envision Acosta growing into a bit of power. He’s raw at shortstop but can probably stick there, considering his athleticism and excellent arm. Acosta is a classic projectable athlete, and San Diego has had success in the past developing middle infielders. It’s unclear what position Acosta might end up playing, but he has all the tools necessary to stick up the middle somewhere. If his bat develops too, the Padres might have another big-time athlete to plug into the mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincones went from Plant HS in Tampa, alma mater of Wade Boggs and Kyle Tucker, to St. Petersburg JC. After two seasons there, he moved on to Florida Atlantic and put up huge numbers to land in the third round of the 2022 Draft with the Phillies. After a decent first full season, a torn thumb ligament shelved him for a large chunk of the 2024 campaign. The son of a former Mariners Minor League pitcher, Rincones played a full 2025 in Triple-A, earning a spot on the 40-man roster following the season. Rincones is a big, strong left-handed hitter with huge raw power he’s still learning to tap into. He can hit the ball extremely hard, with both his max exit velocity (116.4 mph) and his 90th percentile EV (108.6) near the top of the charts last year. Considering his ability to do damage, he manages to keep the strikeouts relatively in check and continues to draw a ton of walks. What he hasn’t been able to do is hit lefties, with a .323 OPS against southpaws in 2025. Rincones will never be confused with a burner, but the big man knows how to run the bases and he’s stolen over 20 bases in each of his three full seasons of pro ball. He’s a decent defender in an outfield corner, working to become average on the grass. He might be on the long side of a platoon with his ability to crush right-handed pitching and he could be a regular if he can refine his approach against lefties.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years of junior college, Rincones went on to Florida Atlantic University and parlayed a big junior year into becoming the Phillies’ third-round selection in 2022. After a solid first full season, he seemed poised to make a big leap to the upper levels following a stint in the Arizona Fall League, but a torn thumb ligament limited him to just 68 games in 2024 with Double-A Reading, though he did make a return engagement in the AFL. A 6-foot-3 left-handed hitter, Rincones has the frame, strength and capacity to be a good hitter with plenty of power. But while he did hit 11 homers in his shortened season with Reading last year, he still has a hit-first mentality at the plate. His metrics are solid, with good exit velocities and walk rates, and he rarely chases, giving him the chance to hit at the next level. The key will be for him to find ways to tap into his natural strength without sacrificing any of that hit tool. Rincones’ baserunning abilities have perhaps been undersold in the past. He’s far from a burner, but despite getting very low run grades, he’s been an instinctual basestealer, with 55 steals over his two full seasons, and he takes great pride in impacting the game that way. He’s an acceptable defender in an outfield corner and he’s close to knocking on the door; if the power starts to show up more consistently, he could be a regular at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Rincones was drafted late by the Padres after two years at St. Petersburg Junior College, he moved on to Florida Atlantic University. He put up huge numbers in his one season there and his 1.110 OPS helped him land in the third round of the 2022 Draft with the Phillies. He was unable to play the summer after signing because of a shoulder issue, but turned in a full season across two levels of A ball in 2023 before finishing up with a solid showing in the Arizona Fall League. Rincones is a big and strong left-handed hitter who looks like he should be able to produce the kind of power numbers (19 homers) he put up at FAU in 2022. He did hit 15 balls out during his first season of pro ball, but there might be much more in the tank if he can make some mechanical adjustments. Rincones has utilized a fairly flat swing that has produced a lot of line drives, and as he learns to add more loft, the pop should show up. Defensively, Rincones is limited to an outfield corner, with some thinking first base might eventually be a better fit. His now-average arm would work from right and he saw time at both corners in 2023, something he’ll continue moving forward as his bat carries him up to Philadelphia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a former Mariners Minor League hurler, Rincones should easily outstrip his dad’s one year of pro ball. The younger Rincones began his college career at St. Petersburg Junior College, earning All-America status there in 2021 and getting drafted late by the Padres. He then transferred to Florida Atlantic and took home Conference USA Newcomer of the Year honors with a 1.110 OPS that catapulted him to the Phillies in the third round of the 2022 Draft. While he didn’t make his pro debut last summer, Rincones did show off his offensive upside at instructs, and the Phillies believe he has the chance to show he’s one of the best hitters in the system once he gets going. The left-handed hitter has the chance to be solid at the plate with potentially plus power, using an advanced approach to drive the ball to all fields. He limited his strikeouts at FAU and walked a bunch, too, allowing him to tap into that power more consistently, especially to the pull side. The bat is what will carry Rincones up the organizational ladder. The Phillies will continue to have him play the corner outfield, and he’s really limited to left with a below-average arm, mostly to maintain some versatility, trying to keep him from a first base/DH only box for as long as possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 70 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Still 17 on Draft Day in 2024, Payne was one of the youngest and fastest players in his class, and though he was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 53 prospect that year, he went 17th overall to the Brewers in July, signing for $3.44 million. He spent his entire first full season with Single-A Carolina, hitting .240/.354/.382 with eight homers and 31 steals in 77 games. Payne was one of only 11 players in their age-18 seasons or younger to get 300 or more plate appearances at Single-A in 2025, joining fellow Brewers Jesús Made, Luis Peña and José Anderson on that list. Payne’s plus-plus wheels continue to pop most on the diamond, and while he wasn’t always the most efficient attempted basestealer, his speed still gave opposing defenders plenty to consider. He glides well between the gaps in center field and could become a plus defender in the middle of the grass with more work there. The lefty hitter’s exit velocities have brought some intrigue to the offensive side of his game, and that added strength hasn’t come with the loss of any athleticism. Payne takes his walks by not expanding the zone, but after employing a leg kick, he can pull out of his swing quickly, leading him to be out of sync. His 30.1 percent strikeout rate in 2025 was no mirage with high whiff rates against all pitch types, and the choppiness of his swing led to a lot of ground balls. There could be more of a focus on waiting for pitches in the heart of the zone -- rather than generally swinging at most strikes -- that could help Payne build on his potential as a power-speed threat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the fastest players in the 2024 class, Payne was also one of its youngest with his 18th birthday coming one month after the Draft itself. He was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 53 prospect in the group but became a Day 1 shock when he went 17th overall to Milwaukee. Payne signed for below slot at $3.44 million, allowing the organization to spread savings for later in the Draft, and he played briefly for Single-A Carolina, including two games in the Carolina League postseason. Payne’s plus-plus speed is a game-changer as he proved in that quick dip in the pros with four steals in five attempts. Batting from the left side, he can explode out of the box and often opens up early in his swing to give himself a head start on the way to first. That can often lead to ground balls -- some of which he’ll beat out with his legs -- and it’ll be important for him to add some more lift on his swings as he enters the pros over a larger sample. To his credit, he impressed some Brewers coaches with his physicality after reporting, and his exit velocities have been better than expected out of the gate, offsetting some strikeout concerns in 2025. Because of his speed, Payne can track down balls gap to gap in center field, and he should get plenty of looks there throughout his career. Once considered fringy, the former Houston commit should also have an average arm to help his defensive work. Payne’s speed should work well in the modern game and gives him a decent floor, and considering he’ll be 18 for much of his first full season, he’ll be given plenty of space to fill out the rest of his game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Salas followed in older brothers Jose and Ethan's footsteps by moving to Venezuela at a young age from Florida and signing for big money. He earned the largest bonus of any player coming out of Venezuela in 2025 ($3.7 million) and skipped Rookie ball entirely during his debut season. Salas, 17, was more than a year younger than any other hitter in the Single-A Florida State League and understandably took his lumps (.564 OPS) against competition that was, on average, four years older than him. Despite being physically overmatched, Salas showed glimpses of why he was the No. 5 prospect in his class. The switch-hitter had one of the highest walk rates on the circuit and struck out at a league-average rate, thanks to a patient approach with vanishingly little chase. He handled secondary pitches well and made good contact from both sides of the plate, though his bat speed was better from the left side. While he flashed above-average power, he did not consistently impact the ball and struggled to keep weight on as the season progressed. Salas is aggressive on the basepaths, where he uses his above-average speed well. That speed also serves him well on defense, and the Marlins played him at six different positions. He currently looks best in center field where his athleticism and arm play up, although he'll be given every chance to stick on the infield dirt -- he signed as a shortstop -- and potentially develop as a multi-position defender. Salas deserves high praise for staying afloat in an ultra-aggressive assignment and would likely have been a first-round pick in a Draft scenario.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a baseball family that included a father, uncle and grandfather who played in the Minors and a pair of brothers (Jose and Ethan) who were recent international bonus babies, Salas was one of the most highly regarded prospects in the 2025 class. Born in Orlando, he moved to Venezuela and trained at the family's complex there before signing with the Marlins for $3.7 million in January. Some scouts believe he's more athletically gifted than his brothers, and like them he earns praise for his maturity and high baseball IQ. Much more advanced at the plate than most 17-year-olds, Salas is a switch-hitter who recognizes pitches well and makes good swing decisions. He has a compact stroke and doesn't hunt home runs, instead seeking to make contact, use the entire field and focus on getting base. He has a wiry 6-foot-2 frame and has the hitting ability and projectable strength to provide 15-20 homers per season in his prime. Salas has solid to plus speed and the savvy to use it well on the bases. His quick feet also make him a quality defender at shortstop, where he has fluid actions and the strong arm to make plays. Some evaluators think he could be even better in center field, which has been his primary position while he has made his pro debut in Single-A at age 17.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally drafted out of the Texas high school ranks in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft, Raya didn’t make his official pro debut until 2022, with the pandemic ruining any chance of him pitching after he signed and then a shoulder strain forcing him off the mound for all of 2021. He showed glimpses of potential on limited workloads the next two seasons, then took off and reached Triple-A in 2024, earning a spot on the 40-man roster. A return to Triple-A St. Paul in 2025 did not go as well as planned. A combination of size, concerns about durability and command issues are now pointing Raya towards a future in the bullpen, a transition that started at the end of last year. One of the big adjustments will be to pare down a repertoire that has had as many as six pitches in it. The fastball-sweeper combination will likely lead the way, with the heater coming in around 95-97 mph and the 86-mph slider missing a lot of bats even while he scuffled last year. His mid-80s curve can also make hitters look bad and he has a 90-91 mph cutter as well. The curve gets misses against left-handed hitters, so he might not need to worry about developing his changeup, which had good action to it, but he couldn’t land in the zone. There could be more ticks in the four-seamer coming in shorter stints, and he won’t have to worry as much about his command. If he can settle on a smaller menu in his new role, he could develop into a starter-turned-effective reliever kind of like former Twin Ronny Henriquez.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins did an excellent job scouting Raya heading into the shortened 2020 Draft, knowing what it would take to sign the Texas high schooler away from his Texas Tech commitment. Since taking him in the fourth round that year, he's run into some injury issues, with a shoulder strain keeping him on the shelf for all of the 2021 season. The next two seasons, the right-hander was on a super-cautious workload plan throwing just 127 2/3 innings combined in 2022 and 2023. Things started to click a bit more in 2024, with Raya reaching Double-A and finishing with close to 100 IP, earning a spot on the 40-man roster as a result. Raya has always excited with his pure stuff, but concerns about durability have dampened enthusiasm. He'll throw as many as six pitches at hitters, with both a four- and two-seam fastball that topped out at 97 mph and averaged over 94 in 2024. His best pitch is his plus mid-80s slider, a sweeper that misses a lot of bats. He still has a solid low-80s curve, and while his changeup wasn't used as much and was inconsistent, it still has solid characteristics. Last year, he added a 90-91 mph cutter that can be effective, though he needs to work on keeping it from blending with his sweeper. In addition to keeping his pitches distinct, Raya also needs to improve his control after walking 4.1 per nine last year. An area of focus for him this year will be his fastball command, with the belief that higher in-zone rates for his heater will bring that walk rate down. Now on the roster, it will be interesting to see how Raya responds as the workload constraints are loosened.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Twins selected Raya in the fourth round of the pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft, they knew they might have to be patient with the Texas prepster's development. It didn't help that a shoulder strain kept him from the mound for all of the 2021 season and the Twins were super cautious upon his return in 2022 and 2023, throwing a combined total of 127 2/3 innings over two years, though he did reach Double-A in the process. While the Twins erred on the side of caution and continued to closely monitor Raya's workload in 2023, they were very pleased with how his stuff progressed, leading to his promotion from High-A to Double-A before his 21st birthday. He's always had plenty of fastball, a pitch that was averaging around 96 mph, with high spin up in the zone. His real out pitch is his slider, missing a ton of bats at 84-85 mph, also with elite spin rates. He can land his slightly slower curve with depth to give hitters a different look, and the Twins think his changeup has improved the most, going from a below-average pitch when he was in Single-A to an offspeed offering that flashes plus with fade and depth. He's working on a cutter to round out his arsenal and has had good early returns with it, a harder Walker Buehler-ish kind of pitch. Not only has Raya's stuff improved, but he was landing all of it in the zone more consistently, with solid command in the zone, especially when he was with Cedar Rapids. He still needs to prove he can handle a full workload as a starter, and the gloves should start coming off a bit in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patience isn't always easy, but sometimes it's needed, especially when it comes to high school pitching talent. Case in point is Raya, the Twins' fourth-round pick out of the Texas prep ranks in 2020. He didn't pitch competitively in 2021 because of a shoulder strain, but while he was on a monitored workload in 2022, he showed exactly why the Twins were excited to get him with a strong debut in the Single-A Florida State League. There's a chance Raya could have a legitimate four-pitch mix at his disposal. His fastball is already an impact pitch, a four-seamer thrown with high spin rates that topped out at 97 mph. He can miss bats with a very good slider thrown mostly in the 82-83 mph range, also with elite-level spin rates, and has a slightly slower curve with good depth to it that can play against left-handed hitters. One of his main areas of focus has been developing his changeup to give him something else to attack lefties with and he's made progress in finding a grip that works for him. Raya has been around the strike zone with all of his offerings, and that, along with further development of that changeup, will help him maintain a true starter profile. As an undersized pitcher who has had some injuries, he'll have to prove to skeptics that he can handle the workload as the developmental gloves come off, but there's a reason why the Twins have fielded plenty of calls from other teams asking about Raya.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2022 season was the first time Raya pitched in affiliated games since the Twins selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft due to a shoulder strain that sidelined him for most of last season, and the Twins were eager to see how the relatively polished stuff of the 19-year-old from Laredo, Texas, was going to play in live action after he passed up a commitment to Texas Tech to sign with the organization. Raya didn't disappoint, throwing extremely well with Single-A Fort Myers. There could be a little bit of physical development left on the 6-foot, 165-pound frame, but his body is already twitchy and athletic. He knows he's on the smaller side and is said to love to model himself after Marcus Stroman, though he's got a fundamentally different profile reliant on a big four-seamer alongside three high-quality secondary pitches that entered the organization with great pitch profiles, with the Twins feeling like there's not too much work needed on those. The fastball sat in the low 90s while he was in high school but was said to be up to 95-96 and touching 97 entering '22. Raya pitches with a chip on his shoulder and is said to have made big strides in his mental development toward the end of '21, and as is the case with many young pitchers, the Twins hope he'll simplify and attack the strike zone with his quality stuff, which he's done in the past. He has the ability to quickly build his stock with strong live outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Raya was a bit of an under-the-radar high school right-hander from Texas when the 2020 Draft rolled around, one who didn’t quite make MLB Pipeline's Top 200 Draft prospects list and who many felt would go on to continue his amateur career at Texas Tech. Despite a shortened spring, the Twins' scouting staff had seen enough to take him in the fourth round last June and then saw him throw well during instructional league play last fall. While he's a bit undersized at 6-feet tall, Raya's combination of stuff, athleticism on the mound and feel for pitching give him the chance to start. He has a legitimate four-pitch mix, five if his two- and four-seam fastballs are separated out. In high school, he was up to 93 mph with his sinking two-seamer and was up to 96 mph with his four-seamer at instructs last year. The Twins liked that Raya entered pro ball with two distinct breaking balls, a tight curve that touches the upper-70s and a sweeping mid-80s slider. His changeup, another future average pitch, has good fade and sink. Raya's stuff plays up even more because of very high spin rates on his fastball and breaking stuff and he does a nice job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. Super young for a high school draftee, he was still 17 at the time of the Draft, Raya has the Twins excited for what he can do as he physically matures and climbs the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A hamate bone injury caused Tresh to miss the start of his 2020 collegiate season, but he put himself back on the radar at North Carolina State in 2021, when he homered 15 times in 56 games and helped the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. The Royals selected him in the 17th round and gave him a high bonus – $423,000 – to sign him away from returning to school. Tresh posted an .828 OPS between High-A and Double-A in his first full pro season in 2022, with 14 homers and 54 RBI. Tresh is a strong hitter who generates impressive exit velocities with his raw power and bat speed. He made more contact in 2022 with a 24.3% strikeout rate between both levels. Tresh is still aggressive, and there are still improvements to be made in his approach, especially with pitches on the outer part of the plate, but he has a lot of power potential. Behind the plate, Tresh showed significant improvement with his receiving last year. He has a plus arm and should become at least an average defender. Tresh receives high marks for his ability to run a pitching staff, a quiet competitor who leads by example. How far he goes and what his ceiling ends up being depends on whether he can continue his improved approach and contact at the higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At North Carolina State, Tresh caught sparingly behind Patrick Bailey, the No. 13 pick in 2020, and Tresh missed the start of the 2020 season with a broken hamate bone in his left hand. He put himself back on the radar and filled Bailey’s void in ’21, homering 15 times in 56 games last spring and helping the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. It felt like a steal when the Royals selected him all the way down in the 17th round, but Tresh stuck to his signability and wasn’t afraid to go back to school if needed. The Royals were able to sign him for $423,000, roughly the slot of a fourth-round selection. Tresh posted a 1.143 OPS in six games in Rookie ball after he was drafted, earning him a quick promotion to Low-A Columbia, where he struggled more in 10 games. Tresh has obvious raw power and consistently high exit velocities thanks to massive strength and bat speed. He’s aggressive at the plate and will need to do a better job of consistent contact, but the Royals see room for improvement as he spends more time with the hitting development program. Behind the plate, Tresh is inexperienced for a college catcher, but he showed significant improvement as a receiver in the fall. He has a plus arm to keep the running game in check and should become at least an average defender if the Royals keep him at catcher. Tresh earns praise for his leadership, ability to run a pitching staff and his quiet competitiveness. He still has a lot of ceiling for a college player, which was appealing to the Royals in the Draft. How far he will go depends on his improvement with contact and time behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Francisca was the centerpiece of the Guardians' 2023 international class and landed a $1,375,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He very much fits the club's favored profile as a switch-hitting middle infielder, although he's grown well beyond his listed 5-foot-8 size to nearly 6-foot, which gives him a higher ceiling than other Guardians infield prospects. The 2025 season was a step back in production, though, as he slashed just .229/.320/.302 in his first full campaign at Single-A after posting a wRC+ of 144 and 141 in his first two pro seasons, largely in Rookie ball. At his best, Francisca has flashy tools, led by a special knack for finding the barrel. With a more consistent approach, his pitch recognition and ability to adjust could give him a potentially plus hit tool. A natural right-hander, the team hopes to get more power from his righty swing, although some scouts like him better from the left side, so there could be discussion down the line of him focusing on just the left side. His once-precocious bat speed backed up in 2025 -- perhaps in part due to a shoulder injury -- but there's potential for power as he continues to grow. Francisca is an athletic, aggressive runner who gets the most out of his impressive speed on the basepaths. He has the tools to play shortstop, but throwing issues plagued him last season. Francisca can show plus arm strength, but he wasn't able to access it fully because his feet were often out of position and his accuracy was lacking. Things are trending more toward him playing second base long-term, although he'll have to continue to remain versatile with the bevy of infield prospects in the lower rungs of the Guardians' system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians target switch-hitting infielders with advanced bat-to-ball skills on the international market, and Francisca fit that profile when he received the highest bonus ($1,375,000) in their 2023 class. Signed out of the Dominican Republic, he went 5-for-7 with a homer, triple, five runs and three RBI in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and hasn't stopped hitting since. He slashed .323/.414/.483 in his first two years as a pro and had no trouble handling Single-A pitching at age 18 in the final six weeks of last season. Francisca has bat speed and tremendous feel from both sides of the plate and makes repeated contact to all fields with ease. He'll chase pitches on occasion but does a good job of working counts and drawing walks for a teenager. Though he's just 5-foot-8 and needs to add strength, he has surprisingly solid raw power and could provide 15-20 homers per season if he learns to drive the ball in the air more regularly. Francisca is a solid runner but will flash plus or better run times on occasion, and he has the instincts and aggressiveness to steal bases. He's a twitchy athlete with smooth actions, range to both sides and reliable hands at shortstop. His average arm strength is a tick light for short but he projects as a solid defender there and plus at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians collect switch-hitting infielders with advanced hitting skills, so it was no surprise they gave the largest bonus in their 2023 international class to someone fitting that profile. After signing for $1,375,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Francisca broke into pro ball by going 5-for-7 with a homer, triple, five runs and three RBIs in his first pro game in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He batted .316/.419/.500 with three home runs and 11 steals in his 40-game debut. Francisca exhibits feel for the barrel from both sides of the plate, allowing him to barrel balls repeatedly. Though he got a bit pull-heavy in his debut, he's a fairly patient hitter who will work counts and draw walks. He's undersized but his bat speed and aptitude for turning on and lifting pitches should translate into 15 or more homers per season once he adds some strength. Francisca has average to solid speed and plays quicker than that thanks to his instincts and aggressiveness. He has similar arm strength and a chance to stick at shortstop, where he has good actions, range to both sides and sure hands. If he loses a half-step as he matures physically, he'll probably wind up at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds signed Lin for $1.2 million in June 2023, they were committed to allowing the Taiwanese two-way standout to play both ways out of the gate. They took an interesting approach, having him only hit in competition in 2024, when he played short and third and finished with an .837 OPS in the Arizona Complex League, then having him focus on pitching with a sprinkling of DH at-bats back in the ACL in 2025. He pitched his way to full-season Daytona and showed enough on the mound that the decision was made for him to commit to the pitching-only path in 2026. Though his focus had been split until this point, the 5-foot-11 athletic right-hander has already shown an impressive feel for pitching with a three-pitch mix he can use to fill up the strike zone. His fastball sits in the low 90s, but he’s shown the ability to reach back for 96 mph in the past, and the pitch plays up thanks to its life that leads to good miss rates. His low-80s changeup might be his best secondary offering, a cambio that drops off the table, and there’s confidence he has enough feel for spin to have an average breaking ball in the future. Lin already shows an ability to throw strikes, and get hitters to chase, with all of his repertoire. There might be limited ceiling because he’s not the typical tall and projectable young arm, but there could be more in the tank coming now that he’s a pitcher only, with a growing understanding of things like between-starts routines and how to get to his premium stuff likely to help his overall profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds signed Lin in June of 2023 for $1.2 million, he had been a teenaged two-way standout in international competition, and it wasn’t immediately clear whether he should hit or pitch professionally. The answer for now, it seems, is both. A hamstring injury kept him from doing much in terms of a debut the summer after signing, but he returned to the Arizona Complex League in 2024 and, as a position player only, put up a .308/.418/.419 line while playing third and shortstop. But he had spent all season on a pitcher’s throwing program so he could hit in the ACL and pitch in instructional league play, leading to the decision to have him pitch and DH in 2025. While Lin only threw three or four innings at instructs, it was really impressive, helping pave the way for him to pitch and hit. Lin almost instantly showed off a real three-pitch mix on the mound, starting with a fastball that sat low 90s and touched 97 mph, but played up to above-average because of its life. His 79-83 mph slider is fringy now and his 82-85 mph changeup is average, but all three of his pitches have the chance to be at least above-average. What was the most impressive is that the athleticism that’s present as a position player allowed him to repeat his delivery and command of all of his pitches right from the get-go. At the plate, Lin will continue to get to show a left-handed swing geared for contact and some sneaky pop and his plus speed is an asset on the basepaths as well. It’s still an experiment, but it’s one of the more fascinating storylines to follow in the Reds system in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds went all-in at the start of the 2023 international signing period by signing catcher Alfredo Duno for $3.1 million on January 15. They had enough left in their bonus pool in June to make a splash in Asia as well, giving $1.2 million to add Lin to the fold. Then just 17, Lin was a two-way player for Taiwan in international competition that generated internal conversations about whether they should send him out as a pitcher or as a position player and, if that, at which position. Some of those questions will start to truly get answered this year for the first time after a hamstring injury kept him from doing much at instructs after a nine-game debut in the Arizona Complex League. For now, the decision has been made to focus on Lin the position player, at least partially because it’s easier to go back to pitching as opposed to trying to hit after being only on the mound for a while. He’s a left-handed hitter with a contact-oriented approach, one who has produced well in international competition. While he’s only 5-foot-11, there’s some sneaky pop in his swing, and there could be more as he matures. He’s a plus runner who should be a threat to steal. With a plus arm that fires low-90s fastballs from the mound (he also has a mid-70s slider and low-80s changeup), Lin has the chance to stick at shortstop. His athleticism is an asset there and also in center field, and he saw time in both spots during his brief debut. Lin is still acclimating to life in the United States and he’ll continue that adjustment as an 18-year-old for nearly all of the 2024 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Georgia high school standout, Johnson began his college career in his home state, with the University of Georgia. But after a freshman year that saw him pick up just 46 at-bats, he transferred to Chipola Junior College and went off. His 1.079 OPS in 2019 garnered plenty of attention, with the Reds able to nab him in the fourth round that June. He played his way from Low- to High-A in 2021, his first true full season, but because he missed a month on the injured list, he got more reps in the Arizona Fall League. Residual hand pain led to eventual hamate surgery this offseason. Johnson is a switch-hitter who can handle the bat from both sides of the plate. The left-handed swing is better, particularly in terms of power, though he did some damage right-handed as well in the AFL as he hit six homers total in 17 games. He can get overly aggressive and needs to refine his overall approach so he can do more damage in hitter’s counts. Johnson has played more shortstop than anticipated, but few think he’ll play there long-term. He’s better suited at second, with the chance he could end up showing enough thump to move to third. The hand surgery slowed him out of the gate a bit, but he was swinging the bat well when some shoulder inflammation landed him back on the injured list in August.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chipola Junior College has built a reputation as one of the best two-year baseball programs in the country, with alumni like Russell Martin and Jose Bautista. Johnson, taken from the Florida school by the Reds in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, hopes to be the first Chipola product to make it to the big leagues since 2012 draftee Andrew Toles. Johnson had a solid, if unspectacular, pro debut in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, then opened a lot of eyes with strong instructional league play in 2020. A switch-hitting middle infielder, Johnson has the chance to really hit, with excellent bat speed from both sides of the plate. His swing might be a touch better from the left side, and his raw power has shown up more left-handed as well, particularly to his pull side. While he’s not a burner, Johnson uses what speed he does have smartly on the basepaths. Most thought Johnson was destined to be a second baseman as a pro, and that might still be the case as his range might be a bit light. But he’s surprised some with his abilities at short, making some body control plays at instructs that stood out. He’ll get a chance to play his way off of short, with his bat potentially profiling just fine at second, where he’s seen time, or even at third.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A solid tools guy who is considered to have great makeup, Johnson will likely be more offensive minded, and he has some thump in his bat with good gap power from the right side. He is a switch-hitter who hit for average and power in junior college, with some easy power from the left side of the plate. But while not as skilled defensively as someone like former Reds elite prospect Jeter Downs (now with Boston by way of the Dodgers), Johnson is viewed as a shortstop first by the Reds and would likely have to play his way off that position. If that were to happen, he would be a candidate as a second baseman, a position he played in junior college after he was a high school shortstop. The Reds’ fourth-round pick in 2019, Johnson is a good, but not great, baserunner and is otherwise average across the board. He has a solid chance to reach the big leagues as a utility infielder who could provide offense, when needed, from the bench, if he doesn’t settle in as an offensive-minded regular at a middle infield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zobac was a two-way player at Cal before he switched his focus to solely pitching his junior year, and the Royals selected him in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft. He seemed primed for a breakout season in ‘25, but a knee injury severely hampered that idea and limited Zobac to just 14 starts between Double-A Northwest Arkansas (11) and his rehab stint in Arizona (three). When he was on the mound, Zobac allowed 36 earned runs in 44 2/3 total innings, and opposing hitters crushed him with a .346 average. He made his last start of the season on Aug. 7 and had surgery shortly after. The Royals still added him to their 40-man roster ahead of the Rule 5 Draft. Zobac is more of a command guy than anything, with his stuff playing up because of it. His above-average fastball sits at 93-94 mph but touches 96 with good life on it. He threw his mid-to-upper-80s slider harder in his small sample size last year, and it has tight break that misses bats, while his curveball is just below average and sits in the upper 70s. Zobac’s work with a fringe-average changeup is ongoing as he tinkers with the grip. Zobac’s delivery is clean and repeatable, and he’s athletic down the mound, although his knee issue in ‘25 hindered how he was moving. Now fully healthy and not bogged down by the lingering injury, Zobac is pitching freer. He’ll continue to develop as a starter but will need that changeup against lefties, and there’s also intrigue to how his stuff would play in short stints. He’ll likely head back to Double-A to begin ‘26, but a quick rise is not out of the question as long as he stays healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zobac pitched sparingly at the University of California until his junior season, splitting time on the mound with hitting as an outfielder. When he turned his focus to only pitching, he showed enough potential that the Royals took him in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft, signing him to a $500,000 bonus. The Royals had an innings limit on Zobac in his first full year of pro ball, and he split it between Single-A and High-A. In 2024, they took off the reins and Zobac broke out, posting a 3.64 ERA between High-A and Double-A across 126 innings en route to Royals’ Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors. Zobac’s stuff plays up because of his plus command. He knows where to put the ball and goes right at hitters, evidenced by his 5.6% walk rate in 2024. His strikeout rate between the two levels was 23.8%, and he doesn’t blow hitters away, but his pitchability and command has helped him. Zobac’s fastball is a high-spin 92-94 mph heater with good carry that touched 97 at Double-A. His mid-to-upper 80s slider is a plus pitch that misses bats with good shape and location to the glove side, and he flashed a fringe-average mid-80s changeup that he needs to continue to refine. He changed the grip on that pitch a few times in ‘24 but is still tinkering to find something he’s most comfortable with, and he’ll need it against lefties at the higher levels. Better accustomed to a starter’s workload in 2024, Zobac held up throughout a career-high year in terms of innings. He’s athletic with a repeatable and simple delivery that helps him command the ball so well, and he gets high marks for his intelligence on the mound and in-game prep. From becoming a full-time pitcher in 2022 to reaching Double-A by his second full pro season, Zobac has moved quicker than maybe even the Royals originally thought he would. His fastball-slider combo would fit well in a Major League bullpen, but the development of a third pitch will be key to his upside as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An outfielder who pitched sparingly until his junior year at the University of California, Zobac showed enough upside when he focused on pitching his junior season that the Royals took him in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft, signing him to a $500,000 bonus. In his first full season, he dominated Single-A and faded down the stretch at High-A, with a 3.47 ERA across the two levels over 90 2/3 innings. He made 22 appearances (18 starts) and had just a 6.4 percent walk rate. Zobac sits 93-95 mph with his fastball, but he can flash upper-90s with good carry. He has an above-average slider in the mid-80s that misses bats. His changeup is fringe-average as a work in progress but it has the potential to get lefties out. Zobac has a smooth and repeatable delivery with impeccable command -- he knows exactly where to locate his stuff and usually executes it. As he’s relatively new to pitching, the Royals built Zobac up cautiously through the season, but he still fatigued at the end getting used to a starter’s workload. With the foundation from last year, he should be more accustomed and in line to make more starts from the beginning of the season. Even as a college pitcher, Zobac might not move as quickly because of his newness to the mound, though it's been impressive to see him reach (and succeed at) Double-A in 2024. But he possesses some exciting pitchability, and evaluators see starter upside if he continues to work on his changeup for a third pitch. His fastball-slider combination would fit well in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of an NFL lineman, Bateman had the size (he’s 6-foot-8) and skills (he throws left-handed) to get noticed coming out of the Southern California prep scene even if he didn’t have the ability. But he does. The Padres selected him in the second round of the 2024 Draft and signed him to an over-slot $2.5 million bonus. Bateman was working through a nice full-season debut in the Single-A California League when he was sent as part of the huge package of prospects to the Orioles in exchange for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the 2025 Trade Deadline, and he finished the year at High-A Aberdeen. Bateman’s stuff befits the enormous high-makeup package it comes in. His fastball can live in the low-to-mid-90s and touched 98 mph during his debut, part of a four-pitch mix that features a pair of breaking balls. The best is a slider that flashes plus. While he needs more reps throwing his 1-to-7 curve and developing changeup, he is seen as having the aptitude to tackle his developmental needs and potentially add pitches to that mix with time. Bateman did a decent job throwing strikes before his walks spiked at Aberdeen at the very end of the year, though that can probably be attributed to fatigue more than anything. He still has work to do overall to get to average control, though if he gets there, he'll look like a mid-rotation starter given his ability and pitch mix. The heater and breaking ball alone give him a floor of a big dominant left-hander out of the ‘pen, which wouldn’t be a bad outcome either.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Of course, Bateman was going to make for a close follow everywhere he went as an amateur. For starters, he’s 6-foot-8. Secondly, he’s a left-handed pitcher. But he proved to have more than just those two attributes with quality appearances in the PDP League and Area Code Games heading into his senior year at Adolfo Camarillo (Calif.) High School -- the alma mater of 2003 No. 1 pick Delmon Young. Bateman joined the Padres as a second-round pick and signed for $2.5 million, roughly the slot of a selection 15 picks higher. He was more than holding his own during his full-season debut in the Single-A California League when he was sent as part of the huge package of prospects to the Orioles in return for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the Trade Deadline. Scouts dreamed on Bateman’s size and praised his makeup as part of the evaluation process, but the stuff was plenty good too, and it’s shown up so far as a pro. He touched 97 mph with his fastball and generally sat 91-93 during summer showcases and has again been up to 97 mph during his debut season. He throws from a high three-quarter slot and has both a slider and more of a 1-to-7 curve, though he doesn’t really throw the latter breaking ball. He continues to work on developing his changeup, a pitch he didn’t need much in high school. Bateman improved his strike-throwing heading into the Draft, and while his history with walks isn’t perfect, his trendlines should get him to average control with advanced instruction, and he did a solid job of finding the zone in 2025. He’ll only be 19 for the duration of the 2025 Minor League season, and the upside is significant, especially if he carries his impressive work ethic into the pros. There’s always the fallback of being a big, dominant lefty out of the bullpen with that heater and breaking ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a year at Western Kentucky and a very strong sophomore season following a transfer to Indiana, Sinnard looked like he could take a huge leap forward in 2024. But when he blew out his elbow in a 2023 regional start and needed Tommy John surgery, he missed all of what should have been his junior season. He threw bullpens for clubs and the Braves, in the third round, saw enough to take a chance on him coming back to full strength. The early returns -- 72 1/3 innings and getting to High-A Rome during the regular season before 15 2/3 more in the Arizona Fall League -- are making it look like it might have been a worthwhile gamble. Sinnard's stuff all seems to be trending in the right direction. His velocity continues to tick up, averaging 93 mph with his fastball during the regular season, then finding more in the AFL, with an average fastball around 95 and touching 98-99. His fastball has always played up with high spin rates and carry to miss bats, and he added a sinking 2-seamer late in the year. His upper-80s slider has cutter-like action; it's short and hard and it elicited close to a 35 percent miss rate at all stops last year. He has a distinct low-80s curve that he no longer uses very often, and his low-80s splitter gives him an effective offspeed offering that also misses bats. All of his stuff comes from Sinnard's 6-foot-8 frame and high three-quarters arm slot, making it hard for hitters to pick up the ball. He tends to be around the zone, and the next step in putting TJ behind him is refining his command so he can be a starter long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a freshman year at Western Kentucky where Sinnard pitched sparingly and poorly, he transferred to Indiana and had a huge sophomore season, with a Hoosiers record 114 strikeouts in 86 1/3 innings to put himself firmly on the early-rounds map for 2024. But he blew out his elbow in a 2023 regional start and missed all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. He did throw bullpens for clubs leading up to the Draft and the Braves liked what they saw enough to take him in the third round. Coming from his 6-foot-8 frame and high three-quarters arm slot, Sinnard does not give hitters a comfortable at-bat. While his fastball sat 91-93 mph before he got hurt, topping out at 96 mph, the heater played up with high spin rates and carry to get a lot of swing-and-miss. He has two distinct breaking balls: His 78-82 downer curve missed a lot of bats and his mid-80s slider with cutter action got more chases. His low-80s changeup with depth was a distant fourth pitch he didn't use frequently. Sinnard did a nice job in 2023 in keeping his mechanics in sync despite his size and filled up the strike zone consistently. The 2025 season will be about seeing if he can get his stuff all the way back and eventually refine his command so he can reach his ceiling as dependable big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his three years at Texas A&M, Cortez spent more time relieving than starting. He really shined in his junior year as a multi-inning bullpen guy, especially during a dominant postseason run to help the Aggies finish as the runners-up in the 2024 Men's College World Series. That led to him being taken in the second round of that summer’s Draft and the Angels sent him to High-A Tri-City as a starter in 2025. There were a lot of things that went well for Cortez. His stuff largely held up over 26 starts and 113 2/3 innings, and he missed bats largely with his sinker-slider combination. It’s a power two-seamer, sitting in the upper 90s and touching triple digits. Hitters just can’t square it up, a big reason why he produced a 61.8 percent ground-ball rate in 2025. His upper-80s slider can feature horizontal and vertical action and serves as a true put-away pitch, missing a ton of bats. There have been rare sightings of a mid-to-upper 80s changeup. The biggest thing standing in Cortez’s way to being a starter, which he’ll keep developing as for the time being, is his command. He walked 6.7 per nine and that’s a number that must come down, even if he ends up back in a bullpen. He could have multi-inning or setup potential with a good combination of strikeouts and ground balls if that move occurs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not typical that a college pitcher’s performance in the College World Series impacts his Draft stock that year, but it’s hard to imagine that Cortez’s run coming out of Texas A&M’s bullpen as the Aggies finished second in Omaha didn’t help him. Cortez had started and relieved over his three years, and he took off with a multi-inning bullpen role last year, dominating postseason play (1.18 ERA, 29 strikeouts in 15 2/3 inning) to cap off a very strong junior campaign. The Angels nabbed him in the second round of last year’s Draft and signed him for $1.6 million but didn’t send him out to pitch at all after his long year. Cortez enters pro ball with two plus pitches that really play. He actually threw his 86-92 mph power slider more than his fastball last year, and it’s easy to see why. It features horizontal and vertical action and elicited a 56-percent miss rate, according to Synergy. His fastball averaged a tick over 98 mph in 2024 and topped out at 101, thrown with power sink that’s extremely difficult to leverage. He has an upper-80s changeup, but it gathered a lot of dust on the pitching shelf. The 6-foot-1 right-hander generates those premium pitches without much effort, so there is some thought that he could be stretched out to start in pro ball. For that to work, he’s going to have to find the strike zone a lot more consistently (5.1 BB/9 last year was an improvement from 2023) and develop a third pitch. If he sticks in the bullpen and can be around the zone at all, he could zoom through a system in an organization that likes to get guys to the big leagues in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aloy’s rise from unheralded Hawaiian recruit to one of the most accomplished players in college baseball culminated in a dominant 2025 season at Arkansas, where he won both the Golden Spikes Award and SEC Player of the Year honors. After transferring from Sacramento State, he continued to build momentum as a sophomore and then took a significant step forward as a junior, playing his way into first-round consideration before the Orioles selected him No. 31 overall and signed him for full slot value ($3.04 million). He then enjoyed a productive pro debut at Single-A Delmarva, logging an .856 OPS in 20 games. Offensively, Aloy offers uncommon power for a middle infielder. He generates plus raw pop with a combination of bat speed and strength that produced 35 homers in two seasons at Arkansas and eight in only 21 games in the Cape Cod League in between his sophomore and junior seasons. The power plays to all fields and against quality pitching, though it's especially potent to his pull side. His hit tool is less advanced. His right-handed swing can get overly uphill and become susceptible to swing-and-miss, particularly against breaking balls outside the zone, but improved pitch selection could unlock more of his overall offensive profile. Despite fringy speed, Aloy should be able to stick at shortstop given his smooth actions, reliable hands and strong arm, and his range and instincts allow him to project as at least an average defender up the middle. If a move becomes necessary, his skill set would fit comfortably at second base or third, where his offensive upside would be an asset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies were looking to fill a future outfield at the start of the 2024 Draft, taking those who patrol the grass with four of their first five picks. The first two were high schoolers, with Dante Nori in the first and Burkholder in the second, and both signed for the same $2.5 million bonus as the Phillies went well over slot to lure Burkholder away from the University of West Virginia. He hasn’t been able to get as many on-field reps as hoped, with a hamstring issue ending his summer debut after signing following just two plate appearances. He was limited to just 34 total games during his first full season. It’s hard to not like Burkholder’s physicality and athleticism, and even with the lost year, he’ll play nearly all of 2026 at age 20. He is capable of making very hard contact, registering high-end exit velocities when he’s been on the field, with at least plus raw power. He has made some swing adjustments and found better angles, but he struggled with his overall approach with too much swing-and-miss, particularly against breaking and offspeed stuff. Missed development time because of the injuries has not helped in this regard. Healthy again, Burkholder will hopefully be able to get back to using his speed well. He’ll turn in some 70-grade run times, but it doesn’t translate the same on the basepaths in terms of stolen bases. It’s also looking like he’s better suited for a corner outfield spot rather than center, and he’s gotten most of his time in right field to date.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Phillies were able to sign 2024 first-round pick Dante Nori under slot, they were able to use their savings to also bring Burkholder, their second-rounder, into the fold. The Virginia high school standout turned a strong summer showcase circuit and excellent senior season to rise up Draft boards, enabling him to land a $2.5 million bonus from the Phillies. He tripled in his first professional at-bat last summer with full-season Clearwater but got shut down after just one more plate appearance because of a hamstring issue. Big, physical and athletic, the Phillies have taken to calling Burkholder “Captain America” because he can do everything well. There’s a ton of raw power for him to tap into, but in high school he didn’t always find the barrel consistently. He’s shown off early aptitude by already making the most swing adjustments of anyone in the system, eliminating some length in his swing and fixing some angles, allowing him to barrel up the baseball much more frequently. Assuming the hamstring is fine, Burkholder has close to top of the scale speed that works on both sides of the ball. He has the skills to play center field long-term, and could trade off with Nori for the time being, with the Phillies very excited if they can form a dynamic duo in the big leagues with Nori in center and Burkholder in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tibbs emerged as one of the best college hitters in the 2024 Draft by continually improving during three years at Florida State, where he slashed .363/.488/.777 as a junior while winning Atlantic Coast Conference Player and Scholar-Athlete of the Year accolades. The Giants signed him for $4,747,500 as the 13th overall pick that July before sending him to the Red Sox as part of the shocking Rafael Devers trade just 11 months later. Six weeks after that, Boston packaged him with outfield prospect Zach Ehrhard to acquire Dustin May from the Dodgers, after which Tibbs raked in Double-A. Tibbs had an up-and-down .243/.373/.429 season between High-A and Double-A while getting dealt twice, and both his bat and power earned fringy to solid grades from scouts depending on when they saw him. He offers an enticing combination of swing decisions and hard contact, not to mention a fluid left-handed stroke with bat speed and strength. He felt like he got too rotational with his swing when the Red Sox had him focus on exit velocity, but he looked more like his better self with the Dodgers and drew a healthy amount of walks at all three of his stops. While he possesses below-average speed, Tibbs has good instincts on the bases and in the field. He can swipe an occasional bag, provides decent range on the outfield corners and handles himself well at first base. He has average arm strength with a quick release, helping him record 11 assists in 93 outfield starts last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Tibbs the third-best offensive prospect in Georgia's 2021 class behind first-rounders Brady House and Harry Ford, but his bat-over-athlete profile sent him to Florida State rather than pro ball. He improved throughout his college career and slashed .363/.488/.777 in 2024 while leading the Seminoles to the College World Series and earning Atlantic Coast Conference player and scholar-athlete of the year honors. The Giants signed him for $4,747,500 as the 13th overall pick last July before including him in the stunning Rafael Devers trade with the Red Sox 11 months later, and then Boston shipped him and fellow outfield prospect Zach Ehrhard to the Dodgers to acquire Dustin May at the Trade Deadline. Tibbs offered one of the best combinations of swing decisions and hard contact in the Draft. He has a smooth left-handed swing with plenty of bat speed and strength, giving him solid power to all fields. While at Florida State, he closed the holes he once had against breaking pitches, shrunk his strikeout rate from 32 percent as a freshman to 12 percent as a junior and boosted his walk rate from 12 percent to 18 percent. He has stood out more with his pop than his hitting ability at High-A, though he has drawn a healthy amount of walks. Tibbs has bounced from left field as a freshman to primarily playing first base as a sophomore to right field as a junior and his first taste of pro ball. He has the solid arm strength to handle right field, though he'll need to maintain every bit of his presently below-average speed to have viable range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rojas was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 24 prospect on the 2022 International Top 50, and he received a $1.3 million bonus to sign with the Padres on Jan. 15, becoming San Diego’s second-highest signee of the class behind only Jarlin Susana ($1.7 million). The Cuba native moved to the Dominican Summer League and quickly caught some eyes by walking more times (26) than he struck out (23) while hitting .279/.373/.357 over 46 games. To put that in further context, Rojas’ 1.13 K/BB ratio ranked 16th among 255 qualifiers in the DSL, and he has the advanced knowledge of the strike zone and short left-handed swing to back up those numbers. He also wasn’t afraid of using the whole field, going the opposite way roughly a third of the time, as he tried to protect the plate. Rojas’ performance came with zero homers, but there’s always been a belief that something close to average pop could come as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-1 frame. An average runner, the teenager wasn’t afraid to press the issue on the basepaths with 14 steals, though that will be tested as he gets off the complex. He played only shortstop -- and the Padres believe he can stick there -- but he has the arm strength to handle third, where he might be a better fit long-term. San Diego officials think they might be able to get aggressive with Rojas in year two because of his approach, and he could see full-season ball at some point before 2023 is up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An intriguing combination of power and speed, Rojas signed with the Padres for $1.3 million on January 15, 2022. The 17-year-old, ranked as the No. 24 prospect on MLB Pipeline’s International Top 50, reminds some of a young Yoán Moncada with his projectable 6-foot-1, 190-pound frame. Rojas, a Cuban native, already flashes some power and has a chance to develop into an above-average hitter with his advanced approach and plate discipline. Described as a pure hitter, Rojas has a quick, compact swing and uses the whole field better than most hitters in his age group. An average runner with a strong arm, Rojas will start his career at shortstop, but some feel he may eventually shift to second or third. He has an enticing skill set and there’s a lot to dream on, but he’s still a ways away.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed the Venezuela native on his 16th birthday in 2019, but Arias couldn't make his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League until '21 due to the pandemic. After finally jumping stateside in 2023, his breakout came in '24 when he posted a line of .283/.390/.443 over 87 games between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver. Those numbers took a slight step back in ‘25 between High-A and Double-A, but Arias remains one of the most exciting outfield prospects in a group that’s quickly growing deeper in Toronto. Arias’ upside as a left-handed hitter is a great starting point and he is one of the better young defensive outfielders in the organization. He’ll need to prove his offense can hold up against more advanced pitching at the upper levels, but he drives the ball loudly, thanks to a swing with a ton of intent, and could end up being a bat that produces 15-20 homers per year if it all comes together and he can learn to elevate more on contact. One of the first things you’ll hear from anyone when asked about Arias is that he’s a “bulldog,” playing with incredible intensity and grit. The Blue Jays had been waiting for one of their young outfielders to click, and from that crowded group, Arias will still have every opportunity to rise to the top. He did undergo a procedure on his non-throwing shoulder, so he’ll be late to start this season, but there’s still plenty of time and talent to work with here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed the Venezuela native on his 16th birthday in 2019, but Arias couldn't make his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League until 2021 due to the pandemic. He was a DSL repeater in '22 before finally jumping stateside in '23, but his breakout finally came in '24. Last season, Arias posted a line of .283/.390/.443 over 87 games between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver. Now just 21, he’s thrust himself onto this list and become one of the Blue Jays’ better development success stories in a hurry. There’s a ton of upside here. Arias posts impressive walk rates as a left-handed hitter and is one of the better young defensive outfielders in the organization, so that’s a fine place to start. He’ll need to prove his offense can hold up against more advanced pitching at the upper levels, but he drives the ball loudly, thanks to a swing with a ton of intent, and could end up being a 15-20 homer bat if it all comes together and he can learn to elevate more on contact. One of the first things you’ll hear from anyone when asked about Arias is that he’s a “bulldog,” playing with incredible intensity and grit. The Blue Jays had been waiting for one of their young outfielders to click, and Arias is now going on two consecutive years of impressive production at full-season levels. Having reached Double-A in his age-21 season, Arias could be an option for the Jays as early as 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez had a long history of performing in game action as a Dominican amateur, which contributed to him receiving the largest bonus ($1,097,500) in the Rangers' 2025 international class. That trend continued in his pro debut, when he earned all-star accolades in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He slashed .337/.473/.506 with six homers in 46 games. Rodriguez has a stocky 5-foot-10 frame with short levers and a quick, compact left-handed swing. He works counts well and uses the entire field, making him one of the more advanced young hitters in the system. He lacks projection and doesn't hit the ball particularly hard, so he may max out at 15 homers per season. Though his high baseball IQ helps him play faster than his average speed, Rodriguez may not make much of an impact on the bases or in the field. He split his pro debut between center field, where his range looked fringy, and second base, the only infield position his so-so arm strength is suited for. He may profile best in left field, which would raise the demands on his power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez turned pro for $1,097,500 out of the Dominican Republic in January, receiving the largest bonus in the Rangers’ 2025 international class. They believe in his bat because of his long track record of performing in game action as an amateur. Though he’s a stocky 5-foot-10, he’s more athletic than he appears and also has a high baseball IQ. Rodriguez’s short levers translate into a quick, compact left-handed stroke. He controls the strike zone exceptionally well for a 17-year-old and uses the entire field. His hitting ability stands out more than his raw power, but he projects to grow into 20-homer pop. An average runner out of the batter’s box, Rodriguez plays quicker than that on the bases and in the field. Signed as a center fielder with fringy arm strength, he has the instincts to potentially stay there and also saw action at both outfield corners as well as second base as an amateur. Scouts praise his makeup and intelligence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 40 | Field: 40 | Overall: 50 The Brewers took Adamczewski from the Indiana high school ranks with their 15th-round pick in 2023 -- the same year they took Bishop Letson from the same state four rounds earlier -- and talked him out of a Ball State commitment with a $252,500 bonus. As a cold-weather hitter, he wasn’t pushed aggressively in his first full season, but he dominated the Arizona Complex League all the same. In his age-20 season, he roared past Single-A Carolina in 2025, hitting .359/.459/.569 with five homers in 46 games, but he missed about two months with a lower back injury. Adamczewski saw a late turn at High-A Wisconsin and rounded out the year with a .953 OPS in 20 Arizona Fall League games. Adamczewski lowered his hands in his stance in his second full season, allowing him to stay on plane with the baseball, and he appropriately cut his ground-ball rate by 10 points from 2024 to ’25. There’s decent bat speed already in his 6-foot frame, and the quality of contact helps him get to much of his raw power. From an approach standpoint, he hasn’t often chased against any pitch types, driving good OBPs in his young career, but he’ll need to handle sliders in the zone a bit better when he reaches the upper levels. Adamczewski was focused on second base to begin his career but wasn't quite a fit on the dirt with subpar hands. The Brewers decided to give him looks in left field in the Fall League, and that’s where he profiles best given his below-average arm strength and the expanded area out there to roam. That puts extra pressure on the bat, but the early returns and tool set give him starting upside on the grass.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Santos joined the Mets system for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic just before the 2017-18 international period closed. He has been slowly working his way through the system, playing for one club per season in his last three campaigns. He spent 2022 entirely at High-A Brooklyn, throwing a career-high 116 2/3 innings for the Cyclones. Santos posted a 4.47 ERA with 105 strikeouts in 116 2/3 innings in the South Atlantic League and was left unprotected and unpicked in the offseason Rule 5 Draft. The lack of a stellar strikeout rate doesn’t tell the whole story because Santos was nearly elite at one thing -- keeping the ball on the ground. His 58.7 percent ground-ball rate was the third-highest in the Minors among the 311 pitchers with at least 100 innings in 2022. A 93-96 mph fastball is the main culprit because its impressive sink made it difficult for batters to square the ball up, enabling the pitch to play up to plus level. His low-80s slider shows some promise but still lacks the depth to be more than average, while an upper-80s changeup drops some but didn’t prevent Santos from getting lit up (.295 average-against) vs. lefty hitters. The 6-foot-7 right-hander has always been projectable, and the velocity and movement have certainly come, along with a little better control than many his size. There’s something to be said for a pitcher that elicits ground balls by the bucketful in an age when hitters prioritize lifting the ball in the air, but a lack of surefire secondary pitches -- and the ticking roster clock -- could make 2023 a make-or-break year for Santos.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of the 2017-18 international signing period, seeing the 6-foot-6 right-hander as a projectable arm. He ascended quickly stateside after only 11 Dominican Summer League outings as a 17-year-old in 2018 but took a step back at Rookie Advanced Kingsport (5.09 ERA, 36 strikeouts in 40 2/3 innings) the following year. Following the missed 2020 season, Santos saw full-season ball for the first time with Low-A St. Lucie and didn’t miss a ton of bats, striking out 79 in 96 innings. He finished with a 4.59 ERA. Heading into just his age-20 season, projection remains the name of the game for Santos. Previously sitting at 92-93, he added a little velocity to be in the 93-96 mph range with his fastball now. The pitch typically shows promising sink, so it’s not straight velo either. Everything else remains in development. A low-80s slider shows promising spin, but lacks the consistency to be more than an average pitch. An upper-80s changeup does little more than show separation from the heater and remains his third pitch by far. Santos got better at throwing strikes in the second half last season, and with an 8.9 percent walk rate, that remains less of a concern than it did entering '21. The Mets are still working with Santos on developing consistent mechanics to help him command the ball better in general, because as his low strikeout rate proved, he could be quite hittable inside the zone. His size, youth and fastball still give Santos some promise, and discussions about a move to the bullpen remain at least a year away.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
