mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets saw plenty to dream on when they signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in September 2017. At 6-foot-8, Santos stood out in more ways than one in his first taste of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, prompting a move stateside in the midst of his age-17 season. His results took a step back in 2019 at Rookie Advanced Kingsport – namely his 5.09 ERA, 1.75 WHIP and 25 walks in 40 2/3 innings – and he missed out on more chances to develop due to the pandemic and a broken toe suffered not long after leaving Spring Training. He was healed in time for instructional league in the Dominican Republic and salvaged some time throwing there. As is true of many tall pitchers, Santos’ fastball is the star of his arsenal. It usually sits around 92-93 and can touch 95 and earns extra points for the way he bears down on hitters with it thanks to his massive extension. There could be even another tick of velocity in the tank as he adds more strength to his frame. As he showed in the Appalachian League, control can be an issue at times because of his size, however, and that’s something Santos will have to find the more he throws. The breaking ball and changeups are works in progress. The former was a particular point of emphasis last spring before camp broke and can look the better of the two offerings because of its promising spin, though it’s not yet a plus pitch. Mechanics and secondary pitches will be what decides how much of a role Santos can play in the Majors. If he can only keep the fastball as a plus pitch, then he could head to the bullpen like fellow 6-foot-8 Met Dellin Betances. If he can develop a better breaking ball, then starting could be a real option. With an August birthday, he will still be a teenager for much of the 2021 season, an indication that time is very much on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses during the 2017 international period, signing shortstop Ronny Mauricio and outfielders Adrian Hernandez for $2.1 and $1.5 million, respectively. Santos, on the other hand, received a $275,000 bonus that's already looking like a bargain for the Mets after the teenage right-hander finished his professional debut at 17 in the rookie-level Gulf Coast League. Long and lanky, Santos has grown since he signed and now stands at 6-foot-8. Unlike many young pitchers of that size, however, he has a very good delivery and knows how to command his developing three-pitch mix. Using a high three-quarter slot, Santos fills up the strike zone with a fastball that sits in the low 90s and touches 95 mph. It has riding life because he generates huge extension toward the plate, while all signs point to the big right-hander adding more velocity to his plus fastball. When he signed with the Mets, Santos didn't have a breaking ball, but he has quickly gotten a good feel for a slider that he throws with power and depth, giving it the look of a future out pitch. His changeup is below average right now, but with his feel for pitching, the Mets are confident it will come on as a third effective offering. Santos' tantalizing combination of youth, size and plus command all point to a career as a strike-throwing starting pitcher, possibly even one who pitches near the front of a big league rotation. So it's been no surprise the Mets have received multiple calls from teams looking to make deals asking about him as his first full season in the United States awaits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If not for Roki Sasaki (and his $6.5 million bonus), Peña would have been the talk of the 2025 international signing class after he joined the Mets organization for $5 million that January. (New York only had a bonus pool of $6,261,600.) He was closely watched in the Dominican Summer League, only to open 0-for-26 in his first nine games. Peña hit .342/.463/.618 with nine homers in 46 contests the rest of the way and had the DSL’s only two three-dinger games of the 2025 season. He was one of only two age-17 players with nine or more homers in the DSL, Detroit’s Cris Rodriguez being the other. When it was going right for Peña last season, he was the poster boy for the “elevate and celebrate” mentality, often turning on inside pitches and driving them in the air for extra-base hits. He wasn’t getting wild with his approach either in search of such contact, exhibiting good swing decisions, but more experienced pitchers might attack his uppercut swing differently. How his exit velocities hold up stateside after another year of physical maturation will deserve monitoring. Despite the high steal count last year, Peña doesn’t project to be a burner by the time he reaches the Majors, and his future position splits evaluators. Some believe he’ll have the actions to be a solid shortstop, noting that his above-average arm strength works from the left side of the infield, while others believe he’s headed elsewhere on the dirt down the line. It’ll likely be the bat that drives Peña’s value toward becoming an everyday player in Queens, and improved consistency in the box would go a long way in ’26 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Azua, Dominican Republic might sound familiar to anyone who has followed baseball in the last decade or so. Sure, established Major Leaguers like Yainer Diaz and Maikel Franco hail from there, but it also came up as the hometown of top 2024 international signing and current Top 100 prospect Leodalis De Vries. The city came up again this January when Peña signed for $5 million with the Mets, who only had a $6,261,600 bonus pool this year. Only Roki Sasaki ($6.5 million) signed for more under the 2025 international rules. Peña wowed evaluators as an amateur with his elite plate discipline, often refusing to expand the zone in showcase settings, much like De Vries did a year earlier. He has ample bat speed from the left side too, and he’s shown a capability of spraying the ball to all fields when he finds a pitch worthy of a swing. There could be even more power to come as he continues to mature and fill out his 5-foot-10 frame, but it already projects for at least average. Peña is a solid runner, though some scouts are concerned he’ll slow down as he ages. His footwork, hands, arm strength and overall actions certainly fit shortstop right now, and if he needs to move on the dirt to either second or third, he could be above-average defensively there too. Anything could happen on the long road of development – and a big bonus isn’t indicative of future success on its own – but Peña has all the pieces to become a prominent piece of the Mets’ current pipeline and future Major League club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Getting a nickname like “Tommy Tanks” as an amateur player can potentially set unfair expectations. But White set a Division I freshman North Carolina State record in 2022 with 27 home runs and then backed it up with 48 more over two years at Louisiana State. Since the A’s went over slot to sign him for $3 million in the second round of the 2024 Draft, however, he hasn’t lived up to that moniker, showing some feel for hitting while reaching Double-A and playing in the Arizona Fall League but without the same kind of impact. White still has terrific raw power from the right side of the plate and is capable of driving the ball to all fields, but he’s focused on his hit tool rather than tapping into that pop. He can let the ball travel deep and go the other way, relying on his ability to make contact. He almost never strikes out (13.7 percent K rate in 2025), but he also almost never walks (7.3 BB percent). It’s a rare statistical feat to see someone with a 20 percent miss rate to go along with a robust 34 percent chase rate. More selectivity should allow that power show up again organically. There is more pressure on that part of his game to grow because he’s destined for an infield corner. He’s played a lot of third base, but he got more reps at first during his AFL stint, with most believing that’s where he and his well-below-average speed will fit best long term. There is a Nick Kurtz-sized obstacle there in the big leagues, but for now, White can focus on becoming the all-around run producer the A’s hoped they were getting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White was a solid high school prospect in 2021, but his commitment to North Carolina State was too strong and teams wouldn’t meet his bonus ask. After setting a Division I freshman and school record with 27 homers, he transferred to Louisiana State for his sophomore year, going yard 24 more times and leading D-I hitters with 105 RBIs as the Tigers won the Men's College World Series. He equaled that home run total again as a junior, and while his name was mentioned as a potential first-round pick, he landed in Round 2 with the A’s, who went over slot to sign him for $3 million and sent him to Single-A Stockton to get his professional feet wet. White’s right-handed power is legitimate and he can hit the ball a long way to all fields thanks to his strength and bat speed. He might be known for his home run totals but he’s a better overall hitter than people think, finding the barrel consistently and limiting strikeouts. His knack for contact can lead to him expanding his strike zone, but he doesn’t swing and miss very often. It will be White’s bat that carries him to the big leagues. He’s a well-below-average runner who likely lacks the range and tools to stick at third base, where he toiled as a sophomore and junior, earning praise for playing through a shoulder injury at LSU in 2023. He’s likely headed to first base long term, which could give the A’s a glut of serious offensive talent between him and first-rounder Nick Kurtz.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox planned on giving an Oppor, a Wisconsin prepster who played for their Area Code Games team, an over-slot bonus in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft, but the Athletics took him seven picks in front of them. He didn't sign, allowing Chicago to land him a year later out of Gulf Coast State (Fla.) JC with a fifth-round choice and over-slot $550,000 bonus. After spending two seasons in Rookie ball and focusing on adding strength, he logged a 3.08 ERA, .199 opponent average and 116 strikeouts in 87 2/3 innings during his full-season debut between two Class A levels in 2025. Oppor could have three plus pitches once he's a finished product, starting with a fastball that sits at 93-97 mph and tops out at 100 with run and sink. His low-80s slider has so much sweep that it's hard to control and often misses the plate by two much to entice chases, but it can be unhittable when it's on. His changeup has similar velocity and more reliability, neutralizing right-handers with its tumble. The most athletic pitcher in the system, Oppor provides a lot of deception with an upright delivery, a low three-quarters arm slot, low release height and some crossfire. He's doing a better job of repeating his unorthodox mechanics as he has added muscle, though his walk rate jumped back up to 13 percent in High-A. He still needs time to develop but could be yet another frontline southpaw starter for Chicago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers spread their international bonus pool around more than usual in 2022, with Munoz their top signing at $757,500 out of the Dominican Republic. He finished seventh in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in batting (.347) during his pro debut, then continued to hit when he came to the United States last year. Los Angeles is excited to see how he handles full-season ball in 2024. More advanced at the plate than most teenagers, Munoz focuses on making hard, line-drive contact with a quick, smooth left-handed stroke. He recognizes pitches well and controls the strike zone while using the entire field. As he continues to add strength to his projectable 6-foot-3 frame and learns to incorporate his legs and increase the leverage in his swing, he could develop average power. Munoz played some third base as an amateur but has become a full-time outfielder as a pro. He has surprised the Dodgers with his instincts and how well he handled center field in 2023, but with below-average speed he's headed for a corner. While his arm strength is merely average, he did notch six assists in 34 games in right field during his first two pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Munoz received the largest bonus in the Dodgers' 2022 international class, signing for $757,500 out of the Dominican Republic. His feel for hitting was apparent in his pro debut, when he finished seventh in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League batting race at .347. Extremely advanced at the plate for an 18-year-old, Munoz has a smooth left-handed swing with a precocious feel for the barrel and the strike zone. He doesn't try to do too much and just focuses on making contact, much of which goes to the opposite field. He has the hitting ability and bat speed to develop average power once he adds some strength and leverage to his stroke and learns to lift balls to his pull side. Though Munoz played some third base as an amateur, the Dodgers see him strictly as an outfielder. He spent most of his debut on the corners, with some brief time in center field. He's a fringy runner with average arm strength, so his best fit may be left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was a tooled-up South Carolina high schooler when the Cubs selected him in the sixth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him for $325,600, and he's continued to flash major offensive potential since the Guardians traded Eli Morgan for him a little over a year later. The Dominican native has steadily climbed the rungs, making it to Double-A at age 21, and he tied for second in the Guardians' system in homers (21) and ranked ninth in OPS (.806). Big, strong and athletic like a linebacker, 6-foot-2 Rosario stands out for his power, with plenty of raw strength and bat speed. Getting to that power is the major question, as he ran a 33.1 percent strikeout rate with a simply unworkable 59 percent contact rate at Double-A. His approach could use work, as focusing on pull power maximizes his damage when he makes contact but has left him vulnerable to secondary offerings. Rosario is larger than most center fielders but will be given the opportunity to stick there because of his foot speed. There's a chance he'll continue to fill out his already-stout frame and slow down, which would push him to right field. The good news is he displayed the best arm strength of any player during a brief stint in the Arizona Fall League last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in the Dominican Republic, Rosario grew up in New Jersey before moving to South Carolina for his high school senior season in 2023. The younger brother of Padres infielder Eguy Rosario, he stood out with his physicality and raw tools on the showcase circuit, though he also was dogged by swing-and-miss issues and lasted until the Cubs took him in the sixth round. He finished fourth in the Single-A Carolina League in both homers (16) and strikeout rate (32 percent) in his first full pro season before Chicago traded him to the Guardians for Eli Morgan in November. Rosario is a study in extremes as a right-handed hitter. On the positive side, he has more bat speed and strength and generates more raw power and higher exit velocities than most 20-year-olds. But he's also overly aggressive, tries to launch every pitch he sees to his pull side and struggles to recognize or deal with non-fastballs. Rosario's big swing slows him down coming out of the batter's box, but he can flash well above-average speed once he gets going and he knows how to use it on the bases. His quickness gives him a chance to remain in center field if he can hone his defensive instincts. If not, his plus-plus arm strength is perfect for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers got creative by announcing Warren -- a shortstop out of Central Michigan -- as a catcher when they selected him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. The switch-hitter caught some in high school and had put himself on the map with a .502 OBP as a sophomore in 2019, followed by a productive trip to the Cape. The catching experiment seemed to wane in his first taste of the Minors, however, with Warren donning the tools of ignorance only three times in his final 39 games. He finished with a .258/.367/.442 line and 13 homers over 89 games between Low-A and High-A. The decision to move Warren away from catching and into the corner-infield spots was influenced, in part, by the Brewers noticing he made more impact offensively when he wasn’t being tasked at a more demanding defensive position. At his best, Warren can work deep counts that tax a pitching staff, and he’s capable of driving balls to the gaps with a short stroke from either side of the plate, though he’s a little more productive as a left-handed hitter. The power remains mostly in the park to this stage, but he has 15-20 homer upside if he can tap into his raw pop more. The Brewers like Warren’s hands on the infield, and there is a chance he could play some second base. In any event, he’ll need to hit even more if his future lies anywhere on the dirt, and Milwaukee has hope that that can happen the more catching gets put in the rearview.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have been creative in recent years in an effort to find talented catchers, keeping an open mind about players without long track records at the position if they like the bat. Warren qualifies. He caught the attention of scouts with his hitting and on-base ability in the Mid-American Conference in 2019, then boosted his stock with a standout summer in the Cape Cod League. Primarily a shortstop at Central Michigan, he caught in high school and the Brewers announced him as a catcher when they selected him in the third round in 2020, making him the highest-drafted Chippewa since Kevin Tapani was a 1986 second-rounder. Warren signed for $575,000 and played over the summer in the Michigan pod of a pop-up independent league, allowing Brewers catching coordinator Charlie Greene to monitor Warren’s progress behind the plate. A switch-hitter with a sound, quick stroke from both sides and excellent hand-eye coordination, Warren makes repeated line-drive contact. He drives balls to the gaps more than over the fence and set a Central Michigan record with 22 doubles in 2019. He works deep counts and draws walks, and his fringy-to-average speed plays better than that on the bases because he's aggressive. There are mixed reviews of Warren's ability as a catcher, though he has the hands, arm and athleticism to make it work as he gains more experience -- and there is no doubt about his eagerness to master the position. The Brewers are committed to giving him a chance to stick there. His so-so range and funky arm action aren't particularly suited for shortstop, so he's received some looks at the corner infield spots with Low-A Carolina. In the worst-case scenario, he winds up in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Cappe defected from Cuba in late 2018, he didn't make his pro debut until mid-2021. By the time MLB declared him a free agent, teams had committed most of their bonus pool money for 2019-29, so he opted until the next international signing period opened in January 2021 before joining the Marlins for $3.5 million. He earned physical comparisons to Carlos Correa as an amateur but has struggled to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame since turning pro. Cappe's sound right-handed stroke and feel for the barrel give him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. But while he does a good job of putting the ball in play for a youngster facing older competition, he chases and pulls too many pitches and is hapless against breaking balls. With his frame and bat speed, it's easy to project him developing 20-homer power if he can gain more strength. Cappe possesses solid speed but still is learning the nuances of basestealing. Primarily a shortstop in his first two pro seasons, he spent more time at second base in 2023 and projects as a solid defender there once he develops more consistency. He continues to baffle scouts with his throwing, as his arm strength flashes plus at time but plays below average at others.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cappe defected from Cuba in late 2018 and by the time MLB cleared him as a free agent, most teams already had committed their bonus pool cash for the 2019-20 signing period. One of top prospects in that class, he opted to wait until the 2020-21 period opened in January 2021 and landed a $3.5 million bonus from the Marlins. He slashed .290/.328/.438 with nine homers and 13 steals in his 67-game U.S. debut last season, split between Rookie ball and Single-A. Cappe has a sound right-handed swing and good feel for the barrel, giving him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. Though he has had no problems making contact, his aggressive, pull-happy approach does cut into his walk totals and could be exploited at higher levels. As a 6-foot-3 shortstop, he garnered physical comparisons to Carlos Correa as an amateur, but he needs to add strength in order to make good on his power projection and deliver 20 or more homers per season. There's some question as to whether Cappe may outgrow shortstop and he has spent more time at second base in 2023. He has solid speed and nice actions at short, but he could lose a step if he eventually adds 40 pounds of muscle to his lean frame. His plus arm is an asset at any position, though the game sped up on him a bit when he played third base in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cappe left Cuba in late 2018 and became one of the top prospects in the 2019 international class, but most clubs already had committed their bonus pool money to other players. He decided to wait for a bigger bonus in the 2020 signing period, which the pandemic pushed back to January 2021. After signing for $3.5 million on the first day, he enjoyed a solid debut against lesser competition in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. As a 6-foot-3 shortstop with a ton of projection remaining, Cappe drew comparisons to Carlos Correa as an amateur. He has already begun to add strength and makes repeated hard contact while also showing the ability to launch balls in the air. He does a good job of keeping his right-handed swing under control and managing the strike zone, though he can get overly pull-conscious. Presently a solid runner, Cappe could lose some quickness as he fills out and may outgrow shortstop. That may be a moot point because the presence of Kahlil Watson and Jose Salas in the Marlins system may push Cappe to third base anyway. He does have quick actions and plus arm strength, though like a lot of young shortstops, he needs to improve his defensive consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After defecting from Cuba in late 2018, Cappe quickly became one of the top prospects in the 2019 international class. Because most teams had already committed the bulk of their bonus pools to other players, he opted to wait for more money in the 2020 signing period, which didn't open until January 2021 because of the coronavirus pandemic. He inked with the Marlins for $3.5 million on the first day. As a shortstop with an extremely projectable 6-foot-3 frame, Cappe draws repeated physical comparisons to Carlos Correa. He has a chance to hit for power and average once he's physically developed, as he already shows the ability to make hard contact to all fields. He'll need to watch the length of his naturally long right-handed swing but has a mature approach and understands the strike zone. Cappe presently has solid speed but could lose some quickness as he adds muscle, making it possible that he'll outgrow shortstop. He'll begin his pro career at short and may be able to remain there because he has quick actions and hands as well as a plus arm. Third base would be his fallback position and he has all the tools to fit that profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Romero family produces talented hitters: sisters Sierra and Sydney were college softball stars, while younger brother Mikey was the 24th overall pick in the 2022 Draft. Signed for a well-below-slot $2.3 million, he was hampered by persistent back issues in his first two full pro seasons but finally was completely healthy and played a career-high 111 games in 2025. He led the system with 54 extra-base hits and 76 RBIs while reaching Triple-A at age 21, but he also struck out at a 27 percent clip. Considered one of the best pure hitters in his prep class, Romero concentrated on working the ball from gap to gap as an amateur. He changed his approach after he put his back issues behind him, focusing on using his quick left-handed stroke to launch balls in the air to his pull side. He has added about 20 pounds since turning pro and now has plus raw power, but his aggressive approach leads to a lot of chases and empty swings, especially against non-fastballs. Romero has slowed down as he has added muscle, though his high baseball IQ helps him play quicker than his below-average speed. Signed as a shortstop, he has fringy range and average arm strength. He saw most of his action at third base last season but his tools fit better at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox spent three straight first-round picks on California prep middle infielders: Nick Yorke (2020), Marcelo Mayer (2021) and Romero (2022). The younger brother of former college softball sensations Sierra and Sydney Romero, Mikey signed for a well-below-slot $2.3 million as the 24th overall pick. Persistent back issues that included a stress fracture limited him to 34 games in his first full pro season and sidelined him until mid-May in 2024, but he finally got healthy afterward and hit his way to Double-A at age 21. Romero earned acclaim as one of the best hitters in the 2022 high school class by focusing on making contact from gap to gap with a quick left-handed stroke. He showed an entirely different approach last year, relinquishing control of the strike zone while aggressively looking to launch balls to his pull side. He has added about 20 pounds since turning pro and become more of a power-over-hit guy with some opposite-field thump on occasion. Romero's high IQ helps his tools play up on the bases and in the middle infield. He's an average runner who's more likely to take an extra base than steal one. His actions, range and arm are all average at shortstop, where he finds a way to make plays, but they're better suited for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After drafting Marcelo Mayer fourth overall in 2021, the Red Sox took his good friend and fellow California prep shortstop Romero with the 24th overall choice a year later. The younger brother of former college softball superstars Sierra and Sydney Romero, he signed for a well-below-slot $2.3 million. After a strong pro debut, he played in just 34 games last year because of persistent lower-back issues. One of the best hitters in the 2022 high school class, Romero concentrates on making contact from gap to gap with his quick left-handed swing. He wasn't at his best at 2023, when his back problems underscored his need to add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame. He won't be a slugger but more muscle could create 15-homer power and would ease concerns about how much impact he'll offer at the plate. When healthy, Romero has average speed and plays quicker than that thanks to his high baseball IQ. Many scouts believe that his average range and arm aren't enough to make him a regular shortstop, but Boston believe his finely tuned internal clock and quick release give him a shot. Mayer likely will push him to second base when they're both in Boston, and Romero could be a solid defender at the keystone whose quick hands would help him turn double plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox have used their first-round pick in each of the last three Drafts on sweet-swinging high school middle infielders from California: Nick Yorke (17th overall) in 2020, Marcelo Mayer (fourth) in 2021 and Romero (24th) last July. Romero also joined Gerrit Cole, Cole Winn and Garrett Mitchell as first-rounders who played at Orange (Calif.) Lutheran HS. Signed for $2.3 million, he comes from a family of hitters that also includes a pair of former college softball superstars in older sisters Sierra and Sydney. Romero's quick left-handed swing and mature approach gave him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the 2022 prep class. He focuses on making contact from gap to gap and isn't very physical, leading to some concerns about how much impact he'll provide at the plate. He does have bat speed and hitting aptitude and has gotten stronger in the last year, so he should be able to provide 15-20 homers on an annual basis. There are also questions about Romero's ability to stay at shortstop, though that may not matter much in the long run with his good friend Mayer also in the organization. He has average speed and arm strength, leaving both tools light for the position, but he compensates with advanced instincts and a quick release on throws. He does show good actions at short and is a polished defender with reliable hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez’s Draft stock wasn’t hurt without a high school season in 2020, with the Royals still selecting him in the second round and signing him for a $1.45 million bonus. He had already proven himself in ’19 at the inaugural Prospect Development Pipeline League when he worked six hitless innings over three outings. The Chicago native tossed 31 1/3 innings with a 4.31 ERA in Low-A Columbia last season before being shut down with fatigue. Hernandez did make it back to finish the season in the Arizona rookie league. Hernandez’s delivery features very little effort and is very repeatable, showcasing deceiving velocity with his 90-94 mph sinking fastball. But his changeup is his calling card, a devastating pitch that has tremendous fade and generates whiffs. Hernandez put an emphasis on improving his breaking ball last season, which also may have led to his 4.88 walks-per-nine ratio. But the mid-70s curveball did look improved, and it has the makings of being a plus pitch if he can throw it consistently with more power. He’s also learning how to manage his velocity and can see the ball elevate more than he wants, which also may have led to the 17 walks last season. Hernandez has great mound presence and the foundation to remain a starter with his athleticism and advanced feel for pitching. He needs to get a full season of work in for the Royals to see what they really have in him, but he has a high floor and the chance to move quickly if it begins to click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez didn’t get a high school season in 2020 because of the pandemic, but that didn’t affect his Draft stock. He had proven enough for the Royals to take him in the second round and sign him for a $1.45 million bonus. Hernandez was the best pitcher at the inaugural Prospect Development Pipeline League in 2019, working six hitless innings over three outings while walking one and striking out seven. He also struck out the side in a perfect ninth inning at the Under Armour All-America Game. The Chicago-area native finally donned a Royals uniform at their instructional league in Arizona in the fall. Hernandez easily had the best changeup in the 2020 Draft. The pitch is devastating, and he showed in the fall that he can get swings and misses with it. It sits in the low 80s and has tremendous fade. His 90-95 mph fastball has some sink to it that plays up because of his command. His mid-70s curveball is his third offering and has the makings of being a plus pitch if he can throw it with better arm speed and power. Hernandez’s delivery features little effort, and he can repeat it very well. Hernandez has an advanced feel for pitching and the body and athleticism to remain as a starter. The Royals eased him into the season at Low-A Columbia because of his low innings count from last year, but he has a higher floor and the chance to move quicker than a typical prep pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As conservative as they typically are with prospects, the Rays put Urbina on the fast track. The Venezuelan right-hander has surprised at every turn, starting with the scouting process that saw him sign with Tampa Bay for just $210,000. He was throwing only 88-90 mph in early events and tryouts, then his velocity jumped to 94-98 just before he signed in 2023. His stuff was ahead of his performance in the early going, as the Rays rushed him to the Rookie-level Florida Complex League at age 17 with no professional experience, but it may all be coming together for him now. After two thoroughly fine seasons in the complex league, Urbina reported to Single-A Charleston last year and put together a 2.05 ERA and a 1.06 WHIP with 96 strikeouts and 30 walks in 92 1/3 innings over 19 starts. His strikeout rate improved. His walk rate dropped. He gave up fewer hits and homers. In short, from a performance standpoint, he delivered everything you’d hope to see from someone with his pure ability. He has arguably the best fastball in the system, a heater that averaged 96 mph and touched 100 last year, and he’s developed a feel for a tighter breaking ball in the mid-80s and another with more sweep to it in the upper 70s/low 80s. His changeup has been effective at times, but he doesn’t use it much. The most encouraging aspect of Urbina’s development has been the gradual decrease in his walk rate. Last season, he issued free passes to only 7.9 percent of the hitters he faced, down from 10.6 percent the year before. If he can maintain that trend, he’ll soon dispel all the questions about reliever risk that tend to follow young, hard-throwing pitchers and establish himself as another starter worth following.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina’s performance has yet to catch up to his raw ability, but the way the Rays have pushed him should be enough of a sign of what he’s capable of, despite his unusual path to a full-season assignment. At the beginning of the scouting process, the Venezuelan right-hander -- showcased at events and tryouts in Colombia -- was throwing 88-90 mph. But that jumped to 94-98 mph when the Rays saw him one last time before international signing day in 2023. He still signed for a $210,000 bonus, a modest sum for an international prospect with that kind of arm talent, and bypassed the Dominican Summer League to pitch in the United States at age 17 with no professional experience. Urbina’s results were fine, if uninspiring, through two seasons spent mostly in the Florida Complex League. He posted a 4.87 ERA with 78 strikeouts and 41 walks in his first 88 2/3 innings as a pro. But he is still stunningly young, and he’ll spend this whole season as a 19-year-old. And he still has stuff to dream on, with a big-time fastball in the mid-90s (touching triple-digits), a sweeping breaking ball and a changeup that has occasionally flashed plus. Urbina averaged nearly five walks per nine innings in the Complex League, although he cut back on that (while giving up more homers) during his brief stint in Charleston last year. That's a trend that has carried into 2025, and thanks to heavy whiffs on the slider, his strikeouts have picked up as well. There's less of a reliever risk now in Urbina's age-19 season, leading to him surging up the rankings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina presented a truly unique scouting situation for the Rays. When they began scouting the Venezuelan right-hander, who pitched in showcases and tryouts in Colombia, they liked what they saw but weren’t necessarily blown away by his 88-90 mph fastball. Then he took off like a rocket ship, running his fastball 94-98 mph by the Rays’ last look leading up to international signing day in 2023. He signed for a $210,000 bonus -- well below what the top international prospects got -- and could wind up being a huge success story for the Rays. The Rays believed in Urbina so much that even at age 17 with no professional experience, they had him bypass the Dominican Summer League to pitch stateside in the Florida Complex League. The results were middling, with a 5.32 ERA and 21 strikeouts against 12 walks in 23 2/3 innings over 11 outings, but again, he was 17. Urbina still has the big-time stuff of a power starter, which is rare to find in someone his age: the mid-90s fastball, a sweeping breaking ball that looked at times like a plus offering and a changeup that also occasionally flashed plus. But there is, of course, a ton of uncertainty regarding Urbina’s future, especially given the hit rate on international pitchers. The 18-year-old didn't prove himself at the complex level, like fellow Rays prospect Santiago Suarez, during his first go, and his results have been similarly just OK in his age-18 season in 2024. He could live up to his potential as a starter, or he could eventually transition to the bullpen as a hard-throwing reliever. But Urbina is young and powerful with a ton of upside, and it bodes well for him that the Rays were so aggressive with his initial assignment.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Rays began scouting Urbina, a Venezuelan pitcher who got on the mound for showcases and tryouts in Colombia, they knew he would be good. They just didn’t expect him to be so good so quickly. The right-hander was throwing his fastball at 88-90 mph in his early looks, then his stuff exploded. The last time the Rays evaluated him before international signing day, Urbina was throwing his heater at 94-98 mph. Thus, Urbina could wind up being the steal of Tampa Bay’s Jan. 15 class as he joined the organization for a $210,000 bonus. If his velocity gains stick, Urbina’s mid-to-upper 90s fastball will be his biggest draw and the reason he climbs up this list. But the Rays are intrigued by the whole package he presents. He throws strikes, works hard, competes well and has the ingredients of a power starter. He showed feel for a slider from a start, and the sweeping, two-plane breaker looked like a plus pitch in his late looks. He also quickly developed a changeup that flashed plus at times. Perhaps the greatest sign of the Rays’ belief in Urbina is that he’s likely to begin his first professional season in the Florida Complex League, bypassing the Dominican Summer League, which is rare for an international prospect in his pro debut. The Rays already evaluated him in game scenarios before signing him and liked what they saw. Of course, he has to prove himself in affiliated competition, and it’s a relatively low rate of success for international pitchers making it to the Majors. But Urbina looks like the top international amateur arm signed by the Rays in 2023, and there was a lot of buzz around him entering the year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez was in the Top 10 of the 2024 International Prospects list and was paid accordingly, getting $2.7 million from the Reds when that signing period opened in January of ‘24. He didn’t put his best foot forward, scuffling during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, finishing with a .701 OPS and a 33.9 percent strikeout rate. Repeating the DSL in 2025 was the right call because Sanchez did a 180, hitting .339 with a .978 OPS before a minor leg injury kept him from a planned move to the Arizona Complex League. The biggest reason for the turnaround was the tweaking of his setup and mechanics, especially pre-swing. He had previously had a lot of movement with his bat early, which contributed to the high swing-and-miss rate. He worked with the Reds to cut down the movement, getting into a better position to hit earlier. He shaved his K rate down to 13.6 percent as a result while continuing to draw walks. The left-handed hitter is capable of very hard contact with some ability to loft the baseball, with more power to come if he can continue to slow things down in the box. Sanchez played both center and right field in 2025 and he’ll continue to get reps in both outfield spots moving forward. The hope is that he can stay up the middle, but he might slow down too much for that to be a realistic projection. A full-time move to a corner puts more pressure on that bat, but if his mechanical adjustments from 2025 are for real, he could profile just fine there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a perfect world, a prospect ranked in the top five of an international signing class who gets a seven-figure bonus would hit the ground running in his Dominican Summer League debut and then be ready to take the United States by storm the following season. But development isn't always the straight line teams desire it to be and Sanchez, who signed for $2.7 million in January of 2024, really struggled in the DSL, finishing his debut summer with a .216/.356/.345 line. Sanchez still has plenty of projection and physical ability that he needs to learn how to use consistently. He entered pro ball with the reputation of having a simple left-handed swing that can produce hard contact and a solid approach. He's shown some loft in his swing with more gap power now, but the thinking was more would come with maturation. He needs to learn to get his bat into a better position so he can stay through the zone and be on time more consistently which would help him reduce his nearly 34 percent strikeout rate during his debut. After getting most of his defensive reps in center field during his debut, Sanchez will keep playing there and right field mostly going forward. He's an average runner but has good instincts in the outfield, giving him the chance to stick up the middle depending on how much he slows down. For now, he'll try to hit the reset button for 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thought to be one of the best hitters in his class, Sanchez was ranked No. 5 on MLB Pipeline's Top 50 International Prospects list when the 2024 signing period opened in January. The Reds never shy away from going after top talent on a yearly basis and the $2.7 million they gave Sanchez to sign is the fifth straight signing period they've given out at least one seven-figure bonus. Sanchez has a simple and mechanically sound swing from the left side of the plate, showing the ability to drive the ball to all fields with consistently hard contact, while exhibiting a solid overall approach. He has some loft in his swing and while he's wiry right now -- he sprays the ball into the gaps -- there should be more power to come with that swing as he fills out his 6-foot-1 frame. While he's just an average runner, Sanchez has good instincts with solid reads and routes when tracking flyballs. That could give him the chance to stick in center field long-term, though his plus arm would be an asset should he have to move to right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sims was a killer reliever for Mississippi State's 2021 national championship team, posting a 1.44 ERA with 100 strikeouts in 56 1/3 innings, and was moving to the Bulldogs' rotation a year later when he sustained an elbow injury in his third start. The issue required Tommy John surgery for the junior, but believing in the stuff, the D-backs selected Sims with the 34th overall pick in 2022 and signed him for above-slot at $2,347,050. Sims made his Minor League debut in June and totaled 15 appearances between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia. Arizona officials note that Sims showed up for instructs with good added weight that he had lost as he worked through rehab. That adds to the belief that he'll get back to the 94-96 mph, high-spin fastball that was such a strong pitch in college after throwing closer to the low-90s in the Minors. His mid-80s wipeout slider still gets awkward swings and can play off the high heater. Sims stuck mostly to his bread-and-butter in his return, but he'll need something of a changeup as he attacks higher levels in 2024 and beyond. Sims walked 12 batters in 24 2/3 innings last year, showing the shaky control typical of a Tommy John pitcher coming off so much missed time, and the D-backs made the decision in ’24 to move him back to the bullpen, where he thrived in college. He continues to show closer-type stuff in that role, even with some continued control questions, and in climbing to High-A, he could be in position for relief looks in The Show in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sims headed to Mississippi State after his stock in the 2019 Draft dropped due to concerns about his secondary stuff. He was a downright dominant reliever in his second season with the Bulldogs, saving 13 games while posting a 1.44 ERA with 100 K's in 56 1/3 innings, helping lead the program to the 2021 NCAA national title. Sims was moving to the rotation (and had a 27/2 K/BB ratio) when he suffered an elbow injury in his third start and needed Tommy John surgery. The D-backs still selected him 34th overall and signed him above slot for $2,347,050. The 6-foot-2 right-hander has been on the rehab path, and he finally made it to a Minor League mound in June. In school, collegiate batters stood little chance against his 94-96 mph fastball with high spin and fiery life up in the zone. His mid-80s wipeout slider may be even better as a pure quality pitch, and it plays well off the high heat. Sims says he believes in his changeup, but he didn't need much of one at Mississippi State, though he will in the pros. The Georgia native walked only 7.3 percent of the batters he faced at school, and that control has Arizona believing he has a shot to be a starter. His makeup, which was on display when he became the Bulldogs' first-base coach when injured, receives raves from scouts and evaluators, and that will come in handy after the long layoff. Still, his two plus pitches would get him to the Majors quickly once he's healthy, should he slide back to relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stevenson’s trajectory has been steady and deliberate. The North Carolina native turned down top-five-round money out of high school in 2023 to attend North Carolina, and he quickly validated that decision by seizing the Tar Heels’ starting catching job as a freshman. That year, he launched 14 homers and earned a spot on the U.S. collegiate national team. His sophomore season only strengthened his profile, as he clubbed 19 homers and emerged as one of the premier catching prospects in the class. The Mariners wound up selecting him with their Competitive Balance Round A pick in 2025 for a $2.8 million bonus. A physical, left-handed hitter, Stevenson’s calling card is impact. He consistently produces loud contact and naturally lifts the ball, with power that plays from left-center to the right-field line. There’s legitimate 25-homer potential if the hit tool reaches average. His approach is generally disciplined, but quality velocity and well-located offspeed can expose swing-and-miss tendencies that will need refinement against pro pitching. That said, the Mariners were really encouraged about his first 100 plate appearances at Single-A Modesto, where he had just a 19 percent K rate. Stevenson won’t wow on the bases -- he’s a well-below-average runner -- but he has reshaped his body and vastly improved his conditioning since high school. Defensively, the strides have been notable. His receiving has cleaned up, and he now projects as a dependable defender. His arm strength stands out, and his throws carry both velocity and accuracy, giving him a chance to control the running game at higher levels. Because he turns 22 in July, Stevenson is already far more seasoned, and as such, could be on a faster trajectory. His upside was one reason why the club was comfortable trading away Harry Ford, its first-round pick in 2021 and a former Top 100 prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz wasn't drafted in 2017 after his senior year at George Washington High School in New York, but the Phillies took a flier on him and his raw power after seeing him playing for the New York Nine Scout Team that summer. Things started to click in 2022 when he got to Double-A and mashed 17 homers before hitting well in the Arizona Fall League. A full season spent with Reading in 2023 yielded 24 more long balls, but he was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft this past offseason and went unselected. At 6-foot-8, there's no question about De La Cruz's raw power, and he started to learn how to make adjustments to better pitching in Double-A to get to it more. While there's always going to be swing-and-miss to his game, he actually cut his strikeout rate in 2023 and upped his walk rate, controlling the zone better and not chasing as much as the idea that more consistent contact will lead to more home runs sunk in. De La Cruz runs well, especially once underway, and has shown he can handle all three outfield spots. He saw more time in center field with Reading after Johan Rojas got called up and looked fine up the middle. He'll keep getting reps across the outfield and at first base to give the Phillies more options should they deem his power bat ready for Philadelphia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It may seem impossible for a 6-foot-8 player to fly completely off the radar, but that’s exactly what happened with De La Cruz. A product of George Washington High School in New York, the alma mater of Manny Ramirez, De La Cruz went undrafted in 2017. The Phillies noticed when he put up gaudy numbers that summer for the New York Nine Scout Team and took a flier, signing him as an undrafted free agent. He was nothing more than a feel-good story until 2022, when he played his way to Double-A, hitting 17 homers in the process, then performed well in the Arizona Fall League. Especially given his size, De La Cruz has a solid feel to hit with a clean swing from the right side of the plate. There is work he needs to do in terms of his overall approach, with better pitch selection and discipline allowing him to tap into his considerable raw power, which could be plus with those adjustments. While he’s an average runner, he’s better once he gets underway. De La Cruz is a better overall athlete than you might imagine given his size, and he does post good sprint speed numbers once he gets going. That allows him to track balls well underway in the outfield, and he’s shown he can handle all three spots out there, playing a better-than-expected center field, while also providing a very big target at first base when needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blanco didn’t attract much attention when he was just a 5-foot-6, switch-hitting shortstop hailing from Caracas, Venezuela’s capital city. But Rays scouts were nonetheless impressed every time they saw him even then, believing at times he was the best player on every field he took, even when he was physically outmatched by his peers. They offered him a $1 million bonus when others weren’t as interested, then saw him shoot up to 5-foot-11 and become a Top 50 prospect in the 2026 international class before they signed him. Now with much more physicality than he possessed before his growth spurt, Blanco is viewed as a complete player with tremendous makeup. He has above-average bat speed and contact skills thanks to his quick hands, and he could develop above-average power from both sides of the plate. Pitch selection will be an issue, and he’ll need to gain more experience as a right-handed hitter as he enters professional baseball. He’s a solid runner and not afraid to be aggressive on the basepaths, but he wasn’t a huge stolen-base threat as an amateur. Blanco has a strong arm and quick feet, so he should be able to stick at shortstop. He’ll have to compete for reps there with top international prospect Victor Valdez, among others, but he is highly regarded for the way he handles himself at a premium defensive position. If he continues to improve like he did before signing, he’ll become a prospect to watch no matter his size.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alderman was one of the top power hitters in the 2023 Draft, one year after he was a key member of Mississippi's Men's College World Series championship team. After signing for a below-slot $1.4 million as a second-rounder, he slugged just .391 in his first full pro season across three levels in part due to a broken hamate bone. A strong Arizona Fall League campaign portended more power for a healthy 2025 campaign, as he produced a career-best 22 homers and 22 steals with an .819 OPS while reaching Triple-A. The right-handed slugger produces top-of-the-scale exit velocities and has done a better job of tapping into that strength lately while slightly decreasing his strikeout rate. Alderman retains his power-over-hit profile, and the Marlins are continuing to work on his swing decisions as he has a tendency to chase, which cuts into his walk rates. Big improvements against secondary pitches in 2025 give hope that his high-load swing will hold up against big league competition. Alderman will need to hit well because he's limited to a corner outfield spot on defense. He's fairly athletic for a stocky frame but his reads aren't great on the grass, and he mostly shines in the field for a strong throwing arm befitting an amateur pitcher who once hit 94 mph on the mound. Alderman has improved his speed in pro ball -- he'll flash above-average sprint speeds -- though his efficiency on the bases is a work in progress.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of Mississippi's 2022 College World Series championship team, Alderman featured some of the best raw power and highest exit velocities in the following year's Draft. Signed for a below-slot $1.4 million in the second round, he lost the first two months of the 2024 season to a broken hamate that still sapped his power for a while after he returned. Fully healthy in the Arizona Fall League, he bashed six homers in nine games and produced the hardest-hit ball (119.5 mph) of the season before leaving to get married. At 6-foot-2 and 250 pounds, Alderman possesses massive strength and leverage and has drawn physical comparisons to Hunter Renfroe. Some evaluators grade his raw power at the top of the 20-80 scouting scale, and he's capable of blasting the ball out of the park from foul pole to foul pole. He has a surprisingly compact right-handed swing considering the size and damage he does, though he's prone to chasing all types of pitches out of the zone, which results in a lot of strikeouts and groundball contact. More athletic than most players his size, Alderman has below-average speed but isn't a baseclogger and can steal an occasional base. He gets the job done on the outfield corners and has a strong arm that pumped fastball up to 94 mph when he pitched sporadically for the Rebels. He caught some in high school and college, which offers an intriguing possibility, though the Marlins want to make the most of his power potential for now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alderman barely played as a freshman at Mississippi before helping the Rebels win the 2022 national championship by providing three multihit games at the College World Series. His raw power and exit velocities compared favorably with anyone's in the 2023 Draft class, prompting the Marlins to select him in the second round. After signing for a below-slot $1.4 million, he looked rusty at the plate during his pro debut in Single-A. Alderman has drawn physical comparisons to Hunter Renfroe in the past and at 6-foot-3 and 250 pounds, he has huge strength and leverage. Some scouts give him top-of-the-scale grades for his raw power, which plays to any part of any ball park. Though strikeouts will be a part of his game, he did a better job of keeping his right-handed stroke more compact in his final college season, which he finished with a 49-game on-base streak. Despite his massive frame, Alderman is more athletic than expected, producing fringy run times out of the batter's box and at least average speed under way. He's a capable corner outfielder with a strong arm that ran fastballs up to 94 mph when he pitched briefly at Mississippi. He also spent some time catching in high school and started some midweek games behind the plate for the Rebels, though Miami is going to focus on fully tapping into his power for now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Padres for $125,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019, Baez had to wait two years just to make his Dominican Summer League debut due to the pandemic. His full-season debut in the Minors didn’t come until 2023, when he posted a 3.84 ERA with 99 strikeouts across 98 1/3 innings between Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne. Last season, he joined the A’s organization as part of the return for Mason Miller and JP Sears at the Trade Deadline. Baez had a 1.96 ERA in 20 starts for Double-A San Antonio and was leading the Texas League in ERA, WHIP (1.00) and batting average against (.195) at the time he was traded, but after making three starts with Double-A Midland, he sustained a forearm injury that cut his season short. Baez made a full recovery this offseason and joined the A’s for big league Spring Training. Baez has increased his velocity over the years, running his fastball up to 99 mph last season and sitting around 94 for most of the year. The heater also carries good sinking action, leading to his high ground-ball rates. What was once a curveball has evolved into more of a slider that generates a decent amount of swing-and-miss. His upper-80s changeup provides good separation from his fastball, though it’s clearly less effective than the slider. He’s tinkered with a cutter that remains a distant fourth pitch at this point. Baez’s control has remained encouraging as the innings build up for him. That quality will likely keep him in a starting role for the time being, though the A’s might be intrigued to see what he looks like as a reliever at the Major League level with his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez signed with the Padres for $125,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019 but couldn’t debut in the Dominican Summer League until two years later due to the pandemic. He didn’t make a full-season debut until 2023 when he split the season between Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne, finishing with solid numbers (3.84 ERA, 99 strikeouts in 98 1/3 innings). He wasn’t added to the 40-man roster that offseason when Rule 5-eligible, however, because of his distance from the Majors. Baez enjoyed his big breakout last year, winning Padres Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors after posting a 2.99 ERA and a 1.09 WHIP with 109 strikeouts in 26 1/3 innings between Fort Wayne and Double-A San Antonio, and San Diego added him to the 40-man in November. His success continued with San Antonio in 2025 and he was leading the Texas League in ERA, WHIP and batting average against when he was included in the prospect package sent to the A’s in return for Mason Miller and JP Sears at the Trade Deadline. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has gained velocity steadily in his years as a pro and has touched as high as 99 mph this season. He typically sits around 94 mph, working north-south with the pitch while getting most of his whiffs up and to the armside. He played off that with a 76-79 mph curveball that could have more slurvish tendencies, but at its best, it snapped downward to fool batters sitting on the high heat and it had produced a 47 percent miss rate at the time of the trade. He also utilizes an 83-86 mph split-change to miss bats, but it stands out more for its separation than movement profile. Baez took a major jump in workload but didn’t let his control improvements suffer. That certainly helps his starting chances, as does his 50.1 percent ground-ball rate from 2024. He’s still only 22, but with his place on the roster now set, the A’s (never afraid to move guys quickly) could try to see what it looks like in the big leagues in a relief role to ease him in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at San Diego, Braun transferred to Cal State Northridge and it wasn’t until his senior season in 2023 that he was a full-time member of the rotation. The Braves thought he could be a valuable senior sign with starter potential, so they took him in the sixth round of that July’s Draft. He reached Double-A in his first full season and then Triple-A in Year 2, proving to be one of the most durable starters in the Minors with the fourth-highest total of innings pitched (293 1/3) among all Minor Leaguers in 2024 and '25 combined. A 6-foot right-hander, Braun is more of a “kitchen sink” starter than he is one with plus stuff; he’ll throw as many as six pitches to keep hitters off-balance. His fastball sits at around 92 mph and tops out at 96, but he’ll throw both a four-seamer with armside run and a two-seamer with sink that he added at the end of 2024. He throws his low-80s slider a lot, and misses bats with it, while also folding in an upper-70s curve and mid-80s changeup. He started to incorporate an upper-80s cutter in 2025 to give a harder fastball-esque look for left-handed hitters. Braun continues to show he can throw all of his offerings for strikes, helping his largely average stuff play up. His ceiling might not be that high without a single plus pitch, but he’s had success at the upper levels and should get the chance to show he can be a back-end big league starter soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Braun, who transferred to Cal State Northridge after two years at San Diego, became the first Matadors pitcher to be taken in the top 10 rounds since 2017 when the Braves selected him in Round 6 of the 2023 Draft after a senior season that saw him start full-time for the first time. He was able to jump on a slightly faster developmental track by pitching his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season, topping all Braves pitching prospects in a host of categories, from innings pitched and strikeouts to K-BB percentage and xFIP. Braun may not have wow stuff, but he sure has a lot of it with a bit of a kitchen sink-type approach to pitching. The six-footer now has as many as five pitches he mixes well to keep hitters guessing. His four-seamer averaged 93 mph in 2024 and topped out at 95 mph with some arm-side run to it and he added a two-seamer with sink at the end of the season and into instructional league play. His 83-84 mph slider is his go-to secondary offering and it elicited a 39-percent miss rate last year, and he also mixes in an upper-70s curve and mid-80s changeup effectively. All of Braun’s stuff plays up because he can throw any pitch for strikes, with a 67-percent strike rate in 2024, and it was encouraging to see him be more effective as he moved up a level with the promotion to Double-A. He doesn’t have that high of a ceiling because of the lack of big stuff, but his feel for pitching gives him a pretty high floor, with a chance to be a solid back-end starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at San Diego as a seldom-used reliever, Braun transferred to Cal State Northridge. He worked as a starter and out of the bullpen in 2021, then moved into the rotation the following season, showing a feel for pitching and a full arsenal, albeit with mixed results. It was enough for the Braves to take him in the sixth round of the 2023 Draft, and he threw 27 effective innings during his pro debut. Braun has a four-pitch mix and can land all of them for strikes, even though none of them jump off the page. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, topping out at 95 mph with some occasional arm-side run. He missed bats at Northridge with his low-80s slider that can flash above-average while mixing in an upper-70s curve and showing solid feel for a low-80s changeup. The six-foot right-hander has a simple and repeatable delivery, throwing from the stretch, and he’s long been a solid strike-thrower, something that continued during his pro debut. The ceiling is limited without a true out pitch, but the feel for his craft gives him the chance to perhaps be a back-end starter, giving the Braves another solid senior sign who makes the big leagues, a la Dylan Dodd.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners originally took Schreck in the ninth round as a money-saver, signing him for just $75,000 in 2023. In the middle of a strong ‘24 season, he was dealt to the Blue Jays for Justin Turner. Since then, Schreck has proven to be more than many expected, emerging as one of the top outfield prospects in the system. He's an excellent fit for the Blue Jays’ offensive identity, which became much clearer during their 2025 World Series run. Schreck is a heady hitter who puts together excellent game plans, which shows in his advanced plate approach from the left side. That’s his calling card, and with 17 and 18 home runs over the past two seasons, there’s at least enough pop there to work with if he can keep his on-base tool comfortably above average in the big leagues. The Blue Jays feel like they’ve found a rock-solid, all-around player who can legitimately handle all three outfield spots defensively. Think Nathan Lukes, but with maybe even a higher ceiling. Schreck adds to a long line of hitting prospects with advanced plate approaches. He hit right-handed pitching very well in '24 and ‘25, which would represent a path to the big leagues if Schreck continues to profile as a fourth or fifth outfielder. Being a lefty bat matters here, too, given Toronto’s current roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After four years at Duke, Schreck had an additional year of eligibility after the pandemic and transferred to Vanderbilt, where he put up a .306/.454/.588 line in his fifth collegiate season. The Mariners took him in the ninth round as a money-saver, signing him for just $75,000 in 2023, and in the middle of a strong ‘24 season, Schreck was dealt to the Blue Jays for Justin Turner. Schreck finished the season with a combined line of .251/.388/.462, including 17 home runs in 114 games. Schreck is a heady hitter who puts together excellent game plans, which shows in his advanced plate approach from the left side. That’s his calling card, but he’ll need that power tool to continue growing and the Blue Jays have been encouraged by his offseason work there. Schreck is a fundamentally sound outfielder who won’t be a problem defensively and is a fine athlete, so he’s working with a strong baseline skill set if one or more of his tools can truly pop. Consider Schreck another very “Blue Jays-style” hitter, adding to a long line of hitting prospects with advanced plate approaches. He hit right-handed pitching very well in '24, which would represent a path to the big leagues if Schreck continues to profile as a fourth or fifth outfielder. He’s been productive and comes from plenty of NCAA experience, though, so Schreck should have no trouble making the final jump to Triple-A, where he’ll work to separate himself from the pack as an MLB option in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ko starred at the 18-and-under World Cup in his native Taiwan in September 2023, going 11-for-20 with seven walks while earning a silver medal. At the press conference announcing his signing for $650,000 nine months later, Dodgers director of Pacific Rim scouting Jon Deeble likened him to Cody Bellinger. He earned Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his U.S. debut in 2025, pacing the Rookie circuit in wRC+ (175), on-base percentage (.487) and OPS (1.026) before making his Single-A debut at age 18. Ko displayed an advanced approach for his age, rarely chasing while working counts and waiting for pitches to drive. His hitting ability and plus raw power could translate into 20-25 homers annually once he's fully developed. Even when he struggled following his promotion to Single-A, he still managed the strike zone well and was able to drive balls in the air. Already 6-foot-3 and 215 pounds, Ko is more physical than twitchy but moves well for his size. He'll steal and take extra bases when given the opportunity, and he has enough quickness and instincts to play a capable center field. Still, he fits better on the corners and has the solid arm strength for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ko excelled at the 18-and-under World Cup in his native Taiwan in September 2023, going 11-for-20 with seven walks while winning a silver medal. When the Dodgers signed him nine months later for $650,000, director of Pacific Rim scouting Jon Deeble compared him to Cody Bellinger. Ko made a brief pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, reaching base 18 times in nine games as a DH. Ko has all the ingredients to hit for average and power. He has a quality left-handed swing with a mature approach, showing the ability to draw walks without becoming too passive at the plate. With his bat speed, present strength with the room to add more and aptitude for pulling balls in the air, he offers plus raw pop and should have the hitting ability to get to most of it. Though he already carries 215 pounds on his 6-foot-3 frame, Ko moves well for his size and should settle in as an average runner once he's physically developed. Los Angeles will give him the opportunity to show what he can do in center field, though he'll probably end up in a corner in the long run. With his offensive upside and solid arm, he profiles well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Doughty could have been selected in the top three rounds of the 2019 Draft after being named Gatorade’s Louisiana high school player of the year but chose to attend LSU, where he was the third member of his family to play for the Tigers after his father, Richard, and brother Braden. The Blue Jays selected Doughty 78th overall in 2022 and were immediately impressed when they brought him in for a post-Draft camp. Doughty has kept that momentum rolling since. With High-A Vancouver in 2023, Doughty launched 18 home runs in 102 games, batting .264 with an .801 OPS. These numbers didn’t get as much attention as they should have -- perhaps because Doughty isn’t the flashiest prospect -- but it was particularly impressive in the Northwest League, where he adjusted well while facing the same pitchers over and over. Strikeouts could be holding him back, with 126 whiffs to only 35 walks a year ago. If he’s going to be that aggressive, Doughty can’t afford to have his power numbers dip any lower than they are now. There could be a future for him at third base, where he takes pride in his defense. He’ll mix in some second, as well, and Doughty could give himself an even quicker path up the ladder as a power-hitting utility player, but he should be given the opportunity to focus on third to begin with. Double-A pitching will be an interesting challenge for Doughty, particularly with his aggression at the plate, but he’s a good example of a prospect with enough present-day talent to put up big numbers while still having some upside down the road.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Doughty could have been selected in the top three rounds of the 2019 Draft after being named Gatorade’s Louisiana High School Player of the Year, but chose to attend LSU, where he was the third member of his family to play for the Tigers after his father, Richard, and brother, Braden. The Blue Jays selected Doughty 78th overall in 2022 and were immediately impressed when they brought him in for a post-Draft camp. Over 26 games for Single-A Dunedin, Doughty hit .272 with an .865 OPS and six home runs. At LSU, Doughty had a wider stance to put an emphasis on controlling the zone and limiting strikeouts. Since joining Toronto, though, that stance has narrowed, which has enabled him to use his legs more and produce more power. That could come with an increased strikeout rate, but it would raise Doughty’s offensive ceiling significantly. Doughty will continue to split time between second and third base but has the potential to be an above-average defender at the hot corner. Combine Doughty’s high ceiling and the polish he enters pro ball with from his NCAA experience, and he could be one of the organization’s more productive players in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If Pan had been able to stay healthy, he might have impacted the Phillies’ big league bullpen by now. He pitched his way to High-A in his debut season of 2023 after signing that January for $350,000. The Taiwanese right-hander then missed nearly three months to kick off the 2024 season with a broken pinky, then missed out on a planned trip to the Arizona Fall League to make up for lost time because of his elbow, which needed Tommy John surgery that November, so he missed all of the 2025 season. The Phillies are excited to see how quickly Pan’s high-end stuff comes back now that he’s healthy again. His fastball plays well with a good angle coming from a little higher slot, sitting in the 96-97 mph range and touching 99 with some ride before the surgery. He’s mostly a two-pitch guy, with a plus splitter that kills spin and gets a ton of swing-and-miss. He started throwing his slider a little harder, around 84-85 mph, and it was effective, but it’s average at best as a distant third offering. Before the injury, Pan had made some good strides in his control and command. It doesn’t need to be pinpoint for him to land high-leverage innings in a big league bullpen in the future, something that could happen sooner rather than later if he can shake the TJ rust off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $350,000 out of Chinese Taipei when the 2023 international signing period opened that January, Pan opened eyes right away that summer, pitching his way from Single-A Clearwater to High-A Jersey Shore in relief. A broken pinky kept him off the mound in 2024 until late June, but he did make it back to the BlueClaws near the end of July. A planned trip to the Arizona Fall League was canceled because of elbow issues, resulting in November Tommy John surgery, so he’ll miss the 2025 season. When he’s healthy, Pan has the kind of power arsenal that could land him in a big league bullpen. He threw his fastball up to 99 mph in 2024 and averaged 96.7 mph with his heater, according to Synergy. His mid-80s splitter is a true out pitch, one that kills spin and elicited a ridiculous 63 percent miss rate in 2024. He made some strides in firming up his slider, averaging 84.4 mph with it and the added velocity made it a more effective bat-misser. Focusing on just those three pitches, Pan did a solid job of finding the zone more in 2024, cutting his walk rate. He may never have pinpoint command, but won’t need it with his stuff in relief. Once he returns in 2026, he should be able to move quickly and has the chance to handle high-leverage situations in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While most of the attention at the start of an international signing period is given to Latin America, there are other places on the planet that produce good talent. When the 2023 period started, there were two Taiwanese pitchers who commanded six-figure bonuses. The Giants signed Chen-Hsun Lee for $647,500 and the Phillies inked Pan for $350,000. He made a very strong first impression by dominating out of the bullpen for full-season Clearwater in his pro debut, earning a late bump up to High-A Jersey Shore. Pan has a power repertoire that can miss a lot of bats, and he struck out 12.4 per nine innings during his pro debut. He touched triple digits with his fastball last year, throwing with excellent armside run. His best secondary pitch is his 84-85 mph splitter that is a real spin-killer. His slider has improved and he's worked on firming it up. It has the chance to be very good pitch if he can get it up to the mid-80s consistently from the upper 70s and low 80s where it lived in 2023. While Pan has used a slower curve and a regular changeup at times as well, they are likely to get shelved moving forward to help him simplify things on the mound. He tends to be around the zone, albeit without pinpoint command. He'll be working toward giving starting a try and could get stretched out to three- to four-inning outings to help build him up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $775,000 as the Rangers’ third-rounder in the shortened 2020 Draft, Roby has mixed promise with a checkered health history in the six years since. He has exceeded 100 innings in a Minor League season only once, in 2022 with then-High-A Hickory. Texas traded him to the Cardinals a year later as part of the Jordan Montgomery swap at the ’23 Deadline in Roby’s first of two seasons in which shoulder issues held him back. He looked on track to break through to the Majors perhaps in ’25 with 16 starts -- including six at Triple-A Memphis -- before he needed Tommy John surgery in late July, a procedure that will keep him out for much, if not all, of 2026. Roby’s four-seam fastball ran 94-97 mph and despite some ride and cut on the heater, Triple-A batters read it pretty well from his high release and average extension. A sinker at least generated more soft, ground-ball contact. The real star of the show remained his breaking pitches. An 80-83 mph curveball can confound lefties with 4 1/2 feet of drop and classic 12-to-6 shape.
