Vukovich slashed .263/.333/.485 with 24 homers and 20 steals over 115 games, making him one of Arizona’s two 20-20 Minor Leaguers last season alongside Jordan Lawlar. Vukovich rounded off ’23 with 20 more games in the Arizona Fall League, where he posted just a .663 OPS. The right-handed slugger has shown at least above-average raw power throughout his career, but it’s becoming a bigger question of how it will play in games. Of Vukovich’s 24 homers in 2023, 18 of them came in Amarillo’s hitter-friendly confines, and he slugged just .362 away from HODGETOWN, in part because he ran a 48.9 percent ground-ball rate. Getting more consistent elevation will be an issue as he heads into his 40-man roster decision season. On the positive side, Vukovich did a better job of easing his aggression in the box and posted a career-high 9.1 percent walk rate by spitting on his fair share of breaking stuff outside the zone. His troubles with high velo might dull the offensive ceiling, but at least the approach is trending upward. An average runner, Vukovich moved from third base to the outfield on a more full-time basis in ’23 and didn’t touch the dirt at all defensively in the AFL. The extra room to roam is a better fit for his athleticism, but he’s still likely limited to a corner with arm strength that can play in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vukovich was just as notable for playing hoops in high school when he was a finalist for Wisconsin’s Mr. Basketball award after averaging 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game. Originally recruited to Louisville for baseball, he instead went in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft to the D-backs, who gave him a $1.25 million bonus – almost $800,000 above slot. After splitting 2021 at two A-ball levels, Vukovich hit .274/.308/.450 and tied for fifth in the Northwest League with 15 homers in 106 games for High-A Hillsboro last year. He spent 11 games with Double-A Amarillo late in the season. The right-handed slugger has at least plus raw power from the right side emanating from his 6-foot-5 frame, and he has enough loft in his swing to tap into it, even on a pitcher-friendly circuit like the Northwest League. What may keep Vukovich from putting up more eye-popping stat lines, however, is his aggression at the plate. He may cover the strike zone well enough when he swings, but he severely lacks patience. His 4 percent walk rate and 0.17 BB/K ratio were second-lowest among 137 High-A qualifiers. The Badger State native still has the athleticism he showed on the court in his basketball days, and that should serve him well as he continues getting looks in the outfield, where he made 32 starts in 2022. He's become more of a full-time outfielder in 2023, in part as he's bumped up against Deyvison De Los Santos and Ivan Melendez, and his athleticism might be a better fit out there anyways. His bat should certainly play in a corner outfield spot moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A finalist for Wisconsin's Mr. Basketball award, Vukovich was a two-sport athlete in high school who averaged 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game. On the diamond, the D-backs liked his power and selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft, going well over slot with a $1.25 million bonus to sign him away from a commitment to Louisville. He made his professional debut with Low-A Visalia and got off to a slow start, but started to hit as the summer wore on and worked his way up to High-A Hillsboro in August. He finished his first full season with a .272/.320/.446 slash line and 13 homers over 92 games. Vukovich has long levers and a lot of projectable strength in his 6-foot-5 frame, which combines with the bat speed and loft in his right-handed stroke to produce the well-above-average raw power. He opened eyes in 2020, showing not only his power, but also a hit tool that was better than expected. Vukovich has a chance to develop into an impact bat at the highest level, but needs to refine his approach a bit and eliminate some of the swing-and-miss as he continues to climb the ladder. Drafted as an outfielder, the D-backs moved Vukovich to third base and it was a rough go initially. However, he’s made noticeably big gains over the past two years and it appears the game is starting to slow down for him. He’s shown enough growth that club officials believe he’ll be able to stick long term at the hot corner, where both his bat and strong arm profile well. If necessary, he has the tools and athleticism needed to play a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A finalist for Wisconsin's Mr. Basketball award, Vukovich was a two-sport athlete in high school. He averaged 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game. On the diamond, the D-backs liked his power and selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft and went well over slot at $1.25 million to sign him away from a commitment to Louisville. He made his professional debut with Low-A Visalia and got off to a slow start, but started to hit as the summer wore on and worked his way up to High-A Hillsboro in August. Vukovich has long levers and a lot of projectable strength in his 6-foot-5 frame, which combine with the bat speed and loft in his right-handed stroke to produce the well above-average raw power that was on display as he slugged 10 homers over 62 games with Visalia before his promotion. Vukovich opened some eyes during Instructional League in 2020, flashing the big-time power, but also showing an excellent hit tool. The D-backs stuck him at third base for the first time and it was a rough go initially, but he made huge strides this season and is continually improving at the hot corner. It’s starting to look as if he can stick there long term, and both his bat and strong arm would profile well. If necessary, he has the tools and athleticism needed to play a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Izzi was teammates with White Sox left-hander Noah Schultz at Oswego East HS in Illinois before the big lefty was taken in the first round and the right-hander was selected by the Mariners in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft. A $1.1 million bonus was enough to get Izzi to sign away from his Wichita State commitment. After making only nine Arizona Complex League starts in 2023, he emerged more on the scene with a 2.85 ERA and 95 strikeouts in 110 2/3 innings with Single-A Modesto a year later. Izzi opened 2025 with an oblique injury and was slowly building back into his own with High-A Everett when the D-backs acquired him at the Deadline in a move for Josh Naylor. Standing 6-foot-3, Izzi gets good extension down the mound and shows average four-seam velocity around 94 mph, touching 97. He’ll also mix in a sinker for another fastball look, but he doesn’t miss many bats with his heater. He throws two forms of a breaking ball in a mid-80s gyro slider and low-80s sweeper, and he’ll go to the vertical break of the former against batters from both sides. That’s useful because his changeup still needs more consistency to become an MLB weapon. Izzi works exclusively out of the stretch and positions himself on the first-base side of the rubber. There aren’t too many moving pieces in his delivery, and as he got built up just before and after the trade, his control really took off down the stretch in the Northwest League with a 4.9 percent walk rate in his final eight starts. He should head to the upper Minors for the first time in his age-22 season aiming to develop a plus pitch that could turn him into a back-end Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oswego East High School in Illinois may not seem like a factory for high-end arms, but it was in 2022. That’s where Noah Schultz -- now the top left-handed pitching prospect in the game after the White Sox took him in the first round of that Draft -- and Izzi were teammates. Izzi showed enough for the Mariners to take him in the fourth round, going over slot with $1.1 million to sign him away from his Wichita State commitment. It was a slow rollout for the right-hander, not pitching after signing and throwing just 18 1/3 innings in the Arizona Complex League in 2023. But the gloves came off in 2024 and Izzi threw well, topping 100 IP for full-season Modesto. After opening 2025 with an oblique injury, he came into his own by midsummer and was then dealt to the Diamondbacks as part of the Deadline deal for Josh Naylor. Izzi is pitching at age 21 for the 2025 season, and the 6-foot-3 right-hander built a pretty good foundation to work from. His fastball typically sits at least 94 mph and can touch as high as 97 at times, and he does a very good job of separating his four-seamer up in the zone and his sinking two-seamer down. His low-80s sweeper has the chance to be a solid pitch that misses bats. He didn’t have a great feel for his changeup with Modesto. Whether that necessitates a move to the bullpen remains to be seen, although there is some thought that because of his excellent separation between his two fastballs, he might be able to stay in a rotation without a changeup. His splits were near-even before the trade, and his control had shown steady improvement, aiding the belief that he should still get rotation looks with Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Izzi wowed ahead of the 2022 Draft when area scouts attended one of his high school outings to see a teammate, which prompted the club to do more homework and eventually select the highly projectable righty in the fourth round for over-slot value at $1.1 million, enough to sign him away from his Wichita State commitment. It’s more upside than floor with the youngster, who didn’t throw competitively the rest of the year after being drafted -- a by-design, health-related effort with the rest of Seattle’s high school pitching selections. He was among the many invited to the club’s high-performance camp, with the goal of putting on more weight and strength. Beyond conditioning, it’s about throwing more strikes and being consistent, because he can already reach 97 mph with his four-seamer, while sitting in the low-90s with modest life. The heater gives him a far higher ceiling than most his age. His low-80s slider also has good depth and is a pitch he can build upon, though his higher arm slot might be more conducive to a curveball instead. The path to starting long term will require polishing those two pitches, but more so fortifying the changeup, which is still a bit off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morlando had a highly decorated amateur career between international tournament success and a star-making performance at the 2023 All-Star Game when he won the High School Home Run Derby and the MVP award at the High School All-American Game. His pro career has failed to launch in two years since the Marlins drafted him 16th overall and signed him for a below-slot $3.4 million, though. Morlando suffered a season-ending back injury in his pro debut and played only 58 games in 2025 (posting a .702 OPS) because of elbow surgery and a hamstring injury. He went to the Arizona Fall League to make up for lost time but was often overmatched. Although primarily known for his power as a high schooler, that has not yet translated to pro ball. Some scouts had concerns about how often Morlando tapped into his power in games before he was drafted, but his top-line power hasn't even shown up sporadically. His max exit velocity (109 mph) ranked in just the 63rd percentile for the Single-A Florida State League, and he didn't put the ball in the air frequently enough. Perhaps that will return with health and consistent play, and Morlando is also looking for the contact skills that regressed when he tweaked his stance. He's had trouble against secondary pitches of all kinds and sliders in particular (.388 OPS, 61 percent whiff rate). Although Morlando is largely an average runner, he will flash above-average sprint speeds and has been efficient stealing bases. He's played some center field, but his range and arm make left field his likely home, and he could be a candidate for first base as well. Ultimately, his chances of playing in the big leagues will come down to his bat, and this will be a key season to prove whether he still has that impact power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morlando had a long track record of amateur success, including starring with the U.S. 18-and-under team in 2022 and 2023, and winning the High School Home Run Derby and the MVP award at the High School All-American Game at the 2023 All-Star Game. Though he added Gatorade's South Carolina prep player of the year award in 2024, his stock took a hit because of questions about his usable power and athleticism. The Marlins may have liked him more than any club, and when the college bats they wanted came off the board before their pick at No. 16, they pivoted to Morlando and signed him for a below-slot $3.4 million. He suffered a stress reaction his back during his first pro game, ending his season after one at-bat, but fully participated in the club's development camp in the Dominican Republic in November. There's no question that Morlando was one of the more advanced hitters in the 2024 prep class, showing the ability to work counts, make two-strike adjustments and deliver consistent contact against quality pitching. He has a quick left-handed swing, already has added 20 pounds since turning pro and can put on an absolute show in batting practice, like he did at the MLB Draft Combine, so he has 30-home run upside. But he went deep just twice while he got pitched around and got to spread out as a high school senior, so some evaluators question if he'll get translate his well above-average raw power into more than average game pop. Morlando also creates mixed opinions with his speed, with grades ranging from fringy to sneaky solid and flashes of plus run times. Miami will try him in center field, though most scouts who saw him as an amateur projected him as a left fielder or first baseman. His arm strength is presently average but could be suitable right field if it ticks up a bit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted in the second round in 2020 out of Florida State, Van Eyk was one of the more encouraging long-term arms in the system before Tommy John surgery derailed his development and cost him the entire ‘22 season. Van Eyk returned to the mound in ‘23 and had a unique season, seeing some early spurts in Single-A and the Florida Complex League before a late assignment to Double-A New Hampshire, where he posted a 4.15 ERA with just seven strikeouts over 13 innings. A stint in the AFL brought some encouraging steps. Finally healthy and enjoying a “normal” season for the first time in years, Van Eyk has been circled by several people within the Blue Jays organization as one of the most exciting arms in the system, even at 25. Toronto is seeing all the building blocks that made him a second-round pick again, and now that he’s finally escaped the complex, Van Eyk can begin his long-delayed climb, even if it’s a few years behind schedule. Van Eyk is throwing two shapes of a fastball now, working in a two-seamer, and is sitting 93-95 mph. This sets up his curveball, an excellent pitch that could be effective against MLB hitters tomorrow, and a slider that plays well. Van Eyk’s workload will need to be closely monitored, given how his past few seasons have gone, but there is a surprising amount of internal belief that Van Eyk can get this back on track, and quickly, if his health cooperates.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Eyk drew plenty of attention prior to the 2017 Draft as a prep arm out of Florida, but missed some time with arm soreness as a senior and decided to head to Florida State instead of signing with the Mets, who selected him in the 19th round. Van Eyk developed into one of the best starters in the ’20 Draft class and was selected by the Blue Jays in the second round, signing to an above-slot bonus. After pitching to a 5.83 ERA over 80 1/3 innings in High-A Vancouver in ’21, though, Van Eyk underwent Tommy John surgery. The Blue Jays were immediately impressed with what they saw following the Draft in instructs, with Van Eyk showing a potential plus curveball and a low-90s fastball. His changeup slotted in as his third pitch while his slider, which was still developing, is key to his long-term success, especially if that can develop into a strikeout pitch. With strong reviews of Van Eyk’s poise and maturity on the mound, too, all of the right pieces are in place for when he returns from his rehab process. There will be a clearer timeline on Van Eyk later in the summer as he continues to work his way back, but once he’s fully healed, he’ll have an opportunity to move up the ladder as quickly as his workload will allow. The injury was an unfortunate setback for one of the more talented arms in the ’20 class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Eyk generated some buzz prior to the 2017 Draft as a high school pitcher out of Florida, but missed time with some arm soreness as a senior and decided to head to Florida State instead of signing with the Mets, who selected him in the 19th Round. After developing into one of the top starters in the 2020 class, Van Eyk was picked by the Blue Jays in the second round and signed to an above-slot deal. The Blue Jays got another brief look at Van Eyk as part of their fall instructional league, and those within the organization already praise his poise and maturity. Van Eyk comes with a full arsenal that’s headlined by a plus curveball, while he spots his fastball well in the low-90s. Van Eyk’s changeup is his third pitch, and while it could benefit from some added depth, his arm speed keeps hitters off-balance. The development of that slider will be key long-term, especially late in counts. Van Eyk will have an opportunity to move quickly once he’s in full-season ball, given the depth of his arsenal and his maturity on the mound. The athleticism in his delivery, which the Blue Jays always love, leaves evaluators optimistic that he'll keep a clean, repeatable delivery. The Blue Jays are very comfortable with the right-hander sticking as a starter long-term, and the ’21 season will offer the first extended look at Van Eyk in pro ball. He’s a candidate to make a jump over the next season, especially as some of Toronto’s more advanced arms graduate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: January of 2023 was an exciting month for the Salas family. First, Ethan Salas signed with the Padres as the top player in the amateur international class, then a few days later, older brother Jose was traded from the Marlins to the Twins as part of the deal for Luis Arraez. The older Salas grew up in Florida and moved to Venezuela to continue in the family business -- his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally -- before signing with the Marlins for $2.8 million as one of the top prospects in the 2019-20 international class. He played across two levels of A ball as a teenager in 2022. The Twins are excited to have Salas and his offensive upside in their system. He’s a switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides of the plate and a solid overall approach in terms of pitch recognition and discipline. The Twins have already been impressed with his feel for what he needs to work on as he’s focused on better swing decisions, especially from the left side, where he’s shown more pop to date. That should help him tap into the raw power he’s starting to develop as he gets stronger. A plus runner, Salas should be a base-stealing threat, another area in which his baseball IQ helps his tools play up. He’s gotten more reps at shortstop than anywhere else, but he saw considerable time at second and third last year. He’s fully bilingual and his leadership skills and maturity jump off the page, not only in the way he’s mentored his younger brother, but in how he jumped into getting up to speed in his new organization during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Florida, Salas grew up in Orlando before moving as a teenager to Venezuela, where his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally. The Marlins' primary target on the 2019 international market, he signed for $2.8 million and stood out with his strength and athleticism during their instructional league program in the fall of 2020. He boosted his stock further when he made his pro debut last summer, tearing up the Rookie-level Florida Complex League for a month before earning a promotion to Low-A at age 18. He became a Twin in January, when he was sent to Minnesota in the deal for Luis Arraez. A switch-hitter, Salas has a quick swing from both sides and recognizes pitches better than most hitters his age. He has gotten stronger since signing and could produce 20-25 homers per season once he adds some polish at the plate. He has a good understanding of the strike zone but can get aggressive and pull-conscious, and presently makes more ground-ball contact than is optimal. Salas combines physicality with twitchy athleticism, showing plus speed and solid arm strength. His proponents think his finely tuned internal clock will help him stick at shortstop, while other scouts believe he'll lose some quickness as he fills out and wind up at second base, third base or center field. His background has given him a high baseball IQ and made him fluent in both English and Spanish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally in Venezuela, Salas was born in Florida and grew up in Orlando. After moving back to Venezuela, he became the Marlins' primary target in their 2019 international class and signed for $2.8 million. Ticketed to make his pro debut in the United States last summer until the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League season, he impressed with his strength and athleticism during instructional league last fall. A switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides, Salas is more advanced than most hitters his age and already recognizes pitches well. He put on a show in batting practice at Marlins Park after he signed and has the upside of 20-25 homers per season in his prime. He currently has plus speed but could lose some quickness as he continues to add strength. Some international scouts wondered about Salas' long-term ability to remain at shortstop, but the Marlins believe he has the actions, twitchy athleticism, solid arm and good internal clock to make it happen. He has the tools to handle the defensive responsibilities and fit the offensive profile at second base or center field if he moves off short. Because of his background, he has a high baseball IQ and is fluent in both English and Spanish, both of which should expedite his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Though his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally in Venezuela, Salas was born in Florida and grew up in Orlando. He moved back to Venezuela and became the jewel of the Marlins' 2019 international class, signing for $2.8 million last July. Because of his background, he has advanced feel for the game and is fluent in English as well as Spanish, which should expedite his development. A switch-hitter, Salas has a quick swing from both sides of the plate and recognizes pitches better than most teenagers. He put on a show in batting practice at Marlins Park after he signed, hinting at 20-homer power once he adds some much-needed strength to his 6-foot-1 frame. He presently has plus speed, though he might slow a bit as he matures physically. While there are some questions about Salas' long-term ability to stay at shortstop, the Marlins believe he has the actions and twitchy athleticism to do so. He has solid arm strength and a good internal clock that help him make plays. He should provide enough offense to profile at second base or center field if he has to move.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting .332 over his first two years at Virginia Tech with a little pop, despite a labrum injury that required offseason surgery in 2023, DeMartini turned on the power as a junior, slamming 21 homers for the Hokies in 2024 while sacrificing some of his approach. He joined the Phillies as a fourth-rounder in 2024 and had a solid debut after signing, then followed that up by hitting well with High-A Jersey Shore for the first half of 2025 before struggling with a promotion to Double-A Reading. A left-handed hitting infielder, DeMartini is capable of driving the baseball with a power-over-hit approach. He can register some big exit velocities, with over-the-fence pop mostly showing up to his pull side. His ability to take in information and make adjustments can be a blessing and a curse as he does have a tendency to tinker too much with his setup and approach. He draws walks, but he’ll need to figure out who he is and find a repeatable swing that allows him to cut down on his swing-and-miss, especially against softer stuff. He also really struggled against left-handed pitching. DeMartini continued to surprise people both with his baserunning acumen, stealing 45 bases despite having below-average speed, and his defense. He could be a plus defender at third and even got reps at shortstop during his first full season, though that’s not a long-term home for him. He could mix in some more second base to help him reach his floor as a power-hitting utility type, though it’s not out of the question he figures out upper-level pitching and settles in at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: DeMartini was part of an upsurge of hitting talent at Virginia Tech and put up numbers for three years with the Hokies. After a shoulder injury limited him in 2023 and required labrum surgery after the season, he returned to hit 21 homers last spring, though with the power uptick came a regression in his overall approach. The Phillies liked the offensive potential enough to take him in the fourth round, and while it was brief, he impressed during his pro debut with Single-A Clearwater, posting a .315/.385/.478 line over 104 plate appearances. While DeMartini has a power-over-hit profile from the left side of the plate, he has a good swing, doesn’t chase a ton and can hit the ball very hard. His strikeout rate jumped back up in his last year in college, but the Phillies were thrilled at how he integrated data and made adjustments during his pro debut. When told that his in-zone contact was particularly low in the spring, he turned that around with an in-zone contact rate of 87.6 percent with Clearwater, giving confidence that he’ll be able to get to his power more consistently, while a healthy shoulder should allow him to repeat his swing path. Perhaps the biggest surprise was how good DeMartini looked defensively. While the industry consensus may have been that he was an average defender at the hot corner, the Phillies think he has the chance to be at least plus with his glove and their defensive coordinator thought he had the chops to play shortstop. He may not have the quickness to stay there long-term, but how he showed on both sides of the ball made him the surprise of the Draft class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Kansas City area native, Kudrna attended Blue Valley Southwest HS in Kansas and went pro when his hometown team selected him in the second round of the 2021 Draft, right before Carter Jensen. Kudrna’s journey through the Minor Leagues has been steady, and he finished ‘25 in Triple-A, where it was a little rocky over four appearances. The majority of his season was spent in Double-A, where he posted a 4.21 ERA across 20 appearances (19 starts), striking out 96 and walking 33 in 94 innings with a 1.29 WHIP. The Royals added Kudrna to the 40-man roster in November. Kudrna’s peak velocity in high school hasn’t returned as a pro, sitting around 92-93 mph with flashes of more velo at times, but it can be vulnerable to hard contact. His best pitch is his plus 85-88 mph circle changeup that gets plenty of fade and drop with good chase rates. That’s usually paired with a mid-80s gyro slider that is hard, tight and gets chase. He’s developing a curveball that he can throw in the zone early in the count. Kudrna has always been physical, but he focused over the offseason on getting his diet back on track so his weight wouldn’t fluctuate during the season and mess with his delivery. His command is around average as long as his delivery is in sync, and the Royals are working on moving him on the rubber to create more angle. Now that Kudrna is on the 40-man roster, anything can happen in terms of role, and some evaluators would like to see how his stuff ticks up in the bullpen. He needs more seasoning in the Minors, though, and that will have to wait until 2027 after he underwent an olecranon stress fracture repair on his elbow that ended his season in April.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Kansas City area native who went to Blue Valley Southwest (Kan.) High School, Kudrna won Kansas baseball Gatorade Player of the Year honors as a senior as his Draft stock climbed. He was a Louisiana State commit but decided to go pro when the Royals selected him No. 43 overall in the 2021 Draft and gave him an over-slot $3 million. He’s had a steady climb in the Minor Leagues, reaching Double-A in 2024, his third full season of pro ball. Kudrna threw 115 1/3 innings between two levels last year, with a 3.49 ERA at High-A (14 starts) before the jump to Double-A, where he got hit around a bit more and posted a 5.32 ERA in nine appearances (eight starts). Kudrna throws from a three-quarters arm slot and has always had solid strikeout and walk rates. His four-seam fastball sits at 92-95 mph, a few ticks down from his peak prep velocity, but he can flash in the upper 90s at times. He’s bigger and stronger than he was in high school, but there still might be a bit more in the tank. The pitch was more vulnerable to slug at Double-A in ‘24, likely a result of command. Kudrna’s best secondary pitch is his changeup, a plus to double-plus pitch that plays well off his fastball. He also features a mid-80s gyro slider with late bite, and consistency with the pitch was his biggest offseason focus. Kudrna introduced a two-seam fastball into his repertoire in 2024, a pitch that has the same velocity as his four-seam but with more run -- and something he’s very comfortable throwing. Kudrna’s delivery is good overall, although the Royals targeted his hip-shoulder separation as needing to be more consistent, and he focused on that this past offseason too. His physical frame makes him a durable and reliable rotation arm, projecting as a back-end starter, although his velocity might tick up more if he’s in the bullpen. He needs to adjust a little more to a higher level, so he’ll head back to Double-A this year with a chance for a Triple-A promotion later in the season depending on performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kudrna grew up in the Royals’ backyard, a Kansas City-area native pitching for Blue Valley Southwest HS. He won Kansas' Gatorade Player of the Year his senior year as his Draft stock climbed, and the Royals selected him No. 43 overall in the 2021 Draft, causing him to forgo his Louisiana State commitment. The Royals have not rushed Kudrna’s development, and he returned to Single-A Columbia to start 2023. Once he began dominating hitters there -- he posted a 3.56 ERA in 14 games -- he was promoted to High-A, where he had a 5.36 ERA in eight starts. Kudrna has a physical frame that continues to add strength as he matures. He threw hard in high school but has less zip now, with his fastball sitting at 93-94 mph and without a ton of swing-and-miss capability. Kudrna pounds the zone, though, and had a 22.2 percent strikeout rate and 9.6 percent walk rate between the two levels last year. His best secondary pitch is a sinking mid-80s changeup that flashes plus after focusing on it heavily when he got into pro ball. Kudrna also possesses a gyro slider with late bite. The right-hander looks the part of a starter with a physical frame that got stronger after the Draft. He seems durable and can be counted on for innings at the back of a rotation right now, but he could grow into a mid-rotation starter if he gets that swing-and-miss on his fastball back. His development will continue to take time, but he reached Double-A this summer as hoped.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals knew all about Kudrna given that he grew up in the Kansas City area, pitching for Blue Valley Southwest High School about 30 miles south of Kauffman Stadium. He broke out at the Area Code Games in August 2020 and his Draft stock continued to grow his senior season when he earned Gatorade state high school player of the year honors in Kansas. The Royals selected Kudrna No. 43 overall in ‘21 and lured him away from Louisiana State with a $3 million bonus. Both Kudrna and fellow top pick Frank Mozzicato were brought along slow to start their careers, not making their official debuts until May ‘22. Kudrna’s first season was promising, posting a 3.48 ERA in 17 starts for Single-A Columbia. Kudrna’s 6-foot-3 frame has added strength since he was drafted, and he’ll get stronger as he grows. He attacks hitters with a fastball that plays up in the zone and is generally 93-95 mph with the ability to get in the upper 90s if he’s fresh. The Royals tasked Kudrna to work on his mid-80s changeup coming into the 2022 season, and it ended up a better pitch than his slider because of how quickly he took to the grip and how much he threw it. With more deception, Kudrna’s changeup could be a plus pitch for him. He will have a similar goal of improving his late-biting slider now this season; the key will be to throw it with some power without losing its shape and vice versa. Kudrna’s three-quarters arm slot and quick arm makes hitters uncomfortable, and his delivery is clean and repeatable. With a durable arm and workhorse-type mentality, Kudrna projects as a mid-rotation starter. The Royals won’t rush his development given his age, but officials couldn’t be happier with what he showed in his first full season of pro ball. His focus will be on improving his slider as part of the rotation in High-A Quad Cities.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kudrna was more on the radar than Frank Mozzicato in the 2021 Draft class, but he seemed destined to attend Louisiana State University until he broke out at the Area Code Games in August 2020 -- and his Draft stock continued to grow his senior season. He threw a three-hit shutout to win the Kansas 5-A championship game for Blue Valley Southwest High School -- just outside of Kansas City -- and earned Gatorade state high school player of the year honors, leading the Royals to take the local product No. 43 overall and nearly double the slot value to sign him for $3 million. He made his unofficial debut in instructional league last fall. At 6-foot-3, Kudrna is an imposing presence on the mound, and he attacks hitters with a 95-97 mph heater. The Royals believe there’s more velocity in the tank as he grows into his broad-shouldered frame; he has already put on 25 pounds of muscle since arriving at their facility in Arizona. His three-quarters arm slot and quick arm creates some angle and movement with his fastball, which makes hitters uncomfortable, and he shows a good rhythm in his delivery. Kudrna has shown a sharp slider, but he’s still developing the pitch, learning how to finish it and throw it for strikes when behind in the count. He has also shown an advance feel for a changeup and began incorporating it more during instructs, with many believing it has a chance to be a plus pitch for him. Kudrna looks the part of a big league starter, and there’s still projection in his frame as well as a durable arm and a workhorse-type mentality. That gives him a high ceiling as a top- or mid-rotation starter, but much like Mozzicato, there’s no rush. Kudrna also should see a full-season assignment in 2022. A solid start at Single-A Columbia this summer has only helped his claim as the best pitching prospect in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going deep just five times in his first two seasons at Tulane, Hoese exploded for 23 homers (fourth in NCAA Division I) in 2019 and mashed his way into the first round of the Draft. He had a solid pro debut before spending 2020 at Los Angeles' alternate site and instructional league program, then endured a rough first full season last year. He tried to play through a left intercostal strain before missing nearly two months and batted just .188/.241/.245 with two homers in 59 Double-A games. When he's going good, Hoese displays an athletic right-handed swing and a disciplined approach while driving balls from gap to gap. But for much of 2021, his stroke looked longer and slower and he got too aggressive at the plate, which the Dodgers attribute to his injury and trying to dig himself out of a hole during a challenging assignment to Double-A. He continued to struggle in the Arizona Fall League, but he made some swing adjustments during the offseason that the club hopes can unlock a solid hitter with similar power. Though he moves well for a large man, Hoese is still a below-average runner and a fringy defender at third base. He has decent range and hands, while his arm strength fluctuates from fringy to solid. He'll need more consistency on both sides of the ball to profile as a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hoese didn't homer as a Tulane freshman in 2017 and went deep just five times as a Draft-eligible sophomore before ranking fourth in NCAA Division I with 23 homers in 2019. He set American Athletic Conference records for homers, total bases (183), slugging percentage (.779) and runs (72) while mashing his way into the first round and a $2,740,300 bonus. He batted .299/.380/483 while advancing to low Class A, then spent 2020 in alternative camp and instructional league. Hoese has an athletic right-handed swing, plenty of strength and does a nice job of using the leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame. He's a disciplined hitter who focuses on driving the ball from gap to gap, so he should hit for average as well as power. But he hasn't looked like his normal self in 2021 while battling an intercostal strain and struggling in Double-A. Hoese moves well for his size, though he's still a below-average runner. There's no reason he shouldn't be able to remain at third base, but he'll need to improve the consistency of his defense and his arm strength, which fluctuates from fringy to solid. If he had to move to first base, he still should provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player at the less demanding position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going homerless as a Tulane freshman in 2017 and going deep just five times as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2018, Hoese powered his way into the first round of the 2019 Draft by finishing fourth in NCAA Division I with 23 dingers. The American Athletic Conference player of the year, he set league records for homers, total bases (183), slugging percentage (.779) and runs (72). A year after he went in the 35th round to the Royals, he signed for $2,740,300 as the 25th overall choice and hit .299/.380/.483 in his pro debut while reaching Low-A. Hoese displayed a nice right-handed swing and the ability to use the leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame during his first two college seasons, and he began to realize his power potential once he added strength. He drives the ball from gap to gap and employs a disciplined approach. While his power is his most attractive tool, he should hit for average as well. Though he's a below-average runner, Hoese moves well for his size. He has solid arm strength and enough range to remain at third base, though he needs to improve his consistency on defense. If he had to move to first base, he should provide enough offense to profile as a regular there as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Venezuela but raised in British Columbia, Canada, Palmegiani was first selected by the Blue Jays in the 35th round of the 2018 Draft but chose to play at the College of Southern Nevada, where he improved his stock and was reselected by Toronto in the 14th round in ’21. After breaking out with 24 home runs in his first full pro season in ‘22, Palmegiani kept rolling in ‘23, hitting 23 home runs with an .842 OPS over 128 games between Double-A and Triple-A. This has landed Palmegiani on the doorstep of the big leagues, right in the middle of a crowded depth group. Palmegiani’s power is real, and looking at his frame, it’s not difficult to see why. After giving the 6-foot athlete time at third and first base, the Blue Jays are eager to try him more in left field. If that experiment goes well, it opens plenty more doors, but even on the infield corners, Palmegiani has a path to the big leagues. He’s taken strides at third defensively, playing a much more solid brand of defense than when he was drafted, but his ticket will always be the bat. Palmegiani has the potential to crush left-handed pitching, which showed in 2023 with a .949 OPS against lefties compared to an .806 mark against righties. That doesn’t point to him being a platoon player by any means, but as he tries to separate himself from Toronto’s upper-level infield depth, his ability to hit left-handed pitching could be the edge he needs. It’s easy to label Palmegiani as the ‘24 version of Davis Schneider -- a late-round pick who flies under the radar before bursting onto the scene -- and he could have the opportunity to play his way onto the roster this season. The same comment came back a half-dozen times with Palmegiani in camp this spring: “He’d be a fan favorite.”

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Venezuela but raised in British Columbia, Canada, Palmegiani was first selected by the Blue Jays in the 35th round of the 2018 Draft but chose to play at the College of Southern Nevada, where he improved his stock and was reselected by Toronto in the 14th round in ’21. He had committed to play at Arizona the next season, but the Blue Jays signed him away from that with a $157,500 bonus. Palmegiani made a productive debut over 17 games in the Florida Complex League in 2021, batting .333 with a pair of homers. His power really showed in 2022, though, as he split the season between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver over 118 games, hitting 24 home runs with an OPS of .815. A success story for a Blue Jays’ development staff who always liked his power, the organization believes he can unlock even more by improving his plate approach. Likely to stay splitting time between first and third base, he’s looked stronger on the right side of the diamond but has focused heavily on the hot corner. Entering the 2023 season at 23 years old, Palmegiani will be challenged by more advanced pitchers through the upper levels, but he has some of the best in-game power in the system. There’s a reason the Blue Jays stayed on him and drafted him twice, and if his approach and contact tools follow his power, there’s plenty of room left for him to climb.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Alfonzo signed with the Pirates in August 2019 for $150,000, he was following in the footsteps of his father, Eliezer, and his younger brother, Eliezer Jr., both of whom had -- and are having -- long professional careers. Omar didn’t make much noise until he reached full-season ball for the first time in 2023, then hit well across both levels of A ball in 2024. He garnered more attention by hitting his way to Double-A for the first time in 2025. Alfonzo checks off a box sought after by all teams as a left-handed-hitting catcher. He’s capable of hitting the ball extremely hard and is starting to figure out how to translate that into more power, setting a career high with his 14 homers a year ago. Most of the over-the-fence pop comes to his pull side, but he is able to drive the ball for extra bases to all fields. He can still add more loft to his swing and cut down on the groundball rate, and while he draws a ton of walks and generally makes good swing decisions, his strikeout rate did tick up a bit in 2025 (now 26 percent in his career). He can struggle against spin, especially out of the zone. Compact and strong, Alfonzo has worked on his conditioning and physicality, which should help him behind the plate. He’s improving defensively, with work still needing to be done on receiving at the bottom of the zone. He’s bilingual and works with pitchers well, and his arm has allowed him to throw out 29 percent of potential basestealers to date. Taking the next step maturity-wise, specifically not bringing bad at-bats with him behind the plate, could help him raise his profile even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of longtime professional catcher Eliezer Alfonzo and younger brother of Tigers Minor League backstop Eliezer Alfonzo Jr., Omar started following in the family business when the Pirates signed him in August 2019. His first two summers of pro ball -- the Dominican Summer League in 2021 and the Florida Complex League in ‘22 -- didn’t make anyone sit up and take notice, but that changed when he hit his way to full-season ball in 2023, then managed to perform well across two levels of A ball in '24. Alfonzo is a strong left-handed-hitting catcher who is starting to punish the ball more consistently as he physically and emotionally matures. He hits the ball very hard and could be just a little more consistent elevation away from being an impact-type hitter. He started tapping into his power to his pull side mostly in 2024, but Alfonzo is still hitting a lot of ground balls and low line drives, and some small adjustments should allow him to drive the ball to all fields. He’s always been willing to draw walks and work counts. Growing up around the game and the craft of catching, Alfonzo has a strong sense of what he’s doing behind the dish. He’s working to improve his throwing accuracy, but he has enough arm strength to have thrown out 30.7 percent of potential basestealers in his career heading into 2025. He works well with pitchers, is bilingual and is a solid overall receiver. If he starts lofting the ball at the plate more, he could take off as a catching prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eliézer Alfonzo caught professionally for 15 years, at least touching the big leagues in six of them with the Giants, Padres, Mariners and Rockies. Now, it’s his son Omar’s turn. The younger Alfonzo was signed by the Pirates in August 2019 for $150,000. He wasn’t able to make his pro debut until 2021, but he immediately showed off his approach at the plate in the Dominican Summer League. After struggling in the Florida Complex League, he took a nice step forward, getting bumped up quickly from the FCL to full-season Bradenton. A left-handed-hitting catcher with a big frame, Alfonzo has the chance to have some serious impact offensively. He’s shown a willingness to work counts and draw walks from the outset of his career, carrying a .380 on-base percentage into the 2024 season. He recognizes spin well and doesn’t chase much. It’s a hit-over-power profile, kind of like his dad, but there is some strength he can learn to tap into. Behind the plate, Alfonzo can be a solid average defender. He receives well with decent hands, has a strong enough arm that has done a good job of controlling the running game and he handles a pitching staff very well -- thanks in part to him being bilingual and having grown up around the game. He’s also shown some versatility in playing first base. It might be a backup profile, but if he can unlock more offensive impact, he could develop into a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has been a bit of a pattern with Rockies young international hitters over the last few years, having early success at the lower levels, then struggling as they move up the ladder. There was hope that Calaz, who signed for $1.7 million in January 2023 and posted a 1.113 OPS across the rookie-level Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex Leagues in 2023 and 2024, would disrupt that trend, especially after he hit well in first taste of full-season ball at the end of the ‘24 season. But a return to Single-A Fresno in 2025 netted rougher results due to a lack of an approach and too much swing-and-miss. Just 20 for all of the 2026 season, there’s still plenty of time for Calaz to figure things out at the plate. He’s a strong, right-handed hitter with a ton of raw power, but he needs to figure out a gameplan to stick with in order to get to it. He likes to attack pitches early in the count and showed he could still do damage if he got a pitch to hit in the first two or three offerings, but if he chased early and fell behind, he was done. He needs to learn he can have impact in all counts and cut down his chase because when he does connect, he still registers elite-level exit velocities. While Calaz saw considerable time in center field at the outset of his career, he’s starting to slow down as he fills out his frame. He’s working on his conditioning and nutrition, but it’s looking like right field, where he saw a lot of time in 2025, is the best spot for him long-term. He has the power potential to profile there if he can find a bit more discipline at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies have had their fair share of young prospects signed from the international market who make a big first impression at the lower levels of the system and then hit a bit of a stumbling block as they reach higher levels. So they’ve been trying to talk in more hushed tones about Calaz, who they signed for $1.7 million at the start of the 2023 signing period. But they’re having a hard time containing their enthusiasm after he posted a .984 OPS during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, then hit his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season Fresno and finished with a combined .344/.446/.633 line last year. That doesn’t mean Calaz -- who will play all of the 2025 season at age 19 -- is a finished product. Far from it, and what amazed the Rockies is that he managed to win the ACL Triple Crown without really having an idea of what he’s doing at the plate yet. Already strong and physical, Calaz hits the ball about as hard as anyone in the system, posting elite-level exit velocities, with tremendous raw power he’s still learning to tap into. He draws walks but still needs to tone down his swing tendencies as he is susceptible to breaking stuff away and out of the zone in particular. The Rockies feel like Calaz is starting to show the makings of being a five-tool player and he’ll continue to get reps in center field. Most feel that his 6-foot-2 frame will continue to fill out and he’ll slow down more, necessitating a full-time move to right field, where his power production should profile perfectly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Professional debuts in the Dominican Summer League following signing as an international free agent have to be taken with a grain of salt because the DSL tends to be very hitter-friendly. But it’s hard not to get excited about the tools Calaz used after signing with the Rockies for $1.7 million at the start of the 2023 signing period. The teenager put up a .325/.423/.561 line to whet everyone's appetite for his United States debut in 2024. While many young players from the international market scream projection but lack present strength, Calaz is already very physical. The power was showing up a little bit during his debut, but that's just scratching the surface of unlocking his right-handed raw pop. He's developed the beginnings of a pretty good approach with a feel to hit, too, allaying some early concerns about his abilities to find the barrel consistently. Calaz is still learning his body and how to use it efficiently, but he's an above-average runner and has the chance to stay in center field. A move to a corner could happen in the future if he slows down, but for now, the Rockies are mostly working with him on slowing the game down and helping him to learn about routines and preparations to maximize his very loud tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peete was a two-way standout as a Georgia prepster but focused on hitting in his senior spring, when he showed as much bat speed as any other high-schooler in the country. The Mariners selected him 30th overall and signed him for $2.5 million. Peete showed tantalizing tools at Single-A (2024) and High-A (2025) in his two seasons in the Seattle system but struck out more than 30 percent of the time at both spots. Despite a career-high 19 homers with Everett last year, he registered just a 79 wRC+ in the Northwest League. The M’s traded him to the Cardinals as part of the prospect return in the Brendan Donovan trade. Several components make Peete a high-ceiling prospect and an interesting rebound candidate for the rebuilding Redbirds. He’s built like a wide receiver with a slender 6-foot-2 frame and packs a punch as well with plus raw power. He retains his plus arm strength from his pitching days, and after beginning his career on the dirt, he moved to center field in 2025 to strong reviews because his plus speed helps him gallop gap to gap to chase down balls. But so much comes down to Peete’s ability to make contact. Opposing pitchers have eaten him alive with non-fastballs. His left-handed swing can look pretty, but he’ll yank over the top of inside breakers and swing over changeups on the outer half with little hope for contact. Recognizing offspeed earlier out of the hand could certainly help, and to Peete’s credit, he did a better job of lifting and pulling when he did put bat on ball last year. It isn’t a hit tool that can be fixed overnight, but in its talent acquisition and development phase, St. Louis can take its time getting Peete to hit just enough for an everyday role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners took high school hitters in the first round for three Drafts in a row, ending with Colt Emerson in 2023. They also took three straight prep bats that year, following Emerson with Jonny Farmelo and then Peete, all taken in the Top 30 picks. Peete signed for a little under slot, $2.5 million, and the former Georgia two-way standout split his brief pro debut between the Arizona Complex League and full-season Modesto as he focused on hitting only. He spent his first full season back with Modesto and showed flashes of the tools that made him a top prospect, but also inconsistencies that need to be addressed. He still didn’t quite click offensively at High-A in 2025 and was traded to the Cardinals in the offseason as part of a three-team deal for Brendan Donovan. A premium athlete with a wide receiver's 6-foot-2 frame, Peete has a left-handed swing geared to do damage at the plate. He has immense raw power and showed flashes of it in 2024, with an approach that could let him crush balls to all fields. But he just as easily can get out of that approach when he tries to sell out for power, and while he does draw some walks, the 30.7 percent strikeout rate he registered in 2024 and 30.6 percent mark in ’25 aren’t going to work as he moves up the ladder. He doesn't have great rhythm and feel at the plate and could be an ambush power-over-hit type of offensive player. Peete uses his speed well on the basepaths, and he stole 70 bags over his first two full seasons in pro ball. He's seen time at shortstop, third base and in the outfield, and he might fit best long term in center, where he saw the bulk of his duties in the summer before his move to St. Louis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Touted as arguably the most athletic prep position player in the 2023 Draft, the Mariners were extremely bullish on Peete's potential, to the point where they took him in Competitive Balance Round A at No. 30 overall and signed him for $2.5 million, earmarking him to be a huge part of their offensive future along with many of his peers taken in that year's class. A two-way player in high school in Georgia, Peete dialed his velocity up to 95 mph off the mound but will transition exclusively to the hitting side in the pros. With a 6-foot-2, 193-pound frame, Peete has the look of a small forward or wide receiver and probably could've pursued a path in either sport. He has an electric left-handed swing that taps into tape-measure power, evidenced by grand slams in consecutive innings at Low-A Modesto last August, which were also the first two homers of his pro career. He also runs extremely well and has decent range, which keeps his options open at shortstop, third base and center field and makes him a potential premium player should he fully realize his potential. The knock on Peete in his incredibly early stages is that he can be susceptible to peaks and valleys at the plate. He rarely uses the opposite field and can get out of a solid approach when trying to pull balls. Those moments make him an easy target for quality pitchers, which he'll need to improve upon to continue climbing up the system. But the tools are all there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bratt went from suburban Toronto to Georgia Premier Academy -- the same path taken by Mets right-hander Jonah Tong -- for his senior year and added more experience in the MLB Draft League. The Rangers selected him in the fifth round in 2021. The left-hander earned an early spot on Canada’s 2023 World Baseball Classic team at just 19 and continued to build from there, reaching Double-A a year later. He spent all of 2025 in the Texas League with Frisco and Amarillo, having been traded from the Rangers to the D-backs in the Merrill Kelly Deadline deal. His 29.3 percent strikeout rate and 25.1 K-BB percentage were tops among Double-A qualifiers. The 6-foot-1 left-hander has one major piece working for him: he commands everything extremely well around the zone. His 90-93 mph fastball comes with subpar velocity, but he can place it repeatedly above bats right at the top rail. He can play off that with a low-80s slider that moves below the lower third of the zone and to his glove side, and in recent years, he’s made better use of an upper-80s cutter that, with limited horizontal movement, he can command even better than the heat. His upper-70s curveball and mid-80s changeup have been less effective but at least provide other movement looks. As he honed that command, Bratt posted the lowest walk rate of his career in the Texas League at just 4.2 percent. He also gave up 1.3 home runs per nine innings because the lack of velo and special movement make him hittable when he doesn’t get to his precise spots. The D-backs added Bratt to the 40-man as Rule 5 protection this offseason, making him a current and future piece of Arizona’s starting depth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When pandemic restrictions made it tough to scout Canadian prepsters in 2021, Bratt left suburban Toronto to pitch his senior season as the Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.). After he performed well there and against older hitters in the inaugural season of the MLB Draft League, he signed for a well-over-slot $850,000 as a fifth-rounder. The youngest player (age 19) on Canada’s 2023 World Baseball Classic team, he reached Double-A shortly after turning 21 last summer. He returned to Frisco for 2025 and put up big strikeout numbers before being dealt to the D-backs at the Trade Deadline in the deal for Merrill Kelly. Bratt hasn’t added as much velocity as hoped since turning pro, but his low-90s fastball that tops out at 95 is still effective because it rides well up in the zone and he can command it where he wants. He plays off the heater with a low-80s slider with nice depth, a mid-80s cutter, an upper-70s curveball and a mid-80s changeup. The slide piece shows the most promise, and mixing in the cutter gives him a bridge pitch to work off that. Bratt’s athletic delivery features little effort and allows him to provide constant strikes. He can move his pitches around the zone and can read hitters’ swings to determine how to get them out. His craftiness and mound presence stand out more than his pure stuff, giving him a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because pandemic restrictions made it difficult to scout Canadian high school prospects, Bratt left suburban Toronto and spent his senior season at the Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.). He pitched well there and against older competition in the inaugural season of the MLB Draft League, earning a well-over-slot $850,000 bonus in the fifth round in 2021. He was the youngest regular starter in the Single-A Carolina and High-A South Atlantic Leagues the past two seasons, as well as the youngest player (age 19) on Canada's 2023 World Baseball Classic team. Though his fastball sits in the low-90s and reaches 95 mph, it worked well against Class A hitters because it has carry and he can spot it where he wants. He added a 78-82 mph sweeper during instructional league in 2022 and it became his primary breaking ball last summer, when he pretty much scrapped his soft mid-70s curveball. His low-80s changeup features depth as well and gives him a third average offering. Bratt's advanced feel for pitching, intelligence and mound presence stand out more than his arsenal. He pounds the strike zone with a low-effort delivery and has a knack for reading hitters' swings and figuring out how to get outs. He has a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation piece but he has to prove that his stuff will play against higher-level hitters and that he can handle a full season's workload after missing six weeks last summer with a lat strain.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pandemic restrictions made it hard to scout Canadian prep prospects in 2021, so Bratt moved from suburban Toronto and spent his senior season at the Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.). After he pitched well there and against older hitters in the inaugural MLB Draft League, the Rangers signed him for a well-over-slot $850,000 in the fifth round. Only two other pitchers worked as many innings (80 2/3) with a lower ERA (2.45) in the Carolina League last year, and he was the youngest regular starter in the Single-A circuit. Bratt enjoys a lot of success pitching off of a low-90s fastball that reached 95 mph and plays better than its velocity thanks to its carry up in the zone and his ability to command it. All of his stuff grades as average at the moment, with some debate as to whether his mid-70s curveball or his low-80s changeup, both of which feature depth, is his best secondary pitch. He made encouraging progress with a low-80s slider he added during the instructional league last offseason. Bratt's delivery has little effort and he repeats it well, throwing strikes with all four of his offerings. He's cerebral and extremely advanced for his age, but he gets outs with his fastball at the expense of using the rest of his arsenal, and he'll need to employ those offerings more often to refine them. With his projectable stuff, feel for pitching and mound presence, he has the look of a future No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With pandemic restrictions making it difficult to scout Canadian high school prospects in 2021, Bratt headed south to spend his senior season at the Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.). He impressed there and against older competition in the inaugural MLB Draft League, prompting the Rangers to draft him in the fifth round and sign him for a well over-slot $850,000. He posted a 0.00 ERA with 13 strikeouts in six innings in Rookie ball, then continued to stand out during instructional league. Bratt aggressively challenged hitters with an 88-90 mph fastball that topped out at 94 as an amateur, with his four-seamer playing better than its velocity because it has good carry at the top of the zone and he commands it well. He's already starting to add strength and worked at 90-95 mph during instructs. He has aptitude for spinning a mid-70s curveball that should become a solid or plus pitch once he adds more power, and he also has feel for a low-80s changeup with depth that can get a bit firm at times. Bratt repeats an efficient delivery that features little effort and throws strikes with his entire arsenal. He's more advanced than a typical high school pitcher and stands out with his presence on the mound. He has the projectable stuff, control and moxie to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A junior-college transfer, Melendez joined Texas for the 2021 season and showed good power with 13 homers but only went in the 16th round to the Marlins that summer. After not signing, he put together one of the most powerful college seasons in recent memory with 32 homers (most in NCAA since BBCOR bat restrictions were adopted in 2011) and led Division I in total bases and slugging percentage on his way to winning the Golden Spikes Award. The D-backs took Melendez in the second round in 2022, and while some questions remain about the entire profile, he lived up to his reputation with 30 homers over just 96 games between High-A and Double-A in his first full season before finishing up with a stint in the Arizona Fall League. The right-handed slugger has the natural strength for at least double-plus raw power, so much so that coaches have advised him he just needs to “tap the ball” to send it screaming around the ballpark. To wit, he topped out with a 115.5 mph exit velocity in the AFL; only Ketel Marte (117.1) had a higher EV among D-backs Major Leaguers in ’23. Melendez has an uphill swing that creates the loft needed for his high homer total, but that also creates major contact concerns. He had whiff and chase rates above 30 percent on every pitch type he saw at Double-A, including fastballs. Melendez was primarily a first baseman at Texas, but the D-backs have held out hope for him at third base in the pros. He still needs a lot of work there due to below-average speed and range, and he still might be best at the cold corner or even DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Melendez translated two impressive seasons at Odessa (Texas) Junior College into a move to Texas in 2021, but even though he led the Longhorns with 13 homers that spring, he still dropped to the Marlins in the 16th round. He used his status as a fourth-year junior and won the Golden Spikes Award, leading Division I in homers (32, most in NCAA since BBCOR bat restrictions were adopted in 2011), total bases (214), slugging (.863) while managing a 51/52 K/BB ratio over 67 games. The D-backs selected him in the second round, signed him for below slot at $1.4 million and sent him for a 25-game spell at Single-A Visalia, where he tripped up some after a long spring and summer. Melendez’s uphill right-handed swing is designed to drive the ball to all fields and let his natural strength do the rest. Adding to Melendez’s offensive promise is the way he improved his plate discipline in his final spring in Austin, and while the other numbers weren’t there, he still managed just an 18.9 percent K rate in his first taste of a full-season level. Concerns about bat speed may blunt his performance and make him an average overall hitter in the end. A below-average runner, Melendez primarily played first base at Texas but got some looks at third in pro ball. While he can make plays on balls hit/thrown to him, his range is limited and should keep him at first base long-term. After the hiccup in the California League, Melendez will have to show his bat can carry a 1B/DH profile, but he has a recent history of proving himself at the right time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knowing how difficult it can be to acquire prospects once they’ve put themselves on the radar, the Rays have no reservations about pushing to land them a year early rather than waiting for a breakout. That was the mentality with Johnson, whom they picked up alongside Santiago Suarez in a November 2022 trade with the Marlins for Xavier Edwards and JT Chargois. Johnson was a reliever at Duke in 2021, didn’t pitch well as a starter during his final season with the Blue Devils, went to Miami in the fourth round of the ’22 Draft and had a mostly forgettable professional debut. But in Johnson, the Rays saw a big, physical strike-thrower with the command to potentially be a big league starter. The 6-foot-6 right-hander mostly delivered on that promise in his full-season debut last year, posting a 3.74 ERA while walking only 3.9 percent of the hitters he faced for Single-A Charleston, a level where he was expected to succeed as a polished college pitcher. He has three average-or-better pitches, puts them all where he wants them with pinpoint control, knows what he’s trying to do and works quickly. His 82-85 mph slider is his best pitch, while his fastball has sat between 90-94 mph (with a tendency to flatten out when it’s on the lower end of that scale) and his changeup clocks in around the mid-80s. Johnson handled a starter’s workload last season, knocking down 130 innings over 26 outings. But there was some concern when he lost weight as the season went on, making his tall frame look even more wiry. He put on 10-15 pounds of muscle over the offseason, which enhanced the velocity (and carry) on his fastball at the outset of the spring; if that holds up, Johnson could take another step toward his potential as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After serving as the top reliever at Duke in 2021, Johnson only spent one season in the Blue Devils’ rotation and didn’t perform well during his platform season, going 1-8 with a 5.61 ERA in 13 outings. But scouts were still intrigued by his size, physicality and starter traits, so the Marlins picked him in the fourth round of the ’22 Draft and signed him for $507,500. Although he posted mediocre-at-best results in his brief organizational debut for Miami, the Rays were pleased to land Johnson alongside righty Santiago Suarez in November 2022 as part of a trade for Xavier Edwards and JT Chargois. The lanky, 6-foot-6 righty has a three-pitch arsenal headlined by a high-spin slider that sits between 82-85 mph with two-plane depth. He’s also implemented a mid-80s changeup more often since moving into the rotation. The real question is about Johnson’s fastball, which sat between 90-94 mph last spring, down from his days as a reliever. It has some arm-side run and carry, but the pitch flattens out and can be barreled up when he’s not locating it well at the top of the strike zone. Johnson still has plenty of room to add strength to his tall frame, and he’s athletic enough to keep his long limbs in sync and repeat his clean delivery. He has a lot of traits that Tampa Bay likes -- specifically his size, stamina, strike-throwing and ability to spin the baseball -- so they can look past his stats and dream on what he’s occasionally shown he can be, like when he struck out 10 over five innings in his final start last season. He's been one of the Minors' best strike-throwers in 2023, and that ability to fill the zone helps those Tampa Bay dreams.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Conley was initially slated to head to Miami for college, but he decided to transfer to Texas Tech, sitting out the 2019 season as a result of the NCAA’s transfer rules. He made a strong first impression with the Red Raiders with an OPS over 1.000 in the shortened 2020 season, then backed it up by slashing .329/.393/.587 in 2021, enough to land him in the fourth round of that summer’s Draft. After a very slow start with Single-A Augusta to kick off his first full season of pro ball in 2022, Conley played his way to High-A and performed well in the Arizona Fall League. The son of former Minor Leaguer Brian Conley, Cal is the kind of player who is better than the sum of his parts. A switch-hitter, Conley has displayed a knack for contact, particularly from the left side of the plate. While the undersized infielder is a hit-over-power, gap-to-gap, use-all-fields type, there’s more extra-base pop than you might think, with the 16 homers he hit in 2022 not an aberration at all. While he’s not a burner, Conley does have solid speed and he maximizes it with excellent instincts and aggressiveness on the basepaths, not to mention a “gamer” mentality that has his engine going full throttle at all times. Those instincts help him play a capable shortstop, the spot he’s seen the most time at thus far, but some see a move to second base in his future, where he might have the best chance at being a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Brian Conley was a Minor League player for the Cubs and Reds in the 1990s and went on to coach in the Cincinnati organization. His son Cal starred at Texas Tech after transferring from Miami, and an uptick in power (15 homers) in 2021 helped land the steady middle infielder in the fourth round of last summer’s Draft, signing for $422,500 and making his pro debut with Low-A Augusta. Conley is a switch-hitter who has very good bat-to-ball skills, though the contact rate is better from the left side and right side features a bit more swing-and-miss. He is hit-over-power, though his added strength did translate into more pop in his last year at Texas Tech and he showed that it translates with a wood bat in his hands during his first full season with the Braves. With above-average speed and very good instincts, Conley is capable of playing a solid shortstop, though his arm might be a bit short for him to be an everyday player at the premium spot. He’s mostly played short as a pro, though he’s gotten times on the right side of second base, and second is the more likely spot where he could develop into a big league regular, with a more likely outcome of being a heady utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fischer was constantly on the move in college, picking up notable slugging benchmarks along the way. He set the Duke freshman record with 11 homers in 2023, led Mississippi with 20 homers in 2024 and finished third in all of Division I with 25 homers for Tennessee in 2025, just in time for his Draft year. The lefty slugger went to the Brewers with the 20th overall pick, signing for below slot at $3.5 million, and there were some in the Milwaukee Draft room that believed him to be the best college hitter in his class. Fischer wrapped up ’25 with 19 games with High-A Wisconsin, hitting .311/.402/.446 in that span. Fischer’s calling card is going to be his power as he consistently gets to hard-hit contact with good bat speed, strength and lift in his swing. His ability to launch the ball carried over into pro ball quickly, and he could be a 25-homer threat with that optimization. Fischer’s approach took a nice jump during his time as a Volunteer. He became the Tennessee batter other teams had to plan around, and he proved less willing to chase bad pitches than he was at his previous stops, leading to 63 walks (tied for the most in a single season in program history). He’ll be a bit more challenged on breaking stuff against pro arms, but it’s a promising trendline. Fischer, who also saw time in left field as a collegian, played primarily first base in Knoxville, but the Brewers already intend to give him a chance to stick at the opposite corner. His above-average arm will work there, but his range is a better fit for the cold corner. It’s going to come down to the bat regardless, and Fischer has the offensive makings of a potential quick mover in a strong-development organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 118 Draft prospect in 2019, Mears showed off some late-blooming loud tools that helped him surge into the second round to the Padres that summer. After finally getting to move up to full-season ball in 2021 due to the lost pandemic season, he’s logged over 50-plus games at both Single-A and High-A, while striking out at least 39.2 percent of the time at both spots. His 14 homers and 121 wRC+ in 52 games at Fort Wayne last summer pushed him to Double-A, where he was young at 21, and it showed with a mind-numbing 47.9 percent K rate. When Mears does make contact, it’s incredibly loud with exit velocities routinely above 110 mph, and perhaps it came as no surprise that he finished 2022 with nearly as many homers (22) as singles (28). But unless a pitch is in his sweet spot in the zone, Mears fans far too often with a 43.9 percent K rate and 21.6 percent swinging-strike rate that ranked first and eighth among the 1,031 Minor Leaguers with at least 300 plate appearances in 2022. The Padres have worked with Mears on altering his swing to find any way to more contact, including a midseason trip back to Arizona last year, but nothing has caught yet. To his credit, Mears’ profile isn’t all wrapped up in his pop. He has more speed than many think, earning above-average runtimes from some scouts, and he can play a capable center field, where he made all 24 of his Double-A defensive starts. But perhaps more than anyone else in Minor League Baseball, he needs to increase his contact rates by at least 10 points to have any chance of meeting his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mears was a relatively unknown high school player from the Pacific Northwest until a late breakout landed him in San Diego with the 48th overall pick in the 2019 Draft.
