De Los Santos, ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list at the time, led the class with his $1.2 million bonus. He then went out and had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League to whet the Pirates’ appetite. A strong and physical infielder, De Los Santos has the chance to be an impact hitter from the right side of the plate. His surface numbers in the DSL don’t jump off the page, but the metrics underneath, things like his exit velocity, did stand out. He has a good idea of what he’s doing at the plate, especially for someone his age, drawing walks and limiting strikeouts. There’s bat speed and strength to come, which could mean plenty of power. Right now, De Los Santos is rangy and athletic, and the Pirates saw improvement in his defense last year. He’ll be given a chance to play shortstop for as long as he shows he can handle it, though there’s some reason to believe he’s going to fill out and slow down, which could necessitate a move to third, a spot he saw some time at during his pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Florida prep prospect who had Draft interest as both a hitter and pitcher, Petry headed to South Carolina as a full-time position player, and that proved quickly to be the right decision when he set the Gamecocks freshman record with 23 homers in 2023. He clubbed 21 more homers in 2024 and followed that up as the Cape Cod League MVP and Top Prospect that summer after producing 11 long balls and a league-best 1.240 OPS. A sprained left shoulder limited him to 44 games as a junior, including only one after April 27, but he still went to the Nationals in the second round and signed for $2.09 million. Petry made up for the lost time with stints at Single-A Fredericksburg and as the rare 2025 Draft pick in the Arizona Fall League. Despite slugging only .298 in the desert, Petry gave a taste of his plus-plus raw power in the AFL with his 114.8 mph max exit velocity, and he proved he had moved beyond the shoulder issue by regularly recording bat speed measurements above 75 mph. That comes from the massive strength in his 6-foot-4 frame. That said, the concerns about his collegiate chase rates didn’t go away in either of his two stops on the pro side, and the uphill and long nature of his swing could be a problem against elevated fastballs the higher he climbs. Petry has well-below-average speed and won’t be counted on to push the envelope on the basepaths. That said, the Nationals still plan to run him out to the corner outfield spots, knowing his above-average arm strength could play there, while getting him work at first base. Most evaluators expect him to land full-time at the cold corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chance Sanford was a late-round Draft pick of the Pirates in the early 1990s who played in parts of two big league seasons with the Buccos and the Dodgers. His son, Wyatt, beat his Draft status by 25 rounds when the Pirates went back to the Sanford well in the second round of the 2024 Draft. The Texas high schooler received an over-slot bonus of $2.5 million to forego his commitment to Texas A&M and he showed signs of a solid all-around game, playing his way from the Rookie-level Florida Complex League to Single-A Bradenton before a groin injury ended his season at the beginning of August. While Sanford entered pro ball with strong tools across the board, the Pirates kept him back in the complex longer so he could work on recognizing spin. There’s still work to be done there as he registered 38 percent miss and 32 percent chase rates on breaking stuff once he got to full-season ball last year. He made strides in understanding how to stay on time for the fastball and give himself enough time to adjust to breaking balls, giving confidence that will keep improving as he gets more reps. He’ll always be a hit-over-power type but there is impact to come, at least in the form of gap-to-gap extra-base pop. A plus runner who finished fourth in the organization with 34 steals last year, Sanford likes to wreak havoc on the basepaths. The Pirates feel he has a very good chance to stick at shortstop with excellent actions, good range and an above-average arm. Everything plays up because of those strong instincts and grinder mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were four Texas high schoolers taken in the top three rounds of the 2024 Draft, with outfielder Braylon Payne and shortstop Theo Gillen going in the first round, left-hander Dasan Hill being taken in Competitive Balance Round B and Sanford coming off the board between them in Round 2. The son of former big leaguer Chance, Wyatt went to one of his dad’s teams, the Pirates, receiving an over-slot bonus of $2.5 million to begin his pro career. He didn’t get into an official game after signing, but did play in instructs. The Pirates have already worked with Sanford on his setup at the plate, as the left-handed hitter had spread out with his legs too far during his senior year of high school, putting too much pressure on himself to make contact, while also trying to pull the ball more at times. He does have good bat-to-ball skills and still made a good amount of contact, but the focus is now on closing the spread, loading on his back hip and being on time for the fastball, which should also help him unlock some of his power. He’s also a plus runner who knows how to use that speed on the basepaths. There are no questions about Sanford’s defensive ability. He was thought to be one of the best shortstops with the glove among prepsters in the 2024 class and he immediately showed why, with rangy and smooth actions to go along with plenty of arm and outstanding instincts. If the bat comes along, he has every chance to be a starting shortstop in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 60 | Run: 30 | Arm: 40 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Burke had an accomplished career at Tennessee that included tying the program's freshman record with 14 homers in 2022 and winning SEC Tournament MVP honors and a national title as a junior in 2024. He slugged .702 with 20 homers in 72 games that spring, and that power led the Brewers to take him 34th overall and sign him for $2.1 million. The first baseman hit .292/.379/.453 with 16 homers in 132 games between High-A and Double-A in his first full season, and his 139 wRC+ was tops among Brewers full-season qualifiers. It was a fascinating 2025 campaign for Burke because he took off following his move to Biloxi, where he clubbed 11 homers in 37 games. His power has long been evident dating back to his time in Knoxville, but the jump to producing it in pro games coincided with him elevating much more on contact with his ground-ball rate dropping an even 10 points between High-A and Double-A. The lefty slugger stands tall in the box and doesn’t need a big load to unleash big hacks, relying on his upper-body strength. He was more swing-happy in Biloxi than in Wisconsin, putting him back at the level of his time in Tennessee, and even if it leads to some chase and whiffs, he might be best at his most aggressive. A below-average runner, Burke will be limited to first-base duty when he is in the field. He can hold down the position fairly enough with decent scoops and movement to and from the bag, but few evaluators or analysts expect him to be a true asset there. Burke needs to hit rockets, and after a brief pause, he’s back to trending toward doing just that at the MLB level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burke got his Tennessee career off to an astounding start by tying a school freshman record with 14 homers in only 95 at-bats in 2022. His performance dipped as a sophomore a year later, but he was back to his slug-heavy dominant ways as a junior last year, slashing .379/.449/.702 with 20 homers and 30 doubles (most in Division I) in 72 games. He also picked up another school record with a 31-game hitting streak, won SEC Tournament MVP and led the Volunteers to their first national title. The Brewers took Burke 34th overall in July and signed him for slightly below slot at $2.1 million before sending him out to High-A Wisconsin for five games. The left-handed slugger has plenty of bat speed and strength that help him generate high exit velocities. It’s plus-plus raw power, and he got to more of it over his time in college because he was less pull-prone and more willing to send the ball screaming all over the yard. He’ll still get swing-happy, however; he ran a 35 percent chase rate in his final season with the Vols and was willing to expand the zone on a variety of pitch types. The hard contact should help keep his average afloat, but better pro pitching will take advantage of that approach. Burke is a well-below-average runner, and he lacks even average arm strength. That should keep him at first base, where the bar for power production only goes up. Milwaukee has other first-base options in the system too between Mike Boeve, Tyler Black, Luke Adams and Eric Bitonti, so Burke may have to keep proving himself at every stop to rise in that crowd.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Keys in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft and signed him for right around slot value at $569,700, targeting the offensive upside they saw in his bat. Keys put up an .829 OPS and drove in 20 runs over 22 games at Single-A in his brief pro debut, and in his first full season in 2025, hit .217 with 19 home runs and a .773 OPS over 119 games in High-A Vancouver. His metrics were stronger than the numbers, though, and with climbing exit velocity, the club feels that Keys is still digging into that impressive power potential. Keys’ power comes easy. An analytics darling coming out of the Draft, he is big and barrel-chested, producing pop without needing a max-effort swing. Whether Keys’ raw power shows up in games consistently will be a deciding factor on his long-term ceiling, but either way, his profile is heavily tied to his bat. This system is lush with position player prospects easily defined as “solid across the board,” so Keys is a rare case of a profile leaning heavily on the slug. Defensively, his glove at third base is still a work in progress, but the Blue Jays are confident it can be solid, even if it’s not flashy. First base remains an option for Keys, but the goal here will be to get his defense up to a level that’s at least solid. The club is betting heavily on Keys’ bat carrying him up the ladder, though, and being enough to overshadow those other parts of his game. Now that Keys has adjusted to the grind of a full pro season, his adjustments will be key. If his power takes the next step and Keys launches 25-plus homers, he’ll keep his prospect buzz alive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bucknell University in Pennsylvania has had just one player get drafted and reach the big leagues -- right-hander Eric Junge, a 1999 pick -- and just three players get taken in the top 10 rounds in school history, now including Keys. Coming off a fantastic showing in the Cape Cod League, which the Blue Jays have always valued highly, they selected Keys in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft and signed him for right around slot value at $569,700. Keys put up an .829 OPS and drove in 20 runs over 22 games at Single-A in his brief pro debut. Keys has easy power. An analytics darling coming out of the Draft, he is big and barrel-chested, producing pop without needing a max-effort swing. In the same vein of past development projects like Spencer Horwitz and Alan Roden, Keys has an excellent approach at the plate and could keep a walk total close to his strikeouts. Whether Keys’ raw power shows up in games consistently will be a deciding factor on his long-term ceiling, but either way, his profile is heavily tied to his bat. Defensively, his glove at third base is still a work in progress. First base remains an option for Keys, but the goal here will be to get his defense up to a level that’s at least solid. The Blue Jays are betting heavily on Keys’ bat carrying him up the ladder, though, and being enough to overshadow those other parts of his game. In his first full season, he's gone from a high-contact hitter in college to a loud-contact hitter in the pros, and marrying the two concepts would go a long way as he reaches for the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a year at Chipola Junior College, Baker moved to Auburn and threw just six relief innings in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season before going back to Chipola in 2021. The Phillies liked his arm strength enough to go over slot to sign him for $200,000 in the 11th round of that summer’s Draft. The reliever has moved quickly since, pitching his way to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball. Baker has always had premium stuff that could be very effective in the back end of a bullpen with a two-pitch mix that could get big league hitters out now. His fastball touched 102 mph last year and averaged 98.5 mph and he couples it with a power breaking ball that hovers in the mid-80s. It’s a hard downer curveball, though some of the metrics read it as a slider, and it’s a true out pitch, one that elicited a 60 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2022. He’s fiddled with a cutter as well to give hitters a different look, but that’s a work in progress. The only thing that has held Baker back at all, both as an amateur and early on in his pro career, has been his command. But while he did walk 4.8 per nine overall in 2022, something clicked for him after a couple of months and he walked just 2.56 per nine from July 1 until the end of the year. If that trend continues, he has the chance to close games in the big leagues one day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Queens native, Sime was a source of constant intrigue on the summer showcase circuit for his elite velocity, and he started to show a little more polish during his senior year at Brooklyn’s Poly Prep Country Day School, including in two outings at USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational. He made three appearances in the MLB Draft League (including one at Citi Field in an All-Star matchup against the Cape Cod League) to round out his résumé, and the Nationals selected him in the fourth round last July. The LSU commit signed for $2 million, almost triple the slot value for the 111th overall pick. The 6-foot-4 right-hander first touched triple digits when he was 16 years old, and he’s continued to pump premium heat since then, eclipsing 100 mph five times during his stint in the Draft League. Sime has good life on the four-seamer too, and he was able to blow it by batters in multiple settings. His low-80s curveball shows off his feel for spin with nice drop and a little sweep, and in his first spring, he’s toying with a gyro slider that would give him a harder breaking ball on top of that. His 85-88 mph changeup can fool batters with its velo differential and armside movement, but it’s likely to be his third pitch at best. Sime can have a long arm action, and he struggled as an amateur at times to land his stuff consistently in the zone. Professional batters will be more willing to lay off his power arsenal if he can’t throw more strikes, so there’s real reliever risk here even for someone who will still only be 18 on Opening Day 2026. Sime should be an interesting project for the Nationals’ new player development apparatus in its first year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: By getting a $700,000 bonus to sign out of Venezuela, Sarmiento received the third-largest bonus of the Mets' Jan. 15, 2021 class, trailing only Simon Juan ($1.9 million) and Willy Fañas ($1.5 million). He moved straight to the Dominican Summer League and proved to be one of the Mets’ most exciting shortstop prospects. Sarmiento batted .295/.374/.393 with eight extra-base hits and nine steals in 34 games during his introduction to affiliated ball in the DR. A plus-plus runner when he signed, Sarmiento has become one of the most no-doubt shortstops in the entire New York system. His ability to track down balls in the hole would make him a special defender alone, and his remarkable arm strength adds to his ability to convert outs from a premium position. He impressed Mets officials early on with his ability to make consistent contact, posting a 16.8 percent K rate in the DSL, and his 9.9 percent walk rate showed he’s willing to take the free passes that come to him too. Power is going to be a major issue for Sarmiento as he works his way toward Queens. He’s listed at a light 160 pounds right now, which affects his ability to impact the ball with any major pop, but it’s still early in his career. If he can get to even below-average slugging ability, his glove and wheels will do more than enough to give him a promising floor as a fast defense-first shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Memorial High School in Evansville, Indiana, will always be known for producing Don Mattingly, but Fisher represents the first player from the school to be drafted since 1993. While he didn’t quite surpass former Indiana prep pitchers Ashe Russell and Nolan Watson as a first-round pick, the two-sport standout -- he also starred at quarterback at Memorial -- did get close to second-round money ($1.25 million) from the Phillies to sign as a seventh-rounder in the 2025 Draft. Fisher is already a presence on the mound at 6-foot-3 with a combination of stuff and projection. He can really spin the baseball, both with his heater and a pair of distinct breaking balls. He tends to work in the 92-93 mph range, touching 95 with a high-spin fastball that has good carry and natural cut that allows it to play up. The spin rates on both his top-to-bottom upper-70s curve and traditional low-80s slider are also very high, and he can miss bats with both. It’s his fourth pitch, but he has some feel for a fading changeup as well. The athleticism that made him stand out on the gridiron helps him on the mound, where he repeats his delivery with good extension and throws a lot of strikes. He has room to add strength, which should lead to more consistent velocity, helping him reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best contact hitters in the 2025 college class, Cohen set a Big Ten Conference record with 56 hits in league play (30 games) and a Rutgers mark with 24 doubles last spring while batting .387 with a 5 percent strikeout rate. He gave Rutgers a player drafted in the first three rounds for the third straight year, following Ryan Lasko and Joshua Kuroda-Grauer (both Athletics) and signed for an under-slot $847,500 in the third round. He batted .327 in 28 regular-season games and .438 in the playoffs to help Single-A San Jose win the California League championship. Cohen's efficient left-handed stroke and disciplined approach continued to translate into repeated contact during his pro debut. While he has undeniable bat-to-ball skills, he's also an extreme ground-ball and opposite-field hitter who totaled four homers in three college seasons and slugged .402 at San Jose. A 410-foot blast at the Draft Combine and surprisingly high exit velocities hint at perhaps average raw power, and San Francisco believes it can help him add some strength and elevate balls more often to get to 12-15 homers per season. Cohen enhances his solid-to-plus speed with keen instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He played mostly right field at Rutgers but has enough range for center, where he played well at Single-A, which prompted another club to tell the Giants he gave them Steve Finley vibes. While he has average arm strength and can play all three outfield spots, he'll profile best if he can stick up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you see the 6-foot-6, 255-pound Quick and think he looks like an offensive lineman, it’s because he was, in high school, and a good one who could have played college football. He opted to focus on pitching at Alabama, but after a solid freshman year as a reliever, needed Tommy John surgery as a sophomore in 2024. He made a speedy recovery and turned in 14 starts for the Crimson Tide helping him land with the Twins as the No. 36 overall pick in the 2025 Draft, signing for a full-slot bonus of $2.69 million. Quick’s stuff is downright electric, with a sinking fastball that sits at 96-97 mph and touches 99. He holds his velocity deep into his starts and was already sitting at 95 mph in early bullpens before Spring Training. The Twins are already working with him on his fastball usage, leaning on the sinker against right-handers and a four-seamer against lefties. They also want him to use his nasty secondary stuff more, especially in two-strike counts after he threw his heater almost 50 percent of the time in those situations in 2025 with Alabama. His mid-80s slider features two-plane depth and he can manipulate it into a harder cutter in the low 90s. Those two, and his upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks, miss a ton of bats. While he’s built like a workhorse, Quick doesn’t have a track record yet of handling a full workload, with just 87 total college innings on his resume entering pro ball. Learning routines as a professional starter, along with refining his command to maximize his raw stuff, will be keys for him to reach his ceiling as part of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After landing in the international penalty box for exceeding their bonus pool in 2016, the Astros were limited to paying no more than $300,000 for anyone in the next two years. They gave the maximum to Gonzalez in 2018, and the Dominican has emerged as the best prospect in that crop. He made his U.S. debut last summer and needed just three weeks to merit a promotion to Low-A. Listed at 6-foot-3, Gonzalez continues to grow and is closer to 6-foot-6 today. His frame gives him tremendous leverage and combines with his bat speed to produce outstanding exit velocities that could increase further as he matures physically. If he can keep his right-handed swing from getting too long, develop some plate discipline and learn to drive more balls in the air, he could produce 20 or more homers per season. Gonzalez has a rocket arm at shortstop and his throws across the infield have been clocked up to 99 mph. An average runner, he has a quick first step and more than enough range to stay at shortstop. If he slows down too much as he fills out, his power potential and arm would fit the right-field profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fajardo signed with the White Sox for $400,000 in February 2024 and has been a steady performer ever since, starting with his 26 percent K/BB rate in the Dominican Summer League that first season. The industry has taken notice as he’s been acquired in trades twice before his 20th birthday. The first came when he was moved to the Red Sox for the DFA’d Cam Booser in December 2024, and then one year later -- after climbing to Single-A in his first stateside season -- when he was traded to the Cardinals as part of the Willson Contreras deal. After adding strength, the 6-foot-3 right-hander pushed his four-seamer and two-seamer up to the 93-95 mph range, touching 96, before his move to the Cardinals. A lack of standout movement made them easier to touch at Single-A, but the velocity trajectory is promising. For now because the fastballs don’t really pop, Fajardo has leaned heavily on his mid-80s slider. He’s able to wear out the low, gloveside area with that breaking ball, and it could be a future plus pitch. Fajardo also delivers plenty of whiffs with his 85-87 mph changeup with fading action, and he appropriately ran equal splits in '25 because of it. Fajardo was pushed so aggressively by Boston because his control was more advanced than most 18-year-old pitchers (with many of them still pitching in American high schools). The chase on his secondaries helps him deliver strikes consistently, though that could be challenged when he reaches the Majors. There is an argument to be made for him as the headline of the return in the Contreras trade considering his ceiling as a potential No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nearly 19 years old when he signed for $10,000 out of Venezuela in July 2023, Martinez made a steady if unspectacular pro debut the following summer. Named Arizona Complex League pitcher of the year when he returned there in 2025, he led the Rookie-level circuit with 67 strikeouts in 47 1/3 innings and would have topped the ACL in ERA (1.90), strikeout rate (35 percent), walk rate (5 percent) and K/BB ratio (6.7) if he hadn't fallen two outs shy of qualifying. He finished his season by contributing to a California League championship at Single-A San Jose. Martinez's stuff made a jump last season, with his fastball sitting in the mid-90s and reaching 98 mph with armside run, showing carry at times and downhill plane at others. He also added sweeping action to his low-80s slider, giving him a pair of plus pitches. While his upper-80s changeup is too firm and lags behind his offerings, it does flash some interesting fade. While Martinez lacks physicality at 6-foot-1 and a listed 165 pounds, he's strong and athletic. He gets down the mound well, providing deception via extension and a low release height. He didn't pound the strike zone as much in the Cal League as he did in the ACL, but he should have at least average control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Obermuller had the chance to begin his pro career after his sophomore season at Iowa but opted to return to the Hawkeyes for his junior year rather than entertain signing with the Rangers, who took him in Round 19 of the 2024 Draft. It turned out to be a wise decision as the son of five-year big leaguer Wes Obermueller went in the same round as his dad did, the second, with the Phillies in 2025, signing for $1.2 million. Obermueller has a slender, wiry frame and is a plus athlete on the mound with a little bounce. The left-hander employs a low arm slot that helps provide excellent metrics on his fastball and slider. The heater sat at 91-94 mph, topping out at 98 and he’s able to manipulate the pitch for carry, run or sink coming from a flat approach angle. He’ll use his low-80s slider with a ton of horizontal break against hitters on both sides of the plate. He has a sinking mid-80s changeup he didn’t use much in college, but the Phillies think it can be a usable third pitch in the future. Standing around 6-foot even and 170 pounds, Obermueller will have to prove he can handle the workload of a starter. His improvement in the strike-throwing department as a junior helps his case there and he brings a very calm demeanor to the mound. He’ll get the chance to develop as a starter, but moving him to the 'pen would put him on a faster track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cook is an eye-popping athlete. Recruited as a two-way player at Southern Mississippi, he focused on pitching and reached 96 mph with his fastball, but his inability to throw strikes led to him redshirting in 2023 and working just two innings last year. Converted to a center fielder in the spring of 2025, he batted .350 with a 6.7 percent strikeout rate and displayed some of the best speed and outfield range in college baseball. The Blue Jays selected him in the third round and signed him for $922,500. Cook immediately becomes the fastest player in the Blue Jays’ organization, and they’re ready to let him run wild. He’s not here to slap ground balls and sprint, though. Toronto, already excited by what Cook was able to do in his final year of college ball -- which was essentially just him in “reaction mode” -- is working with him to develop more of a conscious approach that lets his exciting tools shine. This will be a case study for the difference between fast guys and true base stealers. If Cook develops a true feel for reading deliveries and getting jumps, then look out. He’ll already be a plus defender with the potential to be one of the better ones in Toronto’s system, but if he can tilt games on the bases, that’s when his potential will really become unlocked. Cook is still extremely raw, so leave room for more patience than you’d give the average 22-year-old, but if you’re ranking this system on how “fun” of a development project each prospect could be, Cook is No. 1.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shores has always been able to throw hard dating back during his Texas high school days, when he could have been a solid prep pick in the 2022 Draft if he wasn’t intent on honoring his college commitment at Louisiana State. His time with the Tigers was interrupted early by Tommy John surgery in April of his freshman year, and he missed all of 2024. The velocity came back, but he struggled to find a rhythm as a starter, though he did get two saves (including the championship winner) in the Men's College World Series last year en route to becoming the Angels’ second-round pick. Signed for a full slot bonus of $2.08 million, Shores brings a ton of arm strength to the Halos’ system. He’ll work his heater in the 94-98 mph range and touch triple digits, but upon his return from TJ, the fastball had less armside run and didn’t overpower hitters as much. His mid-80s slider still featured good depth and missed bats, but his command of the pitch wavered. He has an upper-80s changeup, but it hasn’t been an effective offering. Though he’s 6-foot 8 and 245 pounds, Shores is quite athletic on the mound and there’s optimism that the further removed from elbow surgery he gets, the more in sync he’ll become in order to repeat his low three-quarters delivery and find the zone more consistently. Similarly to Angels’ 2024 second-rounder Chris Cortez, Shores could get a chance to start, with most feeling he eventually lands in a bullpen where his fastball-slider combination could be nasty.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of speedster Jeremy Owens, who stole 399 bases in 18 years between the Minors and independent ball, Josh has a similar offensive profile -- but also a potential future on the mound. He won two games as a pitcher and also played some left field for the U.S. national team that earned a gold medal at the 18-and-under World Cup qualifier in Panama in 2024. Hailing from the same part of Tennessee where the Rangers found Evan Carter, Owens will get the chance to play both ways after signing for an over-slot $1.1 million in the third round last July. Most clubs preferred Owens as a position player with plus speed and the chance to grow into comparable raw power. While he has some natural loft in his left-handed swing that allows him to drive balls in the air, he got too aggressive and pull-happy in his brief debut, striking out 11 times in 24 at-bats. He offers good actions and a strong arm at shortstop, though some amateur scouts believed he'd have more defensive impact in center field. Owens has a relieverish delivery that makes him look like a shortstop throwing sidearm, but it creates an extremely low release height and life on his pitches without hurting his ability to provide strikes. During instructional league, he worked at 93-96 mph and touched 98 with heavy sink on a two-seam fastball and in the low 80s with promising sweep on his slider. He also imparts sink on an upper-80s changeup that's a work in progress.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally trained as an outfielder in Venezuela, Cayama didn't attract much scouting interest until he shifted to the mound and quickly began reaching the low 90s with his fastball. After signing for $147,500 in 2024, he had to overcome a bout with pneumonia before working in short stints in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He earned Rookie-level Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his U.S. debut after leading the circuit in average-against (.191), WHIP (1.06) and strikeout rate (28 percent), then made a Single-A cameo at age 18. Cayama has more feel than most teenage pitchers, showing the ability to work up and down with his fastballs and throw his two secondary offerings with horizontal action in opposite directions. He rides four-seamers up in the zone and sinks two-seamers at the knees while working at 92-94 mph and touching 97 with his heaters. His solid low-80s slider has tight spin and breaks away from righties, while his mid-80s changeup fades and sinks toward them. Cayama uses his athleticism to repeat his three-quarters delivery and provide regular strikes. His control and fastball command weren't as sharp as usual when he got rocked at Single-A, though that was more a matter of fatigue than a long-term concern. He's not very physical but has the stuff and polish to succeed as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 45 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Ebel has baseball roots as the son of Dodgers third-base coach Dino Ebel, and he put them to good use as a showcase standout at the Area Code Games and High School All-American Game in 2024. He was part of a loaded and widely seen Corona High School squad featuring top 2025 picks Seth Hernandez and Billy Carlson, and while his stock may have slipped a bit as a senior, he still went 32nd overall to the Brewers with the Draft pick Milwaukee picked up for losing Willy Adames in free agency. Ebel signed just below slot at $2.75 million. Entering pro ball, the 6-foot-3 infielder may not have a lot of huge offensive tools, but there are enough pieces to like here. His left-handed swing is a smooth one with good barrel control, and he doesn’t need much of a load to get it going. Ebel faced many questions about his overall impact after hitting the ball on the ground too much as a Corona senior, but he has size to dream on. Average pop could come down the line with added strength under a pro program. Ebel played third base in high school because Carlson was such a wizard at shortstop, and as a below-average runner with a plus arm, he might just end up there long term. Brewers VP of amateur acquisition Tod Johnson noted after the Draft, however, that Ebel's shortstop actions mimicked Corey Seager, who worked with the senior Ebel in Los Angeles, and his overall IQ could paper over some of the other tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $200,000 signing out of Venezuela in 2023, Virahonda played in the Dominican Summer League in both '23 and '24, and with a .510 OPS in the latter campaign, he didn’t look like a player primed for a breakout with a move stateside. Fortunately, that’s exactly what happened after making adjustments heading into his age-19 season. He pushed past the Arizona Complex League in 2025 with a .347/.464/.455 line in 37 games and then held his own with a .256/.362/.357 performance and 108 wRC+ in 33 games at Single-A Visalia. Batting from the right side, Virahonda stays short to the ball with a simple operation and minimal load. He got a bit swing-happy against offspeed pitches in the California League, but nothing overly worrisome for a player making the large jump from the complex to full-season ball. It’s just average raw power right now, but Virahonda did a nice job of upping his line-drive rate with his move to the U.S., and he keeps the ball off the ground, good news for someone with below-average speed. His overall profile earns a boost for the fact that he looks like an above-average, potentially even plus defender behind the plate. Standing at 5-foot-11, he moves well back there to earn good reviews for his receiving and blocking, and he’s quick with his throws, getting the ball out efficiently to limit the opposing running game. Virahonda has blossomed into the best catching prospect in the Arizona system, but now it’s on him to hold onto that status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 19 years old when the 2025 international signing period opened, Marquez signed that January for just $10,000 out of Mexico. The early returns point to him being a steal. The Phillies skipped him over the Dominican Summer League and sent him to the Florida Complex League for his debut. He threw so well over 10 outings there that he got moved up to full-season Clearwater and continued to miss bats there. Pitching all of this season at age 20, Marquez reminds some in the organization of a third- or fourth-rounder talent-wise. He can throw strikes with three pitches, the best being his 80 mph changeup that features a ton of sink and tailing action away from left-handed hitters, getting an absurd amount of swing-and-miss and chase while also eliciting weak contact on the ground. His fastball, which sits 92-94 mph and tops out at 96, is also a worm-killer, thrown with good sink. His feel for spin isn’t as strong, but there’s faith it will keep improving, with his slider being a bit better when he throws it harder with cutter-like action to it. The 6-foot-2 Marquez does have some projection remaining, and there could be more velocity to come as he fills out his frame. Marquez is athletic on the mound, and despite some excessive head movement, repeats his delivery well and fills up the zone. If he can find a breaking ball to trust and show he can handle the workload, he has the chance to be a back-end starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers hadn’t used a Draft pick in the top two rounds on a college pitcher since Ty Madden in 2021 until they selected Witherspoon with the 62nd overall pick last summer. It was an interesting selection not just because of Detroit’s recent trend toward high school and college hitters on Day 1, but also the type of college pitcher selected. While Witherspoon’s twin brother and Oklahoma teammate Kyson was a sure first-rounder, Malachi’s mercurial results with a similar arsenal had dropped him to third-round projections in some places, with a potential reliever tag weighing on his stock. The Tigers are comfortable looking past results and more toward current and future arsenals, and Witherspoon, who turned down an over-slot bonus from the Diamondbacks as a 12th-rounder out of high school three years earlier, signed with them for a $1,448,700 bonus. There’s a lot to like about Witherspoon’s arsenal, from a power fastball that reaches the upper 90s to a buckling curveball and tight slider. The conundrum that teams faced with him in the Draft was an inconsistency throwing strikes and a struggle to repeat his mechanics. He walked 3.9 batters per nine innings for his college career, and hit 17 batters over 74⅓ innings in his final season at Oklahoma. He worked exclusively out of the stretch with a three-quarters arm slot in college, but there should be some refinement in the pros from the Tigers' pitching development department. The Tigers built a renowned pitching instructional group in part to help get value picks out of the Draft, and Witherspoon will be one of its most interesting tests. Team officials say he’ll get the chance to work as a starter. With improvements in command and a more refined delivery, he would have mid-rotation potential. If not, there are worse fates than getting a late-inning reliever from a second-round pick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $40,000 out of Venezuela in 2024, Azocar started to attract attention after gaining strength following his pro debut and crushing balls in Minor League Spring Training last year. The Red Sox sent him to the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, where he batted .385/.448/.558 in 15 games before earning a promotion to Single-A at age 18. He has some similarities to Justin Gonzales but struggled more against significantly older competition. Azocar weighs closer to 195 pounds than his listed 168, and the added muscle allows him to produce higher velocities than most players his age. He generates plenty of bat speed from the right side of the plate and has the potential for at least 20-homer power once he matures as a hitter and learns to elevate balls more often. He chased too many non-fastballs in Single-A but showed the ability to do damage when he swung at strikes. Azocar has solid speed, can flash plus run times and displays the aptitude to steal a few bases. After playing most of his first season in left field, he spent much of his second in center. He has good instincts and average range in center, but he profiles better in right field and has the solid arm strength necessary there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 That Horvath went undrafted as a high school senior and as a Draft-eligible sophomore at North Carolina had more to do with his asking price than his toolsy combination of power and speed, which has long intrigued scouts. It also had something to do with his inconsistency at the plate, though Horvath dispelled enough of those questions with a strong junior year in Chapel Hill for the Orioles to select him in the second round of the 2023 Draft and sign him for a slightly under slot $1.4 million. Horvath opened his first full season at High-A Aberdeen, where he didn’t hit for average but performed in other ways, and was traded to the Rays in late July as part of a deal that sent Zach Eflin the other way. Horvath uses bat speed and strength to generate at least plus raw power, and he’s especially adept at trusting his quick, powerful hands to turn on inside pitches and hammer mistakes in the zone. The result is an uphill right-handed stroke and extremely pull-heavy batted-ball profile, which helps him to drive the ball out of the park but also works against him with catchable pop flies. He tends not to chase breaking balls out of the zone all that often but is more vulnerable against quality fastballs up in the zone, leading to some significant swing-and-miss. He does know how to see pitches and walked at a higher clip in his debut than he did in college. That on-base ability jives with above-average speed that enabled him to steal 14 bases in 15 attempts last summer. Horvath was drafted as a third baseman and possesses plus arm strength, but struggled with accuracy so much that at this point he doesn’t really have a true position. He moved between third, second and right to begin 2024, and even saw a few games in center. If he can develop defensively, Horvath’s power and speed would be more valuable at an infield spot, though added versatility could also work to his advantage, especially with Tampa Bay.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After helping host Mexico win a bronze medal at an 18-and under World Cup qualifier in November 2022, Gutierrez signed for $32,500 two months later. He batted .352 with a 12 percent strikeout rate in his first three pro seasons, though recurring back issues limited him to just 85 games. He was leading the Single-A California League in hitting (.351), on-base percentage (.445), runs (60) and hits (87) when his 2025 season ended after just 60 contests. There aren't any holes in Gutierrez's compact left-handed stroke or his approach. He rarely chases pitches or misses when he does swing, hangs in well against southpaws and handles all types of offerings while using the entire field. He's not very physical and doesn't pull or lift many balls, so his power upside may be limited to 12-15 homers per year. Gutierrez has solid speed and is an instinctive baserunner who swiped 38 bags in 42 attempts (90 percent) in his first three years as a pro. He may be quick enough to play center field, but he spent most of last season in right in deference to speedier Dakota Jordan. He has average arm strength and is a solid defender on the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Forbes headed to Louisville as a potential two-way player and saw time as a DH/outfielder as a freshman in 2023, even getting at-bats in the Cape Cod League that summer. He broke his left hand in his lone plate appearance of 2024 and didn’t bat again as a collegian after shifting his focus to the mound exclusively that spring. He joined the Cardinals starting corps as a junior, and after working around a flexor strain, he finished with a 4.42 ERA and 117 strikeouts in 71 1/3 innings for Louisville’s College World Series squad. Arizona selected him 29th overall (the pick it received for losing Christian Walker in free agency) and signed him for $3 million. The 6-foot-3 right-hander throws from a low three-quarters delivery that can make him difficult to read. He picked up velocity in the summer before his junior year and sat 94-96 mph throughout the spring, touching 100, with impressive carry and high spin. He has continued to sit mid 90s in workouts heading into his first full season. An 81-85 mph slider shows promising sweep running away from righties and flashes plus. He could turn it into an upper-80s cutter for something sharper in college. Forbes’ upper-80s changeup will require refinement in pro ball as he’ll need a better option than the fastball alone against lefties. Forbes’ delivery comes with energy and verve, and while that might help his explosiveness, it’s also kept him from ever really showing average control to this point. That said, Arizona took him as an upside play considering he isn’t that deep into his time as a full-time pitcher. There could still be more development than your typical big-time college arm with the option of dominating out of the bullpen as a two-pitch righty always a fallback option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pence blew out his elbow pitching summer ball shortly before he enrolled at North Carolina, leading to Tommy John surgery and a redshirt year before he became one of the best relievers in college ball in 2023-24. Signed for an over-slot $350,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2024, he exceeded expectations during his pro debut last season. He logged a 2.73 ERA, .193 opponent average and 32 percent strikeout rate between two Class A levels while improving his secondary pitches. The key to Pence's success going forward will be if a fastball that parks at 91-93 mph and maxes out at 95 can continue to play as a solid pitch thanks to tremendous carry and fine command. He threw his heater three-quarters of the time while in college, and the Rangers had him dial back its usage so he could develop his sweeping slider and splitter/changeup. Both sit in the low 80s and missed more bats with more action last year than they had in the past. Pence uses his athleticism to get down the mound well, creating extension and a low release height. He repeats his delivery well and provides consistent strikes without catching too much of the plate. If he can continue to fool hitters with his fastball, he could be more than a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Cutter: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Hardin spent two years at Daytona State College before transferring to Mississippi State, only to never break out of the Bulldogs' bullpen. The Brewers still took him in the 12th round in 2024, signed him for $147,500 and transitioned him to a starting role on the pro side with impressive early results. Hardin posted a 2.72 ERA and a 1.18 WHIP with 96 strikeouts over 96 innings between High-A and Double-A in his first full season. His 4.4 percent walk rate and 20.4 percent K/BB rate were tops among Brewers farmhands with at least 90 frames in ’25. The 6-foot-2 right-hander sits 92-95 mph with his four-seam fastball, and he makes up for the average velocity by generating decent ride from a low release and good extension. He’ll wear out the top rail of the zone with that four-seamer and then drop in a low-80s slider that gets good sweep to the lower gloveside corner. An upper-80s cutter isn’t quite as sharp as others in its pitch class, but the jump in velo from the slider allows it to sneak up on lefties, leading to soft contact. Hardin has an upper-80s changeup for opposite-side bats, but it’s too firm, leading to issues with splits. Hardin flows well on the mound and kept pumping strikes at each level in 2025. That type of control helped his case not only to start but to remain in a bulkier role in his first taste of the pros. Better batters might have more success against him in the zone, and that’s something that will be tested at the upper levels. If his gains continue, Hardin could factor into Milwaukee’s rotation depth by the second half of his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An Alberta native, Piasentin rose up Draft boards in 2025 after showing off his tools in a swing through Arizona during Spring Training. Continuing to expand their presence with draft picks from their own backyard -- or at least their own country -- Toronto swooped in for him in the fifth round in July and signed him for above slot value at $747,500. At 6-foot-3 and 200 pounds, Piasentin is a presence in the box from the left side of the plate. He is all tools at this point and could continue to grow even stronger, so there’s some serious power upside for the Blue Jays to unlock in the coming years. There are some holes in his swing that come along with that, but Piasentin is the type of project that player development groups love, with an exciting combination of physical attributes and an eagerness to grow. The exit velocities will be interesting to watch early on, but his overall offensive game could be a slower burn. With a plus arm, right field feels likelier as Piasentin's long-term home, but he could continue to see some time at third base going forward. The more the Blue Jays can simplify the development process, the better. If his power really pops, then the sky is the limit, but there’s a wide range of outcomes here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McDonough caught at Moeller High (Cincinnati), which has spawned 14 big leaguers including Hall of Famers Ken Griffey Jr. and Barry Larkin, but found himself blocked at that position at North Carolina State by future first-rounder Patrick Bailey. After transitioning to center field, he priced himself out of the shortened 2020 Draft as a sophomore-eligible and returned to help the Wolfpack place third at the 2021 College World Series, fashioning a 53-game on-base streak that spanned the two seasons. He signed for $828,600 as a third-rounder last July and batted .298/.397/.491 during a month in Low-A. A switch-hitter, McDonough has some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. He added strength and changed his approach in 2021, launching balls more consistently in the air (especially against left-handers) while continuing to control the strike zone well. He lost a half-step of speed as he gained muscle, but he's still a solid runner with good instincts on the bases. McDonough's quickness and savvy translate to center field, where he's a solid defender with average arm strength. He also saw action at second base in college and Boston plans on playing him in both spots and perhaps shortstop and third base. A potential super-utility man, he garners comparisons to former Red Sox fan favorite Brock Holt with his versatility and hard-nosed style of play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Livingston didn’t crack the Hebron Christian Academy (Dacula, Ga.) rotation until his senior year, but he had a lot of interesting traits, including a quick arm, good present velocity and a projectable body at 6-foot-4. The D-backs selected him in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft and signed him away from a Georgia commitment with a $1 million bonus, thus making Livingston the highest-selected prep pitcher from the Peach State since Dylan Lesko went 15th overall in 2022. The big right-hander showed he could sit 92-94 during his final spring as an amateur, and he showed two fastball looks in his four-seamer and two-seamer. He could be higher than that velo in some outings, and it was encouraging when he sat in the mid 90s and touched 97.6 at the Draft Combine in, of all places, Arizona. His feel for spin wasn’t always consistent, but his low-80s slider was ahead of his upper-70s curveball as a potential weapon. He also showed a low-80s changeup that could be effective as a pro. Livingston has added nice strength since signing, and that’s promising because some evaluators believed he was a future 100 mph candidate in high school. His athletic delivery looks like one that should bring at least average control and keep walks from holding him back. He’ll get plenty of runway as a starter in his new organization, and finding an above-average pitch to pair with the fastball will be a deciding factor in his future role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates gave out 16 bonuses of six figures or more after the delayed 2020-21 international signing period opened in January 2021, and it might be the players near the bottom of that long list who provide the biggest dividend. Both outfielder Esmerlyn Valdez ($130,000) and Kelly ($100,000) were added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. A native of Aruba, Kelly didn’t gain much traction in the early going, throwing a grand total of 173 innings and not getting past Single-A Bradenton through the 2024 season. An big uptick in velocity and overall stuff enabled him to go from High-A Greensboro to Double-A Altoona, top 100 innings for the first time and lead the organization in a host of pitching categories. While he’s undersized at 5-foot-10, Kelly is compact and strong, and that added strength has led to a much better fastball, his calling card. It now sits at around 97 mph and he can reach back for triple digits. He commands it well and it can feature some carry to it, though it doesn’t miss a ton of bats. His upper-80s changeup was effective, but he would drop his slot to throw it at times, so he worked on a new split change during the offseason. In early camp this offseason, it was nasty, coming from the same tunnel as the heater. In the past, he threw an upper-80s gyro-type slider as well as a cutter, but the latter pitch has been shelved so he can focus on sharpening the former. Kelly repeats his simple delivery well and threw a ton of strikes overall in 2025, showing no ill effects from the stuff spike. Turning his slider into a true out pitch is the key to the development that will get him to the big leagues, something that could happen as early as this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter pretty much out of the gate at Fresno State, Gray had solid freshman and sophomore seasons, earning Mountain West Freshman of the Year honors in 2023, but something really clicked in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2024, when he hit .329 and got an All-Star nod. When he got hot as conference play started in his junior season, he finished the year with an OPS of 1.037 and landed in Competitive Balance Round B with the Pirates, making him the first Bulldogs hitter to go in the top three rounds since Taylor Ward was taken in the first round in 2015. A big, 6-foot-4 right-handed hitter, Gray is all about impact and contact. He swings a lot, and chases too much (32 percent chase rate in 2025), but he doesn’t miss very often (19 percent miss rate last year). He has a ton of raw power to all fields, typically finding the seats to his pull side. He’ll need to work on some swing modifications and on his swing decisions, as professional pitchers are sure to take advantage of his desire to offer at just about anything near the plate. Where Gray’s bat will fit into a lineup remains to be seen. He has the arm to play third, where he played exclusively in college, but a lack of speed or first-step quickness may push him across the diamond to first base. He’s been working to get his body to be more explosive to give him a shot at the hot corner, but it’s going to be his bat that carries him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wing appeared destined to play shortstop and pitch at Loyola Marymount before his stuff made a jump during his senior season at Scotts Valley (Calif.) HS, which also spawned Robbie Erlin. The Cubs liked his athleticism and projectability enough to select him in the fourth round last July and paid him more than double slot value at $1.5 million. The son of White Sox 2001 second-rounder Ryan Wing, a left-hander who topped out at Triple-A, he'll make his pro debut in 2026. Wing's fastball went from 88-90 mph at the 2024 Area Code Games to 90-96 with high spin rates plus nice carry and armside run last spring. He also tightened his curveball, which shows signs of becoming a plus offering in the upper 70s with downer break. His low-80s changeup has similar action and is still a work progress but looks like it will be a useful third pitch. More athletic than most pitchers, Wing moves down the mound well to create plenty of extension in his delivery, He repeats his mechanics well and provides strikes with ease. He'll need to add some strength but could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers saved international bonus pool money to pursue Roki Sasaki in 2025, and when he signed with the Dodgers, they pivoted and spent $1,200,001 on Kim in May. A two-way standout who projected to go in the first round of the Korea Baseball Organization draft, he played briefly in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League after signing before returning home to complete his high school education. After getting his diploma in January, he'll both play shortstop and pitch in his U.S. debut this year. Scouts are divided as to whether Kim is better as a position player or pitcher. He projects as an average hitter with a good approach and 15-homer power from the right side of the plate, and he could raise his offensive ceiling as he adds strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame. He's a solid defender at shortstop with a strong arm and average speed. On the mound, Kim displays a low-90s fastball that reaches 95 mph. He has a full complement of secondary pitches, with his low-80s slider ranking ahead of his mid-80s splitter and mid-70s curveball. He should add more power as he matures physically and his athleticism should help him throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A center fielder, first baseman, starter and closer at Tulane, Lombardi did it all in college. His Draft outlook was much better on the mound, where he saw a lot of improvement his junior year. That included a velocity increase and led to 73 strikeouts in 42 innings. Lombardi turned that into a second-round selection by the Royals in the 2025 Draft, and he received a $1,297,500 signing bonus. He began his professional career in Arizona, where he pitched in the Royals’ Bridge League and instructional league games. Mainly a reliever at Tulane, Lombardi got things done with his fastball and curveball, which both generated a lot of in-zone swing-and-miss. The heater sits 93-95 mph but runs up to 97 with lots of vert, while the 78-81 mph curveball has a sharp break. Lombardi has some feel for a changeup but he needs to develop it more to turn it into the above-average pitch some evaluators think it might be. He’s added a slider since joining the Royals mainly as a bridge pitch because his other pitches cover different parts of his movement plot, so the slider gives hitters something else to honor in the zone. Lombardi is very athletic -- which makes sense given his time in center field -- and brings that to his delivery, moving well down the mound. He didn’t throw a ton of strikes in college, so finding the zone will be a focus for him as a pro. Lombardi’s two-way status meant he hasn’t spent as much time on the mound as a typical college pitcher, so there’s development to be had here, both with his stuff but also his strength and throwing program. For that reason, the Royals might be a little more cautious with him, but there’s a ton of upside in his raw stuff and athleticism. He’ll develop as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gallagher got off to a promising start at Santa Barbara, earning Big West Conference freshman of the year honors in 2022, but his progress was halted by Tommy John surgery that wiped out what would have been his sophomore season. He came back stronger than ever, posting a 2.22 ERA while leading all Division I pitchers in WHP (0.84), leading to the Cubs nabbing him in the sixth round of the 2024 Draft. He had just earned a promotion from High-A to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball when he was shipped to the Twins in the Willi Castro Trade Deadline deal, finishing off the season with Double-A Wichita. The 6-foot-4 Gallagher is more about his feel for pitching than wow stuff. His fastball sat around 91 mph during his first full season, but it has a chance to play above its velocity because of its impressive induced vertical break and his ability to command it well. He relies on his changeup and slider to miss bats, with an upper-70s cambio that has good depth and a low-80s slider that combined to elicit a 46-percent miss rate in 2025, per Synergy. He’ll still fold in a get-me-over upper-70s curve at times. With a simple and repeatable delivery, Gallagher has always been an excellent strike-thrower. The Twins are hoping there’s a little more velocity to tease out of him so he can be a starter long-term, with some chance of him being an effective multi-inning reliever or swingman, kind of like a Pierson Ohl type with better overall stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The fact that Haley was a Top 100 prospect and one of the better high school lefties in the 2025 Draft class is a testament to his resilience. He had Tommy John surgery before high school, internal brace surgery on the elbow his junior year and a diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma in between. The Mississippi prep standout had a solid -- and healthy -- senior season and the Angels pulled their typical post-10th round magic by taking him in Round 12 and going way over slot with a bonus approaching $900,000 to keep him from heading to Vanderbilt. Haley has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix and enough feel to be a starter. He sits in the low 90s with a fastball featuring plenty of carry and armside run, touching 97 mph during his senior year. His breaking pitches can blur into each other at times, but at their best he has a distinct hammer of a low-80s curve and a slightly harder slider. His low-80s changeup can kill spin, though he hasn’t thrown it a ton. Athletic on the mound, Haley moves down the mound well with good extension. He throws strikes and repeats his delivery, even if it has a bit of a head dunk. There’s no question about his makeup -- not only did he overcome that adversity, he learned to throw right-handed so he could keep playing as a position player while rehabbing his elbow and he played through his chemotherapy and radiation treatments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hitt may have pitched his way into a prominent spot in the 2020 Draft as a high-schooler, if not for the pandemic-shortened spring and the shortened five-round process. Instead, he headed to Alabama and had rough results over his first two seasons before steadying the ship some in the Cape Cod League in 2022. Hitt's big breakout came in fall ball a few months later, and he became a high priority follow as a junior, only to get shut down in April with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. The D-backs took a swing on Hitt with a fourth-round selection and backed up their belief in him with a well-above-slot $1.2 million bonus. Hitt showed a 93-97 mph fastball with better action in the fall. That was up a few ticks from his 90-92 mph heater as a sophomore, and it was a sign that something was up health-wise when the fastball was back to averaging 92 in the spring. What also took the southpaw to another level was a plus upper-80s cutter that might be his best secondary now. Its biggest competition for that is a mid-80s slider, while a mid-70s curveball offers another breaker. Hitt's changeup goes virtually unused and needs to be located on the bottom edge of the zone to be at all effective. His control and command were also ticking closer to average in the fall, but that progress was certainly slowed by the lost TJ time. Hitt's pitch mix gives him mid-rotation upside, despite the injury history, and that's a big reason why Arizona went in for him last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tejeda pitched at both Florida and Florida State in his two collegiate seasons with subpar results at both. After posting a 5.95 ERA in 19 2/3 innings primarily as a reliever in 2024, he headed to the Cape Cod League (where he also spent part of ’23) and struck out 16 in 11 1/3 frames. That performance in the premier summer collegiate league likely helped him go to the Nationals in the 14th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore in ’24, and he signed for $225,000. Washington moved Tejeda into a starting role in the pros, and he handled himself well with a 4.03 ERA, 1.23 WHIP and 79 strikeouts in 87 innings between Single-A and High-A. Entering his age-22 season, Tejeda will pop most for his size at 6-foot-8, and as you might expect, that leads to huge extension that gets him right on top of batters. He sat 91-94 mph with a pair of fastballs from his low three-quarters slot, and early spring reports indicate that he’s been sitting mid-90s more comfortably to begin his second full season, making at-bats even more uncomfortable for hitters. His low-80s sweeper and shorter mid-80s slider gives him two breaking ball variations, and the former is his best whiff generator as it runs away from righties. The fade on his 83-85 mph splitter shows promise, though lefties have given Tejeda a splits problem early in his career. Tejeda’s control numbers are significantly better on the pro side, though he relies on batters expanding the zone horizontally. Because of his limited usage in school and change in role, he’s more raw than the typical collegiate arm, especially one from the 14th round. Holding the velo and control gains would give him a decent shot at being a No. 4/5 starter in D.C.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman reliever at Westmont College in California, Youngerman helped the Warriors win a NAIA Championship, then moved into the rotation as the school moved to Division II status. He went from a very strong showing in the Cape Cod League to Oklahoma State and put up impressive numbers while shuttling between the rotation and bullpen. The Phillies nabbed him in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, signing him for right around slot. A strong 6-foot-3 right-hander, Youngerman could have the goods to start. He leans very heavily on his fastball – he threw it more than 70 percent of the time for the Cowboys last year – which that sat 92-94 mph and topped out at 96, with a little more in the tank when he’s relieving. He commands the pitch well, getting a fair amount of swing and miss as well as a lot of chase on the pitch. His other offerings – a tight mid-80s slider and a fading changeup he throws about as hard – are not as consistently effective, though both can miss bats. He limited walks throughout his college career, another reason why he should get every chance to refine his secondary pitches while developing as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hurley was a three-year starter for Virginia Tech and followed up a breakout sophomore season in 2022 with stints in the Cape Cod League and with the U.S. Collegiate National Team. Upon his return to Blacksburg, the outfielder slashed .320/.414/.714 with 17 homers over 45 games for the Hokies in 2023, trailing only Brock Wilken (.807) and Nick Kurtz (.784) in ACC slugging percentage. The D-backs selected Hurley in the third round and signed him for exact slot at $887,000. He climbed three levels in his first taste of the Minors, topping out at High-A Hillsboro. The left-handed hitter starts from an open stance, kicks his leg high and lands in an attempt to generate kinetic energy and momentum at the dish. It’s certainly helped his power play with promising exit velocities and in-game results; 34 of his 57 hits went for extra bases in his final season on campus. It also leads to some swing-and-miss concerns. Hurley was often late when he saw decent velocity in school last year with no hits and a 41 percent whiff rate on pitches above 94 mph, and a 29.9 percent K rate in his 33-game pro sample raised some eyebrows. There’s still five-tool potential here, though. Hurley is a high-energy plus runner, and once Gavin Cross was out of his way at Virginia Tech, he moved back to center field, where he got the majority of his looks on the pro side. Hurley has the arm for right, if needed, too. Turning down the noise on the swing could set him on a quick road to Phoenix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox failed to sign Ehrhard as a 13th-rounder from a Florida high school in 2021, then nabbed him with a fourth-round selection in 2024 after his power blossomed during his junior season at Oklahoma State. He reached Double-A six weeks into his first full pro season, then went to Los Angeles along with fellow outfield prospect James Tibbs in a July trade for Dustin May. He batted .272/.374/.439 with 46 extra-base hits and 37 steals in 123 games between High-A and Double-A. While Ehrhard may be more of a good fourth outfielder than an everyday player, he can do a little bit of everything and his best attribute is getting on base. He controls the strike zone and grinds out at-bats, making consistent hard contact and showing the ability to launch balls in the air to his pull side. The Dodgers believe they can smooth out his right-handed swing and help him unlock some more hitting ability and power. Ehrhard has solid speed and good instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He has 41 steals in 46 attempts (89 percent) in 145 pro games and can play all three outfield spots while providing average arm strength. He's at least an average defender in center field and solid on the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Franklin spent two years working out of the Kennesaw State bullpen and put himself on a semi-big stage in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2024, but he walked around one batter per inning in both places. That changed when he transferred to Tennessee for 2025. He still pitched out of the Volunteers' bullpen but walked only nine in 38 2/3 innings while posting a 4.89 ERA and 52 strikeouts. The Cardinals found his stuff promising enough to take him 72nd overall and sign him for full slot at $1,145,900. Franklin got in three starts between Single-A and High-A after signing. St. Louis intends to run Franklin out as a starter in the hopes that his stuff holds deeper into outings and makes him even more valuable on the bump. The 6-foot-5 right-hander showed a 94-98 mph four-seamer in Knoxville that got some of the best overall and in-zone whiff rates among all Division I heaters. The pitch can touch 102 but is especially untouchable because of its tremendous ride. It had an 18.5 inch induced vertical break during Franklin’s brief foray into the Florida State League. An 89-92 mph cutter was his most-used pitch beyond the fastball, but he’s shown the makings of a mid-80s sweeping slider and an upper-80s changeup. Franklin toned down the effort in his delivery in his one spring as a Volunteer, causing his walk rate to fall to 6 percent, and that aids St. Louis’ hopes for him as a starter. He’ll need to show he can hold those gains over longer stretches and prove he can be more than a two-pitch hurler in the expanded role. Otherwise, the fastball alone could be dangerous if he slides back to relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Yankees at the start of the 2018-19 international signing period for $350,000, Escotto jumped on prospect radars with an impressive debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, when he finished with a .981 OPS. He was dealt to the Pirates before the 2021 season as part of the return for Jameson Taillon and while he scuffled at times with a leap to full-season ball, there were encouraging signs of development. In many ways Escotto held his own as a teenager in the Low-A Southeast and hit well out of the gate, though he ran into a bit of a wall and his production suffered as the season wore on. He’s strong and physical, showing bat speed and strength to impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. Registering excellent exit velocities, Escotto has the chance to hit for average and plenty of power. There was a good amount of swing-and-miss to his game last year, but the young infielder did offset it somewhat with a solid walk rate. There have been questions about whether Escotto can stick at shortstop given that he’s an average runner, but the Pirates like his footwork, hands and arm and think his body and frame give him the chance to stick there long-term. The makeup and maturity that made the organization feel confident in sending him to full-season ball last year should help him make adjustments from that season and take off from there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers signed five high schoolers as nondrafted free agents following the shortened five-round Draft in 2020, compared to a total of 12 by the other 29 clubs. The two best prospects in Texas' group are right-handers Trevor Stephan and Curry, with the latter foregoing a commitment to Bucknell to turn pro for the maximum $20,000 allowed under pandemic rules. He spent two seasons in Rookie ball before making the leap to Single-A on a full-time basis in 2023 and winning Carolina League Pitcher of the Year honors after compiling a 2.30 ERA, .163 opponents' average against and 99 strikeouts in 82 innings. Curry's fastball parks at 92-94 mph and peaks at 96, playing better than its velocity because of its induced vertical break and the extension he creates with his 6-foot-5 frame. His best secondary pitch is a low-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action that overmatched Single-A hitters. His 82-86 mph changeup cuts and sinks, giving him a reliable third option. Curry has a clean delivery and did a better job of keeping his long limbs in sync in 2023, allowing him to throw more strikes. He still needs to add more muscle to his lanky build, and it's possible that he could have two plus pitches and perhaps solid control if he gets stronger and more consistent. He has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and more upside than most of the Rangers' young pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ayers played three years at the State JC of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota and two at Marshall before he impressed the Cubs in a pre-Draft workout and signed for $50,000 as a 19th-rounder in 2024. In his first full pro season, he slashed .238/.341/.420 with six homers in 65 games as one of the oldest players (age 24) in the Single-A Carolina League before a broken right hand sidelined him in July. He came back and won the Arizona Fall League's breakout player award after hitting .357/.539/.591 with a league-best 22 walks in 20 games. Ayers uses a reasonably disciplined approach to find pitches he can launch in the air to his pull side. His solid raw power and impressive exit velocities portend 20-homer power, though he'll have to show he can do damage against more advanced and age-appropriate pitching. A switch-hitter, he's much better from the left side and has a glaring weakness against changeups. Because he didn't begin catching full time until his final year in college, Ayers needs a lot of work with his receiving and blocking, though he grades well in framing metrics. He regularly recorded sub-1.85-second pop times in the AFL, showing off plus-plus arm strength and a quick release. A below-average runner, he also has played briefly at first base and in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was a dearth of college catching in the 2025 Draft class, and Carmichael stood out as one of the few who landed in the top 100 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 Draft prospects. Following his father, Darby, and brother, Braden, by playing his college ball at Oklahoma, Carmichael used his Cape Cod League All-Star turn (where he won game MVP honors) as a springboard into an outstanding junior season, when he posted an OPS north of 1.000 and showed off improved defensive chops behind the dish. The Pirates nabbed him in the third round and pushed him to High-A Greensboro for his pro debut, where a little wrist issue sapped his production. A right-handed hitter with the possibility of average tools across the board, Carmichael has a disciplined approach, making consistent contact and showing an ability to use the middle of the field. Most of his power -- he hit 17 homers for the Sooners last year -- comes to his pull side, and he has the strength to get to 20 homers annually if he can find a bit more loft. Carmichael is a solid athlete who runs better than most catchers and can steal a base now and again. The Pirates loved the leadership traits he showed right out of the gate, always a plus for the position, and his improved arm strength has already been apparent. There’s work to be done on his receiving in terms of his timing and glove positioning, but the pieces are all there to be a decent all-around big league backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gaston, a Cuba native, earned the No. 18 spot on MLB Pipeline’s list of top international prospects during the 2018 signing period due to his high-octane fastball. Back then, when he was taking part in a showcase circuit that once included fellow countryman Victor Victor Mesa, Gaston’s calling card was elite heat without much control. The Rays took a chance on that upside and signed him for $2.61 million that November, then he went on to strike out 31 with 27 walks and a 6.00 ERA over 27 innings in the Gulf Coast League.
