Gaston’s profile hasn’t changed that much – he’s all about his big fastball, and his control is still a question – but he took a massive step forward in 2021. He shortened his arm stroke to improve his command, but the 6-foot-3 right-hander maintained that 96-101 mph velocity on his heater because he has as much lower-body strength as any pitcher in Tampa Bay’s deep system. He also tightened up his slider, giving him a better chance to land it for strikes as opposed to it only being a two-strike chase pitch. After blowing away hitters in the Florida Complex League, he held his own with a 3.86 ERA, 38 strikeouts and 22 walks in 30 1/3 innings over seven starts for Low-A Charleston. Gaston also throws a curveball and a changeup, but his primary weapons are his fastball and slider. The Rays moved him to the bullpen in 2022 but insist they haven’t given up yet on Gaston’s starting prospects. The move was made to get him as many in-game opportunities as possible per week, in the hopes that the control could improve. If anything, it’s taken a step back. That said, Gaston still doesn’t turn 21 until December, and his heater gives him a lot of promise long-term as a high-leverage relief arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grice homered 18 times and posted a 1.029 OPS over 60 games at the plate and posted a 3.35 ERA with 101 strikeouts in 78 innings during his junior year at Clemson -- numbers that won him the 2023 John Olerud Two-Way Player of the Year Award one year after Paul Skenes claimed the honor. He did punch out 26.9 percent of the time that spring because of his long left-handed swing, and that gave many evaluators pause about his potential at the plate entering the Draft. The D-backs selected Grice 64th overall in July and signed him for $1.25 million before declaring they preferred he stick to the mound. Beyond Grice's size at 6-foot-6, it isn't hard to see why Arizona would express the most excitement about the left-hander's pitching potential. He touched 95 mph in his final spring as a Tiger, and even though the fastball typically sat in the low-90s, there could be more in the tank once he turns his full focus to the bump. His upper-70s slider showed good depth, contributing to his whiff rate, and he sold his mid-80s sinking changeup well out of the hand. Grice doesn't need to show much effort out of his large frame, helping the belief that he'll limit walks even more so on the pro side. There's a lot more projection here than is standard for a college arm, especially of this size, and Grice's development -- particularly when it comes to adding velo -- should be followed closely in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: James had the look of a potential first-round pick after showing out as an underclassman on the showcase circuit and with Team USA’s 18-and-under team in 2023 but couldn’t replicate that same level of success in the summer before his senior year, including going 1-for-12 with six strikeouts at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He rebounded a bit in the spring at Davie County HS and won Gatorade’s Player of the Year honors in North Carolina as a result. Some scouts thought he was headed to Mississippi, but the Nationals selected him in the fifth round and signed him for $2.5 million, tied for the second-highest bonus in their 2025 class. A 6-foot infielder, James added weight going into his Draft year, trading off athleticism for strength in the process. With that additional impact, he profiles as a possible 20-homer hitter, especially if he can maintain his bat speed on the pro side. The focus on driving the ball also came with a regression in swing decisions, and he bit on a good number of non-fastballs outside the zone during his 2024 showcases. His right-handed swing has looked smoother in the past, and getting back to those mechanics would help his ability to hit for average in the pros. James has the actions, hands and above-average arm strength to handle shortstop, but his fringy speed limits his range on the dirt. With Eli Willits also in the organization, James is more likely to be a better fit at second or third base, and his arm could even work in a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holobetz pitched one season at Radford and two at Old Dominion before the Brewers selected him in 2024's fifth round. He made his pro debut last April in Single-A, then went to the Red Sox a month later as the player to be named later in the Quinn Priester trade. He placed second in the Minors in walk rate (4 percent) and K/BB ratio (6.0) in 2025, ending the season with a 2.39 ERA in six Double-A outings. Though Holobetz has gained a couple of ticks of velocity since turning pro and his fastball now sits at 92-95 mph and touches 97, that's not what makes it so effective. He uses his athleticism to get down the mound very well, creating extension and a lower release height in addition to significant carry and armside run, making his heater difficult to barrel. Batters managed just a .514 OPS with one homer against his fastball, repeatedly beating it into the ground. The rest of Holobetz's repertoire is nothing special, featuring an average low-80s slider with two-plane depth at its best and fringy cutter and changeup that both operate in the mid-80s. But his ability to pound the strike zone while providing plenty of deception gives him a high floor. If he can find the more effective changeup he had at Old Dominion, he could become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When teams sign players from the international amateur free agent market, it’s obviously all about projection and the knowledge it may take years before the organization knows what kind of player they have acquired. In 2022, the Twins managed to get very good early returns on their top two acquisitions: Yasser Mercedes, who received $1.7 million to sign, and Acuña, who got the second-highest bonus from the Twins that period ($869K). Acuña, like Mercedes, found immediate success in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .310 with a .409 OBP. You only have to see Acuña swing once to realize he’s the younger brother of Braves star Ronald Acuña Jr., and that he has a similar setup and swing path. Following his success in the DSL, where Acuña showed an affinity for contact and a solid approach, the Twins won’t tinker with his swing much while letting him get acclimated to playing in the United States, though it’s been noted that he tends to flare balls in the upper half of the zone. It would probably be misguided to dream he’ll have his older brother’s power, but there should be some extra-base thump to come as he matures. Having grown up around the game, Acuña’s feel for what he wants to do is apparent on both sides of the ball. He has looked solid and athletic at shortstop, with excellent hands and a strong arm, and he could even be a plus defender at second should he move to the right side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After shining with the bat as an All-Big Ten Conference first-team selection in each of his three seasons at Indiana, Taylor, who set the school's career home run record with 54, then followed that up with a strong showing in the Cape Cod League, was drafted by the A’s in 2025 as a second-round pick and signed over slot with a bonus of $2.5 million. Getting his professional career started at Single-A Stockton shortly after, he flashed some of that pop by hitting .264 with six home runs and five doubles in 28 games, making a solid first impression. Taylor has the tools to become a plus hitter for both average and power with a good feel for the zone. He’s very disciplined during his batting practice and sprays the ball around the field. Once game time rolls around, the power shows up, hitting the ball extremely hard and driving it out to all fields. There is some tendency to chase that he will need to cut down on, but the A’s see a hitter who also happens to bring a ton of power. Defense is a clear point of improvement for Taylor. His speed, arm strength and defensive instincts are lacking in the outfield, and some of that may have been due to limited practice on a regular basis in college. The A’s see some things they can clean up with his footwork and arm, and will work with him on improving that aspect of his game with the belief that he can become at least an average defender, likely in a corner outfield spot. But it’s the bat that has the organization extremely excited for his first full year of pro ball, and it will determine his ability to rise through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A legitimate two-way player during his Mississippi high school days, Morris initially headed to college to both hit and pitch. He put down the bat after his freshman year in 2023 and struggled with his control over his first two seasons pitching out of Ole Miss’ bullpen. Things clicked more during his junior season, helping him land in the third round of the Draft to the Reds, who let him get his professional feet wet with Single-A Daytona. It was only a handful of innings, but he did toss three hitless frames in the playoffs to help catapult the Tortugas into the Florida State League Championship Series. While the Rebels employed him almost exclusively as a reliever, the Reds believe he has every chance to start, and will allow him to develop as such. Moving his arm slot higher helped him find more velocity, with a fastball that topped out at 99 mph, albeit with more downhill plane than life, so it doesn’t miss that many bats. His best pitch, though, is his low-90s cutter that dives, a pitch that led to a 45 percent miss and 40 percent chase rate in college last year. He has an effective upper-80s slider with similar shape that can also miss bats. Morris has a no-nonsense, super-competitive demeanor on the mound and showed in 2025 that he can find the strike zone consistently. He could use a changeup and some improved shape to his fastball, but he has the frame and other pitches to allow him to handle a starting workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A breakout performance in the Cape Cod League in which he batted .344 with a .464 OBP and a strong junior year at the University of Michigan helped Elliott raise his stock in time for the 2022 MLB Draft, where the A’s selected him in Competitive Balance Round B. He was slated to get some action in the Arizona Complex League as part of his intro to the organization, but a quad injury sidelined him after just one game. Elliott has a quick bat that enables him to consistently hit quality fastballs for line drives all over the field. There has been some debate as to how much power he might develop, though an increase in home run totals from five in 2021 to 16 in 2022 should give some hope that he can grow into average power at the very least. He has shown some deficiencies against left-handed pitching that he’ll need to improve. Above-average speed and solid defensive skills make Elliott an asset anywhere in the outfield, though right field was his full-time position at Michigan. The A’s hope to get a good look at him as he enters his first full professional season for a better understanding of his overall game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lewis was a model-based pick by the Yankees as a power-speed athlete out of Queens College, and he quickly exceeded expectations after signing for $150,000 in the 13th round of the 2024 Draft. While old for Single-A and High-A in his age-22 season last year, he slashed .237/.321/.445 (120 wRC+) with 22 homers and 26 steals between the two levels. The Marlins acquired him along with Brendan Jones, Juan Matheus and Dylan Jasso in January for Ryan Weathers. Miami's front office was eager to add Lewis in no small part because of his power potential. The right-handed slugger produces top-of-the-line exit velocities, up to 113.9 mph last year, and has plenty of raw strength. That pop has come with swing-and-miss issues, which could be mitigated with better swing decisions. Lewis chased less as the 2025 season progressed, even against better competition, although some stiff swing mechanics make it likely that he'll maintain a below-average hit tool -- he's had particular struggles with in-zone contact. Lewis is an elite athlete who has been caught just twice in 29 stolen-base attempts in pro ball. Defensively, he shows good burst and speed and has a chance to be an average center fielder or above average in a corner -- likely left since he doesn't have ideal arm strength for right. Lewis earns praise for his makeup and has been a quick learner in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best defenders in the 2022 international signing class, Gonzalez signed with Seattle for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic and could join a long list of success stories the franchise has had there. A slick-fielding shortstop, he projects to have the most potential to stick there long term as he grows and develops as anyone his age and rank within the organization. Despite being known more for his glove, Gonzalez does make hard contact and has a projectable body expected to add strength, which can ultimately add a little more pop to his bat. What he lacks in power, he makes up for in hitting ability and potential. He’s an average runner. On defense, he shows plus hands with smooth actions and is expected to be a plus defender. He projects to have an average arm and his range is improving. Gonzalez makes playing defense look easy. The Mariners are eager to see what he does in his first season of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, which could put him on a fast track to the U.S. and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League come fall.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally ranked No. 246 in MLB Pipeline’s 2022 Draft Top 250 out of Kentucky, concerns about swing-and-miss and his commitment to Louisville led Dickerson to fall to the Twins in the 20th round. Playing sparingly with the Cardinals -- redshirting in 2023 and logging just 17 at-bats in 2024 -- he found traction after a strong summer in the Northwoods League and a transfer to Indiana, where he slashed .314/.381/.632 with 19 home runs. That performance helped him rise to a fifth-round selection by Seattle in 2025. A right-handed hitter, Dickerson stands out for his bat speed and ability to generate premium exit velocities. Scouts see at least plus raw power to all fields, though questions remain about his ability to consistently punish higher-velocity pitching. He tends to pull aggressively but could improve his offensive ceiling by being more selective. Defensively and athletically, Dickerson is a standout. With plus speed and 20/20 upside, he covers ground well in center field and shows the instincts and quickness that give him a chance to be a regular up-the-middle contributor. Arm strength is average but adequate for his position. His small sample in his debut season revealed a highly twitchy, athletic outfielder who aggressively tracks the ball -- a trait that excites evaluators despite a late-season hamstring and quad issue that limited reps. If Dickerson can remain healthy and continue to refine his approach at the plate, his combination of athleticism, speed, and emerging power could make him a dynamic center fielder in Seattle’s system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of two North Atlanta (Ga.) HS players to fit in the first five rounds of the 2023 Draft, Anderson went in the third round to the Red Sox and outfielder Isaiah Drake got popped in the fifth by the Braves. Anderson's offensive upside attracted scouts early in his prep career and landed him a well-over-slot $1.5 million bonus. He made a 12-game pro debut, striking out 15 times and spending a week in Single-A. A switch-hitter, Anderson turns his swing loose more often and does more damage from the right side. He has a balanced setup and displayed the ability to make adjustments and deal with breaking pitches as an amateur. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop into at least a 20-homer threat, though he'll need to launch more balls in the air because he presently makes too much ground-ball contact. While Anderson played shortstop at North Atlanta, he has fringy speed and immediately moved to third base as a pro. His strong arm registered fastballs up to 91 mph as a high school pitcher and fits well at the hot corner. The best case is that he becomes an offensive second baseman, and Boston will see whether he has enough quickness for the keystone in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lodise drew little scouting or recruiting attention as a Georgia high schooler before heading to NCAA Division II Augusta, where he batted .349/.450/.584 with 23 homers and 44 steals in two seasons. Posting similar numbers last spring after transferring to Georgia Tech propelled him into the third round of the 2025 Draft, and he spent a month in High-A after signing for $922,500. His cousin Alex made a similar small college to Atlantic Coast Conference breakout, winning the Dick Howser Trophy at Florida State last spring before the Braves selected him in the second round. Similar to organization favorite Sam Antonacci with his knack for contributing in many phases of the game without loud tools, Lodise has more physical gifts than Antonacci but a little less hitting ability. He's a right-handed hitter with a steady approach, using the entire field and producing surprising exit velocities for a 5-foot-11, 180-pounder. He did struggle in the Cape Cod League and hit .185 during his aggressive assignment to High-A last summer, so he still has to prove he can do damage with wood bats. Lodise combines solid speed with a high baseball IQ, which helped him steal 20 bases in 21 attempts between college and pro ball last year. His instincts also help him get the job done at shortstop, where he displays average range and arm strength. He's a better fit at second base and could wind up as an offensive-minded utilityman who provides constant energy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Summerhill might not have been available to the Rays with the 42nd overall pick in the 2025 Draft had he maintained the momentum he built as a sophomore at Arizona. He led the Wildcats in average, on-base percentage and extra-base hits in 2024 and followed that with an All-Star performance in the Cape Cod League. He played well as a junior, posting a 1.015 OPS and walking more than he struck out, but he missed more than a month with a broken hand and lost more time to a strained hamstring. He wound up with the Rays, signing for a below-slot bonus of $1,997,500, and played 10 Single-A games in his pro debut. When healthy, Summerhill has shown the potential to be a dynamic player on both sides of the ball. He’s strong and athletic, with a mature approach at the plate and a good sense of his strengths and weaknesses. He’s a pure hitter, having cut down on his tendency to whiff each year during his time at Arizona, although he does tend to chase pitches outside the zone. As strong as he is, his raw power hasn’t fully translated into game power since his hand injury, with most of his pop coming to the pull side regardless. Summerhill is an above-average runner but not a burner. He spent his junior season playing right field for Arizona, although the Rays seem inclined to use him in all three spots. He has the arm to play right field, but he’d likely be more valuable in center field if he can handle it in the professional ranks. The Rays generally give good athletes every chance to prove they can play center field, and their outfield philosophy has helped athletic players like Theo Gillen and Aidan Smith take massive strides as defenders. If all goes well, he could develop into a Jake McCarthy-type regular somewhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ovalles signed a little later than many in his class when he joined the Mets in November 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and he missed out on what would have been his first Minor League campaign due to the pandemic the following year. He got off to a solid start with a 2.83 ERA and 0.69 WHIP (third-lowest among the 257 pitchers on the circuit with at least 30 IP) over 35 frames in the Dominican Summer League in 2021 and took a step forward stateside this past season, posting a 4.05 ERA with 66 punchouts in 46 2/3 frames between the Florida Complex and Florida State Leagues. The 6-foot-3 right-hander gained velocity throughout his second pro campaign and was around 93-95 mph, topping out at 97, during his time with Single-A St. Lucie. If the heat wasn’t enough, Ovalles’ fastball also comes with a healthy amount of spin typically in the 2,500-2,700 rpm range, adding to the hope it can be a true plus pitch. His low-80s sweeping slider actually had a higher whiff rate and was dominant against righties. He’d fold in a get-me-over curveball occasionally, and his 83-86 mph changeup can get some swing-and-miss but was pounded by lefties, who had a .948 OPS against Ovalles in a small FSL sample. Ovalles has started and relieved at this early stage, and despite his improved stuff, he’s exhibited decent control too, adding to the hope the arsenal can play over a larger sample. His projectable frame at 6-foot-3 points to the possibility of another level of a repertoire still to come with more experience as he moves into full-season ball for good in his age-20 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the hardest-throwing pitchers on the 2019 international market, Mercedes already reached 95 mph before signing for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He has continued to add velocity and finally got a chance to make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League at age 18 last summer. While he recorded a 5.11 ERA, he also touched 98 mph and ranked fourth in the ACL with 62 strikeouts in 56 1/3 innings. Mercedes' fastball usually operates at 93-96 mph with running and boring action toward right-handers, and he could reach triple digits once he adds more strength to his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-80s slider moves in the opposite direction from his fastball, showing flashes of becoming a plus offering but also lacking consistency. His power changeup in the upper 80s is even more of a work in progress but eventually could give him an average third pitch. While Mercedes has a three-pitch mix to go with size and athleticism, he still may wind up in the bullpen in the long run. He has a slingy delivery with some effort and a long arm action, which compromises his control and command. He'll be 19 throughout the 2022 season, so he still has plenty of time to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top position prospect in Tennessee's 2022 prep class, Godbout went undrafted because of his commitment to Virginia. An immediate starter for the Cavaliers, he became one of the best contact hitters in the college ranks, slashing .321/.415/.514 with an 11 percent strikeout rate in three college seasons. He posted similar numbers during a brief stint in High-A after signing for $1,093,800 as a supplemental second-rounder. Godbout's bat-to-ball skills derive from a compact right-handed stroke, disciplined approach and exceptional hand-eye coordination. He made a lot of groundball contact while producing pedestrian exit velocities in college, but he immediately incorporated some changes after signing and drove the ball in the air more frequently. Boston's demonstrated ability to help players improve their strength, bat speed and ball flight could help Godbout produce at least 15 homers on an annual basis. Godbout has fringy speed at best but compensates somewhat with a high baseball IQ. His average arm strength and range are best suited for second base, where he's a surehanded defender. The Red Sox gave him a little action at shortstop in his pro debut and plan on doing so again in 2026, though most scouts think that's a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals took a liking to the state of Tennessee, taking players from there with their first three Draft picks in 2025. In between fifth overall selection Liam Doyle and 72nd Tanner Franklin -- both University of Tennessee pitchers -- St. Louis went with the state’s Gatorade Player of the Year in Mitchell out of Houston High School in Germantown. Mitchell signed for above slot with a $2.25 million bonus instead of heading to Georgia Tech. Some evaluators believe the left-handed-hitting Mitchell possesses one of the best pure hit tools among prep bats in the 2025 class. Starting with his hands held high, he coils like a spring to generate a quick stroke without much movement from his head. His strike-zone judgment was impressive as an amateur. There’s room to add strength in his 6-foot-2 frame too, and he could get to average pop by the time he reaches the Majors. Mitchell will flash plus speed, but scouts questioned whether he could stick at shortstop long term with average range and arm strength. The Cardinals announced him as a center fielder on Draft Day and intend to cycle him between the grass and dirt beginning in the Florida State League, where he’ll play along fellow shortstop Yairo Padilla. Mitchell took well to a throwing program that could aid his chances at being valuable at either spot up the middle as St. Louis tries to find the right defensive home for his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paniagua was a little older than many international signees when he joined the Cardinals at 17 for $160,000 out of the Dominican Republic in December 2017. He didn’t reach full-season ball until 2021 and was primarily a reliever -- and a successful one with 62 strikeouts in 46 1/3 innings -- during that first spin at Single-A Palm Beach. Paniagua returned to the Florida State League as a starter in ’22 and impressed again with a 2.18 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 K’s in 99 frames. He ended the year with eight more mundane outings for High-A Peoria, and the Cardinals chose to leave Paniagua off the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible, though he went unpicked. The 6-foot-1 right-hander works with a four-seamer and a sinker around 91-93 mph, occasionally touching 95, and there’s still the chance more velo could be coming because it looks like he still hasn’t fully grown into his figure. His upper-70s curveball showed great depth and 12-to-6 vertical break, and A-ball hitters -- especially righties -- couldn’t touch it. A mid-80s fading changeup could be helpful against batters from both sides, but lefties still had the lion’s share of success against Paniagua in 2022. Paniagua likely wasn’t much of a Rule 5 threat last year because he lacked success above the Single-A level, but with his three-pitch mix and solid ability to pitch in the zone, there’s still a potential starting pitcher here in the big leagues. That extra velo would go a long way toward helping that projection. Considering Paniagua is entering his age-23 season, the clock is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran was traded to the Blue Jays in August 2022 as a player to be named later in an earlier swap involving relievers Anthony Bass and Zach Pop, and then top prospect Jordan Groshans. Looking back, it was an awfully savvy move to acquire a prospect who has developed into the top catcher in the system. The backstop spent parts of the 2023, '24 and '25 seasons with Single-A Dunedin before finally earning a promotion to High-A Vancouver last summer, where he hit a combined .275 with eight home runs and a .767 OPS over 100 games. Duran lost some steam in Vancouver, so the dip in his numbers could be more about fatigue than talent, but that’s something young catchers need to adjust to. Duran earns very high marks among teammates, coaches and development staff for his leadership and clubhouse presence. He speaks both English and Spanish and has worked on his ability to manage a pitching staff -- which is so often the final piece to the puzzle -- and his defense behind the plate profiles him as a future big leaguer. While Duran’s average exit velocity has crept up, it’s likelier that his power lands in the range of 10-15 home runs, with the majority of his value coming from an on-base ability and his presence behind the plate. A step forward at the plate could still change this, but Duran likely profiles as an MLB backup, which is still a valuable asset for a club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bullard’s stock was on the rise heading into the 2025 Draft but he had what was considered a strong commitment to Texas A&M. The Blue Jays took a swing by selecting him in the 12th round and signed him for $1,697,500 ($1,547,500 of which counted toward their bonus pool), the largest bonus ever given to a player in that round. Since then, the club has only been more impressed as Bullard has packed on 15 pounds of muscle and shown an excellent work ethic in the early days of his development. Scouts who believe in Bullard like his bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate, but the left-handed swing is ahead of the right-handed swing at this point. He employs more of a gap-to-gap approach right now and makes a lot of ground-ball contact, but he also has bat speed and a projectable 6-foot-2 frame, giving the Blue Jays plenty to work with. The question becomes whether Bullard will have true standout tools or if he’ll be solid across the board. That said, Toronto has done well with the “solid” types, tinkering with offensive approaches to fit their identity. Bullard owns plus speed and knows how to use it on the bases and in the outfield. He displays good instincts in center field and should be able to remain there in Toronto's system. He has average arm strength and could handle the other two outfield spots if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roki Sasaki was the center of attention during the 2025 international signing period, and while the Blue Jays were in the running for the Japanese right-hander, they fell short to the Dodgers. Instead, Cristopher Polanco came in with the highest bonus at $2,297,500, but it’s another Dominican Republic infielder in Sanchez, a $997,500 signee, who has become the talk of the class. Sanchez was named a mid- and post-season All-Star in the Dominican Summer League after posting a .341/.439/.565 line with eight homers and 28 total extra-base hits across 56 games. Of the 304 DSL qualifiers, he was one of only seven with an ISO above .220 (.224) and a strikeout rate below 18 percent (17.4). Heading into his age-18 season, Sanchez already has plenty of size at 6-foot-3, but his plus power grades don’t come from physical projection alone. He’s already brought actualized pop into his game with loud contact in the DSL, and he combines his present strength with a balanced right-handed swing. He impressed Blue Jays officials with the way he reacted to being pitched around once the word got out on his ability, and that baseline of swing decisions should serve him well, if he can maintain it stateside. Sanchez will likely be a below-average runner at full maturity, and the Blue Jays have already given him the lion’s share of work at third base because of the amount of young talents they needed to get shortstop reps in the DR. While he’ll still work in time at the six, he’s a better fit at the hot corner, and his arm strength will work there. Sanchez’s early overall traits have already pushed him into prominence on the Toronto infield depth chart, and he’s a decent bet to see full-season ball before his 19th birthday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bragg is a late bloomer who had an uneven few years pitching out of Nebraska’s bullpen before he moved on to Dallas Baptist and became a money-saving senior sign for the Orioles in the eighth round of the 2023 Draft. He spent his entire first full season at Low-A Delmarva as a 23-year-old, opening some eyes with a strong six-start run down the stretch. But he really landed on radars in 2025, pitching to a 1.68 ERA over his first 12 outings and reaching Double-A. His sudden rise was halted by Tommy John surgery in July and is likely to shelve Bragg for the entire 2026 season. Bragg was throwing harder and missing more bats at the upper levels before the injury, impressing with a five-pitch mix that plays up due to plus control. His low arm slot allows him to get ride and run on his four-seam fastball, which averages around 95 mph and can be dialed up higher, and he also throws a two-seamer to generate ground balls. He backs up the heaters with three secondaries which all can miss bats: a low-80s slider, mid-80s changeup and a cutter he can crank into the upper-80s. At least a couple of those offerings have a chance to be plus pitches. Bragg generates excellent scores on stuff and location models and throws a lot of strikes, hinting at the possibility that the Orioles have a legitimate starting pitcher on their hands once he returns from surgery. But Bragg also doesn’t come with a long track record of amateur success, and if he doesn’t return late in 2026, he’ll be 26 years old by the time he gets back on the mound in game action.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best Canadian prospects in the 2021 Draft, Bucknam turned down the Blue Jays as a 16th-rounder to attend Louisiana State (before transferring to Dallas Baptist). Toronto came calling once again in 2025, though, and selected Bucknam in the fourth round, signing him for $678,300. He immediately becomes one of the most exciting long-term projects for this development staff, especially given the recent success stories near the top of the system. Bucknam's tight 85-88 mph slider can reach 91, features high spin rates and is a legitimate wipeout pitch, while his low-80s curveball has more depth and is nearly as effective. His fastball stands out more for its velocity -- usually sitting near 94-95 mph -- than its life or ability to miss bats. He achieves some fade with his upper-80s changeup, though it's too firm and he struggles to land it for strikes at this point in his development. That pitch will be key to his repertoire long-term. The Blue Jays planned to give Bucknam every opportunity to start, but that was put on hold when he dealt with forearm tightness in the spring and later underwent season-ending elbow surgery before he even debuted in the system. Down the road when healthy, the organization could choose to max out Bucknam’s heater and impressive breaking ball in a shorter role, but his talent is worth exploring as a starter first, assuming the stuff and command returns after recovery and rehab.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trimble was one of the most coveted second-year freshmen eligible for the 2021 Draft, emerging as a top-three-round talent by homering twice for Southern Mississippi at the Oxford Regional championship game. Sporting one of the best power-speed combinations in the Draft, Trimble also hit .441 with seven homers in his final 12 games and led NCAA Division I with 72 RBIs to rocket up draft boards by late spring. The Orioles selected him in the Competitive Balance Round B, inking Trimble for an under-slot $800,000. He endured an underwhelming debut at Class A Delmarva and underwent left labrum surgery in December. The injury is expected to sideline him for at least part of 2022. Trimble is a switch-hitter who shows more power as a left-handed hitter and more contact right-handed, using bat speed and wiry strength to drive pitches consistently from both sides of the plate. His power is more all-fields left-handed and sneaky to the pull-side righty, but it can make him over-aggressive at times, leading to some swing-and-miss against advanced pitching. Trimble is an above-average runner who runs the bases well, giving him 20-20 potential if he can tap into his power effectively at the next levels. A high school shortstop, Trimble played center field both at Southern Miss and Delmarva, and is considered a solid defender there. The Orioles are committed to keeping him in the outfield for now, but his athleticism and plus arm mean he might be able to move back to the dirt at some point if they desire. At the very least, Trimble is capable of playing all three outfield positions and his offensive upside gives him the ceiling of an impact regular at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Belyeu really established himself as a college hitter to watch as a sophomore at Texas in 2024 when he hit .329 with 18 homers. He was off to a strong start to his junior year when he fractured his left thumb diving for a ball in March. Though he finished with nine homers and a .303 average in 32 games, it was really his sophomore production that got him drafted No. 74 overall by the Rockies. He struggled during his pro debut with High-A Spokane, though it was too small of a sample to draw any conclusions. A hamstring issue shut down any action at instructs for the outfielder. While Belyeu isn’t a total free swinger, he did get more aggressive during his junior year, and his strikeout rate did climb, something that continued during his stint with Spokane after signing. The left-handed hitter has some strike-zone awareness and there’s damage in there, with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, but he’s going to have to work to try not to do too much at the plate, which takes him out of his approach. The Rockies’ new hitting group values contact and will work with him to be a hitter first. Belyeu is a solid athlete with decent speed and should be able to handle a corner outfield spot capably, with a plus arm that fits in right field. He plays with intensity, sometimes being too hard on himself, and he’ll get to show what he can really do over a full, healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2025 international signing period, the Dodgers’ gain turned out to also be the Pirates’ gain. When Los Angeles committed to signing Roki Sasaki, they could no longer also sign Morel. The Pirates were able to jump in and ink the infielder for $1.8 million, then watched him make a very solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, posting a .287/.425/.414 line to go along with 26 steals. Morel oozes athleticism and projection from his lean 6-foot-4 frame that he’s just starting to fill out. The teenager is a left-handed hitter who is already showing a solid approach. He’s willing to work counts, wait out at-bats and draw walks while also showing plenty of bat-to-ball skills. There’s plenty of bat speed to work with, and it’s easy to dream on him getting to his raw power as he gets more physical. Despite his size, Morel has a legitimate chance to stick at shortstop. He might only have average speed, but his instincts allow that to play up on the bases as well as defensively, showing excellent lateral range and more than enough arm for the premium position. Just 18 for the 2026 season, there’s the chance he’ll outgrow the spot, but there’s no need to worry about moving him yet. With his offensive upside, the Pirates are hoping perhaps Morel can follow a similar track to Top 100 prospect Edward Florentino.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player during his high school days in Maine, Bowker hit and pitched in the Appalachian League before heading to Georgetown. He did both as a freshman, then started focusing on pitching only in 2024. He was a Cape Cod League All-Star that summer before transferring to Vanderbilt and spending his junior year in the Commodores’ weekend rotation. Leaning heavily on his fastball, Bowker pitched well enough to land in the third round of the 2025 Draft, where the Phillies signed him for $700,000, a bit under slot. While his heater sat 92-93 mph and topped out at 95 at Vanderbilt, it plays up well beyond the velocity. Thanks to a drop-and-drive delivery and a low arm slot, he delivers the pitch from a low release height and a ton of carry. It rises above the barrel and he gets misses and chases on the offering. The rest of his repertoire isn’t as exciting, though he has average spin on his slider and it plays off his fastball pretty well. He has a slightly harder, shorter cutter that might just be a different version of his slider and he can sink a changeup but didn’t throw it much, something the Phillies plan to have him work on. While Bowker commands his fastball well, his control of his other offerings is not as consistent, though he does get a decent amount of chase out of the zone. He’ll need to refine his secondary stuff to have the chance to start long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lamkin was on Draft prospect lists as a prep pitcher in 2022, but he was considered unsignable away from his Texas A&M commitment. He went to college and was an immediate contributor, pitching in big SEC and NCAA moments. Lamkin was one of the best college lefty options in the 2025 Draft, and the Royals selected him with their Competitive Balance Round B pick at No. 71 overall. He stayed in Arizona after he was drafted and pitched in the Royals’ fall instructional league. With some funkiness in his delivery, Lamkin’s 91-93 mph fastball plays up quite a bit, but he also showed up to spring in ‘26 with a little more velo. He’s big and strong and put on some good weight over the offseason, which helps, so whether that sticks throughout the season remains to be seen. His above-average, 83-85 mph gyro slider might look a little cutter-ish, but it’s short and tight. Lamkin sells his 84-86 mph changeup well and is continuing to work on that pitch, and he added an upper-70s curveball when he joined the Royals to give him something with more depth against right-handed hitters. Lamkin’s delivery has some moving parts to it, but it helps his game; he hides the ball well, has a short arm action and it gets on hitters quickly. He’s a solid strike thrower, so the delivery doesn’t seem to hinder him much right now. Lamkin has a good foundation and is advanced as a college pitcher who knows what he’s doing on the mound. He receives high marks for the way he evaluates himself and his outings. As long as those secondaries keep developing, he has back-end rotation potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henderson was a two-time All-Mountain West First-Team selection during his time at Fresno State and was the Bulldogs’ Friday night starter as a junior in 2023, when he posted a 3.74 ERA with 100 strikeouts in 89 innings. The Cardinals took him in the eighth round that year and signed him above slot for $230,000. He enjoyed a solid first full season at two A-ball levels and held his own in the hitter-friendly Arizona Fall League to boost his status further. Henderson was the Texas League Pitcher of the Year in 2024 after finishing with a 2.59 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 134 strikeouts in 132 innings for Double-A Springfield. Standing 6-foot-2, the southpaw uses a diverse arsenal as the foundation for his success. The cornerstone of that is a fastball that took a velocity bump up to 93-94 mph and touching 96 in 2025. He can spot the heater well with carry up in the zone, driving above-average whiff rates, and makes the pitch work above its weight with a deceptive three-quarters arm slot. His 79-82 mph sweeping slider can be effective against batters from both sides, but a mid-80s changeup helps hold off splits issues the best. He doesn’t zone the cambio as well as the other two, but righties still couldn’t touch it for big impact. A mid-70s curveball and upper-80s cutter offer other (albeit less-used) looks. Henderson needs to live on the periphery of the zone, but in so doing, he hasn’t run into major issues with free passes at any pro stop yet in his career. The velo uptick made his future as a No. 5 starter more likely, but he hit a pause this spring with a flexor strain when he seemed ready to knock on St. Louis’ door.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Harber hit 54 homers in 206 college games between Georgia and North Carolina, he went undrafted before signing with the Yankees for $50,000 in July 2024. Though a wrist injury sidelined him for six weeks midseason, he still slashed .323/.420/.550 between two levels and ranked second in the Minors (minimum: 300 plate appearances) with a 173 wRC+. Sent to the Giants as part of a Trade Deadline deal for Camilo Doval, he terrorized the Arizona Fall League and led the developmental circuit with 12 extra-base hits in 17 games. A right-handed hitter, Harber generates high-end exit velocities and can drive balls out of the park from foul pole to foul pole. He doesn't pull or lift pitches consistently, however, so there's some question about how much his power will play at higher levels. He shows the patience to work counts and draw walks, though he does swing through some in-zone fastballs and struggles against sliders. While Harber has worked hard to improve his all-around game, almost all of his value will be derived from his bat. He's a limited athlete with well-below-average speed and average arm strength, which will make it tough for him to remain at third base. He has spent nearly as much time at first, a more viable option, while his lack of range makes the outfield corners a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Burlingame, Calif., Moss moved across the country to attend IMG Academy in Bradenton, Fla., when he was in eighth grade. He became a regular on the summer showcase circuit, including appearances at the East Coast Pro Showcase and the Area Code Games, and developed into one of the top-ranked Draft prospects in the state. The Rays reached into their backyard to select Moss with the 67th overall pick in the 2025 Draft, signing him for an above-slot bonus of $2,097,500. Moss’ hit tool is his finest trait, as he seemingly always found a way to get the barrel on the ball in high school despite a number of moving parts in his left-handed swing. He’s a twitchy athlete with plus bat speed, and he combines an ability to control the strike zone with an all-fields approach against all types of pitching. He’s hit-over-power right now, no surprise given his age and experience, but there is some raw power to tap into as he adds strength and learns to leverage his swing more effectively. Moss was primarily a center fielder in high school, and he has shown good instincts in the outfield. He has a solid arm, but the lack of plus speed could push him into a corner spot. The Rays generally give their outfielders a chance to prove they can stick in center, although they’re also quick to expose them to multiple spots in case a move is necessary. Time will tell if his bat can provide corner-outfield power, but the Rays clearly believed in his offensive upside enough to give him the chance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Thompson went undrafted out of high school in Texas in 2022 and instead headed to Vanderbilt, where he became a starter as a sophomore and the Friday night arm as a junior. He posted a 4.00 ERA and struck out 122 over 90 innings in his final spring as a Commodore, and his 32.1 percent strikeout rate ranked fifth-best among SEC arms (one spot ahead of Oklahoma’s Kyson Witherspoon). Thompson was selected by the Brewers in the second round of the Draft and signed for slot value at $1,560,200. The 6-foot southpaw doesn’t pop for velocity with a fastball around 91-94 mph (topping out at 96 in college), but it got incredible induced vertical break from his lowish release point. That, combined with the way he can hide the ball until late, led to a ton of whiff and chase on the four-seamer. He moved more toward a low-80s slider as a junior because it’s a breaking pitch he can throw in the zone more often than his upper-70s curveball. His low-80s changeup gets a ton of separation from the heater, leading to many empty swings in college, but pros may not chase it as much below the zone where the pitch lived frequently. Thompson’s control was solid in college thanks to his repeatable delivery, and if he can land in the zone with more intent, he could unlock perhaps above-average marks in that category in the Milwaukee system. A touch more velocity would send the fastball into easy plus territory with its movement metrics, but even as is, there could be enough here for a No. 4 starter profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known as Leandro Calderon when he signed for $10,000 in 2021, Lopez spent his first two pro seasons at home in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and missed most of 2024 with shoulder fatigue. He improved his conditioning afterward, which led to a breakout 2025 season that earned him a spot on the 40-man roster. He compiled a 2.40 ERA, .198 opponent average and 111 strikeouts in 101 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. Lopez can create quality depth on two different breaking balls, and his upper-80s slider supplanted his low-80s curveball as his best pitch last year. His fastball operates at 93-95 mph and touches out at 97, albeit with more downhill plane than life and a tendency to catch the heart of the plate too often. He's still learning to locate his mid-80s changeup where he wants but it misses bats with tumble when it's on. Getting in better shape allowed Lopez to repeat his delivery, provide consistent strikes and maintain his stuff better than he had previously. His upright delivery and high arm slot help him stay on top of his breaking pitches but detract from his fastball shape. Upgrading his heater and continuing to refine his control would help enhance his chances of becoming a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing his high school ball at Calvary Christian in Florida, Nelson headed to Florida State rather than entertain signing with the Phillies, who had taken him in the 39th round of the 2019 Draft. A three-year starter for the Seminoles, Nelson didn’t show a whole lot with the bat until 2021 when he tied for the Division I lead with 23 homers. That earned him several collegiate accolades and landed him in the Competitive Balance Round A, where the Reds gave him full slot ($2.1 million) to sign. His pro debut was uneventful and brief, as a thumb injury on his glove hand limited him to just 10 games and he struggled with the bat during his first full season in 2022. Nelson has an exciting power combination in his bat and arm that many teams love to see from catchers. He’s capable of being short to the ball and drive it to all fields, with his plate discipline leading to walks and good hitter’s counts that help him get to his plus power when he was at Florida State. With the power does come some swing-and-miss and there are some holes in his swing he’ll have to continue to address at the pro level. Nelson’s plus arm is an asset behind the plate and has helped him control the running game wherever he’s been. He’s also shown flashes of good receiving and blocking skills, though he’s a bit streaky defensively. He needs to keep trying to find consistency on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Oregon State, Forrester left campus with a career .326 average and a .970 OPS. A very strong junior season in 2023 made many scouts think he was one of the best college hitters on the West Coast in the class. The son of former Minor League infielder Gary Forrester, Garret went in the third round of the Draft and played briefly with full-season Bradenton during his pro debut after signing for an under-slot bonus of $772,500. Forrester is an advanced right-handed hitter who knows what he’s doing at the plate. He makes sound swing decisions and left Oregon State with more walks than strikeouts. He didn’t get to show it much during his stint in the Florida State League, but he has the ability to drive the ball to all fields with opposite-field power. He’s added some strength during the offseason, which hopefully will add to his power profile moving forward. Almost exclusively a first baseman in college, Forrester had seen a little time at third where his solid arm plays well, and the Pirates had him at the hot corner during his debut even though he’s not exactly fleet afoot. That will continue, as will another defensive wrinkle -- Forrester worked out at the Draft Combine behind the plate, and the Pirates have liked what they’ve seen from him at catcher, with plans to build him up and give him time there, first and third in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Hechavarria, a Cuba native, out of the Dominican Republic in June 2024, nearly three months after his 21st birthday. He got his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League shortly thereafter with the results one would expect for an older arm in that circuit (1.84 ERA, 57 strikeouts in 49 innings) and jumped stateside for 2025, first in the FCL before moving to Single-A and High-A. With a combined 2.28 ERA and strong peripherals over 86 2/3 innings, Hechavarria’s second season as a pro was a success in nearly every way. Hechavarria stands 6-foot-4, bringing plenty of mound presence, and he throws from a high release. His four-seam fastball touches 96-97 mph and is generally 93-95 with good carry out of the high slot with some armside run to boot. He’ll mix in a sinker around the same velo for a different look, too. An upper-80s slider actually acts as his primary weapon. It’s a tight offering with less than an inch of gloveside movement on average and it tunnels well off the heaters until it’s too late, diving below bats. It gets a ton of whiffs against lefties, helping Hechavarria run reverse splits despite a subpar changeup. Coming off a nice jump in workload, the Blue Jays could look to push Hechavarria past 100 innings this season, and he’s ready to be challenged more. He has seemed to improve as the seasons went on -- and with each promotion in 2025 -- which left the Blue Jays very impressed. If Hechavarria can miss more bats, this is a different conversation entirely, but he currently profiles as a back-end starter who could eat some serious innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones played football at Stanford, where he was a safety who played special teams, explaining his impressive speed, range in the outfield and pure strength. Once he focused on baseball as a sophomore, though, his ability began to shine through. He hit 18 homers and stole 14 bases for Stanford in 2021, played for Team USA that summer then turned things around as a junior to hit .324/.451/.664 with 21 homers in 65 games. As a result, the Rays selected him in the second round of the 2022 Draft and signed him for a full-slot bonus of $1,077,600. Jones has said he’s trying to “stop ‘athlete-ing’ baseball,” meaning he wants to further refine his all-around game. The biggest step will be cutting down his swing-and-miss rate, something that’s always been a part of his game but could be the only issue holding him back. But if he can hit enough to get to his power, pairing good swing decisions with his strong hands and pull-side power, there’s a potentially useful player here. Jones is close to maxed out physically, but he already has plus speed – with good instincts on the basepaths -- and raw power. Defensively, Jones plays center field like he’s in a one-high safety formation. He makes good reads and takes good routes to balls, with a fringy arm being the only drawback. Tampa Bay is also thrilled with Jones’ makeup, noting how he worked out with fellow prospect Xavier Isaac in Miami over the offseason. Maybe he settles into more of a platoon role eventually, but the Rays hope Jones can develop into an everyday center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hugus’ path has been anything but linear, leading to a variety of opinions about him from scouts, other than the 80-grade put on his mustache. A two-way standout at Cardinal Newman High in West Palm Beach, Fla., he began his college career at Cincinnati as both a reliever and left-side infielder before transitioning to full-time pitching. After uneven results, he transferred to Miami, where a strong showing in the Cape Cod League earned him a rotation opportunity. And he seized it, opening the year as the Hurricanes’ Saturday starter before moving into the Friday night role by March and ultimately landing with Seattle in the third round, signing for under-slot at $640,000. The Mariners will have to wait to see what kind of pitcher they acquired as he blew out his elbow early in his first Spring Training and required Tommy John surgery. He doesn’t overwhelm with pure velocity, but Hugus offers the foundation of a starter’s mix. His fastball typically sits 92-93 mph and will touch 95-96 mph, playing better than the radar gun suggests because hitters struggle to square it up. His mid-80s slider is currently his primary weapon, though some evaluators believe his mid-70s curveball -- added during his time on the Cape -- could develop into the more consistent swing-and-miss offering. He also flashes a mid-80s changeup that could round out a legitimate four-pitch arsenal. Seattle’s interest goes beyond the stat line. Internally, there’s belief that Hugus fits the mold of a “posted” college arm -- someone with innings under his belt and room for targeted development tweaks, once he returns to the mound. The Mariners see areas where modest velocity gains or pitch-shape refinements could unlock another level. Pair that with strong makeup, curiosity and a reputation as a good teammate, and there’s quiet optimism that Hugus could take a meaningful step forward once fully integrated into the organization’s pitching program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Things didn’t start clicking for Middleton as a pitching prospect until he got to Southern Mississippi, as his velocity and stock rose together. He was a solid reliever, albeit with command issues, as a sophomore, but really shot up boards with a very successful move into the rotation as a junior in 2025. After ranking second among all NCAA Division I pitchers with a 0.85 WHIP, he became the highest-drafted pitcher in school history when the Rockies took him No. 45 overall in the second round and signed him for $2.07 million. After a long college season that saw him top 100 innings, the Rockies didn’t have Middleton do much after signing. Middleton is an undersized right-hander who has the three-pitch mix to make a go as a starter. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph, sitting in the 93-95 mph range, and it can play above its velocity at times with his ability to both sink it or throw it with carry up in the zone. It gets a fair amount of miss and chase, but not nearly as much as his secondary offerings. His upper-80s slider has two-plane depth and is sometimes cutter-ish. Both that and his 86-88 mph tumbling and fading changeup miss a ton of bats both in and out of the zone. The six-foot Middleton isn’t the most physical hurler, but he’s athletic, repeats his delivery well and showed a vastly improved ability to find the zone compared to his time in the Southern Miss bullpen. The Rockies love that he pitches with a chip on his shoulder and is super-competitive, knowing that he’s going to hate whatever workload limitations they put on him during his first year of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Based on early returns, Lopez is the best prospect from Miami's 2023 international class. He signed out of the Dominican Republic for $650,000, the second-highest bonus in that crop, and surprised the Marlins by how quickly he acclimated to pro pitching. He homered three times in his first 11 contests in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and slashed .265/.327/.405 with 15 steals in his 49-game pro debut. As an amateur, Lopez attracted scouts with his defensive ability and he has the makings of a Gold Glove shortstop. He has good action and covers plenty of ground to both sides. He also has quick hands and solid to plus arm strength, and his tools would allow him to play several positions if needed. A switch-hitter who's proficient from both sides of the plate, Lopez has bat-to-ball ability and an all-fields approach but can get overly aggressive at the plate. He already displays some aptitude for driving the ball in the air, which could translate into 15-20 homers annually once he gets stronger. He possesses solid speed and looks to make things happen on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cali’s path to pro ball was long and winding. It started at Florida State during the COVID year and he redshirted, not appearing any games. He transferred to Hillsborough Community College and then caught fire at the College of Central Florida in 2022, slashing .438/.533/.826 with 17 homers, which caught the eye of the University of Arkansas. After posting a .923 OPS with the Razorbacks in 2023, the Mariners took him in the 16th round of the Draft and he quickly hit his way from Modesto to High-A Everett, finishing with 16 homers, 81 RBIs and a 128 wRC+. Cali’s numbers do come with the caveat that he was old for the levels, turning 24 last August, but he did show off some savvy from the right side of the plate. It’s not premium bat speed or pop, but there is a little power there and he gives professional at-bats. The strikeouts were a little high (27 percent) but he also drew a ton of walks (14.3 percent). He’s not a slug on the basepaths, but he’s just fringy in terms of his speed. After playing third base almost exclusively with Arkansas, that is where Cali has seen most of his time in his year-plus of pro ball. He might be a little stretched thin there defensively, but he’s the kind of gamer who’ll do anything to help his team win. He’s probably best defensively at first, and he’ll keep getting reps there, but he’s unlikely to have the thump to profile as a right-handed regular at the spot. His best chance is to move around a little bit and hope he gets to enough impact to find a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After an uneven college career that began at Texas Tech, the Orioles drafted Wells in the fourth round out of Texas State in 2023, betting they could add polish to Wells’ tantalizing raw stuff. He struggled in his first full season of pro ball, finishing with a 6.71 ERA and .280 BAA over 60 ⅓ IP, but seemed to turn a corner last season following offseason workouts with Nathan Eovaldi. Wells returned to the mound throwing harder and proved more durable, seeing much better results by pitching his way to Triple-A by the end of the year. Wells is a right-hander with a bulldog mentality on the mound who throws everything hard. His fastball lives in the upper-90s and can hit triple-digits, and Wells has the ability to ride it up in the zone or sink it to generate ground balls. He’ll employ three secondary offerings with a low-80s curve that features depth and a harder sweeper, and he swapped in a 90 mph cutter last year in place of a changeup he grew out of the habit of using. Wells commanded everything better in his second season and throws enough strikes, but there is also a feeling his pure stuff is good enough to miss more bats than he did. Though the Orioles have developed him as a starter, Wells only completed more than five innings in two of his first 46 pro starts. His premium fastball and solid breaking stuff could be nasty in relief, and may destine Wells for more of a multi-inning fireman or swingman type of role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Becker’s path to pro ball is rooted in baseball family ties and projection. A native of Thiells, New York, he crossed into New Jersey to attend Don Bosco Prep -- the same program that produced big leaguer Caden Dana -- following in the footsteps of his older brother, Eric. Their father, Jeff, played at Duke and logged time in Cleveland’s Minor League system, giving Nick a foundation in the game from an early age. Seattle believed enough in his upside to select him in the second round and sign him away from a commitment to the University of Virginia for $2.75 million, well above slot value. At 6-foot-4 with an athletic, projectable build, Becker already pairs present skill with long-term ceiling. A right-handed hitter, he shows advanced bat-to-ball ability and mature hitting instincts, consistently finding the barrel and making in-game adjustments. His swing is fluid and under control, and there’s confidence that more impact will come as he adds strength and learns to better leverage the ball in the air. The expectation is at least average future power without compromising his contact ability. Becker is a solid runner with room to grow into plus speed as he continues to mature physically. Defensively, he offers a strong foundation -- smooth actions, reliable hands and plenty of arm for the left side. All signs point to him sticking at shortstop long term, and he spent a few weeks with longtime Mariners infield coach Perry Hill in Arizona in early February. With his blend of tools, makeup and projection, Becker slots comfortably into Seattle’s deep infield pipeline with a chance to rise quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $290,000 at age-17 out of the Dominican Republic, Sanchez put together his first big year in the system, climbing all the way from the Arizona Complex League to High-A Everett. Why he’s been so under-the-radar and finally found himself is largely rooted in the Mariners’ player development program, which has constantly preached persistence and patience with the middle infielder. After he signed, Sanchez’s hips got a little wider and the defense and range took a dip. But he arrived in 2022 in much better shape, and it translated well into his profile at shortstop. He’s blossomed into a legit defender at the premium position -- arguably the best middle infielder in the system, which could greatly benefit his long-term trajectory. Beyond the glove, a big part of his step forward was simply trusting his approach at the plate. He may not hit for as high of an average as he progresses, but the sneaky power could lead to some surprising production that, coupled with his strong defense, will make up for it, and he’s definitely a high-ceiling player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high schooler who saw his velocity spike during his senior year, raising his Draft profile in 2023, Ellwanger moved on to Dallas Baptist knowing he’d be eligible again in two years as a sophomore. A flexor strain in his elbow forced him out for a couple of months as a freshman, though he made up for lost time with a solid Cape Cod League performance that summer. He missed a ton of bats, albeit with spotty command, showing off enough ingredients for the Twins to take him in the third round of the 2025 Draft and sign him for $1 million, a bit over slot. Tall, projectable and athletic, the 6-foot-4 Ellwanger has some exciting raw stuff and can be dominant when he’s locked in. His fastball sat in the 95-96 mph range last year and flirted with triple digits and he’s capable of throwing it with good carry and armside run. His best secondary offering is his low-80s curve, a pitch that elicited a 41-percent miss rate, according to Synergy. He can land his mid-80s slider for strikes, but it got hit hard in 2025, so he started trying out a harder, low-90s cutter. He has a firm, seldom-used changeup as well. Ellwanger needs innings to develop from pure thrower to pitcher, starting with learning to repeat his delivery and compete in the strike zone more consistently. The Twins will work with him on some usage patterns to find the right mix, knowing there could be more velocity to come as he fills out. He has the stuff to pitch in a rotation if he can hone his command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mace almost signed with the Reds for fourth-round money as a 12th-round pick out of a Florida high school, and he could have gone in the first two rounds in 2020 if his price tag hadn't scared off teams in that shortened five-round Draft. After returning for a fourth college season at Florida, he improved his slider/cutter and posted a career-best strikeout rate of 11.3 per nine innings. Signed for a slightly over-slot $1.1 million in the supplemental second round, he'll make his pro debut in 2022. Mace struggled to find a reliable breaking ball in his first three years with the Gators, but now his mid-80s slider/cutter is his best pitch and grades as plus at its best. While his four-seam fastball can reach 97 mph, it's fairly straight and gets hit, and his low-90s two-seamer with sink is more effective. His 78-82 mph curveball has regressed and he doesn't have much trust in a mid-80s changeup that's too firm and has modest fade. While Mace lacks overpowering stuff, he uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create good extension that enables his pitches to get on hitters more quickly than expected. His track record of throwing strikes helps his chances of making it as a back-of-the-rotation starter, though he'll likely need a second better-than-average pitch to go with his slider/cutter. He'll be 23 when he throws his first professional pitch, so he could move quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliz made a strong first impression in 2021 during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he had an .813 OPS and five homers in 46 games. Signed in 2019 for $900,000, the richest contract among that international class for Seattle, Feliz is still growing into his body and filling out, which has made him a more physical player in recent years. As his body continues to mature, it’s possible he can emerge with 55s for his tools across the board. None of those tools necessarily play above the other, making him one of the Mariners’ more well-rounded outfield prospects. Described as very smart and instinctual, Feliz has the potential to stick in center field due to those attributes. At the plate, Feliz’s swing mechanics are somewhat inconsistent and remain a work in progress. It’s not the cleanest or most compact swing and there are a lot of moving parts, especially in his lower half, but despite those hiccups, he showed more feel for hitting than scouts anticipated. However, it’s likely that he profiles more as a power than average hitter long term. Because of all of his tools projecting as above-average, Feliz probably has more upside than floor. But because his swing has a ways to go, his timeline for the Majors is probably a little longer too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Cutter: 50 | Splitter: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Only three players have ever been drafted out of Cary-Grove HS in Illinois, and just two have ever signed. Both enter the 2026 season as Brewers: Major Leaguer Quinn Priester (2019) and Dorchies. The latter was much less heralded coming out of the prep ranks than his predecessor and went in the 10th round of the 2024 Draft before signing away from a University of Illinois-Chicago commitment with a $162,500 bonus. Only 17 on Draft Day, Dorchies came flying out of the gate in his first full season, blowing past the Arizona Complex League and reaching Single-A Carolina by mid-June. He finished with a 2.74 ERA, a 1.05 WHIP and 89 strikeouts over 82 innings between both spots. Dorchies checks in at 6-feet-5 and uses that size to generate around 7 feet of extension, putting his five-pitch mix right on top of hitters. His four-seamer and sinker only sit in the 90-93 mph range right now, but the ride on the former and the run on the latter help them play beyond the velo. Still only 19 for all of his second full season, Dorchies could stand to add strength and get that heat closer to the mid-90s with regularity in time. His low-80s, low-spin splitter dives late to generate whiffs at his best rates, but he’s been more focused on throwing a low-80s sweeping slider as his most-used secondary. An upper-80s cutter serves as a bridge pitch. The teenager’s walk rate inflated about four ticks once he got away from the complex, but he doesn’t overthrow and should deliver a decent amount of strikes, especially if that strength comes around. Dorchies already displays desirable traits and promising future projection for a 10th-round pick and could become one of Milwaukee’s better development stories by the time he reaches The Show.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gelof is following the same path that took his older brother Zack to the big leagues with the Athletics, going to Virginia as a relatively unheralded recruit and blossoming into a second-round pick. Jake set Cavaliers records for single-season and career homers (23, 48) and RBI (90, 186) in 2023 before signing for $1,334,400. Rusty and not in peak shape after a layoff between the end of the college season and his pro debut, he hit .225/.314/.433 with five homers in 30 Single-A games. One of the best power prospects in the 2023 Draft, Gelof puts a charge into the ball with his combination of bat speed, strength and loft in his right-handed swing. He has an aggressive approach and focuses on launching balls in the air, yet he also uses the entire field and doesn't chase pitches or strike out excessively. He's a 30-homer threat who could hit for a decent average and he'll draw walks if pitchers won't challenge him. Gelof has below-average speed and lacks athleticism, so most of his value will come from his bat. There are questions about his ability to remain at third base, where he has been error-prone and his range and arm may be a bit light. If he has to move, left field and first base would be his fallbacks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his pandemic-shortened 2020 season saw him pitch sparingly at Florida State, Hubbart made a successful move into the Seminoles' rotation in 2021. He really put himself on the prospect map with a very strong performance in the Cape Cod League that summer, then served as FSU’s effective Saturday starter in 2022, showing enough for the Reds to take him in the third round of the Draft, where he signed for $522,500. As a lefty from the ACC, the easy thing might be to compare Hubbart to new organization-mate Andrew Abbott, though while the two have similar builds and resumes, they have very different personalities. Hubbart will use a three- or four-pitch mix to set up hitters well. His fastball only averaged around 90 mph in his last year at Florida State and topped out at 91 during his brief time with Single-A Daytona after signing, but it plays up a bit beyond the velocity thanks to solid spin rates and carry up in the zone. He can add and subtract from his stuff, manipulating his breaking stuff and showing a distinct curve and slider at times, though he showcased more of the latter during his pro debut. He does a nice job of killing spin on his 79-80 mph changeup. Hubbart profiles as a prototypical college lefty, one who has already impressed the Reds with his feel for pitching. He’s become a very good strike thrower, one who might have a ceiling as a No. 4 or 5 starter but could reach further if he adds some velocity or improves his secondary offerings with pro instruction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Washington state, Watson spent one season apiece at Cal Lutheran and San Joaquin Delta College and got drafted by the Mariners in the 20th round of the 2023 Draft before heading to USC. He moved from the Trojans' bullpen to their starting rotation, and he flashed enough promising stuff in the longer role for the Mets to take him in the seventh round and sign him for around slot at $281,300 in 2024. Watson climbed from Single-A to Double-A in his first full season and finished with a 2.60 ERA over 121 1/3 innings; his 142 strikeouts were fourth-most in the New York system. Despite the increased workload in the Minors, Watson experienced a velocity bump across the board in 2025. He averaged around 95 mph with a pair of fastballs, and his four-seamer shows promising ride and a flat approach angle from a relatively low release. His mid-80s slider gives him a gloveside option that can force opponents to expand the zone, while his upper-80s change moves even more horizontally armside. Because of the latter, he ran reverse splits last year, holding lefties to a .186 average and .561 OPS. Watson also shows an 88-91 mph cutter for a bridge pitch, but it can get hit hard with limited movement. With some length in his delivery, Watson lacks pinpoint accuracy with his arsenal, and he walked more than 10 percent of his batters faced at each level in 2025. As things currently stand, he may lack a true plus pitch, though it’s possible the fastball velo would play up in shorter stints. Still, a bevy of above-average options will keep getting him starting looks in a system loaded with upper-level arms.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest bargain in the Dodgers' loaded 2023 international class, Nieves signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic that March. He repeated the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, logging a 5.43 ERA in two seasons there before taking off in his U.S. debut last summer. He was one of the more unhittable pitchers in the lower Minors, holding opponents to a .171 average with a 27 percent strikeout rate between Rookie ball and Single-A. Nieves' fastball velocity made a jump in 2025, sitting in the mid-90s and reaching 99 mph, and he found more success after switching from a fairly straight four-seamer to a two-seamer with run and sink. His mid-80s slider features devastating sweep at its best and he can also tighten it into a harder cutter. His nascent mid-80s changeup can flash some intriguing fade and sink. Nieves has a quick, whippy arm action and a lean 6-foot-3 frame that can add plenty of muscle, so there may be more velocity to come.
