mlb_pipeline.text: Repeating the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League used to be a developmental kiss of death. But it’s been happening more in recent years, with fewer short-season options in the United States and sometimes it really helps a young prospect figure some things out. Arguelles, whose $700,000 bonus in January 2024 was the second-highest the Rockies handed out during that international signing period, held his own during his pro debut in the DSL the summer after signing, but without any impact. He stayed for a second summer, and after adding some strength, earned DSL MVP honors after winning the batting title (.422) and leading the circuit in OPS (1.180). Arguelles hit so well the Rockies considered flying him stateside last summer, but they’re excited to have him in country now. He already has a very strong feel for hitting, using the whole field. He grinds out at-bats, takes walks and shows excellent balance at the plate. The left-handed hitter is going to keep getting stronger and has mistake-type power with a hard rate of contact, but it’s more gap than over-the-fence kind of pop. While he’s not a runner, he has solid instincts defensively and his average arm can play up a little when he attacks the ball. He’s played mostly center field thus far, and the Rockies will still give him reps there to maximize his athleticism, but he’ll start getting time at all three spots, with a corner the most likely home for him long term if he develops into a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shoulder problems limited Ingrassia to 10 innings in two seasons at San Diego State before he transferred to Cal State Fullerton and became the Titans' closer in 2023. A 14th-round pick that July, he dominated in his 2024 pro debut, topping all Minor League pitchers who worked as many as his 58 1/3 innings in strikeout rate (40 percent) while finishing second in strikeout minus walk rate (31 percent) and compiling a 1.85 ERA. He missed six weeks in the second half of that season with elbow inflammation, then didn't pitch after April last season because of more shoulder woes, though he did return for the Arizona Fall League. Ingrassia's fastball has below-average velocity, sitting at 91-94 mph and reaching 95, but it plays better than that because he operates from a low slot with crossfire and extension and creates plenty of carry, armside run and deception. He's throwing a harder, tighter slider in 2026, working with a mid-80s breaker and occasionally turning it into an upper-80s cutter. He produces a ton of fade on his mid-80s changeup, generating a lot of empty swings but also having difficulty landing it for strikes. Ingrassia doesn't have a pretty delivery and throws with some effort, yet he generally throws strikes. He began his pro career as a reliever before earning an opportunity as a starter. His lack of size and durability probably will land him back in the bullpen, though he could move quickly in that role if he stays healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shoulder problems held Ingrassia to 10 innings in two seasons at San Diego State before he moved to Cal State Fullerton and became the Titans' closer in 2023. A 14th-round pick that July, he dominated in his 2024 pro debut while earning Single-A Carolina League All-Star honors. He led all Minor League pitchers who worked as many as his 58 1/3 innings in strikeout rate (40 percent) while ranking second in strikeout minus walk rate (31 percent) and posted a 1.85 ERA. Though Ingrassia's fastball sits at 91-93 mph and tops out at 95, it plays better than its below-average velocity because he throws from a low slot with crossfire and extension that create sink, horizontal action and deception. His low-80s slider has similar movement with more break and works as a back-foot pitch against right-handers. His best offering is a plus mid-80s changeup that fades in the opposite direction as his heater and slider. Ingrassia throws with some effort and doesn't have the most picturesque delivery, yet he's able to trick hitters without costing himself control. He began 2024 as a reliever before getting stretched out as a starter, thriving in both roles but missing six weeks in July and August with elbow inflammation. His size and durability questions probably will land him in the bullpen, but he could move quickly in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the harder-throwing pitchers in the 2021 international class, Maldonado touched 92 mph before signing for $145,600 out of Venezuela as a 17-year-old. He touched 97 mph during his U.S. debut the following year and 99 when he advanced to full-season ball in 2023. He blew out his elbow that July and had Tommy John surgery in December that sidelined him for all of 2024, but returned to reach 101 mph in Single-A last season. Now that he has regained his health, Maldonado sits at 96-99 mph with high spin rates, late hop and some armside run on his fastball. He didn't dominate Single-A hitters with his heater, however, as they slashed .261/.404/.326 against it in 2025. They had much more trouble handling his 82-85 mph slider, which features formidable sweep. Though he has been a starter to this point, Maldonado is a two-pitch guy who projects as a reliever, possibly a closer if he can learn to harness his stuff. He has a compact arm action that hides the ball from batters, but he has trouble keeping his mechanics in sync and logged a 16 percent walk rate last year. He carries at least 50 pounds more than his listed 170 and will have to watch his conditioning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maldonado flashed a low-90s fastball when he signed for $145,600 out of Venezuela in 2021 and pushed it as high as 97 mph during his U.S. debut the following year. He reached 99 mph when he reached full-season ball in 2023 but blew out his elbow in late July and had Tommy John surgery in December. After rehabbing all of last year, he'll be ready to return to the mound at the beginning of this season. Before he got hurt, Maldonado was sitting at 95-97 mph with late hop and some armside run on his fastball. His 82-85 mph slider was more unhittable, generating a 54 percent swing-and-miss rate against Single-A hitters. He didn't show much feel for his fading upper-80s changeup, which was too firm and rarely found the strike zone. Maldonado's compact arm action hides the ball from hitters, making him even tougher to hit. He needs time to figure out his control and command and very well could end up in the bullpen, but he'd have closer upside if he does. At least 50 pounds heavier than his listed weight of 170, he'll have to stay on top of his conditioning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Miller was a Wisconsin high schooler, scouts viewed him as a less physical but more athletic version of his older brother Owen, who has seen big league action with three teams in the past five seasons. After the Twins signed him for $1.7 million as a 2021 supplemental first-round choice, he has developed into a better defender and lesser hitter than anticipated. Swapped to the Dodgers for Manuel Margot and infield prospect Rayne Doncon in February 2024, he slashed .255/.290/.352 between Double-A and Triple-A last year. One of the best defensive shortstops in the Minors, Miller has all the ingredients to win a Gold Glove in the Majors. He has fluid actions, range in every direction, a strong and accurate arm, soft hands and good instincts. He's dependable too, committing just 11 errors in 212 games at short during the past two seasons. A switch-hitter who's more productive as a righty, Miller shows bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate but undermines his offensive game by chasing way too many pitches. While he doesn't strike out excessively, his aggressiveness cuts into his walk totals and produces a lot of weak groundball contact, and he offers well below-average power and just average speed. The best-case scenario is that he develops into something similar to World Series hero Miguel Rojas, as he'll have a difficult time cracking a loaded lineup in Los Angeles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Rockies infielder Owen Miller, Noah profiled as a less physical but more athletic version of his sibling when he was coming through the Wisconsin high school ranks. Since signing with the Twins for $1.7 million as a 2021 supplemental first-rounder, he has provided much more defense and less offense than expected. Traded to the Dodgers for Manuel Margot and infield prospect Rayne Doncon in February 2024, he slashed .244/.318/.315 between High-A and Double-A last season. Some club officials believe Miller could win a Gold Glove in the big leagues this season if given the opportunity. With his slick actions, strong and accurate arm, soft hands and finely calibrated internal clock, there's not a play he can't make at shortstop. He's as reliable as he is spectacular, committing just six errors in 123 starts at short in 2024. A switch-hitter, Miller makes consistent contact but has provided little impact from either side of the plate. The Dodgers hope they can help him develop double-digit home run pop by improving his swing and approach, but he slugged just .317 in his first four pro seasons. He has average speed with good instincts on the bases, though he was a bit slower than that last year while playing through a meniscus injury in his left knee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Miller was a Wisconsin high schooler, scouts considered him a less physical version of his older brother, big league utilityman Owen. Since signing with the Twins for a below-slot $1.7 million as a supplemental first-round pick in 2021, Noah has been more dazzling in the field and less productive at the plate than expected. The Dodgers acquired him and cleared some needed 40-man roster space in February by sending Manuel Margot and infield prospect Rayne Doncon to Minnesota. Miller won a Minor League Gold Glove in 2023 and is equipped to do the same in the Majors. He can make all the plays at shortstop with smooth actions, a strong and accurate arm, soft and reliable hands and an outstanding internal clock. He's a reliable and spectacular defender who could fit almost anywhere on the diamond if he winds up in a utility role like his brother. Though Miller batted just .220/.326/.318 in his first three pro seasons, Los Angeles hopes to unlock more impact by helping him improve his swing and his approach. He's a switch-hitter with bat speed from both sides of the plate and shows the patience to draw walks, but he makes a lot of soft contact and rarely drives the ball with authority. He's an average runner with good instincts on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller is trying to follow in the footsteps of older brother Owen, who was a big league regular for the Guardians in 2022. The younger Miller was the Twins’ pick in the 2021 Competitive Balance Round A, signing for $1.7 million. The Wisconsin high school standout showed some signs of an excellent approach at the plate, albeit without much impact, while playing strong defense in his first full season of pro ball with Single-A Fort Myers in 2022. There are ingredients for Miller to be a strong all-around infielder. The switch-hitter controls the zone well, drawing walks at an impressive clip, but as often as he was able to work counts, he wasn’t able to show an ability to do damage from either side. Some of that might come with added strength, and fatigue was certainly a factor, but Miller has also worked to make adjustments at the plate to create better angles and more impact. His right-handed swing had improved by the end of last season, but his left-handed one still needs some improvement. Miller’s calling card will always be his defense. His tools and plus instincts will enable him to play shortstop for a long time, with a strong, accurate arm and the chance to eventually be a plus defender at the premium position. Those bullish on Miller’s all-around skills look at fellow Badger state prep product Gavin Lux, who had modest offensive production in his first full season of pro ball then took off with the bat a year later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins went very college-heavy in the 2021 Draft, with 19 of their 21 picks coming from the four-year or junior college ranks. The first two, however, were high schoolers, with Chase Petty going in the first round, followed by Miller, from the Wisconsin prep ranks, going No. 36 overall. The younger brother of Guardians infielder Owen, Miller signed for $1.7 million and made his pro debut in the Florida Complex League last summer. When most talk about Miller, the first things that come up are his baseball IQ and instincts on both sides of the ball. While his contact skills were a bit behind as he adjusted to the speed of the game, he did show a good approach from both sides of the plate. He has shown the ability to make consistent contact in the past with a good bat path. He focused on his left-handed swing during the offseason as well as strengthening his lower half, and he did add good weight. As he works through minor tweaks in his swing, don’t be surprised to see more pop, though it’s hard to know yet where the hit-power balance will end up. Miller shows very good awareness on the dirt. While he’s not a burner, those instincts lead to good jumps and solid range. He has a good arm and a quick release with every chance to stick at the premium position for a long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barriga signed for only $20,000 out of Mexico in January 2022 but pushed himself into notability with a strong debut in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old that year. A broken leg limited him to only 10 stateside games the following summer before he picked right back up in 2024, moving as high as Single-A Visalia as a teenager. He really struggled in his return to the California League last season, hitting just .199 with a 28.8 percent strikeout rate and 83 wRC+ over 99 games, but he's been much more productive at High-A Hillsboro to begin his age-21 campaign in ’26. The catcher may stand only 5-foot-9, but he can be a real standout to watch behind the plate. An above-average runner on the basepaths, he moves well behind the dish and often looks fluid at such an important position. This comes to bear most on steal attempts, during which Barriga gets into throwing position quickly and often delivers a throw right on target for the easy tag for his infielder. As of May 2026, his career caught-stealing rate was 43 percent, and that’s been consistent throughout his time in the Minors. A right-handed hitter, Barriga often flicks the bat in preparation for the pitch before getting into a leg raise in his load. He appears to be swinging with more intent in the Northwest League this season, and his power is ticking up as a result. He may never be a big homer threat given his size, but his swing and approach are so tailored to lift and pull that he could reach double-digit homers with everyday at-bats. Barriga is Rule 5-eligible this offseason, and his defense alone could get him a 40-man spot or Rule 5 look from another club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just a $20,000 addition out of Mexico in January 2022, Barriga immediately put up solid numbers in the Dominican Summer League that year with a .380 on-base percentage and 117 wRC+ over 42 games. He was going to make for an interesting follow as he headed stateside, but a broken leg ended his 2023 campaign after only 10 games in the Arizona Complex League. He returned to the ACL in ’24 and looked no worse for wear with a .276/.362/.432 line, four homers and 12 steals in 46 games. He joined Single-A Visalia for a seven-game spin after the ACL postseason. Just 5-foot-9, Barriga brings above-average speed to the table, a rarity for a full-time catcher. He could still learn to pick his stolen-base spots a little better, having gone 12-for-17 in his attempts in ’24, but no other qualified backstop on a domestic complex circuit had more than five thefts last year. He utilizes that athleticism well with good movement behind the plate, even for a smaller target, and his plus arm strength consistently nails attempted basestealers. Entering 2025, he has a 49.5 percent caught-stealing rate in his career. With a smaller strike zone, Barriga hasn’t punched out much yet in his career, but he was exposed for a high chase rate in that first bite of the California League. His bat-to-ball skills can make up for that, and his speed can help him beat out infield hits. He’ll need them with below-average power from the right side. Barriga will be 20 for the entire 2025 season as he tries to nail down his place as a potential athletic catcher for Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top player in the Angels’ 2023 international signing class, Morrobel received $900,000 to sign. Perceived to be one of the better shortstops in the class and ranked on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list, Morrobel had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing and was off to a good start during his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League, but he hurt his shoulder diving for a ball and was shut down after just 15 games. A switch-hitter, Morrobel has an extreme hit-over-power profile from both sides of the plate. He makes a ton of contact with good barrel control, striking out in only nine percent of plate appearances in his brief career so far. He needs to add strength to his frame so he can impact the ball a little. He has just seven extra-base hits in 57 professional games entering 2025, and his flat swing has led to too much groundball contact. It does look like Morrobel will be able to stay at shortstop long term. The arm is now plus, and while he’s an average runner, he has good actions and instincts for the premium position. With a clean bill of health, he’ll play this season at age 19, and there's hope that there’s a little more juice in his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels have never been shy about spending on the international market, often bringing in high-end players with seven-figure bonuses, something they’ve done in six of he last seven signing periods. The one exception was in 2023, but it’s not like they took the year off. They inked Morrobel, a Top 50 prospect in that class according to MLB Pipeline, for $900,000, and then saw him have a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League. Since signing, Morrobel has made a ton of contact from both sides of the plate. He’s slightly better left-handed, but he puts the ball in play from both sides. He has very good barrel control and delivers professional at-bats. There’s no power to speak of yet, with a line-drive approach, but he’s starting to grow into his body and there could be some thump to come. He’s a very aggressive hitter who rarely strikes out, but he also doesn’t draw many walks. Morrobel is an average runner, maybe a tick above, and is able to steal a base. It looks like he’s going to be able to stick at shortstop, with excellent actions and instincts, footwork and a potentially plus arm in the future. There’s some projection here, and if he can impact the ball more, he could grow into a legitimate everyday shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins gave Mercedes, one of the highest-ranked outfielders in the 2022 international signing class, $1.7 million to sign in January of that year, banking on his raw offensive tools. He's shown glimpses, performing well in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then struggling stateside the following summer in the Florida Complex League. The next two years saw him hit well in the FCL but fail to figure out the Single-A Florida State League, with swing-and-miss troubles being a particular problem. The 2026 season opened as a different story, as he dominated FSL pitching and earned a bump up to High-A Cedar Rapids in May. Mercedes can be a very dangerous hitter from the right side of the plate, showing off outstanding bat speed and raw power he can get to, especially when he stays with his approach. The power has shown up mostly to his pull side, and when he's locked in, he limits the whiffs and draws a lot of walks, something he was doing well during the start of this season. While Mercedes have had some injuries that have hampered him in the past, and he might have slowed down a touch, but he's still an above-average runner who knows how to steal a base. He's still getting plenty of time in center field, and his plus arm -- he had 10 assists in 2025 -- works well from right field, where he continues to get reps. Still only 21 for all of this season, the Twins are hopeful Mercedes is starting to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since joining the Twins in January 2022 for $1.7 million as an outfielder ranked in the top 20 of that year’s Top 50 international prospects list, Mercedes has shown off some very impressive tools in fits and bursts. He put up good numbers in the Dominican Summer League after signing, but struggled during his U.S. debut in the Florida Complex League in 2023. A return to the FCL went extremely well a year ago, earning a bump up to full-season Fort Myers, but he struggled there in a very small sample size. When he’s locked in, Mercedes has looked like a very dangerous right-handed hitter. He has excellent bat speed with a ton of raw power to tap into when he sticks to a gameplan. In the DSL and last year in the FCL, he made better swing decisions, limited his swing-and-miss and worked counts well to draw a lot of walks. When he got his feet wet for 10 games in full-season ball, the strikeouts spiked. Mercedes was nursing a quad strain at the end of the year that likely hampered him. Injuries have held back his development, including a minor hamstring issue during his debut and a shoulder injury that plagued him in 2023 and at the start of the 2024 season. He’s slowed down a touch, but he’s going to keep seeing a lot of time in center field while his plus arm would work well in right. For now, the focus will be for him to put in a full, healthy season of at-bats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Puerto Rico but raised in the Dominican Republic, Mercedes was one of the top players on the international market when the signing period opened in January 2022. The Twins gave him $1.7 million to join the organization and he pushed past a hamstring issue to be one of the best offensive performers in the Dominican Summer League, finishing with a .975 OPS. His move to the United States and the Florida Complex League in 2023 did not go as well as he struggled with his approach while dealing with a nagging shoulder issue all summer. The Twins are optimistic they’ll see more of the DSL version of Mercedes now that he’s fully done rehabbing his right shoulder. He has plenty of tools to tap into, starting with outstanding bat speed. As he matures, the 6-foot-2 outfielder should grow into a whole lot of home run power, especially if he can get back to a solid gameplan at the plate, having shown better pitch recognition and swing decisions in the Dominican. Mercedes runs very well and is aggressive on the basepaths -- he stole 30 bags in 41 DSL games in 2022 -- and he has the chance to stick in center field. He did see some time in right in the FCL, which could become his eventual home if he outgrows center. Assuming his shoulder bounces back, he has the kind of hose that could fit well there and could grow into the corner outfield run-producing offensive profile as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2022 international signing period opened, Mercedes was one of the most highly rated outfielders in the class. A Puerto Rican native who grew up in the Dominican Republic, thus making him eligible to sign, received $1.7 million from the Twins when things got going in mid-January. Though he was initially slowed by a hamstring issue, he dominated the Dominican Summer League during his debut, finishing in the top 10 in batting average, slugging percentage, OPS and stolen bases. Mercedes is a veritable tool chest and it was encouraging to see him access them in competition right out of the gate. The projectable 6-foot-2 outfielder has tremendous raw power and impressed evaluators with his swing decisions in the DSL, showing a natural feel for the barrel and some strike-zone knowledge, even if his swing and overall approach are still a bit raw. It’s more extra-base thump right now, but there’s a good chance that will develop into plenty of over-the-fence pop as he physically matures and continues to develop his game plan. He runs well and is aggressive on the basepaths. Big and physical, Mercedes will continue to play as much center field as possible as he comes stateside. There is a chance he’ll outgrow the position and need to slide to a corner, but his easily plus arm, not to mention his potential offensive production, should profile fine in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of four baseball-playing brothers, Southisene has a twin (Tee) who pitches at CC of Southern Nevada, a younger sibling (Tate) whom the Braves drafted in 2025's first round and an even younger brother (Troy) who's a 2026 prep prospect committed to Oregon State. A fourth-rounder in 2024, Ty was one of the least physical players in his class but earned an over-slot $1 million bonus thanks to his high baseball IQ and long track record of performing well with USA Baseball and on the showcase circuit. He batted .244/.387/.276 with 41 steals in 90 Single-A games during his pro debut, ranking fifth in the Carolina League in runs (69) and on-base percentage. Southisene employs a very patient and sometimes passive approach to make a lot of contact, especially against fastballs, and get on base. But his flat right-handed swing and utter lack of strength resulted in the third-worst isolated power (.032) and seventh-worst ground-ball rate (60 percent) in the full-season Minors last year. He can put the bat on the ball vs. secondary pitches but rarely hits them with any authority, slashing .159/.261/.167 against them in 2025. Southisene's profile is similar to Nick Allen's with better on-base skills and quickness but not quite the Gold Glove-caliber defense. Not only does he have solid speed and twitch athleticism, but he also has the instincts to make the most of them. He compensates for his average arm strength with a quick release and was drafted as a shortstop, though he spent all of his time in Single-A at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Southisene was one of the least physical players in the 2024 Draft class at 5-foot-9 and 170 pounds, he stood out with his high baseball IQ and long track record of performance on the showcase circuit and with USA Baseball. The Cubs popped him in the fourth round and paid him an over-slot $1 million bonus to lure him away from a Tennessee commitment. His twin brother Tee is a right-hander at Southern California and younger sibling Tate was the Braves' 2025 first-round pick. More advanced than most prep products, Southisene has a disciplined approach and a penchant for using the opposite field. He has a good feel for the barrel, though his relatively flat right-handed swing and lack of strength may cap his power production at 10 homers per season and he has made next to no impact at the plate in his pro debut. He lapses into swinging for the fences at times and must recognize that his role is to make contact and get on base. Southisene's instincts allow him to make the most of his solid speed and twitchy athleticism on the bases and in the field. He has quick hands and feet and he makes up for merely average arm strength with a fast release. Though he was drafted as a shortstop, Chicago's system is overflowing with shortstop prospects, so he has spent 2025 at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes slow and steady can win the race in player development. That’s what the Phillies are hoping is true with Graves, who they took as a raw high school pitching prospect back in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft. There have been some bumps along the way, like with his pro debut in the Florida Complex League in 2023, but he bounced back with a move to Single-A Clearwater in 2024. Another rung up the ladder in High-A Jersey Shore in 2025, Graves started slowly, with a 6.50 ERA, .270 BAA and 1.83 WHIP through June, but he turned a corner once July hit, posting a 1.93 ERA, .189 BAA and 1.18 WHIP for the remainder of the season. A 6-foot-6 southpaw, Graves’ fastball typically sits around 90-91 mph, topping out at 94-95 mph, and he’ll throw both a four-seamer up in the zone and an occasional two-seamer with sink, though he’s yet to grow into more consistent velocity. His bread-and-butter is his ability to spin the baseball, with elite-level spin rates on his breaking stuff, an upper-70s sweeper and a harder cutter-like slider, both of which miss a lot of bats. Graves has a low-80s changeup that can be effective against right-handed hitters, but the Phillies are working with him to commit to throwing his best pitch -- that slider -- against hitters on both sides of the plate. He’s going to need to be more consistent in the strike zone to remain a starter, though it would be interesting to see if he gains a few ticks on the fastball in shorter stints and uses that slider to neutralize lefties.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies rolled the dice in the 2022 Draft when they took Graves, a tall project of a high-school left-hander out of South Carolina, in the sixth round, and it’s looking like a gamble that could pay off. They slow-rolled him, with Graves not making his pro debut until 2023 in the Florida Complex League, and that didn’t go well. But a move to full-season ball in 2024 provided the first glimpse of what the future might look like, with a 31.8 percent strikeout rate over 84 innings with Clearwater as a 20-year old. There are few players in the Phillies system who made more strides in one year than Graves did in 2024. The 6-foot-6 southpaw can attack hitters with as many as five pitches. He’ll throw both a four-seamer up in the zone and a two-seamer with sink in the 90-95 mph range, getting a lot of groundballs with the latter. He’s already added some strength, with room for more, so it’s easy to dream on him living more in the 93-95 mph range and holding it, making the fastball more playable. Graves can really spin a breaking ball, registering spin rates north of 3,000 rpm with his slider. He has a separate cutter, though the two pitches run into each other, both missing a ton of bats in the low-80s. His changeup took a nice step forward, killing spin with it. Graves also improved dramatically in finding the strike zone, lowering his walk rate to 3.9 per nine in 2024. Continued work on his command, especially the secondary stuff, along with expected velocity gains, could allow him to keep evolving into a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An alumnus of MLB Develops programs like the Hank Aaron Invitational and Breakthrough Series, Drake was a toolsy outfielder from Atlanta who went to the MLB Draft League to test his mettle ahead of the 2023 Draft. He performed well over a small sample there ahead of the Braves taking him in the fifth round of that July’s Draft and going over slot -- close to $750,000 -- to sign him away from his commitment to Georgia Tech. The younger brother of former NFL running back Kenyan Drake, Isaiah really struggled in his first full season of pro ball, but made some great adjustments in 2025 to perform his way from Single-A Augusta to High-A Rome in his age-19 season. The Braves knew it might take a while for things to click for Drake, and when they sent him to Augusta in 2024 to sink or swim, he sunk, hitting .163 with a 35.5 percent strikeout rate in 69 games in the Carolina League. He slashed that last year with just a 21.3 percent K rate across two levels, and his overall miss and chase rates also went down. Strong and physical, the next step in his development with his improved ability to make contact might be tapping into his considerable raw power more consistently. Drake loves to run, swiping 46 bags last year, with some scouts putting an 80 run grade on him. That helps him go get the ball in center field and he’s improved in that facet of the game as well. There’s work to be done still, but he could be a plus defender when all is said and done. This was a bit of a lottery ticket for the Braves, but if his aptitude keeps trending in this direction, they could cash in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drake’s older brother Kenyan has had a fairly lengthy NFL career, but Isaiah chose the baseball route. Playing his high school ball in the Braves’ backyard, it looked like he might be heading to Georgia Tech for college, but after performing well in the Draft League and the Combine, the Braves decided to go way over slot and give him close to $750,000 in the fifth round to sign him away from campus. He had a brief, and uneventful, debut in the Florida Complex League after signing. Young for his Draft class, Drake is a left-handed hitter who could develop an exciting power-speed combination. He might be the fastest player in the system now and that should help him on both sides of the ball. He has raw power aplenty to tap into and will have to work on his approach and his ability to barrel up the baseball to get to it as he advances. Drake’s speed allows him to cover a ton of ground in center field and he should be able to stick there, especially as he improves his reads and routes and doesn’t simply outrun the ball. Patience is going to be key here, as he’s a bit of a project, but the payoff could be considerable considering the raw tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas was navigating through his first full year of full-season ball and setting a career high in innings (64) in 2023 when he hurt his elbow. That turned into Tommy John surgery and he missed all of the 2024 season as a result. The Rockies had invested $500,000 to sign Vargas out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021 and had the expectation bar raised after a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, followed by a summer that saw him pitch his way from the Arizona Complex League to Single-A Fresno in 2022. In an organization trying to uncover any gem in developing pitchers for the big leagues, his return is highly anticipated. Once he can really put the elbow surgery in his rearview, Vargas can get back to being one of the more exciting and projectable pitching prospects in the system. He has good command of his lively low-90s heater. It has good carry at the top of the zone and hitters don’t square it up, plus there’s hope for more consistent velocity in the future. He can really spin his breaking ball, a curve with bite and depth that misses a lot of bats. He has good feel for his tailing changeup as well. Vargas’ slender frame may not be able to add on that much weight and strength, but with more maturity, the hope is he can prove durable enough to handle a starter’s workload because he has the ability to throw his entire repertoire for strikes with a loose arm action. The first order of business is to get a full year in without incident, knowing he’s still only 21 for the 2025 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: July 2023 was not a great month for pitching development in the Rockies organization, with three pitchers having Tommy John surgery: Gabriel Hughes, Jackson Cox and Vargas, putting a pause on the promising start to Vargas’ pro career. Signed for $500,000 in January 2021, Vargas made a strong first impression in the Dominican Summer League that year, then pitched his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season ball in '22. He was back with Single-A Fresno when he was shut down 13 starts into his 2023 season. When he’s healthy, Vargas might be the best pitching prospect in the system in terms of being able to pound the strike zone with a solid three-pitch mix. He can command his low-90s fastball to both sides of the plate, and the carry it has in the top of the zone helps it play up and keeps hitters from barreling it up. He can get a little fastball-heavy in his pitch mix, but he was making strides in his secondary offerings, especially in focusing in on one breaking ball. Instead of trying to create a distinct slider and curve only to have them run into each other, he’s recognized that the biting slider has a real chance to be an out pitch. There’s a solid changeup in there as well. With a narrow and slender frame, it remains to be seen if Vargas can put on weight and add strength in order to be durable enough -- and maintain his stuff enough -- to be a starter. There’s also work to be done in terms of professional maturity and not letting his emotions get the better of him on the mound. For now, though, rehabbing his elbow is the top priority with an eye towards a full return in 2025 when he’ll still be just 21 years old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dominican Summer League is typically known as being very hitter-friendly. Vargas, who signed for $500,000 in January 2021, didn’t get that memo and made a very strong first impression during his pro debut in the DSL. He came stateside in 2022 and showed that was no fluke, pitching his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season Fresno. He had returned to the California League club to start the 2023 season but was shut down at the beginning of July and had Tommy John surgery at the end of the month. Just 19 for all of the 2023 season, Vargas has already impressed with his potential three-pitch mix and feel for how to use it to get hitters out. Coming from a slight and narrow build -- one evaluator said he’s built like a fungo -- he has a low-90s fastball that plays up a bit because of his ability to command it to both sides of the plate and the ride it gets at the top of the zone. Lower-level hitters haven’t been able to square it up, and he’ll have to learn not to rely on it as much as he faces better competition, having thrown the pitch close to 70 percent of the time in 2022. The good thing is he has secondary offerings to go to. He can really spin a breaking ball, and while it sometimes gets caught between a slider and curve, it has depth and bite. It’s a pitch he can land early for a strike and also use as an out pitch. He has good feel for his changeup too, and sometimes it’s better than the breaking ball. Vargas goes right after hitters and should be able to continue filling up the strike zone. It remains to be seen how much strength he can add to his wiry frame, with any physical maturity only adding to his potential starting pitcher profile, something he’ll try to continue building once he’s fully recovered from his surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big league reliever Yorkis Perez, Vargas signed with the Rockies for $500,000 when the 2020-21 international signing period opened in January 2021. The right-hander made an immediate impression by spending the summer dominating the Dominican Summer League at the age of 17, with a 1.30 ERA over 34 2/3 innings. Having thrown all summer, the Rockies didn’t bring Vargas to instructs last fall, building anticipation for his United States debut in 2022. He can already touch the mid-90s with his fastball, throwing it with good spin rates and resulting life. His curve has the chance to be a plus pitch, with outstanding downward action and spin. Working on a changeup will come with time. At 6-foot-3, Vargas has the type of projectible frame that should be able to handle a lot more strength, with more velocity highly likely as he matures. He already has a good idea of his delivery and is largely around the strike zone. Like a lot of young pitchers with premium stuff, he can get into trouble by hunting strikeouts, but as he learns to be more of a pitcher than a thrower, Minor League hitters better watch out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies got one of the fastest players in the 2022 Draft class in the first round when they took Justin Crawford, but they weren’t done adding premium speed that July. In Round 11, they plucked Boyd from the Mississippi high school ranks and signed him for an above-slot $647,500. After a brief summer debut following his signing, Boyd played most of the 2023 season alongside Crawford with Single-A Clearwater, finishing second in the Florida State League with 56 steals. From a pure speed standpoint, Boyd is elite, and it helps him on both sides of the ball. He’s an obvious threat to steal, and he racked up those totals without really knowing what he was doing on the basepaths. He often just took off on the first pitch every time he was on, one of the reasons he got caught 18 times, so there’s some ceiling to reach as he hones his craft. At the plate, the right-handed hitter makes a ton of contact, striking out in fewer than 15 percent of his plate appearances in 2023. How much impact he’s going to have is still a question. He keeps adding good weight, and there’s an expectation his ability to drive the ball will improve with time, though power will never be a huge part of his game. While he played more left field than anything in 2023, the plan for Boyd moving forward is to get a lot more reps in center field, where his speed should enable him to be an excellent defender. How his strength gains translate into more impact will help determine whether he can be more than a different type of big leaguer than fellow Mississippian Billy Hamilton.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The history of drafted high school hitters coming out of Mississippi has been a bit spotty, with exceptions like Austin Riley. Boyd fits in the Billy Hamilton mold as a speedster, with the same questions about offensive impact. He played well enough on last summer’s showcase circuit and in his senior season to attract the attention of the Phillies, who took him in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft and went way over the $125,000 slot value for Day 3 picks to sign him for $647,500. Boyd is known for his speed and his ability to make a lot of contact, with both skills on display during his brief pro debut last summer. He has a short and quick right-handed swing geared to put the ball in play, rarely striking out while also showing a feel for the strike zone, understanding his game is to get on base and use his elite-level speed on the basepaths. He’s never going to be a huge power guy, but the Phillies were encouraged that he gained 20 pounds in good weight over the offseason and feel with his bat-to-ball skills, he’ll start driving the ball more as he continues to add strength. That plus plus speed also helps him track down balls in center field. He has a long-term future in center field thanks to those wheels and improved instincts in tracking fly balls. His ceiling is that of a speedy table-setter, one he can reach if he can translate the strength gains to impact at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better outfielders in the 2023 international signing class, Guanipa sat at the top of the Braves’ wish list, and they signed him for $2.5 million at the start of the signing period in January of that year. Things started off relatively well, with glimpses of his raw tools in the Dominican Summer League and stateside in 2024. There was hope he’d make adjustments from his tough move to Single-A Augusta that year into 2025 while repeating the level, but he managed to play in just 35 games because of a hand fracture from a hit-by-pitch and a quad strain. Guanipa will try to take a mulligan for his lost season while still being just 20 years old for all of the 2026 season. An aggressive hitter from the right side of the plate, he’s shown a knack for contact with plenty of bat speed. He limits his swing-and-miss but does have a tendency to chase out of the zone too much, especially on offspeed stuff. His game is about putting the ball in play, and it seems like it’s not going to come with a ton of impact, so it would serve him well if he could draw more walks to get on base more frequently. Then Guanipa could use his plus speed to greater advantage, something he wasn’t able to do last year. He has the chance to stay up the middle in center field, and the hope is his ceiling is an up-the-middle table-setter type who is a base hit machine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guanipa was ranked No. 34 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2023 signing period opened up, and the Braves nabbed him as the gem of the crop they brought in, giving him a $2.5 million bonus to start his pro career. His raw tools were on display during his debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing, and he played well in the Florida Complex League to kick off his United States debut in 2024, though a bump up to full-season Augusta did not go well. Guanipa is an aggressive right-handed hitter who has shown off excellent bat speed and the ability to make loud contact at times. He swings at just about everything and chases too much, leading to a bit more swing-and-miss when he moved up a level (25.7 percent strikeout rate in 32 games with Augusta). It’s looking more like he’s not going to have that much power, so he’ll have to refine his approach and be a contact-oriented hit-over-pop type to succeed. While there might be questions about his bat, there’s confidence about Guanipa’s speed and defense. He should run well enough to be a threat on the basepaths and he has the chance to be at least an above-average defender in center field. He’s just 19 for all of 2025, with time to reach the ceiling expected of someone so highly regarded on the amateur market, with some seeing a bit of a Manuel Margot profile in him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 65 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Since the Braves got out of the penalty box for international signing violations, they have not hesitated to go after high-end talent who commanded large bonuses. In 2021, that was Ambioris Tavarez. In 2022, Diego Benitez and Douglas Glod got seven-figure deals. When the 2023 signing period opened in January, the Braves targeted Guanipa, who was in the middle of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list and signed him for $2.5 million. He showed off his considerable tools, and his rawness, during his Dominican Summer League debut after signing. Guanipa plays bigger than his listed height of 5-foot-11. The Venezuelan outfielder has impressive bat speed and the ball can jump off his bat. He doesn’t get cheated at the plate and there’s plenty of raw power for him to continue to tap into as he matures, with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, though while he draws walks he will have to learn to refine his approach. A plus runner who has good defensive instincts, Guanipa should continue to be a threat on the basepaths after swiping 20 bags in the DSL a year ago while being able to stick in center field for a long time. The Braves are excited to see what he can do stateside for the first time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves are active players on the international market, giving a seven-figure bonus to Ambioris Tavarez in January 2021 and handing out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to Diego Benitez and Douglas Glod a year later. The top acquisition from the most recent international class is Guanipa, a toolsy Venezeulan outfielder who trained with Omar Alvarez and Johan Hidalgo. Guanipa’s potential of power and speed had him ranked among the best outfielders in the 2023 international signing class. The Braves certainly thought so, signing him for $2.5 million when the period opened in mid-January. While Guanipa is undersized, listed at 5-foot-11, he’s the kind of prospect who plays “big.” A lot of that assessment comes from his plus bat speed and how the ball jumps off his bat. He can drive the ball to the gaps now and has raw power that will certainly develop, with the ability to hit the ball to all fields. He’s also a plus runner, one who has excellent instincts defensively. That should allow him to stay in center field for a long time. There’s a lot to dream on here, with the hope that he can develop into a dynamic up-the-middle player who can both run and rake.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of college baseball's best two-way performers as a sophomore in 2023, Mathis topped the College of Charleston in OPS (1.014) and ERA (3.45) before ranking second in the Cape Cod League with 11 homers in 38 games. He focused on hitting as a junior while dealing with an elbow injury, became the highest pick in school history (second round) and had Tommy John surgery shortly after signing for $1,681,200. Rehab and a subsequent elbow sprain limited him to 29 Single-A games in his 2025 pro debut, and he didn't play the field until the Arizona Fall League. Mathis has an easy right-handed stroke and the upside of a solid hitter with raw power to match, though he hasn't gotten much of a chance to show what he can do when fully healthy in pro ball. He strings together quality at-bats and hangs in well against breaking balls and changeups. He was more aggressive at Single-A than he was in college, showing the ability to elevate balls to his pull side but not hitting the ball as hard as he did at Charleston. Though the Cubs announced Mathis as a third baseman when they drafted him, he spent just one game there in college and most scouts think he lacks the quickness and athleticism to handle the hot corner. He has a chance to be an average first baseman but won't cover a lot of ground at either corner. Before he got hurt, he had a low-90s fastball with armside run and a mid-70s downer curveball that he located well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mathis broke out as one of college baseball's best two-way players as a sophomore in 2023, when he led the College of Charleston in OPS (1.014) and ERA (3.45) before finishing second in the Cape Cod League with 11 homers in 38 games. He concentrated on hitting last spring while dealing with an elbow injury, bouncing back from a slow start to slash .335/.472/.650 en route to becoming the highest pick in Cougars history. After signing for $1,681,200 as a second-rounder, he had Tommy John surgery in August. Mathis employs an effortless, if not picturesque, right-handed stroke and a very patient approach to produce hard contact to all fields. He rarely strayed from the zone or swung and missed in college, though he may need to turn his bat loose more often in pro ball because he takes a lot of strikes. He has enough pull power to get to 20 homers per season, drives the ball the other way for doubles and draws a healthy amount of walks. The Cubs announced Mathis as a third baseman when they selected him, but he played just one game at the hot corner at the College of Charleston and his fringy quickness and athleticism seem like a stretch for the hot corner. Most clubs thought he was strictly a first baseman despite his strong arm. As a pitcher, he featured a low-90s fastball with armside run and got outs with a mid-70s downer curveball that he located well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest notable shortstop prospect to come out of San Pedro de Macorís, Muñoz received the largest bonus ($1.45 million) of any international Marlins signing this year as the No. 27 prospect in his class. He's a dynamic athlete hoping to turn his basket of intriguing tools into production heading into his debut season. The Dominican Republic native offers electric hand speed from the right side of the plate and sprays line-drive contact to all fields. At 5-foot-11, he has a strong lower half and notable pull power. Time will tell whether he's able to get that raw pop to show up in pro ball since he has had trouble in the past making consistent contact, but the Marlins are confident they'll be able to improve his swing decisions. Muñoz is agile on the bases and in the field, and his quick hands and footwork point to him having a chance to stick at shortstop long term. He's played some second and third before and likely will in pro ball as well, and he has the arm to play anywhere. Muñoz is a safer prospect than Miami's other 2025 bonus baby, Santiago Solarte, but still offers plenty of upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Conticello got a $500,000 bonus to sign out of Stoneman Douglas HS in Florida as an eighth-round pick in 2021, setting aside a South Florida commitment to do so. He’s essentially climbed one level per season from the Arizona Complex League in 2022 to Double-A Amarillo, where he spent all of his age-22 campaign in '25. He hit .275/.369/.435 with 12 homers in 121 games with the Sod Poodles, good for a 110 wRC+ while only getting 30 plate appearances against pitchers younger than him. The lefty batter, who has a long finish in his hacks a little similar to Cody Bellinger, still has above-average raw power and a good chance to get to it at full maturity, even if he didn’t post the big-time slugging others do in hitter-friendly Amarillo. Part of that is because of his approach. He expands the zone a lot against lefty sliders and righty changeups, essentially the pitches running away from him, but he doesn’t whiff as much as might be expected because of it. (His 21.3 percent K rate was actually pretty sensible for a power-first bat.) Being more selective than a 56 percent swing rate would help his strengths shine. An average runner with good arm strength, Conticello began his career as a third baseman, began to split time at both corner infield spots in 2023 and then moved to the outfield full-time in '24. He’s made some starts in center but fits better in right field, and the D-backs are comfortable enough in his progress there that he won’t have to move back down the defensive spectrum to first base. He’ll still have to slug in a corner though, and he’s added good weight ahead of his age-23 season to help his cause all the more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Stoneman Douglas HS in Florida, Conticello signed for well above slot with a $500,000 bonus as an eighth-round pick in 2021. He hit 17 homers between Single-A and High-A two years ago but put in a more well-rounded breakout campaign in 2024, hitting .282/.346/.428 with nine homers and 20 steals in 126 games for Hillsboro. He rounded out his age-21 season with six games for Double-A Amarillo, adding one extra dinger. The left-handed slugger cuts a lean figure in the box at 6-feet-3 and already shows raw power with good bat speed. Some believe he’s still growing into his strength and could continue to fill out as he gets deeper into his 20s. Moving back to the hitters' haven that is Amarillo for 2025 could find Conticello putting up career bests in most slugging categories. His overall contact rate was solid for his age despite a lengthy swing, but he struggled against lefties. None of his homers came against same-side pitching and he slugged just .302 against it. Conticello may just be an average runner, but he’s a lively one who knows when to pick his stealing spots. He began his career playing the two corner infield spots but moved to right field primarily in ’24. His reads and routes remain in transition there, but his plus arm strength and accuracy absolutely fit the position as he recorded 14 outfield assists last season. The former South Florida commit headed to the upper Minors for the first time in 2025, but his issues against lefties have continued.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez began his college career at Miami Dade, pitching two years at the JC level before moving on to be a part of the University of Miami rotation. He missed bats, but with inconsistent command, something that continued in his first year of pro ball after the Braves took him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft. He spent the past year with High-A Rome, finishing second in the South Atlantic League in strikeouts (127) and would have been among the leaders in batting average against (.193), ERA (3.57) and K/9 (11.1) had he thrown enough innings to qualify. A bit undersized at 5-foot-10, Hernandez does have some traits that give him a chance to start. Pitching last year at 21, he flashed an effective four-pitch mix. His fastball is an average offering which sat around 93 mph and touched 97, a tick more than in college, and it does miss some bats with good riding life to it. His slider is his go-to, a low-80s breaker that elicited a 40 percent miss rate according to Synergy. He has an upper-70s curve that he doesn't throw as often, and he started showing signs of a solid splitter, though he's still getting the feel for it. The Braves think there's more upside to tap into given that Hernandez really didn't pitch much until he got to Miami Dade. He'll have to find the strike zone a lot more consistently after walking 5.9 per nine in his first full year to have any chance of starting, though that fastball-slider combination could work really well in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 After two years at the junior college level, pitching for Miami Dade, Hernandez headed to the University of Miami rather than sign with the Reds as a Day 3 draftee in 2023. He had an inconsistent season pitching in the Hurricanes' weekend rotation, but the Braves liked his arsenal enough to take him in the fourth round of the Draft, then sent him out to get his professional feet wet with a few innings with Single-A Augusta and High-A Rome. While he's just 5-foot-10, Hernandez could have the chance to be a left-handed starter thanks to a robust repertoire. At Miami, he had four pitches he could go to, though he might simplify it a bit at the next level. He has an average fastball that averaged just over 92 mph in 2024, topping out at 95 mph. His feel to spin breaking stuff really supports his heater, with his low-80s slider that missed bats at a 43-percent rate last year perhaps being the focal point in pro ball. He had a distinct upper-70s curve that missed bats too, though he didn't command it as well. HIs firm changeup is his fourth pitch. For Hernandez to stick as a starter, he'll have to improve that offspeed offering and cut down on the walks. Though he's undersized, he's strong and has the chance to be a durable innings-eater, though there is some reliever risk, with the chance of his breaking stuff really playing well out of the pen should that move be necessary.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suárez was a big-time standout in his native Cuba before moving to the Dominican Republic three years ago. He was the youngest member of the silver-medal-winning Cuban roster at the U15 World Cup in Mexico in 2022 and upped his game by hitting .355/.495/.605 in Cuba’s U16 National League in ’23. Ranked as the No. 22 international prospect in the 2026 class by MLB Pipeline, Suárez signed with the Royals for $1,647,500 this past winter; only Angeibel Gomez ($2,797,500) signed for more with Kansas City this cycle. After heading to the D.R., Suárez trained with Javier Rodríguez in Santo Domingo East under the same program that helped develop Cubs outfielder Kevin Alcántara and Mets shortstop Elian Peña. The right-handed slugger, who will be 17 for the duration of his first Minor League season, has shown more pop as he’s matured, and that loud contact layers nicely over the impressive discipline he showed as a teenage amateur, though the latter will be tested against better arms on the pro side. Standing at 6-foot-1 already, Suárez could have an intriguing power-speed combination at full maturity if he holds onto his at least above-average wheels. His plus arm strength is his best defensive asset at this point, and it could help his case to stick at shortstop, where he has solid actions for now. If he needs to move over to third base, his slugging and throwing ability would make him a natural fit at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After three collegiate seasons with at least a .300 average and 1.000 OPS, Taylor became the highest position player drafted in TCU history when he went 19th overall to the Rays in 2023. He was a Midwest League end-of-season All-Star in his first full season after slashing .269/.389/.513 with 14 homers and 26 steals in 84 games at High-A Bowling Green and overcame a 36.8 percent K rate to produce a 113 wRC+ in a late 30-game assignment to Double-A Montgomery. With 20 total homers and 29 steals, he was one of two 20/20 players in the Tampa Bay system alongside Carson Williams. Batting in the left side of the box, Taylor raises his right leg fairly high and stamps it down in time to generate lift and pull consistently. It helped make him a power threat both in college and the early days of the pros, and it was notable that 11 of his 21 hits went for extra bases (including six homers) during what may have been an otherwise tough time in the pitcher-friendly Southern League last year. He’s returned to Montgomery for 2025 with even more struggles, often whiffing through secondary pitches or popping the ball up leading to a low BABIP and overall average. Taylor may be just an average pure runner but he’s a solid athlete, capable of picking his stolen-base spots and moving around the infield. In other words, he’s a good fit for the Rays. He stopped playing shortstop after the promotion in deference to Carson Williams, and he’s a capable fit at third base with his arm strength. He also moves well enough for second, though that will take some transitioning to learn to read balls on the other side of the dirt. The Rays still have hopes that Taylor can move past the first baseball lumps of his life and adjust to upper-level arms, but his stock has undoubtedly taken a hit in his second full campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of his Utah high school, Taylor went to Texas Christian University and developed into the program’s first-ever position player selected in the first round. A well-rounded infielder without the loud tools of his fellow top prospects in the system, Taylor’s bat stood out as he finished with double-digit home runs, a batting average north of .300 and an OPS higher than 1.000 in each of his three collegiate seasons. The Rays selected him with the 19th overall pick in the 2023 Draft and signed him for a slot-value bonus of $3,880,100. Taylor’s ability to hit is his carrying tool, as he features a sweet left-handed swing with excellent bat-to-ball skills. He uses the entire field, controls the strike zone and rarely chases outside the zone. He’s willing to work deep counts but since he’s more of a hitter with power than a power hitter, he sacrificed some batting average while looking to pull and drive more balls near the end of his time at TCU. That trend followed him into the Rays’ system, as he hit just .242 with a 31.5 percent strikeout rate, but he managed 12 extra-base hits (including five homers) in his 25-game professional debut. Taylor is an average runner and a solid defender. He is probably best suited for third base, where he spent most of his time in college, but he’ll play some shortstop in his full-season debut. He’s not the quickest player in the field, but he has the instincts and arm to make it work on the left side of the infield. The Rays were quickly impressed by Taylor’s makeup, and while he likely won’t wow you with any one tool, his overall value and high floor put him near the top of a system loaded with infield prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis' five-tool potential earned him the largest bonus in Boston's 2021 international class, as he signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic. The consensus top prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League during his U.S. debut in 2022, he subluxated his left shoulder on a swing the following May, had season-ending surgery and hasn't made much impact at the plate since. He slashed .222/.300/.385 with 14 homers and 27 steals in 107 games between High-A and Double-A last year. The bat speed and loft in Bleis' right-handed swing create plus raw power that's more obvious in batting practice than during games. He chases too many pitches and tries to yank too many to left field -- his 62 percent pull percentage led the Minors in 2025 -- an approach that results in too many strikeouts and too much suboptimal contact. He hasn't been able to add strength as easily as the Red Sox hoped but still has the ingredients to generate 25 homers per season if he settles down at the plate. Even while struggling offensively, Bleis can impact a game on the bases and in the field. Boston's 2025 baserunner of the year, he displays consistent plus speed, flashes better than that and runs consistently hard. He has improved his defensive instincts and become a quality center fielder with a strong arm that registered 10 assists in 99 starts last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis showed five-tool center-fielder potential as an amateur in the Dominican Republic and parlayed it into the largest bonus ($1.5 million) in Boston's 2020-21 international class. He ranked as the consensus top prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League during his 2022 U.S. debut, but his progress came to halt when he subluxated his left shoulder on a swing the following May and required season-ending surgery. He slashed .221/.303/.354 with a system-best 38 steals in 95 games between two Class A stops last year while continuing to showcase the best all-around tools in the system. Bleis combination of electric bat speed, still-growing strength and the loft in his right-handed stroke give him more raw pop than most 21-year-olds. He could produce 25 or more homers per year without swinging for the fences, but he sells out for power with an overly aggressive approach focused on launching balls to his pull side. He generates impressive exit velocities when he connects but will need to improve his swing decisions to find consistent success. Though he has gained at least 25 pounds of strength since turning pro, Bleis has retained his plus speed and turns it loose on the bases. He makes some shaky decisions at times in center field but also has the quickness to overcome a lot of his mistakes and plays as a solid defender there. His plus arm strength helped him notch 22 assists in 174 outfield starts during his first four seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top signing in Boston's 2020-21 international class, Bleis earned a $1.5 million bonus on the basis of his electric bat speed and potential to become a five-tool center fielder. Excitement grew when the Dominican was clearly the best prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in his U.S. debut in 2022, seemingly setting the stage for a full-season breakout last year. But he swings so hard that he subluxated his left shoulder last May and required season-ending surgery. Bleis already has jaw-dropping raw power at age 20 thanks to his bat speed, still-developing strength and the loft and leverage in his right-handed swing. He aggressively looks to launch balls to his pull side, producing high exit velocities for a 20-year-old but also leading to chases and strikeouts. He'll need to improve his swing decisions and his patience as he starts to face more advanced pitching. Evaluators give Bleis solid-to-plus grades for his speed, arm and center-field defense. He already has gained 20 pounds since turning pro and could lose a bit of quickness as he continues to add muscle, but even so his instincts will enable him to continue to be an asset as a runner and defender. He looks to make things happen on the bases and makes good reads in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis landed the largest bonus in Boston's 2020-21 international class, signing for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic as a center fielder with the potential for at least solid tools across the board. That's exactly what he looked like in his U.S. debut last summer, when he batted .301/.353/.542 with 23 extra-base hits and 18 steals in 40 games in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. The Red Sox's best international prospect since Rafael Devers, he subluxated his left shoulder on a swing in late May and had season-ending surgery. Built to hit for power, Bleis has a quick right-handed swing with loft and a 6-foot-3 frame with plenty of projectable strength and leverage. He also has an aggressive approach geared to launch balls to his pull side, which helps produce impressive exit velocities for a teenager but also portends the need for adjustments and better swing decisions against more advanced pitching. He does have some feel for recognizing pitches and discerning strikes, so there's optimism that he can become at least an average hitter, which would make him a star. Bleis' present speed earns 55-65 grades on the 20-80 scouting scale, and he likely will settle on the lower end of that range once he matures physically. He uses his quickness well, stealing and taking extra bases and effortlessly covering ground with long strides in center field. He also features solid to plus arm strength and would be an asset at any outfield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021, securing the largest bonus in Boston's 2020-21 international class. He made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, batting .252/.331/.420 with four homers and seven steals in 36 games at age 17. He has one of the highest ceilings in the system with the potential for solid tools across the board. Bleis has a sound right-handed swing and a feel for the strike zone at a young age. His bat speed, projectable strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-2 frame give him plus raw power. He makes a lot of hard contact already and shows the ability to drive balls in the air to his pull side. Though Bleis currently has plus speed to match his raw pop, he likely will slow down a bit as he matures physically. His gliding strides eat up a lot of ground in center field, and he should have the quickness and instincts to stay there. If he had to move to a corner, his solid to plus arm strength would work in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Porter had a decorated high school career at St. Mary's Prep (Orchard Lake, Mich.), winning three state championships in three seasons, Gatorade state player of the year honors in 2021 and 2022 and Gatorade's national award in his senior season. Though he was MLB Pipeline's top-rated pitching prospect in the 2022 Draft, the Rangers managed to float him to the 109th pick, where they used the savings from taking Kumar Rocker at No. 3 to pay Porter a fourth-round-record $3.7 million. He logged a 2.47 ERA with a .160 opponent average and 95 strikeouts in 69 1/3 Single-A innings during his 2023 pro debut, though he also walked 42. Porter's fastball and changeup ranked among the best in the 2022 prep class, and the latter pitch continues to confound hitters with its tumble and fade. But after operating at 94-97 mph and touching 100 with his four-seamer in the past, he has sat at 90-93 mph for much of 2024, and his command and confidence with his heater have plummeted as well. He made just three starts in High-A in April before Texas sent him to the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, where he didn't appear in a game for another two months and continued to struggled when he returned. After showing inconsistent feel for spinning the ball in high school, Porter has scrapped an upper-70s curveball to focus on a mid-80s slider that's becoming a solid offering. But his control has gone from below average last year to a disaster this season, making him a wild card as a prospect. He once looked like he'd pitch in the front half of a rotation, but even before his struggles in 2024, several scouts outside the organization were projecting him as more of a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated pitching prospect in the 2022 Draft, Porter won three state titles in three seasons at St. Mary's Prep (Orchard Lake, Mich.) and was Gatorade's state player of the year in both 2021 and 2022. He also earned Gatorade's national award last spring, when he went 9-0 with a 0.41 ERA, 115 strikeouts in 58 innings and three no-hitters for a 44-0 team. After the Rangers saved money by taking Kumar Rocker with the third overall pick last July, they floated Porter all the way down to pick 109, where they destroyed the fourth-round bonus record by paying him $3.7 million. Porter had the best fastball and one of the best changeups in the 2022 high school class. He's able to sit at 94-97 mph for several innings at a time and reach triple digits with plenty of run and carry on his four-seamer. He achieves excellent velocity separation between his fastball and his low-80s changeup, which has devastating tumble and fade. Porter upgraded his slider significantly as a high school senior, flashing some plus mid-80s slide pieces, and also has a downer curveball in the upper 70s. His strong 6-foot-4 build should lend itself to durability and still has some remaining projection, and he does a nice job of repeating his low-effort delivery. Though Texas decided to defer his pro debut until 2023, he still should advance quickly for a prep pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Honeyman enjoyed a breakout sophomore year at Boston College in 2022, one in which he posted a .908 OPS with only 16 strikeouts in 41 games and carried that straight into the Cape Cod League, where he caught additional eyes. He maintained his momentum as a junior with a .304/.383/.534 line through 39 games, but a shoulder injury ended his season early in May. The Cardinals took him in the third round and signed him for around slot at $700,000. Unfortunately, shoulder issues continued to dog Honeyman into pro ball, and he underwent surgery that limited him to 20 games in the Florida Complex and Florida State Leagues in what should have been his first full season. The lost season certainly doesn’t help Honeyman’s growth and development on the pro side, but the scouting report remains much the same until he proves himself more on the field. He bats with an open stance from the right side and swings his front leg forward with a kick to get his momentum moving forward. He can cover most areas of the plate with his bat-to-ball skills, even if he’ll occasionally expand the zone in search of contact. His pop was a work in progress in school but projected as average before the shoulder woes. Honeyman flashed plus home-to-first times during his brief Florida State League stint, and his wheels shouldn’t be affected by the time off. A throwing program was considered his last piece of rehab in his second offseason, and it’ll be worth monitoring how his arm strength holds up after the surgery. The former Eagle seems likely to move around the grass in his return, but the focus will be on getting on the field consistently in the first place.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Honeyman broke out as a Boston College sophomore in 2022, hitting .329/.402/.506 with only 16 strikeouts in 41 games, and carried that performance forward with a standout turn in the Cape Cod League that summer. He got off to another quick start as a junior, slashing .304/.383/.534 through 39 games, but went down with a shoulder injury in early May. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 61 Draft prospect in 2023, Honeyman went to the Cardinals in the third round (90th overall) and signed for around slot at $700,000. He did not play for a St. Louis affiliate last year. The right-handed hitter has a kinetic appearance in the box, starting with an open stance and then beginning his momentum forward with a leg kick. All that movement helps him especially protect the outside of the plate, and while he did chase breaking balls at an elevated rate as a junior Eagle, his outstanding bat-to-ball skills kept his strikeouts in check. He was learning to tap into pullside power in school, and his wiry strength could get him to average in-game power in the pros. Honeyman is a little bit better than an average runner but wasn’t seen as a big threat to steal bases in college, though he did go 10-for-11 in attempts in 2023. He has some experience in center field but played mostly in right last spring. With Chase Davis a more prominent member of his Draft class and Victor Scott II ahead of him on the CF depth chart, Honeyman is likely headed for the corners long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lesko underwent Tommy John surgery in April 2022, a tough break for someone who had earned a ton of buzz after becoming the first-ever player to be named the Gatorade National Baseball Player of the Year as a junior the year before. Still, the Padres believed in the hype enough to select him 15th overall and sign him for $3.9 million. Lesko worked his way back from surgery and debuted in June 2023, flashing signs of dominance and reaching High-A despite posting a 5.45 ERA over 33 innings. He struggled even more last season, walking 19.2% of the batters he faced and hitting 14 more in 84 innings. The Rays saw an opportunity to buy low and landed him as part of their return for reliever Jason Adam. Lesko’s apparent loss of control since returning from surgery is an obvious issue. His stuff isn’t. He has an elite changeup, which clocked in around 79 mph last year with incredible movement off his fastball.
