It’s a devastating swing-and-miss pitch, and he showed the ability to land it for strikes despite his otherwise problematic control. He throws a tighter-spinning slider that shows some promise as well as a curveball. His fastball has the velocity and movement profile to be effective, too, sitting in the mid-90s and touching 97 mph. Joining the Rays didn’t immediately solve his issues with strikes, as he walked 31% of the batters he faced with Bowling Green. The Rays have been evaluating Lesko since his Draft year, though, and learned a lot from a pitching coordinator in their system who came over from the Padres. The hope is that he can shake off the post-TJ rust and get back to Top 100 form as a potential mid-rotation starter. If not, he’s bound for the bullpen, where perhaps he can command his fastball enough to let his changeup play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 70 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Lesko entered his senior season at Buford (Ga.) High School in 2022 with plenty of hype after becoming the first-ever junior Gatorade National Baseball Player of the Year the prior spring. He was delivering on his promise, only to undergo Tommy John surgery in late April. The Padres still selected the right-hander 15th overall and signed him for just under slot at $3.9 million. Lesko made his pro debut in June 2023 – nearly 14 months after surgery – and despite a 5.45 ERA, showed his high potential again with 52 strikeouts over 33 innings across three levels, ending the season at High-A Fort Wayne. He returned to High-A for 2024 but never dominated as he was capable of doing, and the Padres traded him to the Rays at the Trade Deadline as part of a three-player package for reliever Jason Adam. Lesko sits 92-96 mph with his fastball, touching 98, and makes the offering play even better with impressive carry up in the zone. That’s not even his best pitch. That remains his low-80s changeup with tremendous separation off the heater and movement that gets some silly swings, earning it consistent plus-plus grades. (Lefties hit just .186 with a 38.8 percent K rate off Lesko in 2023 as a result.) His mid-70s curveball shows with 12-to-6 movement and promising spin rates but is still developing consistency. A mid-80s slider might end up becoming the better of his two breaking pitches as he gets to work with the Rays pitching group. The 6-foot-2 right-hander experienced control problems in his first year back from surgery in 2023, and those issues have continued into this summer. That created an opportunity for Tampa Bay to buy low, with the Rays hoping to harness his promising stuff and get Lesko back to filling the zone with more regularity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lesko was the first junior to win the Gatorade National Baseball Player of the Year award in 2021 after posting a 0.35 ERA with 112 strikeouts in 60 innings at Buford (Ga.) High School, the alma mater of Brandon Marsh and Joey Bart. Lesko continued to shove the following spring as a senior, heightening the belief that he could be the top arm drafted in the Class of 2022, but Tommy John surgery in late April made him a question mark. He still ended up being the first prep pitcher taken when San Diego selected him 15th overall and signed him for just under slot at $3.9 million. Before the elbow procedure, the 6-foot-2 righty was already throwing 92-95 mph, touching 97, with a fastball that carried up in the zone, and as he builds back up, there’s the chance he adds even more velo with age and physical maturity. His low-80s changeup was arguably the best of the Draft and will be one of the best in the San Diego system once he throws it again, on account of its separation and two-plane movement that can make hitters look downright silly. His upper-70s curveball will need work to reach consistency, but its high spin rates carry promise. Lesko will have to show he can pitch with the same strong command as he continues to build back innings. That’s easier than it once was for Tommy John pitchers, but still no small task. The good news is he’s been getting innings at both the Arizona Complex and California Leagues and could be primed for a bigger takeoff in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 11 prospect in the 2024 international class, Radney was Arizona’s top signing last year when he joined the D-backs for $1.85 million out of the Dominican Republic, just a smidge above the $1.8 million given to countryman Belfi Rivera. The outfielder split his time between both of the organization’s Dominican Summer League affiliates, hitting just .225/.331/.288 with three triples and two doubles in 34 games. It was a tale of two seasons for Radney. The outfielder batted .296 through his first 16 games, missed two weeks and then hit .158 in his final 18. He was going to be graded on a curve anyway since he turned 17 that June. On the positive side, he walked at a decent clip (10.8 percent) against wild DSL arms. The right-handed slugger’s value has always been in long-term projection as many believe he’ll fill out his 6-foot-3 form and become an above-average power threat. He’ll need to elevate better on contact too after putting the ball on the ground 54.1 percent of the time in 2024. Radney made 22 of his 23 defensive starts in right field. That’s typically not ideal for an athletic outfielder so young -- you’d rather have him in center -- but his power profile and above-average arm strength still fit in that specific corner. The 2025 season -- still just his age-18 season -- will bring more clarity on where the youngster belongs in Arizona’s outfield hierarchy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs had a $7,114,800 bonus pool for the 2024 international window and used a sizable allotment to target two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 prospects in the class -- outfielder Belfi Rivera (No. 24) and Radney (No. 10). The higher ranked of the pair joined the organization for a $1.85 million bonus, just beating out Rivera’s $1.8 million mark to make him the official head of the D-backs' contingent. Radney doesn’t turn 17 until June of his signing year but he already stands in at 6-foot-3. There’s a ton of room to fill in that frame -- his official weight after signing was 180 pounds -- and that level of projection is something that excites Arizona officials. Batting from the right side, Radney has a relatively quiet approach that helps him hit for average, but once more muscle comes, his slugging ability should hit another level. The Dominican Republic native has solid speed for now, and it’s expected that he’ll get a good amount of center-field looks early in his career to keep that valuable lane open. His arm strength would certainly work in right field, however, should he need to move in deference to a better defender or if he loses a step, and the potential pop would play anywhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were few college players in the 2024 Draft class better than Honeycutt in terms of his raw tools, and he left North Carolina as the Tar Heels' single-season (28) and career (65) home run leader. He turned in a 28-homer, 28-steal junior season, but it came with concerns about his ability to make contact after a 27.5 percent strikeout rate. The Orioles rolled the dice on the tools and took him No. 22 overall, and the contact concerns were warranted during his first full season, as he struck out more than 40 percent of the time and finished with a .171/.284/.275 line with High-A Aberdeen. Strikeouts are always going to be a part of Honeycutt's offensive profile, and it's going to be a question of whether he can control the zone just well enough to use his bat speed and leverage to get to his easily plus raw power enough to be a productive hitter. There were some signs this spring, aside from the four Grapefruit League homers in his first four at-bats, of improvement, with more consistent contact, less swing-and-miss and getting to deeper counts. A superior athlete, Honeycutt's speed still showed up despite his struggles, with 32 stolen bases in 2025. He uses it in center field as well as a two-time ACC Defensive Player of the Year and a potential Gold Glover. He'll try to hit the reset button in 2026, and if it clicks at all, his power-speed-defense combination could allow him to climb the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After almost a half-decade of lottery picks, the Orioles picked lower in the Draft the past couple of years as they grew into contenders in the American League East, and they’ve used those mid-to-late first-round picks on athletic outfielders with big tools. Honeycutt, who Baltimore grabbed with the No. 22 overall pick in 2024, is the embodiment of that idea. A high school quarterback who won North Carolina state titles in football and baseball, Honeycutt then posted multiple 20-20 seasons at the University of North Carolina and left college with both the school single-season (28) and career (65) home run records. He didn’t perform nearly as well during a very brief pro debut after signing for a slightly over-slot $4 million. A dynamic athlete with plus tools almost across the board, Honeycutt fell to the Orioles in the Draft because of concerns over his bat. At 6-foot-3 and 205 pounds, he generates enough bat speed, leverage and loft to create well-above-average raw power, though his armsy swing and pull-happy approach lead to serious contact issues that can make him too easy to pitch to. As it was, Honeycutt struck out in more than a quarter of his plate appearances in college and in 42.8 percent of his plate appearances during his 13-game pro debut. In college, Honeycutt was a two-time ACC Defensive Player of the Year and the first player from a Power Five conference to pair 60 career homers with 70 steals. His upside is providing similar impact at the highest level, where his well-above-average speed and plus arm make him a potential Gold Glover in center field. He simply needs to make more contact, enough for his big tools to play. How he develops in that area will determine if Honeycutt becomes a Drew Stubbs type or exceeds that production.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frasso showed first-round potential heading into the 2020 season at Loyola Marymount, but he strained his forearm during the pandemic-shortened schedule and dropped to the Blue Jays in the fourth round. He had internal brace surgery on his elbow in June 2021, returned to the mound in May 2022 and then joined the Dodgers along with lefty pitching prospect Moises Brito in a trade for Mitch White and infield prospect Alex DeJesus two months later. He blossomed into Los Angeles' best pitching prospect in 2023 before tearing the labrum in his pitching shoulder, necessitating surgery that November that sidelined him for all of last season. He has returned to the mound this year in Triple-A, and his ability to miss bats and throw strikes have regressed significantly. A healthy Frasso can overpower hitters with a fastball that parks at 94-97 mph and peaks at 100 with armside run and impressive extension that make it tough to barrel. He flashes a plus mid-80s changeup with fade and sink so hitters can't try to sit on his heater. His hard upper-80s slider features good depth and can be overpowering, though it lacks the consistency of his other two offerings. But none of those pitches have been as good in 2025 as they were two years ago. Frasso creates a lot of deception with his extension and crossfire delivery, and he has the athleticism to repeat his mechanics and pound the strike zone. He looked like a possible frontline starter before he got hurt, but he also had two major arm surgeries in 29 months and has worked just 152 innings in four pro seasons. Given his history and the Dodgers' rotation depth, he'll likely contribute as a multi-inning reliever in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A potential first-rounder going into his junior year at Loyola Marymount, Frasso strained his forearm during the truncated 2020 season and fell the to Blue Jays in the fourth round. He had the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow repaired with an internal brace in June 2021 and returned to the mound in May 2022 before getting dealt with lefty pitching prospect Moises Brito to the Dodgers for Mitch White and infield prospect Alex DeJesus two months later. He emerged as Los Angeles' best pitching prospect in 2023 before tearing the labrum in his pitching shoulder and having surgery in November that will sideline him for all or most of this season. Frasso’s fastball usually ranges from 94-97 mph and tops out at 100 with arm-side run, and the impressive extension he creates enables his heater to get on hitters more quickly than expected. His mid-80s changeup can be a plus pitch at its best, fading and sinking and confusing batters who are trying to sit on his heater. His mid-80s slider has the makings of a solid offering with sweep and depth, though it’s not as reliable as his fastball and changeup. Frasso has an extremely deceptive delivery thanks to his extension and crossfire action, and he also has the athleticism to repeat it. He has a long history of throwing strikes and held up while working a career-high 93 innings in 2023. Durability is the only real question he has to answer to become a mid-rotation starter, and he has the stuff to have a fallback as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Contenders don't often acquire quality prospects at the Trade Deadline, but the Dodgers did just that last August when they grabbed Frasso and fellow right-handed pitching prospect Moises Brito from the Blue Jays in exchange for Mitch White and infield prospect Alex DeJesus. Frasso was a potential first-rounder entering his junior season at Loyola Marymount in 2020, but he strained his forearm during the shortened season and fell to the fourth round of the five-round Draft. He had elbow surgery in June 2021 but returned to the mound 11 months later and displayed an explosive fastball. Frasso can devastate hitters with his heater, which sits at 95-97 mph, touches 100 and plays even better than its velocity thanks to armside run and impressive extension in his delivery. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink continues to improve as he uses it more often, showing flashes of becoming a plus pitch. His mid-80s slider also misses bats with a combination of sweep and depth, though he has trouble landing it for strikes. Frasso didn't go past four innings in an outing during his first two pro seasons, so he still has to prove that his stuff will last deeper into games and over a full season. He uses his athleticism to repeat his delivery well and has a history of throwing strikes. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter and his fastball alone could make him a high-leverage reliever if he winds up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of Palos Verdes Peninsula High School in Southern California, Frasso was a tall and gangly basketball player and a pitcher with a ton of upside, but who had difficulty making the transition from one sport to the next, which kept his velocity down for much of the spring. He looked like the type of pitching prospect who needed college, and that's proven to be true. Focusing on baseball at Loyola Marymount, Frasso started catching up to his upside over his first two years, though an elbow injury suffered before the shutdown put his Draft stock a bit more in question. He was reportedly throwing and working his way back when the season stopped, and the Blue Jays liked his untapped potential on the mound enough that they selected Frasso in the fourth round in June, signing him for below-slot value. Frasso’s athleticism is a plus, as you don’t often find starting pitchers who can dunk a basketball. His fastball has been sitting in the range of 93 mph but reaching up into the 95-97 mph area, and some added strength to his projectable frame could help his sustain that better going forward. That pitch is especially effective up in the zone. Frasso throws a sweeping curve that's an average pitch at this stage with a changeup that lags behind. With long arms, there’s plenty of extension on his releases, too. Frasso’s delivery isn’t the smoothest visually, but his athleticism allows him to repeat it well enough and get to his release point consistently. The physical development of Frasso’s wiry frame will be interesting to track now that he’s in the Blue Jays hands, and while there’s certainly bullpen potential down the road, the organization will explore his potential as a starter first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: What's better than one member of the De Los Santos family in your system? Two. The Pirates signed Yordany De Los Santos in 2022, then circled back to sign his younger brother Johan in 2025, who was No. 23 on MLB Pipeline's Top 50 International Prospects list for that signing period. After getting $2.25 million to join his brother in the system, Johan had a very strong professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .353 with a .911 OPS while not turning 17 until late July. He came stateside and got off to an equally solid start in the Florida Complex League in 2026. Swinging the bat from the left side of the plate, De Los Santos has a feel for the barrel with a line-drive approach and solid bat speed. He's athletic and twitchy in the box, and while he's hit-over-power, he could add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame with impact to come. He's an above-average runner who has already shown he likes to be aggressive on the basepaths. Primarily a shortstop as an amateur, De Los Santos has the actions and an above-average arm to give him a chance to play the premium position going forward. He's been splitting time between short and second base thus far in his blossoming pro career, as the Pirates like to encourage versatility to their young prospects, giving them options if De Los Santos' bat develops like it looks like it might as he rises through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The De Los Santos family must be doing something right. At least the Pirates think so. In 2022, they gave Yordany De Los Santos $1.2 million to sign. Three years later, at the start of the 2025 international signing period, they signed his younger brother Johan for $2.25 million. The younger De Los Santos ranked No. 23 on MLB Pipeline's 2025 Top 50 international prospects list and was one of the youngest players in the class, not turning 17 until late July. A left-handed hitter with a feel for finding the barrel, De Los Santos has a line-drive approach with a sound swing and bat speed. He's athletic with twitchy actions and could add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame with perhaps more impact to come, though he's likely to always be a hit-over-power type of offensive performer. He has good speed with the chance to make plays on the basepaths. With good actions and an above-average arm, De Los Santos has largely played only shortstop and will likely get plenty of reps at the premium position as he embarks on his professional career. The Pirates like to introduce multiple positions to players at a young age to encourage versatility, so don't be surprised if the younger De Los Santos sees some time at second base in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The jewel of the Marlins' 2024 international signing class, Cova landed a $1.5 million bonus out of Venezuela as a remarkable athlete with standout speed. His introduction to pro ball was rocky with a .239/.376/.348 slash line in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, and he returned to the level in 2025. As concerning as it was that the Marlins did not promote him, another year of maturing paid massive dividends as he tied for third on the circuit in homers (nine) and posted a .959 OPS. Cova added strength to his 6-foot-1 frame and loft to his swing in his return to the DSL, which enabled him to tap into his natural power more. The right-handed swinger still has a good knack for finding the barrel, even after trading some contact for impact. He walked nearly as much as he struck out and showed strong swing decisions. How his contact holds up after his first promotion will be key to watch. Cova's renewed pop makes him a true 20/20 threat since he uses his plus speed well on the bases and isn't afraid to run aggressively. A converted infielder, he looks like a potentially plus center fielder with impressive speed underway and solid reads, and there could be untapped strength in his arm. Cova remains a toolsy prospect who has impressed with his maturity and ability to make adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cova originally worked out for teams as a shortstop but didn't distinguish himself until he moved to center field. He starred in center on Venezuela's 15-and-under World Cup team in 2022 and became the headliner of the Marlins' 2024 international class. He signed in January for $1.4 million, the largest international bonus paid by Miami since it gave $3.5 million to Yiddi Cappe three years earlier. Cova makes repeated contact with a quick right-handed stroke. While he's more geared to producing line drives, he has enough bat speed and room to add muscle to perhaps have average power once he's fully developed and learns to launch more balls in the air. His plus speed gives him 20-20 potential. With his quickness and instincts, Cova should be able to remain in center field. His average arm could get stronger as he does, and he should provide enough offense to profile as a regular on a corner if he can't stick in center. Scouts praise his intelligence and maturity as well as his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wallace had an eventful two years at Arkansas, tying the school’s freshman homer record with 14 in 2021 and then helping the Razorbacks reach the College World Series a year later. He was Draft-eligible as a sophomore and went to the Royals in the second round in 2022. He reached Double-A Northwest Arkansas in his first full season and returned to the level to begin 2024, only to suffer a right oblique strain in late May. While rehabbing in Arizona, he suffered a broken rib on a hit-by-pitch and was traded to the Nationals eight days later as part of the return for Hunter Harvey. Wallace got in 11 games with Double-A Harrisburg and three more in the Arizona Fall League before being shut down with a back issue. All of the injuries made Wallace a difficult evaluation in 2024, though the main tenets of his profile remain true. His feel for the barrel from the right side helps him the ball to all fields, and there’s above-average raw power here that could make him a threat to hit 15-plus homers at peak. He chased too much against all pitch types during his Double-A looks last season and especially struggled to lay off (and make contact with) low-and-away sliders. Honing in that approach may be as simple as getting consistent at-bats again. The Royals were impressed by Wallace’s defensive gains before the trade, and the Nationals have come away from their early looks believing he won’t have any trouble handling the position for any club. His arm strength certainly fits there, and he has the accuracy to hit the target on a line. There’s everyday potential here at the hot corner, but Wallace will need the bat to catch up to the glove to reach that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wallace made an immediate impact at Arkansas when he tied the school's freshman home run record (14) for his home state Razorbacks. He led Arkansas to the College World Series as a Draft-eligible sophomore, and then the Royals took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft while giving him a $1.7 million signing bonus. In his first full pro season, the 22-year-old had a strong start in High-A before a late-season bump to Double-A. His performance dipped slightly at the higher level, but he slashed .254/.331/.414 over 130 games total in 2023, with 27 doubles, seven triples, 13 homers and 84 RBIs. Wallace was dealt to the Nats in July in a deal for Hunter Harvey. Wallace goes to the plate with a calm demeanor and simple mechanics, in addition to a compact and efficient right-handed swing. He has a true feel for the barrel and has power potential to all fields, although he struggled with breaking balls in 2023 and could have gotten pull-happy in an attempt to create more power. He projects as more of a gap-to-gap hitter than a home run hitter, but as he adds strength, he might tap into that above-average raw power. More than anything in 2023, Wallace showed he could handle the hot corner. He’s a natural third baseman with a strong, plus arm. His throws are accurate with good carry -- even the balls he fielded close to the line made it across the diamond with plenty of zip. Wallace has solid baserunning skills to help his average speed, which will lead to more stolen bases. Wallace, who has dealt with an oblique injury and broken rib after the trade, is now in an organization with other third-base options in Brady House and Yohandy Morales, but he has the well-rounded profile to carve out his own role in DC.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted in 2020 because of his commitment, Wallace made an immediate impact at Arkansas when he tied the freshman home run record (14) held by former first-round picks Zack Cox and Heston Kjerstad. After he led Arkansas to the College World Series, the Royals made Wallace, the Draft-eligible sophomore, their second-round pick and gave him a $1.7 million bonus. He made his pro debut last summer with three games in the Arizona Complex League before moving up to Single-A Columbia. There, he slashed .293/.379/.466 with two homers. Wallace has a compact and efficient right-handed swing with a traditional setup, and he has a true feel for the barrel. He generates impressive exit velocities and easy power with his bat speed and strength. Big and broad-shouldered, most of his power right now comes from the pull side, but he’s flashed the ability to go the other way. A point of emphasis will be his swing decisions and recognizing the pitches he can do damage with to let that power play. He has a strong arm and good instincts, impressing the Royals in the fall with his third-base defense. Wallace is about an average runner but will be able to steal bases. Wallace played a lot of outfield in college, but the Royals see him as a third baseman for the foreseeable future. As long as he makes the proper adjustments with his approach, Wallace should move quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acevedo became one of the headliners of the 2026 international signing period when he signed with the Orioles for $2.3 million, narrowly topping Luis Almeyda for the largest international bonus in club history. The well-rounded shortstop was the big name of a standout haul for the Orioles, who nabbed five of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects on signing day. A supremely gifted hitter with a smooth right-handed swing, Acevedo stands out with an advanced hit tool built on quick hands, natural bat-to-ball skills and a precocious ability to control the barrel. He generates easy bat speed, stays balanced through his swing and can square up pitches to all fields. He’s mostly gap-to-gap right now, but there is some developing power there to the pull side that he might get to more as he adds muscle and matures physically. He is extremely aggressive in the box and will likely need to refine his swing decisions to acclimate to more advanced pitching. Even amongst a class of talented shortstops, Acevedo is advanced defensively. He shows good actions and a natural feel for the position and generates routinely accurate throws with a plus arm. While he isn’t a burner on the basepaths, he has quick feet and moves well laterally, athleticism that should allow him to remain up-the-middle long-term. Acevedo will play his entire first pro season as a 17-year-old, so there is a lot of projection here. But with the ceiling of a surefire shortstop with an impact bat, there is also a lot to dream on.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres have typically been heavy hitters on the international market. They certainly made waves by bringing in Ethan Salas in 2023 and Leo De Vries in 2024 when both were the top international prospects in their class, and they made a run for 2025 No. 1 Roki Sasaki before he joined the Dodgers. San Diego’s 2026 class is more spread out in terms of talent, but leading the way is Cuban shortstop Hernandez, who trained in the Dominican Republic before signing for $1.4 million in January. The right-handed slugger has a “whippy” swing that comes with a lot of bat speed and easy power on which to dream. Standing 6-foot-1, 180 pounds, he has plenty of room to add extra muscle too, and there’s a shot for him to get plus power at fully maturity. The looseness and length in his swing comes with some hit-tool questions, however. He can swing around breaking balls and offspeed pitches, and that’ll need tightening up as he faces pro-level pitching. After signing Hernandez, Padres amateur and international scouting director Chris Kemp mentioned a “6.3-6.4 60[-yard dash]” as one of the things that stands out most about the youngster. That would give him top-line speed, and even if he slows down as he adds muscle, he could settle into plus wheels all the same. That type of athleticism should help him at shortstop or possibly center field, and if he needs to slide to third base down the line instead, he has the arm strength and pop for that too. Early indications are that he’s improving the hit tool, but don’t expect Hernandez to be a quick mover a la Salas and De Vries.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates went over slot to sign White away from playing football and baseball at Penn State in 2021, they knew they’d have to be patient with an athlete from a cold-weather state who had been splitting his focus among multiple sports. What they didn’t know is how hard it would be to keep him on the field. A number of injuries limited White to 11 total games in 2021 and 2022 but even though he didn’t get started until June of 2023, he saw his first extended action, mostly with full-season Bradenton, allowing him to finally to show a little bit of what the fuss was all about. White has teased with his physicality and athleticism since signing; in 2023, he got to put all of it to use for 61 games. Considering how much development time he missed, it was encouraging he shook off the rust and kept his strikeout rate under 30 percent while also drawing a lot of walks. He can be quick to the ball and find the barrel with pretty good power, with more to come. The former wide receiver is an easily plus runner, so his ability to get on base should help him be a threat to steal. It also helps him cover a lot of ground in center field, where he has a chance to be an excellent defender for a long time. He still has a ways to go, but last year was the first positive steps forward he’s been able to take. If he can put the injuries behind him and continue to stay on the field, he could really start sharpening all of those tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams interested in White’s baseball ability knew he would be a tougher sign because he had the chance to go to Penn State to play football and baseball. Because the Pirates saved on signing Henry Davis atop the 2021 Draft, they were able to get not only two high-ceiling arms in Bubba Chandler and Anthony Solometo, but also White, giving him $1.5 million after selecting him in Competitive Balance Round B. Since then, it’s been tough for him to stay on the field, with injuries allowing him to play just 11 games since signing. Athletic and physical, White still has the raw tools that made him such an intriguing prospect in the first place. The former wide receiver can really run, which should allow him to steal bases and cover a lot of ground in center field. He’s shown glimpses of an approach at the plate, with a short swing from the right side and an ability to barrel up the baseball. Playing multiple sports meant he was a little more raw at the plate, but there’s power to tap into, and there’s been confidence things would smooth out with a baseball-only focus. What White has needed more than anything else as a multi-sport athlete from a cold-weather state is reps, and he’s missed a lot of development time because of what’s largely been soft-tissue kind of injuries. The Pirates don’t feel it’s a long-term concern and if he adjusts to the full-time baseball calendar, his body will respond, with the hope he can truly start showing what he’s capable of with a healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White was a three-sport standout at his high school outside of Philadelphia, one who had the chance to go to Penn State to play football and baseball. The Pirates had other ideas, using their bonus pool wisely and taking the savings from signing No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis below slot and applying it to a number of high-ceilinged prep players. It took $1.5 million to sign White away from the Nittany Lions, and he went and had a brief pro debut in the Florida Complex League. As a former Division I football recruit as a wide receiver, White obviously brings athleticism and physicality to the Pirates system. And while some baseball tools are understandably raw given his previously split focus, he does have a shorter right-handed swing and tends to be on time at the plate. There are some swing-and-miss issues to iron out, but that might come with professional reps, and he has shown he can leverage the baseball and get to some solid power. White’s speed plays on both sides of the ball. He should be a basestealing threat and he can cover a ton of ground in center field with a combination of those wheels and excellent instincts. He might have a long way to go, but the Pirates are excited to see how his athleticism plays as a full-time baseball player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers are the most productive organization at identifying, signing and developing young international talent, so when Frias joined the system as a $350,000 signee out of the Dominican Republic in January 2025, there should have been at least some intrigue about next steps for the outfielder. Frias was a solid performer in the Dominican Summer League with a .316/.411/.400 line and one homer over 27 games, prompting him to move stateside to the Arizona Complex League for his age-18 season this year. Upon his arrival this spring, the right-handed-hitting Frias quickly impressed Brewers officials with both his current power production and future pop potential, and that’s carried into the season, with him recording Statcast-measured exit velocities as high as 117 mph. That would be at least plus-plus raw power already. Frias has also displayed some early bat-to-ball skills, but his swing can be a little flat, keeping his rockets lower to the ground than needed to drive huge homer totals. If he can elevate more, then this level of loud contact would make him one of the best sluggers in a deep Milwaukee farm system. Frias doesn’t have the speed needed to play center field, with fellow 2025 signing Brailyn Antunez getting those looks instead. However, his arm strength makes him a perfect fit in right field, and he’s already proven capable of collecting outfield assists in bunches from out there. The slugging ability would slot in nicely in the corner, but with Frias still several years away, he still has much to prove that he can do more than light up Statcast tech.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a growing contingent of Bahamians in the Marlins organization, Lewis has drawn comparisons to countryman Jazz Chisholm for his package of power, speed and twitchy athleticism in a compact frame. Signed for $950,000 in 2019, he had his pro debut delayed until 2021 because of the pandemic. Personal issues and a broken hamate limited him to just 51 games in Single-A at age 19 last year and his performance has declined while he has repeated the level in 2023. A switch-hitter, Lewis has good bat-to-ball skills and a decent understanding of the strike zone. He exhibits electric bat speed from both sides of the plate and has gotten considerably stronger since turning pro, but he hits too many groundballs and has yet to figure out how to tap into his plus raw power. He can get overly pull-conscious and needs to make adjustments to better handle breaking balls. Lewis has well-above-average speed and uses it aggressively on the bases, stealing 16 in 17 attempts last season. His quickness doesn't play quite as well in the field, where he has average range at second base and perhaps a tick better than that at third. His average arm is better suited for second, where his fast hands help him turn double plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lewis signed for $950,000 in 2019, receiving the highest bonus among Bahamians in that international class. Though the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season and what would have been his pro debut the following summer, he impressed in instructional league that fall. When he finally got a chance to play in 2021, he batted .302/.354/.497 with 18 extra-base hits and nine steals in 43 games as an 18-year-old in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Lewis is reminiscent of countryman Jazz Chisholm with his combination of twitchy athleticism, power and speed in a compact frame. A switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides of the plate, he has gotten stronger since signing and opened eyes by displaying at least average power in his debut. His hand-eye coordination and patient approach allow him to make consistent contact, though he'll have to prove he can handle quality breaking balls at higher levels. With his well-above-average speed, Lewis is a base-stealing threat and covers ground in the middle infield. The Marlins believe he has the actions and solid arm strength to handle shortstop, though he probably won't get much of a chance as he rises through the Minors alongside Kahlil Watson and Jose Salas. Lewis spent most of last summer at second base, where his quick hands help him turn double plays, and he can become an average or better defender as he develops more consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Pirates All-Star David Bednar, Will was named most outstanding player at the 2021 College World Series after dominating in three starts as Mississippi State won its first national title. After signing him for a below-slot $3,647,500 as the 14th overall pick that July, the Giants expected him to move quickly through the Minors. But his first full pro season in 2022 ended after two months because of a stress reaction in his lower back and related issues have sidelined him for most of this year. When he starred in college, Bednar bullied hitters with a 92-97 mph fastball that could feature either good carry up in the strike zone or heavy life at the knees and an 82-85 mph slider with horizontal and vertical action. Rarely at full health last year, he mostly worked at 90-93 mph with his heater and had less power and movement with the slider. His truncated season gave him little opportunity to work on a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink that he barely used in college and can struggle to throw for strikes. Bednar pounded the strike zone at Mississippi State but his back issues also took a toll on his control and command. He features some effort in his delivery but has a strong 6-foot-2 build that should lend itself to durability. His intelligence and competitiveness should help him get the most out of his ability, though he'll need to regain his health and his college stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Bednar brothers will remember 2021 fondly after David compiled a 2.23 ERA as a rookie reliever with the Pirates and Will won most outstanding player honors at the College World Series after leading Mississippi State to its first national title. The latter struck out 15 in six one-hit innings against Texas in his first CWS start and won the final with six more scoreless frames against Vanderbilt, then went 14th overall in the Draft and signed for an under-slot $3,647,500. His stuff and control haven't been as sharp in 2022 while he has battled some lower back issues. Bednar has spent much of his first full pro season working at 90-93 mph with his fastball after operating at 92-95 mph and reaching 97 in college. He can throw his heater with good carry up in the strike zone as well as with heavy life at the knees. His best offering is a slider that reaches the mid-80s with plenty of horizontal sweep as well as depth when it's on, and he'll occasionally dust off an upper-70s downer curveball to give hitters a different look. Bednar also has the makings of an average changeup with fade and sink, though he's still honing his ability to throw it for strikes. His physical frame should give him the durability to succeed as a starter, though there is some effort to his delivery and his control has wavered at times this summer. He also stands out with his intelligence and competitiveness and could be a late-inning reliever if starting doesn't work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramírez joined the Mets for $2.05 million out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019 and jumped straight to full-season ball in 2021 after missing out on his first full campaign due to the pandemic. Until this year, he had yet to make it out of A-ball and slashed .221/.310/.317 with seven homers and 21 steals in 120 games for High-A Brooklyn last season. The Mets added him to the 40-man roster in November 2023 but nontendered him just one year later after a down year at Double-A Binghamton. He re-signed as a Minor League free agent in December 2024. Ramírez can still flash the promising tools that once made him a Top 100 prospect. He can show promising raw power from the right side, especially on pulled fly balls, and at 6-foot-3, there is room for the 21-year-old to add more strength. His above-average speed helped him string together consecutive 20-steal seasons in 2022-23, and while his routes can be circuitous, he can still eat up enough ground with his long legs to be a potentially above-average center fielder. His strong arm, which enabled him to record 11 outfield assists in 2023, is another asset. But he’s going to have to hit to get those skills into a Major League lineup, and while he may have been more selective last season, he still had difficulty finding the barrel with a swing that can be vicious but tends to be all over the place. Only 29 of his 101 hits went for extra bases, and that wasn’t only because of Brooklyn’s pitcher-friendly environs -- he slugged .317 on the road too. Ramírez is still young for the upper Minors, but he's gone from exciting name to a questionable project in a short span.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez signed for $2.05 million as MLB Pipeline’s No. 26 international prospect on July 2, 2019, and after missing out on 2020 like everyone else, he’s only played full-season games, starting with Single-A St. Lucie in 2021. He repeated the Florida State League last year, hitting .284/.359/.443 in 67 games, before finishing up his age-19 season with a 106 wRC+ in 54 games with High-A Brooklyn. The Dominican Republic native is a toolsy center fielder that scouts and player-development types love to dream on. His biggest development in 2022 was cutting his K rate from 31.1 percent the previous year to 22.1 percent while still moving up a level, and that has strengthened the belief that he can hit enough to be an impact player, even if he has a noisy setup at the dish. He has wiry strength that should only increase as he matures, but it's still yet to show up in games. Standing at 6-foot-3, Ramirez uses his size and above-average speed to glide to balls in center, and he can make plays look effortless, sometimes to his detriment. He has enough arm strength for right field, giving him another route to Queens. While he’ll be Rule 5-eligible next offseason, Ramirez is still only 20 years old heading into his third campaign with a full-season club. He still has some road ahead of him, but the 2023 season has represented a step back in some ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets used their highest bonus of the 2019-20 international period on Ramirez (MLB Pipeline’s No. 26 prospect in that class) by signing him for $2.05 million. The Dominican outfielder has been moved about as aggressively as a player in that signing class could, going from instructional league play in 2020 straight to Low-A St. Lucie as an 18-year-old in 2021. Ramirez hit .258/.326/.384 with five homers in 16 steals over 76 games in his first taste of full-season (or any Minor League) action. The Mets remain enthusiastic about who Ramirez could be in time, but it’s still more about potential than present skills. Ramirez is an above-average-to-plus runner right now, one who is willing to use those wheels to good effect in center field and on the basepaths. (A strong arm will also help him move over to right field, if necessary, and he did play 22 games in that corner in 2021.) He stands 6-foot-3 and could fill out more than his current 170-pound frame. His power has started to show up in promising ways at Single-A and High-A this season, and there’s still room for more in-game pop as he matures and gains experience. Ramirez’s long-awaited breakout has begun to bear fruit in 2022, leading to his placement on the MLB Pipeline Top 100 for the first time. Ramirez doesn’t need to be added to the 40-man roster until November 2023, and another big jump could be coming before then, if he continues on this current trajectory.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Andujar got the largest bonus the Rockies handed out during the 2024 international signing period, joining the organization for $1.7 million. He fared well during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, hitting .292 with a .376 on-base percentage. He was still 17 when his United States debut began in the Arizona Complex League, and the Rockies were thrilled with how he carried himself, as he once again hit well (.319) and got on base (.370 OBP), but with virtually no impact either summer. Andujar is a switch-hitter who has already has shown an ability to make a lot of contact. He carries a career strikeout rate of just 13.9 percent into the 2026 season, routinely finding the barrel. He's better from the left side, but some of that is that he just hasn't gotten many reps the other way against left-handed pitching. What he's lacking more than anything else is strength. He has just 17 total extra-base hits in his two stops so far and has not shown the ability to drive the ball. He does have every chance to stick at shortstop with terrific hands and enough arm for the spot. He had a little trouble with the speed of the game when he first got to the ACL, but as he got his legs under him, his internal clock kicked in and he let his defensive instincts take over. This one may take some patience as a deep projection, with the strength piece critical for him to reach the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies don't shy away from going after middle infielders on the international market, with Ezequiel Tovar the biggest success story of the past several years. They added Andujar to the system when the 2024 signing period opened, giving him $1.7 million to sign. One of the top infielders in the class, he went to the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut and showed off some good contact skills, hitting .292 with a .376 on-base percentage, but leading to some concerns about future impact. One of the youngest players in the class who didn't turn 17 until late July, Andujar certainly has time to figure things out. He starts out with a pretty good feel for hitting from both sides of the plate. He can find the barrel routinely and makes a ton of contact. He struck out just 13.5 percent of the time, isn't afraid to hit behind in the count and even drew some walks. He needs to add strength so he can impact the ball more, even if power isn't ever a big part of his game after slugging .352 in his debut. More strength should also augment Andujar's speed. He likes to run despite having just average speed at present and he moves well defensively at shortstop. He has good hands and an arm that could develop into a plus for him at the premium position. His ability to slow the game down gives him an even better overall defensive package and something he can lean on to help his team win if his bat is slow to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In July 2017, it was Ezequiel Tovar. Two years later, Adael Amador led the class. Dyan Jorge was next up in 2022. So it should have come with little surprise when the Rockies again went after, and signed, one of the top shortstops in this year's international amateur class. Andujar, who was No. 17 on MLB Pipeline's Top 50 International prospect list when the 2024 signing period opened in January, got $1.7 million to sign, and like Tovar and Jorge, he will get his pro career started in the Dominican Summer League. Andujar is a switch-hitter who has shown some offensive upside from both sides of the plate. He finds the barrel consistently with high contact rates, rarely strikes out and isn't afraid of hitting with two strikes. Right now it's gap-to-gap thump, at best, but if he can add strength to his frame, there should be more power to come in the future. While he isn't a burner, that added strength should allow Andujar to add speed as he matures as well, and he's already aggressive on the basepaths and likes to steal. He has all the makings of a solid shortstop, with soft hands and an arm that could eventually be plus. His defensive tools play up because he has excellent instincts and awareness to go along with a good internal clock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ foray into the international market under executive VP and GM Mike Elias has resulted in some flashy acquisitions and some of the biggest bonuses handed out in franchise history. The team is seeking success developing bargain gems such as Bencosme, who signed for only $10,000 in August 2020 and then played his way to High-A Aberdeen as a 19-year-old the following year. After jumping three levels in 2022, he was given all of 2023 to develop at High-A and held his own, walking nearly as much as he struck out and swiping 28 bases in 34 attempts. Bencosme is a left-handed batter with excellent contact skills that could make him an average hitter. He rarely strikes out, displaying an approach, understanding of the strike zone and ability to draw walks uncommon in hitters his age. He’s also a really good bunter. The drawback is a dearth of pop. Bencosme generates enough strength from his wiry frame to drive the ball into the outfield and leg out some extra-base hits, but his below-average exit velocities and only average wheels emphasize his need to hit line drives at a high clip. His below-average raw power is only to the pull side, though he might grow into a little more as he continues to add strength to his projectable frame. His strong decision-making on the bases enables him to collect more steals than other players with similar footspeed. Bencosme is primarily a shortstop, but his actions could be cleaned up a little and he’s athletic enough to move around the infield. He essentially split 2023 between short and second base, sprinkling in some time at third as well. His average arm is accurate and strong enough to handle the throws necessary at all those positions. He could probably be average at second and slightly below average but playable at short or third. If he can add a little more thump to his game, Bencosme’s age, athleticism and advanced bat-to-ball skills give him the ceiling of a future infield regular with a useful utility-type floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ transformation under executive VP and GM Mike Elias from absentees to legit players in the international free-agent market took some time to result in high-end acquisitions. But they might have found themselves a bargain gem after signing Bencosme for only $10,000 in August 2020. He made a strong first impression in the Dominican Summer League in 2021, then after playing only two games at the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, jumped to full-season Delmarva and hit .336 in 59 games in 2022. He finished the year at High-A Aberdeen as a 19-year-old. A left-handed hitter with elite bat-to-ball skills, Bencosme is a career .311 hitter in 117 games across four levels already. He almost never strikes out, showing a precocious approach and willingness to draw walks not often seen in very young hitters. So far he does so without much pop, though there is hope he can add more extra-base impact as he continues to grow and add strength to his wiry build. Bencosme’s primary position is shortstop and he played most of his games there at both affiliates last summer, but has also moved around the infield and looks comfortable at second and third as well. He’s a good runner who is already showing some ability to steal bases. Hope remains he can grow into a 8-to-10-homer guy as he matures at the plate. If he’s able to add that thump to his game, he looks like a future regular on the infield with the floor of a useful utility-type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes there are college starters who are clearly ticketed for the bullpen. And sometimes, college relievers are given a chance to start at the next level. Then there are hurlers like Minacci, who did nothing but relieve in three years at Wake Forest, saving 13 games in 2023 en route to being the Angels’ sixth-round pick that summer, and will continue to pitch his way to the big leagues exclusively out of the bullpen. Minacci pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball last year, saving 18 games in the process. There’s nothing fancy about Minacci’s approach on the mound. He goes right after hitters with two plus pitches in his mid-90s fastball that peaks at 98-99 mph and his upper-80s slider. The heater misses a good amount of bats thanks to some serious armside run, and his slider misses even more with depth more than horizontal action. While Minacci’s delivery features some effort and he’s never likely to have pinpoint command, he’s tended to be around the strike zone. There’s some confidence that he’ll throw enough strikes to handle high-leverage situations in the big leagues, something he did effectively in multiple seasons with the Demon Deacons and in his first year of pro ball. It shouldn’t take him too much longer to be deemed big league ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wake Forest has developed into one of the best college baseball programs in the country, famous for its pitching lab and churning out starters like first-rounder Rhett Lowder (2023, Reds) and second-round pick Sean Sullivan (2023, Rockies). The Demon Deacons also produce relief prospects, with Minacci leading the way after serving as the school’s closer for two years and saving 13 games in 2023. That resulted in the Angels taking him in the sixth round of last summer’s Draft and sending him to Single-A Inland Empire for his debut. Minacci is a two-pitch reliever who could move pretty quickly through the Angels’ system, especially given their penchant for pushing college arms aggressively up the ladder. Both of his offerings are plus: a fastball with armside run that sits 94-96 mph and tops out at 99, and a mid-80s slider that touches 90 mph with more depth than horizontal action that misses a ton of bats. There is no third pitch in Minacci’s arsenal and there’s some effort in his delivery, so there’s no question of his future role. He has the intense mentality that can serve a reliever well late in games. His strike-throwing improved over the course of his college career, providing more confidence of him being able to handle high-leverage situations, perhaps as a future setup man in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's Maryland High School Player of the Year in 2021, Heubeck offered one of the best curveballs and was one of the most polished pitchers in that year's prep class. Since the Dodgers signed him away from a Wake Forest commitment with an over-slot $1,269,500 bonus in the third round, he has gained velocity but lost some feel for pitching. He missed the last two months of the 2025 season with rotator-cuff inflammation, and his strikeout rate (28 percent) ranked fifth in the Double-A Texas League and his walk rate was the eigth-highest (12 percent) among pitchers who worked at least as many as his 66 1/3 innings. Heubeck's fastball operates at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with huge induced vertical break that helps it ride by barrels up in the zone. Both of his breaking balls grade as plus pitches and get lefties and righties out when they're on, though he also has difficulty landing his upper-70s downer curveball and tight mid-80s slider for strikes. He also struggles to locate a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Heubeck filled the strike zone as an amateur and should have at least average control given his athleticism and clean arm action. Instead of his letting his stuff play naturally, he'll lapse into overthrowing his fastball and overspinning his breakers. Though Los Angeles still hopes to develop him into a starter, it's more realistic to project him as a bat-missing reliever whose ability to throw strikes will determine what role he fills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's Maryland high school player of the year in 2021, Heubeck stood out with one of the best curveballs and some of the best polish in that year's prep class. Since signing for an over-slot $1,269,500 as a third-rounder, he has retained his feel for spin while adding velocity and losing control. He posted a 3.05 ERA at High-A last year with the best average-against (.181) and second-highest strikeout percentage (30 percent) among Midwest League pitchers with at least 90 innings, but he also had the worst walk percentage (17 percent). Heubeck now operates with a 92-95 mph fastball that reaches 97 with huge induced vertical break that creates significant carry. Both his upper-70s downer curveball and his tighter mid-80s slider can be plus pitches that work against both lefties and righties when he lands them for strikes, which he hasn't done consistently in pro ball. He also has a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink that could be an average pitch if he learns to harness it. Heubeck has a clean arm action and an athletic delivery that should be conducive to at least average control. He sometimes overspins his breaking balls and needs to find a better balance between trying to create nasty stuff and throwing strikes. The Dodgers still think he could develop into a No. 3 or 4 starter, even if takes longer than they expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heubeck earned Gatorade's 2021 Maryland high school player of the year award after leading Gilman School (Baltimore) to the state Class A title, fanning 15 in a complete-game victory in the semifinals and saving the finale. The Dodgers drafted him in the third round, making him the Old Line State's highest prep pitcher pick since 2005, and signed him away from a Wake Forest commitment for an over-slot $1,269,500. He quickly stood out with his aptitude during his four-inning pro debut and in instructional league, with one club official describing him as \"plug and play.\" Heubeck already possesses a plus curveball with upper-70s velocity and legitimate 12-6 break. It plays well off his fastball, which sits at 90-93 mph and tops out at 95 with good induced vertical break and carry up in the strike zone. He also shows promising feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink. With a clean arm action and athletic delivery, Heubeck should provide at least average control. His strike-throwing and velocity should improve as he adds some much-needed strength to his skinny 6-foot-3 frame. A potential No. 3 or 4 starter, he could move through the Minors more quickly than most high school pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before Nolan McLean and Carson Benge were notable two-way prospects at Oklahoma State, Campbell was a finalist for the John Olerud Award -- given to NCAA Division I's best two-way player -- in 2021. The California native went on to focus solely on pitching and performed well enough as a junior for the Guardians to select him 37th overall and sign him for a below-slot $1.7 million in '22. However, Campbell did not make his pro debut until April 2026 because of May 2023 right elbow surgery to relieve pressure on his ulnar nerve, April 2024 Tommy John surgery on the same elbow and October 2024 right wrist surgery. Campbell was a polished arm in college and stands out at the start of his pro career for his broad five-pitch mix, with each offering at least average. After averaging 91-92 mph on his fastball at Oklahoma State, he's now sitting 94-95 mph and touching 97. He throws the pitch more than half the time, but opponents have trouble with it because of the extension he gets on his 6-foot-5 frame and the uncomfortable approach angle from his delivery. He pairs that well with a mid-80s changeup that can pick up a lot of whiffs and chase at its best. Campbell can spin a pair of promising breaking balls, with the curve currently ahead of the slider, in part because it gets nearly 40 inches of vertical separation from the fastball. His low-90s cutter is new since college and has been a promising fifth option. Campbell is an excellent strike-thrower, and his athleticism and delivery have helped him maintain his above-average control, even after all of those surgeries. The big question, though, remains health, since there are very few cases of pitchers not throwing for four years and developing into long-term starters, so the Guardians will continue to build him up slowly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campbell was a finalist for the John Olerud Award given to NCAA Division I's best two-way player in 2021 before focusing solely on pitching as an Oklahoma State junior last spring. He ranked seventh in D-I with 141 strikeouts in 101 1/3 innings before going 37th overall in the Draft and signing for a below-slot $1.7 million. He has yet to make his pro debut, however, because he had surgery to relieve pressure on the ulnar nerve in his pitching elbow in May. Campbell has two secondary pitches that stand out more than his fastball: a plus upper-70s changeup with plenty of fade and a mid-70s curveball with significant depth. His heater sits at 91-93 mph and occasionally reaches 97, featuring high spin rates and armside run that generate a lot of weak contact. He can mix in a low-80s slider but usually works with three pitches. Due to his 6-foot-7 frame that creates unusual angle and deceptive delivery, hitters don't see the ball well against Campbell and take a lot of awkward swings against him. Very athletic for his size, he repeats his mechanics and pounds the strike zone. A tough competitor who had one of the highest floors among pitchers in the 2022 Draft, he should become at least a No. 4 starter with the chance for more if the Guardians can work their Shane Bieber magic on him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies had 12 picks in the top 10 rounds of the 2022 Draft and they used 11 of them to take college-aged players. The one exception was Cox, their second-round selection who got a slightly over-slot bonus of $1.85 million to sign. He was just getting started finding his way in pro ball in 2023 when he needed Tommy John surgery and he missed all of 2024. He came back to log 85 innings under close medical supervision with Single-A Fresno in 2025 and the Rockies were very encouraged with what they saw. Cox’s stuff started coming back once he was on the mound, running his fastball up to 95 mph routinely and reaching back for more at times with good life up in the zone, but it’s his curveball that is still the talk of the town. He registers elite spin rates with the 1-to-7 breaking ball that features sharp bite, missing plenty of bats with it. He was way too fastball-heavy when he first entered pro ball, and in 2025, he found a better balance between the heater and the curve. He has a changeup, but it’s too firm and he doesn’t pronate all that well, leading some to think that he might be a candidate to add another pitch, perhaps bringing the cutter he had worked on previously back into his repertoire. There could be more consistent velocity from Cox as he gets further removed from Tommy John and he did a nice job of being around the zone and repeating his delivery well during his first season back. The gloves will come off a bit more and there’s a chance that Cox, at age 22, could reach a different plane as a pitching prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies had four picks in the top two rounds of the 2022 Draft and used the first three to take college players, one pitcher and two bats. Cox was one of the better high school pitchers on the West Coast that year and the Pacific Northwest native became the Rockies’ second-rounder and was signed away from his Oregon commitment for an over-slot $1.85 million bonus. The organization was excited to see what he could do in full-season ball after impressing in instructional league play the fall after signing, but after pitching in shorter stints over 10 outings with Single-A Fresno, he was part of the Rockies' Tommy John surgery trifecta with Gabriel Hughes and Jordy Vargas. It was Cox’s feel for spin that really helped him stand out as a prepster and during the infancy of his pro career. It’s a plus 1-to-7 curveball with elite-level spin rates, a true out pitch with sharp bite. His other offerings aren’t bad, either: a lively fastball up to 95 mph and some feel for a changeup. The athletic right-hander also tinkered with a slider and cutter after showing acumen for manipulating the spin and break on his curve. Added strength was already a plus for Cox and should help him get his stuff back -- and perhaps add more -- once he’s put the elbow surgery behind him. He has clean mechanics and the ability to pitch to both sides of the plate. It won’t be until 2025 before the Rockies know what they have on their hands, but he could still get back to reaching his ceiling as a mid-rotation type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts looking for good high school pitching in the state of Washington were busy in 2022, with both J.R. Ritchie and Cox getting a lot of attention as right-handers who had first-round potential. Ritchie went No. 35 overall to the Braves, while the Rockies were thrilled to get Cox in the second round, giving him an over-slot bonus of $1.85 million to sign him away from his commitment to Oregon. He didn’t pitch competitively after signing, but he did impress his new organization in instructional league play. He was being handled carefully during his first full season of pro ball in Fresno in 2023 when he needed Tommy John surgery in late July. One of the early things that stood out with Cox is his competitiveness on the mound, with a no-nonsense approach and a desire to attack hitters with what could be a very good three-pitch mix. He can get his fastball up to 95 mph with good running life, but it’s his curveball that has everyone buzzing. It’s a 1-to-7 breaking ball that registers elite-level spin rates and can be a real hammer out pitch with sharp bite to it. He has good feel for his changeup as well. Cox has already added strength to his athletic frame since signing, which could lead to more consistent velocity once he's back to full strength. He’s already shown an ability to command the ball to both sides of the plate and manipulate the spin and break on his curve, with some thinking he might eventually develop a distinct slider. His combination of pitchability and potential power stuff points to a future as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Though he could have turned pro as early as January 2021, Burrowes waited until he nearly completed high school in Panama before signing for $75,000 in April 2022, and he returned home after his pro debut that summer to finish his degree. He broke his hand when hit by a pitch during Spring Training in 2024, which led to a disappointing first foray into full-season ball. He rebounded last year and also improved his effort level, earning a promotion to High-A at age 20. Burrowes has a quick right-handed stroke, makes reasonable swing decisions and hits the ball hard for his age. He does damage against fastballs and consistently turns on pitches, with most of his power playing to left field. He chases too many breaking balls and changeups and struggles to put them in play, so he'll have to make adjustments. Burrowes has plus speed and is an aggressive baserunner who stole 47 bases in 53 attempts (88.6 percent) last year. After spending most of his first two seasons in the United States at shortstop, where the game sped up on him, he looked more comfortable at second and third base in 2025. He has solid arm strength and also has seen action in left and center field. He could fill a super-utility role if he can become a more reliable hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible to turn pro in January 2021, Burrowes waited to nearly finish high school in Panama before signing for $75,000 in April 2022. He attracted immediate attention when he made his pro debut two months later in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, with other clubs asking for him in trade talks. He completed his high school degree that fall before coming to the United States and hitting .259/.330/.386 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last summer. Burrowes already produces impressive exit velocities for a teenagers and has the room to add a lot of muscle to his wiry 6-foot-2 frame. He has a sound right-handed swing with bat speed but is still a work in progress offensively. He was overly aggressive in his U.S. debut and wasn't able to turn on pitches consistently. Burrowes owns plus speed and likes to make things happen on the bases. His quickness gives him range at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength but also a tendency to get flashy. An organization favorite, he's bilingual and stands out with his intelligence and leadership.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eligible to sign in January 2021, Burrowes waited until he had nearly finished high school in Panama before turning pro for $75,000 last April. He made his pro debut two months later and immediately stood out in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, prompting other clubs to ask for him in trade talks. He returned home in the fall to complete his high school degree and will make his highly anticipated U.S. debut in 2023. Burrows' advanced hitting ability and projectable 6-foot-2 frame give him one of the highest offensive ceilings in the system. He recognizes pitches and manages the strike zone better than most teenagers, repeatedly barreling balls with a sound right-handed swing. He generates high exit velocities for someone so young and could develop at least 20-homer power as he gains strength and experience. A solid runner with good instincts on the bases, Burrowes went 12-for-12 stealing bases in the DSL but may slow a bit as he fills out. He has the athleticism and solid arm strength to possibly stick at shortstop, and if he outgrows the position, he'd profile well at third base. He's bilingual and draws praise for his intelligence and charisma in addition to his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fabian left high school early to enroll at the University of Florida and was a second-round Draft pick by the Red Sox in 2021, but didn’t sign. The Orioles nabbed him in Competitive Balance Round B the following year, signing the toolsy outfielder for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million. He’s since flashed the exciting combination of power and speed that made him a marquee name in college, mainly by enjoying a 24-homer, 31-steal performance in his first full season. But he has also struggled against better pitching at every level jump and seriously slumped after reaching Triple-A for the first time down the stretch in 2024. Belying Fabian’s enviable tools is all the swing-and-miss in his game, which was once viewed as a stomach-able tradeoff to his power-speed upside. But Fabian’s inability to make consistent contact has severely cut into his upside as he’s reached the higher levels, due to an uppercut right-handed swing that struggles against pitches at the top of the zone. Fabian struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances at Double-A and in 41 percent at Triple-A. All those whiffs undercut his ability to get on base and get to his power regularly in games. No such glaring holes sabotage Fabian defensively. His plus speed and strong instincts give him excellent range, and his ability to read fly balls and run efficient routes make him a plus defender in center field. He also possesses one of the stronger outfield throwing arms in the O’s system. Given the athleticism, baseball IQ and purse of loud tools, Fabian could be an impact player if he makes enough contact against quality pitching; if not, the swing-and-miss might limit him to a part-time player capable of providing a spark off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 60 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Fabian has been a legit prospect since graduating high school early to enroll at the University of Florida for the 2019 season, and he was drafted twice: first by the Red Sox in the second round in 2021 and by the Orioles in Competitive Balance Round B the following year. He signed with Baltimore for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million, and after an exciting debut, reached Double-A Bowie in 2023, though he struggled against better pitching. His entire career, Fabian has displayed a tantalizing combination of power and speed aside of the holes in his game. He generates legit bat speed and power from the right side of the plate and has good wheels and excellent instincts on the bases. He racked up 27 homers and 32 steals in only 142 Minor League games – including 15 and 12 respectively last summer in only a half season at Bowie. The tradeoff is his swing-and-miss, which was always a part of Fabian’s game. He struck out in 45 percent of his at-bats at Bowie. He’s shown he can make consistent contact without sacrificing power at times, but all the whiffs severely cut into Fabian’s upside. His speed and instincts benefit him as a defender. Fabian’s ability to read balls off the bat and run efficient routes point to a long-term future in center field, and he possesses one of the better outfield throwing arms in the Orioles system. The athleticism, baseball IQ and all those loud tools should enable Fabian to grow into a middle-of-the-field impact bat in the big leagues if he can consistently handle high-quality pitching and cut down on the swing-and-miss.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fabian graduated from high school early to enroll at the University of Florida for the 2019 collegiate season, then reestablished himself as a early-round prospect with a strong summer in the Cape Cod League. The Red Sox made him a second round draft pick in 2021, but he returned to campus after he and Boston could not come to terms. Fabian hit 24 home runs the next spring in Gainesville, this time lasting until the Competitive Balance Round B when the Orioles swooped in and signed him for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million. Fabian then enjoyed an exciting debut, hitting .333/.455/.615 in 22 games across three levels and reaching High-A Aberdeen. Everywhere he’s played, Fabian has shown serious offensive upside as well as the holes in his game. He generates legit bat speed and power from the right side of the plate, connecting for 44 homers over his final two years in college. The tradeoff is some swing-and-miss; Fabian finished college with a 24.3 percent K rate, while also posting a strong 17.6 percent BB rate over his last two years. He’s shown he is capable of making more consistent contact without sacrificing power at times, including during his 2022 debut (19-21 BB/K ratio). Fabian isn’t a burner on the bases, but does possess above-average wheels and excellent instincts. His ability to read the ball off the bat and run efficient routes points to a long-term future in center field. Fabian will still be only 22 when he enters his first full season of pro ball, giving him significant upside; if he keeps cutting the whiff rate, he could grow into an up-the-middle impact bat at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though college football teams were interested in him as an edge rusher, Nwogu decided to stay home in Ann Arbor and accepted an academic scholarship from Michigan, where he walked on the baseball team. He was the Wolverine's most productive hitter in both 2019, when they finished second at the College World Series, and 2020, after which the Cubs made him a third-round choice. He made his pro debut in Low-A last summer, batting .148/.257/.227 with a 41 percent strikeout rate in the first two months before improving to .285/.376/.451 with a 24 percent whiff rate in the final three.
