At 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds, Nwogu offers an impressive combination of power and speed. He crushes tape-measure shots and posts impressive exit velocities, and he did a better job of getting to his power once he got more disciplined and less passive. He's a plus runner who's aggressive on the bases, giving him 20-20 potential. The rest of Nwogu's game is less polished. Chicago has worked with him to clean up his right-handed swing, which can get stiff and disjointed, though he overcomes that with his fine hand-eye coordination. His athleticism doesn't translate well to his defense, as his inefficient reads and routes coupled with his fringy arm likely will keep him in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nwogu drew college football interest as an edge rusher but opted to accept an academic scholarship to stay home in Ann Arbor to attend Michigan, where he walked on the baseball team. He was the Wolverines' top offensive performer on their College World Series runner-up team in 2019 and again in 2020, when the Cubs signed him for $678,600 as a third-round pick. He got his introduction to pro ball at instructional league, where one club official noted that he was as tooled up as any prospect the organization has had in years. At 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds, Nwogu has impressive strength and generates exit velocities to match, showing the ability to knock a fastball out of any part of the ballpark. His right-handed swing and bat path are unorthodox, with his lower half looking out of sync with the rest of his body, yet he manages to make hard contact thanks to his bat speed and hand-eye coordination. He manages the strike zone well but needs to do a better job of recognizing and dealing with quality breaking balls and changeups. Nwogu has unusual quickness for his size and uses his plus speed aggressively on the bases. His athleticism doesn't translate well to the outfield, however, as he doesn't get good jumps and struggles going back on balls. While his arm strength improved while he was in college, it still grades as fringy and he'll likely stick in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Injuries have made it difficult to judge Zamora fully over the last three years. A two-year starter at Miami entering 2020, the Hurricane infielder didn’t play at all that spring in part due to a torn left ACL. The Brewers overlooked that, selected Zamora in the second round that summer and saw him get off to a slow start in his pro career at Single-A Carolina as he continued to try to gain strength coming off such a major knee issue. He entered 2022 with some momentum, only to hit .209 with a .556 OPS in his first 24 games at Double-A Biloxi, then suffer a season-ending subluxed left shoulder injury. Zamora’s best grades before the shoulder issue came on the defensive side. Given his above-average speed when fully healthy, he has the range to track down grounders at shortstop, and he also possesses the good hands needed to make plays. His plus arm strength is a big asset as well. Offensively, Zamora has a short swing geared toward making contact, and that’s helped keep his strikeout and swing-and-miss rates relatively in check in the Minors. Power is a real issue, and given he’s entering his age-24 season, there isn’t a ton of projection left to get him beyond scraping past double-digit home run totals at best. Shortstops who can put the ball in play tend to find regular places in lineups, and that gives hope that Zamora could still find his way into a Major League role. The No. 1 thing he needs is health, and if Zamora gets that in 2023, his future should be all the clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zamora started immediately upon arriving at the University of Miami in 2018 and put together a .300 average with more walks than strikeouts in his first two seasons. A torn left ACL, along with a minor team-rules violation suspension, kept the shortstop from appearing at all for the Hurricanes in 2020. The Brewers still selected him in the second round and signed him for just below slot at $1.15 million. Following some rehab work in the fall of 2020, Zamora needed some time to get acclimated to pro ball in his first full season and was a slow starter at Low-A Carolina. The healthier he got, the more he caught fire, and he finished with a .300/.404/.421 line, six homers and 10 steals between Low-A and High-A. Unfortunately, the injury bug bit again in 2022, and a subluxed left shoulder required season-ending surgery after only 24 games at Double-A Biloxi. Before the latest health concern, it was clear Zamora just needed to regain confidence in the knee for everything to click in 2021. When he’s on, he shows a contact-oriented approach with a short swing. Zamora has been trending in a positive direction with his slugging, but low double-digit home runs might be his ceiling because extra-base hits haven’t come in bunches. His above-average speed can help his offensive game. The Brewers saw more and more why Zamora will be a defensive asset at shortstop with good hands and range. His plus arm provides yet another reason why he can stick at the six. Prospects, like Zamora, who can play at a premium position and put the ball in play have a solid floor as low-impact starters/useful bench options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a delayed start to pro ball due to the coronavirus pandemic and a knee injury, Freddy Zamora finally gets to follow his father’s footsteps in professional baseball. Freddy Zamora Sr. played professionally in Nicaragua, but his son has a chance to go much farther as one of the top pure talents coming out of the 2020 Draft. He was a collegiate starter at Miami from the moment he set foot on campus and went into his junior season with a chance to be a first-round Draft pick, only to fall to the Brewers near the bottom of the second round in 2020. Zamora was first suspended for a violation of team rules -- it emerged that the offense was minor -- then he suffered a left knee injury in practice that shelved him for the rest of the year and required ACL surgery. Still, the Brewers made Zamora their second-round pick and signed him for slot value. He wasn’t ready to play in the fall instructional league, but the Brewers assigned him to the program anyway to begin acclimating to pro ball, and about halfway through the program, Zamora was cleared for some light infield work and to track live batting practice. Despite some negative buzz about Zamora’s makeup at Miami, the Brewers found him to be a model rehabber. At his best, Zamora has the skillset to be an everyday player at a premium position. He can be a plus defender at times, with a lot of body control, range and wingspan and a plus arm. Zamora’s contact-oriented approach that makes him tough to strike out in college, and he started showing more extra-base pop during his sophomore year before tailing off late in the season. He has shown the ability to steal bases in his early days at Class A Carolina.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2026 international signing period, the Reds jumped in by handing out a total of 11 bonuses of six figures or higher. At the top of that list was Nuñez, who came in at No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list and received $3 million to join the organization. A national team standout who starred for the Dominican Republic’s team in the U15 World Cup in 2024, hitting .350 with 11 RBIs across eight games, Nuñez brings a high energy and swagger that matches the vibrant and eclectic streets of his home city of Santo Domingo, to the Reds' system. A left-handed hitting 5-foot-10 sparkplug, Nuñez has already shown a feel to hit with an advanced approach at the plate. With an open and upright stance, Nuñez uses his quick hands to propel the bat through the zone, showing early acumen at spraying line drives to all fields. While he isn’t that big, there is some power for him to grow into, though it will likely be a hit-over-pop profile. Nuñez is easily a plus runner who has recorded some elite-level 60-yard dash times. He has the ability to use that speed on the basepaths, stealing nine bases in 10 tries during that World Cup, and in the outfield. He combines his wheels with excellent instincts to track down balls in center field, where he’ll be able to play for a long time with his strong arm an added bonus.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hertzler teamed with Trey Yesavage at Boyertown (Pa.) HS ,and after three years of college, he went four rounds behind him in the 2024 Draft, joining the Astros as a fifth-rounder. A two-way player in his first two seasons at Liberty, he focused on pitching as a junior and became the Flames' No. 1 starter. He has worked just 21 innings as a pro because he sprained his forearm last April and made just one more appearance five months later. Hertzler's best offering is a low-80s changeup with significant fade. It helps him maximize the effectiveness of a fastball that sits at 91-94 mph and tops out at 97 with carry and armside run. He showed better feel for his tight mid-80s slider than his 78-82 mph curveball during his brief action last season. With a 6-foot-4 frame and high arm slot, Hertzler's pitches come out of a higher release point than usual. His control and command improved as he got more experience at Liberty, and he has no problem providing strikes. He'll need to show he can handle a starter's workload after totaling just 142 innings in the last four years but should be fully healthy for 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyertown (Pa.) High's 2021 pitching staff featured two arms who would go early in the 2024 Draft -- Blue Jays first-rounder Trey Yesavage and Astros fifth-rounder Hertzler. A two-way player in his first two college seasons at Liberty, Hertzler became the Flames' No. 1 starter when he focused on the mound last spring. His pro debut consisted of two brief appearances at Single-A. In his lone season as a college starter, Hertzler showed the ability to get chases and miss bats with four average pitches. His fastball operates at 91-94 mph and touches 97 with carry and armside run, and it could become a solid offering if he finds more velocity. His fading low-80s changeup is his best secondary pitch, followed by a tight mid-80s slider with occasional depth and a low-80s curveball. Hertzler's strong 6-foot-4 frame and high arm slot created a higher release point than hitters are accustomed to. As he got regular innings in 2024, he did a good job of cleaning up his delivery and providing strikes. He has more untapped potential than most college pitchers and could develop into a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arkansas was the SEC regular season and tournament champion in 2021, and Franklin, as a junior, was the team leader with a .964 OPS. Swing-and-miss concerns at the time dropped him to the Cubs in the fourth round, and he missed the entirety of 2022 due a torn patellar tendon in his left knee suffered in Spring Training. By 2024, Franklin climbed to Double-A but couldn’t crack the 40-man roster at the time of his first Rule 5 eligibility. Amid a strong 2025 season at Triple-A Iowa, he was traded to the Nationals at the Deadline for Michael Soroka and was added to Washington’s 40-man in the offseason. Owner of a career .393 on-base percentage, the 5-foot-9 Franklin has long stood out for his discipline on the pro side, and his strong swing decisions were drivers of his International League success last season. After hitting the ball on the ground 60.3 percent of the time at Double-A in ’24, he improved his angles off the bat enough to get to his plus raw power more often, and his 106.3 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity would be comfortably above-average in the Majors. That said, he’s still more likely to spray the ball around the yard than yank homers in the air, and he projects for closer to 10-12 long balls over a full season. An average runner, Franklin could steal 15-20 bags per year in the Majors if given the playing time. He’s spent time in all three outfield spots in recent years with average range in center and better in the corners, and his above-average arm strength helps his case anywhere on the grass. Franklin will be 26 for the 2026 season and has the tools to be a fourth outfielder, if he can crack Washington’s deep positional group in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Franklin was the most productive hitter on an Arkansas team that ranked No. 1 in the nation for most of the 2021 season and he was one of the toolsier players in that year's college crop, yet he slid to the fourth round amid swing-and-miss concerns. He tore the patellar tendon in his left knee while pursuing a flyball during his first Spring Training, requiring surgery that cost him the entire 2022 season. He showed flashes of talent without posting loud numbers the next two years and went unpicked in the Rule 5 Draft in December after the Cubs opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster. Up in Triple-A for the first time in 2025, Franklin started hitting the ball with more authority and was dealt to the Nationals at the Trade Deadline in a three-player swap for Michael Soroka. Franklin hits the ball hard and has a disciplined approach that helped him lead the Double-A Southern League in on-base percentage (.398) and walks (71) last year, but he also makes a lot of ground-ball contact and struggles with sliders and changeups, leading to inconsistent offensive production. He displays plus raw power in batting practice, yet doesn’t drive the ball in the air in games, and four of his five homers last year snuck out down the right-field line. His right-handed swing gets long and he'll miss some hittable pitches in the zone. An average runner out of the batter's box but quicker underway, Franklin stole 34 bases in 41 attempts last season. He makes good reads and takes good routes in the outfield, where his range grades as average in center and solid on the corners. He played all three outfield spots in 2025 with a primary focus on center. His arm plays from anywhere, aiding his chances at being a fourth outfielder in his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most productive hitter on an Arkansas team that ranked No. 1 in the nation for most of the 2021 season, Franklin sported some of the best all-around tools in his college class. But concerns about his hitting ability dinged his Draft stock and caused him to slide more than expected. The Cubs were thrilled to find him on the board with the 123rd overall pick in the fourth round and signed him for $425,000, but he'll miss his entire first full pro season after tearing the patellar tendon in his left knee in Spring Training. Franklin's bat speed and strength produce plus raw power to all fields and impressive exit velocities. His right-handed stroke gets long, however, and he will swing through some hittable pitches in the zone at times. Though he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact, he did improve his plate discipline during his college career and walked 20 times in his 24-game pro debut. Franklin clocks average run times out of the batter's box but shows solid-to-plus speed once he gets going on the bases and in center field. He's a 20-20 candidate with good instincts as a base stealer and a defender. His range and solid arm strength make him an asset at any outfield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two members of the Reds’ college-heavy 2021 Draft class have already made significant first impressions in the big leagues, with Matt McLain and Andrew Abbott turning in strong rookie seasons in 2023. Allen was the only high schooler taken in that class, signing for $2.4 million, selected with the compensation pick for losing Trevor Bauer to the Dodgers via free agency. After an excellent debut in the Arizona Complex League that summer, Allen has had trouble staying healthy and gaining any traction, missing time in 2022 with an oblique issue and a bulk of the 2023 season with a thumb injury suffered very early on. Because Allen split his focus among three sports in high school, there was an understanding that it might take time for his baseball skills to come to the forefront, so the fact he’s missed so much development time has been particularly unfortunate. He probably needs a mulligan for his at-bats last year because he likely wasn’t at full strength even when he came off the injured list. He seems to still be growing and filling out, so there could be some raw power for him to tap into if he can get into a groove. There’s some strike zone judgement as well, with decent walk rates, but there’s also been a lot of swing-and-miss. Allen’s plus speed makes him a legitimate basestealing threat and he can cover a ton of ground in center field. The goal is to try and keep the right-handed-hitting outfielder on the field for an entire season to see if he can start moving towards his very high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds were super college heavy in the 2021 Draft, making all but one of their 22 selections from the college or junior college ranks. The one exception was Allen, a three-sport prep star from Florida who was taken No. 30 overall and signed away from his commitment to the University of Florida. He missed some time in his first full season with a minor oblique issue, but while he had mixed results at the plate, the Reds gave the chance to see how his athleticism would play up a level in High-A at the end of the year. Allen has good bat speed from the right side of the plate and a line-drive approach. He didn’t impact the ball as much as some had hoped, though there is raw power to tap into if he can continue to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. He has a feel for the strike zone and drew a good amount of walks in 2022. His speed is a huge offensive asset, and he finished fifth in the Single-A Florida State League in steals even though he played in just 73 games there before his promotion. That speed also serves him well in center field where he can really go get the ball and has the chance to stay there long-term. Like with many multi-sport athletes, there’s a ton of unlocked potential here, with the full-time baseball reps he’s now getting sure to help him turn his plus athleticism into performance more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Allen was a three-sport star at his high school on the east coast of Florida, one who was a good enough football player to get college interest in that sport as well. He was committed to go to the University of Florida for baseball only, but the Reds liked his athleticism and overall tools enough to use the compensation pick they got for losing Trevor Bauer to the Dodgers via free agency to select him and sign him for just shy of $2.4 million before watching him make a very strong first impression in a brief pro debut in the Arizona Complex League. Allen is capable of doing a lot of things well on the baseball field with a chance to impact the game on both sides of the ball. He has the chance to be at least an average hitter, with a simple setup and good bat speed. Especially given how his focus was divided among three sports, he showed an advanced approach at the plate and feel to hit during his debut, making consistently hard contact from the right side of the plate. He’s sure to get to more power as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. He runs well, occasionally with plus run times, and showed in the ACL he isn’t afraid to steal a base. After playing center field in high school and during his pro debut, Allen does have the chance to stay up-the-middle, and the Reds believe he can stay there long-term, though some amateur scouts thought he’d be better suited for a corner in the future. He has the chance to be an everyday regular somewhere in a big league outfield if it continues to click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Guardians went under slot to sign their first three selections in the 2022 Draft, they splurged on Humphries in the eighth round, giving him fourth-round money ($600,000) to convince him to forgo his commitment to Campbell. Early returns were positive in his first full season, as he showed his strikeout stuff in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, but the next two years were a wash. An illness caused him to lose significant weight in 2024, and he could not find his control in '25 and walked nearly a batter per inning. Humphries is starting to look like his old self again now that he's diligently grown stronger over the offseason and refined his delivery. While he used to have an extreme over-the-top delivery, he's dropped his release point to a high-three-quarters slot that still enables him to reach nearly 20 inches of induced vertical break on his fastball while also adding more armside run. The southpaw throws his heater about half the time and sits 91-93 mph -- he can reach back and touch 96 mph -- and the hope is that his added strength will help him maintain velocity late into the season. The North Carolina native has a pair of distinct breaking balls -- an upper-80s slider and high-70s curve -- that each have a chance to be plus. His changeup has rare vertical movement and pairs well off the fastball because of 10 mph of velocity separation. However, much of his value will come down to his control. After throwing strikes just 54 percent of the time in 2025, he's been consistently in the zone in 2026, thanks in part to a less effortful delivery and better direction to home plate. Humphries' stuff could play up in relief if the walks don't dissipate, but he has the foundation to be a mid-rotation starter, and Cleveland is likely to keep developing him in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Humphries flashed top-three-rounds talent as a North Carolina high schooler before an inconsistent senior season in 2022 dinged his stock a little bit. The Guardians still gave him third-round money ($600,000) as an eighth-rounder that July, and he responded by standing out as the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League during his pro debut the following summer. He had a lost season in 2024, coming down with a virus early in the season that cost him 20 pounds as well as significant velocity and athleticism. When he's at full strength, Humphries shows the potential for three plus pitches. His fastball can operate at 92-95 mph and touch 97 with sink and run, and he can show a pair of high-spin breaking balls, an upper-70s curve with quality depth and a sharp low-80s slider. Even his low-80s fade changeup could become a solid offering. Last year, Humphries worked around 90 mph with his fastball and lost power on his curve and slider, though he still managed to strike out 97 in 79 Single-A innings. His arm action isn't the cleanest and he doesn't repeat his delivery on a consistent basis, so he might be limited to average control and fringy command at best. Assuming he can regain the stuff he had before he got sick, he has a higher ceiling than most of the system's other pitching prospects as a potential mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Humphries looked like a potential top-three-rounds pick when he led Fuquay-Varina HS to the North Carolina 4-A state championship as a junior and impressed at the Super 60 Showcase in February 2022. An up-and-down senior year dinged his stock a bit, though the Guardians gave him third-round money ($600,000) in the eighth round to divert him from a Campbell commitment. He stood out as the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League during his 2023 debut, then displayed improved control following a mid-August promotion to Single-A. While Humphries shows the potential for three plus offerings once he's fully developed, he rarely has been at his best in 2024 while battling a stomach virus that sapped his strength. His fastball already sits at 92-95 mph and reaches 97 with sink and run. He creates high spin rates on two distinct breaking pitches, an upper-70s curveball with quality depth and a low-80s slider with sharper action. Humphries has just begun focusing on his low-80s changeup, which fades and shows flashes of solid upside. He doesn't have the prettiest arm action or most consistent delivery, so he may never have more than average control or fringy command. While he'll need time to develop, he has a higher ceiling than most of Cleveland's mound prospects and could blossom into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crawford led the Big East Conference with 13 homers at Connecticut in 2021 while pitching just 13 2/3 innings between the Huskies, the Cape Cod League and Team USA, yet he was a potential No. 1 overall pick on the mound until he blew out his elbow that fall and had Tommy John surgery in November. Though he missed all of 2022, the Giants spent the 30th overall choice and $2,297,500 on his massive upside that July. He has dominated pro hitters in the 37 1/3 innings he worked in 2023-24 while losing time to mononucleosis, an oblique injury, a lat strain and a labrum tear that required shoulder surgery last September, sidelining him for all of this year. Crawford throws harder than most left-handers, parking at 95-97 mph and peaking at 101 with riding action, and the extension he creates with his 6-foot-4 frame and athleticism make it even more explosive. His slider ranges from 82-88 mph with so much horizontal and vertical action that he struggles to land it in the strike zone. He has similar issues with a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks and could be a solid offering if he can harness it. While Crawford has the stuff and athleticism to become a frontline starter, he has seen just 57 1/3 innings of game action in the last five years, so it's unrealistic to project him as more than a reliever at this point. If he can stay healthy and improve his control and command, he could become a closer. Pitching exclusively out of the stretch in 2024, he still walked 12 batters in 18 1/3 frames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An ultimate risk/reward first-round pick, Crawford went 30th overall in 2022 thanks to his immense ceiling and despite his limited track record. Though he led the Big East Conference with 13 homers at Connecticut in 2021 and pitched just 13 2/3 innings between the Huskies, the Cape Cod League and Team USA, he was a potential No. 1 overall pick on the mound. But he hurt his elbow that October, had Tommy John surgery in November and missed the entire 2022 season. Signed for $2,297,500, he struck out 32 in 19 innings between two Class A levels last year, while losing time to mononucleosis and an oblique strain. Few left-handers can match Crawford's power stuff. His fastball operates at 95-97 mph and reaches 100, with his 6-foot-4 frame and athleticism creating extension that helps his heater explode on hitters. His mid-80s slider tops out at 88 mph and can be just as devastating with its two-plane depth. He began working on a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink during his Tommy John rehab and while he's still learning to throw it for strikes, opponents managed a .000 OPS against the 43 cambios he threw in 2023. Crawford is more physical and athletic than most pitchers, leading to hope that he'll develop average control as he gets more experience. While he offers upside as a potential frontline starter, he pitched just 39 1/3 innings in game action (including summer ball) in the last four years and has been slowed by a lat strain and a tired arm in 2024. San Francisco may be tempted to expedite him to the Majors as a high-leverage reliever, but he lasted just six weeks pitching one or two innings every three or four days before getting shut down in early June. He does have at least plus raw power as a lefty-hitting first baseman but after getting sporadic at-bats in his first two pro seasons and in the Arizona Fall League, he's going to focus almost entirely on pitching this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No player in the 2022 Draft could match Crawford's combination of lofty ceiling and limited track record. He topped the Big East Conference with 13 homers in 2021 but scouts liked him more as a pitcher. He totaled just 13 2/3 innings between Connecticut, Team USA and the Cape Cod League, striking out 30 of the 56 batters he faced. A potential No. 1 overall pick before he hurt his elbow that October and missed all of 2022 following Tommy John surgery, he still went 30th overall and signed for a slightly under-slot $2,297,500. Few left-handers can match Crawford's pair of power pitches, beginning with a 95-97 mph fastball that hits 100 with high spin rates and tremendous carry up in the strike zone. He also can overwhelm hitters with a mid-80s slider that peaks at 88 mph and features impressive depth. He's more physical and athletic than most pitchers and has thrown strikes during his limited experience on the mound. Because he has worked just 20 1/3 innings (counting summer ball) in three years of college and is coming back from elbow reconstruction, the Giants will handle him carefully in his 2023 pro pitching debut and just focus on getting him some reps and keeping him healthy. They'll worry about developing his changeup, refining his command and building up his workload in the future. He also offers at least plus raw power as a lefty-hitting first baseman and will continue to get some sporadic at-bats after going 3-for-19 in Rookie ball last summer, though his future definitely is on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $900,000 out of Venezuela, Velasquez received the highest bonus in the Giants' 2021 international class thanks to his advanced bat-to-ball skills. He earned All-Star accolades in the Single-A California League in 2023 and in the High-A Northwest League last season, which he concluded by hitting .313 in 42 Double-A games at age 20. He's not overly toolsy but has the highest ceiling among San Francisco's middle-infield prospects. Velasquez has a controlled approach at the plate, making consistent contact to all fields while rarely chasing pitches out of the zone. A switch-hitter with a quick, compact swing from both sides, he does more damage as a righty. He did a better job of lifting pitches in 2024 but still lacks the strength to hit more than 10 homers per season. Velasquez's instincts allow him to play a bit quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has been a steady defender at shortstop in the past but his average arm and range are better suited for second base, where he has spent almost all of 2025. He'll project more as a contact-hitting utilityman than a big league starter unless he can provide some more offense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Velasquez signed for $900,000 out of Venezuela, landing the highest bonus in the Giants' 2021 international class because of his advanced hitting ability. He earned a promotion to Single-A at the end of the 2022 season at age 18 and earned California League All-Star honors when he returned there last year. He topped the circuit in hits (127) and doubles (32), while ranking second in batting (.298), extra-base hits (41) and total bases (185). A switch-hitter, Velasquez has a quick swing and makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate. He controls the strike zone well and his on-base skills give him a high floor, but his power potential remains in question because he lacks strength and has yet to show much affinity for pulling pitches or driving them in the air. He'll need to add muscle and make some adjustments to even provide 10 homers per season. Velasquez has average speed and looks to make things happen on the bases, stealing 23 bases in 29 attempts a year ago. After spending most of his first two seasons at shortstop, he split time between short and second base in 2023. He has sure, quick hands but his range and arm are better suited for the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez began his professional career after signing with the Yankees for $50,000 out of Venezuela. He quickly established his defensive bona fides in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and Florida Complex League while providing modest offensive production. The bat didn’t keep up with the glove when he moved to full-season Tampa, and that continued when he moved down the West Coast of Florida to Bradenton when the Pirates acquired him in the Trade Deadline David Bednar deal. At present, Perez offers two elite skills: his swing decisions and his defense. He’s shown an advanced knowledge of the strike zone, especially for his age, with more walks (18.8 percent rate) than strikeouts (17.8) in his young career, with the Yankees doing excellent work in teaching zone control to their young hitters. There is some impact in there, but Perez is more of a hit-over-power type and the Pirates think perhaps he was too focused on leverage, taking him away from making consistent contact. Defensively, Perez is a natural receiver with fantastic hands and excellent blocking and receiving skills to go along with plus arm strength and accuracy. Young Pirates arms are going to enjoy throwing to him, and he’s already shown a knack for calling a game. His glove gives him a high floor as a backup, and if he can find some offensive consistency, he could develop into more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees usually prefer offensive-minded catchers, but Perez stands out most for his ability behind the plate. Signed for just $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2023, he was arguably that system's best defensive backstop before making his full-season debut. He came to the United States last summer and placed second in walks (45) and third in on-base percentage (.444) in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. A move to full-season ball in 2025 has been a challenge, but he’ll get the chance to hit the reset button with the Pirates, who acquired him as part of the prospect package in return for David Bednar at the Trade Deadline. Taller and significantly stronger than his listed 5-foot-10 and 155 pounds, Perez has the upside of plus receiving and blocking skills. His arm strength already is at that level, and he boosts it with a quick release that helps him shut down the running game. More athletic than most catchers, he's agile behind the plate and shows below-average speed on the bases. Though his defensive prowess stands out the most, Perez has offensive potential as well. A right-handed hitter who's more disciplined than most teenagers, he has the strength to provide 15 homers annually once he learns to launch balls in the air to his pull side more often. His approach can border between patient and passive, but he makes his share of hard-hit contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gastelum signed with the Cardinals for only $30,000 out of Mexico as a 21-year-old in April 2023 and headed stateside immediately. His big emergence came a year later when he posted a 2.81 ERA and struck out 34.5 percent of batters faced over 48 innings at Single-A Palm Beach, and he continued to dominate in the Mexican Winter League after that. The Cardinals pushed Gastelum past High-A for his age-23 season in 2025, and while his 4.02 ERA didn’t pop on the surface, his 35.4 percent K rate and 1.10 WHIP still did. Gastelum’s 28.8 K/BB percentage was sixth-best among 952 Minor Leaguers with at least 60 innings in ’25. Gastelum’s success to this point stems from one pitch: his low-80s changeup. It’s a mesmerizing offering with negative induced vertical break and plenty of armside run. It practically works like a left-handed breaking ball, but instead emerges from the 6-foot-2 right-hander’s low three-quarters delivery. Because of that action, the cambio was even more effective against righties than lefties last year with a 64 percent whiff rate against same-side bats. (Not that lefties fared that much better.) Gastelum can throw a mid-90s fastball, but with ordinary movement, it only works to set up his beast of a change. He’ll occasionally work in a mid-80s sweeper too for something with big gloveside movement. Gastelum has posted excellent walk rates at every stop to this point, and a big reason for that is that he consistently gets batters to bite on changeups diving out of the zone. He pitches exclusively out of the stretch, so this isn’t a complicated operation. Without an average fastball, Gastelum might have a limited ceiling, but his uniqueness should earn him some role in St. Louis’ bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Mexico as a 21-year-old in April 2023, Gastelum jumped stateside as a reliever and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 in a 48-inning stint with Single-A St. Palm Beach. His 29.1 K-BB% led the Florida State League among 112 pitchers with at least 40 frames, while his 34.5 strikeout percentage ranked second and his 2.47 FIP third. Gastelum fanned three of his four batters faced (including the final one) in Palm Beach’s FSL championship clincher on Sept. 18, and he’s continued his momentum in the Mexican Winter League. The 6-foot-2 right-hander proved so dominant because of his special changeup. The 81-84 mph cambio averaged -1.6 inches of induced vertical break and 15.5 inches of armside movement, giving it two planes with which to menace hitters. Gastelum threw 317 changeups tracked by Statcast; 161 of them (50.8 percent) ended up as called strikes or whiffs. No one else in the FSL had a CSW rate higher than 41.1 percent (min. 50 changeups), and no one in the Majors had one higher than 41.0 (Angel Chivili) over the same minimum. Gastelum threw his change 47.9 percent of the time because it was so effective. The other side of the coin: the righty’s fastball is much less remarkable as a 91-93 mph offering with ordinary movement, and his mid-80s slider is the closest pitch to flashing above-average. Devin Williams comps would be misguided because at least the Yankees reliever has more fastball velo and usage, but that type of change-heavy profile out of the bullpen gives the righty a profile on which to dream. The Cards prospect will be 23 for the majority of the 2025 season, so it’ll be time for St. Louis to see just how quickly he can ride that changeup toward The Show.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Webb spent two seasons as a starter at Sinclair (Ohio) CC and two as a reliever at Miami (Ohio) before the Red Sox picked him in the 14th round in 2021. In his first full pro season, he compiled a 3.18 ERA with 88 strikeouts in 56 2/3 innings while rising from Single-A to Double-A. The first pitcher from Boston's 2021 Draft to reach Double-A, he also performed well in the Arizona Fall League. Webb works with two pitches and misses bats with both of them. His fastball sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with significant carry and some arm-side run. He backs it up with a low-80s slider that has good sweep at times and is tighter with more depth at others. Physically imposing at 6-foot-5 and 246 pounds, Webb has an extremely low release point for someone so large and creates good extension. There's effort in his crossfire delivery and his short arm action isn't the prettiest, but they provide a lot of deception and his pitches get on hitters in a hurry. He threw strikes in college but has lacked reliable control as a pro, and he could help Boston's bullpen in the near future if he can find the zone more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Webb has the chance to become the first player in the history of Tabor College, an NAIA school in Kansas, to reach the big leagues. Initially an infielder, he moved to the mound when his bat didn't progress, and he landed in the 18th round of the 2014 Draft after an outstanding spring in Tabor's rotation. He's put 2015 Tommy John surgery in his rear view mirror, moving into the bullpen upon his return and pitching his way up to Triple-A in 2018 to earn a spot on the 40-man roster last offseason. Webb relies on two power pitches to get hitters out as a short reliever. His fastball has ticked upwards in those shorter stints, sitting in the 95-96 mph range, thrown with deception thanks to a quick arm. His breaking ball, a power slider, flashes above-average with good depth, though it's not always consistent. He cut his walk rate down in 2018, but he kept missing bats and carries a 11.1 K/9 rate into the 2019 season. Webb led the organization with 18 saves in 2018, but without further consistency of his breaking ball and command, he's unlikely to close in the big leagues. He does have the stuff to pitch in the seventh inning, at the very least, in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for $75,000 out of Aruba in 2022, Albertus slashed .303/.449/.415 in his first three pro seasons. He fractured his left tibia a month after getting promoted to Single-A at age 19 in mid-2024 and joined the White Sox shortly thereafter in a three-team trade that shipped Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to Los Angeles. He had surgery on his leg in November 2024 and has been slow to recover, playing just eight games on a rehab assignment in Rookie ball last year. One of the more advanced young hitters in the system, Albertus recognizes pitches well and employs a disciplined approach. He makes regular contact to all fields with a quick right-handed stroke and hangs in well against breaking balls. He was making progress learning to drive balls in the air when he got hurt and should provide 15 homers per year once he returns to health and adds more strength. While Albertus had below-average speed even before his leg injury, his high baseball IQ allowed him to play better than that on the bases and in the field. He has the solid arm strength, reliable hands and enough range to get the job done at third base. He has worked hard to improved his defense and also has seen action at shortstop and second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Dodgers for $75,000 out of Aruba in 2022, Albertus flew under the radar while spending most of his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After he gained some strength and made his U.S. debut in late July 2023, teams repeatedly asked about him in trade talks. The White Sox acquired him last July in a three-team swap that sent Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to Los Angeles. He didn't play after the deal because of a fractured left tibia that required surgery in November. A career .303/.449/.415 hitter in three years at the lowest levels of the Minors, Albertus stands out with his quick right-handed swing, disciplined approach and bat-to-ball skills. He continues to improve at lifting balls in the air and did a better job of using the opposite field last year. The next step will be to add more muscle to his 6-foot-1 frame so he can develop 15-homer power to go with his hitting ability. Though Albertus has below-average speed, his high baseball IQ helps him play a bit faster than that on the bases and in the field. His solid arm strength, reliable hands and lack of quickness make him best suited for third base, where he's a decent defender with the work ethic to become better. He divided his time equally between the hot corner, second base and shortstop in his first two years as a pro, and Chicago plans on giving him a chance to show what he can do in the middle infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Albertus initially flew under the radar in the Dodgers' 2022 international crop, signing for $75,000 out of Aruba and hitting a soft .304 in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After starting to add some much-needed strength, he batted .309/.447/.479 last summer between the DSL and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Other teams took note and his name came up repeatedly in trade talks until the White Sox landed him in the three-team deal in July that shipped Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to the Dodgers. Even taking into consideration that Albertus has yet to face much in the way of advanced pitching, he has one of most patient approaches in the system, drawing 70 walks versus just 40 strikeouts in his first 85 pro games. He improved the quality of his contact last year, hitting the ball harder and launching it in the air much more consistently. A right-handed hitter, he can get pull-happy at times but offers the upside of a high on-base percentage guy who provides 15-20 homers per season. Albertus has a high baseball IQ that allows him to play faster than his fringy speed on the bases and in the field. He has solid arm strength and divided his time almost equally between third base, second base and shortstop in his first two pro seasons. He profiles best at second base and could be an average defender there or at the hot corner, while sticking at short is more of a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For most of his three years at Miami, McFarlane pitched out of the bullpen, often showing glimpses of electric raw stuff, with enough of a repertoire where scouts thought he had a chance to start if he could learn to harness it. When the Phillies took him in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft, they gave him that opportunity and broke out of the gate well in 2023. That didn’t last and an elbow issue that shut him down turned into Tommy John surgery that knocked him out for all of 2024. He came back in 2025 in High-A Jersey Shore’s rotation and struggled, eventually getting moved back to a relief role late in the year, finishing things off with Double-A Reading. While the surface stats during his 10-game bullpen stint don’t jump off the page, McFarlane’s stuff did tick up in those shorter outings. His fastball, which averaged around 95 mph for the year, but tracked over 97 mph and topped out at 101 mph as a reliever. He’ll throw four-seamers and two-seamers at about the same rate, but got a more groundballs with the harder heater out of the pen. His slider also had more mustard on it, and for the year the sweeping breaker elicited a 45-percent miss rate. One of the reasons it was believed he had a chance to start is that McFarlane had an improving split-changeup as an offspeed offering. He wasn’t throwing it a ton upon his return and it basically was shelved as a reliever. Now on the 40-man roster, he can probably focus on his fastball-slider combination as a full-time reliever, with an eye on impacting the big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McFarlane spent three years at Miami, teasing evaluators with impressive pure stuff but uneven results, especially in the command department and most of it coming out of the Hurricanes bullpen. After taking him in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft, the Phillies decided to develop the right-hander as a starter and after a decent start to his first full season, he faded early on and eventually needed Tommy John surgery that August. He missed all of 2024 as a result but now has a clean bill of health. Scouts have long thought McFarlane could have a chance to start because of his size, elite arm strength and legitimate three-pitch mix. It starts with his fastball that touches triple digits and a move to a two-seamer has worked with his lower arm slot and allowed him to get groundball outs in 2023. He can miss bats with his upper-80s slider, a breaking ball that flashes plus, and his split-changeup was improving before he got shut down with the elbow injury. The biggest thing McFarlane needs to work on, and the reason why he hasn’t stuck in a rotation to date, is his command of all of his offerings after walking 6.8 per nine in 2023. He reportedly added 10-15 pounds of muscle over the course of his TJ rehab and the Phillies think he might be a bit under the radar after the layoff, even if he does eventually land in the back end of a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McFarlane went from the U.S. Virgin Islands to Georgia for his senior year of high school and then on to the University of Miami. Working out of the Hurricanes bullpen for the most part, he showed off enough raw stuff and arm strength to land in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft. The Phillies gave him a chance to start in 2023 and he showed some glimpses early on, though he was shut down in July and threw sparingly in August, eventually needing Tommy John surgery. Even though he had three years at an ACC school, McFarlane profiles more like a raw high schooler after throwing just 91 innings combined at Miami. The power stuff is plenty good enough, starting with a fastball that was up to 101 mph last year, though command of it was spotty. His lower arm slot has been better suited for his two-seamer, and he proved adept at getting ground-ball outs during his first full season. He backs the heater up with an upper-80s slider that flashes plus, and he worked on a split-changeup as he tried to find a complete starter's arsenal. Likely to return in 2025, the Phillies could let McFarlane continue to start so he can make up for lost reps and work on his repertoire, not to mention his below-average command. Seeing him as a multi-inning reliever does seem like a more likely long-term path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of the U.S. Virgin Islands, McFarlane popped up on Draft radars when he moved to Georgia for his senior year of high school before going on to Miami for college. Pitching mostly as a reliever for the Hurricanes, his premium stuff missed a ton of bats. After throwing very well in the Cape Cod League last summer, he landed a slightly over-slot bonus from the Phillies in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft before making a brief pro debut with Single-A Clearwater. McFarlane is a long, loose right-hander with a combination of now stuff and projection, one who has not logged a ton of innings. Though he worked out of Miami’s pen more often than not, he has the chance to start with a legitimate three-pitch mix. While his fastball is up to 98-99 mph and averaged north of 95 mph in college last year, he’s still learning how and when to use his fastball, and he worked at instructs in incorporating both his two- and four-seamers, with the former sinking heater an effective option against right-handed hitters. His upper-80s slider could be a plus out pitch, and he showed off good feel for a split-changeup at instructs. The 6-foot-4 righty has a long arm action in the back of his delivery, which can lead to trouble repeating his mechanics and finding the strike zone. Some pro instruction and refinement could help correct that, and he has the upside to be a big league starter, a reason why the Phillies have already been asked about him in trades.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because of his acumen behind the plate, Flores has been aggressively pushed by the Angels since they signed him for $280,000 at the start of the 2023 international period. After his debut in the Dominican Summer League, he advanced from the Arizona Complex League to full-season ball during his first year in the States. In 2025, he got pushed up to High-A and struggled on both sides of the ball over the first half of the season, but he played much better baseball in the second half, then performed well as one of the younger players in the Arizona Fall League. Flores is likely always going to be known for his work behind the dish ahead of what he does at it. This spring was his third big league camp in a row because he really knows how to handle pitchers. He’s a plus receiver who blocks well and already shows advanced game-calling skills. His plus arm wasn’t quite as effective as controlling the running game in 2025, but he gets rid of the ball and down to second base in a hurry. Flores was completely lost as a hitter over the first half of the season and was hitting just .158 with a .480 OPS and 46 wRC+ through June as he lost the strike zone completely while he tried to sell out for power. He still needs to refine his approach -- his strikeout rate in the second half remained high -- but he posted a .780 OPS and 113 wRC+, getting to his power more organically with eight of his 10 homers coming from July 1 on. His glove should get him to the big leagues. If he can replicate what he did at the plate in the second half, he could be a defense-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better defenders behind the dish in the 2023 international signing class, Flores received a $280,000 bonus to sign when the period opened that January. So far, he’s moved more rapidly up the ladder than shortstop Felix Morrobel, the top of the Angels’ crop that winter. Flores' ability behind the plate will enable him to keep advancing and he’s shown a little more acumen that could make him an even better prospect than expected. Compact and strong, Flores has shown some ability to drive the ball from the right side. He bested expectations with the bat in full-season ball to start off the 2024 season after skipping over the Arizona Complex League. He’s too aggressive at the plate and can chase too much, especially softer stuff, though he can punish a fastball. What pop he has shown has been to his pull side, and with too high of a ground-ball rate, he could stand to find ways to leverage the ball more in the air. The Angels have felt comfortable moving Flores aggressively and inviting him to big league camp in Spring Training two years in a row -- even though he just turned 19 in February -- because of his defense. His strong arm has thrown out 40 percent of potential basestealers in his pro career to date. He’s turning into an excellent receiver who blocks and calls the game well, looking like he’s going to be a plus overall defender with that plus arm and plus instincts. If he can get his bat close to average, he has the chance to be a standout regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Flores drew attention from scouts in Venezuela because of his advanced skills behind the plate. That’s a big reason why the Angels gave him $280,000 to sign at the start of the 2023 international signing period. He made his debut in the Dominican Summer League and showed that word of his defensive acumen was not greatly exaggerated, while he also shook off a slow offensive start to provide a little more with the bat than anticipated. Flores’ calling card will always be his glove work. The skills are there for him to perhaps be a plus receiver in the future and he already has a plus arm, one that threw out 53.1 percent of potential basestealers in the DSL during his debut. The Angels thought so highly of his work behind the dish they thought he’d be able to handle higher-level arms and invited him to big league camp this spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going unpicked in the truncated five-round 2020 Draft, Stephan bypassed his Stephen F. Austin State commitment and signed as a free agent because he wanted to launch his pro career despite pandemic rules capping his bonus at $20,000. He worked his way to Double-A at age 22 two years ago but missed two months that summer with a stress fracture in his back and two more last season with elbow inflammation. He returned to rank second in the Arizona Fall League with a 2.25 ERA, though the Rangers declined to protect him on their 40-man roster. Stephan’s slider easily stands out as his best weapon, a plus offering that sweeps at 82-85 mph, and he shown the ability to turn it into a tighter upper-80s cutter in the AFL. He throws strikes but doesn’t miss many bats with his fastballs, a sinking two-seamer that sits at 91-93 mph and touches 95 and a slightly harder four-seamer with carry. His mid-80s changeup gained velocity but lost some movement and effectiveness in 2024. Stephan’s deception and feel for pitching are the keys to his success. His low arm slot and release height add deception and life to his pitches, while his ability to repeat his easy delivery gives him plus control and the potential for solid command. He needs more strength, but if he can stay healthy, he has a future as a back-of-the-rotation starter or slider happy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just 17 high schoolers signed as nondrafted free agents in the wake of the shortened five-round 2020 Draft, and the Rangers landed five of them. The best of those is Stephan, who gave up a commitment to Stephen F. Austin State because he wanted to start his pro career despite pandemic rules capping his bonus at $20,000. He excelled in High-A last year with a 2.17 ERA, .175 opponents' average against and 73/12 K/BB ratio in 62 1/3 innings, but he sustained a stress fracture in his back during fielding drills after his first Double-A start and missed the final two months. His overall 0.84 WHIP led all Minor League pitchers who worked at least 60 innings. Stephan doesn't light up radar guns but he can really pitch with his low-90s fastballs, creating run and sink on a two-seamer that sits at 91-92 mph and carry and run on a four-seamer that's a tick harder. They tunnel well with his plus low-80s slider, which has more depth than horizontal action. He also has advanced feel for a fading low-80s changeup. Stephan features an easy delivery that he repeats well, giving him plus control and the makings of solid command. His low arm slot and release height create life and deception without costing him strikes. He needs to add some strength and falls in love with his slider at times, but his pitchability and competitiveness give him a high floor and the upside of a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the aftermath of the shortened five-round Draft in 2020, 17 high school players signed as nondrafted free agents and the Rangers grabbed five of them. A Texas high school product, Stephan had committed to Stephen F. Austin State but wanted to launch his pro career despite pandemic rules capping his bonus at $20,000. He impressed in his first extended taste of full-season ball in 2022, recording a 3.14 ERA and 115/31 K/BB ratio in 103 1/3 innings between Single-A and High-A at age 20. Stephan's low arm angle and release height create sink and run on a two-seam fastball in the low 90s and carry and run on a four-seamer than can sneak into the mid-90s. His heaters work well in tandem with his tight low-80s slider, which features more depth than sweep. He also exhibits good feel for a changeup with similar velocity and fading action. Stephan repeats his easy delivery, enabling him to fill the strike zone. He shows the makings of at least average command and his biggest need is to gain some strength so he can add more power to his stuff. One of the more advanced young pitchers in the system, he has a high floor and the potential to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though it was Arteaga's athleticism and defensive ability that earned him a $1 million bonus out of Venezuela in 2019, he has made a habit of showing up on offensive leader boards in the Minors. He topped the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 43 RBI in his 2021 pro debut, topped the Single-A California League with 136 hits and 35 doubles in 2022 and paced the High-A Northwest League with 49 extra-base hits at age 20 in 2023. His slash stats have dipped each year, however, and he batted just .209/.308/.319 in 24 games last season after missing most of the first four months recovering from thoracic outlet surgery. Arteaga has lived up to his defensive billing and is a no-doubt shortstop built along the lines of Elvis Andrus. He has fluid actions, covers ground to both sides and makes plays with quick hands and plus arm strength. He can pull off spectacular plays and is improving his consistency as he gains experience. Arteaga's fine hand-eye coordination could translate into average hitting ability, but he's too aggressive at the plate. His combination of bat speed and sneaky strength give him average raw power that he seeks to maximize by looking to launch and pull pitches regardless of where they're located. He has solid speed but is more of a heady baserunner than a daring thief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur in Venezuela, Arteaga impressed scouts with his athleticism and defensive prowess, earning him a $1 million bonus in 2019. He led the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 43 RBIs in his 2021 pro debut, the Single-A California League with 136 hits and 35 doubles in 2022 and the High-A Northwest League with 49 extra-base hits at age 20 last year. His slash line did drop to a career-worst .235/.299/.410 in 2023 and he'll miss the first half of this season following surgery to alleviate thoracic outlet syndrome. A no-doubt shortstop built along the lines of Elvis Andrus, Arteaga has smooth actions, range to both sides, quick hands and plus arm strength. He's capable of providing web gems and is getting more consistent at executing routine plays. In Baseball America's annual manager surveys, he was rated as the best defensive shortstop in the Cal and Northwest Leagues the past two summers. Arteaga has the hand-eye coordination to be an average hitter, but he chases too many pitches and piles up strikeouts in pursuit of power. He does have more pop than initially expected and his combination of bat speed, sneaky strength and ability to launch balls to his pull side could translate into 15-20 homers per year from the right side of the plate. He possesses average to solid speed and will steal an occasional base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arteaga's father played basketball professionally in Venezuela and handed down his quick-twitch athleticism to his son, who signed for $1 million in 2019. Better known for his defense when he turned pro, he has provided more offense than initially expected. He batted .276/.350/.450 in his first two seasons, leading the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 43 RBIs in his 2021 pro debut and topping the Single-A California League with 136 hits and 35 doubles last year at age 19. Arteaga's glove has been as good as advertised and there's no doubt that he'll be a standout shortstop. With smooth actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a plus arm, he's equipped to make all the plays. In a Baseball America survey of Cal League managers last summer, they rated him the best defensive shortstop (over Top 100 prospects Edwin Arroyo and Adael Amador) and the best infield arm on the circuit. Despite an aggressive approach, Arteaga repeatedly barrels balls from the right side of the plate thanks to his hand-eye coordination. With his bat speed, deceptive strength and ability to launch balls in the air, he could deliver 20 homers per season in his prime. He has solid speed and is still learning the nuances of base stealing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants invested heavily in Venezuelan shortstops on the 2019 international market, giving their two biggest bonuses to Arteaga ($1 million) and Anthony Rodriguez ($800,000). Arteaga's father player professional basketball in Venezuela and passed his quick-twitch athleticism to his son. Better known for his defense, he showed surprising power in his 2021 pro debut, leading the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in RBIs (43) while ranking second in extra-base hits (22) and total bases (99) and third in homers (nine). Despite his ACL slugging exploits, Arteaga still stands out most as a no-doubt shortstop. He has smooth actions and plenty of range, as well as the fast hands and plus arm strength to get rid of throws quickly and make them from a variety of angles. He also has fine instincts that allow him to get the most out of his tools. Arteaga has an aggressive approach but has the bat-to-ball skills to get away with it, repeatedly barreling balls and displaying a knack for launching them in the air. More advanced pitchers may force him to be selective, and his quick right-handed stroke should help him adapt. He's also a plus runner with some basestealing aptitude, giving him 20-20 upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants concentrated on Venezuelan shortstops in their 2019 international class, paying their two highest bonuses to Arteaga ($1 million) and Anthony Rodriguez ($800,000). A quality defender, Arteaga inherited his athleticism from his father, who played professional basketball in Venezuela. The coronavirus pandemic wiped out plans for his pro debut in 2020, when his participation was restricted to San Francisco's Dominican instructional league program. A no-doubt shortstop, Arteaga stands out most with his defensive ability. His quickness and instincts give him plenty of range, and he has the fast hands and solid arm strength to get rid of the ball quickly and make any throw needed. If he doesn't provide enough offense to become a regular, he has the tools to play all over the diamond in a utility role. There aren't concerns about Arteaga's bat, however, because he has an easy right-handed stroke that allows him to make regular contact. With his ability to square up balls and his projectable strength, he has more pop than the Giants initially realized and homered seven times in the first month of his 2021 debut. His plus speed will help him get on base and be a threat to steal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants paid the two largest bonuses in their 2019 international class to Venezuelan shortstops, $1 million for Arteaga and $800,000 for Anthony Rodriguez. The latter may have more offensive potential, but Arteaga is a superior defender and no slouch at the plate. He inherits his athleticism from his father, who played professional basketball in Venezuela. Arteaga has the tools required to stick at shortstop and be an asset there. His quickness and instincts allow him to gobble up plenty of ground balls, and he also fast hands and solid arm strength to make all of the necessary throws. If he doesn't hit enough to become a regular, he's athletic enough to play all over the diamond in a utility role. Arteaga should hit enough, however, because he makes consistent contact with an easy right-handed swing. His ability to barrel balls and his projectable strength could translate into 15 or more homers per season. His plus speed should help him reach base and steal a few bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of the Hawaiian baseball scene, Saltiban was one of the few high school players to compete in the 2023 MLB Draft League. He showed enough for the Phillies to take him in the third round of that summer’s Draft and there were some solid early returns. He was among the Single-A Florida State League’s leaders in home runs (17), slugging percentage (.428) and ISO (.191). He did not build off of that with a move up to High-A Jersey Shore in 2025, struggling to find a rhythm in a year interrupted by a nearly two-month stay on the injured list. He made up for lost time by hitting very well in the Australian Baseball League, winning Championship Series MVP honors as the Adelaide Giants won the title. With a quick right-handed swing that generates plenty of bat speed, the 5-foot-9 Saltiban is capable of doing damage when he’s swinging well. He can make loud contact with over-the-fence juice mostly to his pull side and is capable of driving the ball to all fields. His overall approach unraveled in 2025, with his strikeout rate increasing and his walk rate shrinking, though he made more consistent contact in Australia. Saltiban has plus speed and uses it efficiently on the basepaths, with 46 steals in 54 attempts in his career heading into 2026. He’s also back in the outfield, where he played in high school. The Phillies thought he had a chance to play second base, and while they’re not going to take him off the dirt entirely, they like how instinctive he looked in center field, where he played exclusively in Australia. That might take a little pressure off his bat and could be a better fit long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Saltiban was the best player from Hawaii in the 2023 Draft class. After he held his own as one of the youngest performers in the Draft League that summer, he was taken by the Phillies, who didn’t have a second-round selection, in the third round of that Draft, signing for an under-slot bonus of $602,500. After a brief debut in the Florida Complex League last year, Saltiban went to the Florida State League in 2024 and more than held his own, finishing in the top four in homers (17), slugging percentage (.428) and ISO (.191). Strong and compact, Saltiban has more juice in his 5-foot-9 frame than many anticipated. It’s a quick right-handed swing with plenty of bat speed, and he swings with intent to do damage, regularly registering high exit velocities. Most of his home run pop has come to his pull side so far, though he can drive the ball to all fields. He absolutely punishes fastballs and has shown a solid approach at the plate, drawing a good amount of walks, though he’ll need to improve against spin. A plus runner who went 22-for-24 in stolen-base attempts last year, Saltiban was an outfielder in high school, but the Phillies thought he had a chance to make it on the dirt and played second base exclusively in 2024. He’s probably a fringe-average defender right now, and though his athleticism points to him being average at the keystone in the future, he might get some reps in the outfield moving forward. He has as much upside as any hitter in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nearly all Hawaiian hitting prospects at some point work with Kaha Wong, Kolten and Kean’s father, and Saltiban was no different. The best player from the Aloha State in the 2023 Draft class, Saltiban held his own as one of the youngest players in MLB’s Draft League. He was nabbed in the third round by the Twins, no strangers to Hawaiian prep hitters having taken Kala’i Rosario in the fifth round of the 2020 Draft, making Saltiban the first from the state to go in the top three rounds since Shane Sasaki was a Rays third-rounder in 2019. While Saltiban isn’t the biggest player at 5-foot-10, he’s strong and compact. There is a lot of confidence in his right-handed bat. He has a quick swing and excellent bat speed that was on display during his brief debut in the Florida Complex League last summer. The Phillies believe there’s going to be power to come as well as he adjusts to professional pitching. An outfielder in high school, Saltiban now has the opportunity to show he can play on the dirt. He played shortstop in the FCL, and given that he’d never really played the position at any high level, he showed off good hands and a solid enough arm with his plus speed helping him cover ground. He’ll see most of his time at shortstop and second base, which could be his eventual home if the left side of second proves too much of a challenge, with perhaps him getting enough reps in the outfield to keep those skills sharp.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from Puerto Rico, Luciano used good performances at the PDP League and MLB Draft Combine to help his Draft stock going into his senior year in 2024. The D-backs selected the then-17-year-old in the second round that July, making him the highest prep player selected from the island since Edwin Arroyo also went in the second round in 2021. After signing for $990,000, Luciano spent most of his first full season in the Arizona Complex League, hitting .275/.398/.382 with two homers and a 31/28 K/BB ratio over 44 games. He was promoted to Single-A Visalia for three games in the final week of the season. Luciano seems to see the ball well out of a simple left-handed setup in the box, featuring a load with his legs. He was willing to take his walks against wild ACL arms, not an unexpected skill for a backstop who sees so many pitches on defense anyways. Standing only 5-foot-10, he isn’t a big power threat at this very early stage of his career, but he’s impressed D-backs officials with how he’s hitting the ball harder in early spring work, thanks to improved lower-half strength and body efficiency. His best defensive asset entering Year 2 is his above-average arm strength, and he used it to throw out 28.8 percent of attempted basestealers in the ACL. That improved lower-half foundation should help his work behind the plate too, and he briefly shared a Puerto Rican Winter League roster with Gold Glove winner Martín Maldonado in the offseason. Tackling a true full summer season will be Luciano’s next hurdle as he gains steam in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most famous Puerto Rican catcher to enter professional baseball through the Draft is potential future Hall of Famer and 2000 fourth-rounder Yadier Molina, but others like Geovany Soto, Martín Maldonado and Christian Vázquez give the list extra heft. Luciano could be next in line after good showings in the PDP League and MLB Draft Combine pushed him into the second round to the D-backs last July. He signed below slot for $990,000, the seventh-highest bonus given to a Puerto Rico native since the bonus-pool era began in 2012. Left-handed-hitting catchers will always garner attention from scouts, and Luciano checks that box straight out of the gate. He can make consistent hard contact and shows a solid approach. It’s hit-over-power right now, but he showed a better ability to tap into his pullside pop as a senior heading into the Draft. Though he’s a below-average runner, Luciano has enough athleticism to keep the carousel moving when he’s on base. The 5-foot-10 backstop brings plenty of arm strength to the table, and if he can improve his exchanges, he could give opposing runners plenty to consider. His receiving and framing will also need attention as he enters pro ball, but it’s important to remember he was only 17 at the time of the Draft. Luciano even worked on the defensive side of his game with Molina, notable considering Arizona thought of him as a bat-first catcher at the start of his career. Luciano will have plenty of time and space to become a well-rounded player at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For most of his pro career since the Padres took him in the third round and gave him an over-slot bonus of $3 million to sign, Head has been a bit of a cautionary tale about raw toolsy high schoolers who can’t quite figure things out at the next level. After a pretty solid pro debut after signing in 2019, he reportedly looked good at San Diego’s alternate site, but for most of his two years with the Pirates after they got him as part of the Joe Musgrove deal, it’s been a struggle. There might have been signs of life in 2022, however, as Head slashed a much more solid .264/.355/.472 from July 1 on after posting a .650 OPS in the season’s first three months. Head is a tinkerer at the plate, one who was constantly changing his setup to try to unlock his considerable raw tools. He moved his hands often and found a spot that helped him use his athleticism more, and rather than change it the second something went wrong in the second half of 2022, he stuck with it and found more consistency than he’d had previously. There are still approach issues, as he struck out more than 30 percent of the time, even when things were going better, but there’s a lot of potential impact in his left-handed swing. He also made progress on the other side of the ball. He’s always had good speed, but in 2021, his defensive metrics were not good. In 2022, he graded out very well in center field. It remains to be seen if Head’s mechanical changes and his commitment to his craft will allow him to climb to the next level, but it’s the first glimmer of hope in a while.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Head didn’t have a lot of experience against top competition as a two-sport standout who also was a quarterback at his Texas high school. He did show off some impressive tools as the 2019 Draft approached and the Padres jumped ahead of the industry by taking him in the third round and going way over slot to sign him for $3 million. He had a solid pro debut in rookie ball that summer and impressed the higher ups at the club’s alternate site in 2020. He made his full-season debut with the Pirates, who acquired him in Jan. 2021 as part of the Joe Musgrove trade, and he struggled offensively. The Pirates still feel Head has considerable tools; he just needs to learn how to unlock the shed. His power did show up, as he hit 15 homers, impacting the ball more than you would think someone with his smaller frame should be able to. In 2021, he struggled against good fastballs, leading to a lot of the strikeout issues, and most of his power came off of him crushing secondary stuff. He’s worked to stabilize his stance and let his natural athleticism play so he can more regularly time up velocity. Head also has very good speed, though it’s yet to translate to the basepaths, and his athleticism is a big asset in the outfield. He’s played all three spots thus far and might have the skills to play center field. He does have the arm for right and could have the power profile as well if he can learn to make more consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout at his high school in Texas, Head jumped on scouts’ radars when he hit .615 as a senior. The Padres loved his athleticism and set a then-record for third-round bonuses by giving him $3 million in the 2019 Draft, despite his relative lack of track record.
