His pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League (.283/.383/.417) made it seem like a worthwhile investment, and even though he was slowed by a hamstring issue in 2020, he still showed off some loud tools during his time at the Padres’ alternate training site before joining the Pirates courtesy of the Joe Musgrove trade. Head has now become one of the best athletes in the Pirates' system. The left-handed hitter has tremendous bat speed and raw power, though he’ll have to keep working to rein in his swing to get to it. He does have a good overall approach at the plate with a feel for hitting, but the alternate training site has been the only time he’s really faced advanced competition heading into the 2021 season. With plus speed, Head should provide value on the basepaths, and he has a very good chance to play center field for a long time, especially as he gets more reps to work on his reads and routes. Should a move be needed, his arm, not to mention his potential offensive profile, could work well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seeing an opportunity to add an ultra-athletic, five-tool player to an already loaded system, the Padres went all-in in their pursuit of Head, taking him in the third round in 2019 and then signing him for $3 million, a record bonus for a third-round pick. A little-known commodity with barely any track record against quality competition, Head batted .615 as a senior at Churchill High School in Texas. After being drafted, he went on to post an impressive .283/.383/.417 slash line in Rookie ball. He impressed as one of the younger players at the Padres’ alternate camp last summer, then was the highest-ranked prospect dealt to the Pirates in the deal for Joe Musgrove in January. Wiry strong with good snap in his wrists, Head brings premium bat speed to the Pirates’ system. He has raw power, too, giving him serious upside from the left side of the plate if he can harness the moving parts in his swing. Head has an advanced feel for hitting, and his ceiling is extremely high. But he’s yet to face serious competition. If Head continues to develop and improve, he could wind up with average or better tools across the board. He has plus speed and should have no problem sticking in center field once he improves his reads and routes. His strong arm will allow him to play anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez went from a $10,000 signing in June 2022 to a must-follow Brewers prospect just one year later after hitting .370 in an All-Star year in the Arizona Complex League. He ended his age-18 season with Single-A Carolina and returned to the Mudcats for 2024 but was limited to 81 games due to an injured right shoulder suffered on a dive back to the bag. He hit .272/.331/.361 with only one homer in that span, good for a 106 wRC+ in the Carolina League. To make up for the lost at-bats, Baez headed to the Arizona Fall League and thrived as one of the younger players in the desert with a .295/.402/.474 line and two homers in 22 games. Baez starts from an open stance as a right-handed hitter and closes into place with a big leg kick that looks like something designed to launch balls beyond the left-field fence. Despite all that movement, he has good hand-eye coordination that helps him put the ball in play. He handled fastballs well with Carolina but was more prone to being blown away by heat against more advanced AFL arms, and while his walk rate improved nicely overall in ’24, he still looked prone to chasing soft stuff. He doesn’t wow with exit velocities at this stage, and there is some concern he’s already maxed out physically. An average runner, the Dominican Republic native went just 11-for-22 in stolen base attempts last year during the regular season but was uncaught in three AFL attempts. Roster requirements pushed him to second base in the Fall League, but he’s still a better fit at third with relatively limited range. It’s possible Baez takes another jump in a healthier 2025 as he’ll still be a teenager for half the summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It was easy for Baez to get lost in the international shuffle when he signed with the Brewers for only $10,000 in 2022, but his first stateside season cemented his place as a Top 30 prospect in a burgeoning system. The infielder was named an Arizona Complex League All-Star after finishing second on the Rookie-level circuit with a .370 average and 71 total hits over 48 games. He ended his age-18 season with nine more contests with Single-A Carolina, where he was humbled by going 7-for-30 (.233). Baez has a pronounced leg kick to begin his swing from the right side, but the noise hasn’t affected his ability to make contact in the early going -- his 11.2 percent K rate was lowest among ACL qualifiers. Because of his good hand-eye coordination, he can tend to go hunting for that contact and expands the zone, hurting his walk rate (just 3.9 percent in the ACL) and OBP in the process. He flashed decent raw power at the complex, and getting more patient in search of drivable pitches could help that pop play even better in games. The Dominican Republic native is an average but aggressive and savvy runner, swiping 19 bags in 21 attempts in 2023. His relatively limited range was likely going to push him more toward third base full-time in an organization loaded with low-level shortstops, and overall defensive inconsistencies -- even on simple plays like transferring the ball out of the glove -- put his glovework behind his bat. He’ll head back to the Carolina League for his age-19 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Greg W. Harris, who pitched eight seasons in the Majors, Harris spent three years at High Point as a third-baseman/right-hander before his elbow blew out in 2021 and required Tommy John surgery. He missed most of the next season after transferring to NCAA Division II UNC Pembroke, then performed well as a fifth-year senior in 2023 but went undrafted because he was 24 years old. After he earned Coastal Plain League pitcher of the year honors that summer, the Giants signed him for $10,000 as a nondrafted free agent, and he zoomed to Triple-A midway through his second full pro season. Harris' over-the-top arm slot allows him to stay on top of his 79-82 mph curveball and impart tremendous depth, though his bender wasn't as sharp or effective after he got to Triple-A, leading to problems against left-handers. His arm angle also produces difficult carry and ride on a fastball that ranges from 93-97 mph. His mid-80s slider has similar shape to his curveball, and he'll mix in a low-80s splitter on rare occasions. Harris uses his athleticism to get down the mound well and create a highly unusual combination of a high release point and quality extension. He has thrown strikes throughout his college and pro career, and he didn't stop challenging hitters when he ran into some adversity in Triple-A. San Francisco has toyed with the idea of trying him as a starter but decided he'd be best off as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big league pitcher Greg W. Harris, Harris played three years at High Point as a third baseman/right-hander before his elbow gave out in 2021 and required Tommy John surgery. He transferred to NCAA Division II UNC Pembroke, missed most of the next season before performing well as a two-way player in 2023, going undrafted in large part because he was 24 years old. Signed as a nondrafted free agent for $10,000 after he earned Coastal Plain League pitcher of the year accolades that summer while topping the circuit with a 0.30 ERA, he posted a 1.52 ERA and a 36 percent strikeout rate while advancing to Double-A in his first year-plus as a pro. Harris's fastball explodes on hitters, coming out of an over-the-top arm slot and arriving at 94-97 mph with tremendous carry and riding action. His 79-82 mph curveball and 83-85 mph slider both play very well off his heater thanks to their quality depth, with his curve slightly more effective and grading as well above-average at times. He has shown a low-80s changeup with some fade and tumble in the past but has mostly scrapped it in pro ball. Harris is athletic and gets down the mound extremely well, creating a combination of a high slot and quality extension that is highly unusual. He has provided strikes throughout his college and pro career, and he shouldn't need much more time in the Minors. The Giants are tempted to try him as a starter, though he might be best suited for overpowering hitters for two or three innings at a time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2023 as MLB Pipeline's No. 3 international prospect. He batted .316/.415/.513 in his first two years as a pro, winning championships in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex leagues. His jump to full-season ball didn't go nearly as well in 2025, as he had hit .221 with a 30 percent strikeout rate in 29 games at Single-A, missing much of the year with a stress fracture in his left wrist. A switch-hitter early in his amateur career, Vargas now bats solely right-handed and creates plus raw power with his bat speed, growing strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame. His approach is geared to drive balls in the air to his pull side, but it's much too aggressive. He chased way too many pitches last year, fastballs and secondary pitches alike, and rarely made quality contact. Though Vargas moves well on the bases, he's bigger than most shortstops and still growing, so it's unclear whether he'll retain the quickness to remain at the position. He has good actions and his strong arm is beyond approach, but he's probably destined for third base in the long run. He could be a solid defender at the hot corner and has the power to fit the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 3 prospect on the 2023 international market, Vargas signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic that January. He played well in his first two seasons, hitting a combined .316/.415/.513 with 11 homers and 30 steals in 86 games. He also won a pair of championships in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex Leagues the past two years, homering three times in 10 playoff contests. A switch-hitter early in his amateur career, Vargas now bats solely from the right side of the plate with a quick, compact stroke that produces a lot of hard contact. He has a lot of leverage and room to gain strength in his 6-foot-3 frame, and he improved his ability to drive ball in the air consistently in 2024. He could provide 25 or more homers per season, though his strikeout rate rose from 15 percent in his first pro season to 23 percent in his second, so he'll have to prove he can do damage against more advanced pitching. Bigger than most shortstops, Vargas has average speed and good instincts on the bases, though he could slow down as he continues to add muscle. He has good actions and plenty of arm for shortstop, though his range could be an issue if he loses any quickness. If he eventually has to move, he could be a solid defender at third base and should have no problem fitting the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's third-ranked prospect in the 2023 international class, Vargas signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic that January. He made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, slashing .328/.423/.529 with seven homers and 19 steals in 48 contests. He also batted .310 with a pair of homers in seven playoff contests to lead the Dodgers Bautista squad to the championship. A former switch-hitter who now bats solely right-handed, Vargas owns a quick, compact swing and a mature approach. He controls the strike zone exceptionally well for his age and focuses on making hard contact. Once he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame and learns to lift balls in the air more frequently, he could provide 25 or more homers per season. Bigger than most shortstops, Vargas has good actions and range to both sides, giving him a chance to remain at the position. He's an average runner with good baserunning instincts, but he could lose a step as he matures physically. If he has to slide over to third base, he has the offensive profile and the plus arm to succeed there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers pull one of the top prospects out of nearly every international signing class, with Vargas the latest example. Ranked No. 3 in the 2023 crop by MLB Pipeline, he signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic in January. He's just 17 years old and will need time to develop, but in a system loaded with shortstops, he has the highest ceiling of any of them. A former switch-hitter, Vargas now bats exclusively right-handed. He has a sound swing and an advanced approach, patiently stroking line drives to all fields. With his bat speed and the oodles of projectable strength in his 6-foot-4 frame, he could grow into 25-homer power while also producing high batting averages. Though he's bigger than most shortstops, Vargas has good actions, range to both sides, reliable hands and plus arm strength. He's one of the more polished hitters and defenders in his international class. An average runner who could lose some quickness as he matures physically, he'd profile well at third base if he had to move off shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox's father Blane reached Double-A as an outfielder and coached his son and Lakeland Christian HS to Florida's state 3-A championship in 2019. The Guardians selected Jake in the third round of the 2021 Draft and signed him away from a Florida commitment for an over-slot $850,000. He started slowly while dealing with an elbow injury in High-A last season but rallied to bat .288/.355/.443 in the final two-plus months. With his whippy left-handed stroke and fine hand-eye coordination, Fox has the tools to hit for average. He projects as more of a tablesetter than a middle-of-the-order masher, though he didn't control the strike zone as well in 2023 as he had in the past. While he has added strength and bat speed since turning pro and has learned to turn on pitches and lift them in the air, he still hasn't developed much power and may top out at 12-15 homers per season. Fox combines plus speed with constant energy, though he was less aggressive on the bases last year and still is figuring out the nuances of basestealing. A prep shortstop who spent most of his first two pro seasons at second base, he became a full-time outfielder in 2023. His high baseball IQ helped him make the transition easily, and he displays solid range with average arm strength in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many evaluators inside and outside the organization tab Fox as their pick to click among Cleveland prospects in 2023. His father, Blane, reached Double-A as an outfielder and coached him to Florida's state 3-A championship at Lakeland Christian HS in 2019. A third-rounder in the 2021 Draft who signed for an over-slot $850,000, Fox ranked sixth in the Single-A Carolina League with a .381 on-base percentage at age 19 in his full-season debut and also impressed by taking quickly to playing center field. Fox has a whippy left-handed swing and the hand-eye coordination to barrel balls on a regular basis. He recognizes pitches well and controls the strike zone, and he could be an on-base machine who fits near the top of the lineup. He has improved his strength and bat speed since turning pro, surprised the Guardians with his exit velocities in 2022 and could hit 12-15 homers per season with more added muscle. A plus runner with a nonstop motor, Fox stole bases at a 90 percent success rate in his first two seasons. A shortstop in high school, he has spent the majority of his pro career at second base, where he's a surehanded defender with an average arm. Cleveland's stockpile of infield prospects at the lower levels necessitated trying him in center field last year, and his high baseball IQ helped him look so natural there that center will be his primary position going forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox's father Blane got to Double-A as an outfielder and coached his son Jake to a 2019 Florida state 3-A championship at Lakeland Christian High. Two years later, the Guardians drafted Jake in the third round and signed him away from a Florida commitment for an over-slot $850,000. He batted .405 with seven steals in 13 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League and continued to impress in instructional league. Though Fox has a hitch in his left-handed stroke, it's a whippy swing with bat speed and his hand-eye coordination allows him to barrel balls consistently. His feel for hitting exceeds his power potential, though he did add some strength during the offseason. If he improves at turning on pitches and launching balls in the air, he could deliver 12-15 homers per season. With solid speed and a high baseball IQ, Fox can make things happen on the bases. A shortstop in high school, he divided his time between second base, short and third base in his brief debut. With his first-step quickness and average arm strength, he probably fits best at second base, and some scouts think he could wind up in center field after seeing extensive action there in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz came out of the shortstop factory of San Pedro de Macoris in the Dominican Republic that produced All-Stars such as Tony Fernandez, Jose Offerman and Fernando Tatis Jr., signing with the Cubs for $2.3 million as the headliner of their 2025 international class. He was in the midst of his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League when the Orioles acquired him at the ‘25 Deadline for reliever Andrew Kittridge in what turned into a low-risk deal for Baltimore after it reacquired Kittridge last offseason. That means the Orioles are playing with house money with De La Cruz, who commanded the ninth-highest bonus in the entire ‘25 international class. He’s a switch-hitter with a disciplined approach and the offensive upside to profile as a regular at several positions, with scouts divided over whether his hit tool or power will outshine more in the long run. He has room to grow and fill out his athletic 6-foot-2 frame, hinting at the potential for plus raw power in the future. Adding muscle could slow down De La Cruz, who right now is only an average-to-solid runner, and perhaps move him to the hot corner as he matures. He has enough arm strength to be a quality defender at the position if necessary but features the hands, instincts and footwork to remain a shortstop at least for the moment.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz signed for $2.3 million in January, landing the largest bonus in the Cubs' 2025 international class and the ninth highest on the entire market. He's part of the shortstop factory of San Pedro de Macorís in the Dominican Republic that has produced All-Stars such as Tony Fernandez, Jose Offerman and Fernando Tatis Jr. De La Cruz may eventually move off short but has the offensive upside to profile as a regular at several positions. He got off to a slow start during his debut in the Dominican Summer League but then started figuring some things out, posting an OPS of 1.031 in July when he was sent to the Orioles in return for Andrew Kittredge at the Trade Deadline. Scouts debate whether De La Cruz will stick out more with his hitting ability or power in the long run. He's a switch-hitter with a disciplined approach who focuses on making line-drive contact rather than swinging for the fences. His stroke also features promising bat speed and loft and his still-growing 6-foot-2 frame can get stronger, so he could grow into plus raw power and provide 20 or more homers per season. De La Cruz's twitchy athleticism, smooth actions, soft hands and solid arm strength are suited for shortstop. Presently an average-to-solid runner, he could slow a bit as he develops physically, which would dictate a move to third base. He has the tools to be a quality defender at the hot corner and meet the offensive demands of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz tied a Nationals record by signing for $3.9 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021, one that’s since been bested by Cristhian Vaquero. After hitting just .232 with a 73 wRC+ in the Dominican Summer League later that year, the young shortstop transitioned stateside with a little more offensive performance, batting .275/.320/.362 in 52 games in the Florida Complex League before getting a brief stint as an 18-year-old at Single-A Fredericksburg. The 5-foot-10 middle infielder continues to wow with his defensive work at a premium position, showing the footwork, hands and strong throwing arm that could play at any level in short order. Continuing the theme of his athleticism, Cruz is an above-average runner, though he needs to be a more efficient base stealer after going 6-for-11 in theft attempts last year. As good as Cruz’s glove prowess is, he’ll need to hit to become a larger part of the Nats’ future plans. He makes a good amount of contact -- again leaning into his quick hands -- as he proved with a 16.9 percent K rate in 2022, but that contact is far from loud with only 13 of his 48 hits going for extra bases. There could still be some power coming as he matures in his age-19 season and beyond, but as it stands, it would be a stretch for him to reach double-digit homers in the Majors. The 2023 campaign has only seen him be more challenged with the stick, and it's an open question how far he can get on his glove alone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz signed for $3.9 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021, tying him with Yasel Antuna for the highest international bonus in Nationals history at the time. (Fellow Top 30 prospect Cristhian Vaquero has since moved into the top spot.) He began his Minor League career, as did many in his signing class, in the Dominican Summer League, where his .232/.292/.305 line did not set the world on fire but established a baseline performance. Cruz made a lot of contact (13.7 percent K rate), at least, and swiped 11 bags in 15 attempts. Think of your favorite Major League glove-first shortstop, and that’s who Cruz is in very early form. His footwork and hands at such a premium position have drawn raves since before he signed, and he was considered the best defender of his class. He vacuums up balls, and he has more than enough arm to make proper throws across the diamond. That makes it a well-rounded defensive package. The jury remains out on how much he can hit. Cruz utilizes his quick-moving hands to make a good amount of contact already, and the Nationals came away from his DSL time optimistic that they can help him build an average offensive profile from here. He’ll need to add more strength to improve the quality of contact, but he’ll likely never hit for much power at the top level. Cruz’s glove gives him a floor as a backup infielder with the bat determining if he can do more than that. More professional at-bats will help that future take shape in 2022 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz was Washington’s biggest priority of the 2020-21 international signing period, and the organization proved it by signing the Dominican Republic native for $3.9 million, tying Yasel Antuna for the biggest signing bonus for an international prospect in club history. Because the opening of the international market was pushed back to Jan. 15 of this year, Cruz is still awaiting his first true introduction to the Nationals on the field. The 5-foot-10 infielder was arguably the best defender at any position in this year’s international group, and his glove will be his carrying tool in the early days of his career. Cruz draws praise for both his footwork and hands at the shortstop position, allowing him to get to most balls hit in his general direction, including those that result in highlight-level plays. His arm projects to be plenty strong enough to be a weapon as well. The bat remains the big question. His promising hands translate fine to the box and he could be an average hitter in time, though he doesn’t project to hit for much power. Cruz’s glovework at a premium position gives him a higher floor than most prospects who have just signed internationally. His ceiling will be determined by how well he can develop offensively and if he can get to the point where his bat is worth carrying in the lineup every day. Otherwise, a spot as a bench infielder who can provide value defensively might be in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marceaux jumped on the national stage as a Louisiana prepster who pitched for Team USA’s 18U squad in 2017, then stayed home to play for Louisiana State. He spent three years in the Tigers rotation and saved the best for last, topping 100 innings and finishing with a 2.54 ERA to help him land in the third round of the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. He hurled his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season, though he was only able to make two starts for Rocket City because of back issues. He returned to Double-A in 2023 and was traded to the Mets in June in a package for Eduardo Escobar. Marceaux uses a combination of feel for pitching and a huge competitive streak to succeed. His fastball plays up a bit because it has good run and he can command it to both sides of the plate even though it averages around 91-92 mph. He has two distinct breaking pitches, manipulating the shape of his slider and curve and keeping hitters off balance with both. His low-80s changeup has very good fade and is often his best secondary pitch. As evidenced by his 1.72 groundout-to-flyout ratio and just a 7.2 per nine strikeout rate, Marceaux is much more about generating weak contact than missing bats. The Angels feel he might have the best pitch execution in the system, which he’s going to need to continue to have success with his average stuff at the upper levels and reach the big leagues as a No. 5-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler, Marceaux was one of many standout pitchers on USA Baseball’s 18-and-under team in 2017, a Louisiana area prepster who had an advanced feel for pitching with stuff that didn’t wow anyone. He came out of Louisiana State three years later very much the same pitcher, but with a much better resume. After adding a strong 2021 season to it, he landed in the third round in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft, but barely pitched after signing due to his heavy college workload. He jumped on the fast track in his first full season, however, pitching his way to Double-A in 2022. The six-foot Marceaux uses pitchability, command and competitiveness to get the most out of his four-pitch mix. His fastball averaged just a tick over 91 mph in 2021, topping out at 94, but it’s a successful pitch because it has good run to it and he commands it well. He throws both a slider and a curve in the low-80s, and both are above-average offerings. He has a fading changeup, also thrown in the low-80s like his breaking stuff, missing bats with all three and generating a lot of groundballs. Marceaux’s command coming from a simple and repeatable delivery, along with his makeup, are going to help him maximize his potential. The ceiling isn’t high, but his floor is, and he could move quickly and make it up to the big leagues as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of several Cubans signed by the Astros in recent years, Gomez landed a $775,000 bonus in 2022. He made a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before injuries limited him to 16 games when he came to the United States a year later. Jumping to full-season ball in 2024, he hit .267/.333/.403 with 37 extra-base hits and 20 steals in 107 games between two Class A stops. Gomez has the potential to hit for average and power, though he needs more selectivity at the plate. He keeps his left-handed swing in the hitting zone for a long time but chases all types of pitches off the plate too often. He's strong and shows the ability to pull and lift balls, yet he's still learning to be judicious about which ones he should attack. While Gomez has solid-to-plus speed, he's still learning the nuances of basestealing. His instincts are better in the outfield, where he gets better jumps and takes direct routes to flyballs. He's a plus defender with a playable arm in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros are more active in the Cuban market than most clubs and mined it for three players in the 2022 international class: shortstop Alberto Hernandez ($950,000), Gomez ($775,000) and right-hander Carlos Espinosa ($480,000). Gomez made an immediate impression with his advanced offensive and defensive skills. He batted .294/.402/.500 with 10 steals in 37 games during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Gomez prioritizes making contact at the plate with a disciplined approach and a left-handed swing that stays in the zone for a long time. Though he's a hit-over-power guy, he does have the bat speed and projectable strength in his compact 5-foot-11 frame to grow into 15-20 homer pop. He showed the aptitude to turn on pitches and drive them in the air against DSL competition. Gomez's plus speed will enable him to steal bases and remain in center field. He stands out with his instincts as well as his quickness in the outfield, making quality reads and taking efficient routes. He has fringy arm strength but it's playable in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best defensive shortstops in the 2020 Draft, Tolentino starred at the High School All-Star Game in Cleveland that July and won a silver medal with Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in South Korea two months later. The son of former Astros first baseman Jose Tolentino, he turned down a UCLA scholarship to sign for an over-slot $800,000 in the fourth round. He posted an .857 OPS in the first two months of the 2022 season in Single-A, then dipped to .676 following a promotion to High-A. Tolentino has lived up to his reputation with the glove since turning pro. He has advanced actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a plus arm capable of making throws from any angle needed at shortstop. His combination of tools, consistency and high baseball IQ make him an asset anywhere on the diamond, and he also has seen extensive action at second and third base. How much Tolentino develops offensively will determine whether he's a big league regular vs. a defensive-minded utilityman. A left-handed hitter, he has added strength to his lower half since turning pro but still has below-average power and needs to focus on making contact, getting on base and utilizing his solid speed. He has struck out at a 28 percent rate in his first two seasons and had difficulty lifting balls in the air in High-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Astros first baseman and current Angels broadcaster Jose Tolentino, Milan was one of the best defensive shortstops in the 2020 Draft. He played well at the inaugural Prospect Development Pipeline League in 2019, starred at the High School All-Star Game in Cleveland that July and won a silver medal at the 18-and-under World Cup in South Korea two months later. Signed for an over-slot $800,000 in the fourth round, he batted .269/.333/.425 and reached Low-A in his 2021 pro debut. Tolentino stands out most with his glove, and he's as good as any shortstop defender in a Guardians system loaded with middle-infield prospects. He has advanced actions and instincts, quick feet and hands and a plus arm capable of making throws from a variety of angles. With his tools and high baseball IQ, he could play almost anywhere on the diamond, and he did see time at second and third base last season. A left-handed hitter, Tolentino employed a more contact-oriented approach as an amateur but struck out at a 30 percent rate while homering seven times in his 48-game debut. While he has added strength to his lower half since signing, he's better suited to focus on hitting line drives and getting on base. He has average speed with good baserunning instincts, though he's not much of a threat to steal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After not being heavily recruited out of his Ohio high school, Ross headed to Division II Notre Dame College near Cleveland to extend his career. He was the first two-time All-American in school history and made enough noise to get the Twins' attention, and they took him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft, signing him for an under-slot $220,000. He put up relatively pedestrian numbers over his first couple of seasons, though he did spend a year-plus in Double-A. He went back to Wichita to start 2026 and raked, earning a bump to Triple-A in late April. While Ross very much has a utility role profile, it comes with legitimate tools on both sides. He's reined in the swing-and-miss that plagued him a bit early in his pro career, draws a ton of walks and has been consistently hitting the ball hard. He can drive it to all fields for extra bases and has been tapping into his home run pop to his pull side more routinely. He really punishes fastballs, though he does have more trouble with soft stuff. Ross' defense at a number of positions has always been an asset. The above-average runner plays a solid shortstop, with enough arm for the premium position. But he seamlessly moves around the dirt, seeing time at third and second as well this season, while also having turned himself into a quality defender in center and left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A soccer and baseball standout at his Ohio high school, Ross wasn’t heavily recruited and stayed in state, traveling northeast to Division II Notre Dame College outside of Cleveland. With a .405 average and an OPS north of 1.200, he became the first player in program history to be given All-American honors and left campus after the Twins took him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft. He didn’t quite put up those kinds of eye-popping numbers in his first full season, but he was productive with High-A Cedar Rapids and earned a late bump up to Double-A. Lanky and athletic, Ross has some legitimate tools on both sides of the ball. His profile changed a little bit during his first full season, as there was a bit more swing-and-miss than expected. But he also got to his excellent raw power a bit more, finishing tied for second in the Midwest League with 19 home runs. He’s working on refining his approach and swing angle as he especially had a tendency to hit the ball in the air too much on fastballs up in the zone, with the hope he can keep a line-drive angle on those. Ross’ speed and arm do work well at shortstop, his primary position in college, and he’ll continue to see time as he nears the upper levels. He’s also shown the ability to move around the field as needed, even playing more first base than anticipated because of other high priority infielders in Cedar Rapids. His future is likely as a utilityman, but one who can stay up the middle at short and even in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Notre Dame College is a Division II school that doesn’t exactly have a long track record of producing professional talent, with only lefty Travis Scott previously coming from the school, and he transferred to a junior college for his Draft year. So when the Twins took Ross, who was considered to be the best college hitter in Ohio in his class, in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft, he became the first Falcons product to be drafted. He left Notre Dame with a career .405 average and an OPS over 1.200, then held his own with Single-A Fort Myers in his pro debut. Ross brings some twitchy athleticism, speed and a feel for the barrel to the Twins organization. The right-handed hitter doesn’t chase a ton and draws walks. He can drive the ball, but he entered the pro ranks with a setup at the plate with his lower half that made it difficult for him to cover the outer half. He’s made some small adjustments to have better direction to the middle of the field and a better bat path overall. Tall and lanky, he’s already added at least 10 pounds of strength, which could help him impact the ball more. Primarily a shortstop in college, Ross has a strong arm and plus speed that not only should enable him to be a threat on the bases but give him range defensively. He’ll keep getting reps at the premium position, but like he did during his pro debut, he’s going to move around the infield and see more time in the outfield, where his athleticism might really play well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Playing at Alabama is a family affair for the Wilson brothers, with the oldest, Parker, playing football for the Crimson Tide, and Ross and Peyton playing baseball. The Royals drafted Peyton 66th overall in 2021, and he spent his second full season at Double-A Northwest Arkansas in ‘23, where he was the everyday second baseman and slashed .286/.366/.411 with a Texas-League leading 33 doubles in 128 games. He finished the year with a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League, posting an .822 OPS in 21 games. Small but mighty at 5-foot-8, Wilson has a strong frame with a short, compact swing that makes hard contact from both sides of the plate. However, it’s not power contact -- he’s not going to be hitting a ton of balls over the fence. Wilson is pretty aggressive in the strike zone for as little power as he has, although his 18 percent strikeout rate was the lowest of his career last year. What Wilson loses in power, he makes up for in speed as a plus runner who easily stretches singles into doubles. He has the speed to swipe more bags than he has so far, but that comes down to instinct. Defensively, Wilson’s above-average arm strength should allow him to play in the infield and outfield, but the Royals had him almost exclusively at second to get repetitions and settle in there. Wilson’s work ethic and makeup are off the charts, and there’s no question he’s mentally going to be able to move around to different positions in the field if that’s what the Royals need. He doesn’t possess the hit or power tool of an everyday player, so he could use more experience as a utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peyton comes from an athletic family, with his oldest brother, John Parker, a former Alabama quarterback and other brother, Ross, a former Crimson Tide baseball player. Peyton followed in Ross’ footsteps at Alabama, playing center field as a freshman and moving to second base in ‘21 before the Royals selected him in Competitive Balance Round B that summer. Wilson got off to a slow start because of a hamstring injury, missing about three weeks in April and running cautiously until later in the season. He finished strong with a .268/.359/.456 line at High-A Quad Cities. Wilson has a small frame at 5-foot-8, but he’s strong with a short, compact swing that makes hard contact as a switch-hitter. His best tool is probably his speed, which he can use on the bases and in center field. Wilson’s arm is plus-plus, too, which allows him to play center field without a problem, but he's gotten more time at second base, where he can also be a great defender. He’s still getting a feel for the strike zone and what pitches he can do damage on, so if he tones down the aggressiveness, he could unlock a high average with some sneaky pop. Of Wilson’s 14 homers in 2022, eight of them came in August and September last year, and of his 23 stolen bases, 15 of them came in the final two months of the season, too. So he and the Royals were looking forward to seeing what he can do over a full season, and he's been about league-average in the box in the Texas League in 2023. While center field has taken more of a backseat, he can still be a future utilityman for the big-league club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peyton was the third Wilson brother to star at Alabama; John Parker set records as a quarterback, and Ross still shares the freshman home run mark with 15. After catching and playing center field as a freshman, Peyton moved to second base in 2021 and hit .290/.353/.460 with nine homers in 58 games. The Royals selected him with the 66th overall pick and signed him for exactly slot at $1 million, and Wilson made his professional debut last summer, posting a .733 OPS between rookie ball and Low-A Columbia. At 5-foot-9, Wilson’s strength is deceiving, and his short, compact swing makes hard and loud contact from both sides of the plate. He has a chance to hit a lot of extra-base hits because of his speed, which earns plus-plus grades from scouts. If he tones down the aggressiveness he showed in college ball, he profiles as a leadoff hitter, allowing him to cause havoc on the bases. More toolsy than the typical second baseman, Wilson has great instincts and range at the position, and he has a well-above-average arm that has served him well as he’s gotten looks in the outfield this summer. With his athleticism, speed and overall scrappiness, Wilson fits the mold of a typical Royals player. After bouncing around as much as he did in college, the Royals’ plan is to get him as much time as he can at second base in full-season ball, and as he slows the game down, the organization will likely begin to move him around the field. If he can’t stick at one position, Wilson has the ability to play almost anywhere on the field as a utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas native who had a commitment to TCU lined up as a high school senior, Willems impressed the Orioles so much at a pre-Draft workout in Baltimore in 2021 that they convinced him to turn pro with a $1 million bonus as an eighth-round pick. After a difficult adjustment to pro ball, Willems began to turn a corner in 2023 and reached Double-A as a 21-year-old in '24, capping things off with an impressive showing in the Arizona Fall League. He spent all of 2025 back at Double-A. A left-handed-hitting catcher with plus raw power, Willems has produced at least 16 homers in each of the past three seasons. It’s power-over-hit in a strong and stocky package, with a simple swing built to drop the barrel on pitches low in the zone, but he can get pull-happy and prone to slumps when he strays from using the big part of the field. There is also some swing-and-miss, though Willems has cut his strikeout rate the past four years and kept it below 20 percent in ‘25. He’s not a liability on the bases despite poor footspeed. Willems has always had a strong arm -- he touched 90 mph from the mound as a prepster and recorded a 1.90-second pop time in the AFL -- but his future behind the plate is muddied by clunky mechanics, mobility issues and concerns about his receiving and blocking. Though he always played 60-70 percent of his innings at catcher, that number fell to around 50 last year as Willems saw more time at first base and DH. The power remains his driving tool as he reaches the upper levels, but Willems will need to improve defensively to catch everyday and/or probably hit a little more to become a regular at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The impression Willems made at a pre-Draft workout in Baltimore convinced the Orioles to make him an eighth-round Draft pick in 2021, and an overslot $1 million deal convinced the Lone Star State native to bypass a commitment to Texas Christian and turn pro. The adjustment wasn’t the smoothest, but things began clicking at Single-A Delmarva in 2023 and Willems hit himself to Double-A in 2024 as a 21-year-old before capping the year with a solid stint in the Arizona Fall League. His 2025 was more uneven, though he did hit 16 homers, and the Orioles left him off the 40-man roster, but he was not selected in the Rule 5 Draft. Willems has an attractive profile as a left-handed hitting backstop with excellent raw power, and he’s been able to get to it in games to an impressive degree as a young player, socking 17 homers in each of his first two seasons, followed by the 16 last year. It’s power-over-hit in a strong and stocky package, with a simple swing built to drop the barrel on pitches low in the zone and drive them with authority. Willems can swing and miss quite a bit, but his approach is maturing and he sliced his strikeout rate in Double-A and the AFL, and still kept it under 20 percent in 2025. Willems is a decent baserunner despite poor footspeed, taking extra bases when he can and rarely running into outs. Willems touched 90 mph as a two-way prep player and that strong arm has kept him behind the plate despite questions about his receiving and blocking. He isn’t an elite defender, but he’s ironed out those edges somewhat and caught better than scouts expected in the Fall League. He’s also played about a quarter of his defensive innings at first base, though a full-time move there would put more pressure on the bat to develop even further.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 30 | Arm: 65 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 Willems was a two-way player as a Texas high schooler who appeared to be en route to Texas Christian for college ball before the Orioles swooped in and made him an eighth-round Draft pick in 2021. Baltimore kept Willems from heading to campus with an overslot deal of $1 million. He didn’t hit much at Single-A Delmarva in his first full season of pro ball, but things began clicking back at that level in 2023, when Willems hit his way to High-A Aberdeen and socked 17 homers between the two levels. Left-handed-hitting catchers are always a coveted demographic, and Willems brings youth and tremendous raw power to the profile. He is strong and stocky, using a simple swing to drop his barrel on pitches to drive them with authority, especially ones low in the zone. His results improved this year with a revamped approach and better pitch recognition skills. He also walked more, making him a productive hitter despite ample swing-and-miss. That element might always be a part of Willems’ game, but he also has a chance to grow into plus power by the time he’s fully developed. Willems had a strong enough arm as a high schooler to generate 90 mph velocity readings from the mound, and it’s still a weapon for him behind the plate even as questions remain about his receiving and blocking. He improved in both of those areas in 2023 while also seeing time at first base. If he continues his development behind the plate and with his approach in the box, he could develop into a power-hitting backstop at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles tend to covet bat-to-ball skills at the top of the Draft, but they pivoted big time by taking toolsy outfielder Vance Honeycutt with their first pick of the 2024 Draft. Ten picks later, they reverted back to their comfort zone by selecting O’Ferrall with the PPI pick they were awarded for Gunnar Henderson winning 2023 AL Rookie of the Year Award. O’Ferrall was fresh off a college starring turn for Team USA and the University of Virginia, where he set the single-season hits record as a sophomore and was named the nation’s top shortstop as a junior. But he was challenged in his first full season of pro ball, finishing with a .626 OPS, though he briefly reached Double-A at the end of the year. In college, O’Ferrall’s contact skills made him a steady performer whose excellent fundamentals elevated his game. He’s shown good plate discipline in the pros, as well as an ability to grind out at-bats and get on base. But his lack of impact at the plate drags down his overall offensive ceiling. He doesn’t hit the ball particularly hard despite making a lot of contact, and needs to drive the baseball more consistently to be an average hitter. His footspeed is a tick better than average but plays up because he’s a smart baserunner, helping him swipe 42 bases last season. O’Ferrall has enough quickness and range defensively to handle shortstop, though his just-average arm may fit better at second. His strong instincts, makeup and baseball IQ should help him move around, enhancing his floor. Though he lacks eye-popping tools, O’Ferrall plays hard and does a lot of little things well, making him the kind of player who is greater than the sum of his parts, but he probably needs to hit more to be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest in a long line of quality Draft talent to come out of the University of Virginia, O’Ferrall set the school’s single-season hits record as a sophomore, starred for Team USA that summer and was named the nation’s top shortstop as a junior. The Orioles took him with their second Day 1 selection in the 2024 Draft (No. 32 overall), using the PPI pick they were awarded for Gunnar Henderson winning Rookie of the Year to bring in a steady performer whose excellent fundamentals elevate his game and allow him to get every ounce out of his ability. While he showed good plate discipline during his first full season, he lacked impact, finishing with a .626 OPS, almost entirely with High-A Aberdeen. From Adley Rutschman to Colton Cowser to Enrique Bradfield Jr., the Orioles have consistently coveted bat-to-ball skills at the top 42 b of the Draft (with a few exceptions) under their current regime. O’Ferrall has impressive abilities in this category. He walked more than he struck out in college, has very good feel for the barrel and makes sound swing decisions, which allow him to grind out at-bats and get on base. That continued in 2025, with an 11.4 percent walk rate and just a 14.9 pct K rate. He relies on being a tough out because his power is limited, and while the lack of pop might drag down O'Farrell's overall offensive ceiling, he could develop into an above-average hitter. His footspeed is a tick better than average, and he can steal bases and rarely makes mistakes between the lines, leading him to swipe 42 bases last season. Defensively, too, O’Ferrall is greater than the sum of his parts. Good footwork, positioning and quickness help him overcome a just-average but accurate arm, and while he has enough range to stick at shortstop, those skills would help him move around the infield if necessary, and he saw time at second base in 2025. While O’Ferrall doesn’t have eye-popping tools, he has plus instincts, makeup and a high floor with probably enough upside to develop into an everyday player, and a floor as a utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ second-round pick in 2017, Hall signed for an above-slot $1.3 million bonus after starring for the Canadian junior national team, and seemed to put himself on the fast track with impressive seasons at Low-A Aberdeen in ’18 and Class A Delmarva in ’19. But he was affected more than most prospects by the pandemic, unable to attend Orioles’ secondary site camp in 2020 due to border regulations between the U.S. and Canada. He then experienced a down year at High-A Aberdeen in 2021, hitting .248 with three homers and a .672 OPS as a 22-year-old. The Orioles opted not to protect him from the Rule 5 draft in his first year of eligibility. Hall’s best tool is his plus speed, which he’s used to swipe at least 22 bases in each of his three full professional seasons. He’s more of an all-fields, gap-to-gap hitter than a power threat, with a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions. Even so, the lack of power at High-A in 2021 was concerning, given how Hall’s walk rate and extra-base output also slid considerably when exposed to better pitching. Hall's a scrappy hitter who routinely puts together good at-bats, but he might need to add strength to compete more consistently at the higher levels. Hall couples his speed with savvy instincts on the bases, stealing 26 bases in 27 attempts last summer at Aberdeen. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, though the bat might require him to move around the diamond at the highest level. The arm is good enough to play any of the three infield spots, and Hall also got some experience in center field with the Ironbirds. That versatility helps project Hall to reach the Majors in a utility role, especially if he adds muscle to his wiry frame and can stay out of the trainer’s room. That’s proven challenging in the past, with Hall having three of his four professional seasons disrupted by soft-tissue injuries.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall has improved steadily since the Orioles, enamored with his play for the Canadian junior national team, landed him with an above-slot $1.3 million bonus in the second round of the 2017 Draft. An oblique injury limited Hall to just two games that summer, and he struggled initially in the New York-Penn League before breaking out down the stretch in 2018. Healthy again, Hall jumped a level and was one of the more productive hitters in the Class A South Atlantic League in 2019, hitting .298/.385/.395 with five homers and 33 stolen bases. He attended O’s instructional camp in 2020 and seems to be a fair bet to begin 2021 at Double-A. Hall benefits from a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions, relying more on an all-fields, gap-to-gap approach rather than plus power. There are questions about whether he’ll grow into more, but Hall assuaged some of those doubts by improving his extra-base-hit output and walk rate at each new level. His best tool is his plus speed, which Hall couples with good instincts on the bases. He is a scrappy hitter who consistently puts together competitive at-bats and demonstrates strong on-base skills. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, where Hall has a chance to stick at the highest level. Whether that’s on an everyday basis depends on how his bat develops as he adds muscle to what is still a wiry frame. Hall possesses enough arm strength to play all over the diamond if not, and has shown capable of handling second base and center field in small samples. This versatility leads him to project to reach the Majors in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall has improved steadily since the Orioles, enamored with his play for the Canadian junior national team, landed him with an above-slot $1.3 million bonus in the second round of the 2017 Draft. An oblique injury limited Hall to just two games that summer, and he struggled initially in the New York-Penn League before breaking out in the second half, hitting .358 with a 19-game hit streak down the stretch in 2018. Healthy again, Hall jumped a level and was one of the more productive infielders in the Class A South Atlantic League in 2019, hitting .298/.385/.395 with five homers and 33 stolen bases. Hall benefits from a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions, relying more on an all-fields, gap-to-gap approach rather than plus power. There are questions about whether he’ll grow into more, but Hall assuaged some of those doubts by more than doubling his extra-base-hit output and improving his walk rate last season. His best tool is his plus speed, which he couples with good instincts on the bases, and is a scrappy hitter with a tendency to grind out at-bats. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, where Hall has the chance to stick at the highest level. Whether that’s on an everyday basis probably depends on how his bat develops as he matures and adds muscle to what is now a wiry frame. Hall possesses enough arm strength to play all over the diamond if not, in which case he would project to reach the Majors in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After strong performances with the Canadian junior national team had pushed him up Draft boards in 2017, Hall landed an above-slot $1.3 million signing bonus from the Orioles after they took him the second round. An oblique injury limited him to just two games that summer, and Hall struggled at the outset of 2018, hitting .212 with a .524 OPS during his first month in the New York-Penn League. He broke out in the second half, raking at a .358 clip (.913 OPS) over his final 36 contests, and authored a 19-game hit streak along the way. Hall has natural feel to hit, demonstrating good bat speed and the ability to hit to all fields from the right side of the plate, albeit with below-average power. He does have some pop to the gaps, however, and should be a consistent source of doubles and triples as he adds strength to his athletic frame. Plus speed might be Hall's best tool, and club officials rave about his baserunning instincts. Hall's defense and arm have improved considerably in the professional ranks to the point where scouts now view him as an above-average defender who can stick at shortstop. With his slow start and torrid finish, Hall arguably was Baltimore's most improved prospect in 2018. Club officials are quick to praise infield coordinator Dave Anderson and hitting coordinator Jeff Manto for their role in his development, as they each spent a lot of time working with Hall and made him a more confident player overall. He doesn't have a very high ceiling, but the tools and skills are all there for Hall to develop into an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canada has produced a fair share of Draft talent over the years, with Josh Naylor and Mike Soroka the most recent examples to get taken in the first round (both in 2015). There hasn't been much in the way of middle infielders to come from north of the border, but the Orioles are hopeful that Hall, who signed for $1.3 million as a second-round pick, will be the first to reverse that trend. Hall made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he tallied six hits in nine at-bats before an oblique injury prematurely ended his season. Hall might be a bit unpolished, but he has considerable tools and upside. He has a decent approach at the plate for his age and experience level, with a natural feel to hit and good bat speed. There should be some gap power in the future as well, and he should compile plenty of doubles and triples thanks to his plus speed and sharp baserunning. Hall is capable of making the spectacular play defensively, and while his arm might grade out as average, he can reach back for more when needed and he's usually very accurate. He will struggle at times with the backhand play, but most feel he can stick at short. If not, his tools also would fit nicely at the keystone. Hall needs to add strength to his athletic frame, but that should come as he matures physically. Having turned 18 not long before the Draft, he'll have plenty of time to fulfill his fairly high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Messina became the starting catcher at South Carolina as a sophomore and hit 17 homers that season in 2023. He upped his game in 2024, hitting 21 more long balls and winning the Johnny Bench Award, given to the top catcher in college baseball. The power potential and defensive work were enough to get him selected in the third round of that summer's Draft and he made it to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball. It's a power-over-hit profile for Messina, with more strength than bat speed in his right-handed swing. He can punish mistakes, though he didn't get to much power in 2025, and he did limit his strikeouts while drawing walks. There are a lot of moving parts to his swing with a leg kick, and at times, a bat wrap to go along with questions about his ability to make adjustments. Because of his catch-and-throw skills, Messina has a high floor as a future backup at the big league level. More athletic than you'd think -- he stole 14 bases in 2025 -- pitchers love throwing to him. He's an excellent receiver who calls a good game and has an arm that threw out 40 percent of potential basestealers last year. If he can iron out his swing and his approach to improve the offensive part of his game, he could be a glove-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After not playing much as a freshman at South Carolina, Messina became the Gamecocks' starting catcher as a sophomore, smashing 17 homers in 2023. He won the Johnny Bench Award as the top NCAA catcher in 2024, hitting 21 more homers and finishing with a 1.166 OPS. That helped him land in the third round with the Rockies. He then got to watch younger brother Carson, a high school pitcher, go in Round 12 to the Blue Jays. Messina is a strong right-handed hitter who put up those good power numbers despite struggling with his approach during his junior season. There was a lot more swing-and-miss overall compared to his 2023 campaign, with higher whiff rates against fastballs than previously, and he's always had a hard time with softer stuff. There's plenty of power for him to tap into, especially to the pull side, and he may always have a power-over-hit approach with some walks thrown in. With a take-charge attitude behind the plate, Messina has the right mentality to catch at the next level. He's a solid receiver with an average arm and shows enough agility to block well even though he's not fleet of foot. He didn't hit during his pro debut after signing, but a 15-game sample is not enough to draw any conclusions from.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Swan was a tall prep shortstop at Oakland High School in Murfreesboro, Tennessee but showed flashes of greatness on the mound, including one March 2020 outing in which he sat in the mid-90s. He became a full-time pitcher at Middle Tennessee State after the pandemic, and despite not finding consistent results, he went to the Dodgers with in the fourth supplemental round in 2023. Oblique and arm injuries limited Swan’s first full season before he looked on the brink on a breakout in the Arizona Fall League. Swan was healthy at High-A Great Lakes when the Dodgers traded him to the Nationals in the Alex Call deal at the Deadline. He finished with a 4.42 ERA, 102 strikeouts and 63 walks in 91 2/3 innings at two High-A levels. Working exclusively out of the stretch and primarily from the first-base side of the rubber, Swan sits 94-97 mph with his four-seam fastball and touches the occasional triple-digits from his high release point. The movement is more ordinary than the velocity, making it less of a swing-and-miss offering. That said, Swan gets heavy whiffs on his low-80s sweeper that wears out the gloveside half of the plate, and it was his primary pitch against righties. A harder upper-80s slider worked as his preferred breaker for lefties, and a grip-and-rip 86-88 mph changeup showed promise for the velo difference but was little used in ’25. Swan’s walk rates at both Great Lakes and Wilmington were both above 15 percent, a worrying trend as he heads to the upper Minors. He’s simplified his mechanics – thus the removal of his windup – but still can’t get in the zone consistently enough. The new Nationals player-development apparatus might be best set letting him lean on the fastball and sweeper in relief and letting him dominate in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a shortstop as a Tennessee high schooler, Swan's fastball velocity jumped about 10 mph into the upper 90s when he became a full-time pitcher at Middle Tennessee State. Though he posted a 6.54 ERA in three seasons with the Raiders, his athleticism and arm strength ranked among the best in the 2023 college pitching class and the Dodgers selected him in the supplemental fourth round. After a strained left oblique and minor arm soreness limited him to 28 1/3 innings in his 2024 pro debut, he was one of the most impressive pitchers in the Arizona Fall League. Swan was at High-A Great Lakes for 2025 when Los Angeles traded him to the Nationals at the Deadline for Alex Call. While it looks like he's just playing catch, Swan works at 94-97 mph and tops out at 101 with his fastball while maintaining his velocity deep into games. His heater features more downhill plane than life and he has yet to develop consistent command of it, so it can get hit hard when he doesn't locate it well. He also can miss bats with two different sliders, one in the low-80s with more depth and a tighter upper-80s version that can climb to 90 mph. Swan also will flash some solid upper-80s changeups with interesting fade, though he doesn't use it very often. He's extremely athletic for a 6-foot-6, 240-pounder and works exclusively out of the stretch. But outside of last year’s AFL, he doesn’t have a long history of throwing strikes as a pro. Washington should develop him as a starter for now, but it's more realistic that he becomes an overpowering reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Messina in the 12th round and signed him away from his commitment to South Carolina for $550,000 in 2024, a sharp move by Toronto’s amateur scouting team to add a top prep arm to the system. Unfortunately, Messina was limited to just one outing in the Florida Complex League and dealt with arm issues throughout the summer, so we’re still left with his Draft profile and little competitive data to work with. When the Blue Jays landed Messina, he’d been up to 97 mph in high school and had touched 99 soon after, which he’s working to get back to now at the club's complex. His slider was showing the potential to be a legitimate plus pitch, with a changeup that trailed behind, all of which is a fairly standard profile for a top prep arm. But it still remains to be seen how these pitches play against young pro hitters. Messina has a thick, powerful build that should hold up to workloads as long as his arm can stay healthy. For 2026, getting into competitive games with some level of regularity would be a success, setting him up for a big ‘27 season. Whether he starts long-term is for his health to determine, but the base-level tools are there for an exciting relief profile down the road, too. Messina remains one of the biggest projects for the development staff in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It looked like Messina would play NCAA ball for South Carolina like his brother, Cole, whom the Rockies drafted in the third round in 2024, but the Blue Jays selected him in the 12th round and signed him away from that commitment for $550,000. This was a smart, aggressive move by the Blue Jays' Draft team, adding another high-upside high school arm to the system, where they hope he can benefit from their player development complex and new pitching philosophy. His 2025 was severely limited, though he was back to throwing bullpens by the end of the season. Messina was touching 97 mph in high school and regularly sits in the 93-95 range with his heater. (He's been up to 99 since then.) His breaking ball is his most advanced secondary pitch right now and shows legitimate potential, but like most high schoolers, he'll need to develop his feel for a changeup in the coming years. Messina has a strong build at 6-foot-2, 225 pounds, so while that may already be toward the ceiling of his physical projection and leads to Messina throwing with max effort, there's plenty to work with here. When fully healthy, Messina will be developed as a starter, of course, but if his control doesn't hold up to that consistently, there's some real potential for Messina to excel as a maxed-out, back-end bullpen arm. One advantage the Blue Jays have right now is time, making Messina one of this development staff's most important projects in 2026 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Graham and Jace Jung were good friends, college rivals and even roommates on their way into the 2022 Draft, and the Tigers made them organizational teammates by following their first-round pick of Jung with a second-rounder on Graham. His 20-homer, 34-steal season at Oklahoma was historic, but Graham has struggled to translate that dynamic offensive package to the pros, partly due to injuries that limited him to 84 games over a year and a half in the Tigers' system. Though Graham has learned to temper his aggressive approach at the plate, it has yet to translate into consistent quality contact, particularly against breaking balls and offspeed pitches. He still hits a fair amount of balls on the ground. He had surprising struggles against left-handed pitching last year, from strikeout rate to limited extra-base power. Though the Tigers moved Graham around the infield last year, they had him primarily at his natural position at short, where his athleticism, body frame and arm play better than at third. This could be a key season for Graham, who needs to start moving up the system. His reputation as a hard-nosed player and tough competitor is well-earned, so watching him take on the challenge should be interesting to watch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers went heavy on college bats in the 2022 Draft, and while Jace Jung was the highest-profile one, Graham fit their hitters' prototype. Though he wasn’t a top recruit and went undrafted out of high school, he made himself into a top-class college bat, becoming the first NCAA Division I Player in 18 years with 20 homers and 30 stolen bases in the same season. The Tigers selected him in the second round, signed him to an above-slot $1.8 million bonus and assigned him to Single-A Lakeland for a challenging introduction to pro ball. Though Graham has a solid line-drive swing that produces power without having to push for it, he can still fall into bouts of overaggressiveness at the plate, hunting fastballs at the expense of vulnerability to breaking balls. His plus speed plays well on the basepaths, but that hasn't translated into doubles and triples yet. He showed an ability to hit to the opposite field during his short stint in Lakeland. He has been rated average defensively at shortstop, but his strong arm could lead to a move to third base, especially if he adds more strength. He even played outfield in the Cape Cod League during college. Ultimately, Graham’s athleticism could fit him into the Tigers’ mold of infielders who can play all over the diamond and provide offensive impact at multiple positions. Ankle issues and muscle strains have kept him from truly getting going in 2023, but the raw pieces of his profile remain exciting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many saw Moore, the son of current Rangers senior advisor Dayton Moore, as a potential first-round pick after he posted a .942 OPS and smashed 16 homers for Arkansas in 2021. He did not back that up with another strong season in 2022 as his OPS dipped to .801 with a .232 average. The Brewers liked his bounceback potential enough to take him No. 72 overall that July, but his first full season in High-A was fairly nondescript. He’ll get to try to rediscover his groove with a new organization after joining the Phillies in November in the trade that sent Oliver Dunn to the Brewers. At his best, Moore is a savvy middle infielder whose whole maybe be better than the sum of his parts. He switch hits but has historically been better with more thump from the left side, though he was a bit more impactful the other way during what was largely a rough first full season. Even though he’s listed at 5-foot-9, there is some raw pop in there and he tends to have a solid idea of the strike zone, limiting strikeouts and drawing his fair share of walks. With solid contact skills, he’ll need to rediscover the ability to impact the ball to take the next step. Moore is showing he is a very capable defender on both sides of second base, where his instincts, hands and ability to slow the game down are assets. An above-average runner, he has more than enough range for short, but if he’s going to stick in one spot as an everyday player, it’s likely going to be second base because of his fringy arm strength. His feel for the game and defensive acumen give him a high floor as a utility infielder-type in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Royals exec and current Rangers advisor, Dayton Moore, Robert looked like he was hitting his way to Draft prominence when he homered 16 times and finished with a .942 OPS in 61 games in his first full season at Arkansas in 2021. His dinger output halved the following spring, and he hit just .232 with an .801 OPS, causing his stock to fall. But he was still taken in Competitive Balance Round B by the Brewers in July 2022 and signed for a little below slot at $800,000. After playing at Single-A Carolina during his pro debut, Moore went to Australia for winter ball and showed signs of his old self with a .294/.378/.516 line in 40 games with Brisbane. He wasn’t able to follow that up with a move to High-A Wisconsin in 2023, finishing with a .682 OPS, and is now hoping a change of scenery will help ignite his bat after he got traded with Hendry Mendez to the Phillies in return for Oliver Dunn in November. A switch-hitter, Moore has been more powerful and productive from the left side, though that trend flipped a bit in 2023. Listed at 5-foot-9, it’s sneaky pop overall but likely to be below-average compared to his peers. He typically does a good job of not expanding the zone and should make enough contact with good bat speed from either side to be a potential average overall hitter in the end, though his High-A experience was relatively rough. The former Razorback has the hands, internal clock and instincts to be an impressive defender up the middle. He moved over to second in college in deference to Jalen Battles but got a few more looks at the six in his first taste of the Minors. Fringy arm strength will likely keep him at the keystone long term, and he could be an absolute asset there. That glovework and his high motor give him a high floor, and he could be everyday quality if he can swing it like he did in Australia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morales was a solid performer in his first two seasons at Miami but broke out even bigger with a .408/.475/.713 line and 20 homers as a junior in 2023. The Nationals were pleased to see him still available in the second round, took him there and signed him for $2.6 million. Morales’ first full season was limited by a serious left thumb injury, and he returned to Double-A Harrisburg briefly to begin 2025. After an early promotion to Triple-A Rochester, he hit .249/.330/.401 with 11 homers in 95 games at the Minors’ top level. A productive stint in the Puerto Rican Winter League (three homers in 15 games) helped buoy his stock heading into 2026. A hulking presence, Morales still brings the plus raw power that made him a college star. His 105.9 90th-percentile exit velocity and 48.8 percent hard-hit rate at Triple-A both rated above the Major League average and speak to his slugging ceiling. But when he did make contact, so much was on the ground or hit the other way because of a long swing that it kept his power from showing up as it should have in games. The same length also made him late on fastballs, leading to heavy whiffs on four-seamers, and he looked at times more ready to swing hard than to swing at good pitches. Morales looked like he was pulling the ball in the air more efficiently in PR this winter, a hopeful sign for his age-24 season. Though he has plus arm strength, he’s been trending toward first base since reaching Rochester. The Nationals plan to get him time at both corners but note that Morales could be more of a defensive asset as a big target at the cold corner, where the offensive bar to slug is even higher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morales performed all three years at the University of Miami and exploded in his junior year with a .408/.475/.713 line and 20 homers in 61 games. The Nationals were happy to take him when he was available in the second round in 2023 and signed him for above slot at $2.6 million. Continuing with that enthusiasm, Washington opened Morales at Double-A Harrisburg in his first full season, only for the corner infielder to suffer a serious left thumb injury on a plate at the plate in his 37th game on May 18. He didn’t return to the Senators lineup until Aug. 9 but hit .304/.412/.426 over his final 32 games. So much of Morales’ 2024 was defined by the thumb, even after he returned because of the mental battle dealing with an injury to a key piece of the hitting apparatus. There’s hope that a full offseason of additional rest and recovery will help take away the concerns of a ghost injury and get Morales’ plus raw power to play in games again. At his best, he’s a large presence in the box with significant strength that could produce loud contact. At his shakiest, he struggles against sliders and changeups and gets on top of the ball too much, leading to groundball contact. With his good arm strength, Morales could sprinkle in some third base still, but with Brady House ahead of him and Cayden Wallace acquired last year, his best chance for upper Minors at-bats is at the first base spot. He’s still learning the nuances of the position but will need the power to return to collegiate levels soon if he’s going to be valuable at the cold corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 131 prospect in the 2020 Draft, Morales had a strong commitment to the University of Miami and went undrafted in the shortened process as a result. He was a three-year performer for the Hurricanes -- with some Team USA time sprinkled in -- and enjoyed his best spring as a junior in 2023, slashing .408/.475/.713 with 20 homers in 61 games. The Nationals selected Morales (now ranked 20th in his second class) in the second round of the 2023 Draft and went above slot to sign him for $2.6 million.
