Diaz tries to do too much at the plate, chasing all types of pitches out of the zone and trying to yank them all to left field. The right-handed hitter somewhat makes up for those flaws with his ability to put the bat on the ball and generate high exit velocities when he makes contact, and he could develop 20-homer power if he tones down his approach. He crushes fastballs but flails against breaking balls, so he's going to have to make adjustments. A solid runner, Diaz enhanced his value by improving his basestealing aptitude and proving he could play center field in 2025. Mostly a corner outfielder in the past, he has good instincts and can remain in center going forward. His strong arm helped him notch 25 assists in 212 outfield starts during his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cuban-born Diaz has exceeded expectations since signing for $50,000 in July 2023. He produced in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2023 and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last year before making the jump to Single-A at age 18 in June. He slashed .279/.333/.434 with 21 extra-base hits in 55 games as one of the California League's youngest players. An aggressive right-handed hitter, Diaz looks to pull pitches and chases too many outside the strike zone. He hits the ball hard when he makes contact and already shows solid raw power that could grow as he continues to fill out his 6-foot-2 frame. He raked against fastballs but scuffled against breaking balls in Single-A, and he'll need to make adjustments to survive against more advanced pitching. Diaz has average speed and is a bit quicker once he gets going. He has a knack for chasing down balls in the outfield, providing solid range on the corners and warranting a look in center field. His strong arm adds to his right-field profile and he registered 11 assists in 40 starts there last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken fifth overall by the Nationals and signed for $6.5 million in 2022, the son of Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green was a high-ceiling prospect out of IMG Academy. It’s been a slow build through Green’s first two full seasons, both of which came at Single-A Fredericksburg. The outfielder was limited to 75 games due to a wrist issue in 2023 and returned to slash just .208/.293/.355 with 13 homers and 39 steals in 106 games last season. His .257/.332/.450 line and 127 wRC+ from July 1 onward provided a light at the end of the season, though it came with a 42.5 percent strikeout rate. For all the good that remains in his profile, you still can’t talk about Green without mentioning the strikeouts. Green’s 44.0 percent K rate on the season was tops among Minor League full-season qualifiers, and he missed on 47 percent of his swings. He especially struggled against non-fastballs, highlighting that part of the issue stemmed from pitch selection. Batting with a closed front side, a leg raise and his hands held out, Green is geared-up to shoot rockets when he does make contact, and the exit velos are some of the loudest in the Nats system, occasionally topping 115 mph. When Green’s bat meets ball, the ball tends to go a long way. Green has also retained the plus-plus speed that made him a huge Draft prospect. He’s a constant and efficient threat on the bases, and some believe he could play center field in the Majors tomorrow if needed. His plus arm has helped him pick up 15 outfield assists in the last two seasons. Washington believes in Green’s work ethic and desire to improve, but as his career continues, he’ll face tougher and tougher tests in the box.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green was MLB Pipeline’s No. 3 Draft prospect in 2022 because of a multi-tooled, high-ceiling profile he built at IMG Academy and various stops of the showcase circuit. The Nationals selected him fifth overall and signed him for slot at $6.5 million, hoping he could be the club’s next homegrown superstar. The right-handed slugger’s first full season, however, was a rough one. His 41.6 percent strikeout was fourth-highest among Minor Leaguers with at least 300 plate appearances, while walks and power helped him salvage a .218/.336/.327 line. He was limited to 75 games at Single-A Fredericksburg due to a midseason wrist issue. The Nats have cautioned anyone who would listen not to give up on Green because of just how loud four out of his five tools have been. He’ll pop the occasional exit velocity north of 110 mph because of his quick wrists and immense strength, and he can drive the ball to all fields when he gets the barrel on the ball. Green also makes 70-grade speed look easy on the basepaths -- he stole 30 bags in 2023 -- and he can track down balls all over center field. What’s more, he has a strong arm out there, registering seven outfield assists in 71 defensive starts from the grass. So much comes down to the right-handed slugger’s bat. Green can struggle with pitch recognition -- from missing on pitches outside the zone to sitting on hittable pitches inside it -- and he’s been off-kilter in his directionality at the plate, hurting his ability to make contact. Considering Green would be entering his sophomore year had he gone to school, there is time to correct the mistakes, but the climb to superstardom is a lot more uphill now than on Draft Day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green, Elijah Green had one of the highest ceilings in the 2022 Draft class after standout turns on the showcase circuit and at IMG Academy that spring. He headed into July as MLB Pipeline’s No. 3 Draft prospect, trailing only top two picks Druw Jones and Jackson Holliday on the board, and he eventually went fifth to the rebuilding Nationals, who could use all the ceiling they could get and signed him for slot money at $6.5 million. Green produced a .939 OPS in 12 Florida Complex League games but also struck out 40.4 percent of the time, heightening concerns about his biggest weakness. Start with Green’s strengths because there are many. His raw power could be double-plus in the end, and he makes it play in games with quick wrists and immense strength that drives the ball to all fields. What’s more, his speed is 70-grade now, giving him another elite athletic tool, and that will be a big help in his ability to stick in center for the long term. The same could be said for the plus arm strength that will be another asset from the grass. Green did show struggles against high fastballs even during his prep days, and his early swing-and-miss issues in the pros portend a long road of development ahead. The Nationals believe he just needs more exposure to advanced pitching to improve his swing decisions, and that will be the focus in the early days of Green’s budding career. The other four tools are ample enough to carry him until the bat comes around, and if it does, Green could have superstar potential in the capital.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known more for his hitting and wrestling prowess than his pitching in high school in Virginia, Grammes became a two-way player at Xavier and showed enough promise on the mound to become a fifth-round pick in 2019. The four years since have been a rocky road, to say the least. He lost his first full season to the pandemic and then made eight High-A appearances before needing Tommy John surgery in July 2021. Grammes returned to Hillsboro late last July, and while the results were a mixed bag (17 earned runs, 33 strikeouts in 18 innings), his stuff still showed the same promise. The 6-foot-1 right-hander is back up to the upper 90s, touching triple digits, so velocity has not been a concern coming off the elbow procedure and long rehab. His upper-80s slider is a wipeout pitch too, making sure hitters can’t just sit on the heat, and it might be only a touch better than his low-80s curveball, at least when it comes to bite. The deuce is still at least an above-average pitch, which is more than can be said for a changeup he doesn’t use much in relief. Command was a relative difficulty for Grammes before Tommy John, and that continued to be true last year as he tried to play catch-up. In the offseason, the D-backs have worked with him on landing pitches more consistently. If he can, the quality of his arsenal could point to a high-leverage role out of the bullpen. Grammes was already left exposed to the 2022 Rule 5 Draft (and went unselected), so time is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: More of a power hitter than a pitcher in high school, Grammes won nearly as many Virginia state wrestling titles (two) as he pitched innings (three), and he received a walk-on opportunity at Xavier only after emailing the program. While he has posted much gaudier numbers at the plate than on the mound with the Musketeers, he'll definitely become a full-time pitcher as a pro. He turned down the Orioles as a 35th-rounder last year as a sophomore and should go about 30 rounds higher this June. Grammes offers some of the best fastball velocity in the Draft, working at 95-99 mph as a reliever in the past and at 93-95 as a starter this spring. It doesn't feature a lot of life and he struggles to command it, so his heater can get hit when he leaves it over the plate. Similarly, he can throw some sharp low-80s sliders and also get into trouble when his breaking ball flattens out. Grammes has shown little feel for a changeup while trying to incorporate a third pitch as a starter this year, and he'll probably scrap it as a reliever at the next level. Though he throws with some effort, he has made some progress cleaning up his delivery and has the athleticism to continue to improve. He has little history of providing strikes or consistency, though he never has concentrated solely on pitching either.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Only two pitchers cracked MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list in 2024, and the highest-ranked arm on the list came at No. 25 in Franco. The Dominican right-hander signed with the Cardinals for $800,000, and while he’s since been outshined by other members of his signing class in Rainiel Rodriguez and Yairo Padilla, it’s worth remembering that he was the one who received St. Louis’ highest bonus in 2024. Franco didn’t flash impressive numbers out of the gate with a 6.16 ERA, a 1.63 WHIP and 37 strikeouts in 38 innings in the Dominican Summer League, but he showed some of the promise that made him a notable addition in the first place. Officially 16 on signing day, Franco was all about projection when he first joined the St. Louis system, and his arsenal has already shown an upward trajectory in year one. After sitting 91-93 mph with his tailing fastball as an amateur, he’s closer to the 93-95 mph range now, and entering his age-18 season, there’s still likely more room for velo. He improved a high-70s slurve to be more of a low-80s sweeping slider while his mid-80s changeup needs more refinement. DSL pitchers are typically wild, and Franco was no exception with a 13.3 percent walk rate in year one. Harnessing his pitches will be just as important as improving their individual pitch quality, and that’ll be part of the process as he expands his professional workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2024 international class was much more heavy on bats than arms. In fact, only two pitchers featured among MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list this offseason, and the highest-ranked of the pair was Franco at No. 25. The Dominican Republic native signed with the Cardinals for $800,000 at the start of the signing window on Jan. 15, becoming the organization’s most high-profile addition of the period -- one in which it was down $500,000 in pool money after signing Willson Contreras in 2022. Having only turned 17 back in February, Franco is all about projection. He already stands 6-foot-3 and is expected to fill out as he heads toward and into his 20s. Even so, he already sits 91-93 mph with a tailing fastball that can help generate ground balls now, and considering his present arm speed, there’s a good chance he could be adding a few more ticks to that heater in time. He can sell his 85-87 mph changeup well out of his three-quarters arm slot, and he shows a high-70s slurve that he uses as his preferred offspeed weapon for now. The right-hander can pitch in the zone well from a fairly low-effort delivery at his current stage of development, though that deserves following if he does end up adding velocity. Creating better separation across his fastball and changeup will help too, but in general, he has the tools to be a potential Major League starting pitcher down the road.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going over their allotted bonus pool on the international market, the Reds weren’t allowed to spend more than $300,000 on any prospect during the 2017-18 signing period. They did hand out four six-figure bonuses, but they might have found a deep sleeper bargain in Vellojin, who joined the organization out of Colombia for just $10,000 in January 2018. A second season in the Dominican Summer League helped him get his bat going in 2019, and while he’s had trouble producing consistently at the plate since, he did reach Double-A in 2022 and opened some eyes with a strong performance in the Colombian Winter League this past offseason. While it’s taken him a while to get going, Vellojin has the chance to be a solid all-around big league backstop. Already working in his favor offensively -- even if the surface stats don’t always reflect it -- is his outstanding approach at the plate. He’s walked in 16.9 percent of his plate appearances, including 15.5 percent in 2022 across three levels. The left-handed hitter is capable of making hard contact, and there’s raw power he’s starting to tap into, with it really showing up over the winter as he slugged .597 while walking as much as he struck out. He also caught for Colombia in the Caribbean Series. Vellojin continues to improve as an overall receiver and blocker, but he has always impressed with his plus arm strength and his willingness to take charge behind the dish. It might be a backup profile, but a big year at the upper levels could change that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vellojin joined the Reds out of Colombia for just $10,000 in Jan. 2018 and proceeded to struggle in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the summer after signing. A return engagement to the DSL led to better results and a postseason All-Star nod. Post-shutdown, Vellojin skipped over rookie ball and went to Low-A Daytona and was named an organizational All-Star by MiLB.com The Reds think they might have gotten a potential big leaguer behind the plate at a bargain price. Defensively, his plus arm is his carrying tool, and he threw out nearly 43 percent of potential basestealers in 2021. While there’s work to be done on his blocking and receiving, he does have good hands, already calls a good game and has that “it” factor teams like to see from their backstops. A left-handed hitter, Vellojin is just starting to come into his strength. He makes good, hard contact and has a very good approach that saw him walk nearly as often as he struck out a year ago. There could be more power to come as he continues to get more physical. He has the floor of a Major League backup, but the Reds aren’t ruling out continued growth into a solid all-around regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soler was the D-backs’ third-largest signing in the 2023 international class when he joined the organization for $425,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He’s been solid at every stop since then, though he’s still searching for a true full season of Minor League success. Soler was slow out of the gate as a 19-year-old with Single-A Visalia but caught fire after May, hitting .278/.386/.494 with eight homers and a 143 wRC+ over his final 48 games with the Rawhide. The right-handed slugger has a relaxed look in the box to the point where he’ll actually lay the bat down briefly on his back shoulder as he awaits the pitch from the mound. He’ll coil and get a leg kick going before unleashing his cuts. His strikeout rate has climbed about five percentage points per year, to the point where he fanned 22.3 percent of the time in the California League. Some of that is Soler’s willingness to jump on pitches outside the zone, leading to ground-ball contact, though he got a tad less aggressive during his hot streak. He has a compact build in his 5-foot-11 frame, and there’s already present strength there that could lead to 18-20 homers per year in the future if he can improve his angles off the bat. Soler isn’t any kind of a stolen-base threat with below-average speed, but he’ll show in flashes that he has the right hands for third base, the only position he’s played in pro ball so far. His above-average arm strength certainly fits the position, but he’ll rush his whippy throws sometimes, leading to inaccuracy. Soler is entering his 20s in 2026, just as he’s putting together the sum of his pieces as a classic power-first corner infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $425,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2023, Soler was the D-backs’ third-largest addition in that class in terms of bonus and has continued to carve out an impressive standing for himself in the organization. He was a solid performer in the Dominican Summer League in his first season with a 97 wRC+ in his first 37 games and took off more stateside last year. The third baseman hit .303/.351/.472 with six homers in 53 games in the Arizona Complex League in his age-18 campaign and even got in a pair of games with Single-A Visalia to round out 2024. Soler looks relaxed from the right side of the box, lifts his lead leg a little and then relies on his hands to fire. It works because he’s able to manipulate the barrel well and put bat on ball consistently. His 17.2 percent strikeout rate in the ACL was solid for a player with his age and experience, though he did start to expand the zone much more than he had in the DSL. He’s already well built in his 5-foot-11 frame, and the raw power is above average. But he gets on top of the ball too often (50.3 percent ground-ball rate in the ACL), and he’ll continue to need to add lift to get to that pop. Soler has been third base-only at this early stage in his career, and D-backs officials feel like he’s a good fit for the position with good reads and reactions off the bat and plenty of arm strength for throws across the diamond, despite below-average speed overall. He’ll head to full-season ball for a longer look in 2025 and to potentially solidify his standing in Arizona’s infield corps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox were split on whether Cason had a brighter future as a right-hander or a shortstop when they drafted the Georgia prepster in 2024's eighth round and gave him the opportunity to do both after signing him for second-round money ($1.25 million). Most other teams preferred him on the mound, but he wanted the opportunity to play both ways. After a two-inning outing and a game at DH last May, he developed elbow soreness that eventually led to Tommy John surgery in August. He won't pitch in 2026 but possibly could get some at-bats. As an amateur, Cason showcased a 93-95 mph fastball, topped out at 97, and displayed the aptitude to carry it up in zone or sink it down at the knees. He showed better feel for killing spin on a split-grip changeup in the low 80s than producing it on a tight slider with similar velocity. His athleticism helps him get down the mound well, though he'll rush his delivery at times and lose some control.ss Cason also offers an intriguing combination of solid raw power and speed, though he comes with questions about his hitting ability. He struggled against breaking balls and changeups on the high school showcase circuit, and his right-handed stroke gets too long when he gets aggressive. He has fluid actions and an obviously strong arm at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest in a recent line of Georgia prep two-way talents that includes big leaguers Taj Bradley, Michael Harris and Josh Lowe, Cason starred in four sports at the Greater Atlanta Christian School. The Red Sox were truly divided on whether he was better as a right-hander or a shortstop and still aren't sure after signing one of the youngest prospects in the 2024 Draft for late second-round money ($1.25 million) as an eighth-rounder. Most clubs preferred him as a pitcher, but he wants to play both ways and Boston will make a sincere effort to let him try. Gatorade's Georgia high school player of the year, Cason features a 93-95 mph fastball that reaches 98 and shows the feel to ride it up in the zone or sink it down at the knees. He also has advanced aptitude for killing spin on his low-80s split-grip changeup, which tumbles at the plate and could become a plus offering. His tight slider has similar velocity and solid upside. While he's obviously athletic and gets down the mound well, he can rush his delivery at times and lose some control. Cason asked to showcase himself solely as a shortstop at the MLB Draft Combine, where he impressed scouts with his solid raw power and speed. There are some questions about his hitting ability after he struggled against non-fastballs on the showcase circuit, and his right-handed swing can get too long when he gets overly aggressive. There obviously aren't any questions about his arm strength at shortstop, where he displays fluid actions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The early returns on the Rangers' 2020-21 international class are promising, with outfielder Yeison Morrobel, third baseman Gleider Figuereo and Cueva all making this Top 30 list and right-hander Leandro Lopez not far behind. Based on his potential at the plate, Cueva landed a $1,025,000 bonus. The Venezuelan finished third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting race (.330) in his U.S. debut last summer. Cueva has a quick left-handed stroke and a knack for putting the bat on the ball and using the entire field. He'll need to improve his swing decisions against more advanced pitching, however, because he chases a lot of pitches and that leads to strikeouts and suboptimal contact. His bat speed already translates into high exit velocities, and if he can add strength and learn to drive ball in the air, he could grow into 15-20 homer pop. Cueva has average speed and isn't particularly adventuresome on the bases. He has worked to enhance his quickness and his chances of remaining at shortstop, where he has good actions, quick hands and solid arm strength. His range may be closer to average, which may make him more of a second baseman in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cueva received the second-highest bonus in Texas' 2020-21 international class, signing for $1,025,000. He's one of three Venezuelan shortstops on our Rangers Top 30, joining Luisangel Acuna and Maximo Acosta. He batted .282/.375/.381 in his pro debut as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Cueva will require time to develop but could become a solid hitter with average pop. He has a nice left-handed swing and shows the makings of bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline. To reach his power potential, he'll need to add strength and learn to drive balls in the air more consistently. While Cueva can flash plus speed, he'll probably settle in as a solid runner once he matures physically. He has worked hard to improve his quickness and his chances of staying at shortstop, where his actions, hands and arm are all up to standard. If he and Acosta team up this summer in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, Cueva likely will get much of his playing time at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez was the fifth-ranked prospect in the 2021 international class as a big-bodied shortstop with power potential and signed with the Cubs for $3 million. The Venezuela native has yet to tap into his natural power in pro ball with just 24 homers in 430 games, but he's made slow, steady progress and posted a 99 wRC+ in his first full season in High-A at 21 last year. The Marlins acquired him as part of the return for Edward Cabrera and will be tasked with unlocking his potential after the one-time bonus baby was not protected from or selected in the Rule 5 Draft over the winter. The 6-foot-2 righty swinger has a wiry frame and plenty of room to add strength. Hernandez has excellent bat speed which should enable upward of 20-homer thump. However, he has consistently hit the ball on the ground, which could prevent him from reaching that power potential. He took a more aggressive approach in 2025, especially on pitches in the zone, which helped him strike out less but also cut into his walks. But a longer swing and mediocre footwork continue to hold his hit tool back. Hernandez has long been an above-average runner and performed better on the bases every season, culminating in a career-high 52 swipes on 61 attempts in 2025. He uses that quickness on defense well, although his footwork again can be an issue at short. That might force him to second base, where he would be an above-average defender. He should have plenty of arm for any infield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez generated as much hype as anyone in the 2020-21 international class, drawing physical comparisons to Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado, while some scouts rated him the best prospect available. Signed by the Cubs for $3 million out of the Dominican Republic, he fared well in his 2021 pro debut but struggled in his first two seasons in the United States. He fared better at two Class A stops in the past two years before Chicago shipped him and two other prospects to the Marlins in exchange for Edward Cabrera in January. Hernandez has some of the best bat speed in the system and could translate it into 20 homers per season as he continues to add strength and learns to lift balls in the air more consistently. A much more disciplined approach fueled his growth at the plate in 2024, as he chased less and did a better job of using the entire field. The next step will be improving his timing and shortening his right-handed stroke so he can catch up to quality fastballs. A solid runner with good instincts, Hernandez has stolen 98 bases in 117 attempts (83.8 percent) in 315 pro games. He has the quickness and arm strength to play at least an average shortstop, though like most youngsters he needs to improve his defensive consistency. He's more than capable at second base as well and has the tools for third base if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez elicited physical comparisons to Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, with some scouts rating him as the best prospect in the 2020-21 international class. When the Cubs signed him for $3 million, they believed he had a higher ceiling than any international amateur they had landed in years. But he has struggled since a successful pro debut, slashing .223/.302/.301 with a 27 percent strikeout rate in Single-A last year. With his lightning-fast right-handed swing, it's still easy to dream about Hernandez providing 25 or more homers per season. But he hasn't been able to make much of his plus power yet because he still lacks strength and makes too much ground-ball contact. He needs a more selective approach that concentrates on making hard contact because his pop should come naturally if he lets it. Hernandez has solid speed and is aggressive on the bases, stealing 27 bases in 32 attempts last year. With his quickness and solid arm strength he should be able to stay at shortstop, though he shifted over to second base once Jefferson Rojas came to Myrtle Beach in June. He's a fine defender at second base, more average at shortstop and should be able to handle third if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some evaluators considered Hernandez the top prospect in the 2020 international crop, and he drew physical comparisons to Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado. The Cubs signed him for $3 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021 and believe he has more upside than any international amateur they've signed in more than a decade. He made his U.S. debut last year, slashing .261/.320/.357 with a 30 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. With electric bat speed from the right side of the plate, Hernandez has 25-30 homer upside. He's not tapping into his power yet because he needs to add strength and drive balls in the air more regularly. He has yet to learn to let his pop come naturally rather than pulling too many pitches and chasing too many out of the strike zone. Hernandez possesses solid speed and plus arm strength, and he should retain enough quickness and range to remain at short. He has seen more time at second base this year in deference to Jefferson Rojas and looked good there. If Hernandez slows down more than expected as he matures physically, he could wind up at third base or the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez drew repeated physical comparisons to a young Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, and some scouts considered him the best prospect in the 2020 international class. The Cubs signed him for $3 million in January 2021 and believe he has more upside than any international player they've landed in at least a decade -- including Willson Contreras, Eloy Jimenez and Gleyber Torres. He debuted in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League at age 17, batting .285/.398/.424 with five homers and 21 steals in 47 games. An extremely advanced hitter for his age, Hernandez has a smooth right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed. He has good feel for the barrel and exhibits patience at the plate as well as a willingness to use the entire field. While he should have plus raw power once his projectable 6-foot-2 frame fills out, he'll have to make some swing adjustments to make the most of it after sporting a 2.0 ground/fly ratio in his debut. Hernandez is a plus runner who can make things happen on the bases, though he could lose a half-step as he gets stronger. Even so, he should still be athletic and quick enough to remain at shortstop, where he displays the requisite actions and instincts as well as a plus arm. He'd also profile well at third base and on the outfield corners if he slows down more than expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some scouts considered Hernandez the best prospect in the 2020 international class. The Cubs say he offers more upside than any international player they've signed in recent memory -- including Eloy Jimenez and Gleyber Torres in 2013. The recipient of a $3 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic, he draws constant physical comparisons to a young Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado. Hernandez has the tools to hit for average and power and could become a .300 hitter with 30 homers on an annual basis if everything comes together. He has a fluid right-handed swing with quality bat speed and also exhibits feel for the barrel and a mature approach. He has a track record of producing in game action and his projectable frame should allow him to add plenty of strength. Hernandez presently has plus speed, though he might lose a half-step as he matures physically. Even if that happens, he has the athleticism and actions to remain at shortstop for the long term. His quickness and arm strength would allow him to play all over the field if needed and he'd have no problem fitting the offensive profile wherever he winds up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Having a full set of tools is great, but only if you can get them out of the box consistently. Brannigan has flashed all of them since his two-way days at Notre Dame. He continued as an infielder only after the Pirates took him in the third round of the 2022 Draft, though he’s struggled to stay on the field. He missed time with a quad injury in 2023, a left shoulder issue in 2024 and last year it was his right shoulder, which required labrum surgery that limited him to 59 games. Despite that and inconsistent performance, the Pirates decided his tools were important enough to protect on the 40-man roster this past offseason. When he’s healthy, Brannigan does offer an exciting combination of athleticism, defense, speed and raw power at the plate. He really racked up the strikeouts early in his career and has a 27.4 percent strikeout rate heading into 2026 to show for it. He’s worked to change some things with his setup and bat path to get to more contact but just hasn’t had the at-bats to put it consistent use. Brannigan’s athleticism really shows up defensively. Originally signed as a third baseman where he’s an easily plus defender, he’s shown as a pro that he can also play an outstanding shortstop. It remains to be seen whether the shoulder that once fired upper-90s fastballs as a college reliever comes all the way back post-surgery, but there should be enough to still be an asset on the left side of the infield. He’ll be 25 for the 2026 season, putting more impetus on staying healthy to see if he can translate those tools to production over a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at Notre Dame as a third baseman and reliever, the Pirates selected Brannigan in the third round of the 2022 Draft as an infielder only. He showed off his power-speed combination in his first full season, finishing a home run shy of a 20/20 campaign despite missing a month with a quad injury. He spent the 2024 season with High-A Greensboro trying to make adjustments to his approach and setup at the plate with some success that didn’t necessarily translate to his stat line, and he again landed on the injured list, this time with a left shoulder issue. After he struck out in 30 percent of his plate appearances in 2023, Brannigan focused on cutting down the swing-and-miss, mostly by lowering his attack angle. He was way too steep in the zone and flattened his bat path, resulting in a 26.1 percent K rate in 2024. He did trade some power while working on contact, but given his strength and bat speed, there’s hope he can put the two together and still get to plenty of that pop without the strikeouts piling up. A tremendous athlete who can steal a base, Brannigan could be an easily plus defender at third base, the spot he played in college. Because of his range, instincts and an arm that touched the upper 90s as a reliever, the Pirates wanted to see what it looked like at shortstop, and it turns out it looks pretty good. If he can stay committed to his swing changes, he could take off this year, while profiling as a toolsy everyday shortstop who might be 24 for the 2025 season, but is young in terms of professional reps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brannigan played third base and served as a relief pitcher for three years at Notre Dame, even playing both ways during his stint in the Cape Cod League in 2021. While some scouts thought his arm strength would serve him well on a professional mound, the Pirates drafted him in the third round of the 2022 Draft to let him hit and play the infield. He played his way from Single-A Bradenton to High-A Greensboro and finished a home run shy of a 20-20 season, even though he missed a month early with a quad injury, before finishing things off with a stint in the Arizona Fall League. The right-handed hitting infielder has some serious tools; it’s just a matter of him using them consistently. Yes, he fared well in Greensboro’s friendly park, but the underlying data on exit velocity and contact quality point to it not mattering what ballpark he’s in: Brannigan just hits the ball hard with excellent raw power when he makes contact. And that’s the issue. While he’ll draw walks, Brannigan struck out nearly 30 percent of the time in 2023 and limiting that will be the key to his offensive success. He also has the chance to be a plus third baseman, but the Pirates’ decision to give him some time at other positions, initially at second and shortstop, but then exclusively at short in the AFL, might have changed his trajectory some. His arm that fired upper-90s fastballs from the mound works from anywhere, his hands are solid and he has plus instincts. If he can just increase his range a bit moving forward, he could end up profiling as a regular at the position, where there won’t be quite as much pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of two national championship teams at Parkview HS (Lilburn, Ga.) before attending Troy, Cerny was one of the better college athletes in the 2021 Draft. He dropped to the Phillies in the 10th round because of signability concerns, but he turned pro for $146,100, then got traded to the Astros for Garrett Stubbs in November. He slashed .197/.293/.401 in Single-A during the first two months of 2022, then surged to .297/.404/.513 in the next two before getting shut down with a bruised right thumb. Cerny has some of the best all-around tools in the system but he also comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He has a busy right-handed swing geared to hit balls as far as he can, though his bat speed and strength would provide plenty of power even if he didn't swing for the fences. To reach his 25-25 upside, he'll need to learn to stop chasing balls out of the strike zone and figure out how to handle quality offspeed pitches, and he was making some mild progress last year when he got hurt. Cerny's aggressiveness carries over to the bases and the outfield as well. He has plus-plus speed and looks to steal and take extra bases. His quickness and instincts give him the range to remain in center field and his solid arm strength helps make him an asset at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cerny played on two national championship teams at Parkview High (Lilburn, Ga.) before heading to Troy. One of the better college athletes in the 2020 Draft, he fell to the Phillies in the 10th round because of signability concerns and turned pro for $146,000. A thumb injury restricted him to 13 games in his pro debut, after which Philadelphia dealt him to the Astros for Garrett Stubbs in November. Cerny has 25-25 upside with bat speed and strength that creates legitimate pop from gap to gap. But he also comes with swing-and-miss concerns because he has a lot going on in his right-handed swing and a grip-it-and-rip-it approach. He can crush fastballs but chases too many pitches out of the strike zone and struggles with breaking balls and changeups. With plus-plus speed and an aggressive mindset, Cerny is a basestealing threat. His quick-twitch athleticism and instincts allow him to cover ground and play a quality center field. He also offers solid arm strength and some added intrigue with some catching experience in high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies were investing in McGowan’s stuff and upside when they went over slot to sign the junior college product in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft. Injuries have prevented him from providing any true sense of what the return on that investment might be, with Tommy John surgery ending his first full season after two starts. He returned to toss a combined 42 2/3 innings between the regular season and the Arizona Fall League in 2023 and was limited again to 40 1/3 IP in 2024, this time because of a back issue. He did make it back to the AFL again to make up for some lost mound time but was shelved with a labrum injury that will likely cost him all of 2025. When he’s been healthy, McGowan still teases with a legitimate arsenal. It’s almost all sinker-slider, with a two-seamer that averaged north of 95 mph and topped out at 98 mph in '24 and it’s a worm-killer, leading to a career 1.70 GO/AO heading into 2025. His slider has gotten harder, now more consistently in the upper-80s with depth, and it can miss bats, and his firm upper-80s changeup is a third pitch he doesn’t use as frequently. McGowan needs more mound time to hone his craft and refine his command, and his strike-throwing regressed in '24, though it’s hard to know how much his injury impacted his ability to repeat his delivery and land his stuff in the zone. He has the mentality to fit in the bullpen should the Phillies move in that direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Eastern Oklahoma State Junior College, McGowan was a Top 200 Draft prospect in 2021 and went in the seventh round to the Phillies, who more than doubled the slot value to sign him for $577,000. They haven’t truly gotten a sense of what kind of pitcher they have because he needed Tommy John surgery after two starts of his first full season. He did return to throw 25 2/3 innings in 2023 before adding 17 more in the Arizona Fall League, but had his 2024 interrupted by nearly two months on the injured list with a back issue. Strong and physical, McGowan has legitimate power stuff when he’s fully healthy, led by a very effective sinker-slider combination. His two-seam fastball tops out in the upper 90s and sits around 94-95 mph with excellent sinking action that generates high ground-ball ratios. He can miss bats with his low-80s slider with good depth, and he has shown decent feel for a changeup, but he throws it too hard. Because of the three-pitch mix, the Phillies thought McGowan had a chance to start, and he could continue to get the opportunity to do so now that surgery is firmly in his rearview mirror. He could end up in the bullpen -- given the injury, the lack of consistent command and the fact that he’s strong but not that big -- where his competitiveness and sinker-slider duo could play up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McGowan spent two years pitching at Eastern Oklahoma State Junior College, opting to return to the Mountaineers' rotation rather than transfer to Kansas State for the 2021 season. He pitched well as part of a deep staff and caught the eye of the Phillies, who went over slot in the seventh round to sign him away from heading to Texas Tech for $577,000. There’s been very little return on investment so far as he barely pitched during his summer debut and then needed Tommy John surgery after just two starts in his full-season debut in 2022. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has the build and the three-pitch mix that should point to a future as a starter. At full strength, he can touch the upper-90s with his fastball, though he tends to comfortably sit around 93-94 mph and he’ll show both a two- and four-seamer. There’s good depth on his low-80s slider and he has shown solid feel for a fading mid-80s changeup, though he hasn’t thrown it as much and it can get too firm at times. McGowan gets high marks for his athleticism and competitiveness on the mound and while he can be around the zone, there was a lot of effort and recoil in his delivery as he entered pro ball, which impacted his command. Adding strength to his frame will help him iron out some of those delivery issues, with hope he can reach his big league starter ceiling once he fully returns from the elbow injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez was the Royals’ top international signee in 2021 and signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic and the club sent him to Single-A Columbia right away in '22 as an 18-year-old. It has been a slow progression from there, spending three seasons in Columbia before making it to High-A Quad Cities in ‘25. He slashed .260/.333/.351 across 116 games, which also included six games on a rehab stint in the ACL and five games at the end of the year in Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Vazquez was the Royals’ best hitter in the Arizona Fall League, though, with a .928 OPS in 22 games and nearly as many walks (19) as strikeouts (20). Vazquez has always been a solid defender, but his bat has been slower to develop. It’s coming along, though, with harder contact recently. He’s gotten a lot stronger in the past year or so and really grown into his 6-foot-2 frame with broad shoulders. Vazquez is starting to have an understanding of the zone and hasn't been so fooled by breaking balls, allowing him to make more contact. He’s a potential plus defender with good hands and instincts with a strong arm to boot. Some think that as he’s filled out, he might be better suited for second base or even third, but you’d like to see a little more pop if you move him to the corner. An above-average runner with good instincts on the bases, Vazquez has the profile of a utility infielder if he can continue the positive trend with his bat. He was in big league camp this spring, which allowed him to learn a lot about the Major League routine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals’ top signee in the 2021 international signing period, Vazquez signed out of the Dominican for $1.5 million. The team was aggressive with him early, sending him right to Single-A Columbia in 2022 as an 18-year-old. He has spent three seasons there making incremental progress with his game. In 2024, Vazquez slashed .253/.353/.289 with a 13.2% walk rate, 22.2% strikeout rate and a 99 wRC+. He missed about six weeks with a hamate injury and finished his season in the Arizona Fall League, hitting .298 with a .744 OPS in 14 games. Vazquez has always been a defense-first shortstop with good hands, instincts and agile movements that make the Royals believe he can stick at the position. Offensively, Vazquez has made slow but steady progress just with his hit tool and really increased his line-drive rate in ‘24. He’s in a better neutral position with his swing, which helps, and he’s also stronger and more physical after four seasons in pro ball. Vazquez flashed raw power when he was an amateur and still has good bat speed now, but the power has yet to show up in games. It might be more extra-base hit potential than anything. Vazquez has a strong arm and is an above-average runner. After three years, Vazquez headed up to High-A Quad Cities for 2025. His defense plays, and the Royals will stick with him as a shortstop, but he’ll have to show just a bit more offensively to reach his ceiling, which is likely as a utility player who can get on base unless he really finds something with his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez was in high demand during the 2020-21 international signing period because of his tremendous upside, and he signed with the Royals for $1.5 million. He came to the United States a year later, which was ambitious for his age-18 season, and he was overmatched at Single-A Columbia in ‘22. He returned in ‘23 and made modest gains, with a .618 OPS, 15 doubles, 32 stolen bases, a 13.2 percent walk rate and 22.7 percent strikeout rate in 113 games. Vazquez is a glove-first prospect right now, although some evaluators still believe the power is coming because of the capability to add strength to his athletic frame. He shows good actions on the left side of the infield, makes agile movements and exhibits a plus arm with accurate throws. More repetitions will lead to fewer mental mistakes and make him a reliable defender over a flashy one. Vazquez had a line-drive profile when he first signed, and he’s slowly starting to get there with his smooth and repeatable right-handed swing. He needs to show improvement in his swing decisions to make the most of his physical gains. Still young with upside, Vazquez has had a slow start to his pro career, and the Royals knew they were being aggressive when they pushed him to Columbia. His defense will play, so it’ll be his hit tool that will determine his role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez received comps to Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado during the 2020-21 international signing period and was coveted by teams because of his enormous upside. The Royals were able to sign him for $1.5 million and brought him over to the States a year later, where he went straight to Single-A Columbia in 2022. The Royals acknowledged that was ambitious for his age-18 season, and it wasn’t without struggles: Vazquez slashed just .195/.262/.229 with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate, 10 doubles and no homers in 77 games. He’s been sent back to the Carolina League for 2023 and has shown modest gains with the bat but still hasn’t been league-average. Vazquez looks the part with his athletic frame that has only added strength since he became a Royal. His defense wows with agile movement, exceptional reads, quick hands and good footwork. He profiles as a starting shortstop, but it remains to be seen what the Royals have with Vazquez offensively. He has a smooth, repeatable swing that should produce line drives as he matures. He’s shown nice rhythm and timing to his at-bats, but little has come into focus with the results. Vazquez looked overpowered and overmatched in Columbia last year as an 18-year-old facing a lot of older pitchers. The Royals were impressed with how Vazquez held himself despite the struggles last season. His tools give scouts something to dream on. Vazquez is still all upside in his projection and will need to show some offensive breakthroughs to be able to understand what kind of player he could be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2020-21 international signing period, Vazquez received comps to what Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado looked and played like when they were teenagers. The Royals signed Vazquez, who was ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list, in the early days of the signing period for $1.5 million. After spending his first season in the Dominican Summer League, Vazquez skipped right over the Arizona Complex League and moved to Single-A Columbia for his age-18 season. Results with the Fireflies have been hard to come by, but the Royals maintain the teenager is just getting going with plenty of room to grow. Vazquez has already put on strength since he was signed, and that led to improved impact at the Dominican Academy last summer; despite the lack of results, reports mentioned how much louder the ball sounded off his bat. His smooth, repeatable swing makes a healthy amount of contact, and he should add more extra-base hits as he matures. He has average speed with above-average baserunning skills, and he’s an excellent defender with exceptional reads, a quick release and good footwork. He should remain at shortstop, and the Royals have yet to play him anywhere else in his first two seasons. Scouts see the long, lean and athletic prospect hitting at the top or even near the middle of the order as he develops, and he has a solid ceiling as a well-rounded player. Even with Vazquez’s 2022 struggles, Kansas City officials continue to point out that he moved to the Carolina League at the same age as an American high-school senior. A full-season breakout could be on tap for 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list in 2020-21, Vazquez is built like a young Fernando Tatis Jr. and compares favorably to a teenage Manny Machado. The Royals were able to sign the Dominican amateur in the early days of the international signing period, which was pushed back to January due to the pandemic. Long, lean and with an athletic frame, the 16-year-old Vazquez has a lot of room to grow. A smooth and repeatable swing makes consistent contact, and he projects to have average power. Some believe he will be able to hit around 15-20 home runs while hitting at or near the top of the batting over, and he has solid speed with projected above-average baserunning skills. Vazquez should remain at shortstop to start his pro career, with quick hands and great instincts. He gets exceptional reads on ground balls, features a quick release, has the ability to throw from all angles and shows good footwork at the position. Vazquez has reported to the Royals’ Dominican academy, and game action will determine more of a plan for his development. The projection is there but there’s still a long way to go for the young player. His hit tool and defensive ability give him a carrying asset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally a walk-on at Brigham Young, Pintar played his way into a Diamondbacks fifth-round pick in 2022 despite losing much of that year to a right shoulder injury that required two surgeries. A broken ankle truncated his first full pro season, but he returned to earn High-A Northwest League all-star honors (.304/.403/.516) before scuffling in Double-A in 2024. Sent with slugging prospect Deyvison De Los Santos to the Marlins for A.J. Puk at the Trade Deadline in July, he won Arizona Fall League defensive player of the year accolades during the offseason. When he's on, the righty-hitting Pintar controls the strike zone, gets on base and shows the ability to drive homers to his pull side and doubles to right field. He got abused by non-fastballs in Double-A, however, and did little damage while making contact against heaters. He has flashed hitting ability and 15-homer power, but he'll need to make adjustments or else be relegated to a platoon role. Finally healthy in 2024, Pintar turned his plus speed loose on the bases and swiped 33 bases in 35 attempts (94 percent) between the Minors and AFL. A middle infielder in college, he made a smooth transition to full-time center fielder last year. His reads and routes continue to improve and he's at least a solid defender in center, though his shoulder issues left him with below-average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pintar went from a BYU walk-on in 2020 to one of the program’s best performers a year later after he slashed .333/.433/.556 with nine homers and more walks (32) than strikeouts (29) in 48 games. He hit just .209 with a .613 OPS in 17 games to begin his junior year and then underwent shoulder surgery that shut him down the rest of the way. Relying mostly on what they saw in 2021, the D-backs took Pintar in the fifth round and signed him for below slot at $316,950. The former Cougar was back to hitting and taking ground balls as part of his rehab process heading into the spring, adding to Arizona’s optimism. How much the shoulder affected his 2022 performance remains in question, but the raw tools are certainly enticing enough. He’s a plus runner running down the line and has some promising raw power from the right side. Pintar drew praise from BYU coaches for his improving approach in college, starting with laying off breaking stuff below the zone, and if that upward trajectory continues, it should help ease his transition to the Minors. A shortstop in 2021, Pintar moved to second base-only last year out of concern for his below-average throwing arm. The D-backs say they expect to continue to move him around the infield, hoping to take advantage of his athleticism and range, but second still seems most likely in the long run. If the shoulder was nothing but bad timing and Pintar can get his performance to match his tools again, he could be a mid-round steal for Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The cousin of former Cubs All-Star Starlin Castro, Cruz ranked fifth on MLB Pipeline's 2024 International Top 50 and signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. He injured his left shoulder on a headfirst slide two weeks into his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, which led to offseason surgery that sidelined him for the first month of the 2025 Rookie-level Arizona Complex League season. He fared poorly in his U.S. debut, batting .165/.247/.316 with a 47 percent strikeout rate. Cruz still possesses some of the best all-around tools in the system and Chicago hopes that they'll begin to translate better during a fully healthy 2026 season. He has more bat speed and strength than most teenage shortstops, and he shows the ability to elevate balls to his pull side while also flashing opposite-field power. To get to more of his solid-to-plus raw power, he'll need to learn to recognize pitches better, tone down his long right-handed swing and adopt a more measured approach. Cruz features plus speed and some basestealing savvy, though he wasn't as daring last year, perhaps in an attempt to protect his shoulder. He has fluid actions, plenty of range, quick hands, solid arm strength and a finely tuned internal clock at shortstop, and some club officials believe he's their best defensive prospect at the position. His twitchy athleticism would allow him to play almost anywhere on the diamond, and he also saw action at second base last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Starlin Castro signed with the Cubs out of the Dominican Republic for $50,000 in 2006 and made four All-Star Games in a 12-year big league career. Cruz, his cousin, hopes to follow the same path after turning pro in 2024 for $4 million, the second-largest bonus for an international amateur in franchise history (Jorge Soler landed a $6 million bonus as part of a $30 million contract in 2012). Cruz injured his left shoulder on a headfirst slide early in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and wasn't fully healthy until Dominican instructional league in the fall. With strong hands and forearms, and a build that carries 25 pounds more than his listed 155, Cruz has more bat speed and power than most 18-year-old shortstops. He already shows the aptitude to drive balls in the air to his pull side, can hit the ball out of the park to the opposite field and could grow into 25-homer power in his prime. His right-handed swing looked long and his approach looked aggressive while he was slashing just .215/.326/.329 with a 27.2 percent strikeout rate in the DSL, so he has adjustments to make. Cruz's twitchy athleticism makes him an asset on the bases and at shortstop. He used his plus speed to steal 11 bases in 12 attempts during his 25 games in the DSL. He has smooth actions, very good body control, solid arm strength and a good internal clock at short, and there's no reason he won't be able to remain there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz is a cousin of Starlin Castro, who signed with the Cubs for $50,000 in 2006 and made four All-Star teams. His price tag was considerably higher, as his $4 million bonus in January was the second-largest in franchise history for an international player behind only the $6 million Jorge Soler received as part of a $30 million contract in 2012. The No. 4 prospect in MLB Pipeline's 2024 international rankings, he's more advanced than Chicago's other recent big-money Dominican shortstops, Cristian Hernandez and Derniche Valdez. With strong hands and forearms, Cruz creates plenty of bat speed and more power than most shortstops. Closer to 180 pounds than his listed 155, he has room to add more muscle and could produce 25 or more homers annually once he's fully developed. Though he has an aggressive approach and his right-handed swing can get a bit long at times, he also exhibits good feel for the barrel. Cruz's plus speed and athleticism will allow him to make an impact on the bases and in the field as well. His smooth actions, quick first step and solid arm strength should enable him to remain at shortstop for the long term. If he slowed down a bit and his range diminished to the point at which he had to move, he'd profile well at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays handed MLB Pipeline's No. 23-ranked prospect in the 2021 international class a $2.35 million bonus due to their faith in Beltre's maturity as a player and a person. He was one of the most experienced players in the class, which showed in his approach soon after his pro debut with more walks (42) than strikeouts (33) over 53 games in the DSL. The past two seasons have seen Beltre continue to develop a strong base with his already-impressive fundamentals, but the focus has shifted to getting more out of him offensively. Beltre hit just .231 with Single-A Dunedin in 2023 with his six home runs and .675 OPS representing the ceiling of his power potential at the time. The Blue Jays have challenged Beltre to increase his exit velocities and start impacting the baseball more consistently. The early reviews are positive, as Beltre has put on nearly 15 pounds, but we’ll need to see if that can translate to power in actual games. Thirty home runs isn’t the goal here, but if the Blue Jays can get Beltre to drive the ball, some of those will start sneaking through the infield and some singles could turn into doubles. He has impressive zone control, so if there’s any power to come, he should have no trouble getting to it. Beltre is not a flashy defender, but he could stick at shortstop. This projection is all about his power, frankly, because Beltre’s entire profile is being a solid, across-the-board prospect otherwise. If the ball starts leaving his bat at 100 mph more often, his ceiling could change, and there’s still time for that to happen as he enters his age-20 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays handed MLB Pipeline's No. 23-ranked prospect in the 2021 international class a $2.35 million bonus due to their faith in Beltre's maturity as a player and a person. He was one of the most experienced players in the class, having played internationally with the Dominican Republic and travel ball teams in Florida. That summer, Beltre got in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .225 with a .391 OBP. In 2022, Beltre played 54 games, mostly in the Florida Complex League, and hit .250 with a .357 OBP. He’d begun driving the ball more, which will be key to his long-term value as a smaller hitter at 5-foot-9, but his exceptional fundamentals give the Blue Jays optimism on multiple fronts. He’s praised widely for his worth as a teammate and many within the organization believe these traits will enable him to raise his game with each promotion he earns. Beltre should be able to stay at shortstop, where his athleticism and instincts mesh well. There’s still plenty of development ahead for him, but he’s earned plenty of trust and profiles as a player who should self-teach well, absorb good coaching and make the proper in-game or in-season adjustments. It hasn't been a stellar season for him at Single-A Dunedin in 2023, but he is taking his walks and putting the ball in play at good rates as he establishes himself in full-season ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 24 prospect in the 2021 International class by MLB Pipeline, Beltre signed with the Blue Jays for $2.35 million. He was arguably the most experienced prospect in that class after playing internationally with teams from the Dominican Republic and playing extensively with travel ball teams in Florida. Debuting in the Dominican Summer League in ’21 at 17, Beltre hit .225 with two home runs and a .737 OPS, but impressed by taking more walks than strikeouts and finished strong. Many within the organization view Beltre as a potential “culture driver” given his natural leadership abilities and charismatic personality at such a young age. He pairs this with advanced fundamentals across the board. There is still room for him to mature physically, but Beltre should have enough arm to stick on the left side of the infield. His power is worth monitoring as he develops to see whether that develops into line drives or home runs, but he’s already shown the potential for an advanced plate approach and strong contact rate. While his athleticism is slightly above average now, that’s also worth monitoring as his 5-foot-9 frame fills out. At this point, Beltre simply needs reps. The Blue Jays are looking forward to seeing a full season from him, given his ability to analyze and adjust from game to game. He’s still far off with years of development ahead of him, but his sound fundamentals give the Blue Jays player development staff an exciting package with which to work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 24 prospect in the ’21 international class by MLB Pipeline, Beltre signed with the Blue Jays for a bonus of $2.35 million. Beltre was arguably the most experienced 16-year-old in the class, having played internationally with teams from the Dominican Republic and moving on to travel ball teams in Florida. Many who have seen Beltre play immediately point to the charismatic teenager’s personality, work ethic, and dedication to his own growth, which they feel will help develop Beltre into an excellent leader as he matures. At the plate, Beltre is a natural hitter with a quick, efficient swing. It's a hit-over-power profile for now, but that could change as he matures physically. His throwing arm is just ahead of his fielding tool right now, but the Blue Jays believe he’ll stay up the middle long-term. Beltre has plenty of development ahead, but it’s easy to see the appeal of his tools and his intangibles fit what the Blue Jays love. In a system that’s not lacking for talent up the middle, Beltre represents the next wave with his bat as his likeliest carrying tool.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Hawaii native, Lomavita broke out as a sophomore at Cal in 2023, performed well with wood bats in the Cape Cod League that summer and kept on trucking with a career-best .981 OPS as a junior in Berkeley. The Nationals selected the catcher with the 39th overall pick in 2024 and signed him around slot at $2.325 million. He managed a .275/.339/.364 line with four homers in 99 games with High-A Wilmington in 2025, resulting in an above-average 112 wRC+, and rounded out his first full season with nine more contests with Double-A Harrisburg. The right-handed slugger has a pronounced leg kick that dangles almost over the plate before he gets to two strikes and then he’ll shorten it up a bit when facing a potential strikeout. His defining offensive characteristic was being swing-happy in his first extended taste of the Minors with hacks against 53.4 percent of his pitches seen. His overall contact rates were generally fine, but by swinging so much, he dulled his otherwise decent power with a lot of rolled-over groundballs against undrivable pitches. Lomavita has above-average athleticism for his position, and he has good arm strength for the position. Continuing to learn the nature of framing was a goal coming into pro ball, and he can look stabby as a receiver. (Inconsistent messaging from the previous Nationals front office on the one-knee-down stance likely did him no favors.) There are clear areas to clean up and improve under Washington’s new player-development setup, and despite being in his second full season out of college, Lomavita still has the raw tools to become at least a backup catcher in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Lomavita hailed from St. Louis High School in Honolulu – the same Hawaii program that produced Benny Agbayani, Brandon League and Jordan Yamamoto – and headed across the Pacific to Cal, where he was a three-year performer who especially took off as a sophomore. He also helped his stock with two impressive summers with Cotuit in the Cape Cod League and then produced a .322/.395/.586 line with 15 homers in 55 games as a junior heading into the 2024 Draft. The Nationals selected the backstop with the 39th overall pick in July, signed him for around slot at $2,325,000 and gave him 22 games (including the postseason) with Single-A Fredericksburg in his first taste of the pros. It was an improved bat that really pushed Lomavita into the periphery of the first round. His stance moved from an open one in college to more closed-off in the Carolina League, though his leg kick remained. His swing remains optimized to launch balls on contact, and he showed good bat-to-ball skills in school that helped the power play. That was important because his chase rates ebbed and flowed – better in 2023, back to high levels in 2024 especially against non-fastballs. Cutting that down will go a long way toward Lomavita reaching his offensive ceiling. The former Golden Bear runs well for a catcher, and he shouldn’t be an afterthought on the basepaths unlike many others at his position. His athleticism is an asset behind the plate, at least when it comes to future projection because he’s still learning the nuances of framing after showing up to college with an undefined role. His pure arm strength is plus, and as he’s learning to quicken his release, he threw out seven of 18 (38.9 percent) of attempted basestealers with Fredericksburg.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor required surgery to remove a cancerous kidney at age 5 but recovered to become a multisport star, turning down college basketball offers to play baseball at Polk State (Fla.) CC. After starring for the Eagles and giving up a Florida State commitment to sign for an over-slot $300,000 bonus in the 11th round in 2023, he immediately stood out as one of the best all-around athletes in the system. He got off to good start in High-A last year before batting just .185 with a 29 percent strikeout rate in the final three-plus months, then fared even worse in the Arizona Fall League. As they have with several players, the Red Sox helped Taylor increase his strength and bat speed after he turned pro, and he's capable of producing high exit velocities. He's willing to work deep counts and led the South Atlantic League with 81 walks, but he also has a busy left-handed swing and doesn't make enough in-zone contact, especially against breaking balls and changeups. His solid raw power and ability to elevate balls to his pull side could translate into at least 20 homers per season, but he'll have to make significant adjustments at the plate to get there. One of the top defenders in the system, Taylor's plus speed and fine instincts allow him to chase down balls from gap to gap in center field. He'll flash plus raw arm strength but it plays down some because he lacks a quick release and throwing accuracy. He's an aggressive runner but still is learning the nuances of basestealing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor overcame surgery to remove a cancerous kidney at age 5 to become a multisport star as a Florida high schooler, receiving college basketball offers but turning them down to play baseball at Polk State (Fla.) CC. He helped Bourne win the Cape Cod League championship during a late-summer cameo in 2022 before hitting .353/.467/.620 and topping Florida juco players with 31 steals in 48 games as a sophomore the next spring. He gave up a Florida State commitment to sign for an over-slot $300,000 bonus in 2023, then won Red Sox Minor League defensive player of the year accolades in his first full pro season. Boston has helped Taylor improve his bat speed and strength since he turned pro, and his explosive left-handed swing generates high exit velocities. His pull-heavy mindset and uphill stroke allow him to turn on pitches and drive them in the air, contributing to his solid raw power. He makes good swing decisions but has a lot going on with his stroke and needs to improve his in-zone contact, especially against non-fastballs. If Taylor hits, he has the tools to be a star. He has well-above-average speed and is aggressive on the basepaths, giving him 25-25 upside. He's a no-doubt center fielder with the quickness and instincts to run down most flyballs and his fringy to average arm strength is more than playable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A catcher at the outset of his high school career, Hurd blossomed into a top-two-rounds prospect on the mound but went undrafted in 2021 because he was determined to attend UCLA. He fared well as a Bruins freshman before coming down with a stress fracture in his lower back, then transferred to Louisiana State. Inconsistent as a sophomore before winning the clinchers in the semifinals and finals of the College World Series, he entered 2024 as a projected first-rounder but battled his control and command while getting hammered for a 6.55 ERA. After he went in the third round, he had Tommy John surgery in February 2025 and won't make his pro debut until this year. When he's healthy and dialed in, Hurd can overmatch hitters with a 93-96 mph fastball that climbs to 98 with significant armside run and carry. If they try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with a high-spin mid-80s slider that touches 91 mph with plenty of horizontal and vertical action. He threw just two changeups as a LSU junior, preferring to attack hitters with a 78-82 mph curveball with formidable depth but little consistency. Hurd is athletic and there's nothing glaringly wrong with his delivery, so he should have at least average control and be able to pitch in the front half of a rotation. But he never provided consistent strikes at LSU and working exclusively out of the stretch didn't help, and his lack of command meant he got hit harder than his pure stuff indicated he should. The Yankees develop pitchers better than most organizations, and he'll be an interesting project.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hurd started his prep career as a catcher before moving to the mound and would have been a top-two-rounds pick in 2021 if he wasn't set on attending UCLA. He pitched well as a Bruins freshman before missing the final two months with a stress fracture and transferring to Louisiana State, where he was inconsistent throughout 2023 before rallying to win the clinchers in the Men's College World Series Semifinals and Finals. Projected as a likely first-rounder in 2024, he once again battled his control and pitched his way out of the Tigers' rotation, which dropped him to the third round and an $836,400 bonus. He won't make his pro debut until 2026 after having Tommy John surgery in February. Hurd has a pair of quality pitches when healthy, beginning with a fastball that parks at 93-96 mph and reaches 98 with significant armside run and carry. His high-spin slider sits in the mid-80s and reaches 91 with plenty of horizontal and vertical movement. He threw just two changeups as an LSU junior, trying instead to combat left-handers with his 78-82 mph curveball. With his athleticism and a delivery that features arm speed rather than effort, Hurd should have at least average control, which would land him in the front half of a big league rotation. But he never has shown the ability to provide consistent strikes, his slider gets bashed when he doesn't command it and he hangs his curve too often. Many scouts believe his lack of reliability will land him in the bullpen, where his fastball and slider could become well-above-average offerings in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz signed with the Rangers for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent out of Puerto Rico in July 2021, and after training with Carlos Delgado and wearing contact lenses in games, he really started to take off by the 2023 season. He was named South Atlantic MVP and Rangers’ Minor League Player of the Year that campaign after going deep 33 times and slugging .619 across 109 games (80 of which were with High-A Hickory). Ortiz needed a second-half rebound with Double-A Frisco in ’24, returned there in ’25 and hit .283/.388/.565 with nine homers in 41 games with Triple-A Round Rock after an early August promotion. The Rangers added him to the 40-man roster as Rule 5 protection and traded him to the Nationals in January as part of the prospect return for MacKenzie Gore. Standing 5-foot-10, Ortiz packs a punch from the left side of the box with significant strength. It’s already plus raw power (as evidenced by a 106.6 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity), and he gets to it in games with strong lift-and-pull tendencies. There is 25-30-homer potential here at peak. Ortiz isn’t the most selective hitter though, and he’s struggled against left-handers in the upper Minors. He’s also liable to really undercut balls, leading to a lot of infield popups that hurt his BABIP and overall production. Ortiz is a bottom-of-the-scale runner too, so he won’t pick up extra bags on balls to the gap or many infield singles. Any production from his bat will come from its thunder. He’s moved between first base and right field in recent years, but his lack of range and arm make him a better fit for the cold corner. Washington has an opening there, and he could slide in as the broad (and powerful) side of a platoon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2021, Ortiz looked overmatched in his first full pro season before improving rapidly once he started training with fellow Puerto Rican Carlos Delgado, shortened his left-handed stroke and began wearing contact lenses during games. He won High-A South Atlantic League MVP and Rangers Minor League player of the year honors in 2023, when he topped the Minors in slugging (.619) and ranked fourth in homers (33) and OPS (.990). He recovered from a rough first half at Double-A last year to bat .309/.412/.636 with 15 homers in his final 43 games. Ortiz’s power took him to Triple-A in 2025, and after he was added to the 40-man roster in November, he was traded to the Nationals two months later as part of the MacKenzie Gore deal. Ortiz's bat speed in his lefty stroke and his strength give him well-above-average raw power that plays to all fields, and he began to tap into it more often when he stopped swinging for the fences. A more selective approach helped him find better pitches to attack, enabling him to hit them harder and drive them in the air more frequently. He tightened his strike zone in 2024, cutting his K rate to 22 percent from 27 percent the year before, but struggled against breaking balls and left-handers.
