Most of Ortiz's value will come from his offense because he's a well-below-average runner with fringy arm strength. He's a decent defender at first base, though he needs to reduce his errors. While he has looked better than expected as a right fielder in the Arizona Fall League and Double-A, the outfield corners are still a stretch because of his limited range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz attended high school and trained at the Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy in his native Puerto Rico before following the program's pipeline to Florida Southwestern State JC. Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2021, he didn't do much in his first full pro season but has taken off since shortening his left-handed swing and beginning to wear contact lenses during games. He led the Minors in slugging (.619) and ranked fourth in homers (33) and OPS (.990) in 2023, then shook off a rough first half in Double-A last season to slash .309/.412/.636 with 15 homers in his final 43 games. Ortiz's strength and bat speed create well-above-average raw power. He began to tap into it more in games by toning down his approach, which allowed him to hit the ball in the air and with premium exit velocities on a more regular basis. Strikeouts always will be part of his package but he's showing more discipline than he had in the past and will draw his share of walks. Because Ortiz is a well-below-average runner with fringy arm strength, there's a lot of pressure on his bat. He's an adequate defender at first base who needs to cut down on his errors. He looked better than expected in right field during the Arizona Fall League and in Double-A, but the outfield corners are still a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best college athlete in the 2019 Draft, Bishop went 10th overall to San Francisco, signed for a below-slot $4.1 million and had a solid pro debut. But he barely played in the next two years because the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season in 2020, when he came down with COVID-19 during Summer Camp, and he strained his right (throwing) shoulder in his third game of 2021, limiting him to just 16 contests. He's the younger brother of big league outfielder Braden Bishop, who spent most of last season at the Giants' Triple-A Sacramento affiliate. Bishop's bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed swing produce well above-average raw power that plays to any part of the ballpark, but he has yet to show that he can make enough contact or stay healthy enough to take advantage of his pop. He always has come with swing-and-miss concerns, and they've worsened in 2022 as he's gotten more aggressive and pull-happy. He also missed another month of needed at-bats with an oblique injury. A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a recruited walk-on at Washington before deciding to concentrate on baseball at Arizona State, Bishop has plus speed and at least 25-25 upside. He's still learning to make the most of his quickness as a basestealer and a center fielder, and his inactivity hasn't helped. He should be at least a solid defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable and accurate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a preferred walk-on at Washington, Bishop changed his mind and opted to play baseball at Arizona State. The younger brother of Giants Triple-A outfielder Braden Bishop exploded as a junior in 2019, batting .342/.479/.748 with 22 homers and 12 steals in 57 games, which prompted the Giants to draft him 10th overall and sign him for a below-slot $4.1 million. He recorded an .867 OPS in his pro debut, participated at San Francisco's alternate training site and in instructional league last year and missed most of the first three months this season with a right shoulder injury. Bishop had some of the best raw power in the 2019 Draft, with his bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed stroke enabling him to crush the ball out of any part of the ballpark. He did a better job of translating his pop into production once he settled down his approach, worked deeper counts and began using the opposite field, but he still comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He struck out in 27 percent of his plate appearances during his debut, though he also had an encouraging walk rate of 26 percent. Add in plus speed that he's still learning how to get the most out of on the bases, and Bishop has 30-30 potential. After playing the corners during his first two college season, he took quickly to center field in 2019 and should be at least a solid defender there. His arm is fringy to average but he makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A star wide receiver in high school, Bishop initially committed to play football as a preferred walk-on at Washington before deciding to focus on baseball at Arizona State. After two promising but inconsistent seasons, the younger brother of Mariners outfielder Braden Bishop broke out as a junior last spring by hitting .342/.479/.748 with 22 homers and 12 steals in 57 games. He went 10th overall in June and signed for $4.1 million, then continued to show a blend of power, speed and patience in his pro debut. Bishop's bat speed and strength plus the leverage in his 6-foot-5 frame and the loft in his left-handed swing gave him more raw power than most players in the 2019 Draft. He began to translate it into production more frequently once he calmed his approach, worked deeper counts and became more willing to use the opposite field. He still needs to make adjustments to reduce his strikeouts, but he improved his contact rate last year and offsets his whiffs with a healthy amount of walks. Also one of the best athletes in the 2019 Draft, Bishop has plus speed that he's still learning how to maximize on the bases. His quickness is more obvious in center field, where he already looks comfortable after playing the corners during his first two college seasons. His arm stands out more for its accuracy than its strength, which earns fringy to average grades.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the younger players and considered one of the most advanced hitters on the 2025 international market, Cedeno received the largest bonus in the Yankees' class. After signing for $2.5 million out of the Dominican Republic, he endured a rough pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. He batted .183/.371/.305 and led the Rookie circuit with 76 strikeouts in 47 games. For someone who struck out 37 percent of the time in his first taste of pro ball, Cedeno has a surprisingly compact right-handed swing and relatively good bat-to-ball skills. His problems last summer stemmed from an overly passive approach that put him behind in too many counts and an extremely pull-happy mentality that leaves him vulnerable to pitches on the outer half. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to reach 15-20 homers per season provided he can overhaul his approach. Cedeno has plus speed and knows how to use it, swiping 21 bases in 23 tries (91 percent) last summer. He has fast hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, though his quickness translates into just average range. It's possible that he'll fit better at second base in the long, which would put more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: San Pedro de Macoris in the Dominican Republic may have produced more All-Star infielders per capita than any other city, including Robinson Canó, Tony Fernandez, Pedro Guerrero, Alfonso Soriano and Fernando Tatis Jr. Cedeno has the tools to follow in that tradition after signing for $2.5 million in January. One of the youngest prospects and most advanced hitters in the 2025 international class, he'll play most of the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League schedule at age 16. Cedeno has a compact right-handed stroke and is balanced at the plate, but he has struggled to make contact during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League because he has gotten way too pull-happy. He has shown a willingness to draw walks but also has gotten too passive at times. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to provide 15-20 homers on an annual basis if he refines his approach. Cedeno's infield actions are as smooth as his swing. His speed, shortstop range and arm strength all grade as solid and could get better as he physically develops. He uses his feet well at short and makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bruns has teased with his upside since his days as an Alabama high schooler, when he displayed one of the best arsenals in the 2021 prep class but rarely the ability to harness it. Since signing for $2,197,500 as the 29th overall selection, he has continued to mitigate enticing stuff with a lack of control and health. He has totaled 235 strikeouts and 139 walks in 174 2/3 pro innings over four seasons, missing a month with a lat strain in 2022 and three months with back and rib issues last year. Bruns can overmatch hitters with three different offerings, including a mid-90s fastball that climbs as high as 98 mph with significant induced vertical break that carries it past barrels. His mid-80s slider with depth can be a wipeout pitch at its best, and he favors it over an upper-70s downer curveball that can be a hammer at times. He'll also flash an interesting mid-80s changeup with fade and sink but struggles to land it in the zone and doesn't trust it much. Though the Dodgers have helped Bruns clean up his mechanics, switching him from an over-the top delivery to a high three-quarters slot, that and working more out of the stretch hasn't produced more strikes. He might become a No. 3 starter if he could develop even fringy control, but he has yet to show that he can do that or handle a rotation workload. He's still intriguing as a lefty reliever with power stuff, though he'd have to locate his pitches better to be trusted in a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the biggest enigmas in the 2021 Draft, Bruns showcased some of the best pure stuff in that prep class but rarely displayed the ability to harness it on a consistent basis. He did win Gatorade's Alabama prep player of the year award as a senior and the Dodgers loved his upside enough to select him 29th overall and sign him for $2,197,500. He continued to display a tantalizing arsenal and a lack of control while going 0-12 with a 4.92 ERA in 51 starts over his first two-plus years as a pro. Bruns throws harder than most left-handers, operating in the mid-90s and topping out at 98 mph with a fastball that's tough to barrel thanks to its combination of velocity and carry. Both of his breaking pitches grade as well above average at their best, as his upper-70s curveball can be a true hammer and his mid-80s slider features plenty of sweep. His fading mid-80s changeup has the potential to become average, though he doesn't use it very often. Bruns has made some strides with his pitchability, cutting his walk rate from 9.1 per nine innings in his first full pro season to 6.2 in his second, though he'll need to refine his control much more to remain a starter. Los Angeles has helped him clean up his strong 6-foot-2 frame and his mechanics, having him use a high three-quarters slot rather than the over-the-top delivery he employed in high school. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but a greater likelihood of becoming a power reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bruns was an enigma as an Alabama high schooler, displaying some of the best pure stuff in the 2021 class but also little track record of taming it. He showed more consistency as a senior, winning Gatorade state player of the year honors before Los Angeles selected him 29th overall and signed him for $2,197,500. He opened his first full season with 18 strikeouts versus just two walks in 8 1/3 innings in April before his control fell apart in May, and he never got back on track after missing a month with a mild lat strain. Bruns continues to show three pitches that can grade as well above average when they're on. His fastball can sit in the mid-90s and top out at 98 mph with good carry up in the zone, his upper-70s curveball can be a hammer and his mid-80s slider can sweep past hitters. He shows the makings of an average low-80s changeup with fade but barely has used it while working abbreviated outings as a pro. The Dodgers have helped Bruns clean up his body and his delivery, and he now throws from a high three-quarters slot rather than straight over the top like he did in high school. He still needs to improve the timing and consistency of his mechanics. He has the stuff to pitch in the front half of a rotation with even fringy control and command but has a long ways to go after walking 52 batters in his first 49 1/3 pro innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bruns had some of the best pure stuff in the 2021 high school class but also a mixed history of being able to harness it. After struggling to find the strike zone on the showcase circuit, he did a better job last spring en route to being named Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year and becoming the Dodgers' first-round pick. The first of 14 straight pitchers selected by Los Angeles last July, he walked seven in five innings in Rookie ball after signing for $2,197,500. When Bruns is dialed in, he can work with a mid-90s fastball for several innings and reach 98 mph with good carry up in the strike zone. He also can spin a pair of plus breaking balls, an upper-70s downer curveball with quality depth and an 83-85 mph slider with nice tilt. He didn't need his low-80s changeup much as an amateur and will have to use it more often and improve its action against more advanced hitters. Bruns has a dynamic delivery with a high three-quarters arm slot and the ingredients to become a frontline starter if he can develop reliable control and command. He repeatedly lost feel for the zone in the summer before his senior season and had to dial his pitches back in order to try to get them over the plate. The Dodgers have a track record of helping prospects maximize their talents and were encouraged by the early returns from instructional league and winter camp.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Another in a string of interesting late-round arms taken by the Twins, Culpepper was a 13th-rounder in a 2022 Draft class that has provided a bounty of arms for the organization. It’s never completely clicked for the 6-foot-3 right-hander out of Cal Baptist, but he has been solid -- first across two levels of A ball in 2023, then reaching Double-A in 2024 and again back with Wichita in 2025. Injuries have played a part in the inconsistency, with a forearm strain sidelining him in ‘24 and a nerve injury in his finger delaying him for two months last year. Culpepper has never been a big stuff guy, and that nerve injury caused things to tick down. His fastball has typically been around 94 mph, but he’d been able to reach back for 97-98 mph, something there wasn’t much of in 2025, though there’s hope that a fully healthy version of him will allow him to get back to the delivery that helped him get to that more premium velocity. His low-80s sweeper is his best pitch in terms of missing bats. He can mix in the occasional curve and changeup, but he might be best served by focusing on his two-seamer to get groundball outs, the sweeper and his 88-90 mph cutter. More than anything, Culpepper needs to stay healthy and log innings -- he failed to top 60 IP in either of the last two seasons -- to get a sense of what kind of role he might be able to play long-term. He tends to be around the plate and has the repertoire to be a back-end starter, but given the durability concerns, using that sinker-slider combination out of a bullpen might make sense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Culpepper's move into Cal Baptist's rotation in 2022 after two years as an effective reliever, put him more solidly on some Draft radars. The Twins got him on Day 3, in the 13th round, part of a Draft class that has produced big leaguer Zebby Matthews as well as fellow pitching prospects Connor Prielipp, Andrew Morris and Cory Lewis. Culpper had a solid, but unspectacular first full season in 2023, then pitched his way from High-A to Double-A with better stuff in 2024, though he missed two months with a forearm strain and a pinched nerve in his right wrist delayed his 2025 debut until the end of May. With a bit of a kitchen sink repertoire, Culpepper can offer many different looks to get hitters out, even if he lacks any purely plus stuff. His fastball averaged around 94 mph last year and topped out at 98 mph, and he can throw his four-seamer up in the zone, then sink a two-seamer to get groundball outs. A key part in developing that part of his arsenal will be to maintain velocity deeper into outings. His low-80s sweeping slider can miss a lot of bats, and he's worked to improve his 89-90 mph cutter; blending the latter pitch with his four-seamer more will help him at the upper levels. Culpepper's walk rate can get elevated against left-handed hitters at times, and being able to land his changeup in the zone against them more should help while giving them a softer look away. There might be more to unlock as Culpepper tweaks some things with his delivery in terms of his lower half load and being more aggressively downhill as he comes off the mound. A few more consistent ticks of velocity could help cement him in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Culpepper spent most of his first two seasons at Cal Baptist as a reliever, saving 13 games for the Lancers in 2021, with four more in the Cape Cod League that summer. He got the chance to start in 2022 and threw well enough to capture the Twins' attention, going in the 13th round of that summer's Draft. His stuff ticked up out of the gate in his first full season, though he tired by season's end following a promotion up to High-A ball. Still, the Twins were encouraged by his step forward and think they might have another late-round pitching find on their hands, though his progress was slowed in 2024 by a forearm strain that sidelined him for nearly two months. When everything is clicking, Culpepper has a five-pitch mix with which to attack hitters. He came out in his full-season debut with Fort Meyers throwing harder than he did in college, averaging 95 mph and touching 97 mph with his fastball, a four-seamer with good action to it. He can throw his two-seamer almost as hard to get a lot of groundball outs as well. He has excellent feel to spin both his sweepy mid-80s slider and a newer, harder cutter that he throws around 90 mph. He can mix in a slower curve, and his mid-80s changeup is an effective spin-killer. As Culpepper progresses, he'll need to show he can maintain his better stuff over a full season's workload after his velocity dropped as his first year wore on. While he's generally around the plate, working on his pitch usage and using his breaking ball and changeup more effectively in the zone are on his to-do list. He's trending in the right direction, with the chance to be a workhorse-like starting pitcher in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Rangers for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, Vargas topped the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 11 homers, 27 extra-base knocks and 112 total bases during his U.S. debut in 2023. He made the jump to full-season ball last year and put himself all over the Single-A Carolina League leaderboard with 178 total bases (first), 108 hits (second), 40 extra-base hits (second), a .454 slugging percentage (second) and 14 homers (fifth). He's the best of the three prospects the Marlins acquired in exchange for Jake Burger at the Winter Meetings in December. Though he's just 5-foot-11 and 170 pounds, Vargas hits the ball much harder than most players his size. He uses a big leg kick and an aggressive right-handed stroke to turn on pitches and launch them in the air, allowing him to get the most out of his solid raw power. He'll need to tone down his approach against more advanced pitching after his chase rate ballooned to 42 percent last year and he struggled against non-fastballs. Vargas has solid speed and good instincts on the bases, giving him 20-20 potential. He has solid arm strength as well but more average range at shortstop, where the game sped up on him at times in 2024 as he committed 27 errors in 86 contests. He fits better at second base, also can handle third base and profiles as a power-hitting utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vargas lacks size and signed with the Rangers for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, he had made an outsized impact at the plate in his first two pro seasons. He debuted by posting an .878 OPS and ranking fourth in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 28 extra-base hits in 54 games, then came to United States last year and topped the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 11 homers, 27 extra-base knocks and 112 total bases. Following his successful transition to Single-A in 2024, the Marlins traded Jake Burger to acquire him, fellow middle-infield prospect Max Acosta and left-hander Brayan Mendoza at the Winter Meetings in December. A right-handed hitter, Vargas uses a big leg kick and aggressive hacks to hit the ball much harder than expected from a 5-foot-11, 170-pounder. He has an affinity for turning on pitches and driving them in the air, allowing him to squeeze nearly every drop out of his raw power and giving him 20-homer upside. He has the hand-eye coordination to make that approach work without compromising his timing at the plate, though his strikeout rate did jump from 12 percent in the DSL to 22 percent in his first two seasons in the United States. Vargas has average-to-solid speed with good instincts and an aggressive nature on the bases. He has reliable hands and solid arm strength but limited lateral range at shortstop and is a better fit at second base. He's also a capable third baseman and projects as a slugging utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $30,000 out of Panama in 2018, Ramos made an instant impression in his U.S. debut three years later, mashing a pair of homers with exit velocities of 111 and 114 mph in his first game in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. He has gone deep 44 times while advancing from Single-A to Double-A during the last two years, but the Dodgers have opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster either time. He was one of Panama's top performers at the 2023 World Baseball Classic, going 5-for-16 with a homer. Ramos weighed just 150 pounds when he turned pro at age 17, but he since has added 50 pounds and is one of the strongest players in the system. He also has tremendous bat speed and a pull-heavy mindset that contribute to well above-average raw power, tape-measure blasts and high exit velocities. However, his right-handed swing gets long and uphill and he chases too much, leading to too many strikeouts and rolled-over groundouts. Though he has slowed down some as he has gotten stronger, Ramos still possesses average speed. He spent most of 2023 in center field, where he has fine instincts and is an average defender. He's solid in right field, a good fit for his plus-plus arm strength that baserunners know better than to test.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $30,000 out of Panama in 2018, Ramos didn't make his U.S. debut until three years later but made an immediate impression by homering twice with exit velocities of 111 and 114 mph in his first game in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. He slammed 25 homers between Single-A and High-A at age 21 last season, but his batting average dropped from .329 to .249 and his strikeout rate rose from 25 to 31 percent compared to 2021. Los Angeles likes his upside but declined to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, successfully deducing that his bat was too raw to get plucked in the Rule 5 Draft. Just 5-foot-11 and 150 pounds when he signed as a 17-year-old, he has added two inches and 50 pounds and resembles fellow Dodgers outfield prospect Andy Pages in terms of physicality and tools. Ramos has tremendous bat speed and strength that allow him to hit tape-measure shots and could produce 30 or more homers per season in the big leagues. But his uphill right-handed swing and extremely aggressive approach make him vulnerable to breaking pitches and result in a lot of wasted at-bats and strikeouts, so he'll have to tone things down at higher levels. Ramos has slowed down as he has gained muscle, though he's still an average runner with good outfield instincts. He split time between right field and center field last season, and he's a solid defender at all three outfield spots. His plus-plus arm is a weapon that has notched 30 assists in 223 games in his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain signing at $30,000 out of Panama in 2018, Ramos didn't get a change to play in the United States before last season. He made an immediate impression, homering twice with exit velocities of 111 and 114 mph in his first game in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. He needed just three weeks to earn a promotion to Low-A at age 20 and batted .329/.396/.577 with 11 homers in 62 games between the two stops. Just 5-foot-11 and 150 pounds when he signed as a 17-year-old, Ramos has added two inches and 50 pounds since then and now resembles fellow Dodgers outfield prospect Andy Pages with his physicality and tools. Both offer well above-average raw power from the right side of the plate and arm strength to match. Ramos has an efficient swing and some feel to hit, though he'll need to tighten his strike zone and prove he can handle quality breaking balls at higher levels. Though Ramos has lost some speed as he has gotten stronger, he's still an average runner with good instincts in the outfield. He spent most of his early career in center field but played solely in right field in Low-A, projecting as a solid defender on the corner. Baserunners have not had much success testing his arm, as he recorded 20 assists in his first 112 outfield starts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though he signed for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, Ventura has been brimming with potential for years, beginning in 2019, when he climbed three levels out of the Dominican Summer League and into stateside ball. He missed all of 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic shutdown and Tommy John surgery respectively, and when he returned last June, it was only for four starts before a pectoral injury ended his 2022 early. Ventura went unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft, and while the Mets were concerned someone would grab and stash him, he went unpicked and stayed in the New York system. The 6-foot right-hander flashed his typical promise during his brief time in the Florida State League, striking out 10 of 29 batters (34.5 percent) before the most recent injury. He topped out at 97.3 mph on the radar gun and sat 93-95 mph from a high release slot. His mid-80s changeup got good separation off the heater, and while it did show some firmness, it projects as a potential above-average offering that got almost as many whiffs as the fastball and curve combined. Speaking of which, after Santos toiled with a breaking ball for years, his 79-81 mph curveball flashed as average with vertical drop, but he used it only 14 percent of the time. Ventura’s athletic delivery has long given Mets officials hope that he can throw strikes, and that didn’t change after the brief look in ’22. The right-hander still has the upside of a back-end starting pitcher, especially if he can lock the breaking ball into place, but he absolutely needs to get innings to meet that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for only $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, Ventura shot up through three Rookie-level affiliates (one Dominican, two domestic) a year later and finished with solid numbers -- a 3.78 ERA, 54 strikeouts, 19 walks in 52 1/3 innings. Following the missed 2020 season, he had the potential to break into full-season ball last year but underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring, causing him to miss the entire 2021 campaign. The good news: Ventura returned to Single-A St. Lucie this season with a fastball that averages 94 mph. That’s even more promising because the 6-foot right-hander had really leaned on the heater to find his success early in his career. When he was previously healthy, he had also been working on finding a consistent breaking ball instead of one that showed slider shape at times and curveball depth at others. A mid-80s changeup has been his most oft-used secondary in 2022, and while it has a higher whiff percentage than the other two offerings, it does get too firm to be more than an average pitch. Ventura always earned points for an athletic and repeatable delivery that helped him throw strikes at the lower levels, and those characteristics should help him re-find the command post-Tommy John. A pectoral strain suffered in late June has put off that timeline a little further, but it’s less of a concern than the elbow was. Regained health and additional work on the secondaries could push him into becoming one of the Mets’ best prospect arms by the middle of 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ventura signed with the Mets for only $20,000 shortly after his 17th birthday in July 2018 and moved directly to the Dominican Summer League from there. He returned to the DR complex circuit in 2019 but was moved stateside after only three impressive starts. The right-hander climbed to Rookie Advanced Kingsport in that age-18 campaign, finishing with strong numbers (including 54 strikeouts against 19 walks in 52 1/3 innings) across the board at three levels. He underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring and won’t see a Minor League mound again until likely the middle of next summer. The Mets are fans of Ventura’s overall athleticism and repeatable delivery prior to the procedure. He uses both to throw a fastball around 92 mph that features some cut to it. The pitch alone has guided the 6-foot hurler’s early trips to the Minors to the point where he has used it 80-90 percent of the time at the lower levels. That pitch selection will change as he faces tougher bats, and the Mets are optimistic that his other offerings will be good enough to handle more usage. The breaking ball, particularly, will remain a focus. Sometimes, it can come out of his hand with slider-like action. Others, it has the depth of an above-average curveball. The Mets teamed with Ventura to find the breaking pitch that works best off his heater. The changeup can be an out pitch, but like any young pitcher, it needs to be thrown more to complete its true development. It wasn’t killer stuff from Ventura before Tommy John surgery. But it all came from a promisingly athletic frame, and Ventura’s ability to throw strikes across the board was a promising first step. A move away from the fastball and into the secondary pitches needed to get upper-level bats out should come next in his journey to find a spot in the back end of a Major League rotation, once he regains his elbow health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mets for $20,000 on July 25, 2018, Ventura made his pro debut two weeks later in the Dominican Summer League. When the right-hander returned to the level in 2019, it took him all of four starts to convince the Mets that he was ready for a greater challenge. A strong performance over 33 innings in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League came next and led to another promotion -- this time to the Rookie-level Appalachian League, where he allowed one run and three hits in two starts to close out the season. Though he lacks the type of size or physicality like some of the other teenage hurlers in New York’s system, Ventura does have some room to grow into his lithe, athletic frame. Those physical gains should help the right-hander add more velocity to a fastball that already sits in the low-90s with natural cutting action. A slider that flashes above average gives Ventura a quality secondary pitch to complement his fastball, and he also shows some aptitude for turning over a tumbling changeup. A good athlete with a quick arm, Ventura already repeats his delivery better than most hurlers his age. That should allow him to develop above-average control and at least average command as he works his way through the Minors. If it all comes together for him, Ventura could be a No. 5 starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cluff missed his sophomore and junior seasons at BYU because he was on a mission trip in Atlanta. When he returned to the Cougars as a senior in 2019, he batted .325/.458/.515 and had almost as many walks (37) as strikeouts (39), leading the Nationals to select him in the sixth round that year and sign him for below-slot at $200,000. Two years later, Cluff’s first full Minor League season was interrupted by a broken thumb and a broken hamate bone, and he managed only a .190/.278/.278 line in 35 games with Double-A Harrisburg. Cluff bounced back nicely (and healthily) in the Arizona Fall League, where he batted .342 in 22 games and was named the circuit’s Defensive Player of the Year. It would be too easy to get caught up in Cluff’s Harrisburg numbers and consider him a lost offensive cause, just like it would be too easy to see his resurgence in a hitter-friendly AFL and say he’s back. The answer, of course, lies somewhere in the middle, and we’ll need to see how the bat plays further away from multiple hand injuries. At his best, Cluff shows good bat-to-ball skills and incorporates some pullside power that could help get to double-digit homers in the Majors. The 25-year-old’s defense at shortstop remains stellar, thanks to solid range, good hands and a strong arm. That certainly helps lower his floor as a glove-first type, and these are defensive skills that could translate anywhere on the dirt if his offensive limitations force him into a utility role. More answers on the bat should be coming when Cluff returns to the upper Minors in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cluff was a senior sign out of BYU in the sixth round of the 2019 Draft, having spent the 2017 and 2018 seasons on a mission trip in Atlanta. His .325/.458/.515 line and 39/37 K/BB ratio that final spring on campus put him on the Nats’ radar, and the club signed him for a below-slot $200,000 bonus. Cluff immediately jumped to Class A Hagerstown, where he hit .229/.320/.367 with five homers and 11 steals in 62 games. The former Cougar is as good an infield defender as can be found in the system. His hands and plus arm work at any spot on the dirt, and he has the ceiling defensively of an everyday shortstop because of those skills. The bat will determine whether he deserves to get the at-bats that would come with such a profile. A late addition to the alternate site, Cluff showed average bat speed and a little more power than expected in Fredericksburg, but the pop remains solidly below average. His speed is above-average to plus, and that helps him cover a bit of ground on the dirt and pick up the odd extra base offensively. Because of the questions about how the bat will hold up, Cluff profiles right now as a utility infielder capable of providing value with the glove. Some more power in the upper levels would make an everyday spot more of a realistic option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cluff appeared in 43 games as a Brigham Young freshman before departing on a two-year mission trip in Atlanta. A much stronger and explosive player when he returned to BYU in 2019, Cluff produced a .325/.458/.515 line with 27 extra-base hits and 12 steals to catch the attention of Nationals scouts. Believing he was merely scraping the surface of his potential after a long layoff, Washington selected Cluff in the sixth round in June and sent him straight to Class A Hagerstown for his pro debut. Cluff may be raw, but he looks the part of a future big leaguer with his quick-twitch athleticism and chiseled physique. He’s a steady, confident defender at shortstop with good range and instincts as well as a plus arm that should allow him to play anywhere on the infield. He gets out of the box well and knows how to use his above-average speed once he’s on base. While Cluff’s hitting ability is behind his defense, the Nationals expected that much after his two-year hiatus from the game. He has sneaky raw power from the left side of the plate and began to drive the ball more consistently late in his pro debut. Improving his bat-to-ball skills and trimming some of the swing-and-miss from his game are Cluff’s biggest areas for improvement, though club officials think some of those gains will come naturally as he gains experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a big junior season as Campbell’s Friday night starter, Keuhler was selected by the Braves with the No. 70 pick in the 2023 Draft, making him the third of three college pitchers the organization took to kick off their class. He was off to a solid start to his first full season, with Single-A Augusta, albeit without missing many bats. But after one start with High-A Rome, he was shut down and needed Tommy John surgery in July, so he’s likely out until the 2026 season. While he’s undersized at 6-foot, Kuehler has more than enough options in his repertoire. His fastball had been up to 98 mph in college, with excellent spin rates and carry, and while he was more 91-93 mph in 2024, the damaged elbow might have been the cause. He can mix in a two-seamer as well, and he backs up the fastballs with a mid-80s slider with depth that was plus pre-injury. He also throws a shorter, harder cutter and an above-average low-80s curve, and he’s toyed with both a splitter and a more traditional changeup. Kuehler’s size, short arm action and high three-quarters slot create deception, but he hasn’t always shown the ability to repeat it, leading to issues finding the strike zone. That combined with the elbow surgery may have some thinking he’s destined for a bullpen role, but he’ll have to get healthy before moving in any direction on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Campbell’s reputation for generating draftable talent has taken a large step forward over the past several years, starting with Seth Johnson going No. 40 overall to the Rays in 2019, followed by 2022 first-rounder Zach Neto and sandwich pick Thomas Harrington. Kuehler extended the run by landing No. 70 overall to the Braves in 2023 after pitching for the U.S. Collegiate National Team in the summer of 2022 and having a huge junior year as the Fighting Camels’ Friday night starter. He tossed seven shutout innings over two appearances during his brief pro debut with full-season Augusta. Kuehler can throw as many as seven pitches depending on when you see him. His four-seam fastball, which averaged 94 mph in 2023 and topped out at 98 mph, has plus spin rates and carry, and he’ll mix in some two-seamers as well. His mid-80s slider has depth that misses bats and he can manipulate it into a shorter, harder cutter. He has an above-average low-80s curve, a traditional low-80s changeup with fade and a mid-80s splitter/changeup, though he leaned on the fastballs and breaking balls mostly at Campbell. The six-foot right-hander can get hit at times when he’s not commanding his arsenal consistently. There’s deception stemming from his short arm action and high three-quarters slot, but he hasn’t always been able to repeat his delivery to throw strikes. Working from the stretch during his pro debut seemed to help, but he’ll have to prove he can find the zone enough to remain a starter as he moves up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips’ raw stuff has intrigued evaluators for some time, but injuries have largely kept it in the mythical category. The Braves took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft because of his upside despite the fact he had Tommy John surgery in April of his senior year of high school. He spent the 2023 season rehabbing and then was sent to the Mariners in the trade for Jarred Kelenic and others. Phillips had an eye on taking the mound competitively in 2024 when he needed a second TJ leading up to Spring Training, so he enters the 2025 season without having an official professional pitch on his résumé. It’s hard to know exactly what Phillips might be because it’s possible he hasn’t been truly healthy since his junior year of high school in 2021. The Texas native has shown high-octane stuff, with a fastball that has good run and sits in the mid 90s, touching close to 100. His breaking ball is a bit of a hybrid, thrown with slider-like velocity around 85 mph, but with curveball depth. There is feel for a fading changeup, but he hadn’t used it much nor had time to develop it. All of Phillips’ grades are hypothetical and on-paper numbers at this point. The hope is to get him on the mound at some point during the 2025 season, and while it will likely be '26 before anyone will be able to get any sense of what kind of pitcher he might be, the potential that intrigued the Braves three years ago is still too good to completely forget about him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips was high on the Mariners’ radar ahead of the 2022 Draft, but the Tommy John surgery he underwent in April impacted his status and led him to being taken by the Braves in the second round for $1.5 million. He wound up in Seattle’s system as the upside return in the 2023 trade that sent Jarred Kelenic to Atlanta, but then he underwent a second TJ leading up to Spring Training in ‘24 that will further prevent him from making his pro debut. Part of what may have led to his injuries is also what made him so enticing, which is the fastball with elite velocity that sits in the mid-90s, flirts with triple digits and features strong running action. His best secondary pitch is a power breaking ball that he gets up to 85 mph, a pitch that has curveball depth with slider velocity. With that type of combination, he doesn’t often use the changeup that he has in his back pocket that possesses good fade. The most notable comparison Phillips has drawn is to Nathan Eovaldi, who was also high on Draft boards back in 2008 as a Texas high schooler before sustaining an elbow injury. The focus for Phillips in 2024 will again be to get healthy after another brutally unfortunate setback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips was rushing up Draft boards in the spring of 2022 as reports flowed in of the Texas prep right-hander hitting triple digits with his fastball. He seemed like he had a shot at being a first-round pick until the train was derailed temporarily by Tommy John surgery in April. He had been scouted regularly prior to the injury and the Braves felt comfortable enough to take him as their third straight high school arm in the 2022 Draft, signing him for $1.5 million as their second-round pick. He never threw an official pitch for the Braves, who sent him and fellow right-hander Jackson Kowar to the Mariners in the December trade that sent Jarred Kelenic, Evan White and Marco Gonzales to Atlanta. The hope is that Phillips will get back to the improved stuff he showed before the elbow injury. His fastball can sit in the mid-90s, reach the upper 90s and touch 100 mph with good running action. His breaking ball, a power curve with depth thrown up to 85 mph, could be a plus pitch. Like many prep hurlers with that kind of fastball-breaking ball combination, he didn’t use his changeup much, but he has shown feel for a mid-80s offering with fade. Compared by some to big leaguer Nathan Eovaldi, a Texas high schooler who blew out his elbow as a junior, Phillips’ improved strength has led to a repeatable delivery and more strikes. He’ll get his first true professional test in his new organization in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic, Baez landed the largest bonus in the Astros' 2022 international class. At 18 years old, he was older than most prospects who command seven-figure deals on that market, but he has advanced quickly. He finished 2024 in Double-A at age 20 and his 21 homers last season ranked fourth among Minor Leaguers his age or younger. Baez features more bat speed and strength and hits balls considerably harder than most players his age or in Houston's system. A right-handed hitter, he has no problem turning on pitches and launching them to his pull side and possesses at least 30-homer upside. But his swing-at-everything approach results in a lot of chases and in-zone misses and he's a sucker for sliders, so he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact against more advanced pitching. While the Astros envisioned Baez as a possible center fielder when they signed him, he has slowed down as he has gained weight and is now a below-average runner. He has good instincts but limited range on the outfield corners, where he's an adequate defender who could get more out of his plus arm if he could get to balls quickly. He'll have to stay on top of his conditioning to avoid losing more quickness and winding up at first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez received the largest bonus in Houston's 2022 international crop, turning pro for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic. At 18, he was older than most players who get seven-figure bonuses in that market, and he broke into pro ball by ranking second in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 19 doubles and 30 extra-base hits. He smacked seven homers in 17 games in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer to earn a promotion to Single-A Fayetteville, where he batted .239/.324/.413. Baez has more bat speed and strength than most teenagers -- he's at least 20 pounds heavier than his listed 205 pounds -- and it gives him more usable power than anyone in the system. He already has an affinity for launching balls in the air to his pull side and could provide 30 or more homers per season. He has a sound right-handed stroke but may need to moderate his approach after striking out at a 27 percent clip in Single-A. The Astros thought Baez had a chance to play center field when he signed, but he has lost speed as his weight has fluctuated, reaching a high of 240 pounds a year ago. He's now a below-average runner and an adequate corner outfielder who could make better use of his plus arm strength if he got to balls more quickly. If he slows down any further, he risks winding up at first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez signed for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic, landing the largest bonus in Houston's 2022 international class. Older than most players who get seven-figure bonuses in that market, he turned 18 four days before inking his deal in January. In his pro debut, he ranked second in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 19 doubles and 30 extra-base hits while slashing .305/.351/.552. Baez's bat speed and the strength in his 6-foot-1, 205-pound frame give him natural power that could translate into 25 or more homers per season. He already shows the aptitude to drive balls in the air to his pull side. He has a sound right-handed stroke, but he may need to temper his approach when he faces more advanced pitchers. Presently an average runner, Baez could slow down as he physically matures. He spent most of his debut in right field, where he's an average defender with plus arm strength. He also saw some time in center but projects strictly as a corner guy who could wind up at first base if he loses too much quickness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez received the largest bonus in Houston's 2021-22 international crop, turning pro for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic. Relatively old for his class, he turned 18 four days before inking his contract in January. Baez landed a seven-figure bonus in large part because of his right-handed power potential. A right-handed hitter, he looks to launch balls to his pull side and also generates opposite-field pop with bat speed and projectable strength. Though he's a power-over-hit guy, the Astros like his swing and think he'll make plenty of hard contact. An average runner, Baez could slow down as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. For now, he projects as an average right fielder with a plus arm. If he loses too much quickness, he could wind up at first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Gutierrez for $1.9 million in January 2023, making the Venezuela native the largest signee of their international class that year. The catcher needed to repeat the Dominican Summer League after posting just a .565 OPS in 50 games in his first taste of the Minors, but after stronger early returns in 2024, he headed stateside for the first time and finished the season at Single-A St. Lucie. He spent all of ’25 in the Florida State League, hitting .242/.362/.309 with four homers and a 98 wRC+ in 91 games. Gutierrez was considered a power-over-hit prospect entering pro ball, but that categorization has flipped as he heads into his 20s. Starting from an open stance with his hands held high, the right-handed batter manages to make a lot of contact in zone, despite kicking his back leg out at times, in part because he won’t let drivable pitches sail by without a swing. That said, he can expand the zone a bit much, and while he’ll get the bat on the ball, it’s far from loud contact. His 100.5 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity was on the low side even for someone his age. The Caracas native has retained the above-average arm strength he had as an amateur but has yet to put up the caught-stealing rates to match. His throws can wander, especially toward right-center, and improved accuracy should be a priority. Gutierrez otherwise shows enough promising attributes behind the plate as a receiver to become a backup option in The Show with a few more years of development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gutierrez was the Mets’ big international addition in 2023 as a $1.9 million signing out of Venezuela, giving him the third-highest bonus among catchers behind other notable prospects Ethan Salas ($5.6 million) and Alfredo Duno ($3.1 million). His development got off to a rough start when he batted .186 with a .565 OPS over 50 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first season, but he bounced back right out of the gate back in the DSL in 2024, earning a promotion stateside in late June. He continued to pound the ball (.317/.463/.537) during a short stint in the Florida Complex League and even saw Single-A ball for eight games at the end of the season. The right-handed slugger starts from a very open stance and sweeps his lead leg over as part of his load. He was lauded for plus raw power coming into pro ball, and he certainly got that to play with a strong focus on lifting and pulling the ball in the air. He clubbed two homers and 13 doubles in his 37 games, and as he continues to mature, more of those gappers should head over the fence. Gutierrez got that pop to play even more as he made much more contact in year two, tightening his swing to get the barrel on the ball while fanning in only 13.4 percent of his plate appearances (a number that was inflated by his aggressive FSL time). The Caracas native has above-average arm strength, and while his caught-stealing numbers haven’t been great in the early going, they should improve as he works with more veteran arms who can be quicker to the plate themselves. He has the body of a catcher at 5-foot-11 and should get every chance to stick there heading into his 20s.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his four years at the University of Virginia, McGarry racked up strikeouts, with a career 12.5 K/9 rate, and walks, leaving Charlottesville with an 8.8 BB/9 rate. The Phillies took a chance on the arm strength in the fifth round of the 2021 Draft, and McGarry struggled to balance his elite stuff with his control issues over his five years in the Phils system. He was moved to the Triple-A bullpen for 2024, only to walk 24.5 percent of his batters faced, and went unprotected and unpicked in that year’s Rule 5 Draft. McGarry moved back to starting (this time at Double-A) for ’25 with modest strike-throwing gains that helped him get taken by the Nationals in Rule 5 in December. McGarry still has a repertoire of power stuff to miss bats with. His fastball averaged around 94 mph in 2025 and was up to 99, and it can be effective thanks to his vertical approach angle, aided by his extension and ability to get low down the mound. He can show two variations of a slider -- a low-80s sweeper with a big tail (17-18 inches of horizontal movement) and a more traditional mid-80s breaker. Both can get upwards of 2,800 rpm and miss a health amount of bats. There’s also an upper-80s cutter, 79-81 mph curveball and 86-89 mph changeup that are rarely used. McGarry’s mentality might be better suited for starting over relieving, as he proved in the Arizona Fall League in ’24 and the regular season in ‘25. He’ll show flashes of finding the zone in those longer outings when he isn’t letting his arsenal fly, and the Nationals are leaving the door open to a potential spot in the rotation as they sort through their plans for the new acquisition. McGarry will need to stick in the Majors for all of 2026 to remain in the Washington organization moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McGarry spent four years at the University of Virginia tantalizing with his premium raw stuff while struggling to throw strikes. The Phillies signed him for his arm strength for a bit under slot in the fifth round of the 2021 Draft, and the results have been much of the same, McGarry missed a ton of bats and reached Triple-A in his first full season, then struggled even more in a regressive year in 2023. A move to the bullpen this season did not help in the command department. The right-hander's raw stuff is still worth not walking away from. He is capable of getting outs with as many as five pitches, albeit not consistently. His fastball averaged close to 95 mph and touched 99 in 2023, and it generates swings-and-misses thanks to his vertical approach angle. His mid-80s slider is a true out pitch when he can land it in or near the strike zone, with a 52 percent miss rate last year. He throws his 80-mph curve less frequently but gets swings-and-misses with it as well. He doesn't throw his cutter or changeup that much, but they can be effective. What McGarry hasn't been able to do is throw any of them for strikes consistently enough for prolonged success, with a career 6.1 BB/9 rate entering 2024. He worked with the Phillies to remap and shorten his arm path in the hopes of improving his command this season. The hope is that the move to the bullpen will allow him to carve out some kind of big league role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McGarry has been a prospect since his high school days, when he was a late-round pick of the Rangers before honoring his commitment to Virginia. With the Cavaliers, he showed off his premium arm strength as well as a lack of familiarity with the strike zone, making him an intriguing, yet enigmatic college arm in 2021. The Phillies thought McGarry's stuff was worth taking in the fifth round, and he pitched his way from High-A to Triple-A in his first full season of pro ball. If you’re just evaluating pure stuff, McGarry could be considered one of the better pitching prospects in the game. He’s flirted with 100 mph in the past and was up to 99 mph at the upper levels in 2022, averaging over 95 mph. It’s an elite pitch not just because of velocity, but because of his vertical approach angle as well. His mid-80s slider can be plus at times, missing a ton of bats, and he fools hitters with an upper-70s curve too. He doesn’t throw his changeup nearly as much as the breaking stuff, but it has characteristics of a plus pitch. He added a hard cutter at the end of last year to give him a potential five-pitch mix. How often McGarry can land his elite-level stuff in the strike zone will determine exactly what he can be in the big leagues. A 13.9 K/9 rate to start off his pro career shows he can fool pro hitters, but even with some improvements since joining the Phillies, he’s walked 5.4 per nine entering 2023. There’s hope that as he adds mass to his loose 6-foot-2 frame, he can keep refining his delivery and throw enough strikes to start, a role he’ll continue for now unless there’s a need as a reliever in Philadelphia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since his high school days in California, there’s never been any question about McGarry’s pure stuff, but he was almost as likely to walk a hitter as he was to strike one out during his four years at the University of Virginia. Even though he had some big outings in postseason play for the Cavaliers, it was a little tough to figure out where McGarry belonged on Draft boards. The Phillies took a flier on the raw arm strength in the fifth round, signing him for a bit below slot, then saw him be dominant, and more efficient, during his pro debut. McGarry’s stuff is elite, plain and simple. His fastball touched triple digits in college and he was regularly up to 98-99 mph during his pro debut and at instructs. He was known for a nasty slider in college, one that produced a 67 percent miss rate in 2021, but he also has a very good and distinct curve that can miss bats as well. McGarry continued working on his changeup, which flashes plus as well. It was a small sample size, but McGarry cut his walk rate from 8.8 per nine in his college career to a more manageable 5.2/9 during his pro debut. The Phillies think his command and control are trending up as he continues to streamline his delivery, finding a lower arm slot that seems to work more consistently for him. He has the pitches to start, and he’ll get the chance to work on all his offerings in that role, with a more likely outcome being an elite-level bullpen piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of longtime Major League starter Trevor Wilson, Paul was poised to stay close to home in the Pacific Northwest with a commitment to Oregon State. The Tigers changed his plans by drafting him in the third round in 2023 and going above slot to sign him to a $1.7 million bonus. He began his pro career in 2024 on a once-a-week schedule in the Florida Complex League, where he showed flashes of potential along with the need for polish. Wilson has a nice, fluid delivery with a three-quarter arm angle. His fastball plays up from its low to mid-90s velocity with explosiveness out of his hand, but he has command of the pitch needs improvement. Until he can consistently throw the fastball for strikes, his power curveball and changeup won’t reach their potential. On the bright side, he does a skilled job of keeping the ball in the park and had far fewer hit batters than one would expect for his control. Plenty of high school pitchers have experienced rough introductions to pro ball before settling down and enjoying fruitful careers. Wilson has the pitches and pedigree to do the same with a little patience and some work with the Tigers’ pitching instruction department.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amidst a run of bats in the first two days of the 2023 MLB Draft, the Tigers pulled a sneaky pick by grabbing Wilson in the third round and signing him away from an Oregon State commitment with an above-slot $1.7 million bonus. The Tigers waited until 2024 to get him his pro debut, but the combination of a strong prep career and impressive family ties -- his dad, Trevor, pitched eight years in the Majors -- has Detroit officials excited about his potential. Wilson said after being drafted that his dad helped mold his mechanics, and the polish shows. The younger Wilson has a nice, fluid delivery with a simple leg kick and a three-quarter arm angle. His fastball generally sat in the low-90s out of high school but approaches the mid-90s when he amps up. He complements it with a power curveball, as well as a changeup that needs some refinement but has potential. Wilson pitched a lot in his prep career before taking a break coming out of the Draft. The combination of rest and instruction makes Wilson an interesting pitcher to follow in the years to come. He has the ingredients and influences to become a Major League starter, and even though the southpaw has taken some lumps in his first pro summer, the Tigers still see the individual parts that could make him a promising piece of their future rotations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Bryce Rainer was the headliner of the Tigers’ 2024 Draft class, team officials were just as pleased to land Hall in the middle of the second round. Detroit pried him away from a commitment to Vanderbilt with a signing bonus just below slot at $1.75 million. After his pro debut last spring, he made just four starts for Single-A Lakeland, battling command and pitch counts in two of them, before a stress reaction in his shoulder sidelined him for the rest of the season. Before the shoulder injury, Hall came out with a lower three-quarters arm slot than his prep days while throwing a heavy dose of two-seam fastballs, averaging around 94 mph and topping out at 96. His four-seamer has good induced vertical break. His mid-80s slider has a solid whiff rate and movement. He threw a mid-70s curveball in high school with mixed results. His upper-80s changeup is an occasional offering for him. The Tigers have exercised patience with hurlers drafted out of high school, particularly those with injuries. Hall will get another chance in Lakeland to establish himself as a pro and refine his command before potentially moving up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Bryce Rainer was the headliner of the Tigers’ 2024 Draft class, team officials were just as pleased to land Hall in the middle of the second round. Detroit pried him away from a commitment to Vanderbilt with a signing bonus just below slot at $1.75 million. He didn’t pitch in the Minors over the summer, but spent the offseason working out with Jackson Jobe at PitchingWRX in Oklahoma City. Hall relies heavily on a fastball that sits at 91-94 mph and reaches 98 with explosive life up in the strike zone and induced vertical break out of a high arm slot. With his athleticism and projectable 6-foot-3 frame, he could regularly deal in the mid-90s once he gets stronger. He throws two distinct breaking balls, with his low-80s slider showing more promise and getting more chases than his mid-70s curveball, which lacks consistency but elicits swings and misses. Though Hall barely used his mid-80s changeup as an amateur, it could become an average pitch once he employs it more and gains more velocity separation from his fastball. The Tigers have exercised patience with hurlers drafted out of high school, Jobe among them. That continues for Hall, who worked in only four starts for Single-A Lakeland before suffering a right shoulder stress reaction that kept him out of official games the remainder of the 2025 summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jordan was well-known for his power as an amateur, having gone viral for a pair of 500-foot homers when he was 13, and he moved up a year by reclassifying into the 2020 Draft where he was selected by the Red Sox in the third round before signing for $1.75 million. Jordan didn’t pop off in the upper Minors until 2025 in his third go-round at Double-A Portland, forcing a promotion to Triple-A Worcester at age 22. He was holding his own there when Boston traded him to the Cardinals at the Deadline for Steven Matz, and he struggled down the stretch, hitting .198/.242/.366 in 41 games for Memphis (though with a .185 BABIP). Jordan has an interesting mix of tools that can make his skill set a bit of a roller coaster to evaluate. His in-zone contact rate was exceptional both before and after the trade, leading to K rates below 12 percent at both of his Triple-A stops, but he got much more swing-happy in Memphis, leading to a chase rate in the 40 percent region. His raw power remains plus, but his overzealous swing decisions led to a lot of ground balls (56.4 percent with Memphis) that kept that pop from playing in games. Jordan was at his best in Portland when he was much more selective, and he’s talked about working on his bat speed and angles to get his pop back again. He still hit a career-high 19 homers in 2025 and could repeat that number with the right adjustments. Jordan has the arm strength for third but with well-below-average speed, he best fits at first base. St. Louis didn’t add him to the 40-man roster when he was Rule 5-eligible after the trade, but he’ll still only be 23 for the entire 2026 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jordan was a legendary power hitter as an amateur, winning his first competition at age 11, blasting a pair of 500-foot homers at an event when he was 13 and prevailing at the High School Home Run Derby at the 2019 All-Star Game. He reclassified from the 2021 Draft to 2020 and went in the third round, signing for an above-slot $1.75 million. He has been more controlled and less dangerous than expected in pro ball, batting .296/.350/.481 with 18 homers between High-A and Double-A last season at age 20. Jordan still hits the ball harder than most players his age, but he has taken a more measured approach as a pro than he did as an amateur. Though his bat speed and strength create well-above-average raw power, he has focused more on putting the ball in play early in counts and using the entire field rather than driving balls in the air. He's not going to fully tap into his pop unless he gets more selective hunting for pitches to launch and turning his right-handed swing loose when he gets them. While Jordan has worked hard to improve at third base, his well-below-average speed and substandard range limit his effectiveness there. He has soft hands and decent arm strength, but first base is his likely defensive home, which puts even more pressure on his bat. He's an adequate, if not especially rangy defender, at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A legend in power-hitting competitions, Jordan won his first event at age 11, slammed a pair of 500-foot homers at another when he was 13 and took top honors at the High School Home Run Derby at the 2019 All-Star Game. After reclassifying from the 2021 Draft to 2020, he signed for an above-slot $1.75 million in the third round. He took a more measured approach in his 2022 full-season debut, batting .289/.363/.445 with 12 homers between Single-A and High-A. Jordan's aggressive right-handed stroke and struggles against older competition on the high school showcase circuit created swing-and-miss questions that hurt his Draft stock, but he managed an 18 percent strikeout rate last year while focusing on making hard contact from gap to gap. He impressed with his patience and pitch recognition while producing notable exit velocities for a teenager, albeit with more ground-ball contact than is optimal. His combination of bat speed and strength produces well above-average raw power, though it didn't translate into tape-measure shots in 2022 like it had in the past. Jordan also gets credit for working diligently to improve his conditioning, quickness and defensive prowess at third base. He has soft hands and maybe enough arm strength for the hot corner, but most scouts believe his below-average speed and range will dictate a full-time move to first base, where he already has seen considerable action. His size, power and defensive limitations have earned him comparisons to Matt Holliday and Mark Trumbo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jordan was a legend in amateur home run derby circles, winning his first at age 11, crushing a pair of 500-foot homers at another when he was 13 and prevailing in the High School Home Run Derby at the 2019 All-Star Game. He reclassified from the 2021 Draft to 2020, landing an above-slot $1.75 million bonus in the third round as one of the youngest players and top power hitters in his class. He went deep six times in his 28-game pro debut last summer, including twice in nine Low-A contests. Jordan's massive power has been good as advertised, as he crushes tape-measure shots to all fields and produces huge exit velocities with a right-handed stroke loaded with bat speed, strength and loft. While his struggles against older competition on the high school showcase circuit led to swing-and-miss concerns that depressed his Draft stock, his hitting and approach were better than expected in his introduction to pro ball. He's always going to be more slugger than pure hitter, but he has shown some willingness to use the opposite field and the ability to make adjustments. Though most of Jordan's value will come from his bat, he has worked hard to improve his conditioning, quickness and defense at third base. He has soft hands and might become adequate at the hot corner, but his average arm and below-average speed and range fit better at first base. His size, power and defensive limitations have prompted comparisons to Matt Holliday and Mark Trumbo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top high school prospects expected to be in the 2021 class until he reclassified in May 2019, Jordan became one of the youngest players (17 years, five months on Draft day) and best power hitters in the 2020 crop. He won his first national home run derby at age 11, smacked a pair of 500-foot homers at another when he was 13 and won the High School Home Run Derby at the 2019 All-Star Game. After the Red Sox cut a below-slot deal with first-round pick Nick Yorke in the 2020 Draft, they took Jordan with their next choice in the third round and used the savings to pay him $1.75 million (the equivalent of early second-round money). Jordan's value centers around his prodigious power, the product of impressive bat speed and strength that allow him to hit tape-measure shots without a lot of loft in his right-handed swing. He generates huge exit velocities and his pop already plays to all fields. There are concerns about his swing-and-miss tendencies after he struggled against older competition on the prep showcase circuit, though the Red Sox thought he showed a promising feel for hitting and the ability to adapt his approach during his introduction to pro ball in instructional league last fall. Jordan has worked diligently to lose weight, gain quickness and improve at third base, and he spent a good deal of time in instructs focusing on his defense. He has soft hands and average arm strength but his below-average speed and range have most scouts believing he's destined for first base. Regardless of his position, most of his value will come from his offensive game, which has drawn him comparisons to Matt Holliday and Mark Trumbo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hawkins was limited by COVID protocols at the University of British Columbia in 2021 and turned to a stint in the MLB Draft League (where he struck out 32 and walked only two in 24 innings for Trenton) to boost his stock. The Padres took him in the ninth round that summer, and he was on a steady climb through the San Diego system when he underwent Tommy John surgery in August 2024. Hawkins returned as a full-time reliever at High-A and Double-A and dominated in the role, posting a 1.50 ERA and 0.85 WHIP with 80 strikeouts in 60 innings. The Padres added him to the 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible last offseason. There’s a reason why they call the fastball numero uno. The 6-foot-5 Hawkins really leans into his four-seamer and for good reason. It’s a pitch that can sit in the mid-90s with exceptional ride up in the zone, thanks to his over-the-top mechanics. He threw the pitch at least 69 percent of the time against both sides of batters, and Midwest and Texas League hitters couldn’t help but swing under it. A low-80s sweeper was his most-used secondary as a chase pitch versus righties, and there were the makings of a changeup that lacked consistent results. Hawkins pumped strikes at High-A but saw his control take a hit in a 13-game sample at Double-A, but considering he’s sticking in relief anyways, he can live with some walks. Ideally, he’ll need the slider to take a step forward to make him less predictable, but the heater is so good that he should get a chance to be at least a middle reliever in the San Diego bullpen beginning in his age-26 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canadian COVID protocols meant that Hawkins had a limited NAIA career at the University of British Columbia. His path took a trip to Trenton in the MLB Draft League, putting him on the radar in 2021, and he did so with a 2.63 ERA and 32/2 K/BB ratio in 24 frames. The Padres made him a ninth-round pick that July, signed him for $75,000 and moved him straight to full-season ball a year later. Hawkins dominated at Single-A Lake Elsinore, leading the California League with a 16.7 percent swinging-strike rate but was humbled with a move to High-A Fort Wayne (8.80 ERA, 2.09 WHIP in 15 innings). The 6-foot-5 right-hander owns a 92-95 mph fastball that explodes up in the zone from his high delivery point and tall frame. That helps it play above its already solid velocity, and Single-A hitters stood no chance. His mid-80s changeup plays well off the fastball with the way it drops late off anyone thinking they’re getting the high heat, and it was a big reason why lefties posted just a .661 OPS against him (compared to .830 for righties). He also shows a slider, but it isn’t nearly as close to the other two. Hawkins has a history of throwing strikes, and while that control backed up on him at High-A, that may have been the result of fatigue at the end of a long season. The bigger concern might be his lack of a quality third pitch, and that will determine whether he can find a spot in the back end of a Major League rotation or is better utilized as a two-weapon reliever. He made four starts back in Fort Wayne to begin 2023 before an oblique and forearm strain moved him to the IL, stopping his development chances for a time this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Villarroel has an unusual profile as a 5-foot-8 catcher who can flash solid speed once he accelerates and has started games at five different positions in each of the last two seasons. Originally signed by the Astros for $10,000 out of Venezuela in 2022, he batted .259/.351/.388 with 20 steals in 100 games between two Class A levels in 2025. The Giants acquired him straight up for Kai-Wei Teng in January. For a compact guy, Villarroel has a quick right-handed stroke that generates surprising exit velocities and at least average raw power. He makes decent swing decisions and enough contact, but he gets so pull-conscious that he produces too many rolled-over grounders. He oddly struggles against lefties, and 17 of his 18 homers in his first four seasons came against righties. Quicker than most catchers, Villarroel will lose some speed as he spends more time behind the plate. He's not a lock to stay at catcher, however, because his receiving, blocking and throwing all need considerable work. He does have solid arm strength and has played every position in pro ball except for shortstop and pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $10,000 out of Venezuela by the Astros in 2022, Villarroel features one of the more unusual profiles in the Minors. He's a 5-foot-8 catcher with solid speed who started games at five different positions over the past two seasons. The Giants acquired him in a trade for Kai-Wei Teng in January. Despite his lack of physicality, Villarroel packs surprising strength in his compact frame and has a quick right-handed swing that generates higher exit velocities than most players his age. He could produce 15-20 homers per season once he adds more muscle and starts driving balls in the air more regularly. He has decent plate discipline though he can get pull-happy and roll over grounders to the left side. If Villarroel remains at catcher, the physical demands of the position will take a toll on his offensive production as well as his quickness. He has solid arm strength but will need time to polish his receiving, blocking and throwing. He also has seen action at every other position besides shortstop and pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baumeister was a highly touted prospect coming out of The Bolles School in Jacksonville in 2021, ranking among MLB Pipeline’s Top 100 Draft prospects that year despite the former catcher’s fairly recent (at the time) move to the mound. But he revealed on Draft Day that he would honor his commitment to Florida State, so he went undrafted until the Orioles took him 63rd overall in 2023 and signed him for an over-slot bonus of $1.61 million. They sent the advanced prospect to High-A for his full-season debut, and the Rays watched him dominate for Bowling Green after acquiring him in the Trade Deadline deal for starter Zach Eflin. Baumeister is coming off an odd year that delayed a widely expected breakout. He had a terrible April and an up-and-down May before going on the injured list with a shoulder injury that kept him out until August.
