When he returned, he was lights out, with a 0.78 ERA and 20 strikeouts compared to seven walks in 20 innings over five starts for Double-A Montgomery. Then came an underwhelming stint in the Arizona Fall League, where he was fine despite taking a comebacker off his head. The righty leans mostly on his fastball, a mid-90s heater with good life and upper-90s velocity in the tank if needed. His arsenal has evolved to the point where his cutter/slider is now his top secondary pitch, although his curveball has typically been his out pitch. The Rays were encouraged with the work he did on his changeup in the AFL, and he’ll need it to create separation with his fastball, especially against lefties. Baumeister is big and strong, standing 6-foot-4 with plenty of extension down the mound, and his physicality paired with his fastball can create uncomfortable at-bats for hitters. If he can stay healthy, improve his changeup and limit walks, he’ll give the Rays another starting pitching prospect to watch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baumeister could have been picked pretty high in the 2021 Draft out of high school, having ranked among MLB Pipeline’s Top 100 Draft prospects that year as a former catcher who moved to the mound. But the Jacksonville native announced on Draft day that he would honor his commitment to Florida State and, thus, went unselected. Two years later, the Orioles took him 63rd overall, signed him for an over-slot bonus of $1.61 million and pushed him to High-A for his first full season. He was off to a nice start there before the Rays landed him as part of a three-prospect haul for starter Zach Eflin, and he turned in a dominant stretch to finish the year. Baumeister’s arsenal isn’t quite as elite as fellow Trade Deadline pickup Brody Hopkins, but he features a good combination of stuff, strike-throwing and command. He’s a fastball-dominant starter, using his heater more than half the time, and he throws that pitch in the mid-90s with good life and 97 mph in the tank if he needs it. But his curveball is his go-to out pitch, and it’s up there with the best benders in the Rays’ system. The right-hander has a starter’s frame, listed at 6-foot-4 and 224 pounds, and he’s got the makings of a full arsenal with a cutter-y slider and a changeup. It's a little bit challenging to get a read on Baumeister, in part because of how his performance fluctuates. He struggled to limit his walks as a reliever early in his college career, then he got them somewhat under control in the rotation as a Draft-eligible sophomore despite mixed overall results. He was averaging 5.5 walks per nine innings in Baltimore’s system before the trade, then only walked five batters in 29 innings (while, by the way, striking out 44 and only allowing 12 hits) with the High-A Bowling Green. A shoulder injury has kept him from taking that next leap in his first full season as a Ray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A converted catcher ranked as a high school prospect on MLB Pipeline’s Top 100, Baumeister had a chance to be picked fairly high in the 2021 Draft. But he went unselected after announcing on the day of the Draft that he was honoring his commitment to Florida State, and it wasn’t until two years later that the Orioles took him in Competitive Balance Round B with the 63rd overall pick in 2023. Baumeister signed for an over-slot $1.61 million bonus and moved to High-A Aberdeen for his first full season, posting a 3.06 ERA with a 29.5 percent strikeout rate over 70 2/3 innings. The Rays picked him up as part of a three-prospect return for Zach Eflin at the Trade Deadline. At 6-foot-4 and 224 pounds, Baumeister is a tall, physical right-hander with exciting raw stuff. His best pitches are a low-to-mid-90s fastball that can get as high as 97 mph and a playable mid-70s curve he uses to keep hitters off balance. He also can dunk in a developing cutter-like slider at times as well as a fringy changeup, but both those pitches are behind his primary offerings. The fastball shows some good riding quality up in the zone, and it’s not hard to believe Baumeister will be able to get to consistently plus velocity with it as he grows and develops. Baumeister began his college career pitching in relief and then had mixed results in the rotation as a Draft-eligible sophomore, in part because he’s had trouble at times limiting walks. He might be able to clean up those issues because of his fairly simple delivery and his size suggests he can be durable. That remains a work in progress on the pro side, but his overall pitch shapes should make for exciting additions to the Tampa Bay pipeline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres inked Contreras out of Mexico for $50,000 in July 2017, then watched as he became one of their steadiest risers. After posting a 3.61 ERA in 25 appearances (23 starts) at Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, Contreras’ stock continued to trend upward with a very impressive showing at the team’s instructional camp. That is, until he blew out his right arm during his final outing and underwent Tommy John surgery. Added to the 40-man roster last offseason, Contreras is still finding his footing in his post-procedure return to the mound at High-A Fort Wayne. Contreras doesn’t come with much physical projection to his thicker, undersized build, but his stuff has steadily ticked up since he entered the pro ranks. His fastball sits in the mid-90s, and he commands it with ease for a pitcher his age. He uses that heater to help set up one of the best curveballs in San Diego’s system, and he also has a quality changeup at his disposal to combat left-handed hitters. The clean and repeatable delivery that fuels Contreras’ strike-throwing ability also leads evaluators to project him for well-above-average command. Everything sounds promising, but first he needs to get back on the mound. Once he’s able to make up for lost time and get back on track, Contreras has the look of a future back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres inked Contreras out of Mexico for $50,000 in July 2017, then watched as he became one of their steadiest risers. After posting a 3.61 ERA in 25 appearances at Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, Contreras’ stock continued to trend upward with a very impressive showing at the team’s instructional camp. That is, until he blew out his arm during his final outing and required Tommy John surgery in November. Despite the setback, team officials remain high on Contreras, who should still be only 22 years old when he returns. Contreras doesn’t come with much physical projection to his thicker, undersized build. But his stuff has steadily ticked up since he entered the pro ranks. His fastball sits in the mid-90s, and he commands it with ease for a pitcher his age. Contreras uses that heater to help set up arguably the best the curveball in San Diego’s system, and he also has a quality changeup at his disposal to combat left-handed hitters. The clean and repeatable delivery that fuels Contreras’ strike-throwing ability also leads evaluators to project him for well above-average command. First thing’s first: Contreras needs to attack his rehab process. But with a knack for attacking hitters and an impressive blend of big league caliber pitches, Contreras has the look of a future backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansen was Mr. Reliable during his days at Texas, especially when he moved into the rotation as a sophomore and junior. He posted a 3.76 ERA with 120 strikeouts and only 19 walks over 107 2/3 innings as a junior in 2022, despite limited velocity, and that was enough to make him a third-round pick that summer. He signed for exact slot at $629,800. Hansen spent his first full season with Single-A Palm Beach, where he had a 3.12 ERA and 126 K’s in 112 2/3 frames in a rather lax assignment. He did make one late-season appearance for Triple-A Memphis, retiring all three batters he faced. The 6-foot-2 southpaw continued to sit in the 88-92 mph window with his four-seam fastball but didn’t shy away from the pitch because he could command it so well. He also showed a sinker around the same velocity. Hansen played off those with his best pitch -- a 78-82 mph sweeper that batters missed both in and out of the zone. His mid-80s changeup got a healthy amount of his chase and helped him limit righties to a .594 OPS (compared to .722 for lefties). An upper-70s curveball was a distant fifth pitch in terms of usage, but it was good for the occasional swing-and-miss too. Given his profile, Hansen needs to be able to spot the ball well if he’s going to stay effective, and so far so good on that score. He’s a pitchability lefty through and through who could settle into the back-end of a rotation, but he needs bigger challenges than the FSL to prove himself.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If \"pitchability lefty\" was in the dictionary, you might find Hansen’s picture right next to it. The southpaw was an effective hurler in all three of his years at Texas despite limited velocity, and he took a 3.76 ERA, 120 strikeouts and only 19 walks over 107 2/3 innings as a junior into the 2022 Draft. He went to the Cardinals in the third round, becoming the organization’s third straight collegiate southpaw at the top of the Draft, and signed for exact slot at $629,800. Hansen’s fastball barely reached over 90 mph for much of his time as a Longhorn and was in the 88-92 mph range, occasionally tickling mid-90s, in his final spring in Austin. But his 78-82 mph slider helped drive up his K count, thanks to plus horizontal and vertical action that made it difficult to touch against batters from either side. He also mixed in an 72-76 mph curveball, though he's mostly pocketed it so far at Single-A Palm Beach. His low-80s changeup with decent fade keeps righties honest. The former Texas ace makes it all work because of his control coming out of a near-effortless delivery. He knows exactly where he wants to put it, and he puts it there with relative ease. That feel for location gives hope that he could be a potential No. 5 starter, even without the velocity, but he needs to see higher levels soon heading into his age-23 season in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Hit: 40 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 The Padres were one of the finalists for Roki Sasaki in 2025, and if they had landed him, he would have fit right in alongside Ethan Salas (2023) and Leo De Vries (2024) as top international prospects who joined the San Diego system in successive seasons. When they didn’t land the big fish, the Padres pivoted and added three of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects, including No. 35 Coronil, who signed for $900,000 out of Venezuela. He got his career off to a slow start in the Dominican Summer League, where he slashed .186/.327/.214 with no homers in 45 games. A switch-hitter, Coronil shot up to 6-foot-3 before signing and is still maturing physically as he builds out that frame, so some growing pains were to be expected out of the gate. That said, his 27 percent strikeout rate would set off alarms at any level, especially the DSL where pitchers are equally raw. Coronil barely got work as a righty bat and went 3-for-22 (.136) from that side, highlighting how he’ll need many more reps. He could get to average power as he adds strength but will need to improve the contact alongside the slugging development. Coronil drew strong reviews for his actions and instincts as an infield defender as an amateur, and with above-average speed, he should have decent range too. He actually spent the bulk of his time at third base in the DSL, and he has the arm strength for the deep throws there. But his athleticism should get him looks at shortstop throughout his Minor League time. Coronil will still be the age of an American high-school senior in his second pro season, so he isn’t worth writing off yet as he continues to build a foundation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two straight years of taking big international swings with Ethan Salas and Leodalis De Vries, the Padres changed tact after losing out on the Roki Sasaki sweepstakes to begin 2025. The organization had its complete $6,261,600 international signing pool open to it and spread the signings around, including giving $900,000 to Coronil – a Venezuelan shortstop who had trained with David Concepción Jr. at his academy in Cagua. A switch-hitter, Coronil moves quickly through the zone from both sides of the plate, though he looked inconsistent in the box at times before signing. His impact potential is very much dependent on his projection. Only 17 at time of signing, he shot up in height to 6-foot-3 and is still working to add on muscle. He has the frame for at least average pop, but his swing was geared for contact as an amateur, making some believe he’d work best as a future tablesetter. Even as he’s grown, Coronil has still drawn strong reviews for his defensive work at shortstop. He has fluid actions for the premium spot on the infield, and his instincts give him another leg up. Mix in above-average speed and arm strength, and there’s the potential for him to be an elite fielder. If he can improve his strength to go with the overall athleticism, there is tremendous upside and ceiling in Coronil’s profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bastardo had grown into one of the Red Sox highest-upside pitching prospects since they signed him out of Venezuela for $35,000, but underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2024. The Blue Jays, chasing his long-term upside, selected him in December’s Rule 5 Draft. Bastardo sported a 5.36 ERA through 10 starts at Double-A before going under the knife, but now that he’s with the Blue Jays, he’ll have most of the 2025 season to round out his rehab process. When healthy, Bastardo has a very advanced changeup for his age, potentially his best offering. That was one of the Blue Jays’ main attractions to Bastardo, on top of a heater that sat 93-95 mph while touching 97. His breaking balls are closer to average, but there’s clearly a starter’s arsenal in there, and if that doesn’t work down the road, the Blue Jays could try to max out his arm talent as a reliever. The rehab will slow any process, of course, but Bastardo got up to 119 1/3 innings in 2023. This is a fascinating piece of roster management by the Blue Jays, who tend to get creative the odd time they dip into the Rule 5 Draft. If they can find a way to keep Bastardo long term, it’ll be a major win for the organization as it looks to add high-upside pitching talent any way possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest bargain in Boston's 2018-19 international class, Bastardo signed for $35,000 out of Venezuela. He didn't reach full-season ball until 2022 but has been one of the better Red Sox pitching performers in the lower Minors the past two years. He had one of the best outings in their system last year, striking out 14 in a seven-inning shutout in High-A in late July, but tired down the stretch. He made 10 starts for Double-A Portland in 2024 before needing Tommy John surgery. When the Red Sox left Bastardo off the 40-man in the offseason, the Blue Jays selected him in the Rule 5 Draft as an upside pick. Bastardo's best offering is a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink that helped him limit left-handers to a .190 average last season. He sets it up with a 93-95 mph fastball that reaches 97, though it doesn't feature good shape and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it well. He sports a pair of average breaking balls, with his low-80s curveball perhaps slightly better than his tight mid-80s slider. If Bastardo can develop more consistency with his arsenal and his ability to command it, he could be a back-of-the-rotation starter. He’ll spend much of his Rule 5 year rehabbing, allowing Toronto to keep closer eyes on him without the Major League pressure out of the gate. But he’ll still have to prove his stuff has returned post-TJ to give himself a true MLB shot in his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 As an amateur, Haskin drew comparisons to George Springer, another toolsy right-handed center fielder who starred at Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School. He was drafted in the 39th round in 2018 by the A’s and then by the Orioles with the 39th pick in 2020 out of Tulane, signing with Baltimore for full pick value ($1,906,800) after shooting up Draft boards as an eligible sophomore. He’s displayed both power and speed, but rarely both at the same time. A hamstring injury and then a left hip impingement that required surgery kept him from showing much in 2023, leading the Orioles to leaving him unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft, though Haskin went unclaimed. Haskin stood out in college for excelling with an unorthodox swing, featuring a dynamic, divey load that sometimes resulted in an awkward finish. He’s quieted his front side quite a bit since then, but has tinkered with his swing continuously as a pro. Standing taller and ditching the leg kick led to a breakout year in the power department at Double-A Bowie. Haskin then resurfaced an abridged version of the leg kick last year at Norfolk. He’s always managed the strike zone well (career .376 on-base percentage) and barreled balls consistently, and his power spike at Double-A came without any increase to his strikeout rate. However, Haskin did swing-and-miss a lot more in a small sample at Triple-A before the injury last spring. Haskin broke Springer’s stolen-base record in high school and his best tool is still his speed. He has good defensive instincts and a nose for the ball in the outfield, and is athletic enough to potentially remain in center field long term. He’ll need to get past his rash of injuries and prove durability behind a mass of outfield depth in the big leagues and at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of high school and then the 2020 Draft, Haskin was compared to All-Star outfielder George Springer, another toolsy right-handed center fielder who starred at Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School. Unlike Springer, though, Haskin was drafted twice — first by the A’s in the 39th round in 2018 and then by the Orioles with the 39th pick in the 2020 Draft. The O’s signed Haskin for full pick value ($1,906,800) after he shot up draft boards as a draft-eligible sophomore at Tulane. Haskin then displayed both power (five homers) and speed (22 steals) during a solid debut season in 2021, despite being limited to 83 games by a thumb fracture. He built on those results in 2022 at Double-A Bowie, where, propelled by a three-homer game in April, Haskin socked 15 homers with a .821 OPS in 109 games. The uptick in power didn’t come at the expense of plate discipline (.367 OBP), but Haskin did run much less (five steals in eight attempts) at Bowie than he did at lower levels. While Haskin did reach Triple-A in 2023, he missed time early with a hamstring injury, then was shut down again in late June and ended up requiring surgery to repair a left hip impingement. Haskin excelled in college with an unorthodox swing, utilizing a dynamic, divey load and sometimes awkward finish that drew comparisons to Hunter Pence. He’s quieted it up significantly since college, ditching the leg kick he used at Tulane and starting from a taller, less crouched position that allows him to leverage his contact against better pitching. Haskin has always managed the strike zone well and barreled balls consistently; with that better leverage, the power he used to flash showed up more regularly in 2022. In addition to that offensive potential, Haskin’s best tools are his glove and his speed. He’s a plus runner who broke Springer’s school stolen-base record in high school, with good instincts and a nose for the ball in the outfield. His athletic skillset suggests he will be able to remain in center field long term, giving Haskin the ceiling of a big league regular who can do a little bit of everything offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An athletic center fielder with both power and speed, Haskin has long drawn easy comparisons to All-Star outfielder George Springer, who preceded Haskin at Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School by a decade. One difference between them is Haskin was drafted twice, first by the A’s in the 39th round in 2018 and then by the Orioles with the 39th pick in the 2020 Draft. Haskin signed for full pick value ($1,906,800) after two years at Tulane, rocketing up draft boards as a draft-eligible sophomore. Haskin held his own at Baltimore’s instructional camp in 2020 and then enjoyed a solid debut season in 2021, posting a .381 on-base percentage with five homers and 22 steals while reaching High-A Aberdeen. He was, however, limited to 83 games by a thumb fracture. The easiest thing to notice about Haskin is his unorthodox swing, which has drawn comparisons to Hunter Pence. It’s dynamic and divey, with Haskin striding from a significantly crouched stance and sometimes finishing in awkward positions. He’s quieted it up some since college, ditching the leg kick he used at Tulane for better timing after showing some swing-and-miss during his first pro season. But Haskin also manages the strike zone well and barrels the ball consistently, and the power he flashed at Tulane showed up in spurts during his debut summer as well. He is a potential double-plus runner who broke Springer’s stolen base record at Avon Old Farms, and shows good instincts and an average arm defensively. The athleticism and skillset lead many to believe Haskin will be able to stick in center field long-term, giving him the ceiling of a big league regular who can do a little bit of everything offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School produced an athletic center fielder in 2008 who went on to become a first-round pick after three years in college and an eventual star with the Astros -- George Springer. A decade later, the Beavers spawned another toolsy center fielder who should go early in the 2020 Draft as a sophomore-eligible. A 39th-round pick by the Athletics in 2018, Haskin batted .372/.459/.647 as a Tulane freshman and helped his cause by performing well with wood bats in the New England Collegiate Baseball League during the summer. Though Haskin's right-handed swing can get long at times, he still manages to barrel the ball consistently. His stroke is quick and has nice loft, and once he fills out his lean 6-foot-2 frame he could produce 20 or more homers annually. He manages the strike zone well, though his ability to make contact with ease does cut into his walks. Haskin's speed grades as at least plus. Though he broke Springer's stolen base record at Avon Old Farms, he hasn't been especially aggressive on the bases in college. He tracks balls well in center field, showing good instincts and an average arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee’s top signing in the 2023 international class, Rodriguez turned pro for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic. He held his own as the youngest regular (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League last season, slashing .250/.343/.383 with 36 extra-base hits in 110 games. The Red Sox acquired him along with a Competitive Balance Round A Draft pick and a player to be named in exchange for Quinn Priester this April. Rodriguez stands in the box as a 6-foot-1 left-handed hitter and twists slightly in before uncoiling on his swings. One of his standout traits in 2024 was his ability to focus on pitches in the zone, thus limiting chase and producing a healthy walk rate, especially for someone with his limited experience. His power should be average as he catches up to more age-level competition, but the Brewers were working to add a little verticality to his swing to produce more line drives and fly balls that will allow the power to play more. Rodriguez is a solid runner who may lack the speed to stick in center field over the long haul. His arm, which stands out more for its accuracy than its pure strength, would work in right field if needed. The teenager has plenty of developmental runway ahead of him and will get the time and space needed to become a potential well-rounded outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have done well with top international signings in recent years. Jackson Chourio (2021) is the obvious example, as he’s climbed from the Dominican Summer League to become one of the best prospects in the sport, and Luis Lara (2022) took a similar path to reach High-A at just 18 years old. Fellow outfielder Rodriguez -- the top Milwaukee signing in 2023 at $1.5 million -- could follow in their tracks and in a few ways already has. He slashed .253/.393/.449 with six homers and more walks (41) than strikeouts (40) over 52 games in the DSL last season. The left-handed slugger has already impressed Milwaukee officials with how easy he can make the game look, showing off above-average power without much effort or posting impressive sprint speeds without straining. His approach, as evidenced by the BB/K ratio, might be the most advanced part of his game as he doesn’t expand the zone often and shows solid bat-to-ball skills when he does swing. The raw pop is at least above average, but as Rodriguez’s swing stands, it results in more ground balls (44.9 percent) so elevation will be worth following as he matures. Rodriguez’s speed makes him a solid fit in center field, and he has enough arm strength to play the corners -- an important quality considering Milwaukee’s organizational depth up the middle. There was some discussion about sending the then-17-year-old stateside for a late-season challenge in 2023, but that will come this summer instead as Rodriguez forges his own path in the Brewers’ fast lane.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Serna signed with the Yankees for $10,000 out of Mexico in 2019 before the pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021, allowing him to play the first two seasons of his career alongside his cousin, righty pitching prospect Luis Serna. After two years in Rookie ball, Jared broke out with 19 homers in 95 Single-A games in 2023, then climbed to Triple-A by the end of last season. After acquiring him in a three-prospect package for Jazz Chisholm Jr. last July, the Marlins protected him on their 40-man roster in November. Though he's just 5-foot-7 and 168 pounds, Serna surprisingly has solid raw pop and wants to make the most of it. He focuses on hitting balls hard to his pull side, and he might reach 20 homers per season if he learns to drive them in the air more consistently. Despite his power-seeking mentality, he still makes consistent contact with his compact right-handed stroke, though more patience would help against more advanced pitching. Serna's max-effort swing slows him down coming out of the batter's box, but he can flash solid speed underway and looks to make things happen on the bases. More dependable than flashy at shortstop, he has fringy range and arm strength, making him better suited for second base. He also has seen action at third base and both outfield corners in the past, adding to his versatility as a potential utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The cousin of Yankees pitching prospect Luis Serna, Jared signed with New York for $10,000 out of Mexico in 2019 but didn't make his pro debut until two years later because of the pandemic. He made the Single-A Florida State League postseason All-Star team after batting .283/.350/.483 with 19 homers in 95 games there in 2023, though he didn't go deep in 27 contests following a promotion to High-A. He rediscovered his pop at that level this year before the Yankees included him in a three-prospect package to acquire Jazz Chisholm Jr. from the Marlins in July. Serna has a naturally compact right-handed stroke and makes good swing decisions, allowing him to make repeated contact. He looks to pull the ball and hits the ball harder than expected for a 5-foot-7, 168-pounder, creating surprisingly solid raw power. He can get too pull-conscious and will put pitches in play that he'd be better off avoiding, leading to some suboptimal groundball contact. Though he's slow out of the batter's box, Serna can flash plus speed once he gets going and is aggressive on the bases. With average range and arm strength, he's best suited for second base, but has seen more action at shortstop in 2024. He made 11 errors in 52 games at short last year, compared to just one in 60 contests at second, and also has played third base and both outfield corners in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels inked Ortiz out of the Dominican Republic for $150,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period that January. He had a so-so debut in the Dominican Summer League but handled the move stateside fairly well, showing off his carrying tool by leading the Arizona Complex League in steals with 30. He held his own with a move up to full-season ball in 2024, while also showing the areas of his game that need the most work. Ortiz just started switch-hitting in 2023 and in some ways was better from the left side, with a higher average and on-base percentage than he did from his natural right. He shook off an awful April to hit .288 with a .369 OBP from May 1 through the end of the year and made progress with his overall offensive game. While he’s never going to be a power guy at all, finding a way to add strength to his rail-thin frame would help him have a little more impact at the plate. He also needs to cut down on the swing-and-miss; his strikeout rate was a touch lower than in 2023, but he’s still has a 27.3 percent K rate in his career, not ideal for a guy who needs to get on base and run. One of the fastest players in the system, the Angels would actually like Ortiz to use his speed more, thinking the 22-for-30 in stolen base attempts showing in 2024 isn’t enough. His defense took a nice step forward in 2024, with more confidence he’ll be able to stick at shortstop long-term, and he could even be a regular if he can improve his contact and instincts on the basepaths.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It remains to be seen how good the Angels’ class from the 2022 international signing period is in the long run, but it might be the fastest. Nelson Rada, the top player signed, led the California League in stolen bases in 2023. Ortiz, who signed for $150,000 right when the period opened, had a pedestrian debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing, but then topped the Arizona Complex League in steals (30) during his United States debut in 2023. Signed as a right-handed hitter, Ortiz started to learn how to switch-hit last year and incorporated it into games with decent early results. Thin and projectable, he needs to add strength and be more physical so that he can be more than just a slap hitter. There was too much swing-and-miss in his game in the ACL, something hitting left-handed might have had to do with. Added physicality will also help his already-elite speed, which some already see as an 80 on the scouting scale. His athleticism plays in the field as well. He has good actions and range at shortstop, to go along with the arm strength to play the premium position, but it can be inconsistent and raw. He should be able to stay up the middle no matter what, even if that means a move to second base or perhaps a look at what his speed might look like in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heredia joined the Phillies in the winter of 2021, signing for $300,000, and the early returns were very positive. He played well in the Dominican Summer League in '22 and performed well enough to climb from the Florida Complex League to full-season Clearwater the following year. He struggled with his approach -- and with staying healthy -- in '24, while better production in '25 with High-A Jersey Shore was cut short by a broken pinky. He got off to a solid start, albeit with similar approach issues, with a move to Double-A in '26. A strong and athletic right-handed-hitting outfielder, Heredia has shown glimpses of using all five tools, with hard contact from the right side of the plate and the ability to get to his power. He improved his bat-to-ball skills in 2025 after having worked with Luis Arraez's hitting guy in the offseason prior, but he'll have to watch his swing-and-miss and chase rates if he wants to keep being productive. Heredia isn't a burner and isn't much of a basestealing threat, but the strong and compact outfielder runs better than you might think. He has the kind of plus arm teams like to see in right field, and he continues to get work in both outfield corners. If he can refine his approach at the plate, he might have the offensive profile to fit in one of those spots at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies signed Heredia for $300,000 not long after the 2021 international signing period, but it wasn’t until 2022 that the organization got to see what he could do. He had a solid debut that summer in the Dominican Summer League, and then he really put himself on the map in the United States for the first time in 2023, going from the Florida Complex League to full-season ball and finishing with a .314/.392/.493 line, making him the most productive member of that signing class to date. A strong and athletic right-handed hitter, Heredia shows glimpses of all five tools. He can make hard contact and has impressive raw power that he is already showing he can get to. It’s a power-over-hit profile for sure, and he’ll have to cut his strikeout rate as he moves up the ladder and faces better pitching. He runs better than you might think given his strength/power profile. That speed helps Heredia be a solid defender in an outfield corner, which is where he’ll end up even though he’s seen some time in center early on in his career. His plus arm works from there, and if he can refine his approach, he could develop into that athletic right-field run-producer type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $350,000 in January 2022, Plaz immediately raised the expectations bar by hitting .382 with a 1.206 OPS in 32 Dominican Summer League games. There were some bumps, both of the production and injury variety, when he came to the United States, though he did start to find his power stroke in 2024 when he homered 15 times in the Florida State League, albeit with a ton of swing-and-miss. The injury bug bit again in 2025 with a fractured finger on his left hand limiting him to just 66 games, though he made up for lost time and swung the bat well in the Arizona Fall League. When Plaz is healthy and squares up the ball, the right-handed batter hits the ball really hard. He was in the upper echelon of Florida State League hitters in terms of data like exit velocity, barrel and hard-hit percentages. In 2025, he even cut down his strikeout rate, which had been an issue, while sticking to a better overall approach. There’s plenty of power to spare and to all fields, but he’s going to have to learn better pitch recognition after a 40 percent chase rate last season. There’s work to be done for Plaz on the defensive side of things as well. He has plenty of arm for the position, but the consistency of his receiving has been lacking. His power bat might profile at first base, but there aren’t too many sub-6-foot right-right players at that infield corner in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yordany De Los Santos and Tony Blanco Jr. were the top two bonus-getters in the 2022 international class for the Pirates, but they gave out 14 bonuses of six figures or higher. Plaz, hailing from San Felix, Venezuela, was in that mix, getting $350,000 in January and then putting up huge numbers in the Dominican Summer League. He followed up that 1.206 OPS summer with a rough go of it stateside, limited to 33 games because of injuries and finishing with a .144/.359/.237 line. He was one of the better power hitters in the Florida State League in 2024, finishing with 15 homers, but also showed what he needs to work on both in the box and behind the plate. Strong and compact, Plaz can really impact the ball with quality hard contact from the right side of the plate. He has good bat speed but is a bit of a free swinger, leading to a 28.4 percent strikeout rate and overall high miss-and-chase rates while with Bradenton. He does draw walks, but he'll need to refine his approach so he can get to his power more consistently with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, though most of his over-the-fence pop has come to his pull side. Plaz's best tool defensively is his arm, which is at least above average, but the rest of his catching needs work. Some of it is focus-related and could improve with maturity and more reps, but he doesn't always block or receive well and has seen time at first, where a right-right 5-foot-11 profile might be tough. If the light switches on, he could be a power-first, power-armed backstop in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Rhodes became one of the top sophomore-eligible hitters in his class after the 2021 Draft was moved from June to July that year, going in the third round to the Orioles and signing for an above-slot $1.38 million. Rhodes was coming off a down year at Kentucky after breaking out as a freshman the previous year and raking in the Northwoods League that summer. The Orioles decided to bet on that small sample and then saw Rhodes enjoy a solid debut and reach Double-A down the stretch in 2022. He plateaued a bit back at Bowie in 2023 and didn’t hit much during an extended stay in the Arizona Fall League. Rhodes did tap into his raw power more in ‘23, hitting 17 homers with 22 doubles in 108 games at Bowie. But more than two full seasons in, he’s yet to duplicate his early success at Kentucky. The power stood out last summer as the most improved of the blend of tools that have always been Rhodes’ calling card and still has a chance to be solid across the board. But he’ll need to keep working to refine his overall approach and avoid the extended slumps that have zapped his productivity for long stretches. Where Rhodes is not searching for success is on the bases. He doesn’t run all that often, but when he does, he’s used his plus straight-line speed to convert 30 of 31 stolen-base chances as a pro. That speed and his strong arm help him profile at either corner outfield spot, and while he is athletic enough to handle center in a pinch, those opportunities dried up entirely last year. The versatility is a plus, and points to a possible fourth-outfielder role in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles went all-in on college outfielders in the 2021 Draft, selecting four with their first five picks in executive vice president and general manager Mike Elias’ third Draft at the helm. Their third-round selection was Rhodes, who had become one of the top sophomore-eligible hitters available after the Draft was moved from June to July that year. Rhodes was coming off a down year at Kentucky, after bursting onto the scene with a .426/.485/.672 line in 17 games as a freshman and then raking in the Northwoods League that summer. The Orioles signed him for an above-slot $1.38 million, and after a solid debut, watched him reach Double-A Bowie down the stretch in 2022. He slumped initially at the level after hitting .259/.389/.428 with five homers in 58 games at High-A Aberdeen, despite missing three weeks with a minor wrist injury. Rather than one otherworldly tool, Rhodes’ calling card is a blend of tools with the potential to be solid across the board. He’s strong enough to flash power that could be at least average, with a quick right-handed swing but an inconsistent approach that leads to slumps. He’s always had the ability to work the count and showed good plate discipline both at Kentucky and throughout his Minor League career. Rhodes began using his plus straight-line speed more on the bases last summer, swiping 16 bags without being caught (he owns a 100 percent SB success rate in pro ball, with 16 steals in 16 tries). He shifted from third base to left field to right field during his time at Kentucky but is strictly an outfielder now, playing predominately right during his first two seasons. His strong arm profiles well out there, and he’s athletic enough to move across all three spots and even play center in a pinch. That versatility should help him develop into a bat-first regular who swings his way into the lineup if he continues to hit consistently at the higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles have shown an appetite for drafting college bats under executive vice president and general manager Mike Elias and in 2021 went big on college outfielders, selecting four with their first five picks. Their third-round pick was Rhodes, who became eligible for the 2021 Draft after it was moved from June to July and quickly became one of the top sophomore-eligible hitters available in his class. Rhodes had turned heads by hitting .426/.485/.672 in 17 games during his shortened freshman season at Kentucky, and continuing to rake in the Northwoods League that summer. Then his slumped in ’21, but still signed for an above-slot $1.38 million. Rhodes next got his feet wet at Low-A Delmarva, posting a .343 on-base percentage and two homers in 23 games alongside fellow ’21 draftees Colton Cowser, Reed Trimble and Donta’ Williams (all outfielders), then reached Double-A in his first full season in 2022. Rhodes stands out for his potential for solid tools across the board, with the strength for at least average power and a strong but inconsistent approach. Rhodes’ slumps at Kentucky came when he tried selling out for power, compromising the quick right-handed swing that made him look like an advanced hitter as a freshman. He’s always had the ability to work the count and showed good plate discipline at Delmarva, walking at an impressive clip in a small sample. Rhodes has plus straight-line speed but doesn’t show it much on the bases, and a strong arm that’s allowed him to move around defensively since starting college. He shifted from third base to left field to right field during his time at Kentucky, and played mostly right field during his pro debut. The Orioles also gave Rhodes some early reps at first base; he’s athletic enough for the versatility to be a good thing, with some believing he may be quick enough to even merit a look in center field. If Rhodes hits consistently, he has a chance to develop into a bat-first regular who swings his way into the lineup every day at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hendrick had an up-and-down summer showcase circuit in 2019, at times looking like one of the top high school power hitters in the country and at times looking lost, though he did play for USA Baseball’s 18U team that won silver at the World Cup in Korea. His 2020 season in the Pittsburgh area was all but wiped out by the pandemic, but the Reds bought his power potential at No. 12 overall that summer and signed him for $4 million. Since then, the outfielder has had trouble finding his groove at the plate. After shaking off an injury-riddled first full season, Hendrick’s prodigious power did show up in games in 2022 as he homered 21 times in 388 at-bats. That unfortunately also came with a 37.2 percent strikeout rate across two levels of A ball, but there were some signs of things clicking, albeit inconsistently, cutting down the swing-and-miss a little and getting to his power over the last month and change of last season. He needs to slow himself down and let his barrel stay in the zone a bit longer, with more than enough strength if he can focus with a left-center-field approach, the left-handed hitter has a chance to produce more regularly. Hendrick is a good athlete who runs pretty well and can steal a base. While he’s best suited in right field -- where his strong arm also profiles well -- he’s shown he’s more than capable of playing center field if needed. He’ll need to find a way to make consistent contact to profile well as a regular in either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds certainly haven’t been afraid to take hitters with their top pick in Drafts over the years, going the position player route with their first selection in five of the last seven years. Three of those have been college players and two have been high school, with catcher Tyler Stephenson going No. 11 back in 2015 and Hendrick going No. 12 overall in 2020. The Pittsburgh area prep standout’s debut in 2021 was a bit of a mixed bag, showing off some of the offensive tools that made him worth a $4 million bonus, but also struggling to make contact and dealing with a leg injury that limited him to just 63 games in Low-A in 2021. Healthy in 2022, the power showed up, but consistency remained elusive. Hendrick still has the raw tools as a left-handed hitter that got scouts excited when he was in high school, with elite bat speed and strength which leads to tremendous raw power. He showed flashes of getting to that power during his debut, and while he showed patience (19.2 percent walk rate) he also struck out way too much (37.6 percent), a trend that continued in 2022. It was more about focusing too much on launch angle power to his pull side than it was about chasing out of the zone or poor pitch recognition, and there’s hope he can make adjustments to get back to a gap-to-gap approach that allows him to get to his power more naturally. Hendrick has trimmed down and is more agile and mobile than he’d been previously, with some thinking he’s moving well enough to play center field. He likely fits better in right field, where his above-average arm would play well, with the hope that he can find a level of consistency to fit the power profile for the corner spot as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Pittsburgh area isn’t exactly known as a huge amateur baseball hotbed, there have been some first-round quality bats to come out of the high school ranks in the region. Back in 2003, the Pirates took Neil Walker No. 11 overall and more recently, Alex Kirilloff went 15th to the Twins in 2016. In 2020, it was Hendrick’s turn when the Reds took him at No. 12 and signed him for $4 million, then saw him impress late in the alternate camp and during instructional league play. At his best, Hendrick’s left-handed bat is what stands out the most. He has as much raw power as anyone from the 2020 Draft and when he’s on time at the plate, it’s shown up in games against very good competition. He has very quick hands and plus bat speed, with leverage and loft and the ball jumps off his bat, while the bat head going through the zone sounds like a helicopter. He has, at times, listened to too many people in terms of his setup at the plate, forcing him get out of sync and leading to more swing-and-miss. There’s some rawness to his game, but that will be offset by the plus work ethic that was on display last summer after he signed. Hendrick isn’t a burner, but he is very athletic and runs well. The Reds will let him continue to play center field for now until he shows he can’t handle staying up the middle, but he has the arm and bat to profile well in right, so don’t be surprised to see him get time in both spots in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto originally signed with the Rockies out of Venezuela in July 2019 for $120,000, and came to the Blue Jays organization along with Raimel Tapia in the Randal Grichuk deal in '22. Since then, Pinto’s career has been defined by a string of injuries, but the flashes we’ve seen in between those moments have been tantalizing. Pinto appeared in just 19 games with High-A Vancouver in 2025, but launched seven home runs with a .985 OPS. Don’t expect Pinto’s power to look like that over the course of a full season, as he’s listed at just 5-foot-6. But his offensive upside, speed and ability to play multiple positions still have real value, even with so little game action in recent seasons. The Blue Jays are planning to simplify things for Pinto, focusing much more on second base alone, and you may not see him running as often, even though he has the ability to steal 30-plus bags a season. If the organization can get him to play in 100 contests, then they can expand his game again in ‘27 and beyond. Pinto remains a favorite among coaches and staff who have seen these glimpses. He plays the game with his hair on fire, which might not help on the injury front, but there’s still an exciting bench player in here -- and a fan favorite -- if he can stay on the field and develop some actual routines. That health aspect is one of the biggest “what if's” on this list, but Pinto’s raw ability keeps him ranked for at least one more season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto originally signed with the Rockies out of Venezuela in July 2019 for $120,000, but due to the pandemic and the lost 2020 Minor League season, he didn’t make his professional debut until 2021. Pinto won the Dominican Summer League MVP award that season, batting .360 with a .487 OBP and 41 steals in 54 games. When Pinto was dealt to the Blue Jays with Raimel Tapia for Randal Grichuk, he was an immediate organizational favorite and that hasn’t changed, even as injuries slowed his development. This is a young player who Blue Jays staffers are extremely excited -- and hopeful -- to see for a full season. Pinto dealt with a rib injury in 2024, which limited him to just 26 games, but he hit .330 with a .951 OPS. He rolled that into an Arizona Fall League season nearly as long, at 25 games, in which he put up a line of .274/.392/.357. Now it’s time for the Blue Jays to see what Pinto can do across 100+ games as a prospect who could pile up stats in several categories. Pinto is just 5-foot-6, but generates enough power to be more than just a speed-and-contact threat. He’s focusing on becoming a better basestealer too, using the athleticism that also makes him a sharp defender all over the diamond. All of the raw tools and the flashes we’ve seen from Pinto have been very encouraging, but again, they’ve only been flashes. If it all comes together for Pinto, he could someday profile as a fantastic bench piece on a good MLB roster, bouncing between the infield, outfield and pinch-running spots. Pinto gives it everything he's got and surely would become an immediate Blue Jays fan favorite, but the first step is a full, healthy season. Games played will be the most important stat for Pinto in 2025, but if that number finally starts to climb, he’ll command some attention in this system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto originally signed with the Rockies out of Venezuela in July 2019 for $120,000, but due to the pandemic and the lost 2020 Minor League season, he didn’t make his professional debut until 2021. All Pinto did was win the Dominican Summer League MVP that season, batting .360 with a .487 OBP and 41 steals in 54 games. When Pinto was dealt to the Blue Jays with Raimel Tapia for Randal Grichuk, some within the organization believed this could eventually be known as “the Adrian Pinto trade.” Pinto was challenged with a Single-A assignment in 2022 and hit .242 with a .375 OBP, 24 walks and 32 strikeouts over 47 games. These numbers were a step back, but the Blue Jays loved the playing style they saw in Pinto, who buzzes all over the field at top speed. That matches well with his instincts, and despite the injury-shortened ’22 season due to a hamstring issue, he spent plenty of time at the complex over the winter to make up for lost time. Listed at just 5-foot-6, there isn’t much size or power projection to Pinto, but his speed and on-base ability should make him a leadoff man at each level. He’ll continue to move all over the diamond, where his raw athleticism gives him potential in both the infield and outfield. Pinto was a candidate to make a major jump in 2023 but quad injuries have kept him on the injured list again for much of the summer. He needs to stay healthy and on the field to reach his otherwise intriguing potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals had a $5,179,700 international signing pool in 2022 and used $4,925,000 out of it to add Cuba native Vaquero that January. The outfielder had learned how to switch-hit after a move to the Dominican Republic and was a solid producer in the Dominican Summer League and Florida Complex League over his first two seasons of pro ball. He jumped to Single-A Fredericksburg late in 2023 and returned to the Carolina League a year later with subpar results: a .190/.291/.303, five homers and 29 steals in 103 games. He injured his left shoulder diving back to the bag in a Championship Series game on Sept. 18 and underwent surgery. Vaquero’s strikeout rate exploded in his age-19 season from 20.4 percent to 34.2 percent, the eighth-highest mark among 111 Single-A qualifiers. It wasn’t exactly a splits issue either. He struggled to make consistent contact as a batter from either side of the box, though he did a slightly better job of handling breaking balls as a righty. He has a more pronounced leg kick as a lefty, one he’ll tone down with two strikes. Given his size at 6-foot-3, there’s still room for power in his frame, and he should muscle up balls better in his 20s. A plus-plus speedster, Vaquero played all three outfield spots with the FredNats but would have likely gotten more center-field looks if not for Elijah Green’s defensive skills up the middle. His plus arm strength plays everywhere as he registered 14 outfield assists in 2024. Getting Vaquero healthy will be the primary objective to begin this season, but until he adjusts to full-season pitching, the space between his ceiling and floor remains immense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known to swing big on center fielders in recent years, the Nationals used $4.925 million of their $5,179,700 international signing pool in 2022 to bring in Vaquero, a Cuba native who moved to the Dominican Republic before signing. He learned how to switch-hit in his second country and has been relatively solid in his two years of pro ball, first in the Dominican Summer League and then split between the Florida Complex League and Single-A Fredericksburg last season. He hit .279/.410/.393 with one homer, 15 steals and a 118 wRC+ over 42 games in the FCL before his late-August promotion to full-season ball. Standing at a listed 6-foot-3, 180 pounds, Vaquero still sticks out more for his projection and potential than current production. The son of an Olympic swimmer mother and judo-fighting father, Vaquero is a true plus-plus runner who should constantly give pitchers and catchers something to think about on the basepaths. His wheels also serve him well in center, and he has enough arm strength for right, where he played mostly in Fredericksburg because of the presence of Elijah Green. There’s still plenty of room for him to fill out as well, so while he’s managed only two homers to this point, Vaquero still projects for above-average power as he matures. It'll take some offensive development to get there, however, on top of the physical. Vaquero remains more advanced from the left side (where he has a more open stance) as he acclimates to switch-hitting; he struck out in 40 percent of his right-handed plate appearances over a relatively small 2023 sample. He shows continued patience at the dish though, and as he returns to the Carolina League for his age-19 season, the Nats will continue to exhibit their own patience in his ascent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals had $5,179,700 in their international signing pool for the 2022 period and used $4,925,000 on Vaquero alone, making him the highest signee in his class. The Cuba native had moved to the Dominican Republic, where he picked up switch-hitting before signing, and stayed in the DR for his first taste of the Minors, hitting .256/.379/.341 with nine extra-base hits and 17 steals in 55 games in the Dominican Summer League. Vaquero’s mother was an Olympic swimmer and his father a judo fighter, and it’s clear the 18-year-old picked up their athletic genes. He’s already a plus-plus runner, and the Nats leaned into that by placing him exclusively in center field in the DSL. His arm should work in center as well. However, Vaquero didn’t show a ton of power at the Minors’ lowest level, in part because he hit a plurality of balls on the ground, and the pop he did exhibit came from his natural left-handed side (slugging .358 there compared to .250 as a righty) as he continues to get comfortable as a switch-hitter. Listed at 6-foot-3, 180 pounds entering 2023, Vaquero has plenty of projection remaining to get to his at least above-average power potential, and his overall approach, in which he walked nearly as much as he struck out, adds to that promise. He’ll still only be 18 for much of his first summer playing stateside, where he’ll pick up the at-bats to develop into a potential star up-the-middle talent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Cuba, Vaquero comes from an athletic family -- his mother is an Olympic swimmer and his father is a competitor in judo. He moved to the Dominican Republic and learned to switch-hit there before becoming eligible for the latest international signing window. The Nats spent $4,925,000 of their $5,179,700 signing pool to add MLB Pipeline’s No. 2 international prospect to their potential farm-system rebuild in January. Vaquero, who turned 17 last September, is as skilled as Washington’s heavy investment would indicate. He has true five-tool potential, starting with plus speed that should translate well to the basepaths and center field in the pro game. Those wheels stand out all the more given Vaquero’s size at 6-foot-3. As he grows even more into that frame, true plus power at the plate should be possible as well. His move to switch-hitting has improved his pitch recognition, but he’ll need more time to prove he’s just as capable of hitting from the right side as he is from his more natural side on the left. Vaquero has the potential to be the face of the Nationals farm system for a long time. It’s worth remembering that he’s still the age of an American high-schooler as he begins his Minor League career, and he may need some developmental space to get his many tools in line, as most teenagers do. If it all clicks, he could be the organization’s biggest international success story since Juan Soto.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching well as a reliever at South Carolina, Mahoney had to wait until 2023 to show what he could do for an encore after Tommy John surgery knocked out his sophomore season, though he did get some at-bats while he was rehabbing. He was an effective starter in the Gamecocks rotation upon his return in 2023, showing enough stuff and athleticism to land in the third round with the Rockies. He spent most of the year with Single-A Fresno and earned a late bump up to High-A Spokane, showing good command of his stuff over 120 innings. With a sturdy 6-foot-3 frame, Mahoney appears built to eat innings. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph, sitting more around 93 mph, and it has good natural sink to it that helps him get ground-ball outs. His changeup might now be his best secondary offering, thrown in the mid-80s with good fade and the ability to miss bats and get weak contact. His slider, also around the mid-80s, can also be an out pitch at times, with horizontal and vertical break. A former high school quarterback and position player, Mahoney’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and fill up the strike zone, providing a good combination of pitching to contact to get ground balls and miss bats. His time with Spokane wasn’t as smooth, so he’ll have to work on his overall command within the zone, but he has the makings of a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mahoney started putting his name on the map for the 2023 Draft back in '21 with a dominant freshman year spent mostly in relief. But he became a question mark when he blew out his elbow that May and Tommy John surgery kept him off the mound for all of 2022. He was in the Gamecocks' rotation in 2023 and was their best starter, showcasing a three-pitch mix and athleticism on the mound that helped him land in the third round with the Rockies, who didn’t have him do much after signing following a heavy workload during the spring in his first year post-surgery. A 6-foot-3 right-hander, Mahoney saw his stuff bounce back pretty well upon his return. It starts with a fastball that tops out at 97 mph and sits in the 92-95 range with late natural sink to it. His mid-80s slider can be inconsistent, but at its best, it has horizontal and vertical break. He throws his changeup with the same velocity, and when it’s on, it features good fade. He has the ability to get outs early in counts on the ground, as well as strike guys out. Mahoney is a good athlete who quarterbacked his high school football team and even hit a couple of home runs in 2022 for South Carolina while he was rehabbing his elbow. He has a feel of what he wants to do on the mound, though he’ll need to keep refining his command and control of his repertoire. It’s a pretty good rotation piece starter kit, with perhaps a leap forward to come another year removed from the elbow surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best college bats in the 2021 class and the Pacific-12 Conference Player of the Year that spring at Oregon, Zavala went in the second round that July. A post-Draft physical revealed a mass at the top of his cervical spine, a medical anomaly that left him with a well-below-slot $830,000 bonus but hasn't affected him in pro ball. After a successful first full pro season in 2022, he blew out his right (throwing) elbow in the Arizona Fall League and had internal brace surgery that cost him the first six weeks of last season. His left-handed swing got out of whack and he never recovered, slashing .194/.343/.284 with a 37.3 percent strikeout rate at Double-A. Known for making consistent hard contact with bat speed, hand-eye coordination and a disciplined approach, Zavala never looked like himself in 2023. He got too passive and his contact rate and exit velocities plummeted when he did swing the bat. Assuming that he does return to previous form, to win an everyday job he'll have to demonstrate that he has more than fringy power and that he can handle southpaws after they dominated him in each of the past two seasons. Zavala is a decent athlete with average speed but he isn't very daring on the bases. He gets the job done on the outfield corners and has seen more action in right field during pro ball, though his average arm may be better suited for left. The Rangers are stacked in terms of young outfielders, so he risks getting buried if he doesn't bounce back quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zavala established himself as one of the best college bats in the 2021 Draft, winning Pac-12 Conference Player of the Year honors after setting Oregon records for on-base percentage (.525), runs scored (64) and walks (50). The Rangers selected him in the second round, making him the highest-drafted Ducks position player since the program resumed in 2009, but a post-Draft physical revealed a mass at the top of his cervical spine. The medical anomaly left him with a well below-slot $830,000 bonus but wasn't an issue last year, when he led qualified hitters in the system in OBP (.420) and ranked second in OPS (.873) while reaching Double-A in his first full pro season. Zavala makes contact with ease thanks to his quick left-handed stroke, hand-eye coordination and patient approach. Though he's clearly a hit-over-power guy and lets balls travel deep while judiciously using the entire field, he does hit the ball hard and could produce 20 homers per season if he turns on and lifts pitches more regularly. The only concern with him at the plate is his ability to handle left-handers after he slashed .183/.318/.269 against them last year, compared to .309/.454/.515 versus right-handers. An average runner and athlete, Zavala has decent instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He has spent most of his college and pro career in right field, though his average arm may be better suited for left. He injured his right (throwing) elbow in the Arizona Fall League, requiring internal brace surgery that cost him the first six weeks of the 2023 season, and he hasn't looked like his normal self at the plate for much of the year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best bats in the 2021 college class, Zavala was named Pacific-12 Conference player of the year after setting Oregon records for on-base percentage (.525), runs (65) and walks (50) last spring. The Rangers popped him in the second round, making him the highest-drafted Ducks position player since the program was brought back in 2009. After a medical anomaly was revealed during his post-Draft physical, he signed for a well below-slot $830,000, but he looked like his normal hitterish self while advancing to Low-A in his pro debut. Zavala has advanced bat-to-ball skills and makes repeated contact with his quick, compact left-handed swing and disciplined approach. He concentrates on drilling line drives from gap to gap and controlling the strike zone, but Texas thinks he has untapped power. He worked on some adjustments to his stance and setup during instructional league to unleash some more pop, and he might be able to deliver 15-20 homers on an annual basis if he looks to launch more balls in the air. Zavala's speed, arm and outfield defense all grade as average and he fits best in left field despite spending most of his 22-game debut in right field. He also caught in high school and played mostly third base during the truncated 2020 college season. His hitting ability and strong makeup could allow him to rise quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two years ago, Bitsko was considered a top prospect in the 2021 Draft class, but he chose to reclassify and become eligible for the Draft in 2020. Bitsko said he made the decision to reclassify “to further my career,” but he was dealt a significant setback before it really even began. In December 2020, a matter of months after the Rays took Bitsko 24th overall and signed him for an above-slot $3 million bonus, he underwent surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right shoulder. It’s been a slow recovery and return process for Bitsko since that procedure. He was healthy coming into the season, but the Rays have used him cautiously, beginning with an assignment to the Florida Complex League in early June. He’s made abbreviated and inconsistent starts in the Sunshine State since, though he was starting to show his old self in flashes entering late August. Still, the Rays picked Bitsko in the first round for a reason and remain confident in his upside. He’s big and strong, listed at 6-foot-4 and 225 pounds, and when he’s on, he has “now” stuff. His fastball reached 96-97 mph at the East Coast Pro Showcase, sitting between 92-96, and he throws a hard curveball that should be a plus, swing-and-miss pitch. He also throws a slider, shows a feel for his changeup and has the potential to develop plus command of all his pitches. He’ll need a lot of time to get healthy and develop, and the Rays are already hesitant enough to rush their young pitchers. But if he comes all the way back, he has a considerably high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The scouting industry had seen a good amount of Bitsko, even though he was thought to be one of the top high school arms in the Class of 2021. But when the big right-hander from Eastern Pennsylvania announced that he'd be graduating early, that made him eligible for this year's Draft and put him right up with the top prep arms in the country. Bitsko is 6-foot-4, 220 pounds, with plenty of projection and now stuff. He stood out particularly at the East Coast Pro Showcase over the summer, but he has shown consistent ability at every stop. Bitsko was up to 96-97 mph at East Coast Pro, with all fastballs in the 92- to 96-mph range. He combines it with a hard breaking ball that shows plus shape, thrown in the 78- to 82-mph range to get a lot of swings and misses. While he doesn't throw it as much, he does have solid feel for a changeup. Bitsko isn't pure power, either, showing the ability to throw all three pitches for strikes with a chance for future plus command. Teams were going to have to play some catch-up with Bitsko this spring because they weren't bearing down on him over the summer as much as they were with the incoming senior class, something that couldn't happen beyond an early bullpen session because of the shutdown. He's committed to the University of Virginia, which could come into play, but he has the chance to be an early first-round pick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De Jesus was one of the top prospects from the 2018 international class, and he started to play some shortstop after the Dodgers signed him for $500,000. He eventually came to the Blue Jays in a ‘22 trade from the Dodgers along with Mitch White and made good on his potential in ‘23 with a full-season assignment to High-A Vancouver. There, De Jesus put up an .806 OPS and played through a shoulder injury which required a procedure at the end of the season, so it will be interesting to see how his game develops when fully healthy. De Jesus played more freely in ‘23, letting his natural athleticism show. He’s far likelier to end up at third base long term than shortstop and will work in some first base in 2024. He has a very strong arm, which helps at the hot corner. Some added power would bolster this projection after he hit 11 home runs a year ago, and while his start to ‘24 could be slowed by last year’s injury, there’s enough pop in there for De Jesus to hit at least 15 annually. There’s still belief that De Jesus, who turns 23 in March, could take another step as he climbs to Double-A, but he’ll need one of his skills to pop if he’s going to stand out from the rest of Toronto’s infield depth. He did a better job of limiting strikeouts in ‘23, but that was an issue for him the year prior (151 in 114 games), so that is worth monitoring as he faces more advanced pitching. This feels like a fork-in-the-road season for De Jesus.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De Jesus was one of the top prospects from the 2018 international class, and he started to play some shortstop after the Dodgers signed him for $500,000. He chased power at times early in his Rookie-level debut, batting .281 with a .732 OPS over 57 games, but he came on strong late. Some of that power came in 2021 at Single-A Rancho Cucamonga, where he hit 12 home runs while posting a .268 average and .834 OPS over 87 games. De Jesus was in the middle of another nice season at High-A in 2022 when the Blue Jays acquired him from the Dodgers alongside Mitch White. While his Blue Jays debut was underwhelming over 24 games at High-A Vancouver, the club was very impressed with his maturity, as the fully bilingual De Jesus quickly bought in and became a good teammate. Toronto’s program has also helped him physically, with optimism that more power will follow at the plate. Defensively, De Jesus can play short and third base but is likelier to end up at the hot corner, where his plus arm can make any necessary throw. He’ll need to cut down his strikeout rate at the plate, though, after whiffing 151 times in 113 games last season. If that happens alongside a power surge, De Jesus is another candidate to jump in 2023. Alongside Adrian Pinto, the Blue Jays have done a solid job of acquiring prospects in Major League trades recently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top third-base prospects in the 2018 international class, De Jesus moved to shortstop after signing for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His 2021 full-season debut as a 19-year-old was a tale of two halves. He got too power-hungry early on and batted .210/.315/.395 with a 38 percent strikeout rate in the first two months, then made adjustments and hit .314/.440/.490 with a 25 percent whiff rate afterward. De Jesus has enough strength and bat speed that he doesn't have to lengthen his right-handed stroke and swing for the fences to hit for power. He did a better job of using the opposite field in 2021 and could become an average hitter with solid pop if he stays under control. He drew 45 walks in his final 54 games and made more consistent hard contact once he started making better swing decisions. Six-foot-2 and more physical than his listed 170 pounds, De Jesus started getting more looks back at the hot corner in 2022. He has below-average speed, though his surprisingly smooth actions and well above-average arm strength help him make plays at shortstop. His range projects as fringy at best at short but he could be at least an average defender at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best third-base prospects in the 2018 international crop, DeJesus moved to shortstop after signing for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic. When he made his pro debut the following summer, he earned a swift promotion to the Rookie-level Arizona League and didn't look overmatched despite being the circuit's second-youngest batting qualifier (age 17). The coronavirus pandemic robbed him of a chance to build on that momentum in 2020, though he did attend the Dodgers' Dominican instructional league program. Though DeJesus is young and inexperienced at the plate, he shows the potential to hit for both average and power. He has a compact right-handed stroke and already has begun to add strength and bat speed that eventually could pay off with 20 homers per season. To reach his offensive potential, he'll need to improve his pitch recognition and tone down his aggressiveness. Presently a fringy runner, DeJesus will have below-average speed at best once he fills out. He's smoother and has more range at shortstop than expected thanks to a quick first step, and he has reliable hands and solid arm strength. While he has a chance to stick at short or handle second base, most scouts outside the organization think he'll end up on the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top third-base prospects in his international crop, DeJesus moved to shortstop after signing for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2018. During his pro debut last summer, he quickly earned a promotion to the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he held his own as circuit's second-youngest batting qualifier (age 17). DeJesus has a chance to hit for both average and power. He'll need to improve his pitch recognition and discipline, but he has a compact right-handed stroke and an idea at the plate. He already has added strength and bat speed since turning pro and will continue to do so, giving him 20-homer upside. Already just a fringy runner, DeJesus figures to slow further as he matures physically. Considering his run times, he's smoother and rangier at shortstop than would be expected, and the Dodgers are working to improve his anticipation and explosiveness. His plus arm and offensive profile easily would fit at third base, where most scouts think he'll wind up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unsigned during the 2018-19 international period, Dominguez moved from Venezuela to the Dominican Republic to focus on improving his velocity. The venue change paid dividends when the Mets inked the right-hander just before his 18th birthday in November 2019. The 2020 shutdown kept Dominguez from seeing the Minors in his first season, though he did stay stateside that summer and work out with other Venezuelans at the Mets’ Spring Training facility. Dominguez remained in Florida in 2021 but was highly limited, making only 10 appearances (12 innings) in the Florida Complex League while the Mets had him focus on developing routines and getting in better shape to handle the rigors of a starting role. Dominguez underwent Tommy John surgery in March and is in line to return for 2023. There remains ample stuff on which to dream here. Dominguez stands 6-foot-5 and uses every bit of that size to throw in the mid-90s, touching as high as 99. The heater works well up in the zone too, when Dominguez is at his best with his command. A low-80s slider -- previously deemed a curve -- shows promising spin and break, but it lacks consistency compared to the fastball. He technically possesses a changeup with some movement, but it has a long way to go to become an average offering. Between last year’s and this year's surgery, Dominguez’s inexperience could mean there’s still room for ample growth, especially when it comes to his secondary pitches. But early results make the 20-year-old look more and more like a future reliever who relies on his velocity to blow by hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It isn’t often a great sign when an international player (outside of Cuba) signs a year after he is first eligible, but the plan has worked out well for Dominguez so far. Originally eligible for the 2018-19 signing period, the Venezuela native finally inked a deal with the Mets in November 2019 following a move to the Dominican Republic, where he focused on improving his velocity. Dominguez has yet to appear in a Minor League game but has some experience stateside after the coronavirus pandemic forced him and other Venezuelans to work out of New York’s Spring Training facility in Port St. Lucie last summer.
