The 6-foot-5 right-hander uses his size to his advantage to sit in the mid-90s and has touched as high as 99 in the past. The Mets have been pleased with the way his breaking ball – previously classified as a curveball but now looking more like a slider – has progressed because of the way he can spin it. It shows above-average potential with late break. The changeup made strides in 2020 and now shows promising movement of its own. The command needs to be the next thing to come for the tall righty, and New York hopes improvements with his release point will aide in that category once he is able to get in games more consistently. Dominguez has the pieces and physicality in place to be a starter. He just needs the game action to put all of those into place against actual opponents. If the command doesn’t quite come around, the velocity gives him a good shot at seeing Major League time in a bullpen setting, but as a pitcher still only entering his age-19 season, that conversation remains far off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible to sign during the 2018 international period, Dominguez instead decided to move to the Dominican Republic and focus on his training, with the goal of improving his prospect stock. The right-hander did exactly that, as his fastball quickly jumped from the low 90s to the mid-90s in a matter of months. The Mets took notice of the Venezuelan hurler’s rapid velocity gains and signed him a few weeks ahead of his 18th birthday, then watched him run his fastball up to 99 mph during the Dominican instructional league. Dominguez is physically strong and advanced for his age, with a 6-foot-5, 195-pound frame that leaves plenty of room for projection. He already knows how to spin the ball and flashed a plus curveball during the instructional league. Like many tall, hard-throwing young pitchers, Dominguez will need to fine-tune his mechanics and delivery as he begins to develop in the pro ranks. Getting stronger should help him in that process, and club officials already like how his arm works. The Mets believe they found a steal in Dominguez, who will pitch at age 18 for all of 2020. He will need to develop a changeup and continue to add strength, though the final product could be a big league starter with electric stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $1.5 million signing by the Cubs in July 2019, Made skipped over complex-level ball completely with an assignment to Single-A Myrtle Beach in 2021 after the pandemic-canceled season. He was in the midst of a second season at High-A South Bend in 2023 when the Nationals acquired him in a three-player deal for Jeimer Candelario that also brought over DJ Herz. Made finished out the year in Wilmington and returned to the South Atlantic League for 2024, hitting .239/.353/.327 with one homer and a 103 wRC+ over 72 games. He was promoted to Double-A Harrisburg in early July but batted just .158 in 21 games there (albeit with a low .204 BABIP). Made was passed over for the 40-man roster when he was Rule 5-eligible in both 2023 and 2024 because of his distance from the bigs and overall questions about his bat. A right-handed hitter, he showed decent contact and chase rates in his High-A repeat but started to fan more against quality breaking stuff in Double-A. He’s generally been good at taking his walks, and even that started to dwindle with Harrisburg, though it’s still an early small sample. The Nationals had hoped he would add strength to bring closer to average power, but that hasn’t come to fruition yet. Made can fly open at times in his swing, thereby cutting on top of pitches and leading to heavy groundball rates. The Dominican Republic native is just an average runner, but his saving grace is on the defensive side. He plays a strong shortstop with a good first step and impressive reactions at hands, and his arm strength gives him another weapon. Made has a fallback as a utility infielder with that glovework, but he needs the bat to come around in his age-22 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Made signed with the Cubs for $1.5 million in 2019, and even after he missed out on a potential first full season because of the pandemic, Chicago got aggressive with the shortstop with a move to Single-A at 18 years old in '21. He returned to the level a year later and had his best offensive showing anywhere with a .266/.354/.450 line and nine homers in only 57 games for Myrtle Beach. He hit only .162 over 37 games after a midseason promotion to High-A, returned to the Midwest League in 2023 and was still slashing just .240/.328/.355 in 70 games when Chicago moved him to the Nationals in a three-player deal for Jeimer Candelario at last year’s Trade Deadline. He slashed just .137/.232/.192 after the swap, though he was hurt by a .182 BABIP. The Dominican Republic native has needed to be graded on a curve throughout his career because of the aggression of his assignments. On the optimistic side, he has developed a better approach at the plate and has produced solid contact rates. On the pessimistic side, it’s still gap power at best, and while the plurality of his batted balls are on the ground, even those he does elevate aren’t big threats to leave the park yet. The Nats are hopeful added strength will lead to better exit velocities and bat speed in his age-21 season and beyond. Made has the first step, reactions and hands to remain at shortstop, and his plus arm would certainly play at third, where the Cubs gave him some run. He could also slide over to second without issue. Made could be a future utilityman with that glove, but offensive work remains to get him there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Made signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, but the pandemic delayed his debut until 2021. Chicago's logjam of young shortstops resulted in them aggressively assigning him to Single-A at age 18 for his introduction to pro ball and pushing him to High-A at age 19 in mid-2022. The Cubs sent Made back to High-A for 2023, and he was roughly a league-average bat before being moved to the Nationals in a Deadline deal for Jeimer Candelario. Made's quick right-handed swing and advanced bat-to-ball skills have helped him survive against much older and experienced competition. He has shown the ability to make adjustments as he has gotten acclimated to a level and his walk rate soared from 2 percent in his debut to 11 percent last year, a very encouraging sign. He has projectable strength and shows the ability to turn on pitches, so he could provide 15-20 homers per season once he begins driving the ball in the air more regularly. A solid runner but not much of a base stealer, Made could be a big league regular with just modest offensive production because he's a gifted defender. He has smooth actions and quality instincts at shortstop, where he covers ground to both sides and has a well-above-average arm. He could play almost anywhere on the diamond if he winds up in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chicago added to its collection of promising young shortstops when they signed Made for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2019. The pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until 2021, when their depth at his position led the Cubs to send him straight to Low-A at age 18. He held his own by batting .272 as the second-youngest regular in the Low-A East, but he played in just 58 games while dealing with forearm and hamstring strains. With his quick right-handed swing and advanced bat-to-ball skills, Made was able to survive against much older and experienced competition last year. He has some projectable strength and already shows a propensity for turning on pitches, so he could hit 15 or more homers per season once he's fully developed. To reach his offensive ceiling, he'll need to develop some plate discipline and improve his quality of contact after posting a 2 percent walk rate and hitting a lot of grounders in his debut. Because he played on the same club as 2020 first-rounder Ed Howard, Made also saw some action at third base last summer, but he's a no-doubt shortstop. He has the actions and instincts to make all the plays and throws at short with an arm that garners well-above-average grades from some scouts. He's presently a solid runner but could add some quickness as he matures physically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chicago spent the bulk of its $5.1 million international bonus pool in 2019 on two players from MLB's Trainer Partnership Program in the Dominican Republic, giving $2.9 million to catcher Ronnier Quintero and $1.5 million to Made. Though the coronavirus pandemic put his pro debut on hold, Made began to add some muscle during the layoff and stood out with his increased ability to drive the ball during instructional league last fall. The Cubs have a wealth of young shortstop prospects and he rivals 2020 first-rounder Ed Howard as the best defender in that group. Made makes consistent line-drive contact to all fields with a quick right-handed swing. He has a more advanced approach and better feel for the barrel than most 18-year-olds. While he'll always be a hit-over-power guy, his hitting ability, bat speed and projectable strength should translate into 15 or more homers per season. Presently a solid runner, Made could have plus speed once he's fully developed physically. He has the actions and instincts to play a quality shortstop and his tools will enable him to play all over the diamond as needed. His arm earns well above-average grades from some evaluators and plays better than its pure strength because he gets rid of the ball quickly and with impressive accuracy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The two best players in the Cubs' 2019 international crop came from MLB's Trainer Partnership Program in the Dominican Republic. Catcher Ronnier Quintero signed for $2.9 million and Made received $1.5 million, eating up the bulk of Chicago's $5.1 million bonus pool. If the latter fills out his 6-foot-1 frame as expected, he has the potential for at least average tools across the board. Made possesses fine hand-eye coordination and a more advanced approach than most players his age. A right-handed hitter with a line-drive swing, he controls the barrel very well and uses the entire field. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to provide 15 or more homers per season. Scouts believe that Made could go from present solid speed to a plus runner once he's physically mature. His most impressive tool is his arm, which earns some well above-average grades and plays up because of his quick release and throwing accuracy. With good actions and instincts at shortstop, he should be able to stay there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in Puerto Rico's 2020 high school class, Ceballos went unpicked in the shortened five-round Draft and spent two years at San Jacinto (Texas) JC. He declined to turn pro with the Angels as a 14th-rounder in 2022, then set Oregon records for homers (18) and RBI (70) the next spring before the Braves signed him in the third round. Traded to the Giants last July in a package for Jorge Soler and Luke Jackson, he boosted his High-A OPS from .707 before the deal to .914 afterward and was Puerto Rico's best hitter (.412/.500/.882) at the Premier12 tournament in November. A physical 6-foot-3, 225-pounder with bat speed and strength, Ceballos hits balls hard but has yet to fully tap into his power potential with wood bats. He did a much better job of driving the ball in the air after switching organizations and could offer 20 or more homers per season if he can sustain it. A right-handed hitter, he controls the strike zone reasonably well but struggles against curveballs and sliders. Ceballos' value will be tied to his defensive home. He has a strong arm but has well-below-average speed that hampers his agility and range at third base. His only realistic alternative may be first base, which would increase the demands on his bat, though he did catch briefly in the MLB Draft League in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better prospects in Puerto Rico's 2020 high school class, Ceballos spent his first two college seasons at San Jacinto (Texas) JC. After turning down the Angels as a 14th-round pick in 2022, he transferred to Oregon and set school records for single-season homers (18), RBIs (70) and slugging (.643) the following spring before turning pro as a third-rounder with the Braves. The Giants acquired him in July as part of a package for Jorge Soler and Luke Jackson. Though he's a physical 6-foot-3, 225-pounder with a quick right-handed swing, Ceballos is a hit-over-power guy. He does a reasonable job of managing the strike zone and making the contact, and he has the upside of a .275 hitter with 15-20 homers per year. He did a better job of driving the ball in the air after the trade, and San Francisco is eager to see if he can maintain that improvement in 2025. Ceballos' best pure tool is his plus arm strength, which enables him to make all the necessary throws from third base. He's a well-below-average runner who lacks range and agility, however, and first base may be his only realistic alternative. Some scouts are intrigued by the idea of using his arm behind the plate, and he caught briefly in the MLB Draft League in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates handed out 17 six-figure bonuses during the 2018-19 international signing period. Nolasco was right in the middle, getting $235,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic. He immediately opened eyes with a very strong Dominican Summer League performance in 2019, finishing with a .302/.373/.472 line. His highly anticipated United States debut was delayed, first by the pandemic in 2020, and then a minor injury in the spring of 2021 that kept him from going to full-season ball. He spent the summer posting a .961 OPS in the Florida Complex League. Nolasco has the chance to be an impact hitter from the right side of the plate. He has ridiculous raw power, with the chance for it to be plus in time as he improves his approach. Already showing present strength, he needs to refine his movements in the box so he can get the bat head out front more, but he does show some strike zone discipline and the willingness to draw walks and work counts to get to pitches he can do damage with. In his short time as a pro, he’s already put up impressive Trackman data in terms of things like exit velocity. Not particularly speedy, Nolasco is limited defensively to an outfield corner. He does have enough arm for the prototypical right fielder and he’ll likely see time moving forward in both spots to see which is a better fit. Wherever he plays, it’s the bat that has the chance to move him up the ladder, with physicality and youth on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates went after talent during the 2018-19 international signing period, they clearly targeted hitters, with 10 of their top 11 bonuses being handed to position players. One of them was Nolasco, a physical outfielder who got $235,000 to sign. He made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League and immediately showed some of his offensive upside by hitting .302/.373/.472 over 54 games. Nolasco is lean and ripped and can really impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. He makes consistent, really hard contact, recording a maximum exit velocity of 110 mph in the DSL. He has a solid approach at the plate with the chance to hit for average and power. He’s not a burner, but runs well enough and throws well enough to be a solid outfielder, though he’s definitely a corner outfield type. In the end, it’s going to be all about his bat, which he’s bringing to the United States for the first time as an 18-year old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reifert has bounced all over the map, signing with the Brewers for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2020 and then getting flipped to the Rays a year later for Mike Brosseau. After a 2022 season in which he was sent back to the Florida complex to iron out command issues, he experienced his big breakout in the Arizona Fall League by striking out 25 and allowing only one hit over 11 2/3 scoreless innings. Right shoulder inflammation limited him in 2023, but he got back on the horse with a 1.96 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 41 1/3 innings at Double-A Montgomery in 2024. The Rays didn’t add him to the 40-man roster in the offseason, and the Nationals selected him in the Rule 5 Draft but returned him in Spring Training. Reifert has been dominant for Triple-A Durham since his return to the organization. The 6-foot-4 right-hander’s 83-86 mph slider is the star of the show, and he pitches like it, throwing it two-thirds of the time. Its sharp vertical drop out of a lower three-quarters delivery befuddles hitters, and they whiffed on 70 percent of their swings against the breaking ball last year. It’s so effective at backfooting that Reifert even throws it plenty against lefties, whom he held to a .117 average in ’24. He throws a pair of 92-95 mph fastballs, reserving his running sinker for righties and the straight four-seamer for lefties. Reifert has experienced serious control issues at times in his career. He’s at his best when he isn’t nibbling and lets natural movement get his pitches to the edges of the zone. The slider alone gives him a shot at contributing to Tampa Bay’s bullpen, and the organization isn’t afraid of letting its arms rely heavily on their best pitches no matter the type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reifert took an unusual path to prospect status. Selected by the Rangers in the 30th round of the 2018 Draft out of North Iowa Area Community College, the right-handed reliever returned to school and transferred to Central Missouri for the 2020 season. He only pitched 2 2/3 innings there before that spring season was cut short by the COVID-19 pandemic. Reifert went unselected in the shortened ‘20 Draft but signed with the Brewers for $20,000. He pitched one season in Milwaukee’s system, striking out 103 batters in 60 innings while posting a 2.10 ERA across two levels, then the Rays picked him up in a November 2021 swap for utility infielder/postseason hero Mike Brosseau. Reifert’s first year in Tampa Bay’s system couldn’t have begun much worse or finished much better. He lost his command in April, walking seven and hitting five of the 24 batters he faced for Double-A Montgomery, and earned a demotion to the Florida complex to get right. He moved to High-A Bowling Green and pitched fine, with a 3.67 ERA and 43 strikeouts in 20 appearances. Then he went to the Arizona Fall League and blew everyone away with his wipeout slider, striking out 25 of the 40 batters he faced with only four walks and one hit allowed in 11 2/3 innings over eight scoreless appearances. There might not be a player in the Rays’ big league camp with a wider variance of possible outcomes for this season. He’s likely to begin the season back in Double-A, but if he’s the incredible pitcher he was in the Fall League -- some evaluators say as good as any reliever they’ve seen in the AFL -- he could be a big league bullpen weapon this season. If his command falters again, he may be a middle reliever in the Minors. With a mid-90s fastball and a low-80s slider that frequently freezes hitters in the box, it’s just a matter of control for Reifert.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $1.1 million out of Venezuela on his 16th birthday in July 2018, Garcia managed to play only 56 games through his first three seasons due to a broken ankle in 2019 and the pandemic-lost campaign in 2020. His first true full season came last year, as he opened with a .262/.309/.403 line in 85 games at Single-A Carolina before finishing his age-19 at High-A Wisconsin, where he was even more challenged offensively (.688 OPS in 26 games). The reason Garcia is a prospect at all is his defensive work at shortstop. The 6-foot-2 athlete may show below-average raw speed, but his combination of reactions, hands and overall footwork makes him a potential plus defender at a premium spot on the diamond. Once he vacuums up the ball, his impressive arm strength plays well deep in the hole, too, giving him yet another defensive weapon. Perhaps because of the missed time earlier, Garcia still hasn’t developed an approach that would make him a surefire everyday player. His 20.3 percent swinging strike rate was fifth-highest among the 387 Minor Leaguers with at least 450 plate appearances in 2022, and he didn’t walk in any of his 108 High-A plate appearances (while fanning in 40 of them). He can make loud contact when he does put bat on ball -- as evidenced by his career-high 15 homers last season -- but it isn’t often enough to justify the high K rate. Garcia was unprotected and unpicked when he became Rule 5-eligible last fall and needs to start showing more at the plate to prove he can be more valuable than his floor as a late-game defensive replacement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked 24th in his international class by MLB Pipeline, Garcia had to wait eight days until his 16th birthday on July 10, 2018, to sign with the Brewers for $1.1 million. He was off to a strong start in the Dominican Summer League a year later, going 10-for-32 (.313) with six walks in 10 games, before suffering a broken ankle that ended his first season early. He participated in Milwaukee’s alternate training site in 2020 and made his Minor League stateside debut in the Arizona Complex League, where he hit .252/.327/.474 over 150 plate appearances. Garcia finished his age-18 season with a brief cameo at Low-A Carolina. Brewers officials were impressed by Garcia’s glovework before he even signed, and he still projects as a surefire shortstop nearly four years later. Even without average speed, his reactions help him showcase promising range at the premium position. It’s that defensive work that drives the profile right now. Garcia has gotten more patient at the plate as he’s gained experience, and he’s tapping into more of his power as he’s matured physically. But his approach isn’t there quite yet -- he struck out 28.6 percent of the time in 2021 -- and he has some road ahead of him before he can project to be even an average Major League bat. The ankle and pandemic-missed season still make Garcia a raw prospect. He’ll get to experience a full Minor League season just before he’s eligible for the Rule 5 Draft next offseason. The defense will earn Garcia chances long after that, and some offensive improvements could make him a potential everyday player in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in his class during the 2018-19 international signing period, Garcia signed with the Brewers for $1.1 million on his 16th birthday after MLB Pipeline ranked him as the No. 24 prospect for that period. The projectable Venezuelan shortstop impressed Brewers scouts with the across-the-board tools he showed during MLB prospect showcases in Colombia and the Dominican Republic and was off to a smashing start in the 2019 Dominican Summer League (.313/.450/.469 in 40 plate appearances) while impressing in the field and on the bases before his season ended abruptly after just 10 games in mid-June when he suffered a broken ankle while sliding into second base. He spent 2020 making up for lost time, first appearing with Major Leaguers during the 2020 Cactus League while on loan from Minor League camp, and then as a member of Milwaukee’s Alternate Training Site beginning in mid-August. When he signed, Garcia was considered one of the premier defenders on the international market, with all-around tools that projected to improve if he filled-out physically. At the onset, he drew physical comparisons to former Brewers shortstop prospects Alcides Escobar and Orlando Arcia, but those have waned as Garcia has filled out his frame, and it appears he will continue to get stronger. Garcia projects to stick as a shortstop long term thanks to a slick glove and plus arm strength, and club officials have been impressed with his composure and quick first step, which gives him more range than his average speed suggests. If his frame fills out too much, the Brewers think Garcia will eventually have the power to be a productive third baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in his class, Garcia signed with the Brewers for $1.1 million on his 16th birthday after MLB Pipeline ranked him as the No. 24 prospect for the 2018-19 international period. The projectable Venezuelan shortstop impressed Brewers scouts with the across-the-board tools he showed during MLB prospect showcases in Colombia and the Dominican Republic, and everyone in the organization was eager to see Garcia in action during his 2019 pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. As if on cue, Garcia impressed in all facets of the game during a hot start in the DSL, though his season end abruptly (after just 10 games) in mid-June when he suffered a broken ankle while sliding into second base. Garcia was considered one of the premier defenders on the international market, with all-around tools that project to improve as the teenager matures and his body develops. He projects to stick as a shortstop long term thanks to a slick glove and plus arm strength, and club officials have been impressed with his composure and internal clock on the infield. He has good instincts and a quick first step that gives him more range than his average speed suggests. At the plate, Garcia has sound hitting mechanics and already knows how to efficiently incorporate his lower-half into his swing, with an approach that is advanced for his age. The Brewers think he will develop some pop, too, as those inside the organization peg him for future average game power that could lead to seasons with 15-plus home runs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in his class, Garcia signed with the Brewers for $1.1 million on his 16th birthday after ranking as MLB Pipeline's No. 21 prospect for the 2018-19 international period. The Venezuela native has a good frame and exhibits lots of growth potential with impressive tools that he displayed during MLB prospect showcases in Cartagena, Colombia, and Santo Domingo. Assigned to the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut in 2019, Garcia got off to a hot start before suffering a season-ending broken ankle in mid-June. The teenager was considered one of the premier defenders on the market, and those tools are projected to improve as Garcia matures and his body develops. He'll also eventually be an average runner. At the plate, Garcia is not considered a \"big power guy,\" but the belief is that he will build on his doubles and gap power. Scouts also like his hitting mechanics -- the way his hands and lower half work in during his swing -- and his approach at the plate. There's a belief that Garcia will hit 10-12 home runs in the big leagues one day, but it will be his glove more than his bat that will propel him through the Minor Leagues and make him an everyday player. There's a chance he could also develop into an average run producer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic when they stumbled upon Morel, whom they signed for $97,500 in 2023. He tore up the Dominican Summer League in his pro debut, hitting .344/.417/.644 and topping the Rookie-level circuit with 17 doubles, eight triples, 32 extra-base hits and 116 total bases. He continued to excel when he came to the United States last year, slashing .307/.407/.575 to rank third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in slugging and fourth in OPS (.982). Significantly larger and stronger than his listed 180 pounds suggests, Morel hits balls harder than most teenagers and has plus raw power. He has had less success tapping into it in 2025, when he hasn't launched balls in the air to his pull side as easily and his plate discipline has regressed. His right-handed swing can get too long at times and his aggressive mindset results in strikeouts. Morel draws comparisons to a more athletic version of Marcell Ozuna. He presently has solid speed and looks to make things happen on the bases, though he may slow down if he gets much bigger. His plus arm contributes to his right-field profile, though his defensive instincts and effort need improvement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sebastian Walcott's $3.2 million bonus absorbed most of Texas' 2023 international bonus pool, but they also may have found a bargain in Morel, who signed for $97,500 and was discovered while the Rangers were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic. He batted .344/.417/.644 in his pro debut, topping the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 17 doubles, eight triples, 32 extra-base hits and 116 total bases. He puts on one of the best batting-practice shows in the system and draws some comparisons to two-time All-Star Marcell Ozuna. Morel has a quick right-handed swing, more strength than most teenagers and room on his 6-foot-2 frame to add more muscle. He has plus raw power and gets to most of it, already showing the aptitude to drive balls in the air to his pull side. He'll need to tighten up his plate discipline as he faces more advanced pitching, but he doesn't strike out excessively. Morel is fairly athletic but could slow down a bit as he matures physically. He's presently a solid runner but hasn't shown much feel for stealing bases. He has arm strength to match, adding to his right-field profile, though his defensive instincts need some work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Petersen was an all-Big Ten honoree as an Iowa sophomore in 2023 and looked set to achieve similar status by hitting .333 and slugging .571 in 33 games as a Hawkeyes junior, only to see his ’24 season cut short by stress reactions in both his shins. The Nationals took him in the eighth round and signed him for slot at $230,900, and a similar story of good results mixed in with injuries carried over to pro ball. Petersen missed the start of his first full season with a hamstring issue and managed only 44 games with High-A Wilmington, hitting .297/.398/.490 with a 161 wRC+ in that span. He made up for the lost time in the Arizona Fall League with a .305 average and a .934 OPS in 17 contests there. The right-handed hitter is constantly shifting in the box, making him look eager to get things going. There were some red flags in his Fall League performance, despite the promising surface-level numbers. He carried only a 65 percent overall contact rate on his swings and tended to get overzealous to expand the zone against fastballs. That said, he did surprise by showing better impact at the plate, a continuation of a trend from college, and his swing can come with optimal angles that make some swing-and-miss easier to stomach. Petersen is a plus runner who went 18-for-18 in steals attempts with Wilmington, though he didn’t push the envelope in the AFL. He could be an average defender in center field with that speed but would be above-average if he needs to land in a corner. Left field seems like his best fit due to subpar arm strength. Petersen’s potential as a fourth outfielder will be tested further with his first move to the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Iowa rotation drew plenty of attention in recent years, especially for Brody Brecht, but Petersen stood out in his own right among the position-player group. An all-Big Ten selection in 2023, the outfielder got off to a strong start as a junior last year, hitting .333/.459/.571 with five homers and 17 steals in 33 games before stress reactions in both his shins ended his season in late April. The Nationals selected him in the eighth round, signed him for slot at $230,900 and got him seven games later in the summer with Single-A Fredericksburg. Batting from the right side, Petersen can make for a kinetic at-bat as a constant waggler in the box. He improved his plate discipline over time in college, and he also made harder consistent contact. He slugged just .329 with wood bats in a trip to Cape Cod in 2023, and he struggled against velocity above 94 mph even with metal. There might just be enough power for 12-15 homers, and it was notable that, while he didn’t go deep with the FredNats, four of his eight hits went for extra bases in the small sample. Petersen is a plus runner who has good baserunning instincts; he had a 90.9 percent success rate in steals in college and was 5-for-5 in the pros. Subpar arm strength pushed him primarily to left field with the Hawkeyes, and he might need to stay in a corner with superior defenders like Dylan Crews and Elijah Green options up the middle. With Petersen’s on-base ability and speed alone, he could fit nicely as a Major League fourth outfielder – a solid return for his Draft spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 20 international prospect in the 2024 class, Hurtado joined the Nationals for $2.7 million at the opening of the signing period on Jan. 15. That figure was tied for the sixth-highest international bonus and was $900,000 more than anyone signed by the Nats last year (Angel Feliz being second). Hurtado battled knocks throughout his first taste of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, including a shoulder issue that ended his season on Aug. 5. He showed signs of breaking out in July before that, slashing .261/.346/.464 with three homers and five doubles in 21 games. Still, he finished with just a 76 wRC+ across 155 plate appearances. Much of Hurtado’s scouting report from the day he signed remains true. At a listed 6-foot-3, 175 pounds, there is a ton of projection remaining in Hurtado’s skinny frame, and his left-handed swing is already geared to hit the ball pullside and in the air. There continues to be hope that he’ll be an above-average power hitter as he continues to fill out and bulk up. There is length in his swing, and that probably led to a 28.1 percent strikeout rate in June out of the gate, but Hurtado cut that down as he gained more DSL experience. Hurtado played primarily in left field in 2024 because the DSL Nats employed absolute speedster Dashyll Tejeda in center. A solid runner, Hurtado could get more center field looks in his second season, but the power would play in a corner if needed. A 16-year-old at signing, he’s still only the age of an American high-school senior entering 2025 and will get all the space he needs to meet his considerable slugging ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals had a $5,284,000 signing pool at the start of this year’s international period, and they used a large chunk of it to add two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 25 prospects in the class. The most notable of the pair is Hurtado (No. 20), a Dominican outfielder who joined the system for $2.7 million. Hurtado was 16 at signing -- he’ll turn 17 in May -- making him one of the youngest players in this year’s class. Standing at a listed 6-foot-3, the left-handed slugger brings plenty to dream on to a Nationals organization that could use as much upside as possible. His swing is already smooth and geared for lift, helping the case that he’ll be at least an above-average hitter by the time he fills out his frame. There is length to the swing that could be an issue in time, but for now, he makes enough consistent contact that Washington evaluators envision him hitting from the middle of the lineup. Even if Hurtado has to move to an outfield corner eventually, his offensive trajectory should still work there. He has excited his new organization with his confidence, makeup and work ethic, and he should get the most attention when he takes to the Dominican Summer League in his first taste of the Minors this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guilarte joined the Brewers system for $1 million out of Venezuela as part of the organization's 2021 signing class, the same group headlined by Jackson Chourio from the same country. The infielder missed out on his first season due to a left shoulder surgery but still jumped stateside in 2022, slashing .306/.403/.371 with eight steals in 36 games in the Arizona Complex League. Guilarte headed to full-season ball for the first time last summer and was roughly a league-average bat as a 19-year-old for Single-A Carolina with a .269/.377/.314 line, 107 wRC+ and 26 stolen bases in 58 contests. The right-handed hitter continued to demonstrate a strong knowledge of the strike zone in 2023 with a 13.2 percent walk rate -- equal to his BB percentage the season before -- and while his strikeouts climbed a bit, he still didn’t swing-and-miss much with an 8.8 percent swinging-strike rate that ranked 16th among 99 Carolina Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances. The contact he did produce was generally weak, though, as 55.9 percent of his Single-A batted balls were on the ground and almost half were to the opposite field. Someone with Guilarte’s plus speed can still pick up hits on wormburners -- he had a .377 BABIP last season -- but the lack of impact is becoming glaring as he’s still yet to homer in pro ball. The good news is he has the range and actions to be an above-average defender at shortstop and plus arm strength to boot. The Brewers gave Guilarte more looks at second base at Carolina in deference to Gregory Barrios (a high-quality defender in his own right), and the youngster could be plus there if need be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson Chourio is likely going to be the headliner of the Brewers’ Jan. 15, 2021, international signing class for years to come, but Guilarte, who signed for $1 million out of Venezuela, is making a name for himself too. He moved stateside to the Arizona Complex League in 2022 with promising results – a .306/.403/.371 line and eight steals in 36 games against competition roughly two years older than him on average. Brewers officials quickly started paying more and more attention to Guilarte the longer he performed in the domestic complex circuit. He demonstrated a strong knowledge of the strike zone by walking in 13.2 percent of his ACL plate appearances, and he tended to make contact on pitches that did land in the zone. That contact was mostly on the ground, however; his 64.1 percent ground-ball rate was highest among all Brewers Minor League qualifiers. There is some physical projection remaining in his 6-foot, 160-pound frame, but it may take more than just added strength to give him anything close to average power. That said, Guilarte has a promising floor because of his overall athleticism. He’s a plus runner already, and his range, defensive actions and significant arm strengths should keep him at the six the higher he climbs. Those skills could also translate well at second and third base, where he got some looks in 2022. He’ll be an asset on the dirt no matter what, and any more impact out of the bat would send him flying up the Brewers' prospect ranks in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a five-year defensive end for the Seahawks in the early 2000s, King joined the Padres as a 2022 fourth-rounder out of the Maryland high-school ranks. His career got off to a slow start with concussion and shoulder problems in 2023 and shoulder surgery delaying his start to 2024. He was limited to first-base/DH duties upon his return but got to return to the catcher position for ’25, when he got through a full season for the first time as a pro. King hit .274/.353/.384 with four homers and 21 steals in 105 games between Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne. The most promising fact of King’s age-21 season was that he avoided the injured list for the entire summer. He even got in 17 extra games of action in the Arizona Fall League when fellow backstop Ethan Salas was a late scratch. Starting from a relaxed and open stance with the bat resting on his back shoulder, the right-handed slugger does a fine job making contact on pitches in the zone, and he won’t chase that often for his experience level. He can be vulnerable to sliders and changeups when he does expand the zone, however, and despite solid top-end exit velocities, his power primarily plays to the gaps. King draws strong reviews for his athleticism as a catcher, and he can move better than most backstops, something that aids his work behind the plate. The shoulder issues have affected his throwing, and while he’s regained some strength, he still only caught 10 percent of attempted basestealers in the 2025 regular season and 11 percent in the AFL. After starting behind the eight ball, King needs experience, and continued time at first base (and maybe even adding some in the outfield) will help.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: King’s father played five seasons as a defensive end for the Seahawks in the early 2000s, but the younger edition is trying to make his way on the diamond. A standout as a high-schooler in Maryland, the backstop went to the Padres in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft and signed for $502,800, but it’s been a slow start to his pro career. Concussion and shoulder problems limited him to 84 plate appearances in the Arizona Complex League in 2023, and shoulder surgery delayed his start to 2024 and kept him in a first base/DH role all summer. He moved to Single-A Lake Elsinore in late July and finished with a .271/.379/.421 line and two homers in 62 games between there and the ACL. King has always shown an ability to work a walk during his brief early looks in the Minor Leagues, and he made decent swing decisions in his first trip to the California League. He’s worked to tighten his right-handed swing heading into his second full season, and that could help him tap into the above-average raw power that made him such a promising prep prospect in the first place. There’s the potential that a healthy King could be ready to break out once he gets enough at-bats under his belt. Staying healthy is a big issue beyond his offensive work. The Padres plan to deploy King back as a catcher, as he’d be more valuable behind the plate than at first base. He showed decent arm strength before the shoulder issues, but that will be closely monitored in his return. King will be 21 for the duration of the 2025 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: King’s name might look familiar to football fans from the early 2000s. His father played defensive end for the Seahawks for five seasons and finished with 12 career sacks, including six in 2000 alone. The younger King gravitated toward baseball instead as a Maryland prep standout, and the Padres selected him in the fourth round in 2022 before signing him for exact slot at $502,800. The catcher received only 84 plate appearances in the Arizona Complex League last season due to a concussion and shoulder problems, but he did slash .324/.440/.397 in that abbreviated span. He’s received more playing time in 2024, splitting the summer between the ACL and Single-A Lake Elsinore. San Diego officials know King’s development is going to be a long-term project and consider last year’s problems speed bumps, though the shoulder issues have pushed him to first base/DH duties in 2024. The right-handed slugger showed an advanced willingness to take a walk in the ACL, and while his swing can get long, thus hurting his ability to make consistent contact, there’s still potentially above-average power in his 6-foot-3, 215-pound frame. Perhaps not shocking given his bloodlines, King moved well for his size behind the dish when he did play there and provided a big target for his pitchers. He earned bonus points entering pro ball because of his history of already calling games as an amateur. There is arm strength here, but King was only 2-for-29 in caught-stealing attempts during his game time in the Complex League in 2023. San Diego officials continue to marvel at the physical presence King can bring to the box and the diamond, and his pop alone could make him valuable even at a less premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: King’s father of the same name was a 22nd overall pick in the 1999 NFL Draft and played five seasons as a defensive end for the Seahawks, registering six sacks in his best season in 2000. His son took to the diamond instead, and he was a standout at Calvert Hall College (Maryland) High School and in summers with the Canes National Team. The Padres grabbed King in the fourth round last July, making King the highest-selected player from his home state in the 2022 class, and they added him to their system for exact slot money at $502,800. The right-handed slugger certainly got some of his father’s size at 6-foot-3, 215 pounds, and his already promising strength should help him hit for power through the pro ranks. Coming from a mid-Atlantic state, he is rawer with the bat than some of his warmer-weather counterparts, and his swing has length that might hurt his chances of making repeated contact against pro pitching. Given his size, King provides a large target for his batterymates, and he moves better behind the plate than might be expected based on his frame alone. His above-average arm strength is likely to be his best defensive asset right away, but his experience calling his own games in high school should help ease the transition as well. Evaluators are still split on whether King can be an everyday catching presence or if he’ll profile better as a slugging-first backup, but the Padres will give him plenty of road to develop his skills through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 A reliever for his first two years at Clemson, Weatherly moved into the Tigers’ rotation in 2020 and threw extremely well in four starts before the pandemic-induced shutdown. The Rockies saw enough to take him in the third round of the 2020 Draft and sign him for full slot, then saw him look extremely good in instructional league play last year. Shoulder issues have slowed him over his first two full seasons, but he’s shown glimpses of his overpowering stuff. Weatherly stands out for his pure stuff and his athleticism, to the point where the Rockies think he’s one of the best overall athletes in the entire system. The left-hander’s fastball touched 97 mph at instructs, but the high-spin heater sits more comfortably in the low 90s. His slider is his go-to pitch, a plus wipeout that gets both left- and right-handed hitters to swing and miss on a regular basis. He didn’t need his changeup much in college, especially when coming out of the bullpen, but it’s something he’s continued to work on to improve. The left-hander has had trouble commanding the baseball at times, often because of timing issues with his delivery, which can be remedied. He’s smart to a fault on the mound, sometimes thinking too much rather than just trusting his stuff. The Rockies think he has all the ingredients to be a Robbie Ray-like starter, but also know that he could get big league hitters out in the bullpen right now, with a Josh Hader-type career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clemson University has had more than its fair share of high-end Draft picks, including first-round bats like Logan Davidson in 2019 and Seth Beer in 2018. But Weatherly, who used a dominant move to the rotation in his shortened junior season in 2020 to climb up to the third round and sign for full slot with the Rockies, is the first pitcher to get taken in the top three rounds since the A’s selected Daniel Gossett in the second round of the 2014 Draft. The left-hander then went on to make a very good first impression during instructional league play last fall. Weatherly is all about power, with two potentially plus pitches at his disposal. His high spin-rate fastball was typically in the low-90s at Clemson, occasionally touching a bit higher, but he was up to 97 mph consistently at instructs. His best pitch is his wipeout slider that gets swings and misses from hitters on both sides of the plate. His changeup is behind -- he didn’t need it as much when he was pitching out of the bullpen for Clemson early in his college career -- but he showed improved feel for it as he used it more. There’s confidence that Weatherly has the stuff to start and the Rockies love his pitching IQ and competitive nature, but there are questions about him throwing enough strikes to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter. If not, he could become a very good lefty setup type out of a big league pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox more than doubled Dalquist's third-round slot value, paying the California high schooler $2 million to forgo an Arizona commitment. After getting just three innings in his first two years as a pro because the pandemic wiped out the 2020 Minor League season, he stayed healthier and outperformed fellow big-money prep right-handers Jared Kelley and Matthew Thompson at Low-A Kannapolis. He didn't exactly dominate, however, with a 4.99 ERA and 56 walks in 83 innings. Dalquist has added velocity since signing and now sits at 92-94 mph and reaches the mid-90s more often with his fastball, with the extension in his delivery adding deception that's more notable than his heater's life. His low-80s slider with depth has surpassed his mid-70s downer curveball as his best breaking pitch, though he hangs it too often. He's also making progress with a fading low-80s changeup that can get too firm at times. Dalquist stood out more with his polish than his pure stuff as an amateur, but the reverse was true in 2021, when he struggled to harness his improved stuff. Fastball command was a particular problem, as he regularly missed up and to his arm side. He's a potential four-pitch mid-rotation starter if he can figure things out, but he has yet to show many signs of doing so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox invested heavily in high school right-handers in the last two Drafts, spending $2.1 million on Matthew Thompson and $2 million on Dalquist in 2019 and $3 million on Jared Kelley in 2020. A California high school product, Dalquist received more than double his slot value in the third round to give up an Arizona commitment. He pitched three innings in his pro debut before spending 2020 at Chicago's alternate training site and instructional league program. Though Dalquist stands out more with his polish than his pure stuff, his pitches have gotten better as he has gained strength. He's reaching the mid-90s more often with his fastball and sitting around 92-94 mph, with the extension in his delivery creating deception that's more notable than the life on his heater. His mid-70s curveball and harder slider both have gotten sharper since he turned pro and show flashes of becoming plus offerings. Dalquist also shows some feel for a changeup that he didn't need much as an amateur. More athletic than physical, he has a whippy arm action, repeats his delivery and usually fills the strike zone, though he has had difficulty harnessing his improved stuff in 2021. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After drafting Spencer Adams in 2014's second round, the White Sox shied away from taking prep arms with early picks until they spent their 2019 second- and third-rounders on Matthew Thompson and Andrew Dalquist. One of the few pleasant surprises in a lackluster California high school class, Dalquist signed for $2 million -- more than double his slot value in the third round. Chicago had him make just three one-inning starts in his pro debut and will turn him loose this year, likely developing him alongside Thompson. Heading into Dalquist's senior season, scouts regarded him as a projectable right-hander who lacked the present stuff to buy him away from a commitment to Arizona. That changed when his fastball velocity jumped to 91-95 mph last spring, with the extension in his delivery creating deception that's more notable than the life on his two-seamers and four-seamers. He has good depth on a mid-70s curveball that will be at least a solid offering once it adds more power, and also has a slider and a changeup that he didn't utilize much as an amateur. While Dalquist isn't physical, he's athletic and has a whippy arm action. He repeats his delivery and provides consistent strikes. His polish gives him a higher floor than most high school arms, and his ceiling could rise because he still has a good deal of projection remaining in his 6-foot-1 frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jimenez was a Top 50 international prospect and one of the best catchers in his class when the Tigers signed him for $1.25 million as the period opened in January 2023. After a solid debut that summer in the Dominican Summer League, he came stateside in 2024 and had a good start in the Florida Complex League, then cooled off and went back to the FCL to kick off '25. The Twins got him at the Trade Deadline in the Chris Paddack deal and Jimenez responded with a .982 OPS over 23 games with a bump up to full-season ball in his new organization. A compact, stocky switch-hitter, Jimenez has a quick swing with short levers, showing a combination of strength and some bat speed at times. He’s always had a good feel for the zone, drawing a lot of walks and limiting strikeouts. He started tapping into his power more in 2025, particularly after the trade. It showed up mostly from the left-hand side of the plate, displaying the ability to create some loft to his pull side. While there’s work to be done on his overall defensive craft, Jimenez does have the makings of a decent backstop with average catch-and-throw skills. The Twins rave about his makeup, work ethic and desire to improve in all facets of his game. He might be a solid big league backup, but in just his age-20 season, it’s too soon to know exactly who he might become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers signed the switch-hitting Jimenez out of Venezuela for a $1.25 million bonus as the headliner of their 2023 international class. He made steady if quiet progress since then as a catcher, culminating in his stateside debut last summer in the Florida Complex League. He had a hot start in the FCL before fading down the stretch, then was putting up moderately improved numbers in a return engagement back at the complex when he was sent to the Twins in the Chris Paddack trade. Jimenez isn’t a big body behind the plate at 5-foot-9 and 170 pounds, and his presence at the plate fits accordingly. He has a good eye for the strike zone, though he can be prone to passiveness as a hitter at times, and makes contact with a quick swing and short levers. Using a slightly open stance, there is some solid raw bat speed and strength for him to tap into in the future. Though he’s had more at-bats hitting left-handed, he’s been more effective in limited at-bats from the right side off southpaws. Defensively, he commands the game and handles pitchers well, and he answered the challenge of the running game in the FCL well by throwing out 33 percent of potential base stealers in his two summers combined. While the Tigers were dealing from an area of depth behind the plate, the Twins have had some difficulty developing backstops in recent years. Jimenez doesn’t offer a huge ceiling, but he does give Minnesota someone with a fairly decent floor as a potential big league backup, even though he’s still far away from reaching that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers didn’t have a big-name signing in the 2023 international market, but they delved into a deep crop of Venezuelan catchers and signed the switch-hitting Jimenez -- the No. 32 prospect on the international market according to MLB Pipeline -- for a $1.25 million bonus. The reviews from his early work in the Dominican Summer League suggested a sound investment, from a good eye at the plate to a good arm behind it. Jimenez is an athletic presence behind the plate and a respectable hitter at the plate, with a smooth, compact swing, good zone judgment and promising extra-base power. He was a bit passive at the plate early last season but settled into a good all-fields approach, though his ground-ball rate was a bit high. He’s a mobile catcher who can smother balls in the dirt. He has a quick release on throws to second. The Tigers are thin on catching prospects below Dillon Dingler in their system, despite some teases over the last few years, so there’s an opportunity for Jimenez if he can continue to mature. He’s a long-term play, but his first taste of Minor League ball in the States should give a better idea of how far he has to go.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 international signing period could turn out to be a very productive one for the Phillies for a number of reasons. Top acquisition Starlyn Caba (who got $3 million) and Top 100 prospect Eduardo Tait have been used in trades to bring in big league help, while pitcher Wen-Hui Pan and Ferrebus, who signed out of Venezuela for just $70,000, are current Top 30 prospects. Ferrebus debuted in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then returned there in 2024, eventually playing his way to the Florida Complex League. He began his 2025 there before earning a bump up to full-season Clearwater, the first time he struggled anywhere offensively. While injuries -- an elbow sprain in 2023, an ankle sprain in 2024 and what turned out to be a broken second metacarpal in his left hand last year -- have cut into his playing time since he signed, Ferrebus has consistently shown a knack for contact when he's been on the field. The right-handed hitter does not swing-and-miss much and can hit the ball extremely hard, though he's going to have to learn to find a better angle to get the ball in the air more. He's also an overly aggressive hitter who chases way too much, something that was exposed in his first taste of the Florida State League. While Ferrebus has seen time behind the plate and at first base, the Phillies are bullish about the defensive progress he's made in his brief career. There's confidence he can catch long-term with decent hands and enough arm. He just needs reps, something he got more of as part of a Phillies prospect contingent that helped the Adelaide Giants win an Australian Baseball League title over the winter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 international signing period might be the year of the bargain-price catcher for the Phillies. They landed Eduardo Tait out of Colombia for $90,000 while they scouted Ferrebus in Venezuela and signed him for just $70,000. He spent parts of two summers in the Dominican Summer League, hitting his way stateside and continuing to rake in the Florida Complex League. He carries a career .345/.437/.504 line into the 2025 season. A right-handed hitter, Ferrebus has a good swing and is already showing a penchant for barreling up the baseball and registering big-time exit velocities. He’s strong and physical with a good swing geared for contact. He limits swing-and-miss with a career 14.4 percent strikeout rate to show for it and has shown the ability to drive the ball to all fields. Next up in his development will be to get him to add some loft with more consistency, with conviction there’s plenty of power to unlock. Whether Ferrebus can stick behind the plate remains to be seen, though the Phillies like his catching frame and his internal motor. He’s not going to move the needle defensively, but his hands and arm should be playable enough. He has seen time at first as well, and should a move be necessary, that does put more pressure on the bat to develop, something the organization thinks will happen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After earning national freshman of the year accolades at Arizona in 2021, Berry followed coach Jay Johnson to Louisiana State and had another monster year. He offered one of the best combinations of hitting ability, power and plate discipline in the 2022 Draft, so the Marlins selected him sixth overall and signed him for $6 million. He has surprisingly struggled at the plate in his first three years as a pro, though he did have his best stretch of success yet in the second half of 2024. A switch-hitter, Berry has a quality swing from both sides but lost his patient approach and chased too many pitches out of the zone while trying to make up for a slow start in 2023. The same was true when he posted a dismal .155/.205/.217 line in the first two months of this season, but he looked more like his college self while batting after the all-star break. There were some worries that his pedestrian exit velocities in college might mean that he'd be more of a hit-over-power guy as a pro, and he looks like he might top out at 15-20 homers per season. Drafted as a third baseman, Berry has below-average speed and average arm strength at the hot corner, with most scouts questioning whether he was athletic enough to remain there. He has decent range and can make some nice plays, but he also made 20 errors in 69 starts at third in 2023. Miami had him play more first base in Double-A last season to lessen his defensive load, and he started to hit better once he became primarily a right fielder in the second half of this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Berry earned national freshman of the year honors at Arizona in 2021 before following coach Jay Johnson to Louisiana State. He continued to thrive in Baton Rouge, posting a 1.094 OPS with more extra-base hits (24) and walks (27) than strikeouts (22), en route to going sixth overall in the 2022 Draft and signing for $6 million. He shockingly has struggled to make much impact at the plate in his first two pro seasons. Berry offered perhaps the most tantalizing combination of hitting ability, power and patience in the 2022 college crop, drawing comparisons to a switch-hitting version of Andrew Vaughn. He has a quality swing and advanced approach from both sides, showing more pop as a left-handed hitter, though those attributes have yet to translate into pro production. His relatively pedestrian exit velocities were the lone concern about him in college and he hasn't hit the ball hard in the Minors, while his approach has regressed significantly. After Berry spent most of his freshman year at DH and split his sophomore year between third base and right field, there are questions about where he will wind up defensively. He has below-average quickness and average arm strength, and most scouts think he lacks the athleticism to play the hot corner in the big leagues. He could be adequate in an outfield corner and most likely will wind up at first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boeve was a king of contact over his three years at University of Nebraska-Omaha, and that was never clearer than in his junior campaign when he finished among the top five nationally with a 4.3 percent K rate and a 0.28 K/BB ratio while hitting .401 over 47 games. The Brewers took him in the second round in 2023, making him the highest pick in school history, and he came firing out of the gate in his first full season by going 21-for-38 (.553) in his first 13 games with High-A Wisconsin. Milwaukee promoted Boeve to Double-A Biloxi in late April, and he slashed .306/.374/.447 with six homers in 66 games the rest of the way while missing some time with a right shoulder injury. Batting from the left side, Boeve gets into a slight crouch, using only a minimal load and whipping a short swing to put the barrel on the ball. Even at Double-A, he’s shown an ability to handle most pitch types, and he’s as comfortable shooting balls the other way as he is pulling them down the line. However, his current power projection is for 10-12 homers over a full season because most of his pop comes on doubles to the gaps. Whether it's due to the shoulder or the Southern League, Boeve hasn't been as sharp at the plate in 2025 and has mostly been carried by a decent OBP. Boeve is a below-average runner and a non-threat to steal bases. He can still get his glove to balls at third base but won’t wow anyone there with his range or arm strength. The Brewers gave him more looks at first base in the Southern League, and he has a better chance of being average there, albeit with an added need for power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boeve was one of the best contact hitters in Division I baseball in 2023, ranking fifth among qualifiers with a 4.3 percent K rate and third with a 0.28 K/BB ratio at Nebraska-Omaha. He finished with a .401/.512/.563 slash line over 47 games in his junior spring. Those numbers, along with strong summer performances in the Cape Cod and Northwoods Leagues, pushed Boeve to become the highest UNO player ever drafted when he went in the second round to the Brewers and signed below slot for $1.25 million. He got his feet wet in pro ball with stops in the Arizona Complex and Midwest Leagues. Batting from the left side, Boeve shows a quick and compact swing that prioritizes putting the ball in play. His ability to focus on balls in the zone helps him build a solid on-base percentage on top of the strong average, and that’s the entire foundation of his offensive profile. Because he does focus so much on protecting the plate over driving the ball with his short swing mechanics, he doesn’t get into his average raw power as much as he could, and his exit velocities suffer. He did tee off with four homers in nine games against less-advanced ACL competition but was back to hitting the ball on the ground 60 percent of the time in his short High-A sample. A below-average runner, Boeve improved defensively over time at third base in school but still lacked the arm strength to pop there. He was also drafted into the same organization as Brock Wilken, and as a result, the Brewers tried Boeve out more at second in pro ball where his arm is a better fit. His lack of wheels could push him to first or left field in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The win-now Padres didn’t seem like an obvious Rule 5-picking club at the start of the 2022-23 offseason, but San Diego decided it was worth a small risk to take Lopez, a $100,000 signing by the Rays out of the Dominican Republic in October 2016 -- who now has a real Major League opportunity. The left-hander earned his chance to The Show with a full-time move to the bullpen in 2022, when he posted a 2.60 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 55 1/3 innings at Double-A Montgomery. His 38.7 percent K rate and .164 average-against ranked fourth and fifth, respectively, among Double-A pitchers with at least 50 innings pitched. Lopez’s move to relief corresponded with added velocity, and he was around 94-96 mph as he got deeper into his new role. The 6-foot-1 southpaw paired that with a low-80s sweeping slider that also was a plus pitch last year and was downright unfair to lefties, who often flailed as it dove down and away from their whiffing bats. His upper-80s changeup may have lacked much separation off the heater, but it was effective enough to help him limit righties to a .170 average and .522 OPS last season. If there’s one aspect of Lopez’s game that will truly hinder his Rule 5 chances, it’s his rough control. A 14.9 percent walk rate in Montgomery showed the troubles the southpaw can face against more advanced and patient hitters, and those will only increase against Major League bats. The contending Padres won’t be able to carry Lopez should strike-throwing continue to be that much of an issue, but his two plus pitches, promising splits and whiff-heavy tendencies give him a solid floor as a bullpen arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lopez hurt his elbow during his junior year at Seton Hall and ended up needing Tommy John surgery. Reds scouts had liked what they had seen before he got hurt and took a flier on him, drafting him in the sixth round of the 2014 Draft. The team understandably took it slowly with him post-rehab, but things clicked for him in 2017, as he pitched his way to Double-A and got added to the 40-man roster. Lopez had both started and relieved in college, and the Reds put him in a rotation initially mostly to allow him to build up innings and get regular rest. He took to it much better than the organization thought he would, showing much more pitchability than anticipated. He throws his fastball in the 90-94 mph range and he backs it up with a solid slider and an average changeup. He's shown the ability to mix his pitches well and throw them for strikes, with hitters not getting good looks at his stuff, leading to him striking out just over a batter per inning in his career heading to 2018. After two straight healthy years, it looks like the flier on Lopez is going to pay off in some capacity. He has the chance to be a back-end starter or perhaps a middle reliever, reminding some of a Sam LeCure type of profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 3 in the 2024 international class by MLB Pipeline, Santana earned Julio Rodríguez comparisons for his tools and personality before signing for $1,297,500 out of the Dominican Republic. After performing well in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and winning MVP accolades in the DSL all-star game during his pro debut, he faced more adversity when he came to the United States in 2025. He was decent in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League but overmatched as an 18-year-old in Single-A, where he struck out 29 times in 60 at-bats. Santana controlled the strike zone well in the DSL but didn't in his U.S. debut, struggling to recognize pitches and getting completely bamboozled by non-fastballs in Single-A. He has a quick right-handed stroke but swung through too many offerings when he wasn't chasing them out of the zone. He hit the ball hard when he did connect, and his bat speed and projectable strength give him the chance to develop 20-homer power. Santana has solid speed but still is learning the finer points of basestealing. He got most of his DSL action in center field but spent more time in left field last season, and he may fit better on a corner unless he refines his instincts. He has fringy but playable arm strength at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born and trained in the Dominican Republic, Santana spent some time on the U.S. high school showcase circuit and performed well at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in Florida in October 2024. No. 3 in MLB Pipeline's 2024 international rankings, he garnered comparisons to Julio Rodríguez for his five-tool potential and personality. After signing for $1,297,500, he slashed .292/.465/.364 in the Dominican Summer League and won MVP honors in the Rookie-level circuit's All-Star Game. An advanced right-handed hitter, Santana showed the ability to recognize pitches, manage the strike zone and make adjustments at the plate in his pro debut. He had much more difficulty making contact when he came to the United States in 2025, with his strikeout rate doubling from 15 to 30 percent. He didn't homer in 53 games in the DSL but has the bat speed and projectable strength to grow into at least 20-homer power. Santana has plus speed and the instincts to make use of it on the bases and in center field. He has solid range in center along with a playable if fringy arm. He's bilingual and earns plaudits for his high baseball IQ and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 2 prospect in MLB Pipeline's 2024 international rankings, Santana signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1,297,500. He got better as the signing period approached and earned comparisons to Julio Rodríguez for both his five-tool potential and his personality. He's advanced enough to possibly reach Single-A during his pro debut, just as the gem of the Rangers' 2023 international class (Sebastian Walcott) did last summer. Santana performed well at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in Florida last October, showing the potential to hit for average and power while competing against top U.S. high school prospects for the 2024 Draft. A right-handed hitter, he controls the strike zone with an extremely mature approach and shows the ability to make adjustments at the plate. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to grow into plus pop and drives the ball to all fields. Santana also has the plus speed to make an impact on the bases and in center field. The only obvious weakness in his game is his arm, which grades as below-average-to-fringy but should be playable in center. He's bilingual and earns raves for his work ethic and intelligence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing for $820,000 in July 2019, Quintana has endured a slow road up the Washington chain. After 2020 was lost to the pandemic, the Venezuela native was limited to only seven games in the Florida Complex League in 2021 due to multiple hamstring injuries. He lasted a full campaign in his FCL return last year and showed some promising results with a .289/.342/.439 line, five homers and a 116 wRC+ in 50 games. Now that Quintana has been able to stay on the field more consistently, we have a slightly clearer view of who he can be in the box. He has plus raw power from the right side and uses it to the pull side as well as right-center. Listed at 6-foot-1, 175 pounds, Quintana’s strength and power production should be his carrying tools on his way to the capital. Though he can make hard contact, he expanded the zone too much last year at the complex and walked only 4.5 percent of the time, lowest in the FCL among those with at least 190 plate appearances. An average runner with just a decent arm, Quintana was moved to first base for Single-A Fredericksburg early in 2023 to get out of the way of an outfield logjam. However, the defensive move may have placed an additional burden on his performance because he started to hit again after moving back to grass. First base would put extra weight on his bat, and he still might need to lock in there long-term if he wants to crack the capital with this core of prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quintana was the Nationals’ third-highest signee of the July 2019 international class with an $820,000 bonus. (Fellow Venezuelan Andry Lara was part of the same group.) The 6-foot-1 outfielder is still waiting to make an impact in the Minor Leagues. He was limited to instructional-league play in 2020 and played only seven games in last year’s Florida Complex League before suffering hamstring issues that kept him off the field the rest of the way. He’s gotten a lot more playing time this season in the FCL and has taken advantage with strong production across the board. Quintana displays impressive raw power from the right side and doesn’t show much of an issue driving the ball toward right-center. He has shown quality plate discipline in the past, but that hasn’t been a huge part of his game in 2022. An average runner, he was already expected to slow as he aged and filled out his 175-pound frame. That speed will be worth monitoring even more so following the hamstring concerns. Quintana has played right field only during his looks in Minor League Baseball, and that’s where his long-term home was expected to be anyways. His 2022 success establishes a base layer of both health and production, and he could be a breakout candidate over a fuller campaign in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quintana was overshadowed by fellow Venezuela native Andry Lara among the Nationals’ July 2, 2019 crop, but he received an $820,000 bonus -- third-highest in the organization’s class. He has yet to play in the Minors in an official capacity, but does have experience in instructional league already, following last year’s cancellation of the season. He got in three games in the stateside Florida Complex League this summer before a significant hamstring injury sent him to the injured list. Quintana draws fullback comparisons for his thicker frame at 6-foot-1, strength and physicality. His raw power, particularly to right-center, already jumps out for his age and experience level, and the Nationals are pleased with the way he has been able to show plate discipline at such a young age against more advanced competition at instructs. His speed is average now but is likely to slow a tick as he matures, meaning a move from center to the corners should be in the cards down the line. His arm is impressive enough to handle such a transition. The right-handed slugger is set to see the Minors at age 18 and could take off once he starts playing against more age-appropriate competition. With no true negatives on the board yet, Quintana has a chance to be a solid Major League outfielder, regardless of which spot he ends up at on the grass. He just needs to start picking up the experience necessary to reach that projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals locked up a pair of promising 16-year-old Venezuelan prospects at the start of last year’s international period in right-hander Andy Lara and Quintana, the latter of whom received an $820,000 bonus that marked the third-largest given out by the organization to a player in the 2019-20 class. Brought to the U.S. to participate in the organization’s fall instructional league, Quintana opened eyes with his physicality and tools on both sides of the ball. An athletic and physically gifted young player, Quintana packs a lot of strength into his thicker frame. That strength shows in his bat speed and ability to impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. He can drive the ball to all fields and impressed club officials last fall with his pop to the opposite-field gap.
