He has a clean swing and sound approach for a young player, with the potential to hit for both average and power as he matures. Quintana is an average runner and will likely begin his career in center field, though physical development may eventually force him to an outfield corner. His average arm is better suited for left field than right. The Nationals are high on the teenager’s defensive ability and see him as a potentially dynamic outfielder regardless of position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It should come as no surprise that Cleveland's biggest international signing in a deep 2026 class was another switch-hitting shortstop. Reinoso fits the bill after signing for $820,000 out of the Dominican Republic, although he is more physical than some other recent signings and is already listed at 6-foot, 200 pounds. It's quite early, but his raw tools, particularly on offense, are exciting. Reinoso was initially just a left-handed swinger but learned to switch-hit and is making rapid strides from the right side. He controls the zone well for his age and has a good feel for contact. He already does a good job of putting the ball in the air, so there's a chance for above-average power as he physically matures. Cleveland's system is full of middle infielders, so Reinoso will likely need to move around the diamond, but he'll have a chance to stick at shortstop. His arm is plenty strong for the left side of the infield, and he's a pretty fluid mover despite not being overly speedy. If he does have to shift to the hot corner, there's reason to believe he'll have the bat to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite the Mariners’ possible logjam of quality arms competing for just a handful of bullpen spots, the club liked Clarke enough to pry him away from the Cubs in last December’s Rule 5 Draft, making him a strong candidate to contribute ASAP. Clarke’s numbers didn’t jump off the page at Double-A Tennessee last year, but Mariners GM Justin Hollander suggested that the under-the-hood metrics are above average, saying, “This is a guy we feel like there’s some dials to turn” at the Winter Meetings. Entering his age-25 season with three years of Minors experience, Clarke relies on his massive 6-foot-7 frame to his advantage, paired with a low three-quarters arm slot that creates a quirky angle and makes it challenging to decipher out of hand, especially for righties. And given his size, the repeatability of his mechanics and the athleticism and body control also stand out. He throws his fastball in the 92-94 mph range and tops out at 96 mph with much run and sink, making him one of the top ground-ball pitchers in the Minors. His best pitch is an off-the-table curveball, which is effective against both righties and lefties. He complements those with a mid-80s slider that ranks average. And he throws all of them for strikes, which makes him an ideal arm for the Mariners’ mantra of \"Dominate The Zone.\"

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs spent back-to-back 2019 Draft picks on college closers with starter traits, then moved Louisville's Michael McAvene (third round) and Southern California's Clarke (fourth) into the rotation as soon as they turned pro. Clarke got knocked around when he started for the Trojans early in his college career, but recorded a 1.96 ERA and a 26/4 K/BB ratio during his 23-inning pro debut. He participated in instructional league in 2020, making two game appearances there but spending most of his time in Chicago's pitching camp. He then missed the first three months of 2021 with with a hip impingement. Clarke's hammer curveball is the best in the system and works against both left-handers and right-handers while arriving in the low 80s with power downer break. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph and peaks at 96 with run and sink that produce groundouts. His mid-80s slider gives him another solid pitch and is further testament to his feel for spin, and he's refining a changeup with some sink. Clarke's 6-foot-7 frame and low three-quarters arm slot create unusual angle that makes it tough to pick up his pitches, especially for righties. He's athletic and has good body control, allowing him to repeat his delivery and provide consistent strikes. He can't match McAvene's pure stuff but has more polish and a better chance to succeed as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs used consecutive picks in the 2019 Draft on standout college relievers with starter traits, taking Louisville's Michael McAvene in the third round and Southern California's Clarke in the fourth. Clarke missed his junior high school season following Tommy John surgery and got knocked around while shuttling between roles in his first two years with the Trojans, but he logged a 1.03 ERA in a full-time bullpen role last spring. Chicago eased him into pro ball with short starts and will keep him in the rotation going forward. Clarke's hammer curveball ranks as the best in the system and is effective against both left-handers and right-handers with its powerful downward break. He elicits a lot of ground balls with his fastball, which parks at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 with run and sink. His feel to spin also translates into a solid slider and he's working on refining his changeup after not using it much as a college reliever. Clarke's 6-foot-7 frame and low three-quarters arm slot create angle that makes it difficult to pick up his pitches, especially for right-handers. He's athletic for his size, repeats his delivery well and provides regular strikes. His pure stuff isn't as loud as McAvene's but he has a better chance to make it as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Yankees for $100,000 in May 2021, a few months after the start of the delayed 2020-21 international signing period, Delgado got off to a very good start to his pro career, with an OPS over 1.000 during his debut in the Dominican Summer League, followed by an .899 OPS in the Florida Complex League in 2023 and a combined 70 steals in his first 101 professional games. He was preparing for his 2024 season when he was sent to the Pirates as the player to be named later in the J.T. Brubaker deal and made his full-season debut with Bradenton in early May, with less success at the plate. Delgado is a switch-hitter who showed off a very disciplined approach over his first two summers as a pro, rarely swinging or missing or chasing out of the zone. But in his first go-round with the Pirates, he tried to get to more impact, and it didn't work as his strikeout rate soared to 21.5 percent from the 12.4 percent he posted in 2022 and 2023 combined. He still makes good swing decisions and has a strong sense of the strike zone but needs to get back to being a contact-first type of hitter. An average runner who steals bases because of instincts, Delgado has seen equal time at both middle infield positions, with second base his best landing spot were he to settle in at one position because of a fringy arm. He might get some reps at third in 2025 as well with an eye towards a future career as a super utility guy on the dirt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Delgado has earned All-Star recognition in each of two seasons after signing for $100,000 out of Venezuela in 2021. He ranked second in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with a .504 on-base percentage and third with 34 steals during his 2022 pro debut. He came to the United States last summer and led the Rookie-level Florida Complex League with 54 runs and 36 steals while finishing fourth with eight homers. He'd yet to make his 2024 debut when he was sent to the Pirates as the player to be named later in the JT Brubaker deal. A switch-hitter, Delgado is equally skilled from both sides of the plate and batted .301/.459/.495 in his first two years as a pro. With an extremely disciplined approach and good feel for the barrel, he rarely swings and misses or chases pitches out of the zone. Despite his FCL slugging exploits, he's small and doesn't hit the ball hard or in the air particularly often, so he'll probably max out at 10-15 homers per season. Similarly, his lofty steal totals (70 in 85 attempts over 101 games through two years) are more the result of his instincts than his average speed. He fits best at second base, where his average range and fringy arm strength work better than at shortstop. He reminds some club officials of a smaller and more patient version of Thairo Estrada, who began his career with the Yankees before carving out a niche with the Giants.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perdomo was No. 4 on the 2024 Top 50 International Prospects list when that year’s signing period opened up, the second-highest ranked shortstop behind only Leo De Vries. The Braves went all in, giving Perdomo $5 million, the highest bonus awarded in the class, to join. Since then, they haven’t really gotten a true look at who he is; hamstring issues shut him down after just eight games during his debut in the Dominican Summer League and limited him to 54 more in the Florida Complex League in 2025. The injury bug hit again, though this time it was his knee, an injury suffered in his second game of 2026 that will cost him the season. The Braves really don’t know what kind of player they have on their hands at this point, not wanting to put too much weight on 62 total games and a combined .546 OPS. When he was entering pro ball, he was considered to be one of the best pure hitters in his signing class, a right-handed hitter who is capable of making hard contact. He’s overly aggressive and can chase too much, but there had been a semblance of a plan at the plate with decent pitch recognition, which didn’t necessarily show up stateside last year. All of the missed reps certainly didn’t help him find a rhythm or get to any of his raw power. It remained to be seen if Perdomo, once he got past the hammy bug, could utilize his above-average speed on the basepaths, something even more in question now with his knee injury. Before he went down again, there was confidence he could play a reliable shortstop with a good arm. His age-19 season now scrapped, he'll try to get the ship moving in the right direction in 2027, at age 20.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Imagine getting a premium sports car but not being able to see how it runs for an entire year because it broke down seemingly before you drove it off the lot. That’s kind of how the Braves are feeling with Perdomo, considered one of the best prospects in the 2024 international class who received the largest bonus anyone in the class received, $5 million, to sign. But he suffered a hamstring injury that shut him down after just eight games, leaving the Braves a little unsure what kind of player they actually have on their hands. The good news is that Perdomo should have a clean bill of health and be able to truly get going in 2025. Thought to be one of the best pure hitters in his signing class, the right-handed hitter does not swing-and-miss much and can make consistently hard contact. With his knack for finding the barrel comes an over-aggressive approach at times, chasing out of the zone, but he seems to have good pitch recognition skills and the ability to handle all kinds of stuff. He can drive the ball to all fields and there could be plenty of power to come as he matures. Perdomo was at least an above-average runner before the injury and the hope is that will still be an asset on the basepaths post-injury. He also has a good foundation to play shortstop long-term thanks to good range and arm strength. He’s just 18 for the 2025 season, so there’s still plenty of time for him to reach his ceiling, with the Braves eager to see him get through a full, healthy year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perdomo was ranked No. 3 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2024 signing period opened in January. The Braves had a bonus pool of $5.284 million for the period and put nearly all of their chips in, giving the shortstop $5 million -- the largest bonus anyone in the class received -- to join the organization. A right-handed hitting infielder, Perdomo was considered to be one of the best pure hitters in this international signing class. He rarely strikes out and has a knack for making hard contact with a quick and simple swing. While he’s an aggressive hitter, he has a solid approach, showing good pitch recognition skills and an ability to drive fastballs and soft stuff to all fields, with his power just starting to come. He’s at least an above-average runner who should be able to impact the game on the basepaths as well. It's looking now like Perdomo will be able to play shortstop for a very long time. He’s fundamentally sound with plenty of range and enough arm for the premium position. He’ll be 17 years old for the entirety of his pro debut this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peluse, a ninth-round Draft pick by the A’s out of Wake Forest in 2019, transformed his body during the pandemic by strengthening his legs while also refining his mechanics, leading to a fastball that was up to 98 mph. The increased velocity helped him rack up 109 strikeouts in 101 combined innings between High-A and Double-A in 2021. He regressed a bit last season, posting a 5.38 ERA with only 92 strikeouts in 118 2/3 innings at Double-A Midland. Peluse’s fastball ticked down last season, sitting around 92-94 mph for the most part. He rounds out his three-pitch mix with an above-average slider and decent changeup, though both offerings were likely affected by the decrease in velocity. Command has always been a strength for Peluse dating back to his college days. Even in a down 2022, he only walked 28 batters at Double-A. Between his strong build and ability to consistently pound the zone with strikes, the A’s still see a path for him to stick as a starter, though they hope he can regain some of that lost velocity in the coming season. Given his repertoire, a move to the bullpen could also be in play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick by the A’s in 2019, Peluse went to the New York-Penn League later that summer and posted a 2.25 ERA. He utilized the pandemic as an opportunity to strengthen his legs and refine his mechanics, and the result was a return to baseball throwing a fastball harder than he’d ever thrown before. After lighting up the radar gun in the instructional league, the increased velocity helped him rack up 109 strikeouts in 101 combined innings at High-A and Double-A in 2021. Peluse’s 95-98 mph fastball is accompanied by a strong slider that has flashed plus at times and a solid changeup that continues to improve, giving him a good three-pitch mix to work with. Command is also a strength, evidenced by his low walk numbers that date back to his college days at Wake Forest. Proving to be durable with a big body and having just thrown by far the most innings over a single season in his baseball career, Peluse is expected to develop into a starter at the Major League level. His advanced repertoire and consistent ability to pound the strike zone should help him knock on the big league door soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick in 2019, Peluse has put himself on the prospect radar for the A’s after showing up to the instructional league that consistently hit 97-98. The increased velocity was a credit to his hard work during the baseball shutdown in 2020 as he focused on strengthening his legs. Now carrying a power fastball, Peluse also brings a strong slider that flashes plus, as well as a changeup that is still developing. His command has always been solid going back to his days at Wake Forest, and it showed up in his debut season in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League, walking just six batters across 24 innings. Approaching his first full season in the Minors in 2021, Peluse will get a chance to show what he can do with his improved repertoire. His repeatable delivery projects him to stick as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 14 prospect in the 2022 international signing class, Mejia signed with the Cardinals for $2 million out of the Dominican Republic, thus getting almost one-third of the organization’s $6,262,600 bonus pool. Unlike many young players who need to ease into pro ball, the switch-hitting shortstop found success almost immediately in the Dominican Summer League with a .267/.418/.479 slash line and five homers in 45 games. His 145 wRC+ ranked in the 90th percentile among qualified 17-year-olds in the DSL. Mejia’s impressive bat speed lived up to the hype, and he proved not to be overly aggressive with his hacks either by walking 15.9 percent of the time. There’s some natural lift in his swing too -- he hit flyballs on 46.8 percent of his batted balls -- and that helped the power play quickly in pro ball. He was a bit more productive batting from the left side against righties, but that could balance out as he gets more experience against professional southpaws moving forward. The Cardinals got aggressive with Mejia in his first stateside season, mixing in stints in the Florida State League along with his work at the complex, and his performance has cratered, though low BABIPs in small samples could be to blame. Stil, Mejia hasn't performed to the same level in the FSL or FCL, making his age-18 season a difficult one to swallow. An average runner, Mejia was a potential candidate to move off short even before he signed. The Cardinals will be invested in keeping him there as long as possible, but his arm strength could be a fit at third base too. Both he and the organization will have to flush his 2023 away in the hopes that the exposure to stateside ball lays the groundwork for future gains. Mejia, after all, still won't turn 19 until next April.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals had a bonus pool of $6,262,600 for the 2022 international period and used roughly $2 million of it to sign Mejia out of the Dominican Republic. He was ranked No. 14 among MLB Pipeline’s top prospects for his signing class and instantly became one of the system’s most promising shortstops. A switch-hitter, Mejia already shows an ability to cover the plate well from both sides of the box, and he’s capable of hitting the ball hard already due to impressive bat speed. He’s capable of showing good raw power already, but the skill projects to be just average by the time he dives deeper into the pros. Besides the hit tool, Mejia’s other above-average skill is his arm with some grading it out as plus. It’s his best defensive asset right now, and there is a feeling among some that, with average speed, he’ll have to move off shortstop in time. The arm would help with a transition to third base, or he could be a candidate for second base if his overall athleticism holds up. As is the case with many international signees, Mejia’s range of outcomes is vast. The Cardinals’ investment shows they believe he can be a solid infield regular in the end, and given his present skill set, don’t be surprised if he takes off quickly offensively during early tastes of the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a notable freshman year at Arizona State in which he was honorable mention All-Pac-12, the Louisiana native transferred closer to home to Mississippi. He proved to be one of the more disciplined hitters in the Southeastern Conference, and his high floor helped him go in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, where the Guardians signed him to an above-slot $722,600 bonus. The infielder thrived during a 15-game cameo at Single-A, where he slashed .347/.459/.510 with seven steals and as many walks as strikeouts. Built strongly at 6-foot-1, 200 pounds, Hill retains a hit-over-power profile. His combination of strong swing decisions and in-zone contact enables him to run high walk rates, although he can struggle with whiffs when he does swing out of the zone, in particular on secondary pitches. He has a sound right-handed swing and consistently makes strong contact, but his habit of hitting the ball on the ground and the other way caps his power ceiling. If he is able to catch the ball out front more, he could project to hit more than 15 homers per season. Hill has below-average speed, his weakest tool in a well-rounded skillset, although he's a heady baserunner who may be able to nab double-digit bags in the big leagues. That lack of range caused him to shift from shortstop in college to third base and second, where he's currently splitting time. His average arm should be enough for either position, and he could also see time at first base (or an outfield corner) for increased defensive versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brannon had a monster high school senior season, leading the nation with 20 homers and 91 RBIs in 34 games while carrying Randleman (N.C.) HS to its second consecutive 2-A state title. He tied the state record for long balls set by his father, Paul, in 1989 and signed for third-round money ($712,500) as a ninth-rounder. A left thumb injury and back problems limited him to 17 games in 2023, though he did go deep six times in 72 at-bats. Already quite physical at 5-foot-11 and 210 pounds, Brannon stands out with some of the best raw power and highest exit velocities among Red Sox farmhands. He has a quick right-handed stroke and looks to do damage with an aggressive approach at the plate. He didn't face much quality pitching as an amateur, so there's some question as to how he'll fare against better stuff, especially if he doesn't develop more discipline at the plate. With plus arm strength and quick feet behind the plate, Brannon is equipped to combat the running game. He's overly active as a catcher and his framing and blocking skills will have to improve, but he has the hands and the work ethic to become at least a decent receiver. Though he's a well-below-average runner, he might be able to handle third base or left field if he has to switch positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brannon led national high school hitters with 20 homers and 91 RBIs in 34 games last spring while helping Randleman HS (N.C.) pick up its second straight 2-A state championship. His 20 long balls also tied the state record -- set by his father, Paul, in 1989 en route to becoming a Mariners fourth-rounder. Brooks went in the ninth round last July and signed for $712,500, the equivalent of third-round money. An extremely physical teenager at 6 feet and 210 pounds, Brannon has some of the best raw power and produces some of the highest exit velocities in the Red Sox system. He generates impressive bat speed and shows an encouraging willingness to use the entire field. He's extremely aggressive at the plate and likely will have to tone down his approach against pro pitching. Brannon's plus arm strength and quick feet behind the plate result in pop times around 1.9 seconds and should enable him to control the running game. He has the work ethic and the hands to become at least an adequate receiver, but he's overly active and his framing and blocking skills are raw. He's a well-below-average runner but might be able to handle third base or left field if he can't make it as a catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working just 5 2/3 innings in two seasons at Purdue, Whitman transferred to Kent State and took off under the tutelage of pitching coach and former big leaguer Mike Birkbeck. He won Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year accolades, developed into the best college southpaw in the 2023 Draft and went in the supplemental second round. He struggled in Double-A last year, posting an Eastern League-worst 5.29 ERA, though he did strike out 124 in 117 1/3 innings. Whitman struggled because Double-A hitters crushed his fastball, which parked at 91-93 and topped out at 96 without much life. His best pitch is a low-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action, and he commands it better than his heater. He also can make hitters look bad with a sinking low-80s changeup, though he struggles to land it in the zone consistently. Whitman comes with enough pitches and strikes to make it as a starter, but his ceiling appears lower than it did when he entered pro ball. Unless he improves his fastball velocity and shape, he probably won't be more that a back-of-the-rotation option. He also could become a lefty reliever who depends heavily on his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitman worked just 5 2/3 innings in two seasons at Purdue before transferring to Kent State, where he blossomed under pitching coach and former big leaguer Mike Birkbeck, becoming the Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year and the consensus best college left-hander in the 2023 Draft. He lasted a bit longer than expected and the Giants were delighted to grab him with their supplemental second-round choice at No. 69 overall. He divided his first full pro season between two Class A levels, logging a 4.63 ERA with a 108/37 K/BB ratio in 103 innings. All three of Whitman's pitches grade as at least solid at their best, highlighted by a low-80s slider with horizontal and vertical movement that he commands better than his fastball. He does a good job of locating his heater too, operating at 92-94 mph and touching 97 with riding and tailing action. His low-80s changeup lacks the consistency of his fastball and slider but still misses bats with its fade and sink. Whitman couldn't find the strike zone at Purdue but cleaned up his mechanics at Kent State and now has a more fluid delivery. He struggled with his control in the first half of last season but sliced his walk rate from 12 percent in Single-A to 5 percent in High-A. A legitimate three-pitch starter, he could fit into the middle of a big league rotation if he continues to improve his changeup and strike-throwing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working just 5 2/3 innings in two seasons at Purdue, Whitman transferred to Kent State for 2023 and took off under the tutelage of pitching coach and former big leaguer Mike Birkbeck. He won Mid-American Conference Pitcher of the Year accolades and became the consensus best college left-hander in the Draft. The Giants were surprised to find him available in the supplemental second round, signed him for $805,575 and saw him pitch well in a brief pro debut. A true three-pitch starter, Whitman owns a fastball that sits at 91-94 mph and touches 96, playing better than its velocity because of its ride and tail and his ability to command it. His best option is a low-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action, and he does an even better job of locating it than his heater. Though his low-80s changeup isn't as consistent as his other two offerings because he hasn't used it as much, it fades and sinks and misses bats. Whitman didn't throw strikes at Purdue but that's no longer an issue. He cleaned up his delivery at Kent State, and while it still features some effort, he now fills the zone with his fastball and slider. If he continues to refine his changeup and control, he could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A star on Panamanian youth teams, Sugastey signed for $525,000 in 2019 but had his pro debut delayed by the pandemic. He broke in by winning the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting title (.358) in 2021 but has had his development further delayed by quadriceps and knee injuries the last two seasons. He's the best catching prospect in the system, though the Giants declined to protect him on the 40-man roster last November because he's not close to ready for the Majors. Sugastey stands out more with his defense than his offense. He moves well behind the plate and continues to improve as a receiver and game-caller, though he still needs more consistency. With well-above-average arm strength and a quick transfer, he'll be able to combat the increased reliance on the running game. Sugastey consistently puts the ball in play with his short right-handed swing, though he's going to have to make adjustments and add strength in order to do damage. He produces mediocre exit velocities and struggles to drive the ball in the air, so he may not produce double-digit home run totals. He has a soft-contact approach that yields some gap power and few walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring in international play for Panamanian youth teams, Sugastey signed for $525,000 in 2019. The pandemic pushed his pro debut back until 2021, when he won the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting title with a .358 average. He found the jump to full-season ball more difficult, hitting .240 in Single-A last summer while dealing with a quadriceps injury. In a system full of aggressive sluggers, Sugastey stands out with his bat-to-ball skills and hit-over-power approach. He repeatedly puts the ball in play with a compact right-handed stroke, though he doesn't hit the ball especially hard and must add more strength. He did a better job of avoiding ground-ball contact in 2022, but still slugged just .334 and may max out at 10-12 homers per season. More athletic than most catchers, Sugastey still is learning behind the plate. His receiving improved last season but still has a ways to go. He combats the running game with well-above-average arm strength and a quick transfer, and he also shows promise as a game caller.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing a potentially special 2018 international class, the Giants landed another deep crop the following year headlined by shortstop Aeverson Arteaga. Sugastey landed the fifth-highest bonus ($525,000) in that haul after starring in international play on Panamanian youth teams. The pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021, when he won the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting title by hitting .358/.405/.439 at age 18. Sugastey excels at putting the bat on the ball with a compact right-handed swing, though he almost does so too easily. He hits a lot of ground balls and displays average raw power at best, so even if he continues to add strength, he might top out at 12-15 homers per year. His ability to make contact also cuts into his ability to draw walks, so much of his offensive value could come from his batting average. Sugastey owns one of the strongest arms in the system, earning plus-plus grades from some evaluators, and threw out 30 percent of basestealers in the ACL. He's more athletic than most catchers yet still a work in progress behind the plate. He needs to clean up his receiving but shows promise as a game-caller.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCullough helped Wingate win the NCAA Division II national championship in 2021 and repeated as an All-American as a senior in '22, when he caught the Cubs' eye while outpitching Carson Whisenhunt (now with the Giants) in a heavily scouted Cape Cod League matchup. A 10th-round pick that July, he compiled a 3.44 ERA with 108 strikeouts in 86 1/3 innings between two Class A stops in his first full year as a pro. He missed the start of the 2024 season while recovering from offseason knee surgery, then made just four appearances (three starts) before getting shut down with a lat strain. McCullough's fastball misses bats despite its pedestrian 91-95 mph velocity because it has flat approach angle with carry and natural cutting action. His sweeping low-80s slider features good depth and shows signs of becoming a solid offering. The fade and depth on his 83-86 mph changeup contrast nicely with the movement on his heater, though he doesn't use it or his mid-70s curveball very often. While McCullough has a bit of a herky-jerky delivery, he creates extension and deception without costing himself control. He has a nice variety of pitch shapes and good feel for sequencing his offerings. Often requested in trade talks, he has one of the higher floors among the system's starting pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCullough starred at NCAA Division II Wingate (N.C.), helping the Bulldogs win the 2021 national championship and earning All-America accolades in each of his final two seasons. He proved himself further with five strong starts in the Cape Cod League before the 2022 Draft in which the Cubs selected him in the 10th round. He breezed through Single-A in his first full pro season, got knocked around in his initial two High-A outings, then logged a 2.57 ERA in his last seven starts. McCullough attacks hitters with his fastball, which ranges from 91-95 mph and plays better than its velocity with its flat approach angle. His low-80s slider should give him a second solid offering once it becomes more consistent. His upper-70s curveball and low-80s changeup with some fade are both fringy and he doesn't have much faith in either. Though he doesn't have the smoothest delivery, McCullough creates good extension and deception without compromising his control. He doesn't stand out with his ceiling but he has a high floor as one of the better bets in the system to remain a long-term starter. Other teams bring his name up repeatedly in trade talks and he should become at least a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Brewers for an over-slot $255,900 as a 14th-round pick out of a Nevada high school in 2021, Avina won the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League MVP award and home run title (10 in 36 games) in his pro debut the next summer. The Yankees acquired him and fellow outfield prospect Brian Sanchez in a November 2023 trade for Jake Bauers. After a torn labrum ended his 2024 season a month early and required offseason surgery on his left shoulder, he split last year between High-A (.295/.412/.506) and Double-A (.224/.314/.341). Avina's carrying tool is his plus raw power from the right side of the plate, which mostly plays to his pull side. He doesn't sell out for home runs, rarely chasing pitches as he waits for ones he can drive in the air to left field. Though he has improved his selectivity, he still has issues making reliable contact because he struggles to catch up to in-zone fastballs. Avina has lost some quickness as he has added strength and is now an average runner who doesn't make much of an impact on the bases. He split his time between all three outfield positions in 2025, and he's an average defender on the corners whose range is a bit stretched in center. He features solid to plus arm strength and has a knack for throwing out baserunners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Avina was committed to playing at the University of Nevada when the Brewers selected him in the 14th round in 2021 and signed him for sixth-round money with a $255,900 bonus. He won Arizona Complex League MVP honors in his 2022 pro debut after leading the Rookie-level circuit with 10 homers in 36 games before going deep five times in 28 Single-A contests at the end of that season. In 2023, Milwaukee shipped him and fellow outfield prospect Brian Sanchez to the Yankees to acquire Jake Bauers in November. Avina shows double-plus raw power from the right side, and he’s capable of crushing some absolute moonshots to the pull side. It’s that slugging potential that made him command the attention of scouts and fans alike in his first taste of the Minors. What soured many was that the blasts came with more-than-unhealthy strikeout rates around 35 percent. The right-handed slugger would get swing-happy in search of his next dinger and expand the zone so much that he would still punch out when pitchers wouldn’t dare throw him a strike. He’s improved the strikeout rate slowly in 2023 but not enough yet to project for better than a 40-grade bat at this stage. A 6.7 60-yard runner in high-school showcases, Avina should keep enough speed to feature well at all three outfield spots. He spent more time on the corners in 2023, partly in deference to Luis Lara, but he picked up 12 outfield assists from left and right, highlighting how his arm can work out there. There is a wide chasm of outcomes for the Nevada native, all depending on his contact rate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hidalgo began his pro career almost as an afterthought for the Angels at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, joining the organization for just $30,000. He wasn’t able to make his official pro debut until 2021, logging just 27 Arizona Complex League innings and missing some time with arm issues. He moved to full-season ball in 2022, but the injury bug bit again, with a rotator cuff strain shutting him down for the year in June. He returned for instructs before getting dealt to the Twins in November in return for Gio Urshela. While Hidalgo’s pure stuff doesn’t necessarily jump off the page, he does have some good ingredients to work with. His fastball sits around 92 mph, but it has some good riding life to it and he attended the Twins’ velocity camp to streamline his delivery in order to squeeze a little more velo out of him. His changeup is now his best secondary offering, a low-80s offering sold with good arm speed that elicited a 44 percent miss rate last year. In the past, Hidalgo has had more of a curve-like breaking ball that was slurvy and blurred into a slider at times. He’s worked with the Twins to scrap the curve action and focus on a firmer, harder true slider. His walk rate ticked up in 2022 to 4.4 per nine innings, but he has shown an overall feel for pitching and an ability to find the zone, with the streamlining of his delivery sure to help his overall control and command. If he can find a few ticks of velocity for the heater and continue to tighten up his breaking stuff, he could find his way into the back end of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels were aggressive on the international market when the 2019-20 signing period opened, handing out seven-figure bonuses to a pair of shortstops in Arol Vera and Adrian Placencia. At the other end of the spending ledger was Hidalgo, who joined the organization for just $30,000. After throwing well at instructs during the fall of 2020, he made his official pro debut in the Arizona Complex League, missing a little time with some arm issues. He made his full-season debut in 2022 with Single-A Inland Empire, though he was shut down for the year in late June. He did return to throw at instructs, and the Angels sent him to the Twins in a deal for infielder Gio Urshela in November. Not turning 20 until May, Hidalgo currently uses a two-pitch mix to get hitters out. His fastball sits in the low-90s, touching 94 mph at times, and he has a curve that he has a good feel to spin -- a breaking ball that could be above-average in time. He does have a changeup and sells it well with good arm speed, but it’s fringy right now. Hidalgo has impressed with advanced pitchability at times, especially for his age, showing an ability to throw his arsenal for strikes with a repeatable delivery. While his walk rate ticked up in 2022, he has the chance to have average overall command. He gets high marks for his competitiveness on the mound. Advancements in his fastball execution and development of his third pitch could help determine his future role with the Twins.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shortstops were all the rage for the Angels in the 2019-20 international signing period, with Arol Vera, Adrian Placencia and Jose Bonilla at the top of the bonus list for the organization when the period opened on July 2. That class also netted the Angels Hidalgo for $30,000, and he already opened eyes with his performance at instructs last fall. Hidalgo packs a combination of an advanced feel for pitching for his age and projection into his athletic 6-foot-1 frame. While he averaged around 92 mph and topped out at 94 with his fastball at instructs, added strength should lead to more velocity in the future. He features both a curve and a changeup, with good feel for spin for the former and a good idea of how to sell the latter with good arm speed, giving him two secondary pitches that also have some upside. What stood out more than anything at instructs was Hidalgo’s pitching know-how. He lands all three pitches for strikes, and he has a simple and athletic delivery he repeats well. If his first impression is any indication, Hidalgo should see his name rise up prospects lists as he continues to physically mature.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A North Carolina prep product, Martin planned on going to East Carolina to play shortstop until Los Angeles spotted him on the mound at the end of his 2022 senior season, drafted him in the 17th round and signed him for $125,000. His stuff made a jump in his pro debut after he focused on pitching full-time, but an offseason car accident and other outside factors led him to regress physically in 2024. He got off to a poor start in High-A last April, necessitating a month to recalibrate at the Dodgers' training facility in Arizona, Martin's best pitch is a tight upper-80s slider that elicits plenty of chases and empty swings, and he trusts it and uses it more than a fastball that parked at 92-94 mph last year and peaked at 99. His heater has some carry but is fairly straight and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it well. He's still developing feel for a mid-80s changeup with some depth and has mostly shelved an upper-70s curveball. Martin has a quick arm and works with an up-tempo delivery that creates some deception. Though he's just 6 feet tall, he has the athleticism and strike-throwing to succeed as a starter if he can refine his fastball command and changeup quality. Added strength and durability would help as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally committed to East Carolina as a shortstop, Martin sporadically pitched as a reliever before making a handful of starts on the mound as a North Carolina high school senior in 2022. Los Angeles saw enough to take a flier on him in the 17th round, and his desire to join the organization led him to give up college for a $125,000 bonus. His stuff has made a significant jump since he started concentrating on pitching and began to add strength, and he posted a 2.04 ERA with 48 strikeouts in 39 2/3 innings in Single-A during his pro debut last summer. Martin's fastball velocity increased from the low 90s in 2022 to 94-96 mph with a high of 98 in his first full year as a pro, and his heater comes with carry and armside run. He always has shown feel for spinning the ball and has added power to a mid-80s slider that features plenty of depth. His upper-80s changeup is a bit firm but continues to improve as he uses it more often, grading as a solid offering at its best. The Dodgers loved Martin's athleticism when they scouted him as an amateur and haven't made any adjustments to his clean delivery. After showing the ability to throw all three of his pitches for strikes in 2023, he has fought his control and command throughout this season. He'll need to straighten out his strike-throwing and prove his durability but has the upside of a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers couldn’t complete a big deal at last year’s Trade Deadline when Eduardo Rodriguez declined a move to the Dodgers, but Detroit still snagged a prospect by acquiring Leonard -- designated for assignment by Los Angeles -- for cash. Signed for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in the 2017-18 international class, Leonard struggled at Double-A Tulsa, and the Dodgers needed a 40-man roster spot. The Tigers gave Leonard a fresh start and promoted him to Triple-A Toledo, and he took full advantage, showing the potential he had flashed in years past and placing himself firmly in the Tigers’ roster conversation. Leonard is a high-energy, hyper-aggressive player who has learned to temper the latter as he has progressed up the development ladder. He has the bat speed to catch up with his fastballs and strength to pound mistakes for damage, though he tended to hit sinkers into the ground. Much of his power in Toledo down the stretch came from punishing sliders. He had much more success against lefties last year, a departure from his near-even platoon splits for most of his career. After playing shortstop almost exclusively for his final two years in the Dodgers' system with mixed results, the Tigers found success moving him around the field. While Leonard can handle shortstop for stretches, his future in the Tigers' system likely lies in an offense-first super-utility role. His ability to crush pitches will earn him a look, even though he chases outside the zone a bit too much, and that's continued in 2024 with strong exit velocities. Leonard dealt with multiple hamstring injuries earlier this season at Triple-A but got hot late in the summer to salvage what could have been a lost campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite being limited to paying no more than $300,000 to individual players in the 2017-18 international class as a penalty for spending $96 million on that market two years earlier, the Dodgers still hauled in four quality position players. Miguel Vargas and Andy Pages (both from Cuba) entered 2023 as Top 100 prospects, Jorbit Vivas (Venezuela) is the best contact hitter in the system and Leonard (Dominican Republic) was considered the most athletic of the group. Signed for $200,000, he recovered from a slow start last season to lead the High-A Midwest League in runs (80), hits (131), extra-base hits (51) and total bases (216), but he wasn’t quite turning the corner in 2023 at Double-A Tulsa when he was designated for assignment in July. The Tigers acquired him for cash considerations on the day of the Trade Deadline. Leonard's quick hands and whippy right-handed swing generate electric bat speed, and he also has gotten significantly stronger by adding 35 pounds since turning pro. Those attributes give him 20-homer potential, though he can get himself into trouble with an aggressive, pull-happy mentality. He'll have to make adjustments against more advanced pitchers who will be able to exploit his approach more easily. While Leonard has good athleticism, average speed and solid arm strength, his long-term defensive home remains in question. He lacks the range and consistency to play shortstop regularly in the big leagues, and he also hasn't wowed scouts at second base, third or center field. His best paths to Detroit are as an offensive-minded second baseman or utilityman, but he’ll need to start hitting again in his new organization to meet that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though they were limited to maximum $300,000 international bonuses in 2017-18 as a penalty for spending $96 million on that market two years earlier, the Dodgers still found several talented position prospects, including Andy Pages and Miguel Vargas (Cuba), Leonard (Dominican Republic) and Jorbit Vivas (Venezuela). Signed for $200,000, Leonard is the most versatile athlete among that group. He batted .297/.390/.539 with 22 homers as a 20-year-old getting his first extended taste of full-season ball in 2021, earning a spot on the 40-man roster. Bigger and stronger than his listed 160 pounds, Leonard has quick hands and a whippy right-handed stroke that produce electric bat speed. While he can get a bit pull-conscious, he makes consistent hard contact and is showing at least 20-homer potential as he learns to drive the ball more consistently. He recognizes pitches well and manages the strike zone effectively. Leonard possesses solid arm strength and similar speed that has translated more into defensive versatility than stolen bases at this point. He played primarily at shortstop last season but also had double-digit starts at second base, third base and center field. He needs to cut down on his youthful errors but projects as an average defender at shortstop, potentially plus at second and somewhere in between at third and center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Top 50 international prospect in 2023, Martinez signed with the Mariners for $600,000 when that signing period opened in January. He pitched well, albeit with poor control in his first two stops as a pro, the Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex Leagues. His transition to full-season ball was rough, plagued by poor command in and out of the zone. His July was much better and then he was sent to the Pirates in return for reliever Caleb Ferguson. Martinez is a big, physical 6-foot-4 right-hander with a huge fastball. His heater sat around 95 mph in 2025, touching 97, and he can throw it with decent sink to get ground-ball outs. His mid-80s slider has the chance to be an out pitch, but it was very inconsistent and the Pirates sent Martinez to pitch design camp to help turn it into more of a bat-misser. He’ll flash a good upper-80s changeup but didn’t throw it a lot last year and really struggled to land it in the zone. That’s the biggest thing standing in Martinez’s way. Per Synergy, he threw just 58 percent strikes overall in 2025, leading to a 5.8 BB per nine rate, and when he was in the zone, he got too much of the plate, leading to getting hit. He’ll pitch at age 20 for all of 2026, so there’s time for him to work with the Pirates to turn this upside play into a big league contributor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez was one of just seven pitchers on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the 2023 signing period opened. While the Mariners may have made more noise in signing some elite-level hitters on the international market, they weren’t afraid to go after Martinez, whom they signed for $600,000 in January 2023, adding to a class headlined by Felnin Celesten. In Martinez's two stops heading into 2025, the Dominican Summer League and the Arizona Complex League, he showed his raw stuff can get hitters out -- when he knows where it’s going. He struggled to find consistency for much of his first taste of full-season ball this year, but was having his best month in July when he was sent to the Pirates in the Caleb Ferguson trade. There are still plenty of reasons to be high on Martinez: his athleticism, his size -- he’s 6-foot-4 -- and his power stuff. The teenaged right-hander has seen velocity gains in the early stages of his career, and his fastball now sits around 94-95 mph and touches the upper 90s, and he can really sink it to get ground-ball outs. While his changeup was his better secondary pitch in the DSL, his slider has now caught up and surpassed it. In the DSL, Martinez did a nice job of being in and around the strike zone, even with his upticks in velocity. He didn’t replicate that when he came stateside and his command issues after walking seven batters per nine in the ACL -- and 5.5 per nine in the California League at the time of the trade -- have raised some reliever-risk flags. He's pitched all of the 2025 season at age 19, so there’s no reason to restrict him just yet, but he’ll need to seriously refine his command to remain in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez ranked No. 42 among MLB Pipeline’s international prospects when he signed with Seattle for $600,000 out of Mexico in 2023. He blossomed onto many teams’ radars after playing in the showcase circuit in the U.S., with long-term starter potential -- particularly after a stellar debut season in the Dominican Summer League, where he carried a 1.72 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 30.7 percent strikeout rate in 47 innings. At just 17 years old during his debut, while leveraging a huge 6-foot-4 frame, Martinez’s fastball made a huge velocity jump in just one year, from sitting in the 89-90 mph range all the way up to 93-94, even touching 97 thanks to a combination of getting onto the Mariners’ Dominican campus and making a small mechanical tweak. Through it all, Martinez retained his plus strike-throwing ability, which can often be sacrificed among youngsters growing into velocity. Among his secondaries, the changeup was better than the slider in the DSL. The Mariners haven’t had nearly as much success with pitchers on the international market in the Jerry Dipoto era -- those have mostly come via the Draft -- but there’s more than a strong chance that Martinez could blossom into one of the organization’s best in the coming years, with the ceiling of being a mid-to-high-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as an infielder for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, Castro became a full-time outfielder when he made his post-pandemic pro debut two years later. He has made steady progress through the Minors as a switch-hitter who can do a little of everything and works hard but lacks a better-than-average tool. After getting more aggressive in 2024, when he slammed a career-high 15 homers but batted a career-low .229, he dialed back his approach last season in Double-A. Castro makes more contact and does a lot more damage from the left side of the plate. While he makes good swing decisions and decent contact, he won't profile as a big league regular unless he can provide more offense. He can produce promising exit velocities but doesn't catch up to good fastballs or elevate balls consistently. Castro gets the most out of his average speed with good instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He's a capable center fielder but probably lacks the range to play there on a daily basis in the big leagues, and his average arm strength allows him to play anywhere in the outfield. His lack of ceiling has prompted the Red Sox to leave him off their 40-man roster in the last two offseasons and other clubs to bypass him in the Rule 5 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed as an infielder for $100,000 out of Dominican Republic in 2019, Castro had become an outfielder when he made his post-pandemic pro debut two years later. A switch-hitter who does a little of everything but lacks an above-average tool, he adopted a more aggressive approach in 2024. He slammed 15 homers, exceeding his total of 13 in his first three seasons, but also hit a career-low .229 and got overwhelmed by Double-A pitching following a mid-August promotion. Castro has better bat-to-ball skills and more power as a left-handed hitter, with 14 of his 15 homers coming from that side last summer. He makes good swing decisions and can work counts to draw walks, though he got too passive in Double-A. He hit the ball harder than ever in 2024, but he also struck out more frequently and still didn't pull balls in the air with much consistency. Castro has average speed out of the batter's box, moves quicker once underway and shows good instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He plays a decent center field, though his range probably would fit best in Fenway Park's spacious right field, and his arm grades as an average. Boston declined to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, and his floor as a reserve outfielder stands out more than his ceiling as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as an infielder for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, Castro was a full-time outfielder by the time he made his pandemic-delayed pro debut in 2021. He has advanced quickly, reaching High-A last July just two months after turning 20, and his name has begun to come up in trade talks. He steadily improved throughout last season before tiring in September. A switch-hitter, Castro makes more consistent contact and drives the ball with more authority from the left side of the plate. One of the more disciplined young hitters in the system, he controls the strike zone and focuses on hitting pitches from gap to gap. While he homered just 13 times in 207 games over his first three pro seasons, he's significantly stronger than his listed 170 pounds and his exit velocities portend perhaps 20-homer power in his future. An average runner out of the batter's box, Castro is quicker once he gets going and has good instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He covers enough ground to play an average center field but probably would fit better in Fenway Park's atypically spacious right field. His average arm works at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Anderson was blocked defensively by Kyle Teel until his junior year at the University of Virginia, where he produced a career 1.001 OPS and walked more than he struck out over three seasons. He was a full-time catcher for the first time in 2024, when he earned first-team All-Atlantic Coast Conference honors before the Orioles made him a second-round pick in the ‘24 Draft. The Orioles announced him as a catcher, and he was behind the plate for more than half his games during his full season debut. But Anderson struggled offensively, with a .677 OPS between High-A Aberdeen and Double-A Chesapeake, before bouncing back a bit in the Arizona Fall League (.300/.398/.443 in 19 games). Anderson is a switch-hitter who seemed to get to more power from the left side in college, but he didn’t tap into much from either side in his pro debut and doesn’t torch the ball with super-high exit velocities. Instead, his strengths lay in his ability to control at-bats and make solid swing decisions. He doesn’t strike out much and reaches base at a strong clip. His bat is his carrying tool but it’s a hit-tool-driven profile, meaning Anderson could benefit from impacting the ball with more authority. Plus makeup lifts the overall profile, but Anderson is still something of a tweener -- he’s a fringy defender behind the plate and might not provide enough thump to be an everyday option at first base. He does have a solid enough arm and can be a good receiver at times, leading to a belief he can grow into an average catcher with more defensive reps. His ceiling seems highest behind the plate, where Anderson could grow into a switch-hitting backstop with some positional flexibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Anderson produced a career 1.001 OPS with more walks than strikeouts over three years at the University of Virginia, where he was blocked behind the plate defensively by Kyle Teel until his junior season. He earned first-team All-Atlantic Coast Conference honors that year before the Orioles took him in the second round of the 2024 Draft, announced him as a catcher and signed him for an under-slot $1.17 million. Anderson then hit well (.288/.361/.438) during a brief debut that ended at High-A Aberdeen. His first full season was less successful, with a .677 OPS over 90 games between Aberdeen and Double-A Chesapeake, but he did hit .300 with an OPS of .840 over 19 Arizona Fall League games. The switch-hitting Anderson seems to get to more of his power from the left side, while he’s more of a line-drive hitter from the right side. But he brings a strong approach and good on-base skills to both, with a feel for the barrel and an idea for how to control his at-bats. The ball doesn’t fly off of his bat velocity-wise, so if he develops into an above-average hitter, it’ll be on the basis of those bat-to-ball skills and swing decisions. The bat is his carrying tool along with his plus makeup. Anderson saw time at other positions as an underclassman because of Teel and didn’t catch full-time as a junior, at which point he was considered a fringy defender with an average arm. But his ceiling is highest behind the plate, especially if he doesn’t provide enough thump to profile at first base. The Orioles continue to give him reps at the position to develop into a solid bat-first everyday option there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Serrano comes from the same Jaime Ramos Academy in San Cristóbal, Dominican Republic, that helped produce Top 100 prospects in Dodgers shortstop Emil Morales and Giants shortstop Josuar Gonzalez. The outfielder was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 26 prospect in the 2026 international class, and he signed with the Nationals for $1,969,000, becoming the organization’s biggest January 15 addition this year. Isaias Suarez (No. 40) was the only other prospect from MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 to join Washington. The left-handed hitter repeatedly earned praise from Nationals officials for his sweet swing from the left side. He can maintain his timing despite a wider stance than most of his peers, and he can repeat his swing with impressive loft. He already stands at 6-foot-3 entering his age-17 season, and with the right strength gains, he could get to at least average power, given that propensity to put the ball in the air already. Serrano is just an average runner as he enters the affiliated ranks, but he has a nose for the ball in center field and takes clean routes to generate outs. The Nationals should give him plenty of looks in center field to begin his career, knowing that he could be above-average in a corner should he need to move when he bumps into speedier defenders higher up the chain. That will add some pressure to the bat, though there’s enough promise there to make him a potential average regular in the years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After eschewing the international market for years under previous management, the Orioles have become legit players in Latin America under GM Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, handing out seven-figure bonuses every year and reeling in some of the region’s top-rated prospects. Their biggest splash yet was Almeyda, who signed for a franchise-record $2.3 million bonus to headline the club’s 2023 class. Born in Paterson, New Jersey, Almeyda moved to the Dominican Republic as a 15-year-old and performed well in both the U.S. and the D.R. as a teen and was expected to transition more smoothly to pro ball than other international prospects. But Almeyda was limited to 19 games in the Dominican Summer League due to a left shoulder injury that required surgery in 2023, though he did play 53 games in the Florida Complex League in 2024. Almeyda is a tall, athletic shortstop with solid future tools across the board, but his impact will be made as an offensive player. He has a quick right-handed swing and hits the ball hard, generating a lot of line drives and power from a 6-foot-2, 180-pound frame that should strengthen as his body matures. He struggled with his approach in a small sample during his debut, but the injury played a big factor in that, and he is considered to have a good feel for the strike zone and hitting in general. He’s a good runner who can handle himself on the bases. Almeyda played most of his games during his debut at shortstop, and while he has the chance to play there long-term, there was always the possibility he’d outgrow the position, and he played a lot more third in 2024. He’s considered athletic enough to eventually adjust if necessary, given the strong arm, soft hands, good footwork and quickness he already shows in the middle of the diamond. Almeyda has flashed all five tools, but he needs time to develop on both sides of the ball for a better gauge of how high his ceiling really will be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: ﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ It took a while for the Orioles to get established in the international market after committing to doing so for the first time under general manager Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, but now that they are, they are legit players, handing out seven-figure bonuses every year. The latest example is Almeyda, who signed for a franchise-record $2.3 million as the headliner of their 2022-23 class. A native of Paterson, New Jersey, who moved to the Dominican Republic as a 15-year-old, Almeyda was a familiar name in amateur circles after performing well both in the D.R. and the United States as a teen. He is expected to transition more smoothly to pro ball than many international prospects given his familiarity with the U.S. A tall, athletic shortstop with a good approach at the plate, Almeyda generates power from a quick right-handed swing that could develop into a plus tool. His other tools are solid across the board, with a chance to improve as his body matures and he grows accustomed to professional pitching. He’s a good runner who can handle himself on the bases. Almeyda projects as a strong defender with a plus arm, soft hands, and good footwork in the middle of the diamond. He’ll play shortstop every day in pro ball, though at 6-foot-2 and 180 pounds, it’s possible he’ll outgrow the position in time due to his size. Even so, he’s considered athletic enough that an adjustment to a new position shouldn’t be a problem. He’ll need time to develop on both sides of the field, but Almeyda has a chance to develop into a five-tool player if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lin is an international star back home in Taiwan, having stood out for Chinese Taipei at the 2021 U-23 World Cup before signing with the D-backs for $525,000 that December and throwing four scoreless innings against Japan just this winter in the WBSC Premier12 gold-medal game at the Tokyo Dome. In between, he’s been a steady performer in the Arizona system. His 2024 campaign was put on pause when he suffered facial fractures on a foul ball hit to the Double-A Amarillo dugout, but he still managed a 4.28 ERA with 90 strikeouts in 94 2/3 innings in the Texas League before making one start for Triple-A Reno. Lin rounded out his stateside season with three Arizona Fall League starts before heading abroad for Premier12. The 5-foot-11 southpaw steps to the side and rocks a bit to begin his delivery out of the stretch with a little flair. He throws both a four-seamer and a sinker in the 90-92 mph range (occasionally touching 95-96). Without stellar velocity, he needs the different movement profiles to keep hitters off balance. He also has to locate the pitches well, because when he doesn’t, they can be crushed. But the depth of the arsenal reveals more promising offerings, like an 80-82 mph changeup that fades well off the heat and a mid-70s curveball. Both are options against righties, while a 79-82 mph sweeper is his go-to secondary against lefties. Both breaking balls play with extreme spin with the curve, in particular, averaging above 3,000 rpm at Triple-A Reno in 2025. Lin has also worked on incorporating an upper-80s cutter to keep hitters guessing further. He needs to live on the edges of the zone if he’s going to achieve whiffs because he can’t blow pitches by batters. His four-seamer has been particularly crushed in the Pacific Coast League. Lin’s outing against Japan showed he doesn’t back down from challenges, though, and he has enough offerings to make it work as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Cutter: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 A standout performance at the 2021 U-23 World Cup for Chinese Taipei, along with his previous international experience, helped Lin sign with the D-backs for $525,000 in December of that year. He’s been dominant at virtually every level since and pitched his age-19 season at High-A and Double-A, finishing with a 3.86 ERA and an organization-best 140 strikeouts in 121 1/3 innings. Considering Amarillo is a hitter’s paradise, it was even more impressive that Lin posted a 3.89 ERA and 1.01 WHIP in six home starts (34 2/3 innings) for the Sod Poodles. Standing a mere 5-foot-11, Lin has one of the deepest and most interesting repertoires in the Minor Leagues. Rocking back in his throwing motion, he delivers a fastball that typically only sits in the 88-92 mph range. That said, the pitch has good ride up in the zone, making it play better than the velo alone, and he touched 94 at Double-A. D-backs officials believe the southpaw has added strength in the offseason, and even if he isn’t pumping mid-90s, a little more heat would go a long way. That’s because his secondaries are so impressive. A low-80s changeup shows tremendous fade and got a 49 percent whiff rate at Double-A. A 75-77 mph curveball is tough for hitters to track with its spin and vertical drop, while a low-80s slider glides more horizontally. He’s added a mid-80s cutter for a harder breaking ball as well. The Taiwanese left-hander got good chase rates on the changeup and cutter specifically, and while he spots the ball well, it’s worth wondering what happens when hitters lay off the low cambio. Still, the results at a young age, quality of stuff and early durability all give Lin mid-rotation upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lin’s ample international experience with Chinese Taipei certainly put him on the map, but his performance in the 2021 U-23 World Cup sealed his fate as a potential pro pitcher stateside. The southpaw led his country with 14 strikeouts over 8 2/3 innings against the likes of Cuba and Venezuela, all while just 18 years old. The D-backs signed Lin for $525,000 in December 2021 and he fanned 91 batters over 56 1/3 innings between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia. His 40.3 percent K rate was sixth-best among the 1,343 Minor Leaguers with at least 50 frames in 2022, three spots behind Tink Hence (41.5) in a similar sample size. The 5-foot-11 left-hander is all about movement on the mound from the leg kick in his delivery to the profile of his pitching repertoire. His fastball is only around 89-92 mph, but there’s room for more velo if he adds strength, as Arizona expects him to do. The D-backs believed his vertically breaking curveball to be his best pitch entering the system, but his hard slider proved to be its equal in quality. Now his best offering looks to be a diving changeup with armside movement that makes hitters look silly. Driving home the kitchen-sink feel, Lin can add in a splitter and screwball-like pitch to keep hitters guessing. All that movement caught up to the lefty a bit in the California League, where he averaged a walk roughly once every two innings, but he still projects for average control. While Lin sends many low-level batters back to the dugout shaking their heads, his lack of velocity might catch up to him the higher he climbs. If he adjusts as he ages, he has at least mid-rotation upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt and some mechanical adjustments put Reyes on international radars a bit later than others in his 2025 international signing class. So while he wasn’t ranked on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50, his arm strength got him a $1.8 million bonus from the Braves, the second-largest figure given to a pitcher in the class behind only Roki Sasaki. He showed off his arm's potential, along with just how much he has to work on, during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. Reyes is now a 6-foot-4 pure thrower, one who will be 17 for nearly all of the 2026 season. It’s all about his fastball, and he can crank it into triple digits consistently, having topped out at 102 mph in the past. He doesn’t have much else he can rely on yet, but he started taking a step away from being a one-trick pony by improving his slider over the course of his DSL debut. Giving him grades on that and his control would be pure projection. He walked 29 (while striking out 35) in 27 DSL innings last year, so there’s obvious work to be done on learning how to repeat his delivery and find the zone. The Braves will let him keep starting for now so he can get reps in, but he likely will be a fireballing short reliever in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2025 international amateur class was extremely hitter-heavy, with only four pitchers in MLB Pipeline’s Top 50. That quartet was headlined, of course, by Roki Sasaki. Reyes wasn’t on the list, but thanks to a growth spurt and some tweaks in his mechanics, his arm strength got some late love from teams. The Braves, who also signed highly regarded outfielder Diego Tornes for $2.5 million, swooped in to get Reyes for just under $1.8 million, the largest bonus given to a pitcher not named Sasaki in the class. Now standing 6-foot-4 and 210 pounds, Reyes is all about arm strength and not much else at this point. He was one of the youngest players in this class, will be 16 for most of the 2025 season, and he enters pro ball about as raw as a pitcher can be. What he can do is throw very, very hard. His fastball has already touched triple digits, maxing out at 102 mph with some riding life coming from a three-quarters arm slot. The rest of Reyes’ repertoire is a bit of guesswork. He does have the makings of an 86-90 mph slider with cutting action and a mid-80s changeup with some fade, and the Braves think he has the feel to spin to add a power curve. He’ll hit the ground running, motivated to learn secondary stuff and how to find the strike zone consistently, though the Braves say he has an idea of how to command the baseball overall and a fierce desire to move up the ladder quickly. The Braves player international scouting staff gave their player development colleagues an impressive piece of clay. Now it’s up to them, and Reyes, to see how it gets sculpted.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston College's only two-time baseball All-American, Morissette fell short of pulling off the trifecta in 2021 after injuring his hand in a home-plate collision with Louisville catcher and No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. He did rally to finish his college career with a 16-game hitting streak before Miami selected him in the second round and signed him for $1,403,200. He batted just .234/.312/.401 in his first full pro season, though he did homer six times in June just before fouling a ball off his left ankle and sustaining a fracture that sidelined him for six weeks. After standing out with his bat-to-ball skills in college, Morissette has made changes to his left-handed swing to help him drive the ball more consistently as a pro. Instead of focusing on making line-drive contact and using the entire field, he has concentrated on launching balls to his pull side since joining the Marlins. His new approach might result in 15 or more homers per season, but he also batted just .226/.311/.372 in his first two professional years. That kind of production won't cut it for a player projected as an offensive second baseman. His instincts are more notable than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has a quick first step and gets the job done at the keystone, but his average arm is stretched at third base and he doesn't have the range desired at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston College's only two-time baseball All-American, Morissette didn't put up loud numbers last spring, in part because he injured his hand in a home-plate collision with Louisville catcher and No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. He rallied to finish the season with a 16-game hitting streak before signing for $1,403,200 in the second round. Former All-Star Joe Panik was his favorite player growing up and Morissette projects as a steady player in the same mold. Though Morissette batted just .204/.308/.299 while making his pro debut in Low-A, the Marlins remain confident in his bat-to-ball skills. He employs a compact left-handed swing with a patient all-fields approach that should enable him to produce high batting averages. His power is more in question because he has solid but not plus bat speed, needs more strength and frequently hits the ball on the ground, which may limit him to 10-12 homers per season. Morissette's instincts on the bases and in the field stand out more than his average speed. After he spent most of his college career at second base while also seeing action at third for the Eagles and at shortstop in summer ball, the Marlins plan on trying him all over the infield. He's a solid defender at second base, but his range is a bit lacking at shortstop and his average arm is stretched on the left side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a relatively pedestrian freshman season at Virginia Tech, Schobel hit over .300 in the Cape Cod League that summer, using that as a springboard into a big Draft-eligible sophomore season. Hitting in the middle of the Hokies' powerful lineup, he smashed 19 homers and posted a 1.134 OPS while playing shortstop and ended up being taken by the Twins No. 68 overall. He performed well enough with High-A Cedar Rapids during his first full season to get a bump up to Double-A in mid-July, though he scuffled a bit up a level. Schobel is the kind of player whose whole might be greater than the sum of his parts, one who can do a lot of things pretty well, but nothing plus. Even when the results didn't stand out in Wichita, his underlying numbers were good, including his penchant for making a ton of contact from the right side of the plate and limiting his strikeouts. He controls the zone well and draws plenty of walks and has worked to add depth to his swing, allowing him to drive the ball a little more effectively. While Schobel played shortstop at Virginia Tech and could fill in there if needed, his best position now is second base, where he could be an excellent defender, and he split time between the keystone and third base in 2023, something that should continue to maintain his positional flexibility moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schobel put himself on the map as one of the top Draft-eligible sophomores in the 2022 class after hitting well in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2021. He kept on raking as Virginia Tech's shortstop the next spring, hitting in the middle of a potent college lineup, finishing with 19 homers and a 1.134 OPS, enough to land him in the Competitive Balance Round B and the Twins signed him for $1 million. He spent most of his pro debut with Single-A Fort Myers. A right-handed-hitting infielder, Schobel's contact skills already stand out.
