He struck out in just 14.2 percent of his plate appearances and registered an overall miss rate of just 14 percent on all pitches, according to Synergy, during his sophomore year with the Hokies. He displayed that skill, as well as his ability to control the strike zone, during his relatively modest pro debut. He worked during instructs to add some depth to his swing, as he had a tendency to be too out in front with a pushy swing, with the hope he can impact the ball more as a pro and adjust to breaking stuff more consistently. Schobel is a good athlete who could potentially play shortstop with decent actions and a solid arm. He played a lot of second base during his pro debut, and he'll likely keep moving around, with the Twins' depth at shortstop as much of a reason for that as Schobel's inability to stick there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending two years at Sacramento City Junior College, Costeiu transferred to Arkansas and showed off the ability to miss bats in a relief role in 2021. The Angels took him that summer in the seventh round and decided to stretch him out as a starter. There were some positive early returns with High-A Tri-City, but he blew out in July and needed Tommy John surgery. He missed all of the 2023 season and returned to amass 74 1/3 innings in a solid post-surgery return. One of the reasons why the Angels thought he had a chance start despite being a six-footer is because he does have a real four-pitch mix, even if he doesn’t have one offering that jumps off the page. His low-90s fastball can be effective because of good spin rates and carry up in the zone. His changeup might be his best pitch, a low-80s cambio that can get swing-and-miss and groundball outs. His upper-70s curve was his go-to when he started his career, and he’s since added a distinct slider. Costeiu was an outstanding strike-thrower in 2022 before he got hurt and he wasn’t as sharp upon his return in 2024. If this command returns, he could have a chance to start, though the size and the elbow history will have some thinking a move to the bullpen is in the offing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Costeiu’s work in relief at Arkansas in 2021 -- transferring there after two years at Sacramento City JC -- helped him land in the seventh round of the Angels’ all-pitching Draft. After a solid debut missing a ton of bats out of the bullpen after signing, he was given the chance to start with High-A Tri-City in his first full season, but his early success was cut short by an elbow injury in July that required Tommy John surgery, knocking him out for all of the 2023 season. Though he’s a bit undersized, the 6-foot right-hander’s combination of stuff and feel for the strike zone has some evaluators thinking he has the chance to start. When he was stretched out, he was throwing his fastball in the 92-94 mph range, with good life and carry up in the zone thanks to high spin rates. His low-80s changeup flashes plus, a pitch that misses bats and gets weak contact. He entered pro ball with a big upper-70s curve, but he had started working on a slider that might be a better option long-term. In his brief time starting, Costeiu did a very nice job of throwing his arsenal for strikes, leading to an impressive 4.26 K/BB ratio, which makes it tempting to exhaust the starting pitcher possibilities. But between his size and the elbow surgery, there are a lot of reliever profile signs here, and his stuff would tick up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Sacramento City Junior College, Costeiu moved on to the University of Arkansas and missed a ton of bats pitching out of the Razorbacks bullpen. His arm strength was enough to land him in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft with the Angels. He struck out close to 16 per nine innings in his pro debut that summer, then got the chance to start with a move to High-A for his first full season. He pitched effectively, though his season ended prematurely in July due to an elbow issue and he didn’t throw a pitch in 2023 because of the injury. As a starter, Costeiu’s stuff did back up a bit. His fastball was more in the 92-94 mph range with Tri-City in 2022. There could be more consistent velocity for him to rediscover, especially if he eventually ends up with shorter stints again. The fastball plays up because of its high spin and carry up in the zone. His low-80s changeup can miss bats and get weak contact on the ground, and he brought an upper-70s big curve with him from college. He’s also worked on adding a slider this offseason. Because of the chance to have a complete repertoire and the fact he’s generally around the zone, Costeiu could keep getting the opportunity to start. But the 6-footer does have more of a reliever profile, where the stuff would likely tick back up once he returns to full strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals selected Roccaforte in the supplemental second round of the 2023 Draft at pick No. 66, and the Louisiana-Lafayette product quickly became the best center field prospect in the system. He won the organization’s Defensive Player of the Year Award in back-to-back seasons in 2024 and '25. After spending all of ‘24 in High-A, Roccaforte went back there to begin ‘25 and saw more power, with 13 home runs and an .830 OPS in 82 games. He joined Double-A Northwest Arkansas in July and was even better there, with a .290/.387/.475 slash line in 45 games. Roccaforte found his power stroke in 2025, and seeing it translate to Double-A at the end of the year was an encouraging sign. However, seeing his strikeouts go up (29.4 percent from 26) and his contact rate (69.6 percent from 74.1) go down are trends to monitor. Roccaforte stands tall at the plate, and keeping his weight balanced in between his legs helps put him in better positioning to succeed. A natural center fielder, he has an above-average arm and takes efficient routes on the grass. He’s not a burner of a runner, but he does have above-average speed that helps him in center and on the bases, where he swiped 43 bases in 2025 while only getting caught 12 times. Roccaforte’s development is coming along nicely, especially with his offense, but he still has work to do to profile as more than a fourth outfielder; however, it’s not out of the question for the Royals to talk about him potentially helping in Kansas City soon if the production remains consistent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Roccaforte was drafted in the supplemental second round (No. 66 overall) in the 2023 Draft, he became the highest-drafted player from Louisiana-Lafayette since 1995. He got his feet wet in pro ball with a stint in Single-A at the end of ‘23, then went to High-A Quad Cities in ‘24. Roccaforte spent the whole season as the River Bandits’ center fielder, logging 1,042 innings with just one error. That performance earned him Kansas City’s Minor League Defensive Player of the Year honors. It was more of a struggle offensively as Roccaforte slashed .208/.293/.342 with 23 doubles, 10 homers and an 85 wRC+, along with 34 stolen bases. Roccaforte is the Royals’ best center-field defender, a glove-first player who has good instincts and jumps and knows where the ball is going to be. He’s not a burner; rather, he seems to just glide in the grass. He takes efficient routes and above-average arm strength helps him out there. Offensively, there’s more to unlock. He had some good bat-to-ball skills in college but has been aggressive in pro ball and struggles especially with spin. Some of the problem in ‘24 was getting caught on his back side, causing him to rush to pitches or carry forward too much and have poor swing angles. He’s made an adjustment to tone down his leg kick and work on keeping the weight in between his feet. But he does have quickness in his hands, which leads to better contact rates, and if he’s able to keep better positioning, there should be more room for success. With his athleticism and instincts, Roccaforte has the tools to stick in center field all the way up to the big leagues, but his bat will need to improve some in order to get there. He has strong makeup and is a quick learner and a hard worker. Double-A, where he arrived in the second half of ‘25, is a good test for him both offensively and defensively as he gets used to better pitchers and hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roccaforte became the highest-drafted player from Louisiana-Lafayette since 1995 when the Royals took him in the supplemental second round (No. 66 overall) in 2023. His 26 doubles in his final season as a Ragin’ Cajun ranked fourth-best in Division I ball, and when he begin pro ball later that summer, he continued the momentum. He went 8-for-15 with five stolen bases in Rookie ball before finishing the year in Single-A Columbia with a .733 OPS. Possessing good bat-to-ball skills, Roccaforte is more of a gap-to-gap hitter than home run slugger, especially early on in his career. His hands are high in his compact setup at the plate, and he has a leg kick, but it’s a smooth movement with a good bat path. Roccaforte might be a tick behind other outfielders in the system in terms of pure hitability right now, but his overall game is more well-rounded because he plays center field and can stick there. He’s not a burner out there, but he moves better than he looks, with good instincts and jumps and a keen perception of where the ball is going to be. That makes him an above-average defender with an average arm, so he’ll likely play all three outfield spots. He also has good speed and instincts on the bases. Roccaforte will need to hit more to reach and stick in the big leagues, especially after a rough start at High-A Quad Cities, but his defense will carry him far. He projects as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles think they might be in the process of unearthing a diamond in the rough from their 2022 international class in Sosa, who signed for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Sosa flashed enough potential in the Florida Complex League the next year that the Orioles began challenging him, assigning Sosa to affiliates where he has routinely been one of the youngest players. He seems destined for a big league role of some kind after reaching Double-A in 2025 as a 20-year-old. Sosa is a left-handed-hitting, left-handed-throwing outfielder with size, projectable power and upside, garnering early comparisons to former Pirates outfielder Gregory Polanco. He consistently registers some of the organization’s best 90th percentile exit velocities and hard-hit rates, though issues making contact and with his approach have made the power slow to show up in games so far. He proved to be a better runner than expected by stealing 30 bases in 2024, but was limited on the bases last year due to a knee injury. Defensively, Sosa became more or less a full-time corner outfielder last season and seems suited to right field, where his plus throwing arm profiles well. Otherwise, this is a bat-first skillset, with Sosa’s ceiling dependent on the extent to which he can polish his approach and develop into a well-rounded hitter, rather than a panoply of pop and potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 Sosa wasn’t one of the highest-ranked players in the 2022 international class and didn’t get an earth-shattering signing bonus ($400,000), but the Orioles feel they may have struck gold with the Villa Mella, Dominican Republic, native. After a forgettable debut, Sosa turned heads in the Florida Complex League in 2023 and performed well at Single-A Delmarva in '24. He earned a late-season promotion to High-A Aberdeen but experienced growing pains there as a 19-year-old. Sosa has been compared to former Pirates outfielder Gregory Polanco because he is a left-handed-hitting, left-handed-throwing outfielder with size, projectable power and intriguing upside. He generates loud contact and produces high exit velocities with probably plus raw power, though it's yet to really show up in games because Sosa’s swing and approach remain unrefined. He’s already gotten bigger and stronger since signing, with room to add more size and strength, and Sosa also might be a better runner than expected after totaling 30 stolen bases in 93 games in his first season stateside. Defensively, Sosa gets reps at all three outfield positions, including center field, though he’s probably destined for a corner. His plus arm strength profiles well for right field. Sosa is raw enough that there is still real risk here, but his skill set is the kind that could develop into a bat-first regular if a few things go right, and a star if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Villa Mella, Dominican Republic, Sosa signed with the Orioles for $400,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period. He didn’t hit much in his Dominican Summer League debut that summer but began turning heads in 2023 in the Florida Complex League, where he showed an intriguing mix of upside and production as part of a talented Baltimore club. A left-handed hitting, lefty-throwing outfielder, Sosa draws comparisons to former Pirates outfielder Gregory Polanco for his size, build, stance and makeup. He is long and lanky with a solid approach and flashes of line-drive power that should increase as his body fills out. That’s already begun to happen as he’s grown a lot in the two years since signing, adding at least 3 inches and 20 pounds. He’s a solid runner at this point with good instincts on the bases. A natural center fielder, Sosa got experience at all three outfield spots last year and could potentially move to a corner one day. If that happens, he has the power and arm strength to profile well at either left or right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Soto signed with the Angels for $250,000 in January 2023, he was still only 16 and didn’t celebrate his 17th birthday until he was already into his Dominican Summer League debut. He ended up spending two years in the DSL, adding strength and stuff so that he’d be ready to come stateside in 2025. His U.S. debut was a mixed bag of big stuff, missed bats and iffy command, though he had more success in six outings with Single-A Inland Empire than he did in the Arizona Complex League. As he’s filled out his 6-foot-2 frame, Soto has added velocity to his fastball, beginning his career in the upper 80s and now sitting in the low 90s and touching 97 mph. The four-seamer plays up because he gets really good extension and there could be more consistent velo to come. Beyond the heater, things are a bit more inconsistent. His low-80s changeup does miss bats and could be a solid offspeed offering but his upper-70s curve wasn’t as effective in 2025, and he could be a candidate to add a slider. At times, Soto has shown enough feel for the strike zone where it’s possible to project him as a starter, but that too was inconsistent last year. If he can refine his command and find a better breaking ball, he still could profile in a rotation, with plenty of time for him to figure it out in his age-19 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The Angels gave out five six-figure bonuses to hitters at the top of their list at the start of the 2023 international signing period before they got to their first pitcher. Soto received $250,000 to be that arm and he was still only 16 when he made his professional debut in the Dominican Summer League. While his surface numbers looked good (like his 1.64 ERA), his youth and lack of velocity led to the Angels erring on the side of caution and sending him back to the DSL, where added strength and stuff led to even better results in 2024. After packing some weight onto his 6-foot-2 frame, Soto's velocity jumped from sitting 86-89 mph and touching 92 to more in the 92-94 mph range and topping out at 97. At first it seemed like his 82-85 mph changeup was his best secondary offering, but more power behind his curve -- now up to 77-80 mph from the low 70s in 2023 -- might have caught it up to the cambio. Both have chances to be solid-to-average pitches for the right-hander. In addition to missing a fair amount of bats overall, Soto improved his feel for the strike zone, cut his walk rate down considerably in 2024 and is showing some feel for pitch usage. All of this has added excitement over what he might do for an encore as he pitches in the United States for the first time this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros are adept at finding worthwhile older international pitchers at bargain prices. Tamarez signed for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic as a 19-year-old in March 2019, lost a year to the pandemic and since has climbed from Single-A to Triple-A in three full seasons. His control and command regressed last season, but he did make some progress while posting a 3.32 ERA in the final two months in Triple-A. Tamarez has one of the deeper repertoires among Houston's pitching prospects, starting with a fastball that sits at 94-96 mph, reaches 100 and comes out of a high arm slot with plenty of induced vertical break. His heater pairs well with his tight upper-80s slider/cutter that grades as a plus pitch at its best, parking at 86-88 mph and peaking at 92. He can flash a solid upper-80s changeup with fade, though his low-80s curveball doesn't fool many hitters. Tamarez's up-tempo delivery provides power and deception, yet it also hampers his ability to throw strikes. He's better at getting chases than landing pitches in the zone, and he averaged 5.1 walks per nine innings through his first four pro seasons. He's athletic and has three viable pitches but probably is less a starter and more a multi-inning reliever -- a role in which he might help the Astros this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Another older pitcher whom the Astros uncovered in the international bargain bin, Tamarez signed for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic as a 19-year-old in March 2019. He made his U.S. debut four months later and rose from Single-A to Triple-A in the two seasons following the 2020 pandemic layoff. He ranked second in the system last year in innings (121 1/3), strikeouts (142) and average-against (.191), finishing the season with a 2.50 ERA in four Triple-A starts. Tamarez uses a quick arm and high slot to unleash mid-90s fastballs that top out at 99 mph with uncanny vertical movement and boring action in on right-handers. His heater works well in tandem with his mid-80s slider, which reaches 90 mph and features more vertical than horizontal action. His upper-80s changeup is a bit firm but gets swings-and-misses as well as groundouts thanks to its combination of plane and fade. Tamarez is athletic but his high-tempo delivery produces more deception than strikes. He works solely out of the stretch yet averaged 5.2 walks per nine innings in 2022. He has enough pitches to start but likely will become a multi-inning reliever if he can't do a better job of locating them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have repeatedly hit on signing older pitchers for small bonuses on the international market, uncovering Luis Garcia, Cristian Javier and Framber Valdez. Tamarez may follow the same path after signing for $15,000 out of the Dominican as a 19-year-old in March 2019. He made his U.S. debut four months later and impressed at two Class A levels in 2021, whiffing 103 in 76 2/3 innings with a 3.76 ERA. Tamarez's fastball parked in the low 90s during instructional league in the fall of 2020, then jumped to the mid-90s and touched 99 mph last season. His heater has a flat approach angle and good carry up in the zone, and it plays well in tandem with a mid-80s slider that overmatched lower-level right-handed hitters. He also can flash a solid changeup with fade and mix in a power curveball with more depth than his slider. Tamarez battled the strike zone until he got to High-A, where he issued just 10 walks in 33 2/3 innings. He has the athleticism and strength to develop average control, though he'll have to prove he can provide consistent strikes in more than just a sample size. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter but could wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working as both a starter and reliever through his first three collegiate seasons, Saenz became a full-time member of the starting staff for Texas A&M in 2021, and while he was inconsistent that spring, he impressed enough late to get the Nationals to take him in the fourth round, signing for $500,000. He has worked his way methodically though the Washington system since with in-season promotions in each of his first two seasons after repeating the level from the campaign before. He dominated High-A early in 2023 and moved to Double-A, where he finished with a 4.44 ERA, 42 strikeouts and 19 walks in 73 innings. Saenz’s strikeout rate plummeted from 27 to 14 percent after the promotion, but he was still able to stay effective by throwing strikes and eliciting ground-ball contact. His 89-91 mph fastball certainly lacks velocity, but he hides the ball well to get it to play up, keeping it in line with his side just before release. His low-80s changeup separates nicely off the heater and drifts armside as it fades, getting some right-handers to chase down and away. He threw an 82-85 mph slider more than the changeup because of its movement away from lefties, but it could backfoot righties, too. An upper-70s curveball served as more of a get-me-over look to shake things up. The 5-foot-11 southpaw has thrown strikes consistently at every Minor League stop and won’t beat himself when it comes to allowing free passes. He’s proven plenty durable too, adding to the hope he can contribute to Washington’s starting depth; but without sharp stuff, it’s a limited ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Saenz worked as both a starter and a reliever in his first three seasons at Texas A&M, and after going undrafted in the truncated 2020 Draft, he officially moved into a starting role for good as a senior last spring. He was inconsistent for much of the season but ended on a high with striking out eight and allowing one run on two hits over eight innings against LSU in his final outing. The Nationals selected the southpaw in the fourth round a few weeks later and signed him for just below slot at $500,000. He made brief appearances (mostly in relief to save his arm) in the Florida Complex League and with Low-A Fredericksburg in his first taste of the pros. Saenz tends to lean on his low-80s slider because of its two-plane break. It’s easily his best pitch, and some analysts say it had some of the best metrics among similar pitches in the 2021 Draft class. His fastball doesn’t quite pop in terms of velo at 90-93 mph. It does come with some decent sink, however, and Saenz has little issue spotting to any side of the plate. A low-80s changeup with depth gives him enough to work as a starter, but he didn’t use that specific offering much at A&M. At just 5-foot-11, Saenz isn’t a classic candidate to add more gas in the pro game. There’s a chance the fastball could play up if he’s moved back to the bullpen and given shorter stints. For now, his promising command and control will give him a puncher’s chance to start, at least early in his journey through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bergolla has the same profile as his father William Sr., a contact-hitting, speed-and-defense middle infielder who played 17 games with the 2005 Reds. Signed for $2.05 million out of Venezuela by the Phillies in 2022, William went to the White Sox in a July 2024 trade for Tanner Banks. He won the High-A South Atlantic League batting title (.300) in 2024 and led the Minors in strikeout rate (5 percent) last season, when he hit .522 in the Double-A Southern League playoffs to help Birmingham win its second straight championship. With a compact left-handed stroke, Bergolla employs a contact-over-everything-else approach. He's not especially selective but almost never swings and misses, ranking second in the Minors in swinging strike percentage (3 percent) last year. He also rarely walks or drives the ball in the air, and he's a career .345 slugger with one homer in 293 pro games. He's an excellent bunter who laid down 36 bunts in fair territory in 2025, good for 14 hits and 21 sacrifices. Bergolla has plus speed and has become more comfortable stealing bases as he has gained experience, swiping 40 in 51 tries (78 percent) last year. Primarily a second baseman in the Phillies system, he has become a regular shortstop after switching organizations and has played solid defense at the more challenging position. He covers ground to both sides, and his ability to use his quickness to get behind throws helps his solid arm strength play up. The best-case scenario is that he's Luis Arráez with much more defensive value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: William Bergolla Sr. was a contact-hitting, speed-and-defense middle infielder who played briefly in the big leagues with the 2005 Reds. Signed for $2.05 million out of Venezuela by the Phillies in 2022, his son has a very similar profile. Traded to the White Sox for Tanner Banks last July, he won the High-A South Atlantic League batting title by slashing .300/.359/.381 with 27 steals in 89 games in High-A between the two organizations. Bergolla has a compact left-handed stroke and focuses on putting the ball in play, ranking seventh in the Minors in swinging strike percentage (4 percent) and eighth in strikeout rate (11 percent) last year. He generates extremely low exit velocities and a lot of opposite-field grounders, and he'll need to get a lot stronger and change his swing and approach to ever produce much power. He homered just once in 168 games and slugged .354 in his first three pro seasons. Growing up around the game, Bergolla developed a high baseball IQ that adds to his value as a runner and defender. He has plus speed and swiped 27 bases in 33 attempts last year after going 4-for-8 in his first two pro seasons. After playing primarily at second base in the Phillies system, he spent most of his time at shortstop with the White Sox. He has range to both sides and exhibits average to solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the former big leaguer of the same name, Bergolla ranked fourth on MLB Pipeline's 2022 International Prospects list and signed with the Phillies that January for $2.05 million. He established himself as one of the best contact hitters in Philadelphia's system, batting .292 with an 8.7 percent strikeout rate in his first three seasons. The Phillies dealt him to the White Sox at this year's Trade Deadline to acquire Tanner Banks. The lefty-hitting infielder stands out with his high baseball IQ, plus instincts and innate knack for contact. Bergolla rarely chases pitches out of the strike zone and draws a decent amount of walks. The big question surrounding him is how much offensive impact he'll have because he produces a lot of ground balls, generates below-average exit velocities and homered just once in 146 games in the Phillies system. Bergolla's instincts, hands and feet all give him the chance to play shortstop, and he has enough arm for the premium position. He has played primarily second base this year, and some think the keystone may be a better spot for him long-term because of his range. He's a solid runner who's doing a better job of using his speed on the bases in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: William Bergolla Sr. was a solid prospect who played 10 years in the Minor Leagues and briefly made it to the big leagues with the Reds in 2005. His son, William, was one of the top international prospects in the 2022 class and has the chance to do a lot more than his dad professionally. The Phillies signed him for $2.05 million last January and then saw the talented infielder make a strong first impression in the Dominican Summer League that summer, as he hit .380/.470/.423 over 71 at-bats. In the very early stages of his pro career, Bergolla has already shown off outstanding bat to ball skills, plus instincts in all facets of the game and a very high baseball IQ. He’s a left-handed hitter who -- small sample size alert -- only struck out three times in 71 ABs last summer while displaying good discipline with 11 walks. He has quick hands and uses a quick, direct swing to find the barrel. It’s a gap-to-gap line-drive approach and there should be solid extra-base authority. He may not have a ton of over-the-fence thump, but he’s already added strength. While he’s not a burner, the Phillies are confident Bergolla can stick at shortstop long-term. He has great hands, quick feet and enough arm for the position, and those instincts allow his defensive tools to play up. His feel for the game could help him move a little more quickly as he makes his United States debut in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bergolla was ranked No. 4 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2021-22 international signing period officially opened on January 15, 2022. The son of former Reds prospect, and brief big leaguer, of the same name, Bergolla’s all-around skillset and ability to stay on the dirt led to him signing with the Phillies for $2.05 million. A left-handed hitting shortstop, Bergolla already has a strong reputation for his ability to make contact. He uses his hands very well with a simple, direct swing to barrel up the baseball, with an advanced approach and strike zone knowledge that belies his years. He has more of a line drive approach right now, with the ability to drive the ball to the gaps, and he should be able to add some pop as he matures, though that might be limited given his smaller frame. Defensively, Bergolla displays very good instincts and actions at shortstop, with soft hands, good footwork and enough arm to give him a good chance to stick at the premium position. Because of his baseball IQ and awareness, there’s confidence he’ll maximize the tools he has.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Diaw is on the field, he hits. That was true when he was Loyola Marymount, putting up very good numbers in 2023 (.314/.396/.500), but that came sandwiched between a lost freshman season because of a back fracture and playing just 20 games in 2024 because of a broken left thumb. He did produce in 20 games when he was on the field, then performed well in the Cape Cod League and at the Draft Combine, leading to the Twins taking him the third round of the ‘24 Draft. The story carried over to his first full season of pro ball, where he hit for average and got on base but played just 39 games for High-A Cedar Rapids, first going down with a broken wrist and then a hamstring injury shortly after his return. Diaw is always going to be a hit-over-power type, focusing on contact first, particularly early in counts. When he was in the box, he showed an advanced approach and also drew walks while limiting his swing-and-miss as well as chase, but without much thump. He worked on swing changes while he was rehabbing his wrist to unlock some power to his pull side and was having some good results, only to be derailed by the hamstring issue. An athletic backstop who moves around well enough to also play some outfield, Diaw gets high marks for his cerebral approach to the game, and he made strides with his defense behind the dish. The hope for 2026 is for him to stay healthy to see if the swing changes stick, giving him a chance to be a big league regular catcher or a valuable backup who can see time there and in the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Hailing from the Notre Dame High School in California that Giancarlo Stanton and Hunter Greene called home, Diaw went to Loyola Marymount for college but missed nearly all of his freshman year in 2022 after suffering a fracture in his back. He had a solid full season in 2023 for the Lions, slashing .314/.396/.500, but the injury bug hit again in '24 when he broke his left thumb on a foul tip and then sprained his wrist at the end of the year. He did manage a 1.216 OPS in 20 games, then hit well in the Cape Cod League and impressed at the Draft Combine, leading to the Twins signing him under slot in the third round. He also impressed the organization with how he carried himself during his pro debut with Single-A Fort Myers. Diaw entered pro ball with a reputation for making a lot of contact as an aggressive right-handed hitter who likes to attack pitches early in counts. He continued to control the zone well during his debut, rarely swinging and missing while drawing a good amount of walks. He’s had a lengthy bat path in the past -- mostly because he starts slow -- with decent speed through the zone that led to better-than-average exit velocities in the Florida State League. There’s strength to tap into that might be more extra-base authority than home run pop. Young for his Draft class, Diaw will play most of 2025 at age 21, and he’s very athletic for a backstop. He’s working on his arm strength so that he has more of a chance to stick behind the plate, but he’s an average runner who can steal a base and has seen time in all three outfield spots if catching doesn’t pan out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dollard probably would’ve made his big league debut in 2023 (at the very least for a few spot starts that surfaced), if not for the torn labrum in his pitching shoulder. He made just three starts with Triple-A Tacoma and tried other forms of rehab before undergoing season-ending surgery in June, which put a huge halt to the momentum he’d built in 2022, when he won Pitcher of the Year honors in the Texas League. There’s still hope for Seattle’s fifth and final pick in the shortened 2020 Draft. Recovery from that surgery has taken longer than hoped, with Dollard missing all of the 2024 season as well. A reliever-turned-starter at Cal Poly, Dollard doesn’t possess overpowering stuff -- but it’s how he’s harnessed it that could carry him to the next level. His fastball sits in the low-90s, and he supplements it with an upper-70s slider that can miss bats when generating chases out of the zone and a slower curve that possesses good depth. He also throws a changeup, creating a four-pitch mix that profiles him better as a starter long-term. Dollard had been touted as the most reliable arm in the system for his strike-throwing and innings-eating abilities before the shoulder injury, having cleared 144 frames in his last full season. With a lack of velocity, he’ll have to continue leaning on command and location -- but first, the focus will be on getting and staying healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seattle’s final pick in the five-round 2020 Draft, Dollard had made a positive transition from relief -- the role he mostly held at Cal Poly and in the Cape Cod League -- to the rotation. Part of it had been the profile of his stuff, but perhaps an even bigger part had been his self-awareness of how it plays, helping him succeed in Double-A in 2022. All that progress came to a screeching halt when he required labrum surgery, ending his 2023 season in April. Dollard had been touted as arguably the most reliable arm in the system, with his durability a key aspect of that before the shoulder injury. When healthy, he throws strikes and has a good feel for pitching, making 27 starts and compiling a whopping 144 innings in 2022. The big righty doesn’t wow with his fastball, and he’s more regarded for his feel for pitching than pure stuff. He averaged around 91 mph with his heater but has an upper-70s slider that misses bats and a slower curve that has decent depth. He also has a changeup that rounds out a decent four-pitch mix, another reason he could remain a starter longer term. Because he lacks velocity, a positive transition to the Majors will hinge heavily on command and location. He was considered to have a very high floor, but now he’ll have to see if he can work his way back to his earlier success post-surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A promotion to High-A Everett in 2021 was a little bit of a wakeup call for the former Cal Poly product after he struck out 36.4% of the batters he faced at Low-A Modesto. For a righty who consistently fills up the strike zone, a dip in velocity as the season wore on -- from 92-94 mph to 90-92 -- could have played a part. And there’s also an adjustment curve with the 23-year-old, given that he was mostly a reliever in college and in the Cape Cod League before the Mariners took him for full pick value in the fifth round of the 2020 Draft. At 6-foot-3, Dollard has an ideal frame and a four-pitch mix that he utilizes well, though he has more feel for pitching than pure stuff. His fastball tends to sit around 90 mph and can touch a bit higher, and it plays up because of his command and the sink the pitch has. His upper-70s slider misses bats and will even flash plus occasionally and he folds in a slower curve with decent depth as well. He has good feel for his changeup, giving him four very usable offerings. Given that he’s a little older, the 2022 season will be a big one for Dollard, who has the ceiling of being a back-end starter in the big leagues and the floor of a swing-man out of the bullpen. He’ll need to find better ways to limit extra-base hit power and continue fortifying his secondary pitches to realize his full potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One would be hard-pressed to find another pitcher in Seattle’s system who has endured as many obstacles since Draft Day as Carlson. Since being selected in the second round in 2017 out of a Minnesota high school, the righty underwent Tommy John surgery one year later, then came back in an emotional return in Spring Training in ‘20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. More than one year after that, he finally began his first full pro season. That topsy-turvy start to his career gave him a more grounded mental approach, and in his first full season, he impressed by making every start. The quirky Minor League schedule actually helped ease him into a no-limits workload, and he reached 100 innings over 19 starts with a 4.77 ERA. Essentially, everything was finally consistent for the 23-year-old, who is in the same age range as some of Seattle’s other top arms, such as George Kirby and Emerson Hancock, who were drafted after him. That gives Carlson a good outlook and strong upside. Before the shutdown in 2020, Carlson had added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which allowed him to reach back into the high 90s on his fastball. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above-average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. There’s a lot to like about his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carlson was always going to be a case of patience for the Mariners, who selected the righty out of high school in Minnesota in the second round in 2017, given that he was raised in a cold-weather state. But they didn’t anticipate that he would weather the significant setbacks, with just three professional innings so far. He underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2018 and was sidelined all of ’19, but returned in Spring Training in ’20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. But Carlson enters 2021 completely healthy – and that will be the biggest thing for the 22-year-old. Beyond the physical toll, there’s the mental factor of being back on a field again consistently. It understandably will take time for Carlson to regain feel for his three-pitch mix, but there is confidence that it all will eventually come back. Before the shutdown, he’d added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which gives the Mariners optimism that he’ll be able to get back up to the 93- to 97-mph range he showed on his fastball as a high school senior. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. Carlson is likely headed to High-A Everett or Low-A Modesto to start the regular season. He'll need time to get his command and control back to his pre-injury levels, but the Mariners are excited to finally see what kind of pitching prospect they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners knew they would need to be patient when they selected Carlson out of the Minnesota high school ranks in the second round of the 2017 Draft, given he was coming from a northern, cold-weather state. They obviously weren’t thinking it would take him this long to get going, as the big right-hander has thrown just three professional innings from his summer debut. Tommy John surgery in July 2018, before he had pitched that year, then kept him off the mound for all of 2019. The good news is Carlson is 100 percent healthy for 2020, leaving the Mariners facility last fall ready to go. It will understandably take time for him to regain feel for his three-pitch mix, but there is confidence it will all eventually come back. He’s added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, so seeing him get back to the 93-97 mph fastball he had as a high school senior doesn’t sound far-fetched. He’s always had a very good changeup, thrown with a ton of fade. His slider also flashed at least above-average at times, though it’s a more inconsistent pitch than his changeup. Carlson had always shown an advanced feel for his stuff, especially coming from cold weather. It will understandably take some time for him to get his command and control back to his pre-injury levels, but the Mariners are excited to finally see what kind of pitching prospect they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Minnesota's Gatorade Player of the Year in 2017, Carlson skyrocketed up Draft boards that spring as his velocity improved to go along with his advanced pitchability. Unfortunately, the Mariners haven't gotten to see him pitch competitively much, as he made just a few outings during his summer debut, then needed Tommy John surgery last July without throwing a pitch in a game. Carlson was just finishing his rehab as pitchers and catchers were getting set to report to Spring Training and was playing catch out to 120 feet. The Mariners obviously won't rush the process, but they are eager to see how Carlson's stuff plays, especially because he's filled out his 6-foot-4 frame and is more man than kid now. During that senior year, Carlson's fastball sat in the 93-97 mph range and there's no reason to believe he can't get back to that, if not beyond that once he gets going, and he pairs it well with his fading changeup. His slider would flash plus before the injury, but it was inconsistent, so that will likely be an area of focus, and he always was able to fill up the strike zone with all three pitches. If all goes well, Carlson will get some mound time at the end of the summer in the rookie-level Arizona League. The 2020 season will be the first time the Mariners will get to see exactly what kind of pitcher Carlson might become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked by MLB Pipeline as the No. 15 prospect in his class, Carlson became the fifth ever Minnesota prep to be taken in the second round when the Mariners selected him in June 2017. Carlson signed for $2 million, well above the recommended value of $1,206,900 for his slot, and made his professional debut the following month in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he impressed scouts with two strong outings before Seattle shut him down for the season as a precautionary measure. Carlson would end up undergoing Tommy John the following July, effectively wiping out his 2018 season and putting '19 in jeopardy as well. After pitching at 88-92 mph with his fastball on the summer showcase circuit after his junior year, Carlson began to grow into his projectable frame and had his velocity pick up as a result. He sat in the low 90s and touched 95 at the WWBA World Championships in October and then worked at 93-97 mph as a senior during the spring. Scouts expect Carlson to tack on even more velocity in the coming years, while also noting that his heater already plays above its velocity because it has sinking and running life and he commands it well. Carlson also fills the strike zone with his slider, an above-average pitch, and his changeup, which features fade and sink. Unlike most high school pitchers, he trusts his changeup and uses it liberally. Though his future definitely is on the mound, the Florida recruit was also an interesting prospect as a right fielder with bat speed, power potential and arm strength -- a testament to his overall athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Marlins for $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022, Vargas was an on-base machine at the Dominican and Florida complexes in his first two Minor League seasons, and he popped enough to be included in the July 2023 trade with the Mets for David Robertson. His first full season in the Mets organization was limited to only 37 games because of wrist tendinitis, but he got a fuller workload in 2025, where he zoomed past Single-A St. Lucie after 13 games and finished with a .239/.328/.296 line, one homer and 38 steals in 95 contests with High-A Brooklyn. At 5-foot-11, Vargas isn’t a commanding presence in the box, and his best offensive asset is the fact that he doesn’t expand the zone much at all for someone his age. After he slugged just .238 in the Florida State League in 2024, he got a mulligan for his power because of the wrist injury, but the pop didn’t show up much at all in ’25 either. That wasn’t just an issue with Coney Island (where lefty sluggers tend to struggle); he slugged .330 at home and .260 on the road, in part because of a batted-ball profile that’s overly focused on going the other way. There’s still an intriguing floor here. Vargas can flash impressive home-to-first times when he gets a jailbreak run out of the box, and while he won’t slug, he can add extra bases by stealing bags in bunches. Some consider him the best defensive shortstop in the system with good hands and range, and because of roster crunches, he got time at second base in Brooklyn. He could be above-average to plus with the glove at either spot, lowering his need to show much more than a strong OBP at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas may have signed for only $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022, but he hit the ground running in the Marlins system with a .319 average, .421 on-base percentage and .877 OPS in 53 games as a Dominican Summer League All-Star that season. He was again an on-base fiend in the Florida Complex League in 2023, and that was enough for the Mets to acquire him that July in a deal for David Robertson. Vargas got a little time at Single-A late in 2023 and was set to take on full-season ball for a longer stretch but was limited to only 37 games because of various bouts with wrist tendinitis. The left-handed hitter slashed just .208/.369/.238 over 168 plate appearances in his age-19 season, but the wrist problems basically made that campaign a wash. When Vargas did play, he continued to display the advanced approach at the plate that excited New York officials in the first place, and his 20.2 percent walk rate was ninth-best among 499 Single-A hitters with at least 100 PA. His already below-average power was sapped by the wrist problem , and it didn’t exactly return during his run at High-A in 2025. Vargas has fringy speed but has shown solid baserunning acumen to this early point in his career. He split his time between shortstop and second base in 2024 with some time at third mixed in, and he’s likely a better fit at second, where he could be above average if he sticks there. He might be best served as an OBP-driven middle-infield option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas signed with the Marlins for only $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022 (the same month he turned 17) and instantly became of Miami’s best lower-level hitters, producing a .319/.423/.456 line over 53 games in the Dominican Summer League that helped become a league All-Star. Vargas kept producing stateside during his time in the Florida Complex League and joined the Mets in the David Robertson trade at the Trade Deadline. New York got the infielder time with Single-A St. Lucie before the year was out, and he finished 2023 with a .275/.432/.389 line with two homers, 53 walks and 38 strikeouts over 54 games. The 6-foot left-handed slugger was the only Minor Leaguer aged 18 or younger who walked more than he struck out over 250 plate appearances or more, emphasizing how strong his approach and plate discipline were compared to his peers. If anything, Vargas may not have swung enough on pitches in the zone, leaving some potential hits on the table in favor of those walks. While his power value comes more in the gaps, he makes that profile work by distributing the ball almost evenly to the pull side, center and opposite way. Vargas will swipe some bags with his fringy speed, but that’s more out of savvy than wheels. Both the Mets and Marlins have moved him around the dirt with time at short and third base, but he’s best fit for second where his actions and arm strength are a solid fit. He projects as a high-OBP-type who can play up the middle, while adding strength to his profile would make him an even more complete offensive threat.

mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas may have signed for only $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022, but he hit the ground running in the Marlins system with a .319 average, .421 on-base percentage and .877 OPS in 53 games as a Dominican Summer League All-Star that season. He was again an on-base fiend in the Florida Complex League in 2023, and that was enough for the Mets to acquire him that July in a deal for David Robertson. His already below-average power was sapped by the wrist problem and getting healthy and comfortable with loud contact in the box will be a big priority for ’25. Vargas has fringy speed but has shown solid baserunning acumen to this early point in his career. He split his time between shortstop and second in 2024 with some time at third mixed in, and he’s likely a better fit at second, where he could be above-average if he sticks there. New York’s infield situation remains crowded, but Vargas’ high-OBP profile remains one of the more intriguing in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals took a risk selecting Charles in the final round of the 2022 Draft because it looked like he was headed to UC Santa Barbara, but they were able to lure him away from his commitment with a $429,000 signing bonus. He comes from a baseball family and actually impressed scouts just as much on the mound in high school, but the Royals have only had him hit in the three years since he was drafted. Charles improved upon repeating Single-A in 2024, slashing .257/.353/.386 with 10 homers, 15 doubles and 36 stolen bases in 117 games. Charles is an extreme athlete with tons of tools, including a plus arm and raw power. He’s tall at 6-foot-5, which doesn’t help his hit tool, but he made some adjustments with his swing this year, getting his hands to load back for a better firing position. The goal is to eliminate some of the length in his swing, helping him make better contact on fastballs and walk more. He still struggles with offspeed, but a tweak in his game planning helped him with his recognition and win counts. Finding stability in his swing will allow him to tap into his raw power. Charles’ frame doesn’t make him your typical shortstop, but he has good movements and a strong internal clock that helps him handle the position, while also getting time at third base in Columbia in ‘24. He’s an average runner, but quick-twitch movements help him on the bases. After two seasons in Single-A, Charles made significant progress but really struggled with a move to High-A in 2025 while also dealing with injuries. He is only in his age-21 season and still has untapped potential with his tools and athleticism, but the Royals are excited about what it all could look like if he turns things around as he develops.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Charles looked like he would honor his commitment to UC Santa Barbara before the conclusion of the 2022 Draft, but the Royals selected him in the 20th round and signed him for fifth-round money with a $429,500 bonus. He impressed scouts on both sides of the ball in high school, but the Royals are having him focus on being a hitter. Charles stayed behind in extended spring training last year and played two games in Rookie ball before he joined Single-A Columbia, where he slashed .230/.290/.356 with three homers in 69 games. Charles is one of the best pure athletes in the Royals' system, with a plus arm and raw power. There’s swing-and-miss in his game, and he struggles with breaking balls. But the Royals focused on functional strength with him last year before diving deep into his swing, and that allowed him to tighten up his body movements and find more stability. Now he’ll go into a full season stronger and making better contact. At 6-foot-4, Charles is not your typical shortstop, but he has the skills to handle the position with good movements and a strong internal clock. He saw time at third base because of the shortstop depth in the Royals’ system and he has the ability to become a solid defender on the left side of the infield. He could even move to center field because of his athletic ability and average speed. Charles faced older and better pitchers in Columbia and will likely go back there this season. There is tons of potential for Charles based on his tools and athleticism; he simply needs more time and development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just when it looked like Charles would honor his commitment to UC Santa Barbara last summer, Kansas City took him in the 20th round of the 2022 Draft and signed him for $429,500, roughly fourth- or fifth-round money. Charles impressed scouts with his skills on both sides of the ball, and the Royals were thrilled to get the high-upside high schooler in their system. Charles will stay as a shortstop, and he made his debut last year in the Arizona Complex League, going 3-for-11 in three games. A two-way player in high school, Charles is an elite athlete, with a plus arm and raw power. At 6-foot-4, he’s not your typical shortstop. But he's gotten some early looks there and has started to see more of third base because of Kansas City's loaded depth chart at short in the lower levels. Offensively, Charles is still tapping into his hit tool and raw power. The Royals will work with him on being more consistent at the plate, allowing him to make hard contact more often. Charles has the potential to be a dynamic player for the Royals, although it’ll likely take some time to develop him as he grows. He has all the tools to stay at shortstop, but he could play third base or the outfield as well. He was one of the Royals' best performers in extended spring training early in 2023 and forced his way to Single-A Columbia by early June.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lasko provided hope as potentially the next quality Major League hitter to come out of Rutgers, a school that produced talent such as Todd Frazier and David DeJesus, by hitting .314 with a .988 OPS across his three years in college. Drafted by the A’s in the second round of the 2023 Draft, Lasko took a big step forward last year by reaching Triple-A Las Vegas and performing well there over the final couple of weeks of the season to help the Aviators reach the Triple-A National Championship. After the season, he went to the Arizona Fall League and hit .357 in 21 games. Lasko is still trying to learn his craft from an offensive standpoint. He brings good plate discipline and bat speed, but pitch recognition is something he’s still working to improve. The A's have also worked with him to rein in his high intensity during games. The power element he showed in college has also yet to show up much in pro ball. Defense is Lasko’s calling card. He’s a plus defender in the outfield with a great arm and plays center field fearlessly with high energy. His speed is evident in his range, as well as on the basepaths. He’s another talented center fielder in the A’s system who could one day provide stellar defense in the Majors, but the hit tool is something he’ll have to continue improving to become anything more than a fourth outfielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutgers University has developed some quality Major League hitters over the years such as Todd Frazier and David DeJesus. Lasko provided hope as the next in line for the program, hitting .314 with a .988 OPS over his three-year college career. That strong showing, along with showcase opportunities at the Team USA trials and in the Cape Cod League, led to the A’s selecting him in the second round of the 2023 Draft. His first full professional season last year brought mixed results. Overall, he combined to hit .232 with six home runs, 26 doubles, 47 RBIs and 33 stolen bases in 124 games between Single-A Stockton and High-A Lansing. Despite the up-and-down numbers, Lasko showed good plate discipline, though there are some swing-and-miss and pitch recognition issues the A’s would like to see him correct, especially against pitches up in the zone. There was intrigue over his power potential coming out of college, but that has yet to truly translate to the pro ranks. Lasko’s defense is clearly ahead of his offense right now as the standout trait of his game. He has a plus arm that allows him to cut down baserunners, and his good speed also allows him to cover plenty of ground in center field, giving him a real chance to stick at the position long-term. The A’s love the toughness and blue-collar nature of his playing style. How much he can improve his hit tool will likely determine what type of role might eventually await him at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lasko was a standout hitter at Rutgers University, a school which has developed quality Major League bats such as Todd Frazier and David DeJesus over the years. After a strong three-year college career, mixed in with some time at the Team USA trials and Cape Cod League in ‘22, the A’s liked him enough to take him in the second round of the 2023 Draft, signing him under slot for a bonus of $1.7 million. His first full season of pro ball was up-and-down, but he showed off plate discipline, speed and defense that give him a pretty high floor. Lasko gives off a blue-collar vibe for his toughness and plays the game hard. He also is an above-average athlete who brings an intriguing power-speed combo, though the pop has yet to show up in his brief pro career. His overall approach is solid and helped him hit .330 with 11 homers as a junior. While he drew a ton of walks in his first season with the A’s, concerns about swing-and-miss issues linger, as he has struggled some with pitch recognition, particularly ones with spin. Lasko runs well with speed that translates to the ability to steal bags. That speed is also an element of his elite defense. He has every chance to play center field long-term, with a plus arm that has already cut down baserunners, though he’s shown the ability to handle all three outfield spots well, important in case he doesn’t hit enough to be a regular in one spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With the Braves free and clear of any penalties following their international signing infractions, they aggressively went after talent when the 2022 signing period opened. Benitez was the big catch, ranked No. 10 overall on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list and given $2.5 million to sign. He hasn’t exactly set the world on fire yet production-wise, but did take some nice steps forward from a rough Dominican Summer League debut after signing to his first taste stateside in the Florida Complex League in 2023. Even though he’s still learning to use it consistently, Benitez has an exciting offensive toolkit. There’s bat speed to spare with a good right-handed swing. He was overly aggressive at times in the FCL last year, but improved as the summer wore on, getting back to the more solid approach he had shown in the DSL. It remains to be seen how much he can tap into his raw power, but evaluators feel he can really drive the ball. While Benitez, who will be 19 for all of the 2024 season, has only played shortstop over his first two summers of pro ball, some feel he’s going to need to move off the premium position in the future. His strong arm would work well from third, though that would put more pressure on his bat, with confidence there’s still plenty of untapped potential in that regard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some top international prospects hit the ground running and put up gaudy numbers in the Dominican Summer League. Others stumble a bit out of the gate to translate their raw tools into production. Benitez, who signed for $2.5 million in January 2022 at the start of that signing period, fits into the latter category. The athletic infielder struggled in the DSL, but the Braves are still bullish on his tools. There were some very encouraging signs from Benitez, even if he didn’t impact the ball consistently during his pro debut. He still has excellent bat speed and showed impressive control of the strike zone, keeping his strikeouts down and drawing a ton of walks while never chasing out of the zone, even when he was scuffling. It’s a pretty good swing with the chance to drive the ball if he can get back on track. Benitez is a solid defender at short with an arm that flashes plus. The Braves see a little Manny Machado in him -- body-type wise -- and there is the chance he’ll outgrow the premium position and need to move to third base. For now though, he’ll continue to play short until he shows he can’t handle it while working to turn his potential into performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves were fully out of the international signing penalty box when the 2021-22 signing period opened up on January 15 of this year, and they wasted no time, signing six players to bonuses of six figures or higher. Benitez, who came in at No. 10 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list, was the headline, getting $2.5 million to sign and add his considerable tools to the organization. Big, strong and athletic, there are some evaluators who see a little young Manny Machado in Benitez. With excellent bat speed, he can drive the ball to all fields and there’s a chance he could have better than average power when all is said and done as he matures and gets professional reps. Plate discipline and pitch recognition should also sharpen as he gets instruction and sees competitive pitching on a regular basis. Right now, Benitez has the actions, footwork, hands and especially the arm to play shortstop. It’s possible that he could have to move over to third if he fills out his frame and slows down too much. That’s a question for a day down the road as he’ll make his pro debut this summer in the Dominican Summer League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aponte signed with the Blue Jays out of Venezuela in 2021 and has been all about projection from the start. Aponte was a hot name near the bottom of the system after a strong debut in the Dominican Summer League that year but had a down year in ‘22 in the FCL and seemed to lose steam for a while. Back in the FCL in ‘23 with a brief taste of Single-A, Aponte hit .244 with nine home runs and an .841 OPS over 50 games, restoring some of his prospect shine. Talent isn’t an issue for Aponte, who produces impressive exit velocities and is still a popular bet to have a breakout season in terms of power numbers. An assignment to Single-A could set up Aponte to double his workload after a career-high 50 games a year ago, and if the Blue Jays can get Aponte that many reps, the counting stats could begin to pile up quickly. What Aponte needs to avoid is strikeouts, which will be a difficult balance. There’s not as much contact ability to balance out Aponte’s power right now, but that equation could change if his power really pops. With enough arm to play right field defensively, Aponte does not profile as a plus defender but will work to get that area of his game up to a level where it is not a detriment. Now 20, he will be challenged by more advanced pitching and is no longer surviving on the hype surviving his raw offensive talent alone, so the Blue Jays will need to see him nail his day-to-day routines and make adjustments as the season wears on. The upside is very real, though, if Aponte can unlock it, and this system could use a success story or two in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Venezuela in 2021, Aponte had the attention of the Blue Jays’ player development staff, who brought him in for a look in Spring Training. Immediately impressed with his raw physical tools and day-to-day work at the complex, the Blue Jays sent Aponte to the DSL, where he hit .240 with a .393 OBP and .749 OPS over 38 games. Time will tell if Aponte can play center field, but the Blue Jays already like what they’ve seen defensively from the 17-year-old, and his power is expected to fill out as he ages. The Blue Jays’ strength program should be especially beneficial to him over the next couple of seasons, but the organization was encouraged by some of the contact metrics Aponte showed early. Aponte is still far off, given his age, but his upside is already generating some early buzz. Outfielders haven’t exactly littered Toronto’s top prospect lists in recent years, so any level of potential is good news for the organization at this point, but Aponte should be on your short list of prospects to monitor at the lower levels this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Manon is originally from the same city that brought the baseball world Elly De La Cruz -- Sabana Grande de Boya in the Dominican Republic. He moved to Santo Domingo to train with the MLB Trainer Partnership Program's Amaurys Nina and was No. 15 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the Braves signed him for right around $1.5 million when the signing period opened in mid-January of this year. Strong and physical, Manon is a right-handed hitter who makes a ton of contact with an aggressive approach at the plate. There’s a definite feel for hitting, which he showed off in places like the Amateur Scouting League in 2024, batting .308 over nine games. He uses a small leg kick to stay on time and has shown the ability to drive the ball to all fields, with most of the juice showing up to his pull side. He’s reminded some of a young Aaron Hicks in terms of his swing and projected impact as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. Manon is a solid defender with good lateral movement and the ability to get to all the balls he should at shortstop. He might not have the arm to stick there, but work can be done to build up strength so he can stay at the premium position. He’s an above-average runner who maximizes his speed with strong instincts on the basepaths.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The prize acquisition in the 2026 international signing period for the Phillies was outfielder Francisco Renteria, who got $4 million to join the organization, but he’s not the only top Venezuelan player to enter into the system. Parra, who trained at Bobby Abreu’s academy in Carabobo, was No. 39 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list and got $550,000 to start his Phillies career. Compared by a scout to 2025 first-rounders Steele Hall and Daniel Pierce in terms of his stock, Parra is a switch-hitter who has a real feel to hit from both sides of the plate. While he’s just a 6-footer, there is projection in his loose frame that should allow him to add strength, with more power to come as he matures. A solid athlete with above-average speed, Parra is a sound defender with smooth actions that give him a chance to stay up the middle. He should get every chance to play shortstop, but there’s a chance he’ll eventually be better suited for second base, where he could be an outstanding defender. He gets high marks for his work ethic and makeup, giving confidence he’ll maximize his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bigbie hit the prospect radar in 2023 coming off an eye-opening season that vaulted him three levels and garnered comparisons to another former Tigers 19th-round Draft pick, Kerry Carpenter. Bigbie spent the 2024 season at Triple-A Toledo but struggled to carry the momentum in a frustrating season, including just four home runs in 135 games. The Tigers left him off their 40-man roster at season’s end. Bigbie climbed the Tigers' system with an all-fields approach that allowed him to stay on time for fastballs, still be aggressive on offspeed pitches and remain patient for high walk rates. That approach was tested in Triple-A. Bigbie actually improved his plate discipline, boosting his walk rate while making more consistent contact in the strike zone. But while his contact rate improved, his ground-ball rate soared, comprising more than half of his balls in play. He also oddly struggled to hit left-handed pitching. Defensively, the converted first baseman has shown steady improvement as a corner outfielder, though his arm strength limits his ability to hold runners. Bigbie is a prime example of why the Triple-A level and its more experienced pitching remains a critical step on the way up the system. He could yet be a late bloomer and break into the Majors as an extra outfielder if he can get back to spraying line drives to all fields. But at 26, this is a big year for his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It's hard to see Bigbie’s rise up the system and not think of Kerry Carpenter. Both were 19th-round picks, but Bigbie was a four-year player at Western Carolina after going undrafted out of high school and after his junior season in a pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft. Following an up-and-down 2022 campaign, Bigbie connected with hitting instructor Richard Schenck, who worked with Carpenter a year earlier. Bigbie's 2023 season was a breakout, with a .343 average, 19 homers and a .942 OPS across three levels, culminating with a late-season look at Triple-A Toledo. He kept on hitting in the Arizona Fall League. Not only does the right-handed-hitting Bigbie have an affinity for the opposite field -- where more than 40 percent of his balls in play went at Double-A and Triple-A -- he hits there with authority. That approach allows him to be patient on fastballs, though he has worked on opening up and tapping into more pull power. He gets aggressive on offspeed, sometimes becoming susceptible to breaking balls. All that damage came while drawing high walk rates, including a .421 on-base percentage at Double-A and as many walks as strikeouts over 20 games in the Fall League. Bigbie converted from first base to corner outfield (mainly left) last year and handled the transition well, tempering his lack of speed with decent reads and routes. He catches the balls he can reach and has worked on improving his arm. Despite a crowded outfield roster, the Tigers invited Bigbie to Major League camp for Spring Training to see how he might react to yet another bump in level. He hasn't maintained his momentum at Triple-A Toledo in 2024, though many of his underlying numbers are average or better (except when it comes to pulled fly balls), and he might have a better chance at breaking through next summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $20,000 in July 2019 in the same international period that brought Emmanuel Rodriguez into the organization, Olivar skipped over the Dominican Summer League following the long pandemic-related layoff and didn’t make his pro debut until 2021 in the Florida Complex League. That didn’t go well, but a repeat of the level in 2022 led to an MVP award and an OPS north of 1.000 for the summer. He hit well in a full season with Single-A Fort Myers in 2023 then continued to swing the bat well in 2024, reaching Double-A for the first time. A right-handed hitter, Olivar has made excellent progress at the plate over the past two seasons. He has the chance to perhaps be an above-average hitter, one who has kept the strikeouts in check while improving his overall approach and walking at a career 13.4 percent clip heading into 2025. Better swing decisions have continued to enable him to barrel up the baseball and get to his power more consistently. He can drive the ball to all fields, though his home run pop has come mostly to his pull side. His defense hasn’t come along as quickly as his bat, though the Twins do think he has the chance to catch in the big leagues. He’s a tireless worker who is bilingual, works with pitchers well and calls a good game. There’s still work to be done on his arm strength and receiving, but there’s hope it’s trending toward Major League average. He’ll continue getting reps in the outfield, with the versatility giving his bat a better chance of reaching the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins handed out seven bonuses of six figures or more during the 2019-20 international signing period, led by Emmanuel Rodriguez’s $2.5 million. They added Olivar when the period opened in July of 2019 for just $20,000, then had to wait until after the pandemic for his official pro debut, which was a rough 34 games in the Florida Complex League. He won FCL MVP honors when he repeated the level in 2022 and had a solid year at the plate with the full-time move up to Single-A in 2023. After back-to-back solid offensive years, there is some confidence that the right-handed hitter is going to hit as he progresses. He’s improved his overall approach considerably since signing, continuing to make better swing decisions, drawing a lot of walks and limiting his strikeouts, which led to him finishing second in the pitching-friendly Florida State League in on-base percentage and third in OPS. There’s some impact in the swing with solid extra-base pop. Olivar will continue to work on his catcher/outfielder profile, and the Twins think he’s athletic enough to make it work. His arm won’t wow anyone, but he’s working to improve his receiving and game-calling skills behind the dish and he got most of his outfield reps in left field last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the top of the Twins’ international prospect acquisitions in the 2019-2020 signing period was Emmanuel Rodriguez, now one of the best prospects in the system, who got $2.5 million to sign. Near the bottom in terms of bonus amount was Olivar, who joined the organization out of Venezuela for just $20,000 in July 2019. After struggling in his 2021 debut in the Florida Complex League, something clicked in 2022 as he led the circuit with a 1.047 OPS over 40 games and finished the year in full-season ball. The reigning FCL Most Valuable Player, Olivar has a unique profile as a catcher who also plays center field. The right-handed hitter worked to improve his swing decisions, and it paid off. He impacted the ball on a more regular basis while limiting strikeouts and drawing a good amount of walks. He still chases a bit too much and struggled with pitchers on the outer half, but the Twins like his swing and think he has the chance to hit with his excellent bat-to-ball skills. An athletic catcher, Olivar will continue to get as many reps behind the plate as possible, but the Twins want him to continue to use that athleticism to play a solid center field, and he even played a little second base last year. It’s not common, but the Twins are bullish on his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hightower was a pop-up player out of the North Carolina prep ranks, and San Diego surprised many by swooping in to take him in the third round of the 2024 Draft, paying him slot money at $852,300 to go pro. He looked like one of the best players in the Arizona bridge league the summer after he signed, but then scuffled out of the gate in his official pro debut at Single-A Lake Elsinore. He was traded to the Orioles as part of the return for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the Trade Deadline and didn’t hit much in 24 games with his new organization at Single-A Delmarva to finish the year. Scouts were bullish on Hightower’s offensive potential coming out of the Draft. He looks athletic and hitterish in the box with a high leg kick, has good bat speed and barrel control and a good feel for the strike zone. There was hope he could develop into at least average power, but he didn’t impact the ball much in his debut as he struggled to square balls consistently against advanced pitching. Hightower does show on-base acumen, as well as a mature approach and a strong baseball IQ that hint at an ability to make the necessary adjustments. Hightower can impact the game with his legs, as he is at least an above-average runner who has run the 60-yard dash in 6.6 seconds. He played exclusively shortstop with the Padres but split time between short and second base after the trade. He should still get opportunities at short, though he looks more like a second baseman long term. Wherever he ends up defensively, it’ll be the bat driving the profile -- that is, if he can develop offensively.
