mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hightower helped lead East Rowan High School to a 3A North Carolina state championship last spring and was a consistent performer during his time in school but tended to be overlooked in many Draft circles. Padres area scouts had interest in him, however, and he popped all the more in a South Carolina workout before the Draft. Still, San Diego surprised many when it swooped to take Hightower in the third round last summer and paid him slot money at $852,300 to go pro. After hanging back in extended spring training, Hightower scuffled over his first two months with Single-A Lake Elsinore, but had righted the ship with a solid July when he was sent to the Orioles as part of the return for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the Trade Deadline. The former UNC commit stays back on balls well with a high leg kick and can find the barrel with a repeatable swing. His strike-zone knowledge is solid for his age, adding to the belief he could be an above-average hitter in time. There’s at least average power potential too, especially if he can continue to square balls against more advanced pitching. A 6.6 runner in the 60-yard dash, Hightower can also impact the game with his speed. He should get every chance to play shortstop for the time being, but some view him as a future bat-first second baseman too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals drafted Cross ninth overall in the 2022 Draft after a proven college track record at Virginia Tech. It hasn’t exactly played out that way since, with injuries and illness – including a bout with Rocky Mountain spotted fever in 2023 – slowing Cross’ progress. He got back on track in ‘24 and had a good year at Double-A, but his performance regressed there in ‘25. Cross logged 114 games with the Naturals and slashed .241/.291/.413 with a career-best 17 home runs. He missed a couple of weeks in June with a back injury and hit better upon his return. Cross made a ton of quality contact in college and had a good feel for the strike zone, but he’s gotten away from that skill set in pro ball, walking at just a 6.5 percent clip in ‘25 while striking out 26.4 percent of the time. He’s still strong and has power, evidenced by the 17 homers, but it’s less of a line-drive approach now and is very pull heavy, so the Royals continue to work with him on hitting the ball to all fields. Cross is an average defender with a tick-above-average arm, profiling best in right field. He’s not a speed guy but does have good instincts on the bases and swiped 23 bags in ‘25. There was a lot to like out of the Draft with Cross, but it really has been a slower progression because of the bumps he’s encountered along the way. He could still be a fourth outfielder type of player if his bat takes a step forward in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cross was an experienced college hitter by the time the Royals selected him No. 9 overall in the 2022 Draft out of Virginia Tech and looked like he might move pretty fast when he hit the ground running that summer in his first taste of pro ball. But it came to a screeching halt when Cross slashed just .203/.298/.378 primarily at High-A in ‘23, a disappointing year caused by a variety of issues, including a serious tick-borne illness called Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever that zapped Cross’ strength and ended his season. He was still dealing with slight effects by the time the ‘24 season kicked off, but he got back on track with a .261/.342/.428 slash line and 15 home runs in 101 games at Double-A. In college, Cross had a strong contact ability and was highly regarded for his command of the strike zone but he got away from that a bit and struck out at a 24.1% clip with a 10.3% walk rate in 2024. Cross’ up-the-middle approach has the best impact, and the Royals have really emphasized the direction of his swing to be more forward and linear, which allows him to have better space to get to pitches and find the strength in his left-handed swing. He was able to eliminate some of the swing-and-miss with breaking balls last year but needs to keep working on that approach and game planning. That’s especially true against lefties to avoid becoming a platoon player. Cross is an average runner but possesses baserunning instincts and feel that make him a stolen base threat, and he swiped 30 bags in 32 attempts in ‘24. A solid defender with good jumps in the outfield, Cross has an above-average arm but lacks the true speed needed in center field. The Royals might have him continue to play all three outfield spots for now, though he profiles best in right. Cross needed that bounce-back season in ‘24 but has seen his stock slip with a return to Northwest Arkansas this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cross hit the ground running when he went to Virginia Tech in 2020 and kept producing for the Hokies over his college career. In the summer of 2021, he was a standout on the USA Baseball squad, and the next year, the Royals made him the No. 9 overall pick in '22. Cross did nothing but produce in his first taste of pro ball after the Draft, but the 2023 season was the exact opposite. He slashed .206/.300/.383 at High-A Quad Cities with 12 homers and a 27.8 percent strikeout rate. He was promoted to Double-A in early August but lasted just two games before falling ill, and that illness seemed to zap his strength and ended his season. He returned for instructional league action in the fall and eight games in the Arizona Fall League, but he was slowed by a hamstring injury. Cross made a name for himself in the ACC because of his command of the strike zone and above-average power to all fields. But his plate discipline vastly diminished in High-A, and he sold out for power too much. When he’s right, he has the tools to hit for average and power, and he made mechanical adjustments in the instructional league, like getting his direction aligned when he’s in his stance to try to get back to his smooth, left-handed swing. That’s allowed him to stay in the middle of the field with loft instead of hooking ground balls. Cross has average speed, but he’s aggressive on the bases and not afraid to swipe a bag. His range and reads help his play in center field, although he has good enough arm strength to move to right. It’s hard to tell what kind of hitter Cross will be in pro ball after the lost ‘23 season, so this is an important campaign for the 23-year-old. How he bounces back, and if he gets back to his old self, will determine if he remains on track as a future star of the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Minor Leaguer Adam Cross, Gavin Cross put himself on the scouting map by hitting .369 over 16 games as a Virginia Tech freshman in the shortened 2020 spring. He continued to perform with the Hokies and was arguably the best hitter on the USA Baseball squad in the summer of 2021, leading the Royals to take him ninth overall last July. After signing for full slot at $5,202,900, Cross was too advanced for his late-season assignment to Single-A Columbia, where he hit .293/.423/.596 with seven homers in 26 games. Batting from the left side, the two-time All-ACC first-teamer has opened up his stance since his high-school days, allowing him to elevate balls better and take advantage of his solid bat control. The result has been above-average power potential. However, his K rate crept up to 25.2 percent in Single-A, and it has stayed high with High-A Quad Cities in his first full season, calling into question his ability to hit for average in the pro ranks. Cross has slightly above-average speed, and the Royals have hopes that his range will allow him to stay in center field. He began his career on campus in right field and might eventually move back if he finds himself next to a teammate with more wheels to burn. His overall offensive profile should still fit in a corner, though he’ll need to turn things around in the box to make that the case after his slow Midwest League start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Padres out of the Dominican Republic for $300,000 in 2018, Angeles jumped out to a promising start in his pro career by hitting .301/.359/.376 and striking out just 19 times in 44 games the next year in the Dominican Summer League. A continued breakout in 2021 in which he hit a combined .329/.392/.445 between Low-A and High-A made him an attractive prospect for the A’s, who acquired him last March along with Adrián Martínez as part of the Sean Manaea deal. Playing his first season with Oakland at High-A Lansing as a 20-year-old, he hit .278/.316/.353 in 97 games. Angeles is a strong, physical player despite what his 5-foot-11, 175-pound frame might suggest. While there’s not a ton of power to his game, the ball really comes off his bat hard and he uses a quick swing to hit high quality line drives. He has continued to post low strikeout totals, demonstrating good bat-to-ball skills throughout his Minor League career. Angeles can utilize his above-average speed to steal bases. He still plays shortstop and second base, though he does get lackadaisical defensively at times. With an overall talent the A’s remain high on, he’ll get a chance to continue progressing through the system, with second likely his future full-time role should he settle into one spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres, as a penalty for overspending in the 2016-17 international signing period, were unable to sign anyone for more than $300,000 in 2018, but that didn’t stop the organization from inking Angeles. Signed for the full $300,000, the infielder has looked like a bargain and is off to a fast start in his pro career. He hit .301/.359/.376 with only 19 strikeouts in 44 games in the Dominican Summer League during his 2019 pro debut, then raked over 105 games in 2021, hitting .329/.392/.445 over two levels of Class-A ball. The contact skills caught the eyes of the A’s, who acquired him along with Adrian Martinez in the April trade that sent Sean Manaea to San Diego. Listed at 5-foot-11 and 175 pounds, Angeles doesn’t hit for a ton of power, but puts that ball in play with strong bat to ball skills and an aggressive approach. The right-handed hitter hit .354 against right-handers in 2021, suggesting he’ll be tough to match up against as he continues to climb the ranks. There’s some uppercut in Angeles’ quick swing, but that translates more to doubles and triples as he uses his above-average speed to take the extra base. He also knows how to steal a bag when the opportunity presents itself, swiping 36 over his first 149 professional games. While Angeles is most comfortable at shortstop, the position he played prior to signing, it’s likely he’ll wind up at second base. He’s played second, third and shortstop early in his career and that versatility may help expedite his path to the big leagues -- especially if he keeps hitting at his current pace. Angeles has quick feet, solid hands and the arm strength to play anywhere on the infield, though his accuracy needs to improve. Of course, if he continues to rake, the A’s will find a spot for him to play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teodo didn't pitch much as a Dominican amateur and signed for just $10,000 in 2020, but he quickly made a name for himself by reaching 102 mph with his fastball during instructional league following his 2021 pro. He was named Arizona Fall League reliever of the year in 2023 and a year later became the first pitcher ever to work two perfect innings in a Futures Game. Seemingly poised to make his big league debut in 2025, he instead was stymied by a shoulder impingement that cost him half a season and he never looked like his best self. The one constant for Teodo last year was that he still had a devastating upper-80s slider with downward break, a weapon that generated a 57 percent swing-and-miss rate. He throws one of the hardest sinkers in baseball, operating at 97-99 mph and touching 102, but it got hit hard when he didn't command it well. Though he doesn't use his upper-80s changeup much and it lacks consistency, it can be a plus pitch with fade and depth when it's on. Compared to the late Yordano Ventura because of his small stature, big stuff and electric arm speed, Teodo never has provided regular strikes and walked 19 percent of the hitters he faced last season. He's athletic but his delivery features effort, and some scouts projected him as a reliever even while he was dominating as a Double-A starter in 2024. If he can stay healthy and have even fringy control, he has the arsenal to close games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers found a pair of $10,000 pitching bargains in their 2019-20 international class, stealing both Winston Santos and Teodo out of the Dominican Republic. The latter didn't pitch much as an amateur but quickly opened eyes by pushing his fastball to 102 mph at the instructional league in the fall of 2021. He had his best season yet in 2024, logging a 1.98 ERA and 31 percent strikeout rate at Double-A and becoming the first hurler to spin two perfect innings in the Futures Game, making it a no-brainer for Texas to protect him on its 40-man roster in November. Teodo has the filthiest stuff in the system and one of the hardest two-seamers in the game, a sinker that somehow sits at 97-99 mph, climbs to 102 and is fairly impossible to lift. His tight upper-80s slider is even more devastating, breaking straight down and generating a 58 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2024. His changeup is his worst offering and still grades as plus, operating in the upper 80s with fade and depth. Likened to the late Yordano Ventura because of his small frame, electric arsenal and lightning-fast arm speed, Teodo still has yet to harness his stuff. He's athletic but his delivery has some effort to it, so he never has provided regular strikes and his walk rate rose to a career-worst 14 percent even while he dominated last year. He has the pitches to front a rotation, but his control may land him in the bullpen, where he would have obvious closer potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect from the Rangers' 2019-20 international class was relatively ancient at nearly 19 years old and signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Teodo had limited pitching experience as an amateur but created instant buzz when he came to the United States for his 2021 pro debut and even more when his fastball touched 102 mph during the instructional league that fall. He missed most of the first two months last year with a forearm strain, then averaged 12.3 strikeouts per nine innings primarily as a starter for the second straight season before earning Arizona Fall League Reliever of the Year honors. Teodo has electric arm speed that generates four-seam fastballs that sit at 95-98 and reach 103 mph, but they tended to flatten out at higher velocities, so at midseason last year he switched to a two-seamer with similar heat and plenty of sink. He has more trust in his mid-80s breaking ball, which combines curveball depth with slider power and approaches 3,000 rpm at times. He can miss some bats with an 88-92 mph changeup with splitter action but doesn't have faith in it and doesn't land it for strikes. Compared to the late Yordano Ventura because of his smaller frame and power stuff, Teodo is athletic but lacks physicality and has significant effort in his delivery. He did throw more strikes after switching to a sinker, and even more while coming out of the bullpen in the AFL, but he has yet to prove he has more than below-average control. The Rangers considered expediting him to the big leagues as a reliever in 2024 before continuing to develop him as a starter, and he has looked like a potential mid-rotation option a year or two from now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though the Rangers spent $3.9 million on Dominican outfielder Bayron Lora and $1.65 million on Venezuelan shortstop Maximo Acosta in their 2019-20 international class, the best prospect from that crop is Teodo, who signed for $10,000 at the relatively advanced age of 18 years and 11 months. The Dominican right-hander began to open eyes when he came to the United States for his 2021 pro debut, then drew more attention by pushing his fastball to 102 mph during instructional league. He continued to light up radar guns in Single-A last year while striking out 115 in 84 1/3 innings. Compared to the late Yordano Ventura because of his smaller frame and nasty stuff, Teodo has electric arm speed that produces fastballs that park at 95-98 mph and reach 103 with late hop and carry, though they can flatten out at times. He spins his power breaking ball at 3,000 rpm, combining downer curveball break with slider velocity (mid-80s with a peak of 90 mph). While he can miss bats with a 88-92 mph changeup with splitter action, he doesn't trust it and has trouble landing it for strikes. Control and command are issues for Teodo, who can lose feel for his fastball and averaged 4.9 walks per nine innings in his first two pro seasons. He's athletic but isn't physical and features a lot of effort in his delivery. He may never locate his pitches well enough to fit in a big league rotation, but he does have closer upside if he shifts to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yet another international pitcher signed at a lower price and higher age by the Astros, Ullola turned pro for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 18 in 2021. He reached Single-A in 2022, and in his first four years in full-season ball, he posted the lowest opponent average (.189) and highest strikeout (30 percent) and walk (15 percent) rates among pitchers with at least 400 innings. Houston has developed him as a starter, but his big league future almost certainly will be as a reliever. Ullola has one of the most unhittable fastballs in the Minors even though it sits at 92-94 mph and tops out at 97. With its combination of a flat approach angle and exceptional carry, it seems to explode at the plate. His secondary pitches vary in quality, with his upper-80s cutter and sweeping low-80s slider his most effective options in 2025. His low-80s curveball features depth and his upper-80s changeup has some fade but neither is very reliable. Ullola isn't tall but he has a strong 6-foot-1 frame, plenty of arm speed and the athleticism to get down the mound and create a low release height with quality extension. He has no glaring red flags in his delivery but never has been able to repeat it well enough to provide consistent strikes, and he landed his fastball in the zone just 36 percent of the time last season. He's on the same career path as Bryan Abreu, who battled his control as a starter in the Astros system before claiming a vital role in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding older international pitchers at bargain prices and developing them into big leaguers has played a large role in the Astros' eight consecutive playoff appearances, and Ullola could be the next in line. Signed for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 18 in January 2021, he struck out 32 percent of the batters he faced in his first four pro seasons while climbing from Rookie ball to Triple-A. He led the Minors in opponents average (.163) while ranking third in strikeouts (171 in 130 1/3 innings) and sixth in K rate (31 percent) last year. Ullola's electric fastball can be unhittable, parking at 92-96 mph and peaking at 98 with a flat approach angle and tremendous carry up in the zone. He sharpened his mid-80s slider and threw more strikes with it in 2024, giving him a solid second offering. His low-80s curveball has more depth but isn't as devastating or reliable, while his upper-80s changeup has its moments but lacks consistent movement. Ullola has a quick arm and gets down the mound well, creating premium extension with a low-release height. He's athletic and his delivery isn't glaringly effortful, but he never has provided regular strikes and his 14 percent walk rate last year represented his career best. He has a special fastball and could become a mid-rotation starter if he can find more control, or perhaps will follow the Bryan Abreu path to Houston's bullpen if he can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have had a lot of success signing older pitchers on the international market and refining them into big leaguers. If he can add some polish, Ullola could follow that same path after signing for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic as a 18-year-old in January 2021. He averaged 13.2 strikeouts but also 6.7 walks per nine innings in his first three years as a pro. Ullola has an electric fastball that he can throw repeatedly and still leave Minor League hitters helpless to do much against it. His four-seamer can sit at 92-95 mph and reach 97 with a flat approach angle and exceptional carry up in the zone, though he often has to dial back his velocity in an attempt to throw strikes. His next-best pitch is a short slider that stands out more for its power (peaking in the upper 80s) than its shape. Ullola also sports an improving mid-80s changeup and a fringy low-80s curveball, though he doesn't trust either offering. He has a quick arm but lacks a smooth delivery, so he has no history of throwing strikes despite working out of the stretch all the time. There's a low probability that he makes it as a big league starter, but his fastball is special, and Bryan Abreu had similar early career control issues before becoming a key part of Houston's bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have made a habit of signing older international pitchers to modest bonuses and turning them into big leaguers. They have another candidate in Ullola, who signed for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 18 in January 2021. He fanned 120 batters in 72 Single-A innings last year, finishing second in strikeout rate (15.0 per nine innings) among all Minor Leaguers with at least that many frames. Reminiscent of when Cristian Javier was advancing through the system, Ullola can throw his fastball over and over again and batters are helpless to do anything with it. He sits at 93-95 mph and reached 98 with a four-seamer that features a flat approach angle and tremendous carry. His second-best offering is a short slider that stands out more for its ability to climb into the upper 80s than its shape. Ullola's low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup don't have as much upside and he doesn't trust them as much as his fastball and slider. He has a quick arm but doesn't have a smooth delivery, and he has trouble finding the strike zone even while working out of the stretch on a full-time basis. He needs a lot more polish and comes with considerable reliever risk, but it's difficult not to fall in love with his electric fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After transferring from Southeast Polk HS (Pleasant Hill, Iowa) to IMG Academy (Bradenton, Fla.) for his 2024 senior season, Larson emerged as the best prospect at the prep powerhouse. The White Sox made him yet another of their Area Code Games players to join the club with a seven-figure bonus, signing him for an over-slot $1,397,500 in the supplemental second round. Set to make his pro debut in 2025, he injured his elbow in a January minicamp and had Tommy John surgery the following month. Compared to Max Fried, Shane McClanahan and Chris Sale, Larson has the potential for two plus pitches. Before he got hurt, his fastball sat at 92-94 mph and hit 96 with run and sink, while his high-spin slider operated in the low 80s with two-plane depth at its best. He barely threw his upper-80s changeup as an amateur, and it will be a point of emphasis when he returns to the mound in 2026. Larson's extremely low arm slot creates wide angle and a flat approach, providing plenty of deception, though some scouts wonder if his delivery and effort will allow him to throw enough strikes to remain a starter. He struggled with his control and command on the high school showcase circuit before showing improvement as a senior. He has used his downtime to add significant strength, which should help him repeat his mechanics more efficiently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Larson transferred from Southeast Polk HS (Pleasant Hill, Iowa) to IMG Academy (Bradenton, Fla.) for his 2024 season, becoming the best prospect at the perennial powerhouse. Yet another player to earn a seven-figure bonus from the White Sox after showcasing with their Area Code Games club, he signed for an over-slot $1,397,500 as a supplemental second-round pick Chicago acquired from the Mariners in a trade for Gregory Santos. He added 17 pounds by the end of instructional league and was set to make his pro debut in 2025 before injuring his elbow in a January minicamp and requiring Tommy John surgery. Larson offers the potential for two plus pitches, including a fastball that presently parks at 92-94 mph and peaks at 96 with run and sink. He can spin his low-80s slider up to 3,000 rpm, giving it two-plane depth when it's on, though it can get more slurvy at times. He's just beginning to refine an upper-80s changeup that needs more action and velocity separation from his fastball. While he struggled with his control and command on the showcase circuit, Larson made strides with harnessing his fastball and slider during his senior season. His low arm slot creates wide angle and a flat approach that create deception, though some scouts believe his mechanics and effort hamper his strike-throwing and could land him in the bullpen. He'll need time to return to health and develop but has drawn some comparisons to Max Fried and Shane McClanahan.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals drafted Dabovich in the 18th round in 2018 after he flashed a 98 mph fastball as a Central Arizona CC freshman, but he turned them down to transfer to Arizona State. The Sun Devils shifted him from the rotation to the bullpen midway through his sophomore season and he became their closer before the Giants selected him in 2020's fourth round. He averaged 14.1 strikeouts per nine innings while advancing to Triple-A in his first two pro seasons but he worked just four games last April before undergoing season-ending hip surgery. Dabovich attacks hitters with two pitches, working up high with four-seam fastballs before dropping hammer curveballs through the bottom of the zone. His curve is a legitimate plus-plus pitch with mid-80s power and huge depth that produced a 52 percent swing-and-miss rate and 43 percent chase rate in 2022. His fastball also grades as a well-above-average offering at its best, though it's less inconsistent and parked at 93-96 mph with a peak of 97 two years ago. Hitters can't get comfortable against Dabovich, who works out of a high arm slot with a flat approach angle and doesn't always know where his pitches are headed. An intense competitor who has trouble repeating his delivery, he has walked 26 in 27 1/3 innings during his short time in Triple-A. He can show closer stuff but needs to prove he can harness it and stay healthy after also missing time in 2021 with back issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dabovich flashed a 98-mph fastball as a Central Arizona CC freshman in 2018, then turned down the Royals as an 18th-rounder and transferred to Arizona State. He transitioned from starter to reliever with the Sun Devils before signing as a fourth-rounder in 2020. He averaged 14.1 strikeouts per nine innings in his first two seasons while climbing from High-A to Triple-A. Both Dabovich's fastball and curveball can grade as plus-plus pitches when at their best, though his former wasn't as sharp in 2022, when he dealt with hamstring issues. He lost a bit of velocity and riding action on his heater, though he still sat at 93-96 mph. He likes to work up top with his four-seamer and then mess with batters' eye level by dropping mid-80s curveballs through the bottom of the zone. Hitters have trouble adjusting to Dabovich's pitches coming at a flat approach angle out of a high arm slot. He presents an uncomfortable at-bat because he has overpowering stuff but doesn't always know where it's going. He has trouble keeping his mechanics in sync, which led to 20 walks in 24 2/3 innings, and he'll need to throw more strikes to be a late-inning reliever in San Francisco.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals drafted Dabovich in the 18th round in 2018 after he touched 98 mph with his fastball as a Central Arizona CC freshman, but he turned them down and transferred to Arizona State. He transitioned from starter to closer while with the Sun Devils and pitched his way into the fourth round of the 2020 Draft. He struck out nearly two batters per inning and reached Double-A in his pro debut last summer, though his control disintegrated during a stint in the Arizona Fall League. Dabovich challenges hitters with a 93-97 mph fastball that peaks at 99 and has a flat approach angle coming out of his high arm slot. He works up top with his four-seamer, then changes batters' eye level by dropping mid-80s curveballs through the bottom of the zone. Both pitches can grade as plus-plus when at their best. It's tough for hitters to get comfortable against Dabovich because his stuff is overpowering and he doesn't harness it consistently. Counting the AFL, he issued 25 walks in 43 innings last year, and he'll need to get more dialed in to fill a high-leverage role in San Francisco. As soon as he gets his mechanics in sync and provides consistent strikes, he'll be ready for the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Righty-hitting catchers can be fighting an uphill battle in terms of Draft status, and you have to go back to Reds backstop Tyler Stephenson from the 2015 class to get a player in that profile who's found good MLB success. (Harry Ford, of the 2021 class, could join that list in time.) Like Stephenson, Harvey showed out in front of southeast scouts – this time coming from the Florida ranks – and he was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 153 prospect in the 2025 Draft. The Padres took him right around that slot in the fifth round but gave him their second-highest bonus at $1.5 million to sign away from a Florida State commitment. Harvey has strength and power in his 6-foot-2 frame and continually showed that off in high school, summer showcases and the Draft Combine. At the latter event, he hit three balls at 400-plus feet, tied for the most on Day 2 and maxed out with an exit velocity of 110.5 mph. Scouts were split on whether he would have the hit tool to get to that pop before the Draft, and Harvey’s limited contact in a short seven-game sample with Single-A Lake Elsinore didn’t help the cause. In that time however, he didn’t expand the zone much, and there’s hope the dip in the California League could open him to adjustments in his first full season. Harvey’s good hands and receiving skills will get him plenty of looks behind the plate, and his above-average arm strength fortifies the case, especially if he can clean up some of his mechanics. The Padres took fellow prep backstop Truitt Madonna in the Draft last year and will have to balance the workloads for both, but Harvey has more upside with his slugging advantage.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carela created some buzz by pushing his fastball to 96 mph shortly after signing with the Yankees for $335,000 in July 2018, but he hasn't picked up any additional velocity since. He now leans heavily on his slider and it helped him record a 3.71 ERA with 145 strikeouts in 106 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A in 2024, his first full season in the White Sox system. They picked him up in a 2023 Trade Deadline deal for Keynan Middleton and added him to their 40-man roster last November. He was on track to reach the big leagues this year but instead will miss the season after having Tommy John surgery in March. The Yankees specialize in teaching pitchers to throw sweeping sliders, and Carela's low-80s version induces plenty of chases, though it does get pounded when he doesn't locate it down in the zone. He uses his slider more than his two-seam fastball, which usually ranges from 92-94 mph and generates a lot of weak groundball contact with its sink. He also mixes in a cutter and an occasional fading changeup, both of which arrive in the mid-80s. Carela has the athleticism to repeat his delivery and provide consistent strikes. If he can improve his command and develop a second better-than-average pitch, he could become a No. 4 starter. If not, he has a future as a slider-happy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carela's fastball touched 96 mph shortly after he signed with the Yankees for $335,000 in July 2018, but it hasn't added any velocity since. He logged a 6.90 ERA in his first two pro seasons before improving his slider, which has allowed him to successfully navigate both Class A levels the last two years. The White Sox acquired him in an August trade for Keynan Middleton. The Yankees love sweeping sliders, and Carela picked up a solid low-80s version that he can turn into a more traditional slide piece in the mid-80s. He falls in love with his sweeper too much and will have to use his 91-96 mph two-seam fastball with sink more often against more advanced hitters. His upper-70s curveball and mid-80s changeup are average offerings. Carela is athletic and has a clean delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to throw consistent strikes. If he can refine his command and find a second better-than-average pitch, he could slot in the back of a rotation. Otherwise, he'll probably wind up as a slider-happy middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros lost their first two picks in the 2020 Draft as part of their punishment for sign stealing, and they spent their top selection (supplemental second round) and an over-slot $1.25 million bonus on Santos. Though he was one of the best high school arms to come out of New York City in the last decade, his conditioning, stuff and control all regressed in the early years of his pro career. He got hammered for a 7.83 ERA in Double-A during the first month of the season before getting sidelined by an elbow strain, but he looked like a different pitcher when he returned to tie for the Arizona Fall League lead with 26 strikeouts in 17 2/3 innings. Small sample size aside, Santos' AFL performance provided cause for optimism as he averaged 95 mph and touched 98 with his fastball, getting good carry on his four-seamer and effective sink and run on his two-seamer. His low-80s slider was unhittable at times with two-plane depth and he mixed it with a tighter upper-80s cutter. His upper-70s curveball wasn't as reliable as his other offerings, and he didn't throw a single changeup. Houston had Santos lower his arm slot a bit, and he looks more comfortable while throwing with greater velocity and spin. He also demonstrated better control in the Fall League than he had in the Minors. If he can sustain that stuff and strike-throwing, he still might be a big league starter if he can find a way to get lefties out reliably.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best high school arms to come out of New York City in the last decade, Santos didn't get a chance to pitch as a senior in 2020 because of the pandemic. He had performed well on the showcase circuit the previous summer, which was enough for the Astros to spend their top pick (supplemental second round) and an over-slot $1.25 million on him. They handled him carefully in his pro debut last year, when he struggled to throw strikes during 41 2/3 innings in Low-A. Santos reached 96 mph with his fastball in 2021 but sat more around 90-91 later in the season, though he still had good carry on his four-seamer and nice sink on his two-seamer. His curveball has greater potential, showing signs of becoming a plus pitch with upper-70s velocity and plenty of depth. He's gaining aptitude for using a fading changeup that should give him an average third offering. Though Santos is athletic and doesn't have much effort in his delivery, he had difficulty repeating his mechanics in his introduction to pro ball. The hope is that he'll get more consistent as he fills out his lean 6-foot-4 frame, allowing him to provide enough strikes to remain a starter. He'll be 20 throughout the 2022 season, so he has plenty of time to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros lost their first two choices in the 2020 and 2021 Drafts as sign-stealing punishment, and they used their first choice (supplemental second round) last June on Santos. Scouts consider him and 2018 Indians supplemental first-rounder Lenny Torres the two best prep arms to come out of New York City in the last decade. Santos didn't get a chance to pitch in the spring because of the coronavirus shutdown, but he proved himself enough on the high school showcase circuit the previous summer to earn an over-slot $1.25 million bonus. Santos has the type of high-spin four-seam fastball that Houston emphasizes, usually dealing at 90-94 mph and touching 96 with little effort in his delivery. His curveball may have even more upside, flashing as a true plus pitch with upper-70s velocity and quality depth. He shows aptitude for throwing a changeup with fade despite having little use for the offering as an amateur. Santos is athletic and has plenty of projection remaining in his 6-foot-4 frame, so he could have a plus fastball and curve along with a solid changeup as he gets stronger and more consistent. He repeats his delivery well and should have no difficulty throwing strikes. He's one of the better bets to make it as a starter among Astros pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers’ international scouting department did an excellent job finding Herrera and signing him for just $10,000 in August of 2019. It wasn’t until 2023 that he gained any real traction, pitching well in his second go-round in the Single-A Carolina League. Things clicked more the following year as he made his way to High-A ball when he was sent to the Rockies in the Nick Mears trade that July. He threw very well upon his arrival, but got shut down after six starts and he needed Tommy John surgery, so he missed all of the 2025 season. Herrera did return in time for instructional league play and was providing some optimism by dialing his fastball up to 97-98 mph in shorter stints. Before the injury, he was usually in the 92-94 mph range, getting groundball outs when he sinks it, but relying on his hard slider as his main out pitch. His feel to spin also helps him land a slightly slower curve and he has a changeup that he hadn’t committed to before he got hurt. The new pitching group with the Rockies are excited about working with Herrera because of his ability to shape different pitches, all coming out of the same slot. He got in some competitive innings in winter ball and he’ll pitch most of the 2026 season at age 22, trying to show he has the stuff and command to stick in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herrera got just $10,000 to sign with the Brewers in August 2019 and didn’t really make any significant waves until 2023 when he turned in a solid season in the Carolina League, his second year at the level. He broke out in 2024, pitching his way to High-A when he was sent to the Rockies as part of the return for Nick Mears in a July trade; Herrera then made six more solid starts for his new organization. Excitement for Herrera’s acquisition was dampened when he needed Tommy John surgery at the end of the year, forcing him out for all of 2025. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has three pitches in his arsenal that he was just starting to really learn how to use effectively when he went down. He typically throws his fastball in the 92-94 mph range and uses his hard above-average slider with bite as his go-to pitch. He misses plenty of bats with the pitch, showing the ability to backfoot lefties with it. He has a changeup, but it’s behind the other two offerings. Because of that slider, Herrera’s strikeout rate took a nice step forward in 2024 and he uses the two-seam variation of his heater to get a lot of ground-ball outs. He threw a lot more strikes as well last year, but the Rockies will have to wait until 2026 to see if that sticks and if he can refine a third pitch so that he can stick in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the A’s out of Chinese Taipei in November 2021 after playing in the U-23 Baseball World Cup, Zhuang is a bit of a late-bloomer, having signed at the age of 21. He bounced back from shoulder surgery by touching three levels in 2024, then spent last year at Double-A Midland, where he upped his workload further removed from the surgery to 28 games (26 starts) and 145 2/3 innings. Joining the A’s for big league camp this spring, Zhuang was selected to represent Team Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic alongside fellow A’s prospects Wei-En Lin and Tzu-Chen Sha. Zhuang leans heavily on his four-seam fastball that he can change speeds quite a bit with, throwing heaters that range anywhere from 86-96 mph, though it generally sits in the low-90s. His low-80s changeup has emerged as his best secondary pitch. He also brings a mid-70s curveball, low-80s slider and mixes in a low-80s splitter, providing a decent starter repertoire. Zhuang, nicknamed ‘Z-Man’ within the organization, did a good job of staying healthy last season to silence some previous injury concerns. But while he has above-average command and enough pitches to remain a starter in the Minors, questions still remain about the effectiveness of his offspeed stuff, especially against higher competition, which could eventually lead to him switching to a bullpen role where his fastball can play up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zhuang signed with the A’s out of Taiwan in November 2021 after participating in the U-23 Baseball World Cup. On the older side as a 21-year-old at the time of his signing, he has risen through the system with success at each level. His 2024 campaign began at Single-A Stockton, went through High-A Lansing and ended at Double-A Midland. Across the three levels, he combined to post a 2.09 ERA in 23 games (15 starts) with 84 strikeouts and 12 walks over 86 innings. His surge through the organization helped him earn a spot on the Chinese Taipei roster for the WBC qualifiers this spring. Zhuang relies heavily on his four-seam fastball, which can touch 95 mph but normally hovers in the 90-93 range. He also throws a low-80s split-finger offering with good diving action. His arsenal is rounded out by a low-80s slider, a mid-70s curveball with good bend and a low-80s changeup. Zhuang does have a history of injuries, which brings some real concern as to whether he can hold up as a starter despite having the necessary pitch mix for the role. He can command it well, as evidenced by his low walk numbers. For now, the A’s are enjoying watching the rise of the man many in the organization have nicknamed ‘Z-Man.’ He is firmly on their prospect radar, and his age could actually help him move up quickly if the success continues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valencia, Venezuela already has spawned big league catchers Francisco Cervelli, Carlos Perez, Salvador Perez, Wilson Ramos and Luis Torrens, and it may have another on the way in Graterol. He landed the largest bonus in Chicago's 2026 international crop, turning pro for $1.6 million. He was the top-rated backstop (No. 31 overall) on MLB Pipeline's International Top 50. Graterol offered some of the best raw power on this year's international market, generating it with a combination of bat speed and strength. He uses a simple stride from the right side of the plate and looks to do damage. He's aggressive and his potential to produce 20 or more homers per season stands out more than hitting ability at this point. Most athletic than most catchers, Graterol can post solid 60-yard dash times and shows average speed once he gets going, though he'll probably slow down a bit as he matures physically and accrues wear and tear behind the plate. His strong arm is his best defensive tool, while his receiving and blocking are still rudimentary. The White Sox envision him developing into at least an average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto joined the Tigers organization for $897,500 out of Venezuela in January 2024, making him the second-highest-paid international signing by Detroit in that year’s window behind only Nestor Miranda ($1,497,500). Pinto hit the ground running nicely with a .275/.403/.438 line and four homers in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first season but was limited by a hamstring issue in his move stateside in 2025. He did finish his age-18 campaign with Single-A Lakeland, however, and has returned to the Florida State League with more sustained results this season. A right-handed hitter, Pinto stays very much in control with the front side of his lower half, using just a toe tap to remain in rhythm and get himself in position to be short to the ball. He can kick out his back leg once he fires, and as a result, he has pushed the ball the other way a plurality of the time -- and on the ground the majority of the time at Single-A, to boot. Still, because of his quick movements, he has been among the FSL leaders in in-zone contact to begin 2026, and despite the subpar angles, his raw exit velocities have been solid too. Pinto is just an average runner right now, and while he has enough instincts to track down balls in center, he seems likely headed to a corner long term once he shares the grass with speedier defenders. That said, his arm is an absolute hose both in terms of strength and accuracy and remains an asset from anywhere on the grass. Pinto would need to show better slugging ability to be an offensive fit in left or right, but he still has plenty of development ahead as he won’t turn 20 until March 2027.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New York's best prep prospect in 2022, Kennedy worried clubs with his commitment to Louisiana State but turned pro for a well-over-slot $1 million when the Pirates drafted him in the fourth round. Pittsburgh handled him with care and he compiled a 3.11 ERA with a 158/44 K/BB ratio in 130 1/3 innings at the lower levels of the Minors in his first two pro seasons. After acquiring Spencer Horwitz from the Blue Jays in the Andrés Giménez trade at the Winter Meetings in December, the Guardians immediately spun Horwitz to the Pirates for Luis Ortiz, Kennedy and lefty pitching prospect Josh Hartle. Kennedy's fastball averaged just under 90 mph and peaked at 93 last season, though it was effective because he creates deception and carry with a flat approach angle. Hitters also can't sit on his heater because he has a pair of solid secondary pitches that elicit a lot of chases. His sweeping low-80s slider keeps left-handers in check and his sinking low-80s changeup keeps right-handers at bay. Kennedy's lack of overpowering stuff leaves him with little margin for error, but he rarely makes mistakes. More athletic than physical, he ranked third among teenagers in the full-season Minors (minimum: 80 innings) with a 6 percent walk rate last year, but his control has regressed in 2025. His floor stands out more than his ceiling, and he'll have to prove he can get higher-level hitters out without huge velocity, but his feel for pitching is impressive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New York's top high school prospect in 2022, Kennedy dropped to the fourth round because of his commitment to Louisiana State but signed with the Pirates for a well-over-slot $1 million. Pittsburgh handled him carefully and didn't turn him loose in full-season ball until 2024, when he pitched well at two Class A levels and posted a 95/19 K/BB ratio in 83 2/3 innings. The Guardians acquired him along with Luis Ortiz and lefty pitching prospect Josh Hartle in exchange for Spencer Horwitz at the Winter Meetings in December. Kennedy has good feel for a legitimate three-pitch mix, even if he lacks true wow stuff at present. His fastball tops out at around 92 mph, though it plays up a bit because of deception in his delivery and life up in the zone. He also shows a two-seamer with some sink at times, though not consistently. His slider is his best pitch, a low-80s offering that misses bats and is particularly effective against left-handed hitters. He sells his changeup with decent arm speed and it will be an area of focus to improve that pitch and get more velocity separation from his fastball. Kennedy’s ability to repeat his delivery, throw strikes and set up hitters creates a good foundation to be a big league starter, though at 6-foot-1, he doesn’t offer too much projection. There's hope that with natural maturation, there could be more in the tank, which could raise his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kennedy was the top talent in upstate New York in the 2022 Draft, having put himself firmly on the map with a strong summer showcase circuit, including pitching for USA Baseball’s 18U National Team. He was throwing well as the spring wore on, but many teams thought his commitment to LSU was too tough of an obstacle. The Pirates went well over slot in the fourth round of last year’s Draft to overcome that, giving the high school lefty $1 million to sign. Kennedy didn’t make his official debut in 2022, but the Pirates know they’ve gotten a prep arm with more of a college feel for pitching. He has a three-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that right now tops out at around 92 mph, but the combination of deception and riding life up in the zone helps it play up beyond the velocity. His upper-70s slider can miss bats, and he’ll throw his 80-81 mph changeup to all hitters, selling it with good arm speed. With a repeatable delivery, Kennedy should be able to throw a lot of strikes and has already shown a feel for how to set up hitters. The ceiling might be a little limited because of his size, but as a young pitcher who turned just 18 last November, there should be some projection to come from physical maturity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles tend to sign more position players than pitchers from the international market, but they’ve made good decisions with the hurlers they’ve targeted, seeing prospect success with arms like lefty Luis De Leon and righty Esteban Mejia. They think Hidalgo is more advanced at his age than either of those guys were, making him a highlight of their 2026 class when they signed him out of the Dominican Republic for $700,000. A 6-foot-4, 170-pound left-hander, Hidalgo has a great frame for a 16-year-old pitcher, more space to fill out and already features premium stuff for his age. His fastball gets up into the mid-90s, and he also throws a sharp slider that has potential to be a plus pitch. He may work to develop a changeup down the line as he faces better competition but doesn’t need one very much right now. Hidalgo is still learning to control his body and throw strikes consistently, but he has a low-effort, repeatable delivery and creates some deception with his long limbs. He was young for his class and has a long road of development ahead but has an extremely high ceiling if the command part clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player who played shortstop and was largely a reliever at Hanover High School in Virginia, Keller jumped on prospect map as a pitcher with a 16-strikeout performance at the 2022 National High School Invitational and then continued to raise his profile in Hanover’s rotation the rest of the spring. His athleticism and arm strength helped him land with the Braves in the sixth round of that summer’s Draft, getting well over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Old Dominion. It was looking like a wise investment when he posted a 1.17 ERA and .180 batting average against over his first six outings with Single-A Augusta, but after a month on the injured list due to elbow inflammation, his stuff backed up and he got hit hard in the 23 innings he pitched the rest of the year. Keller is hoping to hit the reset button as he continues to learn how to be a pitcher only. The sub-six footer has quick-twitch athleticism working in his favor on the mound, and when he’s right, he’s shown a low-90s fastball with run that he can crank up to 95 mph. He’s shown good feel for a low-80s changeup with fade and thrown with deception thanks to Keller’s arm speed. A low-80s slider with 11-to-5 break gives him a third at least average pitch. While his athleticism should help him repeat his delivery, Keller struggled with his command and control, especially after he came off the injured list. There is some effort there and that, along with his size, had some evaluators dubious about his ability to start long-term and he did a fair amount of relief work during his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keller might have been known to area scouts in Virginia as a high school shortstop who also served as a reliever at Hanover High School. His profile changed when he stepped in as a starter at the 2022 National High School Invitational and struck out 16 early in the spring, then taking over in the rotation when Levin Huesman got hurt. The Braves liked the two-way standout’s athleticism and arm strength on the mound enough to go well over slot -- close to $700,000 -- to sign him in the sixth round of last summer’s Draft. The Braves are banking on Keller’s quick-twitch athletic actions playing as he focuses on pitching only for the first time. The undersized right-hander can touch the mid-90s with his fastball, though he’s not up there consistently, sitting a tick below that with good run. The Braves think his low-80s fading changeup is his best secondary pitch, which comes with good deception thanks to Keller being able to maintain his arm speed well. He has a solid low-80s slider with decent 11-to-5 break as well. There is optimism Keller’s stuff will mature as he adds strength, and he should be able to repeat his delivery well and find the strike zone consistently thanks to that athleticism. There’s been some effort in the delivery in the past and because of his size, he’ll have to show he can handle a starter’s workload, but that’s not a conversation the organization has to worry about yet.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Liranzo trained with Fernando Tatis Jr. before signing with the Orioles for $500,000 as part of their international class, and raised his stock enough during his first year in the system to the point where he was targeted by clubs in trades the following winter. A solid showing in his pro debut as one of the youngest players in the Dominican Summer League gave him helium heading into 2024, but he lost most of the year to a knee injury. The younger brother of Tigers prospect Thayron Liranzo, Joshua’s tenacious style of play earned him a killer early-career nickname: “Animalito” (“Little Animal”). The bat is Liranzo’s loudest tool. He turned heads after signing by showing the potential for plus raw power, producing high exit velocities and barreling balls consistently for a young player. His bat speed and strength hint at the potential for plus raw power, and he’s drawn comps to Teoscar Hernández at the same age, only with better bat-to-ball and pitch-recognition skills. That package gives Liranzo a chance to develop into an average hitter with more reps and polish. His bat will carry him further than his legs, as Liranzo was a below-average runner before the knee issue. Liranzo signed as a shortstop, outgrew the position quickly and settled at third, where he has adequate arm strength to project as an average defender, assuming the knee problem doesn’t hinder his mobility. He’s still young and inexperienced, but with enough seasoning, Liranzo could still develop into an impact run-producer at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Nicknamed “Animalito” (“Little Animal”) for his tenacious style of play, Liranzo is the younger brother of Dodgers prospect Thayron Liranzo as well as the offseason roommate and training partner of Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. He wasn’t the headliner of the Orioles’ 2023 international class, but Liranzo showed enough potential to command a $500,000 bonus and raised his stock so much during his first year in the system that he was targeted by clubs for trades this winter. Liranzo turned heads in his debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he finished with a .393 on-base percentage as a 16-year-old and one of the youngest players on the circuit. The debut reminded some observers of fellow Dominican Republic native Samuel Basallo, who enjoyed similar success in the DSL a few years prior before rocketing up prospect lists, giving Liranzo helium heading into what should be his stateside debut in 2024. The most exciting thing about Liranzo is the way the ball leaves his bat. He hits it harder than most players his age, using above-average bat speed to produce excellent exit velocities while driving the ball consistently. He’s already grown about 3 inches and gotten considerably stronger since signing, now standing 6-foot-3 and using his strength to leverage his right-handed swing. His precocious power draws comparisons to Teoscar Hernández at that age, but Liranzo’s approach and hand-eye coordination are more advanced than Hernández’s were then. Liranzo is not a burner with below-average speed. The converted shortstop has already outgrown the position and profiles better at third base, with the arm strength, footwork and reaction time to succeed at the hot corner. He projects as an average defender there but his ceiling is of a bat-first player who can grow into a middle-of-the-order run producer at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Juan showed an intriguing mix of power and speed as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, where he trained with three-time All-Star shortstop Rafael Furcal. He was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 16 prospect in the 2022 international class and signed with the Mets for $1.9 million -- more than a third of their pool money -- when the window opened on Jan. 15. Juan’s early results didn’t quite meet the hype as he hit .219/.310/.323 with a 77 wRC+ in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League, but his potential remains. The teenager’s plus speed certainly played early in his transition to pro ball, as he swiped 16 bags in 17 attempts and made 45 of his 47 defensive starts in center field. Batting from the right side, the 6-foot-2 slugger shows good raw power with impressive bat speed in his BP sessions. But to this point, that’s where much of his slugging ability remains, in part because he puts the ball on the ground a lot (51.1 percent GB rate in the DSL). Squaring up the ball a bit more and focusing on pitches he can drive should be focuses as he gains experience against pro arms. Juan drew early comparisons to Byron Buxton and George Springer as an amateur, and those certainly flatter him coming off the DSL time. The outfielder will only be the age of an American high school senior in 2023, so he has ample time to sharpen his considerable tools and become a potential everyday player at the top level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Power and speed working in combination will open any scout's eyes. Juan has the potential to show both in the pro game, and training with 3-time All-Star shortstop Rafael Furcal bolstered his case to be MLB Pipeline’s No. 16 prospect in the 2022 international signing period. The Mets made the right-handed slugger their biggest signing of the cycle when they inked Juan to a $1.9 million bonus, using more than one-third of their pool money to haul him in. Juan already shows at least above-average wheels in all aspects of the game, and that should give New York hope that he will be able to remain in center field for the long haul. As if that wasn’t enough, he already shows good power in batting practice, and there remains room for the lanky 6-foot-2 slugger to add more as he matures. His future value could come down to how well his hit tool plays, but early reports indicate Juan could be an average overall hitter if everything clicks. Juan drew initial comparisons to a young Byron Buxton and George Springer. That’s not exactly fair to a 16-year-old just about to get his professional feet wet, but it does paint a picture of who Juan could be at his absolute best in the pros. A word of caution, however: Buxton and Springer overcame severe strikeout concerns early in their careers. If those same issues pop up for Juan and he doesn’t properly adjust, it could be an uphill battle toward Queens, no matter how good the rest of his profile is.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pacheco signed with the Cardinals as a 19-year-old out of Venezuela in November 2017 and instantly became a reliever. After walking more than one batter per inning at Single-A Peoria in 2019, the right-hander had his breakout coming off the missed pandemic year when he climbed three levels in 2021, finished at Triple-A and had a 44 percent K rate (second-best among Minor Leaguers with at least 50 innings). That got him on the 40-man roster that November, and Pacheco was once again effective in the upper Minors in 2022, finishing with a 3.05 ERA, 1.05 WHIP and 84 strikeouts in a career-high 62 frames between Double-A and Triple-A. The Tigers claimed him off waivers from St. Louis in March. The 5-foot-11 righty generates impressive velocity given his frame with a fastball that seems to burst out of his hand around 95-98 mph, touching 99. It’s great heat up in the zone, fitting modern pitching philosophies well. He pairs it with a mid-80s slider that tunnels well off the fastball and can buckle the knees of anyone trying to sit on numero uno. While the slider is behind the fastball, it helps fuel what have been exceptional K rates from Pacheco the past two years. While he’s sparingly used a changeup, the lack of a true third pitch continues to leave him vulnerable to lefties, though he was improved in that department in 2022. Pacheco’s extreme control issues seem to be behind him, and his 9.1 percent walk rate in Memphis helped ease a lot of concerns that he would suffer against more advanced and patient hitters. There’s true setup potential entering Pacheco’s age-25 season, but even if that control backs up again, he could still be solid in middle relief shortly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals signed Pacheco as a 19-year-old out of Venezuela in November 2017 and immediately made him a reliever. The right-hander exploded on the scene in full-season ball in 2019 when he fanned 90 batters over 54 2/3 innings at Class A Peoria, but he walked more than a batter an inning there as well (56 free passes), leading to a 4.12 ERA and 1.72 WHIP. Pacheco was finally able to show modest control gains in 2021 and climbed from High-A to Triple-A, while finishing with a 3.67 ERA, 95 K’s and 29 free passes in 54 innings. His 44.0 percent K rate was second best among the 1,132 Minor League pitchers with at least 50 frames in 2021. Out of concern they’d lose him in the Rule 5 Draft, the Cardinals added Pacheco to the 40-man in November. It’s essentially a two-pitch arsenal from Pacheco but a very effective one. His fastball explodes out of his hand at 95-98 mph, and he lands it well up in the zone, befuddling hitters. The mid-80s slider can sometimes lose its shape and look more slurvy, but when it’s on, it buckles batters and can be dropped in for strikes against those sitting heat. Without much of a quality third pitch, lefties tend to hit him harder than righties. Five of his six homers allowed in 2021 came off the bats of left-handed hitters, and their .378 slugging percentage was nearly double the .193 of right-handers. Pacheco’s walk rate dropped from 21.5 percent in 2019 to 13.4 last season, but even that is dicey when trying to project it against Major League hitters. There is late-inning reliever potential, but barring split/control improvements, a middle-inning profile might fit best -- and it’s one Pacheco is close to reaching in his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Birdsell got drafted three times, pitched at three colleges (Texas A&M, San Jacinto JC, Texas Tech) and overcame Tommy John surgery and a rotator-cuff strain before turning pro as a Cubs fifth-rounder in 2022. He won the organization's Minor League pitcher of the year award while advancing to Triple-A in 2024, putting him on the cusp of the big leagues, before adversity struck last year. He missed the first two months of the season with a lat strain and blew out his elbow in August, leading to a second elbow reconstruction that will sideline him for all of 2026. Birdsell's 94-96 mph fastball can reach 98 with a mix of carry, armside run and command that yields plenty of chases and empty swings. His mid-80s slider also grades as a plus pitch at its best, featuring two-plan depth. His upper-70s curveball has similar shape and does a better job of throwing off hitters' timing than an upper-80s changeup with modest fade that he barely utilizes. Batters don't get a good look at Birdsell, who employs an upright delivery with one of the shortest arm actions in baseball and very little extension. He repeats his unusual mechanics well, enabling him to pound the zone and locate his fastball where he wants. He has No. 3 or 4 starter upside but will be 27 years old and coming off his second Tommy John surgery when he returns to the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Birdsell pushed his fastball into the low 90s as a Texas high school freshman, blew out his elbow as a sophomore, missed his junior season following Tommy John surgery and turned down the Astros as a 39th-rounder in 2018. He barely pitched as freshman at Texas A&M before spending a year at San Jacinto (Texas) JC and then strained his rotator cuff at Texas Tech in 2021. After avoiding surgery and spurning the Twins as an 11th-rounder that summer, he won Big 12 Conference Pitcher of the Year accolades and turned pro as a Cubs fifth-rounder in 2022. He won their Minor League Pitcher of the Year award in 2024, but he missed the first two months of this season with a lat strain before blowing out his elbow in August, resulting in Tommy John surgery that will cost him all of 2026. Birdsell gets a lot of swings and misses in and out of the strike zone with his fastball, which sits at 94-96 mph and tops out at 98 with a nice mix of carry, armside run and command. His mid-80s slider features two-plane depth and grades as a plus pitch at its best. His upper-70s curveball has similar shape and is a more effective change of pace than his actual upper-80s changeup with mild fade that he barely uses. Hitters don't see the ball well against Birdsell, who has an upright delivery with one of the shortest arm actions you'll see and precious little extension. He repeats his mechanics well, pounds the strike zone and locates his fastball with precision. His medical history may have hurt his stock in the 2022 Draft, but he has been healthy for the last three years and looks like an innings-eating No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Birdsell first attracted scouts when he reached the low 90s as a Texas high school freshman, but he blew out his elbow as a sophomore and missed his junior season following Tommy John surgery. He spurned the Astros as a 39th-rounder in 2018, barely pitched as a freshman at Texas A&M, spent a year at San Jacinto (Texas) JC and then strained his rotator cuff at Texas Tech in 2021. After avoiding surgery and turning down the Twins as an 11th-rounder that year, he returned to the Red Raiders, won Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year honors and finally turned pro as a fifth-rounder with the Cubs in 2022. He reached Double-A in his pro debut last year and contributed a postseason victory as Tennessee won the Southern League title. Birdsell's fastball sits at 93-96 mph and can reach 99, comes with plenty of carry and he commands it well. His best secondary offering is a mid-80s slider with good depth. He favors his upper-70s curveball with similar shape against left-handers and also has a below-average upper-80s changeup that will flash some fade on occasion. Though he has a stiff delivery, Birdsell repeats his mechanics well, throws plenty of strikes and locates his fastball where he wants. His medical history may have knocked him down a couple of rounds in the 2022 Draft, but he's not too far away from helping the Cubs as a back-of-the-rotation starter or multi-inning reliever. If Chicago shifts him to the latter role, he could arrive in Wrigley Field later this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz’s long journey in pro ball began all the way back in February 2017 when he signed with the Dodgers for $60,000. He advanced to full-season ball as a starter in 2019, then had to wait through the pandemic to return in 2021. He threw just 11 2/3 innings before needing Tommy John surgery, and between that and other injury setbacks, didn’t throw another competitive pitch for three years. After 11 innings in 2024, he pitched his way from High-A to Triple-A in 2025 as a reliever and earned a spot on the 40-man roster. The Dodgers faced a roster crunch and sent him to the Mariners this past offseason in a trade for Minor Leaguer Tyler Gough. Now 26, Ortiz has the chance to impact a big league bullpen soon. The Mariners really liked his slider, a firm mid-80s breaker with good action to it -- a pitch they think could have even better characteristics. He pairs it well with a 94-95 mph fastball that gets a decent amount of miss and chase. He’ll also work in a hard 90 mph cutter. Command has been one issue for Ortiz, and that might limit what his ultimate bullpen role is, but he also missed so much time from the mound that there could be some improvement to come in terms of his strike-throwing ability. He could fit the Mariners’ need for a lefty reliever this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz signed for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the end of the 2016-17 international period. He helped win a championship in the Rookie-level Arizona League in his 2018 U.S. debut, then made a successful jump to low Class A at age 19 in 2019. He opened eyes with improved velocity during Spring Training last year but didn't participate at Los Angeles' alternate site or instructional league program after the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the Minor League season. Ortiz worked at 94-97 mph during live batting practice last spring after previously operating at 90-93 and topping out at 95 with running action on his fastball. He uses his heater to set up a solid changeup with fade and sink that he throws with the same arm speed. His slider has its moments but gets slurvy at times and is clearly his third-best pitch. Ortiz isn't especially big or projectable but he's athletic and repeats his delivery well, which should allow him to throw strikes. His walk rate nearly doubled from 2.2 per nine innings in his first two pro seasons to 4.2 in low Class A, but Los Angeles believes some minor mechanical adjustments will improve his consistency. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter and has elicited comparisons to a smaller version of Caleb Ferguson, though a strained forearm in May put Ortiz's development on hold once again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz went unsigned for most of the 2016-17 international signing period before landing a $60,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic in June 2017. He made his U.S. debut at age 18 last summer, averaging 11.7 strikeouts per nine innings while helping the Dodgers win the Rookie-level Arizona League championship. He has drawn comparisons to a smaller version of Caleb Ferguson, who jumped from high Class A in 2017 to Los Angeles last year. Ortiz shows the potential for three solid pitches once he matures physically. He operates at 90-93 mph and reaches 95 with running action on his fastball, setting up an advanced changeup that he throws with the same arm speed. His curveball has more shape than power at this point. His athleticism allows Ortiz to repeat his delivery, which bodes well for his ability to provide strikes and stay healthy. While he doesn't have a ton of projection remaining, his combination of stuff and savvy gives him a ceiling of a No. 4 starter. He also has a higher floor than most teenaged southpaws and could start to advance quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fitterer one of the more polished high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, and he drew comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff. Since signing for an over-slot $1.5 million as a fifth-round pick, he has been slower to acclimate to pro ball than expected. He lost the 2020 season to the pandemic and missed time with back and shoulder issues in 2021 before finally getting a full season in High-A last year. Fitterer's fastball usually ranges from 92-95 mph with natural sink and cut, and it stands out more for its ability to generate weak contact than for missing bats. His best secondary pitch is a sinking low-80s changeup that helped him have more success against left-handers than right-handers in 2022. He has some feel for spinning the ball, though his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider can blend together at times. Fitterer's athleticism hasn't translated into reliable strike-throwing. He doesn't attack hitters, and his average stuff doesn't leave him with much margin for error when he catches too much of the plate. He needs to get stronger and more consistent to make it as a starter, and he faces an important year in Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more polished prep pitchers in the 2019 class, Fitterer slid to the fifth round amid concerns about his UCLA commitment but signed for $1.5 million (the equivalent of early second-round money). He has been compared to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff, though he has only pitched 53 innings in three years because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and back issues last season. The Marlins tried to get him more innings in the Arizona Fall League, only to see him develop shoulder soreness after two starts. Fitterer imparts a lot of natural sink and cut on a fastball that ticked up a bit last year, when it sat at 92-94 mph and touched 96 while generating a lot of weak grounders. He has aptitude for spinning the ball, producing solid 78- to 82-mph curveballs with good depth and some tighter sliders in the low 80s. He's also making progress with a sinking low-80s changeup. A good athlete who offered some intriguing right-handed power as a two-way player in high school, Fitterer repeats his delivery with ease and provides consistent strikes. He exudes a calm demeanor on the mound and has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter with three solid pitches and control to match. To reach it, he'll need to get stronger and prove he has the durability for the role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fitterer one of the more polished high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, but his UCLA commitment clouded his signability. He fell to the fifth round before signing with the Marlins for $1.5 million, the equivalent of early second-round money. He posted a 2.38 ERA in his 2019 pro debut in Rookie ball and performed well in instructional league last fall while continuing to draw comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff. Fitterer uses a fast arm to generate 91-93 mph fastballs and top out at 95 with natural sink and cut that produce weak grounders, and he could add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His best secondary pitch is an upper-70s curveball with good shape. He also has a tighter slider in the low 80s and a changeup with similar velocity and some sink. A good athlete who flashed some intriguing right-handed power potential as a prep hitter, Fitterer repeats his delivery consistently and throws strikes. If he adds strength and refines his arsenal, he could fit into the middle of a big league rotation. His polish will help him make the jump to full-season ball in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fitterer caught the attention of scouts with a 12-strikeout complete game at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October 2018, setting the stage for a strong high school senior season. Signability concerns related to his UCLA commitment knocked him down to the fifth round last June, but the Marlins landed him for a well-over-slot $1.5 million, the largest bonus after the top three rounds. He pitched well in his pro debut, adding to his comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better pure stuff. With a quick arm, Fitterer produces 91-93 mph fastballs that top out at 95 with natural sink and cut that elicit a lot of weak ground-ball contact. He shows the potential for three solid secondary pitches, headlined by an upper-70s curveball with nice shape. He also utilizes a sharper slider in the low 80s and a changeup with similar velocity and some sink. A good athlete who displayed some interesting right-handed power potential in high school, Fitterer repeats his delivery well and should have no trouble providing strikes. He's more polished than most young pitchers, and his main needs are to get stronger and develop more consistency with his pitches. If that happens, he could blossom into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
