mlb_pipeline.text: Wolkow projected as a likely 2024 first-rounder before he reclassified during his sophomore year at a suburban Chicago high school. That made him one of the youngest and most physical prospects in the prep class in 2023, when he lasted longer than anticipated but received third-round money ($1 million) in the seventh round. The youngest regular (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League in 2024, he returned there last year and ranked second in homers (13) and RBIs (69). At 6-foot-7 and 239 pounds, Wolkow has more strength and leverage than most players his age, and they combine with his bat speed and ability to launch balls in the air to give him as much raw power as anyone in the Minors. The big question is whether he'll make enough contact to tap into his pop, because he has a naturally long left-handed swing, chases too many pitches and has problems catching up to non-fastballs. He struck out 30 percent of the time in 2025, but that was down from 40 percent the season before, and the White Sox think he can continue to get improve by refining his swing decisions. While Wolkow looks more like a tight end than a typical baseball player, he has at least average speed once he gets going and pilfered 33 bases in 39 attempts (85 percent) last year. He moves well enough to provide average defense on the outfield corners and hasn't looked overmatched when he has filled in as a center fielder. He features plus arm strength and recorded 11 assists in 71 right-field starts in 2025. Besides his high ceiling, he also earns praise for his intelligence, maturity and competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rated as a probable first-rounder in 2024, Wolkow reclassified to the 2023 Draft during his sophomore year at a suburban Chicago high school. One of the youngest and most physical prospects in the '23 prep class, Wolkow lasted longer than expected but landed early third-round money ($1 million) in the seventh round. He tore up Rookie ball for two weeks to start his 2024 season, then slashed .241/.342/.428 with 11 homers in 76 games as the youngest regular (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League. Wolkow has a massive 6-foot-7, 239-pound frame with more strength and leverage than most players his age. Add in his bat speed and he has as much power upside as anyone in the Minors. He's still growing and showing some aptitude for launching balls in the air, and he could produce 40 homers annually if he makes enough contact. That's a question, however, because his size results in a naturally long left-handed stroke. He'll miss some fastballs in the strike zone and chase non-fastballs more than he should, resulting in a 40 percent strikeout rate in 2024, though he improved throughout the year and the White Sox believe he'll make adjustments as he gains experience. Built like a tight end, Wolkow takes time to get out of the batter's box but moves well for his size and is at least an average runner underway. He played well at third base during the 2022 Area Code Games and some scouts think he could handle the hot corner, but he's more comfortable in right field and has the solid arm for the position. Club officials love his makeup, repeatedly praising his intelligence, maturity and competitive will.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Projected as a likely first-rounder in 2024, Wolkow reclassified to the 2023 Draft in March of his sophomore year at a Chicago-area high school. He lasted longer than expected before the White Sox selected him in the seventh round, though he landed top-of-the-third-round money ($1 million) to forego his commitment to South Carolina. He played briefly in Rookie ball and immediately impressed club officials with his maturity at age 17. One of the youngest and most physical prospects in the 2023 crop, Wolkow earns comparisons to Top 100 Prospect Spencer Jones of the Yankees. His massive 6-foot-7, 239-pound body gives him the strength and leverage that can produce top-of-the-scale raw power, and he's still growing. His size adds length to his left-handed stroke and his plate discipline is a work in progress, so he swings through some fastballs in the strike zone and gets fooled by offspeed pitches. Wolkow is built like a tight end and is athletic for his size, slow to get started out of the batter's box but displaying at least average speed once he gets going. He handled third base well at the 2022 Area Codes and some scouts believe he could make it there, but he's much more comfortable in right field and has the solid arm strength needed there. He'll be 18 throughout his first full pro season and will need time to develop, but his ceiling is as huge as his frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz was the 19th-ranked international prospect in the 2018 class, according to MLB Pipeline, before the Tigers signed him for a $1.8 million bonus. His much-anticipated debut in the States was delayed a year by the pandemic and arguably led to him being rushed to Low-A Lakeland, where his .127 average and 74 strikeouts over 158 plate appearances promoted a midseason second-guessing. He had a much more respectable second half one level down in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. As an athlete, De La Cruz is a physical specimen who keeps getting stronger; he already boasts some of the best raw power in the organization. As a hitter, he’s still unrefined with a violent, uppercut swing. He has enough power to go to all fields. He has shown improvement in his plate discipline but struggles against offspeed pitches. He runs well for his body but isn’t an instinctive base stealer. He has the strong arm to play a corner outfield spot but needs time to hone his accuracy. Considering De La Cruz’s age, he has plenty of time to learn the skills necessary to take advantage of his raw skills, but the Tigers have to avoid the temptation to push the timetable with him. His second chance at the Florida State League hasn’t quite proven that much better than the first, and the 20-year-old is in danger of never meeting his ceiling of a power-first Major League bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the Tigers spent just shy of $3 million each to sign Roberto Campos and Cristian Santana, they gave De La Cruz – then the 19th-ranked international prospect by MLB Pipeline – a $1.8 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He made a strong first impression in 2019 in the Dominican Summer League, batting .307 with 11 home runs, 16 stolen bases and a .931 OPS in 225 at-bats. He was on track to compete in the Gulf Coast League when the pandemic scuttled the Minor League season. De La Cruz continues to fill out his athletic frame, reporting to instructional ball last fall with more muscle following the shutdown. He has all-fields power with an aggressive approach at the plate, possibly too aggressive given his 75 strikeouts in the DSL. The Tigers believe his approach will mature, allowing him to maintain average while adding power. He played center field in the DSL but will likely shift to a corner as he continues to fill out. Though the recent Campos and Santana signings have overshadowed De La Cruz, the Tigers see similar upside with a stronger body than expected out of a teenager. He opened 2021 at Low-A Lakeland but bounced down to the Florida Complex League in late June to find his offensive stroke.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers’ shift toward bigger-ticket international signings began in 2018, when they signed De La Cruz – ranked 19th by MLB Pipeline in his international class -- out of the Dominican Republic for a $1.8 million bonus, a then-record for the team under the current system. His stint in the Dominican Summer League didn’t disappoint, including 11 home runs, 16 stolen bases, a .307 average and a .931 OPS in 225 at-bats. The physical tools with De La Cruz are evident, from all-fields power in batting practice to a strong outfield arm to surprising speed. His body has filled out well for his age while still providing room to add muscle. He has good instincts for the game, though his 75 strikeouts in the DSL created some concern about his aggressiveness at the plate. Though De La Cruz played center field in the DSL, he’s expected to eventually shift to a corner spot, where his arm could play. He’ll head to the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hartle was one of the top prep lefties in the 2021 Draft class and entered his junior season at Wake Forest as perhaps the top college pitcher, but his stuff and control backed up and caused him to slip in the '24 Draft. He ended up signing for $850,000 as a Pirates third-rounder before the Guardians acquired him and fellow southpaw Michael Kennedy for Luis Ortiz. The North Carolina native made it to Double-A in his first full pro season and earned High-A Midwest Pitcher of the Year honors after logging a 2.35 ERA with 100 strikeouts and a 1.05 WHIP in 103 1/3 frames for Lake County. While he doesn't have overpowering stuff, Hartle throws strikes with a deep repertoire and creates unique angles from his 6-foot-6 frame and horizontal release. His best pitch is a slurvy slider that gets plenty of chase against lefties, and his changeup gets a decent amount of chase and miss but rarely lands for strikes. Hartle has a four-seam and two-seam fastball that each sit in the low 90s, although he could add more power as he fills out his 207-pound frame. He often works with his upper-80s cutter in the zone and limits hard contact on the pitch. Hartle repeats his delivery well and throws plenty of strikes. He profiles as a back-end starter currently, although the Guardians have had success developing this type of pitcher in the past. He's done a great job of preventing hard contact -- and home runs, in particular -- to date, but without velocity gains, that will be difficult against more advanced hitting. Hartle's 2025 season ended two weeks early with a shoulder injury, but he's unrestricted heading into 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some clubs rated Hartle as the best left-hander in the 2021 prep class, but he went undrafted because he was set on attending Wake Forest. Following an All-America sophomore season, he entered 2024 as a consensus first-rounder before all four of his pitches and his control regressed. The Pirates drafted him in the third round, then sent him to the Guardians five months later as part of a package for Spencer Horwitz. At his best, Hartle exhibits advanced feel for a plus slider, solid cutter and average fastball and changeup. His heater sat at 89-92 mph and topped out at 94 with less life and command last spring, and he became reluctant to throw it when it got pounded. His low-80s slider and upper-80s cutter weren't as sharp as in the past, and his sinking mid-80s changeup rarely landed in the zone. As a sophomore, Hartle used his athleticism to repeat his easy delivery and spot his pitches wherever he wanted. Diminished stuff with less command was a recipe for disaster in 2024, when he also gave up four runs and recorded just five outs in his lone pro outing. He once looked like a lock to be at least a No. 4 starter with the upside of a No. 2, and now he's a reclamation project for an organization renowned for its ability to develop pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals surprised many by selecting Mozzicato at No. 7 overall in the 2021 Draft, taking the Connecticut prep pitcher higher than some thought but also leaving flexibility to draft Ben Kudrna and Carter Jensen after the first round. It hasn’t been the smoothest of journeys for Mozzicato since the Draft, plagued by command issues and inconsistent results. He returned to High-A Quad Cities to begin 2025 and was excellent there, posting a 1.24 ERA in seven starts. Mozzicato faced more challenges in Double-A, where he recorded a 7.46 ERA in 17 games (13 starts), saw his walk rate balloon to 19.4 percent and strikeout rate dip to 17.6 percent, while batters hit .278 against him. Mozzicato has yet to find the velocity that many thought would come in his development, averaging around 90 mph in 2025 and getting hit hard. His 86 mph circle changeup is fringe-average. His curveball, though, has never let him down. It’s a plus pitch, has tons of spin and misses bats. Mozzicato introduced a 90 mph cutter this past offseason, which gives him more confidence in the zone and misses the barrel, although how he uses it in games and how it opens up his arsenal remains to be seen. What has hurt Mozzicato the most, though, is his delivery, and it’s what the Royals have worked extensively on with him. His long stroke never allowed him to sync up, and while he doesn’t have a short arm stroke now, it has tightened and timed up better. The Royals want to continue to see Mozzicato as a starter for now, but there’s clear reliever potential here. Some say the curveball is ready for the Majors; Mozzicato just needs to be able to get his fastball to a place where he can trust it up there, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals took Mozzicato at No. 7 in the 2021 Draft, making him the highest-drafted Connecticut prep player since Bobby Valentine in 1968, and signed him to an under-slot bonus. His development since has been slow and inconsistent, and he returned for a full season at High-A in 2024 after struggling there at the end of ‘23. Last year, Mozzicato posted a 3.45 ERA across 101 2/3 innings, limiting batters to a .203 average. But he walked 62 batters while his strikeout rate fell to 21.3%. Mozzicato’s best pitch remains his plus low-80s curveball with downer movement. He’s always been able to spin the ball well, but the command was not consistent in 2024. It doesn’t help that his fastball velocity continues to fluctuate as Mozzicato struggles to keep weight and strength on during the season. His heater was 87-90 mph and was out of the zone too often in '24, but it does have some high vert with a good approach angle. He has increased the usage of an average circle changeup, but it doesn’t have a ton of velo separation from his fastball. If the heater is performing well one night, so is his changeup, and vice versa. Mozzicato’s numbers weren’t bad in 2024, but the Royals worked with him a lot on some under-the-surface aspects after the season so he can be better set up for success at the higher level. The priority was reworking his long arm action that really hindered not only his command but also his velocity, officials believed. Specific drills helped him shorten up the arm stroke, and he was having better results by Spring Training. But Mozzicato will have to show it in games and see if his control issues can be ironed out because that and the low velocity will hold him back from starter projection. They looked better at High-A Quad Cities to open 2025 but regressed again after a promotion to Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-drafted Connecticut prep player since Bobby Valentine in 1968, Mozzicato went No. 7 overall to the Royals in 2021 and signed for an under-slot bonus. They’ve taken his development slow, but Mozzicato got off to a strong start in Single-A Columbia in ‘23; through his first nine starts, he had a 2.14 ERA with a 40 percent strikeout rate and a vastly improved walk rate. But a collision with a teammate during batting practice in early June caused Mozzicato to miss some time, and he struggled to find his rhythm after that with three more starts in Columbia, and then posted a 7.12 ERA in nine starts with High-A Quad Cities. Mozzicato has always been able to spin the ball with a plus curveball that has downer movement, sitting in the upper-70s. His fastball fluctuates with his strength. When he’s at his best, it can hit 94 mph with deception. When it’s not, he’s in the upper-80s and low-90s. Strength has been a big focus for him, as he struggles to keep weight on during the season. Like most of their high school pitchers, the Royals urged Mozzicato to learn a changeup, and he threw it more last year. It has a chance to be an average pitch. Mozzicato has had control issues since he was drafted because of long arm action, but he really struggled after the collision last year with a 16.2 percent walk rate last season. But Mozzicato is extremely athletic with a lean frame that should add strength as he continues to mature. After a funky year that saw highs and lows, Mozzicato still has tons of ceiling because of his weapons, and the Royals see a mid-to-late rotation starter if he irons out the control issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals pulled off a surprise pick when they selected Mozzicato seventh overall in the 2021 Draft and made him the highest-drafted Connecticut prep player since Bobby Valentine (fifth) in 1968. Mozzicato’s Draft stock increased during his senior season at East Catholic (CT) High School, when his velocity jumped and he pitched four consecutive no-hitters with one of the best curveballs in the country. The Royals were able to sign him for a $3,547,500 bonus, about $2 million under slot, and Mozzicato made his professional debut alongside Kudrna in May 2022. Mozzicato made 19 starts for Single-A Columbia, posting a 4.30 ERA. Mozzicato can spin the ball well, with a plus downer curveball that has a good depth and the potential to be plus-plus. His fastball was anywhere from 87-94 mph in 2022, but it landed mostly around 90-92 mph. The Royals are hoping for more velocity as Mozzicato grows into his tall, lean and athletic frame. He is still developing a changeup, which showed improvement early in 2022. He sells it well with his arm speed, and the pitch has the chance to be average or above-average with more repetitions. Developing that third pitch will continue to be a priority. Mozzicato has a free and smooth delivery that should allow him to command the ball well, although sometimes he can lose control of his front side. Command was an issue in his first full season, walking 6.7 per nine in Columbia. Hitters barreled the ball against him, too, so spotting the ball better is a point of emphasis as he moves forward. Mozzicato still has a high ceiling and won’t be rushed in his development, likely moving one level per year. He projects as a back-end starter, although some see a bullpen arm in the future with his fastball/curveball combination. Some of his command issues might have stemmed from losing stamina later in starts, so adding strength is a priority. That will also happen naturally as he matures physically. He repeated Single-A Columbia in 2023 and moved up to High-A Quad Cities, where control continues to be a real issue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mozzicato’s Draft stock soared during his senior season at East Catholic (CT) High School when he showed a jump in velocity and pitched four consecutive no-hitters with one of the best curveballs in the country. The Royals still pulled a surprise when they selected him seventh overall in the 2021 Draft, making him the highest-drafted Connecticut prep player since Bobby Valentine (fifth) in 1968. Mozzicato signed for a $3,547,500 bonus, about $2 million under slot, and reported to the Royals' training facility in Arizona to make his unofficial debut during instructional league. Mozzicato’s curveball is his selling point, a plus breaker with high spin, sharp bite and good depth, and many scouts believe it could eventually be plus-plus, especially after seeing how he can throw it for strikes and expand the zone with it. Mozzicato’s velocity used to sit in the upper-80s, but after working out at Cressey Sports Performance, he came out last spring throwing 91-93 mph consistently. With a projectable frame and his athleticism, he should be able to add more velocity. The Royals were impressed with Mozzicato’s improved changeup in the fall, a pitch he didn’t use much in high school but one that’s hard for hitters to read thanks his arm speed. It has the potential to be a solid offspeed pitch and will be a focus for him going forward. Mozzicato is an athletic lefty with a free and smooth delivery, though his control has wavered in his early days of pro ball. The Royals went against the grain taking Mozzicato as high as they did given his relatively low profile, but with the weapons he has, his room for growth and overall competitiveness, he has the potential to be a mid-rotation starter. He’s been at Single-A Columbia since late May, working on honing a fuller arsenal that will help meet his ceiling. With how deep the Royals system is right now, there’s no rush with Mozzicato, giving the club time to develop him into a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nezuh went from working just 18 innings in two seasons at Florida State to becoming Louisiana-Lafayette's top starter in 2023. The Astros put more stock in his pitch metrics than his 6.25 career ERA in college and selected him in the 14th round. He ranked 10th in the Minors with a 30 percent strikeout rate in his 2024 pro debut between two Class A levels but wasn't as effective while dealing with elbow issues in Double-A last year. Nezuh's upper-70s changeup has improved a lot since his college days, with its splitter action baffling both lefties and righties. It creates tremendous vertical separation from his fastball, which parks at 91-94 mph and touches 96 with huge carry. To remain a starter, he'll need to find a reliable third pitch from among a sweeping low-80s slider, a mid-80s cutter and a mid-70s curveball he has mostly shelved. Nezuh works from a higher arm slot that costs him some deception. Since battling the strike zone at Florida State, he has developed average control and good feel for playing his fastball and changeup off each other. Those two pitches alone could make him a useful multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nezuh worked just 18 innings in two seasons at Florida State before transferring and becoming Louisiana-Lafayette's top starter in 2023. He pitched well down the stretch and held his own in an NCAA regional playoff game against Texas, prompting Houston to draft him in the 14th round. He raised his stock with a strong pro debut that included leading the Single-A Carolina League with 105 strikeouts in 81 2/3 innings before his mid-July promotion and ranking 10th in the Minors with a 30 percent K rate. Nezuh has significantly upgraded his changeup since college and now owns one of the best in the Minors, a low-80s cambio that plunges at the plate and confounds both lefties and righties. It has tremendous vertical separation from his fastball, which sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 with the flat approach angle and carry that the Astros covet. He needs to improve his below-average breaking balls, a sweeping low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball with similar shape. After not throwing strikes in his two years with the Seminoles, Nezuh has done a better job of harnessing stuff since. His biggest need is to find a reliable third pitch, and he has begun toying with an upper-80s cutter. If he can't stick in the rotation, his fastball/changeup combination could make him a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff and won Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year award in 2017, but dropped to the Yankees in the 37th round because he was strongly committed to Auburn. He succeeded 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' No. 1 starter in his final two seasons before signing for a below-slot $1.6 million as a supplemental first-rounder in 2020. He performed well while advancing to Double-A in his first two years as a pro but missed time with a sore elbow in 2021 and a shoulder strain last season. After working with a 92-95 mph fastball and touching 97 with some armside run on his fastball in 2021, Burns spent much of last year operating more at 90-93, though he still commanded his heater well. His most dependable pitch is a mid-80s slider with depth, and he can turn it into a harder, tighter cutter as well. He lands his upper-70s curveball for strikes and also mixes in a low-80s changeup with sink. Burns flashed solid control in the past but his walk rate jumped from 3.4 per nine innings in his first pro season to 4.6 last year, when he didn't challenge hitters as much with slightly diminished stuff. He's small for a starter and has durability concerns that date back to college, where he had shoulder issues in 2019. If he can regain some velocity and stay healthy, he might be a No. 4 starter, though he's starting to trend toward becoming a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff as Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year in 2017, but he was strongly committed to Auburn and followed 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' Friday-night starter in his final two college seasons. The Guardians selected him 36th overall in 2020, the highest pick they've spent on a college arm since taking Drew Pomeranz at No. 5 a decade earlier, and signed him for a below-slot $1.6 million. They handled him carefully in his successful 2021 pro debut, starting him once a week in High-A and giving him two weeks off when he came down with elbow soreness in midsummer. Burns usually works at 92-95 mph and touches 97 with some run on his four-seam fastball, and his ability to spot it on either side of the plate may be more impressive than its velocity (which fluctuated after his stint on the injured list) or life. His best secondary pitch is his plus slider/cutter, which arrives in the upper-80s and helped him to have more success against lefties than righties in High-A. He also throws a 78-82 mph downer curveball that has gotten more consistent in pro ball and has some feel for a low-80s changeup with some sink. With the ability to throw four pitches for strikes and advanced command of his fastball, Burns has a high floor as well as the upside of a mid-rotation starter. The biggest concern is his durability because he's small for a starter, had shoulder issues in 2019 before his elbow flared up last year and his stuff has declined at the end of his last two full seasons. If he can stay healthy, his biggest backers believe he could be similar to fellow former Southeastern Conference standout Sonny Gray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff when he was Gatorade's Alabama High School Player of the Year in 2017, but worries about his size and signability dropped him to the Yankees in the 37th round. He didn't sign with New York, then worked his way into Auburn's rotation as a freshman and succeeded 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' ace during the next two seasons. The Indians signed him for a below-slot $1.6 million as the 36th overall choice last June, the highest they've taken a college arm since grabbing Drew Pomeranz at No. 5 a decade earlier. When he's on, Burns can feature two plus pitches in his fastball and breaking ball. His four-seamer sits at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with some run, and he shows the ability to locate it on either side of the plate. His breaker can combine curveball depth with slider velocity in the low 80s at times and devolve into a slurve at others. Burns also has a sinking changeup that can become an average third offering. He throws strikes but comes with some durability concerns because he's 6 feet tall, had shoulder problems in 2019 and his stuff tends to dip late in the season. The highest-ranked college pitcher on this list, he has a higher floor than the high school arms ranked ahead of him and his biggest backers see similarities between him and another smaller former Southeastern Conference standout, Sonny Gray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were high hopes for Hackenberg, whose athletic brothers have been drafted in baseball, football and soccer, as he entered his Draft-eligible sophomore season at Virginia Tech. He had uneven results but the Braves liked him more than the industry did, taking him in the second round of the 2023 Draft. It looked like a smart decision after a first full season saw him top all Braves arms in ERA (3.07) and batting average against (.212) as he pitched his way to Triple-A. Year 2 was a disaster by comparison as Hackenberg missed time with an oblique issue that limited him to 74 total innings and he had trouble finding any consistency on the mound with Double-A Columbus. Hackenberg’s stuff ticked down in 2025 and it’s hard to know how much the injury played a part. His fastballs -- he throws both a four- and two-seamer -- averaged just around 92 mph and topped out at 94. The sinker does help him get ground-ball outs at a steady clip, but his heater didn’t miss many bats last year. He can still miss some bats with his low-80s two-plane curve and his 90 mph cutter can be effective at times. He didn’t throw his mid-80s changeup much. In addition to his strikeout rate diving compared to 2024, Hackenberg’s command and control suffered. His walk rate soared to 6.6 per nine as he struggled to land most of his repertoire consistently in the zone, and when he did, he got hit. He’s hitting the reset button in his age-24 season; it’s a big year that could result in a 40-man roster spot or exposure to the Rule 5 Draft in the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a very athletic family, with brothers taken previously in the MLB, NFL and MLS Drafts, Hackenberg was coming off of an uneven Draft-eligible sophomore season at Virginia Tech as the 2023 Draft approached. The industry had the big right-hander pegged for more like a 5th-7th round pick, but the Braves liked him more than that, taking him in the second round. So far, it’s looking like they were right as Hackenberg pitched his way from High-A to Triple-A in his first full season, leading qualified Braves arms in ERA and batting average against. With as many as five pitches at his disposal, Hackenberg has provided an intriguing combination of missing bats and getting groundball outs in the Minors. He throws both a four- and two-seam fastball, with the former up to 97 and averaging 94.7 mph last year and the latter averaging over 93 mph and leading to high groundball rates. He was sinker heavy in college but started to feature the four-seamer up in the zone more in pro ball with solid results. His best secondary offering is his power two-plane curve that can miss bats, though his changeup also got some swing-and-miss along with weak groundball contact, and he mixes in a hard 90-mph cutter as well. The most encouraging thing with Hackenberg was that his stuff got better and he threw harder as the year went on despite blowing by his season innings high from college. His strike-throwing hasn’t been as consistent as it was with the Hokies, but there’s confidence he’ll be in and around the zone enough to be an innings-eating workhorse in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Cutter: 45 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 The Hackenberg family does pro sports. Adam is a catcher in the White Sox organization, Christian was a quarterback taken by the Jets in the second round of the 2016 NFL Draft and Brandon was a first-round pick in the MLS Draft. It became Drue’s turn in 2023, though he wasn’t as solid in his Draft-eligible sophomore season as he was as a freshman at Virginia Tech in 2022. The Braves thought there was enough to work with to take him in the second round of the 2023 Draft and sign him for an over-slot bonus of $2 million. He made two good, but short, appearances with Single-A Augusta, then lost the zone in a one-start showing in Double-A. A 6-foot-2 right-hander, Hackenberg looks like he could be an innings-eating kind of starting pitcher. He leans mostly on his fastball-breaking ball combination. The heater is a heavy sinker that sat around 93 mph in 2023 and tipped out at 95-96 and it has excellent sink that led to a 55.6 percent groundball rate in his two years with the Hokies. He couples it with a low-80s slider that can miss bats and get chases, though it’s an average pitch. He utilizes a little cutter and a changeup that also has some sink to it as well. His Double-A debut aside, Hackenberg has a track record as a strike-thrower. The Braves like his athleticism and think he’ll be able to refine his overall command within the zone, something that caused him to get hit too much in his sophomore season. The ceiling is a little limited without a plus pitch, but he could move quickly thanks to his pitchability and settle in to the back end of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suisbel signed with the Mariners out of Venezuela for $350,000 in July 2019. He didn’t get off to a very promising start to his pro career in 2021, spending two summers with very modest numbers in the Dominican Summer League. Things started to click a little bit in 2023 as he hit his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season Modesto and finished with a .951 OPS. He wasn’t quite as consistent in his return to the Nuts in 2024, though he did help them win the California League title after topping the circuit with 15 homers and 90 RBIs. A switch-hitter with strength at the plate, Suisbel has the chance to have above-average raw power in the future. He got too aggressive at the plate in 2024, getting a bit too swing-happy, leading to fairly high miss and chase rates. His strikeout rates have always been elevated, but because he was performing better in 2023 and last year, the Mariners didn’t want to mess with it too much. But there remains work to be done in refining his approach so he can tap into that pop. Suisbel does have some interesting defensive traits that work well from the left side of the infield, with a very strong arm, good hands and footwork. He’s not particularly athletic, though, so that probably means an eventual full-time move to first base, where the power will have to show up against better pitching for him to have the chance to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suisbel signed with the Mariners for $350,000 out of Venezuela during the 2019-20 international signing period, though he wasn’t able to play competitively until '21, and even then, he got off to a slower-than-ideal start. He played two seasons in the Dominican Summer League, with minimal production over a decent sample size. He took off when he came stateside in 2023, scorching through the Arizona Complex League with a 1.044 OPS and six homers in 36 games, which led to a promotion to Single-A Modesto, where he had a few big moments -- none more so than a walk-off grand slam in early September. Suisbel switch-hits and plays both corner infield positions, both of which are attributes that already give him a leg up within an organization that covets versatility. At the plate, he’s shown a better feel to hit from the left side, but he can do more damage from the right. The knock on him early is the swing-and-miss, particularly after posting a 29.9 percent K rate at Modesto. There’s a decent chance Suisbel could stick at third, particularly with an above-average arm. But he’ll need to show more athleticism, better range and speed to do so. If he can get to more consistent contact, he could be a really valuable switch-hitting corner bench bat with some thump.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Breaux smacked 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC while also hitting 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever, a combination that made him the best junior college prospect in the 2018 Draft. After signing for $1,497,500 in the second round, he missed half of his first full season with elbow problems that dogged him at McLennan and lost all of 2020 to the pandemic. He returned last year to homer 23 times in 90 games while advancing to Double-A, though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster in November. Breaux resembles recently traded Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically. He has a strong presence at the plate, where his well above-average bat speed and extremely aggressive approach create plus-plus raw power but also a propensity to swing and miss. He did a better job of turning on pitches to crush them out of the park last season, but his swing decisions still leave a lot to be desired. His elbow issues prevented him from catching much in 2018 or 2019 before the pandemic wiped out the 2020 season, so Breaux still has considerable work to do behind the plate. He's still raw in terms of receiving and blocking, while his slow transfer and inconsistent accuracy mean that his arm plays down and he threw out just 17 percent of basestealers last year. He's a bottom-of-the-scale runner, so his only other defensive option would be first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top junior college prospect in the 2018 Draft, Breaux bashed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC while also clocking 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever. He went homerless in his 30-game pro debut after signing for $1,497,500 in the second round but bounced back to go deep 13 times in 51 low Class A contests in 2019, missing half the season with elbow problems that also bothered him at McLennan. His on-field development last year consisted of five games in the independent Constellation Energy League. Similar to Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically, Breaux has a lofty ceiling but is a long ways from reaching it. His well-above-average bat speed and strength coupled with an extremely aggressive approach give him the raw pop to deliver 35 or more homers per season. But he also swings and misses excessively, and he'll need to make better swing decisions and loft more balls in the air to fully tap into his power potential. Elbow soreness meant Breaux spent more time at DH than at catcher in 2018-19 and he had next to no game reps last year, costing him the time behind the plate he needs to improve his receiving and blocking. While few catchers can match his pure arm strength, he has a slow transfer and inconsistent accuracy that led to him throwing out just 16 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. He's a well-below-average runner, so his only other position options would be first base or DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The consensus top junior college prospect in 2018 after turning down the Astros as a 36th-rounder the year before, Breaux slammed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC and also hit 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever. The Yankees used their top two picks that June on catchers with entirely different profiles, taking Anthony Seigler in the first round and signing Breaux for $1,497,500 in the second. Elbow soreness that limited him as a sophomore sidelined him for nearly three months in 2019, though he did homer 13 times in 51 games in low Class A. Breaux resembles Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically. He has huge raw power and an extremely aggressive approach, displaying well above-average bat speed and strength but also swinging and missing excessively. He produces high exit velocities from the right side of the plate and could have 35-40 homer upside if he makes better swing decisions and puts the ball in the air more often. Breaux's elbow problems meant he spent more time at DH than at catcher in 2018-19, and he needs more reps behind the plate to polish his receiving and blocking. Few catchers can match his pure arm strength, though he must quicken his transfer and improve his throwing accuracy after erasing just 16 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. Despite his radar-gun readings at McLennan, pitching isn't really a fallback option because he has a violent delivery that would make it tough to keep him healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees used their first two 2018 Draft picks on catchers with different profiles in 2018, a polished athlete (Anthony Seigler) in the first round and a raw slugger (Breaux) in the second. The consensus top junior college prospect after turning down the Astros as a 36th-rounder in 2017, he slammed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC. He also reached 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever for the Highlanders, though elbow issues limited him to four innings and prevented him for catching for a month as a sophomore. Extremely aggressive at the plate, Breaux has well above-average bat speed, strength and raw power. While his approach has yet to result in excessive strikeouts, pro pitchers exploited it and held him homerless and to a lot of weak contact in his 30-game debut last summer. He had shown that his pop will play with wood bats and against better competition when he ranked fifth in the Cape Cod League with six homers in 2017. Though Breaux improved significantly behind the plate from his freshman year to his sophomore year at McLennan, he still requires more polish to become a dependable receiver. Despite his pure arm strength, he threw out just nine percent of basestealers in his first taste of pro ball and won't be able to control the running game until he improves his throwing accuracy. Pitching is less of a fallback than it might seem because he has a violent delivery that would make it difficult to keep him healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins' pick at No. 33 overall in the 2024 Draft out of Lousiana-Lafayette, DeBarge has a knack for stealing bases, something he did successfully 66 times during his first pro season. The rest of his offensive game was less consistent, but he also proved valuable by capably playing multiple positions as Cedar Rapids reached the High-A Midwest League championship series. During his huge junior season with the Ragin’ Cajuns, DeBarge had shown an advanced approach at the plate, a penchant for contact and a quick right-handed stroke with sneaky pop to his pull side that resulted in 21 homers. He still saw a lot of pitches and drew a ton of walks with Cedar Rapids in 2025, but his strikeout rate more than doubled compared to his last season in college, and the impact wasn’t present, with an inflated ground-ball rate. DeBarge is a 5-foot-9 sparkplug who isn’t just aggressive on the basepaths, he’s successful, going 66-for-74 in steal attempts in ‘25. He won a Minor League Gold Glove at second base, showed he can help out at shortstop occasionally and played a good center field, giving him a floor as a high-energy utility type. If he can get to a little more offensive impact, there’s still a chance he could be a regular presence in a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If the Twins were trying to corner the market on college infielders who performed at the plate in the 2024 Draft, they did a very good job out of the gate, getting Kaelen Culpepper in the first round, Billy Amick in Round 2 and DeBarge right between them. The Lousiana-Lafayette standout had been a catcher at Barbe High School in Louisiana before moving to short and parlayed a huge junior season for the Ragin’ Cajuns (1.117 OPS) into being the No. 33 overall pick in the Draft. He got his professional feet wet with just over 100 at-bats with Single-A Fort Myers after signing. The Twin were clearly coveting advanced hitters with an idea of what they’re doing at the plate and DeBarge, like Culpepper, typically does a fantastic job at making a ton of contact without chasing out of the zone. He has a quick right-handed stroke with some sneaky pop to his pull side, but he does tend to hit a lot of ground balls with a flatter swing, something that happened more when perhaps he was pressing a bit during his brief pro debut. There’s confidence he’ll be able to rediscover his knack for finding the barrel and driving the ball without sacrificing his approach. An impressive athlete with plus speed, DeBarge should be able to steal bags as a pro. That quickness along with excellent hands, good instincts and a strong arm give him all the tools to play shortstop, but the Twins are eager to continue seeing how he looks at second, third and perhaps even in center field to expand his paths to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have been the kings of international scouting and development in recent years, and the organization went back to Maracaibo, Venezuela -- Jackson Chourio’s hometown -- to add Antunez in January 2025. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 42 international prospect, the outfielder signed with Milwaukee for $900,000. Antunez hit just .215/.353/.282 with one homer and 21 steals over 55 games in the Dominican Summer League during his first foray into the pros, but the Brewers have pushed him stateside for 2026 (his age-18 season) all the same. Early performance aside, there’s still a ton of potential in the 6-foot, right-handed slugger’s game. Antunez utilizes a leg kick to get going at the plate, and the power he’s shown to this point has come to all fields; he’s particularly impressed evaluators with his ability to drive the ball the opposite way, given his age and experience level. The raw power could end up being above-average in the end, but he needs to curtail his young aggressiveness at the plate to get to it in the full-season levels. Antunez has above-average speed and was willing to display it with 27 total stolen-base attempts last year in the DSL. He’ll need to hold onto those wheels to stick in center field, his only position in pro ball entering 2026, and that remains an open question depending on how his body matures into his late teens and early 20s. Sticking up the middle would be huge for his overall profile, but if he does get into more regular in-game pop with added strength, that could be useful in the corner outfield spots too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have proven to be not only good at scouting internationally but honing in on Venezuela specifically. Jackson Chourio remains the poster boy for signing and development for the system in recent years, while top 2025 prospect Jeferson Quero also hailed from the same South American nation. Milwaukee went back to Chourio’s hometown of Maracaibo to sign Antunez, who ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 42 international prospect in the 2025 class, for $900,000 at the opening of the signing period in January. Antunez uses a leg kick to get into his extra-base power, and as an amateur, he displayed abilities to drive the ball to all fields. He already has quality bat speed, adding to the level of offensive excitement, and he has the power potential to hit 20-plus homers down the road. There is some length to his swing, however, stemming from his desire to pound the ball on contact, and that could lead to some early hiccups on the pro side. Antunez transitioned from the infield as a youngster to the outfield, much like Chourio did after signing, and he has the overall athleticism and energy to fit in center field. It’s going to be a process for him out there as he continues to learn reads and routes, but Milwaukee officials highlighted that everything is trending in the right direction as Antunez enters pro ball. Once comfortable and fully established in the outfield, he could be Milwaukee’s next international success story.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Tommy John surgery as a high school senior in 2020, Carr redshirted in his first college season at San Diego and barely got on the field as a two-way player in his second. He transferred to Palomar (Calif.) JC, emerged as the top junior college prospect in the 2023 class and became a third-round pick. His stuff has regressed since he turned pro, though that didn't stop him from becoming the 2025 South Atlantic League pitcher of the year and leading the High-A circuit in ERA (1.96) and opponent average (.190). Carr worked with a 91-97 mph fastball at Palomar and now operates at 90-92 and maxes out at 95, and while he doesn't miss many bats with his two- and four-seamers, he also generates a lot of weak contact. His slider has lost some power and sweep as well, going from the low 80s to the upper 70s, and it's now more of an average offering. He has switched to a harder changeup that sits in the mid-80s with decent sink. Carr compensates for a lack of physicality with athleticism and arm speed. He pounded the strike zone in junior college but has become more of nibbler working with a diminished arsenal against pro hitters. He has flashed bigger stuff in offseason workouts the last two years, so the Yankees hope he'll show improved velocity in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following Tommy John surgery as a California high school senior in 2020, Carr redshirted at San Diego in his first year in college and got a brief run as a two-way player in his second. He pitched well in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2022, transferred to Palomar (Calif.) JC and ranked as the best junior college prospect in the 2023 Draft after going 12-1 with a 2.31 ERA and 111/19 K/BB ratio in 78 innings. A third-round pick, his stuff and control regressed during his pro debut last year at High-A. After dealing at 91-95 mph and touching 97 with his fastball at Palomar, Carr worked more at 88-92 and topped out at 94 with his two- and four-seamers in 2024. His once-solid low-80s sweeper also lost some velocity and life, playing as more of an average pitch. He has yet to show much aptitude for a changeup that dropped into the low 80s last year while featuring inconsistent depth. Carr's walk rate also doubled from 6 percent in junior college to 12 percent at High-A as he became reluctant to attack hitters with diminished stuff. His athleticism and arm speed help him overcome a lack of physicality, and offseason workouts have the Yankees optimistic that he's recapturing his Palomar form. If that happens and he adds some strength and polish, he still could become a No. 3 or 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carr had Tommy John surgery as a California high school senior in 2020 before redshirting at San Diego in his first college season and seeing brief action as a two-way player in his second. He pitched well in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2022, then transferred to Palomar (Calif.) JC and became the top junior college prospect in the 2023 Draft after going 12-1 with a 2.31 ERA and 111/19 K/BB ratio in 78 innings. He bypassed a Texas Christian commitment after the Yankees selected him in the third round and will make his pro debut in 2024. Carr's stuff has backed up in his first full pro season, and he has lost about 3 mph off his two- and four-seam fastballs, averaging around 90 mph and topping out at 94. He doesn't always stay on top of his slider, which has dipped in terms of both velocity and spin and now sits around 79 mph. His mid-80s changeup gets too firm and has only mild fade, so he doesn't trust it much. Carr's athleticism and arm speed help him compensate for a lack of physicality. After filling the strike zone at Palomar, he has been more tentative in 2024. He'll need to improve his strength and polish to make it as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez signed with the D-backs for $1.25 million in January 2023, making him Arizona’s top international addition of that year. A strong introduction in the Dominican Summer League complete with a .363 OBP caught the attention of many, including the Mets, who acquired him in a one-for-one swap for Tommy Pham at the ’23 Trade Deadline. Rodriguez caught even more fire with New York's DSL affiliate after the deal and had a solid stateside debut in the Florida Complex League last season, slashing .282/.355/.400 with three homers and 17 steals in 50 games. A left-handed hitter, Rodriguez stays on time with a leg lift and snaps into place at the right moment to drive his impressive bat-to-ball skills. With a 17.1 percent K rate, he was one of only two players aged 17 or younger to strike out less than 18 percent of the time in stateside complex ball in 2024 -- Phillies catcher and preseason Top 100 prospect Eduardo Tait (14.6) was the other. Rodriguez’s slugging output did drop a touch from the DSL to the FCL and his exit velocities weren’t exactly at a promising level. Considering he’s still only entering his age-18 season, he has time to mature physically and produce more than gap power, but the trend lines aren’t established yet. Rodriguez possesses above-average arm strength that remains his best defensive asset at shortstop, but even as an average runner, he has the footwork and hands to handle the position at this early stage in his career. He continues to get looks at second base to keep him up the middle, and he even played a few games at third, where the arm would work as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was the D-backs’ biggest international addition in 2023, signing with the club for $1.25 million out of the Dominican Republic in January. He didn’t last long in the organization after a strong walk rate and OBP in the Dominican Summer League caught the Mets’ eye, and New York acquired him in a one-for-one swap for Major League outfielder Tommy Pham at the Trade Deadline. Rodriguez went 19-for-45 (.422) with eight extra-base hits, 11 walks and four strikeouts in 13 games for a Mets’ DSL affiliate after the move, further solidifying his status as a prospect to watch in his new organization. Batting from the left side, Rodriguez was nearly stellar at protecting the plate in his first professional season, especially considering he didn't turn 17 until July. His 1.06 BB/K ratio ranked third among the 15 qualified DSL players playing in their age-16 seasons in '23. With only three of his 18 extra-base hits leaving the yard, his power plays best to the gaps, but it was always likely he’d need some time to get the pop to play in games. The 6-foot infielder boasts above-average arm strength needed for long throws from shortstop, and while he’s just an average runner, he has the hands and footwork to keep getting work at the six. Notably, the Mets got him some looks at second base to keep his athleticism up the middle. Rodriguez will take his advanced approach stateside with plenty of development still to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Messinger spent most of his college career as a reliever at Virginia before the Yankees signed him for an above-slot $225,000 as a 13th-rounder in 2021. They had him spend that summer reshaping his fastball and slider before making his pro debut in 2022. His improved stuff has translated into 232 strikeouts in 194 innings over his first two seasons, and he finished last year with a start in Double-A. After sitting at 90 mph with his fastball in his final year with the Cavaliers, Messinger now deals at 92-94 mph with bat-missing run and carry, and he touched 99 in 2022. His slider also has jumped from the upper 70s in college to 81-84 mph with high spin rates and nasty sweep. He also has increased the power and gets good depth on an upper-70s curveball, though he doesn't use it very often. Messinger's sinking mid-80s changeup lags behind the rest of his repertoire because it doesn't have enough velocity separation from his fastball and he struggles to throw it for strikes. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create angle and extension that make life difficult for hitters, but he's still learning to harness his upgraded stuff. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter with a fallback of becoming a multi-inning reliever who could lean even more heavily on his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a reliever in college at Virginia, Messinger signed for an over-slot $225,000 as a 13th-rounder in 2021. He spent time remaking his fastball and slider before embarking on his pro debut last season in Single-A. He showcased some of the most interesting stuff in the lower levels of the Yankees system while moving into the rotation in late May and striking out 112 in 83 2/3 innings. After averaging 90 mph with his fastball in his final college season, Messinger operated at 92-94 and touched 99 with armside run and carry on his four-seamer in 2022. His slider went from parking in the upper 70s with the Cavaliers to sitting at 81-84 mph with high spin rates and dastardly sweep. He also has good shape on an upper-70s curveball that added power but doesn't find the strike zone consistently. Messinger's changeup is a work in progress, showing some sink but coming in too firm in the mid-80s. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create difficult angle and extension, though he's still learning to harness his improved arsenal. He has the ceiling of a No. 4 starter but will have to refine his changeup, control and command to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A projected 2023 first-rounder after transferring from Kansas to Tennessee, Ahuna fell to the fourth round after trying to do too much at the plate while dealing with a stress reaction in his back. The Giants saw a lot of parallels between him and another slick-fielding college shortstop who had fallen to them in the fourth round 15 years earlier: Brandon Crawford. Ahuna has had a difficult time making good on that comparison because he injured his elbow early in his 2024 pro debut, requiring Tommy John surgery, and played just 97 games in his first two seasons. Crawford earned four Gold Gloves with San Francisco and Ahuna has the talent to do the same. He has fluid actions, a quick first step, plenty of range and fast hands. He also possesses a strong arm, though it graded more as solid than its usual plus in his first year back from elbow reconstruction. Ahuna has sneaky pop for a 6-foot-1, 170-pounder and could provide 15-20 homers per season, but it comes at a price. He swings for the fences with a big leg kick and a left-handed stroke that gets too long and uphill, leading to too many empty swings on strikes and too many grounders when he does make contact, and he particularly struggles against southpaws. He has solid speed and some basestealing aptitude but needs to focus on reaching base more often to take advantage of them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ahuna transferred from Kansas to Tennessee for his junior season, entering 2023 as a projected first-rounder before trying to do much at the plate while playing through a stress reaction in his back. San Francisco pounced on him in the fourth round, just as they had done in 2008 with another slick-fielding college shortstop who stock fell after a down spring: Brandon Crawford. The Giants see a lot of parallels between the two, but Ahuna didn't get to show much in his 2024 pro debut after injuring his elbow and requiring Tommy John surgery. Crawford won four Gold Gloves with San Francisco and Ahuna has the same kind of defensive ability. He has smooth actions, outstanding body control, quick hands and a strong arm. If he doesn't hit enough to be a regular, his prowess with the glove and versatility would make him a useful utilityman. There are questions about Ahuna's bat because he sells out for power, letting his left-handed swing get too long and uphill while trying to pull every pitch he sees. He does have enough sneaky pop to translate into 15 homers per season, but he produces a lot of rolled-over grounders and struggles to make contact against non-fastballs. He has the quick first step and plus speed to steal bases but isn't especially daring in that regard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brandon Crawford projected as a first-round pick in 2008, then had a rough spring at UCLA before dropping to San Francisco in the fourth round and developing into a two-time World Series champion, three-time All-Star and four-time Gold Glover. San Francisco is hoping that history will repeat itself with Ahuna, who slipped from a mid-first-rounder to signing for a below-slot $497,500 as a fourth-rounder last July after transferring from Kansas to Tennessee and trying to do too much at the plate while playing through a stress reaction in his back. The Giants were excited at how good he looked in camp after adding 20 pounds during the offseason, but his 2024 pro debut was marred by an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. Ahuna is similar offensively and defensively to Crawford and has the tools to win Gold Gloves of his own. The best shortstop in the system, including the big leagues, he can make all the plays and all the throws with smooth actions, outstanding body control and a strong arm. He has a quick first step and well-above-average speed, though he's not much of a basestealer. An aggressive hitter who employs a leg kick, Ahuna tried to do too much at the plate last spring, let his left-handed stroke get too long and didn't make adjustments. His college strikeout rate jumped from 21 percent in his final season with the Jayhawks to 31 percent with the Volunteers, and he's going to need to tone down his approach to succeed against pro pitching. His uphill swing produces some sneaky power that plays to all fields and could translate into 15 or more homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A well-regarded high school pitching prospect, Champlain honored his Southern California commitment in 2018 and stayed close to home. Three years later, the Yankees selected him in the ninth round of the 2021 Draft and then traded him to the Royals as part of a three-pitcher package for Andrew Benintendi in 2022. Champlain returned to Double-A in ‘24 and showed he had mastered it with a 3.50 ERA, a 0.92 WHIP and a 34.5% strikeout rate in seven starts. The move to Triple-A was more challenging; Champlain made 28 appearances (27 starts) there for a 5.61 ERA, 15.5% strikeout rate and a 1.56 WHIP while batters hit .283 against him. Champlain’s average cutting fastball sits 91-94 mph, touching 97 in 2024. He spins the ball well and has improved his upper-70s curveball into a solid weapon. That pitch is different from his low- to mid-80s slider which has good depth and got some chase in ‘24 in a limited sample. Champlain also shows a cutter, which could be an out pitch eventually because of his natural movement, and his mid-80s changeup is still a work in progress, as it has been for several years. The lack of a pitch against lefties has hindered Champlain as he’s faced better hitters. He has some effort in his delivery which affects his command at times, but he showed up to Spring Training over 10 pounds lighter. Champlain has the look and mentality of a workhorse on the mound and has proven durable in the Minors, throwing 135 and 140 innings the past two seasons respectively. But he’ll need to develop a weapon against lefties for him to reach his ceiling, otherwise there’s thought he would have more in the tank as a multi-inning reliever with a fastball-curveball combination. He wasn’t added to the 40-man when eligible for the Rule 5 Draft, but he’ll return to Triple-A, be part of the Royals’ depth and could make his debut in ‘25.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Well-regarded as a pitching prospect at a Southern California high school, Champlain struggled for three years at USC, but he showed enough stuff for the Yankees to take him in the ninth round in 2021. A year later, he was traded to the Royals as part of a three-pitcher package for Andrew Benintendi at the ‘22 Deadline. Champlain had a tough first impression in High-A Quad Cities, but his 2023 season was much better. With 25 starts and 135 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A Northwest Arkansas, Champlain posted a 3.33 ERA with a 22.8 percent strikeout rate and a 7.8 percent walk rate. Champlain spins the ball extremely well and has a 91-94 mph cutting fastball that showed improved velocity last year. He can throw his upper-70s curveball for strikes, and it has above-average spin and good shape to it. His 83-86 mph slider shows some sweep and got better last year. He’s shown a feel for a changeup, but it needs more work. The split-finger grip he had last year on the change had moderate success in limited usage, but he struggled to master it, leading to a grip change this spring. The mental side of changing speeds is something that will be a focus for Champlain this year. At 6-foot-5, Champlain has the look of a workhorse and he has been able to pitch innings. There is a little bit of effort in his delivery, but he has deception. Champlain profiles as a back-end starter, and without overpowering stuff, he will have to continue to locate well and keep working on his changeup to stick there. Otherwise, Champlain has the weapons and presence to fit in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Champlain was a top high school pitching prospect out of California in 2018, but he went to USC instead, where things didn’t go quite as expected. He wasn’t a starter until his junior year, but the Yankees still saw enough to draft him in the ninth round in 2021, signing him for around slot at $150,000. He didn’t make his debut until last year and was solid for Single-A Tampa until the Royals acquired him as part of a three-pitcher package for Andrew Benintendi at the Trade Deadline. After some inconsistencies at High-A after the trade in 2022, Champlain returned to Quad Cities to begin 2023 and has taken off with Double-A Northwest Arkansas in the second half of the season. Champlain spins the ball extremely well and has a cutting fastball that sits in the mid-90s with flashes of upper 90s when he’s fresh. His upper-70s curveball has above-average spin and good bite, while his slider also features tight spin and two-plane movement while sitting 82-84 mph. Champlain has shown feel for a changeup that could be an occasional weapon for him, but it needs more development. He is 6-foot-5 and sturdy, certainly looking the part. He has a quick delivery, which helps his deception off the mound. Champlain has done a nice job of rebounding in 2023 and has been almost unhittable at times following his midseason promotion to the Minors' second-highest level. His ceiling is as a back-end starter if he can iron out his fastball command and develop another secondary pitch, but his weapons and presence could fit in a bullpen as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller comes from a football background. His father, Mike Miller, was a wide receiver in the NFL. But Cole took the baseball route growing up in Southern California. After standing out at Newbury Park High School, he was selected by the A’s in the fourth round of the 2023 MLB Draft, pulled away from a commitment to UCLA with an over-slot signing bonus of $1 million. Recovering from Tommy John surgery that wiped out his entire 2024 season, Miller finally debuted as a professional this past season and ended up appearing in 11 games (nine starts) for Single-A Stockton. Miller’s fastball velocity has been diminished so far since returning from surgery. He previously was up to 96 mph pre-surgery. Last year in his return, the heater hovered around 90 mph and maxed out at 92. His mid-80s changeup and slider are both decent secondary pitches that continue to improve. If there was one silver lining to Miller’s velocity decrease, it’s that it did force him to learn how to pitch a little more as he kept the walk rate low last season. His long-term future hinges largely on the velocity, and the A’s believe it will tick back up the further he gets away from surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former NFL wide receiver Mike Miller, Cole took his athletic talents to baseball. He was viewed as an intriguing right-hander from Newbury Park High School in Southern California whose raw stuff likely needed further development at the college level, but by the end of his junior season, an uptick in velocity and overall improved stuff led to him committing to nearby UCLA. It took an over-slot $1 million signing bonus as a 2023 fourth-round Draft pick for the A’s to move him off that commitment. He was set to make his pro debut in 2024 until an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery derailed those plans. After continuing his rehab this spring, he finally made his organizational debut in June. The A’s were working on some mechanical adjustments with Miller prior to his injury. His electric fastball ticked up to 96 mph in high school and displayed excellent movement down in the zone. The mid-80s slider is a hard breaker and was showing signs of improvement. His low-80s changeup showed some potential as an average third pitch. There was real excitement within the organization for Miller’s professional debut. His three-pitch mix and large 6-foot-6 frame give off the potential of a workhorse-type starting pitcher in the big leagues. The A’s also loved the competitiveness they saw from him on the mound while scouting him. After an unfortunate delay, he finally got his first opportunity to make an impression this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller entered the 2023 high school season viewed as an intriguing, raw high school right-hander who likely needed further development at the college level. By the end of the season, though, an uptick in velocity and overall enhanced stuff, along with some athletic bloodlines -- his father, Mike, was an NFL wide receiver -- boosted him up Draft boards. The A’s took him in the fourth round in 2023, going over slot to sign the UCLA commit for $1 million, making him the first Newbury Park (Calif.) HS product to go in the top five rounds since Andrew Lambo was a fourth-rounder back in 2007. He was set to get his pro career started in 2024 but went down with an elbow injury this spring that required Tommy John surgery. Before the injury, the A’s had been working on some mechanical adjustments with Miller. He currently brings a fastball that was up to 96 mph in high school and has excellent movement down in the zone. His slider is improving as a hard breaking ball around 81-84 mph with more consistent action, and he has demonstrated good feel for his low-80s changeup. Miller entered his pro debut season carrying some buzz for his promising three-pitch mix that, along with his 6-foot-6 frame, gives him a good chance to develop into a durable innings eater in the Majors. Lauded for being super-competitive on the mound, he will have to wait until 2025 look to make a strong first impression.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis showed off monster power numbers in his final two seasons on campus at the University of Arizona, including a .742 slugging percentage and a 1.231 OPS as a Pac-12 All-Conference honoree in 2023. The Cardinals selected him 21st overall that July and signed him for slot at $3,618,200. St. Louis played it fairly passively with Davis out of the gate in 2024 with an assignment to Single-A Palm Beach, and he didn’t crack out of the level for 74 games, hitting .232/.337/.401 with eight homers in that span. He was much better after a late July promotion to High-A Peoria (.301/.388/.451 in 30 games) and even finished things out with a quick trip to Double-A Springfield. The left-handed slugger worked through numerous swing and approach changes in his first full season but appears to be at his best with a swing that often draws comparisons to Carlos Gonzalez with his hands starting high near his head, his stance open and his front leg kicking to generate forward momentum. His raw power numbers are still clearly above average and he can pull the ball well, especially heaters. But soft stuff tailing away from him can be an issue when it comes to whiffs or quality contact. Even during the good times at High-A, he ran a 55.6 percent ground-ball rate, and he's continued to miss on a ton of offspeed pitches in 2025. Davis gets most of his reps in center field, but with average speed and plus arm strength, he figures to land in a corner full time as he closes in on St. Louis. That puts added pressure on the raw power to come through in games, and with his whiff rates with Springfield, that's becoming a tall order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted in 2020, Davis hit 39 homers between his sophomore and junior years at Arizona, sandwiching those powerful performances between summer excursions in the Cape Cod League and at Team USA trials. A Pac-12 All-Conference member and tournament MVP, Davis led the conference with his .742 slugging percentage and 1.231 OPS in 2023. The Cardinals snagged him with the 21st overall pick and he signed for slot at $3,618,200. Davis slowed down post-Draft with a .212/.366/.269 line in 34 games with Single-A Palm Beach. Putting that first pro stint aside, the left-handed slugger still stands out most for his impressive raw power that can play to all fields. It’s a fast, twitchy swing that often draws comparisons to Carlos González. He improved his approach as a junior in order to get to that power more, but swing-and-miss concerns remain, especially after that first trip through the Florida State League. An average runner, Davis was pushed to left field with the Wildcats, but the Cardinals kept him exclusively in center after the Draft. His plus arm strength would certainly work in right too if he needs to move again, and his power-first profile fits either corner. The Cardinals like getting their outfielders versatility early and have moved Davis around the grass in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Dodgers for $397,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, Perez tied for first in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League during his U.S. debut the following year. He joined the White Sox in July 2024 as part of a three-team deal that sent Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to the Dodgers. He spent last season in High-A at age 20 and topped the South Atlantic League in doubles (24), homers (22), extra-base hits (50) and total bases (215). Perez has extremely quick hands that generate some of the best bat speed and exit velocities in the system. A right-handed hitter, he's aggressive and looks to launch balls to his pull side, but he doesn't get out of control at the plate and tones down his approach with two strikes. His mindset has resulted in declining walk rates as he has risen through the Minors, so most of his offensive value will come from his 20-homer power. Perez isn't especially quick on the bases or rangy in the middle infield. He looks more comfortable at second base than he does at shortstop, where he sometimes has to rush plays because his arm is merely average. He could fill a bat-first utility role, though his arm also is stretched at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for $397,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, Perez tied for the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League lead with 11 homers while making his U.S. debut the following summer. He finished that season in Single-A at age 18 and returned there last year to hit .262/.370/.423 with 12 homers in 105 games. His production was similar before and after he joined the White Sox in a three-team trade in July that shipped Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to Los Angeles. Perez's lightning-quick hands produce some of the best bat speed in the system and allow him to make harder contact than most players his age. A right-handed hitter, he's not afraid to turn his swing lose but controls the strike zone reasonably well. He already displays the ability to launch balls in the air to his pull side and could grow into 20-homer power. Perez has fringy speed and doesn't take many chances on the bases. The Dodgers shuttled him between second base, third base and shortstop in his first two pro seasons before deploying him mostly at the keystone in 2024, though the White Sox used him more at short after the trade. He needs more defensive consistency and fits best at second base with his so-so range and average arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coffey was a two-way prospect who touched 94 mph with his fastball, but the Red Sox preferred him as a position player when they took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft. Moved to the Blue Jays at the 2024 Deadline for Danny Jansen, Coffey is one of the Blue Jays’ most tooled up position player prospects. After struggling in High-A down the stretch in ‘24, Coffey looked better in ‘25, hitting .273 with 11 home runs and a .786 OPS over 99 games, and he carried some momentum into a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League (.328/.427/.406). There’s some serious power to be unlocked here if Coffey can put it all together, and many of these conversations feel like the same ones people had about Addison Barger a few years ago. Breaking balls were tough on Coffey, which is a hole he’ll need to shore up, but the Blue Jays feel he’s taking that next step and the tools are there for him to push past 20 home runs if he’s making more contact. Defensively, Coffey will be at third base with second base still part of his profile, and his throwing arm is more than enough for the hot corner. The athletic profile here is exciting. Coffey’s plate approach needs work, and those exceptional physical tools need to show up in games more consistently, but this is the type of prospect that development staffs love to work with. Coffey is one of the best bets to really pop if it all comes together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better two-way high school prospects in the 2022 Draft, Coffey displayed a low-90s fastball and a sharp low-80s slider on the mound. Most clubs preferred him as a position player, however, and the Red Sox made him a full-time hitter after signing him for $1,847,500 in the second round. He's one of four California prep middle infielders whom Boston has given seven-figure bonuses in the past three Drafts.
