Coffey has more raw power than most middle infielders, and his bat speed and strength could produce 20 or more homers on an annual basis if he can develop more consistency at the plate. At times, he'll show the ability to recognize pitches and make adjustments, leading to hope that he'll be at least an average hitter. But his right-handed swing also can get long and he can struggle to handle velocity up in the strike zone, so he may be prone to strikeouts. In his 11-game pro debut, Coffey shuttled between shortstop, third base and second base. His athleticism, good infield actions and plus arm strength give him a chance to stick at short, though his fringy speed may land him elsewhere, especially if he loses a step as he continues to mature physically. He could become a solid-to-plus defender at the hot corner or wind up as an offensive-minded second baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bostick and his older brother Marcus attended three junior colleges in three years, with Josh playing shortstop at Howard (Texas) in 2021, hitting and pitching at Hillsborough (Fla.) in 2022 and emerging as the best juco arm in Texas while at Grayson in 2023. He ranked third in the NCAA in strikeout rate (15.3 per nine innings) for the Vikings before signing for a double-slot $397,500 bonus as an eighth-rounder. He has led his circuits in strikeout percentage in his two pro seasons (26 percent in the Single-A California League in 2024, 28 percent in the High-A Northwest League last year), recovering from a rough start to log a 2.45 ERA in his final 11 starts in 2025. Bostick can miss bats with four different pitches when they're on, starting with a low-80s slider with impressive sweep. It pairs nicely with a mid-90s fastball that reaches 99 with huge induced vertical break. He made progress last season with his upper-70s curveball and low-80s changeup, which both drop at the plate. The Giants made changes to Bostick's delivery that spurred his second-half turnaround, moving his hands away from his body and changing his leg kick to enable him to get down the mound better and improve his extension. He works exclusively out of the strength, with his strength and athleticism allowing him to maintain his stuff and mechanics deep into games. He has only been a full-time pitcher for three years, so he has room to continue to improve, but his development will be put on hold after he ruptured an Achilles tendon while lifting weights during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bostick and his older brother Marcus attended three junior colleges in three years, with Josh playing shortstop at Howard (Texas) in 2021 and pulling double duty at Hillsborough (Fla.) in 2022 before establishing himself as the best juco arm in Texas while at Grayson College. He ranked third in the NJCAA with 15.3 strikeouts per nine innings in 2023, and the Giants believed in his combination of stuff, size, athleticism and data to give him a double-slot $397,500 bonus as an eighth-rounder. He broke into pro ball by leading the Single-A California League in strikeout rate (26 percent) last year. Bostick blew away Cal League hitters with a four-seam fastball that parks at 92-96 mph, has reached triple digits in shorter stints and comes with significant induced vertical break and carry. His heater's movement pairs nicely with the depth on his sweeping low-80s slider, which can be a plus pitch when he commands it. He's gaining feel for his low-80s changeup with tumble as he uses it more regularly. After working out of the stretch at Grayson, Bostick did the same last summer and threw a decent amount of strikes. His combination of strength and athleticism allows him to maintain his stuff deep into games and should help him refine his control and command. He comes with reliever risk but also just started focusing on pitching in 2023, so he has more room for development gains than most 23-year-olds.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres took Williams in the third round of the 2022 Draft out of Duke despite him having Tommy John surgery about seven months beforehand. He worked his way back to the mound with Single-A Lake Elsinore in late May last year, and the Royals acquired him in the Scott Barlow trade at the Deadline. The Royals stuck to his post-rehab program when he joined Single-A Columbia, proceeding cautiously with his workload, and he made five starts (24 innings) with a 3.38 ERA, 22.8 percent strikeout rate and 12.9 percent walk rate. Williams was in the mid-90s with his fastball as an amateur, but he’s been more in the 92-94 mph range post-surgery, with officials believing there’s more velocity in there as he gets farther away from the procedure. His potentially plus slider is a short, tight, low-80s gyro shape with the chance for more power behind it. Williams also shows an average changeup and could show average control in time from his athletic delivery. Injury history might limit Williams’ upside if he’s unable to regain his stuff. If he does, he has a No. 4 or 5 starter ceiling. Williams is very cerebral, analytically-inclined and detail-oriented, and the Royals are already impressed with his execution and routine. His weapons and presence on the mound could find a fit in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres have no problem drafting a Tommy John pitcher if they believe the talent is there. They proved that by taking Dylan Lesko (perhaps the best prep arm in the class) in the middle of the first round last July, and they went back to the strategy in the third round, taking Williams out of Duke. The Connecticut native managed only 37 2/3 innings as a Blue Devil, but he was showing promising signs in the fall of 2021 before undergoing the elbow procedure that December. He still signed above slot at $800,000. Williams worked his way back to the mound with Single-A Lake Elsinore in late May and was still trying to regain his stuff when he headed to the Royals at the 2023 Trade Deadline. Part of the pre-TJ excitement with Williams was his added velo in the fall, as his fastball picked up from 90-92 mph the previous spring to regularly being around 94-95 mph. His low-80s slider could get a healthy amount of swing-and-miss as it dove down and away from right-handed batters. A mid-80s changeup also flashed above-average potential but could sit a little too close for comfort to his fastball velo at times. Williams stands 6-foot-5, making him a presence on the mound, and he has the athletic delivery to keep throwing strikes. The Tommy John surgery isn’t the only health issue on his docket, however, after arm soreness and a forearm strain popped up in 2020 and 2021 respectively. The elbow reconstruction could go a long way toward putting all of that in his past, and if he can stick on the mound, there’s mid-rotation upside. It’ll be on Kansas City to mold him into that moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strumpf played in the same JSerra Catholic HS (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield as 2017 No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis and 2019 supplemental first-rounder Davis Wendzel before becoming an immediate starter at UCLA. The best second-base prospect in the 2019 Draft, he homered in an NCAA regional playoff game immediately after Chicago took him in the second round, later signing for $1,050,300. More of a hit-over-power guy in the past, he sold out for power in 2022 and batted .236/.378/.463 with 22 homers and 162 strikeouts in Double-A. Amateur scouts compared Strumpf to Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner because both were right-handed hitters who drilled line drives from gap to gap and controlled the strike zone while starring in the Pacific-12 Conference. Strumpf has gone from using an inside-out stroke and the entire field at the start of 2021 to looking to pull and launch almost every pitch he sees. He does have real 20-homer power and mitigates his strikeouts with a healthy amount of walks, but he's extremely vulnerable against offspeed pitches. A fringy runner with average arm strength, Strumpf has split his pro career between second and third base. He improved his range at second last season and grades a solid defender there. Chicago has a greater need at the hot corner, where he does a passable job.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the same JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield as Royce Lewis (No. 1 overall pick by the Twins in 2017) and Davis Wendzel (a Rangers supplemental first-rounder in 2019), Strumpf became an immediate starter at UCLA. The consensus top second base prospect in the 2019 Draft, he homered in an NCAA regional playoff game immediately after the Cubs drafted him in the second round. Signed for $1,050,300, he earned a promotion to Double-A one month into his first full pro season in 2021 but hit just .211/.335/.380 at that level. Amateur scouts likened Strumpf to fellow Pacific-12 Conference star and Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner because both were right-handed hitters who focused on driving balls from gap to gap while controlling the strike zone. Strumpf has been a different guy in pro ball, however, and his production has suffered as he has aggressively tried to launch balls out of the park to his pull side. He's still drawing walks and making hard contact when he connects but Chicago would like to see him make some adjustments to keep his bat in the zone longer. Because he's a fringy runner with average arm strength, Strumpf derives most of his value from his bat. He's not particularly notable on the bases or in the field, and he played mostly third base last year because of team needs in Double-A. The Cubs still view him as more of a second baseman, though he did prove capable at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strumpf starred in the same JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield with Royce Lewis (the No. 1 overall pick in 2017) and Davis Wendzel (a Rangers supplemental first-rounder in 2019), playing shortstop and pushing Lewis to second base. He immediately started at second base for UCLA as a freshman and was the consensus top prospect at the position in the 2019 Draft. He homered in an NCAA regional playoff game immediately after the Cubs drafted him in the second round and reached Low-A in his pro debut after signing for $1,050,300. Coming out of the Draft, Strumpf was considered similar to fellow Pacific-12 Conference product and Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner, a right-handed hitter who focused on lining balls from gap to gap while controlling the strike zone. But he has been a different guy in pro ball, struggling to provide consistent production while getting too caught up trying to pull and lift pitches. He has the hitting ability, bat speed and strength to hit 20 homers per year if he lets his power come naturally. Most of Strumpf's value will come from his bat, so his early-career difficulties have been alarming. He has fringy speed and won't rack up many stolen or extra bases. He has fringy to average range and arm strength at second base, his position at UCLA and in his debut, and his arm has been stretched at third base, where he has seen most of his action in Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 At JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.), Strumpf teamed in the same infield with Royce Lewis (the No. 1 overall pick in 2017) and Davis Wendzel (a Rangers supplemental first-rounder in 2019), manning shortstop and pushing Lewis to second base. He became an instant starter at second base for UCLA and rated as the 2019 Draft's best prospect at the position. He homered in an NCAA regional playoff game moments after the Cubs took him in the second round, and he had a solid pro debut after signing for $1,050,300. Strumpf's offensive game has drawn comparisons to Ian Kinsler's and is similar to that of Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner. He employs a compact right-handed swing and drills line drives from gap to gap while controlling the strike zone. He has a hit-over-power profile, but he has the hitting ability, bat speed and strength to produce 20 homers per season, especially if he looks for more pitches to attack. Strumpf has fringy speed and isn't much of a threat to steal. He gets the job done at second base, though his fringy arm and range would be stretched on the left side of the infield. He should hit enough to be an everyday player but won't fit the utility profile well if he doesn't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because of the pandemic, Maier threw just 19 innings in 2020 and none in 2021 at British Columbia. But he jumped on radars with a strong Cape Cod League performance in the summer of ‘21 and transferred to Oregon. He made just three starts before a partially torn UCL ended his season, leading to internal brace surgery. The Braves rolled the dice by taking him in the seventh round of the 2022 Draft, going way over slot to sign him for $1.2 million. He didn’t pitch in 2023 because of the elbow and an oblique issue, finally making his pro debut in 2024 and making 19 starts across two levels of A ball before capping things off with a handful of outings in the Arizona Fall League. It’s hard to know if there’s more to come stuff-wise from Maier, an athletic 6-footer, as he gets more innings and puts the elbow injury further behind him. He can throw his four-seamer up to 95 mph with good spin up in the zone but hurled more sinkers in the 90-93 mph range that did help elicit ground-ball contact. His best pitch is his slider, also thrown with super high spin rates with good downward break and the ability to miss bats. His 83-84 mph changeup can offer some sink, but it’s behind the slider. As a former infielder, Maier’s athleticism on the mound had helped him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone fairly consistently. His feel did regress, however, with a move to High-A and during his AFL stint, when his walk rate went up. The 2024 season was important because he made it through healthy, now it’s time to see if there’s anything more in the tank.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves bought a $1.2 million lottery ticket when they drafted and signed Maier in the seventh round of the 2022 Draft. The Canadian right-hander started out at the University of British Columbia as a two-way guy but threw just 19 innings before the pandemic hit. The school cancelled its 2021 season, too, although Maier was able to open some eyes with 25 2/3 innings in the Cape Cod League that summer, then transferred to Oregon, where he made just three starts before he partially tore his UCL. He had an internal brace put in rather than have Tommy John surgery, but he's yet to throw a professional pitch, both because of the elbow and also an oblique issue in 2023. With just over 60 innings of amateur pitching to work from, it's hard to know exactly what Maier might be. He is a strong and athletic six-footer who had thrown his fastball up to 95 mph with good spin and command when he was healthy. His low-80s slider also registered high rpm, a potentially plus pitch that misses bats with good downward break. His sinking changeup gives him a third very effective pitch, thrown with good arm speed. Maier's athleticism as a former infielder shows on the mound as he repeats his delivery well and should be a solid strike-thrower. The big thing he needs now is time on the mound, as those innings on the Cape represent his highest season total to date. He'll still be just 22 for all of the 2024 season, so there's time, with a healthy year the primary objective.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 It's been an unusual path for Maier, whom the Braves signed to a way-over-slot deal of $1.2 million as a 2022 seventh-round pick. He began his college career as a two-way player at the University of British Columbia, but that was short-lived because of the pandemic-truncated 2020 season and UBC's canceled season in 2021. Scouts were excited by his Cape Cod League performance that summer and were hoping to see more in 2022 when Maier transferred to Oregon, but he suffered a partial tear in his UCL after just three starts. Rather than have Tommy John surgery, Maier had an internal brace put in with an eye toward making his debut in 2023. Maier has a light pitching resume after being an infielder -- in addition to the missed time -- but the 6-footer is strong and athletic. When he's been healthy, he throws his fastball up to 95 mph with high spin rates and excellent command of the pitch. The right-hander's best offering is his low-80s slider, a plus pitch also with outstanding spin rates that misses bats with good downward break to it. There's a lot of feel for a sinking changeup too, sold with solid arm speed. When he's been on the mound, Maier's athleticism has been apparent, with the ability to repeat his delivery and fill up the strike zone consistently. The Braves will get their first real look at Maier at some point in 2023, with reps needed more than anything else to get a sense of what he can become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hicks starred for two years at Crowder (Mo.) JC before transferring to South Carolina for 2022, only to blow out his elbow in his second start and have Tommy John surgery that March. He turned down the Orioles as a 15th-rounder, came back for his redshirt junior year and joined the Astros as a 13th-rounder in 2023. A line drive broke his right forearm in April last season, costing him three months, though he returned to win Arizona Fall League pitcher of the year honors with 19 strikeouts in 14 scoreless innings. Hicks succeeds with command over pure stuff, with his two- and four-seam fastballs ranging from 91-94 mph but playing as average pitches because he locates them so well. His stuff is mostly average across the board, with his sweeping low-80s slider and fading mid-80s changeup his best secondary offerings. He also mixes in a tight mid-80s cutter and a fringy upper-70s curveball. While he lacks a true weapon, Hicks' arsenal is more effective than the sum of its parts because he mixes pitches and locations so well. He creates some deception with an upright delivery and low three-quarters slot that creates wide angle and a flat approach on his pitches. He has one of the highest floors among the system's pitchers and could help Houston at some point this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring for two years at Crowder (Mo.) JC, Hicks transferred to South Carolina for the 2022 season but blew out his elbow in his second start and had Tommy John surgery that March. The Orioles still selected him in the 15th round, but he returned to pitch well in a variety of roles for the Gamecocks the following spring before signing with the Astros as a 13th-rounder. He demonstrated some of the best command in the system while reaching Double-A midway through his first full pro season last year. Hicks' best pitches are his low-90s two-seam fastball with sink and a mid-80s changeup with fade and depth. Since turning pro, he has added a slightly harder four-seamer and a low-80s slider with more sweep to an arsenal that also includes a curveball in the upper 70s and a more traditional slide piece in the low 80s. His breaking stuff pales in comparison to the rest of his repertoire. None of Hicks' six offerings grades as better than average, but they work because he sequences them well and works all four quadrants of the strike zone. His low three-quarters slot creates wide angle and a flat approach trajectory that provides deception. He's on track to help the Astros as a back-of-the-rotation starter or middle reliever sooner than initially expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Twins prospect Jake Rucker, Carson was a two-time winner of the Mr. Tennessee award as the state’s top prep baseball player. He seemed poised to stay in the state and play collegiately at Tennessee like his older brother, until the Tigers selected him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him above slot for $772,500. Injuries have stalled his career since then, including labrum surgery on his left shoulder last summer that limited him to 13 games at the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Rucker earned his status on Draft boards with right-handed pull power but has had precious few opportunities to show it as a pro. The pull-heavy approach is still apparent, along with a good eye at the plate. Though Rucker has been primarily a shortstop when he has played, he is expected to eventually shift to third base. The Tigers still believe in Rucker’s potential despite the injuries. He’ll turn 21 in August, but in many ways, 2025 is an introductory season for Rucker to develop an everyday routine as a pro player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Draft under president of baseball operations Scott Harris and amateur scouting director Mark Conner saw a number of high school players signed away from college commitments. One of them was Rucker, a two-time Mr. Tennessee winner who looked set to join the Vols until the Tigers went above slot to sign the fourth-rounder for $772,500. He made his pro debut with nine games in the Florida Complex League, showing a mix of run production, plate discipline and aggression. Rucker earned his status on Draft boards with right-handed pull power. Despite a 43.5 percent ground-ball rate in his brief 2023 stint, he had virtually equal rates of pull and oppo hitting in his small sample size. The power should become more apparent as he physically matures without having to sell out what is a productive swing and keen eye at the plate. Though Rucker is expected to eventually shift to third base, he stayed at shortstop for most of his FCL stint with good numbers. While top picks Max Clark and Kevin McGonigle project to be high-risers up the Tigers' system, Rucker could involve more patience. That’s even truer after he suffered a separated shoulder four games into his 2024 season, prompting a move to the full-season injured list. Once he returns to play, his upside for pure hitting and power could prove well worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $700,000 signing out of Mexico City in January 2022, Verdugo has shown what can be exciting and cautionary about pushing a young prospect quickly early in his career. He ran a 116 wRC+ over 52 games in the Arizona Complex League in his age-17 season in ’22 after skipping over the Dominican Summer League completely, but his move to Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2023 was a struggle with a .220/.308/.332 line in 113 games. He returned to the Storm with much better numbers (.250/.363/.407 in 81 games) before hitting another wall as a 19-year-old with High-A Fort Wayne, finishing with a .561 OPS and 29.4 percent strikeout rate in 25 games. Watch Verdugo hit, and you can see why the Padres have pushed him so far. He doesn’t overly complicate matters with his setup from the right side, keeping things nice and quiet until he unleashes quick hands through the zone for a sound swing. He showed a better understanding of the strike zone between his first full season and his second, cutting down his chase by a good margin, but he still struggled to make consistent contact. When he did, he got under the ball too much. Without significant strength, many of his batted balls were catchable flies rather than stung line drives. In 2025, he's started to drive more of those balls over the wall back with Fort Wayne and looks more like a 15-plus homer threat as he enters his 20s. A below-average runner, Verdugo has had to move away from shortstop and spend time at second and third. He continues to see time at those last spots, and even the departure of Leo De Vries won't likely lead to more Verdugo looks at the six moving forward. He's still building his offensive game, but the home run gains are promising at this still early stage.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 47 international prospect, Verdugo was considered the top player from Mexico in the 2022 signing class, and he joined the Padres for $700,000 out of the Diablos Rojos del Mexico academy in Mexico City. After Verdugo turned 17 in February, San Diego moved him straight stateside to the Arizona Complex League, and he was the only person with a 2005 birthdate to get enough at-bats to qualify for a batting title in the circuit. He finished with a .251/.338/.467 slash line, seven homers and a 116 wRC+ over 52 games. The right-handed slugger showed loud contact in the ACL that mostly played in-game to the pull side, but that's backed up some with a move to Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2023. He isn’t a hulking presence in the box at a listed 6 feet, but perhaps power could return as he ages and gets more upper-level experience. His strikeout rate has dropped around 10 points year to year, so that's a positive sign of development at the plate. While he got some time on the left side of the infield in his pro debut, Verdugo lacks the footwork for short and the arm strength for third to make either his long-term home. He’s a better fit at second base, where he may still only be average, and he'll have to get back to hitting to be at his most valuable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolters signed for an over-slot $2.8 million as the Royals’ second-round selection in 2023 out of Mahomet-Seymore (Ill.) HS. He was an intriguing prospect right away because of a 99 mph fastball and high-spin slider, but it’s been slower going for Wolters. He was shut down in ‘24 after hitting his innings limit, and he dealt with shoulder weakness in ‘25 that limited him to just 12 starts with Single-A Columbia. In those outings, Wolters posted a 3.99 ERA but had identical walk and strikeout rates (19.3 percent). In two full seasons since he was drafted, Wolters has only recorded 103 innings in affiliate ball. The Royals had Wolters on a dedicated strength program this past offseason to hopefully help his shoulder issues, which never required surgery or even much past rest and recovery. His fastball averaged just 93 mph in 2025, way down from when he was drafted. His shorter slider also had lower spin in ‘25 than in previous years, and throwing from an inconsistent slot with just about every pitch didn’t help matters as the pitch also sometimes looks like a curveball. Wolters did get some good whiffs on his mid-80s changeup. He has a repeatable delivery and the Royals are hoping better strength helps him with his command. Wolters is still only 21 and has a ton of upside, and the Royals will exhaust every option to keep him as a starter. If he regains the velocity and spin that he had as an amateur, there’s still potential for a mid-rotation starter in there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Putting together a strong senior season at Mahomet-Seymore (Ill.) HS, Wolters became the Royals’ second-round selection in the 2023 Draft, signing for an over-slot $2.8 million and decommitting from Arizona. Wolters spent the rest of ‘23 pitching at the Royals’ facility in Arizona and made his pro debut last year, going to Single-A Columbia to start the season instead of being held back in extended spring training like the Royals have done with their prep pitchers in the past. Wolters was solid for the Fireflies with a 4.20 ERA across 14 starts at 55 2/3 innings, and the Royals shut him down in August after he had minor tendinitis and was nearing his innings limit. Strong and physical, Wolters stands 6-foot-4 and certainly looks the part of a starting pitcher. His fastball features ride and run, sitting in the mid 90s during starts last year, but he has touched 99 mph. That velo was down a touch in the early going of 2025 with him sitting more in the 92-94 mph range. His slider has the potential to be his wipeout pitch, a plus offering in the mid 80s that’s tight with hard break. He’s learning how to throw it and trust it more. Wolters worked on his changeup quite a bit in 2024, but it was up and down when he used it in games. That will continue to be a focus pitch for him because he needs a third offering to stick as a starter. With improved consistency, it has the potential to be above average. Wolters has a clean and efficient delivery, repeatable from a three-quarters arm slot. Wolters has the upside of a front-end starter, and he is extremely intelligent and advanced for his age when it comes to preparation and the way he digests information. But it will still take some time for him to develop as he works on pitch execution. He returned to Single-A for 2025 and was slowed after a shoulder issue in the first half.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolters jumped onto the scene his senior year at Mahomet-Seymour (Ill.) HS with more strength and increased velocity. He set a Super 60 showcase record with 98 mph on consecutive pitches in February 2023, and a few months later, the Royals took the Arizona commit in the second round while going over-slot to sign him at $2.8 million. Wolters didn’t pitch in an official game last season, but he was impressive at the Royals’ fall camp and showed up to Spring Training hitting upper-90s on the radar gun. At 6-foot-4 with a strong frame, Wolters is a physical presence on the mound. His fastball touches 98 mph with good life, but he’ll likely sit 95-96 during starts. He possesses an above-average 82-84 mph slider that has a hard break, landing on both sides of the plate. A big focus for him will be a changeup, like most pitchers his age. He looks the part of a starter -- a mid-rotation arm or better at that -- but will need that third pitch to get there. Wolters’ delivery is clean, smooth and repeatable. He pitches easy and is incredibly mature for a high school draftee. Officials rave about his mind, how he digests information and prepares, which will take time off his development timeline. The Royals got more aggressive with Wolters than they typically do with prep pitchers, pushing him out to Single-A Columbia in April, and they've been pleased with how he's handled his first full season from there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Toman grew up around the game as the son of longtime college coach Jim Toman, so it’s no surprise that he was one of the most polished and mature high school hitters in the 2022 Draft class. Toman was committed to play NCAA ball at LSU, but the Blue Jays selected him 77th overall and signed him for a well-above-slot $2 million. Trusting Toman’s pedigree, the Blue Jays assigned him to Single-A Dunedin for his first full season in 2023, when he hit .208 with five home runs and a .633 OPS. Those numbers, including Toman’s 135 strikeouts in 114 games, were underwhelming, but the Blue Jays came away impressed with how he dealt with the challenge at the very least. His maturity showed, and while the numbers need to improve significantly, the organization continues to believe in Toman’s upside because of those intangibles and his dedication to his development. The switch-hitter continues to find more success hitting from the left side (.658 OPS in 2023) than the right (.549). Toman’s body is in a better spot than when he was drafted and he’s looked sharp at third base, which feels like his future home over shortstop. Still just 20, there’s still plenty of time for him to develop into a solid all-around prospect, but the numbers will need to improve in 2024. For now, Toman’s foundation and some positive internal evaluations on how he’s managed his first year-and-a-half in pro ball keep him afloat in rankings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Toman grew up around the game as the son of longtime college coach Jim Toman, so it’s no surprise that he was one of the most polished and mature high school hitters in the 2022 Draft class. Toman was committed to play NCAA ball at LSU, but the Blue Jays selected him 77th overall and signed him for a well-above-slot value of $2 million. Toronto gave the switch-hitting Toman a taste of pro ball in the Florida Complex League, where he hit .290 and worked seven walks over 11 games. He’s already earned rave reviews throughout the organization for how much time he’s spent at the club’s player development complex. In fact, the Blue Jays sent him home at one point over the offseason for a mental break from baseball, but they love what they’ve seen early. He’s expected to continue to split time between shortstop and third base, but his instincts give him a shot to stick at short. His body will play a role in that too, as he’s already added some natural build and is benefiting from the Blue Jays’ program. Toman has a smooth, sweet swing from the left side. His right-handed swing wasn’t as fluid, but that had taken noticeable strides since he was drafted. However, Toman has struggled out of the gate with Single-A Dunedin, where he's walked a decent amount but has also punched out at a higher rate than desirable. There's still the potential for an all-around game here, but it's going to be a longer climb than first envisioned when Toman entered the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was far from a big name on the international stage when he signed with the Cardinals as a 19-year-old in January 2016, but he commanded attention after hitting .322/.400/.580 with seven homers over 40 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first Minor League season. He climbed steadily through the system and earned a Florida State League midseason All-Star spot in 2019 before jumping to Double-A Springfield. He was set to return to that level in 2021, only to break his hamate bone playing winter ball back home in the Dominican Republic. Following February surgery, he played briefly for Springfield in May, suffered a setback and came back for good in late July. The right-handed slugger hit just .196/.252/.299 with three homers over 29 games in Double-A last season, numbers that were clearly affected by the hamate injury, which can typically sap players of their power in the early stages of recovery. Still, Rodriguez has a history of being aggressive at the plate, and while his bat-to-ball skills keep the strikeout rates from being high, that aggression also keeps him from developing much power. It’s an all-defensive-type profile anyway. Rodriguez’s arm has always been effective at limiting the running game, and even with the hand issues, he threw out 9 of 14 (64 percent) of attempted basestealers with Springfield last season. He’s a quality blocker and receiver out of his 6-foot, 245-pound frame, and it’s clear Cardinals pitchers enjoy working with him behind the plate. It’s a clear glove-first backup profile, and after Rodriguez was passed over twice for a 40-man spot when Rule 5-eligible, a healthy 2022 could get him closer to achieving that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in January 2016 as a 19-year-old, Rodriguez was initially expected to be an organizational roster-filler but has surpassed expectations thanks in large part to his offensive development. He hit .322 with seven homers over 40 games in the Dominican Summer League in his professional debut and has continued his upward trajectory in the Cardinals’ system, including midseason All-Star honors in the Florida State League in 2019. Rodriguez suffered a broken hamate bone after being hit by a pitch in winter ball. He underwent surgery in February and after getting off to a late start in his 2021 campaign, he found himself on the injured list once again, though he returned in early August. Rodriguez’s defensive skillset is what drew the Cardinals to him initially. The backstop has a strong, accurate arm and has thrown out 69% of attempted basestealers over the first four years of his professional career. Offensively, Rodriguez has an overly aggressive approach, but flashes some power -- he hit a combined 16 homers in 2017 and ’18 -- and has made noticeable strides since signing. There’s certainly value to having a defensive-minded catcher like Rodriguez in a system keen on developing pitching prospects. If he continues to improve his overall game and reaches the Majors, it’s likely he’ll do so in a reserve role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An older international prospect whom the Cardinals signed at age 19 in January 2016, Rodriguez was originally viewed as an organizational roster-filler based on his defensive merits. But the Dominican catcher proved a more complete player than initially thought during his pro debut, showing feel to hit and power potential in the Dominican Summer League, and has continued to make strides offensively while incrementally climbing through the Cardinals' system. After a solid first full season at Class A Peoria, Rodriguez moved up to Class A Advanced Palm Beach in 2019 and garnered midseason All-Star honors in the Florida State League before receiving a late promotion to Double-A. Rodriguez's abilities behind the plate are obvious. He does a good job controlling the running game with his plus, accurate arm, and has been praised by evaluators for his catch-and-throw skills, with many noting his consistent footwork and quick release. He moves well in spite of his stocky frame and is regarded as a good receiver and framer who also can handle a pitching staff. Offensively, Rodriguez has feel for finding the barrel and will flash some pull-side power from the right side of the plate, albeit with an overly aggressive approach that can at times undercut his pure hitting ability and on-base skills. Cardinals officials view Rodriguez as a valuable player to have in a system that is always looking to develop pitching prospects. He appears ticketed for a backup role at the highest level if he can continue to make strides on both sides of the ball, and there's a non-zero chance that he will achieve such a role based simply on his defensive chops.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziehl turned down the Cubs as an 11th-rounder out of a New York high school in order to attend Miami, where he was the Hurricanes' best starter as a sophomore and junior. A Yankees fourth-rounder in 2024, he made his pro debut last year and logged a 4.12 ERA with a 90/19 K/BB ratio in 107 innings, mostly in Single-A and High-A. He already has changed organizations twice, going to the White Sox last July in exchange for Austin Slater and to the Red Sox in February as part of a Jordan Hicks salary dump. Ziehl's fastball got rocked last year, sitting at 91-94 mph and topping out at 96 with modest ride and run. He used his heater less than his sweeping mid-80s slider, which shows flashes of becoming at least a solid pitch, and an upper-80s cutter that's more ordinary. He pounds the zone with all three of those offerings but has less success controlling a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Though Ziehl had below-average swing-and-miss rates on all of his pitches last year, he can get chases with them. Considering his ability to fill the strike zone with ease, Boston might have something if it can help him improve his velocity. He's a tough competitor with a high floor but a current ceiling of no more than an end-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cubs 11th-round pick in 2021 as a New York high schooler, Ziehl put his pro career on hold to attend Miami. He led the Hurricanes in appearances as a freshman, then became their best starter during the next two seasons before the Yankees took him in 2024's fourth round. He already has been traded twice, going to the White Sox last July in exchange for Austin Slater, then to the Red Sox along with a player to be named for Jordan Hicks, righty pitching prospect David Sandlin and two players to be named in February. Ziehl's ability to command his fastball stands out much more than its velocity and life, as it operates at 92-94 mph and reaches 96 with modest ride and run. He misses more bats with a sweeping mid-80s slider that grades as a plus pitch with two-plane depth at its best, and he used his slide piece and an upper-80s cutter more than his heater during his 2025 pro debut. He imparts fade and sink on a mid-80s changeup but has difficulty keeping it in the zone. At 6 feet and 223 pounds, Ziehl is compact but strong and durable. He's a tough competitor who repeats his high three-quarters delivery with ease, enabling him to rank seventh in the Minors last year (minimum: 100 innings) with a 4 percent walk rate. He comes with a high floor but his inability to keep hitters off his fastball limits his ceiling to back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burkhalter's Draft stock took off during his junior year at Auburn, when his command improved enough for him to take over as the Tigers' closer as he saved 16 games. The Braves signed him with an under-slot bonus with their compensation pick after the second round of the 2022 Draft, with the plan to develop him as a starter. They had to press pause when he needed Tommy John surgery shortly after he got started, but he came back with a solid 2024 season with High-A Rome, then pitched his way from Double-A to Triple-A both as a starter and reliever last year. The thinking behind allowing the 6-foot Burkhalter to start was his pitch mix and feel for the strike zone. His four-seamer plays -- averaging 94 mph and touching 98 -- by getting good carry and missing bats up in the zone. His upper-80s cutter that's hard and short can be effective at times and it tends to be his go-to secondary offering. His gyro-like 84-85 mph slider is hit or miss and his kick-change worked at times. The Braves moved Burkhalter to the 'pen when he got to Triple-A, but his stuff didn't tick up all that much. He's around the strike zone, but without the kind of command you'd like to see from a starter, and he doesn't feature the kind of bat-missing stuff to profile as a reliever. There was a little buzz about him ahead of the Rule 5 Draft, but he wasn't selected, so he can focus on carving out a multi-inning/swingman/spot starter type of role in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burkhalter spent three years pitching exclusively out of Auburn's bullpen, but it wasn't until his final season in 2022 when his command improved dramatically, which allowed him to step into the closer role and save 16 games. The Braves took him with a compensation pick after Round 2 of that summer's Draft, but he needed Tommy John surgery shortly after he had begun his first pro season. He had a solid return to the mound with High-A Rome in 2024, logging 72 total innings for the year. Though he's just 6-foot and has that impressive relief resume in college, the Braves are continuing to give Burkhalter the chance to start. That's because he now has a viable four-pitch mix and the ability to land all of them in the strike zone. His velocity was back upon his return, up to 98 mph with a fastball that features good carry. A cutter that he can get up to about 91-92 mph is hard and short, and he throws it all hitters. At one point he shelved his slider, but he brought it back with better results command-wise, and it's more of a gyro-type pitch with more depth than the cutter. He has a changeup but doesn't throw it as much. Burkhalter was able to show that the improvements he made control-wise in college have stuck, which was even more impressive considering it was his first year back from elbow surgery. The gloves should come off more now, and while he may still end up back in a bullpen one day, the Braves are excited to see what he can do taking the ball in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two seasons pitching out of the Auburn bullpen, Burkhalter showed off good stuff but little idea of where it was going. In his final season with the Tigers, he took a huge step forward in finding the strike zone and became of the nation's best closers, saving 16 games and posting an eye-popping 10.1 K/BB ratio. Seen as the kind of college reliever who could potentially move quickly through a system, he was the Braves' selection with the No. 76 overall pick in the 2022 Draft, but heading into the 2024 season, he has just three outings from that summer on his professional resume because he tore his UCL in Spring Training in 2023 and needed Tommy John surgery. He returned at the end of May and pitched well with High-A Rome. The six-foot right-hander was up to 98 mph before the injury and sat around 93 mph at Auburn in 2022 with a fastball that has good carry and arm-side run. Shelving a slider he couldn't command in favor of a cutter he can crank into the low-90s was a good move as it's a pitch he lands for strikes and uses to miss both right-handed and left-handed bats. He also has a solid low-80s fading changeup with sink. While he has been getting the opportunity to start to get innings in, Burkhalter is seen by most as a reliever in the future despite his three-pitch mix because he's bit undersized and has some effort in his delivery. If he can show that the control gains he made in his last year of college are real, he has the chance to pitch impactful innings as a set-up man in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two seasons pitching out of the Auburn bullpen, Burkhalter got outs but struggled with the strike zone. That all changed in 2022 as his command vastly improved and led to him finishing second in Division I baseball with 16 saves. His combination of missing bats and improved pitchability helped him land at pick No. 76 in the Draft, where the Braves signed him for an under-slot bonus of $647,500. Burkhalter has three pitches he now can throw for strikes, and all three have the chance to be above-average offerings. He can run his fastball up to 98 mph, typically sitting in the 92-95 mph range, throwing the four-seamer with good carry and arm-side run. He switched from throwing a slider he couldn't command to an upper-80s cutter he throws to hitters on both sides of the plate, and his low-80s changeup features good fade and sink. Because Burkhalter is just 6-feet tall and has some effort in his delivery, most feel he's a reliever only -- he never started a game in college -- even though he has a three-pitch mix with good control. He has the ceiling of a setup man, one who could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyzelman underwent Tommy John surgery as a San Francisco freshman in 2020 and couldn't find the strike zone as a sophomore, then overpowered hitters as a reliever after transferring to Louisiana State and worked his way into 2022's fifth round. He worked just 8 2/3 innings in his first two years as a pro while dealing with a cyst on his back that required three operations before compiling a 1.16 ERA, .136 opponent average and 41 percent strikeout rate while rocketing to Double-A in 2024. His stuff and strikes went way backward in Triple-A last season, when he missed the final two months with a mild back strain. When he was rolling two years ago, Reyzelman paired a 94-97 mph fastball that hit 99 and featured good carry with a tight low-80s slider with significant horizontal action. In 2025, his heater dropped 2 mph and lost life while his sweeper lost 4 mph and often didn't come close to the strike zone. He had an effective low-80s changeup with huge fade in 2024 but it became so unreliable that he abandoned it last season. Reyzelman works solely out of the stretch and uses a three-quarters arm slot to create a low release height and wide angle that's tough on right-handers. He struggled to keep his mechanics in sync last year, when his walk rate spiked to 22 percent from 12 percent the season before. He may never have more than below-average control and command, so he'll need to regain his sizzling stuff from 2024 to succeed in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyzelman had Tommy John surgery as a San Francisco freshman in 2020 and couldn't throw strikes as a sophomore before transferring to Louisiana State in 2022. His mid-90s fastball and success as a reliever got him drafted in the fifth round that July, but he barely pitched in pro ball before last year because of a cyst on his back that required three operations. Finally healthy in 2024, he posted silly numbers (1.16 ERA, .136 average-against, 41 percent K rate) in 31 appearances between three stops, mostly at Double-A. When he dominated in 2024, Reyzelman showcased two plus pitches in a 94-97 mph fastball that touched 99 with more ride than armside run and a tight low-80s slider with significant horizontal break that worked against both lefties and righties. His changeup showed similar velocity and big fade in the opposite direction, though it lacked the consistency of his other offerings. But his arsenal has backed up this year, with his fastball losing 2 mph, as well as life, his sweeper often missing the zone by a wide margin and his changeup becoming unreliable. After throwing 94 percent fastballs at LSU, Reyzelman has changed his approach and cleaned up his mechanics in pro ball. He works out of the stretch, creating a flat approach angle with a low three-quarters arm slot. If he can recapture his 2024 stuff and do a better job of keeping his delivery in sync and providing more strikes, he could join New York's bullpen in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more advanced hitters in the 2023 international crop, Cespedes landed the largest bonus in the Red Sox's class when he signed for $1.4 million out of the Dominican Republic. He won the organization's Latin program player of the year award after his debut that summer and batted .337/.395/.578 in Rookie ball during his first two seasons. He earned a promotion to Single-A at age 18 in 2024 but never played because of a broken left hamate, then made it there in 2025 and struggled to a .227/.292/.376 line in his full-season debut. Long compared to Howie Kendrick because of his hitting ability and stocky build, Cespedes mitigates his bat-to-ball skills by venturing out of the strike zone too often and flailing against changeups. When he does make contact, his bat speed and strength allow him to produce high exit velocities. His right-handed swing and mindset are geared to drive the ball in the air to his pull side, and his best-case scenario may be as a power-over-hit guy who can provide 20 or more homers per season. Cespedes ran a little better than he gets credit for in 2025, showing average speed, though he's not much of a basestealer. Primarily a shortstop in Rookie ball, he became a full-time second baseman in Single-A. His lack of fluidity and range and his average arm are less of an issue at second than they were at short, though some scouts still think he could wind up in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox gave Cespedes the largest bonus ($1.4 million) in their 2023 international class because he was one of the more advanced hitters on the market. He won their Latin program player of the year award after hitting .346/.392/.560 in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in his pro debut. He posted similar numbers in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last spring, earning a promotion to Single-A at age 18, but he never played at that level because of a broken left hamate. Cespedes earns Howie Kendrick comparisons for his hitting ability and stocky build. With his quick right-handed swing and fine hand-eye coordination, he regularly barrels balls and produces high exit velocities. He already displays the aptitude to launch pitches in the air to his pull side, which could result in 20-homer power. His aggressive approach and ease of contact may mean that he'll need to adjust and lay off more pitches at higher levels. Though Cespedes played mostly shortstop in his first two pro seasons, like Kendrick he's more of a second baseman. He has fringy speed and range at short, and his arm is merely average. He has played mostly at second in 2025 and some scouts wonder if he might wind up as a left fielder in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more advanced hitters in the 2023 international class, Cespedes landed the largest bonus in Boston's crop. Signed for $1.4 million out of the Dominican Republic, he earns Howie Kendrick comparisons for his hitting ability and stocky build. The Red Sox named him their Latin program player of the year after he slashed .346/.392/.560 in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in his pro debut, during which he also stood out with his baseball IQ and work ethic. Extremely advanced for an 18-year-old hitter, Cespedes recognizes pitches and manages the strike zone well. He has a quick right-handed stroke and fine hand-eye coordination, enabling him to barrel balls with ease. He also hits harder than most players his age and already shows the aptitude to drive the ball in the air to his pull side. While there's little doubt Cespedes is equipped to hit for average and power, there are questions as to whether he's a long-term shortstop. He has average speed and arm strength, which aren't quite up to the standards for the position, and he could slow as he matures physically. He projects as more of a second or third baseman but would have no problem fitting the offensive profile at either position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 1 prospect in the 2022 international class. Arias signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. Wrist and thumb injuries shortened his first two pro seasons, though he was one of the more dynamic players in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2023. He struggled in his first taste of full-season ball, batting .233/.335/.393 with 13 homers and Single-A Florida State League highs in steals (37) and strikeouts (171) last summer. While Arias will work counts and produces plus raw power with his bat speed and growing strength, he also has an overly aggressive, pull-happy approach that leads to many chases and empty swings, including on pitches in the zone. He's a switch-hitter who has a much better stroke from the left side (.776 OPS in 2024, compared to .544 from the right side), and all 22 of his homers in his first three seasons came as a lefty. He still could produce 20 or more homers per season, more than most shortstops, but he has created serious concerns about his bat and ability to make adjustments. A plus runner who's aggressive on the bases, Arias stole 64 bags in his first 183 pro games but needs to improve upon his 75 percent success rate. He has smooth actions and one of the strongest infield arms in the system, but his attention to detail slipped last year as he made 22 errors in 84 games at shortstop. He paled in comparison to Tampa teammate George Lombard Jr. at short and looked better at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2022 international crop, Arias turned pro for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. His debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League was alarming, as he hit .194/.379/.370 with a 33 percent strikeout rate after missing the first month with a wrist injury. He looked much more dynamic in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2023, batting .267/.423/.505 with six homers and 17 steals in 27 games before he broke his right thumb. The switch-hitting Arias works counts looking for pitches to drive and has the bat speed and developing strength to punish them when he gets them. He has a pull-happy mentality and did a much better job of making hard contact and lifting balls in the air during his second pro season than he did in his first, though he has regressed in 2024. It's a power-over-hit approach that could produce 20-25 homers per season once he's fully developed. Arias not only possesses uncommon power for a middle infielder but also tools to impact the game in a variety of other ways. He's a plus runner who's very aggressive on the bases and has 30-30 upside. He's a solid shortstop with smooth actions, instincts and a plus-plus arm who could play almost anywhere on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 1 prospect in the 2022 international class, Arias signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. He may have the best all-around collection of tools among the Yankees' stockpile of shortstops, though he'll need time to develop. He missed the first month of the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with a wrist injury, then slashed .194/.379/.370 with a 33 percent strikeout rate in his pro debut. Though Arias didn't post big numbers in his introduction to pro ball, he showed the ability to use the entire field and hit the ball hard from both sides of the plate. He may have returned too soon and tried to do too much once he did, but he displayed a quick bat, the ability to identify breaking balls and promising patience. He drew walks at a 20 percent rate and could develop plus power once he gains more strength and experience. Beyond his offensive upside, Arias has exciting all-around ability. He has run the 60-yard dash in 6.5 seconds, should be at least a plus runner even after he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame and is aggressive on the bases. With his quickness, instincts, smooth actions and a plus-plus arm, he's a no-doubt shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2021-22 international class, Arias signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic in January. He added to the greatest position of strength in a Yankees system headlined by standout shortstops Anthony Volpe and Oswald Peraza. He has the potential for at least solid tools across the board and could be significantly better than that if he reaches his ceiling. Arias is extremely advanced at the plate for a teenager. A switch-hitter, he has feel for the barrel, recognizes pitches well, makes good swing decisions and uses the entire field. He makes consistent hard contact that could develop into plus power once he adds more strength and experience, and his pop currently plays better from the right side of the plate. Arias' secondary tools may be more exciting than his offensive gifts. He can run the 60-yard dash in 6.5 seconds and should retain at least plus speed once he's physically mature. He's also a no-doubt shortstop with instincts, smooth actions and a plus-plus arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees first spied the Cuban-born Mayea training in the Dominican Republic in 2020, and he immediately became their top priority in the 2023 international class. They signed him for $4.35 million, the third-highest bonus in that cycle, with one scout comparing him to a smaller version of Gary Sheffield. Expectations have been revised downward after he hit .282/.370/.326 with 19 steals in 35 games during his U.S. debut in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. A right-handed hitter with a reputation for advanced bat-to-ball skills, Mayea struggles with pitch recognition and often is off balance when he makes contact. That flaw produces a lot of soft grounders and reduces his impact, not letting him take advantage of his bat speed and projectable strength. He used his quickness to beat out a lot of infield hits in the FCL, something that won't be as easy to do against better defenses. Mayea's best tool is his plus speed, which allows him to create havoc on the bases and chase down balls in center field. He's a solid defender who can become better than that if he can refine his reads and routes. His strong arm is an asset anywhere in the outfield and notched nine assists in his first 66 pro starts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees began targeting Mayea when they first saw the Cuban training in the Dominican Republic in 2020, and they signed him for $4.35 million as soon as he became eligible in January 2023. He offered one of the best combinations of tools and skills in his international class, with one scout comparing him to a smaller Gary Sheffield. He made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, slashing .276/.382/.400 with 22 steals in 38 games. Mayea has advanced bat-to-ball skills and uses his quick right-handed swing to make hard contact to all fields. With his combination of hitting ability, bat speed and projectable strength, he could have average or better power when he's fully developed. To get there, he'll have to learn to pull pitches and launch them in the air more consistently than he did in the DSL. Mayea's speed earns 70-80 grades on the 20-80 scouting scale and it was evident on the bases and in center field during his first taste of pro ball. His quickness allows him to cover plenty of ground in center, where his fine reads and routes enhance his range. He also features plus arm strength and would be an asset at any outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mayea is a premium athlete with advanced tools for his age, and the team that signs him is getting one of the most exciting players in the class. He has the type of uncommon bat speed and power that scouts like to see. One evaluator described him as “mini Gary Sheffield” and others praised his advanced approach at the plate. He’s very aggressive in the batter’s box, and he's getting a better understanding of the strike zone. He has a mature frame, but there is still plenty of upside because he is strong and twitchy. On defense, there’s a chance he stays in center field, but a move to a corner spot could be possible, according to scouts who have seen him play. Mayea trains with Jaime Ramos in the Dominican Republic. The Yankees have shown interest in him. Ramos is a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Galiz originally agreed to sign with the Yankees for $1.5 million, but they backed out of the commitment in November 2020, nine days after his father Edgar died of COVID-related complications. Two months later, the Dodgers signed the top-rated catcher in the 2020-21 international class for the $812,500 they had remaining in their bonus pool, adding him to their collection of Venezuelan catching prospects that also includes Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. Galiz made his U.S. debut at age 18 last year and slashed .235/.343/.471 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. A former middle infielder, Galiz is quicker and more athletic than most catchers. He moves well behind the plate, has the hands to become at least a solid receiver and can deter the running game with plus arm strength. He impressed with his framing ability during his first season in the United States and also earns praise for his intelligence and maturity. Galiz's defense is ahead of his offense at this point. He does offer 20-homer potential from the right side of the plate thanks to his bat speed, growing strength and feel for driving balls in the air to his pull side. But he'll need to address swing-and-miss concerns because he gets overly aggressive and tends to pull off pitches, resulting in a 25.3 percent strikeout rate last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top catching prospect in the 2020-21 international crop, Galiz originally committed to sign with the Yankees for $1.5 million. But they backed out of the agreement in November 2020, nine days after his father Edgar died of covid-related complications. The Dodgers signed him two months later for the $812,500 they had left in their bonus pool, adding him to a collection of Venezuelan catching prospects that also includes Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. Galiz's .218/.286/.287 batting line in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League belies his offensive potential. He's a right-handed hitter with bat speed and a patient approach who already makes consistent contact. He shows some feel for launching balls in the air and could develop 20-homer power once he gets stronger. A former middle infielder, Galiz is more athletic than most catchers. He's quick and agile behind the plate, where he shows soft hands and solid arm strength. He'll need time to develop but has the intelligence and maturity to make the most of his physical gifts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Galiz's world was shattered last November, when both his father Edgar died of covid-related complications and the Yankees backed out of an agreement to sign him for $1.5 million out of Venezuela. The top catching prospect in the 2020 international class, he wound up joining the Dodgers in January for the $812,500 they had remaining in their bonus pool. He adds to the club's strong collection of Venezuelan catching prospects that also includes Keibert Ruiz, Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. Galiz is advanced enough on both sides of the ball that he could have come to the United States for his debut this summer. A patient hitter with a quick right-handed stroke, he's content to spray line drives to all fields. As he gets stronger and gets more aggressive with his swing, he could develop 20-homer power. A former middle infielder who's quite athletic for a catcher, Galiz is quick and agile behind the plate. He has the soft hands to become at least a solid receiver and has the arm strength to match. He also earns praise for his intelligence, leadership ability and maturity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his two years at North Carolina, Sabato did two things really well: hit for power and get on base. He set a Tar Heels freshman record with 18 homers in 2019 and slugged .708 as a Draft-eligible sophomore in the shortened 2020 season, all while getting on base at a .459 clip over the two years. That skillset was enough for the Twins to take him at the end of the first round of the 2020 Draft. He struggled for much of his first full season in Low-A, but made adjustments and performed much better in 22 games up in High-A to finish the year. Sabato clearly had issues adjusting to the speed of the pro game and with swinging a wood bat. The right-handed hitter was focused on driving the ball the other way, to right-center field, early on and was often very late, unable to catch up to good fastballs. It took a while, but when he shifted his approach to center and left-center, he started to time up better velocity, which led to better results down the stretch. While the swing and miss is a concern, he also showed strong knowledge of the strike zone, drawing a lot of walks even when he struggled. The expectations around Sabato’s defense were pretty low and while he still has work to do there, the Twins were encouraged with the progress he made. They also felt he showed some mental toughness working through the start of his first full season, with the hope he can use that to turn a corner and hit his way to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lightly recruited and undrafted as a high schooler in Connecticut in 2018, Sabato put his name on the map by setting a North Carolina freshman home run record with 18 long balls in 2019. He couldn’t play summer league ball because of shoulder surgery, but returned for a shortened Draft-eligible sophomore year in 2020 and added to his power bona fides by homering seven times in 19 games for the Tar Heels. That offensive potential carried him to the back end of the first round, where the Twins gave him a full pick value bonus of just over $2.5 million to sign. The Twins didn’t send any 2020 draftees to their alternate training site last summer, but Sabato did get some work in instructional league play. Sabato’s value comes from his bat from the right side of the plate. He is very strong and has excellent bat speed to go along with loft in his swing, ingredients to give him the best raw power in the Twins system. It’s a power-first approach, but he’s more than willing to take walks and he keeps his strikeouts relatively low, particularly given his power potential. As a right-handed first baseman, there is a lot of pressure on Sabato to be a run producer, especially since he’s limited athletically, has a below-average arm and while he’s worked on his defense, he’s fringy at first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pham was a 19th-round pick in the 2021 Draft as a senior reliever out of the University of San Francisco and signed for just $25,000, so he wasn’t really on anyone’s radar when he broke out in 2023, leading Orioles hurlers in a host of major statistical categories and finishing the year at Double-A. He spent all of 2024 back at that level, and after getting off to a slow start, pitched to a 3.00 ERA with more than a strikeout per inning over his last 18 starts. Undersized and lacking huge stuff, the 5-foot-11 Pham makes up for those shortcomings and gets the most out of his ability with a deep arsenal of pitches and a bulldog mentality. He operates with a low-90s fastball that is average velocity-wise but can be difficult to square up because its high spin and Pham’s low arm slot give it the illusion of rising action. He supplements that pitch with an array of secondary offerings. None are plus pitches on their own, but Pham is effective when he mixes them up. He draws high marks for his makeup, competitiveness and moxie. He’s become a better strike thrower since transitioning full-time into a starter, though he struggled early last year when his walk rate began creeping back up. Whether he can reach his low ceiling as a back-end starter will hinge on his ability to command all of his pitches consistently and maintain his strength and stuff, both deep into starts and throughout the season. Anything less and he could emerge as a swingman type who is able to cover innings relatively soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Cutter: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Pham was a reliever for four years at the University of San Francisco and pitched out of the bullpen for parts of two seasons after the Orioles signed him for just $25,000 after selecting him in Round 19 of the 2021 Draft. Given the chance to start last summer, Pham put himself on the prospect map with a 2.57 ERA across 112 innings. He led organizational pitchers in ERA, xFIP (3.68), WHIP and K/BB (19.9 percent) and finished the year at Double-A Bowie. Undersized at 5-foot-11, Pham doesn’t have the typical build of a starter. But he has five pitches at his disposal and uses his height to his advantage, throwing from a low slot and angle that helps his hoppy fastball play up and makes him difficult to time. That fastball lives at 92-93 mph and can touch 96 with good spin. But his success comes from his assortment of secondary offerings, which all individually grade out as average but are effective when Pham mixes them up. His cutter and curve are his best pitches to lefties, his slider can be a plus offering against righties and he has an average changeup that he folds in on occasion. Pham didn’t have a huge track record of throwing strikes when converted into a starter, but he posted the lowest walk rate of his career (including college) last year and sliced it even lower after a midseason promotion to Bowie. Drawing high marks for his competitiveness and moxie, he was able to maintain his stuff as a starter, both over the course of five- to six-inning starts and six months of the season. Whether he stays in that role long term hinges on whether he can keep developing the feel for his secondary pitches and continue throwing all his offerings for strikes on a consistent basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2020, Monegro has compiled a 2.57 ERA and 33 percent strikeout rate since arriving in full-season ball in mid-2023. After shoulder weakness cost him most of the first two months of the 2024 season, he rebounded to not permit an earned run in his final 41 2/3 frames. He was thriving in Double-A last year when he blew out his elbow in June and had Tommy John surgery that will sideline him for all of 2026. Monegro spins the ball better than most Red Sox farmhands, producing upper-80s sliders/cutters and low-80s curveball that are hard to lay off and just as difficult to hit. He got overly slider-happy last year, preferring it to his two- and four-seam fastballs that both operate around 93-95 mph with a peak of 97. He also shows feel for an upper-80s splitter that serves as his changeup. Monegro has improved his control as he has cleaned up his delivery, and he has enough pitches and strikes to make it as a starter. He found more success with his fastball by emphasizing his sinking two-seamer over his fairly straight four-seamer, and he did a better job of maintaining his velocity before he got hurt. If he winds up in the bullpen, his stuff could tick up and give him the upside of a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Monegro turned pro for $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2020, a month before the pandemic shutdown that delayed his pro debut until the following year. He has thrived since arriving in full-season ball in mid-2023, logging a 2.55 ERA with 155 strikeouts in 116 2/3 innings between two Class A stops. After shoulder weakness cost him most of the first two months of last season, he went 41 2/3 consecutive frames without allowing an earned run from in the final two months. Monegro added a mid-80s slider/cutter in 2023 and it added depth and became his best pitch last year, though he fell in love with it so much that he used it 44 percent at the time. His four-seam fastball ranges from 92-96 mph early in games, but it loses velocity and lacks good shape, so he has begun using a low-90s two-seamer more often. His upper-70s curveball once ranked as the best in the system but has regressed since he started favoring his slider, while his improving upper-80s splitter/changeup is becoming an effective chase pitch. Though Monegro has size and athleticism in his favor and has toned down his delivery while improving his control, there are questions about whether he can survive as a long-term starter. He pitches backwards because his fastballs don't have much movement or deception, so he needs to find more life or add velocity as he continues to fill out his 6-foot-4 frame. If he can't, he'll probably be a slider-heavy reliever, and those concerns contributed to the Red Sox not protecting him on the 40-man roster during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Monegro signed for $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2020, a month before the pandemic shutdown that pushed his pro debut to 2021. He reached full-season ball last June, pitching 18 straight scoreless innings upon arriving in Single-A. He posted a 2.06 ERA, .194 average-against and 93 strikeouts in 65 2/3 frames between three levels during the regular season and won his lone playoff start to help High-A Greenville capture the South Atlantic League championship. Monegro carved up lower-level hitters with one of the best curveballs in the system, an upper-70s bender with true 12-6 break that's effective against both lefties and righties. His four-seam fastball will range from 92-96 mph in the early innings, but it drops off later in games and lacks life, so he has begun to fiddle with a two-seamer as well. He also added an average mid-80s slider/cutter in 2023 but didn't make much progress with an upper-80s changeup that lacks velocity separation and life. The downside to Monegro's curveball is that he falls in love with it at the expense of developing is other offerings. He did improve his delivery and strike-throwing last season, adding to hope that he can become a No. 4 or 5 starter. There's still projection remaining in his athletic 6-foot-4 frame, so he could add velocity and boost his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring on the high school showcase circuit in 2019 and winning Gatorade's national baseball player of the year award in the shortened 2020 season, Kelley established himself as a first-round talent. But signability questions and the industry's reluctance to take prep right-handers that high dropped him to the second round, where he signed for $3 million. Poor conditioning led to a dreadful 2021 pro debut, but he looked significantly better last season, which he concluded by pitching well in Double-A during the organization's Project Birmingham. Kelley can run a four-seam fastball up to 98 mph but is more comfortable and generates more weak contact with a 92-96 mph two-seamer. He has regained his feel for a changeup that ranked among the best in the 2020 Draft, a low-80s weapon with fade and tumble. He lacks natural feel for spin but has made strides with an 82-85 mph slider with more than depth than sweep, and it could become at least an average third option with more consistency. Kelley was significantly overweight during his pro debut, which cost him arm speed and led to shoulder fatigue and forearm tightness. After improving his shoulder and core strength and dropping some weight, he did a better job of repeating his deliberate delivery in 2022. He cut his walk rate from 9.9 per nine innings in his debut to 5.5 last season, but his control and command still have to get much better for him to remain a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelley dominated the high school showcase circuit in 2019 before winning Gatorade's national baseball player of the year award the following spring. Though he was a consensus first-round talent, his signability and the industry's general skittishness about prep right-handers dropped him to the second round in the 2020 Draft, and the White Sox signed him for $3 million.
