His 2021 pro debut went poorly, as he dealt with shoulder fatigue and forearm tightness while logging a 7.61 ERA with 26 walks in 23 2/3 innings between Rookie ball and Low-A, but he has fared better this season. Kelley still shows the pure stuff that scouts loved as an amateur, starting with a four-seam fastball that ranges from 93-98 mph with running action and a low-90s two-seamer that induces groundball contact. His mid-80s changeup remains an advanced weapon with fade and sink. After showing inconsistent feel for spin in high school, he has made some progress with a sweeping slider that shows flashes of becoming at least an average third option. Kelley's conditioning started to go south during his truncated senior year and got worse in 2021, when he was significantly overweight and lost some arm speed. His ability to repeat his delivery and locate the strike zone also fell apart. He focused on improving his shoulder and core strength during the offseason, which has helped him throw more strikes, but he's going to have to make significant further gains with his control and command to be a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 Refugio (Texas) High never has produced a drafted player, though that's about to change in a big way in 2020. Kelley entered the year rated as the nation's top high school prospect and is regarded as Texas' best prep pitcher since Jameson Taillon went No. 2 overall in 2010. He repeatedly dominated on the showcase circuit last summer, including an Area Code Games performance that some scouts said was the best in the long history of the event. Few pitchers can create as much velocity with as little effort as Kelley, who can pump 93-96 mph fastballs and reach 98 with some running action. He already owns an advanced changeup with fade and sink, and he's willing to throw it in any count. His third-best pitch at the moment is a hard slurve in the low 80s that lacks consistency but should develop into at least a solid offering. Kelley combines his now stuff with feel for pitching. The Texas recruit pounds the strike zone and has the look of a frontline starter who could reach the big leagues before he turns 21. His strong, physically mature frame and the ease of his delivery should allow him to log plenty of innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 Sanabria was selected by the Padres in the 18th round of the 2022 Draft after two years at Indiana River State (Fla.) JC, and he signed for only $50,000 to go pro. His breakout season came in 2024 when he climbed three levels while leading the San Diego organization in on-base percentage (.396) and doubles (30), and he earned a look in the prospect-heavy Arizona Fall League after that. Sanabria got off to a hot start with Double-A San Antonio in ’25 but wilted after June, finishing with a .257/.309/.376 line and 12 homers in 119 games. Sanabria became a good amount more aggressive in his more extended stay in the Texas League, jumping his full-season swing rate from 42.3 percent in ‘25 to 49.3 in ’26. His chase rate, as you’d expect, also took a jump, particularly against fastballs and sliders, and that took away one of his strengths as a high-OBP type. There is raw power here, and the Padres are hoping improved strength and conditioning help the left-handed slugger show it in games over the course of a long season in the warm Texas (or eventually San Diego) sun after the way his results fell off last season. After a very brief dalliance with catching in 2022, Sanabria has been locked in at first base as a professional, and that’s where he’ll remain with well-below-average speed. He simply has to hit at that position to make himself a Major Leaguer, even as part of a platoon at the cold corner. Now in his age-24 season, Sanabria has already been overlooked in the Rule 5 process, both on the 40-man roster and the Draft itself.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 Sanabria played two years at Indian River State (Fla.) JC and slashed .400/.471/.578 as a sophomore in 2022. The Padres took him in the 18th round that July and signed him for just $50,000. He slowly solidified himself on the prospect radar and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 in which he climbed three full-season levels from Single-A to Double-A. He finished with a .288/.396/.427 line, 11 homers and 30 doubles over 125 games. He led the organization in on-base percentage and two-baggers and finished second in average and hits (130). Sanabria got in 15 extra games in the Arizona Fall League, where he batted .276 with a .709 OPS. From the left side, Sanabria looks relaxed at the plate and hits out of an open stance before getting in line with a leg kick. He ran a solid in-zone contact rate in 2024, and while he’ll whiff at the occasional secondary, he can handle fastballs well. When he gets beat, it tends to be toward the outside half. With typical solid plate discipline, he’s been a solid OBP producer, and some in the organization are wondering when or if he’ll stop hitting. That said, it’s hit-over-power right now. He topped out with a 109.1 mph exit velocity in the Fall League, but typically his pop plays best in the gaps. Sanabria got some brief catching experience after signing, but as a 30-grade runner, he’s basically locked into first base. Improving his footwork over there will be a priority moving forward, so that he can provide value beyond what he shows in the box. Generating more power would also help his case to be a future starter at the cold corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Joseph received the fourth-highest bonus of anyone in the 2024 international signing class, getting $3.3 million from the Mariners in January of that year as one of the perceived best shortstops in the entire crop. He had grown since first being scouted years prior, sprouting up to 6-foot-2 and 185 pounds, but he wasn’t able to use his size or tools with any consistency during a rough professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, when he hit just .133 with a 29.1 percent strikeout rate. The Mariners would like to give Joseph a mulligan and hope he can hit the reset button in 2025, but there could be a long way to go for the right-handed-hitting infielder to figure things out. There were always some concerns for his pure hit tool, but the raw power was significant and something to work on tapping into. But Joseph didn’t show much feel for contact during his debut, and even when he did, he wasn’t squaring up the ball with much impact. Additionally, it appears like Joseph might outgrow shortstop. He’s slowed down after growing, and as he fills out, it seems more likely that he won’t have the quickness to stay at the premium position. If he can hit the reset button and start tapping into that power the Mariners liked, perhaps he can eventually profile as a third baseman, though there’s a lot of work to be done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners started following Joseph three years ago, when he was just 5-foot-10. By the time they brought him in during the 2024 international signing period for $3 million, he had grown to 6-foot-2 and 185 pounds. Given that young frame, most weren’t sure if he’d profile as an outfielder or infielder, with some thinking he had a similar build to Twins center fielder Byron Buxton. Joseph now exhibits much more body control, with better hands at shortstop. It's more of a power-hitting offensive profile than before, and overall, he’s a physical athlete who projects to play a position up the middle. And just as importantly, he can really control the zone with a simple swing, direct mechanics and projectable power. He’s lost some of the top-end wheels through his growth spurt but still is touted with at least above-average speed, with the ability to be a threat on the basepaths. Now for the No. 7 prospect from his international class will come the opportunity to play in the Dominican Summer League, where he’ll face stiffer competition and look to incorporate some of the work he’s done with respected trainer Cristian Batista, a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former standout at Seminole State (Junior) College of Florida, Levenson moved into a DH/bench role for Miami in 2022 and became a starting outfielder with a .292/.397/.554 slash line and 14 homers over 63 games as a junior. The Cardinals took him in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him for exact slot at $381,300. Levenson put in a solid turn at Single-A Palm Beach in his first taste of the pros and spent his first full season with High-A Peoria, slashing .215/.317/.367 with eight homers and a 100 wRC+ over 70 games. He didn’t play after July 20 after being hit by a pitch on the left wrist. It was a perplexing year for Levenson. On one hand, his contact numbers were generally solid with some struggles against changeups in particular, and his 11.2 percent walk rate was above-average for the Midwest League. That’s notable because he tends to stay back in his stance and use a quick toe tap for a load, and pitchers will attack him outside because of that. On the other, he popped a ton of balls up; his 41.9 percent infield flyball rate was third-highest among 1,312 Minor Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances in 2024. He had shown above-average exit velos in the Florida State League in ’23, and there is still decent raw power in his 6-foot frame, but he needs to improve the quality of contact to get to it. With fringy speed and glovework, Levenson got most of his looks in left field, and many expect that’s where he’ll remain. Being in a corner means he’ll need to hit all the more, and after being robbed of an opportunity to improve in the second half, he’ll be under a microscope in his second full campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Levenson went from a junior college standout at Seminole State College of Florida in 2021 to a solid DH/bench option for Miami in 2022 to a starting outfielder/team captain for the Hurricanes in 2023. He made the most of his playing time in his final spring on campus, slashing .292/.397/.554 with 14 homers and a decent 18.8 percent strikeout rate over 63 games. The Cardinals selected Levenson in the fifth round in July and signed him for exact slot at $381,300. He was an above-average hitter during a 34-game spin with Single-A Palm Beach, slashing .268/.331/.480 with six homers and a 114 wRC+. The right-handed hitter’s setup at the dish isn’t overly complicated. He stays back in his stance, slightly lifts his legs and lets his arms and hands fire. It’s a process that works for him as he pulverized fastballs as a Miami junior and didn’t even whiff on a pitch 95 or above in that collegiate season. The misses he did experience came more on breaking stuff, and that trend continued in the Florida State League. Levenson will show average power -- standing more to the pullside -- and ran a 40 percent hard-hit rate at Single-A at a time when many other college picks show fatigue. The Florida native needs to hit because with speed and arm strength that can both be called fringy, he’s likely locked into left field long-term. That’s where he made 21 of his 27 defensive starts with Palm Beach with fellow 2023 picks Chase Davis and Travis Honeyman also on the roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blanco began his pro career when he signed with the Pirates for $900,000 in January 2022. The son of the late Tony Blanco, who spent 17 years in pro ball, Blanco Jr. has shown that he can get to his immense power with 18 homers over 362 career at-bats but he’s had trouble both making contact and staying healthy. He’s yet to play more than 40 games in a season, and while he did reach full-season ball for the first time in 2025, he missed much of the year with a hamstring injury. He made up for some lost time in the Arizona Fall League, where he put on a show in winning the Fall Stars Home Run Derby. A mountain of a young man at 6-foot-7 and over 240 pounds, Blanco’s calling card is, and always will be, his immense raw power. He hits the ball extremely hard, with a max EV of 120 mph in the Florida State League last year. When he makes contact, it’s impactful, and even when the ball isn't hit squarely, he can send it out of the park to all fields with elite-level barrel and hard-hit percentages. Unfortunately, he doesn’t make enough contact to establish confidence that it’s going to work even if he can stay on the field and move up the ladder. He has a career 35.1 percent strikeout rate, and that’s just at the lowest levels of the Minors. Continuing to work on his conditioning so that he can keep working on that approach and avoid the injured list is essential. While there had been talk of him playing some corner outfield, where his strong arm would profile well, his limited time has been at first base, a more likely long-term home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tony Blanco spent 17 years in pro ball, several in Japan, getting a cup of coffee with the Nationals back in 2005. Now his namesake is trying to work his way through the Pirates’ system. Blanco Jr. signed for $900,000 back in January 2022 and since then has shown glimpses of his tremendous offensive potential along with what he needs to work on, spending two years in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and then making progress in his first taste of playing in the United States, with a .890 OPS in 30 Florida Complex League games, but that came to an end with a hamstring injury in July. Blanco is a monster of a human now standing at 6-foot-7 and more than 240 pounds. With that frame comes an absurd amount of raw power, huge exit velocities and leverage. But that's only when he makes contact, something that has been an issue in his early career. The good news is he cut his strikeout rate by about 10 percent in 2024, leading to better numbers overall. He's always going to be power-over-hit, and the Pirates will live with some swing-and-miss, knowing that if he can even find the barrel at a fringy rate, he's going to put up big power numbers. More than anything for his development, Blanco has to stay on the field so he can get reps in order to refine his approach. He worked this offseason on his conditioning to enhance the odds of him staying healthy. Playing a corner outfield spot still isn't completely out of the realm of possibility, but he'll be getting a lot more time at first to keep his bat in the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it’s too early for the 2018-19 international signing class to have made a big league impact in Colorado, the Rockies' efforts during that period are showing up on the prospect landscape. Warming Bernabel is in the organization’s top 10 and Juan Brito was dealt to bring in Nolan Jones. Guerrero, who signed for $650,000 in July of 2018, is perhaps a step behind Bernabel, but has pretty much hit everywhere he’s been, from his Dominican Summer League debut in 2019 to his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021 and his step up to full-season ball in 2022. Since signing, Guerrero has displayed a knack for finding the barrel. It’s kind of a controlled aggression at the plate as he’s not one to see a ton of pitches, but he rarely strikes out, with a 15.6 percent K rate heading into the 2023 season. He’s slight and wiry, but he started tapping into some raw power more consistently in 2022, though it still remains to be seen how much strength he can add to maintain that extra-base authority. Though he’s just an average runner, Guerrero is an aggressive baserunner and can steal a base. He’s played all three outfield positions since moving from the infield in 2021, but is mostly likely a corner guy long term and his defense has improved markedly. That puts more pressure on his bat, but the Rockies like his confidence and his response to things like late-game pressure to make them a bit more bullish about his offensive upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies handed out nine bonuses of six figures or higher during the 2018-19 international signing period. Guerrero was closer to the top of the list when he received $650,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the period. Since then, he’s done nothing but hit, with a .319 average in the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut in 2019 and then a .318 average in his United States debut in 2021 in the Arizona Complex League. Guerrero has already shown a very good feel at the plate and even though it’s more of a “see the ball, hit the ball” approach, he’s limited his strikeouts and even drawn some walks. How much he can add muscle to his ultra-lean frame will help determine how much impact he has at the plate, with the Rockies expressing confidence he’s going to grow into more extra-base thump. Signed as a shortstop, Guerrero mostly played third during his DSL debut and shifted to the outfield in 2021 where he used his athleticism more than he exhbited any idea of how to actually play the position. He’s an aggressive baserunner who plays with super-high energy but has average speed, so a corner spot makes the most sense. He might just be scratching the surface, with the ceiling to eventually grow into a big league regular with an exceptional bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of 1971 Heisman Trophy winner and NFL quarterback Patrick Sullivan, Joseph spent time as a safety and wide receiver in high school before realizing his future was in baseball. He posted an unspectacular .271/.436/.528 batting line in three seasons at South Alabama and went undrafted as a sophomore-eligible in 2023, but the Astros liked his all-around ability enough to pick him in the seventh round the following July. He reached Double-A while slashing .244/.368/.403 with 44 extra-bases hits and 27 steals in 116 games during his first full pro season. Sullivan has some of the best on-base ability among Houston prospects, regularly making good swing decisions from the left side of the plate and ranking 10th in the Minors in walk rate (18 percent) while also getting hit by 20 pitches in 2025. He may not hit for a high average because he doesn't make consistent contact against non-fastballs, and his struggles against left-handers could relegate him to platoon duty. He does have the bat speed and strength for at least average power if he can cut down his strikeouts and elevate more pitches. Sullivan possesses solid speed and an aggressive nature on the basepaths, swiping 42 bags in 51 attempts (82 percent) last year. Solely a left fielder at Alabama, he has played primarily center in pro ball and is an average defender there with arm strength to match. He plays with constant energy, and the Astros love his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of 1971 Heisman Trophy winner and NFL quarterback Patrick Sullivan, Joseph played safety and wide receiver in high school before deciding to focus on baseball. He batted a modest .271/.436/.528 in three seasons at South Alabama, went undrafted as a sophomore-eligible in 2023 and was hampered by a right hamate injury last spring before signing with the Astros as a seventh-rounder. After he showed all-around ability during his pro debut, his name repeatedly came up in trade talks. Sullivan makes good swing decisions from the left side of the plate and enhances his on-base ability by drawing walks and getting hit by more than his share of pitches. He has the bat-to-ball skills along with the bat speed and strength to become an average hitter with power to match if he can refine his approach at the plate. He tends to pull a lot of balls on the ground and can be more selective about which strikes he puts into play. Sullivan is aggressive with his plus speed and looks to steal and take extra bases. Though he played mostly left field at South Alabama in deference to Red Sox seventh-rounder Will Turner, he's a legitimate center fielder with an average arm. Besides his skills, he earns praise for his constant energy and strong makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 21 years old when he signed with the Angels for just $10,000 in late June of 2022, Hurtado brought his arm strength to full-season ball in 2023 after a brief Dominican Summer League debut after signing. He had inconsistent results as a swingman type with Inland Empire, and a move to full-time starting up a level with High-A Tri-City led to similar surface numbers. Things clicked a bit more in Double-A in 2025, with Hurtado walking far fewer batters while also striking out less, finishing with a solid start in Triple-A. The Angels rolled the dice and didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster and nobody took him in the Rule 5 Draft. Hurtado has always been able to throw hard, and that didn’t change last year despite missing two months of the season. His fastball sits at around 95 mph and typically tops out in the upper-90s, though he’s no stranger with triple digits. The two-seamer is the effective one, thrown with good sink to routinely elicit groundball rates of 50 percent or higher. He has an 85-86 mph hard slider that can be effective but doesn’t miss as many bats as it should, especially since his fastball isn’t about whiffs. He’s continued to try to find a changeup that works, with limited success. The 25-year-old right-hander did improve his strike-throwing considerably last year, with just a 2.7 BB/9 rate all season. That, plus the ability he’s shown to log innings and hold his stuff deep into outings, gives him the chance to start, though he needs a third pitch and more missed bats to thrive. He could otherwise find some success as a sinker-slider type out of a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Several months into the 2022 international signing period, the Angels landed Hurtado for the bargain price of $10,000. He was older, already 21 when he signed, so after getting started in the Dominican Summer League after signing, he went straight to full-season ball in 2023, starting very slowly but then figuring things out in the back end of the season. After starting and relieving with Single-A Inland Empire, he was a mainstay in High-A Tri-City’s rotation in 2024 with mixed results, though he did lead the Northwest League in innings pitched (138 2/3) and strikeouts (134). Now 24, it feels like in many ways Hurtado is still figuring out who he is as a pitcher. The 6-foot-2 right-hander can light up the radar gun, flirting with triple digits and sitting in the mid-90s with ease, throwing two-seamers with sink to get groundball outs. His slider, which he can run up into the upper-80s, has become his breaking ball – he’s all but scrapped a slower get-me-over curve – and he misses a lot of bats with it. He continues to try to find a third pitch, some kind of change-of-speed, that can work for him. Hurtado’s ability to land his two potentially plus pitches for strikes regressed in 2024 and he walked 5.3 per nine as a result. The Angels may not want to pull the plug on him starting just yet so he can work on his command and that third offering, but it’s hard not to dream about him as a sinker-slider reliever who’s throwing 100 mph-plus in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2022 international signing period opened in January of that year, the Angels found some high-price-tag talent right out of the gate, signing outfielders Nelson Rada and Randy De Jesus for seven figures apiece. They did some bargain shopping later on, getting Hurtado (then already 21 years old) for $10,000 at the end of June. He got his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League after signing and then came stateside for full-season ball in 2023. After really struggling out of the gate, he was very effective with Inland Empire, capping things off with seven innings of one-hit, shutout ball in a playoff start. After giving up 19 runs in six innings in April 2023, Hurtado posted a 3.50 regular-season ERA from May 1 on, striking out 10.3 per nine while walking just 2.8. He does it mostly with a fastball-slider combination. He sits around 95-96 mph with his heater and can flirt with triple digits, and he started throwing more two-seamers with sink as the year went on. Hurtado's mid-80s slider, which can touch 88-89 mph, is his go-to breaking ball that can miss bats. He has a little get-me-over 82-84 mph curve, and he’s working on a changeup, though he didn’t bring it into games in 2023 much. As Hurtado gained confidence and got stretched out as a starter during his U.S. debut last year, he started filling up the strike zone more consistently. Continued development on that front, along with finding an offspeed offering, could give him a chance to stay in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three seasons at Vanderbilt both starting and relieving as well as a strong MLB Draft Combine showing led the Royals to take Owen in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft, signing him for $631,700, He might have gone higher if not for injury concerns in his final season at Vandy. Owen put those aside by throwing 102 innings across 23 games (22 starts) for High-A Quad Cities in his first pro season. He had a 4.20 ERA with a 1.20 WHIP, an 18.9% strikeout rate and a 7.5% walk rate. Owen is a presence on the mound at 6-foot-6 and 260 pounds. His fastball is 90-94 mph with solid carry and vert to it and uses the top of the zone well. His 86-89 mph slider is smaller, almost cutter-like, misses bats and has potential to be his out pitch, while his 75-76 mph curveball is still developing after he wasn't able to land it much in 2024. His 83-85 mph changeup is near average with sink and gets some chase on it. Owen’s delivery is simple but does have some effort because of his bigger frame, although he likes using that strong presence to his advantage on the mound. Owen looks the part of a big-bodied rotation guy who’s built like a workhorse, so it was good to see him stay healthy across a full season with a lot of innings and a jump from what he had in ‘23. He’ll head to Double-A in 2025 and projects as a back-end starter if he can keep developing his secondaries, but that stuff might tick up in a bullpen, especially against lefties.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Owen was Maine’s top prep prospect in 2020, but he opted to attend Vanderbilt rather than turn pro right away. He was a reliever his first two seasons, then a starter in ‘23, but he could not stay healthy with a tired arm after flashing first-round stuff in the spring. A strong showing at the MLB Draft Combine eased some concerns, and the Royals took him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft. Owen didn’t pitch last year with the Royals after the up-and-down nature of his season. All of the stuff Owen flashed early on last spring was impressive. His 92-94 mph fastball has good carry, while his upper-70s curveball is above-average. A mid-80s slider missed bats with a whiff rate of 46 percent as a junior, and a mid-80s sinking changeup grades out as average but has potential to improve. Owen is an effective strike-thrower with all his pitches. He’s a big guy at 6-foot-6 and 261 pounds, but he has a simple and athletic delivery despite the sometimes uneven tempo to it. The former Commodore faces major question marks about his health and durability entering his pro career. As a college pitcher coming out of a program like Vanderbilt, one might hope to accelerate his development a bit quicker, as long as he can stick on the mound. He’ll begin his career as a starter, but his stuff and presence would fit in a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Hit: 35 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Tears didn’t get consistent playing time until his junior year at Tennessee and broke out for that Men’s College World Series championship team, hitting .324/.427/.643 with 20 homers in 71 games. The Padres used their first compensation pick after the fourth round (a selection they received for losing Josh Hader in free agency) on the outfielder and signed him for $525,200. Tears dealt with a right hamstring strain in his first spring and never quite got going at Single-A Lake Elsinore, finishing with a .227/.320/.385 line, 13 homers and a 96 wRC+ in 107 games. The left-handed slugger gets going with a big leg kick that helps him generate big bat speed, but he got exposed for being too rotational and getting too long with his swing in his first campaign against pro pitching. Tears especially struggled against changeups with a whiff rate of 58 percent against them, per Synergy, often showing an inability to manipulate the barrel going down and away from him, and that led to reverse splits in the California League. When he does make contact, it can be loud, and there’s still hope to be found in his exit velocities. Tears is a better runner underway than he is out of the gate, and he was only 6-for-11 in stolen-base attempts in 2025. Once he gets the legs going -- and isn’t being bothered by the hamstring -- he can get moving in the outfield and he has the arm strength for right field. Tears spent much of last season at DH, however, and even mixed in three starts at first base. His priority in year two will be tightening up the swing in search of getting back to being the toolsy star he was as a Volunteer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 55 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 Tears redshirted at Tennessee in 2022 and then got only 56 at-bats due to hamstring and oblique injuries in 2023. No bother. Facing Draft eligibility last spring, the outfielder became one of college baseball’s toolsiest players and was a force for a Volunteers squad that went on to win the Men's College World Series. He finished with a .324/.427/.643 line and 20 homers in 71 games. The Padres selected Tears with their first compensation pick after the fourth round (the selection they got for losing Josh Hader in free agency) and signed him for slot value at $525,200. Standing tall in the box as a left-handed hitter, Tears loads with a big leg kick and generates big bat speed that helps him drive the ball all over the park. He has at least plus raw power that helped him generate impressive exit velocities, even when adjusting for college and metal bats, and that pop was a huge piece of his Draft profile. There are more questions about his overall hit tool. He showed improved swing decisions as a junior but still ran just a 69.6 percent contact rate on his swings. A flat bat path could be partly to blame and could cap his overall offensive profile. Tears is a better runner underway than he is out of the box or off the bag, so he may not be a huge stolen-base threat. But the running ability certainly helps him in the outfield. For Tennessee, he played mostly right field, where his plus arm strength certainly is an asset, but he could be average in center as well. Tears hasn’t played an official Minor League game entering 2025, and pro pitching will test just how much he can rely on his pure strength as a hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout on Cuba’s 15U national team back in 2016, Nunez signed with the Cardinals for $300,000 in July 2018 and immediately dominated the Dominican Summer League and won a batting title with his .415 average. He hasn’t been able to reach that very high bar since, scuffling a bit during his United States debut in 2019 and putting up pedestrian numbers in 2021. He found his footing with Double-A Springfield a year ago before being sent to the Pirates in the José Quintana deal and finished the year in Triple-A. The Bucs rolled the dice and didn’t put him on the 40-man roster, but he wasn’t selected in the Rule 5 Draft. His case to land a spot on the roster in 2023 wasn’t helped by missing two months of the season with a shoulder impingement. Compact and strong, Nunez tapped into his considerable raw power more consistently in 2022 than he has since that stunning DSL debut. He makes a lot of contact, with a strikeout rate under 20 percent for his Minor League career and even his small uptick in whiffs during his power breakout last year was offset by a walk rate of 14 percent. While he still tends to hit the ball on the ground too much, the improved patience has given him better counts to drive the ball on a regular basis. Although Nunez doesn’t have the footspeed to play third on a regular basis, he does have more than enough arm for the hot corner, and he’ll continue to get some reps there. He has really good hands, which will help him be a solid defender at first, where he’s most likely to fit long term if he’s going to play one spot every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nuñez posted Cuba’s best batting average during a gold medal-winning turn at the 2016 15U World Cup in Japan and won the 2018 Dominican Summer League slash-line triple crown (.415/.497/.774) after signing with the Cardinals for $300,000 that July. Following some stateside stumbles as an 18-year-old in 2019, Nuñez popped much better at High-A Peoria to open last season, hitting .285/.351/.453 over 151 plate appearances. He was pushed once more to Double-A Springfield, and while his 91 wRC+ was below-average, his 224 plate appearances were second-most among 20-year-olds at Double-A in 2021 behind Riley Greene’s 373. He was spending a full season at Double-A and showing more power when he was sent to the Pirates in return for José Quintana close to the Trade Deadline. Listed at 5-foot-11, 205 pounds, Nuñez shows impressive raw power and bat speed out of his boxier frame, and it’s that pop that will continue to fuel his ascent toward the big leagues. He shows good bat-to-ball skills as well with strikeout rates regularly below 20 percent. That said, the lack of K’s had been in part due to his overly aggressive nature at the plate, and that leads to more ground balls than should be expected of someone with his strength. Experience has helped and he started showing more patience and tapping into his power more consistently as a more age-appropriate for his level in 2022. Nuñez has the strong arm for third base, but he lacks the speed or relative athleticism to make him a surefire fit for the position. He seems destined for a first base/DH role or even left field where the arm could be of use, and he’ll have to hit to be valuable at any of those spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez put himself on the international radar while playing in Cuba’s youth national leagues and then recorded the team’s highest batting average as he led Cuba to a gold medal during the 2016 15U World Cup in Japan. He signed with the Cardinals for $300,000 in July 2018 and won the Dominican Summer League triple crown (.415/.497/.774) in his professional debut. The Cardinals pushed Nunez to Low-A Peoria in 2019, but some holes in his game were exposed and he was demoted to the Rookie Appalachian League, where he hit .254 over 37 games. That experience proved fruitful for Nunez as he made adjustments to his approach and worked his way up to Double-A as a 20-year-old in 2021. Nunez’s calling card is his raw power and ability to impact the baseball. The 5-foot-11 Nunez generates impressive exit velocities, but doesn’t hit a ton of balls in the air, something he worked on at the alternate training site in 2020 and has continued to work on this season. Nunez’s approach can get overly aggressive at times, though that can be attributed to his lack of experience and he’s been receptive to coaching early in his career. Defensively, questions remain about Nunez’s long-term home. While he has spent the vast majority of his career at third base, he’d need to both refine his mechanics and improve his athleticism to stick at the hot corner. Nunez, who possesses a solid arm, may ultimately wind up at first base, with left field also being a potential option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez established himself as a rising international prospect while playing in Cuba’s youth national leagues and led Cuba to a gold medal while recording the highest batting average at the 2016 15U World Cup in Japan. He continued to rake after signing with the Cardinals for $300,000 in July 2018, as Nunez captured the Dominican Summer League triple crown (.415/.497/.774) as a 17-year-old while racking up 13 homers and 59 RBIs in 44 games. The big performance inspired the Cardinals to challenge Nunez with an assignment to Class A Peoria in early 2019, but he was overmatched in the Midwest League and batted just .183 in 21 games before being demoted to the more age-appropriate Rookie Appalachian League, where he slashed .254/.336/.385 with two homers in 37 games. Nunez might lack physical projection, but the big-bodied teenager has a ton of present strength in his 5-foot-11, 205-pound frame. He generates plus raw power as well as some of the best exit velocities in the Cardinals’ system, combining plus bat speed with an explosive swing. Club officials believe Nunez’s power will start to show as he learns to elevate the ball, though, right now, he makes too much ground-ball contact. The aggressive, free-swinging approach that worked for him in the DSL was exposed against advanced pitching in 2019, as Nunez struggled to control the strike zone and make consistent quality contact. Much of that can be chalked up to his youth, though, and the Cardinals expect to see improvement as Nunez gains experience. Nunez is more athletic than he appears and has the above-average arm strength needed for third base, though it might be a challenge for him to remain there on account of his below-average speed and limited range. While most evaluators expect him to end up at first base, such a move down the defensive spectrum would come with greater offensive demands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez was known in international scouting circles because he was a standout in Cuba's youth national leagues and one of the stars of the 2016 15U World Cup in Japan, where he posted the tournament's top batting average (.667) while leading Cuba to a gold medal. Facing signing restrictions in '18 after spending heavily on international talent the year prior, the Cardinals managed to sign Nunez for $300,000 in July 2018. Subsequently assigned to the Dominican Summer League, Nunez hit .415/.497/.774 with 13 home runs and 59 RBIs in 44 games to win the circuit's triple crown. Nunez is physically mature for his age, with a broad, thick frame that's loaded with strength. It helps him generate plus raw power that he should be able to get to in games because he's also an advanced hitter with a plus bat speed, feel for the barrel and a swing that stays in the zone for an extended period of time. He recognizes pitches and demonstrates an understanding of the strike zone, albeit with an aggressive approach. Nunez is more athletic than he appears and has the above-average arm strength needed for third base, but it might be a challenge for him to remain there on account of his below-average speed and fringe glove. Players who are physically strong tend to excel in the Dominican Summer League, and Nunez's impressive production there should be viewed in that context. However, club officials all rave about the teenager's innate hitting ability, viewing him as someone who will continue to hit for both average and power, regardless of his defensive home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been eight high schoolers drafted and signed out of Hawaii to make it to the big leagues this century, the most recent coming in 2017 (Joey Cantillo). The last two prep hitters to come from the Aloha State to reach the highest level were both taken in 2013: Kean Wong and Isiah Kiner-Falefa. Rosario, the Twins’ final selection in the shortened 2020 Draft hopes to end that drought. He’s provided up-and-down production since winning Midwest League MVP honors in 2023, then missed a chunk of '24 with an elbow injury that dampened his output. He bounced back with 25 homers in Double-A during his age-22 season. It’s becoming clear that Rosario’s power is for real, with 20-plus homers in two of his last three seasons while being young for his level. The right-handed hitter routinely hits the ball hard, with plus bat speed, and can find the seats to all fields. With that power comes a healthy dose of strikeouts (27.5 percent K rate in 2025), especially against softer stuff, but he also draws a ton of walks (12.6 percent). He has fringy speed, but for the first time in his career, he used what he has to swipe 32 bases last season. Rosario hasn’t been protected on the 40-man roster and hasn’t been selected in the Rule 5 Draft largely because of those strikeouts and his fringy, at best, defense. If he can improve that part of his game, his power could profile as a big league corner outfielder soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was the top prospect in Hawaii ahead of the shortened 2020 Draft and ended up being the second one taken when the Twins selected him in the fifth round. (The Red Sox took pitcher Jeremy Wu-Yelland in Round 4.) Rosario has shown flashes of offensive potential, like when he won the Midwest League MVP and then tied for the Arizona Fall League lead in home runs in 2023. That raised expectations for 2024, but an elbow injury that forced him out of action for two months somewhat derailed his progress, though he did make up for lost time with a return engagement in the AFL. Since entering pro ball, Rosario has displayed the ability to hit the ball very hard, but he’s also been one to get off to slow starts and then heat up as the year goes on. That was happening again in 2024 when he landed on the injured list as he started to show he could make adjustments to the sharper breaking balls he saw in Double-A. Early on, his swing had gotten flatter and he was chasing more than he used to. There is always going to be swing-and-miss to Rosario's game with a power-over-hit profile, but he was starting to figure things out and he always offsets the K’s with a healthy dose of walks. As a right-handed-hitting corner outfielder, Rosario is on the wrong side of a platoon and he’s going to have to really consistently mash to be an everyday player. The Twins didn’t protect him from Rule 5 Draft last December and he wasn’t taken, but he has the kind of work ethic in which he can use that to earn a 40-man spot this year, when he’ll still be just 22 for most of the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been just two Hawaiian prep hitters who signed out of high school to go on and make any real impact in the big leagues: Shane Victorino, a 1999 sixth-round pick, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa, who went in the fourth round in 2013. Rosario is hoping he can join that short list after the Twins took him with their final pick in the shortened 2020 Draft and has moved one rung at a time. He's gone from the Florida Complex League in 2021 to Single-A Fort Myers in 2022 and then on to High-A last year, when he had his most productive year to date, earning Midwest League MVP honors. He finished off 2023 by tying for the Arizona Fall League lead in home runs. The Twins’ patience with Rosario’s development appears to be paying off. He made a big adjustment with his setup at the end of 2022 and it really clicked in 2023, using a spread out base to cut down his movement, recognizing he didn’t need to do that much to tap into his natural strength and raw power. He also cut down on his chase rate and drew a lot more walks as his overall approach improved, helping him to lead the Midwest League in homers. While he did a really good job at punishing fastballs, he still missed breaking stuff at a pretty high clip, his front hip can leak out early, leading to struggles with pitches away, and he’s still learning to be adjustable with his swing. Now a corner outfielder only, Rosario has shown off an accurate arm that racked up 14 assists with Cedar Rapids. Upper level pitching will be the next challenge, but he seems to make improvements at each step as well as anyone in the system and could very well profile well as a power-hitting right fielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Instead of trying to be taken in the 2021 KBO Draft back home in South Korea, Cho moved to Atlanta one month after his 18th birthday and signed with the Cardinals in January 2022. He had a limited run in the Florida Complex League that first summer before taking to full-season ball last year with Single-A Palm Beach, where he was a solid performer. Cho slashed .270/.376/.389 with seven homers and 32 stolen bases over 105 games, finishing with an above-average 114 wRC+ in the pitcher-friendly FSL. Don’t be overly alarmed by Cho’s slugging percentage just yet. The left-handed slugger topped out with an 111.1 mph exit velocity – equal to the 2023 max EV of Adley Rutschman, Mac Muncy and Eugenio Suárez – and considering the 6-foot-1 outfielder is barely in his 20s, there could be more in the tank as he matures. Getting to that raw pop might take a slight change in mechanics and approach as Cho too often showed a willingness to spray the ball around, leading to a ground-ball rate of 50 percent. With a 14.2 percent walk rate, he also figured to be fairly selective, aiding the belief that he’ll be an average overall bat at each stop up the ladder. Cho is likely to settle in as an average runner, and the Cardinals have already moved the majority of his starts from center field to right. With his previous experience as a pitcher, he has the arm to work out there, and if he can turn more of his raw pop into in-game slugging ability, he’ll have the overall profile as well. A rough go at High-A Peoria in 2024 has dulled Cho's profile, but the Cardinals caution he was still only the age of an American college sophomore this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cho could have been selected in the 2021 KBO Draft in his native South Korea. Instead, he moved to Atlanta one month after his 18th birthday that fall in search of showing off for Major League scouts and a stateside deal. That came when the Cardinals signed Cho at the start of the 2022 international period on Jan. 15. The outfielder was limited by injuries to 26 games in the Florida Complex League during his rookie summer and hit .211/.400/.316 with five extra-base hits during his time there. Cho’s simple left-handed swing is part of the reason why the Cardinals were excited to add him to their mix. He flashed good power with it during a November 2020 showcase event at Globe Life Field in which he homered 15 times. It’s still mostly pop to the gaps in games now, however, but given his 6-foot-3 size as a teenager, there’s a belief that above-average power could come in time. He showed a willingness to walk early in his career, bordering on passivity, which helped fuel his OBP but may change if he gets more aggressive on pitches to drive. A solid runner early in his career, Cho is likely to slow down enough to move him out of center for good. Indeed, the majority of his defensive Minor League starts have come in the corners. A former pitcher, he has the arm for the corners, and while it’ll take some to develop, he could have the bat to fit there too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 De Andrade was in the top half of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list when he signed with the Twins in January 2021 for $2.2 million. After a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, he held his own stateside in the Florida Complex League. In 2023, he moved to full-season ball for the first time and showed off some of his tools with 11 homers and 20 steals in pitching-friendly Fort Myers. He wasn’t able to build off that in 2024 when an ankle injury that required surgery ended his season with High-A Cedar Rapids after just 29 games. He was supposed to head to the Arizona Fall League, but wasn’t ready, though he’s been given a clean bill of health for 2025. With the injury behind him, the hope is De Andrade can get back to building off a decent foundation of contact skills and ability to control the zone. He limits strikeouts, draws walks and was making better swing decisions overall, though his knack for contact has led to higher chase rates. He’s continued to try to get better swing angles, and while the surface numbers don’t show it during his small Midwest League showing in cold weather, his ground-ball rate went down as he started leveraging the ball in the air more. De Andrade was a fringy runner before the injury and he’ll have to work to maintain his athleticism. He has the hands and arm to play shortstop, which is where he’ll mostly play in 2025, though he’ll continue to get work at third and second as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects on the international market when the signing period opened in January 2021, De Andrade received a $2.2 million bonus from the Twins to sign then went about showing off his solid fundamental skills, even if they didn’t show up in eye-popping numbers. He was solid in the Dominican Summer League during his debut, showed some abilities to make adjustments when he came to the United States and played in the Florida Complex League in 2022 and continued making some progress during his full-season debut in 2023. His move to High-A in 2024 ended after just 29 games with an ankle injury that required surgery. From the outset of his pro career, De Andrade has shown off excellent bat-to-ball skills. He had stretches early on when he was making too much contact, chasing pitches out of the zone and getting himself out. Work he started putting in during his FCL season to cut his chase rate carried over to the Florida State League last year as he continues to refine his approach, make better swing decisions and draw more walks, all while still keeping the strikeouts relatively in check. He also made some subtle adjustments with his mechanics to get better swing angles and not hit the ball on the ground as much. He’s continuing to learn how to get the ball in the air more and hit the ball harder, which should help increase his power output. With good hands and a strong enough arm, combined with excellent instincts, De Andrade has a chance to stick at shortstop even though he’s a fringy runner. He’ll have stay on top of his conditioning so he doesn’t slow down too much to stay at the premium position. Though he played short exclusively in 2023, he has seen some time at third, which would put more pressure on his bat to produce.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 14 on MLB Pipeline’s Top International Prospects list when the signing period opened in January 2021, De Andrade was one of two players to get seven-figure bonuses from the Twins. The Venezuelan infielder signed for $2.2 million and had a solid, if unspectacular, debut in the Dominican Summer League. He came stateside in 2022, and after a rough start, showed improvement as the Florida Complex League season wore on. De Andrade’s knack for making contact is a blessing and a curse. He has very impressive bat-to-ball skills, having struck out in just over 15 percent of his plate appearances over his first two summers of pro ball. The down side is that he’s fallen into the habit of expanding the zone too much, something he got away with in the DSL, but then he was chasing and missing at the start of the FCL season. He focused on hunting pitches over the plate after his first month, and that cut his chase rate in half while sharply boosting his walk rate. He’s made some small swing adjustments as well, because he used to enter too steeply, which led to too many ground balls. That tweak plus added strength should help him turn his contact into more impact. While De Andrade doesn’t run particularly well, his instincts, hands and arm give him the chance to stick at shortstop, especially if he follows through with his conditioning. He’s seen time at third base already and could slide over if he slows down more, though that will put a little more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the good things about the international signing deadline not starting until January the last couple of years is that teams can get an almost immediate first impression of their new player that summer. That’s what happened with De Andrade, a Venezuelan infielder who had been training in the Dominican Republic. Ranked right in the middle of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list, De Andrade signed with the Twins for $2.2 million and then went out and had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League. De Andrade has the chance to be a plus hitter in time from the right side of the plate and stood out with his ability to control the strike zone, especially given his age (17) and lack of experience. There is bat speed and the ability to use all fields, though he’s content right now to focus on contact, and he did that well, rarely striking out even if he was a bit over-aggressive. The next step in his offensive development will be to work on driving the ball and doming more damage, something that will come as he physically matures. The teenaged infielder saw time at shortstop and third during his debut. The Twins think he has the chance to play up the middle for a while because of his actions, hands, arm and instincts. He’s not particularly speedy, so there is some thought that sliding over to the hot corner eventually might be in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2020-21 international signing period, which officially opened in mid-January, featured a class that was particularly deep at shortstop. De Andrade, a Venezuelan infielder who had been training in the Dominican Republic, was ranked No. 16 overall on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects rankings, the eighth shortstop on the list. The Twins liked his size and athleticism enough to give him $2.2 million to sign. De Andrade has the ingredients to develop into an impact hitter. He shows off excellent bat speed from the right side of the plate and can drive the ball to all fields. There are flashes of average power now, with above-average pop in the future possible as he adds strength to his lean frame. Added strength would also help him get close to being an average runner. Because of his soft hands, good footwork and arm, there’s a chance De Andrade could stick at short. It’s more likely, given his speed, that he’ll eventually slide over to third as he physically matures, where his actions and instincts could make him an above-average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets weren’t necessarily big spenders during the 2021 international signing period, but the organization was excited to see what Díaz could do as he entered pro ball out of the Dominican Republic. He shot out of a cannon that summer, posting a 0.54 ERA with 63 strikeouts and only nine walks over 50 1/3 innings in the Dominican Summer League, making him the only qualified Minor Leaguer with an ERA below 1.00 in 2021. His 2022 was much bumpier following an aggressive assignment to Single-A St. Lucie (5.86 ERA in 55 1/3 frames), but it was notable that he pitched the entire 2022 campaign at just 18 years old. Díaz underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring, causing him to miss the entire 2023 season. The 6-foot-2 right-hander showed a touch-above-average velocity last year with a fastball around 92-95 mph, reaching as high as 97. The offering’s ride up in the zone makes it work well in this modern age of pitching, and the Mets are hopeful more velocity could still be in the tank. His 79-81 mph curveball flashes plus potential with some steep vertical drop. Díaz gained more confidence in his mid-80s changeup as the summer wore on, and the sink on the cambio was good enough to keep whiffs coming. In fact, Díaz didn’t allow a single extra-base hit on his change in games measured by Statcast. Díaz didn’t flash the same stellar control he had in the DSL, but there were no signs that strike-throwing should be a major issue when healthy. That control will be worth monitoring when he returns from the elbow procedure at some point in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets didn’t ink any of the big names or spend big money on Jan. 15, 2021, but if there was one new prospect the player development staff was most eager to see, it was Diaz. The 6-foot-2 right-hander backed up that excitement with one of the best statistical Minor League pitching performances of the year, sporting a 0.54 ERA (making him the only MiLB qualifier with a mark below 1.00) while striking out 63 and walking only nine over 50 1/3 innings in the Dominican Summer League. Since 2010, only Sixto Sánchez (0.50) has posted a lower qualified ERA in his age-17 season. Diaz’s fastball is the star of the show at this very early stage of his career. He throws it in the low-90s now and touches as high as 96. The pitch already shows impressive ride up in the zone, making it well-suited for modern pitching philosophy. Diaz flashes a little more than just the fastball with a curveball with solid vertical break and a changeup with decent sink. Both could be average to plus pitches in time, but he has room to grow with both. Strikes were not an early issue with a 4.7 percent walk rate, though it’ll be interesting to see how that holds up against more advanced hitters. Diaz is very much a lottery ticket at this early stage of his career. If the velocity holds over a fuller season and the secondary stuff improves, he could be a star of the system in short order. So much else (health concerns, loss of stuff, fluctuating command) could happen in the meantime that would challenge that status. At minimum, he should be a fun follow to see what he can do for an encore in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs quickly became enchanted by Valdez's bat when they began scouting him in the Dominican Republic, and they signed him for $2.8 million after he developed into one of the best prospects in the 2023 class. When he turned pro, Chicago vice president of international scouting Louie Eljaua said Valdez had the potential to grown into a Starlin Castro build with Hanley Ramirez production. He scuffled in his pro debut, however, batting .234/.328/.477 with a 41 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. A right-handed hitter, Valdez has quick hands that produce plenty of bat speed and allow him to control the barrel well. He undermined himself in the DSL by chasing way too many pitches and trying to launch them as far as he could to his pull side. He does have plus raw power and could produce 20 or more homers per season, but he's going to have to significantly tone down his approach to survive against more advanced pitching. Valdez possesses solid speed but still has a lot to learn about basestealing. His instincts and actions should enable him to stick at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength. If he loses some quickness as he gains strength, he should be able to handle second or third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs fell in love with Valdez's bat soon after seeing him in the Dominican Republic. He blossomed into one of the top prospects in the 2023 international class and signed with Chicago for $2.8 million in January. Cubs vice president of international scouting Louie Eljaua said Valdez could grow into a Starlin Castro build and provide Hanley Ramirez production. While he doesn't have the all-around upside of fellow Dominican shortstop Cristian Hernandez, who signed for $3 million two years earlier, Valdez does have more pure hitting ability. A right-handed hitter, he's very advanced at the plate with gifted hands that produce plenty of bat speed and enable him to manipulate the barrel well. He uses the entire field and focuses on driving the ball from gap to gap with the promise of at least average power once he matures physically. An average runner, Valdez has good instincts and actions at shortstop. He should be able to remain at the position, but if he slows a bit as he gets stronger, he should have enough quickness and the solid arm strength to handle either second or third base. If he reaches his ceiling, he'll profile well offensively at any position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nuñez joined the Twins for $25,000 in November 2019 and dominated the Dominican Summer League when he made his debut in 2021. He was off to another solid start in the Florida Complex League a year later when Minnesota dealt him to the Orioles as part of the four-pitcher return for Jorge Lopez at the 2022 Trade Deadline. He finally got a full season’s worth of innings (104 2/3) in 2023 between Single-A and High-A and was back with Aberdeen for 2024, posting a 2.45 ERA with 38 strikeouts in 29 1/3 frames when he went down with a shoulder injury. After going unprotected, Nuñez went to the Padres in the Rule 5 Draft but was returned to Baltimore at the end of Spring Training. The right-hander’s stuff plays bigger than his size at 5-foot-11. His fastball can touch the occasional 97 mph but typically settles in the mid-90s, though High-A hitters slugged .481 against it. Nuñez almost threw his gyro slider as often as the heater against righties, and they couldn’t much handle it with a 47 percent whiff rate and 35 percent chase rate. Thought to be a developing pitch entering the year, Nuñez’s changeup was a similar menace, tunneling well off the fastball only to dive armside late. It stood out more for its movement than its separation, but both lefties and righties couldn’t touch it in limited usage. Nuñez did a better job of cutting down walks in the short 2024 sample, but control had been a serious issue before that. The arsenal is interesting, but the hurler is also entering his age-24 campaign with only one season above 100 innings, no upper-level experience and a recent injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the four pitching prospects acquired by the Orioles when they sent Jorge Lopez to the Twins at the 2022 Trade Deadline, Nuñez had to wait two years before throwing his first official pitch after signing with Minnesota in November 2019 for just $25,000. The pandemic erased what should’ve been his debut in 2020, and he was throwing well in the Florida Complex League at age 21 when the Orioles picked him up. Nuñez then pitched his way from Single-A Delmarva to High-A Aberdeen in his first full season with his new organization, flashing power stuff but iffy control. He was off to a promising start back with Aberdeen this year before being shut down for the year in May with a shoulder issue. After Nuñez was left off the O’s 40-man in the offseason, the Padres selected him in the Rule 5 Draft, giving him a shot at the Majors for 2025. Nuñez may only be 5-foot-11, but his stuff is big. He has the ability to miss bats with everything in his four-pitch mix, working his secondary stuff off a fastball that can flash 96-97 but typically settles consistently in the mid-90s. He throws a power curve and a gyro slider that flash plus, as well as a developing changeup that could become at least an average pitch. He pitches with quick arm action but there is some effort to his delivery. While he’s strong and compact, sub-6-footers often have trouble making it to the big leagues as a starting pitcher. Control is also a problem after Nuñez walked 13 percent of batters last summer. He’ll need to reverse that trend and prove his health if he’s going to stick in The Show in ‘25, especially with San Diego’s plans for contention in mind.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres didn’t have too much time to show what he could do at North Carolina State, with the pandemic shortening his freshman year and him leaving after the 2021 season as a Draft-eligible sophomore. He played enough to convince scouts his glove alone was worth drafting, and his power production as a sophomore helped him land in the third round of that summer’s Draft. After a solid pro debut, his first full season in High-A in 2022 was rough offensively. There are some things Torres can do well from the right side of the plate when he stays within himself. He uses his hands well with some feel for the barrel, with some seeing a little Tim Anderson in his setup and mechanics. At his best, he’s shown good feel for the zone and a gap-to-gap swing, but he doesn’t see enough pitches and gets into trouble when he tries to do too much and sells out for power, leading to too many swings and misses. If Torres can simplify things at the plate, he’ll be able to impact a big league team sooner rather than later because of his glove. He’ll be a shortstop for a long time, with outstanding actions and hands to go along with a plus arm and terrific instincts. He saw a lot of time at second base in 2022, both because of personnel on the same team and the fact that the lack of offensive profile points to a likely career as a defense-first utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres was Maryland’s best high school prospect in 2019, but opted to head to North Carolina State for college. The Dominican-born shortstop was Draft-eligible in his second year of college in 2021 and while he didn’t go in the first round, like former Wolfpack shortstops Trea Turner and Will Wilson, he did land in the third round with the Reds, then went out and had an impressive pro debut, mostly in Low-A. Torres’ calling card in defense was, and continues to be, his work at shortstop. Though he’s a fringy runner, he has excellent instincts that help him cover a lot of ground to go along with smooth actions, plus hands and a plus arm. While there were concerns about how his bat would play at the next level, the Reds have been pleasantly surprised with his right-handed swing. He’s always had good bat speed and some sneaky power, but got into trouble in college by getting overly aggressive at the plate. In the brief sample of his pro debut, Torres showed good plate awareness, didn’t chase too often and showed off an excellent gap-to-gap line drive swing. If he can continue to perform offensively like that, he has the chance to be a big league regular at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Viars entered his senior season of Texas high school baseball as a bit of an unknown because he wasn’t a presence on the summer showcase circuit, but his power and athleticism opened the eyes of some scouts in the spring of 2021. That led to the Phillies taking him in the third round of that summer’s Draft and going a little over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Arkansas, and they were encouraged by early returns from his pro debut. He was greatly slowed in 2022 by a bad ankle sprain and by getting hit in the hand by a pitch. The Phillies are still high on Viars’ set of tools. He’s a strong and physical right-handed hitter who has the chance to hit, and hit with power. He sees the ball very well and has a decent overall approach, and while he was out of sync for much of the 2022 season, he still showed the ability to impact the ball when he made contact. His swing features bat speed to go along with leverage and loft that points to solid future power. Viars runs well for his size, with decent straight-line speed, though he might slow down a bit as he physically matures. After playing first base and the outfield during his summer debut, he was exclusively a left fielder last year, which could be a good long-term fit. The Phillies are hopeful a full, healthy season will help Viars tap into his considerable offensive potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Viars was a bit of an off-the-radar prospect out of the Texas high school ranks as the 2021 Draft approached, albeit one with a commitment to Arkansas, mostly because he didn’t hit the summer showcase circuit before his senior year. A strong senior season brought some interest and the Phillies nabbed him the third round and signed him away from heading to play for the Razorbacks. He had a solid, but brief, debut in the Florida Complex League. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Viars is big and physical with a ton of now strength. He sees the ball really well and uses a swing with leverage and loft that has the chance to deliver a lot of power. It started to show up during his senior year of high school and he showed a solid overall approach during his summer debut. Viars is a better athlete than you’d think and is a pretty good straight-line runner, though he might slow down some as he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame. He’s shown some positional versatility, with the ability to play some center field, the outfield corners (a more likely long-term fit) and some first base, but it’s his power bat that will carry him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meza was one of the top catchers on the 2022 international market and signed with the Blue Jays for a bonus of $2,050,000. The No. 33 prospect in that class per MLB Pipeline, he joined a system that had recently produced Gabriel Moreno and Alejandro Kirk as potential stars after signing each to much smaller bonuses. Meza’s 2022 debut was a learning experience. Pressing at times as he tried to produce early, he hit .229 with a .559 OPS over 28 games in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old. The Blue Jays still like his foundational tools, though, and expect him to bounce back. There will be plenty of patience too as catchers typically take longer to develop, and he still has years of growth ahead of him. It still may be a year or two until you see Meza with a full-season affiliate, but the Blue Jays will continue to bring him along at his own pace. Like all new international signings, he should benefit greatly from having access to the Blue Jays’ new player development complex and their physical program from such a young age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meza was one of the top catchers available on the International market, signing with Toronto out of Venezuela in January of ’22 for $2.05 million. The young backstop was ranked as the No. 33 overall prospect in the class and joined a system that’s begun to regularly produce talent at the premium position. The Blue Jays were attracted to Meza’s potential as a defender behind the plate, where he’s showing early signs of strong catch-and-throw skills along with the potential to be an above-average receiver and blocker. Scouts are also high on Meza’s baseball IQ and fundamentals across the board for a player his age. While he’s listed at 5-foot-10, Meza comes with a broad frame that should allow him to add some muscle and hold up against the wear and tear of catching as he develops. Meza can drive the ball to all fields, but the development of his power long term will be worth monitoring. At such a young age, Meza is further from the Major Leagues than any prospect on this list, but he has some high-upside building blocks for the Blue Jays’ development staff to work with.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays targeted Barriera with the No. 23 overall pick in the ‘22 Draft, signing him to an above-slot bonus of $3,597,500. Barriera had development staffers buzzing in early ‘24, but he suffered an elbow injury early in the season that required a hybrid Tommy John and internal brace procedure. Soon after he returned in ‘25, he was sidelined again with a fracture in his forearm, so this has been a long and frustrating stretch of Barriera being forced to start over. It’s time to begin again, though, and Barriera only turns 22 in March. There’s plenty of time for the Blue Jays to work with here and the optimism is back. He’s been living at 96-98 mph with his fastball on the backfields, but the key is for Barriera to find a consistent release point, which was a struggle in his brief time back on the mound in 2025 (eight walks in 5 2/3 innings). At this point, more game action is needed to see if Barriera’s plus slider is back to where it was before the injuries, but he finally has a shot at a healthy season. Expect him to be built up very carefully. The numbers won’t matter much for Barriera in 2026. The Blue Jays simply want the young left-hander to get out there and compete again, which would set him up with a foundation for ‘27. Barriera feels like an arm who could generate some serious buzz (again) a year from now if it all goes well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barriera was one of the top prep pitchers in the 2023 class and represented a sort of middle ground between high school and college arms with a rare combination of upside and polish. The Blue Jays targeted Barriera with the No. 23 overall pick in the ‘22 Draft, signing him to an above-slot bonus of $3,597,500. Barriera had development staffers buzzing in early ‘24, but he suffered an elbow injury early in the season that required a hybrid Tommy John and internal brace procedure. After losing a crucial year of development, Barriera is scheduled to return to game action in May or June. Prior to that injury, Barriera’s stuff was all the way back. He was hitting 97 mph in spring games a year ago, paired with a slider that projects as a legitimate out pitch at the next level. While the surgery was a major setback, Barriera used the time to get his body in better shape, and the Blue Jays believed they were getting the best version they’ve seen of him yet. He made five rehab starts in the Florida Complex League in 2025 before suffering yet another unfortunate injury -- this time a small fractured piece of his forearm -- and that ended his season in July. Barriera will still only be 22 entering 2026, but his prospect status is wearing thin, regardless of how he's looked in various comebacks. Getting healthy and sticking to the mound in games will be paramount next season, especially with the Jays' pitching pipeline getting all the stronger this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barriera had generated plenty of buzz on the showcase circuit leading up to the 2022 Draft and represented an exciting middle ground between the upside typically found in high-school arms and the polish typically found in NCAA pitchers. The Blue Jays targeted Barriera with the No. 23 overall pick in the ‘22 Draft, signing him to an above-slot bonus of $3,597,500. The organization has hoped to get Barriera to the same jumping-off point that Ricky Tiedemann experienced a year prior, but injuries slowed that process. That continued into 2024 when the southpaw made one Single-A start before suffering a left elbow injury that required a hybrid Tommy John and internal brace procedure. He will miss the rest of the season as a result. Barriera’s pro debut in 2023 was slowed by a separate pair of arm injuries, and his velocity lived more in the 92-93 mph range, a step back from the 95-96 fastball that excited scouts leading up to the Draft. Barriera had a reputation for a solid low-80s slider and upper-80s changeup, but as he continued to work around physical issues, the young left-hander never quite settled into a groove or found the momentum he needed. His 20 1/3 innings (3.98 ERA) didn’t offer much of a snapshot. Barriera got his body right this offseason and looked better physically than he did a year ago, but the elbow issue came all the same. Given that he only turned 20 in March, there is plenty of time for the development staff and Barriera to build something exciting together when he gets back on the mound in 2025. He should still have the polish to attack hitters and put up excellent numbers in the lower levels when healthy, but staying that way and maintaining his stuff are the keys for Barriera, now more than ever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: American Heritage High School in Plantation, Fla., has been known more for its hitters (Eric Hosmer, Triston Casas) than its pitchers over the years, but Barriera could change that. The southpaw was a showcase circuit standout heading into 2022, highlighted by a perfect inning at the High School All-American Game in Denver. MLB Pipeline’s No. 15 Draft prospect in 2022, Barriera went to the Blue Jays at No. 23 in July (eventually signing for an above-slot $3,597,500 bonus). While not a massive or projectable presence on the mound at 6-foot-2, Barriera does show promising stuff in his quest to be a Major League starter. His fastball sat in the low-90s as a high schooler, and after not pitching officially in the Minors post-Draft, he was touching 97-98 during fall bullpen sessions. The heater has late movement too, which can help it play up. He mixes in a low-80s slider with promising sweep that acts as his primary off-speed pitch, and his mid-80s changeup looks like the fastball out of the hand, giving it above-average potential too. Jays coaches have come to appreciate how Barriera isn’t afraid to attack hitters in the strike zone, and that mentality, mixed with the quality of his stuff, makes him a future rotation candidate. His size calls into question whether he’ll be durable enough to handle that load, and those questions have gotten louder as he's missed time in 2023 with elbow, shoulder and biceps issues. Gearing up for a true full season will be a priority moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever at Southern Miss and in the Cape Cod League, the 2022 sixth-rounder moved to a starting role in the Mets organization and took off quickly with a 2.20 ERA and 112 strikeouts in 110 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A in his first full season.
