He was off to a solid start back in Binghamton to open 2024 when he was traded to the Nationals in late July in a one-for-one deal for outfielder Jesse Winker. He split his remaining eight starts between Double-A Harrisburg and Triple-A Rochester, stumbling a bit with a 7.56 ERA at the Minors’ top level. At 6-foot-9, Stuart will be one of the Majors’ tallest pitchers immediately upon arrival; only Bailey Ober and Sean Hjelle were that height or taller in 2024. But he doesn’t stand out for his physical presence on the bump so much as he does for his special breaking stuff. Stuart twirls an 82-85 mph slider with good two-plane break. He commands the pitch well in spite of the movement, and the slider got a 41 percent whiff rate across all levels in 2024. He’ll use it like a primary pitch at times. That’s a sensible move considering his 93-95 mph sinker is more prone to be hit hard when it catches too much of the zone. There’s also an 85-87 mph changeup and harder 89-91 mph cutter to play with. Stuart’s walk rate climbed to 13.2 percent during his four-start stay in Triple-A, but the control has been at least average at every spot. Despite his large frame, it can look like he’s playing catch with the backstop. Stuart battled elbow issues for much of 2025, making only 10 appearances (nine starts) across three levels, before undergoing Tommy John surgery that will knock him out for much (if not all) of 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stuart worked mostly as a reliever at Southern Miss and in the Cape Cod League, but after his selection in the sixth round in 2022, the Mets transitioned him to starter -- and a statistically impressive one at that. The right-hander led full-season Minor League qualifiers with a 2.20 ERA and ranked 12th among the 183 on that list with his 1.10 WHIP over 110 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. That said, his numbers at the higher level were closer to pedestrian (3.60 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 19.3 percent K rate) as he faced more advanced bats. He was a solid starter back at Binghamton in 2024 and was dealt to the Nationals in late July in a straight-up swap for outfielder Jesse Winker. Standing 6-foot-9 (yes, 6-foot-9), Stuart tends to start with his low-80s slider, which he threw roughly half the time in 2023, and for good reason. The pitch can show good two-plane break and sweep, leading to above-average whiff rates especially when it’s located on the edges of the zone. But it can hang in the zone at other times and get thumped. His 91-94 mph fastball shows sink and run in the other direction and can be tough to square up from his low three-quarters arm slot, giving him two potentially above-average pitches. Stuart’s changeup remains a distant third option. Stuart didn’t walk more than 7.6 percent of his batters faced at either level in 2023, and he fills the zone better than expected for someone his size. That control is one reason why the Mets wanted to give him starting looks in the pros, but he needs a more well-rounded arsenal to lock in that status. He’ll continue that work at the upper levels of the Washington system with his sights set on a potential debut next spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez stood out as a teenager for a high baseball IQ befitting a player whose father, Jose, is a scout for the Brewers in their home country of Venezuela. Gabriel signed with the Guardians for $500,000 in 2024 and carried his amateur success over to his pro debut, where he posted a .904 OPS in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He played well in his stateside debut in the Arizona Complex League (.795 OPS) last year but only played 28 games between a hamstring injury and extra time in the weight room. Rodriguez, who was born in Florida, is taller than most Guardians infield prospects and continuing to grow. He signed with the team at 6-foot, 145 pounds, and has already grown an inch and added 25 pounds. Rodriguez does not yet hit for much power but has plenty of projectability in his lanky frame. He shows traits for an above-average hit tool with a pretty left-handed swing geared for low contact, good barrel feel and a discerning eye. Although the Guardians have played him at short, third and second, Rodriguez projects as at least an average shortstop, where his instincts and hands stand out, and his speed and arm strength are above-average. Added impact at the plate will determine his ceiling, but his impressive defense for his age gives him a solid floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Florida, Rodriguez grew up in Venezuela, where his father Jose scouts for the Brewers. As an amateur, he impressed with his performance against high-level competition (he batted .400 without a strikeout in 23 plate appearances at a 15-and-under World Cup qualifier in 2022) and the high baseball IQ he developed while being raised around the game. Signed for $500,000 in 2024, he ranked second in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with a .506 on-base percentage in his pro debut. Rodriguez recognizes pitches and makes better swing decisions than most players his age. A left-handed hitter, he uses the entire field well and shows some aptitude for pulling pitches and lifting them in the air. His bat-to-ball skills could translate into 20 homers per season once he fills out his lean 6-foot-frame. Rodriguez's instincts help him play quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the middle infield. More sure-handed than spectacular at shortstop, he committed just two errors in 26 games there last summer. He also saw action at second base, which may be a better long-term fit for his average range and arm strength, and has gotten some time at third base in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez signed out of Venezuela in 2018 for $2.1 million, which remains a Guardians record for an international position player. He batted .234/.300/.331 in his first two pro seasons, though he was younger than most of his competition. He made his U.S. debut at age 17 at the end of the 2019 season, and he was the fifth-youngest regular in the Low-A East last year at 19. The raw ingredients are there for Rodriguez to hit for some average with 20 or more homers per year. He has a compact right-handed stroke with bat speed that produces high exit velocities when he connects, and he shows a willingness to use the entire field. To reach his ceiling, he'll need to get stronger while improving his ability to recognize pitches and manage the strike zone. Rodriguez split most of his first full pro season between third base and shortstop while also getting brief action in right field and at first base. With average speed and solid arm strength, he fits best at the hot corner. He does have good instincts and body control for a youngster, but he probably won't have enough quickness and range at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez might have the highest ceiling among all of the international middle infielders in whom Cleveland has invested heavily in recent years. He signed out of Venezuela in 2018 for $2.1 million, which remains a franchise record for an international position player. He was advanced enough to venture to the United States at the end of his 2019 pro debut, though Rookie-level Arizona League pitchers exposed his lack of patience at the plate, and he participated in instructional league last fall. Rodriguez employs a compact right-handed stroke and shows a willingness to use the entire field. He has the hitting ability and solid bat speed for 20 homers per season as he continues to add strength, starts to pull more pitches and learns to drive more balls in the air. To reach his offensive potential, he'll have to do a better job of recognizing pitches and controlling the strike zone, two areas in which he struggled when he came to the AZL. Presently an average runner, Rodriguez could slow down as he fills out. Nevertheless, the Indians believe his actions, body control and solid arm may enable him to stay at shortstop. Scouts outside the organization think it's more likely that he'll move to third base, where he made 15 of his 48 starts during his debut, and he should provide enough offense to fit there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians have invested heavily in several international middle infielders in recent years, and Rodriguez has the highest ceiling of all of them. They signed him out of Venezuela in 2018 for $2.1 million, a franchise record for an international position player. He was advanced enough to come to the United States at the end of his 2019 pro debut but may not reach full-season ball until 2021. Rodriguez has the potential for at least average tools across the board and stands out most with his offensive potential. He has a compact right-handed stroke, some patience at the plate and a knack for using the entire field. His hitting ability, solid bat speed and projectable strength could translate into 20 homers per season if he makes some adjustments to pull the ball more often and drive more balls in the air. Presently an average runner, Rodriguez could lose a step once he matures physically. Cleveland believes his infield actions, body control and solid arm give him a chance to stick at shortstop. Other scouts believe he'll likely wind up at third base, where he made 15 of his 48 starts during his debut, and his bat should profile at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez's all-around potential and his track record of hitting in tournament competition made him the Indians' top target in the 2018 international crop. They signed the Venezuelan as soon as he became eligible for $2.1 million, a franchise record for an international position player. Cleveland has invested in several shortstops from the worldwide market in recent years, and none has a higher ceiling than Rodriguez. While he doesn't have a wow tool, Rodriguez has average to solid ability across the board and the instincts to get the most out of it. He's an advanced hitter for a teenager, displaying a disciplined approach and a willingness to use the entire field. His hitting acumen, solid bat speed and projectable strength give him a good chance to develop average power. Rodriguez has average speed but could lose a half-step as he matures physically. If that happens, most scouts think he'll wind up at third base, where his bat and solid arm would fit nicely. The Indians think his body control, actions and arm can keep him at shortstop and they'll try to do so as long as possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mattison has flashed a world of potential in small doses since the Tigers drafted the former Northeast Conference Pitcher of the Year out of Bryant. After missing a chunk of the 2022 season due to arm fatigue, he showed enough strikeout potential in the Arizona Fall League to warrant a promotion out of Single-A Lakeland, setting up a dominant 2023 campaign between High-A West Michigan and Double-A Erie. He seemed on the fast track to Detroit when Tommy John surgery ended his 2024 season before it could start. Mattison is a classic big-framed power pitcher, with a fastball that creeps into the upper 90s, an upper-80s changeup and a hard slider. He can be prone to walks at times but did well to temper that down the stretch in 2023. How that command looks post-surgery is a big question that could guide his path to Detroit. Even with Mattison’s rehab stretching into 2025, the Tigers thought enough of him to protect him on the 40-man roster and bring him into big league camp for Spring Training to work with Tigers pitching coaches while finishing his rehab. A midseason return seems likely, but if his arsenal returns to form, the Tigers might not hesitate to move him aggressively, putting him in line for a potential debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bryant University has produced just two Major Leaguers, most recently James Karinchak, but the Tigers saw a potential hard-throwing reliever in Mattison when they drafted the former Bulldogs starter and Northeast Conference Pitcher of the Year in the fourth round in 2021. After throwing just 39 2/3 innings in a 2022 season interrupted by arm fatigue, Mattison used the Arizona Fall League to build momentum for a breakout '23 campaign, averaging 6.0 hits and 13.7 strikeouts per nine innings. He tossed 11 hitless innings to begin his Double-A Erie tenure before helping power the SeaWolves to an Eastern League title. Mattison is a prototypical power reliever with a mid-90s fastball, but he can reach into the upper-90s when he’s going right. His combination of quick arm action and high arm angle creates some deception, allowing the fastball to play up. His fastball command progressed markedly last year as he learned to work up and down in the zone. He complements the heater with a low-80s curveball and a mid-80s changeup that improved last year. Though the fastball is his dominant pitch, he’s confident enough to throw secondary pitches to steal early strikes. Mattison has the arsenal to become a Major League reliever if he can continue to use all parts of the strike zone with his fastball and command his secondary pitches, both of which he’ll need to do against older hitters in Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers saw a potential small-college gem when they drafted Mattison in the fourth round in 2021 out of Bryant, where he had a dominant senior season to earn Northeast Conference Pitcher of the Year honors. Three walks over two innings in his pro debut raised concerns, but after a two-month break due to arm fatigue, he bounced back with a solid stretch run at Single-A Lakeland, followed by 19 strikeouts over 11 1/3 innings in the Arizona Fall League. Mattison uses his 6-foot-4 frame well in his delivery, bringing a fastball down on hitters from a high arm slot. It generally sat at 93-95 mph but reached 96-97 on occasion. His upper-80s changeup played well off the velocity bump, and he throws a cutter/slider and an 82-84 mph curveball. The big concern is his command, especially with the fastball, evidenced by eight walks in the AFL. Between a four-year college career and a shortened first pro season, Mattison had been on the older side for everywhere he played until reaching Double-A Erie this summer. His walk rate remained in check while the strikeouts remained high, leading him to see the upper Minors for the first time. A 2024 debut could be in the cards if he keeps up this momentum.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last and least expensive player signed in the Astros' 2021 international crop, Fleury turned pro for $10,000 that December out of the Dominican Republic. He made a spectacular pro debut in 2022, compiling a 1.42 ERA and 60/4 K/BB ratio in 38 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, then jumped from Single-A in 2023 to Double-A the following year. He posted a 1.82 ERA in Double-A in the first half of 2025, missing a month with shoulder issues, then tasted adversity for the first time when he got rocked for a 6.95 ERA in Triple-A. Fleury's success stems from his changeup, which sits around 80 mph with plenty of fade and depth, parachuting through the bottom right-hand corner of the strike zone. He struggled in Triple-A when hitters sat on his cambio because his other fringy pitches couldn't make them pay. His fastball features good carry but sits around 90 mph and peaks at 94. His low-80s cutter, 78-82 mph slider and mid-70s curveball all lack power and get barreled. The 6-foot Fleury lacks physicality but his athleticism helps him repeat his high arm slot and provide regular strikes. It also allows him to get down the mound well and create atypical extension for his size. He has some of best feel for pitching in the system but will have to upgrade his arsenal to claim a regular role in Houston.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The final and cheapest player signed in Houston's 2021 international class, Fleury turned pro for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic that December. He broke into pro ball by logging a 1.42 ERA with a 60/4 K/BB ratio in 38 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2022. He continued to dominate in Single-A in his U.S. debut the following year, then skipped a level and held his own in Double-A last year despite a thigh injury that sidelined him for two months. Fleury's changeup has fueled his success, operating in the low 80s with fade and huge depth while deceiving both lefties and righties. It drops through the bottom of the strike zone and pairs nicely with a 90-92 mph fastball that tops out at 94 and stands out much more with its carry than its velocity. He trusts his low-80s slider more than his upper-70s curveball, though neither is as effective as his cambio or heater. Fleury makes up for a lack of physicality with athleticism and a fluid, high three-quarters delivery that he repeats well. He adds deception by getting down the mound well and creating a low-release height with quality extension. He doesn't have a high ceiling but can be a No. 4 or 5 starter if he can find a little more velocity or improve his breaking stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last and least expensive player signed by the Astros in their 2021 international class, Fleury turned pro for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic that December. He made a spectacular pro debut in 2022, recording a 1.42 ERA with a 60/4 K/BB ratio in 38 innings in the Dominican Summer League. He came to the United States last year and earned All-Star accolades in the Carolina League, where his strikeout rate (12.7 per nine innings) and average-against (.181) would easily have topped the Single-A circuit if he hadn't fallen just short of qualifying. Fleury's low-80s changeup has significant fade and has keyed his early career success. It helps him make the most of a fastball that stands out more for its induced vertical break and carry coming out of a low release height than it does for its velocity, operating at 90-92 mph and topping out at 94. He throws two breaking balls, with his upper-70s curveball grading better than a tight 78-82 mph slider, though both need work. Though he lacks physicality, Fleury is athletic and repeats his delivery well. While his walk rate jumped from 0.9 per nine innings in his debut to 4.4 in 2023, he should have at least average control once he's fully developed. Adding some velocity and refining his breaking stuff would help raise his ceiling, but he's on a promising path to becoming a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fleury was the last and least expensive player signed by the Astros in its 2021 international class, turning pro in December for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He broke into pro ball in spectacular fashion, posting a 60/4 K/BB ratio with a 1.42 ERA in 38 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He continued to impress during instructional league, building anticipation for his U.S. debut in 2023. Fleury's best offering is his low-80s changeup, which features plenty of fade and plays well off his fastball. He doesn't throw especially hard, sitting at 90-92 mph and touching 94, but his heater has outstanding vertical movement and good carry coming out of a low release height. His breaking pitches need significant work because his 75-78 mph curveball gets slurvy and blends with his tight 78-82 mph slider. Though young DSL hitters don't exactly have refined plate discipline, Fleury's strike-throwing numbers are nonetheless impressive. He lacks physicality but is athletic and repeats his delivery well. He needs to refine a better breaking ball and is years from the Majors, but he has starter traits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers planned to sign Mata in July 2015 before a groin injury scuttled the deal, and he turned pro with the Red Sox instead six months later for $25,000. He blossomed into Boston's best pitching prospect before losing 2020 to the pandemic and 2021 to Tommy John surgery. He recaptured his stuff and pitched well in Triple-A by the end of 2022, but he worked just 27 innings last year while plagued by shoulder inflammation and an inability to throw strikes. Mata sits at 94-96 mph and reaches triple digits with both his two-seam and four-seam fastballs, and the former is more effective because of its power sink. His mid-80s slider can be a plus pitch with significant sweep, though he turned it into more of an upper-80s cutter last year. He lost trust in his mid-80s changeup with late fade as well as in an ineffective upper-70s curveball he should discard. Mata's delivery features effort, and he has trouble keeping it in sync, resulting in a lack of fastball command and an inability to land his secondary pitches for strikes. He walked just two batters in nine Arizona Fall League innings, but he also surrendered nine runs on 11 hits. Once viewed as a mid-rotation starter, he's out of options and likely will stick with the Red Sox in a relief role that won't give him the innings he needs to work out his issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mata originally agreed to sign with the Brewers in July 2015 before they declined after he suffered a groin injury, so he turned pro with the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. He established himself as Boston's top pitching prospect before losing two years of development to the pandemic in 2020 and Tommy John surgery in 2021. He returned to the mound last June and recaptured his previous stuff, but he has been waylaid by shoulder inflammation and control woes this season. Though Mata can run his four-seam fastball up to 101 mph, it lacks life and isn't nearly as effective as his 94-96 mph two-seamer with power sink. While his heaters generate more weak contact than swings and misses, his upper-80s slider dodges plenty of bats with its horizontal action. His mid-80s changeup grades as a plus pitch with late fade at its best, though it can get too firm and straight at times, and he should scrap his ineffective upper-70s curveball. Despite three quality pitches, Mata isn't a slam-dunk starter. He's not as dominant as his stuff suggests he should be, and he's not efficient because he lacks consistent control and doesn't command his secondary pitches well. There's an increasingly strong possibility that he's more of a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mata planned on signing with the Brewers in July 2015 before they backed out when he suffered a groin injury, and he inked with the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. The Venezuelan was the youngest pitcher (age 19) in the 2018 SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and established himself as Boston's top pitching prospect while reaching Double-A the following year. He lost two years of development to the 2020 pandemic shutdown and 2021 Tommy John surgery but should return to the mound by the middle of this season. Before he got hurt, Mata had electric sink and unusual velocity on a two-seam fastball that sat at 93-97 mph and created a lot of weak groundball contact. Both his upper-80s slider and fading mid-80s changeup graded as plus pitches at times, with his slider more reliable because he trusted it more. He also has a four-seam fastball that reaches 100 mph but lacks life and a slurvy curveball he never has shown much feel for. Boston brought Mata to its alternate training site in 2020 to work on simplifying his delivery so he could provide more frequent and better strikes. His control had gone haywire in 2018 and his command regressed when he reached Double-A the next summer, so he's seeking more consistency. He still has the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter but could end up as a multi-inning reliever if he can't add more polish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Brewers backed out of a deal to sign Mata in July 2015 when he came down with a groin injury, the Venezuelan landed with the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. He was the youngest pitcher (age 19) in the 2018 SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game but also dealt with a sore back and severe control issues that summer, then dominated high Class A but struggled in Double-A in 2019. Throughout those ups and downs, he has established himself as Boston's best pitching prospect, and he reinforced that status with his performance at the club's alternate site last year. Mata has electric sink and unusual velocity on his two-seam fastball, which sits at 93-97 mph and generates more weak groundball contact than swings and misses, and he also throws a four-seamer that reached triple digits in the Arizona Fall League in 2019 but features ordinary life. Both his upper-80s slider and fading changeup can be plus pitches at times, with his slider more reliable because he uses it more. He never had much feel for spinning a curveball that predates his slider but still has the curve in his repertoire. While Mata slashed his walk rate from 7.3 per nine innings in 2018 to 3.6 in 2019, he got knocked around when his control and command weren't as sharp in Double-A. The Red Sox helped him simplify his delivery at their alt site and were impressed by the increased frequency and quality of his strikes. He has the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter, but his development is on hold after he was diagnosed with a small ligament tear in his elbow during Spring Training and underwent Tommy John surgery in April.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Mata was set to sign with the Brewers out of Venezuela in July 2015 before a groin injury quashed that deal, setting the stage for him to join the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. The youngest pitcher (age 19) in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in 2018, he battled a sore back and severe control issues that summer. He bounced back to dominate last year in Class A Advanced, though he struggled after a promotion made him the second-youngest arm in the Double-A Eastern League. Mata's two-seam fastball is notable for both its velocity, sitting at 93-97 mph when he starts, and its electric sink, which helped him produce a 2.2 groundout/airout ratio in 2019. After struggling to refine his curveball, he has found much more success with a power slider in the mid-80s. He also has a fading changeup that he throws with deceptive arm speed, though he doesn't employ it as often as he did before he had a reliable breaking ball. As he grew to 6-foot-3 and 240 pounds, Mata needed time to adapt to his larger frame. He cut his walk rate from 7.3 per nine innings in 2018 to 3.6 last season, though his control wavered in Double-A. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but also reached triple digits with his fastball and pushed his slider into the upper 80s as a reliever in the Arizona Fall League, showing closer potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Mata expected to sign with the Brewers at the start of the 2015 international signing period that July, but a groin injury squashed that deal and he wound up joining the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. He was the youngest pitcher (age 19) in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in 2018, though his rocky season ended shortly afterward because of a sore back. He has come back better than ever this year, adding a slider and improving his velocity and control. Mata has the potential for three solid or better offerings, starting with a fastball that ranges from 93-98 mph with late sink that induces a lot of swings and misses as well as weak grounders. He didn't have much success with his curveball in 2018 and now relies more on a power slider in the mid-80s. He also sells a fading changeup with deceptive arm speed. At least 50 pounds heavier than his listed weight of 160, Mata has learned how to adapt to his bigger body. After displaying advanced pitchability in the past, he saw his walk rate jump from 3.0 per nine innings in 2017 to 7.3 last year, but he's back to throwing strikes. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Though he was eligible to sign out of Venezuela in July 2015, Mata had to wait six months before the Red Sox offered him a $25,000 bonus. His success during his 2016 pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League prompted Boston to jump him to low Class A last season, when he was the youngest player in the South Atlantic League at age 18. He handled the challenge with aplomb and helped Greenville win the SAL championship, then encored by pitching in the SiriusXM All-Star Future Game in 2018. Mata combines promising present stuff with projectability and pitchability. He already has a 90-94 mph fastball that reaches 97 mph with late life, and his quick arm and room to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame bode well for developing a consistent plus heater. His changeup is his best secondary offering, as he throws it with deceptive arm speed and fade, and has similar upside. Mata has good shape to his curveball and can throw it for strikes, and it shows flashes of becoming a solid pitch now that he has added power to it in 2018. He misses bats, generates a lot of ground balls and has the upside of a No. 3 starter. After showing advanced pitchability for a teenager in the past, his control has regressed this season, which could slow down his timetable for arriving in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dohm worked out of the bullpen at both Ball State and Mississippi State as a freshman and sophomore, respectively, before joining the Bulldogs rotation as a junior in 2024. A forearm strain slowed an otherwise hot start, but after re-establishing his health later in the spring and participating in the MLB Draft Combine, he went to the Mets in the third round and signed for below slot at $797,500. He put up solid numbers at Single-A and High-A to begin his first full season in 2025 and was moved to the Cardinals at the Trade Deadline as part of the return for closer Ryan Helsley. Dohm couldn’t find similar results at High-A Peoria after the deal and returned to the Midwest League to begin ’26. The 6-foot-4 right-hander shows a 93-96 mph four-seamer that can zip past batters at the top of the zone with impressive carry. He could reach 99 as a reliever in college in a sign that the pitch could be even more explosive in shorter stints if and when he needs to head back to the bullpen. His 83-86 mph slider can flash hard, late bite to get something move gloveside and similarly generate whiffs. He has much more trouble landing a changeup for strikes, and lefties have become a concern in pro ball without the third pitch. Dohm had started to show improved control as a Mets starter but hasn’t been able to replicate that in either of his Peoria stints so far. He needs batters to chase the high heaters and diving breaking balls to be effective, and that could be a challenge as he climbs. He has the chance for two above-average, bat-missing pitches though and could let them fly to their full potential with a move back to relief, if the control never comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dohm pitched in relief at Ball State as a freshman in 2022 and transferred to the Mississippi State bullpen a year later. He finally got a chance to start with the Bulldogs as a junior and started fast with a 1.50 ERA and 32/4 K/BB ratio through his first four starts. But a forearm strain slowed him for much of the spring, and he mostly made short appearances when he fully returned in late May. He helped his case with two dominant innings against Texas A&M in the SEC tournament, participated in the MLB Draft Combine and went to the Mets in the third round before signing for below slot at $797,500. After Dohm posted solid numbers at Single-A and High-A to begin his first full season, New York traded him to St. Louis in a big move for closer Ryan Helsley at the Deadline. The healthy version of Dohm utilizes a 93-95 mph fastball with impressive carry to blow past hitters up in the zone. He ran the heater up to 99 in shorter stints as a sophomore reliever -- a sign of what’s in the tank -- and he relied heavily on the heater throughout his college career. His 82-85 mph slider plays off the heater well, darting late gloveside to get a healthy amount of whiffs. He’s mostly kept his upper-70s curveball in his pocket as a pro, but the offering gives him a vertical option too. His upper-80s changeup is often too firm and doesn’t stand as a huge weapon against lefties, leading to splits concerns. Dohm was a tremendous strike-thrower in his two years in Starkville, but because of the forearm issues -- including more during his sophomore campaign -- evaluators hadn’t seen that control hold up over long stints as a starter. He quieted some of those concerns in the first half of the 2025 season before the trade. The lack of a cambio could hurt him down the line, but there’s still starter upside here given his ability to fill the zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vilorio signed for $1.75 million out of the Dominican Republic, landing the highest bonus in the Yankees' 2024 international class. He offered some of the best raw power on that market but had difficulty getting to it in his pro debut. He batted just .196/.294/.345 with a 33 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Vilorio already is stronger and hits the ball harder than most 18-year-olds, and there's still room to add more strength to his 6-foot-4 frame. The bat speed he generates with his right-handed swing contributes to projections of plus-plus raw pop once he's fully developed. He has at least 30-homer upside, but he'll have to tone down his chase-heavy approach and make a lot more in-zone contact to succeed at the plate. With solid-to-plus speed and good instincts, Vilorio can steal a few bases and has a chance to remain in center field. He'll probably lose a step as he matures physically, which would dictate a move to the corners. His arm strength grades out as at least plus and easily would work in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Instead of investing most of their international bonus pool in one player like they often do, the Yankees spread their cash around their 2024 class. Their highest-priced signee was Vilorio, who turned pro for $1.75 million out of the Dominican Republic. He fits the classic right-field profile and will break into pro ball in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in June. A right-handed hitter, Vilorio is stronger than most teenagers and still has more room to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame, so he could have explosive raw power. He has plenty of bat speed as well and already exhibits 25-30 homer upside. There are some mixed opinions about his bat-to-ball skills, but the consensus is that he should be at least an average hitter. Vilorio's solid to plus speed gives him a chance to remain in center field. If he loses some quickness as he matures physically, his plus-plus arm strength is more than enough for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guerrero pitched for three different Washington colleges in his home state, but it was a solid season for the Washington Huskies that caught the Royals’ attention and led them to select the lefty in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft. He was limited early in his pro career because of injuries but jumped onto the radar with two consistent seasons. Guerrero returned to Double-A in 2024 and posted a 3.69 ERA across 102 1/3 innings and 22 games (all starts). He jumped to Triple-A at the end of August and didn’t finish well, allowing 21 earned runs in 20 2/3 innings with 14 walks and 14 strikeouts in his final five starts. Armed with a four-pitch mix, Guerrero sits 91-93 mph with a fastball that runs up to 96. He has two breaking balls, an 83-84 mph slider and a 77-78 mph curveball, the latter of which has downer action and flashes plus on some nights. The slider with sweeping action is probably his best secondary right now and tunnels off his fastball well. His changeup is fringe average and still developing after an inconsistent year. Guerrero is usually a strikethrower who keeps the ball in the ballpark. Guerrero has more of a smaller build, but his stuff would probably tick up in the bullpen. There’s likely more opportunity there for him as a multi-inning reliever as he gets closer to Kansas City. He began the 2025 season in the Triple-A Omaha rotation but lasted only three starts before undergoing Tommy John surgery. Already left off the 40-man when Rule 5-eligible in 2024, he'll miss out on an opportunity to push for that status this season as he undergoes recovery and rehab for the remainder of the campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: From Lower Columbia (Wash.) CC to Washington State to Washington, Guerrero moved around his home state quite a bit in college, but his 2.96 ERA for the Huskies in 2021 led to the Royals selecting him in the 12th round that year. Guerrero had a limited start to his pro career because of shoulder injuries, but he stayed on the field in 2023 and had a solid year, making 18 appearances (17 starts) for High-A Quad Cities with a 3.63 ERA and 106 strikeouts with just 29 walks across 84 1/3 innings. He ended the season with a late promotion, making three starts for Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Guerrero sits 91-94 mph with his above-average fastball and throws a ton of strikes with the pitch. His best secondary pitch is a slider with sweeping action that grades out as plus and tunnels with his fastball well. His curveball differs from the hard breaking ball with downer action and low-80s velocity. Guerrero does have a changeup, but it’s inconsistent and will be a focus for him in Double-A. He’s an efficient strike-thrower with good control. Guerrero will need that changeup to neutralize right-handers, as hitters will challenge him more at the upper levels. But he has the tools and composure to keep starting, profiling as a back-end rotation pitcher. Evaluators could see Guerrero’s stuff ticking up in the bullpen, and he’d probably get to Kansas City quicker that way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid prospect from the Pennsylvania high school ranks, Holman never seriously considered forgoing his commitment to Alabama by signing in 2021. After a year as a reliever and a solid season in the Crimson Tide rotation, Holman hit the transfer portal (following a good showing for the U.S. collegiate national team) and headed to Louisiana State. A strong junior season led to him being taken by the Reds at No. 71 overall in the 2024 Draft. He was sidelined by an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery just nine innings into his pro debut in 2025. A 6-foot-4 right-hander with a four-pitch mix when healthy, Holman won’t wow with velocity but had success in college thanks to his feel for pitching. At LSU, he maxed out at 95 mph and sat around 92, but a combination of induced vertical break, ride at the top of the zone and command helped the pitch play up. His low-80s slider with two-plane depth is his bread and butter, eliciting a ton of swing-and-miss, and while his upper-70s curve and mid-80s changeup are underutilized and underdeveloped, both can be effective at times. Holman has shown he can throw all of his pitches in and around the strike zone fairly consistently, and there could be some more velocity to come if he can add some strength to his long and lean frame. The first order of business is getting back to health so he can resume trying to develop into a future big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holman could have been a legitimate high school draftee in 2021, but didn’t go until the very end of the Draft because he was determined to go to Alabama. After relieving as a freshman, he had a successful turn in the Crimson Tide’s rotation in 2023 then was the U.S. collegiate national team’s top performer that summer, before transferring to Louisiana State. Another strong campaign at his new school helped him move up Draft boards and land in Competitive Balance Round B. The Reds shut him down, as they often do with their college arms, rather than send him out for a pro debut last summer. His debut was delayed even further when he missed all of 2025 following reconstructive elbow surgery. While Holman may never light up the radar gun, the 6-foot-4 right-hander has a good feel for using his four-pitch mix to get outs. His fastball sat 92 mph last year with LSU, topping out at 95, but excellent command, ride at the top of the zone and induced vertical break make it better than its pure velocity. He throws his low-80s slider with two-plane depth for strikes, eliciting a 48-percent miss rate according to Synergy in 2024. His upper-70s curve and mid-80s changeup aren’t as advanced in terms of his ability to land them for strikes or throw them frequently. With his long and lean frame, it’s possible that Holman’s stuff could tick up under pro instruction once he returns to health. Because of his fastball-slider and his command of them, Holman has every chance to stick in the back end of a big league rotation. If more velocity or better feel for his other secondary offerings come, he could be more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moore's steadfast Stanford commitment made him the highest-ranked position player (No. 57 on MLB Pipeline's Draft Top 250) to go unpicked in the 2022 Draft. After homering 31 times in two seasons with the Cardinal, he became the second catcher selected in 2024, signing for $3 million as the 30th overall choice. His first full pro season was rough as a foul tip broke a finger on his right hand in early April, sidelining him for two months and contributing to a .198/.293/.271 line in High-A. While at Stanford, Moore made consistent contact, hit for power and drew plenty of walks. During his time in High-A the last two years, the lefty hitter has been overly aggressive, swung and missed much more often, been hopeless against non-fastballs and generated no pop against southpaws. He still produces high exit velocities when he does barrel balls, but that hasn't happened frequently enough. Moore needs to produce at the plate because scouts have questioned his ability to stay behind it since high school. He's not very athletic or agile, though he has made some progress with his defense at Stanford and in pro ball and earns praise for his leadership skills. He still may not be more than a fringy receiver with arm strength to match, and first base and DH are his only other options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With teams unable to sway Moore from his Stanford commitment, he became the highest-ranked position player (No. 57 on MLB Pipeline's Draft Top 250) to go unselected in the 2022 Draft. He smashed 31 homers and improved his plate discipline in two seasons with the Cardinal while continuing to get mixed reviews for his defense behind the plate. He became the second catcher drafted in 2024, going 30th overall and signing for $3 million before breaking into pro ball with a month at High-A. Moore offered one of the best all-around offensive profiles in last year's college class, displaying the ability to hit for average and power while drawing a healthy amount of walks. But he has struggled much more than expected in High-A during his first full pro season, getting too passive at times and having trouble turning on pitches. When he's at his best, his bat speed and strength produce hard contact to all fields from the left side of the plate. Scouts have questioned Moore's ability to stay at catcher since high school, and some still think he'll max out as a below-average defender with arm strength to match. He's slow-footed and not very agile, but he also made some progress with his defense at Stanford and draws praise for his work ethic and ability to communicate with his pitching staff. While his lack of quickness makes first base and DH his only fallbacks, he has the offensive upside to be an everyday player at those spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners did a good job of scouting Gough and understanding what it would take to keep him from heading to Oregon State after pitching at California high school power JSerra Catholic. They inked him for $275,000 in the ninth round of the 2022 Draft and he only threw 30 innings during his pro debut in '23 as the Mariners built him up slowly before he missed three months with an oblique injury. A return to Single-A Modesto in 2024 was much more successful, especially over the season’s first three months (3.21 ERA, 10 K/9). He faded in the second half, then was shut down at the end of August with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. The Mariners will have to wait until 2026 to see if Gough can build off of his gains in '24, when he showed a legitimate (though far from eye-popping) four-pitch mix. His low-90s fastball plays up a little with good ride up in the zone and induced vertical break. Of all his secondary offerings, his changeup probably has the best chance to be an out pitch and it’s ahead of his breaking stuff. He has a traditional slider and curve, but now leans on the trendy sweeper. Gough’s walk rate has been high in his two years of pitching, though he had improved that during that strong April-June stretch in 2024. He repeats his delivery well and there was confidence his command would continue to improve. The Mariners were getting calls from other teams about him when the elbow issue occurred, so they will eagerly wait for his return to the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gough so badly wanted an opportunity to pitch in the Mariners’ system that he opted to forgo a commitment to Oregon State, culminating with the club selecting him in the ninth round in ’22 and giving him an over-slot bonus of $275,000 to sign him. He raved about all the success stories of pitching in the Seattle pipeline, and in turn, the club was impressed with his big performance at the MLB Draft Combine, where he K’d each of the five batters he faced. They also loved his social and emotional makeup. Since then, player development can’t stop raving about the arm, aptitude and work ethic. His fastball can touch 95 mph, but typically sits 91-94 mph, thrown with good spin rates up in the zone. While he typically features a slurvy breaking ball in the upper-70s, he showed a distinct slider and curve. Like the rest of Seattle’s high school pitching selections, he didn’t pitch competitively at an affiliate or in the Arizona Complex League the rest of the year, a health-dictated decision. How the Mariners deploy Gough in the coming years will be of great intrigue. Stuff-wise, he profiles more for relief, and he has the go-right-after hitters mentality for the role, but he does have the arsenal and is around the zone enough to give him an opportunity to start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After drafting Vrieling in 2022's third round out of Gonzaga, the Yankees had him focus on gaining muscle, and he added 20 pounds in advance of his planned pro debut in 2023. He missed all of that season with a stress fracture in his pitching elbow, however, before returning to the mound in the Arizona Fall League. He finally broke into the Minors last season at Double-A, leading the Eastern League in wins (13) while ranking second in innings (147 1/3) and sixth in strikeouts (132). Though Vrieling's best attribute is his feel for spin and his 78-82 mph curveball and mid-80s slider/cutter both can grade as plus pitches at their best, they were merely average in Double-A. He gets some carry on his low-90s fastball that maxes out at 96 mph, but it can straighten out at times. His upper-80s changeup is too firm, and he has trouble landing it in the zone despite its modest movement. A reliever for the first two years of his college career, Vrieling held up under a full starter's workload last summer and threw more consistent strikes than ever before. He's doing a better job of repeating his three-quarters arm slot as a pro. He looked like a potential No. 3 starter in the first part of his junior season at Gonzaga, but he'll have no more than a back-of-the-rotation ceiling unless he can develop a better-than-average offering.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzaga's 2022 weekend rotation produced three early picks in that year's Draft, with Hughes going 10th overall to the Rockies and Vrieling (Yankees) and William Kempner (Giants) factoring in the third round. New York had Vrieling focus on adding strength after signing and he gained 20 pounds in advance of his planned 2023 pro debut. He wound up missing all of last season after coming down with a stress fracture in his pitching elbow, though he did return to work 10 2/3 innings in the Arizona Fall League. Vrieling has good feel for spin, with both his 78-82 mph curveball and mid-80s slider/cutter grading as plus pitches at their best, though they've played as more average in Double-A this season. He fell in love with his breaking pitches too much while transitioning from the bullpen to the rotation at Gonzaga in 2022, costing him run and sink on a low-90s fastball that tops out at 96. He's vulnerable without his best life on his heater but has recaptured it since turning pro. Vrieling has a lot to prove to remain a starter, beginning with durability. He needs to improve an upper-80s changeup that's much too firm, as well as his fastball command and overall control. If that doesn't work out, his breaking balls could make him a useful multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: All three members of Gonzaga's 2022 weekend rotation went in the first three rounds of the Draft, with the Rockies taking Gabriel Hughes 10th overall before Vrieling (Yankees) and William Kempner (Giants) became third-rounders. Vrieling spent his first two years with the Bulldogs as a reliever before overpowering hitters as a starter early last spring, then tailed off in the second half of the college season when he got away from using his fastball. New York had him focus on building strength after signing and he added 20 pounds before making his pro debut in 2023. Vrieling has high spin rates on his low-80s downer curveball, his best chase pitch, and his tight mid-80s slider, his top offering in terms of getting swings and misses. Both can be plus offerings at their best and he can turn his slider into a harder cutter with even more upside. When he fell in love with his breaking pitches last spring, he lost some of the sink and run on a fastball that parks at 90-93 mph and peaks at 96, and it got hit. To survive as a starter in pro ball, Vrieling will need to find some more velocity or life for his heater, and his strength gains should help. He also needs to improve and develop more trust in his changeup, which is too firm in the upper-80s, and throw more strikes. If he returns to the bullpen, his breaking stuff could make him a multi-inning weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $10,000 find in the Dominican Republic by the Dodgers in 2021, Batista pitched well in the Rookie ball the next two summers. When Los Angeles needed extra international bonus pool money to sign Korean right-handed Hyun-Seok Jang in August 2023, it packaged Batista with fellow righty pitching prospect Maximo Martinez to acquire $1 million from the White Sox. He had a strong first season with his new organization, but after he made his first start in 2025, a stress fracture in his elbow sidelined him for 4 1/2 months. When he's fully healthy, Batista has a pair of 92-94 mph fastballs that top out at 96, favoring sinking two-seamers down at hitters' knees to running four-seamers at their letters. He has one of the best changeups in the system, a mid-80s weapon with fade and tumble that creates a lot of weak contact. His mid-80s slider is effective and features two-plane depth at its best. Batista is deceptive too, operating from an extremely low arm slot that doesn't prevent him from providing strikes. His stuff was down when he returned late last August to make seven brief appearances, so he'll need to prove he can recapture what he had. He's a potential No. 4 starter who could boost his ceiling if he adds more strength and velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2021, Batista fared well in Rookie ball during the next two summers. Los Angeles needed more international bonus pool money to sign Korean right-hander Hyun-Seok Jang in August 2023, so it traded Batista and fellow righty pitching prospect Maximo Martinez to the White Sox for $1 million in funds. He has pitched well at two A-ball levels since while displaying one of the system's best changeups. Batista utilizes two fastballs that operate at 92-94 mph and max out at 96, preferring sinking two-seamers down at hitters' knees to running four-seamers past them at the letters. He slings mid-80s changeups that fade and tumble, generating a lot of weak contact. He has an effective mid-80s slider that will flash some two-plane depth at its best. Batista is athletic and works from a low slot that's a tick above sidearm, creating deception without harming his ability to throw strikes. If he can add more muscle to his slender 6-foot-2 frame, he might add more velocity and boost his stuff and ceiling. He has the upside of a No. 4 starter but will need some development time to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bright was a key member of Auburn’s 2022 College World Series team and signed with the Orioles for a below-slot $400,000 as a senior after they made him a fifth-round selection in that year’s Draft. After a brief debut, Bright struck out more than one-third of the hitters he faced at High-A Aberdeen in 2023, though he wasn’t young for the level, and reached Double-A by the end of his first full pro season. He spent all of 2024 sort of stagnating back at the level, pitching to a 4.18 ERA but missing fewer bats and finishing with an ugly 0-11 record. Bright has always stood out more for his pitch traits than his stats, which weren’t sensational in college either. He’s a 6-foot-4 righty with a traditional delivery and a four-pitch mix, the best of which is a plus curve that he learned to spin harder in ‘24. He pairs it with an average heater that lives between 92-95 mph but can play up because he tunnels it well and throws it with carry at the top of the zone. He also throws a harder breaker that’s morphed from a slider into more of a pure cutter and an improving changeup that has a chance to be an average pitch. Bright has never been a very good strike thrower, and the Orioles were hoping he’d improve at limiting free passes and learn to come out of the gate stronger over a full year at Double-A. But that didn’t necessarily happen. Bright’s walk rate stayed on the high side, his strikeout rate declined, and falling behind often in counts made him more predictable, leading to more hits allowed. With more consistency, he still has a chance to develop into a back-end starter, but if the control issues persist, they limit his upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bright never put up overwhelming numbers in college, but he was a mainstay in Auburn’s weekend rotation in 2022 and helped the Tigers pick up their first College World Series win since 1997. That helped him catch the attention of the Orioles, who were intrigued enough with his pitch shapes to select him in the fifth round of that year’s Draft and sign him for a below-slot $400,000. He became the highest drafted pitcher Baltimore signed that year after it failed to bring third-rounder Nolan McLean into the fold. Bright then broke out at High-A Aberdeen, where he struck out more than one-third of the hitters he faced before finishing his first full season strongly at Double-A Bowie. Bright is a 6-foot-4 right-hander with a traditional delivery and over-the-top slot who spent his first full season adding to his pitches and learning how to best utilize them. His 92-94 mph fastball is average velocity-wise but plays up by getting above barrels due to its plane and carry. Bright’s best secondary offering is a plus mid-70s curveball that he tunnels well off the heater and can throw to both sides of the plate with depth. He also incorporates a changeup that flashes above average and two sliders, including a hard mid-80s gyro. If Bright can improve his feel for them, all three of those pitches have a chance to be average offerings. The area Bright needs to improve the most on is his command. He’s had high strikeout rates in college and through his pro career so far, but that comes with high walk rates that threaten to limit his upside. Cutting down the free passes and learning how to come out of the gate stronger in the first inning could lead to better consistency overall and give Bright a chance to develop into a back-end rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buelvas signed with the A’s out of Colombia during the 2018-19 international signing period for $100,000. He has experienced several ups and downs while developing in the organization. Last season saw a bit of a resurgence for him as a prospect, as he moved back to High-A Lansing to begin the year before advancing to Double-A Midland. Between the two levels, he combined to hit .267/.352/.421 with eight home runs, 28 doubles, seven triples and 62 RBIs in 113 games. Then he went back home to play winter ball and was one of the top hitters in the Colombian Winter League, hitting .361 with a .986 OPS, nine homers, seven doubles and 35 RBIs in 34 games. Buelvas still strikes out a ton, but his overall approach has improved, leading to an ability to draw a decent amount of walks. His power is below average, though he can drive the ball to all fields. Keeping that line-to-line approach is how the A’s believe he can maximize his potential at the plate. The A’s are still dreaming of a Ramón Laureano-type defensive arc for Buelvas. Though he may not ever reach that kind of physicality, he is still a very good defender in his own right who can handle all three spots. His ability to cover ground with good speed and a solid arm have helped him stick at center field in the Minors. The intriguing tools are still there for Buelvas, even if they have developed a bit slowly, and a carryover of his recent success could boost his chances of getting another bump through the system, with the potential to develop into a fourth outfielder at the Major League level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buelvas signed out of Colombia for $100,000 in 2018 and got off to a hot start in 2019 by hitting .300 as a 17-year-old playing in the Rookie-level Arizona League. After an encouraging 2021 in which he showed off his raw tools with 31 extra-base hits, 16 home runs and 17 stolen bases over 88 games with Low-A Stockton, he took a bit of a step back last season, hitting just .195 in 69 games at High-A Lansing. He continued to play into the winter with Vaqueros de Monteria in Colombia and hit .214 with four homers and 15 RBIs in 33 games. Buelvas has displayed qualities of a good approach at the plate at a young age with a decent ability to draw walks, even in a down season last year. He has shown off an intriguing speed and power combo, with the hope he can tap into that pop as he develops more into his wiry 5-foot-11 frame. A very good outfielder who can play all three spots well, Buelvas likely will continue to move around out there to maintain that versatility. The A’s are not too concerned about his down year, partially attributing the struggles to him being a bit worn out from his workload the previous year, which also included winter ball. They still see a bit of a Ramón Laureano-type skill set with him and hope he can bring more energy throughout the 2023 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 out of Colombia in 2018, Buelvas quickly made a good impression in 2019 by hitting .300 in the Rookie-level Arizona League as a 17-year-old. He really showed off his raw tools in 2021 with a total of 31 extra-base hits, 16 home runs and 17 stolen bases over 88 games in his first full season at Low-A. He spent some time in the Caribbean Series playing for Colombia and hit .273 with three RBIs in seven games, but didn’t carry that over to 2022, when he struggled offensively and missed considerable time with a hamstring injury. The A’s think Buelvas has the chance to have a good approach at the plate. For a player his age, he’s shown good plate discipline at times with his ability to draw walks. While the solid speed has always been there, the uptick in power was a pleasant surprise, given his wiry 5-foot-11 frame. With time, he has the chance to develop into a very good hitter. Able to play all three outfield spots, Buelvas projects to stick in center field, with the A’s believing he could evolve into a Ramón Laureano-type player without the amazing arm. His passion for the game is clear, which should help him advance through the system and ultimately establish himself as an everyday player at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buelvas signed for $100,000 out of Colombia in July 2018 and put himself firmly on the prospect map in 2019, when he went to the Rookie-level Arizona League as a 17-year-old and shined with a .300/.392/.506 slash line and 20 extra-base hits in 44 games. He made a fairly successful jump to full-season ball as a teenager in 2021, reaching double-digits in home runs and stolen bases. The A’s have been impressed with how well Buelvas has handled everything that's been thrown at him at such a young age. He’s expected to develop into a plus hitter in due time, already showing an advanced approach with a willingness to draw walks. He’s an aggressive runner on the basepaths with a touch above average speed. He struggled some in the instructional league in 2020 after perhaps putting extra pressure on himself, but it appears he was able to learn from older players and use those lessons during his full-season debut. Buelvas can play all three outfield spots well, though he has the chance to stick in center field. The A’s love the passion he plays with just as much as his tools, which showed up consistently in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When opportunity knocks, one has to be ready to answer. That’s exactly what Buelvas, an athletic outfielder who signed for $100,000 out of Colombia in July 2018, did during his debut summer in 2019. While playing in the Dominican Summer League, Buelvas was summoned to the United States to play in the rookie-level Arizona League just a few weeks after his 17th birthday because they needed more bodies stateside. He then proceeded to hit .300/.392/.506 with 20 extra-base hits in 44 games to jump firmly onto the prospect map. One of the youngest players in the AZL, Buelvas handled being thrown into the fire with the aggressive assignment with aplomb. The A’s think he has the chance to be a plus hitter in time, with an advanced approach especially given his age and a willingness to draw walks. While he’s likely not going to be a big over-the-fence type of hitter, he did show extra-base authority to all fields and a penchant for going the other way. He may settle into being an average runner over time, but he’s aggressive on the basepaths. Buelvas has seen time in all three outfield spots, something that’s likely to continue, but he’s a true center fielder who should be able to play there long term. As much as his tools excite the A’s, they also love his makeup and his passion for the game. He won an award for being the most valuable player at instructs after the season, leaving the organization very excited to see what he does for an encore in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Of the 16 prospects who received six-figure bonuses from the Pirates at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Tsung-Che Cheng has jumped out as the best prospect to date. Castillo was close to the bottom of that list, getting $140,000 to sign in July 2019. He jumped on the map when he won the Florida Complex League batting title (.352), and while he wasn’t nearly as productive with a move to full-season Bradenton in 2023, he joined teammate Termarr Johnson as two of the eight players in the Minor Leagues to walk 100 or more times. Since signing, Castillo has shown off impressive bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate. He’s registered very low strikeout rates at each stop, carrying a 17.3 K rate into the 2024 season. He doesn’t give away at-bats and isn’t afraid to hit with two strikes. He couples that with excellent patience to be an on-base machine, when he can then use his speed to be a basestealing threat. What he lacks, however, is any impact at the plate, and he’s working to get more physical without taking away his all-fields approach, though he’s never going to have more than gap power. Castillo is so sound defensively, the sentiment is that he could handle playing in a Major League game at shortstop if need be. He’ll continue to get plenty of reps there, but he’s also proven to be a bit of a Swiss Army knife, one who did everything but catch for Bradenton in 2023. The Pirates love his aggressive style of play and his contact skills. If he can add just a little strength, he could carve out a future as a utility player in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castillo begain his career with the D-backs, signing back in August 2011, but was dealt to the Cubs in February '13, before he had even pitched in the United States. He was on the move again at the Trade Deadline in '16, joining the Angels courtesy of the Joe Smith trade, with his new organization sending him to full-season ball for the first time. He broke out in '17, pitching across three levels and reaching Double-A, earning a spot on the 40-man roster as a result. His return to the Southern League did not go as well in 2018, a season that also included close to a month on the disabled list. With just average stuff across the board, Castillo has to rely on command and generating weak contact to succeed. While he still managed a solid ground-ball rate in 2018, thanks to his 90-91 mph fastball with heavy sink, he missed fewer bats and also saw his walk rate tick up. His secondary stuff, an upper-70s curve and a changeup he is capable of throwing with good arm speed and deception, is average at best. Deception and extension in his delivery have helped him in the past, and he's always been a solid strike-thrower. Castillo went to the Arizona Fall League to make up for lost innings and it was more of the same, as he gave up more than 13 hits per nine innings. He does have relieving on his resume from his previous organizations and that might end up being his best ticket to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castillo has twice been involved in relatively small trades that didn't receive much fanfare. Initially signed by the D-backs back in 2011, he was sent to the Cubs before the 2013 season. After three summers of gaining little traction in the lower levels of Chicago's system, he was dealt to the Angels in the August 2016 Joe Smith deal. Things clicked in 2017, as Castillo pitched well across three levels, reaching Double-A, and was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Castillo is all about pitchability and command of his average stuff. His fastball is average from a velocity standpoint, around 90-91 mph, but he throws it with extreme sink and gets a ton of ground-ball outs as a result. Both his curve and changeup have the chance to be average pitches and he throws his upper-70s breaking ball for strikes while maintaining good arm speed on his changeup. Castillo repeats his delivery very well, leading to above-average control, and gets more swings and misses than you'd expect thanks to deception and big-time extension out front. With the D-backs and Cubs, Castillo had both started and relieved. The Angels' decision to commit to him as a full-time starter seems to be paying off. He might have the ceiling of a No. 4 or 5 type in the big leagues, but if his secondary stuff improves or he adds strength and velocity, he could outstrip that projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of former Astros great José Cruz and son of former first-round pick and longtime MLB center fielder José Cruz Jr., Trei Cruz was a third-round pick in the shortened 2020 Draft whose career seemed stalled at Double-A Erie, where he spent parts of four seasons. After adding outfield to his position list and becoming more of an impact hitter, Cruz won over Tigers officials by becoming the pinnacle of versatility, a switch-hitter who can play all over the field and defend well nearly everywhere. That didn’t get him to Detroit in 2025, but it earned him a spot on the 40-man roster in the offseason and a long look in Spring Training. While Cruz has always been a switch-hitter, he’s much more dangerous from the left side, where he hit all of his home runs in 2024 and 2025. He adjusted his swing two years ago with help from his dad to produce more power from his hips and lower body, yet he doesn’t chase home runs, taking more of a doubles mentality. He has the bat speed to keep up with rising velocity and produce a high hard-hit rate, yet stays very disciplined at the plate with a low chase rate and swing rate overall. His high walk rate, even against lefties, enables him to utilize above-average speed on the bases. While he doesn’t have a standout defensive position, he’s athletic and instinctive enough to play just about everywhere. As a switch-hitter who can be that versatile, Cruz profiles as the ultimate player for manager A.J. Hinch’s bench. Hitting a little stronger against lefties would help his cause, but it’s not hard to envision Cruz as a fill-in for an injured Zach McKinstry should the need arise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz may have the most extensive big league pedigree in this year's Draft, as his father Jose, grandfather Jose and great-uncles Hector and Tommy all played in the Majors. His uncle Enrique started at second base for the 2003 College World Series champions at Rice, where Trei has spent the last three seasons. Selected in the 35th round out of high school by the Astros in 2017 and in the 37th round as a sophomore-eligible by the Nationals in 2019, he should fit in the first five rounds after improving several aspects of his game. A switch-hitter, Cruz has toned down his approach after selling out for home runs in the past. He has modified a big leg kick he used from the left side of the plate and displayed better strike-zone discipline during the truncated 2020 season. Scouts see him as a hit-over-power guy who could provide 15 homers on an annual basis. Cruz posted below-average running times in the past but now flashes average speed, especially once he gets going, and shows aggressiveness and savvy on the bases. His average arm and fringy range don't lend themselves to sticking at shortstop, though he may get a chance to play there for a while in pro ball after displaying more quickness this spring. His best fit is at second base, where he played well as a freshman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodden’s professional profile is built around versatility, competitiveness and high baseball IQ. After two years at Seminole State College in Oklahoma, he transferred to Wichita State, where he posted a huge senior season that earned him American Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors. Though originally drafted as a junior in the 10th round by the A’s in 2022, he returned to school and elevated his stock, leading to a fifth-round selection in 2023 by the Mariners, who signed him for $200,000. Rodden hit well with High-A Everett in his full-season debut, earning a bump to Double-A. He returned there in 2025 and kept the bat going, finishing with an .822 OPS despite injuries getting in the way. An undersized switch-hitter, Rodden has consistently shown bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline, though the jump to Double-A saw strikeouts rise and contact become less consistent. Over two years at Wichita State he hit 34 home runs, and he added 14 in his first full pro season. But Rodden projects as a low-power bat as he moves up, with just five homers at Arkansas. His game will rely heavily on making consistent contact and drawing walks to create offensive value, and he did a better job at that while hitting .342 during an 11-game stint in the Arizona Fall League. Defensively, Rodden has the versatility to play second base, third, shortstop and potentially the outfield, and his plus speed helps him defensively and on the basepaths, where his strong instincts make him a base stealing threat. Scouts are particularly encouraged by his sneaky utility potential at the Major League level. Among big league comps, Leo Rivas has been floated. Beyond tools, Rodden brings leadership and a grinder mentality that sets the tone for younger teammates, making him a candidate to contribute as a versatile, switch-hitting option on a future big-league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodden took the junior college route out of high school, then went to Wichita State after two years at Seminole State College in Oklahoma. He was one of just three players taken in the Top 10 rounds of the 2022 Draft that opted to go back to school, returning to the Shockers after the A’s took him in Round 10. He had a huge senior year to win American Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors and he jumped up to the fifth round, where the Mariners signed him for $200,000. After hitting very well with High-A Everett during his full-season debut, he got pushed to Double-A at age 24, though he struggled at the level. An under-sized switch-hitter, Rodden has shown good bat-to-ball skills and a disciplined approach at the plate, though that unraveled a bit and the strikeouts piled up more once he got to Arkansas. He hit 34 homers over two years at Wichita State and finished his first full pro season with 14, but there’s not going to be a ton of power as he keeps moving up, so he’s going to have to really make a ton of contact and draw a lot of walks. Rodden is a plus runner and combines that with good instincts on the basepaths. He’s best suited to play second base defensively, but his bat is unlikely to profile as an every day player at the position. He’s seen time at third and at shortstop, which also won’t work at the highest level, so there’s a chance the Mariners give him the chance to see how his athleticism plays in center field so that he can possibly carve out some kind of utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going unselected in four straight Drafts while moving from Okeechobee (Fla.) HS to Florida SouthWestern State JC to Jacksonville, Adams led the Atlantic Sun Conference with 108 strikeouts in 90 innings in 2022. Signed for $75,000 as a 13th-round senior, he quickly established himself as one of the more polished pitchers in the system. On the verge of making the Majors in 2025, he injured his flexor tendon during Spring Training and had Tommy John surgery in April, costing him the entire season. Adams stands out with his ability to spin the ball and fill the strike zone. When healthy, he features a plus low-80s curveball with downer break and a solid if less reliable mid-80s slider with similar shape. He throws his breaking balls more than his fringy two- and four-seam fastballs, which park at 90-93 mph and peak at 94. He improved his upper-80s changeup in 2024, having more success with splitter action than the mild fade it had in the past. Adams excels at sequencing his pitches, working all four quadrants of the strike zone with the varying movement profiles of his offerings. He gets down the mound well, creating deception with extension and a flat approach angle. His No. 4 or 5 starter floor is more impressive than his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adams went unselected in four straight Drafts while going from the Florida high school ranks to Florida SouthWestern State JC to his junior season at Jacksonville. He finally got noticed when he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with 108 strikeouts in 90 innings in 2022, and the White Sox gave him $75,000 as a 13th-round senior sign. One of the most polished pitchers in the system, he paced Chicago farmhands with a 3.9 K/BB ratio last season and would have led the Double-A Southern League in ERA (2.44) if he hadn't fallen a few innings shy of qualifying. Adams had very good feel for spin, producing a plus low-80s curveball with downer break and a solid if less consistent mid-80s slider with two-plane break at its best. He uses his breaking ball as much as he employs his fringy two- and four-seam fastballs, both of which sit at 90-93 mph and top out at 94. He improved his upper-80s changeup, finding more success with improved depth rather than the mild fade he had in the past, though it's still a bit firm. A crafty right-hander, Adams mixes his pitches well and can work all four quadrants of the strike zone with the different movement profiles of his offerings. He creates deception with a flat approach angle and relentlessly fills the strike zone. He got roughed up in five Triple-A starts at the end of 2024, so he'll have to prove himself at that level, but he's not far from joining the big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 From his senior year as a Florida prepster to two seasons at Florida SouthWestern State JC to his first at Jacksonville, Adams went unselected in four straight Drafts.
