After he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with 108 strikeouts in 90 innings in 2022, the White Sox signed him for $75,000 as a 13th-rounder. He reached Double-A and established himself as one of the best strike-throwers in the system during his first full pro season. Adams' money pitch is his low-80s curveball with true downer break, a plus offering that he can locate for strikes or use to get chases outside the zone. His feel for spin extends to a mid-80s slider with two-plane depth, though it's not nearly as reliable as his curve. He uses both two- and four-seam fastballs in the low-90s, with his fringy sinker the more effective choice. Adams also has a mediocre mid-80s changeup with mild fade and not enough velocity separation from his heater. His ability to pound the strike zone and create deception with a flat approach angle help him get the most out of his less than overwhelming stuff. He could be a back-of-the-rotation starter if he can miss enough bats with his fastball, and a curveball-dependent reliever if he can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: JSerra Catholic HS (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) has sent Austin Hedges and Royce Lewis to the big leagues and featured 13 NCAA Division I recruits on its 2021 team. The highest pick among that group was Silva, who gave up a UCLA scholarship to sign for $1,497,500 (nearly triple slot value) in the third round. Though he got tagged for a 5.88 ERA in Single-A during his first full pro season, he impressed scouts with what could be the best four-pitch mix in the system. Silva's quick arm generates 92-95 mph four-seam fastballs that reach 97 with a low release height that produces plenty of riding action up in the zone. He has good feel for spin and his plus 82-85 mph slider with horizontal and vertical life misses more bats than his solid upper-70s curveball with more depth. He's making progress with a mid-80s changeup with fade, though it gets too firm at times. Silva isn't very physical at 6-foot-1 and 185 pounds, and his control and command wavered when he tired in the second half of 2022. He needs to get stronger so he can do a better job of maintaining stuff and strikes. More shortstop than pitcher at the start of his high school career, he's a quality athlete.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: More of a shortstop than a pitcher when he first got to Laguna Beach (Calif.) High, Silva knew his future was on the mound when he transferred to JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) for his 2021 senior season. The Lions have spawned Austin Hedges and 2017 No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis, and Silva was one of 13 NCAA Division I recruits on their team last spring. The highest pick among that group, he gave up a UCLA commitment to sign for $1,497,500, nearly triple his slot value in the fourth round. Silva isn't particularly physical at 6-foot-1 and 185 pounds, yet he has a quick arm that produces 92-95 mph four-seam fastballs that peak at 97 and feature a flat attack angle that provides tough carry up in the zone. He has a pair of quality breaking balls that miss bats, with his low-80s slider with horizontal action and depth perhaps slightly better than his upper-70s curveball with more downer break. He shows some feel for throwing a changeup with fade, though it needs more consistent velocity separation from his fastball. Silva provides strikes but like most young pitchers, he'll need to refine his command as he faces more advanced hitters. Despite his size, his arm speed and athleticism can help him remain a starter. To do so, he'll have to show that his stuff will hold up over a long pro season, and he has done that in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Joining the organization for $750,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2022, Santana was Arizona’s third-highest signing of the class, trailing only Abdias De La Cruz ($1.1 million) and Yerald Nin ($900,000). It’s the same class that brought fellow infielders Jansel Luis and Cristofer Torin into the fold. Santana produced a 142 wRC+ in the Dominican Summer League during his first taste of the Minors that summer and moved stateside for 2023, slashing .316/.389/.487 with four homers and seven steals in 52 games in the Arizona Complex League. The right-handed slugger cut his walk rate nearly in half, going from 15.3 percent to 8.1 between the DSL and ACL, and his strikeout rate bumped slightly from 20.2 percent to 23.7, elevating some concerns that his hit tool will be more challenged by pitchers with better control and command. Santana still maintains above-average raw power in his 6-foot frame, and that could take another step forward if he can reel in some of the swing-and-miss concerns. Entering his age-19 season, Santana shows above-average speed for now, though concern that he’ll slow down eventually remains. That agility still serves him fairly well at third base, and his plus arm strength is an even bigger asset. The D-backs gave Santana seven starts at first base in the ACL, but any long-term move there remains far away. The power and early performance makes Santana an interesting follow ahead of his debut with a full-season affiliate in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abdias De La Cruz ($1.1 million) and Yerald Nin ($900,000) were the D-backs’ two highest-paid international additions on the first day of the 2022 signing period. Coming in right behind them was Santana as a $750,000 signee out of the Dominican Republic. The right-handed slugger proceeded to slash .316/.436/.436 with 10 extra-base hits, 15 steals and a 142 WRC+ over 43 games in the Dominican Summer League during his first pro season, solidifying his status as a Top 30 prospect in a deep Arizona system. Santana doesn’t get as swing-happy as many young players do when they enter the Minor League ranks, as proven by his 15.3 percent walk rate in 2022. That’s going to come in handy because he already has plenty of raw power from the right side and should grow to be above-average in slugging by the time he enters his 20s. The more selective he is on pitches he can drive, the better that pop will play. He’s also an above-average runner now but might still slow down a tick if he does add more bulk. Santana’s plus arm certainly plays well at third base -- his only defensive position in 2022 -- and his overall agility helps him make rangy plays and have quick reactions when needed. There are still some areas that need tightening, but he could be an average defender in the end. The long road ahead works both for and against Santana, but at the least, he deserves close following as he moves stateside this summer for his age-18 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bohrofen was a highly ranked player out of high school in 2020 and could have landed in the top three rounds but opted to play college ball at Oklahoma. A strong showing in the Cape Cod League and a strong finish in ‘23 with Arkansas revived his Draft stock. The Blue Jays landed Bohrofen in the sixth round and they were thrilled with the value. Coming off an impressive start to his pro career that year, Bohrofen hit 14 home runs with a .796 OPS over 116 games in High-A Vancouver in 2024. Down the stretch in ‘24, Bohrofen turned a corner and was one of the hottest hitters in the Blue Jays’ system, which has reignited the optimism around his long-term potential. Bohrofen has made an adjustment with his front foot to help him see the ball better and it’s been paying off. He’s built to mash, with excellent upper-body strength, but he isn’t too rigid in the field. The Blue Jays believe he’ll be just fine in the outfield and play solid defense, allowing his bat to shine if he takes that next step. The power numbers haven’t quite been there yet, but if Bohrofen ever truly breaks out, that’s going to be his headlining tool. Cutting down on his swing-and-miss will continue to be a priority, but Bohrofen is still a fine candidate to climb a couple of levels in 2025 and could give the Blue Jays an outfield depth option by next spring. His power will need to pull him up the ladder a bit, so this is a major season for Bohrofen and he’ll need to carry that strong finish from ‘24 over.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bohrofen was a highly ranked player out of high school in 2020 and could have landed in the top three rounds but opted to play college ball at Oklahoma. A strong showing in the Cape Cod League and a strong finish in ‘23 with Arkansas revived his Draft stock, and the Blue Jays landed Bohrofen in the sixth round, where they were thrilled with the value. He carried the power of his 16-homer season in college right into pro ball, putting up a 1.080 OPS and seven home runs over just 24 games between the complex league and Single-A. Bohrofen balances the Blue Jays system well. Many of their higher-ranked hitters, like Alan Roden or Spencer Horwitz, profile more as contact hitters who reach base at a high rate, while Bohrofen has the potential to mash. The big, well-built outfielder moves well enough to play a sturdy corner outfield position and let his bat shine. Bohrofen has excellent upper body strength and can produce power in multiple zones, which leaves the Blue Jays optimistic that this area of his game will sustain itself as he climbs levels. This will be challenged in High-A Vancouver, where he will face the same pitchers over and over. There’s nothing complicated about Bohrofen’s projection. He’ll go as far as his bat takes him, and so far that bat looks exciting, though swing-and-miss against softer stuff presents some reason for pause. He should continue to benefit from the Blue Jays’ player development complex to hone his swing and represents one of the higher-upside power bats outside of the Orelvis Martinez and Arjun Nimmala tier.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baum’s pro career is playing out as quite the feel-good story. Selected by the A’s in the second round of the 2019 Draft after three years at North Carolina as a starter, he returned from the pandemic unable to even play catch and spent nearly two years at the club’s Minor League Complex in Arizona trying to figure out how to throw a strike again. Sent to High-A Lansing to begin the 2023 season, he took off by posting a 2.59 ERA with 37 strikeouts and 14 walks in 31 1/3 innings before ending the year at Double-A Midland. Baum’s strong three-pitch mix suits his role as a reliever. He sits between 95-98 mph with his fastball and also brings a 12-6 curveball that flashes plus and a lights-out changeup that has been described by some as Trevor Hoffman-esque when it’s on. Baum utilizes his unorthodox over-the-top arm slot to his benefit since regaining his feel for pitching. His command was scattered early last season yet was still around the zone enough to get hitters to chase, and it improved as the year went along. After virtually two lost seasons, he is back on the big league radar, and it would not be a surprise to see him pitch his way to Oakland’s bullpen at some point in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After forgoing a chance to be a possible first-rounder in the 2016 Draft out of high school, Baum turned in three solid seasons at the University of North Carolina before the A’s selected him in the second round in 2019. He debuted in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League and posted a 4.70 ERA in 11 starts. Baum carries a solid four-pitch mix, bringing a fastball that can touch 94, and reached a bit higher at the A’s alternate camp in 2020, to go with two distinct breaking balls, an upper 70s curve and a low 80s hard slider that breaks low. He also throws a changeup that has some fade to it. Baum’s velocity mysteriously curtailed last year at the A’s alternate training site. After getting cleared during medical examinations, Oakland opted to shut him down for the year rather than sending him to the instructional league. A strike-thrower who has shown good command in the past, Baum projects as a mid-rotation type, though his fastball-breaking ball combo could eventually make him a candidate for the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In every Draft, players slide because of signability issues tied to strong college commitments. Baum could’ve been one of those players in the 2016 Draft after a strong high school career in Florida, but he removed his name from the Draft because he was set on attending the University of North Carolina. He spent three solid, though unspectacular, years as a starter for the Tar Heels, showing enough promise for the A’s to draft him in the second round of the 2019 Draft and he made his pro debut in the Short-Season New York-Penn League. Baum doesn’t have eye-popping stuff, but he does have a four pitch mix at his disposal. He’ll touch 94 mph with his fastball, throwing it with good armside run. He has two distinct breaking balls thrown from his high-three-quarters arm slot, with his upper-70s curve a bit ahead of his harder, more lateral-breaking low-80s slider. His changeup gives him a fourth at least average pitch, an offspeed offering that has some fade to it. Baum’s strike-throwing improved during his junior year at North Carolina and it carried over during his pro debut. Though there’s some crossfire in his delivery, the improved command gives him a better chance to start, as a No. 4 type in a rotation, long term, though his fastball-breaking ball would play up should he have to move to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays signed Colmenarez, a highly regarded Venezuelan shortstop, for $3 million as the headliner of their 2021 international signing class. It’s been a tough road for him so far, with most issues completely out of his control. He couldn’t join the Rays in 2020 because the signing period was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, couldn’t properly train with them during the shutdown, then fractured his right hamate before his first season began. Still young (he’ll be 19 all season) and plenty raw, Colmenarez will likely be further challenged with a necessary but challenging promotion to Single-A Charleston this year. It's easy to write off the .247/.319/.289 slash line Colmenarez produced as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League, because the hamate injury sapped his strength even after he returned for 26 games. His numbers were better, but not dominant, as he moved to the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He hit .254/.379/.381, still displaying a sweet left-handed swing, but his 26.8 percent strikeout rate and lack of power inspired some concerns about how he’ll fare against upper-level competition. He should gain more power as he grows into his projectable frame, and that would enhance his overall offensive profile. It's the rest of Colmenarez’s game, though, that suggests he still has a big league future. He looks like an above-average shortstop with soft hands, good actions, a strong arm and impressive instincts. That would make him, at worst, a lefty-hitting utility infielder if he hits enough -- and it’s not hard to find a place for those on Major League rosters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Look no further than his $3 million signing bonus to understand the Rays’ optimism regarding Colmenarez, a highly touted Venezuelan shortstop who headlined their 2021 international signing class. And understand the number of obstacles that he faced leading up to his professional debut: He couldn’t join the Rays during the first summer of the COVID-19 pandemic due to the delayed signing period, couldn’t properly train during the shutdown, then fractured his right hamate bone just before his first season began. With his debut pushed back to mid-August in the Dominican Summer League, Colmenarez hit for essentially no power as the hamate injury sapped his strength. That led to a .247/.319/.289 slash line in 26 games for the 17-year-old, but the Rays remain excited internally about his potential despite those pedestrian numbers. His hamate is not considered a long-term issue, and Tampa Bay expects him to bounce back as he moves to a domestic affiliate this year. Colmenarez is still projectable, listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds. He has a sweet left-handed swing with a balanced profile, a good blend of hitting for contact and power, that should include more pop as his body continues to mature. Colmenarez has displayed soft hands with good actions at shortstop, and evaluators expect he’ll remain up the middle as an above-average shortstop even as he grows. He also has plus arm strength, enhancing his defensive potential. Despite a delayed and disappointing debut, there’s still plenty of reason to believe Colmenarez will develop into a well-rounded shortstop with above-average tools across the board.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The shortened 2020 Draft only brought six picks to the San Diego system, and all six signed, including future Top 100 prospects Robert Hassell III and Owen Caissie. Of that half-dozen, only one remains in the organization, however, and that’s the final pick: fifth-rounder Haynes who signed for $300,000 as a North Carolina prepster. Tommy John surgery knocked his pro debut back to April 2023, and blister/shoulder issues that summer meant he didn’t cross the 100-inning threshold until 2024. Last season, Haynes spent the entire summer with Double-A San Antonio and finished with a 4.11 ERA, 101 strikeouts and 62 walks in 103 innings. Haynes regained some of his previously lost velocity in ’25 but still only sat 91-94 mph with his fastball. He’s shown both a four-seamer and sinker early in the spring, but neither has standout movement. The 6-foot-3 southpaw is much more effective with his low-80s slider, his best pitch by whiff and chase. Lefties missed on more than half their swings against the breaking ball, which features low spin, while righties found it difficult when he ran it down and hit on the tops of their feet. Haynes’ mid-80s changeup also showed promise versus opposite-side bats, but he needs to bury it lower in the zone; the pitch has more ride than typical changeups and sometimes can act like a slower, more armside sinker. Haynes has held steady with walk rates around 14 percent the last two seasons, and his command can be just as inconsistent; righties have proven to punish any of his pitches that catch too much of the plate. Unprotected and unpicked in last year’s Rule 5 Draft, Haynes might be headed toward last-chance saloon territory as a starter before seeing how he plays as a lefty-dominant reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Haynes was a projection fifth-round pick as a 17-year-old based in remote North Carolina in 2020, and the Padres wanted to see what they could make of him with a $300,000 bonus. The southpaw experienced elbow issues in what would have been his first pro season and underwent Tommy John surgery. He didn’t officially debut until April 2023 and then made only 11 abbreviated starts for Single-A Lake Elsinore that summer due to blister and shoulder issues. That made 2024 his first truly full Minor League campaign and he amassed 110 2/3 innings at High-A Fort Wayne, posting a 4.64 ERA with 114 strikeouts and 66 walks. The important bit was that Haynes stayed on the mound throughout ’24, never going on the IL. His four-seam fastball lost a little bit of velocity in the process, sitting 90-92 mph and touching 94. (It's back up to 91-94, touching 96 in 2025.) It has some armside run to it, but it isn’t a whiff-heavy pitch. Those swings-and-misses came primarily from his low-80s gyro slider -- a straight dropper that can often look like a curveball -- and 81-84 mph changeup. The latter posted a 47 percent whiff rate but was gettable if he didn’t bury it below the zone. Righties could handle that and also jumped all over Haynes’ fastball, leading to notable splits issues. Haynes battled control issues, seemed to iron them out in the middle of the season and then lost the zone again late as his workload piled up. Getting the command to return is all part of the process in TJ recovery, so that will be all the more under the microscope in 2025. Haynes was left unprotected and unpicked in the Rule 5 Draft after 2024, but another year of health and experience could make him a 40-man candidate after this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Haynes was a bit of a wild card in 2020 as a raw left-hander who needed to show innings out of remote West Columbus High School in North Carolina and who didn’t turn 18 until after the Draft. Of course, the pandemic robbed him of those opportunities, but the Padres saw enough of him previously to take a fifth-round shot and landed Haynes with a $300,000 bonus. It’s been all promise and little production since. After experiencing elbow issues and undergoing Tommy John surgery, the southpaw didn’t make his pro debut until 2023 with Single-A Lake Elsinore, and even then, he was only limited to 25 1/3 innings over 11 starts due to blister and shoulder problems. When he did get back on the mound for the Storm, the 6-foot-3 hurler showed solid velocity, touching 97 and generally sitting 92-95. It was a solid bounceback from the elbow injury, but considering Haynes didn’t throw more than 56 pitches in any of his California League starts, it’s still worth wondering how that heat will hold over longer outings. His mid-80s curveball helped play off the fastball and generate a 26.6 percent K rate, while he’s had the workings of a changeup dating back to his amateur days. Haynes’ 11.0 percent walk rate in the small sample isn’t a huge concern yet because of the missed time off. He was trending in the right direction before hitting the IL again, and that’s the main story here. He’ll still be on the young side as a 21-year-old on Opening Day 2024 and has the upside of a Major League starter, but he’ll need to prove both his stuff and his health over a longer term this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Haynes felt like the ultimate high-risk, high-reward prospect entering the 2020 Draft, and that remains true almost three years later. The southpaw needed innings to impress scouts out of remote West Columbus High School in North Carolina, and the 2020 pandemic wiped away that opportunity, and considering he wouldn’t turn 18 until after the Draft, he was considered somewhat of a wild card. The Padres and their area scouts believed enough in Haynes to take him in the fifth round, making him the youngest player selected that year, and signed him for a little below slot at $300,000. Left elbow issues and eventual Tommy John surgery have kept him from making a pro debut entering 2023, though his rehab process shows promising signs. During his healthier days, Haynes threw out of an athletic and easy delivery. His fastball was already touching 94 mph, and at 6-foot-3, he had the size and projection to add a few more ticks to the heater as he aged. His average slider represented some feel for spin, while his changeup looked like a potential above-average weapon, helping his case to start in the pros. After all the missed time, Haynes got back to pitching for Single-A Lake Elsinore this summer, and San Diego officials felt comfortable with how he was tracking before he hit the shelf with a blister issue in July. Haynes is going to need time to build up his repertoire as he enters his 20s.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the same remote county in North Carolina that produced fellow lefty MacKenzie Gore, whom the Padres selected with the No. 3 pick in the 2017 Draft, Haynes came with much less fanfare when San Diego took him in the fifth round in ‘20. The fact that Haynes’ senior year at West Columbus High was wiped out by the pandemic made him even more of a wild card, and at 17 years, 8 months old, Haynes was the youngest pitcher selected in the entire Draft. Unfortunately, left elbow issues and subsequent Tommy John surgery have kept Haynes from making his professional debut. Much like Gore, Haynes is an athletic left-hander with a free and easy delivery, albeit without the same raw stuff. Haynes can run his fastball up to 93-94 mph, and given his age and remaining physical projection, it’s easy to envision more velocity in the future as he adds strength and gains much-needed experience. He shows a feel to spin the ball and has a pair of promising secondary pitches in a slider and changeup. The Padres believe they landed a steal in Haynes and are quick to note that he likely would have shot up other team’s Draft boards had he been able to have a normal senior year. Because he’s so young, Haynes may need extra time to develop his craft in the Minor Leagues. He has enough qualities to profile as a starter long-term. But as a left-hander who is expected to throw hard, a spot coming out of the bullpen could be an option as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the same remote county in North Carolina that produced fellow lefty MacKenzie Gore, whom the Padres selected with the No. 3 pick in the 2017 Draft, Haynes came with much less fanfare when San Diego took him in the fifth round of the ’20 edition. The fact Haynes’ senior year at West Columbus High was wiped out by the pandemic made him even more of a wild card. At 17 years, 8 months old, Haynes was the youngest pitcher selected in the entire Draft. Unfortunately, elbow issues have kept Haynes from pitching for an affiliate in 2021. Much like Gore, Haynes is an athletic left-hander with a free and easy delivery, albeit without the same raw stuff. He can already run his fastball up to 93-94 mph, and given his age and remaining physical projection, it’s easy to forecast more velocity in Haynes’ future as he adds strength and gains much-needed experience. He has a pair of promising secondary pitches in a slider and changeup and was able to refine both offerings during his training this past spring. The Padres believe they landed a steal in Haynes and are quick to note that he likely would have shot up other team’s Draft boards had he been able to have a normal senior year. Because he’s so young and given the health of his elbow, Haynes may need extra time to develop his craft in the Minor Leagues. He has enough starter qualities to profile in that role long-term. But as a left-hander who is expected to throw hard, a spot coming out of the bullpen could be an option for him as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard led his Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) club to the Little League World Series Finals in 2014, six years before becoming just the third local product drafted by the Cubs in the first round. Signed for $3,745,500 as the 16th overall pick in 2020, he struggled offensively and missed time with a hamstring strain when sent to Single-A at age 19 to make his pro debut the following year. He didn't get much of a chance to rebound in 2022, severely injuring his hip in early May and requiring season-ending surgery. Howard's outstanding defense and makeup have prompted Chicago to challenge him with aggressive assignments. He hasn't disappointed with the glove, showing twitchy actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a plus arm capable of making strong throws from a variety of angles. He complements his tools with instincts and intelligence and looks like a future Gold Glover. Though amateur scouts had mixed opinions about Howard's offensive upside and he hit just .229/.287/.315 in 103 games during his first two pro seasons, the Cubs saw some encouraging signs before he got hurt last year. A right-handed hitter, he hit the ball significantly harder and controlled the strike zone better than he did in 2021. He could develop at least 15-homer power to go with his solid speed, but he's going to have to learn to recognize and deal with breaking balls and make adjustments to avoid producing weak ground-ball contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard starred at shortstop on the Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) club that advanced to the Little League World Series finals in 2014, six years before the Cubs made him just the third Windy City-area product they've ever drafted in the first round. Signed for $3,745,000 as the 16th overall pick in 2020, he's so advanced defensively that he headed directly to Low-A for his pro debut at age 19 last year. Initially overmatched at the plate before rallying in the final two months, he didn't get much of a chance to develop further in 2022 because he injured his left hip in a baserunning mishap in May and required season-ending surgery. One of the best defenders in the entire Minors, Howard is a legitimate plus-plus shortstop. He has quick-twitch actions, fast hands and a plus arm capable of making quality throws from a variety of angles. He has instincts and intelligence to complement his physical tools, and the only reason he spent time at second base last summer was to give fellow teenager Kevin Made some time at shortstop. After Howard's offensive upside drew mixed reviews on the high school showcase circuit, he didn't answer any of those questions in his debut. He has some promising building blocks in a sound right-handed swing, the bat speed and projectable strength to have perhaps average power and solid speed. But he also has a long ways to go with his plate discipline and pitch recognition, which leads to too many strikeouts and too much ground-ball contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The starting shortstop on the Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) team that advanced to the 2014 Little League World Series finals, Howard became just the third Windy City-area product selected in the first round by the Cubs. The top true shortstop in the 2020 Draft, he followed in the footsteps of Brian Rosinski (1975) and Don Schulze (1980) when Chicago took him 16th overall last June. Signed for $3,745,500, he impressed the Cubs with his physical and mental maturity during instructional league. The best defensive player in the system, Howard is a no-doubt shortstop. He has smooth, athletic actions as well as quick hands and a solid to plus arm capable of making throws from a variety of angles. He has the high baseball IQ to make the most of his tools and the internal clock to slow the game down on both sides of the ball. While Howard drew some mixed reviews as a hitter on the high school showcase circuit and again while making his pro debut with a challenging assignment to Low-A, he has an efficient right-handed swing and mature approach that should allow him to make consistent contact. He generates promising bat speed and is adding strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame, so he could develop average power. He's a solid runner who's an asset on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October 2021, Wagner moved from suburban Chicago to the P27 Academy (Lexington, S.C.) to face better competition. He thrived and went in the sixth round, where the Dodgers paid him their second-highest bonus ($597,500) in the 2022 Draft. He has barely played as a pro, getting into just 57 games in his first three seasons because he broke his right hamate in 2023 and his left hamate last year. A switch-hitter, Wagner has a more fluid and contact-oriented stroke from the right side and a more aggressive lefty swing that provides more damage. He arrived in pro ball with more physicality than most prep products, has bat speed to go with his strength and has shown the ability to launch balls to his pull side during his brief action. His 18 extra-base hits and 27 walks in 38 Single-A games last spring hinted at his power potential and on-base ability. Wagner played shortstop in high school and has seen action at second base this year, but he's better suited for the infield corners. Though he's a fringy runner, he has worked to improve his agility and become a capable defender at third base, though he played more first base last year on a Rancho Cucamonga club with a logjam of infielders. He has the solid arm strength to handle the hot corner and conceivably could try left or right field as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of suburban Chicago, Wagner made a name for himself at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October 2021 before moving to P27 Academy (Lexington, S.C.) to face better competition as a high school senior last spring. That decision paid off with the Dodgers selecting him in the sixth round and paying him their second-highest bonus ($600,000) in the 2022 Draft. Several area scouts thought he was comparable -- if a little less polished at the plate -- to fellow Palmetto State prep infielder Tucker Toman, who signed with the Blue Jays for $2 million as a supplemental second-rounder. A switch-hitter, Wagner has a more direct and fluid swing from the right side but barrels balls regularly as a lefty and righty. More physical than most teenagers, he has the strength and bat speed to develop 20-25 home run power. He also has the feel for hitting and the plate discipline to hit for average as well. Wagner played shortstop in high school and immediately moved to third base as a pro while also trying second base in his brief pro debut. With fringy speed and at least solid arm strength, he's a better fit at the hot corner. If that doesn't work out, he should provide enough offensive to profile as a corner outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliz was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 24 international prospect in the 2024 class and signed with the Nationals for $1.8 million that January. Only outfielder Victor Hurtado ($2.7 million) signed for more. Feliz was a Dominican Summer League mid-season All-Star in his first taste of the pros after hitting .310/.381/.468 with four homers and 27 steals in 49 games and handled himself decently well with his move stateside for his age-18 season in 2025. The infielder produced a .264/.366/.358 line in 53 games in the Florida Complex League and produced a 96 wRC+ with Single-A Fredericksburg following a late July promotion. It was notable that Feliz was one of only 30 age-18 prospects to get more than 100 plate appearances in Single-A last season and the only Washington player to meet that criteria. Already standing at 6-foot-3, there’s hope that he can add some strength to that frame and get to at least average power, but to do that, he’ll have to lift the ball at a much better rate. He doesn’t chase pitches outside the zone much for his age, but when he does, it’s often with an empty swing, especially against soft stuff. Starting with his hands held above his head, he can yank over breaking pitches beyond the outer third of the plate right now, but it’s still plenty early in his development cycle. Feliz will flash decent home-to-first times when he’s really pushing it out of the box, but many expect him to land at fringy speed at best by the time he fills out. He isn’t the twitchiest defender, though Nats officials have praised him for his hands on the dirt and arm strength. With Eli Willits likely in his path, Feliz remains a priority infielder, albeit one likely to move to third long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals went for two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 25 international prospects in the 2024 signing class, adding Dominican outfielder Victor Hurtado for $2.8 million and Feliz for $1.8 million out of the same country. The young shortstop was the better performer out of the gate in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .310/.381/.468 with four homers and 27 steals in 49 games. He led qualified DSL Nats in average, slugging, isolated slugging (.158), hits (53) and doubles (nines) and tied for the lead in homers on his way to mid-season All-Star honors. At 6-foot-3 already so early in his development cycle, Feliz drew excitement for his projectable power potential when signing and already put it to use in the DSL, specifically to the pullside. The exit velocities should only get louder from here, and if he can use added strength to elevate more on contact, there’s even the possibility for above-average pop here in time. Concerns about the length of Feliz’s swing were quieted some with good contact rates, but he’ll face much tougher tests against stateside pitching. Feliz ran wild in the DSL but is expected to have below-average speed by the time he reaches the Majors. The Nationals have stuck to their word about intending to play him at shortstop as much as possible, but the thought that he might have to move over to third base eventually remains. His arm strength will fit there. But everything is trending well enough offensively that Feliz moved to Single-A Fredericksburg for a late-season came at the end of his age-18 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Starting with a $5,284,400 signing pool, the Nationals came away with two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 25 international prospects in the 2024 class. Dominican outfielder Victor Hurtado (No. 20) was the headliner with a $2.8 million bonus, but not far behind him was Dominican infielder Feliz (No. 23) with a $1.8 million deal of his own. Both are expected to begin their careers in the Dominican Summer League. Standing in already at 6-foot-3 at just 17 years old, Feliz stood out to Nationals evaluators for his projectable size and strength. His promising pullside power should play pretty quickly when he first sees pro pitching. That right-handed swing can get a bit long, so tightening that up might be one of the early focuses for Washington’s hitting instructors, but the pop alone gives them plenty of positives to work with. The Nats say they believe Feliz can make impressive defensive plays up the middle at for his size, and given that we live in the age of the big shortstop, it’s possible he could stick there in time. It does seem more likely, however, that he’ll eventually have to move to third base, where he’s a more stereotypical fit. His arm strength -- which also drew praise as an amateur -- should help with that transition if and when it comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With some of the best all-around tools on the 2023 international market, Diaz landed a $2.25 million bonus, the highest in the Astros' class. It also ranks as the third-highest international bonus in franchise history and the most Houston ever paid an infielder from that talent pool. The Dominican broke into pro ball by hitting .209/.374/.353 with a 33 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. The 6-foot-3, 208-pound Diaz looks the part of a power hitter, possessing electric bat speed and more present strength than most 18-year-olds. He has 30-homer upside but will need to make adjustments to get there. His right-handed stroke gets too long, he chases too many pitches and he has too many empty swings, so he'll have to adapt to succeed as he faces more advanced pitching. Diaz can flash plus speed but figures to lose a step or two as he continues to fill out his large frame. He doesn't have smooth actions at shortstop and didn't look very rangy there in the DSL, increasing the likelihood that he'll eventually move to third base. He saw some action at the hot corner and has the strong arm required there, but he'll need to settle down defensively after being erratic at both positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz featured some of the best all-around tools in the 2023 international class and landed the highest bonus in the Astros' crop, signing for $2.25 million out of the Dominican Republic. That's the third-highest international bonus in franchise history and the most Houston ever has paid an infielder in that market. He'll likely make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in June. More physical than most 17-year-olds at 6-foot-3 and 208 pounds, Diaz has electric bat speed to go with his present strength and already plus raw power. His size creates a naturally long right-handed stroke and he has an aggressive approach, so he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact against quality pitching. If he can, he could provide upwards of 30 homers per season. Diaz currently has plus speed but could lose a step as he continues to fill out his frame. Between his size and the fact that he has good but not smooth actions at shortstop, he could wind up moving to third base in the future, though the Astros are confident that he'll remain up the middle. With his strong arm and power, he'd profile well at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina was ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list when the 2018-19 signing period began, and the Twins gave the outfielder $2.75 million to sign right out of the gate on July 2, the third-highest bonus given to a player in the signing period. He’s shown some glimpses of ability, especially in terms of his approach at the plate, but it’s come without much impact and his development has been impeded by the pandemic in 2020 and then visa issues that kept him from playing in 2022 until late June. There is no question the right-handed-hitting outfielder knows how to control the strike zone. He makes a ton of contact and draws walks, bringing a 17 percent strikeout rate and a walk rate just over 11 percent with him into the 2023 season. But he’s yet to show a consistent ability to do any damage or tap into any power. He did hit the ball a bit harder in 2022 with more line drives and fly balls, but he’ll have to show more to live up to the initial power projections. Urbina has slowed down some since signing and will have to stay on top of his body and conditioning to maximize his ability. He’s a center fielder by trade, but there is growing concern he won’t maintain his speed to stay up the middle. A move to a corner might be necessary, which puts even more pressure on him to be a more productive hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2018-19 international signing class, Urbina got $2.75 million to sign with the Twins right at the start of the signing period. He showed off his advanced feel to hit and speed during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and got pushed up to full-season ball in 2021, an aggressive assignment that didn’t go so well as the outfielder finished with a .585 OPS. His 2022 debut was delayed until late June because of visa issues. Despite the struggles, Urbina still showed off a strong knack for making contact and controlling the strike zone, with a 12.3 percent walk rate and a strikeout rate of just 18.7 percent. The issue was the quality of contact, with a lack of physicality leading to a lack of impact. He did work this offseason in Venezuela on adding strength and engaging his lower half more to give him a more impactful swing. Adding angle to that swing while having better pitch selection in terms of which ones to put into play will also help his offensive upside. While Urbina appeared to slow down a tick, the strength and conditioning work he put in this offseason should help in that regard as well. He has good instincts on defense and can still play center field even if he’s not quite the burner he was when he first signed. Urbina could have benefitted from a summer in a short-season league last year, but given how young he is, there’s time for him to reach the ceiling the Twins thought he had when they signed him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina was ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list when the 2018-19 signing period began, and he got the third-highest bonus in the class, $2.75 million, to sign with the Twins. He showed off an exciting offensive skill set in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and continued to impress with how he carried himself during his time at instructs last fall. Though he’ll be just 19 for nearly all of the 2021 season, Urbina really stands out for his feel for the game. He has incredible bat-to-ball skills and controls the strike zone very well, walking more than he struck out in the DSL and whiffing in just 6.5 percent of his plate appearances. He has a good swing from the right side of the plate and tends not to chase out of the zone. The only question is how much impact he’ll have, as he needs to add strength to get to what could be decent power in the future. Urbina is a plus runner right now, but beyond his pure speed, his tempo in the game helps him both be a basestealing threat and to play excellent outfield defense. While he played mostly center field during his debut, he looks very comfortable in all three outfield spots, with good instincts and routes, with the Twins thinking he could end up a plus defender in whatever spot he settles into.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Urbina spent several years in the Venezuelan Winter League’s parallel program for young players, showing what he could do against older and more experienced players. That helped make him one of the best players in the amateur crop for the 2018-19 international signing period and led to the Twins signing him for $2.75 million on July 2. He didn’t disappoint in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, showing off impressive all-around skills. Urbina has the chance to be an outstanding hitter, one who could eventually develop into a plus hitter in the future. He makes consistent hard contact and can use all fields well. Right now, he’s showing mostly doubles power, more to the pull side, but the right-handed hitter should grow into more pop as he matures, even though he’s not the biggest guy in the world. He has an advanced approach at the plate, walking more than he struck out during his pro debut. Urbina’s plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball. He’s already a basestealing threat, swiping 19 bags in the DSL in 2019, and he has outstanding range in center field, with the chance to be at least an above-average defender there long-term. Urbina is obviously still far away, but the Twins are excited to see what he can do in the United States for the first time in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the start of the 2018-19 international signing period drew near, Urbina was No. 3 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list. The Twins wasted no time to pounce, inking the talented outfielder for $2.75 million. He'll make his professional debut this season. Urbina has the chance to be a dynamic up-the-middle player who hits at or near the top of a lineup. He's shown an ability to make consistent line-drive contact, performing well against older competition in the Venezuelan Winter League's parallel program for young players over the years. He has plus speed, he's been clocked with premium 60-yard times, that should help him on both sides of the ball. He's already considered an advanced defender who can stay in center field long-term and he continues to make strides with his throwing, with evaluators feeling he'll have an average arm in the future. It will be years before the Twins get a return on their investment with Urbina. But the combination of his instincts, makeup and tools will make it exciting to watch him begin the climb up the Twins ladder in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A California prep product, Barber earned an over-slot $1 million bonus as a 2019 fourth-rounder because the Astros were intrigued by his power/speed combination. But his pop hasn't fully developed and he has lost some quickness, in large part because of shoulder, ankle and hip injuries that limited him to 189 games in his first five years as a pro. He played in a career-high 79 contests in 2023, batting .244/.358/.433 in Double-A. When fully healthy, Barber has shown the ability to work counts, launch balls in the air and employ the entire field from the left side of the plate. He has the bat speed and strength to provide 20 homers per season, and his power plays to all parts of the ballpark. He hasn't produced high batting averages outside of 2022 and he hasn't done much damage against southpaws, so he might not be more than a platoon option. Barber once flashed plus speed but now is an average runner who doesn't take a lot of chances on the bases. After dividing time between all three outfield positions but seeing more action in center field earlier in his career, he only had duty on the corners in 2023. With fringy arm strength, he's better suited for left field than right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have been waiting for Barber to take off since signing him to an over-slot $1 million bonus as a fourth-rounder from a California high school in 2019. He has shown one of the best power/speed combinations in the system when he has taken the field, but the pandemic (2020), shoulder surgery (2021) and shoulder and ankle ailments (2022) limited him to 110 games in four years as a pro. He batted .294/.400/.439, mostly in High-A, while playing in a career-high 66 contests last season. When healthy, Barber has shown a promising ability to work counts, lift balls in the air and use the entire field. He's still learning to drive balls to his pull side, though he has enough bat speed and strength to produce 20-homer power from the left side of the plate. He hasn't been effective against southpaws, though he's an intelligent hitter who could make adjustments once he gets regular at-bats. Barber has settled in as a solid runner as he has matured physically. He's aggressive on the bases and has improved his reads and routes in center field, where he's an average defender. He has arm strength to match and divided his time almost equally among all three outfield spots in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barber's combination of power potential and speed earned him an over-slot $1 million bonus as a fourth-round pick in 2019. Because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and labrum surgery on his right (non-throwing) shoulder in 2021, he accrued just 141 at-bats in his first three years as a pro, including only 42 in full-season ball. The Astros still have high hopes for him and believe his tools and work ethic will allow him to rebound from all that lost time, and one club official likens his intensity to Alex Bregman's. Despite his youth and inexperience, Barber already shows the ability to work counts and launch balls in the air. He has the bat speed and strength to produce at least average power from the left side of the plate, though he can get too pull-conscious. Houston has had him focus on driving balls from gap to gap and he did a better job of using the entire field during his brief 16-game stint last season before getting hurt. Barber presently flashes plus speed but likely will be more of a solid runner once he matures physically. He makes the most of his quickness with an aggressive nature on the bases and in center field, where his reads and routes have improved. His average to solid arm strength fits at all three outfield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barber had one of the better power/speed combinations in the 2019 prep class, which helped him garner an over-slot $1 million bonus as a fourth-rounder. He finished strong in his pro debut and divided his 2020 between the independent City of Champions circuit (where he was the youngest player at age 19), a brief appearance at Houston's alternate site and instructional league. Besides his tools, he has impressed the Astros with his work ethic and focus, with one club official comparing his intensity to Alex Bregman's. Barber has a mature offensive approach for a youngster, showing the ability to work counts and use the entire field. With his quick left-handed swing, projectable strength and propensity for launching the ball in the air, he should develop at least average power. Houston had him focus on driving the ball from gap to gap during instructional league and was pleased with his progress, though his development was limited to just 16 games this year before he injured his shoulder and required season-ending surgery. With present plus speed and an aggressive nature, Barber is a potential 20-20 player. He may slow down a bit as he fills out, which might dictate a move from center to right field. He played all three outfield positions during his pro debut and has the solid arm strength and offensive ability to profile in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2025 international signing period looked to be a particularly fruitful one for the Mariners at the outset. They inked a pair of top 20 prospects in Yorger Bautista and Martínez, who got the organization’s largest bonus of $2.5 million when the period opened in January. Playing at age 17 for his debut in the Dominican Summer League, Martínez struggled mightily, posting a .475 OPS over 37 games, serving as notice that sometimes patience is very much needed in the development of young prospects. Martínez will try to hit the reset button in 2026. He had entered the system with a reputation of having a high floor because of a strong feel for hitting that did not materialize in the DSL. He had gotten rave reviews about his quick left-handed swing and being short to the ball, geared toward contact, but he didn’t find a consistent approach during his debut, striking out in 27.8 percent of his plate appearances. He had just one extra-base hit, but there is projection with the potential to add strength to his frame, with the hope of some impact showing up as he matures. The teenager split time between shortstop and second base last year, actually getting more time at the keystone. He’s shown good defensive instincts at times with average speed and perhaps enough arm to play the left side of the infield. This is looking like a long-term project, and he might need a few years at Rookie levels to find his footing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With as good a track record as any team in terms of signing and developing hitters from the international market, the Mariners may have struck gold again in 2025, two times over. Not only did they sign Yorger Bautista, No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 prospects for the international Class of ‘25, they also picked up Martínez, No. 19 on that list, for $2.5 million. They were one of four teams to land two top 20 prospects when the signing period opened this past January. While Bautista might boast a tremendous ceiling, Martínez is a little more of a whole-is-greater-than-the-sum-of-his-parts kind of prospect with a higher floor. A lot of that stems from what could be a plus hit tool in time, with a clean left-handed swing that’s short to the ball thanks to quick hands. It remains to be seen what kind of power he gets to as he advances, but there is some projection and ability to add strength to his frame, so he could start driving the ball in time given his knack for finding the barrel, albeit with a flatter bat path and up-the-middle approach. Martínez has the chance to stick at shortstop long term. He may not be an electric defender, but his excellent instincts and internal clock help him maximize his average speed and arm to play the premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Parada attended Catcher U at Georgia Tech and was an immediate contributor for the Yellow Jackets, producing a .929 OPS as a freshman in 2021. He set a school record with 26 homers as a Draft-eligible sophomore and slashed .361/.453/.709 over 60 games, pushing him into easy first-round territory. The Mets used the first of their two Top 14 picks on Parada with hopes he could be a quick mover in their system. Parada did reach Double-A by the end of his first full season but finished with a .248/.324/.428 slash line and 14 homers over 105 games. A right ankle injury limited him somewhat, and he made up for the lost time with 18 games in the Arizona Fall League, where he put up a .611 OPS. The plus power potential is still there for the right-handed slugger, especially to the pull side, which was beneficial when he wasn’t aiming for the Coney Island beach in Brooklyn. His exit velocities are still promising, and batting from a relaxed stance with a decent leg kick, he’s able to elevate well on contact. But he exhibited above-average swing-and-miss rates against fastballs and breaking stuff on pitches in and close to the zone, and that will only become more worrisome the higher he climbs against sharper stuff. Parada displayed below-average arm strength in college and professional baserunners ran rampant against him, swiping 115 bags – the 10th-most against any catcher in the Minors – despite getting only 59 starts behind the dish. His framing also remains a focus, though the Mets are happy with how much work he’s putting in, and they haven't made any moves toward another position. Parada’s value still comes at the plate, not behind it, as he tries to refind his Tech form in the pros.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Parada could have been a fairly high pick in the 2020 Draft but was insistent upon going to Georgia Tech, the alma mater of backstops Jason Varitek, Matt Wieters and Joey Bart. The right-handed slugger took to the college game quickly with a .929 OPS as a freshman and then took off with a .361/.453/.709 line and school-record 26 homers as a Draft-eligible sophomore. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 6 Draft prospect, Parada went at No. 11 to the Mets and translated instantly to the pro game with a .455 OBP and 13/12 K/BB ratio in 13 games, mostly at Single-A St. Lucie, where he won a league title. Part of Parada’s pre-swing setup includes a bat wiggle and a decent leg kick, but he has few issues covering the zone, making contact and driving the ball to all fields. His exit velocity topped out at 105.5 mph in his brief FSL stay, but there should be more in the tank over a larger sample as he settles into pro ball. Repeating 20-plus homers isn’t likely to be an issue by the time he reaches the Majors, and his ability to marry average and power will drive his place toward the middle of most lineups. Defense has long been a primary focus for Parada, and that’s notable considering he looked like he was wearing down with additional playing time at Georgia Tech and with Team USA in 2021. His caught-stealing rate gradually improved from his freshman to sophomore years, but his general arm strength still checks in at below-average. While the Mets are pleased with his growth in 2023, he remains a work-in-progress behind the plate. No matter, Parada’s potential with the bat is so good that he profiles as a potential bat-first everyday catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robberse signed with the Blue Jays for $125,000 out of Zeist, Netherlands in July 2019, a few months shy of his 18th birthday and methodically climbed the Toronto system over the next four years. He was with Double-A New Hampshire in 2023 when Toronto dealt him to St. Louis as part of the return for Jordan Hicks at the Trade Deadline. He immediately headed to Triple-A for the first time and was added to the 40-man roster when he became Rule 5 eligible that offseason. Robberse returned to Memphis for 2024 but was limited to 84 1/3 innings there due to elbow tightness, posting a 4.59 ERA with 76 strikeouts in that span. The 6-foot-1 right-hander still hasn’t managed to add much velocity as he’s aged and was still sitting only 90-92 mph and topping out at 93.7 mph with his four-seamer at Triple-A. It was his primary pitch, technically, but without great movement, he only threw it 29.3 percent of the time. That’s a sound strategy considering his sweeping 82-84 mph slider (with an average 12.9 inches of gloveside break) and 86-89 mph changeup were much better at generating whiffs. The latter is particularly interesting because it may not have a ton of separation from the four-seam but has enough run to make Robberse a reverse-splits righty. An upper-80s cutter rounds out the arsenal but was hit hard in Triple-A. Without elite velo, Robberse needs to be able to hit his spots, and his 7.8 percent walk rate at Triple-A was a nice improvement from his 10.6 percent mark at all levels in ’23. The more he leans on the slider versus righties and changeup against lefties, the better chance he’ll have to be a No. 5 starter. The pursuit of such a role will be delayed following the May news that Robberse needed Tommy John surgery. He will miss the remainder of the 2025 season and could be out for a chunk of 2026, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robberse signed with the Blue Jays out of Zeist, Netherlands, in July 2019, and he stayed stateside during the lost 2020 pandemic season. Since then, he's followed a pattern of playing for two teams per season following a repeat of a level and an in-season promotion. In 2023, the 21-year-old had a 4.06 ERA and 86 strikeouts in 88 2/3 innings for Double-A New Hampshire when Toronto dealt him to the Cardinals alongside Adam Kloffenstein for Jordan Hicks at the Trade Deadline. St. Louis moved Robberse to Triple-A Memphis after the transaction, and he posted a 4.84 ERA with 44 K’s and 24 walks in 35 1/3 innings there. With his Rule 5 eligibility looming, the Cards added Robberse to their 40-man roster in November. There has long been hope that the 6-foot-1 right-hander would add velocity as he’s aged, and that hasn’t quite manifested yet. His fastball primarily sat 91-93 mph in 2023, and without much movement, it wasn’t much of a bat misser. However, his secondaries showed a good amount of promise, starting with an 82-86 mph breaking ball with sweep and depth that helped him wear out the low, gloveside corner. An upper-80s changeup may not have the separation of a typically great pitch of that designation but the armside fade was good enough to fool batters en route to a 43 percent whiff and chase rate. Robberse also worked with an upper-80s cutter right around the 0 horizontal movement mark. Because he doesn’t overthrow from his three-quarters slot, the Dutch hurler hasn’t suffered many control issues outside of Triple-A, where ABS may have played a role. Any velo/movement improvement on the heater could get him to St. Louis before his 23rd birthday. He was dealing with elbow tightness in June that led to an extended IL stint.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robberse is a unique development story, originally signed out of Zeist, Netherlands, in 2019. He was able to make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League that season, allowing just one run over 10 1/3 innings. When the pandemic stopped baseball, Robberse was unable to return to the Netherlands and stayed at a hotel near the Blue Jays’ complex with a group of prospects, including many of the Venezuelan players. This added yet another interesting wrinkle to his growth as he was often forced to work out by himself. Coming out of that, Robberse posted a 4.36 ERA over 88 2/3 innings in 2021, split between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver. Each number moved in the right direction in 2022, as Robberse climbed another level to Double-A and finished with a cumulative ERA of 3.23 over 111 1/3 innings, striking out 97. Much of Robberse’s game is self-taught, which gives him a unique ability to adjust on the fly, and the Blue Jays were encouraged with some of his physical growth, too. After trying to keep on weight for years, Robberse finally packed it on in ’22 and is now up above 200 pounds, which was the goal. There’s hope this can bump his fastball up closer to the 93-94 mph range eventually. An increased strikeout ability would serve Robberse well, as at this point he relies on finesse with a promising package of secondaries. Now with the Cardinals after a Jordan Hicks trade at the 2023 deadline, the Futures Game participant can carry his momentum forward in hopes of joining a future St. Louis rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in 2019 out of Zeist, Netherlands, Robberse is one of the most unique development cases in Toronto’s system. The right-hander appeared in just five GCL games as a 17-year-old back in ’19, but when the COVID shutdown hit in ’20, he was unable to return to the Netherlands and instead stayed at a hotel near the Blue Jays’ complex along with other prospects, including a large Venezuelan group. Robberse worked to keep weight on and train his arm with workouts provided by the club, but this threw a wrench into some valuable development time. Back on the mound in ’21, Robberse split time between Low-A and High-A, posting a 4.36 ERA over 88 2/3 innings with 90 strikeouts. Robberse had his fastball up to 93-95 mph at the end of ’21, but dropped a bit of weight and has been building that back up. His curveball sits just ahead of his slider and has the potential to be an above-average pitch while his developing changeup trails behind. The Blue Jays like Robberse’s feel for pitching and his athletic delivery, which comes naturally and is more self-taught than other prospects in these ranks. Coaches also compliment Robberse’s ability to take feedback and immediately implement it on the mound, which lends to their belief that his development will continue at this rate through the upper levels. He also used much of the down time during the shutdown to develop his mental game, diving into pitch sequencing and mound strategies. Now 20, Robberse still needs to add muscle to his frame and sustain that over the course of a full season, but he’s already exceeding expectations, especially when you consider the disruptions he’s been forced to deal with. Now one of the highest-upside arms in the system, Robberse does still have a wide range of outcomes from here, but he’s put himself in a very good place entering ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in late July 2019 as an international free agent out of Zeist, Netherlands, where he spent the entirety of his amateur career and competed for his country internationally, the young right-hander opened eyes quickly in his pro debut. Though he only got into five games in the rookie Gulf Coast League, Robberse offered a flash of what the Blue Jays hope they’ll see more of in the future, posting a 0.87 ERA over 10 1/3 innings, walking none and striking out nine. Given that much of Robberse’s game is self-taught, the right-hander’s delivery is a natural movement that the Blue Jays believe comes with plenty of projection. Robberse’s fastball velocity has moved from the high-80s to the low-90s with room for more growth, and his curveball, a pitch he throws confidently, is well ahead of his developing changeup when it comes to secondaries. One could argue that his mid-80s slider has overtaken the curve as his best breaking pitch in 2021, and it’s helped take his profile to a new level. When Robberse signed with the Blue Jays, he had an extremely wide range of potential outcomes, and that remains true. The potential is there for a breakout, though, especially as he develops his 6-foot-1, 160-pound frame. Robberse is one of the more intriguing long-term rotation projects in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Signed in late July as an international free agent out of Zeist, Netherlands, where he spent the entirety of his amateur career and competed for his country internationally, the young right-hander opened eyes quickly in his pro debut. Though he only got into five games in the rookie Gulf Coast League, Robberse offered a flash of what the Blue Jays hope they’ll see more of in the future, posting a 0.87 ERA over 10 1/3 innings, walking none and striking out nine. Robberse has a three-pitch mix, featuring a fastball, curveball and changeup. His curve is ahead of his changeup in the development stage, with a lot of confidence and feel for his breaking pitch, and he has advanced feel for all of his secondary stuff and a high baseball IQ that helps him on the mound. His velocity ticked up throughout the 2019 season, starting in the mid-to-to-high 80s and getting up into the low 90s, and team officials believe he will continue trending in the right direction. While there are a huge range of outcomes possible for the young right-hander because of his relative lack of experience and flashes of greatness on the mound, he has an incredibly projectable frame and plenty of room for growth. The upside is there to dream on him as a big league rotation member.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the more highly regarded international prospects available for the 2019-20 signing period, Vera commanded a $2 million bonus in July 2019, then was basically stuck in his Arizona apartment and unable to stay in shape during 2020 because of the pandemic. In 2021, he turned his conditioning around and went out and hit well during his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League to earn a late bump up to full-season ball. The 2022 season, however, was a disaster, as Vera struggled out of the gate and let it snowball. Still only 20, there’s time for Vera to right the ship, but after a year in which he finished with a .572 OPS, he has a lot to work on. A 6-foot-2 athletic switch-hitter, Vera had shown a strong feel for making contact in the past, and there was belief he could tap into some raw power as he added strength. In 2022, he chased out of the zone much more than he should have and didn’t make enough contact to overcome that, with a 27 percent strikeout rate far too high for someone without big-time power. He’ll have to work to make better swing decisions moving forward. Vera is still a good defender with excellent actions and a strong arm, enough for him to play shortstop going forward. For now, the emphasis will be on him finding a better approach at the plate if he’s going to have a chance to fulfill his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vera was ranked in the top 10 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospect list when the 2019-20 signing period began and the Angels gave him $2 million to join the organization in July of 2019. The pandemic not only kept him from making his debut in 2020, but he was pretty much stuck in an Arizona apartment for an extremely long time and gained weight as a result. He was able to return to his conditioning, shedding those pounds in time to hit .317/.384/.469 in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, earning a late promotion to Low-A ball at age 18. Vera reported to camp this spring in even better shape and the Angels were thrilled with where he was physically, though that didn’t help his offensive profile as he struggled to find consistency in full-seson ball. He’s still hit over power, and has shown the ability in the past to make contact from both sides of the plate. He doesn’t draw a ton of walks and his strikeout rate crept upward in 2022. There’s plenty of bat speed and his added strength should allow him to start tapping into his raw power, even if he always has a contact-first approach. There is a chance Vera’s 6-foot-2 frame will fill out too much and he’ll become too big for shortstop, though he shows very good actions and more than enough arm for the premium position. He could be a plus defender if he eventually has to move to third and there’s confidence the extra-base authority will come to profile well at the corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A dozen prospects got bonuses of $2 million or more during the 2019-20 international signing period. Vera, one of two to get seven-figure bonuses from the Angels over that time, was at the bottom of that dozen, getting $2 million even to sign on July 2. The shutdown kept him from making his professional debut in 2020. Because he was stuck in one place, he wasn’t able to work out, so he came to instructs with some added weight. The good news is that he still showed off tremendous tools and already has shed the excess pandemic-induced weight. The Angels gave Vera that kind of bonus because they feel he can be an impact player at a premium position. He swings the bat well from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed and an advanced feel for the strike zone that’s geared for contact. There’s definite raw power to tap into, but he’s hit over power for sure, with the chance for him to be a plus hitter in time. While Vera is an average runner, he might be as close to a true shortstop as the Angels have in the system. He moves very fluidly with outstanding actions and instincts, a strong arm and very true hands. The only thing that will keep him from being an above-average defender at short is if he slows down too much in the future, which eventually could necessitate a move to another infield position, though that’s not something being discussed at all internally at this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A shortstop out of Venezuela who ranked highly on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list as the 2019-20 signing period opened last July 2, Vera got $2 million from the Angels to join the organization. With that price tag comes lofty expectations, even if patience is used, and Vera has already stood out at instructs and the Angels’ pre-spring program in Arizona. Vera’s tools and advanced feel for the game, especially given his age, give him the chance to be a true impact player. The Angels love his swing from both sides of the plate and think he could be a plus hitter when all is said and done. He has plenty of bat speed and was already showing plate discipline that belies his age and lack of experience. There’s above-average raw power in there with the chance for it to be at least average game power once he physically matures. The only tool that isn’t going to be above-average is his speed, but he’s a very good defender, with a strong arm, really good hands and excellent range despite the lack of quickness. He’ll have every chance to play shortstop long-term, but will profile just fine at second or third should he outgrow the position. He’ll be 17 as he plays his first professional games in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Simpson was selected by the Pirates in the 18th round of the 2019 Draft but opted to honor his commitment and play at Washington. He didn’t generate enough excitement to get drafted again after his junior season and instead returned for his senior year. He was eventually taken by the A’s in the 15th round (436th overall) and immediately delivered encouraging results in the A’s system, reaching Double-A by the end of his first full season. Looking to add right-handed power to their system, the Rays acquired Simpson along with two pitchers and a Draft pick in return for lefties Jeffrey Springs and Jacob Lopez. Batting with a slightly open stance and his hands high, Simpson makes good use of all the power in his 6-foot-3, 225-pound frame. The 23-year-old has legitimate power, ranking up there with the top hitters in the Rays’ system in terms of bat speed and exit velocity. With the A’s, assistant GM Billy Owens compared his hitting profile to former All-Star Garrett Cooper, another big right-handed slugger. The 23-year-old can barrel balls to all fields, but he’s also shown a good sense of what he’s doing and the adjustments he needs to make during at-bats. Simpson has mostly played first base, but he’s more athletic than many might assume. He could split time between first and the outfield this season, and he even got some work at third base with the A’s. As a right-handed-hitting first baseman who won’t add value on the bases, Simpson’s bat will obviously have to carry his profile. From what he’s shown, it could carry him pretty far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A’s selected Simpson in the 15th round of the 2023 Draft following four solid years at the University of Washington. Shortly after, he began his pro career in the Arizona Complex League and ended the year at Single-A Stockton, where he hit .322/.373/.544 with four homers, 11 doubles and 16 RBIs in 29 games, leaving a strong first impression before embarking on his first full season in 2024. Simpson is a cerebral player with a good understanding of the analytics side of the game and how to gameplan for every at-bat. This advanced approach should help him maintain a decent walk rate while keeping strikeout totals relatively low. There is some good power potential, as evidenced by his 18 homers as a senior at Washington, and his big 6-foot-4 frame has drawn some comparisons to Garrett Cooper. Despite his bigger size, Simpson is a decent defender at first base and is also plenty capable of handling the corner outfield spots thanks to his sneaky effective athleticism. He plays the game hard, which caught the eye of many within the A’s organization who look forward to watching him go through his first full season after a productive first look.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Houck was a two-way star at Parkview HS in Liburn, Ga., the same school that produced Matt Olson and Jeff Francouer. He threw for 2,189 yards as a senior quarterback, earning Power 5 football offers along the way, and was named Gatorade’s Georgia Player of the Year for baseball. The Mets selected the Mississippi State commit with the 32nd overall pick in 2023 and signed for him above slot at $2.75 million. Houck spent his entire first full season with Single-A St. Lucie but struggled with the jump to full-season ball, hitting just .206/.304/.306 with five homers and 171 strikeouts in 112 games. Houck’s 171 K’s were tied for third-most among Single-A batters, and his 36.3 percent K rate was fourth-highest among qualifiers at the level. The punchouts came in a variety of ways. On one hand, the right-handed hitter couldn’t handle breaking and offspeed pitches, whiffing on 53.9 percent of his swings against secondaries. On the other, he had 59 called third strikes because of his passivity; no one else in the FSL had more than 42. When he did make contact, there was still decent pop in there for his age and experience level. An average runner, Houck has plus arm strength, and that helps him on the left side of the dirt.
