He remains a work in progress defensively, however, and saw time at third base earlier than expected. He can rush plays at the corner, either forcing him to bobble on a transfer or throw inaccurately. Houck will be 20 for the entire 2025 Minor League season, making him the age of a college sophomore, but he needs to prove he can adjust off these early issues to get anything close to the potential he showed heading into the 2023 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While at Parkview (Liburn, Ga.) HS – the school that produced Matt Olson and Jeff Francoeur – Houck threw for 2,189 yards and 24 touchdowns as a senior quarterback and was also named Gatorade’s Georgia Player of the Year for his work on the diamond. He turned down Power 5 football offers to commit to Mississippi State only to go 32nd overall in the Draft to the Mets. New York signed Houck for just above slot at $2.75 million and sent him to the Florida Complex League, where he went 7-for-29 (.241) in nine games. Batting from the right side, the 6-foot-2 Houck has had a flummoxing first full season at the plate with Single-A St. Lucie. He's looked passive at the plate at times, even with two strikes leading to a ton of strikeouts looking, and his contact rate against pitches in the zone is general has been rough. He's especially struggled against non-fastballs as he's dug in against pro pitchers over an extended amount of time. His exit velocities when he has managed to make contact have been average at least, which is more in line with his pre-Draft scouting report. Houck has at least average speed, and he has the body control and obvious arm strength to handle plays at shortstop. Some project him to trend more toward third base as he matures, but there will be added pressure on the bat should he need to move to the corner. Houck will seek to rebound, likely back in the Florida State League, in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After getting hammered for a 6.79 ERA in three seasons at Cal State Fullerton, Knorr transferred to Coastal Carolina in 2022, added velocity and pitched his way into the third round of the Draft. He struck out 125 in 98 innings while advancing to Double-A in his first two pro seasons but has had a hard time staying healthy. Persistent shoulder issues sidelined him for the final two months of the 2023 season and the last three months in 2024. Knorr works at 93-95 mph and reached 98 mph with carry on his fastball, though it lacks movement and got rocked last year when he threw it over the plate. His tight mid-80s slider was his most effective chase pitch last year, but it too got hit when he didn't locate it well. He also has an upper-80s curveball and a low-80s changeup with fade and depth, and the latter could be his best weapon if he can command it better. Knorr works exclusively out of the stretch and his short arm action and extension bolster his deception. He pounded the strike zone in college but his walk rate has doubled from 5 percent at that level to 10 percent in his first two pro seasons. His mound presence adds to his starter's package, and the Astros believe they can help him get more out of his stuff, though they're going to have to keep him healthy first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knorr got knocked around en route to a 6.79 ERA in three years at Cal State Fullerton before transferring to Coastal Carolina and discovering more velocity and success in 2022. He topped the Sun Belt Conference in K/BB ratio (6.6), finished second in strikeout rate (11.2 per nine innings) and worked his way into the third round of the Draft. He fanned 78 in 58 1/3 innings between two Class A levels during his 2023 pro debut but missed the final two months with a shoulder injury. Knorr's fastball jumped from 90-92 mph in 2021 to 93-96 and topped out at 98 the following spring, albeit with more downhill plane than carry. He has maintained that velocity in pro ball while adding more power to his breaking pitches, a tight mid-80s slider and an upper-70s curveball with more vertical movement. They're both average offerings, as is his low-80s change with fade and depth. Working exclusively out of the stretch, Knorr features a short arm action that adds deception without detracting from his ability to throw strikes. His control wasn't as sharp in his debut as it was at Coastal Carolina, and he needs to refine his command because his pitches don't have a lot of life. A tough competitor, he could become a back-of-the-rotation starter if he develops a solid second offering and refines his ability to locate his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knorr got rocked for a 6.79 ERA in three seasons at Cal State Fulllerton before transferring to Coastal Carolina and finding more velocity and success in 2022. He led the Sun Belt Conference in K/BB ratio (6.6) and was second in strikeouts per nine innings (11.2) before signing for an under-slot $487,500 in the third round. As they did with all three of the college pitchers they took in the top four rounds last July, the Astros gave him the summer off and will have him make his pro debut in 2023. Knorr went from pitching with a 90-92 mph fastball with the Titans in 2021 to parking at 93-96 mph and peaking at 98 with the Chanticleers. His heater comes with more downhill plane than life, so he has to rely on his ability to command it well to keep it off barrels. His 83-85 mph changeup with fade and depth is his best secondary pitch, and he adds to its deception by selling it with fastball arm speed. Though Knorr missed some bats with his breaking pitches in college they were too soft, and the Astros have helped him add more power to what are now a mid-80s slider and an upper-70s curveball. He works exclusively out of the stretch and employs a short arm action that creates deception without detracting him from solid control. If he can continue to pound the zone while developing a more reliable breaking ball, he could fit in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela, Mogollon has emerged as the best prospect from Chicago's 2023 international crop. He posted a .967 OPS in two different Rookie leagues during his first two pro seasons but didn't enjoy the same success in his full-season debut in 2025. He slashed .220/.347/.387 in 51 games, though some of that performance may be attributed to a hamstring injury that cost him most of May and ended his season in late June. Mogollon has the best all-around tools among the White Sox's relatively deep group of second-base prospects, though it remains to be seen if his approach will work against advanced pitching. He has a reasonable idea of the strike zone but a maximum-effort right-handed stroke that seeks to launch balls as far as he can to his pull side. That mindset results in shocking exit velocities for a player listed at 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds but also a lot of empty swings. Mogollon displays plus speed when healthy and looks to make things happen on the bases, stealing 42 in 50 attempts (84 percent) in his first 144 pro games. He has split his time between second base and shortstop, and while he has enough arm strength for the left side of the infield, his range is better suited for the keystone. He can get out of control at both positions and needs more reliability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela, Mogollon looks like the best prospect from Chicago's 2023 international crop. He batted .289/.412/.555 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons, ranking fourth in the Dominican Summer League with 10 homers in his debut and third in the Arizona Complex League with eight blasts last year. Though he's listed at 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds, he produces some of the best exit velocities in the system. After showing a more measured approach in the DSL, Mogollon adopted a leg kick and focused almost solely on launching balls in the air to his pull side in 2024. With his quick right-handed stroke, he still smoked balls hard and hit some tape-measure shots, but he also posted the third-highest strikeout rate in the ACL at 38 percent. He's not afraid to work deep counts and take walks, and he does show some feel for the barrel when he's not trying to do too much at the plate, but he'll have to tone down his aggressiveness when he faces better pitching. A plus runner with savvy on the bases, Mogollon stole 16 bags in as many attempts in 46 games last season. After playing more second base in his debut, he spent most of 2024 at shortstop. He has solid arm strength, though his range is just average at short and he needs to improve his defensive consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for just $75,000 out of Venezuela, early returns indicate that Mogollon may be the best prospect in Chicago's 2023 international class. He slashed .315/.417/.582 in his pro debut, ranking fourth in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 10 homers. He stands just 5-foot-8 and is a long way from the Majors, but he offers one of the more intriguing combinations of hitting ability and power potential in the system. While he won't be a true slugger, Mogollon has stunning raw pop for his age and size, already producing occasional tape-measure shots -- at age 17, he had a maximum exit velocity of 105 mph. He has a quick right-handed stroke and already shows some feel for driving the ball in the air. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate and has a knack for putting the barrel on the ball. The rest of Mogollon's tools are average, though he's a savvy and aggressive runner on the bases. He plays under control in the middle infield, with his range and arm best suited for second base. He saw some action at shortstop in 2023 and the White Sox want to give him more time during his U.S. debut this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suarez signed for only $10,000 out of Venezuela in May 2018 but became a name to know after posting a 1.79 ERA with 47 strikeouts in 40 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League a year later. He missed 2020 due to the pandemic and then had his momentum further stifled by Tommy John surgery six starts into his 2021 campaign. Suarez didn’t look fully back on track until early summer 2023 and truly took off in his final 15 appearances between High-A Brooklyn and Double-A Binghamton, posting a 2.53 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 98 strikeouts and 21 walks over 74 2/3 innings in that span. To boot, he tossed back-to-back hitless outings over 13 innings in his first two starts in the Eastern League. The 6-foot-3 right-hander averaged 95.2 mph with his fastball in three Binghamton starts, proving he was still strong toward the end of first season with 100+ frames. His command of the pitch seemed to jump once he made a midseason adjustment of moving from the first-base side of the rubber to the third-base side. He also ditched a cutter that acted more like a bad fastball and went toward an 82-85 mph gyro slider that got more swing-and-miss in the zone, leading him to throw it 31 percent of the time at Double-A. Suarez also still has an upper-70s curveball and upper-80s changeup for additional looks. Suarez’s walk rate plummeted from 16.6 percent in his first nine starts to 7.2 percent over those final 15 following the mound change. That’s much more palatable for his rotation chances. He’s ticketed to become a Minor League free agent after 2024 and has a number of similarly aged starters ahead of him on the depth chart. But Suarez’s momentum makes him an interesting follow at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $10,000 signing out of Venezuela in May 2018, Suarez made a name for himself when he posted a 1.79 ERA with 47 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League a year later. After working out stateside during the canceled 2020 season, the right-hander returned to make six starts for Low-A St. Lucie but managed just a 7.66 ERA in 24 2/3 innings. Elbow issues may have been to blame, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in June, ending his 2021 season there. During his Low-A time last season, Suarez was around 92-94 mph with the fastball, and he touched 95.5 mph with his hardest-thrown pitch of the season. Once he’s fully recovered, he could add more velocity, as some do following Tommy John. An upper-80s changeup remained his most-used secondary pitch because he’s shown the most feel for it early in his career, and a developing mid-70s curveball showed some promise with its vertical drop. The 6-foot-3 right-hander did take a step back in terms of his control with a 13.6 percent walk rate in the short 2021 sample, but that could have been related to the elbow issue. The Mets are still hopeful that Suarez, who is back on an early throwing program this spring, can be a serviceable starter in time. He’ll try to back up that optimism with an expected return to the mound in late 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suarez was far from a big name in the 2017-18 international signing period, when he signed for only $10,000 out of Venezuela in May 2018. His stock has steadily risen since then, aided by a promising first trip stateside in 2019. During that campaign, Suarez finished with a 1.79 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 16 walks over 40 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League. The right-hander spent the 2020 shutdown at the Mets’ facility in Florida with his fellow Venezuelans. He made six starts for Low-A St. Lucie before undergoing Tommy John surgery at the start of the summer. Suarez will likely next see a Minor League mound for his age-22 season in 2022. The 6-foot-3 right-hander threw in the low-90s with his fastball in the early days of his career, and given his size, there is some hope he could add more gas to the tank. He was up to 93-94 last fall. The changeup earned solid marks in the early days because of his feel for the offering, while the curve had been the secondary in need of the most development. The Mets were most pleased with how the breaking pitch came along in 2020 after it had been a focus during the entire summer and hope it can grow beyond being just a show-me pitch. Like so many others, Suarez just needs a chance to prove how far his stuff has come against actual competition. It’s unfortunate that the elbow surgery will cause him to miss more opportunities for experience, but the raw ingredients remain there for him to pick his progress back up once he does return.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Echavarria dominated his senior season at Millburn (N.J.) HS by going 8-1 with a 0.28 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 50 innings as a senior. That, along with a strong showing on the showcase circuit, led to the A’s selecting him in the third round (72nd pick) of the 2023 Draft, swaying him away from a commitment to the University of Florida by signing him for first-round money at $3 million. After spending his first professional season with Single-A Stockton, he began the 2025 campaign at High-A Lansing and spent the entirety of his year there. Echavarria’s stuff is tantalizing. His fastball can touch 99 mph, while his mid-80s slider has the makings of a plus pitch. His upper-80s changeup has shown promise as a third offering but remains inconsistent. This past season, he experimented with a low-80s curveball, but it's largely a work in progress. Overall command of his pitches is still an issue at times, which often leads to him running his pitch count up early in his outings. Consistency is something Echavarria is still working to find, which is not uncommon for a high school arm at this point in his career. When he’s on, he’s really good; when he’s off, he really struggles. The A’s worked with him over the second half of ‘25 on relying more on his scouting reports instead of overthinking things by trying to dissect weaknesses of hitters. The arm talent is there, and the club hopes to see some more polish as he continues to rack up more innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout in the New Jersey high school ranks, Echavarria put himself on the Draft radar by impressing on the showcase circuit and dominating his senior season at Millburn High School by going 8-1 with a 0.28 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 50 innings. Selecting him in the third round (72nd pick) of the 2023 Draft, the A’s were able to snag him away from his commitment to the University of Florida with first-round money at $3 million. Getting his pro career underway last season at Single-A Stockton as an 18-year-old, he went through some ups and downs and posted a 6.55 ERA in 19 starts with 59 strikeouts and 36 walks over 57 2/3 innings. The A’s believe Echavarria’s stuff played better than the overall numbers might suggest. His fastball reached 98 mph and sat 95-96 with good ride up in the zone. The issue was struggling to command his arsenal when he would fall behind in counts. His mid-80s slider flashes plus, and his upper-80s changeup continues to improve. He also throws a two-seamer in the 92-93 mph range. He clearly dealt with some control issues, but the A’s are not at all sounding the alarm, instead patiently working with the teenager on adjustments. Echavarria profiles as a starter for the long-term with his 6-foot-1 frame and sound delivery. Previously having shown an ability to consistently throw all of his offerings for strikes prior to the Draft, he will continue to work to rediscover that control in his second season of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Echavarria boosted his Draft stock on the strength of his performances on the showcase circuit and an uptick in velocity that helped him dominate his senior season by going 8-1 with a 0.28 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 50 innings. Though he was committed to the University of Florida, the A’s managed to sway him with first-round money ($3 million) as a third-round selection (72nd pick) in the 2023 Draft. The A’s liked what they saw in the handful of innings he pitched in the instructional league, and there is a lot of anticipation within the organization about watching his first season of pro ball unfold. Echavarria brings a four-pitch mix that features a fastball that consistently hits 96 mph and has reached up to 98, carrying ride up in the zone that lends to a good amount of swing-and-miss. Other pitches in the arsenal include a sweeping slider, curveball and low-80s changeup. He also throws a 92-93 mph two-seamer down in the zone, which should develop more consistent velocity as he grows into his 6-foot-1 frame. For a prep arm in a cold-weather state, Echavarria shows off very good pitchability with an ability to consistently throw all his offerings for strikes. Continuing the recent run of early-round Draft picks from the New Jersey high school ranks, headlined by first-rounders Anthony Volpe in 2019 and Chase Petty in 2021, he enters his first full year as a pro with high expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers broke with their track record of spreading out international signing bonus money across several players to make some big-money deals for a few years. One such example was Santana, whose $2.95 million bonus was a franchise record when the 13th-ranked prospect of his class signed in January 2021. Santana showed some intriguing stretches over his first couple years in the organization to suggest he was worth the attention, reaching Single-A Lakeland at age 18. Then came 2023, a campaign that saw the 19-year-old move all over the infield, bat .156 over 97 games and draw nearly twice as many walks (91) as hits (48). Santana signed with reports of an advanced bat for his age, yet nearly half of his plate appearances ended with walks (21.7 percent) or strikeouts (27.7). He produced 12 home runs in 97 games at Lakeland, including seven at spacious Joker Marchant Stadium, and half his hits went for extra bases, yet he averaged exit velocities in the 80s across a variety of pitch types. He produced a high walk rate but still chased too many pitches out of the zone, a trend he’s working to reverse. He bulked up his frame last year in search of power, but he might have outgrown the shortstop position, at least on a full-time basis. The Tigers still like Santana’s talent and are willing to let him figure things out, but are nonetheless nearing decision time with other infield prospects making their way up the system. He’s still just 20 years old and is determined to play his way back into top status, but he needs to reshape his game as a hitter to give himself a chance, especially if he has outgrown becoming a full-time shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers thought enough of Santana coming out of the Dominican Republic to sign him for a franchise-record $2.95 million bonus as part of their international class in January 2021. MLB Pipeline’s 13th-ranked international prospect didn’t need long to make an impact, tearing up the Dominican Summer League later that year and then making a quick impression in the Tigers’ Minor League mini-camp the following spring. He skipped the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and went to the Single-A Florida State League, where he received enough of a challenge at age 18 to slow his lofty comparisons but showed flashes of what many still believe is impressive potential. Not surprisingly, Santana’s raw power dropped some as expected in a Major League Spring Training park in Lakeland. He still used his strong lower body for an uptick in line drives while better using the whole field. He shows a smooth, quick swing and advanced plate discipline for his age at the plate, reflected in a 15.9 percent walk rate last year, but his strikeout rate also ticked up. His speed has yet to translate into stolen bases or triples. Santana moved around the infield in Lakeland as part of a rotation with Manuel Sequera and Peyton Graham. His speed and quickness enabled him to hold his own at short, but he reportedly gained weight over the offseason in search for more power and the Tigers have moved him around in his return to the FSL with looks at second and third. The Tigers have a logjam in the middle infield at the lower levels of their farm system, but a slow start back in Lakeland has kept him in Single-A for 2023. Santana made an in-season adjustment regarding the position of his hands in the box and his swing path, and the changes have led to a late-season surge. He still has many parts of his game to smooth out, but his raw talent is some of the best in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, the Tigers spread out their bonus money on the international market for several small- and mid-level signings, rather than throwing big money into any particular prospect. They changed course a few years ago for players like Santana, who received a team-record $2.95 million bonus when he signed with Detroit in January 2021. He ranked No. 13 on MLB Pipeline’s prospect list for his international class at the time, then backed it up by posting a .942 OPS as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League later that year. Santana has very strong legs, which provide both the strength of his right-handed swing and the low center of gravity that helps him move smoothly and quickly at short. His above-average bat speed and efficient swing allow him to turn on power pitches and make him difficult to pitch inside. He isn’t afraid to stand up on the plate and was hit by 15 pitches over just 54 games in the DSL. For his power, he doesn’t chase as often as others his age, and he can recognize breaking pitches. He might not make highlight plays at short, but he has the potential to be a reliable defender, earning him comparisons to Jhonny Peralta, though his current build brings some comparisons to former Tigers prospect Willy Adames. Santana has good speed with his leg strength but is still learning how to utilize it on the basepaths. Detroit’s recent investment in the international market has resulted in a class of talented players with Santana at the top, but the Tigers have historically avoided rushing their international prospects. They’ve changed up tactics a bit for Santana, who has spent much of his age-18 season with Single-A Lakeland. It’s been a growing experience for him -- one with plenty of walks but a relatively low average -- but the establishment of some stateside success is good for his future development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have spent more aggressively in the international market the past few years, with Santana as the latest example. The Dominican shortstop ranked 14th on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list when he signed with Detroit for a team-record $2.95 million bonus in January 2021. The Tigers scouted Santana for nearly three years. One evaluator believes he has the natural ability to become an impact hitter once he grows into his body frame. MLB Pipeline’s scouting report compared him to Jhonny Peralta, who played four seasons in Detroit during a 15-year Major League career. He has above-average bat speed with an advanced approach and raw power that should improve with maturity. He’s a steady if not flashy defender with quick feet and an average arm. He has the quickness and speed to be a plus runner. Like slugging outfielder Roberto Campos, Santana faces a long path to reach the big leagues. Also like Campos, his upside sets him apart from others at this point in the system. His bat skills should allow him to chew up lower-level pitching once he gets more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the end of the 2013-14 international signing period, Santana put up big numbers in his first three seasons in the United States. He paced the Rookie-level Arizona League with eight homers in 2016 and encored by hitting a combined .366/.394/.556 at three levels (including the Class A Advanced California League playoffs). He returned to the Cal League in 2018 and slumped during the first half before finishing on a .356/.382/.624 tear with 10 homers in the final six weeks to top the circuit in homers (24) and RBIs (109), then won playoff MVP honors after leading Rancho Cucamonga to the championship. Santana's electric bat speed and strength give him power to all fields, though there's some concern as to how it will translate at higher levels. He has settled his right-handed stroke down somewhat since turning pro, but he still has a hyper-aggressive approach and struggles against breaking pitches. He still overswings and chases balls out of the strike zone too often instead of just letting his natural pop take over. Santana's arm strength is just as impressive as his raw power and he's capable of making any throw from any angle at third base. He has upgraded his range at the hot corner but needs to improve his throwing accuracy. If he slows down much as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame, he could wind up at first base and saw extensive action there last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic as the 2013-14 international signing period came to a close, Santana led the Rookie-level Arizona League with eight homers in his 2016 U.S. debut. A shaky performance in instructional league that fall left the Dodgers wondering if he could survive against better pitching, but he made adjustments and had a spectacular 2017. He batted .537 with five homers in 10 games at Rookie-level Ogden, hit .322 at Class A Great Lakes and then went 7-for-17 (.417) in the high Class A California League playoffs for a combined .366/.394/.556 line. Santana has worked to calm down his right-handed stroke, allowing him to get more out of his electric bat speed. But he has met few pitches that he won't chase and overswings too often, traits that have proven to be his undoing in his return to the Cal League this year. He needs to develop an approach at the plate and realize that he has so much natural pop that he doesn't have to sell out for home runs. Santana has an easy plus arm and the ability to make throws from any angle necessary at third base, though his accuracy needs to improve. His decent speed and quickness have led Los Angeles to play him at all four infield spots, though he's better suited for the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller entered 2025 riding the momentum of a breakout 2024 season in the Tigers system and a spot in the Double-A Erie rotation alongside Troy Melton, among others. He started feeling back tightness early in the season, struggled to find the root cause of it and never really got going. After a rehab setback, he was diagnosed with hip issues -- first on the left, then on the right -- that required hip labrum surgery to repair. The Tigers added him on the 40-man roster in the middle of his rehab to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, a hint at how highly Detroit regards him. When Miller is right, he creates deception from a three-quarters arm angle with a quick delivery. His fastball tops out in the mid-90s and sits more in the 93-mph range, but has good carry that sneaks up on hitters. His low-80s slider generates a high whiff rate with good spin, and his sweeper produces a good amount of movement. His changeup is a good swing-and-miss offering when he’s locating his fastball. He was also working on a sinker during his rehab from hip surgeries to complement the four-seamer. He became a more aggressive strike-thrower during his breakout 2024 season and looks to continue that. Miller has the opportunity to become this year’s version of Melton or Ty Madden, rising from Double-A to a brief stop at Triple-A to the big leagues for the stretch run. But he has to get back on the mound first, then get comfortable with how he’s delivering with two surgically repaired hips. Like Melton, Miller is comfortable as a starter or a reliever, but the Tigers will work him as a starter in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Jackson Jobe and Jaden Hamm were the pitching stars of the Tigers’ farm system in 2024, arguably no hurler in the organization did more for his stock than Miller, an eighth-round pick in 2022 out of Valparaiso who saw his pro career delayed by injuries in 2023. He began 2024 as a reliever at Single-A Lakeland but earned a rotation spot and dominated, rolling off seven straight wins and racking up strikeouts. He advanced to High-A West Michigan in a piggyback role, then made a spot start for Double-A Erie before going to the Arizona Fall League, where he gave up damage but posted a 24-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in just 16 2/3 innings. Miller produces a lot of deception without a ton of velocity from his three-quarter delivery with an arsenal based around his 92-93 mph four- and two-seam fastballs with movement. His slider is a wipeout pitch with late action, and his changeup is difficult for right-handed hitters to pick up, with both producing high whiff rates. He shows solid command and an aggressive mentality, though the Tigers have yet to stretch him out far as a starter. The tricky part with evaluating Miller is determining what role he fills on a Major League team. He has the potential to become an impact reliever, but the Tigers want to see how far he can go as a starter. A back injury kept him from picking up from that momentum for much of 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De Jesus joined the Angels organization in January 2022, getting $1.2 million when that international signing period opened. He’s made slow, incremental progress up the ladder, spending a summer each in the Dominican Summer League and the Arizona Complex League before hitting full-season ball for the first time in 2024. That was an up-and-down season, with flashes of using his tools early and at the end of the year. But while he set a career high with 18 homers with High-A Tri-City last year, that was about the only thing that went well. At 6-foot-4 and almost 240 pounds, De Jesus is a physical specimen with loud raw tools he still hasn’t learned to use consistently. In his two years of full-season ball, he’s shown he can hit the ball hard with good exit velocities at times and there’s more than enough raw power to tap into. Unfortunately, he hasn't made much progress in terms of his overall approach. He drew walks at a better clip, but his strikeout rate shot up to 34 percent last year, still chasing out of the zone too much. De Jesus has the arm strength and the potential power to profile well in right field, and he moves fairly well, especially for someone his size. He’s still only 21 for all of the 2026 season and evaluators liked some of the things they saw from him over the fall, with the hope he can hit the reset button and tap into his tools regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 There is no one path for prospects, even if they’re both outfielders and both signed at the same time. Case in point are Nelson Rada and De Jesus, who both received seven-figure bonuses in January 2022. Rada spent the 2024 season at Double-A with mixed results, while it’s taken De Jesus a longer period of time to find his footing. He’s moved one rung at a time, going from the Dominican Summer League to the Arizona Complex League and then to Single-A Inland Empire in 2024. He got off to a very good start there, then faded before rebounding at the end of the season to post an OPS north of .900 from Aug. 1 on. It’s clear that the 6-foot-4 De Jesus has the raw tools to be an impact hitter. He’s got the projectable frame and he’s already added strength too. There were stretches during his full-season debut last year when his quality of contact and exit velocities were vastly improved. That let him get to his considerable raw power a bit more frequently, though he has to keep refining his approach, cutting down the strikeouts (29.3 percent K rate last year) and improving his on-base skills (just an 8 percent walk rate). De Jesus moves pretty well for someone his size and has the makings of a solid defensive right fielder with a strong arm. For him to profile there as a big league regular, he’s going to have to keep getting to that power so he can be the kind of run producer teams want from that spot on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels pursued outfield talent aggressively when the 2022 international signing period opened that January, giving MLB Pipeline's Top 50 international prospects Nelson Rada $1.85 million and De Jesus $1.2 million. De Jesus had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, was named a midseason All-Star and finished with a respectable .272/.362/.467 line. De Jesus has plenty of tools to dream on and took an encouraging early step forward in using them during his pro debut. The 6-foot-4 right-handed hitter has plenty of size and strength with plus raw power and the ability to make hard contact. He showed a pretty good approach at the plate in the DSL, keeping strikeouts to a relative minimum while getting to his power with 21 extra-base hits (seven homers) in 184 at-bats. He has a power-over-hit profile and will have to work on making adjustments so his big swing doesn’t get too long. In addition to the power and run-production profile, De Jesus’ plus raw arm strength fits well in a corner outfield spot. He’s athletic and should be a solid enough defender, but it’s all going to be about how much he taps into that huge reservoir of power moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 38 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2022 signing period opened, De Jesus was the second of two young outfielders to get a seven-figure bonus from the Angels. While Nelson Rada topped the list with his $1.85 million bonus, De Jesus wasn’t far behind, getting $1.2 million to sign out of the Dominican Republic. While Rada is a hit-over-power type of outfielder, De Jesus might end up being the opposite. He can make hard contact with a solid approach, but it’s his emerging power that really stands out. In 2020, he worked on improving his conditioning, getting in better shape, losing some weight and adding strength to his impressive 6-foor-4 frame. De Jesus is athletic and while he’s not a burner, is a smart and aggressive baserunner. He fits the athletic, power-hitting corner outfield profile well, especially if he continues to make enough contact to tap into his raw power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 Wagner began his sophomore year of college on the bench for Clemson and finished it with Atlantic Coast Conference Player of the Year honors after blasting 17 homers in his final 24 games and tying Khalil Greene’s single-season school record of 27 overall. The surge made Wagner one of the biggest pop-up prospects of the 2022 Draft. He landed in the second round with the Orioles and signed for $1.9 million. Wagner’s pro debut was less impactful, though he reached Double-A Bowie during an otherwise unremarkable first full season in 2023. Offseason left hamate surgery delayed his 2024 debut by a month and after quickly making it to Double-A, he struggled there when he landed on the injured list in late June with a back injury. Wagner is a strong right-handed hitter with a short, quick swing and some power, though probably not the record-setting pop he displayed in college. He made significant improvements to his approach on campus. Similarly, he hit the ball harder last summer compared with his debut even as his contact rate sagged while he adjusted to higher-level pitching. His exit velocities suggest he can be an average hitter with improvements to his barrel path and spin recognition, especially with two strikes. He’s always shown an ability to draw walks and can steal some bases despite average speed. Wagner was considered a capable defender coming out of school and is now seen as at least above average at third base with good range and solid-plus arm strength. He also showed well at second, where he played more than a quarter of his games in ‘23. That defensive versatility adds to what remains a bat-first profile for Wagner, who could grow into an offensive-minded regular or a platoon player at the highest level with more seasoning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the biggest popup prospects of the 2022 Draft, Wagner went from a defensive replacement at the start of the season at Clemson to the Atlantic Coast Conference player of the year after homering 17 times in his final 24 games to tie Khalil Greene’s school record with 27 jacks. His surge landed him in the second round with the Orioles, who gave him $1.9 million to sign. Wagner’s pro debut was significantly less impactful, though he did reach High-A Aberdeen down the stretch and showed good on-base skills in a small sample. Wagner didn’t have much of a track record after struggling at Clemson as a freshman, though he did perform well with wood bats in the Northwoods League that summer and always showed the ability to work counts and draw walks. His raw power is at least plus, though it's considered more strength-based than the result of extraordinary bat speed. He’s a right-handed hitter who made significant improvements to his approach in college, becoming better equipped against breaking balls, particularly with two strikes. Wagner is considered a capable defender at third base with decent range, solid arm strength and good body control, though he could improve his consistency at the hot corner to keep the pro game from speeding up on him. He’s a fringy runner but not a liability on the bases. He has a bat-first profile -- Wagner’s eventual ceiling hinges on his ability to build on his breakout success in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez signed with the Marlins for $850,000 out of the catcher-rich nation of Venezuela in January 2021, and he was traded to the Mets in late July for reliever David Robertson while on his third campaign at a Rookie-level circuit in 2023. He closed out that ’23 campaign with a .476 OBP in the Florida Complex League before jumping to Single-A St. Lucie for the first time. He returned to the Minors’ lowest full-season level, where he slashed .271/.362/.359 with five homers in 98 games, and ended his age-20 season with 10 games for High-A Brooklyn. A switch-hitter, Hernandez evened out his splits pretty well in 2024, showing perhaps a tiny bit more slugging ability from his right side after previously displaying the opposite. He still controls the zone better as a lefty hitter, though he expanded the zone a bit too much against breaking pitches. Hernandez enters 2025 with a career .375 OBP in the Minors, and with his catcher’s eye, that will likely be his best offensive asset. He ran into strong 90th-percentile and max exit velocities in the FSL, but he still projects as a hitter who will scrape double-digit homers over a full season. Hernandez continues to draw strong reviews for the way he works with pitching staffs as a bilingual speaker, and early reports indicate he’s already looked much more in shape in order to be better prepared to catch nine innings night in and night out. His receiving can be solid already, and he’ll need to continue to work on his throwing accuracy as his caught-stealing rates have declined. Mets officials view Hernandez as a steady presence, and with his Rule 5 eligibility hitting next offseason, he remains on track as a potential backup MLB catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez signed with the Marlins for $850,000 out of Venezuela in January 2021 and slowly developed at two complex-level circuits over his first two seasons of pro ball. He returned to the Florida Complex League at age 19 in 2023 and showed signs of taking off on the circuit before he was traded to the Mets in late July for closer David Robertson. Between Miami and New York FCL affiliates, Hernandez slashed .295/.476/.460 with four homers, 47 walks and 37 strikeouts in 45 games before getting a late-season promotion to Single-A. Aided by his innate knowledge of the strike zone, Hernandez ranked third among all 124 complex-level qualifiers with his 24.6 percent walk rate and .476 OBP, and he has the sound swing from both sides to hit for a solid average. He got a lot more time working as left-handed hitter (201 plate appearances) than he did as a righty (29) in 2023, and he was much more productive from a power standpoint from the left side. He could still scrape double-digit homers as he matures and gains more experience in both boxes. Hernandez draws solid reviews for his receiving and communication work from behind the plate – he can speak both English and Spanish with his pitchers -- and he could figure to be above-average defensively. His arm strength is just average, and his caught-stealing rate actually dipped from 33 percent in 2022 to 24 percent last summer. Controlling the running game is all the more important in the current era of baseball, but most of Hernandez's other arrows are pointing up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins signed their two best catching prospects six months apart in 2021, landing Hernandez with an $850,000 bonus out of Venezuela in January before drafting Joe Mack 31st overall in July. Hernandez has less offensive upside but is a more advanced defender. He slashed .236/.329/.321 in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League while making his U.S. debut at age 18 last season. Hernandez was in the middle of a nice FCL rebound when Miami dealt him to the Mets in late July in a deal for closer David Robertson. A steady receiver, Hernandez is agile behind the plate and does a nice job of blocking balls in the dirt. He has solid-to-plus arm strength and showed improved throwing accuracy in 2022, when he erased 33 percent of basestealers. He works hard on his craft, diligently preparing for games, displaying leadership skills and communicating with pitchers in either English or Spanish. While he hadn't posted big offensive numbers until this year, Hernandez has a sound swing from both sides of the plate and makes consistent contact to all fields. He has the patience to work counts and should continue to improve offensively as he adds more strength and experience. He could provide 12-15 homers per season once he learns to turn on and lift pitches more often.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: May's winding college journey brought him to Oregon State -- his third school in as many years -- where he dominated as the Beavers' Friday night starter and raised his stock en route to going 70th overall to the Marlins in the 2023 Draft. The righty has barely seen the field since then, though. May did not pitch after signing for a below-slot $900,000 -- he had a heavy college workload and missed a month with a forearm injury -- and then arthroscopic elbow surgery delayed his pro debut until July 2025. He ended up logging 32 2/3 innings between Rookie ball, Single-A and the Arizona Fall League and heads into 2026 healthy for the first time in years. At 6-foot-2 with a low release point, May has a sinker-slider profile, although he's changed his pitch mix a bit since college. The sweeping slider remains his bread-and-butter pitch with biting action that he can land for strikes or get chases on, and his sinking fastball -- up to 96 mph in starts and 98 in short stints -- has almost equal horizontal movement in the opposite direction. This year, he's been incorporating a high-80s cutter, which is dangerous glove side and a weapon against lefties, and his upper-80s changeup has promise but needs to land for strikes more. May had solid control by the end of his college career, although he walked too many batters in his brief pro debut. Some of that can be chalked up to him working back from injuries in 2025. If he can stay healthy and improve his cutter or changeup as a platoon-neutral pitch, it's easy to see May becoming a back-end starter. If not, he could still profile as a reliever whose movement will play up even more in short stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: May's college career took him from Pima (Ariz.) CC to Arizona to Oregon State. His stuff and control looked better than ever with the Beavers last spring, when he missed a month with an elbow strain before recovering to permit just nine earned runs across his final seven starts. The Marlins signed him for a below-slot $900,000 as a supplemental second-rounder and believe he may emerge as one of the best pitching prospects when he makes his pro debut in 2025. May used his plus mid-80s slider almost half the time at Oregon State, and it comes with high spin rates and so much spin that it locks down both lefties and righties. While his two-seam fastball parks at 93-95 mph and reaches 98, it has more of a sink than carry profile and doesn't miss a lot of bats. His 87-90 mph changeup is firm but drops at the plate and rarely gets barreled. Working from a low arm slot, May creates deception with a flat approach angle but not much in the way of extension. Given his delivery, he might find more success with a four-seamer that carries up in the strike zone and plays better off his slider. He provides consistent success and has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez’s signing, initially scheduled to take place in the 2018-19 international window, had to wait until June 2020 due to the pandemic and an age discrepancy. After joining the Cardinals for $525,000, he moved to Single-A Palm Beach in 2021 and couldn’t break past the Florida State League until '23 when he was promoted to High-A Peoria in late June after showing significant control improvements. Nunez finished with a 3.39 ERA, 65 strikeouts and 30 walks in 63 2/3 innings between the two stops and got in eight more appearances in the Arizona Fall League where he held his own. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has always been on the St. Louis radar because of his velocity. Despite leaving the club midseason, he threw 24 of the 30 hardest pitches for Palm Beach in 2023, topping out at 99.9 mph. He averaged 96-98 mph with the heater, which acts like a sinker, and the lack of rising movement makes it more hittable than the velo alone would indicate. His upper-80s changeup is better at generating swing-and-miss with nice armside fade, and FSL hitters chased it out of the zone 43.1 percent of the time. He’ll throw a low-80s slider too, but even low-level hitters knew to lay off it given his poor command of the breaker. Nunez worked on staying within his delivery, allowing for the overall control improvements last season, but it’s going to take more for him to move beyond 40 control. He has the present stuff to be a quality reliever, and last year’s results give him solid momentum heading into his Rule 5 decision year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez was meant to sign during the 2018-19 international signing window but was declared ineligible by MLB because of an age discrepancy. The Cardinals were finally able to sign him for $525,000 in June 2020, after a pandemic-related pause in the international market. The Dominican Republic native jumped right into full-season ball the following year and showed enticing stuff with lackluster results. There are two ways to best describe Nunez’s experience at Low-A Palm Beach. First, he threw the 109 fastest pitches thrown by Palm Beach pitchers as recorded by Statcast in 2021 -- all at 98.2 mph or above and topping out at 101.1 mph. Second, he walked 56 batters in 53 2/3 innings, nearly equaling his output of 59 strikeouts in the same span. It’s a lot of gas, very few brakes from the 6-foot-3 hurler. Nunez also sports a mid-80s curveball that can flash above-average with decent spin rates and an upper-80s changeup that he doesn’t sell very well just yet. The Cardinals like Nunez’s clean delivery and work ethic and believe his control struggles were the result of inexperience due to lost time and an aggressive assignment. The righty pitched almost exclusively out of relief in 2021, and that’s where his big-time velocity profiles best anyway. If he can even find just 45-grade control in the Minors, his future as a back-end reliever will become even clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves have half of what would have been their normal international bonus pool at the start of the 2020-21 signing period in January of 2021 as part of the penalty for previous signing infractions. That didn’t hold them back from going all in on Tavarez, giving the Dominican shortstop $1.5 million to sign. He didn’t debut until 2022, in the Florida Complex League, and that didn’t come until August because he had thoracic outlet surgery on his non-throwing shoulder. His full-season debut in 2023 was a struggle at the plate. It's still too soon to know exactly what Tavarez might be because of how much time he missed. There are some raw tools to work with, starting with excellent bat speed from the right side of the plate. He’s capable of driving the ball to all fields, with power to come, if and when he makes contact. That was the biggest issue in 2023 as he struck out in nearly 41 percent of his plate appearances. He’s continuing to work on quieting down his setup and swing, something that will have to improve so he can make more contact. At one point, there was concern that Tavarez would outgrow shortstop, but it’s seeming his athleticism, excellent hands and plus arm should allow him to stick at the premium position. That helps raise his floor, but he’s going to have to make some adjustments to make more contact in order to progress up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2020-21 international signing period finally began in January 2021, the Braves couldn’t wait to jump back into the market after the penalties levied as a result of their signing violations ended. They used a majority of that pool on Tavarez, giving the Dominican shortstop $1.5 million to join the organization. With no Braves affiliate in the Dominican Summer League, he didn’t make his pro debut until 2022 in the Florida Complex League, and he briefly performed well there after being delayed by thoracic outlet surgery on his left shoulder. Because of how little he’s played, Tavarez is a bit of a wild card, but the hope is the raw tools that made him a prime target of Atlanta's international scouting staff will start coming to the fore with more reps. While he’s working to learn to quiet down his setup and swing, the right-handed hitter has tremendous bat speed and can drive the ball to all fields, with the chance to have plenty of in-game power as he develops. There were some questions about whether Tavarez could stay at shortstop long term, with some thinking he’d outgrow it and need to move to third. He is a good athlete with a plus arm and the Braves got good reports on his defense from his stint in winter ball in Colombia. He’ll be given every chance to stick at shortstop as he really gets his pro career started.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The start of the 2020-21 international signing period was delayed until January of 2021, so the Braves had to wait to jump out of the penalty box that came as a result of their signing violations. Given half of what would have been their normal bonus pool, they used a huge chunk of it to sign Tavarez in January 2021 for $1.5 million. Because the Braves didn’t have a team in the Dominican Summer League, he wasn’t able to make his pro debut that summer. The start to his career was further delayed when he needed thoracic outlet surgery on his non-throwing arm before the start of Florida Complex League action this year, though he did return to the FCL to make his debut in August. The Braves are excited to see this athletic infielder in action, especially in the batter’s box. Tavarez’s right-handed bat has the chance to carry him up the ladder, with a ton of raw power he’ll learn how to get to as he physically matures. He can drive the ball to all fields with bat speed, but he’ll need to keep working on the moving parts of his swing so he can be sure to access that pop consistently. Tavarez is an excellent athlete with a plus arm and the Braves feel he has every chance to stick at shortstop, certainly with enough arm to play the premium spot. Should he slow down and need to move, it does look like he has the power profile to fit nicely at third.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though he missed his senior season of high school because of the pandemic, the Angels liked Blakely’s raw tools enough to take him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft out of the Detroit area high school ranks and give him $900,000 to sign him away from attending Auburn. He didn’t provide much return on the investment during a rough debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, but things started to click with a move to full-season ball, though he missed time with a hamstring issue and then a hand injury caused by a hit by pitch. He made up for lost reps as one of the younger players in the Arizona Fall League. With the strides Blakely made in 2022, there’s confidence more people will be talking about him with more reps. While he still struck out in nearly 30 percent of his plate appearances in 2022, that was a big step in the right direction compared to his debut, and he continued to understand the value of seeing pitches and drawing walks. There’s raw power for him to tap into, but he’s yet to grow into his body and needs to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. Signed as a shortstop, Blakely moved around the infield during his pro debut, but has settled in at third base, focusing on the hot corner in the California League and the AFL. His defense has been inconsistent, with a strong arm and decent footwork but a tendency to let things speed up on him. Some feel a move to the outfield might make the most sense long term, but if the improvements with the bat are legit, the Angels will find a spot in the lineup for him every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels have hit the Detroit area high school scene twice in the last few years to roll the dice on some high risk, high reward types. In 2018, it was two-way player William Holmes in the fifth round. In 2020, they took Blakely, an athletic, but raw infielder who got an over-slot bonus of $900,000 to walk away from his Auburn commitment. He didn’t play his senior year because of the pandemic and struggled for much of his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League, though the Angels saw steady improvement from start to finish last summer. Blakely has some raw tools to work with, starting with his athletic 6-foot-3 frame. His hit tool is fringy -- he struck out in 37.1 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut -- and he will have to refine his approach to make more consistent contact from the left side of the plate. There’s at least above-average raw power for him to tap into and there could be more if he can add strength. The Angels moved Blakely around the infield during his debut, getting equal time at shortstop, third and second base, largely because of other personnel. He’ll keep getting reps at all three, though he might profile best at third when all is said and done. He let the game speed up on him defensively, but he has a strong arm and good footwork that should allow him to stay on the dirt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Detroit-area high school scene might not be thought of as a hotbed for baseball talent -- the last prepster from there to make it to the big leagues was Daniel Fields, a 2009 draftee who touched the Majors briefly in 2015. But the Angels feel they may have tapped into a bit of a mine, taking high-risk/high-reward type players in the top five rounds twice in the last three years. In 2018, it was two-way player William Holmes. In 2020, it was Blakely, a super-athletic shortstop who got an over-slot $900,000 to sign in the fourth round and then went to instructs for his unofficial pro debut. Blakeley’s size and athleticism are the first things that stand out. He’s 6-foot-3 and has plus speed, which should help him on both sides of the ball. A left-handed hitter, he’s worked to improve his swing to make more contact with some good results, though there are still swing-and-miss concerns, something that could improve with a refined approach and pitch recognition as he faces better pitching consistently. As he adds strength to that athletic frame, there is some power to come if he can learn to make enough contact to get to it. Despite his size, Blakeley has every chance to stick at shortstop, with outstanding range and enough arm for the premium position. This isn’t going to happen overnight, and Blakely has only about 40 at-bats at instructs on his pro resume, but there’s considerable ceiling for the infielder to try and get to in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Knoth and Marcus Stroman share an alma mater in Long Island’s Patchogue-Medford HS, but it was the former that became the first player to sign straight out of the school when he joined the Brewers as the 33rd overall pick in 2023. Knoth, who was 17 on Draft Day, signed below slot for $2 million. He struck out 96 and posted a 4.48 ERA in 84 1/3 innings with Single-A Carolina in his first full season but underwent Tommy John surgery the following offseason. He missed all of 2025 as a result but was back to throwing in the leadup to his third Minor League campaign. Before going under the knife, Knoth showed a 91-95 mph four-seamer that he could blaze by Single-A hitters with impressive ride to the top of the zone. Both his upper-70s curveball and mid-80s slider looked like potential plus pitches with exceptional spin rates, though the latter was better at getting batters from both sides to expand the zone the way Knoth worked it down and glove side. His changeup was rarely used, but he was still more effective against lefties than righties for Carolina. After walking 11.1 percent of his batters faced in ’24, Knoth projects for fringy control, and that’s if the command holds up post-TJ. He’ll still only be 20 years for much of the ’26 season, and the stuff is intriguing enough to make him a breakout candidate if he can maintain the quality of the arsenal over a likely innings limit. Knoth’s upside remains in the middle of a future Milwaukee rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knoth shares a high school alma mater with Marcus Stroman in Patchogue-Medford HS on Long Island, N.Y. But after Stroman chose to head to Duke after going in the 2009 18th round, Knoth headed straight to pro ball, becoming the school’s first player to sign as the 33rd overall pick in the 2023 Draft. His bonus came in below slot at $2 million. Knoth posted a 4.48 ERA with 96 strikeouts in 84 1/3 innings for Single-A Carolina in his first full season but dealt with elbow issues in his second offseason, leading ultimately to Tommy John surgery that will knock him out for the 2025 season. A little undersized at 6-foot-1 but strong for his frame, Knoth sat 91-95 mph with his fastball in the Carolina League but got whiffs with the heater because of good ride up in the zone. His breaking balls remained potentially plus pitches with an upper-70s curveball and mid-80s slider -- both of which came in with impressively high spin rates. The slider was better at generating chase, especially with two strikes. Knoth didn’t use much of a changeup with Carolina but will need one the higher he climbs. Knoth walked 11.1 percent of his batters faced in 2024, and how his control returns from surgery will be worth following upon his return in 2026. That’ll still just be his age-20 season, so time is very much on his side here. But it’s far from an ideal pause in development for a young pitcher who still has significant upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knoth hails from Patchogue-Medford HS on Long Island, N.Y. -- the same program that produced Marcus Stroman before he headed to Duke -- and the similarly undersized right-hander did enough to seize scouts’ attentions despite hailing from a cold-weather state. The Brewers made him the first player selected directly from his school since 2013 when they took him 33rd overall in July and signed him for a below-slot $2 million bonus. Strong for his 6-foot-1 frame, Knoth gained some velocity in his senior spring and was touching the upper 90s, though he was typically a few ticks below that. The real eye-opener was his feel for spin. His 77-80 mph curveball was easily the best in his Draft class -- high school or college -- because of its 3,000+ rpm spin rates and sharp downward action. He also showed a low-80s slider with similar dizzying spin and more two-plane break, though the pair of breaking balls can bleed into one another. Knoth’s changeup wasn't needed much in school and could be a focus in the pros. Knoth has a solid history of finding the strike zone with a repeatable delivery, and his ability to get chase outside of the zone with his breaking pitches should help hold walks relatively at bay. Having only turned 18 in August, he’s very much a lump of clay who could be molded into a reliever if the changeup never comes around or a high-end starter if the stuff takes off further.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Puerto Rico before moving to Florida as a teenager, Montalvo was a shortstop prospect until he took up pitching as a high school senior. He rose from a 20th-round pick in the 2021 Draft to a ranked prospect in the Rangers' system on the strength of swing-and-miss stuff, which held after converting from reliever to starter in 2023. The Tigers liked the pitch shapes and command enough to include him in the return package for Andrew Chafin at the 2024 Trade Deadline. Montalvo shows good command and instincts for someone still relatively new to pitching, reading and reacting to hitters’ swings. His extension out of a relatively low arm angle allows his low to mid-90s fastball to play up, and he can spot it in different parts of the zone. His low-80s slider is his main swing-and-miss pitch, looking like a fastball out of his hand before moving late with sweeping action. He has improved his command on his mid-80s changeup, which he uses to generate weak contact, but might need more deception to handle left-handed hitters. Montalvo fits the profile of pitcher that the Tigers’ player development group has had success polishing in the last few years. If he fills out his frame, polishes his changeup and adds another tick or two of velocity to his fastball, he could become an intriguing prospect for the Tigers to push.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Puerto Rico, Montalvo attended high school in Florida and became the Rangers' final pick (20th round) in the 2021 Draft. A former shortstop who stood out more for his athleticism than his pure stuff as an amateur, he has thrived as a full-time pitcher in pro ball. He transitioned from relieving in his 2022 pro debut to starting last year and logged a 2.83 ERA, .211 average-against and 107 strikeouts in 95 1/3 innings in Single-A. He was enjoying another solid season at High-A Hickory when the Rangers moved him to the Tigers in a Trade Deadline deal for Andrew Chafin. Montalvo's four-seam fastball sits in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph, playing better than its velocity because of its carry and arm-side run and the extension in his delivery, and he's also developing a sinking two-seamer. His best swing-and-miss pitch is a low-80s slider with good depth. He also has nice feel for a fading mid-80s changeup that shows flashes of becoming a solid offering. An athletic mover who gets down the mound well, Montalvo combines quality extension with a low release height and flat approach angle, presenting an unusual look for hitters. He improved his control in the second half of last season, throwing more and better strikes. He profiles as a back-of-the-rotation starter and perhaps more if his stuff gets better as he adds more strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 35 | Power: 60 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 The Brewers took Bitonti out of the California prep ranks in the third round in 2023 when he was only 17 years old, signing him away from an Oregon commitment for $1.75 million, more than double slot value. He showed promise out of the gate with 16 homers (the second-most by a Minor Leaguer age 18 or younger) and a 147 wRC+ in 79 games between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Carolina in 2024 but came back to down to earth with a return to the Carolina League a year later. Bitonti hit .238/.341/.421 with 19 homers in 118 games with the Mudcats in ’25; his 33.5 percent strikeout rate was fourth-highest among Single-A qualifiers. Standing 6-foot-5, Bitonti cuts a massive figure from the left side of the box. He uses that size to generate big bat speed that comes primarily from his upper body, considering he only relies on a toe tap for the bottom half of his load. The levers in his swing create a lot of length despite the sheer velocity of his hacks, and he can run late on pitches, even fastballs in the zone. When he does make contact, it’s loud and often in the air to the pull side, giving hope that he could be a future 30-homer slugger. Originally taken as a shortstop, Bitonti has slid down the defensive spectrum since with some time at third base in 2024 and then primary duty at first in ’25. He makes for a big target there and still retains arm strength that will help on throws across the diamond. Bitonti will only be 20 for the duration of the 2026 season, but adjustments will have to come quick if he’s to power his way up the chain.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bitonti was an inconsistent performer on the showcase circuit in 2022 but received plenty of invitations and attention from scouts. The Brewers took the California native in the 2023 third round, signed him for above slot at $1.75 million and played it slow with him out of the gate considering he was still only 17 on Draft Day. Bitonti opened his first full season in the Arizona Complex League and laid waste to the Rookie level with a .320/.451/.580 line and eight homers in 51 games. He was promoted to Single-A Carolina in late July and continued to slug there with eight more homers in 28 games. His 16 total dingers were second-most in the Minors among players 18 or younger. Standing in the box at 6-foot-4, Bitonti already exhibits absolutely electric bat speed, registering in the mid-70s at times, and he’s already built like a house with the strength to turn most contact into loud contact. (Forty-two of his 83 hits in 2024 went for extra bases.) But with that comes a ton of swing-and-miss concerns at this early stage. His long levers contribute partly to the problem, and the Brewers hold out hope that shortening the swing some could lead to more overall contact. Bitonti was drafted as a shortstop but has primarily slid over to third in pro ball. The majority of his starts with Carolina came at the opposite corner at first base, and many believe that’s where he’ll land full-time as a fairly athletic defender and big target for his fellow infielders. Bitonti’s power will certainly play there as is, and he has plenty of runway to make other tweaks to unlock his hit tool in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bitonti certainly made the rounds on the showcase circuit with stops at the PDP League, Area Code Games, Major League Baseball’s High School All-American Game and Perfect Game All-American Classic in 2022, and while his performance was inconsistent in those environments, he continued to draw scouts last spring. The Brewers selected the infielder in the third round and signed him with an above-slot bonus of $1.75 million. Bitonti went 7-for-39 (.179) with two homers, nine walks and 15 strikeouts during a 12-game run in the Arizona Complex League after signing. Standing in at 6-foot-4 already, Bitonti is certainly a presence on the diamond, and that shows up in his tools as well. The left-handed slugger already shows at least plus raw power, and given his size, he can make it translate into games fairly easily. While he has the plate discipline that can lead to walks, his long levers and swing have hurt his overall hit tool as he can struggle with swing-and-miss. Some amateur scouts believed he needed pro instruction to iron out those concerns. Though we live in the Age of the Big Shortstop, Bitonti has long been pegged for a move from the six to third base, and that’s what happened in the early days of his Brewers career. He had the body control to play an adequate short in school, and that, along with a plus arm, could make him a quality defender at the hot corner. Bitonti is only entering his age-18 season and has the tools (and room to grow) to be an interesting project for the Milwaukee pipeline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An infielder and pitcher on Venezuela's 2015 Little League World Series team, Fernandez later moved behind the plate and became one of the best catching prospects in the 2019 international crop. He signed for $717,500 and didn't make his pandemic-delayed pro debut until 2021, when he batted .355/.414/.488 and advanced to Single-A at age 18. He ranked sixth in batting (.292) when he returned to the California League in 2022 and fifth in the High-A Midwest League (.273) last season. Unlike most catchers, Fernandez stands out most with his bat-to-ball skills and is more athletic than physical. He has a compact right-handed swing, outstanding hand-eye coordination and a disciplined approach that have resulted in a 13 percent strikeout rate through his first three years as a pro. He almost makes contact too easily, however, producing a lot of soft groundballs that give him an extreme hit-over-power profile. Fernandez has close to average speed and more quickness than most catchers, but he must improve defensively to carve out a big league role. He gets the most out of his average arm strength with a fast release and good accuracy, but he's still a work in progress in terms of receiving and blocking. Extremely versatile for a backstop, he's an average defender at second base and also saw brief action at third base and shortstop in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An infielder/pitcher on Venezuela's 2015 Little League World Series team, Fernandez later moved behind the plate and developed into one of the best catchers in the 2019 international class. Signed for $717,500, he had his pro debut delayed a year by the pandemic and came to the United States in 2021, when he hit .355/.414/.488 and reached Single-A at age 18. He had to share time at that level last season with Diego Cartaya and Dalton Rushing, but showed his versatility by playing a nice second base while finishing sixth in the California League batting race at .292. Fernandez has an unusual profile for a catcher, with his hitting ability his standout tool and his athleticism outshining his physicality. A right-handed hitter, he recognizes pitches, manages the strike zone and puts the bat on the ball more easily than most players his age. He won't ever be a slugger, but he did drive the ball in the air more frequently last season and has a quick, compact swing that could translate into 12-15 homers per season if he gets stronger. Close to an average runner, Fernandez is quicker than most backstops and moves well behind the plate. He continues to improve his receiving and blocking with experience and his fringy arm strength plays up a tick thanks to his fast release and accuracy. He can develop into an average defender as a catcher and also handles second base well, a la Dodgers backup Austin Barnes, and there are scouts who think Fernandez might have more upside at the latter position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of three big-ticket signings in a banner Giants 2018 international crop, Pomares has stalled while Marco Luciano and Luis Matos reached the Majors as 21-year-olds. Signed for $975,000 after leaving Cuba, Pomares finished second in the Rookie-level Arizona League batting race (.368) in his 2019 pro debut and slashed .334/.378/.629 with 20 homers in 77 games during his first full season in 2021. His overly aggressive approach didn't work as well in High-A the following year and he played just nine games in Rookie ball in 2023 because of persistent quadriceps and back injuries. Pomares has some of the best bat speed and produces some of the highest exit velocities in the system. But he undermines himself with poor swing decisions, letting his left-handed stroke get too long and uphill as he looks to launch pitches out of the park. He has posted a 33 percent strikeout rate in parts of two seasons in High-A and struggles to make in-zone contact because he's so aggressive. Pomares has to hit because almost all of his value will come from his bat. He's a below-average runner with one steal in 176 games at the full-season level, and he's just an adequate corner outfielder with average arm strength. He has back issues in 2021 as well, so his health is another concern.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of an impact Giants international crop in 2018 that also included Marco Luciano and Luis Matos, Pomares signed for $975,000 after leaving Cuba. He broke into pro ball by finishing second in the Rookie-level Arizona League in hitting (.368) in his 2019 debut and batted .334/.378/.629 with 20 homers in 77 during his first full season two years later. He took a step back in 2022, however, posting a .768 OPS with a 33 percent strikeout rate in High-A and getting left off the 40-man roster. A left-handed hitter, Pomares has exceptional bat speed and hits the ball harder than most of San Francisco's prospects. He has good bat-to-ball skills but he also makes extremely aggressive swing decisions, chasing pitches out of the zone and rarely working walks. Though he hit .300/.368/.523 over the final three months of last season, he now looks like more of a slugger than a hitter and will have to make adjustments to succeed against more advanced pitching. Most of Pomares' value will come from his bat. He has fringy speed and doesn't do much on the bases, swiping one bag in his two years of full-season ball. He has spent most of his pro career in left field, where he has decent range and average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants' bountiful 2018 international crop included not only two Top 100 Prospects in Marco Luciano and Luis Matos, but also a third hitter who has batted .330 in his first two pro seasons. Signed for $975,000 after defecting from Cuba, Pomares finished second in the Rookie-level Arizona League batting race (.368) in his 2019 pro debut. Visa issues during the pandemic prevented him from coming to the United States in 2020 and a back strain delayed the start of his 2021 season, but he came back to hit .334/.378/.629 with 20 homers in 77 games between Low-A and High-A. A left-handed hitter loaded with bat speed, Pomares produces a lot of hard contact and exceptional exit velocities for a young player. While he used more of an opposite-field approach in his debut, he began turning on and launching more balls last year, showing the potential for 25 or more homers per season. He's extremely aggressive and often gets away with it because of his bat-to-ball skills, but he'll have to add more plate discipline to reach his offensive ceiling after striking out 33 times and walking just once in 26 games in High-A. Pomares has one of the highest offensive ceilings in the system, which is good because most of his value will come from his bat.
