He's a fringy runner with similar range and average arm strength on the outfield corners. He split time between left and right field last season and is better suited for left at Oracle Park.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pomares starred in Cuba's 15-and-under league before defecting and signing with the Giants for $975,000 as part of a potentially special 2018 international class that also includes shortstop Marco Luciano and outfielder Luis Matos. Advanced enough at the plate to come to the United States for his pro debut the next summer, he finished second in the Rookie-level Arizona League batting race (.368) and earned a promotion to short-season ball a week after turning 19. Visa issues during the coronavirus pandemic limited his 2020 development to San Francisco's Dominican instructional league program. Extremely advanced for his age, Pomares is one of the best pure hitters in the system and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. He has a quick left-handed stroke, recognizes pitches well and has good feel for using the opposite field. He makes consistent hard contact and has hit for more power in 2021 as he has launched more balls to his pull side, showing the potential for 20-25 homers on an annual basis. Pomares' speed, arm and corner-outfield defense all earn average to solid grades. After he spent most of 2019 in right field, the Giants planned on trying him in center field, though that may be a stretch. He recorded 10 assists in 45 outfield starts during his first pro season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants landed what looks like their best international class in years in 2018, when they landed Dominican shortstop Marco Luciano ($2.6 million), Venezuelan outfielder Luis Matos ($725,000) and Pomares ($975,000). A Cuban defector, he starred in the island's 15-and-under league and continued to impress with his hitting ability in San Francisco's instructional league and Dominican programs after signing. That merited a trip to the United States for his pro debut in 2019, when he ranked second in the Rookie-level Arizona League in hitting (.368) and earned a promotion to the short-season Northwest League a week after turning 19. One of the best pure hitters in the system, Pomares is extremely advanced for a teenager. He recognizes pitches well and doesn't try to do too much with his quick left-handed stroke, showing tremendous feel for using the opposite field. He won't be a slugger, but he makes repeated hard contact and can drive the ball to his pull side, so he should get to most of his average raw power. Pomares earns average to solid grades for his speed, arm and corner-outfield defense. The Giants will give him a chance to show what he can do in center field after he spent most of 2019 in right. He recorded 10 assists in 45 outfield starts during his first pro season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dominican shortstop Marco Luciano was the highest-profile player in the Giants' 2018 international class but not the only potential impact player. Pomares, a Cuban defector who signed for $975,000, might have the best pure hitting ability in the system. He made a strong impression during San Francisco's instructional league and Dominican programs during the offseason, then continued to stand out after coming to the United States for his pro debut. Pomares has a tremendous approach for a teenager. He has a quick left-handed stroke, understands how to recognize pitches and manage the strike zone, and doesn't try to do too much. While's he's content to lash line drives to all fields for now, he has some raw power and should produce 15 or more homers annually as he continues to develop physically. Though Pomares played primarily left field in Cuba's 15-and-under league, the Giants believe he has a chance to stick in center. He's at least a solid runner and quicker once he gets going, though he'll need to improve his reads and routes. He has an average arm and should be capable of at least filling in at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles signed Martinez out of the Dominican Republic for $950,000 as a headliner of their 2024 international class, and he impressed with a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, collecting 13 extra-base hits in 41 games as a 16-year-old. Martinez then made his way stateside and reached full-season ball by the end of his first full season in 2025, the Orioles challenging him more aggressively than is typical for teenage international signs. He had a tough go of it at Single-A Delmarva, but as a just-turned-18-year-old he was also extraordinarily young for the level. Martinez shows better on-base ability and can hit the ball harder than most players his age. At 6-foot-4 and nearly 200 pounds, he’s strong and athletic and capable of producing 90th percentile exit velocities as high as 108 mph, which hint at a chance at plus raw power. Martinez generates similar hard-hit metrics as Samuel Basallo did at his age and can drive the ball to all fields. His bat-to-ball skills are less advanced, with swing-and-miss tendencies evident even before he was overmatched during his short stint with Delmarva. He’ll need to learn to recognize spin and understand the strike zone better to develop into an average hitter. Martinez got reps at all three outfield spots in each of his first two seasons, but his size and fringy speed make him look more suited for a corner spot, where his plus arm would play. Martinez’s ability to impact the baseball gives him the chance to grow into a run-producer, but he will need to work to develop his all-around offensive profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles now have an established presence on the international amateur market, and at the beginning of the 2024 international period handed out six-figure bonuses to 16 players, including Martinez, an outfielder who signed for $950,000 as one of the headliners of that year’s crop. Martinez was ranked on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list entering the period and then enjoyed a solid debut, collecting 13 extra-base hits during a stint in the Dominican Summer League played mostly as a 16-year-old. Strong and athletic with a knack for hitting the ball hard, Martinez stands out particularly because of his raw power. He’s shown he is capable of producing uncommonly high exit velocities for a hitter his age, registering readings as hard as 108 mph off the bat during his pro debut. Those numbers are comparable to the type of pop Orioles top prospect Samuel Basallo exhibited as a young prospect, when he was a little-known teenager turning heads by lighting up the exit velo radars at the O’s training facilities. Martinez generates similar numbers and can already drive the ball to all fields, showing better feel for hitting to the opposite field than Basallo did at that age. It’s clear that Martinez’s 6-foot-4, almost 200-pound frame will be able to add more strength as he matures, but he’s also aggressive at the plate and will need to cut down on the swing-and-miss as he advances to develop into an average hitter. Martinez played mostly center field in his debut and has an easily-plus arm. But he’s only an average runner, and though it's possible he could stick in center, the size and power potential make his ceiling look more like that of a run-producing corner outfielder given the chance he grows out of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A decision to give up hitting and focus on pitching only at Gonzaga catapulted Hughes into first-round conversations in 2022, and he ended up landing with the Rockies at No. 10 overall. When he reached Double-A in his first full season, it was looking like a wise pick, but then he got shut down in July that year and had Tommy John surgery. He made it back to shake off the rust in the Arizona Fall League and pitched his way to Triple-A in 2025. The Rockies saw enough to add him to the 40-man roster during the offseason. While some of Hughes’ surface results were decent in 2025, his stuff has yet to come all the way back post-surgery. His rehab went very well, with no setbacks, but issues started popping up once he was back. He struggled to stay in the same slot, then was shut down with a shoulder issue because of how he was over-compensating. He still gets good sink on his two-seamer to get groundball outs, but his fastball only averaged around 91-92 mph last year, down a few ticks. He does have solid secondary stuff, with a mid-80s slider and a changeup that has a chance to be a solid offspeed offering. His slower, upper-70s curve did miss bats last year, though his strikeout rate tumbled overall. Hughes really struggled with the move to Albuquerque last year and overall, his stuff just wasn’t quite as crisp as it had been pre-surgery. This is a big year for him as the gloves come off a bit and he gets a chance to show if things can bounce back further removed from TJ. There’s still a starter package in here if it clicks, but there is some thought to his sinker-slider combination working in a multi-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After splitting his focus as a two-way player for Gonzaga in his first two seasons of college ball, Hughes took a big step forward when he put the bat down for good and focused on pitching only as the Zags’ Friday night starter in 2022. That led to him beating Marco Gonzales as the highest pick in school history, going No. 10 overall to the Rockies. Hughes reached Double-A in his first full season in 2023, but got shut down in July and needed Tommy John surgery. He returned in time to make six starts in the Arizona Fall League in 2024. Hughes was able to use his 17 1/3 innings in the AFL to shake some of the rust off and the good news is that his stuff looked pretty much back to where it was pre-injury. His fastball averaged 93 mph and touched 96, thrown with good sink to frequently get ground-ball contact. His cutter-like slider was regularly in the mid 80s, a hard breaker that flashed plus in the past, and he has some feel to spin a slower 80-82 mph curve, though it’s behind the harder breaking ball. HIs upper-80s changeup is starting to improve as well. Throw out Hughes’ surface numbers in the AFL given they came from his first post-surgery innings. He generally was around the zone previously, though his up-tempo delivery could get out of sync and cause timing issues, which in turn would lead to control problems. His ceiling might be somewhat limited, but once he really puts TJ behind him, he could be a big league back-end starter soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hughes spent two years in Gonzaga’s rotation and took a big step forward as their Friday night guy in 2022, allowing him to become the Zags’ first first-round pick since the Cardinals took Marco Gonzales No. 19 overall in 2013. Hughes became the highest pick in school history when the Rockies took him tenth overall in the 2022 Draft, thinking there might be some upside from a guy who had been a two-way player for his first two college seasons. He did touch Double-A in his first full year of pro ball but needed Tommy John surgery in July. When he’s healthy, Hughes brings an intriguing combination of size and stuff -- with feel for it -- to the mound. Even right before the elbow injury in Double-A last year, he was up to 97 mph with his fastball, though he sat at around 93. His short and hard mid-80s slider, that has cutter-like action to it, flashes plus and he’s shown feel to spin an effective upper-70s curve as well. He has an 87-88 mph changeup as well, but it’s clearly a fourth pitch. Hughes uses an up-tempo delivery and goes right after hitters. He can sometimes run into timing issues and there’s unintentional cut on his fastball occasionally, and both can impact his command, though he’s generally around the strike zone. All of that is on hold, of course, with Hughes not expected to do much competitively until 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It may go counter to what people think, but the Rockies have had some success when they’ve taken a college pitcher with their first pick, with hurlers such as Tyler Anderson, Jon Gray and Kyle Freeland having some big league success. The Rockies had gone the college arm route just once since Freeland was taken in 2014, with Ryan Rolison in 2018, until they selected Hughes No. 10 overall in 2022. The Gonzaga standout signed for an under-slot $4 million and pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season before getting shut down in early July with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. A former two-way player, Hughes only started pitching full-time in 2022, so there could be some serious growth potential once he's healthy. He already has the makings of a very good three-pitch mix coming from a solid starting pitcher’s frame. His fastball touches the upper 90s with some riding life to it, with more velocity to come. His slider is short and hard with cutter action to it, a pitch that flashes plus and misses bats. His changeup is probably his worst pitch, mostly because he didn’t throw it much in college, but there’s feel for it. Hughes has already impressed the Rockies with his mound presence, work ethic and intelligence -- he was a biology major who was on pace to graduate in three years. He goes right after hitters, and there’s confidence he’ll continue to be a solid strike-thrower the more time he has focusing on the craft, though first he'll focus on rehabbing post-surgery. He’s the type of college arm who could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The selection of Perez as a college senior out of Texas Christian in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft didn’t draw too much attention, and there wasn’t much buzz around him after a solid first full season of pro ball spent mostly at the Single-A level. He suffered through a tough 2024 campaign in High-A, but things started getting a little interesting last year, when he pitched his way from High-A to Double-A. The Mariners didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster, and he went unselected in the Rule 5 Draft. The 5-foot-10 Perez will never be confused with a flamethrower, but he does have a feel to pitch and for the strike zone. His fastball averaged around 93 mph last year, and he showed the ability to hold his velocity deeper into starts. But whatever success he has, he owes to his sliders. He throws them more than the heater, and he’ll use both a hard, short gyro-like pitch up to 87 mph as well as a low-80s sweeper. He’s tinkered with a variety of changeup grips and styles but hasn’t found one he can command. Perez continues to be an extreme strike-thrower, carrying a career 2.5 BB/9 rate into the 2026 season. He’ll get the opportunity to keep starting for now, but he’s pitching this year at age 26, so the clock is ticking. With younger starting pitching prospects coming behind him, there could be a time soon where the Mariners put Perez in a bullpen as a slider monster who maybe can gain a few more ticks in velocity in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez was selected as a reliever by the Angels in the late rounds of the 2021 Draft but he opted to return to Texas Christian University, then upped his stock to the 11th round, where the Mariners took him one year later and signed him for $125,000. He had a solid debut season in ‘23, making 15 starts at Single-A Modesto before a late-season promotion to High-A Everett. Undersized at 5-foot-10, Perez nonetheless possesses athleticism for his build. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, with good ride and break, which allows it to play up more than the radar gun shows. It’s also possible that he continues to grow into more velocity. It’s the slider that really took off in his first year, particularly the command of the pitch that has good two-plane break. It’s already consistently missing bats in the pros. Perez has exclusively started in his short stint in the organization, but for him to remain there, he’ll need to fortify at least one more pitch, the clearest offering being the changeup that he’ll drop in occasionally. Even with just a two-pitch mix, there’s a good foundation for him to eventually work as a reliever in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays made Bonilla one of their biggest international signings in years, handing the young Dominican slugger a $4.1 million bonus in 2023. Bonilla was billed as one of the top offensive talents in that year’s class and showed some early flashes in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .307 with an .836 OPS over 50 games. Bonilla’s numbers took a significant step back in ‘24, though, which was surprising after he’d generated so much positive buzz coming into the year. In the Florida Complex League, Bonilla hit just .186/.257/.299. The organization isn’t putting too much stock into those results and still believes in Bonilla's physical upside, which remains among the highest in the organization. Bonilla was a popular breakout pick a year ago for a reason, and many of those reasons still apply, but in 2025 that stat line will start to matter. Bonilla’s profile is all about his bat. He could develop into a dynamic offensive threat with legitimate plus power, but he’ll need to cut down on the swing-and-miss significantly to be more consistent. At 19, he remains a bit of a long-term project, but is still a name that brings out as much excitement as nearly any hitting prospect in the system. Likely destined for a corner outfield spot, the Blue Jays are still rolling out Bonilla in center field for now. A year ago, Bonilla felt like a dark-horse pick to catapult himself into the Top 100 conversation, and while the exact opposite happened, Bonilla is a talent worth being patient about. Few prospects in this system have a bigger gap between their potential floor and ceiling than Bonilla, so this should be a fascinating 12 months for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays made Bonilla one of their biggest international signings in years, handing the young Dominican slugger a $4.1 million bonus in 2023. Bonilla was billed as one of the top offensive talents in that year’s class and showed some early flashes in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .307 with an .836 OPS over 50 games. His game power hasn’t quite shown up (three homers) and his 55 strikeouts were an issue, but at 18, Bonilla is still one of the highest-upside prospects in this organization. It’s already jarring to see Bonilla in person. After having the image of a baby-faced teenager when he signed with the Blue Jays, there's a double-take upon seeing Bonilla walking around the Blue Jays’ complex with braids and a full, thick beard. There are raw elements to his game, but the exciting power he flashes in batting practice should start spilling into games this season. His exit velocities are already showing progress from 2023, and while he isn’t quite at the level of Orelvis Martinez in that area, he’s getting there. Bonilla seems destined for a corner outfield spot, which will need to be a greater focus for him in the coming seasons. He still moves very well for his size, so even if the Blue Jays can get Bonilla to the point that he’s playing a passable corner outfield, that’s enough to let his bat truly shine. His plate approach and strikeout rates are worth monitoring this year, but much like Arjun Nimmala, Bonilla is a dream project for this development staff and should benefit as much as anyone in the organization from the resources at the new complex. The long-term nature of said project remains a point of emphasis after Bonilla has struggled in the Florida Complex League this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays made Bonilla one of their biggest international signings in years, handing the young Dominican slugger a $4.1 million bonus in 2023. There are years of development ahead for Bonilla, but the Blue Jays came away impressed with him after he took part in their instructs in the Dominican Republic after the signing. At 6-foot-1, 180 pounds, Bonilla will continue to add strength and size to a physical frame that is already very impressive. His hit tool will need to develop in the coming years as he learns about himself as a hitter and develops a professional plate approach, but his raw power and bat speed were among the very best in the ’22 international class. He will play some center field coming up, but as he continues to mature, Bonilla could soon profile as a corner-outfield thumper, and he’s athletic enough to be a solid fielder in left or right. We’re still a couple of years away from seeing Bonilla with a full-season affiliate, but with his physical tools and age, he is a prospect the organization can dream on. He’ll benefit from climbing the ladder with the Blue Jays’ new player development complex at his disposal as he gets into the team's training program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fountain became the Nebraska high-school career home run record holder when he was a junior at Norris HS and finished with 31 total blasts. An LSU commit, he went to the Padres in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft but signed for second-round money with a $1.7 million bonus. His time in the San Diego system has been marred by injuries – Tommy John surgery in his first pro fall, hamstring and knee injuries in his first full season. He played only 65 games split between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2025, hitting .226/.346/.309 with three homers and 21 steals. Big-framed at 6-foot-5, Fountain still hasn’t found a solid foundation in the San Diego system because of the unfortunate piling up of his injuries. His size and strength still give him tons to dream on, but he hit too many balls on the ground and swung through too many sliders in his California League stint. To his credit, he didn’t expand the zone as much as other high-schoolers jumping to the pros, and those swing decisions point to a more promising offensive future. Fountain can show above-average speed at times, and he was an efficient basestealer in 2025, only getting thrown out once in 22 attempts. He spent the vast majority of his time last year at first base, where he’s a big target, but the Padres moved him to the outfield for '26 in hopes of tapping into his athleticism. Fountain suffered a left shoulder injury in April that required season-ending surgery, adding another health issue to his growing list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 60 | Run: 45 | Arm: 55 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Fountain set the Nebraska high-school career home run record as a junior, surpassing Cole Stobbe (25) and Jakson Reetz (24), and finished with 31 total dingers when he graduated in 2024. He also set state career records with 154 RBIs and 84 stolen bases. On top of the individual success, Fountain helped Norris High School win a state Class B championship as a senior. After all that fanfare, the third baseman went to the Padres in the fifth round of the Draft but signed for second-round money with a $1.7 million bonus. He underwent Tommy John surgery in the fall, slowing his early ability to show out in pro games. Fountain stands at 6-foot-5 and brings massive right-handed power. He has tremendous bat speed and strength, and he can launch balls with loft and leverage in his swing. That cuts both ways in his case. Fountain had rough showings on the summer showcase circuit between his junior and senior years, and some scouts worry that his uphill stroke and strike-zone discipline will hold him back against pro pitching. On the plus side, he didn’t swing-and-miss too much, but that could come without proper adjustments. The Padres were aware of a potential elbow issue because of Fountain’s throwing motion out of school, but at his best, he shows at least above-average arm strength. Some scouts think he should be able to handle third base when healthy, but others believe he doesn’t have the range for the spot and will land at first long term. He's been primarily at the cold corner in his first taste of Minor League action while he's been tested early by full-season arms. The Padres rave about Fountain's makeup, and his work ethic will be put to the test as he moves beyond injuries and the early rough numbers with Single-A Lake Elsinore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds had the No. 7 overall pick and a Competitive Balance Round A pick heading into the 2023 Draft, giving them the sixth largest bonus pool, and they weren’t afraid to spread the money around. They went almost three times over slot in the fourth round to sign Schoenwetter away from his commitment to his hometown Santa Barbara Gauchos. It took a while for the Reds to see what they had on their hands as he headed straight into rehab mode in order to build shoulder strength after the Draft, eventually making his debut in the Arizona Complex League. Numbers aside, the Reds were thrilled he was able to make 18 healthy appearances and spend some time with full-season Daytona at the end of the year. This will be the first year Schoenwetter should be able to show if he can start reaching his potential. He does have three excellent pitches in his arsenal, with a fastball that sat 92-95 mph last year, playing up with good spin rates up in the zone. He has more of a true, hard power curve, thrown anywhere in the 78-84 mph range with good depth, and his 84-87 mph changeup features good fade and he sells it well with arm speed. All three offerings might grade out as average right now, but all three could be plus in time as he physically matures and gets more reps. He struggled a bit finding the zone during his debut, but that might have been the time away from competition as much as it was anything with his delivery, which does have a little effort to it at times. He still has the chance to develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schoenwetter made a name for himself on the summer showcase circuit in 2022, standing out on a national stage at the Perfect Game All-American Classic. A solid senior season at his Santa Barbara-based high school put him in top two round conversations based on talent, but there was a commitment to stay home and go to UC Santa Barbara to contend with. The Reds, by virtue of having the No. 7 overall pick and a Competitive Balance Round A selection, had one of the larger bonus pools in baseball and were able to snag the athletic right-hander in the fourth round by giving him $1.9 million to sign. A prototypical projectable prep pitcher, Schoenwetter enters pro ball with the foundations of an exciting three-pitch mix. His fastball currently sits in the low-90s, but not only could there be more in the tank, it already plays up because he throws it with high spin rates and misses a ton of bats up in the zone. He uses a spike curve to get swings-and-misses as well, typically thrown in the mid-70s with hard, downer depth to it. His fading changeup, thrown with excellent arm speed, is a third at least above-average offering. As the 6-foot-3 Schoenwetter adds strength to his frame, he should be able to continue to repeat his delivery -- which does have some effort at times -- and find the strike zone consistently. There are always things high school arms need to improve as they begin the climb, and if Schoenwetter can maintain his stuff and stay on top of his breaking ball consistently, he has the chance to grow into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following two subpar seasons at South Carolina, Milone transferred to Oregon in 2022 and transformed into a different hitter by earning first-team All-Pac-12 honors as a junior after hitting .337/.405/.545 with 12 home runs in 60 games. The A’s took note of this revelation, selecting him in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft. Since joining the organization, he has quickly climbed up the prospect radar. He spent 2024 at Double-A Midland and hit .278/.361/.441 with 15 homers, 29 doubles and 70 RBIs in 120 games. The A’s initially figured they would have to tweak Milone’s mechanics at the plate given his unconventional setup and swing, but his production thus far at every level has led them to allow him to stick with what is working for him. His power numbers have been decent to this point, and he draws a good amount of walks and has solid bat-to-ball skills to round out an overall solid approach at the plate. Defense has always been the big question mark surrounding Milone. The A’s have tried giving him looks all around the infield, and while they plan to keep him versatile, first base is likely going to be where he ends up. Regardless of position, hitting is what got him this far, and the bat is what will take him to the Majors one day if his offensive output continues as he advances through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Transferring cross-country from South Carolina to Oregon in 2022, Milone earned first-team All-Pac-12 honors as a junior by hitting .337/.405/.545 with 12 homers in 60 games. That performance led to the A’s selecting him in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft. During his first full season of pro ball last year, he catapulted himself up the prospect radar by combining to hit .285/.398/.488 with 17 homers, 28 doubles and 72 RBIs in 114 games between Single-A Stockton and High-A Lansing. Milone’s setup and swing are a bit unconventional, but it has worked for him so far as a pro, so the A’s have no plans to tinker with his hitting mechanics for the time being. His good bat-to-ball skills lead to some homers and are part of an overall solid approach that also includes the ability to draw a ton of walks. Not considered strong with the glove by any means, Milone’s biggest question mark is figuring out his spot on defense. He was mostly a DH at Oregon, and while the A’s have given him looks at second and third base, it seems like first is his best shot if he’s going to play anywhere on the field, which puts more pressure on his bat to continue shining as he progresses through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2021, the Angels used all 20 of their Draft picks on pitchers. Albright was the only high schooler from that group, a Maryland native who moved to IMG Academy and got a way-over-slot bonus of $1.25 million to sign as a 12th-rounder rather than head to Virginia Tech. His first full season was full of bumps, but he returned to Single-A in 2023 and was having much better results when he was sent to the Rockies at the Trade Deadline in the deal for Randal Grichuk and C.J. Cron. He finished the year with a five-start look at what High-A Spokane was like. None of Albright’s four pitches jump off the page, but he has a pretty good feel for how to use all of them effectively. The six-foot lefty usually sits in the low-90s and it’s effective because he has good fastball command and hitters don’t pick it up because of deception in his delivery. When he stays on top of his breaking ball, it’s an effective pitch. He has good feel for a fading changeup and he can mix in a cutter as well. In the past, Albright has been plagued with a long arm action in the back and some inconsistency out front with his delivery that hurt his overall command. But was able to shorten his arm action and find the zone much more regularly in 2023. As his walk rate went down, his stuff ticked up and so did his strikeouts. The ceiling is limited, but if those trends continue, he could land in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 Draft might always be remembered as the one in which the Angels used all 20 of their picks to select pitchers. All but one were from the college ranks, with the lone exception being Albright, a Maryland native who moved to Florida to get exposure at IMG Academy. The left-hander received a way over-slot bonus of right around $1.25 million, second-round money, to join the organization rather than head to Virginia Tech. He tossed eight scoreless innings in the Arizona Complex League in his pro debut before getting more work in at instructs. Albright is not your prototypical high school projection case, as the six-footer is more about his feel for pitching than raw stuff. His fastball typically has been sitting in the 90-92 mph range, though he has shown a little more velocity in the past. It does play up because he can command it and misses bats thanks to deception in his delivery. His curve has the chance to be a solid pitch, though it can get slurvy at times, and he has feel for his changeup. While the southpaw can throw all three pitches for strikes, there is some concern about his long arm action in the back and his consistency out front with his delivery that hampered his stuff and his command. He’s young enough to correct some of those mechanical issues and land in the back end of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fraizer has long teased with impressive raw tools dating back to his days at Arizona when he didn’t produce much as a freshman and sophomore, but he then saw things click as a junior in 2019 before a broken hamate limited him to just 19 games. The Pirates took him the third round of that year’s Draft, signing for a just-below slot of $525,000. When he hit his way from High-A Greensboro to Double-A Altoona in 2021, finishing with a .939 OPS, the Bucs thought they perhaps had a steal on their hands. But his first full season at the upper levels in 2022 -- back with Altoona -- did not go nearly as well. The left-handed-hitting Fraizer still has the ability to hit the ball hard, recording high exit velocities when things are clicking. He really lost his approach in 2022 and it snowballed as he struggled, with the outfielder often trying to do too much. His swing mechanics also went significantly sideways and his tendency to cut himself off on the front part of his swing -- which didn’t hurt him in 2021 -- really caused him trouble against better pitching in 2022. Fraizer’s speed still plays well and he can steal a base, as well as play a very solid center field. He needs to simplify things and just let his natural ability and tools take over. The Pirates didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster last offseason and he wasn’t taken in the Rule 5 Draft. At age 25, the clock is ticking. He may have overperformed in 2021 and underperformed last year; the key will be in finding a middle ground somewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fraizer didn’t have much success in his first two years at the University of Arizona, despite obvious size and athleticism. He was at the start of a breakout season as a junior in 2019 when he broke a hamate, leaving most teams unsure of who he was as a player. The Pirates liked his tools enough to take a flyer on him in the third round of that June’s Draft and he had an understandably rusty return from injury during his pro debut. Unseen by most during the pandemic, Fraizer took off in 2021, going from High-A to Double-A and earning a spot on the second team of MLB Pipeline’s Prospect Team of the Year. Even during his up-and-down days at Arizona, Fraizer has shown an advanced knowledge of the strike zone and a willingness to work counts and draw walks. That continued in 2021 as he walked in over 11 percent of his plate appearances while limiting strikeouts, making consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. He changed his setup in 2021 with obviously positive effects, spreading out a bit more and staying more balanced, which helped him drive the ball and tap into his raw power. Fraizer’s plus speed is an asset on both sides of the ball, as he continues to learn the craft of stealing bases and covers a lot of ground in center field, where the Pirates believe he can stay long term, though he’s continued to get reps in all three spots. The Pirates saw Fraizer’s confidence soar in 2021 and now that he believes in his own ability to produce, he has the chance to continue developing into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fraizer had two relatively nondescript years at the University of Arizona before starting to really click at the start of his junior year. His Draft profile was just starting to rise when he suffered a broken hamate, limiting him to just 19 games. The Pirates liked his tools enough to nab him in the third round of the 2019 Draft and signed him for a below slot $525,000 and he shook off the rust during his pro debut in the short-season New York-Penn League. His production was impacted by a scratch in his glasses, making it hard for him to see, but he’s since upgraded to contacts. The left-handed hitter is physical and athletic with plus speed that helps him on both sides of the ball. He needs to clean up some of his movement at the plate and his bat path, some of which he’s already made gains on, and that could give him the chance to be a solid hitter who can barrel up the baseball consistently. Fraizer is strong and he could start tapping into some power as he further refines that approach. With his speed, Fraizer has the chance to play center field with an average arm. He played all three outfield spots last summer, something that’s likely to continue with a likely ceiling of a fourth outfielder type contributor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: To be filed under “pitching talent can come from anywhere,” Erla was a 17th-round pick of the Angels in their all-pitching 2021 Draft, signing for slot value ($125,000) after spending five years at Michigan State. The organization first thought that perhaps it had a Draft bargain when he was the most exciting arm at instructs the fall after he signed. He missed the first two months of the 2022 season with a shoulder issue but threw well across 16 starts in Double-A once he was healthy. Erla’s arsenal starts with what can be a plus fastball. He sat in the mid-90s during instructs in shorter stints and was around 93-94 mph, touching 97 with the Trash Pandas last year, but the organization thinks there’s more velocity in the tank. With a lower release, he does a good job of sinking it down in the zone to get ground-ball outs but also can get guys out at the top of the zone because of his unique release height. He flashed a solid mid-80s slider and he’s worked on a new one this offseason in the hopes of finding a true out pitch. He has a changeup that can miss bats and get contact on the ground, though it’s too firm at times. The 6-foot-4 Erla has shown he can repeat his delivery well and fill up the strike zone with all of his pitches. He’ll be 25 for most of the 2023 season, so the clock is ticking, and the Angels will continue to let him start because of his strike-throwing ability and the hope he can sharpen his two secondary offerings, knowing the fastball-slider from his slot could be nasty coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Erla spent five years at Michigan State, not getting drafted in 2019 after a rough season in the Spartans rotation and not getting selected in the shortened five-round Draft in 2020. He put up decent numbers in that fifth year to attract a little attention and the Angels made him pitcher No. 17 in their 20-pitcher Draft in 2021. He threw a handful of innings last summer in the Arizona Complex League to get his professional feet wet, then opened some eyes with his performance in instructional league play. The 6-foot-4 Erla may have been the most impressive arm at instructs for the Angels last fall. He’s more about arm strength than anything, with a fastball that sat 95-96 mph and touched 98 at instructs. After that, it’s a bit of a question mark. He showed a good hard slider in the mid-80s that has the chance to be a solid secondary offering and he has a changeup, but it’s well behind the other two as a below-average pitch. While Erla was generally around the plate at Michigan State, he didn’t have great command, but he’s been filling up the strike zone since joining the Angels. He’s already 24, but there’s an interesting combination of velocity and size here. He’ll get the chance to start for now and any future role will depend on the consistency of his secondary stuff and his ability to land them for strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor set a Central Michigan record with 125 strikeouts while winning Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as a sophomore in 2021, then encored by breaking his own mark with 126 the following spring. The Astros selected him in the supplemental second round, making him the Chippewas' highest pick since 1986 second-rounder Kevin Tapani. His strikeout rate (13.5 per nine innings) in his 2023 pro debut ranked fourth among Minor Leaguers who worked as many as his 84 innings. Taylor's low-90s fastball features outstanding metrics because he has a 6-foot-5 frame with a high arm slot and plenty of extension, plus he backspins the ball so well that it has tremendous carry up in the zone. He has added significant strength since turning pro, weighing closer to 225 pounds than his listed 190, and the Astros hope that results in added velocity that will make his heater even more effective. After throwing roughly 80 percent fastballs in college, he's trying to refine the rest of his repertoire. His best secondary pitch is his low-80s slider, though he'll switch to a tighter version after having difficulty controlling a sweepier version in 2023. Both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s changeup are fringy and leave him vulnerable against left-handers, who batted .313/.405/.458 against him last season. He repeats his delivery well enough but will need to provide more strikes to reach his ceiling as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year, Taylor set a Central Michigan record with 125 strikeouts and then broke the mark with 126 whiffs last spring. He left two starts early with elbow tightness but didn't miss a turn in the rotation and looked good in the NCAA regional playoffs against Florida. The Chippewas' highest pick since 1986 second-rounder Kevin Tapani, he signed for $804,700 as a supplemental second-rounder and will make his pro debut in 2023. Taylor's fastball sits around 90 mph and tops out at 94, yet it rarely gets squared up. His heater is an analytical darling because his high spin rates produce tremendous carry and he uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create plenty of extension that throws hitters off. He relied on his fastball roughly 80 percent of the time in college, with his seldom-used 78-82 mph changeup with fade and sink serving as his most reliable secondary pitch. The Astros will work with Taylor to improve his breaking pitches and add strength. His tight 78-82 mph slider is average at best, while his soft mid-70s curveball is more of a fringy offering. He does a good job of keeping his long limbs in sync and repeating his delivery, though he has battled the strike zone more than expected in his first taste of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Padres signed Suero for $325,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period, he's shown glimpses of his tools coming from a frame that now stands 6-foot-6. He had a solid enough debut in the Dominican Summer League, but was struggling to find consistent production during his United States debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in 2023 when he was sent to the Pirates in the Rich Hill/Ji Man Choi deal. He wasn't able to have much more success with a return to the Florida Complex League in 2024, with what turned out to be a broken hamate sapping his impact and shutting him down at the end of July. Suero will be just 19 for nearly all of the 2025 season, and there are ingredients to work with. He's a switch-hitter who has shown the ability to make hard contact with good bat speed from both sides of the plate. He has a decent approach, draws walks and generally makes good swing decisions. What he doesn't do is make enough contact, as he struck out close to 30 percent of the time at the rookie levels. He'll need to find a way to cut down on the swing-and-miss so he can tap into his raw power, with more of that to come as he adds strength to that huge frame. Right now, Suero runs well enough to man center field, and it could be an option moving forward. There is a pretty good chance he outgrows the position and needs to move to a corner, and he's seen time in both. The focus now is staying healthy and getting enough reps to find some offensive consistency to fit the corner outfield profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Suero for $325,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period, and he went out and performed fairly well during his debut in the Dominican Summer League. The move to the United States and the Arizona Complex League was a little bumpier, then he was dealt to the Pirates as part of the return for Rich Hill and Ji Man Choi. He finished up his summer in the Florida Complex League and then got some more work in the Dominican Instructional League. It's hard to miss Suero, now standing at 6-foot-5 and just starting to grow into that frame. As modest as his numbers have been, it should be noted he was still 16 when he played in the DSL and there's a ways to go in terms of his physical development. The upside, though, is considerable. A switch-hitter with all the raw tools, he can make hard contact from both sides and has good bat speed, even with his long arms. He'll need to work on his approach and cut down on the swing-and-miss, but does show some feel for barreling up the baseball out in front. Suero runs well, too, potentially providing an exciting speed-power combination in the future. That speed gives him a chance to play center field, but he could fill out enough where moving to a corner spot will be necessary. He could take off as he learns how to polish those tools, but just ask Oneil Cruz: The Pirates know a little bit about helping a tall, lanky and toolsy player reach the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A big-time college performer who started three years at NC State and helped lead the Wolfpack to a Men's College World Series, Cozart went in the second round of the 2024 Draft and signed with the Guardians a hair over slot for $2,050,000. After his first taste of pro ball was a disappointment offensively following a long college campaign, he bounced back in his first full season with a .235/.341/.371 slash line between High-A and Double-A. Despite being large for a catcher at 6-foot-3, 214 pounds, Cozart stands out most for his defense. Not only is he a strong framer and receiver, but he receives rave reviews for soft skills such as his communication with pitchers, game planning and leadership -- perhaps unsurprising since he comes from a baseball family. He has a strong throwing arm, although he only caught 23.9 percent of attempted runners last year because his throws were sometimes off the mark. Cozart may be no threat to steal bases, but he's plenty nimble behind the plate. His offense trended in the right direction last season, although swing-and-miss is holding him back. Cozart's longer, steep swing can make it difficult to cover the zone, and his strikeout and walk numbers regressed against more advanced pitching; his overall improved production from High-A (106 wRC+) to Double-A (113 wRC+) can largely be attributed to BABIP luck. He has solid raw strength, but his lack of bat speed caps his in-game power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An immediate starter as a freshman at North Carolina State, Cozart earned All-America honors last spring after hitting 19 homers and leading the Wolfpack to the College World Series. The fourth catcher drafted in 2024, he signed for $2,050,000 as a second-round pick. He went just 5-for-42 (.119) in a 13-game pro debut in High-A, though he did throw out eight of 15 basestealers. A left-handed hitter, Cozart works counts in search of pitches that he can drive. He's a potential 15-20 homer hitter whose power plays from left-center to the right-field line, though he generates it more with strength than bat speed. His swing can get long and he has difficulty barreling non-fastballs, so he'll have to prove he can do consistent damage against quality pitching. Taller than most catchers at 6-foot-3, Cozart is an average receiver with good framing skills. While he'll flash solid pop times, his arm plays more as average. He's a baseclogger with well-below-average speed, though he moves well enough behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It looked like Hettiger, who starred on the Los Angeles high school scene, was going to head to Oregon for college ball as the 2023 Draft wore on and he didn’t hear his name called. The Phillies had other ideas, using some extra bonus pool money when Day 3 started, going over slot to sign him for close to $400,000. He hasn’t put up big numbers as of yet, but he made some progress along the way in a rough first full season with Single-A Clearwater, then earning a promotion to High-A Jersey Shore while finishing the year in Double-A in 2025. A former switch-hitter who is now only hitting left-handed to help simplify things at the plate, Hettiger does have the makings of a solid approach at the plate, seeing a lot of pitches and drawing a lot of walks as evidenced by his career walk rate north of 16 percent heading into 2025. He finds the barrel a lot, and there’s some power for him to get to, but while he limits chase, the swing-and-miss is concerning (29.1 percent K rate). When he first entered pro ball, there were questions about Hettiger’s ability to catch long-term, especially because he hadn’t played much behind the dish in high school. He continues to get reps at first, but he’s become one of the better defenders at the position in the organization, with more than enough arm. If that continues, he could end up catching in the big leagues one day, getting at-bats against right-handed pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the first two days of the Draft came and went in 2023, Hettiger may have thought he was headed to Oregon for college ball. But the Phillies hadn’t quite used up their bonus pool money over the top 10 rounds and were able to nab Hettiger in Round 11, going over the Day 3 slot ($150,000) to sign him for just under $400,000. He made his very brief pro debut in the Florida Complex League last summer after signing. A switch-hitter, Hettiger appears to be better from the left side than the right, though he sees the ball well and has good at-bats from both sides of the plate. He’s used a small trigger in his swing in the past, but tends to be on time and has an advanced approach with excellent pitch recognition. There’s plenty of raw power to tap into, and that shows up more when he’s hitting left-handed. Strength gains this offseason could start showing up at the plate during his first full season. Hettiger didn’t catch a ton in high school, as the solid athlete moved around and played the infield corners quite a bit. There’s work to be done on his receiving, but he sets up well behind the plate. He’s already shown that he has more than enough arm to remain behind the plate, throwing out several potential basestealers in the FCL, with the Phillies having a bit more faith that he can stick there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2020-21 international signing period was delayed from opening until January 2021 because of the pandemic, and that’s when the bulk of the signings occurred and were announced. The Angels weren’t quite done though, as nine months later, they signed Marcheco for $35,000. After tossing nine hitless innings in the Dominican Summer League in his brief debut, he came stateside in 2022 and pitched his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season Inland Empire. He reached High-A over the course of the 2023 season, piling up 121 2/3 innings in the process. The 6-foot-1 right-hander’s success comes from a combination of pitchability and deception. His fastball has below-average velocity, typically sitting 88-89 mph and touching 91, but he hides the ball so well that hitters have not fared well against it; he threw the pitch 70 percent of the time. Both the slider and the changeup will flash average to give him a three-pitch mix that plays beyond its individual grades. Marcheco might have the best command in the organization and uses the funk in his delivery and his understanding of how to keep hitters off-balance to get outs. He did wear down a bit by the end of the year; added strength would help with that and could give him the chance to gain enough velocity to give him the chance to reach the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The delayed 2020-21 international signing period might always be known in the Angels organization for the addition of Denzer Guzman to the system. But nine months after inking Guzman for $2 million when the period opened on Jan. 15, 2021, they also signed Marcheco, giving the Cuban right-hander $35,000 that September to start his pro career. He recorded two short hitless outings at the end of the month in the Dominican Summer League, then threw well in his U.S. debut in 2022, finishing third in the Arizona Complex League in strikeouts with 76 and earning a late bump up to full-season ball. Marcheco’s success has stemmed more from his pitchability than his pure stuff. He has a three-pitch mix with a fastball that currently sits in the 90-92 mph range and plays well because he locates it in the strike zone. He backs it up with an average slider and has decent feel for a changeup. The 6-foot-1 right-hander already has the ability to set up hitters and mix his pitches well, throwing a ton of strikes with all three offerings. There’s some funk and deception in his delivery, a reason why he was able to strike out 13.1 per nine and hold hitters to a .216 average-against in 2022. Now he’ll get to see how his average-stuff profile plays over an entire full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia signed for $850,000 out of Venezuela in 2022 and was off to a hot start in Single-A two years later before tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee while running the bases. He missed a year's worth of action before returning late last May and homering 12 times in 58 games, mostly in High-A. The Red Sox also signed his older brother Jhostynxon for $350,000 in 2019 and sent him to the Pirates in the Johan Oviedo trade last December. Garcia's signature tool is his plus raw power, the product of prodigious strength, and he uses it well by consistently elevating balls to his pull side. There are questions about how much contact he'll make against advanced pitching, however, because he has a big leg kick, a right-handed stroke that gets too long and an aggressive approach. He chases all types of offerings out of the zone and swings through too many strikes. Much heavier than his listed 196 pounds, Garcia gained weight during his layoff and has had trouble shedding it. He's a bottom-of-the-scale runner who isn't moving as well behind the plate as he was before he got hurt. He receives, frames and blocks well enough to become an average defender if he can regain some athleticism, and he features solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three years after signing his older brother Jhostynxon Garcia out of Venezuela for $350,000, the Red Sox landed Johanfan for $850,000. He has become the best prospect from Boston's 2022 international class and batted .385/.467/.596 in the first month in Single-A before blowing out the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee running the bases. He had surgery in May and may not be quite ready for the start of the 2025 season. Garcia stands out most with his plus raw power. He's very strong for his age, has good feel for driving the ball in the air and produces loud exit velocities. Despite his .286 average through three pro seasons, there are some questions about how well he'll hit against higher-level pitching. He employs a big leg kick, his right-handed swing can get long and his chase and swing-and-miss rates are high. Bigger than his listed 196 pounds, Garcia has well-below-average speed and will have to watch his conditioning as he gets older. Nevertheless, he moves well behind the plate and has made strides with his receiving, framing and blocking since turning pro. He can become an average defender with solid arm strength if he continues to improve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Venezuelan outfielder Jhostynxon Garcia for $350,000 in 2019, then added his younger brother, Johanfran, for $850,000 three years later. He received the third-highest bonus in Boston's 2022 class and has emerged as the best prospect among that group. He made his U.S. debut in 2023 and slashed .302/.408/.497 in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, ranking among the top 10 in all three categories, before spending the final month in Single-A at age 18. Garcia is stronger than most teenagers and already displayed aptitude for driving the ball in the air. He lets his power come naturally, managing the strike zone while distributing balls to all fields. While his right-handed stroke can get long, he could hit for a decent average while providing 20 homers per season. Garcia has well-below-average speed yet moves well behind the plate. He made significant improvements with his receiving, framing and blocking in 2023 and looks on course to becoming an average defender. He has solid-to-plus arm strength and threw out 38 percent of basestealers in his first two years as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oklahoma's top high school prospect in 2018, Franklin missed most of his senior season with a broken foot yet still landed third-round money ($450,000) as a sixth-round pick. The nephew of former All-Star closer, Ryan Franklin, he significantly improved his stuff during his first full pro season, then didn't pitch at all the next two years because of the pandemic shutdown (2020) and oblique and shoulder issues (2021). He never got into a rhythm making abbreviated starts every six or seven days last season in High-A, recording a 6.88 ERA with 75 strikeouts in 69 1/3 innings. Franklin had no trouble regaining his fastball velocity in 2022, hitting 99 mph in his first live batting practice in Spring Training and working at 94-97 mph and touching 99 during the season. His fading changeup was still his best secondary pitch, albeit a little less lively because it got a bit too firm at 83-86 mph. After showing limited feel for spin as an amateur, he has developed a 78-82 mph knuckle-curve that's at least a solid pitch when it's on, and he has added a similarly effective sweeping low-80s slider in 2023. While his stuff returned, Franklin had difficulty locating his pitches, issued too many walks and got crushed when he caught too much of the zone. His fastball has more downhill plane than life and gets hit when he doesn't command it, and he can have trouble throwing his secondary pitches for strikes. He still flashes mid-rotation upside, but he's also 23 years old with just 120 innings in his first five years as a pro and may wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former All-Star closer Ryan Franklin, Kohl ranked as Oklahoma's top prep prospect in 2018 but missed most of his senior season with a broken foot. After selecting him in the sixth round and paying him third-round money ($450,000), the Cubs were delighted by the progress he made in his first full pro season in 2019. But he didn't pitch at all the next two years because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 followed by oblique and minor shoulder maladies in 2021. As Franklin has added muscle to his 6-foot-4 frame, his fastball has increased from 86-89 mph in 2017 to 89-93 in 2018 to 93-96 in 2019, and he worked at 97-99 during his first live batting practice in Spring Training 2022. His best secondary pitch is a low-80s changeup with fade that plays well off his four-seamer. He lacked feel for spin as an amateur but added an upper-70s knuckle-curve in 2019, and it shows signs of becoming at least a solid offering. Franklin has the athleticism to repeat his delivery and fill the strike zone, though his control and command have been erratic in High-A this year. He uses his size and high three-quarter arm slot to create downhill plane on his pitches, and club officials praise his maturity and competitiveness. He has the ingredients to become a mid-rotation starter but must prove he can handle the workload after totaling just 50 2/3 innings in his first four pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former All-Star Ryan Franklin, Kohl emerged as Oklahoma's top high school prospect in 2018 but missed most of his senior season with a broken right foot. The Cubs took him in the sixth round and paid him third-round money ($450,000) to divert him from a college commitment to Oklahoma. His stuff took a jump forward during his first full pro season in 2019 but the coronavirus pandemic scuttled plans to build up his workload in full-season ball last year and he has yet to pitch in 2021 while dealing with an oblique injury. As he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame, Franklin continues to add fastball velocity, going from 86-89 mph in 2017 to 89-93 in 2018 to 91-97 the last two years. The Cubs think he eventually could sit at 93-96 mph and back up his heater with a pair of solid to plus secondary pitches. He has advanced aptitude for a hard changeup with fade and has taken to a knuckle-curve he adopted in 2019 after showing inconsistent feel for spin as an amateur. Franklin's athleticism and ability to repeat his delivery allow him to provide consistent strikes. He uses his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane on his pitches. He offers hope for a mid-rotation starter to an organization that has had difficulty developing homegrown pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oklahoma's top high school prospect in 2018, Franklin missed most of his senior season with a broken right foot and dropped to the sixth round. The nephew of former All-Star Ryan Franklin, he signed for $540,000, the equivalent of third-round money. His stuff took a significant step forward last summer and the Cubs are eager to see how he handles a jump to full-season ball in 2020. Franklin's fastball velocity continues to rise as he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame, climbing from 86-89 mph in 2017 to 89-93 in 2018 to 91-97 last summer. After not showing much aptitude for spinning the ball as an amateur, he switched to a knuckle-curve grip in 2019 and flashed a solid to plus breaker with increased depth. He has advanced feel for his fading changeup, giving him a quality three-pitch arsenal. Franklin still has room to add strength, so his stuff could continue to add power. He's athletic, repeats his delivery well and throws strikes on a steep downhill plane created by his size and high three-quarters arm slot. He's young and will need time to develop, but he offers hope for a mid-rotation starter to an organization that has struggled to develop pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox might have taken Kath with their 2021 first-round pick if Colson Montgomery hadn't been available, so they were delighted to grab him as their second-rounder with an over-slot $1.8 million bonus. Gatorade's Arizona player of the year, he led Desert Mountain HS (Scottsdale) to the state 5-A title and crushed a long home run at the Angels' Spring Training stadium in the championship game. He hasn't thrived in pro ball, batting .227/.325/.367 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in his first two pro seasons. Scouts considered Kath one of the more advanced hitters in the 2021 prep class, but he has struggled to catch up to quality fastballs and to recognize breaking balls as a pro. Chicago helped him simplify the load with his left-handed swing, and while he did a better job of drawing walks and avoiding ground-ball contact last season than he did in his debut, his propensity for swinging and missing remains a huge concern. He still has plus raw power that could translate into 20 or more homers per season if he can put the bat on the ball more regularly, but he also needs to add more strength after his bat speed diminished late in the year. Kath played shortstop in high school but his below-average speed and quickness prompted an immediate move to third base in pro ball. He has the potential to become at least an average defender with soft hands and plus arm strength at the hot corner, though he'll have to improve his agility and consistency. He has a ways to go to catch Bryan Ramos as Chicago's third baseman of the future, which eventually could prompt a move to first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kath factored into the White Sox's possibilities for the first round of the 2021 Draft, so they were thrilled to find him available in the second. Gatorade's Arizona player of the year, he carried Desert Mountain High (Scottsdale) to the state 5-A title and smashed a long homer at the Angels' Spring Training park in the championship game. Signed for an over-slot $1.8 million, he hit just .212/.287/.337 with a 37 percent strikeout rate during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Kath was one of the more advanced hitters in the 2021 high school crop, employing an easy left-handed swing and a mature approach to make consistent hard contact to all fields. He tried to do too much in the ACL, chasing and trying to pull too many pitches and producing a lot of weak contact when he did connect. If he gets back to focusing on driving the ball from gap to gap and can add some loft to his stroke, he could become a solid hitter with average or better pop. A shortstop in high school, Kath immediately moved to third base after turning pro. Though he's a below-average runner, he has enough range to go with soft hands and plus arm strength at the hot corner. His debut may have been rockier than expected, but the White Sox still envision him and 2021 first-rounder Colson Montgomery locking down the left side of their infield in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Having signed for $1 million on Jan. 15, 2021, Montesino was one of the Padres’ two seven-figure additions to begin the 2021 international period, the other being Samuel Zavala, who has become an even more prominent name in the two years since. The Venezuela native got off to a promising start in the 2021 Dominican Summer League but missed the opportunity for his first stateside season after undergoing Tommy John surgery before the 2022 campaign began. The left-handed slugger flashed a good amount of power in the DSL, ranking among the top 15 qualifiers (out of 190) with his .489 slugging percentage and .934 OPS. A selective approach led to a quality walk rate and on-base percentage, but as is true of many young hitters, there was still plenty of swing-and-miss when he did take his hacks, leading many to believe he’ll eventually settle in as a power-over-hit type. Montesino was a defensive question mark even before needing the elbow procedure. Originally signed as an outfielder, he already got the majority of his defensive starts at first base in the DSL, and unless he can improve his routes on the grass, he’ll likely end up at the cold corner long term. Below-average speed and arm strength did him no favors there either. Montesino is still only 19 entering 2023, and it’ll be important for him to pick up right where he left off offensively given how much of his value is tied into his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montesino, along with Samuel Zavala, is one of two left-handed-hitting outfielders who signed for seven figures in the Padres’ 2020-21 international class. Montesino, who signed for $1 million, projects as a power hitter and showed as much in his professional debut last summer. The Venezuelan slugged .489 over 56 games in the Dominican Summer League. He underwent Tommy John surgery before the season and has missed the 2022 campaign as a result. Montesino’s easy left-handed swing produces plenty of pop, though there’s some swing-and-miss to his game. He’s a strong hitter with a selective approach, but needs to control the strike zone better as he matures. He’s a power-over-hit prospect, but the Padres think there’s still plenty to like about his overall hit tool and the Padres feel he could develop into an above-average hitter. This was an offense-first signing as Montesino’s defensive skill set is a work in progress. He projects as a below-average defender who needs to refine his routes and his reads and is likely to wind up in either left field or first base. His arm and his speed leave something to be desired as well, though they should both be passable. Regardless, his bat is his carrying tool and his offensive development will ultimately determine his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of two lefty-hitting outfielders to sign for seven figures in the Padres’ 2020-21 class, Montesino joins Samuel Zavala as big-time talents out of Venezuela. Montesino, who signed for $1 million, projects as a power-hitting corner-outfield type in the mold of fellow Padres prospect Tirso Ornelas. Montesino’s easy left-handed swing should produce plenty of pop. Though there might be a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, he’s a big, strong hitter with few moving parts and a decent understanding of the strike zone. The Padres expect him to be able to hit for average and power as he progresses. But make no mistake: This was an offense-first signing. Montesino’s defensive skill set is raw, and he projects as a below-average defender who needs work cleaning up his routes and his reads. Montesino’s arm and his speed leave something to be desired as well, though they should both be passable. Still, if the Padres can hone Montesino’s corner-outfield skills toward respectability, they feel his bat will be able to carry him the rest of the way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paulino turned 16 the same day the 2018 international signing period opened, and he celebrated by turning pro for $205,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He made his U.S. debut by batting .336 in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2021 and led the Single-A Carolina League in doubles (35), triples (10), extra-base hits (58) and total bases (217). He made the jump to full-season ball the following year, and his numbers weren't as big in 2023 but he held his own in High-A at age 20 and helped Greenville win the South Atlantic League championship. He was a solid performer at Double-A Portland to begin 2024 and was traded to the Blue Jays in a four-player deal involving Danny Jansen at the Trade Deadline. Paulino has the ingredients to hit for average: a pretty left-handed swing, fine hand-eye coordination and more discipline than most players his age. But he hasn't been able to add much muscle to his slight 5-foot-10 frame, so his quality of contact dipped against better pitching last year. His hitting ability should enable him to tap into most of his average raw power, so he could deliver 15 or more homers per season if he gets stronger. Though he has just average speed, Paulino can steal bags, though he became less efficient at that skill in 2024. Almost half of his starts last year came at shortstop, though he has fringy range there and his arm stands out more for its accuracy than its strength. He also saw action at second base (his best position) and third (where his arm is a bit light), and he played briefly in center field in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paulino celebrated his 16th birthday in 2018 by signing with the Red Sox for $205,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His best attribute was his pure hitting ability, and that has translated into a .281/.377/.468 slash line through his first three pro seasons. He made his full-season debut at age 19 last year and led the Single-A Carolina League in doubles (35), triples (10), extra-base hits (58) and total bases (217). After recognizing pitches well and repeatedly making good swing decisions in 2022, Paulino has been less patient and productive in High-A. His sweet left-handed stroke and fine hand-eye coordination should allow him to make consistent contact, but he has regressed and has been feeble against southpaws. There are some questions about his lack of physicality and how much power he'll have, though he should have the hitting ability to get to most of his raw pop and produce at least 15 homers per season. Paulino plays faster than his average speed on the bases thanks to his instincts and aggressive nature. Signed as a shortstop, he started games there and at second and third base, and left and center field in 2022. With his average quickness and arm strength along with his hit-over-power profile, he fits best at the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paulino turned 16 on the day the 2018 international signing period opened, and he celebrated by turning pro with the Red Sox for $205,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His biggest selling point was his pure hitting ability, which was evident when he batted .336/.436/.549 as a 19-year-old in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League making his U.S. debut last summer. Originally signed as a shortstop, he moved to third and second base in the FCL to accommodate slicker defenders Marcelo Mayer and Brainer Bonaci. Paulino is built to hit for average with a smooth left-handed stroke, fine hand-eye coordination and advanced pitch recognition and swing decisions for a teenager. He makes a lot of contact but also shows the ability to work walks. Though he didn't homer in his first two pro summers, he did have 20 extra-base hits in 36 FCL games and his bat speed and ability to barrel balls could produce 15 or more homers annually once he adds some much-need strength. An average runner, Paulino displays good instincts on the bases. He has reliable hands and some twitchy athleticism but his quickness and average arm strength are a bit stretched at shortstop. He profiles best as an offensive second baseman and also might see some outfield action to enhance his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves were excited to see what Bagwell could do in his first full season of pro ball in 2025 after giving him third-round money ($822,500) in Round 6 to sign him away from his Missouri commitment. The Illinois high school standout had shown glimpses of upper-90s velocity early on in his senior season but didn’t maintain that. He hasn’t shown a return to that kind of crisp stuff since, though an oblique injury that cost him three months didn’t help and put the organizational enthusiasm on hold. Bagwell is a big, strong 6-foot-4, 230-pound right-hander with a feel for pitching and a potentially deep repertoire. When he was on the mound in 2025, his fastball sat at around 92 mph and topped out at 95, with some carry up in the zone. He needs to sharpen his secondary offerings, though his low-80s slider that features some sweep can miss bats at times and was particularly effective against right-handed hitters. He does have an 86 mph changeup he’ll use more against lefties that he’s still learning to trust, but it can get groundball outs. With a football player’s build, Bagwell’s physicality is a plus, even if there’s not much projection in there. There’s some effort in his delivery, though he managed to be around the zone more often than not. He’ll need to find a true out pitch as he looks to turn in a full, healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It seemed likely that Bagwell, a strong right-hander from the Illinois high school ranks, was going to honor his commitment to Missouri as the 2024 Draft approached. He had opened eyes by touching the upper 90s at the very start of his senior season but did not keep that kind of velocity up all year. He did head to the Draft combine and hit 96 mph during his brief outing. The Braves, never one to shy away from high-ceiling prep arms, took him in the sixth round and were able to keep him from heading to Mizzou by giving him $822,500, third-round money. For most of his senior season, the 6-foot-4, 230-pound Bagwell sat 89-94 mph with his fastball with decent carry up in the zone. His secondary stuff isn’t as consistently effective, with his 78-82 mph sweeping slider the best of his options. His upper-80s changeup is too firm, and like with many prep arms, he hasn’t thrown it a lot nor does he trust it much. Bagwell’s delivery does have some effort to it and that has led to command and control issues at times, even when pitching out of the stretch full time. He doesn’t offer much projection to his frame, but he’s more physical than many high schoolers, giving him upside to go along with some reliever risk.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After four years at the University of San Diego, the last of which saw him homer 16 times and hit .373, Ricketts was taken in the seventh round of the 2022 Draft by the Phillies. He’s managed to play his way to the upper levels of the system in his first two years of pro ball, though injuries have hampered his development and he’s yet to top 275 at-bats in a single season. Hopes that making up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League in 2023 would serve as a springboard were dashed when he posted a .670 OPS with Double-A Reading in 2024. While Ricketts’ numbers with Reading were disappointing, he still checks off some boxes and has some traits the Phillies like.
