Only 19 for the duration of the 2023 season, the right-hander has seen his K rate crater at High-A Fort Wayne, but there's still enough to dream on moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for a $1 million bonus on March 1, 2021, Lizarraga was certainly one of the more intriguing names in the Padres' 2020-21 international class. Regarded as the top pitching prospect from Mexico, the 18-year-old features an exciting three-pitch mix and struck out 35 over 30 innings in Rookie ball during his brief professional debut. Lizarraga’s fastball sits in the low-90s, but Padres officials believe his velocity will tick up as he adds strength to his 6-foot-3, 180-pound frame. The right-hander also shows some feel to spin his upper-70s curveball, though the pitch needs more refinement to reach its ceiling. He rounds out his arsenal with a changeup that features downward action and shows flashes of becoming a real weapon in the future. Confident from competing against older competition in Mexico, Lizarraga shows good poise on the mound. His natural athleticism is apparent in his smooth delivery, which allows him to command his pitches and throw plenty of strikes. Referred to by some as a “projection dream”, it’s easy to see a high ceiling as a starter for Lizarraga. In order to get there, he’ll need to add some strength and continue to improve both his off-speed offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After landing a few prospects when the international market opened, the Padres were thrilled to add Lizarraga on a $1 million signing bonus in late February to put a cap on what they feel was a strong 2020-21 international class. Regarded by many as the top pitching prospect out of Mexico, Lizarraga features an intriguing blend of athleticism and three pitches. Lizarraga’s fastball currently sits at 89-92 mph with solid life, and as he grows into his lean frame – he enters his debut season at 6-foot-4 and just 185 pounds – the Padres believe that fastball could reach the mid- to high-90s. To go along with the heater, Lizarraga has feel for a changeup that projects as at least average, with fade and drop. His current go-to secondary weapon is a curveball that bites hard. Lizarraga’s delivery is smooth and repeatable, and his raw athleticism is readily apparent. Combine that with a three-pitch mix, and it seems fairly clear that he’s destined for a starter’s role in the long-term. First, however, Lizarraga needs to bulk up a bit to get the most out of his fastball, while continuing to progress in developing his two offspeed weapons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his college career at Clemson, Amick transferred to Tennessee so he could play third base. He manned the hot corner all spring, slammed 23 homers and helped the Volunteers win the College World Series. His production helped him land in the second round of the 2024 Draft, where he signed for a full-slot $1.45 million. While he hit .310 with an OPS of .873 with High-A Cedar Rapids in his first full season of pro ball, oblique and shoulder injuries limited him to just 59 games for the entire season. An attempt to make up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League went poorly as Amick went 1-for-30 with 20 strikeouts. Amick’s plus raw power and ability to tap into it to drive the ball to all fields were supposed to be his calling cards as a pro. He showed some glimpses here and there during the regular season but never consistently, and the injuries didn’t help him get in sync. While he cut down his chase rate some compared to his season with Tennessee, his miss rate went up. The damage he did do came against fastballs, and he struggled to do much with breaking and offspeed stuff. It was generally thought that Amick would hit as a pro, but there was less clarity about his defensive home, and he’s yet to answer those questions. A combination of lack of range and inconsistency with his hands makes a move to first base, where he’s played some as a pro, possible. He works hard to improve his defense at the hot corner, and there’s more pressure on his power bat should he become a first baseman only.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amick spent the first two years of his college career at Clemson, barely playing as a freshman, then being stuck in a DH/first-base role once he finally got a shot to play as a sophomore. After a strong showing in the Cape Cod League, the son of former NASCAR driver Lyndon Amick transferred to Tennessee, where he hit 23 homers and helped the Volunteers win the College World Series. The Twins bought the power potential in the second round, signing him with a full-slot $1.45 million bonus and letting him get his feet wet with Single-A For Myers. With bat speed and plenty of strength, Amick’s offensive calling card entering pro ball was his plus raw power and ability to get to it to all fields. Though he can be very aggressive at the plate and often chased pitches out of the zone in college, he showed he could routinely barrel up the baseball, and the Twins were pleased during his pro debut that to see him do a better job at laying off bad secondary stuff, showing better pitch recognition than anticipated. The other question surrounding Amick is whether he will be able to stick at the hot corner, which he finally got to play with the Volunteers. Though he’s a below-average runner with fringy-to-average defensive tools, the Twins are bullish on that part of his game as well after seeing him make solid strides in his brief time with the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was already a Perez-Brewers connection considering Hedbert’s father, Robert, played for the club in 2001. The younger Perez joined Milwaukee for $700,000 out of his native Venezuela in July 2019, and after the lost pandemic season, he got off to a quick stateside start in 2021, slashing .333/.394/.575 with six homers in 32 games in the Arizona Complex League before a brief promotion to Single-A Carolina. He returned to the Mudcats for his age-19 season last year and showed some pop (15 homers) but struggled overall with a .216 average, .272 OBP and 82 wRC+. There is an obvious positive in Perez’s game in his raw power. He’s bulked up in his 5-foot-10 frame from his days playing back home, and the result has been loud exit velocities and a significant portion of his hits going for extra bases when he puts the bat on the ball. Pitch recognition and selection have been issues at this early stage, and those problems not only led to a 29.9 percent K rate in Carolina, but also have kept him from reaching the hitter’s counts that would allow him to swing away more freely. As Perez has grown out at the lower levels, he’s become progressively less toolsy overall. Once a 55 runner, he’s closer to average now and isn’t likely to be a huge stolen-base threat moving forward. The lack of speed and a weak arm have made left field his primary position, and he’ll face a higher offensive threshold there. There are worse places to start than with plus raw slugging ability, and considering Perez will still only be 20 for the entire upcoming season, he has time to improve his overall approach at the dish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of six-year Major Leaguer Robert Perez signed with the Brewers -- for whom his father played briefly in 2001 -- for $700,000 out of Venezuela in July 2019. It hasn’t taken Perez long to stand out in an organization getting more loaded with outfielders by the year. In 2021, the left-handed slugger slashed .333/.394/.474 with six homers over 32 games in the Arizona Complex League and earned a bump to Low-A Carolina in his age-18 season. Full-season pitchers were able to keep him much more off-balance (25 strikeouts in 65 PA), thus ending Perez’s 2021 on a sour note. An alternate training site participant at just 17 in 2020, Perez struggled with pitch selection and found himself down in a lot of counts at Carolina, leading him to fight off pitches instead of putting good swings on hittable offerings. He is capable of making good strong contact, and he exhibits a good amount of raw power from a bulky 5-foot-10 frame. It plays in games as well, as he showed in Arizona. The Brewers are hopeful that the Carolina bumps are growing pains because if it does come together, Perez still has the chance to be an average hitter at the top level with the way he can pound the ball on contact. Perez looked toolsier upon signing, but as his body has matured, his power remains his only plus skill. His speed and fielding ability are above-average now, though they could grade downward if he continues to prioritize strength, and his arm isn’t seen as much of a weapon these days. While he has years of development ahead of him, Perez is trending toward becoming a power bat in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prince Fielder moved fast through the Brewers’ Minor League system thanks to a mix of talent and pedigree; he knew his way around professional baseball because he grew up in the game. Now along comes another left-handed hitter with eye-popping tools and impressive poise for his age in Perez, whose father, Robert Perez, wasn’t a player the caliber of Cecil Fielder but nonetheless logged six seasons in the Major Leagues with five different teams including the Brewers in 2001. Hedbert Perez received the second-highest bonus ($700,000) among players signed by Milwaukee during the 2019-20 international period and immediately made an impact during a batting practice session in Milwaukee, launching a series of long home runs to Fielder’s former landing spots before departing for that fall’s instructional league. Despite being denied his official pro debut in 2020, Perez continued to impress with tools on both sides of the ball. At 17 years old he was the youngest player at the Brewers’ alternate training site, getting experience against far more experienced pitchers and some of the Brewers’ tough left-handed pitching prospects like Antoine Kelly and Aaron Ashby. Perez finished the year in the instructional league, then once again was the youngest player in the room when the Brewers included him among 15 players invited to their Minor League mini-camp at the start of Spring Training. Perez has a quick, compact left-handed swing and advanced plate discipline for his age combined with the raw power. In the field, he has an arm for the corners but the speed and instincts to play center field. The Brewers, who prioritize up-the-middle defenders, believe he will stick in center. If his tools and poise lead to production in his long-awaited pro debut, then Perez could continue to rise to the top of the Brewers’ prospect list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Robert Perez, an outfielder who played six Major League seasons (1994-2001) with five different teams, Hedbert Perez received the second-highest bonus ($700,000) among players signed by Milwaukee during the 2019-20 international period after he impressed scouts with his athleticism, tools and advanced feel for the game as a Venezuelan amateur. The Brewers brought him to Miller Park for batting practice after he signed, and Perez made the most of the opportunity by hitting some long, big league-esque home runs before opening even more eyes during instructional league. Across-the-board tools highlight Perez’s impressive profile and fuel his impact potential on both sides of the ball. One of the better pure hitters in his class, Perez has a pretty swing for a player his age, combining bat speed and feel for the barrel with a quick, compact left-handed stroke. Those qualities, along with his discerning eye, have led scouts to project Perez as a future above-average hitter, and the fact that he already shows above-average raw power as a teenager makes it easy to dream on his offensive ceiling. More than just a promising young hitter, Perez has the potential to remain in center field long term with his blend of athleticism, plus speed and range, and it certainly doesn’t hurt that he also has great instincts and gets good jumps. His accurate, above-average arm is a weapon up the middle and qualifies him to play either outfield corner. Overall, Perez has one of the highest ceilings in the Brewers’ system and should offer a glimpse of that potential when makes his highly anticipated debut in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players the Dodgers signed in their 2018-19 international class, Rodriguez turned pro for $15,000 out of Mexico. The pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021 and he spent all but one game of his first three seasons in Rookie ball. Finally turned loose in full-season ball at age 22 last year, he posted a 3.38 ERA between two Class A stops and the best strikeout (33 percent), strikeout minus walk (25 percent) and swinging strike (20 percent) rates in the system (minimum: 90 innings). Rodriguez features the best changeup among Dodger farmhands, a low-80s cambio with tremendous fade and some depth as well. He throws both two-seam and four-seam fastballs, ranging from 92-95 mph and topping out at 97, with ordinary life. Refining his tight low-80s slider was a point of emphasis in 2024, and he also can mix in an upper-70s curveball. Though he's a lanky 6-foot-6, Rodriguez repeats his mechanics well enough to provide consistent strikes. He creates 7+ feet of extension with his delivery, which enables his pitches to get on hitters much more quickly than expected. He hasn't been able to add much strength since turning pro, and if he can, his stuff could kick up and enhance his chances of becoming a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $650,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period, Rodriguez made a very strong first impression during his pro debut that year in the Dominican Summer League. The outfielder led the circuit in home runs (13) and RBIs (49), finishing with a .966 OPS. He wasn’t quite as productive during his debut stateside in the Florida Complex League in 2023 (.737 OPS), but he still showed off some offensive tools that could be building blocks for a better future. The key to success for Rodriguez moving forward will be his ability to tap into his easily plus raw power. He’s shown to date that he can get to it with a willingness to take walks and get to better counts. It was encouraging that he managed his strikeouts well in the FCL as well, but there’s still work to do on his plate discipline and swing decisions with cutting down on his tendency to chase. Developing an ability to make adjustments, especially as the pitching gets better as he moves up, will be important. The other essential ingredient for Rodriguez is for him to stay on top of his body and conditioning. He’s already big, physical and slowing down, so he’s at best limited to an outfield corner. He mostly played right in the FCL, but it remains to be seen if he can stay there, and he also got some reps at first base in 2023. Wherever he goes defensively, it’s his power bat that will enable him to climb the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If Dominican Summer League performance is any indication of future success, the Twins might have a bumper crop of talent from their 2022 international signing period class. Top bonus getters Yasser Mercedes and Bryan Acuña performed well, and so did Rodriguez, who signed when the period opened for $650,000. The teenage outfielder led the DSL in home runs and RBIs while finishing fourth in slugging percentage. There’s no question about Rodriguez’s raw power, and he might have more of that than anyone in the system, with perhaps the exception of Matt Wallner. The only question is how much he’ll be able to tap into it as he progresses. He clearly did a fine job of that in his pro debut and there’s a willingness to draw walks, but he is going to have to improve his swing decisions, especially as he sees better breaking stuff. Getting him to focus on punishing pitches over the plate and not expanding the zone will be a key developmental piece. Rodriguez is big and physical and lacks the speed or instincts to play center field. He spent most of his time in right during his debut in deference to Mercedes, and he could fit the profile of a power-hitting corner outfielder well, with the Twins likely to keep giving him reps in center for now to help him work on his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Rodríguez has vaulted to the head of the White Sox's 2017-18 international class. He surprised scouts with his power in his 2019 U.S. debut, slugging .505 and placing sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League with nine homers in 44 games. He continued to impress during his first taste of full-season ball in 2021, batting .301/.338/.469 and reaching Double-A at age 20. Not physically imposing at 5-foot-11 and 175 pounds, Rodríguez has a quick right-handed swing and deceptive strength that give him solid raw power to his pull side. It wasn't quite as evident in games last year, when he made more ground-ball contact than he had in the past, but he has a knack for driving the ball out of the park when he launches it to left field. He'll make some curious swing decisions at times, but he shows some feel for using the entire field and shortening his stroke with two strikes. A solid runner, Rodríguez is aggressive on the basepaths and led Sox farmhands with 30 steals and 41 attempts last season. He has solid arm strength but just average range at shortstop, where he needs more consistency. Club officials believe he makes enough plays to stay at short, but he might be better suited for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most promising member of Chicago's 2017-18 international class, Rodríguez signed for just $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He showed surprising power in his 2019 U.S. debut, slugging .505 and finishing sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League with nine homers in 44 games. He also displayed the best athleticism among the infielders whom the White Sox brought to instructional league last fall. While he's not physically imposing, Rodríguez has a quick right-handed stroke and deceptive strength that give him solid raw power to his pull side. To maximize his offensive potential, he'll need to calm down an overly aggressive approach and make better swing decisions when facing more advanced pitchers. Though most of his present power goes to his pull side, he does show some feel for using the entire field. Rodríguez lacks a true plus tool but could wind up as average across the board. With average speed, range and arm strength, he's likely best suited for second base. The White Sox think he makes enough plays to remain at shortstop and also have deployed him at third base and right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gerardo clocked a 102-mph throw from the outfield as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, leading the Marlins to wonder if they should make him a full-time pitcher, but they ultimately decided to sign him as an outfielder. They spread their 2022 international bonus pool money around and gave 13 players six-figure bonuses, including $180,000 for Gerardo. He opened eyes by slamming nine homers in his first full month in the Dominican Summer League and finished third on the Rookie-level circuit with 11 in 50 games. Not only does the righty-hitting Gerardo feature more bat speed and present strength than players his age, but he also has room to add more muscle to his 6-foot-1 frame. The question is how he'll fare against better quality pitching because he's extremely aggressive. He looks to pull and launch almost every pitch he sees, and his 30 percent strikeout rate in the DSL underscores his need to develop a better approach. More than just a masher, Gerardo has some of the best all-around tools in the system. He presently has solid speed and could get quicker once he's physically mature. His top-of-the-scale arm strength is well-suited for right field, where he spent the majority of his pro debut, and his defensive instincts give him a chance to play center as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Hall of Famer Jeff Kent, Kaeden has the same profile as an offensive-minded infielder who fits best at second base. He was a part-time player for most of this first two years at Texas A&M before an injury to first-round pick Braden Montgomery thrust him into the lineup during the 2024 NCAA tournament, and Kent provided a grand slam in the super regionals before hitting .417 in the College World Series. He started at shortstop for the Aggies as junior, then went in the third round and struggled during an aggressive pro debut assignment to High-A. Kent's best attributes are his high baseball IQ, quality left-handed swing and penchant for making line-drive contact. He tries to do much at the plate at times and got too more chase- and pull-happy in High-A, though he still put balls in play fairly easily. He could enhance his offensive profile if he drove more balls in the air and tapped into more of his 15-20 homer potential. Kent makes up for below-average speed with advanced instincts on the bases and in the field. Though the Yankees will give him every chance to stay at shortstop, his fringy range and average arm are better suited for second base. He's at least an average defender at the keystone and his internal clock allows his arm to play up enough that he may be able to handle third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coret was already physically advanced when the Rays signed him out of the Dominican Republic in January for $1.6 million. The ninth-ranked prospect in a 2025 international amateur class headlined by Japanese ace Roki Sasaki, Coret stood 6-foot-4 and weighed in at 187 pounds as a 17-year-old. He was also regarded well for his mental maturity, approaching the game with passion and dedication and somewhat of an edge despite his prospect status. But the most intriguing thing about Coret is his talent in every phase of the game. Prospects like him are signed so young -- with so much time and development standing between them and even the Minors, much less the Majors -- that they are notoriously difficult to project. Coret has standout physical tools across the board, though, so there is understandable excitement as he enters Tampa Bay’s system. He clocked in at 6.6 seconds in the 60-yard dash. His above-average bat speed generated exit velocities up to 104 mph, giving him a chance for top-of-the-scale power as he fills out his frame, and he’s shown signs of a discerning eye at the plate. He has a strong arm, chucking 96 mph throws from the outfield, and he has the range and instincts to be a plus defender in center field. His ceiling is undeniable, but it will take time and patience to see if he can reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray chose baseball over the chance to be a Division I quarterback, thinking he had more of a future on the mound. Raw but electric, the athletic right-hander excited scouts with what he could potentially become once he left the gridiron behind. The Angels' scouting department was definitely in that camp, giving him third-round money -- a bonus of $1.25 million -- to sign the North Carolina high schooler as a fifth-rounder in the 2025 Draft. With tremendous arm speed, Gray can light up radar guns with his fastball up to 98 mph, sitting in the 92-96 range with sink. He featured an upper-70s sweeper of a slider in high school, often having trouble harnessing it, and leading some to think his power profile would be better suited for a tighter, harder slide piece in the future. Surprisingly, he has some feel for an 80 mph changeup with some fade. Gray’s athleticism helps him drive down the mound, but his mechanics are rarely in sync and he has trouble repeating his delivery, leading to poor control and command. This is a bit of a lottery ticket that might take extra time to cash in, but the payout could be huge eventually.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top seven bonuses the Twins handed out at the start of the 2025 international signing period were all given to hitters. You have to go down to a tie (with another bat) for eighth to find Castellanos, who signed in January of that year for $247,500. He opened a lot of eyes with a sizzling Dominican Summer League debut, where he finished with a 2.79 ERA, .215 batting average against, 1.10 WHIP and 11.2 K/9 rate over 29 innings. If Castellanos fit the 6-foot-3 projectable mold, he might be considered the best pitching prospect in the DSL. The 5-foot-10 right-hander was still just 16 when he got things going and showed off an exciting four-pitch mix at times during his debut. His fastball currently sits in the low 90s, occasionally bumping up to 95-96, but it plays up because of its life and deception, getting some swing-and-miss. His sweeper is his best pitch with huge horizontal break, an offering that produced a 63-percent miss rate in the DSL. He also has shorter and harder cutter to go along with an effective changeup. While Castellanos threw a good amount of strikes, his in-zone rates weren’t great, with a lot of that swing-and-miss coming from chasing that sweeper out of the zone. He’s athletic on the mound, and if he can show he can get his fastball to sit in the 94-95 mph range, he has a solid starting pitcher package.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Barrios for $1 million out of Venezuela in January 2021, but a fellow Venezuelan of the same age turned out to be the biggest prospect in that international class for Milwaukee: Jackson Chourio. While Chourio rocketed to the Majors, Barrios advanced one level per season from the Dominican Summer League in 2021 to High-A ball in ‘24. As they began a summer sell-off in July, the Rays sent starter Aaron Civale to the Brewers and landed Barrios in the one-for-one swap. Barrios’ greatest strength is his defense. He’s a no-doubt shortstop, grading out in the Rays’ system behind only top prospect Carson Williams. His movements are smooth and fluid, his instincts are impressive for his age and his actions are clean. He also has a strong arm, giving him the ability to make most every throw, including many from deep in the hole. The Brewers pushed the 6-foot shortstop to High-A Wisconsin despite subpar results in Single-A primarily to let him play the position every day, and he proved to be more than up for the challenge in the dirt. Barrios uses his speed well on the bases, swiping 90 bags in his first four seasons while only being caught 18 times. He gave up switch-hitting after the 2022 season and didn’t hit much in the Carolina League the next year, but he got off to a hot start with High-A Wisconsin in 2024 by slapping the ball around the field for singles and the occasional double. Barrios doesn’t swing and miss much, with a roughly 13 percent strikeout rate in the Minors, and he can hit with two strikes. So if he improves his pitch selection to key in on the stuff he can do damage against, he could hit for a decent average as a bottom-of-the-order hitter with some baserunning value and plus-plus defense at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals spent nearly their entire international signing bonus on Hernandez in July 2017, when they signed him for $200,000. He made his full-season debut in Single-A Columbia in ‘21 and was solid there, but his real offensive breakout came as a 21-year-old in 2022. Hernandez slashed .284/.347/.407 between High-A and Double-A, with nine homers and 40 stolen bases. His defense was solid enough to have Kansas City add him to the 40-man roster in the offseason to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. Hernandez suffered an unfortunate injury at the beginning of his first big league Spring Training, when he dislocated his right shoulder diving for a ball in center field, delaying his season until mid-June Hernandez is an elite athlete with plus-plus speed and stellar defense in the outfield. He hits the ball on the ground a lot, but he’s able to pick up base hits out of it with his speed. Hernandez is still learning the strike zone and what pitches he can handle, but he’s worked on elevating the ball more. He walked at a decent clip in 2021, but that number dropped in ‘22. Hernandez hit nine homers in 2022 and won’t be a power threat, but he could unlock more if he adds strength to his frame. Hernandez still needs more time to develop his bat in the Minors, but he’ll be a defensive depth option for the Royals soon. His glove gives him a floor as a defensive replacement and runner. If he can improve more with his offense, he could be a leadoff candidate in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Musgrove played both ways at the NAIA program at the University of Mobile, and in his three years with the Rams, he finished with a .398/.505/.668 line over 489 plate appearances and a 4.70 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 99 2/3 innings. The Padres took him in the seventh round in 2023, signing him for just below slot at $175,000, and initially intended to keep him on a two-way path. However, Musgrove underwent Tommy John surgery soon after signing and didn’t appear in a game for a San Diego affiliate until April 2025, by that time cementing his place as a pitcher-only. He managed 20 innings for Single-A Lake Elsinore (striking out 26 in that span) before continuing to build up with six more appearances in the Arizona Fall League. The 6-foot-3 right-hander can run his fastball up to triple-digits, and he has a few of them – a four-seamer with good riding action up in the zone and a sinker that can equally come in the 97-99 mph range over shorter outings with more armside run. He also possesses a cutter for another fastball look. Musgrove pitches with upwards of seven feet of extension, shortening the decision window further for hitters. He can spin a mid-80s sweeper with impressive horizontal break and can mix in another slider with more vertical drop and a slower curveball in the low-80s. After dropping a splitter, he’s working on a rarely thrown changeup. Dating back to his days as a collegiate center fielder, Musgrove has athleticism to work with on the mound but is still finding his command post-surgery. He’s come back stronger though and with enough velocity to garner attention across the game in his initial relief looks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Wideman was a four-year starting center at Clemson and played basketball in multiple countries overseas, including Spain where his son Ryan was born. The younger Wideman was a standout for two years at Georgia Highlands JC but went undrafted before heading to Western Kentucky, where he was the Conference USA Player of the Year in 2025. He notched 36 extra-base hits and 45 steals in 60 games for the Hilltoppers, becoming the first Division I player to eclipse 35 and 45 in those categories since 2001. The Padres selected Wideman in the third round, signed him for below slot at $650,000 and gave him 26 games at Single-A Lake Elsinore. Standing at 6-foot-4, Wideman was one of the most physical players in his Draft class and instantly became one of the most athletic in the San Diego system. He can show plus-plus speed and uses his size to display plus raw power from the right side. He can go and get balls in the gaps from center field with those wheels, and tellingly, the Padres only played him in the middle of the grass after the Draft. With average arm strength, he could be a fit anywhere in the outfield. But so much will come down to his hitting mechanics and approach. Wideman chased out of the zone a ton in his one season at the Division I level, and there were only slight improvements during his time in the California League. He typically uses a giant leg kick to get going – though he’ll sometimes tamp it down – and can chop at the ball, leading to a lot of groundball contact that dulls his power. The Padres have hopes they can alter Wideman’s directionality, and there’s everyday upside if he can improve that and his selectivity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly bounced around a bit as an amateur, going from a two-way high school standout in Northern California to starting his college career at Texas A&M. After a redshirt year, he moved to McLennan Community College and played both ways, then was on the move again, this time to Arizona State as a pitcher only. He missed a bunch of bats as a reliever, helping him land in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, and he headed up to High-A to get his feet wet professionally. He capped things off by striking out the side to get the save that gave Everett a Northwest League championship. The 6-foot-4 Kelly is strong and physical and comes at hitters largely with a two-pitch mix and a funky delivery. His four-seam fastball topped out at 99 mph in college, and it misses bats thanks to its carry up in the zone. He backs it up with his 79-84 mph slider that can have good depth and bite to it at times, a breaking ball that could be at least above average if he can find the strike zone with it more. He had a changeup for lefties on occasion at ASU, but he might not need it, and there was some talk of him bringing a two-seamer he used to feature back into his repertoire. Kelly’s unusual mechanics come with a ton of effort and a low three-quarters arm slot and cross-body delivery. But he tends to get down the mound well and throw a decent amount of strikes. If he can be around the zone enough, especially with his slider, it’s not out of the question to see him in high-leverage relief situations in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A late addition to Chicago's 2018-19 international class, Sanchez signed for $80,000 out of Venezuela. He made his U.S. debut in 2021 at age 19, earning a promotion to Low-A after just a month in Rookie ball. He has one of the higher ceilings among White Sox position prospects, though he'll also need plenty of development time. Sanchez's most noticeable tool is his plus-plus speed, which he used to swipe 17 bases in 18 attempts over 53 games last year. After employing a patient, contact-oriented approach in his 2019 pro debut, he got much more pull-conscious and launch-happy last year. A right-handed hitter, he needs to make better swing decisions, focus on getting on base and let his modest home run power come naturally. Sanchez plays with constant energy and is arguably the best infield defender among White Sox farmhands. He's extremely reliable and made just three errors in 70 games at shortstop last season, a remarkable performance for a shortstop. He has the actions, quickness and plus arm to remain at short and the tools to play all over the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If ever there was an example that it's not always a straight path to pro ball, it’s Craig. He started things out at Tyler JC in Texas in 2020, went to Texas A&M and ended up redshirting in '21, returned to Tyler in '22, then spent three years pitching out of Baylor's bullpen. He was virtually unhittable in his final season, finishing with a 0.56 ERA, .124 batting average against and an absurd 51/3 K/BB ratio in 32 innings. The Phillies made him a very intriguing money-saving senior sign in the fifth round, landing him for just under $200,000. A 6-foot-5 right-hander, Craig didn't allow an extra-base hit all spring before being drafted, and he has his wipeout slider to thank. He throws it in the mid 80s and it touches 88 mph with huge sweep and some depth. Opponents managed to hit just .111 with 43 strikeouts against the pitch. It pairs well with his 93-95 mph fastball that reaches 97, featuring some carry and armside run in the opposite direction of his slide piece. He's working on adding a two-seamer that will play off those offerings. A come-at-you reliever who works only out of the stretch, Craig filled the zone with his two pitches coming from a high release point. He's already 24, but he’s expected to move quickly, with the Phillies thinking he could progress in an Orion Kerkering kind of way, potentially making it to the big leagues in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for a mere $45,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Luciano quickly has become one of the most intriguing players in Houston's 2022 international class. He earned Rookie-level Dominican Summer League All-Star honors in his pro debut, then ranked second in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League with 10 homers after coming to the United States last summer. He smokes balls harder than most teenagers, already producing average exit velocities by big league standards and maxing out at 110 mph. Luciano's power is his most obvious tool, as he not only hits balls hard from the right side of the plate but also has a penchant for driving them in the air to his pull side, giving him at least 25-30 homer upside. Though he batted just .238 in his first two pro seasons, the Astros are encouraged by his bat-to-ball skills. His swing got out of whack and he was making too much suboptimal contact in the first half of the 2024, so Houston had him spent a month on the development list to get back on track. Heftier than his listed 170 pounds, Luciano currently has fringy speed and will have to watch his conditioning so he doesn't lose his quickness and limit his defensive options. Houston would like to see him get leaner and more athletic to enhance his chances of sticking at third base, where he has average-to-solid arm strength. Right field would be Plan B if he slows down and he saw action there last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Quebec native, Langevin came to the United States for college ball at Wabash Valley (Ill.) Community College before transferring to Louisiana-Lafayette his junior year. He struck out the world there, maintaining a nearly 40 percent strikeout rate. The metrics on his fastball in particular were part of the reason the Royals took Langevin in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for $597,500. It’s no secret that Langevin’s fastball is what makes him stand out. It’s a unique pitch that has baffled hitters so far, although not because of velocity -- it sits 92-96 mph. The pitch has extremely high spin rates and features plenty of ride and run from a lower vertical approach angle. Langevin’s deceptive delivery definitely helps the pitch play up too, as does his quick arm. His secondaries are fringe average at best, as he didn’t really need or use them in college, so that will be a focus for him in his first pro season. The slider has some sweeping action to it, but it varies in speed and he needs to work on landing it in the zone. He has a feel for a changeup but needs to develop it more. If it translates to results in pro ball, Langevin’s fastball could dominate, and he could move quickly as a reliever. Officials love his makeup and fiery competitiveness on the mound. He’s a one-trick pitcher right now, though, and needs to improve his secondaries and control to reach his ceiling as a potential back-end bullpen arm. Langevin will likely begin his pro career at High-A in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knipp spent most of his time over his time at Campbell University as a catcher, becoming the starter and putting up big numbers at the plate in 2024. He also returned to the mound to make four relief appearances that year, showing off tremendous arm strength that intrigued several teams. The Mariners initially announced him as a two-way player when taking him in the sixth round of the 2024 Draft, but it seemed like they were inclined to have him focus on the mound only. He didn’t make much progress as elbow trouble in Spring Training resulted in Tommy John surgery, and he missed the 2025 season. Not only is Knipp coming back to pitch at some point in 2026, the Mariners have decided to let him also get at-bats as a DH after seeing him swing it well last spring, taking since-traded prospect Jurrangelo Cijntje deep twice. As a hitter, he’s strength over bat speed with raw power and questions about him making enough contact to get to it. On the mound, he had been up to 96 mph with his fastball last spring, showing good ride and induced vertical break on the pitch to go along with an interesting sweepy 84-85 mph slider. It will be interesting to see how long the Mariners conduct this two-way experiment, with Knipp in his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels may have found a real sleeper in Quintero, whom they signed at the start of the 2024 international signing period for just $25,000 out of Panama. He immediately established himself as one of the best catch-and-throw backstops in the system, first in the Dominican Summer League after signing in a year truncated by a broken hamate, and then when he came stateside in 2025, helping the Angels win the Arizona Complex League championship. Following that, he moved up to Single-A Inland Empire to play a part in the 66ers’ playoff run. Quintero is always going to lead with his glove. Compact at 5-foot-8, he’s agile behind the dish with excellent receiving and blocking skills. His arm is at least plus, using its strength and accuracy to throw out 49 percent of potential basestealers across both stops in 2025. Playing all of 2026 at age 19, Quintero does have some offensive qualities to work with. He has a line-drive approach to all fields and his exit velocity took a nice step forward last year. He doesn’t strike out much, but he needs to cut down on his chase to become a more complete hitter. That will determine his ultimate ceiling because his defensive work might be special enough to carry him to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners took Beilenson as a money-saving senior sign in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft, with his $25,000 under-slot bonus helping pay to sign Ryan Sloan. But Beilenson had success in college, especially once he moved to Duke after three years at Brown, saving 12 games for the Blue Devils while getting a pair of graduate degrees. While he was old for the High-A level where he began his first full season of pro ball, he pitched well enough to earn a promotion to Double-A after 20 appearances, putting him on the prospect map. Now 26, Beilenson is more a sum-of-his-parts kind of pitcher than a reliever who is going to blow hitters away. He has a foundation of three pitches but manipulates them into different shapes to give him a repertoire of as many as five. He’ll throw both a four- and a two-seam fastball, averaging around 93 mph. His best pitch is his kick-change that has splitter-like action to it. He’ll throw both a sweeper and a shorter, harder slider around 81 mph with cutter-like action. Beilenson can throw a ton of strikes with all his offerings, but it’s control over command, and he got hit more once he got to Double-A. If he can find a bit more consistency from one outing to the next, he could be knocking on the door to a big league bullpen job.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres were considered one of the three finalists for 2025’s top international prospect Roki Sasaki, only to see the Japanese right-hander sign with the NL West rival Dodgers. San Diego still signed three members of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects in Carlos Alvarez, Deivid Coronil and Jhoan De La Cruz but managed to have international pool money left over come October when it signed Su for $775,000. The Taiwanese right-hander had most recently pitched for Chinese Taipei in the 18U World Cup in Japan in September, when he struck out 14 batters and held opposing batters to a .192 average in 7 1/3 innings. Drawing comparisons to fellow past top international signing Humberto Cruz, Su is super projectable at 6-foot-1 and a rail-thin 150 pounds at the time of signing. His fastball works 89-94 mph right now, but there is ample room for that velocity to jump as he adds strength within the Padres development program. He showed good feel for spin with a pair of breakers in his upper-70s curveball and 79-83 mph slider in the World Cup, and there were the makings of a decent changeup that he can sell well out of the hand, though it was a distant fourth offering in terms of usage. Because he isn’t overthrowing, Su has a natural feel for throwing strikes, and that will aid his starting chances as he moves stateside. Maintaining that control while adding a few ticks of velocity will be key in the early years of his career, but at a time when the farm system needs depth after years of aggressive trades, the Padres are excited to add Su to their pitching depth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's got a close look at Diaz as a local amateur when he played at Acalanes HS (Calif.) and liked what they saw back then, leading to his selection by the club years later coming out of Vanderbilt in the eighth round of the 2024 MLB Draft. He's been on a steady climb through the system since joining the organization. Jumping from Single-A Stockton to High-A Lansing in 2025, he made another leap early on in '26 with a promotion from High-A to Double-A Midland after a strong performance in first 29 games with the Lugnuts. Diaz stands out at the plate for his impressive bat-to-ball skills and overall patience in the batter's box. That has translated to a low strikeout rate and solid on-base numbers early in his pro career. The contact skills help mitigate the lack of power he's shown thus far, though he has increased his frequency of extra-base hits this season, which gives some hope that there is some more pop in that bat to unlock. The A's raised some eyebrows when they decided to utilize Diaz, primarily a third baseman in college, as a catcher, a position he hadn't played since high school. So far, that decision is looking great as he's demonstrated clean mechanics behind the dish along with a strong arm and ability to control the run game. Still showing off his versatility by getting some time at third, second and even some first base, Diaz is quickly emerging as an intriguing super-utility player with enough tools to eventually make a big league impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marquis Grissom was a two-time All-Star and four-time Gold Glover across his 17 seasons in the Majors. His son headed to Georgia Tech to make it as a starting pitcher but didn’t produce high-quality results, leading to him being taken by the Nationals (the same organized that selected his dad as an Expo in 1988) in the 13th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2022. He’s been a reliever in the Washington system ever since and a dominant one at that. Grissom split 2024 between High-A Wilmington and Double-A Harrisburg, finishing with a 2.21 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 56 strikeouts in 53 innings. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s best pitch is easily his 82-85 mph changeup. It gets roughly 10 mph separation off Grissom’s 92-95 mph fastball and also fades incredibly well to the armside, holding lefties at bat. Even right-handed hitters whiff on 49 percent of their swings against the changeup last season, per Synergy Sports. The fastball has just average life but can touch 96 when Grissom really needs it. A mid-80s slider gives him a breaker with gloveside action. Grissom struggled with strikes over longer outings as a collegiate starter but has reined that in as a pro. He can use the fastball to steal early strikes and then put batters away by getting them to chase over and over with the changeup. More fastball velocity would help his case to be a high-leverage reliever, but the cambio alone should help him punch his ticket to working out of an MLB bullpen. Considering when he was drafted, he might have more runway of development than a typical college relief arm anyways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mullins ranked among the best high school left-handers in the 2019 Draft but had elbow problems that spring that persisted through his three seasons at Auburn, where he worked just 53 1/3 innings before having Tommy John surgery in 2022. A 12th-round pick that July, he posted some of the best numbers (2.21 ERA, .177 opponent average, 30 percent strikeout rate) in the Red Sox system last year despite missing three weeks with shoulder fatigue in May. Boston gambled by not adding him to its 40-man roster in November and was glad that he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft without getting taken. Mullins has one of the better bat-missing fastballs among Red Sox farmhands, thanks to tremendous carry that helps it play significantly better than its 91-95 mph velocity. While his low-80s slider can feature big sweep and grade as a plus pitch at its best, it was more of an average offering last year. His sinking low-80s changeup is similarly effective, and he also has begun working on a cutter with similar velocity. There's a lot going on in Mullins' delivery, which features a big leg kick, a twist that hides the ball behind him and a low release point. All of that provides deception but hampers his ability to find the zone, and he never has demonstrated better than fringy control or command. He could be a No. 4 starter if his secondary pitches and strikes improve, and he may be of more immediate big league help as a multi-inning lefty out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After one year in the George Mason bullpen, Salina – a native of Rochester, N.Y. – moved closer to home with a transfer within the Atlantic 10 to St. Bonaventure ahead of the 2024 season. He pitched out of the Bonnies rotation in his first spring and became the team’s No. 1 starter as a junior. His time atop the depth chart didn’t last long; he struck out 26 batters over 17 1/3 innings in his first four starts but suffered an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in April 2025. The Padres selected him in the fourth round and signed him for slot value at $571,500. The 6-foot-1 righty was showing steady gains with his fastball velocity during his days as a collegian and was sitting 94-96 with his heater as a junior, even touching as high as 102 mph. He also got excellent extension that made the fastball play better than the heat alone and generate a healthy amount of whiffs. His mid-80s slider shows short, hard break and looks like an absolute weapon against fellow righties. There was some feel for an upper-80s changeup, but he’ll need a better option against lefties in the pros. Salina pitches exclusively out of the stretch and used a fair amount of effort late in his delivery to squeeze that velocity. That said, he was showing a little better control before TJ, and the Padres are hopeful that a year of recovery and rehab may only make him stronger, as can happen for pitchers after the elbow procedure. Salina should be an interesting arm with upside when he debuts in the San Diego system in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lambert didn’t stay long at any one location as a collegian, moving from North Iowa Area CC to Missouri State to Oklahoma between 2022 and '24. He also worked as a closer in the MLB Draft League ahead of his Draft eligibility in 2024. The Mets took him in the eighth round that July and signed him for below slot at $172,500, but it didn’t take long for Lambert to look like a mid-round steal. He moved quickly through High-A Brooklyn after striking out 17 in eight innings there to begin 2025 and spent the rest of the season with Double-A Binghamton, finishing with a 1.62 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 50 innings between both spots. His 39.5 percent strikeout rate was fifth-highest among 1,383 Minor Leaguers with at least 50 innings last season. Lambert describes himself as “an adrenaline guy,” and it isn’t hard to see why. Working exclusively out of the stretch, he throws a 95-98 mph four-seamer with a ton of spin and carry that’s capable of touching triple digits. The heater had a 38 percent whiff rate in 2025, giving it the swing-and-miss tendencies of a breaking ball rather than a primary pitch. When the fastball is that good, you don’t need a ton of secondaries, and Lambert only has one: an 86-88 mph slider that breaks sharply downward and keeps batters from looking for the high four-seam alone. Lambert’s lack of a third pitch leads to predictable left-right splits, but opposite-side bats swing through their fair share of heaters and sliders too. The former Sooners reliever has the look and walk rates of a grip-it-and-rip-it reliever, and no one will confuse him for a pinpoint artist anytime soon. But with two absolute MLB-quality weapons, Lambert has high-leverage upside and could get important outs in Queens.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Signed for $300,000 in January 2021, Perez toiled away in relative anonymity for two summers in the Dominican Summer League. He opened some eyes in his first Spring Training stateside in 2023 and held his own with a jump to full-season Fresno, albeit without much offensive impact. The Rockies sent him back to Single-A to start the 2024 season and some of that impact started showing up, which earned him a late nudge up to High-A Spokane, where he played shortstop for a championship-winning team. Perez is a left-handed hitter who is gradually and continually adding strength. He’s considerably bigger than his listed height and weight, with team officials thinking he’s closer to 6-foot-4 and 210 pounds now. The left-handed hitter has a strong offensive foundation built on making a ton of contact, and despite chasing too much, he rarely strikes out. There’s confidence the combination of that added strength and a little more refinement in his approach will lead to a greater power output after he took a big step forward by hitting 10 homers in 2024. An average runner, Perez can steal a base. And even at his size, he moves very well on the dirt defensively. There is conviction internally that he can stay at short for the long term, but if the impact at the plate keeps coming, he could profile well even if he has to move to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners went shopping for hard-throwing senior signs on Day 2 of the 2024 Draft and may have found a couple of potential big league bullpen pieces in Hunter Cranton and Moore. Moore bounced from Danville Community College to Menlo College in the NAIA ranks to Oregon for his final collegiate season at age 24. He brought a ton of velocity to the system and to Single-A Modesto for his pro debut after signing in the seventh round, posting four shutout relief innings in the Nuts’ championship run. Moore is all about power coming from his enormous 6-foot-6 frame. His fastball averaged around 96-97 mph at Oregon, and after seeing him hitting 101 on pull-downs in early pitching camp, the Mariners think he could sit in the 99 mph range out of the bullpen. He can also really spin his firm 82-85 mph sweeper and he has a firm 85-88 mph changeup, though it’s unclear if feel for it will be there long term. That won’t matter if Moore can find a way to limit the walks just a little bit. He does not have a great record of strike-throwing, with a career 4.9 BB/9 rate at Menlo and Oregon combined. He’ll need to be tested quickly at the upper levels given his age, but the physical talents are too impressive to ignore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez left Cuba in 2024 but took a while to get cleared by Major League Baseball, so he didn't turn pro until January. He signed for $900,000, the second-highest bonus in the Cubs' 2026 international class. He stands out with his all-around ability and high baseball IQ. A switch-hitter, Martinez has a slight 5-foot-10 build that seems built more for contact than profile. While he does focus on lining balls to all fields and getting on base, he also hits balls surprisingly hard for his size. He won't be a slugger but could provide 15 homers per season once he gets stronger. Martinez has quick-twitch athleticism and plus speed that serves him well on the bases and in the field. He has good actions and solid arm strength at shortstop, where he should have no difficulty remaining. He also earns praise for his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Munoz joined the Mariners during the 2019-20 international signing period for $195,000, then was among the many impacted by COVID interrupting the following season, which prevented him from pitching competitively until an assignment to the Dominican Summer League, where he spent 2021-22. The first year was inconsistent, but he rebounded in the second and made the midseason All-Star team. A projectable righty with room to keep adding strength, Munoz is another arm that Seattle’s player development staff has been banging the drum on. He’s up to the mid-90s on his fastball with decent arm-side run and above-average hop. He’s also shown flashes of a plus slider that generated a ton of whiffs and strikeouts with. It’ll probably need more depth as he progresses, but, so far, he commands it better than the heater. Now it’s a matter of if he can develop a third pitch and remain a starter, because there were a lot of positive signs with his strike throwing. It’s a changeup right now, but he doesn’t throw it often because of how good the other two have been. If he does go down a relief road, his path to the Majors could be accelerated.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Growing up in a suburb of Montreal, Pitre admitted he was “kind of an outlier” in one sense: He never played hockey. The Quebec native preferred soccer and, of course, baseball. Specifically, he loved hitting. He played travel ball as a teenager, his first time playing in the United States, and starred on Canadian provincial teams before playing for the National Junior Team. That made him Quebec’s top position player prospect in 2021, but the undersized infielder -- he said he weighed 130 pounds in high school -- needed an opportunity to grow in college. He learned English in Ontario during the pandemic and wound up playing at Kentucky, despite having never visited the campus, where he eventually turned into the Rays’ second-round pick in the 2024 Draft. Pitre went straight to Single-A Charleston to make his professional debut, and he was as advertised there. He has a mature approach, excellent hand-eye coordination and a lot of strikezone awareness. All that allows him to make contact to all fields, and his surprising strength gives him playable power at the plate even though his flat left-handed swing might top out at 10 homers per season in the professional ranks. Pitre is a solid runner and uses his speed aggressively on the bases, like when he swiped 26 bags for Kentucky in his final season there or when he stole seven down the stretch for Charleston. He is regarded as a quality defensive second baseman, and he showed enough range in the Rays early looks that he could get some time at shortstop this year. His arm strength will likely limit his overall effectiveness if he winds up in a utility role, but he has the defensive ability and offensive profile to hold down a job at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last 40-round Draft could very well be the 2019 edition. One year before that, the Mets used their 40th-round selection on Metoyer out of NAIA program Louisiana State University of Alexandria. He was dominant in relief for High-A Brooklyn in 2021 with a 2.18 ERA, 0.91 WHIP and 46 strikeouts in 33 innings with the Cyclones and made a late two-game appearance at Double-A Binghamton. The right-hander closed out his age-24 season in the Arizona Fall League, where he fanned 17 but walked 10 while allowing 12 earned runs in 10 1/3 innings. Lanky at a listed 6-foot-3 and 173 pounds, Metoyer earns the biggest praise for his curveball, a plus-plus offering that could play in the Majors right away. The 79- to 81-mph deuce regularly pops 3,000-plus rpm, and he posted the 35 highest spin rates as measured by Statcast in last year’s Fall League. The vertical break toward the bottom of the zone helps generate a high ground-ball rate, and his 69.2 GB percentage was tops among Mets pitchers with at least 30 innings in 2021. The right-hander is typically around 94-96 mph with a cutting fastball, helping keep balls on the dirt. Metoyer went to the AFL to work on a changeup, but that remains a distant third pitch. Because of all the movement, Metoyer can struggle to stay in the zone. That lack of control (along with the lackluster third pitch) keeps him in relief, and it played into the Mets’ decision to leave him off the 40-man roster last November when he became Rule 5-eligible. The velocity and spin of the curveball give him enough of an arsenal to feature in a Major League bullpen, and a back-end role is possible if he can land more strikes in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kevin Alvarez wasn't the only Astros outfield prospect to make a strong impression in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League last year. Signed for $472,500 out of Venezuela, Millan had a history of performing well at amateur events, so his easy transition to pro ball wasn't much of a surprise. He batted .279/.407/.419 with 11 extra-base hits and 13 steals in 42 games. More advanced than most 17-year-olds, Millan controls the zone and makes consistent contact. While he's not very physical at 5-foot-11 and 170 pounds, he hits the ball surprisingly hard for his size and generates plus raw pop. His right-handed-stroke is relatively flat, so he'll need to add some loft to fully tap into his 20-homer potential. A plus runner, Millan uses his quickness well on the bases and in center field. He has the instincts to steal bags and chases down balls from gap to gap. He also features solid arm strength and recorded six assists in 40 outfield starts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mikolajchak set a Sam Houston freshman record with 13 saves in 2017 and split the next two seasons between the bullpen and the rotation before the Guardians selected him in the 11th round of the 2019 Draft. They sent him to Double-A for his full-season debut after the pandemic layoff and he responded by posting a 3.18 ERA with a 57/9 K/BB ratio in 39 2/3 innings. Mikolajchak has upgraded his stuff since turning pro, beginning with a fastball that has gone from 92-95 mph in college to 94-97 with riding action and induced vertical break that make it tough for hitters to get on top of. He has turned an average low-80s slider into a plus mid-80s slide piece, and he also can morph it into a shorter, harder cutter. His upper-70s curveball has become an average offering and he also can mix in a low-80s changeup with some fade. Not only does Mikolajchak have more pitches than most relievers, but he also throws more strikes. His biggest need is to find a way to hold left-handers in check after they battered him for an .835 OPS (compared to .555 by right-handers) in 2021. Though he'll open 2022 with just 64 2/3 frames in the Minors, he may not need many more before he's ready to help Cleveland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Venezuela native didn’t sign with the Mets until he was a 19-year-old in August 2021 but moved quickly, reaching Single-A St. Lucie the following year. New York used him as a reliever that first full season in the Florida State League with promising results: a 3.78 ERA and 54 strikeouts in 47 2/3 innings. Gomez generated a ton of buzz in his second Spring Training, averaging 100 mph during one backfields outing. He made three starts for High-A Brooklyn as the Mets hoped to see him transition into a rotation, but he needed Tommy John surgery after that and missed the rest of the season. Gomez’s fastball sat 96-98 mph before surgery and regularly touched triple digits. The heater had plenty of ride up in the zone too, making it more than just a radar-gun darling. He also showed an upper-80s slider that could break over two planes, leading to some buckled knees from anyone trying to time their swing on the fastball. An upper-80s changeup remained very much a work in progress, and that will continue when he returns in 2024. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s velo increase coincided with control issues as he walked nine batters in his seven innings with Brooklyn. The ability to limit walks was closer to average at the lower levels, and there’s hope it would have improved as the sample grew larger in the South Atlantic League. Regardless, Gomez had arguably the best two-pitch profile in the Mets system pre-injury, and he could be dominant in a move back to the bullpen when healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the baseball factory that is Stoneman Douglas HS in Florida, Dubanewicz looked like he was set to honor his commitment to the University of Florida in 2024 when the Brewers swooped in to take him in the 15th round that July. He signed for $665,000 on the day of the deadline with $515,000 of that counting toward its bonus pool. The 6-foot-3 right-hander got off to a solid start in pro ball in 2025 with a 2.40 ERA and 1.12 WHIP over 82 1/3 innings in the Arizona Complex League and at Single-A, and after a delayed beginning this spring, he’s been even more dominant at the same levels in ’26. As expected for someone with his size and potential, Dubanewicz has added velocity in his age-20 campaign, now sitting 93-96 mph with his four-seamer and touching 97.8 mph in the early going. He’s also getting better extension (around seven feet), and with good ride on the heater, it’s been difficult for low-level batters to touch. He plays off that with a late-diving low-80s slider to generate whiffs against same-side bats, and he also has an upper-70s curveball with more break downward and to the gloveside. His upper-80s changeup stands out more for its armside movement than its fade. Dubanewicz’s control was stellar in 2025 but has taken a step back early on in ’26, though it’s coincided with more swing-and-miss for a fine trade-off. His delivery is loose and free enough that strikes shouldn’t be a major problem for him. He has leaked a little velocity over starts this spring, and that will need monitoring. But as he shows an improved arsenal over a larger workload, the potential for midrotation upside becomes clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Werner pitched and hit his first two years of college at Texas A&M before transitioning to hitting full-time in ‘22 and ‘23. Scouts were still intrigued by his 90-plus mph arm, and the Royals drafted him as a two-way player in the seventh round of the 2023 Draft. But he made his pro debut as a hitter with four games in the Arizona Complex League before heading to Single-A Columbia. There, he simply produced and produced some more. Werner won the Carolina League Player of the Month in September, when he had a 1.328 OPS and paced the league in hits (15), runs (12) and RBIs (14). There were some questions about the swing-and-miss in Werner’s game leading up to the Draft, and he did strike out at a 23 percent clip in the small sample at Single-A last year. Werner holds his hands high, and he’s not totally smooth in his setup or follow-through. But he’s done a good job of freeing up his swing with the work he did this offseason, and that should help to unlock his impressive power. Werner has athleticism and an ease with which he moves about third base, although he made eight errors in 20 games at Single-A. He has a cannon of an arm and should be able to stick there at least for now. Werner receives high praise for his work ethic and cerebral approach to the game, his routine and his preparation. He’s a physical presence at 6-foot-3 and 225 pounds. It certainly was a small sample size in Columbia last year, but it rightfully garnered some attention. Werner has some tools to work with, which excites the Royals long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2019-20 international signing period, the Braves weren’t allowed to sign any amateur free agents for more than $10,000 as part of the penalty for previous signing infractions on the market. That doesn’t mean they weren’t able to find any talent. They nabbed Joseph in November 2019 when he was already closing in on his 19th birthday, and he wasn’t able to make his pro debut until 2021. He spent three years either in the Florida Complex League or with Single-A Augusta until 2024, when he managed to pitch his way from High-A Rome to Double-A Mississippi. It’s not difficult to figure out what Joseph, 24 for all of the 2025 season, is all about. He’s a two-pitch-only reliever who offers power and more power. His fastball sat at 98 mph in 2024 and touched triple digits, missing bats at a 36 percent clip thanks to good ride up in the zone. He unfurled his slider, topping out at 89 mph, more than his fastball and it’s easy to see why: The nasty breaking ball produced a 45 percent miss rate last year, according to Synergy. The one thing that has held Joseph back has been his control, and he enters 2025 with a career 5.9 BB/9 walk rate to go along with his 12.2 K/9 rate. He found the zone a bit more consistently to start the year, which enabled him to reach Double-A for the first time, but there’s a reason why the Braves didn’t put him on the 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft and why he wasn’t taken. It’s clear his stuff would be good for the backend of a bullpen, but he won’t see any high leverage situations unless he can improve his command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $20,000 out of Venezuela in 2021, Agreda spent the first four years of his career in Rookie ball, including three straight seasons in the Arizona Complex League. He made a successful jump to Single-A in 2025, fashioning a 2.64 ERA with a .163 opponent average and 95 strikeouts in 82 2/3 innings. The Rangers opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster during the offseason, surmising correctly that his distance from the big leagues would sneak him through the Rule 5 Draft. Agreda relies heavily on a mid-90s fastball that reaches 100 mph with good carry but not much armside run. He creates high spin rates on his heater as well as a mid-80s slider and low-80s curveball that can be unhittable but also catch the zone only one-third of the time. He dabbles with an upper-80s changeup with fade and depth, though he almost never lands it for strikes. The 6-foot Agreda lacks starter size, and his short arm action has more of a reliever look. He can miss bats with four different pitches yet struggles to throw any of them for consistent strikes. He has the upside of a No. 4 starter or late-inning reliever, though he also has pitched just one game above Single-A five seasons into his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chalas’ $10,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in January 2023 barely made a blip on the international radar, considering he was about to turn 19 a month later. But he’s made a big impression through two seasons, first on both the Dominican and Arizona complex circuits in ’23 and then between Single-A and High-A last year. Chalas posted a 4.09 ERA with 72 strikeouts and 26 walks in 50 2/3 innings (all in relief) between Visalia and Hillsboro in his age-20 campaign. His 32.1 percent strikeout rate was third-highest among 40 D-backs Minor Leaguers with at least 50 frames in 2024. Standing 6-foot-3, the right-hander drops and drives well from atop the bump, generating plus-plus velocity that regularly touches the upper 90s. Low-level hitters just can’t handle that level of velocity, and right-handers struggled with Chalas’ heater coming up and in. He plays off it with a mid-80s slider that flashed plus with sharp gloveside dive out of a lowish arm slot. Chalas didn’t have a changeup in ’24, and lefties punished him appropriately with a .463 slugging percentage, compared to .291 for righties. The D-backs challenged him to find a third pitch, and it looks like a sinker-splitter hybrid (i.e., the splinker) may win out after offseason work. That would be a good fit for such a hard thrower with that release point, but picking up such a unique pitch isn’t as easy as Paul Skenes or Jhoan Duran make it look. Still, Chalas’ continued breakout has many across the industry intrigued, including Arizona, which won’t rule out trying Chalas as a starter the more he proves himself stateside. His control was solid for a reliever, especially late in the 2024 season, and it’s worth trying out Chalas’ stuff in a longer role before he knocks on the door of the desert.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Spence spent his first two college seasons at Black Hawk (Ill.) CC, where he batted .368/.442/.600 while also seeing action on the mound. He continued to play both ways at Southern Illinois-Edwardsville, where he won the Ohio Valley Conference batting title (.385) in 2024 before the Astros signed him for $150,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He reached Double-A in his first full pro season, hitting a combined .244/.368/.403 with 10 homers and 27 steals in 116 games between three levels. Spence rarely chases pitches and could fit at the top of the order with his on-base skills and basestealing ability. While the left-handed hitter doesn't miss fastballs, he struggles to make contact against breaking balls and changeups and has been overmatched by southpaws in pro ball. He has some sneaky pop but also hits a lot of grounders, so he'll probably top out at 10-12 homers per season. Though there's some question about how much offense Spence can provide, he can help a team win in a variety of ways. He knows how to use his plus speed to reach base, steal bags and chase down balls in the outfield. He's a solid defender in center with plus arm strength that translated into a low-90s fastball in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With fewer options for Rookie or short-season ball available to teams, it’s become more common for young international signees to spend multiple seasons in the Dominican Summer League. The Reds did just that with their top three signings from the 2024 class: Adolfo Sanchez and Naibel Mariano, who both got seven-figure bonuses, and Morillo, who signed for $420,000. Morillo put up solid numbers both summers and is ready to come stateside. Morillo is a switch-hitting catcher who will play all of his 2026 season in the United States at age 19. His bat is definitely ahead of his glove, with an advanced approach that led to more walks than strikeouts over two summers in the DSL and helped him hold his own against older competition in the Australian League this offseason. His swing works from both sides of the plate with more gap-to-gap thump right now, though there’s power for him to get to. He needs to tighten up his zone a little bit and his swing can get long, but there are building blocks for him to be an average hitter with average power. While Morillo has more work to do behind the dish with maybe an average arm and more rudimentary receiving skills, the Reds love the intangibles and leadership qualities he possesses, including improving his English and showing up in Arizona early to get to work for the season ahead. There might come a time when they’ll want to move him from behind the plate so his bat can advance, but that decision isn’t coming any time soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phoenix-born De La Torre grew up in Mexico before attending high school in Utah and showcasing himself to big league teams in the Dominican Republic. Signed for $10,000 in July 2023, De La Torre spent two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before making his U.S. debut last year. He was leading the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 62 strikeouts in 38 2/3 innings when he was promoted in early July to Single-A, where he logged a 1.77 ERA in seven starts before starring in the playoffs as San Jose won the California League title. De La Torre's 94-96 mph fastball touches 98 and explodes on hitters because the extension and low release height in his delivery create plenty of carry. His heater generated a 32 percent swing-and-miss rate at Single-A; to put that in perspective, big league left-handers Aroldis Chapman and Brendon Little posted identical marks in 2025. He backs it up with a mid-80s slider that can be a plus pitch with big sweep at its best. De La Torre operates mainly with two pitches and has yet to show much faith in his fading mid-80s changeup. He compensates for a lack of physicality with some of the best athleticism in the system, getting down the mound very well and filling the strike zone. If he's as good as he looked last year, he could be a mid-rotation starter and climb quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Compared to George Springer as an amateur in Venezuela, Rivas signed for $950,000 in January 2025. He flashed five-tool potential during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, where he hit .258/.393/.384 with 12 extra-base hits and 18 steals in 46 games. He'll make his U.S. debut shortly after turning 18 this year. Rivas stood out with his ability to recognize pitches, make consistent hard contact and draw walks in his first taste of pro ball. The next steps will be to add strength and make adjustments to his bat path so he can tap into his potential plus raw power. His right-handed swing is more notable for its bat speed than its loft, resulting in a lot of groundball contact. Rivas' speed, arm and defense all earn plus grades from evaluators, giving the upside of a 20-20 center fielder. He's an aggressive baserunner who has posted 6.5-second times in the 60-yard dash. His quickness and instincts leave no doubt that he can handle center, where his unusually strong arm for the position notched seven assists in 42 games last summer.
