mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barnett headed to Division II Wingate as a two-way player before exploding offensively as a junior in 2024. His 26 homers were second-most for that level of collegiate baseball, while his .739 slugging percentage placed 32nd among qualifiers. He posted a .349 average and 1.138 OPS over his 59 games with the Bulldogs while also making six appearances out of the bullpen, striking out seven and walking six over five frames. The Padres took him in the 11th round in the '24 Draft and signed him for $175,000 ($25,000 of which counted toward their bonus pool). Barnett only hit and played corner outfield with Single-A Lake Elsinore after joining the organization, but he pitched in late workouts and turned more than a few heads on the mound. He ran his fastball up to 97 and averaged closer to the mid-90s. His slider sat in the upper-80s with a hard cutter-like break, and that pitch could easily be a weapon, too. The ball comes out of his 6-foot-2 frame easily, and his delivery isn’t overcomplicated. With his position-player background and athleticism, he could get to average control with the right professional instruction. As much as many in the organization prefer Barnett’s work on the mound, the Padres will still give him a chance to DH part-time to begin his first full season. His power is undeniable from the right side, but he really struggled against non-fastballs in the California League last year. Had Barnett shown this level of stuff more consistently, some believe he would have gone several rounds earlier as a pitcher alone, and that’s likely where his future lies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After barely playing during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, Sprinkle was co-Big West Conference freshman field player of the year the following spring and played for the U.S. collegiate national team during the summer. UC Santa Barbara's best position prospect since 2006 third-rounder Chris Valaika, Sprinkle entered 2022 with first-round buzz but slipped to the fourth round after struggling at the plate. He batted .237/.290/.301 in a month in Single-A after signing for $452,900. Scouts considered Sprinkle the best defensive shortstop in the 2022 college class. He's quick with range to both sides and reliable hands, and he increased his arm strength last year to where it now grades as solid to plus. He enhances his throwing ability with a fast release and has a good internal clock. Sprinkle batted .353/.402/.536 at UCSB in 2021 but got out of whack when he added strength and hunted home runs for much of his draft year. He has bat speed but gets overly aggressive at the plate, lengthens his right-handed swing and leaves himself vulnerable to offspeed pitches. He needs to focus on getting on base to take advantage of his plus speed and basestealing aptitude.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Facundo has worked just 148 innings in his first five years as a pro after signing for $20,000 out of Venezuela in May 2021. He missed all of 2022 with shoulder issues and had Tommy John surgery in May 2024. He may be worth the wait, however, because he's the rare left-hander who can reach triple digits with his fastball. Coming back from his elbow reconstruction, Facundo threw harder than ever, working at 94-96 mph and touching 100 with his heater. He has more success with a two-seamer with sink because his four-seamer is fairly straight and doesn't miss many bats. His mid-80 slider lacks consistency but could become a solid offering with more development, while he barely uses a changeup that sits around 90 mph without much action. Because he's currently a two-pitch guy who has yet to show any durability, Facundo projects more as a reliever than a starter. He works solely out of the stretch and with an upright delivery and three-quarters arm slot. The Yankees opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, and his relative inexperience allowed him to sneak through the Rule 5 Draft without getting popped.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Draft picks taken after the 10th round are automatically assigned a slot value of $150,000. When a college senior gets taken in Round 11, as Clohisy was out of St. Louis in 2024, and signs for that exact slot amount, it tends to fly under the radar. But when that senior plays his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season and finishes third among all Minor Leaguers with 79 steals before stealing 22 more to lead the Arizona Fall League, as Clohisy did in 2025, folks tend to sit up and take notice. Clohisy’s future in the big leagues is directly connected to his legs. In 2025, regular season and AFL combined, he stole 101 bases in 120 attempts (84.2 percent success rate) in 152 games. Not only does he have great speed, he’s aggressive in using it, wreaking havoc at all times. His wheels also help him cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He can no doubt play center field, but has and will continue to get time in all three spots. That’s important because his future role would be as a fourth or fifth outfielder if it all clicks. And that will depend on how the left-handed hitter swings the bat. There is a little extra-base ability, but his job will always be to put the ball in play and get on base, and it will be interesting to see whether he can carry over the offensive success he had in Double-A and Arizona to lift him up to Atlanta.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts placed himself squarely in the Draft conversation by slashing .270/.442/.476 with 10 homers and more walks (44) than strikeouts (41) over 55 games as a UNC junior outfielder in 2021, and the D-backs selected him in the fifth round that July, announcing him as a catcher, where he had summer league experience. After spending most of his first full season at High-A, the left-handed slugger broke out some with Double-A Amarillo in 2023, slashing .278/.383/.523 with 17 homers over 97 games. The former Tar Heel rarely expands the zone with a strong approach, resulting in a 13.4 percent walk rate last season. He particularly shows strong contact skills against fastballs, thanks to a simple and quick swing, but swing-and-miss issues against softer stuff and right-left splits (.930 OPS vs. .751) will likely keep him from being an average hitter at higher levels. Roberts also took advantage of Amarillo’s friendly confines, hitting 14 of his 17 homers there with a .677 SLG at home, but he has solid raw power and the lift needed to push for 12-15 dingers annually. Roberts rotated through the outfielder corners and catcher at Double-A and during a stint in the Arizona Fall League. His arm strength helps play at those spots, but he’s still a work in progress behind the plate with his bat pushing him faster than his glove can follow. His left-handed stick, power potential and multiple mitts would give him value on a Major League bench should his offensive trends continue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has never been a player from Uganda to make it to the big leagues, though there is a growing baseball presence in the African nation. The Dodgers signed two Ugandan players in 2022, Ben Serunkuma and Umar Male, and since then the Pirates have inked two more, most recently Armstrong Muhoozi and Matoma, who received $20,000 in January 2023. Matoma got his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League that summer but really jumped on radars when news of his arm strength spread and he put up outstanding numbers, albeit in a small sample, in the Florida Complex League. Matoma may only be a six-footer, but he has a super-fast arm and tons of arm strength. He's touched triple-digits with his fastball and routinely is in the 97-98 mph range, though he does tend to fatigue pretty quickly. His 87-88 mph gyro-like slider could be a true out pitch in time, one that already misses a good amount of bats, and when he can keep his heater at the high end of his range, there's good velocity separation there. He has an upper-80s splitter, but it's a distant third pitch that doesn't kill enough spin. Considering that Matoma has played so little baseball, he's done an impressive job throwing strikes consistently. He has a reliever-like mindset, with a slow heartbeat, but the Pirates don't want to limit what he could become. He showed up this spring more physical with much more muscle on his frame, which could help him maintain his stuff as he takes his next step.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $47,500 out of Venezuela in 2022, Osorio spent his first two years as pro in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and his third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. When he finally made his full-season debut in 2025, he ranked third in the Single-A Carolina League with a .393 on-base percentage at age 20. He returned to Hickory this spring and was one of the top offensive performers in the early part of the season. Osorio's skills stand out more than his physical tools, beginning with his ability to put the bat on the ball. With a compact left-handed stroke and advanced feel for the barrel, he rarely swings and misses. He's hitting balls harder and launching them in the air to his pull side more frequently in 2026, allowing him to homer 10 times in his first 45 games after going deep just six times in 178 contests during the previous four seasons. Osorio has fringy speed but good baserunning instincts. His high baseball IQ has also led to some playing time in center field despite his lack of quickness, though he's better suited for the corners. He's an average defender in left or right field with decent arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high school all-state performer, Peters began at Temple Junior College before transferring to Dallas Baptist University, where he earned second-team All-Conference USA honors. Primarily a reliever, he led the Patriots with four saves and made key spot starts, including a six-inning, 10-strikeout outing as part of a combined no-hitter against Liberty to close the regular season. Strong performances in Regional play helped propel him to Seattle’s fourth-round selection in 2025, when he signed for below slot value at $550,000. At 5-foot-11, Peters is an athletic left-hander with the potential to develop into a starter. His fastball sits around 93 mph and can touch 96 mph, featuring natural ride that challenges hitters up in the zone. Behind it, he mixes an upper-70s curve that generated high whiff rates in 2025 and a low-80s sweepy slider, though the slider is used less consistently. Peters pairs his repertoire with a repeatable delivery and solid arm action, allowing him to command all his pitches and attack the strike zone effectively. The next step for Peters as a starter will be refining a changeup and demonstrating he can handle a rotation workload, as he did not report to an affiliate after being drafted. Even if that path proves challenging, he projects as a high-floor left-handed reliever with three effective pitches. Paired with other top picks like Griffin Hugus and Kade Anderson, Peters represents another promising pitching piece in Seattle’s 2025 Draft class, offering both present value and long-term upside out of the bullpen or potentially in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Smith's combination of stuff, athleticism and arm speed landed him in the third round of the 2023 Draft, the Tennessee high school product had Tommy John surgery shortly after turning pro. He missed all of 2024 and worked just 21 innings in his pro debut last year, but he's finally making regular starts this season. While he'll need time to develop and to add some strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame, he has some of the best upside among Los Angeles' starting pitching prospects. Smith has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks, and he shows the ability to land it for strikes or use it as a chase pitch. His fastball sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with quality carry and should join his cambio as a plus offering once he learns to command it better. His upper-80s slider, low-90s cutter and upper-70s curveball are all works in progress but show some promise. Smith explodes off the mound and tunnels his pitches well from a three-quarters arm slot. He still has to prove that he can maintain and harness his stuff, and the Dodgers think his athleticism will help him do so. They'll try to bring him along carefully while also realizing that he'll need to be protected from the Rule 5 Draft following the 2027 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to hitters Bralyn Brazoban and Adbiel Feliz at the start of the 2024 international signing period, but a couple of prospects a bit further down the list have come to the forefront a bit more. One is Edward Florentino, now a Top 100 prospect, and the other is Navarro, an electric left-hander who got $270,00 to sign, the third-highest bonus given to a lefty in the class. In both his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2024 and in his first trip to the United States in '25 (where he reached full-season ball), he showed that he is very tough to hit, if he can find the plate. There is no doubt that Navarro has the stuff to dominate hitters, with a 15.8 K/9 rate and .120 batting average against over 56 total innings heading into the 2026 season. Thus far, it’s been all about the lefty’s fastball-slider combination. He’ll throw his heater in the 95-100 mph range, and the four-seamer elicited a 47 percent miss rate. His mid-80s slider has been even nastier, with a 50 percent miss rate. He does have a seldom-used changeup that he didn’t throw last year, but the plan is to be intentional to up his usage on the pitch this season. As unhittable as Navarro is, his inability to command his stuff makes it hard to project what he might be. He only threw his fastball for strikes 54 percent of the time last year and his slider came in under the 50 percent mark. If the walks start to trend down, he could start to move. He’s almost certainly a reliever long-term, but the Pirates will keep him on a starting routine so the 19-year-old can work on harnessing all three of his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitts was a “famous” high schooler in the Atlanta area at a very early age, and he actually committed to the University of South Carolina as a shortstop before he even began his high school career. By the time his Draft year came around in 2025, he had moved to the outfield and changed his college commitment to the University of South Florida. He might have had the chance to move up boards more during his senior year, but a hamstring issue slowed him considerably. After being able to work him out a couple of times and getting to know more about his makeup, the Reds rolled the dice and took him in the fifth round, going a little over slot at $575,000 to sign him. Pitts didn’t make his pro debut after signing and he was slow coming out of the spring as he continued to nurse his hamstring back to health. The Reds think this was a good upside play based on his athleticism and potential to stay up the middle. A right-handed hitter and thrower, Pitts’ carrying tool is the speed he wasn’t able to showcase much his senior year, getting 70 grades from some evaluators when he’s healthy. He’s shown off solid raw power at times and a decent feel for hitting that gives some hope he can tap into that pop consistently in the future. That plus speed is also an asset defensively, and Pitts has the athleticism to play center field at the next level, albeit with an arm that needs work. It’s a bit of a lottery ticket given that he wasn’t seen that much in 2025, but if he can get past the hamstring problems, there’s some ceiling for him to grow into.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more athletic players in Illinois' 2025 high school crop, Wheeler played third base and pitched for Morris (Ill.) HS, while also pulling duty as a wide receiver and defensive back in football and setting the school's career scoring record in basketball. His varied sporting interests didn't leave much time for the prep showcase circuit, so he flew a bit under the scouting radar. The Rangers waited until the sixth round to take him and paid an over-slot $525,000 to sign him away from an Illinois commitment. Texas believes in Wheeler's offensive upside because he makes good swing decisions and consistent contact while producing better exit velocities than most players his age. He has a simple right-handed stroke and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Once he adds more strength to his athletic 6-foot-5 frame and learns to elevate balls more regularly, he could produce 20 or more homers per year. Wheeler presently has solid speed but may lose a step as he fills out. He moves well at third base and features a strong arm that ran fastballs up to 92 mph when he took the mound. If he can't stay on the dirt, his power and arm strength would profile well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better two-way players in the 2022 Draft, Mule displayed raw power, arm strength and athleticism at shortstop and hit 100 mph with his fastball on the prep showcase circuit. He displayed increased polish as a pitcher during his New Jersey high school senior season, leading most clubs to believe he had more upside on the mound. He gave up a Miami scholarship to sign for an above-slot $1 million in the fourth round, but Tommy John surgery in March 2023 will push his pro debut back to mid-2024. Though Mule can reach triple digits with his fastball, he has learned that he's better off ignoring radar guns and working at 93-96 with increased riding action. He showed a more consistent slider last spring and his low-80s breaker features more depth than sweep. He barely needed a third pitch as an amateur but can flash a low-80s changeup with intriguing fade. Mule did a better job of pitching under control as a high school senior, and his athleticism should help him throw strikes. Though he'll need plenty of time to refine his secondary pitches, control and command, he has one of the more electric arms in the system. The Cubs have said they plan to develop him as a pitcher but will remain open-minded about how his role might evolve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyd didn't get on the field during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season in his first year at Oregon State and made just 19 starts in his second. But he broke out last spring, hitting .373/.490/.577, and led the Pac-12 Conference with 24 steals before the Reds signed him for a slightly under-slot $847,500 as a supplemental second-round pick. He spent most of his pro debut in Single-A before Cincinnati traded him to Cleveland for Will Benson in February. A disciplined right-handed hitter, Boyd focuses on making contact and reaching base. He features at least plus speed, which he uses to beat out bunts, turn grounders into singles and create havoc on the bases. He has a bit of pull power but makes a lot of ground-ball contact and hasn't shown much power with wood bats, so he could max out at 10-12 homers per season. Boyd's quickness, solid arm strength and keen instincts give him plenty of versatility. Though he played primarily right field at Oregon State, he spent most of his pro debut in center and the Guardians project that he'll develop into a quality center fielder. The Beavers recruited him as a shortstop and it's possible he could handle second or third base in a super-utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 6-foot-7 Storm was better known for his basketball exploits than his pitching at Madison (Miss.) Central HS, where he worked just 14 varsity innings in four years. He put himself on the prospect map with a crucial victory over Louisiana State to help send Southern Mississippi to the NCAA Super Regionals in 2022, then won the Sun Belt Conference tournament finale and three of the Golden Eagles' five NCAA playoff wins last spring. He made four relief appearances in Rookie ball after turning pro as a seventh-round pick last July. Solely a reliever, Storm gets ahead of hitters with his fastball and puts them away with his slider. Though his fastball usually ranges from 90-93 mph and maxes out at 95, it plays better than its pedestrian velocity because it comes out of a very high release point and features plenty of carry up in the zone. His plus slider is his best pitch, sitting at 82-85 mph and missing bats with a combination of horizontal and vertical action. His unusual arm angle and crossfire delivery create plenty of deception without costing Storm control. He has the upside of a set-up man and could move quickly through the system. He had repeated success in long outings in the last two NCAA postseasons, so there could be some temptation to try him as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants have signed a number of intriguing arms on the international market in the last few years, including Rodriguez for $10,000 as a 19-year-old out of Venezuela in 2025. He carved up Rookie-level Dominican Summer League hitters in his pro debut, logging a 2.41 ERA with a .138 opponent average and 46 strikeouts in 41 innings. He has continued to impress after coming to the United States and pitching in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in 2026. Rodriguez operates at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with a fastball that features sinking and tailing action. He backs it up with a hard, short slider in the mid 80s. He also shows the making of an average low-80s changeup with some fade. At 5-foot-11 and 212 pounds, Rodriguez is more physical than projectable. He has a simple delivery with a low release height, and his control is improving as he gains more experience. He has a chance to pitch in the back of a big league rotation if he can upgrade his secondary pitches and command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez turned pro for $250,000, earning the largest bonus given to a Dominican catcher on the 2019-20 international market. Because of the pandemic and two years in Rookie ball, he didn't reach full-season ball until 2023. He batted .299/.360/.393 between Single-A and High-A but tired noticeably down the stretch and wasn't protected on the 40-man roster in November. One of the best contact hitters in the system, Perez laces balls to all fields with a compact right-handed stroke. He has enough strength and bat speed for at least 12-15 homer power, but his approach yields a lot of soft contact and he went deep just four times in 158 games over his first three seasons. He does make good swing decisions and controls the strike zone well. Perez needs to clean up his defense after giving up 24 passed balls in 62 games a year ago, and he may never be more than an adequate receiver and blocker. He has well-above-average arm strength but can improve how quickly he gets rid of throws. Despite below-average speed, he managed to steal 23 bases in 27 attempts in just 75 games last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins' Rookie-level Dominican Summer League roster is filled with big pitchers with upside, including 2025 signees Kevin Defrank and Adrian Pena, who have some of the best stuff in the system. Santana, who signed for $67,500 in 2023, fits right in as a 6-foot-7 physical specimen. The Dominican Republic native showed plenty of promise early on before undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2024, 13 games into his pro career. He returned 13 months later to make five starts with even more velocity. Santana was touching the high 90s before his elbow injury and spent his time rehabbing adding significant muscle. The right-hander is now up closer to 250 pounds, compared to his listed weight of 200, enabling him to top out at 102.6 mph on his fastball with impressive ride. His upper-80s cutter-like slider is his best secondary pitch with the potential to be plus, and his low-90s changeup also has promise. Santana's control has wobbled before and after the injury, but the hope is that added strength will make his delivery more consistent and coordinated. This is one of the highest-upside arms in the system, albeit one who turns 21 in October, has yet to pitch stateside and has to be added to the 40-man roster after the 2027 season or be exposed to the Rule 5 Draft. This will be a key season, more than a year after the surgery, to see how his powerful stuff plays against better competition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he played on the same Goodpasture Christian HS (Nashville) as Tigers fourth-rounder Carson Rucker in 2023, Elkins flew somewhat under the radar because he was also an all-region running back in football who didn't spend much time on the showcase circuit. Teams recognized his tools but didn't have much history with him, allowing the Dodgers to land him in the eighth round with an over-slot $407,500 bonus. After making a one-game pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he returned there last summer and batted .285/.412/.457 with 20 steals in 57 games. Elkins has a strong 6-foot-1 frame and a quick right-handed swing that give him plus raw power with the potential for more. He has a pull-happy approach and looks to drive the ball in the air, enabling him to tap into most of his pop. He'll have to prove he can hit advanced pitching because he tied for the ACL lead with 80 strikeouts while whiffing at 35 percent clip, though he did show a willingness to work deep counts and take walks. Elkins may have the best combination of power and speed in the system. He's a plus-plus runner who's aggressive on the bases and in the outfield. Both his center-field defense and arm strength grade as at least plus, and the Dodgers have some internal 70 grades on both tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Phillies as a 14th-rounder in 2024 to transfer to Texas, Spencer emerged as the best college senior in the 2025 Draft before injuring his shoulder in April and undergoing season-ending surgery. The Blue Jays selected him in the 11th round last summer and signed him for $165,000, a big swing on landing a talent who could have landed in the top three rounds of the Draft if he was healthy. There’s risk, but these are the types of gambles organizations should be taking outside of the first 10 rounds. Spencer added two mph to his fastball in the spring of 2025, sitting at 93-96 and touching 98 while maintaining his velocity deep into games, albeit with more downhill angle than carry or run. His sweeping slider always has been his best pitch, and it became a wipeout offering after it picked up five mph compared to a year ago, averaging 88 and reaching 91. His changeup had developed into a solid, mid-80s offering before the surgery. Spencer will open 2026 on the IL, so if he simply gets into some game action and sets himself up for a “regular” offseason next winter, that will be a success. This is a longer-term project for the Blue Jays, which is rare to say about a senior pick, but this has the potential to pay off in a major way if Spencer returns to his old self following rehab.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing as a 17th-round pick from a Puerto Rican high school in 2023, Rodriguez spent his first three seasons in pro ball in Tampa. Minor injuries limited him to 90 plate appearances in 2023-24 with the Yankees' Rookie-level Florida Complex League team there, and he returned to the FCL to start last year. He earned a promotion to their Single-A Florida State League affiliate after six weeks and slashed .237/.342/.392 with two homers in 30 games before missing the final month with a sprained wrist. Rodriguez has a quick left-handed stroke, makes reasonably good swing decisions and generates a lot of contact and promising exit velocities. Overly pull-conscious in his first two years as a pro, Rodriguez settled down his approach in 2025. He began to understand that he doesn't have to launch every pitch he sees to right field, which resulted in fewer rolled-over grounders, and he should develop 20-homer pop as he continues to get stronger. Rodriguez possesses solid speed and some basestealing savvy. He has spent most of his early pro career on the outfield corners, where he's a solid defender with average arm strength. He may be quick enough to handle center field and should get more of an opportunity to show what he can do there in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: By the standards of a drafted high-school player, Cox may have been a relatively late bloomer. He was a member of the JV team as a sophomore at Rock Hill High School (Texas), and it took breakouts as a junior and senior to make pro scouts think he could be signed away from playing at the University of Texas. The Nationals took on that risk by selecting Cox in the fourth round and inked him to a nearly double-slot $1 million bonus. With his upright stance, Cox sports a classic left-handed swing that could translate nicely on the pro side. He went 10-for-35 with a homer in 10 Rookie-level Florida Complex League games to boost that argument, and it’s notable that he only batted out of the leadoff spot there. There isn’t a ton of power at present, but his 6-foot-3 frame indicates more pop could be in store as he matures physically. Cox was a two-year starting quarterback and touched 94 mph on the mound during his prep days, so he should be able to handle any of the three outfield spots from an arm perspective. On top of that, he’s a plus runner and impressive overall athlete. Cox has already bumped a bit into Washington’s logjam of athletic outfielders -- he made eight of his 10 starts in left field in deference to Elijah Green -- but while he’s raw, he still has the skill set to elbow his way further into the conversation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs have long loved their athletic and toolsy center fielders with Corbin Carroll and Alek Thomas graduating in recent years, Druw Jones joining as the second overall pick in 2022 and Adriel Radney entering the fold internationally this January. Zapata fit the description in January 2023 when he signed with Arizona for $950,000. The teenager debuted in the Dominican Summer League and was a midseason All-Star there before finishing with a .254/.364/.522 line and 126 wRC+. The left-handed-slugging outfielder measured in at 6-foot-4 and 195 pounds upon signing, and his size led to belief that he’d get to above-average power down the line. That pullside pop actually came quickly in 2023 with nine home runs and a .269 ISO, each of which ranked fifth in the DSL. Zapata, however, struck out in 29.1 percent of his plate appearances, and he’ll need to reel in that approach significantly as he heads stateside. The Dominican Republic native runs well for someone with his frame, and the D-backs gave him the majority of his defensive starts in center field. He also got ample time in right because of his plus arm strength, and he might end up there long-term should he slow down a tick as some expect. His powerful profile would play in a corner, but he’ll have to make adjustments at the plate as he climbs the ladder toward Phoenix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Preparing for the possibility that Roki Sasaki might sign at the end of the 2024 international period, New York stockpiled bonus pool money and acquired some more from the Red Sox in the Carlos Narvaez trade that November. When Sasaki opted to wait, the Yankees spent $1.65 million on Dec. 17 to sign Marinez, who had planned to turn pro in 2025. He batted .275/.424/.375 and looked good at shortstop in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. A left-handed hitter, Marinez has a sound stroke and patient approach. He drew 41 walks in 47 DSL games but also can get too passive and fall behind in counts more than he should. He needs to add significant strength so he can turn on more pitches and hit them harder, but New York believes he can grow into at least 15-homer power with more muscle and some adjustments to his swing path. Marinez features plus speed and likes to turn it loose on the bases, stealing 22 bases in 28 attempts (79 percent) in the DSL. His quickness helps him cover ground to both sides and he has the solid to plus arm strength to finish plays. Like most teenage infielders, he needs more defensive consistency, which should come with experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lara joined the Mets for just $25,000 in June 2021 and has been a level-per-year player since. After posting an OPS below .700 in both the Dominican Summer and Florida Complex Leagues the previous two seasons, he broke out some in his first trip to full-season ball with a .264/.362/.452 line, 14 homers and 17 steals in 99 games with Single-A St. Lucie last summer. His 122 wRC+ tied for seventh-best in the Florida State League while he was one of only seven players in all of Single-A ball with at least 14 homers and 14 steals. The right-handed slugger keeps his lower half relatively quiet in his batting setup, relying on his arms and wrists to fire through the zone. He can be caught chasing occasionally and was especially prone to whiffing on offspeed stuff, but he was aggressive on fastballs for good reason, slugging .653 off four-seamers. His exit velocities were roughly league average for the Florida State League, a solid showing for a 19-year-old, and his 90th percentile EV (101.5) was in the same neighborhood as more notable prospects Jett Williams (102.2) and Jacob Reimer (101.6). Lara ranked in the 82nd percentile for speed among his fellow FSLers, and the Mets put those wheels to use all over the diamond with time everywhere except for pitcher and catcher. He has the arm strength for either right field – where he topped out with a 100.5 mph throw – or third base, but a more permanent move to a corner puts a strong focus on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lohman was a steady buildup at Fort Zumwalt North HS, northwest of St. Louis. He didn’t show much velocity with a fastball only in the upper 80s as a junior, and that initially made him a low priority with many figuring he was set to honor his commitment to Missouri. Instead, he turned heads with a little extra heat as a senior, along with a pair of interesting breaking balls, and he attended the MLB Draft Combine in Arizona. The Mets selected him in the eighth round and signed him for well above slot at $797,500 (late third-round money) to keep him out of the SEC. That improved velo pushed Lohman’s fastball into the 91-95 mph range, and with his size at 6-foot-4, he can create downhill plane from a high release point. He’ll work with both a mid-70s curveball and low-80s slider that have promising two-plane depth. The curveball might be a better fit for his over-the-top delivery, but both pitches have the chance to become at least average Major League quality. His low-80s splitter was a work in progress but looks like a pitch with some promise. Lohman uses short strides on the mound, rather than getting big extension, and that’s what leads to the high release. He’ll either need to improve the shape of his fastball and slider or locate them exceptionally well in pro ball to get the most out of both offerings against pro bats, but as a prep arm, he’ll be given plenty of time and space to work on both goals. There could be even more strength coming in his projectable frame, and the Mets, who have a run of pitching development success, could be the right org to get the most out of Lohman’s budding potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of San Diego’s St. Augustine HS, Boles got time on the showcase circuit in 2024 and even started the High School All-American Game in his native city at Petco Park that August, picking up a pair of strikeouts in his lone frame. He had a commitment to Texas and looked likely to head to Austin as the 2025 Draft passed before the Royals selected him in the 18th round. Kansas City eventually signed the right-hander for $500,000 ($350,000 of which counted toward its Draft pool), and that was the sixth-highest bonus in the organization’s 2025 class. Already standing in at 6-foot-5, Boles is all about projection. He ran his fastball up to 94 mph in his final amateur season, and it’s easy to dream on him sitting mid-90s more regularly as he fills out that frame with strength in the pros. His low-80s slider also shows present and future promise with impressive spin and sharp movement to the glove side. He can also flash a solid mid-80s changeup to give him an offspeed pitch going the other way while his slow curveball doesn’t look like a true weapon. Boles could be all around the zone at times heading into the Draft, and tightening up his slinging delivery should be a focus on the pro side. The Royals tend to take things slowly with prep arms early in their careers, and Boles will be no exception as he’ll open his age-19 season in the Arizona Complex League with the goal of cracking Single-A Columbia at some point in 2026. He has received positive reviews from Royals officials for his willingness to take pro-level instruction, and that combined with his stuff gives him higher upside than a traditional 18th-round flier.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Leach had two elbow surgeries in high school and a third to remove screws from the joint while in college, where he compiled a 5.50 ERA in 54 innings during two seasons at Creighton and one at Miami (Ohio). His medical history and lack of success left him unselected in the 2023 Draft, but his arm strength and feel for spinning the ball spurred the Astros to sign him for $125,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He missed most of last May and June with a shoulder strain but also added 4 mph to his fastball last year, which helped him shoot from High-A to Triple-A before he impressed in the Arizona Fall League. Leach can exceed 3,000 rpm on a power curveball that operates in the low 80s, features huge downer break and can be unhittable when it's on. His heater went from sitting at 91-94 mph in 2024 to working at 95-97 and touching 99 with nice carry and some mild armside run. He also employs an upper-80s cutter that stands out more for its velocity than its action. Pitching solely out of the stretch, Leach has a drop-and-drive delivery that provides a low release height and good extension. The depth of his curve can make it hard to harness and Triple-A hitters punished his fastball and cutter when he didn't locate it well. If he can improve his control, he could contribute to Houston's bullpen this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed from the Mexican League's Yucatan Lions in May 2021, Serna landed a $50,000 bonus and has excelled ever since. He posted a 2.25 ERA in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in his pro debut and a 1.96 mark in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. He topped the FCL with 56 strikeouts in 41 1/3 innings, while whiffing 32 percent of the batters he faced. Serna has confounded younger hitters with a mid-70s changeup that drops at the plate and has huge velocity separation from his fastball. His heater operates at 90-91 mph and reaches 93 and he could throw harder if he adds more strength to his small frame. His sweeping upper-70s slider stands out more for its spin rates than its power and he also throws a mid-70s curveball with more depth. Serna has a clean delivery, throws strikes, misses bats and generates weak ground ball contact. Listed at just 5-foot-11 and 162 pounds, he'll have to prove he can handle a starter's workload over a full season. He has gained nearly 20 pounds since turning pro and is the most polished of the Yankees' teenage pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you’re a high-ceiling high school pitcher who hasn’t heard his name called in the top 10 rounds and think you’re headed to college, the Angels can always give you hope. On an almost annual basis, extra bonus pool money is available to take and sign some prep arms. In 2025, they targeted a pair of intriguing high school lefties, taking Talon Haley in the 12th round and Mitchell a round later. Rather than head to Texas, Mitchell signed for $872,500, heading down a baseball path despite coming from a football family that includes an uncle who quarterbacked in the Canadian Football League and a brother who was a wide receiver at Arizona. After pitching for Team USA the summer before his senior year, Mitchell got off to a good start back at school but was shut down with shoulder fatigue after a month, so building up strength will be a key. He can sit 90-92 mph with his fastball, touching 94, and the fastball plays up because of deception in his delivery and carry up in the zone. He has a good feel to spin an upper-70s curve with depth that works well off of his heater. Like with a lot of high school pitchers, he hasn’t used a changeup much, but he’s shown glimpses of a decent cambio in the low-80s with fade and sink. Mitchell is athletic on the mound, repeating his delivery well and filling up the strike zone. There’s room to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame, which could help all of his stuff tick up as he gets his pro career going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Armas played in the 2015 Little League World Series before attending San Diego, where he hit a soft .265 in three seasons but won Rawlings NCAA Division I Gold Glove recognition in 2024, when he permitted just 15 steals and allowed only one passed ball in 55 games. His prowess behind the plate led the Cubs to draft him in the fifth round that July and he has ranked among the best defensive catchers in the Minors ever since. He slashed .234/325/.347 at High-A during his first full pro season. While Armas has below-average speed, he moves exceptionally well behind the plate. His framing metrics are outstanding, and he's also a quality receiver and blocker who committed just two passed balls in 79 games last year. He has a strong arm and makes accurate throws, erasing 34 percent of basestealers in 2025. Armas profiles as a quality backup because he's unlikely to provide enough offense to become a big league regular. He has a sound right-handed stroke and a decent approach, but he struggles against changeups and is hapless against breaking balls. He showed some aptitude for launching balls to his pull side in 2025, but he doesn't barrel enough to provide more than 8-10 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson missed almost all of his 2024 Mississippi high school senior season while recovering from internal brace surgery before staying local to pitch at Pearl River (Miss.) CC. In his lone season with the Wildcats, he tied a school record with 12 wins while posting a 2.28 ERA with 70 strikeouts in 71 innings. The Rangers paid him a double-slot $300,000 bonus in the 11th round last July to divert him from attending Auburn. Johnson's fastball sat at 89-90 mph at the end of his high school career before parking at 90-93 mph and touching 96 last spring, generating a lot of grounders with its heavy sink and armside run. He backs his heater up with a tight low-80s slider that he can land for strikes or use to create chases. He barely uses his mid-80s changeup with fade but controls it well. With Johnson's long, whippy arm action and ultraprojectable 6-foot-3 frame, Texas believes more velocity gains are in his future. He's athletic and moves down the mound well, creating deception with extension and a low arm slot and release height. He'll be just 19 at the start of the 2026 season, so the Rangers will be patient with his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Geraldo received the sixth-highest bonus ($600,000) in the Cubs' 2026 international class, he may have a higher offensive ceiling and a stronger arm than any of his counterparts. A late bloomer physically out of the Dominican Republic, his stock was rising as the January opening of the signing period approached. Geraldo has the ingredients to develop 25-homer power. He has a quick right-handed stroke, a knack for barreling balls and room to add plenty of strength to his 6-foot-1 frame. He's an advanced hitter for his age who shows some ability to recognize pitches. An average runner who doesn't have typical shortstop quickness, Geraldo compensates with plus arm strength. Given the four of the five Cubs 2026 signees who landed higher bonuses also play shortstop, he likely will get some reps at second and third base when he makes his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He probably fits best at the hot corner in the long run and should have the pop to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stovall could have had the chance to be an early-round selection out of the Louisiana high school ranks in 2021 but chose to keep his commitment to play for Arkansas. He under-performed over his first two seasons with the Razorbacks, trying to play through a torn labrum in his throwing shoulder in 2023. He missed the start of the 2024 season with a broken left foot, but when he returned, his bat clicked, finishing with a .944 OPS, and he played better second base defense. He landed in the fourth round with the Reds, who sent him to full-season Daytona for a brief pro debut after signing. Stovall’s left-handed swing still stands, out and he used it to find the barrel much more consistently during his junior year at Arkansas. He has excellent strike zone awareness and showed more overall patience in 2024, allowing him to get to better pitches to drive. The power hasn’t shown up as much, but he does have extra-base authority to the gaps and some over-the-fence juice to his pull side. While speed isn’t a part of his game, Stovall makes the most out of that and his fringy arm thanks to plus makeup and excellent instincts. He should be able to stay on the right side of the infield, at second base and perhaps at first, where he played exclusively as a freshman in college. He could even see a little time at third, though his arm strength will likely limit him there. The plan is to let him go hit and find ways to get that bat into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $42,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2024, Laroche pitched just three innings during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He returned to the DSL last year and stood out with some of the best stuff in the circuit, posting a 2.11 ERA with a 34/6 K/BB ratio in 38 1/3 frames. He'll make his U.S. debut in 2026 and could push his way to full-season ball at the end of the summer. LaRoche features an explosive sinker that operates at 93-95 mph and maxes out at 97, and he also uses a four-seam fastball with similar velocity and armside run. His tight 82-85 mph slider has the potential to become a solid offering. While he has yet to use it very often, he also shows some feel for a mid-80s changeup. Though Laroche stands just 5-foot-11 and doesn't have a smooth delivery, he's very athletic and deceptive. He flies down the mound, producing plenty of extension for his size as well as a unusually low release height. He has no problem filling the strike zone but will need to refine his command as he climbs the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Undrafted in 2021, Bazzell was slated to head to Dallas Baptist out of high school but transferred to Texas Tech after only one semester, causing him to miss the 2022 season. He hit the ground running as a Red Raiders third baseman in 2023, hitting .343 with a 1.025 OPS, and transitioned to the catching spot when it became open for 2024. He dealt with mononucleosis early in the spring but managed a .307/.401/.473 line in 49 games, and that performance pushed him to the Nationals in the third round. He got in 19 games for Single-A Fredericksburg, including the postseason, after signing. Batting from the right side, Bazzell keeps things simple in the box with a controlled stroke and calm load. He rarely swung and missed in college, especially against fastballs, but started to whiff a bit against more high-quality sliders in his early looks in the pros. Still, he brings discipline to a lineup and could carry high OBPs at each stop moving forward. He’ll hit balls hard but without optimal launch angle, dulling his power projection to more of the gap variety until he adjusts for more elevation. Bazzell is fairly athletic – a big reason why he could play both third and catcher in college – but will likely slow down the more he focuses behind the plate. He’s still wet behind the ears back there, and the Nationals intend to prioritize getting him work there to improve his receiving. He has a quick release to help keep runners in check, and his arm strength could be useful elsewhere should he need to move again later in his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Romero received the second-largest bonus in Chicago's 2026 international class, signing for $1.5 million out of Venezuela in January. He's a more advanced hitter than most 17-year-olds, and his tools are roughly comparable to those of Jaden Fauske, who landed an above-slot $2,997,500 bonus as second-rounder last July. He'll likely spend his first pro season in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. A left-handed hitter, Romero has a fluid stroke and showed the ability to put together quality at-bats and make consistent contact as an amateur. He has a projectable 6-foot-2 frame that could add significant strength, and he should develop at least 15-20 homer power. He'll require time to develop but could blossom into one of the best offensive prospects in the system. Romero has solid speed and athleticism, which should allow him to steal some bases. He also should be able to handle center field and has the arm strength to handle right field if he shifts to a corner. He has been clocked up to 88 mph on throws from the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 An All-Big Ten Second Teamer for Penn State in 2021, Wood followed up a solid sophomore year with a stellar junior campaign in which he finished second in the conference in average (.379) and OPS (1.147) and helped Nittany Lions pitchers strike out a program-best 503 batters. Milwaukee made him the highest-picked position player in Penn State history when it selected him in the fourth round and signed him for below slot at $347,500. Already known for a strong approach, Wood boosted his stock by walking more times (36) than he struck out (26) during his final spring on campus, and his jump from four to 12 homers opened some eyes as well. His current power plays best to the pullside and comes more as a result of his natural strength than his overall bat speed. That brings along some concerns about how the bat will translate, and some evaluators believe Wood’s performance says more about his quality of college competition than his own potential. Wood can be a solid catcher but isn’t likely to wow anyone with his defensive work. Decently quick pop times and solid arm strength will be helpful, and he’ll need an adjustment period to handling better stuff day in and day out in the pros. That said, lefty-hitting catchers who can reach base at a good clip are always in demand, so there’s a path to being at least a Major League backup here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Columbia, Mo., native and Missouri State product, Nivens was the Royals’ fifth round selection in the 2023 Draft, signing for just above slot at $472,500. He was slowed out of the gate in ‘24 with High-A Quad Cities, dealt with a hamstring strain in April and didn’t hit well in the first half with a .168 average through June and a high strikeout rate. He absolutely turned it on in the second half, though, and especially in August, when he hit 13 home runs alone. In all, Nivens slashed .243/.333/.475 with 20 homers and 17 doubles. Nivens clearly has power, especially pull side, and can drive the ball, but he was more aggressive in his first full season of pro ball than what he showed in college, striking out at a 26.9% clip. A lot of that was the inconsistency in his stance with a hand pump, a leg kick that can turn into a hang and a lot of moving parts that get exposed as a pro. He toned that down some in the second half and is continuing to simplify and sync up the movements to get on time, because when he does, it’s above-average power. Nivens fits best in the corner outfield with his power, and most likely left field with his below-average arm strength and average speed once he gets going. There weren’t many hitters who did what Nivens did in August 2024, and his second half surely could give him momentum as he likely heads to Double-A in ‘25. Nivens needs to stay consistent with his movements and keep hitting to reach the big leagues and stick there as a fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star who excelled on the football field in high school, Campbell focused on baseball only when he headed to the University of Texas. He improved each year and the Dodgers took him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft after he posted a 1.039 OPS as a Longhorns junior. He spent his first full season of pro ball with High-A Great Lakes and was one of a handful of hitters in the Minors to hit 20 doubles and 10 homers while stealing 40 bases. The Dodgers sent him to the Phillies in January to get international bonus pool money used to sign Roki Sasaki. Strong and compact, Campbell has a well-deserved reputation for spraying line drives to all fields and was among the best in the Dodgers system last year with his 24.3 percent line-drive rate. His strikeout rate did go up, but he typically has had good pitch recognition and a solid approach, making good swing decisions and there’s confidence he’ll be able to make adjustments as he progresses. He’s not a burner, but he runs well and used his instincts to steal 42 bags in 2024. While he saw some time on the dirt at the start of his college career, and played a few games at second last year, Campbell has developed into a defensive outfielder. He used his plus arm to pick up 11 outfield assists a year ago and his speed allows him to cover a lot of ground. Right field might be his best spot, but his ability to play all three outfield positions points to a future career as a fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Owusu-Asiedu had a background in the United Kingdom, Canada and Wisconsin before landing at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. A promising turn in the 2022 Appalachian League (.965 OPS) preceded a junior year breakout with the Cougars in ’23 (.986 OPS, 15 HR, 24 SB), and both performances helped push him to the ninth round that July. Owusu-Asiedu really struggled with Single-A Clearwater in his first full season with a 36.1 percent strikeout rate, but he cut that by more than 12 points in his return in ’25 and then held his own in High-A Jersey Shore after an in-season promotion. He was dealt to the D-backs in the offseason in a straight-up swap for lefty reliever Kyle Backhus. Listed at 6-foot-4, the right-handed slugger has an interesting profile from a tools standpoint. He moves quickly as a plus-plus runner and regularly posted sprint speeds above 30 ft/sec in the Florida State League. That helps him cover ground well in center field, and he’s seen some time in the corners, where evaluators believe he’d be plus if he has to slide over full-time eventually. Clocked up to 97 mph from the grass, he can give opposing runners something to think about and he even threw out top prospect Konnor Griffin on a play at the plate last season. The bat could be what holds him back. Owusu-Asiedu can post impressive exit velocities -- topping out at 112.7 mph with Clearwater in 2025 -- but he struggles more on making contact in the zone than is desirable, in part because said zone is so big. The trend line is promising, but entering his age-23 season, he’s still yet to be tested in the upper Minors. He’ll make for an interesting development case in his second organization as Arizona tries to get him enough bat to be a potential fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like Fernando Rodney, a fellow native from Samana, Dominican Republic, De Jesus was a wild card in the Tigers farm system. He spent two-plus years in the Dominican Summer League and didn’t reach full-season ball until 2019, three years after signing. From there, his power fastball and high strikeout rate caught attention, allowing him to advance quickly. By the end of 2021, he was closing at Triple-A Toledo, and combined for 80 strikeouts over 64 2/3 innings with just 38 hits allowed between the Mud Hens and Double-A Erie. De Jesus’ fastball picked up some life last year, sitting in the mid-90s but topping out at 97-98 mph. There’s enough late movement on it and enough deception in his three-quarter delivery that hitters struggle to pick it up. He complements that with a mid-80s slider that moves late. Command and consistency have always been his questions; he rarely gives up home runs in part because he rarely leaves mistakes over the middle of the plate. The Tigers thought enough of De Jesus’ potential to add him to their 40-man roster at the end of last season. Detroit has had success turning hard-throwing but inconsistent relievers into Major Leaguers, including Gregory Soto and Jose Cisnero. With a little work, De Jesus could be next up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon was three months shy of his 17th birthday when he signed with the Cardinals for $70,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2019. His stateside debut didn’t come until three years later, and while he looked like a workhorse with back-to-back seasons of 132 2/3 innings in ’23 and ’24, he didn’t become a breakout arm with swing-and-miss stuff until this past season, in which he posted a 3.92 ERA with 108 strikeouts in 96 1/3 frames at High-A and Double-A. Despite that, he went unprotected and unselected in the Rule 5 Draft when eligible in the offseason. The 6-foot-2 right-hander bumped up his velocity just a bit to sit 91-94 mph with his fastball, but the pitch only gets ordinary ride and doesn’t come with big extension. While it doesn’t produce whiffs, he can spot it well to get ahead in counts and bring in his more dangerous weapons. Rincon tinkered with his changeup grip and clearly found something that worked because the mid-80s pitch shows a lot of armside run and generated a ton of whiffs. (Lefties pounded the heater though, making splits still an issue.) He’d also work in a low-80s gyro slider with nice drop versus righties, who’d often lunge at breakers low and away from them. Rincon throws free and easy from a fluid delivery, and he’ll even use a bounce in his right knee when he gets into the windup that gives him a throwback look from a different era. He was better at limiting walks in his climb to Double-A Springfield, something Cardinals officials credit for better sequencing rather than any overhaul in mechanics. Entering his age-24 season, Rincon may need to rely even more on his secondaries if he’s going to break through to the Majors because they are the moneymakers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels may have a reputation of drafting college players who can get pushed to the big leagues in a hurry, but they broke away from that script when Day 3 of the 2023 Draft commenced. They had some bonus pool money left over to sign Wimmer -- a toolsy but raw high school shortstop from South Carolina -- away from his commitment to The Citadel as their 11th-round pick for close to $400,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games in the Arizona Complex League. It's likely going to require patience for Wimmer to grow into his raw tools. He’s a plus quick-twitch athlete and right-handed hitter who can use the whole field. His swing works and there might be some power to tap into in the future if he can add some strength to his lean frame. An above-average runner, he shows good instincts on the basepaths. While there’s work to be done on his footwork defensively, there’s some confidence he can stick at shortstop in the long run. It’s possible the Angels will move him around the diamond some, but don’t be surprised to see him stick up the middle -- at second or in center field -- if shortstop doesn’t work. He’s a bit like a piece of unmolded clay, one that the Angels can dream on becoming a Rodin.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Another reason 2025 was a very strong international signing class for the Royals, Calcaño ranked as the 38th-best prospect on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list heading into the signing period. The Dominican native signed for $1,847,500. His 2025 season was cut short because of a shoulder injury, but he stood out in his nine-game sample, hitting .346 with a 1.052 OPS, seven stolen bases and eight walks to 10 strikeouts. A switch-hitter, Calcaño is a bit better from the left side but overall possesses a line-drive approach and good understanding of the strike zone. He has a wiry and lean frame, and as he adds strength, there’s power potential beyond doubles in the gap. But the early excitement about Calcaño comes on the dirt. He’s a plus defender with good hands and he'll be able to stick at shortstop. There are questions about how his arm strength returns following the shoulder injury, but it was plus before. Calcaño also has good speed and instincts on the bases. Because of their position and ages, there will be comparisons between Calcaño and Ramcell Medina as they grow up through the system together. Calcaño probably is the better defender, while Medina has the higher upside with his bat. Calcaño could make his stateside debut in ‘26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meola was named Atlantic Sun Conference Tournament MVP as a sophomore after homering three times in four games and earned ASUN defensive player of the year accolades as a junior in 2025. The cousin of former U.S. national soccer team goalie Tony Meola, he went in the fourth round, making him Stetson's highest-drafted position player since 2003 first-rounder Brian Johnson. He took over at shortstop for an injured Maui Ahuna at Single-A San Jose and helped win a California League title. With solid speed and quick feet, Meola covers plenty of ground at shortstop. His smooth actions, soft hands and strong arm help make him a plus defender at short. Factor in some sneaky power, and some Giants officials think he has J.J. Hardy upside. Meola hits the ball surprisingly hard for a 5-foot-11, 172-pounder and can drive the ball out of the park to all fields, giving him the potential for 15-20 homers per season. He does get overly aggressive and pull-happy, however, resulting in strikeouts and rolled-over ground balls. He's most effective when he focuses on driving balls from gap to gap.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Almost all of Boston's promising catchers are congregated at the lower levels of their system, and Rodriguez is the best of the bunch. Signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2023, he was advanced enough to defensively to get a taste of Single-A the following year at age 18. After adding strength and bat speed before last season, he showed more power and finished with three homers in 22 games in Single-A during the final month. A right-handed hitter with good bat-to-ball skills, Rodriguez will be more effective at the plate as he becomes more selective. He doesn't strike out much but chases more pitches than he should, lowering his quality of contact. He not only added muscle but also improved his ability to drive balls in the air, giving him 12-15 homer potential. Rodriguez is stocky but has some sneaky athleticism, moving well enough on the bases and showing agility behind the plate. His receiving needs more consistency but he blocks and frames well to project as a solid defender. He has at least as much arm strength to match and erased 35 percent of basestealers in his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rossi spent six years in college, bouncing from West Florida to the State JC of Florida (Manatee-Sarasota) to UNC Charlotte. After missing all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery, he came back to reach 97 mph with his fastball and destroy college hitters with his slider in 2024 but went undrafted because he was 25 years old. Signed as a nondrafted free agent for $10,000, he posted a 2.18 ERA, .119 opponent average and 34 percent strikeout rate in his pro debut last season. Rossi's slider tore up hitters at two Class A levels with its combination of mid-80s velocity and huge sweep, producing an elite 52 percent swing-and-miss rate. His fastball works in the mid-90s and maxes out at 98 mph with armside run. He works east and west with his heater and slider, then can drop an upper-80s splitter though the bottom of the zone. A physical 6-foot-3, 230-pounder, Rossi combines a low release height and extension to provide deception. He can't always maintain his delivery and has little history of providing consistent strikes. If he can develop decent control, he certainly has the stuff to find a bullpen role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $350,000, Labrada made his debut among the Mariners’ Top 30 prospects for the first time in spring 2022 after wowing with his speed the season prior. Though the consensus is that Jonatan Clase might be the fastest player in Seattle’s system, Labrada led all Mariners Minor Leaguers with 32 stolen bases last year over 99 games. At 5-foot-9 and 165 pounds, he may be short in stature but he packs physicality. He possesses a good, compact swing from the left side, but is certainly more of a hit-over-power prospect. With his glove, Labrada profiles in center field given that he has advanced range, great jump, and again, elite speed. After graduating in 2021 from Low-A Modesto to High-A Everett, Labrada saw a dip in offensive production, but not an astronomical one. He still showed decent on-base skills and will continue to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivas earned NCAA Division II All-America accolades at Indianapolis in 2022 before transferring to Mississippi, where he was the Rebels' best starter as a junior before missing all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. The Yankees still drafted him in the 16th round because they were intrigued by the deception of his pitches. He returned to the mound last year and recorded a 3.38 ERA with a .166 average-against and a 31 percent strikeout rate while advancing from Rookie ball to High-A. Rivas doesn't fool hitters with a riding fastball that sits at 90 mph and maxes out at 92, but he utilizes it well enough to set up a pair of baffling secondary pitches. He does an excellent job of killing spin on a low-80s changeup with splitter action that generated a 41 percent chase rate and 57 percent swing-and-miss rate in his pro debut. Hitters also consistently swung over the top of his tight low-80s slider. Though Rivas spent his first pro season as a starter, he profiles better as a tricky left-handed reliever. He has to nibble with his below-average heater and get chases with his slider and changeup, so only a third of his pitches landed in the strike zone last year. His competitive makeup also would work well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Callahan was a career .351 hitter at St. Joseph’s and posted an OPS above 1.000 in both his sophomore and junior years with the Hawks. But questions about how he’d hold up against better competition dropped him to the 13th round in 2023, and the Tigers picked and signed him for $197,500. He’s shown flashes of dominance at virtually every stop since but has struggled with injuries, including a dislocated finger and right lower leg hematoma in 2024 and a pulled quad in 2025. He finally cracked Double-A to begin 2026 -- his age-24 season -- with positive results out of the gate. A left-handed hitter, Callahan has long shown promising raw power as a professional, and he proved that this spring in limited Grapefruit League looks with a pair of home runs hit above 105 mph and one batted ball at 112.2 mph. But an overly aggressive approach early in his career seriously put into question how much of that pop translated into game action at the upper levels. Callahan, who has gone from an open stance to one more straight-on while keeping his leg kick, has been less swing-happy to begin ’26, allowing his walk rate to double in the season’s first month and making a potential MLB future all the clearer. Standing 6-foot, the former Atlantic 10 first-teamer can get moving out of the box, and he’s proven capable of making strong throws from the grass. The Tigers have rotated him around the outfield because of both skillsets, and he could prove to be above-average defensively in a corner. Much will come down to maintaining his early swing-decision improvements, especially with Rule 5 eligibility coming up this offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pacheco headlined the 2022 international signing period for the Athletics, signing out of Caracas, Venezuela, as a 17-year-old for $1.2 million. Confined to the Dominican Summer League for his first two professional seasons as he acclimated himself to pro ball, he stood out in extended spring training and finally made his way to the Arizona Complex League last season. He held his own as a 19-year-old by hitting .257 with an .801 OPS, three homers, 10 doubles and 11 stolen bases in 48 games. On the smaller side at 5-feet-11, 150 pounds, Pacheco makes up for his lack of size with dynamic fast-twitch athleticism. He is selective at the plate with decent on-base skills, particularly for his young age. He has an athletic swing and good bat speed, which lead to good contact rates. His power numbers have been below average thus far, though he can spray line drives to all fields, giving the A’s hope that he could develop into 20-homer potential as the 20-year-old grows into his body. With plus speed that enables him to cover plenty of ground and a solid arm, Pacheco is gifted enough as a defender to stick at center field for the long term. With a well-rounded set of tools and a strong foundation to work with, Pacheco will get an opportunity to continue honing those physical tools in full-season ball as he looks to climb toward reaching his high and exciting ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fernandez is yet another small, contact-oriented, switch-hitting infielder for the Guardians, having exceeded expectations after signing for $215,000 out of Venezuela in 2024. He looked overqualified for the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last year as he hit .333/.398/.558 with six homers and 16 steals in 43 games before a brief cameo at Single-A Lynchburg. This well-rounded skillset starts with strong contact skills. Fernandez is an aggressive swinger who puts the ball in play a lot, which causes him to rarely strike out -- or walk. He is undersized and doesn't have a ton of physical projection, but his line-drive approach could lead to 15 homers at maturation with added strength, since he's still plenty athletic. To date, he has been much more productive from the left side, partially a product of seeing far more consistent playing time against right-handers. Fernandez has played across the infield and will likely continue to do so as the Guardians try to find his long-term home. His above-average speed that plays well on the basepaths is also an asset at second, short and third, and he has ample arm strength too. He has been somewhat error-prone and looks most comfortable to date at second base but has a real chance to stick at short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hedges was a presence in Southern Cal’s lineup for nearly all of his three years on campus. He turned in a big junior season, not only as the best hitter on the team who posted a .346/.462/.619 line with 14 homers but also serving as the Trojans’ closer and racking up nine saves. With former big leaguer Andy Stankiewicz at the helm, there tends to be a comfort level from MLB teams in terms of taking USC infielders, and the Rockies didn’t shy away from nabbing Hedges in the third round of the 2025 Draft, sending him to High-A Spokane for a brief pro debut. While his time at instructs after the season was cut short because of a concussion, the Rockies are intrigued with what Hedges might bring to the table. He has a good feel to hit from the right side of the plate, with a line-drive approach and a knack for barreling up the baseball. It can be loud contact at times and while it’s more extra-base authority right now, the hope is the jump in the bat the Rockies saw can translate to more over-the-fence pop in the future. Hedges moves well enough to play third base capably, though it’s the arm that fired low-90s fastballs as a reliever for the Trojans that really stand out. His instincts help all of his tools play up across the board.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abeldt was one of college baseball's best relievers in his first two years at Texas Christian, recording a 2.81 ERA with 125 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and spending both summers with the U.S. collegiate national team. The Horned Frogs planned on turning him into a starter in 2025, but he blew out his elbow just before the beginning of the season and required Tommy John surgery in February. The Rangers still popped him in the fifth round and signed him for $450,000. Abeldt relies heavily on a 91-94 mph fastball that peaks at 96 and is much more effective than its ordinary velocity would indicate. His heater has riding action and plenty of deception coming out of a crossfire delivery, and it's nearly impossible to lift when he works down in the zone. He can't overpower hitters with a slider that sits around 80 mph, but it can baffle them with its sweeping action when it's on. While he doesn't use it much, Abeldt has the makings of an effective low-80s changeup with sink. He looks like a shorter, stronger version of Chris Sale with his slingy delivery, and it generates a lot of empty swings and groundballs. It remains to be seen if he can succeed as a starter, but he comes with a high floor as a quality lefty reliever once he returns to full health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Etzel spent a semester at Texas A&M then played two seasons at Panola (Texas) JC, but it was actually a stint in the MLB Draft League that set him up for his professional future. He slashed .371/.463/.586 with 25 steals in 33 games there in 2022, putting himself on scouting radars a year before signing with the Orioles as a 10th-rounder out of Southern Mississippi. Baltimore sent him to the Rays as part of a three-prospect package for starter Zach Eflin in July 2024, then Tampa Bay shipped him to the Marlins for Nick Fortes a year later. Etzel’s performance dipped after a promotion to Double-A and fell off when he joined the Rays, as he batted .232 with a .692 OPS and a 35 percent strikeout rate in 36 games for Montgomery. The swing-and-miss jump was somewhat alarming, as Etzel typically makes a fair amount of contact (especially against fastballs) and already puts a lot of balls on the ground. Granted, he has the speed to make that work and added value by stealing 45 bases over 119 games last year, but it will require him to boost his slugging percentage with doubles and triples, not home runs. Despite his above-average speed, Etzel seems likely to settle in at a corner position. He played all three outfield spots at an almost exactly even rate last year and even saw time at first base in an effort to keep his bat in the lineup. He hasn't made much progress at Double-A this year, a telling sign that probably caps his ceiling as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez signed with the D-backs for $50,000 as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in January 2023, and entering 2026, he’s yet to post a seasonal ERA above 4.00 during his steady climb through the lower Minors. In 2025, his 2.40 ERA in 105 innings between Single-A Visalia and High-A Hillsboro was best among D-backs Minor Leaguers (min. 100 IP) and ranked 10th among MiLB hurlers who met that requirement. He accomplished that despite striking out only 88 in that span. The right-hander returned to the Northwest League for his age-20 campaign in ’26 and poured on the strikeouts at much better rates, furthering his push into Arizona prospect prominence. The 5-foot-10 hurler shows a pair of promising pitches in his four-seam fastball and sweeping slider. The heater comes in at 92-94 mph, giving it just below MLB average velocity, but it plays above that with cut-ride action and enough induced vertical break to keep it consistently above bats. The mid-80s breaking pitch comes with high spin and good horizontal movement and has regularly fooled batters, getting both ample whiffs and chases early on this season. Sanchez has worked on incorporating a bridge cutter and a changeup, though the latter hasn’t quite helped him fend off splits issues against lefties at this stage of his career. Starting from the extreme first-base side of the rubber, Sanchez has steadily improved his control numbers throughout his time as a pro, aided by opponents expanding the zone against the slider in particular.
