He lacks the power stuff to blow his arsenal past opponents, and given his size, it’s unlikely that will ever come, so he’ll need to keep locating well. The results are becoming undeniable though, and he looks more like a possible backend MLB starter with each passing year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rogers bounced from Southeastern Louisiana to Jones (Miss.) JC to Southern Mississippi in three years of college. Used exclusively as a reliever by the Golden Eagles in 2022, he struck out 57 in 37 innings while limiting opponents to a .128 average. After he made two short starts in the Cape Cod League, the Red Sox drafted him in the third round and signed him for a below-slot $447,500 with the intention of moving him into the rotation. Rogers threw 85 percent fastballs at Southern Miss and the metrics on the pitch are elite. His 5-foot-11 frame and drop-and-drive delivery result him in delivering at an extremely low height and flat plane that create exceptional carry on his heater, which also has some running action while sitting at 91-94 mph and topping out at 96. His low-80s changeup plays off his fastball well because of its velocity separation and depth, though he struggles to throw it for strikes. To succeed as a starter, Rogers will need to refine his breaking ball and control. He shows some feel for changing the shape of his low-80s slider depending on whether he's facing a lefty or a righty, but he rarely used it as an amateur because he could dominate with his fastball alone. He averaged 5.5 walks per nine innings in college and will have to be much more efficient to be able to handle a rotation workload, especially considering his slight build.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nankil was a seventh-round selection by the A’s out of Cal State Fullerton in the 2023 MLB Draft as part of a class headlined by No. 6 overall pick Jacob Wilson. After a strong first full professional season, he began 2025 at High-A Lansing and ended with Double-A Midland, combining to hit .278 with a .724 OPS in 124 games. Nankil’s overall approach at the plate is solid, having shown a good ability to draw walks and limit the strikeout totals at a decent rate. His raw power excited the A’s when he entered the organization, but that aspect of his game has yet to fully show through. While he does hit the ball hard, he tends to hit the ball on the ground too often. He also has some trouble picking up on offspeed pitches at times. Nankil is an average defender who can cover a decent amount of range in the outfield with his athleticism, while also bringing a strong arm. He ideally profiles as a corner outfielder, but he will have to hit for more power to continue progressing through the system. The A’s believe he has at least 20-homer power potential, and they plan to work with him on getting the ball in the air more to try to unlock some more of that pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring as a Texas prep junior, Leeper underwent two Tommy John surgeries and an ulnar nerve transposition that limited him to 2 2/3 innings over his senior season and first two years at Oklahoma State. He persevered and eventually became the Cowboys' closer before signing with the Cubs for $20,000 as a 23-year-old nondrafted free agent in 2020. He made a spectacular pro debut last summer, recording a 1.29 ERA with 53 strikeouts in 35 innings between Double-A and Triple-A, though he was shut down in August with elbow inflammation. Leeper goes after hitters with two pitches. His four-seam fastball sits at 94-96 mph and touches 99, and it features a flat approach angle and riding life that make it tough for hitters to barrel. If they try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with an 86-88 mph slider that features tremendous depth. After averaging 7.0 walks per nine innings during his college career, Leeper more than halved that rate to 3.3 in his pro debut. His stuff is real and if his control is as well, he could help Chicago in the near future and eventually fill a high-leverage role. The biggest question is his health, as he didn't pitch on consecutive days in 2021 before missing the final two months, though the Cubs say his shutdown was precautionary more than anything else.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robert Calaz was the big get for the Rockies when the 2023 international signing period opened in January of that year. Four months later, the organization might have found a bargain in Dali, who signed for $70,000 in May. It took a while for him to get going, spending two summers in the Dominican Summer League, but he hit .327/.445/.450 there in his second summer, then showed it might not be an aberration by coming stateside in 2025 and hitting his way from the Arizona Complex League up to Single-A Fresno, finishing with a combined .308/.399/.468 line. Dalis gets some high praise from those who have been around the Rockies a while, earning comps to Ezequiel Tovar at a similar age in terms of how he plays the game. The switch-hitter has shown the ability to swing it from both sides of the plate, though he was stronger as a left-handed hitter in 2025, with a hit-over-power profile. He has gap power now with doubles-type pop, but he also isn’t close to being physically mature, so there could be more power to come in the future. Hopefully, that doesn’t come at the expense of his speed and athleticism. He can steal a base and he has the agility to stay up the middle defensively, with an ease of operation defensively that’s fun to watch. He’ll keep seeing time at three infield positions and while he played he’s played mostly on the left side of the infield, some think second base might be his best shot as a long-term home if he turns into a table-setting every day type of player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An inability to throw strikes limited Potter to 8 2/3 innings in two seasons at Crowder (Mo.) JC. He still battled the zone after transferring to Wichita State in 2025 but also established himself as one of the harder throwers in NCAA Division I. The Astros signed him for a below-slot $336,600 as a fifth-rounder and will have him make his pro debut in 2026. Potter used his fastball three-quarters of his time with the Shockers, operating at 95-97 mph and reaching 100 with impressive carry. He complements his heater with a tight 82-85 mph slider that could become a solid offering if it adds more movement. He threw only a handful of cutters and changeups during three years in college, and Houston will look to expand his arsenal this season. Potter works exclusively out of the stretch, with a big leg kick and a long arm action that help him generate power but hurt his ability to find the zone. He'll work as a tandem starter to get him regular innings to work on his arsenal and his control, but he projects as a two-pitch reliever. He'll need to add considerable polish to become a late-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curley was a 16th-round pick by the Pirates in 2024 after two years at Virginia Commonwealth but didn’t sign and instead transferred to Georgia. He began as the Bulldogs’ closer but became the club’s No. 1 starter later in the spring, finishing with a 3.55 ERA, 1.05 WHIP and 85 strikeouts in 66 innings. That pushed him into the third round last summer, and he signed with the D-backs for below slot at $700,000. The 5-foot-10 right-hander sure makes for an interesting watch. When pitching out of the windup, he looks like he hesitates a bit in his gather before rushing toward the plate with high effort. (In the stretch, he gets things moving a lot quicker, as you’d imagine.) He runs his fastball up to 100 mph and generally sits 94-97 with high spin rates, thanks to added velo as a junior. He can work a few different breaking ball looks -- the best of which is a mid-80s slider with good depth. There’s a harder version in the upper 80s with cutter-like tendencies too and a 79-81 mph curveball with more vertical snap. Curley didn’t show a changeup or other armside offspeed pitches in Athens, using his curve to neutralize lefties instead. That, along with the exertion in his delivery for his size, give him a relief projection in the Majors. But in their search for depth, the D-backs should still give him plenty of starting chances to open his career, knowing the stuff could be high-leverage quality if Curley needs to slide back.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wherever Anthony has been, he’s hit. Over two years at Iowa, he posted a combined .372/.476/.686 line, but he wasn’t drafted because he had been suspended for betting on college sports (not his own team). Since the Phillies signed him as a nondrafted free agent in the summer of 2023 for $125,000, he’s continued to rake, making his way all the way to Triple-A in 2025 and carrying a career .324/.402/.467 line as a pro into the 2026 season. Anthony is a smart right-handed hitter with a knack for contact. He limits his swing-and-miss, with a career 17.8 percent miss rate as proof, and loves going the other way for base hits. He’s cleaned up his body and added some strength, registering better hard-hit rates last year, and he can drive the ball to all fields for extra bases. But he has a tendency to hit the ball on the ground too much, and his chase rate (38 percent) went up when he went to Triple-A. He’s a hit-over-power guy for sure, but finding a bit more loft and leverage would help. That’s because he’s limited to first base only, putting pressure on him to be more of a run producer. He’s a fine defender at first, but he’s not super athletic, and the right-right profile at the position is tough. Because of that, he gives off some Darin Ruf type vibes, and Ruf did carve out a career that included parts of nine seasons in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes teams take a college senior early on Day 2 of the Draft solely to save money for other signings. Occasionally, those bargains turn out to be pretty good. That might be the case for Cranton, who signed for just $50,000 in the third round of the 2024 Draft after a solid season saving games for Kansas. The right-hander was sent to Modesto for his pro debut, and after throwing well in the regular season, tossed four hitless innings and picked up three saves to help the Nuts win the California League title. His 2025 debut was delayed by a concussion suffered on a comebacker in Spring Training, but he was in the midst of dominating at High-A Everett when the Mariners traded him to the D-backs in the Eugenio Suárez deal in July. Cranton has all the makings of a big league reliever. His fastball has interesting characteristics in terms of ride up in the zone and it’s a pitch that sits 97-98 mph and can top out in triple digits. His upper-80s gyro-like slider can be a plus out pitch at times, though it flattened out and got hit at Kansas occasionally. The 24-year-old right-hander has a long arm action and moving parts in his delivery, which can impact his control and command. That improved with the Jayhawks in 2024, but it’s definitely a work in progress. If he can get to throwing more consistent strikes -- and early returns were good in that regard -- he could find himself in the back end of a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best sleeper in the Giants' 2024 international class, Tejada signed for $147,500 out of the Dominican Republic. Known most for his power when he turned pro, he turned in a nifty all-around offensive performance in his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He slashed .300/.405/.488 with 19 extra-base hits, 22 walks and 13 steals in 46 games. Tejada has plenty of strength in his stocky 5-foot-11 frame and generates impressive bat speed and high exit velocities with a simple right-handed stroke. In the DSL, he showed the ability to drive balls in the air to his pull side and the possibility of 25-homer seasons in the future. Though he has a power mentality, he also displayed some feel for hitting and for managing the strike zone. Tejada makes the most of his average speed with an aggressive nature on the bases and good instincts in the outfield. He spent his pro debut in center field, yet his quickness is better suited for the corners in the long run. Though he has average to solid arm strength, he didn't record an assist in 42 games last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tatum spent his first three seasons at North Carolina State as a part-time player, then hit .317/.423/.543 with 12 homers and 16 steals as the Wolfpack reached the College World Series semifinals in 2021. He hit a massive home run to beat Jack Leiter and Vanderbilt, 1-0, in Omaha shortly before the White Sox made him a 16th-round pick. He played just 42 games in his first full season because he drew a 50-game suspension after testing positive for amphetamines, and an ankle injury limited him to just six contests in the Arizona Fall League. Tatum collected just 600 at-bats in the past five years between college and the Minors, so he has more untapped potential at the plate than most 23-year-olds. He has a quick left-handed swing and a willingness to work counts and draw walks, but he also strikes out way too much (30 percent of his plate appearance in his first two pro seasons), puts the ball on the ground far too often (28 percent) and uses the opposite field almost to a fault. He has enough bat speed and wiry strength to produce at least 15 homers per season but will need to turn on and lift more pitches to get there. With his well-above-average speed, Tatum is dangerous on the bases and covers plenty of ground in center field. His below-average arm is playable in center and left but limits his usefulness in right. His speed and defense could help make him a useful fourth outfielder if he doesn't provide enough offense to be a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top high school left-handers in the 2021 Draft, Coppola went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Florida. He struck out 38 percent of the batters he faced with the Gators, but he also worked just 49 1/3 innings in four years because of back and shoulder ailments. After the Cubs made him a seventh-round pick last July, he fanned 14 in eight innings at Single-A. Coppola uses his huge 6-foot-8 frame and a low arm slot to create wide angle on his fastball, which sits in the low 90s and tops out at 96 with carry and armside run. He could have more velocity in the tank if he can stay healthy and add strength. He also operates with an upper-70s slider with sweep that made it unhittable in college, though it may need more power to succeed in pro ball. Though Coppola has toyed with a mid-80s splitter, he's mainly a two-pitch guy. He doesn't have a smooth delivery and doesn't repeat it well, which has led to injuries and below-average control. He'll begin his pro career as a starter to get some much-needed innings, but the likely best-case scenario is that he cleans up his mechanics and adds some power en route to a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Millar’s stock rose quite a bit during his senior season at Alhambra HS in Martinez, Calif., and the Royals jumped at the chance to get him in the third round of the 2025 Draft. He signed for an over-slot $1,497,500 bonus to keep him from an Arizona commitment. Millar didn’t go out to affiliate ball after he was drafted, but he did pitch in the organization’s instructional league games in the fall. Similar to a lot of prep pitchers the Royals have drafted recently, Millar is young and raw with intriguing stuff that needs development. His fastball was in the low-to-mid-90s in high school until it spiked to 97 mph his senior year, and the Royals have seen that velocity recently, along with good ride. Millar’s slider hovers around 83-85 mph and is more bullet-like and not quite average yet. His changeup was his best pitch in high school, a low-80s offering with lots of tumble. He’s working on throwing it from a more consistent slot, and one of his cues is to throw it harder and more like his fastball. Millar pitches from a higher slot. although there’s some inconsistency he’s working on, but it’s mostly a clean delivery with a quick arm. He went to the Royals’ strength and conditioning camp over the offseason with hopes that some of the benefits could be found in his delivery and velocity. Millar’s development will be a slower one, but it’ll be as a starter to begin his career with the potential for a mid-to-back-end rotation member there. He gets high marks for his competitiveness on and off the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Floyd pitched only one year at Texas Tech, following two years of JuCo in the same state, but he made enough of an impression as a reliever to get the Brewers to select him in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft. Following the 2020 Minor League season cancelation, he made his full-season debut last year and was effective at both the High-A and Double-A levels, posting a 2.89 ERA and 1.11 WHIP with 84 strikeouts in 56 innings across the two spots. He also made nine appearances in the Arizona Fall League, but he suffered tougher results in the hitter-friendly circuit (seven earned runs, 10 K’s in 8 2/3 innings). The 6-foot-1 right-hander throws out of a low sidearm slot that borders on being a submarine delivery. There’s nothing secondary about his slider. Floyd often goes to the 77-79 mph offering as his primary pitch, because its hard break leads to a ton of swing-and-misses. His 90-92 mph fastball won’t wow with velo, but it does feature a ton of sink, causing batters to hit the ball straight into the ground when they do make a contact. He only occasionally will sprinkle in a low-80s changeup and can sometimes be left vulnerable by batters not willing to swing on movement out of the zone. Floyd ranked among the top three Brewers Minor League pitchers (minimum 50 innings) in both strikeout rate (37 percent) and groundball rate (50.4 percent) in 2021, highlighting his strengths perfectly. The Brewers feel he’s capable of pitching in high-leverage situations because of those typical outcomes, even if it isn’t high-octane stuff, and Floyd might not be far off from helping the Milwaukee bullpen with his version of funk.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grinsell made a big leap between his sophomore and junior seasons at Oregon, lowering his ERA by a full run and cutting his walk rate in half while becoming just the sixth pitcher in Ducks history to post 200 career strikeouts. While he wasn’t overpowering, his ability to miss bats and his athleticism -- he was a very good two-way player in high school -- led the Tigers to take a sixth-round pick on him in the 2025 Draft and sign him for $297,500. Deception is the name of the game for Grinsell, who doesn’t have a dominant pitch but has a good feel for sequencing and reading hitters. His fastball sits in the low 90s but plays up thanks in part to extension and location. It also sets up an 80 mph changeup that he hides well with a similar delivery. His slider was his third pitch in college. While he fits into the Tigers’ pitching philosophy of commanding the strike zone, he could also add velocity if the club can improve his delivery. Projection can be difficult with a college pitcher, but Grinsell’s athleticism provides some potential for upside if he can find another tick or two on his fastball, which could then make his changeup that much better. He’ll need an effective breaking pitch to make it as a starter, but a good fastball-changeup combination could be the foundation for a potential crafty lefty reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the stricter penalties for their international signing violations weren’t levied until the 2019-20 signing period, the Braves still couldn’t sign any prospect for more than $300,000 during the 2018-19 period, the typical penalty for having exceeded their bonus pool (in 2016-17). That doesn’t mean they didn’t find talent, such as prospects like Royber Salinas -- traded to the A’s for Sean Murphy -- and Quintero, who signed in February 2019 for just $40,000 and is coming off a solid full-season debut that allowed him to reach High-A in 2022. Quintero is a bit of a throwback type player as an undersized infielder who can do a lot of little things well on the diamond. A switch-hitter, Quintero has shown a knack for making contact and getting on base, walking in 11.8 percent of plate appearances and striking out just 16.2 percent of the time in his brief pro career. That’s going to have to be his game because there’s not much power there, with relatively low exit velocities. Quintero’s best tool is his speed, and he’s registered some 30 ft/sec sprint speed times, something that should become more of an asset the more he learns the nuances of basestealing. He doesn’t have the actions to play shortstop, with second and maybe third base the best options, and a future as a speedy utility-type the most likely outcome.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two seasons at Southeastern Louisiana, Burke transferred to Miami and earned all-Atlantic Coast Conference accolades in 2022 before the White Sox selected him in the 11th round. He missed the first month of last season with a lower back injury, then returned to hit .294/.392/.439 between two Class A levels. He made up for some lost at-bats in the Arizona Fall League and will advance to Double-A to begin 2024. Burke looks to smack line drives to all fields with his quick right-handed swing. He projects to hit in the bottom third of a big league batting order because he has only modest pull power that may not translate into more than 10-12 homers per season and his aggressive approach doesn't yield many walks. He doesn't strike out excessively but can improve his quality of contact. Burke makes the most out of his solid speed on the bases and in the outfield, enhancing his chances of making it as a fourth outfielder. He has spent most of his pro career in center field, exhibiting solid range and playable if fringy arm strength. A two-time all-state linebacker as a Louisiana prepster, he plays baseball with a football mentality and endears himself to club officials and coaches with his intensity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big league caliber talent can be found just about anywhere and Diaz has the chance to prove that true. Taken in the 27th round of the 2019 Draft out of Michigan State, where he relieved for a year after two years at Iowa Western Community College, Diaz put himself on the map in 2021 with a huge full-season debut that saw him earn a promotion from High-A to Double-A and strike out 16.6 per nine for the year. He wasn’t as dominant post-promotion and he struggled to find the strike zone during his time in the Arizona Fall League, a trend that continued in Double-A in 2022. Diaz is a 6-foot-5 right-hander who profiles as a reliever only. He can get his fastball up to 97 mph, but typically sits around 92-93 mph. It plays up because of its carry in the zone and his extension coming down the mound. His power breaking ball can get slurvy, and it has good depth, but because of the mid-80s velocity, it plays more like a slider. Diaz generally had shown a penchant for throwing strikes somewhat consistently, generally attacking the zone and going right after hitters, but his walk rate continued to climb with Mississippi in 2022. He doesn’t need pinpoint command to fill a prominent role in a big league bullpen, something he should be able to do once he shows he can handle the upper levels of the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highlight of Boston's 2024 international crop, Asencio signed for $1 million out of the Dominican Republic. He trained at the same Mejia Top 10 facility that also spawned Miguel Bleis, the top signee in Boston's 2020-21 class. He'll make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League later this year. Asencio's advanced bat-to-ball skills are his calling card. He recognizes pitches, consistently barrels balls with his sound right-handed swing and already has a penchant for using the opposite field. His lack of physicality leads to questions about his power potential, and he may top out at 15 homers per season -- and he'll have to add muscle to get there. Asencio's speed earns average-to-solid grades from evaluators, and he could get quicker as he gets stronger. His instincts enhance his range in center field, and he should be able to stay there long term. With average arm strength, he's capable of handling all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ozuna was the latest standout to train at the Niche Baseball Academy in Santo Domingo North, Dominican Republic, where stars such as Juan Soto, Elly De La Cruz and others have trained at under Cristian Batista. Drawing rave reviews by those who watched him closely there, he came in at No. 16 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list for 2025 and signed with the A’s for $850,000 when the signing period opened in January. He got his feet wet in pro ball with 35 games in the Dominican Summer League but was limited production-wise because of a hamate injury. Listed at 6-foot-3 and 185 pounds, Ozuna is a presence that is hard to miss when walking through the A’s Dominican complex. He reminds some within the organization of a young Vladimir Guerrero Sr. in terms of how he looks standing in the box for batting practice. His physical attributes lend to impressive power as a right-handed hitter that could reach plus-plus levels as he continues growing into his body. Ozuna’s cannon of an arm and natural athleticism gives him a shot at being a decent defensive right fielder. The obvious question here is whether he will make enough contact to fully unleash that tremendous raw power. The A’s are hopeful that he will come back this year in a healthier form and continue his valuable development time as a teenager.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Rosa signed with the Yankees out of the Dominican Republic for $400,000 last April, receiving the third-highest bonus given to any left-hander on the 2025 international market. He quickly stood out with his stuff and strikes during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing immediate trade interest. Three months after he turned pro, the Giants acquired him in a four-prospect package in exchange for Camilo Doval. De la Rosa works with a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96 with significant carry as well as armside run. Both of his secondary pitches also show promise. He throws both a tight slider and a sweepier version in the low 80s, and his fading changeup is a tick harder. While De La Rosa has three legitimate pitches and posted a 7 percent walk rate in his first taste of pro ball, there are questions about his ability to remain a starter in the long run. He's undersized and works uphill with some funk in his arm action, though his delivery provides deception without costing him control. If he does land in the bullpen, he has the upside to work in a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pena has been a reliever in the Padres system ever since signing for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2022, 10 days before his 21st birthday. After one season in the Dominican Summer League, he’s been on a fast track toward San Diego, having played for all five stateside affiliates between 2023 and ’24. In his most recent campaign, he finished with a 2.43 ERA and 64 strikeouts over 63 innings across the top three levels of the Minors. Like many Padres pitching prospects, his numbers jumped at hitter-friendly El Paso but not enough to be overly concerning. Pena cuts a thin figure at 6-foot-1, setting up out of the stretch from the first-base side of the rubber. But he generated over 7 feet of extension at Triple-A, putting himself close to the plate with dynamic stuff. He throws a pair of fastballs, both in the 94-97 mph range -- a sinker with more than 11 inches of armside run and a straighter four-seamer. He leaned on the former more at Triple-A, which makes sense given his other offering. In 2025, his most oft-used secondary is an 86-89 mph two-plane slider that he uses to get a ton of whiffs. Walks weren't a huge issue for Pena in the Minors until his extended time at Triple-A in '25. The sinker helps him run a heavy ground-ball rate. The lack of a changeup may make him a questionable fit against lefties at the top level, but the slider has served him well enough so far. He has to find more strikes if he's going to earn that MLB debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds are always active players on the international market and it was no different during the 2024 international signing period. They focused much more on bats, with seven of their top bonuses – all six figures or more – going to hitters. Down the list was Torres, a six-foot right-hander who got $30,000 to sign with the organization when the period opened in January of that year. He was among the Dominican Summer League’s leaders in ERA, WHIP and batting average against, then came stateside in 2025 and was equally dominant over 38 1/3 Arizona Complex League innings. While a bit undersized, Torres is strong and stocky and his intriguing combination of feel for pitching and solid all-around stuff points to a future as a starter. He has three usable pitches, all of which are average but could be better as he progresses. His fastball sits in the 91-94 range, and he’s shown the ability to maintain his velocity throughout outings, he spins a low-80s curve very well and has good feel for an 85-87 mph fading changeup. All of his offerings play up because he’s shown a very strong feel for throwing them all for strikes, especially for his age. He’s walked just 1.9 per nine in his brief pro career heading into 2026, with the hopes of him having at least above-average command in the future. He’s yet to show he can answer the bell in a full-season rotation, but the Reds are bullish on his ability to start long term. Other organizations have definitely noticed his early success as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coley faced plenty of adversity in his college career at Rhode Island, striking out in more than half his at-bats as a freshman in 2019, losing most of the 2020 season to the pandemic, missing all of 2022 because of a school credit snafu and half of 2023 after breaking his jaw in a collision at first base. He homered eight times and stole six bases in 25 games last spring, graduated with a mechanical engineering degree and signed with the Marlins for $50,000 as a 17th-rounder. He made his pro debut by batting .265/.395/.480 in Single-A and helping Jupiter win the Florida State League title. Coley's bat speed and strength rank among the best in the system and create plus raw power. A right-handed hitter, he looks to make the most of it by launching balls to his pull side, though his approach also yields strikeouts and rolled-over groundballs. More raw than most 23-year-olds because he had only 305 at-bats in five years in college, he could do a lot of damage if he learns to be more selective. He didn't run much at Rhode Island but Coley possesses plus speed and swiped nine bases in 10 tries during his 33-game pro debut. His quickness allows him to cover plenty of ground of center field and he has solid arm strength that could improve a tick if he cleans up his throwing motion. Besides his tools, he draws raves for his intelligence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $10,000 back in July 2018, Castellano didn’t pitch officially until 2021 in the Dominican Summer League and then spent two years in the Florida State League, mostly as a reliever. In 2024, he jumped on the map when he was given the chance to start, pitching his way to Double-A while recording a 31-percent miss rate. The Phillies didn’t protect him on their 40-man roster, and the Twins selected him in December’s Rule 5 Draft, but he was returned to the Phillies on March 25. A huge amount of that 2024 swing-and-miss came from Castellano’s curveball, an 80-82 mph pitch with power and depth that showed a lot of improvement in 2024, eliciting a 49 percent miss rate. His changeup has long been an effective offering for the 6-foot-3 right-hander, thrown in the mid-80s with sink and fade that also can be an out pitch (39 percent miss rate, according to Synergy). He mixes both of them well with a fastball that averaged just over 94 mph last year, touching 98, and is thrown with good extension. The biggest leap forward for Castellano has been his command and control. After walking 4.1 per nine in his two years in Single-A Clearwater, he cut that rate to 2.5/9 last year, while still racking up strikeouts (11.8 K/9 in ‘24), giving him the potential to start long term, something he’ll get back to doing with the Phillies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Michigander during his high school days, Steensma headed to Boone, North Carolina, home to Appalachian State, for college ball. After pitching out of the bullpen as the Mountaineers' closer, racking up seven saves as a freshman in 2023, he moved into the rotation as a sophomore, finishing among the Sun Belt Conference top 10 in a host of pitching categories. An elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in December 2024 kept him off the mound in '25, but a combination of Mariners scouts and their analytics department saw enough potential from his performance the year prior to take him in the ninth round of last July's Draft. Now healthy, he got off to a very good start during his pro debut at Single-A in 2026. A strong 6-foot-4 right-hander, Steensma has a potential four-pitch mix that gives him a chance to start. While his fastball sits 92-93 mph and touches 95, it plays up and misses bats thanks to riding life that comes as a result of the combination of good extension and low release height. His tight mid-80s slider has ticked up since his college days and could be an out pitch in time. He'll mix in an 80 mph curve, and while he does have a potentially serviceable changeup, he wasn't throwing it much at the outset of his pro career. The Mariners are bullish about Steensma because he's still learning how to mix his pitches effectively. He was throwing a ton of strikes out of the gate, with the organization thinking he could have future plus command. They don't want to put unfair expectations on him, but the Mariners have done excellent development work with formerly injured college arms taken later on Day 2 of the Draft, like sixth-rounder-turned-All-Star Bryan Woo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: High school pitching can be one of the riskiest demographics in the Draft, but occasionally a late-round flier can emerge as a true gem. That appears to be the case with Payne, whom the Marlins signed away from his George Mason commitment for $235,000 as a 2024 18th-rounder and now looks like a bargain. The southpaw cruised through the Rookie-level Florida Complex League by striking out more than a third of the batters he faced and ended the year with six solid Single-A outings. Payne can really spin a pair of breaking balls and leaned on his low-80s slider and high-70s curve to rack up whiffs and chases. Both pitches have significant downward movement from his higher three-quarters delivery, which has helped mitigate platoon concerns. His fastball is still a work in progress, though, with a 91 mph average and sinking shape in 2025. He was more consistently hitting 95 over the offseason and has the build to add more velocity. Payne has a little-used cutter and a changeup with splitter-like movement that have had modest success in the mid-80s, but the breaking balls remain his meal ticket. The Marlins tried to ramp up his stuff at the cost of his control early on, and it will be key to see him throw more strikes to avoid bloated walk rates. Still, Payne has No. 4 starter upside thanks to his workhorse size, repeatable delivery and breaking balls -- or perhaps more if his added velocity sticks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of Corona Del Mar High School in California, Schwartz headed to UCLA, where he redshirted his freshman year and only saw 15 games in the shortened 2020 season. His big breakout finally came last spring when he hit .396/.514/.628 with eight homers and a 28/37 K/BB ratio in 44 games for the Bruins. Those numbers made him the Pac-12 batting champion and earned him a spot on the All-Conference Team. The Mets selected Schwartz in the fourth round and went slightly under slot to sign him for $475,000. He walked more than he struck out (13 vs. 12) but otherwise saw minimal results with a .195 average and a .576 OPS in his first 25-game trip to the Minors with Low-A St. Lucie. Despite standing in the box at 6-foot-4, Schwartz isn’t your typical slugging first first baseman. He’s shown an advanced approach everywhere he’s played over the last four years, including in summer-ball circuits, and as he proved in his final season on campus, he makes enough quality contact to sustain a good batting average. However, he doesn’t have a long history of hitting the ball over fences, and before the Draft, some evaluators were concerned that previous shoulder, knee and hip problems would keep him from showing even average power in games. Schwartz is first-base only on defense, and the Mets secured that by giving him all 24 of his defensive starts at the cold corner with St. Lucie. He faces a high offensive threshold there, and simply producing a solid average and OBP might not be enough to meet it. Schwartz is staring up at Pete Alonso on the Mets’ first-base depth chart, so he needn’t press to expedite his route toward Citi Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hodge is a product of Crespi Carmelite HS (Encino, Calif.), which has sent seven players to the big leagues, most notably Rick Dempsey, Jeff Suppan and Trevor Plouffe. He was considered the most athletic catching prospect in the 2025 Draft , just as White Sox starter Kyle Teel was in the 2023 class. A fourth-round pick, he foresook a Louisiana State commitment to sign for a well-over-slot $1,097,500. Hodge has a disciplined approach geared to work balls from gap to gap. While he has a quick, compact left-handed swing, he comes up empty on pitches in the strike zone more than he should, especially fastballs on the outer third. He had contact issues against quality pitching on the prep showcase circuit and will need to improve his timing and add strength to realize his ceiling of an average hitter with 15-homer pop. With his agility behind the plate, developing receiving skills and solid arm strength, there's no doubt that Hodge can stay at catcher. He can get better with the technical aspects of his craft and has the work ethic to do so, not to mention strong leadership skills. An average runner, he's quick enough to play second base or the outfield corners if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Caple spent two years as a reliever at Stephen F. Austin before transferring to Lamar and becoming a starter. The Cubs drafted him in the ninth round in 2024 after he won Southland Conference pitcher of the year honors and ranked among the NCAA Division I leaders in WHIP (0.87, third), ERA (2.40, eighth) and opponent average (.170, eighth). The velocity on all of his pitches has increased in pro ball, and he has blossomed into one of the system's top pitching prospects. Caple's fastball sat at 90-91 mph during his senior season at Lamar but now averages 94 mph and touches 98 with high spin rates that produce bat-missing carry. He utilizes an 86-88 mph cutter, 78-80 mph curveball and 83-85 mph slider in that order of frequency, though his sweeping slide piece is the most effective offering of that trio. He also has a fading mid-80s changeup. The shape of Caple's fastball combined with the extension in his delivery make it very difficult to hit. He works from a three-quarters arm slot and high release point while providing consistent strikes. He's a potential No. 4 starter if he can maintain his stuff and success against upper-level hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Michigan's top high school prospect in 2021, Mooney elicited top-two-rounds interest but ultimately went undrafted because of his commitment to Duke. He stood out as one of the best position players in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2022 and earned all-Atlantic Coast Conference honors as a sophomore last spring before signing for a well-over-slot $1 million in the seventh round. He batted just .152/.263/.212 in his 17-game pro debut in Single-A. A right-handed hitter, Mooney initially struggled as a college freshman but found consistent success after settling down his approach. He's making more consistent and higher quality contact, though he'll still chase pitches and struggles with changeups. He has bat speed, some sneaky strength and feel for driving the ball in the air to his pull side, giving him 15-homer potential. Like many of Cleveland's middle-infield prospects, Mooney distinguishes himself with his fine instincts, and he also earns praise for his nonstop energy and leadership ability. He has solid speed and is opportunistic on the bases. He has good hands and solid arm strength but just average range at shortstop, so he projects more as a second or third baseman in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing Dominican shortstop Cristian Hernandez for $3 million in January 2021, the Cubs came back a year later and inked his younger brother, Alexis, for $1.3 million. He wasn't as physical or considered as advanced at the plate as his older sibling at the same stage, but Hernandez had a much productive U.S. debut. He batted .315/.407/.515 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last summer, while Cristian managed a .261/.320/.357 line in the ACL in 2022. Hernandez's .494 average on balls in play was the second-highest in the Minors (minimum: 150 plate appearances) last year and obviously isn't sustainable. A right-handed hitter, he'll need to show more patience after striking out at a 33 percent rate in 2023 but he has a knack for making hard contact when he connects. He shows some aptitude for driving balls in the air to his pull side, so he could grow into 15-20 homer power. With solid speed, Hernandez will steal an occasional base. He's an average defender with a solid arm at shortstop, though like many youngsters he needs to play more under control. He also has seen action at second and third base, and some scouts who saw him as an amateur thought he might wind up in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-ranked member of Florida's 2019 recruiting class to make it to Gainesville, Rivera could have factored in the top five rounds had he been signable. He did little offensively in his first three years with the Gators or with wood bats in the Cape Cod League, then broke out with 19 homers to help Florida reach the College World Series finals in 2022. He proceeded to High-A almost immediately after turning pro as a third-rounder and slashed .250/.320/.402 in 25 games. Rivera was aggressively pushed to Double-A Tennessee for his first full season but struggled (in part due to a low BABIP) before being traded to the Blue Jays in late July in a deal for Nate Pearson. Rivera developed more patience and hit the ball significantly harder in 2023 than he had previously. He always had displayed a quick right-handed swing and he did a better job of keeping it on plane, allowing him to drive the ball with authority to all fields. He has the upside of a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per season, but he’ll need to do a better job against upper-level pitching to get there. Rivera plays quicker than his average speed thanks to his instincts. More steady than spectacular at shortstop, he has decent range and solid arm strength. The Jays like his defense at the six and are hopeful they can squeeze enough offense out of their acquisition with more exposure to the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The big splash, headline-grabbing international signings every year tend to happen right when the period opens in January. But sometimes hidden gems are found, and the Reds are hoping Villafana is one of them. Signed in July 2024 for $20,000, Villafana was older than most international prospects, signing at age 21. He made his brief pro debut after joining the Reds in the Dominican Summer League, then came to the U.S. and posted a nifty 42/9 K/BB ratio in the Arizona Complex League, though he also gave up 78 hits over 46 2/3 innings. Villafana has a legitimate three-pitch mix that he’ll throw to hitters on both sides, coming from a projectable 6-foot-4 frame that points to more in the tank to come. Coming from a three-quarters slot and upright delivery, his fastball typically sits in the 92-96 mph range, occasionally touching as high as 98. It doesn’t offer a ton of life, typically offering more horizontal than vertical break, and proving to be hittable in the ACL. He lands his 85-mph changeup for strikes consistently, getting above-average chase and a ton of groundballs with the cambio. His 82-mph gyro slider isn’t a super-high spin breaker, but it has a little sweep because of his arm slot and also elicits a good amount of chase. It’s an interesting package, with solid shapes for his secondary offerings and a clear ability to fill up the zone with all three pitches. The key to his success will be some kind of pitch design for his fastball to keep it away from barrels, especially as he starts to move up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you wanted to see young outfielders who really had a feel to hit, you should have headed to Inland Empire in the California League in 2023. That’s where Nelson Rada and Ruiz called home as teenagers. Rada was a big-ticket purchase prospect who got seven figures in January 2022; Ruiz got just $10,000 to sign in May 2021, but he’s hit every where he’s played, going one rung at a time to date: the Dominican Summer League in '21; the Arizona Complex League in '22 and Single-A last year. He was hitting over .300 in July when a wrist injury sustained while diving for a ball in the outfield ended his season. Like Rada, Ruiz has shown in the early stages of his career that he has a knack for getting the barrel to the ball. Because of that impressive contact skill, he’s shown the ability to hit righties and lefties alike with a line-drive, all-fields approach. He rarely strikes out (12.8 K rate heading into 2024) with a firm knowledge of the zone and the ability to get on base. There’s never going to be much power, but a little added strength would help him impact the ball more. While he’s not a burner, Ruiz is capable of stealing a base, and while he played left field mostly in deference to Rada at Inland Empire, he could be at least an above-average defender in center if given the opportunity. He could be a fourth outfielder type with an old school slashing contact profile, the kind of guy who finds his way into the lineup more than expected because of that feel to hit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kling displayed five-tool potential as a Pennsylvania high schooler and could have gone in the first three rounds in 2022 if he hadn't withdrawn from the Draft to head to Louisiana State. He was part of a national championship team as a freshman but after struggling for two years and going unselected as a sophomore-eligible, he transferred to Penn State. He slashed .358/.470/.632 with 13 homers and 15 steals with the Nittany Lions, spurring the Rangers to sign him for an over-slot $375,000 as a seventh-rounder last July. A right-handed hitter, Kling tried to do too much at the plate at LSU, getting pull-happy and struggling to make contact against non-fastballs. He did a better job of using the entire field at Penn State, though he still swung and missed at a 40 percent clip against non-heaters. His plus raw power and ability to drive balls in the air give him 25-homer upside, though his hitting ability remains a question. Kling possesses plus speed but isn't especially daring on the bases. He's a versatile defender with the range to cover center field and the arm strength to handle right. He has a higher ceiling than most Rangers prospects but also a lot to prove at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The two best prospects signed by the Giants in their 2017 international class are Dominican right-handers who turned pro for just $50,000 each: Randy Rodriguez and Cruz. The latter didn't stand out in his first three pro seasons but progressed rapidly in 2022, leading all Minor League relievers (minimum 50 innings) with a .119 average-against and ranking second with a 43 percent strikeout rate. Though he spent the entire season in Single-A at age 22, San Francisco protected him on its 40-man roster in November rather than risk exposing him to the Rule 5 Draft. Cruz creates exceptional armside run with his fastball and changeup, both of which are consistent plus pitches and sometimes better than that. His heater sits at 94-96 mph and touches 98 while running away from left-handers and in on right-handers, and his low arm slot creates carry up in the zone. His mid-80s changeup has a tad more horizontal movement and also some tumble, helping him limit lefties to a .085/.207/.169 line last season. Cruz doesn't have as much feel for spinning the ball, as his third pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that's fringy at best. Though his career has moved slowly to this point, San Francisco will begin expediting his path to the big leagues in 2023. He'll have to prove that his stuff will play at higher levels and also needs to improve his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colleran wasn’t really on a ton of radars entering the 2024 Draft after an inconsistent season at Northeastern. But the Royals were intrigued by his fastball and selected him in the seventh round that summer. He climbed three levels in 2025, ending the year with an inning in Double-A and with a 2.85 ERA across all affiliates. He was especially dominant in High-A Quad Cities, where he made 21 appearances, posted a 1.83 ERA and struck out batters at a 25 percent clip. He also pitched in the Arizona Fall League, where he struck out 11 in 7 2/3 innings. Colleran’s heater is probably the best in the Royals’ system, given that it sits upper 90s and touched 101 mph in 2025. It’s a plus-plus pitch with really good sink and is hidden well in his delivery with his big leg kick. He throws an above-average 90-91 mph cutter that sometimes registers as a slider depending on the location, as well as an average mid-80s sweeper with big horizontal break. Colleran can get a little wild with high walk rates, but consistency with his secondaries could help with that. He’s focusing on the breaking ball especially, as well as controlling the running game; that big leg kick gives him some deception and power, but it can also get him in trouble. There’s obviously a lot to like with the velocity on Colleran’s fastball, and he has setup man or closer upside if he can continue to develop the secondary weapons and have better command. The Royals had him in big league camp this spring, so he’s on the radar and could move quickly if he keeps improving.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players the Astros signed in their 2018-19 international class, Batista signed for $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His career started slowly, with a pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League followed by the pandemic shutdown and then a 7.46 ERA in a brief stint in the United States in 2021. He took a huge step forward last year, posting a 2.67 ERA with a .178 opponents' average against and 127 strikeouts in 107 2/3 innings while earning a late promotion to High-A at age 20. Batista works at 91-94 mph and tops out at 96 with the projectability to add more velocity, and his fastball also features the flat approach angle with carry and armside run that's in vogue. His best pitch is a plus low-80s slider with two-plane break and he also throws an upper-70s curveball with similar shape. He shows some feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade but it's still a work in progress. More polished than most of Houston's younger pitching prospects, Batista has a sound delivery and generally repeats it well. He could have average control and at least decent command once he's fully developed. He has the ingredients to become a four-pitch starter and also could be a bullpen asset who concentrates on his fastball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The state of Ohio's top prospect in the 2025 Draft, Vidourek hit 14 homers and stole 39 bases (in 40 tries) as a Cincinnati junior before putting on a show in batting practice at the Draft Combine. The Dodgers targeted him with their third-round choice and signed him for a below-slot $552,750. He has some of the best all-around tools in the system and played well in a 16-game pro debut in Single-A. There's nothing subtle about Vidourek at the plate. He combines strength and bat speed to generate well above-average raw power, and his left-handed stroke is designed to launch balls great distances to right field. He will take pitches and draw walks, but his aggressive mentality leads to too many swings and misses against all types of pitches, even when they're in the zone. Vidourek's plus speed and basestealing aptitude give him 30-30 upside. His quickness doesn't translate as well to his defense, as he played mostly right field in his last two college seasons and in his first taste of pro ball. He's an average corner outfielder with tremendous arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two seasons at Samford, Walton transferred to Arizona, where he had a career-best season with a 1.026 OPS, 14 homers and 19 stolen bases. Cleveland snagged him with the 66th overall pick in the 2025 Draft and signed him for $1.1 million, after which he played 16 games at Single-A with a solid .238/.324/.397 slash line but surprising strikeout issues after big improvements through his college years. Walton is a power-speed threat from the right side who is built at 6-foot-3 like Captain America -- and he has the makeup to match. His bat speed is among the best in the Guardians' system, which he deploys with a big leg kick and a closed-off stance. Walton has become more selective with time, and how his somewhat noisy swing fares against more advanced pitching will be key, especially given how he has been vulnerable to pitches away. Walton uses his swift legs well on the bases and in the field. He pushed 2025 supplemental first-rounder Brendan Summerhill off of center at Arizona, and Cleveland will give him every shot of sticking there, even if he may fit better in a corner. The Tennessee native is fearless and has solid instincts, but there are mixed reviews about his routes. Right-right outfielders who can even pass in center are rare, though, which gives him a decent floor as a bench bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Dominican Republic native, Sanchez was the Orioles’ highest-ranked signee (No. 31 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list) and received the highest bonus of their 2024 international class at $1.3 million. He made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he walked more than he struck out and ran rampant on the basepaths in his first taste of professional baseball. Sanchez is a left-handed hitter with athleticism and an advanced approach at the plate for his age. His pitch recognition and plate discipline stood out in his pro debut, as Sanchez drew 13 more walks than strikeouts over his first 203 plate appearances, and though he didn’t impact the baseball much, his patience and bat-to-ball ability hint at a solid offensive skill set. Adding strength as his body matures should help Sanchez develop more raw power, though he’s already showing signs of some to the pull side. He’s a strong runner who swiped 29 bases in 31 attempts in the DSL. Sanchez flashes his athleticism on the basepaths and in the infield, where his actions, range and arm could give him the chance to stick at shortstop. At 6-foot-1 and 160 pounds, he still has room to grow and fill out, and he’s already seen some time at third base if that happens and requires him to move to the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres are one of the most heavily involved -- if not the most heavily involved -- teams in Mexico as part of the international signing process. That’s where the club headed to sign Serna in January, two months before the southpaw turned 17. Serna gained some international notoriety at the 2024 WBSC U15 World Cup in Colombia, where he struck out 12 and allowed only one earned run on one hit and four walks in seven innings against the host nation. He signed for $1 million. The 6-foot-3 southpaw throws free and easy from a smooth delivery, and while he only sits 88-91 mph with his fastball now, he has the size to add strength and get that velocity up to at least Major League average in the years to come. His best present pitch is an upper-70s slider with short, controllable depth, and it should help fuel any immediate Minor League success. There’s a feel for a low-80s changeup too, though he barely used it in the World Cup. Serna excelled on the international stage because he could hit his spots at an advanced level, and he was willing to go right after hitters. The Padres brought up his strike throwing on signing day as the most exciting part of the early profile, and if Serna can sharpen his stuff with physical maturity -- not a given considering the wide error bars on young arms -- he could be a midrotation option in the Majors in the next decade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thach could have started his pro career out of high school when the Giants took him in the 18th round in 2022, but the great-nephew of Hall of Famer Catfish Hunter headed to UNC Wilmington instead. He's all over the Seahawks' record books, setting the freshman home run mark (15) in 2023 and then the single-season record with 27 as a sophomore. The power kept showing up with wood bats in the Cape Cod League (eight homers), but enthusiasm dampened a bit when the pop didn't show up as much in 2025. Still, his 54 career homers are a school record, and the Rockies took a flier in the eighth round of last summer's Draft, going a bit over slot to bring him into the fold. He got off to a very good start during his first full season of pro ball with Single-A Fresno. The big left-handed hitter offers an intriguing combination of strength and bat speed coming from his 6-foot-4 frame that provides optimism he can send the ball a long way and catch up to good velocity. He hits the ball very hard, registering high exit velocities and his well-above-average raw power can show up to all fields, though most of his home run thump comes to his pull side. He doesn't strike out a ton, especially given his power, but he does chase out of the zone too much, something that will have to improve as he moves up the ladder. A former two-way player who was up to 90 mph on the mound, Thach's well-below-average speed almost certainly limits him to first base, though he has seen a little time in right field as a pro. He'll have to keep getting to that raw pop to profile well in either corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was a July 2019 signing out of the Dominican Republic who joined the Mets as part of the same international class as Alex Ramirez. The southpaw missed out on the 2020 season like every other Minor Leaguer, but New York showed enough confidence in him to push him to the Florida Complex League and Single-A St. Lucie in 2021, when he fanned 16 in 12 1/3 innings. Rodriguez was set to take off in 2022, only to undergo Tommy John surgery in March that knocked him out for the entire campaign. There was promising stuff to generate excitement in Rodriguez’s abbreviated stateside look before he hurt his elbow. He typically sat in the mid-90s with his fastball and touched 97 mph during his brief turn in the Florida State League. His low-80s slider showed promising sweep to help him generate whiffs and give him another above-average offering. He didn’t throw his changeup at all with St. Lucie, and it will remain a major point of focus moving forward. Tommy John surgery isn’t what it used to be in terms of scariness, but the Mets have experienced another concern with Rodriguez getting shut down in August due to forearm inflammation. There's still enough stuff here for the southpaw to develop into a potential backend starter, but New York will be extra cautious with him as arm issues continue to pile up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Angelo spent three years at Cal State Bakersfield, finally cracked the Roadrunners’ rotation in 2021 and then transferred to Fresno State for two more years. Playing as a COVID senior in 2023, he was an All-Mountain West Second Team selection with a 4.39 ERA and 72 strikeouts in 80 innings with the Bulldogs but didn’t get drafted. The D-backs signed him as a free agent in July, and a year later, he ranked second in the system with 151 strikeouts while sporting a 3.49 ERA over 121 1/3 innings between Single-A and High-A. A 6-foot-5 right-hander, Angelo gave Arizona some size to dream on despite his advanced age, and he put that to good use early in his career. He averaged just 90.1 mph on his fastball in his final collegiate season but was typically up closer to the 93-94 range at Visalia and Hillsboro. He throws different types too between his four-seamer and sinker. It’s a deep arsenal as well, highlighted by a mid-80s changeup that ran a 51 percent whiff rate in his first taste of the pros. His slider was his next-best option for swing-and-miss, and he’ll also incorporate curveballs and cutters for different shapes. Angelo walked 17 in 25 innings with Visalia before his promotion but showed much closer to average control at the higher level. He can rush his delivery a bit, and given that he’s already entering his age-25 season, he won’t have a super-long leash as a starter. But the ingredients are there, and he has enough offerings to keep hitters constantly on their toes as he heads toward the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kouba spent his first two college seasons at North Central (Texas) CC and opened 2021 in Dallas Baptist's bullpen, pitched his way into the rotation by midseason, earned all-Missouri Valley Conference honors and became a 12th-round pick. He doesn't dazzle anyone with his stuff but compensates by being the best strike-thrower in the system. He was named Double-A Texas League pitcher of the year in 2023 and finished the season in Triple-A. Kouba's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and tops out at 94 but doesn't get hit hard because he has all the traits the Astros target with pitchers: low release height, flat approach angle, significant extension in his delivery. It also plays up because he keeps batters off balance with his best pitch, a solid low-80s changeup with fade and sink. He has a pair of ordinary breaking balls, a sweeping low-80s slider he uses vs. righties and an upper-70s curveball he employs against lefties. With his combination of deception and control, Kouba could be a No. 5 starter. His stuff works better than it grades because he mixes his pitches well, commands his fastball and throws his secondary offerings for strikes. He was in line to get an opportunity if Houston needed rotation help in 2024 before missing two months with an elbow injury that didn't require surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patick stood out more with his projection than his present stuff when the Dodgers made him an 18th-round pick out of a suburban Los Angeles high school and signed him for an over-slot $347,500 in 2023. An illness requiring hospitalizing sidelined him for what would have been his first Spring Training and limited him to 31 2/3 innings in 2024, but he bounced back to successfully navigate Single-A last year. His 27 percent strikeout rate ranked third in the California League among pitchers who worked at least as many as his 85 1/3 innings. Patick's fastball sits at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with more downhill plane than life, and he uses it to set up a wide variety of secondary pitches. His best offering is a mid-70s curveball with depth that confounds both lefties and righties but also makes it difficult to land for strikes. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with plenty of sweep that he can turn into a tighter cutter that climbs as high as 93 mph, as well as an 85-88 mph changeup with some fade. Patick has good feel for spinning the ball and mixing his pitches. He creates deception by utilizing a big leg kick, rotating his upper half and throwing from a crossfire angle, and that doesn't stop him from throwing strikes. He has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and his ability to neutralize hitters from both sides with his breaking pitches could make him a useful bullpen piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peck was an undersized shortstop in high school until a senior-year growth spurt and a visit to Pepperdine’s camp earned him his only Division I option. Former Tigers shortstop Danny Worth, then a coach on Pepperdine’s staff, recruited Peck to the Waves and then reworked his swing to get more impact. It paid off with an all-West Coast Conference sophomore season in 2022, but a tough summer in the Cape Cod League and a subpar junior season sent him falling down Draft boards. The Tigers were the beneficiary, getting him in the seventh round in 2023 and then watching him break out in 2025 to climb all the way to Double-A Erie and earn a non-roster invite to Major League camp, where his work made an impression on Detroit’s staff. While Peck’s calling card is his defense, he has enough impact at the plate to punish pitchers for mistakes. He has a relatively quiet swing other than a leg kick for timing, but he’s capable of hard contact for line drives around the field. His walk rate dropped a bit last year as he took a slightly more aggressive approach, but his strikeout rate remained relatively steady. He’s opportunistic on the basepaths and capable of sneaky speed to take an extra bag. Peck is an elite defender with smooth movements, good pitch anticipation and a fairly strong arm. He can play around the infield. Though Peck might be the best defensive shortstop in the Tigers system, his bat will determine how much Detroit can do with that, whether he has a chance to compete for a shortstop role in the big leagues or fits better as a utility infielder who can hit lefties hard. He’ll likely open the season back at Double-A Erie but could advance quickly given his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals signed Rodriguez in July 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and the start of his pro career was bumpy because of the pandemic. It didn’t seem to slow him down, as he was named the DSL Royals Blue Player of the Year in 2021 and then brought his high energy to the States in 2022, slashing .306/.395/.514 between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A. Rodriguez’s best tool is hitting, with innate bat-to-ball skills, an efficient swing and a simple approach at the plate. He doesn’t fear velocity and has an excellent idea of the strike zone for someone who just finished his age-19 season -- his 10.8 percent walk rate and 16.2 percent strikeout rate were better in Columbia than Rookie ball. The switch-hitter has a good approach from both sides of the plate, but most of his pop -- which is below average right now -- comes from the left side. That could change with more reps on the right side and more strength. Rodriguez is an above-average defender at second base with quick hands and good footwork. Rodriguez has tools and youth on his side right now. The ingredients are there to make good on that upside as long as his contact skills and zone control continue. He seems to be limited to second base right now, but he could probably handle the left side of the infield if needed; certainly if he gets stronger and there’s emphasis on versatility. As a second baseman without a lot of thump, Rodriguez has a high floor as a utility infielder, but if the high average and on-base numbers continue against better pitching, perhaps there’s a leadoff candidate in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz slugged .771 with 34 homers in his two years at Walters State CC in Tennessee and showed out nicely in separate stints in the Appalachian (2023) and MLB Draft Leagues (2024) to establish himself on the Draft radar. The Cardinals took him in the 16th round and dipped a little into their bonus pool to make him a JUCO signing for $200,000. Ortiz ripped through the Florida State League in his first full season with a .285/.406/.446 line and 10 homers in 77 games and produced a .938 OPS over 30 contests with High-A Peoria following a July promotion. The 6-foot-1 right-handed slugger has an interesting stance at the plate that starts with him leaning back and then launching forward with a leg kick. It’s a swing designed for contact in the air, and his 29.7 percent line-drive rate was highest among Cardinals full-season qualifiers, while his 29.3 percent ground-ball rate was lowest. His 105.3 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity in the FSL was also comfortably above average, and Ortiz could be a threat to hit 20+ homers pretty easily if trends hold. Ortiz was beatable with good velocity and sliders in the zone, however, and that will be a more worrisome trend against better arms in the upper Minors. The Puerto Rico native ran subpar sprint speeds in the FSL but picked his spots well against Single-A catchers, going 31-for-34 in steal attempts there. (That dropped to 8-for-14 in the Midwest League, perhaps a better sign of what to expect.) The Cardinals believe Ortiz has enough athleticism to keep getting looks at third base, where his above-average arm strength fits, but have already mixed in plenty of first. It’s likely he lands down the defensive spectrum and needs to keep his offensive production high to be valuable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCollum spent three seasons at Division II Wingate University, pitching almost entirely out of the bullpen and helping the team win a national championship in 2021. He went undrafted, but signed a free agent contract following the Draft and made his pro debut that summer with full-season Clearwater, recording inconsistent results over nine appearances. A return to the Single-A level in 2022 reaped much better results with a 1.45 ERA and a .111 average-against before a bad ankle sprain ended his season at the end of June. The 6-foot-5 right-hander might end up with three quality pitches. He throws his fastball in the 94-97 mph range with solid carry and offers a hard and short slider. His splitter is a developing third pitch, but there’s a chance it could become an out pitch in time. Command and control have held McCollum back, though. He walked more than seven per nine in college and really struggled during his pro debut. But he’s already improved his ability to find the zone since he signed, dropping that walk rate to 4.6 in 2022 while striking out 15.1 per nine. More strides in that direction could give him the chance to impact a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Copen's 6.30 ERA in three seasons at Marshall belied his power and physicality, which the Dodgers liked enough to grab him in the seventh round of the 2023 Draft. A line drive struck him in the face and cost him the vision in his right eye in August 2024, but he returned for Opening Day last year. He ranked 12th in the Minors in strikeout rate (29 percent) and opponent average (.200) while splitting his year between High-A and Double-A. After working with a 91-94 mph fastball during his final college season, Copen now operates at 95-98 mph and touches 100 with bat-missing carry. His high-spin mid-80s slider has so much depth that it's difficult to hit and even harder to land in the strike zone. He uses a low-90s cutter as his third pitch and threw just four changeups in 2025. The 6-foot-6 Copen has a long arm action with a deep plunge in the back, and he has trouble keeping his long limbs in sync. He walked 13 percent of the batters he faced at Marshall and 15 percent his first three years as a pro. He may never harness his stuff well enough to make it as a starter, but his fastball and slider could make him a dynamic bullpen weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After splitting time as a starter and reliever at Illinois, Lavender headed to the MLB Draft League with Mahoning Valley in 2021 for another opportunity to boost his stock. The Mets selected him in the 14th round, signed him for $125,000 and immediately gave him a full-time role in the bullpen. The southpaw appeared for all five domestic affiliates in his first three seasons, topping out at Triple-A Syracuse in 2023. After posting a 3.27 ERA with 67 strikeouts in 44 innings in the International League and ranking second among Mets Minor Leaguers (min. 50 IP) with a 36.9 percent K rate last season, Lavender was diagnosed with ligament damage this April. Lavender is the rare reverse-split reliever -- he held righties to a .164/.265/.336 line in 2023 compared to .241/.366/.374 for lefties. A big reason is the deception in his three-quarters-slot delivery. He hides his 90-92 mph fastball (touching 95) exceptionally well, and it sneaks up in the zone against righties, who missed on 48 percent of their swings against the heater. For that reason, Lavender went to the fastball 66 percent of the time against righties and 65 percent overall in 2023. His 78-81 mph changeup got an even better whiff rate (56 percent) against other-side batters because of the velo separation and way he sells it out of his hand, but its usage lags well behind the fastball. He also has a low-80s slider with some sweep, but it’s not nearly as effective as batters slugged .463 off it in ’23. The effort in Lavender’s delivery can get him off line at times, and he’ll run into some problems with location and control. That – and his lack of standout velo – may keep him from serving a prominent role in future Mets bullpens, but he’s essentially ready to get out Major League batters from both sides now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colon grew up in Puerto Rico and came to the United States for his senior year of high school in the Miami area. He caught the attention of the Reds, who had some bonus pool money left over as Day 3 began in 2024. They went about $100,000 over the post-10th-round slot to sign him in Round 11. He learned a lot in going to full-season ball during his first full season in 2025, then returned to Daytona and was making big strides in the Florida State League to kick off 2026. A strong and athletic right-hander who is about an inch taller and 20 pounds heavier than his listed height and weight, Colon has future rotation potential if he can improve his command. Right now, he leans heavily on his fastball-split-change combination. It's a plus heater that currently sits around 96 mph and touches 98 mph, getting outstanding induced vertical break on the pitch to elicit strong swing-and-miss rates. He can kill spin and gets good horizontal action on his upper-80s changeup that also can miss bats. His slider thrown at about the same velocity continues to improve. Colon is athletic on the mound, with a short stride that leads to less-than-optimal extension. In addition to rounding out his arsenal with a dependable breaking ball he trusts, Colon needs to continue to improve his control and command. He showed some improvement in that regard to kick off 2026 and he gets high marks for his maturity at age 20, providing optimism he can figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taurek redshirted his freshman year at St. Mary’s in 2023, then played sparingly the next season. He made it count in 2025, earning second-team All-West Coast Conference honors while hitting .328 with 11 homers and helping the Gaels win the WCC tournament and reach NCAA Regional play. The Mariners liked his swing enough to take a $150,000 flier on him in the 13th round of the Draft, and he went out and hit some more, posting a .336 average over 27 games with Single-A Modesto during his pro debut. The one thing that seems certain about Taurek is that he can make a lot of contact with a chance to hit at this level. He’s small and compact and so is his right-handed swing, with simple mechanics and direct to the ball action. He does not strike out much -- just 9.5 percent with the Gaels in ‘25 -- and while he’s very aggressive at the plate and doesn’t walk a ton, he also limits chase. He’s not all that projectable from a physicality standpoint, and it’s unclear whether he’ll have that much impact. Taurek is a bit of a tweener defensively. He doesn’t have enough speed to play center field regularly -- he played left exclusively at St. Mary’s, and that’s where he spent most of his time during his pro debut. But he doesn’t have enough thump to profile as an everyday guy in a corner. The right-right undersized profile is a tough one, but he’s swung the bat well enough to make him interesting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
