mlb_pipeline.text: A Wisconsin high schooler with a big fastball, Snead started his college career at Wichita State, but then moved on to Tennessee where, as a sophomore, he helped the Volunteers win the 2024 Men's College World Series, picking up a key save and hold in the Finals. He came out of the bullpen again as a junior, but his combination of a full arsenal and ability to throw strikes could give him the chance to start, something the Angels no doubt were contemplating when taking him with their compensation pick following the third round of the 2025 Draft. There’s no doubt that Snead can throw hard -- he sat around 95-97 mph and touched triple digits. But the heater often lacked life, with sink over carry, so if he wasn’t locating it down in the zone well, it was very hittable. He’s already gotten to work on differentiating his two- and four-seamers (which often blended together), as well as improving his low-90s cutter. His low-80s curve evolved into his best secondary offering in 2025. There’s also a mid-80s slider and low-90s changeup in Snead’s bag of tricks, though he didn’t pull them out often. He has a bit of a slinky delivery coming from a low three-quarters slot, and while he finds the strike zone, it’s control over command. The Angels could give him a chance to start out of the gate, knowing that he could also develop into a late-inning reliever with better fastball characteristics.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kohn immediately claimed a role in Mississippi State's bullpen as freshman before missing all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery. He showed average stuff when he came back as a starter and went undrafted in 2024, then improved his stuff and strike-throwing as a redshirt junior last spring. One of the best fourth-year collegians in the 2025 Draft, he went in the fourth round and will make his pro debut this year. Though Kohn's fastball has pedestrian velocity at 91-95 mph, hitters don't see it coming out of his low three-quarters arm slot and flat approach angle, and he has the aptitude to work it with carry up in the zone or spot it down at the knees. He also has advanced command of a sweeping low-80s slider that he can locate on either side of the plate. While he works almost exclusively with those two pitches, he does show a promising low-80s changeup with fade that could give him a third solid offering. Kohn improved his athleticism in 2025, allowing him to get down the mound better and repeat his delivery more consistently. That led to improved extension and deception as well as control and command. He has a high floor as a three-pitch lefty starter with advanced feel for his craft and strong mound presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamilton played little in his first four seasons at Wright State, redshirting when he arrived, coming off the bench the next two years and having the 2020 season shortened by the pandemic. He finally got a chance to show what he could do in 2021, when he was named Horizon League Player of the Year and ranked third in NCAA Division I in runs scored (78) and OPS (1.306). Signed for a well-below-slot $47,500 in the fifth round that July, he slashed .308/.425/.508 between Single-A and High-A in his first full pro season before dropping to .206/.320/.341 in the final six weeks in Double-A. Hamilton has one of the best approaches among Astros farmhands, controlling the strike zone while making consistent contact and drawing a healthy amount of walks. His left-handed swing is geared more for hitting line drives than launching balls, but he has enough bat speed and strength to generate 12-15 homers per season. He handles same-side pitchers well, adding to his usefulness as a potential fourth outfielder. Hamilton has plus speed and uses it well on bases, swiping 27 bases in 31 tries last year. He possesses average range in center field, where he played most often in 2022, and could be a solid defender on the corners, where he also saw a lot of action. He has average arm strength, gets rid of throws quickly and registered 11 assists last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians landed two talented high school arms with well-over-slot bonuses in the middle rounds of the 2022 Draft, signing left-hander Jackson Humphries for $600,000 in the eighth round and Zibin for $1.2 million in the 10th. The top Canadian prospect and youngest player in the Draft, Zibin set a record for his round and received the equivalent of second-round money. A veteran of the Canadian junior national team, he spent his senior season at the TNXL Academy (Ocoee, Fla.) to increase his exposure. Zibin already works at 92-94 mph and touches 97 with armside run on his four-seam fastball, which should gain more velocity as he adds weight to his projectable 6-foot-4 frame. He has advanced feel for a low-80s changeup with fade and sink, selling it well with deceptive arm speed. His 77-82 mph slider can flash some promising sweep but also gets slurvy at times. While Zibin throws strikes, he can refine his delivery and command. He'll focus on gaining strength and building up innings early in his career. He'll need time to develop but has the upside of a mid-rotation starter, especially if he can upgrade the consistency of his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitaker is the latest prospect to come out of Bishop Gorman High (Las Vegas), which has spawned 10 big leaguers, including Joey Gallo and former American League Rookie of the Year Marty Cordova. He was a shortstop/right-hander before shifting to the outfield last spring and winning Gatorade's Nevada player of the year award. Signed for a well over-slot $1.5 million as the Astros' top pick (third round) in the 2021 Draft, he batted .202/.263/.327 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Whitaker's bat speed and the leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame create plus raw power with the potential for more as he gets stronger. He made a more concerted effort to drive the ball in 2021, though his right-handed stroke gets too long at times, leading to swing-and-miss concerns. To make the most of his pop, he'll need to make more contact and learn to turn on more pitches and drive them in the air. A quality athlete, Whitaker offers solid to plus speed and a strong arm. While he played right field in a loaded Bishop Gorman outfield, he shifted to center field in pro ball and may have enough quickness and instincts to stay there. Houston also was pleasantly surprised at how he looked in brief action at third base during his debut and has played him at shortstop this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the top 10 rounds of the 2025 Draft, the Phillies took nine pitchers, eight of them from the college ranks. The lone hitter in the group was Ferrara, a high school shortstop from Toms River East High School in New Jersey. The athletic middle infielder had shown off some tools on the summer showcase circuit and turned in a strong season in the New Jersey Shore Conference. The Phillies had some bonus pool money to play with in the ninth round when they took Ferrara, who signed for an over-slot bonus close to $600,000, or fourth-round money. The Phillies pushed the six-foot right-handed hitter to full-season Clearwater for a 15-game debut that did not go particularly well, though little should be read into thrusting an 18-year old kid from the Northeast into that level of competition. What was impressive was that even in the small sample, he was starting to make some small adjustments that should help him in the future. He wasn’t on time, launching his barrel too late, which led to poor barrel accuracy. When he got more synced up, his barrel accuracy and zone contact improved. He’s already added strength and physicality since signing, which could help him get to more impact. While Ferrara only played second base during his debut, the Phillies think his athleticism gives him the chance to stick at short. He’s an easily plus runner with decent actions defensively. He’ll continue to see time on both sides of second base, and it’s not out of the question that he gets some run out in center field at some point in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2024, the Mariners signed Chia-Shi Shen out of Chinese Taipei. They hit that pitching market again in 2025, signing Lin for $460,000 when the signing period opened in January. A former two-way player who pitched well in international competition, Lin looked really good in Spring Training after signing, but then wasn’t able to make his pro debut because of a lat strain, though he did get some innings in the bridge league at the end of the year, once again raising expectations. Lin had played both the infield and outfield previously, and he brings that athleticism to the mound. The 5-foot-11 right-hander has the chance to have a full starter’s repertoire, with his splitter the standout pitch. It flashes plus and can fall off the table with excellent depth while also throwing a distinct changeup. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, but he’s shown the ability to reach back for more, and there could be more velocity in the future. He has some feel to spin with a more traditional slider, though it’s behind the other offerings, and there’s been some talk of adding a sweeper to his mix. Lin’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone consistently. His stuff may never wow anyone, but his feel for pitching and full array of offerings gives him the chance to start, with the Mariners getting to see what he’s like in competition this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quinn had an uneven two-year tenure at Mississippi, cracking the Rebels’ weekend rotation as a freshman but battling blister and oblique issues as a sophomore, before transferring to Georgia. He found success as a swingman for the Bulldogs before the Orioles took him in Competitive Balance Round B in the 2025 Draft and signed him for $1.15 million. He didn’t pitch for the organization after the Draft. Quinn is a 6-foot-6 power righty. He throws a fastball that lives in the mid-90s and touches 98 mph with armside run, and his main putaway pitch is a mid-80s slider that breaks down and away from right-handed hitters. He throws a curveball in the upper 70s with significant depth but has trouble landing it with any consistency. He has a much better grip on his fastball command, as he’s able to run that pitch past hitters up in the zone or throw it with downhill plane toward the bottom of the zone to induce ground balls. Overall, it’s fringy control of what is basically a fastball-slider package at this point, and Quinn also operates exclusively from the stretch -- all of which gives him the look of a power reliever who would be best running his raw stuff wild in short sprints. It stands to reason he’d need to learn to throw more strikes and develop an offspeed pitch to succeed as a starter in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Neville’s commitment to Arkansas as a Las Vegas high school standout pushed him to the end of the 2022 Draft, so he headed to play for the Razorbacks. After getting just 27 at-bats as a freshman, he transferred to Oregon and immediately showed he could get to some power with 16 homers as a sophomore. He tightened up his swing as a junior, cutting down his strikeouts, which helped him tie for the Division I lead with 26 homers. Worries about his feel for hitting followed him into the Draft, so he was available for the Reds in the fourth round and his debut with Single-A Daytona, albeit brief, did not assuage those swing-and-miss concerns. Neville does offer up ever-exciting raw power from the left side of the plate to go along with excellent overall athleticism. After striking out 33.5 percent of the time as a sophomore with the Ducks, he trimmed that to 23.6 percent as a junior before whiffing 31 times in 90 pro plate appearances during his debut. He can impact the ball for extra bases to the gaps, with his over-the-fence thump showing up mostly to his pull side. He can feast off fastballs but one of his areas of focus as a pro will be to recognize spin and cut down whiffs on softer stuff overall. Neville played a solid center field at Oregon and there are those who feel he has a chance to stick there. He’ll get time at all three spots as he gets going in earnest and might best be suited for right, where his above-average arm would play well. His ceiling is directly tied to how much he can manage the strike zone and make contact in order to get to his very real power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Florida State, Parrish did enough to warrant the Royals’ attention in the 2019 Draft, when they took the southpaw in the eighth round and signed him for slot at $184,700, shortly after he dominated Arkansas in the College World Series. After the 2020 season was canceled due to the pandemic, Parrish shoved in Double-A Northwest Arkansas last year, striking out 95 in 83 innings with a 3.36 ERA across 18 games as one of the most consistent starters in the Royals’ system. He even earned a spot with Team USA’s Olympic Qualifying team. Parrish might have been overlooked in the Draft due to his 5-foot-11 frame and lack of velocity, throwing in the high 80s for most of college, but he’s up to low 90s consistently now -- and even flashed 94-95 mph in 2021. Parrish’s headliner is his changeup, an upper-70s pitch that consistently misses bats. He didn’t have to use his curveball much as an amateur, but he’s significantly improved the pitch to be at least average. Parrish doesn’t have a fast arm, but it’s extremely efficient. He can spot the ball to all four quadrants and walked just 25 batters in 83 innings in 2021. Parrish’s ceiling may be limited because of his velocity, but Royals officials love the way he pitches and his overall craftiness. His dominance last season also proved that velocity isn’t everything. A back-end starting role is an attainable goal, but Parrish could end up filling a lot of roles for the Royals -- starter, bulk pitcher out of the bullpen or a middle-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working just 19 1/3 innings in two seasons at Oklahoma State, Reid transferred to Abilene Christian and set the program's NCAA Division I record with 112 strikeouts in 88 1/3 innings last spring. He allowed only one run in his final starts, including seven shutout frames with 12 whiffs against Utah Valley in the Western Athletic Conference tournament, and worked his way into the third round of the 2025 Draft. He signed for a below-slot $649,125 as the Wildcats' highest selection since 1969 third-rounder Bill Gilbreth, the lone big leaguer in school history. Reid led all NCAA D-I pitchers with 66 strikeouts via a changeup. His plus cambio operates at 82-84 mph with fade and sink, and he'll double and triple up on it, even against same-side hitters. He sets it up with a 91-94 mph fastball that touches 96, and he can create carry at the letters or sink at the knees. He's mainly a two-pitch guy, showing little faith in a slurvy low-80s breaking ball that doesn't fool hitters. Reid has a strong 6-foot-3 build that lends itself to durability and an athletic delivery that he repeats well and translates into regular strikes. His fastball doesn't overpower hitters and can catch too much of the plate, so he needs to command it well to set up his changeup. Set to make his pro debut in 2026, he probably will need a better breaker to remain a long-term starter as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herrera not only earned a berth on Venezuela's team at the 2022 18-and-under World Cup qualifiers when he was just 15, but he also led the squad with a homer and nine RBI in eight games. One of the best power hitters in the 2024 international class, he signed in January for $1.8 million, the top bonus in the White Sox crop. He'll probably make his pro debut this summer in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Already 6-foot-3 and 212 pounds at age 17, Herrera is built to hit for power. He has a relatively effortless right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed and leverage that produce pop to all fields. His pure hitting ability draws mixed reviews, earning below-average grades from some evaluators while others laud his ability to make adjustments and handle offspeed pitches. Herrera moves OK considering his size, but he's a below-average runner who could lose more speed if he continues to add muscle. He already has outgrown shortstop and could develop into an average defender at third base if he can retain his present quickness. He has solid arm strength and some experience at catcher, though Chicago would rather expedite his bat than try him behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Molina stood out in two years at Texas Tech and transferred to Arkansas as a junior in 2024. He dealt with ankle and control issues with the Razorbacks, causing him to go to the Brewers in the seventh round of the 2024 Draft. The Rangers acquired him in his first offseason in a deal for Grant Anderson, and he was moved again to the Cardinals at the 2025 Trade Deadline as part of the Phil Maton return. He finished with a 3.10 ERA, 119 strikeouts and 43 walks in 95 2/3 innings across Single-A and High-A in his first full season. The 6-foot-2 southpaw sat 90-93 mph with his four-seamer in 2025 but got a healthy amount of whiffs on it thanks to impressive ride up in the zone. He showed improved velocity this spring, averaging 93.2 mph on the heater (touching 95.8) in a pair of Grapefruit League outings, and with the 18-20 inches of induced vertical break, the extra heat could make the fastball a plus pitch in his age-22 season. Molina typically earns his best grades for his low-80s changeup that gets almost exactly 10 mph separation from the four-seamer and a ton of fade and armside run, but he drops the release enough on the pitch that it could become a tell for upper-level bats. He showed both 82-85 mph sliders and 79-82 mph sweepers this spring and occasionally sprinkles in a slow mid-70s curve. Even with the improved stuff, Molina must show he can find the zone more consistently as he climbs the ladder. His walk rate moved to the double-digits at High-A before the trade and escalated to 16.1 percent. He’ll need the breaking stuff, particularly the sweeper, to help keep batters off the predictability of his fastball-changeup mix and improve his starting chances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aracena was a long play for the Mets when they signed him out of the Dominican Republic for $70,000 as part of their 2022 international class. He was super raw, even for a young pitcher, walking 20.2 percent of his batters as recently as 2024. But Aracena took a big step forward as a 20-year-old in the Florida State League in 2025 and was pitching very well when the Orioles acquired him as part of the return for Gregory Soto near the Trade Deadline. He pitched to a 1.95 ERA over his first 27 2/3 innings in his new organization, finishing the year at High-A Aberdeen, but was traded again in the offseason to the D-backs as part of the return for Blaze Alexander. Aracena’s stuff makes it clear why he was a project worth waiting for. The 6-foot-3 right-hander brings serious heat to the mound, sitting 96-99 mph with his four-seam fastball and topping out at 101. He also throws a razor-sharp cutter at 92-94 mph with significant gloveside run, as well as two breaking balls: an upper-80s slider with depth and a developing curve. He’s had a two-seamer and a changeup, but throws neither pitch often enough to be a factor. The control of those offerings was so erratic that Aracena’s 13.6 percent walk rate in ‘25 indicated marked improvement. He’s still able to blow his stuff past batters for now, but upper-level hitters won’t provide that luxury. As it stands, it’s a high-risk/high-reward package -- when Aracena commands his stuff, he dominates; when he doesn’t, the walks make him vulnerable to implosion. How well he learns to locate will ultimately dictate his true ceiling, though he looks like a high-leverage reliever in the making if he can learn to harness even a fraction of his tantalizing stuff consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ravelo signed for $545,000 out of the Dominican Republic, landing the third-highest bonus in Boston's 2021 international class. Though he batted just .197/.303/.265 in his U.S. debut last summer, his defense earned him a promotion to Single-A for the final week of the season at age 18. His offensive game needs more work, though he shows some promise as a switch-hitter with bat speed from both sides of the plate. Despite his youth, Ravelo already displays the consistency to make routine plays at shortstop and the tools and instincts to produce web gems. He has twitchy athleticism, classic shortstop actions, quick hands and solid arm strength. He's an average runner at best, but still shows range to both sides and is one of the best infield defenders in the system. More effective as a left-handed hitter, Ravelo needs to make adjustments to his offensive approach. He employs a leg kick and is overly pull-conscious, leading to too many strikeouts and weak ground balls. If he can get stronger and improve his pitch recognition and swing decisions, he could produce 10-15 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wichrowski worked as both a starter and a reliever as a junior at Bryant in 2023 and didn’t wow scouts with a 4.50 ERA and 64 strikeouts in 50 innings. The Brewers took him in the 13th round that July, signed him for $100,000 and were taken aback by the jumps in stuff Wichrowski showed that fall and the following spring. He was promoted from High-A Wisconsin to Double-A Biloxi after only four starts (in which he struck out 21 and walked three) and posted a 4.12 ERA with 61 strikeouts in 74 1/3 frames in the Southern League the rest of the way. He ended the year on the injured list with a dead arm but is expected to be good to go to begin 2025. The 6-foot-2 right-hander reminds some of Joe Kelly for his ability to light up radar guns from a lither frame. He was touching triple-digits at times before the season started and still touched 98 at times, though his velocity wavered a bit because of the arm down the stretch. He’ll throw a pair of heaters too between a blazing four-seamer and a sinker to give batters different looks. Wichrowski can twirl an 83-85 mph sweeping slider down and gloveside to elicit some funky swings against batters from both sides. There are two upper-80s pitches in his cutter and changeup, but the latter isn’t nearly as reliable as the others. Wichrowski walked 11.1 percent of his batters faced in Double-A, and even as his stuff has jumped, there remains a concern that he won’t corral it well enough to remain a starter. Milwaukee is already enthused by his early jumps in pro ball, however, and some in the organization believe the righty can build on 2024’s gains with a fully healthy ’25.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-hander Nehomar Ochoa Sr. pitched in the Expos system from 2003-05 until falling off a horse and injuring his shoulder, and his son was born in Venezuela shortly before his career ended. The younger Nehomar moved to the United States at age 10 and blossomed into a physical and toolsy outfielder at a Houston high school before signing with the local Astros for $300,000 (double slot value) as an 11th-rounder in 2023. In his first full pro season, he slashed .222/.317/.359 with 10 homers and 17 steals in 103 games as the second-youngest batting qualifier (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League. Extremely physical at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Ochoa has a quick right-handed swing and at least plus raw power that plays mostly to left field because of his pull- and launch-heavy mindset. He has enough natural pop to hit 25 or more homers per season without swinging for the fences. He'll have to moderate his approach as he advances because he chases too much and is overmatched by breaking balls from righties. Very athletic for his size, Ochoa has average speed and is aggressive on the bases. He's still a work in progress as a corner outfielder, but he has the quick reactions to become at least an average defender and may get a trial in center field. He has plus arm strength, reaching 95 mph with his fastball as a prep pitcher and throwing out 12 runners in 76 starts in right field last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heuer had some of the best physicality and projectable fastball velocity in the 2023 Draft, but he turned down the Guardians as a 16th-rounder to attend Texas Tech. He served as the Red Raiders' No. 1 starter and pushed his fastball to 98 mph last spring, but he also logged a 6.28 ERA as a Draft-eligible sophomore. That didn't deter the Yankees, who signed him for an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round. Heuer operates at 93-95 mph with cut and carry on his fastball, which is effective up in the zone but gets pounded when he doesn't command it well. His mid-80s slider with sweeping action can be a solid offering when it's on, though he has trouble landing it for strikes and it sometimes flattens over the heart of the plate. His mid-80s changeup with fade and depth was his most effective offering as a sophomore, though he didn't use it much. Scouts don't love Heuer's delivery, which features a short arm action, high release point and some crossfire. He presently has fringy control and below-average command, which may make him more of a reliever than a starter in the long run. If he doesn't make it in baseball, he has his own livestock business with his brother and raised ewes that won grand champion titles at the 2020 and 2022 Georgia National Fairs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets added Fañas -- then on the older side at 18 -- for $1.5 million as their second-biggest signing of the 2022 international period, behind Simon Juan, who joined for $1.9 million. The Dominican Republic native didn’t get off to the greatest statistical start in the Dominican Summer League, hitting just .257/.330/.297 with a 79 wRC+ over 32 games, but he did flash enough potential to keep Mets player development officials excited. It’s all about potential with Fañas heading into his second Minor League campaign. Listed as 6-foot-2, 190 pounds, the outfielder has plenty of power projection remaining, so while he didn’t homer at all in the DSL, there’s hope that at least average pop is coming down the line as he gains strength and experience against pro arms. A switch-hitter, he did a decent job protecting the plate and had fairly even splits from both sides in a small sample. Fañas’ athleticism and above-average running ability helped him swipe 10 bags in 13 attempts and provide him with another avenue to be valuable until the overall hitting ability comes around. Even if he needs to move from center field to right, his arm strength should help ease that defensive transition. Fañas turned 19 in January, making him the same age as many American collegiate freshmen, and he stands to move stateside for the first time. The larger the sample on his Minor League playing time, the more answers Mets' and other club evaluators will receive on his chances to turn potential into performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After showing the ability to command his fastball and miss bats with his secondary pitches as a freshman at Cloud County (Kan.) CC and a sophomore at Nebraska, McConnaughey positioned himself as an early-round pick in 2025. But his elbow gave out after three starts last spring and required Tommy John surgery in March. He still rated as the top prospect in the Cornhusker State and went in the fourth round to the Rangers, signing for a below-slot $495,825. McConnaughey's fastball sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 mph, though it plays up a bit because he can ride it up in the zone and sink it down at the knees. He can manipulate his low-80s slider, landing a tight version for strikes and getting chases by burying them in the dirt or sweeping them away from righties. He also has good feel for a tumbling 82-85 mph changeup that neutralizes left-handers. McConnaughey has an easy, clean delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to place his pitches where he wants. Pitchers often throw harder after adding strength during the Tommy John rehab process, and adding more velocity to his present polish would raise his ceiling. Scouts praise his mound presence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyle was a reliever for much of his college career at Suffolk (N.Y.) CC and Dallas Baptist before signing for $10,000 as a 25th-round senior in 2018. He consistently has outperformed expectations as a pro and finally became a full-time starter last year. He led the system in wins (13), innings (155 1/3) and strikeouts (160) while successfully navigating Double-A and Triple-A, though he was left off New York's 40-man roster for the second straight offseason. Boyle relies heavily on the type of sweeping slider that the Yankees love, operating in the low 80s with enough horizontal action that it works against both righties and lefties, and he also can morph it into an upper-80s cutter. His two-seam fastball sits around 90 mph and maxes out at 94, and while it doesn't miss bats, its sink does create weak ground-ball contact. His fading mid-80s changeup shows flashes of becoming a solid offering but he needs to do a better job of controlling it and creating velocity separation from his sinker. His lack of overpowering stuff leaves Boyle little margin for error and he was tagged for a system-high 25 homers last year. He helps his cause by minimizing his mistakes and pounding the strike zone, though his floor always will stand out more than his ceiling. He continues to beat the odds associated with his Draft pedigree and could find a role as a slider-heavy middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending four years at St. John’s, Antico transferred to Texas as a pandemic senior for the 2021 season and made sure he was on the Draft map this time by hitting .273/.437/.489 with 10 homers while leading Division I with 63 walks and ranking second with 41 steals. The Cardinals took him in the eighth round and signed him well below slot at $20,000. Antico split his first full season between High-A Peoria and Double-A Springfield, hitting .245/.344/.395 with 14 homers, and his 67 steals led all St. Louis farmhands and tied for sixth-most in the Minors. Antico finished up with 23 more games in the Arizona Fall League as a taxi-squad member. Dating back to his college days, Antico’s whole offensive role has been about getting on base. He has a normal, quiet setup at the plate, and the lack of noise helps him see the ball well and take his walks (11.9 percent BB rate in 2022). Standing at 5-foot-10, there isn’t a ton of power, but he could threaten for double-digit homers over a full Major League season with an uphill swing that put the ball in the air 46.7 percent of the time -- the highest fly ball rate among Cardinals full-season qualifiers last year. That also takes away his ability to snap up infield hits, though. A plus-plus runner, Antico’s value will stem from his feet. He’s the perfect type of base runner to take advantage of new rules encouraging stealing, as he proved in 2022, and he can track down balls between the gaps in center too. Because of his extensive collegiate experience, his second full season will be his age-25 campaign, so he’ll need to get to his ceiling as a speedy fourth outfielder soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing high school baseball at Westlake HS (Ga.), Nowlin went to Chipola Junior College in Florida, and while he didn’t throw a ton -- 60 innings in total over two seasons, almost all in relief -- he impressed with his ability to miss bats. The left-hander didn’t hurt his stock by throwing well in the Cape Cod League in 2021, with the Twins taking him in the 19th round of the Draft that year and going a bit over the Day 3 slot to sign him for $160,000. Developing him cautiously, he both started and relieved in his first full season, reaching High-A at the end of the year. Because of Nowlin’s lack of deep resume, he’s still pretty raw, but his performance as a pro has spoken for itself. He struck out about 36 percent of batters he faced in 2022. His fastball averaged around 92 mph and topped out at 95-96 with high spin and good arm side life, with the potential for more consistent velocity as he gets more physical. He missed a ton of bats with both his low-80s slider, which is more of a north-south pitch with depth than a sweeping breaker, and a mid-80s changeup that was effective more because of the velocity differential than the action of the pitch. Nowlin is going to have to refine his command, with an inflated walk rate (4.6 BB/9 in 2022), especially as he moves up the ladder and faces hitters less likely to chase out of the zone. If he does that, he has the chance to start. If not, his stuff could play well as a lefty reliever in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most advanced prospect in Miami's 2022 international crop, de la Cruz turned pro for $150,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Making his U.S. debut last summer, he needed just two starts in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League to earn a promotion to Single-A. The only 18-year-old to work double-digit innings in the Florida State League, he held his own with a 4.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts in 43 1/3 innings. While de la Cruz still is refining his entire repertoire, both his fastball and curveball show the potential to become plus pitches once fully developed. His riding fastball parked at 92-95 mph and touched 97 before he tired late in his first full pro season, and he should add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-70s curveball has good shape with plenty of depth and some horizontal action but also would benefit from more power. De la Cruz's changeup has some interesting fade, though it gets too firm in the mid-80s and he needs to use it more often so he can refine it. He's not as physical as Edward Cabrera was as a teenager, but he reminds some club officials of their big league starter with his repertoire and delivery. His control was spotty versus much older competition in the FSL but should be fine as he adds more strength and experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hood overcame some pandemic-impacted challenges at Penn, mainly in that his 2020 season was cut short after just eight games and that it was canceled altogether in ‘21. His performance as the 2019 Ivy League rookie of the year caught some eyes, including those of the Red Sox, who drafted him in the 20th round in 2021. But Hood instead opted to transfer to NC State, where he jumped on Seattle’s radar and prompted the club to take him in the sixth round in 2022 and give him $250,000 to sign. The 22-year-old has above-average raw power and has the chance to remain an infielder, perhaps even at shortstop, though he profiles better at third. He also plays a decent outfield defense, which collectively has drawn comparisons to big league super utilityman Dylan Moore but with more power. That type of versatility could only help his case to ascend quickly. Hood has legit strength and an aggressive approach, with some impressive exit velocities already. But one critique is that he can too often hunt the homer. He’ll also need to make adjustments against secondary pitching, especially as he rises the ranks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crossland bounced from Division II Ouachita Baptist (Okla.) to Weatherford (Texas) JC to the University of Oklahoma in a three-year collegiate period. Just when he was about to show off with the Sooners, he strained a back muscle in fall practice, and it affected his performance with a 6.32 ERA in 68 1/3 innings. He struck out 26.6 percent of his batters faced, though, and buoyed himself with nine strikeouts and just one unearned run allowed in seven innings against Nebraska in the NCAA Regionals. The Cardinals selected him in the fourth round and signed him above slot at $729,500. The 6-foot-2 southpaw touched 98 mph in his one SEC spring but generally sat 91-94. He could elicit a healthy amount of chase by climbing the ladder effectively with the heater from a simple side-step delivery. Holding bigger velocity without the back problems should be a goal in pro ball. Crossland’s most dominant pitch was easily his 83-85 mph changeup that generated special fade, and hitters swung over it again and again. He sells it well out of the hand, only for it to die just as it reaches the plate. His low-80s breaking pitches didn’t have great spin rates or feel for the zone, but he could work a slider or humpier curveball in for different looks. Crossland slowly improved his control rates during his various stops in school, but even with the simple mechanics, he still walked 10.4 percent of batters faced with OU. At least the changeup should help him run reverse splits in the pros, and that’ll help his chances of finding a spot in the back of a future St. Louis rotation, especially if he gets to a little more velo with full health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a two-sport standout who didn't stop playing football until his senior year of high school. He was on scouts' radars in southern California but headed to pitch at UC Irvine. Although Injuries interrupted his progress over his two first years with the Anteaters, a chance to move into their rotation in March of his junior year allowed him to take off. He landed in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, and while he didn't pitch officially after signing, he got in some good work during instructs. An athletic 6-foot-5 right-hander, Kelly entered pro ball with three pitches and might now have four at his disposal. The Rockies are hoping there might be another tier of velocity to reach with his fastball, which currently sits in the 91-94 mph range, occasionally touching 96. It has some good metrics with some ride and finish to the pitch. But Kelly's really all about the spin. His upper-70s curve has 11-to-5 shape and regularly tops 3,000 rpm, and he can miss bats with his low-80s changeup as well. During instructs, he found a slider grip that works for him, giving him a fourth pitch that could be Major League average. Kelly started throwing better quality strikes when he became a starter during his junior year, and the hope is that trend continues. He has the pitch mix to start and will be given the opportunity to stick in a rotation if he can hold the zone consistently throughout his outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for only $17,500 out of Colombia in January 2022, Liñan spent his first three years in the Los Angeles system primarily working out of the bullpen. His big breakout came as a starter in 2025, and he had a 2.78 ERA with 101 strikeouts in 74 1/3 innings across three levels heading into the Trade Deadline, when the Dodgers moved him to the Nationals as part of the Alex Call deal. Washington dealt him again eight months later, shipping him to the Yankees for Jorbit Vivas right before the start of the regular season. Liñan has a legitimate claim for the best changeup in Minor League Baseball. The 6-foot right-hander throws the 79-82 mph offering like a screwball with significant drop and armside run, and oddly, it’s also his highest-spin pitch. Batters whiffed on 60 percent of their swings against the cambio that earns Devin Williams comps from virtually all that witness it. But how far can Liñan can go on that one pitch alone? He throws a 90-93 mph four-seamer and sinker with ordinary movement that got crushed in ’25; at their best, he can sneak them by batters waiting for the lower-velo changeup. Liñan also has a mid-80s cutter/slider with only slight armside movement. Liñan looked like he could deliver enough strikes at Single-A and High-A, but his brief runs in Triple-A and the Fall League made that less of a certainty. He could stand to add some extra velocity, and considering he’s only entering his age-21 season in 2026, that remains a possibility. But for now, he’s trending a one-pitch relief role, albeit with that one pitch being excellent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds handed out 10 bonuses of six figures or more at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, including two north of $1 million. In terms of early returns, it’s been Confidan, who signed for $200,000 out of the Domincan Republic, who has stood out. He came to the United States to make his professional debut in 2021 and promptly hit .315/.359/.573 to earn Arizona Complex League MVP honors. The left-handed hitting outfielder has the chance to be a very good offensive performer. He has a handsy swing and manipulates the bat well and has a ton of raw power, especially to the pull side. The biggest surprise may have been how much he accessed it right out the gate, with 11 homers in 178 at-bats in 2021. He will need to work on his overall approach as he advances to cut down on his tendency to chase, though there may always be some swing-and-miss to his game. Defensively, Confidan has a strong arm that might be plus in time, one that allowed him to pick up seven outfield assists in the ACL. Improvement on his reads and routes will come with more reps and he could fit the athletic right fielder profile well. Just 19 for all of the 2022 season, he reminds some of fellow Reds prospect Elly De La Cruz as an under-the-radar prospect whose tools translated better, and faster, than expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's 2025 Delaware high school player of the year, Mitchell won a state championship at Cape Henlopen HS (Lewes), a program that has produced big leaguers Mason Fluharty and Zack Gelof. The Astros drafted him in the seventh round, making him the state's highest selection since 2012 Rangers second-rounder Jamie Jarmon. Mitchell signed for $797,500, tripling his slot value and breaking Jarmon's Delaware record of $601,500. More physical than most high schoolers at 6-foot-3 and 205 pounds, Mitchell features plus raw power. He needs to learn to let that pop come naturally rather than hunting home runs, which leads to his left-handed stroke getting too long and uphill. He hits balls hard but doesn't have much experience facing quality pitching, so he'll have to prove that he can hit premium velocity and breaking pitches. As a catcher, Mitchell stands out most with solid arm strength that will play better once he improves his footwork. He needs to clean up his receiving and blocking and may need some time to adjust to handling pro pitchers. He's a below-average runner but not bad for his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roki Sasaki took up virtually all of the pitching oxygen in this year’s international class, and much of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 ranking was loaded with players at other premium positions. The second-highest ranked arm – and the only left-hander on the list – was Alvarez out of Santo Domingo East, Dominican Republic. The southpaw was one of two players to sign with the Padres for $1 million, shortstop Jhoan De La Cruz being the other. Alvarez would stand out plenty for his handedness and his size at 6-foot-4, but he caught plenty of scouts’ attentions as well with a fastball that already works consistently in the low-90s. It isn’t hard to envision him adding a few ticks more as he ages and matures more physically. He also shows a biting slider and fading changeup that could become average pitches in time. A former outfielder who only recently converted to full-time pitching, Alvarez is still raw on the mound, but that works to his credit here as he still has a fresh arm. Using a short arm action from his big frame, he can land strikes decently well for his experience level, and that will help his starting chances early in his career. Alvarez will be 17 for the entirety of his first professional season and has plenty of time to develop into a promising young lefty in the San Diego system alongside Kash Mayfield and Boston Bateman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brazoban was ranked No. 38 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2024 signing period opened this past January. The Pirates made him their top target, and he became one of nine prospects in the class to get a bonus of $2 million or more by getting that amount exactly. He’ll get his first taste of professional baseball in the Dominican Summer League. A left-handed-hitting and -throwing outfielder, Brazoban has already shown a solid approach and strike-zone knowledge to go along with a knack for consistent hard contact. He has quick hands with excellent bat speed, allowing him to drive the ball line-to-line with authority. There are flashes of over-the-fence power, with more to come as the teenager matures. Lean and athletic, Brazoban runs well, especially underway. He has the kind of frame that should be able to add strength, which could mean more pop and speed. He looks like he could have a chance to stick in center field, but if he slows down as he gets older, a move to the corner isn’t out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee has been hailed as one of the most effective clubs when it comes to international scouting in recent years, and its top signing from the start of the 2025 international window was Fenelon out of Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic. The 17-year-old signed for $1.3 million, making him one of only two seven-figure additions for the Brewers’ 2025 class. Brewers director of international scouting James Armstrong described Fenelon’s power as “top of the market” when his Jan. 15 signing was announced. The right-handed slugger uses an uppercut swing to bring the pop into his game, though some evaluators have expressed concern about how his mechanics will play against pro-level arms. Power isn’t his only above-average tool, however. Fenelon also draws excitement for his wheels, and that power-speed combination could be special if it all comes together offensively. Standing at 6-foot right now, Fenelon earns quality reviews for his work in center field. He already shows the instincts to get good jumps on balls and then can track those in the gaps with his speed as well. That should help him get long looks at the position moving forward. Below-average arm strength might point to a future in left if and when he bumps into bigger talents up the middle, but the power should still be valuable in that spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tunink enticed scouts with his left-handed stroke and athleticism as an Illinois high schooler, his strong Notre Dame commitment clouded his signability in the 2024 Draft. The Dodgers floated him down to the eighth round and were able to land him for $412,500, the equivalent of fifth-round money. He earned Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his pro debut last summer after finishing fourth in the Rookie circuit in wRC+ (152), slugging (.550) and OPS (.967), but he also struck out at a 30 percent rate. Tunink's bat speed, growing strength and propensity for driving the ball in the air to his pull side generate high exit velocities and plus raw power. He's not overly aggressive in terms of chasing pitches, but he has holes in his swing that lead to too many in-zone misses. Viewed as more of a hit-over-power guy as an amateur, he flipped that projection in the ACL. Tunink features at least plus speed that makes him a basestealing threat and a solid center fielder. He has below-average arm strength and didn't record an assist in 35 outfield starts last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ross moved all over the collegiate spectrum with time at Eastern Kentucky (2020), Northwest Florida State College (2021) and Georgia (2022). But he lasted only two starts with the Bulldogs before needing Tommy John surgery, and the elbow procedure pushed him down into the 13th round, where the Mets took and signed him for $125,000. A TJ revision pushed his pro debut back to September 2024, and after a trip to the Arizona Fall League, he was ready for a healthy breakout in ’25. Ross accomplished just that, posting a 2.17 ERA with 80 strikeouts in 54 relief innings across three levels before getting called up (but going unused) by New York in late September. The 6-foot-5 right-hander came back with a vengeance in 2025. He ran his four-seamer up to 102 mph and generally sat 96-98 with it. The heater also came with roughly seven feet of extension on average, putting it right on top of hitters. But the velocity is the biggest standout there, and it didn’t miss as many bats as expected in his 28 Triple-A outings, making it more plus than plus-plus. Ross uses his 88-91 mph splitter as his primary weapon against lefties; it averaged only 708 rpm at the Minors’ top level, making it a real spin killer. Ross’ upper-80s slider dominated righty bats with limited gloveside movement, just enough to give him something the other way. He also occasionally flipped in a mid-80s curveball. Ross’ walk rate exploded to 17.3 percent at Syracuse; without a big breaker or armside runner, the movement profile might make him more predictable horizontally, limiting the chase he needs to dominate. His control will be the biggest determining factor in his future MLB role because batters can’t touch his stuff when they do swing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the best left-handed high-school pitchers in the country headed into the 2020 Draft, Savino was so committed to the University of Virginia that he graduated a semester early and headed to Charlottesville that spring instead. He wasn’t wowing scouts the same way in college, but after some promise in the fall of 2021, he enjoyed the best spring of his brief Cavaliers career, posting a 3.69 ERA with 79 strikeouts in 78 innings. The D-backs selected him in the third round and signed him for just below slot at $700,000. Savino underwent shoulder surgery before his first full season began, meaning his pro debut will wait until 2024. The 6-foot-3 southpaw added some velo to his fastball last spring, ranging from 90-94 mph after it averaged just 87.4 mph in 2021, and his slider also moved from the upper 70s to the low 80s while showing more sharpness. An effective changeup rounded out the pitch mix, and as the stuff looked better, so did his punchout rates. That said, Savino wasn’t always consistent with the velocity as a junior, and scouts had serious questions about who he would be over a larger sample in the pro ranks. The good news is he largely throws strikes, having walked 9.4 percent of his batters faced in 2022, and his delivery is simple and athletic enough that that shouldn’t change even against more advanced bats. Even if it’s just average stuff across the board, that’s enough to make Savino a possible Major League backend starter with the possibility for more if the D-backs can squeeze more velo out of him upon his return next season .

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019, Saladin still didn’t see the Dominican Summer League until 2021 due to the pandemic and repeated the level after becoming a starter in 2022. He moved stateside in 2023 and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 with a 2.62 ERA that ranked second among St. Louis Minor League full-season qualifiers. He also struck out 134 and walked 33 over 123 innings between Single-A and High-A. He was Rule 5-eligible in the offseason but went unprotected and unpicked due to his distance from the Majors. Standing only 5-foot-11, Saladin still stands out for his fastball that comes out of a low release height and has a flat vertical approach angle, causing more swing-and-miss than expected for most four-seamers. The pitch played in the 92-94 mph range in the Florida State League but lost some steam late with Peoria, understandable considering Saladin’s workload. His mid-80s changeup comes with enough armside run and deception off the fastball to get some whiffs too and hold lefties relatively at bay. A low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball aren’t at the same standard. Saladin kept his walk rates fairly low at both levels in 2024, and while he relies on some chase on all of his pitches (particularly the changeup), he has the control to remain a starter. Despite his Rule 5 status, the hurler is only entering his age-22 season and should get heavier 40-man consideration if he enjoys repeat success in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Mathison showed off some legitimate pop at various stops, first as a high school senior and then when he stayed in-state to play college ball for the Hoosiers, homering 19 times as a freshman. He was more inconsistent his next two years but he still finished sixth on Indiana’s career home run list with 42 and the Phillies took the power potential in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft, going a little over slot to sign him and sending him to full-season Clearwater for a very brief pro debut. It remains to be seen what kind of impact Mathison can ultimately have at the plate. The left-handed hitter has plus raw juice and can drive the ball to all fields, but while he was willing to take walks in college, he also got too passive at times and took too many strikes. His swing also got long and he’ll have to show he can be dangerous with a wood bat after not doing much during his time in the Cape Cod League in 2023. Mathison has plus speed but wasn’t much of a basestealer with the Hoosiers, but his wheels were a definite asset in the outfield. He has every chance to play center field for a long time and might be plus there when all is said and done. He can play all three outfield spots well, something he did during his debut and which should continue while he works to develop his offensive game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While big-money international signings are usually wrapped in January, De La Cruz didn’t officially join the Nationals organization until April last year. All the same, the Dominican Republic native’s $500,000 bonus was the third-highest for a new Nationals prospect in the 2025 signing cycle. He backed that up quickly in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .294/.448/.450 with two homers, 15 steals, 30 walks and only 17 strikeouts over 39 games. A left-handed hitter, De La Cruz certainly put up a performance that would jump off any page at any level. His 1.76 BB/K ratio was 13th-best among 363 hitters with at least 140 plate appearances in the DSL last year. However, evaluators believe some of that success came from an all-too passive approach at the plate. In a league with young, wild arms like the DSL, oftentimes the best decision is not to swing. That can be promising discipline. It can also be worrisome if it’s a trend that carries over to leagues with arms that boast much better control. De La Cruz could also get to at least average power if he adds strength to his 6-foot frame in his move stateside. An average runner, De La Cruz got the vast majority of his starts in center field in the DSL, as one might expect for the bigger-money signing on the grass, but he also saw time in both corners. He seems likely to slide over to left or right more permanently higher up the Nats’ chain. De La Cruz has certainly put himself on the map entering year two, and how he answers the passivity question will determine his place in Washington’s growing outfield depth chart.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After LaCombe posted a 1.74 ERA with 97 strikeouts in 67 1/3 innings at Cochise (Ariz.) CC in 2023, he became the second native of France ever drafted when the White Sox took him in the 12th round. Signed away from a Louisiana-Lafayette commitment for fifth-round money ($450,000), he dealt with a shoulder impingement and lat issues and didn't make his pro debut until 2025. He thrived in Rookie ball but battled the strike zone in Single-A. LaCombe has a pair of bat-missing weapons, beginning with a fastball that parks at 93-95 mph and touches 98 with carry and armside run. He has improved his low-80s slider since turning pro, and it features some of the best sweeping action among Chicago's farmhands. His mid-80s splitter has nice tumble when it's on but lacks consistency. LaCombe's low arm slot produces wide angle and a low release height, not to mention life on his pitches. It also makes it difficult to stay on top of his secondary offerings, and he struggled in Single-A when he landed his slider and splitter in the zone just 30 percent of the time. He looks like a mid-rotation starter when he's at his best, but he'll also be 24 this season and has pitched just 17 2/3 innings above Rookie ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Southern California’s Notre Dame HS helped produce Hunter Greene and Giancarlo Stanton, and Gurevitch is aiming to be the next big name from the program, though his path took him in state to the University of San Diego before the pros. He showed steady gains over his three years with the Toreros before exploding with a .371/.477/.681 line and 17 homers in 56 games as a junior. The Cardinals took him in the third round, signed him for slot at $879,000 and sent him to Single-A Palm Beach for 22 games where he struggled in the late summer. Gurevitch has a straight-on stance from the left side of the box, featuring a crouch and hands held high. He relies on those hands to drive his contact, without a big load in his lower half, but that was enough to make lots of loud impact during his final spring on campus. His clean mechanics made him look like a potential above-average hitter coming out of school with at least average pop. Fair or not, some of his reddish flags from college glowed crimson in the Florida State League, namely his high chase and whiff rates on sliders and his inability to catch up to pitches at 94 mph or above. That exposure, along with an offseason to prepare, could help Gurevitch erase those concerns in his first full campaign in ’26. Gurevitch got some time at third base with San Diego, but many believed he was always headed to first base. Indeed, all of his starts with Palm Beach came at the cold corner. He’ll need to hit to be valuable there, but he earned good reviews for his leadership coming out of school, adding to the belief that he could take well to St. Louis’ hitting development department.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals’ 2024 international class was headlined by shortstop Yandel Ricardo, ranked No. 17 on MLB Pipeline’s international prospects list, and the club handed Ugarte a $1,312,500 bonus to sign out of the Dominican Republic just two months before he turned 17. Ugarte jumped onto the radar later that year in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .299 with an .818 OPS and nearly as many walks (30) as strikeouts (36) in 46 games. He then participated in the Royals’ instructional league that fall. Ugarte has an efficient bat path and line-drive swing, with some quickness to the hands as he makes contact. He starts in an athletic stance with his front foot slightly back, using a toe tap to get into a firing position. He’s already grown into a sturdy frame, but there might be another level he can get to with his power. While DSL pitchers can get wild, Ugarte has already shown a good awareness for the strike zone, although he struggled with breaking balls like many young hitters do. Ugarte is strong and looks more like a third baseman or even a corner outfielder, but the Royals will develop him as an infielder. He has above-average arm strength and good instincts, and he should be a solid defender wherever he lands. Ugarte doesn’t turn 18 until March, after which he’ll make his stateside debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2025. He’s young and his development will take time, but the potential for an everyday third baseman is certainly there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had a compensation pick after the fourth round of the 2025 Draft after losing Max Fried to free agency. They used it to pick up Williams, a middle infielder who was coming off a solid junior season at East Carolina, finishing with 14 homers and an OPS over 1.000 before going 8-for-20 and being named to the all-tournament team at the NCAA Greenville Regional. He signed for just under $500,000, a bit under slot, becoming the earliest-drafted hitter from the Pirates program since Connor Norby was a second-rounder in 2021. Williams brought his solid approach from the left side of the plate with him during his relatively brief 28-game pro debut last summer with Single-A Augusta. He could be an average hitter in the future with solid on-base skills and strike zone control. He drew more walks than strikeouts in his last year of college, part of what helped him get to his power more, with his over-the-fence pop coming mostly to his pull side. His debut with Augusta was solid, but the Braves think the underlying data points to even better contact rates to come. A plus runner who swiped 22 bases in 25 tries last year at East Carolina, Williams could have a potentially intriguing power-speed combination in the future. Where he ends up defensively is still up in the air. He played second and third in college, and his arm might be a tad short for the hot corner. His best bet long term to stick in one spot might be as an offensive-minded player at the keystone. But he’ll likely move around some, with center field one day not out of the question for a more likely utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants drafted Heliot Ramos in the first round out of the Leadership Christian Academy (Guaynabo, P.R.) in 2017, then went back there six years later to take Ortiz in the 13th round. He impressed with his athleticism on the U.S. high school showcase circuit and continued to do so in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League the last two years. Promoted to Single-A last August, he banged up his knee running into the outfield wall in his first game, ending his 2024 season. Ortiz isn't very physical, so he focuses on making contact and getting on base. He has good feel for his right-handed swing and the strike zone and looked more comfortable against pro pitching during his second stint in the ACL. He did a better job of turning on pitches and lifting them last summer, so he could grow into 12-15 homer power once he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. Ortiz earns plus grades for his speed, arm and center-field defense. He has the mentality and aptitude to steal bases, and the instincts enhance his range in center. His arm is stronger than most at his position, adding to his credentials as the system's best defensive outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After an up-and-down freshman year at Clemson in 2023, mostly in relief, Smith really put himself on scouts' radars with an outstanding performance in the Cape Cod League that summer. The Draft-eligible sophomore had an up arrow next to his name with how he was throwing during the 2024 season, but an ankle injury that forced him out for a month slowed his progress a bit. The Reds made him the third college pitcher they took in last summer's Draft, going over slot in the fifth round to sign him for $600,000. As they typically do with their college arm draftees, the Reds didn't pitch Smith competitively after he signed and he managed just a handful of outings in 2025 after dealing with illness then knee discomfort following his return. In some ways, Smith is the same pitcher who was a top South Carolina prep talent, a left-hander with a fastball that sits 91-94 mph and touches 96 mph, one who can ride it up in the zone or sink it down. His low-80s slider has a lot of sweep, and he lands it in the zone consistently with high spin rates to miss a good amount of bats. He had a really good feel for a slinking low-80s changeup in high school, and he's not afraid to throw it to hitters on both sides of the plate. While he has the arsenal to start long-term, it remains to be seen if he can throw enough strikes to be in a big league rotation. His delivery can get out of sync, and he loses his direction to the plate, impacting his control and command. The Reds will have to wait until 2026 to get their first prolonged look at him, and he still has a starting pitcher ceiling if he can repeat his delivery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coba wouldn’t have popped on many radars as a $10,000 signing out of Venezuela in May 2024, and he was initially used out of the Tigers’ Dominican Summer League bullpen in his first season with rough results (14 ER, 11 BB, 14 K in 12 1/3 innings). He returned to the DSL as a starter in ’25 and was much more in control there. Coba has moved to the Florida Complex League this season for his first taste of affiliated stateside ball, and his early work in the Sunshine State has solidified his standing as one of the more intriguing young arms in the Detroit system. All three of the 6-foot right-hander’s pitches show promise. Coba can run his four-seamer into the mid-90s while generating 18-20 inches of ride, but right now, he can leak some of that velocity over the length of his outings. If he can continue to build strength and sit 94-96 rather than 92-95, the heater would become a true plus pitch. His 79-83 mph slider shows gyro shape, dropping more downward than to the gloveside, but it can play well off the heat running up and in on righties. His 83-86 mph changeup kills spin while showing similar armside run to the four-seamer except it tumbles more, leading to empty swings when it’s on. Coba throws with some energy on the bump -- the arm speed helps sell the changeup -- and when he misses, it’s because he’s yanking the ball a bit too much to his gloveside. Still, it was promising to see him cut his walk rate by more than half between his two DSL stints, and with three potentially above-average pitches in his arsenal, he’ll deserve more starting looks as he climbs the domestic ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Warwick’s path from Downers Grove North High School in Chicago to Michigan State took a detour when Detroit drafted him in the 12th round in 2024 and wooed him away from Big Ten baseball with a $247,500 bonus. He did so well at the Florida Complex League that the Tigers gave him a chance at full-season ball at Single-A Lakeland, where his command of the strike zone was tested. He still showed plenty of reason to climb the prospect rankings and became the latest shortstop in the Tigers’ potential pipeline. Warwick is a speedy, solid-fielding shortstop with a disciplined approach at bat. His parents enrolled him in dance classes as a child, which reflects in his solid footwork and ample range at short, though he also saw time at second. At the plate, Warwick stays upright in his stance before employing a toe tap to generate some momentum in his swing. He showed solid swing decisions and contact rates in the FCL but struggled with the jump. That said, he needs to add strength to his 6-foot-1 frame. He’s at least an above-average runner with both aggression and savviness in picking his spots on the basepaths. The Tigers have enough shortstop prospects that Warwick can easily get overlooked, and he’ll likely continue to until he makes a bigger offensive impact. That could require physical growth. Even if it doesn’t happen, his left-handed bat and defensive range could ultimately find him a utility infield role in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 Dickinson certainly had an interesting path to pro ball. He didn’t make his varsity team at Kennewick HS (Wash.) until he was a junior and headed to Utah Valley for college as a walk-on. He was a two-time All-Western Athletic Conference first-team honoree with the Wolverines and set school records with 18 homers and 32 steals in 2024. He had stints in Cape Cod and with the U.S. Collegiate National Team that summer and transferred to LSU as a junior, helping the Tigers win a Men's College World Series title while hitting .315/.458/.525 with 12 homers and a 42/40 K/BB ratio in 68 games. The Brewers took him in the sixth round and signed him for $325,000. Batting from the right side, Dickinson looks relaxed at the plate and employs a simple right-handed swing and excellent hand-eye coordination to put lots of pitch types into play. His chase rate in his final year of college was just a tad below the MLB average, and his ability to get that bat on the ball kept strikeouts in check. His raw power is just average at best, however, and he didn’t slug much with wood bats before his move to Baton Rouge -- something worth watching in his introduction to the pros. As an average runner with average arm strength, Dickinson bounced around a good amount defensively as a collegian with most of his looks for Utah Valley and LSU coming at second base. With other priority shortstops Jesús Made, Luis Peña and Cooper Pratt already in the system ahead of him, it’s likely Dickinson will settle in back at the keystone. Down the road, he might project best as a contact-heavy utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis worked out of the Sam Houston State bullpen for two years, got a taste for starting in the Cape Cod League in 2023 and transferred to Oklahoma for the '24 season. He posted a 4.30 ERA with 117 strikeouts in 92 innings during his time in Norman, and the Cardinals took him in the fifth round that summer before signing him for $485,700. He led all Cardinals farmhands with 153 strikeouts and finished with a 2.85 ERA over 110 1/3 innings between Single-A Palm Beach and High-A Peoria last season. The 5-foot-11 southpaw picked up velo from his days as a Sooner and sat 90-94 mph with his fastball, touching as high as 96.9 in the Florida State League. There was a ton of ride and run on the pitch that lower-level hitters just couldn’t handle. But its below-average velo also comes with below-average extension, and it’s likely that more experienced bats will read it better. Davis’ best pitch is a killer 80-82 mph changeup that had a 61 percent whiff rate across both levels. It moves much like the heater and has only a smidge less spin, but the velo differential fooled batters and led to dominance against righties. A low-80s slider also showed some depth as an option moving gloveside, and a mid-80s cutter bridged the repertoire. As untouchable as he could be in terms of hits and strikeouts, Davis struggled to stay in the strike zone consistently, and his 16.6 percent walk rate was the highest among any Minor League full-season qualifier. He can pitch like he’s trying to be fine at the corners, only to miss with uncompetitive pitches. The reverse splits and nasty changeup still make him intriguing, but the lack of control could shorten his leash as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ibarguen was announced as a shortstop when he signed with the Brewers for only $60,000 out of Venezuela in January 2023, but he’s yet to play there in pro ball as he’s bopped around all three outfield spots as well as second and third base. His bat did the early talking at the outset of his career anyway, as he hit .311/.437/.447 with three homers and seven steals over 43 games with Milwaukee’s Dominican Summer League affiliate. Batting from the right side, Ibarguen did a nice job of adjusting to pro-level pitching and was named the Brewers’ Complex Player of the Month in August, when he hit .341/.436/.659 with more extra-base hits and walks (seven each) than strikeouts (five) over 14 games. With a slight leg kick and early bat movement, his swing is geared to provide pullside power, and that’s where most of his batted balls land. There’s the potential for at least average power eventually, though his size is a little limited at 5-foot-10. (Note: Ibarguen turned 17 in July after signing, so time is on his side when it comes to physical maturation.) The Brewers’ 2023 international class was too loaded at shortstop and pushed Ibarguen all over the diamond. He has the arm strength to play anywhere in the outfield and even some third base. The majority of his looks came on the dirt as Milwaukee wanted to try him up the middle. If he does land in a corner, he’ll have to replicate his DSL numbers or develop even more power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brailer Guerrero was the big name in the Rays’ 2023 international signing class, but they may have landed another player to watch in Monzon. The infielder from La Guaira, Venezuela, was signed for $300,000 by Rays scouts Marlon Roche and William Bergolla. Initially viewed as a defensive-oriented shortstop who could also make contact at the plate, he immediately performed well in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old and jumped onto the prospect radar. Monzon is one of the Rays’ best young players coming out of the DSL, and his .281/.395/.421 batting line reflects some of the things he does well. His hit tool stands out ahead of his power, which is more gap to gap at this point, but he controls the strike zone well from the left side of the plate and he ultimately had more walks (35) than strikeouts (30) in 205 plate appearances during his 46-game professional debut. Considering he was signed as a glove-first prospect, it’s an especially interesting offensive profile for someone his age -- but he’s obviously yet to be tested by even Florida Complex League pitching. Monzon played 25 games at shortstop, 10 at third base and nine at second last season. He’s a shortstop for at least the short term, with above-average actions, solid instincts in the field and enough arm to hold down the spot. The question is more about how he grows physically, as he bulked up quickly to 6-foot and 160 pounds with some projection remaining on his frame. If he gets bigger, it’s more an issue of lateral quickness and whether he’s better suited for one of the other infield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tillero signed for $497,500 out of Venezuela, making him the most expensive pitcher in the Dodgers' 2023 international class. Los Angeles hadn't spent that much on an arm in that market since giving Jerming Rosario $650,000 and Osvanni Gutierrez $600,000 five years earlier. In his pro debut, Tillero earned the starting nod in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League's All-Star game and logged a 1.47 ERA with 34 strikeouts in 30 2/3 innings. Before he tired later in the summer, Tillero displayed a 94-95 mph fastball that touched 97 with plenty of induced vertical break. His slider parks at 83-86 mph at its best and could become a solid or better offering once he improves its consistency. He also has the makings of a decent changeup but hasn't used it much in game action. Tillero already repeats his sound delivery with ease and walked just six batters in 10 DSL starts. He's not very big or physical, so he'll have to prove that he and his stuff can hold up over a full-season workload. But he's off to a promising start and could turn heads when he makes his U.S. debut in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy was technically still a freshman in 2021, despite him being Draft eligible and in his third year as a Vanderbilt student. The right-hander had needed Tommy John surgery after his senior year in high school, so he redshirted and rehabbed with Vandy in 2019, then threw two innings total in the shortened 2020 season. He emerged as the Commodores’ closer in 2021, saving nine games and performing very well in postseason play. The Angels loved the arm strength and took him the fourth round of their pitching-only 2021 Draft, going over slot to sign him for around $750,000. While he didn’t pitch much for the Angels after signing, Murphy has the chance to move quickly through the system in a relief role. He gained velocity in his time at Vanderbilt and now features a four-seam fastball that touches 99 mph and has good riding action up in the zone. His slider is his go-to second offering, a power breaking ball thrown in the low-80s that misses bats, but that he hasn’t always commanded so well and that can flatten out when he overthrows. He does have feel for a sinking changeup that could be a good option against left-handed hitters if he can find the strike zone with it more consistently. The 6-foot-5 right-hander creates good plane and uses his high three-quarters arm slot well to stay on top of his breaking ball. He’s never going to have pinpoint control, but he doesn’t need it in a bullpen role. Because of the chance to have three pitches, he could develop into an intriguing multi-inning reliever in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies targeted college pitching in the 2025 Draft, using 13 of their 20 selections on that demographic. Their first six picks were all college arms, with Tallon the last of the half-dozen. The big left-hander spent three years at Duke, almost entirely as a reliever, showcasing swing-and-miss stuff albeit without the ability to command it consistently. A 12.5 career K/9 rate for the Blue Devils stood out and the Phillies took a chance on his bat-missing arm in the sixth round, signing for right around slot. While there was some talk about Tallon being given the chance to start out of the gate, it’s looking like he’s going to be a reliever to kick off his pro career. The 6-foot-5 southpaw is all about his unhittable fastball, a pitch he threw more than 70 percent of the time last year at Duke.
