It sits in the low 90s and tops out at just 95 mph, but it elicited a miss rate of 34 percent and a 35-percent chase rate in 2025 thanks to a deceptive delivery and a low release height. He’ll need to improve his breaking ball, though his cutter-like slider did miss bats at times. Tallon did throw a mid-80s changeup now and again in college, but will likely focus on his top two pitches as a professional reliever. He needs to harness his command after walking 4.7 per nine last year, but if he can do that and improve his ability to spin the ball, he could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the advanced age of 18 in 2023, Florentino drew little attention while spending his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He made a spectacular U.S. debut in 2025, earning Cubs Minor League Pitcher of the Year accolades. He posted a 2.43 ERA, .201 opponent average and a 30 percent strikeout rate despite a lack of physicality and velocity. Florentino has a slender 6-foot frame and a fastball that sits around 90 mph with a peak of 92 without notable carry or run. But lower-level hitters haven't done damage against his heater because his low arm slot and ability to get down the mound produce an elite low release height and quality extension. His slider parks in the mid-70s but missed a lot of bats last summer with high spin rates and plenty of sweep. Florentino relies mainly on his fastball and slider, occasionally turning the latter into a mid-80s cutter and also fiddling with a mid-80s changeup with fade, though neither of those offerings fool hitters at this point. He has a simple, effortless delivery that has allowed him to provide consistent strikes throughout his career. He could be very intriguing if he can find some more power for his main two weapons, and the fact that his heater gained 5 mph from 2024 to 2025 is an encouraging sign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson utilized a low slot at Virginia Commonwealth before the Yankees selected him in the 15th round in 2021. Following his lackluster first full pro season in Single-A, they had him drop down further and overhaul his arsenal. The changes paid off as he led all Minor League relievers (minimum: 60 innings) with a 1.58 ERA and ranked second with a .138 opponent average while reaching Double-A. Watson creates unique deception as a 6-foot-7 sidearmer with an upright delivery. Batters struggle to barrel his fastball, which parks at 90-92 mph and tops out at 94 but features tremendous carry and armside run. He has scrapped a tight slider and a changeup and now works with a mid-80s cutter that shows flashes of becoming a solid offering and a fringier 78-82 mph sweeper. The new arm slot not only upgraded Watson's stuff, but he's also throwing more strikes. The changes also helped him log a .393 OPS against left-handers in 2023 after they teed off on him for a 1.019 OPS the year before. He could reach New York in 2024 if his unusual look can continue to baffle hitters in Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his high school career in Champaign, Illinois, Munroe stayed in-state to keep playing at the junior college level, setting both single-season and career home run records at John A. Logan College. He parlayed that to an invite to play for Louisville in 2025 and continued to perform with an OPS over 1.000 and a spot on the College World Series All-Tournament Team. The Angels took him in the fourth round of last summer's Draft, signing him for an under-slot bonus of just less than $600,000. He got his professional feet wet with a dozen games in the California League after signing and got off to a solid start with High-A Tri-City in his first full season. Munroe is a 6-foot-2 right-handed hitter who has shown a feel to hit throughout his college career and early on with the Angels. With more of a choppy approach as an amateur, even though he found the seats at that level, he profiles more as a contact-first bat with good plate discipline, one who uses the whole field with some gap power, though he was showing some over-the-fence juice early in 2026. A below-average runner who didn't show much in the way of quick-twitch athleticism at Louisville, there were some concerns about his ability to stick at third base at the pro level. So far, though, he's shown off average defensive tools with an average arm, giving him the chance to stick at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McKenzie looked like he was well on his way to Draft prominence after hitting .389 his first two seasons at Baylor, only to drop off with a .225 average and .561 OPS in 30 games on the Cape in the summer of 2021. He got off to another slow start back with the Bears before a late surge allowed him to finish with a .288/.388/.517 line in 54 games as a junior, albeit with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate. The Nats grabbed him in the fifth round, and McKenzie looked like his old self by going 28-for-70 (.400) with 10 extra-base hits and 11 steals in 17 games at Single-A Fredericksburg. McKenzie has a sweet-looking swing from the left side, one designed to spray line drives all over the field. That said, the same swing hasn’t done a great job the past two years of generating power, especially in wood-bat leagues, as he seems to prioritize contact over impact. McKenzie can get too aggressive in trying to put his bat on the ball, and that approach found him walking only once in 73 plate appearances with the FredNats. An above-average runner, McKenzie got more aggressive on the basepaths in the Carolina League, and he would be a decent bet to stick in center in most systems because of his instincts and jumps from the grass. However, James Wood’s presence pushed him to the corners last summer, and because of fringy arm strength, he’s a better defensive fit in left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fisher redshirted at Mississippi in 2020, helped Walters State (Tenn.) CC make the Junior College World Series in 2021 and cranked 18 homers (including two grand slams in one game) at Charlotte in 2022 but went undrafted because of worries about his stroke and strikeout tendencies. Then he set 49ers marks for single-season (30, third in NCAA Division I) and career homers (48), including a record six while winning MVP accolades at the Conference USA tournament, powering his way into the fourth round. He batted .273/.396/.500 with five homers in 31 games in Single-A in his pro debut. There's nothing subtle about Fisher's approach. He stands upright at the plate and looks to launch balls to his pull side with an uphill left-handed stroke. His combination of bat speed and strength, extreme pull-focused mentality and high exit velocities led one amateur scout to call him the mid-major version of Kyle Schwarber. Though he ranked fifth in D-I with 64 walks and generally makes good swing decisions, his mentality results in a lot of strikeouts and some difficulties against non-fastballs. Fisher isn't the prettiest runner, but he has surprisingly solid speed and succeeded on all 15 of his steal attempts between college and pro ball last year. His athleticism should translate into defensive ability as well, but he's just adequate as a corner outfielder with an average arm. A part-time catcher in junior college, he played mostly right field at Charlotte and in his debut but is better suited for left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels drafted McIntosh in the 34th round after he swatted 16 homers as a Motlow State (Tenn.) CC freshman in 2018, but he chose to transfer to West Virginia rather than turn pro. He had modest success with the Mountaineers but performed well in the inaugural year of the MLB Draft League in 2021, landing him a $20,000 bonus from the Marlins as a nondrafted free agent. He quickly has become an organization favorite and spent his first full pro season in Double-A, where he helped Pensacola win the Southern League championship. A right-handed hitter, McIntosh produces some of the best exit velocities in the system and works deep counts in search of pitches he can drive to his pull side. Though he fits the power-over-hit profile, he draws plenty of walks and doesn't strike out excessively. He's surprisingly quick for a catcher, can flash solid run times and displays good instincts on the bases. It may be a stretch for McIntosh to remain behind the plate, however. He earns raves for his leadership and preparation skills, but he's a decent receiver at best, struggles to block balls and has below-average arm strength. He surrendered 97 steals (at an 85 percent success rate) in 67 games last year, and Miami plans on giving him time at first base to get him more at-bats in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 40 | Slider: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 The Rangers made Hales the third reliever taken in the 2023 Draft, selecting him in the fourth round out of Santa Clara. He finished his pro debut in the High-A South Atlantic League playoffs, then advanced to Double-A midway through his first full season before getting some extra work in the Arizona Fall League. He could reach the big leagues in 2025 if he can find a reliable pitch to complement his fastball, which can be unhittable at times. Hales turns to his heater about two-thirds of the time, operating at 94-97 mph and reaching 100 with tremendous carry and deception as well as some armside run. His mid-80s slider is his most trusted secondary pitch and features sharp horizontal action at its best, though it doesn’t result in many chases or empty swings. He got roughed up in the AFL while fiddling with a low-80s curveball he couldn’t throw for strikes and an upper-80s cutter that didn’t fool anyone. Hales works from a low slot with a short arm action in back, and his mechanics allow his fastball to get on hitters more quickly than they expect. He has a history of filling the strike zone when he comes out of the bullpen, and his competitiveness contributes to his ceiling as high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peterson bounced from Purdue to Wabash Valley (Ill.) CC to Connecticut in four years of college, earning All-America honors in his final season in 2022 when he ranked second in NCAA Division I with 11 wins and third with a Huskies-record 147 strikeouts in 110 1/3 innings. His performance stood out more than his stuff, so he lasted until Cleveland drafted him in the ninth round. He shook off a so-so 2023 pro debut to lead the Minors with 14 victories and a 0.89 WHIP last year while placing second in K/BB ratio (7.6) and walk rate (4 percent) and advancing to Double-A. Relying heavily on deception, Peterson uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create plenty of extension and has the feel to manipulate the ball to produce three solid secondary pitches. His low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball both feature downward action, as does his fading mid-80s changeup, and all three elicit a lot of chases. He has added strength since turning pro and his fastball has gained a couple of ticks velocity to average 92 mph and top out at 95, and it's effective when he locates it up in the zone. Repeating his easy three-quarters delivery with precision, Peterson has the best control and command in the system. He'll still have to prove he can keep Triple-A and big league hitters off his fastball and get them to fish outside the zone for his secondary pitches, which he can fall in low with a bit too much at times. He comes with a high floor as a likely back-of-the-rotation option, and the Guardians believe they can help him find more velocity and ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the D-backs out of the Dominican Republic three months after his 18th birthday in January 2021, Yan worked his way through the organization’s Dominican and Arizona Complex-level affiliates, combining for 50 2/3 innings between the two spots before enjoying his breakout performance this past season. Pitching in his age-20 campaign, the right-hander tied for third in the organization with 138 strikeouts over 103 2/3 innings and led D-backs Minor Leaguers (min. 100 IP) with a 31.9 percent K rate between Single-A Visalia and High-A Hillsboro. It's all about east-west movement for the projectable 6-foot-4 right-hander. Coming out of a lower slot, his fastball only touches the low-90s currently, but it’s a sinker that can run in hard on the hands of right-handers, making it play above the velo. It also helped lead to a 51.3 percent ground-ball rate, 24th best among 272 Minor Leaguers with at least 100 frames in 2023. Yan’s best pitch is a sweeping slider that darts the opposite way of the sinker and can make hitters look foolish if they guess wrong because of the deceptive delivery. His low-80s changeup can flash above average, but it remains inconsistent in terms of location. Notably, lefties slugged .428 off Yan in 2023, compared to only .197 for righties. After early control issues in the DSL, Yan didn’t get too much in his way in terms of walks last season, and that helped him stay in a starting role. More advanced hitters might lay off the slider, though, causing walks to creep back up, along with relief concerns. He could absolutely continue to dominate righties in shorter stints, but given his trajectory and projection, the D-backs have every reason to keep him in the rotation moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gavin Lux, Jarred Kelenic and JD Dix have been the most prominent high school bats to come out of Wisconsin in the last decade, and the state deserves credit for being the home of 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin before he shipped off to Missouri State. But the Badger State has been considerably lighter on prep arms, at least until 2025. Kussow was Wisconsin’s top prospect heading into last year’s Draft and ended up being the only player from the state selected when the Mets took him in the fourth round. His $897,500 bonus was more akin to mid-third-round money and was the highest-ever paid to a Wisconsin high school pitcher. New York has favored college arms higher up in the Draft in recent years, but it isn’t hard to see what they see in Kussow to change strategy. Standing 6-foot-5, the right-hander generates good extension and gets down the mound to create a low release point that make him difficult to read. He showed a low-90s fastball as a prepster and touched 97 with carry and armside run. An upper-80s, high-spin slider gives him a breaking-ball weapon that could take off under the Mets’ guidance, and there are the workings of a mid-80s changeup in there. Kussow’s delivery was under some scrutiny as an amateur, and he’ll likely need to smooth out his mechanics to deliver strikes consistently on the pro side. As a cold-weather arm, he has a lot of potential that the Mets, who have made tremendous gains in pitching development in recent years, could tap into in the coming years. That in-game development will have to wait until 2027 after preseason labrum surgery on his pitching shoulder pushed him to the full-season injured list for '26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Girton played three springs at Texas Tech but never found a regular spot in the rotation -- an injury-marred 2022 didn’t help -- and transferred to Oklahoma in '24. Ten of his 16 appearances with the Sooners were starts, but success was still limited with a 7.32 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 31 walks in 35 2/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the 10th round -- two rounds after taking OU teammate Ryan Lambert -- and signed him for below slot at $122,500. Girton dominated High-A Brooklyn in his first full season, posting a 2.59 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 76 1/3 innings, before slowing down in his final four starts with Double-A Binghamton. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches with bounce in his delivery and throws from a high three-quarters slot. His four-seam fastball can move in the mid 90s and acted like a downright weapon with cut-ride action at the top of the zone, getting whiffs on one-third of opponents’ swings against it across both levels in 2025. Girton works with two slider variations -- a mid-80s sweeper with a ton of horizontal break and a tighter upper-80s option that practically acts like a cutter. He has talked about adding a splitter but went to very little offspeed last season. Luckily for him, the sweeper can backfoot lefties well and helped fend off splits issues. Girton really struggled to deliver consistent strikes in school and looked to correct course midseason in ’25, only to struggle again after his move to the Eastern League. He’s already entering his age-24 season and might not have too long of a leash for starting, now that he’s seen the upper Minors, unless the control is ironed out or he finds a split/change. Even so, the fastball/sliders could put him on the fast track to Queens on their own.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Entering the 2021 season, Ferguson was considered Tennessee’s best hitting prospect since Nick Senzel, who was selected second overall in 2016, but he slumped and fell to the Padres in the fifth round of the Draft. Just like he did in his final season with the Volunteers, he has drawn walks and made things happen on the bases but also has been too passive at the plate in pro ball. He was batting .221 and ranked third in the Minors with 55 steals in 91 games between two Class A stops in 2022 before the Padres sent him to the Red Sox with Eric Hosmer and outfield prospect Corey Rosier in exchange for 2016 first-rounder Jay Groome at the Trade Deadline. When at his best in college, Ferguson displayed a sweet left-handed swing, controlled the strike zone and barreled balls with ease. In the past two years, he has tried to drive the ball in the air more often, his stroke has looked slower and he has made less contact. He needs to add some strength, stop worrying about power and focus on getting on base. Ferguson has good instincts and makes the most of his plus speed on the bases. A quality defender at the keystone in his pro debut, he has seen more action at shortstop in 2022 and looks solid there. His finely tuned internal clock helps him compensate for average arm strength at short, and he also should be capable of playing all three outfield spots if he winds up in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Overshadowed in a deep 2022 Wisconsin high school class headlined by future first-rounder Gavin Kilen, Fox was also an all-state quarterback on a championship football team. Recruited by Notre Dame primarily as a shortstop, he didn't play much as a freshman before becoming a full-time starting pitcher the next two seasons. After he led the Atlantic Coast Conference in opponent average (.187) last spring, New York signed him for an over-slot $411,100 in the sixth round. As a Fighting Irish junior, Fox operated at 91-94 and topped out at 96 with bat-missing carry and armside run on his fastball. His best offering is a tight low-80s slider that yields a lot of called strikes and in-zone misses. He also employs a mid-80s changeup with sink and fade and an upper-70s curveball that both need more refinement. The younger brother of Dodgers lefty pitching prospect Luke Fox, he's more athletic than most pitchers and has a long history of throwing strikes. There's room to add more strength to his 6-foot-3 frame and the Yankees are known for their ability to help pitchers upgrade their stuff. He already has pushed his fastball to 98 mph during offseason workouts and could have the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez was working his way back from a knee injury in the spring, but despite not being scouted much, he still looked like the best Draft prospect out of Puerto Rico in the 2023 class. That status was cemented when he headed to the Draft Combine in June, and by Draft day, he'd established himself as MLB Pipeline’s No. 213 prospect in the class. The Padres liked him even more than that, selecting him in the third round and signing him for $550,000. Gonzalez became the first Puerto Rican catcher selected in the first 10 rounds since 2017 (Santis Sanchez, A’s). He opened with Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2024 and was traded to the Rays at the Deadline as part of a three-player return for reliever Jason Adam. There are plenty of interesting parts of Gonzalez’s profile, starting with his status as a left-handed-hitting backstop. The Combine was the perfect place for him to show above-average raw power with a steady rate of exit velocities above 96 mph, and there’s a chance he could add even more pull-side pop in pro ball. The biggest raves he earns are reserved for his arm strength, with one evaluator noting he has a “bazooka” behind the dish. His blocking and receiving skills could end up being solid with professional work, and therein lies the rub. Having only turned 18 in October of his Draft year, Gonzalez faces a potentially long developmental path, and the history of prep catchers isn’t terrific across the game. But the building blocks, in this case, are worthy of some early excitement and intrigue, and that’s what the Rays were buying into with this acquisition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gourson spent three years starting for UCLA (mostly at second base), earning a reputation as a gamer who maximized what tools he had, even earning a spot on Team USA after his sophomore campaign in 2023. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular junior season, finishing with a .909 OPS, and the Pirates took a low-risk flyer on him in the ninth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for a touch under $190,000. After a nondescript pro debut after signing, he was one of the pleasant surprises of the Pirates' system in 2025, performing well in all facets of the game with High-A Greensboro and Double-A Altoona. Gourson earned a ticket to pro ball because of his approach at the plate, swing decisions and contact skills. There was enough bat-to-ball skill to think he had a chance, and that was apparent in 2025; he kept his strikeouts relatively low, despite a little more swing-and-miss once he got to Double-A, while also posting a walk rate north of 10 percent. What wasn’t expected was the increased impact from the left side of the plate. He gained a few miles per hour in bat speed and that resulted in a huge uptick in exit velocity, allowing for more quality contact. Gourson's instincts and aggressiveness make him an average runner or perhaps a slight tick above that as he stole 31 bags in 34 tries in 2025. He’s seen time at three infield positions -- all but shortstop -- and he should get some reps in the outfield corners as well. If he takes another step offensively, he has a utility role kind of future in the big leagues, and it’s hard to bet against him given his intangibles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were certainly bigger names and bigger players than the 5-foot-9 Rivero in the Nationals’ 2018-19 international signing class, and in part because of the 2020 canceled season, it took the shortstop a little longer to prove himself within the system. That opportunity came last summer when Rivero hit .270/.409/.416 with three homers and more walks (19) than strikeouts (17) over 32 games in the Florida Complex League. Rivero was signed in the first place primarily because of his glovework at the premium position of shortstop. He shows exciting fluidity at the six and has looked like a smooth natural at that spot on the diamond ever since he entered pro ball. He gets rid of the ball quickly with a good arm too, giving him multiple ways to impact the game defensively. What earned Rivero his spot on this list, however, was his offensive improvements. He thrives on making a good amount of contact, and the Nationals have been enthused by how well he’s protected the plate at this early stage. The bat doesn’t come with much power, however, and for all Rivero’s defensive strengths, he isn’t much more than an average runner underway. Good, if light, hitters that are also no-doubt shortstops tend to find their ways onto Major League rosters. Rivero’s fit of that profile will be tested when he sees full-season ball for the first time in 2022, just before he becomes Rule 5-eligible in the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kohlhepp is a unique all-around pitcher, from his delivery to his background. He was the top-rated shortstop in Wisconsin out of high school, but pitched effectively -- and hard -- out of the same sidearm angle he threw as an infielder. The package earned him a chance at the University of Tennessee, but his command woes left him little used as a freshman. He was wild again at Iowa Junior College, but his 30 batters faced over 21 1/3 innings caught the attention of Notre Dame, which slotted him into a bulk relief role and gave him a chance to thrive. He became one of the best pitchers in the ACC and helped the Irish reach the NCAA Super Regionals. The Tigers have sought unique bullpen arms in recent years, but viewed Kohlhepp as a potential starter when they drafted him in the fourth round and signed him for a $400,000 bonus. Kohlhepp generates a lot of velocity from his near-sidearm delivery with late whip action. His fastball sits in the mid-90s with movement and can top out higher in a pinch. He throws a changeup in the mid-80s out of the same slot to attack left-handers and a harder slider to eat up right-handers. The question with Kohlhepp has always been command of the strike zone. The result isn’t necessarily a high-strikeout arsenal, but hitters struggle to square him up. Kohlhepp already has the ingredients to become an effective reliever, providing a different look in a Tigers bullpen currently stocked with traditional hard-throwing righties. However, team officials are open to giving him a chance to start and see how he can mix his pitches. Either way, he has a chance to fit in on a Major League staff in some role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After three years of relief work at Kansas State, including a junior season that catapulted him onto Draft boards, he went in Round 14 in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. Los Angeles challenged him with a Double-A assignment in his first full season and he responded. The left-hander led the Southern League in saves and was named its Reliever of the Year, missing a ton of bats and giving up very few hits in the process. Torres does it from a 6-foot frame and with average stuff, but his combination of a lower slot -- the ball looks like it’s coming from the first-base dugout -- and feel for using what he has helped him strike out 14.3 per nine innings and hold hitters to a .143 average in 2022. His fastball only sits around 90 mph, but the angle and carry up in the zone helped it elicit a 36-percent miss rate last year. His low-80s slider can also miss bats, a sweeping breaking ball that flashes above average. He continues to work on a changeup to give him another look for right-handed hitters, but no one squared him up from either side in the Southern League. The Angels love Torres’ athleticism and competitiveness on the mound, and while he could stand to cut the walk rate down a little, he’s around the zone enough to project future success. The overall stuff might mean he doesn’t get the ball in high-leverage situations in the big leagues, but he’s not far from getting the chance to impact the Los Angeles bullpen and he’s shown he is far from afraid of the spotlight.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cebert spent his first three college seasons at South Florida before transferring to Texas Tech for his senior season last spring. He led the Raiders with seven wins as a long reliever before the Yankees selected him in the 15th round. His stuff jumped during his brief pro debut, during which he struck out 11 of the 25 batters he faced at High-A. At Texas Tech, Cebert sat in the low 90s and topped out at 96 mph with a two-seam fastball that he backed up with a 78-82 mph slider and an upper-80s cutter. He didn't miss a lot of bats with any of his offerings, relying on throwing strikes and inducing ground balls to succeed. At High-A, he went to a four-seamer that averaged 95 mph and touched 98. His high-spin slider added a couple of ticks of velocity and some sweep, while his cutter parked around 90 mph. Cebert started as a sophomore and a junior in college, and New York may return him to the rotation in 2026. He'll have to refine a mid-80s changeup with occasional fade to keep left-handers in check. His control is more impressive than his command, and he'll have to improve his location against pro hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players signed in the Guardians' 2018-19 international class, Antunez turned pro for $10,000 out of Venezuela in April 2019. He played 15 games in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League that year, then lost 2020 to the pandemic and didn't see any game action in 2021 while dealing with leg injuries. He got back on the diamond last season and impressed scouts with his all-around tools but hurt his leg again on an awkward slide shortly after arriving in Single-A in late July. Antunez has the potential to hit for both average and power. He possesses a quick left-handed stroke and works deep counts looking for pitches he can drive. While he's aggressive, he also makes a lot of hard contact, shows the ability to drive the ball in the air and draws walks. Antunez likes to use his plus speed on the bases, swiping 13 bases in his first 41 pro games and exuding 20-20 upside. With his quickness, instincts and solid arm strength, he can provide quality defense at all three outfield spots. He has spent most of his early pro career in center field and should be able to remain there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hynes took a leap as the top Canadian prep pitcher in the 2025 Draft by adding four ticks of velocity last spring and performing well against professional teams, including a group of Guardians prospects. Months later, Cleveland drafted him in the second round and signed him away from his Wake Forest commitment for $950,000. He did not pitch after signing, similar to how the club has treated high school hurlers in the past. Considering how few reps he had as a teenager from Ontario heading into pro ball, Hynes has quite a good feel for his delivery and creating spin. His best pitch to date is a potentially plus slider that operates in the low 80s with plenty of horizontal movement from his low three-quarters release. Hynes' sinking fastball now touches 95 mph and figures to have another gear in it, as he has a lot of room to fill out his 6-foot-2 frame. His changeup fits his arsenal well with sink and run but has a ways to go to reach its potential. Hynes is a quality strike-thrower, and his athleticism and sound delivery portend above-average command to pair with his promising control. The Guardians are generally cautious with prep arms, so he will likely start in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, but he has the pitchability to take off pretty quickly and a solid chance to stick as a starter. While Hynes lacks the high-end traits of 2024 picks Braylon Doughty and Joey Oakie, he's a nice combination of the two.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keith won Western Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors in 2021, posting a 1.021 OPS and leading the league with 13 homers before Los Angeles drafted him in the 18th round. He has the tools to become the first California Baptist position player to reach the big leagues. In his first full pro season, he slashed .277/.411/.478 with 17 homers between two Class A levels. Not only does Keith have one of the best right-handed swings in the system, he also features one of its best combinations of power and patience. His combination of bat speed and strength produces plus raw power that he'll tap into more efficiently if he can lift the ball in the air more consistently. While he struggled in the final six weeks last season following a promotion to High-A, he continued to work counts and draw walks. Keith has solid speed but isn't much of a basestealer. He needs to upgrade his reads and routes in the outfield, though he's a decent defender on the corners and has the plus arm strength for right field. He also has seen action in center field and might have enough quickness for the position if he can improve his instincts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jimenez bounced around Florida as an amateur with four years at Archbishop McCarthy HS followed by one season each at Miami and Central Florida. After only limited playing time with the Hurricanes, he was an All-Big 12 Second Team selection with the Knights in 2025 after hitting .329/.407/.575 with 11 homers and 11 steals in 55 games. He was Draft-eligible as a sophomore, and the Mets, who love such a profile, took him in the third round with their second overall choice of last year. Jimenez signed for below slot at $564,000 before getting in 26 contests with Single-A St. Lucie. Jimenez has strength in his 6-foot-1, 200-pound frame, and his above-average raw power was something the Mets highlighted as a reason they took him where they did. It’s not exactly all-fields pop though, and he’s at his best when he’s getting out in front of balls and driving them with authority to the pull side. (Ten of the right-handed slugger’s 11 homers in 2025 went to left or left-center.) Jimenez handled fastballs well with UCF but expanded the zone against sliders and changeups, and both trends carried over into the Florida State League. Entering his first full season of pro ball, Jimenez earns his strongest grades for his plus arm strength as he’ll unleash absolute ropes from anywhere on the dirt. He has the right actions for shortstop right now after improving his defensive game in college, and while he can look too flashy at times, he should get plenty of chances to stick at the six. An above-average glove would lessen the need for him to improve his plate discipline at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Venezuela natives Brayan Rocchio (Guardians) and Ezequiel Tovar (Rockies) have taken their slick-fielding ways at shortstop to the Majors in recent years with varying levels of effectiveness. Cortesia is several years behind his countrymen at the position but could very well follow in their footsteps in time. The 17-year-old was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 14 prospect in the 2025 class and became Washington’s top international signing at the start of the 2025 period when he joined the organization for $1.92 million. Nationals officials said they targeted hit tools at the top of this year’s international group, and Cortesia has a solid one with a level right-handed swing that can send the ball all over the diamond. It’s been hit-over-power at this early stage, but he’s been growing into his frame, adding to the hope that average pop could be in the tank by the time he fully matures. Cortesia earned his best amateur grades on the defensive side. His hands, footwork and arm strength all look above-average at this early stage, and as the brother of a member of the Venezuelan national track-and-field team, he’ll flash plus-plus run times in the 60-yard dash right now. Even if he slows down as he fills out, he should still be good for above-average wheels. The Nationals will take that defensive profile and hope to build a stronger and sustainable hitter in Cortesia, starting with their Dominican Summer League program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Belgrave's lack of polish led to him redshirting in his first college season at Maryland and recording a 6.79 ERA with 51 walks in 51 2/3 innings during the next two. The Marlins still saw enough promise to draft him in the 15th round last July and he posted a 2.16 ERA in Single-A during his pro debut, though he still battled the strike zone. He allowed one run in three playoff appearances during Jupiter's run to the Florida State League championship. Both of Belgrave's pitches looked better than ever during his brief debut. His primary weapon is a late-biting slider that sat at 86-88 in his first taste of pro ball after parking at 82-84 mph during the spring. His fastball also jumped form 93-95 mph with the Terrapins to 95-97 with the Hammerheads, and its heavy life induces groundouts. Belgrave has a short arm action and considerable effort in his delivery, so he has trouble repeating his pitches and throwing strikes. He's going to work on adding a changeup as Miami considers trying him as a starter, but he's probably going to wind up as a two-pitch reliever. If he can improve his control and command, he could be a seventh- or eight-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the former All-Star shortstop of the same name, Ramirez was born in New Jersey but grew up in the Dominican Republic. He signed with the Guardians for $800,000 in 2022 and is one of the more physical middle-infield prospects in the system. He made his U.S. debut last summer in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, where he ranked second in walks (50) and seventh in on-base percentage (.453). He was off to a slow run with Single-A Lynchburg to begin his age-18 season when Cleveland dealt him and two other youngsters to Washington for Lane Thomas. At least 15 pounds heavier than his listed 159, Ramirez has the developing strength and the bat speed to produce 15-20 homers per season. He already displays the aptitude for turning on pitches and launching them in the air. He'll need to make more consistent contact after logging a 28 percent strikeout rate in the ACL, but he has the sound left-handed stroke and bat-to-ball skills to do so once he refines his approach. Like many sons of former big leaguers, Ramirez has a high baseball IQ. He's an average runner who gets the most out of his speed on the bases. He exhibits quick hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, though he may slow a bit as he matures physically and wind up at second or third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A transfer from Kirkwood (Iowa) CC, Krob ascended to the TCU starting staff in his second year there in 2021 and placed at No. 250 on the MLB Pipeline Draft rankings that summer. No team took him, however, and he returned to the Horned Frogs, only to flip between the rotation and bullpen in '22. The Padres believed in him enough to take the left-hander in the 12th round that July and signed him for $125,000, the max allowed without dipping into their bonus pool. Pitching in his age-23 season, Krob was dominant for both Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne in his first full season, finishing with a 2.72 ERA, 1.34 WHIP and 124 strikeouts in 109 1/3 innings. In many ways, Krob dominated those levels as he should for someone his age and experience, but the Padres came away believing he set himself up for a potentially solid pro career. The 6-foot-3 southpaw still has his 81-85 mph sweeping slider that’s gotten an even longer tail in pro ball and helped him pick up consistent K’s. His low-80s changeup also shows decent fade, and it was notable that Krob held righties to a .316 slugging percentage and .629 OPS across his 22 outings last season. The sinking fastball only sits 89-92 mph, but the action on it helped force a lot of weak contact as Krob ranked ninth among Minor League qualifiers with a 55.2 percent ground-ball rate. The former Horned Frog pitches out of the stretch, beginning with his back almost turned to the batter, and his delivery looks relatively free and easy, heightening the belief that he’ll stick as a starter. After making a pair of Double-A postseason appearances, Krob has faced more challenges upon his Texas League return this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies handed out a dozen six-figure bonuses when the 2025 international signing period opened in January of that year. Espinosa, who was still 16 years old at the time he signed, was on the back half of that list with his $250,000 bonus. He more than held his own during his debut in the Dominican Summer League, finishing with a .282/.363/.430 line over 41 games to set the stage for his United States debut in 2026. Tall and wiry with long levers, the 6-foot-4 Espinosa reminds many of a young Elly De La Cruz in terms of his physical build. The young infielder's athleticism stands out more than anything else, and that permeates all parts of his game. The right-handed hitter showed off very solid bat-to-ball skills during his debut and his bat speed graded out as above-average as one of the youngest players in the DSL. There should be a lot more power to come in the future as he packs on strength to that long frame. He's raw in some facets of the game, particularly in chasing too much and not recognizing spin. Even with his size, the Phillies think he has a good chance to stick at shortstop because of that athleticism, actions and enough arm, not to mention at least above-average sprint speed. He's a little bit of a lump of clay, but there's plenty to be molded with the chance for an exciting big leaguer when all is said and done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lovich was one of the older players in the 2024 prep class and carried just 185 pounds on his 6-foot-4 frame, so most teams viewed him as a projectable project they'd like to see develop in college at Arkansas. A couple of clubs were intrigued enough to try to lure him away from the Razorbacks, and the Cubs did so by selecting him in the 11th round and paying him a fourth-round bonus ($650,000). He fared well during the instructional league and will make his official pro debut in 2025. With a quality left-handed stroke that's relatively short considering his size and the ability to recognize pitches better than most players his age, Lovich is equipped to hit for average. He shows promising bat speed that should increase once he adds some much-needed strength, giving him the potential to develop 20-homer power. Some evaluators aren't as sold as much on his pop because he doesn't turn on many pitches and the fact that he hit a lot of opposite-field grounders on the showcase circuit. Lovich is more athletic than his gangly frame might indicate and has solid speed. The Cubs were impressed by how well he tracks ball in the outfield and will give him every chance to stick in center field, though he projects more as a right fielder with solid arm strength. He also created some interest as a three-pitch left-hander with an upper-80s fastball in high school, though his future clearly was brighter as a position player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The Brewers have set up a connection in New Jersey by taking four pitchers from the state in the past two Drafts, including top-70 picks Bryce Meccage and Chris Levonas in 2024 and Cairone and Sean Episcope in ’25. Cairone joined the organization from Delsea HS as the 68th pick last year -- the same selection Milwaukee picked up for not inking Levonas -- and signed him below slot for $1,097,500. The 6-foot-2 left-hander struck out 94 batters in 44 innings as a senior and helped his cause with a nice showing at the MLB Draft Combine in Arizona. His fastball touches 95 mph but plays up with ride generated from a low release, and his extension close to 7 feet puts that heater right on top of batters. Holding the velocity will be a test on the pro side. Cairone’s low-80s slider sat between 2,900-3,000 rpms during the Combine, making it easy to dream on the breaking ball as a future plus pitch with good sweep. A solid cutter acts as a bridge pitch, and he can kill spin with a mid-80s changeup that still sits behind his other pitches in quality. Only 17 on Draft Day, Cairone fits a lot of the Milwaukee bill when it comes to Draft arms: young for the class, projectable and armed with pitches that plug nicely into models. Unfortunately, he was hospitalized after a serious car accident in the middle of the offseason, and while reports have been good about his initial recovery, he’ll likely need to be eased into his first full season. Once fully healthy and built up, Cairone will get plenty of runway to take off as a Brewer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Choate led NCAA Division II with 16.3 strikeouts per nine innings in 2022, including games with 19 and 18 whiffs, the Giants took him in the ninth round, making him the first Assumption (Mass.) player drafted in 29 years. Signed to a discount $87,500 bonus, he breezed through the lower levels of the system with a 2.59 ERA before arriving in Double-A last August. His finesse approach didn't translate immediately at that level, as he got tagged for a 5.82 ERA in eight starts. Using his 6-foot-6 frame and low arm slot to create extension and a flat approach angle, Choate manages to get chases and miss bats with a fastball that operates at 89-92 mph and peaks at 94. His 78-82 mph changeup baffles hitters with its sweeping shape and grades as his best pitch. His slider features similar velocity and shape with more horizontal action, and though he can struggle to throw it for strikes or get batters to chase it, they don't catch up to it when lands it in the zone. The 6-foot-6, 249-pound Choate patterns his mechanics after Chris Sale's and uses his athleticism to keep his long limbs in sync. His repertoire gives him little room for error, so he got into trouble when his control and command wavered in Double-A, allowing hitters to tee off on his fastball when he didn't locate it well. A classic crafty lefty, back-of-the-rotation type, he'll have to make adjustments when he returns to that level in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mikulski had offers to go toward the end of 2020's shortened five-round Draft, but he decided to bet on himself and return to Fordham. He improved his delivery and control, led NCAA Division I in strikeout rate (16.3 per nine innings), set Rams records for season (124) and career (272) whiffs and won Atlantic 10 Conference pitcher of the year honors last spring. The Giants signed him for $1,197,500 in the second round, making him the second-highest pick in school history behind only 1987 supplemental first-rounder Pete Harnisch. After shortening his arm action and making his delivery more compact, Mikulski saw his stuff get better across the board in his final college season, with his fastball sitting in the mid-90s and reaching triple digits with plenty of carry up in the zone. His velocity has backed up in his first full year as a pro, with his heater parking around 90 mph and his formerly mid-80s slider and changeup dropping into the low 80s. His slider still shows flashes of being a solid offering with sweep and depth, while his sinking changeup is more average. Cleaning up his delivery also helped Mikulski improve his control, though he still has lapses at times and will need to refine his command. His new mechanics have given him more deception as well, as his pitches jump on hitters quicker than they anticipate. The funkiness in his delivery has helped him miss bats in Single-A, but he also has been hit hard and looked more like a future reliever than a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keener logged a 6.31 ERA in his first two seasons at Wake Forest before earning all-star honors in the Cape Cod League. He allowed just three earned runs in his first 42 2/3 innings last spring and ranked second in NCAA Division I in WHIP (0.87) and third in opponent average (.167) while serving as a swingman on college baseball's best pitching staff. The White Sox signed him for $800,000 in the third round and definitely see him as a full-time starter on the pro level. The key to Keener's success is a mid-80s slider with two-plane depth that can be a wipeout pitch, and he has the aptitude to both throw it for strikes and get chases outside the zone. He used his slider more than his fastball at Wake, a pattern he'll need to reverse as a starter. He has a 91-95 mph heater that maxes out at 97 with riding action and uses a fading mid-80s changeup to keep left-handers in check. Keener has the sound delivery and strike-throwing ability to make it as a starter. To do so, he'll have to prove he can maintain his stuff and control deeper into games and over the course of 150 innings in a season. If Chicago changed course and deployed him as a reliever, he'd probably race through the Minors and could become a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After growing up in the Dominican Republic, Rodriguez moved to Boston in 2020 and lived in New England for two years before heading to the Georgia Premier Academy. He became the program’s first hitter to be drafted when the Angels took a $100,000 flyer on him in Round 19 of the 2023 Draft. Following two uneventful summers in the Arizona Complex League, things clicked in 2025 with a move up to the Single-A California League, where he finished among the league leaders in several categories and his 130 wRC+ was good for third in the circuit and led the Angels' organization. He wasn’t done, either, going to the Arizona Fall League and hitting .433 while taking home Fall Stars Game MVP honors. The Angels think Rodriguez’s leap forward isn’t an anomaly. There’s a good amount of swing-and-miss in his power-over-hit game, but he has an approach and takes his walks to help offset the strikeouts. He’s just scratching the surface in getting to his power in games, with excellent bat speed producing high-end exit velocities and allowing him to drive the ball to all fields. Not only did he hit 14 homers in 2025, he also legged out 14 triples, a sign of his speed and athleticism. The speed that allowed him to swipe 38 bases last year should help him defensively in the outfield as well. He’s probably a corner guy long-term, but he’s shown it’s not out of the question that he could spend some time up the middle. If he can keep the whiffs in check, he has the chance to have big league value as an athletic corner outfielder with pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The pandemic and injuries limited Wehunt to 11 innings in three years at Southern Mississippi before he transferred and became Kennesaw State's Friday-night starter in 2023. His combination of size and strikes attracted the Red Sox, who signed him for a below-slot $100,000 in the ninth round that July. He posted better numbers in his first full pro season than he did with the Owls and finished 2024 in Double-A. Wehunt added a little velocity and missed more bats with his fastball as a pro, operating at 92-94 mph and touching 96 while showing the ability to carry it by hitters at the letters or leverage it down in the zone for grounders. He has switched from a low-80s changeup in college to a mid-80s splitter in pro ball, and it could become a plus pitch if he learns to harness it better. He threw his sweeping low-80s slider almost as much as his heater last year, and he also can morph it into an upper-80s cutter. Wehunt is more athletic than most 6-foot-7, 240 pounders and gets down the mound extremely well, producing plenty of extension that allows his pitches to get on hitters quickly. He keeps his long limbs in sync and repeats his three-quarters delivery well, providing consistent strikes. Boston believes he can add more strength to his frame and more power to his pitches, which would enhance his chances of becoming a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because Sanchez had a 5-foot-11, 150-pound build and a mid-80s fastball as an amateur, he received just a $17,500 bonus when signing out of Venezuela as an amateur. He's still not very physical, but his stuff has improved dramatically in pro ball. He posted a 46/7 K/BB ratio in 34 1/3 innings during his U.S. debut last summer at age 18, spinning four shutout frames in a playoff start to help the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League Dodgers win a championship before becoming the youngest pitcher to make a start in the Single-A California League. Sanchez now operates at 92-94 mph and can push his fastball to 97 while producing difficult carry from a high arm slot. He has advanced feel for killing spin and creating sink on a plus mid-80s changeup that already ranks among the best in the system. He's still refining his breaking pitches with a mid-70s curveball with more depth than power and a tight low-80s slider that blend into each other at times. More advanced than most pitchers his age, Sanchez repeats his efficient delivery and pounds the strike zone. He needs to add more strength and has to prove he can handle a starter's workload. He generates his stuff with arm speed, athleticism and little effort, which helps his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fairly anonymous when he signed with the Yankees for $30,000 out of Venezuela in 2022, Ramirez batted .319 in two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before attracting attention in his U.S. debut last year. He earned Florida Complex League All-Star accolades after ranking second in the Rookie-level circuit in hitting (.348) and on-base percentage (.447) and fourth in OPS (.960). The Marlins acquired him as part of a three-prospect package for Jazz Chisholm Jr. at the Trade Deadline last July. Ramirez employs a leg kick at the plate and makes consistent contact with a disciplined approach and a compact right-handed stroke. He's learning to turn on pitches but hits a lot of ground balls and may not provide more than 10-12 homers per season. Though he puts the bat on the ball with ease, he makes good swing decisions and draws a healthy amount of walks. Ramirez's solid speed plays better on the bases than in the field, though he's not a prolific basestealer. His average arm and range are best suited for second base, though he spent the majority of his time last year at third base, where he committed nine errors in 36 starts. He also has seen action at left field and shortstop and projects as a utilityman with a sparkplug mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting himself on the Draft radar with three solid years at South Florida, Boser transferred to the University of Florida and boosted his stock as a senior with an impressive season. Entering the 2025 MLB Draft on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 list, Boser landed with the A’s as an 11th-round pick. Ahead of his first full season as a pro, he got his feet wet with 32 games at Single-A Stockton. Boser has an intriguing profile as a hitter. He’s got some power to all fields and showed he can do some damage with the bat in college with good bat speed and balance at the plate. There’s also a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, which he’ll have to improve to tap into that power as a pro. Boser fits the mold of a versatile utility player who can provide strong defense at multiple positions that the A’s traditionally value highly, similar to past prospects such as Jeremy Eierman and Max Schueman. He has a good, accurate arm that should allow him to get plenty of reps at shortstop, third base and second base. He also worked to improve his athleticism in college, and that shows through on the bases as a decent runner. There is a solid floor here as a productive super-utility type, and the A’s liked what they saw from him at first glance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The prize acquisition for the Braves during the 2023 international signing period was outfielder Luis Guanipa, who got $2.5 million to sign. But the organization handed out seven additional six-figure bonuses when the period opened in mid-January, including the $240,000 they gave to Baez. A strong debut in the Dominican Summer League is not a full return on investment just yet, but the infielder made a very good first impression by posting a .311/.393/.422 line with 24 steals. A 5-foot-9 sparkplug kind of a player, Baez is a right-handed hitter who has shown a knack for making contact in the early going. He struck out in just 12.1 percent of his plate appearances during his debut and showed a solid approach, walking nearly as often, especially for someone who didn’t turn 17 until the end of March. He’s never going to be mistaken for a cleanup hitter, but there is some extra-base authority in his compact swing. Baez is a plus athlete who has already shown a propensity for effective basestealing. That speed and agility helps him defensively as well. He’s a little undersized for what most big league teams are looking for at shortstop, but his above-average arm plays there and the Braves will keep running him out there until it no longer seems viable, at which point a move to second base would make the most sense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest in the line of pitching Leiters, Cam has a father (Kurt) who reached Double-A and two uncles (Al, Mark) and two cousins (Jack, Mark Jr.) who took the mound in the Majors. After spending his first college season at Central Florida in 2023, he transferred to Florida State and showed first-round stuff early in his sophomore season before developing shoulder issues in March 2024. He underwent cleanup surgery that October and never pitched again for the Seminoles, but the Dodgers still took him in 2025's second round and signed him for $1,346,600. When he last pitched for the Seminoles, Leiter worked with a 95-96 mph fastball that touched 99 mph and featured carry and armside run at times and heavy sink at others. His 78-82 mph curveball and 85-89 mph slider/cutter both graded as plus pitches with quality depth at their best. He even showed signs of a solid upper-80s changeup/splitter that earned more strikes than either of his breaking balls. Besides his health, the biggest question with Leiter is whether he can provide enough strikes to remain a starter. More physical than athletic, he operates from an upright delivery that lacks deception and carried a 15 percent walk rate in college. He comes with a lot of risk but also has a huge ceiling and was back throwing in the mid-90s and reaching triple digits during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years of inconsistent work at the University of Maryland, Staine transferred to Central Florida for the chance to have a more certain role. While a minor back issue and a blister slowed him down some, his ability to pitch well -- mostly as the Knights’ Friday night starter -- allowed him to land in the fifth round with the Rockies. While he didn’t pitch competitively after signing, he did make a good impression with the club's player development staff during instructs. A 6-foot-4 right-hander with a loose arm and some athleticism on the mound, Staine has four pitches that give him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 93 mph and touches 96 and it features good ride to it, which plays well at the top of the zone when he needs it to. His low-80s slider should be an average breaking ball, and he has a slower curve he can land early in counts. He’ll flash a decent changeup, but will need to commit to it more after not throwing it much in college. More than anything, the Rockies love how Staine goes right after hitters with a repeatable up-tempo delivery. He’ll need to refine his command to remain a starter long term, but the organization feels like he has the mentality to develop into a guy who can navigate through a lineup multiple times and be a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After saving $1.3 million in bonus pool with 2024 first-round pick PJ Morlando, whom they coveted, the Marlins used most of that cash to sign Johnson in the second round for a well-over-slot $2.8 million. The latter garnered some comparisons to fellow Alabama prep shortstop Gunnar Henderson, though the 2023 American League Rookie of the Year had more athleticism and power potential at the same stage of their careers. The game sped up a bit on Johnson in his pro debut, when he batted .221 with a 33 percent strikeout rate and made nine errors in 24 games as one of the youngest players (age 18) in the Single-A Florida State League. Johnson earned a reputation as one of the better hitters in the 2024 prep class by making consistent contact to all fields with a controlled left-handed swing and advanced approach. He didn't look like himself in the FSL, chasing pitches out of the zone much more than normal and struggling with non-fastballs. He doesn't stand out in terms of bat speed, present strength or exit velocities, but his hitting ability could translate into 15 or more homers annually once he matures physically. Though he'll flash slightly above-average speed, Johnson probably will slow down a bit as he gets stronger, and he isn't adventurous on the bases. He has smooth actions, reliable hands and a solid arm at shortstop but may not have the quickness or range to stay there. He'll return to the FSL in 2025 on the same team with gifted defenders Starlyn Caba and Andrew Salas, so he'll also see action at second and possibly third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick in 2022 out of Iowa, Williams has always been an upside play on his long-term power. Nicknamed “The Iowa Meat Truck”, you won’t find a larger human being in the Blue Jays’ organization … or many organizations. Listed at 6-foot-5, 255 pounds, Williams looks even larger than that in the box, but it hasn’t turned into the eye-popping power numbers you’d expect just yet. He homered 14 times in 2023 (83 games) and 11 times last season (87 games), but with a strong finish and a successful stint in the Arizona Fall League, there’s buzz in the system about him finally unleashing more of that pop. Outside of Vladimir Guerrero Jr., there may be no player in the organization who hits the ball harder than Williams. He’s still a proper hitter, fully capable of shooting a line drive when the situation calls for it, but the Blue Jays are eager to get Williams taking more shots in the right counts. There’s also been a focus on getting him to drive the ball in the air more often. While Williams is a sturdier defender at first base than you’d expect, all of the upside here is clearly and fully tied to his bat. The Rowdy Tellez comps are easy, and given the breakout season Tellez had at Double-A New Hampshire in 2016, you’ll probably be hearing more of them. Similar to outfielder Dasan Brown, whose value leans on elite speed and defense, Williams gets on this list because he does one thing extremely well. He’ll need to hit his way to the top, but there’s a chance he does just that. He’s already an organizational favorite and would be a fan favorite in Toronto if he ever puts on that uniform.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green showed off an exciting power-speed combination across three seasons at Cal by swiping 45 bases and crushing 34 home runs in 151 games. The A’s had plenty of looks at those raw tools while scouting him just down the road over the years and were thrilled to land him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, going over slot value to sign him for $1 million. Getting his feet wet at Single-A Stockton last year, he hit .289 with an .832 OPS, three homers, eight doubles and nine stolen bases in 24 games. Green falls in line with recent A’s Draft picks such as Denzel Clarke and Henry Bolte who stand out for their exciting raw tools. The ball really jumps off the bat with his ability to drive it to all fields, and the A’s still believe there is more raw power he will tap into. The big concern has always been his lack of consistent contact, as his strikeout rate hovered around 30% in college, which could be attributed to his unorthodox mechanics at the plate. But the A’s have been encouraged by his improvements in that respect, and he has shown a decent eye by drawing a fair amount of walks. A plus runner who can cover a ton of ground with a solid arm, Green has a chance to stick in center field, though some scouts see an eventual move to left. The A’s saw Green as a first-round talent with a ceiling that is just about as high as any other prospect in the organization, but he will have to overcome the swing-and-miss issues that plagued him throughout his amateur career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dombroski established himself as a prospect while winning Cape Cod League most outstanding pitcher accolades in 2021, when he led the summer circuit in ERA (0.85), strikeouts (45 in 31 2/3 innings) and K/BB ratio (22.5). He set a Monmouth record with 120 whiffs in 95 frames and ranked seventh in NCAA Division I with an 8.6 K/BB ratio the next spring, becoming the third-highest pick in school history when Houston selected him in the fourth round. He topped the Single-A Carolina League in strikeouts (148), average-against (.216) and WHIP (1.12) in his 2023 pro debut. Dombroski's lone better-than-average pitch is his low-80s changeup with depth, but he succeeds thanks to his ability to command his entire four-pitch arsenal. His fastball is nothing special, sitting in the upper 80s and topping out at 93 mph with some riding action. His breaking balls both can flash average and have added a bit more power since he turned pro, with his downer upper-70s curveball maybe a tick ahead of his 78-81 mph slider with sweep. A classic finesse left-hander, Dombroski depends on his ability to locate and mix his pitches. His control wasn't as sharp as usual in the first two months of his debut before he locked in and issued just 15 walks in his final 14 starts. He's a high-floor guy who profiles as a No. 5 starter for now, though the Astros have helped several pitchers unlock more velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers paid eight of the nine largest bonuses in their 2022 international class to Venezuelans, including $247,500 to Torres. He ranked third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 23 steals and fifth with seven homers in his U.S. debut last summer, the only player in the league to place in the top five in both categories. He was overmatched in a 10-game promotion to Single-A as an 18-year-old, going 4-for-37 (.108) with 18 strikeouts. Torres has one of the quickest bats among Rangers farmhands, and the loft in his left-handed stroke and his growing strength produce some of the best raw power. There are some questions about how much contact he'll make because his swing can get long and uphill, and he didn't do much damage against southpaws last year. He does display some characteristics of a good approach, mostly concentrating on balls from gap to gap and showing reasonable patience for a teenager. Torres flashes plus straight-line speed but projects to be more of an average runner once he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. He steals more with savvy than quickness, so he likely won't be as much of a factor on the bases at higher levels. He's an average defender with similar arm strength in left and right field and at first base, the three positions he played (in order of frequency) in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A mainstay in UNC Wilmington’s rotation over his four years there, Taylor produced one of the best seasons in school history as a senior in 2025 by leading NCAA Division I in K/BB ratio (9.6) and WHIP (0.76), while also ranking second in walk rate (1.0 per nine innings) and fourth in ERA (1.98). Entering the 2025 Draft as one of the top senior arms in the class, he was selected in the fifth round by the A’s and signed at a full-slot bonus of $513,900, becoming the highest-drafted pitcher out of UNCW since supplemental first-rounder Bradley Holt in 2008. With Triple-A Las Vegas in need of a starter at the end of the season, Taylor was called upon for his pro debut with a start for a playoff-bound Aviators squad. Taylor pleasantly surprised the A’s by showing up with a bit more velocity than they expected, working with a fastball that reached up to 98 mph and sat 93-95. His low-80s changeup has good fade and is probably his best secondary pitch right now. He also brings a low-80s curveball, mid-80s cutter and a sweeper he learned shortly after getting drafted. He has good command of all his pitches and was one of the top strike-throwers in all of college baseball. Taylor is a bit undersized, reminiscent to some within the A’s organization of Sonny Gray in that aspect. He will enter his first full season as a professional as one of the more intriguing A’s pitching prospects, and given that he’s basically a finished product, the potential is there for him to rise quickly through the system and eventually reach the Majors, where he profiles as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson spent his first three years of collegiate ball with Division III North Carolina Wesleyan and transferred to UNC Greensboro for the 2024 season. He spent two additional years with the Spartans and closed out his time there with a 3.79 ERA and 87 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings as a reliever. The Blue Jays took him in the eighth round as a fifth-year senior sign, and his $5,000 bonus was the lowest in Toronto's 2025 class. Thompson popped nicely at Single-A Dunedin with one run allowed and 15 K's in 13 2/3 innings after the Draft, and he has joined the High-A Vancouver staff in his first full season, showing enough stuff to get his first extended starting look since 2023. The 6-foot right-hander has already taken nice steps forward in his professional development under the Blue Jays' guidance. His fastball velocity is up a bit in his first full season, sitting 93-95 mph, and he can staple the four-seamer to the top of the zone from a lower-than-average release height, making it tough for High-A hitters to pick up. Thompson also works with a promising upper-80s slider with harder action, and he's folded in a sweepier breaker in '26 too (one he calls a curveball but is likely closer to a sweeper). He's struggled to land his upper-80s changeup in the zone. It might be more of a command-over-control profile for Thompson moving forward. He can place the ball in the right spot to miss bats consistently, but if batters can learn to lay off the fastballs up and the sliders down, Thompson could find more trouble the higher he climbs. As it sits early in '26, he's been a K-BB% standout with a possible back-end starter profile and another potential win for the improved Toronto pitching department.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A true gamer who rose to prominence at Kansas State for his speed, discipline and defense -- he led the Big 12 in steals (40) and walks (55) as a junior while being named a Gold Glove finalist -- Jones signed with the Yankees for $150,000 as a 2024 12th-rounder. He's hardly missed a step in pro ball with 69 stolen bases and nearly as many walks (111) as strikeouts (130) across his first two seasons of pro ball, and ended 2025 at Double-A. The Marlins acquired him along with three other prospects in January for Ryan Weathers to add to their outfield depth on the farm. Jones holds his hands high and maneuvers his barrel around the zone to make frequent contact on all pitch shapes. He controls the zone well and rarely chases, taking pride in getting on base. The Tennessee native has not made much hard contact, though, and doesn't have much projection left in his 5-foot-10 frame. The Marlins hope a mechanical change will make him more powerful so he can at least fill a Brett Gardner-like role. Not only does Jones possess impact speed, but he's also highly efficient and isn't afraid to take an extra base. He's similarly an intellectual defender in center field -- and a quality defender in the outfield corners -- with a good sense of how to position himself and average arm strength. Jones is a high-character player who gets high marks for his motor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a deep Red Sox international class headlined by shortstop Dorian Soto, outfielder Harold Rivas and right-hander Sadbiel Delzine, Ramos signed for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He offers an interesting combination of shortstop defense with unusual switch-hitting pop for the position. He batted .254/.384/.443 with four homers in 36 games during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Ramos hits the ball hard for a teenager and already shows feel for driving balls in the air to his pull side, so he could become a 20-homer threat once he adds more strength to his projectable 6-foot-1 frame. He has good hand-eye coordination, which allows him to turn his swing loose and still make consistent contact. In his first taste of pro ball, he displayed power from both sides of the plate but did a much better job of controlling the strike zone as a lefty. Though Ramos possesses just average speed, he runs the bases well and plays a smooth shortstop. He has good actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a strong, accurate arm. Though it's possible he could slow a bit if he gains considerable muscle, Boston believes he's stay at short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reed didn’t get much traction as a swingman over his first two years at West Virginia, but he really opened eyes with his power stuff as the Mountaineers’ closer in 2023. Reed always felt he had the ability to start, even going to the Draft League to do it a few times as the Draft approached; the Pirates agreed, taking the right-hander in the fourth round of that summer's Draft, allowing him to develop in a rotation out of the gate. The early returns were better than expected as he pitched his way from Single-A Bradenton to High-A Greensboro while leading all hurlers in the system with at least 100 innings pitched in ERA (1.99) and BAA (.173). With two fastballs and very real secondary offerings coming from a 6-foot-4 frame, Reed does have a future rotation piece starter kit. His fastball sat around 93-94 mph last year, and touched 97, and it wouldn’t surprise anyone if there was a velocity jump coming. He throws a four- and two-seamer, missing some bats up and getting ground-ball outs down. Both of his secondary offerings -- an 83-84 mph sweeper with high spin and his spin-killing changeup -- miss bats and could be plus pitches in the future. The one thing that could keep Reed from remaining a starter is his command, as his longer arm action has led to high walk rates. He’s ironed out some issues with his delivery, and he did a better job of finding the zone in his six Greensboro starts, perhaps a sign of things to come away from the ABS system. There’s currently no talk of moving to the 'pen, with the Pirates excited to see what he does for an encore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted in the seventh round as a Puerto Rican high schooler in 2023, Melendez gave up a Rice scholarship to sign for an over-slot $400,000. He spent his first two years as a pro in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, slashing a combined .263/.374/.410 with 22 extra-base hits and 11 steals in 63 games. He's still raw but is one of the more intriguing young hitters in the Cubs' system. Melendez has a relatively compact left-handed swing considering his gangly 6-foot-3 frame and he produces better exit velocities than most teenagers. He shows some feel for driving the ball in the air to his pull side and could grow into 25-homer power once he gains some much-needed strength. He comes with contact concerns because he chases pitches and swings through strikes, so he'll have to prove he can handle more advanced pitching. Presently an average runner, Melendez will lose some quickness as he fills out. He displays quick hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, but his fringy range will necessitate a change of position at higher levels. He played more under control at third base and second base than he did at short last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hunt never found a full-time spot in the Mississippi State rotation during his four years in school, and after choosing not to sign with the Pirates as a 12th-rounder in 2022, he posted an 8.54 ERA as a reliever the following spring. He boosted his stock with a solid showing as Falmouth’s closer in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2023 and signed with Milwaukee as a nondrafted free agent in July. He broke out in a big way in his first full season of pro ball, moving from Single-A Carolina to starting spots with High-A Wisconsin and Double-A Biloxi. His 2.03 ERA and 0.93 WHIP each ranked fourth best among Minor Leaguers with at least 100 innings, while his 34.7 percent K rate placed fifth. The former Bulldog’s dominance stemmed from heavy slider usage last season. Hunt can wear out the low, armside corner with the 84-86 mph pitch that has gyro shape, dipping below bats at just the right moment. Hunt threw it almost half the time against righties, but the breaker was also effective against lefties, who batted just .163 against the hurler during the season. His 91-93 mph fastball (occasionally touching 96) doesn’t pop for velo but can work well at the top of the zone, especially to set up the slider. Hunt also works with an upper-70s curveball and a firmer mid-80s changeup. Hunt really struggled with control in college but was a control artist last season with a 6.2 percent walk rate. That will likely creep up if hitters can hold off against the sliders outside the zone, but the improvements have helped his case at reaching -- and sticking in -- a pro rotation as a potential future No. 5 in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies spread their 2025 international bonus pool money around when the signing period opened in January, handing out a total of 19 six-figure bonuses to help restock the lowest levels of the farm system.
