Blanco got the fourth-highest bonus ($600,000) to join the organization, and he’s the one who has jumped to the foreground in the early going after a terrific Rookie-level Dominican Summer League debut. The infielder slashed .345/.449/.453 over 54 games to raise excitement for his United States debut in 2026. Blanco is a 6-foot-1, solidly built middle infielder who has already shown a solid approach and feel for hitting. He walked nearly as often as he struck out during his debut, really limiting his swing-and-miss. He has bat speed with a short right-handed swing and has already displayed some ability to drive the ball with carry off his bat. He made good swing decisions during his debut which led to a ton of quality contact, and there could be more power to come as he fills out. The infielder, who will play all of 2026 at age 18, manned shortstop almost exclusively last year and has a chance to stay there with average speed and excellent instincts. He likely could handle moving anywhere on the infield in the future because of his feel for the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery ended Patteson’s 2022 college season early at Central Florida, but the Royals were convinced enough in their scouting of him and his makeup that they still drafted him in the fifth round that year. It took Patteson time to come back from the injury and start to make an impact, but his stuff shot up in 2025. He made 13 starts in High-A with a 1.99 ERA, while holding batters to a .199 average. He finished the year with 11 appearances (eight starts) in Double-A, where he had a 4.41 ERA. Patteson’s fastball hovered around 90-92 mph over the past few years, but once he got to Double-A in ‘25, he started running it up to the mid 90s and touching 97. The velo spike, which was more about a return to his pre-TJ form, also helped his main breaking ball become more firm as a mid-80s average slider that tries to be gyro but can get a little sweepy. Patteson also throws a curveball with good depth and feel to land it for strikes. His best weapon, though, is a mid-80s changeup with plus potential. Patteson throws strikes and has a clean delivery, hiding the ball well with short arm action. Lauded for his pitchability and being a student of the game, Patteson might be a late bloomer but is really coming into his own now that he’s reached the upper levels. He needs to show more consistency at Double-A and continue to refine his secondaries, but if the stuff continues to look like what it did there in ‘25, he has back-end rotation potential. The Royals might try him in the bullpen to see whether the stuff ticks up even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene signed for just $17,500 as a South Alabama senior when the Yankees took him in the eighth round of the 2019 Draft. After missing out on his first full season due to the pandemic, he proved to be a steady performer as a reliever at the High-A, Double-A and Triple-A levels in 2021 and 2022. He spent all of last season with Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, posting a 3.42 ERA, .199 average-against and 96 strikeouts in 68 1/3 innings, but he was still left off the Yankees' 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible due to a roster crunch. The Mets swooped in during the Rule 5 Draft, and in order to keep him, Greene must remain in their Major League bullpen for all of 2023. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches out of the stretch at the extreme first-base side of the rubber, and he fires in a low-90s fastball that can be deceptive with its apparent rise and cutting action. Despite the fastball being closer to average velo, that ride can make the heater extremely difficult to pick up, and hitters often hopelessly swung below the pitch at Triple-A. An upper-70s slider kept opposing batters from sitting on the fastball and played well into the Yankees’ pitching philosophy of prioritizing sweep on breaking pitches. An upper-80s changeup kept lefties honest but was a distant third pitch. If hitters can learn not to chase the high heat or the solid breaker, they can earn the occasional free pass from Greene, who walked 11.1 percent of the batters he faced in 2022. That control has been one reason why the righty has stayed in relief in the pros, but his two best pitches make him an MLB-ready bullpen option for the Mets.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The state of Missouri produced three quality prep shortstop prospects in the 2024 class. D-backs fourth-rounder Tytus Cissell was seen as having the best athleticism of the trio, Drew Dickerson was the most physical but went undrafted on his way to the University of Oklahoma and Snyder – Missouri’s Gatorade high school player of the year -- had the most polish and highest floor. He went to the Mets in the fifth round (12 picks after Cissell) but signed for roughly second-round money with a $1,322,500 bonus. Snyder played in six games with Single-A St. Lucie to mark his pro debut. The former Tennessee commit impressed amateur scouts with his good swing decisions as a righty hitter. That hit tool is part of the reason why New York decided to give him a quick look at the Florida State League, and the approach could help him take off even more quickly in a return there this spring. There was some concern about his power coming into his senior year, and that remains to some degree even after he added strength. His exit velocities have run cold in 2025, but he is doing a better job of limiting chase and making contact in the zone. Snyder could flash plus run times when he really got going as a high schooler, but his added strength did slow him down some when it came to going home to first. He has the hands and internal clock for shortstop, while his arm strength and limited range have seen him move to second and third in his first full season back in the FSL.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman signed for only $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in September 2022 and played in the Dominican Summer League the two following seasons without standing out much statistically -- his highest seasonal OPS down there was .691. He came stateside all the same for 2025 and broke out in a big way with a .302/.375/.524 line and 10 homers in 75 games between the Florida Complex League and Single-A St. Lucie. His 18 extra-base hits in 26 games following his debut in full-season ball on July 25 were second-most in the Florida State League over that span, trailing only Top 100 prospect Alfredo Duno’s 22. Standing 6-foot-4 and batting from the right side, Guzman begins with his hands held high above his head before loading up with a toe tap to unleash his power. He’s up there to hack -- he ran a 43 percent chase rate in the FSL -- but he can show adaptability on spin inside the zone too. When he runs into a ball, he really runs into it with his strength. Guzman ran a 108.5 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity at Single-A, better than Konnor Griffin’s 107.7 in the same league. It’s always going to be that pop that intrigues most, though the overall approach will be a restrictor plate unless he makes more adjustments. A well-below-average runner, Guzman has seen time at all four corners of the infield and outfield during his three professional seasons. His primary focus was at first base in 2025 with some left and right field mixed in. He’s almost certainly going to be locked into the cold corner long-term, but his slugging ability gives him a fighting chance to clear the high offensive bar there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia signed for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of the Orioles’ 2024 international class and he made an impact immediately, producing a .943 OPS with 12 steals and more walks than strikeouts in the Dominican Summer League in one of the organization's best debut performances of the year. That set the stage for the switch-hitting shortstop to come stateside in 2025. Garcia is an athletic infielder with a line-drive swing and a knack for making solid contact, with a varied skill set that can make him intriguing as he matures and adds strength. He’s hit-over-power, but he has an advanced approach for his age and can work deep counts, avoid strikeouts and barrel balls from both sides of the plate. He’s a good runner and his athleticism serves him well on the basepaths. He is an advanced fielder with good instincts, actions and quickness up the middle, and a strong arm that gives him a chance to stay at shortstop long-term. Garcia will be 18 for the entire '25 season and there is a lot of projection here, but if he continues to develop, he has a chance to grow into an up-the-middle regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valencia is the latest example of catchers sometimes needing more time to develop, though his development seemingly came out of nowhere. Far from a top prospect, the Venezuelan was a 2018 international signing for a $10,000 bonus. After five seasons in the States, he had played one game above A-ball, often serving as a backup or platoon mate. Then came 2025, when he got in better shape, looked for more launch angle, found his power stroke at the plate at Double-A Erie, then carried it to Triple-A Toledo. The breakout earned him a spot on Detroit’s 40-man roster in November, at the additional position of first base to help keep his bat in a lineup. Valencia, with help from Tigers instructors, changed his swing after the 2024 season to lower his hands and add more lift. A big leg kick helps with his timing, but he also became more selective with pitches, looking for balls he can launch after struggling with ground-ball rates for years. He has solid pitch recognition and can read what pitchers are trying to do against him, though he still struggled against breaking balls. Defensively, Valencia receives well but isn’t especially agile, and he struggled to control the running game in Toledo. Valencia’s work ethic and resulting rise made him one of the more popular players in the organization among coaches and instructors who worked with him over the years. He’s clearly in the Tigers’ sights, possibly even as a third catcher behind Dillon Dingler and Jake Rogers if he continues to hit, but shoring up his work behind the plate could be his best ticket to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis never could claim a regular turn in Oklahoma State's rotation, battling injuries and his control and command while logging a 5.61 ERA in three seasons. As a junior, he missed fall practice after breaking his collarbone in a fishing accident and lost a month last spring to shoulder issues. But he was still a 6-foot-9 right-hander with power stuff, so the White Sox selected him in the fifth round last July and signed him for an over-slot $587,500. Davis can work at 94-97 mph and touch 100 with his fastball, which features more downhill plane than armside run, so it can get hit when he doesn't command it. His tight upper-80s slider climbs as high as 92 mph, and he can turn it into a harder cutter. His mid-80s changeup lacks consistency but will flash some intriguing fade and tumble. With room to add more strength to his huge frame, Davis could add even more velocity. He still has starter upside, but to get there he'll have to prove he can stay healthy and keep his long limbs in sync well enough to put his pitches where he wants them. If he does head to the bullpen, he has the fastball and slider to fill a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers saw a chance to build organizational depth and some offensive upside at catcher when they drafted Crouch in the 11th round in 2021 following a breakout junior season at Central Florida. But even they weren’t expecting how well he adjusted to the pro game. After two strong weeks at Single-A Lakeland, Crouch moved to High-A West Michigan and helped lead a Whitecaps turnaround, taking ownership of a young pitching staff while providing clutch hits. That earned him a September promotion to Double-A Erie following a season-ending injury to Dillon Dingler. Crouch doesn’t really have one standout tool so much as he does a lot of things well. He’s sneaky athletic behind the plate with a strong enough arm to control a running game. He improved his receiving skills as the season went on but still has a lot of room to grow there. Similarly, he has enough power in his quick swing to punish mistakes but is more effective as a situational hitter. He batted .346 with 51 RBIs with runners in scoring position at West Michigan despite just eight extra-base hits. More impressively, he struck out just 14 times in those situations. Crouch was one of the more intriguing players in the Tigers system for some evaluators, thanks in part to his sudden emergence. With a strong work ethic and an effort to get stronger, he has a chance to reach the Majors in time, likely profiling as a backup. It’ll be interesting to see how the Tigers move Crouch and Dingler, who aren’t far apart in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Dyan Jorge may have been the cream of the Rockies' crop at the start of the 2022 international signing period, getting $2.8 million to sign. But Hidalgo, another middle infielder who received a $500,000 bonus, has jumped to the forefront a bit more. It didn’t happen overnight as Hidalgo repeated the Dominican Summer League, but things really clicked for him in Round 2 in 2023, finishing with a .980 OPS en route to being named the DSL MVP. He performed well during his U.S. debut in 2024, earning a late bump up to Single-A Fresno, albeit with less impact at the plate. A right-handed-hitting infielder, Hidalgo showed a knack for finding the barrel in the DSL. But while he still made some loud contact in 2024, more chase showed up in his game. There’s a good amount of raw power for him to tap into, but he’ll need to tone down his approach more so he can get pitches to drive, instead of wave at soft stuff out of the zone too much. Hidalgo is a solid runner with good instincts on the basepaths, which helps him be a threat to steal. There is some question over whether he’ll be a shortstop long term -- his arm works from the left side of the infield and no one is pushing him off short for the time being, but he likely will get introduced to second base this year after he’s also received time at third at the outset of his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed only one player to a seven-figure bonus when the international window opened in January 2021, and that was Pena, who inked for $1.2 million out of the Dominican Republic. He got off to a solid start at the Dominican Summer League in his first Minor League campaign. Arizona got aggressive with the infielder in 2023, sending him to both the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia in his age-18 season. That aggression caught up to Pena in the California League, where he slashed just .248/.344/.314 in 36 games, but that early taste of full-season ball could set him up well for a return in 2023. The pieces that Arizona evaluators first loved from Pena as an international amateur are still there, for the most part. He shows a smooth swing from the left side, and even when he was struggling with Visalia, he was still taking walks at a 12.7 percent clip. The power remains in the projectable department, considering he homered only four times in 2022 (none of them in Single-A), but his size at 6-foot-1, 170 pounds gives hope that at least average pop is coming. Pena’s lack of speed at this early stage of his career has pushed him from shortstop to second base, and he might end up being average there with the lesser defensive demands. D-backs coaches and evaluators have always loved Pena’s baseball IQ, and that’s part of the reason why they’ve pushed him so quickly to this point. He’ll get a crack at his first full Minor League campaign during his age-19 season in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foster rated as the second-best shortstop in the 2020 Texas high school class behind Masyn Winn (who reached the Majors in 2023), but he went unselected in the shortened five-round Draft and attended Auburn. He barely played as a freshman and started at second base as a sophomore, then boosted his stock considerably last spring by improving his approach and returning to shortstop. He scuffled offensively and defensively after turning pro as a third-round selection, batting .230 with a 32 percent strikeout rate in Single-A. After Foster took off at Auburn by focusing on making consistent contact to all fields rather than trying to launch out of the park, he got too aggressive and his swing got too uphill in his first taste of pro ball. He'll need to settle back down to reach his ceiling of a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per season and a decent amount of walks. A switch-hitter, he did damage from both sides of the plate in college but went just 1-for-24 with 12 strikeouts against southpaws in his debut. Foster's instincts allow him to play quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the middle infield, though he's not much of a threat to steal. While he's a sure-handed defender with a strong arm, his average range at shortstop may not be enough to keep him there. He's a solid defender at second base and also could handle third base if he winds up in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz hails from La Vega, Dominican Republic, the country’s fourth-largest city and hometown of Major Leaguers Jonathan Villar and Ronald Guzmán. The outfielder was the biggest prospect from there in the 2025 international class and ranked No. 27 in MLB Pipeline’s list heading into the January signing period. He was Arizona’s biggest addition -- and only seven-figure signing -- with a $1.1 million bonus. The right-handed slugger brings an uphill swing from a stance that features an inward-facing front foot. He gets into his power through his back leg, generating good bat speed ahead of the point of contact, and some evaluators said he reminded them of Marcell Ozuna as a player who uses his pop as his carrying tool. There’s a solid approach here too, although the plane of the swing might be challenged against pro pitching. With decent wheels, De La Cruz could cover center field, but many expect he’ll be pushed to a corner by rangier players. The D-backs happen to have plenty of those already in the system between Slade Caldwell and Druw Jones, among others. He could play closer to average defensively once he moves, and his wheels should be good enough to make him a potential basestealing threat. De La Cruz has a long way to go, but the pieces are there for him to be a middle-of-the-order bat who also adds value in other areas.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Contreras signed with the Royals as part of their 2025 international signing class for just $147,000 out of the Dominican Republic, and he didn’t turn 17 until Aug. 10 -- right before he wrapped up an excellent Dominican Summer League season. He posted a 3.30 ERA there, striking out 37 batters across 30 innings with 13 walks. He also started for the American League in the DSL All-Star Game, although he allowed four earned runs and recorded just two outs. Listed at 5-foot-11, Contreras might not be super tall in stature, but he’s very strong and throws effortlessly from the mound. Answering the questions about his durability and velocity because of his smaller size, he already sits 95-98 mph with his heater, pairing it with a downer curveball that has great spin and an average changeup that plays off his fastball well. Contreras threw strikes in the DSL and has a repeatable delivery that helps with his command, as the ball comes out of his hand free and easy. Contreras is young and still has far to go with his development, but there’s upside of a mid-rotation starter. He arrived stateside for the 2026 season but suffered an elbow injury that required season-ending UCL surgery in the spring. Contreras will likely still only be 18 by the time he returns to a Minor League mound with plenty of promise still ahead.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Had things gone differently, Barr might now be a part of the University of Tennessee rotation. But the top junior college player in the 2025 Draft class threw well enough at Niagara County Community College, now known as SUNY Niagara, to catch the attention of the Twins. They went over slot in the fifth round to sign the right-hander for $762,500, making him just the second Thunderwolves player to go in the top five rounds, joining 2023 Brewers fifth-round pick Ryan Birchard. The 20-year-old Barr is a 6-foot-6 poster child for projection with some good now stuff. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph and it features very good life up in the zone. He has a pair of distinct breaking pitches with his slider and curve, and both missed a lot of bats en route to him dominating the NJCAA DIII level. His breaking stuff registers elite-level spin rates and his heater plays up because of spin on that as well. Barr has a loose, easy and athletic delivery, so there’s belief that he can improve what’s been spotty command and control. He’s on the raw side and as good as he is at spinning the ball, he hasn’t always had a feel for consistent grips. There’s a lot of upside here, given that he has plenty of room to fill out both his frame and his repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moss has spent most of his baseball career flying under the radar. After playing sparingly over two years at Seton Hall, he transferred to Division II St. Leo University in Florida and hit .340 with an 1.107 OPS in his final season there. He cemented his unofficial title as the \"Mayor of the Appalachian League\" and earned Player of the Year honors by posting a 1.254 OPS there in 2024, his third summer in the wood-bat MLB-run collegiate league. That led to a contract with the Royals as a nondrafted free agent. Moss was in the middle of his first pro season when the Pirates acquired him from Kansas City at the 2025 Trade Deadline in the Bailey Falter deal. A right-handed first baseman, Moss absolutely raked in the Pirates organization post-trade, hitting .339 with a .993 OPS over 30 games with High-A Greensboro. He's always shown excellent contact quality, but he could be poised to take another step forward as he registered high-end max exit velocities all spring. When that's combined with good bat-to-ball skills, solid plate discipline and decent chase rates, Moss has the chance to add up to a solid overall hitter. Moss has below-average speed but is an excellent baserunner, with his instincts allowing him to swipe 17 bags last year. He's worked hard to become a capable defender at first, but his bat will always be his calling card. For him to have the chance to be a big league regular, he'll have to get to more power, but if he doesn't, it won't be from lack of effort. Moss plays with a chip on his shoulder and gets praise for his work ethic and leadership characteristics as he enters his age-22 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olejnik started his college career at Triton College in Illinois before heading to Oklahoma for his sophomore year. After pitching sparingly for the Sooners, he was on the move again, this time to Miami (Ohio), where he missed bats in a swingman/multi-inning reliever role. He threw really well over five starts in the Draft League in 2024, helping him land in the sixth round with the Angels, where he signed for a below-slot bonus of $197,500. He proved to be durable during his first full season of pro ball, amassing 128 2/3 innings with Single-A Inland Empire, capping things off with a playoff win. The thing that stands out the most with Olejnik is his size, with the right-hander coming in at 6-foot-11. He does a solid job with his four-seam fastball, coming from a lower slot. He backs it up with a decent sweeper and a changeup, both of which can flash above-average at times. He needs tighter action to miss more bats on his breaking ball and his changeup needs more depth. There are some who feel the addition of a cutter and a two-seam fastball would help round out his repertoire. For a guy his size, Olejnik does a decent job repeating his delivery and he tends to be around the zone. Timing up his mechanics will always be an issue, as they are for any super-tall pitcher. There are starter characteristics here, especially if Olejnik can get some more bat-missing action out of his secondary offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Tanner hit 15 homers as a sophomore at Mississippi State, including one in the game that clinched a 2021 College World Series title against Vanderbilt, he was more known for his work behind the plate. He didn’t hit as well as a junior in 2022, but his glove work was the main reason why the Reds took the Bulldogs standout in the second round of last year’s Draft. Tanner is always likely to be a defense-over-hit backstop. He loves to throw and who can blame him, with one of the strongest arms in the Minors. It’s plus-plus with some amateur scouts hanging an 80 on it, the kind of hose that can shut down a running game. A good leader behind the plate who works well with pitchers, Tanner is a solid receiver and blocker, giving him all he needs to catch in the big leagues for a long time. How often he’s able to do that will depend on how his bat develops. There’s strength and bat speed from the right side, with a solid knowledge of the strike zone and a willingness to draw walks, although he needs to get the ball in the air more to put that raw power to better use. In his brief pro debut, he was a little pull happy; the Reds think an emphasis on staying in the middle of the field, trusting his hands and believing he has the goods to stay on the fastball away and breaking stuff moving away from him to go opposite field will serve him well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top acquisition for the Angels in the 2025 international market was the highest-ranked catcher in the class, Gabriel Davalillo. But the organization was also jazzed to get De Paula, a shortstop from Santo Domingo, for $900,000. He got off to a hot start on offense, one that was equally as encouraging as Davailillo’s, in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .387/.525/.484 over his first 10 games. But his debut ended when he hurt his left shoulder diving for a ball on defense. The Angels are excited to see what a healthy De Paula can do stateside. He’s shown an early penchant for contact, with solid knowledge of the strike zone, limiting strikeouts and taking some walks. He’s a switch-hitter with some ability to drive the ball, though it’s a hit-over-power profile. De Paula runs well and can steal a base, and that athleticism will help him stay up the middle defensively. He has the chance to be a plus defender at shortstop in the future, one with a table-setter type of offensive profile. He might be a half step ahead of 2026 international signee Jeyson Horton for now, and it will be interesting to see which one of them sticks at the premium position and which one slides over to the keystone, a competition the Angels won’t have to worry about for a while.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A top prospect in the Royals’ stacked 2025 international class, Medina slipped onto MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 list at No. 49, and he signed with the Royals for $947,500 out of the Dominican Republic that January. Medina earned an All-Star selection in the Dominican Summer League in 2025, slashing .260/.398/.404 in 44 games with two homers, seven doubles and four triples. He walked more (31) than he struck out (26), not uncommon in the DSL, but still impressive and a nod to his skill set. He came to the States after the ‘25 season for the Royals’ fall instructional league program. Medina already looks leaner and has gotten stronger in his short time as a pro, and there’s plenty of projection in his frame still as an 18-year-old. A twitchy athlete, he has a compact right-handed swing with power potential, along with a good approach at the plate for such a young hitter. Defensively, Medina probably profiles best as a corner infielder, likely third base because of his arm strength, range and quickness. The Royals do want to see how he handles shortstop, though. Because of their position and ages, there will be comparisons between Medina and Warren Calcaño as they grow up through the system together. Calcaño is probably the better defender, while Medina has the higher upside with his bat. Medina figures to see plenty of reps stateside in ‘26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If the early returns mean anything. Pena might be the bargain of the Twins’ 2023 international signing class. Signed for just $40,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Pena has done nothing but hit at two stops. He batted .382 with a .949 OPS in 39 Dominican Summer League games during his debut after signing, then came stateside and slashed .282/.386/.410 as an 18-year old in the Florida Complex League. An undersized right-handed hitter, Pena makes an almost absurd amount of contact. In his first two summers of pro ball he struck out in just 6.5 percent of his plate appearances, obviously reminding many of former Twin Luis Arraez in his knack for finding the barrel. He has shown a willingness to draw some walks (11.8 BB percentage) and while he’s never going to be a big power guy -- how much he does end up impacting the ball is a question -- he did show a bit more extra-base authority in the FCL and can drive the ball to the gaps. Finding a spot for Pena’s bat in the lineup might be more of a challenge. He’s played second base, his most likely full-time home should he land in one spot, as well as third and left field. He’ll likely spend most of his time at the keystone and in left, but it’s been a bit of an adventure defensively thus far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scull’s father, Antonio, won three Olympic medals playing as a first baseman for Cuba. Anthony started his own path in baseball by signing with the Angels for $235,000 in September 2021. It took a while for the outfielder to show the Angels anything, getting into just 10 games in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then missing most of the 2022 season with a shoulder injury sustained when diving for a ball in the outfield. He did play a full slate of Arizona Complex League games in 2023, showing glimpses of some playable tools. Scull has a strong and athletic frame with the ability to do some damage from the left side of the plate. He makes a lot of hard contact, registering some of the better exit velocities in the lower levels of the Angels' system. He doesn’t strike out a ton, but he can be a bit too aggressive at the plate. It’s more of a line-drive swing right now, but there’s raw power to tap into with the potential to hit around 15 homers annually once he matures physically and with his approach. An above-average runner, Scull can play all three outfield spots with an average arm. He saw more time in center field than anywhere else in 2023 and he does have a chance to stay there should he develop into a regular at one position. A more likely outcome is for him to be a solid fourth outfielder type who moves around and provides a left-handed bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies had spent $6.1 million of their close to $6.7 million international bonus pool as the 2026 season opened, but they knew they wanted to land Park, a projectable 17-year-old right-hander from South Korea, to their organization. So they traded Griff McGarry to the Dodgers and Andrew Baker to the Rockies for a total of $750,000. That gave them enough room to sign Park for just over $1.2 million in May and keep him from being one of the top pitchers in the KBO Draft. Park wanted to pursue a career in the United States rather than head to the top league in Korea, and now he'll get his chance. He's still growing and now stands at 6-foot-3 and 195 pounds with as many as five pitches in his arsenal. Throwing from a three-quarter slot, he can get up to 94 mph with his fastball, generally sitting in the 91-93 range, with late ride at the top of the zone. He can also run and sink it occasionally against right-handed hitters. He has feel to spin two distinct breaking pitches in his curve and slider, the latter registering 2,800 rpm spin rates. He has a changeup and splitter for offspeed options to kill spin -- using the fading change more frequently -- against hitters on both sides of the plate. The Phillies really like Park's ease of operation on the mound, showing an ability to repeat his delivery. He's athletic, with a feel to pitch and an ability to execute that belies his years. That gives him a very good chance to start long-term, and given how much strength he can add to his frame, there's excitement about his ultimate ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It has been well documented several times on the current Angels' Top 30 that this organization likes rolling the dice on high-end high school pitchers in later rounds of the Draft. In 2025, they did it five times, acquiring a group that included LaCourse in Round 6, making him the first Michigander prep pitcher to be taken in the top 10 rounds since Brock Porter was a fourth-rounder in 2022. The Angels went about $120,000 over slot to sign the right-hander away from his commitment to Michigan State. LaCourse’s size, projection and feel for spin all stood out to the Angels scouting staff. The 6-foot-3 starter routinely hits elite spin rate levels with his slider, registering consistently north of 3,000 RPMs with what could be a true out-pitch in time. While he had touched 93-94 mph in short stints in high school, he was more around 88-92 mph with his fastball as a starter, though Angels player development staff have been pleased to see that his velocity is starting to creep up. He throws the heater with a lot of spin for good carry up in the zone to miss bats. His changeup has also improved under pro supervision in the early going. A strong athlete who played basketball in the winter and shortstop when he wasn’t pitching as a prepster, LaCourse does an excellent job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. If the early gains are for real and he can continue to add strength and velocity, he could turn into an inning-eating starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez has built a reputation for outstanding bat-to-ball skills ever since his high school days in Georgia. He brought them with him to Georgia Tech, where he hit .332 and had a .932 OPS the spring after finishing second in the Cape Cod League with a .331 average. The skillset intrigued the Pirates enough for them to take him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft and he continued to do his thing, hitting .325 during his pro debut in Bradenton. He quickly made his way from Bradenton to High-A Greensboro while he continued to build on his hit-over-power profile. The left-handed-hitting outfielder has a fairly high floor because of his knack for contact and lack of strikeouts, especially when combined with his plate discipline and willingness to draw walks. What’s lacking thus far has been impact; his exit velocities have been a little light and he’ll need to find a way to add more physicality and drive the ball more without sacrificing his contact skills. Gonzalez is a better baserunner than his average speed would indicate, and those instincts make him a thread on the basepaths. The lack of speed makes it seem unlikely that he can stick in center field, and he’s seen time in all three outfield spots. If he can’t play center, the offensive profile without more extra-base thump is a little tougher, but his feel for hitting gives the chance to perhaps be a fourth or fifth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of La Romana, Dominican Republic, in 2017, Nunez put up underwhelming numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2019, but there was already some early intrigue with his power potential heading into the lost 2020 season. Nunez grew into some of that in 2021, hitting six home runs with an .848 OPS between the Florida Complex League and Single-A, then his breakout finally came in 2022. Last summer, Nunez climbed from Single-A to High-A, hitting a combined 19 home runs with a .304 average and .824 OPS. He carried this into a successful Dominican Winter League stint, showing some of the pop that the Blue Jays have long dreamed on. At 6-foot-3 with a big frame, Nunez is limited to first base, where he’s just an OK defender. He needs to improve his chase rate at the plate and work more walks, but his exit velocities are among the best in the organization. Nunez will be challenged by more advanced pitching, especially as older arms use more polished breaking balls against him, but there’s no denying his pop from the right side. Much like Spencer Horwitz or any other prospect in the organization likely to stick at first base, he’ll need to hit his way up the ladder. The Blue Jays believe there’s far more potential in there physically, though, making Nunez a name many are watching for another potential breakout if he can clean up his plate approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Elissalt had an outstanding first pro season after the Tigers made him a Day 3 Draft pick and wooed the former Chipola College hurler away from Southern Miss with an above-slot $187,500 bonus. The lanky right-hander opened the season in the Single-A Lakeland bullpen before moving to the rotation by the end of April. He allowed just two earned runs in a 40-inning span from mid-May to the All-Star break, including 21 2/3 consecutive scoreless innings, before securing a promotion to High-A West Michigan's run to the Midwest League title. He earned Florida State League Pitcher of the Year honors, vaulted up prospect rankings and worked his way into the Tigers’ long-term pitching picture. Elissalt isn’t an overpowering pitcher, but uses his long frame for extension that gets his pitches on the hitter sneaky quick. His fastball generally sits around 91-93 mph but still gave up little damage despite a pedestrian whiff rate. His dominant pitch is a 77-80 mph curveball with good spin, nearly 5 feet of drop and another foot of gloveside movement. His lesser-used slider generates a similar whiff rate with less spin and good vertical movement, while his kick change has potential against left-handed pitchers. He has occasional off nights for command but generally attacks the strike zone when he’s in form. Part of Elissalt’s standing comes from projection for a velocity bump with refinements and physical growth; he won't turn 22 until July. He has potential as a back-half starter if he gets a tick more on his fastball and continues to locate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Phillies as 31st-rounder out of an Arizona high school in 2019, Murphy worked just 14 innings in three years at Chandler-Gilbert (Ariz.) CC because of the pandemic and Tommy John surgery. The younger brother of former big league pitcher Patrick Murphy, he parlayed a short stint in the MLB Draft League into getting drafted by the White Sox in the 14th round in 2022. He flew under the radar until last season, when he reached Triple-A, led the Minors in WHIP (0.89) and ranked second in ERA (1.66) and eighth in walk rate (5 percent). Murphy's success came despite not having a single pitch that grades as average. He has the best control and command in the system, and he keeps hitters off balance by expertly sequencing his offerings and locations. He's a tremendous competitor who studies scouting reports and reads swings to exploit opponents' weaknesses. Murphy's fastballs sit at 90 mph and don't exceed 94, avoiding hard contact thanks to the carry on his four-seamer, the sink on his two-seamer and the precision with which he spots them both. His best secondary offering is a mid-80s changeup with depth, followed by a low-80s slider that he can turn into a mid-80s cutter and an upper-70s curveball. Whether all that's enough to get big leaguers out remains in question, but he has put himself in position to find out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz signed with the Yankees for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022 and was one of several standouts on a prospect-laden team in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. The youngest batting qualifier in the circuit at age 17, he led the FCL with 47 RBI and ranked second with 10 homers. The Marlins acquired him in a three-team trade in March, sending Jon Berti to New York and also receiving outfield prospect Shane Sasaki from the Rays. After looking launch-happy and passive during his 2022 pro debut, Cruz displayed a better approach and more power last year. His quick left-handed stroke produces loud contact when he connects, and he could grow into plus pop if he fills out his projectable frame and adds more polish as a hitter. He controls the strike zone fine for a teenager, but his aggressiveness leads to less-than-ideal contact. Cruz presently has solid speed but is still learning to make the most of it on the bases and in the outfield. He's not an instinctive defender and spent most of his FCL time in right field, where he displays solid arm strength. To make it in center, he'd need to improve his reads and routes while retaining his quickness as he matures physically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins were very active at the start of the 2023 international signing period, inking three members of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list. That trio was led by Castro, the Cuban outfielder, who was No. 11 in the rankings. After training with Jaime Ramos in the Dominican Republic, Castro signed with the Twins for $2.4 million. Castro stands out because of his raw tools, projectable frame and left-handed swing. He has a good knack for contact and has shown off a solid approach at the plate at times with a smooth stroke. From time to time, he will get overly aggressive, which is common for a hitter his age. He has the kind of body that should be able to add plenty of strength and some project above-average power when all is said and done. He already displays excellent raw pop in batting practice. Reminding some in the organization of outfield prospect Yasser Mercedes, Castro has the opportunity to stick in center field, where he has good instincts. There is a chance he’ll slow down more as he physically matures and he could slide over to be a run-producing athletic right fielder with a solid arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies have long sought potential impact hitters on the international market, with an eye on up-the-middle-type players. Ezequiel Tovar is a recent success story, while others have reached the big leagues -- like Adael Amador -- without establishing themselves yet. They're hoping De Los Santos can rise through the ranks as well after they signed him for $1 million at the start of the 2026 international signing period in January. One of the younger players in the class, De Los Santos doesn't turn 17 until right before the Dominican Summer League season starts. He's already started adding some strength to his projectable and lean 6-foot-1 frame, which should help his overall offensive profile. He has clean mechanics in the box, showing he can be on time with his smooth left-handed swing. He uses a slight front-foot toe tap for timing, and there's some ability to drive the ball starting to surface. The hope is that De Los Santos, with a good first step and improving arm strength, will be able to stick at shortstop. Some scouts feel he doesn't always have the cleanest slot and might eventually need to move to third as a result, though that's obviously not something the Rockies have to worry about just yet.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Um’s father, Um Jong-soo, played one season in the Braves’ system back in 2001, and with Um’s signing with the Royals in 2022, it made the pair the first South Korean father-son duo to join Major League organizations. After going back to Rookie ball in Arizona to start ‘24, Um showed he was ready for the next level by hitting .310 with a .900 OPS. In his final 50 games of the season in Single-A Columbia, Um slashed .205/.333/.307 with four homers and a 100 wRC+ while sharing catching duties with 2023 first-rounder Blake Mitchell. Um has a simple setup with a little bit of a higher positioning with his hands, getting them back in a decent position to hit, and a leg kick that lifts and coils into his hip for a better load. It’s an efficient swing from the right side with line-drive power right now and the potential for more extra base hits and average power as he grows into his frame. His solid bat speed and quick hands help him get to pitches on the inner half of the plate. Um is still learning how to navigate an at-bat and can struggle with breaking balls. Defensively, Um is athletic and moves well behind the plate. His receiving is a work in progress, but he has above-average arm strength and the foundation to stick at backstop. Um adds to the Royals’ catching depth in their system with four catchers in the preseason Top 30. With a strong makeup, he is smart and wants to learn, and the Royals are eager to get him to a full-season affiliate. With time and more development, Um has the potential to be a backup Major League catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners’ activity in the 2024 international signing period started with Dawel Joseph being the headliner, getting $3.3 million in January. Six months later, they added Shen, signing the Taiwanese right-hander, for $175,000 in July. Pitching at age 21, Shen was rolled out cautiously, making his debut in the Arizona Complex League last May. After 28 dominant innings over seven appearances, he earned a bump up to full-season ball for nine more starts. Right out of the gate, Shen displayed a feel for commanding all three of his pitches. His fastball sits in the low 90s, touching 95 mph now and again, and he throws it with sink to help get ground ball outs. His mid-80s changeup also gets weak contact on the ground and gets a lot of chase. He can spin an 81 mph slider decently, and it missed bats at the lower levels, but a little more power could make it even nastier. Shen filled up the strike zone in both stops during his debut, though he was getting too much of the plate during his time in Modesto. Some added strength to his 6-foot-3 frame would help not only that slider, but all of his offerings trend upwards. He has back-of-the-rotation potential based on his pitchability and projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some teams might have been content with nabbing the No. 5 prospect in the 2024 international class, like the Reds did by signing Adolfo Sanchez for $2.7 million. But Cincinnati was able to go big a second time, nabbing the No. 42 prospect in Mariano for $1.65 million, both of whom they got when the signing period opened in mid-January. It’s the second time in three years the Reds have doled out multiple seven-figure bonuses in one signing period, having done so to bring Ricardo Cabrera and Anthuan Valencia into the fold in 2022. Mariano is a long and lean 6-foot-3 infielder with lots of room to add strength. He’s already shown good contact skills from the right side of the plate, though like with many young players, improved plate discipline and pitch recognition will help. With his aggressive approach, he’s shown the ability spray the ball in the gaps and the thinking is he’s going to fill out that frame and plenty of power is going to come. That will be an important part of his development because most feel he isn’t destined to stick at shortstop long-term. He has good hands and plenty of arm for the premium position, but if he matures physically as expected, he’s likely to slow down too much and will need to move to third, where he should be a capable defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCoy should make for one of the most interesting prospect follows in the Padres system in 2026, and not just because he stands 6-foot-5 and is listed at 260 pounds. The Baltimore-area native spent two years at the University of Maryland-Eastern Shore before transferring to Hofstra, where former 14-year Major Leaguer Frank Catalanotto coached him. After going unselected in the 2024 Draft, McCoy signed as a nondrafted free agent with the Padres. He dealt with hamstring and quad injuries in his first full season but he left a mark in his time with Single-A Lake Elsinore, hitting .318/.394/.513 with six homers in 53 games. The right-handed slugger's raw power is the best in the San Diego pipeline and some of the best in the entire Minors. There's a ton of strength in his base and upper body, and he maxed out with an 118 mph exit velocity in the California League -- a number that would fit at the top of many teams' leaderboards in the Majors. There is some feel for hitting here too. McCoy doesn’t lash out to get to that pop, and his swing can be short and controlled to whack stuff inside. He did swing a fair amount through sliders and changeups away, and upper-level pitchers will try to take advantage of that. McCoy is a decent mover under way -- someone who can push for extra bases on balls to the gaps -- but can take a bit to get moving up the first-base line. He was primarily in left field last year in Lake Elsinore, a decent fit for his speed and arm strength, but could eventually become a bigger target at first base, where he spent the first two years of his NCAA career. McCoy will need to mash at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like his father, Eric, the 1992 National League Rookie of the Year, Karros played collegiately at UCLA before turning pro with the Dodgers. He pitched just 41 innings in three years with the Bruins because of the pandemic and persistent back issues that sidelined him for all of 2022, when Los Angeles drafted him in the 16th round. He has filled the strike zone while climbing from Single-A to Double-A the past two seasons, though he missed nearly three months last summer with mild flexor soreness. Karros' fastball parks at 91-93 mph and reaches 96 but stays off barrels because his 6-foot-7 frame creates an unusually high release point and plenty of extension. He'll spot his heater where he wants, then catch hitters off balance with a solid low-80s changeup that he leverages down in the zone. He also can miss bats with a low-80s slider that has depth and occasionally will flip in a fringy upper-70s curveball. Karros stands out more for his pitchability and deception than his pure stuff. He repeats his simple delivery with ease and provides consistent strikes, though he nibbled at the zone a bit too much when he got hit harder in Double-A. He has a high floor and could become a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 While Joswa Lugo received the highest bonus of any player from the Angels’ signing class at the start of the 2024 international signing period, De La Rosa received the most of any pitcher signed by the organization, getting $300,000 to get his pro career started. He did that in the Dominican Summer League and put his best foot forward out of the gate, finishing with a 2.79 ERA, .211 BAA and a 9.9 K/9 rate in a typically hitting-friendly environment. At 6-foot-4, the hope is De La Rosa can develop into an innings-eating workhorse-type starter. His fastball maxes out at 96 mph and typically sits 91-94, though the hope is more velocity will come as he matures. He has a solid 77-82 mph slider that flashes above average and could develop into an out pitch. There’s an upper-80s changeup in there, but it’s too firm and it’s behind the other two offerings. For his first time out, De La Rosa did a decent job of being in and around the strike zone. He’ll be just 18 as he comes stateside for the 2025 season and he’s a long way away, but with improved command and velocity to go along with a solid third pitch, he has a big league starter ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s important not to put too much stock into Dominican Summer League numbers as the Rookie-level circuit tends to be very hitter-friendly. But when a new prospect has a huge debut there, it also shouldn’t be ignored. Beltre put a huge first foot forward after signing for just under $1.5 million, shaking off an early wrist injury to post a 1.071 OPS and finished tied for second on the circuit with 11 homers. Beltre showed, at least during his debut, that his right-handed swing can do a lot of damage. He makes hard contact to all fields, and it’s clear he can already get to his raw power. He entered pro ball with a reputation of being a very aggressive hitter, and his strikeout rate was a little high (23.8 percent), but he also had better plate discipline than expected, offsetting those K’s with a healthy dose of walks (15.5 pct). Strong and compact, Beltre’s athleticism stood out on both sides of the ball. He was introduced to all three outfield positions in the DSL, and while it was once thought he was certainly destined for a corner where his strong arm would work well, there’s now some conviction that he could stick in center field. He’ll be 18 for all of his U.S. debut in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Armbruester wasn’t very well known coming out of the Seattle prep ranks. He turned into quite an accomplished collegiate pitcher, first at Division III Pacific Lutheran and then at New Mexico State, for whom he claimed WAC conference pitcher of the year honors in 2021. That success caught the attention of the Orioles, who took him in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft and signed him for $100,000. He pitched well enough to reach Double-A in his first full season and Triple-A in 2023, but stalled a little in Norfolk down the stretch last summer. At 6-foot-5 and 250 pounds, Armbruester is a big, physical right-hander with intriguing stuff that he tinkers with frequently, sometimes with immediate success. He added an upper-80s cutter in 2022, and missed more bats with it that year than any other pitch in his arsenal. Last season, he shelved his changeup and added a curveball. In 2024, he plans to revive the change to give him another weapon against left-handed hitters. The cutter is the best of those offerings. Armbruester plays them all off a hoppy low-to-mid-90s fastball with ride and a sweepy slider, both of which he demonstrates plus feel for. Armbruester uses an awkward delivery and funky arm slot to hide the ball well, using that deception to help his stuff play up. His success really hinges on that and his command. When he locates everything well, he controls the zone and can miss bats with multiple pitches. But he can sometimes get hurt throwing too many strikes when ahead in the count and his walk rate spiked down the stretch last year against Triple-A hitters. If he can continue developing his secondary stuff and throwing strikes with all his offerings, he could still fit in as a back-end rotation piece at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia, a cousin of Wilmer Flores (both the Giants infielder and the Tigers pitching prospect), joined the Mets system out of Venezuela in June 2021 and made it to full-season ball last year with mixed results. His 5.04 ERA in 80 1/3 innings between Single-A St. Lucie and High-A Brooklyn didn’t quite pop, but he did strike out 106 batters in that span. His 31.9 percent K rate in the Florida State League ranked third among the 46 pitchers on the circuit with at least 60 frames. The 6-foot right-hander throws a 92-94 mph two-seam fastball (topping out at 96.7) out of a low slot that lower-level batters just found difficult to pick up, leading to a strong whiff rate and some weak contact. He primarily paired that with a low-80s sweeping slider that gave him an option with good gloveside break as compared to the armside movement of the two-seamer. He showed the occasional low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup too, but he understands which pitch is his bread and butter. Garcia walked 14.6 percent of batters faced between those two levels. That’s a slight improvement from 15.6 percent in 2022 but an example of why many believe he’ll remain in a relief role. He’ll still only be 21 years old as he heads back to the High-A level, and there are some in the organization who believe he’s on the precipice of a breakout as he continues to rack up K’s and finetune his command with more stateside experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest acquisition for the Reds on the international market when the 2023 signing period was catcher Alfredo Duno, who received $3.1 million, and the organization gave a seven-figure bonus later in the period to ink Sheng-En Lin. Third on the 2023 bonus list was Alcantara, signed initially as a shortstop out of the Dominican Republic for $640,000 in January of that year. He performed well enough during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League to come stateside in 2024 and struggled with the Arizona Complex League assignment. A return to the level the year after paid dividends, and he earned a bump to full-season Daytona for the first time. The Reds saw enough to move him to High-A Dayton to kick off his age-20 season in 2026. Alcantara, an undersized infielder at 5-foot-9, is a right-handed hitter with an aggressive approach at the plate. After striking out over 36 percent of the time during his U.S. debut, he's worked to refine his approach, cutting down on his swing-and-miss considerably in 2025. He has gap-to-gap power right now, with some ability to impact the ball, and limiting chase and continuing to see pitches and draw walks should help him maximize his offensive potential. While he was signed as a shortstop and saw plenty of time at the premium position over the first three summers of his career, Alcantara doesn't have the range to stick there long-term. He has the arm strength for third, and he's splitting time between the hot corner and second base, which might be the best option for him should he settle into one position permanently in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After getting $600,000 to sign with the Pirates out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Terrero couldn’t play until 2021 because of the pandemic. He showed off a solid approach during his Dominican Summer League debut that year, then posted an .890 OPS in the Florida Complex League when he came to the United States for the first time. He was streaky during his full-season debut in 2023, fading down the stretch, but showing off some of his offensive potential. With a smaller frame, Terrero has yet to display a ton of impact from the left side of the plate. But there were some gains in terms of exit velocity last year, which gave the Pirates hope there could be more of that to come with some pop to his pull side. He’s made a ton of contact in his brief career, though his strikeout rate did climb a bit in Single-A Bradenton. He tends to have a consistent approach and draws walks, with a 13 percent walk rate in 2023. Terrero runs well enough to steal some bags, and it also gives him the potential to stick in center field. He’s an average defender there now who still needs to work on his reads and routes. He’s actually a plus defender in an outfield corner, but he’s not going to have the kind of offensive impact teams like to see from that spot, which could make him a bit of a tweener if center doesn’t work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benitez's $225,000 bonus ranked fourth among left-handers in the 2023 international class, and the Dominican has emerged as the best prospect from the Marlins' crop that year. He made his U.S. debut last May but needed just three starts in Rookie-ball to merit a promotion to Single-A four days after his 18th birthday. He logged a 3.12 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 57 2/3 innings as the youngest starter in the Florida State League. Extremely advanced for his age, Benitez already owns a plus low-80s changeup with significant fade and sink. He has added 20 pounds since turning pro, boosting his two- and four-seam fastballs into the low 90s with a peak of 96 mph, though both could use more consistent action. He improved the shape of his upper-70s slider last year, turning it into a sweeper that should become a solid pitch once it gains more power. With a quick arm and explosive movement down the mound, Benitez creates more extension than most 6-foot-1 hurlers. His control and command can waver at times, but he's athletic and repeats his delivery well, so he should gain more consistency as he gets stronger. Another member of Miami's deep stable of potential lefty starters, he could fit in the middle of a big league rotation once he's fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Randall was a catcher growing up before taking his strong arm out from behind the plate and onto the mound. After two years in the bullpen at the University of Arizona, he transferred to the University of San Diego and became a workhorse starter and hit the scouting radar. The Tigers selected him in the third round and signed him for a $700,000 bonus. Randall made 16 starts at Single-A Lakeland in his first full season before earning a promotion to High-A in late July. He was traded to the Nationals shortly after in a Deadline move for Kyle Finnegan. Randall is a classic power sinker-slider pitcher with a low three-quarter delivery and rotation, but he actually saw an uptick in his strikeout rate when he became a starter at San Diego. His heavy sinker sits around 94-95 mph but can ramp up to 98 and induce a ton of ground balls. His high-spin slider is a nice swing-and-miss pitch off the sinker. He has a feel for a changeup, but his ability to develop it could determine whether he ends up a starter or reliever as he advances. Part of what separated Randall as a starter in college was his ability to repeat his stuff and hold his velocity late into starts. Randall, who threw a ton of strikes in Lakeland, drew comparisons to former Cleveland starter Justin Masterson during his time in the Detroit system. But with Randall’s big body frame and sinker/slider approach, there’s still a decent chance he ends up in a bullpen role down the road with Washington, one who needs to play in front of a good defensive infield given his propensity for grounders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Florida high school product, Hermann was headed to play college baseball at South Florida before the Yankees took him in the 14th round and gave him a slightly over-slot $135,000 bonus in 2021. Because he was the lightest player in the Draft at 160 pounds, they had him initially focus on adding strength before making his pro debut in 2022. He needed little more than a month before earning a promotion from Rookie ball to Single-A, where he recorded a 2.66 ERA in four starts. Hermann's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and peaks at 94, playing better than its velocity because it has a flat approach angle that produces carry up in the zone. He has advanced feel for a sinking 83-88 mph changeup that yields ground-ball contact, though it could use more velo separation from his heater. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with encouraging shape and spin rates that he can morph into an upper-80s cutter. While he lacks physicality, Hermann is athletic and has projection remaining. He has good extension in his delivery, allowing his pitches to appear quicker than they are, and he provides plenty of strikes. If he can get stronger and add more power to his stuff, he could become a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros play the Cuban market as much as any team and handed the largest bonus in their 2024 international class to an outfielder from the island. Hernandez signed for $1.7 million and likely will make his pro debut in the United States this summer. As an 18-year-old in 2022, he batted .233/.398/.301 as a semi-regular in Cuba's top league. Houston is bullish about Hernandez's potential to hit for both average and power. He already has produced maximum exit velocities of 110 mph and has plus raw pop that plays to all fields. There's more question about his hitting ability because some scouts with other organizations don't love his left-handed swing. Hernandez has plus speed and is plus-plus once he gets going, giving him 25-25 upside. He projects as a center fielder, though his reads and routes could use some improvement. With average arm strength, he's capable of playing all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mobley established himself as one of the best prep pitchers in the 2024 Draft early in his career at Durant HS (Plant City, Fla.) and stood out last spring as one of the youngest, most projectable and hardest-throwing high school hurlers available. Armed with the largest bonus pool ($18,334,000) since those rules came into play in 2012, the Guardians floated Mobley all the way down to the 295th overall pick, where they signed him for $1.8 million. That obliterated the 10th-round bonus record Cleveland set two years earlier by paying Jacob Zibin $1.2 million. Mobley already reaches 92-95 mph and reaches 99 with armside run and carry on his fastball, which gains deception coming out of a low three-quarters arm slot and low release height. Because he could overmatch most high schoolers simply by using his heaters, he didn't need to rely on or develop his secondary pitches very much. His slider and tumbling changeup both park in the low 80s and have solid upside, while his mid-70s curveball needs more power. There still plenty of projection remaining in Mobley's 6-foot-5, 205-pound frame, so he could add even more velocity as he gets stronger. He's still in the process of learning how to keep his long limbs in sync, maintain a consistent regular point and land his secondary pitches in the zone. He comes with some reliever risk and will need time to add polish but could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a Marlins' 2024 Draft class filled with prospects hailed for their bat-to-ball skills as amateurs, Trimble stands out as the club's best selection as a fourth-rounder who signed for a below-slot $550,000. After amassing high OBPs with few strikeouts at James Madison, he carried that over to pro ball. Trimble reached Double-A in his first full season and slashed .253/.372/.402 between three levels in his age-22 season. Although he missed two months with a strained hamstring, he made up for lost time with a strong Arizona Fall League performance. While he doesn't have any single standout tool, Trimble is above average in many aspects of the game. Chiefly, he does a lot of the small things quite well. Trimble makes good swing decisions, takes his walks and rarely whiffs. Pitchers haven't found an easy way to get him out, and he proved even more disciplined against more advanced pitching. But while his swing is smooth, he doesn't offer a ton of bat speed. Until he can elevate the ball more, there are questions about his ability to hit more than 10-15 homers in a season. Trimble uses his above-average speed well on the bases to leg out hits and take extra bases. He's a solid athlete on defense who has a chance to stick in center and could be very good in left, even if his arm strength is fringy at best. Trimble is a well-rounded prospect who is quite likely to be a Major Leaguer, even if he may top out as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campos shot out of the gate with a .357 average and an .869 OPS over 45 games as a freshman at Arizona State and never much looked back. He finished with a career .369/.465/.554 slash line over his three springs as a Sun Devil and had significantly more walks (94) than strikeouts (66) over the 147-game span. He was a two-time Buster Posey National Collegiate Catcher of the Year Award semifinalist. The Cardinals selected him in the fourth round in 2024, signed him for exact slot at $669,300 and assigned him to the Florida State League, where he slashed .319/.396/.407 with a 13/13 K/BB ratio over 26 contests. It's astounding how consistent Campos has been, both in the pros and in college. As a left-handed hitting catcher, he’d hold a certain value already, but he adds to that with good swing decisions, excellent pitch recognition and strong bat-to-ball skills. He doesn’t whiff on many pitch types and especially succeeds against fastballs. However, the 5-foot-8 backstop doesn’t project for much pop at all, despite an uptick in collegiate homers in ’24, and he’ll likely always be hit-over-power. At that size, Campos doesn’t make for a huge target, and his defensive skills – from his receiving to his arm strength – are considered fringy. He played some corner outfield in school, but his best value will be behind the plate. Evaluators rave about his baseball IQ though, and his overall offensive approach gives him a good shot at being a future backup catcher in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vasquez signed for only $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2023, and three years later, he’s proved to be a lesson in the power of patience. Vasquez sported an unseemly 13/24 K/BB ratio over 27 innings in his first pro season, forcing him to repeat the Dominican Summer League in 2024. With a better foundation under him, he found success stateside in 2025 with a 3.80 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 64 innings between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia. His 28.1 percent strikeout rate was 10th-best among 42 Minor Leaguers aged 19 or younger (min. 60 IP). The 6-foot-2 right-hander sits 94-96 mph with his four-seamer and can run it up to 98 already, a big driver of the excitement on his profile. There’s room for even more power behind the heater as he enters his 20s, and he mixes in a sinker for a different fastball look too. His slider shows good sweep and spin, running away from righties with regularity. It flashes at least above average, but Vasquez’s command of it could use improvement with too many missing the mark. He added a kick-change that shows early promise but wasn’t often used in the California League. Vasquez clearly has arm talent, the type that earns you long looks at starting. But until he establishes more consistent command of the breaking ball, his control is going to be a major question mark. Entering 2026, he’s walked at least 11 percent of the batters he’s faced at every level, and that number was up to 15.4 in his five Single-A starts. He’ll be the age of a college sophomore as he returns to Visalia this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holton’s commitment to Vanderbilt meant he slid out of serious Draft consideration in 2021, and he headed to Nashville and established himself immediately in the Commodores’ weekend rotation. After a solid start to his final college season in 2024, he faded and saw his stuff diminish, missing the SEC Tournament and making just one relief appearance in Regional play. He made one appearance as a pro after signing with the Braves as a second-rounder, then needed Tommy John surgery, meaning he’ll miss the 2025 season. When he’s healthy, Holton has a legitimate four-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that sits 93-95 mph and tops out at 98. His low-80s slider -- a plus breaking ball with horizontal and vertical action that misses bats -- is particularly effective against left-handed hitters. He’s had a solid upper-70s curveball in the past and can throw a sinking changeup in the mid-80s. Holton is super competitive on the mound, but there are questions about whether he can be a starter at the next level. The 5-foot-11 lefty has an unorthodox delivery and high arm slot, and his mechanics haven’t always led to consistent strike-throwing. For now, the focus is on rehab, and the Braves will get their first real look at what he might be in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Waddell’s first experience with the Draft came in 2019, when he was eligible as a sophomore at Georgia Tech and was selected in the 32nd round by the D-backs. He went back to school, only to see the season shortened by the pandemic and did not have his name called in the truncated five-round Draft in 2020. He had a solid 2021 season and was taken in the fifth round this time around as a senior sign, and the Braves saved some bonus pool money by signing him below slot. He went straight to High-A and hit six homers in 21 games before getting a bump to Double-A and then finishing off his long year with a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League. He began the year in Double-A to start his first full season, but a back strain forced him out of action at the end of May. Waddell has a contact-first approach from the left side of the plate with excellent strike zone judgment, leading to very low strikeout rates and good walk rates, something he brought with him during his pro debut and in the AFL. He added some strength that helped him impact the ball more in 2021, though he’s likely never going to be a huge home run guy. The infielder showed he can play a capable shortstop at Georgia Tech, then spent time at three infield positions during his debut. He likely has the ceiling of a utilityman, but his floor is pretty high and it shouldn’t take him too long to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A California high school product, Huezo didn't turn 18 until three months after the Astros signed him for $397,500 as a 12th-round pick in 2023. Injuries and strikeout issues resulted in him spending most of his first three years as a pro in Rookie ball, but he does offer one of the more interesting combinations of power and speed in the system. After overcoming hamate surgery early in 2025, he played the final month of last season at Single-A, where he batted .301 with a pair of homers in 22 games, then led the Australian Baseball League with a 1.031 OPS during the offseason. One of the strongest hitters in the system, Huezo hits balls exceptionally hard with a left-handed swing designed to crush balls to right field. He has 30-homer upside, but to get there he'll have to make a lot of adjustments at the plate after striking out at a 32.7 percent clip his first three pro seasons. His stroke gets too long and uphill, he chases too many pitches and he struggles to connect with non-fastballs. Huezo has solid speed and is aggressive on the bases, swiping 27 bags in 35 tries (77.1 percent) in 127 pro games. He played all three outfield spots in 2025, spending the bulk of his time in center field, where he's an average defender. He profiles best in right with his power and solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After selecting just two position players in the 2021 Draft, the Dodgers needed some more bats and farm director Will Rhymes liked Gauthier's swing and selectivity. Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent, he has ranked in the top 10 in the Minors in both walks and on-base percentage in each of his two full pro seasons. He batted .316/.435/.475 with 12 homers and 19 steals while reaching Double-A in 2023, and he soon could become Hofstra's first big leaguer since mid-1970s Mets right-hander Hank Webb. Gauthier understands the strike zone and makes better swing decisions than most players, rarely giving away an at-bat. He understands his right-handed stroke and doesn't try to do too much with it, lacing line drives while using the entire ballpark. He focused on adding strength after his first full season and hit the ball harder in the second, though he won't have more than 12-15 homer power unless he looks to turn on pitches and drive them in the air more frequently. While Gauthier doesn't have loud tools, he makes the most of them and is surprisingly versatile for someone with average speed and arm strength. He started 18 or more games at five different positions in 2023: third base, shortstop, second base, left field and right field. He fits best and provides averageish defense at second base, grades as fringy elsewhere and profiles as an offensive-minded utilityman who excels at getting on base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Georgia's best prep pitching prospects in 2019, David slid to the Diamondbacks in the 35th round amid signability concerns and opted to attend Auburn instead. He never pitched for the Tigers during the pandemic-truncated 2020 season before bouncing from Gordon State (Ga.) JC to Northwest Florida State JC to NAIA program Southeastern (Fla.) before the Astros drafted him in 2024's 10th round as a fifth-year senior. He moved from Single-A to Double-A in his first full pro season, compiling a 3.47 ERA with 87 strikeouts in 85 2/3 innings. David's fastball parks at 95-96 mph and peaks at 98, and he maintained that velocity throughout 2025. It features carry and armside run. His tight mid-80s slider doesn't get a lot of chases but does generate a lot of in-zone swings and misses, and he can turn it into an 89-91 mph cutter on occasion. After focusing primarily on his heater and slider in college, he has worked on incorporating a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup with depth but has trouble landing both for strikes. There's effort in David's delivery that has prevented him from throwing consistent strikes, so he's more of multi-inning reliever than a starter in the long run.
