He spent the first two months of 2025 in the rotation at Single-A Fayetteville before shifting to the bullpen. He'll pitch at age 25 this season, and the less challenging role will accelerate his timetable to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Candiotti rode the knuckleball to a 16-year career in the Major Leagues. His son, Clark, utilizes a very different arsenal that took him on an interesting ride as a college player. Candiotti played for five schools in five years between St. Mary’s (2020), Vernon (Junior) College (2021), Grayson County Community College (2022), Wichita State (2023) and finally Arizona (2024). He was a Pac-12 All-Conference selection after posting a 3.39 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings with the Wildcats, and that helped push him to Padres with the 135th overall pick in the '24 Draft, where he signed for $80,000. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has the look of a durable starter. He added fastball velocity between his time at Wichita State and Arizona, averaging around 93 mph with the latter while touching 96. The heater can feature good carry, eliciting chase above the zone. Candiotti, however, leaned even more heavily on his 83-85 mph slider, throwing it 45 percent of the time and using it against batters from both sides. It has sharp, short movement, allowing him to wear out the gloveside half of the plate. He mixed in a 78-82 mph curveball for a different breaking look and barely used his mid-80s changeup in ’24. Candiotti did a great job of throwing strikes in each of his last two collegiate seasons, but a significant portion of that was getting batters to expand the zone. That ability will be tested against pro bats. There is a certain temptation to throw Candiotti in the bullpen because of his age -- he'll be 24 entering his first full season -- but given his late college trajectory, he could have a fighting chance to stick in future rotations, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pentecost was one of the NAIA's top pitchers in 2025, ranking among the national leaders in wins (12, sixth), strikeouts (116, sixth), K/BB ratio (5.5, second), K rate (13.1 per nine innings, fifth) and walk rate (2.4 per nine innings, third). He set Taylor (Ind.) school records for victories and whiffs and became the Trojans' first Draft pick in a decade. After he signed for a below-slot $297,500 in the sixth round, a shoulder impingement delayed his pro debut until 2026. Pentecost's four-seam fastball averages 92 mph and tops out at 96 with more carry than life, but it plays up because of his command and extension. He also has good feel for locating a sweeping low-80s slider that he can use to get both chases and in-zone strikes. His 78-82 mph curveball and low-80s changeup with fade are decent complementary pitches. His athleticism allows Pentecost to repeat his delivery and get down the mound well, leading to a lower release height and consistent strikes. He'll need to prove himself against more rigorous competition, but he exhibits some of the best feel for pitching in the system. A potential back-of-the-rotation starter, he'll attempt to join Dave Wickersham as the only big leaguers ever to come out of Taylor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hainline spent two seasons at Washington State before transferring to Oregon State, where he formed a double-play combination with No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana in 2024. A below-slot seventh-rounder that July, he played at all four levels of the Dodgers system in 2025, counting the Double-A Texas League playoffs. He earned All-Star honors in the High-A California League and played well enough during an emergency Triple-A assignment in June that the Oklahoma City coaching staff wanted to keep him. A right-handed hitter, Hainline has a good eye at the plate but swings and misses at strikes more than he should, especially against non-fastballs. His sneaky raw power and ability to turn on pitches could translate into 15 or more homers per season, though he produces more groundballs than are desirable. He hits the ball consistently hard but needs to improve his quantity and quality of contact. Hainline has average speed and good instincts on the bases, and he swiped 31 bases in 39 attempts (79 percent) last year. He played shortstop, second base and third base and his glovework earned differing reviews from inside and outside the organization. The Dodgers see him as a solid defender with arm strength to match, while other scouts grade him as more average in both regards.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams generally want junior college hitters to prove they can handle better pitching, so Miller went undrafted despite batting .394 in two seasons at Bishop State (Ala.) CC and winning a Perfect Game Collegiate League MVP award in between. He had no problem making the jump to the Southeastern Conference last spring, batting .381/.474/.702 at Alabama before the Marlins signed him for $800,800 as a third-rounder. He expanded his strike zone during his pro debut, resulting in a .240/.305/.298 line between two Class A stops. Miller found success throughout college and in Single-A by understanding how pitchers were trying to attack him, adjusting accordingly and making consistent hard contact to all fields. He diverted from that approach when he got off to a slow start in High-A, aggressively tried to pull everything and piled up strikeouts and weak groundballs. When he's not trying to do too much, he shows the feel for the barrel, bat speed and strength to hit for a high average with 20 homers per season from the right side of the plate. It's unclear where Miller, who has below-average speed and fringy arm strength, will wind up defensively. He was adequate at best at third base for the Crimson Tide and may not have the quickness for second base, where he spent most of his debut. The Marlins believe his work ethic will help him get the job done at the keystone, while most scouts project him as a left fielder or first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were two Indiana natives on the World Cup-winning US 18-and-under national team in 2022: Max Clark and Tilly. While Clark went third overall to the Tigers in the 2023 Draft, Tilly was unselected as MLB Pipeline’s No. 208 prospect in the class and headed to Auburn instead. He pitched primarily out of the bullpen in his two years in the SEC and sported a 5.48 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 46 innings as a Draft-eligible sophomore last year. The Mets took him in the seventh round and signed him for above slot at $397,500 to keep him from heading back to school. The Mets have early interest in developing Tilly as a starter because of his interesting pitch mix. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph, touching 97, and because of the average velocity, he was willing to go liberally to his secondaries in his final season on campus. Since his amateur days, Tilly has earned praise for the high spin rates on his low-80s slider, and he’s developed his mid-80s splitter into arguably an even better pitch, one with enough dip and movement to cause lefties fits. Tilly also worked in another high-spin curveball in the mid 70s with Auburn but saved it mostly for early counts. Tilly walked 13.4 percent of the batters he faced in his two years at Auburn -- a rate that would keep anyone in the bullpen early in their collegiate career -- but the Mets believe there’s untapped pitchability there, especially if they can tame some of his spinnier options. There’s a good chance Tilly would have gotten starting looks as junior anyways, and now that can happen under the eye of a New York organization that has specialized in pitching development in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cardenas walked right into UCLA’s starting lineup as a freshman in 2019 largely because of his defense and surprised a lot of people with a .976 OPS that season. He didn’t come close to that kind of production again over his next two years as the Bruins’ backstop, but his glove enabled him to go in the eighth round of the 2021 Draft to the Twins. He’s largely been the same player professionally, moving one rung at a time. Possessing the kind of skills that could point to a long career in the big leagues, Cardenas is a plus receiver with plus instincts that go along with excellent blocking skills. He also has a huge arm, one that has thrown out 30 percent of potential basestealers heading into the 2024 season. Pitchers love throwing to him, and it’s not a big surprise that he was behind the dish when High-A Cedar Rapids won the Midwest League title. It isn't that Cardenas is a complete zero as a hitter. He makes a ton of contact and draws a lot of walks, leading to lofty on-base percentages. It’s an unorthodox swing that might make hitting coaches cringe, but he puts the ball in play, albeit without much impact. He’s worked to clean up his swing to get to a little more thump, which would help him stick as a big league backup for a long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding big lefties with good stuff isn't always so easy, so Eaton got plenty of attention during his time at George Mason University. He worked out of the Patriots' rotation for two years, missing bats but with poor command. The Rockies thought he was worth a flier with their sixth-round pick in the 2024 Draft, and after sending him out that summer as a reliever for a brief pro debut, there was a lot of internal talk about putting him in the bullpen. That thinking has been shelved, however, after Eaton made 27 starts and amassed 140 innings while reaching Double-A in his first full season of pro ball, leading the organization in strikeouts, K/9 and strikeout percentage. Eaton is now showing an ability to throw three pitches for strikes and that, along with showing acumen for finishing hitters, gives him a chance to start. His fastball sits around 93 mph and he can reach back for 95-96. He'll carry his velocity deep into starts, and the pitch has occasional cut or tail to it. His mid-80s slider is his best pitch, eliciting a miss rate north of 40 percent last year. He'll manipulate its shape, sometimes throwing it with sweep, sometimes with the tilt and depth of a more traditional slider. A big reason for his success thus far has been his conviction in throwing his low-80s changeup more. The big left-hander struggled with the strike zone throughout his college career, a big reason why the Rockies weren't the only ones thinking he belonged in a bullpen. It's not pinpoint command, but he's around the zone enough where the organization thinks he might have the ability to stick in a rotation for a long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Martinez out of Venezuela in 2018 and started him in the Dominican Summer League the next summer, when he hit .239 with a .664 OPS over 58 games but showed some raw tools that kept the organization intrigued through the lost 2020 season. In 2021, Martinez played in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and got a brief taste of Single-A, hitting .330 with as many walks (22) as strikeouts in 34 games. Last summer, Martinez broke out over the course of 96 games, mostly with Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver, hitting .293 with an .832 OPS. Most impressive was his power jump, as he launched 14 homers after showing very little pop earlier in his pro career. This placed Martinez squarely on the radar for the Blue Jays, who have been starving for a star outfield prospect for years. Martinez has borrowed some swing mechanics from Bo Bichette. They help him tap into his natural athleticism, and he showed a very good feel for the barrel of his bat before a difficult 2023 season with High-A Vancouver, where he still hasn't struck out much but has lacked impact. Defensively, his range in the outfield needs to improve, which likely limits him to a corner spot, but his bat-first profile puts the young Venezuelan on the map in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estanista joined the Phillies after signing for just $10,000 in November 2019. Because of the pandemic, the Curacao native wasn’t able to debut professionally until 2021, but he made a solid first impression in the Dominican Summer League. He followed that up with perhaps an even more impressive showing during his U.S. debut in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2022. The right-hander screams projection from his 6-foot-3 frame. He’s long and loose, coming at hitters with a high slot delivery. He can already run his fastball up to 97 mph, and it’s easy to dream on more consistent velocity to come. The pitch has good carry to it and cuts because of that arm slot. His secondary stuff is a work in progress, and while he’s shown some feel to spin a decent slider, his best secondary offering might end up being a newer cutter he throws in the upper 80s, a tight pitch with late depth to it. He’ll continue to work on developing his changeup as well. Between extended spring training and the FCL last year, Estanista probably topped out at around 50 innings, and he needs a lot more reps to improve his command. When he’s in the zone, hitters do not square up the baseball, and the Phillies are excited to see what he can do as he builds up his innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pedro Strop pitched eight seasons as a reliever for the Cubs and even had a brief run in the Reds bullpen in the COVID-shortened season of 2020. His son Royelny, at least to begin his career, is sticking in the NL Central. The outfielder, who trained with his father in their native Dominican Republic, signed with the Cardinals for $1.4 million in January, becoming St. Louis’ top international addition in the 2025 signing period. Only 16 at the time of his signing, Strop is seen as mighty projectable moving forward as a lefty-hitting, lefty-throwing outfielder. St. Louis scouts dream that he’ll have at least average power at full maturity once he bulks up, and he already shows quality pullside pop. His hit tool is somewhat split with some seeing strong present bat-to-ball skills and others concerned about his mechanics. If he can continue to hit the ball hard, he could live with a few strikeouts. With that ability to bulk up also brings questions about where Strop lands defensively. He’s a good runner right now who can handle center, but he may slow down as he ages, necessitating a move to the corners. It’s likeliest that his bat is what pushes him through the St. Louis system in the years to come, and Strop got to show that off late in the Dominican Summer League, going 13-for-26 (.500) with seven extra-base hits in his final six games after sporadic opportunities throughout the summer. He hit for the cycle in his final contest of 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Salcedo was arguably the revelation of the Tigers organization on the pitching side with a spectacular stateside debut. Signed for $70,000 out of Venezuela in January 2023, he spent two years in the Dominican Summer League, then dominated the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer, racking up more than twice as many strikeouts (53) as hits allowed (22) over 45⅓ innings, including a 10-strikeout gem over five scoreless innings of one-hit ball against the Blue Jays. He jumped to Single-A Lakeland for the stretch run and helped the Flying Tigers win a Florida State League title, not allowing more than one run in six of his seven starts and two hits or fewer in all of them. Salcedo has a good fastball and sinker that average around 95 mph and top out at 97-98 but don’t miss many bats. His secondary pitches were the key to his high strikeout rate, including a mid-to-upper-80s slider with sharp movement and a better than 50 percent whiff rate, plus a split change that plays off of it with even better swing-and-miss. His walk rate was a concern in the FCL as well as in the DSL, but he tempered it upon promotion to Single-A. His body has filled out since turning pro, enabling him to maintain his best stuff deeper into games but could lead to delivery issues if he gets too big. The Tigers need pitching depth in their system to go with their abundance of bats, and Salcedo has a chance to be the next to emerge. He’ll likely return to Lakeland to begin the season but could move to High-A West Michigan if he makes improvements with command while maintaining his high-strikeout arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his four years at Princeton, Smith both relieved and started. He had his strongest year in the Tigers' rotation as a senior, enough for the Angels to take a low-risk flier on the left-hander in Round 18 of the 2019 Draft, signing him for just $3,000. After pitching out of the bullpen during his pro debut that summer, Smith took the opportunity to start in 2021 and ran with it, pitching across four levels to finish in Triple-A. Smith does have four pitches at his disposal, all coming from his strong, though undersized, 5-foot-11 frame. His fastball averaged around 92 mph in 2021, touching 94, but it plays up some because it has good ride up in the zone. His slider, a sweeper with a ton of horizontal movement, is his best secondary offering that can miss bats, a big reason why he struck out 10.6 per nine last season. His slower curve isn’t as good, but serves as a good get-me-over pitch for strike one and he uses his changeup effectively while starting to mix in a new cutter as well. Throughout his college career, Smith struggled with command, walking 4.4 per nine. He threw a ton more strikes in 2021, nearly cutting that walk rate in half. He’s on the map now, with the chance to serve as a No. 5 starter/long reliever type in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels gave seven-figure bonuses to outfielders Nelson Rada and Randy De Jesus at the start of the 2022 international signing period, but they also brought in some intriguing young pitching talent. No one got a higher bonus than Encarnacion, who signed for $500,000 and then struck out nearly 11 per nine innings during his Dominican Summer League debut. A plus athlete on the mound, Encarnacion’s fastball currently sits around 92-93 mph and can touch 96. His slider is his best secondary offering, a low-80s breaking ball that has the chance to be better than average in the future. He’ll throw his changeup up to 87-88 mph, giving him a true three-pitch mix, though he could use some more separation between his heater and the offspeed offering. The two things Encarnacion needs to work on the most are his command and physicality. He walked 5.3 per nine in his debut and adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame will help him repeat his delivery, which in turn will lead to more strikes. There’s projectability here to go along with some intriguing stuff, giving him the chance to develop into a starting pitcher long term as he comes stateside for the first time in 2023 at age 18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watters transitioned from pitching in the bullpen his first two years at West Virginia to starting in 2022. The stuff he showed in the Mountaineers' weekend rotation was tantalizing, highlighted by a 15-strikeout performance against Texas, and it was enough for the A’s to take him in the fourth round of the 2022 MLB Draft. Getting his feet wet with a couple of outings at High-A Lansing, he’ll look to begin his ascent as a starter through the system in his first full season as a pro. Watters is a strong presence on the mound at 6-foot-4. His fastball was up to 99 mph during his junior year and touched triple digits in his time as a reliever. He also possesses a plus pitch in his power curve, missing plenty of bats as a true 12-to-6 that sits in the mid-80s. There’s also a mid-80s changeup in there, though it’s less polished compared to his other two offerings. Command will need to improve for Watters to have a chance to start at the next level. While the stuff was high-octane in college, he usually had little idea of how to locate it. Given his track record as a reliever, there’s a strong chance he ends up back in the bullpen, where he can rear back and overpower hitters with two plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted by the Blue Jays out of McNeese State in the 11th round of the 2023 Draft, Rogers’ development has slid under the radar because there are no eye-popping strikeout numbers or 100 mph radar readings. Rogers is a throwback, a starter who already has the ability to eat serious innings by filling up the zone and letting his defense work behind him. This is the type of prospect who coaches and teammates will always appreciate more than some external rankings do. Rogers works quickly, and despite his massive frame at 6-foot-7, he repeats his mechanics well and rarely “loses it” mid-start. Between High-A and Double-A in 2025, Rogers posted a 3.47 ERA over 150 1/3 innings, and while his strikeout rate (6.9 K/9) won’t blow anyone away, his walk rate (2.3 BB/9) was very impressive. Rogers leads with a fastball that can reach up to touch 94-95 mph and typically lives just below that, but he has a great feel for his repertoire and adjusts well throughout games. Prospect lists are stocked with hard-throwing arms who run into health problems or end up in bulk roles, but Rogers is a different profile entirely. This almost feels like a pitching prospect from the 1980s and 90s, one capable of throwing 170-plus innings each season and posting every five or six days. If Rogers can miss more bats, that opens up more conversations about his big league potential, but even with his current traits, he has a path towards being a reliable depth arm from Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former catcher, Hall redshirted his freshman year at Division II Central Missouri and moved into the Mules’ bullpen as a sophomore with rough results (9.20 ERA in 14 2/3 innings) in 2024. He was showing signs of a big breakout as a junior starter, fanning 19 of the 62 batters he faced, before suffering an elbow injury that required season-ending internal brace surgery. He showed enough in that limited look for the Mets to take him in the sixth round and he signed for below slot at $297,500. Some evaluators believe that, if healthy, Hall could have gone closer to the third round based on his talent. He showed a four-seam fastball up to 98 mph in February before getting hurt, and he threw the pitch out of a low release height, generating a good vertical approach angle. If that velocity -- he was typically closer to the mid 90s early in starts before tapering off -- and movement hold, it could be a plus pitch at maturity. Hall also flashed some good low-80s sliders and upper-70s curveballs with promising depth, and he showed he could at least turn over a decent changeup. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is still very much finding his way as a pitcher, and the elbow surgery put his collegiate development on pause. Mets officials have praised how well Hall has tackled his rehab, and coming out of the Draft, they believe he has enough promising athleticism to deliver strikes and earn starting looks. Hall could be a fun pick to click if his stuff returns to form and holds up in his first taste of the pros in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boissiere arrived on the University of Arizona campus in the fall of 2018 and never stopped hitting from there, finishing with a .355/.434/.488 line over 117 career games with the Wildcats. His best numbers (.369/.451/.506, five homers) came as a junior, prompting the Nats to select him in the third round and sign him for below slot at $600,000. Boissiere stumbled out of the gate at Low-A Fredericksburg, going 17-for-85 (.200), but that’s not unheard of for a college player settling into the pro game after a long spring. Boissere earned solid reviews in the Grand Canyon State for his impressive approach against collegiate pitchers. He posted near-equal K/BB ratios all three years, an indication of his willingness to work a walk while limiting his punchouts. His slugging numbers won’t open any eyes on their own, but he’s capable of above-average raw power from the left side. It’s pop that plays to all fields too, so he could see 15-20 homers in the Majors at his peak. The left-handed thrower, who will be 22 for the entire season to come, had some experience as a corner outfielder in his early NCAA days but was a full-time first baseman in college and the pros last year. He possesses the agility to be an above-average glove at the cold corner, adding another way he can provide value. He’ll still need to fulfill every bit of his hitting potential and maybe squeeze a little more power to meet the offensive requirements of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rios was the Pac-12 Player of the Year in 2023 after finishing with an OPS of 1.191 while helping Stanford reach the College World Series. This was an amazing development given the fact that Rios appeared in eight games combined over his first two years in college. He became one of the more intriguing college bats on the West Coast last year and the Angels were piqued enough to take him in the third round of the Draft. It was a small sample, but he struggled out of the gate during his pro debut, mostly with Single-A Inland Empire. Even though his résumé was light, amateur scouts had some conviction that Rios would hit at the next level. The right-handed hitter is short and quick to the ball and he displayed a very advanced approach, drawing a ton of walks, as well. The combination of pitch recognition, discipline and finding the barrel enabled him to use his raw power consistently, with 18 homers last spring. For Rios to make it, he’s going to have to hit because he doesn’t have a real defensive home. He played left field at Stanford but the Angels started working with him behind the plate -- he spent a lot of his non-playing time catching bullpens in college -- and they liked his leadership and his good hands behind the dish, though his arm is below-average. He’ll still get some reps in the outfield, but he’d obviously have more value -- and there’d be less pressure on his bat -- if he can catch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butterworth started his college career at Western Carolina, spending two years as the Catamounts' second baseman before transferring to North Carolina State for his junior year. He got the chance to play shortstop every day for the Wolfpack, and while he put up pedestrian numbers offensively, he showed enough for the Padres to take him in the 12th round of the 2024 Draft. He was having a solid first full season of pro ball in High-A, playing both middle infield positions, when he was sent to the Orioles at the Trade Deadline as part of the prospect package received in return for Ramon Laureano and Ryan O'Hearn. The Orioles bumped him up to Double-A after the trade, and that's where he started his first full season in the organization in '26. An undersized and athletic right-handed hitter, Butterworth has the makings of a future utility-type in the big leagues. He can find different ways to beat opponents offensively, starting with a contact and on-base-oriented approach at the plate. His swing is geared for line drives, and he puts the ball in play a lot, while also showing solid plate discipline and an improved walk rate. It's going to be hit over power, but there are some flashes of pop, particularly to his pull side, registering exit velocities up to 108 mph. Butterworth is a plus runner who can steal a base, and that athleticism helps him move around the diamond defensively. He'd been an infielder exclusively in college and at the outset of his pro career, and the Orioles have continued using him on the dirt. They've also given him time in center field because of that agility and he'd seen action at five positions over the first month of the 2026 season, pointing to a future as a flexible role player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor split time between catcher and first base in two seasons at Virginia Tech, and he was one of college baseball's top performers (.431/.541/.690) during the shortened 2020 season. A Draft-eligible sophomore, he went in the fourth round that summer and made his pro debut in 2021. He batted .278/.371/.433 in High-A and posted similar numbers as a late replacement in the Arizona Fall League. First and foremost an offensive player, Taylor controls the strike zone, puts together some of the best at-bats in the system and makes a lot of line-drive contact. A switch-hitter, he had a loopier swing from his natural left side when he entered pro ball but has tightened that up. He has solid raw power that currently translates mostly into doubles, but he could produce 15-20 homers on an annual basis if he learns to pull more pitches in the air. Taylor's 55 starts at catcher in High-A more than doubled his total at Virginia Tech, so he's still a work in progress behind the plate. His receiving has improved significantly and could become solid or better, but he's not particularly agile and still is learning the nuances of blocking balls in the dirt and calling pitches. He has average raw arm strength but needs to upgrade his accuracy after throwing out just 19 percent of basestealers last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 50 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Japanese-American Balzer was primarily a position player growing up in Japan but saw time on the mound as a high schooler, and that’s where he got interest from evaluators on both sides of the Pacific. The Padres signed him for only $10,000 in January 2023, and Balzer spent the start of his career rehabbing from Tommy John surgery. He didn’t debut until July 2024 and went to Single-A Lake Elsinore last season, posting a 7.92 ERA and a 1.78 WHIP with 49 strikeouts in 50 innings. The 6-foot-1 right-hander is still plenty raw, but he generated excitement by reaching the upper 90s last spring. He worked closer to 93-96 mph, touching 98, with a running sinker in the California League. Despite some nice movement on the heater, he couldn’t command it well, often leaving it to be slammed in the zone. His mid-80s sweeper was his best swing-and-miss offering, mirroring the horizontal movement of the sinker (plus a few extra inches) while running away from righties. His split-change is very much a work in progress to find consistency, and lefties teed off on Balzer with a .971 OPS against him at Single-A. At this stage, Balzer, who pitches solely from the stretch, is a control-over-command arm. His 11.6 percent walk rate with Lake Elsinore was modest for someone with such little pro experience, but his misses were in sluggable spots for opponents. He’ll be 21 for the 2026 season and enters the campaign still two years away from Rule 5 eligibility, meaning he’ll be given ample time and space to find the results that match the quality of his fastball-slider mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees' decision to select Jackson in the fifth round last July drew criticism after reports surfaced that he drew a swastika on the dorm room of a Jewish student when he was a freshman at Nebraska in 2021. He transferred to South Mountain (Ariz.) CC as a sophomore and spent his final two college seasons at Utah, where he was charged with impaired driving in 2024. He batted a combined .363/.455/.577 and earned first-team all-conference honors in his two years with the Utes before signing for a well below-slot $147,500. A left-hander who made consistent hard contact college despite an aggressive approach in college, Jackson was unusually passive in High-A during his pro debut. He usually crushes fastballs but had trouble making contact against in-zone heaters last summer, though he may have been overwhelmed by his challenging assignment. He has the ingredients for at least 15-homer power, especially if he can learn to elevate more pitches. Jackson was more impressive defensively in his first taste of pro ball. He displays smooth actions, solid range and plus arm strength, leaving no doubt he can remain at shortstop. He has average speed with good baserunning instincts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seven years after the Tigers took a Draft flier on a college pitcher with mixed results a year removed from Tommy John surgery (Tarik Skubal), they went a similar route with Leys, who missed the 2024 season recovering from surgery before taking the mound for the University of Maine in 2025. Leys won America East Pitcher of the Year with a 2.69 ERA and 74 strikeouts in 67 innings, better than his first two seasons with the Black Bears. The Tigers drafted him in the fourth round, five rounds earlier than Skubal, and signed him for $574,900. While Leys isn’t big for a pitcher, he has a quick, fluid delivery with a big leg kick and a three-quarters arm angle. His fastball can touch 96 mph, setting up a slider and a changeup both in the low 80s. Leys greatly improved his strike throwing and command upon his return from surgery, cutting his walk rate in almost half from his first two seasons while ticking up his strikeout rate. The Tigers have been aggressive at times starting out college pitchers in full-season ball, and could do the same with Leys, who made an impression in Spring Training. If he can hold his command while adding more swing-and-miss, he could force his way up the system quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round selection by the A’s in the 2024 MLB Draft out of Boston College, Leary underwhelmed a bit in his first taste of pro ball upon joining the organization. His first full season as a pro went much better, as he began the year at Single-A Stockton and earned a promotion to High-A Lansing, where he held his own over a 33-game stint. Between the two levels, Leary hit .269 with a .798 OPS in 126 games. Leary has above-average power potential which showed up in stints last season, with an ability to hit to all fields after working with the A’s to tighten up his swing. He can draw a decent amount of walks, but his 130 strikeouts last year highlight some swing-and-miss issues that will need to be corrected for him to fully take advantage of that power. Leary might be one of the better baserunners in the entire organization, evident by his 56 stolen bases in ‘25 while getting caught only eight times. Defensively, he can move around well, but his below-average arm likely limits him to left field, though the A’s plan to work with him on his quickening up his release to see if his positional versatility could expand to the other two outfield spots. The A’s are still trying to figure out just what type of player Leary might end up being, but there were some encouraging signs in his first full year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Auerbach turned down the Rockies as a 40th-rounder out of Saddleback (Calif.) CC in 2018 and transferred to Alabama instead. The co-MVP at the 2019 Cape Cod League All-Star Game, he batted .388 with 12 steals in 17 games while making starts at four positions during the shortened 2020 college season before signing for $20,000 as an undrafted free agent. His offensive production and versatility quickly made him a favorite among Giants officials during his pro debut in 2021, when he forced a promotion to High-A after two months and hit .288/.379/.529 overall. A classic greater-than-the-sum-of-his-parts type, Auerbach is a gritty right-handed hitter who works deeps counts and repeatedly finds his way on base. Though he's just 5-foot-9 and comes with ordinary bat speed, he understands how to turn on pitches and launch them in the air, giving him at least 15-homer power. He possesses fringy speed but has outstanding instincts on the bases, allowing him to steal 30 bases in 37 attempts last year. Auerbach's savvy is obvious on defense as well. He started games at second base, catcher, third base, left field and center field in his first year in pro ball and also appeared in right field. He has average arm strength and profiles best at second base, though he's a legitimate option behind the plate and likely has a super-utility role in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Cedeño for $300,000 out of Venezuela in July 2018, the max they were allowed due to previous overages in the international period. He showed a good approach in the 2019 Dominican Summer League with a nearly equal K/BB ratio but hit just .193 in 47 games. There was hope a breakout would come when he moved stateside in 2021, only for a meniscus tear to limit him to 18 games in the Arizona Complex League. He jumped to a full-season affiliate last year in Single-A Lake Elsinore and produced a .256/.362/.400 line in 71 contests before getting 12 games in during the Arizona Fall League. Because of his distance from the Majors, the Padres left Cedeño unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft. Cedeño is still more about potential than production. To watch him take batting practice and even swing during the game is to see a switch-hitter with a patient approach, promising bat speed and enough power to reach around a dozen homers in a Major League campaign. In reality, he still hasn’t hit above .256 in a season, perhaps because he trades line drives for more catchable fly balls and still looks a little more comfortable hitting from the left side. An average runner with a decent arm, Cedeño has seen time at all four infield spots, including a little bit of first base in 2022. He’s adequate enough with the glove to handle second base, and that would represent his best opportunity to provide value. Cedeño will be 21 for all the 2023 season, and that will be a proving ground to show his physical gifts can turn into actual performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Regarded as one of the top infielders of the 2025 international signing period, Johnson, a Nassau, Bahamas native, received a $1.5 million signing bonus from the A’s. His arrival to the organization comes with considerable hype, with some talent evaluators labeling him as arguably the Caribbean nation’s most polished prospect to ever enter pro ball. Johnson is fully bilingual and has been training with Jose Fortuna, which afforded him the opportunity to play in the United States and the Dominican Republic. Joining his brother, Paris -- a current member of the Dodgers organization -- in the pro ranks, Johnson will get his career started in 2025. Johnson is a bat-first prospect. He has a clean setup at the plate from the right side and utilizes a quick and crisp bat path, which leads to spraying the ball to all fields. He hunts for his pitch and looks to do extra damage, and the power should start to show up as he continues to grow into his 6-foot-2 frame. Johnson is not a burner but his speed is solid. While some evaluators see him as an eventual third baseman, the A’s will get him plenty of reps at shortstop, where he is considered a steady defender up the middle, to begin his journey as a professional.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last New Hampshire high schooler to make it to the big leagues was outfielder Ryan McKenna, an Orioles fourth-rounder back in 2015. Carey, who was a two-sport star in the Granite State (hockey), signed with the Braves for $150,000 as a 15th-round pick in the 2024 Draft and opened eyes with a very solid first full season of pro ball, playing all year with Single-A Augusta. Especially for a teenager from New England, Carey showed off a good feel to hit from the left side of the plate. He displayed excellent contact skills during his first full season, striking out less than 16 percent of the time, with a smooth stroke. He hit the ball on the ground too often, but there’s a feel for loft and raw power for him to tap into, even if it hasn’t shown up yet. He uses a leg kick that can help him get the ball in the air to his pull side, but there hasn’t been any resulting in-game production in-game yet. Carey will have to find a way to elevate consistently and do more damage in order for him to fit a corner-outfield profile. He’s a good defensive outfielder who saw time at all three spots and has above-average speed, but he probably doesn’t have the chops to play center field regularly, putting a bit more pressure on the power to materialize at some point during his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles under Mike Elias love to draft college players, and the 2024 Draft was no different, with Baltimore taking each of their first six picks from the collegiate ranks. But they tend to break that pattern once or twice per Draft for a prep player they really believe in, and in 2024, that was Layton. An athletic infielder from Charlotte Christian HS in North Carolina, Layton was the only high schooler the Orioles took in the top 10 rounds when they made him a sixth-rounder. They then went more than twice over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Southern Miss for $715,800. The Orioles decided to wait for 2025 for Layton to make his pro debut. But they are bullish on the athletic switch-hitter with a few interesting raw tools. He’s shown some ability to make consistent contact from both sides of the plate, and he uses all fields with a gap-to-gap approach and a solid swing. Layton’s athleticism plays on both sides of the ball, and on the basepaths, he has the kind of speed that should make him a basestealing threat. Layton was clocked at up to 93 mph as a prep pitcher, plus arm strength that would help him play anywhere in the middle of the field. Though he was drafted as a shortstop, he lacked defensive polish and area scouts weren’t convinced Layton had the chops to stick there. Even if he gets the chance to prove them wrong off the bat, Layton’s speed, athleticism and arm strength may be best suited long-term for center field, where those raw tools can play more freely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey took a truly unique path to the Rays’ Minor League system. He pitched for two years at Walters State (Tenn.) CC and struggled a bit the following season at UNC Charlotte, at which point he decided to give up baseball. He took a job digging ditches and repairing roads and took the spring of 2022 off, but coaching a youth team renewed his love of the game. He pitched in the Appalachian League that summer, transferred to Tennessee and pitched his way into the Volunteers' rotation. He wound up being their most reliable starter, logging a 2.90 ERA in 21 outings, and went to the Marlins for a below-slot bonus of $340,000 in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft. He only made two professional starts in the Florida Complex League before Miami flipped him to Tampa Bay alongside Erick Lara and Jake Mangum for Calvin Faucher and Vidal Bruján. Lindsey added velocity across the board as a fifth-year college pitcher last spring, and he’s now a power sinker/slider-type starter who covers the entire width of the plate and hides the ball well before throwing from a lower arm slot. His fastball sits in the mid-90s with the potential to reach back for more. But the Rays were more enamored with his slider, a tight upper-80s breaker that can tick above that while landing in the zone for strikes or outside for chases. It’s a different profile for the Rays, who often target pitchers with big fastballs that carry up in the zone. Lindsey also throws a curveball and a lesser-used changeup, giving him a starter’s arsenal. He also has the physical strength to log innings in the rotation. He could evolve to handle a variety of roles for the ever-creative Rays, with the ceiling of a starter and a solid floor as a sinker/slider reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect in Boston's 2022 international class, Encarnacion signed for $1.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. He debuted as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, hitting .255/.355/.369 and leading his club with three homers in 41 games. He'll need plenty of time to develop but features some of the best power potential in the system. With a quick right-handed swing and a projectable 6-foot-2 frame, Encarnacion could have at least plus raw power once he matures physically. He can lift pitches without selling out for home runs, and his pop plays to all fields. He also shows promising feel for hitting and managing the strike zone. Presently a fringy-to-average runner, Encarnacion could slow a bit as he adds muscle. Reduced quickness could push him from shortstop, where he spent most of his pro debut, to third base, where he also got some playing time. His quick hands and strong arm would be well suited to the hot corner, and he should be able to fit the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guedez headlined a group of 2025 international signees for the A’s along with Shotaro Morii and Ayden Johnson, signing out of Venezuela for around $1.5 million. He was regarded as one of the top hitters in the class, and that showed through in a very successful pro debut as he hit .359 with an .885 OPS in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old. Next up for him is to make his stateside debut. Guedez has a knack for hitting. His swing is smooth through the zone with good barrel control and impressive hand-eye coordination that allows him to get to pitches both inside and outside of the zone. He does tend to chase at a high rate, though that is not uncommon for a teenager. There isn’t much power to his game at this point, and the A’s are unsure how much will come even as he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. Guedez’s defense is considered average with an average arm, which likely limits him to a corner outfield spot. He was one of the more fun players to watch for the A’s player development staff down in the Dominican Republic this past summer, but with his no standout defensive attribute and underwhelming power, he will have to rely on his strong hit tool to carry him through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After racking up seven saves as Ohio State’s closer as a freshman, then being named a Cape Cod League All-Star in 2023, Beidelschies led the Buckeyes’ rotation as a sophomore. A transfer to Arkansas didn’t go well from a results perspective, as the left-hander lost his spot in the Razorbacks’ rotation. Once considered a potential top-five round pick, Beidelschies went in the sixth round in the 2025 Draft, signing for just under $300,000, a little below slot. With a potential three-pitch mix, Beidelschies does have the ingredients to start at the next level. His fastball sat in the 92-94 mph range with Arkansas and topped out at 96, occasionally missing bats with armside run up. He can throw his 83-85 mph slider with a lot of depth, a pitch he uses a lot against left-handed hitters. He has a mid-80s changeup that isn’t as consistent, but it has good fade and tumble when it’s on. There’s some hope that the 6-foot-3, 230-pound Beidelschies might have some untapped velocity and stuff to come as he gets pro instruction, strength and conditioning, and he was up into the mid 90s during fall practice with the Razorbacks. He repeats his short-armed delivery and fills up the strike zone, though it’s more control over command. His ceiling is probably as a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dominican-born Reyes' $450,000 bonus was the fifth-highest given to a pitcher on the 2024 international amateur market. He broke into pro ball by not allowing a run in four June starts in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, striking out 17 and walking just two in 16 innings. He came down with a tired arm and worked just one more frame in the next two months as the Red Sox had him concentrate on gaining strength. Reyes already can park in the low 90s and reach 94 mph with run and sink on his fastball while exerting little effort, and he could operate in the mid-90s once he fills out his extremely projectable 6-foot-5 frame. Just 18, he already has the makings of a pair of solid mid-80s secondary pitches in a slider and a fading and sinking changeup. Boston may have him add a cutter to his arsenal as well. Quite advanced for his age, Reyes does a nice job of keeping his long limbs in sync and producing a clean delivery that he repeats well. In his pro debut, he not only provided strikes but also showed the ability to command his pitches and manipulate their shapes. He'll need time to add muscle and develop, but his combination of stuff and pitchability gives him one of the higher ceilings among Red Sox pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes buying low on a prospect can provide a huge payoff. That's what the Pirates are hoping they can get from Ager, who had dropped to the sixth round of the 2024 Draft after a subpar junior season at Santa Barbara. Considered one of the top college arms on the West Coast heading into the year after pitching for Team USA over the summer, his stuff and performance regressed, though he did settle in as the Gauchos closer. It turned out he had been trying to pitch through an oblique issue, so the Pirates are hoping a healthy Ager will rebound quickly in pro ball. When he was at his best, Ager had a solid four-pitch mix and the ability to throw strikes with all of them, with a fastball in the 92-93 mph range that topped out at 96. His low-80s slider flashed plus in the past, with the potential to miss a lot of bats. He uses a slower mid-70s curve as a get-me-over type of breaking ball, and while his changeup has been his fourth pitch, it has the chance to be an average offering. As a sophomore, Ager repeated his delivery and threw a lot of strikes, giving him the chance to start long term. He's 6-foot-6 with some projection, and the Santa Barbara program has a history of producing solid big league rotation pieces, with the Pirates curious to see what he might do now that he's 100 percent healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paplham went undrafted after only 12 appearances at the University of New Orleans in 2022 and had a rough go with Mahoning Valley in the MLB Draft League shortly after, giving up seven earned runs in four innings. Still, the Padres believed there was enough to work with there because of elite velocity and signed Paplham as a free agent that August. He was a quick mover in his first taste of the pros, jumping from Single-A Lake Elsinore to Double-A San Antonio while finishing with 11 saves, a 3.60 ERA and 36 strikeouts over 30 innings. Paplham rounded his first full season with eight appearances in the Arizona Fall League. Always pitching out the stretch, the 6-foot-3 right-hander threw a 95-97 mph fastball -- touching 99 -- during the regular season, carrying over that velo he showed in the Draft League. His 85-87 mph sweeping slider could also look like a plus pitch at times with promising break, and it was a good enough second pitch on its own to help Paplham limit lefties to a .489 OPS in the Minors. Paplham walked 12 batters in 21 innings in the California League, and while he didn’t run into as many control issues higher up in-season, the AFL was a good reminder that his let-it-fly look on the mound will be an issue against more advanced batters. Still, he already has the two-pitch profile needed to be a solid Major League reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holiday bounced between two Florida junior colleges in 2022 and 2023, leading JuCo pitchers with 141 strikeouts in 88 innings for Junior College World Series champion Central Florida the latter year. He moved to Oklahoma State as a junior and led the Big 12 with 128 punchouts in 113 frames. Holiday delivered a complete-game two-hitter in the postseason against Florida in the NCAA Regionals, and the Cardinals selected him in the third round that July. He signed for $800,000, a little below slot, as St. Louis’ second pick of the 2024 Draft. The 5-foot-11 right-hander may have only sat 90-93 mph (touching 95) with his fastball in college, but his impressive command of the pitch, particularly with carry up in the zone, made it closer to an average offering. His low-80s slider caused batters from both sides of the plate to expand the zone, and he could land it especially well low and to the gloveside. His mid-70s curveball was a serviceable third pitch, while his low-80s changeup was used only against lefties and with unreliable results. Holiday uses an extremely high leg kick that could rival that of Bronson Arroyo and he makes a stabbing motion with his front foot as it lands, adding some deception. At his size, he isn’t a candidate to add a ton of velocity in pro ball, so he’ll need to continue to pound the zone and throw hitters off in other ways to stick as a starter. Holiday underwent Tommy John surgery last spring and has yet to make his pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castro signed out of the Dominican Republic for $450,000 in 2024 with a prototypical slugging corner outfield profile, and he's beginning to fulfill that potential after a second stint in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After struggling to make contact as a 17-year-old, he became one of the most productive players on the circuit in 2025 with a single-season-record 16 homers (six more than any other player last year) and a .264/.399/.585 slash line. At 6-foot-3, Castro was already larger than most Rookie-ball players, but his power began to show up in games after he added 20 pounds in the past year. The right-handed slugger has plenty of raw strength and bat speed -- with further room to fill out his frame -- and his pull-happy approach plays up the game power even more. Swing-decision issues that plagued his debut season have lessened but remain, and refining his approach to key in on hittable pitches in the zone should enable him to tap into his team-best exit velocities more consistently. Castro is fairly athletic for his size but has not been an efficient basestealer. Defensively, he stands out most for his strong arm, which fits well in right field and could get even stronger as he adds weight. He's occasionally played in center but is a better fit for a corner long term. Castro is an organizational favorite and gets high marks for his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dumesnil looked like he could be a high-round Draft pick after an eye-opening sophomore season at Cal Baptist, including a .362/.440/.702 slash line with 19 homers, and an All-Star season in the Cape Cod League, hitting .311 and leading the circuit in steals (26). A difficult junior season changed his momentum, but the Tigers snagged him in the eighth round, signed him for $214,300 and immediately put him at Single-A, where he made an impact for Lakeland in the Florida State League playoffs. Strong and athletic, the 6-foot-2 Dumesnil showed the ability to hit with power in college, but his 2025 season came with struggles against spin, notably sliders, and inconsistent power. Both of those continued in Lakeland, where he hit fastballs well but not for much power while whiffing on breaking balls. He’s not a fluid runner but has enough speed and aggressiveness to swipe bases, which he did often in a small sample size for the Flying Tigers. Dumesnil’s speed does help him cover ground in the outfield and he’s shown he can be solid at all three spots defensively. Some feel he can play center long term, but others feel he’s best suited for a corner, with left being a better option because of his fringy arm strength. Even with the struggles he’s had, the Tigers will try to get him back to 2024 Cape form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lara wasn’t a big-time prospect when the Marlins signed him for just $85,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of their international signing class in January 2023. But his performance as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League caught the Rays’ attention, and they landed him from Miami as part of a three-prospect return for infielder/outfielder Vidal Bruján and reliever Calvin Faucher. This could be the latest in a long line of moves in which the Rays have acquired a young Complex League prospect and watched him take off. Lara, hailing from Bani, has excellent bat speed and a loose, whippy swing from the left side of the plate that allows him to drive the ball well. He had enough skills and polish to perform in his professional debut in the DSL, slashing .305/.416/.445 with 23 walks and 37 strikeouts in 154 plate appearances. He’s skinny, at 6-foot-2 and 165 pounds, but he could develop above-average power as he fills out his frame. Where Lara lands defensively is another question. He started most of his games at shortstop last year, and he has the arm strength to handle the left side of the infield. It’s not out of the realm of possibility that he’ll stick at the six, but if he gets big enough, he might be a better fit at third base and could be athletic enough to handle a spot in the outfield. He’ll likely spend the season at the Rays’ Spring Training complex, first for extended spring camp then in the Florida Complex League. The Rays love his upside, but it’ll be years before his developmental path is totally clear.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams took off after transferring from Alabama to Florida State and hammered 33 homers with a .975 OPS across his sophomore and junior seasons. Known for his massive raw power and free-swinging approach, he was a natural fit for the Marlins in the third round of the 2025 Draft and signed for a below-slot $897,500. He finished the year at Single-A with a .269/.359/.284 slash line across 19 games. The lefty slugger can produce plenty of thump from a crouched stance as he fires his hands with impressive speed. Williams was able to succeed in college with an overly aggressive approach -- he chased all secondary pitches at least 40 percent of the time -- but will have to tighten that up in pro ball. Although the power didn't show up in his brief pro cameo, success in wood bat leagues while in college gives hope that it will come. He did make more contact than usual at Single-A and frequently walked, which will be key to his offensive profile. Despite being a solid athlete, Williams didn't use his average speed much on the bases in college. He'll play all three outfield positions but will be more suited for a corner long term unless he improves his routes. Williams' offense will drive his profile, so sticking in center would merely be a plus, and he could be an above-average defender in right with a strong arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery was well-known as an Orlando-area high schooler and slotted in at No. 34 on MLB Pipeline’s 2020 Draft rankings. The shortened Draft and his strong commitment to Florida State kept him from being drafted that year, but he never found consistent success with the Seminoles as a starter or a reliever. The Padres still took him in the 11th round in 2023 and signed him for $200,000. Montgomery needed Tommy John surgery after only three appearances with Single-A Lake Elsinore in '24, and he didn’t return to a mound in an official setting until the 2025 Arizona Fall League, where he allowed two earned runs, struck out seven and walked seven in 10 1/3 frames. He has opened his age-23 season as a starter with High-A Fort Wayne. The 6-foot-1 right-hander showcases both a four-seamer and sinker. He can sit 92-95 mph with the heat, though he’s been below that at times in the cold Midwest League this spring. The sinker has decent tail running in on righties, while the four-seam will flash promising ride, and both were significant chase pitches in the AFL. His 83-86 mph slider is back as a whiff generator in 2026, flashing enough depth to look like a potential above-average offering, while his upper-80s changeup lacks enough separation to be a serious weapon against lefties at this stage. Montgomery had control problems dating back to his first year in Tallahassee but has actually tightened up his command coming out of his TJ recovery and rehab, enough to keep getting starting looks. He’s already facing Rule 5 eligibility this upcoming offseason though, and unless there’s a significant jump in stuff in 2026, he might not be far off from seeing if the sinker-slider combo can play up as a righty-heavy option in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The University of North Carolina at Pembroke has never had a player from its Division II program make the big leagues, though it now has two pitchers in pro ball with that chance. River Ryan is getting close to Los Angeles with the Dodgers. Bowen has just one year of pro ball on his résumé after the Mariners took him in Round 13 of the 2022 Draft, and he spent the year with Single-A Modesto after an up-and-down college career in which he mostly started as a sophomore and mostly came out of the bullpen as a junior. The Twins saw enough upside potential to get the right-hander in the late January Jorge Polanco deal. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has more projection than the typical college arm. With a lanky and wiry build, Bowen is a terrific athlete with room to add strength to his frame, giving hope that his stuff could tick upward as he matures. Right now he has a fastball that’s typically in the 91-94 mph range but touched as high as 97 at times in 2023. He has both a sweepy upper-70s slider that could eventually be an out pitch as well as a shorter, harder cutter that's thrown around 85 mph. He also has a changeup with depth typically around 84 mph. Bowen will need to refine his control and command for him to have the chance to start at the next level. He’s a good athlete on the mound, so there’s hope he can learn to repeat his delivery and find the zone more consistently. He’ll get the chance to prove he can stick in a rotation, though his stuff would tick up even more in shorter stints coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers spread out their international spending during the January 2023 window, adding Dominican outfielder Yophery Rodriguez ($1.5 million) and a pair of Venezuelan shortstops in Kevin Ereu ($1.4 million) and Di Turi ($1.3 million). Di Turi started the Dominican Summer League strongly, batting .338 over 19 games in June, and even when he faded over his final 13 in August, he was still walked 14 times and struck out only seven. He finished with a .282/.414/.354 line, 12 steals, 38 walks and 32 K’s in 52 games on the international complex circuit, good for a 119 wRC+. The switch-hitter has a smooth and mechanically sound swing that helped him make a healthy amount of contact in his first pro campaign. He also showed a relative unwillingness to expand the zone against wilder DSL arms. That will certainly be tested against arms with much better command, but the Brewers were pleased with the foundation he set with his approach. Power remains a question mark. Di Turi put 47.6 percent of his batted balls on the ground and only picked up 11 extra-base hits in his 52 games, none of which were homers. Standing 5-foot-11, Di Turi doesn’t have burning speed and might be asked to ease up on stolen bases if he doesn’t become more efficient (60 percent success rate). His best defensive weapon is his plus arm. That helped him get the majority of his starts at shortstop, but the Brewers also tried him at second base to keep him up the middle. He could also see time at third down the line based on his cannon, but Di Turi will need more pop to be a viable offensive option at the corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barreto received the next-highest bonus behind Josuar Gonzalez in San Francisco's 2025 international crop, signing for $1,118,700 out of Venezuela. Though he received more attention for his shortstop play as an amateur, he slashed .322/.449/.394 in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He also spent most of his time at second base in deference to Anthony Marquez. A right-handed hitter, Barreto has advanced bat-to-ball skills. He makes good swing decisions though he can get overly pull-happy, resulting in too many rolled-over grounders. Though he only went deep once in his first 53 pro games, he packs some sneaky pop in his compact frame and could provide 15 or more homers per year if he improves his quality of contact. An average runner with a thick lower half, Barreto could lose some quickness as he matures physically. He has the actions, hands and plus arm strength to play shortstop if he maintains his current quickness. The Giants will give him some time at short but project him as more of an offensive second or third baseman. rate of just 8.9%. He didn’t make much impact on contact, however, and most of his power will likely be limited to doubles on balls to the gaps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After not being recruited during his high school career, Yeaman took the junior college route to play for College of the Canyons. Though he missed a lot of time over two years there because of multiple injuries and non-throwing shoulder surgeries, he did manage to hit .400 and showed enough in his limited time for UC Irvine to join the Anteaters lineup. He had a big 2025, finishing with an OPS over 1.000, and as college performers tend to do, he rushed up Draft boards. The Orioles took him in the fourth round and signed him for just over $600,000, sending him out to get his professional feet wet with Single-A Delmarva. Yeaman brings a strong track record of hitting to the Orioles organization. He's adept at finding the barrel, doesn't chase and draws walks. He can really punish fastballs, and he puts up good in-zone contact numbers. There's some strength and bat speed, helping him drive the ball to all fields, with some home run juice to his pull side. He's a fringy runner who likely won't be a basestealing threat at the next level. Because of that lack of speed, Yeaman's range is a bit shy for shortstop long term, and his average arm also could hold him back. He played more third than short during his brief debut with Delmarva. Carving out a career as a utility type might be the best outcome, though he could potentially be an offensive-minded second baseman should the O's shift him to the right side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching out of the bullpen as a freshman, Marriott joined Baylor’s rotation for two years beginning in 2023 but didn’t find consistent success in that role and finished his junior season with a 5.94 ERA, 65 strikeouts and 37 walks in 69 2/3 innings. The D-backs still found some intriguing traits and selected him in the sixth round in 2024 before signing him for below slot at $241,000. Marriott was playing a different tune in his initial taste of pro ball with a 2.29 ERA, 25 K’s and eight walks in his first four starts with High-A Hillsboro to open his first full season, but he needed Tommy John surgery after that. Before undergoing the elbow procedure, Marriott could run his fastball up to the mid 90s, often sitting a touch below that for basically average fastball velo. His high release point helped him command the ball better to the upper part of the zone, where he could get some swing-and-miss. His best pitch was a low-80s, high-spin curveball, and its tight break was toughest on lefties who struck out 15 times in 41 plate appearances against him in the small sample. His feel for spin should help him find at least an average slider, and he’s flashed a changeup that could give him something arm side. Marriott showed much better control in pro ball, having tamed some of the rushing he did late in his delivery in college. He is expected back in the middle of the 2026 season, and the D-backs believe he should continue his upward trajectory toward the back end of an MLB rotation once he’s returned to full starting status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez flew under the radar in the 2016-17 international class, signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela. He took a few years to find his footing, but he absolutely wowed in 2022, especially when making the jump to High-A Everett, where he slashed .342/.477/.583 with seven homers and 27 RBIs in 35 games to give him 27 homers and 114 RBIs (second among all Minor League hitters) in total. There’s a chance he taps out because of his speed and defense, but the Mariners are bullish on how he finished the season, which he capped off with time in the Arizona Fall League. The big focus for him into 2023 will be finding better counts to continue to do damage, which should help him better tap into his considerable raw power. He can be aggressive and expand the zone too often at times, though he offsets the swing-and-miss with a willingness to take walks. When he’s putting the ball in play, he’s found far more line drives and fly balls, a big reason why he surpassed his 2021 season home run total by June last year. Likely destined for first base, Perez has legit pop from the right side and the exit velocities to show for it, but he’ll need to continue raking to progress -- his big league trajectory depends on it, especially given the defensive limitations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smaller-college outfielders like Strong can easily get overlooked in the Draft, but the numbers he posted during his junior season at Canisius got attention, from an 1.104 OPS and 11 home runs to more walks (41) than strikeouts (38) and 42 stolen bases in 48 games. That combination of athleticism and plate discipline drew the Tigers to take a shot with a seventh-round pick in 2024, signing him for a $222,500 bonus to see whether his skills could translate to pro ball. After a cameo appearance at Single-A Lakeland in 2024, he posted a respectable first full season, including a .370 on-base percentage, 20 stolen bases and 20 doubles between Lakeland and High-A West Michigan, all while playing solid defense. Strong shows good bat speed from his left-handed swing and produces high line-drive and lift rates for a hitter with below-average power. He’s a patient, disciplined hitter with a low swing rate, but there was a concerning uptick in strikeouts last year due to a low contact rate and a high number of called strikes. He has very good speed that he uses on the bases as well as in the outfield, where his defense is the strength of his game. Strong profiles as a fourth outfielder in the Majors given his defensive versatility. He’ll have a chance to roam the vast outfield gaps of West Michigan this spring, but his offensive improvement -- particularly in contact -- will determine how quickly he advances up the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cohen spent five years at George Washington and was the Colonials' best starter in the final three before signing for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2022. Since missing the first half of the 2024 season with a back strain, he has been one of the most unhittable relievers in the Minors during the past two years, logging a 1.62 ERA and .155 opponent average. Though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft and will compete for a big league bullpen job in 2026. Cohen's money pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that hitters can't lay off or catch up to when it ventures into the strike zone. His fastball is fairly ordinary, ranging from 92-94 mph and reaching 96 with nice carry at times but also below-average command that can make it vulnerable. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink can be a solid offering at it's best. Cohen hides the ball well with an up-tempo, upright delivery with a high leg kick. While his mechanics provide deception, they also hamper his control and have resulted in a 12 percent walk rate in pro ball. He profiles more as a middle reliever than a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more unheralded Day 3 picks of the 2023 Draft by the A’s who signed for $150,000 as a 13th-rounder out of Texas A&M, Johnston exceeded expectations after an inconsistent four-year career with the Aggies, beginning his first full pro season at Single-A Stockton and continuing through High-A Lansing before finishing at Double-Midland. Combined at the three levels, he posted a 3.88 ERA in 27 games (15 starts) with 137 strikeouts and 40 walks over 99 2/3 innings. Johnston appears to have a much better feel for his three-pitch mix than he did in college. His fastball velocity typically varies from 89-94 mph and can touch up to 96. His split-changeup flashes plus as it continues developing as a true out pitch. His low-80s slider is improving but still a work in progress as it sometimes gives off the look of a slurvy-type offering. Big-bodied at 6-foot-3 and 215 pounds, Johnston has the size and arsenal to stay in a starting role, something that may have seemed like a long shot before he was drafted. His strike-throwing ability has clearly improved as a professional, which helped him quickly rise through multiple levels last season. Maintaining that control along with tightening up the breaking ball as a solid third pitch will be the keys to developing into a possible back-end rotation piece, with a floor of a multi-inning lefty reliever out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansell was in the Royals’ backyard at Wichita State before he transferred to Arizona State for his sophomore and junior years, and they selected him in the 16th round of the 2023 Draft, signing him to a $150,000 bonus -- the max allowed without dipping into their bonus pool. A reliever mostly in college, Hansell pitched in the bullpen during his first full season in 2024, but he transitioned to a starter’s role in '25. He made eight starts at both Single-A Columbia and High-A Quad Cities but saw a better ERA at the higher level with a 2.81 mark for the River Bandits. A stress reaction in his back ended his season in July. Hansell came to the Royals fairly raw in his development, even as a college pitcher, but with really intriguing stuff. His fastball sits around the low-to-mid-90s but can run up to 97 mph. His potentially plus curveball is in the upper 70s with good downer action, getting consistent whiffs. Hansell has a harder breaking mid-80s slider that is average on most days, while his mid-80s changeup is still developing but can get some chase if he’s ahead. Hansell has some work to do on his delivery, which is inconsistent in its tempo. The Royals are working with him on moving quicker and more efficiently. There’s still a bit of development to go with Hansell, but the Royals really like his weapons and potential. While he needs reps and innings to help with that development, Hansell may end up as a reliever by the time he reaches the Majors, with his stuff ticking up in shorter spurts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castañon broke out with a 1.208 OPS during his senior year at UC Santa Barbara in 2021 but was limited to only 28 games by a broken hand, hurting his Draft stock. The Padres picked the infielder in the 12th round that summer, signed him for $125,000 and have seen him hit at every Minor League stop since. Castañon was a California League end-of-season All-Star for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first full campaign, then slashed .287/.352/.491 with 13 homers in 77 games for High-A Fort Wayne to begin 2023. His numbers at Double-A San Antonio were much closer to average (.280/.335/.436) over a 54-game stint to end the year. The right-handed hitter has put up solid batting averages at every stop, staying on time with the ball even with a large leg kick. That leads to hard contact that helps fuel the numbers, despite below-average speed that would otherwise help pick up extra hits here and there. Castañon was especially good at elevating and spraying the ball to all fields at Fort Wayne but got more pull- and ground-ball heavy at San Antonio, hurting his power. There’s still potential for 15-plus homers though, if he can even out those approaches. Castañon needs to hit because he’s a major question mark defensively. His lack of agility makes him a rough fit for second base, and his lack of arm strength makes him a stretch for third base. Those have been his two primary positions in pro ball, and barring a full-time move to first base, there isn’t a great place to hide his glove. Castañon might be best at being a right-handed part of a DH platoon and bench infielder, provided he carries his previous results to the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted coming out of high school despite being a standout in the Louisiana area and as a Breakthrough Series alum, Huggins continued his baseball career at Chipola Junior College in Florida, where he became teammates with Cam Collier. The two went on to be Draft classmates for the Reds in 2022, with Collier going to Cincinnati in the first round and Huggins in the fourth. After Tommy John surgery in June 2023, he returned near the end of the ‘24 campaign. Beginning the 2025 season at Single-A Daytona, he was dealt to the A’s at last year’s Trade Deadline for Miguel Andujar, finishing his season at High-A Lansing. Huggins has an electric arm with a fastball that can reach up to 97 mph and sits 95-96. His hard slider is by far his most effective secondary pitch. He also recently reintroduced an upper-80s changeup into his repertoire. All this comes from a high release point that creates some good deception. Command has been an issue for Huggins in the past, though he seems to be emerging as more of a consistent strike thrower the further removed from surgery he gets. He’ll get a chance to continue starting for now, but his limited pitch mix could lead to him in a bullpen role long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
