mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not always a straight line of progress and development for young players -- especially pitchers -- and repeating a level can be just what the doctor ordered. Such seems to be the case for Acosta, who didn’t make any waves when he signed for $10,000 in April 2022 and struggled with his first professional action in the Dominican Summer League. But a return to the DSL last year paid dividends as he led the hitting-friendly circuit with a 1.17 ERA while striking out 12.4 per nine. Acosta is a strong and athletic 6-foot-1 right-hander who might have the chance to stick in a rotation. He improved the command of his 92-96 mph fastball in 2023, a big reason for his more consistent success. He complements the heater will with a low-80s slider that flashes above-average and served as an out pitch. He continues to work on finding a changeup, but it’s a distant third. Being able to find that third offering will be key for him if he wants to remain a starter. So will his ability to find the strike zone more consistently. He made strides in that regard in 2023 and continued refinement will help him stay in games longer. Still a teenager, there’s time for him to iron those things out as he comes stateside for the first time, with his fastball-slider combination likely playing up in shorter stints should he need to move to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The big catch of the 2023 international signing period for the Phillies is no doubt Starlyn Caba, who fetched a $3 million bonus. But it might be a much more productive class than just the shortstop and the Phillies have done it with some bargain shopping, getting Eduardo Tait for $90,000 and De La Cruz for just $20K. The big right-hander put his name on the map with a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, striking out nearly 12.5 per nine over 31 1/3 innings of work. De La Cruz has size and arm strength already working in his favor at 6-foot-6. He already had plenty of fastball, getting his heater routinely into the mid-90s. He couples it with a solid mid-80s slider with sweep that misses a lot of bats. He has shown some feel for a changeup, but it’s well behind the other two offerings. A former basketball player, De La Cruz is relatively new to pitching, so while he needs to refine his command, the fact that he showed any feel for pitching out of the gate is encouraging. His athleticism plays on the mound in a Taijuan Walker kind of way (Walker’s first sport was also basketball) and the Phillies are excited to see what he can do stateside for the first time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers swiped Pacific Northwest prep pitchers away from Oregon State commitments in consecutive Drafts. The more recent, Swanson, was a two-sport star in Washington, the son of a high school basketball coach who was the top-ranked high school player in the state. The Tigers drafted Swanson in the ninth round and wooed him to pro ball with an above-slot $722,500 bonus. Swanson’s athleticism has allowed him to blossom as a pitcher at a later stage than others. His fastball ranged from the low-to-mid 90s in high school but is more of a power offering with carry since working with the Tigers’ pitching department to refine his delivery. His high-spin slider has a lot of movement and depth. His changeup needs work but could be the difference between starting and relieving. The Tigers drafted Swanson fully knowing he could take longer to develop but believing in the athlete and competitor. His introduction to pro ball will be delayed after he underwent Tommy John surgery ahead of the 2025 campaign, knocking him out for what would have been his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Johnson jumped on scouts’ radars as the 2019 Draft approached, most felt the Mississippi prep right-hander was going to head to Mississippi State. The Braves, however, thought they had a chance to keep him from going and were able to do so by taking him in the 14th round and going over slot to sign him for $257,500. He threw well during his brief debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League that summer, but while he missed bats with the jump to full-season ball in 2021, he struggled in other areas of his craft. He’ll have to wait to refine those things, as Tommy John surgery this spring will knock out his entire 2022 season. Johnson added strength to his 6-foot-2 frame during the 2020 shutdown, helping him throw harder than he had before the Draft. He can sit in the mid-90s and has been up to as high as 99 mph with his fastball at times. He also has a solid power slider, which flashes above-average with good sweep to it. His changeup remains his third pitch, something Johnson will have to focus on if he wants to start long-term. He’s also going to have to throw more strikes after walking 5.6 per nine innings in 2021. He needs reps to find consistency in repeating his delivery and landing his secondary stuff in the zone, because even at the lower levels, people can hit a fastball. He’s still young -- just 21 for the 2022 season -- so there’s time for him to come back from surgery and show the Braves what kind of pitcher they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have made a habit in recent drafts under amateur scouting director Mark Conner and assistant general manager Rob Metzler of targeting high school pitchers with second-day picks and signing them away from college commitments. Schiefelbein was one of the more notable ones last year, a California prep star at Corona High School and seemingly headed for UCLA before Detroit selected him 72nd overall and signed him above slot for a $1,797,500 bonus. While Schiefelbein is neither physically imposing nor overpowering, he has an advanced pitch mix that hitters do not like to face, based around a low-90s sinker and two breaking balls. He used his mid-70s looping curveball more often in high school, flipping it into the zone to steal strikes and burying it for chase with a delivery that sometimes left him falling off the mound. His harder slider might have more potential as a swing-and-miss pitch in the pros with more deception. His low-80s changeup plays well off his fastball. Physical maturation will be big for Schiefelbein as he gets into the pro ranks, but his ability to adapt and adjust provides more than typical upside. While he could end up as the prototypical crafty left-hander, his grasp of pitching could create a hurler who outperforms his stuff. He's battled a shoulder strain in his first full season that limited him to only three Rookie-ball appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for just $10,000 out of Colombia, Bella is the best pitching prospect from the Cubs' 2022 international crop. He compiled a 3.21 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 89 2/3 innings in Single-A during his full-season debut last year, surrendering just five runs in his final seven starts. The Astros acquired him in the January trade that sent Ryan Pressly to Chicago. Bello's best weapon is a mid-70s curveball that generated a 50 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2024 thanks to its huge downer break and some horizontal action as well, and it could become a plus pitch with more power. His fastball also could use more velocity but works while sitting in the low 90s and topping out at 94 because he commands it well up in the zone with carry. He gets chases with his low-80s slider and mid-80s changeup but doesn't consistently land them for strikes, which is also the case with his curve. Bello operates with a lower three-quarters arm slot and a flat approach angle, and he'll have to show that he can succeed against better hitters who are less likely to stray out of the strike zone. He's not very physical at 6-foot-1 and needs more strength so he can work deeper into games and hold up over a full season's workload. Added muscle could provide a boost to his stuff and bolster his chances of making it as a four-pitch starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fontenelle bounced around during his college days, starting at the University of Washington in 2021, then moving to McLennan Junior College the following year and then on to Texas Christian for his Draft year in 2023. He went to the College World Series that year and finished with an OPS over 1.100, helping him land in the seventh round with the Angels. In a very unsurprising development for anyone who follows the organization, Fontenelle went up to Double-A to start his first full season and was playing well when his season ended after just 22 games after a slide into second caused both a dislocated ankle and fractured fibula. He made it back to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he really struggled to shake off the rust at the plate. A big switch-hitter the Angels think just fell through the cracks as teams focused on Horned Frogs teammate Brayden Taylor, Fontenelle has the chance to fit the corner-infield profile well offensively. When he’s healthy, he can hit the ball very hard with excellent exit velocities. He didn’t swing and miss much in college with a solid overall approach, and while his strikeout rate ticked up during his pro debut and in the AFL, it’s too small of a sample size to draw any conclusions there. Fontenelle has only played third with the Angels, and while he’s big and a below-average runner, he has good instincts (which help him steal some bases despite the lack of quickness) and actions, with enough arm to have a chance to stick at the hot corner. He’s played first base and even a little left field in the past, so there are some options should a move be needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palma trained in the same Venezuelan program that produced Willson Contreras and Keibert Ruiz. He signed for $300,000 in 2018, receiving the maximum bonus the Astros could pay while in the penalty box for blowing well past their international pool two years earlier. He batted .274/.340/.409 in High-A last year while missing seven weeks with a calf strain, then struggled offensively and defensively in the Arizona Fall League. Palma provides quality work behind the plate, where he moves well and is one of the best receivers, framers and blockers in the system. He also earns praise for his game planning, pitching calling and leadership ability. His lone drawback defensively is his below-average arm, which led to 112 steals in 129 attempts (87 percent) in 48 games at catcher between the Minors and AFL in 2023. Young for every league he's played in, Palma has shown the ability to manage the strike zone. He has some raw power but struggled to turn on pitches or lift them in the air last season compared to the past. The right-handed hitter doesn't have a huge offensive ceiling but could bat .250 with 10-15 homers per year with solid defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith pitched at a Houston-area high school (Bellaire) and college (Rice) before the Astros selected him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft. The Owls' top starter in his last two college seasons, he didn't make his pro debut until late May 2025 because of a back injury. He fashioned a 3.32 ERA with 55 strikeouts in 59 2/3 innings in Single-A. While Smith doesn't miss a lot of bats with a low-90s sinker that can reach 96 mph, its movement yields a lot of harmless grounders. His best offering is a mid-80s changeup that grades as plus at its best but also has so much fade that he can struggle to land it near the zone at times. His low-80s slider stands out more for his ability to throw it for strikes than its sweep. At 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Smith is strong but also maxed out physically and unlikely to add much more velocity. His slingy, low three-quarters delivery adds life to his pitches without costing him control. He stands out more of his floor than his ceiling and projects as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kent State is an underrated pitching factory that has produced multiple big leaguers over the past decade. Albright should be the next in line after making a successful transition from relieving to starting. The D-backs selected Albright in the sixth round of the 2021 Draft and signed him for slot value ($301,600) before sending him to Low-A Visalia to begin his professional career. His debut was brief as he threw just 23 1/3 innings, but he struck out 22 and posted a 3.47 ERA. A hard worker, Albright throws a low-90s fastball which is expected to increase in velocity as he tightens up his mechanics. As is, the pitch plays up because he uses his 6-foot-4 frame and three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. An upper-70s curveball and sinking changeup are Albright’s best offspeed weapons, with both offerings grading out as above average. He rounds out his arsenal with a sharp, low-80s slider, though sometimes the pitch has more cutterish actions. A fully developed slider will give Albright an intriguing mix of four above-average pitches. His command could still use some refinement, though he has shown an ability to adjust as necessary. His competitiveness adds to his No. 4 starter upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Karpathios played both ways in his one season at Maryland’s Harford Community College in 2022, and the Padres (via area scout Danny Sader, who scouted Jackson Merrill from the same area) preferred his bat. Looking to go pro rather than stay in school, Karpathios signed with San Diego as a nondrafted free agent that July, just one month after his 19th birthday. While he was a decent performer early in his career, his big breakout came in 2025, when he hit .249/.357/.413 with 15 homers and 73 walks in 124 games between High-A and Double-A. Karpathios ended the year with time in the prospect-rich Arizona Fall League. The Pennsylvania native stands tall from the left side of the box before getting into a leg kick. He rarely chased pitches outside the zone during the 2025 regular season despite increasing his overall swing rate a tad. His exit velocities were loud with a 90th-percentile EV of 105.8 mph, leading to a jump in home-run production. He can hit the ball well to all fields too, although he went the opposite way more than he pulled the ball once he reached Double-A. Getting the barrel out front more often will be a focus when he returns to the upper levels, or else he’s probably limited to 15ish homers per season. Karpathios also whiffs at high levels against non-fastballs, and he swung and missed more across the board in the Fall League (albeit after a long summer). A below-average runner, he has experience in all three outfield spots but is the best fit in right, thanks to his above-average arm strength. Ahead of his Rule 5 decision year, Karpathios is trending toward a lefty bench bat/fourth outfielder, and that’d be a nice development win for an NDFA signing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: German signed for $400,000 last year out of the Dominican Republic, giving him the joint fourth-highest bonus of Washington’s 2025 international class but well behind the seven-figure deals for Brayan Cortesia ($1.92 million) and Daniel Hernandez ($1.1 million). Only year later, the switch-hitting infielder has surged in stock to become the best prospect of the group at this very early stage of his career. German was a Dominican Summer League mid- and post-season All-Star with a .283/.479/.513 line, eight homers and 33 steals in 53 games. While many of his age can be undisciplined at the plate, German showed an advanced approach from both sides of the plate, leading to a 42/43 K/BB ratio. He shows better ability to slug from the left side to this point -- all eight of his dingers came against righty pitchers – but that might also speak to his lack of gametime against southpaws (only 49 plate appearances in 2025). German stands only 5-foot-10, but what he lacks in stature, he makes up for in his early tendency to lift and pull the ball, helping the pop show in games. By getting on base so much, German gives himself plenty of chances to steal bags, and he certainly took advantage by showing off his above-average wheels in the DSL. That athleticism has helped him stay up the middle on the dirt to this point, and he has the arm strength to make that a defensive asset as well. Nationals instructors have been impressed by his teenage work ethic and aptitude with the glove early on, and he should be a priority middle infielder at the Florida complex when he arrives stateside this spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benny Agbayani spent parts of five seasons in the big leagues after being a late-round Draft pick out of Hawaii Pacific University in 1993. When the Twins took his son Bruin out of the Hawaiian high school ranks in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, he beat his dad by 24 rounds, signing with the Twins for just over $380,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games with Single-A Fort Myers after signing. A 6-foot-2 left-handed hitter who earned Hawaii Gatorade Player of the Year honors last year, Agbayani enters pro ball with a very good feel to hit. He routinely finds the barrel with outstanding bat speed and while he’s a hit-over-power type, there is some thump, especially to his pull side, which was on display when he ripped a 106 mph triple to right-center field in the MLB Draft Combine High School Game last June. There should be extra-base impact to come in the future as well. Agbayani likes to use his above-average speed on the basepaths, but few think he has the ability to stay at shortstop -- his high school position -- not only because of a lack of range, but also because he doesn’t possess the actions or hands for the premium spot. He’ll still get reps there, but his best chance of staying on the dirt will likely be second base, though some amateur scouts thought an outfield corner will make the most sense long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias originally signed as a shortstop for $10,000 with the Blue Jays in July 2018, but he never played in an official game before getting released in May 2020. The Cubs picked him up as a pitcher in January 2021 and he spent most of the next two seasons figuring out how to throw strikes in Rookie ball. He broke out in 2023, fanning 110 in 81 1/3 innings between two Class A stops, but his control regressed significantly during a rocky 2024 season before the Cubs designated him for assignment this January and dealt him to the Yankees for cash considerations. Arias presents an unusual look to hitters, working from a nearly sidearm slot and slinging fastballs that sit at 94-97 mph and touch 99 with heavy sinking and tailing action. He struggled to locate his heater well in 2024, however, and it got pounded. His changeup shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch with upper-80s velocity to go with fade and sink and his low-80s slider devours righties when he stays on top of it and creates some late bite, though he often missed badly with both offerings. While Arias' low arm slot and whippy arm action create deception and electric life, they also limit his ability to provide strikes. The movement on his pitches makes them difficult to land in the zone at times and he may never have enough control or command to be a starter. Making him a full-time reliever in 2024 didn't improve his strike-throwing, but he could become a late-inning option if he figures it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonzagni worked just 23 1/3 innings in two seasons at Weatherford (Texas) JC after coming back from Tommy John surgery, then operated mostly out of the bullpen after transferring to Southern Illinois in 2023. The Rangers thought he had one of the best sinkers in that Draft and selected him in the 12th round. In his first full pro season, he compiled a 3.64 ERA with 95 strikeouts in 89 innings between two Class A stops. Bonzagni’s two-seam fastball operates at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 while burrowing at the plate, and its heavy sink is the reason why he posted an excellent 2.0 groundout/airout ratio in his first two pro seasons. He also throws a four-seamer that reaches 98 mph with more armside run and carry. He gets good depth on a sweeping low-80s slider, giving him a solid second offering. A good athlete, Bonzagni repeats his simple side-step delivery and provides a steady stream of strikes. He has yet to show much feel for his too-firm changeup in the mid-80s and almost never uses it. He’ll project more as a sinker/slider multi-inning reliever unless he can refine his cambio, but he might advance quickly in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his college career at Southern Mississippi as a two-way player in 2023, Monistere focused on hitting and played six different positions as a sophomore. He became a full-time second baseman in 2025 and won Sun Belt Conference player of the year honors after slashing .323/.410/.623 with a league-best 21 homers. The Astros made him a fourth-round pick because they liked his athleticism and versatility, though he looked less refined than expected on both sides of the ball during his introduction to pro ball. Monistere uses an aggressive right-handed swing to produce high exit velocities, though he needs to tone down his approach. He rolls over on too many fastballs and comes up empty while chasing too many breaking balls and changeups. His solid-to-plus raw power could translate into 20 homers per season if he can become more selective and less pull happy. Monistere features average quickness and solid arm strength that produced fastballs up to 94 mph when he pitched as a freshman. The game sped up on him when he spent most of his pro debut at shortstop and third base, and he began 2026 by mainly playing second base. That's his best position and he projects as an average defender there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 45 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Hailing from Carabobo, Venezuela, the same hometown as former All-Star and World Series champion Pablo Sandoval, León is the son of longtime Twins scout Jose León. So it should have come as no surprise that Minnesota was the team that landed the shortstop ranked No. 24 on MLB Pipeline’s 2025 Top 50 International Prospects list when the signing period opened on Jan. 15. León, one of four Top 50 players signed by the Twins, received just under $1.7 million to join the organization. Some of the Twins staff have known León since he was a little kid, so they didn’t have to do too much digging to understand what makes him tick. He’s a right-handed hitter who shows that he grew up around the game with an advanced aptitude for contact and having a selective approach, standing out as the top performer in the 2024 Carabobo Prospect League. He’s hit-over-power right now, but some scouts think there could be a lot more pop to come as he continues to refine his strike zone and understands when he can drive the ball. An average runner now, León has good actions, hands and enough arm for the left side of the infield. He could slow down a tick as he matures, which might mean a move to third base eventually. For now, though, he’ll focus on getting his professional feet wet this summer at age 17.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: William Bergolla was the crown jewel of the Phillies’ international signing class in 2022, getting over $2 million to sign. Segura received just $80,000 to sign when the period opened in January, but if early returns are any indication -- he was one of the better pitching prospects in the Dominican Summer League -- he could help make it a bumper crop. The right-hander out of San Pedro de Macorís is all about projection, though he has some new offerings that helped him succeed in his DSL debut. The 6-foot-3 hurler hits 92-95 mph with his fastball, throwing it with good life especially down in the zone, which enabled him to get a good amount of ground-ball outs. It’s easy to dream on him adding strength to that frame, and there should be an increase in velocity as he physically matures. He already has a solid slider with good depth that could eventually develop into a true out pitch. There’s a long developmental road ahead for Segura, but he doesn’t turn 18 until December, so the Phillies can be as patient as needed. If it all comes together -- the added velocity, harnessing of his stuff, adding a third pitch -- he could rise up the rankings as he gains experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merejo was born in Florida and grew up there before moving to the Dominican Republic late in his high school career and signing for $340,000 in 2023. He followed up a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League by coming to the United States at age 18 last year. After beginning the season in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he concluded it by batting .282/.372/.466 in the final month Single-A as one of the Carolina League's youngest players. Unlike most of the Guardians' international signings, Merejo stands out more for his power than his hitting ability. His physicality and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke produce plus raw pop, and he taps into most of it by concentrating on driving balls in the air to his pull side too. He has some feel to hit and is willing to take walks, though he'll have to tone down his approach because it leaves him vulnerable to non-fastballs. Most of Merejo's value will come from his bat. Though he stole 11 bases in 77 games last year, he's a below-average runner who's probably limited to first base. He committed 10 errors in 53 starts there in 2024 while also getting time on the outfield corners, where he displayed solid arm strength but substandard range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies are no strangers in trying to find bullpen help via the Rule 5 Draft. Anthony Molina was a 2023 selection who spent parts of the next two seasons in the big leagues. Back in 2020, they gave Jordan Sheffield a shot, and he appeared in 30 games the following season. This year, they’re hoping Petit will be their Rule 5 lightning in a bottle. While he was a starter in his last year at Charleston Southern, Petit has done nothing but relieve as a pro since the Tigers drafted him in the 14th round in 2021. After reaching Triple-A in 2025, he was left off the 40-man roster for the second straight year, and the Rockies made him the No. 1 pick in the Major League phase. Petit is a mountain of a man, standing at 6-foot-8 and 300 pounds, though he’s a good athlete, especially for his size. He can touch as high as 98 mph with his fastball, sitting around 95 and using a steep downward plane to get ground-ball outs. His 84-mph gyro slider is his out pitch, missing a lot of bats and getting a lot of chase, a breaking ball the Rockies think might work in Coors Field. He does have an upper-80s changeup that tunnels off the fastball effectively. The big right-hander has shown an ability to get hitters on both sides of the plate out and has kept his walk rate in check. His best chance of sticking with the Rockies will likely be as a bulk reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading Vanderbilt with 15 homers as a junior and turning down the Marlins as a 31st-rounder in 2018, Scott bashed 14 more longballs and won a College World Series championship with the Commodores the next spring. A $50,000 senior sign taken in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft, he became an organization and fan favorite last year when he raked in Low-A and High-A while living in a camper with teammate Joe Davis. He finished his first full pro season by batting .338/.430/.606 with eight homers in 39 games in High-A. Scott not only has one of the better bats in Boston's system, but he also has one of the best approaches as well. He has an efficient left-handed swing, controls the strike zone and uses the entire field. His strength creates plus raw power and he lets his home runs come naturally rather than swinging for the fences. Scott made 39 starts at first base, 25 on the outfield corners, 18 at catcher and 14 at DH last year. Boston will give him more time behind the plate in 2022 and he has the desire and work ethic to make it as a backstop. He's a potentially average to solid receiver with some aptitude for framing, though he has fringy arm strength at best. With well below-average speed and a subpar arm, he doesn't offer much defensive value elsewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 Dalena shares an alma mater of Montoursville Area (Pa.) HS with Mike Mussina and was mentored by the Hall of Fame pitcher growing up in the Keystone State. After a stint at Monmouth in 2021-22, he played both ways at Division II Shippensburg in 2023, turned toward pitching in ’24 and posted a 3.36 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP with 99 strikeouts in 83 innings as a graduate student in ’25. The Padres took him in the sixth round, making him the first Shippensburg player selected since 2018 and the highest since 1999, and signed him for $10,000. Dalena made three brief appearances for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his pro debut. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is entering his age-24 campaign in his first full season but has some upside given his limited background. He was sitting mid-90s with impressive ride up in the zone after signing, and it’s a pitch he uses to set up the rest of his repertoire. It’s likely to be a true north-south look with an upper-70s curveball that drops off the table and a low-80s slider that stands out more for its drop than sweep. The deuce has better action and got more whiffs in his final collegiate season, but finding a consistent preferred breaking pitch will be a priority in ’26. Dalena also worked with a cutter and a changeup, the latter of which he struggled to command in his brief pro look in the California League. Dalena has a history of landing multiple pitches in the zone though, and he’d come up in offseason trade talks with other clubs intrigued by his early mix. He must prove his stuff can play beyond Division II, but the quality of the arsenal could make him a quality low-money, middle-round sign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts went undrafted after his junior year at Utah in 2023, when he batted just .266 with three homers over 46 games, but he started to show out for Mankato in the Northwoods League that summer (.346/.476/.555), creating some momentum for himself. He built on that with a Pac-12 All-Conference nod after slashing .356/.430/.562 with seven homers in 55 games for the Utes as a senior. His 33 steals were most among Pac-12 players. The Padres selected him in the seventh round and signed him for just $10,000, but Roberts continued to show out with a .340/.414/.470 line in 24 games with Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first taste of the Minors. Roberts cuts a stunning figure in the field at 6-foot-5, 205 pounds, and he moves exceptionally well for that size, notching 60-yard dashes in the 6.5-second range. He was a perfect 14-for-14 in steal attempts during that short run in the California League, and the Padres don’t have much doubt that his speed will continue to play as he reaches higher levels. With those wheels, Roberts is a comfortable fit in center field and has just enough arm for the position, too. That said, the left-handed hitter hasn’t been a huge power threat despite his size, though San Diego officials were intrigued by the good weight he put on during in his first offseason. He struggled to make contact against sliders and changeups as a senior and will need his speed to help run high BABIPs that can make up for some of the contact issues. Roberts already enters his first full season at age 24 and doesn’t have a long runway, but his best skills could be useful in the Majors in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays have done some great work on the nondrafted market in recent years and Coleman looks like one of their gems. Coleman had some hype going into his time with LSU, but ran into some injuries along the way and never quite established himself with the Tigers. Something has been unlocked with Toronto, though, and Coleman is suddenly the top lefty among the organization's pure bullpen prospects. Between Single-A and High-A in 2025, Coleman posted a 3.00 ERA with 85 strikeouts over 54 innings. Coleman got stronger as the season went on, too, leaning on a fastball that sits 94-96 mph and can reach a tick higher. That fastball comes from a bit lower of a release point than you typically see and it has some deception to it; when paired with a slider that can at least be a solid pitch in the future, it’s an intriguing package. Coleman pitches with an edge, too, and feels like a perfect fit for a true relief role. That role should also allow him to climb the ladder quicker than as a starter. If Coleman can keep his walk rate close to where it was in his pro debut (3.8 BB/9), that’s a safe enough number to let his strikeout rates shine. Expect to see him remain in one-to-two inning stints, and while others on this list have the advantage of starting, Coleman’s path to the big leagues is shorter and straighter than many others.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers spent much of the 2022 Draft stocking up on college bats. Gold was among the most polished, a three-year performer at Boston College who posted a .940 OPS as a sophomore and .958 as a junior. The Tigers’ front office has changed since drafting Gold, but his combination of hitting ability and zone control fit the mold of hitter that new president of baseball operations Scott Harris has touted as the model for the organization. Though Gold struggled in a late-season stint at Single-A Lakeland last summer, his quick swing and line-drive approach to all fields is expected to translate well once he gets acclimated to pro ball and develops a routine. The bigger question might be power. He never reached double digits in home runs at BC, and just two of his 13 pro hits last summer went for extra bases, both doubles. He doesn’t tend to chase much. Gold alternated between second and third base in Lakeland, but his strong arm and body frame could work better at third. Gold turned 22 last fall, and the Tigers could aim to push him if he can handle pitching in Lakeland early in the season. He’ll have to fight his way through a crowded group of infielders in the Tigers farm system, but for an organization that badly needs offense, Gold’s hit-first resume should get a fair shot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jimenez’s $480,000 bonus was the fourth-highest the Mariners handed out in the 2019-20 international signing period. Like with all signees from July 2019, he had to wait through the pandemic to make his pro debut in 2021, spending two summers in the Dominican Summer League. He then ended up in the Arizona Complex League for parts of another two years before having a bit of a breakout in 2024 that allowed him to reach full-season ball for the first time. He repeated the level in 2025 and showed off an intriguing, if still unpolished, set of tools. While he’s not the biggest guy in the world at 5-foot-10, Jimenez has shown that he can impact the baseball at times from the left side of the plate. He started barreling up the baseball more consistently in 2025 and can show solid bat-to-ball skills overall when he sticks to his approach. He also tapped into his power more effectively last year, showing leverage to his pull side, but has to make sure he doesn’t sell out for that pop and lose his approach. He can get caught in between being a guy to drive the ball with some swing-and-miss and a guy to get on base -- he does draw a good amount of walks -- who puts the ball in play. The Mariners would love to see him be more of the second guy, letting the power come naturally, so he can keep taking advantage of his speed and athleticism on the basepaths. He can also run the ball down in center field but will likely be the kind of guy who sees time in all three outfield spots as a potential fourth outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Binelas established himself as a potential first-rounder when he slugged 14 homers as a Louisville freshman in 2019, but he played just two games in the shortened pandemic season before breaking the hamate bone in his right hand and slumped at the start of his junior year. He recovered to hit 19 homers in 50 games before the Brewers selected the Wisconsin native in the third round and signed him for $700,000. After he batted .314/.379/.636 with nine blasts in 29 games in Low-A, Milwaukee traded him along with Jackie Bradley Jr. and shortstop prospect David Hamilton to the Red Sox for Hunter Renfroe in December. Binelas' strength and bat speed create solid power to all fields. While he has a reasonable approach at the plate, drawing his share of walks and avoiding chasing too many pitches, he's also a streaky hitter who batted just .272 in three college seasons. His left-handed stroke can get long and uphill, leading to concerns about his ability to handle velocity up in the zone and prolonged slumps when his timing gets out of whack. Where Binelas plays with his fringy speed and average arm remains to be seen. He's erratic and lacks range at third base, his primary position in his debut, and scouts don't like his hands, footwork or funky throwing motion. Louisville moved him to first base three weeks into this junior season but he also looked rough there and may wind up in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019-20 international signing period might always be known for the addition of Francisco Álvarez for $2.7 million in July. One month later -- after New York added international bonus pool money in a deal that sent Jeurys Familia to Oakland -- the club also picked up Lugo for $475,000 as an infielder out of the Dominican Republic. After a mundane introduction to stateside ball, Lugo broke out offensively in 2022 with Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .261/.347/.427 with 10 homers in 84 games before moving up to High-A Brooklyn, where he was also an above-average hitter with a 115 wRC+ in 28 contests. Lugo’s power is better than his Florida State League numbers indicate as he regularly registered exit velocities above 95 mph. His 41.1 percent hard-hit rate on that circuit was on par with Major League sluggers like Ian Happ and C.J. Cron in 2022, and the 20-year-old -- who stands out for his strength more than bat speed -- may only get stronger from here. Batting from a slightly closed stance, Lugo can sometimes expand the zone, leading to strikeouts in about one-quarter of his plate appearances, and hitting for average likely won’t be a strong suit. At 6-foot-3, Lugo was large for shortstop, even by modern standards, and as a below-average runner, he’s a better fit at third base. He has the arm for that spot, and he has enough pop to provide offensive value away from a premium position. The 20-year-old was Rule 5-eligible this offseason but went unprotected and unpicked as he’s at least two years away from the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clarke tied for the Division I lead with 23 homers as a junior for South Carolina in 2021, apt timing considering he missed much of his sophomore campaign the previous year due to the pandemic. The Brewers selected him in the 10th round that summer and signed him below slot at $75,000. The right-handed slugger was a solid performer between High-A and Double-A his first full season, finishing with 14 homers and a 116 wRC+ in 99 games, but truly took off in a return to Biloxi this summer with a Southern League-best 26 homers and an .889 OPS that placed third on the circuit. A strong Arizona Fall League campaign solidified the breakout. Power, power, power -- that’s long been Clarke’s calling card and will continue to be the closer he gets to Milwaukee. His uphill swing enables the pop to play as 50.2 percent of his batted balls were flyballs in 2023, but it also can affect his overall contact rate as he struck out 29.2 percent of the time. Clarke balances the punchouts with a lot of walks, but even he’s admitted he needs to get to the power earlier in counts to keep the offensive profile balanced. A well-below-average runner, Clarke initially impressed Brewers officials with his improvements behind the plate, but he’s still viewed as a long-term first baseman, especially as he plays next to Jeferson Quero and bumps into William Contreras’ shadow. He has decent arm strength but lacks accuracy on throws, leading to a 10.3 percent caught-stealing rate in 2023. A full-time right-right first baseman has a high offensive bar to clear, but Clarke just might have the power to handle it. If he can serve as a third catcher on the roster too, all the better.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signing as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in May 2018, Rodriguez began his career in the bullpen because of major control issues (51 walks in 50 1/3 innings) during his first two years in the Dominican Summer League. After the lost pandemic season, he moved into the rotation at Single-A Palm Beach and had success with a 3.36 ERA and 88 strikeouts in 69 2/3 innings. His 2022 season in High-A Peoria (4.59 ERA, 119 strikeouts in 121 2/3 frames) was a bumpier ride, but it was notable that he nearly doubled his previous career-high workload. The Cardinals did not add him to the 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in the offseason, and he went unselected in that process. The 6-foot right-hander’s velocity has picked up in recent years as he’s matured and gotten stronger. He can sit 95-96 mph earlier in outings but typically settles in closer to 93-94 as he goes deeper, which makes sense for a pitcher still getting built up as a starter. He’ll showcase a quality mid-80s slider that he can work to either side of the plate while also mixing in an upper-70s curveball offering a slower breaking look. His mid-80s changeup still lacks consistency, and there are the makings of a cutter for another diversified offering. Rodriguez doesn’t have the same control issues he did earlier in his career, but his delivery lacks consistency and can make him to fly open, causing his command to waver. His career might go full circle with a return to the bullpen as a result, which could allow him to open the velo even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, scout Billy Milos scoured independent leagues and found quality players for the Twins. Now with the Rockies, Milos’ last hurrah for his old team might be Eeles, who spent four years at Division II Cedarville University in Ohio, then got a fifth season at Coastal Carolina because of the pandemic. He was 23 and only 5-foot-5, so he went undrafted and headed to the American Association and then the Atlantic League to start 2024. That’s where Milos found him and he joined the organization for just $500, then became one of the best stories of the year, hitting his way to Triple-A and finishing with a system-leading .932 OPS. The left-handed-hitting Eeles combines a terrific feel for hitting with a “hair on fire” approach to the game. He really controls the strike zone, drawing walks and limiting his swing-and-miss (16 percent in 2024). It’s a hit-over-power approach, but he barrels up baseballs routinely and uses all fields. There’s surprising pop, and he has shown the ability to hit the ball out in all directions. Eeles doesn’t have plus speed but he’s smart and aggressive on the bases, which enabled him to steal 41 bases last year. He played every position but first base and catcher during his debut season, and his path to the big leagues is probably as a super-utility type. No one wants to undersell him at this point, though, and second base seems like his most likely landing spot should he be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mariners management was relieved when Kuhn remained in the organization after clearing the Rule 5 Draft despite not being added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. That’s because they view him as a possible big league bullpen piece, perhaps as soon as 2023. It was emblematic of his career path to this point, because wherever the big righty has played, he’s had to prove that he belonged, dating all the way back to when he was a walk-on at the University of San Diego. Kuhn’s fastball is a legit heater, sitting 95-96 mph and topping out near 99 mph with good run and sink on it. He also throws a hard, short slider that lands in the upper-80s and has become a true out pitch in the Minors. Both offerings from his small yet stocky frame make him the prototypical come-right-after-you reliever. Entering his age-25 season, Kuhn is a little older and one of the many whose development was stalled due to the Minors season being canceled in 2020. But if the command takes a step forward, he could be a viable shuttle guy between the Majors and Triple-A Tacoma sooner than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Scoyoc comes from Iowa baseball royalty, with a grandfather who was a coach immortalized in the film “The Final Season,” a dad who played pro ball and a brother who was drafted by the Phillies in 2019. Connor was committed to Arizona State after earning Iowa Gatorade Player of the Year honors, but the Angels went well over slot, giving him $400,000 in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft to keep him from heading to campus. He didn’t make much noise over his first couple of years, but he found some success in A-ball in 2022 and got some exposure in the Arizona Fall League. He was pitching well at High-A in 2023 when he was sent to the Rockies in exchange for Mike Moustakas and he finished the year with eight starts at Double-A. A 6-foot-6 right-hander, Van Scoyoc could have a three-pitch mix that gives him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 92 mph, though he can reach back for a few more ticks on occasion. It can be an effective pitch because of it’s cut and sink, a reason why he produces solid ground-ball rates. He’s shown the ability to spin a decent upper-70s curve that can flash above-average at times. He has a mid-80s changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much and it’s well behind the other two offerings. Pitchers this size can often find it difficult to repeat their delivery and Van Scoyoc struggled with finding the zone consistently in the early stages of his career. He improved dramatically on that front in 2022 and was a decent strike-thrower in '23. He was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft last offseason and wasn’t selected, making this a big year for the 24-year old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A South Carolina high school standout who stayed nearby to go to Clemson for college ball, Gordon was an outstanding reliever for the Tigers as a freshman, then spent his sophomore year in their weekend rotation. He lost his starting gig as a junior, though he did get into a bit of a groove closing games, finishing with 11 saves. The Angels sent him out as a starter in his first full season after taking him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft and he missed bats and limited walks, but he got hit over the course of the year with High-A Tri-City. Gordon has a potential four-pitch mix coming from a 6-foot-5 frame, ingredients to be a starter long-term if things click. Nothing in his repertoire is better than average at present, limiting his ceiling. He’ll typically throw his fastball in the 92-93 mph range, occasionally touching 96-97. He still has two breaking balls -- a mid-80s slider and upper-70s curve -- and both can miss bats but don’t profile as true out pitches. He still doesn’t throw the mid-80s changeup he has very often. Gordon can fill up the strike zone, walking just 2.9 per nine during his pro debut. It’s definitely control over command, and he often got too much of the zone, with Northwest League hitters combining for a .260 average against him. There’s a starter profile in there, but he’ll have to improve his secondary offerings to get to the big leagues as a back end of a rotation type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Juan was relatively unheralded when he signed out of the Dominican Republic with the A’s for just $10,000 in 2017 as an 18-year-old. Struggling through some command issues early in his professional career, he returned from the year off due to the pandemic and unexpectedly broke out in Single-A in 2021, showcasing an uptick in velocity that led to a promotion to High-A Lansing before a flexor strain cut his season short. The A’s liked his power arm enough to add him to the 40-man roster this past offseason, but they had to release him after designating him for assignment in early May, then re-signed him a week later. He again missed time rehabbing the same arm issue, but showed similar ability to miss bats when he was on the mound. Juan utilizes his big 6-foot-8 frame to fill up the zone with a fastball that can reach up to 99 mph and consistently hits 95-97 mph. He also brings a wipeout slider and an offspeed pitch that has the makings of a solid changeup but can be thrown too hard at times, which is why the A’s had encouraged him to focus on it by throwing the pitch more over the past year. When he did pitch in 2022, Juan did a better job of finding the strike zone, but command still remains an overall issue. That, combined with his injury history, could lead to him moving to the bullpen full-time in the future, where that fastball-breaking ball combination could play up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gutierrez signed with the Padres for $750,000 out of Venezuela on July 31, 2019 -- the day he turned 16 years old. The timing couldn’t have been tougher since he missed out on a professional debut in 2020 due to the pandemic and repeated the Dominican Summer League in 2021 and 2022. He was still at Single-A Lake Elsinore to begin 2025 but zoomed up all four full-season levels, posting a 3.31 ERA with 115 strikeouts in 125 innings. The 6-foot left-hander showed he could spot his 91-95 mph fastballs extremely well, and he added a little extra zip to touch 97 in his age-21 season. The sinker he showed in his one Triple-A start was in the deadzone, and the life on his four-seamer wasn’t all that much better, so Gutierrez needs to land those on a dime to be effective as he pushes toward San Diego. His low-80s slider shows nice depth, and it’s a pitch that he can glide nicely away from lefties. An upper-80s changeup has similar armside movement to the sinker but more drop; however, it wasn’t quite as effective against righties as it needs to be. No one will accuse the southpaw of overthrowing any time soon, as his delivery looks relatively free and easy albeit maybe a bit rushed in its final movements. He sets up on the extreme first-base side of the rubber, giving that slider the full width of the plate over which to break. Gutierrez may have gone unprotected and unpicked in last year’s Rule 5 Draft, for which he was eligible, but he’s still young at only 22 entering 2026. With the right adjustments, he could be a part of San Diego’s MLB depth soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros paid the two highest bonuses in their 2025 international class to a pair of players who trained together in Santo Domingo, D.R. Cuban outfielder Kevin Alvarez signed for $2 million, while Venezuelan infielder Manzueta turned pro for $847,500. The latter slashed .224/.405/.392 with 42 walks in 47 games during his pro debut as one of the youngest players (age 16) in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Manzueta stands out with his advanced feel for the barrel and his control of the strike zone. He has a sound right-handed stroke and recognizes pitches well. He won't be physically imposing and needs to add strength to his 5-foot-10 frame, but his ability to turn on pitches and square them up gives him some sneaky power that could translate into 12-15 homers per season. While Manzueta trained as a shortstop, his below-average speed and average arm strength aren't suited for the position. He played there briefly in the DSL while spending most of his time alternating between second base and third base. He profiles best at the keystone and could wind up a utilityman who derives much of his value from his on-base skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 65 | Control: 40 | Overall: 40 The Rangers have had more success than any organization with signing high schoolers as nondrafted free agents in recent years. Curtis gave up a commitment to Barry University (Fla.) to turn pro for $125,000 in 2022, working just 6 2/3 innings in his pro debut the following summer because he was too wild. His control was still sporadic last year but he posted a 2.85 ERA with a .194 average-against at Single-A. Much of Curtis’ success stems from his high-spin low-80s changeup that dives and fades under barrels, generating a 56 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2024. He also does a good job of spinning a solid upper-70s curveball and a tight low-80s slider that get chases but landed in the zone only a third of the time last year. His fastball has some carry but misses few bats, sitting in the low 90s and topping out at 96 mph in the early innings but parking at 88-90 by the middle frames. While Curtis is a good athlete, he has yet to figure out how to harness his stuff. He could become a No. 4 starter if he gets stronger and discovers more strikes, though he also has to prove he can do more than trick Single-A hitters with his array of secondary pitches. Texas will continue to be patient with his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cerda was born in the Bronx but signed out of the Dominican Republic when he joined the Rays' system for $325,000 in July 2019. He debuted in the Dominican Summer League in 2021 due to the pandemic and was in the midst of his first stateside campaign in 2022 when the Rays dealt him to the D-backs for outfielder David Peralta at the Trade Deadline. Finally in full-season ball last year, Cerda slashed .247/.402/.397 with 11 homers over 108 games between Single-A and High-A. His 93 walks ranked second among all Minor League catchers, trailing only Harry Ford's 103. That knowledge of the strike zone and unwillingness to expand it remain Cerda's best offensive attributes. The right-handed slugger starts with his lead leg slightly open from a hunched-over position but he drags the toe into place instead of incorporating a leg kick. The muted movement keeps him seeing the ball well and allows the free passes to pile up. When he does make contact, Cerda tends to hit the ball in the air with an uppercut swing; his 44.4 fly-ball percentage was second-highest among Arizona full-season qualifiers. There's enough raw power, too, that he should challenge for double-digit homers over a full year. Through his background, Cerda is bilingual, and he earns strong reviews for his ability to work with a pitching staff. He still has some room to grow with blocking and receiving, but the pieces are there for at least an average Major League defensive backstop. Cerda has arm strength, but a lack of accuracy helped opposing runners steal 139 bags off him in 2023. Despite being left off Arizona's 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in 2024, Cerda is trending upward and could serve as an adequate backup in The Show in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Panamanian pipeline to Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.) highlighted by Guardians 2019 first-rounder Daniel Espino, Rodriguez was one of the older prep prospects (19 years, seven months) in the 2023 Draft. The Cubs didn't mind his age because they had some third-round grades on him, and they took him in the 13th round. His development has progressed more slowly than expected, but he finally reached Double-A at the end of last season. Rodriguez operates at 92-95 mph and touches 99 with his fastball, but he's often tentative with it because it lacks good shape and gets whacked when it grabs too much of the plate. He shows much better feel for strikes with his upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Like the rest of his arsenal, his tight mid-80s slider plays as an average pitch. Rodriguez works solely out of the stretch with a low release height that creates some deception. He has improved his strike-throwing every season as a pro, though his control and command still need more work if he's going to succeed as a starter. He gets more ground balls than he misses bats and is more likely to wind up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cermak had some of the best all-around tools from the college ranks in the 2022 Draft class, which led the Rays to select him 71st overall out of Illinois State and sign him for a below-slot $750,000 bonus, but he’s still raw in some ways. He led his college team with 11 homers during his first full season in 2021 then became a more well-rounded player in his final spring by controlling the strike zone better. He spent most of his first college season and the beginning of his second at third base, then moved to the outfield and became Missouri Valley Conference’s defensive player of the year two years in a row. Wrist and knee injuries limited him in 2023, but he was productive for Single-A Charleston, finishing with a 129 wRC+ in 39 games. Cermak hit for big-time power in college but still hasn’t faced a lot of high-level competition. His right-handed swing comes with effort and an uphill path, leaving him vulnerable to high fastballs, although he’s done more consistent damage by cutting down on his chases outside the zone. He looks to drive the ball, and he has the bat speed and pure strength to generate above-average power. He’s shown a pull-heavy mindset that can lead to strikeouts. Cermak has well-above-average speed, having been clocked down the first-base line in less than 4.1 seconds, and an arm that lit up the radar guns up to 95 mph during a brief stint on the mound in college. The Rays gave him time at all three outfield spots in 2023, but the majority of his looks came in right because of the arm. That will put more pressure on his bat to help him climb through the Minors as he works to stay healthy for a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gordon began his time at Oregon as a two-year reliever before undergoing internal brace surgery that wiped out his junior year in 2023. He returned to the Ducks as a starter but posted a 5.13 ERA in that role, leading him to land in the 13th round to the Mets in ‘24. He enjoyed a breakout first full season in the High-A and Double-A rotations, finishing with a 3.36 ERA and 147 strikeouts in 128 2/3 innings. Gordon was one of only 13 Minor League pitchers to post a K rate above 27 percent (27.3 in his case) over at least 120 frames. The 6-foot righty isn’t going to blow many batters away with his 91-94 mph fastball, but he has the strong set of secondaries to get outs as a starter. His 83-86 mph slider was his most-used pitch in 2025 (per Synergy), and that’s understandable because he commands its tight break to the gloveside edge of the zone so well. An upper-70s curveball gives him something with a bit more of a hump that he can get for swings below the knees. Gordon deserves credit for moving to a kick-change after barely using a cambio in his last year at Eugene, and the 83-85 mph pitch is a natural fit for his supination tendencies. With the addition of the armside offering, he ran reverse splits in ’25. Gordon used his breaking pitches to get batters to expand the zone in Binghamton and actually improved his walk rate as he climbed up the Mets' system. His mechanics are loose and easy, and he could even get to above-average control if this trend holds. Gordon’s lack of velo holds back his ceiling, but his development into a backend starting option would be a massive win for a 13th-rounder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited as a catcher by Boise State, Buxton moved to the mound with the Broncos, redshirted in 2019 and pitched in just four games during the shortened 2020 season. Boise State dropped baseball afterward, so he transferred to Lipscomb, where he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with seven wins in 2022 before getting drafted in the 15th round that July. He reached Double-A for one start at the end of his first full pro season and soaked up more experience in the Arizona Fall League afterward. Buxton relies heavily on his fastball, a power sinker that operates at 93-95 mph, reaches 97 and creates a ton of groundball contact -- his 2.06 groundout/airout ratio would have ranked fourth in the Minors last year if he had enough innings to qualify. He can flash a solid low-80s slider with nice sweep at times but he struggles to land it in the zone. He has made some strides with an 82-85 mph changeup with similar sink to his heater, and it could become an average offering if he uses it more often. To remain a starter, Buxton will need to throw more strikes. His control improved a bit during his six weeks in High-A last summer but remains fringy at best. He could wind up fitting toward the back of a big league rotation or wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Puerto Rico, Ortiz slid over to Florida’s IMG Academy for high school ball as a two-way player who was initially known more as a shortstop. The Nationals took him in the 20th round of the 2022 Draft, as a pitcher, but he opted to head to junior college instead, playing both ways for Chipola. The Reds took him as a draft-and-follow in 2023, then saw enough progress on the mound back at Chipola to sign him for $225,000 that May. He got his feet wet the summer after signing, then threw over 90 effective innings with full-season Daytona in 2025. An athletic six-foot right-hander, Ortiz continues to get better the longer he’s been focused on pitching only. His fastball is gaining velocity and he throws it mostly in the 90-95 mph range with some armside run, and there could be more consistent velo to come in the future. The Reds feel his 84-87 mph changeup is ahead of his 83-86 mph slider but not by much, and there’s conviction he could end up having three above-average pitches down the road. In addition to the stuff ticking up, Ortiz used his athleticism to find the strike zone more consistently in 2025 and it’s not difficult to believe that he will eventually display average command. He has full-time starter upside with the organization excited to see how he handles a climb up the ladder and a heavier workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers appreciated Lopez's defensive ability as a catcher and signed him for $347,500 out of Venezuela in 2022. He made his U.S. debut last summer and homered three times in four games at the end of June but played just once more before getting shut down with a sore arm. He slashed .289/.396/.644 in 13 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. A no-doubt catcher, Lopez looks natural and more advanced than most teenagers behind the plate. He moves well, receives and blocks well and threw out 39 percent of basestealers in his first two seasons thanks to plus arm strength and impressive accuracy. He's intelligent, already exhibits good feel for calling pitches and can communicate with hurlers in either English or Spanish. There's nothing subtle about Lopez's left-handed stroke and approach, which are geared to launch balls to his pull side. His strength and exit velocities portend 15-20 homer power, with strikeouts a product of his swinging for the fences. He does exhibit some patience at the plate and could provide enough offense to go with his quality defense and become a starting catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Indiana State might best be known for producing NBA great Larry Bird, but there have also been more than 20 big leaguers to come from the school, most recently left-hander Sean Manaea. Hayden hopes to be the next after the Reds took him in the eighth round of the 2024 Draft. He started his college career at Indiana before transferring to start for the Sycamores, where he had his real success, albeit with command issues. He made four relief outings for full-season Daytona after signing. Hayden’s best offerings are his fastball-slider combination. While he sat in the low-90s as a starter during his junior season, he’s already shown he can push his fastball up to 98 mph. His mid-80s slider is actually better than the heater, a pitch that elicited a 45 percent miss rate during his junior season, according to Synergy. He does have a firm changeup up into the upper 80s, but it’s a distant third pitch he doesn’t rely on. The Reds may let Hayden develop as a starter for now so he can work on his entire repertoire and try to refine his command after his 5.4 walk per nine rate in 2024 was an improvement from his first two seasons of college ball. He profiles best as a reliever and he could see his stuff tick up while moving quickly through the system, if and when he gets shortened up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Jennings in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft out of Louisiana Tech, and while it’s taken some patience, he's developed into one of the most interesting arms in the upper levels of Toronto’s system. It all came together for a healthy Jennings in 2024, when he opened the season at High-A Vancouver and eventually slid into a bullpen role with Double-A New Hampshire, posting a combined 1.93 ERA with 68 strikeouts over 60 2/3 innings. He followed that up with an excellent showing in the Arizona Fall League (10 IP, 0 ER, 14 K). Jennings leads with a fastball that sits 95-96 mph, reaching up to touch 98, and while his mid-80s slider projects as a legitimate MLB pitch, the depth of his arsenal (with an added curveball and changeup) is what continues to tempt the Blue Jays to keep him stretched out. Jennings could help the MLB bullpen in the short term, but if he stays in the rotation and reaches 100 innings in 2025, that could give the Blue Jays some attractive depth going forward. Team need will dictate this to a certain extent, but Jennings has developed from a stuff-first pitcher into one with a better feel for his own game. Jennings turns 26 in June, so there’s no need to slow play anything development-wise. Regardless of how he gets there, he is a good bet to be a big leaguer and is getting close to being a success story for the player development staff. Jennings is a name that comes up often around the organization as a prospect who deserves some more shine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee’s 2024 international class came with a big seven-figure name in Jorge Quintana ($1.7 million) and a future Top 100 prospect in Jesús Made. Anderson’s $60,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic barely would have registered from an outside perspective. But Brewers evaluators had Anderson down as an early breakout candidate, and he achieved that status by leading Milwaukee Dominican Summer League prospects in homers with eight (two more than Made) while slashing .283/.403/.512 over 201 plate appearances. His .916 OPS was fifth best by a Brewers DSL prospect since 2010. Anderson has impressed Milwaukee hitting instructors with his ability to stay balanced at the plate, especially compared to other teenagers with his level of pro experience. That helps his above-average power play in games already, and there could be even more coming as he continues to fill out his 6-foot frame. Anderson walked 14.4 percent of the time against often wild DSL pitchers but has seen that approach challenged more with an aggressive jump to Single-A Carolina this season. Anderson is a solid runner at this stage and swiped 15 bags in 19 attempts in 2024. He might slow down a touch as he matures, and he's already seen time in both center and right at this early stage of his career. He’s expected to head to a corner full-time as he joins clubs with faster players up the middle, and his arm strength and power would be fine fits in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olson earned second-team all-Big Ten Conference honors and an invitation to try out for the U.S. national team as a Nebraska sophomore in 2022. He boosted his Draft stock with a strong performance against Michigan in front of a crowd of scouts last April and went in the fourth round, where he signed for a well below-slot $460,000. He made just one brief appearance after turning pro. A finesse left-hander, Olson has his most success when he's in command of his breaking pitches. His mid-70s curveball has a lot of downer break but lacks power and rarely lands in the zone, while his low-80s slider is more reliable in terms of strikes and chases. His fringy low-90s fastball peaks at 95 mph and doesn't miss many bats, and his mid-80s changeup has depth but gets too firm. Olson features a high-three-quarters arm slot and provides consistent strikes with all of his pitches except for his curve. He's physically maxed out at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, so he's unlikely to add significant velocity. He has a decent floor as an end-of-the-rotation starter with little margin for error with his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited by Auburn as a left-handed pitcher, Snell redshirted there while injured in 2021 before transferring to Wallace-Dothan (Ala.) CC and becoming the national junior college player of the year in 2023. He played both ways on Alabama in 2024 before becoming a full-time left fielder in his final college season. As a Southeastern Conference performer with intriguing data and no college eligibility remaining, he was one of the better discount hitters available in the 2025 Draft and went in the fifth round. After displaying one of the best combinations of swing decisions, contact and exit velocities in the 2025 college crop, Snell continued to stand out in those areas even while slashing just .167/.268/.219 at High-A during his 27-game pro debut. He drives the ball to all fields and handles all types of pitches with a quality left-handed swing. His biggest need is to learn to launch balls in the air more regularly, or else he'll be a hit-over-power corner outfielder who will top out at 15 homers per season. Snell can show close to average speed at his top end but he's more of a below-average runner with limited outfield range. He reached 93 mph with his fastball as a redshirt junior and the Cubs deployed him on both outfield corners after Alabama utilized him solely in left field. Most of his value will come from his bat, though he also receives high marks for his leadership skills and competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trying to prove that a local kid can make good, Tolve went from the Georgia high school ranks to Kennesaw State for college. He parlayed a solid 2021 season (.319/.393/.498) to get drafted by his hometown Braves in Round 17 of the 2021 Draft. He showed off some interesting tools during a solid first full season with High-A Rome in 2022, but his climb to Double-A in 2023 was interrupted by a quad strain that limited him to just 50 games. He made up for some lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. When he’s healthy, Tolve has been an athletic left-handed hitting catcher, a demographic that’s often in high demand. He is capable of making loud contact, though there’s too much swing-and-miss in his game. He did improve his strikeout rate a bit in 2023 (27.2 percent, compared to 32 percent in 2022), and he will draw some walks. There’s raw extra-base pop there if he can be a bit more consistent in finding the barrel at the plate Tolve runs very well, especially for a catcher, and he’s been athletic enough to play other positions in the past. His agility is an asset as a backstop; he’s a solid receiver with good arm strength. If he can continue to refine his approach at the upper levels, he could be a solid big league backup in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally drafted by his hometown D-backs as a 19th-rounder in 2022, Turley instead opted to play college ball at Oregon State, where he had a big year as a freshman with 14 home runs and an OPS above 1.100. After crushing another 19 homers in 2024 and performing well in the Cape Cod League that summer, the A’s drafted him in '25 as a fourth-round pick, following a 20-homer junior year, signing him below slot at $600,000. Ahead of his first full professional season, Turley got his feet wet with 27 games at Single-A Stockton. Turley falls in line with similar A’s draft picks in recent years -- like Denzel Clarke and Rodney Green Jr. -- as a toolsy outfielder with some concerns about his ability to make consistent contact. He’s got big power and is able to drive the ball out to all fields with great bat speed, but his strikeout rates throughout his career with the Beavers were somewhat alarming. The question over whether he can hit enough to tap into that raw power is something he’ll have to prove early in his pro career. He has a tendency to chase breaking stuff often, though he mitigates that issue somewhat with his strong ability to draw walks. A big knock on Turley coming out of college was poor defense, but the A’s believe he is plenty athletic and speedy enough to improve and envision that happening as he grows into his 6-foot-1 frame. His body type and look in the box remind some within the organization of Mark Canha, and he’ll look to move through the system as a power-hitting corner outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Mason Martin, a former Pirates farmhand who ranked fourth in the Minors with 35 homers in 2019, Martin also stands out with his well-above-average raw power. Signed for an over-slot $250,000 in 2023 as an 11th-rounder from a Washington high school, he struggled for two years in Rookie ball before doing more damage in Single-A last year and drawing significant trade interest from other clubs. He earned Carolina League all-star honors after leading the Single-A circuit in extra-base hits (43) and ranking second in slugging (.440) and third in homers (12) and OPS (.783). Martin can drive the ball out of the park to all fields with an impressive combination of bat speed and strength, and he hits the ball harder and farther than most Rangers farmhands. In 2025, he did a better job of attacking hittable pitches in early counts and launching them in the air to his pull side, allowing him to make better use of his pop. How much he'll be able to tap into his 25-30 homer upside at higher levels will depend on his ability to improve his swing decisions and handle secondary pitches. Though Martin stole 15 bases in as many attempts last year, he has fringy speed with good instincts on the bases. He has limited range and below-average arm strength, relegating him to left field and diminishing his value outside of the batter's box. He's adequate at first base and can fill in in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An accomplished amateur player who starred for the U.S. national team that won a gold medal at the 2017 18-and-under World Cup, Young nonetheless went undrafted as a Washington high schooler after slumping offensively on the showcase circuit the following summer. He hit 16 homers in his first full season at Vanderbilt but also led NCAA Division I in strikeouts while battling a left shoulder injury that required offseason surgery. Healthy again, his offensive struggles persisted last spring as Young continued to sell out for power and pile up whiffs, batting .207/.327/.383 as a junior. The Orioles took a no-risk flier on him in the 17th round in the 2022 Draft, signing him for just over $1.3 million when it became clear they weren’t going to be able to come to terms with third-round pick Nolan McLean. Young got his feet wet but didn’t hit much during a brief debut in pro ball, finishing the year at Single-A Delmarva. Young is a different player than he was in his prep days, having added 20 pounds and a more upward angle to his swing from both sides of the plate. He now has average power that plays to his pull side as a righty and to all fields as a lefty, but it comes with a ton of swing-and-miss due to poor pitch recognition. He’ll need to tidy up his approach and stop chasing pitches out of the strike zone if he’s to realize his 20-homer potential in pro ball. Young is much more polished defensively, with advanced instincts and a strong internal clock that allows him to play quicker than his average speed. Good range and a strong arm help make him a solid and reliable defender. Right now it’s a glove-over-bat profile, with questions about whether Young will hit enough to develop into a regular. If not, he has the versatility and skills to fill a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs took Giesting in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft after he’d struck out 104 in 74 1/3 innings that spring and signed him for $400,000 (roughly fifth-round money) as a Draft-eligible sophomore with leverage. He spent his entire first season with High-A Hillsboro, where he posted a 4.00 ERA with 124 strikeouts and 71 walks in 117 innings, and returned to the Northwest League with much more dominance and control (1.50 ERA, 67 K, 13 BB in 60 IP) in 2024. Giesting rounded out his age-22 season with 15 starts for Double-A Amarillo, and his 154 strikeouts across 141 1/3 total frames were tops in the Arizona system and tied for 13th-most in the Minors. Setting up from the first-base side of the rubber, the 6-foot-4 left-hander gets down the bump well, creating some flat angle on his 89-91 mph fastball and enabling it to play above velocity alone.
