His 78-82 mph slider can be a menace with ample sweep; even righties whiffed on 45 percent of their swings against it, per Synergy. His feel for spin also ties into a curveball that can bleed into the slider but is as effective. Giesting added an upper-80s cutter in 2024 and used it with solid effect when he needed more of a pinpoint offering to get back into a pitcher’s count. His 85-87 mph changeup is too close to the fastball to be truly effective. Giesting significantly improved his control numbers year to year at High-A, and even his 8.7 percent walk rate at Double-A shouldn’t scare anyone. He’s proven plenty durable through two Minor League seasons and moves well enough in his mechanics that he could be a backend starter, even with subpar velo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Active players in the international amateur market, the Phillies have handed out at least one seven-figure bonus in each of the past four signing periods, with three signees in the previous two alone already ranked highly in the organization’s Top 30. Arias became the latest addition, signing for $1.45 million when the 2024 signing period opened in January. Already 6-foot-3 and having added strength, Arias is a long-limbed outfielder who has the chance to hit for a ton of power. The right-handed hitter uses an explosive uppercut swing and has gap-to-gap pop, with more certainly coming as he continues to fill out his frame. While he does have an idea of what he wants to do at the plate, he will have to watch the swing-and-miss, especially with those long arms. He has a power-over-hit profile right now. Arias runs well enough for his size and is a solid athlete with smooth defensive actions and an average arm. He might have the chance to play some center field at least early on, but chances are he’s going to continue to slow down a bit as he matures and will need to slide over to a corner. There he’ll have the chance to fit the power-hitting profile well if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz has a lot of similarities to Bryan Ramos, as both are power-over-hit third baseman who starred as youngsters in Cuba before signing with the White Sox. The MVP at the 15-and-under world qualifying tournament in Venezuela in 2022, Cruz played with Cuba's 18-and-under team at age 16 the following year. Signed for $2 million shortly after turning 18 this January, he's expected to begin his pro career in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Cruz has a projectable 6-foot-3 frame with a relatively compact right-handed swing with loft. He already shows some aptitude for working counts and using the entire field. He has present pull power and could produce 20 homers annually as he gains strength and experience. While Cruz currently has plus speed and shows some basestealing ability, he'll probably lose a step and be more of an average-to-solid runner once he matures physically. He displays good actions at third base and could be a better defender than Ramos in the long run. He earns average to solid grades for his arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Powell got just 35 at-bats as an Oklahoma freshman, prompting him to transfer to Seminole State (Okla.) JC, where he became the national junior college player of the year as a sophomore in 2024. He topped NJCAA Division I in slugging (1.088), OPS (1.649), homers (32) and RBI (104) before giving up an Oklahoma State commitment to sign with the Astros as sixth-rounder. He slashed .264/.331/.442 in Single-A before breaking his left hamate last May, then missed two months and hit just .209/.358/.358 afterward. Powell features well above-average raw power, the product of a fierce right-handed stroke and an aggressive mindset that looks to crush balls to his pull side. He exhibits reasonable plate discipline and hits balls extremely hard when he makes contact -- but there are major questions about whether he can do so consistently against advanced pitching. He had a swing-and-miss rate of 29 percent against the strikes he saw in 2025, including 33 percent against in-zone fastballs. While Powell is slower out of the batter's box, he flashes solid speed underway and stole 32 bases in 38 attempts (84 percent) in 84 games last year. He played mostly shortstop in junior college and spent the majority of his time there last year, but his quickness is better suited for third base. He was erratic at both spots in 2025, committing 16 miscues in 61 starts, and has average arm strength. The organization will focus on getting him reps in the outfield this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trentadue spent a season at NCAA Division III Southern Virginia before moving to the JC of Southern Idaho, where he topped national junior college pitchers in strikeout rate (16.0 per nine innings) in 2023. A 14th-round pick that July, he earned High-A South Atlantic League honors in 2025 after posting a 1.15 ERA, .148 opponent average and 34 percent strikeout rate in the first four months of the season. He got roughed up in seven Double-A starts to finish the year, so he'll return there in 2026. As Trentadue has gotten stronger, his fastball has gone from averaging 88 mph at Southern Idaho to sitting at 92-95 mph and touching 97. Beyond its velocity, hitters have trouble handling his heater because it features quality carry and bores in on right-handers. He also made improvements with his sweeping low-80s slider and sinking mid-80s changeup, though he's still figuring out how to locate the latter where he wants. Trentadue uses his athleticism to get down the mound very well, creating a low release height and extension that add to his deception. He has decent control but looked more tentative while getting knocked around in Double-A. He has the ceiling of a No. 4 starter but his ability to make adjustments against advanced hitters will determine whether he stays in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cleveland didn’t get much mound time at Central Arkansas until 2021, his third year on campus, becoming the Bears’ closer and saving nine games. He pitched well as a starter in 2022 to close out his college career, and the Mariners took him in the 14th round that July. He actually spent the 2023 season still working as a starter, but a combination of moving to the bullpen and dropping his arm slot even further has helped him get some traction, and he made it to Double-A for the first time in July 2025 before capping things off in the Arizona Fall League. Nothing Cleveland does is conventional on the mound, and while his mode of operation isn’t the same, his stuff -- and the surprising effectiveness of it -- evokes some Tyler Rogers vibes. Once just a sidearmer, Cleveland has dropped down further to submarine levels, and there’s even more deception with a delivery that has him stepping all the way to the third-base side of the mound while slinging his two-pitch mix back across his body. His fastball hovers around 85 mph but hitters don’t pick it up, his sweepy low-70s slider also misses a fair amount of bats and he was virtually unhittable in 2025 (0.87 ERA, .128 BAA). Cleveland throws enough strikes with his funk to believe it’s something that could work at the highest level. It might have to be in limited stints, but teams are often seeking out different looks coming out of the 'pen to keep hitters off balance, and Cleveland is as different as they come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: “I am tomorrow, or some future day, what I establish today. I am today what I established yesterday or some previous day.” The other James Joyce could have very well been talking about pitching prospects, including the Mariners one who shares his name. This Joyce has always flown under the radar among a pitching-heavy pipeline, particularly given that he was a 16th-round pick in 2021, signed for just $25,000 and entered his pro career on the heels of struggling to find consistency at Hofstra University. Those challenges continued in his first full pro year at High-A Everett, but he took a notable leap forward in 2023 despite missing the season’s first two months with a forearm strain, climbing all the way to Double-A Arkansas. Joyce operates with a three-pitch mix via a funky delivery. His fastball sits around 93 mph from a lower arm slot, and it's thrown with plenty of life. His 83-84 mph changeup runs and has hard fade to it and his 82-83 mph curveball gets big top to bottom action on it. That combination of funk and movement has allowed him to miss a fair amount of bats despite less than plus stuff. The cause for Joyce’s turnaround last season? A big step forward with command. He dropped his walk rate from 10 to seven percent in the span of a year while keeping hitters in the ballpark, with just one homer surrendered in seven starts after the Double-A promotion. With many questions about his trajectory entering the year, he probably steered back into an arm with starter upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed a then 17-year-old Aquino for only $16,000 out of the Dominican Republic on the first day of the 2021 international period and have seen him steadily climb the ranks one level a year since. After stints on the Dominican and Arizona Complex circuits, the right-hander posted a 2.75 ERA and 1.26 WHIP with 86 strikeouts over 88 1/3 frames for Single-A Carolina this summer. That inning output more than doubled his total from 2021 and '22 combined (78 1/3), so Milwaukee officials found it particularly promising that Aquino was still growing into himself toward the end of his age-20 campaign. Aquino shows largely average fastball velocity around 92-94 mph but can crank it up as high as 96 at times. His low-80s slider is his best pitch with impressive two-plane movement that can drive his whiff rate. Despite averaging less than a K per inning, his 14.5 swinging-strike percentage was ninth-best among 29 Carolina Leaguers with at least 80 innings in 2023. The vertical drop, in particular, can make the breaker look closer to a curveball at times, but it’s still effective. Aquino’s mid-80s changeup remains behind the other two offerings, and without a quality third pitch, lefties batted .288 with a .381 OBP off the hurler in 2023. The 6-foot righty found the zone with better regularity as the season wore on, walking only five batters in his final six outings (27 IP). More disciplined upper-level hitters could hold off chasing the diving sliders out of the zone, pushing that walk rate back up in years to come, but the improvements at least help Aquino’s odds of starting for now. Even so, his best chance of being an impact Major Leaguer might be as a two-pitch reliever who leans into his best tools in shorter appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s way too soon to know what kind of return the Angels will ultimately get for their investments in the 2023 international market, but the early signs are encouraging. The class, led by shortstop Felix Morrobel, also includes Juan Flores behind the plate and Texido on the mound. The left-hander signed for $250,000 in March and then found himself all over the leaderboard in the Dominican Summer League, finishing in the top 10 in strikeouts (61), WHIP (0.95), ERA (2.31) and strikeouts per nine (10.8) as the Angels' club in the league went 37-18 and made the playoffs. None of Texido’s three pitches currently jump off the page, but he already has an idea of how to use them. The left-hander’s fastball sat around 88-89 mph and touched 92. His 80-82 mph changeup has the chance to be an above-average pitch with some sink and he’ll need to add some power to his 75-78 mph slider, a pitch he also struggled to command in the zone consistently. Other than those issues with his breaking ball, however, Texido did a very nice job in throwing strikes overall. There’s a little funk in his delivery, which helps in the deception department, and he has a projectable frame, giving the potential for him to add strength and some oomph to his fastball-slider combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays found Shaw in the ninth round of the 2023 Draft out of Lambrick Park Secondary School in British Columbia and signed him away from an NCAA commitment to Xavier with a $282,500 bonus. This was a strong piece of scouting by the Blue Jays' staff, who knew Shaw well going back to his appearance in their Canadian Futures Showcase. Shaw got a brief look at pro ball in ‘23, appearing in nine games in the FCL. Shaw profiles between second base and the outfield defensively, with some projecting the outfield as his likeliest landing spot after he’s worked out some throwing issues. The Blue Jays already like the style of at-bats they see from Shaw, grinding out deep counts and competing consistently. He’s naturally athletic in the box, too, not getting bogged down by rigid mechanics. Right now, Shaw’s contact tool is comfortably ahead of his power, but the Blue Jays are optimistic that he can develop some pop in the coming years. Shaw represents upside, which is exactly what the Blue Jays need more of in their system, particularly when it comes to players with the potential to play the outfield long-term. This will be a fun development project for the Blue Jays’ staff, particularly if Shaw’s pop can step forward as his leading tool and pull him up through the Minor Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2022 international signing class’ Top 50 list included two players from Panama: The first was catcher Adan Sanchez, who got $1.5 million to sign with the Cubs. Pineda stayed in the NL Central as well, as the No. 49 prospect received $800,000 to join the Reds organization. He had a solid, albeit brief, debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing and then continued to show some hitterish tendencies in his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2023. A former standout in international youth competition, Pineda is a compact and strong right-handed hitter. He has a good feel to hit with the ability to find the barrel consistently while hitting the ball hard. He hasn’t started finding the seats yet, but he did start tapping into his extra-base authority in the ACL with a bunch of doubles. As he moves along, those could translate to long balls and he could eventually have average power. Pineda is a corner outfielder only because he’s a fringy runner and not overly athletic. His plus arm fits in right field and he’s a capable defender there. Now it’s a question of whether his run-producing capabilities manifest as he matures so he can profile as an everyday guy in that spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No player had been drafted from Seattle’s Ballad HS since 1997 and no one had signed from there since 1989 before Madonna headed to the MLB Draft League out of hope he could build up his stock to end both streaks. He hit .279/.360/.512 with two homers and four doubles in 12 games for Frederick on the summer showcase circuit while being roughly four years younger than its average player. The Padres saw enough from there and his time in the Pacific Northwest to take him in the 11th round and sign him away from a UCLA commitment with a $654,000 bonus (closer to fourth-round money). Madonna flashed good power in that short time with the Keys, topping out with a 107.8 mph exit velocity on one of his two dingers and finishing with a 90th-percentile EV of 104.3 (close to MLB average) in the small sample. It's gap-to-gap power that led to six of his 12 hits falling for extra bases. The right-handed slugger was left exposed against high-end velocity, and he struggled against Draft League breaking stuff. That was a trend that carried into his short spin with Single-A Lake Elsinore, where he had just a 57.3 percent overall contact rate in 14 games. All that said, Madonna faced aggressive assignments as an 18-year-old amateur and pro last summer and deserves to grow into more age-appropriate competition in his first full season. Defensively, some scouts believe he's close to maxed out physically and might have to move to first base eventually in his 20s, though his average arm strength and good accuracy should help limit opposing running games behind the plate. The Padres will rotate Madonna with 2025 fifth-rounder Ty Harvey at catcher while getting them enough at-bats to develop offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long winding path for Mejia, who started his college career by redshirting at Arizona in 2019, then transferred to Pima Community College in 2020, but made just five starts there because of the pandemic. The right-hander went to New Mexico State after that, mostly relieving in 2021 then stepping into the rotation in 2022. He signed for $100,000 as an 11th-round pick that summer, spent all year with High-A Rome in 2023 and then had another solid, and durable, season with Double-A Mississippi in 2024. Mejia’s feel for pitching and the ability to mix his offerings to keep hitters off-balance stands out more than any of his pure stuff. His fastball averaged around 92 mph last year and maxed out at 94 mph. It doesn’t feature a ton of life, but he commands the pitch consistently. His low-80s slider is his go-to pitch, and he threw it almost as much as his heater in 2024, missing bats at a 42-percent clip. His 83-84 mph changeup is a decent third offering and he’s been working on a splitter as well. The 6-foot-3 Mejia does a nice job of repeating his delivery and has a history of throwing strikes, especially in 2022 with the Aggies and during his first pro season. His walk rate did jump a bit in 2024, but he’s posted consistently, topping 120 innings in each of his two full seasons. His ceiling is probably as a No. 5 type starter because of the lack of wow stuff, but he’s close to showing if it can work in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: St Joseph’s most successful product has been left-hander Jamie Moyer, who spent a quarter century in the big leagues. There’s been one other catcher, Brian O’Keefe, who touched the Majors in 2022-23, but Cossetti is hoping to be the next. After four years at the Philadelphia-based school, Cossetti certainly didn’t hurt his stock with a strong showing in his second stint in MLB’s Draft League in 2022, helping him land in the 11th round of that year's Draft. He posted a .960 OPS across two levels of A ball in 2023, with a 163 RC+ that placed second among all catchers with more than 300 plate appearances, before finishing up with a defense-focused stint in the Arizona Fall League. Cossetti has the chance to be a productive right-handed hitter because he has a solid combination of strength and approach at the plate. He limits strikeouts and draws a ton of walks, getting him into better counts where he did fairly consistent damage. He registers high exit velocities, and there’s good power he should be able to continue to get to. Whether he can defend well enough to stay behind the plate is more of a question. He’s improved his arm strength to average, and he works very hard at his craft, but he’ll need to keep grinding to become an adequate receiver. The Twins don’t want to bet against his work ethic, but they’ll also keep getting him some reps at first base to get his bat in the lineup more regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: High school catching is a tough demographic, with perhaps as much risk as prep pitching. The Braves weren’t afraid to roll the dice after seeing Montgomery excel on the summer showcase circuit, at events like MLB’s PDP League and the Area Code Games, along with the Draft Combine. They took Montgomery in the fifth round but went way over slot to sign the California high schooler away from his Arizona State commitment, giving him third-round money to begin his pro career. The 6-foot-4 Montgomery’s standout offensive tool is his raw power from the right side of the plate. He showed he can get to it against good pitching at showcase events, using a small leg kick for timing. There is some length in his swing and he opens up prematurely at times, leading to some questions about his overall feel to hit, though there was some confidence from scouts that he would make enough contact to get to that pop as a pro. Given his size, it’s unclear if Montgomery will be able to catch. He has at least an above-average arm that plays, and he’s not a terrible receiver, but his lack of agility could have the Braves looking at first base or maybe a corner outfield spot in the future, which would put more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to his senior season, Steinmetz wasn’t known that well outside the region of Long Island, New York. The big projectable right-hander opened a lot of eyes, however, by heading the ELEV8 Baseball Academy in southeast Florida and became the first Orthodox Jewish player ever drafted when Arizona selected him in the third round. He signed for a below-slot $500,000 and showed more polish than expected in subsequent workouts. There’s plenty of projectability with Steinmetz and the teenager already shows the potential to develop two plus pitches. The fastball sits in the low 90s now, but it’s believed that number will tick up as he adds muscle to his 6-foot-5 frame. Steinmetz’s best secondary offering is his high-spin-rate curveball and his sinking changeup also shows promise. As a Northeast prep pitcher without a track record against top competition, Steinmetz is understandably raw. He’s struggled at times in finding the strike zone consistently, though scouts like his delivery and arm action enough to think he’ll figure it out with reps and instruction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morfe wasn’t a headliner of the Orioles’ 2023 international class, signing for $207,500 out of Venezuela as an undersized right-hander, and he struggled to throw strikes in his Dominican Summer League debut later that year. But he made a big leap forward in 2024, proving quickly he was too good for the DSL in his second go-around there before finishing the year with four starts at Single-A Delmarva as an 18-year-old. He racked up 49 strikeouts over 32 2/3 innings across the two levels, the equivalent of 13.5 strikeouts per nine. Morfe surprised a lot of evaluators with his ascent last summer and has surprisingly high-octane stuff for a pitcher his size. He only stands around 5-foot-8 but can dial his fastball up near triple digits, and it consistently lives in the upper 90s. What Morfe lacks in height he makes up for in athleticism and flexibility, using those qualities in tandem with a whippy arm to generate velocity that belies his size. His two secondary offerings are both hard, too: a mid-80s sweeping slider that can miss bats and a low-90s changeup with fade. The change especially showed big improvement last summer, going from a fringy offering to a potential plus pitch. It’s an advanced arsenal in an unpolished package, as Morfe’s command remains a work in progress. That’s not unusual for a young power pitcher, and Morfe was better at throwing strikes last year than his stats might imply because they were skewed by one ugly blow up start at the very end of the season. His three plus pitches and bulldog mentality remind some evaluators of Carlos Martinez, but to reach that ceiling, Morfe will need to prove he can throw enough strikes and that his body can handle a starter’s workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Endersby was recruited as an infielder but moved to the mound at Cal State Fullerton, where he totaled 16 2/3 innings in three years before transferring to Concordia (Calif.). He made just five starts at the NCAA Division II level during the shortened 2020 season, yet impressed the Astros enough to sign for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Double-A and struck out 110 in 97 innings. Endersby employs the north-south attack pattern that Houston favors. He goes after hitters with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball with high spin rates and carry up in the zone and an upper-70s curveball with downer break. He also has a harder slider with sweeping action and a nascent changeup that lags behind the rest of his offerings. Endersby lacks physicality but he's athletic and has a quick arm. His control and command come and go, as does the consistency of his secondary pitches, so it's more likely that he winds up as a reliever than a starter. If he moves to the bullpen and concentrates on his fastball and curveball, he could reach the big leagues in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 NCAA Division II player of the year after batting .408/.506/.901 with a school-record 28 homers at Point Loma Nazarene (Calif.), Christian transferred to San Diego for his Draft year. The Toreros' best power prospect since Kris Bryant, he slashed .364/.460/.828 with 26 homers to win West Coast Conference player of the year honors. He played briefly in Single-A after signing for $397,500 as a fifth-rounder. Christian's 6-foof-5, 225-pound frame gives him tremendous strength and leverage, and his right-handed stroke provides plenty of bat speed and loft. That combination results in well above-average raw power that allows him to smash balls out of any part of the ballpark. He does come with an aggressive approach and swing-and-miss concerns, especially against non-fastballs, and he struggled to produce with wood bats in college summer leagues. Christian moves well for his size, displaying fringy speed with decent instincts on the bases. After playing first base at Point Loma Nazarene, he moved to right field at San Diego and spent most of his short pro debut in left field. He has adequate range and average arm strength on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 The Reds have had success on the international market in recent years finding talent among five-figure signings, headlined by Elly De La Cruz. Jimenez looks to add to that collection after joining the organization in April 2024 for $82,500. After an impressive five-game showing in the Dominican Summer League later that year, the D.R. native got a full run through the circuit last season and posted an .819 OPS across 35 games. He played for the Sydney Blue Sox in the Australian Baseball League over the winter and hit four home runs with 18 RBIs across 38 contests while being nearly 6 years younger than the average competitor. A right-handed hitter, Jimenez shows excellent athleticism in the box and a feel for extra-base pop, although it’s not appeared consistently during game action. There’s some length to his swing and he’ll need to become more selective after running a 25.9 percent strikeout rate (with just a 9.5 percent walk rate) during his extended look in the DSL. But when he squares the ball up, it can really jump off his bat. He posted a 29.2 percent line-drive rate in 2025, which ranked him fourth among all Reds Minor Leaguers with at least 100 plate appearances. As can often be the case at the lower levels, he’s a pull-side fiend with a 58.5 percent rate for his balls in play last year. Jimenez played strictly shortstop during his time in Australia, but the Reds split his time almost 50/50 last year between there and the hot corner. With premier defensive shortstops at the lower levels like Liberts Aponte and Steele Hall, it’s likely that Jimenez moves around a bit, including seeing time at second base. He has average actions on the infield but a solid arm and quick first step, the latter evidenced his 16-for-17 mark on stolen-base attempts through his first 40 pro games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Reds 2023 rookie standout Matt McLain and Dodgers infield prospect Sean McLain, Nick redshirted at UCLA (Matt's alma mater) with a back injury in 2022 before transferring to Arizona State (Sean's alma mater). He broke his right hamate in 2023 and his left hamate last spring before finishing his college career with a 20-game hitting streak. Signed for an under-slot $800,000 as a third-rounder, he'll break into pro ball in 2025. A switch-hitter with bat speed and solid raw power from both sides of the plate, McLain ranks sixth in Sun Devils history with a career .658 slugging percentage. Though he's relatively compact at 5-foot-10 and 190 pounds, he drives the ball in the air with authority as both a lefty and righty. He makes consistent contact while controlling the strike zone and produced with wood bats in the Cape Cod League. McLain lost a touch of speed as he gained strength while in college, but he's still an average runner out of the box and quicker underway. While he's not a burner, the White Sox believe his instincts and fearlessness give him a chance to play center field in pro ball after he barely did at Arizona State. If he can't, his solid arm strength will fit well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While fellow infielder Nestor Miranda was the Tigers’ headline signing of the 2024 international class, Dickson had the better introduction to pro ball after signing for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He was one of the more impressive performers for the Tigers in the Dominican Summer League and earned a spot in the DSL All-Star Game. Dickerson has a lanky, athletic build with a solid swing that becomes more formidable as he physically matures. He had a leg kick when he signed, but the Tigers worked to quiet his stance. He was pull heavy in the DSL with a high rate of ground balls and fly balls and good extra-base power without a home run, but his aggressive approach was tempered by a good eye at the plate for his age. He’s an opportunistic baserunner whose high stolen-base total in the DSL came with a good success rate. He moves well at shortstop but could move positions as he fills out. Dickson’s success in the DSL should move him to the Florida Complex League as an 18-year-old. He has the tools to become a promising prospect, but his physical maturation will have a big impact on his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hipwell played just 76 games in three seasons at Santa Clara and had little experience with wood bats in summer ball, so he was tougher to evaluate than most collegians in the 2024 Draft. He lost the final three weeks of his sophomore year and the first two months of his junior season to a suspension for performance-enhancing drugs, which he attributed to an over-the-counter supplement. Signed for $345,700 as a sixth-rounder, he batted .196/.360/.402 with five homers and 40 strikeouts in his 29-game pro debut in Single-A. Hipwell is built to hit for a power with a quick left-handed stroke with loft, a strong 6-foot-3 frame and a pull-focused mindset. He has a patient-bordering-on-passive approach that results in walks, but it also leaves him behind in counts too often and leads to strikeouts. He pounds fastballs but had a 38 percent swing-and-miss rate against non-heaters in his debut. With below-average speed, Hipwell offers little value on the bases and limited range at third base. His solid arm strength fits the hot corner, but he's an erratic defender who may have to move. He played some right field and first base with the Broncos and also dabbled at second base in the MLB Draft League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez reached a deal with the A’s for $800,000 during the 2022 international signing period, a figure that was only topped among the club’s agreements that year by outfielder Carlos Pacheco, who signed for $1.2 million. After playing 44 games in the Dominican Summer League last year, his second summer there, he should make his United States debut in 2024. Gonzalez has outstanding bat-to-ball skills and an overall advanced approach at the plate. He has been described as hitterish in the box with an ability to drive the ball to all fields, and his power should show up more as he grows into his 6-foot-2 frame. Though young, he does seem to already be drawing his fair share of walks while also limiting the strikeout totals. While Gonzalez is considered more of a bat-first catcher, the A’s have been pleased with his defensive skills thus far, though there is certainly room for improvement behind the plate. He has an above-average arm and should stick as a backstop, but the A’s also will get him some time at first base this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Older than most Draft picks, Kopps had to bide his time before bursting onto the radar. He redshirted in 2016, missed 2018 after undergoing Tommy John surgery and then the pandemic shortened his 2020 campaign. However, he was nearly unhittable in 2021, pitching to a 0.90 ERA with a 0.76 WHIP, both of which led NCAA Division I. After racking up 131 strikeouts in 89 2/3 innings, Kopps was named the SEC Pitcher of the Year and also won the Dick Howser Trophy as the College Player of the Year. The Padres grabbed the Arkansas product in the third round and signed him to a below-slot $300,000 bonus. As a result of his workload in college, Kopps only threw 14 2/3 innings in his professional debut, but was just as dominant. Kopps has four pitches in his repertoire, but it’s his cutter that’s been the key to his success. The mid-80s offering has late movement and the right-hander is able to vary its depth depending on whether he wants to throw it in the zone, or try to get a hitter to chase. He also throws a low-90s fastball, an average curveball and a developing changeup. Kopps has shown decent control early in his career, but doesn’t always command his fastball as well as he’d like. Kopps has been 25 for the duration of the 2022 season and hasn’t moved as quickly as many would have hoped coming out of college, having been just OK at Double-A thus far. He’ll need to work on getting more swing-and-misses against advanced bats if he’s going to break through to San Diego as a 26-year-old in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foley worked as a freshman reliever for Indiana and got his collegiate career off to a solid start with 42 strikeouts in 29 innings. After a quick spin in the Appalachian League, he moved to the Hoosiers rotation for 2024 and got off to a strong start with four scoreless starts in his first eight only to suffer a back problem in his ninth. He missed two weeks and didn’t show the same control in his return, eventually finishing with a 4.71 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 82 strikeouts and 49 walks in 63 frames. The D-backs selected him in the fifth round as a Draft-eligible sophomore and went well above slot to sign him for $1 million. Foley touched 99 and showed a 93-95 mph fastball in both of his roles at Indiana, and the fact that his velocity held despite the back issues was promising. The heater plays well with good induced vertical break out of his over-the-top delivery, and batters from both sides struggle with it up in the zone. He plays off it nicely with a low-80s changeup that tumbles away arm side with so much separation it can look like it’s in slo-mo compared to the fastball. His short mid-80s slider was reserved for right-handers and was less effective. Standing 6-foot-5, Foley is a former all-state tight end in Indiana and brings a physical presence to the mound, but his command and control woes after the back issue heightened the concern that he’s still a reliever long term. Eliciting more chase outside the zone would help alleviate some of that as he gets going in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez-Gomez pitched one season each at San Bernardino Valley (Calif.) JC and Temple (Texas) JC before the Cubs signed him for an under-slot $100,000 in the 10th round, using some of the savings to land since-traded Zyhir Hope with their next pick. Used primarily as a reliever as a pro, he got torched in his debut and spent most of his first two seasons in Rookie ball. He broke out in 2025 with a 1.46 ERA and 29 percent strikeout rate at two Class A stops, which may earn him a chance to show what he can do as a starter this year. The key to Martinez-Gomez's success was developing a low-80 splitter that's a weapon, as he does an excellent job on killing spin before it dives under barrels. The splitter plays well off his fastball, which parks at 93-95 mph and touches 97 with sink and armside run. He also spins a fringy slider in the low 80s. Martinez-Gomez's athleticism helps him get down the mound well and create extension in his delivery, though it hasn't helped him repeat mechanics well enough to provide regular strikes. He has a career 16 percent walk rate in pro ball before slicing that mark to 6 percent at High-A during last season's final month. If he can maintain average control, he might become a back-of-the-rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts and recruiters mostly ignored Bush when he was a Texas prepster, but he went in the 16th round of the 2023 Draft after slashing .357/.510/.615 as a freshman at Tyler (Texas) JC. He earned High-A South Atlantic League all-star honors last year, though his OPS dropped from .812 there to .671 after he was promoted to Double-A in early August. He profiles as an offensive-minded backup catcher. The strength in Bush's 6-foot-4, 235-pound frame and the loft in his left-handed stroke give him solid to plus raw power that translates into high exit velocities and plays to all fields. He could provide 20 homers on an annual basis if he makes enough contact, though he has to prove he can catch up to quality fastballs and handle spin. Strikeouts will always be part of his package, though his patient approach also yields a fair amount of walks. Bush needs reps behind the plate to improve receiving and blocking skills, but those were hard to come by when he played alongside 2024 first-rounder Walker Janek in High-A. He's a well-below-average runner who isn't very agile as a catcher or at first base. His solid arm strength is his best defensive attribute, though he needs to improve his throwing accuracy after erasing just 17 percent of basestealers last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schubart has been a major power prospect for years, falling two hits shy of the Big 12 Conference triple crown as a sophomore before finishing his Oklahoma State career with 59 homers and a 1.169 OPS. His prodigious power has come with swing-and-miss concerns, though, which led to Cleveland grabbing him in the third round of the 2025 Draft and signing him for just under slot ($730,000). The Michigan native made a brief cameo at Single-A, where, true to his three-true outcome profile, 63.6 percent of his plate appearances ended with a homer, walk or strikeout. Standing at a hulking 6-foot-5, 223 pounds, Schubart has double-plus raw power -- where the vast majority of his value derives. It's more than just brute strength; the lefty slugger's bat speed and penchant for pulled air contact make him a home run machine. He's selective and waits for pitches he can hunt, which leads to impressive walk rates, but he often struggles to make contact in the zone. The Guardians are working to shorten his swing to counteract that problem, especially early in counts, even if whiffs will likely always be a part of his game. Schubart was still fairly productive against fellow southpaws in college, and maintaining that will be key to his future deployment. Given his massive size, Schubart is likely a first baseman long-term, although the Guardians will give him a chance to play an outfield corner several times per week. He doesn't have a great first step or the speed to make up for it, and his arm likely limits him to left if he can pass in the outfield. His lack of range also leaves him as a below-average defender at first. The good news is that if he's limited to DH, he has the type of raw power to still potentially make an impact there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever for most of his college career at the University of Nevada, Morris got a shot as a starter full-time in 2023 and racked up 85 strikeouts in 81 1/3 innings. Showing off stuff that looked much better than his 5.42 ERA might have indicated that year, Morris was selected by the Mets in the third round of the ‘23 Draft. Midway through his first full season as a professional, Morris was moved at the 2024 Trade Deadline to the A’s, who were high on the right-hander ever since scouting him as a somewhat local product at Pitman HS in Turlock, Calif., for right-hander Paul Blackburn. Morris proved to be a workhorse in his first full year in the A’s system last season, racking up a career-high 150 innings pitched as he began at Double-A Midland and ended at Triple-A Las Vegas. Morris can run his fastball up to 97 mph, while his sinker sits in the mid 90s with good armside run and generates a ton of ground balls. He’s added a low-80s sweeper as a variation from his mid-80s slider. His mid-70s curveball has improved, as has his upper-80s changeup, though that pitch remains behind his other offerings in terms of effectiveness. Morris’ demeanor as he struts his wiry 6-foot-3 frame around the mound reminds some within the organization of Mark “The Bird” Fidrych. He is a tenacious competitor and brings some personality whenever he toes the rubber. While he can throw up to seven different pitches, the A’s may try to work on simplifying his arsenal to three or four quality pitches, which should give him a better chance against big league hitters when his time comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending two years pitching mostly out of the bullpen for the University of Nevada-Reno, Morris worked his way into the rotation in 2023 and posted a 5.42 ERA with 85 strikeouts across 81 1/3 innings. Drafted by the Mets in the third round of the 2023 Draft, he began his first full professional campaign last season at Single-A St. Lucie and was promoted to High-A Brooklyn after six starts before getting sent to the A’s at the Trade Deadline in exchange for right-hander Paul Blackburn. Between Single-A, High-A and even a couple of outings with Triple-A Las Vegas, he combined for a 4.50 ERA with 121 strikeouts and 45 walks over 136 innings. Morris runs up his four-seam fastball to about 95-96 mph and also throws a sinker with good arm-side run in the 92-95 range. His mid-80s slider has developed into an above-average secondary offering. His mid-70s curveball provides a good variation of pitch speeds, though he is still working to make it a more consistent pitch, along with his improving upper-80s changeup. Morris is athletic with his 6-foot-3 frame. His competitive drive stands out whenever he takes the mound. Discovering the right arm slot that allows for the most consistency is the next big step in his development. How that pans out as he moves through the system will likely determine his long-term role, though he profiles as a back-end starter given his overall pitch mix and solid control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Way began his college career at NCAA Division II Belmont Abbey (N.C.) in 2019, then excelled at Northwest Florida State JC in the shortened 2020 season. The Yankees saw enough of him there and in the Cape Cod League the previous summer to take him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft. Way was having a good start to 2022 and continued that after he was one of three pitchers traded to the Royals for Andrew Benintendi at the Trade Deadline. Way finished the season in High-A Quad Cities and posted a 3.79 ERA in 35 2/3 innings with a 30.7% strikeout rate but an 11.1% walk rate. Utilizing a four-seam fastball with ride and a two-seamer with sink, Way is a power pitcher with a three- to four-pitch mix. He sits around 95 mph with his fastball and the low-80s with his plus slider, which features sweeping action and could be labeled as the best slider in the Royals’ system. Way’s tumbling changeup is his third pitch that he’ll need to use more as he moves up levels, but it has potential. There is some effort in Way’s delivery, but his lack of control and command are his biggest issues. While his stuff misses bats, he often finds himself out of counts and out of the zone. The Royals will develop Way as a starter until he shows them he’d be better suited out of the bullpen. Evaluators do see relieving in his future, where he can let his fastball and slider go in shorter stints. But at 6-foot-4 with a durable frame along with a three-pitch mix, Way will continue to start and see if he can fix the command issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Way spent his first season in college at NCAA Division II Belmont Abbey (N.C) at 2019 before impressing scouts in the Cape Cod League that summer, prompting him to transfer to Northwest Florida State JC so he'd be eligible for the 2020 Draft. He ranked third nationally among juco pitchers in wins (five), fourth in strikeouts (58 in 40 innings) and eighth in ERA (0.67) during the shortened season, then gave up a Louisiana State commitment after the Yankees selected him in the fourth round. He showcased a live arm during his pro debut last year, exhibited improved control to begin 2022 and was traded to the Royals at the Deadline in a deal for Andrew Benintendi. Way utilizes both four-seam fastballs with ride and two-seamers with sink and both gained velocity over the course of last season, each sitting around 93-96 mph with his four-seamer topping out at 99 late in the year. He also added some power and sweeping action to his low-80s slider, which shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch. His mid-80s changeup with tumble has potential as well but lacks consistency. Though Way dominated as a starter in junior college, many scouts believe he's more of a reliever. His lack of control and command are the biggest issue, and New York kept him in extended spring training for most of May last year so he could work on locating his pitches. There's effort in his delivery and he may be more effective just airing out his fastball and slider in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Way pitched at NCAA Division II Belmont Abbey (N.C.) as a freshman in 2019 before impressing in the Cape Cod League that summer and transferring to Northwest Florida State JC, making him eligible for the 2020 Draft. One of the top two-year college prospects in last year's crop, he ranked third nationally among juco pitchers in wins (five), fourth in strikeouts (58 in 40 innings) and eighth in ERA (0.67). He passed up a Louisiana State commitment to sign with the Yankees in the fourth round for an above-slot $600,000. Way sits at 91-95 mph and touches 97 with riding action on his four-seam fastball, and he still has room to add strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which could bring more velocity. His mid-80s changeup tumbles at the plate and grades as a plus pitch at times. His low-80s slider lags behind his other two pitches in terms of consistency and missing bats. While Way starred as a starter in junior college, some scouts believe he's destined to become a reliever. He'll need to refine his slider, maintain the improved control he showed as a sophomore and upgrade his command. He features some effort in his delivery and struggled to throw strikes while coming out of the bullpen at Belmont Abbey and on the Cape.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Groover was a consistent producer in his one year at UNC Charlotte and two years at NC State with a .349 combined average, and after the D-backs selected him in the second round in 2023, he’s carried that reputation right on through to pro ball. The corner infielder suffered a broken left wrist at High-A Hillsboro in his first full season but managed to still hit later at Double-A Amarillo and in the Arizona Fall League in ’24. He returned to the Texas League last season and spent the entire campaign there, hitting .309/.399/.434 with 12 homers in 123 games. Batting from a straight-up stance, the right-handed slugger keeps things loose but controlled in the box and doesn’t have much trouble shooting all pitch types into play as a result. He can catch up to velocity when needed and adapt to breaking stuff while also generally keeping his swings to the strike zone, except for with two strikes when he relies on his bat-to-ball skills to just get something on anything that’s close. He’s still yet to strike out more than 15 percent of the time in either of his first two full seasons. With that contact comes fringy pop, so it remains a hit-over-power profile. Groover saw time at first and second base in 2024 (and even played some outfield in college), but the D-backs gave him only starts at third last season to focus his development on the hot corner. He made some gains in agility and range there, but with a move to Triple-A in ’26, he’ll go back to mixing in first base as Arizona assesses its corner-infield options. With just average arm strength, Groover will need his bat to force the issue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A .351 hitter in his one season at UNC Charlotte, Groover never stopped hitting after transferring to NC State. He slashed .332/.430/.546 with 13 homers as a junior member of the Wolfpack, numbers that pushed him to the D-backs in the second round of the 2023 Draft. He looked set for a potentially big first full season before suffering a broken left wrist on a play at first base in his fourth game with High-A Hillsboro in 2024. He didn’t return to the Hops for three months, got a late-season promotion to Double-A Amarillo and dominated in hitter-friendly environs there with a .340/.400/.600 line in 13 games. Groover rounded out the year with a .339 average and .767 OPS in 18 Arizona Fall League contests. The right-handed hitter stands tall in the box, patiently waiting for his pitch with his hands behind his head ready to fire. He ran a 91 percent contact rate against Minor League fastballs in '24, per Synergy, to continue a trend going back to his collegiate days. Only changeups seemed to give him much trouble. His swings lack big oomph, however, and he continues to trend as more of a doubles hitter than a homer threat when away from the winds of Amarillo. A below-average runner, Groover has made some gains defensively at third base, where he’s quickened his release to make up for below-average arm strength, and the D-backs plan to keep getting him looks at second base as well as a potential Max Muncy type. It’s still possible, perhaps even likely, he lands at the cold corner long term or as a bat-first utilityman off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Groover hit .351 as a freshman at UNC Charlotte in 2021, transferred to NC State the following year and never stopped hitting for the Wolfpack. He produced a .332/.430/.546 line with 13 homers and a 26/36 K/BB ratio over 57 games as a junior last year and was selected by the D-backs in the second round that July, signing for exact slot at $1.783 million. Groover went 23-for-87 (.264) and struck out only nine percent of the time over a 23-game stint with High-A Hillsboro to end the summer. The right-handed slugger has a quiet and simple stance at the plate, letting his hands do the firing because of their impressive quickness. He manipulates the barrel well, too, helping him make contact against pitches of all types, and he especially feasted on fastballs, whiffing on only nine percent of his swings against heaters in college in 2023. His swing can be grooved, leading to solid line drives across the park, but he has 20-homer upside if he can elevate a bit more. Groover’s defense was his biggest drawback going into the Draft. Below-average speed made him a first baseman as a freshman and sophomore, and while his fast reactions helped him move to third base last year, he still lacks the range and arm strength (with a short throwing motion) to project as anything more than below-average at the position. His plus bat would hold up at the cold corner, second base or the outfield, where he also got looks in school. It was at first that he suffered a broken left wrist on April 9, an injury that kept him out for three months of his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout in high school who didn’t start pitching until he was 17, Natera had three uneven seasons at New Mexico State where he missed a lot of bats and walked a lot of hitters. The Angels took a low-risk flyer on the left-hander in the 17th round of the 2022 Draft, and he kept striking guys out and giving them free passes during his pro debut with High-A Tri-City in 2023. A sprained elbow kept him off the mound for all but 15 innings during the regular season, but he opened a lot of eyes with his work over five Arizona Fall League outings. It was a small sample size spanning just 12 innings, but Natera’s combination of size, stuff and better feel for the zone made people sit up and take notice. His fastball averaged around 94-95 mph and touched 98, and it plays up because of its life that allows it to get a lot of swings and misses. His 82-85 mph slider has good sweep to it, giving him another bat-missing offering. He has a changeup, but he doesn’t throw it very often. While Natera is already 25, he has very low mileage on his arm between starting late, the pandemic and the missed time in 2024. In his brief mound time last year, he was finding the strike zone with more consistency, raising the bar a little bit more. Left-handers who are 6-foot-4 and have two out pitches tend to make it to the big leagues, so everyone is intrigued to see how Natera follows up his AFL breakout.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick in the 2021 Draft after he grew from a reliever into a starter at Tennessee, Chad “Cheese” Dallas opened his pro career with what you could call a learning experience in ‘22. That year with High-A Vancouver, Dallas posted a 4.60 ERA over 88 innings, with a walk rate of 5.2 BB/9 holding him back. Some improvements to Dallas’ body and repertoire helped him regain some momentum in ‘23, as he posted a 3.65 ERA over 123 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A, cutting that walk rate along the way. Dallas’ projection is still more about the overall package than overwhelming stuff, though his slider could be a plus pitch that misses serious bats in the big leagues. He threw the low-80s offering 40 percent of the time during his stint in New Hampshire. He’s added a bit of velocity over the years and is doing a better job of maintaining it now, but Dallas has been sitting near 93 mph and could benefit from a bit more because of the movement profile. He’ll need to spot that fastball with top-end precision to make everything else work. One new wrinkle is the cutter that Dallas has developed, which should help him against left-handed hitters. This is the type of pitcher the Blue Jays could benefit from developing in waves, particularly after a few years of thin rotation depth. Dallas may not match the ceilings of some of the names higher on this list, but he’s given himself a good shot with a strong floor and deep mix of pitches. He’ll have every opportunity to position himself well behind that first wave of Ricky Tiedemann, Bowden Francis, Yariel Rodriguez and others in Toronto’s depth picture if he gets off to a strong start. He’ll need to hit his spots, though, because Dallas won’t get away with as many misses on his fastball as some other starters might.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After striking out 71 batters in 39 innings as a freshman at Panola Junior College (Texas) in 2019, Dallas was recruited by Tennessee as a reliever. Instead, he developed into the Volunteers’ No. 1 starter and helped pitch them to their first College World Series since 2005. The Blue Jays made him a fourth-round selection in ’21 and signed him slightly over slot value at $497,500. Nicknamed “Cheese,” Dallas has gotten the velocity on his fastball to tick up since the Draft, and it now sits around 93 mph, touching 95 mph. There could be room for a bit more, too, which would leave Dallas’ arrow pointing up into ’22. The biggest addition for Dallas has been a mid-80s cutter that’s tough on right-handers while his low-80s curveball is a pitch he’s comfortable with in any count, too. At 5-foot-11, Dallas is a different look physically than many of the larger-built starters in the Blue Jays’ organization, but he makes it work by pounding the zone and competing. In '22, left-handed hitters will be one challenge to monitor, which is where an improved changeup would really benefit him. There’s bullpen potential here, of course, and that’s something Dallas would be familiar with, but he’ll be rolled out as a starter and could move quickly given his experience against quality NCAA competition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCambley has impressed scouts with his feel for spin since he was a Pennsylvania high schooler, though he went undrafted in 2017 because he had a minor knee injury and was considered unsignable. A strong summer in the Cape Cod League followed by a dominant if shortened 2020 college season propelled him into the third round that June, making him the second-highest drafted pitcher in Coastal Carolina history. He carved up High-A hitters in his 2021 pro debut, but battled his control and command after a promotion to Double-A in mid-July. McCambley had arguably the best curveball in the 2020 Draft, and his breaker now sits at 82-85 mph with high spin rates, plenty of depth and so much horizontal action that some scouts call it a slider. He also imparts plenty of spin on his four-seam fastball, which parks at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with riding action up in the strike zone. He ran into trouble in Double-A when more advanced hitters chased his curve less frequently and teed off on his heater when he didn't command it well. Though the Marlins will continue to develop McCambley as a starter for now, he likely will wind up as a reliever. His mid-80s changeup is too firm and lacks consistent life, and the effort in his delivery detracts from his ability to locate his fastball and curveball with much precision. He has the stuff to play a high-leverage role coming out of the bullpen, especially if he adds more velocity working in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCambley lacked consistency while shuttling between the rotation and bullpen in his first two years at Coastal Carolina, then broke out with a strong summer in the Cape Cod League and dominated during the shortened 2020 college season. Part of the Marlins' all-pitching Draft last June, he signed for a below-slot $775,000 in the third round. The second-highest drafted pitcher in Chanticleers history, he got his first pro experience during instructional league. Some scouts thought McCambley had the best curveball in the 2020 Draft, a low-80s bender with high spin rates that dives at the plate and grades as a plus-plus weapon at times. He also imparts a lot of spin on his fastball, which parks at 90-94 mph, tops out at 96 and has carry up in the strike zone. His changeup isn't nearly as effective as his two best pitches, partly because he didn't use it much as an amateur. McCambley comes with reliever risk because the effort in his three-quarters delivery detracts from his fastball command and his curveball breaks so much that more advanced hitters may lay off it when he can't land it in the strike zone. In order to remain a starter, he'll need to refine his changeup and his ability to locate his pitches with more precision. If he winds up in the bullpen, his fastball and curveball could land him a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bowen could have played baseball and football at Michigan State coming out of an Ohio high school, but the Pirates tempted him into pro ball instead with an over-slot $392,500 bonus as an 11th-rounder in 2019. He flashed an intriguing power-speed combination in the Bucs' system -- most evident in a 23-homer, 26-steal campaign at High-A and Double-A in '23 -- but didn’t reach Triple-A until '25. The Padres signed Bowen as a Minor League free agent back in November and saw him take off in Spring Training and the first month of action at Triple-A El Paso. The right-handed-hitting outfielder bops his front leg in his slightly open stance before getting going with a leg kick. He’s been hitting the ball harder with El Paso with a max exit velocity of 112.6 mph and a 90th-percentile EV of 106.4 entering late April. He can elevate well to help him pick up extra-base hits in bunches too; in fact, he hit for the cycle in just his fifth game of 2026. But while he’s reeled in some of the aggression he showed early in his career, he still expands the zone too much, which would limit that power and overall hitting potential in The Show, and he’s particularly vulnerable on breakers down and away out of the zone. Even so, Bowen is at least an above-average runner capable of pushing for extra bases on balls to the gap or stealing bags when opportunities arise. That athleticism helps him on the grass too, and the Padres have played him at all three outfield spots to take advantage of it with an early emphasis on center field. With his twitchy toolset, Bowen could finally be pushing for an MLB debut as a fourth/fifth outfielder in his age-25 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There’s long been a complaint that baseball hasn’t been doing enough to attract premium athletes to the pro game. The Pirates did their part at the start of Day 3 of the 2019 Draft when they took Bowen, a two-sport star from the Ohio high school ranks, in Round 11. They went over slot with a $392,500 bonus to sign him away from playing football and baseball at Michigan State. He’s shown off an improving power-speed combination in three years of full-season ball, reaching Double-A in 2023 and capping things off with a solid showing in the Arizona Fall League. Bowen brings a football mentality to how he attacks the game, both in terms of his work ethic and how he’d run through a wall while playing center field. While his numbers were no doubt helped by hitting-friendly High-A Greensboro in 2023, the metrics under his 20-20 season were very good. He routinely registers high exit velocities with quality contact and does damage more consistently from the right side of the plate. There’s still work to be done on his approach as he continues to focus on not chasing and expanding the zone, with sweepers from right-handed pitchers particularly his kryptonite. With above-average speed and that aggressiveness a plus on the basepaths, Bowen continues to be a legitimate basestealing threat. He’s an excellent defender who can definitely play center and also looks good in the corners with a strong arm, and he’s also proven to be a capable first baseman. He likely profiles as a fourth outfielder, but the quality of his at-bats in the AFL was encouraging, and if he can cut down the K’s and up his walk rate, there could be more here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arroyo was one of the youngest players in the 2021 Draft class when he was the best player coming out of Puerto Rico and selected by the Mariners in the second round. He was having a solid first full season of pro ball at age 18 when he was part of the prospect package sent to the Reds for Luis Castillo at the 2022 Trade Deadline. Arroyo made a nice step up in 2023, reaching Double-A briefly, but then was derailed by a torn left labrum that cost him his 2024 season. He turned in a full 2025 campaign, and though reduced impact at the plate has led to some questions about his ultimate ceiling, he was added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. The Reds view the fact that Arroyo played 120 games at Double-A in 2025 as a win coming off that injury, then he added some more productive at-bats playing winter ball in Puerto Rico. He’s a switch-hitter who can make a ton of contact from both sides of the plate. It looked like added strength was contributing to more power, which didn’t reappear in 2025, perhaps because of the injury. He’s an aggressive hitter who is prone to chase too much and can struggle with softer stuff, but he also didn’t elevate the ball nearly as consistently last year compared with his pre-injury performances. One thing that has never been questioned is his defense and he still very much has the chops to play shortstop, with the actions and arm to stay there for a long time. He did get introduced to second base last year and he’ll continue to focus on both sides of the bag, giving the Reds options should they need help in Cincinnati now that he’s on the roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because Arroyo was just 17 years old when the Mariners drafted him in 2021, the native of Puerto Rico has always been very young for every level he's reached so far. So even after two full seasons in 2022 and 2023, the latter of which including getting dealt to the Reds in the Luis Castillo deal, and a missed 2024 season because of a torn left labrum suffered in Spring Training, he'll still be only 21 years old for the bulk of the 2025 season. Arroyo had touched Double-A in 2023 with a big up arrow next to his name, and he was able to shake off the rust from the layoff by holding his own in the Arizona Fall League in 2024. Arroyo’s time in the AFL was more about him starting to get his timing back at the plate while proving to himself that he put the injury behind him, so even though his offensive numbers were modest, those missions were accomplished. The switch-hitter swings the bat well from both sides with a contact-first approach that allows him to send line drives to all fields. Before the injury, his power started to show up more consistently and there should be more of that in the tank to come. A very aggressive baserunner with above-average speed, Arroyo likes to steal bags and take extra bases. The one thing that wasn’t rusty at all during his Fall League stint was Arroyo’s glovework. He’s a smooth defender with excellent body control, showing the ability to make all the plays and throws from all angles, with evaluators thinking he could play shortstop defensively in the big leagues right now. For now, though, he’ll get to focus on playing a full healthy year at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest members of the 2021 Draft class, Arroyo got more exposure to scouts when he relocated from Puerto Rico to Florida for his senior year of high school. Drafted at age 17, he went in the second round to the Mariners and was having a solid first full season of pro ball when he was sent to the Reds in the Deadline deal for Luis Castillo. He struggled initially after the trade and had just a .576 OPS through the end of May 2023, after which he righted the ship. He slashed .276/.356/.474 the rest of the way, including a bump up to Double-A to close out the season. That momentum came to a halt when he needed surgery to repair a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder in March, ending his 2024 season before it began. Before the injury, the Reds felt everything was trending up for the switch-hitting shortstop, who was set to play at age 20 for almost all of the 2024 season. He has a good swing from both sides of the plate, with a line-drive approach that produces hard contact to all fields. He started really coming into some \"man strength\" as the 2023 season progressed, and he started tapping into his extra-base authority more consistently, with some thinking he’s going to have at least average power eventually. After his rough start, he tightened up his approach and cut his strikeout rate considerably, all while raising his walk rate. Arroyo has swiped 56 bases over his first two full seasons of pro ball and should be a threat to steal as he continues to the upper levels of the Reds' system. He’s worked very hard on his defense at short, especially on balls to his glove side, exhibiting impressive body control and leaving no doubt about his ability to play the premium position. The Reds were impressed with his emotional maturity as much as his physical growth, leaving some thinking he’s primed for a breakout season once he’s fully returned from the shoulder injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arroyo was just 17 when the 2021 Draft rolled around and after impressing on the summer showcase circuit, the Puerto Rican infielder relocated to Florida for his senior year of high school for more exposure. The Mariners liked what they saw and took him in the second round of that summer’s Draft, and he was giving an early return on investment with a strong first full season in the Single-A California League when he was sent to the Reds in the Luis Castillo deal. Still only 19 years old for nearly all of the 2023 season, Arroyo has the chance to be a dynamic up-the-middle player. He swings the bat well from both sides of the plate and was productive each way, showing the ability to make hard contact with a line-drive approach. He’s added a good amount of strength to his wiry build already, and that led to more power than anticipated out of the gate, though he’s still more of a hit-over-power type. He could become even more of an impact hitter as he tightens up his approach, something that got away from him post-trade as he was likely pressing too much. If he continues to hit at all, Arroyo could be an elite-level player because there’s no doubt he’s going to be able to play shortstop for a long time. He has excellent hands and actions at the premium position, with more than enough arm to make throws from all over the infield. Assuming he gets his bearings with his new organization, he should continue to prove he has the tools to be an everyday shortstop in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the younger players in the 2021 Draft class, at age 17, Arroyo quickly established himself as the best player from Puerto Rico on the showcase circuit the summer prior. The potential shortstop got the chance to be evaluated more closely last spring after coming to Florida to attend Central Pointe Christian Academy for his senior season, which led to the Mariners taking him in the second round in 2021 and signing him for $1.65 million. He was having a stellar first full season, sitting in the Top 10 among California League hitters in a host of offensive categories when he was sent to the Reds as part of the package for Luis Castillo. Arroyo has an intriguing package of athleticism, defense and offensive potential, and he was making a quicker-than-expected transition to full-season ball in 2022. A switch-hitter who is a bit better from the right side, Arroyo has good contact skills and is a solid line-drive hitter. While he entered pro ball lacking strength, Arroyo has been praised for his sneaky wiry-strong build, and he was already starting to grow into some extra-base pop, with potentially more to come. Defensively, Arroyo has every chance to stick at shortstop, with plenty of arm strength, good hands and easy actions at the premium position. Arroyo can actually throw with both hands and has pitched left-handed, though that doesn’t necessarily mean he’ll do so professionally. Arroyo certainly had a wake-up call with his first taste of pro ball in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, hitting .211/.337/.324 (.661 OPS) with a 30.2% strikeout rate in 21 games, and used that lesson to work on his offensive game. If the bat continues to come along, he has the chance to eventually be an everyday shortstop in the big leagues.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 5’11″, 175 | Bat/Throw: S/R | 2nd Round (48), 2021 (SEA) | ETA: 2026

Arroyo missed the entirety of the 2024 regular season due to labrum surgery during Spring Training. He turned in a fine 2025 campaign, but struggled to produce much power. Mechanical adjustments and added strength have helped Arroyo tap into much more power in 2026 as the glove and defensive versatility continue to stand out.

A switch hitter with a similar set up from both sides of the plate, Arroyo simplified his operation from both sides. Previously featuring a very crouched setup that would cause his weight to sway, pushing onto his front side prematurely. Arroyo is now more upright with his setup, coiling over his back side, rather than teetering over it and pushing out.

Staying taller on his back side has helped him leverage the ground more effectively, aiding both his raw power and batted ball angles. His setup was even more dramatically crouched from the left side, with his front knee bowed and open. His hands are also closer to his launch position from both sides, compared to the previous lower starting point, below his back shoulder.

The quality of contact shift through the first half of 2026 is impossible to overlook, not just on the surface where he nearly matched his career-high home run total through his first 50 games, but in the raw power and batted ball angles as well.

Arroyo upped his 90th percentile exit velocity by two MPH, while cutting his ground ball rate by nearly 20% and doubling his Air Pull percentage. Previously featuring below average exit velocities, Arroyo’s now average raw impact paired with the improved angles makes 20 home runs an attainable plateau.

The contact skills are above average for Arroyo from both sides of the plate, with the aforementioned swing adjustments improving his ability to handle secondaries as well. Though the contact skills are strong, Arroyo can hurt himself with his aggressive approach, consistently running a chase rate at or around 35%.

Above average hit and leaps in the power department give Arroyo the upside to be an above average contributor offensively, but the swing decisions could hold him back some.

An above average runner and sure-handed defender with a plus arm Arroyo provides plenty of value in the infield, with the ability to play an above average shortstop with comfort moving all over the diamond. Arroyo has improved his efficiency as a base stealer and should be a threat for around 20 bags annually.

Though losing out on his 2024 campaign was a tough blow for his development, Arroyo proved to have his feet back under him in 2025 before appearing to really put things together in his age 22 season in 2026. Arroyo’s offensive improvements give him the upside of an everyday shortstop, as even league average production with his glove and speed should give him a reasonable path to 3-WAR. If the bat stalls at the highest level (would likely be due to swing decision issues and the power uptick perhaps not translating against big league competition), Arroyo has the fallback of a quality infield utility piece, giving him a high probability of sticking on a big league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez starred in college at Mississippi, winning national freshman of the year accolades in 2021 and a College World Series championship in 2022 while also starting for the U.S. collegiate national team both summers. When questions about his athleticism creeped up during his junior season, he slipped from a potential top-five pick to No. 15 overall, where he signed for an under-slot $3.9 million. He has done little damage as pro, slashing .232/.310/.335 in his first three seasons while reaching Triple-A. While Gonzalez has continued to control the strike zone and consistently put the ball in play just like he did with the Rebels, he has lapsed into a defensive approach at the plate and makes too much soft contact. After displaying 25-homer power potential in college, he rarely turns his left-handed stroke loose and rarely drives the ball with authority. Adjustments to quicken his load, improve his bat path and allow him to pull more pitches won't make much difference unless he swings with more intent. Gonzalez has below-average speed but his instincts allow him to play better than that on the bases and in the field. He has sure hands, solid arm strength and a finely calibrated internal clock, though he's not particularly rangy. Primarily a shortstop in his first two years as a pro, he spent more time at second base in 2025 and may not be more than utilityman unless he gets his bat going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez had a decorated college career at Mississippi, winning national freshman of the year honors in 2021, helping lead the Rebels to their first-ever College World Series title in 2022 and starting for the U.S. collegiate national team during both summers. Questions about his athleticism arose during his junior season, so he dropped to the 15th overall pick, where the White Sox signed him for $3.9 million. He has slashed just .233/.313/.326 while reaching Double-A in his first two pro seasons, though he did star in the Southern League playoffs last September as Birmingham won the championship. After controlling the strike zone and making consistent contact in college, Gonzalez has continued to do the same in pro ball. But the 25-homer upside he showed as an amateur hasn't translated, and it now looks like he'll have to add some strength and use a more selectively aggressive approach to produce 12-15 per year. Even after making adjustments to quicken his load and give him a better left-handed swing path, he still struggled to pull pitches or drive them with much authority in 2024. Gonzalez is a below-average runner with solid instincts on the bases but questions about his ability to remain at shortstop. He's a sure-handed defender with solid arm strength and a good internal clock, and the White Sox think he can cover enough ground at short. Others think he's better suited for second base (where he saw some action last season) or third base, which would put more demands on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
