As he’s grown and gained strength, he’s been running better and shows good instincts on the basepaths. Those instincts carry over to his work on the dirt as well. He has excellent actions and more than enough arm to play shortstop long-term. Given that he might still grow and add strength, when coupled with his advanced feel for the game already, there’s a lot of upside to dream on as Amador begins his pro career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Waldrep spent two years at Southern Miss before transferring to Florida for his junior year. He showed off premium stuff, albeit with mixed results, in the Gators’ weekend rotation, enough for the Braves to make him their first-round pick in 2023. He kind of was the college version of AJ Smith-Shawver in that the Braves pushed Waldrep quickly, up to Triple-A during his summer debut and then calling him up to the big leagues in 2024, though elbow inflammation slowed him at the highest level. Like Smith-Shawver, Waldrep has shown he has legitimate swing-and-miss stuff in his race to Atlanta, and while AJSS might have the better fastball, Waldrep’s secondary stuff is superior. That’s especially true of his 85-86 mph splitter, which routinely misses bats with spin rates under 1,000 rpm. He can fall in love with it a bit too much on occasion, but it’s hard to find fault with that given how effective it is. He also has a hard upper-80s slider that flashes plus and his heater is plenty hard enough, up to 99 mph, even though it doesn’t feature a ton of life and can get squared up. There’s long been some effort in Waldrep’s up-tempo delivery, leading to command issues. He walked 4.3 per nine in 2024 and will have to show he can throw his impressive secondary stuff for strikes more consistently in order to be a starter long-term in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years of showing dominant stuff at Southern Miss, one as a reliever and one in the weekend rotation, Waldrep entered the transfer portal and moved to the University of Florida for his junior year. The Team USA alum served as the Gators’ Saturday starter and continued to show off an impressive power repertoire, with uneven results. He showed enough for the Braves to take him with their first-round pick, then watched him race up the organizational ladder, touching all four full-season stops and finishing at Triple-A. There is no question about Waldrep’s stuff playing against good competition. He left college with a career 13.5 K/9 rate, then struck out 12.6 per nine during his pro debut last summer. His bread-and-butter is an absolutely unhittable splitter, an upper-80s pitch that generated a miss rate north of 60 percent both at Florida and at the upper levels of the Braves system. He doesn’t always command his fastball well, but it has plenty of velocity, up to 99 mph consistently. He also has a hard upper-80s slider that is plus at times and misses a lot of bats as well. Waldrep has used an up-tempo delivery with some effort in the past, something he’ll have to keep working on so he can land his premium stuff in the zone more consistently. There’s a little reliever risk here, but if he can iron things out, his frontline starter stuff could play in a big league rotation soon. Even if it doesn’t quite click, his stuff in shorter stints could be downright nasty in high-leverage bullpen situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Povich turned himself from a hardly-recruited highschooler into a first-team All-Big Ten hurler in 2021, when the Twins took notice, drafting him in the third round that year. He was making a name for himself missing a ton of bats at High-A when the Twins dealt him to the Orioles at the ‘22 Trade Deadline for Jorge Lopez. He finished his first full season at Double-A Bowie and reached Triple-A in 2023, flashing occasional brilliance, but he’s also been maddeningly inconsistent at both upper levels with Baltimore. Povich racked up at least nine strikeouts in five of his starts last summer -- including a 13-strikeout one-hit performance in June -- and allowed at least five runs or lasted three innings or fewer in eight others. Between Double- and Triple-A, he owned a career 5.34 ERA entering the 2024 season, but more consistency with Double-A led to his first call up to the big leagues. The left-hander has four distinct pitches and when he’s commanding them, he’s one of the best pitching prospects in the system. His heater is a high-spin fastball that gets swings and misses up in the zone despite average-ish velocity, but can flash as hard as 96 mph. He also relies on a big, sweeping slider and a changeup with depth off his fastball that flashes plus and helps neutralize right-handed hitters. When Povich loses the feel for that changeup, hitters can sit on his fastball and he struggles. Being able to spot the slider and curveball with more consistency would help, but his ability to locate his offspeed stuff wavers. The 6-foot-3 Povich’s wiry, broad-shouldered build and good mechanics suggest he will be able to refine his mechanics with more reps. Walks can still remain an issue, as they did during his first time up with Baltimore. He needs to throw more strikes with all his pitches and continue refining his secondary stuff. If he does that, his combination of stuff and pitchability give Povich the ingredients to develop into a mid-to-back-end starter who still has a chance to pop beyond that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hardly recruited out of high school, Povich pitched in junior college in Arizona for a year before transferring to Nebraska, where he grew into a first-team All-Big Ten hurler by 2021. That success prompted the Twins to snag him in the third round that year, and he parlayed a tantalizing small-sample debut into a solid start at High-A in 2022. Povich wasn’t dominating, but was missing a ton of bats when the Twins dealt him to the Orioles at the ’22 Trade Deadline for Jorge Lopez. Povich racked up 148 strikeouts in 114 innings with a 4.50 ERA across two levels in his first full season, finishing the year at Double-A Bowie. Povich’s stuff ticked up when he first entered pro ball compared to pre-Draft expectations. He mostly works in the low 90s but can flash 96 mph with the fastball, sitting more in the 92-93 range consistently. He can throw strikes with his entire five-pitch arsenal, which also features a changeup with depth off his fastball, a big sweeping slider, a slower curveball and a distinct cutter. It’s a clean delivery that should, with more reps, help hone the consistency of the fastball movement, allowing that pitch to play up even more. His solid walk rate at both levels last year and good mechanics project at least above-average command. Povich was hit harder upon the jump to Double-A last summer, which the Orioles believe was somewhat attributed to bad luck in a small sample. He’ll be just 23 years old for ’23, with all the ingredients to develop into a mid-to back-end starter or better. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see his stock continue to rise as he continues to gain exposure to professional hitters, especially if the fastball keeps trending up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones was the Rays’ first-round pick in 2019, signed for $3,027,000, and entered their system with high expectations due to his speed, switch-hitting and power potential. He lived up to the hype in his professional debut and kept it going in High-A after the lost pandemic season, but he hasn’t matched that production since. He was talented and toolsy enough for the Rays to place him on their 40-man roster after a disappointing 2022 season in Double-A. He was sent to the Rockies in March in return for pitching prospect Joe Rock. Jones reached Triple-A last year and performed well, albeit with an unsustainably high .440 batting average on balls in play, then his season ended early due to a right hamstring strain. He struggled in Double-A before that and still struck out in 38.8 percent of his plate appearances overall. A certain level of swing-and-miss will always be part of his game, but his continued struggles against offspeed pitches combined with an inability to stay healthy makes Jones a frustrating prospect to evaluate. He hits fastballs well enough but has just enough bat speed and raw power to get himself in trouble, as he might occasionally be better served just putting the ball in play and wreaking havoc with his elite speed. The Rays saw him as an above-average defender at two premium positions -- shortstop and center field -- but the numbers and eye test don’t necessarily agree. He has piled up errors at short throughout his career, with a case to be made that he’s getting to balls nobody else would even attempt a play on due to his range, and he only just moved to the outfield last spring. He could carve out some sort of role as a speed-and-defense option off the bench, but it’s all theoretical if he doesn’t stay healthy or start hitting, questions that have now followed him for years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A first-round pick as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2019 who signed for $3,027,000, the speedy, switch-hitting shortstop impressed the Rays in his professional debut and spent some time at the alternate training site in 2020. Then he performed well at High-A Bowling Green in 2021 after recovering from an early quad strain before appearing overmatched with Double-A Montgomery. His 2022 showing in Double-A was underwhelming, as he hit .238/.318/.392 with only eight homers and a nearly 36 percent strikeout rate in 79 games but ended the year with a spot on Tampa Bay’s jam-packed 40-man roster. Optimistically, you can point to Jones’ sheer athleticism, natural ability and tools that could lead to him being a productive big leaguer in a lot of different ways. He has impressive bat speed and surprising power for someone who’s also a plus-plus runner. You could argue his struggles last season were the result of a wrist injury that was more limiting than he let on, and if he hits enough to get to his power, everything else takes care of itself. Similarly, you could argue that his range at shortstop – which leads to some spectacular plays -- almost makes him look worse than he is; he’ll get to balls that he can’t realistically turn into outs, but he’ll try anyway, which is how errors pile up. But the concerns are obvious, especially about his bat and his ability to handle offspeed pitches. He’s a good enough shortstop to stick there, but now that he’s on the 40-man roster, he must find a way to become a potential big leaguer -- and he’s not about to take Wander Franco’s job or surpass Taylor Walls as a defensive shortstop. That could mean finally introducing him to center field, where his elite speed would play well, and creating different paths to playing time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones was Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2019 and became the highest ever pick out of UNC Wilmington when the Rays selected him 22nd overall. After signing for full slot value at $3,027,000, the speedy switch-hitter made a strong first impression with a 163 wRC+ and 19 steals in 48 games with Class A Short Season Hudson Valley. Jones got a few weeks in at Tampa Bay’s alternate site in 2020 before making his true full-season debut last summer. After suffering an early quad strain, Jones was a promising age-23 performer at High-A Bowling Green (.291/.389/.527, 13 homers, 27 steals) and received a late promotion to Double-A Montgomery, where he was overmatched in a short sample. Jones isn’t your typical speedster prospect. His plus-plus wheels indeed catch scouts’ eyes first, and the Rays say he might have the best straight-line speed in the organization. However, he also possesses impressive bat speed capable of resulting in some rockets out of the box. Swing-and-miss concerns, however, have only gotten worse in 2022 and have caused his stock to tumble as a 24-year-old. The Rays came away most impressed by Jones’ defensive improvements at shortstop last season, and while it was thought he would eventually move to center field, that has become less of a concept as he’s made more highlight and 50-50 plays at the premium position. Once a quality up-the-middle talent, Jones brings too many offensive questions to be looked at as a potential regular now. The rest of his many tools will still give him chances in The Show, perhaps next year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones, the highest Draft pick ever out of UNC Wilmington, landed with the Rays as a sophomore-eligible prospect in the first round in 2019. He developed a reputation in the Colonial Athletic Association as a switch-hitting speedster, having ranked fifth among all Division I players in steals, and he lived up to that reputation during his professional debut in the New York-Penn League. Playing at 21 years old in 2019, Jones hit .335/.413/.461 with 19 steals in only 48 games. Jones joined the Rays’ player pool on Sept. 1, 2020, missed most of their instructional league camp with a minor injury and reported to big league Spring Training this year. Jones’ athleticism and knack for stealing bases aren’t in question, and the Rays believe there’s significant upside in his bat. His speed has helped him leg out hits that others might not get, but he also makes hard contact from both sides of the plate. He already had the bat speed and strength necessary to project he’ll hit for average power, although he hit just one home run in his pro debut, then he added what he called “10 pounds of good weight” in 2020. With that extra muscle on his frame and additional loft to his swing that the Rays believe will come in time as he develops, Jones has the potential for above-average power to go along with his plus-plus speed. Jones has dynamic tools across the board, so he has the range and arm to handle shortstop. Some scouts wonder if he might be better served in center field, where his speed would also play well. Even with their system stacked with middle infielders, though, the Rays are going to give him every opportunity to stick there to see how his tool set plays over the course of a full season. Wherever he winds up in the field, Jones has the look of a future everyday player up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best sophomore-eligible prospect at a four-year college in the 2019 Draft, Jones benefited from some late spring helium after he garnered the Colonial Athletic Association's Player of the Year and tournament MVP awards. The Rays made Jones the highest-drafted player in UNC Wilmington history that June, selecting the switch-hitting speedster with the No. 22 overall pick, and he rewarded the organization with an impressive pro debut in the New York-Penn League, finishing among the circuit leaders with a .335 average (third), .413 OBP (third) and 19 steals (tied-fourth). With his elite athleticism, plus-plus speed and basestealing prowess, Jones knows how to create havoc when he gets on base and did a better job of doing so in 2019. He controls the zone and makes hard contact from both sides of the plate, with his wheels enabling him to steal hits on the ground. Jones’ bat speed and strength give him average raw power from both sides of the plate during batting practice that has yet to translate it into over-the-fence pop. He’s more likely to be a source of extra-base hits than home-run power, though double-digit dingers isn’t out of the question. Jones’ athleticism and blazing speed make him a rangy defender at shortstop and he has the raw arm strength required for the position. His stiff hands and inconsistent throws leave something to be desired, though, and some scouts already wonder whether he’ll end up as a plus defender in center field. Regardless of his future defensive home, Jones has a bright future as an everyday player with his athleticism, tools and skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An eighth-round pick in 2019, Herz signed with the Cubs for $500,000 (roughly fourth-round money) to set aside a commitment to North Carolina in his home state. Four years later, he was repeating Double-A Tennessee with strong results (3.97 ERA, 80 strikeouts in 59 innings) when Chicago traded him to the Nationals in a three-player deal for Jeimer Candelario. Herz continued to generate whiffs at Double-A Harrisburg, and a solid showing in the hitter-friendly Arizona Fall League sealed the southpaw’s 40-man-roster status ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility this offseason. The 6-foot-2 left-hander picked up a Vulcan changeup grip from Cubs senior pitching coordinator Casey Jacobson, and the pitch perfectly fit his natural pronating motion. The 79-81 mph cambio separates nicely off Herz’s low-90s fastball and drops nicely off the table as it approaches the plate, leading to impressive whiff and chase rates at Double-A. Late life on the heater helps it get more whiffs than the velo alone would indicate. His 81-85 mph slider is the more consistent of his breaking balls, and because he can’t land his upper-70s curveball for strikes as often, he’s more vulnerable to walking righties despite the changeup advantage. Post-AFL, Herz admitted he needs to work on his directionality toward the plate and get less “crossfire-y” to help his control. His 13.9 percent Double-A walk rate hinders his chances of starting, now that he’s knocking on Washington’s door, but the arsenal is there for him to get a rotation look or settle in as a two-pitch bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts thought Herz had the most live arm among North Carolina high school pitchers in 2019, but his murky signability dropped him to the eighth round. The Cubs surprised other teams when they got him to give up a North Carolina scholarship for $500,000, the equivalent of fourth-round money. After a rough first turn at Double-A Tennessee in 2022, the left-hander returned to the Southern League this season with much better results, including 80 strikeouts in 59 innings, before he moved to the Nationals at the Trade Deadline in a deal for Jeimer Candelario. Herz barely used a changeup as an amateur, but now it's his best pitch, as he sells his low-80s cambio with fastball arm speed before it vanishes at the plate. His heater sits at 91-94 mph and tops out at 96 with late life that keeps it off barrels. He was able to thrive at the lower levels with mainly those two offerings before his inability to land his upper-70s spike curveball caught up to him in Double-A, prompting him to work on a low-80s slider last offseason that fits better with his low arm slot. Herz's extreme crossfire delivery with a long arm swing creates a lot of deception but also compromises his ability to repeat his mechanics and throw strikes. After he walked 33 batters in 31 2/3 Double-A innings in 2022, Chicago tried to help him get more directional to the plate, which could lead to improved control -- and also could detract from his stuff. Most evaluators believe he’s headed for the bullpen, but Washington has every reason to keep trying out the 22-year-old as a starter in its rebuilding farm system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herz had the most electric arm among North Carolina prep pitchers in 2019, but he also came with signability questions that caused him to slide to the eighth round. The Cubs surprised other clubs when they landed him for $500,000, the equivalent of fourth-round money, and he has blossomed into one of their top pitching prospects. In his first extended taste of pro ball last summer, he reached High-A at age 20 while striking out 131 in 81 2/3 innings. Herz's stuff keeps getting better, with his fastball jumping into the low 90s when he was a high school senior and reaching 95-96 mph more often with late finish during his first full pro season in 2021. He didn't use a changeup much as an amateur but has developed one that has become a true weapon that just disappears at the plate. After throwing a promising low-80s slider in high school, Herz has switched to an upper-70s spike curveball with more depth that plays well off his heater. In addition to bat-missing stuff, Herz also creates plenty of deception with a crossfire delivery that's extremely difficult on left-handers and produces good carry on his fastball that that leaves hitters from both sides struggling to get good swings. His mechanics do compromise his control, however. His ability to locate his pitches will determine whether he remains in the rotation rather than head to the bullpen, where he could fill a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Herz had the most electric arm in North Carolina's 2019 high school crop, questions about his signability caused him to drop in the Draft. The Cubs selected him in the eighth round and surprised other teams when they landed him with a $500,000 bonus, the equivalent of fourth-round money. He worked 10 1/3 innings in his pro debut before his 2020 development was restricted to Chicago's pitching camp during instructional league. Herz added about 5 mph to his fastball as a high school senior, when he sat at 90-93 mph and touched 95. His lean 6-foot-2 frame has room to add strength, and he has been throwing in the mid-90s more regularly in 2021, his first full pro season. He generates a lot of ugly swings with a low-80s slider that features sharp horizontal break and has also added a spike curveball that shows promise. Herz is gaining feel for a changeup he didn't need as an amateur. He throws across his body, which adds deception and life to his pitches but also hurts his command. Some scouts believe the effort in his delivery and long arm action have him destined to become a reliever, but the Cubs like the way his arm works and think his strength and athleticism will help him make it as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mazur spent his first two college seasons at South Dakota State before a breakout summer in the Cape Cod League led him to transfer to Iowa. The 2022 Big Ten Conference pitcher of the year, he signed with the Padres for an under-slot $1.25 million in the second round. He reached the big leagues last June after just 153 innings in the Minors but got pounded for a 7.49 ERA with San Diego and traded to the Marlins in a package for Tanner Scott and Bryan Hoeing a month later. Mazur works at 94-96 mph and reaches 98 with his four-seam fastball, though it has only average carry and below-average armside run. His best weapon is a tight upper-80s slider/cutter, and it was his lone effective offering during his introduction to the Majors. His low-80s curveball is his only pitch with much depth to it, while his fading upper-80s changeup regressed significantly last year. Because his pitches don't feature a lot of movement, Mazur has to be precise with his location. He has compiled an excellent 5 percent walk rate in his first two seasons in the Minors, but that figure jumped to 13 percent in the big leagues, where he got tagged when he caught too much of the plate and became reluctant to challenge hitters. He operates from an upright delivery with a high three-quarters arm slot, so batters get a good look at his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mazur went from a decent starter at South Dakota State to the 2022 Big Ten Pitcher of the Year for Iowa, and that momentum carried into that year's Draft, where he went to the Padres in the second round and signed for slightly below slot at $1.25 million. He reached Double-A by the end of his first full pro season and San Diego two months into his second. After he scuffled in three short stints with the Padres, they sent him to the Marlins in the Tanner Scott/Bryan Hoeing deal in July. Standing at a wiry 6-foot-2, Mazur sits at 94-96 mph and touches 98 with his fastball. His control of the pitch was stellar in the Minors out of a fairly high slot, and because he could get ahead of so many batters, he could work in his solid secondaries. A mid-80s slider remains the star with tight, late break, allowing for a healthy amount of chase. His upper-80s changeup has stepped forward, giving him an armside option with fade and sink when it's on, while his 78-81 mph curveball splits the plate with decent vertical break. Mazur's athletic delivery helps him repeatedly pump strikes into the zone, though he didn't pitch with the same confidence in San Diego. He didn't challenge big league hitters, fell behind in the count and got hit hard. A lack of more than two above-average pitches dilutes his ceiling some, but so long as he can get through a lineup twice, he should still fit the modern mold of a starting pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mazur had one of the most interesting collegiate paths in the 2022 Draft, having gone from an OK starter at South Dakota State to a Cape Cod League breakout All-Star to a spot in the Iowa starting rotation. During his one year with the Hawkeyes, he was named 2022 Big Ten Conference Pitcher of the Year after posting a 3.07 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 98 K's in 93 2/3 innings. That helped vault him into a spot in the second round and to the Padres at No. 53 overall, where he was Iowa's highest pick since 1990. The 6-foot-2 right-hander stands out as a starter for his deep five-pitch arsenal, headlined by an 82-86 mph slider that comes in with tough two-plane break. He sports two different types of heaters between his 93-95 mph four-seamer and 90-94 mph sinking two-seamer, and he can touch as high as 99 when he needs it. His mid-80s changeup and upper-70s curveball grade out much more average, but both give a diversity of looks that can keep hitters off-balance. Mazur's control improved over his three years in the NCAA, and he sported just a 5.4 percent walk rate during his time on the Cape. He has a wiry frame now, giving some scouts hope that more strength and velocity could still be coming. If it does, Mazur's status as a potential mid-rotation Major League starter would be all the more secure.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dunn played just about every sport in the Michigan high school ranks. He gave up football, basketball and track when he went to Western Michigan, playing baseball for four years (including the pandemic-shortened 2020 season). A broken hamate in 2021 limited his exposure, but the Reds thought his athleticism was worth a low-risk flier in Round 15 that summer. Injuries plagued him throughout his first year-plus in the system, but a healthy 2023 enabled him to take advantage of more playing time, and he turned in a stellar 20-50 season across High-A and Double-A. Dunn was truly able to showcase his athleticism while avoiding the injury bug. It was unclear what kind of playing time he was going to get last year, but when Jay Allen got hurt, Dunn took the opportunity and ran with it. The right-handed hitter has a solid approach -- he will take a walk but also isn’t afraid to be aggressive in order to do damage. That improved approach allowed him to tap into his raw power consistently for the first time. Dunn’s above-average speed plays up because he’s aggressive and smart on the basepaths, and he was able to swipe 54 bags in 61 tries in 2023. He can play all three outfield spots, and the Reds love his all-out grinder mentality and willingness to do anything the team needs to win. He’s the type of player who might profile as a fourth or fifth outfielder in the big leagues, but it would surprise no one if he willed himself past that limited ceiling and found a bigger role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing sparingly as a freshman at East Carolina and then losing most of his second season to the pandemic, Norby batted .415 and led NCAA Division I with 102 hits in 2022. Signed for $1.7 million as a second-round pick by the Orioles, he continued to produce in the Minors but found it difficult to crack a loaded big league lineup. That won't be an issue with the Marlins, who acquired him and Kyle Stowers in exchange for Trevor Rogers in July. A right-handed hitter with a simple, compact swing, Norby is quick to the ball and makes consistent loud contact. He punishes fastballs and is adept enough at recognizing spin to more than hold his own against breaking stuff, which he slugged .459 against last year (Triple-A average slugging against non-fastballs: .394). Furthermore, subtle changes to his approach have turned what looked like solid extra-base power into at least 20-homer pop. Norby has average speed and the ability to sneak a stolen base when the opportunity presents itself. He's a fringy defender with arm strength to match at second base. Baltimore began playing him on the outfield corners the last two seasons because it had a logjam of infielders, but he profiles best as an offensive second baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Norby put himself on the map as an East Carolina sophomore when he hit over .400 in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season. He showed it was more than a small sample size with a slash line of .415/.484/.659 with 15 homers in a full 2021 campaign, landing him with the Orioles in the second round. He’s had no issues adjusting to the pro game, smashing 29 homers and playing across three levels in his first full season in 2022. The right-handed hitter has always been quick to the ball and shown the ability to make consistent loud contact. He absolutely punishes fastballs, batting .368 and slugging .735 against heaters between Double- and Triple-A in 2022. Some small changes to his approach have turned what looked like solid extra-base power to at least above-average over-the-fence pop and he can hit it out to all fields. Norby is an aggressive baserunner, one who can steal a base despite having just average speed. He’s a capable defender at second base, where his average arm works fine and he’s athletic enough to handle left field as he did at times last year. It’s his bat, though, that put him on the fast track to Baltimore, and he should be knocking on the door soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his shortened year in 2020 and in 2021 at East Carolina, Norby didn’t get the memo that hitting over .400 isn’t the norm. He hit .403 in ’20 and followed that up with a .415/.484/.659 line and 15 homers in his Draft year, leading to some first-round buzz. He ended up landing in the second round, and after getting his professional feet wet in the Florida Complex League, he posted an .847 OPS in 26 games with Low-A Delmarva. More than anything, Norby stands out for his bat and his “gamer” approach. He’s quick to the ball from the right side of the plate and makes a ton of hard contact to all fields. He rarely misses a fastball, and while it’s likely going to be more extra-base authority than over-the-fence thump in the pro game, he did show the ability to hit the ball out all over the ballpark in 2021. His bat speed and strength should help him hit some home runs at the highest level. An average runner, Norby maximizes his speed by being smart and aggressive on the basepaths, showing he’s capable of stealing and taking extra bases. Defensively, he’s a second baseman only because he doesn’t have the arm strength for the left side of the infield, but he looks like he has the bat to be a solid offensive-minded second baseman in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: President of baseball operations Scott Harris’ first trade with the Tigers remains arguably his best, bringing Malloy -- a fast-rising but blocked prospect in Atlanta’s system -- to Detroit for reliever Joe Jiménez. After Malloy climbed three levels in the Braves' organization, he spent all of his 2023 season at Triple-A Toledo, where he backed up what Tigers evaluators saw in him. His 110 walks led all Minor Leaguers, while his 23 home runs and 83 RBIs led the Mud Hens. The Tigers opted not to extend a September callup, partly for 40-man roster management, but made it clear he’s part of their picture. Malloy brings elite hand-eye coordination and a studious approach to the plate. He knows his strike zone to the point that teammates in Toledo joked he was more accurate than the automated ball-strike system at Triple-A. That occasionally made him a tad passive at the plate, knowing he can wait for his pitch and work a walk, but he showed more aggressiveness in Spring Training. He has an all-fields approach and improved his line-drive rate, but the vast majority of his power comes to the pull side. The Tigers tried him at third base in Toledo, but his big frame and inconsistent throws led to a move to the corner outfield, the same decision Atlanta made a year earlier. His strong arm plays well when he gets behind fly balls, and he worked with Tigers coach George Lombard in the offseason on range. Malloy perfectly fits the Tigers’ offensive identity of zone control with power. Now Detroit has to find a fit defensively in spacious Comerica Park. If Malloy can make it work, he gives the Tigers an ideal right-handed run producer to lengthen and balance a lefty-heavy lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scott Harris arrived at Comerica Park as the Tigers’ new president of baseball operations preaching domination of the strike zone as one of his core values. Fitting then that Malloy was one of the first prospects Harris traded for, acquired from Atlanta in the Joe Jimenez trade. The former Georgia Tech standout ascended three Minor League levels in his first full pro season, culminating with a brief stint at Triple-A, then made a further impression in the Arizona Fall League. His on-base and slugging rates remained surprisingly consistent at each stop. Some hitters who rack up walks on their way up the Minor Leagues do so at the expense of hitting, looking to reach base by taking advantage of a young pitcher’s command. That’s not the case with Malloy, who put up 17 homers and 28 doubles to go with his 97 walks. Nor did his patience lead to more strikeouts; while his walk rate held in the mid- to upper teens, his K rate ranged from 20-25 percent in the Braves system. Where he could improve is the quality of contact. Though Malloy's a solid pull hitter for power, he hit more ground balls and fewer line drives than one might expect for his strength. That’s expected to improve as he works on launch angle and mechanics. Defensively, Malloy's 6-foot-3 frame sometimes works against him. He moved from third base to left field once he reached Double-A last summer. Unlike the Braves, the Tigers have no clear answer at third and every reason to try Malloy there. Some scouts see him as a potential first baseman. If he continues to progress at his current rate, he could find his way into Detroit’s lineup sometime during the 2023 season, especially if he can make third base work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the 2013 Draft, Westbook has been working to be the local kid done good. A native of the greater Phoenix area, Westbrook was signed away from his Pepperdine commitment by his hometown team in the fifth round. A big offensive year in the California League in 2015 raised his profile some, though he didn't completely back it up with the move to Double-A in 2016. Compact but strong, Westbrook showed surprising power with a low strikeout rate during his breakout season in Visalia. The extra-base ability didn't return in the Southern League, though it should be noted he was very young for the level, turning 21 mid-year. He's aggressive at the plate and doesn't draw a ton of walks, but he also doesn't strike out much. An average runner who can steal a base here or there, he's a capable defender at second. Westbrook participated in the Arizona Fall League last year and started seeing regular time in left field. At the very least, it could provide some positional flexibility that big league managers seem to covet more these days.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Should Loutos make a future Cardinals bullpen, he should be a fun local story. The right-hander was a starter at Washington University, helping the St. Louis school make the 2021 Division III World Series with a stellar senior year. He went undrafted and was set to start a career as a software engineer when the Cardinals offered to sign him for $20,000 with a dual role of working as a developer for other arms in the system. He became more than an interesting story when he rocketed up three levels in his full-season debut, finishing with a 3.96 ERA and 72 strikeouts in 63 2/3 innings and closed out the year in the Arizona Fall League. Loutos’ velocity has ticked up since he was a junior at Wash U and entering his second spring, he’s capable of sitting in the mid-90s from a deceptive over-the-top delivery that hides the ball from opposing batters. The heater works especially well up in the zone, and lower-level batters struggled to climb the ladder against it. Loutos’ low-80s sweeping slider played off the heater during the regular season, and he started working in a tighter 89-90 mph cutter and low-80s curveball during the AFL to see if they’d stick as potential secondary offerings. The 6-foot-5 hurler shows decent control for a reliever, especially for his size, but he’ll remain in a bullpen role entering his age-24 season. The experimentation with breaking and off-speed stuff could help him find an easier route back to St. Louis while the fastball alone gives him a decent shot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 16th-round pick by the A’s in the 2019 Draft, Basso has come a long way from his college days at Oklahoma State, where command issues were a theme of his three-year career. Overcoming Tommy John surgery in 2021, he truly put himself back on the prospect radar in 2023 by earning a 40-man roster spot and broke through last season. His 2024 campaign began at Double-A Midland and went through Triple-A Las Vegas before his first call to the Majors. The left-hander had a few different stints with the A’s, appearing in seven games (four starts) and posting a 4.03 ERA with 19 strikeouts and five walks in 22 1/3 innings. Before Tommy John, Basso could rev up his fastball up to 98 mph. His heater, which averaged just over 92 last year, is enhanced by his vastly improved ability to command it. He threw it for a strike close to 70 percent of the time across all three stops in 2024. His mid-70s wipeout curveball is a strong secondary pitch. He rounds out his four-pitch arsenal with a good mid-80s cutter and a mid-80s changeup that has become more defined but still could use some tinkering. Basso profiles as a solid back-end lefty starter, a role he has already gotten a taste of in the Majors, with sound mechanics and control that has shifted from what once was a weakness to an asset. He also has some experience working out of the bullpen, which presents the opportunity to be utilized in a swingman role if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mostly a reliever due to shaky command during his three years at Oklahoma State, Basso was taken in the 16th round of the 2019 Draft by the A’s, and he's come a long way since. After undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2021, he returned to action last season on a limited workload and earned a spot on Oakland’s 40-man roster on the strength of a strong campaign in which he posted a combined 2.42 ERA in 20 games (17 starts) with 64 strikeouts and 15 walks over 63 1/3 innings between High-A Lansing and Double-A Midland. There was a point earlier in his career when Basso was hitting 98 mph with his fastball. Nowadays, he tops out around 94 with the heater to go along with a wipeout curveball in the mid-70s, cutter in the mid-80s that generates ground balls and swing-and-miss and a changeup that continues to improve. That gives him a solid lefty starter mix. Basso is mechanically sound on the mound with good control, which is evident by his low walk totals. Now on the 40-man roster, he will look to stay healthy and potentially earn a chance to appear in the A’s starting rotation at some point this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schwellenbach was a good enough high school player in Michigan to get taken late by Cleveland, but even though he was a two-way guy as a prepster, he went on to Nebraska and spent his first two years only hitting and playing the infield for the Cornhuskers. He got back on the mound as the school’s closer in 2021 while also playing shortstop, doing both well enough to win the John Olerud Award for the best two-way player in college ball. The Braves wanted him for his arm and took him in the second round in that summer’s Draft, but had to wait until 2023 to see him pitch because he needed Tommy John surgery right after signing. He pitched across two levels of A ball in his first return to action. Especially since it was his first competitive work post-surgery, Schwellenbach’s feel for pitching and potential four-pitch arsenal was particularly impressive. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and he can reach back for more. He has two breaking pitches with a hard mid-80s slider and a slightly slower curve, with the former a bit better, though both can be very effective. He has feel for a mid-80s changeup with sink. The athleticism that allowed Schwellenbach to play shortstop at the Division I level shows up in his ability to repeat his simple delivery consistently. That leads to a lot of strike-throwing, and he was commanding all of his offerings well (2.2 BB/9 rate in 2023) right out of the gate. The hope is the gloves will come off now further removed from surgery and there’s considerable ceiling given his stuff, feel for it and relative lack of mound time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at shortstop for Nebraska, Schwellenbach had also pitched in high school, but didn’t take to the mound for the Cornhuskers until 2021. As a very effective closer during his junior year, he was the John Olerud Award winner as the best two-way college player and landed in the second round of that summer’s Draft as a pitcher. Because he needed Tommy John surgery right after joining the Braves, the 2023 season marks the first time he’s throwing competitive innings. While he was a reliever for that one year at Nebraska, Schwellenbach has a three-pitch mix and a feel for how to use it that give him the chance to start. It’s big stuff, with a fastball that topped out at 99 mph and sat in the mid-90s in shorter stints and a low-80s slider that can miss bats. He also has a mid-80s changeup that features a lot of sink. All three pitches are at least above-average. With a simple delivery, Schwellenbach showed an ability to throw strikes with all three of his offerings. As someone who hasn’t pitched a lot or gotten a lot of instruction, there’s upside here, and there’s some hope he can follow a Jacob deGrom-like path as a two-way player who didn’t pitch much in college and had Tommy John surgery shortly after signing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schwellenbach spent three years as Nebraska’s shortstop. Because of an elbow injury in high school, he didn’t pitch for the Cornhuskers until 2021, when he served as the closer, saving 10 games and pitching 31 2/3 innings en route to winning the John Olerud Award as college baseball’s best two-way player. While it was a small sample, the Braves liked what they saw on the mound enough to take him in the second round as a pitcher. Signed for well below slot, Schewellenbach needed Tommy John surgery shortly after joining the Braves organization. In the brief time Schwellenbach was on the mound, often coming in from shortstop to finish games, he showed three quality pitches and command of all of them. All three would at least flash plus, with a fastball that sat 94-97 mph and topped out at 99, a low-80s slider and a mid-80s changeup with power sink. He could throw all three of them for strikes with a simple delivery. Because of his repertoire and feel for pitching, there is some thought he has the chance to start, and the Braves will likely develop him as such once he returns to the mound. He’ll probably be back in time for instructional league play in the fall of 2022, with 2023 a target for regular season action. Some see a lot of Jacob deGrom in him, who was also a college shortstop who didn’t pitch much before his junior year of college, and also needed Tommy John surgery the summer after he signed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Venezuela in 2016 for just $40,000, Montero languished on the fringe of prospect rankings -- and at High-A West Michigan for two full seasons -- until a stronger body frame and boost in velocity sent him vaulting up the system in 2023, culminating in a late-season stint at Triple-A Toledo. His strikeout rate of 11.3 per nine innings was by far his career best, and he maintained it through a career-high 26 starts and 127 1/3 innings. The Tigers avoided losing him in Minor League free agency by adding him to their 40-man roster. Montero has a steady mid-90s four-seam fastball that can reach 97 mph when he needs it, setting up a duet of high-spin breaking pitches. While his slider sits around 2700 rpm, his buckling curveball can cross the 3000 rpm threshold. Both move enough that he can struggle at times to control them, placing pressure on him to use his fastball to get ahead in counts. A mid-80s changeup provides a different look. He has had to learn to stay out of the middle of the zone, where he can be prone to home runs. Though Montero could end up as a reliever, where his fastball might play up more consistently, he showed durability as a starter last year. That’ll get him another look in Toledo’s rotation and another chance at older Triple-A hitters. His arsenal bears some similarity to Reese Olson, whose ability to adapt turned a midseason callup into a rotation spot last year. Either way, Montero has shown a lot to get this far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers signed Montero out of Venezuela during the 2016 international signing period, then kept him in the Dominican Summer League for two years while he worked on his control. Their patience paid off with an impressive 2019 season in short-season ball, including a 2.08 ERA and 49 strikeouts over 47 2/3 innings in 10 starts. He seemingly entered 2021 with momentum from a strong stint in the Florida Instructional League, but struggled at High-A West Michigan before being shut down at the end of July with arm issues. Montero has a fastball that can hit the mid-90s, but his strikeout pitch is a big curveball with a high spin rate that not only drops but can move across the plate and away from right-handed hitters. He also has been working on a changeup with good late movement. He has improved his command with refinement of his delivery. Montero’s .394 BABIP reflected a bit of hard luck, especially with low line-drive and home run rates. Still, he needs to translate his arsenal into more swings-and-misses. Though Montero struggled last year, he was a 20-year-old in High-A ball, three years below the average pitching age for the league, and coming off a lost 2020 season. The Tigers left him off their 40-man roster but invited him to their Minor League minicamp, where he seemingly put last year’s struggles behind him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rather than entertain starting his pro career as a Day 3 pick by the Red Sox, Bliss opted to go from the Georgia high school ranks to Auburn. He was a three-year starter with the Tigers and landed in the second round with the D-backs after hitting 15 homers and posting an OPS over 1.000 in 2021. He struggled in his first full season of pro ball (82 wRC+) but made some adjustments in 2023 that enabled him to turn in a 20-50 season (127 wRC+), go to the Futures Game and reach Triple-A, all while catching the eye of the Mariners, who acquired him with Dominic Canzone in return for Paul Sewald at last year's deadline. Don't let Bliss' 5-foot-6 frame deceive you. While he doesn't have the most raw power, he's found a way to tap into it without selling out for it, something he did in his first full season with a big leg kick, closing off his stance more in 2023 and staying shorter to the ball. That led to more consistent hard contact and the right-handed hitter has the chance to approach average power at the highest level. He's an above-average runner who is aggressive on the basepaths, making him a legitimate threat to steal. Bliss has continued to see time on both sides of second base and he's acceptable at shortstop, but his best chance to be a regular in the big leagues is probably at the keystone, where he played exclusively during his Arizona Fall League stint last autumn. At worst, Bliss is poised to be a super-utilityman who can impact the game offensively in a number of ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Red Sox as a 30th-rounder from a Georgia high school in 2018, Bliss became an immediate starter at Auburn. A second baseman on the Tigers' 2019 College World Series team, he shifted to shortstop as a sophomore and ranked sixth in NCAA Division I in hits (29 in 18 games) while playing errorless defense. He adopted a more aggressive approach in 2021 and tripled his previous career home run total with 15. The D-backs then selected him in the second round of the Draft (42nd overall) and he signed for $1.25 million. It took some time to get acclimated to pro ball, but Bliss found his footing late in the year and thrived over the final month of the season with Low-A Visalia. Though he's just 5-foot-9 and 165 pounds, Bliss is strong for his size and has quality bat-to-ball skills. He has added some loft to what had been a relatively flat right-handed stroke and uses a big leg kick to make the most of his modest raw power. He remains a hit-over-power prospect with a good approach and a knack for making hard contact. A solid runner, Bliss has good hands and instincts on defense. He covers ground at shortstop and tries to compensate for fringy arm strength with a quick release. He has the tools to play some shortstop, but profiles better at second base and could become a plus defender at the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in September 2012 out of the Dominican Republic for a modest $50,000, Garabito has moved slowly through the Royals' system. The six-foot right-hander spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League before making his United States debut in '15 and it took until '18 for him to get to the Class A Advanced Carolina League. He made the most of it, earning the league's ERA title, though he was left unprotected for the second straight year in the Rule 5 Draft and wasn't selected. Garabito's stuff is largely average across the board and when he's on, he mixes all three of his pitches well to keep hitters off balance. His fastball is a tick above average, especially when he's commanding it well, thrown with good movement and his upper 70s curveball has good depth to it. His changeup gives him a third average pitch he uses effectively. The key for Garabito to make it as a back-end starter in the big leagues will be to continue improving his fastball command. He was particularly effective in the second half of the 2018 season and the Royals hope that carries over as he attacks the upper levels of the system, with an Arnaldo Hernandez-type breakout the best-case scenario. He doesn't have the stuff to profile well in shorter stints, so if starting doesn't pan out, work as a long reliever might be his only way to get to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2012, Garabito spent his first three seasons in Rookie ball. When he finally made the jump to low Class A in 2016, he went 2-11 with a 4.80 ERA, though the Royals thought he showed more promise than that record indicated. He looked much better when he returned to Lexington last year, slicing his ERA to 2.81, though he missed more than two months with shoulder tendinitis. Garabito's upper-70s curveball has depth and often serves as his most effective option. He showed more trust in his fading changeup during 2017, when he held left-handers to a .584 OPS. His fastball parks at 90-93 mph, peaks at 95 and is relatively straight, which makes it both easier to command and to hit. While Garabito lacks a plus pitch, he can throw strikes with all three of them despite a relatively long arm action. He's not very physical or projectable, so his ceiling is limited to a back-of-the-rotation starter. He does have some of the best pitchability and one of the better floors among Kansas City farmhands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yet another potential Royals bargain signee from Latin America, Garabito got a $50,000 bonus when he turned pro out of the Dominican Republic in 2012. He spent three years in Rookie ball before making the jump to low Class A in 2016, where he went 2-11 but showed an arsenal that was more impressive than his record. He pitched better when he returned to that level this year before missing more than two months with shoulder tendinitis. Garabito's best pitch usually is his curveball, which features good depth. His fastball is the definition of average, sitting at 91-93 mph and topping out at 95 with ordinary life. There are games when Garabito's fading changeup is his most effective offering, though there are others when he lacks confidence in it. While Garabito has the requisite three pitches needed in a starter, he's still refining his control and command. He's reasonably athletic and has a sound delivery, so he should be able to do so. There's not a lot of projection remaining in Garabito's 6-foot frame, so he'll have a ceiling as a back-of-the-rotation starter unless he gets an unexpected surge in velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two things have changed for White since he jumped into the Rays’ Top 30 Prospects list last spring: He’s now on their 40-man roster, having been added in November, and his ETA shifted from 2022 to ’23 because he had Tommy John surgery last April. After blowing through all four full-season levels of Tampa Bay’s system in 2021, White is now hoping to return to affiliated games by May and potentially break into the Majors by midseason. If he's anything like the shutdown reliever he was in 2021, when he posted a 1.44 ERA with 104 strikeouts over 43 appearances, it won’t be long. Early in the rehab process, White noted that his arm hadn’t felt so good in years. It’s too soon to say how fully his stuff will return or how long that might take, but the Rays are optimistic he’ll regain his form and impact their bullpen sooner than later. The 6-foot right-hander, a Mississippi native, grew up as a big fan of longtime Braves closer Craig Kimbrel -- and it shows. He’s not a towering presence, but he throws hard. His primary weapon is a 95-98 mph that generated a ton of swinging strikes in 2021, and he complements that with an above-average slider he refined during the 2020 shutdown as well as a still-developing splitter that he broke out in High-A and used against lefties. White is strictly a reliever and has been since he pitched at Pearl River Community College and Mississippi State, where he became the Rays’ sixth-round pick in the 2019 Draft. His health will determine his immediate future, but he has the electric stuff, all-out competitiveness and mentality to get high-leverage outs in the late innings. He likely would have done that last year, in fact, if not for the injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: DeLoach won the 2019 Cape Cod League batting title (.353), then hit .421 with six homers in 18 games at Texas A&M during the shortened college season in 2020 before landing a $1,729,800 bonus as a Mariners second-rounder. After two so-so pro seasons, he set career highs in most categories last year, when he hit .286/.387/.481 with 23 homers in Triple-A. Seattle packaged him with Prelander Berroa and a supplemental second-round pick to acquire Gregory Santos from the White Sox in February. DeLoach's best attribute may be his disciplined approach at the plate. He works counts, uses the entire field and draws a healthy amount of walks. His willingness to take pitches also led to a Pacific Coast League-high 173 strikeouts and a 28 percent K rate in 2023, and he could do a better job of tapping into his solid raw power to all fields if he turned his left-handed stroke loose more often. DeLoach has average speed and is capable of spot duty in center field while being better suited for the corners. He parlayed his average arm into 11 assists in 104 games in right field last year. Without a better-than-average tool, he profiles as an extra outfielder rather than a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick out of Texas A&M during the shortened Draft in 2020 who signed with the Mariners for $1,729,800, DeLoach has had a solid Minor League career but perhaps not to the level of his Draft pedigree. He climbed to Double-A Arkansas in his first pro year and remained there for all of ‘22, putting him on the big league doorstep, but his ceiling might be as a fourth outfielder. He successfully navigated Triple-A in 2023 before Seattle traded him along with Prelander Berroa and a supplemental second-round pick to the White Sox for Gregory Santos in February. DeLoach’s success in the Majors will also hinge on him hitting consistently and then some, because there’s nothing really in the secondary tools that prop him up if he’s not hitting in the high-.200s. He's had good on-base ability (with a .371 OBP) in his first two seasons and he hits left-handed, which both play in his favor. But the power hasn’t emerged the way most might’ve envisioned, which could be a byproduct of being almost too selective. All said, if DeLoach can hit consistently and handle all three outfield positions, there’s a good chance he’ll play in the big leagues. Even if there’s not a lot of speed and power, he decently does a combination of things that could help a ballclub. And the makeup and maturity are already in his favor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though his numbers in his first two seasons at Texas A&M weren’t overwhelming (a .239 average and just five homers), DeLoach began to catch scouts’ eyes in 2019, when he won the Cape Cod League batting title with a .353 average. He followed that up in the truncated 2020 season with the Aggies by hitting .421 with six homers in 18 games and ranked 11th in NCAA Division I with a 1.336 OPS. It all created a promising yet unclear product, but the Mariners liked the bat enough to select him in the second round of the shortened Draft and sign him for a full slot bonus of $1,729,800. That mixed portrait continued during his first pro year in 2021, when he had a .930 OPS at High-A Everett and .722 clip after earning a promotion to Double-A Arkansas in July. Arkansas is well known as one of the toughest hitters’ parks in the Minors, and DeLoach mentally handled the transition well, swinging at the right pitches and flashing more extra-base potential, even though it didn’t translate to ideal results. Comped by some scouts to Kole Calhoun, DeLoach has a solid overall skill set despite lacking overwhelming upside. His hit and power tools are graded as average and his above-average running ability as a corner outfielder should set his floor as a fourth outfielder or DH. Some scouts believe his ceiling gives him the chance to run into an All-Star-type season in his prime.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: DeLoach began to catch scouts’ eyes in 2019, when he won the Cape Cod league batting title with a .353 average and also starred in the Northwoods League later that summer. His numbers at Texas A&M weren’t as overwhelming -- he put up a .239 average and just five homers over his first two seasons. But in the truncated 2020 season, he hit .421 with six homers in 18 games and ranked 11th in NCAA Division I with a 1.336 OPS. It all painted a somewhat mixed picture, but the Mariners took a shot by drafting him in the second round last year and offered full slot value ($1,729,800). DeLoach has been described as streaky. He’s at his best when he turns his left-handed swing loose, which he did more frequently during his brief junior year. Seattle clearly believes he can be the guy seen on the Cape who drove the ball with authority with wood bats, even if his stock didn’t truly rise until the final 12 months before he was drafted. A swing change installed at the Cape helped DeLoach with controlling the strike zone and putting the bat on the ball, but he too often adopted an almost defensive approach and settled for weak contact in his first two seasons with the Aggies. More of an average runner in the past, DeLoach flashed some plus times from home to first last spring. That helps his chances of staying in center field, though his so-so instincts likely will land him on a corner. His average-to-solid arm should fit in either left or right field, positions that will increase the demands on his bat. The Mariners believe that DeLoach’s floor is high, whether it’s as a fourth outfielder or as a DH -- but they are adamant that he knows how to hit, and that he could conceivably fit right in a lineup featuring Jarred Kelenic and Julio Rodriguez.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hodge mostly flew under the scouting radar while winning Utah 5-A state championships at Cottonwood HS (Salt Lake City) as a sophomore and senior, but the Cubs popped him in the 13th round of the 2019 Draft. He recorded a 6.44 ERA in his first two pro seasons sandwiched around back surgery in 2020, then broke out and tied for the system lead with 141 strikeouts in 2022 after he dedicated himself to improving his conditioning and athleticism. He hit the wall as a starter in Double-A but pitched better after becoming a full-time reliever in late June, earning a spot on the 40-man roster. Hodge's fastball parked at 90-92 mph before he got into better shape, and now it operates at 93-96 and touches 98 with late life and carry up on the strike zone. He also bolstered his slider, an 82-86 mph sweeper that destroys right-handers. He essentially scrapped his average upper-70s curveball after shifting to the bullpen and barely used his below-average upper-80s changeup even as a starter last year. With his 6-foot-4 frame and the quality extension in his delivery, Hodge's pitches get on hitters more quickly than expected. He has yet to prove he can harness his souped-up fastball and slider, which contributed to his change in roles. If he can throw more strikes, he could develop into a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hodge went mostly unnoticed by scouts and recruiters while winning Utah 5-A state championships at Cottonwood HS (Salt Lake City) as a sophomore and senior, though the Cubs saw enough to sign him for $125,000 in the 13th round of the 2019 Draft. He posted a 6.44 ERA in his first two pro seasons with 2020 back surgery in between, then took a huge step forward last year. He tied for the system lead with 141 strikeouts in 109 1/3 innings and kicked his stuff and control up a notch following a promotion to High-A in late July. After Hodge dedicated himself to improving his conditioning and athleticism, his fastball went from sitting at 91 mph in 2021 to parking at 93-96 and touching 98 with late life and good carry up in the zone. He upgraded his slider to an 82-86 mph offering with wicked sweep that destroys righties and works as a back-foot pitch against lefties. He also has an average upper-70s curveball and an upper-80s changeup that's too firm and straight, but he struggles to throw them for strikes. Hodge's 6-foot-4 frame gives him the strength to handle a starter's workload and creates plenty of extension in his delivery, allowing his pitches to get on hitters quickly. There's some mixed opinion on whether he can cut it as a big league starter, and he'll need to refine his control and a third pitch to do so. If he ends up as a reliever, his fastball/slider combination might make him a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 14th-round pick out of a Puerto Rico high school in 2017, Vazquez didn't stick on a full-season roster until four years later. Though he was one of the better defensive infielders in their system, the Cubs didn't protect him on their 40-man roster after the 2021 or 2022 seasons. They did last November after he set career highs in most offensive categories while batting .271/.361/.456 with 20 homers between Double-A and Triple-A. Vazquez makes all the plays at shortstop with range to both sides, quick hands, plus arm strength and a good internal clock. He's so good at short that Chicago rarely has deployed him at other positions, though his tools also make him a quality defender at second and third base. He's blocked by Dansby Swanson in the Majors and still has to prove his bat is real, but he could be an asset as a glove-first utilityman. Lowering his hands at the plate keyed Vazquez's offensive breakout, helping him to keep his right-handed stroke on plane and enabling him to hit balls harder and farther than before. He also looked to turn on pitches more often and exceeded his combined home run total of 16 from his first five pro seasons. He's still overly aggressive at the plate but boosted his walk rate to 10 percent in 2023 as pitchers had to respect his newfound power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2017 Draft (17 years, seven months), Rodriguez went in the third round but didn't reach full-season ball before his fifth year as a pro or claim a roster spot on the 40-man roster until after his seventh. He ranks second in the Minors with 84 homers in the last three seasons and had his best year yet in 2024, winning International League MVP honors. He topped the Triple-A circuit in wRC+ (140) and RBI (94) while finishing second in homers (29), total bases (237), slugging (.540) and OPS (.930), third in on-base percentage (.390) and fifth in batting (.301). Rodriguez switch-hit when he turned pro but has batted solely right-handed since 2019 and developed into one of the best sluggers in the system. His prodigious bat speed and strength produce high-end exit velocities and well-above-average raw pop that plays to all fields. While he does sell out for home runs and is definitely a power-over-hit guy, he did make some progress last year by chasing fewer pitches and swinging and missing less within the strike zone. Though he's a below-average runner who offers little value on the bases, Rodriguez covers enough ground to play a decent corner outfield. His plus-plus arm strength is a weapon in right field and he notched 27 assists in 225 outfield starts in 2023-24. His overall profile is quite similar to that of 2004 Guardians playoff hero Jhonkensy Noel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2017 Draft at 17 years and seven months, Rodriguez was a third-round choice out of the Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy in Puerto Rico. He didn't reach full-season ball until his fifth year as a pro in 2021 and went unselected in the Rule 5 Draft despite being unprotected after '21 and '22. After homering 55 times in the past two seasons, he finally claimed a spot on the 40-man roster in November. A switch-hitter when he turned pro, Rodriguez has batted solely from the right side since 2019 and has become one of the few true sluggers in the organization. He creates the highest exit velocities in the system and well-above-average raw power that plays to all fields with his combination of prodigious strength and bat speed. Instead of letting his pop come naturally, he repeatedly chases pitches out of the strike zone, leading to strikeouts and suboptimal contact. He did show more patience in 2023, taking walks when opponents declined to challenge him. Despite below-average speed, Rodriguez covers enough ground to be an average defender on the outfield corners. He spent the majority of last season in right field, where his plus arm enabled him to record 13 assists in 91 games. He should get an opportunity with the Guardians at some point in 2024 after they finished last in the Majors in home runs last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The second-youngest player in the 2017 Draft class, Rodriguez didn't celebrate his 18th birthday until November. That youth, along with his highly projectable frame and loud but raw tools, put him firmly on the Indians' radar, and the club was thrilled to land the Puerto Rican prep in the third round. They were even more thrilled with his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where Rodriguez proved a more advanced hitter than initially expected while exhibiting a mature approach. Scouts rave about Rodriguez's athleticism and projectable 6-foot-3 frame, one that leaves room for him to add considerable strength in the coming years. Once he's done so, the switch-hitting Rodriguez could offer plus raw power, though not before shortening the length of his swing and refining his overall hitting mechanics. Defensively, Rodriguez has a strong arm that receives plus grades from evaluators and profiles as a clean fit in right field. Rodriguez is raw and will need time to develop his game in the Minor Leagues, but the overall package offers club officials plenty on which to dream.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017-18 international signing class for the Rockies may always be known as the group topped by Ezequiel Tovar, who led with his $800,000 bonus. Carreras has been in that shadow, starting with signing for just $15,000 in February 2018 and continuing as the pair progressed together, with Tovar jumping ahead developmentally. Carreras started making more of a name for himself in 2022, shaking off a shoulder injury that hurt him in 2020 and '21, reaching Double-A for the first time and getting added to the 40-man roster. Rangy and athletic, Carreras has always exhibited some positive offensive traits with good bat speed and the ability to make hard contact out front. He’s been overaggressive to a fault, however, and will need to make better swing decisions and be more selective to reach his offensive ceiling. He did start using the leverage in his swing to tap into some of his raw power, and there’s reason to believe that the doubles he was hitting in bunches could turn into more home runs if he can refine his approach. Carreras can play a solid defensive shortstop, with good instincts and plenty of arm for the position, and he’s also shown in the past that he can handle sliding over to third base, something that might have to happen with Tovar establishing himself at short. Even if it’s eventually as a utility type, Carreras is the type who is already showing leadership and other intangibles to make him a valuable big leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carreras signed with the Rockies for just $15,000 in February 2018 as an 18-year-old, which is a touch old for the typical international prospect. He went out and hit well in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 (.867 OPS), then turned in a solid debut stateside with a .294/.369/.466 line in the Rookie-level Pioneer League the following summer. Both the pandemic and a shoulder injury limited his development time in 2020. Surgery required to fix that issue delayed his 2021 start and hampered his overall production as he moved to full-season ball. Tall, lean and athletic, Carreras has shown excellent bat speed from the right side of the plate with an ability to make hard contact out front when he’s healthy. There’s leverage in his swing and as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame, there should be a good amount of power to come. He was a bit tentative with his swings after coming back, but the pop showed up at times and the next step for him tapping into that power is to make more adjustments and eliminate his tendency to chase. Carreras has played mostly on the left side of the infield, with more than enough arm to stay there, and opinions are split over whether he can play shortstop or third regularly. The latter puts more pressure on the bat to develop, but his makeup and intangibles point to him maximizing the tools he has.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the very top of the 2017-18 international signing period, in terms of bonuses, stood Wander Franco, now the game’s No. 1 prospect, who got $3.825 million to sign with the Rays. Close to the other end of the spectrum was Carreras, who received just $15,000 in February 2018 to join the Rockies. He’s looked like a bargain find so far, hitting well both in the Rookie level Dominican Summer League in 2018 and during his United States debut in the Rookie Advanced Pioneer League in 2019. A left shoulder injury limited his time on the field at instructs in 2020, but he’s been given a clean bill of health. Carreras provides an exciting combination of size, strength and athleticism to both sides of the ball. He has plenty of bat speed with present leverage to his right-handed swing and when he grows into his 6-foot-2 frame more, there’s bound to be more power to come. Carreras is able to extend and make hard contact out front, all while showing a solid approach at the plate. The 21-year-old infielder creates buzz with his defense as well. He has quick reactions and one of the best infield arms in the system. Carreras has shown the ability to play second, third and short capably, but given his physical and offensive projection, he might profile at third base the best in terms of a long-term home, though the Rockies love positional flexibility from their infielders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017-18 international signing period is looking like it might be a very fruitful one for the Rockies, both in terms of high-bonus players, like Ezequiel Tovar and Eddy Diaz, and guys who might have seemed like afterthoughts. Carreras fits into the latter category, having signed in February 2018 for just $15,000. After a solid pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the summer after he signed, he kept on performing with a move to the United States and the Pioneer League in 2019. Of all the young players from Latin America in the system, Carreras might have the most upside in terms of his hit and power tools. He has long levers and bat speed, with leverage to his swing. Though he’s not overly physical and hasn’t grown into his man strength, his power is already showing up. He gets good extension and makes hard contact out front, creating good whip with this swing. An average runner who is aggressive on the basepaths, Carreras has played all over the infield. He’ll continue to play all three spots for now, but as he fills out, finding a home at the hot corner could make a lot of sense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the shortened 2020 Draft, many teams did a fair amount of shopping for non-drafted free agents. Few, if any, have as interesting a background story as Hurtubise. The pandemic-shortened season that spring was Hurtubise’s fourth playing for Army and when he signed for just $20,000 after the Draft, he became the first academy player allowed to defer his military service obligation under a new pro athlete exemption policy. He had moderate success in High-A in his first full season, then missed a bunch of the 2022 season with injuries. He went from good story to potential big leaguer in 2023, finishing with a .961 OPS and 45 steals across Double-A and Triple-A. The Reds’ Minor League offensive Player of the Year capped things off with a trip to the Arizona Fall League before being added to the 40-man roster. Since signing, Hurtubise has been one of the fastest players in the Reds’ system, and that speed plays on both sides of the ball. The left-handed hitter doesn’t have the prettiest swing mechanics, but he made it work at the upper levels. He’s never going to hit for a ton of power -- he didn’t homer at Army and didn’t hit his first professional roundtripper until 2022 -- but he can lace balls to the gaps, which quickly can turn into triples, though he’s just as likely to hit a 30-hopper to short and beat it out. Hurtubise’s speed is an asset in the outfield and he’s worked hard to be a serviceable center fielder. He’s a better defender in the corners, though he has a fringy arm, and he has shown he can handle all three spots with all signs pointing to him being a valuable fourth-outfielder type in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Air Force and two summers pitching for Team USA, Skenes transferred to Louisiana State for his junior season, helping lead the Tigers to a Men's College World Series title in 2023. A former two-way player who reached double digits in wins and home runs with Air Force in 2022, Skenes' focus on pitching helped cement him as the best college pitching prospect since Stephen Strasburg. So did an other-worldly junior campaign that earned him SEC pitcher of the year honors while leading all Division I pitchers in strikeouts, K/9 and WHIP. The Pirates set a Draft record by giving him a $9.2 million bonus as last year's No. 1 overall pick and let him get his feet wet with a handful of professional outings that ended in Double-A. Skenes’ velocity started to spike during the fall at LSU. It carried over to his incredible spring in Baton Rouge, averaging 98 mph and topping out at 102 mph with his fastball, with a flat approach angle and carry that make it very difficult to hit, as evidenced by a 30 percent miss rate on it last spring. His slider turned into the best secondary pitch in the class. In the Minors, it's thrown largely in the upper 80s with sharp break that elicited ridiculous swing-and-miss rates (62 percent).
