mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 Smith had spent his first two years at Maryland as a starter at shortstop when he headed to Cape Cod for the summer. It was in that elite wood-bat league that he jumped much more firmly onto the Draft radar with an outstanding performance that led to an All-Star selection and playoff MVP honors. He didn't fare as well as a junior, though it did little to deter Toronto from drafting him in the fourth round in June. Smith was unable to maintain that kind of offensive consistency as a junior this year, with some swing and miss tendencies keeping him from hitting for average. He has shown some aptitude for making adjustments and improving in that regard, something he'll have to do at the next level. He has sneaky power that shows up in games, but while he is capable of driving the ball to all fields, he tends to get too pull-happy. While he is a below-average runner, Smith's instincts and hands should allow him to stay at shortstop. His arm grades out as average, but he has a quick release and is always accurate. There's nothing flashy with Smith's game, but he makes all of the plays consistently. If the bat can improve, he has the chance to be an everyday shortstop at the next level, something the Blue Jays are banking on.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves weren’t allowed to spend more than $300,000 on a prospect on the amateur international market in the 2017-18 signing period because they went over their bonus pool the previous year. Muñoz signed for just $30,000 close to the end of the signing period in June 2018. He’s worked as a starter and reached Double-A in 2022, showing enough to earn a spot on the 40-man roster this past offseason. Atlanta moved him into the bullpen in ’23 and designated him for assignment in July before Washington picked him up. The Nats have slowly worked him back into the Triple-A rotation, where he’s had rough results but is still young at 23. The 6-foot-2 right-hander has swing-and-miss stuff, relying mostly on a fastball-slider combination to get things done. His four-seamer and sinker both sit around 94-96 mph, topping out at 98, so there’s velo there. He really leans on the low-90s slider, an out pitch that can be a true plus and has cutter-like action to it, missing a healthy amount of bats with it. He has an 89-91 mph changeup, but it's clearly his third pitch. Control was a big part of Muñoz’s push to relief, and it hasn’t gotten any better as a starter with the Nats, though the Triple-A ABS system could be affecting things. He still projects best as a two-pitch reliever, and the fastball-slider combo could make him a quality right-handed option, so long as he finds the zone with some regularity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Leiter declined first-round offers from clubs as a New Jersey prepster in 2019 to attend Vanderbilt, where he became the No. 2 overall pick in the Draft two years later. The son of two-time All-Star and World Series-champion Al Leiter, he tied teammate Kumar Rocker for the NCAA Division I strikeout lead (179 in 110 innings) and pitched the Commodores to the Men's College World Series Finals in his lone full college season, then signed for $7,922,000. Sent straight to Double-A for his 2022 pro debut, he got knocked around there for two years as his delivery, stuff and control all regressed. He rebounded to win Triple-A Pacific Coast League pitcher of the year honors in 2024, though he got roughed up for an 8.83 ERA over five different trips to Texas in his first taste of the big leagues. Leiter's fastball added a little velocity last year, parking at 94-97 mph and peaking at 100 with high-end carry and extension as well as some armside run, though it got rocked when up in the zone at Triple-A and all over the place in the Majors. His nastiest pitch is an upper-80s slider that reaches 92 mph with two-plane depth, though big leaguers didn't chase it as much as Minor Leaguers did. Both his low-90s cutter and low-80s curveball have their moments, while his fading upper-80s changeup pales in comparison to the rest of his arsenal. A dynamic athlete who gets down the mound well, Leiter did a better job of maintaining consistent timing with his delivery last year. He reduced his walk rate to 10 percent, down from 13 percent in his first two pro seasons, but still needs to improve his control and command further. The Rangers still believe in his pitches, pedigree and makeup and think he eventually will pitch in the front half of their rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of two-time All-Star and World Series champion Al Leiter, Jack turned down first-round money as a New Jersey high schooler in 2019 to attend Vanderbilt, where he emerged as the No. 2 overall pick two years later. In his lone full college season, he no-hit South Carolina in his first Southeastern Conference start, tied teammate Kumar Rocker for the NCAA Division I strikeout crown (179 in 110 innings) and pitched the Commodores to the College World Series finals. After signing for $7,922,000, he spent most of the last two years in Double-A struggling with his delivery as his stuff and control regressed. Leiter's fastball continues to sit at 93-96 mph and top out at 98 with plenty of induced vertical break and riding life, but it's not quite the elite pitch it was in college because he hasn't commanded it well and pro hitters have crushed it when he doesn't locate it up in the zone. He has added velocity and depth to a mid-80s slider that was his most effective pitch in 2023. He's now having trouble getting strikes or chases with an upper-70s curveball that used to be his best secondary offering and doesn't show much faith in a mid-80s changeup with modest fade. Leiter spent two stints on the developmental list twice last year, for a week in June and six weeks later in the season, so he could focus on improving his mechanics. He's an explosive athlete who creates plenty of extension, but his timing can get out of whack, leading him to open early and lose direction toward the plate, which hampers his stuff and his ability to locate it. The Rangers are optimistic that his off-field work ironed out those kinks, and he'll need to in order to recapture his previous ceiling of a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Leiter played with top Yankees shortstop prospect Anthony Volpe at the Delbarton School (Morristown, N.J.) and turned down first-round money from clubs in the 2019 Draft to attend Vanderbilt, where he made a spectacular if brief debut in the shortened 2020 season before dominating the following year. He no-hit South Carolina in his first Southeastern Conference start, held Missouri hitless for seven innings before departing in his second, tied teammate Kumar Rocker for the NCAA Division I strikeout lead (179 in 110 innings) and pitched the Commodores to within a victory of their second straight national title. The No. 2 overall pick in the 2021 Draft, Leiter signed for $7,922,000 before scuffling in Double-A during his 2022 pro debut and again at the same level this year. Leiter's 93-98 mph fastball played as an elite pitch with tremendous riding life and induced vertical break in college, making it almost impossible to barrel when he located it up in the strike zone, but it got hit hard at times during his debut due to decreased metrics and command. He threw more strikes and missed more bats with an improved slider that added velocity (sitting in the mid-80s, topping out at 92 mph) and depth. His upper-70s curveball lost a bit of power and he struggled to land it for strikes, while he barely dabbled with a mid-80s changeup with some fade. After overwhelming college hitters with his stuff, Leiter hasn't been able to do the same to Double-A opponents because of his spotty control and command. He'll have to throw more strikes and live up in the zone more often with his fastball, and the Rangers believe he can do so by improving the timing and direction of his delivery, but he hasn't made those adjustments yet. The son of two-time All-Star and World Series champion Al Leiter, he grew up around the game and is more mature and comfortable than most pitchers his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of two-time All-Star and World Series champion Al Leiter, Jack turned down first-round overtures from clubs as a New Jersey high schooler in 2019 and dropped to the Yankees in the 20th round because he was determined to attend Vanderbilt. He made a spectacular but brief college debut in the truncated 2020 season before dominating in 2021, no-hitting South Carolina in his first Southeastern Conference start, tying teammate Kumar Rocker for the NCAA Division I strikeout lead with 179 in 110 innings and pitching the Commodores to within a win of their second straight national championship. After going No. 2 overall and signing for a Rangers-record $7,922,000, he got the rest of the summer off and made his pro debut in Double-A in 2022. Leiter's fastball can play as an elite pitch, not so much because of its 92-98 mph velocity but more because of its tremendous riding life and induced vertical break, which make his heater almost impossible to barrel when it's up in the strike zone. His mid-80s slider has added velocity in his first pro season and has slightly surpassed his downer curveball that sits around 80 mph, though both are solid options with the potential to become plus pitches. He also shows some aptitude for throwing a power changeup with fade that he rarely used in college. Leiter's spin rates and fastball metrics dipped in his first pro season, though the Rangers think it's just a delivery-related issue that he'll be able to rectify. If so, he has the stuff and moxie to be an ace once he refines his command, which gets spotty at times. The only other thing he has to prove is his ability to handle an increased workload in pro ball, because he's small for a starter at 6-foot-1 and his 110 innings at Vanderbilt were easily a career high.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the biggest stories of the shortened 2020 college season, Knack won all four of his starts at East Tennessee State while posting a 1.08 ERA and leading NCAA Division I in strikeouts (51 in 25 innings) and K/BB ratio (51/1). After going unselected despite being eligible in each of the previous five Drafts, he went in the second round and received the highest bonus ever for a fifth-year senior ($712,500). After dealing with hamstring injuries in both of his first two pull pro seasons, he had his best year as a pro and reached Triple-A in 2023, though he was shut down with forearm tightness in late August. Knack touched 98 mph during his college breakout but usually works around 90-94 mph and peaks at 96 with his fastball, which plays up because of his ability to locate it where he wants. It plays as a solid pitch, as do his tight 82-85 mph slider and fading 79-82 mph changeup. He'll break out an upper-70s curveball on occasion to give hitters a different look, but it's nothing special. Knack's stuff took off when he improved his strength and conditioning in his final college season, and after regressing in those areas as a pro, he rededicated himself and found more success in 2023. He can display well above-average control and plus command when he's at his very best. Added to the 40-man roster in November, he could become a No. 4 starter if he can stay healthy and in shape.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knack went undrafted despite being eligible for five straight years before breaking out during the shortened 2020 college season, winning all four of his starts at East Tennessee State with a 1.08 ERA and NCAA Division I bests in strikeouts (51 in 25 innings) and K/BB ratio (51/1). The best fifth-year-senior prospect perhaps ever, he set a bonus record for that demographic ($712,500) after Los Angeles selected him in the second round. Hamstring issues have hampered him in each of his first two full pro seasons, and he followed a strong debut by getting roughed up as his stuff regressed in Double-A last year. After Knack improved his strength and conditioning, his fastball went from 88-92 mph in his first four years of college to 93-95 with a peak of 98 and improved carry in 2020-21, but he dropped a tick of velocity on his heater and didn't command it with his usual precision last year. His tight mid-80s slider remained a solid pitch and was his most effective offering, though he lost some feel for his low-80s changeup with fade and had trouble landing his upper-70s get-me-over curveball in the zone. The key to Knack's success always has been his ability to locate his entire arsenal with precision, but his leg issues led to his walk rate spiking from 1.2 per nine innings in his pro debut to 3.8 last year. He'll need to improve the conditioning of his burly 6-foot-2 frame and stay healthy in order to recapture his past magic. He still has one of the higher floors among Dodgers pitching prospects, but his ceiling of a mid-rotation starter is further away than it was a year ago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted while eligible in each of the previous five years, Knack saw his stuff make a dramatic leap forward during the truncated 2020 college season, winning all four of his starts at East Tennessee State while posting a 1.08 ERA and leading NCAA Division I in strikeouts (51 in 25 innings) and K/BB ratio (51.0). He became the best fifth-year-senior prospect in recent memory and set a bonus record for that demographic ($712,500) after the Dodgers drafted him in the second round. Despite hamstring issues that sidelined him in May, he maintained his improved repertoire throughout his pro debut in 2021, when he reached Double-A and pitched well in the Arizona Fall League. Knack worked with an 88-92 mph fastball for much of his college career before improving his strength and conditioning, which helped him jump to 93-95 and touching 98 with good carry in 2020. His slider climbed into the mid-80s and was sharper as well, and his low-80s changeup with fade played better with increased velocity separation from his fastball. That stuff held up over the course of the 2021 season, with his changeup showing signs of becoming a plus offering and his slider consistently grading as a solid pitch. Knack has a burly 6-foot-2 frame but repeats his delivery so well that he locates his entire arsenal, which also includes an get-me-over curveball in the upper 70s, wherever he wants. He averaged just 1.3 walks per nine innings in college and 1.2 in his debut, when he recorded an 82/8 K/BB ratio in 62 1/3 innings. With his combination of stuff and command, he has a ceiling of No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most improbable success story in the 2020 Draft, Knack became the best fifth-year-senior prospect in years and set a bonus record for that demographic ($712,500) after the Dodgers selected him in the second round. Knack had gone undrafted in each of the previous five years, starting with when he tore the labrum in his pitching shoulder diving into a base as a Tennessee high school senior in 2015, which required surgery that led to him redshirting in his first year at Walters State (Tenn.) CC. He dislocated his non-throwing shoulder when he came back in 2017, costing him most of that year, then went 13-0 on the mound and hit 11 homers to lead the Senators to a runner-up finish at the 2018 Junior College World Series. He focused solely on pitching in two years at East Tennessee State and saw his stuff make a huge leap during the truncated 2020 season, winning all four of his starts while posting a 1.08 ERA and leading NCAA Division I in strikeouts (51 in 25 innings) and K/BB ratio (51.0). After working with an 89-92 mph fastball and fringy secondary pitches in his first year as a full-time pitcher, Knack focused on adding strength and trimming up his burly 6-foot-2 frame. He came out firing 93-95 mph heaters and touching 98 as a senior, tightened his slider into a consistent option and added some power to what had been a get-me-over curveball. His fading changeup became more effective too as it achieved more velocity separation from his souped-up fastball. The brother-in-law of Pirates 2016 first-rounder Will Craig, Knack continued to show premium stuff at Los Angeles' alternate site and instructional league and sat in the mid-90s during offseason workouts, pounding the strike zone all the while. He doesn't have the prettiest body or delivery but repeats his mechanics and averaged just 1.3 walks per nine innings in college. Few pitchers in the 2020 Draft could rival the combination of stuff and command he showed last spring, and if that's for real, he won't need much development time in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A potential first-rounder as a Georgia sophomore-eligible in 2021, missed the first three weeks of the season with mononucleosis, never was at his best and went undrafted. As a junior, he walked just 12 batters in 13 starts and received an over-slot $925,000 in the third round from the White Sox, who desperately needed advanced pitching prospects. In his first full pro season, he earned a midseason promotion to Double-A and worked a scoreless inning in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. Cannon keeps hitters off balance by employing six different pitches, starting with a cutter that sits around 90 mph and grades as plus at its best -- though it wasn't as effective against Double-A hitters. The rest of his stuff is average across the board: two- and four-seam fastballs that park at 92-95 mph and touch 97, an 82-85 mph slider, a 78-82 mph curveball and a mid-80s changeup with sink. He used his two-seamer more often while adding the curve in 2023, which allowed him to work the bottom of the zone and post a 1.6 groundout/airout ratio. Cannon uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create downhill plane and has no trouble keeping his long limbs in sync in his efficient delivery. He pounds the strike zone and sequences his pitches well. He has the highest floor among Chicago's pitching prospects and looks like a surefire No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cannon entered 2021 with a chance to go in the first round as a Draft-eligible sophomore at Georgia, but he missed the first three weeks with mononucleosis and never really got going. He returned to school and walked just 12 batters in 13 starts last spring, though he did miss two weeks in April with a strained forearm. The White Sox need advanced pitching prospects and were delighted to find him available in the third round, where they signed him for an over-slot $925,000. Though Cannon's strike-throwing stands out more than his stuff, he does have an effective four-pitch mix. His best offering is his plus cutter, which improved in 2022, now sits in the upper 80s and misses more bats than the rest of his arsenal. He also has a 92-96 mph fastball with heavy sink, a low-80s slider that also made strides that year, and a mid-80s changeup with similar movement to his heater. Though he's 6-foot-6, Cannon has no trouble keeping his long limbs in sync and repeating his efficient delivery. He pounds the strike zone with his fastball, slider and cutter, averaging just 1.6 walks per nine innings in three years with the Bulldogs. More polished than overpowering, he stands out more for his floor than his ceiling but may not need much time in the Minors to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A late addition to the Cubs' 2012-13 international class, Pereda signed for $7,500 out of Venezuela in April 2013 and spent his first four pro seasons in Rookie ball. He played primarily first base in his 2017 full-season debut and was ticketed to repeat low Class A last year before high Class A Myrtle Beach manager Buddy Bailey wanted Pereda as his starting catcher. He responded with career highs in most categories and earned recognition as a Carolina League midseason all-star. Pereda lacks showcase tools but possesses a high floor as a potential big league backup with a grinder mentality. His best attribute is his plus arm, which he used to erase 38 percent of basestealers in 2018. He has improved as a receiver and framer but still needs to get more consistent in both areas. Though Pereda fits at the bottom of a batting order, he possesses some of the best plate discipline in Chicago's system. He has a flat right-handed swing and uses the entire field, with almost all of his modest power coming to his pull side. He has below-average speed, though that makes him a faster runner than most catchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing for $300,000 in October 2017, Pages has destroyed pro pitching, slamming 89 homers in 401 games and leading his leagues in extra-base hits during each of his first three full seasons in the United States. The Cuban struggled for the first time in 2022 as a 21-year-old in Double-A, yet still ranked third in the Texas League with 26 homers. He improved his approach and athleticism going into last season and got off to a fast start before tearing the labrum in his left (non-throwing) shoulder during his Triple-A debut on May 16, requiring season-ending surgery. Pages' combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his uphill right-handed stroke give him plus-plus raw power. In 2022, Double-A pitchers exploited his aggressive tendency to try to launch balls to his pull side, but he displayed more patience and chased pitches out of the zone less often last season. Though his huge pop is his most obvious tool, he's actually one of the more intelligent hitters in the system and shows the ability to make adjustments and draw walks when he's not trying to do too much at the plate. Pages also improved his conditioning and displayed more quickness in 2023, producing fringy to average run times with good instincts as a baserunner and defender. He makes good reads in the outfield and played mostly center field last spring before he got hurt. He projects more as a right fielder, where he has spent most of his pro career, and his plus-plus arm strength enhances his profile at the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cuban who signed for $300,000 in October 2017, Pages has crushed 86 homers in 367 pro games over his first four pro seasons. Though he struggled more than ever before in Double-A last year, he still led his league in extra-base hits for the third straight time, topping the Texas League with 58 while also ranking third with 26 long balls. He got off to a hot start in 2023 but his season ended prematurely when he tore the labrum in his left shoulder in his Triple-A debut on May 16, requiring surgery. Pages derives plus-plus raw power from a combination of bat speed, strength and leverage with an extremely uphill right-handed swing. He consistently drives the ball in the air to his pull side and has at least 30-homer potential, but Double-A pitchers took advantage of his aggressive stroke and approach. He's an intelligent hitter who will take walks and make adjustments when he's locked in, but he also chases too many pitches and gives away at-bats at times. Pages perfectly fits the right-field profile with his light-tower power and plus-plus arm strength, which led to 14 assists in 127 starts last season. Once an average runner, he has lost a step as he has matured physically, though his instincts enhance his quickness. He reads balls well in the outfield and will steal and take extra bases when he gets the opportunity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $300,000 in October 2017 after leaving Cuba, Pages has destroyed pitchers in his two full years in the United States. He led the Rookie-level Pioneer League in extra-base hits (43) while ranking second in homers (19), RBIs (55), total bases (153) and slugging (.651) as an 18-year-old in 2019, then won High-A Central MVP honors last season after topping the circuit in homers (31), extra-base hits (57), runs (96), RBIs (88), walks (77), slugging (.539) and OPS (.933). The Dodgers would have shipped him to the Angels along with Joc Pederson and Ross Stripling for Luis Rengifo and Taylor Ward as an adjunct to the Mookie Betts trade in February 2020, but Angels owner Arte Moreno got impatient when the Betts negotiations dragged on and nixed the move. Pages has the bat speed and leverage to create well above-average raw pop as well as the loft in his right-handed stroke and aggressive approach to make the most of it by repeatedly launching line drives to his pull side. While his power is his most impactful tool, he also is an intelligent hitter who recognizes pitches, understands his swing and makes adjustments when needed. He improved his plate discipline throughout his introduction to full-season ball in 2021 and could hit .260 with 30 or more homers per season. More than just a masher, Pages has average speed and an arm that earns double-plus grades from some evaluators. He spent most of 2019 in center field, where his instincts enhance his range, but played the majority of last season in right field. Though he still needs to improve his consistency, he projects as at least an average defender on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If the Mookie Betts trade has gone through as originally conceived, Pages would have headed to the Angels along with Joc Pederson and Ross Stripling in a related deal for Luis Rengifo and assorted youngsters. But when the Betts negotiations got more complicated, Angels owner Arte Moreno became impatient and nixed the latter move. Signed for $300,000 in October 2017 after defecting from Cuba, Pages led the Rookie-level Pioneer League in extra-base hits (43) and ranked second in homers (19), RBI (55), total bases (153) and slugging (.651) as an 18-year-old in 2019. While Pages has some loud physical tools in his power and arm strength, the Dodgers also love his intelligence at the plate. He has an advanced understanding of his right-handed stroke, demonstrating the ability to make adjustments as well as create bat speed and leverage to generate well above-average raw pop. There are some concerns about his strikeout tendencies because he has a leg kick and posted a 28 percent whiff rate in 2019, but he has a sound swing, recognizes pitches well and generates explosive exit velocities when he connects. Pages might have the best present combination of power and speed in the Dodgers system, though he projects as more of an average runner once he's physically mature. His instincts boost his range in center field and may allow him to remain at the position. His arm earns plus-plus grades from some evaluators, so he would easily fit the right-field profile if he has to move to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top young hitters in Cuba before he defected, Pages signed with the Dodgers for $300,000 in October 2017. He advanced to the United States as a 17-year-old making his pro debut the next summer, then led the Rookie-level Pioneer League in extra-base hits (43) while ranking second in homers (19), RBI (55), total bases (153) and slugging (.651) in 2019. Reportedly headed to the Angels along with Joc Pederson and Ross Stripling as an offshoot of the original version of the Mookie Betts trade in February, he stayed put when that deal fell through. Still just 19, Pages has an advanced understanding of his right-handed swing and how to create bat speed and use his leverage to generate well-above-average raw power. Though he had a 28 percent strikeout rate in 2019, Los Angeles is confident he'll make enough contact to damage because he has a sound right-handed swing and is an intelligent hitter. He needs to clean up his plate discipline and perhaps tone down his leg kick. Pages offers one of the best combinations of strength and speed in the system, though he'll probably settle in as more of average runner once he's physically mature. His instincts help him cover ground in center field and may allow him to stay there in the long term. He easily profiles in right field with his power and an arm that earns plus-plus grades from some evaluators.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitley reached Double-A and seemed on the cusp of the big leagues one year after the Astros took him 16th overall in the 2016 Draft out of a Texas high school. But he has enjoyed little success outside of two Arizona Fall League stints while dealing with a 50-game suspension for testing positive for a stimulant as well as minor oblique and lat injuries in 2018, shoulder inflammation and command woes in 2019, the pandemic shutdown and elbow soreness in 2020 and Tommy John surgery that cost him all of 2021 and half of 2022. He returned to the mound in June and posted a 7.09 ERA in Triple-A, casting more doubt on his future. Whitley's fastball sat at 94-96 mph and touched 100 mph in Triple-A last year, though it had different shape and less hop than it had in the past. His mid-80s changeup once ranked among the best in the Minors, but his feel for the pitch and its life also regressed in 2022. He couldn't throw his low-70s curveball for strikes, didn't miss bats with his mid-80s slider that's now more tight than sweepy and barely used an upper-80s cutter that scouts once preferred to both his breaking pitches. His control and command never were his strong suits because he tinkered with his delivery and struggled to repeat it, and Whitley walked 27 batters in 40 innings last year. He still flashes the potential for five different plus pitches and created some optimism by throwing well during the offseason, but he has gone from possible No. 1 starter to a total wild card. If he claims a role in the big leagues, it likely will be in the bullpen rather than the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitley has gone from the game's top pitching prospect to its most enigmatic. He reached Double-A and seemed on the verge of the big leagues one year after the Astros made him the 16th overall pick in 2016 Draft out of a Texas high school. But he almost all of his success since then has come in two dominant Arizona Fall League stints because he has missed time with a 50-game suspension for violating the Minor League drug program plus minor oblique and lat injuries (2018), right shoulder inflammation and command issues (2019), the pandemic shutdown and elbow soreness (2020) and Tommy John surgery (2021) that will sideline him until mid-2022. When healthy and at his best, Whitley displayed five pitches that could grade at plus or better. His best weapons were his fastball, which ranges from 92-99 mph with cut and sink, and his mid-80s changeup, which features fade and depth and ranked among the best in the Minors. He also showed a low-80s downer curveball, a mid-80s slider with late bite and a low-90s cutter that some scouts believed was better than either of his breaking balls. During his last extended stretch of pitching in 2019, Houston had Whitley make some mechanical adjustments in order to maintain better upper-body posture to reduce stress on his shoulder and help him throw more strikes. His control and command always lagged behind his stuff and some club officials hope he comes back from his elbow reconstruction with more focus. He still has more upside than any pitcher in the system but also a huge variance in how his career might play out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros rated Whitley as the best high school pitcher in the 2016 Draft, when they selected him 17th overall and signed him for $3,148,000. After reaching Double-A in his first full pro season, a rare accomplishment for a prepster, he seemed on the verge of reaching the big leagues in 2018. But he pitched just 86 regular-season innings and 51 Arizona Fall League frames over the next three years while dealing with a 50-game suspension for violating the Minor League drug program plus minor oblique and lat injuries (‘18), right shoulder inflammation and command issues (‘19) and the shortened recent season plus a sore right elbow (‘20). The biggest blow yet came this March, when he was diagnosed with a torn elbow ligament that led to Tommy John surgery that will sideline him until mid-2022. While Whitley has become something of an enigma, he still has five weapons in his repertoire that all can grade at plus or better at their best. His most reliable offerings are his fastball, which cuts and sinks while ranging from 92-99 mph, and his mid-80s changeup, which features fade and depth and ranks among the best in the Minors. He also has a downer curveball in the low 80s and a late-biting slider in the mid-80s, both with high spin rates, and a low-90s cutter that some scouts think is better than either of his breaking pitches. Whitley made some mechanical adjustments in 2019 in order to maintain better upper-body posture in hopes that it would reduce stress on his shoulder and help him throw more strikes. The quality of his stuff and his ability to harness it fluctuated throughout that year, though he did rebound in the end to lead the AFL in strikeouts for the second straight season. He's still just 23 years old and still can become a frontline starter if he can stay healthy and develop average control and command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros graded Whitley as the best high school pitcher in the 2016 Draft and signed him for $3,148,000 as the 17th overall pick, the sixth prep arm selected that June. He reached Double-A during his first full pro season, a rare feat for a high schooler, but he totaled just 86 regular-season innings the next two years. A 50-game suspension for violating the Minor League drug program plus minor oblique and lat injuries limited him in 2018, then shoulder inflammation and command issues sabotaged his 2019 season. Though consistency can be an issue, Whitley has five pitches that grade as plus or better when they're working. He can cut or sink a fastball that usually ranges from 92-97 mph, and hitters can't try to sit on it because his changeup has fade and depth and ranks as one of the best in the Minors. His downer curveball and late-biting, mid-80s slider both feature high spin rates, and he can morph the latter into a low-90s cutter that may be better than either of his breaking balls. The quality of Whitley's stuff and his ability to harness it varied throughout 2019, though he rebounded to lead the Arizona Fall League in strikeouts for the second straight season. He altered his mechanics to maintain better posture with his upper body, in hopes that will reduce stress on his shoulder and allow him to throw more strikes. If he can maintain average control and command, his stuff will make him a star.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros rated Whitley as the best high school arm in the 2016 Draft and were thrilled that he lasted until they picked at No. 17, where he signed for $3,148,000 as the sixth prep pitcher selected. In 2017, he averaged 13.9 strikeouts per nine innings and joined Zack Greinke, Chad Billingsley, Clayton Kershaw and Dylan Bundy as the only high school first-rounders this millennium to pitch in Double-A during their first full pro season. His encore wasn't as successful, as he worked just 26 1/3 regular-season innings because of a 50-game suspension for violating the Minor League drug program and minor oblique and lat injuries. Whitley got more work in the Arizona Fall League, where he was the developmental circuit's strikeout leader and showed why he's considered the best pitching prospect in baseball. He can make hitters look bad with his entire repertoire, starting with a 93-98 mph fastball with natural life (heavy sink down or cutting action up in the zone) and a devastating changeup with fade and depth. He has a pair of high-spin, power breaking balls with a 12-to-6 curveball and a late-biting slider, and he can turn the latter into a true cutter in the low 90s. Whitley has endured a puzzling 2019 season during which the quality of his stuff has fluctuated at times, and even so he got hit much harder than he should have in his first taste of Triple-A. His command has never been particularly sharp and has regressed this year, with scouts from other organizations raising questions about his focus and maturity. He still has the upside of a dominant No. 1 starter but hasn't looked like one as often as he had in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros rated Whitley higher than any high school pitcher in the 2016 Draft and got him at No. 17 overall -- the sixth one selected -- for a $3,148,000 bonus. Now the top-rated pitching prospect in baseball, he averaged 13.9 strikeouts per nine innings in 2017 and joined Zack Greinke, Chad Billingsley, Clayton Kershaw and Dylan Bundy as the only prep first-round arms this century to advance to Double-A in their first full pro season. He missed the start of this season after drawing a 50-game suspension in February for violating the Minor League drug program, then picked up right where he left off after he returned in June. Whitley can miss bats with all four of his pitches. His best is his fastball, a nasty combination of velocity (92-97 mph), cutting and running action plus steep downhill plane. After doing a terrific job as a high school senior of trimming what had been a soft body, he has room to add more strength and could throw harder once he does. Whitley backs up his heater with a hard 12-to-6 curveball, a power slider that flashes late bite and a fading changeup that he already trusts. Though he has good body control for a young pitcher with a huge frame, Houston had him pitch exclusively out of the stretch at times last season to have him focus on repeating his delivery. He already does a nice job of throwing strikes and should become an ace if he can refine his command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitley stood less than 6 feet tall and had a mid-70s fastball when he entered Alamo Heights HS (San Antonio) in 2012, then grew to 6-foot-7 with a low-90s heater by the spring of his sophomore year. He starred on the high school showcase circuit and with the U.S. national-18-and-under team after his junior season, then dropped 25 pounds and looked better than ever as a senior. The Astros liked him as much as any high school pitcher in the 2016 Draft and were delighted to select him 17th overall and sign him for $3,148,000. Whitley projects to have four solid-or-better pitches, starting with a 92-95 mph fastball that tops out at 97, could have more velocity to come and features cutting and running action. He has a power curveball that peaks in the low 80s with good depth and tight spin, and he can turn it into a mid-80s slider when he wants. He has an advanced changeup for a pitcher fresh out of high school and already trusts it. Though Whitley has good body control for a youngster with an extra-large frame, the Astros still are having him pitch exclusively out of the stretch to help him repeat his delivery. He'll have to watch his weight, but he recognizes the importance of conditioning after firming up his previously soft frame helped his Draft stock soar. He has drawn physical comparisons to former National League ERA leader Josh Johnson, but is more advanced at the same age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clase had long been touted as the fastest runner in Seattle’s system, and he supported that designation with a historic 2023, when he stole 79 bases in 94 attempts between High-A Everett and Double-A Arkansas to pair with 20 homers. He became the first player since records began to be tracked in 1961 to have a 20-70 season in the Minors. It was perhaps a result of Clase finally being consistently healthy after dealing with multiple injuries, albeit minor and more nagging, in recent years. He showed his health again in 2024, bouncing multiple times between Triple-A Tacoma and the Majors but never quite stuck at the latter. The Mariners dealt him to the Blue Jays at the Trade Deadline in a move for reliever Yimi García. Despite his 5-foot-10 frame, Clase can show decent high-end exit velocities, leading to great intrigue on what his overall hit tool will look like when he’s fully developed. Maintaining a sound approach and not selling out for power and getting away from his best abilities will also be vital. Before the trade, he posted a 32.6 percent K rate in The Show, proving that it’ll take some time for him to develop at the plate. Speed will always be Clase’s calling card, and coupling those wheels with improved route running should allow him to play center field in the Majors, though he got a decent amount of time in left in deference to Julio Rodríguez and because of below-average arm strength. That running ability could get him extra value with today’s emphasis on basestealing, but he’ll need the bat to be more consistent to become a true everyday player in Toronto.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clase is probably still the fastest runner in Seattle’s system, a perch that Felnin Celesten may soon challenge -- but not for now. Clase swiped a whopping 55 bags in 107 games in 2022, all for Single-A Modesto. The Mariners knew Clase had wheels when they signed him in 2018, but they weren’t as cognizant of his burgeoning power potential, which he flexed with 13 homers and a .463 slugging percentage last year. Part of the extra-base uptick is rooted in Clase’s conditioning. Despite standing at just 5-foot-8, he’s as strong as any prospect in the system. The term “gym rat” gets thrown around a lot, but Clase truly embodies it, which is why it’s not surprising that he’s developed such premier bat speed. One downside to his development has been nagging injuries through the years, though he played a mostly full season in ‘22. It likely prevented him from climbing quicker, but after a solid season, climbing the ladder rapidly is not out of the realm. Clase isn’t the best route runner, but he makes up for it with his speed, which has allowed him to stick in center field. In ‘21, he used his down time rehabbing an injury to pick up another valuable tool that had been an old habit: switch-hitting, something that nobody in the Mariners’ front office had any idea he could do.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clase might be the fastest runner in Seattle’s entire system. With legitimate 70 speed, the 19-year-old has already stolen 47 bases in just 77 pro games since signing with Seattle in 2018. At that time, he was listed at 5-foot-8 and 150 pounds, a frame that certainly made him overlooked among that year’s international class. In ‘21, he was 16-for-16 on steal attempts, and he had at least two in half of the 14 games he played before suffering a nagging lower-body injury that cut his season short. During his rehab, Clase picked up an old habit: switch-hitting. He opted to swing exclusively from the left side when he was being scouted as an amateur, but when he had down time to recover this past year, he began taking cuts again from the right. Nobody in the Mariners’ front office had any idea he had switch-hitting ability, but now that he does, they’re really bullish on his makeup, work ethic and physical attributes despite being a smaller-stature player. Clase doesn’t have the best route-running ability, but his speed and jump abilities make up for it and allow him to track down more than he might otherwise. He has a very similar makeup to Victor Labrada in that regard. At the plate, the 19-year-old has some punch in the batter’s box, with upside to put on more muscle as he continues to grow beyond his current frame. The uber-competitive Dominican native has been touted for his tireless work ethic, and his Instagram workout videos are enough evidence to indicate as much.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he’s just 5-foot-8 and 150 pounds, Clase pops some punch in the batter’s box, and despite being just 18 years old, the Mariners believe he has tremendous upside to put on more muscle and grow into that frame. Clase already has broad enough shoulders to indicate as much and a strong lower half that he’ll be able to continue to grow into. The uber-competitive Dominican native has been touted for his tireless work ethic, and his Instagram workout videos are enough evidence to indicate as much. Clase has tremendous instincts in the box for his age, with an open left-handed stance and balanced approach. His fluid stroke has all-field ability, and though he could improve his bat speed, he’s had a knack for making consistent contact with sound patience. Power could be a byproduct of aging and strengthening. Clase was injured for part of 2020, but the Mariners finally got him stateside last year for their fall developmental league in Arizona, where he was able to take some live cuts. He’s been touted as the fastest runner in the club’s farm system with the potential to be an above-average fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2018-19 international signing period netted the Mariners shortstop phenom Noelvi Marte, who received the organization’s largest bonus for the period. Close to the other end of the spectrum was Clase, a 5-foot-9 outfielder who signed on the same day as Marte, but for just $35,000. While Marte is clearly the better all-around prospect, Clase certainly opened a lot of eyes with a .300/.434/.444 debut, finishing in fifth in the Dominican Summer League with 31 steals. Upon signing, Clase became the fastest player in the Mariners system, with very close to top-of-the-scale speed. That enabled him to steal a ton of bags in his debut, stretch singles to doubles and doubles to triples, and cover a ton of ground in center field, something that will only improve as he refines his reads and routes. The left-handed hitter can spray the ball to all fields and while his frame doesn’t scream power hitter, he’s already added a lot of strength, and has some surprising extra-base authority. It’s hard to know just yet what kind of prospect the Mariners have on their hands now, but given his size and the size of his bonus, he’s already opened more eyes than expected. Watching how he responds during his United States debut could be a lot of fun.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for an over-slot $200,000 as a 15th-rounder out of a Florida high school in the 2017 Draft, Vanasco got concussed nine innings into his pro career when catcher Sam Huff nailed him in the head with a throw. He also missed time with elbow inflammation in 2018 and blew out his elbow during his final outing at Texas' alternate site in 2020, requiring Tommy John surgery. Back on the mound for game action for the first time in three years in 2022, he recorded a 4.48 ERA with 111 strikeouts in 84 1/3 innings in High-A and made two starts in Double-A. Vanasco worked in the mid-90s and hit 99 mph with bat-missing carry on his four-seam fastball before getting hurt, then operated more at 92-95 last year. The Rangers believe a nagging hip issue saved his velocity and were encouraged when he flashed some 97-98 mph heat this January. His low-80s curveball can reach 85 mph and be a hammer at its best, though it was inconsistent in 2022. Vanasco also throws a slider with some sweep and a changeup with some fade, and both mid-80s offerings could become average pitches. He has a long arm action and never has shown great feel for throwing strikes, so he's probably headed for the bullpen at some point. If his fastball and curveball come all the way back and he can upgrade his control, he has late-inning upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vanasco worked with an 88-92 mph fastball as a Florida high schooler, the Rangers believed his arm speed would translate into significantly more velocity, so they signed him for an over-slot $200,000 in the 15th round of the 2017 Draft. He got concussed nine innings into his pro debut when catcher Sam Huff drilled him in the head with a throw, then missed more time with elbow inflammation in 2018. After dominating the lower levels with a 1.81 ERA and 75 strikeouts in 49 2/3 innings in 2019, he looked like a future frontline starter at Texas' alternate site in 2020 before blowing out his elbow in the final game and requiring Tommy John surgery. Before he got hurt, Vanasco was sitting in the mid-90s and touching 99 mph with impressive carry on his four-seam fastball. He backed it up with a low-80s curveball that can be a hammer at its best. His fastball velocity hasn't been quite as strong in his return this season but his breaking ball has been a weapon. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Vanasco is very much a work in progress because he totaled just 83 1/3 innings in his first five years as a pro. He needs to improve his fastball command, develop more consistent curveball quality and refine a changeup to give him a reliable third pitch. He doesn't have much history of throwing strikes and still has to prove he can maintain a starter's workload, so he may be more likely to become a closer than an ace.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If Vanasco hadn't had Tommy John surgery in September 2020, some evaluators would include him in the discussion about the Rangers' top pitching prospect. Signed for an over-slot $200,000 as a Florida high schooler in the 15th round in 2017, he got concussed nine innings into his pro debut when a throw from catcher Sam Huff hit him in the head, and he missed time with elbow inflammation in 2018. He broke out in 2019 by posting a 1.81 ERA with 75 strikeouts in 49 2/3 innings at the lower levels and continued to showcase one of the best arms in the system at Texas' alternate site last summer before getting hurt. The Rangers correctly bet that Vanasco's impressive arm speed in high school would translate into increased velocity once he got stronger and cleaned up his delivery. After working with an 89-92 mph fastball as a prepster, he was dealing in the mid-90s and touching 99 before his elbow gave out. His curveball also has added power and can be a true hammer when it's on. Once he regains his health, Vanasco has work to do in order to remain a starter. He needs to improve his changeup and develop more consistency with his fastball command and curveball quality. He understandably lacks polish because when he returns to the mound in 2022, he will have worked just 83 1/3 innings in his first five years as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he signed for an over-slot $200,000 as a Florida high schooler taken in the 15th round in 2017, Vanasco's first two pro seasons were cut short. A throw from catcher Sam Huff struck him in the head and concussed him nine innings into his debut, and elbow inflammation cost him time in 2018. He showcased one of the best arms in the Rangers system while compiling a 1.81 ERA with 75 strikeouts in 49 2/3 innings last year but wound up having Tommy John surgery in September 2020. Texas believed Vanasco's arm speed in high school would translate into a velocity jump once he added strength and cleaned up his mechanics, and it has. After working with an 89-92 mph fastball in high school, he now deals in the mid-90s and tops out at 99. His curveball also has added power and can be an absolute hammer at its best. Vanasco still has work to do if he's going to remain a starter for the long term. The Rangers are having him focus on improving his changeup, and he also needs more reliable command with his fastball and quality with his curveball. His control and command are still inconsistent, understandable because he logged just 83 1/3 innings in his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Parker jumped from the late-20s to the fifth round out of San Jacinto JC in 2020 after fanning 64 batters in 30 1/3 innings before the shutdown. He’s averaged more than a strikeout per inning across his three Minor League seasons since and led Washington Minor Leaguers with 150 K’s in 124 innings across Double-A and Triple-A last season. (It wasn’t particularly close with the runner-up at 116.) He did struggle some with keeping runners off base with a 4.72 ERA, 1.42 WHIP and 11.3 percent walk rate, but the Nationals still saw enough in his bat-missing ability to place him on the 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in the offseason. Thrown from a high slot, the 6-foot-4 southpaw’s fastball sits 91-95 mph, and he maintained that velo throughout the season, even sitting in the upper reaches of that band in shorter outings at Triple-A. The pitch rides well with great induced vertical break, and it’s why he leaned on the heater 60 percent of the time in 2023. Parker plays off the high fastball with an 80-82 mph dropping curveball to work both vertical areas of the zone, and he’ll also show a harder slider with velocity a little above that. His mid-80s split-change can be too firm, but he doesn’t have as many split issues as you might expect. Parker has made strike-throwing a big emphasis as he’s closed in on the Majors, and even then, he still led Nationals qualifiers in walk percentage in 2023. He’ll be back in Triple-A this season and serve as Washington’s rotation depth, but if the walks continue to pile up, it might be worth seeing how much more he could squeeze out of the fastball as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A selection in the late-20s rounds the previous two years, Parker jumped up into the fifth round of the 2020 Draft after a stellar second season (64 K’s in 30 1/3 innings) at San Jacinto College, the same junior college as fellow National Jackson Rutledge. The southpaw sported a 4.87 ERA with 144 strikeouts (second-most in the organization) over 101 2/3 innings between Single-A and High-A in his first full campaign. He settled in back at Wilmington, where he had the lowest ERA (2.88) among South Atlantic League pitchers with at least 100 innings, for the duration of the 2022 season. Throwing from a high slot and a windup often reminiscent of Clayton Kershaw’s, Parker is made for the modern game with a low-90s fastball that rides well at the top of the zone, inducing whiffs as batters can’t reach the high stuff. His low-80s dropping curveball can pair nicely with the high heat and generate whiffs of its own. Parker has worked on a splitter and a changeup, and the way the former dives nicely out of the hand gives it a leg up as his best third option. The 6-foot-4 hurler nearly doubled his walk rate from 8.4 percent in 2021 to 15.4 in 2022, so while he was more difficult to touch, he was still giving batters too many opportunities to reach base. His stuff and arm angle could work in shorter stints, and he’ll best be served in the bullpen if he can’t find the zone more often. Parker is Rule 5-eligible in November, so 2023 will be a big proving year for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Parker was selected in the 28th round by the Cubs in 2018 and 27th round by the Rays in 2019 before the Nationals finally landed him for good as a 2020 fifth-rounder. The southpaw made a leap in his second season at San Jacinto College -- the same junior college as fellow Nats hurler Jackson Rutledge -- by striking out 64 over 30 1/3 innings in his second season. After signing for $100,000, Parker finished second among Washington farmhands with 144 strikeouts in 101 2/3 innings at Low-A and High-A. His 3.88 FIP on the season spoke more to his actual performance than his 4.87 ERA at those levels. Throwing out of a high slot, the New Mexico native sits in the low-90s with his fastball, but coaches have praised the carry on the heater that helps it play up. Parker’s curveball gives him another good vertical option, and the pitch pairs especially well with the vertical nature of the fastball. The left-hander has thrown both a splitter and a changeup as a potential third pitch, but early returns are that it’s the former that seems more likely to stick. Parker displays average control in terms of throwing in the zone, but sometimes command issues made him too hittable at High-A. A lack of purely plus stuff doesn’t make him an ideal relief candidate, if he does need to switch roles later in his career, but he could squeeze a little more velocity out of his 6-foot-4 frame if needed. Whether Parker’s ERA normalizes or if it’s the peripherals that make a jump will be worth watching in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nastrini's control woes got him bounced from UCLA's rotation early in his 2021 junior season, but the Dodgers thought they could help him and took him in the fourth round after he performed well in a pre-Draft workout and summer ball. They helped him harness his impressive stuff and turned him into one of their better pitching prospects before packaging him a trade for Lance Lynn and Joe Kelly in July 2023. His arsenal and ability to locate it regressed in his first full season in the White Sox organization, which included going 0-7 with a 7.07 ERA in nine big league appearances. Nastrini operated with a 92-95 mph fastball and topped out at 97 in 2024, down a tick from earlier in his pro career, mitigating a lack of armside run with considerable carry. His best pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that reaches 89 mph with high spin rates, though it also was responsible for 11 of his 24 homers allowed last season. He also throws a solid upper-70s curveball and an average mid-80s fading changeup but has trouble landing both for strikes. Though Nastrini's fastball, curve and slider all can grade as at least plus when they're on, they also can get hammered if he doesn't place them well. His walk rate jumped from 11 percent in his first three years as a pro to 16 percent in 2024, and his command also went backward. The rebuilding White Sox can afford him more chances as a starter, but he's looking more and more like a long-term reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nastrini lost the strike zone as a UCLA junior in 2021, dropping out of the rotation after just five starts, but the Dodgers believed the local product's control issues were fixable. He performed well in a pre-Draft workout and during summer ball, so they signed him for an over-slot $497,500 in the fourth round and helped him quickly develop into one of their top pitching prospects. Now he's the top righty in the White Sox system after Chicago acquired him in a trade for Lance Lynn and Joe Kelly last July. After working at 93-96 mph and popping 98 with impressive vertical break on his fastball in his first two-plus years as a pro, Nastini has pitched at 92-94 mph in 2024. His best secondary offering is a tight mid-80s slider with high spin rates, as does his 78-82 mph curveball that he doesn't land for strikes as consistently. His mid-80s changeup tumbles at the plate and gives him a solid fourth option. While Nastrini has the stuff to pitch near the front of a rotation, how well he harnesses it ultimately will determine his role. He's throwing more strikes than he did at UCLA, but his control and command have regressed this year and are below average. His delivery isn't complicated yet he struggles to repeat it at times.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nastrini began 2021 as one of the best college pitching prospects on the West Coast, but he lost the strike zone and fell out of UCLA's rotation after just five starts. The Dodgers knew the local product well enough to believe that his control issues were fixable, a notion that grew stronger after he performed well in a pre-Draft workout and with the summer Santa Barbara Foresters, so they signed him for an over-slot $497,500 as a fourth-rounder. He led the Los Angeles system in strikeouts (169), strikeout rate (13.0 per nine innings) and opponent average (.180) while shooting to Double-A in his first full season, then went to the White Sox in a trade for Lance Lynn and Joe Kelly midway through his second. Nastrini worked with a 92-94 mph fastball in college but has operated at 94-96 and reached 98 with outstanding carry and pitch characteristics as a pro. His mid-80s slider can be unhittable and features high spin rates, as does his 78-82 mph curveball, which also shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch but doesn't land in the zone as consistently. He's showing increased feel for a mid-80s changeup that bottoms out at the plate and utilized it more often in 2022. There's no doubt that Nastrini's stuff gives him the upside of a frontline starter, but the question is will he throw enough strikes to reach his ceiling. He does have a repeatable delivery, and some minor adjustments to his tempo and catcher targeting helped him reduce his walk rate from 7.4 per nine innings at UCLA to 4.2 in his first full pro season. He'll be an asset in the rotation if he can develop average control and decent command, and still could be an impact reliever if he doesn't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nastrini opened 2021 as one of the best college pitching prospects on the West Coast and a potential second- or third-rounder, but his control evaporated and he pitched his way out of UCLA's rotation after just five starts. The Dodgers scouted the local product enough to believe that his issues were correctable, and their confidence rose when he impressed in a pre-Draft workout for them and also struck out 24 in 13 scoreless innings with the summer Santa Barbara Foresters, whom he helped win the National Baseball Congress World Series in 2020. After they signed him in the fourth round for an over-slot $497,500, he dazzled with his stuff in his pro debut and during instructional league. After sitting at 92-94 mph with his fastball at UCLA, Nastrini averaged 96 mph with outstanding carry and pitch characteristics in shorter stints as a pro. He also delivered high spin rates on both his upper-70s downer curveball and low-80s sweeping slider, which both show the potential to become plus offerings. He also can miss bats with a mid-80s changeup that dives at the plate, though he doesn't use it very often. Nastrini piled up 30 strikeouts in 13 innings in Low-A but he also issued seven walks. He never had pinpoint control at UCLA, but he has a repeatable delivery and the Dodgers think they can help him with some minor tweaks such as tempo and catcher targeting. If he develops average control and command while maintaining the arsenal he showed in his debut, he could pitch in the front half of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winn became the first athlete to win Gatorade Baseball Player of the Year honors in two different states (Colorado in 2017, California in 2018) and was the most polished right-hander in the 2018 high school class. The Rangers brought him along slowly after signing him for $3.15 million as the 15th overall pick and he appeared on the verge of the big leagues after earning Double-A Central Pitcher of the Year accolades in 2021. He has spent most of the last two years struggling in Triple-A and was moved to a long-relief role this June. Winn continues to pitch at 92-95 mph and touch 97 but his fastball has lost riding action and deception up in the strike zone, allowing Triple-A hitters to tee off on it. His 78-82 mph downer curveball also isn't as sharp as it had been in the past. His tight mid-80s slider has become his most effective pitch, with his fading changeup with similar velocity right behind. With his athleticism and clean delivery, Winn should be able to pound the strike zone, but his walk rate doubled from 3.2 per nine innings in 2021 to 6.4 last year and has soared higher in 2023. He finds himself behind in the count too often against PCL hitters and they make him pay when he can't execute his pitches. He still has the potential for four solid or better pitches but is dealing with a second straight lost season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first athlete to win Gatorade baseball player of the year awards in different states (Colorado in 2017, California in 2018), Winn was the most polished righty in the 2018 prep class and signed for $3.15 million as the 15th overall choice. The Rangers brought him along carefully, delaying his pro debut until May 2019, and he continually has gotten better with more experience. He won Double-A Central pitcher of the year honors in 2021 and reached Triple-A at the end of his age-21 season, logging a 2.41 ERA with a .146 opponent average and 107 strikeouts in 86 innings. All four of Winn's pitches grade as at least plus when they're at their best. His two most reliable weapons are his 92-97 mph fastball -- though its riding action and deception up in the strike zone have dipped in 2022 -- and a 78-82 mph curveball with power and sharp downer break. He shows good feel for locating his slider and fading changeup, both of which park in the low 80s. Winn's athleticism translates into a clean delivery that should allow him to command his pitches and maintain quality stuff deep into games. He battled the strike zone at the outset of his pro career before making adjustments to get more online to the plate, though his control has regressed significantly this season. In addition to his physical ability, he also has the intelligence to read hitters and the confidence to throw any pitch in any count, ingredients that should help him become a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winn became the first athlete to win Gatorade baseball player of the year awards in different states (Colorado in 2017, California in 2018) while establishing himself as the most polished right-hander in the 2018 high school class. Signed for $3.15 million as the 15th overall pick, he spent his first pro summer in a deloading program and struggled in his first month after making his debut in May 2019. He since has looked like the pitcher the Rangers believed they were getting, posting a 2.81 ERA in his final 12 starts of 2019 and competing well against veteran hitters at their alternate site last summer. After making some adjustments to get more online to the plate in his pro debut, Winn showcased the stuff that made him a first-round pick. He owns a pair of plus pitches in a 92-95 mph fastball that tops out at 97 with running action and a curveball with 12-6 break. He added a slider as a high school senior that now flashes some wipeout potential and also shows feel for a changeup with fade. Winn's athleticism helps him repeat his clean delivery, allowing him to command his entire arsenal and maintain quality stuff deep into starts. He has the ability to read hitters and the confidence to throw any pitch in any count, and Texas expects that he'll pound the strike zone more often during his second pro season. He has a ceiling of a No. 2 or 3 starter and the combination of stuff and pitchability to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The only athlete to win Gatorade state baseball player of the year in two states, Winn transferred from Silver Creek High (Longmont, Colo.) to Orange (Calif.) Lutheran High for his senior season and established himself as the most polished right-hander in the 2018 prep class. After signing him for $3.15 million as the 15th overall pick, the Rangers put him in a deloading program and didn't have him make his pro debut until mid-May 2019. The layoff seemed to affect him, as he got bashed for a 9.35 ERA in his first six starts before recovering to post a 2.81 ERA in his final 12. Once Winn made some adjustments to get more online to the plate, he showed the stuff that made him a first-round choice. His two best offerings are a 92-95 mph fastball that reaches 97 with some running action, playing up because he locates it well, and a curveball with true 12-6 break at its best. During his senior season, he added a slider that flashes some wipeout potential, and he made progress with his fading changeup during his debut. All four of Winn's pitches could be solid to plus when he's a finished product, and he projects as a No. 3 starter with a high floor. He's athletic and repeats his clean delivery, which helps him command his arsenal and maintain quality stuff deep into starts. Texas' cautious approach means he probably won't rush to the big leagues, but he still could be one of the first prep arms from the 2018 Draft to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first athlete to win Gatorade state Baseball Player of the Year Awards in two states, Winn transferred from Silver Creek High (Longmont, Colo.) to Orange (Calif.) Lutheran High in 2018. He cemented his reputation as one of the most polished prep pitchers in the Draft, leading the Rangers to sign him for $3.15 million as the No. 15 overall pick. Texas had him focus on learning and conditioning during his first pro summer, and he hasn't been as sharp as expected while making his debut in 2019. Winn already possesses two plus pitches in a 92-95 mph fastball that reaches 97 with some armside run and a curveball with true 12-to-6 break. He added a low-80s slider during his high school senior season, and it has already shown flashes of becoming a wipeout pitch. He gets good fading action on his changeup, which should improve as he uses it more against pro hitters. Winn's athleticism should allow him to repeat his clean delivery and maintain his quality stuff deep into games. But in his first taste of pro ball, he hasn't looked like the guy who was supposed to be more advanced than most pitchers his age. If he can reclaim the control and command that helped make him a first-round pick, he still could be the first high school arm from his Draft to make it to the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 20th-round selection by the A’s in the 2018 Draft following a solid three-year career at Eastern Michigan, Schuemann has slowly climbed the organizational ladder over the past few years. Getting a second crack at Triple-A Las Vegas in 2023 after struggling there the previous season, he broke through by hitting .276/.402/.430 with 10 homers, 20 doubles and 51 RBIs in 116 games. The performance earned him an invitation to big league camp in 2024 as a non-roster invite. Schuemann has shown a knack for making consistent contact throughout his pro career by using the whole field to his advantage. He maintains a relatively low strikeout rate and continues to draw a good amount of walks to keep a healthy on-base percentage. He will never be mistaken for a power hitter, though there is some sneaky sting in his bat due to his ability to hit the ball hard with high exit velocities. Schuemann has not approached the 52 stolen bases he posted in 2021. Nonetheless, he is still a good runner with excellent instincts on the basepaths. His versatility is his greatest asset, with a rare ability to play above-average defense at every position on the diamond outside of pitcher and catcher. That supreme positional flexibility will keep him on the big league radar for ‘24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A closer at Illinois, and one of the best in college baseball, Jay went No. 6 overall in the 2015 Draft to the Twins, who saw a four-pitch mix and thought it could work in a starting rotation. He did make it to Double-A as a starter in his first full season, though a neck strain shelved him at the end of the year. Moved to the bullpen for 2017, the injury bug hit again and Jay missed most of the season, though he did make up for some lost time in the Arizona Fall League. The Twins are cautiously optimistic that Jay is starting to find the pitcher he was before the injuries hit. When Jay first got to the AFL, he seemed tentative and afraid to let it fly, with a fastball that was touching the low 90s. In his final outing of the fall, however, he was up to 94-96 mph and felt great about how he wrapped up a lost season. His slider, while still flashing plus, is still a bit inconsistent and he still throws his curve and changeup, with the chance to be more than two-pitch reliever. There is no longer any talk of having Jay start, as his slight build clearly was not suited for it, and there's hope that the clarity in role will help him mentally prepare. If he can take his AFL finish and carry it over to 2018, he can put the injuries behind him and impact the back end of a big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considering that Jay was almost exclusively a reliever during his career at Illinois, the fact the 2015 first-round pick made it to Double-A as a starter in his first full year is impressive. But he missed the final month of his first full season because of a neck strain, and the Twins decided this spring to move back to a bullpen role. That switch barely got off the ground as biceps tendinits and then a shoulder impingement has kept him off the mound for most of the season. Jay does have a four-pitch mix he can use, with a fastball up into the mid-90s. He has a plus slider that's his best out pitch and he'll mix in both a curve and a changeup, both of which can be Major League average. With a less-than-picturesque delivery and a slight build, there have been concerns about his durability, which is one reason, along with his ability to impact the big league club more quickly, to let him relieve once again. Most importantly, Jay needs to get healthy before determining his future. As a starter, he could have the chance to be at least a mid-rotation starter. In relief, he could have both a 70-grade fastball and slider with the ceiling of a future closer, but that's only if he can stay off the DL.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holliday entered his senior year of high school as a potential late first-round pick following an inconsistent summer showcase circuit, but he took off during that spring to vault his way toward the top of most Draft boards. The son of seven-time All-Star Matt Holliday, Jackson set a record for a prep player when he received a bonus of $8.19 million from the Orioles as the No. 1 pick in the 2022 Draft. If it’s possible for a top pick to exceed the hype that comes with that Draft standing, Holliday did it, playing across four levels last season while finishing with a .941 OPS and earning MLB Pipeline Prospect Hitter of the Year honors. It's an easy argument to make that Holliday is the best pure hitting prospect in the game. His incredibly advanced approach at the plate led to him being one of just eight Minor Leaguers who walked 100 or more times in 2023, resulting in a .442 on-base percentage. He combines that discipline with a short left-handed stroke that delivers consistent hard contact and elite-level exit velocities. Still only 20 for the 2024 season, Holliday continues to add strength, and there’s confidence he’ll drive the ball more -- and over the fence -- with greater consistency. A plus runner who can steal a base, Holliday has more than enough range, good enough hands and actions and plus instincts to play shortstop for a very long time. The only thing that might be in question is his arm, which he’s worked to improve since entering pro ball. There’s a chance he’ll need to slide over to second, though that’s as much because of other Orioles personnel as it is any questions about his arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a bit of an up-and-down showing on the summer showcase circuit, Holliday’s stock took a bit of a hit, though scouts routinely predicted he would right the ship once the spring of 2022 started. Matt Holliday’s son did just that, earning Gatorade’s Oklahoma High School Player of the Year honors and setting the national high school record for hits. All of that landed him at the top of the Draft, taken No. 1 overall by the Orioles and given a bonus of $8.19 million, a record for a high schooler. He reached Low-A Delmarva during his pro debut, then hit his way to Double-A in his first full season. The combination of nature and nurture certainly come into play, with growing up around the game clearly helping Holliday’s overall skillset. He has an extremely advanced approach at the plate, and he showed it off by walking more than twice as much as he struck out during his debut last summer. He has a simple left-handed stroke he got back to after his swing got a little long last summer, allowing him make more hard contact than ever, with plenty of power coming organically from his swing. With strength he added before his senior year, and with more to come, Holliday has also gotten faster and is a consistently plus runner. There’s an up arrow next to his arm strength as well and that, along with his improved quickness, means he should be able to play shortstop for a long time. His combination of pure tools and high baseball IQ have helped him move through the system quicker than a typical prep player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arrighetti pitched at three different colleges in three years, moving from Texas Christian to Navarro (Texas) JC to Louisiana-Lafayette before the Astros selected him in 2021's sixth round. Houston has helped him significantly upgrade his stuff since he turned pro, and he led the system with 152 strikeouts in 106 2/3 innings during his first full pro season and reached Triple-A midway though his second. The organization's Minor League pitcher of the year in 2023, he has averaged 11.6 strikeouts per nine innings as pro. Arrighetti's fastball has jumped from 89-91 mph with a peak of 94 with the Ragin' Cajuns to 92-95 mph with a max velo of 97 in pro ball, and his four-seamer's flat approach angle and late hop keep it off barrels. He has turned what was a ho-hum slider with tight break into a low-80s sweeper that's now his best pitch, and he also can morph it into a harder cutter. His upper-70s curveball features good depth, he has a new grip on his mid-80s changeup that produces tumble and he may add a two-seamer in 2024. To reach his ceiling as a No. 4 starter, Arrighetti will have to refine his control and command.
