He threw more strikes with less stuff in college, though he doesn't have to be terribly precise because his low arm slot and the extension in his delivery create a lot of deception. If he can't stick in the rotation, his fastball/slider combination and competitive nature could make him a bullpen weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arrighetti pitched at three colleges in three years, relieving at Texas Christian in 2019 before starting at Navarro JC (Texas) and Louisiana-Lafayette the next two seasons. His stuff has improved significantly since he turned pro as a sixth-rounder in 2021, propelling him to Double-A by the end of his first full season. He led all Astros farmhands with 152 strikeouts in 106 2/3 innings in 2022. After operating at 89-91 mph and peaking at 94 with his fastball at Louisiana-Lafayette, Arrighetti now deals at 92-95 and touches 97 with a flat approach angle and late hop that make his heater tough to barrel. He has upgraded a mediocre slider with tight break into a low-80s sweeper that misses a lot of bats. He also utilizes a mid-70s curveball to give hitters a different look and is trying to refine a mid-80s changeup that has fade but needs more separation from his fastball. Arrighetti still is learning to harness his improved stuff and got tagged for a 5.04 ERA in High-A as he battled control and command at times. He threw strikes in college and doesn't have to be precise because his low arm slot and the extension in his delivery create a lot of deception. He could be a No. 4 starter if he locates his pitches better, and his fastball/slider combination and competitiveness would play well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arrighetti began his college career as a reliever at Texas Christian before transferring and becoming a starter at Navarro (Texas) JC and Louisiana-Lafayette. He made an immediate impression with the Ragin' Cajuns last spring, allowing just four runs while fanning 50 in his first 40 innings, before tailing off and serving as a closer in the Sun Belt Conference tournament. He made six brief pro appearances after signing for $147,500 in the sixth round last July. Arrighetti's fastball sat at 89-91 mph and topped out at 94 mph at Louisiana-Lafayette before ticking up 3-4 mph in his first year as a pro, but it's the flat approach angle and late hop on his heater that make it a plus pitch. His best weapon is a low-80s slider, which showed signs of giving him a second plus offering after Houston tweaked his grip and helped him find more sweep. He also spins a mid-70s curveball and owns a rudimentary low-80s changeup but can't always land them for strikes. While Arrighetti has four pitches and provides a decent amount of strikes, he lacks physicality and will have to prove he can handle the pro workload to remain a starter. He's a potential back-of-the-rotation option but projects better as a multi-inning reliever who could focus on his fastball and slider. His competitive nature fits well in the bullpen, and he might add more velocity working in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Overshadowed in a JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield that also included 2017 Twins No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis and 2019 Cubs second-rounder Chase Strumpf, Wendzel was lightly recruited but blossomed into one of college baseball's best hitting prospects in three years at Baylor. He shared 2019 Big 12 Conference player of the year honors with Josh Jung before the Rangers took them both with their top two picks that June, signing Wendzel for $1.6 million as a supplemental first-rounder. He barely has been healthy as a pro, missing most of his debut summer with a thumb injury and dealing with a broken hamate in 2021. Wendzel seemed to press at times and was bothered by the hamate while batting just .238/.346/.399 between three levels last year. When fully healthy, he works counts and utilizes the entire field with a controlled right-handed stroke. He's still a hit-over-power guy, but he has been more aggressive in pro ball than he was in college, showing enough strength and raw power to deliver perhaps 20 homers per season. Wendzel's impressive work ethic helped him improve his athleticism after he got to Baylor, and he spent much of this offseason getting into even better shape and also consulting with Rangers hitting director Cody Atkinson. His instincts allow him to play faster than his average speed on the bases and in the field. His twitchy athleticism, soft hands and strong arm allow him to play a solid third base and he also started games at shortstop, second base and left field last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wendzel was overshadowed in a JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield that also included 2017 No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis and 2019 Cubs second-round pick Chase Strumpf. He went from being lightly recruited to one of college baseball's top hitting prospects in three years at Baylor, sharing the 2019 Big 12 Conference player of the year award with Josh Jung before the Rangers used their top two picks that June on them both. Wendzel missed most of his pro debut with a minor thumb injury after signing for $1.6 million as a supplemental first-rounder but impressed in 2020 at Texas' alternate training site and in instructional league. One of the more polished hitters in the system, Wendzel isn't afraid to work deep counts in search of a pitch to drive and will take walks if he doesn't get one. He stays inside the ball well and utilizes the entire field, usually working from gap to gap with a controlled right-handed stroke. He has the strength and raw power to hit 20 or more homers per season if he looks to pull pitches more often. Wendzel has worked hard to improve his speed and athleticism since arriving at Baylor and is now close to an average runner who plays faster than that thanks to his instincts. His twitchy actions, soft hands and strong arm make him a solid defender at third base. The Rangers believe he can play an average shortstop after seeing him at their alt site, where they also gave him time at second base and all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wendzel drew little scouting or recruiting attention at JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.), where he was overshadowed by 2017 No. 1 overall choice Royce Lewis and 2019 Cubs second-rounder Chase Strumpf. He blossomed into one of the college baseball's best hitting prospects in three years at Baylor and shared the 2019 Big 12 Conference player of the year award with fellow third baseman Josh Jung. The Rangers used their first two picks last June on Jung and Wendzel, signing the latter for $1.6 million as a supplemental first-rounder and seeing him miss most of his pro debut with a minor thumb injury. Fearless at the plate, Wendzel works deep counts while hunting for a pitch to drive and accepts walks if he doesn't get one. A right-handed hitter, he stays inside the ball well and uses the entire field. He focuses on working from gap to gap rather than selling out for homers, and he could get more out of his solid strength and raw power if he looks to turn on pitches more often. Though Wendzel had below-average speed when he got to college, he worked diligently to become close to an average runner out of the batter's box and his instincts allow him to play quicker than that on the bases. He displays some twitchy action at third base, where he shows soft hands and both his arm and defense earn solid to plus grades. He played all over the diamond for Baylor during games and fall practice, and Texas plans on exposing him to both middle-infield spots and the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals didn't have a pick until the third round of the 2017 Draft because of their free-agent signing of Dexter Fowler and the hacking scandal with the Astros. They did try to strategically use their small bonus pool and went over pick value to sign Jackson out of the Florida high school ranks, and away from playing for the Florida Gators, in the sixth round. He played sparingly on a Gulf Coast League roster that had two other catchers on it during his pro debut. Jackson is a left-handed-hitting catcher, something always in demand, one with power potential at the plate and a power arm behind it. He's capable of making loud contact with solid bat speed, and while there's swing-and-miss potential, he draws walks and can drive the ball, with the chance for future Major League power. His arm will flash plus at times and he threw out 31.5 percent of potential basestealers during his debut, albeit in a very small sample size. He's not overly athletic or agile, so he'll have to work on his overall receiving. Jackson is getting his Cardinals career going in earnest in 2018, with reps and time needed, as they are for any high school backstop to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For a player whose speed has been a hallmark of his game, Perez has had a slow climb up the Tigers' system since signing for $550,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2016. He spent the better part of three seasons in A-ball, then broke out with a .902 OPS between High-A West Michigan and Double-A Erie in 2022 to land back on the prospect map and onto Detroit’s 40-man roster. Just when he seemed on a path to Detroit, lingering back injuries hampered him for much of 2023. He earned a late-season promotion to Toledo, posting an .890 OPS in 35 games. While Perez is fast, his breakout as a prospect came after adding strength to his body and changing his swing to create more lift. He’s an increasingly selective hitter, reflected in a career-high 63 walks last year, but sometimes also struggles to find his best pitch for damage and ends up with softer contact. His power drop last year seemed to coincide with his back issues, though his extra-base production improved later in the year. His switch-hitting capabilities are hampered by a struggle to hit left-handed pitching, including a .197 average last year. Perez has enough speed to steal 25-plus bases, but he can be up and down with success rate, especially after he advances a level. Throwing issues severely hampered Perez at second base last year, but his arm seems to play better as an outfielder, where his speed helps him cover ground in center. Though Perez’s athleticism and versatility have a chance to contribute in the Majors, his appeal is hampered by his platoon splits and defensive issues at second. He has a chance to address these at Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $550,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2016, Perez has ridden a roller-coaster career -- one that is back on the upswing. The switch-hitting infielder showed promise by hitting above .300 in each of his first two seasons and even reached Single-A ball in his age-18 season, only to struggle badly at two A-ball levels in 2019 and 2021. Last season represented a major breakout with a .295/.369/.534 line and career highs in homers (14) and extra-base hits (47) over 94 games between High-A and Double-A. The Tigers protected Perez from the Rule 5 Draft by adding him to the 40-man roster last November. Thanks to a quiet load and good bat speed, Perez has long put up quality contact rates in the Minors but took off last season after adding strength that helped increase his exit velocities and better elevate batted balls, leading to his much-improved slugging rates. The bulk of his power still comes from his at-bats as a lefty, but he hits southpaws well enough to hold off splits issues as a righty. While he won’t likely threaten 20 homers at his peak, his power increases have been promising enough to raise his entire offensive profile. A plus runner capable of stealing 15-plus bags a season, the 5-foot-11 prospect has moved around the infield throughout his career with stops at short and third (where he has enough arm), but the Tigers feel he’s found a home at second, where he can still be valuable up the middle with good footwork around the bag. He's also added some looks in center and left this season in his ascent to Triple-A Toledo. His versatility could come in handy should he settle into more of a utility role, especially now that fellow second baseman Jace Jung is in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez was a relative find on the international market, signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2016 for a $550,000 bonus and advancing to Class A West Michigan by the end of his first season stateside at age 18. A strong month there found him climbing prospect rankings, but he struggled to build on that, batting just .233 with a .613 OPS at the same level the following year. A foot injury sidelined him during Spring Training in 2020 before the shutdown, but he recovered in time for instructional ball. While Perez is a switch-hitter, he bats more comfortably from the right side. He has a quick bat for contact, but his power is limited to line drives to the gaps, allowing his speed to play for triples and doubles. He slumped badly to begin 2019 trying to boost his power, but recovered down the stretch. He’s a daring baserunner at times, but has been slowed by injuries the past couple years. His athleticism and range suggest he has the tools to stick at shortstop, but inconsistent throws led to many of his 33 errors in 2019. Perez faces a critical season in 2021 after being left unprotected for the Rule 5 Draft. While the Tigers have stocked up on left-side infielders in recent amateur Drafts, some see Perez eventually shifting to second base, where his offensive struggles would be less glaring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, the Tigers preferred spreading out their international prospect money to sign several players at mid-range bonuses rather than throw most of it into one prospect, preferring the odds that that one or more of the former group would make it. Perez, a $550,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic, stands as an example why. The speedy infielder wasn’t a high-ranked signing until he made it to the states in 2018 and hit up the rookie-level Gulf Coast League and made the Midwest League at 18. He opened the following season at West Michigan and showed the growing pains of his first full-season pro stop, but continued to flash his athletic potential. While Perez is a switch-hitter, he bats more comfortably from the right side, evidenced in his splits against left-handed pitching. He has a quick bat for contact, but his power is limited to line drives to the gaps, allowing his speed to play for doubles and triples. He slumped badly to begin 2019 but recovered down the stretch. Some scouts see him as an eventual glove-first shortstop. His athleticism and range suggest he has the tools to stick there, but inconsistent throws led to many of his 33 errors in 2019. The results in 2019 dimmed the star on Perez’s rise through the system, but he remains a promising middle infielder in the Tigers system. He has a strong, thick frame for his size, but will have to be careful not to outgrow his position or get away from his strengths.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not every successful international signing has to be a seven-figure expenditure. If the early returns are any indication, Perez, who signed for $550,000 in July 2016 out of the Dominican Republic, will be one of those bargain finds. He showcased natural hitting ability during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League and firmly put himself on the prospect radar in 2018, ascending three levels to finish the season as an 18-year-old in the Class A Midwest League. With his plus bat speed, barrel control and a clean swing from both sides of the plate, Perez shows many of the attributes needed to hit for a high average. He covers the plate well, too, trusting his approach to let pitches travel deep and open up his use of the entire field. He projects for more gap power than true over-the-fence pop, but there's enough raw power and physical projection remaining to think he could produce double-digit homers in his prime. Perez's loudest tool is plus speed that shows up in all facets of the game. He gets out of the box and down the line well and is aggressive on the basepaths, at times to a fault. Those wheels, along with his overall athleticism, translate well at shortstop, where he profiles as an above-average defender with the necessary hands, actions and arm strength to stick at the position long term. Perez's lack of power limits his ceiling, but the pieces are there for him to develop into a glove-first regular up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Henley threw three consecutive no-hitters as a Texas high school senior and was one of the more polished arms in the 2016 prep class, he lasted until the Yankees took him in the 22nd round because of his commitment to Texas. He was a three-year starter for the Longhorns but his stuff didn't improve, so he went undrafted as an eligible sophomore in 2018 and lasted seven rounds last June. He recorded a 1.47 ERA with a 50/9 K/BB ratio in 36 2/3 innings during his pro debut. Henley has elite spin rates of more than 3000 rpm on his curveball, an upper-70s breaker that falls off the table when it's on, and also has aptitude for throwing a low-80s slider with sharp break. The Astros have had a lot of success at souping up fastballs, and they hope to improve the shape and spin on his 88-92 mph heater. His changeup is his clear fourth option but shows signs of becoming an average offering. While it helps him stay on top of his breaking pitches and creates downhill plane, scouts don't love his upright delivery. He didn't always stay online to the plate in college, though he threw more consistent strikes in his introduction to pro ball. If he can build off that momentum, he could advance quickly as a potential back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his junior year at Florida Atlantic in 2019, Pagés was the Conference USA Defensive Player of the Year and a Buster Posey Award semifinalist, and that performance helped push him into the sixth round. His defense elevated him as high as Triple-A in 2022, but his bat lagged behind his glove, leading to a return to Double-A Springfield for 2023. Back in the Texas League, Pagés enjoyed his best offensive season yet, slashing .267/.362/.443 with a career-high 16 homers across 117 games. He was added to St. Louis’ 40-man roster in November, one year after he first became Rule 5-eligible. Pagés starts from a wide base at the plate, then dips his back shoulder as the pitcher delivers but he still manages to stay on time. Last season, he did a tremendous job of not expanding the zone against pitches of any kind and cut down on his swing-and-miss, too, with a Texas League strikeout rate that dropped from 33.5 percent in ’22 to 19.3. He has average raw power, and the improved contact and swing decisions allowed that to play better in game, though considering he was repeating the level, it’s worth wondering how the bat will hold at Triple-A. Entering his age-25 season, Pagés gets his best reviews on his defensive work behind the dish. He’s a terrific blocker and receiver from a one-knee-down stance, and Cardinals evaluators note that he thinks like a pitcher with his work as a gamecaller. He has the arm strength to limit the running game, too, with a 38.2 percent caught-stealing rate that led Double-A qualifiers. Pagés may be third on St. Louis’ catching depth chart entering 2024, but the Cards shouldn’t be afraid to call on his defense quickly if and when they need it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foscue led Mississippi State to the Men's College World Series in both of his two full seasons in Starkville before the Rangers signed him for a below-slot $3.25 million as the 14th overall pick in the 2020 Draft. He homered in eight consecutive games during his 2021 pro debut and has been one of the most productive and disciplined hitters in the system since, though he doesn't have a clear path to a role in Texas. He made his big league debut last year but went 2-for-42 (.048) and lost nearly three months to a left oblique strain. A right-handed hitter, Foscue is a combination of extremes at the plate. He doesn't chase or swing and miss much relative to other hitters, allowing him to control the strike zone and make a lot of contact, but he also rates on the low end in terms of bat speed and exit velocities. Scouts have serious reservations about how his power will play in the Majors, though his strength should translate into 15 homers per season, mostly to his pull side. Foscue's well-below-average speed and athleticism limit his usefulness on the bases and in the field. He has reliable hands and fine instincts, but he has below-average range and arm strength at second base, his primary position. A trial at third didn't go well in 2023, and he's merely adequate at first, where he lacks the pop to profile as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After helping Mississippi State reach the College World Series in his two full seasons in Starkville, Foscue went 14th overall to Texas in the pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft. Signed for an under-slot $3.25 million, he homered in eight straight games during his 2021 pro debut and has performed well in the upper levels of the Minors the past two seasons. He ranked third in the Triple-A Pacific Coast League in walks (85) and fourth in doubles (31) while expanding his defensive horizons last summer. Foscue is a polished right-handed hitter who knows himself and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. He doesn't chase pitches and focuses on using the entire field rather than trying to launch balls out of the park. Even with his disciplined approach, he has enough bat speed and strength to provide 20 homers per season, with most of his over-the-fence power going to his pull side. Foscue has reliable hands and good instincts, but his defensive effectiveness is limited by well-below-average speed and substandard range and arm strength. Mostly a second baseman in his first two pro seasons, he saw increased action at third base (where his arm is too light and the game is too fast for him) and tried first base in 2023. Given that the Rangers have All-Stars at every other infield spot, his only real chances for big league playing time with them are at first and DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foscue helped lead Mississippi State to the College World Series in each of his two full seasons before becoming the third-highest Bulldogs position player ever drafted in his third. He went 14th overall in 2020, trailing only Will Clark (No. 2, 1985) and Hunter Renfroe (No. 13, 2013) in school history, and signed for an under-slot $3.25 million. He homered in eight straight games during his injury-shortened 2021 pro debut before batting .288/.367/.483 in Double-A last year. An offensive-minded second baseman, Foscue did a better job of letting his bat speed and strength translate into power rather than chasing home runs in 2022. The right-handed hitter showed more discipline, made more contact and used the opposite field more often than he did while struggling in Double-A at the end of his debut. He misses few fastballs, hangs in well against breaking balls and changeups and destroys left-handers while holding his own against right-handers. More muscular than most middle infielders, Foscue is a below-average runner who's a little quicker once underway. He does have reliable hands and turns the double play well at second base, though his fringy arm and range limit his effectiveness there. He played third base as a Mississippi State freshman and briefly in 2022 but lacks the arm for the hot corner, and he could wind up in left field given the Rangers' overcrowded infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After helping Mississippi State reach the College World Series in each of his two full seasons, Foscue became the third-highest Bulldogs position player ever drafted behind Will Clark (No. 2, 1985) and Hunter Renfroe (No. 13, 2013). Signed for an under-slot $3.25 million as the 14th overall choice in 2020, he sustained a left ribcage injury three weeks into his pro debut last May and didn't return until early July. Once healthy, he homered in eight consecutive games and finished with 17 blasts in 62 games while reaching Double-A. Foscue is an offensive-minded second baseman whose right-handed power stands out as his best tool, in the mold of Jeff Kent. He has more bat speed and strength than most middle infielders, and he makes the most of it with an approach designed to launch pitches to his pull side. He can get overly aggressive at times and likely will have to tone it down a bit to hit for average against more advanced pitching. Though he's a below-average runner out of the batter's box, Foscue displays close to average speed once he gets going. He has good hands and turns the double play well at second base, where he's a fringy to average defender. His so-so range and arm strength limit his usefulness on the left side of the infield, though he did play third base as a Mississippi State freshman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers used their first-round picks in 2019 and 2020 on infielders with offensive upside and a track record of production at the highest levels of college baseball. They followed Texas Tech third baseman Josh Jung with Foscue, who signed for an under-slot $3.25 million as the 14th overall pick last June. He led Mississippi State to the College World Series in each of his two full seasons and became the third-highest Bulldogs position player ever drafted, behind only Will Clark (No. 2, 1985) and Hunter Renfroe (No. 13, 2013). An offensive-minded player whose right-handed power is his best tool, Foscue has a profile similar to that of Jeff Kent. He has more strength and bat speed than a typical second baseman and attacks pitches with a pull-heavy approach. Though he's aggressive at the plate, he makes consistent contact and should produce 20 or more homers per season without striking out excessively. Foscue records below-average run times from home to first but has close to average speed underway. Though his arm and range are nothing special at second base, he has good hands and turns double plays well. He played third base as a freshman in college but would be stretched at shortstop, reducing his potential value as a utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox grabbed Fernandez in the 23rd round of the 2018 Draft and signed him for $125,000 out of Hillsborough (Florida) CC. The 6-foot right-hander has been relief-only since the lost 2020 season. He lost out on some playing time with elbow inflammation in 2022 and topped out at 54 1/3 innings last year, 30 2/3 of which came at Triple-A Worcester, where he had a 6.16 ERA but struck out 35 and walked only 10. After Boston left him off the 40-man roster, the Cardinals selected Fernandez in the December Rule 5 Draft. Fernandez can touch 99 mph with his fastball and typically sits 96-97, but the pitch doesn’t play to its velocity due to lack of impressive movement. Triple-A batters slugged .594 off the heater alone, so that’ll be a focus of improvement in his shot with the Cards. He throws a pair of hard breaking balls in an upper-80s slider and low-90s cutter, though the two can bleed into one another. The ferocity makes them a pair of potential plus pitches and helps drive Fernandez’s whiffs. He can also show the occasional curveball but lacks a changeup, which hurt him against left-handers. While walks were up across Triple-A, the righty actually kept his free passes in check with a 7.2 percent walk rate with Worcester. Despite turning 26 in June, Fernandez is still more about his raw materials than results, giving St. Louis officials hope they could mold him and his arsenal into a Major League reliever who specializes in facing righties in 2024 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $415,000 signing out of Venezuela in July 2017, Barrosa pushed his way onto Arizona’s 40-man roster five years later after a breakout year at Double-A Amarillo in which he posted an .812 OPS in 110 games. He spent all of 2023 with Triple-A Reno with more solid results (.274/.394/.456, 13 homers). The switch-hitter made his Major League debut on April 1, 2024 with the D-backs but returned to the Pacific Coast League after three games, only to suffer a hamstring injury later that month. Hamstring issues dogged him for a good part of the first half and he didn’t return to the Majors until September before ending the year back in Reno, where he finished with a .781 OPS in 75 total games. The injuries – and concerns about them – slowed Barrosa down in his return to the Aces; most of his top-end Sprint Speeds at Triple-A came in 2023. He’s still an above-average runner capable of pushing for stolen bases, and his great instincts in the field are perhaps his best skill. He can still track down balls and make amazing grabs in center, but without the plus closing speed, it’s a 60 glove instead of a 70. Below-average arm strength also make him a better fit in left than right when he needs to move to a corner. At 5-foot-6, Barrosa doesn’t have a big strike zone, but he expanded it more at Triple-A in 2024. That said, his contact rates were still solid, and he’ll never be a big exit-velocity guy anyway. A natural lefty thrower, he was better hitting from the left side once again in ’24, though his splits have evened out in '25. The D-backs have a thing for short, athletic outfielders, and Barrosa will get another chance to fight through the depth chart in a backup role this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 60 | Arm: 45 | Field: 70 | Overall: 45 Signed for $415,000 in July 2017, Barrosa didn’t truly break out in the Arizona system until five years later over a full season at Double-A Amarillo in which he slashed .276/.374/.438 with 12 homers and 22 steals in 110 games. That earned him Rule 5 protection with a 40-man roster spot in November 2022, and last season, the D-backs sent the outfielder to Triple-A Reno, where he was again a solid performer (.274/.394/.456, 13 homers, 15 steals in 120 games) in a hitter-friendly environment. Barrosa stands in the box at just 5-foot-5, giving him a small strike zone to begin with, and as a switch-hitter, he’s able to place the barrel well to most areas of the zone and sometimes out of it. While he chased some, he only had whiff rates above 30 percent on sliders and curveballs at Triple-A. That’s helped him keep his K rate below 20 percent at every full-season stop so far. Barrosa shows more slugging ability from his left side -- where he hit 11 of his 13 homers in ’23 -- and even so, he packs a modest punch with his .413 SLG away from Reno, a better indication of his true ability. The Venezuela native plays with high energy and is a delight to watch cover the outfield, using tremendous instincts to head toward balls in the gap and plus speed to close them down. Below-average arm strength dulls things a little defensively, but there’s still Gold Glove upside if he plays everyday. That will come down to the impact in Barrosa’s bat, but it isn’t hard to see him being valuable as switch-hitting, glove-first fourth outfielder either.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arizona signed Barrosa for $415,000 in July 2017, and he’s climbed meticulously through the D-backs Minor League ranks in almost six years. While he finally made his full-season debut in 2021, the Venezuela native’s breakout campaign came a year later, when he played 110 games for Double-A Amarillo and hit .276/.374/.438 with 12 homers and 22 steals. The D-backs added him to their 40-man roster in the offseason, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft in his second year of eligibility. Barrosa moved to switch-hitting full time in 2018, and he’s developed well from both sides of the plate, though he has a touch more from the right side (where he is more of a natural in the box). That said, his best offensive asset continues to be his advanced approach and discerning eye, which have helped him post healthy walk and strikeout rates in recent years. Standing just 5-foot-9, he’ll never be much of a power hitter, and it’s worth noting he slugged just .389 away from the hitters' haven that is Amarillo last year. The center fielder is an exceptional defender in the middle of the grass – one with great instincts off the bat and the plus closing speed to chase down balls from gap to gap. He’s long considered to have one of the best gloves in the system, but Corbin Carroll and Druw Jones (two players with better bats and even more speed) have better claims on the starting center-field job in the desert. Barrosa’s average bat could still work in a corner, if needed, or he could be a super sub off the bench with his ability to switch-hit and provide instant impact on the basepaths and in the field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs were aggressive in the international market at the start of the 2017 signing period, with Bahamian Kristian Robinson the big catch, getting a seven-figure bonus. They also got Barrosa, an intriguing outfield prospect in his own right, signing him out of Venezuela for $415,000. Making his pro debut in 2018, Barrosa impressed in all facets of the games in the Dominican Summer League before moving stateside and finishing his age-17 season in the Pioneer League. Barrosa is already showing a good feel to hit, with natural bat-to-ball skills and an advanced approach at the plate. He is now a switch-hitter and took quickly to hitting left-handed for the first time in 2018, all while demonstrating excellent on-base skills but also little power from both sides of the plate. He was successful in 39 of 47 steal attempts thanks to a combination of plus speed and strong instincts that also serve him well in center field, where he has a chance to be plus defender. Barrosa has a long way to go before it's clear what kind of player he will be. If he continues to progress, he has the chance to be a top-of-the-order type in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 26th-round pick by the Giants out of Long Beach State in 2019, Avila got rocked as a High-A starter in his full-season debut in 2021, but found instant success when he became a full-time reliever that August. He led all Minor League relievers (minimum 50 innings) with a 1.14 ERA last season, after which San Francisco declined to protect him on its 40-man roster. After selecting him in the big league phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December, the White Sox must keep him on their big league roster throughout 2023 or pass him through waivers and offer him back to the Giants for half of his $100,000 Rule 5 price. Avila has a more diverse repertoire than most relievers, using five different pitches: two-seam and four-seam fastballs, a distinct cutter, a slider and a curveball. His upper-80s cutter and riding mid-90s four-seamer are plus weapons that generate lots of swings-and-misses, chases and weak contact. His low-90s two-seamer and mid-80s slider are solid offerings, while his 78-82 mph curveball has more depth than his other pitches but is more fringy. Avila provides plenty of strikes coming out of the bullpen, walking just 2.3 per nine innings in 2022 after averaging 4.8 as a starter the year before. He's effective against both left-handers and right-handers, enhancing his chances of sticking in Chicago. He profiles more as a middle reliever than a late-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shenton has taken an up-and-down journey to reach the doorstep of the Majors. A fifth-round pick by the Mariners in 2019, he crushed Minor League pitching in 2021 and wound up traded to the Rays for reliever Diego Castillo. He returned to Double-A in ’22, but a hip injury limited him to 52 games and sapped his power. He returned to better health and top form last year, mashing to the tune of a .304/.423/.584 line with 29 homers and 99 RBIs in 134 games between Double-A Montgomery and Triple-A Durham, then earned a spot on Tampa Bay’s 40-man roster in the offseason. As long as he’s healthy, Shenton is going to hit. He has an advanced approach, and he’s done nothing but hit for average, get on base and display extra-base pop in the Minors aside from his injury-plagued ’22 season. He struck out more in the upper Minors, specifically against offspeed stuff, but not enough to temper the Rays’ excitement about his offensive upside. He has above-average raw power and feel for the barrel, and the underlying data backs up the performance he’s put together. There are some drawbacks, however. He’ll be 26 years old this season. He’s a below-average runner. He’s at best an average defender, perhaps a tick above that at first and a tick below that at third (albeit with enough arm to handle the hot corner), and he could potentially see some time in the outfield this season. His path to playing time is blocked by the likes of Yandy Díaz and Isaac Paredes, not to mention Jonathan Aranda, Junior Caminero and Curtis Mead. But he’s not far from being a big league option, which is why he’s garnered interest from other clubs in trade talks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A local kid who began his college career near home at Bellevue Junior College in Washington, Shenton later transferred across the country to Florida International for his sophomore year. He really jumped on the map in the Cape Cod League after that season, but he couldn’t replicate that success as a junior, undoubtedly impacted by his mother undergoing cancer treatments back home. He started to heat up as the Draft approached, eventually landing with the Mariners in the fifth round in 2019, then he went out and looked like the guy people saw on the Cape during his pro debut, reaching full-season ball in the process. Shenton hit .300/.414/.566 with 12 homers over 67 games between High-A and Double-A in 2021 before being moved to the Rays in a three-player Deadline deal for Diego Castillo. What Seattle liked most about Shenton coming out of the Draft was his pure hit ability and a mature approach with consistent hard contact. As he exhibited in his pro debut before taking a fastball to the jaw that ended his season, Shenton can drive the ball to all fields for extra bases, even if his home run power is more exclusively to the pull side. While Shenton’s ceiling remains somewhat uncertain and hinging upon his development, his floor is very high. The 23-year-old has drawn comparisons to Max Muncy, and he should reach the big leagues purely on his ability to hit. At the alternate training site in 2020, Shenton smacked one of the longest home runs in recent memory at Cheney Stadium, taking George Kirby deep. Part of the Muncy comp comes from Shenton’s room to improve with his run game, as he can look non-athletic at times. His range is limited at third, but he has a solid average arm from the hot corner and gets very high marks for his makeup, so he won’t be outworked in terms of improving his defensive profile. He also won’t complain about moving around, something he accomplished during his debut with time in the outfield corners. It’s that bat that will push him up the organizational ladder – he’s said to be beyond his years with his approach, particularly with a great feel for where his barrel is - and he could continue his quick move up the ladder with Tampa Bay.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shenton began his college career near home at Bellevue Junior College in Washington, but transferred across the country to Florida International for his sophomore year. He really jumped on the map in the Cape Cod League after that season, but couldn’t replicate that success as a junior, undoubtedly impacted by his mother undergoing cancer treatments back at home. He started to heat up as the Draft approached, eventually landing with the Mariners in the fifth round of the 2019 Draft, then going out and looking like the guy people saw in the Cape during his pro debut, reaching full-season ball in the process. What the Mariners were buying was Shenton’s left-handed bat. He has a really good swing with a very good approach at the plate and the ability to make consistent hard contact. He showed in his pro debut that he has the ability to drive the ball to all fields for extra bases, even if his home run power came to his pull side. Shenton doesn’t run well and can look non-athletic at times. His range is limited at third, but he has a solid average arm from the hot corner and gets very high marks for his makeup, so he won’t be outworked in terms of improving his defensive profile. He also won’t complain about moving around, something he did during his debut by seeing time in the outfield corners. It’s that bat that will push him up the organizational ladder, and he could move pretty quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees selected Sauer in the second round of the 2017 Draft and signed him to an over-slot $2.5 million bonus, but health problems have limited him in his professional career. He underwent Tommy John surgery in ‘19 and had another procedure to address elbow and forearm problems in ‘23. He still threw 68 1/3 innings in Double-A last year, with a 3.42 ERA, 29.5 percent strikeout rate and 10.3 percent walk rate, and the Royals snagged him in the Rule 5 Draft, adding a new face to their bullpen. Sauer can spin the ball very well and is mainly a fastball-slider pitcher, with both pitches grading as above-average. His heater sits 93-94 mph and can get to the upper-90s with good ride. His best pitch is an upper-80s slider that misses bats with sweeping action. He does have a curveball and changeup to round out his arsenal. They’re inconsistent at best, and he might not need them if he’s a reliever. Sauer is efficient and throws strikes, which is why the Royals targeted him in the Rule 5 Draft. He has good size, strength and athleticism on the mound, even without the loud stuff he had when he was younger. If Sauer makes the team out of Spring Training -- something he’ll have to do if the Royals want to avoid putting him through waivers or offering back to the Yankees -- he’ll be skipping Triple-A completely. But the Royals think he’s well-balanced and should be able to manage it. His stuff might tick up in shorter outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees took Clarke Schmidt in the first round of the 2017 Draft and signed him to a below-slot bonus because he was coming off Tommy John surgery, then used the savings to pay Sauer an over-slot $2,497,500. He blew out his elbow two starts into his full-season debut in 2019 and required elbow reconstruction that April, but he came back to rank among the system's strikeout leaders in 2021 and 2022. More surgery to address elbow and forearm problems limited him to 68 1/3 Double-A innings in 2023 (3.42 ERA, 83 strikeouts in that span), and after the Yankees left him unprotected, the Royals snagged him in the Rule 5 Draft this December. After touching 97 mph as a Massachusetts high school senior, Sauer mostly worked at 91-93 mph and peaked at 95 with riding life on his fastball. His best pitch is a tight low-80s slider that can get swings and misses in the strike zone and chases outside of it, while his upper-70s curveball no longer shows signs of becoming a hammer like it did in the past. After left-handed hitters batted him around in 2022, he needs to improve a mid-80s changeup that features fade but not enough velocity separation from his fastball. While Sauer flashed louder stuff in the past, he has become more efficient with his pitches. He has the size, strength and athleticism desired in a starter, though he'll have to add some more power to his stuff or refine his command to fit in the back of a big league rotation. If he moves to the bullpen in the Majors with Kansas City, he might gain more velocity and could depend more on his slider in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sauer's Draft stock soared when he started hitting 97 mph with his fastball as a California high school senior in 2017. The Yankees selected Clarke Schmidt in the first round and signed him to a below-slot deal because he was coming off Tommy John surgery, then used the savings to pay Sauer an over-slot $2,497,500 in the second round. They handled him carefully but he still blew out his elbow two starts into the 2019 season, necessitating elbow reconstruction of his own that April. Sauer worked with a 93-96 mph fastball with riding action before he got hurt and showed similar velocity when he returned to the mound last spring. He utilized both a curveball and a slider as an amateur before New York had him concentrate on his curve, which ranges from a low-80s hammer at its best to a slurve at its worst. He has focused on the development of his changeup since turning pro, and his has fade but not always enough velocity separation from his heater. The Yankees believe Sauer's size, strength and athleticism will lend themselves to the control and durability to make it as a starter. Before his elbow gave out, some scouts outside the organization thought he was likely to wind up as a reliever because of the effort in his delivery and the length of his arm action. He worked just 87 1/3 innings in his first four years as a pro, so his future won't become clear until he gains more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sauer was one of the more projectable pitchers in the 2017 high school class until he suddenly started realizing a lot of that projection in his senior year. After sitting around 90 mph the year before, he suddenly started popping 97s and his stock soared along with his velocity. The Yankees took him in the second round and signed him away from an Arizona commitment for $2,497,500 -- $313,200 more than they paid first-rounder Clarke Schmidt. Sauer's fastball sat at 90-93 mph at the beginning of last summer, when he focused on his changeup and dialed down his velocity to throw more strikes, but he was back up to 93-96 toward the end of the season. After he threw both a curveball and a slider as an amateur, New York has had him concentrate on his curve, which can be a low-80s hammer but lacks consistency. He's making encouraging progress with his changeup after not using it much before turning pro. The Yankees like Sauer's combination of size, strength and athleticism, which they think bodes well for having the control and durability to be a starter. Some scouts outside the organization worry about the length of his arm action and the effort in his delivery and think he'll wind up in the bullpen. How he handles the workload in full-season ball in 2019 will shed more light on his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: On the high school showcase circuit before his senior season, Sauer stood out more for his projection than his present stuff. That changed last spring when his fastball suddenly started hitting 97 mph and he became one of the most in-demand prep pitching prospects in the 2017 Draft. The Yankees took him in the second round and signed him away from an Arizona commitment for late first-round money ($2,497,500). After working at 88-92 mph in 2016, Sauer now operates with a 92-95 mph fastball and touches 97, and he maintained his improved velocity through instructional league in the fall. He also showed some power with both a curveball and a slider as an amateur, and New York will have him focus going forward on his tight curve, which has the upside of a plus pitch. His changeup will require more work because he seldom used his as an amateur. Sauer has the size for durability and the athleticism to throw strikes and make adjustments, so the Yankees envision him becoming a mid-rotation starter. Some scouts have concerns about his delivery, which features a long arm action and some head whack and crossfire, and think he'll be better suited to be a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teng landed the largest bonus given to a Taiwanese prospect on the 2017-18 international market, signing with the Twins for $500,000. Minnesota packaged him with Prelander Berroa and Jaylin Davis to get Sam Dyson in a 2019 trade with the Giants. Teng has more strikeouts (475 in 358 1/3 innings) than any Minor League pitcher over the last three seasons, reached Triple-A in 2023 and joined San Francisco's 40-man roster in November. More of a finesse right-hander with a four-pitch mix before the pandemic, Teng has become heavily dependent on what has turned into a well-above-average slider. His mid-80s slide piece features two-plane depth and batters can't barrel it or stop chasing it. His 91-94 mph fastball comes with more sink than carry and grades as fringy, as do a low-80s curveball and a fading mid-80s changeup that he rarely employed last year. Teng is an intelligent pitcher who reads swings well and has shown good feel for sequencing his offerings when he's not slider-happy. He hasn't provided reliable strikes since Single-A and while his fastball generates groundballs, he struggles to command it consistently and it gets pounded when he doesn't. Burly and durable at 6-foot-4 and 260 pounds, he's beginning to look more like a slider-dominant reliever than a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When they traded Sam Dyson to the Twins in July 2019, the Giants received three potentially useful pieces in Teng, slugger Jaylin Davis and live-armed righty Prelander Berroa. Teng originally signed in 2017 for $500,000, the largest bonus given to a Taiwanese prospect in his international class. He dominated low Class A at age 20, going 7-0 with a 1.58 ERA and a .510 opponent OPS, but did not come to the United States amid the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. Teng works with four mostly average pitches, starting with a four-seam fastball that ranges from 90-94 with riding action up in the strike zone. Some scouts believe his fading changeup is his best secondary offering, while others point to his low-80s slider. He also mixes in an upper-70s curveball. Teng's repertoire plays better than the sum of its parts because he possesses tremendous feel for his craft, though his control has taken a significant step back in 2021. He has a knack for reading swings and sequencing his pitches, keeping hitters off balance. He already carries 260 pounds on his 6-foot-4 frame, so he'll have to keep his body in check to reach his ceiling as a back-of-the-rotation workhorse

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teng received the largest bonus given to a Taiwanese prospect in the 2017 international class, signing for $500,000 with the Twins in October. In a trade that could pay significant dividends for the Giants, they sent Sam Dyson to Minnesota last July in exchange for Teng, slugger Jaylin Davis and live-armed right-hander Prelander Berroa. He opened last season in extended spring training before dominating low Class A at age 20, going 7-0 with a 1.58 ERA and a .510 opponent OPS. Teng's four-seam fastball ranges from 90-94 mph with riding action that keeps it off barrels up in the strike zone. There's not much consensus about which of his secondary pitches is the best. Some scouts point to his fading changeup while others prefer his slider, and he also utilizes a curveball. None of Teng's offerings grades better than average, but he succeeds thanks to his tremendous feel for his craft. He has a knack for reading swings, allowing him to sequence his pitches well while throwing all four of them for strikes. Already hefty at 6-foot-4 and 260 pounds, he'll have to maintain his conditioning to reach his ceiling as a back-of-the-rotation workhorse.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones has been on radars for quite some time now as a two-way standout, starring for his La Mirada High School team at the 2019 National High School Invitational and countless showcase events like the PDP League this past summer. While his father, Keith, spent two summers as an infielder in the D-backs system, Jared's future is definitely on the mound. Jones will show three usable pitches, though he's more arm strength than pitchability at this point in his young career. But there's plenty of arm to like, with a fastball that is up to 96-97 mph on a consistent basis, thrown with good tail. He'll flash a solid slider that he adds and subtracts from, but it's at its best when it's the harder 80-82 mph version of the pitch and not the more slurvy 74-78 mph offering. He does miss bats with it, though a lower elbow in his delivery leads to him getting underneath it at times. He doesn't need his changeup much now, and it's a bit firm, but the 85-88 mph offspeed pitch has the chance to give him a third at least average offering. Jones’ command has been inconsistent at best, not unusual for a prep power pitcher. While he's not the biggest guy in the world, he's strong and athletic, getting good genes from both his father and his mother, who played collegiate softball. Initially committed to attend Southern California, Jones switched to Texas when USC coach Dan Hubbs was fired.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A talented two-way player from the California high school ranks, Jones was a University of Texas recruit who could have gone on to show off both his home run pop and premium fastball on the mound. The Pirates had other ideas, going over slot in the second round of the 2020 Draft to sign him for $2.2 million. He showed off his velocity as a thrower in 2021, then took some big strides toward becoming a complete pitcher with a move to High-A in 2022. Jones is still very much a power pitcher, he’s just learned how to use that stuff more effectively. He’s continued to throw consistently harder as he’s advanced in his pro career, with a fastball now consistently clocked in the 96-99 mph range. While they do still blend together, metrics show his hard, sweeping slider and his curve are separating more and more, with more depth to the curve sure to help them set apart moving forward. His changeup has also gotten better, fooling hitters when he throws it in the upper-80s, but he throws it too hard (in the low-90s) at times. While he cut his walk rate considerably in 2022, there’s still work to be done in terms of Jones’ overall command. Super-competitive, Jones has learned to keep his emotions in check on the mound, giving him every chance to continue his evolution as a complete pitcher and reach his ceiling as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones was all about power in high school, with both a high-octane fastball on the mound and impressive raw power at the plate. He could have possibly gone to University of Texas to play both ways, but most MLB teams saw him as a future pitcher. The Pirates agreed with that assessment, going over slot to sign him for $2.2 million in the second round of the 2020 Draft. His first taste of pro ball came with Low-A Bradenton in 2021, where he missed a ton of bats while showing he still has things to work on. Jones’ power stuff dominated Low-A hitters, as he struck out 14 per nine over his 66 innings of work. He throws his fastball in the mid-90s consistently and can reach back for more, with good spin rates up in the zone. He’s gone back and forth on which breaking pitch he wants to focus on, and he committed more to the harder mid-80s slider, landing it for strikes with positive results. There is feel for a changeup, but he still tends to throw it too hard, in the 85-88 mph range. Command remains the biggest obstacle in Jones’ development as a potential starter. His walk rate (4.6 BB/9) wasn’t astronomical given his experience level and there are no glaring issues with his delivery. He just needs reps to improve consistency of execution and to build up the work load. If he can do that, he has the chance to start, with the fastball-slider combination out of a bullpen an interesting backup plan.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones was a two-way standout at his California high school, one who stood out at showcase events with his power potential at the plate and his arm strength on the mound. The scouting industry felt his future was on the mound, and the Pirates were in that boat as well, taking him in the second round of the 2020 Draft and giving him an over-slot $2.2 million bonus to sign him away from his University of Texas commitment. Entering pro ball, Jones was seen as more thrower than pitcher, but with the makings of a three-pitch mix. There’s more than enough fastball to work with, a heater up to 97 mph with good tail. His slider has the chance to be at least above-average if he commits to throwing the harder low-80s version of it rather than the mid-70s slower slurvy offering, and he can get underneath the pitch at times with a lower elbow. Though his changeup can be too firm, in the 85-88 mph range, he has shown some feel for the offspeed pitch. The biggest issue for the young right-hander has been his control, which was inconsistent in high school. He’s strong and athletic with good bloodlines -- his father played pro ball and his mother was a college softball player -- and if he can iron out some of the delivery concerns, he has the chance to start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $60,000 by the Phillies as a 33rd-rounder out of a Long Island high school in 2017, Brown blew out his elbow shortly after arriving in full-season ball two years later. Subsequent Tommy John surgery meant he pitched just 135 2/3 innings (including just 25 2/3 above Rookie ball) his first five years as a pro before he finally broke out in 2022. Traded to the Cubs that August for David Robertson, he surrendered one earned run in four Double-A starts to open last season before dealing with control issues and an oblique injury at Triple-A. There's nothing subtle about Brown, who's 6-foot-6 and can overpower hitters with three pitches coming out of his high arm slot, including a fastball that operates at 94-97 mph and reaches 99 with armside run. His breaking stuff can be even more devastating, highlighted by a power curveball sitting in the mid-80s with true 12-6 action. He also has a harder slider with similar movement and speeds up to 91 mph, though he plans on sticking with one breaking ball and focusing on his curve in 2024. Despite his three plus pitches, Brown has questions to answer to become a mid-rotation starter. He has little feel or willingness to throw a changeup, he struggles to command his fastball and keep his big breaking curveball and slider in the zone, and he never has worked more than 104 innings in a season. The Cubs love his mound presence and will continue to develop him as a starter, but he could provide more immediate help as a reliever with dynamic stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs did a nice job of turning big league relievers into future starters at the 2022 Trade Deadline, dealing Scott Effross to the Yankees for Hayden Wesneski and David Robertson to the Phillies for Brown. The latter signed for $60,000 as a 33rd-rounder out of a Long Island high school in 2017 and succumbed to Tommy John surgery in his first full pro season in 2019. He entered 2022 with just 25 2/3 innings in full-season ball before breaking out, reaching Double-A while compiling a 3.38 ERA with 149 strikeouts in 104 frames. A 6-foot-6 right-hander, Brown uses a high arm slot and blows his fastball by hitters, sitting at 94-96 mph and peaking at 98 with armside run. His power curveball may be an even better pitch, sitting in the mid-80s with downer break and eliciting a lot of swings-and-misses in the zone and chases out of it. He also has a hard slider/cutter that can reach 91 mph and stands out more for its depth than its horizontal action, and he's working on developing more distinct break with it. Because he has missed so much time as a pro, Brown has barely begun work on his changeup and threw just two in 31 innings after the trade. He keeps his long levers in sync but has inconsistent control in part because he tends to work at the very top and bottom of the strike zone. The Cubs love his mound presence and could have a mid-rotation starter or late-inning reliever on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When people show you who they are, believe them the first time. Maya Angelou wasn’t talking about baseball players when she said that, but it fits when looking at Austin Martin’s development path. The former No. 5 overall pick of the Blue Jays out of Vanderbilt in 2020, he went straight to Double-A in 2021 and was sent to the Twins in the José Berríos deal at that year’s Trade Deadline. In that season, along with two injury-riddled ones with the Twins, mostly because of a torn UCL in his non-throwing elbow, he’s been the same kind of player throughout, one who makes a lot of contact but without a ton of impact. From the outset, coaching staffs have worked with Martin to drive the ball more and no adjustments have ever stuck. What he does have is incredible bat-to-ball skills; the right-handed hitter has struck out in just 16.5 percent of his plate appearances heading into 2024. He draws walks and can spray the ball to all fields and, to his credit, did hit the ball on the ground less once he recovered from the elbow injury at midseason last year and he had a big August where he drove the ball more consistently. In addition to his ability to avoid strikeouts and get on base, Martin runs well, can steal a base and while he’s never going to be a superb defender, he’s shown he can handle multiple positions, playing shortstop, second and two outfield spots in 2023. The time has come to just let him be who he is, someone who controls the zone and provides versatility in a utility type role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken No. 5 overall by the Blue Jays in the 2020 Draft as the best pure college hitter in the class, Martin has struggled to show consistent offensive production since signing. After making his pro debut in Double-A in 2021, he was sent to the Twins at the Trade Deadline in the José Berríos deal. He got off to a poor start in 2022, then missed a good chunk of time with a torn UCL in his non-throwing elbow, though he returned and performed better late, which carried over to a strong Arizona Fall League. The right-handed hitter continues to have elite-level contact skills and impressive plate discipline, which leads to high walk rates and low strikeout totals. Martin tried to work on impacting the ball more to start 2022 without much to show for it, holding a .691 OPS when he got hurt. He simplified his approach upon returning by adjusting his hand setup so there was more barrel depth to his path. That didn’t lead to more power, but did allow him to get back to his spray-to-all-fields approach. His .827 OPS in September carried over to his .374/.454/.482 AFL showing, and while hopes for real power have dimmed, there could be a bit more impact thanks to his barrel being in the zone a bit longer. Martin still doesn’t have a true defensive home, though the Twins have put him on a throwing program to help with his arm difficulties. He’s played more shortstop than anywhere else, but with depth at that position in the system, don’t be surprised to see Martin get more time in center field and second base, both of which he has played professionally, to improve his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thought to be the top hitter in the 2020 Draft class, Martin left Vanderbilt with a .368/.474/.532 career line that helped him become the No. 5 overall pick in that year’s Draft, taken by the Blue Jays. After time at Toronto’s alternate training site that summer, Martin went straight to Double-A for his pro debut in 2021 and showcased his impressive on-base skills. He also went to the Futures Game before he was sent to the Twins at the Trade Deadline for right-hander José Berríos. Martin has many desirable attributes as a right-handed hitter. He makes a ton of contact and can use the entire field. He limits strikeouts and has incredible plate discipline, as evidenced by his .414 on-base percentage in his first year as a pro. While Martin did show more extra-base authority from year-to-year at Vandy, there are questions about whether a lack of physicality will limit his power and impact at the plate. A solid athlete with good hands, Martin faces more quandaries about where he might find his long-term defensive home, with throwing issues the main concern. He’s played shortstop and center field as a pro after moving all over the diamond in college, with the outfield perhaps a better overall fit. His contact skills give him the chance to be a good hitter, and added strength could make him a special one, regardless of where he plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martin did not sign with the Indians as a 37th-round pick out of high school in 2017, instead choosing to honor his commitment to Vanderbilt. He led NCAA Division I in runs (87) and the Southeastern Conference in batting average (.392) and on-base percentage (.486) as a sophomore, helping the Commodores win their second College World Series championship and setting himself as a potential No. 1 overall pick for 2020. The Blue Jays were thrilled to find Martin still on the board for the No. 5 overall pick, and even more so after he signed for $7,000,825. He spent the summer getting acclimated to pro ball at Toronto’s alternate training site. He was having a solid pro debut in Double-A in 2021, including a trip to the Futures Game, when he was sent with Simeon Woods Richardson to the Twins in return for Jose Berrios at the Trade Deadline. Scouts felt that Martin was the top hitter in his Draft class. He has an outstanding feel for the barrel and effortlessly makes hard contact with a short, quick right-handed stroke that quickly and efficiently gets into the strike zone. He controls the zone very well and uses the entire field, showing no weaknesses at the plate. Martin is not overly physical and may not possess more than average raw power, but his uncanny hitting ability allows him to make the most of it, and he showed more pop in each successive season at Vanderbilt. Though Martin is a twitchy athlete with soft hands and quick feet, there are concerns about his arm and questions about where he'll find a defensive home. He started games at six positions at Vandy, with throwing issues at third leading to a move to center field in his Draft year. He’s played shortstop and center field as a pro, after getting reps there and at third during his entry into pro ball at the Blue Jays’ alternate site in 2020. Wherever he lands defensively long-term, it’s going to be his bat-to-ball skills that get him to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lipscomb led a dominant 2022 Tennessee team in hits (89), homers (22), total bases (180), slugging percentage (.717) and OPS (1.145), and that level of performance pushed him into the third round where the Nats signed him for slot at $758,900. He split his first full season between High-A and Double-A, finishing with a .272/.311/.419 line, 14 homers and 10 steals over 129 games, and got in 21 more contests in the prospect finishing school that is the Arizona Fall League, though fatigue likely set in there with subpar results. The right-handed slugger stands virtually straight up in the box with his bat vertically parallel to his body, and the noiseless approach helps him react to pitches in all areas of the zone. That said, “zone” is an important word there because while Lipscomb kept the strikeouts in check at all levels (18.8 percent in the regular season), he did post a high 42 percent chase rate in the Eastern League. He even swung at more than half of sliders and changeups outside the zone, leading to a 3.6 percent walk rate (third-lowest among 222 players with at least 300 Double-A plate appearances) with Harrisburg. He has average power upon impact and should continue to be a 12-15-homer threat. The former Volunteer is a surehanded defender on the dirt, and his reactions and strong arm at third base helped him capture a Minor League Gold Glove Award in his first full season. That said, Lipscomb plays in an organization with Brady House and Yohandy Morales at the hot corner, and the Nats also gave him time at all four infield spots in Harrisburg and the AFL. Unless one of his tools becomes truly plus, he profiles best as a utility infielder who slots in wherever needed most.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though Tennessee didn’t qualify for the College World Series, it still enjoyed a special 57-9 season in 2022, thanks in large part to Lipscomb. After taking over the starting third-base gig in his fourth year on campus, the Volunteer star led the team in hits (89), homers (22), total bases (180), slugging (.717) and OPS (1.145), thrusting himself into early-round discussions. The Nationals grabbed MLB Pipeline’s No. 136 Draft prospect in the third round (84th overall), signed him for slot at $758,900 and sent him straight to Single-A Fredericksburg for 23 games. The right-handed slugger was a bit more humbled in his first taste of the Minors (one homer, .392 slugging, .719 OPS), but it was difficult to tell how much of that was his skill set and not just fatigue after a long spring. Lipscomb shows an advanced approach that helps him swing at pitches he can drive to all fields, even though a flat bat path may hinder him to just average power in the pros. Notably, 18 of his 22 homers came at a hitter-friendly environment in Tennessee’s Lindsey Nelson Stadium, so his collegiate numbers won't be so easily reproduced. The Nats have pushed him to both High-A and Double-A in 2023, and he's answered the bell at both stops, answering some of the questions that came with his bat. Lipscomb has the reactions and above-average arm to play a solid third base, and he should stick there, particularly if he improves his instincts with more playing time. He turned 23 in June of his first full season and may have to hit quickly to find an everyday place in Washington’s burgeoning rebuild.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A backup to Joey Bart at Georgia Tech in 2018, McCann took over at catcher in 2019 and raised his stock with 23 homers. That led to the A’s drafting him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft. McCann joined the system and immediately showed that power, though making consistent contact was a bit of an issue. McCann’s power has been called Chris Davis-esque by some, as he’s able to drive the ball to all fields. As expected, his power also comes with a lot of swing and miss. While he may not hit for a high average, he has displayed a good ability to work counts and draw walks. McCann really benefitted from being around veteran catchers like Carlos Perez at the A’s alternate site in San Jose last year. Already possessing a strong arm, McCann's worked hard to improve his blocking and game-calling abilities, and it showed both at the alternate site and in the instructional league. His power as a left-handed hitter reminded some in the organization of Carlos Delgado. Once considered a possibility to move to first base, McCann’s willingness to improve his defense behind the plate keeps him profiled as a power-hitting backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCann spent his first two years at Georgia Tech playing first base because 2018 first-round pick Joey Bart was ahead of him. He took over behind the plate as a junior for the Yellow Jackets and he raised his profile considerably by mashing 23 homers in 2019, landing him in the fourth round of last June’s Draft. He did bring his power to the pro game during his debut, hitting nine homers in his first summer though he struggled to make contact consistently. The left-handed hitter has legit power to all fields, reminding some of the Orioles’ Chris Davis power-wise. He can lift it out to the opposite field and has a little hook to the pull side and like Davis, his power will come with considerable swing and miss (He struck out in nearly 35 percent of his plate appearances in 2019). He may never hit for a high average, but he does mitigate the strikeouts a bit by working counts and drawing walks. McCann caught and played first base during his pro debut, partically because he was nursing a sore shoulder. He showed off a much better arm during instructs, but while his hands work, his blocking and overall receiving are works in progress. If it all clicks, he could fit the profile of a lefty power-hitting backstop, but he also might have enough pop to be a first baseman if the catching end of things doesn’t come together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nuñez was known for his speed and defense when the Marlins took him in the second round of the 2019 Draft and signed him for over slot at $2.2 million, and that very much remains the case. His 183 steals rank second-most in the Minors since his Draft year, and his stellar glovework on the dirt earned him a spot at last year’s SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game, where he won MVP honors with a double and three RBIs. Nuñez spent his entire 2023 season with Double-A Pensacola, where he slashed .224/.341/.286 with five homers and 52 steals in 125 games, and when the Fish kept him off their 40-man roster in the offseason, the Nationals took him in the Rule 5 Draft. Entering his age-23 season, Nuñez still has the reputation as a Gold Glove-caliber middle infielder with incredibly smooth actions moving to all sides. His hands scoop up most of what’s hit in his general direction, and he has the arm strength to make plays going any direction. He’s a natural fit at shortstop but has some second-base experience too as Miami tried to give him more lanes to the Majors. However, the switch-hitter needs to do more to stick on a Major League roster. On the positive side, Nuñez has an approach that could translate to the bigs, as he’s patient enough to lay off pitches outside the zone and doesn’t often miss against offerings of any kind when he does swing. However, his .061 isolated slugging percentage was second-lowest among Double-A qualifiers in 2023, and he’s never slugged above .323 at any Minor League stop, hindering his Rule 5 chances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nuñez rated as the best defensive shortstop in the 2019 Draft and has maintained that reputation since signing for an over-slot $2.2 million as a second-rounder from a Georgia high school. He's one of the most dazzling defenders and prolific base stealers, ranking third in the Minors with 70 swipes in 86 attempts last season. But the 2023 SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game MVP's lack of physicality and impact at the plate may limit him to no more than a utilityman ceiling. The Marlins left him off the 40-man roster this offseason, and the Nationals scooped him up in the Rule 5 Draft, giving him a chance to crack Washington’s Major League roster in 2024. A fast-twitch athlete with smooth actions at shortstop, Nuñez has quality range to both sides, quick hands and the well-above-average arm strength and agility to execute any throw from any angle. His defensive instincts enhance his physical gifts, and he'll contend for Gold Gloves as soon as he's promoted to the Majors. He can improve his consistency, however, after committing 23 errors in 118 games at age 21 last year. Listed at 5-foot-9 and 158 pounds, Nuñez lacks physicality and struggles to turn on pitches or drive them with any authority. He added 10-15 pounds of muscle during the offseason, but scouts still fear he'd be overpowered by big league pitches. A switch-hitter, he knows his limitations and concentrates on getting on base by using his plus-plus speed to beat out hits and by drawing walks -- he ranked 12th in the Minors with 95 last year -- but produced just a .238/.367/.287 batting line in his first three pro seasons. It’s that lack of a bat that will hinder his chances of sticking next season, but the Nats will want to give his speed and glove close consideration.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best defensive shortstop in the 2019 Draft, Nunez has lived up to that reputation since passing on a Clemson commitment to sign for a well-over-slot $2.2 million as a second-rounder. He's an electrifying defender and base runner, but questions persist about his small stature and offensive upside. He batted just .222/.347/.251 his first two pro seasons and his ability to provide offense will determine whether he becomes a regular vs. a glove-first utilityman. Nunez might contend for a Gold Glove in the big leagues right now. He's silky smooth with fast-twitch actions, quick hands and feet and a plus-plus arm that delivers accurate throws from any conceivable angle. He can make plays that most shortstops can't and also is remarkably consistent for a young defender. Nunez lacks physicality at 5-foot-9 and 158 pounds and won't produce any power with his contact-oriented, grounder-heavy approach. The switch-hitter does understand his limitations and focuses on getting on base by beating out grounders and controlling the strike zone. He has plus-plus speed and tremendous instincts on the bases, enabling him to steal 61 bases in 103 games with an 84 percent success rate in his first two years as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best defensive shortstop in the 2019 Draft, Nunez gave up a commitment to Clemson to sign for a well over-slot $2.2 million in the second round. He topped the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League with 28 steals and ranked second with 34 walks in his pro debut that summer, though he recorded just a .565 OPS between too levels.
