The Cardinals protected him from the Rule 5 Draft (and additional free agency) with the 40-man add in November. Gómez always posted some of the best exit velocities in the Rays system when he made contact, and both the player and St. Louis coaches got to work on tamping down some of the moving parts of his swing (namely a large leg kick) to get that double-plus raw pop to play in games. The proof was certainly in the pudding with the way he slugged .705 at Springfield and .541 in Memphis. That said, Gómez still sold out for power too often, leading to a 34.7 percent K rate -- highest among Cardinals qualifiers. Though he was signed as a center fielder, the 24-year-old has slowed out of the position and now profiles in the corners, where he’s still a below-average defender. A strong arm helped him earn nine assists from right field in 2022. Now with his best Major League chance ever, Gómez profiles as a potential right-handed power bat off the bench who can wow crowds with moonshots and frustrate them with punchouts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $40,000 out of Venezuela in 2015, Gomez can get overlooked because he’s a high-risk prospect with huge power and major swing-and-miss issues in a Rays system that’s teeming with high-probability prospects. But he was arguably the Class A Midwest League’s top slugger as a 19-year-old in his first full season -- he led the circuit in extra-base hits (60), ranked second in slugging (.503) and fourth in home runs (19) -- and set a Class A Advanced Charlotte single-season home run record (16) in 2019. Gomez also batted just .220, a marked drop-off from his first full season (.280), and struck out at a 33.5-percent clip, the combination of which led the Rays to pass on adding him to the 40-man roster in November. With his strong, compact frame, explosive right-handed swing and natural fly-ball tendencies, Gomez has the makings of a future big league slugger. He produces some of the best exit velocities among Rays farmhands, showing plus-plus raw power that plays to the big part of the field and results in tape-measure pull-side homers in games. He has good feel for finding the barrel, but struggles to make consistent contact, with an overly aggressive approach and pitch-recognition issues fueling his penchant for whiffing. That, in turn, prompts valid questions from scouts about Gomez’s bat and whether he will ever hit enough to be an effective power-hitter. An average runner who moves well underway, Gomez fits better in left field than right because his arm strength is only slightly above average. He has the power ceiling to profile at either corner-outfield spot but will need to make significant gains as a hitter to reach his potential as a 25-plus homer threat who bats in the middle of a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $40,000 out of Venezuela in 2015, Gomez improved in each of his first two seasons in pro ball before moving up to full-season Class A Bowling Green and breaking out in 2018. At age 19, Gomez led the Midwest League with 34 doubles, 60 extra-base hits, 82 RBIs and 237 total bases. He also hit 19 home runs, good for fourth in the circuit, and finished second with a .503 slugging. He continued to boost his stock during the offseason in the Venezuelan Winter League, garnering Rookie of the Year honors after he delivered six homers and 26 RBIs over 35 games. Gomez is physically put together and looks the part of a future big leaguer. His strength really shows when he swings the bat, as he'll generate huge raw power from the right side of the plate that often translates to tape-measure home runs during games. Gomez's power does come with a heavy dose of swing-and-miss, which in turn raises concerns about his hitting ability, but scouts who saw him last season were impressed by his feel for the barrel and believe he'll make more contact as his pitch recognition improves. He's an average runner, perhaps a tick above, and moves well underway, though he's likely to lose a step or two as he continues to add strength. Gomez fits better in left field than right because his arm strength is only slightly above average. Evaluators believe he'll be an average defensive corner outfielder once he improves his reads and routes, though it's widely agreed that it will be Gomez's bat that dictates his development. If it all clicks, Gomez could be hitting 25-plus homers from the middle of the Rays' lineup in a matter of years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Rosa signed for $300,000 in July 2018, and the Dominican Republic native was already impressing in instructs that fall. He later got another advanced assignment when he was included in the club’s alternate training site at just 18 years old in 2020. He slashed .315/.394/.505 with 10 homers in 69 games at Single-A Fredericksburg in 2022 and after he got a dip at High-A Wilmington, he was added to Washington’s 40-man roster as Rule 5 protection. That roster spot lasted one year. De La Rosa slashed just .240/.324/.361 with seven homers in 93 games back in Wilmington last season and was outrighted off the 40-man in November. The left-handed slugger is capable of showing off above-average raw power in batting practice sessions, and he’ll run into the occasional high-end exit velocity, thanks to the strength in his 6-foot, 215-pound frame. Notably, he was a victim of Wilmington’s hitting graveyard, slugging .288 there compared to .422 on the road in 2023. But his bat path -- starting from a semi-open stance -- needs to be better geared for loft. Instead, it led to a majority of ground balls, and that’s when he made contact, factoring in his 33.7 percent strikeout rate. De La Rosa still runs decently well, and he’s workable in center field. However, he played more games than ever in right field in 2023 because of his organization’s logjam in the middle of the grass, and his arm can work there. De La Rosa is still only entering his age-22 season, so he has time to make adjustments, but he’s already been on the wrong end of roster churn once.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just a $300,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, De La Rosa has impressed Nationals officials at nearly every stop, earning advanced assignments to instructs in fall 2018 and the alternate training site in the lost 2020 campaign. After a down age-19 season in 2021, the left-handed slugger showed promise by hitting .315/.394/.505 with 10 homers over 69 games back at Single-A Fredericksburg. He suffered a broken hamate at High-A Wilmington, and his numbers plummeted (.195/.273/.271), but the non-injured portion was enough to get him added to Washington’s 40-man when he first became Rule 5-eligible last November. Batting from an open stance, De La Rosa does a good job of staying back on balls, and his Single-A strikeout rate notably improved from 34.1 percent to 24.8 in his return to the Carolina League. Even while he struggled with the hamate, he still only punched out 27.8 percent of the time with Wilmington, though that trend has reversed course in 2023. De La Rosa has long shown above-average raw power, and it started to play even more in games in 2022 (see the .505 slugging), even if he still puts the ball on the ground more than most would like at this stage. A plus runner who swiped 39 total bags last year, the 21-year outfielder has gotten the majority of his looks in center field, where he covers ample ground. The trouble is that the Nats are becoming more and more loaded in the middle of the grass, and he may get squeezed to a corner. Though Wilmington is a notorious tough place to hit, De La Rosa has to get back on track offensively or else risk getting lost in Washington's increasingly deep pool of outfielders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Rosa wasn’t a huge name when the Nationals signed him for $300,000 in July 2018 but has shown a strong base level of skills in the close to four years since. Washington liked him enough to send him to American instructs the same year he signed and then to the Gulf Coast League in 2019. At 18, he was one of the Nats’ youngest alternate-training-site participants in 2020 and moved back to Fredericksburg for Low-A play last summer. Even the Nats would agree that may have been a bit too aggressive for the 19-year-old, and De La Rosa backed that up by hitting just .209/.279/.316 with five homers and a 34.1 percent K rate in 87 games with the FredNats. De La Rosa’s scuffles at the plate were mostly approach-based in 2021. Once the strikeouts began to pile up because of chased pitches, the youngster became perhaps too passive and sat back on pitches he could drive. It’s a seesaw battle that many teenaged hitters wage, and without being able to fall back on a non-complex short-season club to find success, De La Rosa rode that up-and-down for much of the summer. The good news is that the raw tools remained in place, and he’s enjoyed a much more productive 2022 back at Fredericksburg and at High-A Wilmington. The left-handed slugger still shows above-average raw power to all fields, and decent speed is an asset he puts to use in center field, where he gets the bulk of his looks. The Nationals came away from De La Rosa’s first taste of full-season ball enthused by his reaction to the lows of the game. He showed strong makeup by acknowledging struggles are part of a budding career and still acted like a leader as the season wore on in Fredericksburg. His rebound in 2022 has gotten him right back on track to be a piece of Washington’s brighter future

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals went a bit under the radar when they signed De La Rosa out of the Dominican Republic for $300,000 in July 2018 and have been fairly aggressive with his assignments ever since. He moved stateside for instructs in his signing year, then played 26 games in the Gulf Coast League in 2019, when many others of his class were in the Dominican Summer League. The 5-foot-11 outfielder played at the alternate site in Fredericksburg last year, during what would have been his age-18 season. De La Rosa’s swing from the left side remains a work in progress, particularly when it comes to getting his hands into position early, but the pieces are there for a solid hit tool. The bat speed produces impressive raw power that can go all over the field, and that should show up more in games as he grows older. His speed is also above-average at present, giving him a promising mix on the offensive side. That run tool helps him in center, where he typically tracks down balls well. But if he needs to move to a corner, the rest of his profile shouldn't make that a problem. The Nats like to challenge De La Rosa because he can show solid tools across the board. All the pieces are there for a solid-hitting outfielder, regardless of exact placement on the grass, and his time against advanced competition at the alternate site in 2020 should help him reach that ceiling moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Rosa made a strong impression on Nationals scouts as a 16-year-old Dominican amateur with his physical strength and pure hitting ability before signing for $300,000 in July at the outset of the 2018-19 international period. He participated in the organization’s instructional league in Florida that fall and then began his career in earnest in '19 in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, albeit after getting a late start so that he could finish high school. Club officials are excited about the combination of physical projection and hitting ability De La Rosa already shows as a teenager. He has plus bat speed and controls the barrel well as part of an explosive left-handed swing that could allow him to hit for both average and power. He is a confident hitter who understands his swing and has a solid foundation for developing a big league approach. Defensively, De La Rosa has the above-average speed to play center field, though physical maturation could eventually force him to an outfield corner. His arm strength is average right now, though the Nationals do expect it to improve as he makes physical gains. The Nationals are among the best in the business in terms of scouting and developing international talent, with Juan Soto and Victor Robles serving as recent examples. De La Rosa’s ceiling isn’t on par with those two, though some club officials view the youngster as the next impact hitter in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many pegged Cronin as a potential quick mover when the Nationals selected the former two-year Arkansas closer in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft. The canceled 2020 campaign got in the way of the southpaw’s first full season, and then he was limited to 30 innings in 2021, in part due to a non-arm-related health issue. Ten walks in 11 1/3 Double-A innings didn’t help matters. Back to being fully healthy, Cronin returned with 14 scoreless appearances at Harrisburg before finishing out with a 3.53 ERA and 34 K’s in 35 2/3 innings at Triple-A Rochester. The 6-foot-2 left-hander’s velocity has backed up a little bit to the low 90s, but it still plays well with good vertical break and spin efficiency. Though he isn’t a commanding size on the mound, Cronin’s high-slot delivery can make it seem like he’s putting the ball right on top of hitters. He shows good feel for spin with an upper-70s, 11-to-5 curveball that can keep opponents off the fastball, while his low-80s changeup provides a third option. Cronin isn’t a typical lefty reliever -- he sported fairly even splits between righties (.174 average, .542 OPS) and lefties (.216 average, .581 OPS) in 2022. He can still run into occasional bouts of wildness, but his control actually improved as 2022 wore on. Having been added to the 40-man roster in November, Cronin is a high-floor bullpen arm who won’t need much seasoning in Rochester before getting his chance to help the Washington relief corps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cronin was dominant in all three seasons at Arkansas and took over the closer’s role for the Razorbacks in his final two years on campus. He finished with 16 saves, a 2.08 ERA and 91 strikeouts in 52 collegiate innings before the Nationals selected him in the 2019 fourth round, a rarity for a relief-only talent. He continued his strong run of form at Low-A Hagerstown (0.82 ERA, 41 K in 22 innings) that summer before taking his 2020 work to the alternate site and instructs. Cronin moved quickly from High-A to Double-A last season but hit a wall with control in Harrisburg and missed six weeks with a non-arm-related health issue. The 6-foot-2 left-hander’s present and future in the bullpen is clear based on his arsenal. His heater comes in the mid-90s and earns extra points for its vertical break and spin efficiency. It can be a truly explosive pitch on its own. His 12-to-6 curveball shows promising depth and can flash plus when he locates it. A split-change is a distant third pitch and won’t be what pushes the southpaw to Washington. Cronin ran into control issues with Harrisburg (10 walks in 11 1/3 innings) against more patient Double-A hitters. Landing the curve in the strike zone will become even more important at the upper levels or else batters will be able to take lengthy free passes/feast on the heaters. The two pitches alone give the former Razorback true late-inning potential, but it hasn’t been as quick a trip to the Majors as may have been expected when Cronin first entered the system three years ago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Relief-only types have to show something special to go in the first five rounds of the Draft, and that’s exactly what Cronin accomplished at Arkansas before the Nats took him in the fourth round in 2019. The 6-foot-2 southpaw recorded 26 saves in his final two years on campus and fanned 101 batters in 77 1/3 innings over that span. He didn’t miss a beat in the pro ranks, posting a 0.82 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 41 K’s in 22 frames at Class A Hagerstown the summer of his Draft year. Cronin pitched at both the alternate site and instructs in 2020. The former Razorback is a classic two-pitch bullpen arm who could move quickly when regular play resumes. The heater comes in at the mid-90s, and he’s able to rely on it heavily because of a 20-inch vertical break and perfect spin efficiency. Those latter aspects are what give the offering explosive life. The 12-to-6 curveball gives another impressive look because of its depth, though Cronin has needed to focus on throwing it more in the strike zone. He has also worked on a split-change that the Nats admit he’ll likely use sparingly. Control, in general, will remain a point of emphasis – as is typical of relievers – after Cronin walked 11 of the 85 batters he faced in Class A two years ago. Cronin’s two best pitches are nearly as Major League-ready as any you’ll find on a pitcher two years out of the Draft – his fastball especially. He has late-game upside in the back of a traditional Nationals bullpen or could be used earlier in bigger spots. Barring any significant setbacks, his stay in the Minors could be a short one.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cronin was a bullpen mainstay for Arkansas since his freshman year and set a school record with 14 saves as a sophomore in 2018, when the Razorbacks finished runner-up at the College World Series. The Nationals made him their fourth-round Draft pick the following year, after Cronin had posted 12 saves and a 1.86 ERA while averaging 13.0 strikeouts-per-nine as a junior, and he rewarded the organization with an excellent pro debut at Class A Hagerstown, pitching to a 0.82 ERA with 41 strikeouts across 22 innings. Cronin attacks hitters with two plus pitches that feature outstanding spin rates. His 92-95 mph fastball gets great carry in the strike zone, appearing to rise as it reaches the plate. His over-the-top arm slot helps him get nice depth on his plus curveball, which can be a true hammer in the mid-70s and was regarded by scouts as one of the best breakers in the Draft. Cronin’s strike-throwing ability requires further refinement, but he has the potential to be effective even if his control is below average. The effort and recoil in Cronin’s delivery along with his two-pitch profile make him a legitimate bullpen prospect. He projects as a high-leverage reliever -- likely a setup man -- at the highest level and could get there quickly, with a chance to close games if he throws more strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gómez made his big league debut at the end of 2023, seven years after signing for $50,000 out of Venezuela. He spent most of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball before losing 2020 to the pandemic and most of 2021 to shoulder and elbow issues, with the latter requiring internal brace surgery that August. He also missed time with shoulder tendinitis in 2023 but stayed healthy throughout last year, working a career-high 95 2/3 innings and spending three short stints in New York. Gómez mixes five different pitches and relies heavily on his two solid offerings, a low-90s fastball that tops out at 96 and plays better than its velocity thanks to its carry and the elite extension in his delivery and a sweeping low-80s slider. He also spins a downer curveball at 79-82 mph and a mid-80s cutter, both of which grade as average. His upper-80s changeup has some fade but is too firm and lags behind the rest of his arsenal. With his velocity and spin rates decreasing a bit in recent years -- he touched 98 mph before his elbow surgery -- Gómez lacks a true plus pitch. His control has slipped a bit as well, and he never has been especially durable. He probably fits best now as a multi-inning reliever in the big leagues, with the possibility of regaining some power if he pitches in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Gómez pitched just 277 innings in the next seven years, including two with the Yankees last September. He spent most of his first three seasons as a pro in Rookie ball, lost 2020 to the pandemic and has battled arm issues since. He had shoulder issues in early 2021, tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his elbow and required internal brace surgery that August and missed the first two months of last season with shoulder tendinitis. Gómez's fastball sits at 92-94 mph and tops out at 97 with some riding action and carry that keep it off barrels. His most effective secondary offering is his 78-82 mph curveball, though he uses it a lot less than his 83-85 mph sweeping slider and upper-80s cutter. He'll throw an occasional changeup to left-handers, but it's too firm in the upper 80s and features just mild fade. Gómez's velocity and spin rates have ticked down a bit in the last couple of years, leaving him without a true plus pitch. His control has regressed too, and outside of his cutter he doesn't have a secondary pitch that he reliably can land for strikes. He once flashed mid-rotation upside but now looks more like a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Gómez spent most of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball before losing 2020 to the pandemic. He dealt with shoulder issues early in 2021 and had a torn ulnar collateral ligament in his elbow repaired with an internal brace that August, but he returned last June and finished the year with a crucial victory in the Double-A Eastern League Finals to help Somerset win the championship. He missed the first two months of this season with shoulder issues. Gómez spins the ball exceptionally well, creating quality carry on a fastball that ranged from 92-96 mph last year and has touched 98 in the past. His feel for spin extends to his breaking pitches, a sweeping 82-85 mph slider that grades as plus at its best and a 79-82 mph curveball that can be a solid offering. His upper-80s changeup has some fade but needs more velocity separation from his heater. Gómez looked rusty last year and his control and command haven't returned to where they were before his elbow surgery. His delivery hasn't been as tight and repeatable, and the Yankees hope he'll return to the best version of himself when he's fully healthy. He worked a total of just 209 2/3 innings in his first six seasons as a pro -- and never more than 56 1/3 in a single year -- so there are questions about his ability to hold up as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela as a projection right-hander in 2016, Gomez spent almost all of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball. The Yankees still added him to their 40-man roster after he lost 2020 to the pandemic shutdown and kept him on there after he worked just 23 2/3 innings in 2021, when he had shoulder troubles early in the season and elbow surgery in August. Despite his lack of development opportunities, he still has the best feel for pitching among New York's international pitching prospects. Gomez has added about 5 mph to his fastball since signing and now operates at 92-95 mph and peaks at 98 with high spin rates that create a lot of carry and riding action. He also generates plenty of spin on his breaking pitches, and his 82-85 mph slider has supplanted his 79-82 mph curveball as his best secondary offering. He trusts his fading changeup but it needs more consistency. Gomez is doing a better job of repeating his clean delivery as he gets stronger. He throws strikes but needs more innings in order to polish his command. He returned to the mound in June and still has mid-rotation upside, though he has to prove his durability after never pitching more than 56 1/3 innings in a single year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest bargain in the Yankees' 2016 international crop, Gomez signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela as a projection right-hander. He spent almost all of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball, skipping a level to jump to low Class A at the end of 2019. New York didn't invite him to its alternate site and didn't hold instructional league in 2020, crimping his opportunity for development last year, but did add him to its 40-man roster in November. Gomez has gained about 5 mph on his fastball since turning pro and usually deals at 92-95 mph and peaks at 97. His heater plays better than its velocity because its high spin rates create riding action and his size and high three-quarters delivery produce downhill plane. He also generates plenty of spin on a hard curveball that's his best pitch, has added a low-80s slider in 2021 and already has learned to trust his fading changeup. Gomez has better feel for pitching than any of the Yankees' top pitching prospects. He has a clean delivery and is doing a better job of repeating it as he adds strength. He's on track to have three solid or better pitches with similar control and command, and he still has projection remaining in his lanky frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Another bargain from the Yankees' 2016 international class, Gomez signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela as an ultraprojectable right-hander. He spent most of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball focusing on adding strength, though he did reach Class A ahead of schedule at the end of 2019. He's one of the more polished young arms in the system. Gomez has added about 5 mph to his fastball since signing and now works with a 92-95 mph heater that touches 97. It plays better than its velocity with high spin rates and downhill plane that he creates with his size and high three-quarters delivery. He also imparts plenty of spin on a hard curveball that has the most upside in his repertoire, and he already shows trust in his fading changeup. Gomez not only has the makings of three solid or better pitches, but he also has the potential for similar control and command. He has clean mechanics and is doing a better job of keeping them in sync as he gets stronger. There's still projection remaining in his lanky frame, so he could continue to gain velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Though Gomez oozed projection with a skinny 6-foot-3 frame and already ran his fastball into the low 90s as a 16-year-old, New York was able to sign him for just $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2016. He's a long-term project who probably won't be ready for full-season ball until 2020, but he added about 5 mph to his heater in his first two years of pro ball. Gomez now operates at 92-97 mph with his fastball, which plays up because of its high spin rate and the downhill plane he creates with his size and high-three-quarters delivery. He also shows feel for spinning a curveball with some power and depth that shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch. He has some fade on his changeup and grasps the importance of using it. While Gomez has a quick arm and a clean delivery, he's still young and figuring out how to keep his mechanics in sync. He has yet to provide consistent strikes but has the ingredients for average control. Given his upside, the Yankees are willing to be patient with his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bowlan followed in his dad’s footsteps and went to the University of Memphis, pitching his way into the second round of the Royals’ pitching-heavy 2018 Draft. His dad, Mark, was a 19th-round pick by the Cardinals in 1989. Jonathan was on a fast track to the big leagues in 2021 until Tommy John surgery stopped him. He returned at the end of ‘22 to make nine starts in Double-A, but his stuff wasn’t all the way back, which the Royals expected after elbow surgery. He’s fully healthy now and on the 40-man roster. Bowlan has a massive mound presence standing at 6-foot-6, with broad shoulders and an imposing frame. Before his surgery, he was an extreme strike thrower, pounding the zone with his 95 mph fastball that speeds up on hitters down in the zone. His 87-89 mph breaking ball tunnels well with his fastball, and his changeup continues to improve. All of his pitches played up before the surgery because he was so aggressive in the strike zone and uses his long extension down the mound to his advantage. Now that he doesn’t have an injury holding him back, the Royals believe he’ll get back to that style of pitcher. Before his surgery, Bowlan was tearing up Double-A. If his stuff comes back in 2023, he’ll likely get back on that track. The Royals truly see him as a starter in their future because of his pitch mix and physicality. If he can stay healthy and get back in the zone, he could see time in Kansas City this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mark Bowlan was a star pitcher at the University of Memphis and 19th-round pick by the Cardinals in 1989, spending two years in pro ball. Three decades later, his son Jonathan followed in his footsteps to Memphis and pitched his way into the second round of the Royals’ college pitching-heavy 2018 Draft. In 2021, the right-hander was on the fast track to the Major League rotation when he suffered an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. He returned to the mound in mid-June and reached Double-A again by the end of July. An extreme strike-thrower, Bowlan was off to an impressive start in Double-A last season, posting a 1.59 ERA with 25 strikeouts in 17 innings. His star offering is his 93-96 mph fastball that has deception and can be sneaky quick because of his imposing 6-foot-6 frame. His low-80s slider tunnels well with his late-breaking fastball, and his changeup continues to improve as a solid offering in his arsenal as a starter. The biggest change for Bowlan in ’21 was the addition of a curveball that has potential, giving hitters a different look than his slider. Bowlan commands the ball extremely well with a clean delivery, which allows all his pitches to play up as he gets aggressive in the strike zone. If Bowlan can stay healthy after his surgery, the Royals truly see him as a starter in their future. Officials rave about his makeup and work ethic, which should help during rehab. If Bowlan can’t stick as a starter, his physicality and weapons would fit well in a big league bullpen. His command hasn’t been great coming off the rehab, but the Royals expect him to return to form by 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Mark Bowlan, a star pitcher at the University of Memphis and a 19th-round pick by the Cardinals in 1989, Jonathan also attended Memphis and pitched his way into the second round of the 2018 Draft, the last of five consecutive college arms the Royals took that year. The big right-hander had a breakout year in 2019, with a 150/23 K/BB rate and a nine-inning no-hitter on July 15 at Class A Advanced Wilmington. Bowlan was a late addition to the Royals' alternate training site in 2020 before taking part in instructional league at Kauffman Stadium. He made four impressive starts at Double-A Northwest Arkansas to open 2021 before suffering an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. He will miss the remainder of the 2021 season and at least part of 2022 as a result. Bowlan, whose 6-foot-6 frame is imposing on the mound, is an extreme strike thrower, pounding the zone with all three of his pitches. He has a plus fastball, which sits at 92-95 mph and can be sneaky quick, getting on hitters more deceptively. His low-80s slider tunnels well with the fastball, has some cutter action to it and will flash plus with tilt and a late break to it, though he needs to work on the consistency of the pitch. Bowlan’s changeup was a major focus of his work in 2020, developing into a solid offering in his arsenal as a starter. His command is excellent, and while he’s learning how to throw inside to right-handers better, he can throw the down-and-away strike as well as anyone in the Royals system. Bowlan might seem more under the radar compared to the pitchers who went higher than him in his Draft class, but the Royals truly see him as a starter in their future. Officials rave about his makeup. Still, much will depend upon his return from Tommy John. If Bowlan is unable to stick as a starter, his fastball-slider combination and physicality would fit well in a big league bullpen, where his stuff could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mark Bowlan was a star pitcher at the University of Memphis who authored a perfect game and was a 19th-round pick of the St. Louis Cardinals back in 1989, spending two years in pro ball. Three decades later, his son, Jonathan, went to his alma mater and pitched his way into the second round of the 2018 Draft, the last of five consecutive college arms the Royals took that year with their first five picks. After an abbreviated pro debut, the big right-hander was a breakout prospect in his first full season, recording a 3.14 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 150/23 K/BB in 146 innings across two levels in '19. The highlight of Bowlan’s season came on July 15, when he fired a nine-inning no-hitter with nine strikeouts in his fifth start at Class A Advanced Wilmington. Bowlan is a physical presence on the mound who intimidates opposing hitters with his hulking 6-foot-6, 262-pound frame. He commands his plus fastball well, sitting at 92-95 mph and touching 97 with sinking action that nets him groundball outs. His low-80s slider will flash plus with tilt and sharp break to it, though he still needs to work on the consistency of the pitch. He has some feel for his changeup, giving him the chance for a third Major League offering. He pounds the zone with all three pitches and led Royals farmhands with a 6.52 strikeout-to-walk rate in his first full season, showing plus control with command that one day could earn a similar grade. Bowlan has the chance to be a workhorse-type starter in the big leagues if he can continue improve his changeup, and scouts and club officials are optimistic that he’ll achieve that projection. If Bowlan is unable to stick as a starter, however, his fastball-slider combination and physicality would fit well in a big league bullpen, where his stuff could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mark Bowlan was a star pitcher at Memphis who authored a perfect game and was a 19th-round pick of the St. Louis Cardinals back in 1989 and spent two years in pro ball. Three decades later, his son Jonathan went to his alma mater and pitched his way into the second round of the Draft, the last of five college arms the Royals took in 2018. He made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Pioneer League, but was shut down a bit early because of fatigue following a long college season. Bowlan didn't get the chance to show the true version of who he was during his pro debut and the Royals are excited to see what the 6-foot-6, 260-plus pound right-hander can bring to the table. At his best, Bowlan pitches well off of his heavy 92-95 mph fastball and can touch a tick or two higher with the pitch. He throws it with sink to get ground-ball outs. His low-80s slider will flash plus with good sharp break to it, though he still needs to work on the consistency of the pitch. He does have some feel for his changeup, giving him the chance for a third Major League offering. Despite his size, Bowlan has a repeatable delivery and has shown an ability to throw strikes consistently. If he can continue to do that and refine his changeup, he has the chance to be a workhorse-type starter in the big leagues. If not, that fastball-slider combination, not to mention his huge presence on the mound, could work well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2017-18 international signing period was coming to a close, the Angels took a low-risk flier on Caceres, signing him for $10,000 in May 2018. Working as a starter and reliever at the outset, he did little to distinguish himself at Rookie-level stops in 2018 and '19, nor did he make much noise when he returned to competitive action following the pandemic in '21. Things started to click a bit with a full-time move to the bullpen in 2022, and after being left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft that offseason, he pitched his way from High-A to the big leagues in '23. While Caceres does have three pitches, he’s definitely a reliever-only now. It’s a power arm from a small, but strong frame, starting with a fastball that sits around 95 mph and touches 99. He has both a four- and two-seamer, the latter of which can get groundball outs. His out pitch is his hard 82-84 mph curve, but he also misses bats with his 88-89 mph changeup. Caceres’ command did improve in 2023, but that’s still a work in progress after he gave up 5.3 walks per nine in the Minors. He doesn’t need pinpoint control to be an effective big league reliever -- something that could happen this year with more ease now that he’s on the roster. If he can find the strike zone a little bit more consistently, his power stuff could help get some high-leverage outs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Veneziano has had a rollercoaster of a professional career ever since the Royals drafted him in the 10th round in 2019 out of Coastal Carolina. The pandemic eliminated his first full season, and he was a breakout player in ‘21, when he struck out 127 batters in 93 2/3 innings for High-A Quad Cities. Then he got out of whack in ‘22 with a 5.72 ERA at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Veneziano got back on track last year and was one pitcher who really benefited from the Royals’ revamped pitching department. He started his 2023 season in Double-A and ended it with 2.1 innings in the Majors. Veneziano’s walk rate dropped to three percent in Double-A last year while his strikeout rate jumped to 28.4 percent. He was challenged more in Triple-A, in part because of the ABS system, but he posted a 4.22 ERA in 18 games (17 starts). Veneziano is 6-foot-5 with long limbs, which helps the deception on his 92-94 mph fastball. He pairs that with an 82-85 mph tight, gyro slider -- still his best out pitch. He worked hard on his 85-87 mph above-average changeup, especially on establishing the velocity separation. This spring, he came into camp with a new ‘slurve,’ that sometimes looks like a sweeper. It’s a get-me-over pitch that he can drop in for strikes, especially against right-handed batters. Veneziano can get out of his three-quarters-slot delivery at times, and cleaning that up helped him immensely last year. Fighting for an Opening Day roster spot, Veneziano built up as a starter this spring, but he's been used in a variety of roles during the season -- a starter, multi-inning reliever, one-inning arm. Considering he turns 27 in September, the southpaw is seeing the clock tick on his time as a rotation option for Kansas City, be his overall stuff could still be helpful in other ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year after Coastal Carolina won the College World Series in 2016, Veneziano joined the program and saw things start to click during the playoffs of his sophomore year. His Draft stock increased during his junior year, and the Royals took him in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft. After spending 2020 working out at his home in New Jersey, Veneziano broke out in ’21 for High-A Quad Cities, posting a 3.75 ERA in 93 2/3 innings and striking out a whopping 127 batters. At 6-foot-5 and 205 pounds, Veneziano is deceptive on the mound and elevates his fastball, which saw a burst in velocity over last season, averaging 94-95 mph with late life and at times hitting 98-100 mph. Working off his fastball, he possesses an above-average slider that gets whiffs and an average changeup that is a major focus for improvement this season. Tall and lanky, Veneziano had some kinks in his delivery to work out last season, mainly not dropping his front arm and staying loaded in his back leg so he could drive through the baseball. He saw it all click around June and took off from there as one of the bigger surprises of the Royals’ Minor League season. There’s no denying what Veneziano showed as a starter last season, so he will continue on that track for now. While he did throw more strikes in ’21 and was able to repeat it, lack of fastball command as a power lefty could eventually drive him to the bullpen, especially if he doesn’t develop that changeup. But even then, a 100-mph throwing lefty would certainly be welcomed in the big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming off a strong year as South Florida’s closer in 2021, scouts were excited to see what Kerkering could do as a starter in 2022. It might have worked to the Phillies’ benefit that the transition didn’t go well and the right-hander returned to the bullpen, enabling them to select him in the fifth round of that year's Draft. His brief pro debut that summer did nothing to prepare anyone for what was to come in his first full season, when Kerkering pitched across all four levels of the Minors, landed in the big league bullpen in September and made seven postseason appearances. Kerkering is already staking a claim to be a true Slider Monster at the highest level. The upper-80s sweeper routinely registers an rpm north of 3,000. It missed bats at every single level, including in the big leagues, registering a 45 percent miss rate from Double-A on up. He threw the breaking ball a lot more than his fastball, especially once he reached Philadelphia, but that doesn’t mean his heater isn’t also a weapon. That pitch with sink flirted with triple digits and elicited a 29 percent miss rate at those same levels. The stuff is good enough to get hitters out in The Show, but Major Leaguers have not yet seen the above-average command of a slider-fastball combination that will make him more than just any old reliever. That, combined with deception in his delivery and the mentality of wanting the ball in tough situations, gives him the chance to eventually pitch in the back of a bullpen and close out games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his first two years at South Florida, Kerkering pitched out of the Bulls’ bullpen, closing games effectively in 2021. He got a chance to start on Friday nights and broke out of the gate well, but returned to relief work when things went sideways. The Phillies were able to add him to their system with an under-slot bonus of $322,500 as their fifth-rounder in the 2022 Draft and he made his brief pro debut, mostly with Single-A Clearwater, last summer. The right-hander’s velocity fluctuated during his final year at South Florida depending on what role he was in. In shorter stints, he can be expected to be consistently in the mid-90s and he’s been working on the playability of his fastball so it’s not as hittable as it has been at times. He has what might end up being one of the best sliders in the system. It has the chance to be consistently plus, with high spin rates, feel to shape it, and the ability to land it in the zone and get hitters to chase it. He does have a mid-80s changeup he doesn’t use as much, but it could be an option against left-handed hitters. Pitching solely from the stretch, Kerkering’s stuff plays up because of deception in his delivery and his ability to hide the ball well. He’s improved his strike-throwing ability and he doesn’t need pinpoint command to serve in what is likely to be a relief role long term. He’ll get the chance to be a multi-inning guy in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Caminero signed with Cleveland in July 2019, but because of the pandemic, he didn’t debut in the Dominican Summer League until two years later, slashing .295/.380/.534 with nine homers in 43 games. Tampa Bay acquired him for Tobias Myers in a 40-man-clearing move in November 2021, and Caminero's breakout came in a big way during his age-19 season in 2023. His 31 homers between High-A and Double-A tied for sixth-most in the Minors (no other teenager hit more than 24). His .591 slugging percentage ranked fifth among MiLB full-season qualifiers, and his .324 average placed 11th. The Rays called up Caminero from Montgomery on Sept. 22 and kept him on their postseason roster as a bench bat. Starting from an open stance, the right-handed slugger routinely unloads on pitches of all kinds (especially fastballs) with exit velocities that would pop up Major League leaderboards right now, nevermind ones adjusted for age. It’s near top-of-the-scale power that plays to all fields -- eight of his 20 Double-A homers went the other way to right -- and it’s a big reason why Tampa Bay wanted him nearby in the playoffs. His plate discipline also improved as he climbed the ladder, and that, combined with his loud contact, should help him be a plus overall hitter, too. A fringy runner, Caminero moved from shortstop to third base more full-time in 2023, and Tampa Bay officials were enthused by how he improved his reactions at the hot corner as the season wore on. He has enough arm for either spot on the left side and should be at least average defensively. Caminero’s bat is what gives him such an elite ceiling, however, and he should be a talent the Rays make room for, even with an already loaded infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays followed a familiar playbook to land Caminero. To resolve a roster crunch before the deadline to protect eligible prospects from the Rule 5 Draft, they traded a nearly MLB-ready pitcher and in return targeted a young infielder with little experience outside of complex-league ball. That’s how they acquired Curtis Mead from the Phillies, and it’s how they snagged Caminero from Cleveland in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tobias Myers in November 2021. Signed by the Guardians in 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, Caminero almost immediately proved to be another hidden gem following Mead’s path into the upper tier of a loaded Tampa Bay system. Only 19 at the start of the 2023 season, Caminero possesses elite bat speed that generates a ton of power to his pull side and impressive bat-to-ball ability that allows hard line-drive contact to all fields. His plus raw power led to 11 homers over 62 games as he hit .314/.384/.498 between the Rookie-level FCL Rays (where he was the organization’s team MVP) and Single-A Charleston in 2022, but there may be more over-the-fence production coming as he continues to grow. Evaluators rave about his offensive traits and mature feel for what he’s doing in the batter’s box, painting the picture of a potentially special bat. Caminero’s best spot defensively is third base, where he spent most of his time in his first season with the Rays and all his time in the Australian Baseball League over the winter. He profiles as an average defensive player at the hot corner in the future, with a solid-average arm, which is more than enough to stick there given his offensive ability. Caminero will have to be added to the Rays’ 40-man roster in December 2023, and the organization has gotten aggressive with him in 2023 by sending the teenager to Double-A already, backing up its confidence with its assignments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: This story might sound familiar: Facing a deadline to protect eligible prospects from the Rule 5 Draft, the Rays flipped an intriguing, nearly MLB-ready pitcher who didn’t fit on their 40-man roster and received a young infielder with no experience outside of complex-league ball. Yes, it sounds like how they acquired a pre-breakout Curtis Mead. But in this case, we’re talking about how the Rays landed Caminero from Cleveland in November 2021. Tampa Bay traded Rule 5-eligible righty Tobias Myers for Caminero, a Santo Domingo native and part of the Guardians’ 2019 international signing class. Caminero barely has any professional experience but showed some intriguing traits while performing well at the plate during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, leading some evaluators to believe the Rays might have unearthed another hidden gem. With a right-handed swing and impressive bat speed, the 5-foot-11 Caminero generated a lot of power to his pull side – he pulled 55 percent of the balls he put in play last year – and hit the ball in the air roughly 60 percent of the time. Caminero projects to have plus power at the plate, although the question for now is whether he’ll continue to make enough contact to get to that power as he’s challenged by higher-level pitching, better stuff and more complex sequencing. Caminero profiles as a future corner infielder, another potential parallel to Mead, although he worked all around the infield in his debut with 18 games at third, 10 at first and the rest up the middle. He has split his time between third and short this season in the Florida Complex League. He has a solid-average arm and is projected to be an average runner. Caminero hit well in the FCL, showing both power and a solid contact rate, and Tampa Bay decided to test him with a move to Single-A Charleston a month after his 19th birthday. In a system loaded with infielders, Caminero has given himself plenty of helium and could shoot higher up prospect boards during his true full-season debut in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A four-sport standout during his time at Turner Ashby (Va.) High, Hanifee blossomed on the mound as a senior before going to the Orioles in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. He signed for slightly above slot value, forgoing his commitment to Eastern Carolina. While a minor back injury prompted the Orioles to delay his pro debut until 2017, Hanifee showed no ill effects as he posted a 2.75 ERA, second among Baltimore farmhands, in the New York-Penn League. He built upon that progress at Class A Delmarva in his first full season, finishing among the top five in the circuit in both ERA (2.86) and innings pitched (132). Hanifee compensates for his lack of a true plus offering by demonstrating advanced feel for his craft. His arsenal is centered on a bowling-ball fastball that registers at 91-94 mph with exceptional late sinking action that has helped him to record ground-ball rates of 58 and 55 percent in his first two seasons, respectively. Hanifee's low-80s slider flashes above average, and he has good feel for locating, and he rounds out his arsenal with a changeup that plays nicely off his fastball and has average potential. Everything he throws plays up on account of his advanced pitchability and command. Tall and athletic with projection remaining, Hanifee has a smooth delivery, clean arm action and uses his height to his advantage, consistently creating angle to the plate. He has all the ingredients to stick in the rotation and possesses a blend of stuff, feel and durability that point to a future as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hanifee was the definition of a multi-sport standout as a prep, playing baseball, football, basketball and golf at Turner Ashby (Va.) High. He came into his own on the mound during his senior year, and the Orioles made him their fourth-round Draft pick that June, giving Hanifee a slightly above-slot bonus of $500,000 to forego his Eastern Carolina commitment. After having his pro debut pushed back to 2017 to account for a back injury, Hanifee impressed when he finally took the mound in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League by posting a 2.75 ERA that ranked second among Orioles farmhands. Hanifee can bump 94 mph with his heavy fastball but usually sits in the 88-92 mph range. He knows how to use his height to create plane to the plate, while the nearly 58 percent ground-ball rate he posted in 2017 speaks to the overall effectiveness of his sinker. A low-80s slider that flashes above average and fringy changeup comprises Hanifee's secondary arsenal, and everything he throws plays up on account of his advanced pitchability and command. Scouts believe Hanifee's velocity will tick up as he adds strength to his lean, 6-foot-5 frame. His smooth delivery and clean arm action lend credence to that thought, giving the young righty a solid foundation to start long term. It's a likely No. 4- or 5-starter profile at maturity, though Hanifee could very well surpass that projection with improved velocity and better feel for his secondaries.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The athletic and projectable Hanifee was a multi-sport star at Turner Ashby (Va.) High, where he played football, basketball and golf to go along with his exploits on the diamond. However, the right-hander didn't see his Draft stock take off until his senior campaign, when he went 7-0 and posted a 0.78 ERA. Having already selected pitchers with three of their first four picks, the Orioles drafted Hanifee, an Eastern Carolina commit, in the fourth round and signed him for slightly more than pick value at $500,000. Hanifee typically works in the 88-91 mph range with his heater and touches 93, but scouts believe more velocity will come as the right-hander adds strength to his lean, 6-foot-5 frame. He features a low-80s slider that flashes above average, as well as a raw, work-in-progress changeup that will need to be developed in the professional ranks. Hanifee's secondary pitches lag behind his fastball, but with time on his side and plenty of physical projection remaining, the right-hander gives the Orioles plenty on which to dream.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Mike Fitzgerald, a first-round pick in the 1983 January and 1984 June secondary Drafts who played briefly in the Majors, Tyler was a fourth-rounder out of Louisville in 2019. He has produced consecutive 20-20 seasons in the upper Minors, earning Triple-A Pacific Coast League All-Star recognition in addition to making his big league debut in 2023. He started nine games in center field for the Giants despite not playing there prior to last year and homered off Ryan Yarbrough and Clayton Kershaw. Fitzgerald homered just 11 times in three college seasons but has developed average power in pro ball by concentrating on launching balls to his pull side. He has a quick right-handed swing and plenty of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame, and his aggressive approach helps him do damage when he connects. He chases too many pitches out of the zone and doesn't make consistent contact against non-fastballs, so he may not hit enough to be a regular. Fortunately for Fitzgerald, he's well suited for a utility role with his plus speed, solid arm strength and fine baserunning and defensive instincts. He has average to solid range at shortstop -- his primary position -- and quickly took to covering ground in center. He's a quality defender at second base, though the game speeds up a bit on him at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants spent two of their top four picks in the 2019 Draft on infielders who helped Louisville reach two College World Series in their three seasons, first baseman Logan Wyatt in the second round and Fitzgerald in the fourth. They advanced through three levels of the system together last summer and finished in low Class A, where Fitzgerald homered in the South Atlantic League playoffs. His father Mike was a two-time first-round choice in the 1983 January and 1984 June secondary Drafts who caught briefly in the big leagues for the 1988 Cardinals. Fitzgerald was the same player in his pro debut that he was in college, a steady performer who showed the potential for at least average tools across the board. A right-handed hitter, he makes consistent line-drive contact to all fields and draws a healthy amount of walks. He has strength in his 6-foot-3 frame and hit the ball harder than ever in 2019, displaying 15-homer power and perhaps more if he starts driving more balls in the air. Fitzgerald has a high baseball IQ, allowing him to play quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the field. While his range is ordinary at shortstop, he's a reliable defender with a strong, accurate arm. His floor stands out more than his ceiling, as he seems a good bet to at least become a utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estes was a 16th-round pick in 2019 out of Paraclete High (Lancaster, Calif.) by the Braves and signed over slot with a bonus of $497,500. He joined the A’s in March 2022 as part of the Matt Olson deal. Beginning 2023 at Double-A Midland, he worked his way up to Triple-A and earned his first call to the big leagues in September, making two starts for Oakland the final month of the regular season. Estes possesses a pitch repertoire that includes a fastball that tops out at around 96 mph with significant ride, a mid-80s slider that varies in shape and a changeup that continues to make strides. He also incorporated a cutter with some late tilt last season, giving him a four-pitch mix that helps him generate a good amount of swing-and-miss. All of this comes from a compact and athletic delivery. The A’s have long been impressed by Estes’ strike-throwing ability and admire his competitiveness on the mound. After getting his feet wet with a couple of Major League starts, he should play a bigger role on Oakland’s pitching staff in 2024, with his improving four-pitch mix giving him a good chance to stick as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estes was committed to Long Beach State out of high school in California until the Braves signed him well over slot value with a bonus of $497,500 as a 16th-round pick in the 2019 Draft. After making his pro debut at age 17 the summer he was drafted, he earned 2021 Low-A East Pitcher of the Year honors in his first full season of professional baseball, making him an intriguing talent for the A’s, who acquired him from Atlanta as part of the Matt Olson deal in 2022. The A’s liked what they saw from Estes as a 20-year-old at High-A Lansing, where he posted a 4.65 ERA with 92 strikeouts in 91 innings. He upped his fastball to around 95-96 mph. He also brings an effective mid-80s slider with good depth and mixes in a changeup that he made strides with last season. Estes is aggressive on the mound and fills up the zone with strikes, continuing to develop a better feel overall for pitching as he matures. He doesn’t necessarily have a plus pitch in his arsenal at the moment, though that could come with time. His ultimate role will likely be determined by how much he can polish his secondary stuff. For now, the A’s are content with keeping him in a starting role and seeing just how much better he can get.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estes was a solid high school pitcher in California who looked like he might end up honoring his commitment to Long Beach State. But the Braves swooped in the 16th round of the 2019 Draft and were able to sign him for a well-over-slot bonus of $497,500 before he turned 18. He made the move to full-season ball in his first true full season in 2021 look easy, earning Low-A East Pitcher of the Year honors after leading the circuit in ERA, strikeouts, WHIP and batting-average-against. That clearly caught the eye of the A’s, who acquired him as part of the prospect package they received from the Braves in return for Matt Olson. All of Estes’ stuff is trending in the right direction. He averaged 93.5 mph with his fastball in 2021, a good tick or two harder than in 2019 when he first entered pro ball, and it has unique characteristics and good life. At times, he relied on overpowering Low-A hitters just with the fastball, and other times, he mixed in an effective slider with better depth as well. There was some variability to it, thrown anywhere in the 82- to 87-mph range, with Estes having more success with it when he started throwing it a little harder. His changeup also improved, though it’s still his third pitch. As encouraging as the stuff gains were, it was equally impressive that Estes filled up the strike zone as much as he did as a teenaged starter. How much the consistency of his secondary stuff improves could dictate his ultimate role, but for now those who thought he was sure to be a reliever have been quieted.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since his college days at Ball State, Nicolas has shown off premium stuff without always known where it was going. He landed in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2020 Draft with the Marlins after throwing more strikes before the shutdown and pitched his way to Double-A in 2021 before getting sent to the Pirates that offseason in the Jacob Stallings deal. He spent all of 2022 back in Double-A and seemed to have stalled back at Altoona in 2023, but he eventually moved up to Triple-A and a switch to a bullpen role helped him reach the big leagues for the first time. The 6-foot-4 Nicolas still has some of the most exciting stuff in the system. It starts with a fastball that averaged close to 96 mph in 2023 and touched 98-99 in shorter stints. It plays up even more because it has a ton of induced vertical break. He has two distinct breaking pitches, with the upper-80s slider that topped out at 92 mph a plus pitch that misses a ton of bats and a low-80s curve that provides a different look to hitters. He typically relied on those three pitches, infrequently bringing out his mid-80s changeup. The biggest thing that’s continued to hold Nicolas back has been his command. Not only does he have the repertoire to start, he’s shown he doesn’t wear down and his stuff holds up deep into starts. But he’s walked 4.6 per nine innings in his Minor League career, and the fact his offerings continue to tick up without as much concern for control in shorter stints could land him a job in the big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nicolas moved back and forth between relieving and starting in his three years at Ball State, showing off good raw stuff but struggling with command. He made only four starts before the shutdown in 2020, but his ability to find the strike zone more consistently helped him land with the Marlins in Competitive Balance Round B. He pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season in 2021, then pitched all season at the level with the Pirates in 2022 after coming over in the Jacob Stallings deal. Nicolas has the stuff to start, with a fastball that has some elite characteristics and two distinct breaking balls. While he’s not throwing quite as hard as he once did, averaging around 93.5 mph and topping out at 97, he maintains the velocity deep into starts, showing the ability to reach back for that 97 mph heater late in games. It plays up because it has 20 inches of induced vertical break, among the highest IVBs in the Minors. Both his mid-80s slider and low-80s curve will show glimpses of being above-average to plus. He does have a changeup, but it remains behind the other three offerings. The one thing that might keep Nicolas from reaching a big league rotation is his inability to land that premium stuff in the strike zone consistently, with a 4.6 walk per nine rate entering 2023. His ability to maintain his stuff will afford him more chances to start, but if the strikes don’t come more consistently, there’s comfort knowing his fastball-breaking ball combination would tick up in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at Ball State, Nicolas had a reputation as a big right-hander who could throw really hard, but didn’t always know where it was going. When he found the strike zone with more regularity during the shortened 2020 season, his Draft stock soared, landing him with the Marlins as a supplemental second-round pick. He used his power repertoire to pitch his way to Double-A in his first full season, then was sent to the Pirates in the Jacob Stallings trade last November. Nicolas’ ability to maintain his stuff deep into games could give him a chance to start. He touches triple digits in shorter outings and holds mid-90s with his fastball in most starts. The heater plays beyond just velocity because of it’s carry up the zone and heavy life when he’s down. He misses bats with a slider that can top out at 90 mph with sharp break and while his breaking pitchers run into each other, he will show a good, distinct curve. His changeup is a distant fourth pitch. The 6-foot-4 right-hander had simplified his delivery at Ball State to improve his command and cut his walk rate. He walked 4.5 per nine in his first full pro season and continued refinement could help his cause as a future starter. If his control doesn’t come along, that premium fastball and slider are plenty to serve a high-leverage role out of a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former NFL quarterback Todd Blackledge, Nicolas used his strong arm to become one of the hardest-throwing starters in the 2020 Draft. He showed improved control during his truncated shortened junior season at Ball State, where he struck out 17 in seven one-hit innings in his final start before the Marlins signed him for $1,129,700 as a supplemental second-rounder. He showcased one of the best arms at Miami's instructional league program last fall and used that to have a successful first full season of pro ball, reaching Double-A, before getting sent to the Pirates at the end of November as part of the Jacob Stallings trade. Nicolas maintains mid-90s velocity deep into games with his fastball, which has reached 100 mph in shorter stints and features good carry up in the strike zone and some heavy life when he works the bottom half. He also can overpower hitters with a slider that parks in the mid-80s, touches 90 mph and has sharp break when it's on. He also flashes an interesting curveball, though his breaking balls blend together at times, while his changeup is very much a work in progress. After simplifying his delivery and understanding that he doesn't have to maximize his velocity to get hitters out, Nicolas slashed his walk rate from 7.6 per nine innings in his first two college seasons to 2.7 in his third and walked 4.5 per nine in his first pro season. More improvements with strike-throwing should allow him to continue to move quickly. He also earns praise for his intelligence and graduated from Ball State in just three years with a degree in business administration.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyle was a bit of an enigma for three years at Notre Dame as a flamethrower who missed a lot of bats and walked a lot of hitters. The Reds took a chance on his power stuff in the fifth round of the pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft. Missing most of the 2021 season due to injury, he got going in 2022 as a starter who reached Double-A. Struggling with command when he was traded to the A’s for Sam Moll in 2023, Boyle figured something out in his new organization and dominated his way to the big leagues, making three starts for Oakland and posting a 1.69 ERA with 15 strikeouts and five walks in 18 innings. Boyle consistently pushes triple digits with an high-octane fastball that also has some riding action to it. That, along with an upper-80s power slider that misses plenty of bats and a solid low-80s curve, gives him a solid three-pitch arsenal to work with as he’s continued to operate in a starting role for the A’s. This upcoming season will reveal whether Boyle’s newfound control is fluky or legit. There is some thought that Boyle’s command issues earlier last season may have had something to do with the experimental baseballs that were being utilized in the Southern League he was pitching in. It could also be that something just clicked for the 6-foot-7 right-hander. Whatever the case, Boyle is now viewed as a potential frontline starter if he can keep this up, while a high-leverage bullpen role could still be in the cards if the command falls apart again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds took Boyle out of Notre Dame with their fifth round, and final, selection of the 2020 Draft, they knew what they were buying. Boyle had spent three years pitching out of the Fighting Irish bullpen, using power stuff to rack up strikeouts while typically not having much of an idea of where the ball was going. While he spent a good portion of his first full season on the injured list, he did make his pro debut in August, cautiously making his way to Low-A. Healthy in 2022, Boyle pitched his way to Double-A. Boyle has shown off the high-octane velocity that made him a Draft prospect, typically sitting 97-98 mph and touching triple-digits. There’s good riding action on the pitch but his delivery doesn’t offer much in the way of natural deception, so he won’t be able to rely on power alone. That means his upper-80s slider, which does have good power and tilt, will have to keep trending upwards, and he did miss plenty of bats in 2022. The biggest question mark around Boyle is his control. He walked a whopping 12 batters per nine innings in his Notre Dame career, and walked 9.2 per nine in his 12 2/3 innings with Daytona. That’s trended in a better direction as the Reds have let him start and if he can find the strike zone even moderately well, he could be a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyle spent three years pitching out of Notre Dame’s bullpen, missing a ridiculous amount of bats and walking nearly as many along the way. A stronger Cape Cod League showing in the summer of 2019 provided a glimpse into what he was capable of, though it didn’t carry over into his shortened junior season. Still, he had the best arm strength in the Draft class of 2020 and the Reds decided to roll the dice on it by taking him with their final selection in the fifth round. The 6-foot-7 right-hander can now compete with fellow Reds prospect Hunter Greene for most velocity in the organization. He’s topped triple-digits on a regular basis and has shown the ability to sit in the upper-90s over multiple innings, with good riding action on the pitch. He couples it with an 85-88 mph slider that has missed a lot of bats, with Boyle leaving Notre Dame with a 14.3 K/9 rate. The issue with Boyle has been, and will likely continue to be, his ability to land either pitch in the strike zone. He walked 12.0 per nine in college and even in his successful turn on the Cape in 2019, he still walked 7.7 per nine. His size helps in terms of being imposing on the mound, but it’s also made it hard for him to repeat his delivery. That will be the biggest focus in his development, and he does have some athleticism to provide hope he can throw enough strikes to pitch in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A player without a regular position during his three years at Rice, Gray saw time at both outfield corners and at just about every infield spot. He improved at the in each season and swung the bat particularly well as a junior in 2017, when the Pirates took him in the 13th round. He signed for $125,000, then turned in a solid pro debut on both sides of the ball in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League. The Rays took notice and acquired him during the offseason in the Corey Dickerson trade, then sent him straight to the Class A Advanced Florida League for his first full season. Gray has projection remaining to his athletic and lanky frame, and evaluators believe he's going to hit for power as he adds strength and fills outs. He flashed his power potential with a loftier swing at Charlotte in his first taste of full-season ball, totaling 53 extra-base hits including 13 homers and 38 doubles from the left side of the plate in the pitcher-friendly circuit. The uptick in power did detract from his feel to hit, however, as Gray crossed the finish line with a .238 average and a strikeout rate just shy of 23 percent. The Rays expect improvement from Gray on that front going forward, though, noting that he still fared well overall in the face of a difficult assignment. The Pirates deployed Gray at the keystone to begin his pro debut, but by the end he was playing shortstop on an almost regular basis. He continued to see time at both middle-infield spots in 2018, and the Rays increased his versatility by working him in at third base. He's a reliable, if unspectacular defender wherever he plays, with good hands and actions as well as an accurate arm. It gives him a realistic floor as a utility infielder at the highest level, though there are some evaluators who think he has everyday upside if he can fully unlock his potential at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kjerstad was off to a hot start (1.304 OPS) at Arkansas in his Draft year, but his season was cut short by the pandemic in 2020. While most of the industry saw him as a legitimate first-rounder, the Orioles reached a little bit to take him at No. 2 and sign him well under slot so they could aggressively go after other talent in the later rounds. He wasn’t able to play until June 2022 because of a diagnosis of myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart. That summer was mostly about just getting him on the field, but he showed he was ready to make the next step when he won Arizona Fall League MVP honors that fall. It carried over to a 2023 season in which he posted a .904 OPS between Double-A and Triple-A while making his big league debut in September. With the ailment clearly in his rearview, Kjerstad is looking very much like the left-handed power bat the Orioles hoped they were picking up. He has a combination of strength and bat speed and makes a ton of hard contact, showing the ability to drive the ball over the fence and for extra bases to all fields. His overall approach improved in 2023, and while he’s an aggressive swinger, he also managed his strikeouts well (18.4 percent K rate in the Minors), giving hope that he might not be as much power-over-hit as some anticipated. While he’s a fringy runner, Kjerstad is an athletic outfielder and fits nicely in right field with an above-average arm. It’s looking like his bat will profile well there in the big leagues too, and he should get every opportunity to prove that soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kjerstad had put his name on the map as a potential impact college bat by hitting 31 homers over his first two seasons at Arkansas. When he broke out of the gate in 2020 by posting a 1.304 OPS over his first 16 games, his Draft stock took a bigger leap and while it surprised many when the Orioles took him No. 2 overall to save money and manipulate their bonus pool, he was a bona fide first-rounder. A diagnosis of myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart, and its lingering effects, kept him off the field until June 2022. He made quick work of Single-A ball, struggled a bit with the move to High-A but definitely righted the ship with an MVP performance in the Arizona Fall League. More than anything, the 2022 season was a win for Kjerstad simply because he got on the field and competed for the first time in over two years. Beyond that, he started to show that his left-handed power bat has the chance to have an impact at this level. There’s strength and bat speed and even though there’s some swing-and-miss that’s still a part of his game that might always make him more power-over-hit, he showed a willingness to work counts and take walks as well as the ability to punish the baseball. His approach suffered a bit when he moved up to High-A and his K rate went up in the AFL, though he hit the ball consistently hard in Arizona. Defensively, Kjerstad fits nicely into an outfield corner, with a strong arm that works in right field. It’s his bat that will continue to carry him up the ladder, though, with the hope that his AFL experience serves as a springboard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles sent shockwaves through the industry when they selected Kjerstad out of the University of Arkansas second overall in the 2020 Draft, as part of a strategy to manipulate their bonus pool and spend on upside picks later on. The fifth Razorbacks hitter to be taken in the first round of the Draft, Kjerstad signed for more than $2.5 million below-pick value after accumulating 37 homers over parts of three seasons in Fayetteville, where he emerged as one of the top sluggers in college baseball. Due to the lingering effects of myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart that surfaced shortly after the Draft, Kjerstad didn't make his pro debut until June 2022. Because of those unforeseen circumstances, Kjerstad remains something of an unknown quantity to the Orioles and the baseball world at large. He was seen as the best left-handed power bat among college hitters in his Draft class, with significant strength and bat speed and well-above average raw power to all fields. He was an aggressive hitter in college with some swing-and-miss attributed to the moving parts in his swing. It’s a herky-jerky swing with a hitch that sometimes made it tougher for Kjerstad to be on time consistently, but that may have been altered in the 23-some months since he left campus. Whether he’s tailored that swing to make more contact and how well he maintained strength during the layoff will be two points of emphasis for the eyes on Kjerstad as he gets acclimated to pro ball. Kjerstad resumed baseball activity at the Orioles’ training complex late last year, and while he went more than two years without playing in a competitive game, he managed to hit his way from Single- to High-A in short order in 2022. He’s just 23, plenty young enough to make up the time missed and climb up the Orioles’ system. He’s still seen as a potential middle-of-the-order hitter, a bat-first corner outfielder with an above-average arm and who moves well enough to profile in right field long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A total of five hitters have been taken from the University of Arkansas in the first round of the Draft, starting with Kevin McReynolds in 1981 and No. 1 overall pick Jeff King back in 1986. After setting a freshman home run record with 14 in 2018, hitting 17 more as a sophomore and starting out his junior year on fire, Kjerstad looked like he was ready to join that pair and 2015 No. 7 overall pick Andrew Benintendi as a Top 10 selection.
