Pereira not only has plus speed, he already knows how to use it on the bases and in the outfield. He shows good instincts in center field and has the solid arm strength to fit anywhere in the outfield. He's advanced enough that he easily has handled making his U.S. debut as a 17-year-old in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baseball offers no shortage of fresh faces who make quick work of the Minor Leagues and reach the Majors at an amazingly young age, but Meadows -- a former second-round pick who signed for a $2.5 million bonus -- might have been last year’s best example of the value of patience with prospects. After three seasons in A-ball, including part of 2022, Meadows finally translated his impressive skill set into consistent on-field production and climbed the rest of system in about a year and a half. He nearly posted a 20-20 season at Triple-A Toledo last year, earned a mid-August callup and looked like he belonged upon arrival, tripling in his second MLB game, hitting a walk-off homer a few days later and racing down deep fly balls in center field at cavernous Comerica Park almost daily. For a 6-foot-5 frame, Meadows flies, both with quick acceleration and long strides that swallow up ground with each step. It’s a great combination for a center fielder at Comerica Park. The flip side of his height is a larger strike zone that he has had to learn to manage at the plate. His breakout in the Minors came with a change to a line-drive approach at the plate, shortening his swing and giving him a better chance against fastballs. His strikeout rate ticked back up last year at Triple-A Toledo and again in his late-season audition in Detroit, but so did his walk rate. His chase rate was well below the MLB average, though big league pitchers had more success flipping him breaking balls near season’s end. With near-elite defense and athleticism, Meadows has every chance to become Detroit’s center fielder. His hitting will determine whether he’s an everyday player -- and a Gold Glover -- or part of a platoon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No Tigers position prospect made more progress in 2022 than Meadows, who had struggled to translate his impressive athleticism into production for three years after Detroit selected him in the second round of the 2018 Draft. After a month back at High-A West Michigan, Meadows received a long-awaited promotion to Double-A Erie and ran with it, batting .275 with 16 home runs, 17 stolen bases and an .820 OPS. While some pointed to the arrival of Meadows’ older brother, Austin, to the Tigers via trade, a lot had to do with a revamped swing, renewed health and simple maturity -- physical and emotional -- for a player who was still nearly two full years under the average age at Double-A. Meadows revamped his swing going into the 2022 season with help from his high-school hitting coach, shortening his path, removing a hitch and taking a line-drive approach. It’s still a longer swing thanks to his lanky frame, but the change allowed him to catch up with high velocity while still giving him time to lay off slower pitches outside the zone. He cut his strikeout rate under 20 percent and pushed his walk rate over 10 percent, the first time in his pro career for both, and he hit almost evenly to all fields. The more he reaches base, the more he can put his speed to use. That also translates in the field, enabling him to hold his own in center field, though many evaluators expect him to eventually move to a corner spot. The Tigers have an abundance of young left-handed hitting outfielders, but Meadows’ late-blooming career demands attention as Detroit looks to become more athletic. Still just 23, he’ll get a chance to further figure himself out as a hitter, and he's continued to add some power at Triple-A Toledo this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Austin Meadows has emerged as a slugger with the Rays over the past few years, his younger brother has endured a rougher path in pro ball since the Tigers took him at the top of the second round in the 2018 Draft. The pandemic-related cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season denied Meadows a chance to apply lessons learned from a rough introduction to A-ball in 2019. He returned to West Michigan, now High-A, in 2021, only to battle similar struggles. Though Meadows is one of the best athletes in the system, his high strikeout rate had cost him chances to put his talent on display. A hitch in his long swing has left him vulnerable against velocity, though he spent the offseason working with a swing instructor to minimize it while maximizing his line-drive rate. He has made more contact in 2022, and his power has also ticked up a touch after he showed up to spring camp looking stronger than ever. His speed enables him to play a rangy center field despite his size, but he needs to read pitchers and defenders better to translate that onto the basepaths. Though Meadows is understandably compared to his older brother, one evaluator likened him to Derek Hill, who needed several years in the Minors to find his identity as a player after being a high pick out of high school. Unlike Hill, Meadows has been relatively healthy in his career, and that’s continued in 2022 at High-A West Michigan and Double-A Erie, where his modest offensive improvements have helped him hold serve in the Detroit system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Parker Meadows has had a rougher introduction to pro ball than older brother Austin had on his way to All-Star status with the Rays. After spurning a college commitment to Clemson to sign for a $2.5 million bonus as the top pick of the second round in the 2018 Draft, Meadows showed glimpses of his potential at Class A West Michigan, but largely reflected a difficult transition in his first full pro season. Then came the cancellation of the Minor League season in 2020, which limited Meadows to a brief stint at the alternate training site followed by an impressive instructional league performance. Meadows has the athleticism of a potentially elite player, combining a 6-foot-5 body frame with very good foot speed. His size leads to power projection, but his swing remains raw and will have to quicken for him to put his strength to work. He can fly in the outfield and around the bases – his first Class A home run was an inside-the-parker -- but like many his size, he needs a few steps to get to top speed. He spent much of 2019 in center field, showing some promise there, before moving to right for 2019 top pick Riley Greene. As Meadows gets stronger, his arm might play better in a corner. Though Meadows is older than Greene, he’s likely to take longer to develop, mainly to find his swing and harness his offensive game. He’s the kind of athlete who could have a major impact in a big outfield like Comerica Park, but he’s going to require patience to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Austin Meadows blossomed into an All-Star with the Rays in 2019, his younger brother endured the growing pains of his first full professional season in the Tigers' system, a year out of high school. Detroit drafted the younger Meadows with the top pick in the second round of the 2018 Draft and used a $2.5 million signing bonus to woo him away from a college commitment to Clemson. His strong Rookie-ball campaign that summer raised some hopes he could move quickly, but the Midwest League was a reminder he has plenty to learn, despite a handful of highlight plays that included an inside-the-park home run. Meadows has the athleticism of a potentially elite player, combining a 6-foot-5 body frame with very good foot speed. His size leads to power projection, but his swing remains raw and will have to quicken for him to put his strength to work. He can fly around the bases and in the outfield but, like many his size, needs a few steps to accelerate. He spent much of 2019 in center field, showing some promise there, before moving to right for 2019 top pick Riley Greene. As Meadows gets stronger, his arm might play better in a corner. Compared to the fast-moving pitchers in the Tigers system, Meadows will require time and patience to develop, from coaches and fans as well as himself. It would not be surprising at all if he takes longer than Greene, 10 months his younger. The combination of Meadows’ athleticism with his family lines, however, justify the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Rays outfielder Austin Meadows, Parker has some similarities to his brother, though he wasn't quite as highly regarded coming out of Grayson High School in Georgia. While Austin went No. 9 overall in the 2013 Draft, Parker did hear his name being bandied about in the back end of the first round and landed with the Tigers as the top pick in the second. He signed for above pick value deal, receiving $2.5 million to forego his commitment to Clemson, and then played at two levels in his pro debut before opening his first full season with Class A West Michigan. Meadows has leverage and projectable strength in his 6-foot-5 frame, giving him plus raw power, and the Tigers believe he'll hit enough to tap into it. Like many young hitters his size, Meadows has some length to his left-handed swing that's led scouts to question the future utility of his bat. He did make some nice adjustments during the spring, which helped raise his overall offensive profile, though he looked hesitant at times. A plus runner with a solid arm and defensive skills, he can handle any outfield position and has the chance to stick in center. Meadows has a tantalizing ceiling as a center fielder with 20-20 potential. He'll need time to develop and will have to make many adjustments along the way, but the final product should be worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken as a fourth-rounder in 2018 out of the Kentucky prep ranks, Rom moved methodically through the Orioles' system and reached Triple-A at just 22 years old in 2022. Baltimore added him to the 40-man roster soon after (fearing a potential Rule 5 selection), and returned him to Norfolk for 2023, when he opened with a 5.34 ERA and 100 strikeouts in 86 innings over his first 19 appearances. His 4.19 FIP indicated he was better than the ERA alone, and the Cardinals acquired the southpaw in the Jack Flaherty deal at the Trade Deadline. Rom debuted for St. Louis in late August and was shelled over eight starts with an 8.02 ERA in 33 2/3 innings. The 6-foot-2 left-hander can make for an interesting, if vexing, watch. He doesn’t have much extension in his fairly simple delivery, but he will mix up his release point depending on the pitch. His low-90s four-seamer -- typically aimed at the top of the zone -- comes from a high three-quarters slot, as does his 82-85 mph splitter. His upper-80s sinker comes much lower, bordering on sidearm, as it tails armside, while a 78-81 mph sweeper can come from either spot. Of those four offerings, the sweeper is the closest to being an average pitch, but the four-seamer can get some chase up in the zone too. Rom is a command-over-control type. He needs to live on the edges of the zone because anything in the zone can be hit hard. More-experienced hitters can lay off the stuff off the black, though, so he really needs to be fine with that location. The first taste of the Majors gave the lefty an idea of what top-level bats will do, and adjustments will need to come if he’s going to lock in a more permanent rotation spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rom rose steadily through Baltimore's system after the O’s plucked him out of the Kentucky prep ranks in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft, signing him for an above-slot $650,000 bonus. The tall, lanky lefty produced at the lower levels, reaching Double-A Bowie in ’21 as a 21-year-old and Triple-A last summer at age 22. The Orioles added him to their 40-man roster in November, hinting at an imminent debut, but that didn’t come early in 2023, and he was traded to the Cardinals at the Trade Deadline in a deal involving Jack Flaherty. Rom relies on deception more than elite stuff, using his 6-foot-2 frame, three-quarters arm slot, long stride and crossfire finish to hide the ball well. Rom’s arm action is quick and tough to time, and the extension he generates enables his stuff to play up and miss barrels with regularity. He works predominately off a high-spin fastball that’s ticked up in recent years and now sits around 89-91 mph, with a flat angle that works especially well up in the zone when he lands it there. His low-80s slider shows enough depth to give him a second average offering, and he also works in a mid-80s split for a third, lower-quality look. A former high school soccer player, Rom also earns high marks for his athleticism and makeup, as well as a delivery that projects durability. Rom excelled at the lower levels thanks to outstanding control, but that wavered along with his results last summer at both Double-A and Triple-A. While he kept his strikeout rate high at the upper levels, his walks increased and his ground-ball rate dropped -- somewhat concerning for a pitcher who thrives on pitchability more than overpowering stuff. In short, Rom’s ceiling looks as high as his command will take it. That continued to take a step back in 2023, and he might end up being more of a swingman in the Majors than a true starter unless he can find better command or a touch more velo in the St. Louis system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles have watched their share of crafty lefties march up their farm system in recent years, graduating several to the big-league level in 2021. The next might be Rom, whom the O’s plucked out of the Kentucky prep ranks in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft and signed for an above-slot $650,000 bonus. They’ve seen the tall, lanky southpaw progress steadily since, parlaying strong showings at Class A Delmarva and High-A Aberdeen into a promotion to Double-A Bowie last summer. The 21-year-old Rom pitched to a 3.83 ERA and more than a strikeout per inning in his first go at the level, where he was nearly four years younger than the average player. Lean and projectable, Rom hides the ball well by creating deception with his 6-foot-2 frame. He releases from a three-quarters arm slot and uses his long stride and crossfire finish to create good extension, which allows his pitches to play up and miss barrels consistently. He works predominantly off a high-spin fastball that lives in the upper-80s but ticked up last summer, and a potential plus slurve he throws in the high 70s with good feel. Rom also features a changeup that functions more like a split-fingered fastball, a pitch that has improved since his draft day but still plays about average. He is comfortable throwing either off-speed pitch in fastball counts as well as mixing up arm angles; he couples this unpredictability with a quick pace and moderate effort delivery that projects durability. A former high school soccer player, Rom also earns high marks for his athleticism and makeup. Rom succeeds despite a lack of overpowering stuff due to his advanced pitchability and solid control, both of which could still improve if he continues to iron out inconsistencies in his delivery. The body also suggests room for growth, perhaps with an accompanying velocity bump. If that arrives, he could grow into a mid-rotation starter at the highest level. If not, his need to rely more on command than stuff probably gives him a ceiling of a spot starter or long reliever with upside to grow into something more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Rom racked up 116 strikeouts in 60 innings as a senior at Highlands (Ky.) High School, the Orioles lured him away from his commitment to Michigan with a fourth-round selection and above-slot $650,000 bonus, then sent him to the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League for his pro debut. Rom impressed enough there (1.76 ERA) to earn a jump to Class A Delmarva for his age-19 season, when the lanky lefty went 6-3 with a 2.93 ERA and 122 strikeouts in 95 1/3 innings for the Shorebirds. His 2020 season was limited to Orioles instructional camp due to the pandemic. Lean and projectable, Rom hides the ball well by creating deception with his 6-foot-2 frame. He’s filled out some in pro ball, though some believe there is still room for Rom to add muscle as he grows more, and that doing so will boost his stuff as he matures. As of now, he works predominatly off a fastball that sits between 89-92 mph and a slurve he throws in the high 70s, with plus feel. Rom also features a changeup that functions more like a split-fingered fastball, a pitch that plays about average but has improved since he entered pro ball. He works quickly and commands well enough to generate early, weak contact with all three pitches. The walks bumped up with Rom’s jump to Delmarva, the result of some mechanical inconsistencies the Orioles believe that he is athletic enough to iron out. The jump also came with a bump in swing-and-misses, despite Rom’s lack of overpowering stuff. That pitchability probably means Rom remains in the rotation, giving him the ceiling of a back-end starter if he can learn to repeat his delivery consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he racked up 116 strikeouts in 60 innings as a senior at Highlands (Ky.) High School, the Orioles lured Rom away from his commitment to Michigan with a fourth-round selection and above-slot $650,000 bonus, then sent him to the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League for his pro debut. Rom impressed enough there (1.76 ERA) to earn a jump to Class A Delmarva for his age-19 season, where the lanky lefty went 6-3 with a 2.93 ERA and 122 strikeouts in 95 1/3 innings for the Shorebirds. Lean and projectable, Rom hides the ball well by creating deception with his 6-foot-2, 170-pound frame. There is still room to add muscle as he grows, which some believe will result in boosting Rom’s stuff as he matures. As of now, he works predominately off a fastball that sits between 87-91 mph and a slurve he throws in the high 70s. Rom also features a changeup that functions more like a split-fingered fastball, a pitch that plays about average but has improved since he entered pro ball. He works quickly and commands them well enough to generate early, weak contact with all three pitches. The walks bumped up last year with Rom’s jump to Delmarva, the result of some mechanical inconsistencies the Orioles believe he is athletic enough to iron out. The lack of overpowering stuff probably means Rom remains in the rotation, giving him the ceiling of a back-end starter if he can learn to repeat his delivery consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rom endeared himself to scouts with solid performances during the summer and fall and continued to improve his Draft stock as a senior, posting a 2.42 ERA with 116 strikeouts in 60 innings for Highlands (Kent.) High. He was believed to have a strong commitment to Michigan before the Orioles selected him in the fourth round and signed him for $650,000, above his slot's recommended value of $483,300. He would make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, posting a 1.76 ERA across 31 innings. Rom may never develop overpowering stuff, but there's a lot to like in the left-hander's present feel for three pitches. He pitches with average velocity, sitting around 88-91 mph. He complements his fastball with a two-plane slider that flashes above average and a quality split-fingered fastball -- used in lieu of a changeup -- that bottoms out as it nears the plate. He throws all three pitches for strikes. Rom's somewhat mature build still requires physical projection, and it suggests that he could develop more velocity in the coming years. His mechanics differ depending on whether he's working from the wind-up or stretch, but he's athletic enough to make the necessary adjustments to consistently repeat his delivery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marte was No. 10 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list when the 2018-19 international signing period opened and he signed with the Mariners for $1.55 million, then made a strong first impression the following summer in the Dominican Summer League. He reached High-A during his U.S. debut in 2021 and was red-hot following a sluggish start to his 2022 season when he was traded to the Reds in the Luis Castillo deal. He hit his way from Double-A to Cincinnati in 2023, finishing the year with a long hit streak and a .380/.417/.544 line from Sept. 1 until the end of the year. He got off to a hot start in winter ball too, but a hamstring issue cut his time with Gigantes short. He was preparing for what seemed like his first full season in the big leagues when he received an 80-game suspension in March for testing positive for Boldenone, a performance enhancing substance. Just 22 for all of the 2024 season, Marte is still a bit mercurial as a player, but he made strides in being a more consistent offensive performer last season. The Reds challenged him to make better swing decisions when he got to Triple-A and he showed more aptitude in making adjustments, which led to his callup to the big leagues. In the Minors, he’s never struck out much and continued to draw walks, which will help him improve his ability to tap into his considerable raw power. It still shows up mostly to his pull side, but he’s shown he has the acumen to drive the ball to all fields. Marte is largely an above-average runner who can steal a base here and there, but he did register some elite-level sprint speeds during his big league debut. While he’s embraced playing third and could be an excellent defender at the hot corner, the Reds didn’t completely take shortstop away from him, which came in handy when he was asked to fill in at his original position last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners originally signed Marte for $1.55 million at the start of the 2018-19 international signing period, and he made an immediate impression with a strong debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019. He was able to play his way from Low-A to Single-A in his 2021 United States debut, and after a slow first half back with Everett in 2022, he had an 1.164 OPS in July, when he was sent to the Reds in the Luis Castillo trade. After finishing off with Dayton in his new organization, he capped things off by trying out a new position in the Arizona Fall League. There are few prospects with more raw power than Marte, and he’s continuing to learn how to tap into it, with 36 homers over the last two seasons. It shows up more to his pull side as he’s good at barreling the ball out front. He draws walks and keeps his strikeouts to a minimum but can still improve on swing decisions and overall consistency in following his gameplan, though it should be noted he’s always been quite young for his level. While Marte has the feel, instincts and arm to play shortstop long-term, it’s unclear if he’s going to outgrow the position. The Reds introduced him to third base in the AFL and were pleased with how that went, even if outside evaluators detected a player who looked more like he wanted to prove he can stick at short. He’s just 21 for all of the 2023 season, with plenty of time for him to figure things out and let his bat carry him to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year after landing Julio Rodríguez on the international amateur market, the Mariners were aggressive again, signing Marte, thought to be one of the best players in the 2018-19 signing class, for $1.55 million. Excitement grew when Marte lit up the Dominican Summer League and then was the youngest player at the Mariners’ alternate training site in 2020. He carried lessons learned there into his United States debut in 2021, earning a late promotion from Low-A to High-A. After a slow start back in High-A in '22, Marte was heating up in a big way when he was sent to the Reds as the top prospect in the trade that sent Luis Castillo to Seattle. Marte has ridiculous raw power, as the young shortstop can go toe-to-toe with just about anyone in batting practice displays. It shows up in games -- he hit 17 homers in 2021 -- especially to the pull side, and he’s naturally good at impacting the ball out front. While he has shown a willingness to draw walks, he can get out of his approach at times, and like many young hitters, he will need to continue to find consistency between at-bats and games. He wore down and is learning how to pace himself for a long professional season. It’s still up in the air if Marte will stay at shortstop forever. His bat would profile at third and he’s athletic enough to handle center field. The focus is now on shortstop, and that’s the only position he’s played as a professional prior to joining Cincinnati.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects on the international amateur market when the singing period began in July 2018, Marte landed in the top 10 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects that year. Seattle signed him for $1.55 million and he made it seem like a sound investment right away in 2019, when Marte led the Dominican Summer League in total bases and RBIs while showing off his power-speed combination and hitting .309/.371/.511 with nine homers in 65 games. The Mariners liked him so much that they invited him to Summer Camp with the big league team before the 2020 season. At 18 years old, he was the youngest of the 60 players there. Though he was understandably overmatched at times, Marte showed that he had gleaned valuable experience by the time he showed up to instructional league last fall. Seattle has been confident in Marte’s ability to impact the baseball, with most of his power coming from his pull side, though he’s shown the ability to drive the ball to all fields. He’s already gotten much more physical since he signed while improving his approach, looking very much like someone who will hit for average and power. While that increased physicality has slowed him down a touch, he’s still a plus runner who can steal a base. Had it not been for the cancellation of the Minor League season, Marte likely would’ve been headed for Class A Short Season or Class A. Instead, he spent 2020 at the alternate training site, where he flashed an assortment of loud tools while gaining the type of experience against older competition that could lead to a breakout campaign in 2021. While it is still unclear exactly where Marte’s defensive home will be, he’s answered many questions with his commitment to his throwing program, syncing up his lower half and his arm action. He made a lot of errors early in his debut, then cleaned things up and was very sharp at the end. He could end up at third base when all is said and done, but that’s an improvement for a player who some doubted would be able to stay on the dirt at all. Even if he had to move to the outfield, his bat is going to play, with some seeing similar offensive traits as Hanley Ramirez at this age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marte was one of four shortstops in the top 10 of MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International prospects list at the start of the 2018-19 signing period. The Mariners liked his power-speed combination enough to give him $1.55 million to sign. The Dominican teenager came to Arizona in the fall to participate in the organization's high performance camp, rather than play in instructional league games, so he'll be making his professional debut in 2019. Two things stood out for the Mariners with Marte from the get-go: his bat speed and his footspeed. He has work to do on his approach, nothing new given his age and experience level, but he's already been making an effort in that regard and will just have to start applying it as he begins his career in earnest. He should have the ability to hit for average and the leverage in his swing points to plenty of power as well. Marte can really run too, with some seeing 80 run times on the 20-to-80 scouting scale. There are some good defensive tools to work with, though at first his actions weren't in sync, with his feet ahead of his hands. He's already shown more maturity in approaching ground balls and keeping his feet under him, giving more confidence he can stay on the dirt with his strong arm. Whether that's at shortstop remains to be seen, as it's hard to know exactly how his body will continue to mature. A move to third or second could be in his future, and the Mariners think his electric speed would play in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken in the second round in 2020, Winn was drafted as a potential two-way player, and he gave pitching a brief shot in pro ball but has stuck to position-player status ever since. His breakout came in 2022 when he hit .283/.364/.468 with 12 homers and 43 steals between High-A and Double-A, earning spots in the All-Star Futures Game and Arizona Fall League along the way, and he showed more power than ever with a career-best 18 homers over 105 games for Triple-A Memphis last season. The Cardinals called up Winn in August but he struggled offensively, going 21-for-122 (.172) with only four extra-base hits. Winn has admitted since that he may have been pressing to make a good impression during that first Major League run, leading to drops in power. The right-handed slugger, however, did post above-average chase, whiff and strikeout rates over his 37-game span, and that overall approach points to a solid bat once he reestablishes himself. His Triple-A pop came by jumping on pitches he could drive earlier in counts, and while the raw slugging ability won’t necessarily stand out, there’s still the potential for around 15 homers in a full MLB season. The Texas native’s arm strength has been legendary in the Minors -- most notably when he threw 100.5 mph in the 2022 Futures Game -- but he’s learned to keep it under control, drawing praise from Paul Goldschmidt. He can absolutely fly, registering home-to-first times in the 4-second range, and that helps his coverage at short, though he struggled some going to his right in the Majors. Even if the power doesn’t reach Memphis levels again, Winn’s multiple ways to contribute should make him St. Louis’ long-term answer at the six.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winn was a fascinating two-way talent in the five-round 2020 Draft, having shown off an arm capable of touching the high-90s and multiple skills at shortstop. The Cardinals selected him 54th overall that July and toyed briefly with keeping him in both roles before choosing to make him a full-time position player instead. After getting settled at two A-ball levels in 2021, Winn broke out a bit with the bat last year, slashing .283/.364/.468 with 12 homers and 43 steals in 119 games at High-A and Double-A, before he held his own in the Arizona Fall League. Any discussion of Winn has to start with his arm, a true 80-grade howitzer. He fired a 100.5 mph seed at the All-Star Futures Game in Los Angeles that broke the Statcast-era record for hardest infield throw. The Cardinals have worked with Winn on knowing when to let it fly and when to be more in control, but he’s still good for a few eye-popping lasers each week. With his near-plus-plus speed and promising hands, Winn has the skills to be a strong overall defender from deep in the hole. What launched Winn into Top 100 standing were his offensive improvements in 2022. He became a more patient hitter in his second full season and also started elevating the ball more, leading to a jump in total home runs from five to 11 and extra-base hits from 29 to 56. Continued gains this season at Triple-A Memphis have only helped the case that he'll add value with his bat too, making him a potential five-tool shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If Winn could be cloned, he would make for two different, yet impressive prospects. He proved that in the 2019 World Wood Bat Association Championship by shoving at 98 mph and homering in the same game in Jupiter (his future Spring Training/Low-A home). After Winn’s senior year at Kingwood (Texas) High School was interrupted by the pandemic, the Cardinals selected the two-way talent 54th overall and went above slot to sign him for $2.1 million. He was a shortstop only for Low-A Palm Beach and held his own at the plate with a .262/.370/.388 line in 61 games. Winn struggled after an aggressive push to High-A Peoria, and while he did make one relief appearance there, the Cardinals plan to keep him focused on being a position player for the foreseeable future. No surprise, Winn’s arm is his most wow-worthy tool. He had 10 throws measured at 95-plus mph by Statcast in Low-A Southeast in 2021 and famously unleashed a 100.5 mph throw in the 2022 All-Star Futures Game that set a Statcast record. As if that wasn’t enough defensively, the 5-foot-11 infielder is a plus runner who shows ample range at a premium position. He used those wheels to steal 32 bags in 2021, and he could be a 25-steal threat in the Majors due to his aggression and efficiency on the basepaths. It all comes down to the bat. Winn has shown offensive improvements in 2022, cutting down a little on his strikeouts while adding some strength and impact in his at-bats, leading to a midseason promotion from High-A to Double-A. He should be at least average offensively, and given how great he can be on the other side, he’s a potential above-average regular shortstop. His pitching days are securely in the rearview.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A prospect with legitimate two-way capabilities, Winn is one of the most intriguing prospects in the Cardinals’ system. The Kingwood (Texas) HS product turned heads at the 2019 World Wood Bat Association World Championship when he homered and hit 98 mph on the mound in the same game. On top of that, he also flashed a pair of plus secondary pitches. The Cardinals selected Winn in the second round (54th overall) in June 2020 and signed him for an above-slot $2.1 million. He made his professional debut with Low-A Palm Beach and although he got off to a slow start, he caught fire in June and was promoted to High-A Peoria as a 19-year-old. St. Louis isn’t ruling out developing Winn as a two-way player, though he’s spent the bulk of his time thus far developing as a shortstop. His arm, easily a plus tool, profiles well at short and he has the quickness and range to stick there as well. Offensively, his approach needs refinement. He has good raw power, but is still learning how to get to it in games. He may ultimately become more of a gap-to-gap hitter than a true home-run threat. He has above-average speed, which could help turn some of those line drives in the gaps into triples. If Winn gets back on the mound, his fastball sits in the low-to-mid-90s and he has a pair of secondary pitches with plus potential. Overall, he has an intriguing set of tools and consistency will determine his ceiling. While his potential in the field is high, there are some questions about whether he’ll hit enough to become an everyday player in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schanuel stayed in his own backyard to play college baseball and hit the second he got on Florida Atlantic University’s campus. After posting a combined 1.081 OPS in his first two seasons, he went off as a junior in 2023, leading all Division I hitters in average (.447), on-base percentage (.615) and walks (71). Taken No. 11 overall by the Angels, who have a reputation for pushing guys quickly up the ladder, Schanuel played just 22 Minor League games before getting called up the big leagues, where he promptly walked more than he struck out and reached base in all 29 games he played. A left-handed hitter, Schanuel has always had an advanced approach at the plate, leaving FAU with a career .516 OBP. He has a keen sense of finding the barrel and doesn’t swing and miss much, with just a 17.6 percent whiff rate during his first taste of the big leagues. He tapped into more power as he made his way through college, homering 19 times last spring, and while the pop didn’t show up over his first 51 pro games, he spent the offseason working to add strength and make some tweaks to his setup and swing to tap into his raw pop without sacrificing any approach. Schanuel is an average runner who has good baserunning instincts, and there’s some athleticism there, though he’s largely played first base both in college and at the outset of his pro career. He’s already reached Los Angeles, and there’s no reason to think his bat won’t be in the lineup daily from here on out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMillon was first drafted out of high school in Texas and then again after his third year at Texas Tech. But he went back to school -- and got unlucky with the pandemic shortening the Draft to five rounds. He signed with the Royals as an undrafted free agent and began a slow climb. Finally in 2023, McMillon broke out: across 51 1/3 innings from Single-A Columbia to Double-A Northwest Arkansas, he struck out 91 batters and walked just 25 with a 2.10 ERA. He was nearly unhittable with a .138 opponents' average against and 0.95 WHIP. McMillon skipped Triple-A completely and made his Major League debut in August, but he was shut down after four appearances because of a forearm strain. He showed up to Spring Training healthy. Explosive is about the only way to describe McMillon’s stuff, and he trusted it more in ‘23. A plus-plus fastball sits in the upper-90s and flashes over 100 mph at times, generating a lot of his whiffs. His 85-87 mph slider misses bats with good bite, leading to healthy swing-and-whiff rates. He has a feel for a changeup, but it hasn’t shown up in games, as his two-pitch repertoire has been very effective. McMillon made improvements to his mechanics last year that helped his command, but it’s still fringe-to-average as the biggest thing keeping him from being a surefire high-leverage reliever. Intense on the mound, McMillon looks the part of a big league reliever. His upside is a closer with his two dynamic weapons. That all hinges on his control, but he’ll compete for a spot in the Royals’ bullpen and will help them out again at some point in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs took Jarvis 18th overall in 2020 after a standout but shortened spring at Duke, but it’s been a bumpy ride since. Oblique issues limited him to 75 1/3 innings in 2021, and he was shelled at hitter-friendly Double-A Amarillo a year later. By all accounts, the 2023 campaign was his best yet, even with a 5.26 ERA over 92 1/3 innings at Triple-A Reno. Jarvis debuted in the Majors on Aug. 15 and was used as a multi-inning reliever for much of his 11-game run, proving adept at limiting runs and runners (3.04 ERA, 0.97 WHIP), but he didn’t miss many bats (12 K's in 23 2/3 innings). Jarvis shows decent velocity with a 93-97 mph fastball, but with only 12.3 inches of induced vertical break, the movement profile makes it play well below that. When Jarvis spots it in the zone, it has a tendency to be hit hard. Luckily, his mid-80s slider is a true plus pitch as it dives low and gloveside, and that’s why it was his most oft-used offering against righties across all levels in 2023. His changeup -- sitting around the same velo -- moves the opposite way, giving him an option for lefties, while a low-80s curveball is a distant fourth pitch. The former Blue Devil showed better in control in the Majors away from the Triple-A ABS system, but his strikeout rate also fell from 23.4 percent to 13.0 in the smaller sample. Because of his fastball, it’s clear why Arizona didn’t want him seeing batters more than once, and he might be best-served leaning even more into the slider in limited roles moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jarvis didn’t get much chance to show off in his junior year at Duke before the 2020 pandemic canceled his spring, but he made the most of it, striking out 40 and walking only two in 27 innings. That upward momentum helped him get picked 18th overall that summer, and he signed for $2.65 million. An oblique issue limited him to 75 1/3 innings, mostly between High-A and Double-A, in his first full season. He returned to Amarillo in 2022, only to get shellacked (8.27 ERA, 1.88 WHIP, 27 homers in 106 2/3 innings) in the hitter-friendly environs there. The 6-foot-2 right-hander epitomizes the phrase “velocity isn’t everything.” Jarvis can sit in the mid-90s with his fastball, but without much movement or deception, hitters can see it well. Sometimes in Amarillo, all batters needed to do was make contact, lift the ball into the air and let the conditions do the rest. Jarvis’ off-speed pitches still grade out well, especially his mid-80s slider and diving changeup around the same velocity. The latter particularly fools left-handers well, and it’s why Jarvis’ 12.8 percent swinging-strike rate (seventh-best in the Texas League) brought cause for optimism. He’ll also spin a decent curve that rounds out the four-pitch mix. Jarvis’ control regressed in ’22 as he walked 11.9 percent of his batters, adding to concerns about his ability to start. His delivery is rather short, and D-backs coaches hope some tweaks will make him more deceptive, allowing the results to match his stuff. The former Blue Devil has a ways to go in that department to live up to his lofty Draft status, through.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jarvis, the son of former big league pitcher Kevin, added muscle to his body and velocity to his fastball prior to the 2020 college season, which caused him to rocket up Draft boards. The D-backs nabbed him with the 18th overall pick, making him just the second Duke player (Marcus Stroman was the other) to be selected in the first round. Arizona signed him for a below-slot $2.65 million bonus and challenged him early. Jarvis immediately impressed at the alternate training site, pitching against advanced competition in 2020. He then got off to a fast start in his professional debut, dominating in High-A and working his way up to Double-A, though he did miss roughly six weeks with an oblique issue. Since being drafted, Jarvis has added 20 pounds to his 6-foot-2 frame and now operates in the mid-90s with his fastball. With an effective downhill plane, Jarvis’ fastball jumps out of his hand. His curveball has continued to progress and his mid-80s slider has developed into an above-average offering, which occasionally flashes plus. His fading changeup remains his best secondary pitch, grading as well-above-average at its best. Jarvis has proven to be the polished pitcher with strong command whom the D-backs selected out of Duke. The 24-year-old shows a good feel for pitching and could move quickly through the system. He’s able to throw all four of his offerings for strikes and could develop into a solid No. 2-type starter when all is said and done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jarvis, the son of former big league pitcher Kevin, added muscle to his body and velocity to his fastball prior to the 2020 college season, which led him to shoot up Draft boards. The D-backs nabbed him with the 18th overall pick, making him just the second Duke player (Marcus Stroman is the other) to be selected in the first round. Arizona signed him for a below-slot $2.65 million bonus and challenged him early. Jarvis immediately impressed at the alternate training site, pitching against advanced competition in 2020, and he worked his way up to Double-A Amarillo in his 2021 professional debut, though he did miss some time with an oblique issue. Jarvis added 20 pounds to his 6-foot-2 frame and operated at 92-96 with effective downhill plane in 2020. His stuff has taken a step forward in 2021 and he’s now working at 95-96 mph. The fastball jumps out of his hand and he's continued to progress with his curveball, which is an above-average offering for him and his slider is effective in the mid-80s. His fading changeup remains his best secondary offering, grading as well above average at its best. Jarvis has proven to be the polished pitcher with strong command whom the D-backs selected out of Duke. As a 23-year-old, he worked his way up to Double-A in his full-season debut and appears to be a quick riser. He can throw all four of his pitches for strikes and has a future of a No. 2-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A year ago, Jarvis was a strike-thrower with a good changeup and big league pedigree (son of former pitcher Kevin), who could have gone toward the end of the top 10 rounds if he were signable as a sophomore-eligible. He wasn't and turned down the Yankees as a 37th-rounder, then opened eyes with a much stronger body and better stuff in the fall. Scouts wanted to see if he could maintain them over a full college season and never got the chance to find out, but he did throw one perfect game and flirted with another in his four starts -- which was enough for him to join Marcus Stroman as the only first-round picks ever out of Duke when the D-backs took him No. 18 overall and signed him for a below-slot $2.65 million bonus. After working with an 88-93 mph fastball at the beginning of 2019 and dipping to 86-91 by season's end, Jarvis added 20 pounds to his 6-foot-2 frame and operated at 92-96 with effective downhill plane last fall and this spring. His breaking ball used to be average at best, and now he flashes a plus curveball in the upper 70s that he can manipulate into a distinct and equally effective slider in the mid-80s. His fading changeup remains his best secondary offering, grading as well above average at its best. Jarvis has improved his control along with his stuff, posting a 40-2 K-BB ratio in 27 innings this season while showing the ability to move his pitches around the strike zone. He repeats his delivery well and long has drawn praise for his competitiveness. He does have a narrow frame and lack of track record, but the D-backs clearly believe the 2020 version of Jarvis is for real.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lopez took an unusual path to becoming a key part of the Rays’ rotation depth entering the 2024 season. He transferred away from San Francisco State to the College of the Canyons and wound up being selected by the Giants in the 26th round of the 2018 Draft -- a round that wouldn’t exist two years later. About a year after signing for $150,000, San Francisco dealt him to Tampa Bay for Joe McCarthy. He broke out with big-time strikeout numbers in 2021, then underwent Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of ’22. He returned last year, put together a 2.68 ERA in 26 upper-Minors appearances, debuted for the Rays on Aug. 14 and started their final game of the regular season. Lopez has a deceptive delivery and excellent extension, meaning he releases the ball closer to home plate than most. That makes him especially tough against left-handed hitters, who recorded just a .584 OPS against him in the Minors last season. His slider is by far his best offering, coming in around 78-80 mph with two-plane break and the best whiff rate of any pitch he throws. His fastball sits in the low-90s, occasionally reaching up to 93-94 mph, with armside run. His low-to-mid-80s changeup is another option against righties, but not a consistently effective one. Lopez had run up some impressive strikeout-to-walk ratios in the past, but his strikeout rate dipped and his walk rate jumped as he transitioned to Triple-A with the ABS system in place. He’ll be 26 years old this season, but he’s valuable as essentially a Major League-ready starter/bulk-inning pitcher who could settle into a role as a back-end starter. How he’s used could depend on what the Rays need, whether it’s rotation depth or a multi-inning bullpen arm to ride the Durham shuttle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Meckler earned just 10 at-bats as a freshman walk-on at Oregon State in 2019, the coaching staff told him it would be in his best interests to transfer. He stayed in Corvallis anyway and became a two-year starter for the Beavers and a money-saving eighth-round pick in 2022. He needed just 92 games to hit his way from Rookie ball to the Majors, batting .232 in 20 games with the Giants in 2023, but a sprained wrist hampered him for most of last season. A career .328 hitter in his first three season in the Minors, Meckler has a compact, controlled left-handed stroke and controls the strike zone. He makes a lot of soft groundball contact, though he did add some strength and hit the ball a bit harder in 2024, showing the potential for perhaps 10 homers per season. He's much more effective against fastballs, making contact on 92 percent of swings compared to just 68 percent against all other pitches last season. Though Meckler has well-above-average speed, he's not a prolific basestealer or a dazzling defender. He's a solid center fielder with fringy arm strength and has seen action at all three outfield spots. He has the same build and extreme hit-over-power profile as fellow Oregon State product Steven Kwan, but Meckler will have to solve non-fastballs and find a bit more impact to compete for a job as a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 60 | Power: 30 | Run: 65 | Arm: 45 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 Meckler collected just 10 at-bats as a freshman walk-on at Oregon State in 2019, prompting the coaching staff to tell him he'd be better off transferring. He decided to remain in Corvallis, became a two-year starter for the Beavers and became a money-saving eighth-round pick in 2022. He needed just 92 games to hit his way from Rookie ball to San Francisco and hit .232 in 20 games with the Giants last summer. His .371 batting average between three levels would have led the Minors if he hadn't fallen just shy of qualifying, while his .456 on-base percentage would have ranked third. Similar to fellow Oregon State product Steven Kwan, Meckler manages the strike zone well and has an extreme hit-over-power profile. He has a compact left-handed swing, rarely chases pitches and almost never swings and misses against a fastball. He does have some trouble making contact against breaking balls and changeups -- he went 2-for-26 with 18 strikeouts against them in the Majors -- but of greater concern is his lack of pop. While he regularly put the barrel on the ball, he hits a lot of soft grounders and rarely drives the ball with authority. It's difficult to project Meckler as a big league regular unless he makes some adjustments to find more power, but he offers value beyond being a contact hitter. He has well-above-average speed but he's somewhat conservative as a basestealer and has good but not great range in the outfield. He's a solid defender on the corners -- more average in center field -- and possesses fringy arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Basabe signed with the Rangers for $550,000 during the 2017-18 international signing period, one of their consolations when they missed out on Shohei Ohtani. He wasn’t the biggest prize then, but he turned out to be the best prospect from that Texas class. He wasn’t even considered the top prospect in the deal when the Rangers acquired Nathaniel Lowe from the Rays after the 2020 season; he was second in line behind Heriberto Hernandez. But Basabe is getting plenty of attention now, as his continued performance earned him a spot on the Rays’ 40-man roster and further recognition as one of the organization’s top prospects. After a couple solid seasons in the low Minors, Basabe took another step forward while splitting the 2022 season between High-A Bowling Green and Double-A Montgomery. The speedy, right-handed-hitting infielder batted .324/.385/.462 while striking out only 59 times in 495 plate appearances over 112 games. He continues to display elite contact skills, finding ways to put the ball in play and get on base, as his .316 career batting average would indicate. He doesn’t have much raw power – he hit eight homers in his first 1,220 professional plate appearances – but his bat speed leads to solid enough contact so that he can use his above-average speed to leg out doubles and occasional triples. Basabe has moved around the infield for the Rays, handling himself well at shortstop, second and third base. He’s a good defender with a strong arm that plays at any spot, which should help him carve out a multi-positional role with Tampa Bay at some point in the near future. The Rays have also been impressed with Basabe’s competitiveness and work ethic, as he played through some injuries and found ways to be productive in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Basabe wound up signing with the Rangers during the 2017-18 international signing period, when Texas missed out on Shohei Ohtani and had to invest its savings elsewhere. Basabe ($550,000) didn’t get the most attention or the most lucrative deal in that Rangers class, but the Venezuelan infielder turned out to be the group’s best prospect. The Rays picked him up as one of three prospects they acquired for first baseman Nathaniel Lowe after the 2020 season, essentially as the second piece in the deal behind Heriberto Hernandez, and Basabe – a cousin of Luis Alexander Basabe (White Sox) and Luis Matos (Giants) -- put together a solid first season in Tampa Bay’s system. Basabe is an up-the-middle athlete with an intriguing blend of tools, and he’s performed well at every level since beginning his pro career in the Dominican Republic in 2018. He spent most of his Rays debut with Low-A Charleston, where he hit .284/.347/.385 in 66 games. He’s still young enough at 21 to hope he’ll add a little more power as he matures, but he’s only slugged .416 in 725 professional plate appearances. He possesses a combination of bat speed, foot speed, bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline that should allow him to hit for a reasonably high average and get on base enough; he worked 28 walks compared to 45 strikeouts in 327 total plate appearances last season, boosting his OBP to .347. The question is whether he’ll develop enough thump to make consistently hard contact against high-level pitching. His plus speed and up-the-middle versatility set him apart. He swiped 18 bags last season and should remain a baserunning threat moving forward. And while he also spent time at second and third base last season, Basabe looked good enough at shortstop – with an above-average arm, to boot -- to believe he can stick at the premium position. Given the Rays’ overwhelming crop of shortstop prospects, the fact that Basabe can play anywhere should only work to his advantage. At the very least, he seems like a potential utility infielder who can hold his own at the plate and challenge opponents on the bases. If things break right, he could be a bottom-of-the-order regular in the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 After the Rangers failed to sign Shohei Ohtani and had leftover money in their bonus pool, they pivoted and landed three other premium international prospects, the best of whom is Basabe. Signed out of Venezuela for $550,000 in December 2017, he has three cousins with the same surname in pro ball, including White Sox outfield prospect Luis Alexander Basabe. In his 2018 pro debut, Osleivis finished third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League batting race at .344. Basabe has some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the Texas system, uses the entire field and controls the strike zone. Some scouts expressed concerns about his hitting ability when he was an amateur but he has calmed down his right-handed swing. He may max out at 12-15 homers per year, though he has some wiry strength and shows occasional pull-side power. With his on-base ability and plus-plus speed, Basabe could become a dynamic basestealer. There were teams that projected him as a center fielder, but the Rangers like his infield actions and believe he can stay at shortstop. He has improved his consistency since turning pro and also looked fine at second base in his debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seeking extra work due to a dislocated elbow that limited him to only 84 Minor League games in 2022, Butler, a sixth-round pick by Oakland out of Westlake High School in Atlanta in the 2018 MLB Draft, parlayed a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League into a spot on the A’s 40-man roster this winter. After hitting .270 with 11 home runs and 31 stolen bases in 81 games with High-A Lansing, he joined the Mesa Solar Sox of the AFL and posted an .833 OPS with two home runs and 16 RBIs over 19 games. Butler’s speed and power to all fields gives him 20-20 potential. He continues to work hard on improving his plate discipline and walked at a higher rate last season, though there is still plenty of swing-and-miss to his game as evidenced by his 31.5 percent strikeout rate with Lansing in ‘22. Butler has worked hard on cleaning up his body, leaning out while adding more muscle over the past year. He’s also changed his tune on defense from when he first joined the A’s, emerging as a solid defender at the corner outfield spots with a good arm and speed and athleticism that enables him to cover a ton of ground. There’s still time to improve the strikeout rate, but even if his punchouts remain at a high clip, his other attributes should help him progress through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 55 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Perhaps no player in the organization took a bigger step in raising his prospect stock over the past year than Butler. A sixth-round pick out of Westlake High School in Atlanta by the A’s in 2018, he bounced back from early struggles in Rookie ball and a tough 2019 in the New York-Penn League with major strides through the pandemic and returned looking like a completely different player in 2021 as he combined to hit .273 with 19 home runs and 75 RBIs while also adding 29 stolen bases in 102 games combined at Low-A and High-A. Butler’s skill set gives him consistent 20-homer, 20-stolen base potential. His plate discipline has dramatically improved over the past year and he can use the whole field as a hitter with monster power to all fields. There is still a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, but the A’s expect him to cut that down over time. Assuming the swing-and-miss is adequately addressed, Butler profiles as a Major Leaguer with improved defensive attributes that should allow him to play both first base and outfield. He should continue to progress through the A’s system as one of the more fun prospects to watch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Danner is one of the most unique development stories in the organization, first drafted as a catcher out of Huntington Beach HS (Calif.) At the time, Danner also had interest as a pitcher but stayed behind the plate, where he struggled offensively, batting just .191 over three seasons between Rookie ball and Single-A. Then came the fun part, as Danner and the Blue Jays began his transition back to the mound. The results were immediate coming out of the lost 2020 season. Danner spent 2021 with High-A Vancouver, where he posted a 2.02 ERA with 42 strikeouts over 35 2/3 innings. The Blue Jays quickly protected him from the Rule 5 Draft, recognizing his potential and polish could be attractive to other clubs. Danner’s 2022 season was limited to just 3 2/3 innings in Double-A, though, as he dealt with an elbow issue. He got into eight games in the AFL, where he allowed three runs and struck out eight over 7 2/3 innings. Danner attacks hitters with a high-90s fastball and a snapping slider, both of which have the potential to be plus pitches, and he’s shown the makings of the occasional upper-70s curveball. His pro experience is extremely limited on the mound, but at 24 and with his experience catching, he’s far more advanced than his 39 1/3 Minor League innings suggest. Danner could make his MLB debut as early as 2023, but the upper Minors will be a good test of his feel for pitching. As the Blue Jays chase more swing-and-miss out of their pitching prospects, Danner is exactly the outcome they’ve been aiming for.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Danner drew scouts as both a pitcher and catcher leading into the ’17 Draft, but the Blue Jays liked him behind the plate and made him a second-round pick out of California’s Huntington Beach High School. Over three seasons as a catcher from ’17 to ’19, Danner hit just .191 with a .633 OPS over 146 games, so a change was in order. The Blue Jays looked at Danner as a pitcher once again in ’20 and gave him his Minor League pitching debut in ’21, which went very well. Danner immediately impressed, posting a 2.02 ERA in High-A Vancouver with 42 strikeouts over 35 2/3 innings. It was enough to convince the Blue Jays to add him to their 40-man roster this past offseason, far earlier than anyone could have reasonably expected. Danner was sitting in the mid-90s with his fastball and even touched 100 mph at instructs last fall. His slider sits in the mid-80s and is still a work in progress, but there’s potential in there for it to be a legitimate out pitch at the Major League level. Those two potential plus pitches, if they continue to develop, could be enough for Danner to succeed in the big leagues. This is one of the most unique development cases in the system. Danner will be tested by more advanced hitters in ’22, and that will be a great learning experience for a pitcher who’s so raw professionally. The talent is there to continue this rapid ascent, though, and that velocity will be awfully tantalizing for the MLB club if he continues to flirt with triple-digits. Danner doesn’t turn 24 until late September, either, so the Blue Jays appear to have uncovered a potential gem here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Once known as a star in the 2011 Little League World Series, Danner evolved into one the better two-way players in the 2017 Draft class, so much so that the scouting industry remained split down the middle all spring on whether he'd be better suited on the mound or behind the plate at the next level. The Blue Jays preferred Danner in the latter role, drafting him in the second round and then signing him for close to $500,000 above slot value. But after a pro debut that saw him hit just .160 with a 26.5 percent strikeout rate over 34 games in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, the jury is still out regarding Danner's positional future. Danner is raw behind the plate but has the chance to be a special catcher. He has good hands and a plus arm defensively -- he was up to 94-95 mph on the mound as a prep -- and while he's a below-average runner, his athleticism helps him move well behind the dish. He swings the bat well from a crouch set up, with quiet pop that could end up being average power in the future, but he'll need to distance himself from his current pull-heavy approach to be successful against pro arms. The one thing scouts agree on is that Danner's grades will improve now that he's focused solely on catching and hitting. At the same time, Danner's pro debut indicated that he would need considerable time to refine his game on both sides of the ball. At the worst, Danner's power arm represents an interesting fallback option should he have trouble sticking as a catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known since starring in the 2011 Little League World Series, Danner was one of the better legitimate two-way players in the 2017 Draft class -- so much so that the scouting industry remained split down the middle all spring on whether he'd be better suited on the mound or behind the plate at the next level. The Blue Jays preferred Danner in the latter role, drafting him in the second round and then signing him for close to $500,000 above slot value. Danner has the chance to be a special catcher. He has good hands and a plus arm defensively -- he was up to 94-95 mph on the mound -- and while he's a below-average runner, his athleticism helps him move well behind the dish. He swings the bat well from a crouch set up, with quiet pop that could end up being average power in the future. The one thing scouts agree on is that Danner's grades will improve once he starts to focus on one craft. But even as the spring unfolded, there was division among scouts whether he should stay on the mound or behind the plate at the next level. At the worst, Danner's power arm represents an interesting fallback option should he have trouble sticking as a catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After an unsuccessful attempt to sign Shohei Ohtani after the 2017 season, the Rangers pivoted and used their surplus of international bonus pool money to spend $2.8 million to land Martinez in March 2018. He had starred in Cuba's top league as a 20-year-old in 2016-17, then spent two seasons in the independent Can-Am League after defecting. In his first year in affiliated ball, he held his own in the short-season Northwest League and starred in the Arizona Fall League, but he has struggled to make consistent contact in 2019. With his willingness to work counts and plus speed, Martinez could fit at the top of a big league batting order. To do so, he'll have to curb a tendency to let his left-handed swing get too long when he tries to hit home runs. While he's not a big guy, he generates solid raw power with his quick bat and deceptive strength in his hands and wrists. Martinez has the speed to be an asset as a basestealer and a center fielder, but he's still learning how to make the most of it. He needs to improve his jumps on the bases and in the outfield. He's capable of playing all three outfield spots, though his fringy-to-average arm would be a bit stretched in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ryan was viewed as a better position prospect than a pitcher as a high school senior even though he could pump a mid-90s fastball. He passed on signing with the Indians as a 40th-round pick in 2014 and honored his commitment to North Carolina, where he would struggle at the plate and make just one appearance on the mound before leaving the team in 2016. The Indians took Ryan in the 30th round that June, signing him for $100,000, then dealt him to the Mets a little over a year later in exchange for Jay Bruce. He excelled with Class A Advanced St. Lucie early in the 2018 season, earning Florida State League All-Star honors along with a promotion to Double-A, where he opened his 2019 campaign. Ryan shows power stuff out of the bullpen. He'll sit at 95-96 mph and touch 98 with a riding fastball that he pairs with a low-to-mid-80s slider that has a high spin rate and earns above-average grades from scouts. He also has a changeup, but it's a distant third pitch that he seldom throws. After issuing 3.6 walks-per-nine in his first full season, Ryan made strides with both his control and command in 2018 before taking a slight step back in '19. The gains Ryan made with his breaking ball and overall feel for pitching last season bode well for his chances of reaching the Major Leagues as middle reliever capable of working multiple frames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hancock hasn’t quite lived up to the lofty expectations affixed to his status as the No. 6 overall pick in the 2020 Draft, but he showed in a short stint in the Majors last year that he can be a viable back-end rotation piece when healthy. Hancock impressed in two starts before suffering a right shoulder strain in his third, which wound up ending his season. Health remains the most critical component to his long-term trajectory, given that he also dealt with shoulder issues in 2021 and a lat strain in 2022. The former Georgia Bulldog doesn’t possess the high-90s velocity he did in college, but he’s harnessed a four-pitch mix and shown above-average command enough to where his stuff should play in the Majors. There’s good feel-to-pitch and strike-throwing ability that have allowed him to eat innings in the Minors when healthy. His four-seamer remains the bread and butter, and his slider possesses some cutter tendencies more than the sweepers that are all the rave, and it consistently induced weak contact. The development of his two-seamer has been encouraging, and he has a usable changeup as well. Hancock was one of three prominent pitchers to graduate from Double-A Arkansas last year, along with Bryce Miller and Bryan Woo, and though he doesn’t possess the overpowering stuff that those teammates do, he nonetheless has the chance to be a quality contributor. It’s just that he has a few notable “ifs” attached to him -- health and the fortification of his entire arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top righties in the 2020 Draft, Hancock battled a shoulder injury in 2021 and a right lat issue to start 2022, ultimately stalling his development. But once he debuted last season, there were no setbacks and he spent the entire season at Double-A Arkansas, where he continued to harness his four-pitch mix. For the former Georgia Bulldog, staying healthy and confident is more paramount than his actual stuff. Hancock’s strikeout and walk rates haven’t matched what he did in college, but at his best, he still has good control and command of his stuff. His fastball velocity has dropped, though, from 96-97 mph to around 94 mph. His slider was much improved, thanks to reverting back to a shorter, firmer shape out of a three-quarter slot like when he was at UGA, opposed to the sweeper that’s more in vogue. The changeup has also taken a big step forward. While he might not possess true plus stuff the way Bryce Miller does, Hancock is a reliable strike thrower in the eyes of most Mariners scouts, and because of his pitch mix and profile, he probably has a more legitimate shot at remaining a starter, even if it’s a mid-to-back-rotation projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thought to be the top college right-hander in the Draft class of 2020, Hancock ended up being the second one taken behind Max Meyer when the Mariners selected him No. 6 overall. That marked the third straight Draft Seattle went with a college righty in the first round. Since signing for $5.7 million, the biggest challenge has been to keep the tall right-hander on the mound, as arm and shoulder issues limited him to just 44 2/3 innings and kept him from attending the Futures Game. From a pure stuff standpoint, Hancock still displays many of the attributes that made him one of the best arms in his Draft class. He can run his four-seam fastball up into the upper 90s and his two-seamer up to 95 mph, though not as consistently in the upper registers. He’ll continue to throw both a slider that flashes plus and a solid curveball, though with good fade and deception, his changeup is likely his best secondary offering. Hancock is capable of throwing strikes with all of his offerings, but he hasn’t always repeated his delivery well and lost reps because arm issues cost him valuable time for refining his mechanics. He didn’t pitch more than five innings in any of his 2021 starts, and even though it was encouraging to see him throw well when he got to Double-A, he only made three starts there. Some feel other pitchers in the system like Matt Brash have passed him up, though a full, healthy season could put doubts to rest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A top high school pitching prospect in Georgia in 2017, Hancock’s commitment to the University of Georgia kept him from being seriously considered in that year’s Draft. For much of 2019, he was the best pitcher in college baseball, though he missed time with a lat issue. He didn’t get to pitch much in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, but was still considered to be one of the best arms in the class. He was taken No. 6 overall by the Mariners, the third straight college right-hander taken in the first round by the organization, signing for $5.7 million, then worked sparingly at the M’s alternate training site over the summer. Hancock has the chance to have four at least above-average pitches when all is said and done. It starts with his fastball, thrown 94-99 mph. It’s actually fastballs, plural, now because in addition to the hard riding and running heater up in the zone, he’s worked to add a hard running, sinking two-seamer, thrown with the same velocity. All three of his secondary offerings can be plus at times, with his mid-80s slider serving as an out pitch ahead of his power curve he used more as a prep standout. His changeup features excellent fade and he commands it well, giving him a third plus pitch right now. He’s a good athlete who can throw all of his pitches for strikes. Some minor tenderness over the summer made the Mariners err on the side of caution during Summer Camp, but if he stays healthy, he has the chance to pitch near the top of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tucker's ascension to Pittsburgh hasn't exactly gone on a straight path. Taken out of the Arizona high school ranks in 2014, a torn labrum cut short his first full season, and a broken thumb kept him from heading to the Arizona Fall League in '17. He struggled for the first half of the '18 season, but things clicked in the second half and he was one of the best players in the AFL, earning a spot on the 40-man roster in the process. Aside from staying healthy, it's always been a matter of Tucker learning to control his 6-foot-3 frame consistently, especially offensively. During his struggles at the start of the 2018 season, his lower half would get off-balance in the box, his stride would get too big and he'd lose connection with his lower half. Late in the year and in the AFL, he was feeling his base better, driving the ball more consistently with extra-base authority. His plus speed plays up on the basepaths and in the field because of his outstanding instincts. He gets off the ball well, with good reads and more than enough arm for the premium position long term. In addition to his physical gifts, Tucker gets high marks for his leadership and work ethic, and he was given the AFL's Stenson Sportsmanship Award as a result. His arrow is pointing up and he should be the Pirates' shortstop for a long time to come once he's ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It might have surprised some when the Pirates took Tucker in the first round of the 2014 Draft out of the Arizona high school ranks, but the Pirates felt they had added a very projectable middle infielder to their system. They were confident he would maximize his potential because of his plus makeup, even if it took a while. Despite a torn labrum suffered during his first full season in 2015, and a broken thumb that kept him from going to the Arizona Fall League at the end of 2017, it's hard to argue Tucker isn't way ahead of the curve after reaching Double-A shortly following his 21st birthday. Cole's offensive game continues to grow as he matures. The switch-hitter is more natural from the left side, but his overall approach has improved and his walk rate has gone up. He makes a lot of contact and there should be more power to come as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. Tucker led the Florida State League in stolen bases even though he was promoted after 68 games and topped the organization in steals with 47 in 2017. That speed helps him defensively as well, and he should stay at short long-term, with an arm that has bounced back to a tick above average since that shoulder surgery. The Pirates have some depth at shortstop at the upper levels with Tucker and Kevin Newman. Watching that competition unfold should be a lot of fun as both come close to knocking on the door.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates took Tucker in the first round of the 2014 Draft -- a bit of a surprise to some -- they knew it might require some patience to watch this extremely projectable shortstop develop. Shoulder surgery to repair a torn labrum during his first full season certainly slowed him, but did nothing to dampen the organization's enthusiasm about who Tucker can become. The further Tucker gets removed from the surgery, the better his arm is at shortstop. He's completely pain-free, though his throws don't quite have the carry yet that they did before the injury. His range and hands all still work extremely well at shortstop. His speed works on both sides of the ball, and he's starting to master the art of stealing a base. Tucker continues to make progress as a switch-hitter, getting more natural left-handed than right-handed because of all the reps he's taken. He's hit over power, but the strength in the bat is coming as he fills out. He's more upright in his stance and learning to leverage the ball more. Increased recognition of off-speed stuff and improved plate discipline will only enhance his offensive profile. Still a bit of a baby giraffe, Tucker has started to grow into his man strength and become a solid all-around shortstop. His makeup and personality are what they feel separate him and will allow him to reach his still enormous potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With his power potential and flashy style of play, Ornelas drew comparisons to Javier Báez as an Arizona high schooler before going in the third round of the 2018 Draft. He sandwiched two so-so years in full-season ball around the pandemic shutdown, then led the Double-A Texas League in hits (157) and ranked eighth in batting (.299) in 2022. The Rangers named him their Minor League Defender of the Year and added him to their 40-man roster. A right-handed hitter, Ornelas improved at the plate last year when he did a better job of using the entire field and made more regular contact. Most of his damage comes against fastballs and left-handers because he's still trying to figure out how to solve breaking pitches.
