A switch-hitting catcher, Rodriguez has shown a solid feel to hit and an idea of what he’s doing from both sides of the plate since he signed. Not only did that continue in Low-A in 2021, the power started to show up more consistently without sacrificing any of his plate discipline or approach, especially as the year went on, with an OPS of .970 from July 1 through the end of the season. His willingness to draw walks (11.1 percent) and knack for contact (17.7 percent K rate) should help him maximize his offensive tools. Rodriguez was equally impressive behind the plate, where his athleticism and agility play well and he’s shown excellent catch and throw skills. His maturity and presence might stand out even more than his tools, so while he’s athletic enough to play the outfield and first base, committing to him as a backstop might maximize his value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez joined the Mets organization for just $10,000 at the start of the 2018-19 international signing period and he immediately set out to outperform the moderate expectations that come with a bonus of that size, making a nice transition from the Dominican Summer League to the Gulf Coast League in 2019. He showed off his athleticism with the Mets during instructional league play in 2020, then headed to the Pirates in the three-team deal that sent Joe Musgrove to the Padres and Joey Lucchesi to the Mets, giving the Pirates their first catcher in the top 30 since 2017. The switch-hitting Rodriguez has already showed off an advanced approach at the plate, with impressive contact skills and the ability to use all fields. There’s more extra-base pop from the left side right now, with good raw power that should show up as he matures physically. He’s hit-over-power right now, but there could be a lot more juice to come in the future. Super-athletic, Rodriguez has played first base and the outfield in addition to catching in games. He's also gotten reps elsewhere, but his value is obviously higher if he can stick behind the plate. He’s very agile back there with a strong enough arm that will get better as he focuses on the craft more. He has a long way to go, but the ingredients for an everyday catcher might be in there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Mets have given out seven-figure bonuses to five different players across the past three international periods, they also have found some serious value in cheaper, under-the-radar signings. Rodriguez, who signed for $10,000 -- an amount that does not count against a team’s international bonus pool -- in July 2018, falls into the latter group. A switch-hitter who has shown an ability to play multiple positions including catcher early in his career, the Dominican native made a smooth transition from the Dominican Summer League to the Rookie Gulf Coast League in 2019, albeit while missing time with a hamstring injury. He participated in instructional league play this past fall before being dealt to the Pirates as part of the three-team deal that sent Joe Musgrove to the Padres and Joey Lucchesi to the Mets in January. Combining an advanced approach and natural bat-to-ball skills, Rodriguez makes a lot of contact and sprays hits to all fields from both sides of the plate. He drives the ball better as a left-handed hitter, showing flashes of raw power that should begin to translate into more usable power as he gets stronger. While a penchant for contact points to more of a hit-over-power future profile, there are some evaluators who think Rodriguez will surprise with his power output. Rodriguez’s bat will become even more valuable if he can remain behind the plate. He’s an athletic and agile defender who moves well behind the plate, with solid catch-and-throw skills that should continue to improve. He runs well enough to play an outfield corner and also has seen time at first base early in his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Priester was one of the best high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, one who played multiple sports at his Illinois school, but the Pirates liked his upside and feel for pitching enough to take him in the first round of the 2019 Draft. After a brief summer debut, he had to wait until 2021 to really get going and he led his league in ERA and went to the Futures Game in that first full season. He was slowed in 2022 by an oblique injury and didn’t make his debut until June, but he still managed to pitch his way to Triple-A and then made up for lost innings in the Arizona Fall League. While the projectable Priester hasn’t quite taken the big steps forward stuff-wise some might have expected, he’s shown that his legitimate four-pitch mix can get hitters out in a number of ways. The right-hander, who will be just 22 for nearly all of the 2023 season, has plenty of time for more velocity to come. His fastball touched 97 mph in 2022 and averaged just over 93. His two-seamer features plenty of sink and has led to a ton of ground-ball outs and he also has a four-seamer he can throw up in the zone to change eye levels. His curve is still his best pitch, a high-spin upper-70s breaker that misses a ton of bats, and he also has a low-to-mid 80s slider as he continues to fold in a mid-80s changeup. Priester is super-athletic on the mound and at times has shown he can be a very efficient strike-thrower, something that will only improve with more reps at the upper levels. Even with his missed development time, he’s knocking on the big league door at a very young age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Typically when a high school pitcher -- especially one from a cold-weather state who played multiple sports -- is taken in the first round of the Draft, there’s a healthy dose of patience that comes along with watching his development. That should certainly have been the case with Priester, the 2019 first-rounder from the Illinois prep ranks, given that there was no competitive 2020 season. But word of his advancement at the Pirates’ alternate site in 2020, coupled with dominant stuff in instructional league play that fall, created a ton of buzz. His first full season was a little up-and-down, but he still led the High-A East in ERA and went to the Futures Game. He was slowed by an oblique issue at the end of Spring Training in 2022, keeping him from making his Double-A debut for more than a month. The Pirates actually feel Priester’s 2021 couldn’t have gone better, scuffles and all, when considering his age (20 for all of the ’21 season) and the fact he’d never come close to the 97 2/3 innings he threw for Greensboro. While his stuff might have backed up a bit, he still showed a very strong four-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that sat mid-90s for most of the year. He can sink it, leading to a lot of ground-ball outs, and throw his four-seamer up in the zone. He has two distinct breaking balls: a plus curve with high spin rates and a newer slider that should be at least average. He’s continuing to work on mixing in his changeup consistently. Priester’s athleticism on the mound points to a future of strike-throwing. The Pirates feel the young right-hander learned valuable lessons about handling fatigue, sticking with his routine and getting outs without his best stuff. All of that still points to him having the chance to be a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the Pirates took Priester in the first round of the 2019 Draft, No. 18 overall, the last time an Illinois high school player had been taken in the first round was when Mike Foltynewicz was the No. 19 overall pick in the 2010 Draft, taken by the Astros. A two-sport star as a prepster, Priester’s athleticism was not only on display during his pro debut in 2019 but also during his time at the end of the alternate training site and in instructional league play in 2020. It’s clear Priester used his first offseason to add strength and the stuff he displayed in 2020 had taken a step forward. Over the summer and fall, he was up to 98 mph, averaging a touch over 97 mph, a four-seamer thrown with a spin rate north of 2,200 rpm in a matchup against Phillies 2020 first-rounder Mick Abel at instructs. He also features a sinking two-seamer that gets ground ball outs. He worked on distinguishing between two breaking balls, a plus low-80s curveball with 2900 rpm spin rate metrics and a slider that could eventually be at least above-average. He has growing feel for his changeup as well. Big, broad and athletic, it’s easy to dream on Priester’s physicality and stuff. The work he did in 2020 on how and when to use all of his pitches and in sharpening all his offerings has as big of an up arrow next to his name as any pitching prospect in baseball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For many years, the Pirates earned a deserved reputation as an organization that didn’t shy away from the high risk, high reward world of drafting high school pitching. They rarely went that route in the first round, however, taking only two -- Jameson Taillon and Shane Baz – since 2010. They added one more in 2019 when they took Priester, a two-sport standout from the Illinois high school ranks, and signed him for $3.4 million. While his pro debut was relatively brief, he showed off his athleticism, stuff and feel for pitching in the Gulf Coast League and earned a bump up to make a start in the New York-Penn League. Priester, who won a state championship in football, showed plenty of stuff during his pro debut. His fastball averaged 93 mph and he’s shown the ability to crank his four-seamer up to 97 mph with riding life and he used his low-90s two-seamer to get a ton of ground-ball outs. He can really spin his 80-mph curveball with good depth, projecting as an out pitch that misses a lot of bats. He hasn’t had to throw his changeup that much, but he did show feel for one in the mid-80s as he continues to work on separating it from his fastball. The Pirates loved the presence and maturity Priester already shows on the mound. His ability to command his stuff and understanding of how to set up hitters belies his age and the fact he comes from a cold-weather state. Combine that with his athleticism and projectability, it’s easy to dream on a future frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Yavapai, a junior college in Arizona, Encarnacion-Strand moved on to Oklahoma State and put up big numbers there, hitting 15 homers and posting an OPS north of 1.100. The Twins thought they had a fourth-round steal on their hands as he posted a 1.022 OPS during his brief pro debut after being drafted in 2021, then hit his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season (.987 OPS). They weren’t the only ones paying attention; the Reds liked his bat enough to make sure he was included in the return for Tyler Mahle at last year’s Trade Deadline, then watched their new acquisition continue to rake after the trade. The Reds knew they were getting someone with very impressive raw power who was already tapping into it, with Encarnacion-Strand finishing his 2022 breakout with 32 homers, a .587 slugging percentage and 114 RBIs to boot. What impressed them even more was a better feel to hit than many expected when he entered pro ball. Sure, he swings and misses some, with a K rate of 25.5 percent in 2022 and he can cut down on his chasing of soft stuff out of the zone, but there’s an advanced approach here. He uses all fields and can hit the ball out everywhere, showing a willingness to go the other way with two strikes. Encarnacion-Strand has more than enough arm strength to stick at third, and he’ll keep getting plenty of reps there, but the strong and physical infielder can be too stiff there at times. He’ll keep getting time at first, mostly to give the Reds options of ways to get him into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: All Encarnacion-Strand did as an amateur was hit, spanning two seasons at Yavapai (Ariz.) College in the JUCO circuit and one year at Oklahoma State, where he was Big 12 Conference newcomer of the year after hitting .361/.442/.661 with 15 homers. He didn't slow down after the Twins selected him in the fourth round in 2021, hitting .391/.424/.598 in A-ball across 22 games in the notoriously pitcher-friendly Low-A Southeast. The bat kept coming during his first full season, and he had hit his way from High-A to Double-A shortly before being sent to the Reds as part of the return in the Tyler Mahle Trade Deadline deal. Encarnacion-Strand can chase outside the zone a little too much, perhaps borne of seeking contact and hits instead of waiting for his pitch, but he's got solid bat-to-ball skills and the ability to drive the ball hard to all fields. The results have obviously spoken for themselves throughout his amateur career and early pro career and he’s made some strides with his plate discipline and selectivity, with some mechanical adjustments with his stride also in play to help his consistency. Though he mostly played first base in his first professional season, the 22-year-old also opened eyes with his defense at the hot corner, where he moves well with his big frame and features strong instincts and angles to the ball and good hands. If he can address the plate discipline, his bat could carry him up the system, with the ability to contribute from either corner infield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2017-18 international signing period, the Phillies handed out 19 bonuses of six figures or more, topped by the $2.5 million they gave Luis Garcia. They found a bargain later on in the period, in January of 2018, when they inked Rojas for just $10K. In each of his two years of full season ball, he’s started slowly but finished well offensively, showing off his plus speed and defense at all stops. He made it to Double-A for the first time in 2022 and then finished with a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League before getting added to the 40-man roster. Rojas has shown he can be an impact player on both sides of the ball thanks to his near-top-of-the-scale speed. He’s an elite baserunner, one who stole 62 bases in 67 tries last season and then went 13-for-13 in the AFL. His speed is an obvious asset in the outfield, where he is a premium defender in center field, one who could be a Gold Glove contender because of his range, instincts and above-average arm. The young outfielder’s ceiling is tied to what advancements he can make at the plate. The right-handed hitter is very adept at making contact, striking out in just 16.6 percent of his plate appearances entering 2023. He’s too often been content to hit the ball on the ground and use his legs to get on base, though he did get the ball in the air a bit more in 2022. The Phillies would love to see him make more hard contact, with line drives to the gaps turning into doubles and triples, to give him a real chance to be a table-setter atop a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the international signing periods typically opened in July before the pandemic, Rojas didn’t sign with the Phillies until January of 2018 and did so for just $10,000. He immediately showed he might be the biggest bargain of that 2017-18 class by putting up a .321/.421/.797 line in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and hit his way across two levels of rookie ball during his United States debut the following year. He had a solid, if unspectacular, full-season debut in 2021 until he absolutely raked after getting moved up to High-A for the final month of the season. Since signing, Rojas has shown an innate ability to make contact, and he struck out in just under 18 percent of his plate appearances in 2021. That standout skill has also been an obstacle, as he’s been too over-aggressive from the right side of the plate. He’s been working on his approach and swing decisions to keep him from not expanding the zone too much, all while learning to get the ball off the ground more. He’s made strides in getting better counts and not being content to beat the ball into the ground. Using his elite-level speed has allowed him to start tapping into his considerable raw power. That speed makes Rojas a very impressive center fielder, with plus range and instincts to go along with a strong arm, with no doubt he can stay up the middle long-term. Rojas could have been even further ahead had he not missed a year of reps because of the pandemic, but he’s the player who often gets asked about when teams call to talk trades.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017-18 international signing period has the chance to be a successful one for the Phillies at both ends of the spending spectrum. At the top end, there’s Luis Garcia and his $2.5-million bonus. At the bottom end, there’s lefty Jordi Martinez, now a Top 30 prospect, and Rojas, who jumped on the map by hitting .320 in the Dominican Summer League in 2018, then hit his way from the Gulf Coast League to the New York-Penn League during his United States debut in 2019. He was one of the top standouts during instructional league play in 2020. Rojas has already impressed with his ability to make consistent hard contact from the right side of the plate, displaying plus bat-to-ball skills along with one of the highest exit velocities in the system. Because of his knack for contact, he’s been very aggressive at the plate. While he doesn’t strike out much, he doesn’t draw walks and is still working on his overall approach so he can get to better hitters' counts and utilize his raw power more effectively. With a strong arm that works well for a corner, Rojas’ plus speed and instincts give him a very good chance to stick in center, showing the ability to play shallow and go deep with ease. He’ll keep getting time at all three outfield spots, with one of the highest ceilings in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies were extremely active on the international market during the 2017-18 signing period, kicking things off on July 2 by signing Luis Garcia for $2.5 million. Rojas signed sixth months later, and for just $10,000, but he’s been very impressive in the early stages of his pro career. After hitting .320 during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, he opened more eyes with a .920 OPS in 18 games in the Gulf Coast League to earn a quick promotion to the short-season New York-Penn League during his United States debut. Rojas makes a ton of hard contact from the right side of the plate, barreling up the baseball very well and has the chance to be a solid hitter with good power. In order to tap into his raw power more, he will have to learn to be more selective at the plate. He doesn’t strike out much, but he swings early and often and will have to learn to lay off breaking and offspeed stuff as he advances. With plus speed, Rojas can steal a base and uses his speed to his advantage in the outfield as well. He’s played more center field than anywhere else to date and has the range and the instincts to stay there, though he’s also shown the ability to play both corners and has plenty of arm strength for right. As exciting as his tools are, the Phillies might love his makeup even more, giving him points for his energy and passion for the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year as a senior at Gonzaga, Jacob dropped to the 16th round because scouts were concerned his low-velocity funk wouldn’t translate to the Minors. Two years after his Draft day, he made his Major League debut on July 15, 2023, and struck out Alec Bohm as his only batter faced. In between, the right-hander transitioned to a relief-only role, climbed three levels in 2022 and posted a 1.32 ERA with 32 strikeouts in 27 1/3 innings for Double-A San Antonio in '23. A minor flexor strain and UCL sprain in his right elbow limited him to only three Major League appearances last summer, but he is back healthy for this season. Throwing out of a low sidearm slot, Jacob is all about running pitches east and west with what can look like Bugs Bunny stuff. His mid-80s sinker won’t light up any radar guns, but it slices enough armside to make right-handers at least a little uncomfortable and drops enough to generate plenty of ground balls. His low-70s sweeper breaks just as hard going the other way, forcing some awkward diving swings from righties, and was his most-used pitch during his limited MLB run. A changeup also fades armside but somehow has the 11-12 mph separation to make it a potential plus pitch too. Despite all the movement, Jacob hasn’t posted a walk rate above 7.5 percent at any Minor League level because he locates to both sides of the plate so well. Entering his age-26 season, Jacob won’t be a back-end Major League option necessarily, but he’s definitely capable of getting outs as a reliever in The Show so long as his command holds.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There are funky pitchers, and then there is Jacob. A four-year hurler and 2021 West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year at Gonzaga, Jacob fell to the 16th round in 2021 because of concerns over his lack of velocity, and he joined the Padres system with a $75,000 signing bonus. Despite those issues, he was one of the quickest risers of his Draft class, climbing from High-A to Triple-A in his first full season and ending it with an assignment to the Arizona Fall League. The bulk of Jacob’s work came at Double-A San Antonio, where he finished with a 1.83 ERA, 1.08 WHIP and 43 K’s in 34 1/3 innings as a reliever. About that lack of velo: Jacob’s fastball only sits in the upper-80s -- atypical for the modern game where bullpen arms throw harder than ever. A difficult sidearm angle, heavy sink and arm-side run make the fastball difficult to barrel, however, and it’s a better pitch than the radar gun alone will tell you. His best offering, however, is a low-70s, Bugs Bunny-esque changeup that stands out for its separation from the sinker and its own fade going down and to Jacob’s right. A slider around the same velocity dives the other way toward his glove side, and the opposite movement can have batters tied up in knots. Though Jacob is capable of filling up the strike zone, the Padres have kept him in relief roles, thus limiting how many times batters can sit on his softer stuff. Right shoulder soreness in the offseason had him delayed to start the season before he earned a Major League debut in July. A minor flexor strain and UCL sprain in his right elbow placed him on the IL soon after, but there's no denying the goofy stuff could still be useful in relief in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big league pitcher Steve Soderstrom, Tyler was one of the best high school bats in the 2020 Draft class, coming out of Steve’s alma mater, Turlock High School. The A’s went over-slot to sign him for $3.3 million at No. 26 overall and despite missing a large part of his first full season, he immediately showed off his offensive upside in 2021, then started in High-A and ended in Triple-A in 2022, mashing 29 homers and driving in 105 runs in the process. A left-handed hitter, Soderstrom has long displayed an excellent feel for the barrel and solid overall approach at the plate. He can make consistent hard contact to all fields, and his combination of strength and bat speed point to the kind of power and run production consistent with his 2022 output, with the ability to hit the ball out to all fields. His strikeout rate did tick up last year, but he spent the first month of the season playing through a thumb injury and the A’s are confident that his feel for hitting will allow him to be more consistent contact-wise as he faces better pitching more consistently. Where Soderstrom plays defensively long-term is more of a question. He has solid arm strength, and while his glove is still behind his bat, the A’s have been pleased with his progress behind the plate. He split time between first base and catcher in 2022 and that should be the case moving forward, giving the organization options to get his bat into the lineup if his blocking and receiving aren’t big league ready, not to mention the presence of Shea Langeliers ahead of him on the depth chart.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Steve Soderstrom came out of Turlock High School in Northern California, went to Fresno State and was the No. 6 overall pick by the Giants in 1993, pitching in the big leagues for them in 1996. His son Tyler went to the same high school, but instead of heading to college, in this case UCLA, he signed with the A’s for an over-slot bonus of $3.3 million as the No. 26 pick in 2020. While an oblique injury limited him to just 57 games and kept him from playing in the Arizona Fall League, he showed off his offensive tools by posting a .957 OPS and went to the Futures Game. While playing as a teenager in the Low-A West, Soderstrom showed off why he was considered one of the more advanced high school hitters in the 2020 Draft class. The left-handed hitter works counts and draws walks (10.6 percent walk rate in 2021), allowing him to drive the ball hard to all fields. There’s plenty of strength and bat speed, to the point where Soderstrom could have plus game power when all is said and done. Soderstrom entered pro ball without a ton of catching experience and that part of his game is still behind the bat, leading some to wonder if it would be better to move him to first, a position he saw some time at in 2021 and played a lot more in 2022, to let his bat advance more quickly. There’s still work to be done, but he had made some progress with his blocking and receiving, as well as using his above-average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Steve Soderstrom, a former big league pitcher who was the sixth-overall pick in the 1993 Draft by the Giants out of Fresno State, Tyler carved out his own path as one of the top high school catchers in California. Concerns from teams over whether he would sign out of high school or continue his amateur career at UCLA led to him dropping to No. 26 to the A’s, who went nearly $650,000 above pick value to sign him for $3.3 million in 2020. Soderstrom’s offense is ahead of his defense at this point. The left-handed hitting catcher has an offensive game that is quite mature for a 19-year-old, with supreme strike zone recognition and plenty of pop in his bat. Though there was talk of a potential move to third base or outfield in the future, the A’s saw a solid improvement behind the plate both at the club’s alternate site and in the instructional league and expect him to stick at catcher. How Soderstrom progresses with his blocking and game management -- two areas he is still raw in -- will determine his long-term position. He has already shown off a strong arm, which helps his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2021 college season, Gelof looked like one of the more intriguing college bats in the Draft class, one who could land in the first round. He got off to a very slow start, hurting his stock, though he righted the ship as the season wore on and he landed in the second round with the A’s. He had a huge pro debut and got off to a very good start in Double-A in his first full season before a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder derailed his train. He did return and made up for lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. When he’s locked in, Gelof provides an exciting combination of approach and raw power from the right side of the plate to any lineup. His swing is a bit unorthodox, but he understands it well and he shows good knowledge of the strike zone. His strikeout rate was a bit high in 2022 (27.5 percent), but it was offset by a healthy walk rate (11.4 percent). The latter helped him get to his power more consistently, even late in the year when he was out of sync overall post-injury. While his speed is just a bit above average, he’s a good baserunner and his overall athleticism is an asset on the field. A third baseman out of college, he shifted over and played a lot of second late in the year and exclusively in the AFL, where he showed solid overall defensive skills. That should be his spot most of the time going forward, though he could see some time in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a strong finish to an uneven junior season at the University of Virginia, Gelof entered the 2021 Draft considered to have some of the best raw power of any hitter in the class, leading to his signing with the A’s for $1,157,400 as a second-round pick. That power bat immediately showed up in pro ball, as he homered seven times in 36 games and was rewarded with a call-up to Triple-A in the final week of the Minor League season. Along with power that is expected to show up even more as he progresses through the system, Gelof brings an advanced approach at the plate with strong strike zone recognition and a good understanding of his swing. While he’s not a burner, he runs well enough and has excellent instincts, making him a legitimate threat on the basepaths. Gelof’s supreme athleticism could lend to him playing multiple infield positions, though the A’s were impressed with his defense at third base, particularly his throwing arm, which had been a question mark entering the Draft due to some injuries. Also earning high praise for his confidence and presence in the clubhouse, Gelof has the makings of a player who could soon find himself on the fast track to Oakland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a journey since Uribe signed for only $85,000 as an 18-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018. His stock began to soar at Single-A Carolina in 2021, when he used his elite velo to fan 52 in 33 2/3 relief innings, but that campaign was limited by a torn meniscus. Following a trip to the Arizona Fall League, he was about to pop again at Double-A Biloxi in 2022, only to suffer another torn meniscus in his left knee in April that required season-ending surgery. A second (and even more productive) trip to the AFL pushed him onto the 40-man roster last November, and he worked in three more appearances in the Dominican Winter League. The 6-foot-2 right-hander is a prospect first and foremost because of his fastball. It was back to sitting 98-99 mph during his Arizona Fall League stint, and he had eight of the 11 hardest pitches thrown in the showcase circuit (in games measured by Statcast) -- all at 100-plus mph. He has been known to touch 103 in the past too, when healthy. Uribe has plenty of confidence in his upper-80s slider with two-plane break and will sometimes lean on it more than the heater because he can land it better in the zone. Therein lies the rub. Like many elite fireballers, Uribe has a mixed history when it comes to throwing strikes. However, he walked only two batters (while fanning 14) in 10 innings during his AFL return, giving hope that he may have turned a corner in that department. His high-tempo delivery may keep him from ever being truly average there, but there’s upside as a high-leverage arm on the quality of his stuff alone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Uribe for $85,000 just a month after his 18th birthday in July 2018 and moved him straight to the Dominican Summer League. His first two seasons, which included trips to the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues, brought uninspiring results (28 strikeouts, 21 walks in 18/13 innings; multiple 9-plus ERAs), but the right-hander’s stock began to shoot up as he added strength with the velocity to match. He posted a 4.01 ERA with 52 strikeouts in 33 2/3 frames for Low-A Carolina in 2021, missing some time with a torn meniscus, and he ended the year in the Arizona Fall League, where he fanned 16 in nine innings but also walked 17. Unfortunately, he suffered another torn meniscus in his left knee early in 2022 and underwent season-ending surgery on April 26 to address the issue. It’s the velo that will always pop for the 6-foot-2 righty, when he is healthy. There were outings when Uribe sat 100-101 mph last season, and he threw 13 of the 14 hardest-thrown pitches of the 2021 AFL as measured by Statcast, all above 98.9 mph. His high-80s slider, which some systems call a cutter, can actually be his best pitch some days, too, and he sometimes relies on that over the heater in tough situations because of his ability to land it in the zone. He used to mix in a changeup, but the fastball and slider have become almost co-primary pitches. It’s going to come down to control. Like many young pitchers, Uribe can chase radar-gun readings and overthrow, causing him to miss the zone with regularity. Considering his delivery is pretty smooth without any major red flags, it might just take a change in mentality and approach for Uribe to improve and find even average control. If that (no small task) happens and everything else returns post-surgery, he could be impactful in the back end of a Major League bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Uribe signed out of the Dominican Republic as an 18-year-old in 2018 for $85,000, so he was eligible to finish that year with the club’s Dominican Summer League team, then came stateside in ‘19 and logged limited innings in the Arizona League and the Pioneer League. In 28 1/3 innings as a pro, he had an uninspiring ratio of 28 strikeouts vs. 21 walks, but his stock shot up in 2020 along with his fastball velocity as Uribe added physical strength to his frame. Uribe’s power fastball can sit 100-101 on some days and even more when he really chucks it. At Uribe’s age and lack of pro innings, it is more arm strength than pitching at this point, and he tends to chase radar gun readings rather than focus on commanding his plus stuff. Uribe was one of 30-or-so players at the team’s complex in the Dominican Republic working to refine his tools as Spring Training began, and after turning 21 in June, he has spent all of 2021 at Low-A Carolina trying to make the most of his elite velocity and honing in his control. Uribe’s path to the Majors is definitely through the bullpen at this point. His low-90s slider is ahead of his changeup at this stage, giving him the two decent options necessary to thrive in relief. A torn meniscus has slowed him down in 2021, but pitchers with that type of velo can always be put back on the fast track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canzone never batted below .323 in any of his three seasons at Ohio State, and he went out with a bang as a junior in 2019 with a program-record 59-game on-base streak. Scouts were still not sold his swing would hold up in the pros, and the D-backs snagged him in the eighth round. The left-handed slugger was a productive High-A and Double-A hitter in his first full season in 2021 and got some time in the Arizona Fall League to boot. He spent the majority of his age-24 campaign with Triple-A Reno, slashing .284/.349/.489 with 16 homers in 88 games, but went unprotected and unpicked in last year’s Rule 5 Draft when eligible. He raked again in Reno in 2023 with an OPS north of 1.000, which led to his first big league callup in July. He was with the D-backs when he was sent along with Ryan Bliss to the Mariners in the Paul Sewald trade. Canzone lifts his leg kick and almost pauses his load before planting as the pitch is delivered, and while he ranked in the bottom third in the Pacific Coast League for swinging-strike rate, he still strikes out less than many in the modern game because he knows how to control the barrel. He has wiry strength at 6-foot-1, 190 pounds, and his 112.6 mph max exit velocity would have put him right alongside Christian Walker’s best mark for the big league club. The former Buckeye shows a penchant for nabbing the occasional bag with back-to-back seasons with 15-plus steals, but his below-average speed limits his defensive value. He’s ticketed for an outfield corner spot and has mixed in more first base into his glove work as Arizona tried to find a spot for his bat in the lineup. He played right field some and DHed more during his time up with the D-backs, but now it will be up to the Mariners to find a spot for his bat in their lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campbell finally found his footing after transitioning to a relief role last June, posting a 1.61 ERA and holding hitters to a .204/.226/.320 slash line over 29 outings. Given his huge workloads in college and the season-ending elbow surgery he underwent in 2021, the 2019 Competitive Balance Round B pick might’ve unearthed his calling card, especially as all his stuff ticked up. The objective for Campbell was to keep his stuff peaking in shorter stints. His fastball has stood out in relief, with velocity sitting around 95-96 mph. His ability to land his slider, which has always been there, really took off; it’s functional and above-average, and he can land it for strikes when he wants to expand the zone later, rather than just use it as an out pitch. All of it has changed the trajectory of his career. The former University of Arkansas standout may have many miles on his arm, and he’s also entering his age-25 season, but Seattle added him to the 40-man roster in November to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, underscoring how much they value the chance of him contributing in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campbell suffered elbow soreness and bone chips at Arkansas that prompted him to come back for his junior season. That wound up being a smart decision as the righty went 12-1 with a 2.13 ERA, enough to become the No. 76 overall pick. But given his 118 1/3 innings that year, the Mariners immediately shut him down, and following the cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season, the club has yet to see him pitch in pro ball. Campbell creates excellent downhill plane with his 6-foot-4 frame and high three-quarters arm slot, allowing his 91- to 95-mph fastball, which occasionally touches as high as 98 mph, to play up. He has two distinct breaking balls. There's a low-80s slider that often becomes more of a mid-80s cutter and is currently better than his curve. His splitter is a relatively new pitch, but it improved in 2019 as his willingness to pitch up in the zone with his fastball enabled it to be even more effective. With a clean and repeatable delivery, Campbell showed he can be an outstanding strike-thrower. The Mariners sent him to Class A Short Season in 2019, but they didn’t have him pitch after a long college season, much like they did with Logan Gilbert in ’18, and then Campbell was cut off from a Minor League season in ’20. His combination of stuff and command could mean the righty moves almost as quickly as Gilbert, who will debut in ‘21. But the fact that the Mariners haven’t seen Campbell pitch professionally yet creates some uncertainty about where he might fit long term, whether it be as a back-end starter or as an important bullpen piece. He might be the biggest mystery in the farm system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campbell missed almost all of his sophomore season at Arkansas because of elbow soreness and bone chips, leading him to take a redshirt year. He threw decently enough as a redshirt sophomore to be a Draft prospect in 2018, but he didn’t go until the 24th round, so he opted to come back for his junior season. It turned out to be a smart decision as the right-hander pitched very well for the Razorbacks in 2019, leading to him being the No. 76 overall pick. Campbell creates excellent downhill plane with his 6-foot-4 frame and high three-quarters arm slot, allowing his 91-95 mph fastball, which occasionally touches as high as 98 mph, to play up. He has two distinct breaking balls, with his low-80s slider that often becomes more of a mid-80s cutter, better than his curve currently. His splitter is a relatively new pitch, but it improved in 2019 as his willingness to pitch up in the zone with his fastball allowed it to be even more effective. With a clean and repeatable delivery, Campbell showed he can be an outstanding strike-thrower. The Mariners sent him to short-season Everett last summer, but didn’t have him pitch after a long college season, much like they did with Logan Gilbert a year prior. His combination of stuff and command could mean Campbell moves almost as quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed Martinez, a former outfielder, for $50,000 in March 2018 out of the belief they could turn his arm strength and athleticism into something on the mound. Martinez opened his pro career as a starter but switched to relief for good after undergoing Tommy John surgery after seven Single-A starts in 2021. After returning the following year and reaching Triple-A, Martinez went to back to Reno for 2023, posting a 4.29 ERA with 67 strikeouts and 48 walks in 49 1/3 innings. He debuted for the big club in July and made 10 walk-filled appearances over three separate MLB stints. There are few humans on the planet who throw harder than Martinez. His 99.9 mph average fastball velocity in Triple-A was highest among hurlers who threw at least 100 pitches at the level in 2023, and he had the 40 fastest pitches thrown by the D-backs during his Major League time, topping out at 102.7 mph. But the heater had very little ride, keeping it from being a true 80-grade pitch, and his command of the fireball was all over the place. If anything, it might be best setting up his upper-80s slider and splitter to righties and lefties, respectively, that each posted whiff rates above 50 percent in 2023. Throwing with below-average extension, Martinez would make for a strong back-of-the-bullpen option if he got to even below-average control, but even that is a stretch. His 21.2 percent walk rate was 19th-highest among 1,832 Minor Leaguers with at least 40 innings last season. He’s still entering his age-22 campaign, so there’s a little time to figure it out and land on the positive side of his boom-or-bust potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez was originally an outfielder during his amateur days in the Dominican Republic, but the D-backs took a flier on him as a pitcher with good arm strength. He came up primarily as a hard-throwing starter and moved to Single-A Visalia for his age-19 season in 2021. The right-hander needed Tommy John surgery after only seven starts with the Rawhide and didn’t return to a Minor League mound until July 2022. Now a full-time reliever, Martinez sprinted through the Minors with stops at four affiliates (including a late-season move to Triple-A Reno) and the Arizona Fall League before he was added to the 40-man roster in November. The 6-foot-3 hurler touched triple digits in the Fall League as he continued to regain his strength and was typically around the 96-99 mph range during his time with Salt River. That was roughly in line with his Triple-A performance too, where he averaged 97.4 mph on his heater. He doesn’t always command the four-seamer as well as he should, causing the pitch to lose a little shine. His mid-80s slider (righties) and upper-80s split changeup (lefties) give him workable secondaries against batters from both sides of the plate, but it’s the latter that’s better at generating whiffs with its armside fade. Martinez has rarely posted a Minor League walk rate in the single digits, and his 15.2 percent mark in the AFL was further evidence that he was likely always headed for relief. His velocity certainly works in the role, and it’s no wonder why the D-backs didn’t want to leave him exposed to the Rule 5 Draft. Now with TJ fully behind him, the right-hander could be a part of Arizona’s bullpen mix soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez spent most of his amateur career in the Dominican Republic as an outfielder before moving to the mound late in 2017. The Diamondbacks took a low-risk gamble on his athleticism and arm strength, signing him for $50,000 the following spring, and Martinez rewarded the organization by reaching the mid-90s with his fastball during an otherwise shaky pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. The right-hander’s velocity continued to improve during his age-17 season, helping him climb three levels up to the Rookie Appalachian League. Stronger and even more athletic in 2019, Martinez was sitting in the mid-90s and bumped 98 mph with his explosive fastball. His athleticism shows in his arm action and delivery, but as is the case with so many young, raw hurlers, he’s still learning how to repeat them both consistently. He complements his heater with a power slider that flashes above average with late bite and rounds out his promising three-pitch mix with a firm, work-in-progress changeup. Martinez is very young and therefore will need time to refine his delivery and stuff, but the Diamondbacks think he has the ingredients needed to become an above-average starting pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more advanced players in the 2015 Dominican crop, Fermin signed for $500,000 that July. He made contact but didn't have enough strength to do much damage in his first two years in Rookie ball, then took a positive step forward last summer in the short-season New York-Penn League. He ranked among the NY-P leaders in several categories, including finishing second in walks (39) and lowest strikeout rate (8 percent) and fourth in on-base percentage (.391). One of the things that attracted the Indians to Fermin in the first place was his mature approach, as he uses a simple right-handed swing and mastery of the strike zone to lace line drives to all fields. He won't ever be a huge power threat, but he'll need to continue to get stronger so he can hit the ball with authority against more advanced pitching. He has average speed with keen instincts as a runner and basestealer. Fermin's smarts also help his tools play up on defense. Signed as a shortstop, he spent most of his first two seasons there before seeing more time at second base in 2018 while playing alongside Tyler Freeman. His internal clock helps him play an average shortstop but his arm and quickness fit better at second, where he can be a solid defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Rays out of the Dominican Republic in June 2015, it took six years for Felipe to reach full-season ball as a reliever, and he entered Minor League free agency after posting a 2.59 ERA with 78 strikeouts in 62 2/3 innings at Single-A and High-A in 2021. The Padres signed him in January ’22 and moved him to Double-A for the first time. Felipe finished his first year as a San Diego prospect with a 3.63 ERA and 30.7 percent K rate in 62 frames between San Antonio and Triple-A El Paso, and he was added to the 40-man roster in August, though he’s still awaiting his MLB debut. The 6-foot-5 right-hander is as hard a thrower as they come in the Padres' system with a four-seamer and sinker that both averaged 99 mph in the Pacific Coast League. He registered 71 of the 72 highest velocities measured by El Paso pitchers (per Statcast), topping out at 101.2 mph in late September. While the heat still makes up the plurality of his pitch mix, he throws a mid-80s slider around a third of the time, and it had the highest Triple-A whiff rate because of its great depth. He’ll also sprinkle in an upper-80s changeup that can get firm but has the separation needed to fool the occasional lefty. Felipe has a long, circular arm action that accelerates as he moves toward the plate, and that hurriedness can affect his control. His Minor League walk rates have never dipped below double-digits, and strike-throwing will likely hold him back from being a more prominent bullpen arm. His stuff is electric enough that he’s ready for an MLB look early in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With the noticeable exception of top prospect Jackson Holliday, the Orioles have been very bullish on college hitters over the last few years of the Draft, a run that began with Adley Rutschman in 2019. It continued with Heston Kjerstad in 2020 and extended to Cowser as the No. 5 overall pick in 2021, and like Kjerstad, he was signed at a discount. Cowser hasn’t performed like a bargain, touching Triple-A in his first full season, then dominating back at that level in 2023 (.937 OPS), though he didn’t take advantage of his first chance to prove himself in the big leagues. Despite the small hiccup over 61 Major League at-bats, Cowser still profiles as an everyday presence in a big league lineup. He has a smooth left-handed swing and good overall approach and draws plenty of walks, even during his time in Baltimore. He can drive the ball to all fields and consistently hit the ball hard in 2023. He also cut down his strikeout rate a bit, though he still had some difficulty with spin, with a 45 percent miss rate on breaking stuff while with Norfolk. Cowser runs well and has shown he can play a solid center field with excellent instincts, something he was called upon to do in Baltimore last year. With a strong arm, he might be best suited for a corner spot should he settle in at one position, though his first order of business will be trying to find a way to break through the logjam of talent to land in the big leagues full time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cowser was the top-ranked college hitter in the 2021 Draft class, coming in at No. 10 overall, and the Orioles took him No. 5 overall that summer to make him the second first-round pick in Sam Houston State history. He signed for a below-slot $4.9 million and made a very strong first impression with a .982 OPS in his professional debut. He kept it going in his first full season, making his way from High-A to Double-A, where he absolutely raked to earn one more move up to finish the year in Triple-A. A 6-foot-3 left-handed hitter, Cowser combines an outstanding swing, bat speed and good plate discipline to make him a dangerous all-around hitter. He was known more as a hit-over-power type, but the pop is very real and showed up in his first full season. He understands the strike zone, leading to 94 walks in 2022, but there was also more swing-and-miss to his game than anticipated. He struggled with softer stuff at the upper levels, with a 44 percent miss rate on breaking stuff, though that didn’t keep him from driving the ball to all fields. While he’s not a burner, Cowser uses his tick-above-average speed well on both sides of the ball. He’s shown he can play solid center field with good instincts, but long term he might be better suited in a corner, where he could be a very good defender with an above-average arm. He jumped on the fast track and impacted Baltimore’s lineup for the first time in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sam Houston State has produced two first-round picks in school history. The first was Glenn Wilson, the No. 18 pick back in 1980 who spent parts of 10 years in the big leagues. Cowser became the second when the Orioles took a college outfielder high in the Draft and went under slot to do so for the second straight year. Cowser signed for $4.9 million as the No. 5 overall pick and then posted a .375/.490/.492 in his pro debut, mostly in full-season ball, to provide a very strong early return on that investment, following it up by hitting his way to Double-A in his first full season. A big and strong left-handed hitter, Cowser has a tremendous feel to hit and an advanced approach at the plate that allowed him to walk more than he struck out not only in his college career, but in his pro debut as well. He can send line drives to all fields and while he was known as a hit-over-power type of performer, the Orioles see some serious power coming from the 6-foot-3 outfielder. Cowser runs pretty well, especially for his size, but might eventually settle into being an average runner in the future. He has enough instincts to play a decent center field, but he’s likely to move to a corner if a better center fielder, someone like Cedric Mullins in Baltimore, is on the team, and he could be a plus defender there should a permanent move take place. With his feel, maturity and advanced approach, it might not take long for O’s fans to find out where he’ll fit into the big league outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians signed not one but two players with strong right arms named Mejia out of the Dominican Republic in 2013. Francisco Mejia blossomed into one of the best catching prospects in baseball after signing for $350,000 and was traded to the Padres for Brad Hand and Adam Cimber last July, while Jean Carlos (no relation) spent his first three years as a pro in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League after signing for $45,000. The latter finally made his full-season debut in 2018, impressing enough in low Class A to earn a spot on Cleveland's 40-man roster. Though the Indians didn't make Mejia a full-time starter until last season, he definitely has the attributes to stay in the rotation. His heavy sinker is a plus pitch that sits at 91-94 mph, touches 96 and helped him log a 1.5 groundout/airout ratio in 2018. His curveball and slider have similar potential, and he also has feel for using his changeup. Mejia is doing a better job of repeating his delivery now that he has grown into his extra-large frame, showing aptitude for commanding his breaking pitches as well as his fastball. He'll still have to prove he can handle a starter's workload after missing time last year with elbow soreness. If he can hold up, he eventually could fit in the middle of Cleveland's rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palencia was relatively ancient at age 20 when he became the final player the Athletics signed in their 2019-20 international class, turning pro for a mere $10,000 out of Venezuela. The pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021, when he made six Single-A starts before Oakland traded him for Andrew Chafin. That deal now looks like a steal for the Cubs, who expedited him to the big leagues this summer by moving him to the bullpen. Though he stands just 5-foot-11, Palencia is much stronger than his listed 160 pounds and has an exceptionally quick arm that produces fastballs that park at 96-98 mph, top out at 102 and blow by hitters up in the zone. He relies heavily on his fastball and a tight upper-80s slider, though his mid-80s knuckle-curve is nearly as effective as his slide piece and a wipeout pitch at its best. Palencia's delivery includes a long arm action and some effort, and he averaged 4.6 walks per nine innings in his first two pro seasons. His control regressed during his first stint in the Majors, though he still has closer upside if he can harness his overwhelming stuff. If he returns to starting, he'll need to refine an upper-80s changeup that has some fade and throw a lot more strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last player the Athletics signed in their 2019-20 international class, Palencia turned pro out of Venezuela for a mere $10,000 at the relatively ancient age of 20. The pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until 2021, when Oakland traded him and Greg Deichmann to the Cubs for Andrew Chafin in July. He finished the season by allowing two runs and improving his strike-throwing in his final three Low-A starts. The 5-foot-11 Palencia is a short guy with a strong frame and a big arm, sitting at 96-98 mph and reaching triple digits with a four-seam fastball that rides through the zone. He showed better feel for spin than Chicago initially expected, unleashing some mid-80s knuckle-curves that were wipeout breaking balls at their best. He's in the nascent stages of developing an upper-80s changeup with some fade. Palencia has a chance to remain a starter but also a lot to prove. His delivery features effort and a long arm action and he goes through stretches where the strike zone eludes him. If he does end up in the bullpen, his fastball/curveball combo could make him a late-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing both ways at Rice, Myers concentrated on pitching after the Tigers drafted him in 2017's sixth round. Despite a fastball that touched 95 mph and a promising breaking ball, he couldn't solve High-A hitters in 2019 and became a full-time position player after returning from the pandemic in 2021. The Marlins grabbed him in the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December 2022 and he made 17 big league starts in the outfield for them last summer. Myers has a flat right-handed swing that generates too much groundball contact, but he's also strong and hits the ball extremely hard. He slammed 41 homers in his first two full seasons as a position player -- including one off Aaron Nola in his fifth start in the Majors -- and would have even more pop if he learned to drive balls in the air to his pull side more frequently. He uses the entire field well and continues to improve his plate discipline as he gains more experience. Though he's the oldest position player on any of MLB Pipeline's Top 30 lists and will play this season at age 28, Myers has legitimate tools. With plus speed and arm strength, he started at least a dozen games at all three outfield spots and both infield corners in 2023. He's a solid defender in left or right field, average in center and shakier in the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Andrews was a successful two-way player in 2018 as a Long Beach State junior, posting a 1.99 ERA in 15 starts while also batting .302 across 57 games. But as a 5-foot-6 lefty who lacked velocity on the mound and power at the plate, Andrews didn't fit into a neat box as a Draft prospect and fell to Milwaukee in the 17th round. After only pitching during his professional debut, Andrews returned to playing two ways in his first full season, faring well in both roles while climbing to Double-A Biloxi. Andrews pitches with below-average velocity, as he'll typically sit in the upper 80s and occasionally break 90, but his heater plays up because he locates it well to help set up two quality secondary pitches. Andrews' changeup is a plus offering that he throws with tumble and late fading action, and he also has advanced feel for spinning a curveball. He's capable of working multiple innings and has proved comfortable pitching in high-leverage situations. As a hitter, Andrews demonstrates good feel for making contact from the left side of the plate, albeit with bottom-of-the-scale power. He employs a patient approach and isn't afraid to take a walk. Andrews' athleticism stands out in center field, where he's impressed club officials by running down balls in all directions. Despite his size, Andrews has a chance to carve out a bullpen role, if not become a legitimate two-way player at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Previous bonus pool overages meant the Nationals couldn’t sign anyone for more than $300,000 during the 2017-18 international period. They brought in Ferrer for one-third of that on July 2, and it took four-and-a-half years for him to break out in the Minors. The Dominican Republic native climbed three levels in his first full-season campaign, finishing with a 2.48 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 78 strikeouts in 65 1/3 innings between Single-A, High-A and Double-A, and struck out Ceddanne Rafaela as a National League reliever at the All-Star Futures Game. A reliever since signing, the 6-foot-1 southpaw shows short actions on the mound in terms of his arm movements and extension, but he’s still able to throw in the mid-90s consistently and can ramp it up to 99 mph. He complements that with a slider around 82-84 mph that can dive out of the zone and a low-spin mid-80s changeup that also plays well off the carry on his heater. Notably, all eight of the homers he allowed in 2022 came against righties, but the quality cambio still has a chance to keep them at least somewhat honest. Ferrer's strikethrowing ability has taken a step back a bit in 2023, and his mechanics will keep him in the bullpen anyhow. He was protected on the 40-man roster in November and has found a home in the Washington bullpen during the second half of the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pint was one of the most exciting prospects in the 2016 Draft, a big, strong high school right-hander capable of hitting triple digits consistently. There would need to be work done to turn him into a complete pitcher, sure, but the upside was too much for the Rockies to pass up with the No. 4 overall pick, signing him for $4.8 million. He has had trouble gaining traction since, scuffling in his first full year and missing nearly all of 2018 due to first forearm stiffness then a strained oblique. Based on his profile and Draft status, Pint certainly hasn't lived up to expectations thus far. The good news is he's still only 21 years old and the premium stuff that excited everyone coming out of high school is still very much there. The 6-foot-4 righty still cranks his fastball up to 97-100 mph consistently. The Rockies feel he has the best curve in the system, one that flashes as a 70 pitch, though not consistently. His above-average slider also can buckle knees and his fading changeup gives him a fourth pitch that grades out as at least above-average. The one thing, other than health, that has held him back has been his ability to command the baseball. It will come down to him finding a way to control his effort and body, which will allow him to repeat his delivery and find the strike zone more consistently. A full season should help tremendously in him taking a step from thrower to pitcher, with a frontline starter ceiling still not unreasonable to dream about.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pint showcased one of the best high school arms to come along this decade, earning him Justin Verlander comparisons before the Rockies drafted him fourth overall and signed him for $4.8 million in 2016. They've handled him carefully as he makes the transition from thrower to pitcher, limiting his pitch counts as he tries to harness his stuff. He has been sidelined for much of this season, coming down with foreness stiffness in his first start in April and then straining an oblique two starts after returning in June. Pint's pure stuff is exciting, as he has the potential for four plus pitches -- if he can control them. He has an electric fastball that sits at 94-98 mph and has climbed as high as 102 with life and downhill plane, though he has yet to blow pro hitters away with it because he struggles to command it. He also can make hitters look bad with his pair of power breaking balls and his fading changeup but has had trouble getting ahead in the count to set up his secondary offerings. The Rockies have toned down what was considerable effort in Pint's delivery, but he still has trouble repeating his mechanics and finding the strike zone. His first order of business is to locate his fastball more consistently, and then he can spend more time refining his other pitches. Youth and athleticism are on his side, and if he figures everything out, he can be a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the most explosive high school arms in years, Pint drew Justin Verlander comparisons and possessed a higher ceiling than anyone in the 2016 Draft. The Rockies gladly snapped him up with the No. 4 overall pick and signed him for $4.8 million. His talent was evident when he made his pro debut against older competition in the Rookie-level Pioneer League, and so was his need for more polish. Pint's fastball alone would make him intriguing, because it sits at 93-98 mph and climbs as high as 102, but there's much more to his arsenal. His power curveball already is a plus pitch, sometimes grades better than that, and he can alter it into a harder slider when he desires. Though he didn't need a changeup as an amateur, he already shows flashes of a plus change with some fade. The caveat with Pint is that his control and command lag behind his stuff. He throws with considerable effort, leading to worries about his ability to stay healthy and locate his pitches in the long run. If he can learn tone down his delivery and do a better job of repeating it, he can become the homegrown ace the Rockies have tried to develop for years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marsh was Arizona State’s Friday night starter his junior year and showcased a high ceiling, leading Kansas City to take him in Competitive Balance Round B in 2019, adding to the list of college pitchers in their system. Marsh’s pro career got off to a bumpy start -- first without games in 2020, then an arm injury around the biceps area limited him to just six games in ‘21. So his first full pro season was in ‘22, when he had a 7.32 ERA in Double-A, allowing 27 homers and 137 hits in 114 1/3 innings. He still flashed upside, and the Royals added him to their 40-man roster last winter ahead of the Rule 5 Draft. Marsh knows how to utilize all his weapons, and he pounds the strike zone with all his pitches. The problem he encountered in ‘22 was too much hard contact, specifically with his 95-96 mph fastball. His slider has developed into his primary breaking pitch, coming in the upper-80s with two-plane movement, and his low-80s curve offers another look. Marsh still needs to develop his changeup because he needs a pitch to get lefties out -- they hit .353 off Marsh last year. Marsh’s results were not great in 2022. But the Royals were happy he got through a full season healthy and still believe in the arm. He worked with the club’s new pitching coaches this spring, which could help unlock better performance, and he breezed through Double-A and Triple-A on his way to a Major League debut in the club's rotation. Marsh has still run into control problems at the top level, but his arrival is a potential success story for the organization's pitching development system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After serving as Arizona State’s Friday night starter his junior year, the Royals drafted Marsh in the supplemental second round in 2019 and signed him for full pick value. His velocity soared in 2020 despite no games, showing up to the alternate training site looking like a different pitcher. Arm soreness around the biceps kept him from building on that momentum, though, and he only pitched six games in 2021. The Royals erred on the side of caution by shutting him down after one start in the Arizona Fall League, and he entered the spring fully healthy. Marsh has a powerful arm with a true feel for five pitches, and he can throw strikes with all of them. He touches 99 mph with his fastball and complements it with a two-seamer that sinks. His curveball is his best secondary pitch with good shape and depth. Marsh’s slider is tight and could be plus with more development, and his average changeup has natural sink to it. A repeatable delivery has helped his control improve when he’s healthy. Before his injury, Marsh profiled as a solid, reliable mid-rotation starter, but he’s been much less reliable in 2022 as his mistakes haven been punished in the Texas League. The stuff is still there to dream on Marsh as a starter, as his strikeout numbers indicate, but it wouldn’t be a surprise to see him get relief looks before long in order to make the most of the arsenal in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marsh continuously got better throughout his time at Arizona State, throwing well during a brief stint in the Cape Cod League after his sophomore year and serving as ASU’s Friday night starter his junior year. The Royals took him in the supplemental second round in 2019 -- their first of six college pitchers taken in the top 10 rounds -- and signed him for full pick value. Marsh hasn’t had a full professional season with the Royals, but after pitching a few games in a pop-up league in Texas in 2020, he reported to the Royals' alternate training site late in the summer -- and looked like a different pitcher. Unfortunately, arm soreness has limited him in 2021 and kept him from building on that alt-site momentum. Fastball velocity was Marsh’s biggest improvement during 2020. He is now touching 99 mph with his four-seamer and complements it with a two-seamer that sinks. He has a powerful arm and demonstrates an advanced feel for a deep arsenal. His slider is tight and averages 86 mph, which he pairs with a power 80-mph curveball that has good shape and depth. The breaking balls are now two distinct pitches and are usually both there for him on any given day. He has a feel for an average or better changeup with natural sink that still needs some developing. But Marsh can throw each of his four pitches for strikes, and he throws from the same arm slot with a clean, repeatable delivery that has helped his control improve. Marsh made his full-season debut in 2021, but the injury concerns have hurt his chances to reach higher this summer. When he's on, Marsh gets high marks for his mechanics, work ethic, competitiveness and ability to learn quickly. With four pitches that could all be Major League average or better, he profiles as a solid, reliable mid-rotation starter once he's able to get fully healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he went undrafted as a Wisconsin prep in 2016, Marsh turned in a nondescript freshman season at Arizona State, pitching mostly in relief. He took a nice step forward as a sophomore with the Sun Devils, however, and then threw well during a brief stint in the Cape Cod League that summer. That success carried over into Marsh’s junior year, when the right-hander served as ASU’s Friday night starter. The Royals took him in the supplemental second round that June -- the first of six college pitchers taken in the top 10 rounds -- and signed him for full pick value. He threw well during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Pioneer League, demonstrating advanced feel for a deep arsenal. Marsh can throw each of his four pitches for strikes. While he'll typically sit around 92 mph, he can dial his four-seamer fastball up to 95-96 mph with some late cut and complements it with a two-seamer that sinks. His 78-83 mph slider is better than his average curveball, and he has the command to land it for a strike or bury it outside the zone. He also has feel for a changeup, though it’s a clear fourth pitch for him that will need to be developed in the pro ranks. Marsh’s control improved in each of his three years at Arizona State. It was even better in the Pioneer League, with the right-hander’s clean and repeatable delivery translating to 38/4 K/BB. In addition to having four pitches which could all be Major League average when all is said and done, scouts love the way Marsh competes on the mound, with many pegging him as a No. 4 starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It took three times for Vines to start his pro career, first getting drafted late out of high school by the Astros, a year later by the Cubs out of Oxnard Junior College and then, finally, in the seventh round by the Braves in 2019 out of Cal State Bakersfield. He was added to the 40-man roster after reaching Triple-A in 2022 and while shoulder inflammation shelved him in 2023 until the end of June, he pitched his way to Atlanta for the first time, appearing in five games during the stretch run. Vines has been able to do quite a bit without overpowering stuff. It’s an average fastball, at best, usually around 90-91 mph, topping out at 93 mph, but he actually throws his secondary stuff more frequently. His 81-mph changeup has depth and deception and he’s shown a willingness to throw it in any count and he continued to get chases out of the zone with it in the big leagues. When he was up, he featured his newer mid-80s cutter, and he still has a usable slider, which might be his fourth pitch by now. Athletic on the mound, Vines has a simple delivery he repeats consistently, leading to plenty of strike-throwing. The ceiling isn’t very high given the lack of a true out pitch, but his ability to mix his pitches and keep hitters guessing in and around the zone gives him a decently high floor, with a future as a No. 5 type starter or effective long man out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of the California high school ranks, Vines was a late-round pick of the Astros as a prepster in 2016, then was taken again out of junior college the following year by the Cubs before transferring to Cal State Bakersfield for the 2019 season. He became the highest-drafted player in Roadrunners history when the Braves selected him in the seventh round that summer. He’s moved methodically through the system, reaching Triple-A in 2022 and earning a spot on the 40-man roster in the offseason, though he was held out of action in 2023 until the end of June because of shoulder inflammation. While Vines is never going to wow with electric stuff, his feel for pitching has enabled him to get outs at the upper levels of the system. His secondary stuff is better than his fastball, starting with a plus changeup, thrown around 81-82 mph with deception and depth. He’ll throw it at any point and commands it well, getting swings-and-misses in and out of the zone. His low-80s slider isn’t quite as exciting, but it’s an average pitch that misses bats as well. He does have a slower curve he doesn't throw as much. He’s just as likely to use one of those offerings as his average-ish fastball that's usually around 91-92 mph and tops out at 94-95. A solid athlete who played different sports in his high school days, Vines repeats his delivery well and has above-average control of his arsenal. He’s kind of a “throw the kitchen sink at you” pitcher, with a limited ceiling, but his ability to mix those offerings well gives him the chance to sit in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For Vines, the third time was indeed the charm. He was drafted late by the Astros out of high school in 2016, went to junior college in his home state of California and was drafted by the Cubs in 2017, then went on to Cal State Bakersfield and landed in the seventh round of the 2019 Draft, finally signing with the Braves. His pro debut that summer did not go well, but he had a solid first full season after the 2020 shutdown, pitching his way across two levels of A ball in 2021. Vines didn’t pitch at the Braves’ alternate site in 2020, but the work on his own clearly paid off. All of his stuff plays up because of his ability to command four pitches. He typically sits around 92 mph with his fastball, but can go get a 95 mph heater when he needs it. Both his slider and his changeup have the chance to be above-average when all is said and done, and while the latter is ahead of the former as a pitch with depth that plays well off of his fastball, he’s made progress with his low-80s slider as well. His bigger, slower curve is more of a get-me-over, steal a strike kind of pitch, but it’s effective. Vines is super-athletic, a former two-way player who played multiple sports in high school, which helps him repeat his delivery and throw a ton of strikes. His ceiling is somewhat limited, but he might be a “whole is better than the sum of his parts” type who lands in the back end of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming off a year in which Alu hit .339 with only four homers and an .877 OPS at Boston College, he was a cheap senior option for the Nationals in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft and signed for just $10,000. Following the lost pandemic year, he showed decent signs that his bat could translate to the pros with a .303/.357/.490 line at High-A and finished the year in the upper Minors. He returned to Harrisburg last season and truly broke out with a .299/.365/.506 line in 132 games between Double-A and Triple-A, leading Nationals full-season qualifiers in average, slugging, OPS, doubles (40), extra-base hits (62) and total bases (254). Washington rewarded that work by adding Alu to its 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible. Improvements in approach aided the infielder’s offensive improvements in 2022. Alu grew more patient, leading to a jump in his walk rate from 5.7 percent to 9.0, while still protecting the plate well with two strikes. The tone back in aggression also helped the left-handed slugger tap more into his power -- his 20 homers doubled his career high -- but that came more from an ability to put the barrel on the ball than any pure raw pop. Listed at 5-foot-10, Alu is smaller than a typical third baseman, and while he’s played some second, he lacks the footspeed required to be a regular up-the-middle defender. Even though his arm is tested at the hot corner, he should still be part of the conversation there for Washington in his first 40-man year, and he’ll need to press that issue considering he's entering his age-26 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After not getting much mound time as a freshman at the University of Michigan in 2016, Karcher transferred to Walters State Junior College in Tennessee, where he caught the eye of Cincinnati scouts with his raw arm strength. The Reds thought he was worth a $125,000 flier in the 13th round of the 2017 Draft, and while it’s taken him a while to get going -- he didn’t touch full-season ball until 2021 after having Tommy John surgery in 2019 -- he was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason after reaching Triple-A. Karcher began his pro career developing as a starter, but it was a move to the bullpen in 2021 that has allowed him to take off and his power arsenal to play up. His fastball averaged around 97 mph for the 2022 season and touched triple digits. His power upper-80s slider has improved and is now at least average, and it produced a 41 percent miss rate last year. He’ll even fold in a firm changeup, now up to 90 mph, from time to time.
