Karcher’s relationship with the strike zone has been spotty at best, but he took a big step forward in that area in 2022, walking fewer batters in Triple-A than before he was promoted. His control might keep him from handling too much in the way of high-leverage situations, but it’s looking like that 2017 Draft flyer is going to turn into a big league reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending three years as part of Mississippi’s rotation, McArthur became a 12th-round Draft pick of the Phillies in 2018, getting an over-slot $215,000 to keep him from going back to Ole Miss for his senior year. He started and relieved in his first full season and spent most of the 2021 season starting in a hitting-friendly home park in Reading. He added innings in the Arizona Fall League and while he was inconsistent there, he finished well and showed enough to earn a spot on the Phillies’ 40-man roster. McArthur still has the four-pitch mix and the size (6-foot-7) that made the Phillies like him in the first place. He was throwing his fastball in the 92-95 mph range, sometimes touching 96, with some sinking action to it during his AFL stint. Making some adjustments to how he grips his slider has allowed him to add more sweep to it, an above-average breaker that has the chance to be a consistent swing-and-miss pitch for him. He still has the slower curve and a changeup, both of which he uses more against left-handed hitters. The right-hander did a better job of finding the strike zone during the 2021 regular season, though he needs to keep refining his command and breaking stuff. That could give him the chance to start as a back-end starter, with a chance to serve in a swingman role as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vallimont is among several in the Twins' system who had problems with wildness coming out of a lost 2020, with his strikeout-to-walk ratio plummeting from 3.66 in '19 to 2.23 in '21. The Twins couldn't pinpoint anything in the mechanics that led to Vallimont's career-high 61 walks, but they hope the former fifth-rounder from Division II Mercyhurst College will get back to pounding the zone following a more normal offseason. That's the biggest step that could help him get back to the form that the Twins liked when they acquired from Miami at the 2019 Trade Deadline in the Sergio Romo deal and saw him impress in 2020 instructional play. The right-hander does have four pitches that can flash plus at times, all of which can miss bats. He doesn't throw as hard as his 6-foot-5 frame would suggest, with his fastball largely sitting around 92 mph, occasionally touching as high as 96 with good movement and ride. The slider is his best secondary pitch while the consistency of the curveball and changeup continue to develop. The quality of his stuff noticeably tailed off as he went deeper into his 2021 outings and he tended to spray his pitches around the zone. He needs to put himself in counts where he can leverage them for strikeouts. The control issues have some wondering an eventual move to the bullpen could help, but the Twins, who added Vallimont to the 40-man roster this past offseason, continue to see him as a starter because of the quality of his stuff and mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three pitchers from Division II power Mercyhurst College in Pennsylvania have made it to the big leagues, most recently Dan Altavalia. Vallimont, a fifth-round pick by the Marlins from the school in 2018, hopes to be the next with the Twins, who acquired him from Miami as part of the Sergio Romo deal close to the 2019 Trade Deadline. Vallimont made a very strong impression in a brief post-trade sample size, then threw well during instructional league play in 2020. While Vallimont is 6-foot-5, he’s more about his complete repertoire than he is about power. The velocity of his fastball can fluctuate, sometimes touching 95-96 mph and sometimes floating below-average, though he always throws it with a lot of movement. His hard slider is his best weapon, a hard breaking ball with depth the Twins are trying to get him to throw more, especially to right-handed hitters. He mixes in an average curve and his changeup gives him a legitimate four-pitch mix. Vallimont did a much better job of throwing strikes in his first full season of pro ball after struggling with command for parts of his college career and during his summer debut in 2018. If he continues to throw enough strikes with all four of his pitches, that’s more than enough for him to be a No. 4 or 5 starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 When the Twins traded prospect Lewin Diaz to the Marlins close to the 2019 Trade Deadline, the key target was big league reliever Sergio Romo, who bolstered a playoff-bound bullpen. But they also got Vallimont, who had been a fifth-round pick of the Marlins in 2018 out of Division II powerhouse Mercyhurst College in Pennsylvania. Valilmont pitched across two levels of A ball during his first full season, and the Twins liked what they saw in his four post-trade starts, leading some to believe he might be a more meaningful piece in that trade than anticipated. In high school in Pennsylvania, Vallimont was a tall and gangly pitcher who topped out in the upper-80s. His velocity has improved steadily since and he now employs a 92-96 mph fastball. His slider is his best secondary pitch, a mid-80s sweeping breaking ball that elicits swings and misses. He’ll also mix in a hard curve, with both breaking balls much tighter now than when he entered pro ball, and a changeup that could give him four average or better pitches when all is said and done. Whether Vallimont can start long-term will largely be dependent on his strike-throwing ability. That’s been a challenge for him at times, though he did a better job of finding the zone in 2019. His stuff would play up, with more velocity for sure, in shorter stints out of the bullpen should a move be deemed necessary.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No pitcher in Seattle’s organization has had a more topsy-turvy go the past two years than Then, whom president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto said took as big of a leap as any in 2020, prompting the club to add him to the 40-man roster and protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. But Then stumbled mightily in the two years since, with a 6.10 ERA in that stretch and not reaching Double-A Arkansas until this past August. A huge component of his issues has been health, specifically elbow problems that have limited him to just 66 1/3 innings the past two Minor League seasons. Even when he was on the mound, he still couldn’t get right, so he was the classic case of one step forward and two steps back. But he finished 2022 on a high note in the Arizona Fall League, sitting 94-96 mph on his fastball with a really good changeup, while showing enough promise that warranted a return to the Top 30 after being left off in ’22. Then will need to keep pounding the zone to get back on track, which he did in the AFL. The big questions with him are if the fastball will be impactful enough and if there’s going to be enough on his breaking ball to succeed against better hitters. Those answers will hinge on Then being fully healthy and trusting his stuff, but there is enough evidence that Then possesses a solid middle-reliever profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Last year, Mariners GM Jerry Dipoto said no pitcher had taken a bigger leap in the organization than Then, who was placed on the 40-man roster ahead of the 2021 season and appeared to be on a fast track to the Majors. That type of projection made his ensuing season all the more confounding. He stumbled to a 6.46 ERA in 14 starts for High A Everett and remained there all season. The Mariners still believe that Then's stuff is there and real, and the fact his solid slider was still hitting 97 mph with 59 strikeouts in 54 1/3 innings indicate as much. It was almost as if he was throwing too many strikes at times and left a bevy of pitches over the plate, which led to a 1.601 WHIP. When his fastball is at its best, it misses bats and has good riding life to it, yet he found himself using it often in hitters’ counts. Then's best secondary pitch is a hard slider that can serve as an out pitch, but he couldn’t get to it enough. He has a changeup that shows flashes of being a good pitch, but he doesn’t always throw it with conviction and it’s often too firm. Then is just 22 years old and possesses high-90s velocity, which will continue to make him intriguing. But because he’s on the 40-man, his situation will face more urgency in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mariners GM Jerry Dipoto admired Then so much that he acquired him twice. The righty initially signed with the organization for $77,500 in July 2016 but was traded to the Yankees in November 2017 after he had made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. But when the Mariners dealt Edwin Encarnacion to the Yankees in June 2019, they centered their return on Then. He pitched his way from short-season to full-season ball for the first time after the trade. The pitcher they got back was one whose stuff had improved dramatically since they first got him, beginning with a fastball that keeps growing, from the low 90s initially to up to 100 mph as recently as the Arizona fall developmental league last fall. When it’s at its best, it misses bats and has good riding life to it. Then's best secondary pitch is his hard slider that can serve as an out pitch. He has a changeup that shows flashes of being a good pitch, but he doesn’t always throw it with conviction and it’s often too firm. Dipoto said that no player in Seattle’s farm system took a bigger step forward in 2020 than Then -- even among the big league roster. Then, who was added to the 40-man roster to protect him from December’s Rule 5 Draft, spent last season at big league Summer Camp, then alternate training site, then in Arizona in the fall, where he continued to develop his slider that could be a true plus pitch. There’s hope that will get better as he continues to add strength and that he can slow down his changeup to separate from his fastball enough for him to remain a starter. With his status on the 40-man, Then could be in the Majors sooner than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners liked Then so much they acquired him twice. He signed initially with the organization in 2016 for $77,500 in July 2016 but was traded to the Yankees in November 2017 after he had made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. When Seattle dealt Edwin Encarnacion to the Yankees in June 2019, they knew who they wanted in return, getting Then back in the fold. He pitched his way from short-season to full-season ball for the first time after the trade. The Mariners got a pitcher back whose stuff had increased since they first got him, starting with a fastball that keeps growing. He’s now consistently in the 92-94 mph range and given his age and experience, there could be more in the tank. When it’s at its best, it misses bats and has good riding life to it. Then's best secondary pitch is his hard slider that can serve as an out pitch. He has a changeup that shows flashes of being a good pitch, but he doesn’t always throw it with conviction and it’s often too firm. Then has shown a penchant for throwing strikes, though he does struggle with maintaining his arm slot on his delivery at times. There’s hope that will get better as he continues to add strength and that he can slow down his changeup to separate from his fastball enough for him to remain a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees acquired Then (and lefty J.P. Mears) from the Mariners in November 2017 in return for Nick Rumbelow. Signed for $77,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, Then has successfully navigated two years of Rookie ball thanks to advanced pitchability. In his first season with his new organization, he led the Gulf Coast League in WHIP (0.98) and finished third in opponent average (.210). He was waiting to make his 2019 debut when he was sent back to the Mariners in June's Edwin Encarnacion deal. Then doesn't miss a lot of bats with his 90-95 mph fastball because it's fairly straight, though that allows him to command it better than most teenagers can. He also throws strikes with a changeup that's advanced for his age. He has promising depth on his curveball, which ranks as his third-best pitch yet has solid potential. Then isn't very physical, but he could make it as a No. 4 or 5 starter because he keeps his pitch counts down and limits his mistakes. He has a high floor, and it's possible that he could develop a plus pitch or two as he matures. He probably won't make his full-season debut until 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees have so much depth that they faced a 40-man roster crunch this offseason, prompting them to trade four players whom they couldn't protect in November -- and they still had four players chosen in the big league phase of the Rule 5 Draft for the second straight Winter Meetings. One of those deals sent Nick Rumbelow to the Mariners for two promising pitchers, Then and bat-missing left-hander J.P. Sears. Signed for $77,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, he had a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Then offers a combination of projectability and pitchability. His fastball currently ranges from 90-95 mph but New York believes he'll add significant velocity as he adds strength and becomes more consistent with his delivery. He also has a feel for throwing strikes with his advanced changeup and shows promising depth on his curveball, though it's presently his least reliable offering. Once Then puts on 25 pounds or so of muscle, he could have three solid or better pitches. He pounded the strike zone during his 2017 debut and should be able to remain a starter despite being a little shorter than desired.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutherford entered 2016 as the top-rated high school position player in the Draft but lasted 18 picks in June because of worries about his signability and age (19 years, one month at the time of his selection). The Yankees signed him for $3,282,200, still a franchise record for a drafted hitter, and shipped him to the White Sox as the headliner in a four-player package for Todd Frazier, Tommy Kahnle and David Robertson a year later. Chicago has tried to unlock his power but he slugged just .383 in his first two-plus seasons after the trade. Rutherford still has the smooth left-handed stroke, strong 6-foot-3 frame and all-fields approach that scouts loved during his amateur days. But he has shown little power since slugging .570 in his pro debut, most of it coming to his pull side while he makes too much weak groundball contact. He encouraged the White Sox by doing a better job of backspinning and driving balls and incorporating his lower half in his swing at their alternate site last summer, but he still has to prove he can do so in games that count. An average runner, Rutherford can steal an occasional bag but doesn't stand out on the bases or in the outfield. Though he broke into pro ball as a center fielder and has spent most of his time in Chicago's system as a right fielder, his fringy arm strength eventually will land him in left. His bat will have to carry him if he's going to be a big league regular and he has a ways to go to become even a platoon player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After entering 2016 as the top-rated prep position player in the Draft, Rutherford lasted 18 picks because of questions about his signability and age (he was one of the oldest high school players in his class at 19 years, one month on Draft Day). He signed for $3,282,200 -- a Yankees record for a drafted hitter -- and posted a .570 slugging percentage in Rookie ball during his pro debut. Sent to the White Sox in a four-player package for Todd Frazier, Tommy Kahnle and David Robertson in July 2017, he slugged .383 in his first two-plus seasons after the trade. Rutherford still has the smooth left-handed stroke and all-fields approach that attracted scouts when he was an amateur, but his power has yet to come close to materializing as hoped. Almost all of his modest in-game pop comes to his pull side and he makes a lot of weak ground-ball contact. He spent time in the Arizona Fall League during the offseason trying to use his legs more in his swing to create more power, but he hit just .179/.281/.385 in 21 games. Compared to Andre Ethier and David Justice when he was younger, Rutherford will have to step up his production to become a big league regular. He's an average runner who's good for an occasional steal, but he's nothing special on the bases or in the outfield. Though he broke into pro ball as a center fielder and has spent most of his last two years as a right fielder, his below-average arm figures to land him in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutherford entered 2016 as the top-rated high school position player for the Draft, then dropped to the Yankees at No. 18 because of concerns about his signability and his age (at 19, he was old for a prepster). He slugged .570 in Rookie ball after signing for $3,282,200, a franchise record for a hitter, but managed just a .395 mark at two Class A levels the next two seasons. The White Sox acquired him in July 2017 as the headliner in a four-player package for Todd Frazier, David Robertson and Tommy Kahnle. Rutherford still impresses scouts with his smooth left-handed swing, pitch-recognition skills and willingness to use the entire field. He makes repeated contact and club officials believed he could start to hit for more power in 2019 after adding strength in the offseason, though that hasn't happened. He has the size, strength and bat speed to produce 20 homers per season if he can stop hitting so many grounders and drive the ball more consistently. Compared to the likes of Andre Ethier and David Justice, Rutherford could have at least average tools across the board when he's fully developed. After playing primarily center field in his first two pro seasons, he spent the bulk of his time in right field last year. His average arm isn't a liability but ultimately could land him in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutherford began 2016 as the top-rated high school position player, then got surpassed by fellow California outfielder Mickey Moniak (who went No. 1 overall) and fell to the Yankees at No. 18 because of worries about his age (19 years, 1 month on Draft day) and signability. He tore up Rookie ball after signing for $3,282,000, a franchise record for a hitter, but batted just .260/.326/.348 with two homers in 101 Class A games in his first full season. New York sent him to the White Sox in July as part of a four-player package for Todd Frazier, David Robertson and Tommy Kahnle. Though Rutherford failed to post big numbers in 2017, there were positives. He recognized pitches, made consistent contact and showed a willingness to use all fields, all of which bode well for him hitting for a high average. Chicago believes his size, strength, bat speed and left-handed stroke will translate into at least average power once he learns which pitches he can drive. Sometimes compared to a more athletic version of David Justice, Rutherford could have average or better tools across the board. He figures to slow down a bit as he matures physically, so he's unlikely to remain in center field despite spending most of his first two pro seasons there. He has enough arm strength to handle either outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After entering 2016 as the top-rated prep position player in the Draft, Rutherford got passed by fellow California outfielder Mickey Moniak and slipped all the way to the Yankees at No. 18 overall amid concerns about his age (19 years, 1 month when he got picked) and signability. Signed for $3,282,000, a franchise record for a hitter, he immediately looked like a steal by batting .351/.415/.570 in Rookie ball. He has continued to impress in 2017, and the Yankees used him as the key prospect to swing a July trade with the White Sox for Todd Frazier, David Robertson and Tommy Kahnle. The most productive offensive player on the U.S. national 18-and-under team that included three other seven-figure bonus babies and won the 2015 World Cup in Japan, Rutherford is a rare talent who has the chance to hit for plus average and power. He has a smooth left-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed, recognizes pitches well, shows signs of patience and uses the entire field. While he currently employs a line-drive approach, he has big raw power and will tap into it once he adds some loft to his swing. Rutherford entered pro ball as a solid runner and a center fielder, but he should slow down as he starts to fill out and most scouts believe he'll wind up on an outfield corner. Evaluators grade his arm anywhere from fringy to above average. He has drawn comparisons to a more athletic version of David Justice.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The professional version of Mederos thus far has been very similar to the one who pitched for Miami and then Oklahoma State in college. The Angels’ sixth-round pick in the 2022 Draft created a lot of buzz at instructs the fall after he signed, but his first full year of pro ball was more of the same: an arsenal that could rank with some of the better pitching prospects in the game and results that did not match up with the pure stuff. He did make his big league debut in 2023, but had a 5.67 ERA in 20 Double-A starts. Mederos is a big, strong and physical right-hander who has a legitimate four-pitch mix. His fastball averaged 94 mph last year and touched as high as 99, a heater thrown with pretty good sink. His mid-80s slider features two-plane depth and missed a lot of bats last year, and while he didn’t throw his low-80s curve nearly as much and didn’t land it for strikes with a high frequency, it can be effective at times. He has a fading 87-88 mph changeup that he throws even less than his curve. Because of his repertoire and ability to maintain his velocity, it’s hard to give up on Mederos as a starting pitcher. But the combination of his arm action and effort in his delivery have led to command issues, both in and out of the strike zone. In shorter stints, he could be sporting a triple-digit sinker and slider combination that could be really nasty.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Throughout his college baseball journey, first at Miami and then Oklahoma State, Mederos teased with premium velocity and intriguing stuff, but the results never matched the promise. He was nudged out of the Hurricanes rotation and got hit hard the year he pitched for the Cowboys. The Angels thought he was worth a flier and took him in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft, signing him for a bit under slot. It's a small sample size for sure, but Mederos was the talk of instructional league play last fall, giving the Angels hope they can help the strong right-hander get better results. He’s always had fastball velocity, sitting in the 94-97 mph range in college. During instructs, it was in the upper 90s and routinely hit 99 mph. His improved command of the pitch was an encouraging development. In the past, he’d have to take something off in order to land it in the strike zone and it would get hit. With two-plane depth, his hard 83-86 mph slider was much more consistent in the fall than it has been. He has a downer low-80s curve, but hasn’t been able to throw it for strikes and there’s a seldom-used changeup in there as well with some fade. Given Mederos’ struggles in the past in terms of command in and out of the zone, not to mention the effort and arm action with his delivery, he probably will end up in a bullpen. But with a potential four-pitch mix and the early strides he showed at instructs, he could get the opportunity to start for now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Triolo was a starter from day one at Houston but really jumped on the map with a big 2019 season, posting a .931 OPS to go along with his outstanding defense, enough to land him with the Pirates in the Competitive Balance Round B of that year's Draft. Because of the pandemic, he couldn’t make his full-season debut until 2021, when he raked with High-A Greensboro. He put up solid numbers in 2022 with Double-A Altoona, particularly in the second half, earning him a spot on the 40-man roster this past offseason. Since joining the Pirates, Triolo has adjusted his right-handed swing, changing the setup of his hands to be in a better position to hit, which has resulted in him more consistently finding the barrel. He regularly takes professional at-bats, seeing pitches and drawing a good amount of walks while limiting strikeouts. He’s big and physical, but he still doesn’t always tap into strength and raw power enough; he could do so if he would commit to elevating the ball more. He’s a smart baserunner who can steal a base. There isn’t much separating Triolo and big league highlight-reel regular Ke’Bryan Hayes defensively at third, as Triolo has plus hands and instincts to go with a strong arm. Because of Hayes’ presence in Pittsburgh, Triolo has started moving around the field more, showing he can play a capable shortstop and getting time in the outfield as well, with second base also a possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Houston, Triolo established a reputation as a solid, if unspectular, infielder, one who could hit, without a ton of power, and play a solid third base, all while earning praise for his makeup. The Pirates liked the sum of his parts enough to take him in the second round of the 2019 Draft and his rather pedestrian debut in the short-season New York-Penn League prepared no one for the huge breakout he had with High-A Greensboro in 2021. Triolo has long had an advanced approach with excellent plate discipline, but some swing adjustments really allowed him to take off. His hands are in a better spot now and he’s closed the loop in his swing path that was evident in college. That’s allowed him to barrel up the baseball on a much more consistent basis and he can drive the ball, with the next step in his evolution as a hitter being an ability to backspin the ball to his pull side. With great hands and instincts, Triolo won a Rawlings Gold Glove at third last year. With Ke’Bryan Hayes in the big leagues, Triolo could start seeing more time at shortstop and was even getting some reps in the outfield this spring. He’ll get to see if his improvements can carry over to the upper levels in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Triolo became an immediate starter for Houston as a freshman in 2017 and has been one of the best hitters in the American Athletic Conference the last two seasons. He also proved himself with a strong summer in the Cape Cod League a year ago and has one of the higher floors among college position players in the 2019 crop. He projects to go in the top four or five rounds and perhaps even higher to a club that believes it can unlock more power. Triolo has a prettier swing than most right-handers and uses it to make consistent contact while controlling the strike zone. He has strength and leverage in his impressive 6-foot-3 frame, but his bat speed is merely average and has limited his power production. Unless he can quicken his stroke and perhaps add more loft, he may max out at 30-35 doubles and 15 homers per season at the next level. Athletic for his size, Triolo can produce some plus run times but likely will wind up with average speed as he gets older. He provides steady defense at third base, displaying average range and solid arm strength. He doesn't have any plus tools or glaring flaws, and scouts love his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 After helping Mississippi State go to the College World Series in 2018 and 2019, Westburg played very well in the Cape Cod League and raised his profile even more with a good start over 16 games in 2020 until the pandemic ended the college season. The Orioles had seen enough to take him at the start of the Competitive Balance Round A. He’s hit his way up to the top of the system, knocking on the door particularly loudly with his 27 homers and 106 RBIs between Double-A and Triple-A in 2022. At 6-foot-3 and around 200 pounds, Westburg is a strong and athletic infielder with legitimate power that has really showed up in games. He can drive the ball to all fields and hit the ball out anywhere, though the over-the-fence pop shows up more to his pull side. It’s a power-over-hit profile, with some swing-and-miss to his game -- though his strikeout rate actually went down a little bit in 2022 from his first full season -- and he offsets it with a healthy dose of walks (11.3 BB rate last year). He’s not a burner, but he runs well enough to take an extra base and steal a few. Westburg has seen most of his time as a pro at shortstop, and he has the arm strength and moves well enough to play capably there. At second base or third base, he could be at least an above-average defender, and it’s looking like he’s going to have the power-hitting offensive profile that fits well at the hot corner. He should hit his way to the big leagues sooner rather than later and might keep moving around the infield to get that bat into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Westburg was a star who helped lead Mississippi State to College World Series appearances in 2018 and 2019 when he emerged as one of the top collegiate infielders in the country alongside future Rangers prospect Justin Foscue. Impressed with his combination of athleticism, power and speed, the Orioles selected Westburg with the No. 30 overall pick in 2020, 16 spots after Foscue went to Texas. He signed for full pick value ($2,365,500), immediately becoming one of the best infield prospects in a Baltimore system lacking them. Since, Westburg has done little to alter that perception. He opened eyes at Baltimore’s instructional camp in 2020 then excelled across three levels in 2021, hitting .285 with a .868 OPS, 15 homers and 17 steals. Flashing a blend of tools from his 6-foot-3, 200-pound frame, Westburg’s most notable attribute is his combination of strength and bat speed. He has a compact right-handed swing that can drive the ball gap-to-gap and with power, particularly to the pull side, and an aggressive approach that led to occasional struggles with pitch recognition in college. He’s quelled most of those concerns as a pro despite showing some swing-and-miss, reaching base at a .389 clip in his first full season. All told, it’s an offensive profile some believe could produce 20 or more homers annually in the big leagues. Defense isn’t Westburg’s calling card given his size and average speed, but he’s a reliable defender at short and athletic enough to move around if need be. His arm strength is plus; that and his power potential could forecast a move to third base somewhere down the line. Baltimore’s lack of high-level infield prospects made Westburg a candidate to move quickly and so far he’s lived up to that billing, reaching Double-A in 2021 and looking like a potential impact player at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though neither was a heralded prospect or drafted out of high school in 2017, Mississippi State's Westburg and Justin Foscue have developed into college baseball's best double-play combination. Foscue has been a more consistent hitter but Westburg has a higher ceiling and more defensive value. He tied a College World Series record with seven RBI in one game in 2018 and helped the Bulldogs return to Omaha last season. Westburg has a compact right-handed swing and possesses the bat speed and strength to provide 20 or more homers on an annual basis. He lacks consistency at the plate because he has a very aggressive, pull-happy approach and sometimes struggles with pitch recognition and managing the strike zone. After he failed to make the U.S. collegiate national team last summer, he settled down nicely in the Cape Cod League and was one of the circuit's more productive hitters. Westburg has solid speed and arm strength to match, giving him a chance to stick at shortstop at the next level. He's big for the position at 6-foot-3 and if he adds more strength to his frame, he could slow down and necessitate a move to third base. With his power potential, he still could profile offensively at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wong put himself on the prospect radar with a series of strong performances on back-to-back Western Athletic Conference regular-season championship clubs at Grand Canyon and in the Cape Cod League. He went in the third round of the 2018 Draft, making him the Antelopes' earliest pick since Tim Salmon went in the same round in 1989. After signing for an above-slot $850,000, he cruised through his first two pro stops before getting knocked around in high Class A last summer. In his first full pro season, Wong lost a couple of ticks of velocity on his two-seam fastball, which sat around 91-94 mph and topped out at 96. His heater features heavy sink when it's on but wasn't at its sharpest in the second half of 2019. He switched from a slider to a curveball in 2018 but he's back to throwing both breaking pitches after his curve lacked consistency last year. Wong still is developing feel for his changeup, which has some fade but can get too firm in the mid-80s. He has a strong frame and repeats his delivery well enough to provide strikes. If he doesn't regain the plus fastball and solid breaking ball he showed at the beginning of his pro career, he'll need to upgrade his command to work his way into a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wong helped put Grand Canyon's newly minted NCAA Division I program on the map with a series of strong performances against ranked opponents in 2017-18, including six shutout innings against Texas Christian when the Antelopes debuted their new ballpark last February. He became the program's highest-drafted player since Tim Salmon in 1989, signing with the Giants for an over-slot $850,000 in the third round. In his abbreviated pro debut last summer, he did what he does best: miss bats and get groundouts. Wong sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 mph with his fastball, which features heavy sink when he keeps it down in the strike zone. He switched from throwing a slider in 2017 to using a curveball in 2018, and its power and depth give it the makings of a potential plus offering. His changeup has some fading action but can get too firm at times. With Wong's size, strength and sound delivery, he should have the durability to handle a starter's workload over a full pro season. While he throws a reasonable amount of strikes, he needs to refine his command because he'll get hit harder than his stuff indicates he should at times. He comes with a higher ceiling but a lower floor than Sean Hjelle, the fellow college righty whom San Francisco selected a round ahead of him last June.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since he was taken No. 7 overall in the 2020 Draft after putting up huge numbers at hitter-friendly New Mexico State and winning the Cape Cod League MVP in 2019, Gonzales’ pro career has moved forward in fits and bursts. In both of his full seasons, he’s had to deal with injuries – a broken finger in 2021 and a heel injury in 2022 – that cost him a lot of development time. He’s also overcome slow starts in each season to finish well, including hitting .286/.408/.505 post-injury in Double-A a year ago, and he ended both years by making up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League. Gonzales still shows off the plus bat speed and fast hands that made him such an alluring Draft prospect, with an ability to be very quick to the ball. He relies on rhythm and timing at the plate, and he’s struggled to get in sync at times -- missing reps hasn’t helped in that department. There is plenty of raw power to tap into and he’s willing to draw walks, but he’s swung and missed much more than someone who looked like such a tremendous pure hitter, with close to a 28 percent strikeout rate. Known as a bat-first infielder as he entered pro ball, that’s still the case, but he’s worked hard on his defense to improve his footwork and reads. He’s likely a second baseman only, but he has filled in at shortstop at times and played third for the first time in the AFL. More than anything, he needs a full, healthy season to show whether he can reach his offensive potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Anyone who wondered how much Gonzales’ career .399/.502/.747 line at New Mexico State was a product of the hitting-friendly environment of his home field in college was convinced his bat was for real when he won the Cape Cod League MVP in 2019. A 1.765 OPS in the shortened 2020 season helped him go No. 7 overall in the 2020 Draft and a slow start after coming back from a broken finger during his 2021 debut in High-A was offset by a torrid finish, followed by being one of the best hitters in the Arizona Fall League. Thanks to super-fast hands, Gonzales has elite-level bat speed that allows him to be very quick to the ball and send line drives to all fields, with some believing he might be a 70 hitter on the 20-to-80 scouting scale when all is said and done. Gonzales is a rhythm and timing hitter, something that was lacking right after his injury but showed up consistently after he got settled in. He routinely puts up huge exit velocities with sneaky pop, perhaps average or a tick better down the road. He got to more power than many expected in 2021, but that also came with a higher strikeout rate than anticipated, though there’s confidence Gonzales will find the balance between extra-base authority and swing-and-miss. While it’s his bat that will get him to the big leagues, the Pirates have been pleased with how much progress Gonzales has made defensively at second base, benefitting from time with former infield coordinator Jamey Carroll during the year and former Pirates shortstop Jack Wilson in the offseason. His advanced feel to hit should help him get to Pittsburgh quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzales racked up serious numbers during his college career at New Mexico State, including a ridiculous .448/.610/1.155 line in 16 games during his shortened junior year in 2020. Since the Aggies are known for playing in an extreme hitters’ paradise, Gonzales’ MVP performance in the Cape Cod League, where he hit .351/.451/.630 with wood in his hands, did as much to put him high on the Draft radar and land him No. 7 overall to the Pirates, who gave him full pick value to sign before sending him to their alternate camp and instructs to get as many reps as possible. Few question Gonzales’ ability to swing the bat from the right side of the plate. Talk to anyone who watches the 5-foot-10 infielder swing and they rave about his bat speed, how fast his hands are and how quick to the ball he is. He demonstrated during his time at the alternate training site that he can hit any fastball, with 60 percent of the fastballs he put in play in Altoona registering exit velocities of over 100 mph. He did a nice job of recognizing spin as well, though that’s a steeper learning curve as he faced advanced breaking stuff for the first time. There’s every confidence he’ll adjust to that as well and with his bat speed, he could eventually have average power. While he was drafted as a shortstop, the spot he played as a junior, and got some time there in Altoona, Gonzales played second base almost exclusively at instructs, with nearly everyone believing that to be his long-term home. He runs well and is athletic enough to be acceptable there, but it’s his bat that will get him to the big leagues in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walter was Delaware's best starter as a freshman in 2016, then hurt his elbow the following spring and missed all of 2018 after Tommy John surgery. He fronted the Blue Hens' rotation again as a redshirt junior in 2019, signed for $35,000 as a 26th-rounder and attracted little notice during a ho-hum pro debut. His stock soared after he returned from a year of at-home development during the pandemic shutdown with better stuff, but it has backed up since a bulging disc in his upper back ended his 2022 season in June. Walter added velocity during his layoff, pushing his slider into the low 80s while adding tremendous sweep that overmatches left-handers. His fastball went from 87-91 mph in his debut to 92-97 while keeping its heavy sink in 2021, though it has parked more at 90-92 the last two seasons and is getting whacked. His tumbling low-80s changeup helps keep right-handers in check but has been less effective with less velocity separation from his diminished heater. There's effort in Walter's short-arm, crossfire delivery, yet it provides deception, as does the extension he creates. After pounding the strike zone earlier in his career, including a 68/3 K/BB ratio in 50 Double-A innings in 2022, he has been less aggressive challenging hitters as his fastball has regressed. He might profile best as a multi-inning reliever now and had some success in that role with the Red Sox in July.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Delaware's best starter as a freshman in 2016, Walter blew out his elbow the next spring and missed all of 2018 following Tommy John surgery. After he headlined the Blue Hens rotation again as a redshirt junior in 2019, he signed with the Red Sox for $35,000 as a 26th-rounder and made an unremarkable pro debut. Following a year of at-home development, he opened 2021 in the bullpen before forcing his way into the rotation and posting a 2.92 ERA with a 132/20 K/BB ratio between Low-A and High-A. Walter came back from the pandemic layoff with improved velocity, as his fastball went from 87-91 mph in his debut to sitting at 92-94 with a peak of 97 while retaining its heavy sink. His best pitch is a slider that also has gotten hotter, sitting in the low 80s and destroying left-handers with its sharp horizontal life. He uses a tumbling low-80s changeup to combat right-handers, though they too have difficulty with his slider. In addition to his stuff, Walter also has upgraded his control, averaging 2.0 walks per nine innings last year compared to 3.2 in college. He has a better arsenal than any southpaw in Boston's system and a high floor as at least a multi-inning lefty reliever. If he can build off his breakout season and improve his changeup, he might be significantly more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams popped 95 mph with his fastball as a North Carolina high schooler and 100 mph as an East Carolina freshman, but his development stalled and he went undrafted as a junior in 2020. He finally broke out as a senior, earning American Athletic Conference Pitcher of the Year honors and ranking fifth in NCAA Division I strikeouts per nine innings (14.4) before the Guardians drafted him 23rd overall. Signed for a below-slot $2.25 million, he advanced to Double-A while leading the Minors in opponent average (.173) and ranking third in ERA (1.96) in a spectacular 2022 pro debut. Williams still stands out most with his fastball, which can sit at 94-97 mph late into games and continues to reach triple digits. The biggest reason for his surge is that after years of struggling to spin the ball effectively, he has developed two solid breaking pitches, with his tighter mid-80s slider landing in the zone and missing bats more frequently than his upper-70s curveball with good shape and depth. He also has a solid mid-80s changeup with fade, though it can get too firm at times. Besides upgrading his breaking stuff, Williams also has dramatically improved his control after battling the strike zone in his first three college seasons. He cleaned up his delivery and began repeating it better in 2021, and that carried over into pro ball. Once he gets more consistent with throwing his secondary pitches for strikes, he'll be a mid-rotation starter in Cleveland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams hit 95 mph as a North Carolina high school senior and 100 mph as an East Carolina freshman, but he couldn't grab a rotation role in his first three years of college. Then he dramatically improved in 2021, earning American Athletic Conference pitcher of the year honors and finishing fifth in NCAA Division I in strikeout rate (14.4 per nine innings). The 23rd overall pick in the Draft, he signed for an under-slot $2.25 million and will make his pro debut in 2022. Williams still can light up a radar gun, holding 94-97 mph fastball velocity for several innings and tickling triple digits. After showing little feel for spin before last year, he suddenly added power and shape to his curveball, which now sits in the upper 70s with outstanding metrics. He also turned a mediocre slider into a mid-80s offering that shows flashes of becoming solid while retaining his aptitude for throwing a mid-80s changeup with fade. In addition to improving his breaking pitches, Williams also upgraded his strike-throwing, cutting his walk rate from 4.2 per nine innings in his first three college seasons to 2.3 in his fourth. He cleaned up his delivery during his time at East Carolina and began repeating it better last spring. If his breakout is sustainable, he won't need much time in the Minors before becoming a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamilton led the Big 12 Conference with 31 steals and helped Texas make the College World Series as a sophomore in 2018, but he missed the entire next season after rupturing his Achilles tendon in a motorized scooter accident. The Brewers paid him an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round of the 2019 Draft, and he ranked third in the Minors with 52 steals while reaching Double-A in his 2021 pro debut. Acquired by Boston in the Hunter Renfroe trade that December, he set a Red Sox Minor League record with 70 steals in 2022 and led the Triple-A International League with 57 swipes last year while also making his big league debut. Hamilton's plus-plus speed and savvy on the bases has allowed him to succeed in 85 percent of his steal attempts through three pro seasons, even though opponents know he's going to run. His quickness also enables him to cover plenty of ground in the middle infield, though his fringy arm strength prevents him from making some of the more difficult plays at shortstop. He did display better defensive instincts in 2023, and he also exhibited solid range in some brief time in center field. While Hamilton is a gamechanger on the bases and an asset in the field, he probably doesn't make enough impact offensively to warrant an everyday job. A left-handed hitter, he can use his speed to beat out infield singles and draws a healthy amount of walks, yet he strikes out too much and makes a lot of weak contact. He occasionally can ambush a high fastball but has below-average power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading the Big 12 Conference with 31 steals and helping Texas reach the College World Series as a sophomore in 2018, Hamilton ruptured his Achilles tendon in a motorized scooter accident and missed the following season. Signed by the Brewers for an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round of the 2019 Draft, he ranked third in the Minors in triples (11) and fifth in steals (52) while advancing to Double-A in his 2021 pro debut. Sent to Boston that December as part of the Hunter Renfroe trade, he set a Red Sox Minor League record and placed third in the Minors with 70 steals last year before getting added to the 40-man roster. Hamilton's plus-plus speed is unquestionably his best asset, and he excels as a base stealer, succeeding on 88 percent of his attempts in his first two pro seasons. His quickness also gives him range as a middle infielder, though his fringy arm strength restricts his ability to make some of the more difficult plays at shortstop. He's better suited for second base, where he spent the majority of his time in 2022, but his hands and instincts are average at best, and some evaluators like him more as a potential center fielder. Hamilton's offensive focus should be getting on base to wreak havoc with his speed, yet instead he tries to turn on and launch balls far too often. A left-handed hitter, he draws a decent amount of walks but strikes out too much for a player with his quickness and below-average strength. He does have some mild pull power, but it will be difficult for him to achieve regular playing time in the big leagues unless he overhauls his approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamilton shot up Draft boards with a solid sophomore season at the University of Texas, where he was named to the All-Big 12 second team and the Austin Regional All-Tournament Team after finishing second on the squad with a .291 average to go with a .404 on-base percentage and 31 stolen bases, the most for a Longhorn in 16 years. He was also named Texas’ defensive player of the year. Hamilton missed his junior season after rupturing his Achilles tendon in a scooter accident, but the Brewers love athletic shortstops and they liked this one enough to draft him in the eighth round. Milwaukee persuaded him to sign with a $400,000 bonus, well above slot value of $162,000. It was the second straight year the Brewers tried such a strategy with a high-ceiling college player. They drafted Oregon State pitcher Drew Rasmussen in the sixth round a year earlier when he was recovering from Tommy John surgery. Hamilton reported to 2020 Spring Training at 100 percent, only to be denied his debut season by the coronavirus pandemic. Hamilton’s calling card is some of the best raw speed and baserunning instincts in the organization, but he was also a pleasant surprise with the bat when he reported to the Brewers' fall instructional league as a 23-year-old finally getting a taste of pro ball. Hamilton has little power, but he does hit line drives and reaches base enough to access his speed. His average arm makes him a stretch for shortstop at the highest level, but he has plenty of defensive ability to play a good second base or center field. Wherever he lands, scouts see Hamilton as an up-the-middle defender. The Brewers like his makeup enough that they have pushed him aggressively with a move to Double-A in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An undrafted free agent out of tiny San Joaquin Delta junior college, Denoyer was more or less unknown when the Orioles signed him out of the Northwoods League in 2019. Thanks to the pandemic, he didn’t really burst onto the scene until two years later, when he opened enough eyes to reach High-A Aberdeen as a 23-year-old in 2021. Then, Denoyer was one of the organization's surprise breakouts in 2022, reaching Double-A in May and pitching to a 2.79 ERA with a 69-11 strikeout-to-walk ratio for Bowie. He made up some reps lost to injury with a solid showing in the Arizona Fall League before the Orioles added him to their 40-man roster prior to the Rule 5 Draft in December. The 6-foot-5, 225-pound Denoyer has a starter’s build and a three-pitch mix: a fastball that touches 95 mph and averages 93, a low-80s sweeping breaking ball and a splitter in the mid-to-upper-80s. That combination has allowed him to generate whiffs wherever he’s pitched, including 12.0 strikeouts-per-nine at Bowie and more punchouts (21) than innings (20) in the AFL. He did so while not issuing a ton of walks (2.1 per nine in ’22). So far most of Denoyer's work has come out of the bullpen, but he started in the AFL and pitched at least four innings in eight of his final 10 starts at Bowie. The solid control he’s shown would also seem to bode well for a future multi-inning role. While Denoyer’s ascension may have caught some off guard, his age, frame and repertoire suggest a potential big league swingman with a bulk reliever floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis was the top-ranked college bat in the Draft class of 2021, one who used a huge junior season that spring to catapult him to the top of the Pirates’ board. Pittsburgh was able to save some money by taking the Louisville product No. 1 overall, but they also coveted his bat and work ethic. He showed glimpses of both during his first full season, with wrist injuries limiting him to just 59 games, though he did make up for some lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. Davis’ setup at the plate is a bit unorthodox, but even though he missed considerable time in 2022, he still showed that he’s likely going to hit, and with plenty of power. He has a good approach at the plate, showing off excellent pitch recognition, and he can hit the ball hard to all fields. The right-handed hitter does crowd the plate, a big reason why he got hit 20 times in 2022 (which led to the wrist ailment) and it’s something he might need to adjust to avoid the injury bug. Scouts from other organizations have voiced doubts about Davis’ ability to catch long-term in the big leagues, as he can be a bit stiff behind the dish. The Pirates love his work ethic -- he headed to Florida in January to work with pitchers before Spring Training and his plus-plus arm is an asset. He did get a taste of right field in 2022, where his arm and instincts worked well in case catching doesn’t stick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis put himself on the map as a top college bat for the 2021 Draft class when he posted a 1.179 OPS for Louisville in the shortened 2020 season. He moved into the top of the Draft contention with a .370/.483/.663 line with 15 homers in 2021. The Pirates loved his bat and were blown away by his makeup, vaulting him to the top spot. They saved money to boot, allowing them to get three high-end high school prospects later in the Draft. Davis hit three homers in eight games during his pro debut, though an oblique injury cut his first summer short. While he doesn’t do it conventionally, with a bit of an unorthodox setup and right-handed swing, few doubt he’s going to hit. He walked more than he struck out at Louisville, recognizing pitches well and making consistent hard contact. He can hit it out to all fields and though he can get a little pull-happy at times, he manages his strikeout rate quite well. There were more questions about Davis’ defensive ability, though he has one of the strongest arms in the game. The Pirates were encouraged by his early work behind the plate, with pitchers in the system appearing to like throwing to him. He’s a natural leader, one who not only wants to catch but wants to be the best catcher in baseball, giving the Bucs confidence that he’ll put in the work to be fine as a big league backstop while putting up huge offensive numbers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dubin's college career took him from Erie (N.Y.) CC to Buffalo to Georgetown (Ky.) College, and he earned NAIA All-America honors in 2018 before becoming Georgetown's first Draft pick in 21 years. Signed for a mere $1,000 as a 13th-rounder, he led the High-A Carolina League with 132 strikeouts in 98 2/3 innings in his first full pro season and was part of Houston's postseason player pool in 2020, though he didn't appear in the playoffs. He has continued to miss bats in Triple-A the last two years and likely would have made his big league debut if he didn't miss chunks of both seasons with forearm tightness. Dubin has added 25 pounds and done a better job of using his lower half in his delivery since turning pro, and his fastball has gone from averaging 90 mph at Georgetown to parking at 95-97 mph and touching 101. His mid-80s slider can devastate hitters with its two-plane break, but he went to more of a harder, tighter cutter last year even though the latter is more of an average offering. He also has a low-80s curveball that he struggles to land for strikes and barely uses an upper-80s changeup that's too firm and doesn't have much fade. Despite adding weight as a pro, Dubin is still smaller and skinnier than most starters and projects more as a multi-inning reliever than as rotation fodder at this point. The effort in his delivery leads to additional concerns about his durability and restricts his ability to throw strikes at times. If he can stay healthy, his electric fastball/slider combination should make him a useful bullpen asset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dubin bounced from Erie (N.Y.) CC to Buffalo to Georgetown (Ky.) in college, earning NAIA All-America honors in 2018 and becoming Georgetown's first Draft pick in 21 years. Signed for just $1,000 in the 13th round, he led the High-A Carolina League in strikeouts (132 in 98 2/3 innings) in his first full pro season and made the Astros' postseason pool in 2020, though he didn't appear in the playoffs. He missed two months with forearm tightness last season but returned in late July and dominated Triple-A hitters when healthy, earning a spot on the 40-man roster. Since adding 25 pounds and doing a better job of incorporating his lower half in his delivery as a pro, Dubin has seen his fastball go from averaging 90 mph to sitting at 93-96 and topping out at 99. His mid-80s slider can be devastating with two-plane break that makes it effective against left-handers and right-handers. He relies heavily on those two pitches but also will mix in a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup that gets too firm and has modest fade. Even though he has added strength, Dubin is still shorter and skinnier than a typical starter, and the effort in his delivery creates additional concerns about his ability to hold up in that role. He provides a decent amount of strikes but his control and command are average at best, another reason that he'll likely wind up in a big league bullpen. His fastball/slider combination can be electric when he's healthy, so he could succeed as a high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dubin concluded a nomadic college career that included one year at Erie (N.Y.) CC and two at Buffalo by spending his 2018 senior season at Georgetown (Ky.), where he won NAIA all-America honors and became the school's first Draft pick (13th round) in 21 years. Signed for $1,000, he boosted his stock tremendously in his first full pro season, when he led the high Class A Carolina League with 132 strikeouts in just 98 2/3 innings. He continued to open eyes at Houston's alternate site and pitched his way into the club's 40-man postseason pool, though he was not on the active roster for the playoffs. Dubin has added 25 pounds and done a better job of incorporating his lower half in his delivery since turning pro, and his four-seam fastball has gone from sitting around 90 mph to parking at 93-97 mph and approaching triple digits. His mid-80s slider is an even better pitch, featuring so much movement that it tied up left-handers and right-handers alike in the lower levels of the Minors. He also has added power to his curveball and is working to improve his changeup. Because Dubin is smaller and skinnier than a typical starter and has some effort in his delivery, there are concerns about his ability to hold up as a starter. To remain in the rotation, he'll also have to upgrade his fringy control and command. The Astros could choose to expedite his path to the big leagues as a multi-inning reliever who has the fastball and slider to succeed in high-leverage situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dubin played at three colleges in four years, spending one season at Erie (N.Y.) CC, two at Buffalo and his senior year at Georgetown (Ky.). After he won NAIA All-America honors with a 2.09 ERA and 128 strikeouts in 94 2/3 innings as a senior in 2018, the Astros made him Georgetown's first Draft pick (13th round) in 21 years. He was a revelation in his first full pro season, limiting opponents to a .547 OPS while averaging 12.3 strikeouts in nine innings, mostly in high Class A. Dubin has gained about 3 mph of velocity since turning pro and now deals with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball that tops out at 97. Despite that added heat, his best pitch is a plus slider with high spin rates and so much movement that it has wiped out lefties and righties alike at lower levels. He also has improved his curveball and is working to upgrade his changeup. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 154 pounds, Dubin is extremely skinny and about 50 pounds lighter than a typical big league starter. To remain in the rotation, he'll need to add some strength and refine his control and command so he can work deeper into games. His slider gives him a chance to become a high-leverage reliever, and he might throw even harder in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a fifth-year senior in 2021, Hartwig led Miami (Ohio) pitchers -- a group that included 2021 first-rounder Sam Bachman -- in innings pitched (73 1/3) and finished with a 3.42 ERA and 82 strikeouts, but he went unselected in that July's 20-round Draft. The Mets snagged him as their first non-drafted free-agent signing and moved him to the bullpen. Hartwig led Mets Minor Leaguers with 13 saves and finished with a 1.75 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 83 K’s in 56 2/3 frames across all four full-season levels in 2022. He added seven more appearances in the Arizona Fall League to end the season. The 6-foot-5 right-hander’s 35.5 percent strikeout rate led Mets Minor Leaguers with at least 50 frames in 2022, and a big reason for that was his low-80s slider with good vertical and horizontal break. The pitch could dive away from lunging right-handers or cut sharply to the back foot of a lefty hitter, and it was actually the latter who struggled most against Hartwig, hitting just .150 with a 38.5 percent K rate against him in the regular season. His 93-95 mph fastball played closer to average, but sinking action on it helped him keep healthy ground-ball rates and allow just one homer over his 39 appearances. His mid-80s changeup lags behind the other two in usage but offers at least something of a third option. Hartwig’s walk rates got worse the higher he climbed as hitters knew to lay off the breaking stuff out of the zone. The slider is still so good it’s worth the risk going for that chase, and it has the former RedHawk on the doorstep of the New York bullpen entering 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Balazovic started his pro career as the Twins’ fifth-round pick in the 2016 Draft out of the Canadian high school ranks, he was a projectable right-hander who quickly gained strength and put his name on the map as a Top 100 prospect who went to the Futures Game in 2019. He was added to the 40-man roster after the 2020 shutdown and he pitched pretty well in Double-A in 2021, though a back issue kept him from pitching until June. A knee injury in 2022 sidelined him until May and he clearly wasn’t ready for Triple-A as he struggled for most of the year. He did finish the year well, but was delayed building off of that in 2023 when he suffered a broken jaw in an off-field altercation at the start of Spring Training. When Balazovic first returned from his knee injury, he was not as physical as he had been and his stuff regressed across the board. His upswing at the end included an uptick of his velocity in the right direction, though his average fastball dipped from 96 mph in 2021 to about 94 mph. His power breaking ball can still miss bats but wasn’t as sharp, and his changeup also got hit hard. Not only did Balazovic’s walk rate jump, his command within the zone wasn’t sharp, leading to him giving up 13 hits per nine innings in 2022. All of the numbers looked a bit better in the season’s final month and the hope is that once he returns to the mound in 2023, he can get back to looking like he'll be headed to the middle of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect in Canada from the 2016 Draft class, Balazovic inspired the Twins to take him in the fifth round and go over slot value to sign him. Then, he was a thin, super-projectable high school right-hander. He’s made steady progress since, making his full-season debut in 2018, pitching across two levels of A-ball and going to the Futures Game in 2019 and pitching well at the Twins’ alternate training site and in instructs in 2020 to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. Although a back issue kept him from making his Double-A debut until June 2021, he still managed to miss bats while setting a career high in innings pitched. He was slowed out of the gate in 2022, this time by a knee injury, and never really got on track. As Balazovic has advanced, he’s gotten stronger and thrown consistently harder. That trend continued once he returned to the mound in 2021, with a fastball that averaged 96 mph in Double-A and has good life up in the zone to miss bats. His power breaking ball is also harder and flashes plus to give him another swing-and-miss offering. Balazovic started throwing a splitter as his changeup, with good results, a pitch with more depth off his fastball. Balazovic’s walk rate went up in 2021, and his command in the zone suffered a bit, leading to a higher hit rate, partially because he’s learning to harness his now firmer stuff. But he repeats his delivery well, and there’s deception, making for a tough at-bat. Further refinement of his splitter to go along with a return to his excellent command should allow him to reach his mid-rotation ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the past 10 years, there have been five pitchers drafted and signed in the top five rounds of the Draft out of Canada. Only one, the Braves’ Mike Soroka, has made it to the big leagues. Balazovic, signed as a thin, projectable high school right-hander as a fifth rounder in 2016, has the chance to be the next. After pitching across two levels of Class A ball, and in the Futures Game, in 2019, Balazovic joined the Twins’ alternate training site late in the summer of 2020, throwing well there and in instructional league play last fall, impressing enough to get added to the organization’s 40-man roster. Balazovic has add two inches in terms of height and a ton of good weight since he’s signed, with his stuff ticking up as a result. His fastball now sits consistently in the mid-90s and he can get swings and misses at the top of the zone with life on his four-seamer. When he’s down in the zone, it has good life and generates weak contact, with his high front glove side providing deception for his fastball so hitters don’t pick up the ball well. He throws a hard breaking ball that looks like a slider when he’s locked in, flashing plus and missing more bats. His changeup, once a distant third pitch, has caught up and might be a tick above-average when all is said and done. All of his stuff plays up because of his penchant for throwing strikes, with his fastball command really separating him from other young power arms. Balazovic worked hard to earn his way up to the alternate camp last summer, paving the way to the upper levels of the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Twins selected Balazovic in the fifth round of the 2016 Draft, the hope was that the projectable, but raw Canadian high schooler would eventually grow and develop into a legitimate big league starting pitcher. That's why they went above slot to sign him away from Auburn. It's been a slow process -- it took him three summers to get to full-season ball -- but he's been dominant across two levels of Class A ball and pitched in the 2019 Futures Game, providing confidence that the Draft investment is going to pay off. Not only has Balazovic grown as a pitcher, he's literally grown, adding two inches and 45 pounds of good weight so that he's now a 6-foot-5, 215-pound specimen on the mound. He's thrown consistently harder as he's progressed to the point where he was consistently in the 95-97 mph range with his fastball. It's a heavy sinking heater that elicits weak contact on the ground. His breaking ball can be a bit of a hybrid at times, but at it's best, it's a hard slider that misses a ton of bats and flashes plus. He's worked very hard on his changeup and there's enough separation from his fastball that it's a third at least average offering. Despite his size and his relative inexperience entering pro ball, Balazovic has largely been a solid strike-thrower throughout his pro career, something that should serve him well as he moves up the ladder. He's been treated somewhat cautiously from a workload perspective, but all signs are pointing to him reaching that big league starter ceiling the Twins envisioned when they signed him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2016 Draft approached, Balazovic traveled to Florida with his fellow Canadian high school standouts. The right-hander separated himself with his performance and projectability and the Twins took him in the fifth round that June, going above slot to sign him away from his Auburn commitment. After two summers in the Gulf Coast League, he took a nice step forward while pitching full-season ball for the first time, then another leap in 2019. Balazovic made very good strides during extended spring training and that carried over into his 2018 Midwest League debut. The big right-hander had plenty left in the tank at the end of the year, living in the 92-94 mph range and consistently up to 95 mph with his fastball, and he's been up to 97 mph consistently this season. He throws it with good sinking action to get ground-ball outs. His changeup has improved quite a bit, and while he can still throw it a bit too hard, in the 85-86 mph range, it has more movement and there's more separation between the two pitches because of his uptick in velocity. The slider is still his go-to breaking ball and it flashes plus. There could still be more in the tank as Balazovic continues to fill out his 6-foot-4 frame, giving him considerable ceiling. He's taken a nice step in the right direction toward reaching it, with a big up arrow next to his name, this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 24th round doesn’t even exist anymore, but that’s where the Blue Jays grabbed Horwitz after three productive years at Radford, and he’s carried that level of success throughout the pros. Sporting a career .302 average and .407 OBP in the Minors, the 26-year-old pushed his way onto the 40-man roster in November 2022. He backed that up with his best season yet at Triple-A Buffalo, where he posted a .337/.450/.495 line with 10 homers and more walks (78) than strikeouts (72) over 107 games. He got in 15 contests with the Major League club over two separate stints in June and September. The left-handed slugger has built a reputation on his strong knowledge of the strike zone, and that’s a big reason why he thrived in Triple-A, where the automated ball-strike system helped define that zone more clearly. His .450 OBP was third-highest among full-season Minor League qualifiers. Horwitz rarely whiffed on fastballs with Buffalo and continued to show an all-fields approach that helped him pick up hits aplenty, although his swing lacks the lift that would help him push for average power production. A well-below-average runner, Horwitz has made some strides defensively at first base but has also gotten looks in left field (away from Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s shadow) as the Jays try to find a spot for his bat in the lineup. He remains a better fit at the cold corner, and given his pressing age and roster status, he’s likely a left-handed bat-first option off the bench in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Horwitz put together three productive seasons for Radford in the Big South Conference, and while he didn’t have a flashy Draft profile, he has made the Blue Jays’ scouting crew look smart after selecting him in the 24th round in 2019. Horwitz’s NCAA experience immediately translated that summer as he split 60 games between the Appalachian and Northwest Leagues, batting .307 with an .808 OPS. Following the lost 2020 Minor League season, Horwitz spent most of 2021 at High-A Vancouver before earning a taste of Double-A, batting .294 with 12 home runs and an .862 OPS over 110 games. That included more walks (70) than strikeouts (68). Then Horwitz starred in the Arizona Fall League, where he hit .375 over 16 games. In 2022, Horwitz split 114 games between Double-A and Triple-A, batting .275 with a .391 OBP. He has one of the best plate approaches and abilities to control the strike zone in the organization. That hitting tool and plate approach will need to carry Horwitz, who is solid at first base but may not move well enough to play the outfield in the big leagues. Horwitz offers a very mature at-bat at 25, though, and should adapt quickly to Major League pitching if injuries open up an opportunity for him at some point in 2023. He profiles as a player who will continue to play up to the level he’s assigned to.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Horwitz put up some nice, consistent numbers at Radford University in the Big South, hitting .288 with 25 home runs and an .850 OPS over three seasons. The Blue Jays picked him up all the way down in the 24th round, which has proved to be one of their best selections in the ’19 Draft. Horwitz debuted that summer, hitting .330 over 51 games in the Appalachian League and getting a taste of Low-A. He kept hitting in ’21, batting .294 with 12 homers and an .862 OPS over 105 games in High-A and five in Double-A, but really broke out in the AFL. There, Horwitz hit .375 with a .944 OPS against some of baseball’s best prospects. An above-average plate approach allowed Horwitz to walk (70) more than he struck out (68) in ’21, and that’s where everything starts for him. With good control of the zone, Horwitz works his walks and hits for average, but unlocking more power will be the next step, especially for a prospect splitting time between first base and left field. Horwitz answered that bell by slugging .517 and posting a .930 OPS in 70 games at Double-A New Hampshire to open 2022 -- production that carried him to Triple-A. Without adding surplus value as a defender or runner, Horwitz’s value will be tied closely to his bat, so he'll need to keep the power coming. First base remains the primary position for Horwitz, but he’ll continue to experiment with the corner outfield. He’s earned plenty of fans within the organization with his plate approach and overall offensive improvements.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for an over-slot $247,500 in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, Amaya quickly made an impression with his plate defense and plate discipline. He set a career high with 17 homers and reached Triple-A in 2022 before the Marlins acquired him in a trade for Miguel Rojas in January 2023. He made his big league debut over four games with Miami last June, but got designated for assignment this April and traded to the Astros for right-handed pitching prospect Valente Bellozo. Amaya is a quality defender at shortstop with smooth actions, quick and sure hands, a solid and accurate arm and a good internal clock. He has average speed but solid range and is working to enhance his first-step quickness so that he can cover more ground. He's also quite capable at second and third base. A right-handed hitter, Amaya is at his best when he keeps his stroke under control and focuses on getting on base. He added strength during the pandemic layoff, which enhanced his power but also has led to lapses where he starts hunting home runs and chasing pitches. He makes consistent contact when he swings at strikes and could provide on-base ability with 15 homers per year if he maintains a disciplined approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Amaya out of a suburban Los Angeles high school for an over-slot $247,500 in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, and his plate discipline and defense quickly made him an organization favorite. He bounced back from his worst pro season in 2021 to hit a career-best 17 homers between Double-A and Triple-A last year before the Marlins acquired him for Miguel Rojas in January. He could be Miami's shortstop of the very near future and for the long term. Amaya is most effective when he employs a controlled right-handed stroke and concentrates on getting base. He got stronger during the pandemic layoff, but his newfound power can get him into trouble when he starts hunting home runs and chasing pitches. He settled down more in 2022 and projects as a .250 hitter with 12-15 homers per season and plenty of walks. That type of production would be more than enough to make Amaya a big league regular at shortstop, because he's a quality defender. Not only does he have quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm, but his high baseball IQ and nonstop energy allow him to get the most out of his physical tools. He also is an asset at second and third base and would be a useful utility man if he doesn't hit enough to play regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of former Dodgers middle-infield prospect Frank Amaya, Jacob signed for an above-slot $247,500 out of a suburban Los Angeles high school in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft. His keen batting eye and his glovework quickly made him an organization favorite, and he bounced back from his worst season as a pro in 2021 to hit a career-high 17 homers in 2022. The Marlins acquired him in a January deal for Miguel Rojas.
