He spent 2020 at Chicago's alternate training site, improving his pitch-calling and communication under the tutelage of veteran backstops Jose Lobaton and P.J. Higgins. Amaya stands out most with his work behind the plate. He demonstrated more consistency as a receiver last summer while continuing to frame and block pitches well. His arm rated as average when he turned pro and now grades as solid to plus, and he erased 35 percent of basestealers in 2019. Though Amaya batted just .243/.334/.375 in his first four pro seasons, he has been younger than most of his competition and has shown the ability to manage the strike zone and get on base. He has good feel for the barrel and uses the entire field well, though most of the right-handed hitter's pop comes to his pull side. If he learns to drive the ball more consistently, he could develop into a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Cubs gave out $16.4 million in bonuses (and paid $13.2 million in penalty tax) in the 2015-16 international period, second only to the Dodgers. That haul included seven-figure bonuses for seven position players, the best of whom is Amaya, who signed for $1 million out of Panama. The high Class A Carolina League's youngest batting qualifier in 2019 at age 20, he has played in the last two SiriusXM All-Star Futures Games. Though Amaya's offense and defense are still works in progress, he projects as an all-around contributor. He needs more consistency with his receiving but displays the aptitude to frame and block pitches well. His arm strength has improved from average to at least solid since he has turned pro, and he threw out 35 percent of basestealers in 2019. Amaya shows impressive control of the strike zone, especially for a player who has been much younger than most of his competition. A right-handed hitter, he has good feel for the barrel and is beginning to tap into his solid raw power. He could develop into a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per year and quality defense behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Chicago invested heavily in the international market during the 2015-16 signing period, signing eight players to seven-figure bonuses, including $1.25 million for Amaya. They have pushed him aggressively, assigning him to the short-season Northwest League at age 18 and having him make his full-season debut at age 19 in 2018. He was up to the challenge, playing his way into the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and the low Class A Midwest League all-star game. Amaya's defensive ability and makeup are the traits that initially attracted the Cubs, and he hasn't disappointed in those areas. He's a better receiver and moves better than most catchers his age, already showing the aptitude to frame and block pitches well. His arm has gotten stronger since he turned pro and now grades as solid with a chance to become plus, and it plays up because he gets rid of the ball quickly and makes accurate throws. Amaya's offensive potential also has grown and he has the upside of a solid hitter with power to match. He has nice feel for the barrel, is getting better at managing the strike zone and makes repeated contact from the right side of the plate. He's developing a better understanding of how to tap into his raw power, though he'll need to get stronger after wearing down toward the end of his first year in full-season ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 The Cubs handed out seven-figure deals to eight international prospects during the 2015-16 signing period, including $1 million to land Amaya out of Panama. They were attracted to his work behind the plate and his intangibles, traits that led them to promote him to the short-season Northwest League for his U.S. debut last summer. He was the league's best defensive backstop as an 18-year-old and this year has emerged as one of the game's best catching prospects, earning a spot in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. With his agility and soft hands, Amaya is an advanced receiver for a teenager, framing and blocking pitches well. His arm strength is average but plays better than that because he makes quick and accurate throws, and he erased 41 percent of basestealers in the NWL. His arm strength has improved since he has signed and he could be a plus thrower once he's fully developed. Amaya is starting to make the same type of impact offensively, showing feel for the barrel and the ability to make consistent contact from the right side of the plate. He's doing a better job of waiting for pitches he can do more damage against, allowing him to tap into his power. He moves decently for a catcher but isn't a factor on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been 13 big leaguers who hail from Mercer University, the most recent being Mariners outfielder Kyle Lewis. Cox could be No. 14. In the college-pitching-heavy 2018 Draft, Cox was the Royals’ fifth-round pick and had one of the best full-season debuts in ’19, walking only 38 batters in 130 2/3 innings. Back in game action in 2021, Cox posted a 3.00 ERA with 56 strikes and 25 walks across 63 innings at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. He worked through some arm fatigue, which led to a lower average on his fastball and struggles with control. Cox’s arsenal includes three above-average pitches, starting with his low-90s fastball that has good life to it and misses bats on both sides of the plate. His main secondary pitch is his curveball, which is one of the best in the system. It has true 12-to-6 action to it and flashes plus with power behind it. Cox’s feel for spin allows him to have a new distinctive slider in the low-80s, and he rounds out his arsenal with a changeup that’s he’s been working on getting a feel for on the mound. Cox features a repeatable delivery and arm action. While he hasn’t moved as quickly as some of the others from his Draft class, Cox put together a solid year in Double-A despite the arm fatigue and higher walk rate. The Royals were faced with a roster crunch this past offseason and left Cox off the 40-man, exposing him to the Rule 5 Draft, but he’s still high on their radar and has a future in the big league rotation if he can get completely healthy. He also wouldn’t be out of place as a big arm in the bullpen, especially if he’s limited to his fastball and curveball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cox’s alma mater, Mercer University, has produced 13 big leaguers since the program’s inception in 1897. Mariners outfielder Kyle Lewis is the most recent. Cox could be next. The Royals drafted him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft, and the lefty was a model of efficiency in his first full season between Class A and Class A Advanced. Cox had a tough summer working at the Royals' alternate training site in 2020, adjusting to more advanced hitters and working on his secondary pitches, but he left in a good spot heading into 2021. Cox operates with three Major League-caliber pitches that he controls well. He usually sits in the low 90s with his fastball, but he can dial the above-average pitch up to 95-96 mph. His curveball is one of the best in the system, a true plus pitch thrown with power and 12-to-6 downer action that gets him whiffs on both sides of the plate. His feel for spin also translates into a distinctly different slider that sits in the low 80s and can be a solid pitch at times. His average changeup has improved, and he’s been able to command it better recently with fastball-like arm speed in the mid-80s. His stuff shows natural bat-missing ability, and he’s able to repeat his delivery and arm action, which has lowered his walk rate from college. Cox bulked up some before going to the alternate training site, and it might have led to some of his battles in 2020. He struggled with getting the ball down, which led to a ton of contact against him. But the Royals were encouraged with where he left things, and he's enjoyed a bounceback year for the most part at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. He has the makeup and talent to project as a big league starter but would not be out of place as a big arm near the back of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mercer University has produced 13 big leaguers since the program’s inception in 1897, the most recent being 2016 first-round pick Kyle Lewis, who made his Mariners debut in 2019. Cox, whom Kansas City took in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft, could be the next to join that exclusive list. After he struggled to throw strikes while pitching to mixed results in college seasons, Cox was a model of efficiency in his first full season, posting a 2.76 ERA as well as strong strikeout and walk rates while totaling 130 2/3 innings between Class A Lexington and Class A Advanced Wilmington. Cox’s stuff has improved across the board in pro ball, as he now operates with three Major League-caliber pitches that he controls well. The big left-hander can reach back for 95-96 mph but usually sits in the low 90s while pitching to both sides of the plate with his fastball. He complements his above-average heater with one of the better curveballs in the system. It’s a true plus pitch, thrown with power and 12-to-6 downer action that nets him whiffs against hitters on both sides of the plate. Cox rounds out his arsenal with an average changeup that he throws with fastball-like arm speed in the mid-80s. Cox’s ability to repeat his delivery and arm action have improved in lockstep with the 6-foot-4 left-hander’s physical gains, and he issued 2.9 walks-per-nine in his full-season debut after posting 4.5 BB/9 during his Mercer career. He has shown natural bat-missing ability throughout his career and does a good job keeping the ball in the park despite being a fly-ball pitcher. The Royals see him as a future big league starter and think Cox will continue to move quickly through the Minors in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mercer University has produced a handful of big leaguers, most recently reliever Cory Gearrin, and might best be known recently for producing first-round pick Kyle Lewis, now with the Mariners. Cox parlayed a very strong junior season at the Georgia school into a fifth-round selection and above-slot bonus in the 2018 Draft, then went out and pitched extremely well during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Appalachian League. The Royals think they might have gotten a steal in the big left-hander, as his stuff during his debut all ticked up. He looked like a late-first-round type of college lefty, showing flashes of four above-average pitches across the board with plus command of it, albeit in a small sample size. His fastball touched 95 mph with good run and sink, and he used his slider very effectively, backdooring and backfooting it at will. He mixed in his power curve and changeup very effectively. Cox got to spend some time with fellow lefty and 2018 draftee Daniel Lynch and should benefit from working with the other college arms from the Draft class. He pitches with a bit of a small-school chip on his shoulder, something that could help propel him up the ladder, and up this list, quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following standout turns in the Northwoods and Cape Cod Leagues, Pfaadt became the second-highest player selected in Division II Bellarmine history when he went in the fifth round to the D-backs in the shortened 2020 Draft. He established a good baseline by playing at three levels in his first full season in 2021 before exploding last year. The Arizona hurler became the first Minor League pitcher to strike out more than 200 batters since 2011 when he fanned 218 batters over Double-A and Triple-A, and his 167 frames also led the Minors. The 6-foot-4 right-hander topped out at 96.2 mph in the Pacific Coast League but is typically more around 93-94 mph with his fastball. The pitch has enough carry to work up in the zone, giving another tick or two of quality. Pfaadt utilized his mid-80s slider the most among his secondary pitches (roughly 28 percent of the time at the Minors’ top level), and it got a healthy amount of swing-and-miss because of its promising sweep across the zone. A mid-80s changeup moved the other way toward his arm-side and dove enough out of the zone to have a higher whiff percentage than the slider, while his upper-70s curveball is mostly used for show and little else. Pfaadt had the lowest walk rate (4.8 percent) among D-backs full-season qualifiers, and while his ability to pitch in the zone made him hittable in the past, he did a better job of working its periphery and letting the quality of his stuff do the work. His arsenal, durability and strike-throwing prowess have gotten Pfaadt to the Majors in 2023, and he needs to build on what he showed in the Minors to stick as a prominent piece of the Arizona rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from NCAA Division-II Bellarmine, Pfaadt made a name for himself in the Northwoods and Cape Cod leagues over the 2018 and ’19 summers. He was off to a strong start in 2020 (1.38 ERA with 27 strikeouts over 26 innings) before the coronavirus pandemic canceled the rest of the season. The D-backs selected the 6-foot-4, 220-pound right-hander in the fifth round of the 2020 Draft and signed him for a below-slot $100,000. It didn’t take long before the pick looked like a steal as Pfaadt pitched his way across three levels and worked his way up to Double-A in his 2021 professional debut. Pfaadt operates with a 92- to 97-mph four-seam fastball that cuts and a 93- to 95-mph two-seamer with armside run. The heavy sink generates a lot of ground-ball outs for the 6-foot-4 right-hander and he complements the fastballs with a changeup and a pair of breaking balls. Some evaluators feel the fading changeup is his best pitch, while the curveball and slider grade out as average offerings. The two breaking balls used to blend together at times, but Pfaadt has begun to separate them, getting vertical break on the curveball and more horizontal action on the slider. As the two pitches become more defined, he may be able to miss even more bats after posting a 10.9 K/9 in 2021. A throwback pitcher who brings both hands up over his head in his delivery, Pfaadt can throw all of his pitches for strikes and holds his velocity deep into his starts. With above-average-to-plus command, he’s been guilty of throwing too many strikes on occasion and will work his way through the system as a starter. He has the potential to develop into a mid-rotation starter, but if he has to transition to the bullpen, his heavy fastball and ability to miss bats would play well in high-leverage situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever in his first two years at Central Arkansas, Stone got just four starts as a junior in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season but finished with a 13-strikeout no-hitter and became the highest-drafted pitcher in Bears history. After the Dodgers signed him for a well below-slot $97,500 with the penultimate pick in the truncated five-round Draft, they helped him significantly upgrade his stuff, which allowed him to lead the Minors with a 1.48 ERA in 2022. He regressed a bit last season as he struggled through a rough first half, yet he made his big league debut in May and spent four stints in Los Angeles. Stone barely employed a fading changeup in college before the Dodgers outfitted him with a more powerful mid-80s version with devastating tumble at its best that grades as a plus-plus weapon. The only downside is that he falls in love with his cambio, using it more often than any of his other pitches, and big leaguers weren't fooled by it as much as Minor Leaguers were. His low release point produces good carry with a 93-95 mph four-seam fastball that reaches 97, but his heater lacks life and got mashed in 2023, when he had more success with a little-used sinker with similar velocity. His mid-80s slider shows flashes of becoming a solid pitch but lacks consistency, and he has a less effective 89-91 mph cutter that he can throw for strikes more easily. Stone's fastball dodged more barrels and his slider had better shape when he dominated in 2022, and he still could be a No. 3 or 4 starter if he can recapture that form. Using his heater more often could help him improve its movement and command, which would make his changeup even more effective. He's not very physical but his athleticism and efficient delivery help him maintain his stuff and throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stone led Central Arkansas with six saves as a sophomore in 2019 before moving to the rotation, where he authored a 13-strikeout no-hitter against Southeastern Louisiana in his fourth and final start of the pandemic-shortened 2020 season. Though he didn't get a lot of scouting exposure, the Dodgers made him the highest-drafted pitcher in school history, selecting him in the fifth round with the penultimate pick in the truncated Draft. His stuff has made a huge leap since he signed for a well below-slot $97,500, and he ranked first in the Minors in ERA (1.48) and fifth in strikeout rate (12.4 per nine innings) in 2022. Stone barely used a fading changeup in college but he now has a harder, mid-80s cambio with devastating tumble, a plus-plus pitch that he threw more than his four-seam fastball in 2022. After averaging 92 mph with his heater at Central Arkansas, he now sits at 94-96 mph and peaks at 98, and his low release point creates plenty of induced vertical break. He also has scrapped a downer curveball and developed a solid slider that showed improved shape while parking in the mid-80s last season. While Stone is less physical than desired for a starter, he's athletic and has an efficient delivery that helps him hold his stuff and provide consistent strikes. His biggest need is to add some life to his fastball, which doesn't miss as many bats as metrics suggest it should. He has little left to prove in the Minors and projects as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading Central Arkansas with six saves and a 1.52 ERA in 2019, Stone moved to the rotation as a junior and spun a 13-strikeout no-hitter against Southeastern Louisiana in his final outing of the shortened 2020 college season. The Dodgers made him the highest-drafted pitcher in school history, selecting in the fifth round with the penultimate pick of the truncated Draft. Signed for a well below-slot $97,500, he showed improved stuff in his pro debut while reaching High-A and averaging 13.6 strikeouts per nine innings, which would have ranked fifth in the Minors if he weren't five innings short of qualifying. Stone went from working with a 90-94 mph fastball as a college starter to averaging 94 mph and touching 98 in his first season as a pro, and his low release point creates induced vertical break that leaves hitters scuffling to get on top of his heater. He barely used a mid-80s changeup with some fade in college but now has a harder, devastating cambio that drops off the table. He has scrapped his downer curveball to focus on a harder mid-80s slider/cutter and is working to add more sweep to help combat right-handers. Stone aggressively attacks hitters with all three of his pitches and provides strikes. Though he's less physical than a typical starter, his efficiency and twitchy athleticism may help him remain in that role. Los Angeles also could try to expedite him to the big leagues as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Irvin overlapped with top Nationals pitching prospect Cade Cavalli on the 2018 Oklahoma staff and went to the Nationals in the fourth round that year after two solid seasons as a Sooners starter. After spending all of his first full season at Single-A, he missed out on 2020 like everyone else and then didn’t pitch in a Minor League game in 2021 due to Tommy John surgery. Irvin returned to the mound last year and lasted 103 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A, posting a 4.79 ERA over 15 starts with a more promising 25.5 percent K rate at Harrisburg. The 6-foot-6 right-hander showed encouraging velocity in his return from the elbow injury, sitting in the mid-90s while topping out around 97 mph. The velocity waned as he worked deeper into games, but that likely had something to do with the workload after such a long layoff. A low-80s curveball displayed promising break, and he landed it for enough strikes and whiffs outside the zone to help push his strikeout-an-inning pace. An upper-80s changeup remains fringy but hasn’t hurt him too badly against lefties. Irvin’s 6.6 percent walk rate ranked second among Nationals Minor Leaguers with at least 100 frames in 2022, and that will keep him in a starting role. Washington added him to its 40-man in November, and he is entering his age-26 season -- signs he’ll need to push for the Majors soon, perhaps as a two-pitch reliever if he runs into starting snags in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It will be some time before we see results from Irvin on the mound. The 6-foot-6 right-hander was a standout at the University of Oklahoma, where he pitched Friday nights. Irvin posted a 3.41 ERA with 115 K’s and 28 walks in 95 innings as a junior, prompting the Nationals to grab him in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft. He spent his first full season at Class A Hagerstown and held his own in the South Atlantic League with a 3.79 ERA, 1.25 WHIP and 113 strikeouts in 128 1/3 frames. Irvin looked like he was making improvements at the Nationals’ alternate site in Fredericksburg, but developed forearm and elbow issues that required Tommy John surgery in October. He will be out for the entire 2021 season as a result. Before the injury, the former Sooner was showing promising signs of using his size to pump fastballs with increased velocity in the mid-90s, touching 97 mph at times. The high-70s curveball has been a plus pitch at times and was only held back by its inconsistency, while the changeup sat behind the heater and breaker. Irvin’s arm action could get long at times, but the Nationals weren’t overly concerned that would inhibit his stuff over the long term. It all comes down to what kind of pitcher Irvin can be coming back from the surgery. Returning from Tommy John is not as difficult as it once was, but Irvin will have the added task of proving he can maintain the velocity jump he showed in 2020. If he does, his Major League chances are all the better. If that fastball doesn’t hold, there is much more pressure on the secondaries to prove his worth as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Irvin moved into Oklahoma’s rotation as a true freshman and improved in that role in each of the next years, ultimately garnering Big 12 All-Conference honors as a junior in 2018, when he ranked among the conference leaders in strikeouts (1st, 63), opponent batting average (1st, .197) and ERA (6th, 2.94). The Nationals made the Sooners’ Friday night starter their fourth-round pick in June, signing him for $550,000. Irvin overcame a slow start to finish strong at Class A Hagerstown in '19, posting a 2.95 ERA over his final 20 starts, then showed more velocity in ’20 while pitching at Washington’s alternate training site. But after experiencing a bout of forearm tightness during fall instructional camp, Irvin underwent Tommy John surgery late in October that will sideline him for all of 2021. At 6-foot-6, 225 pounds, Irvin has the size and durability needed to start. He began to use his body to generate velocity late in the season and saw his low-90s fastball jump to 94-96 mph. His fastball command also took a step forward after the Nationals encouraged him to start attacking hitters on the inner half of the plate. Irvin threw a slider in college but has scrapped it as a pro in favor of a curveball that can flash plus but lacks consistency. His changeup is a work in progress and will need to be developed, especially after he permitted a .273/.320/.439 slash line to left-handed hitters in the South Atlantic League. While Irvin doesn’t miss as many bats as his stuff suggests he should, Nats club officials believe the whiffs will start to come as he improves his pitch mix, reins in his fastball command and develops a more effective changeup. If it all clicks, Irvin could start to move quickly en route to backend starter or long-relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller began his college career at Blinn College, a junior college in Texas, then moved to Texas A&M after one year. He pitched out of the Aggies' bullpen for two years before getting the chance to start in 2021. He showed his premium stuff could potentially play enough as a starter to go in the fourth round of the Draft to the Mariners, then jumped on the fast track by pitching his way to Double-A in his first full season, finishing with a combined .195 batting average against while striking out 11 per nine. Over the course of a full season and more than 133 innings, Miller showed his stuff will hold up. He has at an easily plus fastball with high spin, a pitch that averaged 95 mph in Double-A and touched triple digits. He has a distinct hard mid-80s slider with power and depth and a slower upper-70s curve that can both miss bats, with the slider ahead of the curve. He also has an effective heavy mid-80s changeup. There were those who thought Miller was destined to head back to the bullpen because he had struggled with command and has a high-tempo delivery. But he’s made huge strides in his ability to find the strike zone while repeating his delivery that features a ton of arm speed, giving him a very good chance to join a big league rotation soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite being just a fourth-round pick less than 12 months ago, Miller has more makings than arguably any pitcher in the system to make an aggressive leap. He flashed 99 mph in Minor League Spring Training and has a gnarly slider that could probably play in a big league bullpen sooner than later. His trajectory will likely be determined by what profile the Mariners view him as long term. Miller went the JUCO route in college, transferring from Blinn (Texas) after one season to Texas A&M, where he had to prove himself a full-time reliever before finally getting the chance to start in his final season. That opportunity was a big part of why he turned down his 38th-round selection by the Marlins in 2018 and other opportunities in the shortened ‘20 Draft. Despite the transition from the bullpen, Miller held his velocity and featured some of the best fastball metrics in last year’s Draft. He has three effective secondary offerings, the best of which is a mid-80s slider with power and depth. He also utilizes an upper-70s curveball as an offspeed pitch and mixes in a heavy mid-80s changeup. Though he has a high-tempo delivery, Miller generates his stuff with arm speed more than effort. He has shown the ability to maintain the quality of his pitches deep into games. His arm action is a bit long and leads to some inconsistencies with his control and command that he'll need to iron out to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2018 supplemental first-rounder from a Florida high school, Edwards signed with the Padres for an over-slot $2.6 million and quickly established himself as one of baseball's top second-base prospects. After the Rays acquired him in the Jake Cronenworth trade in December 2019, he lost 2020 to the pandemic before his performance took a downturn the next two seasons. Tampa Bay declined to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, instead dealing him and J.T. Chargois to the Marlins for righty pitching prospects Marcus Johnson and Santiago Suarez. Edwards displayed advanced feel for the barrel while hitting .320 in his first three pro seasons, then slumped to .246 while striking out at a 19 percent clip in Triple-A last season. The switch-hitter lost his approach and got too aggressive in 2022 but has gotten back to what makes him successful this year while ranking among the Minor League leaders in hitting and contact rate. He matched his previous career total of six homers in four years by early August, though he still features well below-average power. While Edwards once had double-plus speed, he was more of a plus runner in 2022 before ticking up a bit this season, when he has shown better basestealing aptitude than ever. His quickness allows him to cover ground in the infield but his fringy arm strength limits his effectiveness at shortstop and third base. He's more reliable than flashy at second, the position at which he has the best chance to become a big league regular, and the Marlins have deployed him in center field for the first time in his pro career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres paid Edwards an over-slot $2.6 million as a 2018 supplemental first-rounder from a Florida high school, then traded him along with Hunter Renfroe and Esteban Quiroz to the Rays in December 2019 to acquire Jake Cronenworth and Tommy Pham. After losing the '20 season to the pandemic, Edwards has seen his prospect stock dip significantly in the last two seasons. Rather than protect him on its 40-man roster in November, Tampa Bay dealt him and J.T. Chargois to the Marlins for right-handed pitching prospects Marcus Johnson and Santiago Suarez. A career .320 hitter entering 2022, Edwards batted just .246 in Triple-A. While he exhibited elite bat control in the past, he struck out at a career-high 18.8 percent clip this year. He has limited offensive upside because he rarely drives the ball and produces little power, and his ability to make contact cuts into his walk totals. Edwards' best tool remains his plus-plus speed, though he never has been a particularly prolific basestealer and ran less than ever this season. While his quickness gives him range, his fringy arm strength limits his effectiveness on the left side of the infield and leaves him best suited to play second base. He may be more utilityman than regular, and he'll have to regain his past hitting ability to claim a role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres went well above slot value to get Edwards in the 2018 Draft, signing him for $2.6 million and away from a Vanderbilt commitment after selecting him No. 38 overall. He followed up his strong pro debut with an even better first full season, batting .322 with 34 steals between Class A Fort Wayne and Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, while also finishing tied for the third in the Minors with 162 hits. After the season, the Padres traded Edwards to Tampa Bay, packaging him with Hunter Renfroe to get Tommy Pham and Jake Cronenworth in a December 2019 deal. The Rays added Edwards to their alternate training site group in August, then got their first extended look at the young infielder in fall instructional league. Edwards has several leadoff-man qualities in his natural hitting ability, approach and speed. He will hit the ball to all fields from both sides of the plate, showing a penchant for making quality contact and a discerning eye, with an approach that leads to minimal swing and miss. Edwards is a threat to run whenever he gets on base and stole 56 bases with an 82.4 percent success rate across his first two seasons. The Rays think Edwards will develop more pop as he gets stronger and learns to generate more bat speed, but even then, he’s unlikely to offer anything more than well-below-average home-run power. Edwards is a capable shortstop but profiles as more of a true second baseman in the pro ranks. He’s at least an above-average defender at the keystone, one with smooth actions, soft hands and average arm strength that was stretched thin as a shortstop. Edwards isn’t flashy but does all the little things needed to help a team win, projecting as a top-of-the-order regular at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Edwards spurned his Vanderbilt commitment to sign with the Padres for $2.6 million -- more than $700,000 above his slot's value -- after they selected him with the No. 38 overall pick in the 2018 Draft. He reached the Class A Short Season Northwest League and batted .346 with 22 steals across two levels during a strong pro debut, then posted a .322 average with 34 steals and finished tied for third in the Minors in hits (162) while climbing from Class A Fort Wayne to Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in his first full season. However, it will now be up to the Rays to further Edwards' development after they acquired him, Hunter Renfroe and a player to be named later from the Padres in December in exchange for Tommy Pham and Jake Cronenworth. Edwards has prototypical leadoff-man tools with his plus-plus speed, advanced approach and innate feel to hit to all fields from both sides of the plate. A burner out of the box and a threat to run whenever he's on base, Edwards has already proven to be a gifted basestealer in the pro ranks, swiping 56 bases with an 82.4 percent success rate between his first two seasons. He projects as a true plus switch-hitter, one who makes a ton of quality contact, coaxes his share of walks and rarely swings and misses. He recorded 47 multihit games in his first full season and finished tied for ninth in the Minors (400 PA min.) in swinging-strike rate, whiffing at just above a 4-percent clip. While Edwards will never offer much in the way of over-the-fence power, his wheels and knack for hitting line drives should net him plenty of extra-base hits. After being deployed as a shortstop to begin his career, Edwards spent most of his first full season manning second base. He profiles as an above-average defender at the keystone on account of his smooth actions, soft hands and average arm strength that was stretched thin as a shortstop. And while he currently trails both Wander Franco and Vidal Brujan on Tampa Bay's middle-infield depth chart, evaluators tend to agree that Edwards possesses the ingredients needed to become a quality everyday player at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Edwards passed on a Vanderbilt commitment to sign for $2.6 million with the Padres in 2018, more than $700,000 above his slot's value. The switch-hitting speedster opened his career in the Rookie-level Arizona League and then advanced to Class A Short Season Tri-City, batting .346 with 22 steals across the two levels during an impressive pro debut. He was equally impressive in his first full season, posting a .322 average with 34 steals while climbing from Class A Fort Wayne to Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore. But it will now be up to the Rays to further Edwards' development after they acquired him and Hunter Renfroe and a player to be named later from the Padres in December in exchange for Tommy Pham and Jake Cronenworth. Edwards is a bit undersized at 5-foot-10, but his skill set makes that easy to overlook. He stands out most for his speed, an easy plus-plus tool that can legitimately impact games. At the plate, Edwards uses all fields well, and he owns an advanced knowledge of the strike zone. While he's not likely to be a home run threat, he could grow into his frame for more extra-base pop with an Eric Young-type build. He has excellent actions and footwork at shortstop and has shown he has enough arm to stay on the left side of the infield. With a combination of a mature approach, strong contact skills from both sides of the plate and nearly elite speed, Edwards has all the requisite tools to hit atop a lineup for a long time. An ability to stick up the middle adds even more value to his profile and gives him a realistic Major League floor to go along with a high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fletcher was one of college baseball's best outfield defenders during his three seasons at Arkansas and the Razorbacks' top hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost in the finals to Oregon State. A 2019 supplemental second-round pick by the Diamondbacks, he batted .301/.350/.441 in his 28-game big league debut last summer before breaking his left index finger in late August. The younger brother of the Braves' David Fletcher, he joined the White Sox in a February trade for righty pitching prospect Cristian Mena. Fletcher continues to stand out most with his defense. Though he's just an average runner, he's faster under way and possesses tremendous instincts, allowing him to cover a lot of ground in center field. A plus defender at all three outfield spots, he also has solid arm strength and recorded four assists in 24 starts in the Majors. Because he offers less impact at the plate, Fletcher projects more as a fourth outfielder than a regular. He has some sneaky strength in his 5-foot-6, 185-pound frame but ordinary bat speed and not the smoothest left-handed swing. He fishes for too many pitches outside the strike zone and doesn't turn on pitches or drive them in the air on a consistent basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter in center for Arkansas and key part of the 2018 College World Series finalist squad, Fletcher became the 75th overall pick in 2019 when he joined the D-backs. Arizona added Fletcher to its 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in November 2022, and Team Italy selected him for the World Baseball Classic roster (along with brother David) last spring. He made his big league debut in 2023, slashing .301/.350/.441 in 28 games, then went to the White Sox in a February trade for righty pitching prospect Cristian Mena. Fletcher’s improvements in picking his pitches and protecting the plate correlated with his offensive performance in 2022 and continued last season. The hitter-friendly environments flatter his power performance as a 5-foot-9 left-handed hitter who is better known for spraying the ball the other way, but there’s still enough pop for him to hit double-digit homers in The Show. While Fletcher is just an average runner, he gets great reads off the bat and is efficient with his routes to the ball, translating into outs for his team. He has the plus range and arm strength to handle all three outfield positions. He's 26 and doesn't come with a high ceiling, but he should get the chance to establish himself with a rebuilding White Sox club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter in center for Arkansas, Fletcher was the Razorbacks' best hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost to Oregon State in the Finals. As with older brother, David, an infielder with the Angels, Dominic’s skills still stand out more than his pure physical ability. The D-backs took Fletcher 75th overall in the 2019 Draft and sent him straight to Low-A, where he produced an impressive .318/.389/.463 line with 20 extra-base hits in 55 games. Bumped up to Double-A for his 2021 full-season debut, Fletcher got off to a slow start and had a bit of an up-and-down season, but made some adjustments throughout the year and finished strong, hitting nearly .400 in September. Arizona likes Fletcher’s left-handed swing and is pleased with the way he uses the entire field. The 5-foot-9, 185-pounder has surprising power for his size and could develop into a 15-homer guy in the Majors. He’s still improving and fine-tuning his approach, but overall Fletcher is a polished hitter who puts together quality at-bats. He makes up for his average speed with tremendous instincts. Fletcher consistently gets good jumps and some club officials believe he’s one of the best defenders in the entire organization. He’s primarily played center, but has the skill set to be an above-average defender at all three outfield spots with a strong, accurate arm. Fletcher has a floor of a fourth outfielder and the D-backs have fallen in love with the way he plays. Given the career his brother has put together and the fact that Dominic has superior tools, the D-backs are bullish on his chances to finish closer to his ceiling than his floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter in center for Arkansas, he was the Razorbacks' best hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost to Oregon State in the finals. As with his older brother David, an infielder with the Angels, his skills still stand out more than his pure physical ability. The D-backs took Fletcher with the last of their seven picks on Day 1 of the 2019 Draft and sent him straight to Class A Kane County, where he produced an impressive .318/.389/.463 line with 20 extra-base hits in 55 games. Fletcher got off to a slow start in 2021 as he was bumped up to Double-A, but after a few weeks, he adjusted to the new level and started to perform better offensively. Though he won't wow you with any one of his tools, the combination, along with his instincts, should carry him far. The Diamondbacks like Fletcher’s left-handed swing and how he uses it to hit to all fields with some surprising power for a 5-foot-9 guy. He puts together very consistent at-bats and competes hard. He could develop into a 15-homer guy in the big leagues. Fletcher is an average runner but receives above-average grades for his center-field defense because he has excellent instincts and consistently gets good jumps that allow him to track down balls from gap to gap. While he’s primarily played center, he has the skill set to be an above-average defender at all three outfield spots and possesses a strong, accurate arm that flashes plus at times. Fletcher has a floor of a fourth outfielder and the D-backs have fallen in love with the way he plays and think he could have more potential than that. Given the career his brother has put together and the fact that Dominic has superior tools, the D-backs are bullish on his chances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fletcher one of the top defensive outfielders in the 2016 prep class, but his lack of profile tools and commitment to Arkansas left him undrafted. A three-year starter in center for the Razorbacks, he was their best hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost to Oregon State in the finals. As with his older brother David, an infielder with the Angels, his skills still stand out more than his pure physical ability. The D-backs took Fletcher with the last of their seven picks on Day 1 of the 2019 Draft and sent him straight to Class A Kane County, where he produced an impressive .318/.389/.463 line with 20 extra-base hits in 55 games. The Diamondbacks like Fletcher’s left-handed swing and how he uses it to hit to all fields. He has a surprising amount of raw power for a player who is listed at 5-foot-9 and can get to it during games, albeit in streaks rather than consistently. That could translate to 15-plus homer seasons for him at the highest level, though he will first need to trim some of the swing-and-miss from his game after striking out at a 21-percent clip in his pro debut. To go along with the power, scouts also think Fletcher could develop into an average hitter. Fletcher is an average runner but receives above-average grades for his center-field defense because he has excellent instincts and consistently gets good jumps that allow him to track down balls from gap to gap. He has displayed plus arm strength in the past, though it played closer to average in 2019. The potential is there for Fletcher to develop into a second-division regular, though his offensive package may fit better for a fourth outfielder than an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bolton was a projectable high school right-hander from California who would have headed to the University of Michigan had the Draft not worked out. The Pirates, never an organization to shy away from high-upside prep arms, kept him off campus by going slightly over slot to sign the right-hander in the sixth round of the 2017 Draft. Despite missing much of his first full season with a forearm issue, Bolton was able to pitch his way to Double-A in 2019 and then pitched well at the Pirates’ alternate training site in 2020. Bolton has a three-pitch mix that’s trending upwards -- four considering he uses two distinct fastballs effectively. His four-seamer is up to 97 mph and thrown with high spin rate that leads to ride up in the zone. His two-seamer is more in the 93-95 mph range with good sink that has led to a lot of ground-ball outs. His slider has become sharper and less slurvy, flashing signs of being an out pitch and his changeup gives him another at least average offering. While he’s a good strike-thrower, Bolton needs to continue to refine his fastball command within the strike zone. That, plus continued sharpening of and trust in his secondary stuff, should allow him to reach his ceiling as a No. 3-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2017 Draft approached, many felt Bolton, a Northern California high school standout, was set on heading to the University of Michigan for college. The Pirates, never ones to shy away from aggressively acquiring prep pitchers in the Draft, knew he was signable, and went just a bit above slot to sign him for $300,000 in the sixth round. He was able to advance to full season ball in 2018, though he was shut down in July with forearm tightness. Bolton is healthy and back on track for 2019 so he can get back to developing his interesting three-pitch mix. He'll actually throw a pair of fastballs in the 90-95 mph range, a two-seamer with sink that can elicit weak contact on the ground as well as a four-seamer. As he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame, there could be more velocity to come. Like many young pitchers, his secondary stuff still needs work, but his feel for his slider and changeup all point to them being at least solid average pitches in the future. There's not a lot of track record, but Bolton has thus far filled up the strike zone consistently. A tireless worker, Bolton could be poised to make a large jump up this list as he continues to refine his stuff and mature physically and mentally. The key in 2019 will be to get in a full season's worth of healthy innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New Mexico State is a college hitters' paradise, so scouts weren’t sure what to make of Ortiz’s gaudy numbers as a three-year starter there, particularly his .422/.474/.697 line as a junior. The Orioles figured at least his defensive acumen was worth taking in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, but it took a while to really know what kind of all-around player they had on their hands, between the pandemic in 2020 and a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder cutting his 2021 season short. He took a big step forward with a healthy 2022 in which he reached Triple-A, then hit .321/.378/.507 with Norfolk last year while making multiple stops in Baltimore. He was traded to the Brewers as part of the Corbin Burnes blockbuster in February. Since being drafted, Ortiz has added a lot of strength that’s enabled him to consistently register high exit velocities. He hasn’t sacrificed any of his elite bat-to-ball skills, striking out just 17.2 percent of the time in his Minor League career while showing the ability to drive the ball to all fields with solid in-game pop. There’s never been any question about his ability to defend. He has plus hands, actions, instincts and the ability to slow the game down, not to mention more than enough arm for shortstop. He’s shown the ability to play a plus second base and can even slide over to third, something that could come in handy given Milwaukee’s larger need at the hot corner with Willy Adames handling short. Adames is a free agent next season, however, and Ortiz could slide over to his natural position for the long haul in Milwaukee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
