He throws plenty hard enough, frequently touching 96-97 mph in the big leagues last summer, and gets hitters to swing under the pitch with regularity. He’s added more sweep to his slider as a pro and has an excellent fading changeup. Both are thrown in the low 80s and flash plus, and he also folds in an upper-70s curveball that does blend with his slider at times. There’s deception in the 6-foot-4 lefty’s delivery thanks to his lower three-quarters arm slot, not to mention his angle and extension. He’s struggled with his command at times, but made some nice strides in the strike-throwing department in 2022, helping him look more and more like a mid-rotation big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a dominant sophomore season at Saint Mary's in 2018, Waldichuk scuffled the following spring as he tried to throw harder, allowing the Yankees to draft him in the fifth round. He has found more velocity since turning pro and hit 98 mph while working out on his own during the pandemic shutdown in 2020. That led to a spectacular full-season debut in 2021, when he opened the year by not allowing a run in 30 2/3 innings in High-A. He finished fourth in the Minors in strikeouts (163 in 110 innings) and strikeout percentage (36.0). He was having another big season in 2022, reaching Triple-A and being named to the Futures Game, when he was sent to the A’s as the top prospect in the Frankie Montas deal close to the Trade Deadline. Waldichuk has scrapped the 89-92 mph two-seam fastball he had in college in favor of a four-seamer that sits at 92-95. His heater's shape and carry up in the strike zone are even more impressive than its velocity, and hitters repeatedly swing under it. He also has made progress with his slider, adding sweep to it since signing, as well as his fading changeup, and both low-80s offerings grade as plus at their best. Waldichuk also employs an upper-70s curveball to give him a pitch with more depth, though it gets slurvy and blends with his slider. He does a nice job of using his 6-foot-4 frame and low three-quarters arm slot to enhance his deception, and his angle and extension are especially tough on left-handers. He throws a reasonable number of strikes but is still learning how to command his improved stuff, which could make him a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Saint Mary's has sent Kyle Barraclough, Corbin Burnes and Tony Gonsolin to the big leagues in the last decade and could have a fourth pitcher on the way in Waldichuk. After dominating as a sophomore in 2018, he got caught up seeking more velocity, which led to a so-so junior season that allowed the Yankees to get him in 2019's fifth round. He posted a 49/7 K/BB ratio in 29 1/3 Rookie-ball innings in his pro debut that summer and hit 98 mph in bullpen workouts on his own last year during the pandemic shutdown. After operating with an 89-92 mph two-seam fastball during his college career, Waldichuk has adopted a four-seamer and repeatedly has hit 95-96 as a pro. His heater plays as at least a plus pitch because it features quality shape and life, and hitters just don't seem to be able to see it well. Scouts debate which of his breaking balls is better, but both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider show the potential to become solid offerings. Waldichuk also displays some feel for a changeup with fade, though it still needs more work. He uses his 6-foot-4 frame and low three-quarters arm slot to create angle and extension that makes it difficult to pick up his pitches, especially for left-handers. He has a history of throwing strikes but will need to refine his command to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a while since the state of Alabama has produced a high school player who was drafted, signed and had a big impact in the Major Leagues, with the 2005 tandem of Colby Rasmus and Desmond Jennings the most recent. Henderson is ready to jump to the front of the list. The Orioles’ second-rounder in 2019, Henderson had a strong year in 2021, his first full season due to the pandemic and then really took off in 2022, dominating Double- and Triple-A, going to the Futures Game and holding his own over the last month-plus of the season as a 21-year old in the big leagues. Following his first promotion to Double-A in 2021, Henderson struggled, particularly with his approach at the plate. In an indication of his future ability to make adjustments, the left-handed hitter greatly upped his walk rate and cut his strikeout rate in 2022 compared to the previous year, eliminating much of his chasing out of the zone. That let his impressive bat speed play with even more consistent hard contact and extra-base power, with additional over-the-fence pop certainly coming. A premium athlete who was a basketball star as well in high school, Henderson’s solid speed makes him a threat to steal, and he couples aggressiveness and instincts to take extra bases. That athleticism, along with an easily plus arm, could help him continue to play shortstop despite his size, and Henderson has Gold Glove potential at third, where he played mostly for Baltimore last year. If he’s not on your short list for Rookie of the Year honors, he should be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019 Draft may always be known in Baltimore as the one where Adley Rutschman became an Oriole, but it would be short-sighted to forget the scouting staff also managed to bring in Henderson to kick off the second round. A tremendous high school athlete who starred in basketball and baseball in Alabama, Henderson signed for an over-slot bonus of $2.3 million and had a solid pro debut that summer. After playing well as one of the youngest players at the O’s alternate site in 2020, Henderson started the 2021 season in Low-A and finished in Double-A, then made it up to Triple-A, and the Futures Game, in 2022. Henderson has always been young for his level and the Orioles have been pleased with how he's responded with the challenges each promotion presented. The left-handed hitter is capable of making loud contact with at least plus power potential. Questions about whether he could cut down on his swing and miss to reach that ceiling have abated as he’s whittled down his strikeout rate and continued to make strides on pitch selection, chasing out of the zone and maintaining his emotions in the box as he's moved up the ladder. With a cannon for an arm and off-the-charts athleticism, there is confidence Henderson could play shortstop long-term despite his size. He’s also shown he can handle playing third base and has gotten enough work in the outfield for the Orioles to believe he could play all three spots if needed. He has superstar potential if he can continue to refine his approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first pick of the second round in the 2019 Draft, Henderson was the Alabama basketball and baseball player of the year before the Orioles signed him for $2.3 million to forgo his commitment to Auburn. Henderson showed well in the Gulf Coast League as an 18-year-old, then turned as many heads as anyone at the O’s alternate training site and instructional camp in 2020. There, he impressively flashed an array of loud tools against exclusively older and more advanced pitching than he would’ve faced during a normal season. A physical left-handed hitter, Henderson produces good bat speed from his projectable 6-foot-3 frame, which has elicited comparisons to Corey Seager. The power upside is big, potentially plus at the highest level. He also has a plus arm, good speed for his size and strong instincts on the bases, to go along with strong makeup and work ethic. The jury is still out on whether Henderson sticks at shortstop or will require a move to third as his body continues to mature. But the Orioles believe there is enough athleticism there to move him around out of choice, not need, after he held his own defensively at third and even center field at times during instructional camp. Henderson’s age and athleticism should give them more than enough time to sort out those particulars; at this moment, he owns the highest ceiling of any O’s position player prospect not named Adley Rutschman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport prep star at Morgan Academy in Selma, Alabama, Henderson was the state’s basketball and baseball player of the year before the Orioles took him with the first pick in the second round of the 2019 Draft. The Orioles convinced Henderson to forgo his commitment to Auburn with an above-slot $2.3 million bonus. He then put together a nice showing in the Gulf Coast League as an 18-year-old, flashing what were considered some of the louder offensive tools among prep players in his Draft class. A revelation of the pre-Draft showcase circuit, Henderson produces good bat speed from his projectable 6-foot-3 frame, which has elicited comparisons to Corey Seager. There is a little length to his left-handed swing and some hope his approach matures with age, but the power upside is big, potentially plus at the highest level. Henderson also runs well, especially for his size, and possesses strong instincts on the bases. The jury is still out on whether Henderson sticks at shortstop or will require a move to third base as his body continues to mature. He has a plus arm either way, and the glove and hands to play third base if necessary. Still, some believe he has the chops to remain at shortstop long-term, where his power would project even better. Henderson’s age and inexperience make him largely an unknown quality, but he has the potential to jump as much as any Orioles prospect with a big first full season of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter for three years at UCLA, Toglia’s power showed up in a big way when he slugged 19 homers as a junior in 2019, helping him land in the first round with the Rockies, who had taken a late-round flier on him out of high school three years prior. He reached Double-A and hit a home run at Coors Field in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in his first full season in 2021, before tapping into his power enough to hit 30 homers in the Minors in 2022 en route to making his big league debut. The signs are pointing towards Toglia being a three true outcomes kind of hitter. He has at least plus raw power from both sides of the plate, and he’s shown he can get to it at all levels and hit the ball out to all fields. While he did that more consistently in 2022, he also struck out at a 30.1 percent clip in the Minors and he’ll need to cut down on his tendency to chase early in counts to have lasting success in the big leagues. He does offset the K’s by drawing a lot of walks (13.1 percent walk rate in his Minor League career). Defensively, Toglia has the chance to be a Gold Glover at first base, moving with ease and excellent range, terrific hands and a very strong arm. He’s played some right field, including during his time up in Colorado and is more than athletic enough to handle a corner outfield spot as needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies liked Toglia when he was a high schooler coming out of the Pacific Northwest, taking him in Round 35 in 2016 before he went on to UCLA. His Bruins career was inconsistent, but his power surge as a junior in 2019 was well-timed, helping him land in the first round and once again with the Rockies. His first full season in 2021 after the shutdown brought mixed results, though he did reach Double-A and hit a home run in his future home ballpark during the Futures Game. Toglia’s offensive profile is all about his power. He’s a threat to leave the yard in every at-bat and can do so from both sides of the plate, hitting 22 homers in 2021. He might always be a higher walk, higher strikeout kind of hitter, as he walked in 13 percent of his plate appearances a year ago and struck out in 28.5 of them. At times he can be too patient and find himself quickly behind in the count, especially when he faced more advanced pitching in Double-A, and the key will be continuing to eliminate swings and misses in the strike zone. Toglia is athletic enough and has solid instincts to be a good corner outfielder, but he has the chance to be a Gold Glove caliber first baseman. He does everything with ease in and around the bag with excellent hands and a strong arm to boot. He could be Colorado's first baseman of the future if he can make enough adjustments to hit the ball out of the park consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid, but raw, high school prospect from Washington State, Toglia went to UCLA rather than entertain signing with the Rockies as a 35th-rounder in 2016. He had an up-and-down college career with the Bruins and didn’t hit well in two summers in the Cape Cod League, but got hot in his junior season in 2019, finishing with 17 homers. This time, the Rockies got their man, drafting and signing Toglia in the first round of the Draft, then watched his pop translate to the Class A short-season Northwest League during his pro debut. A switch-hitter, Toglia’s power from both sides of the plate stands out. The 6-foot-5 first baseman can drive the ball to all fields with tremendous raw pop. The question has always been his ability to make enough contact to tap into that power in games consistently because even though he draws walks, he does swing and miss quite a bit. He did make some small adjustments, particularly to his right-handed swing, at the Rockies’ alternate training site last summer, with positive results in terms of in-game power production. Very athletic, especially for his size, Toglia could play an outfield corner, something he did at times in college and on the Cape, but he’s a very good defender at first with an above-average arm and excellent hands. If he can continue to make adjustments at the plate, he should fit the profile of a power-hitting, run-producing first baseman in the big leagues quite well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2016, the Rockies had an idea Toglia would be a good professional player. That's why they took him late in that Draft as a high schooler from the Pacific Northwest, even though he was raw and had a strong commitment to UCLA. Three years later, Toglia emerged as one of the better college bats in the 2019 Draft class, and while his junior year with the Bruins was uneven, he got hot as the Draft approached and the Rockies were happy to draft him again, this time in the first round. He showed glimpses of his power potential by finishing among the leaders in home runs in the short-season Northwest League during his pro debut. A 6-foot-5 athletic first baseman, Toglia is still growing into his frame and is still maturing as a player. He has tremendous raw power from both sides of the plate with the chance to eventually have plus pop in games. How much he's able to do so will be contingent on how much he'll hit. There are some swing-and-miss tendencies, and he did strike out in 26 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut. He does offset that with a willingness to draw walks, and the Rockies believe he has enough feel to hit to perhaps be an average hitter in the future. Toglia moves well enough to play the outfield, but is a plus defender at first base, with a strong arm, excellent range and great hands -- the kind of first baseman who will save runs with his glove. He was young for his Draft class (20) and has more upside than the typical college bat, with the ceiling of an everyday run producer in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching just four innings as a North Carolina freshman in 2016, Little broke out in the Cape Cod League that summer and transferred to the State JC of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota in order to become eligible for the 2017 Draft. The Cubs used both of their 2017 first-round choices on college arms, Little and since-traded Alex Lange, and both have seen their stuff regress in pro ball. Signed for $2.2 million, Little made only 12 starts in 2019 while dealing with a lat strain and has a 5.05 ERA after three pro seasons. When he starred on the Cape and in junior college, Little paired a 91-96 mph fastball that featured life and downhill plane with a low-80s hammer curveball. He'll occasionally flash those plus pitches but too often pitches with a straight 91-93 mph heater and a curve with less shape. He's at his best when he aggressively goes after hitters, but when he tries to work on the finesse aspects of his game, he winds up pitching more tentatively. Since turning pro, Little has improved his changeup and added a slider/cutter, though he might be better off ditching the latter and focusing on his curve. He's still learning to repeating his delivery so he can throw strikes and maintain his best stuff on a more consistent basis. While he continues to offer upside, he also may be the most enigmatic arm in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: North Carolina gave Little just four innings of work as a freshman in 2016 but he impressed scouts with electric stuff in the Cape Cod League that summer. He transferred to the State JC of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota in order to become eligible for the 2017 Draft as a sophomore, and the Cubs signed him for $2.2 million as the 27th overall choice. Like Alex Lange, Chicago's other 2017 first-rounder, he saw his stuff decline in his first full pro season. At his best, Little has two plus offerings in a low-80s hammer of a curveball and a 91-96 mph fastball with life and downhill plane. He rarely overwhelmed hitters in 2018, often sitting around 90 mph with his heater and having a good-not-great curve, though his stuff has bounced back somewhat this season. He's slowly making progress with his changeup, which the Cubs have emphasized after he had little need for one as an amateur, and he also has added a slider. Because Little had just 89 innings of college experience, Chicago knew he would require time to develop. For now, he's focusing on repeating his delivery and keeping it in sync so he can maintain his best stuff. He throws with effort and has little history of throwing strikes, so he may have average control at best.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A highly regarded recruit who got just four innings as a North Carolina freshman in 2016, Little opened eyes by starring in the Cape Cod League that summer. His success prompted him to transfer to the State JC of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota, which made him Draft-eligible as a 2017 sophomore. He ranked second among national juco pitchers with 133 strikeouts before the Cubs selected him 27th overall and signed him for $2.2 million. Little's best pitch is his 12-to-6 curveball, a low-80s hammer when he stays on top of it. His fastball is close behind, ranging from 91-96 mph with impressive movement and downhill plane. He rarely used his changeup as an amateur, so Chicago had him focus on it during his introduction to pro ball, which partially explains his 9.21 ERA in his debut. The Cubs see considerable promise in Little's changeup and see him developing into a starter with three quality pitches. He does feature effort in his delivery and has trouble keeping his mechanics in sync, a problem that cropped up again in his first summer as a pro. If he winds up in the bullpen, he has closer upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs rated Estrada as a second-round talent in the 2017 Draft and were elated to get him with a sixth-round pick and a $1 million bonus. He barely pitched in the next five years, working just 40 innings while dealing with a sore elbow (2018), Tommy John surgery (2019), the pandemic shutdown (2020) and a bout with COVID (2021). Finally healthy last year, he ranked second among Minor League relievers (minimum 40 innings) with a 1.30 ERA and struck out 86 in 54 innings while zooming from High-A to the big leagues. With his physical issues behind him, Estrada worked with a fastball that sat at 95-97 mph, touched 99 and seemed even harder thanks to its vertical movement and the extension in his delivery. His 82-85 mph slider can reach 89 and also has unusual life with both sweep and carry. His fading mid-80s changeup also can miss bats though he doesn't use it very often, and he has a mid-70s curveball that he utilizes as a chase pitch. While he has a four-pitch mix, Estrada works mostly with his fastball and slider and is purely a reliever. After not always being dedicated to his conditioning in the past, he got in better shape in 2022 and did a better job of throwing strikes with his two primary pitches. If he can stay healthy and locate his arsenal with more precision, he might be Chicago's closer of the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estrada flashed first-round talent on the showcase circuit in 2016 but confounded scouts when he didn't pitch up to that standard as a high school senior. The Cubs rated him as a second-rounder and were thrilled to get him in the sixth round, even if he cost them more than four times his assigned pick value at $1 million. He signed right at the July deadline because the Cubs had to wrap up negotiations with first-rounder Alex Lange first, clearing money for Estrada so they wouldn't lose a future first-rounder as a penalty for exceeding their bonus pool. In his brief pro debut, Estrada showed the 92-96 mph fastball that excited scouts the previous summer, not the reduced 88-92 mph heater he had during the spring. He also reclaimed a changeup that shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch. His breaking pitches are less advanced after he relied more on a slider during his senior season and detracted from what had been a solid curveball. While Estrada is shorter than desired for a right-hander and has some effort in his delivery, his athleticism gives him a good chance to remain a starter. He repeats his mechanics and should have at least average control. He began 2018 in Extended Spring Training and came down with elbow soreness that lead the Cubs to shut him down as a precaution.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the best athletes of the 2019 Draft class, Carroll has consistently performed when he’s been on the field since. The 2020 canceled season and a 2021 labrum tear in his right shoulder kept him out of games, but his true breakout came last year, when he hit .307/.425/.610 with 24 homers and 31 steals between Double-A Amarillo and Triple-A Reno (two hitter havens). Following a late August promotion to the Majors, the outfielder more than held his own in virtually all phases of the game, and he heads into 2023 as a National League Rookie of the Year favorite. Carroll is already in the conversation for the fastest player in the Majors; his 30.7 ft./sec. average Sprint Speed on competitive runs was tops in the bigs (min. 10 opportunities), while his 31 Bolts (runs at 30+ ft./sec.) were second-most on the Arizona roster despite his late start. He puts that speed to good use on the grass, where he can cover acres in any direction, and after making arm strength a focus, he’s above-average in that area and can keep runners honest. The wheels and glove would be enough to make Carroll a special prospect, but what places him among the best in the game is his work in the box. Starting from an upright stance, the left-handed hitter then drops down to look almost springloaded, which helps generate the bat speed necessary to spray the ball all over the park. His slugging performance has improved as he’s added strength in pro ball, and he could be capable of multiple 20-homer seasons if this progress continues. Even if the presence of Alek Thomas or (way down the line) Druw Jones pushes Carroll to a corner, he carries the offensive capability to provide across-the-board impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts generally agreed Carroll was among the best hitters and better athletes in the 2019 high school class. After an MVP-winning performance at the Perfect Game All-American Classic, the Pacific Northwest prep star solidified his spot in the first round with a strong senior season at Lakeside High in Seattle. The D-backs took Carroll 16th overall that June, then gave him $3,745,500 to forgo his commitment to UCLA. Carroll looked advanced during his pro debut, posting a .299 average with an .896 OPS and 18 steals while reaching Class A Short-Season Hillsboro. He was even more impressive at Arizona’s alternate training site in 2020, standing out against much more advanced competition in the uniquely competitive environment. It then came as no surprise that he got off to a fast start in 2021, slashing .435/.552/.913 through seven games at the High-A level before shoulder surgery abruptly ended his campaign. Carroll has all the qualities scouts look for when projecting a player as a plus hitter. He has an advanced approach and controls the zone well, showing the ability to make adjustments and excellent swing decisions at a young age. Carroll makes consistent hard contact and drives the ball to all fields from the left side of the plate. The strength Carroll has added since signing has already helped him unlock more power. He may always have more of a hit-over-power profile, but there’s enough pop in Carroll’s left-handed bat to project him for double-digit home runs in the big leagues. Carroll’s plus-plus speed is a game-changing tool. He’s a threat to steal and swiped 21 bags (he was caught just twice) over 49 games in his first two seasons. That speed also gives him plenty of range defensively, where he’s an easy plus defender in center field. Carroll’s across-the-board tools and overall maturity could help him reach the Majors faster than the typical prep pick. Developing more power could heighten a presently lofty ceiling, as he already shows the hitting ability, speed and defensive prowess needed to become a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts generally agreed that Carroll was among the best hitters and better athletes in the 2019 high school class. After an MVP-winning performance at the Perfect Game All-American Classic, the Pacific Northwest prep solidified his spot in the first round with a strong senior season at Lakeside High in Seattle. The D-backs took Carroll 16th overall that June, selecting him with the first of their seven picks in the top 75 slots, then gave him $3,745,500 to forgo his commitment to UCLA. Carroll looked advanced during his pro debut, posting a .299 average with an .896 OPS and 18 steals while reaching Class A Short-Season Hillsboro. He was even more impressive at Arizona’s alternate training site in 2020, standing out against much more advanced competition in the uniquely competitive environment. Carroll was off to a fast start in 2021, but season-ending shoulder surgery halted his campaign in May. Carroll has all the qualities scouts look for when projecting a player as a plus hitter. He has an advanced approach and controls the zone well, showing the ability to make adjustments and excellent swing decisions at a young age. Carroll makes consistent hard contact and drives the ball to all fields from the left side of the plate. The strength Carroll has added since signing has already helped him unlock more power, and some D-backs club officials felt that he showed as much raw power as any player at the team’s alternate site. He may always have more of a hit-over-power profile, but there’s enough pop in Carroll’s left-handed bat to project him for double-digit home runs in the big leagues. Carroll’s plus-plus speed is a game-changing tool. He’s a threat to steal whenever he gets on base and has range for days as an easy plus defender in center field. There is no doubt that he will be able to stay at the position long term. Carroll’s across-the-board tools and overall maturity could help him reach the Majors faster than the typical prep pick. Developing more power could thrust Carroll into the conversation as one of baseball’s best prospects, as he already shows the type of hitting ability, speed and defensive prowess needed to become a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though some teams were turned off by Carroll's undersized frame leading up to the 2019 Draft, amateur scouts generally agreed that the Pacific Northwest prepster was among the best hitters and better athletes in the class. A strong season as a Lakeside High (Seattle) senior helped to keep Carroll, who had garnered Perfect Game All-American Classic MVP honors the previous summer, firmly in the first-round conversation, and the D-backs, who had seven of the first 75 picks in the Draft, were thrilled to get him with the No. 15 overall pick. He signed for slot value, forgoing a UCLA commitment, then posted a .299 average, .896 OPS and 18 steals while reaching Class A Short-Season Hillsboro in his pro debut. Carroll's approach and pure hitting ability stood out among his high school peers. A potential plus hitter, he already controls the zone well and can spray the ball to all fields from the left side of the plate. Carroll's game power may never be more than below average, but he does have the ability to drive the ball with line-drive loft and shows flashes of developing some usable pop to his pull-side. Plus-plus speed is Carroll's loudest tool. It makes him a threat to steal when he's on base as well as a rangy, plus defender in center field, where he's expected to stay long term. Carroll has a similar profile to that of 2018 second-round pick Alek Thomas, albeit with more speed. It could help him move through the Minors more quickly than the average prep, though the D-backs are expected to exercise patience with Carroll's development and remain hopeful that he'll grow into more power in the pro ranks. Even if he doesn't, Carroll's bat, speed and defensive chops at a premium position give him a high floor as a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly won 27 games in 46 starts over four years at NCAA Division II Concord (W.Va.) and Newberry (S.C.) before hooking on with the Athletics for $500 as a nondrafted free agent in 2017. After getting released by Oakland the next spring and the Angels in 2020, he had elbow surgery and signed with the Red Sox in January 2021. He became a full-time reliever, struck out 141 batters in 95 Minor League innings the next two seasons and made his big league debut last August. Kelly's fastball dodges barrels because it features good carry coming out of a lower release height, and he has boosted it from the low 90s as a starter to 94-95 mph with a peak of 97 as a reliever. It pairs well with his low-80s changeup, a plus offering that drops at the plate with plenty of velocity separation from his heater. He'll also work in a fringy mid-80s slider against right-handers. Though Kelly's control can get inconsistent at times, he can throw strikes with all three of his pitches and had no issues while recording a 3.95 ERA in 13 appearances with Boston. He's not overpowering but generates a lot of swings-and-misses as well as weak contact. Following his humble beginnings in pro ball, he's positioned to become an effective middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 6 Draft prospect heading into the shortened 2020 process, the UCLA star ended up going to the Brewers with the 20th overall pick, in part because of concerns around his Type 1 diabetes. It only took him two years to reach the Majors, having risen from Double-A Biloxi and Triple-A Nashville (while missing some time with an oblique injury) to Milwaukee in 2022. He went 19-for-61 (.311) with two homers and eight steals in 28 games following his Aug. 27 ascent to The Show and enters 2023 as the internal favorite to be the club’s Opening Day center fielder. Mitchell became one of the Majors’ fastest players the second he arrived. His 4.01 home-to-first time (as measured by Statcast) was fastest among 529 qualifiers, and his 30.2 ft./sec. average Sprint Speed on competitive runs was sixth-highest, one spot behind Trea Turner. Those wheels certainly come in handy in center field, where he can track down balls gap to gap. If that wasn’t enough of a defensive weapon, he also has plus arm strength that helps limit the opposing run game. Batting from an open stance, the former Bruin tends to slice the top of balls, and as a result, his 59.5 percent ground-ball rate was ninth-highest among the 1,251 Minor Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances last season. He has raw power and made solid contact with an average exit velocity of 92.9 mph in his small sample of the Majors, but constant worm burners hurt that slugging output. An increase in launch angle and consequent power production would seal Mitchell’s place as an outfield regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mitchell came into his own as a UCLA sophomore in 2019, hitting .349 with a .984 OPS, and he was off to a strong start before the 2020 season was cut short. The California native was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 6 2020 Draft prospect but fell to the Brewers at No. 20, in part due to concerns about his Type 1 diabetes. He dominated High-A to open his Minor League career in 2021 but hit a wall following a July promotion to Double-A. He finished with a .186/.291/.264 line at the higher level and was limited to only 64 games overall between the two spots by a knee injury and non-COVID illness. What makes Mitchell such a promising prospect is his athleticism. He’s a plus-plus runner who can steal a base (17 in 19 attempts last season) and turn balls hit to the outfield into extra-base hits. He covers lots of ground in center and showcases a plus arm that makes him an overall defensive asset. The bat remains in question, even more so now after the trip to Biloxi. The left-handed slugger can show good raw pop in batting practice, but his in-game swing leads to a lot of ground balls. His 61.7 percent GB rate was highest in the system (min. 200 PA), blunting his overall offensive impact. Worth noting: his 17.2 percent walk rate was also third-best. The Brewers don’t want to get Mitchell too far away from what made him successful in college. That could be delaying an inevitable swing change, but a healthier 2022 would go a long way toward that return to hitting promise. The rest of the tools give Mitchell a promising floor as a fourth outfielder with burning speed and plenty of glove.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Mitchell was a solid high school prospect at Orange (Calif.) Lutheran and firmly in the middle of the Draft Top 100 in 2017, concerns about his ability to consistently tap into those tools and his strong commitment to UCLA led to him not being selected until the 14th round (by the A's). He started to make good on his potential during a strong sophomore season with the Bruins and was expected to play for USA Baseball’s College National Team before a leg injury forced him off the roster. The injury continued to limit Mitchell the next fall, but he still impressed scouts with his batting practice sessions, then showcased his across-the-board tools in earnest early in his junior year. The Brewers were thrilled to land Mitchell, whom MLB Pipeline had ranked as the sixth-best 2020 Draft prospect, with the 20th overall pick, and they signed him for slot value. He got his first taste of pro ball during Milwaukee’s fall instructional league, though a quad injury limited his time on the field. Mitchell has done his part to assuage concerns about his hitting ability by making real strides with his left-handed swing. He hit consistently for the first time in 2019, and he was doing it again early in his junior season, even transferring the plus raw power he showed in batting practice to games. Big and strong, Mitchell is an easy plus runner who can steal bases and cover a ton of ground in center field, a premium position he'll be able to play long term, with the chance to develop into at least an above-average defender in time. Mitchell has been playing with Type 1 diabetes since being diagnosed in third grade and has shown he can be a premium athlete while dealing with the disease. He featured perhaps the best collection of tools in the entire 2020 Draft class, and the Brewers believe he will be able to use those tools consistently in games once he’s healthy. If it all clicks, Mitchell could become an above-average regular at the pro level, perhaps even more if he can come close to reaching his offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former two-way player at Oklahoma, Cavalli showed better potential on the mound, pushing to the 22nd overall pick with the Nationals in the shortened 2020 Draft. He led the Minors with 175 strikeouts and reached Triple-A in his first full season but didn’t find the same level of consistency back in Rochester in 2022, though he was able to make his Major League debut at home on Aug. 26 that year. It remains his only MLB outing after Tommy John surgery wiped out his 2023 season, and after three rehab starts in 2024, he didn’t pitch again last summer due to the flu and dead arm, according to the organization. Both Cavalli and the Nationals as a club have cautioned that not every pitcher recovers from TJ on the same timeline. After building back up late in the season, Cavalli is expected to be ready to go for a healthier 2025. Before the surgery, he had a 95-97 mph fastball that touched triple-digits but lacked stellar movement. His 82-85 mph curveball had good bite, leading to plenty of whiffs, while an 85-88 mph slider had gyro movement with ample drop to keep hitters off. An upper-80s changeup also flashed plus with ample swing-and-miss and helped stave off lefties. Command issues have dogged Cavalli as a pro and are the second thing to keep him from his considerable ceiling, beside the injuries. He was still feeling his way back to form during his abbreviated rehab looks, and that work will continue headed into his age-26 season in 2025. If everything clicks, he could be a key contributor to Washington’s rotation, but after the missed time, it’ll be an uphill climb to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cavalli transitioned from being a two-way player at Oklahoma to sticking to the mound only, and after flashing great potential before the 2020 shutdown, the Nationals selected him 22nd overall that summer. He led the Minors with 175 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings in his first full season but was much more inconsistent at Triple-A Rochester in 2022, though he did make his Major League debut that August. Right shoulder inflammation ended that campaign early, and as Cavalli worked toward an MLB return in spring 2023, he suffered a Grade 3 UCL sprain in his right elbow that required Tommy John surgery. His rehab has been a slow process in 2024, in part because he's dealt with the flu and a bout with \"dead arm.\" Before the procedure, the 6-foot-4 right-hander showed off a 95-97 mph fastball that could tickle the occasional triple digits. It was a velo-over-movement offering, but that type of heat is still rare. A mid-80s curveball was his best bat-missing pitch in 2022, earning whiffs on 41 percent of swings, thanks to its sharp downward bite, while his upper-80s cutterish slider could get chase down and on the gloveside. An upper-80s changeup also developed enough fade to keep lefties relatively in check. Cavalli fought off command issues early in his Triple-A tenure in 2022 but was trending upward by the time he reached The Show. His first priority this year will be getting healthy, and it’s possible that his location still wavers as he refinds his form in rehab outings. There’s still a high degree of upside if he hits his spots and remains on the mound, but even with the high TJ success rate these days, nothing is guaranteed coming off the surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at the start of his NCAA career with Oklahoma, Cavalli settled best on the mound and looked like he was on the precipice of a breakout as a junior in 2020, when his season was canceled after only four starts. The Nationals saw enough promise to grab him 22nd overall, and the former Sooner showed how worthy he was by leading the Minors with 175 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings across three levels in his first full season. The 2022 campaign was one of fits and starts at Triple-A Rochester (3.71 ERA, 104 strikeouts in 97 innings), but Cavalli did manage to improve enough to earn a Major League debut on Aug. 26. He suffered right shoulder inflammation shortly after and didn’t pitch again in 2022. The injury bug bit again this spring when Cavalli suffered a Grade 3 sprain of the UCL in his right elbow, an issue that required Tommy John surgery. He will miss the 2023 season as a result. The 6-foot-4 right-hander sits 95-97 mph with his fastball and is capable of touching triple digits. The four-seamer relies more on velocity than movement, considering it can come in fairly straight, but that level of heat still makes it a promising pitch. His mid-80s curveball breaks sharply downward and has separated itself as Cavalli’s best breaker over his upper-80s slider that features late cutterish break. His upper-80s changeup has been a work in progress in pro ball but has developed enough fade to be a pitch to hold off lefties. Though he usually avoids walks in large bunches, Cavalli struggled most in 2022 when he couldn’t find consistent fastball command. He was trending in the right direction before his injury with a 1.47 ERA in his final seven Rochester starts. The elbow procedure throws another wrench in that progress, but the rebuilding Nats have said they plan on Cavalli playing a prominent role in future MLB rotations after his return in '24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally drafted in the 29th round by the Braves in 2017, Cavalli instead headed to the University of Oklahoma, where he opened as a two-way player. He moved to the mound full-time as a sophomore, suffered a stress fracture in his arm that season and then showed exciting results as a junior before the pandemic ended his 2020 spring after four starts. The Nationals saw enough to take him 22nd overall and gave him long looks at the alternate training site and fall instructs. He had one of the most promising debut seasons in 2021, leading the Minors with 175 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings while climbing three levels. Cavalli has added velocity and now sits around 96-97 mph with the heater. He’ll touch triple digits, as he did three times in last year’s All-Star Futures Game (the most of any participant). The 6-foot-4 hurler also can manipulate the ball well, with both his mid-80s curveball and upper-80s slider showing plus potential. The curve has more depth while the slider has some cutter action to it, and both were big pieces in driving Cavalli’s K rates. An upper-80s sinking changeup is still a work in progress, but Washington was pleased with its growth. Where Cavalli struggled in 2021 was in his ability to fill up the strike zone, especially against upper-level bats. Lower-level hitters were flummoxed by his velocity and movement, but those in Double-A and Triple-A were more patient, leading to a 13.2 percent walk rate. The Nationals are hopeful Cavalli can continue to refine his command and work on his pitch sequencing. If it all clicks, they could have the next big piece of their rebuild.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cavalli was Oklahoma's top prep pitching prospect in 2017, but he turned down the Braves as a 29th-rounder to attend the University of Oklahoma. After spending the early part of his college career as a two-way player, he shifted his focus more to pitching as a sophomore and emerged as a likely first-rounder in ‘20 after his stuff had ticked up early in his junior year. Viewing Cavalli as someone who is only scraping his potential on the mound, the Nationals took the right-hander with the No. 22 overall pick and signed him for $3,027,000. The electric stuff Cavalli showed at Washington’s alternate training site and fall instructional camp left an indelible impression on club officials, and there even was some speculation that the hard-throwing righty might have finished the year in the Nationals’ big league bullpen had the team stayed in the playoff race. Despite being relatively new to pitching, Cavalli already has shown that he can both throw strikes and miss bats with his entire four-pitch mix. Cavalli knows how to use his powerful 6-foot-4 frame and lightning-quick right arm to generate easy velocity. He sat comfortably in the mid-90s and topped out at 99 mph with his riding fastball in his first pro exposure. Cavalli can make hitters look bad with his 82-85 mph curveball, a plus pitch that he throws with power and depth, and he has developed an upper-80s slider/cutter that has similar out-pitch potential. An upper-80s changeup that Cavalli throws with conviction gives him yet another weapon, and some within the organization think it could become the right-hander’s best secondary offering. Where Cavalli has struggled at times is in the command department. Lower-level hitters were flummoxed by his velocity and movement, but those in Triple-A have been more patient, leading to a higher walk rates and some punished balls that are more squarely in the zone. The Nationals are hopeful Cavalli can continue to refine his command and work on his pitch sequencing. He’s shown modest gains there as the season has gone along, and he still holds No. 2 starter upside..

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Rosario for $300,000 in August 2015 but he didn’t find full-season success until joining High-A in 2019. After climbing a level per year, his best statistical season came with Triple-A El Paso in 2022, when he hit 22 homers and stole 21 bags while slashing .288/.368/.508 in a hitter-friendly environment. He got in seven games with the Major League club that summer, but a broken ankle sustained during Winter League workouts kept him out for a chunk of the 2023 campaign. He delivered a .769 OPS in 43 games back in the Pacific Coast League and managed 11 more contests in The Show after rosters expanded in September. With a small zone due to his 5-foot-7 stature, Rosario has never been a huge strikeout type, but he still swung and missed at his fair share of breaking stuff and offspeed. Still, he can generally find contact with good bat speed, especially against fastballs, and he could hit for a decent average if given enough at-bats. Rosario has decent raw power with an 111.3 mph max exit velocity, but he won’t challenge for 20 homers again outside the PCL in all likelihood. The Dominican Republic native showed improved wheels the further he got from the ankle issues in 2023, and his home-to-first and sprint speeds point to him being an above-average runner again. That agility comes in handy as he’s moved around the dirt and does well been moving in on grounders. He can handle third with his arm strength or second with his quickness, but at this juncture, he best profiles as a bench infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in August 2015, Rosario didn’t grow into a full-season success until four years later at High-A Lake Elsinore in 2019, when he finished with a .743 OPS over 122 games. He has climbed one level per season since (excluding the missed 2020 pandemic campaign) and is coming off his most successful year yet when he was a 20-20 player at Triple-A El Paso, including a career-best 22 homers, .508 slugging percentage and .876 OPS. The Dominican Republic native was called up to the Majors for seven games in August and September but was only used minimally as infield depth. He suffered a broken ankle during Winter League workouts and has been slow to get going during his return in 2023. Rosario lacks size at 5-foot-7, but his good bat speed from the right side, along with improving pitch selection and bat control, have helped turn him into a high-contact hitter. His 19.3 percent K rate as a 22-year-old at Triple-A last year was his lowest mark with a full-season affiliate and coincided with his jump in power. That said, don’t expect Rosario to be a 20-plus homer guy moving forward, considering a good part of that jump was related to extreme hitter-friendly conditions in El Paso (he slugged just .416 on the road). Rosario has acted more like a below-average runner at Triple-A coming off the ankle injury. He’s moved around the dirt a lot in recent years, and while he has a strong arm for third base, his traditional athleticism might be best served at second base; that’s if he needs a full-time position. Rosario’s versatility and hit-over-power profile point toward a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in August 2015, Rosario posted gaudy numbers in both rookie ball and the Dominican Summer League. It took some time for that bat to translate as he progressed, but he put forth a solid 2019 season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, hitting .278/.331/.412. After losing the 2020 season to the pandemic, Rosario played in the Venezuelan Winter League, where he hit .327 with an .821 OPS in 27 games. He continued to hit in 2021, mashing a career-high 12 homers and slashing .281/.360/.455 over 114 games in his first taste of Double-A before finishing up the year in the Arizona Fall League. Rosario, listed at 5-foot-9 and 150 pounds, is undersized, but he has an innate feel to hit, showing good bat speed from the right side of the plate and the ability to drive the ball all over the field. Improved pitch selection helped him set a career-high for homers last season, but he's still more of a hit-over-power type who drives the ball into the gaps. When he reaches base, Rosario knows how to use his speed and has swiped 20 or more bases in four of his five Minor League seasons. A plus arm stands out as Rosario plays all over the diamond defensively. He spent the bulk of his time in Double-A at second base and shortstop, though also got plenty of reps at the hot corner in the Arizona Fall League. Third base may wind up being his best position long-term, but the overall versatility will certainly help Rosario carve out a place on a roster, especially if his bat keeps trending upward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in August 2015, Rosario posted gaudy numbers in rookie ball and the Dominican Summer League. It took some time for that bat to translate as he progressed, but he put forth a solid 2019 season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, hitting .278/.331/.412. After losing the 2020 season to the pandemic, Padres officials were pleased to see Rosario challenge himself in the Venezuelan Winter League. He thrived there, too, hitting .327 with an .821 OPS in 27 games. Rosario is undersized, but he has an innate feel to hit, showing good bat speed from the right side of the plate and the ability to drive the ball from line to line. He has gap-to-gap pop -- though his pitch selection and overall contact rate leave something to be desired. Rosario has a strong arm, and when he reaches base, he knows how to utilize his plus speed as a baserunner. After splitting time mostly between second and third base early in his career, Rosario was deployed in a utility role in 2020. He's played primarily at second and short this season at Double-A San Antonio as the Padres cling to the hope he can stick up the middle. If Rosario’s bat continues its upward trajectory, he has the makings of a big league-caliber utility piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robinson batted just .202 with three homers as a part-time catcher in his first two seasons at Southern Mississippi, then worked his way into the lineup and hit .288 with seven homers as a junior in 2016. The Astros liked his power and arm strength enough to select him in the 21st round and sign him for $100,000. He showed off both tools by homering 15 times and throwing out 41 percent of basestealers in low Class A last year, then went deep four times in the playoffs to help Quad Cities win the Midwest League championship. Robinson carries a lot of strength in his 5-foot-11, 225-pound frame and has bat speed as well, giving him impressive raw power. His right-handed stroke can get long as he takes very aggressive hacks, leading to questions about whether he'll be able to succeed against more advanced pitching. His below-average speed is better than most catchers and surprising for his size. Though Robinson's arm strength is obvious, he had to work to shorten his arm action after entering pro ball. His receiving still has a long ways ago, but Houston believes his makeup and work ethic will allow him to become at least adequate behind the plate. If that happens, he could serve as a power-hitting backup in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs scout Mexico more heavily than most clubs and landed Assad in July 2015 in a $150,000 deal with the Mexican League's Yucatan Lions. He recorded a 2.87 ERA in the Rookie-level Arizona League during his 2016 pro debut, then led the short-season Northwest League in strikeout rate (9.8 per nine innings) last summer. He finished his year by whiffing nine in six scoreless innings during the NWL playoffs. Assad has a four-pitch mix, starting with a heavy 90-94 mph fastball that tops out at 96. He throws two separate breaking balls that show flashes of becoming solid offerings, with his slider rated slightly ahead of his curveball. He also displays promising feel for his changeup. Assad has a thicker frame without much projection, so he may not develop a true plus pitch. But he can throw his entire repertoire for strikes and keeps the ball down in the zone, enhancing his chances of remaining a starter. He could wind up as an innings-eater toward the back of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Plassmeyer quickly worked his way into Missouri's weekend rotation as a freshman in 2016 but pitched his way out of it midway the following year. After working during the offseason to add velocity to his fastball and sharpness to his slider, he rebounded to become the Tigers' best starter in ‘18. The Mariners made Plassmeyer their fourth-round pick that June, then traded him to Tampa Bay during the offseason along with Mike Zunino and Guillermo Heredia. He pitched his way from Class A Bowling Green up to Triple-A Durham in his first full season, finishing second in the Minors (120 IP min.) with a 1.91 ERA. Plassmeyer has below-average velocity on his fastball, which sits 89-90 mph and peaks at 93, but it plays as an above-average pitch because its high spin creates running action and he commands it so well. His slider is average, but he manages to sneak it by more hitters than would be expected. A changeup that has some late fade gives Plassmeyer a third average pitch that he threw with more confidence in 2019. He's not afraid to pitch inside despite lacking swing-and-miss stuff. Plassmeyer’s effectiveness is largely, if not entirely tied to his plus-plus control. After issuing 35 walks in 203 1/3 innings (1.5 BB/9) in three years at Missouri, he’s allowed 27 free passes across 156 frames (1.6 BB/9) as a pro. Plassmeyer’s stuff limits his ceiling, but he has a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter who will compete and gobble up innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Waters was taken in the second round of the 2017 Draft by his hometown team, was the Southern League MVP in ‘19 and made the Futures Game roster in ‘21. But the jump to Triple-A was rough, and he again struggled in Triple-A Gwinnett to start ‘22. The Royals have had their eye on Waters since he was in high school, though, and in July 2022, they were able to land him and two other Minor Leaguers by sending a supplemental first-round Draft pick to the Braves. Waters made an immediate impact, posting a .940 OPS with Omaha before finishing the year in Kansas City, where he had an .803 OPS with five homers in 32 games. The change Waters made when he came to Kansas City was not mechanical. Rather, the Royals emphasized his approach and making better decisions at the plate. His walk rate nearly doubled from Gwinnett to Omaha and then settled at 11% in Kansas City. Waters has power from both sides of the plate and is continuing to tap into that despite his lean frame. He is still too aggressive at times, but that will be a work in progress as he gets into his second Major League season. Waters has elite speed that allows him to swipe bags and play center field, where he can showcase his plus fielding skills and plus arm. The Royals see 2023 as the year to find out if they have their center fielder of the future in their organization, and Waters is still in that conversation despite a left oblique strain wiping out his spring and delaying his season. He can also play right field or serve as a valuable defensive replacement if his bat doesn’t hold up in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken in the second round of the 2017 Draft and signed for a slightly below-slot bonus of $1.5 million out of the Georgia high-school ranks, Waters moved rapidly up his hometown team’s ladder, picking up accolades along the way. He was the Southern League MVP in 2019 and made the Futures Game roster in 2021. Outside of that trip to Denver in the midst of a very strong July, however, Waters' production dipped considerably in Triple-A last year, though the Braves were sure to protect his five-tool potential on the 40-man roster during the offseason. In the midst of another rough year, Waters was traded to Kansas City in early July, and he’s shown promising signs of a turnaround in the weeks since. After the lost 2020 season, Waters tried too hard to show he was ready for the big leagues in 2021, and he didn't consistently drive the ball from both sides of the plate. He’s always been an aggressive hitter, one who swings and misses a good amount, with plenty of raw power he still is learning to get to. He actually cut his strikeout rate and upped his walk rate in Triple-A in 2021 compared to his time there in 2019, and also cut down his chase rate considerably, even if that didn’t show up in his other numbers. A positive sign of maturity in 2021 was that Waters didn’t let his offensive struggles impact the other aspects of his game. He swiped a career-high 28 bags and played plus defense consistently in all three outfield spots. He still doesn’t turn 24 until December and will use the time before then to press upon his new organization just how much of a piece of its future he can be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Braves went into their own backyard to draft Waters, a Georgia high schooler, in the second round of the 2017 Draft, he’s done nothing but perform well, showing off all five tools as he’s made a quick ascent up the organizational ladder. Often playing alongside, or a half step behind, fellow Braves outfield prospect Cristian Pache, Waters has won a batting title and MVP award, both in the Double-A Southern League in 2019, while reaching Triple-A at age 20. He spent 2020 working on his game at the Braves’ alternate training site. Waters is a switch-hitter, better from the left side, but able to drive the ball to all fields from both sides of the plate. An aggressive hitter, he can use his quick, whippy swing to hit for a high average. He spent much of his time at alternate camp working on his overall approach, one that has produced a career 26.2 percent strikeout rate and just a seven percent walk rate, and the Braves feel his time facing so many advanced arms last summer will benefit him and allow him to be a more advanced hitter and to tap into his raw power more consistently. Because of Pache, Waters might not play center field in the same outfield as him, but he certainly has the skills, with plus speed, excellent range and strong instincts. He’s played all three spots and would be a plus defender with a very strong arm in any spot he plays. If the gains in his approach are for real, he’ll be an impact player on both sides of the ball soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Georgia high school scene has become a hotbed of talent on both sides of the ball over the last several years. In the outfield alone, players like Austin Meadows and Clint Frazier have reached the big leagues while Taylor Trammell and Brandon Marsh are among the game's best prospects. They are led on the prospect front now by Waters, a 2017 second-round pick who has raced up the organizational ladder to reach Triple-A at age 20 in 2019 and won both the batting title and MVP honors in the Double-A Southern League. A switch-hitter with tremendous tools, Waters has shown he can impact the baseball from both sides of the plate. He's better from the left side, but he is capable of driving the ball to all fields each way, especially when he's on time with his loose, buggy-whip of a swing. He's still learning to tap into his raw power and there's confidence that many of his doubles (40 in 2019) will turn into home runs as he matures and refines his approach at the plate. That's the only concern about Waters offensively right now, as his strikeout rate spiked in 2019. His walk rate went up a bit, but his overall 164/39 K/BB ratio will have to improve for him to have prolonged success in the big leagues. Waters' speed is a plus on both sides of the ball. He has more than enough range and the instincts to stay in center field, though he saw time in all three outfield positions a year ago as he played alongside fellow prospect Cristian Pache. He's been overshadowed by Pache at times, but just like his organization-mate, he's way ahead of the curve developmentally and also has the chance to be an impact player in his own right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Braves deservedly have a reputation for developing young pitching, with many exciting arms reaching Atlanta in 2018 and many more to come. But it would be a mistake to look past the outfield pipeline as well. Ronald Acuna Jr. made a huge splash in Atlanta last year, Cristian Pache is ready to attack the upper levels of the system and Waters, taken from the Georgia high school ranks in the second round of the 2017 Draft and coming off a very successful first full season that included a South Atlantic League All-Star nod and a promotion up a level, caught up to Pache and played alongside him in Double-A in 2019. Waters has the chance to be an impactful hitter from both sides of the plate. Mechanical adjustments on his swing, particularly his stride, allowed him to be on time with his buggywhip stroke. He's better from the left side currently, but has shown the ability to make hard contact and drive the ball both ways, with raw power sure to turn into more consistent in-game pop as he matures. Waters' plus speed works on the basepaths, where he is a threat to steal, and in the outfield, and he has every chance to stick in center field long-term. After a first full season in which Waters' considerable tools showed up perhaps ahead of schedule, the Braves are excited to see what the young outfielder can do as an encore. He has the chance to be a dynamic, elite-level performer, and seeing a young outfield of Acuna, Pache and Waters -- yes, he has the arm and offensive profile for right field -- in Atlanta should excite all Braves fans.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Waters emerged as one of the best high school prospects from the state of Georgia, winning Gatorade state player of the year honors, the obvious landing place for him in the 2017 Draft was of course the Braves, who love bringing in talent from their own backyard. After a hot start in the Gulf Coast League, the second-round pick struggled with a promotion to the Appalachian League. But he clearly learned some lessons and has had a fantastic full-season debut in the South Atlantic League in 2018. The toolsy outfielder made some solid adjustments at instructs last fall and it carried over into 2018, with the tweaks he made to his mechanics at the plate clearly helping him. He had tinkered quite a bit with his setup and they worked with him to stay with one approach, closer to what had worked for him in high school. He has a buggywhip of a swing, and work he did on his stride has helped him be on time more consistently, and that should continue to help him tap into his considerable raw power more consistently. Waters has plus speed, which will continue to aid him on the basepaths and in center field, where he has the chance to stick. Waters is a veritable toolshed who needs time and reps to use those tools consistently and have them turn into performance. All the pieces are there for him to potentially develop into a dynamic everyday player and he took a large step in the right direction in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Anyone going from a $5,000 signing as a 19-year-old to a Major League starter is a success story, and Butto certainly fits the bill. The right-hander has been a steady performer throughout his time in the Mets system since signing in June 2017 and earned a 40-man spot in November 2022 after reaching Double-A. He sported a 3.56 ERA with 138 strikeouts in 129 innings between Binghamton and Triple-A Syracuse last year to continue his string of successful seasons, and he made his Major League debut on Aug. 21 in Philadelphia, surrendering seven earned runs on nine hits over four rough innings against the future National League champions. The Venezuela native touches 97 mph with his four-seam, high-spin fastball but is more likely to sit around 92-95 mph in most starts. The heater might be best when it’s setting up his 82-85 mph changeup, which has long been the best in the Mets system because of its separation and depth. Butto added a low-80s slider to fend off concerns about his lack of a true biting breaking pitch, but both that and his curveball still don’t do much to fend off righties. He continued to do better against lefties (.742 OPS) than righties (.747) in ’22. On one hand, Butto has a history of Minor League success and is already a starting depth option for the Major League club. On the other, he has a limited ceiling as a two-pitch hurler who isn’t a clear option to have his stuff play up in shorter spurts. He could be valuable as a bulk pitcher out of the bullpen and occasional emergency starter, a role he could handle right away for New York.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butto signed for just $5,000 as a 19-year-old in June 2017. Five years later, he has worked his way to New York’s 40-man roster and now stands on the cusp of the Majors. After starting 2021 at High-A Brooklyn, the 6-foot-1 right-hander sported better numbers at Double-A Binghamton with a 3.12 ERA, 1.04 WHIP and 50 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings. That performance helped earn him Rule 5 Draft protection when he became first eligible in November. The Venezuela native is around 92-94 mph with his fastball, touching 96 mph at times, and it comes with an above-average spin rate as well. Perhaps the fastball’s greatest asset, though, is the way it plays off Butto’s low-80s changeup, which is easily his best offering. The change already gets tremendous separation off the fastball and fools hitters further with its depth. The righty will also mix in a low-80s curveball, but throws it with below-average consistency and bite. Butto hides the ball well in his delivery and throws a healthy amount of strikes, aiding his quest to be a potential Major League starter. The changeup keeps his splits in line -- lefties had a .712 OPS against him in '21, compared to a .699 OPS for righties -- but the lack of a third pitch means he might struggle seeing Major League hitters a second or third time through the order. Now on the Mets' 40-man roster, Butto, who was promoted to Triple-A Syracuse in August, should be knocking on Queens’ door by the first half of next year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butto signed late out of Venezuela as a 19-year-old in June 2017 and signed for very little with just a $5,000 signing bonus. It didn’t take long for him at all to look like a bargain. The 6-foot-1 right-hander posted sub-2.00 ERAs in the Dominican Summer and Appalachian Leagues before stumbling some with Class A Short Season Brooklyn in 2018. He regained ground again in 2019 by showing durability and promising results with a 3.62 ERA and 109 strikeouts in 112 innings at Class A Columbia. Only two Mets full-season pitchers posted a WHIP lower than his 1.17. Any discussion of Butto’s repertoire must begin with the change. The 6-foot-1 right-hander really sells the pitch with the same hand speed upon delivery, only for it to show 10-11 mph of separation from the fastball with depth thus making hitters look bad when they swing early. Speaking of the heater, Butto was averaging 93 mph on the fastball during his time at last year’s instructs, about in line with what he showed early in 2019 (when he had also been touching as high as 96). That left the Mets enthused after concerns he might lose some velocity in the otherwise lost year. Butto also sports a two-seamer that the organization has worked with him on, making sure it provides different movement from his four-seam. The breaking ball is a work in progress. It had shown slurvish tendencies with some sweeping action, and both he and the Mets have tried to give it more vertical break. Butto throws a good amount of strikes with the entire repertoire. The promising velocity and near-elite changeup have given Butto a much brighter future than the one predicted for him when he first signed. He will need the breaker to become more of a consistent pitch if he’s going to face batters multiple times at the top level, but the two pitches he does have could eventually work in middle-relief role at the bare minimum.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butto received the lowest bonus of any player in the Mets’ 2016-17 international class, signing for just $5,000 at age 19 in December '16, but it hasn’t taken the Venezuelan right-hander long to emerge as a potential steal. After spending most of his first two seasons in Rookie ball, Butto moved up to Class A Columbia in '19 and steadily improved throughout his first full season, compiling a 2.72 ERA over his final 14 starts. Overall, he finished fourth among qualified Mets pitchers in ERA (3.62) and fifth in strikeouts (109). Butto’s breakout second half corresponded with an uptick in velocity. His low-90s fastball began to creep into the mid-90s more consistently after the All-Star break and was bumping 96 mph in the season’s final weeks after the Mets began limiting him to two innings per start. Butto complements his heater with the best changeup in the Mets’ system. It’s a true plus pitch, thrown with late diving action and a near 11 mph demarcation in velocity compared to his fastball. He does have a third pitch in a curveball, but it’s below average and lags well behind his fastball-changeup pairing. Butto’s devastating changeup is a weapon against left-handed hitters, and they batted just .199 with a .581 OPS against him in the South Atlantic League. The fact that righties fared better (.264 average, .748 OPS) underscores Butto’s need for a better breaking ball and leads some evaluators to wonder whether he can stick as a starting pitcher. If that doesn't work out, Butto has the velocity and requisite out pitch to be successful in a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 3 on MLBPipeline.com's list of the top 30 international prospects for 2016-17, Ruiz was declared a free agent in September following an impressive three-year career in Cuba's Serie Nacional, during which he posted a 2.55 ERA in 374 1/3 innings. In December, the A's secured the right-hander's future with a $2 million signing bonus. After visa issues delayed the start of his season, Ruiz made his U.S. debut in June in the Rookie Arizona League, where he logged one start before advancing to Class A Advanced Stockton. Ruiz's fastball sits in the 91-94 mph range and touches 95, and he's adept at creating late movement on the pitch thanks to his varying arm angels. His changeup arguably is his best secondary offering, flashing plus at times, and he also has advanced feel for a slider and a splitter. In general, he's a ground-ball pitcher who doesn't miss many bats but knows how to change speeds and keep hitters off balance. While not physically intimidating, Ruiz knows how to pitch and evaluators praise his bulldog mentality on the mound. Improving his control and command and generating more whiffs could go a long way in helping him carve out a role as a backend starter, though he could also offer plenty value coming out of the bullpen, where his stuff stands to play up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox envisioned Aybar as a potential five-tool center fielder when they signed him for $450,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, but he batted just .241/.279/.345 in his first four pro seasons and his strikeout rate ballooned to 35 percent when he finally reached full-season ball. He always exhibited one of the strongest arms among the system's position players, so Boston decided to try the outfielder-to-lefty reliever conversion that worked well with Williams Jerez, who made his big league debut after going to the Angels in the Ian Kinsler trade last July. Aybar was understandably raw in his first year on the mound but improved during the course of 2018. Aybar threw 90-93 mph fastballs when he first took the mound but was sitting at 94-97 and hitting 99 at the end of the season and in instructional league. Though he's still gaining feel for his secondary pitches, he'll flash some sharp sliders in the mid-80s when he's on. His changeup is rudimentary but can leave right-handers off balance on occasion. Aybar's athleticism has helped him in his career change, as he throws a decent amount of strikes while he's still learning to keep his delivery in sync. It's still too early to know what he'll become, but his pure stuff could make him a late-inning weapon if he can develop consistency. One club official watched him work out and said it was the best bullpen session the system had seen since Michael Kopech, who was part of the Chris Sale trade with the White Sox and might have the most devastating fastball/slider combo of any current prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Comparably old as a 19-year-old high-schooler, Baty’s age may have caused him to slip some in the 2019 Draft, but his considerable tools have shone brightly at every Minor League stop. He hit .312/.406/.544 with 19 homers in 89 games at Double-A last season, prompting an August promotion to Triple-A. He lasted only six games in Syracuse before joining the Mets in The Show, where he homered in his first at-bat. The Texas native struggled to reproduce that magic over his 11 total games in the Majors and was shut down after that time due to a torn UCL in his right thumb that required surgery. Baty finished his 2022 Minor League season with a .315 average between his two stops on the strength of a smooth left-handed swing and an approach that doesn’t see him expand the zone too often. His biggest bugaboo throughout his career has been his ground-ball rate, and that did drop to a more manageable 43.5 percent (down from an organization-worst 55.8 percent in 2021) after he made it a priority to get behind the ball more and lift it more efficiently on contact. That’s important because Baty can hit the ball hard with at least plus raw power, and more airtime means more extra-base hits. A three-sport athlete in high school, the 23-year-old still looked rough around the edges defensively when he made the Majors, and increasing his range will remain a priority perhaps for much of his career. A plus arm certainly helps his defensive case and also eases his time in left field, where he’s made 29 Minor League starts. Baty’s ceiling is at its highest at the hot corner, however, and after the Mets’ Carlos Correa deal fell through, his path to third in Queens should be clear for the taking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baty’s age at 19 might have been the only thing that allowed him to slip to the Mets at No. 12 overall in the 2019 Draft. He quickly got to work across three affiliates that first summer, finishing with a trophy-raising turn with Class A Short Season Brooklyn. He returned to Coney Island for the alternate site in 2020 and played once more with the Cyclones as a High-A affiliate last summer. He hit .292/.382/.473 with 12 homers at High-A and Double-A and picked up more at-bats in the Arizona Fall League. Baty works well to all fields utilizing a smooth swing from the left side. He typically has little issue staying behind the ball and making solid contact off the bat, and when he doesn’t, he can still work a walk. The Texas native is capable of putting on a powerful show in batting practice, but it hasn’t translated into eye-popping slugging numbers. A 50-plus percent ground-ball rate has kept him from making the most of that strength, but there’s hope that more upper-level experience could iron out those issues. A better runner than one might expect given his size, Baty has grown to be a capable defender at third base, where his plus arm fits the bill. The Mets gave him time in left field in Binghamton, and he has enough athleticism to work there. Notably, he was third-base-only in the Fall League. If Baty can turn his dreamlike raw pop into actual game power, New York could have its next long-term third baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baty was old for his class as a 19-year-old high school senior, and that deterred some clubs from taking him early in the 2019 Draft.
