The Mets weren’t one of them, as they made Baty the first third baseman to be taken by the organization in the first round since Chris Donnels in 1987, selecting the Lake Travis (Texas) High product No. 12 overall. Baty posted a .821 OPS with 25 extra-base hits (seven homers) while climbing three levels in his pro debut after signing for $3.9 million, then arrived at the Mets’ alternate training site in '20 looking physically stronger and leaner. Hitting for power from line-to-line from the left side is Baty’s calling card. He’s shown early in his career that he can get to it during games, even hitting his longest and most impressive home runs to the opposite field, though he’s still learning how to turn on the ball. Baty’s swing mechanics and bat path do lead to swing-and-miss issues that raise questions about his hit tool, but he also employs a patient approach and controls the zone well enough to project him as an average hitter with plus game power. The athleticism that made Baty a three-sport standout as a prep shows up on the diamond, and he showed improved agility and more speed last summer at the alternate site. He could develop into an average defender at third base, where his plus arm strength -- he was clocked at 92 mph off the mound in high school -- is an asset, though, overall, Baty will need time to develop on both sides of the ball to reach his ceiling. Having climbed to Double-A in 2021, Baty has seen some time in the outfield with the Mets hoping to get his bat in the lineup anyway they can in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Baty technically was old for the 2019 Draft class as a 19-year-old high school senior, it didn't deter the Mets from making him the franchise's first third baseman selected in the first round since Chris Donnels in 1987. Fresh off a monster season at Lake Travis (Texas) HS in which he batted .615 with 19 home runs, Baty furthered his reputation as an advanced hitter by posting an .821 OPS with 25 extra-base hits (7 HR) while climbing three levels in his pro debut after signing with the Mets for $3.9 million. Baty's raw power was among the best in the 2019 Draft, the product of his bat speed, strength and lofty left-handed swing. He drives the ball with authority to all fields and already generates big league-caliber exit velocities, and scouts were especially impressed with the true opposite-field power he showed during his first pro exposure. More than just a slugger, Baty also employs a patient approach, does a good job controlling the zone and recognizes spin well enough for scouts to project him as an above-average hitter with 25-plus homer power. A multi-sport standout at Lake Travis, where he played both basketball and football in addition to his exploits on the diamond, Baty is a much better athlete than his 6-foot-3, 210-pound frame and below-average speed suggests. He could develop into an average defender at third base, where his plus arm strength -- he was clocked at 92 mph off the mound in high school -- is a clear fit. He'll need time to develop his game on both sides of the ball, but also stands to move faster through the Minors than the typical prep pick because of his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tarnok was a two-way player for most of his amateur career at Riverview High School in Florida, but success on the mound as a senior led to the Braves going well above slot with a bonus of nearly $1.45 million as a third-round Draft pick in 2017. After a brief Major League stint in 2022, he was traded to Oakland that December in the Sean Murphy deal. Working his way back from a Spring Training shoulder issue, he made five appearances (one start) in 2023 for the A’s before a calf strain cut his season short. Tarnok’s low-80s changeup has emerged as a solid put-away pitch that misses plenty of bats, complementing a fastball that sits around 95 mph and can top out at 98. His curveball continues to be an effective pitch, while a newer slider showed encouraging signs during his time in the big leagues last season. Tarnok’s repeatable, athletic delivery helps him consistently stay around the zone and command the ball well. The A’s continue to build him up in a starting role, though recent injury history -- he entered 2024 Spring Training recovering from hip surgery last August -- could lead to considerations for a possible bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player for most of his amateur career at Riverview High School in Florida, Tarnok’s success as a pitcher in his senior year was enough for the Braves to go well above slot, signing him for nearly $1.45 million as a third-round Draft pick in 2017. Utilizing the pandemic in 2020 as an opportunity to work on his body and refine his mechanics, he rapidly ascended through Atlanta’s system upon returning, reaching Triple-A in 2022 and making his Major League debut before getting traded to Oakland in the Sean Murphy deal. Tarnok increased his stock in the Braves’ system thanks to a return of his stuff that had regressed earlier in his pro career. His fastball sits around 95 mph, topping out at 98. While his curveball has long been an effective pitch and he added a slider more recently, he did struggle a bit landing them for strikes in 2022, but his low-80s changeup took a nice step forward and missed a good amount of bats. Tarnok tends to be around the zone with a repeatable, athletic delivery and commands the ball well enough to get plenty of swing-and-miss, evidenced by his 10.5 whiffs per nine innings in ‘22. With a 6-foot-3 frame that looks to be durable, he figures to get a good look in Oakland’s pitching staff at some point in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tarnok hadn’t pitched a ton in high school as a two-way player at Riverview High School in Florida, he did have some helium in his senior year on the mound. The Braves liked his projection and athleticism enough to give him double slot and sign him for nearly $1.45 million. He showed glimpses early on, then regressed, both in terms of velocity and effectiveness, in 2019. His home workouts in 2020 seemed to pay off as he reached Double-A and pitched well there, earning a spot on the 40-man roster. He made it to Triple-A in 2022 and made his big-league debut before being sent to the A’s in the three-team deal that brought Sean Murphy to Atlanta. Tarnok was one of the most improved pitchers in the Braves’ system prior to the trade. His stuff ticked back up after that early regression, starting with his fastball that averages around 95 mph. He’s long had an effective curve and, like many pitchers in the system, he more recently added a slider, with positive results. His average changeup is effective, especially against left-handed hitters. He’s missed a lot more bats over the past two seasons, including whiffing 10.5 per nine in 2022 and while his command isn’t pinpoint, he’s generally around the strike zone. His athleticism should help him continue to repeat his delivery and refine his command and he should get the opportunity to impact the A’s big league staff at some point in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player from the Florida high school ranks who seemed likely to head to Division II Tampa for college, Tarnok’s athleticism on the mound, though raw, caught the attention of the Braves, who went well over slot in the third round of the 2017 Draft to put the infielder on the mound full time. He’s been able to move fairly well, especially considering how little time he spent pitching as an amateur, hitting full-season ball in 2018 then moving up to High-A in 2019. He pitched well there after returning from a lat injury. Working out at home on his own during the shutdown, Tarnok continued to fine-tune a delivery that’s been a work in progress. After his velocity backed up a bit in 2019, the first year he topped 100 innings, it was trending back up, sitting more in the mid-90s while maxing out at 99 mph in bullpen sessions. There’s room to keep adding strength to his 6-foot-3 frame so he can maintain those velocity gains. He complements the heater with a power breaking ball with tight spin, a pitch that could be better than average in time, and an average changeup he uses mostly against lefties. Tarnok has improved his strike-throwing as he’s developed in the Braves system, something he’ll have to keep doing as his stuff ticks up. He’ll have to show better command within the zone as well as he gets to the upper levels if he wants to reach his ceiling as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tarnok didn’t pitch a ton during his high school career in Florida, a two-way guy known more for being an infielder. But the Braves liked his upside on the mound enough to take him in the third round of the 2017 Draft and give him a well above-slot bonus of $1.445 million to keep him from heading to college. Given his lack of experience, he’s moved well through the lower levels of the system, pitching in a tandem system in the South Atlantic League for his first full season of pro ball, then moving up to the Florida State League in 2019, where he topped 100 innings for the first time as a full-time starter and showed marked improvement in the second half of the season after missing a month to a lat injury. A good athlete with an ideal pitcher’s frame, Tarnok can still add strength which should mean velocity gain to a fastball that sits around 93-94 mph and touches 96 at times. When it’s at its best, Tarnok’s breaking ball is a power pitch with tight spin. It will flash above-average, but not consistently yet, and he shows feel for a solid changeup. One of the biggest negatives for Tarnok has been his command, but he took a big step forward in 2019, slashing his walk rate from 2018 and giving up just under two walks per nine innings in the second half. He impressed during the Braves’ pitching camp in January and is poised to make a jump to the upper levels of the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves were the high team on Tarnok at the 2017 Draft and were able to convince the Florida high school two-way standout to focus on pitching, taking him in the third round that June and going well over slot to sign him for $1.445 million. Knowing he was a bit of a project, the projectable right-hander didn't pitch much his first summer of pro ball and was held back in extended spring camp to start the 2018 season. But Tarnok took a big step forward by pitching well in full-season ball last summer. The more the Braves see Tarnok, the more confidence they have in his ability to pitch at the highest level and withstand the rigors of a long season, with the chance to be a starter. He's starting to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame, which should help him maintain his stuff deep into starts. He tops out at 96 mph and should settle in at 93-94 mph, a pitch that plays up because of his excellent extension and finish. His power breaking ball should be at least average, and he continues to improve his changeup. More than anything, Tarnok needs innings as someone who didn't pitch until his junior year of high school. Whether he starts or relieves long-term remains to be seen, but given his progress, his raw stuff and his athletic frame, seeing him make another leap forward as the gloves come off a little bit is very realistic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tarnok was a solid two-way player in the Florida high school ranks, one with some upside but whom many figured would go on to Tampa for college. The Braves, never wary of pitching projects, took him in the third round and gave him $1.445 million, more than double his pick value, to start his pro career. He pitched sparingly in the Gulf Coast League during his pro debut, but he has shown some glimpses of the kind of pitcher he can become. Tarnok's Draft profile jumped because of an increase in velocity with his fastball. He will now sit in the low-90s and touches 95-96 mph at times, and with his projectable 6-foot-3 frame, it's easy to dream about more velocity to come as he fills out. His fastball already plays up some because of his extension and ability to throw downhill, with good finish at the end. He has a good feel to spin his breaking ball, a power curve that should be at least average, and he's already shown progress with his changeup. A solid athlete who didn't pitch until his junior year, Tarnok still has a lot to learn, but that athleticism should allow him to find a repeatable delivery and to throw strikes. Based on the fact he is now focusing on pitching only for the first time and has so much room for added strength, Tarnok's ceiling is considerable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins drafted Garrett in the eighth round out of the Texas high school ranks in 2014, targeting the athletic outfielder for his loud tools as well as his untapped potential after playing multiple sports as an amateur. He quickly proved more advanced than originally thought, pacing the New York-Penn League in home runs (11), RBIs (46) and OPS (.933) in his second professional season. But he was unable to build on that performance in 2016, as a wrist injury delayed the start of his full-season debut until late April, and a botched knife \"prank\" by then-teammate Josh Naylor in early June resulted in a right thumb laceration and subsequent surgery, costing Garrett more than two months during the heart of the season. Garrett has good strength to his athletic frame and generates impressive bat speed from the right side of the plate. He has plus raw power, especially to his pull side, and has worked with the Marlins to simplify his swing mechanics since signing. His approach and pitch recognition remain raw, however, and there's some concern that his penchant for whiffing will impede his ability to make contact and get to his power in games. Garrett is an above-average runner with enough range to handle all three outfield spots, but with below-average arm strength, he's more likely to end up in left field if he's unable to stick in center. Garrett made up for some of his lost time with a strong offseason campaign in the Australian Baseball League, tying for the league lead with seven home runs. Though healthy in 2017, Garrett struggled to build on his offseason progress in the Florida State League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees signed Cabrera out of Venezuela for $100,000 in 2015, a year after they signed his older brother Leobaldo for $250,000. While they released Leobaldo in 2018 -- he's now an outfielder in the Twins system -- Oswaldo has slowly developed into one of their better prospects. After totaling 22 homers in his first four years as a pro, he broke out with 29 in 2021, winning Double-A Northeast League MVP honors and going deep five times in nine Triple-A games at the end of the season. A switch-hitter, Cabrera returned from the 2020 pandemic layoff with more strength and more pronounced loft in his swing. His power surge only came from the left side, where he batted .290/.350/.612 compared to .227/.277/.333 as a righty. He's using his legs more at the plate and has taken a more aggressive approach without sacrificing much in the way of contact, though he's a fringy hitter at best. Cabrera's added muscle cost him some quickness, though he's still an aggressive runner who makes the most of his fringy to average speed on the bases. His quick hands, solid arm and finely-tuned internal clock help him make plays in the field, though his range is a bit stretched at shortstop. He saw more action at second and third base in each of his last two seasons, and he's a solid defender at both spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thanks largely to his defensive prowess behind the plate, Langeliers was thought to be the second-best catcher in the 2019 class, behind only eventual No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman. The Braves were a bit ahead of the industry when they took him No. 9 overall and signed him for an under-slot $4 million bonus. A solid debut in full-season ball and a strong performance at the Braves’ alternate site in 2020 allowed Langeliers to jump to Double-A in 2021, finish in Triple-A and earn the trust of the organization enough to be the catcher on the club’s taxi squad throughout its postseason run. It’s also why the A’s wanted Langeliers to be one of the headliners in the deal that sent Matt Olson to Atlanta. Langeliers’ power bat and arm were on full display during his first full season. His right-handed pop started to show up at the alt site in 2020 and continued in Mississippi, where his 22 homers stand out even more because it’s such a tough place to hit. While there is some swing-and-miss to his game (26.8 percent K rate), that was right about average for his level and he routinely registered high exit velocities, was near the top of the organization in terms of the quality of his contact and showed the ability to recognize and hit breaking stuff. Improvement in handling velocity up in the zone will help his development as a hitter. Even if he doesn’t hit, Langeliers’ defense will make him a big leaguer. He has one of the best arms of any Minor Leaguer at any position and he threw out 42 percent of potential basestealers a year ago. He’s a strong leader and works very well with pitchers and after his experience on the postseason taxi squad, he’s close to being ready for a job as a big league regular, receiving his first call up in mid-August.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For most of his college career at Baylor, Langeliers was known as a glove-first backstop and for good reason. Even though he missed part of his junior year with a broken hamate in his left hand, he answered enough questions about his offensive profile to make him the second best catcher in the class, behind No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman. Thought by many to be more of a middle-of-the-first-round type of player, Langeliers ended up going No. 9 overall to the Braves, who signed him for below pick value. He held his own with a debut assignment to full-season Rome in 2019 and performed very well at the club’s alternate camp in 2020. He hit 22 homers in Double-A his first real full season, then spent the entire postseason on the big league club’s taxi squad. He was in Minor League Spring Training when he was part of the quartet of prospects sent to the A’s for Matt Olson. There’s no question that Langeliers’ defense is still his calling card. His athleticism and agility allow him to be a plus blocker and receiver and he perhaps has the best arm of any catcher in the Minor Leagues, one that allowed him to throw out 42 percent of potential basestealers heading into 2022. He is a strong leader who worked very well with more advanced pitchers at the alternate training site and frames pitches extremely well. While his glove is ahead of his bat, the Braves loved the strides Langeliers made from the right side of the plate. He has a good setup and solid swing mechanics that point to consistent hard contact and plenty of raw power, which he got to fairly consistently in 2021, with excellent velocity on balls in play to the opposite field. He has every chance of being an outstanding starting catcher in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known mostly for his defense at Baylor University, Langeliers turned a stronger offensive season as a junior, despite missing time with a broken hamate in his left hand, into being one of the top prospects in the 2019 Draft. If it weren't for No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, he would've been the top catcher in the class. He still went No. 9 overall to the Braves, who signed him for a below pick value bonus of $3,997,500. Langeliers rewarded Atlanta's faith by going straight to full-season ball during his pro debut. While most of the talk around Langeliers is about his defense, he has the chance to be a very good all-around backstop. He has plenty of raw power to tap into and has a solid right-handed swing that should continue to allow him to make consistent hard contact once he settles into the pro game. Speed isn't a big part of his game, but he moves better than most catchers. That athleticism certainly helps him behind the plate. He's extremely agile, helping him be an outstanding blocker and receiver. His cannon for an arm can shut down the running game and he threw out 41 percent of potential basestealers during his pro debut. He frames pitches well and is a strong leader. Those defensive skills alone should be enough to allow him to be a big league regular. If his offense continues to develop, he has the chance to be an elite-level backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The MVP of the 2016 Connie Mack World Series as an Atlanta high schooler, Curry stayed home to pitch for Georgia Tech for three years before the Guardians selected him in the seventh round of the 2019 Draft. Between shoulder inflammation that summer and the pandemic, he didn't make his pro debut until 2021. It took him just 15 months to climb from Single-A to Cleveland, where he made a pair of starts last summer. Curry's 91-94 mph fastball reaches 96 and plays better than its average velocity because it has all the characteristics the Guardians crave, coming out of a high arm slot with plenty of induced vertical break and efficient spin. His four-seamer overmatched hitters in the lower Minors but wasn't nearly as dominant in Triple-A or the big leagues. He has helped himself by improving the velocity and depth on what is now a mid-80s slider, giving him a second solid offering. Curry's mid-70s curveball lacks power and his mid-80s changeup often is too firm and straight, and both grade as fringy. His lack of a reliable third pitch and physicality leads to questions as to whether he's more of a back-of-the-rotation starter or a multi-inning reliever. He has a history of throwing strikes but his control regressed a bit last year when he became reluctant to challenge more advanced hitters when they knocked him around.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curry won MVP honors at the 2016 Connie Mack World Series before pitching for three years at Georgia Tech and going in the seventh round of the 2019 Draft. Shoulder inflammation that summer and the cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season delayed his pro debut until May 2021, but he made up for lost time quickly. He reached Double-A and ranked third in the Minors in K/BB ratio (7.7) and sixth in ERA (2.30) and walks per nine innings (1.5). Curry's fastball sits in the low 90s and touches 96 mph, playing as a solid to plus pitch with all the characteristics that the Guardians covet. He releases it from a high arm slot with plenty of efficient spin and induced vertical break, and hitters couldn't catch up to his heater last year. He relies heavily on his four-seamer, with his low-80s slider showing flashes of becoming an average pitch because he locates it well and his downer curveball and changeup grading as fringy. Just 5-foot-11 and 190 pounds, Curry lacks the physicality desired as a starter, though he repeats his delivery well and pounds the strike zone. He's riding a lot of momentum from last season, but he still needs to find a reliable secondary pitch or two in order to make it as a big league starter. Otherwise, he'll wind up as a fastball-heavy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall was one of the best high school lefties in the 2017 Draft class, ranking only behind MacKenzie Gore. The Orioles drafted him accordingly, taking him No. 21 overall that June. Throughout his climb up the organizational ladder, which included his first trip to the big leagues in a relief role, he’s shown off elite-level stuff that dominates hitters, though his ability to find the strike zone has hampered him at times. He put an elbow strain that sidelined him for much of 2021 in his rear view with a healthy 2022, largely in Triple-A, to earn that first callup. Throughout the 2022 season, Hall continued to show off a four-pitch repertoire and an ability to miss bats. Hall’s fastball touches triple digits and averages over 96.5 mph. His fading mid-80s changeup is a plus offering at times and it elicited a 49 percent miss rate. He still has two separate breaking balls, throwing his upper-80s slider a lot more frequently than his slower curve. No one has questions Hall’s stuff and ability to get big league hitters out, but there are concerns about his ability to find the strike zone enough to do it as a starter. His walk rate ballooned to 5.3 per nine in the Minors in 2022, though he was more efficient during his big league debut. The O’s still think he can use his athleticism to improve his command and start, with the stuff to pitch in the front half of a rotation, though there is still some reliever risk here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Orioles took Hall out of the Georgia high school ranks No. 21 overall in the 2017 Draft, the left-hander has shown off premium pure stuff and the ability to dominate Minor League hitters. The 2019 Futures Gamer had gone a level at a time, spending all of 2018 in Low-A and all of 2019 up a level with High-A Frederick before pitching at the alternate site in 2020. His 2021 in Double-A was off to a very good start, but an elbow strain limited him to just 31 2/3 innings all year. The Orioles added him to the 40-man roster in the offseason and a healthy 2022 led to his first call up to the big leagues in August. At full strength in 2022 after a rebuilding program and the organization erring more on the side of caution with holding him out for so long a year ago, Hall’s stuff has continued to be absolutely nasty, with a fastball routinely up to 101 mph and a fading changeup that flashes plus. He does have distinct breaking pitches, throwing the slider more frequently than the curve. Hall’s main obstacle, other than health, has been his command. He did throw more strikes in 2021 (4.6 walks per nine) and he’s worked to streamline his delivery, though his walk rate ticked back up in 2022. He’s one of the best athletes at any position in the system, something that should help him continue to find consistency in that regard. Further refinement will allow him to reach his ceiling as a dynamic lefty starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were three high school lefties taken in the first round of the 2017 Draft: MacKenzie Gore, who went No. 3 to the Padres; Trevor Rogers, the No. 13 pick by the Marlins who made his big league debut in 2020; and Hall, the Orioles' pick at No. 21. He’s shown dominant stuff across Class A and Class A Advanced during his first two full seasons of pro ball, adding in a perfect Futures Game inning in '19 for good measure, before spending the summer of '20 at Baltimore’s alternate camp. As Hall has progressed through the Orioles' system, he’s continuously added velocity. He was consistently at 96-99 mph last summer, throwing his heater with excellent life. His changeup can be a true out pitch, thrown in the low-80s with good fade. Hall has worked hard to separate his curve and slider and has defined the shape and speed of each pitch consistently now, with the curve flashing plus with excellent spin and bite. One of the few things holding Hall back has been his command, as his walk rate spiked along with his strikeout rate in 2019. The Orioles liked what they saw in terms of improvements in his delivery during his work at the alternate training site, and he showed a greater capacity to make in-game adjustments. He’s yet to top 100 innings in a season, so he needs more reps, but there’s an up arrow next to his name in terms of his starting pitcher ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heading into the 2017 Draft, MacKenzie Gore was clearly the top high school lefty in the class. Hall, a Georgia area standout, wasn't too far behind and while Gore was the No. 3 overall pick that June, Hall went No. 21 overall to the Orioles. After a slow start to his first full season, he showed dominant stuff in the South Atlantic League, then continued to be tough to hit with a move to the Carolina League in 2019, a season that also included a perfect inning in the All-Star Futures Game. Hall continues to add velocity to what was a plus fastball entering his pro career. His heater now sits 95 mph and touched 97 mph in 2019 and he was 96-98 mph during his Futures Game frame. His changeup has improved tremendously and some see it as his best secondary offering, a fading offspeed pitch that at times is as effective as his lively fastball. His curve flashes plus, thrown with excellent spin and bite. His walk rate spiked in 2019, but much like he did in his first full season, he was much better in the second half in terms of finding the strike zone. More than anything, Hall just needs innings to learn how to harness his stuff as he has a clean and repeatable delivery. He's been treated with kid gloves workload-wise and missed the end of 2019 with an oblique injury, so he's yet to top 100 innings in a season. The command should improve as he continues to mature and he still has a ceiling as mid-rotation starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching at Valdosta (Ga.) High School as a freshman, Hall transferred to Houston County High (Warner Robins, Ga.) in 2016 and helped the program win a 5-A state title. He returned to Valdosta for his senior year, established himself as one of the top left-handed pitchers ahead of the 2017 Draft and became the fourth southpaw to come off the board when the Orioles took him with the No. 21 overall pick. He signed for above slot at $3 million. Making his full-season debut in the Class A South Atlantic League in 2018, Hall scuffled initially but dominated during the second half, posting a 0.84 ERA with 64 strikeouts and a .171 BAA over his final 53 2/3 frames (11 appearances). Hall already pitches with a plus fastball, sitting at 92-94 mph and reaching 96, with late life that makes the pitch difficult to barrel. His curveball is above average but can flash plus, thrown with a high spin rate that gives it late bite, and the same can be said about the fading changeup he's made strides in developing. Meanwhile, that he does a good job repeating his simple delivery and knows how to find his release point with each pitch suggests he could develop above-average command. The Orioles kept Hall on a tight leash during his first full season and never allowed him to throw more than 90 pitches in a start. While the training wheels should come off a bit more going forward, it wouldn't be surprising if the club employed a similar approach to managing Hall's workload in 2019. That could lead to a slower climb through the Minors for the young lefty, who has the upside of a mid-rotation starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Houston County High (Warner Robins, Ga.), Hall returned to Valdosta (Ga.) High, where he pitched as a freshman. While he was gone, he helped Houston County win the 2016 state 5-A title and established himself as one of the top left-handed hurlers in the 2017 Draft. Hall only confirmed that assessment with an impressive senior campaign, and he became the fourth southpaw selected in the Draft when the Orioles took him with the No. 21 overall pick. The Florida State commit signed for above slot at $3 million and then had an uneven professional debut in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, but he's looked every bit the first-round pick during an impressive full-season debut in the Class A South Atlantic League. Hall already pitches with a plus fastball, operating at 92-94 mph and touching 95, and scouts expect him to add more velocity as he grows into his projectable frame. His curveball is at least an above-average offering, thrown with a high spin rate that gives it late bite, while his changeup, though still in its nascent stages, projects to be average. Hall's arm slot can be inconsistent at times, thus limiting his command, though he did make strides in cleaning up his delivery during the club's fall instructional league. Hall draws comparisons to Scott Kazmir for his build, live arm and overall upside. The Orioles, meanwhile, will be patient in developing the young southpaw, whom they view as a future mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick out of Oklahoma State in 2019, Battenfield already has been traded twice, by the Astros along with outfield prospect Cal Stevenson to the Rays for Austin Pruitt in January 2020 and to the Guardians for D.J. Johnson and Jordan Luplow last July. After relieving in college, he has found success as a starter in pro ball, logging a 2.53 ERA with a 131/19 K/BB ratio in 103 innings while advancing to Double-A in his first full season last summer. He struck out 10 in seven innings of one-hit ball in the opener of the Double-A Northeast championship series to help Akron win the title. Battenfield's fastball sat around 90 mph in shorter stints in college, but now he's operating at 91-95 and touching 97, with his four-seamer playing up thanks to its carry and his command. His heater pairs well with his upper-70s downer curveball and an upper-80s cutter/slider with short horizontal break, both of which can be solid offerings. He also has a low-80s changeup with fade that flashes similar upside. The younger brother of White Sox pitching prospect Blake Battenfield, he keeps batters off balance by mixing four pitches that move in four different directions and locating them where he wants. He has improved his conditioning and athleticism since turning pro, resulting in improved stuff and a better ability to repeat his delivery. He doesn't have the prettiest arm action but he pounds the zone and misses bats, giving him a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and a high floor of a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Casey was a two-way player at Boston College but told teams he preferred hitting, despite posting better numbers on the mound. He fell to the Dodgers in the 20th round in 2017 as a result. Inconsistent success marked his first two seasons in pro ball before he managed 23 homers at High-A and Double-A in 2019. He was hitting .296/.362/.462 over 73 games as a 25-year-old back in Tulsa last season when Los Angeles sent him to Washington in the six-player deal involving Trea Turner and Max Scherzer. Shortly after, Casey ran into a roadblock at Triple-A, hitting .179 with a 38.8 percent K rate over 38 games. Eligible for the Rule 5 Draft for a second time, he was added to the 40-man in November after strengthening his case in the Arizona Fall League. Casey still possesses a strong arm from his days as a BC pitcher, and he uses it to great effect from the outfield grass. He also boasts plus speed that makes him an annual candidate to swipe 15-plus bags in a full season. While he played a lot of right field in the Dodgers system, it was notable that Casey played primarily in center for the Nationals following the trade. He could likely step right into the Washington outfield mix without the MLB club missing a beat defensively. There are legit questions about Casey’s bat, however. He has shown K rates right around 30 percent for much of his time in the upper Minors. That hinders his ability to tap into his solid raw power, as does his history of putting the ball primarily on the ground. Casey isn’t far from being a fourth-outfield type in the Majors because of his wheels and defense. But his age at 26 and performance in the box might keep him from ever being more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams were split on whether to draft Casey as an outfielder or a right-handed pitcher after he played both ways at Boston College. Though he made more of an impact for the Eagles on the mound and reached 94 mph, he wanted to play every day and turned down overtures to pitch, which partially explains why he lasted 20 rounds last June. After signing for $137,500, he batted .403/.453/.604 in Rookie ball. Though he's a 6-foot-2, 190-pound athlete loaded with tools, Casey batted just .287 with four homers in three years of college. The Dodgers helped him make some adjustments to his right-handed swing that helped him start to translate his solid bat speed and plus raw power into production, and there's still plenty of room for improvement because he hits a lot of ground balls. He's also making more consistent contact but could use more patience. Casey has two more plus tools in his speed and arm strength. He became more aggressive as a basestealer in 2017 and has 20-20 upside, though he's a long way from that ceiling and still has to prove he can hit more advanced pitching. He divided his pro debut among all three outfield positions and fits best in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2019, the main attraction at Hagerty High School in Florida was Riley Greene, who went No. 5 overall that June to the Tigers. Grissom was that school's shortstop, and while he wasn’t as highly regarded, the Braves liked him enough to go over the $125K limit in the 11th round and sign him for $347,500. He’s rewarded their investment by hitting pretty much everywhere as a pro -- from his summer debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League to the alternate site, where he was one of the youngest players, to a full-season debut in 2021 in which he raked in A ball and earned a late promotion to High-A. Grissom routinely displays outstanding bat-to-ball skills with a very good approach. He has a strong feel for the barrel from the right side of the plate, manages his at-bats well, draws walks and rarely strikes out. He’s short to the ball with relatively simple hitting mechanics and has solid bat speed. The Braves hope he’ll continue to fill out his 6-foot-3 frame and grow into more power as he matures. As solid as Grissom has been at the plate, it’s been less clear where he might belong long-term defensively. He’s still seen more time at shortstop than any other position, but he’s also played a fair amount at third as well as a little at second. He has the arm to stay on the left side of the infield, where he’s more comfortable and while he doesn’t always have silky-smooth actions, he’s a solid defender. If he can’t play short, he might need to raise his power profile a bit to be a fit at the hot corner as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the 2020 season, Hagerty High School now has two big leaguers on its alumni list, with Orioles outfielder Ryan Mountcastle joining Phillies right-hander Zach Eflin at the highest level. Chances are Tigers 2019 first-round pick Riley Greene will be next, but Grissom, his teammate and 11th-rounder that same June, might not be far behind him. After getting an above-slot bonus to keep him from attending Florida International, he had a solid pro debut in the Gulf Coast League, then performed well as one of the youngest players at the Braves’ alternate site in 2020 before continuing his good work at instructs. Facing a slew of 40-man roster-caliber arms at the alternate site, Grissom showed that the advanced approach he displayed in the GCL was for real. He consistently had quality at-bats, with the ability to repeat a simple load and swing with good bat speed. He’s simplified his setup from his days as an amateur and that should help him make hard contact and tap into his power more as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. Just how much he does that might help decide what infield position he ends up at long term. A shortstop in high school and during his pro debut, he has good hands and a strong arm. He’ll likely see time at second, third and short moving forward, with the hot corner the most likely landing spot should he develop enough to be a regular at one position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the 2019 Draft, the biggest claims to fame for Hagerty High School outside of Orlando was Phillies right-hander Zach Eflin and Orioles prospect Ryan Mountcastle. The 2019 Draft class has the chance to add two names to that list: Tigers’ first-rounder Riley Greene and Grissom, whom the Braves did a great job of scouting and signing for an above-slot $347,500 bonus in the 11th round. He then had a solid debut in the Gulf Coast League. The Braves like Grissom’s potential on both sides of the ball, even if it’s unclear where he’s going to play defensively just yet. At the plate, the right-handed hitter has good bat speed and showed a pretty good approach at the plate during his pro debut, limiting his strikeouts and drawing some walks along the way. He came to pro ball with a little leg kick and some other moving parts to his swing, things he worked on cleaning up at the Braves’ hitting camp this offseason, which should help him tap into his raw power more. While Grissom exclusively played shortstop during his pro debut and the Braves think he could handle the position for a while, he also played some third base during instructs. Some of that is because the organization has some depth at the position in the lower levels, but some of it is because the 6-foot-3 Grissom could outgrow the position. The good news is the Braves feel his hand, arm strength and power potential all could profile well at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stevenson transferred to the University of Arizona as a junior after he had spent his freshman and sophomore seasons at Nevada and Chabot College. A starter in both years for the Wildcats, Stevenson proved to be an on-base machine, amassing 83 walks against 52 strikeouts. That plate discipline earned Stevenson a selection by the Blue Jays in the 10th round last June, and he signed for just $5,000. The deal already is looking like a bargain after Stevenson produced a .369/.511/.523 line with 73 runs scored, 21 steals and almost three times as many walks as strikeouts across two levels in his pro debut. Stevenson's penchant for drawing walks and reaching base has followed him throughout his career. His feel for the strike zone is as good as any player in the system, and he's advanced in his ability to recognize pitches. Stevenson has hitting ability, too, with a knack for finding the barrel and staying inside the ball that enable him to rope line drives to all fields. Power will never be a big part of Stevenson's game, but he does have consistent pop to the gaps, with speed that fuels his extra-base potential and earns him praise as one of the organization's better baserunners. Club officials also see Stevenson as one of the system's better defensive outfielders, noting that he gets great reads off the bat and has instincts that allow him to get the most of his abilities. While those qualities give him a chance to remain in center field, Stevenson's mature game and vast skill set have led many to forecast him as a future fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Charles has steadily climbed up the organization since signing with the A’s in March 2015 out of the Dominican Republic. The right-hander’s breakthrough came in 2019, when he rose through three levels to end the season at Double-A Midland as a reliever. Possessing the highest average velocity in the organization, Charles is still learning how to pitch as he looks to graduate to the highest level. Bringing a power fastball that can touch triple digits to go along with a wipeout slider, Charles showed improvement at both the A’s alternate site and in the instructional league. If he can put it together, Charles has the makings of a strong-armed reliever who can fill the back end of a bullpen. Lowering his walk rate and throwing more strikes could speed up his call to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Georgia State player ever to make the U.S. collegiate national team, Gaddis also became the highest pick in school history when Cleveland drafted him in the fifth round in 2019. He topped the High-A Central with 127 strikeouts in 97 1/3 innings during his first full pro season in 2021, then scooted from Double-A to the big leagues last season. He allowed seven homers and 15 runs in 7 1/3 innings over two starts with the Guardians, who believe he was tipping his pitches by altering his arm angle when he threw his changeup. Gaddis' best pitch is his upper-70s change, which elicits a lot of empty swings with plenty of fade and some sink as well. His changeup pairs well with his four-seam fastball, which parks at 92-95 mph, can reach 98 in short stints and has effective carry when he maintains his high three-quarters arm slot. His mid-80s slider/cutter plays as a solid pitch because he locates it well and is much more effective than his mid-70s curveball. Gaddis throws strikes and uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create deceptive angle that is tough on right-handers, but he struggled against left-handers in 2022. He's vulnerable to home runs when he doesn't locate his pitches well, and he gets in trouble when he drops his arm slot and loses action on his fastball and depth on his breaking balls. He could serve as an innings-eater at the back of a rotation or a long reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ragans pitched only 7 2/3 innings in his pro debut after signing for $2,003,400 as the 30th overall pick in 2016, but he showed why the Rangers made him a first-round selection the next summer when he led the short-season Northwest League with 87 strikeouts in 57 1/3 frames. Texas was set to turn him loose in full-season ball in 2018, until he was diagnosed with an elbow injury in Spring Training and missed the entire year following Tommy John surgery. He reinjured his elbow just before he was set to return to game action this May and had to have his elbow reconstructed a second time. Ragans patterned his delivery after former Rangers ace Cole Hamels and often gets compared to the four-time All-Star for his repertoire and lanky 6-foot-4 build. He has advanced feel of a plus changeup and sets it up nicely with a 91-95 mph fastball that plays better than its velocity because of its high spin rate and how well he hides the ball. His curveball has good shape and could become a solid third offering if he can add more power to it. The athletic Ragans repeats his mechanics well and uses his size to deliver his pitches with downhill plane. Though he has all the ingredients for better than average control, he surprisingly averaged 5.7 walks per nine innings during his first two years as a pro. The Rangers believe those issues may have been related to the health of his elbow and he could take off once he's back to full strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers not only have Cole Hamels in their rotation, but also the next version of him coming through their system in Ragans, who patterned his delivery after the four-time All-Star's and started earning comparisons to him in high school. Signed for $2,003,400 as the 30th overall pick in 2016, he topped the short-season Northwest League in strikeouts (87) last summer and easily would have led in strikeout rate (13.7 per nine innings) if he had enough innings to qualify. His encore will be delayed until 2019, however, because he was diagnosed with an elbow injury during Spring Training that required Tommy John surgery. Ragans' fastball sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 mph, but it plays as a plus pitch because it features a high spin rate that creates riding life and he also hides it well. He added some velocity during his first full year of pro ball and could pick up more as he continues to strengthen his lean frame. His changeup is similarly effective and his downer curveball should become a solid third pitch once it develops more power. Ragans has sound mechanics and employs a high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. Though he's athletic and repeats his delivery, his control and command are still works in progress. He walked 5.7 batters per nine innings in his first two pro seasons, and if he can pound the strike zone more efficiently once he returns to health, he could become a No. 2 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A projectable, athletic left-hander, Ragans draws comparisons to a young Cole Hamels and modeled his delivery after him. He'll get a chance to one day join him in the Texas rotation after the Rangers drafted him 30th overall and signed him for $2,003,400 last June. The club plans on bringing him along slowly and had him pitch just 7 2/3 innings in his pro debut. Ragans has the potential for three solid-or-better pitches. His fastball currently sits around 90 mph and tops out at 94, but he figures to add more velocity when he gets stronger and already misses a lot of bats because it features a high spin rate that creates riding life. His curveball has downer action when he stays on top of it and could turn into a plus offering if it adds more power as expected, and his changeup has similar upside but less consistency. Ragans has a sound delivery and uses a high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. He does a good job of repeating his mechanics, though his command still wavers, as is true of most young pitchers. If he can add the necessary polish, he could become the most well-rounded lefty starter among Texas' deep group of southpaw mound prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A quarterback who totaled 43 touchdowns as an Alabama high school senior and sparked interest from Southeastern Conference football programs, Thompson decided to focus on baseball. The Rangers spent the 26th overall pick in 2017 and $2.1 million to land his athleticism and upside, but a series of injuries (tendinitis in both knees, broken hamate, ankle) and the cancelled 2020 season held him to just 171 games in his first four years as a pro. He enjoyed full health and the best season of his career in 2021, though his plate discipline remains an issue and Texas opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster in November. Thompson's best tool remains his well-above-average speed. It helped him lead the Double-A Central with nine triples and 48 extra-base hits last season, and he also swiped 25 bases in 33 attempts. He has improved his reads and routes and become a plus defender in center field, though the former quarterback surprisingly lacks arm strength and didn't register a single assist in 93 games a year ago. With his hand-eye coordination, bat speed and strength, Thompson has the physical tools to be productive at the plate. But his lack of pitch recognition and plate discipline continue to hold him back, and the right-handed hitter may not do enough damage against same-side pitchers to be more than a platoon player. His work ethic and personality have made him an organization favorite and earned him its True Ranger Award in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A quarterback who drew interest from Southeastern Conference football programs, Thompson accounted for 43 touchdowns as an Alabama high school senior before commiting to Alabama for baseball only. His five-tool potential earned him $2.1 million as the 26th overall pick in 2017 but repeated injuries have impeded his development. Tendinitis in both knees hampered him his debut, and a broken hamate and an ankle injury limited him to 57 games and a .573 OPS in high Class A last year. Thompson has the bat speed, strength and well above-average speed to become at least a 25-25 player if everything clicks. That hasn't happened yet because his struggles with pitch recognition and plate discipline undermine his fine hand-eye coordination, and totaling just 714 plate appearances in his first three pro seasons hasn't helped. After his strikeout rate rose to a career-worst 32 percent in 2019, he spent time in the Arizona Fall League working on developing a more consistent load, shortening his right-handed stroke and creating a better swing path. Thompson's quickness already has translated into basestealing prowess. He's less polished in center field, where his reads and routes need improvement but his speed allows him to outrun his mistakes. He has an average arm that allows him to play all three outfield positions if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A quarterback recruited by Southeastern Conference football programs, Thompson totaled 3,860 yards and 43 touchdowns while leading McGill-Toolen High to the Alabama state 7-A championship game in the fall of 2016. He committed to Alabama for baseball only before playing his way into 2017's first round with a strong senior season. Signed for $2.1 million as the 26th overall pick, he was slowed by tendinitis in his knees during his pro debut, but his five-tool potential was evident in his first full season. While Thompson isn't as raw on the diamond as a lot of two-sport stars, he will also need time to refine his tools into skills. He has impressive hand-eye coordination and bat speed from the right side of the plate, though he's still working on pitch recognition and plate discipline and lost some needed development time in 2019 to a broken hamate and an ankle injury. He's starting to drive the ball more consistently and could produce 25 or more homers annually as he gets stronger. Thompson's most obvious tool is his well-above-average speed and he shows the aptitude to become a premium basestealer. His reads and jumps are less polished in center field, though he has the quickness to outrun a lot of his mistakes and should get better with more experience. His solid arm strength fits anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson quarterbacked McGill-Toolen High to the Alabama state 7-A championship game in the fall of 2016, totaling 3,860 yards and 43 touchdowns while drawing football scholarship offers from Mississippi and Tennessee. He committed to Alabama for baseball only, but that didn't matter after he played his way into 2017's first round and signed for a slightly under-slot $2.1 million as the No. 26 overall selection. Though he was bothered by tendinitis in his knees during his pro debut, his upside was apparent. For an athlete who divided his attention between multiple sports, Thompson isn't nearly as raw as might be expected. His impressive hand-eye coordination should allow him to make consistent contact from the right side of the plate, and his pitch recognition and selectivity are surprising considering his inexperience. Scouts entered his senior season unsure about his power potential, but he began to drive the ball more consistently and has the bat speed and strength for average pop. Thompson's well above-average speed and his strong arm can make him a quality defender anywhere in the outfield. He's still learning as a basestealer and needs to upgrade his reads and routes in center field. The Rangers are known for their ability to polish high-ceiling prospects, and he could be a 20-20 up-the-middle player when fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas starred as an amateur in Cuba, driving in the gold medal-winning run off Team USA's Hunter Greene at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup, before defecting with his father Lazaro (the DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions) in November 2015. He waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000 and has established himself as the best hitter in the system. A career .313 hitter in the Minors, he won the Double-A Central batting title (.321) in 2021 and doubled off Alex Cobb in his first big league at-bat last August. Vargas is an extremely advanced hitter with elite bat-to-ball skills and a good understanding of his right-handed swing and what he's trying to do at the plate. He controls the strike zone, uses the entire field and handles fastballs and breaking balls with ease, though he did struggle a bit against changeups in 2022. He's more hitter than slugger, but his bat speed, strength and penchant for making hard contact should allow him to get to all of his solid raw power and produce 20-25 homers per season. Known mostly for his bat, Vargas has put in the time to improve his speed, athleticism and defense. Regarded as a fringy to average runner, he nonetheless recorded sprint speeds in the 94th percentile during his introduction to the Majors. He has fringy range but solid arm strength at third base, his primary position, but spent most of his big league time at first base and left field. He's decent at first base, a work in progress in left field and comfortable (albeit with subpar range) at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Lazaro Vargas, the DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions, Miguel drove in the gold medal-winning run off Team USA's Hunter Greene at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup in Mexico. After defecting with his father in November 2015, he waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000. The best pure hitter in the system, he owns a career .316 average in his first three years as a pro and won the Double-A Central batting title last season at .321 as a 21-year-old. Vargas is well equipped to accrue more batting championships in the future because he has advanced bat-to-ball skills, understands the mechanics of his right-handed swing, controls the strike zone and hits balls where they're pitched. He's figuring out how to tap into his solid raw power, improving from seven homers in 2019 to 23 last year by turning on and lifting more pitches. He has shown the ability to handle high-velocity fastballs and isn't fazed by quality breaking balls. Vargas' bat definitely should play but the question is where because he lacks speed and quick-twitch athleticism. He has improved his conditioning and his range at third base since turning pro, and he does possess solid arm strength. The Dodgers also have given him time at left field, second base and first base the last two seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Cuban team that also included Adrian Morejon and Athletics outfield prospect Lazarito Armenteros, Vargas drove in the gold medal-winning run at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup in Mexico. He defected in November 2015 with his father Lazaro, the DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions, and waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000 in September 2017. He hit .314/.387/.447 while reaching high Class A in his first two pro seasons before spending 2020 in instructional league. Los Angeles has pushed Vargas aggressively because he has the advanced bat-to-ball skills to handle the challenge. He understands his right-handed swing mechanics, controls the strike zone and uses the entire field. He began driving the ball in the air more regularly in 2019 and has shown solid power this year as he has gotten more aggressive and turned on more pitches. Because Vargas lacks speed and quick-twitch athleticism, his defensive home is in question. He has worked diligently to improve his conditioning and his range at third base, where he displays solid arm strength. The Dodgers are pleased with his progress at the hot corner, while scouts in other organizations wonder if he's destined for first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Playing on a Cuban team with Lazarito Armenteros (now in the Athletics system) and Adrian Morejon (Padres), Vargas won a gold medal at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup in Mexico. He defected in November 2015 along with his father Lazaro, a DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions, and waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000 in September 2017. He easily handled two Class A levels as a 19-year-old in 2019, batting a combined .308/.380/.440 with a system-best 38 doubles. Vargas possesses some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system, the main reason why Los Angeles hasn't been afraid to push him. He has a fine understanding of his right-handed swing, manages the strike zone well and has an affinity for using the entire field. The Dodgers do a nice job of squeezing the most out of their prospects' power potential and helped him drive the ball in the air more regularly in 2019, and some of those doubles could turn into homers as he gets stronger and turns on more pitches. Vargas lacks speed and quick-twitch athleticism, but he has worked hard to improve his body and range at third base. Despite his solid arm strength, scouts in other organizations question whether he can stay at the hot corner, though Los Angeles is pleased with his progress. First base is his only realistic fallback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas played on a talented Cuban 15-and-under national team with Lazarito Armenteros (now with the Athletics) and Adrian Morejon (Padres) before defecting in November 2015 along with his father Lazaro, who won gold medals as a DH on Cuba's Olympic teams in 1992 and 1996. Miguel waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers, receiving $300,000 in September 2017. He batted .400/.464/.592 between two Rookie levels in his 2018 pro debut but dropped to .213/.307/.253 following a promotion to low Class A. Vargas stands out most for his bat-to-ball skills, which were advanced enough to land him on Cuba's 18-and-under team when he was just 15 years old. He understands his right-handed swing very well, controls the strike zone and likes to use the opposite field. He has some raw power but has yet to tap into it, prioritizing contact with an inside-out stroke and rarely pulling the ball with authority. Most of Vargas' value is going to come from his bat, so he'll need to hit more home runs in order to become a big league regular. His solid arm works at third base but he lacks quickness and range. To his credit, he improved his body last offseason and has shown more speed and defensive ability at the hot corner this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A supplemental second-round choice out of a Southern California high school in 2017, Freeman has established himself as one of the best pure hitters in the Minors. He hit .292 or better in each of his first four pro seasons, won the short-season New York-Penn League batting title at .352 in 2018 and entered 2022 with a career .319 mark along with a tiny 9 percent strikeout rate. He was contending for another batting crown in the Double-A Northeast last June when he slightly tore the labrum in his left shoulder on a swing, leading to surgery that ended his season after 41 games, but he still claimed a spot on Cleveland's 40-man roster in November. His younger brother Cody is a catcher in the Rangers system with similar tools. A right-handed hitter, Freeman possesses exceptional bat-to-ball skills that produce line drives to all fields on a regular basis. He rarely swings and misses, but the ease with which he makes contact cuts into his on-base ability because he owns a career 4 percent walk rate. He also homered just nine times in his first 272 pro games, so he might fit a Nick Madrigal high-average/low-impact profile, though he does drive some balls to the gaps and offers some doubles power. Freeman's bat is his lone plus tool, and his speed, arm and defense all grade as average. He does have good instincts that allow him to play above his physical ability on the bases and in the field. He's an aggressive baserunner and a sure-handed fielder with a quick release on his throws, though many scouts think he'll eventually shift from shortstop to second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Southern California's best high school hitters in 2017, Freeman gave up a Texas Christian scholarship to sign with the Indians as a supplemental second-round Draft pick. One of several sweet-swinging infielders with a high baseball IQ in Cleveland's system, he won the short-season New York-Penn League batting title (.352) in ‘18 and batted .306/.368/.410 between two Class A levels as an encore. He continued to excel in Double-A this year, but sustained a slight tear in his labrum in his left shoulder on a swing, necessitating surgery that ended his season after 41 games. His younger brother Cody was a Rangers fourth-rounder in ‘19 and possesses similar tools. While Freeman's hitting ability is his only plus tool, he does have some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the entire Minor Leagues. He batted .319 with a 9 percent strikeout rate in his first three pro seasons, lashing line drives to all fields from the right side of the plate. He could develop 15-homer power if he adds strength and learns to drive the ball in the air more often, though he may never walk much because he makes contact so easily. Freeman's instincts allow him to play quicker on the bases and at shortstop than his average speed. He's an aggressive baserunner with a knack for stealing bases and is a reliable defender with sure hands at short. He enhances his average arm strength by getting rid of the ball quickly, though many scouts think he's destined for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best high school hitters in Southern California in 2017, Freeman appeared headed to Texas Christian until the Indians drafted him in the supplemental second round and signed him for $816,500. After a solid pro debut, he led the short-season New York-Penn League in hitting (.352), slugging (.511), OPS (.916), runs (49), hits (95), doubles (29), extra-base hits (35) and total bases (138) in 2018. He made the jump to full-season ball last season and continued to produce, batting .306/.368/.410 between two Class A levels. Though Freeman's hitting ability is his lone plus tool, his elite bat-to-ball skills could make him a big league regular. He excels at making line-drive contact to all fields from the right side of the plate, and he could develop 12-15 home run power if he gets stronger and drives the ball in the air more frequently. He could stand to draw more walks, but he puts the ball in play so easily that he rarely works deep counts. An average runner, Freeman plays quicker than that on the bases and in the field thanks to his high baseball IQ. He's an aggressive baserunner who knows how to pick his spots to steal. He's a reliable defender with sure hands at shortstop, enhancing an average arm with a quick release, though he ultimately might wind up at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top high school hitters in Southern California in 2017, Freeman passed up a strong commitment to Texas Christian to sign for $816,500 as a supplemental second-rounder. After a solid pro debut, he had a spectacular '18, topping the short-season New York-Penn League in hitting (.352), runs (49), hits (95), doubles (29), extra-base hits (35) and total bases (138). He has the highest offensive ceiling among Cleveland's deep pool of young infielders, not to mention some of the best leadership ability and work ethic in the system. Freeman's elite bat-to-ball skills produce repeated line-drive contact from the right side of the plate. He has such advanced feel for hitting that he could develop close to average power once he adds more strength and drives the ball in the air more often. If there's a knock on his offensive game, it's that he puts the ball in play almost too easily, as he drew only eight walks in 301 plate appearances last year. Freeman's instincts also stand out on the bases and in the field, where he plays better than his average speed. He's an aggressive runner and proficient basestealer. He has sure hands and makes up for an average arm at shortstop with a quick release, though his tools may fit better at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians made Freeman the highest-drafted player in Etiwanda (Calif.) High history in 2017 when they took him with the No. 71 overall pick in the second Competitive Balance Round. After signing for slot value and forgoing a commitment to Texas Christian, Freeman impressed with his well-rounded game during a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League. The Indians targeted Freeman in the Draft for his pure hitting ability and potential to stick at an up-the-middle position. He's a high-contact, line-drive hitter from the right side of the plate, one who should naturally grow into some power in the future. Though not a burner, he is an above-average runner, especially once underway. Defensively, Freeman shows range and a decent arm as a shortstop, with both tools playing up thanks to his strong instincts. But because his tools aren't overwhelming, many evaluators foresee a move to second down the line. Regardless of his future defensive home, Freeman's bat suggests the floor of a utility player who might perform his way into an everyday role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henry vaulted onto the radar with his first five starts of 2019, including a complete-game one-hitter with 13 strikeouts against The Citadel on just 88 pitches. The D-backs took Henry with the No. 74 overall pick in the Draft, then watched as the southpaw fired a 10-strikeout three-hit shutout against Florida State to help lead Michigan into the College World Series Finals. Henry’s stuff ticked up at the alternate training site in 2020 and he carried that momentum into 2021, when he made his full-season debut with Double-A Amarillo. Pitching in an offense-friendly league, Henry posted a 5.21 ERA and struck out 135 over 115 2/3 innings with multiple D-backs officials saying he threw better than the numbers indicated. Henry's stuff has improved since his time at Michigan. After throwing in the mid-80s as a freshman and sophomore, his fastball now sits between 90-94 mph and can touch 95-96. He locates the fastball to both sides of the plate and impressed with his ability to miss bats in Double-A (10.5 K/9). His fading changeup has grown more than any of his other offerings over the past two seasons and his low-80s slider serves as his out pitch. Henry has also developed a curveball, and although it needs refinement, it shows promise. An underrated athlete, Henry has an easy delivery -- though his mechanics, and therefore his velocity, fluctuate at times. That being said, plus control allows Henry to throw all his pitches for strikes. He fared well when the D-backs challenged him with an aggressive assignment to Double-A in his professional debut, showing growth throughout the season and improving as the year went on. A consistent performer, Henry has already pitched his way to Arizona with a strong season at Triple-A Reno and should get consideration for a long-term Major League rotation spot the rest of the way in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henry was steady as a freshman reliever and sophomore starter at Michigan, but he wasn't a priority target after sitting in the mid-80s with his fastball in the Cape Cod League. Then he was spectacular in his first five starts of 2019, including a complete-game one-hitter with 13 strikeouts against The Citadel on just 88 pitches, looking like the Wolverines' best pitching prospect since Jim Abbott. The D-backs took Henry with the No. 74 overall pick in the Draft, then watched as the southpaw fired a two-hit, 10-strikeout shutout against Florida State to help lead Michigan into the College World Series finals. Henry’s stuff ticked up at the alternate training site in 2020 and he carried that momentum into 2021, when he made his full-season debut with Double-A Amarillo. Henry's stuff has improved since his time at Michigan. While his fastball still sits in the low 90s, he’s also shown an ability to dial it up to 95-96. He locates the fastball to both sides of the plate and has impressed with his ability to miss bats in Double-A. He also throws a changeup with good fading action and a slider with depth, with both offerings registering in the upper 70s to low 80s. He’s a good athlete with an easy delivery that he repeats well. Henry is an underrated athlete, one of those guys who can drive a golf ball or kick a field goal and he has a tremendous competitive streak. The D-backs challenged Henry, assigning him to Double-A in his first full season, and he responded well. A consistent performer, he has a chance to move quickly through the system and develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Henry was steady as a freshman reliever and sophomore starter at Michigan, but he wasn't a priority target after sitting in the mid-80s with his fastball in the Cape Cod League last summer. Then he was spectacular in his first five starts of 2019, including a complete-game one-hitter with 13 strikeouts against The Citadel on just 88 pitches, looking like a potential supplemental first-rounder and the Wolverines' best pitching prospect since Jim Abbott. The D-backs took Henry with the No. 74 overall pick in the June Draft, then watched as the southpaw fired a two-hit, 10-strikeout shutout against Florida State to help lead Michigan into the College World Series finals. Though nothing he throws is overpowering, Henry knows how to be successful by commanding all three of his pitches well. He sits in the low 90s with a fastball that he locates to both sides of the plate and can induce swings and misses with a changeup and a slider. He throws the former with good fading action and latter with depth, with both offerings registering in the upper 70s to low 80s. He’s a good athlete with an easy delivery he repeats well. Henry floods the zone with strikes and generates a bunch of ugly swings when he's on top of his game. However, he'll need to answer questions about his durability in pro ball after his fastball dipped into the upper 80s and his secondary pitches weren't as sharp late in his junior campaign. If Henry can check those boxes, he could be one of the first college hurlers from his class to reach the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benson excited scouts with his size and power/speed combination leading up to the 2016 Draft, earning comparisons to Jason Heyward as an Atlanta-area high schooler with a similar build and athleticism. After signing for an under-slot $2.5 million as the 14th overall pick that June, he hit just .201/.329/.409 in his first three pro seasons. He led the Class A Midwest League with 22 homers and ranked third with 82 walks in 2018, but his .180 batting average was the second-lowest among full-season batting qualifiers in the Minors. Benson offers massive raw power, the product of a quick bat, prodigious strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-5 frame. He's also extremely selective at the plate, able to recognize offspeed pitches and refrain from chasing them out of the strike zone. But there are mechanical and timing issues with his left-handed swing, resulting in way too many swings and misses at hittable strikes. If Benson can solve his hitting issues, he would have some of the highest upside in the system. He's very athletic for his size, displaying solid speed and a plus arm. He has the tools to be an asset in right field, though he needs to smooth out some rough edges first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout for USA Baseball's gold medal-winning team in the 2016 18U World Cup in Japan, Benson continued to boost his Draft stock during the spring as he led The Westminster School to its first Georgia 3-A championship since 1975. Targeting offensive upside, the Indians selected Benson, a Duke commit, with the No. 14 overall pick in June, and he made his pro debut later that month after signing for $2.5 million. Spending all of 2017 with Class A Short-Season Mahoning Valley, Benson tied for the New York-Penn League home run lead with 10, while his 36 RBIs ranked third in the circuit. Benson's combination of bat speed and sheer physical strength translates to prodigious raw power from the left side of the plate, and he's already shown that he can apply it to his pull-side during games. Making consistent contact, however, has been a struggle for Benson, who has struck out one-third of the time in his first two seasons, though he does work his share of walks. The Indians will continue to work with Benson to clean up his swing, with the goal of getting him in a better position to hit. Benson is an impressive athlete for his size as well as an above-average runner, but he's likely to lose some of that speed with physical maturation. It's also why Benson, a center fielder in high school, is best suited to play right field in pro ball, where he's an average defender with a plus arm. He may be a bit of a project, but all the ingredients are there for Benson to develop into a middle-of-the-order hitter who also adds value with his baserunning and defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benson endeared himself to scouts with his loud tools while playing for USA Baseball's gold medal-winning squad in the 18U World Cup in Japan. As a senior, he batted .454 with eight home runs and 41 RBIs and led The Westminster School to a Georgia 3-A championship, the Wildcats' first title since 1975. Targeting offensive upside, the Indians selected Benson, a Duke commit, with the No. 14 overall pick in June, and then saved nearly $500,000 by signing him for $2.5 million. He struggled at times in the Rookie Arizona League during his pro debut but still showed the ability to impact games in a variety of ways, finishing second on the team in doubles (10), home runs (6), walks (22) and stolen bases (10). Benson's bat speed and strength give him well-above-average raw power from the left side of the plate, and he already shows the ability to get to it during games. He's at his best when he stays short to the ball and uses the whole field, and the Indians have worked to get him into a better position to hit. And while strikeouts may always be a part of his game, Benson impressed club officials during his pro debut with his ability and willingness to coax walks.
