Benson is a standout athlete with slightly above-average speed, although he's likely to lose a step or two as he fills out physically. It's also why Benson, a center fielder in high school, is best suited to play right field in pro ball, where he profiles as an average defender with a plus arm. Benson has the tools to develop into a middle-of-the-order hitter, but he may require extra time to refine his skills in the Minor Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite hitting just .249 in three seasons at Sacramento State, Outman showcased an interesting package of tools that enticed Los Angeles to select him in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft. He homered 11 times in the final month of the 2019 season in Single-A and has continued to get better after returning from the pandemic layoff in 2020. He batted .294/.393/.586 with 31 homers between Double-A and Triple-A last season, leading all Dodgers farmhands in slugging and OPS (.978), and homered off Germán Márquez in his first big league at-bat in July. Outman has taken off at the plate after making significant adjustments to his left-handed swing, gained a better understanding of it and calming down his approach. He still prioritizes damage by looking to launch balls to his pull side, but his ability to tap into his bat speed and strength could result in 25 or more homers per season. His aggressive hunt for power does lead to strikeouts, though he offsets his whiffs by consistently drawing walks and getting hit by pitches to post high batting averages. Outman has the ability to contribute in all phases of the game. One of the best athletes in the system, he has plus speed and has stolen bases at a 77 percent clip in the Minors. He's a quality center fielder who can fit anywhere in the outfield with his ability to cover ground and his strong arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Outman batted just .249 in three seasons at Sacramento State, the Dodgers bought into his intriguing all-around tools and selected him in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft. He began to break out with 11 homers in the final month of the 2019 season in Low-A and took another step forward in the second half of 2021, batting .297/.392/.568 while advancing to Double-A. He built on that momentum in the Arizona Fall League and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Outman began to perform better at the plate as he gained a better understanding of his left-handed swing. He still aggressively looks to launch balls to his pull side, but slowing things down enabled him to chase fewer pitches out of the zone and access his plus raw power more consistently. He still strikes out too much to post high batting averages, though he compensates by drawing plenty of walks and hit by pitches. One of the best athletes in the system, Outman is a 6-foot-3, 215-pounder with plus speed and arm strength. He has aptitude for stealing bases and swiped 23 in 27 attempts last season. He has instincts to go with his quickness in center field and provides plus defense at any of the three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Orioles assistant general manager Sig Mejdal broke into baseball with the Cardinals, he famously targeted a college infielder for the team’s top pick in the 2005 Draft, believing the player was undervalued. That player was Jed Lowrie, whom St. Louis passed on and who went on to enjoy a productive big league career as a versatile switch-hitting second baseman. Mejdal never forgot that oversight, and now, the system he oversees sports a player with a similar profile in Terrin Vavra. The story goes a long way toward explaining why the Orioles targeted Vavra as part of their return package in the 2020 Mychal Givens trade with the Rockies. A bat-first second baseman who can also play some outfield, Vavra was Colorado’s third-round pick in 2018 out of the University of Minnesota. His baseball family ties run deep: He is the son of former Twins and Tigers hitting coach Joe Vavra, and has two brothers who also played pro ball. He had a standout career at Minnesota and built on that success immediately, earning South Atlantic League MVP honors in ’19. He then had a productive but incomplete first year in Baltimore’s system, posting a .388 on-base percentage at Double-A Bowie in ’21 but missing more than two months with back issues. The Orioles added him to their 40-man roster in November. On the field, Vavra’s natural feel to hit stands out more than anything else. He works counts and knows the strike zone extremely well, walking nearly as much as he's struck out in his Minor League career. He’s known as a gamer who manipulates the bat head well and rarely gets fooled, consistently squaring up the baseball from both sides of the plate. The power is only fringe to average, though he’s shown more from the left side of the plate thus far. Defensively, Vavra profiles best at second but also showed well in center field in a small sample last summer. He’s likely to move around at the highest level rather than settle at one position, profiling as an offensive-minded utility type who hits his way into the lineup every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies' 2018 third-round pick after a standout career at the University of Minnesota, Vavra built on that success immediately in pro ball, earning South Atlantic League MVP honors in 2019. He arrived in the Orioles system the following year, as part of the Mychal Givens trade prior to the 2020 Deadline. Vavra is known as a gamer whose baseball bloodlines run deep: He is the son of former Twins and Tigers hitting coach Joe Vavra, and has two brothers who also played pro ball. On the field, Vavra’s natural feel to hit stands out more than anything else. He works counts and knows the strike zone extremely well, walking as much as he struck out in 2019. The switch-hitter manipulates the bat head and doesn’t get fooled, consistently squaring up the baseball and spraying line drives to all fields from both sides of the plate. It is a hit-first profile with fringe to average power, though he’s shown more from the left side of the plate thus far. Described by Orioles people as a “Moneyball-style second baseman,” Vavra profiles better defensively at the position than at short. The likelier scenario is that he moves around, seeing time at third and in the outfield as well in ’21, with an eye toward maximizing his versatility. Even if he doesn’t settle into one position, he could easily be an offensive-minded utility type who hits his way into the lineup every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In three years at the University of Minnesota, Vavra earned a reputation as a gamer with good instincts and a feel to hit. He’s been as good as advertised in his year plus of pro ball since the Rockies took him in the third round of the 2018 Draft. The son of Tigers hitting coach Joe Vavra had two brothers who also played pro ball, but after his MVP campaign in the South Atlantic League in 2019, he looks primed to outperform his siblings, something he’ll have to do with the Orioles after being acquired as part of the Mychal Givens trade on the eve of the 2020 Trade Deadline. Vavra’s natural feel to hit stands out more than anything else. He works counts and knows the strike zone extremely well, walking as much as he struck out in 2019. The switch-hitter manipulates the bat head and doesn’t get fooled, consistently squaring up the baseball and sending line drives to all fields, with more power coming from the left side of the plate so far. The only reason Vavra spent all year in Asheville, other than giving him the chance to compete in a playoff push, was to work on his defense. He’s played both shortstop and second base, the latter being his best spot for him to be a big league regular in one position, and he could start seeing time at third in 2020. Even if he doesn’t settle into one position, he could easily be an offensive-minded utility type who hits his way into the lineup every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Vavra family just keeps churning out professional baseball players. Terrin Vavra is the third of three brothers to head into pro ball, following their father Joe, who is still coaching in pro ball as the Tigers' quality control coach, into the family business. Terrin's also the best prospect of the trio, and after a big junior season at the University of Minnesota in 2018, he became the Rockies' third-round pick and kept on hitting during his pro debut in the short-season Northwest League. Put simply, Vavra just hits wherever he goes. Utilizing a short stroke from the left side of the plate, he always stays within himself, focusing on using the middle of the field. The result is line drives to all fields, consistently professional at-bats with a strong strikeout-to-walk ratio, and some sneaky extra-base authority. On the other side of the ball, Vavra is a steady, but not flashy, defender who makes all the plays from multiple positions. He can handle shortstop, but his arm and range might not be a fit to be a regular there. He plays a very good second base as well. The Rockies love infielders with positional flexibility, and Vavra will mix some third base in as he moves forward. Some in the organization compare him favorably to fellow infield prospect Garrett Hampson, without as much speed, with the competitiveness and makeup similar to, but with more offensive potential, another Rockie infielder, Pat Valaika.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sierra was overmatched during his first taste of full-season ball as a teenager in 2015. He rebounded in his return to the Class A Peoria the following year, when he finished ninth in the Midwest League in batting average and tied for third in stolen bases. Sierra built on that success in 2017, beginning the season in the Class A Advanced Florida State League before jumping to the Major Leagues in May. He ultimately batted .317 over parts of 22 games (and four stints) with St. Louis, which then dealt him to the Marlins in December with Sandy Alcantara, Zac Gallen and Daniel Castano as part of the Marcell Ozuna trade. With his knack for making consistent, hard contact and his well-above-average speed, Sierra has the raw ingredients to become a future top-of-the-order-type hitter, and he stands to solidify that profile even more with a more refined approach and improved on-base skills. Sierra will never offer over-the-fence power but has enough strength to hit the gaps, with his speed enabling to him to routinely take extra bases. He receives high marks for his baserunning, though his ability as a basestealer leaves something to be desired. Sierra is an elite-level defender in center field, the kind who regularly makes highlight-reel plays, and he has a plus arm to boot. While he doesn't have the ceiling of Miami's other recently acquired outfielders like Lewis Brinson and Monte Harrison, Sierra, with his four average-or-better tools, certainly has the highest floor. He's a key part of the rebuilding Marlins' future as well as a candidate to see significant time in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baseball development isn't always a straight path and sometimes prospects need to take a step back to move forward. That seems to be the case with Sierra, who wasn't ready for full-season ball in 2015, righted the ship after a move back to the Rookie-level Appalachian League, then handled the Midwest League in 2016 by finishing ninth in batting average and tied for third in stolen bases. He jumped on the fast track in 2017, moving up to Double-A early in the season and even making his big league debut in May, and then joined the Marlins in December with Sandy Alcantara, Zac Gallen and Daniel Castano as part of the Marcell Ozuna trade. While Sierra could stand to refine his approach and draw more walks, especially since he profiles as a top-of-the-order type hitter, he does have a knack for making consistent hard contact. He doesn't have over-the-fence power, but Sierra has enough strength to hit the gaps. From there, his speed allows him to take extra bases and he should become a more efficient basestealer as he progresses. Sierra is an elite-level defender in center field, the kind who regularly makes highlight-reel plays, and he has a plus arm to boot. Seeing a young player show they can bounce back after struggling, that they can demonstrate and learn from adversity, is important in development. That skill, along with his natural tools, has allowed Sierra to make progress up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading Vanderbilt to the 2019 College World Series title while pacing NCAA Division I with 27 homers and 192 total bases, Bleday signed for $6.67 million as the No. 4 overall pick in the Draft. He was overly aggressive in his pro debut in High-A and batted just .212/.323/.373 with 12 homers in 110 Double-A games last season, when he generated a lot of harmless flyball contact. He did rake in the hitter-friendly Arizona Fall League and looked more like the guy who dominated in college, but has exuded a power-over-hit vibe while earning his first big league callup in 2022. Bleday has said that he tried to do too much in 2021, when a slow start snowballed on him, and he believes he has made the necessary adjustments (lowering his hands, using his legs more, regaining a disciplined approach) to be productive going forward. With his smooth left-handed swing and his bat speed, strength and leverage, he has the tools to hit for both average and power. After reporting to Spring Training looking stronger than ever after adding 20 pounds of muscle, he has launched more fly balls to his pull side than in the past while also striking out at a higher rate than ever before. While his offensive performance has been puzzling, Bleday has upgraded other aspects of his game such as his quickness and defense. He's a fringy runner out of the batter's box but average underway, and his instincts help him play faster on the bases and in the outfield. He's a capable center fielder but fits best in right field, where he's at least a solid defender with a plus arm that once made him a two-way prospect as a Florida high schooler.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts voted Bleday the top prospect in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2018 and he rode that momentum to a banner junior season, leading Vanderbilt to a College World Series championship while topping NCAA Division I in homers (27) and total bases (192). The Marlins put him on the fast track immediately after drafting him fourth overall and signing him for a then-franchise-record $6.67 million, sending him to high Class A for his pro debut. Though his only experience last year came at Miami's alternate training site and the instructional league, he seemed on course to reach the big leagues at some point in 2021 but instead has endured a rough season in Double-A. In college, Bleday first emerged as an advanced hitter with a quality left-handed swing and a disciplined approach. His power began to emerge on the Cape and he projected as a potential 30-homer threat thanks to his bat speed, strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame. While the Marlins aren't overly concerned with his performance this year and attribute it to struggling with some mechanical adjustments, evaluators outside the organization note that he has lost weight and isn't making quality contact as much as he did in the past. Bleday used his pandemic downtime to improve his conditioning and quickness. He's a fringy runner whose instincts allow him to play faster than that on the bases and in the outfield. While he saw time in all three spots last summer, he fits best in right field, where he can be a solid defender with a plus arm that made him a two-way prospect as a Florida high schooler.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleday was Vanderbilt's best hitter as a sophomore in 2018 but didn't start to tap into his power potential until that summer, when scouts voted him the top prospect in the Cape Cod League. He built on that success last spring, topping NCAA Division I with 27 homers and 192 total bases and leading the Commodores to their second College World Series title. After going fourth overall in the Draft and signing for a then-Marlins-record $6.67 million, he proceeded straight to high Class A. Before he broke out as a slugger, Bleday first emerged as an advanced hitter with a sweet left-handed stroke and a disciplined, all-fields approach. His bat speed, strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame give him power to all parts of the ballpark. He walked more than he struck out in each of his three seasons at Vanderbilt and the only hole in his offensive game is that he's a below-average runner who won't do much on the bases. Bleday makes up for his lack of speed with good defensive instincts, projecting as a solid right fielder. He was a two-way prospect as a Florida high schooler, and his plus arm adds to his right-field profile. Expected to open 2020 in Double-A, he should make his debut in Miami at some point next year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trying to address an organization-wide shortage of mound talent, Chicago chose college arms with 13 of its first 14 Draft picks in 2016 and its top five in '17. That haul includes Uelmen, who signed for $382,300 as a fourth-rounder out of Cal Poly last June. Though he worked just 17 2/3 innings in his pro debut, that was long enough to establish as one of the best ground-ball pitchers in the system. Uelmen pounds the bottom of the strike zone with a heavy 90-94 mph sinker that has the Cubs wondering if he might be the second coming of Derek Lowe. They're going to have him add a four-seamer he can elevate to change batters' eye level. He can get some swings and misses with his average slider but he needs more work on his changeup. Uelmen operates from a low three-quarters arm slot and has effort in his delivery, so some scouts project him as a reliever. Chicago will develop him as a starter, believing that his athleticism and strike-throwing ability can keep him in the rotation. He could succeed as at least a middle reliever with his sinker, giving him a nice fallback and one of the higher floors among its recent college pitching selections.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring for three seasons at Minnesota, Meyer matched Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history when he went third overall and signed for $6.7 million in 2020. He won Double-A South pitcher of the year accolades and ranked fifth in the Minors with a 2.27 ERA in his 2021 pro debut before reaching the bigs the following July. His elbow gave out in his second start with the Marlins, leading to Tommy John surgery that sidelined him throughout 2023, but he made a triumphant return to the Majors this April. Meyer long has been famous for his wipeout slider, which sits in the upper 80s with plenty of horizontal movement as well as two-plane depth. His fastball sits at 94-96 mph with riding action and reached triple digits when he worked shorter stints in college. He has improved his feel for his changeup since turning pro, a solid offering that can get a bit firm in the upper 80s. Though Meyer lacks size and his elbow reconstruction will add to questions about his long-term durability as a starter, he helps his cause with his strength and athleticism. He has a fluid delivery that he repeats well and never has had any issues throwing strikes. His competitiveness enhances his package as possible No. 2 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meyer starred for three seasons at Minnesota before going third overall in the 2020 Draft, matching Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history and signing for a Marlins-record $6.7 million. Sent to Double-A for his 2021 pro debut, he answered the challenge by winning Double-A South pitcher of the year honors and ranking fifth in the Minors in ERA (2.27). He missed a month with nerve irritation in his elbow last season yet still made his big league debut in July, only to have his elbow blow out in his second start with Miami and result in Tommy John surgery that will sideline him for all of 2023. Meyer's slider wasn't quite as dominant as advertised in his pro debut but returned to wipeout status last year, sitting in the upper 80s with outstanding horizontal action and two-plane depth as well. His fastball added a couple of ticks of velocity, parking at 94-96 mph with riding action, and he has reached triple digits in shorter stints in the past. He also upgraded his feel for his changeup, which is a bit firm in the upper 80s but features good fade and serves as a solid third pitch. His lack of size did lead to concerns about Meyer's durability, and his elbow reconstruction will create more questions, though he does have the strength and athleticism to remain a starter. He repeats his fluid delivery well and made progress with his control and command in 2022. If he can't last in the rotation, he has the stuff and competitiveness to be a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meyer tied a Minnesota record with 16 saves as a freshman in 2018 before dominating as a starter in his next two college seasons. He went third overall in the 2020 Draft, matching Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history, and he signed for a Marlins-record $6.7 million. Challenged with a Double-A assignment at the outset of his 2021 pro debut, he responded by capturing Double-A South pitcher of the year honors and ranking fifth in the Minors in ERA (2.27), including two overpowering starts in Triple-A to cap his year. Meyer made his big league debut this July but two weeks later was diagnosed with a torn elbow ligament that required Tommy John surgery. Meyer's slider was the consensus best pitch in the 2020 Draft, and while it wasn't quite as dominant last summer, it was still a well-above-average offering that usually ranged from 85-89 mph with tremendous horizontal break and some depth as well. His fastball sits at 92-95 mph and can reach 100 with riding action up in the strike zone. While he had little need for a changeup in college, his fading mid-80s cambio shows potential but needs more consistency. Though he's just 6 feet tall, Meyer is strong and athletic and repeats his fluid delivery well. After battling the strike zone in his first two months as a pro, he did a better job of trusting his stuff afterward. Now the next step will be refining his command. While there's no reason he shouldn't pitch in the front half of a big league rotation, his stuff and competitive makeup could make him a lights-out closer if so desired.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meyer made an immediate impact at Minnesota, tying a school record with 16 saves as a freshman in 2018 and leading the U.S. collegiate national team with seven that summer, then continued to dominate after moving into the rotation as a sophomore. He posted a 1.95 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 27 2/3 innings during the truncated 2020 college season and went third overall in the Draft, matching Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history. After signing for a Miami-record $6.7 million, he participated in alternate camp and instructional league. Meyer had the best pitch in the 2020 Draft, a wipeout slider that reaches the low 90s and with which he can add and subtract depth. He also can blow away hitters with a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-97 mph, clocked at 98 in the ninth inning of one start last spring and tops out at 100. He surprised the Marlins with his feel for a changeup that he didn't need much in college, and his mid-80s offering with fade could give him a solid third option. Though Meyer is listed as just 6 feet tall, he has erased any concerns about whether his size would prevent him from becoming an impact starter. He's strong and athletic, showing the ability to repeat a fluid delivery and fill the strike zone with premium stuff. A tough competitor who got semiregular at-bats in Minnesota's lineup, he should move quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As Garcia has risen in the Royals’ farm system, so has his potential. The cousin of Royals postseason hero Alcides Escobar and Braves star Ronald Acuña, Garcia signed with the Royals out of Venezuela in 2016. He burst onto the scene in 2021 as he got stronger and developed a contact-oriented approach at the plate, leading the Royals to add him to the 40-man roster. His stock only continued to rise in 2022, when he made his debut on July 15, playing in nine big league games. He finished the year in Triple-A Omaha, where he posted an .804 OPS. Over the winter, he just kept hitting: Garcia slashed .323/.444/.498 in 58 games in winter ball, walking more times (46) than striking out (31). With an unorthodox setup at the plate, Garcia is a contact-oriented hitter who has excellent hand-eye coordination and uses the entire field. He hit 11 homers in 2022 -- six more than the previous four seasons combined -- but he isn’t a home run hitter. Instead, he relies on his gap-to-gap power with speed, which helped him to 34 doubles last year. He brings a consistent approach to the plate and gets on base, where he can then cause trouble because of his plus speed. Garcia is one of the best shortstops in the Royals’ system with a quick first step, above-average arm and great range. He is instinctual at the plate and in the field. There is still projection in Garcia’s wiry frame, but he showed up this spring stronger as he continues to physically mature. Evaluators see strength as the difference between him becoming a utilityman or a starting middle infielder. Garcia will compete for a roster spot this spring, but it’s likely he returns to Triple-A and serves as infield depth knowing he’ll get a callup at some point in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The cousin of Royals postseason hero Alcides Escobar, Garcia signed with the Royals during the 2016-17 international signing period and is looking to follow in his cousin’s footsteps with Kansas City in the coming years. Like Escobar, Garcia is a shortstop, and he burst onto the scene in 2021 with a lot of contact and tons of walks between Low-A and High-A this year. That ability, plus his defense, earned him a spot on the 40-man roster in the offseason for protection from the Rule 5 Draft. Garcia’s skillset is contact over power -- he hit .291 last season with only four home runs -- and he can get on base, posting a .380 on-base percentage across the two levels in 2021. As he’s risen in the system, he’s seen his walk rate improve and his strikeout rate decrease. And when he’s on base, he creates havoc with his speed. He stole 35 bases last season and has 83 in his Minor League career. Defensively, Garcia is as consistent of a shortstop as the Royals have in their system with a quick first step, above average arm and great instincts. The Royals aren’t lacking depth at shortstop, and Garcia is near the top of that list. Some see the lack of physicality in his small frame as the biggest hurdle for him to be a big leaguer. But he does have wiry strength, and being only 21 years old, there’s still projection in his body. The Royals put Garcia on the 40-man because of his contact skills and glove, and that’s already born fruit as they gave him his Major League debut on July 15. Bobby Witt Jr.’s presence at short complicates matters a little, but Garcia gives Kansas City another potential everyday player at the six -- a good problem to have for a team building around its youth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Toffey was a standout in both baseball and hockey at Salisbury (Conn.) Prep before he turned down the Yankees as a 23rd-round pick in 2014 in favor of his commitment to Vanderbilt. A three-year starter for the Commodores, he was Vandy's best hitter as a junior -- he led the team in all three slash categories (.354/.475/.602) and hit 12 homers -- and the A's made him their fourth-round pick that June. Toffey was in the second half of his first full season with Class A Advanced Stockton when he was sent to the Mets in July's Jeurys Familia trade. Promoted to Double-A upon joining New York's system, he made a greater impact at the plate in the Eastern League than he had in the hitter-friendly California League. Toffey controls the strike zone very well and shows power potential in his left-handed swing. He improved his walk and strikeout rates each year at Vandy and hit for more power than ever in 2017. He's been an on-base machine, but hasn't shown that pop as a pro, though the Mets believe he'll develop more game power by incorporating better use of his lower half in his swing. While his power plays best to his pull side, Toffey hit his most impressive home runs to left-center field last season -- an encouraging sign for a player whose big league profile at the hot corner depends on his power output. Though he's a fringy runner, Toffey provides above-average defense and plus arm strength at third base. Toffey receives comparisons to Colin Moran as a left-handed-hitting third baseman who plays quality defense, gets on base consistently and has untapped potential with the bat. There is some question about whether he will hit for the average and power demanded of third basemen at higher levels, but even those who question his tools give him credit for his ability to process the game, his makeup and his competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A baseball and hockey star at Salisbury (Conn). Prep, where his brother John coached him in both sports, Toffey turned down the Yankees as a 23rd-rounder in 2014 to attend Vanderbilt. He started from day one with the Commodores, playing on their 2015 College World Series runners-up team before slumping as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2016, when the Orioles took a flier on him in the 25th round. He rebounded in the Cape Cod League that summer and was Vandy's best hitter as a junior, when he paced the team in all three triple-slash categories (.354/.475/.602) and belted 12 homers. That led to the A's taking him in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft and he was in the second half of his first full season in the California League when he was sent to the Mets in July's Jeurys Familia trade. Toffey controls the strike zone very well and shows power potential in his left-handed swing. He improved his walk and strikeout rates each year at Vandy and hit for more power than ever in 2017. While he hasn't shown that pop as a pro, he has been an on-base machine. Though he's a fringy runner, Toffey provides quality defense and solid arm strength at third base. There is some question about whether Toffey has enough bat speed to hit for the average and power demanded of third basemen at higher levels. However, even those who question his tools give him credit for his ability to process the game, his makeup and his competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Massey -- no relation to the Royals second baseman of the same name -- was a dominant reliever at Wake Forest in 2023, striking out 76 batters over 41 2/3 innings while holding opponents to a .161 average before converting to a starter in his junior season with mixed results. After hamstring and back injuries, he moved back to the bullpen in late May, but he dropped to the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, where the Tigers signed him for a $522,500 bonus. Massey combines the core ingredients of a potentially dominant reliever with secondary pitches that could allow him to grow into an effective starter; the Tigers tweaked his pitch usage to aid him in the latter. His fastball ranges from 93-97 mph but plays big with a lot of ride, allowing him to beat hitters to the top of the strike zone. His 82-85 slider has plenty of drop, allowing him to work the bottom of the zone. His starting arsenal includes a changeup to attack left-handed hitters and a curveball. The Tigers plan on having Massey work as a starter to begin his pro career. Still, they have a history of finding successful late-inning relievers out of converted starters, from Michael Fulmer to Shane Greene to Alex Lange. How Massey develops his secondary pitches will likely determine his career path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A back injury that limited his time in the field during his junior year at Illinois caused Massey’s Draft stock fall, but he was still able to post an .831 OPS. The Royals jumped at the chance to take him in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, signing him for just below slot at $312,500. Massey was still hindered by the back injury during Rookie ball and his first instructional league, but his work with the Royals' training staff and increased focused on his mobility saw him enjoy a strong and healthy campaign in High-A Quad Cities in 2021 -- with his 21 homers more than he hit in all three years at Illinois. The Royals knew Massey had power as an amateur, but they didn’t know what they would get after the canceled 2020 season. Finally healthy, Massey tapped into his power after working with the Royals hitting development program, but he didn’t lose the contact skills that got him drafted, either, posting an .882 OPS in 99 games for the Bandits. He employs a sweet swing from the left side and makes hard contact to all parts of the field. He may be limited to second base defensively, but he’s made himself into one of the best second basemen the Royals have, winning the Minor League Gold Glove at the position in 2021. He has more range there now that he’s healthy and has shown improved arm strength. Massey picked up right where he left off in 2021 with another powerful season this year at Double-A and Triple-A, where he slugged above .500 and posted an OPS above .900 before joining the big club potentially for good in early August. The offensive improvements over the last two years, along with Massey’s steadiness at second, could make him another sizable piece in KC’s youth movement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pratto entered last year in a similar bucket to his fellow 2017 draftee MJ Melendez. That year’s 14th overall pick had a solid first full season at Class A Lexington, only to hit .191 with nine homers over 472 plate appearances at Class A Advanced Wilmington in 2019. The Royals believed Pratto learned from the experience and were pleased with his performance at the alternate training site in 2020, preceding his breakout. The left-handed slugger swatted 36 homers and finished with a .265/.385/.602 line in 124 games at Double-A and Triple-A last summer. His 71 total extra-base hits were second-most in the Minors, trailing only teammate Bobby Witt Jr.’s 72. Kansas City added Pratto to the 40-man roster in November, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. Pratto’s jumps in 2021 were more based in changes to his approach than physical adjustments. Beginning at the alternate training site, he learned to avoid pitches below the knees and mash those more up in the zone. As a result, his ground-ball rate went down, and his fly-ball rate jumped, leading to better power numbers. He also became a more patient hitter. That patience and intent to drive the ball have kept his K numbers high, and that blunts his hit tool. But overall, he possesses an above-average offensive ceiling with the potential for 30-plus homers. His speed is fringy, but he has strong instincts that have helped him swipe 10-plus bags every season thus far. Since his Draft days, the California native has been considered a gifted defender at first base and should provide value there with his athleticism and plus arm. Now back on track, Pratto has the pieces in place to play a large role in the Royals’ next foundation of contention.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pratto was a two-way standout at Huntington Beach (Calif.) High School before emerging as a better hitting prospect as a senior in 2017, when the Royals selected him in the first round of the MLB Draft. He looked like one of the more advanced prep players from his class in his first full season, turning in a strong second half at Class A Lexington to finish with 14 homers and 22 stolen bases, though he lost much of that progress with the move up to Class A Advanced Wilmington in ‘19. Pratto was one of the organization’s most improved and impressive players at the alternate training site in ‘20. After deviating from his strengths in 2019 as he tinkered with several components of his left-handed swing to no avail, Pratto looked like a different hitter in 2020, and that carried into 2021 as well. Employing a more confident approach that led to better decisions, Pratto’s hard-hit rate has shot up, and his whiffs have decreased sharply. After hitting only nine homers at Wilmington two years ago, he cleared 20 with ease in 2021 and shows at least 25-homer potential for the future. One of the best and most efficient baserunners in Kansas City’s system, Pratto compensates for his fringy speed with excellent instinct on the basepaths. Pratto has long been revered for his defensive prowess as a first baseman, with many evaluators giving his glove a 70 grade on the 20-80 scouting scale. His athleticism translates well at the position, while the plus arm that he used to fire upper-80s fastball as a prep is an underrated weapon. Given that defensive ability and his increased offensive production, Pratto has turned himself back into one of the best first-base prospects in baseball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more well-known prep prospects in the 2017 Draft class, Pratto was a two-way star at Huntington Beach (Calif.) High and also played for USA Baseball’s national gold medal-winning teams. He emerged as a better hitting prospect than pitcher as a senior en route to a first-round selection by the Royals, who viewed Pratto as one of the top pure hitters on the board. He got off to a slow start at Class A Lexington in 2018 but turned it on in the second half, slashing .322/.394/.518, and he finished the year with 14 homers and 22 steals. A move up to Class A Advanced Wilmington brought more early struggles, but Pratto was unable to dig himself out of the hole this time. Though he had a poor first half in the Carolina League, batting .167/.262/.230, Pratto did fare a bit better after All-Star break (.218/.295/.401). His overall line of .191/.278/.310 was disappointing, as was his 34.7 percent strikeout rate. He spent much of the year tinkering with his hand positioning and it resulted in an inconsistent swing path and an alarming amount of soft contact -- most notably, a plethora of weak flyouts to the opposite field. In addition to creating more extension and a better barrel path, club officials would like to see him make better swing decisions. The Royals still believe in Pratto’s offensive potential, viewing him as someone who will offer at least average hitting ability and game power at maturity. While Pratto has fringy speed, he is one of the better baserunners in the organization, with excellent instincts that fuel his aggressiveness on the basepaths. His athleticism makes him a rangy defender at first base, where a plus arm that used to fire upper-80s headlines a solid set of defensive tools. Of course, Pratto will first need to figure things out at the plate to profile there at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler, Pratto was a two-way star who attended Huntington Beach High School, a program that has produced big league hitters like Daric Barton and Hank Conger. He was also a teammate of 2017 second-round pick Hagen Danner, now with the Blue Jays, and a frequent member of USA Baseball national teams winning gold medals. As a senior, his bat jumped ahead of his arm and the Royals took him in the middle of the first round to hit and he did just that in his first full year, finishing with 14 homers and 22 steals. While Pratto struggled out of the gate in the South Atlantic League, he showed just why he was considered one of the best high school bats in the 2017 Draft class with a .322/.394/.518 line in the second half. He dug an even deeper first-half hole in 2019, hitting .167/.262/.230 in the Carolina League before slowly finding himself in the second half. He has shown a solid overall approach at the plate and can drive the ball to all fields, but there's been more swing and miss to his game than some anticipated, though that did improve in his strong finish to the 2018 season. He started tapping into his left-handed power more, with the chance to grow into even more as he matures and refines his approach. While Pratto has fringy speed, he might be the most instinctive baserunner in the system, allowing him to be aggressive on the basepaths. His athleticism also plays well at first with excellent defensive tools, including a plus arm that used to fire upper-80s fastballs from the mound. He has every chance to follow in Eric Hosmer's footsteps as a homegrown first-round pick who plays first base every day in Kansas City.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 60 | Overall: 50 Pratto has a long history of starring in international play, hitting a walk-off single to beat Japan in the 2011 Little League World Series, defeating Japan as a starting pitcher to help the United States win the 2015 18-and-under World Cup and starring again for Team USA to capture a gold medal at the 2016 18-and-under Pan Am Championships. One of a number of legitimate two-way prospects in the 2017 Draft, he drew interest as a pitcher until it became clear that he might be the best pure prep hitter available. He joined Eric Hosmer as the only first basemen ever taken in the first round by the Royals, signing for $3,450,000 as the 14th overall selection. While Pratto slumped at the end of his high school senior season and had a so-so pro debut, that hasn't stopped scouts from comparing him to Joey Votto and Brendan McKay (the No. 4 overall pick in 2017). Like them, Pratto is a hit-over-power first baseman who bats left-handed and has a mature approach at the plate, though he has struggled while trying to do too much in his first full season. He owns a pretty swing with plenty of bat speed, has an affinity for using the entire field and is beginning to tap into his considerable raw power. Pratto is a better athlete than most first basemen. He's a potential Gold Glover who moves well around the bag and has a stronger arm than most players at his position. On the mound, he was very similar to McKay at the same stage of their careers, displaying an upper-80s fastball, promising secondary pitches and advanced feel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ruiz signed with the Royals in July 2015 out of the Dominican Republic for $100,000. He was sent to the Padres two years later in a six-player trade in the midst of a standout year that earned him 2017 Arizona League MVP honors after slashing .350/.395/.602 with 34 extra-base hits and 26 stolen bases in 52 games between two organizations. Moved again in a 2022 Trade Deadline deal with the Brewers for Josh Hader, it was his overall performance last season that featured a Minor League-leading 85 stolen bases that really caught the attention of the A’s, who acquired him in the three-team deal that sent Sean Murphy to the Braves last December. Ruiz improved across the board as a hitter in ‘22, even showing an uptick in power. His chase rate also went down with better decision-making on pitches outside of the strike zone, which in turn led to career highs in several categories over his 114 games between Double-A and Triple-A. Ruiz’s 80-grade speed is his most tantalizing attribute, and the value shows up in his Minor League stolen-base totals. His legs have also enabled him to transition from second base to center field, a position the A’s feel confident in his ability to handle on an everyday basis. He’ll likely get a shot to prove that belief with Oakland in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ruiz signed with the Royals in July 2015 out of the Dominican Republic, and only two years later, he was a prospect piece in a six-player deadline deal with the Padres centered around pitchers Trevor Cahill and Brandon Maurer going the other way. Staying in the same Minor League circuit after the trade, Ruiz captured 2017 Arizona League MVP honors after hitting .350/.395/.602 with 34 extra-base hits and 26 stolen bases in 52 games divided between the Royals and Padres affiliates. His numbers fell off away from the complex, and he ended up with a .239/.300/.357 line over 98 games at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in 2019, though his speed (34 steals) did help him earn a spot on the mid-season California League All-Star team. As such, Ruiz was left unprotected and went unpicked in last year’s Rule 5 Draft. Still only 22 years old, Ruiz has the promising bat speed and strength to dream on better offensive production as he matures and climbs the ladder toward San Diego. However, plate discipline has been an issue and not just because of a lack of walks. The right-handed slugger can struggle to stay away from swinging at pitches outside of the zone, leading to weak contact and less power than he’s capable of exhibiting. His glove and arm were below-average at second base, and the Padres have tried to give him a new outlet by getting him time in left field in 2021 at Double-A San Antonio. The move puts an even bigger burden on his bat to produce, but at least the extra space gives Ruiz a better chance to make the most of his above-average speed. Those wheels make up easily his best tool at this stage, until his offensive approach improves. Given his age, there is still time for Ruiz to make the necessary adjustments and get back to his status as one of the most promising prospects in the Padres system. With his bat and speed, the upside is certainly there, but the improvements will need to come fast if he’s ever going to be more than a utilityman/pinch runner at the top level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered more of a good college player than a prime prospect in his first two seasons at Ball State, Call boosted his stock by hitting 13 homers and winning Mid-American Conference player of the year honors in 2016. The White Sox loved his talent as well as his makeup, so they popped him in the third round and promoted him to Class A a month into his pro career. He made the jump look easy, batting .308/.361/.449 with 20 extra-base hits and 10 steals in 46 games, though an intercostal strain has held him back in his first full season. One of the better college athletes in the 2016 Draft, Call could have average or better tools across the board once he's fully developed. He doesn't have a pretty right-handed swing, yet he makes consistent hard contact and controls the strike zone well. His worst tool is his power, though he still has enough strength to provide 15 homers per year while hitting for average and getting on base. Call manned right field in college because Ball State valued his strong arm there, but he may be quick enough to handle center field. He's a solid runner out of the batter's box and even faster once he gets going, though his reads and routes still need work in center. He has the speed and instincts to steal a few bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2014-15 international crop, Garcia got the largest payout ($3 million) in a Yankees spending binge that exceeded $17 million in bonuses. Though power is his carrying tool, he didn't homer in his '15 pro debut before bouncing back with 30 homers in 120 games over the next two seasons. Garcia also struck out in 32 percent of his plate appearances, making him the biggest boom-or-bust prospect in the system. Garcia's outstanding bat speed and strength give him top-of-the-scale raw power, though it remains to be seen how much he'll be able to tap into it against more advanced pitching. He still has trouble with recognizing pitches and handling offspeed offerings, and he has yet to prove he can make consistent contact. Garcia has displayed a willingness to accept walks, though he still chases pitches out of the strike zone with alarming frequency. Garcia has plenty of arm strength for third base, but he's a well-below-average runner with limited range and a history of errors at the hot corner. He has seen most of his action at first base in 2018, but he may never be more than an adequate defender there. New York has begun trying Garcia on the mound in bullpen sessions, during which he has shown a mid-90s fastball and some feel for spinning a curveball and using a changeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Multi-sport high school stars are not uncommon, but those who stand out in hockey and baseball are a bit more unusual. Jones played hockey at a high level before leaving the ice to become one of the best high school hitters in the 2016 Draft class and getting first-round money as Cleveland’s second-round pick that June. He was buzzing his way through the Minors, including going to the Futures Game in 2019, when a combination of struggles and a serious ankle injury slowed him in 2021. Ankle surgery slowed his return in 2022, but he did make it up to the big leagues for the first time and then was sent to the Rockies for Juan Brito during the offseason. Big and strong with tremendous leverage in his left-handed swing, Jones’s raw power has always been apparent, though he hasn’t always been able to tap into it. There’s some length to his swing, which leads to some swing-and-miss, and while he draws walks and works deep counts, that can lead to him being too passive at the plate. He made some adjustments last year to handle breaking stuff better, and he spent the offseason in Scottsdale, with the Rockies preaching more aggression at the plate. The Guardians had moved Jones to the outfield, largely because of the presence of José Ramírez in Cleveland. He’ll still get reps in both outfielder corners, with the athleticism and arm to do so, but he’ll get back to seeing time on the dirt, both at his natural third as well as first base, with the chance to get his bat into the big league lineup regularly while moving around the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout hockey center before concussion issues forced him to leave the sport, Jones emerged as one of the best high school hitters in the 2016 class and landed first-round money ($2.25 million) as a second-rounder. After performing well throughout the Minors, including leading the short-season New York-Penn League in OPS (.912) in '17 and the Minors in walks (96) in '19, he spent time playing the outfield during instructional league in '20 and appeared on the verge of filling a void in Cleveland. Jones struggled in Triple-A in '21 and sustained a left high ankle sprain that required surgery that kept him sidelined until May 2022, but he bounced back to solve Triple-A pitching and earned his first big league callup in July before being sent to the Rockies for Juan Brito in November. With his bat speed, strength and the leverage in his left-handed swing, Jones has tremendous raw power and a patient approach. At the same time, his naturally long stroke and willingness to work deep counts always will result in strikeouts. He has made some adjustments to better deal with breaking balls in 2022, though the Guardians protected him by using him almost exclusively against right-handers in the Majors. Though he possesses below-average speed, Jones is reasonably athletic for his size and worked hard to become a competent third baseman. His arm strength never has been a question, and he has improved his footwork, agility and range. Cleveland had moved Jones to the outfield because of José Ramírez at the hot corner, and he's at least an adequate defender in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout hockey center before concussion issues forced him to focus on baseball, Jones developed into one of the best prep hitters in the 2016 Draft and signed for first-round money ($2.25 million) in the second round. He has performed well everywhere he has played as a pro, and in 2019 he led the Minors with 96 walks, advanced to Double-A at age 21 and played in both the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and the Arizona Fall League's Fall Stars Game. His only action in 2020 came at alternative camp and in instructional league, and he stood out in both places with his offensive approach and dedication to improving his defense. Jones exudes patience at the plate, waiting for pitches he can hammer and taking walks if pitchers decline to challenge him. His combination of bat speed and strength plus the loft and leverage in his left-handed swing give him well above-average power that plays to all fields. His willingness to work deep counts and the length in his naturally long stroke do lead to strikeouts, an acceptable tradeoff for his pop and on-base ability, though he'll have to make adjustments to solve left-handers after hitting .167/.316/.286 against them in his first two years of full-season ball. Jones has more athleticism than his below-average speed would indicate and has worked to transition from a high school shortstop into an acceptable third baseman. He has the strong arm desired at the hot corner and his footwork, agility and range all have gotten better since he turned pro. Because the Indians have José Ramirez at third and need outfielders, they began working him at the latter position during instructional league.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones initially stood out as a hockey center before concussion issues led him to focus on baseball, where he developed into one of the best high school hitters in the 2016 Draft. After lasting until the second round amid signability concerns but landing a first-round bonus ($2.25 million), he has produced everywhere he has gone in pro ball. He led the Minors with 96 walks in 2019, reaching Double-A at age 21 and getting selected to the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and the Arizona Fall League's Fall Stars Game. Jones utilizes a patient approach at the plate, waiting for pitches he can punish and using the entire field. His bat speed and strength could translate into 30 homers per season, especially since he started to add more loft to his left-handed stroke in 2019. The length in his swing and his willingness to work deep counts result in a strikeout rate that has risen as he has climbed through the Minors, but his ability to draw walks should lead to healthy on-base percentages if not high batting averages. A better athlete than his below-average speed might indicate, Jones has worked hard to transition from high school shortstop to pro third baseman. He has the strong arm required at the hot corner and he has improved his footwork and agility. He's on his way to becoming an average defender at third base and has a fallback of playing the other infield or outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the premier prep hitters in the 2016 Draft, Jones likely would have been a first-round pick if not for signability concerns that ultimately led to his selection by the Indians in the second round. After signing for nearly twice slot value, Jones made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League before advancing to the Class A Short-Season New York-Penn League in 2017, leading the circuit in on-base percentage (.430) and OPS (.912) while also pacing all Indians farmhands with a .317 average. A left-handed hitter, Jones combines bat speed with a fluid stroke and natural feel for the barrel to generate hard contact across the field. He knows how to get on base, too, showing advanced plate discipline and an age-defying approach that helped him lead the NY-PL in both walks (43) and OBP as a teenager. And while Jones' impressive raw power has yet to translate during games, scouts do expect him to develop above-average power as he adds strength to his athletic and highly projectable frame and trims some of the swing-and-miss from his game. The Indians moved Jones off shortstop, his position as a prep, to third base upon his entering the pro ranks. His size and physicality are clean fits at the hot corner, as are his plus arm strength and average speed, though some evaluators believe his inconsistent glove work will eventually land him in right field. Regardless of his future defensive home, Jones has the bat and offensive ceiling needed to become an impactful everyday player at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones took to hockey before baseball and showed promise as a center before concussion issues caused him to focus on the diamond. One of the better high school hitters in the 2016 Draft, he dropped to the second round amid signability concerns but landed first-round bonus money ($2.25 million). After a so-so pro debut, he led the short-season New York-Penn League with a .912 OPS in 2017, ranked third in the Class A Midwest League with an .858 mark last year and posted a .910 OPS during the final month in Class A Advanced. Jones has an advanced approach at the plate, patiently working counts and using the entire field. He has a smooth left-handed swing and impressive feel to hit, and he shows the ability to produce high batting averages despite working deep counts that lead to some strikeouts. His bat speed and strength give him promising power potential that could produce 25 or more homers per season, especially if he adds some loft to a stroke that's currently more geared for line drives. Though he's a below-average runner, Jones is a decent athlete and has worked hard to make the transition from amateur shortstop to pro third baseman. He has a strong arm and has improved his footwork, but still needs to increase his range in order to become an average defender at the hot corner. If he can't, his alternatives would be first base or an outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bello has gone from getting passed over in the 2015 and 2016 international signing periods to turning pro for a mere $28,000 in 2017 to ranking as Boston's top pitching prospect five years later. He initially struggled when he skipped two levels and jumped to Low-A in 2019, but he finished strong that summer and then looked better than ever at the Red Sox's instructional league program in 2020 following the pandemic layoff. He maintained his improved stuff throughout 2021, when he reached Double-A, pitched in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. After using his pandemic downtime to get stronger, Bello has seen his fastball go from sitting at 92-95 mph in 2019 to parking at 95-97 and pushing triple digits. His heater is fairly straight and is vulnerable when he doesn't locate it where he wants, so he might benefit it from mixing in some two-seamers with sink. He has refined his changeup into a consistent plus offering in the mid-80s with fade and depth, and his slider features similar velocity and upside. Bello has three quality pitches, throws enough strikes and generates plenty of swings and misses as well as weak groundball contact. He has the potential to pitch in the front half of a big league rotation, and to get there he'll have to refine his command and show that his fastball will work well against more advanced hitters. If not, he still has a high floor as a multiple-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bello signed for $28,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively advanced age of 18 in 2017. He dominated the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in his pro debut the following year but struggled for three months when he skipped two levels and jumped to low Class A in 2019. He finished strong down the stretch that summer and showed some of the best pure stuff at Boston's instructional league program in 2020. Bello's four-seam fastball sat at 92-95 mph during the 2019 season and parked at 95 while touching 98 in shorter stints during instructs. His heater features modest life and can get hammered when he struggles to command it, so he might be better off trying to sink a two-seamer, which he has shown some aptitude for. Both his slider and fading changeup reside in the mid-80s and show flashes of becoming plus pitches, with the changeup having the most upside in his entire arsenal. With the ability to throw strikes, miss bats and elicit ground-ball contact with three solid or better pitches, Bello has mid-rotation upside. Some scouts don't love his fastball characteristics and wonder how well it will play against more advanced hitters, however. He's athletic and still has some projection remaining, so he could add some more velocity in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: First eligible to sign out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Bello had to wait two years before hooking up with the Red Sox for a $28,000 bonus. After he dominated younger competition in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League at age 19 in his 2018 pro debut, Boston skipped him two levels to low Class A last season. He logged a 7.78 ERA in the first three months but recovered to post a 3.05 ERA with a 63/14 K/BB ratio in 59 innings over the final two. Bello shows the potential for three solid or better pitches, though they can vary in their effectiveness. He works around 92-95 mph and reaches 98 with good sink on his fastball, though he got hit hard early in 2019 when it lacked life and command. Scouts had preferred his low-80s slider to his fading mid-80s changeup in the past, but he was much more effective against lefties than righties last season. Bello is far from a finished prospect but demonstrates the ability to throw strikes and get groundouts. He still has room to add strength, so he could gain some more velocity in the future. If that happens and he can improve the consistency of his offerings, he eventually could fit in the middle of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bello looks like one of the better investments in the Red Sox's deep 2017 international class, signing for $28,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively advanced age of 18. In his 2018 pro debut, he finished among the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League leaders in WHIP (0.73, second), opponent average (.162, third) and K/BB ratio (6.8, sixth). Boston deemed him suitably advanced to bring him to the United States for the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League playoffs. Though Bello is very much a work in progress and has been knocked around in Class A this year, he displays the potential for three solid or better pitches. His fastball presently sits at 91-93 mph and touches 96 with some sink, and he could add more velocity as he gets stronger. His low-80s slider stands out more for its velocity than its bite but he will flash some sharp ones. Bello also shows some feel for a changeup with some fade, though it's not as consistent as his other offerings. While he was a bit old for the DSL, his ability to throw strikes and keep the ball down in the zone was apparent. He has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter but will need plenty of development time to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hill was a bit of a late bloomer in the Tigers system, though not for lack of results. He was 22 years old when Detroit drafted him in the 26nd round in 2018, posted a 2.25 ERA and 129 strikeouts across Class A ball in 2019, lost 2020 to the pandemic, then fanned 99 batters over 75 2/3 innings between High-A West Michigan and Double-A Erie last year. He backed it up with 21 strikeouts over 13 2/3 innings in the Arizona Fall League, which caught scouts’ attention. Hill’s fastball sits in the low 90s, but he has an assortment of breaking balls to go with a nasty splitter. When he does allow contact, it tends to be on the ground. He has allowed just eight home runs over 237 1/3 innings in his Minor League career. The big question with Hill has been how much advantage he has gained being an older pitcher at each level, though he looked solid against Detroit’s top prospects in Minor League minicamp. Despite Hill’s success, the Tigers left him off their 40-man roster going into 2022. He forced his way onto it with impressive upper-level performances to begin the season, earning his Major League debut on July 4. Because of his solid command, he’s been able to overcome a lack of standout stuff and could continue to be a reliable backend starter for Detroit in the years ahead.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stefanic put up huge numbers at Westmont College, an NAIA school in California, leaving the school as the career leader in a host of offensive categories, including hits and total bases. Despite hitting .392 his senior year, he went undrafted in 2018, signing as a free agent with the Angels. He managed to hit his way to Triple-A in 2021, finishing the breakout season with a .336/.408/.493 line across two levels. As the numbers show, Stefanic has pretty much hit wherever he’s been. He makes a ridiculous amount of contact, with a miniscule 12.7 percent strikeout rate in his pro career heading into 2022. He didn’t sacrifice any of that in 2021 even with some power starting to show up. There’s a little more pop to his pull side, but he showed in Triple-A (where he hit 16 of his 17 homers last year) that he can drive the ball the other way as well. While there is growing confidence that Stefanic would hit Major League pitching, there are large questions about how to get that bat into the lineup. He’s a below-average defender with a below-average arm who has played several positions in the Minors. He’s played second base the most and the hope is he can be acceptable enough there to earn big league at-bats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A part-time player in his first two college seasons at California, Lee had a huge year in 2019 batting behind No. 3 overall pick Andrew Vaughn. Most clubs regarded Lee as more of a third-round talent, but the Astros loved his massive raw power and arm strength and made him a surprise first-round pick, signing him for a below-slot $1.75 million at No. 32. He made his big league debut with 12 games with Houston in 2022 but spent all of this season in Triple-A before getting traded to the White Sox for Kendall Graveman in late July. The Astros worked with Lee to quiet his load and shorten his stride after he turned pro, but he was still an extreme power-over-hit guy before 2023. After previously trying to get the most out of his well above-average raw power by launching balls to his pull side, he has settled down this season. Though he's making more contact, he's doing a lot less damage. Lee didn't become a full-time catcher until 2019 and has yet to start more than 73 games behind the plate in a pro season. While he's quicker and more athletic than most backstops and features plus-plus arm strength, his receiving and blocking skills draw mixed reviews. He has done a better job in 2023 and the consensus is that he's an average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee went from posting a .724 OPS as a part-time player in his first two college seasons at California to batting .337/.416/.619 in 2019 while batting behind No. 3 overall pick Andrew Vaughn. Though most teams evaluated Lee as more of a third-round talent, the Astros bought into his raw power and arm strength and selected him 32nd overall, where he signed for a below-slot $1.75 million. After losing a year of development to the pandemic layoff, he moved from High-A to Triple-A during his 2021 full-season debut and demonstrated improvement on both sides of the ball. Since turning pro, Lee has quieted his load, shortened his stride and added more balance at the plate, which has allowed him to drive balls in the air from gap to gap more easily. A right-handed hitter, he still can tap into more of his well above-average raw power if he can further reduce his tendency to make ground-ball contact. His approach has deteriorated in 2022, as he has gotten more pull-happy and looked helpless against breaking balls. Lee didn't become a full-time catcher until 2019 and continues to develop behind the plate. He's quicker and more athletic than most backstops and the hope is that he can become an average receiver and blocker as he gains more experience. The Astros have helped him get more out of his plus-plus arm strength by shortening his throwing stroke, and he erased 43 percent of basestealers last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After batting .243/.332/.392 as a part-timer in his first two college seasons at California, Lee surged to a .337/.416/.619 line in 2019 while hitting behind No. 3 overall pick Andrew Vaughn. Though most clubs viewed Lee as a third-round talent, the Astros loved his raw power and arm strength and made him a surprise first-rounder, signing him for a below-slot $1.75 million at No. 32. He bought a pitching machine for his home, which enabled him to work on his hitting and receiving during the pandemic layoff, before making a brief appearance at Houston's alternate site and participating in instructional league last fall. While in instructional league, Lee focused on maintaining some mechanical changes at the plate. He has quieted his load, shortened his stride and improved his balance, allowing him to drive the ball from gap to gap more easily. His bat speed and strength give him raw pop to all fields from the right side of the plate, and home runs should come naturally if he just concentrates on making hard contact and managing the strike zone. Lee also saw time at both infield corners and DH in college and didn't become a full-time catcher until 2019. He has the athleticism and quickness to remain behind the plate and is making strides with his receiving, which should become at least average with more experience. The Astros have shortened his arm stroke, making him even more effective at deterring the running game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winder entered pro ball as a pitchability right-hander, a seventh-rounder in 2018 from Virginia Military Institute who carved up lower-level hitters because of his impressive feel for pitching. Since that time, his stuff has consistently improved, and in 2021, he showed that the physical gains he made during the shutdown were for real as he pitched his way from Double-A to Triple-A and appeared in the Futures Game. Only a shoulder strain, which ended his season in late July, put a cloud over the breakout performance, but he was still added to the Twins’ 40-man roster and given a clean bill of health. The 6-foot-5 Winder has seen his velocity uptick since signing, sitting in the low-90s during his first full season in 2019 and averaging 95 mph (touching 98 mph) last season, maintaining the burst he had shown in instructional league play after the shutdown. His mid-80s slider flashes plus, and he has very good feel for his changeup, an offspeed pitch that doesn’t offer huge speed differential but does feature excellent depth and elicited a 53-percent swing-and-miss rate last year. He folds in an average curve as well. Winder’s improved stuff has not come at the sacrifice of his command as he walked just 1.6 per nine a year ago. The biggest question is the health of his shoulder. If he can put the injury behind him, he has the chance to be a mid-rotation type big league starter in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins’ seventh-round pick in the 2018 Draft out of Virginia Military Institute, Winder provides an interesting test case in terms of how to evaluate developmental progress during 2020’s lost season. A touch-and-feel kind of right-hander entering pro ball, one who led the Midwest League in ERA and WHIP during his first full season, Winder showed up for instructional league play last fall more physical and throwing a lot harder, something that carried over into his 2021 season, and he earned a Futures Game nod for his efforts. Winder worked hard during the shutdown to add strength to his 6-foot-5 frame, and it showed. After sitting in the low 90s throughout the 2019 season, he was up to 98 mph consistently during instructs, albeit in a smaller sample size, throwing it with good riding life. He added velocity to his curve as well, touching the low 80s with more spin, giving him a second above-average pitch. He still throws a distinct slider, and his average changeup now potentially has a better separation in terms of velocity from his fastball. The big right-hander has always had a knack for finding the strike zone, with a 2.0 BB/9 rate in the Minors entering the 2021 season after a 1.7 rate at VMI. The velocity and stuff gains seem to be for real, allowing Winder to keep climbing the charts as one of the biggest starting pitcher sleeper prospects in the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Virginia Military Institute has had just three players make it to the big leagues, most recently adding Reed Garrett to the ledger in 2019. Winder hopes to be the next in line. The right-handed starter had an up-and-down junior season at VMI, but the Twins liked the combination of his size, stuff and feel for pitching enough to take him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft. He rewarded their faith by leading the Midwest League in ERA and WHIP during his first full season. While none of Winder’s stuff will blow scouts away, he does have a solid four-pitch mix. He’ll work in the 91-94 mph range with his fastball and it’s played up a bit thanks to some tweaks he made to add more ride to it since he was drafted. He has two distinct breaking balls and does a good job of using both, employing his low-to-mid 80s slider against righties and using his mid-70s curve more against left-handed hitters. One of Winder’s biggest areas of improvement came with his changeup. It had flashes of good movement, but wasn’t separated enough velocity-wise from his fastball for it to be effective, but that took a big step forward in 2019. Strong and durable, Winder has always been a huge strike-thrower. His ceiling is limited, but he has the chance to be a dependable back-end starter if it continues to click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maryland's top high school prospect in 2015, Morris had Tommy John surgery a week before the Draft and redshirted during his first college season at South Carolina. He has performed well since the Guardians made him a seventh-round pick in 2018, but he also has worked just 106 innings combined in the past two seasons because of repeated shoulder issues. He made his big league debut last September, allowing a total of five runs in five starts and pitching two scoreless frames against the Yankees in the American League Division Series. Morris threw harder than ever in 2022, working at 93-95 mph and peaking at 98 with high spin rates and good carry on his four-seam fastball. He has a second plus pitch in a tumbling 81-85 mph changeup that dies at the plate, and big leaguers went 2-for-18 with 11 strikeouts against it. His breaking balls lag behind the rest of his arsenal, though both his 87-92 mph cutter and 78-82 mph curveball are average offerings. Though Morris has a long arm action, he repeats his delivery well, provides strikes and locates pitches well. With his arsenal and history of throwing strikes, he could fill a variety of roles in Cleveland from mid-rotation starter to late-inning reliever. The Guardians would like to deploy him as a starter but his inconsistent health may land him in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maryland's best high school prospect in the 2015 Draft, Morris had Tommy John surgery a week before the Draft and redshirted in his first year of college at South Carolina. A seventh-round pick in 2018, he made a strong pro debut the following year but lost 2020 to the pandemic shutdown and came down with a sore shoulder last spring. He looked better than ever when he returned to the mound last July, logging a 1.62 ERA with 93 strikeouts in 61 innings between Double-A and Triple-A to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. When he's 100 percent, Morris works at 92-95 mph and reaches 97 with high spin rates and good carry on his four-seam fastball. His tumbling 82-85 changeup disappears at the plate and gives him a second plus pitch at its best. After he showed little feel for a slider in college, he has reshaped it into a solid upper-70s curveball with downer break, and he's also beginning to unveil an upper-80s cutter. While Morris has a long arm action, he did a better job of repeating his delivery and commanding his repertoire in 2021. With three solid or better offerings and a history of throwing strikes, he offers the upside of a mid-rotation starter. To get there, he'll have to show that he can stay healthy and maintain quality stuff throughout a full pro season, and he missed the first three months of this season after straining his shoulder during Spring Training.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morris ranked as Maryland's best high school prospect in 2015 but wound up having Tommy John surgery and sat out his first college season at South Carolina. A seventh-round pick in 2018, he wore down toward the end of his pro debut the following year but was back throwing in the mid-90s in instructional league last fall. He came down with a sore shoulder this March and didn't pitch in a game until July, but he earned a swift promotion to Triple-A once he returned. When he's fresh and healthy, Morris can operate at 92-95 mph and touch 97 with high spin rates and good riding action on his four-seam fastball. After he showed little aptitude for throwing a slider in college, the Indians helped him reshape it into a solid upper-70s curveball with downer break.
