A switch-hitter, Fox has thrived on spraying line drives around the field at his best, but he got away from that approach some last season with a 56.5 percent groundball rate and .242 average for Triple-A Omaha. He is capable of squaring balls up and making hard contact, but by putting the ball on the ground, he blunts his power. Fox’s best offensive assets remain his willingness to take a walk (13.1 percent in 2021) and his plus-plus speed that allows him to earn infield hits and be a 20-plus stolen-base threat. An impressive defender at shortstop, Fox saw more time at second base in deference to Bobby Witt Jr. in Omaha and even played center field for the first time over the season’s final month. His athleticism will allow him to play up the middle, and that’s what so many teams have bet on in the last seven years. Without a significant offensive adjustment, Fox, who was called up by the Royals briefly but was never given his official MLB debut, remains a bench piece at best, albeit one that is ready now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he moved from Florida’s American Heritage High to his native Bahamas ahead of his senior year, Fox signed with the Giants as an 18-year-old in 2015. Less than a year later, the Giants traded him to Tampa Bay for Matt Moore at the Trade Deadline. Fox earned an All-Star Futures Game selection in ’17. After opening the 2020 season at the Rays’ alternate site, he was traded to Kansas City for Brett Phillips and joined the Royals' alternate site before seeing time during fall instructs. A member of the 40-man roster, Fox struggled for part of the year at Triple-A Omaha but used a hot run in the closing weeks to end up a league-average bat at the Minors’ top level. He was recalled by Kansas City briefly in July but is still awaiting his official Major League debut. He was claimed off waivers twice this offseason, first by the Orioles and most recently by the Nationals. Fox can spray line drives from both sides of the plate. Prior to Fox’s most recent moves, the Royals learned that his hard-hit rates were better than what his power numbers suggest; he hits hard line drives, they just don’t find themselves over the fence. Fox shows patience at the plate and has quality chase rates, and his on-base skills have continued as he’s moved levels and organizations. He also knows how to use his plus-plus speed on the bases. He stole a career-high 39 bases in 2019 and added 19 in 57 games with Omaha this past summer. Fox’s running and defensive profile have made him attractive to multiple clubs in the past few years, and he’s a quick learner with a high baseball IQ. He was considered an above-average shortstop with good hands and a strong arm entering 2021, but the rise of Bobby Witt Jr. has made him more of a utility option. Fox saw time at second base and center field with the Storm Chasers, and his athleticism helped in that transition. Now a part of Washington’s quick rebuilding efforts, Fox’s proximity to the Majors and ability to help out in multiple areas off the bench could make him a better option for the Nats than your typical waiver claim.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants signed Fox for $6 million as an 18-year-old in 2015 after he had moved from Florida, where he spent three years at American Heritage High (Delray Beach, Fla.), to his native Bahamas ahead of his senior year. He had been in the Giants’ system for less than a year when they flipped him to Tampa Bay for Matt Moore at the 2016 Trade Deadline. Though a foot injury sidelined Fox for the rest of that season, he returned healthy and performed well in ‘17, earning a SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game selection, and then made even greater strides the next year before struggling in Double-A to finish the season. While those struggles continued for Fox in ‘19, the Rays still pushed him up to Triple-A Durham for a bit in August and added him to their 40-man roster in November. After opening the 2020 season at the Rays’ alternate site, he was traded to Kansas City for Brett Phillips in August. Fox focuses on making line-drive contact from both sides of the plate and does a good job using the entire field. The quality of Fox’s contact is underwhelming, though, and he struggles to drive the ball consistently, even though he’s fairly strong, hitting mostly singles. He’s maintained strong on-base skills as he’s climbed the ladder thanks to a penchant for walking and knows how to use his plus speed on the bases. After recording at least 25 steals in each of his first three seasons, Fox swiped a career-high 39 bags in 2019. Fox is a rangy, above-average defensive shortstop with good hands and an above-average arm. The Rays began to increase his versatility with reps at both second (13 games) and third base (nine) in 2019, and he saw more time in center field ahead of the 2020 season. While he is unlikely to do enough damage at the plate to be an everyday player, Fox’s on-base skills, speed and glove could make him the type of utility player that teams love to have on their roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox chose to move back to his native Bahamas rather than fulfill his senior year at American Heritage High (Delray Beach, Fla.). It proved a wise move, as MLB ruled him an international free agent in April 2015, and he signed with the Giants on his 18th birthday three months later for $6 million, a record bonus for a non-Cuban international amateur. Fox struggled during his pro debut at Class A Augusta, albeit after an 18-month layoff from game action, and the Giants shipped him to Tampa Bay with right-handed pitcher Michael Santos and big leaguer Matt Duffy for Matt Moore at the 2016 Trade Deadline. It was learned that he had been playing through a foot injury, and the Rays shut him down for the remainder of the season. Fully healthy in 2017, Fox made his Rays debut with Class A Bowling Green before a late-season promotion to the Class A Advanced Florida State League. Along the way, he represented the World Team in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. Fox is a top-flight athlete with plus-plus speed and three more tools that should be at least solid. The switch-hitter profiles as a future leadoff-type hitter, as he employs a solid approach, produces line-drive contact from both sides of the plate and knows how to use his impressive wheels once on base. Fox won't offer much in the way of over-the-fence power, but he does have some strength and can drive some balls to the gaps, making him a source of doubles and triples. Fox's range, quick hands and arm fit easily at shortstop, though, like any young shortstop, he needs to fine-tune his game and learn the nuances of the position. Some scouts don't love his middle-infield actions and think he'll fit better in center field, though the Ray believe he can stay at short, lauding his super athleticism and ability to learn quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox chose to move back to his native Bahamas rather than fulfill his senior year at American Heritage High (Delray Beach, Fla.). It proved a wise move, as MLB ruled him an international free agent in April 2015, and he signed with the Giants on his 18th birthday three months later for $6 million, a record bonus for a non-Cuban international amateur. Fox struggled with an aggressive assignment to Class A Augusta for his pro debut, after an 18-month layoff from game action, and was shipped to the Rays with right-handed pitcher Michael Santos and big leaguer Matt Duffy for Matt Moore at the Trade Deadline. Fox admitted that he had been dealing with a foot injury shortly thereafter, and the Rays shut him down for the remainder of the season. Fully healthy in 2017, he made his Rays debut with Class A Bowling Green before suiting up for the World Team in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. Fox is a top-flight athlete with plus-plus speed and three more tools that should be at least solid. A switch-hitter with a line-drive stroke, he has the approach and the wheels to become a leadoff hitter and prolific basestealer. He won't be a homer threat but he does have some strength and can drive some balls to the gaps. Fox's range, quick hands and arm fit easily at shortstop. Some scouts don't love his middle-infield actions and think he'll fit better in center field, though the Rays, much like the Giants, believe he can stay at short, lauding his ability to learn quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals say they were lucky to snap up Pasquantino in the 11th round of the 2019 Draft. The Old Dominion slugger broke out late with the power for the Monarchs, slugging .573 with 16 homers in 56 games as a junior. He carried that to Rookie-level Burlington, where he hit .294/.371/.592 with 14 homers in 57 contests, but his momentum stopped momentarily in 2020. When he returned in 2021, Pasquantino was arguably better than ever, producing a .300/.394/.563 line, 24 homers, 64 walks and 64 strikeouts in 116 games at High-A and Double-A. His 64 total extra-base hits were sixth-most in the Minors. Pasquantino was a remarkably consistent hitter at two different levels and racked up more walks than strikeouts after his move up to Northwest Arkansas. Batting from a slightly open stance, Pasquantino stays on time and sees balls well through the zone. He draws positive reviews for the way he utilizes his lower half to create the necessary lift on contact that leads to extra-base hits by the bunches. He doesn’t quite create the same damage against fellow lefties (three of his 24 homers came off southpaws), but the overall package of contact and pop is refreshingly rare in today’s game. His makeup and clubhouse presence are often the first things mentioned by Royals officials, even above his hitting exploits. A well-below-average runner, Pasquantino is locked into first base, but those in Kansas City believe he’s more athletic there than he’s gotten credit for in the past. Sticking there or slotting into DH keeps the offensive bar high. The 24-year-old has shown he can clear it to this point, and anything close to a repeat performance in 2022 should get him to Kauffman Stadium by season’s end.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big leaguer Mike Capel, a pitcher who appeared in 49 games over parts of three seasons, and the godson of Roger Clemens, Conner showed scouts everything they wanted to see from him as a high school senior in 2016, leading to his selection in the fifth round by Cleveland. After ranking among the Midwest League leaders with 22 home runs (third) and pacing all Indians farmhands with 73 runs scored in his first full season, Capel took a step back in 2018 and became Cardinals property in July when they acquired him and Jhon Torres for Oscar Mercado. With his combination of strength, bat speed and an improved bat path, Capel showed in his first full season that he could hit the ball out to the deepest part of any ballpark, albeit at the cost of more swing-and-miss. In 2018, he made a concerted effort to make more contact and utilized a shorter, less-fluid swing that in turn zapped both his raw and game power, as he followed up his 22-homer campaign by tallying 34 extra-base hits over 118 games in Class A Advanced. Capel's above-average speed and strong instincts are qualifiers for him on the basepaths and in center field, and he has the arm strength -- he generated 90-mph fastballs off the mound in high school -- to play either corner spot. His bat, however, profiles best up the middle, as any move to a corner would come with a higher threshold for production.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big leaguer Mike Capel, a pitcher who appeared in 49 games over parts of three seasons, Conner showed scouts everything they wanted to see from him as a high school senior in 2016, but was widely believed to be difficult to sign given his strong commitment to Texas. The Indians nonetheless took a gamble on Capel in fifth round, and then surprised the industry by signing him for slot value. Assigned to Class A Lake County for his first full season, Capel's bat heated up with the weather as he overcame a slow start and improved with each month while flashing impresses tools. He finished among the Midwest League leaders with 22 home runs (third) and slugging (.482), and paced all Indians farmhands with 73 runs scored. While he reversed that script in 2018, hitting well early and scuffling late, the Cardinals saw enough to get him and Jhon Torres in a trade for Oscar Mercado. Capel has already made strides as a professional in cleaning up his left-handed swing, a good sign for any young hitter. Those adjustments helped Capel tap into his plus power in full-season ball, as he showed that he could hit the ball out to the deepest part of any ballpark with his combination of strength, bat speed and an improved bat path. And although Capel's uptick in power resulted in more strikeouts, he continued to recognize spin as part of a mature approach while also making plenty of hard contact. Capel's above-average speed and strong instincts are qualifiers for him on the basepaths and in center field, and he has the arm strength -- he generated 90-mph fastballs off the mound in high school -- to play either corner spot. He saw time at all three outfield positions in 2017. Capel stands to offer the most value if he can remain up the middle, where his power-speed combo would be a premium, but he also should produce enough to profile as a regular in either right or left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a senior at Lee's Summit West High in 2013-14, Harrison accounted for 29 touchdowns on a Missouri Class 5 state champion football team and averaged 16.4 points per game on a basketball squad that finished third in the state. He turned down a scholarship to play wide receiver at Nebraska to sign with the Brewers for $1.8 million as a second-round choice in 2014, then came to the Marlins as part of the Christian Yelich trade in January 2018. He led the Minors with 215 strikeouts in his first season with his new organization, then showed some progress in 2019 before fracturing his right wrist in June. Few players can match Harrison's all-around tools, though he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact in order to reach his lofty ceiling. He did tone down his leg kick and do a better job of using the whole field in 2019, reducing his strikeout rate to 29 percent from 37 percent the year before. The bat speed in his right-handed swing and the strength in his 220-pound frame create well above-average raw power and exit velocities, though his career 1.6 groundout/airout ratio (2.1 last year) reduces his effectiveness at driving balls over the fence. Harrison has plus speed and knows how to use it, stealing bases at an 84 percent success rate in his first six pro seasons and projecting as a 30-30 threat if he can continue to make adjustments at the plate. His quickness makes him at least a solid defender in center field, where he has spent most of his pro career, and an easy plus on the corners. His plus-plus arm strength ranks among the best in baseball for his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-sport standout in high school, Harrison opted to play baseball over accepting a football scholarship from the University of Nebraska. The Brewers made him their second-round pick in 2014, swaying him with a well-over-slot $1.8 mllion bonus. After ankle and hamate injuries sidetracked his first two full pro seasons, Harrison broke out with 21 homers and 27 steals in 2017, then got traded to the Marlins along with Lewis Brinson, second baseman Isan Diaz and right-hander Jordan Yamamoto for Christian Yelich during the offseason. In terms of pure athleticism and brute strength, Harrison has tremendous upside. A career .242 hitter who led the Minors with 215 strikeouts in 2018, he must demonstrate he can make consistent contact to reach his true potential. Even when he struggled in his first season in the Miami system, his upside was evident with 19 homers and 28 steals. According to Marlins metrics, 20 percent of the balls he put in play in Double-A had exit speeds of more than 105 mph, nearly three times the MLB average of 7 percent. Defensively, he has the quickness for center field and a cannon for an arm that easily would fit in right. Harrison made some adjustments in the Arizona Fall League, reducing his leg kick and producing more regular contact. He continued to show improvements in 2019, though he fractured his right wrist making a diving catch in June and subsequent surgery was expected to sideline him for most or all of the rest of the season. If he stays healthy and keeps refining his swing, he could develop into a 30-30 player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Revered as one of the 2014 Draft's premier athletes, Harrison was set to pursue a career in both baseball and football at Nebraska before the Brewers offered him nearly $700,000 over slot value as their second-round pick. Although a grim ankle injury prematurely ended his first full season and a broken hamate limited him the following year, a fully healthy Harrison blossomed in 2017, earning Midwest League All-Star honors before advancing to the Carolina League. He finished the season with 21 home runs and 27 stolen bases over 122 games between the two levels, and then firmly put himself on the Major League radar with a standout campaign in the Arizona Fall League. Harrison's breakout caught the attention of the Marlins, and they acquired him with Lewis Brinson, Isan Diaz and Jordan Yamamoto for Christian Yelich in January. Harrison might have the loudest tools in Miami's system. He generates plus raw power to all fields thanks to a combination of physical strength and plus bat speed that enables him to turn around velocity. That power does come with some strikeout concerns, as Harrison's swing will get too long at times and he'll struggle to recognize spin, causing him to expand his zone. Harrison's plus speed makes him a basestealing threat as well as an above-average defender, either in center field or in right, where his cannon for an arm is a clean fit. Harrison offered a taste of his potential during his breakout 2017 campaign, and the Marlins are justifiably excited about what the future may hold for their new outfielder. If he can stay healthy, Harrison could develop into a perennial 20/20 player who also offers considerable value with his defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the premier athletes in the 2014 Draft class, Harrison passed on an opportunity to play two sports at Nebraska to sign for nearly $700,000 over slot value as the Brewers' second-round pick. Injuries impacted his progress early in his career, as a grisly ankle injury in July prematurely ended Harrison's first full season, and a broken hamate limited him to just 75 games at Class A Wisconsin in 2016. When Harrison was healthy in 2017, his on-field results finally reflected his immense physical tools, as he was named a Midwest League All-Star before advancing to the Carolina League. He finished the season with 21 home runs and 27 stolen bases, and then continued to make strides during an impressive turn in the Arizona Fall League. Harrison's breakout caught the attention of the Marlins, who acquired him, Lewis Brinson, Isan Diaz and Jordan Yamamoto for Christian Yelich in January. Harrison has excellent bat speed and should develop at least average power as he matures and gains much-needed experience. His penchant for whiffing stems from a long swing and pitch-recognition issues, though his overall approach is solid. Harrison's plus speed makes him a basestealing threat as well as an above-average defender, either in center field or in right, where his cannon for an arm is a clean fit. Harrison offered a glimpse of his potential during his healthy 2017 campaign, and that production should continue to translate as he gains experience. The final product could be that of an All-Star-caliber outfielder who also offers considerable value with his defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After joining the Rays out of Mexico as a 17-year-old during the 2015-16 international signing period, Aranda eased into his professional career. He didn’t play in a full-season league until 2019, and even that year brought only 273 plate appearances of a fine average, a respectable on-base percentage and little power. But the Rays were encouraged with what they saw from Aranda in the Mexican Pacific Winter League after the canceled 2020 Minor League season, as the infielder hit .333/.390/.458 over 40 games. That, it turns out, was just the start of Aranda’s breakout. Aranda put together a 1.004 OPS in 21 games for High-A Bowling Green last year and earned a promotion to Double-A Montgomery, where he hit .325/.410/.540 over 79 games. Aranda was named the 2021 Double-A South Most Valuable Player and the Rays’ team MVP for Montgomery, and his big year ended with him on Tampa Bay’s 40-man roster. He’s not a prototypical left-handed slugger, standing at just 5-foot-10, but he has a simple swing and has always possessed a good approach with plenty of bat speed. He’s still a hit-over-power player, likely only reaching solid-average power, but he started hitting the ball in the air more over the last year and set a career high with 14 homers in 2021. He’s lined up plenty at second and third base, but his most likely long-term home is at first base, where he made most of his starts in Montgomery. Aranda’s track record doesn’t scream “highly touted prospect,” but if he can sustain the gains he made last season in Triple-A and the Majors this year, his hit tool and defensive flexibility should carry him into the Majors with a pretty high floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $325,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Sosa came to the United States at age 17 for his pro debut the following summer and has consistently been one of the youngest players in his leagues. He finally broke out in 2022 after adopting a more disciplined approach, leading the system in hitting at .315 while slamming 23 homers (more than double his previous career high) between Double-A and Triple-A at age 22. He had two brief stints with the White Sox, homering off Jonathan Heasley in August and making himself a candidate for their open second-base job in 2023. Sosa's hand-eye coordination and bat-to-ball skills allow him to make a lot of hard contact despite an aggressive mindset. He settled down his right-handed stroke and made better swing decisions in 2022, and while he's still not patient, his walk (7 percent) and strikeout (17 percent) rates were easily his best in three years in full-season ball. He has the bat speed and strength for average power, and he might find more than that if he can become more selective. Sosa displays good actions and reliable hands as an infielder, but his below-average speed leads to fringy range, and his arm strength is merely average. He has played primarily shortstop in the Minors, but his range would be stretched at that position in the big leagues, and his arm may be a bit light for third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox have promoted Sosa aggressively since signing him for $325,000 out of Venezuela in 2016. They brought him to the United States for his pro debut the following summer, have consistently made him one of the youngest regulars in his leagues and sent him to Double-A at age 21 last August. He finally caught his breath in 2022, breaking out as one of the system's top prospects and making his big league debut in June. A right-handed hitter, Sosa owns some of the best hand-eye coordination and bat-to-ball skills in the system. He began to reach his offensive potential this year by making better swing decisions, and while he still doesn't walk much, he's not getting himself out by making weak contact. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to deliver 15-20 homers per season if he can maintain a decently selective approach. Sosa has good actions, reliable hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, but his below-average speed leads to subpar range. He fits better at second or third base, though those positions will demand more offense. Given the strides he has made this year, that shouldn't be a problem.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox considered Sosa advanced enough to come to the United States for his pro debut in 2017, a year after he signed for $325,000 out of Venezuela. He held his own as one of the youngest regulars in his league in each of his first three seasons and ranked second in the low Class A South Atlantic League with 35 doubles at age 19 in 2019. His development experience last year consisted of instructional league. Sosa already shows the ability to make consistent contact thanks to his fine hand-eye coordination. The next step will be to add some strength and some loft to his right-handed swing to make the most of what could be 15-20 home run power. Developing more patience to wait for better pitches to put into play also would help his cause. Sosa's fringy speed throws his ability to remain at shortstop into question, though his instincts help him get to balls and make plays. He has reliable hands and solid arm strength and may fit best at third base, with second base another possibility. He'll likely spend this year in high Class A as a 21-year-old and could wind up as a bat-first utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing Sosa for $325,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, the White Sox considered him advanced enough to bring to the United States for his pro debut the next summer. While he didn't post lofty numbers in his first three seasons, he managed to hold his own as one of the younger regulars in his league each year. He hinted at his offensive upside by finishing second in the low Class A South Atlantic League with 35 doubles as a 19-year-old in 2019. Sosa's quick right-handed swing and fine hand-eye coordination enable him to make consistent contact. If he gets stronger and adds some loft to his stroke, he could produce 15-20 homers per season. Developing a more patient approach also will help him reach his offensive potential. With average speed and the possibility of losing a step as he matures physically, it's unclear if Sosa can remain at shortstop. However, his instincts help him make plays and his hands are very reliable. His solid arm would allow him to move to third base, though that would place greater demands on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jorge Alfaro might currently be the best-known catcher from Colombia in the big leagues, but the Royals are hoping Viloria can join him full-time soon. Signed in July 2013 for $460,000, the third-highest international bonus the organization doled out in that signing period, Viloria has shown abilities on both sides of the ball at times and the Royals thought enough of his maturity to call him up from the Class A Advanced Carolina League to the big leagues last September. Because of his potential on both sides of the ball, some evaluators think Viloria has the chance to be an everyday catcher in the big leagues. He's shown an advanced approach from the left side of the plate and doesn't strike out much. While it hasn't shown up much in the stat line yet, there is some raw power for him to tap into. Viloria has a very strong arm behind the plate, one that has thrown out 35.7 percent of potential basestealers. He's a good blocker, but the rest of his receiving needs to get more consistent. At times, he'll be very good, then he'll do something like let a fastball tip off his glove. Viloria's tendency to see himself as an offensive-minded catcher has kept him from developing all of his skills fully. His time in the big leagues, where he saw how All-Star Salvador Perez prepares, should help him realize the work he needs to put in to be Salvy's eventual successor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $460,000 out of Colombia in 2013, Viloria went from failing to produce an extra-base hit in 45 games in 2015 to winning Pioneer League MVP honors in 2016 after leading the Rookie league in batting (.376), doubles (28) and RBI (55). He didn't make the same impact last year, though he did hold his own offensively and threw out 40 percent of basestealers as the youngest catcher (age 20) in the low Class A South Atlantic League. Viloria has bat speed and a knack for barreling the ball from the left side of the plate. His gap-to-gap approach and relatively flat swing cut into his power, though he has the potential to produce double-digit home run totals. He needs to hone his plate discipline after posting career worsts in strikeout rate (20 percent) and walk rate (6 percent) in 2017. A shortstop when the Royals first spotted him, Viloria still is refining his defense behind the plate but shows promise. He has a strong if sometimes inaccurate arm, has the soft hands to become a solid receiver and has impressed the club officials and pitchers with his leadership and English-speaking skills. He weighs more than his listed 175 pounds and will have to watch his conditioning to avoid losing agility behind the plate and becoming a baseclogger.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Viloria's offensive potential warranted a $460,000 bonus when he signed out of Colombia in 2013, but it wasn't always evident when he went through the entire 2015 season without an extra-base hit in 45 games. He exploded last year, earning MVP honors in the Pioneer League after leading the Rookie league in hitting (.376), doubles (28) and RBIs (55) while also homering six times in 58 games. While the Pioneer League is a hitter's haven, Viloria shows a patient approach and makes repeated hard contact. He drives the ball to both gaps and has some home run power to his pull side. As a left-handed hitter who could bat .275 with 12-15 homers per year, he has more offensive upside than the typical catcher. A shortstop when the Royals first worked him out, Viloria still is learning the nuances of catching. Though he led the Pioneer League backstops with 14 errors, he has solid arm strength and the hands to become an average receiver. He'll have to watch his weight -- it's more than his listed 175 pounds -- to retain his agility behind the plate and avoid becoming a true baseclogger.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 70 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Signed for $450,000 in July 2012, Barrera took a long journey through the A’s system before really breaking out in 2016. After earning Texas League All-Star Game MVP honors in ‘19, a left shoulder injury temporarily hindered his ascent. Making a full recovery and standing out at the alternate site in 2020, Barrera finally got his first taste of big league action in 2021, appearing in six games for the A’s. Barrera is a pure hitter with an ability to slash the ball from line to line. While the home run totals have been low, he is able to use his left-handed stroke to hit line drives to all fields. His great hand-eye coordination allows him to put the ball in play often and keeps his strikeout rate low, even if he does not draw a ton of walks. Not only is he a speedster on the bases, he’s also displayed good instincts when running, allowing him to consistently put up double-digit stolen base totals. Barrera’s passion for the game makes him one of the more fun A’s prospects to watch. He plays good defense, though he is a little slow in his transition getting the ball out of his glove. The A’s still love his athleticism, and he projects as an outfielder who can play all three spots in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barrera signed for $450,000 in July 2012, but it wasn’t really until 2016 that he really took off in the A’s system. The outfielder played across two levels in both ‘17 and ‘18, earning a spot on the 40-man roster following his ‘18 campaign. The Texas League All-Star Game MVP in ‘19, Barrera’s rapid push to the big leagues took a hit later that year due to a left shoulder injury that required surgery. He made a full recovery in 2020 and was by far considered the best performer at the alternate site by A’s officials. A slasher from line to line, Barrera is a pure hitter. Although there isn’t a ton of power there, he brings a level left-handed stroke and the ability to hit line drives to all fields. His plus speed comes with good instincts on the bases, and his solid defense allows him to play all three outfield spots. Barrera plays with a lot of passion and brings excitement. He does not walk much, but he also does not strike out at a high rate due to great hand-eye coordination. Barrera will chase sometimes, which could expose him at the higher levels, though he seems determined to work on improving that area of his game. Once that comes, Barrera should develop into a starter at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $450,000 back in July 2012, Barrera hasn’t exactly taken a rapid or direct path to the big leagues. He didn’t reach full-season ball until late in 2016, but then things started happening a bit more quickly for the outfielder after that, playing across two levels in both 2017 and 2018, earning a spot on the 40-man roster following that ’18 season that saw him reach Double-A. A 2019 season that could have led to the final jump to the big leagues was interrupted and eventually ended in late June because of an injury to his non-throwing shoulder that eventually required surgery. Even when he was trying to play through his injury, Barrera was still doing what he does best: hit. The left-handed hitter is aggressive at the plate and makes a ton of contact with a line-drive, slashing kind of approach. He doesn’t walk a ton, but he also doesn’t strike out much. He’s never going to be a big home run guy, but he has shown the ability to hit the gaps on a regular basis, with his extra-base thump showing up more in Double-A last year. Barrera is a plus runner who can steal a base and is as aggressive on the basepaths as he is at the plate. Barrera’s passion for the game shows up on defense as well and his shoulder injury wasn’t helped by diving for balls in the outfield. He’s probably best suited for an outfield corner, where his above-average arm plays well, but he’s also shown the ability to play center field if needed and the A’s love how fearless he is. He might break in as a fourth outfielder, but he has the ability to be a big league regular on both sides of the ball if the opportunity arises.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barrera was the biggest international sign by the A's in the 2012-13 signing period, with his $450,000 bonus in July 2012 the top among five players who received six figures from the organization. He's moved methodically, not touching full-season ball until his fourth summer in 2016. Since then, he's earned in-season promotions in '17 and '18 and really jumped more firmly on the prospect map by hitting his way to Double-A in '18 and earning a spot on the 40-man roster. Perhaps the most improved player in the organization, Barrera came into his own in 2018 in terms of his approach and consistency in his at-bats. With a line-drive, slashing style, Barrera is showing he has the ability to hit for average with excellent bat control, a decrease in his strikeout rate and an increased willingness to draw walks. He won't be a home run hitter because of his flat bat path, but there could be a bit more pop to unlock at some point. Aggressive with good instincts, Barrera uses his speed well to steal bases. He also uses it to play all three outfield positions and his defensive play has improved nearly as much as his bat has. Barrera does have the tools to play center field regularly. If his step forward offensively is for real, he could shed the fourth outfielder profile and become a regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees were the favorites to land Castillo at the outset of the 2015-16 international period before an issue with the Venezuelan right-hander's physical caused the deal to fall through. He instead signed with the Blue Jays in September, and did so for just $10,000. Castillo made both his pro debut and U.S. debut the next year and then in 2017 advanced to Rookie-level Bluefield, where, at age 18, he won six of his 10 starts and posted strikeout and walk rates of 26.0 and 3.5 percent, respectively. Castillo is already physically mature for his age, with a stocky frame that leaves little room for projection. His feel for pitching is similarly advanced, as Castillo operates at 89-92 mph with a fastball that has run and late sinking action that nets him both whiffs and ground balls. Castillo can spin a solid breaking ball but does so inconsistently, while a changeup gives him a distinct third pitch. Castillo's strike-throwing ability is one of his strengths, but he needs to improve his fastball command so as to better set up his secondary pitches, with the goal of getting hitters to expand the zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Encarnacion didn't land a deal in the 2014 international signing period, and the Marlins were tracking other players in the Dominican Republic when they stumbled upon him and inked him for $78,000 in September 2015. Nagging injuries and a propensity for strikeouts dogged him until he broke out in 2019, when he led the system with 71 RBIs and ranked second in with 43 extra-base hits before clubbing the decisive home run in the Arizona Fall League's championship game. He reached Double-A last year but hit just .222 with a 38 percent whiff rate while knee issues and a broken finger limited him to 63 contests. Encarnacion fits the right-field profile with some of the best power and arm strength in the system. His combination of bat speed and the strength and leverage in his massive frame give him 30-homer upside that he has yet to fully tap into. A long right-handed swing and pitch-recognition issues prevent him from making consistent contact, and he'd be more dangerous if he turned and lifted pitches more consistently. Though Encarnacion is more athletic than the typical 6-foot-4, 250-pounder, he's still a fringy runner who doesn't provide much value on the bases. He has decent range in right field and notched 33 assists in his first 200 starts there, but he's also error-prone. He played on a Double-A Pensacola team last year that also featured outfield prospects JJ Bleday, Peyton Burdick and Griffin Conine, so he saw semi-regular action at first base, allowing enough at-bats for everyone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miami stumbled upon Encarnacion while pursuing other players in the Dominican Republic and signed him for $78,000 in September 2015, a month before he turned 18. Nagging injuries and swing-and-miss issues prevented him from making much of an impact until 2019, when he led the system in RBIs (71) and ranked second in extra-base hits (43) while playing at two Class A levels and swatted the decisive home run in the Arizona Fall League championship game. He spent 2020 at the Marlins' alternate site before they protected him on the 40-man roster in November. Encarnacion generates at least plus raw power with his combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his 6-foot-5 frame. He did a better job of translating his pop into production in 2019, when he improved his plate discipline and pitch recognition, but he regressed in those areas this year in Double-A. He also has made adjustments to help him pull and lift pitches more frequently. Though Encarnacion is more athletic than most players his size, he doesn't do much on the bases with his fringy speed. He has a plus arm that helped him register 18 assists in 118 games in 2019, though he must improve his decision-making and accuracy after committing 15 errors. Once he settles down, he should be an average defender on the outfield corners, and he also has seen time at first base this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Marlins were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic when they stumbled upon Encarnacion, who was nearly 18 when he signed for $78,000 in September 2015. Held back by nagging injuries and swing-and-miss issues at the beginning of his pro career, he broke out last year by leading the system with 71 RBIs and ranking second in extra-base hits (43) while playing at two Class A levels. He homered in the Class A Midwest League all-star game and provided the decisive grand slam in the Arizona Fall League championship contest. Encarnacion's bat speed and the strength and leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame give him at least plus raw power to all fields, and he did a much better job of tapping into it in 2019. He made more consistent contact with his simple right-handed swing and turned on and lifted pitches more regularly. He also did a better job of dealing with breaking balls and improved his plate discipline, allowing him to make more consistent contact. Encarnacion is a better athlete than most players his size, though he's not much of a factor on the bases with his fringy speed. He has a plus arm that notched 18 outfield assists in 118 games a year ago, though he must improve his accuracy and decision-making after committing 15 errors. If he can settle down, he'll be at least an average defender in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene was an impressive prep hitter, leading to a gold-medal-winning turn with USA Baseball's 18-and-Under National Team in the Pan-American Championships in 2018. The Tigers grabbed him with the fifth overall pick the following year and signed him to a slot $6.18 million bonus. The Florida native saw three levels in the summer of 2019, was a standout at Major League camp the following spring and continued to the alternate training site before his 20th birthday. In 2021, the slugger hit .301/.387/.534 with 24 homers and 16 steals over 124 games at Double-A and Triple-A. A trip to the Arizona Fall League was canceled after he experienced concussion-like symptoms, but he cleared protocols in October. Greene exhibits a potent combination of hit and power tools from the left side. His swing is often described as fluid, but it also comes with plenty of violence, thanks to the way he utilizes his lower half. He exhibits a mature approach as well, one that helps him pick up walks at a good clip. While his strikeout rate has sat on the high side, there is hope it will trend back down as he sees more upper-level pitching. Perhaps most promising in his development has been the power that has gone from raw strength to in-game prowess with some added muscle. Primarily a center fielder at Double-A, Greene played all three outfield spots with Toledo. His instincts help make up for average speed, and he has the arm to work anywhere on the grass. The Tigers have sought new challenges for Greene since signing him, only for him to clear every bar. Whether it’s in center or a corner, he’ll be an impact bat alongside Torkelson in the heart of a Detroit lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a standout turn with USA Baseball's gold-medal-winning 18-and-Under National Team in the Pan-American Championships, Greene strengthened his case as the best pure prep hitter in the 2019 Draft by batting .422 with eight homers as a Hagerty HS (Oviedo, Fla.) senior. The Tigers took Greene with the No. 5 pick that June, signing him for $6.18 million, then watched him climb three levels to finish his pro debut at Class A West Michigan. He was the biggest standout among Tigers prospects in his first big league camp, slashing .417/.611/.917 with two homers and six walks in seven games, and continued to make an impression on Tigers officials during Summer Camp and at the alternate training site. Scouts love Greene's left-handed swing because it’s as fluid and balanced as it is explosive. His bat speed and path through the zone yield plenty of hard contact, and he already demonstrates an advanced approach. He shows huge raw power in batting practice, especially to the pull side, and has started to get to it more regularly as he’s gotten stronger. He should have at least above-average game power, along with a plus hitting ability, once developed. Greene is an above-average runner who can hold his own as a center fielder, although most scouts believe he eventually will move to an outfield corner. His strong arm would fit in either left or right, as would Greene’s offensive profile. Greene is advanced for a recent high school pick, possessing a unique combination of tools, skills and instincts that could help him move through the Minor Leagues relatively fast. The final product could be that of an above-average Major League player, if not better, who hits for average and power from the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene cemented his status as perhaps the best pure high school hitter in the 2019 Draft with a strong performance on the summer showcase circuit and with USA Baseball's gold-medal-winning 18-and-Under National Team in the Pan-American Championships. He garnered Gatorade Player of the Year Award honors in Florida as a Hagerty HS (Oviedo, Fla.) senior the following spring, batting .422 with eight homers, and signed with the Tigers for $6.18 million after they selected him with the No. 5 overall pick. Greene hit the ground running in his pro debut, climbing three levels to finish the season at Class A West Michigan. Greene's left-handed swing is as fluid and balanced as it is explosive. His bat speed and path through the zone yield plenty of hard contact, and he already demonstrates an advanced approach. He shows huge raw power in batting practice, especially to the pull side, and should have at least above-average game power, to go along with a plus hitting ability, once developed. While Greene is an above-average runner and held his own as a center fielder in his pro debut, most scouts believe he'll eventually move to an outfield corner. His strong arm would be a fit in either left or right, and he has the offensive profile for either position. Greene's advanced feel to hit and solid approach give him a solid foundation for developing game power, and club officials believe it'll start to show as he adds strength to his projectable frame and gains experience. He'll need time to develop (though possibly not as much as the typical prep pick), but the final product could be that of a middle-of-the-order run producer who hits for both average and power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a tale of two competitive seasons for Peguero since he came to the Pirates from the D-backs in the 2020 Starling Marte trade. After impressing as one of the youngest players at the team’s alternate site that year, he made the leap to High-A in 2021 and helped Greensboro make the playoffs as one of the youngest regulars in the league. The move to Double-A in 2022 wasn’t as kind, though he was called upon to be an emergency fill-in and make his brief big league debut and was still very young for his level. Peguero started his Double-A debut with a hot bat, albeit one that was too aggressive, with an OPS of .853 through May. But when the Eastern League adjusted, he largely wasn’t able to. He needs to see more pitches at the plate, and the right-handed hitter often chased out of the zone, relying too much on his knack for making contact and thus diminishing his ability to impact the ball consistently. It’s still in there, with good bat speed, but his power only came to his pull side last year, and he struggled against breaking stuff. Peguero’s speed is still an asset on both sides of the ball, and he likes to run, with 56 steals over the past two years combined. While he has plenty of range and arm strength, he’s struggled with defensive consistency but will continue to see time at shortstop while adding in second base and perhaps even some outfield moving forward. The good news is at just 22 years old for all of 2023, there’s plenty of time for him to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates looked to trade Starling Marte before the 2020 season, they wanted to make sure they got some high-end talent, even if it meant waiting for a return on the investment. They found what they were looking for with the D-backs, sending the All-Star outfielder to Arizona in return for right-hander Brennan Malone and Peguero, who had signed for $475,000 back in July 2017 and was coming off a scintillating United States debut in Rookie ball in 2019. After Peguero opened a lot of eyes at the Pirates’ alternate training site in 2020, he was challenged in '21 with a move to High-A, where he was the regular shortstop of a playoff team and nearly three years younger than his contemporaries in the league. A right-handed hitter, Peguero routinely shows the ability to hit the ball with outstanding exit velocities and premium bat speed, giving him the chance to eventually be a plus hitter. He continues to get stronger as he matures and could also have at least average power, especially if he can figure out who he is as a hitter. He can get over-aggressive and try to do too much in each at-bat, but he improved in terms of his consistency from AB to AB as the 2021 season wore on. Peguero is a plus runner who has shown he can steal a base and uses that speed to cover plenty of ground at shortstop, a position he should be able to play long term. He gets as high marks for his aptitude and passion for the game as he does his tools, and he’ll play all of 2022 at age 21, with the Pirates excited to see him continue bonding with his future double-play partner, Nick Gonzales.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed Peguero for $475,000 back in July 2017, and it didn’t take him long to put himself on the map, playing his way from the Dominican Summer League to the United States in his debut summer in 2018. In 2019, he was impressive as one of the youngest prospects at his level, earning a promotion from the Rookie-level Pioneer League to the Short-Season Northwest League. The Pirates took notice, making sure to get him as part of the return for Starling Marte before the 2020 season began. He was the youngest, and perhaps the most exciting, prospect at the Pirates’ alternate training site in 2020. After getting his footing at the alternate site, Peguero’s performance really stood out and carried over to his play during instructional league play. The right-handed hitter posted elite-level exit velocities consistently at instructs, topping out over 109 mph. Because of his bat speed and knack for barreling up the baseball, he has the chance to be a plus hitter down the line. The power will come more as he keeps adding strength to his 6-foot-1 frame, and his advanced approach for his age has separated him from other young prospects. Peguero’s speed is an asset on both sides of the ball, with the chance to steal bases and the ability to cover a ton of ground at shortstop, a position he could play for a very long time because of his instincts, footwork, hands and arm. If he outgrows the position, his offensive profile could work in a lot of places and his infectious energy will be welcomed wherever he’s penciled into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When international amateur free agents are signed at age 16, it can often take a while for projected tools to show up. Then there are players like Peguero, who signed with the D-backs in July 2017 for $475,00, who come out of the gate swinging a hot bat. He hit his way out of the Dominican Summer League to the United States during his pro debut in 2019 and then dominated the Pioneer League in 2019, earning a promotion to the short-season Northwest League in the process. The rest of his development will now be up to the Pirates, who acquired him along with pitching prospect Brennan Malone in the Starling Marte deal. Peguero could be a plus hitter when all is said and done. He can really impact the baseball from the right side of the plate, with plus bat speed that enables him to smash good velocity and make consistent barreled contact. The extra-base ability is already showing up and there’s more power to come as he adds strength to his projectable frame. He has an advanced approach for a teenager and already shows the ability to recognize spin and control the strike zone, with his plus speed that aids him on both sides of the ball. The infielder has also made strides defensively and he has every chance to be a shortstop long-term thanks to his actions, hands and arm strength. While his remaining physical projection could lead to a move off of the position down the road, Peguero's bat could enable him to profile at a host of positions on the diamond. For now, though, he'll be given every opportunity to stick up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first player to be selected out of Millville (N.J.) High School since Mike Trout in 2009, the D-backs picked Kennedy in the fifth round of the 2017 Draft. He signed for $500,000, forgoing his commitment to North Carolina, then impressed over 50 games in his professional debut. Kennedy was named a Pioneer League midseason All-Star and slashed .327/.396/.465 over 57 games in 2018. He put together another solid campaign in 2019 and added strength to his frame before the 2021 season. The results were obvious as he slugged a career-best .523 and more than tripled his previous best of seven homers with 22. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 190 pounds, there’s a lot to like about Kennedy’s offensive profile. His quick bat and barrel control enable him to consistently square up the baseball and make line-drive contact. While he started to hit the ball more in the air last season, his biggest improvement came with his approach. Kennedy drew more walks and gained confidence working pitchers and hitting in deeper counts. He projects to be an average hitter who gets on base and collects 20 or so homers at the highest level. A decent athlete, Kennedy is an average runner with good instincts on both sides of the ball. He’s not a burner, but he uses his speed well and swiped 16 bags last season (he was caught four times). He’s made strides defensively since signing and has spent time at first, second and third in the Minors, paving the way for him to ultimately be someone who can fill a variety of needs for a club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the D-backs took oKennedy in the fifth round in 2017, they made him the first player to be drafted out of Millville (N.J.) High since Mike Trout in 2009. Kennedy signed for $500,000, forgoing his commitment to North Carolina, then showcased innate feel for squaring up the baseball during his pro debut. That continued for him in 2018 with a move up to the Pioneer League, where Kennedy produced a .327/.396/.465 line and garnered honors as a mid-season All-Star. Kennedy may be stocky and lacking in physical projection, but there is plenty to like about his offensive profile. His quick bat and excellent control of the barrel enable him to make consistent line-drive contact from the right side, where he covers the plate well and shows a discerning eye. Those qualities should help him succeed at higher levels and, in general, give him the upside of an above-average hitter who's capable of hitting 15-plus homers and reaching base at a high clip. A better athlete than his stout frame suggests, Kennedy is an average runner with good instincts on both sides of the ball. He impressed club officials last year with his improvements at third base, and he'll likely add more positions to his resume going forward as the D-backs look to increase his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marinan was a \"pop-up\" guy as a Florida high schooler as the 2017 Draft approached, a young two-way player who saw a velocity spike raise his profile. A two-way player who was going to head to Miami, the Dodgers took him in the fourth round and gave him second-round money to sign him, as a pitcher, away from joining the Hurricanes. He was in his first full year with the Dodgers in 2018 when they sent him to the Reds in early July. Marinan's velocity spike brought his upper-80s fastball to one that typically sits 92-96 mph with some sink. He has two distinct breaking pitches, an upper-70s curveball with good depth and a sweeping slider. The curve will flash plus, but is inconsistent as he sometimes has trouble commanding the pitch. His changeup, which he rarely used in high school, is now his best secondary offering in terms of its consistency. Marinan has the chance to add strength to his large 6-foot-5 frame and while he's still learning to find the strike zone regularly, he has the athleticism to be able to repeat his delivery in the future. The Reds like upside arms like this, knowing that had Marinan gone to college he wouldn't be eligible for the Draft until 2020, and they know they'll have to be patient to see what he might become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 A two-way player at Park Vista Community High in Boynton Beach, Fla. -- Trea Turner's alma mater -- Marinan created debate as to whether he had a brighter future as a sweet-swinging first baseman or a projectable right-handed pitcher. When his velocity spiked during his senior season last spring, it became clear that his future was on the mound. The Dodgers popped him in the fourth-round and gave him late second-round money ($822,500) to divert him from a commitment to Miami, then traded him to the Reds in July 2018. Marinan's fastball jumped from the upper 80s on the showcase circuit during the summer before his senior year to 92-96 mph with sink last spring. He also has added more power to his breaking pitches, an upper-70s curveball that features good depth when he stays on top of it and a sweeping slider. He rarely used a changeup as an amateur but shows encouraging feel for the pitch. With a strong 6-foot-5 frame and a clean delivery, Marinan is equipped to remain a starter. Though he battled his control during his brief pro debut, he has the athleticism to do a better job of repeating his mechanics and throwing strikes. The Reds will develop him patiently and he likely won't make his full-season debut until 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 After his freshman year at Cameron University (Okla.), Tetreault transferred to State College of Florida Manatee - Sarasota, where he showed improved stuff as a member of the program's starting rotation in 2017. Intrigued by Tetreault's present ability and remaining projection, the Nationals signed him for $300,000 after selecting him in the seventh round. Working exclusively as a starter in his first full season, Tetreault exhibited a blend of stuff, pitchability and durability en route to a late promotion to Class A Advanced Potomac. A 6-foot-5 right-hander, Tetreault has a clean delivery and fast arm help him generate a fastball that reaches the mid-90s but typically sits a few ticks lower. He has feel for spinning a curveball that can flash above-average at its best, and he's made strides developing a changeup that's at least average, with room for improvement. Meanwhile, after facing questions about his control and command heading into the season, Tetreault did his part to assuage those concerns by trimming his walk rate from 3.8 to 2.8 BB/9, all while missing a healthy number of bats. Tetreault impressed Nats officials with his steady, season-long development in 2018. Specifically, they like how he learned to command his fastball to different parts of the strike zone as the season progressed -- he had elevated it too often and was hit around early in the year -- and how the right-hander effectively mixed in his secondary pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Tetreault spent his freshman year at Cameron University (Okla.) before transferring to State College of Florida Manatee - Sarasota ahead of his sophomore campaign. He showed improved stuff as a member of the starting rotation that spring, and the Nationals, intrigued by his present ability and potential, drafted him in the seventh round. After signing for above-slot at $300,000 and forgoing a South Florida commitment, Tetreault had a successful pro debut between the Rookie-level Gulf Coast and Class A Short-Season New York-Penn Leagues. Listed at 6-foot-5, 170 pounds, Tetreault has considerable physical projection remaining. His stuff is plenty good, too, as the quick-armed right-hander will reach 95 mph with his fastball while flashing a sharp, above-average curveball and showing feel for a changeup. Tetreault has considerable physical projection remaining, though some scouts do worry about his ability to maintain velocity and work deep into games. Given his limited college track record and remaining physical projection, it shouldn't come as a surprise that Tetreault's control and command are both below average. The Nationals, however, are excited about his upside, viewing him as a late-bloomer who has the potential to stick in the starting rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Talk about perseverance. Bride was nowhere near the prospect radar as a 23rd-round pick by the A’s in 2018. In fact, his struggles in 2019 as a 23-year-old had the A’s thinking they might need to demote him to Low-A. However, he returned from the pandemic and put together a solid 2021 season in which he showed supreme versatility while hitting .265 with nine home runs and 49 RBIs for Double-A Midland. Bride is considered to have the best fastball contact of any player in the entire system, particularly against fastballs in the zone. There is some power in his game, and he’s always been able to get on base at a high clip. The definition of super-utility, Bride can play third, first, second and left field well. This past season, he added catcher to his list of positions, getting extra reps behind the plate in the Fall League due to the injury to Tyler Soderstrom. Known to be a great teammate who is hard-nosed and has already overcome several challenges in his career, he’s moved his way up the system and reached the big leagues in June as a solid utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles have binged on college outfielders in the Draft under executive vice president and general manager Mike Elias, adding a bevy of such players to their system during their current rebuild. The first was Stowers, whom the Orioles took out of Stanford with the No. 71 overall pick in 2019, the first of three Cardinal players they’d select with their first 12 picks that season. He also was the first of that group to reach the Majors after leading Baltimore’s system with 27 homers and reaching Triple-A Norfolk in 2021, then getting called up for the first time in mid-June. The surfer-haired, sweet-swinging Stowers showed as much growth as any prospect in Baltimore’s system last season, jumping three levels and sharing its co-Player of the Year honors with Adley Rutschman. Most of his damage came at Double-A Bowie, where Stowers hit .283/.377/.561 with 17 homers in 66 games. Stowers’ loudest tool is plus raw power, which results in consistently strong exit velocity readings and translates better to the pull side of his left-handed swing. He generates it with good bat speed, though there is some length to his path that creates some swing-and-miss in his game. Stowers struck out at a 32-percent clip in 2021 but his 14-percent walk rate also indicated refinement in his approach. Stowers is an average runner with a decent arm who projects best as a bat-first corner outfielder. The likeliest landing spot is left field, especially if he can develop the type of all-fields approach he’ll need to hold his own against left-handed pitching. If it all clicks, Stowers could grow into an everyday, impact bat at the highest level -- as early as this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a breakout sophomore season at Stanford, Stowers shot up Draft boards with a strong showing in the Cape Cod League the following summer, when he ranked among the premier wood-bat league’s leaders in hitting and homers. He got off to a slow start offensively as a junior, but the Orioles saw enough maturation and promise to snag Stowers with the No. 71 overall pick in the 2019 Draft, making him the first of three Cardinal players they’d choose with their first 12 picks. Stowers then got off to a slow start in his pro debut, hitting .216 with six home runs and 53 strikeouts in 55 games with Class A Aberdeen. He participated in Orioles instructional camp in 2020. The Orioles are confident Stowers’ numbers at Aberdeen don’t reflect the quality of contact he made, citing consistently strong exit velocity readings and bad batted-ball luck. Stowers’ loudest tool is his plus-raw power, which translates better to the pull side of his left-handed swing. He generates it with good bat speed, though there is some length to his path that creates some swing-and-miss issues at times. Stowers is an average runner with a decent arm who projects best as a bat-first corner outfielder. The likeliest landing spot is left field, especially if he can develop the type of all-fields approach he’ll need to hold his own against left-handed pitching. If it all clicks, Stowers could grow into an everyday, impact bat at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 75 | Curveball: 55 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Capable of hitting triple digits with his fastball, Zabala has arm strength that can't be taught. The Dominican right-hander was the definition of a project during his two pro seasons but made progress in his second tour of the Rookie-level Arizona League, recording 10.8 strikeouts-per-nine with a .167 opponents average that ranked third in the circuit among relievers. Zabala made strides with his heater last summer, sitting at 96-99 mph with an improved downhill plane helped him generate more than twice as many outs on the ground than in the air in the AZL. He complements his fastball with a hard, downer curveball that scouts view as an above-average pitch, and he showed the ability to miss bats with both offerings for the first time in 2016. Though his stuff is electric, Zabala struggles to harness it within the strike zone, with well-below-average control that has resulted in 5.7 walks-per-nine in 102 1/3 career innings. The good news is that Zabala, who will be 20 for all of 2017, still has age on his side, and it gives him plenty of room improvement in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Moreno for only $25,000 out of Venezuela in August 2016, and he has recently blossomed into one of the game’s most promising catching prospects. He first got onto external scouts’ radars when he hit .413 over a 23-game span in the Gulf Coast League, prompting a push off the complex in his age-18 season. He followed that up with a strong showing at Class A Lansing in 2019 and was a standout at the alternate training site a year later. His biggest breakout came last summer when he hit .373/.441/.651 with eight homers in 32 games at Double-A New Hampshire before a fractured left thumb cut that short. He returned in time for the Arizona Fall League (where he led the circuit in doubles) and a short spell in the Venezuelan Winter League. The Jays gave the 22-year-old his Major League debut this summer, but a crowded catching group has caused him to stay at Triple-A Buffalo for much of the summer. The right-handed slugger shows a quick and compact swing that he uses with promising hand-eye coordination to make a good amount of contact, and he should always hit for a decent, if not impressive, average. His .600-plus slugging percentage flattered him last year, and a high groundball rate could take the shine of what would otherwise be at least average pop. Moreno has made promising developments behind the plate as well. An infielder at the time of signing, the 22-year-old puts his athleticism to use with blocking, receiving and throwing. He has a plus arm with a quick release, capable of controlling the running game as he did with a 40 percent caught-stealing rate last year. Moreno saw some time at third base in the AFL, but his ceiling behind the plate is immense as a potential All-Star.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 60 | Power: 55 | Run: 35 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 55 One of the organization’s savviest international signings in recent years, the Blue Jays landed Moreno for $25,000, seeing the fundamental tools and athleticism to develop into a catcher. Five years later, Moreno is one of the most intriguing young players in the organization, and teams around baseball are quickly taking notice of what the Blue Jays have seen for years. After a rough debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2017, Moreno hit everything he saw in the GCL in ’18, earning him a bump up to the Appalachian League. With Class A Lansing in ’19, Moreno put himself squarely on the prospect map by hitting .280 with 12 home runs and an .823 OPS over 82 games. He was off to a killer start in 2021, hitting .373/.441/.651 with eight homers in 32 games at Double-A New Hampshire before he suffered a fractured thumb in June. At the alternate training site in 2020, Moreno didn’t just turn coaches' heads. Fellow players raved about the young catcher, who was making louder contact and consistently driving the ball in the air with his quick, compact swing. With low strikeout and walk rates, Moreno puts plenty of balls in play with his very advanced hand-eye coordination and has added even more power as he’s matured in the pro game. He should be above-average in both the hit and power categories, a scary scenario considering his position. Behind the plate, it’s Moreno’s quickness and athleticism that appeal most to evaluators. Those skills, along with an above-average arm, are what give the Blue Jays confidence in Moreno as a catcher not just today, but in his development going forward, as well. Moreno is young with development still ahead of him, but he has a path to becoming a Major League starter. Even with the lost time due to injury this year, Moreno is young and looking like he may not be far from helping Toronto at the top level. He’s become one of the game’s most exciting catching prospects before his 22nd birthday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 43 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 The Blue Jays signed Moreno for $25,000 in August 2016 because they liked the athleticism and tools and believed he could develop into a well-rounded catcher. After a nondescript pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2017 and an unbelievably incredible start at the plate in the Gulf Coast League in ’18 that earned him a promotion to the Appalachian League, Moreno got into 82 Midwest League games last year. He hit .280/.337/.485 for the Lansing Lugnuts, adding 12 homers, 17 doubles, five triples and 52 RBIs at just 19 years old. Moreno’s knack for making hard contact is a product of his outstanding hand-eye coordination and his preternatural feel for getting the barrel to the ball. He’s cognizant of those strengths to a fault at times, as he’ll attack pitches outside of the zone simply because he can reach them. At the same time, he neither strikes out nor walks all that often and he has the ability to use the whole field. There’s enough juice in his bat to safely project double-digit home run totals though he more likely will profile to hit more for average than for power. Defensively, Moreno impresses club officials with his athleticism and energy behind the plate, and they believe he has a chance to stay there long term. His arm strength is average but plays up because he has solid catch-and-throw skills which culminate with a quick release. Like any young catcher, there are improvements to be made with his blocking and receiving, but all the ingredients are there for Moreno to develop into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 The Blue Jays signed Moreno for $25,000 in August 2016 because they liked the athleticism and tools and believed he could develop into a well-rounded catcher. After a nondescript pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, the Venezuela native moved stateside in 2018 and promptly raked to the tune of .413/.455/.652 in the Gulf Coast League, earning a promotion to the Appalachian League after his first 23 games. Moreno's knack for making hard contact is a product of his outstanding hand-eye coordination and his preternatural feel for getting the barrel to the ball. He's cognizant of those strengths to a fault at times, as he'll often attack pitches outside of the zone simply because he can reach them. At the same time, Moreno neither strikes out nor walks all that often. There's enough juice in his bat to safely project double-digit home run totals, though his profile likely will be hit-over-power. Defensively, Moreno impresses club officials with his athleticism and energy behind the plate, and they believe he has a chance to stay there long term. His arm strength is average but plays up because he has solid catch-and-throw skills which culminate with a quick release. Like any young catcher, he has a ways to go with his blocking and receiving, but all the ingredients are there for Moreno to develop into a big league backup, perhaps even a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds selected Okey in the second round out of Clemson in 2016, they figured he'd be a light hitter with the chance to improve while playing good defense. However, Okey's bat has regressed in many ways as his anemic 2017 and 2018 numbers have shown while his prospect stock continues to trend the wrong way. Part of that might have been because of a right wrist/hamate injury that he tried to grind through on his own for a long time before he alerted the medical staff. Okey doesn't have the statistics to show it, but there was a feeling he took some better at-bats in Double-A. Now the consistency of his approach really needs to come into focus for 2019 to give him a chance to get back to the decent hitter with some extra-base pop to tap into that he showed glimpses of before the injuries hit. Behind the plate, Okey has impressed with his defensive play and it appeared to improve in 2018. He has gotten good marks for being able to work well with pitchers and call a good game while showing solid blocking and receiving skills. His best bet at a big league career will be as a defensive-minded backup, but he'll have to improve his offensive profile to reach that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heading into the 2016 Draft class, there were catchers who had better offensive profiles, and there were backstops who were better defensively, but no one seemed to have a better chance of being a solid all-around big league catcher than Okey. The Clemson product went in the second round as a result, then saw his prospect stock plummet with a dreadful first full season in 2017 and he was not able to bounce back offensively in 2018 as an injury to his other wrist delayed his start and clearly impacted his production. A natural leader who prides himself on being tough behind the plate, it turned out Okey had hid a right hand and wrist injury from the organization, self-treating it at night and playing through it. It clearly impacted his hitting as he batted only .185 and slugged .265, but he hasn't been able to get back to being the average hitter that he was pre-injury, one with some power to tap into. While he hasn't handled the bat, Okey has impressed the organization with his defensive play. He's great working with pitchers, calling a good game to go along with solid blocking and receiving skills. His throwing has improved, and he'd thrown out just over 33 percent of potential base stealers in his career heading into 2018. Okey deserves some slack because of the injuries, but he does have to show he can stay healthy and be productive at the plate. If he can do that, he could shoot back up this list and reclaim his mantel as one of the best overall catching prospect from his Draft class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds had their eyes on two college catchers in the 2016 Draft class, Will Smith from Louisville and Okey, from Clemson. Smith went to the Dodgers at the end of the first round, but that was just as well for the Reds, who liked Okey's history better. They were able to nab him at the beginning of the second round and he advanced to full-season ball before his summer debut was over, the organization trying to pair him with first-rounder Nick Senzel. Okey was the best all-around catching prospect in the Draft class, with tools on both sides of the ball. There is some swing and miss to his offensive game, and he struggled during his first full season, though he has the tools to hit, and with some power, more from strength than bat speed. He's a good baserunner, especially for a catcher, and that athleticism plays behind the plate as well. While his arm is average, it's accurate and he's done a solid job of controlling the running game as a pro. Okey is a natural leader behind the plate, the type who still could be a big league regular for a long time despite his sluggish first full year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
