More polished than the average high school pick, Thomas could move relatively quickly through the Minors now that he's focused on baseball. His game earns him comparisons to the likes of Andrew Benintendi and Jacoby Ellsbury, though Thomas is more advanced at the same stage of their careers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The second of three straight college right-handers taken in the first round by the Mariners, Kirby came out of Elon University as a strike-throwing machine, a command-over-stuff guy who walked just 1.9 batters per nine innings over three years. After a brief debut in 2019, time at the Mariners’ alternate training site in 2020 and a full-season debut that saw him reach Double-A in 2021, Kirby still fills up the strike zone, but his prospect stock has skyrocketed thanks to his stuff improving exponentially since signing. Kirby appeals to evaluators of all types thanks to the quality of stuff and the ease with which he does it, blowing up any and all internal metrics in terms of things like velocity, movement, command, swing and miss and lack of hard contact. He can now run his fastball up to 100 mph, turning what was a low-90s heater into one that sits in the 96-98 mph range consistently. He has two distinct breaking pitches, both of which are plus at times, and he sinks a solid changeup as well. The velocity gains have done nothing to hamper Kirby’s ability to drop the ball on a dime, as the right-hander walked just 2.0 per nine in 2021. The only thing that’s holding him back is experience, and he did miss some time with shoulder fatigue, but he’s looking more and more like a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s now been five Drafts in a row that the Mariners have gone with a college player in the first round, the last three coming in the form of right-handed pitchers. Kirby, the No. 20 overall pick in 2019, was the first-ever first-round pick out of Elon University and was sandwiched by Logan Gilbert in 2018 and Emerson Hancock in 2020 as the Mariners try to draft and develop a future rotation. Kirby gave a glimpse of what he’s about during his pro debut in short-season ball in 2019, then threw well at the Mariners’ alternate training site last year. While Kirby is known more for his command than anything else, he has more than enough raw stuff at his disposal. He delivers a four-pitch mix from a 6-foot-4 frame, starting with a fastball that sits in the low-90s with good running life, but that he can get up to 98 mph at times. He’s worked on adding strength which will lead to more consistent velocity as well. Kirby throws both a curve and a slider, with the former slightly ahead, and both have the chance to be out pitches. He does a nice job of selling his sinking changeup with excellent arm speed. All of Kirby’s stuff plays up because of his command, which might be as good as any pitcher in the Minor Leagues. He walked virtually no one during his last season at Elon and then walked literally no one over 23 innings of his pro debut in 2019. His combination of improving stuff and elite-level control all point to him moving very quickly up the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the last four Drafts, the Mariners have gone the college route with their first-round pick, with solid success. Kyle Lewis' bat started contributing in Seattle in 2019 and Evan White, taken a year after Lewis in 2017, just signed a long extension. Logan Gilbert had an outstanding first full season and it's looking like Kirby, taken No. 20 overall out of Elon University last June, is ready to use his solid stuff and plus command to join Gilbert in moving quickly through the Mariners' system. The 6-foot-4 Kirby has four pitches that all have the chance to be at least above-average when all is said and done. It starts with his fastball, which he can crank up to 97-98 mph at times, especially in shorter stints, and typically sits in the low-90s with good running life. As Kirby adds strength, there could be more consistent velocity, similar to how Gilbert has developed. Kirby has two distinct breaking balls, with his curve slightly ahead of his slider now, but both show flashes of being potentially plus. He has feel for his sinking changeup as well. To call Kirby a strike-thrower would be an understatement. As a junior at Elon, he led all Division I pitchers in strikeout/walk ratio (17.8) and walk rate (0.6 per nine innings), then didn't walk a single batter in 23 innings during his pro debut. He was very fastball-reliant in college and will have to continue to refine his secondary stuff, but he has all the makings of a mid-rotation starter who can get to Seattle in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of Alex Rodriguez, Dunand has some physical mannerisms that resemble those of his famous uncle. He was a divisive player in the 2017 Draft, with some clubs projecting him as a power-hitting third baseman and others seeing him as more of a one-tool player with a questionable bat. The Marlins fell into the former camp, signing him for $1.2 million as a second-round choice. Dunand's most obvious tool is his raw right-handed power, which he creates more with strength than bat speed. He'll have to control the strike zone and make more contact to get the most out of it, however, and he had a 30-percent strikeout rate in Double-A last year. He never has hit for a high average, batting .268 in three years at North Carolina State and .246 in his first two pro seasons, and he walks infrequently. A fringy runner with a thick lower half, Dunand played exclusively at shortstop in his first two years as a pro but doesn't project to stay there. The Marlins like his defensive instincts and will let him play his way off the position. He's a better fit at third base, where his power potential and solid arm fit the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of Alex Rodriguez, Dunand was one of the more divisive players in the 2017 Draft, with some scouts pegging him as a future power-hitting third baseman, and others seeing him as more of a one-dimensional player with questions about his hit tool. Dunand's big, raw power was too enticing to pass over for the Marlins, who secured his future with a $1.2 million bonus after selecting him in the second round. He hit his way up to the Class A Advanced Florida State League in his pro debut and swung the bat well there to open 2018, ultimately earning promotion to Double-A just a year into his career. Dunand's intrigue lies in his potential to hit for both average and power. The latter is more strength-driven than it is a product of his bat speed, though he does know how to get to it. Dunand hit for more average during his final two NC State campaigns, as well as in the Cape Cod League, but he'll need to control the zone better and make more contact to be successful as a pro. As a fringy runner with a thicker lower half, Dunand isn't a clean fit on paper at shortstop. However, Marlins club officials have been impressed with his performance there so far, noting that he has the instincts and feel for the position despite a lack of outstanding defensive tools. He'll be given every chance to prove he can stick up the middle, but it's widely believed that he'll end up at the hot corner, where his glove, strong arm and power potential are all fits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2017, Lewis was a bit of a surprise No. 1 overall pick, though the Twins coveted him. He made a very strong impression playing across two levels of A ball in his first full season. After a rougher 2019 campaign, Lewis won MVP honors in the Arizona Fall League, but then didn’t play a game for two years because of the 2020 shutdown and a torn ACL in 2021. He hit well upon his return in Triple-A in 2022 to earn his first callup to the big leagues. The comeback story was short-lived as he tore the same ACL after crashing into the center-field wall during his second time up with Minnesota, knocking him out for another year. All of the tools that made Lewis a potential All-Star caliber player are still there. It remains to be seen if his elite-level speed will still be intact after his second knee surgery, but Lewis’ rehab work following his first injury actually increased his speed. He had struggled with his approach at times during the early stages of his career, particularly in 2019, but was much more refined and patient at the plate in 2022, with simpler swing mechanics -- minus his old leg kick -- allowing him to barrel up the baseball more consistently and get to what could be above-average or better power in the future. Lewis has continued to primarily play shortstop as a pro and has the defensive chops to stay there long-term, with more than enough arm and range for the premium position. He showed off the ability to play a very good center field in the AFL and then in 2022, though there might be some concern given that’s where he reinjured his knee in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 1 pick in the 2017 Draft, out of the Southern California high school ranks, Lewis played up to advanced billing in his first year-plus of pro ball, with a .292/.352/.451 slash line across two levels of A ball in his first full season. He struggled in '19, though he went to the Futures Game and reached Double-A. He seemed to right the ship with an MVP performance in the Arizona Fall League, but he didn’t play a competitive game for two years because of the pandemic and a torn ACL suffered in Spring Training of '21. He made a triumphant return to competitive play in '22, earning his first callup to the big leagues, only to tear the same ACL when he crashed into the center-field wall in his second Major League stint. Lewis has tremendous upside when he’s healthy. He had close to top-of-the-scale speed before he hurt his knee that made him a dangerous baserunner. With a lot of moving parts to his swing and a big leg kick, Lewis got out of sync in 2019, but he seemed to get his timing back in the AFL and at the Twins’ alternate training site in '20. He’s worked to quiet his setup and smooth out his swing, and losing the leg kick helped his timing before his second knee injury. He is capable of driving the ball to all fields and there’s plenty of raw power for him to tap into. Drafted as a shortstop, Lewis has mostly played the premium position as a pro, and had made enough improvements for most to believe he and his above-average arm can stick there in the big leagues. He also showed off positional flexibility in the AFL, including some plus defensive ability in center field. He was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason, but now Lewis and the Twins will have to wait 12 months from his June surgery to get him back into action again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it was a mild surprise when Lewis was the No. 1 pick in the 2017 Draft, he certainly played like the top player in the class during his pro debut that summer when he reached full-season ball as a high school draftee and continued excelling across two levels of Class A ball during his first full season. He dealt with failure for the first time in 2019, though he did reach Double-A, finishing with a .661 OPS. Lewis erased some of that with an MVP performance in the Arizona Fall League that fall and continued to play well at the Twins’ alternate camp in 2020. His progress was derailed when he required surgery for a torn right ACL at the start of Spring Training. When he’s locked in and healthy, Lewis shows off all five tools on the field, all of which can play up because of his plus makeup and instincts. The main variance might be with his hit tool. He spent most of 2019 struggling being on time at the plate as he utilizes a big leg kick and has a busy swing, leading to a loss of approach. He was able to get it back for his time in the AFL and it carried over to his alternate camp work this past season. Lewis is able to drive the ball with hard contact to all fields and the power is just starting to show up. Lewis’ plus speed makes him a basestealing threat and his athleticism helps him on the defensive side. He showed he can move seamlessly around the field in the AFL, seeing time at second, third and center field in addition to shortstop. That’s the spot he played exclusively at the alternate camp, working with infield coordinator Billy Boyer and has every chance to stick there long-term, though the Twins know they can plug his bat into any number of positions when it’s deemed ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There’s a certain level of expectations that comes along with being the No. 1 overall pick in the Draft and in many ways Lewis, the top pick in 2017, has lived up to them. He reached Double-A at age 20 while representing the Twins at the All-Star Futures Game, though he struggled at times during his 2019 campaign. He put all of that behind him when he was the top prospect in the Arizona Fall League, taking home MVP honors and helping the Salt River Rafters win the title. Lewis is an exciting combination of impressive tools and high baseball IQ, all of which was on display during his time in Arizona. He uses a high leg kick at the plate with a busy swing and his timing can be off at times, something that happened during his 2019 regular season. He made some adjustments in the second half and while his regular-season numbers don’t reflect that, it did help him regain his timing in Arizona. He can make hard contact to all fields and there’s plenty more power to come as he continues to mature. One of the fastest players in the Minors with excellent instincts, he should also continue to be a basestealing threat. Capable of handling shortstop with good range, hands and a strong arm, Lewis moved around the diamond quite a bit during his AFL stint, showing defensive acumen at second, third and center field. The Twins plan to continue to have Lewis play multiple positions, which could help get his bat into the lineup sooner rather than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it surprised some when the Twins took Lewis with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2017 Draft, the toolsy infielder has shown quickly that he was worthy of being taken in the top spot. The California high schooler made it to the full-season Midwest League in his summer debut, then performed his way up to the Florida State League in his first full season. While he may have been fatigued down the stretch, he did homer three times in helping Fort Myers win the FSL title at the end of the year. A premium athlete, Lewis has impressive tools across the board combined with instincts and makeup that allow them all to play up consistently. He consistently makes hard contact with an advanced approach at the plate, drawing walks while not striking out a ton. He can drive the ball to all fields and his over-the-fence power started showing up, with more to come. His speed should allow him to continue to be a serious basestealing threat. He had a very positive year at shortstop defensively, showing a ton of improvement. There's still room for him to improve the consistency of his throws, but the Twins think he could be an above-average defender when all is said and done. Lewis was the youngest player in the Florida State League when he got there at age 19, so he's already well ahead of the curve. Seeing him in Minnesota at age 21, with a future as an All-Star level player, seems completely reasonable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though ranked as the top high school position player in the 2017 Draft class and often mentioned as a potential top pick, it nonetheless took some by surprise that the Twins took Lewis No. 1 overall. He signed for $6.725 million, $1 million under pick value, then repaid Minnesota's faith in him by performing extremely well in the Gulf Coast League and all the way up in the full-season Midwest League after a late promotion. Lewis has outstanding athleticism on both sides of the ball. When you combine that with his baseball IQ, it's easy to see a future star. At the plate, he barrels the ball up consistently and has extra-base authority to all fields, with more power to come for sure. He showed an advanced approach at the plate with the ability to draw walks, which should give him more opportunities to use his plus speed on the basepaths. There were some questions about whether Lewis would be a shortstop long term, or need to move to center, but he has good range and hands and might have just enough arm to stay on the dirt. The Twins plan to keep him there, at least for the time being. Lewis will be an impact up-the-middle player in either case. After his strong pro debut that saw the prepster jump on a slightly faster track by getting his feet wet in Cedar Rapids, watching his full-season encore should be a treat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hjelle is on the cusp of making it to San Francisco, and when he does, he'll match Jon Rauch as the tallest big leaguer ever at 6-foot-11. The Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year as a Kentucky sophomore in 2017, he signed for $1.5 million as a second-round pick after his junior season. After mostly breezing through the Minors, he got rocked for a 5.74 ERA in 10 starts after he arrived in Triple-A last August, though that didn't dissuade the Giants from placing him on their 40-man roster. Hjelle's biggest weapon remains his hard knuckle-curve, an 82-85 mph breaker with power and depth that was his lone effective pitch in Triple-A. His fastball continued to sit at 92-94 mph and top out at 96, but the extension and angle that his extra-large frame creates didn't throw Triple-A hitters off as much as it had lower-level opponents. His sinking changeup can be an average third offering when he keeps it in the low 80s and lands it in the zone, but it lacks consistency. With excellent body control for his size, Hjelle has a long track record of providing strikes, though his walk rate jumped from 2.3 per nine innings before he got to Triple-A to 4.9 afterward. He keeps batters off balance by sequencing his pitches well, but he must locate his fastball and changeup with more precision in order to succeed. He has displayed No. 4 starter ceiling in the past but looked more like a future curveball-dependent reliever at the end of 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year as a sophomore in 2017, Hjelle signed for $1.5 million as a second-round pick the following year and advanced to Double-A in his first full pro season. Despite the lack of a Minor League season in 2020, he wasn't invited to the Giants' alternate site (because they focused on pitchers who could help in the Majors imminently) or instructional league (because they didn't want to ramp him back up and alter his offseason program in advance of big league camp). While throwing simulated innings at home, he was on hand for the birth of his first child and completed his college degree from Kentucky. If Hjelle makes it to The Show, he'll match Jon Rauch as the tallest big leaguer ever at 6-foot-11, but unlike a lot of gargantuan pitchers he's more polished than intimidating. His fastball parks around 92-94 mph and tops out at 96, playing better than its velocity because of the extension and angle his huge frame creates. His low-80s knuckle-curve can be a plus pitch at times and he has made progress with a sinking changeup since turning pro. Hjelle has exceptional body control for his size, which allows him to provide consistent strikes and pound the bottom of the zone. He sequences his pitches well, adding to his ability to keep hitters off balance. He should help the Giants in the near future and comes with a high floor as a good bet to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If Hjelle makes it to The Show, he'll match Jon Rauch as the tallest big leaguer ever at 6-foot-11, but unlike a lot of gargantuan pitchers he's more polished than intimidating. He has a history of success, including winning Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year honors as a sophomore in 2017, a year before signing for $1.5 million as a second-rounder. He advanced from low Class A to Double-A in his first full pro season. Unlike many tall pitchers, Hjelle stands out more for his polish than intimidating stuff. His fastball sits around 92-94 mph and touches 96, playing above its average-ish velocity because of his command and the unusual angle his height creates. His low-80s knuckle-curve can be a plus pitch at its best, and he made strides with a sinking changeup in 2019. Hjelle has uncanny body control considering his size, repeatedly throwing strikes and pounding the bottom of the zone. He improved at sequencing his pitches last season, particularly in the way his changeup plays off his fastball. He has a high floor with a good chance of becoming at least a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If Hjelle can make it to the big leagues, he'll equal 6-foot-11 Jon Rauch as the tallest pitcher in MLB history. He compiled an impressive college résumé, setting a Kentucky freshman record with eight saves in 2016, winning Southeastern Conference Pitcher of the Year honors as a sophomore and posting the best numbers of his career as a junior. Kept on tight pitch counts after signing for $1.5 million as a second-rounder, he could advance quickly once the Giants turn him loose Hjelle doesn't fit the protoype of a tall pitcher because his polish stands out much more than his power. His fastball sits at 91-94 mph and peaks at 97, with the unusual angle he creates with his extra-large frame more notable than his velocity. He has outstanding body control for someone his size, allowing him to repeat his delivery with ease and throw strikes with all of his offerings. Hjelle's best pitch is his low-80s knuckle-curve, which earns plus grades from some evaluators. He also uses a cutter/slider to give him a harder breaking ball and shows feel for a changeup. While he still could add some strength to his lanky frame, his floor stands out more than his ceiling and he's likely to settle in as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No one in the Cardinals' system did more to put himself on the radar in 2021 than Yepez. Originally signed for $1 million by the Braves in July 2014, the Venezuela native was traded to St. Louis in May 2017 for Matt Adams. He didn’t hit more than 10 homers or sport an OPS above .789 until that 2021 breakout, where he sported a .286/.383/.586 line with 27 blasts between Double-A and Triple-A. The Cards added Yepez to the Major League roster for the NL Wild Card Game against the Dodgers and afterwards sent him to the Arizona Fall League, where he hit .302/.388/.640 in 23 games. Yepez added muscle in 2021 and used it to fuel his power increase at the upper Minors. He also shortened his swing to make the most of that pop and make more quality contact. The result was a strikeout rate below 20 percent, not typical for someone with that much power. Improved strike-zone awareness and an advanced approach could make him an above-average hitter at the top level, should this trajectory continue. The Cardinals have given Yepez time at all four corner spots -- left, right, third and first. A lack of speed and his increasing strength make him more of a first baseman, and it was noteworthy that 16 of his 20 defensive starts in the AFL came at that spot. He might need to access the versatility (or a DH) to find playing time with Paul Goldschmidt on the roster, but the hitting gains and new roster spot should mean he’ll help St. Louis in some way soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves signed Yepez as a 16-year-old for $1 million in 2014. He made his full-season debut in 2016, but missed nearly three months with an injury. The Venezuela native continued to work his way up the ladder in the Braves’ system, but was dealt to the Cardinals in exchange for Matt Adams in 2017. Yepez showed an advanced approach and promising hitability upon his arrival to the Cardinals organization. Yepez shed some fat and added some muscle to his frame, which quickly paid dividends as things really started to come together for him in 2019 and continued in 2021 as he set a career high for homers and reached Triple-A Memphis. While he doesn’t always get to it in games, there is power in Yepez’s 6-foot-1, 200-pound frame. Yepez drives the ball well to the gaps and consistently posts high exit velocities, so the Cardinals expect more home runs to come as he continues to make adjustments in the batter’s box. Among those adjustments, Yepez has shortened his swing since the Cardinals acquired him and also increasingly shown a better understanding of the strike zone as a whole, as well as which pitches he’s able to drive. The fact that he’s been able to transform both his body and offensive approach speaks to a work ethic that could help speed up his timeline. Yepez’s size and lack of speed limits him on the defensive side of the ball, but he’s still shown some good versatility. Originally signed as a third baseman, Yepez also spent time at first base early in his career and added outfield to his skillset in 2019. While his arm will play at any of the positions, his range will likely limit him to first base in the future. The development of his power will certainly be important if Yepez is to profile at first base. While his bat will allow him to contribute, the power may determine whether he’s an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves gave Yepez the largest bonus of any player in their 2014-15 international class, signing the then-16-year-old Venezuelan for $1 million at the outset of the July 2 period. He made a relatively quick climb through Atlanta’s system for a young player, with his advanced approach carrying him up to full-season Class A Rome at age 18 in 2016. Yepez continued to show a promising blend of hitting ability and power potential after the Cardinals acquired him in exchange for Matt Adams in 2017, and after working to improve his physique, he began to realize his power potential as a 21-year-old in ’19 while reaching Double-A. While Yepez has traded some of his big right-handed power for hitting ability in recent years, it still shows in his batting practice, and when he does connect during games, it’s often a tape-measure blast to left field. He does a good job controlling the zone for a young player, albeit without drawing many walks, and has made a concerted effort to trim some of the swing-and-miss from his game since he joined the Cardinals. The Cardinals like how Yepez challenges himself and think that he will eventually put up big numbers. For a player whose size limits him to corner positions, Yepez is surprisingly versatile. After bouncing between first and third base during his first four seasons, Yepez added the outfield to his resume in 2019, appearing in 37 games between right and left. But as a below-average runner who is likely to lose a step with physical maturation, Yepez’s ultimate defensive home likely will be first base. He has the bat to profile there, but will need to hit for power to be a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Faedo is nearly five years removed from his dominant run through the College World Series at the University of Florida. He was once among a quartet of pitching prospects who comprised the heart of the Tigers’ rebuilding effort, but the combination of the pandemic and a torn elbow ligament that led to Tommy John surgery halted his progress the last couple of years while Casey Mize, Tarik Skubal and Matt Manning graduated to Detroit. Faedo’s slider has always been his out pitch, which he has leaned on to varying degrees since his college days at the University of Florida. He can throw it like two different pitches, whether he’s trying to spot it for a strike or induce a hitter to chase. His fastball dropped to 90-91 mph in 2018 but bounced back to the mid-90s with an improved spin rate thanks to a more upright delivery and consistent arm slot. How that pitch mix, especially his slider use, changes after surgery will be closely followed. The Tigers will have to weigh carefully how to progress Faedo. He hasn’t thrown a regular-season pitch since 2019 at Double-A Erie, and he’ll likely face the same growing pains with command that many pitchers -- including fellow Tigers prospect Joey Wentz last year -- encounter their first year back from surgery. Faedo is also 26 years old, and with the Tigers ready to progress into contention, the organization has to figure out where he fits in its plans.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Faedo’s career has progressed in stops and starts since the summer of 2017, when he was the Tigers’ first-round pick and the Most Outstanding Player of the College World Series just weeks apart. Faedo didn’t pitch the rest of that year, struggled through his first pro season in 2018, matured into a more polished prospect in 2019, then saw a chance at the Majors vanish during baseball’s spring shutdown. Last year included a COVID bout that cost him a spot in Summer Camp, a forearm strain that shut him down at the alternate training site and eventually a diagnosis of a torn elbow ligament. He underwent Tommy John surgery and will miss the 2021 season while rehabbing. Faedo’s slider has always been his out pitch, which he has leaned on to varying degrees since his college days at the University of Florida. He can throw it like two different pitches, whether he’s trying to spot it for a strike or induce a hitter to chase. His fastball dropped to 90-91 mph in 2018 but bounced back to the mid-90s with an improved spin rate thanks to a more upright delivery and consistent arm slot. How that pitch mix, especially his slider use, changes after surgery will be closely followed. Tigers officials were impressed with Faedo’s progress and maturity and saw him as a real contributor for the near future, until an essentially lost 2020 was followed by a lost 2021. He’ll be 26 years old when he resumes pitching in 2022, at which point former Double-A Erie teammates Casey Mize, Tarik Skubal, Matt Manning and even Joey Wentz all might be in Detroit. How he reacts will determine whether he’s left behind or pulled forward to join them. If he doesn’t crack the rotation, his arsenal could play in a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers landed Faedo in the 2017 Draft just before he helped pitch the University of Florida to a College World Series title and earned Most Outstanding Player honors in the process. His struggles as a pro the following season, from a flattened slider to a drop in velocity, left some wondering whether that postseason run was simply a hot stretch or if his arm wore down; Faedo insisted he felt fine. His 2019 season at Double-A Erie restored some faith as well as his prospect standing. The slider has always been the dominant out pitch in Faedo’s arsenal, with enough late movement to draw swings and misses or soft contact. The pitch betrayed him in 2018, as did a fastball that fell to 90-91 mph. Faedo came back in 2019 with a more upright delivery and consistent arm action, bringing his fastball back to the mid 90s with improved spin rate. His slider acts at times like two different pitches with varying speeds and break, depending on whether he’s trying to locate it for a strike or draw a swing and miss. The resulting mix and improved command pushed his strikeout-to-walk ratio from 3.14 in 2018 to 5.36 the following year. His changeup, a little-used pitch in college, improved with his fastball. Faedo might never be the front-line starter some envisioned coming out of the College World Series, but he has the tools, frame and pitching instincts to fill a big-league rotation. His 2018 struggles forced him to grow into a professional pitcher, a lesson that could help keep him focused through challenges against more experienced hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A pair of knee surgeries after Faedo's sophomore year at Florida led to a sluggish start for the junior in 2017. But he finished strongly, turning in a dominant performance as the College World Series' Most Outstanding Player shortly after the Tigers took him at No. 18 overall in the June Draft. He didn't pitch after signing for $3.5 million, as Detroit erred on the side of caution after Faedo's long college season. Assigned to high Class A Lakeland for his debut, Faedo pitched well in the Florida State League but struggled in Double-A, allowing 15 home runs in 60 innings after receiving a mid-June promotion. By the end of his final season with Florida, Faedo was back to full strength, featuring his plus fastball and one of the best sliders in the class. In his first pro season, though, he underwhelmed with his raw stuff, showing a slower arm that affected the life on all of his pitches and made him susceptible to the long ball in Double-A. After working at 92-95 mph as a junior, Faedo hovered around 90-91 mph with a flatter fastball in 2018. His slider regressed as well, showing less depth and bite and netting him fewer whiffs, and he struggled to execute his changeup without a lively fastball to work off of. He did throw a lot of strikes, though it's more control than command right now. It's not uncommon for college pitchers to experience diminished velocity in their first full professional season, only to bounce back the next year once they have a better understanding of the physical demands of a full season. That's precisely what happened with Faedo, whose fastball and slider picked up again in 2019 in his return to Double-A. Faedo's return to form has his stock back on the rise, and he could be knocking on the door of the big leagues before long.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Faedo's spot atop 2017 Draft boards was initially hurt by minor knee surgery the fall before his junior year and slightly lackluster stuff as a result at the start of his season. He did finish strongly and dominated in the College World Series shortly after the Tigers feel he dropped in their lap at No. 18 overall in the June Draft. He didn't pitch after signing as Detroit erred on the side of caution. By the end of his final season with Florida, Faedo was back to full strength, featuring his plus fastball and one of the best sliders in the class. He'll sit around 93 mph and touch 95 regularly with good sink. He threw his slider too much in college, but it is a true out pitch that gets a lot of swings and misses. He'll flash a very good changeup, something he'll have to throw more often as a pro. He generally throws strikes, though it's more control than command right now. Even though the Tigers went slightly over pick value to sign Faedo, he could prove to be a first-round bargain, a top-of-the-Draft talent found in the middle of the round. His Gators teammate A.J. Puk made it to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball, and Faedo's stuff allowed him to follow a similar fast track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few Minor Leaguers did more to rebuild their stocks in 2021. The Florida native was a Royals second-round pick in 2017, signing for above slot at $2.1 million, and enjoyed a solid first season at Class A Lexington a year later. His 2019 season, however, was a massive offensive struggle. Melendez hit just .163 with nine homers and a 39.4 percent K rate at Class A Advanced Wilmington. He spent 2020 reworking his swing and approach at the Royals’ alternate training site and put that to good use in his breakout 2021. Melendez led the Minors with 41 home runs and finished with a .288/.386/.625 line and 21.7 percent strikeout rate over 123 games at Double-A and Triple-A. The bulk of the left-handed slugger’s improvements came down to him lessening the severity of his leg kick and improving his pitch recognition with the added time at the plate. His power plays to all fields, and Melendez can really drive balls the opposite way when needed. He has been considered a plus defender behind the plate since his prep days, though his framing still needs work entering his age-23 season, and his arm is right there with his pop as his loudest tool. Melendez threw out 31 percent of attempted Double-A and Triple-A basestealers and owns a career 40 percent caught-stealing rate in the Minors. Melendez is back to being one of the most complete catching prospects in the game. With Salvador Perez still in the frame, Melendez’s ceiling as a first-division backstop only gives the Royals a good problem -- one they might have to solve early in the summer of 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a 2017 Draft light on catching prospects, Melendez stood out as MLB Pipeline’s No. 72 prospect. The Royals took him No. 52 overall and signed him well above pick value to get him away from playing for his father, Mervyl, at Florida International. While Melendez has always performed well behind the plate, he struggled offensively in 2019 and posted a .163/.260/.311 slash line in Class A Advanced. He spent the summer at the Royals’ alternate training site followed by instructs at Kauffman Stadium to get as many at-bats as possible while also working on mechanical changes to his swing, and the work has showed up in a big way in 2021 as Melendez has chased the Minor League home run lead for much of the summer. Melendez has serious raw power that even the Royals say might be the best in the system. In 2020, he toned down the big leg kick that causes him to over-rotate with his upper half and commit to pitches earlier -- which hurt pitch recognition and had been a reason for his 39.4 percent strikeout rate in the Minors. The Royals don’t want to take away the leg kick completely and have worked with Melendez to improve his posture in the box, trying to get him to be squarer with the pitcher and calm the movement in his swing down. He worked hard to improve his contact point and reduce the amount of pitches he chases out of the zone. Melendez’s best tool defensively is his cannon of an arm with a quick release that helps stymie the running game. He already has impressive blocking and receiving skills, and he knows how to call a game and manage a staff. The Royals were confident in his offensive adjustments made last year and have been elated to see them turn into production in 2021. Melendez always had the defensive ability to be a Major League catcher, but these improvements make his future as a starting backstop all the clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked by MLB Pipeline as the No. 72 prospect heading into the 2017 Draft, Melendez stood out in a class that featured a dearth of catching prospects. The Royals took him in the second round (No. 52 overall) and gave him a bonus north of $2 million, well above pick value, to sign him away from playing for his father, Mervyl, the coach at Florida International. After a promising first full season at Class A Lexington in which Melendez performed well behind the plate and finished among the system leaders with 73 RBIs (third) and 19 home runs (fourth), he struggled mightily and posted one of the Minors’ worst slash lines (.163/.260/.311) as a 20-year-old at Class A Advanced Wilmington in 2019. The left-handed-hitting backstop has some serious raw power, with bat speed and loft that could translate to average game power if he can learn to make contact. Melendez has fanned at 33.8 percent clip in the Minors and had a 39.4 percent strikeout rate -- with an alarming 24.4 percent swinging-strike rate -- in the Carolina League. At the root of Melendez’s swing-and-miss issues is a big leg kick that causes him to over-rotate with his upper half and keeps him from being on time with his swing. The Royals like the leg kick and therefore have worked with the youngster to improve his posture in the box. The early returns have been encouraging, with Melendez showing better direction in his swing along with an improved contact point. Melendez could be a monster if he can figure it out at the plate because the defensive tools and skills are already there. An impressive athlete who’s agile behind the plate, he is a good blocker and already knows how to call a game and manage a staff. A combination of plus arm strength and excellent catch-and-throw skills help Melendez stymie the running game, and he threw out 60 percent of basestealers in 2019, bringing his career mark to 43 percent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Melendez headed into the 2017 Draft ranked as the No. 72 prospect by MLB Pipeline. In a class that lacked catching prospects, Melendez stood out, and the Royals took him No. 52 overall and gave him a bonus north of $2 million, well above pick value, to sign him away from playing for his father, Mervyl, the coach at Florida International. If his first full season of pro ball is any indication, it will be money well spent, as Melendez finished third in the system in RBIs and fourth in homers, all while learning the nuances of catching. The left-handed-hitting backstop has some serious raw power to tap into, with bat speed and loft that will allow him to continue to show over-the-fence pop. There is too much swing and miss to Melendez's game, with a strikeout rate of more than 30 percent heading into 2019, and he'll have to continue to refine his approach at the plate to keep reaching his power as he advances. Melendez is very athletic, running better than most catchers, and uses that agility behind the plate. He is an excellent blocker and already shows an ability to work with pitchers to call a good game. His plus arm allowed him to throw out nearly 42 percent of potential base stealers in 2018. Developing high school catching is often a crapshoot, but Melendez, thanks to his all-around skills and having grown up around the game, has a chance to buck the trend, though he'll have to erase a rough 2019 season. Luckily there's time as he played all season at age 20.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a 2017 Draft thin in catching prospects, Melendez stood out with his defensive brilliance and flashes of power. The Royals made him the second backstop taken, selecting him 52nd overall and paying him a well over-slot $2,097,500 to give up a commitment to Florida International, where his father Mervyl is head coach. He lived up to his reputation during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Melendez has more athleticism than most catchers, and it's obvious in all phases of his defensive game. He's a quality receiver who moves quickly to block balls in the dirt, and his footwork enhances his plus arm. Because he grew up around the game, he's a more advanced game-caller than most teenagers. Melendez creates solid raw power with the bat speed and loft in his left-handed swing. His stroke can get too long and uphill, however, leading to a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first taste of pro ball and questions about how consistently he'll produce at the plate. He has close to average speed now, but figures to slow down as he gets bigger and endures the rigors of catching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins took Miranda in the Competitive Balance Round B of the 2016 Draft and the Puerto Rican high school product progressed slowly, spending two summers in rookie ball and putting up moderate numbers across two levels of A ball in 2018 and 2019, though he did touch Double-A at the end of the year. He wasn’t put on the 40-man roster following 2020, nor was he selected in the Rule 5 Draft, decisions all 30 teams might be regretting after Miranda had one of the best offensive seasons in the Minor Leagues in 2021, leading the Minors in hits and finishing with a .973 OPS between Double- and Triple-A. Miranda has always been a contact machine with a very low whiff rate. In 2021, he was much more selective, drawing more walks and working counts in his favor, which allowed him to use his plus bat-to-ball skills to drive the ball much more frequently and finish with 30 or more doubles and homers for the season. The power came without a sacrifice in terms of strikeouts as he whiffed in just 12.5 percent of his plate appearances. He rarely misses a fastball, and he registered above-average exit velocities during his time in Triple-A. As certain as the Twins are now about Miranda’s bat, and yes, he was added to the 40-man this past offseason, it’s less clear where Miranda might fit defensively. He has good hands and has worked this offseason to improve his arm strength, but he’s very limited range-wise. He’s played mostly third and second, with some first base mixed in of late, though few doubt he’ll get his bat into the lineup more often than not in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins drafted and signed at least one player from Puerto Rico every year from 2007-18, with Eddie Rosario ('10) and José Berríos ('12) the most successful to date. Miranda, a 2016 draftee, was the first Puerto Rican player taken in the top two rounds by the club since Berríos and is one of four players taken from the island in rounds 1 or 2 from 2016-20. He’s made incremental progress, touching Double-A for the first time in 2019. He wasn’t protected on the 40-man roster and wasn’t taken in the Rule 5 Draft last December, but turned in a good instructional league performance last fall and hit well in a brief stint in the Puerto Rican Winter League, something that has carried over to a breakout 2021 performance. Miranda’s biggest strength, and perhaps weakness, had been his ability to make contact. He’s struck out in less than 12 percent of his plate appearances over the course of his career entering 2021, using a short, compact swing to drive the ball to all fields. The flip side of that coin is that he swings at virtually everything, often putting balls out of the zone into play and rarely working counts. The Twins challenged him to work on his approach and tighten up his strike zone at instructs, with positive results that helped lead to his power breakthrough in 2021. Miranda has mostly played second and third defensively, and has seen time at those two positions as well as first base in 2021. It’s now looking like there might be enough pop to profile at an infield corner, but he could still fit a role as an offensive-minded utility player whose bat finds its way into the lineup on a daily basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After being taken by the Twins with the 73rd overall pick in the 2016 Draft as part of the Competitive Balance Round B, Miranda struggled during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League. He took a nice step forward with a move to the Appalachian League in 2017, then performed well enough in his full-season debut the following year to earn a promotion from the Midwest to the Florida State League. A return to the FSL in 2019, however, didn’t go as well as hoped, and the infielder managed just a .663 OPS with Fort Myers. Miranda still has offensive attributes to like, he just needs to work on using them more efficiently. He has a great swing with the ability to make a lot of contact from the right side of the plate. He rarely strikes out, something that continued even as he struggled in 2019 with an 11.3 percent K rate. He has the ability to drive the ball to all fields, though his home run power comes mostly to his pull side. While his contact rate is impressive, it also can be his downfall. He needs to shrink the strike zone more and learn not to swing at everything, as he gets himself out on pitcher’s pitches too often. With better decision-making, he could approach average power. Defensively, Miranda has split time between third and second over the last couple of years and that will continue, though the hot corner will get more of his focus. He played very well at third in 2019, doing an outstanding job of making plays on the run. That’s likely his best spot to be an everyday player at one position and if he refines his plate discipline, he could fit the offensive profile there as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2012, Puerto Rico had a pair of first-round picks, headlined by No. 1 overall selection Carlos Correa. The island didn't have another selection in the top two rounds until 2016 when the Cardinals took Delvin Perez in the first round and the Twins took Miranda in the second. Miranda scuffled during his pro debut, but bounced back as one of the better hitting prospects in the Appalachian League in 2017, finishing tied for the home run lead. Miranda was really able to settle in and adjust to pro ball in his second summer after looking unprepared in the Gulf Coast League the year prior. He showed off outstanding bat-to-ball skills, striking out less than 10 percent of the time while showing good overall plate discipline. For that reason, many feel he'll be an above-average hitter in time, one who can drive the ball to all fields and approach Major League average power. He's not much of a runner, but he has the chance to be an average defender at second. He's also played some third base and he might move around a bit defensively. The Twins feel they saw the player they drafted in 2017 and there is excitement to see how those adjustments play in full-season ball. Regardless of where he plays defensively, it's his offensive upside that should help him move up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins have had some success mining the considerable talent in Puerto Rico over the years, drafting Eddie Rosario in 2010 and Jose Berrios in 2012. They got Miranda in the second round of the 2016 Draft and after struggling out of the gate, he went on to be an Appalachian League All-Star in 2017 and have a solid full-season debut last year, making it seem more likely that he will join his island-mates in Minnesota. Miranda has one of the best pure swings in the organization with the chance to be a plus hitter down the line thanks to outstanding bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline from the right side of the plate. He rarely strikes out and can spray the ball to all fields. He's shown more power than expected, with most of his over-the-fence damage coming to his pull side. He's played mostly second and third, and should continue to see an even split between the two spots going forward, though the Twins got him a little time at shortstop in 2018, where his range is limited, but his hands and arm work fine. Miranda's tweener profile limits his ceiling a bit, and he might be a utilityman when all is said and done as a result. But if his bat keeps progressing, he could hit his way into a regular spot in a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Sands missed a lot more bats in his third year as a starter for Florida State in 2018, that led to him creeping up Draft boards, landing to the Twins in the fifth round. He’s missed some time with injuries -- some arm-related, some not -- but has shown he can get professional hitters out. He pitched across two levels of A-ball and touched Double-A in 2019, then came back post-pandemic in 2021 and found success in Double-A, where his 2.46 ERA would have led the Double-A Central had he pitched enough innings to qualify. Sands was a consistent performer pretty much from start to finish, using a solid, if unspectacular, three-pitch mix in the process. He doesn’t have the more typical north-south profile, with a lower slot bringing fastballs that averaged 93 mph and topped out at 97. He worked in the offseason to add more movement and there was good run on the pitch last year, leading to missing more bats. His curve is a bit slurvy, with more of a sweepy break at around 80 mph, and he’s worked to throw it a bit harder, but it’s a successful pitch, and his changeup features solid fade. With a very repeatable delivery, Sands was a big-time strike-thrower in the early stages of his career and his uptick in walks in 2021 caught some by surprise, though that might be attributed to the 2020 layoff. His ceiling might be limited to the back end of a rotation, but he could be ready to help out in that role very soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sands spent three years in Florida State’s rotation with somewhat uneven results. A combination of two strong summers in the Cape Cod League and a junior season that saw him miss bats at a much higher rate led to the Twins taking the right-hander in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft. He didn’t make his professional debut until '19 because of some arm issues and even though his workload was somewhat limited during that first full year, he pitched his way across three levels to Double-A. His official work in '20 was limited to instructional league play. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has the chance to have three at least average pitches, all of which he can throw for strikes. After featuring more of a sinker down in the zone in college, Sands has found success with a low-90s fastball that touches 95-96 mph with life up in the zone. His breaking ball, a curve with solid three-quarters break to it, has improved, and he continues to work on adding velocity to it and commanding it in the strike zone more consistently. His changeup gets swings-and-misses as well as weak contact. While Sands’ control was intermittent in college, he was an extreme strike-thrower during his first full season of pro ball, walking just 1.8 per nine innings, with a very repeatable delivery. His ceiling might be limited as a back-end starter, but he’s not far from reaching it, with the chance to be a bit more than that if his stuff keeps ticking upwards.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sands is the younger brother of Carson Sands, a one-time Cubs pitching prospect who signed out of high school. Cole entered the pro ranks after three years in Florida State’s rotation and two solid showings in the Cape Cod League, with the Twins taking him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft and signing him for a well-over-slot $600,000 bonus. Biceps tendinitis kept him from making his debut until 2019 and between the Twins managing his workload, a blister issue and a calf strain, he managed to pitch his way up to the Florida State League and finished with a start in Double-A. Over his 18 starts in his first full season, Sands showed the ability to throw three effective pitches for strikes. His fastball will hit as high as 96 mph with good life up in the zone, and he threw it more in 2019 after featuring a sinker in college. He can miss bats and get weak contact with his above-average changeup and his curve has good three-quarters break to it. It’s a pitch he particularly worked on at the Twins pitching camp in January and it could give him a third above-average pitch if he can learn to land it in the strike zone more consistently. Sands showed a propensity to attack the strike zone and did not hurt himself with walks during his debut season. He repeats his delivery well and the Twins like the way he competes. He’s more of a high floor kind of arm, but one who has every chance to fit into the back part of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles opted for a bulk package of pitching prospects when they traded Dylan Bundy to the Angels in December 2019, acquiring Bradish along with Kyle Brnovich, Zack Peek and Isaac Mattson. All have a chance to reach the big leagues (Mattson already has) in short order. But the highest ceiling of the group belongs to Bradish, a sizable righty with a starter’s build and a developing four-pitch mix. A former fourth-round pick of the Angels in 2018, Bradish spent three years as a weekend starter at New Mexico State before impressing in his only season in the Angels’ system. He was one of the top performers at Orioles’ instructional camp in 2020, then spent most of 2021 at Triple-A Norfolk, posting a 4.26 ERA with 105 strikeouts in 86 2/3 innings. Baltimore added him to its 40-man roster in November. At 6-foot-4 and 220 pounds, Bradish is an imposing presence on the mound with a max-effort delivery that creates natural deception and an uncomfortable look, especially for right-handed hitters. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and touches 97 at times, pairing with a power curve in the mid-80s he uses to miss bats. Bradish also features a hard changeup and slider-like cutter, which he throws in the high 80s and darts away from righties. The changeup has made strides and gives him an additional weapon, though it remains a work in progress. Bradish struggled with command at times as a younger pitcher due to his size, stuff and all-out delivery. Control remains a growth area, but improved at Triple-A to quiet speculation about a potential long-term move to the ‘pen. He may end up there or as a swingman in the short term, given his chance to break camp with the Orioles this spring. But his four-pitch mix gives Bradish the ceiling of an impact starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick of the Angels in 2018 after spending three years as a weekend starter at New Mexico State, Bradish was the highest rated of the four prospects the Orioles acquired from the Angels for Dylan Bundy in December 2019. He performed well in one season in the Angels system, compiling 120 strikeouts in 101 innings in the Class A Advanced California League, looking like a potential mid-rotation starter when he was sent to Baltimore along with Isaac Mattson, Kyle Brnovich and Zack Peek. There is a sense now, though, that Bradish could grow into much more. His fastball velocity increased from 88-94 mph before the trade to 92-97 mph after, numbers Bradish showed regularly at the O’s alternate training site in 2020 and has largely maintained into the 2021 season. The 6-foot-4 righty pairs it with a power curve in the mid-80s he uses to miss bats, and features a hard changeup and slider-like cutter as well. The slider, which Bradish throws in the high 80s, may develop into his best secondary pitch with time. He fires it all from a unique delivery that creates natural deception and an uncomfortable look, especially for right-handed hitters. The combination of Bradish’s size, stuff and max-effort delivery gives him a lot of moving parts on the mound; as a result, he’s struggled with command and control issues both in collegiate and pro ball. He has enough weapons though, at this point, to silence any prior chatter about potentially ending up in the ‘pen. He advanced to Triple-A after three Double-A starts at the beginning of 2021, moving quickly thanks to his four-pitch mix and impact starter ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-rated of the four prospects the Orioles acquired from the Angels for Dylan Bundy, Bradish was a three-year weekend starter at New Mexico State and Cape Cod League All-Star before the Angels plucked him in the fourth round in 2018. Bradish signed for slightly below pick value ($397,500), then compiled 120 strikeouts in 101 innings in the Class A Advanced California League in his first full pro season. He was sent to Baltimore along with Isaac Mattson, Kyle Brnovich and Zach Peek for Bundy. Bradish’s unique delivery creates deception that allows his low-90s fastball to play up, though it can reach 95 mph at times. The 6-foot-4 right-hander pairs it with a power curveball in the low-80s he uses to miss bats, and he features a changeup and slider-like cutter as well. The slider, which Bradish throws in the high-80s, may develop into his best secondary pitch with time. The combination of Bradish’s size, stuff and max-effort delivery give him a lot of moving parts on the mound; as a result, he’s struggled with command and control issues both in collegiate and pro ball. Those may ultimately land him in the bullpen, where his fastball-breaking ball combination may translate better in shorter stints. But the Orioles are expected to keep Bradish starting at least for now, given his four-pitch mix and middle-of-the-rotation ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of the Hawaii prep ranks, Tom spent one year at Fort Scott CC before transferring to Kentucky, where he showed improvement over two seasons before going to the Indians in the fifth round of the 2015 Draft. He made his full-season debut with Class A Lake County the next year, but ultimately appeared in just 28 games before requiring season-ending surgery on his left shoulder in July. Fully healthy in 2017, Tom broke out over a full season in the Class A Advanced Carolina League and continued to impress in the Arizona Fall League, showing an intriguing blend of hitting ability, power and speed. Tom is a sum-of-all-parts player who also has some nice tools. He has feel to hit from the left side of the plate as well as consistent pop to the gaps that translated to more over-the-fence power in the Carolina League, where he delivered a career-high 10 homers. Tom's above-average speed is an asset, one that helped him compile 48 extra-base hits while going 23-for-29 on the basepaths in '17, and he receives high marks for his approach and on-base skills ability despite having some swing-and-miss to his game. Tom played all three outfield positions in the Carolina League, showing versatility which, along with his solid offensive tools, could help him to carve out a role as a valuable fourth outfielder in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: First drafted out of Chipola College by the D-backs in the 18th round of the ’16 Draft, Francis went in the seventh round to the Brewers the next summer and signed for an above-slot bonus of $235,000. Francis’ first full season in Milwaukee’s system (’18) saw him post a 4.50 ERA between Low-A and High-A, but he came back with a stronger ’19 season between High-A and Double-A, posting a 3.97 ERA with 165 strikeouts over 142 2/3 innings. The Blue Jays acquired Francis alongside reliever Trevor Richards in a deal for Rowdy Tellez in July of ’21. Francis filled a valuable role for the Blue Jays immediately in terms of upper-minors depth. With a sinking fastball that comes from his 6-foot-5 frame in the low-90s, Francis works to set up his slider, which has been his most effective pitch of late when he needs a strike. He’ll feature a curveball and changeup to a lesser extent, but Francis’ value lies mostly in his steady outings. Much like former rotation-mate Zach Logue, who was traded to Oakland in the spring, Francis doesn’t do much in a flashy manner but gets the job done consistently. Also added to the 40-man roster this past offseason, Francis should be one of the first young arms the Blue Jays turn to if they have a need at the Major League level. After needing to convert starters into relief roles in recent seasons, the Blue Jays are now looking at a nice Triple-A depth group. Turning 26 in March, Francis could be called on at any point in ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Taft High School in Chicago, most thought Suwinski was headed to Indiana for college. But the Padres swooped in, taking him in the 15th round of the 2016 Draft and signing him for an above-slot $550,000 to keep him from ever suiting up for the Hoosiers. He spent two years in Low-A ball and one up a level in 2019, with little success, before having a bit of a breakout in 2021 in his first taste of Double-A, then getting sent to the Pirates in the Adam Frazier deal at last year’s Trade Deadline. The Pirates liked the bat enough to add Suwinski to the 40-man roster in the offseason. The left-handed-hitting Suwinski showed off an improved approach at the plate in 2021 that led to much better results. His walk rate went up and his strikeouts decreased, which helped him get to his plus raw power on a more regular basis, and he set career highs in several offensive categories. He hits the ball hard and with loft, especially to his pull side, and it’s not hard to dream about how his left-handed swing might work with the short porch in right field at PNC Park. Suwinski has average speed, but moves well for his size. He’s never going to wow anyone with his outfield play, but should be capable enough to play an outfield corner in the big leagues. He might be more of a platoon or fourth-outfielder type, but don’t be surprised if he works his potent bat into a lineup more often than not.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palacios comes from a baseball family that already has produced a pair of big leaguers in his uncle Rey and brother Josh. The highest-drafted player in Towson history, he set school records for single-season (32) and career (76) steals before the Guardians selected him in the third round of the 2018 Draft. After missing all of 2019 following labrum surgery on his right (throwing) shoulder and losing 2020 to the pandemic, he came back last year to reach Triple-A in his first full pro season and grab a spot on Cleveland's 40-man roster. Palacios posted a career .318 batting average and .409 on-base percentage in his first two seasons as a pro, thanks to his quick left-handed stroke, bat-to-ball skill and patient, all-fields approach. He uses his plus speed to get on base and is a threat to steal, adding to his tablesetter profile. He has added some strength since signing but prioritizes contact over power and won't provide more than 12-15 homers per year. Though he spent most of his first two pro seasons at second base and has more than enough quickness for the position, he doesn't have smooth infield actions and possesses fringy arm strength. Cleveland has an abundance of middle-infield prospects, so he's probably headed for the outfield. He played some center field last season and only left and center in the Arizona Fall League, showing the potential to become an average to solid defender if he moves.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palacios comes from a baseball family, with his father Richard a former Tigers' farmhand, his uncle Rey an ex-big league catcher and his brother Joshua an outfielder in the Blue Jays system. Richie starred at Towson, setting school career records for hits (205) and steals (76) and becoming the highest-drafted position player in the program's history when the Indians popped him in the third round last June. He batted .361 between three levels in his pro debut, advancing to low Class A, though he has yet to play in 2019 following offseason shoulder surgery. Palacios profiles as a potential leadoff hitter with his bat-to-ball skills, on-base ability and baserunning savvy. He has a quick left-handed swing and could develop 15-homer power as he continues to get stronger. Though he's just an average runner out of the batter's box, he's a plus runner underway and has a knack for stealing bases. Though he's athletic and quick, Palacios is in search of a defensive home. He played shortstop at Towson but his fringy arm makes that a stretch in pro ball, where he spent almost all of his debut at second base. He has reliable hands but not the smoothest actions, which leads some scouts to believe he'll wind up in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick out of South Alabama in 2018, Donovan was one of the Cardinals' breakout stars in 2021. Playing in his age-24 season, the left-handed slugger climbed three levels to Triple-A Memphis and finished at the top of the system in average (.304), OBP (.399), OPS (.854) and wRC+ (134). He continued to hit during a trip to the Arizona Fall League, where he went 16-for-52 (.308) with more walks (10) than strikeouts (eight) and won a fan vote to be named to the Fall Stars Game. The Cardinals rewarded Donovan for his efforts with a spot on the 40-man roster ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility. Utilizing the smallest of toe taps, Donovan relies on the quickness of his hands to generate a healthy amount of contact from the left side. He shows a patient approach that also helps drive his walk rates, and the shortness of his swing keeps him from striking out all that often too. Since the approach is geared toward contact, he doesn’t exhibit a ton of power, and his 12 homers from 2021 are about what to expect from him in a potential full Major League season. Donovan doesn’t exhibit great speed by any means but knows how to pick his spots on the basepaths; he finished with 19 steals in 2021, third-most among St. Louis full-season farmhands. Donovan saw time at six different positions last season -- all four infield spots, along with left and right -- and that was almost out of necessity because the Cards wanted his bat in the lineup somehow. With his below-average speed and arm, he isn’t a natural fit anywhere and is likely best served to continue moving around based on daily need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Riley Greene wasn’t exactly a surprise as the Tigers’ Minor League Player of the Year in 2021, nobody would’ve expected Brieske -- a 27th-round pick in 2019 -- to win Pitcher of the Year honors going into the season. He didn’t begin pitching full-time until his senior year in high school, then went to Glendale (Ariz.) Junior College before his high strikeout rate caught scouts’ attention at Division II Colorado State-Pueblo. A solid introduction to the Tigers system in 2019 backed up the pick, and after losing a season to the pandemic, he returned to action in 2021 as a more well-rounded pitcher and hit the fast track up the system. By season’s end, he was arguably the most effective starter at Double-A Erie, and in the conversation for pitchers who could eventually contribute in Detroit. With a high arm angle and a delivery that starts on the first-base side of the rubber, Brieske essentially takes the shortest path to home plate and throws downhill from there. His four-seam fastball averages 92-94 mph, but he commands it well to all parts of the strike zone and complements it with a changeup about 10 mph slower. That was his primary arsenal when he entered pro ball, but his breakout 2021 season came after adding a tight slider that he can locate and a 12-6 curveball that can freeze hitters as it breaks. The total package is four pitches at different speeds with different movement. Brieske is the kind of pitching prospect who can make a good organization great if he makes the big leagues. His cerebral approach and work ethic have enabled him to better his game and earned him an opportunity to tap the Tigers’ player development resources. Brieske came to Spring Training intent on adding an extra mph or two of velocity on his pitches through training and technique. If he can do so without sacrificing the rest of his game, that could be the factor that eventually lands Brieske in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Padres' $78 million international spending spree in 2016-17, Arias signed for $1.9 million out of Venezuela. He had the highest ceiling among the six youngsters San Diego sent to the Guardians in the nine-player Mike Clevinger trade in August 2020, and he may have more upside than any of Cleveland's position prospects. His performance dipped in 2022, in part because of a broken right hand that cost him eight weeks in Triple-A, but he still made his big league debut, homered off Tyler Glasnow in September and started three American League Division Series games at first base in October. With impressive bat speed and strength, Arias has more raw power than most shortstops and 30-homer upside. To reach that potential, he'll need to develop a more selective approach and do a better job of driving the ball in the air. He doesn't strike out excessively, but he gets himself out on pitches he should avoid and rarely walks. Arias gets average-to-solid grades for his speed, which plays better in the field than on the bases. He's a quality defender at shortstop with range to both sides, reliable hands and double-plus arm strength that ranks among the best in the Minors. He played all four infield positions in Cleveland last year as well as left field in Triple-A, and he might be able to claim a role as a slugging super-utilityman on a big league club loaded with infield options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias has the highest ceiling of the six players the Guardians acquired in the nine-player Mike Clevinger trade with the Padres in August 2020 -- and some evaluators believe he has the highest ceiling of any position player in Cleveland's system. He was part of San Diego's $78 million spending spree on the 2016 international market, signing for $1.9 million out of Venezuela. The youngest batting qualifier (age 21) in the Triple-A East last season, he posted an .802 OPS with 13 homers while also standing out with his defense. A right-handed hitter, Arias has impressive bat speed and strength that give him more raw power than most shortstops, but he'll need to make some adjustments at the plate to reach his 25-30 homer upside. While he doesn't strike out excessively, he's overly aggressive at the plate and makes too much weak groundball contact. He'll have to make better swing decisions and learn to launch more balls in the air to his pull side. Arias earns average to solid grades for his speed, which is more apparent in the field than on the bases. He has good actions and instincts at shortstop, where he's a plus defender, and he's also an asset at third and second base. He has one of the strongest arms in the Minors and is capable of making any throw needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres shelled out $78 million in bonuses and penalty taxes for their 2016 international class, with Arias' $1.9 million bonus ranking as just their seventh-highest. They promoted the Venezuelan aggressively, sending him to high Class A at age 19 in 2019 and watching him hit .302/.339/.470 and lead the California League with 224 total bases. He has the highest ceiling of the six players acquired by the Indians in the nine-player deal that sent Mike Clevinger to San Diego in August 2020. Loaded with tools, Arias has more raw power than most shortstops and is capable of driving the ball out of the park to all fields thanks to his bat speed, strength and leverage. How much he'll tap into his 25-30 homer potential will depend on his ability to refine his approach at the plate. He needs to improve his pitch recognition, keep his right-handed swing from getting too long and curb a tendency to chase pitches out of the strike zone. An average to solid runner, Arias makes better use of his quickness in the field than on the bases. He's a plus defender at shortstop, where he displays quality instincts and actions, and he also gets the job done at second and third base. His best pure tool is his arm, which earns top-of-the-scale grades from some evaluators and ranks among the very best in the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Padres' $78 million international spending spree in 2016-17, Arias signed for $1.9 million out of Venezuela. San Diego promoted him aggressively, and he finished third in the high Class A California League in total bases (224) as its second-youngest regular (age 19) while batting .302/.339/.470 in 2019. He was the top prospect acquired by the Indians in the nine-player August trade that sent Mike Clevinger to the Padres. Arias offers more power than most shortstops and could develop into a 25-homer threat if he adds some polish at the plate. A right-handed hitter, he often gets too long with his swing and needs to improve his plate discipline. He has average to solid speed and his quickness is more apparent in the field than on the bases. A quality defender at shortstop, Arias has all the tools needed to remain at the position. He has smooth infield actions, plenty of range and soft hands, and his strong arm may be the most impressive part of his defensive package. If he doesn't hit enough to become a regular, he could become a slugging utilityman capable of playing almost anywhere on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias, one of the top prospects in the 2016-17 international class, received $1.9 million as the Padres blew past their spending pool during the signing period. At age 17, he was promoted to Class A Fort Wayne and held his own, hitting .276 in the Midwest League playoffs before turning in a strong showing in the Australian Baseball League. Arias remained with Fort Wayne for the entirety of the '18 season, and he slumped to a .654 OPS. But he remained an expert defensively, and he came on strong offensively toward the end of the season. Arias has all the tools to become a plus defender at short, where he has very good hands, footwork and control of his body. His arm strength and range make it clear he's cut out for the position long-term. He has strides to make at the plate, however. A right-handed hitter, Arias' swing can get long and his plate approach needs a bit of work. If he can refine his swing, Arias is expected to generate some power as he develops physically. He already hits the ball hard, gap-to-gap. Arias' defensive value gives him a relatively high floor, but it's the entire package on both sides of the ball that has club officials excited about the teenager's bright future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Arias to be one of the top prospects from Venezuela available in the 2016-17 international signing class, praising him for his easy and natural actions on offense and defense. Ranked No. 11 on MLBPipeline.com's list of the Top 30 international prospects in 2016 , Arias received $1.9 million as the Padres blew past their international spending pool. After beginning his pro debut in the Rookie Arizona League, Arias, at age 17, was promoted to Class A Fort Wayne and held his own, hitting .276 in the Midwest League playoffs before a turning in a strong showing in the Australian Baseball League. A right-handed hitter, Arias displays a smooth, balanced stroke that is expected to generate more power as he develops physically.
