He spent all of his first two pro seasons in center field and is presently an average defender there, thanks more to his quickness than his instincts. He projects as a right fielder in the long term and has the power and plus arm to profile well there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramos starred on the high school showcase circuit, winning MVP honors at the Under Armour All-America Game in July 2016 and wowing scouts when he ran a 6.42-second 60-yard dash at the Excellence Games a month before the 2017 Draft. He offered one of the best power/speed combinations available, which prompted the Giants to draft him 19th overall and sign him for $3,101,700. He continued to perform well in his pro debut, leading the Rookie-level Arizona League in slugging (.645) and finishing second in batting (.348) and OPS (1.049). While he needs a few years of development time, Ramos has the highest ceiling of any Giants prospect since Buster Posey. His bat speed and strength generate well-above-average power from the right side of the plate, and he already shows the ability to drive the ball out of the park to all fields. Part of an athletic family that includes brothers in the Dodgers system (Henry, an outfielder) and on Puerto Rico's national soccer team (Hector), Heliot has at least plus speed as well as solid arm strength. The biggest question with Ramos is whether he can develop a more patient approach and make consistent contact so he can realize his offensive potential. He also needs to refine his reads and routes in order to stay in center field. Time is on his side, as he'll play the entire 2018 season at age 18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long, methodical march to the big leagues for Bautista, who first signed as a teenager with the Marlins in 2013 and reached Triple-A Norfolk in 2021 for the first time. He’ll also turn 27 in June, making him about a decade older than the youngest prospects in the Orioles’ system. That’s not a typical profile, but Bautista is not a typical prospect. He is a 6-foot-5 right-hander who jumped three levels in ’21, striking out 40 percent of the batters he faced to leapfrog from obscurity onto the Orioles’ radar. The club added Bautista to their 40-man roster in November; prior to ’21, he’d never pitched above Class A. Now, Bautista looks not only like a candidate to make Baltimore’s Opening Day roster, but to potentially be closing games come 2022. He’s an imposing presence on the mound with an electric arm, sporting a triple-digit fastball and a slider in the low 90s. That arsenal led to eye-popping strikeout numbers in the Minors but remains very raw, with Bautista issuing 30 walks in 46 2/3 innings last summer. The control issues are nothing new; Bautista spent five seasons in Rookie ball and remained in the low Minors into his mid-20s largely due to spotty command. The upside with Bautista is that when he does throw strikes, his stuff is virtually unhittable. The question is whether he can do it consistently at the highest level, where hitters quickly learn to time even the hardest heaters. With a little polish, Bautista profiles as a late bloomer who might be able to dominate late in games, particularly in short stints. For a rebuilding team like the Orioles with persisting bullpen issues, it’s a gamble worth taking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes in the 2016 international class, Rosario signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1.85 million as part of the Padres' $78 million spending spree. The third-youngest regular (age 19) in the high Class A California League in 2019, he never put up big numbers while being promoted aggressively during his first three years in pro ball but did post consistently high on-base percentages. The Red Sox acquired him and infield prospect Hudson Potts in exchange for Mitch Moreland in August. Rosario has natural hitting ability thanks to a combination of bat speed, barrel control and hand-eye coordination. But his left-handed swing has a few moving parts, which makes it tricky to repeat. If he can simplify things, Rosario has quick hands and makes a lot of hard contact from the left side of the plate, and he could grow into some power. Rosario’s above-average speed enables him to cover ground with graceful strides in the outfield, giving him a good chance of remaining in center. He still needs time to develop in the Minors, mostly to fill out his lean and athletic frame. But the finished product could be that of a big league regular, with the athletic capabilities to do dazzling things on the baseball field -- including his trademark backflips to celebrate victories.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was viewed by scouts as one of the best athletes in the 2016 international class, and he's done nothing to prove those scouts wrong. That athleticism, along with his promising bat and feel for the game, led the Padres to sign Rosario for $1.85 million. During his 2017 professional debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League, he finished with a .299 average and a .404 on-base percentage, the latter a product of him walking (33) nearly as often as he struck out (36). His impressive debut earned him a promotion to the Class A Midwest League as an 18-year-old in 2018. He didn't disappoint, notching a .368 on-base percentage while showcasing an incredibly advanced plate approach for his age. Rosario has natural hitting ability thanks to a combination of bat speed, barrel control and hand-eye coordination. He has quick hands and makes lot of hard contact from the left side of the plate, and he could grow into average power. Rosario's above-average speed enables him to cover ground with graceful strides in the outfield, and club officials are optimistic about his chances of remaining in center field. Rosario still needs time to develop in the Minors, mostly to fill out his lean and athletic frame. But the finished product could be that of a big league regular, with the athletic capabilities to do dazzling things on the baseball field - including his trademark back flips to celebrate victories.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline list of the Top 30 international prospects for 2016, Rosario was viewed by scouts as one of the best athletes in his class. It was that athleticism, along with his promising bat and present feel for the game, which led the Padres to sign him for $1.85 million on July 2. He showed all of those qualities during his 2017 professional debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he finished with a .299 average and a .404 on-base percentage, the latter a product of him walking (33) nearly as often as he struck out (36). Assigned to the Midwest League for his first full season, Rosario was one of several talented 18-year-old prospects to suit up for Class A Fort Wayne on Opening Day. Rosario has natural hitting ability thanks to a combination of bat speed, barrel control and hand-eye coordination. He has quick hands and makes lot of hard contact from the left side of the plate, and it is believed that he could develop average power as he grows into his lean and athletic frame. Rosario's above-average speed enables him to cover ground with graceful strides in the outfield, and club officials are optimistic about his chances of remaining in center field. Rosario, like so many of his fellow J2 Padres peers, proved to be an advanced all-around prospect in his first pro campaign. He will need considerable time to develop in the Minors, but the finished product could be that of an everyday bat-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 12 on MLBPipeline.com's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2016-17 period, Rosario was viewed by scouts as one of the best athletes in his class. It was that athleticism, along with his promising bat and present feel for the game, which led the Padres to sign him for $1.85 million on July 2. Rosario has natural hitting ability thanks to a combination of bat speed, barrel control and hand-eye coordination. He has quick hands and makes lot of hard contact from the left side of the plate, and it is believed that he could develop average power as he grows into his lean and athletic frame. Rosario's above-average speed enables him to cover ground in the outfield, and club officials are optimistic he may be able to remain in center field. If he can't, he has the necessary arm strength to play right field. Rosario will need considerable time to develop in the Minors, but the finished product could be that of an everyday bat-first outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs have some catching depth at the bottom of their system, especially after they added a pair of backstops from the 2016 Draft in second-rounder Andy Yerzy and the suspended Ryan January in the eighth round. Herrera, an international signee out of Venezuela, has the chance to be the best all-around catcher in the system if he can find a way to avoid the injury bug. Last year, it was a hamate injury that knocked Herrera out of action, and thus from important development time behind the plate. Even with the missed reps, Herrera has matured as a defender, showing an ability to handle pitchers, often much older than he is, capably. He's learned English rapidly to be able to communicate better and understands the importance of calling a game. While there is still work to do, he receives the ball as well as anyone in the system. At the plate, he is a switch-hitter who uses a short, simple swing and is gaining strength and bat speed. Staying healthy will be key to helping Herrera take the next step. But he's just 20 years old for the entire 2017 season, and as catching coordinator Bill Plummer likes to preach, you shouldn't pay attention to the age of catching prospects because it can take a bit longer for them to fully develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After redshirting his freshman year at Santa Clara and missing his senior season because of Tommy John surgery, Wilson was granted a sixth year of collegiate eligibility and used that year to establish himself as the Broncos’ No. 1 starter. The Padres selected Wilson in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft and pushed him aggressively because of his age. He went from High-A Lake Elsinore straight to Triple-A El Paso during his 2019 full-season debut, then spent most of this past season in El Paso again, pitching to a 3.21 ERA with 71 strikeouts over 42 innings out of the bullpen. Wilson has a prototypical bullpen profile, attacking hitters with a pair of above-average offerings. His fastball is notable for its velocity and movement, sitting in the mid 90s and touching 97 mph with late action that helps him miss barrels and generate whiffs. Wilson also throws a solid slider in the low- to mid-80s. Wilson’s command has improved considerably since he was drafted. After issuing 5.66 walks per nine innings in 2019, that number dropped to 3.20 in 2021. He doesn’t have the truly elite stuff a team would expect from a closer, but his fastball-slider combination plays well enough to translate into a role as an effective reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilson’s amateur path made him a late arrival to pro ball. He redshirted his freshman year at Santa Clara, then missed his senior season due to Tommy John surgery, before receiving a sixth year of NCAA eligibility. It was in that sixth season where he emerged as Santa Clara’s top starter and became an eighth-round pick of the Padres in 2018. They pushed him quickly. He thrived at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in 2019 and made the leap to Triple-A El Paso. Then, after spending the ’20 season at the team’s alternate site, he was excellent in the Dominican Winter League, where he posted a 1.88 ERA across 14 outings. Wilson has a prototypical bullpen profile, attacking hitters with two pitches. His plus fastball is notable for its velocity and movement, sitting in the mid 90s and touching 97 mph with late action that helps him miss barrels and generate whiffs. Wilson pairs his heater with a solid slider in the low to mid 80s. Wilson has refined his command of both pitches significantly since the Padres drafted him. But he’ll need to prove he can keep his walk rate down at the higher levels. Though he may not have closer stuff, Wilson’s profile is unique enough and he misses enough bats to become an effective big league reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marinaccio missed what would have been his first college season at Delaware in 2014 while recovering from Tommy John surgery, then became a mainstay in the Blue Hens' rotation the next three years. The Yankees signed the redshirt junior for $100,000 as a 19th-rounder in 2017 -- they took Garrett Whitlock the round before -- and have watched him develop into one of their best relief prospects. He recorded a 2.04 ERA with 107 strikeouts in 66 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A last season to grab a spot on New York's 40-man roster. Marinaccio's fastball went from sitting around 90 mph before the pandemic layoff to averaging 94 mph and topping out at 97 with improved carry up in the zone last season. His best pitch is a plus changeup that approaches the plate at 82-85 mph before taking a dive. He also has a sweeping low-80s slider that flashes as a solid offering at times. While he generally throws strikes, Marinaccio gets so much action on his changeup and slider that he can't always locate them where he wants. He utilizes a low arm slot that provides deception and adds life to his pitches. He's old for a prospect at 26 but is ready to help the Yankees as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts broke Tennessee Tech's saves record with 13 as a sophomore and again with 15 as junior in 2018, when he helped the Golden Eagles win their first NCAA regional playoff tournament ever. The Cubs made him the highest pick in school history that June, signing him in the fourth round for a below-slot $130,000 that helped them afford outfielders Brennen Davis and Cole Roederer and right-hander Kohl Franklin. He has continued to thrive as a pro, reaching Triple-A and grabbing a spot on the 40-man roster in 2021 before making his big league debut this year, though he blew out his elbow in June and required Tommy John surgery. Roberts is a spin-rate monster who can top 2700 rpm with his fastball and 3100 rpm with his breaking ball. His heater sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 but plays well above its velocity because it features natural cut and appears to rise as it nears the plate. His breaker combines slider velo in the low 80s with curveball depth, playing nicely off his fastball. Roberts lacks physicality at 5-foot-10 and 180 pounds, but his size works for him by contributing to a flat approach angle for his heater and a compact delivery that he repeats well. He's a competitor who challenges hitters, though getting touched up for a 4.50 ERA in Triple-A underscored his need to refine his command. He doesn't have the overpowering stuff or ceiling of fellow Cubs relief prospects Ben Leeper and Cayne Ueckert, but he does have a higher floor with a longer track record of success and strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While there’s no question Rodriguez has made the $1.75 million investment the Mariners made in him back at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period seem very shrewd, there were some question marks surrounding the uber-talented outfielder heading into the 2021 season. He had broken his wrist at the Mariners’ alternate training site and did not perform well in winter ball upon his return. Rodriguez answered those questions and then some by hitting .347/.441/.560 between High-A and Double-A, while also going to the Futures Game and helping the Dominican Republic earn a bronze medal in the Olympics. Outside of that small sample in winter ball, Rodriguez has hit pretty much wherever he’s been, carrying a career .331/.412/.543 line into the 2022 season. He’s long had an advanced approach at the plate with impressive pitch recognition and plate discipline and can hit the ball hard to all fields. He has prodigious power he’s tapping into more and more, but he doesn’t sell out for that pop, giving him every chance to be a double-plus hitter with double-plus pop. Not content with just being a bat, Rodriguez has worked hard on his speed and is an excellent and aggressive baserunner who can steal a base. Rodriguez has played more right field than anything, which should be a very good long-term home for him that will allow him to use his plus arm, though he’s also shown he can handle roaming center field when needed. All of his incredible tools play up because of his makeup, work ethic and passion for the game. Loved by old-time scouts and analytics-minded folks alike, he has all the makings of a big league superstar.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2017-18 international signing period began, Rodriguez was ranked No. 10 on the MLB Pipeline Top 30 international prospects list. The Mariners were thrilled to sign him for $1.75 million on July 2 and the outfielder quickly served notice that he was one of the best players in the class by posting a .929 OPS in the Dominican Summer League in 2018. Despite a left hand fracture in 2019, Rodriguez played across two levels of A ball during his United States debut before playing in the Arizona Fall League. He was playing well in the Mariners’ summer camp last July when he fractured his wrist diving for a ball in the outfield, though he recovered in time to get some winter ball at-bats under his belt. Rodriguez has every chance to be a plus hitter with plus power at the big league level. The Mariners felt comfortable pushing him as a teenager across levels and to the AFL largely because of his advanced approach from the right side of the plate, something that allows the big, physical outfielder to already tap into his tremendous raw power. While he’ll never be a big basestealing threat, Rodriguez has worked very hard to improve his speed and moves very well for his size. Just 20 for all of the 2021 season, Rodriguez has played both center and right field during his pro career. He can handle playing up the middle, but is better suited for a corner, where his plus arm plays well, especially given other personnel in the organization. In addition to his obvious on-field tools, Rodriguez brings a passion and joy to the game that should help him become a superstar in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 ﻿ One of the top talents on the international amateur free agent market in the 2017-18 signing period, Rodriguez joined the Mariners with a $1.75 million bonus. He immediately started living up to expectations with a strong pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the only thing that slowed him during his United States debut in 2019 was a fastball to the left hand in April. Once he recovered from the hairline fracture, he tore up the South Atlantic League and was extremely impressive in the California League before more than holding his own as an 18-year-old in the Arizona Fall League. He was participating in the Mariners’ summer camp in July when he suffered a hairline fracture in his left wrist after diving for a ball in the outfield. Rodriguez has about as much offensive upside as any hitter in the Mariners’ organization, and perhaps all of the Minors. He should continue to be able to hit for both average and power and his already advanced approach will allow him to continue to get to his prodigious raw power consistently, giving him every chance to hit in the middle of a big league lineup. Strong and physically imposing, Rodriguez will never be a burner and speed isn’t a huge part of is game, but he moves very well for his size. The teenager has played both center and right field, including during his stint in the AFL. While he’s capable up the middle, right field seems to be the best fit for him long-term, where his cannon of an arm will play very well. Rodriguez has matured, both physically and mentally, much more quickly than anyone could have anticipated. A leader on and off the field, Rodriguez has the tools, and the personality, to be a superstar once he reaches the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 An older international prospect whom the Cardinals signed at age 19 in January 2016, Rodriguez was originally viewed as an organizational roster filler based on his defensive merits. But the Dominican catcher proved a more complete player than initially thought during his pro debut, showing feel to hit and power potential in the Dominican Summer League, and has continued to make strides offensively while incrementally climbing through the Cardinals' system. After a solid first full season at Class A Peoria, Rodriguez moved up to Class A Advanced Palm Beach and garnered midseason Florida State League All-Star honors in 2019. Rodriguez's abilities behind the plate are obvious. He does a good job controlling the running game with his plus, accurate arm, and has been praised by evaluators for his catch-and-throw skills, with many noting his consistent footwork and quick release. He moves well in spite of his stocky frame, and is regarded as a good receiver and framer who also knows how to handle a pitching staff. Offensively, Rodriguez employs an aggressive approach from the right side of the plate, with a knack for making consistent contact to all field fields to go along with some pull-side raw power. Rodriguez appears ticketed for backup role at the highest level if he can continue to make strides on both sides of the ball, and there's a non-zero chance that he'll achieve such a role based simply on his defensive chops.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 With his big and athletic body, along with his projectable frame and tools, it's easy to see why Rodriguez ranked as MLB Pipeline's No. 9 prospect for the 2017-18 international signing period. The Mariners certainly agreed with that assessment, as they inked the 16-year-old outfielder for $1.75 million on July 2 and then began to acclimate him to the professional ranks with an assignment to the Dominican instructional league in the fall. Rodriguez has a chance to be a special hitter, one who projects to hit for average and already shows robust raw power during batting practice. Rodriguez does have a pre-pitch waggle in the batter's box that can get his timing out of sync at times and results in some swing-and-miss, but his advanced approach at the plate and his overall bat speed helps solve some of the issues caused by his developing batting mechanics. Overall, he has the ability to drive the ball to all fields and he consistently makes hard contact. On the other side of the ball, Rodriguez shows the makings of an everyday right fielder because of his solid defensive skills and above-average arm strength. His offensive profile is a clean fit at the position, and scouts believe Rodriguez has the potential to be a middle-of-the-order type of run producer once fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torkelson broke Barry Bonds’ Arizona State freshman record with 25 homers in 2018. He led the Pac-12 in dingers as a freshman and sophomore and slugged at least .700 in all three seasons as a Sun Devil. Mix in star turns in Cape Cod and two Team USA stints, and Torkelson entered the 2020 Draft as a consensus No. 1 talent. The Tigers agreed and made him the first corner infielder to go No. 1 overall since Adrian Gonzalez in 2000. Torkelson signed for $8,416,300, which still stands as a Draft record. He backed up that investment with a stellar first season, climbing from High-A to Triple-A while hitting .267/.383/.552 with 30 homers over 121 games. He finished the year in the Arizona Fall League before a right ankle sprain cut that assignment short after only seven games. Thanks to impressive physical strength, Torkelson has some of the best raw power in the Minors, and it shows in both batting practice and game settings. He isn’t just a modern free swinger either. Torkelson is patient in the box, willing to take a walk and able to control the zone with a sound swing. The Tigers were impressed that he didn’t seem willing to rest on his previous laurels and constantly found ways to improve as he moved up the chain, including an added emphasis on going the other way at Triple-A. During the Draft, Detroit announced Torkelson as a third baseman, and he was OK there. However, he primarily stuck to first base in Toledo, and in September, Tigers manager A.J. Hinch said, “there’s no secret that the first baseman of the future is going to be Spencer Torkelson.” The 22-year-old has the offensive capability to be an elite middle-of-the-lineup talent in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torkelson was a three-sport standout as a California prep but went unselected in the 2017 Draft and ended up at Arizona State, where he hit 25 home runs to shatter Barry Bonds’ freshman record. Torkelson continued to perform well for USA Baseball and in the Cape Cod League, then led the Pac-12 in home runs (23) as a sophomore before another turn with Team USA. After an abbreviated junior campaign in 2020, the Tigers made Torkelson the first corner infielder in 20 years to be drafted No. 1 overall, announcing him as a third baseman. He signed for $8,416,300, becoming the first No. 1 pick in the bonus-pool era (since '12) to receive more than slot value, then spent the summer at Detroit’s alternate training site before participating in the team’s fall instructional program. Torkelson has a special bat, with the ability to hit for both average and power from the right side. He’s extremely patient and controls at-bats well, drawing plenty of walks. When Torkelson does swing, he combines physical strength and bat speed to generate massive power from line to line, including elite raw power to his pull side. He gets to that power during games with relative ease, too, thanks to natural hitting ability that allows him to hit all different pitch types to all fields. Torkelson had not manned the hot corner since high school before the Tigers drafted him as a third baseman and deployed him there at the alternate site. Club officials were surprised by how agile and athletic Torkelson looked at the position, noting that he improved over the summer thanks to his work with Alan Trammell. Being able to stay at third base will only maximize Torkelson’s future offensive value, and he should have no trouble meeting the offensive demands that come with playing first base at the highest level should he be forced to move down the defensive spectrum.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abrams was named Georgia’s Gatorade High School Player of the Year as a senior at Blessed Trinity Catholic High (Roswell, Ga.) in 2019, when he also separated himself from his Draft class peers with his elite blend of athleticism, speed and pure hitting ability. The Padres took Abrams with the No. 6 overall pick that June and signed him for a below-slot $5.2 million. Abrams continued to garner accolades as he won the Rookie Arizona League MVP Award after hitting .401 and stealing 14 bases over 32 games. He built on that success in ‘20, impressing at the Padres’ alternate training site and held his own when aggressively pushed to Double-A as a 20-year-old in 2021. However, a fractured left tibia and sprained left MCL limited him to just 42 games last season. Abrams’ 80-grade speed allows him to impact the game on both sides of the ball and he’s shown an early ability to use that speed, swiping 28 bags over his first 76 professional games. He’s also added strength to his 6-foot-2, 185-pound frame and projects to have at least average power in the future. A plus hitter, Abrams is still fine-tuning his pitch selection, but possesses good bat-to-ball skills and has shown the ability to make adjustments in the box. A naturally gifted athlete, Abrams has made big strides defensively since signing. That top-of-the-scale speed gives him plenty of range, and his hands, coupled with his strong arm, give him the tools needed to make all the necessary plays. He has the skills to stick at shortstop and be an impact player long-term, but a position change may ultimately occur if San Diego keeps Fernando Tatis Jr. at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abrams garnered honors as Georgia’s Gatorade High School Player of the Year as a senior at Blessed Trinity Catholic High (Roswell, Ga.) in 2019, when he also separated himself from his Draft class peers with his elite blend of athleticism, speed and pure hitting ability. The Padres took Abrams with the No. 6 overall pick that June and signed him for below-slot value at $5.2 million, then watched him win the Rookie Arizona League MVP Award -- batting .401 with 23 extra-base hits and 14 steals in 32 games -- and reach Class A Fort Wayne in his pro debut. He was even better in ‘20, showing more polish and strength to go along with his loud tools, albeit at the Padres’ alternate training site and fall instructional league camp. San Diego pushed Abrams to Double-A for his age-20 season. He held his own despite his youth, but a fractured left tibia and sprained left MCL suffered in early July ended that campaign early. Abrams’ top-of-the-scale speed is a game-changing tool that makes him an impact player on both sides of the ball. The strength Abrams has added to his ultra-projectable frame since signing shows in his ability to drive the ball and do damage from the left side, and scouts now like his chances of developing at least average game power to go along with a plus bat. Abrams’ speed and penchant for making hard contact give him both a high ceiling and floor as a hitter -- the latter a product of his ability to steal hits on the infield and stretch singles into extra bases. Abrams’ biggest improvement in 2020 came on the defensive side thanks to his work with the coaching staff at San Diego’s alternate training site. His speed and quickness give him tremendous range in all directions, and he has the hands, actions and plus arm strength needed to make all the plays. And while a move to either second base or center field in deference to Fernando Tatis Jr. may be unavoidable, any such position change shouldn’t keep Abrams from reaching his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the same Blessed Trinity Catholic High (Roswell, Ga.) program that produced big leaguers Tyler Flowers and Matt Skole, Abrams separated himself from most of his 2019 Draft class peers with his blend of elite speed, athleticism and natural hitting ability. After garnering honors as Georgia's high school player of the year as a senior in 2019, Abrams signed with the Padres for $5.2 million, below slot value, after they selected him with the No. 6 overall pick. He immediately rewarded the organization's investment in him with a stellar pro debut, winning the Rookie Arizona League MVP Award -- batting .401 with 23 extra-base hits and 14 steals in 32 games -- before a late promotion to Class A Fort Wayne. Abrams truly has game-changing speed, with 80-grade wheels that enable him to make an impact in all facets of the game. He's also a very impressive left-handed hitter, one who consistently finds the barrel with a short, fluid stroke that yields hard contact to all fields. More than a slap-and-dash hitter, Abrams already shows some pop and will develop even more as he adds strength to his wiry-athletic frame. Scouts project him for at least average game power at maturity, and there are some who think he'll surpass that projection. Abrams' defensive outlook comes with a few more question marks, but only because he has the speed and tools to profile just about anywhere on the diamond. That speed gives him outstanding range as a shortstop, and he has the hands, actions and above-average arm strength needed to stick at the position. A move over to second base or even center field is a possibility if that doesn't work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting up solid numbers in three years at UNLV, Stott became the first Rebels first-rounder in five years, and the first position player from the school to go that high since Matt Williams went No. 3 overall back in 1986. Strength gains made during his time at the Phillies’ alternate training site in 2020 paid dividends in his first full season of pro ball, as the infielder went from High-A to Triple-A before capping it off as one of the best prospects in the Arizona Fall League and topping the circuit in RBIs. Since his college days, Stott has exhibited an advanced approach from the left side of the plate with the ability to hit the ball hard to all fields. He draws a ton of walks and walked more than he struck out in the AFL, much like he did in college. That helps him get in more favorable counts to let him drive the ball with more extra-base authority than he’s had in the past, with the chance to get to average in-game power in the future. Stott has the arm, hands, footwork and instincts to play shortstop at the big league level, with enough speed and range to stay there long term. He’s also shown he can slide over to second or third with ease should the need arise, giving the Phillies many options of getting his solid bat into the Major League lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at UNLV, Stott parlayed a huge junior season in which he finished with a .997 OPS to land in the middle of the first round, where the Phillies took him No. 14 overall in the 2019 Draft. He had a solid debut, mostly in the short-season New York-Penn League, then showed improved strength facing a much higher level of competition at the Phillies’ alternate site in 2020. A left-handed-hitting shortstop, Stott has shown a knack for making contact and using all fields and an advanced approach at the plate that enabled him to walk more than he struck out in college. He uses all fields well and the added strength led to an increased ability to drive the ball at the alternate site, something that only will improve as he continues to mature. The Phillies were particularly impressed with his recognition of spin and his ability to handle left-handed pitching. A solid runner, Stott is a natural shortstop who got some experience playing second and third at the alternate site to add versatility to his resume. But he has the range, arm and instincts to stick at shortstop long-term and the upside to be a big league regular at the premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best player ever to be drafted out of UNLV was undoubtedly Matt Williams, who was an All-Star third baseman with a 17-year big league career. He was a shortstop in college and was taken No. 3 overall in the 1986 Draft. The Rebels didn't have another hitter taken in the first round until Stott, also a shortstop, was taken 14th overall in 2019. He hit all three years as a starter, culminating in a huge junior year that resulted in him being the first of five college shortstops taken in the first round. He went on to have a solid debut in the Short Season New York-Penn League. While none of Stott's tools jump off the page as obviously plus, he can do a lot of things very well. The one tool that has the chance to be plus in time is probably his hit tool. He makes a ton of contact and can drive the ball to all fields, working counts and drawing a ton of walks as well. He doesn't sell out for power, but it did show up more during his junior year and during his pro debut, particularly to his pull side. An above-average runner, Stott has worked hard on the defensive side of the game as well. He has plenty of arm for shortstop and excellent instincts, giving him a chance to stick there long term. Should he slow down as he matures, he could be an excellent defender at second or third. Alec Bohm, the Phillies' first-round pick from 2018, reached Double-A in his first full season and Stott is a fellow college bat who could follow a similar path up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins acquired Duran from the D-backs, who had originally signed the right-hander for just $65,000 in 2018, when he was making his full-season debut. He pitched his way to Double-A and onto the Twins’ 40-man roster in 2019 and after pitching well at the club’s alternate training site in 2020, he seemed poised to contribute to the big league staff in 2021. However, elbow issues limited him to 16 Triple-A innings, though he was healthy and throwing extended live batting practice sessions at the end of the year. Duran has long had a dominant combination of pitches in his fastball and hybrid splitter-sinker called a “splinker.” Even in his brief time on the mound in 2021, his fastball touched 101 and averaged 96.4 while the splinker averaged 90 mph and touched 94. Both pitches miss bats and generate a ridiculous amount of ground balls. He started working on a slider last year to go along with the big, hard curve he’s always thrown, but that he hadn’t always landed consistently in the strike zone. Duran didn’t have enough time to see if the slider would be a usable weapon in game action, though there were positive early indications. He’ll have to show his elbow is sound, but if he can throw that slider for strikes and continue to refine his overall command, he still has a good chance to start in the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran originally signed back in Dec. 2014 with the D-backs for just $65,000 and originally moved slowly, finally reaching full-season ball in 2018 when he was sent at that year’s Trade Deadline to the Twins in the Eduardo Escobar trade. The right-hander took off in his first full year with the Twins, pitching his way to Double-A and getting added to the 40-man roster following the 2019 season, then was the best pitching prospect at the Twins’ alternate site in 2020. Physically imposing at 6-foot-5, 230 pounds on the mound, Duran attacks hitter with an exciting power arsenal featuring two pitches that could get big league hitters out right now. The first is his fastball, a heater that sits around 97 mph and hit triple-digits regularly at the alternate site. He complements it with a a filthy “splinker,” a splitter-sinker hybrid pitch he cranks up to 94 mph that gets both swings and misses as well as weak contact on the ground. The key to Duran reaching his ceiling will be the continued development of his hard curve. He’s made strides in throwing it for strikes more consistently and his overall command has improved. There isn’t concern internally about reliever risk, with belief Duran will have the three-pitch mix to be a very successful big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Twins traded Eduardo Escobar to the D-backs at the Trade Deadline in 2018, they were sure to get Duran as part of the return. At the time, he was a tall and projectable, but raw, right-hander experiencing his first taste of full-season ball. The 2019 season saw him take a big step forward both in terms of stuff and performance, reaching Double-A at age 21 and getting added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. Duran always had very good power stuff and it all ticked up in 2019. His fastball averaged 97 mph for most of the 2019 season and he often touched triple-digits. He backs that up with an absolutely nasty splitter/sinker hybrid pitch, thrown 88-94 mph, which falls off the table, missing bats and getting ground-ball outs. He worked to improve his curveball and it has better characteristics, with good depth. It’s a hard breaking ball, thrown around 84 mph, and he’s working on commanding it in the strike zone. It’s not the typical starter profile, but so far there’s no reason whatsoever to consider moving him out of a rotation. The keys for him will be to continue to refine his command -- his walk rate did tick down a bit overall while his strikeout rate went up -- and, given his all-power repertoire, finding ways to keep hitters off balance. If he can do that, he could be a mid-rotation workhorse in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When deals are made at the Trade Deadline, it can often be years before the trade can be truly evaluated. The D-backs knew they would get immediate help when they got Eduardo Escobar from the Twins in July 2018, but the Twins knew they'd have to wait a while to see how good the key parts of the return, outfielder Gabriel Maciel and Duran, would be. Duran did show glimpses of his enormous upside during his full-season debut in 2018, leaving the Twins very excited to see what he can do in his first full season in the organization. Duran has an exciting repertoire that points to a future in a big league rotation. He relies heavily on two distinct fastballs, a four-seamer that sits at 94-96 mph and touches 98 mph and a two-seamer that's a cross between a sinker and a splitter, thrown 90-93 miph, that misses a ton of bats and drives his strikeout rate. He can spin a curveball, flashing a plus breaking ball, and it's a point of focus for him in 2019. His changeup still needs work, but it has the chance to be an average pitch eventually. He's continued to refine his delivery and improve his command and control. There's still more in the tank for the 6-foot-5 Duran and he could make a big leap up prospect lists as he moves up another level in 2019. He could be the next big high ceiling arm in the Twins system after Brusdar Graterol.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you were to look up the definition of projectable right-hander, there might be a picture of Duran next to it. The 6-foot-5 Dominican, who signed back in December 2014 for just $65,000, made his United States debut in 2016 and made an incremental step forward a year later. The results haven't caught up to the potential, but there's a lot to like here. The Twins agreed, acquiring his upside in the Eduardo Escobar trade. Duran has an exciting three-pitch mix he is still in the process of learning how to use consistently. His mid-90s fastball jumps out of his hand and features heavy sink, which leads to a lot of ground-ball outs. The 20-year-old knows how to spin a breaking ball and it has the chance to be an above-average pitch in the future. Even his changeup, which is behind the other two, flashes above-average at times. His command and control remain a work in progress, but the hope is they will come as he grows into his frame and learns to trust his stuff. It can take time for a young arm with this much upside to click, so patience will be the key. But Duran has the tools and the body to develop into a No. 3-type starter if everything comes together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With some pitchers, just watching them throw a bullpen can make you sit up and take notice. Duran, who made his United States debut in 2016 after his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the year prior, is one of those kinds of young arms -- one with a ton of upside. The ball really jumps out of Duran's hand, delivering a fastball that sits in the mid-90s now. He throws it with a lot of life, with heavy sink down in the zone that generates groundball outs. He can spin a good curveball, albeit not always consistently, though it looks like it could eventually be at least an above-average breaking ball. He has some feel for his changeup, giving him a potentially third Major League-average (or better) offering. He has a clean and smooth delivery that points to a future of throwing strikes. Duran has plenty of room to add strength to his 6-foot-5 frame, which could lead to even more velocity. Put a star next to his name, as he's a right-hander who could make a leap up prospect rankings in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez hit 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider as a Florida high school senior in 2017, but he had a sore shoulder for much of the spring and learned right before the Draft that he would require Tommy John surgery. The Astros were one of the few teams that preferred him as a hitter when he was healthy, so they took him in the second round and signed him for an above-slot $1.6 million. More injuries and the pandemic pushed his full-season debut back until 2021, but he rose from Single-A to Houston in 11 months, getting an at-bat with the Astros last April while providing emergency depth. Perez creates at least plus raw power with a combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his right-handed stroke. He hasn't been able to tap into it consistently at higher levels, however, producing a lot of ground-ball contact and just 15 homers in 567 at-bats across Double-A and Triple-A the past two years. He has matured as a hitter during that time, showing more discipline at the plate and using the opposite field more often. Though Perez works hard on his conditioning, he's still limited athletically and defensively. He's a well-below-average runner who lacks range at third base and on the outfield corners. He has regained his arm strength but is erratic at the hot corner and could wind up at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez drew plenty of pitching interest as a Florida high school senior who reached 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider in 2017, but he battled shoulder soreness that spring and learned just before the Draft that he required Tommy John surgery. One of the few teams that preferred him as a position player when he was healthy, the Astros still selected him in the second round and signed him for an above-slot $1.6 million. Further injuries and the pandemic delayed his full-season debut until 2021, when he slammed 18 homers and forced his way to Double-A and onto the 40-man roster. Perez has well above-average raw power thanks to his bat speed, strength and the loft in his right-handed stroke, and he created optimism that he'll be able to tap into it by maturing as a hitter last season. He did a better job of controlling the strike zone and using the entire field, though he still can get more consistent in both regards. His swing can get long and uphill, so he'll always be a power-over-hit guy. Though Perez used the pandemic layoff to improve his conditioning, he's still limited athletically. He's a well below-average runner who lacks range at third base, where he made 21 errors in 88 games last year. He has recovered his arm strength but probably will wind up at first base in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez hit 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider as a Florida high school senior in 2017, but he came down with a sore shoulder in March and learned just before the Draft that he needed Tommy John surgery. That didn't deter the Astros, one of the few teams that preferred him as a position player when he was fully healthy, and they signed him for an above-slot $1.6 million in the second round. Because of his elbow reconstruction, some soft-tissue injuries and the coronavirus pandemic, he played just 54 games in his first four years as a pro. Perez's bat speed, strength and the loft in his right-handed swing give him easy plus raw power, though he still has to prove he can tap into it. His stroke gets too long and uphill, and he gets too aggressive and pull-focused, which led to a .188 batting average and a 28 percent strikeout rate in short-season ball in 2019. He produces high exit velocities when he connects, and he has done a better job of making contact while advancing to Double-A in his full-season debut in 2021. The Astros were pleased that Perez used the pandemic layoff to improve his conditioning, and he reported to instructional league in the best shape of his career. He's still a well below-average runner and has limited range at third base but has a better chance of becoming at least an adequate defender there. He still has well above-average arm strength, so pitching could still be a fallback if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez reached 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider as a high school senior last spring, but he came down with shoulder soreness in March and learned shortly before the draft that he'd need Tommy John surgery. That didn't bother the Astros, one of the few teams who preferred him as a position player even when he was fully healthy. They drafted him as a third baseman and paid him an above-slot $1.6 million in the second round. Part of three Florida state 6-A championship teams at Archbishop McCarthy High (Southwest Ranches), Perez saw more action and had more success as a hitter than he did as a pitcher. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power, and he showed it off by homering at spotlight events such as the Area Code Games and the National High School Invitational. He has a sound right-handed swing and did a better job of making contact and using the whole field as a senior, so Houston believes he can hit for average and pop. Perez obviously has the arm strength for third base. His lack of quickness and range eventually could prompt a move to first base, though the Astros will give him every opportunity to make it at the hot corner. If hitting doesn't work out, he'll always have pitching as a fallback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sousa compiled a 5.50 ERA in four college seasons as a reliever at Virginia, turning down the Nationals as a 34th-rounder in 2017 before signing with the White Sox for $10,000 in the 10th round the following June. He has thrown a lot more strikes in pro ball than he did in college, and his stuff made a leap when he returned from the pandemic layoff last season. He claimed a spot on the 40-man roster in November after recording a 3.61 ERA with 71 strikeouts in 47 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A. Sousa's money pitch is a plus slider that went from parking in the low 80s at the start of 2021 to averaging 88 mph and touching 91 in Triple-A. It features both horizontal and vertical action, destroys same-side hitters and is effective against right-handers. His fastball velocity also improved over the course of the year, ranging from 94-98 mph in Triple-A, though his four-seamer gets straight and doesn't dodge a lot of bats. Outside of an early-2021 blip in Double-A, Sousa has had no control issues as a pro, averaging 2.4 walks per nine innings in his first three seasons -- down from 5.8 at Virginia. He hides the ball well in his high three-quarters delivery, making it harder for hitters to get good swings against him. If he continues to dial in the strike zone and maintains his Triple-A stuff, he could play a key role in Chicago's bullpen this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a 16-year Major League pitcher, Witt already had a high stock before he saw his first pro pitch as a star in showcase and international events. The 2019 Gatorade National High School Player of the Year was selected second overall by the Royals and signed for a franchise-record $7,789,900. An early trip to the Rookie-level Arizona League provided lackluster statistical results (but strong underlying data), and Witt built on that with standout trips to Kansas City’s 2020 alternate site and fall instructs. He busted out for good in 2021, hitting .290/.361/.575 with 33 homers and 29 steals at Double-A and Triple-A. He fell one theft shy of being the Minor Leagues’ ninth 30-30 player since 2000. Little Witt does on the diamond is surprising anymore. Utilizing a slightly open right-handed stance and small leg kick, the Texas native generates impressive bat speed with a compact swing capable of generating power to all fields. He also gets good lift through the zone, and that -- combined with improved strength -- helps him to project for plus-plus power. He has shown that additional pop while cutting his K rate down from 24 percent at Double-A to 22.5 percent at Triple-A. A plus runner coming out of high school, Witt has already put his wheels to good use, and he should continue to be a base-stealing threat. Witt covers ground well, shows quick hands and makes the most of his plus arm from the premium position of shortstop. He’ll bump up against Adalberto Mondesi and Nicky Lopez quickly in 2022 and could move to third, where he made 17 starts in 2021. The rest of the tools make Witt, who only turns 22 in June, a potential star and the future (if not the present) face of the franchise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline ranked Witt Jr. as the 2019 Draft’s No. 2 prospect behind Oregon State catcher Adley Rutschman. The two players came off the board in that order, with the Royals taking Witt, the son of former 16-year Major League pitcher Bobby Witt, at No. 2 and then signing him to a franchise-record bonus worth $7,789,900. He produced mixed results during his pro debut in the Rookie Arizona League, but the 20-year-old proved advanced beyond his years in 2020, excelling in the face of older, more advanced competition at the alternate training site and the Royals’ fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Witt drives the ball to all fields with excellent barrel control and outstanding bat speed. He has made significant gains in improving his approach in pro ball, becoming more aggressive while also trimming swing-and-miss tendencies from his game, and he already knows how to make difficult adjustments within at-bats. Witt has long shown plus raw power to his pull side and tapped into it more consistently in 2020, applying it from line to line against advanced pitching. He should generate even more power as he adds strength to his projectable frame and continues to refine his approach. Witt is also a plus runner who is aggressive on the basepaths, giving him a high-end combination of power and speed at a premium position. There’s no question Witt will also be able to stay at shortstop, with that speed allowing him to have plenty of range. He has very quick hands and an arm that allowed him to throw in the mid-90s off the mound in high school. Club officials rave about his makeup, instincts and passion for the game as much as his tools, giving him as much chance as anyone to reach his enormous potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top of most boards heading into the 2019 Draft had Oregon State catcher Adley Rutschman at the top and Texas high school shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. right behind him, including on MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 200 rankings. The top of the Draft went exactly that way with the Orioles selecting Rutschman with the No. 1 pick and the Royals thrilled to get Witt at No. 2, signing former big league pitcher Bobby Witt’s son for full pick value at $7,789,900, the third-highest Draft bonus in history. After scuffling a bit out of the gate during his pro debut, he finished strongly in the rookie-level Arizona League. In the past, there had been some concerns about the swing-and-miss tendencies in the toolsy shortstop’s game, but he improved on that front a good deal during his senior year. He’s capable of driving the ball to all fields with excellent barrel control and outstanding bat speed. As he continues to refine his approach, there are few concerns about his ability to hit for average. That, in turn, will help him tap into his plus raw power more consistently. He’s also a plus runner who is aggressive on the basepaths, giving him 20-20 potential. There’s no question Witt will also be able to stay at shortstop, with that speed allowing him to have plenty of range. He has very quick hands and an arm that allowed him to throw in the mid-90s off the mound in high school. Scouts rave about his makeup and passion for the game as much as his tools, giving him as much chance as anyone to reach his enormous potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-drafted position player in University of Maine history, Peña went in the third round in 2018, when he was considered one of the best college defenders in his class. The son of former big league second baseman Geronimo Peña, he has gotten stronger and provided more offense than expected since turning pro. He injured his left wrist diving for a grounder in Spring Training last year and had surgery that cost him much of the season, but he returned to set a career high with 10 homers in just 30 Triple-A games and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Peña remains the best defender in the Astros system, getting to plenty of balls at shortstop with his quick first step and plus range. He has solid arm strength, unloads the ball quickly and makes accurate throws. He also has soft hands and sound fundamentals and is capable of playing anywhere in the infield if needed. After looking feeble with wood bats in college summer leagues, Peña has gotten much stronger and is hitting the ball much harder as a pro. He also has gotten better at controlling the strike zone and does a nice job of using the entire field, though he still needs to add more loft to his right-handed swing because he makes a lot of groundball contact. Factor in his solid speed and basestealing mentality, and he has the upside of a 20-20 player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While his father Geronimo played seven seasons in the Majors as an offensive-minded second baseman, Pena is best known for his glove at shortstop. One of the top college defenders in the 2018 Draft, he became the highest-drafted position player in University of Maine history when the Astros took him in the third round. He has proven a better hitter than expected in pro ball and batted .306/.349/.430 in the Dominican League this winter, but he didn't get a chance to build on that in 2021 because he injured his left wrist diving for a grounder in Spring Training and required surgery that cost him most of the season. The best defender in Houston's system, Pena is a legitimate shortstop with a quick first step and plus range. His arm strength draws grades anywhere from fringy to plus, but the bottom line is he has a quick release and doesn't have any problems making the necessary throws. He has soft, reliable hands and can provide quality glovework all over the infield should he wind up as a utilityman. Though he struggled with wood bats in college summer leagues, Pena has gotten much stronger in pro ball and now is making more frequent and higher quality contact from the right side of the plate. The Astros believe he'll hit enough to be a regular on contending teams and see some untapped power that eventually could produce 15 or more homers per season once he incorporates some mechanical changes. A solid runner out of the batter's box, he's faster once he gets going and has a basestealing mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Geronimo Pena played seven seasons in the big leagues as an offensive-minded second baseman, while his son Jeremy stands out more with his glove at shortstop. One of the best college defenders in the 2018 Draft class, he became the highest-drafted Maine position player ever when the Astros selected him in the third round. Following a pedestrian pro debut, he hit .303/.385/.440 with 20 steals between two Class A levels in his first full season. Pena covers plenty of ground with a quick first step and plenty of range. There are mixed reports on his arm strength, with grades ranging from fringy to plus, but he both gets to balls and gets rid of his throws in a hurry. He has soft, reliable hands and would provide quality defense all over the infield if he winds up in a utility role. Since struggling with wood bats in college summer leagues, Pena has added significant strength and did more damage in 2019. A right-handed hitter, he looks like he'll produce enough offense to merit an everyday role now that he's doing a better job of working counts and driving the ball in the air as a pro. He shows solid speed out of the batter's box and is quicker underway, and he has the aggressive mentality to steal bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The son of offensive-minded second baseman Geronimo Pena, who played seven seasons in the big leagues, Jeremy is also an infielder but has a totally different profile. One of the best defensive shortstops in the 2018 college class, he became the highest-drafted position player in Maine history when the Astros took him in the third round. He earned short-season New York-Penn League All-Star honors in his pro debut but missed the final month with a leg injury. Pena is the top defender among shortstops in the Houston system. His quick first step and smooth actions give him plenty of range, and he has a plus arm to make all of the necessary throws. His tools will allow him to play anywhere in the infield and serve as a utilityman if he doesn't hit enough to become an everyday player. Pena makes regular contact to all fields and has a patient approach. He has the strength to do some damage at the plate and the Astros are working with him to try to unlock some power in his right-handed swing. He has solid speed and an aggressive nature on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams will try to develop starting pitching as much as possible; it's a reason why a prospect with arm strength will be allowed to start for a long time in the Minors in the hopes that it works. Arano started his first two seasons after signing with the Dodgers and then one more year after joining the Phillies in the Roberto Hernandez trade. A move to the bullpen after that however, has allowed the right-hander to take off and he threw well as a reliever in the big leagues during his debut last September. Arano had started the year with an arm injury, and it took a while for his stuff to bounce back. He has two legitimate Major League weapons right now in his fastball and slider. He throws the former up into the mid-90s when he's at his best and he can finish good hitters with it when he's commanding it well. His slider is a legitimate out pitch that misses bats with sharp break. He'll mix in an occasional changeup against left-handed hitters. He's always been a solid strike-thrower. Arano's numbers in Reading last year, post-injury, don't do him justice and the Phillies feel what he did in the big leagues in September is exactly who he can be. He should get the chance to prove them right in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Dodgers, Arano joined the Phillies via the Roberto Hernandez trade in 2014. After a year as a starter with his new organization, Arano moved to the bullpen in '16 and saw his stuff and results take off. His progress was delayed at the start of 2017 due to biceps tendinitis, but he joined the Double-A Reading bullpen at the end of May. The Phillies struggled with the decision to move Arano because he did have four usable pitches as a starter. Arano embraced the move to the bullpen and it showed. His fastball jumped to the mid-90s and touched more when he needed it. Arano needed some convincing to focus on his slider instead of throwing both breaking balls, but he did it and it's now a swing-and-miss pitch for him, a big reason why he missed so many more bats in '16. He doesn't use his changeup as much now, but it does give him a weapon against left-handed hitters. He's always been a strike-thrower and that continued in his new role. The Phillies have developed some big relief arms internally over the last couple of years, including Ken Giles and last year, Edubray Ramos. They think Arano might be next in line as a power reliever who will help out the back end of the bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees went all-in during the 2014-15 international signing period, handing out a total of seven seven-figure bonuses. After that tier came 15 six-figure bonuses with Castillo at the higher end of that group, getting $750,000 to sign out of Venezuela. Outside of a solid Dominican Summer League debut in 2015, the Yankees didn’t get a whole lot of return on their investment until 2021, when his bat took off in Double-A in time for him to be included in the return the Pirates got for Clay Holmes at last year’s Trade Deadline. He hit his way to Triple-A and on to the Pirates’ 40-man roster last fall. Castillo earned his way onto his first 40-man roster because of advancements he made at the plate. He’s always made a ridiculous amount of contact, with a career strikeout rate under 11 percent, but added strength and more patience, combined with a willingness to add loft, led to a power outburst of 19 homers, more than double his career total heading into last season. That it came without sacrificing contact rate points to it being something that could be sustainable. His bat is going to have to carry him to the big leagues because it’s unclear where he fits defensively. Signed as a shortstop, he’s seen time at all three infield spots over the last few seasons. He might fit best as an offensive-minded second baseman, and maybe he’s developing the power to fit the third base profile, but it’s more likely he carves out a role as a bat-first utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays have challenged Castillo since they signed him for $64,000 at age 20 in 2014, pushing him through the system at an accelerated pace. He responded as hoped every step of the way before breaking out in earnest in 2017 with a 2.76 ERA, 15 saves, a .216 opponents' average and 90 strikeouts in 71 2/3 innings between Double- and Triple-A. The big right-hander represented the World team in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game along the way, and the Rays added him to their 40-man roster in November. A physically mature pitcher with a stocky but strong frame, Castillo is absolutely loaded with arm strength. He'll run his fastball up to 101 mph and consistently sits in the upper 90s, even imparting some late sinking action that nets him ground balls. He pairs his electric heater with hard slider that makes him devastating against right-handed hitters, who collectively batted .206/.273/.336 with a 34 percent strikeout rate against him in 2017. That Castillo is a max-effort thrower further enhances his bullpen profile, and despite occasional bouts of wildness, he's generally around the zone with his fastball-slider combo. And although he's had success in the Minors as a closer, Castillo likely projects better in a seventh- or eighth-inning role in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A steady performer but overshadowed on an Oregon State 2018 College World Series championship team that included three first-round picks, Kwan went in the fifth round that June. He did little to shed his reputation as a slap-hitting complementary player in his first two years as a pro before coming back as a different guy after the 2020 pandemic shutdown. He batted .328/.407/.527 with 12 homers in 77 games between Double-A and Triple-A, prompting the Guardians to place him on their 40-man roster. Kwan has elite contact skills, the product of a short left-handed swing, uncanny hand-eye coordination and a disciplined approach. He added a more pronounced leg kick in 2021 and began pulling more pitches and hitting them harder, and his 12 homers last year doubled his total from three years in college plus his first two in the Minors. He's not very physical and scouts still question how much impact he'll provide at the plate, with most believing he'll top out at 12-15 homers per full season. A solid runner out of the batter's box and quicker once he gets going, Kwan projects as a leadoff type who can provide high on-base percentages and a few stolen bases. His quickness and instincts allow him to cover plenty of ground in center field, where he has a fringy but playable arm. If he doesn't offer enough thump to be a regular, his broad array of skills would make him a useful fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Venezuela back in October 2012, Azocar initially opened eyes by using his tools well in his second season in the Venezuelan Summer League in 2014 and then again during a very successful United States debut. His full-season debut a year later was OK, but he wasn't able to replicate it in 2017 with a move up to Lakeland, where his .220/.246/.292 line left some evaluators scratching their heads. He got back on track in 2018, hitting well in the Midwest League before a return to Lakeland in June. After the start to his career here in the States, the Tigers thought Azocar would have gained more traction by now. The key culprit has been a lack of any kind of approach at the plate. There's a lot of swing and miss because he chases pitches out of the zone, and he's now walked exactly 14 times in back-to-back years. When he does make contact, it can be loud, and there is some raw power for him to tap into if he can find a way to stop getting himself out. An above-average runner, Azocar has shown he can play center and has a plus arm that looks very good in right. The Tigers still believe in Azocar's tools. It hasn't clicked for him yet, but they think it will. He's young enough to get headed in the right direction, with an improved approach No. 1 on his priority list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Venezuela back in October 2012, Azocar initially opened eyes by using his tools well in his second season in the Venezuelan Summer League in 2014 and then again during a very successful United States debut. His full-season debut a year later was OK, but he wasn't able to replicate it with a move up to Lakeland in 2017, leaving some evaluators scratching their heads. After the start to his career here in the States, the Tigers thought Azocar would have gained more traction by now. The key culprit has been a lack of any kind of approach at the plate. There's a lot of swing and miss, he chases pitches out of the zone and drew only 14 walks in 2017 (compared to 122 strikeouts). When he does make contact, it can be loud, and there is some raw power for him to tap into if he can find a way to stop getting himself out. An above-average runner, Azocar has shown he can play center and has a plus arm that looks very good in right. The Tigers still believe in Azocar's tools. It hasn't clicked for him yet, but they think it will. He's young enough to get headed in the right direction, with an improved approach No. 1 on his priority list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As Azocar has made slow progress in the Tigers system -- two summers in the Venezuelan Summer League, then his 2015 United States debut in the Gulf Coast League -- he has shown glimpses of his considerable set of tools. His first two years of full-season ball have been more of the same, with the Tigers excited to see what comes next. Azocar plays the game with passion and without fear. He's very aggressive at the plate and definitely doesn't go up looking to walk. Breaking balls still give him some trouble, and he chases pitches out of the zone too frequently, but when he's under control, he has considerable offensive skills. He has the ability to make solid contact to all fields and while he hasn't shown any semblance of power to date, the Tigers feel there's a chance he'll still grow into some. His speed allows him to steal some bases. He's also an outstanding defender with a strong arm, one who has shown the ability to play both center and right. Azocar might have as much ceiling as any position player in the Tigers system, even if he's still far away from reaching it. The end result could very well be a solid everyday outfielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A surprise 2016 first-rounder as a Texas high schooler, Potts signed with the Padres for a below-slot $1 million as the 24th overall selection. In his first full pro season, he and Fernando Tatis Jr. became the first 18-year-olds to hit 20 homers in the low Class A Midwest League in three decades, but Potts has leveled off since and struggled in Double-A in 2019. He and outfield prospect Jeisson Rosario went to the Red Sox in an August trade for Mitch Moreland. Potts' quick right-handed bat and strength give him plenty of raw power, but he has yet to show he can make enough contact against quality pitching to tap into it. He'll always be a power-over-hit guy, but he'll need a more disciplined approach to do enough damage to claim an everyday job in the big leagues. He doesn't walk much and he's a fringy runner, so almost all of his offensive value comes from his pop. Drafted as a shortstop, Potts lacked the quickness for the position and moved to third base when he played alongside Tatis in 2017. He has solid arm strength, sure hands and decent range at the hot corner. The Padres also gave him some playing time at second base in 2019, though he fits there more as a fill-in than as a potential regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Potts bypassed his Texas A&M commitment and signed with the Padres for $1 million in 2016 as the No. 24 overall pick, making him Southlake Carroll (Texas) High's highest-drafted player ever. After finishing his professional debut in the Class A Short Season Northwest League, Potts spent his first full season with Class A Forty Wayne, where he and Fernando Tatis Jr. became the first 18-year-olds to hit at least 20 home runs in the Midwest League since 1987. Potts finished with an even 20 homers, 14 of which he hit during a torrid second-half stretch that also saw him slash .278/.325/.512 over 65 games. Potts has a knack for making hard contact at the plate, with a quick right-handed bat and plenty of strength to his frame, though there is some swing-and-miss to his game. He projects as fringe-average hitter, but scouts expect him to develop at least average power as he continues to add strength. San Diego drafted Potts as a shortstop but has since shifted him to third base, where he shows the necessary hands, footwork and arm strength for the position. Potts has proved to be more advanced than expected early in his career, most notably in his capacity to make adjustments and get to his power during games. Though he'll need to tighten his approach and clean up his defensive some, Potts appears on the right path towards becoming a future middle-of-the-order third baseman at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Potts impressed evaluators with his hitting ability against high-level competition on the summer showcase circuit, though some teams worried that he couldn't be signed away from his Texas A&M commitment. The Padres ended up giving Potts $1 million as the No. 24 overall pick, making him Southlake Carroll (Texas) High's highest-drafted player ever, and he rewarded them with a strong pro debut in which he reached the Class A Short Season Northwest League at age 17. Potts has a knack for making hard contact at the plate, with a quick right-handed bat and plenty of strength to his frame, though there is some swing-and-miss to his game. He projects as an above-average hitter, and scouts expect him to develop at least average power as he continues to add strength. San Diego drafted Potts as a shortstop, where he has the necessary hands, range and arm strength, but he's since shifted over to third base, where his size and tools are a better fit. Potts proved to be more advanced than expected to begin his career, and though he didn't light the Midwest League on fire in 2017 like some of his Fort Wayne peers, the Padres believe he has a chance to be a future middle-of-the-order hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Signed for $450,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Solis surprisingly reached the advanced Rookie-level Appalachian League as a 17-year-old making his pro debut the next summer. He continued on the fast track and moved to Class A in 2018, giving up one or fewer earned runs in eight of his 11 starts before blowing out his elbow in August. Following Tommy John surgery, he returned to the mound in the Astros' Dominican instructional league program last October. Solis went from throwing 89-91 mph when he signed to dealing at 93-95 and touching 97 before he got hurt, with late hop and cutting action on his fastball. He hit 97 mph again last fall and could add more velocity because elbow reconstruction often leaves pitchers stronger than ever after they rehab. He has a promising four-pitch mix that also includes a 79-81 mph curveball with depth, an 84-86 mph slider that's more powerful than sharp and a developing changeup. Solis has a smooth delivery that he repeats well, and he had a history of throwing strikes until his elbow began barking. Significantly bigger than his listed 6-foot-2 and 160 pounds, he has long arms that create good extension and downhill plane on his pitches. Despite his youth and layoff, he's one of the more polished starting pitching prospects in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Solis moved faster than expected after signing for $450,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, reaching the Rookie-level Appalachian League during his pro debut the following summer. He overcame some early-season control issues to pitch well in Class A in 2018 until he blew out his elbow in August. He had Tommy John surgery and may not return to game action until 2020. Solis went from working with an 89-91 mph fastball when he signed to sitting at 93-95 mph and touching 97 with late hop and cutting action when he got hurt. He could add more velocity because he still has physical projection remaining and Tommy John rehab often leaves pitchers stronger than ever. His hard slider has the potential to become a plus pitch and he also shows promising feel for his changeup. His long arms allow Solis to create good extension and downhill plane on his pitches.
