Following a strong debut that summer, he moved slowly through the lower levels during his first two full seasons of pro ball, then missed a large chunk of the 2019 season because of an ankle injury. He wasn’t protected from the Rule 5 Draft in either 2019 or 2020, but wasn’t selected. He finally reached Triple-A in 2021 and was called up to make his big league debut with the Reds last September. When Friedl remembers who he is as a hitter, he has success. The left-handed hitter is at his best when he focuses on working counts, getting on base, making hard contact with line drives to all fields and using his plus speed and high energy to be a table-setter. He got into trouble trying to get to his pull side power with too much lift rather than going gap-to-gap and let his power come naturally. Friedl can play all three outfield spots extremely well. A fringy arm would make it tough for him to play right field on a daily basis, but it’s playable in center and left. If he can commit to maintaining his approach, he has the chance to be a solid fourth outfielder in the big leagues in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a sophomore at Nevada, Friedl hit .401 and finished with an OPS over 1.000, but no team realized he was a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2016. That information came to light as he was playing well for the U.S. Collegiate National Team that summer and the Reds, who had some bonus pool money left over, were able to sign him for $735,000, a record for an undrafted free agent. After a scintillating pro debut after signing, he methodically made his way up to Double-A and was scuffling there in 2019 when an ankle injury that required surgery ended his season early. Friedl, who was at the Reds alternate site in 2020, but was left off the 40-man roster and not selected in the Rule 5 Draft both after the 2019 and ’20 seasons, won’t wow anyone with his size or tools. He does have a very good feel for contact and keeps his strikeouts down while drawing a fair amount of walks. Some saw a little Adam Eaton in the left-handed hitter when he first entered pro ball, but he lacks the same kind of bat speed, which limits how much he can impact the ball. From a pure speed standpoint, he might just be above-average, but it plays up on the basepaths because of his instincts and aggressiveness. Friedl has seen time at all three outfield spots and can play all of them very well, albeit with a fringy arm. That bodes well for him as his profile is likely as a fourth outfielder type, but one who could be valuable in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Friedl had a nearly lost season at Double-A Chattanooga in 2019, as he was limited to 65 games full of struggle at the plate. It turned out that he was playing with an extra bone in his right ankle and it broke while he ran the bases. The added issue of Friedl playing with the injury for about six weeks didn’t help and he had season-ending surgery in July to remove the bone. The Reds left Friedl exposed in the Rule 5 Draft but he wasn’t taken. He also wasn’t invited to big league camp for 2020 like he was in ’19. But he still has several tools that could make him a strong fourth outfielder or a platoon guy in the Majors. A lefty hitter, Friedl still needs to work on his gap-to-gap hitting, situational hitting and using his speed with better bunting. He runs the bases well but also needs to improve his base stealing skills. The clock is ticking and this will be a big season for him to show improvement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Friedl's start to professional baseball was indeed irregular. He hit over .400 at Nevada-Reno as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2016, but he went undrafted because teams didn't realize he was eligible until after the Draft. A bidding war took place as he was playing for the U.S. National Collegiate Team, and the Reds were able to give him $735,000 to sign as a free agent. He played his way up to Double-A in his second full season of pro ball in 2018. Friedl needs to figure out how to maximize his offensive value and do the little things -- such as bunting, slashing hits on the ground, the hit-and-run and moving runners -- enhancing his chances to reach his floor as a really good fourth outfielder. But with his speed, personality and ability to provide maximum effort, he could work himself into becoming an everyday center fielder. He doesn't strike out much and draws a decent amount of walks. While he's never going to be a huge home run guy, he does have a little sneaky pop and might run into a few homers. One issue for Friedl currently is personnel related: There are other center field prospects ahead of him, namely Taylor Trammell and Jose Siri. Friedl has seen time in all three outfield spots, so he will be ready to fill that backup role if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It doesn't happen often for a college hitter to go through a season hitting over .400 and not be noticed or taken in the Draft. That's because most didn't realize Friedl was a Draft-eligible sophomore at Nevada-Reno until after the Draft. He was playing well for the U.S. National Collegiate Team when a bidding war of sorts ensued, won by the Reds, who gave him $735,000 to sign. Friedl hit well in the Midwest League (.850 OPS) during his first full season, then fizzled a bit after a promotion to the Florida State League. Friedl has a good idea of what he wants to do at the plate, with a contact-oriented approach. He puts the ball in play, sending line drives to the gaps without striking out much and drawing a decent amount of walks. While he's never going to be a huge home run guy, he does have a little sneaky pop and might run into a few homers. His plus speed works on both sides of the ball, allowing him to take an extra base as well as steal a few of them. It also plays well in the outfield. He's seen time in all three outfield spots, but he's better suited in center or left because of his fringy arm. In all likelihood, Friedl will fit the fourth outfielder mold really well. If his bat comes around a little bit more, he could be an everyday outfielder, though it would have to be in center since he doesn't fit the offensive profile for a corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Friedl went through his redshirt sophomore season at Nevada-Reno without too much fanfare, though he did hit over .400. It was unbeknownst to anyone, it seems, that he was actually Draft eligible. That fact was discovered as he was playing well for the U.S. National Collegiate Team, with several teams expressing interest. The Reds won out, signing him for $735,000 as a non-drafted free agent. Friedl is a fast-twitch athlete who went out in his pro debut and did what he had done all spring and early summer: hit. He has a solid approach at the plate, one that is geared to line drives and hitting the gaps. He does have some raw power, but he has a firm understanding of what his game is. That's getting on base and causing damage with his plus speed. That speed works in the outfield as well, where he covers a lot of ground and plays an above-average center field. Friedl might profile best as a fourth outfielder type, one who can play good defense at all three spots and impact the game with his speed. If he hits enough, though, he could end up being a table-setting regular in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies’ first selection in the 2017 Draft, Vilade was a high school product from Oklahoma who was taken in the second round. Since that time, the son of former coach and scout James Vilade moved steadily up the organizational ladder, spending a year at each A ball level, performing well at the Rockies’ alternate site in 2020, then jumping to Triple-A, going to the Futures Game and making his brief big league debut in 2021 before wrapping things up with a trip to the Arizona Fall League. He spent a so-so year in Triple-A in 2022, and when the Rockies put him on waivers in November, the Pirates decided to buy low and claim him. Throughout his professional career, Vilade has always shown an innate knack for contact. He rarely strikes out, with a career 17.4 percent K rate to show for it, and he’s not afraid to work counts or draw walks. He’s long been hit over power, not changing his approach too much by adding launch angle that would diminish his hit tool. He’s added a lot of strength as he’s matured, so there’s still confidence the power, which hasn’t shown up consistently, will come, especially if he can start making contact out front more regularly. Initially an infielder, Vilade made the move to the outfield in 2020 and played there almost exclusively a year ago, with a little first base mixed in. He’s likely a left fielder when all is said and done, with the chance for the power to come as he’ll play all of 2023 at age 24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies didn’t have a first-round pick in 2017, thanks to the free-agent signing of Ian Desmond. But they feel they may have gotten a first-round talent in Vilade, the son of former college coach and current Marlins scout James Vilade, who signed for full pick value as the No. 48 overall selection, and has moved one level per year in his first two full seasons, making progress offensively at both stops. That continued in 2020, as he was the best hitting prospect at the Rockies’ alternate site in Denver. Over the last year and a half, Vilade had evolved from a good hitter with solid bat-to-ball skills and an advanced approach to one who can really damage the baseball. He’s added strength and very good weight without sacrificing any athleticism and might now have 70 raw power from the right side of the plate. Because of his approach and plate discipline, he’s a safer bet to get to that power, with the Rockies thinking he might be a 25-30-homer guy in the future. Vilade has moved around a bit defensively, starting his pro career at shortstop, moving to third and then focusing more on playing left field, where he could be an average defender. He’s likely done with the hot corner, but he could get some reps at first, where he played a bit during instructs. He does have the chance to be an everyday run producer in left field, reminding some of former Rockie Matt Holliday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two full seasons of pro ball since joining the Rockies as their second-round selection in the 2017 Draft (but first pick thanks to the free-agent signing of Ian Desmond), Vilade has started out the year relatively slowly, then clicked in the second half. The son of former college coach, and now Marlins scout, James Vilade, Ryan Vilade appears like he’s turned a corner towards becoming the impact performer the Rockies were hoping they were getting. Vilade really came into his own as a hitter in 2019, particularly in the second half, then took another stop forward during the Rockies’ informal instructs program last fall. He’s added a lot of strength, which in turn has helped him impact the ball more as he’s made mechanical adjustments to barrel up the ball more consistently. His uptick in extra-base authority was not a product of playing in Lancaster or the California League, but rather his maturity as a hitter. He doesn’t strike out much and draws walks, is very comfortable driving the ball the other way and uses all fields while also developing a much better feel for pulling the ball with power. While Vilade doesn’t have great speed, he has very good instincts on the basepaths. Where Vilade will end up defensively long-term remains to be seen. His days as a shortstop are more or less over after an up and down season defensively overall, and he started to see a lot of time at third in 2019. The Rockies introduced the outfield corners to Vilade over the fall and he should play a lot of both in 2020, with his bat likely to force its way to Colorado sooner rather than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies didn't pick for the first time until No. 48 overall in the second round of the 2017 Draft, courtesy of signing free agent Ian Desmond, but they feel they got a first-round talent in Vilade, an Oklahoma high school infielder who signed for full pick value rather than join his father, an assistant coach at Oklahoma State. After a strong summer debut, Vilade really struggled out of the gate during his full-season debut in 2018, but righted the ship with a .310/.370/.419 second half. Vilade's ability to shake off a terrible start in the South Atlantic League as a teenager speaks volumes about his ability to learn and make adjustments as a hitter. He has a tremendous feel to hit with excellent bat speed and a quick swing from the right side of the plate. There's a lot of raw power to tap into, with the chance for Vilade to eventually have plus pop that he'll get to thanks to his approach. While few doubt he'll hit, there is more question about what position he ultimately plays. The Rockies like moving infielders around during development, doing it with top prospect Brendan Rodgers, for example, and Vilade will do the same moving forward after only playing shortstop in his first year-plus as a pro. Vilade will have the opportunity to stay at shortstop, but given that he's already bigger and stronger than he was when last season ended, it's easy to see him outgrowing the position. He could slide over to third or across to second full-time in the future. One thing the Rockies love about positional flexibility is that it will be easier to get Vilade's potent bat into a big league lineup once he's ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies didn't have a first-round choice in the 2017 Draft after signing Ian Desmond as a free agent but were thrilled to find Vilade in the second round. He had a history of success as an amateur, including winning the home run derby at the Under Armour All-America Game in 2016 and starring for the U.S. 18-and-under team that won a gold medal at the Pan American Games later that year. He signed for $1,425,400, turning down the chance to play at Oklahoma State, where his father James is an assistant coach. Vilade grew up around the game and gets universal praise for his makeup and instincts, and he also has a chance to be a dynamic offensive performer. He has a quick right-handed swing that already produces pull power and should deliver home runs to all fields once he gets stronger. He has shown the ability to make adjustments at the plate and his patience was obvious when he walked 27 times in a 33-game pro debut shortened by a lower back injury. Most amateur scouts projected that Vilade will outgrow shortstop, though he looked a little better than expected in his debut. He's an average runner who may slow a bit as he fills out and doesn't have the quickest first step, but his instincts and strong arm help him make plays. Colorado plans on trying him at third base and he also could fit at second base or in the outfield, but there are no immediate plans to move him off shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Fortes didn't become a full-time starter behind the plate until his third college season at Mississippi in 2018, when he won Southeastern Conference tournament MVP honors and went in the fourth round. He stood out defensively but did little offensively as a pro, batting .232/.318/.333 in three Minor League seasons, until the Marlins called him up in mid-September last year when Jorge Alfaro injured his calf. He homered in each of his first two starts and four times in 34 plate appearances. Fairly athletic for a catcher, Fortes is agile behind the plate and a capable receiver and blocker. His arm strength is merely average but plays better than that because he has a quick transfer and makes accurate throws. He also has the leadership and intelligence desired in a backstop, and he graduated from Mississippi with a finance degree in just three years. Despite his power outburst in September, Fortes is more a guy who ambushed some fastballs from unsuspecting big leaguers than a real slugger. He did start launching balls in the air more often in 2021 and does have enough bat speed and strength to perhaps produce 15 homers per season from the right side of the plate. While he won't hit for a high average, he does make consistent contact and has a knack for getting on base via walks and hit by pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he twice garnered Gatorade Player of the Year honors in Utah, Henry passed on a commitment to Brigham Young to sign with the Brewers after they selected him in the sixth round of the 2016 Draft. He impressed with his power potential and catch-and-throw skills as a Class A Wisconsin midseason All-Star in his first full season, then hit for even more power at Class A Advanced Carolina in 2019 to finish among the Carolina League leaders in home runs (14, tied-fourth) and RBIs (75, third). Henry’s right-handed raw power shows in his ability to drive the ball with authority to the opposite field. He’s still figuring out how to pull the ball, though, and he hit just one of his career-high 14 home runs to left field. Henry’s 29.5 percent strikeout rate and 18 percent whiff rate were among the highest in the Carolina League and led scouts to question whether he will make enough contact to apply his power at higher levels. Club officials do like Henry’s approach, though they also want to see him be more selective and make better swing decisions. Henry should be able to offer defensive value even if his bat doesn’t come to fruition. A quick release and a strong, accurate arm help Henry to combat the running game, and he threw out 38 percent of basestealers in the Carolina League after posting a 44-percent success rate in his first full season. He blocks well, showing athleticism and agility behind the plate, and the Brewers have been impressed with how Henry has developed a receiving style that utilizes his big, athletic frame. Overall, he has the makings of becoming a defense-oriented back who also hits for power at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-time Gatorade player of the year winner in Utah, Henry was headed for Brigham Young before the Brewers made him their sixth-round pick in the 2016 Draft and signed him for $550,600, nearly twice the recommended value for his slot. He showed promise on both sides of the ball the following year in the Rookie-level Pioneer League and continued to make strides in 2018 with the move up to Class A Wisconsin. Henry generates above-average raw power from the right side of the plate. He's already shown some feel for applying it during games, too, hitting some of his farthest home runs to right-center field. While there is present swing-and-miss to his game, as well as some pull-side tendencies, Henry has an advanced approach that nets him walks and suggests he'll hit for more average as he matures. In his first full season, Henry, who is praised for his energy and leadership skills behind the plate, threw out nearly 44 percent (46 of 105) of attempted basestealers and committed just six passed balls. A quick release and a strong, accurate arm help Henry to combat the running game, and club officials have been impressed with how he's developed a receiving style that utilizes his big, athletic frame. Overall, he has the makings of becoming a power-over-hit everyday catcher at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heasley fell to the 13th round in the 2018 Draft after posting a 6.98 ERA in 15 starts at Oklahoma State, but the Royals saw something in the right-hander and went above slot to sign him. He’s steadily improved in stuff, pitchability and presence since he became a Royal. His 3.33 ERA across 105 1/3 innings in Double-A last year earned him a jump to the Majors, where he impressed in three starts. Heasley’s velocity keeps ticking up since he became a pro; he can dial his fastball to 97-99 in short bursts and was averaging 94 mph in the Majors as a starter. He has four pitches, and his best secondary pitch is his above-average, 12-6 curveball. He didn’t throw his slider as much in the Majors, but it should be a solid offering for him moving forward. And he rounds out his arsenal with an effective changeup that he can use on both sides of the plate. Heasley has a repeatable delivery and walked just 34 batters in Double-A with 120 strikeouts, although he faced tougher hitters in the bigs and lost a feel for fastball command at times. Heasley gets high marks for his ability to field his position and control the running game, boasting one of the best pick-off moves in the organization. He received praise for how he handled the jump from Double-A to the Majors last year, and his competitiveness and talent will see him help the starting group this year and even compete for a spot in the Opening Day rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heasley had mixed results in two years at Oklahoma State and posted a 6.98 ERA in 15 starts as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2018. He fell to the 13th round, but the Royals thought he was better than his performance and went above-slot to sign him. He showed better stuff and improved pitchability in 2019 and was a late addition to the alternate training site in 2020 before finishing the year at Kauffman Stadium for the Royals' instructional league program. Heasley has unlocked more velocity as a pro thanks to a higher arm slot. His fastball sits at 92-95 mph with high spin but can get up to 97 mph. His 12-to-6 curveball is an above-average pitch, and he also has a slider that’s distinct from his other breaking ball. Heasley rounds out his arsenal with an effective changeup, and he’s not afraid to throw to either side of the plate with it. He has done a great job of repeating his delivery, and he gets whiffs not only because of his stuff, but also because he knows how to be successful with his sequencing. Heasley receives praise for his competitiveness on the mound and his ability to control the running game and field his position. He’s tightened up his body since he was drafted and looks more like a starter now after a solid beginning to 2021 at Double-A. The Royals project him as one still with his arsenal and makeup giving him the potential to be at the back end of the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heasley pitched to mixed results in two years at Oklahoma State, operating as a swingman as a freshman before moving into the rotation and posting a 6.98 ERA in 15 starts as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2018. The Royals believed he was better than his performance and went above-slot value to sign Heasley after taking him in the 13th round. After a nondescript pro debut, the right-hander showed better stuff and improved pitchability at Class A Lexington in 2019. He finished second among qualified South Atlantic League hurlers in ERA (3.12) and opponents’ average (.222) and made a pair of strong starts in the postseason to help the Legends claim their second straight league title. Heasley knows how to mix his four pitches, though nothing he throws is plus. A slight tweak to his arm slot has helped the right-hander unlock more velocity, and he spent his first full season sitting 92-95 mph with a high-spin fastball. His 12-to-6 curveball is an above-average pitch that can flash plus, and he does a good job turning over a changeup to impart fading action that is effective against both right-handed and left-handed hitters. Though he doesn’t overpower hitters, Heasley gets his share of whiffs because he knows how to be successful with sequencing, often pitching backward. His competitiveness enhances his cerebral approach on the mound, allowing him to profile as a potential back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A switch-pitcher with nearly equal velocity right-handed as left-handed as an amateur in Venezuela, Diaz became a full-time southpaw after signing for $600,000 in 2013. He missed all of 2015 after blowing out his right knee during a fielding drill but has otherwise been healthy. He helped Greenville win the South Atlantic League championship in 2017, then returned to low Class A last year and topped the SAL in wins (11), strikeouts (147) and innings (153). Diaz uses a low arm slot to create a lot of sink on a fastball that plays a grade better than its below-average 89-93 mph velocity, as evidenced by his 1.7 groundout/airout ratio through his first four seasons. Some evaluators think his changeup is his best secondary offering, while others point to a curveball more notable for its depth than its power. He also added a slider last season. None of Diaz's four pitches is better than average, yet he manages to succeed because he mixes and sequences them so well. With an effortless delivery, he repeatedly throws strikes and works the bottom of the zone, necessities for a pitcher with little margin for error. He'll have to keep proving himself at every level but is on the path to becoming a No. 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur in Venezuela, Diaz intrigued scouts with his ability to throw with nearly the same velocity right-handed as left-handed. The Red Sox made him a full-time southpaw after signing him for $600,000 in 2013, and he has shown impressive polish for his age ever since. He struggled for the first time when he posted a 7.03 ERA in his first seven starts in low Class A last year, then posted a 3.02 mark in his final 12, including a scoreless outing in the playoffs as Greenville won the South Atlantic League title. Diaz's fastball has jumped from 85-89 mph when he signed to 89-93 with room for more projection, and it's more notable for its sink than its velocity. He logged a 1.8 groundout/flyout ratio in his first three pro seasons, missing 2015 after blowing out his right knee during a fielding drill. He does a good job of maintaining his arm speed when he throws his solid changeup and also shows some feel for spinning an average curveball. Diaz isn't very physical but is athletic and repeats his effortless delivery. He fills the strike zone but will need to find a way to miss more bats as he faces more advanced hitters. While he doesn't have a huge ceiling, he has a high floor with a reasonable chance to become a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Diaz created intrigue with his ability to throw nearly as hard right-handed as left-handed. A full-time southpaw since signing for $600,000 out of Venezuela in 2013, he has impressed with his aptitude for pitching. He missed the entire 2015 season after blowing out his right knee during a fielding drill, then bounced back to rank second in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in strikeouts (57 in 60 innings) during his 2016 U.S. debut. Diaz's fastball velocity already has improved to from 85-89 mph when he turned pro to 88-93, still has room for more projection and features nice sink and run. He maintains his arm speed when he throws his deceptive changeup, which shows some signs of becoming a plus pitch, and he also has feel for spinning a curveball. While Diaz may lack size, he's very athletic and has a relatively effortless delivery that he repeats well. He not only fills the strike zone but also keeps the ball down, as evidenced by his 1.9 groundout/airout ratio in 2017 while making the jump to low Class A. He has a long way to go and doesn't have a huge ceiling, but he's also advanced for his age and could develop into a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moran remained in the Twins' organization despite being unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft following the wiped-out 2020 season, and the left-hander's performance shone across Double-A and Triple-A following an initially shaky taste of the high Minors in '19. His 109 strikeouts and 2.41 ERA in 67 1/3 innings earned him a late-season promotion to the Twins, where his control issues flared up and made for a challenging first MLB stint, though the stuff is there for the young Puerto Rican to join the Twins' recent pipeline from the island that has featured José Berríos, Eddie Rosario and Jose Miranda. A season missed due to bone chips in Moran's elbow spurred his move to the bullpen in 2017, and that's allowed him to lean heavily on his superb, disappearing changeup that generates huge swing-and-miss numbers against both lefties and righties. His fastball averages 93 mph with life, and he's worked hard to improve his slider from an essentially nonexistent pitch to a somewhat competitive in-game offering, though there's still work to be done there. To this point, his changeup has been good enough that the slider hasn't really mattered as much. He has the chance to occupy a leverage role in the Twins' bullpen sooner rather than later if he continues to progress with the slider and throws more strikes, though walks will always be a part of his game. He has struggled at times when deviating from his routine -- say, with a promotion to a new level -- and could benefit from his '21 MLB cameo in that regard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cal State Fullerton keeps sending strike-throwing machines to the big leagues, with Seabold following in the footsteps of Noe Ramirez, Dylan Floro, Thomas Eshelman and Justin Garza when he made a start for Boston in September. A Phillies third-round pick in 2017, he reached Double-A midway through his first full pro season and boosted his stock by starring in the Arizona Fall League in 2019. After the Red Sox acquired him in an August 2020 deal for Brandon Workman and Heath Hembree, he missed most of the first three months last year with elbow inflammation. Seabold's best pitch is clearly his changeup, a true plus offering (and sometimes better) in the low 80s with late fade and tumble that confounds hitters from both sides of the plate. He sets it up with a four-seam fastball with high spin and induced vertical spin, and though his velocity dipped a bit to 88-92 mph with a peak of 94 in 2021, his heater still didn't get hit hard. He could use a better breaking ball because his low-80s slider is merely average and he lacks trust in his softer curveball. Because he can't overpower hitters, Seabold tricks them by mixing his pitches and locations. He has a simple, efficient delivery and pounds the strike zone, though his control and command weren't quite as sharp last year as they had been in the past. He has a high floor as a likely back-of-the-rotation starter, though he'll have to prove he's durable enough dealing with oblique (2019) and elbow issues in his last two full seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seabold followed in the footsteps of future big leaguers Noe Ramirez, Dylan Floro and Thomas Eshelman at Cal State Fullerton, pitching the Titans to the College World Series in 2015 and 2017 and himself into the third round of the 2017 Draft. He reached Double-A midway through his first full season in the Phillies' system in 2018 but missed most of 2019 with an oblique injury before starring in the Arizona Fall League. Looking to upgrade its bullpen, Philadelphia traded him and Nick Pivetta to the Red Sox in August for Brandon Workman and Heath Hembree. Despite not having eye-popping stuff, Seabold has averaged more than a strikeout per inning as a pro. He’s throwing a bit harder than he did in his college days, typically working at 90-94 mph with his fastball and showing the ability to command it where he wants. His slider is an average offering yet generated a lot of swings and misses in the Arizona Fall League. He worked to improve his changeup while he was rehabbing and it’s an above-average pitch now with excellent downward action. A finesse pitcher, Seabold has to rely on changing speeds and locations to keep hitters off balance. He has continued to pound the zone in pro ball, averaging 2.1 walks per nine innings during his first three pro seasons. His floor stands out more than his ceiling, and he could fit in the back of a big league rotation in the near future if he can build on the progress he made in the AFL.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Phillies took Seabold in the third round of the 2017 Draft, the hope was the Cal State Fullerton product would be the kind of advanced college starter who could move rapidly through the system. While he did struggle a bit when he first got there, he did live up to his advanced billing by reaching Double-A in his first full season. Seabold is all about mixing his pitches, his overall feel for pitching and his command, rather than pure stuff, with three offerings that typically grade out as average. He will show an above-average fastball on occasion, with a tweak to his delivery helping him add a tick, though he usually sits in the 90-93 range. He mixes in his average changeup effectively and he'll show an average breaking ball. His ability to keep hitters guessing and fill up the strike zone will continue to be key for him moving forward. After initially struggling in Reading, Seabold made solid adjustments and pitched very well over the season's final month. If he can continue to show that kind of command and crispness of his pitches, he'll be ready to impact the back end of the Phillies rotation soon now that he's put the injury in his rearview mirror.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beer became a national sensation in his first year at Clemson, garnering honors as the consensus 2016 Freshman of the Year while also taking home the Dick Howser Trophy as national player of the year. He continued to produce over the next two years to finish his Tigers career with a .321/.489/.648 line and 56 homers in 188 games, during which he totaled more walks (180) than strikeouts (98). The Astros took Beer 28th overall in the 2018 Draft, and he continued to mash, hitting 12 homers over 67 games in his pro debut. He, along with J.B. Bukauskas, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas, was dealt to Arizona as part of the Zack Greinke deal in the middle of the 2019 season. Beer impressed at Arizona’s alternate training site in 2020 and then continued to excel in Triple-A last season. He was called up to make his Major League debut last September, but appeared in just four games before hurting his shoulder diving for a ball and undergoing season-ending surgery. Some initial mechanical tweaks that Beer made to his swing upon entering Houston’s system have paid off considerably for the left-handed slugger. He applies his booming raw power from line to line, making loud contact with a leveraged swing that’s conducive to hitting fly balls. He projects as an average hitter, one with an advanced approach, though there is some swing-and-miss in his game. To his credit, Beer made strides in this area in 2021, reducing his strikeout rate to 17.5 percent over 100 games, his lowest mark since his 67-game professional debut in 2018. He’s a below-average runner but moves better once underway. The jury is still out on Beer’s long-term defensive home. He saw some time in the outfield early in his pro career but has primarily played first base in the D-backs’ system. While his initial performance in the outfield was discouraging, Beer dedicated himself to improving defensively and has made notable gains over the past few seasons, giving club officials hope he’ll be at least serviceable in the outfield long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beer became a national sensation in his first year at Clemson, garnering honors as the consensus 2016 Freshman of the Year while also taking home the Dick Howser Award as national player of the year. He continued to produce during the next two years to finish his Tigers career with a .321/.489/.648 line and 56 homers in 188 games, during which he totaled more walks (180) than strikeouts (98). The Astros took Beer at the back end of the first round in the 2018 Draft, and he had already clubbed 16 homers at the Double-A level the following year before Arizona acquired him, along with J.B. Bukauskas, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas, in the Zack Greinke deal. Beer was a standout at Arizona’s alternate training site, showing more consistency on both sides of the ball, and continued to impress with Triple-A Reno in 2021. Some initial mechanical tweaks that Beer made to his swing upon entering Houston’s system have paid off considerably for the left-handed slugger. He applies his booming raw power from line to line, making loud contact with a leveraged swing that’s conducive to hitting fly balls. He projects as an average hitter, one with an advanced approach that nets him walks, although there is some swing-and-miss in his game. He’s a below-average runner but moves better once underway. The jury is still out on Beer’s long-term defensive home. He saw some time in the outfield early in his pro career but has played first base almost exclusively in the D-backs’ system. While his initial performance at the new position was discouraging, Beer dedicated himself to improving defensively at the alternate site and did just that. Club officials are pleased with the progress they’ve seen this season and are now bullish about Beer’s capacity to play the position, viewing his defense as at least serviceable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more prolific college hitters in recent history during his three years at Clemson, Beer was the consensus Freshman of the Year and won the Dick Howser Award as national player of the year in 2016 before finishing his Tigers career with a .321/.489/.648 line, 56 homers and nearly twice as many walks (180) as strikeouts (98). While concerns about Beer's pure hitting ability and overall viability in the field caused him to fall to the back of the 2018 Draft's first round, he still made a strong impression in his pro debut by slugging his way up to the Class A Advanced level after signing for $2.25 million. Beer produced even more promising results in his first full season, and he'd already advanced to Double-A when the Astros packaged him with J.B. Bukauskas, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas to Arizona in a Deadline deal for Zack Greinke. Houston made some mechanical tweaks to Beer's left-handed swing in hopes of enhancing his plate coverage and power, and they have worked well in his first two pro seasons, yielding 38 home runs across his first 189 games. He went deep 26 times in 2019 -- including 16 in his first 63 Double-A games -- and hit half of his homers to either left or center field. That line-to-line game power is Beer's carrying tool, but he also shows at least average hitting ability, with a knack for driving the ball in the air. Beer's power comes with some swing-and-miss and overall strikeout tendencies, though he's long showed a knack for coaxing walks and getting on base and finished tied for second in the Minors last season in hit-by-pitches (31). An underwhelming defensive outfielder with below-average arm strength during his time with Clemson and early in his pro career, Beer, who is a well-below-average runner, played mostly first base upon reaching Double-A, then played there exclusively after the season in the Arizona Fall League, committing five errors in 18 games. Beer has the type of power and hitting ability needed to profile either as a first baseman or a left fielder, but he'll need to develop into at least a passable defender at one of the two positions now that he's in the National League. The D-backs are hopeful that he'll make enough gains to handle first-base duties, noting his inexperience at the position as a reason to expect improvement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beer graduated from high school a semester early to enroll early at Clemson, where he was the consensus Freshman of the Year in 2016 and won the Dick Howser Award as national player of the year. He posted numbers as good as anyone's in college baseball during his three years with the Tigers: .321/.489/.648 with 56 homers and nearly twice as many walks (180) as strikeouts (98). Concerns about his ability to hit with wood and lack of athleticism dropped him to the Astros with the 28th pick last June, though he performed well in his pro debut and reached Class A Advanced after signing for $2.25 million. Beer had already slugged his way up to Double-A in his first full season when the Astros sent him, J.B. Bukauskas, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas to Arizona in a Deadline deal for Zack Greinke. Beer was the most polarizing player in the 2018 Draft. His proponents loved his strength and plate discipline, while his critics didn't like his less-than-smooth left-handed stroke or his persistent struggles with wood bats on the high school showcase circuit and with the U.S. collegiate national team. Houston made some mechanical tweaks to his swing in hopes of enhancing his plate coverage and power, and they have worked well in his first two pro seasons. While Beer set national records in the 50- and 100-meter backstroke as an 11- and 12-year-old, he's a limited athlete whose value will come almost solely from his bat. The Astros are trying to help him improve his quickness, but he's a bottom-of-the-scale runner with fringy arm strength. He showed well below-average range in left field before the Astros played him mostly at first base when he reached Double-A, and he'll need to prove capable at one of those two positions now that he's in the National League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays selected Lowe 13th overall in 2016 on the strength of his athleticism and gave him some early looks at third base. A year later, Lowe moved to the outfield full-time and has remained there ever since. He climbed one level per season from 2017 to 2019 but had yet to post an OPS above .800 until his breakout 2021 campaign at Triple-A Durham. The left-handed slugger produced a .291/.381/.535 line with 22 homers and 26 steals in 111 games and received a two-game cup of coffee with the big club in early September. Lowe sports arguably the loudest collections of skills in a deep Rays system. The 24-year-old has emphasized shortening his swing in recent years to cut down on strikeout issues, and while he can still get lengthy at times, those adjustments (along with some added strength) have helped buoy the hope that he can hit for a decent average. The next step could be evening out his splits with 17 of his 22 Triple-A homers coming off right-handers and a difference of 200 points between the two sides (.763 vs .996). The power could lead to 25-plus homers at the top level. Elsewhere, he is an easy plus runner who has always been a threat to steal in the pros. He draws strong reviews for his ability to cover ground in center, and his plus arm gives him another asset when playing the grass. He could stick up the middle or switch over to right without issue as he did at times for Durham. Lowe has the tools necessary to elbow his way more into a longer Major League look this summer and hold down a spot once there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way standout in high school, Lowe garnered Georgia Gatorade player of the year honors as a senior and was one of the more impressive all-around athletes available in the 2016 Draft. The Rays liked him more as a hitter and selected him with the 13th overall pick, then lured him away from a Florida State commitment with a $2.6 million bonus. He overcame a sluggish start in his full-season debut the next year and ultimately finished on a high note, hitting .296/.350/.415 with 24 extra-base hits and 14 steals over his final 72 games. The performance led to high expectations for Lowe's 2018 campaign, though he was unable to build upon that progress in the Florida State League, where his feel to hit backed up and resulted in below-average production. Lowe's athleticism and physical tools suggest he'll eventually make an impact at the plate, but right now he's still figuring out what type of hitter he is. He knows how to create leverage through the hitting zone and has added some loft since signing, though, so far, it hasn't yet translated to any uptick in usable power. But even as he's scuffled at the plate, Lowe has worked to improve his approach and become more selective. That progress was evident in 2018, as he trimmed his strikeout rate by nearly 3 percent from the previous year while simultaneously improving his walk rate from 8.3 to 10.3 percent. It gives him a solid foundation for further offensive development, and club officials are still bullish about Lowe's potential to hit for average and power. After struggling at third base during his pro debut, Lowe was shifted to center field and immediately proved a natural, covering huge amounts of ground with his plus speed and long, graceful strides. He's developed into the best defensive outfielder in the system and looks like a lock to stick in center field, where his offensive profile offers the most value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the 2016 Draft's more talented two-way players, Lowe garnered Georgia Gatorade player of the year honors as a high school senior after a dominant season with the bat and on the mound. Though he received consideration in both roles, the Rays liked him more as a hitter, so much so that they selected him with the 13th overall pick and gave him $2.6 million to forgo his Florida State commitment. Assigned to Class A Bowling Green for his full-season debut, Lowe overcame a sluggish start to post a .296/.350/.415 batting line with 24 extra-base hits and 14 steals over his final 72 games. Lean and athletic with a projectable frame and loud tools, Lowe has everything teams covet in a high-ceiling Draft pick. His left-handed swing is both quick and controlled, and he knows how to create leverage through the hitting zone with his long arms to generate considerable raw power, even if it is yet to manifest during games. The same bat path leads to quite a bit of swing-and-miss -- his 144 strikeouts in 2017 ranked seventh among Midwest League hitters -- though he is athletic enough to make the necessary adjustments to his swing in the coming years. Once he's done so, it doesn't take much to envision him hitting for both average and power. The Rays are confident in Lowe's abilities as a hitter and see the sky as his ceiling given the remaining physical projection in his ultra-athletic frame. After struggling at third base during his pro debut, Lowe was shifted to center field during fall instructional league and immediately proved a natural, with his plus speed and long, graceful strides fueling his impressive range. The Rays think he has a real chance to stick there, and he certainly has more than enough arm strength -- he pitched with a low-to-mid-90s fastball as a prep -- to handle either outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lowe was Georgia's Gatorade player of the year as a senior, and many scouts viewed him as the most talented two-way player in the 2016 Draft. The Rays liked him more as a hitter, so much so that they selected him with the 13th overall pick in June, and then gave him $2.6 million to forego his commitment to Florida State. They also signed Lowe's older brother Nathan, a first baseman out of Mississippi State, after drafting him in the 13th round. Lowe is lean and athletic, with a frame that oozes projection. The left-handed hitter has a quick, controlled swing and creates leverage with his long arms to generate considerable raw power. Lowe played third base during his pro debut but drew rave reviews for his performance in center field during instruction league, showcasing plus speed with long, graceful strides. The Rays will give him a chance to stick there, and he has more than enough arm strength -- he showed a low-to-mid-90s fastball as a prep -- to handle either outfield corner. The Rays are confident in Lowe's abilities as a hitter, and the view the sky as his ceiling given Lowe's remaining physical projection. Meanwhile, a return to the mound offers an intriguing fallback option for both parties should that not work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not only did Ortega get just $10,000 to sign, he did so in the middle of the 2014-15 international signing period in February. He was also 18, nearly ancient for that market. Suffice it to say that this signing came with little fanfare or expectations and Ortega was basically off the grid for the first four years of his pro career, spending a summer in the Dominican Summer League and one in the Arizona League before missing all of 2017 with injury. He pitched well enough, again with no attention, during his full-season debut in 2018, but then officially jumped on the radar with an All-Star season in the California League and a late promotion up to the Double-A Southern League in 2019. Ortega generates a ton of swing and miss with his fastball and curve, finishing last season with 10.9 strikeouts per nine innings. His fastball sits in the mid-90s now and touched as high as 99 mph last season, showing he can hit those upper levels regularly in relief stints. His curve also flashes plus and he took a big step forward in his feel for both pitches working off each other. While those two pitches are his bread and butter, he does have a slightly below average changeup. His biggest area of focus going forward is his command and control a year after walking 4.6 per nine innings. Ortega could succeed as a starter, even with a fringy changeup, if he can throw strikes because his other stuff is so good. If his control doesn’t improve, watching that fastball and breaking ball come out of the bullpen could be a lot of fun.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring at Jacksonville alongside future Orioles outfielder Austin Hays, Baumann became a third-round selection of Baltimore in 2017, signing for below-slot value ($500,000) and rising quickly. Baumann reached Class A Advanced in his first full season and threw a 10-strikeout no-hitter in ’19 at Double-A Bowie, where he blossomed into a standout in the O’s fast-improving system. But the pandemic and some arm trouble delayed Baumann’s debut until 2021, when he made four inconsistent September relief appearances. He touched the big leagues again in 2022, again in relief, spending most of his time in Triple-A in the bullpen as well. The 6-foot-4, 225-pound righty is an imposing presence on the mound, with broad shoulders and a strong lower half he uses to create a downhill plane that accentuates his stuff. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and flashes 98-99 mph at times. It has angle and carry that generates plus vertical movement, enabling him to miss bats up in the strike zone. Baumann has a simple, repeatable delivery but the arm action is long, leading to inconsistent command at times and risk of injury. Indeed, he was on the fast track before being shut down with a flexor strain late in 2019, and he was limited at the Orioles’ 2020 alternate site due to the issue. Those durability concerns mean Baumann could ultimately end up in the bullpen, where it's easy to envision his heater and plus power slider presenting a dominant combination late in games. But he also has the pitch mix to start, with an improving changeup and developing curve that remains a work in progress. Baumann showed an ability to maintain velocity deep in games in the Minors when healthy, but also struggled with walks, especially post-injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Atlantic Sun Pitcher of the Year at Jacksonville in 2015, Baumann caught the eyes of Orioles scouts when they arrived in north Florida to see former college teammate Austin Hays. The O’s tabbed Baumann in the same round as Hays a year later, signing him for below slot value ($500,000), thus beginning the big, physical righty’s quick climb through the system. Baumann reached the Class A Advanced Carolina League in his first full season, then pitched to a 2.31 ERA and threw a 10-strikeout no-hitter at Double-A Bowie in 2019. Baumann had his 2020 cut short due to an elbow strain that did not require surgery, and it isn’t expected to hinder his status for 2021. Standing 6-foot-4 and 225 pounds, Baumann uses his frame and simple, repeatable delivery to create a downhill plane that accentuates his stuff. His fastball sits 94-95 and flashes 98-99 mph at times, with late life that he maintains deep in games. A plus power slider is the better of his two breaking balls, thrown in the high 80s to elicit swings and misses. Baumann’s changeup has improved immensely since his college days, and he is still working to develop a fringy curve. Both will be integral in whether he ultimately sticks as a starter at the highest level. Baumann’s longer arm action has also led to command issues at times. If those are refined, Baumann’s durability and potential four-pitch mix give him a chance to be a mid-rotation starter in the big leagues. If not, his fastball-slider combination could be devastating late in games, making his floor that of an impact reliever. He’s next in line to debut in a group of exciting young Orioles pitchers that includes Dean Kremer, Keegan Akin, Zac Lowther and others.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Atlantic Sun Pitcher of the Year at Jacksonville in 2015, Baumann caught the eyes of Orioles scouts when they arrived in north Florida to see former college teammate Austin Hays. The O’s tabbed Baumann in the same round as Hays a year later, signing him for below slot value ($500,000), thus beginning the big, physical righty’s quick climb through the system. Baumann reached the Class A Advanced Carolina League in his first full season, then impressed there again before taking a big step forward at Double-A Bowie in 2019. Baumann pitched to a 2.31 ERA in 13 outings (11 starts) in the Eastern League last season, highlighted by a 94-pitch, 10-strikeout no-hitter in July. Standing 6-foot-4 and 225 pounds, Baumann uses his frame and simple, repeatable delivery to create a downhill plane that accentuates his stuff. His fastball sits 94-95 and flashes 98-99 mph at times, with late life that he maintains deep in games. A plus power slider is the better of his two breaking balls, thrown in the high 80s to elicit swings and misses. Baumann’s changeup has improved immensely since his college days, and he is still working to develop a fringy curve. Both will be integral in whether he ultimately sticks as a starter at the highest level. Baumman’s longer arm action has also led to command issues at times. If those are refined, Baumann’s durability and potential four-pitch mix give him a chance to be a mid-rotation starter in the big leagues. If not, his fastball-slider combination has the potential to be devastating late in games, making his floor that of an impact reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year removed from selecting Austin Hays in the third round, the Orioles once again tapped Jacksonville's talent pool in 2017, selecting Baumann, the Atlantic Sun Pitcher of the Year in '14, in the third round. Signing for below slot value at $500,000, Baumann looked like he might move relatively fast through the professional ranks, and he reached the Class A Advanced Carolina League in his first full season, pitching to mixed results there after he had opened the season with Class A Delmarva. With a focus on pitching to his strengths in 2019, the right-hander dominated during his return to Frederick and received a mid-season promotion to Double-A Bowie, where he fired a 94-pitch, 10-strikeout no-hitter in his third Eastern League start. A big and physical right-hander, Baumann can run his plus fastball up to 96-97 mph and will sit 94-95, using his height to his advantage to work on a downhill plane while throwing his heater with a ton of late life. He throws two breaking balls, a fringy curveball and a power slider at 89-91 mph that flashes above average, as well as a changeup that improved in 2019. Baumann misses his share of bats, although the effort in his delivery, along with his longer arm action, does raise questions about his ultimate command profile. Baumann's arm strength, durable frame and potential four-pitch mix will give him a chance to remain a starter, especially if he can make strides with his command and changeup. Should that not work out, shortening Baumann up and putting him in the bullpen would allow his fastball-slider pairing to play up and possibly expedite his arrival in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year removed from selecting Austin Hays in the third round, the Orioles once again tapped Jacksonville's talent pool in 2017 to land Baumann, the Atlantic Sun Pitcher of the Year in '14, in the third round. After an impressive pro debut in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League, club officials are cautiously optimistic that Baumann, like Hays, could move relatively fast through the professional ranks. That certainly was the case in Baumann's first full season, as he earned a promotion to Class A Advanced Frederick after making seven dominant starts for Class A Delmarva. A big and physical right-hander, Baumann can run his fastball up to 96-97 mph, but usually sits more in the 92-94 mph range, also using his height to his advantage to work on a downhill plane. He throws two breaking balls, a fringy curveball and a slider that flashes above average, as well as a promising changeup. Baumann is adept at missing bats, although the effort in his delivery, along with his longer arm action, does raise questions about Baumann's ultimate command profile. Baumann's arm strength, durable frame and potential four-pitch mix will give him a chance to remain a starter, especially if he can make strides with his command and changeup. Should that not work out, shortening Baumann up and putting him in the bullpen would allow his fastball-slider pairing to play up and possibly expedite his arrival in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castro grew up in Venezuela as a catcher and switched to pitching just three months before San Francisco signed him for $100,000 in July 2015. Tommy John surgery in 2017 restricted him to one inning in two years and he didn't make his full-season debut until 2021, when the Giants challenged him with a full-season debut in Triple-A last May. He responded by earning a September callup, allowing just a single unearned run in 13 1/3 innings in the Majors before making a couple of scoreless Division Series appearances, but scuffled this season before the Cubs claimed him on waivers in August. Castro displayed inconsistent fastball velocity and parked around 91-92 mph as a starter in 2019, then used his pandemic downtime to add strength and showed up at the instructional league in 2020 with a 92-97 mph four-seamer. He maintained that heat as a reliever last season, topping out at 98 mph and getting good carry up in the strike zone. He always has demonstrated good feel for his curveball, a low-80s offering with power and depth despite below-average spin rates. Though Castro repeats his simple delivery well and showed solid control in the past, he had bouts of wildness in Triple-A last year with his improved stuff and has struggled to throw strikes in 2022. He flashed an average changeup as a floor-over-ceiling starter and theoretically could try to make it as a starter if a need arose. If he can rediscover the strike zone, he can bolster Chicago's bullpen after the club dealt three relievers at the '22 Trade Deadline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castro grew up catching in Venezuela and moved to the mound just three months before the Giants signed him for $100,000 in July 2015. Tommy John surgery in 2017 cost him all of that season and limited him to one inning in the next, so he didn't make his U.S. debut until 2019. Though he worked just 89 2/3 frames in his first five pro seasons -- none in full-season ball -- San Francisco added him to its 40-man roster in November after he used his pandemic downtime to get stronger and his velocity trended up at instructional league. After Castro's fastball sat around 91-92 mph and its velocity wavered in his first year back from elbow reconstruction, his four-seamer operated at 92-95 and reached 97 last fall. He long has demonstrated feel for spin, and his curveball showed improved power and depth during instructs. His changeup needs more consistency but shows the makings of an average third pitch. Before his stuff took off this fall, Castro impressed the Giants with some of the best control in the system. He repeats his simple delivery well and led the short-season Northwest League in walk rate (1.7 per nine innings) in 2019. He'll remain a floor-over-ceiling starter to open 2021 but could shift to the bullpen in the near future if San Francisco looks to expedite his development now that he's on the 40-man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 22nd-round pick by the Yankees out of Seattle University in 2017, Junk is now on his third organization, having moved from New York to the Angels for Andrew Heaney at the 2021 Trade Deadline and then the Halos to the Brewers in a November 2022 deal for Hunter Renfroe. The right-hander’s breakout came in 2021, when he posted a 1.78 ERA with 68 K’s at Double-A Somerset in his final stop in the Yanks' system, and he spent most of 2022 at Triple-A Salt Lake, where he posted a 4.64 ERA with 69 strikeouts and only 18 walks in 73 2/3 innings. Junk made seven appearances (six starts) during his two years with LA but couldn’t manage to stick in Anaheim. Junk sits around average velocity with a 91-93 mph fastball, but a decent spin rate helps it play better up in the zone. His low-80s slider has become his best offspeed pitch with good sweep across the zone, and he upped its usage in 2022 to the point where he was throwing it about as equally as the fastball. As a result, he relied less and less on his upper-70s, 12-to-6 curveball and was barely using his firm upper-80s changeup by season’s end. Throwing strikes hasn’t been an issue for the 6-foot-1 hurler over the last two seasons, and his 5.8 percent BB rate was sixth-best in the Pacific Coast League (min. 70 IP) in 2022. That will keep Junk a part of Milwaukee’s starting depth heading into his first campaign in the system, and any further uptick in stuff, whether it be more velo or a sharper curve as a third offering, could earn him a longer look as a No. 5.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the first few years of his pro career after the Yankees took Junk out of Seattle University in the 22nd round of the 2017 Draft, he did little to distinguish himself as a prospect. Using the shutdown as a time to really get to work, he emerged in '21 as a different pitcher, one who had a 1.78 ERA and .185 batting average against in 14 Double-A starts when he was sent to the Angels for Andrew Heaney at the Trade Deadline. He took a perfect game into the ninth inning in his fifth start with his new organization, then was called up and made four September big league starts. He jumped between Triple-A and the Majors in '22 before being traded again in November, this time to the Brewers in a four-player deal for Hunter Renfroe. Junk leans heavily on his low-90s fastball, a four-seamer that can touch 96 mph and has high spin rates and carry up in the zone. He features both a slider and a curve, thrown roughly around the same velocity in the 78-81 mph range, with the former a bit better with excellent sweep. As a result, he threw the slider around 38 percent of the time in 2022, almost three times as often as his other breaker. He throws his fringy upper-80s changeup much less frequently than his other three offerings. The 6-foot-1 right-hander’s control took a big step forward in 2021, a big reason for his consistent success. At 26, he’s a bit old for a prospect, but the late bloomer is ready for a more consistent big league role, either as a back-end starter or perhaps in the bullpen where his four-seamer and slider might play up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Tigers 2013 first-rounder Jonathan Crawford, Kutter taught himself a cutter during Christmas break in 2016 before posting the second-best ERA (1.71) and third-most strikeouts (99, trailing two seasons by Chris Sale) in Florida Gulf Coast history. A 16th-round pick in 2017, he reached Double-A before blowing out his elbow late in the 2019 season. Following Tommy John surgery that fall and a second operation to remove bone chips from his elbow in the summer of 2020, he looked better than ever last season and made his big league debut with a September start. Crawford's returned from his elbow reconstruction with a better fastball and curveball than before. His heater added a couple of ticks of velocity, sitting at 92-95 mph and reaching 97 with carry up in the zone, while his upper-70s curve went from an offering he could land for strikes to flashing as a plus offering with improved depth. His mid-80s cutter was his best weapon before he got hurt but played mostly as an average pitch in 2021. Crawford also has a mid-80s changeup with splitter action, but he doesn't trust it much because he struggles to throw it for strikes. He has good control of the rest of his repertoire, though he got knocked around in Triple-A and the Majors when his command faltered. He could be a back-of-the-rotation starter or useful multi-inning reliever if he can figure out a way to handle advanced left-handed hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ironic for a pitcher named Kutter, Crawford didn't begin throwing the pitch until he taught himself one during Christmas break in 2016. The following spring, he recorded the second-best ERA (1.71) and third-most strikeouts (99, trailing only two seasons by Chris Sale) in Florida Gulf Coast history and signed for $125,000 as a 16th-rounder. The younger brother of Tigers 2013 first-rounder Jonathon Crawford, he topped the system with 157 strikeouts and advanced to Class A Advanced in his first full pro season. Crawford gets most of his strikeouts with, appropriately enough, his mid-80s cutter. He sets it up with a fastball that has improved from 88-92 mph in college to 91-95 in pro ball, though it lacks life. His curveball and changeup aren't anything special but he can land them both for strikes. Crawford has good spin rates and delivers all of his pitches from the same release point. He's a fly-ball pitcher without much margin for error, and he has struggled in 2019 as his control and command have regressed. Though he lacks a high ceiling, he eventually could help the Red Sox as a back-of-the rotation starter or middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltner both started and relieved during his three years at Ohio State, with mixed results, though he was virtually unhittable as a closer in the Cape Cod League in 2017. When the Rockies took him in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft, it was because they thought he had the goods to start at the next level. His development on that front was slow going at first, but things clicked a bit more in 2021 as the right-hander started the year in High-A and made his big league debut last September. The 6-foot-4 right-hander does have a solid enough three-pitch mix to give him the chance to start, though there’s still work to be done in terms of command and execution for him to stick in that role. While he can crank his fastball up into the mid-90s in shorter stints, he’s more likely to sit in the low-90s as a starter. Even without premium velocity, he misses bats up in the zone and the Rockies want him to be effective down as well so he isn’t so predictable with his heater. He can land his mid-80s slider for strikes and also will take something off to fold in a get-me-over slower curve on occasion. He has feel for a changeup, but the Rockies would like to see him use it more. Tweaks to shorten his arm action in back paid dividends in 2021 as he repeated his delivery more effectively and showed signs of being able to pitch to both sides of the plate. There’s still hope he can land in a rotation, even if the fastball-slider combination would look very good in the 'pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltner’s three-year career at Ohio State was up-and-down, serving in both starting and relief roles. He was, however, lights out closing in the Cape Cod League in 2017, which undoubtedly opened a lot of eyes. So even though his junior season as a starter for the Buckeyes was inconsistent, he landed in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft. The Rockies have been developing him as a starter and after a strong summer pro debut, he struggled pitching in the hitting haven of Asheville in 2019. He was dominant, albeit as a 24-year-old, during his time in instructional league play last fall. The progress Feltner made in workouts over the summer and then at instructs revolved around his delivery and ability to command his power stuff. He was 95-97 mph with his fastball at instructs and his slider played a lot better than it did in 2019, an 86-87 mph breaking ball with better action and lateness to it. He’s always had a good changeup with good fade. Feltner shortened up his arm circle in back, allowing him to get to a more consistent release point and he was repeating his delivery more last fall. That helped his stuff tick up while he was able to command his pitches relatively well. He has the stuff to start, but if the command gains don’t stick, his fastball-slider combination could be really nasty in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltner worked as a swingman over his first two years at Ohio State, then was absolutely dominant as a reliever on the Cape the summer of 2017, opening the eyes of many scouts. His results as a full-time member of the rotation during his junior year were mixed, but scouts still liked his stuff enough for him to land in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft. His pro debut after he signed made it look like the Rockies had gotten a steal as he didn’t walk anyone and missed a ton of bats, but his first full season was a lot more up and down. Much of the difficulties Feltner had in the South Atlantic League last year can be tied to delivery issues he’s continuing to clean up. He has a tendency to kick out his front leg, tends to be a little too merry-go-round with his body and doesn’t always stay on top of the baseball. When he’s on line and on top, he’s a major strike thrower who can get weak contact and miss bats with a three-pitch mix, headlined by a fastball that’s up to 97 mph and a solid average changeup that has good fade to it. His slider is behind, but has a chance to be his third at least average offering. Feltner fought through some elbow soreness and fatigue during the 2019 season, but was able to come out of it and pitched well over his final five starts of the year. If he can iron out his mechanical issues on the mound, he still has the chance to be the rotation piece the Rockies thought they were getting in the Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltner spent three years mostly starting for Ohio State, with mixed results. But scouts always liked his pure stuff. That, plus a dominant turn in the Cape Cod League in 2017 was enough for the Rockies to take Feltner in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft, and he responded to their faith in him by pitching very well in his brief pro debut in the rookie-level Pioneer League. Feltner's composure and maturity have already made a strong impression on the Rockies, and he's shown, at least early, more feel to pitch than anticipated. He challenges hitters with a fastball that sits at 94 mph and touches 97 regularly. His changeup is his best secondary offering, thrown with fade and excellent arm speed deception. His slider currently isn't a true weapon, and he focused on improving his breaking ball over the offseason so it becomes more viable. Feltner showed better command than he had at Ohio State, with an ability to work to all four quadrants of the strike zone. If that continues, he has the chance to start. If not, he showed that his stuff plays very well when he closed during that stint on the Cape.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Reds for $70,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2012, Siri set a Midwest League record with a 39-game hitting streak in 2017, when he topped the Low-A circuit with 46 steals and added 24 homers, but he couldn't replicate that success. He bounced to the Mariners and Giants on waivers in the spring of 2020 before the Astros signed him as a free agent that November. He tore up Triple-A last summer to earn his first big league callup in September, homered four times in 46 at-bats and wound up starting two games in the World Series. Siri has demonstrated impressive raw tools for years but hasn't been able to find consistent success at the plate. His approach didn't change much in 2021, as he was still very aggressive and pull-happy and struck out at a 31 percent clip. He was able to get to his plus raw power and reach base more than ever before, though it's unclear how sustainable his performance will be if he doesn't add more plate discipline. Siri doesn't have to hit for a high average to help a team. His plus-plus speed makes him a weapon on the bases -- he stole 27 bags in 31 attempts last year -- and an asset in center field. He has the quickness and strong arm to provide quality defense at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he put it all together during a breakout 2017 -- which included 20 homers and 40 stolen bases, not to mention a Midwest League record 39-game hitting streak -- Siri initially struggled in 2018. A left thumb ligament injury suffered early during Spring Training games when he crashed into the wall trying to make a catch made it tough for him to get on track. Brimming with tools and athleticism, Siri could play center field in the Major Leagues right now. With Billy Hamilton departed, there is no center fielder in the system who can get to a fly ball or line drive like Siri can. And his cannon arm also enables him to be a good right fielder. Offensively, he has well above-average raw power, but he still lacks in pitch selection and discipline while being super-aggressive at the plate, keeping him from tapping into that power consistently. Eric Davis has been working with him and had Siri move his hands down on the bat to create more leverage. He possesses great bat speed and can create good backspin on the ball. Now is the time for Siri to put it all together, especially after seven years in the organization and being 23 years old. On any given day, a scout could give him 70 and 80 grades across the board. But he needs to improve his emotional control and be pushed at times to reach what still appears to be a high ceiling. As one scout said, \"He'll show the tools at 5 o'clock, but will it translate at 7?\"

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: To call Jose Siri's 2017 season a breakout might be a bit of an understatement. Always blessed with tremendous raw tools, the outfielder started using them more consistently, finishing with a 20-40 season that placed him first in the Midwest League in stolen bases and second in home runs. He kept his hot bat going with a very strong showing in the Dominican Winter League, but then started the 2018 season on the disabled list after suffering ligament damage in his left thumb. When Siri makes contact, it's loud, and he has the ability to drive the ball, and out of the park, to all fields. His power showed up more consistently in 2017, but whether he'll be able to get to it as he moves up will be dependent on his ability to refine his approach. His strikeout-to-walk ratio needs a lot of work as his aggressiveness at the plate leads to a lot of swings and misses and few free passes. He's a plus runner and then some, one who will continue to steal bases and cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He certainly can play center field long term and his cannon arm plays very well in right. Siri might always be one of those super-aggressive hitters who succeeds because of his ridiculous tools and athleticism. But the abilty to improve his approach at the plate could allow him to become an impact, All-Star caliber player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez piqued the interest of White Sox scouts in high school before batting just .262 in three college seasons at Miami, though he did perform well with wood bats and earn all-star honors in the Cape Cod League in 2017. Looking for a versatile defender in the later stages of the 2018 Draft, Chicago signed him for $125,000 in the 18th round, but he didn't do much while primarily playing the outfield in his first two pro seasons. He shifted to the middle infield last year after coming back from the pandemic layoff, and he batted .283/.364/.532 with 24 homers and 24 steals in 93 games between Double-A and Triple-A to earn his first big league callup. At 6-foot-2 and 215 pounds, Gonzalez is bigger and more powerful than most middle infielders. His strength and bat speed create solid to plus raw pop, and he taps into it with an aggressive approach. His right-handed stroke can get long and leads to swings and misses, so he'll probably always be a power-over-hit guy. Gonzalez has solid speed and translates it into stolen bases. His hands and arm grade as average, and he's more capable of playing several positions than a standout at any of them. He's a decent shortstop who probably profiles best at second base, and he also has seen action everywhere but catcher in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted as a senior out of Division II Cal State Stanislaus in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft, Ryan quickly showed he was much more than a money-saving senior sign when he pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season.
