A pure projection pick out of high school, Greene has filled out his 6-foot-3 frame and how has a premium fastball that sits in the mid-90s with ease and touches triple digits at times. When he is throwing well, he throws downhill and with sink to elicit ground ball outs, but too often the heater has flattened out of late, leading to him being more hittable than he should be. So does his lack of consistent secondary stuff. Both his power breaking ball and his changeup will show glimpses of being average, if not better, but an inability to repeat his release point has made it tougher for him to throw them effectively and has resulted in surprisingly low strikeout rates. Command is still a huge issue for Greene, with his 83 walks in 2017 placing him sixth in all of the Minors. The Cardinals let him start and get his innings at the start of 2018, but moved him to the bullpen when he was bumped up to Triple-A, with the hopes he'll develop into a high-octane reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken by the Blue Jays in the seventh round of the 2013 Draft, Greene spent his first three seasons in Rookie ball before breaking out in '15, when he excelled at both Class A levels and finished the year at Double-A New Hampshire at age 20. While he pitched well in the Florida State League and held his own after a mid-year promotion to Double-A in 2016, Greene's overall control regressed and he missed fewer bats than at any point in his career, a trend that carried over into his return to the Eastern League in 2017. The Blue Jays sent him to St. Louis in January in the Randal Grichuk deal. Pure projection when he entered the Blue Jays' system, Greene started to grow into his athletic frame and saw his stuff tick up as a result. That physical growth shows most through his plus-plus fastball, which, after topping out at 92 mph in high school, now sits in the mid- to upper-90s and routinely hits triple digits, though it can be straight at times. His best secondary pitch is his fading changeup that he throws with convincing arm speed from the same slot as his fastball, giving him a weapon against left-handed hitters. Greene's hard slider in the mid-to-upper 80s is ahead of his fringy curveball, but his release point for both offerings will vary, in turn affecting their shape and action. Greene has struggled to both get ahead of and put away hitters the past two seasons, often picking at corners rather than trusting his stuff and attacking hitters. He's continued to post solid ground-ball rates and keep the ball in the park, and his athletic delivery and high three-quarters slot leave room for improved control and command. If it all clicks, Greene could develop into a starter, though a late-inning bullpen role may be a more realistic option for the right-hander.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The power Terry showed as a Georgia high schooler intrigued scouts but his righty-hitting, first-base-only profile did not, so he lasted 13 rounds in the 2015 Draft. After giving up a Georgia State commitment to sign for $100,000, he didn't reach full-season ball until his fifth pro season, but once there he batted .293./.362/.537 with 25 homers between two Class A stops in 2019. He was the Rangers' best hitter in instructional league last fall, though they opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster for the second straight year. Terry still sticks out most for his prodigious pop, which he creates with bat speed and the strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-2, 258-pound frame. Though he primarily looks to pull balls in the air, he makes a reasonable amount of contact for a slugger -- and most of it's loud. He doesn't draw many walks, however, and may need more patience when he faces more advanced pitchers. Though he works hard to maintain his conditioning and improve his defense, Terry is still an all-bat player. He's a well below-average runner with limited range at first base, and he has a below-average arm while throwing from a low slot. He's not the slam-dunk DH he looked like when he entered pro ball but he's really going to have to hit to become a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a shortstop in his first two seasons at NCAA Division II Le Moyne (N.Y.), Gray became a full-time pitcher in the Cape Cod League during the summer of 2017. He went 11-0 and ranked third in D-II with a 1.25 ERA in ‘18, when he joined the Reds as a supplemental second-round pick in June and went to the Dodgers as part of the Yasiel Puig/Matt Kemp trade in December. Gray reached Double-A and won the Los Angeles' Minor League Pitcher of the Year Award in his first full pro season and spent his second refining his secondary pitches at the club's alternative training site. He made his Major League debut on July 20, 2021, but he was moved to the Nationals nine days later in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner Deadline blockbuster. Having been traded twice already, Gray has been on the move very much because of other organizations looking to bring him in rather than anybody trying to get rid of him. Hitters have difficulty catching up to Gray's 92-97 mph fastball, which seems to explode at the plate with riding and rising life. He sharpened both of his breaking balls at the alternate training site, tightening up and adding some power to his mid-80s slider while improving his feel for his upper-70s curveball. His changeup is more of a work in progress because he didn't use it much in college, and it features some sink but gets too firm at times. The athleticism that made Gray a shortstop translates well to pitching. He repeats his delivery well and shows the ability to harness his electric fastball and slider. He was one of the toughest competitors in the system and brings that tenacity to a Nationals pipeline in need of potential stars.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers executed a masterful trade with the Reds in December 2018, not only clearing roster spots and salary by unloading Yasiel Puig, Alex Wood, Matt Kemp and Kyle Farmer but also adding a pair of players who quickly blossomed into Top 100 Prospects in Gray and shortstop Jeter Downs. Gray spent most of his first two seasons at NCAA Division II Le Moyne (N.Y.) as a shortstop before becoming a full-time pitcher in the Cape Cod League during the summer of 2017. He went 11-0 and ranked third in D-II with a 1.25 ERA to propel himself into 2018's supplemental second round, then reached Double-A and won Los Angeles' Minor League pitcher of the year award in his first full pro season. Gray generates a lot of swings and misses with his 92-97 mph fastball, which seems to explode at the plate with riding and rising action. He has the makings of a second plus pitch in a sharp low-80s slider, and he also has added a curveball to give hitters a softer look. He didn't use a changeup much in college so it still needs work, showing some sink but often lacking enough velocity separation from his heater. The athleticism that allowed Gray to play shortstop at the college level translates well to the mound. His delivery isn't the smoothest but he repeats it well, commands his fastball and is improving his ability to locate his secondary offerings. He's a potential No. 3 starter who should be able to help the Dodgers in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Los Angeles cleared roster spots and salary when it traded Yasiel Puig, Alex Wood, Matt Kemp and Kyle Farmer to Cincinnati in December, and it also landed a pair of quality prospects in middle infielder Jeter Downs and Gray. The latter spent most of his first two seasons at NCAA Division II Le Moyne (N.Y.) as a shortstop before becoming a full-time pitcher in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2017. After he went 11-0 and ranked third in D-II with a 1.25 ERA last spring, he signed with the Reds for $772,500 as a supplemental second-round pick. Gray works with a 90-95 mph fastball that tops out at 97 with nice carry in the strike zone, generating velocity with a quick arm and maintaining it deep into games. His low-80s slider shows sharpness and signs of becoming a plus pitch, and he has recently added an effective curveball. He didn't use his changeup much in college but made some progress with it in his pro debut and the Dodgers believe it could become a solid third offering. The athleticism that made Gray a shortstop also allows him to pound the strike zone with his fastball. If he can refine his secondary pitches and command, he could become a mid-rotation starter. If he winds up in the bullpen, he might sit in the mid-90s with his lively heater.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $30,000 in May 2014, Garcia has moved slowly through the Phillies' system pitching largely in relief, but often being given a chance to start to see if his three-pitch mix could work in a rotation. A full-time move to the bullpen allowed him to reach Triple-A for the first time, and he was rewarded with a spot on the 40-man roster in the offseason. Garcia's fastball-slider combination works extremely well in shorter stints out of the bullpen. With a live arm and athletic delivery, Garcia will throw his fastball in the 92-95 mph range and touches a tick higher regularly. He routinely misses bats with his slider, which flashes plus. His changeup was a work in progress, but as a short reliever, it's possible he can be just a two-pitch pitcher, though that would limit his value. The right-hander won't need pinpoint command, though he'll have to continue to be around the strike zone consistently. If he can do that, and develop his changeup to be a weapon against a lefty, he could pitch late in games in Philadelphia soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed back in May of 2014, Garcia has been brought along slowly by the Phillies by pitching largely in relief. There has long been talk of his skills translating to the rotation -- he did make four starts in the South Atlantic League in 2016 -- and he was moved into the Clearwater rotation in late May in 2017. The 20-year-old Garcia has a fastball that hits 95 mph regularly in shorter stints, and his slider is a true out pitch that misses plenty of bats. He has a changeup that will need to continue to develop for him to remain a starter. A good strike-thrower, Garcia shows a lot of confidence on the mound and goes right after hitters. It might take longer for him to develop as a starter, and the Phillies are more than willing to remain patient. As a reliever, Garcia could follow Edubray Ramos and perhaps Victor Arano in a line of power arms that started slowly then took to a role and moved rapidly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mets for an over-slot $150,000 in the 18th round of the 2015 Draft, Humphreys was breaking out during his full-season debut two years later when he blew out his elbow, requiring Tommy John surgery in August 2017. A second operation to address an ulnar nerve issue in his elbow delayed his return until June 2019 and he pitched only two innings in Rookie ball last year, but he allowed just one run in 11 2/3 Arizona Fall League frames and landed a spot on New York's 40-man roster. He was designated for assignment twice in 2020 and changed organizations each time, going to the Giants in a trade for Billy Hamilton in July and to the Indians via waivers in November. Humphreys' best pitch is his fastball, which plays better than its 90-94 mph velocity because of its riding life and his ability to command it to any quadrant of the strike zone. Both of his secondary pitches presently grade as average but show flashes of becoming better than that. He has a tight upper-70s curveball with promising spin rates and a changeup that he sells well with fastball arm speed. Humphreys pounded the strike zone before he got hurt, averaging just 1.6 walks per nine innings in his first three pro seasons before issuing five in 13 2/3 innings in 2019. He offers the upside of three solid pitches with plus control, though he's also 24 years old and has worked just 11 innings above low Class A. Cleveland probably won't know exactly what it has in Humphreys until he returns to game action in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buford High School, Marsh’s alma mater in Georgia, has produced some solid baseball talent in the past, namely Joey Bart, who went on to Georgia Tech and became the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 Draft. Marsh is the first player to get taken from Buford in the top two rounds, taken No. 60 overall by the Angels. A two-sport star who helped Buford win state titles in football, Marsh’s combination of athleticism and feel for hitting have allowed him to climb to the top of the organizational ladder, though some minor injuries have slowed his ascent. Throughout his pro career, Marsh has shown an ability to make hard contact and get on base, with a walk rate over 10 percent to show for it. With strength and bat speed, there’s always been raw power to tap into, but he hadn’t done much of that until 2019, when a change in his setup at the plate -- standing more upright -- helped him slug .520 in August and .522 in the Arizona Fall League. He continued to get to his power at the Angels’ alternate camp in 2020, hitting seven homers in just over 100 at-bats, showing power to all fields, while still walking at a 20-percent clip. Marsh’s other three tools -- his speed, arm and defense -- are all plus and were all consistently on display at the alternate camp. He has the goods to play center field long-term, but can easily handle either corner to flank Mike Trout in the Angels’ outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport starter who was a wide receiver and outfielder at his high school in Georgia, Marsh has always been blessed with tools and athleticism. The only thing that has slowed him at all have been some minor injuries, a back issue that didn't allow him to debut the summer after he was a second-round pick in the 2016 Draft and a sprained ankle that forced him to miss about a month of the 2019 season. In between, he's performed everywhere he's gone, reaching Double-A last season at age 21, finishing with a very strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. While Marsh has always shown a good feel to hit, he took a big step forward in his overall approach and setup at the plate in 2019. He worked with the Angels to stand more upright from the left side of the plate and that enabled the rest of his swing to click into place. That resulted in a .357/.429/.520 August and carried over into his .328/.377/.522 AFL campaign. He's always been willing to draw walks, but he cut down on his strikeout rate and had an above league average 19 percent miss rate in 2019. That not only will help him continue to hit for average but will also allow him to keep getting to his power more consistently, as he did late in the season. Marsh's plus speed is an asset on the basepaths and in the outfield. He can steal a base and he's proven to be a plus defender in center field to go along with a plus arm. He's obviously not going to play center for the Angels, but luckily has no problem sliding over to either corner for whenever that first call to the big leagues comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Angels took Marsh in the second round of the 2016 Draft, they knew it might take a while for his raw tools and athleticsm to come into focus on the field, especially since his focus was split at his Georgia high school as a standout wide receiver and outfielder. He wasn't even able to start his pro career in earnest until 2017 because of a back injury. The Angels didn't want to get too excited about his debut in the Pioneer League that summer, but it was hard not to be encouraged by his 2018 that saw him play across both levels of A ball. While Marsh had a very productive first taste of full-season ball, what makes him an even more intriguing prospect is that he still has a lot to learn, especially at the plate. He does have a good feel to hit and showed he's more than willing to draw walks, but there is a lot of swing and miss there and he does need to work on the consistency of his swing. Once he does that, he should be able to hit for average and power. His speed works on both sides of the ball, and he showed the ability to steal a base and run down everything in center field. Marsh showed he can be a plus defender at all three outfield positions, and his plus arm certainly would play in right. He and top prospect Jo Adell form a super-athletic outfield prospect duo that could be ready to join Mike Trout in about a year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marsh is a product of a strong high school program at Buford High in Georgia, one who excelled both on the diamond and on the gridiron as a wide receiver. The Angels loved his upside and athleticism enough to take him in the second round of the 2016 Draft, but they had to wait to see him play until 2017 as a back issue was found in his post-Draft physical. The wait was worth it, as he was one of the more exciting players in the Rookie-level Appalachian League. Despite having split his focus among two sports in high school, missing his summer debut and then being out for a short spell with a thumb injury in 2017, Marsh has a very good feel to hit and the Angels feel he could be at least an above-average hitter in time. He makes consistent hard contact, recognizes pitches well and should grow into at least average power. A plus runner who can steal a base, Marsh has more than enough speed to play center field and a plus arm that would fit perfectly well in right. The Angels were excited to see what Marsh could do over the course of a full, healthy season as he continues to grow into his athletic frame, and he hasn't disappointed, playing across two levels of A ball and forming an exciting 1-2 outfield punch with 2017 first-rounder Jo Adell.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It's never a bad thing to try and target up-the-middle athletes in the Draft. For the past two years, the Angels have gone that route early, taking Jahmai Jones in 2015 then taking Marsh a year later, also in the second round. A back issue found in his physical delayed his signing and the Angels erred on the side of caution and held him out of play last summer. Marsh didn't play in games during instructional league games in Arizona last fall, but he did finally see some action in their Dominican instructs program after that and he is ready to hit the ground running in 2017. Marsh has bat speed and strength, with the chance to eventually be an above-average hitter with solid average power from the left side of the plate. Marsh runs well and has a strong arm that would work well in right field, though the Angels believe he could stay in center long term because of his athleticism. He has the kind of build and athleticism that reminds some of a Josh Hamilton type player. Marsh needs reps and to get on the field so he can start sharpening his raw tools and reach his considerable ceiling. If it all clicks, he has a chance to be a five-tool player manning an outfield spot in the big leagues on a daily basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran has blown away expectations since the Red Sox drafted him in the seventh round out of Long Beach State in 2018. He had a scintillating pro debut that summer, played in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and reached Double-A in his first full pro season and arrived in Boston halfway through his second after playing for Team USA in an Olympic qualifier. He struggled in his first taste of the big leagues, however, striking out in 36 percent of his plate appearances. The best athlete and fastest runner in the Red Sox system, Duran has plus-plus speed that allows him to beat out routine grounders and wreak havoc on the bases. Boston has helped him rework his left-handed swing since he has turned pro, allowing him to drive the ball much more consistently as he has added some loft and is doing a better job of using his lower half. While he's now a legitimate 20-homer, 40-steal threat, his stroke got too uphill during his Red Sox debut and he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact to reach his potential. A second baseman in college and during his first month in pro ball, Duran lacks experience in center field and it shows. He has improved his reads and routes but they still need more work, and he often relies on his speed to overcome his mistakes. His fringy arm strength is playable in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran has raised his profile significantly since Boston made him a seventh-round pick out of Long Beach State in 2018. He posted a .910 OPS in his pro debut and hit .387 in high Class A during the first two months of 2019 before appearing in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and spending the second half of his first full season in Double-A. The Red Sox are excited by the offensive and defensive gains he made at their alternate site last summer, which paid off with an MVP award in the Puerto Rican Winter League playoffs and a .400/.500/.640 line at the Caribbean Series. Duran's best offensive tool is his plus-plus speed, which helps him routinely beat out grounders and makes him a dangerous basestealing threat, as evidenced by his 70 swipes in 199 games during his first two pro seasons. Though he showed some ability to backspin the ball, scouts had concerns about how much impact he might have when he slugged just .325 in Double-A. But after he added some loft to his left-handed swing and started better incorporating his lower half at the plate at the alt site, some club officials believe he could produce 20 or more homers per season. Because he spent his college career and his first month as a pro at second base, Duran still is learning the nuances of outfield play. He's making progress with his reads and routes in center field, and his speed helps him overcome some of his mistakes. He has fringy arm strength but could compensate by getting to balls more quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-rounder out of Long Beach State in 2018, Duran is believed to be the lowest Draft pick ever to play in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game during his first full pro season. He posted a .910 OPS in his pro debut, then flirted with batting .400 in Class A Advanced during the first two months of 2019. He struggled in Double-A following a June promotion, but the Red Sox nevertheless are excited by how much he has exceeded initial expectations. With a compact left-handed swing built for contact and plus-plus speed, Duran routinely beats out ground balls for hits and creates havoc when he's on base. After slugging .377 in three years of college, he posted a .527 mark at his first three pro stops and showed some affinity for backspinning balls from gap to gap. Most of his power comes to the opposite field, though it diminished when he got to Double-A, leaving scouts split as to whether he'll be more than a slap hitter. Duran spent his college career and his first month in pro ball at second base before becoming a full-time outfielder. He has been slow to develop instincts for his new position, often taking poor routes to balls and relying on his quickness to overcome his mistakes, and he has fringy arm strength. There's a wide divergence in his possible outcomes, from a solid center-field regular to an extra outfielder with one better-than-average tool.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran's plus-plus speed led the Red Sox to sign him for $189,000 as a seventh-rounder in the 2018 Draft. They weren't expecting much power after he had slugged .377 in three years at Long Beach State, so his .357/.394/.516 debut was a pleasant surprise. He quickly established himself as the fastest player and top outfield prospect in the system, and he built on that by dominating Class A Advanced early in 2019. Duran has a left-handed stroke geared for line-drive contact and his quickness can make routine ground balls a challenge for the defense. While he won't be a slugger, he has the ability to backspin the ball from gap to gap and drove the ball more consistently once he stopped spreading out in his stance like he did in college. He's still honing his basestealing acumen, but he has the speed to be a force on the bases. A second baseman for the 49ers, Duran spent his first month in pro ball at the keystone before shifting to the outfield. He needs to improve his reads and jumps but is fast enough to outrun a lot of his mistakes and should become a solid center fielder once he gains more experience. He has fringy arm strength but it isn't a liability because he gets to balls quicker than most outfielders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Raleigh, whose uncle played for a long time in the Minor Leagues and father played and coached college ball, has more than lived up to the expectations typically laid upon players who grew up around the game. The Mariners’ third-round pick in 2018 out of Florida State, Raleigh made it to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball and led all Minor League catchers with 29 home runs. He followed that up with nine homers at the alternate training site in 2020 in what was perhaps the best offensive performance of any player there. Raleigh has been tabbed as an offensive-minded catcher, and the power he showed at Florida State has carried over to the pro game. He definitely has a better power tool over hit, but he controls the strike zone well enough that his tremendous raw power shows up from both sides of the plate. He can drive the ball to all fields, with more success from the left side. From a raw power numbers perspective, Raleigh ranks right up there with elite catching prospects like Joey Bart. His biggest area of improvement would be cutting down his 23% strikeout rate, but he will likely show better strike zone command with more Minor League reps. Despite his reputation with the bat, Raleigh has made significant strides with his defense. His receiving metrics have been off the charts and his blocking has been great. He also has wowed with his ability to communicate with and lead a pitching staff. Having already formed a close bond with Logan Gilbert, Raleigh has helped pitchers learn their game plans and held them accountable -- signs of a big leaguer in the making. Raleigh’s lowest floor would be a platoon backstop in the big leagues, while his ceiling could be a starting regular, particularly given his switch-hitting ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There is an expectation when you grew up around the game that you’re going to soak up information and use it on the field quickly, perhaps even move quickly in the pro game. Raleigh, whose uncle played for a long time in the Minor Leagues and whose father played and coached collegiate ball, has more than lived up to that expectation. The Mariners’ third-round pick in the 2018 Draft out of Florida State, the backstop made it to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball and led all Minor League catchers with 29 home runs. Raleigh has always had the reputation of being an offensive-minded catcher and the power he showed at Florida State has carried over to the pro game. He’s definitely power over hit, but he controls the strike zone well enough so that his tremendous raw power shows up from both sides of the plate. He can drive the ball to all fields, with more success in finding the seats from the left side. He’s made even greater strides with his defense. While his arm is approaching average and he needs to work on his footwork, he’s accurate and he threw out nearly 30 percent of potential basestealers in 2019. After attending a program the Mariners instituted called GCU -- Game Calling University -- Raleigh showed the ability to take that information and apply it to his game, evolving into an above-average receiver with excellent framing skills. A natural leader who works very well with his pitching staff, Raleigh is looking more and more like a big league starting backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last Florida State catcher to make it to the big leagues was Buster Posey. While the Mariners don't expect Raleigh, taken in the third round of the 2018 Draft after a solid offensive junior season with the Seminoles, to reach that All-Star level, his very strong pro debut on both sides of the ball have them encouraged about his potential. Raleigh has some baseball bloodlines, with a dad who played and coached college ball and an uncle with a long professional resume. It shows in his advanced approach at the plate, with the ability to control the strike zone enough to tap into his considerable raw power from both sides of the plate. He entered pro ball with a reputation as an offensive-minded backstop and though his bat is ahead of his glove, the Mariners were pleasantly surprised with his defensive tools, particularly his framing and game-calling, not to mention excellent leadership skills. The one part of his defensive game that's behind is his arm, but Raleigh was on a throwing program during the offseason and worked on using his lower half more. If that part of his game improves, he has the chance to join Posey as a big league regular behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a decorated amateur career that included MVP honors at the 2013 Perfect Game All-America Classic and an impressive turn with the 18U U.S. national team in the World Cup in Taiwan, Reetz became the first Nebraskan prep to be picked in the top five rounds since 1996 when the Nationals made him their third-round pick in 2014. A myriad of injuries have kept Reetz from developing as Washington had hoped he would, and he played more than 69 games just once in his first five seasons while struggling at the plate. Reetz continued to struggle in his return to Class A Advanced Potomac in 2019, batting .220 with one home run in 46 first-half games. After that, however, he arguably was the Carolina League’s most productive hitter, batting .282 with 12 home runs over his final 50 games. The Nationals attributed Reetz’s improvement to the adjustments he made with his setup and hand positioning, noting that the combination helped him achieve a strong hitting position more consistently. Reetz also did a better job attacking pitches in the zone, and did so without it detracting from an approach that has resulted in a .357 OBP in six pro seasons. Defensively, Reetz stands out most for the arm strength and catch-and-throw skills that helped him throw out a career-high 41 percent of basestealers in 2019. He continues to earn high marks for his makeup and work ethic and became the seventh recipient of the Bob Boone Award -- given annually to the Nationals Minor Leaguer who best demonstrates the professionalism, leadership, loyalty, passion, selflessness, durability, determination and work ethic required to play the game the ‘Washington Nationals Way.’ -- in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reetz had a decorated prep career, garnering MVP honors at the 2013 Perfect Game All-America Classic before starring for the 18U U.S. national team in the World Cup in Taiwan. The Nationals drafted him in the fourth round the following year, making Reetz the first Nebraskan prep to be picked in the top five rounds since 1996. While he has made progress in the subsequent years, especially as a defender, injuries in back-to-back years have kept Reetz from developing as hoped. Despite having a quick right-handed swing that yields line drives across the whole field, Reetz has struggled to hit for average as a pro. The same can be said about Reetz's power, though he does hit the ball consistently harder now after learning how to better apply his lower half in 2016. Reetz continues to show plate discipline and a solid approach at the plate, qualities that some within the organization believe will help his bat to eventually come around. Defensively, Reetz stands out most for the arm strength and catch-and-throw skills that produced a career-best caught-stealing rate of 31 percent in 2017. He continues to earn high marks for his makeup and work ethic, and club officials are quick to note his great relationship with Nats catching coordinator Michael Barrett, who has helped him to improve as a receiver and game-caller. But after logging just 230 games across his first four seasons, Reetz now faces an uphill battle towards reaching the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout during the 2013 showcase circuit, Reetz garnered MVP honors at the 2013 Perfect Game All-America Classic before starring for the 18U U.S. national team in the World Cup in Taiwan. The Nationals drafted him in the fourth round the following year, making Reetz the first Nebraskan prep to be picked in the top five rounds since 1996. After having his first full pro season marred by injury, Reetz moved up to Class A Hagerstown in '16 and flashed his potential on both sides of the ball. While hasn't built on that performance as hoped this season, Washington was pleased enough with Reetz's progress that they promoted him to the Carolina League in July. A right-handed hitter, Reetz has a quick swing that yields line drives across the whole field. The Nationals worked with Reetz to improve his lower-half setup during the season, and it resulted in harder contact and better pitch recognition as the season unfolded. He's physically strong and has average power potential, though it may be a few years before he learns how to get to it in games. Even if the power never arrives, Reetz's plate discipline and approach give him the chance to be a quality hitter. Reetz is a good athlete with a solid set of tools that could help him stick behind the plate, and the Nationals have been pleased with his progress as a receiver and game-caller. Though still quite raw, he has solid-to-average arm strength and promising catch-and-throw skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knehr saw time as a two-way player at Fordham, but he showed more promise as a pitcher and the Padres drafted him as one in the 20th round in 2018. He reached Class A Fort Wayne in his pro debut and spent his first full season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, where he averaged 11.3 strikeouts-per-nine over 17 appearances (12 starts). The Padres had Knehr work out of the bullpen exclusively in that year’s Arizona Fall League, and he built upon that progress with a standout performance at fall instructional camp in 2020. Knehr built on that success in 2021 and made his Major League debut in July, appearing in 12 games and throwing 29 innings. Knehr’s stuff has improved in the pro ranks as the right-hander has shifted his focus to pitching only. He throws his high-spin fastball around 93-95 mph with late movement that helps him induce a mixture of whiffs and weak, ground-ball contact. His changeup is effective against hitters on both sides of the plate, flashing plus on occasion and playing nicely off the fastball. He rounds out his arsenal with an above-average slider. Knehr looks the part of a Major League reliever, with his 6-foot-2 frame, crisp stuff and natural strikeout tendencies, but he will need to improve his control in order to reach his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knehr saw time as a two-way player at Fordham, but he showed more promise as a pitcher and the Padres drafted him as one in the 20th round in 2018. He reached Class A Fort Wayne in his pro debut and spent his first full season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, where he averaged 11.3 strikeouts-per-nine over 17 appearances (12 starts). The Padres had Knehr work out of the bullpen exclusively in that year’s Arizona Fall League, and he built upon that progress with a standout performance at fall instructional camp in 2020. Knehr’s stuff has improved in the pro ranks as the right-hander has shifted his focus to pitching only for the first time. He throws his fastball around 93-95 mph with late movement that helps him induce a mixture of whiffs and weak, ground-ball contact. His changeup is effective against hitters on both sides of the plate, flashing plus and playing nicely off the fastball, and he can miss bats with a useful slider as well. Knehr looks the part of a future Major League reliever, with his 6-foot-2 frame, crisp stuff and natural strikeout tendencies, but he will need to develop more control in order to succeed at higher levels. He showed improvement on that front late in 2020, giving the right-hander some helium heading into the 2021 season and his eventual Major League debut in July.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 70 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 Bruján signed for just $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic in October 2014, and he stood out as a steal almost immediately. When he completed his first full season in 2018, he posted a .320 average with 55 steals (second-most in the Minors) at Class A and Class A Advanced. After a 48-theft season in 2019, he was added to the 40-man roster and spent 2020 at the alternate training site and on the postseason taxi squad. Bruján was with Triple-A Durham for the majority of 2021 (hitting .262/.345/.440) and featured in 10 games with the big club in his debut campaign. Bruján puts bat to ball often, although the drop in average with Durham takes some shine off a plus hit-tool projection, and is a better overall hitter from the left side. Thanks to an increased fly-ball rate, his power did take a jump with a career-best 12 homers in 2021, and he showed off better exit-velocity numbers, enough to bump up his pop ceiling. His best asset remains his plus-plus speed, and he’s as good as anyone in the Minors at putting it to use on the basepaths. The majority of Bruján’s starts came in the outfield for the first time in 2021, and he played all three spots in both the Majors and Minors. His infield work was concentrated at second base -- partly in deference to Wander Franco -- but he saw time at third and short as well. Bruján’s athleticism and above-average arm will make him an option anywhere for the Rays, and his best chance at getting in the lineup every day might be to keep bopping around based on need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brujan came with little fanfare as an international amateur, signing with the Rays for $15,000 in 2014. He looked like one of the biggest steals from that year’s class when he led the Minors in runs (112) and finished second in stolen bases (55) in his first full season, then solidified his top-prospect status by reaching Double-A at age 21 in 2019. The Rays added Brujan to their 40-man roster after the season, and he spent the 2020 campaign at the alternate training site before joining Tampa Bay’s taxi squad in the postseason. Brujan structures his game around the plus-plus speed that helped him rack up 103 steals in his first two full-season campaigns. His quickness is as impressive as his pure speed, and they both allow him to get out of the box well and create hits from both sides of the plate. Solid bat-to-ball skills with a knack for making line-drive contact fuel Brujan's projection as a plus hitter, and he has long demonstrated that he can control the strike zone. He drives the ball more consistently while showing some sneaky pop from the left side of the plate -- all 13 of his home runs in 2018-19 were against righties -- while his right-handed stroke is geared toward putting the ball in play to utilize his wheels. Those wheels also make Brujan a rangy defender on the infield. He profiles as a near plus defender as a second baseman and can hold his own at shortstop even though his solid arm strength is stretched thin there. The Rays also began trying him out in the outfield during Spring Training, giving him starts in center and right field, with the idea of potentially making him an even more versatile, Ketel Marte-type up-the-middle player. He profiles better at the keystone long term and looks the part of a future top-of-the-order hitter with his blend of hitting ability, on-base skills and speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brujan was an under-the-radar international signing in 2014, when the Rays inked the Dominican native for just $15,000, but he's quickly developed into one of the more dynamic top-of-the-order prospects in the game. After a breakout first full season in 2018 in which he led the Minors in runs scored (112) and finished second in steals (55), Brujan continued his climb towards the big leagues in 2019 and reached Double-A as a 21-year-old following an All-Star campaign with Class A Advanced Charlotte. He continued to perform well after the season in the Arizona Fall League, prompting the Rays to add him to their 40-man roster in November. One of the more prolific basestealers in the Minors, Brujan followed up his 55-steal full-season debut by finishing tied for fourth in MiLB with 48 steals in 2019. He wreaks havoc on the basepaths with his plus-plus speed and quick feet, but is still learning how to be an effective basestealer and owns a 72.6 percent success rate (151 of 208) across his first five seasons. His advanced bat-to-ball skills and knack for making hard contact from both sides of the plate fuel Brujan's projection as a plus switch-hitter, and he already demonstrates an understanding of the zone. He drives the ball more consistently and shows some sneaky pop from the left side of the plate -- all 13 of his home runs in the past two seasons have come against righties -- while his right-handed stroke is more contact-oriented, geared towards putting the ball in play so as to utilize his speed. That said, his splits did become more pronounced in 2019, as he batted just .202/.286/.266 against southpaws compared to .301/.365/.429 versus righties. Brujan's speed makes him a rangy defender at second base, where he profiles as a slightly above-average defender with solid arm strength, and he also held his own last season in his first action at shortstop (29 games) since his 2015 pro debut. Brujan's defensive tools and skills are better suited for the keystone long-term, and it's easy to envision him developing into a dynamic top-of-the-order presence with his blend of hitting ability, on-base skills and speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, Brujan made his stateside debut two years later and then flashed his top-of-the-lineup potential in '17 by ranking among the Class A Short-Season New York-Penn League leaders in a host of offensive categories. He was even more impressive last year with the move up to full-season ball, as Brujan led the Minors in runs scored (112) and finished second in steals (55) while hitting .320/.403/.459 with 41 extra-base hits in 122 games between the Midwest and Florida State Leagues. The switch-hitting Brujan is advanced from both sides of the plate. He already knows how to control the strike zone at a young age and recognizes pitches well, with bat-to-ball skills and a knack for making hard contact that lead scouts to project him as a plus hitter in the future. He has sneaky raw power in his left-handed swing, and it was from that side that he hit all nine of his home runs in 2018. His right-handed swing is more contact-oriented. That Brujan rarely strikes out and takes his walks to go along with natural hitting ability underscores his potential as a top-of-the-order presence, a profile that's only enhanced by his plus-plus speed and aggressiveness on the basepaths. Brujan's wheels translate to good range at second base, where he profiles as a slightly above-average defender with average arm strength. The Rays have no shortage of promising middle infielders in their system, though none can rival Brujan's upside as a true leadoff man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brujan quickly has blossomed into one of Tampa Bay's more promising middle-infield prospects since signing for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014. He spent parts of the next two seasons in the Dominican Summer League before finally making his U.S. debut with Class A Short Season Hudson Valley in late 2016. Returning to the New York-Penn League last season, Brujan broke out in earnest, hitting .285 with 23 extra-base hits while ranking among the circuit leaders with 74 hits (first), 51 runs scored (first), 108 total bases (first), 16 steals (fifth) and a .378 on-base percentage (fifth). The switch-hitting Brujan is advanced from both sides of the plate. He already knows how to control the strike zone at a young age and recognizes pitches well, with bat-to-ball skills and a knack for making hard contact that led scouts to project him as an above-average hitter in the future. That Brujan rarely strikes out and has strong on-base skills to go along with natural hitting ability underscores his potential as a top-of-the-order presence, a profile that's only enhanced by his well-above-average speed and impact potential on the basepaths. Brujan's wheels translate to exceptional range at second base, where he profiles as a slightly above-average defender with average arm strength. Tampa Bay's glut of middle-infield depth could complicate his rise through the Minors, though there are many evaluators who believe Brujan could make a smooth transition to center field should the need arise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fairchild's intriguing mix of power and speed prompted the Reds to take him in the second round of the 2017 Draft and pay him full slot value. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular first full season of pro ball, playing across two levels of Class A ball, but then jumped up the rankings after making good strides at the plate and reaching Double-A in 2019. The D-backs were able to acquire him at the Trade Deadline in 2020 in the Archie Bradley deal and, he made his Major League debut with the club on July 6, 2021. Fairchild doesn't have a big flashy set of tools, but he does everything well. He got off to a slow start in 2019 as he made adjustments to his swing that allowed him to recognize pitches sooner and get to the ball quicker. Once he found his swing consistency, it clearly started clicking for him, with an .824 OPS after his promotion in the second half of the season. He controls the strike zone well, hits the ball hard and has above-average speed. Fairchild has a lot of attributes the D-backs value -- strike zone judgement, versatility and good instincts for the game. He can play all three outfield positions and his floor is that of a backup outfielder, but he could grow into more. He spent the winter hitting almost every day with fellow prospect Corbin Carroll. D-backs manager Torey Lovullo values players he can trust and Fairchild is that type of player -- you know what you're going to get from him every game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Reds went high school heavy at the start of the 2017 Draft, taking prepsters with four of their first five picks. The one exception was Fairchild, who brought an intriguing power-speed combination from Wake Forest to the organization as a second-round pick who signed for full pick value. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular first full season of pro ball, playing across two levels of Class A ball, but then jumped up the rankings after making good strides at the plate and reaching Double-A in 2019. With the Reds seeking a playoff berth in 2020, the club traded Fairchild and Josh VanMeter to Arizona in the Archie Bradley Deadline deal. Fairchild got off to a slow start in ’19 as he made adjustments to his swing that allowed him to recognize pitches sooner and get to the ball quicker. Once he found his swing consistency, it clearly started clicking for him, with an .824 OPS after his promotion in the second half of the season. He has mistake power and that pop enabled him to hit 12 homers last season. Fairchild is a plus runner who can move well on the bases, but he must improve his stolen base techniques after being caught stealing seven times in 13 attempts last season. His speed and skills in the outfield allow him to be a plus defender at any of the three spots with a decent arm. He has the skills to be a big league regular, with a floor of being a very valuable fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 An early second-round Draft pick in 2017 who received a bonus of just over $1.8 million, Fairchild had a very solid debut season playing center field for Billings in the Rookie-level Pioneer League. In 2018, he moved up and split the year in low-A and high-A but still needs to figure out who he is as a hitter. Fairchild is kind of a \"tweener\" in that he has middle-of-the-road tools that don't necessarily stand out in any one spot, but he is still a very consistent and sound fundamental player. He has a chance to be a good hitter with solid on-base skills. The power he currently has is less of an asset, and it's unlikely he will grow much more to add more pop. He could likely turn on a ball in a damage count, but if he tries to add power, he could lose some of his on-base acumen and hitability. A very good defender with a good arm and capable of playing all three spots, Fairchild is a smart runner and is a capable basestealer. Put it all together and he could be a good fourth outfielder or a starter on a second-division club because he lacks the power for the corner spots and the burner speed for center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 50 A strong junior season that wiped out a rough sophomore campaign at Wake Forest vaulted Fairchild into early round talk prior to the 2017 Draft. He landed early in the second round and got a touch over $1.8 million, a slight shade below pick value, to sign. He went out and had a very solid debut playing center field for Billings in the rookie-level Pioneer League. The Reds were pleasantly surprised with how good Fairchild's approach was during his debut. There was an expectation of more swing and miss than there was; instead he struck out just 15 percent of the time while drawing a fair amount of walks, with it looking like he should carry a Major League average hit tool with him. Fairchild hit 17 homers in his junior year, but Wake Forest is a very good place to hit for power, so it remains to be seen if those numbers will transfer to the pro game. A plus runner, Fairchild can steal a base and he had better reads in center field than he did in college. If his pro debut is any indication, Fairchild could start moving a little faster and develop into a big league regular in center, perhaps a No. 2 type hitter. If the power shows up, he could have a bigger impact than anticipated.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beasley began his post-high school career on the junior college circuit, at Darton State College in Georgia. He transferred to Clemson and pitched in relief as a junior, albeit not with good results. The Angels liked his stuff enough to take a flier on him in the 30th round of the 2017 Draft. After being sent out as a reliever during his pro debut, Beasley got a chance to start and ran with it, pitching his way across three levels and finishing the year in Double-A. Beasley relies heavily on a fastball-splitter-changeup trio to get hitters out. He'll throw his fastball in the low-90s with occasional life. His split-finger changeup is his out pitch, and it's a good one, thrown in the low-80s with tumble that can miss bats and get weak contact. He mixes in a breaking ball as well and has shown the ability to throw strikes, with all three pitches coming from a quick and repeatable delivery. In all likelihood, Beasley ends up back in the bullpen, where his fastball-split combination could play up. His success as a starter has opened some eyes, and at the very least, he has shown he could be a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox signed Burger for $3.7 million as the 11th overall pick in 2017, making him the first Missouri State position player ever selected in the first round and envisioning that his power would get him to Chicago quickly. Instead, he ruptured his left Achilles tendon running out a ground ball in February 2018, tore it again during rehab three months later and severely bruised his left heel in 2019. After losing those two seasons to injury and 2020 to the pandemic shutdown, he returned last year to bash 18 homers in 82 Triple-A games and go deep once during his 15-game big league debut. Burger's significant strength and solid bat speed create plenty of raw power from the right side of the plate, though he'd be able to tap into more of it if he could shed a propensity for hitting balls on the ground that has marked his brief pro career. He does make a lot of hard contact, as evidenced by his average exit velocity of 98 mph and maximum of 115 mph during his stint with the White Sox, and he uses the entire field. He was more aggressive last year than he was in college or during his pro debut, and he may need a more disciplined approach to succeed against big leaguers. Though he's a stocky 230-pounder and can look awkward at times, Burger is deceptively athletic and got into better shape while recovering from his leg injuries. He can flash average speed out of the batter's box, but he doesn't make much happen on the bases. While his range might be a bit limited at third base, he has soft hands and solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Missouri State position player taken in the first round, Burger has had a star-crossed pro career since signing for $3.7 million as the 11th overall choice in 2017. After a modest debut that summer, he didn't play in an official pro game the next three years after rupturing his left Achilles tendon running out a grounder in February 2018, tearing it again during rehab three months later and severely bruising his left heel in 2019. He did see action last year in the CarShield Collegiate League and at Chicago's alternate site and instructional league program. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Burger generates at least plus raw power with strength and solid bat speed. He made hard contact and drove the ball to all fields while training at the alt site and instructs in 2020. He evokes comparisons to Todd Frazier because he's a stocky right-handed hitter with some arm bar in his swing, though he manages the strike zone better and makes more consistent contact than the two-time All-Star. Burger can look awkward at times, but the White Sox believe he has recaptured most or all of the deceptive athleticism he had before he tore his Achilles. Before he got hurt, he displayed average speed out of the batter's box and was a little quicker once he got going. He has the soft hands, solid arm and enough range to stick at third base, though it won't be easy to displace Yoan Moncada from the hot corner in Chicago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Missouri State position player ever drafted in the first round, Burger signed for $3.7 million as the 11th overall pick in 2017. After a modest pro debut that summer, he missed his first two full seasons with injuries. He ruptured his left Achilles tendon running out a grounder in February 2018, tore it again while rehabbing three months later and lost all of 2019 to a severely bruised left heel. Burger's strength and solid bat speed give him at least plus raw power and helped him rank second in NCAA Division I with 21 homers as a sophomore and encore with 22 more in his Draft year. As a stocky right-handed hitter with some arm bar in his stroke, he draws comparisons to former White Sox third baseman Todd Frazier. He manages the strike zone well and makes repeated contact, so he projects as a better hitter than Frazier. Though he's more awkward than graceful, Burger had deceptive athleticism before injuries stuck. He showed average speed out of the batter's box and was quicker underway, though it remains to be seen how fast he'll be following three leg injuries in two years. He has the soft hands, solid arm strength and enough range to remain at third base, though Yoan Moncada has established himself at the hot corner in Chicago while Burger has been sidelined.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burger slammed 21 homers (second in NCAA Division I) as a Missouri State sophomore in 2016 and 22 as the Missouri Valley Conference's player of the year in 2017, helping him become the first position player in school history ever selected in the first round. Signed for $3.7 million as the 11th overall choice, he missed all of last season after rupturing his left Achilles tendon while running out a grounder in February and tearing it again while rehabbing in May. He lost the 2019 season as well when he severely bruised his left heel during his rehab. Burger has the strength and solid bat speed to provide 25 or more homers on an annual basis, and he was working on making adjustments to hit more balls in the air after a ground ball-heavy debut. As a stocky right-handed slugger with some arm bar in his stroke, he has drawn comparisons to former Chicago third baseman Todd Frazier. He has a patient approach and a penchant for making contact, so he should be a better hitter than Frazier. While Burger can look more awkward than graceful, he's a deceptive athlete who gets the job done in all phases of the game. Before he got hurt, he displayed average speed out of the batter's box and was even quicker underway. He has decent range, reliable hands and solid arm strength at third base and should be able to stay at the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox snagged one of the best power hitters available in both the 2016 and 2017 Drafts, spending first-round picks on catcher Zack Collins and Burger. The latter bashed 21 homers (second in NCAA Division I) as a sophomore and 22 (en route to winning Missouri Valley Conference player of the year honors) as a junior last spring, becoming the first Missouri State hitter ever taken in the first round. Signed for $3.7 million, he had little trouble adjusting to low Class A pitching in his pro debut but missed all of 2018 after rupturing his left Achilles tendon while running out a grounder in February and then tearing it a second time while rehabbing in May. Because he's a stocky right-handed slugger with some arm bar in his swing, Burger draws comparisons to former Chicago third baseman Todd Frazier. With his strength and solid bat speed, he could produce 25 or more homers annually, though he needs to make adjustments to hit more balls in the air after posting a 1.5 groundout/airout ratio in his first taste of pro ball. With his patient approach and ability to make consistent contact, he should hit for average as well as power. Burger isn't the most graceful athlete but gets the job done in all phases of the game, making him sort of a corner-infield version of Hunter Pence. He's quicker than he looks, displaying average speed out of the batter's box and decent range at third base. With a solid arm, reliable hands and a strong work ethic, he should be able to stick at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson performed better as an outfielder than a pitcher at Utah before requiring Tommy John surgery that wiped out his 2017 season. The Dodgers still drafted him in the 12th round and signed him for an over-slot $247,500 that June, brought him along slowly for a year and have seen him make rapid progress since. He led their system in strikeout rate (11.1 per nine innings) in 2019, spent 2020 at the club's alternate site and instructional league program, then rocketed from Double-A to Los Angeles last year. Jackson has more athleticism and arm speed than most pitchers and can reach 98 mph with a four-seam fastball with late finish, though he operated more in the low 90s in 2021. His best offering for much of last season was a plus mid-80s changeup that drops off at the plate. He has replaced a soft downer curveball with a mid-80s slider that has more power than bite in his efforts to find a reliable breaking ball, and he might turn to more of a cutter in the future. Raw on the mound when he began his pro career, Jackson has worked hard to develop a more compact and consistent delivery. It has paid off with better control, as he went from averaging 5.0 walks per nine innings during his first two seasons in the Minors to 2.8 in his third. He could be a useful starter if he regains some velocity and refines a third pitch, and more of a multi-inning reliever if he can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson had more success in college at Utah as an outfielder than he did on the mound, posting a 6.53 ERA in brief action over two seasons before having Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of 2017. The Dodgers still drafted him in the 12th round and signed him for an over-slot $247,500 that June, then didn't have him make his pro debut until May 2018. He led the system in strikeout rate (11.1 per nine innings) in 2019, then jumped on the 40-man roster last November after seeing time at Los Angeles' alternate site and instructional league program. More athletic than most pitchers, Jackson has a quick arm that generates 92-96 mph fastballs that top out at 98 with some late finish. He presently shows more feel for his changeup than he does for spinning the ball, and his low-80s changeup is a plus offering with some sink. His 78-82 mph curveball has its moments and he has developed a mid-80s slider/cutter since turning pro. Still raw on the mound at the start of his pro career, Jackson has worked to develop a more steamlined and consistent delivery. After averaging 5.0 walks per nine innings during his first two pro seasons, he's doing a much better job of attacking hitters and providing strikes in 2021. He has erased questions about whether he can remain a starter and drew a lot of interest from other clubs at the Trade Deadline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at Utah, Jackson had more success as a part-time starter in the outfield than he did on the mound, where he posted a 6.53 ERA in brief action before having Tommy John surgery that cost him all of his 2017 junior season. The Dodgers still took him in the 12th round and signed him for an over-slot $247,500 that June, then delayed his pro debut until May 2018. When they finally turned him loose last season, he led the system in strikeout rate (11.1 per nine innings). Jackson is extremely athletic and possesses a quick arm that delivers 92-96 mph fastballs that reach 98 and feature late finish. Despite his relative inexperience on the mound, he currently shows more feel for his solid changeup than he does for spinning the ball. His 78-82 mph curveball shows some signs of effectiveness and he's also working on a mid-80s slider/cutter. Far from a finished product on the mound, Jackson doesn't always attack hitters or provide as many strikes as he should. He'll continue to get innings as a starter but could wind up as a reliever if he can't add enough polish. Coming up with a reliable breaking option will be key as he faces more advanced hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Reds expected big things from Gutierrez when they signed him in 2016 for $4.75 million, when he was a Top 30 international prospect out of Cuba. However, the right-hander has not consistently performed anywhere near what the expectations have been. The 2019 season was rough in almost every way as he posted a 6.04 ERA and 1.40 WHIP in 27 starts with Triple-A Louisville. His progress took another hit when he was given an 80-game suspension for testing positive for performance-enhancing substance Stanozolol last June. If not for a decent final month of the 2019 season, it would've been a total setback year for Gutierrez. Relying on analytical data more, he learned how his best pitches matched up with hitters and it's something he will have to continue to do in 2020. It's a big year for Gutierrez, who still has good stuff that includes a plus fastball and plus changeup and can pitch effectively when he has the good tempo he showed in 2018. The Reds still feel that Gutierrez has value and potential as a starter once he returns from his suspension. But if a need arose on the big league club, his stuff would play as a reliever and he could transition to a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Reds are no strangers to being aggressive on the international market, particularly when Cuban players become available. They jumped at the chance to sign Gutierrez, who was No. 4 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list when he got $4.75 million from the Reds to sign. After impressing early with his bullpen sessions and showing initial polish similar to fellow Cuban Raisel Iglesias, the right-hander appeared to get away from his strengths during a rocky first pro season in 2017. The 2018 season was a nice step forward for Gutierrez. He did a good job of finding his delivery, which enabled him to stay on top of the ball better and created a better angle. As a result, he had better action on his pitches and a more consistent break on his curveball, which lost its sharpness when he would get under or on the side of the ball. But he wasn't able to repeat that success in 2019. An improved tempo also increased Gutierrez's ability to pound the strike zone in 2018, though his walk rate spiked the following season.. With a three-pitch mix that gives him a good chance to start, Gutierrez's fastball touches as high as 97-98 mph. If he can get back to what led to his success in '18 and continues to refine his pitches, he might not be far from reaching the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Over the years, the Reds have not shied away from spending on the international market, especially bringing Cuban prospects into the fold. Gutierrez was No. 4 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list heading into the 2016 signing period when the Reds gave him $4.75 million. He had an uneven first season of pro ball in 2017, but the Reds feel it created a foundation upon which the right-hander can build. Considering that Gutierrez hadn't pitched competitively in about two years and that he was shut down in August because of fatigue, his peripherals were pretty solid. He showed he can fill up the strike zone (1.7 BB/9) and miss a fair amount of bats (8.2 K/9) at the same time. He does it with a three-pitch mix that gives him a good chance to start. His fastball touches as high as 97-98 mph, but wasn't consistent, more frequently sitting in the low 90s in 2017. He adds and subtracts from his plus curveball without losing bite to it, throwing it for strikes at times and bouncing it as a chase pitch at others. He has feel for a changeup that should be average in time. Now with that experience under his belt, the Reds feel 2018 will be a true evaluation of who Gutierrez is. All the stuff is there; the next step will be for him to put it together consistently from month to month.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 The Reds went all in during the July 2016 international signing period, spending close to $12 million on a pair of Cuban prospects, shortstop Alfredo Rodriguez and Gutierrez. Primarily a reliever when he pitched in Cuba, he would not have been ranked No. 4 on MLBPipeline.com's Top 30 International Prospects list nor would he have gotten $4.75 million from Cincinnati if people didn't think he had the goods to start. Gutierrez has an outstanding fastball-curveball combination that certainly would play up in a relief role. But he has the chance to develop into a solid rotation piece. His fastball will sit in the low-90s and he can reach back for 95-96 mph. His curve is a plus breaking ball and he commands both of them well. The Reds haven't seen a changeup enough since he joined the organization, but he has shown a good feel for it in the past and it should be Major League average. Gutierrez has already impressed with his work ethic as he prepares to make his professional debut. He's tasked with developing as a starter at a full-season level, with the organization knowing he could move more quickly out of the bullpen if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of several left-handers who debuted in Baltimore in 2021, Lowther made the jump without Triple-A experience, then spent the summer bouncing between Norfolk and the big league club to mixed results. It was a bumpy debut for the burly southpaw, who rose quickly through the Orioles system after they made him a second-round selection out of Xavier in the 2017 Draft. But he finished strong, using his first extended look to post three strong starts in September. Lowther enters 2022 in competition for a back-end rotation job in Baltimore. To claim it, it’ll be key for Lowther to miss bats, which he showed a talent for in the Minors on the strength of his pitchability and high-spin fastball. Lowther led the Eastern League in strikeouts and finished second in ERA in 2019. After battling an oblique injury in 2020, he compiled 30 punchouts in 29 2/3 big league frames despite considerable hard contact. Lowther relies more on deception than pure stuff, using big extension and a low release point to augment his low-90s fastball and three offspeed pitches. The fastball is his main weapon, but it was crushed by big league hitters last summer. Lowther also features an above-average spike curve, a useful changeup and a developing slider. He is a polished strike-thrower who draws high marks for his competitiveness and makeup, with the size, frame and skills to suggest a durable mid-rotation-starter ceiling. Whether Lowther gets there probably depends on how well he can balance his pitch mix, become less predictable and get big league hitters off his fastball more effectively. He should get plenty of opportunity in 2022, either as a starter or in a swingman role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ second-round pick in 2017 out of Xavier, Lowther made a name for himself as a strikeout artist in the Big East Conference and hasn’t stopped missing bats since entering pro ball. The burly left-hander has risen quickly through the O’s system on the strength of his pitchability and ultra high-spin fastball, which helped him lead the Eastern League in strikeouts and finish second in ERA in 2019. He was slowed by an oblique injury in 2020, but not enough for the O’s to rethink protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft last November. Lowther doesn’t have dominant pure stuff, instead relying on a combination of deception and his signature heater, which only regularly registers between 87-91 mph but can click slightly higher at times. What it does do is play up due to Lowther’s low release point and big extension, which gives the heater an “invisible” element he uses to get swings and misses both in and above the strike zone. He pairs it with an above-average spike curve and serviceable changeup, and has worked to incorporate a slider into his arsenal. Lowther is considered a polished strike-thrower who draws positive reviews for his competitiveness and makeup. His size, frame and skills suggest a durable back-end starter at the highest level, though Lowther has a chance to surpass those projections as well. His first chance could come in 2021 if Lowther shows well at Triple-A to begin the year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lowther became known as a strikeout artist at Xavier, where he established a school record for career whiffs and led the Big East Conference in the same category as a sophomore. The Orioles made him the No. 74 overall pick in the Draft a year later in 2017, and the burly left-hander has not stopped missing bats since entering pro ball. Consistent performance has allowed Lowther to rise quickly, spending a full All-Star season in Double-A in 2019 and leading the Eastern League in strikeouts and finishing second in ERA. Lowther doesn’t have dominant pure stuff, instead relying on a combination of deception, pitchability and the magic of his ultra high-spin fastball. The pitch only regularly registered between 87-91 mph, though it can click slightly higher at times. But it plays up due to Lowther’s low release point and big extension, which give the heater an “invisible” element he uses to get swings and misses both in and above the strike zone. He plays it off an above-average spike curve, serviceable changeup and has worked to incorporate a slider into his arsenal. The walks ticked up a bit at Bowie, but Lowther is considered a polished strike-thrower who draws positive reviews for his competitiveness and makeup. His size, frame and skills suggest a durable back-end starter at the highest level, though Lowther has a chance to surpass those projections as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles took Lowther with the No. 74 overall pick in the second Competitive Balance round in 2017 after a dominant career at Xavier during which he led the Big East Conference in strikeouts as a sophomore and then established a school record for strikeouts (123) while finishing fourth in NCAA Division I in whiff rate (13.3) as a junior. The left-hander has continued to pile up strikeouts since entering the professional ranks, as he posted a 12.4 K/9 during his pro debut and followed it with 11.0 K/9 in his first full season, much of which he spent at Class A Advanced Frederick. Lowther's track record of missing bats is testament to his dominant fastball. He throws the pitch with only fringy velocity, sitting at 87-91 mph and occasionally bumping a few ticks higher. However, the massive extension he generates to the plate, combined with his fast arm and slightly lower slot, gives the pitch a high spin rate and late riding life that enables him to consistently beat hitters within and above the strike zone. An above-average curveball and a tumbling, low-80s changeup that's at least average comprise Lowther's secondary arsenal, and he keeps hitters off balance with both pitches. Physically mature and durable, Lowther has long shown that he can handle a heavy workload. That trait alone suggests the floor of a No. 5 starter, and it would surprise no one within the organization if Lowther, with his unique profile and arsenal, were to further his success and ultimately surpass that projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lowther led the Big East Conference in strikeouts as a Xavier sophomore and then continued to raise his profile in the Cape Cod League, which he led in strikeouts (54), whiffs per nine innings (13.6) and K/BB ratio (13.5). As a junior, he established a school record for strikeouts (123) while finishing fourth in NCAA Division I in whiff rate (13.3). Targeting Lowther's bat-missing ability, the Orioles took him with the No. 74 overall pick in the second competitive balance round, and he continued his run of dominance by posting a 1.66 ERA with 12.4 K/9 during his pro debut with Class A Short Season Aberdeen. A move up to full-season ball in '18 brought even more success for Lowther, as he received a promotion to Class A Advanced Frederick after six dominant starts with Class A Delmarva. Lowther's best pitch is a fastball that sits at 87-90 mph and tops out at 93. It plays well above its fringy velocity, as he commands it well and creates deception by hiding the ball well before generating massive extension to the plate. He's unlikely to throw much harder because he's already physically mature at 6-foot-2 and 235 pounds. Lowther's ability to pitch off of his fastball increases the effectiveness of his above-average curveball and a changeup that ranges from fringy to average. His control is average, with room for improvement, though he does offset many of his free passes with strikeouts. While the effectiveness of his modest arsenal will be tested at higher levels, Lowther's pitchability and knack for missing bats points to a career as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Deichmann had some of the best power in the 2014 high school class, but a so-so senior season and signability concerns left him undrafted and headed to Louisiana State. After barely playing as a freshman, he slugged 30 homers over the next two seasons and went to the Athletics in the second round of the 2017 Draft. He broke the hamate bone in his left hand during his first full season and hurt his right shoulder diving for a flyball in his second, but he finally stayed healthy in 2021 before joining the Cubs along with righty pitching prospect Daniel Palencia in a July trade for Andrew Chafin. Deichmann's best attribute is his considerable raw power from the left side of the plate, which he generates with bat speed and strength. After batting .232 in his first three years as a pro and leading the Arizona Fall League with nine homers in 23 games after the 2019 season, he has employed a more selective approach in Triple-A this year. He's making more contact and drawing more walks but also homered just four times in 60 games before the deal, and he's no longer clearly a power-over-hit guy. Though he possesses fringy speed, Deichmann has good instincts on the bases and will swipe bags if the defense forgets about him. An infielder in his first two college seasons, he has developed into an average defender on the outfield corners. His solid arm strength plays well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Deichmann hit 30 homers over his final two years as Louisiana State, 11 as a sophomore in 2016, then 19 more as a junior after he headed back to school rather than join the Twins as a 26th-round Draft pick.
