The A’s liked his power bat enough to take him in the seventh round in 2017 and he began his pro career well enough, with a .915 OPS in the Short-Season New York-Penn League. It’s been hard for Deichmann to stay on the field since, however, as hand and wrist issues allowed him to play just 138 games over the next two seasons. A healthy Deichmann did show what he can do when he led the Arizona Fall League with nine homers in 2019. Before the injuries hit, Deichmann was a very stiff-bodied hitter, one who would over-rotate and whose shoulder would fly open too often, with his arms and hands not working independently at all. While he was rehabbing, he focused more on flexibility than just hitting the weight room and being more elastic at the plate allowed for more shoulder and hips separation. Staying on pitches more, keeping his shoulder in and being on time cut down on his swing and miss, allowed his walk rate to go up and he started to show the ability to drive balls to left-center field. He learned that as he barrels up the ball more, he didn’t need to chase power; it was going to come naturally with his strength and natural loft. With a strong arm, Deichmann could fit the power-hitting corner outfielder profile well. Though he has below-average speed, he is a good baserunner who can steal a base. More than anything, though, he needs consistent and healthy reps so he can keep working on getting to his tremendous raw power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known for his power since his high school days in Louisiana, Deichmann found his college power stroke as a sophomore at Louisiana State, hitting 11 homers and getting selected as a Draft-eligible sophomore by the Twins in the 26th round of the 2016 Draft. Deciding to go back to LSU for his junior year was a smart move, as he hit 19 more homers and catapulted into the second round of the 2017 Draft. A solid summer debut did not carry over to his first full season as a wrist injury allowed him to play just 58 games for all of 2018. Even when Diechmann was on the field in 2018, he wasn't fully healthy as he tried to play through the issue. Initially misdiagnosed as tendinitis, it turned out to be an injury near his hamate and sapped him of his best tool when he was able to play. The A's liked what they saw in terms of his power potential in his first summer and at instructs that fall, and they are hoping to have that player back again in 2019. His approach has helped him get to his power consistently and while he will strike out, he'll also draw walks. His strong arm and power profile are good fits in right field, his likely long-term home, and he should be an average defender there. The first order of business for the left-handed hitter is to get a full season of reps in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Deichmann led Louisiana prepsters in homers for three straight years and offered some of the best power among high school middle infielders in the 2014 Draft, but a so-so senior season and signability issues left him unselected and headed to Louisiana State. After playing sparingly as a freshman, Diechmann erupted to hit 11 home runs the next year, then he blew past that total with 19 homers as a junior before going to the A's in the second round. After signing for $1.7 million, Deichmann showcased his impressive power by hitting eight homers in 46 games as Class A Short Season Vermont's everyday right fielder. Assigned to the California League for his first full season, Deichmann logged just 10 games before a wrist injury landed him on the disabled list for nearly three months. Deichmann's power is his calling card. The big left-handed hitter has impressed scouts with his bat speed and strength dating back to his high school days, and he's shown that he can get to it consistently in the past year-plus after shortening his swing and adopting a more selective approach. Deichmann's improved approach also has helped him in using the entire field, though much of his power remains to his pull side. And while strikeouts will always be a part of Deichmann's game given his power-over-hit profile, he does offset some of those concerns with perennially strong walk rates and on-base skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Newcastle, Australia, Wells has a chance to become the third Orioles player to hail from Down Under after signing for $300,000 in August 2015. He’s risen steadily through their system since, his only hiccup coming due to no fault of his own in 2020, which he spent almost entirely in Australia due to the coronavirus pandemic. Wells was the organization’s Minor League Pitcher of the Year in 2017, a SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game selection in 2018, and went 8-6 with a 2.95 ERA and 1.07 WHIP at Double-A Bowie in 2019 before turning heads with a stellar showing in the Arizona Fall League. The Orioles added Wells to the 40-man roster in November, hinting at a potential 2021 debut. With three quality pitches and plus control, Wells succeeds despite a fastball that used to live in the upper 80s, though it consistently clocked in at 90-91 mph late in ’19. His above-average changeup is an equalizer and he pairs it with an improving 12-to-6 curveball that helps keep hitters off balance. Both play up due to Wells’ ability to throw them for strikes to both sides of the plate, and he’s added a serviceable slider to use predominatly against right-handed hitters. Plus-command allows Wells to limit free passes and keep the ball in the ballpark; he’s averaged 1.4 walks-per-nine in over 475 career innings and allowed just 10 homers across 153 innings in 2019. While he will never miss many bats, Wells’ ability to spot three distinct pitches gives him a high floor that should translate to a back-end starter or swingman at the very least. Some believe he has a chance to exceed those projections and potentially become a mid-rotation starter in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Wells family has produced a pair of left-handed pitchers in twin brothers Alex and Lachlan. Though Lachlan signed first, inking with the Twins in 2014, Alex has become the better pro prospect after signing for $300,000 out of Australia in August 2015. Advanced pitchability helped Wells dominate during an impressive full-season debut two years later, when he posted a 2.38 ERA with a 0.91 WHIP over 140 innings to take home the organization's Jim Palmer Minor League Pitcher of the Year Award. Wells scuffled at times early in 2018 after moving up to the Carolina League, but he still earned a selection for the prestigious SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in July, then finished the season with his best month, posting a 1.97 ERA and 0.81 WHIP during five starts in August. Wells pitches with a fringy fastball, operating in the upper 80s and scraping 91 mph, but the pitch plays up thanks to his smooth delivery and because he commands it well. He also has great feel for throwing an above-average changeup in the low 80s that has late fading action and plays nicely off of his heater. Wells' curveball, a 12-to-6 downer in the mid-70s, has improved in the professional ranks, giving him a quality third pitch to keep hitters off-balance. Owner of plus control, Wells has averaged 1.4 walks-per-nine in over 337 career innings heading into 2019. While he will never blow hitters away or pile up many strikeouts, Wells' knack for spotting three distinct pitches gives him a high floor and should allow him to carve out a successful career as a back-end starter or swingman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Wells family has produced a pair of left-handed pitchers in twin brothers Alex and Lachlan. Though it was Lachlan who signed first (with the Twins in 2014), Alex has emerged as the better prospect after signing for $300,000 out of Australia in August 2015. Wells' advanced pitchability led to immediate success with Class A Short Season Aberdeen the next year, and he continued to build on that success in 2017 in his full-season debut with Class A Delmarva. A South Atlantic League mid-season All-Star, Wells pitched to a 2.38 ERA with a 0.91 WHIP over 140 innings to take home the organization's Jim Palmer Minor League Pitcher of the Year Award. He didn't fare as well in 2018 with the move up to Class A Advanced Frederick but still earned a selection for the prestigious SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game at Nationals Park in July. Wells pitches with an average fastball, operating in the upper 80s and scraping 91 mph, but the pitch plays up thanks to his smooth delivery and because he commands it well. He also has great feel for throwing an above-average changeup in the low 80s that has late fading action and plays nicely off of his heater. Wells' curveball, a 12-to-6 downer in the mid-70s, has improved in the professional ranks, giving him a quality third pitch to keep hitters off-balance. Owner of the best control and command in the Orioles' system, Wells' 0.64 walks-per-nine innings in 2017 was one of the better marks among qualified Minor League starters. And while he doesn't blow hitters away or pile up many strikeouts, Wells' knack for spotting three distinct pitches gives him a high floor and should allow him to carve out a successful career as a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Wells family has produced a pair of left-handed pitchers in twin brothers Alex and Lachlan. Though it was Lachlan who signed first (with the Twins in 2014), Alex has emerged as the better prospect since signing the 18-year-old for $300,000 in August 2015. His advanced pitchability was on full display last season at Class A Short Season Aberdeen, and he continued to build on that success in 2017 in his full-season debut with Delmarva. Wells pitches with an average fastball, operating in the upper 80s and scraping 90 mph, but the pitch plays up due to his ability to command it to both sides of the plate. His changeup registers in the low 80s with good fading action, and he sells it with fastball-like arm action. Wells also has made strides with his curveball, a 12-to-6 downer in the mid-70s, since turning pro, giving him a quality third pitch, and his whole arsenal plays up due to his above-average control. Though Wells has some physical projection remaining, he's unlikely to gain much in the way of velocity. But with a solid three-pitch mix and advanced feel for his craft, Wells could develop into at least a back-end starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player as a Virginia high schooler, Lee went to the Royals in the third round in 2016 and became strictly a position player. Pre-pandemic, he was moved aggressively up the system due to his speed (stealing as many as 53 bags at Double-A in 2019) and strong on-base skills. After Lee was added to the 40-man roster in November 2020, Kansas City traded him three months later to the Mets as part of a three-team deal that brought in Andrew Benintendi from the Red Sox. Lee was a statistical Triple-A standout in Syracuse, leading full-season qualifiers with a .451 OBP while finishing with 14 homers and a .951 OPS in 23 games. He was used for an 11-game Major League cameo in May but went 1-for-18 with 13 strikeouts. As his 18.3 percent walk rate indicated in 2021, Lee can be patient at the plate, but that borders too much on passivity. He did get more aggressive as the season wore on and will need that to continue to make the most of his offensive potential. The left-handed slugger has always shown above-average raw power. A high ground-ball rate blunts that slugging potential, and while some gains were made in that department last year, he still hit the ball on the ground 51.5 percent of the time. Lee’s above-average speed and plus arm (dating back to his pitching days) give him defensive assets, and he profiles best in right field, where he spent most of last season. The 5-foot-10 prospect isn’t far from his floor as a bench outfield bat, and he’ll need to continue his improvements on aggression and launch angle to have a chance at being a Major League fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee was a third-round pick by the Royals in 2016 after a stellar two-way showing out of a Virginia high school. Kansas City kept him as a position player only and moved Lee aggressively up the chain, including an assignment to Double-A in 2019 when he opened the season at just 20 years old. Lee held his own with a 112 wRC+ in that campaign but stood out most for his 53 stolen bases, which ranked second in the entire Minors behind only then-fellow Royal Nick Heath’s 60. Lee was added to the 40-man last November and was traded to the Mets three months later in a three-team involving the Red Sox and Andrew Benintendi. Lee is no stranger to two of three true outcomes, having struck out in 28.2 percent and walked in 11.9 percent of his plate appearances at Double-A. That balances out the offensive profile. He loses a few points as well for hitting the ball primarily on the ground with a 59.3 percent ground-ball rate that led the Texas League in 2019. That keeps him from playing into what could be above-average power. As such, elevation was a key focus during his time at the Royals’ alternate training site last year, and it deserves watching whether he can reverse that trend when he returns to play. The other tools are the standouts of the profile right now. Lee showed in 2019 that he can steal bags by the dozens, and that speed gives him a good shot at sticking in center. The arm is even better than the glove and is a true plus tool, so if some route-running issues push him to a corner, he can still help any club defensively. The Mets inserted themselves into the Kansas City-Boston trade in order to pick up Lee, so they were obvious admirers of the outfielder’s skill set. However after a few games with the Major League club in the first half of 2021, Lee has been overlooked while positing an impressive on-base percentage and overall OPS at Triple-A Syracuse. This remains his age-23 season, and after establishing a little more consistency at Triple-A, he could still very well carve out a role as a fourth outfielder in the Majors down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 A talented two-way player as a high schooler in Virginia -- one many teams preferred as a left-handed pitcher -- Lee's athleticism and offensive upside appealed to the Royals, who drafted him in the third round of the 2016 Draft and went over pick value to sign him. He's moved rapidly thus far, making his Double-A debut right after he turned 20 in 2018. Lee has the tools to be an impact player on both sides of the ball and with some adjustments to his offensive approach, he could be a better than average hitter with outstanding power. While he cut down his strikeout rate considerably in 2018 and has excellent plate discipline, Lee's willingness to see pitches can work against him. He'll often take too many hittable pitches early in counts and then hasn't altered his two-strike approach at all. If he can learn to be a bit more aggressive early in counts, then pitchers will start trying to expand the zone early, where his advanced eye will come in handy. All of that should put him in better counts to use his bat speed and loft to get to his power more frequently without his K rate skyrocketing. Defensively, Lee can handle playing center field and will continue to get plenty of time there in the Minors. But he likely profiles better as a right fielder, where his cannon for an arm plays well and he has the chance to be a plus defender overall. The Royals are hoping his time in Double-A and in the Arizona Fall League will help him continue up the ladder quickly after he lost time due to a back injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Though he had a low-90s fastball and a promising slider, intriguing several clubs as a left-handed pitching prospect, the Royals liked his multitool ability more. They made him a full-time outfielder after signing him for an over-slot $750,000 as a third-rounder in 2016, and they have no reason to regret that decision. He led the Rookie-level Arizona League in runs (43), triples (six) and total bases (88) during his pro debut, then ranked second in homers (17) and third in walks (65) in the low Class A South Atlantic League at age 19 last year. If he can make some adjustments at the plate, Lee could have solid or better tools across the board. Though he's not physically imposing at 5-foot-10, the bat speed and loft in his left-handed swing give him surprising raw power. He has some feel to hit and a willingness to work counts, though he needs to tone down his aggressiveness after fanning a SAL-high 171 times last year. With his solid speed, Lee could be a 20-20 player if he refines his basestealing technique after getting caught in 18 of his 38 attempts in 2017. He split last season between center and right field, showing the range to stick at the former position and Gold Glove upside at the latter. His strong arm allowed him to register 14 assists in 119 games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 Lee drew interest from clubs as both an outfielder and a left-handed pitcher in the 2016 Draft. Though he had a low-90s fastball and a promising slider, the Royals liked his bat and made him a full-time position player after signing him for an above-slot $750,000 as a third-round pick. Gatorade's 2016 Virginia high school player of the year, he topped the Rookie-level Arizona League in runs (43), triples (six) and total bases (88) while ranking second in on-base percentage (.396) and fifth in slugging (.484). Kansas City considered Lee the best athlete available with the 103rd overall choice, and he has average or better tools across the board. Though he's not physically imposing, he has some juice in his quick left-handed stroke. He has good feel to hit and a mature approach, plus he already has shown the ability to make adjustments at the plate. An average runner out of the batter's box, Lee shows more speed once he gets going. He played all three outfield spots in his pro debut, getting most of his time in center field, though he may be better suited for a corner in the long run. His obvious arm strength would play well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers selected the Puerto Rican backstop out of Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy with the 75th overall pick in 2016. His breakout campaign came in 2019, when he was named Carolina League MVP after hitting .270/.323/.473 with 19 homers for High-A Carolina. He followed that up with a strong showing at the alternate training site a year later. Milwaukee added Feliciano to its 40-man roster in November 2020, but 2021 was a rough season for him. Feliciano, who appeared in one Major League game in May, missed nearly two months with a right shoulder impingement and hit just .210/.246/.314 (46 wRC+) over 114 plate appearances with Triple-A Nashville. A trip to the Arizona Fall League (.318/.348/.432) helped end the year on a brighter note. Ever since he was drafted, Feliciano has used his bat to raise his prospect profile. He utilizes a compact right-handed swing to drive the ball with authority, and he has the above-average raw power to threaten for 15-20 homers over a full Major League season. Among reasons for optimism in 2021, his strikeout rate did drop a touch at Triple-A, but he isn’t the most cautious swinger with just a 3.5 percent walk rate. Feliciano’s shoulder troubles weren’t a first last season -- he also needed arthroscopic surgery in the 2018-19 offseason -- and it’s becoming a concern whether his injury history will affect his ability to stay behind the plate. At his best, he’s an agile catcher with above-average arm strength, and the Brewers are optimistic he can get back to that level. He needs consistent reps to find that form, and those should come in his second 40-man season in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have not hit big drafting and developing catchers. The last home-grown catcher to represent them at an All-Star Game was Jonathan Lucroy in 2014 and ‘16. Before that, it was Dave Nilsson in 1999, but Nilsson was already an established pro in Australia before he signed with the Brewers. But now the Brewers have a relatively deep crop of backstops led by Feliciano, the No. 75 overall pick in the 2016 Draft. After nagging injuries ruined his 2018, including a shoulder flare-up in the Arizona Fall League that required arthroscopic surgery in the offseason, Feliciano got back on track during a breakout 2019 at the advanced Class A level; he was Carolina League MVP after leading the circuit in home runs (19), RBIs (81), slugging (.477) and total bases (210) at age 20, and he was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Feliciano’s strength is his bat. His clean and compact right-handed swing yields consistently hard contact as well as above-average game power that plays from the left-center gap to the right-field line. There is great potential for more if Feliciano can bring down his 28.8 percent strikeout rate from 2019 and cut down one of the Minors’ highest swinging-strike rates (19.7 percent). Defensively, Feliciano has enough tools to be a catcher long-term, particularly his arm. He’ll be a bat-first guy, but should be able to stick behind the plate at the highest level. A shoulder impingement has limited both his production and game experience in 2021, but the Brewers are still believers that Feliciano can be a productive catcher when fully healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Puerto Rico high schooler, Feliciano endeared himself to Brewers amateur scouts with his hitting ability, power and potential to stick behind the plate. He signed for $800,000, after Milwaukee took him with the No. 75 overall pick in the 2016 Draft, and then offered a glimpse of his offensive upside at Class A Wisconsin the following year. But nagging injuries plagued Feliciano in 2018, limiting him to just 42 regular-season games, and his Arizona Fall League campaign ended prematurely due to shoulder discomfort that required offseason arthroscopic surgery. Fully healthy in 2019, Feliciano broke out to garner Class A Advanced Carolina League MVP honors after he led the circuit in home runs (19), RBIs (81), slugging (.477) and total bases (210) at age 20. Feliciano’s bat is his calling card, and no player in Milwaukee’s system offers a better combination of hitting ability and power potential. His clean and compact right-handed swing yields consistently hard contact as well as above-average game power that plays from the left-center gap to the right-field line. Club officials believe Feliciano will unlock even more power as he tightens his approach. While he did a better job controlling the zone better and chased fewer pitches in 2019, Feliciano still stuck out at a 28.8 percent clip and recorded one of the Minors’ highest swinging-strike rates (19.7 percent). Defensively, Feliciano has the athleticism, agility and tools needed to stick behind the plate, though he does occasionally lose focus from pitch-to-pitch. His framing and receiving have improved in the pro ranks, while his quick transfer and plus arm strength translate to average-or-better pop times. Feliciano’s defense should be good enough to allow his bat-first profile to play at the highest level, but he’ll need to make more improvements on both sides of the ball along the way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high school senior in Puerto Rico in 2016, Feliciano impressed scouts with his hitting ability, power potential and overall athleticism behind the plate. The Brewers took him with the No. 75 overall pick that June, signing him for $800,000. After a solid first full season at Class A Wisconsin that included Midwest League All-Star honors, nagging injuries plagued Feliciano in 2018, limiting him to just 42 regular-season games. He was assigned to the Arizona Fall League after the season so that he could make up some of the lost developmental time but instead experienced shoulder discomfort and underwent arthroscopic surgery in November. The Brewers continue to be high on the young catcher's upside at the plate. Feliciano works with a clean right-handed swing when he's healthy, showing feel for the barrel and the ability to make hard contact to all fields that portend to solid averages in his future. That knack for making contact can also work against Feliciano, at times causing him to expand his zone and make weak contact on pitches off the plate. And while his average raw power hasn't shown up in games yet, the Brewers believe he'll have at least modest over-the-fence power once he adds more strength and learns to better leverage his swing. Feliciano is an impressive athlete who runs surprisingly well and shows agility behind the plate. He's a solid receiver and framer, especially to his glove side, while his quick transfer and above-average arm strength translate to average-or-better pop times. Many of the defensive gains he needs to make should happen organically with health and experience, and club officials are confident he'll make enough adjustments along the way to allow his bat-first profile to play at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Puerto Rico was well represented on Day 1 of the 2016 Draft, with the Cardinals selecting shortstop Delvin Perez in the first round, and the Brewers nabbing Feliciano with the No. 75 overall pick. While the former has yet to play a game above the Rookie level, Feliciano played his entire full-season debut as an 18-year-old in the Class A Midwest League, showing a combination of hitting ability and raw-but-improving defensive skills that have the Brewers excited about what his future may hold. Feliciano stands out for his potential at the plate. With a clean right-handed swing, feel for the barrel and good strength to his frame, Feliciano knows how to generate hard contact, and he does so to all fields. Those qualities, as well as his advanced approach, give Feliciano a chance to hit for average. And although his raw power translates to mostly doubles right now, he's expected to develop at least modest over-the-fence power as he gets stronger and learns to better leverage his swing. Feliciano is an impressive athlete who runs well, especially relative to his position. That athleticism aids him behind the plate, where he's an agile but fundamentally raw defender with an above-average arm. While some scouts question whether he'll stick at the position, the Brewers believe Feliciano will make the necessary defensive adjustments to allow his bat-first profile to play at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliciano and shortstop Delvin Perez headlined a strong crop of talent from Puerto Rico in the 2016 Draft. While Perez went to the Cardinals in the first round, Feliciano, an offensive-minded catcher, remained on the board until Lottery Round B, where the Brewers took him with the No. 75 overall pick. The Brewers are excited about Feliciano's potential at the plate. He has strength in his swing, with over-the-fence potential from the right side of the plate, but he's not an all-or-nothing hitter and shows a solid approach at times. Especially for a catcher, Feliciano runs well, and that athleticism translates in his efforts behind the plate. He has an above-average arm, though some worry about his overall defensive game and ability to catch long term. If he can't stay behind the plate, there's a chance Feliciano could handle left field, though that might be a stretch. Regardless of his future defensive home, Feliciano's offensive potential will be his calling card moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida, Welker was a fourth-round pick back in 2016 and the Rockies went about $300,000 over slot to sign the infielder. He didn’t hit below .329 over his first three summers of pro ball, establishing self as one of the better pure hitters in the Minors. A shoulder injury didn’t help him with a move to Double-A in 2019, though he did earn a spot on the 40-man roster following the shortened 2020 season. He served an 80-game suspension in 2021 for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone (DHCMT), a performance-enhancing substance, returning late and making his big league debut last September. At his best, Welker still shows off the skills of a very gifted hitter. Even when he’s struggled, he’s shown a willingness to work counts and draw walks, keeping his strikeout rate relatively low. He has a knack for contact and can drive the ball to all fields, showing an aptitude for making adjustments during an at-bat. There is raw power to tap into, but he’s struggled when he’s tried to sell out for power and would be better suited just letting it come naturally from his right-handed swing. While Welker has solid hands and a strong arm that work at third, his lack of speed might mean first base is a better home long-term. Either corner puts pressure on his bat and he’ll have to be more consistently productive to profile well as a regular at either corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 35 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The best player to come out of Stoneman Douglas High School to date has been Anthony Rizzo, who was a sixth-round pick in the 2007 Draft. Thirteen years later, Jesus Luzardo was a third-round pick and the most recent alum to make the big leagues. Welker was part of that same 2016 Draft, going a round later than his lefty teammate. For much of his Minor League career, he lived up to his offensive potential, hitting .337 over his first two-plus years of pro ball. He hit a wall, and dealt with a shoulder injury, after a hot start in Double-A in 2019, then struggled in the Arizona Fall League. Still believing in his bat, the Rockies added him to the 40-man roster following the 2020 season, though Walker was given an 80-game suspension after testing positive for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone (DHCMT), a performance-enhancing substance, in May. Still just 23 years old for the 2021 season, there’s plenty of time for Welker to rediscover the swing and approach that made him look like a future plus hitter from the right side of the plate. When he’s in sync, he combines his knowledge of the strike zone with his ability to drive the ball to all fields. He’s willing to draw walks and doesn’t strike out a ton, even when he struggled in 2019. He gets into trouble when he gets out of his game plan and tries to hit for power, rather than let it come naturally. While Welker doesn’t run well, he has the tools to play a solid third base, with good hands and enough arm for the hot corner. He started seeing more time at first base in 2019 because of his lack of speed and, of course, Nolan Arenado. The latter is gone, but Welker should still get reps at both infield corners, once he returns from his suspension.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 35 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Ever since being drafted in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft and signing for an above-slot $855,000, Welker had hit. He put up a .329/.366/.490 line in his pro debut in the Pioneer League, hit .350/.401/.500 in an injury-shortened move to full-season ball in '17, then kept on going with a .333/.383/.489 in the California League. It looked as if he was going to steamroll through his move to Double-A when he hit .356 in April, but he hit just .203/.278/.314 in the second half, missed two months with a shoulder issue and then struggled in the Arizona Fall League as well. At his best, Welker still has the ability to consistently hit the ball hard. He knows the strike zone well, can draw a walk and limits his strikeouts. He has extra-base authority to all fields. There is some over-the-fence pop, though it hasn’t shown up consistently and he can occasionally sell out for power too much. If he can maintain his approach, he still has the tools to be an above-average hitter with average power. A below-average runner, Welker’s arm, hands and footwork all work fine from third and he can make all the routine plays. His lack of speed, not to mention the continued presence of Nolan Arenado, has led to him seeing time at first, both during last regular season and in the Arizona Fall League. That might be his best spot to be a big league regular, though teams typically do like to see a little more run-producing ability from that position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 35 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 50 Welker was a teammate at Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida with Jesus Luzardo, who went from having Tommy John surgery his senior year to becoming the top left-handed pitching prospect in the game. While Welker had an uneven senior year of high school, he's done nothing but hit since the Rockies went over pick value to sign him for $855,000 in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft, winning the California League batting title in '18. Welker continues to show an innate ability to make consistent hard contact, recognizing pitches extremely well and not getting fooled often. While his strikeout rate has gone up, so has his ability to draw walks, and he started tapping into his power more in 2018, with the ability to drive the ball to all fields from the right side of the plate. While speed isn't a part of his game, he's far from a clogger, with good instincts on the basepaths. Welker has more than enough arm to profile well at third and his hands should allow him to stay there. His lack of speed might eventually be an impediment. Nolan Arenado will be a free agent after the 2019 season; his future in Colorado could determine if Welker takes over in '20 or slides over to first, a spot he saw limited time at in '18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 Part of a Stoneman Douglas High (Parkland, Fla.) program that has produced big leaguers Mike Caruso, Matt Fox and Anthony Rizzo, Welker led the Eagles to the Florida 9-A state title and a No. 1 national ranking in 2016. Since he signed for an over-slot $855,000 as a fourth-rounder that June, the only thing that has slowed him is an abdominal strain that cost him two months last summer. His batting average (.350), on-base percentage (.401) and OPS (.901) all would have led the low Class A South Atlantic League if he had enough plate appearances to qualify. With his advanced pitch-recognition skills and feel for the barrel, Welker rarely gets fooled and consistently makes hard contact. Once he adds some needed strength, the bat speed and leverage in his right-handed stroke could generate 20-homer power. He's a below-average runner with decent instincts on the bases. Multiple Rockies officials have noted that Welker reminds them of a young Nolan Arenado because they have similar builds and put up similar numbers in their first two years of pro ball. While Arenado has made himself into an elite defender at third base, Welker still is learning the position after playing shortstop in high school. He has the hands and arm strength to be an asset defensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best position prospect to come out of Stoneman Douglas High (Parkland, Fla.) since Anthony Rizzo, Welker led the Eagles to the state 9-A championship and a No. 1 national ranking in 2016. Colorado immediately moved him from shortstop to third base after signing him for an above-slot $855,000 in the fourth round. He had no problem competing against older competition in the Rookie-level Pioneer League, batting .329/.366/.490 at age 18. He reminds the Rockies of another third-base prospect who didn't get a lot of hype coming out of high school: Nolan Arenado. They're not saying that Welker will blossom into perhaps the best all-around player in the big leagues, but he has a similar build, knack for making hard contact and instincts that allow him to play well above his below-average speed at the hot corner. Extremely advanced at the plate for a teenager, Welker recognizes pitches well, has good feel for the barrel and uses the entire field. His bat speed and leverage in his right-handed swing could translate into 20-homer power once he adds strength. He immediately took to third base, displaying reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Alexy for a well-over-slot $597,500 as an 11th-rounder in 2016, then shipped him along with Willie Calhoun and infield prospect Brendon Davis to get Yu Darvish from the Rangers a year later. After making just five starts in 2019 because of a lat injury and losing 2020 to the pandemic shutdown, he came back and moved from Double-A to the big leagues last year. He won three of his four starts with Texas, logging a 2.79 ERA, though he was shelled in his lone relief appearance. As a starter, Alexy works with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball that reaches 97 with good carry in the strike zone. He flashed a plus curveball with power and depth in the past, but it parked more in the mid-70s and he didn't use it as much in 2021. He has started using a tight low-80s slider and owns a mid-80s changeup with modest life, and both are fringy offerings. Alexy never has been a prolific strike-thrower and issued as many walks as he had strikeouts (17) in his 23 innings in the Majors. He sat at 97 mph and touched 100 with his fastball in short stints during instructional league in 2020, and he might be better suited as a two-pitcher reliever than a starter. For now, he'll contend for a rotation job in Texas.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Alexy for a well-over-slot $597,500 as an 11th-rounder out of a Pennsylvania high school in 2016, then traded him along with Willie Calhoun and infield prospect Brendon Davis to Texas for Yu Darvish a year later. He was progressing nicely until getting shut down with a lat injury five starts into the 2019 season, and his only action since has come at instructional league in each of the last two falls. He showcased maybe the best pure stuff at Rangers instructs in 2020, prompting his addition to the 40-man roster. When last seen as a starter in early 2019, Alexy dealt with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball that topped out at 97, but in shorter instructional league stints he has parked at 97 and touched 100. He has high spin rates on both his heater and his curveball, which combines power with legitimate 12-6 break. His changeup lacks the upside of his other two offerings but can be an average pitch at times. Though Alexy has a big frame and has quieted his delivery since turning pro, he may be better suited for the bullpen than the rotation. In addition to refining his changeup, he also needs to improve his control and command to remain a starter. He could move very quickly as a reliever and become a high-leverage option if he can carry his instructs stuff into the regular season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One month after he threw an infamous 164-pitch complete game for Twin Valley High (Elverson, Pa.), Alexy signed with the Dodgers for a well-over-slot $597,500 in the 11th round of the 2016 Draft. The Rangers acquired him a year later along with Willie Calhoun and infield prospect Brendon Davis in exchange for Yu Darvish. He made just five high Class A starts in 2019 before getting shut down with a lat injury, but he did return with electric stuff in instructional league. Alexy generates high spin rates on both his fastball and curveball and changes the eye level of hitters with four-seamers up in the strike zone and benders that drop through the bottom of it. He usually works at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with his heater, but he sat around 97 and touched 100 during short stints in instructional league. His curve combines power with legitimate 12-6 break. While Alexy's changeup lags behind his two plus offerings, it shows some flashes of becoming a solid third pitch. He has a big frame built for starting and has toned down his delivery since turning pro, but he'll have to improve his control and command to succeed as a starter. Should he move to the bullpen and maintain the velocity he showed last fall, he could become a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alexy signed with the Dodgers for a well over-slot $597,500 as an 11th-rounder in 2016, one month after he threw an infamous 164-pitch complete game at Twin Valley High (Elverson, Pa.). Los Angeles parted with him a year later, sending him with Willie Calhoun and infield prospect Brendon Davis to the Rangers for Yu Darvish. He has legitimate swing-and-miss stuff, averaging 11.0 strikeouts per nine innings in his first three pro seasons. Because Alexy didn't start pitching full-time until he was a high school junior, he still has a lot to learn on the mound. He has reduced the effort in his delivery since turning pro yet he still doesn't keep it in sync consistently, which compromises his control. If he eventually moves to the bullpen, his fastball/curve combo could make him a late-inning weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willie Calhoun was the headliner in the three-prospect package the Rangers received from the Dodgers for Yu Darvish last July, but Alexy quickly asserted himself as one of the best starting pitchers in his new system. Los Angeles signed him for a well over-slot $600,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2016, one month after he infamously threw a 164-pitch complete game at Twin Valley High (Elverson, Pa.). He impressed the Dodgers so much in his first spring training that they sent him to low Class A at age 18, and he struck out 113 in 94 1/3 innings between the two organizations. Alexy added strength during his first full year in pro ball, boosting his high-spin-rate fastball consistently into the low 90s, and his 6-foot-4 frame still has room to add more muscle. His curveball already had good depth and added power as well, becoming a consistent plus pitch. His changeup isn't as consistent as his other offerings but has the makings of an average pitch. Because Alexy didn't become a full-time pitcher until his junior year in high school, he's just scratching the surface of his potential. There's still some effort in his delivery but he's athletic and toned it down in his first full season, so the Rangers think he'll throw more strikes. His curveball and competitiveness will serve him well if he eventually moves into the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his college days, Dohy lived up to the “have left arm, will travel” adage, attending three schools in three years. The Phillies took Dohy, a starter at Division II Cal Poly in 2017, in the 16th round in that June’s Draft and immediately put him in the bullpen with good results. The lefty reliever made it to Double-A in his first full season and up to Triple-A in 2019, though he didn’t pitch particularly well there. Though he didn’t pitch at the alternate training site or in instructional league play, the Phillies still decided to protect his left arm on the 40-man roster this past offseason. The 6-foot-2 lefty brings an intriguing combination of deception and stuff to a future big league bullpen. There’s funk in his delivery, making it hard for hitters to pick the ball up, contributing to his 13.8 strikeout per nine rate in his career heading into 2021. He’s typically topped out in the mid-90s, but was up to 98-99 mph on Rapsodo during offseason workouts. It remains to be seen if those are real velocity gains. He has one of the best changeups in the system, with good separation from his fastball and thrown with excellent deception. At times, his slider is a wipeout pitch, though it’s less consistent. Dohy has shown the ability to miss bats with all three pitches. What he hasn’t been able to do is find the strike zone consistently enough. He’s walked 7.0 batters per nine innings, which will keep him from having any lasting impact in the big leagues. If he can find the strike zone a bit more frequently, his stuff is more than good enough to be a reliever at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Dohy spent his three years in college ball at three different schools, starting at Cal State Northridge in 2015, moving to the junior college ranks (Citrus College) in '16 after not pitching much, then only to Division II Cal Poly. Though he was a starter there, the Phillies moved him to the bullpen after taking him in the 16th round of the 2017 Draft. He pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season, then up to Triple-A in '19, though he struggled more upon reaching the highest level of the system. The left-handed reliever has all the weapons to be very successful coming out of the bullpen, and even though his numbers with Lehigh Valley weren’t pretty, he still struck out 14 per nine innings for the year overall. Dohy has a funky delivery that creates deception and his fastball is consistently touching the mid-90s, he can sell his changeup extremely well and his slider flashes plus at times. The only thing holding Dohy back from being an impact reliever in the big leagues is his command. His walk rate skyrocketed to 7.8 per nine last year (8.6 in Triple-A) and that’s obviously not sustainable. With his stuff, it doesn’t have to be pinpoint and the good news is he’s only 23, so there’s time for him to iron out his delivery enough to find the strike zone more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Dohy began his college career at Cal State Northridge in 2015, but after pitching sparingly, he transferred to Citrus College, a junior college in California. He was on the move again after his sophomore year, heading to Division II Cal Poly, where he started all year. The Phillies took a flier on him in the 16th round of the 2017 Draft, immediately moved him to the bullpen and watched him pitch his way across three levels to Double-A in his first full season. With three pitches that at least flash plus, Dohy has nasty stuff that allowed him to strike out nearly 15 batters per nine innings in 2018. All of it comes from the lefty's aggressive, up-tempo and funky delivery. He gets up to the mid 90s with his fastball consistently and he complements the heater with two excellent secondary offerings. His mid-80s slider is often a plus pitch, and his changeup is more average, though sometimes it's the other way around. With his delivery, command is going to be an issue, and he'll likely always be a control over command type of reliever. Dohy struggled in Double-A, partially because of fatigue at the end of his first full season and partially because the more advanced hitters at the level were laying off his chase pitches out of the zone. He's worked hard on his conditioning this offseason to avoid the first pitfall, and he will work to refine his command enough to allow his stuff to play in the strike zone effectively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $320,000 at the start of a 2016-17 international signing period that saw the Padres spend more than $40 million on the international market, Marcano hit .366 in his first taste of pro ball in the United States in 2018. He hit well in full-season ball in 2019, then jumped from Low-A that season to the big leagues to start the 2021 season. That may have been too tall of an order to fill, and Marcano struggled, though he righted the ship a bit back in Triple-A when he was sent to the Pirates in the deal for Adam Frazier at last year’s Trade Deadline. Contact has, and always will be, the name of Marcano’s game. He carries a strikeout rate of under 10 percent in his Minor League career into the 2022 season and has drawn more walks (152) than strikeouts (135). His knowledge of the strike zone is elite and his short swing from the left side can spray line drives to all fields. There isn’t much power to speak of and it’s unclear how much he’ll drive the ball, though he’ll still be just 22 years old for nearly all of the 2022 season. Marcano’s above-average speed helps him defensively and he’s shown the ability to play shortstop, with good hands. His arm fits better at second and he played all four infield spots as well the two corner outfield positions in 2021, with an eye towards a future as a super-utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres' 2016-17 international spree garnered attention for the money spent, but some of the best pieces from that class weren't big-bonus signings at all. Marcano is a perfect example. Named for the town of Tucupita, where he's from in Venezuela, Marcano signed for $320,000. He’s already shown some of the most advanced knowledge of the strike zone in the organization. Marcano batted .366/.450/.438 at the lower levels in his first full season, while striking out 16 times and walking 30. At Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, he continued to hit -- but not for much power -- and that continued in 2021 as he jumped to Triple-A and made his big league debut before being included as the top prospect in the deal that sent Adam Frazier to San Diego Marcano is a slender and wiry middle-infield type, who still needs to fill out his 6-foot frame. As he has, he has grown into a bit of pop. But his contact skills are the defining characteristic. Marcano's short left-handed stroke produces line drives all over the field. At times, his hand-eye coordination is almost too good, and he’d be better served being more selective within the strike zone, swinging at pitches he can do damage with. Still, Marcano can differentiate balls from strikes as well as anyone, and he complements his excellent plate approach with above-average speed. Defensively, some feel Marcano can remain at shortstop, and he's got the quick hands necessary to be a solid defender. His arm projects as merely average, and that could force a move to second base. But his plate skills could develop into him being a serious on-base threat as a bat-first middle infielder.

His arm projects as merely average, and in a Padres system loaded with shortstop options, that could force a move to second base. mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones both started and relieved at Washington State, with very mixed results, but the Phillies felt his size, raw stuff and left-handedness was worth a flier in the 18th round of the 2017 Draft. After pitching out of the pen during his pro debut that summer, Jones had two fairly successful seasons starting, touching Triple-A in 2019. After being added to the 40-man roster in 2020, he moved back to a relief role in 2021 and made his big league debut before a very strong turn in the Arizona Fall League. The 6-foot-5 lefty has the stuff to get big league hitters out; it’s just a question of landing that stuff in the strike zone enough to do so. His fastball easily touches 95-96 mph and averaged around 94 in 2021 and it often has cutting action to it, leading to solid groundball ratios throughout his career. He’s thrown both a curve and slider in the past, but he focused on the slider especially in the AFL with good results, with the chance for it to be a true out pitch. He’s also had a changeup in his repertoire, but he may not need it as a reliever. That’s the role he’s going to have from now on as his walk rate spiked in 2021. He threw better strikes in the AFL, though he still walked 6.1 per nine in a small sample. With his swing-and-miss stuff (11.3 K/9 in his career in the Minors), he doesn’t need pinpoint command to play a role in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2021 The 2017 Draft has already produced some late-round big leaguers, like Cardinals’ 27th-rounder Kodi Whitley and Angels 30th-rounder Jeremy Beasley, a list that also includes Phillies’ 10th-rounder Connor Brogdon. Jones, a Phillies flier taken in the 18th round that June, is about ready to join them after a 2019 season that saw him pitch his way to Triple-A and a 2020 that included time at the Phillies’ alternate training site and a spot on the 40-man roster. Jones typically uses three pitches, all of which can get outs. It starts with a fastball that’s up to 96 mph with natural cut to it, a pitch that has gotten a groundball percentage well over 50 percent. He misses bats, 12 of them per nine innings in 2019, with a plus curve and a slider that’s above-average. He does have a below-average changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much at this point. That, combined with command issues, he’s walked 4.6 per nine innings, means the 6-foot-5 lefty’s future is very likely in a bullpen. The good news is the combination of that lively fastball and his array of breaking stuff could allow him to play a significant role if he can find the strike zone a bit more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 There’s nothing from Jones’ amateur resume, either at the College of Southern Idaho or in two years at Washington State after he transferred there, that screamed “future professional success.” His size and his left-handedness certainly were attractive and the Phillies took a flier on both in the 18th round of the 2017 Draft. He then proceeded to defy all expectations by pitching across three levels, finishing in Triple-A, in 2019. Jones uses his 6-foot-5 frame extremely well to create excellent extension. That, plus deception in his delivery makes it tough for hitters to pick the ball up out of his hand, leading to swings-and-misses on his fastball that touches 96 mph. He’ll throw a changeup that approaches average, but it’s really his breaking stuff that stands out. His curveball is downright nasty and has evolved into a true out pitch, while he mixes in a slider and changeup that are both close to average pitches for the southpaw. Fastball command will be a key for Jones for him to have a chance to succeed in the big leagues. If he can refine that and continue to hone something offspeed, then he has the chance to start. Otherwise, the fastball-breaking ball combination could be really nasty out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bettinger was more of a reliever than a starter during his four years at the University of Virginia, and he worked exclusively out of the bullpen as a senior in 2017. The Brewers still liked this strike-throwing ability enough to select him in the 10th round and transition him into a starting role. Early results were inconsistent until Bettinger’s breakout season for Double-A Biloxi in 2019, when he finished second in the Southern League with 1.07 WHIP and 157 strikeouts in 146 1/3 innings. The Brewers added the former Cavalier to the 40-man roster in November 2020, and he was solid at Triple-A Nashville last year with a 4.75 ERA, 98 strikeouts and 26 walks in 96 2/3 innings. He made four appearances (one start) for the Brewers in the first half of the 2021 season but is still seeking consistent Major League success. The Virginia native doesn’t boast a true plus pitch as part of his arsenal, but he makes the most of a deep pitch mix. His heater averaged 91.5 mph in the Majors last season, and he’s typically right around that 89-92 mph velocity range. The pitch plays up with some deception out of Bettinger’s 6-foot-2 frame, aided by decent extension toward home plate. He adds in a mid-70s curveball with good break and an upper-80s cutter that works well off the fastball and can be effective against either hitters on either side of the plate. A low-80s changeup remains below average. Bettinger, who turns 27 in July, is yet to walk more than 7 percent of his batters faced at any full-season level, including Triple-A and the Majors, where his BB rates were below 6.3 percent. He will still get starting looks because of that control, but he might be most effective soon as a long reliever for Milwaukee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round pick in 2017 who signed for $10,000 after a strong senior season as a long reliever at Virginia, Bettinger was moved into a starting role upon entering pro ball and has surged to the brink of the big leagues thanks to his penchant for throwing strikes. He struggled in his first full season in ‘18, recording a 5.45 ERA between the two Class A levels, but the Brewers still decided to push the right-hander up to Double-A Biloxi in 2019. After Bettinger got off to another shaky start, he pitched increasingly well and showed more velocity as the season unfolded, putting him on the organization’s prospect map. He finished among Southern League leaders in starts (T1st, 26), strikeouts (2nd, 157), WHIP (2nd, 1.07), innings (2nd, 146 1/3), opponent average (4th, .223) and ERA (6th, 3.44). The Brewers added Bettinger to the 40-man roster in November 2020 and president of baseball operations David Stearns predicted he would contribute at the big league level in 2021. That proved prescient when Bettinger made his Major League debut back in May. Though Bettinger has always featured some deception with crossfire action in his delivery, he found a new level of effectiveness in Double-A thanks an uptick in velocity. With Biloxi, the right-hander was touching 94-95 mph with his fastball early in games and sitting in the low 90s consistently, and that continued in 2020 at the Brewers’ alternate training site. He throws two different breaking balls -- a curveball that flashes above average and a slider with cutter-like action that plays nicely off his fastball. A changeup gives Bettinger a usable fourth pitch. He knows how to mix his pitches and throws a lot of strikes, showing above-average control and solid command. Bettinger could become a back-end starter, though most evaluators believe he will end up pitching as a multi-inning long reliever. That’s a valuable role for a Brewers team known for using the full 40-man roster and blending the lines between starters and relievers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick by the Braves in the 2016 MLB Draft out of the Texas high school ranks, Muller progressed through a farm system that was stacked with pitching talent and earned his first call to the big leagues in 2021. After another short stint in the Majors in ‘22 as the organization’s top-rated prospect, he was one of five players dealt to the A’s in a three-team deal that sent Sean Murphy to Atlanta in December. Muller brings a strong four-pitch mix that includes a fastball that consistently hits 95-97 mph with good carry. His two breaking pitches -- a low-80s curveball and recently added power slider that averages around 87 mph -- have both flashed plus and can generate plenty of swing-and-miss. He’s also developed a fourth offering in a changeup that comes in handy when he lacks a feel for his breaking stuff, though he uses it much less frequently than his other three pitches. Muller’s walk rate improved considerably at Triple-A in 2022, and he often succeeded in limiting damage whenever he found himself in a tough spot. While his path to a starting role was going to be difficult in Atlanta’s loaded rotation, the move to Oakland should allow him plenty of opportunity to build on that early Major League experience and establish himself as a starter with the A’s.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2016, the Braves took four high-school pitchers with their first six picks. While first-rounder Ian Anderson has spent considerable time in the big leagues, the Braves had traded two others from that class, Joey Wentz and Bryse Wilson, previously. Muller, the fourth-round pick, made his Major League debut in 2021, touched the big leagues again in 2022 while making strides on his overall pitchability in the Minors. He then became the third member of this quartet to get dealt, going to the A’s in the three-team deal that brought Sean Murphy to Atlanta in December. The 6-foot-7 southpaw now has four pitches in his arsenal. It starts with a fastball that averaged 93.5 mph in Triple-A and the big leagues in 2021, consistently reaching 95-97. It's a pitch that plays well up in the zone with high spin rates and good carry. He has two distinct breaking pitches and he leaned on his newer power slider more in 2021, a pitch that flashed plus, averaging almost 87 mph and missing a ton of bats. He still threw his low-80s curve and generated swings-and-misses with it, though he threw it for strikes less consistently. His changeup is definitely his fourth offering, one he doesn’t use frequently, but did help him at times when he lost feel for his breaking stuff. Muller is never going to have pinpoint control, but his walk rate dropped considerably in 2022 in Triple-A, and he did a good job of limiting damage. The advancement of that slider is a big reason why he had early success in the big leagues and if he can continue to make strides in finding the strike zone, he has more than enough stuff to be a Major League starter, something he should get to do in Oakland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two other high school pitchers taken by the Braves in the 2016 Draft had already made it to the big leagues through the 2020 season. Fourth-rounder Bryse Wilson was the first to get there and Ian Anderson, the No. 3 overall pick, made a huge contribution in the regular and postseason in 2020. Muller, a lefty taken from the Texas prep ranks who got an above-slot deal to sign in the second round, doesn’t look like he’s too far behind after dominating Double-A hitters in 2019 and throwing well enough at the Braves’ alternate training site in 2020 to get added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Muller started throwing harder back in 2018 and velocity gains have continued since. He was sitting in the upper 90s and touched triple digits during his time at the alternate site in 2020, throwing his four-seamer with a lot of spin and carry to miss bats up in the zone. Already equipped with a curve that can be above-average, Muller added a harder slider last year and it could end up being as good as, if not better than, the curve. He continued to show improvement on his changeup, giving him the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix. The one thing that’s held Muller back has been his command -- he walked 5.5 per nine in Double-A in 2019 -- but the big left-hander has worked hard on the consistency of his delivery and was finding the strike zone with some more consistency last summer. If that trend continues, he has more than enough stuff to join Anderson in the Braves rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Braves took three of the top high school arms in the 2016 Draft class in the first 44 picks, nabbing Ian Anderson No. 3 overall, getting Joey Wentz in Competitive Balance Round A and then selecting Muller in Round 2. Wentz has since been traded but Anderson and Muller, who signed for an above-slot $2.5 million, are on the brink of impacting the big league staff. While Muller missed most of the last month of the 2019 season with a calf strain, he largely dominated hitters in the Double-A Southern League. Muller’s velocity ticked upwards in 2018 following a move to Driveline workouts, and he’s managed to maintain it. He’s regularly up to 95 mph, touching 96-97 at times, and he can still go get mid-90s heat in the seventh inning of starts when he needs it. As impressive as his fastball is, he does fall in love with it too much and can lose command of it when he tries to overthrow. His curveball is better than he gets credit for and if he can commit to using it more, it could become a very solid weapon for him. Muller went to instructs last fall to work on his changeup, which is behind his other two offerings, and both he and the Braves were pleased with the progress when he left. Muller will need that consistent offspeed offering to give hitters varied looks if he wants to keep starting at the highest level. He’ll also have to improve his control, which went in the wrong direction with a spike in walks in 2019. There are a lot of moving parts with his 6-foot-6 frame, but the Braves feel his athleticism will allow him to figure it out and land in the big league rotation soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Braves love to go aggressively after high school pitching and they did that with Muller in 2016, taking him in the second round of that June's Draft and then going over slot to sign him for $2.5 million. Unlike most of their high school draftees, Muller wasn't ready for full-season ball right after his Draft year, instead spending the summer in the Rookie-level Appalachian League. Propelled by strong offseason workouts, he hit the ground running in 2018, pitching across three levels and finishing with a stint in the Arizona Fall League. Muller was able to start moving more quickly because his velocity bounced back to closer to what scouts saw in his high school days. Some of that was because of Driveline workouts this offseason and some of it occurred as Muller consistently found his arm slot and utilized a much more athletic delivery. More free and easy, the left-hander hit 94-95 mph with his fastball consistently, though he would lose command at times when he cranked it up. He could get fastball-heavy at times, trying to blow the ball past hitters, and he needs to learn to more effectively mix in his secondary stuff. More than anything, Muller needs to find a level of consistency. If he can learn to pitch with his rediscovered plus fastball and sharpen his breaking ball and changeup more effectively, he could give the Braves another No. 3- or 4-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 The Braves like pushing their young high school arms to full-season ball the season after they are drafted, and they've recently done so with positive results. The hope was that Muller, to whom they gave an above-pick value bonus of $2.5 million in the second round of the 2016 Draft, would follow that model, but he wasn't ready to make the jump, instead spending his second summer of pro ball in the Rookie-level Appalachian League. Since Muller became a pro, his stuff had been down, with a dip in velocity. Much of that, the Braves believe, was due to a mechanical breakdown in his delivery: His arm had gotten too straight overhand, instead of a more comfortable three-quarters slot. He started showing a little more life to his fastball, closer to what he showed pre-Draft, near the end of his season with Danville, with the hope he's on his way back to sitting at 92-93 mph, in the same ballpark as fellow lefty Joey Wentz. His breaking ball regained some of its shape, showing some good downer action with tight spin, and his changeup showed glimpses of depth. When he's right, he uses his 6-foot-6 frame very well on the mound. Not every pitcher can follow the same exact development path, and Muller may greatly benefit from not being pushed too aggressively. His move to full-season ball will be a good test to see how far he's come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 A tremendous athlete and two-way player during his high school career in Texas, Muller was the Gatorade National Player of the Year in 2016. He parlayed his strong senior season into being the 44th overall pick of the Braves, in the second round, and received an above pick-value bonus of $2.5 million to sign rather than head to the University of Texas to both pitch and hit. As a pro, Muller's future is undoubtedly on the mound, though he's already shown an eagerness to swing the bat whenever he's given the chance. Muller pitched sparingly during his debut, but he was effective even though his velocity was down a bit from the low-90s-to-95 mph spike he showed in high school. Muller uses his 6-foot-6 frame extremely well, throwing downhill and with sink. He also has good deception in his very repeatable delivery, so hitters do not square him up very often. His secondary stuff is inconsistent right now, but he does flash a plus breaking ball at times and has a good feel for a changeup with fade and tumble. Given his size, stuff, feel for pitching and athleticism, not to mention that he's focusing on pitching for the first time, Muller brings a lot of upside to the table. Watching him, Ian Anderson and Joey Wentz develop together could be a whole lot of fun.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rondón signed for only $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2016 and needed two-and-a-half seasons before jumping to full-season ball. His breakout came in 2019 when he was named Cardinals Minor League Pitcher of the Year, having posted a 2.93 ERA with 159 strikeouts in 160 innings between High-A and Double-A. He moved to Triple-A for his age-23 season and put up more pedestrian numbers (4.58 ERA, 68 strikeouts in 76 2/3 innings), but he did make his Major League debut with a pair of relief outings in June. The 6-foot-1 right-hander averaged 93.1 mph on his heater in those brief MLB looks, and that’s around where his fastball was in the Minors as well. He can touch the mid-90s when needed, and the fastball plays up because of some natural deception and late movement. Rondón pitches a bit backward with much better splits against lefties than righties (.223 average-against vs. .329, respectively, at Triple-A) in part because of a low-80s fading changeup. His slider and curveball can flash average with the former looking slightly better than the latter at this stage, but both have suboptimal spin rates and can hang a bit too much, leading to the punishment from fellow righties. To Rondón’s credit, he did improve his control rates in 2021, dropping it from 8.9 percent in 2019 to 6.5 percent. He also deserves plaudits for working with a four-pitch mix that he can sequence well, keeping hitters off even when the raw stuff doesn’t stand out. His pitchability makes him a potential No. 5 starter, and entering his age-24 season, he isn’t far from reaching that role. A focus on just one breaking ball to go with the fastball-changeup could also work in a bullpen setting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rondon’s career got off to a bit of a slow start after he signed with the Cardinals as an 18-year-old for $25,000 in 2016. The native of the Dominican Republic spent two seasons in Rookie ball before he started to rise up the ranks. Rondon reached full-season ball in the second half of the 2018 campaign and followed up the strong showing with an award-winning 2019. He began the year with Class A Advanced Palm Beach, where he was named a midseason All-Star before being promoted to Double-A Springfield and ultimately named the Cardinals’ Minor League Pitcher of the Year after posting a 2.93 ERA with 159 strikeouts over 160 innings split between the two levels. The 2021 season got off to a rough start as Rondon was hit hard and struggled in his first Triple-A experience, though he did make a couple of scoreless appearances in the Majors. Rondon impressed at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020, facing advanced hitters and showing a good understanding of how to sequence pitches. His delivery creates natural deception, which often helps his fastball play above its velocity. The fastball features late movement and sits in the mid 90s, but can also touch 97 mph on occasion. Rondon can vary the shape of his curveball, a pitch with heavy downward action that reminds some of a slider. He’s also shown an ability to keep hitters off-balance with an average changeup. The right-hander needs to improve his command and control, but he has shown he’s capable of handling a starter’s workload. The 2021 numbers have been a bit of a disappointment, but it’s important to remember he’s still just 23-years-old. Rondon’s ceiling seems to be at the back end of a rotation, though his fastball/curveball combo, paired with his pitchability, could also play well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Cardinals for $25,000 as an 18-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in January 2016, Rondon turned in two nondescript seasons across multiple Rookie levels before he finally advanced to Class A Peoria halfway into the ’18 season. He opened eyes with his performance in the Midwest League, then broke out in earnest in 2019, earning midseason All-Star honors at Class A Advanced Palm Beach before advancing to Double-A Springfield in mid-May at age 21. He proceeded to win the Texas League ERA (3.21) title and finished second in the circuit in WHIP (1.23), and the Cardinals named him their Minor League pitcher of the year after he finished second in the system in ERA (2.93) and strikeouts (159). The Cardinals attribute Rondon’s ever-improving blend of stuff, pitchability and deception to his breakout performance and note that the right-hander was unphased against Double-A competition. He generates easy velocity, touching 97 mph and sitting 93-94 with a fastball that has a lot of late movement that helps him evade barrels. His power curveball is an above-average pitch that plays nicely off of his heater, with late, sharp vertical action that can resemble a slider. Rondon can miss bats with both his heater and his breaking ball, and he also demonstrates feel for executing an average changeup. He knows how to mix his pitches and exploit hitters’ weaknesses, traits that help him compensate for control and command that both need more work. The tempo of Rondon’s delivery along with his backside arm action gives his natural deception, and hitters generally struggle to barrel the right-hander’s fastball even though it lacks plus velocity. He has the stamina and durability to handle a starter’s workload -- he finished sixth in the Minors in innings (160) last season after working just 88 frames in 2018 – and should be able to stick in that role so long as his control and command keep improving. If not, it’s almost a given that Rondon's stuff would play up in shorter bursts out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts already viewed Ray as a future first-rounder before he erupted to hit 15 homers and steal 44 bags as a Louisville junior in 2016. The Brewers made him the fifth overall pick that June, signing Ray for $4.125 million. Since then, however, Ray has battled myriad injuries and struggled to produce when healthy, save for a 2018 campaign at Double-A Biloxi in which he totaled 27 homers and 37 steals as the Southern League's Most Outstanding Player. He failed to build upon that breakout performance in 2019, as he spent the spring trying to play through an avulsion fracture in his right hand before finally requiring a month-long stint on the injured list in May. Ray still managed to gain some Triple-A experience, albeit while batting .188/.261/.363 with a 38.7 percent strikeout rate in 53 games, and the Brewers added him to their 40-man roster in November. While Ray still shows a high-end combination of power and speed, the confidence in his ability to apply those tools has waned in conjunction with his strikeout-heavy struggles at the plate. He paced the Class A Advanced Carolina League in strikeouts (156) in his first full season, finished second in the Double-A Southern League (176) in 2018 and owns a career strikeout rate of nearly 30 percent across his first four pro campaigns. While the Brewers think that a reduction in Ray’s pre-pitch movement with his hands and head, along with a subtle adjustment in his approach, will lead to better, more consistent contact, it is unlikely that he will be anything more than a below-average hitter. Ray has plus speed that serves him well on the bases and in center field, where he's an above-average defender with at least average arm strength. While those qualities, as well as Ray’s left-handed power, give him a Major League floor, he will need to trim some of his swing-and-miss and impact the ball more consistently to profile as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a breakout campaign as a Louisville sophomore that he followed with a strong performance for the U.S. collegiate national team, Ray solidified his status as a future first-round pick by hitting 15 homers and swiping 44 bags as a junior. The Brewers made him the fifth overall pick that June, and Ray signed for $4.125 million, the largest bonus in club history. Knee surgery delayed the start of Ray's pro debut, and he never looked right upon returning, hitting for neither average nor power while spending the entire season in the High A Carolina League. Challenged with a Double-A Biloxi assignment in 2018, Ray finally looked like the player the Brewers had drafted, hitting 27 home runs and swiping 37 bags en route to honors as the Southern League's Most Outstanding Player. He was slowed early in 2019 by an avulsion fracture in his right hand that he tried to play through all spring before finally requiring a month-long stint on the injured list in May. Ray's power-speed combo is among the best in the Minors. It didn't show in his first full season because Ray struggled to control the strike zone, often chasing pitches well out of the zone with a lengthy swing that produced a Carolina League-high 156 strikeouts. With an emphasis on picking specific pitches to hit in 2018, Ray regained his confidence at the plate and returned to his strengths, showing above-average game power and feel for using the entire field. He still struck out quite a bit and finished second in the Southern League with 176 whiffs, but the overall quality of his contact, as well as the results, were markedly better. A plus runner, Ray's 37 steals were an improvement over the 24 in his pro debut, and he's a candidate to steal 30 bags at the highest level. Ray's wheels also serve him well in center field, where he's an above-average defender with at least average arm strength. Strikeouts will always be a concern with Ray, but his combination of strong game power, speed and defense should ultimately help to offset concerns about his low batting averages.
