He also features a lot of spin on his 78- to 81-mph curveball (which he mainly uses against lefties) and his 84- to 87-mph slider (his primary weapon against right-handers), both of which flash as solid pitches but got hit hard by big leaguers. Poteet throws strikes but will need to be more precise with his breaking balls to survive as a long-term starter in the Majors. He has pitched to contact more than missed bats during his pro career, which could indicate he's better suited for a multi-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Poteet saw time as a starter and reliever during his three years at UCLA, but pitched mostly out of the bullpen as a junior. The Marlins made him their fourth-round pick in 2015, signed him for $488,700 and then deployed him as a starter in his pro debut. He impressed scouts with his pitchability during his promising full-season debut in the South Atlantic League and was named a Florida State League All-Star in 2017. Poteet's fastball sits at 89-92 mph with good arm-side run, and he can reach back for an extra tick or two when needed. The right-hander's slider, thrown with power and depth in the mid-80s, flashes above average and nets him whiffs, and he understands how to keep hitters off balance with his average curveball. Poteet's fringy changeup is his least-advanced offering, although it stands to improve with increased use as a starter. He has good control, consistently works down in the zone and keeps the ball in the park. Poteet's mature arsenal and pitchability bode well for him becoming a big league starter. Should that not pan out, though, the fastball-slider combo should make him an effective reliever, one capable of working multiple frames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round Draft pick in 2014 out of the Maryland prep ranks, Stokes made slow but steady progress at the outset of his career, spending his first two seasons at a pair of Rookie levels and then advancing to full-season ball in 2016. Assigned to Class A Advanced Carolina in 2017, Stokes, in his age-21 season, erupted to slug 14 home runs over 100 games to earn a late-July promotion to Double-A, where he added another six homers in just 35 games. Those 20 home runs, along with his 30 stolen bases, made Stokes one of 10 players to accrue at least 20 homers and 20 steals on the season. Stokes may be an undersized right-handed hitter -- he's listed at 5-foot-8 -- but his compact frame is loaded with strength, giving him above-average power to his pull side that he can get to in games thanks to a leverage swing. A pull-oriented approach can limit the quality of Stokes' contact at times, while also resulting in too many strikeouts, but the overall approach is sound and he's shown solid on-base skills throughout his career. Stokes is an above-average runner and knows how to apply his wheels on the basepaths and in the outfield. While his well below-average arm strength limits Stokes to a career in left, he has the offensive profile to make it work. With his blend of power, speed and patience, Stokes seemingly is on his way toward becoming a fourth outfielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a perfect world, every trade acquisition takes a step forward in development following the trade. That's what's happened with Madero, who originally signed with the D-backs in October 2013 for $160,000. The right-hander joined the Angels organization via the 2017 Trade Deadline deal for David Hernandez. In his first full year with the Angels, the Venezuelan hurler was a Midwest League All-Star, earned a promotion up to the California League, performed very well there and earned a spot on the 40-man roster. The 6-foot-3 right-hander saw his stuff tick upwards in 2018 and the results followed suit. His fastball is trending up, and he was sitting low-90s last year, touching 94 mph, throwing the pitch with sink to get ground-ball outs. He gets swings and misses with it and his above-average slider also misses bats, with the sharpening of his stuff leading to a higher strikeout rate. His changeup is developing and is behind the other two offerings. Madero has always been a good strike-thrower, and he didn't lose that with the uptick in his stuff. The next step will be command within the zone so he doesn't get hit as much as he has, but even that was trending in the right direction. He could have a chance to start, but that fastball-slider combination could play well coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Oregon State's College World Series team in 2018 had two players taken in the top 20 picks in Nick Madrigal and Larnach. Madrigal went No. 4 overall to the White Sox and reached Triple-A in his first full season. Larnach, who used a huge junior season -- partially picking up the slack from Madrigal when he was hurt, to land in the first round -- isn't too far behind him after a first full season that saw him hit his way to Double-A. Larnach has always been able to hit from the left side of the plate -- hitting for average as a sophomore and in the Cape Cod League. He added power as a junior after he adjusted his swing and he showed the ability to drive the ball to all fields during his first full season as a pro. He can easily use the opposite field, both for extra bases and home runs and was starting to improve turning on the ball to his pull side, all while maintaining his approach and drawing walks. A below-average runner, Larnach is a bit limited range-wise defensively, though his strong arm works well from right field and he's a smart defender. Even if he has to slide over to left in the future, his bat should get him to Minnesota sooner rather than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 College hitters who perform as juniors, particularly for big programs, always rise up Draft boards. Larnach was a prime example of this, going from interesting bat to sure-fire first-round pick as he helped Oregon State win the College World Series. The Twins liked his offensive profile enough to make him the 20th overall selection of the Draft and after his long college postseason run, he turned in a solid pro debut, reaching full-season ball even though he was running out of gas. Larnach had shown an advanced approach at the plate and the ability to hit for average as a sophomore and in the Cape Cod League, but took a huge step forward as a prospect when he added power to his resume thanks to some tweaks to his swing mechanics. The added power hasn't taken anything away from him potentially being a plus hitter, one who draws walks and doesn't strike out a ton, when all is said and done. Larnach's above-average arm works well from the outfield and he looked fine in right field during his debut, though some feel his below-average speed will land him left. In the end, though, it will be his bat that will carry him quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the Royals' aggressive spending spree on the international market during the 2015-16 signing period, they gave seven figures to outfielder Seuly Matias and shortstop Jeison Guzman. They also gave out a half dozen six-figure bonuses, starting with Rivero, a catcher out of Venezuela who was given $450,000 to sign. He spent the 2018 season sharing catching duties with MJ Melendez during his full-season debut. Rivero has the kind of intangibles teams love to see in their catchers. He learned English quickly to help him work with his pitching staff and he's an excellent game-caller and receiver. He also has a plus arm that allowed him to throw out more than 35 percent of potential basestealers in 2018. While the right-handed hitter's offense is behind his glove work, he has shown some potential with the bat. He has displayed excellent bat control and doesn't strike out much. He'll never be a big power guy and understands his role, with the profile of being a bottom of the order hitter. Rivero and Melendez fed off of each other in 2018 and the Royals hope they continue to do so, with Rivero helping Melendez become a better overall defender and Melendez helping to push Rivero offensively. It reminds some in the organization of the relationship between Salvador Perez and then-catcher Wil Myers in the Minors, with the hope Rivero can still develop into a big league regular as a result.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There are certain expectations of a player when he's a top five pick in the Draft and has MLB bloodlines. Gordon, the son of former big league pitcher Tom, and Dee's brother, was taken No. 5 overall in the 2014 Draft and in many ways has been chasing the status attached with his name and position in the Draft. While he hasn't been the elite-level player some hoped he would be, he did perform extremely well in Double-A and reached Triple-A at age 22, though he struggled mightily upon his arrival. Things started off well enough in 2018 for Gordon, who was having a bit of a breakout offensively when he hit .333 with a .906 OPS in the Southern League and earned a bump up a level in late May. After hitting well initially, the wheels came off and his struggles snowballed. One of the biggest causes for the fade, something that also happened in 2017, was a lack of strength that led to questions of durability. To his credit, Gordon learned a lesson last year and worked hard this offseason to add strength. When he's doing well, he has an excellent line-drive approach that leads to good contact, and he showed early on last year that there is some extra-base authority in his left-handed swing. An average runner, Gordon won't wow anyone on the basepaths or in the field, but his plus instincts help him steal bases and be more than capable on both sides of second base and still have the chance to be a solid big-league regular. The game punched him in the mouth in 2018; now it's time to see how much he can punch back.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big league pitcher Tom Gordon and brother of the Mariners' Dee Gordon, Nick Gordon has moved slowly and steadily, one level at a time, up the Twins' organizational ladder ever since he was taken as the No. 5 overall pick in the 2014 Draft. His move to the upper levels of the system in 2017 was largely a successful one, including a Futures Game invite and Southern League All-Star nod, though he did struggle in the second half of the season. Gordon is the type of player who may not jump off the page with any one tool, but does a number of things well. He's typically employed a successful contact-oriented, line-drive approach from the left side of the plate. He did show more extra-base power in Double-A, but with that came a higher strikeout rate, though an increased walk rate offset that to a degree. He's a solid runner with good instincts and will steal a base on occasion, and is a tick above-average defensively, both in terms of his arm and overall actions at shortstop. Many have felt his range points to being a better fit at second base and while he did still primarily play short, he did see more time on the right side of the infield in 2017. Gordon will be 22 for all of the 2018 season and is knocking on the big league door. He's more of a high floor than ceiling type and isn't far away from showing just what kind of solid everyday big leaguer he can be, on either side of second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 With steady infield skills and MLB bloodlines, Gordon was one of the top high school position players in the 2014 Draft class. The son of former big league pitcher Tom Gordon and Dee Gordon's half-brother, ended up being the first one taken, No. 5 overall, and has been making his way up the Twins ladder steadily since. A Florida State League All-Star in 2016, Gordon continued to show an innate ability to make consistent contact from the left side of the plate, both during the regular season and in a strong Arizona Fall League performance. Gordon has a line-drive approach, but he is starting to show more extra-base power and could develop more as he matures. He's shown an ability to steal some bases despite possessing average speed, though some evaluators feel his lack of quickness could necessitate a move to second base in the future. Others feel he will stay there long-term, with good instincts and enough arm for the premium position at the highest level. Gordon continues to be more high floor than high ceiling, a prospect who doesn't have one \"wow\" tool, but who can do everything relatively well. He continued his path toward being a solid everyday big leaguer with a strong move to the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kruger bounced around after his high school days in California, spending his freshman season at Oregon before transferring to Orange Coast College, a junior college. From there, he was on to Mississippi State, where he had a solid junior season, posting a .344/.435/.550 line. In 2016, his battery-mate Dakota Hudson went in the first round to the Cardinals. Kruger went in the 20th, getting an above slot $395,000 to sign. After a solid pro debut at the rookie levels, Kruger had a relatively nondescript first full season across two levels of A ball. The athletic backstop broke out in 2018, reaching Double-A and hitting for average at both stops. It's a contact-oriented approach, with the ability to shoot the ball to all fields, and Kruger did a nice job of managing the strike zone and drawing walks for much of the 2018 season. He's not a big power guy, but does have some juice to his pull side. He runs well for a catcher and can even steal a base, and that athleticsm plays pretty well behind the plate, where he's a solid receiver who has thrown out 27.5 percent of potential basestealers. Kruger is the only catcher on the Angels' preseason Top 30, so there isn't much to stop him from progressing. He has the chance to be a solid backup, perhaps more if the bat keeps improving.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of three first-round pitchers taken by the Royals in the 2018 Draft, when the club selected eight college pitchers in the first six rounds, Lynch was pitching well at Class A Advanced Wilmington in 2019 before a minor arm issue interrupted his first full season. But the 6-foot-6 lefty made a healthy return in late July to finish the regular season on a high note, then opened eyes as one of the best pitchers in the Arizona Fall League. Lynch made even more progress at the alternate training site in 2020, with some club officials pegging him as the camp’s biggest standout. The Royals suggested Lynch throw more fastballs upon entering the pro ranks after he had pitched with a breaking-ball-heavy arsenal in college. It immediately helped Lynch unlock more velocity, and he's been averaging around 95 mph on his fastball this summer. A plus, mid-80s slider represents the left-hander’s best secondary pitch and plays nicely off his fastball with its big depth and sharp bite. Lynch’s changeup was a major focus of his work at the alternate site, and he became more comfortable throwing it against hitters on both sides of the plate. He completes his four-pitch mix with an average curveball that he can throw for strikes but doesn't go to very often. That Lynch also got better at repeating his delivery and arm slot while at the alternate site has inspired even more confidence in his capacity to develop at least average command on top of his present above-average control. Lynch’s feel for locating his power stuff speaks to his high ceiling as a starter, and the Royals have been committed to getting him looks at that role in the Majors in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals accelerated their rebuilding efforts when they selected eight college pitchers within the first six rounds of the 2018 Draft. That group included a trio of first-rounders in Brady Singer, Jackson Kowar and Lynch, whom the Royals took with the No. 34 overall pick. The Virginia product's eye-opening pro debut led to high expectations for his first full season, with many pegging him as a potential fast-riser, and he was pitching increasingly well at Class A Advanced Wilmington before minor arm issues popped up in early June and sidelined him for seven weeks. The layoff, however, was exactly what Lynch needed, and he returned in late July to finish the regular season on a high note that carried over into his Arizona Fall League campaign. Lynch operated with a breaking-ball-forward arsenal and average velocity with the Cavaliers, but he's quickly developed into more of a power pitcher in the pro ranks after the Royals suggested that he throw more fastballs. The new approach helped Lynch unlock more velocity, as he now sits around 94-96 mph consistently with his fastball and has even reached the upper 90s in shorter stints. Lynch's plus slider in the mid-80s is his go-to secondary pitch and plays nicely off his fastball with its big depth and sharp bite, and he'll also flash plus with a changeup that improved during his first full season. An average curveball rounds out the 6-foot-6 lefty's four-pitch mix, and he repeats his clean delivery well enough to project him for above-average control. Lynch works with conviction on the mound and has advanced feel for sequencing his pitches. Those qualities, along with the sheer quality of his stuff, could make Lynch a mid-rotation starter in the big leagues, and there are some who believe he'll ultimately surpass that projection. For now, though, staying healthy and gaining experience are the top priorities.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the Royals work to rebuild their farm system, they likely will look back at the work they did early in the 2018 Draft as a big reason for the turnaround. Targeting college pitching, the quartet of Brady Singer, Jackson Kowar, Kris Bubic and Lynch could form most of a big league rotation in a hurry. Lynch, the last of three first-round picks for Kansas City, opened a lot of eyes during his pro debut and perhaps put himself on a faster track than anticipated, though some minor arm issues kept him off the mound for over a month during his first full season. While it's important to temper enthusiasm over one summer debut, it's hard not to get excited about how Lynch's stuff ticked up as a pro, especially considering he nearly reached 140 innings between his junior season at Virginia and his time in the Minor Leagues. At times last summer, Lynch showed flashes of three plus pitches with plus command. He pitched at 94-95 mph consistently with his fastball, touching 97 mph, well up from his amateur velocity. He threw outstanding sliders and a very deceptive changeup while mixing in his average curve ball extremely well. His advanced feel for pitching and conviction of what he's doing on the mound made it all play up and he came in on right-handed hitters better than most young lefties. Lynch set the bar high for his first full season after his pro debut, but the Royals are confident he can live up to his own expectations. He and the other college arms from the 2018 Draft class should feed off each other and could push each other up to Kansas City in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Thompson won two gold medals with U.S. national teams while in high school and sandwiched three productive seasons at Auburn around missing all of 2016 following Tommy John surgery. The Cubs made him a third-rounder in 2017, when they took college arms with their first five picks, and he reached Double-A by the end of his first full pro season. After throwing five no-hit innings in his first 2019 outing, he spent more than four months on the injured list with elbow inflammation that required a platelet-rich plasma injection, then returned as one of the better starters in the Arizona Fall League. Thompson's slider, changeup and pitchability rank among the best in the system. His upper-70s curveball was his go-to pitch in college, but his low-80s slider has gotten tighter and more reliable since he turned pro. He works at 90-92 mph with his four-seam fastball more notable for command than life, and his heater tunnels well with a changeup that sinks and fades. He can't overpower hitters but Thompson keeps them off balance by sequencing his pitches well and moving them around all four quadrants of the strike zone. He doesn't beat himself with home runs or walks, adding to his high floor as a back-of-the-rotation option. His medical history does create cause for concern, however.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Cubs made Thompson a third-round pick in 2017 in large part because of his long track record of success. He won two gold medals with U.S. national teams while in high school and sandwiched three productive seasons at Auburn around missing all of 2016 while recovering from Tommy John surgery. He reached Double-A midway through his first full pro season and after a tough debut, he allowed a total of five runs over his next eight starts before tiring down the stretch. Thompson's best pitches are his curveball and his slider. His upper-70s curve flashed plus more often in college, while his low-80s slider was his more consistent breaker in 2018. He uses 89-92 mph two-seam fastballs with sink and can reach back to hit 95 when he turns to his four-seamer. Thompson also demonstrates feel for a changeup with some sink. He can't blow the ball by hitters but instead keeps them off balance by mixing his pitches and pounding the strike zone. He has one of the higher floors among Cubs starting pitching prospects, projecting as a workhorse toward the back of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Thompson's lengthy track record of success, which dates back to winning multiple gold medals with U.S. national teams while in high school, played a role in Chicago taking him in the third round of the 2017 Draft. He served as a two-way player as an Auburn freshman in 2014 before blowing out his elbow the next year and missing all of 2016 while recovering from Tommy John surgery. He returned last year and showed he had regained his stuff and command by opening his redshirt junior season with a school-record 22 2/3-innings scoreless streak. As is the case with Cubs 2017 first-rounders Brendon Little and Alex Lange, Thompson's best pitch is a curveball with true downer action that elicits well-above-average grades at times. While he won't dazzle radar guns with his velocity, his two-seam fastball in the high 80s is effective because of its sink and his four-seamer that can reach 95 works because of its high spin rate. He also has good feel for his changeup, a plus pitch at its best. Thompson has become a more mature pitcher since his elbow reconstruction, focusing on getting outs and no longer worrying about velocity. He fills the strike zone with all four of his offerings and understands pitch sequencing. He has a high floor, looking like a safe bet to reach the big leagues as either a workhorse No. 4 starter or a reliever who relies on his curve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mills was the Mariners’ yo-yo in 2021, having been recalled from Triple-A Tacoma seven times during his first season in The Show. As such, his rookie status remained intact after pitching just 12 2/3 innings in mostly low-leverage scenarios, yet it was a bit of a stumble, as Mills was scoreless in just four of the 11 outings and had a 9.91 ERA overall. Seattle is still bullish on his makeup, though. He’s another example of the Mariners’ excellent job of finding money-saving college seniors in the Draft who really perform, having signed for well under slot value at $125,000 after being taken in the third round in 2017. Mills’ low three-quarter-slot delivery has been described as funky, and he’s primarily relied on a fastball-slider combination to miss bats and generate a ton of groundouts. The Mariners want to see Mills continue to use all of that to his advantage and remain in “attack” mode. His fastball sits in the low 90s with sink, and his slider has been his main strikeout pitch, especially against righties. Both offerings have high spin rates and his developing changeup gives lefties a different look, but it’s not a go-to pitch yet. Mills doesn’t need to be pinpoint accurate to be a right-handed specialist or a sixth-inning type of reliever, but if he can improve his changeup and refine his command a bit, he still has the chance to have a larger role. The Mariners love the makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mills is another example of the Mariners’ excellent job of finding money-saving college seniors in the Draft who really perform. Infielder Donovan Walton and reliever Sam Delaplane are other cases, but Mills is an even later selection who has risen through the ranks. A third-rounder in 2017, Mills signed for $125,000 – more than $45,000 under slot value -- then he proceeded to carve up Class A hitters and reached Double-A in his first full season. He scuffled some during the first half of ’19 when returning to Double-A, but he was able to turn things back up and he finished in Team USA’s bullpen during Olympic qualifying that fall. Mills’ low three-quarter-slot delivery has been described as funky and he’s primarily relied on a fastball-slider combination to miss bats and generate a ton of groundouts. The Mariners want to see Mills continue to use all of that to his advantage and remain in “attack” mode. His fastball sits in the low 90s with sink, and his slider has been his main strikeout pitch, especially against righties. Both offerings have high spin rates, and his developing changeup gives lefties a different look, but it’s not a go-to pitch yet. Mills essentially missed all of 2020 after not being selected to Summer Camp or the alternate training site, which may have served as a wakeup moment for him, but he made up for lost time at the club’s fall developmental league in Arizona and wound up on the 40-man roster, showing a nearly 4-mph uptick in fastball velocity. Hitters were said to have no chance with the 97-mph heat with movement. Typically around the strike zone, Mills' walk rate went up a bit in Double-A. He doesn’t need pinpoint accuracy to be a right-handed specialist or a sixth-inning type of reliever, but if he can improve his changeup and refine his command a bit, he still has the chance to have a larger role. The Mariners love the makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners have done an excellent job of finding money-saving college seniors in the Draft who really perform, with infielder Donnie Walton reaching the big leagues and reliever Sam Delaplane, an even later selection, rising up the ranks. Mills signed as a third-rounder of the 2017 Draft for $125,000, more than $450K under slot, then proceeded to carve up A ball hitters to reach Double-A in his first full season. He scuffled in the first half of 2019 in a return to that level, but turned it on in the second, then finished things up in Team USA’s bullpen during Olympic Qualifying last fall. Mills uses a funky low three-quarters slot to get hitters out, largely using his fastball-slider combination to miss bats and get groundball outs. His fastball sits in the low-90s with a ton of sink to it and his slider serves as his main strikeout pitch, especially against right-handed hitters. Both pitches have high spin rates, allowing them to play up. He’s worked on developing a changeup to give lefties a different look, but it’s not a go-to pitch yet. Typically around the strike zone, Mills has seen his walk rate go up a bit in Double-A. He doesn’t need to be pinpoint to be a right-handed specialist or a sixth-inning type of reliever, but if he can improve his changeup and refine his command a bit, he still has the chance to have a larger role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Under the current Draft rules, it's become common for teams to pick college seniors in the top 10 rounds and sign them for under pick value in order to aggressively go after tougher-to-sign talent. Signing Mills as a third-rounder in 2017 following a senior season at Gonzaga that saw him save 12 games and post an ERA well below 2.00 for more than $450,000 under slot allowed the Mariners to go above value to sign a pitcher like Sam Carlson, for example. But Mills is turning out to be more than just a money-saver, using his stuff and funky delivery to get to Double-A in his first full season. Mills did struggle when he reached Double-A in 2018, but there is every expectation he'll make the adjustments necessary, especially after a successful stint in the Arizona Fall League following the season. He uses a low three-quarters slot and will have to develop a changeup for left-handed hitters. He'll also have to deviate from always using his low-90s sinking fastball and ride it in on right-handed hitters to give them a different look. Analytically minded folks love Mills, who has high spin rates on both the fastball and his tight slider that serves as a swing and miss pitch, especially against right-handed hitters, and he routinely finds the strike zone. It might seem like Mills profiles best as a right-on-right specialist or more of a sixth- or seventh-inning reliever. But the same was said about Steve Cishek, whom Mills is often compared to, and Cishek has 125 career saves entering the 2019 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mills passed on signing with the Rays as a 17th-rounder in 2016 and instead opted to return for his senior season at Gonzaga, where he posted a 1.79 ERA and 12 saves to finish with the second-most saves (21) in program history. The Mariners made Mills their third-round pick in June, and he proved to be far more than just a money-saving senior discount during a stellar pro debut in which he reached full-season ball after signing for $454,800 below slot value. Mills draws comparisons to Steve Cishek because he's a lanky, side-armed right-hander with two above-average pitches. His combination of a low-90s fastball, that touches 95 mph, and a tight slider makes Mills highly effective against same-sided hitters, and he's already impressed Mariners club officials with his ability to throw strikes from his unique slot. As a low-slot reliever who features both velocity and control, Mills has the potential to jump on the fast track to the Major Leagues in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sandlin starred as a closer for two seasons at Southern Mississippi, then moved to the rotation in 2018 and led NCAA Division I in ERA (1.06) and WHIP (0.71). The Indians signed him for a below-slot $750,000 in the second round, watched him rush to Double-A as a reliever and considered promoting him in September until he wore down late in the summer. He continued to excel in 2019 before a stress fracture in his forearm ended his season in late June and necessitated surgery in August. A 5-foot-11 right-hander without overpowering stuff, Sandlin keeps hitters off balance by mixing five different pitches from three different arm slots. His best offerings are a low-90s two-seam fastball with nasty life and a sweeping, high-spin slider from a sidearm angle. He mixes in a changeup from a low three-quarters angle and a four-seamer and a curveball from a high three-quarters slot. Sandlin has tremendous feel for pitching, showing the ability to manipulate the shape of his breaking balls and to move all of his offerings around the strike zone. He confounds hitters by changing speeds and eye levels, generating a lot of swings and misses as well as weak contact. Expected to be fully healthy in 2020, he could be a multi-inning relief option for Cleveland in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring as a closer for two seasons at Southern Mississippi, Sandlin moved to the rotation in 2018 and led NCAA Division I in both WHIP (0.71) and ERA (1.06) while also ranking second in hits per nine innings (4.8) and fifth in strikeouts (144). The Indians pounced on him in the second round, signed him for a below-slot $750,000 and watched him dominate as a reliever at three levels before tiring in Double-A. They considered calling him up to the big leagues in September until he wore down late in the summer. Sandlin overcomes being a 5-foot-11 right-hander without overpowering stuff by confounding hitters with a mix of five pitches from three different arm slots. His best offering is a two-seam fastball with unusual velocity (up to 95 mph) with nasty life from a sidearm angle. He also throws a sweeping slider from down low, a changeup from a low-three-quarters slot and a four-seamer and a curveball from a high-three-quarters slot. Sandlin has tremendous feel for pitching, pounding the zone with all of his combinations of pitches and deliveries. He has an uncanny ability to throw hitters off balance by changing speeds and eye levels, and he was more effective against left-handers than right-handers in his pro debut. Cleveland thought he could be a weapon as a multi-inning reliever by midseason, but he instead was shut down for the year with a forearm strain in early July.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: His slight frame made it difficult to attract teams, so Uceta went unsigned in 2015 before landing a mere $10,000 bonus from the Dodgers the next July. The Dominican since has become an organization favorite for his pitchability and competitiveness. A key part of championship clubs in the Rookie-level Pioneer and Class A Advanced California leagues in 2017 and 2018, he allowed one run in two playoff starts last September as Double-A Tulsa fell in the Texas League finals. Uceta's best offering is his hard changeup, which arrives with fade and late tumble after he sells it with deceptive arm speed. He sets it up with a sneaky fastball that ranges from 90-95 mph and stays off barrels thanks to its riding action. He has improved the shape of a curveball that serves as an effective third pitch. Because he lacks physicality and power stuff, Uceta has to keep proving himself as a starter at each level and he has done so through Double-A. He has thrown strikes throughout his pro career and improved his command after Los Angeles helped him take a more direct path to the plate. A potential No. 4 starter, he has good feel for pitching and does a nice job of tunneling his pitches to keep hitters off balance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the advanced age of 18 in 2016, Uceta recorded a 6.59 ERA in his U.S. debut a year later. He did improve over the course of the summer and pitched well in the playoffs to help Ogden win the Rookie-level Pioneer League championship. His 2018 season unfolded in a similar fashion, as he struggled after an August promotion to high Class A but won a crucial postseason game with 5 2/3 scoreless innings to contribute to Rancho Cucamonga capturing the California League title. Uceta's best pitch is a hard changeup with fade and late tumble, and he throws it with the same arm speed as his fastball. His four-seam heater parks at 90-93 mph and reaches 95 with riding life up in the strike zone. He improved the shape of his curveball last year, giving him an average third offering. Uceta has thrown strikes throughout his pro career, and his command improved once the Dodgers got him to stop throwing across his body and take a more direct path to the plate. A dogged competitor, he must be precise with his pitches and confuse hitters by throwing them from the same release point because he doesn't have overpowering stuff or deceptive angle. As a slender 6-footer, he'll have to prove he can maintain his stuff over the course of a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The state of Wisconsin has become a bit of a baseball hotbed lately, with top Dodgers prospect Gavin Lux reaching the big leagues in 2019 and Mariners outfielder Jarred Kelenic not far behind him. Rortvedt was taken in the same Draft (2016) as Lux, a round later, with the Twins knowing that a high school catcher from a cold-weather state might take longer to develop. He’s advanced very nicely as a defender and while his bat has lagged behind, he did reach Double-A in 2019 despite missing time with a meniscus issue. Rortvedt has all the makings of a big league backstop. He has excellent blocking and receiving skills and gets high marks for his ability to frame pitches and work with a staff. His quick release helps his accurate and above-average arm be even more effective, allowing him to throw out nearly 52 percent of potential basestealers in 2019 and 38.7 percent in his pro career heading into 2020. As a hitter, Rortvedt has gotten caught in between being a contact hitter and a power guy. He doesn’t strike out much and draws plenty of walks and had previously employed a line-drive approach from the left side of the plate. There is strength in his swing and he’ll continue to work on bringing that out in his game a little more. He profiles best as a glove-first backup, but if the bat comes, he still has the chance to be more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafting high school catchers can be a risky business, and teams need to play the long game patience-wise in terms of development. That's even more true when that catcher hailed from a cold-weather state. The Twins knew all of this when they took Rortvedt in the second round of the 2016 Draft out of the Wisconsin prep ranks. His defensive work has been exemplary and he took a step forward with the bat in 2018, playing across two levels of Class A. There are few questions about Rortvedt's ability to defend at this point. He's an outstanding blocker and receiver, with some thinking he'll be a plus defender overall. His above-average arm plays up because of its accuracy and his ability to transfer quickly as well as throwing from his feet or his knees, as he's thrown out 32.6 percent of potential basestealers heading into 2019. There could be more in Rortvedt's left-handed bat as well. While he's big and strong, he employs a more conservative, contact-first swing. He did improve offensively in 2018, but the Twins would like to see him let loose a little more to unlock more of his raw power. If that happens, then the Twins could have a very intriguing every day catcher on their hands. But even if he stays the course, he has the tools necessary to have a successful backup backstop career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Rortvedt was a Draft prospect at his Wisconsin high school in 2016, he was thought to be a potential all-around catcher in the future, one whose bat appeared ahead of his glove. After his first two summers of pro ball, he still has a ways to go, but it actually seems like his defense is more advanced than his offensive game. Rortvedt looks like could be a plus receiver down the road and does a lot of things well behind the plate. He's very mobile with soft hands, receiving and blocking well, showing an ability to get really low. He has very good framing skills and is arm is solid average and accurate, allowing him to throw out 36 percent of potential basestealers during his full-season debut in 2017. At the plate, the left-handed hitter does make consistent contact, but hasn't shown the ability to impact the baseball on a consistent basis. He does have strong hands and forearms, but hasn't been able to incorporate what overall strength he does have to drive the ball. Patience is always needed for catchers develop, especially ones from high school, as the added responsibilities can slow your progress. Rortvedt now looks like he at least has the tools to be a capable backup. If the bat can come around as some expected when he was an amateur, there's plenty of time for him to evolve into an everyday catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amateur players coming from cold-weather states often enter the pro game a little more raw than their warm-climate counterparts. That's definitely the case with Rortvedt, the Wisconsin high school product taken in the second round of the 2016 Draft, though the end result could be a big league regular behind the plate. Most believe Rortvedt will hit, and with some impact. He's strong enough to have some pop, with some in the organization thinking he'll reach at least 10 home runs annually down the road thanks to his strong hands and forearms. Defensively, it's likely going to take a while. His arm may be closer to average than the above-average some amateurs initially thought, and he'll grow into being an average receiver. Rortvedt has off-the-charts makeup and loves to catch, with the kind of presence teams covet behind the plate and the leadership to run a game well. Because he won't be outworked, there is a belief he will eventually reach his ceiling. With average grades across the board, he has the chance to be a solid every day catcher at the big league level. Patience might be key, but the Twins do have some experience with developing a high school catcher from the north.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitchers who drop their arm slots to more of a sidearm delivery typically don't throw harder upon making that mechanical shift. But that's exactly what's happened with Lawrence, who struggled to get mound time at Jacksonville as a \"traditional\" pitcher, then dropped down and found some success after transferring to Daytona State College, a junior college in Florida. The Rockies took note and took him in the 12th round of the 2015 Draft. He shook off a slow start to his career and an injury in 2017 to pitch well enough in the California League and the Arizona Fall League in 2018 to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. Lawrence continues to throw harder as he progresses through the Rockies system, thanks to his throwing program and tweaks he's made to his delivery. He's now 97-100 mph with his fastball, routinely hitting triple digits during his AFL stint, coming from a very low three-quarters to sidearm slot. At times, there's some serious sink that elicits a ton of groundball outs. He's already a very uncomfortable at-bat for any right-handed hitter and he's working on tightening up his slider to be a better all-around reliever. With his delivery and arm slot, it's tough for Lawrence to remain consistent in his mechanics, leading to some issues with command. He focused on that during his AFL stint and the Rockies think it will continue to improve with more reps, with the chance for Lawrence to be a back-end bullpen guy in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lin created a stir as an amateur, winning MVP honors at the 2010 World Junior Championships and planning to sign with the Yankees for $350,000 until the Chinese Taipei Baseball Association said it would ban him from playing or coaching in Taiwan if he turned pro before graduating from high school. He stayed to get his diploma and broke the bonus record for Taiwanese position players when the Red Sox gave him $2.05 million in 2012. He posted just a .614 OPS in his first five years in pro ball before 2017, when he broke out in Double-A and served as a competent stopgap solution at third base in Boston. Lin had more success at the plate when he did a better job of balancing selectivity with aggression. He always has controlled the strike zone well and made consistent contact, but now he will pick his spots and hunt pitches to drive. He won't be a power threat but his seven homers in 2017 eclipsed his total of six in his first five seasons. Though his plus speed remains his best tool, Lin never has translated it into many stolen bases. It plays better on defense, where his quickness and average arm allow him to play shortstop, second base, third base and center field. He doesn't have the offensive upside to profile as a regular but could be a useful utilityman if the progress he made at the plate is real.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hendrix missed three months of the 2019 season because of a right elbow strain while with Double-A Chattanooga but it didn’t diminish his rising star potential. The right-handed reliever opened the year with 10 1/3 scoreless innings and 15 strikeouts in April. After returning from his injury in July, he finished the year with a 2.33 ERA over 16 games overall. That helped get him added to Cincinnati’s 40-man roster after the season. Projections for a big league reliever still fit Hendrix, who has a power two-pitch mix: a plus-plus fastball that ranges 94-98 mph but has reached 99 mph, and an above average slider/curveball. He can generate swings-and-misses with a 12.2 K/9 ratio over his pro career entering 2020. He can also generate weaker contact on the ground. It was a short sample size but Hendrix was able to cut down on his walk rate from 4.6 per nine innings to 3.7. He’s also starting to develop the confidence he was lacking when he initially entered pro ball as a 2016 fifth-round pick out of Texas A&M.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds scouted Hendrix at Texas A&M, they thought his stuff as a reliever could have placed him in the top two rounds of the 2016 Draft. But he struggled in his junior year, so he was still on the board when the Reds picked in the fifth round that June. His power stuff has played well in the lower levels of the Minors, and he was a Florida State League All-Star in 2018. With big stuff that projects well for the Major Leagues as a reliever, Hendrix has two effective pitches with a plus-plus 94-98 mph fastball and an above-average power curveball that ranges from 87-90 mph. There is no question he has swing-and-miss stuff, with a 12.3 K/9 ratio entering 2019. He also gets a lot of weak contact on the ground, as evidenced by his 1.60 GO/AO ratio through the 2018 season. Hendrix still has work to do to sharpen his command and control after he had 4.9 walks-per-nine innings last season at Daytona while he posted a 1.76 ERA in 44 games. He doesn't need to have pinpoint control in short relief, but more consistent strikes could lead to him getting high-leverage innings late in games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Santos for $250,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, and then he went with Shaun Anderson to the Giants in a trade for Eduardo Núñez two years later. He showcased power stuff early in his career and kicked it up a notch during instructional league in 2020, propelling him to the big leagues in April 2021. He drew an 80-game suspension that June after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs and never could claim a full-time job in the Majors the last two seasons, after which San Francisco dealt him to Chicago for right-handed pitching prospect Kade McClure in December. Santos featured a heavy 92-98 mph fastball and a plus 82-85 mph slider as a starter earlier in his career, and he has lit up radar guns even more since becoming a full-time reliever in 2021. His slide piece is a true plus-plus pitch that sits at 87-90 mph and touches 93 with two-plane depth, and it generated a 45 percent swing-and-miss rate last season. His heater averages 99 mph and peaks at 102, though it lacks life and gets barreled more than his slider. Now that he's in the bullpen, Santos no longer has to refine what was a mediocre changeup, but he does need to improve his control and command if he's going to play a high-leverage role. After he averaged 2.5 walks per nine innings as a starter in the Giants system, that rate has jumped to 5.4 the last two seasons, during which big leaguers tagged him for three homers in just 5 2/3 frames. The White Sox hope he'll figure things out like Tommy Kahnle did after they acquired him in a 2015 trade for Yency Almonte.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015 before shipping him to the Giants along with Shaun Anderson in a deal for Eduardo Núñez two years later. His stuff took a leap during instructional league in 2020 and landed him in San Francisco in April 2021, but he drew an 80-game suspension that June after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. After he was unable to land a permanent role in the big leagues the last two seasons, the Giants traded him to the White Sox for right-handed pitching prospect Kade McClure in December. Santos had a heavy 92-98 mph fastball and flashed some plus 82-85 mph sliders in the past, then kicked his stuff up a notch during instructs and maintained it after becoming a full-time reliever in 2021. Working in shorter stints, he now parks at 97-99 and regularly climbs into triple digits with high spin rates that produce carry, though his heater is somewhat straight. His slider now operates at 88-90 mph with wicked horizontal and vertical action and both offerings grade as plus-plus. Santos no longer has to worry about refining a mediocre changeup that he scrapped after moving to the bullpen. His biggest need is to improve his control and command after he battled the strike zone last year and big leaguers teed off on him when he didn't locate his pitches well. If he can add some polish, he could become a late-inning weapon and perhaps a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Red Sox for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Santos came to the Giants along with Shaun Anderson in a trade for Eduardo Nunez two years later. He made his full-season debut at age 19 in 2019 but made just eight starts because of shoulder tightness. His only 2020 development experience came in instructional league, where he performed spectacularly to cement a spot on the 40-man roster. Santos already had showcased some of the best stuff in the system prior to last fall, working with a 92-96 mph fastball that touched 98 with heavy sink and flashing some plus sliders at 82-85 mph. In shorter stints at instructs, he dealt at 97-100 mph and displayed a plus-plus slider with increased velocity and sharpness. His stuff looked ready for a high-leverage role in a big league bullpen. When Santos continued to display an overpowering fastball and slider this spring, the Giants promoted him to their bullpen in late April, though he got demoted a week later and drew an 80-game suspension in June after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. As a reliever, he won't have to worry about refining his changeup or his command as much as he would if he remained a starter. Working in shorter stints may help him stay healthier after he accumulated just 174 1/3 innings in his first five years as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trading Eduardo Nunez to the Red Sox in July 2017 netted the Giants two potential future big league starters in Shaun Anderson and Santos. Signed for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Santos made his full-season debut at age 19 last year. He made just two starts before going on the injured list for two months with tightness in shoulder, then came back and made six more before getting shut down in mid-July. When healthy, Santos showcases some of the nastiest stuff in the system. He operates at 92-96 mph and peaks at 98 with heavy sink on his fastball that makes it difficult for batters to lift. His 82-85 mph slider can be a plus pitch as well, though it needs more consistency. Santos struggles against left-handers, reinforcing the need to develop his changeup. His strike-throwing has improved significantly since he switched organizations, but his command is still a work in progress, understandable given his youth. San Francisco believes his shoulder problems last year were more a matter of learning to prepare for a long season rather than any long-term health concerns.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Eduardo Nunez played a role in the Red Sox winning the 2018 World Series, the Giants have no regrets about trading him in July 2017. In return, they received a pair of right-handers who could team up in their rotation of the future in Shaun Anderson and Santos. Signed for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, he made a successful jump to full-season ball this year but has been bothered by persistent shoulder problems. Santos' fastball velocity continues to climb as he matures physically, and he sat at 92-96 mph and touched 98 as an 18-year-old in 2018. His heater comes with heavy sink that makes it difficult to lift, as evidenced by his outstanding home run rate (0.4 per nine innings) and groundout/airout ratio (2.4) in his first three pro seasons. His 82-85 mph slider lacks consistency but shows flashes of becoming a plus offering. Santos shows some feel for his changeup but it still needs a lot of work to keep left-handers from teeing off on him. His control is improving but his command has a long ways to go. Youth is still very much on his side and San Francisco will be patient with his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Eduardo Nunez played the best baseball of his career after the Giants shipped him to the Red Sox, the trade could pay huge dividends for San Francisco. Not only did it land Shaun Anderson, a potential No. 3 starter, but also Santos, who has similar upside but is much further away. Signed for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, he spent his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Santos added about 3 mph to his fastball in 2017, reaching 97 mph and working at 91-94 mph as a 17-year-old. He demonstrates good aptitude for spinning a curveball that shows signs of becoming a plus pitch. His changeup isn't as advanced but he shows some feel for what should be at least an average third offering. Santos does a good job of using his 6-foot-2 frame to create downhill plane, resulting in a 2.4 groundout/flyout ratio in his first two years as a pro. Though his control and command still require a lot of development, the Giants like how he works with a quick tempo and think he'll figure it out. He made a strong impression during instructional league before making a successful U.S. debut in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Short led the Northeast Conference with nine homers and 33 walks as a Sacred Heart sophomore in 2015, lackluster performances in the Cape Cod League and his junior season depressed his Draft stock. After signing for $80,000 as a 17th-rounder in 2016, he regained his power and steadily advanced through the system. He reached Triple-A Iowa in 2019 and was on track to make his Major League debut that summer before his left hand was broken on a hit by pitch, costing him 10 weeks. Short made up for some of that lost time in the Arizona Fall League and was added to the Cubs’ 40-man roster in November, though they traded him to the Tigers for Cameron Maybin at the 2020 Trade Deadline. Short has surprising power for his size, thanks to quick hands and an aggressive approach in which he tries to pull and left everything with his right-handed swing. He will need to shorten his stroke, develop more consistency and make adjustments to catch up to fastballs up in the zone. While he doesn't hit for average, he does work deep counts and draw a lot of walks, fueling healthy on-base percentages. Short can help a team beyond his bat, using his solid speed well on the bases and playing quality defense at a number of positions. He might be the best shortstop in the Tigers' system, and his quickness and strong arm allow him to get the job done at second and third base as well. He has a ceiling as a Zack Cozart-type regular but more likely will be a slugging utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Short put himself on the prospect map by leading the Northeast Conference with nine homers and 33 walks as a Sacred Heart sophomore in 2015, only to slump in the Cape Cod League that summer and again as a junior. He fell to the 17th round of the 2016 Draft, signed for $80,000 and didn't do much in his pro debut. But he has opened eyes since with his power and patience, combining for 30 homers and 176 walks in his first two full seasons while reaching Double-A. Short has quick hands and a pull-heavy approach, giving him more pop than a typical 175-pounder. He's an extreme flyball hitter who makes a lot of loud contact from the right side of the plate, though the Cubs would like to see him cut down his swing and make more regular contact. He works deep counts and draws a lot of walks, giving him healthy on-base percentages despite subpar batting averages. With solid speed and an aggressive nature, Short can steal an occasional base. Some club officials believe he's the best defensive infielder in the system, and his quickness and arm strength allow him to play second and third base and serve in a utility role if needed. If he can put the bat on the ball more consistently, he could be an everyday shortstop in the mold of Zack Cozart.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Short led the Northeast Conference with nine homers and 33 walks as a Sacred Heart sophomore in 2015, intriguing scouts with his combination of pop and patience. But he didn't perform well in the Cape Cod League and slumped as a junior, so he dropped to the 17th round of the 2016 Draft. He got going again offensively in his first full pro season, slamming 13 homers and finishing third in the Minors with 94 walks while reaching high Class A in 2017. While he's just 5-foot-10 and 175 pounds, Short has quick hands and makes repeated hard contact, giving him the ability to produce 12-15 homers on an annual basis. He's an extremely disciplined hitter who walked more than he struck out in his first two years as a pro, though his whiff rate has soared in Double-A this year and his on-base percentages have been much more impressive than his batting averages. He runs well and is aggressive on the bases. Short's athleticism, quickness and solid arm strength give him defensive versatility. The Cubs believe he's a legitimate shortstop and also have played him at third base and second base. There's no reason he couldn't handle some outfield duty as well, which could make for a very interesting utilityman package.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Switch-hitters with power potential who have the chance to play up the middle aren’t easy to find, so the Pirates were excited when they landed Castro for $150,000 in the 2015-16 international signing period. Since then, Castro has shown glimpses of that pop, but has often struggled with other facets of his offensive game. After hitting 19 homers across two levels of A ball in 2019 and performing well at the club’s alternate site in 2020, Castro was added to the 40-man roster. He made headlines when his first five big league hits were home runs in 2021. An extremely physical infielder who has packed on a lot of strength to his six-foot frame since signing, there are no questions about his raw power from both sides of the plate. He’s tended to be better from the right side, though he hit bunch of homers left-handed in 2021. He can hit the ball out to all fields, but the question remains if he can make enough contact to get to it his power consistently. He hits the ball very hard, but also swings and misses a great deal, giving away at-bats and not recognizing spin all that well. Castro is an average runner who used to play a lot of shortstop, but now focuses on second and third, where he’s a fringy defender. It’s possible he could be an offensive-minded second baseman in the big leagues, but it’s more likely that he moves around a bit to find ways to get his power potential into a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates signed Castro for $150,000 during the 2015-16 international signing period, they saw a switch-hitter with power potential who had the chance to play up the middle. That power started to show up consistently when he got to repeat the South Atlantic League, as he hit 14 homers in just 61 games to earn a bump up to the Florida State League. Castro keeps getting stronger and is now a very physical six-foot tall infielder. He can drive the ball from both sides of the plate and can hit the ball out to all fields, though he’s better from the right side of the plate. While he has a fairly clean, low-maintenance swing from both sides, he does need to work on his approach as he is prone to giving away at-bats and pitches. An average runner, Castro quickly moved from shortstop to focusing more on the right side of the diamond. He still sees time at short and has mixed in third base as well, with a likely future as an offensive-minded utility type, with his best chance at being a big league regular at one spot likely coming at second.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Many scouts believed Bukauskas’ fastball and slider were the best combination of pitches in the 2017 Draft, in which he went 15th overall to the Astros and signed for $3.6 million. An automobile accident in his first Spring Training left him with a slipped disc and limited him to three appearances in the first three months of the 2018 season, but his overpowering stuff was apparent down the stretch and in the Arizona Fall League. He was having an inconsistent season in Double-A, albeit while missing plenty of bats, before the Astros packaged him with Seth Beer, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas in a deal with Arizona to get Zack Greinke at the '19 Trade Deadline. Bukauskas has legitimate no-hit stuff when he’s firing on cylinders, with four pitches that grade out as at least average. His best offering is his slider, which combines mid-80s power with late, sharp bite, and he can morph it into an average cutter to give hitters a different look. His heater is also explosive, sitting in the mid-90s, topping out at 98 mph and featuring some sink and run. He can flash plus with his changeup, but he doesn’t get to use it much because he struggles to get ahead in counts consistently. Bukauskas has demonstrated natural bat-missing ability at every stage of his career, averaging 10.7 strikeouts-per-nine in three seasons at North Carolina and 10.5 as a pro, but his control and command backed up in his first Double-A campaign, resulting in an alarming 5.7 BB/9 across 92 2/3 frames. The signs suggest that Bukauskas will end up in the bullpen, where he has the chance to dominate in short bursts, but the D-backs aren’t ready to give up on him as a starter and believe a deviation from his prior mental approach, along with some mechanical inconsistencies, contributed to his 2019 struggles. He may never fit in a clean box as a starter due to his lack of size and control issues, but there is no question that Bukauskas has the raw stuff to be successful in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bukauskas' velocity and prospect status took off in 2014, when he reclassified from a high school junior to a Draft-eligible senior, yet he turned down early-round overtures from clubs in order to attend North Carolina. Many scouts believed his fastball and slider were the best combination of pitches in the 2017 Draft, where he went 15th overall and signed for $3.6 million. An automobile accident in his first Spring Training left him with a slipped disc and limited him to three appearances in the first three months of the 2018 season, but his overpowering stuff was apparent down the stretch and in the Arizona Fall League. He was having an inconsistent season in Double-A, albeit while missing plenty of bats, when the Astros packaged him with Seth Beer, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas to Arizona to get Zack Greinke at the 2019 Trade Deadline Bukauskas' best offering is his slider, which combines mid-80s power with late, sharp bite, though he can fall in love with it and lose some feel for his fastball. His heater is also formidable, sitting in the mid-90s, topping out at 98 mph and featuring some sink and run. He flashed a plus changeup with fade in the AFL, though he needs to throw it more often to improve its consistency, and he also can mix in a cutter. The debate over whether Bukauskas is better suited to be a starter or reliever dates to his high school days. He has settled down his delivery somewhat since then but still throws with effort, and his lack of size and reliable command could point him toward the bullpen. He could move very fast in a relief role, though others see him as a Sonny Gray type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way star who rated as the state of Minnesota's best prospect in 2014, Hentges focused on pitching after signing for an over-slot $700,000 in the fourth round. Waylaid by Tommy John surgery in 2016, he didn't break out until 2018, when he led the Class A Advanced Carolina League in strikeout rate (9.3 per nine innings) while ranking second in ERA (3.27). His jump to Double-A didn't go smoothly last year, as he gave up the most runs (89) and baserunners (213), took the most losses (13) and posted the worst ERA (5.11) among qualifiers in the Eastern League. Hentges has displayed more arm speed since having his elbow reconstructed and now works at 91-94 mph and reaches 96 with some sink on his fastball. His upper-70s curveball features good depth and serves as his best secondary pitch, though it was less effective in 2019 and never has dominated same-side hitters. He also has a mid-80s cutter that he added in 2018 and a fading changeup that he needs to trust more often. While Hentges' 6-foot-8 frame and high three-quarters delivery create steep downhill plane, he was less effective at inducing grounders last year than he had been previously. His mechanics are fairly polished for an extra-large pitcher, but he has yet to repeat them well enough to provide consistent strikes. He can't blow hitters away, so he'll have to command his offerings better to succeed against upper-level hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top prospect in Minnesota in 2014, Hentges was a high school two-way star who became a full-time pitcher after signing for an over-slot $700,000 in the fourth round. He spent most of his first two years as a pro in Rookie ball before blowing out his elbow in '16, with Tommy John surgery sidelining him for most of the subsequent season as well. He finally broke out in 2018, leading the Class A Advanced Carolina League in strikeout rate (9.3 per nine innings) and ranking second in ERA (3.27). Hentges doesn't have a true plus pitch, but he has the potential for four solid offerings. He has shown more arm speed since having his elbow reconstructed and now works at 91-94 and touches 96 mph with his fastball. An upper-70s downer curveball is his second-most reliable option, a mid-80s cutter he began throwing in 2018 has promise and his changeup features some fade and should improve if he uses it more often. Hentges uses his 6-foot-6 frame and high-three-quarters delivery to create steep downhill plane on his pitches, which helped him top the Carolina League in home-run rate (0.3 per nine innings). He has a fairly smooth delivery for an extra-large pitcher but has yet to prove he can throw strikes on a consistent basis. If he can do that and refine his secondary offerings, he could be a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hentges was named Minnesota's Gatorade High School Player of the Year in 2014, the same year that the Indians drafted the big left-hander in the fourth round. He enjoyed a promising start to his career and advanced to full-season ball in 2016, only to require Tommy John surgery in June that kept him out for part of the next year. Fully healthy in 2018, Hentges made the jump straight to Class A Advanced Lynchburg and emerged as one of Cleveland's top pitching prospects behind an impressive campaign in the Carolina League. The 6-foot-6 southpaw has shown improved physicality as well as more arm speed since making his return to the mound, and the result has been a fastball that now touches 96 mph and sits comfortably in the low 90s with significant downhill plane. Hentges' downer curveball flashes plus when it's right, and he's demonstrated better feel for throwing a potentially average changeup post-surgery. He's still learning how to repeat his delivery, and scouts expect both his control and command to improve as he becomes comfortable doing so. The combination of Hentges being one of the youngest players in his Draft class and that he's quickly made up for lost time due to surgery bodes suggests his best is yet to come. He's still a bit of a project and will need time to develop his craft, but the long-term payoff could be that of a mid-rotation workhorse who misses his share of bats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of reliever Phil Maton, now with the Indians, Nick was a seventh-round pick in 2017 out of Lincoln Land Community College, where he had transferred after one season at Eastern Illinois. He was an All-Star in each of his first two full seasons, earning a late promotion to Double-A in 2019. A broken thumb cut short his time in the Arizona Fall League, but even then he had competitive at-bats while trying to play hurt. The Phillies think Maton really has the chance to hit, with a buggy whip of a swing that generates solid bat speed and allows him to catch up to velocity. He controls the zone well, limiting strikeouts and drawing walks at an impressive clip. He’s never going to be a huge power guy, but he’s not going to have the bat knocked out of his hand either, with some extra-base authority from the left side of the plate. He’s not a burner, but he’s aggressive on the basepaths and is still learning how to steal bases more consistently. With solid defensive skills across the board, Maton has the chance to play shortstop regularly. He’s shown he can handle second base more than capably and even mixed in some third base in 2019. His floor is a valuable super-utility type, but don’t give up on him being an everyday player at one position just yet.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If nothing else, the Maton brothers know how to overachieve. Older brother Phil was a 20th-round pick of the Padres in 2015 and has spent the last two years pitching out of their big league bullpen. Nick was a 40th-round pick out of high school in the same Draft as his brother and after a year at Eastern Illinois, transferred to Lincoln Land Community College. A huge season there landed him in the seventh round of the 2017 Draft and he had a solid, albeit unspectacular, first full season in 2018 that included a South Atlantic League All-Star nod. Maton has the chance to have four at least average tools. As a legitimate 6-foot-2 infielder, the easy thing to say is he won't be able to stay at shortstop long-term, but the Phillies haven't seen any reason why he can't, with his hands, arm, accuracy and footwork all working well from the premium position. He has a solid approach at the plate, with the ability to work counts, and while there isn't a ton of over-the-fence-power, he can drive the ball from the left side of the plate. If Maton can continue to develop offensively and gets to be a Major League average hitter, he's at least a solid utility type in the big leagues, and he did play a few games at second in 2018. But there's enough upside here to think he could find a way to be a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Solomon established himself as a potential 2017 first-rounder after a strong summer in the Cape Cod League, but control issues relegated him to Notre Dame's bullpen and the fourth round as a junior. He regained his control and advanced to High-A in his first full pro season, only to blow out his elbow in April 2019 and require Tommy John surgery. He returned last year to win Triple-A West pitcher of the year honors and make his big league debut, posting a 1.29 ERA in six relief appearances, but his stuff has regressed in 2022. Solomon regained the 92-96 mph velocity on his four-seam fastball early in 2021, though his heater sat more in the low 90s at the end of last season and has parked at 91 this year. He has fallen in love with his mid-80s cutter even though his low-80s slider with more depth is a better offering. His formerly solid to plus curveball is now merely an average pitch. To remain a starter, Solomon will need to rediscover his previous stuff as well as the feel for his fading low-80s changeup, which wasn't as effective in 2021 as it had been previously. He'll also need to refine his control and command, which are average at best. He may be more suited to be a multi-inning reliever, the role he filled in his introduction to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Solomon ranked as the state of Maryland's top pitching prospect in 2014, when he was coming out of a Mount Saint Joseph High (Baltimore) program that has spawned eight big leaguers (most notably Mark Teixeira), but fell to the Padres in the 21st round because he was strongly committed to Notre Dame. A strong summer in the Cape Cod League after his sophomore season positioned him as a potential first-rounder for 2017, but control issues landed him in the Fighting Irish bullpen and eventually the fourth round. He rediscovered the strike zone and rose to high Class A in his first full pro season, but he blew out his elbow in April 2019 and required Tommy John surgery. Back on the mound last fall in instructional league, Solomon showed he had regained his 92-96 mph four-seam fastball, and he previously had demonstrated the ability to hold that velocity deep into games and over the course of a full season. While his breaking balls lack consistency, his curveball can be a hammer at its best and he flashes a plus slider that he also can turn into a cutter. His changeup is clearly his fourth pitch, yet helps him keep lefties in check and could become an average offering if he uses it more. Placed on Houston's 40-man roster in November, Solomon could be a mid-rotation starter if he stays healthy and throws strikes. He averaged 5.3 walks per nine innings at Notre Dame but slashed that mark to 2.9 in his lone full season as a pro. Like many of Houston's top pitching prospects, he ultimately may fit best as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maryland's top pitching prospect in 2014, Solomon came from a Mount Saint Joseph High (Baltimore) program that has spawned eight big leaguers (most notably Mark Teixeira) and dropped to the Padres in 21st round because he was set on attending Notre Dame. Starring in the Cape Cod League after his sophomore season gave him a chance to go in the first round, but control problems caused him to slide to the fourth in 2017. He impressed while advancing to high Class A in his first full pro season but blew out his elbow this April and required Tommy John surgery. Solomon has three pitches that grade as plus at their best. His most reliable offering is his four-seam fastball and he can maintain its 92-96 mph velocity deep into starts and over the course of a season. His breaking pitches aren't as consistent, but his curveball can be a hammer at times and he can turn his hard slider into an even harder cutter. Solomon's changeup lags behind his other pitches yet helps keep left-handers off balance and could become an average offering if he uses it more. He averaged 5.3 walks per nine innings during his college career, which got him banished to the Fighting Irish bullpen as a junior, but he sliced his walk rate to 2.9 last season. He has a chance to become a mid-rotation starter once he returns to health, and he could have a mid-90s fastball with power breaking stuff if he lands in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It took three international signing periods for Doval to catch on with a pro team, as he signed for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic as an 18-year-old in 2015. His fastball gained about 10 mph in the three years between him joining the Giants and reaching full-season ball in 2018, and he now has one of the most electric arms in the system. Pitching purely in relief, he averaged 12.8 strikeouts per nine innings in his first four seasons as a pro. Doval doesn't quite have the fastest fastball in the system, but he might have the craziest. He ranges from 93-98 mph and repeatedly reaches triple digits, exceptional velocity coming out of a low three-quarters arm slot, and the angle imparts huge spin rates and nasty cutting and sinking life. He depends heavily on his heater and pairs it with a hard, sweeping slider that can overmatch right-handers. Doval doesn't have a third pitch and could use an option to better combat left-handers, who tagged him for an .876 OPS in 2019 (compared to .447 for righties). His delivery provides deception but also features a lot of effort that makes it difficult for him to throw strikes. His fastball could make him a late-inning weapon, though he'll need a lot more polish before he approaches his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively advanced age of 18 in October 2015, Doval has one of the best pure arms in the Giants organization. He averaged 12.9 strikeouts in his first three pro seasons and made a successful jump to full-season ball in 2018. During that time, his fastball gained about 10 mph. Doval has a filthy heater that sits at 93-98 mph and frequently reaches triple digits. His slings the ball from a low-three-quarters arm slot that makes it hard for right-handers to pick up his heater and imparts natural cutting and running action. He relies heavily on his fastball, complementing it with a hard, sweeping slider that has its moments. Strictly a two-pitch guy, Doval could use something to keep left-handers in check.
