He throws a true 11-to-5 curve with good depth to it, though he commanded it inconsistently. His changeup is underdeveloped -- he was mostly a fastball-curveball pitcher in '16 -- but he can throw it with good arm speed, and it has the chance to be average once he starts using it more, something he'll have to do as he reaches the upper levels. Command and feel often come back a little slower with pitchers returning from TJ surgery, but the Phillies saw enough to add him to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Continued progress could mean Anderson becomes more of a talked-about prospect, one who could impact the big league rotation in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It might seem like Sims has been around forever, having been taken as a high schooler out of the Braves' backyard in Georgia back in 2012. And while his developmental path hasn't necessarily gone in a straight line, including struggling mightily in his first taste of Triple-A in 2016, it should be noted he reached that level before his 22nd birthday. When Sims came back down to Double-A after faltering, he did right the ship considerably, leading the organization in strikeouts and getting added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. The stuff is all still there, but he's still dealing with some mechanical issues, a big reason why he walked 92 in 141 innings in 2016. He still throws across his body too much at times, and the lack of direction impacts his control and his overall stuff. When he's right, his 93-95 mph fastball comes from a downhill plane and he's able to throw it for strikes. The same goes for his nasty curveball, which will be a true plus offering with better command of it. His changeup remains behind the other two offerings. Sims needs to find what's comfortable and let his mechanics work for him. There's plenty to work with and even though he's at the upper levels, there's still time for him to figure it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Flexen's combination of size and strength intrigued the Mets, so they went above the $100,000 bonus limit for selections made beyond the 10th round to sign him out of high school back in 2012. He had Tommy John surgery in 2014, but a fully healthy 2016 put him on the prospect radar. A knee injury delayed the start of his 2017, but he still enjoyed a breakout in Double-A. He was rushed to the big leagues out of necessity and showed he wasn't quite ready for prime time. Everything clicked for Flexen while in Double-A as he mixed three, and occasionally four, pitches well to keep Eastern League hitters flummoxed. His fastball was up to 95-96 mph with regularity. He showed a plus curve at times and an improved changeup, all of which he threw routinely for strikes. In Double-A, he didn't need fine command and could get away with missing spots, but that didn't fly in the big leagues. He tried to be too fine and hit corners and it didn't work for him. His curve regressed and he started going to an average slider with New York. The Mets don't expect Flexen to have the kind of miniscule walk rate he showed in the Minors in 2017. If he can get back to trusting his stuff and stop nibbling, he could be a No. 4 type starter. There's also the knowledge that his high-end velocity and breaking ball would play up as a reliever, but there's no talk yet of moving him to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets liked Flexen enough in the 2012 Draft to give the 14th-round pick out of the Northern California high school ranks well above the $100,000 bonus limit for selections made in the 10th round and higher. Tommy John surgery in 2014 slowed him down, but he logged over 130 innings in his first true full season in 2016 and pitched his way to Double-A in 2017 despite missing more than a month of the season following knee surgery. With a strong and durable frame, Flexen looks like he could be a workhorse the further removed from surgery he gets. He pitched at 93 mph with his fastball in 2016 and touched as high as 96 mph on occasion. The rest of his stuff grades out as average at best. He can spin a solid breaking ball, a mid-70s curve and does have some feel for a changeup. He's around the strike zone with all three pitches, and his command could improve as he's able to log more innings. Flexen has the chance to be a starter long term, with the ceiling of a No. 4 or 5, albeit one who could log a lot of innings. The uptick in velocity could mean he would profile well in relief, coming in and throwing in the mid-to-upper 90s in shorter stints, but the Mets liked what they saw in his progress as a starter enough to call him up to help out the big league rotation in late July.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bader started for three years at the University of Florida and performed well enough to warrant a third-round selection in the 2015 Draft. Thought to be the kind of college performer who could move quickly, the outfielder lived up to that billing, making his full-season debut in Double-A and zipping through the upper levels to make his big league debut in his second full year of pro ball. Bader's tools grade out as all average or a tick above and he can do everything fairly well, though he doesn't have one plus or carrying tool. An aggressive hitter, he has shown a knack for barreling up the baseball consistently. He has done that often without great pitch recognition, with offspeed and breaking stuff giving him problems at times, and he doesn't draw many walks. With solid speed, Bader has enough range to man center field, where he mostly played during his big league callup. He can steal a base, though he hasn't always been efficient. Bader has nothing left to prove at the Minor League level, though it might still be tough to break through a crowded Cardinals outfield. Being able to play center field increases his value, though his first extended stay in St. Louis might have to be as a guy who plays all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals have shown a knack over the years for finding college talent in the later rounds, with Allen Craig, Matt Carpenter and Matt Adams as prime examples. While Bader wasn't the same level of sleeper pick as a third-rounder out of Florida, after making it to Triple-A in his first full season, it's clear he's not far off from contributing like those others have. While Bader doesn't have one plus tool, he can do a lot of things well, and better than one might think after a casual glance. With an aggressive approach at the plate, he doesn't get cheated, and while he's likely to never lose that attitude, he was open to tweaking his approach when Triple-A proved to be a bit more challenging for him. He has more power than one would think, with the chance to be Major League average in that department at the highest level. He's a better defender than people gave him credit for, with the chance to stay in center field long term. With the free agent signing of Dexter Fowler, Bader can't break in at that up-the-middle position. But after a strong Arizona Fall League showing and an impressive 2017 season in Triple-A, he appears ready to help out in any of the three outfield spots when the need arises.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Devers the best left-handed bat on the international market in 2013, and he has lived up to that billing since the Red Sox signed him for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic. The third-youngest regular (age 19) in the Class A Advanced Carolina League in 2016, he scuffled below the Mendoza Line for the first two months before batting .326/.367/.539 in the second half. He has continued to excel in 2017, appearing in his first SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and reaching Triple-A before receiving his first Major League callup in late July. Devers' signature tool is his prodigious power to all fields, the product of impressive bat speed and strength. He's more than just a slugger, however, which he proved yet again with his ability to make adjustments in high Class A. While he can get aggressive at the plate, he recognizes pitches well for his age and understands he's at his best when he tries to drive the ball from gap to gap and just lets his power come naturally. When Devers signed, there was some thought that he'd outgrow third base and wind up at first base, but he worked diligently on his defense and conditioning. He has the hands and arm for the hot corner, and his underrated instincts give him enough range to make plays. While he figures to lose a step from his presently average speed as he physically matures, he shows surprising savvy on the basepaths.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $1.1 million out of Venezuela by the Padres in 2011, Ruiz was one of the top catching prospects in his international class but batted just .203/.239/.240 in five Minor League seasons behind the plate. San Diego converted him to the mound in mid-2016 and brought him to the Majors for an emergency appearance 13 months later, only to lose him on waivers to the White Sox in December 2017. Chicago outrighted him off its 40-man roster last March but added him again when they made him a September callup. Ruiz's strong arm threw out 37 percent of basestealers during his days as a catcher and now generates 94-97 mph fastballs that reach 99. He compensates for his relatively short frame by creating a downward angle with a high-three-quarters delivery. He backs up his heater with an 84-88 mph slider that stands out more for its power than its bite. Ruiz will mix in an occasional changeup but mostly attacks hitters with his fastball and slider. While he throws with effort and never will be able to pinpoint his pitches, he did improve his control and command from his first full season as a pitcher to his second. He has the stuff to work the late innings and could claim that role with the White Sox after spending some time in Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout during his time at Louisiana State where he played alongside Alex Bregman, Stevenson signed for $750,000 as a second-round pick in 2015. He finished his pro debut with Class A Hagerstown and reached Double-A in his first full season before an impressive turn in the Arizona Fall League. He performed well in his return to Harrisburg in 2017 and earned a quick promotion to Triple-A, where his production waned against more advanced arms. He didn't fare any better after his first big league callup in July, ultimately batting .158 and with a .193 slugging over parts of 37 games. Considered to be the best defensive center fielder in college baseball leading up to the 2015 Draft, Stevenson has continued to impress with his reads, jump and range as a pro. Stevenson's below-average arm strength is his down tool. At the plate, Stevenson exhibits a solid approach, with good contact skills from the left side, though some worry about the utility of his hit tool given his lack of strength and bat speed. A plus runner, Stevenson produces plus run times to first base and is a threat to steal once on base. Club officials continue to rave about Stevenson's makeup, leadership and overall feel for the game, all of which help him to get the most out of his tools. A lack of impact potential with the bat will keep Stevenson from becoming an everyday player, but he does enough things well to continue to profile as a fourth or fifth outfielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Louisiana State produced a pair of Day 1 Draft picks in 2015 in Alex Bregman and Andrew Stevenson. While Bregman, whom Houston took with the second overall pick, has already established himself as an impact big leaguer, Stevenson isn't too far behind his former teammate. He signed for $750,000 as a second-round pick, finished his pro debut with Class A Hagerstown and advanced to Double-A in his first full season. Stevenson boosted his stock even more last year's Arizona Fall League, where he finished second in the batting race (.353) and paced the circuit in hits (30), and he spent all of 20 games back in Double-A this season before moving up to Triple-A. Considered to be the best defensive center fielder in college baseball leading up to the 2015 Draft, Stevenson has carried that reputation with him to the professional ranks. His reads and jumps are outstanding and few players show more range, with some scouts grading his defensive ability as a 70 on the 20-80 scale. Stevenson's below-average arm strength is his weakest tool, although it doesn't detract from his overall brilliance in center. At the plate, Stevenson shows top-of-the-order potential from the left side with his knack for quality contact, strong on-base skills and speed that produces plus run times to first base and makes him a threat on the basepaths. Club officials rave about Stevenson's makeup, leadership and overall feel for the game, all of which help him to get the most out of his tools. While defense alone will make Stevenson a big leaguer, he could very well carve out an everyday role with continued progress at the dish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2016, Jorge reached Double-A for the first time, finished among the organization's leaders in ERA and wins and earned a spot on the 40-man roster. For an encore in 2017, the right-hander was once again one of the better pitching prospects in the system numbers-wise and made his big league debut when a spot starter was needed in Minnesota. That Jorge did not pitch particularly well in the big leagues, or during his time in Triple-A, speaks to an issue about his lack of pure stuff to get upper level hitters out. He's an extreme strike-thrower with a career 2.2 walks per nine ratio in his Minor League career, but there is concern he doesn't have the weapons to miss enough bats in the big leagues. He will throw his fastball anywhere in the 90-95 mph range and the Twins think he could throw harder more consistently if he employed his lower half better and have more extension in his delivery. His changeup is his best next option after his fastball, his slider flashes average and he'll mix in a slow curve to try to keep hitters off-balance. While still slender, Jorge has proven to be durable, throwing more than 140 innings in each of the past three seasons. However, right triceps soreness forced him to begin 2018 on the disabled list. If he can refine his delivery to find a bit more velocity or tighten up one of his secondary pitches to get it to plus, he can be more than the back-end starter his ceiling appears to be at this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a season that saw Jorge pitch his way from the Florida State League to the Double-A Eastern League, the Twins debated long and hard about whether to add him to the 40-man roster, partially because they weren't sure anyone would take him after not dominating in the Eastern League. In the end, the organization felt he was worthy of a spot. Still very much a slender right-hander, Jorge has added enough strength where there are no longer questions about his ability to start. He's proven his durability by topping 300 innings over the last two years combined, doing it with a solid three-pitch mix. His fastball is playable, touching 95 mph with light sink that does get some ground-ball outs. His changeup is his best secondary pitch and his slider flashes average and he'll even mix in an occasional curve to keep hitters honest. None of his offerings scare hitters, but he commands the ball, especially his fastball, extremely well, allowing his stuff to play up. Jorge doesn't have a ton of ceiling, looking like a future No. 4 or 5 starter, but the Twins thought his ability to eat up innings in such a role was vital enough to warrant protection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fowler was set to continue his career at Georgia Southern before the Yankees selected him in the 18th round and offered him a $278,000 bonus, the largest above-slot bonus handed out by the organization in the 2013 Draft. He blossomed into a potential five-tool player in the subsequent years, ultimately earning his first big league callup in June 2017 after an impressive Triple-A campaign. But a ruptured patellar tendon in his right knee, suffered when he ran into the wall down the right-field line in his Major League debut, required immediate surgery and prematurely ended Fowler's season. Nearly a month later, he was dealt to the A's with James Kaprielian and Jorge Mateo at the Trade Deadline for right-hander Sonny Gray. Fowler has grown as a hitter in each of his five seasons. Employing a short-but-impactful swing, he makes lots of hard contact, driving the ball across the entire field. Fowler generates good pop for his size and could produce 15 to 20 home runs at the highest level, while his plus speed nets him plenty of doubles and triples and gives him impact potential on the basepaths. Fowler doesn't have much swing-and-miss to his game, though he does stand to benefit from more selectivity in his approach. Fowler's outfield defense improved considerably during his time with the Yankees, thanks in part to his work with outfield instructor Reggie Willits. It's led to more playing time in center field, where he profiles as at least an above-average defender, since the start of 2016. While the impact of his knee injury has yet to be seen, Fowler's across-the-board tools and strong track record of performance points to him becoming an everyday player, if not more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest over-slot signing by the Yankees in the 2013 Draft, Fowler got $278,000 in the 18th round to pass up his commitment to Georgia Southern. He has made steady progress, getting stronger and polishing his all-around tools to blossom into a potential five-tool player. A strong start in Triple-A this season earned him his first big league callup in late June, but he ruptured the patellar tendon in his right knee when he ran into an outfield wall in his first game with the Yankees and was lost for the year. Nearly a month after suffering the injury, Fowler was dealt to the A's with James Kaprielian and Jorge Mateo at the Trade Deadline for right-hander Sonny Gray. Fowler makes repeated hard contact with a short, quick left-handed stroke. His bat speed, strength and plus speed give him 20-20 upside, though he's still learning to be an efficient basestealer. To reach his offensive ceiling, he'll need to get more selective at the plate because he walks infrequently and puts too many early-count pitches in play rather than waiting for one to drive. Fowler has made tremendous defensive improvement since turning pro. He has worked diligently with outfield instructor Reggie Willits to refine his reads and routes, going from spending the majority of his time on the corners in his first two season to being a quality center fielder. He also has bolstered his arm strength to at least average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Andujar's $750,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic was the highest in a Yankees 2011-12 international class that also included Luis Severino. He has improved consistently while being pushed aggressively, batting .315/.352/.498 with 16 homers in 125 games at the upper levels of the Minors last year at age 22. He arrived in the big leagues with a bang, going 3-for-4 with four RBIs against the White Sox in his June 28 debut. With a quick right-handed bat and strong wrists, Andujar offers plenty of pop that shows up against both lefties and righties. He recognizes pitches well for his age and rarely swings and misses, repeatedly barreling balls and producing rockets to all fields. The only knock on him at the plate is that he rarely walks, though that won't matter much if he continues to hit for average and power. Despite his offensive prowess, Andujar's most impressive tool is his cannon arm. He has slightly below-average speed, but more than enough range for third base, though he still needs to polish some rough edges on defense. While he has lapses with his footwork and throwing accuracy, he's making progress.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-priced signee in the Yankees' 2011-12 international class, Andujar landed a $750,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic. His first two years in full-season leagues featured slow starts and fast finishes, but last year he hit well in the early going in high Class A and earned a midseason promotion to Double-A at age 21. He put up the best numbers of his career and continued to hit in the Arizona Fall League. Andujar has a quick right-handed bat that generates impressive raw power, though interestingly most of his pop currently comes against righties. He makes repeated hard contact, though his aggressive approach sometimes leads to him getting himself out on pitches he'd be better off avoiding. He has the upside of a .270 hitter capable of 20 homers on an annual basis. Despite his offensive potential, there's no question that Andujar's most impressive tool is his cannon of an arm. His hands and range are suited for third base, though he still lacks consistency there. While he still has some rough edges to smooth out offensively and defensively, he's easily the best and most advanced hot-corner prospect in New York's deep system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Wade gets overlooked in the shadow of higher-ceiling New York prospects, he'd be on the verge of challenging for a big league starting job in a lot of organizations. He reached Double-A at age 20 and earned Eastern League all-star honors there last season. The Yankees praise his intelligence and leadership skills, and his makeup and his game earn him comparisons to former All-Star Walt Weiss. Wade's quickness, arm strength and smooth actions make him a quality defender up the middle. He can make all the plays at shortstop and turns the double-play pivot well at second base, though he still needs to improve his consistency at both spots. Because he lacks a clear path to middle-infield playing time in New York, the Yankees have also had him play third base and all three outfield spots this year, and he looks capable all over the diamond. Wade's bat doesn't stick out as much as his defensive prowess and versatility. He understands his limitations at the plate, focusing on making contact and getting on base, where his speed and savvy make him a threat to steal. While he won't be a power hitter, he has improved his strength and timing, and his five homers in 2016 were one more than he totaled in his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barreto was fresh off his impressive pro debut when the Blue Jays sent him and three other prospects to the A's for Josh Donaldson in November 2014. He's since blossomed in Oakland's system, as Barreto made the jump straight to the California League the next year before finishing sixth in the Texas League batting race (.281) in 2016. That offensive success would follow Barreto to Triple-A in 2017, although he struggled mightily at the plate overall during two stints in the Majors after homering in his big league debut. Barreto's potent bat is his calling card, as he's long showed the potential to hit for both average and power. His quick right-handed bat and feel for the barrel yields hard, line-drive contact across the entire field, and he's started to tap into more game power as he's climbed the ladder. His propensity to swing-and-miss stems from an aggressive approach and below-average pitch recognition, both of which he'll need to refine in order to adjust to big league pitching. Barreto has slightly above-average speed and likes to run, though he still has many gains to make as a basestealer. A fringy defender at shortstop where he shows a plus arm but inconsistent hands and actions, Barreto is a better long-term fit at second base, where he has a chance to become an average defender. Regardless of his ultimate position, Barreto will need to become a more selective hitter to carve out an everyday role in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barreto was coming off of an impressive pro debut when he became the key return for Oakland in the trade that sent Josh Donaldson to Toronto in November 2014. He's moved quickly since joining the A's system, making the jump directly to the Class A Advanced California League for his full-season debut and then spending much of 2016 in Double-A, where he posted the Texas League's sixth-best average (.281). After beginning 2017 in Triple-A, Barreto, at age 21, homered in his first at-bat in his big league debut against the White Sox on June 24. Barreto projects to hit for both average and power. Though an undersized right-handed hitter, he produces line drives with a short, quick swing and demonstrates good feel for finding the barrel. His approach and bat path are geared more towards spraying the ball across the field rather than hitting for power, although scouts believe he'll clear more fences with improved selectivity at the plate. He has slightly above-average speed and likes to run, though he still has many gains to make as a basestealer. An average defender at shortstop where he shows a plus arm but inconsistent actions, some scouts believe Barreto is a better long-term fit at second base, and he's also shown the ability to play center field in the past. Barreto stands to benefit from more times in the Minors to refine his skills on both sides of the ball, especially on defense, though he showed during his stint in the big leagues that he's already capable of making an impact with his bat. With Marcus Semien holding down shortstop for the time, Barreto's clearest path to everyday playing time could come as a second baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Appalachian State head coach and current Tulane assistant Billy Jones, Ryder turned down the opportunity to attend Stanford after the Giants bucked the industry consensus and made him a second-round pick in 2013. He earned all-star honors in the Rookie-level Arizona League during his pro debut but mostly scuffled in his first three years in full-season ball. The he drilled a career-high 15 homers in 2016, played well in the Arizona Fall League and hit his way to his first big league promotion this June. Jones' strength and loft in his left-handed swing give him considerable raw power. He makes consistent contact and started to perform better at the plate once he became more selective and stopped getting himself out by putting pitches in play that he shouldn't swing at. After never walking more than 26 times in a full season, he matched that total by late June this season. Though Jones has a cannon arm, his well below-average speed and quickness limit his range at third base. He led Double-A Eastern League third basemen with 20 errors in just 91 games last year, when he also played 25 contests at first base. He could become a backup on both infielder corners for the Giants, who have tried to enhance his usefulness by introducing him to left and right field this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pretty much since Paredes signed with the Angels back in March 2012 out of Venezuela, he's followed a certain pattern. A first time at a level, his results won't be quite as strong, and his strikeout rate will go down. Then he'll get a second crack at the level, and the numbers will bounce back up to his career averages. This tendency is important to recognize after the reliever made his big league debut, with mixed results, in 2017. Paredes has come out of the bullpen exclusively since signing and has used a two-pitch combination to pitch his way from the Dominican Summer League up to Los Angeles. He'll throw his fastball in the 92-95 mph range and it plays up because of its movement as well as the deception caused by his low and short arm slot. He backs up the heater with a slurvy slider that does have some depth to it. Hitters don't have comfortable at-bats against him, as evidenced by his Minor League career K/9 ratio of 10.4 heading into 2018. Paredes has done a nice job of filling the strike zone with his two pitches, something he should get to do again in the big leagues in a middle relief role. The Angels are hopeful, as it has been throughout his career, that the second time will be the charm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Throwing out of the bullpen ever since he signed back in 2012 out of Venezuela, Paredes has moved steadily through up the Angels' ladder as a two-pitch short reliever. After a 2016 season that saw him reach Double-A at age 21 and go to the Arizona Fall League, Paredes was added to the 40-man roster to be protected from the Rule 5 Draft. He's rewarded the organization's faith in him by pitching well enough to make his big league debut in 2017. Paredes gets swings and misses on both his fastball and slider, striking out 10.5 per nine innings in his Minor League career heading into the 2017 season. He throws his fastball in the 92-95 mph range and it plays up because of its plus run, sink and spin. His slider is more slurvy than anything else, but it has a lot of depth to it. He's not a sidearmer by any means, but he does employ a low and short arm slot that provides a lot of deception. Hitters do not pick the ball up well coming out of his hands. He's done a very nice job in his career of staying in the strike zone. Paredes has closed games throughout his Minor League career, saving 32 over the last two seasons combined. His stuff is probably a little short to keep doing that in the big leagues, but he's looking like he'll be able to fill a bullpen role there in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally drafted by Baltimore in the 19th round in 2012, Hader was traded to the Astros the following year at the Trade Deadline in a deal for Bud Norris. The 2015 Trade Deadline saw him get moved once more, this time going from Houston to Milwaukee in the Carlos Gomez/Mike Fiers deal, but it wasn't until that year's Arizona Fall League that Hader established himself as one of the game's top left-handed pitching prospects. He opened 2016 with a dominant showing back at Double-A Biloxi but struggled following a mid-season promotion to the hitter-friendly Pacific Coast League. Though he didn't show much improvement back at the level to begin 2017, that didn't stop the Brewers from calling him up and putting him in the bullpen in June. Hader possesses electric stuff, as he'll consistently operate at 93-97 mph with his fastball and complement it with a wipeout slider. The pairing enables him to miss bats with ease, a notion evidenced by his full-season-best 11.5 K/9 in 2016, and that should continue as Hader makes further strides with his changeup. Meanwhile, everything Hader throws plays up on account of his deceptive delivery, especially after he shifted to the first-base side of the rubber during the 2015 season. Hader's control and command backed up a bit last season as Triple-A hitters consistently put pressure on the him to throw strikes early in counts, leading to too many elevated pitch counts and abbreviated outings. With improvement on that front as well as a more effective changeup, Hader could emerge as the Brewers' most dynamic starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros' persistence in scouting the lower levels of the Minors paid off when they asked for Martes as the third prospect from the Marlins in a package for Jarred Cosart in July 2014. Within a year, he had risen from Rookie ball to Class A Advanced and established himself as Houston's best pitching prospect. He got rocked in Double-A at the beginning of 2016 before recovering to record a 2.52 ERA in his final 19 starts, then showing one of the best arms in the Arizona Fall League. Martes' stuff is similar to what Lance McCullers Jr. showed in the Minors. He can work at 93-96 mph and reach 98 with his fastball, and while it doesn't feature a ton of life, he does show some feel for moving it around the strike zone. His curveball gives him a second well above-average pitch, combining power and depth. Martes' changeup has improved a lot in the last two years and shows flashes of becoming a plus offering, and he also can snap off a hard slider when he wants. Whether he reaches his ceiling as a frontline starter will hinge on his control and command, which regressed a bit in 2016. There are no red flags in his delivery, he repeats it well and he's still just 21, so there's cause to be optimistic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The Twins have unfortunately had to deal with more than their fair share of helping young talented arms rehab from Tommy John surgery. Rosario had his back in 2014, and the organization liked what they saw upon his return a year later. He was added to the 40-man roster following the 2015 season. Developing mostly as a starter, Rosario moved to the bullpen late in 2016, with the switch allowing the left-hander to reach Double-A for the first time. The hope was that Rosario's stuff would play up in shorter stints out of the pen and that's exactly what happened. His fastball sat at 94-95 mph and frequently touched 96-97 mph. His slider remains an up-and-down pitch. At times, he'll show a really good one in the mid 80s, but at others, it will have inconsistent break. That should come in time and with more innings, something he missed a lot of because of the elbow injury. Part of the reason Rosario was moved to the pen was because he's on the 40-man roster and there's a certain timetable to get him up to Minnesota, a timetable met when he made his debut in 2017. A hard worker, Rosario should figure out his new role and get there full-time in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cordero jumped on the prospect radar when he showed loud tools during his stateside debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League in 2013, two years after he had signed with the Padres out of the Dominican Republic for $175,000. He spent much of the next two years struggling as an error-prone shortstop with Class A Fort Wayne before breaking out in 2016, when, at age 21 and after a move to the outfield, he began the season at Lake Elsinore, moved up to Double-A San Antonio at midseason and then reached Triple-A El Paso ahead of the Pacific Coast League playoffs. Cordero's resurgence came full circle in 2017 when he made his Major League debut in May, his first of three impressive stints with the Padres. He started 2018 on the 10-day disabled list with a groin strain. Cordero combines physical strength with good bat speed and a lofty left-handed swing to produce above-average raw power to all fields. It translated to a Minor League-leading 18 triples in '17, and he also tallied 17 home runs and 21 doubles, marking his second straight season with double-digit totals in all three categories. Cordero's aggressive approach and lack of strike-zone judgment comes with considerable swing-and-miss tendencies -- he had a 44.4 percent strikeout rate in 99 big league plate appearances -- but he does consistently impact the baseball when he connects. Cordero is a 70-grade runner who is aggressive on the bases and has Statcast-measured sprint speed that ranks among the best in Majors. The Padres moved Cordero to left field from shortstop in May 2015 after he had led the Minors with 52 errors the previous year, then shifted him to center field in '16 with the hope that it may unlock his offensive potential, which it ultimately did. He's quickly proved a natural in the outfield, where his speed and long strides help him cover large swaths of territory. Though best in center field, Cordero's impact athleticism and above-average arm strength are clean fits anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unheralded and undrafted out of a Pittsburgh-area high school, Happ emerged as one of the best hitters in college baseball during three years at Cincinnati and in back-to-back summers when he ranked as the top prospect in the Cape Cod League. The Cubs took him ninth overall in 2015, marking the fourth straight Draft in which they selected a hitter with a top-10 choice (Albert Almora, Kris Bryant and Kyle Schwarber preceded him). After signing for $3 million, Happ reached Double-A midway through his first full year as a pro and finished it by homering from both sides of the plate in the Arizona Fall League championship game. Happ demonstrates balance and bat speed from both sides, though he has been more productive as a left-handed hitter in pro ball. With his deceptive strength, solid speed and baserunning instincts, he has 20-20 upside. He has good plate discipline as well, though he'll have to tighten his strike zone after expanding it once he got to Double-A. Happ has quickness and arm strength, yet those tools don't translate as well as they could to his defense. He moved off second base after his freshman year with the Bearcats before returning there in instructional league after his 2015 pro debut. His infield actions are more stiff than smooth, however, and most evaluators outside of the Cubs organization believe he's most likely to wind up in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bellinger's father Clay parlayed his skills as a glove-first shortstop into two World Series rings with the Yankees and a spot on the 2004 Greek Olympic team. Though Cody can flash some leather as well, it's his bat that has scouts excited. After totaling four homers in his first two pro seasons, he has smashed 56 in the last two while reaching Triple-A at the age of 21. Bellinger focused on hitting for average when he broke into pro ball, displaying a smooth left-handed stroke and patient approach. He since has added loft to his swing and gotten more aggressive about pulling pitches, becoming one of the best power prospects in the Minors. He did reduce his strikeout rate from 28 percent in 2015 (when he broke out with 30 homers) to 20 percent last year while also setting a career high with 60 walks, so there's hope that he could hit for high average to go with his pop. Scouts rarely rave about a first-base prospect's defensive skills, but Bellinger is an exception who's smooth around the bag and excels at digging throws out of the dirt. Considered a future Gold Glover at first base, he moves and throws well enough that he also has seen time at all three outfield positions and hasn't looked overmatched in center field. His versatility will help him crack the lineup in Los Angeles, where All-Star Adrian Gonzalez is still under contract for two more seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though the Giants surprised many clubs when they drafted Arroyo 25th overall in 2013, he wasted little time legitimizing the decision. He won the Rookie-level Arizona League MVP Award after signing for $1,866,500 and has consistently hit for average and gap power throughout the Minors. He tore up Triple-A to the tune of a 1.065 OPS and earned his first big league promotion in 2017, but he lost most of the last three months after his left hand twice was hit by pitches, necessitating surgery in November. Following the season, the Giants sent Arroyo -- with Denard Span and pitching prospects Matt Krook and Stephen Woods -- to Tampa Bay for Evan Longoria. A right-handed hitter, Arroyo has exceptional hand-eye coordination and feel for the barrel, which results in repeated line-drive contact to all fields. Though he never has hit more than nine homers in a pro season, he has enough hitting savvy, bat speed and strength to produce 15 or more homers per year if he looked more often for pitches to drive. His lack of selectivity also cuts into his walk totals because he puts the bat on the ball so easily. Arroyo spent the majority of his first three years in pro ball at shortstop, but his below-average speed and quickness weren't going to work there at the Major League level. His hands and arm strength will play anywhere in the infield, however, and he can be a solid defender at either second or third base. The hot corner looks like his best fit, though he'll have to develop more pop to truly fit the profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest surprise in the first round of the 2013 Draft came when the Giants took the relatively unheralded Arroyo with the 25th choice and signed him for $1,866,500. He won the Rookie-level Arizona League MVP award in his pro debut and has silenced his doubters by establishing himself as one of the purest hitters in the Minors. He tore up Triple-A for the first three weeks of 2017 to earn his first big league callup in April, but he played just eight games after returning to the Minors in June because he injured his wrist and then broke his left hand. Following the season, the Giants sent Arroyo with Denard Span and pitching prospects Matt Krook and Stephen Woods to Tampa Bay for Evan Longoria. Arroyo's tremendous hand-eye coordination allows him to barrel balls with ease from the right side of the plate, producing hard contact to all fields. He puts the bat on the ball almost too easily, because he rarely walks and delivered just 20 homers in his first four years as a pro. If he were to become more selective at the plate and look to drive the ball more often, his biggest proponents believe he could develop at least average power. After spending most of his first three pro seasons at shortstop, Arroyo has divided his playing time between short, third and second. He has the hands and arm strength to play shortstop, but he lacks desirable range and quickness and is better suited for the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 70 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 It's the kind of story that sounds like it comes straight out of a movie script. A young pitcher doesn't even get drafted, signing as a free agent out of high school with the Tigers in June 2013. He then begins a remarkable ascent, pitches in two Futures Games, saves 30 games across three levels in 2016 and makes his big league debut in 2017. Big and strong with terrific mound presence, Jimenez has all of the tools needed to succeed pitching out of the bullpen late in games. He'll throw his fastball consistently in the 95-98 mph range That and his plus slider, which he continues to tighten, both miss a ton of bats. His changeup has come along and it looked good during instructional league play, giving him a potential weapon against left-handed hitters in the future. For a power reliever, he does stay around the zone, though he can over-rotate at times, which impacts his command. Using his changeup more will be key to his development in 2017 and beyond, especially as he knocks on, and knocks down, the big league door. The best Hollywood ending would be to see Jimenez racking up saves in the big leagues, something that does not seem far-fetched at all.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Senzatela broke out as a prospect in 2015 when he was the organization's and the California League's pitcher of the year after leading the Advanced Class A circuit in ERA (2.51) and opponents' average (.229) at age 20. He was putting up better numbers in Double-A last year but made only seven starts while battling shoulder issues that didn't require surgery. Signed for $250,000 out of Venezuela in 2011, he went 41-19 with a 2.45 ERA in his first five pro seasons. Senzatela has one of the best fastball packages in the system, working at 92-95 mph and reaching 98 with modest life but advanced command and difficult downhill plane. The key for him will be developing his secondary pitches, with most evaluators hanging average grades on his slider and changeup but the Rockies retaining more optimism. His slider can touch the mid-80s with late bite, and his changeup has helped keep left-handers in check. Though he never had much success refining a curveball, Senzatela can at least throw his for strikes and uses it occasionally to give batters a different look. He uses his high three-quarters arm slot to pound the bottom of the zone and doesn't beat himself with homers or walks. With more consistent secondary stuff, he could become a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's drafted high school shortstops Addison Russell and Robertson with their first two picks of the 2012 Draft, only to trade both players within six months of each other, with Russell going to the Cubs in July 2014 and Robertson to the Rays in January '15 as part of the deal that sent Ben Zobrist and Yunel Escobar to Oakland. A broken hamate bone in his left hand limited Robertson to just 82 games that year, and he regressed on both sides of the ball with a move up to Triple-A Durham in 2016. Robertson employs a short swing and uses the whole field to hit, with a mature approach that makes him adept at working walks and fuels his on-base skills. His bat speed and feel for hitting give him good power to the gaps but little in the way of over-the-fence power. A below-average runner, scouts have long viewed Robertson as a candidate to move to second or third base. Though he saw increased time at both spots last year, Robertson's best position is still shortstop, where he makes up for a lack of range with excellent instincts and a quick first step. Robertson has the tools and versatility to carve out a solid career as a utility infielder, though he'll first need to get back on track offensively in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a shortstop while growing up in Venezuela, Torrens lacked the speed to profile there but intrigued the Yankees with his potential as catcher. He took quickly to the new position after signing for $1.3 million in 2012, so much so that he earned an assignment to Class A at age 18 two years later. Shoulder problems limited him to 62 games in 2014 and required surgery to repair a torn labrum in January 2015, knocking him out for the entire season. He returned to action in 2016 in mid-June, and then became property of the Padres after they acquired him from the Reds, who had selected him in the Rule 5 Draft. An advanced hitter for his age, Torrens already shows a willingness to work counts and use the entire field. He used his downtime last year to add strength and get in better shape, so he may begin to realize his 15-homer potential from the right side of the plate. Torrens already had a plus arm when he signed and quickly learned the footwork and transfer he needed as a catcher, enabling him to erase 41 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. He has the hands and athleticism to become a solid receiver and worked on improving his English while sidelined in 2015 so he could communicate better with his pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Panama in January 2013, Cordoba impressed during his United States debut in '15, earning Gulf Coast League MVP honors, and then followed it in '16 by winning the Appalachian League batting title with a .362 average. Following the season, the Padres added Cordoba to their system when they selected him with the No. 3 pick in December's Rule 5 Draft. Cordoba stands out because of his advanced feel for hitting. He has a solid approach at the plate and makes consistent hard contact that allowed him to win batting titles in back-to-back seasons. Cordoba has good speed and is a basestealing threat. He's added some strength, and there could be some more extra-base pop in time. Cordoba's quickness gives him range defensively, and scouts feel he has the aptitude to stick at shortstop while also being able to handle moving around the infield if needed in the future. Cordoba has yet to play at a full-season level, but San Diego deemed him advanced enough to gamble on him in the Rule 5 Draft. Time will tell whether he can stick on the big league roster for the full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League after signing out of the Dominican in 2011. The slightly undersized right-hander didn't disappoint in his highly anticipated stateside debut in 2014, when he showed the ability to miss bats with electric stuff en route to recording 10.1 strikeouts per nine innings in the Rookie-level Arizona League. The Brewers expected big things from him in 2015, though he was unable to take the next step as an avulsion fracture in his elbow limited him to just 20 innings. He finally made his full-season debut in 2016, pitching as part of a loaded piggyback starting rotation at Class A Wisconsin. In December, he was selected by the Twins with the first pick in the Rule 5 Draft, only to be traded to San Diego. When healthy, Diaz's lightning-quick arm generates a fastball in the mid-90s with late movement from a high three-quarters slot. His slider, thrown in the 75-77 mph range with good lateral action, has the chance to be an out pitch if he can throw it for strikes. His changeup lags behind his two other offerings, but club officials believe it will become an effective third pitch for him once he creates better velocity separation relative to his heater. He has the ability to miss bats naturally, though his control and command require refinement, as does his mechanics. Diaz's elbow injury required subsequent surgery, but he was not limited by the injury in 2016. Although the Padres may continue to develop him as a starter, his fastball-slider pairing gives him undeniable upside in a late-inning bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts regarded Margot as one of the premier athletes in the 2011 international class before he signed with Red Sox for $800,000. He put himself on the map during his full-season debut in 2014 and then reached Double-A the following year, only to be traded to the Padres during the offseason as part of a prospect package used to land Craig Kimbrel. He advanced to Triple-A in 2016, was named a Pacific Coast League All-Star and suited up for the World team in the SiriusXM Futures Game at PetCo Park before making his big league debut at age 21 in early September. Margot's quick bat and outstanding hand-eye coordination help him to generate hard contact to all fields from the right side of the plate, and his improving feel for managing the strike zone suggests he'll reach his ceiling of a plus hitter. He has good strength to his frame but projects for below-average over-the-fence pop. However, with plus-plus speed, Margot should provide plenty of doubles and triples, as well as stolen bases. Those wheels also enable him to cover a ton of ground in center field, where he's viewed by scouts as one of the top defensive players in the Minors, with a plus arm that produced a PCL-leading 18 assists in 2016. Margot's quick rise through the Minors and brief big league exposure last season seemingly has him primed to contribute from the top of San Diego's order in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves were excited to get Ruiz as part of the package from the Astros in return for Evan Gattis in January 2015. That optimism was dampened by a very ordinary first season in the organization, but Ruiz jumped back on the radar a bit more strongly with a solid Triple-A season in 2016, making his big league debut at age 22. Ruiz still has a very smooth swing from the left side of the plate and shows an advanced approach with the willingness to draw walks. He typically has a left-center-field approach, and while the Braves believe there is still solid power to unlock, it hasn't really shown up in games just yet. His defense has improved as he's gotten in better shape, showing better lateral movement than he has in the past. As a result, questions about his ability to stay at the hot corner have largely abated. Knowing how your swing works is first and foremost, and Ruiz can check off that box. Adding size and strength? That's happening. Power is often the last thing to come. If it does, Ruiz still has the chance to fit the profile of an everyday third baseman in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olson ranked third in the Minor Leagues with 37 home runs in 2014, trailing only Joey Gallo and Kris Bryant, two years after the A's had selected him 47th overall in the Draft. Though his power and overall production regressed in each subsequent season as he climbed the Minor League ladder, Olson performed well enough last year in Triple-A to receive his first big league callup in September, but hit just .095 (2-for-21), albeit with more walks than strikeouts, while appearing in 11 games. Back on track in 2017, Olson has bounced between Triple-A and Majors while showing more consistency at both levels. Though he still possesses big raw power, Olson's penchant for whiffing keeps him from applying it with any consistency, in turn resulting in perennially low batting averages. The left-handed hitter's patient approach continues to net him plenty of walks, though he's often criticized for being overly passive. Meanwhile, Olson's struggles against same-side pitchers portends to a career as a platoon hitter. The A's experimented with Olson in right field at the end of the 2015, and he saw the bulk of his playing time there last season, including in the big leagues. He continued to see time at first base and in the outfield in 2017, and it's that defensive versatility, along with his left-handed power and strong on-base skills, that could make Olson an attractive option off the bench, if not a second-division regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Rockies traded Corey Dickerson and prospect Kevin Padlo to the Rays in January 2016, Jake McGee was the big name they received in return. With much less fanfare, Marquez also arrived in the deal, and he quickly raised his profile by winning the Eastern League pitcher of the year award, finishing second in the Double-A circuit in ERA (2.85) as the second-youngest qualifier and earning his first big league win in September. Marquez has added strength and velocity since turning pro, with his fastball moving from 88-91 mph when he signed to sitting at 93-96 and peaking at 98 last season. It features more run than sink, so he'll have to keep it down in the strike zone at Coors Field. His curveball also has improved, giving him a second plus offering. His changeup has potential but is more of a work in progress. Marquez has an easy delivery and the athleticism to repeat it, so he has little difficulty throwing strikes. He's still refining his command, which is understandable considering that he'll pitch the entire 2017 season at age 22. Some scouts believe he's a better bet to become a frontline starter than fellow Rockies right-handers Jeff Hoffman and Riley Pint.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was drafted as a third baseman out of the Pacific Nothwest high school ranks, but after two summers at the hot corner, he made the move behind the plate and it's proven to be a wise one. He's developed into one of the best defensive catching prospects in the game, and with his bat catching up the past two seasons, both of which concluded with callups to St. Louis, he's turned into a potential all-around standout. Defense will always be Kelly's calling card, with plus tools across the board. He moves well behind the plate, blocks and receives well, calls a good game and exhibits the leadership skills teams covet behind the plate. With a strong arm and quick release, he can help control the running game, having thrown out 31 percent of would-be basestealers in the Minors through 2017. At the plate, Kelly has always had good contact skills and an advanced approach, but he's impacted the ball more of late and has started tapping into his raw power. Kelly has learned under the wing of Yadier Molina for some time now, and with the veteran signed through 2020, he should be able to do so at the big league level for the next couple of seasons. He'd be a regular elsewhere by now and will most certainly be ready to take over after Molina's contract runs out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Cardinals decided to move Kelly, who was initially drafted as a third baseman, behind the plate, they knew the process might take a while. But they hoped eventually he could develop into a potential replacement for Yadier Molina. It's looking more and more likely that their patience will be rewarded. With a tireless work ethic, Kelly has turned himself into a premium defender behind the plate, one who looks like he's been back there for years. He has a plus arm that has thrown out almost a third of would-be base-stealers since he switched positions. He has outstanding hands and footwork, the type of backstop who could win Gold Gloves in the future, and he is the kind of natural leader teams love to have behind the plate. In 2016, his bat started to catch up to his glove. He has some raw power and has really improved his approach and pitch selection, where it looks like he should be able to hit for average and power in the future. Kelly made it up to the big leagues for the first time in 2016, and said the experience was invaluable. He appeared more than ready to take over in St. Louis after Molina's contract was set to expire following the 2017 season, but the veteran's extension through 2020 clouds Kelly's future with the Cardinals.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendez strained his elbow shortly after signing for $1.5 million out of Venezeula in 2011, leading the Rangers to handle him with extreme caution, but he jumped from high Class A to Texas in 2016 once they turned him loose. He has been unable to build on that success, going 4-12 with a 4.86 ERA between four levels last year and winding up back in high Class A at midseason to regroup. His 2019 season was put on hold when he was diagnosed with a sprained ulnar collateral ligament in his elbow during Spring Training, though he won't need Tommy John surgery. Mendez still possesses a deceptive changeup that fades and sinks and can be a well above-average pitch at times. The problem is that the rest of his repertoire is fringy to average and it's not always easy for him to set up his changeup. He has a 90-93 mph fastball that tops out at 95 with some sink and has yet to find a reliable breaking ball while trying both a curveball and slider. Though he throws strikes, Mendez has little margin for error with his repertoire and was hit harder than ever in 2017 and 2018. He has looked tentative in his big league stints, falling behind in counts and getting punished when hitters know he has to come over the plate. Once considered a safe bet to become a No. 3 starter, he now looks like a back-of-the-rotation option at best.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers spent more than $28 million in bonuses and guaranteed contracts for international players in 2011, with Mendez's $1.5 million their biggest outlay for a pitcher. He strained his elbow shortly after signing and totaled just 181 2/3 innings during his first four pro seasons before breaking out in 2016, when he jumped from high Class A to the big leagues. He hasn't been able to duplicate that success in the last two years, becoming somewhat of an enigma. Mendez owns one of the best changeups in the Minors, with fade, sink and deception that add up to a well above-average pitch at its best. He relies on it almost too heavily at the expense of his other pitches, so the Rangers restricted his use of it last year so he could focus on the rest of his repertoire. He has some feel for his 90-95 mph sinker, but not as much for his pair of fringy breaking balls, with his slider more reliable than his curveball. Though he's still not very physical, Mendez has proven his durability since Texas turned him loose. He doesn't have a huge margin for error, leaving him vulnerable when his control and command have regressed in 2017 and 2018. His ability to come up with a solid breaking pitch may determine whether he becomes more than a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers went all in on the international market in 2011, handing Leonys Martin a $15.6 million big league contract and spending another $12.8 million on bonuses for amateurs, including $4.95 million for Nomar Mazara. The most expensive pitcher in that crop was Mendez, who signed for $1.5 million out of Venezuela. Elbow problems and cautious handling slowed his development until 2016, when he rocketed from high Class A to Texas. Mendez owns one of the best changeups among pitching prospects, and its fade, sink and deception help him keep right-handers in check. He throws it with the same arm speed as he does his sinking 90-93 mph fastball, which peaks at 95 and might pick up a bit more velocity if he adds more strength to his lanky 6-foot-5 frame. His breaking pitches don't stand out as much as his other offerings, though he did make strides with his slider last year and it's now more effective with his curveball. Mendez had a history of filling the strike zone before he reached Triple-A and the Majors at the end of 2016, but his control hasn't been as sharp since. He doesn't have a huge ceiling but does have a solid floor and is a good bet to become a No. 3 starter. The only real question is his durability, because his 114 innings last year were a career high and he worked as many as six frames just three times in his first 59 pro starts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox spent $63 million to sign Moncada in March 2015, a record $31.5 million bonus (nearly doubling the previous amateur record of $16.25 million that the Reds gave Aroldis Chapman in 2010) and a matching penalty for exceeding their international bonus pool. He has lived up to that investment so far, earning MVP honors at the 2016 SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and making his big league debut ahead of schedule, 18 months after he turned pro. Boston used him as the centerpiece of a four-prospect package to acquire Chris Sale from the White Sox at the Winter Meetings. A switch-hitter with tremendous bat speed, Moncada made some nice adjustments during his second pro season, adding more loft to his swing and more patience. He has been more effective from the left side of the plate as a pro and showed significantly more pop batting lefty in 2016. With his gifts, he's capable of batting .280/.400/.500 in the Majors, which is why he has been called a faster version of Robinson Cano. Moncada is a well above-average runner who stole 94 bases at an 86 percent success rate in his first two pro seasons, though he still can be a bit reckless on the bases at times. While he could fit almost anywhere on the diamond with his quickness and arm strength, he's more of an average defender than a standout with the glove. Because he was blocked by Dustin Pedroia at second base, the Red Sox began playing him at third base last August, but he'll play second for Chicago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Parlaying an outstanding college career that included one College World Series title and one runner-up finish, Swanson was the No. 1 overall pick in the Draft in 2015. He made more history when he became the first top pick to be traded the year he was drafted when the D-backs sent him to the Braves in the Shelby Miller deal. He went from Class A Advanced to the big leagues in his first full season, and while some worried about him being rushed, he more than held his own, hitting over .300 during his big league debut. A proven winner, Swanson looks every bit the part of the franchise player the Braves hope he will be. He's already shown his approach at the plate will work at the highest level, with an ability to draw walks and make consistent hard contact. He has extra-base power right now and should start clearing fences more as he settles in. His above-average speed and instincts will allow him to steal bases and help him have outstanding range at shortstop. His hands and arm both work very well from the premium position and he has the natural leadership often sought from those who play short. The Braves are hopeful Swanson, a native Georgian, can continue to live up to, and exceed, the lofty expectations placed on him. There's been nothing that says he can't lead the Braves in their current youth movement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyes grew up in Elizabeth, N.J., but moved to the Dominican Republic in order to sign for $950,000 as an international free agent in 2012. He dominated during his full-season debut two years later and reached Double-A for the first time in '15, receiving a promotion after recovering from a minor shoulder issue. A drug suspension during the offseason delayed the start of Reyes' campaign in '16, but he rebounded to make a big league impact later that year out the Cardinals' bullpen, and seemed poised to establish himself in '17 before Tommy John surgery in February wiped out his season and the start of his '18 campaign. Reyes returned to the mound in earnest in early May and quickly pitched his way back to the big leagues, only to suffer a torn right lat tendon that required season-ending surgery in June. When healthy, Reyes has one of the most electric fastballs among all pitching prospects. He easily hits triple digits, especially in shorter bursts, and sits in the mid-to-upper 90s with ease. That and a plus upper-70s curve would be enough for a bullpen gig, but his 88-90-mph changeup gives him a third above-average offering, and he also has developed good feel for throwing a hard slider in the upper 80s. The only negative -- beyond the injury bug -- for Reyes has been his command, though he was doing a better job of repeating his delivery during his truncated '18 campaign. While Reyes still has an exceptionally high ceiling as a potential front-of-the-rotation starter, his checkered medical history makes it fair to question whether he will reach it. The Cardinals were pleased with how the right-hander improved his body while recovering from TJ surgery, and the plan is for him to prepare as a starter ahead of 2019. However, Reyes' role will be dictated by his health, with club expected to carefully manage his workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If things had gone according to plan, Reyes would have graduated from the prospect rankings in 2017. The native of Elizabeth, N.J., who moved to the Dominican Republic in order to sign as an international free agent in '12, had hit some stumbling blocks, including a shoulder issue in '15 and a drug suspension in '16, before rebounding to make a big league impact later that year. Poised to establish himself in '17, he instead required Tommy John surgery in February and missed the season. He began the '18 season on the 60-day disabled list, worked his way back to St. Louis only to have his season lost to a torn lat tendon that required surgery in June. When healthy, Reyes has one of the most electric fastballs among all pitching prospects. He easily hits triple digits and sits in the mid-to-upper 90s with ease. That and a plus upper-70s curve would be enough for a bullpen gig, but his 88-90-mph changeup gives him a third above-average offering. The only negative -- beyond the injury bug -- for Reyes has been his command, and he will have to keep his walk rate relatively in check to reach his potential as a top-of-the-rotation starter. Reyes was throwing well again post elbow surgery and was in excellent shape. He'll have to go through another rehab process now to get back to reaching that extremely high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyes had put his 50-game suspension for marijuana in 2016 behind him, making a huge impact in the big leagues in '16, both as a starter and out of the bullpen. He was going to be counted on to have a large role on the 2017 Cardinals' pitching staff but instead will spend the year rehabbing after being diagnosed with a torn UCL in his pitching elbow in February and undergoing Tommy John surgery. When he's healthy, Reyes is arguable the best pitching prospect in the game, with his combination of elite stuff and missing bats all pointing to a future as a frontline starter. His fastball sits in the mid-to-upper-90s comfortably and he can reach back for more, hitting triple digits at times, something that happened consistently in relief outings. He backs that up with a nasty curve he'll throw in the upper 70s that also elicits swings and misses. Reyes actually threw his improving changeup, 88-90 mph, more frequently than his breaking ball during his time in the big leagues, with tremendous success. Command had been the only thing that had held Reyes back, with a walk rate of 4.5 per nine innings in his career, though most felt that would improve over time. The track record for TJ surgery recovery is good, but it's going to take time for Reyes to build himself back into the star all envisioned.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acquired by Atlanta from the Mets at the Trade Deadline in July 2015, Whalen excelled at the Double-A and Triple-A levels in '16 to earn a big league callup in August at age 22. However, shoulder fatigue combined with a team-imposed inning cap limited the right-hander to just five starts with the Braves, who then sent him and Max Povse to the Mariners for '14 first-rounder Alex Jackson in late November. He returned to the big leagues in 2017 with Seattle, but also missed considerable time with leg and knee injuries early in the season before taking the rest of the year off in July to address mental health issues. Whalen pitches with an average fastball, sitting at 90-93 mph, but it plays up thanks to heavy sinking action that yields a high number of ground balls. His curveball is his lone above-average pitch, and he also mixes in a slider and a usable changeup. The right-hander is around the strike zone with all of his pitches and knows how to keep hitters off balance and guessing by effectively changing speeds. With an advanced feel for four pitches as well as a bulldog mentality on the mound, Whalen shows the makings of becoming a backend starter at maturity. Perhaps more importantly, Whalen, after receiving treatment for depression and anxiety that affected him for much of 2017, has returned to the game as an advocate for mental health and hopes to change its stigma within the sport.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acquired by Atlanta from the Mets at the Trade Deadline in July 2015, Whalen excelled at the Double-A and Triple-A levels in '16 to earn a big league callup in August at age 22. However, shoulder fatigue combined with a team-imposed inning cap limited the right-hander to just five starts with the Braves, who then sent him and Max Povse to the Mariners for '14 first-rounder Alex Jackson in late November. Whalen pitches with an average fastball, sitting at 90-92 mph range, but it plays up thanks to heavy sinking action that yields a high number of ground balls. His curveball is his lone above-average pitch, and he also mixes in a slider and a usable changeup. The right-hander is around the strike zone with all of his pitches and knows how to keep hitters off balance and guessing by effectively changing speeds. With an advanced feel for four pitches as well as a bulldog mentality on the mound, Whalen shows the makings of becoming a No. 4-type starter at maturity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benintendi hit one home run during an injury-marred freshman season at Arkansas before exploding for an NCAA Division I-leading 20 as a sophomore in 2015, when he won every major college-player-of-the-year award. The Red Sox ranked him second on their Draft board and were delighted to get him at No. 7 overall, where he signed for $3,590,400. He tore up four levels of the Minors before reaching Boston 13 months after turning pro, continued to perform well in the big leagues and was the Sox's most impressive hitter in their Division Series loss to the Indians. Though Benintendi isn't physically imposing, he generates surprising power with his quick hands and strong wrists and projects to deliver 20 or more homers on an annual basis. Even so, his slugging takes a back seat to his pure hitting ability. With a pretty left-handed swing and astute pitch recognition and strike-zone management, he repeatedly barrels balls and holds his own against southpaws. A quality athlete who was the Ohio state Division III baseball and basketball Player of the Year as a high school senior, Benintendi has above-average speed and plays a fine center field. He won't get a chance to do that in a Boston outfield with Jackie Bradley Jr. and Mookie Betts, but he could develop into a Gold Glove left fielder with an average arm. He runs the bases well but still is honing his basestealing skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Nationals for a mere $17,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2012, Lopez battled a sore arm early in his pro career and didn't begin to break out until the second half of 2014. He established himself as one of the hardest-throwing starters in the Minors and, in the minds of some scouts, passed Lucas Giolito as Washington's best pitching prospect last year. Lopez outperformed Giolito with the Nats before both were packaged with fellow righty Dane Dunning to get Adam Eaton from the White Sox during the Winter Meetings. Lopez averaged 96 mph and hit 100 with his fastball in the big leagues, though his heater tended to get hit more than his secondary pitches because its life isn't as impressive as its velocity. His curveball features power and depth, and it can be a plus pitch at times and have trouble finding the strike zone at others. His changeup has become an effective third pitch, though it too lacks consistency. Lopez usually throws strikes but can run into trouble with his command because he sometimes overthrows and doesn't stay on line to the plate. Though he's a flyball pitcher who lacks the size to create a lot angle and plane, he still manages to minimize the damage done by home runs. He has made significant progress in each of the last three seasons and is still young, so Chicago is optimistic that he can develop into a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Giolito might have become the first high school right-hander ever drafted No. 1 overall, but he sprained his elbow in the spring of 2012 and fell to the Nationals at No. 16, where he signed for $2,925,000. He had Tommy John surgery after one pro start, made a full recovery and entered 2016 as baseball's consensus top pitching prospect. Despite making his big league debut in June, it was a trying year that included mechanical issues, diminished velocity and control and a December trade to the White Sox as part of a package for Adam Eaton. When he's on, Giolito shows stuff that most pitchers can only dream of. He can sit at 95-98 mph and crack triple digits with his fastball -- which also features running life and downhill plane that make it even better -- snap off power curveballs that are just as nasty and mix in a third plus pitch with his sinking changeup. However, he spent most of last season working with 93-95 mph heaters, battled his control and command for much of the time and got knocked around in the Majors. Giolito has a big frame and some evaluators wonder if he has enough athleticism to repeat his delivery on a consistent basis and get the most out of his pure stuff. He has shown impressive feel for pitching at times in the past, though last summer he never really got into a groove while shuttling between teams on nine different occasions. Chicago's Don Cooper is one of the game's best pitching coaches, so Giolito is in good hands as he tries to deliver on his No. 1 starter potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first of four straight position players Chicago drafted with a top-10-overall pick from 2012-15, Almora signed for $3.9 million (a franchise record for a high schooler) as the No. 6 choice. While he doesn't have the offensive upside of the three hitters who followed him -- Kris Bryant, Kyle Schwarber, Ian Happ -- Almora has value as a defensive standout whose instincts help him play above his tools. He made his big league debut last June and scored the go-ahead run in the 10th inning of Game Seven of the World Series. Almora is the best center fielder in the Cubs organization, and he could have a long-term role as a starter who solidifies the up-the-middle defense while batting toward the bottom of the order. While he's just an average runner, he has well above-average range because he reads balls quickly, gets terrific jumps and takes direct routes to the ball. He also has a strong, accurate arm that enables him to play anywhere in the outfield. Almora's strong suit as a hitter is his ability to make contact, but he still has to show he can do more than hit for average. He can get overly aggressive at the plate, so he rarely walks and has yet to tap into his raw power, which could produce 15 homers per season. He's not a big threat to steal but runs the bases well, and he made a heady play by tagging up and advancing from first to second base on a fly ball in the final inning of the World Series.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tiedemann took an immediate physical jump after the Blue Jays drafted him in the third round of the 2021 Draft out of Golden West JC (Huntington Beach, Calif.). He hasn’t stopped taking those jumps, either, a physical specimen who you can pick out of a group from a field away.
