Injuries are all that have held Tiedemann back from maintaining his spot in the top half of Top 100 lists, and after spending much of 2024 and all of ‘25 rehabbing from Tommy John surgery, he ran into some elbow soreness again ramping up for camp in ‘26. When he’s healthy, Tiedemann’s talent is undeniable. His fastball is back in the 96-98 mph range, and he’s throwing a new slider, one focused on lessening the strain on his elbow after bone chips were also removed during that surgery. It’s going to be a harder, tighter slider that could take some time to re-develop, but paired with a strong changeup, all of the pieces are there for Tiedemann to mow through big league hitters if he can only stay on the mound long enough to build some momentum. Prior to the injury, Tiedemann had come into camp at 245 pounds and was bulked up closer to 255 by mid-season, but now he’s about 15 pounds above his listed weight of 220, a much more natural and athletic size for a pitcher. This has helped him become more fluid on the mound again. While 32 starts and 200 innings may never be in the cards for Tiedemann, that’s just fine. He’ll build up in a bulk role this season when he’s ready to roll, and while all of this comes with a “but” related to his health, he still has as much raw talent as any player in the Blue Jays' system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a dominant year at Golden West (Junior) College (Huntington Beach, Calif.), Tiedemann went to the Blue Jays in the third round of the 2021 Draft. At times, it’s looked like the organization struck gold, but injuries have held Tiedemann back from truly skyrocketing up Top 100 lists. Tiedemann was once again one of the buzziest stories in camp in 2024, but he eventually underwent Tommy John surgery in July and is expected to miss the majority of the ‘25 season. At his best, Tiedemann has the potential to be a truly dominant lefty. In past camps, he’s received the highest praise a young pitcher can, which is veteran starters going out of their way to watch him throw on the back fields. His fastball, which was touching 98 mph while sitting 94-96, is one of the best pitches in the organization, and Tiedemann’s three-quarter arm slot plays up that velocity. His slider and changeup could both be plus pitches in the big leagues. Beyond health, Tiedemann’s only real challenge has been control. He’s been able to overwhelm younger hitters in the Minors with stuff alone, but to carry that success over to the big leagues, he’ll need to be hitting the corners and avoiding the heart of the plate. If the walks do come, Tiedemann has the ability -- like Blake Snell -- to erase them himself. He's eyeing a return to the mound by August or September, so while his ‘26 return to starting is the real story to focus on, his rare physical gifts could make him an intriguing bullpen option later this season if his recovery goes well and the Blue Jays have a spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A dominant arm in his one year at Golden West (Junior) College (Huntington Beach, Calif.), Tiedemann joined the Blue Jays as a third-round pick in 2021 and quickly broke out by striking out 117 batters over 78 2/3 innings across three levels in his first full season. Shoulder and biceps issues limited him to only 44 frames while topping out at Triple-A during the regular season in 2023, but he still managed to finish with a 44.1 percent K rate that ranked second among 1,832 Minor Leaguers with at least 40 innings. He made up for the lost time by looking healthy and productive in the Arizona Fall League, where he was named the circuit’s Pitcher of the Year. Tiedemann opened 2024 with Triple-A Buffalo but struggled with health all summer and ultimately needed Tommy John surgery in July. The 6-foot-4 left-hander can run his fastball up to 98 mph and it generally sat at 93-96 over the top two levels of the Minors this past summer. His low three-quarters arm slot helps the heater play above the velocity too, making the four-seam a true plus pitch. His swings-and-misses, however, come from the offspeed -- a low-80s sweeping slider that has gotten better in pro ball and a mid-80s changeup that can dive below bats. He does well against fellow lefties but was an absolute menace against opposite-side batters in 2023, holding them to a .186 average and a .196 slugging percentage over 123 plate appearances. The length of Tiedemann’s delivery has led to some control issues, and his walk rate climbed from 9.6 percent in 2022 to 12.4 in 2023. That control will be worth monitoring when he returns in late 2025 at the absolute earliest, and it likely won’t be until 2026 that he can truly push for a Major League debut at last.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally a San Diego commit headed into the fall of 2020, Tiedemann chose to go the JuCo route instead, eventually landing at Golden West College. The southpaw struck out 60 batters in 38 innings as a freshman, prompting the Blue Jays to take him in the 2021 third round and sign him for around slot at $644,800. Tiedemann started showing signs of a breakout in the spring before his first full season and carried that improved stuff into the summer, when he posted a 2.17 ERA with 117 strikeouts in 78 2/3 innings across three levels, ending at Double-A New Hampshire. While he sat around 93-94 mph as an amateur, the 6-foot-4 lefty started being around 95-96 mph, touching higher, with his heater after adding muscle in the offseason. The pitch has some sink to it as well and helped Tiedemann force healthy amounts of ground-ball contact. That said, his mid-80s, diving changeup has become arguably his best pitch with the way it generates whiffs, and that helped him limit righties to a .153 average in 2022. His low-80s, sweeping slider shows plus potential, though it needs to be a little more consistent to give Tiedemann his true third weapon. Beyond being difficult to touch, Tiedemann’s control should continue to improve as he gains experience in his delivery, which includes some long levers and a lower arm slot. The next step is adding innings after Toronto carefully managed the California native, including with a brief midseason pause in Florida in 2022. Biceps issues have limited Tiedemann this season, but longer, more frequent starts in the future will keep him on a trajectory toward being a possible No. 2 starter in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted in the five-round 2020 Draft, Tiedemann changed his commitment from San Diego State to attend Long Beach Junior College, making him eligible for the ’21 Draft. Long Beach soon cancelled spring sports due to COVID-19, though, and Tiedemann was on the move again, landing at Golden West College. The end result paid off, though, as the Blue Jays scooped up Tiedemann in the third round and signed him to a bonus of $644,800. After not having much of a detailed strength or throwing program prior to the Draft, Tiedemann took off once the Blue Jays got him into their new player development complex. The lefty added more muscle to his 6-foot-4 frame and his velocity ticked up from the 93-94 range pre-draft, now sitting at 95-96 mph and reaching higher. Tiedemann also mixes in a mid-80s circle change with plus potential and a low-80s slider that’s progressed since he joined the club. That hard slider, in particular, will be key to keeping hitters off his plus fastball. All three pitches have been major parts of Tiedemann’s breakout 2022 season in which he’s climbed from Single-A to Double-A. With as much upward momentum as any prospect in the organization, Tiedemann has already accelerated his development timeline significantly. The Jays have tried to manage Tiedemann’s workload some -- giving him a midseason pause in Florida before his ascent to New Hampshire -- and that’s about the only thing that’s held him back. With his ability to generate whiffs with a stellar three-pitch mix, Tiedemann has quickly become one of the game’s best pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Ricky Cabrera was the cream of the Reds’ international crop in 2022, signing for $2.7 million, he’s not the only prospect from that class who has made some noise in the system. Sanchez signed for just $70,000 and in many ways has outperformed Cabrera, starting with his .947 OPS during his debut in the Dominican Summer League. His debut in the United States was also productive, finishing in full-season ball, and while a rough 2024 stalled his progress, he put up much better numbers while repeating Single-A Daytona, earning a midseason promotion to High-A in the process. Adjustments in his left-handed swing path led to better results last year for Sanchez. Learning better contact points and catching the ball out front has helped him impact the ball more. That and a lot of added physicality has made him a more dangerous hitter, one with extra-base authority he’s still learning to tap into. He continues to draw walks and even limited his strikeouts last year, upping his overall contact rate. Sanchez also made progress defensively, continuing to display valuable positional versatility. The Reds will continue to keep him on the dirt at third and at shortstop, where he played better than expected in 2025. He also got reps in center field, giving him the chance to be a utility type with a solid bat in the future. He’s just 21 for all of the 2026 season, so there could be more to unlock ahead of a decision needed to be made on his 40-man roster status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2022 international signing period might best be known among Reds prospects fans as the time they signed Ricardo Cabrera, who received a $2.7 million bonus. It has a chance to be about more than the top guy they signed thanks to Sanchez, who also signed when the period opened in January of that year for $70,000. He certainly made people sit up and take notice when he posted a .948 OPS in the Dominican Summer League during his pro debut that summer and he continued to impress stateside in the Arizona Complex League, earning a late bump up to full-season Daytona. He then kept it going with a stint in the Australian Baseball League. It's hard to tell which gets the Reds more excited -- Sanchez’s left-handed bat or his makeup and maturity. The left-handed hitter continues to have a very discerning eye at the plate and he walked as much as he struck out en route to a .468 on-base percentage in the ACL. His K rate did creep up, but there’s confidence he’ll make adjustments as he moves up the ladder. He has untapped raw power that hasn’t shown up in games, but he’s adding strength and it’s going to come. Sanchez’s defensive home is still a question. He signed as an outfielder, and he played a bunch of right field in the DSL. He’s seen a lot of time at shortstop (including in Australia), as well as third, and his arm works from the left side of the infield. The prevailing thought is shortstop isn’t going to work long-term, so look for him to see more time at third and probably left field as the Reds find ways to allow his advanced bat to move.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kipp didn't have a distinguished college career at Yale, compiling a 6.95 ERA over just 79 innings in four years while losing much of 2020 and all of 2021 to pandemic cancellations. After graduating with an economics degree in 2022, he planned on attending graduate school at Notre Dame until the Cubs saw him in the Cape Cod League and signed him for $50,000 as a nondrafted free agent. Chicago may not have protected him on its 40-man roster this offseason, but he's a legitimate prospect who spins the ball as well as anyone in the system. Kipp can exceed 3,000 rpm with his low-80s curveball and can manipulate its shape to gets swings-and-misses in the zone or elicit chases with greater depth. His slider has similar shape and spin rates to go with a tick more velocity, though it's a little less effective. The rest of his pitches all grade as below average: a 91-94 mph fastball that touches 96 with some armside run but more downhill plane than carry, an upper-80s cutter and an upper-80s changeup that's too firm and often misses the zone badly. While Kipp has an easy delivery and an amateur track record of throwing strikes, his walk rate has risen as he has climbed through the Minors. He has such little margin for error that he has to nibble around the zone, and he can get into trouble when he falls behind in the count. He has a ceiling of a back-of-the-rotation starter but is more likely to be a multi-inning reliever who concentrates on spinning curveballs and sliders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCabe hit 30 homers combined in 2021 and 2022 at UNC Charlotte, leading to the Braves taking him in the fourth round of the ‘22 Draft. He jumped more firmly on the prospect map with a solid first full season across two levels of A ball (17 homers combined), then finishing up with a decent showing in the Arizona Fall League. His forward momentum was stopped by Tommy John surgery in February, though he did return and struggle at the end of the year in Double-A. He got some more at-bats back in the AFL. A 6-foot-4 switch-hitter, McCabe has long had a solid approach at the plate, with excellent pitch recognition skills and the willingness to take walks. He drew free passes even during his rough Double-A debut last year and enters the 2025 season with a 15.2 percent walk rate in his career. He’s a better hitter left-handed, though when he’s locked in, he’s shown he can drive the ball from both sides. He has a more open stance from that side compared to his right-handed setup, and he’s tamed his leg kick a bit. Primarily a first baseman in college, the Braves were giving McCabe a lot of reps across the diamond at third because of his arm strength. With his elbow 100 percent, he should get time at both infield corners moving forward, with that positional flexibility perhaps his ticket to a big league role unless his power profile takes a step in the right direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing his high school ball in Ontario, McCabe stepped right into the UNC Charlotte lineup, only to see his first year of college ball halted by the pandemic in 2020. He then proceeded to hit 14 homers in 2021 and 16 more in 2022, leaving the 49ers with the second-highest slugging percentage (.679) in school history when the Braves took him in the fourth round of the ’22 Draft. After a fairly nondescript summer pro debut, he hit 17 homers across two levels of A ball before finishing with a stint in the Arizona Fall League. He wasn’t able to build off that as an elbow injury required Tommy John surgery in February. The 6-foot-4 McCabe is a switch-hitter with an advanced approach at the plate that he’s carried over to his pro career. After walking more than he struck out at Charlotte, McCabe walked 81 times in 2023, then posted a .448 on-base percentage in the AFL. He’s better from the left side of the plate, but he’s shown he can drive the ball either way. Even with an open stance and leg kick, he tends to be on time and manages strikeouts well. While McCabe played mostly first base in college, the Braves thought his arm strength might look good at third, and he played the hot corner exclusively in his first full season, then split time between the corners in Arizona. It’s looking like first base is his best shot at a regular spot, and he’ll have to keep using his approach to get to more power to profile well there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCabe didn’t make any kind of impression during his pandemic-shortened freshman year at UNC Charlotte, but the Canadian corner infielder made noise in each of the next two seasons, even if he did miss some time with injuries. He hit 30 homers in 2021 and 2022 combined and left the 49ers with a career .341/.451/.679 line, good enough to land in the fourth round of the ’22 Draft with the Braves. He got his professional feet wet mostly with Single-A Augusta. A switch-hitter, the 6-foot-4 McCabe has a tremendous amount of raw power to tap into. It didn’t show up during his brief pro debut, but he did hit the ball hard without results to show for it at times. He’s better from the left side of the plate and showed an ability to work counts at Charlotte, walking more than he struck out in his college career. McCabe played both infield corners in college, focusing mostly at first base, but the Braves think he and his plus arm could work at third, where he played exclusively during his debut in the organization. He’ll likely get some reps at first, but it’s the power potential at the plate that will determine his ultimate value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs added Elbis to its bat-heavy international signing class in July 2019 for $275,000. The Venezuela native missed out on 2020 like everyone else and then dominated the Arizona Complex League in 2021, prompting a late-season move to Single-A Visalia. He was limited to only three California League starts in 2023 because of right shoulder inflammation, and a year later, he saw an atypical uptick in walks while at High-A Hillsboro. Elbis looked much more like himself in 2024, posting a 3.39 ERA and a 1.19 WHIP over 135 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A, and the D-backs added him to the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible for a second time. Elbis didn’t punch out a ton of batters in his age-21 season, instead relying on his above-average command to draw weak contact. His pair of fastballs sit 91-94 mph, touching 96, and he held that velocity and even built on it well as he worked deeper into the biggest workload of his young career. He plays off the heater with an 83-85 mph slider that wears out the low, gloveside part of the plate, and batters (especially righties) just can’t lay off it. His 79-81 mph curveball has steeper drop and was his most-used secondary against lefties, who slugged just .280 off him. His 84-88 mph changeup can be an armside option but can be too firm. The right-hander perhaps got caught nibbling too much in the past but typically delivers strikes with regularity. That -- along with his deep arsenal -- was a big reason why Arizona chose to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. He’ll need that pitchability to stick as a starter because without a plus pitch he doesn’t easily project as an impact reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs went bat-heavy in the 2019-20 international signing period, but managed to add Elbis to the mix for $275,000. After missing out on 2020 like everyone else, the Venezuela native jumped straight to the Arizona Complex League in 2021 and dominated with 46 strikeouts and only four walks in 39 2/3 innings. That helped him get a late look at Single-A Visalia, and he returned to the Rawhide to make three starts in 2022, only to suffer right shoulder inflammation. The issue didn’t require surgery, and he was back pitching at instructs in January. When healthy, Elbis showed a fastball in the low 90s that he commanded well to all areas of the zone. He succeeded most when he landed it high, keeping with modern practices, and that led to some swings-and-misses despite the average velocity. His fading changeup received the best grades and helped fend off splits issues. He showed some feel for spin with an average curveball that could be landed for strikes and a slider that looked fringier but could offer another breaking look. The right-hander will still only be 20 years for the majority of the 2023 season, and his slim listed measurements of 6-foot-1 and 150 pounds point to a still-developing frame. His profile before the shoulder issue was dependent on his command, but a few more ticks of velocity as he physically matures would go a long way. The D-backs say Elbis has gotten back to his old self post-rehab, and he'll need to show proof of that when he gets back to a Minor League mound this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades (present/future): Hit: 4/6 | Power: 4/5 | Run: 3/3 | Arm: 6/6 | Field: 4/5 | Overall: 4/5 After scuffling in the lower Minor Leagues for a few seasons, Flores broke out in 2012. As a 20-year-old, he moved up to Double-A Binghamton for the first time. He built on that progress in 2013 and made his Major League debut. Flores has made impressive progress at the plate in the last two years. He has a knack for making contact and is extremely tough to strike out. His overall approach at the plate improved, and that helped him tap into his raw power more consistently. Initially a shortstop, Flores now splits his time between second and third base, either of which is a much better home for him, given his lack of quickness. He has good hands and a strong arm, but the lack of range might continue to be an issue. Flores' bat is ready to contribute soon, regardless of his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The five-round 2020 Draft was odd in many ways, including the ability for someone like Flores to go from undrafted free agent status into the Top 100 Prospects discussion. The brother of the Major League infielder of the same name, Flores made only six relief appearances at Arizona Western (Junior) College but stood out enough to get an offer from the Tigers. He laid the groundwork with impressive turns in the Florida Complex and State Leagues (and a turn in the Arizona Fall League) in 2021 and then truly broke out with a 2.79 ERA, 1.01 WHIP and 130 K’s in 103 1/3 innings at High-A and Double-A last season. Standing out of his tall 6-foot-4 frame, Flores has been more around the low-90s with his fastball in 2023, though he locates the pitch well. The command of that heater took a particular leap with the additional innings gained in 2022 and helped Flores work deep into games in September. (A hamstring injury this season will affect his ability to do the same.) His upper-70s curveball gives him another potential plus pitch -- one that drops off the table and generates whiffs or ground balls in the lower reaches of the zone. A mid-80s cutter replaced his changeup in the arsenal pecking order, and its improvement in sharpness helped Flores fend off the stark splits often seen by hurlers without a quality cambio. Improving the changeup was a point of focus in his return to Double-A Erie in '23, and it was showing a few more signs of life before the hamstring injury. After walking 12 in 11 2/3 innings in college, Flores has improved his strike-throwing enough to keep getting starting looks. The Tigers kept him at Double-A this season to work on the quality of his pitches, and he's trending more toward being a reliever until he proves his arsenal can work at Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers tried to complement their abbreviated 2020 Draft class with several low-risk signings of non-drafted free agents who would’ve been later picks in other years. One of them was Flores, the younger brother of the Major League infielder of the same name. He pitched just 11 2/3 innings over six relief appearances in his lone season at Arizona Western College, but struck out 16 batters while allowing just five hits, though he walked 12. With a little polish to his raw talent, he enjoyed an impressive first pro season, striking out 90 batters over 66 innings between the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and Low-A Lakeland. The Tigers saw enough to send him to the Arizona Fall League, where he had nearly as many walks (16) as strikeouts (17) over 12 2/3 innings. Flores’ big frame and delivery produce a fastball that sits solidly in the mid-90s and tops out at 98, and a big, high-spin curveball that he can locate for strikes when he’s on his game or use to chase when he’s ahead. Fastball command can be inconsistent, an issue behind the walks. Flores has worked on a changeup since last year to make his fastball more effective, along with a cutter. Tigers officials believed Flores had Major League stuff at the start of this season, and they’ve felt vindicated by a downright dominant age-21 season by him at High-A West Michigan and Double-A Erie. The lack of a quality third pitch remains a concern, but Flores’ fastball-curve combo has been stellar enough to make his MLB rotation dreams even closer to a reality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Much like that sleek-looking sports car that tempts you when you hear the engine roaring, but always ends up in the shop, Canterino has shown some of the most electric stuff in the Minors when he’s on the mound. The only problem is that since being taken in the second round of the 2019 Draft out of Rice, the right-hander hasn’t been out there much, with just 85 innings since signing. The forearm strain that caused him to miss most of 2021 was a harbinger of a torn UCL, which required Tommy John surgery in August of 2022. Even though the Twins knew he’d be out for the 2023 season, they put him on the 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. When Canterino has pitched, he showed even better stuff than when he starred at Rice, starting with a fastball that averaged 95 mph and touched 97 mph, a heater with very good life. His mid-80s slider is an out pitch, a hard breaker that misses a ton of bats. His 80-mph changeup can be equally nasty with depth and tumble and he even has a slower curve he can fold in occasionally. Canterino’s stuff plays up even more because of his funky, up-tempo delivery, though one has to wonder how that has impacted his arm health. He’s been more control over command and will need to find the zone more with his stuff as he returns from elbow surgery. His medical record, when combined with his delivery and the fact he’s 26 for the 2024 season, could mean that the bullpen is the best place for him to have a big league impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canterino served as the best starter at Rice for three years in a row, reaching triple digits in strikeouts all three seasons. That track record led to him landing in the second round of the 2019 Draft and he’s continued to show off the stuff that made him successful with the Owls. But he hasn't been healthy very often to do so, with a grand total of 85 innings of pro experience under his belt. A forearm strain in 2021 was a precursor to an elbow issue that required Tommy John surgery last August. The rare times he was on the mound, Canterino’s repertoire often looked even more electric than it did in college. His velocity ticked up, averaging 95 mph in 2021 and 2022 with good life. He mostly threw a hard mid-80s slider that missed a ton of bats but has a low-80s curve with depth as well. His 80-mph changeup can be an out pitch at times as well, with depth and tumble to it. Canterino has missed a ton of bats as a pro with a 13.8 K/9 rate while generally being around the strike zone. His stuff has been so dominant the Twins added him to the 40-man roster this past offseason even though he won’t pitch competitively again until 2024 at age 26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canterino left Rice University as a three-year starter who had struck out 100-plus batters in all three seasons, leading him to being taken by the Twins in the second round of the 2019 Draft. Since then, it’s been hard to see him on a mound, with the pandemic in 2020 and a forearm strain in 2021 limiting him to a total of 48 professional innings since being drafted entering the 2022 season. When Canterino has been able to pitch, he’s shown improved stuff with more velocity and a legitimate four-pitch mix. His fastball averaged 95 mph in the 23 innings he did manage to collect in 2021, with good movement. He has both a low-80s curve with a ton of depth and a harder slider that both flash plus. While his changeup is his fourth pitch, it does have good depth and tumble to it. Canterino has shown the ability to miss a ton of bats while filling up the strike zone (11.25 K/BB ratio in 2021). It’s all going to come down to health for the right-hander. The Twins are cautiously optimistic, because the injury has been in the flexor area and there has been no ligament damage thus far. If he can stay on the mound, he could end up being the best pitching prospect in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Once upon a time, Rice University was churning out high-end pitching prospects, with three arms going in the top 10 of the 2004 Draft. But when Canterino went in the second round to the Twins in the 2019 Draft, he was the first pitcher to go in the top three rounds since Jon Duplantier was a third-rounder in 2016. The right-hander made it to full-season ball during his summer debut, then spent most of 2020 working out on his own, showing it was time well-spent with some excellent outings when he joined the Twins’ alternate site late in the year. Canterino has taken steps forward particularly in two areas. The first is fastball velocity, with a heater that sat in the low-90s in college planted in the 94-95 mph range at the alternate site, with good life. The other area is his changeup, which had been his fourth pitch at Rice. It was more of a speed-differential pitch then, but now it has much better depth and excellent downward movement, turning into a weapon that could be used against hitters from both sides of the plate. The right-hander throws both an upper-70s curve with big depth and a hard plus slider, giving him a true four-pitch mix. He’s always thrown a lot of strikes despite an unconventional delivery that features some effort, so there’s confidence he can be a starting pitcher for the long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canterino spent three years in the Rice rotation, quickly establishing himself as the ace of that staff, and he brought along a resume of success to the 2019 Draft. The right-hander reached triple digits in strikeouts all three years in college and also pitched very well for Team USA and in the Cape Cod League to put him even more firmly on the map. That led to him being a second-round selection by the Twins, who managed his workload carefully during his pro debut after a long junior season, but still saw Canterino pitch well in the Midwest League. Canterino has a true four-pitch mix potential. His fastball usually sits in the low 90s and reaches 96 mph with good downward plane. He’d always thrown a slider and a curve in his first two years at Rice, but got away from throwing the latter as a junior because he liked his slider, a plus mid-80s power breaking ball, so much. He focused on bringing back the curve in his first pro summer with success, showing a 77-mph breaker with really big depth, pairing it well with his riding fastball at the top of the zone. He threw his changeup effectively against left-handed hitters during his pro debut, but needs to get comfortable throwing it to righties. With a bit of an unusual delivery that includes a good amount of effort, Canterino has faced questions about his ability to start long-term. But he’s always been a strike-thrower overall and was very durable throughout his college career, leaving no reason to believe he can’t fit very nicely in the middle of a big league rotation in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in the Bahamas, Murray played high school and college ball in Florida, the latter at Florida Atlantic. Part of a baseball family that includes brothers who played in the Giants system (Byron) and independent ball (Brandon), B.J. turned pro as a 15th-rounder in 2021. He was a major part of championship teams at High-A South Bend in 2022 and Double-A Tennessee in 2023, providing the decisive home run in the Southern League clincher last September. Murray's combination of plate discipline and power ranks among the best in the system, and he led all Cubs farmhands in on-base percentage (.410) in his first full pro season and in walks (82) in his second. A switch-hitter, he has a smoother swing as a lefty but is proficient from both sides and makes a lot of hard contact. After putting the ball on the ground too much in 2022, he did a better job of driving the ball in the air and tapping into his power last year, when he ranked third in the Southern League with 54 extra-base hits. Though Murray has below-average speed out of the batter's box, he's an average runner once he gets going and stole 14 bases in 17 attempts last season. After spending most of his first full pro season at first base, he returned to his college position of third in 2023. He has a chance to be an average defender with similar arm strength at the hot corner if he continues to improve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Franklin hit 23 homers in his first two seasons at Michigan, scouts were excited to see what he might do in his Draft year, but even before the pandemic shortened the 2020 season, Franklin broke his collarbone in a skiing accident, so he didn’t play a single game. The Braves thought he could tap into that power as a pro, taking him in the third round of the Draft that summer. He did slam 24 homers and finished a steal shy of a 20-20 season in his first full season in 2021, but Tommy John surgery knocked him out for nearly all of the 2022 season. His return in 2023, in Double-A, featured some power, some speed and a lot of swing and miss. Franklin’s lead tool is still his easily plus raw power from the left side of the plate. He did hit 15 homers in 2023, but the length of and holes in his swing were taken advantage of by Double-A pitchers, and Franklin struck out in early 30 percent of his plate appearances and had a 36-percent miss rate overall. When he does make contact, he is able to drive the ball out to all fields, but he’s going to have to find a way to adjust his approach to find the barrel more to have a usable power-over-hit profile. While he’s not a burner, Franklin runs well enough to steal some bags and his athleticism plays in the outfield as well. He’s continued to see time in all three spots, but if he’s going to hit enough to be an everyday guy in one spot, it’s going to be left field because of his fringy arm. A future as a fourth or fifth outfielder and a power left-handed bat off the bench might be the best outcome at this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Franklin established his power bona fides right away at Michigan, hitting 23 homers in his freshman and sophomore years combined. He missed what ended up being a shortened 2020 season because of a broken collarbone, but the Braves were willing to bite on the power potential, taking him in the third round of that summer’s Draft. The power showed up in his first full season with 24 home runs, along with the swing-and-miss. He was barely acclimating to Double-A in 2022 when a left elbow injury that resulted in Tommy John surgery sidelined him after only 15 games. The missed time for someone like Franklin, who has some holes in his swing, wasn’t ideal. But the Braves are still bullish on his power potential. High-A Rome is not a friendly place for hitters, but Franklin was still able to translate his raw pop to home runs during his first full season. There’s work to be done on his approach, but he did show signs of adjusting as that first full season wore on. A solid athlete, Franklin showed he can steal a base with his above-average speed. He’s seen time in all three outfield spots, but left seems to be the best spot if he were to settle into one outfield position as an everyday player. More than anything, he needs a full season of reps to show whether he can be a power-hitting run producer at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a solid career at Seattle Preparatory School, Franklin hit 23 homers over his first two years at Michigan, becoming more of a power-first type hitter as a sophomore, albeit with a ton of walks. He hit well in the Cape Cod League, but didn’t get to follow that up due to a broken collar bone that wiped out any at-bats in the shortened 2020 season. The Braves had seen enough to take him in the third round of that summer’s Draft and he rewarded their faith by finishing tied for the High-A East lead in home runs and finishing a steal shy of a 20-20 campaign, though he struggled in the Arizona Fall League. He barely got the chance to improve in 2022, playing in just 15 games before being shelved with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. While Franklin’s strikeout rate of around 28 percent in 2021 was too high, it was actually better than league average and was perhaps an acceptable tradeoff for the legitimate power he got to from the left side of the plate. Even with the K rate, his exit velocities and quality of contact were very impressive and he had a .936 OPS after an atrocious May. He still needs to work on his approach, something he was working on in the AFL, leading to a higher walk rate even if it didn’t translate into other positive results. After not being much of a threat in college, Franklin started to use his speed, a tick above-average, to his benefit on the basepaths. He can handle center field if needed, but will continue to be exposed to all three outfield spots as he hits the upper levels. Left field seems to be the best destination for him, with the power profile that works well for an outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid high school prospect from the Pacific Northwest, Franklin headed to Michigan rather than sign with the Mariners in the 37th round of the 2017 Draft. He broke out of the gate well as a freshman, hitting .327/.379/.588 for the Wolverines in 2018, then hitting .302 in the Cape Cod League. Selling out for more power as a sophomore did lead to more homers, but worse overall numbers, though he did help Michigan finish as runners-up in the College World Series. Though he broke his collarbone to wipe out even a shortened junior season, the Braves liked his first two years enough to take him in the third round of the 2020 Draft, and he made up for some lost time at the team’s alternate training site and during instructs. While Franklin doesn’t have any one plus tool, he can do a number of things fairly well. The Braves loved the quality of the at-bats he had from the left side of the plate, especially when facing upper-level lefty prospects like Kyle Muller and Tucker Davidson at the alternate site. There is strength and he’s shown a solid approach at the plate overall, with a chance to hit for decent average with some power if he can avoid trying to hit the ball out too much. Franklin is a touch above-average runner, but he’s never really used it to his advantage on the basepaths or in the outfield. He played mostly center field in college, but will likely see time in all three outfield spots as he gets his pro career started, with a fringy arm best suited for left if he were to settle into one spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziegler was Draft-eligible at 17 years old in 2020, but the pandemic shutdown and shortened Draft hurt his chances. The Ontario native headed south to TNXL Academy in Florida to help his stock, and that paid off when the Mets signed him for $900,000 as a 2021 second-round pick. The 6-foot right-hander’s pro time has been marred by injuries since. Biceps tendinitis limited him to 46 2/3 innings at Single-A St. Lucie in his first full season. Before the 2023 campaign, he underwent surgery to address bone spurs in his right elbow and tore his quad during his rehab. He finally returned to a Florida State League mound on Sept. 9 and struck out all three batters he faced. On a per-pitch basis, there remains a lot to be excited about from the Canadian. Ziegler’s fastball touched 95.7 mph during that brief 2023 outing, and he’s generally been about 92-94 with the pitch in pro ball. The heater plays up too with terrific ride up in the zone. Off that, Ziegler utilizes an 82-85 mph curveball that shows good 12-to-6 drop, giving him a north-south approach. He’s worked with an 83-85 mph splitter that had a healthy whiff rate as well but didn’t use it in his lone 2023 appearance. Ziegler walked 17.6 percent of batters faced in 2022 because of his aggressive delivery. That control was going to be put to the test more in 2024 before injury concerns reared their head again. Ziegler underwent elbow issues early on that required Tommy John surgery, and he’ll miss the rest of the season as a result, wiping out what was looking like a potential breakout season. He’ll still only be in his age-22 campaign in 2025, giving him needed runway to regain his form and health beginning next summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziegler could have been selected in 2020 when he was 17, but the combination of the pandemic shutdown and shortened Draft that summer did him no favors. To give himself a better showcase the next year, the Ontario native went to TNXL Academy in Ocoee, Fla., and that worked out well when he went in the second round and signed below slot at $900,000. Ziegler’s first full season was limited to 46 2/3 innings at Single-A St. Lucie due to biceps tendinitis and other concerns, but he fanned 70 batters in that span. Before the 2023 season, Ziegler underwent surgery to address bone spurs in his right elbow and later tore his quad during his rehab, keeping him out for much of the season. Standing at just an even 6 feet, the right-hander can good fastball velocity for his size in the 92-94 mph range, and he touched 96.5 mph during his time in the Florida State League. He lost some of that velocity as the season wore on, but the perceived rise of the pitch, stemming from its relatively flat angle, helps it play up. His low-80s curveball generated a ton of whiffs, and FSL hitters batted only .032 against it (per Statcast). His 83-85 mph splitter also kept hitters off guard but is still a low-spin work in progress. Ziegler battled control issues before and after his injured list stints, and his 17.6 percent walk rate won’t cut it at any level. He can be aggressive in his motion on the mound, and that can lead to some of the missed spots. The Canadian hurler will likely to have wait until his age-21 season in 2024 before he can show off how his stuff and control is coming along.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziegler was technically Draft-eligible as a 17-year-old out of Ontario in 2020, but the pandemic shutdown, combined with the shorter Draft process, kicked his selection down the road by one year. To improve his 2021 stock, the 6-foot right-hander went south to TNXL Academy in Ocoee, Florida, while still occasionally heading home, and that worked out when the Mets selected him in the second round. Ziegler signed for a below-slot $900,000 bonus and still awaits his Minor League debut. Ziegler displays good arm strength for his (or any) size. He typically sits around 93 mph already but has touched as high as 97. His heater works best down in the zone, thanks to its sinking movement. A low-80s curveball has shown good bite and vertical shape in its early days at Single-A St. Lucie, earning the highest whiff percentage of his three pitches. As is typical of high-schoolers entering the pros, Ziegler will focus on developing a mid-80s changeup, though that has kept hitters off-balance at times too. It should be interesting to see how Ziegler’s command develops under the Mets’ watch. He was inconsistent with his location last spring, despite an aggressive approach from the mound. Those woes would point to a bullpen role should they continue, but such a decision is years away for the right-hander, who will be 19 for the entire 2022 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilson burst on the season in his first year at South Alabama, setting a freshman school record with 17 homers in 2019. By 2021, he had become more of a contact-over-power hitter, but his .947 OPS helped him land in the second round of that summer’s Draft. He has yet to find any kind of offensive groove in his two-plus years in the Phillies system, though there were some signs of life power-wise while spending the 2023 season in Double-A Reading. The left-handed-hitting Wilson did find the seats 17 times in 2023, and while the assumption might be it was because Reading's home park is very hitting-friendly, he actually got to his power on the road as well. He’s going to have to find ways to do that more frequently unless he vastly changes what has been an overly aggressive approach as a pro. He’s shown he can make loud contact but chases out of the zone way too much, and his strikeout rate ticked up last year without the benefit of an increased walk rate. A decent athlete who has shown he can run a little, Wilson is limited to corner outfield spots, and he played more left than right for the first time last year with Reading. If he’s ever going to play one spot regularly, it’s likely to be left because of his fringy arm, but he’s going to have to become a much more consistent offensive performer to be an everyday player in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting a South Alabama record 17 freshman home runs in 2019, Wilson opted for contact over power two years later in his Draft season. His .947 OPS helped him climb to the second round of the 2021 Draft with the Phillies, and he made his debut with full-season Clearwater that summer. While he did reach Double-A in his first full season, he struggled to find any kind of offensive consistency in 2022. Some of Wilson’s issues in 2022 stemmed from him being caught between the power and contact-first profiles, but most of it was a result of poor swing decisions. His strikeout rate wasn’t awful, but he swung at just about everything in his first full season and walked at just over a six percent clip. He regularly offered at pitches out of the zone, leading to weak contact and outs. The left-handed hitter didn’t tap into any of the raw power he has as a result. Wilson is a decent athlete, but is definitely limited to an outfield corner long-term. He’s played more right field to date, but his fringy arm might be best suited to left in the future. Still just 23 for the entirety of the 2023 season, there’s time for him to get straightened out, with the hope he can rediscover the swing that made him an offensive force in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilson burst on the scene as a freshman at South Alabama, destroying former All-Star Luis Gonzalez’s freshman home run record by blasting 17 homers to earn Sun Belt Conference player of the year honors in 2019. He eschewed power for more contact in 2021 and his .947 OPS helped land him in the second round of the 2021 Draft, signing for slot value with the Phillies and making his pro debut in Low-A. It remains to be seen what kind of hitter Wilson will be at the professional level. He showed an ability to barrel up the baseball with an advanced approach in 2021, with high contact rates and a willingness to work counts and draw walks. The left-handed hitter sacrificed some pop in the process, but the Phillies believe there is plenty of power to tap into as he learns to find an offensive balance. Wilson is almost certainly limited to playing a corner spot in the outfield, with left the most likely destination because of his fringe-to-average arm. He should be an average defender there, but it does put more pressure on the bat to produce, though it is the offensive potential the Phillies were buying in the first place.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Santos in 2019 out of Acarigua, Venezuela, but his professional debut was delayed by the lost '20 season. Since he got rolling in ‘21, Santos has flashed the ability to miss bats at a high rate. In ‘22, he struck out a whopping 142 batters over 86 innings between Single-A and High-A. The ‘23 season felt like a jumping-off point for him, but an arm injury limited him to 48 1/3 innings with Vancouver. The results were there with a 3.54 ERA, but his strikeout rate dropped and it was another season that pointed to a potential future as a reliever. Santos has finally added weight, which the Blue Jays have been working on for years. He’s never going to be mistaken for a linebacker, but Santos’ weight is closer to 190 pounds now. That doesn’t need to result in a huge velocity bump above his current spot in the low 90s, but if it helps Santos maintain his stuff through a full season, it’s a big win for both him and the organization. Santos is back to using a slightly lower arm angle that comes more naturally to him, and his slider has the potential to be a legitimate out pitch in the big leagues. That’s the biggest reason many point to a relief profile, where Santos' walk rate wouldn’t be as detrimental. Santos dealt with elbow trouble early on in 2024 and didn't make his season debut until mid-June, eventually reaching Double-A a month later. He's worked exclusively as a reliever since, playing right into what some expected his future role to be anyways. He could be a quick mover in '25, assuming the elbow health holds on, and that slider would be a menace at the top level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Santos out of Acarigua, Venezuela, in 2019, but his professional debut was delayed by the lost 2020 season. He eventually debuted in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and got a taste of Single-A in 2021, posting a combined 5.58 ERA with 58 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings. Santos’ breakout came in 2022, though, when he split his season between Single-A and High-A with a 4.50 ERA and a whopping 142 strikeouts over 86 innings. That strikeout rate of 14.9 per nine innings is where Santos’ appeal lives. Santos is still working to add more weight, which the Blue Jays hope will bump his fastball velocity up as he moves through his early 20s. It currently sits in the low 90s and touches 94 mph. His slider, which he uses heavily at times as a secondary pitch, can produce plenty of whiffs as a low-80s sweeper. As Santos is tested by more disciplined hitters at higher levels, though, he’ll need to continue to hone that slider and improve his changeup. Santos is now working with a lower arm slot which he adjusted in 2022 and it gives him a more natural, athletic delivery as he slings the ball to the plate. There’s certainly some reliever potential if he shortens up his arsenal to a fastball and a slider to chase strikeouts, but he’ll still get plenty of run as a starter as he tries to develop his secondaries. This is a major year for Santos, especially as he faces older hitters who will be more disciplined against his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Acarigua, Venezuela, in 2019, Santos had his professional debut delayed by the lost ’20 season, but the right-hander finally debuted in the Florida Complex League in ’21. There, Santos pitched 35 1/3 innings before getting a taste of Single-A at the tail end of the season, where he was hit hard over five innings. Santos ended the season with a combined 5.58 ERA, striking out 58 batters over 40 1/3 innings. He’s been a breakout hurler for Toronto this summer, striking out close to 40 percent of his batters faced back in the Florida State League. Santos spent most of the winter at the club’s complex and added some good weight, though there’s still plenty of room for him to mature physically. Santos’ fastball sat in the low-90s in ’21, but he’s reaching up to 94 mph early in ’22 with the potential for more. He’s leaned heavily on a low-80s slider with two-plane sweep, throwing it 40 percent of the time in some cases, and it’s gotten twice as many whiffs on a per-pitch bases as the heater. His mid-80s changeup can get too firm, and he’s moved away from it some as the season has gone on. Gifted with an electric arm, Santos is still years away, but his raw potential is impressive. He’ll be tested with moves higher up the chain at some point, but the fastball-slider mix has worked wonders in Dunedin in 2022, making him one of the must-follow arms throughout the summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hardman showed off his power by prevailing in the Cape Cod League home run derby and finishing third in the circuit with eight homers in the summer of 2019, then won the Big 12 Conference batting title (.397) at Oklahoma two years later. A fifth-round pick in 2021, he ranked fourth in the High-A South Atlantic League with 22 homers in his first full pro season and then tied for the Arizona Fall League lead with six. He continued to mash in 2023, leading the Double-A Eastern League with 26 blasts despite playing in just 77 games because an errant pitch broke his right hand in late July. Hardman's 6-foot-3, 230-pound frame provides plenty of strength and leverage, which combine with his bat speed to produce high exit velocities and well above-average power that plays to all parts of the ballpark. His right-handed pop comes with plenty of strikeouts, however, because he has a launch-heavy approach and works deep counts looking for pitches to crush. He whiffed in 32 percent of his plate appearances during his first three years as a pro and may not make enough contact to do damage against big league pitching. Athletic for his size despite below-average speed, he's aggressive on the bases and will steal when given the opportunity. After playing almost exclusively at first base for the Sooners, he moved to third base in 2022 and has fared better than expected. He has good reactions and makes most plays, though his fringy range and average arm strength are a bit less than desired and he needs to improve his consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hardman won the home run derby and finished third with eight homers in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, then won the Big 12 Conference batting title (.397) at Oklahoma two years later. Signed for a well-under-slot $200,000 as a 2021 fifth-rounder, he topped Yankees farmhands and ranked fourth in the High-A South Atlantic League with 22 homers in his first full pro season. He finished 2022 by tying for the Arizona Fall League home run lead with six and played better defense than scouts expected there. With the strength and leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame to go with his quick right-handed swing, Hardman is built to hit for power. He does pile up strikeouts while working deep counts looking for pitches to punish, but he also shows the willingness to use the opposite field. He hits the ball harder than most players in the system and his pop plays to all fields. Though Hardman has below-average speed, he's fairly athletic for his size and stole 14 bases in 18 attempts last season. Almost exclusively a first baseman for the Sooners, he became a full-time third baseman in 2022 and displayed good reactions and average range. His arm strength is merely average, a bit less than desired at the hot corner, but it doesn't prevent him from making most plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 35th-round pick out of a California high school by the Braves in 2019, Hall improved throughout his three-year college career at Oregon and set a school record with a .640 slugging percentage in 2022. A fourth-rounder that July, he broke the hamate bone in his right hand while popping out in his first pro at-bat and then required a second surgery last January after injuring his wrist. He finally returned to the field in mid-April and hit .246/.353/.403 between two Class A levels. Hall has a quick left-handed swing and produces high exit velocities to all fields. He has enough bat speed and strength to create plus raw power, though he didn't make the most of it in 2023 because he didn't lift the ball in the air consistently. He has a patient approach but struggles against breaking balls from left-handers, so he'll have to make adjustments to be more than platoon player. Hall has average tools across the board, though he's a little quicker than that once he gets going. He played center field in his first two years at Oregon before moving to right field in his third, and he split time between the two positions last year. His range is more suited for a corner and he throws well enough to handle right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two so-so seasons at Oregon, Hall impressed scouts with a strong summer in the Cape Cod League in 2021. He built on that momentum last spring, slashing .333/.402/.640 with 14 homers and setting a Ducks record for slugging percentage. The Yankees were pleased to find him available in the fourth round last July, though his pro debut ended quickly when he broke the hamate in his right hand while popping out in his first pro at-bat. Hall has a quick left-handed swing and regularly makes hard contact from gap to gap. His bat speed and strength add up to plus raw power, and he can drive the ball out of the park from left-center to the right-field foul pole. He's an aggressive hitter who pounds fastballs but will need to make adjustments to handle quality breaking pitches. Hall shows average speed out of the batter's box and is quicker underway, albeit not much of a base-stealing threat. He played center field in his first two years at Oregon before moving to right in 2022. His range fits better on a corner and his average-to-solid arm strength plays well in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since being selected out of San Jacinto College in the fifth round of the 2021 Draft, Auer has experienced the highs and lows of life in the Minor Leagues. A former two-way player in college and an unquestionably talented athlete, Auer immediately impressed in his full-season debut with his all-out style of play. But he took a frustrating step backward at the plate in Double-A last year, no longer able to hide the deficiencies in his mechanics with his natural ability against tougher competition. There were already questions about how Auer’s contact rate would hold up against higher-level pitching, and he didn’t do much to answer them in Double-A as he slashed .205/.292/.348 with a 36 percent strikeout rate. He often looked lost, struggling to pick up spin or hit anything on the outer third of the plate. He finished better than he started with better underlying numbers over the final six weeks. Auer spent a lot of time with the club’s hitting coordinators, and he didn’t stop hitting all offseason after working his way to a more comfortable setup and swing. Auer does everything else well. He’s in better shape than anyone in the system, with strength that gives him solid power when he manages to make contact. He is the best defensive center fielder in the Rays’ system and arguably the best defensive player, period. He has elite speed, which allowed him to steal 47 bases even in a year he wasn’t on as often as he would’ve liked. He has a true cannon of an arm in the outfield. He works hard and takes care of himself, with a strong focus on his body and his career, so the Rays aren’t worried about him even after an offensive performance he’d like to quickly forget.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays knew they were getting a talented athlete when they selected Auer out of San Jacinto College in the fifth round in the fifth round of the 2021 Draft. He’d hit and pitched for Missouri State in 2020, then did the same as a juco player in Houston and solidified himself as a prospect to watch while playing for Frederick in the MLB Draft League in ’21. The Rays signed him for $312,500, just under slot, only to discover Auer’s impressive tools and all-out style of play were accompanied by much more advanced skills than they expected. In his first full season, the 21-year-old Auer hit .290/.372/.487 with 15 homers, 12 triples and 21 doubles over 115 games between Single-A Charleston and High-A Bowling Green. He shortened his load at the plate, enhancing his ability to make contact and letting his bat speed help him generate some high exit-velocity readings. He still struck out in 20.8 percent of his plate appearances, plus in 23 of his 78 PAs in the Arizona Fall League, which leads to some questions about how his contact rate will hold up against higher-level pitching -- concerns that have held up with his move to Double-A. But Auer has a ton of strength and athleticism -- he's in the best physical shape of any Rays prospect – and his wide-ranging skill-set allows him to create value with more than just his bat. The Rays figured they could expect a strong arm from the 6-foot-1 outfielder/former pitcher, and indeed, he has the best outfield arm in the system, a true plus-plus cannon. But Auer surprised the club with the accuracy of his throws and the relatively clean routes he took to balls in center and right field. He’s a plus runner -- and more advanced than expected there, too, as he swiped 48 bags in 55 attempts while earning the organization’s Baserunner of the Year award. He still has some more polishing that needs to take place, and his other tools will only travel as far as his bat takes him, but he has the look of a future big league outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have looked at creative ways to add young talent under president of baseball operations Scott Harris, and their trade for Dickerson fits the profile. Essentially, they turned $500,000 of international prospect pool money into a domestic prospect. Dickerson ranked 158th on MLB Pipeline’s Draft prospect rankings last summer, but teams shied away from the Virginia Tech commit until the Padres offered him a $500,000 signing bonus. It was a sharp move, but the Padres needed international money. The Tigers, who had scouted Dickerson along with his Team USA teammates Max Clark and Kevin McGonigle, took the opportunity. While Dickerson throws a 91-93 mph fastball, his tall frame provides plenty of projection for a velocity bump as he physically matures and polishes his mechanics. His slider is a swing-and-miss pitch with sharp break. His changeup is a third pitch at this point but has room for improvement. His stretch delivery has little wasted motion and hides the ball well, but his quick release makes it imperative he generates enough rotation to get the ball in on righties or to the outside corner on lefties. The Tigers see him as a starter, but even if he falls into a lefty relief role, it’s worth the cost of acquisition. The Tigers’ pitching development group has turned out good arms over the last year or two, some of which were undervalued by other clubs. Dickerson is an intriguing project, not just for his physical gifts but his aptitude for pitching. He might need time to blossom, but he’s the kind of addition that can deepen an already good farm system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Phillies drafted Sanchez in Round 12 of the 2019 Draft and went over slot to sign him for $300,000, he had some difficulty gaining traction, playing in the Complex League after signing and starting again there in '21 following the lost year because of the pandemic. He had trouble staying healthy in 2022 and then was sent to the Angels with Mickey Moniak in return for Noah Syndergaard at the Trade Deadline. Sanchez stayed relatively healthy last year, playing in over 100 games in a season for the first time and putting up solid numbers overall while finishing things off with an aggressive assignment to the Arizona Fall League. Finally putting in a full season, Sanchez started to unlock some of his raw tools a bit more consistently. He shook off a rough April, when he hit just .209, to hit .304 for the rest of the season. He’s a switch-hitter who’s a little better from the right side, but he showed some ability in both boxes. He’ll draw some walks, rarely strikes out and he started getting to his raw power for the first time. A corner outfielder only, Sanchez has a very strong arm, but unlike many young players with hoses they like to show off, he combines it with very consistent accuracy, which helped him rack up 15 assists from right field in 2023. He may be a fourth outfielder who plays in either corner at best, but he also might just be figuring out how to be a productive hitter, with more projection to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins needed two tries to land Montgomery, drafting him in the 35th round out of a Washington high school in 2019 and then in the 15th round after he spent a season at Boise State and two at Missouri. He batted .365 as a junior and ranked third in the rugged Southeastern Conference with a .374 average in league games before signing for $75,000. He earned Single-A Florida State League all-star accolades in his first full pro season but didn't fare nearly as well in High-A, slashing a combined .288/.413/.402. Like the other top first-base prospects in the system, Montgomery fits an atypical hit-over-power profile for his position, and he has the platoon disadvantage of batting right-handed. Though he's strong, his stroke is geared more for line drives and he doesn't turn on many pitches or drive them in the air. After his OPS plummeted from .968 in Single-A to .587 in High-A, the Marlins began working on him to improve his swing path to add more loft. With below-average speed once he gets going and average arm strength, Montgomery is limited to first base. He's a fringy defender at first who needs to develop more consistency after committing 12 errors in 94 games last season. He'll need to diligently maintain his 6-foot-3, 245-pound frame or risk lapsing into a DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cooke pitched two years in relief at Louisiana-Lafayette before finding results (2.03 ERA, 90 strikeouts in 79 2/3 innings) as a starter in 2021. The Blue Jays selected him in the 10th round that July, signed him for around slot at $141,900 and transitioned the right-hander back to relief when he joined High-A Vancouver late in 2022. Cooke took some lumps that year, but broke out in ‘23 with 80 strikeouts over 44 1/3 innings and reached Triple-A. You wouldn’t guess it from a reliever, but Cooke is one of the best athletes in the entire organization. If you need a guy who can touch 98 mph and dunk, Cooke is your man. Whether his fastballs live near 96 mph or begins flirting with triple digits again will determine his ceiling, but it’s already exciting in a short relief role and he should have a fairly short path to the big leagues if this track continues. Cooke’s slider can be devastating with impressive sweep and is already good enough to be an out pitch in MLB. The most important thing for Cooke is setting himself up better in counts, because when he has the advantage, he can be dominant. Spotting that fastball will be key and the Blue Jays trust his natural athleticism will enable him to adjust his delivery on the fly without losing the fundamentals. There is serious upside here in Cooke, who is quietly becoming one of this organization’s better development success stories in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brock dealt with injuries in college, so even though he spent four seasons at Ohio State and took two trips to the Cape Cod League, evaluators were left to stitch together his best flashes over the years. Brock’s biggest NCAA workload was 31 innings as a freshman and he threw just 16 2/3 in his Draft year, but the Blue Jays still loved him as an upside play in the sixth round in 2022. In two seasons since, Brock has flashed an incredible ceiling even though the numbers themselves might not reflect that. Across 65 Minor League innings, he owns a 4.85 ERA but has struck out a whopping 109 batters (15.1 K/9). Brock got off to an excellent start with High-A Vancouver in 2023, but got rocked in Double-A, which the Blue Jays are confident he’ll learn from. Some tutelage from star closer Jordan Romano will be part of that. Brock’s stuff is electric. His fastball lives in the upper-90s and his upper-80s slider, thrown 55 percent of the time in Double-A, is one of the best pitches in the system that could get MLB hitters out tomorrow, but as you can gather from his numbers, Brock needs to put himself in dominant counts more often to attack hitters. The organization has a high level of internal optimism that the numbers will move in the right direction this season, and if they do, Brock could move quickly in his age-24 year. There are clearly some command pieces that still need to come together for Brock, which won’t happen overnight, but his potential in a short relief role is massive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2016-17 international signing period, the A’s tied for the largest single bonus to one player, giving Lazaro Armenteros $3 million to sign on July 2. While that hasn’t turned out well, they may have struck gold when they signed Diaz about a month later out of Colombia for $275,000. He didn’t make it to full-season ball until 2021, but he showed enough offensive potential with High-A Lansing to get added to the 40-man roster that offseason. He rewarded Oakland's faith by slashing .326/.366/.515 with 19 homers across the two upper levels en route to his big league debut about a month after his 22nd birthday. With excellent bat speed, Diaz has posted elite-level contact rates in his career, and that continued in 2022 with just a 21 percent miss rate across all levels. His 14.4 percent strikeout rate in the Minors was right in line with his career mark (14.7). With that feel for the barrel has come a very aggressive approach that does not include many walks. He’s ditched a leg kick so there’s less movement at the plate, and he’s really starting to tap into his considerable raw power, showing he can hit the ball out to all fields. While big league manager Mark Kotsay really liked Diaz’s right-handed bat during his time up with Oakland, it is a little unclear where Diaz’s long-term defensive home should be. He’s never going to be a great defender, but the A’s felt he played his best defense in the big leagues and he held his own when asked to play second base. He might best be suited for first base or even DH, with the potential offensive profile to fit at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signing out of Colombia during the 2016-17 international signing period for $275,000, Diaz’s success throughout Short-Season ball transferred over to what was his first season at High-A, where he hit .288 with 13 home runs and 24 doubles in 90 games. The A’s felt he made enough progress to add him to the 40-man roster this offseason. Diaz has shown above average bat speed through the zone, which helps offset his high leg kick during the setup of his swing. He uses the whole field, and now the power the A’s were hoping to see is also starting to show up as he matures and evolves from being more of a gap-to-gap hitter. He already possesses some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the organization. Also showing good plate discipline, Diaz brings quite an advanced approach to the plate, especially for his age. Defense remains a work in progress for Diaz. While it has improved over the last year, the A’s continue to seek a permanent position for him. They tried him out at third base, and while he impressed with his strong arm, lapses in concentration led to him shifting over to first base and even some left field over the past year. Ultimately, Diaz will likely rely on his special abilities with the bat to continue moving up the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz signed out of Colombia for $275,000 during the 2016-17 international signing period. After debuting in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2017, he arrived to the United States that summer. He’s continued to hold his own as one of the younger players in both the Rookie-level Arizona League and Class A Short Season New-York-Penn League. More recently, Diaz performed well in the Caribbean Series this past winter, hitting .368 with three doubles and four RBIs in five games. Considered to have some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the organization, Diaz has displayed good plate discipline as he hits line drives to all fields. His skill set allows him to limit the strikeouts, and although he’s more of a gap-to-gap hitter, the power continues to improve. The big question for Diaz is where he’s going to play. Poor footwork and occasional lapses in concentration have impeded him when playing third base, though he did seem comfortable at first base while playing there during instructional league play last fall. Expected to grow into more power, the A’s will keep moving him through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from Colombia, Diaz signed during the 2016-17 international signing period for $275,000, the last of nine bonuses of six figures or more the A’s handed out during that period. He made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2017, but made his way to the United States that summer. After a full summer in the Arizona League, he moved up to the Short-Season New York-Penn League in 2019 and more than held his own as one of the younger players at the level. Diaz has perhaps the best bat-to-ball skills in the organization. He has an advanced feel to hit with outstanding bat-to-ball skills, limiting his strikeouts. He’s more of a gap-to-gap hitter and he’s not a quick-twitch kind of hitter, though there is potential power in there. While there’s faith Diaz is going to hit, there are more questions about whether he’ll defend. He doesn’t always keep focus there and while his hands and arm work, he needs to improve his footwork to stick at third long term. He can get caught flat-footed and make errors as a result. Some of that can get chalked up to youth, but he’ll need to be more consistent as he moves forward. The power will have to come more for him to really profile at the infield corner, but the A’s feel the bat will keep him going up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2016-17 international signing period is proving to be a fruitful one for the A's organization, at least as it pertains to filling the Top 30 list. Marcos Brito and Yerdel Vargas got seven figures to sign that summer out of the Dominican Republic and, of course, the organization went over the threshold to get Lazaro Armenteros for $3 million. Diaz was a lower-ticket item, getting $275,000 to sign out of Colombia. Like Vargas, he went from the Dominican Summer League to the Arizona League in his first summer of pro ball in 2017, then took a nice step forward in his return to the AZL the following summer. The key to Diaz's progress offensively was an increased understanding of his approach, and the right-handed hitter stayed with it all summer. He had some good exit velocity numbers with a line-drive approach and showed much better discipline, with a solid walk rate to show for it. Diaz didn't try to lift the ball too much, but with a strong, stocky build, there is some power to grow into. He also improved defensively at third, working hard at it and putting aside some lazy tendencies he displayed in his first summer, and he looked like one of the better defenders at the hot corner in the AZL. The A's are excited to see how Diaz's newfound maturity in terms of his approach, work ethic and consistency will allow him to progress moving forward. It's too early to tell exactly what he's going to be, but watching how he builds off of his encouraging 2019 should be interesting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Groome’s journey through pro ball has been an epic saga, and he hasn’t even reached the Majors yet. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 1 prospect in the 2016 Draft, he went 12th overall to the Red Sox due to signability concerns, and then was severely limited by lat and forearm injuries, as well as Tommy John surgery and the lost 2020 pandemic season before finally eclipsing the 60-inning mark in 2021. He moved to Triple-A for the first time in 2022, only to get traded to the Padres at the Trade Deadline in a swap for Eric Hosmer. Forget who Groome was an amateur -- he’s developed into a different pitcher now. His four-seam fastball was around 91-94 mph (touching 96) with some sink in the Pacific Coast League following the trade, making it just an average heater, though he can spot it pretty well. While his upper-70s curveball was considered his best pitch coming out of high school, a low-80s slider has emerged as his better swing-and-miss option, and he likewise upped its usage in his second month with El Paso. A low-80s changeup shows decent sink and separation, and while it isn’t more than average either, it did help him limit righties to a .673 OPS (compared to a .867 OPS from lefties) across all levels in 2022. Groome will have the occasional rough bout with wildness, but he keeps the walks in check enough to stay in a starting role. Without a true plus pitch, it’s tough to say he’s a natural candidate to move into relief, which would otherwise give him a better chance in the Majors; he’s rotation depth for now, with the hope of being a No. 5 someday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 1-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, Groome fell the to the Red Sox at No. 12 because of signability and makeup issues and signed for $3.65 million, still a franchise record for a drafted pitcher. He has avoid any off-field trouble but totaled just 66 innings in his first five years as a pro while dealing with lat and forearm injuries, Tommy John surgery and the pandemic shutdown. He stayed healthy, pitched a career high 97 1/3 innings and led the system with 134 strikeouts in 2021, overcoming a slow beginning to the year in High-A to finish with a strong three-start stint in Double-A. He reached Triple-A Worcester in mid-2022 before he was moved to the Padres at the Trade Deadline as the lone prospect return for Eric Hosmer. Groome's fastball velocity isn't what it once was, as he now operates in the low 90s and usually touches 94-95 mph only for an inning or two at a time.
