His best pitch is a mid-80s slider that he refined at Boston's alternate site in 2020, as it now shows flashes of becoming a plus offering and has surpassed his upper-70s curveball, which scouts considered the best bender in the 2016 Draft. He has developed a low-80s changeup with tumble that helps him handle right-handers, who fared far worse against him (.619 OPS) than same-side hitters (.890) in 2021. Evaluators aren't sure exactly what to make of Groome, who has puffed up to a listed 262 pounds and is less athletic than he was as an amateur. He throws strikes but might find more velocity and consistency if he got into better shape. He’ll try to show San Diego that he can still be a potential No. 5 starter in his second organization, but it might not be long before the Padres give him a look in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, Groome slid to the Red Sox at No. 12 amid huge signability and makeup concerns. He has avoided any off-field issues since signing for $3.65 million, still a franchise record for a drafted pitcher, but he pitched just 66 official innings in his first five years as a pro because of lat and forearm issues, Tommy John surgery in May 2018 and the coronavirus pandemic. He looked better in 2020 at Boston's alternate site than he did in instructional league, where his listed weight was 262 pounds, and he struggled in the first month of the 2021 season before coming on later in the summer. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Groome has worked at 92-95 mph with his fastball for most of 2021 after sitting at 90-92 during instructs. Scouts considered his curveball the best in the 2016 Draft, but it's more of a solid offering now and has been surpassed by his mid-80s slider, which has gained velocity since he added it in 2020. He has developed more confidence in his sinking changeup, which can become an average offering. Known for using his athleticism and clean delivery to pound the strike zone as an amateur, Groome needs to keep his conditioning in check to locate his pitches where he wants. Boston still sees the ingredients of a quality starter and hopes that his finally getting regular innings in 2021 will help him reach that potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Red Sox thought they were getting a steal when they landed Groome, MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, with the 12th overall choice amid major signability and makeup concerns. He has been a model citizen since signing for $3.65 million, a franchise record for a drafted pitcher, but he also worked just 66 innings in four years as a pro. He lost time to a lat strain and forearm soreness during his first full season, missed all of his second following Tommy John surgery in May 2018 and didn't return to game action until last August. Groome has regained the velocity on his fastball, working at 92-96 mph with some arm-side run. He also shows flashes of what scouts rated the best curveball in the 2016 Draft, a well above-average bender with power and depth, though he's still seeking consistency with it. He developed more confidence in his sinking changeup during his rehab process and it could become a solid third offering. Though he battled his control before he got hurt, Groome has the athleticism and clean delivery to provide consistent strikes. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create angle and plane on his pitches, helping keep them off barrels. Boston still sees a potential frontline starter and hopes he'll finally take steps toward becoming one in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, Groome lasted 12 picks amid severe signability and makeup concerns. Since signing for $3.65 million, a franchise record for a drafted pitcher, Groome was hampered by a lat strain and forearm soreness in his first full pro season and missed his second after having Tommy John surgery last May. Before he blew out his elbow, he was throwing as well as he had as a pro, fueling hopes that he was poised for a breakout year in 2018. After working in the low 90s with his fastball while recording a 5.37 ERA during his first two years in pro ball, Groome sat in the mid-90s with armside run last spring. He also showed why scouts considered his curveball the best in the 2016 Draft, displaying a well above-average bender with power and depth. He has displayed feel for a changeup with some sink, but needs more time to refine it into a reliable third offering. Though Groome has yet to throw consistent strikes as a pro, he has the athleticism and clean delivery to do so. His 6-foot-6 frame helps him create plane and angle with his pitches, making them more difficult to barrel. He won't turn 21 until late in the 2019 season and still has the upside of a frontline starter, but he has done little thus far to demonstrate he can reach that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, Groome slipped to the Red Sox at No. 12 because of questions about his signability and off-field issues. After signing for $3.65 million, a franchise record for a drafted pitcher, he did little in his first two years as a pro. Groome made three short starts in his debut before a lat strain and forearm soreness limited him to 55 1/3 innings in 2017, and he won't pitch at all this year after having Tommy John surgery in May. Groome has spent most of his pro career working in the low 90s with armside run on his fastball, though he hit 97 mph as an amateur and should add more consistent velocity as he gets stronger and healthier. Even if his heater climbs into the mid-90s, it will take a back seat to a curveball with power and depth that was the consensus best breaking ball in his Draft class. He has some feel for a changeup that flashes some sink, but it lacks consistency because he hasn't had much experience throwing it yet. Though Groome averaged 4.9 walks per nine innings in his first two seasons as a pro, his athleticism and clean delivery bode well for his ability to provide more strikes in the future. His 6-foot-6 frame lends itself to durability and creating tough downhill plane on his pitches. Despite his rocky introduction to pro ball, he still has the upside of a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 Though Groome was MLBPipeline.com's top-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, he fell to the Red Sox at No. 12 because of serious worries about his maturity and signability. The Padres reportedly promised Groome a $5 million bonus if he got to them toward the end of the first round, but Boston signed him for $3.65 million, a franchise record for a drafted pitcher. He made three brief starts in his pro debut and missed much of the first half of the 2017 with a lat strain before returning to the mound. Groome works with a 90-95 mph fastball that peaks at 97 with armside run, and he could throw harder as he gets stronger. Nevertheless, his best pitch is a curveball with power and depth that many evaluators believed was the best breaking ball in the 2016 Draft. Though he had little use for a changeup during his amateur career, he has some feel for the pitch and it features some promising sink. Groome's 6-foot-6 frame is built for durability and he uses it to generate good downhill plane on his pitches. His athleticism enables him to repeat his clean mechanics and fill the strike zone. He has the potential to become an ace if his makeup issues don't get in his way, and he could be the best pitcher signed and developed by the Red Sox since Roger Clemens.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The vast majority of players to make it to the big leagues from New Hampshire have been pitchers, though Ryan McKenna has spent time in the Orioles' outfield after being a 2015 fourth-round pick out of high school. Lavigne would like to be the next Granite State prep bat to make it. The Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million as a Competitive Balance Round A pick in 2018, then saw him have a tremendous pro debut that summer. It’s taken him a while to find his footing since then, though he started figuring some things out in 2021 and hit his way to Double-A for the first time in 2022, finishing things off with a solid Arizona Fall League showing. Lavigne entered pro ball with a definite hit-over-power profile, but he got into trouble when he started to try to sell out for power too much. He got back to a better overall approach in 2022, drawing more walks and showing the ability to make more consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. The power is going to come thanks to his natural strength and bat speed and the Rockies were pleased with how he adjusted to the Eastern League after his promotion. It’s possible Lavigne will never be more than a fringy defender at first base, one with a below-average arm, but this part of his game improved as well in 2022. He’s a tireless worker, one who will be at the upper levels of the Rockies' system at age 23 for most of the 2023 season and who still has the potential to develop into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lavigne was a bit of a pop-up prospect from the New Hampshire high school ranks, not exactly a hotbed for professional talent, as the 2018 Draft approached. He landed in the Competitive Balance Round A and the Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million. It seemed like a very shrewd investment based on his pro debut in the Pioneer League (.996 OPS), but he really seemed lost for most of his first full season of pro ball in 2019. A return to Low-A in 2021 was a good move as he righted the ship and earned a bump up a level for the final two months of the season. When he was struggling, Lavigne was getting caught between the hitter he’d always been, one focused on contact with excellent plate discipline, and the one he thought he had to be, a power-hitting first baseman. He sold out for power too much in 2019 and got out of his approach. He’s still learning to catch the ball out front and let his natural strength do its thing. In 2021, he started getting much more comfortable with his swing and was adjusting to velocity more consistently. Lavigne is going to have to hit to keep moving up, as he’s a fringy defender at first base with a below-average arm. He’s grown into more of a leadership role, and the Rockies noticed that after he helped Fresno win a ton of games in Low-A, he led Spokane to the High-A West playoffs as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-handed pitcher Chris Carpenter is the highest-drafted high school player ever from New Hampshire, taken No. 15 overall back in 1993. After popping up to land in the Competitive Balance Round A in 2018, Lavigne became just the second prep player since Carpenter (Jeff Locke, 2006) to get taken in the top two rounds from the Granite State. He made a very strong first impression when he posted a .996 OPS in his pro debut, but struggled with the move to full-season ball in 2019, though the Rockies were pleased with his adjustments in instructional league play in 2020. At his best, Lavigne’s strengths as a left-handed hitter are his knowledge of the strike zone and his ability to drive the ball to all fields. While he drew a lot of walks in 2019, he was too passive at the plate and missed too many good pitches to hit. He also got pull-happy and tried to sell out for power, leading to a spike in strikeouts, instead of just letting his natural strength and bat speed do the work. At instructs, he looked more like the 2018 version than the lost ’19 edition, making more hard contact and using the entire field more consistently. It will be Lavigne’s bat that will carry him to the big leagues, as he’s definitely a first baseman only with a below-average arm. The Rockies are optimistic he righted the ship last fall and hope the reps of a full season will fully get him back on track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: How many high school players drafted out of New Hampshire have made it to the big leagues? As of right now, none, but Lavigne is hoping to change that. Taken in Competitive Balance Round A of the 2018 Draft, Lavigne had a huge pro debut that resulted in an All-Star nod in the Pioneer League. He wasn't able to keep that going with the jump to full-season ball in 2019 as he struggled in the South Atlantic League. There's still a lot to like about Lavigne's offensive upside if he can right the ship. He's big and strong, with bat speed and a ton of raw power coming from his 6-foot-4 frame. While he has shown a propensity for drawing walks, he may have been too patient during his first full season, not aggressively going after good pitches to hit. As a result, he didn't drive the ball as consistently as he is able to and he certainly didn't tap into that power, while seeing his strikeout rate spike as well. Given Lavigne's age and experience, some struggles aren't out of the ordinary, and a rediscovery of the balance between being patient and aggressive will allow him to develop into the all-around hitter the Rockies think he can be. Lavigne is a first baseman only on the defensive end of things, and has work to do there, but he's athletic and should be a capable defender, albeit one with a below-average arm. It will be his bat that will carry him and there's confidence in the organization he'll get that going again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Players from cold-weather Northeast states like New Hampshire aren't supposed to be particularly advanced. There's a reason why a high school hitter from the Granite State has never made it to the big leagues. Lavigne, taken earlier than any prep position player from the state when the Rockies selected him 42nd overall in the 2018 Draft, hopes to be the first and showed that he didn't get the memo about not being prepared for pro ball when he led the Rookie level Pioneer League in on-base percentage and finished third in OPS in his summer debut. Scouts lauded Lavigne's raw power as the Draft approached, seeing his bat speed, strength and 6-foot-4 frame all pointing to future over-the-fence ability, some of which showed up during his first taste of pro ball. There's confidence he'll get to that power because of his advanced approach from the left side of the plate. He works counts, draws a ton of walks and rarely gets fooled, giving him the chance to eventually be a plus hitter with plus power. While his below-average speed does limit him to first base as a pro, he's surprisingly athletic given his size and has the chance to be a solid defender. His bat should profile at the typically run-producing spot as well, with the Rockies excited to see what he can do over a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci celebrated his 16th birthday in 2018 by signing with the Red Sox for $290,000. He weighed just 140 pounds when he turned pro out of Venezuela, but has added at least 25 pounds of muscle five years into his pro career. In his first extended taste of full-season ball last year, he ranked second in the Single-A Carolina League in walks (89) and on-base percentage (.397) at age 19 and hit all six of his homers in the final six weeks. Though Bonaci has slowed as he has gotten stronger and is now a fringy-to-average runner, he remains one of the best infield defenders and has one of the strongest arms in the system. His instincts and quick first step still give him solid range to both sides at shortstop, though he played more second base last season as a teammate of 2021 No. 4 overall pick Marcelo Mayer. He also saw action at third and even played an inning in right field. A switch-hitter, Bonaci has been a different hitter in 2023 after being too passive and making too much soft contact in the past. Stronger and more aggressive than ever, he's turning on more pitches, hitting the ball with more authority and showing 15-homer potential. If he can keep this up, he'll provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci had to wait a week into the 2018 international signing period to turn 16 and become eligible to sign, landing a $290,000 bonus on his birthday. The Venezuelan carried just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he turned pro but since has added 25 pounds while still retaining his quick-twitch athleticism. He made his U.S. debut in 2021 and reinforced his reputation as one of the best infield defenders and strongest arms in Boston's system. A switch-hitter, Bonaci displays good bat-to-ball skills and a disciplined approach from both sides. While he won't be a slugger, he has enough hitting ability and bat speed to provide doubles power with 10-15 homers per year as he gets stronger and turns on more pitches. He understands that his focus is getting on base and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Bonaci has slowed down to more of an average runner as he has started to mature physically, but his instincts help him play quicker than that and he stole 12 bases in as many attempts in 49 games last summer. He still moves well enough to have solid range at shortstop, though he might wind up getting more action at second base if he plays alongside 2021 first-rounder Marcelo Mayer. His double-plus arm strength is his loudest tool and enables him to make any throw needed at any infield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci signed out of Venezuela for $290,000 on his 16th birthday in 2018, carrying just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he turned pro. While he's still not overly physical, he has added 25 pounds and played well on both sides of the ball during his 2019 pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, eliciting trade inquiries from other teams. While the coronavirus pandemic wiped out plans for his U.S. debut last year, he did come to instructional league and impressed there. A switch-hitter, Bonaci has good bat-to-ball skills and regularly produces line drives from both sides of the plate. He won't ever be a power threat, but he has the hitting ability and enough bat speed to provide some gap power as he gets stronger. He understands his limitations at the plate and focuses on employing a disciplined approach to get on base. Bonaci's loudest tool is a double-plus arm that allows him to make any throw needed at shortstop. He's a solid runner who's aggressive on the bases and covers plenty of ground at short, where he also displays smooth actions and soft hands. Advanced for his age offensively and defensively, he comes with a higher floor but lower ceiling than fellow shortstop and 2019 second-rounder Matthew Lugo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci had to wait a week into the 2018 international period to turn pro, receiving a $290,000 bonus on his 16th birthday. The Venezuelan carried just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he signed, and while he's still not very physical, he already has added another 20 pounds. He played well offensively and defensively during his 2019 pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing trade inquiries from other clubs. A switch-hitter, he handles the bat well and makes regular line-drive contact from both sides of the plate. He still needs to get much stronger, and has the bat speed and hitting ability to provide some gap power when he does. He understands he won't be a slugger and instead focuses on maintaining a disciplined approach and getting on base. Bonaci has solid speed and an aggressive nature on the bases. His loudest tool is his plus-plus arm, which allows him to make every throw imaginable from shortstop. His smooth actions and soft hands should allow him to remain at the position, and he's a very reliable defender for his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A college starter with elite stuff, Lacy was the No. 4 overall pick in 2020 out of Texas A&M when the Royals paid him a bonus of $6.67 million. Since then, Lacy’s journey has been extremely bumpy. He was injured in 2021 (shoulder) and ‘22 (back). He pitched just 28 innings in ‘22, and he walked 42 batters. Lacy was able to get back to the mound in the fall, and his offseason revolved around strength and health moving forward. With just his stuff, Lacy has elite starter potential. His fastball is in the upper-90s, his upper-80s slider is plus, and his changeup can be plus with time, diving late away from hitters’ swinging bats. He also has a curveball with depth in his arsenal, although his slider is his preferred breaking pitch. The problem is simply control -- although the fix could be anything but simple. Lacy’s delivery isn’t consistent and falls out of sync quickly. Once he loses the zone, it’s hard for him to find it again. The Royals have their work cut out for them when it comes to developing Lacy. He will be 24 in June and is entering 2023 with just 80 professional innings under his belt. There were times last year when he was pulled out of the starter’s routine and pitched out of the bullpen just to get more reps. But Kansas City will continue to develop Lacy as a starter, depending on health and performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lacy gambled on himself ahead of the 2017 Draft, when he went in the 31st round to Cleveland. It paid off three years later when the Royals took him fourth overall and gave him a $6.67 million signing bonus. His first taste of the pros was bumpy at best. He posted a 5.19 ERA with 79 strikeouts and 41 walks in 52 frames before a barking shoulder ended his regular season in July. He made up for some of the lost time with four abbreviated starts in the Arizona Fall League. Lacy again experienced injury concerns this season at Double-A Northwest -- this time with his back -- and has dealt with serious control woes during the times he has been on the mound. On stuff alone, Lacy shows front-of-the-rotation potential. His fastball can sit in the upper-90s, but the Royals say they may even prefer it when he’s at 92-96 with better command. His best off-speed pitch might depend on the day any evaluator sees him. His upper-80s slider jumped past his curveball to become his preferred breaking pitch during his days as an Aggie, and there were times in the past when he showed promise with a changeup that can dive late away from hitters’ swinging bats. That said, Lacy will be limited if he doesn’t find a way to hit his spots more consistently. As part of his delivery, his head movement can throw his motion out of sync, causing the command to waver. The Royals also believe he tried to prove himself too quickly and overthrew at times to show off what made him such a high pick. Unfortunately in part due to injuries, he hasn’t taken a step forward, especially when it comes to finding the zone, and he may be headed to the bullpen long-term for health and results-based reasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lacy showed the talent to go in the first five rounds as a Texas high schooler in 2017, but his $1 million price tag dropped him to the Indians in the 31st round. He opted to attend Texas A&M, where he dominated for three seasons and became the highest pick in school history. The Royals selected him No. 4 overall in June and signed him for $6,670,000, a franchise record for a drafted pitcher. Lacy was limited by an eye issue while at the Royals’ alternate training site but made a healthy return in time for organization’s fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Lacy attacks hitters with a 92-97 mph fastball while using his 6-foot-4 frame to create angle towards the plate. He uses two distinct breaking balls, with his harder, upper-80s slider surpassing his downer curveball during his junior season and becoming a true plus pitch. He can pile up whiffs with both pitches, as well as a fading changeup that is a consistent plus offering and well-above-average at its best. While there are no questions about the quality of Lacy's pitches, he'll need to improve his command and control to reach his ceiling as a frontline starter. There is some effort in his three-quarters delivery and he can't always harness his overpowering stuff -- a problem he's run into a few times with High-A Quad Cities in 2021. Even without precise location, Lacy could still move quickly as a left-hander who can induce swings and misses with four different offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Norge Luis Vera, who won nine gold medals for Cuba (including one at the 2004 Olympics), Norge defected from the Cuban national team while playing in the independent Canadian American Association during the summer of 2019. The top pitching prospect in the 2020-21 international class, he signed with Chicago for $1.5 million in February 2021. He worked just 54 1/3 innings in his first two pro seasons while dealing with mild shoulder soreness (2021) and a lat strain (2022). It's still unclear what exactly the White Sox have in Vera. He displayed a 91-94 mph fastball while working out for teams before he signed, came out blazing at 95-100 while overmatching younger hitters in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2021, but sat at 90-93 in Double-A at the end of last season. His slider is a sharp mid-80s offering at its best but devolved into an upper-70s slurve late in 2022. Vera's changeup is very much a work in progress, featuring modest life and velocity fluctuating from the upper 70s to the mid-80s. He has a loose arm and an easy delivery that could result in average control, but he also struggles to keep his long limbs in sync and often battles the strike zone. On his best days, he can look like a mid-rotation starter, but he needs a lot more consistency to approach that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Norge Luis Vera was a star pitcher in Cuba's Serie Nacional and in international competition, winning nine gold medals, including one at the 2004 Olympics, as well as silvers at the 2000 and 2008 Olympics. His son Norge was starting to follow in his footsteps before defecting from the Cuban national team while playing in the independent Canadian American Association of Professional Baseball during the summer of 2019. The top pitching prospect in the 2020-21 international class, he signed with the White Sox for $1.5 million and overmatched younger hitters in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League during his pro debut, which didn't begin until August because he had mild shoulder soreness. Vera worked with a 91-94 mph fastball while showcasing himself for big league clubs, but he came out firing at 95-98 and touching 100 during his brief debut. His upper-70s curveball shows some flashes of becoming a plus pitch, and he has some aptitude for throwing a mid-80s changeup with fade. He has utilized a low-80s slider and a mid-80s splitter in the past, but Chicago has had him simplify his pitch mix. Vera had trouble finding the strike zone as an 18-year-old in Cuba's top league but issued just five walks in 19 innings last summer. His DSL stint was a small sample size without much in the way of competition, but he displayed a loose arm and easy delivery that should lead to at least average control. The White Sox hope he can become a mid-rotation starter, and they will get a better idea of his future when he makes his U.S. debut in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Norge Luis Vera starred in Cuba and in international play for many years, including winning a gold medal and two silvers in three Olympics appearances. He never pursued pitching in the Majors but his son will chase that dream after signing with the White Sox for $1.5 million in February. He defected while Cuba's national team was playing in the independent Can-Am League during the summer of 2019 and was considered the top pitcher in the 2020-21 international class. Vera's fastball sat at 91-94 mph during showcases for big league teams, and it has reached 96 in the past with the potential for more velocity to come because he has a lot of projection remaining in his 6-foot-4 frame. Scouts generally rate his upper-70s curveball as his best secondary pitch, though his low-80s slider isn't far behind. He used to throw a splitter but now employs a traditional changeup with some fade. Vera is still refining his delivery and doesn't repeat it consistently, though added strength should help in that regard. As an 18-year-old in Cuba's top league in 2018-19, he walked 32 batters in 54 2/3 innings, so he'll have to prove he can throw strikes. He'll need time to develop and is on roughly the same timetable as the high school righties (Jared Kelley, Matthew Thompson, Andrew Dalquist) whom Chicago has collected in the last two Drafts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sequera, a $750,000 signing out of Venezuela in 2019, was one of the surprises of the Tigers' international crop in 2021, when he posted an .823 OPS and 23 extra-base hits in just 46 games to win MVP honors in the Florida Complex League. His promotion to Single-A Lakeland for 2022 left him a bit more exposed, but he still produced 28 doubles and 19 homers in 116 games and had a solid late-season run before fading in the final week. Sequera steps to the plate looking for hard contact to the pull side, an approach that leads to high chase rates and strikeout totals -- though he dropped his strikeout rate 7 percent from 2021 to 2022. He homered on 20 percent of his fly balls in 2021, an unsustainable performance, but answered in 2022 with more line drives and better pitch recognition, if not results. His athleticism has not translated into speed on the basepaths. He moves well at shortstop and has a knack for highlight plays but could eventually shift over to third if he continues to grow. While Sequera has slugged his way alongside Cristian Santana and Roberto Campos to give the Tigers a trio of intriguing international prospects on their way up the system, Sequera is the least heralded of the group. He might never be a high-average hitter, but if he can maintain power numbers, he could work his way into the Tigers’ infield picture. Advanced pitching at High-A West Michigan could temper his aggressiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Roberto Campos was the headline signing of the Tigers’ 2019 international class, Sequera was rather overlooked as a Venezuelan shortstop who received a $750,000 bonus. Despite missing the Dominican Summer League when it was canceled due to the pandemic, Sequera enjoyed an eye-opening pro debut by winning MVP honors in a Rookie-level Florida Complex League well stocked with prospects. He got extra bases on more than half his 42 hits for the season, including 11 home runs, and finished with a flourish, including four long balls, four doubles and 17 RBIs over his final 12 games. Sequera takes an aggressive pull approach at the plate that leads to high strikeout totals but consistently hard contact when he connects. He has enough bat speed to turn on fastballs with authority on different parts of the plate. He shows some pitch recognition, but like many hitters his age looking for power, will also chase breaking balls out of the zone. He moves well at shortstop for his size, especially on balls up the middle, and has worked to improve his range. He could shift to third as his body fills out. The Tigers once had a pipeline of talent coming out of Venezuela, including Avisail Garcia and Eugenio Suarez, but Sequera has the potential to be the best Tigers prospect from the country since those days. He got his first taste of full-season ball with Single-A Lakeland this summer and has shown pop, but little patience at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially a 19th-round pick by the Royals in 2017, Howell climbed seven rounds in a year by going back to Kirkwood (Iowa) Community College and signed with the Brewers for $210,000. He showed signs of a breakout with 16 homers and 24 steals in 97 games between High-A and Double-A in 2021, and while he didn’t get added to the 40-man when Rule 5-eligible, he did capture the attention of the Padres, who acquired Howell in an early 2022 trade for Victor Caratini. Howell was off to a solid start at Double-A San Antonio, posting a 124 wRC+ in 48 games before suffering a wrist ligament injury that required surgery. Howell’s loudest tool by far is his plus-plus speed that’s always kept him on a prospect map in some way. While he’s never been overly aggressive on the basepaths, his skillset could take advantage of the new rules across the game geared toward encouraging stolen bases. Those wheels serve him well defensively, and it’s just a matter of finding him a regular spot. Both the Brewers and Padres liked giving him chances up the middle at center, second and short, but a below-average arm also meant he got 2022 looks in left field, where he can still cover lots of space. Offensively, Howell shows fast hands and around average raw power at the plate to go with a patient approach that helped him earn a .390 OBP in San Antonio. But his overall approach is heavy to the pull side, and he can struggle with swing-and-miss on breaking stuff. Even though he’s been passed over twice for 40-man spots, he still has a future as a fast and versatile right-handed-hitting option for San Diego.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howell bet on himself by heading back to Kirkwood Community College in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, instead of signing with the Royals as a 2017 19th-rounder, and the move paid off when he slid up seven rounds a year later. He signed with the Brewers for $210,000. Howell’s breakout came in 2021 when he hit .248/.361/.465 with 12 homers and 20 steals in 69 games at High-A Wisconsin. His numbers dipped at Double-A (.235/.318/.429), and the Brewers chose not to protect the Rule 5-eligible speedster with a 40-man spot following the season. Prior to the 2022 campaign, the Padres acquired Howell and Brett Sullivan in exchange for Victor Caratini and cash. Howell’s plus-plus speed has made him a prospect since his early days. He’s an easy threat to steal 20-25 bags in any season and could exceed that if he gets even more aggressive on the basepaths. His overall athleticism is something the Padres enjoy taking advantage of when putting together a roster and lineup. The wheels absolutely play in center field, and if he had to stick in a position, that’s likely his best bet. But San Diego has liked the concept of keeping him moving around all three spots up the middle. The bat will be the big question. Howell shows fast hands at the plate, can take a walk and has at least average raw power. But his strikeout rate bloomed to as high as 39.6 percent at Double-A in 2021, and it will continue to be a problem. Now in his age-23 season, Howell is trending toward late-game pinch-runner/defensive replacement territory, but there still exists time and room for a larger utility role if he can find a way to make more contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis hasn’t been seen a ton in recent years, both at the amateur and pro levels. He underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery in July 2020, which knocked him out for many showcase events that summer. The Cardinals still liked enough of what they saw to select the Colorado high-school product in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft and sign him away from a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus. Another arm issue limited him to six appearances (four starts) in the Florida Complex League last season. The 6-foot-5 right-hander has plenty of size on the bump, so while he touches the mid-90s but sits more in the 89-92 mph range these days, there’s still hope he can add a few ticks of velo as he continues to age and mature. (He’ll just turn 20 before Opening Day this spring.) His curveball has long been his preferred secondary, and while he’ll flash an occasional good-looking changeup, it’s still lagging behind the other two offerings. One of the promising signs of Willis’ 2022 was that he walked only two of the 46 batters he faced in the FCL, notable for someone with so much missed time. The Cardinals took it easy with Tink Hence out of the gate too, then watched him blossom into a Top 100 prospect. Willis lacks Hence’s premium stuff and ceiling, but like the other right-hander, he has ample time to blossom into a quality starting prospect, especially if his pitches take a step forward the more he throws them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery on his right elbow in the middle of July 2020, knocking him out of many showcase events. Almost exactly one year to the day later, he was a Draft pick in his home state of Colorado. The Regis Jesuit High School product showed enough health and stuff in his senior spring to get the Cardinals to select him in the seventh round, and St. Louis coaxed him out of a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus, well above the $211,500 assigned to the slot. The right-hander, who made one appearance in the Florida Complex League, stands out for his size at 6-foot-5, and with some projection remaining, there is hope that he can add even more velocity. As it stands, he’s around 90-94 mph, occasionally touching a smidge or two higher. His curveball looks like a solid secondary already, and he sells a sinking changeup well with his arm speed, though it remains behind the curve. Willis remains a work in progress with his command, perhaps no surprise for such a young pitcher his size. Interestingly, he was the only high school pitcher selected by the Cardinals over last year’s 20-round Draft, so it’s clear they see enough moldable parts in him as he begins his pro career. It wouldn’t be a shock if St. Louis took a conservative approach with him early on, just as they did with Tink Hence in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was in his fourth year on campus, Love was still technically a sophomore when he finally joined the North Carolina rotation in 2021, posting a 3.71 ERA with 129 strikeouts in 102 innings just in time for the Draft. The Cardinals selected the right-hander in the third round and moved him to High-A Peoria for his first full season with rough results (5.73 ERA, 1.52 WHIP, 151 strikeouts in 125 2/3 innings). His 4.04 FIP and .366 BABIP indicated Love may have been better than his traditional stats would indicate, and his relatively high whiff rate helps that case too. Love shows just average velocity in the 91-95 mph range, but he can ramp it up to touch the high 90s on occasion. A lack of movement can make the heater hittable, so it’s notable that his mid-80s slider has developed into more of an above-average offering, one that can dive down and away from lunging right-handers. Love showed the makings of a plus mid-80s fading changeup in college and still displays it in flashes, but he leaned more on the fastball-slider combo, perhaps a big contributor in why lefties crushed him with a .343 average and .916 OPS over his 26 starts. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has a short arm action, and despite limiting walks, his profile leans more toward control than command, making particularly hittable in the Midwest League. It might be worth seeing how high he could crank the fastball in a move to the bullpen soon, and considering Love is entering his age-24 season in 2023, that transition might not be far off unless his stuff ticks up quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Love was technically a fourth-year sophomore at UNC in 2021, having redshirted in 2018 and then again during the COVID-shortened spring of 2020. It was his first season as part of the Tar Heels rotation and he handled the move well, posting a 3.71 ERA with 129 strikeouts in 102 innings. The Cardinals selected him in the third round and signed him slightly below-slot at $600,000 before sending him to seven appearances in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and Low-A Southeast. He fanned 13 of the 27 batters he faced in that short Minor League sample. The right-hander earns the biggest raves for a mid-80s changeup that comes with a heavy fade and could be a weapon against batters from either side. He’s typically around 91-95 mph with his fastball, touching as high as 98, but the heater doesn’t come with much movement. An average mid-80s slider/cutter gives him a third pitch, though it’s yet to flash more than average. General command issues have plagued Love in the past, perhaps because of his short arm action, and his fastball and slider can be particularly hittable when they catch too much of the plate. He didn’t show those concerns early in his pro career, but they will be worth watching as he expands that sample. Already 23 before his first full season, the former Diamond Heel may not have as long a runway to prove he can stick as a starter in the pros. This arsenal is a solid start at least, and the fastball, in particular, could play up with more velocity should he eventually move to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it’s a bit too soon to put a final grade on the Pirates’ efforts during the 2018-19 international signing period, it has netted them a big leaguer already in right-hander Luis Ortiz. Lopez, who signed for $400,000 when the period opened on July 2, has put himself on the prospect map more than anyone other than Ortiz, showing off some raw power in his full-season debut in 2021 and continuing to impact the ball in High-A last year, though a dislocated right knee will sideline him for the 2023 season. Power is the 21-year-old infielder’s calling card and he has as much raw pop as anyone in the system. Greensboro is a good place to hit, and the right-handed-hitting Lopez took advantage, slugging .571 in the friendly confines. He has quick hands at the plate and can go to right-center with authority, but he needs to work on his overall approach to get to better counts after walking in just five percent of his plate appearances in 2022. The Pirates moved Lopez around the infield some to help him maintain his athleticism, but after playing a lot of shortstop early on, he played more third base than anywhere else in 2022. He has the chance to stick there, though given his well-below-average speed, first base might be the best fit for a full-time home. He’s still raw, but the offensive tools are there to profile well at either infield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez didn’t produce much initial hype as a 2017 signing out of Mexico, partly because of his size at 5-foot-8, but he immediately earned some attention in his 2018 debut in the Dominican Summer League. There, Hernandez posted a 2.60 ERA over 55 1/3 innings, striking out 64. That momentum quickly evaporated, though, when Hernandez got rocked in Rookie-level the Gulf Coast League in 2019, posting an 8.02 ERA over 21 1/3 innings. But the up-and-down start to his career continued when he bounced back with Los Mochis in Mexico. That set up Hernandez’s true breakout in ’21. That summer, he climbed from Single-A to Double-A, striking out 108 batters with a 2.74 ERA over 62 1/3 innings. That's when Hernandez’s potentially elite changeup truly began to shine, baffling hitters even when they knew it was coming. He was off to a tremendous start in 2022, with a 1.88 ERA over 24 innings while reaching Triple-A, but his season was slowed by a shoulder issue, and he was hit hard upon his return. The Blue Jays are betting on Hernandez’s upside, though, and after he went untouched in the Rule 5 Draft, he has a chance to make his big league debut as early as 2023. It’s all about the changeup with Hernandez, but can that pitch survive on its own against MLB hitters? That question is why the Blue Jays are working with him to add some bulk and get his fastball up to the 92-93 mph range, which would theoretically keep hitters off the changeup a bit more. He also throws a slider, but that’s more to show hitters a different look than create outs. Hernandez’s changeup is one of the best pitches in the organization, though, and his strikeout numbers prove it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Slider: 40 | Changeup: 65 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Hernandez signed as an unheralded pitching prospect out of Mexico in 2017, but showed some immediate promise in the Dominican Summer League that year with a 2.60 ERA over 55 1/3 innings, striking out 64. Moving to the GCL in ’19, though, he got tagged with an 8.02 ERA over 16 relief appearances and appeared to lose any momentum. Hernandez embraced that challenge, pitching for Los Mochis in the Mexican Winter League before earning a Low-A assignment to open ’21. He climbed all the way to Double-A, posting a combined 2.74 ERA across the three levels with a whopping 108 strikeouts over 62 1/3 innings, reintroducing himself as one of the best young arms in the system. Hernandez’s changeup is one of the best pitches in the organization. Even with opposing hitters on it, they often struggled to make much contact against it at all. His fastball sits in the low-90s, approaching 92 mph, and he uses that to disguise the changeup. He’s also thrown a bit of a slider, but his changeup was so effective in ’21 that he rarely needed to stray from that in big situations. There isn’t much more physical projection for Hernandez’s 5-foot-10 frame, but as a strict reliever now, he makes it work. Developing his breaking ball will be a key to his long-term sustainability, but his changeup has the potential to be special. Veteran Triple-A pitchers who have seen advanced changeups before will be a great test for that pitch, but now that Hernandez has been added to the 40-man roster this past offseason, he could put himself on the doorstep of the Major Leagues by the end of ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Targeting projectable, tooled-up prospects at premium positions, the Mets handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to Dominican amateurs in 2017, signing both shortstop Ronny Mauricio and Hernandez, a center fielder, on July 2. While Mauricio was widely viewed as the better prospect and therefore received a higher bonus, Hernandez signed for $1.5 million after he ranked 19th on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list. Hernandez is a premium athlete with a strong frame who has a high-energy style on the field. An aggressive hitter, he has terrific bat speed and outstanding raw power from the right side of the plate. That pop shows up more on the pull side, but he can drive the ball to all fields and should tap into it more consistently as he refines his approach at the plate. Hernandez's plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball. Hernandez is a center fielder for the time being, but there's the chance he could grow and develop more into the prototypical athletic right-fielder mold down the road. Hernandez's power-speed combination has earned him comparisons to Jose Guillen from some scouts, and the Mets would be thrilled if he become that caliber of player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Mets went shopping in the international amateur market last summer, they aggressively went after, and signed, a pair of exciting Dominican position players. One was shortstop Ronny Mauricio; the other was Hernandez, the toolsy outfielder who ranked 18th on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list and signed for $1.5 million. Compared to former big league outfielder Jose Guillen, Hernandez has a power-speed combination that could be special one day. He is a premium athlete with a strong frame who has a high-energy style on the field. An aggressive hitter, Hernandez has terrific bat speed and outstanding raw power. That pop shows up more on the pull side, but he can drive the ball to all fields and should tap into it more consistently as he refines his approach at the plate. Hernandez's plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball as he begins his pro career in earnest. Hernandez is a center fielder for the time being, but there's the chance he could grow and develop more into the prototypical athletic right-fielder mold down the road. He has a long way to go, taking his first official steps in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson's fastball reached 96 mph when he was a Kentucky high school senior in 2015, but he blew out his elbow shortly before the Draft and required Tommy John surgery. He redshirted in his first year at Louisville before dealing with shoulder and control issues during the next two before signing for an over-slot $200,000 in the 11th round in 2018. After emerging as one of the Cubs' top pitching prospects in 2019, he didn't pitch the next two years because of the pandemic shutdown and shoulder soreness, then returned with intriguing stuff but a lack of strikes last season. Thompson's fastball sat at 94-96 mph and peaked at 98 with some running action when he worked three- to five-inning stints as a starter last year and has hit 100 mph in shorter outings in the past. His low-80s downer curveball wasn't as sharp as it was previously, though it still graded as a plus pitch when he could land it in the strike zone, and he also can break out a tighter mid-80s slider. He doesn't show much trust in his mid-80s changeup with fade and sink, but it generated a 59 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2022. After throwing a lot more strikes as a pro than he had in college, Thompson walked 32 in 57 innings last season. He has bat-missing stuff but doesn't command his fastball well and struggles to control his breaking pitches. Given his track record of inconsistent strikes and health, he might be better served by moving to the bullpen, where he'd have late-inning upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson hit 96 mph as a high school senior in 2015 and could have factored in the early rounds of the Draft, but his elbow gave out in late May and required Tommy John surgery. He redshirted in his first year at Louisville and battled shoulder troubles and the strike zone during the next two before signing for an over-slot $200,000 in the 11th round in 2018. He remained healthy and won two championships in his first two years as a pro, but his 2020 development was limited to a pitching camp during instructional league and he has yet to pitch in 2021 because of shoulder discomfort. Thompson sat at 92-95 mph all season and topped out at 97 with his fastball as a starter in 2019, and he reached triple digits in shorter stints during his pro debut. His curveball features some of the best spin rates in the system while ranging from 82-86 mph and sometimes featuring so much depth he has difficulty landing it in the zone. He has developed an effective changeup since switching to a split-finger grip, though he sometimes falls in love with the pitch too much. The Cubs have helped Thompson clean up the lower half in his delivery and he has displayed improved control as a pro. If he can remain healthy and add some polish, he could become a mid-rotation starter, but he also hadn't progressed past Low-A before turning 25 this July. He might get to Wrigley Field quicker and perhaps become a closer if he moves to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Thompson attracted scouts by reaching 96 mph with his fastball as a Kentucky high school senior in 2015, but he blew out his elbow two weeks before the Draft and had Tommy John surgery. He redshirted during his first year at Louisville, then had sporadic success the next two springs while also dealing with shoulder troubles before signing for $200,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2018. He stayed healthy and won two championships in his first two years as a pro, clinching the low Class A Midwest League title last September with 10 strikeouts over five hitless innings. Thompson topped out at 100 mph with his fastball during his pro debut, then sat at 92-95 mph and repeatedly hit 97 last year while working 103 1/3 innings -- 19 more than he totaled in 2016-18. He has some of the best curveball spin rates in the system, contributing to a power downer that ranges from 82-86 mph and sometimes breaks so much he has trouble landing it for strikes. He has made strides with his changeup after adopting a split-finger grip, though he sometimes falls in love with his offspeed pitch. Though he struggled to find the strike zone in college, Thompson has shown average control since cleaning up the lower half in his delivery and getting more regular work. As he continues to build up innings, he could add a bit more velocity. His first full season as a pro couldn't have gone much better and has the Cubs thinking he could become a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Thompson hit 96 mph with his fastball as a Kentucky high schooler but blew out his elbow two weeks before the 2015 Draft and had Tommy John surgery. He redshirted during his first year at Louisville, then produced uneven results over the next two seasons while also battling some shoulder issues. The Cubs signed him for $200,000 as an 11th-rounder last June on the basis of his upside, which was evident during his pro debut and instructional league. Thompson's fastball velocity fluctuated during his final season at Louisville, dipping to the low 90s at times and topping out at 98 mph at others, and his curveball was similarly inconsistent. As a pro, he worked at 93-98 mph and hit 100 with his heater and spun some well-above-average curves with power and depth. He even showed promise with a changeup he didn't utilize much in college. After battling the strike zone at Louisville, Thompson displayed better control after Chicago cleaned up his lower half in his delivery. He still has a long ways to go to prove he can remain healthy, maintain quality stuff and locate his pitches. While the Cubs will continue to develop him as a starter, he could move quickly as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A pre-signing elbow injury kept Patino from joining the Rangers as initially planned in 2017, but he linked up with the D-backs for $985,000 that October instead. Elbow surgery, short-season assignments, the 2020 pandemic season and a strained calf (2021) kept him from playing a true full Minor League campaign entering 2022. But he finally did, compiling a slash line of .290/.365/.432 with nine homers in 94 games between Single-A and High-A. His 67 steals led the organization and ranked sixth among all Minor Leaguers. With at least plus speed and a muscular 6-foot-1 frame, Patino is one of the best athletes and base stealers in the Arizona system, which is saying something for a group that contains Corbin Carroll and Druw Jones. If you isolate his swing from the right side, there’s some promise there with quick bat speed and above-average raw power that can play to all fields. But Patino, who employs a leg kick in his load, struggles with pitches at the lower end of the zone, especially breaking stuff, which led to some strikeout issues while keeping him essentially an average hitter at both of his A-ball stops in 2022. Still entering just his age-21 season, Patino has used his wheels to lock into a center-field spot in the lower Minors, but many expect he’ll need to move to a corner with more high-ceiling-center types in the org. The D-backs chose not to add him to their 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible last fall because of his distance to the big leagues, and no one selected him. That isn’t a concern for someone this young, but Patino will need to turn his tools into genuine performance soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patino had reportedly agreed to sign with the Rangers for $1.3 million during the 2016-17 International signing period before an elbow injury that required surgery led to a voided deal. The D-backs then signed the Venezuelan teenager for $985,000 in October. Patino offered a glimpse of his potential during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the following year, albeit after requiring a second elbow surgery, then emerged as one of the more exciting prospects in the system during a healthy 2019 season between the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues. He missed out on crucial developmental time when the 2020 season was canceled and then a strained calf limited him to just 38 games in 2021. Patino is one of the best athletes in the Arizona system. The son of a former Venezuelan professional basketball player, Patino flashes every tool, he just needs to refine them. The right-handed hitter has a quick bat that helps him generate raw power to all fields that should start to show up in games as he learns to drive the ball in the air more consistently. He already has a solid approach and projects to hit for both average and power as he adds strength and gains experience. A plus runner, Patino can impact the game with his speed on the bases and in center field, where he has a chance to stick long term. The organization has a lot of center fielders in the pipeline but Patino has an above-average arm that will play in either outfield corner if he is moved. Patino has massive tools and just needed a chance to show them off, as he’s done in 2022 with Single-A Visalia prompting a promotion to High-A Hillsboro. That’s helped raise his floor, and he still has a considerable ceiling that could be met with more and more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patino had reportedly agreed to sign with the Rangers for $1.3 million during the 2016-17 July 2 period before an elbow injury that required surgery led to a voided deal. The D-backs then signed the Venezuelan teenager for $985,000 in October. Patino offered a glimpse of his potential during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the following year, albeit after requiring a second elbow surgery, then emerged as one of the more exciting prospects in the system during a healthy 2019 season between the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues. He, along with all Minor Leagues, missed out on crucial development time when the 2020 season was canceled. He played in just 10 games in 2021 before landing on the injured list with a strained calf; however, there’s some hope he’ll be back in time to get some reps toward the end of the season. Patino is one of the best athletes in the Arizona system. The son of a former Venezuelan professional basketball player, Patino flashes every tool and the key for him is to refine them. The right-handed hitter has a quick bat that helps him generate raw power to all fields that should start to come out as he learns to drive the ball in the air consistently. He already has a solid approach and projects to hit for both average and power as he adds strength and gains experience. A plus runner, Patino can impact the game with his speed on the bases and in center field, where he has a chance to stick long term. The organization has a lot of center fielders in the pipeline but Patino has an above-average arm that will play in either outfield corner if he is moved off center. Patino was not on the team's 60-man roster last year and was unable to return to the U.S. from Venezuela during the summer but he showed his commitment by using the time to get stronger and he hit as often as he could. The organization saw increased power as a result when he reported to Instructional League last fall. The key for Patino now is just getting the reps and experience to develop his massive tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Ranked by MLB Pipeline as the No. 26 international prospect for the 2016-17 July 2 period, Patiño had reportedly agreed to sign with the Rangers for $1.3 million before an elbow injury that required surgery led to a voided deal. Seeing an opportunity to get a player that their international department had been particularly high on, the D-backs signed the Venezuelan teenager for $985,000 in October. Patiño offered a glimpse of his potential during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the following year, albeit after requiring a second elbow surgery, then emerged as one of the more exciting prospects in the system during a healthy 2019 season between the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues. The son of a former Venezuelan professional basketball player, Patiño is as athletic as he is with projectable, with the potential to develop across-the-board tools. The right-handed hitter has a quick bat that helps him generate raw power to all fields that should start to come out as he learns to drive the ball in the air consistently. He already has a solid approach and projects to hit for both average and power as he adds strength and gains experience. A plus runner, Patiño can impact the game with his speed on the bases and in center field, where he has a chance to stick long term. If not, he has an above-average arm that qualifies to play either outfield corner. D-backs officials are quick to note that Patiño made big strides -- as big as any player in the system from 2018 to ’19. They think he’s only scratching the surface of his potential, viewing the Venezuelan teen as a true five-tool talent. Though he’ll need to refine his all-around game as he moves through the Minors, the final product could be an impactful regular who contributes in all facets of the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Patino was the No. 26 prospect on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects and had reportedly agreed to sign with the Rangers for $1.3 million before an arm injury led to a voided deal. The D-backs went on to sign him in October, 2017, and he impressed the organization with his development and overall performance the following summer at age 17 in the Dominican Summer League. The Venezuela native is extremely athletic with a projectable body and the potential to have plus tools across the board. He showed an advanced approach during his pro debut, and he's poised to start impacting the ball more consistently as he adds strength and gains experience. A decent runner, Patino has the potential to be a base-stealer and profiles well in center field, where he has impressed scouts with his defensive actions and range. He has plenty of arm strength for the position and could probably play all three outfield positions if needed. The D-backs have been very impressed with Patino's athleticism and by how quickly he's added size and strength since entering their system. He'll need a lot of time to develop, but the final product could be a tooled-up center fielder who hits for power as well as average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez signed with the Red Sox for $550,000 in April 2018 -- a few weeks before his 17th birthday -- after getting some pro experience with Aguascalientes in the Mexican League. He dominated out of the gate, allowing just one earned run in 23 innings in the Dominican Summer League that year, and he was showing signs of a full-season breakout at Single-A Salem in 2021 (2.03 ERA, 32 strikeouts in 31 innings) when he was dealt to the Nationals in a July deal straight up for Kyle Schwarber. He had been limited by elbow tendinitis at the time of the trade, and after doing some rehab work in the Florida Complex League, he underwent Tommy John surgery in spring 2022, meaning he still hasn’t pitched for a full-season Washington affiliate. Before the elbow issues, the 6-foot right-hander was showing improved velocity to the 92-95 mph range and was touching the high 90s from a high slot. He also sported a mid-80s changeup with good fade, and while lefties still hit him better than righties at Single-A, it should help fend off the splits from getting too extreme. An upper-70s curveball with depth rounded out his arsenal and gave him the three quality pitches needed to start. Command was rarely an issue for Ramirez pre-Tommy John, though that ability to spot the ball well all over the zone will be tested in his return. He has gotten back to playing catch this offseason, and evaluators will be paying attention to how well his repertoire returns when he retakes the mound throughout the summer of his age-22 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez had some pro ball experience with Aguascalientes in the Mexican League when the Red Sox purchased his contract for $550,000 in April 2018, just a month shy of his 17th birthday. He dominated the Dominican Summer League that season, giving up just one earned run in 23 innings, and proceeded to strike out 24 percent of the batters he faced at Class A Short Season Lowell a year later. The pandemic delayed a further breakout, but Ramirez showed promise upon his return in 2021 with a 2.03 ERA, 32 strikeouts and eight walks in 31 innings at Low-A. Elbow tendinitis limited his first-half contributions, and he was traded to the Nationals straight-up for Kyle Schwarber at the Deadline in July. He rehabbed in the Florida Complex League late in 2021 and then unfortunately needed Tommy John surgery in the spring of 2022, forcing him out for the entire season. The 6-foot right-hander throws from a high slot and has seen his velocity pick up since entering the Minors to the point where he sits in the 92-95 mph range, touching the high-90s on occasion. The mid-80s changeup is his best secondary with promising fade, and it should help him fight rough lefty-righty splits. He isn’t afraid of going to an upper-70s curve that could be a solid third offering with its downward break. Ramirez’s best asset remains his command and ability to spot the ball both up and down in the zone. On paper, he has all the pieces to be a solid back-end starter, even if nothing is a true plus pitch yet. But the elbow concerns lower that floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez broke into pro ball in the Mexican League as a 17-year-old before the Red Sox purchased him from Aguascalientes for $550,000 in April 2018. He allowed just one run in 23 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League that summer, then ranked sixth in strikeout rate (9.2 per innings) in the New York-Penn League in 2019, when he was the short-season circuit's youngest qualifier at age 18. He used his pandemic downtime to get stronger last year and opened eyes with improved stuff in instructional league. That carried into 2021, when he had a 2.03 ERA with 32 strikeouts and only eight walks in 31 innings at Low-A Salem before hitting the IL in late June with right elbow tendinitis. The injury wasn’t enough to scare off the Nationals, however, as Washington picked him up at the Trade Deadline in a swap for Kyle Schwarber. Ramirez works the top and bottom of the strike zone with four-seam and two-seam fastballs, and his velocity jumped from 91-94 in 2019 to averaging 93.5 mph and topping out at 96 more frequently in shorter stints at instructs. He has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. When he stays on top of his upper-70s curveball, it features nice depth and gives him a solid third offering. The most advanced young pitcher in the Boston system at the time of the trade, Ramirez repeats his clean delivery easily and pounds the strike zone. He has the confidence to throw any pitch in any count, and it's growing as his stuff continues to improve. He has a high floor and the possibility of winding up with a solid fastball and curve to go with a plus changeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez pitched in the Mexican League at age 17 before the Red Sox purchased him from Aguascalientes for $550,000 in April 2018. He allowed just one run in 23 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League afterward, then skipped a level and thrived as the youngest ERA qualifier (age 18) in the short-season New York-Penn League last year. Using both two- and four-seamers to work the top and bottom of the strike zone, Ramirez sits at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96 mph with his fastballs. He gets downer action on his upper-70s curveball when he stays on top of it, and he throws hitters off balance with a mid-80s changeup with some fade and sink. Ramirez has precocious feel for pitching that stands out more than his stuff. He has a clean delivery, repeats it easily, pounds the strike zone and possesses the confidence to throw any pitch in any count. Though he doesn't have much projection remaining in his 6-foot frame, he might have three solid pitches if he can find a little more power and consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Barlovento, Venezuela, in 2019 for $775,000, Machado was one of the biggest mysteries in the system entering the 2022 season after appearing in just one professional game. Machado was part of the Venezuelan group who stayed in Florida through the pandemic, but his Rookie-level Florida Complex League debut was cut short by a hamstring injury. In ’22, Machado appeared in 90 games with Single-A Dunedin, where he hit .263 with a .687 OPS. A full, healthy season made ’22 a success to begin with, but the Blue Jays were also encouraged by some of Machado’s physical maturation in their program. As draftees flooded into Dunedin, he raised his game and continued to work through scrappy at-bats, showing a little more pop than his one home run suggests. Machado is a switch-hitter, but put up far better numbers batting left-handed (.300) than right-handed (.146), which will be important to monitor in 2023 and beyond. Machado will continue to split his time between shortstop and second base with a chance to stick at short long term. Part of his offensive game will need to make a jump, whether that be in the power or on-base department, but his defensive fundamentals give Machado a good base to work from. A sample of 91 pro games is very shallow to draw from, though, so Machado could still have plenty of development in front of him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed alongside Rikelbin De Castro in ’19 for $775,000, the switch-hitting Machado remains one of the more tantalizing mysteries in the Blue Jays’ system. Machado was part of the Venezuelan group that stayed in Florida throughout the COVID shutdown, and when he finally had an opportunity to make his pro debut in ’21 in the Florida Complex League, that lasted just one plate appearance -- a single -- before a hamstring injury cut his season short. With just one trip to the plate as a pro entering ’22, Machado needs reps and lots of them. Without much power to speak of, Machado will be more of a spray hitter, but he comes with the potential to make contact consistently enough for that to work with his broader profile. A solid athlete, the Blue Jays like how Machado looks defensively and trust he’ll stay at shortstop long-term with a quality throwing arm. That defensive ability will be valuable to supporting Machado’s floor while his offence develops. We’ll finally see some longer stretches of Machado in ’22, giving him one of the widest ranges of outcomes in Toronto’s system. Hitting for average and working walks will be key to his rise, given the lack of power, but Machado’s glove is what has the organization excited about a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Machado was signed in 2019 alongside Rikelvin De Castro, and while Machado received the smaller bonus of the two at $775,000, the switch-hitter already profiles as a better bat. Machado was part of the Venezuelan group who stayed in Florida throughout the shutdown and found creative ways to stay physically engaged and work on his game at the hotel. There will be immediate appeal in an athletic, switch-hitting shortstop, and Machado has some legitimate offensive upside from both sides of the plate. Both swings are quick and compact, and there could be some more power for Machado to grow into as his strength naturally develops. Machado will be given every opportunity to stick at shortstop long term, which the Blue Jays believe he’s fully capable of. His throwing arm will be his strongest tool defensively, but the Blue Jays like his defensive actions, too. There’s still plenty of development ahead for the teenager when he gets into Minor League games, but Machado could start to take some serious strides up the board as he puts together his all-around tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays shelled out nearly $2 million to land a pair of promising 16-year-old shortstops at the outset of the 2019 international period, signing Rikelvin De Castro ($1.2 million) and Machado ($775,000) on back-to-back days. While Castro is viewed as the better defender and more likely of the two players to remain at shortstop, Machado, a switch-hitter from Venezuela, could end up as the better hitter. An advanced approach for his age gives Machado a solid foundation as a hitter, and he makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate with a short swing that has little wasted energy. His bat speed and overall ability to impact the baseball should improve as he begins to grow into his wiry-athletic frame, and there are some scouts who believe Machado will develop double-digit home run power. He’s a dynamic athlete on both sides of the ball with average speed that plays up once he’s underway. Machado’s athleticism, tools and feel for the game will give him a chance to stick at shortstop, where he profiles as an above-average defender with range, dependable hands and an above-average arm. Machado’s ceiling is still coming into view and he’ll need years to develop his game in the Minors, but the final product could be an everyday player who contributes in all facets of the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitching in a stacked rotation at Cypress Ranch HS (Texas) with future supplemental first-rounders J.J. Goss (Rays, 2019) and Ty Madden (Tigers, 2021), Thompson flashed first-round stuff but lacked consistency. After the White Sox signed him for an over-slot $2.1 million as a second-rounder in 2019, he worked just two innings in his first two years because of the pandemic. His development has been up and down in full-season ball since, though he did make strides with his control in 2022. Thompson's best pitch is a 78-82 mph curveball that has quality depth and grades as a plus pitch when he stays on top of it. His fastball parks at 92-95 mph and touches 97 with riding action at times, though it gets smacked around when he doesn't command it well. He has added a low-80s slider that can get slurvy but shows signs of becoming an average or better offering, but he needs to spend more time refining a changeup with modest fade that's too firm in the upper 80s. One of the best athletes in the Chicago's system, Thompson did a better job of repeating his delivery last year, cutting his walk rate to 3.3 per nine innings after averaging 4.6 in 2021. He still gets offline to the plate, costing him life and command with his pitches. While he needs more consistency, he still has the best chance of becoming a starter among the high school righties (Jared Kelley, Andrew Dalquist) the White Sox have invested heavily in in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a loaded rotation at Cypress (Texas) Ranch High with future supplemental first-rounders J.J. Goss (Rays, 2019) and Ty Madden (Tigers, 2021), Thompson flashed first-round stuff on the showcase circuit but was inconsistent as a senior in 2019. He went to the White Sox in the second round and signed for an over-slot $2.1 million, then worked just two innings in his first two years as a pro because of the pandemic shutdown. He posted a 5.90 ERA in Low-A last season, though he pitched better in the second half after missing a month with a hip flexor strain. Thompson usually operates at 92-94 mph with his fastball and can reach 97 with good carry, though it gets hit when he doesn't locate it well. He imparts power and depth on his 78-82 mph curveball when he stays on top of it but needs to do so on a more consistent basis. He's working on adding a harder slider to give him an offering with more horizontal action, as well as refining a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink. While Thompson is one of the best athletes in Chicago's system, his delivery has some stiffness. He doesn't repeat it well, losing his tempo and getting offline from the plate, which harms his control and command. The White Sox hope the strides he made down the stretch last year are a sign that he's on the path to becoming a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson flashed first-round stuff on the prep showcase circuit in 2018 but he wasn't as consistent the following spring as a senior. Fellow Cypress (Texas) Ranch High right-hander J.J. Goss surpassed him and went to the Rays in the supplemental first round of the 2019 Draft, while Thompson fell to the White Sox in the second. He has pitched just two pro innings in two years after signing for an over-slot $2.1 million, though he did participate at Chicago's alternate training site and instructional league program last year. The White Sox consider Thompson the best athlete in their system and see him as having the upside for at least a plus fastball and curveball on a consistent basis. The velocity on his four-seam fastball fluctuates at times but can sit at 91-94 mph and touch 96, with room for growth as he adds strength to his projectable frame. His curve needs more consistency but features quality power and depth when he stays on top of it. Thompson is in the early stages of refining a changeup that shows some encouraging deception and sink. He's learning to repeat his delivery and stay aligned to the plate, and his athleticism should help him do that as well as find the strike zone and stay healthy. He does a good job of using his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create steep downhill plane on his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
