mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson looked like a future first-round pick when he hit 95 mph at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship as a rising junior in October 2017, but his stock dipped slightly during an inconsistent senior season. He got surpassed on his own Cypress (Texas) Ranch High team last spring by fellow right-hander J.J. Goss, who went to the Rays in the supplemental first round before the White Sox grabbed Thompson in the second. He pitched just two innings in his pro debut after signing for $2.1 million. Thompson had one of the quickest arms in the 2019 Draft class, helping him sit in the low 90s and reach 96 mph with his fastball. His four-seamer is fairly straight, though he compensates by using his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create steep downhill plane, and there could be more velocity in his projectable frame. He also flashes a plus curveball, though it was inconsistent last spring and turns into a flatter slider when he doesn't stay on top of it. Though Thompson's changeup is in its nascent stages, it does have some promising deception and sink and should become at least an average third pitch. His athletic delivery bodes well for his ability to throw strikes and stay healthy. He has the ceiling of a No. 3 starter but will need time to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez played with Luis Robert on a Cuban 18-and-under team and debuted in the island's top domestic league at age 18, playing three seasons before defecting in 2018. Cleared to sign in February 2019, he chose the path several Cubans have and waited until the subsequent signing period so the White Sox could find more bonus pool cash for him. Signed for $2.5 million in July 2019, he didn't make his U.S. debut until 2021 at age 24 and spent most of last season in Triple-A. Though Sanchez has a compact right-handed stroke and some of the system's best bat-to-ball skills, he prioritizes making contact at the expense of everything else. He puts the bat on the ball almost too easily, producing a lot of harmless ground balls (54 percent of his contact last season) and drawing few walks. His approach also results in precious little power and almost all of his offensive value comes from his ability to hit for average. Sanchez's smooth infield actions help him get the most out of his fringy speed and average arm. He's a solid defender at second base and capable at shortstop and third, which will help him in his projected role as a utilityman. He's more reliable than flashy with his glove.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez teamed with Luis Robert on a Cuban 18-and-under squad and debuted in the island's Serie Nacional at age 18, playing three seasons before defecting in 2018. MLB declared him a free agent in February 2019, but like many Cubans have done, he wanted to join with the White Sox and waited until the next signing period so they could find more bonus pool money for him. Signed for $2.5 million in July 2019, he didn't make his U.S. debut until age 24 in 2021, when he batted .308/.352/.419 overall and hit .343 following a late-July promotion to Double-A. Employing a contact-hitting approach with a compact right-handed stroke, Sanchez shows the ability to catch up to most fastballs and makes nice two-strike adjustments. He has enough strength and bat speed for average raw power, though he rarely launches balls in the air and has little usable pop. His bat-to-ball skills cut into his walk totals, so much of his offensive value will come from his batting average. Sanchez has smooth infield actions but his fringy speed and average arm limit him somewhat defensively. He's a capable shortstop but spent most of 2021 at second base in deference to Romy Gonzalez and Lenyn Sosa. An average defender at second, Sanchez also can handle third base and profiles more as a utilityman than a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez debuted in Cuba's top league at age 18 and played three seasons before defecting in 2018. MLB made him a free agent in February 2019, but he waited until the opening of the 2019-20 signing period to accept a $2.5 million bonus from the White Sox. He spent his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and was limited to instructional league in 2020, so he turned 24 without having been challenged in pro ball. Best known for his quality defense at shortstop, Sanchez didn't stay on top of his conditioning during the pandemic layoff and displayed less than his usual plus range at instructs. He actually has spent more time at second base in 2021 in deference to shortstop prospects Lenyn Sosa and Romy Gonzalez. With smooth actions, quick feet and hands and a solid arm, he's capable of playing anywhere in the infield if he winds up in a utility role. A right-handed hitter, Sanchez showed good bat-to-ball skills but didn't make much offensive impact in Cuba, where he played with Luis Robert on a national 18-and-under team. He doesn't lack strength but makes a lot of soft contact and probably will max out at 10-12 homers per season. His main focus will be getting on base to take advantage of his solid to plus speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez debuted in Cuba's top league at age 18 and played three seasons before defecting in 2018. Though MLB cleared him as a free agent in February 2019, he waited until the beginning of the 2019-20 signing period to turn pro and accepted a $2.5 million bonus from the White Sox. Though he hit .297/.386/.441 last summer, at 22 he was ancient by Rookie-level Dominican Summer League standards, so how he performs in full-season ball this year will shed more light on the type of player he can become. A teammate of Luis Robert on Cuba's 18-and-under team, Sanchez plays quality defense at shortstop. He's capable of making all the plays thanks to his smooth actions, quick feet and hands and solid arm strength. Some scouts think he could handle playing shortstop in Chicago right now. There's less conviction in Sanchez's bat. A right-handed hitter, he showed promising bat-to-ball skills but didn't make much offensive impact in Cuba, and he didn't drive the ball consistently against younger competition in the DSL. He needs to develop just enough pop to make pitchers respect him so he can get on base and utilize his solid to plus speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners coveted Polcovich enough out of Oklahoma State that they used one of their five picks in the shortened 2020 Draft on him. The immediate transition to pro ball, however, was not seamless, especially after he climbed in the second half of ‘21 to Double-A Arkansas, where he slashed .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) and struggled to establish any confidence. But his ‘22 at the affiliate was a big turnaround. He raised his OPS by nearly 300 points and did so with a healthy sample size of 524 plate appearances. He also continued to flash his speed and has drawn praise as one of the best baserunners in the system. He also can play all over the infield and outfield, making him that much more valuable in the eyes of a club that puts a huge premium on defensive versatility all the way up to the Majors. Based on his trajectory, with a few hiccups followed by promise, Polcovich has drawn comparisons to Sam Haggerty. The big thing with him to continue climbing will be showing that his turnaround in ‘22 was legitimate and that he can produce consistently with the bat. The switch-hitter bats more naturally righty, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. And even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A promotion to Double-A Arkansas in 2021 was an eye-opening one for the middle infielder, as Polcovich hit .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) in 149 plate appearances. The Mariners believe their third-round pick from ‘20 still had a solid process, approach and good pitch recognition, but wasn’t seeing results. As such, it took a mental toll that led him to pressing more. The club has chalked up those Double-A struggles to bad luck. He was much better at High A Everett earlier last season with a .980 OPS. Polcovich has a shorter stature at 5-foot-10, and while his tools aren’t incredibly loud, he profiles with solid on-base potential and he’s a switch-hitter. Though he bats more naturally from the right side, he’s been able to make enough contact from the left to stick with both moving forward. The power profile isn’t exactly strong, but he does have some extra-base potential within the gaps rather than over the wall. He’s also described as a solid runner and smart base runner. Defensively, Polcovich came up as a second baseman at Oklahoma State, but the Mariners have used him all over, including shortstop and center field. He’s dependable with an average arm yet doesn’t necessarily stand out at one spot over the others. The Mariners covet that kind of versatility, which could make him a valued commodity if his bat catches up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a former 10-year pro ball player, Polcovich spent one year at the University of Kentucky then moved on to Northwest Florida State College for two seasons and Oklahoma State after that. He began to catch scouts’ eyes after hitting .305 in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, and he was batting .344/.494/.578 with 19 walks and eight steals in 18 games for the Cowboys last spring before the shutdown, which was enough for the Mariners to nab him in the third round and sign him for a below-slot bonus of $575,000. The switch-hitting Polcovich bats more naturally from the right side, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. Overall, he has a solid approach, and even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential, though his power is more gap-to-gap than over-the-wall at this point. He runs well and is a smart baserunner. At various stops, Polcovich has played a number of positions defensively, including second and third at OSU and center field on the Cape. He’s dependable at a number of spots with an average arm, but he doesn’t necessarily profile at one defensive home. That could lead to a future similar to his dad’s, albeit with a bit more thump in his bat. He made a strong first impression on the Mariners during his time at the alternate training site last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies like Williams and his upside so much, they acquired him twice. They first took the Colorado high schooler out of their own back yard in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft, signing him for $450,000. He hadn’t thrown a competitive pitch when the Rockies sent him to the Reds that offseason as part of the deal that netted them Robert Stephenson. He was making his pro debut in the Reds system when he came back to the Rockies in the Mychal Givens trade close to the 2021 deadline. He took a developmental step forward in 2022 across two levels of A-ball before finishing with a 12-strikeout exclamation point in Double-A. Still only 21 for all of the 2023 season, Williams’ projection is looking like it’s starting to turn into performance. The Rockies think he has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix, with all of them being at least average. He’s commanding his low-90s fastball better to both halves down in the zone and showing he can pitch up with it. He’s also learned that he can’t just blow away hitters with his heater and is mixing his pitches much more effectively. He’s always been able to spin a breaking ball with an outstanding power curve and there are makings of a distinct slider. He also started showing conviction in throwing his changeup more consistently. With his delivery more under control, Williams is developing beyond just a thrower, learning to execute his pitches. The next step will be command within the zone but his improved stuff, pitchability and added physical maturity have led to an up arrow next to his name.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams was the top high school player in Colorado for the 2020 Draft, though no one got to see him pitch leading up to it because the coronavirus pandemic shut down the season before it began there. So teams interested in the big, physical right-hander had to mostly go on what they saw over the summer. The Rockies saw enough to take the prepster out of their own backyard in the fourth round of the shortened Draft, and they signed him for a below-slot bonus of $450,000. They never got to see him throw a competitive pitch, as they sent him to the Reds, whose scout team Williams played on in the Area Code Games in the summer of 2019, as part of the deal that saw Jeff Hoffman join the Reds and Robert Stephenson head to the Rockies. Williams has all of the elements of a future big leaguer, but they’re a bit raw and undeveloped at this point in time. The Rockies saw a fastball in the 92-95 mph range coming from his 6-foot-3 frame. His secondary stuff is all inconsistent, but he has a good feel to spin his breaking ball with the chance to have a plus curve down the road. He had not thrown his changeup much in high school, so that will be an area of focus developmentally for him as he starts his pro career. Big and physical, Williams is a solid athlete who should be able to eventually command the baseball well enough to give him the chance to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter. Patience will be key as he’s not logged many innings on the mound, knowing that there have been pitching success stories out of the Colorado high school ranks – Roy Halladay, Kevin Gausman and Kyle Freeland as the prime examples – but that Gausman and Freeland went on to college and it took a while for Halladay to figure it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMahon could have been a pretty high Draft pick out of high school in 2017, but he ended up being just a late-round flier by the Braves because of his commitment to Miami. After missing most of his freshman year with a knee injury, he pitched in the Hurricanes' weekend rotation over the next two years, with his feel enough for the Rockies to take him in the second round of the shortened 2020 Draft. He had a solid first full season in High-A but wasn’t able to build on it in 2022 as a lat strain kept him off the mound for much of the year. There’s confidence that McMahon will bounce back healthy and return to his right-handed pitchability ways. He can get swings-and-misses with all of his offerings, starting with a low-90s fastball that has solid action down in the zone. His changeup is his best secondary offering, with good arm speed and deception, and his slider was tightening up from the slurve he featured in college. While he doesn’t have a true plus out pitch, he doesn’t hunt strikeouts and focuses more on executing pitches. He is willing to throw any of his pitches with two strikes to put hitters away. McMahon’s ability to fill up the zone can hurt him at times because hitters know strikes are coming and he has been too predictable with his pitch usage. Using his changeup more against right-handed hitters, pitching backward occasionally and setting up hitters better in general will help him reach his high floor as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMahon went from the Philadelphia high school ranks into the University of Miami rotation, though a knee injury kept him out for the bulk of his freshman year in 2018. He pitched pretty well in the weekend rotation as a sophomore and showed his solid feel for pitching in the shortened 2020 season enough to generate some first-round looks. He landed in the second round to the Rockies, threw well at instructs that fall and had a solid first full season in High-A in 2021. His progress was delayed in 2022 as a lat strain kept him from throwing a competitive pitch until late July. The right-hander has a solid three-pitch mix with a very good idea of how to use his entire repertoire. He pitches to both sides of the plate very well, starting with a fastball that sits low-90s and touches a bit higher, thrown with good late action down in the zone. His changeup is an above-average pitch that he throws with good deception and arm speed, missing bats and getting ground-ball contact with it. His breaking ball can be a bit of a hybrid/slurve type of a pitch, but it’s trending in the right direction towards more of a tight slider. While McMahon can throw strikes and can keep hitters off-balance by mixing his pitches and tunneling his secondary stuff off his fastball well, he still needs to work on his command within the zone. His fastball can flatten out at times, causing him to get hit, but he has the pitching IQ to reach his ceiling as a No. 4-type tarter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A multi-sport standout in high school out of Philadelphia, McMahon was a solid pitching prospect in 2017, but slid deep into Day 3 of the Draft because of his commitment to the University of Miami. After missing a large chunk of his freshman year with a knee injury and serving as the Saturday starter as a sophomore, McMahon pitched very well for Team USA and continued to throw well during the shortened 2020 season. While he did get some first-round buzz, he landed near the top of the second round, where the Rockies went a bit over slot to sign him before watching him throw very well at instructs. During his time in instructional league play, McMahon really stood out with his pitchability, especially his fastball command. He can run it up to the mid-90s with late action when he keeps it down and he’s shown the ability to reach back for a bit more when needed. While he has good feel for spin, his breaking ball can be a bit of a slurvy hybrid, but should be tight slider with good late three-quarters tilt to it, a potential plus pitch. His changeup gets swings and misses as well as generates weak contact. In addition to the breaking ball consistency, he’ll have to continue to work on shortening his deeper arm action to help keep his stuff from flattening out. Thanks to his athleticism and feel for pitching, he has a very good chance to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palmer helped his Draft stock with a strong showing as a reliever in the Cape Cod League in 2019, and he carried that back to college and into the Jacksonville rotation. The Blue Jays liked him as a starter, though, and selected him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. Palmer’s advanced pitches and deep arsenal helped him to a 3.00 ERA in 2021 with Single-A Dunedin over 63 innings, and he was off to another strong start in 2022, carrying a 3.90 ERA between High-A and Double-A. Unfortunately, Palmer underwent Tommy John surgery late in the season and is expected to miss most or all of the 2023 campaign. It’s a difficult blow for the right-hander, who has one of the most unique mixes of pitches in the organization, creating movement in every direction. That’s helped Palmer post a strikeout rate of 11.6 batters per nine innings in the Minor Leagues, and that should continue to serve him well following his recovery. In a perfect world, Palmer could recover in time to be an Arizona Fall League candidate, which would enable him to see some competitive innings in ’23 and carry momentum into 2024. By then, he should slide right back into the upper Minors and offer the Blue Jays some nice starting depth with the “bulldog” presence on the mound he’s become known for. The surgery is a tough setback, but Palmer remains a unique talent to monitor long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palmer gained momentum with a strong showing in the Cape Cod League as a reliever, posting a 1.45 ERA over 18 2/3 innings before enjoying a strong start to this junior season at Jacksonville in the rotation. The Blue Jays selected him in the third round of the 2020 Draft, signing him to a slightly-above-slot bonus. His pro debut with Low-A Dunedin saw Palmer struggle with control early, but he turned a corner midseason and pitched two seven-inning no hitters over his final five starts of the season, ending with a 3.00 ERA and 83 strikeouts over 63 innings. That successful first step in the Minor Leagues came thanks to one of the most unique and diverse pitch-movement profiles in the organization. Using his deep arsenal, Palmer can comfortably work all quadrants of the zone and uses an above-average changeup to keep hitters off balance from either side. With a fastball that sits in the 92-93 mph range and reaches a touch higher, Palmer also has a slider that's still ahead of his curveball with some good depth. You’ll hear the “bulldog” tag applied to Palmer often, and while his thick build on a 6-foot-1 frame is unique in the organization, the Blue Jays were pleased with how he improved his physicality towards the end of ’21 and through the offseason. In ’22, Palmer’s first task will be proving that his strong ending to ’21 was the start of something. He still walked 42 batters over those 63 innings, which will need to improve regardless of his role. There’s obviously bullpen potential down the line if the Blue Jays choose to explore that, but he’ll be given more opportunities to start for now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jacksonville University has produced a lot of Draft talent over the past several years, including back-to-back third-round picks Michael Baumann (2017) and Austin Hays (2016), both with the Baltimore Orioles. While Palmer wasn’t as scouted as any of his Dolphins predecessors, his arm strength and strong start to his junior season, not to mention a successful turn as a reliever last summer on the Cape, still earned him a third-round selection by the Blue Jays, along with an above-slot signing bonus. At 6-foot-1, 230 pounds, Palmer is a unique build in a Blue Jays system that’s filled with taller right-handers. Palmer makes up for that with great intangibles and competitiveness, described by some as a “bulldog” on the mound. With a fastball that sits in the 92-95 mph range, Palmer uses his strength to maintain that into starts. It’s a heavy ball with sinking action coming from a relatively low slot, which helps keep Palmer away from hard contact. His split changeup is a strong pitch in the 82-84 mph range while his slider has some good depth to it. Palmer’s curveball is still developing as a fourth pitch. Opening at Low-A Dunedin in his first season, Palmer showed real control concerns and was averaging a walk an inning as late as late July before turning things around in that department in the second half. His swing-and-miss rate took off around the same time, confirming what made Palmer such a promising Draft pick in the first place. It’ll take a longer road for the right-hander to prove the control issues are truly behind him. Until he shows more consistency, questions about his ability to start hold down the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $195,000 out of Mexico in 2019, Melendez made a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League later that year and opened eyes by coming back from the pandemic layoff to strike out 38 in 18 1/3 Single-A innings to open 2021. He finished that season as a 19-year-old in Double-A, making him the youngest pitcher in the Texas League, and he retained that status when he returned to Corpus Christi for all of 2022. He battled his control and command throughout last season and has missed most of 2023 with elbow issues. Melendez has gained about 5 mph in fastball velocity since turning pro, now dealing at 92-95 mph and touching 98. His 5-foot-8 build and over-the-top delivery created an unusual look for hitters, and the shape and carry on his heater resulted in a 31 percent swing-and-miss rate on his heater in 2022. His 77-80 mph curveball and tight 82-85 mph slider had shown signs of becoming solid pitches in the past, but he didn't throw them for strikes or miss bats with them last year. Melendez's fading low-80s changeup was actually his second-most effective offering in 2022, though he doesn't trust it much. While his delivery provides a lot of deception, he also struggles to keep it in sync and doesn't have a track record of throwing strikes. With his size and control issues, he's more multi-inning reliever than starter, but his fastball is a true weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Mexico for $195,000 in 2019, Melendez made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After his development was limited to instructional league in 2020, he opened last season by dominating Low-A hitters with a 0.84 ERA and 38 strikeouts in 18 1/3 innings. Just 19 years old, he earned a promotion to High-A in June and another to Double-A in September. Melendez has added about 5 mph to his fastball since signing and now operates at 92-95, though the shape and carry on his heater are more notable than its velocity. He backs it up with a pair of solid breaking pitches, with his 78-80 mph curveball slightly more effective than his 83-85 mph slider. His sinking changeup is still a work in progress but he shows some encouraging feel for it. Melendez has an advanced ability to sequence his four-pitch mix and the deception in his delivery helps his stuff play up. He might be more of a multi-inning reliever than a starter, however. He's shorter than desired at 5-foot-8, he doesn't have a track record of filling the strike zone and he has to prove his stuff will hold up over a full pro season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top pitching prospects in the 2020-21 international class -- and also one of the youngest -- Pinto didn’t debut until ‘22 due to pandemic-impacted issues in his first year and minor injuries in his second. The Mariners instead instilled a conditioning-heavy plan for the Venezuela native, which he ate up. And now that he’s better built up his body, the focus transitions to the Mariners’ mantra of 'Dominate The Zone.' Pinto’s numbers weren’t stellar in his first pro year, but much of that was marred by Jekyll and Hyde performances -- he would dominate for 1-2 innings, then lose it. Yet everything from the naked eye to the under-the-hood numbers suggest that he possesses above-average fastball velocity that can continue to grow. The true out pitch is his curveball, which generates comical swings and takes from his three-quarters arm slot. There’s good bend and depth, suggesting it can be a big league offering. He does a solid job of repeating his delivery, which also bodes well. For all these reasons, the lean and loose Pinto will probably require more patience because the delivery isn’t quite there yet. But if he can transform the dominant flashes into consistency, there could be big upside -- because the pure stuff is certainly there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top pitching prospect signed in the 2020-21 international signing period and basically the youngest, Pinto has yet to pitch in a professional game, mostly due to the limited baseball and physical resources where he was stationed during the peak of the pandemic shutdown. So Seattle instead had the 17-year-old focus exclusively on conditioning and getting in better shape last season. Scouts estimate Pinto is up to 6-foot-4 and really lean and projectable, with an incredibly loose delivery. He’s now hitting the low 90s with plenty of opportunity to keep growing into velocity. His best pitch is a curveball, a tight breaking ball with good depth that has a chance to be at least a plus pitch in the future. He already has solid feel for a changeup. Pinto is long and loose and does a nice job of repeating his delivery, which could eventually lead to better-than-average control and command. There’s a long way to go here, but with patience could come a very exciting left-handed starting pitching prospect -- especially since he’ll pitch a full season in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Things were looking up for Valerio when he went from a $10,000 signing with the Mets in March 2018 to a piece in the Keon Broxton trade with the Brewers in January 2019 to an impressive full-season performer in 2021. Last season, however, changed that narrative when Valerio found himself challenged in the upper Minors for the first time. The Dominican Republic native slashed just .228/.313/.357 with 12 homers in 113 games at Double-A Biloxi. Even with that down year, Valerio still exhibits signs of controlling the zone well. His 16.7 percent K rate may have been a career high, but it was still well above-average by Southern League standards. A 10 percent walk rate was solid too and roughly in line with Valerio’s career marks. He’s added some lift to his swing in the last two years, and while that’s increased his homer output to 23 in that span, a relative lack of overall strength led to some weak fly balls and a .249 BABIP that dulled his whole offensive performance. Valerio needs to hit because he’s yet to lock in as an average defender anywhere. His below-average arm has made second base his primary position, and the Brewers started mixing in more left field last year. Average speed doesn’t help matters at either spot, though he is more aggressive on the basepaths than his raw wheels would indicate with 61 steals on his resume since 2021. Finding the perfect marriage between keeping his K/BB ratio in check and perhaps getting back to what he’s best at with spraying line drives could put Valerio back on track in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valerio signed with the Mets at 17 years old in March 2018 and immediately took to the pro game with a .319 average and 6.9 percent K rate in that year’s Dominican Summer League. The 5-foot-7 infielder caught the attention of Brewers scouts, and Milwaukee acquired the then-teen in a January 2019 trade for Keon Broxton. After a solid stateside debut in 2019, Valerio’s true breakout came at Low-A Carolina last season as he hit .314/.430/.469 with more walks (54) than strikeouts (49) in 85 games. A late-season promotion to High-A Wisconsin saw more power from the 20-year-old. One thing is abundantly clear in Valerio’s career -- he can hit. His career .302 average entering 2022 speaks to that, and his career 113/120 K/BB ratio highlights his plate discipline and bat-to-ball skills. It’s decent power for a player sized at just 5-foot-7, 165 pounds, given how much hard contact he already makes, but his 11 homers in 2021 likely will be his ceiling at higher levels. Valerio isn’t a burner, but he was an active baserunner in the lower levels (where rule changes encouraged action on the basepaths) with 31 steals in 40 attempts. The Brewers want to find Valerio a defensive home, and that’s their next challenge in his development. He has second, third and short on his Minor League resume, but his below-average arm should keep him at the keystone. Milwaukee hasn’t ruled out trying him in center either to see if that can stick. The Dominican Republic native has gone from a low-level trade pickup to a bat his organization wants in the lineup at every level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $428,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, Mieses spent his first three pro seasons in three different Rookie leagues before losing 2020 to the pandemic. He since has produced consecutive 15-homer seasons and was one of the more productive hitters in Project Birmingham, which sent most of the system's best prospects to Double-A for the final month of the 2022 season. The White Sox haven't protected him on the 40-man roster in either of the last two seasons, however, because he's not close to big league ready. Mieses has the ingredients to hit for average and power, though his lack of plate discipline is a concern. He makes consistent contact with a sound left-handed swing, but he's so aggressive that he gets himself out by putting pitches in play that he'd be better off avoiding. At least 40 pounds stronger than his listed weight of 180, he has solid raw power that he could tap into more often if he were more selective. Mieses' added muscle has resulted in decreased speed, making him a below-average runner who's not much of a factor on the bases. Primarily a center fielder in his first two pro seasons, he now spends most of his time in right field, where he's an average defender with plus arm strength. He also saw action in left field and began playing first base for the first time last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox spent a franchise-record $54.2 million on bonuses and penalty tax to lock up their 2016-17 international class, and $53.3 million went to outfielders -- including $51.2 million for Luis Robert and $428,000 for Mieses. A Dominican, he spent his first three years in pro ball in three different Rookie leagues before losing 2020 to the pandemic shutdown. He returned last year to put up career-best numbers (.270/.312/.463, 15 homers) while reaching High-A in his full-season debut at age 21, though Chicago still left him off its 40-man roster because he's still not close to big league-ready. Mieses has a 6-foot-3 frame with a lot of leverage and projectable strength, and he began to tap into more of his solid raw power in 2021 once he became more proficient at launching balls in the air. He has a sound left-handed swing and makes consistent contact, but he could use more patience at the plate. His 5 percent walk rate last year was a career high and he gets himself out by putting pitches in play that he should avoid. Mieses has slowed down as he has started to add some muscle, and he's now a below-average runner. After breaking into pro ball as a center fielder, he's definitely a corner guy now. His plus arm is a weapon in right field, where he has good instincts but somewhat limited range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bradley’s senior year at the University of Georgia got off to a fast start when he had a .397/.513/.730 line through 18 games, only to come to a screeching halt because of the pandemic. The five-round 2020 Draft left him unselected, but he was part of the Royals’ undrafted free agent class that summer. Bradley’s contact rates have fueled his rise, and he slashed .293/.382/.455 with 12 homers at Double-A in 2022. Bradley has a good eye and reacts well to where the ball is thrown, spraying the ball all over the field rather than pulling everything. He uses a slightly open stance and has a smooth left-handed swing, but he doesn’t garner a lot of power, even for an older guy with a bigger frame. He makes up for that with his situational hitting and awareness of the strike zone, lowering his strikeout rate to 18.3 percent in Double-A last year. Bradley has a high baseball IQ, leading to more stolen bases (19 last year) than his average speed originally accounted for. He’s likely limited to left field because of his below-average arm. Bradley has been a solid all-around contributor in his first two years as a Royal. If that continues, he could find a role as a fourth outfielder. Evaluators would like to see a little more power to give him a higher ceiling, but the hit tool could carry him far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Pirates shortstop Oneil Cruz, Rafael Cruz signed with the Twins for $500,000 when the 2020-21 international signing period opened up in January 2021. He struggled out of the gate in the Dominican Summer League that year but righted the ship with a return to the DSL in 2022, hitting well enough to earn a trip stateside to finish the year in the Florida Complex League. Most facets of Cruz’s game are still pretty raw. He has tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate and showed he could get to it with a .558 slugging percentage in the DSL last year. He had a tendency to try to hit every pitch hard, which worked in the Dominican, but he scuffled and pressed a bit when he got to the FCL and had to start refining his approach. There’s some swing-and-miss to his game, but more reps against better pitching should help him learn to make better swing decisions. It's a little unclear where Cruz will play defensively long term. He was a shortstop when he first signed, but the Twins moved him to third base before he even played a game. He has a very strong arm that fits the hot corner and he’s continued to work on his throwing and fielding accuracy. He’s played a good amount of first as well, and while it’s way too early to pigeonhole him, some see a future as a first-base/DH type. Wherever he plays, his offensive potential will carry him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mooney spent three seasons in St. John’s rotation and had success right out of the gate. He was putting together a solid junior season to boost his Draft stock when he needed Tommy John surgery after nine starts. The Twins took him in Round 12 of the 2019 Draft and had him rehab with their staff. He’s dominated hitters at the lower levels but also hasn’t been on the mound that much, brought along slowly in 2021 (42 IP) and missing time with a nerve entrapment in his collarbone in 2022 (60 IP). The 6-foot-1 right-hander fools hitters with a bag of fringy-to-average stuff. Thanks to his lower slot and funky arm path, his 90-ish mph fastball plays up with a very flat vertical approach angle. His frisbee 80-mph slider and changeup with good depth might be his best offerings, and the data points to them being more successful than his heater. He also has a low-80s cutter, and when he’s been on the mound, the combination of pitches and deception has been very tough to hit, with a 13.5 K/9 rate and .183 average-against entering 2023. Aside from needing to stay healthy for a full season, Mooney has to land his stuff in the zone more (4.7 BB/9) to have success at the upper levels. He’s been a good strike-thrower in the past, and if he can rediscover that, he has the chance to start. Already 25, the clock is ticking for a pitcher who was not protected on the 40-man roster and not taken in last year’s Rule 5 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dirden opened his college career at East Carolina in 2016, then went undrafted after his lone season at Jefferson CC (Mo.) and two more at Southeast Missouri State. After missing all but two games with a broken thumb in 2019, he returned as a redshirt senior and ranked second in NCAA Division I with nine homers in 17 contests during the shortened 2020 season. Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent that summer, he led the system in slugging (.558), OPS (.942), doubles (40), extra-base hits (69) and RBIs (101) while advancing to Triple-A in 2022. A physical left-handed hitter, Dirden stands out most with his plus raw power, and he maximizes it by repeatedly driving balls in the air to his pull side. He also can drive the ball the other way with authority, as 11 of his 24 homers last season went to left or center field. His approach leads to strikeouts, though he does have some feel for hitting and works counts well enough to draw some walks. Dirden does most of his damage against right-handers, so he might not be more than a platoon player, but he also offers some sneaky athleticism for a 6-foot-3, 209-pounder. A fringy runner out of the batter's box, he's quicker once he gets going and has average arm strength. Capable of playing all three outfield spots, he's better than expected in center field, where he spent the most time in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mezquita decided to stick with the Braves and re-sign after his original $300,000 bonus in 2017 was nullified as part of the penalty for international signing infractions. His first two summers in the organization -- the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the Gulf Coast League in 2019 -- were fairly nondescript, but his tools showed up a bit more consistently after the shutdown in Complex League play during the summer of 2021. He performed decently in his full-season debut in Augusta in 2022, but he scuffled with a promotion to High-A Rome. There are some raw tools for Mezquita to work with, though he’s still learning how to use them on a regular basis. He has good bat speed from the right side of the plate and raw power to tap into, but it’s yet to show up in games. He’s capable of hitting the ball hard but is often too aggressive at the plate, and while he’s willing to draw some walks, his penchant for swinging and missing continues to be a concern. Mezquita runs well and is capable of stealing a base, but he’s not electric when it comes to his speed and athleticism. That could mean that he won’t stick in center field long term, and while he has a strong enough arm for a corner spot, that would put much more pressure on a bat that has yet to come around.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peguero received the second-highest bonus ($575,000) in the Marlins' 2022 international class when he signed out of the Dominican Republic. The most advanced player in that crop, he batted .286/.355/.424 during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He has struggled mightily in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League after making the jump to the United States in 2023. Peguero makes consistent contact thanks to his quick, short right-handed stroke and his hand-eye coordination. He already displays average raw power with the potential for more as he adds muscle, but he hasn't driven the ball with any authority this summer. He'll need to find more pop to profile as an everyday outfielder in the big leagues. An average runner who may gain more speed as he gets stronger, Peguero has good instincts and an aggressive nature on the bases and in the outfield. He spent most of his first season in pro ball in center field and could stick there, especially if he gets a little quicker. He has solid arm strength that would play well in right field if he winds up on a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Consuegra for $500,000 in July 2017, and it took nearly five years for the outfielder to reach somewhere above the Dominican or Florida Complex Leagues due to various injuries and the 2020 pandemic-canceled season. Finally able to hit triple-digit games played for the first time, the Dominican Republic native broke out at Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .251/.324/.431 with eight homers and eight steals in 66 games before coming back to earth at High-A Brooklyn (90 wRC+), where the pitcher-friendly confines of Coney Island may have played a part. He got an 11-game look in the Arizona Fall League ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility but remained unprotected and unpicked in the early winter. What makes Consuegra such a promising talent is that he’s loaded up with tools. His raw power ranks among the best in the Mets system, and it was certainly notable that he finished with eight balls struck at 110-plus mph during his time in the Florida State League (per Statcast). He’s also an above-average runner who can cover good ground from any of the three outfield spots. His plus arm strength, capable of firing 95+ mph missiles from the grass, helped him pick up 13 outfield assists last season (with two more in the AFL). The separator will be Consuegra’s overall performance with the bat. His swing can get too long, and a 25.9 percent K rate in ’22 is likely only to get worse as he dives into the upper Minors. He’ll get much-needed reps to improve the bat in what is still technically his second full season in 2023, and the rest of the profile gives him a shot at being a fourth outfielder down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Atencio joined the Mets in July 2018 at the same time as top New York prospect Francisco Álvarez, but it’s been a much slower road through the system for the southpaw. The Venezuela native pitched in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and 2021, showing signs of a breakout coming out of the pandemic with 76 strikeouts in 48 innings during the latter season. He jumped to Single-A St. Lucie in 2022 and handled the assignment fairly well with a 2.27 ERA and 48 strikeouts in 39 2/3 innings, though he did walk 23 over that span. The 6-foot left-hander sat in the average velocity range with a 91-93 mph fastball, which did touch 95 at times. He worked hard to establish the four-seamer in his first trip to a full-season affiliate, throwing it 58 percent of the time. His 82-85 mph changeup could get fairly firm but still was average with an ability to get whiffs against righties, while his upper-70s sweeper has enough depth to be a putaway pitch too. Atencio’s 13.6 percent walk rate with St. Lucie marked a career high as he fought wildness. That’s a tough pill to swallow for a hurler without a true plus pitch at present. That said, the three-pitch mix he’s flashed over the past two seasons keeps his starting dreams alive. Despite being passed over for Rule 5 protection in 2022, Atencio enters his age-21 season with a limited workload on his arm, so the potential for further growth certainly exists.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he committed to the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Vela decided to go pro as a 28th-round pick in 2017, signing with the Padres for $125,000 -- the max they could give him without dipping into their bonus pool. After being stuck at the Arizona complex for three straight seasons, the southpaw showed signs of a breakout with 21 Single-A and High-A starts in 2021. He was just as good in his return to Fort Wayne a year later, posting a 3.83 ERA with 101 K’s in 87 innings. He made nine late-season appearances at Double-A San Antonio, where walks (20 in 22 2/3 innings) caught up to him in a big way. Vela’s improvements over the previous two seasons coincided with a jump in velocity, and he’s now touching the mid-90s and usually sitting around 92-94 mph. His low-80s curve comes with enough vertical break to make it an above-average pitch and a definite weapon against fellow left-handers, who can look foolish swinging over it. A mid-80s changeup gives him three solid options and helps fend off splits issues. Vela’s delivery can look too stiff, and he’ll often fly open as he releases, leading to several missed locations. He walked 12.5 percent of his batters faced in High-A last season, and that number exploded to 18.5 percent against the more patient Double-A hitters. Barring any significant changes in his age-24 season, those control woes are going to force him into a relief role, and it was notable that the Padres made five of his nine San Antonio appearances come out of the bullpen already.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former White Sox closer Bill Simas and brother of Red Sox infield prospect Karson Simas, Kohl spent one season each at Fresno CC (Calif.), San Diego and San Diego State before signing for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2021. A reliever in college and during his pro debut, he opened eyes with two strong months as a starter in Single-A to begin last season. After missing a month with a forearm strain, he wasn't as effective afterward, though he didn't finish his first full year as a pro in Double-A as part of the organization's Project Birmingham. When he was rolling, Simas featured three effective pitches in his fastball, curveball and slider. His heater sat at 92-94 mph and reached 96 with armside run, and he showed he could hold velocity over longer stints than he had been accustomed to. His upper-70s curveball has depth and his low-80s slider has sweep when they're on, though they also can blend together at times. The change in roles meant Simas needed a changeup more than he had in the past, and his varied from a low-80s offering with fade and sink to a harder version that was too firm and straight. He also threw a lot more strikes than he had in college, adding credence to the thought that he can become a back-of-the-rotation starter. To do so, he'll have to regain the stuff he showed at the start of 2022 and prove he can hold up over a full season's workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest Cuban prospect to emerge in the White Sox system, Chapelli was named MVP at the 15-and-under World Cup in 2016 and won rookie of the year honors in the island's top domestic league at age 17 three years later. One of a dozen players to defect from Cuba's 23-and-under World Cup team in Mexico in October, he signed for $500,000 eight months later. He tore up younger competition in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League during his pro debut, finishing third in slugging (.636) and OPS (1.084). Built like a slightly taller Jose Altuve, Chapelli's clean left-handed swing and patient approach produce a lot of hard contact. In two seasons as a teenager in Cuba's Serie Nacional, he batted .304/.419/.438, a stat line that doesn't do justice to his power potential. With his hitting ability, bat speed and sneaky strength, he could hit 15 or more homers on an annual basis. After playing the outfield corners in Cuba, Chapelli switched to second base in the DSL. His solid speed, quick hands and decent arm give him a chance to become an average defender at second. He'll be 21 this season and could make the jump to High-A to show what he can do against more age-appropriate competition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barrios will sign as a shortstop, but that does not mean he is going to stay there. Either way, the large-framed infielder has tons of potential on defense. He has shown solid defensive actions, quickness and is best described as a “good twitch” athlete. He could move to third base as he continues to grow and develop, but that’s to be determined. There’s plenty of room on his frame to add strength. He has a solid throwing arm so getting the ball across the diamond from the left side with some authority is not a problem. At the plate, Barrios has a compact swing with a good feel for consistent hard contact. The athletic teen already shows signs of being a plus runner. His work ethic, aptitude and overall makeup are noteworthy. Barrios trains with Carlos Yanez. The Brewers are the favorite to sign him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hiraldo was ranked as the No. 17 prospect in the 2017-’18 International class by MLB Pipeline and was considered by some to be the most advanced hitter in the group. Signed for $750,000, Hiraldo debuted in ’18 in the DSL and GCL where he hit a combined .300 over 64 games. He spent most of ’19 in Rookie League Bluefield, again hitting .300, and came out of the lost ’20 season with an assignment to Low-A Dunedin. That ’21 season was a learning experience for Hiraldo, where he hit .249 with a seven homers and a .727 OPS over 105 games, striking out 111 times. With both Orelvis Martinez and Leonardo Jimenez in Low-A in ’21, Hiraldo played second and third base, but could get some reps back at shortstop in ’22. His defense remains a question mark and his throwing accuracy has been inconsistent at times, so finding a defensive home will be important for Hiraldo at this stage. His offensive dip in ’21 was largely due to pitchers making adjustments against him, which he’ll need to counter. That led to some frustrations for Hiraldo, but the raw hitting talent is still in there and his thick build should continue to give him some natural power. At 21, Hiraldo is entering am important season after seeing several prospects around him shoot up these rankings. The main focus will be his approach so that he can get to his natural power, which can still be above-average, but that tool will need some others to support it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hiraldo was ranked by MLB Pipeline as the No. 17 prospect in the 2017-’18 international class, with some evaluators considering him to be the best hitter available. The Blue Jays signed Hiraldo for $750,000 that summer and the early results have matched those reports. Hiraldo hit .313 with an .834 OPS over 54 games in the Dominican Summer League in ’18, earning a late promotion up to the Gulf Coast League. In ’19, the Blue Jays sent Hiraldo to Bluefield, where he hit .300 with an .829 OPS, before bumping him up to High-A Lansing for a one-game taste late in the season. With a frame that was already naturally strong as a 16-year-old, Hiraldo continues to develop physically and that shows in the type of contact he makes. Add in plus bat speed, and Hiraldo profiles as a hitter who will produce high exit velocities and line-drive contact with legitimate home-run potential. Hiraldo’s hand-eye coordination is impressive, but his aggression at the plate can lead to him pulling the ball often. If he’s able to drive the ball to all fields more consistently, that will open up his offensive profile even further. Hiraldo will continue to move around the infield, where his throwing arm is his strongest tool. As his body continues to mature, Hiraldo’s likeliest landing spot could he third, but the Blue Jays believe in his defensive actions enough to continue giving him time in the middle infield as he develops. The 2021 season will be key for Hiraldo’s development path, especially as he begins to face pitchers with more advanced game plans against his pull-heavy approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 MLB Pipeline’s No. 17 prospect for the 2017-18 international period, Hiraldo earned rave reviews for his bat as an amateur in the Dominican Republic – so much so that some scouts viewed him as the best overall hitter in his class. The Blue Jays secured Hiraldo’s future that July with a $750,000 bonus. So far in his career, he has lived up to his reputation, slashing .300/.348/.481 in the Rookie Advanced Appalachian League in ’19. In 56 games, he hit seven homers, 20 doubles, one triple and drove in 37. Strong beyond his years, Hiraldo has plus bat speed and impacts the ball using a quick, compact swing in which he generates huge extension through contact, driving the ball with back-spin carry. He has an innate feel for finding the barrel, though his approach can be too pull-oriented and he can struggle with spin at times. The gap power he’s shown, along with his swing mechanics, give scouts the impression that Hiraldo could be good for 20-plus home runs annually in his prime. Questions pertaining to Hiraldo’s ability to stick at shortstop long term will continue to follow him as he moves through the Minors, and though he handled the position well during his pro debut thanks to his athleticism and above-average arm strength, he spent more than half his time in the field in 2019 at second base. As a physically advanced teenager with below-average speed and modest defensive actions, Hiraldo is likely to end up at the hot corner, where his bat could profile nicely, provided his development plays out as expected and he makes the necessary adjustments along the way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Hiraldo opened eyes with his bat as a Dominican amateur, and many scouts viewed him arguably as the best overall hitter in the class. That distinction made him one of the most coveted players on the market, and he ranked as MLB Pipeline's No. 17 prospect for the 2017-18 international period before signing with Toronto for $750,000. Hiraldo is a bat-first prospect who has the makings of becoming a special offensive talent. Scouts like Hiraldo's approach and his swing. He's a mature player with quick hands, a plan at the plate and he can hit the ball hard to all fields. He's also been praised for his makeup and how he plays the game. Hiraldo was signed as a shortstop, but he's widely expected to end up at third base once he's added strength his naturally thicker frame. Second base is also a possibility, as is a corner-outfield spot, although neither his athleticism nor his below-average speed are clean fits at those positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 MLB Pipeline's No. 17 prospect for the 2017-18 international period, Hiraldo earned rave reviews for his bat as an amateur in the Dominican Republic -- so much so that some scouts viewed him as the best overall hitter in his class. The Blue Jays signed Hiraldo in July, securing his future with a $750,000 bonus. He lived up to this reputation in his professional debut, finishing in the United States with a taste of the Gulf Coast League after he had raked in Dominican Summer League. Hiraldo's impressive pro debut underscored his potential at the plate. Strong beyond his years, he has plus bat speed and impacts the ball using a quick, compact swing in which he generates huge extension through contact, driving the ball with back-spin carry. He has innate feel for finding the barrel, too, though his approach can be too pull-oriented, and he'll struggle with spin at times. The consistent gap power he showed in 2018, on top of his aforementioned swing mechanics, gives scouts the impression that Hiraldo could be good for 20-plus homers annually in his prime. Questions pertaining to Hiraldo's ability to stick at shortstop long-term will continue to follow him as he moves through the Minors, but he handled the position well during in pro debut, albeit while relying on his sheer athleticism and above-average arm strength. But as a physically advanced teenager with below-average speed and only modest defensive actions, Hiraldo likely will end up at the hot corner. The good news is that his bat could profile nicely there, provided Hiraldo's development plays out as expected and he makes the necessary adjustments along the way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman signed with the Royals for $1.5 million in the 2015-16 international signing period. While he didn’t hit much early in his career, he impressed defensively and the Royals added him to the 40-man roster in 2019, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. He was then non-tendered late in 2020, but re-signed with the Royals on a Minor League deal. His bat started to come around in 2021 as he reached Double-A for the first time. He also played for his native Dominican Republic in the Tokyo Olympics and was the starting shortstop in the bronze medal game victory. He elected free agency after the season and signed a Minor League contract with the D-backs in November. Guzman, who used to switch hit as a kid, just started doing so professionally in 2019. It’s still a work in progress, but he hit well at High-A (.289/.352/.465) prior to his promotion last season, showing signs that hitting from both sides of the plate may stick. He added strength and his .401 slugging percentage last season was a career high, but power still isn’t Guzman’s forte and it’s unlikely he’d hit double-digit homers at the highest level. The 23-year-old is certainly a glove-first shortstop and grades out as a plus defender at the premium position. What’s more, he added to his versatility last season, spending time at both second base and center field. With a plus arm and above-average speed, Guzman has the capabilities to play all over the diamond. It remains to be seen how much he’ll develop as a hitter, but his glove gives him a solid floor and the added versatility could help him reach the Majors as a utility option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals didn’t hold back on the international market for the 2015-16 signing period, handing out a combined $3.75 million to two players: outfielder Seuly Matias and Guzman. The shortstop got $1.5 million to sign and has consistently impressed with his defense in the pro ranks. Though his offense initially struggled to keep up with his slick glove, he showed signs of improvement in 2018, reaching full-season ball for the first time. He made even greater strides back at Class A Lexington in 2019, leading the Legends to a South Atlantic League title. If you remove Guzman’s unproductive April from his final .253/.296/.373 batting line, he was a .273/.313/.404 hitter as a 20-year-old in his first full-season campaign. He’s begun to grow into his projectable frame and was a noticeably stronger player in 2019. The Royals have worked with him to calm down his extraneous movement in the box and give him a more solid base to hit, and the results have been positive so far. Club officials see Guzman’s power starting to come out and note that he drove the ball more consistently as the 2019 season unfolded. He’s also running better than he has in the past, adding speed and being more aggressive on the basepaths. Even if the bat doesn’t come to fruition, Guzman’s glove could carry him up the ladder. He’s capable of making spectacular plays at shortstop thanks to outstanding lateral range and arm strength that’s up there with best in the Royals’ system. His high error totals are a product his range, and club officials think he actually was better on making the types of routine plays he’s struggled with in the past. Whether Guzman will hit enough to be an everyday player remains to be seen, but the Royals are encouraged by the progress he made in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals didn't hold back on the international market for the 2015-16 signing period, handing out $3.75 million to two players, outfielder Seuly Matias and Guzman. The shortstop got $1.5 million to sign and has consistently impressed with his defense, and while his offense has struggled to keep up, he showed signs of improvement in 2018, reaching full-season ball for the first time. There's no question it's Guzman's glove that will carry him up the ladder. He's capable of making spectacular plays at shortstop with an arm that sometimes plays as plus. He has outstanding range, showing he can make the play up the middle or to his backhand side. The organization still believes in his bat from the left side of the plate and thinks he's starting to figure things out. He has had a tendency to get out of his swing, jumping around the box, so the Royals have worked with him to calm things down and give him a more solid base with positive effects. He's also running better than he has in the past, adding speed and being more aggressive on the basepaths. Guzman has the tools to play shortstop defensively without question. Whether he will hit enough to be an everyday player remains to be seen, but the Royals are encouraged by the step forward he made in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals exceeded their international bonus pool for the first time during the 2015-16 signing period, with outfielder Seuly Matias ($2.25 million) and Guzman ($1.5 million) receiving their two biggest bonuses. Part of the same Dominican youth league that spawned Nomar Mazara and Amed Rosario, he batted just .228/.301/.305 in his two years in Rookie ball. Kansas City still likes his potential on both sides of the ball and is encourage that he finished 2017 with his best month as a pro and a strong performance in instructional league. While he has yet to produce much at the plate, Guzman already recognizes pitches and controls the strike zone well for a teenager. A switch-hitter, he has bat speed but needs more strength in order to do some damage. Though he has a groundball-oriented swing, he should grow into some gap power. Though he's not flashy, Guzman has good hands and a solid arm that plays up with a quick release at shortstop. He doesn't have the speed or quickness typical of his position, but the Royals believe his smooth actions will allow him to remain there. They like his maturity and how he has handled adversity in his introduction to pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals have invested heavily in international shortstops this decade. They spent $2 million on Raul Adalberto Mondesi in 2011, $1.3 million on Marten Gasparini in '13, $850,000 on Ricky Aracena in '14 and $1.5 million on Guzman in '15. The other three players have louder tools than Guzman, but he might have the best instincts of the bunch. Guzman has a mature approach for a teenager, showing good pitch-recognition skills and patience. A switch-hitter who enjoyed more success from the left side of the plate in his 2016 pro debut, he makes consistent line-drive contact and should have some gap power once he fills out. Presently a fringy runner, Guzman could gain a step as he gets stronger, but he won't ever be a basestealer. Guzman is not a flashy shortstop, but he has good hands and gets the most out of his solid arm with a quick release. Some scouts outside the organization wonder if he's quick and rangy enough to stay at short, but the Royals like his actions and have no such concerns. They praise Guzman's maturity and how well he handled jumping to the United States for his debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When he was selected in the third round of the 2017 Draft, Tabor was a skinny, baby-faced kid, but the D-backs saw pitchability and the potential for his stuff to tick up. They signed him for an above-slot $1 million. He overcame a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018 to finish the season on a high note, and that success carried over into his age-20 campaign at Class A Kane County, where the right-hander compiled a 2.93 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 101/16 K/BB over 95 1/3 innings spanning 23 starts. Tabor pitched across three levels in 2021, working his way up to Triple-A in the process. His numbers dipped a bit, but the D-backs feel he pitched better than the numbers indicate since pitching in Reno is always tough on the stats. Tabor’s advanced ability and polish are particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a Massachusetts prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, his fastball sits in the low 90s and he can get up to the mid-90s when he needs to. He’s had an advanced changeup since he was drafted and has improved his slider to the point where it can be his best secondary pitch. While he’s capable of missing some bats, Tabor is a command-over-stuff guy and has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career. He can pitch to all four quadrants of the zone and features some of the best command in the Arizona system. The D-backs like what they’ve seen from Tabor and believe he has the tools to remain a starter at the highest level. He’s made big leaps over the past four seasons, so as long as Tabor continues on a similar trajectory -- refining his secondary pitches and continuing to gain experience -- it won’t be long until he’s pitching in the back end of a Major League rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
