While the numbers dipped a bit in 2021, Tabor did work his way up to Triple-A. Tabor’s advanced pitchability and polish at a young age are particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, he is a good student of the game. His fastball has ticked up to where he sits at 92-93 mph and can pop 94 or occasionally 95. He had a plus-changeup when he was drafted and he has improved his breaking ball to the point where it is his best secondary pitch in some games and in others it's his best. He has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career, can pitch to all four quadrants of the strike zone and features some of the best command in the Arizona system. The D-backs liked what they saw from Tabor in Instructional League and believe he has everything needed to eventually be a starter in the big leagues, especially with the recent uptick in stuff. Refining his secondary pitches and gaining experience are the keys now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt before his senior year led to a big uptick in stuff for Tabor, sending his Draft stock rising and scouts pouring into New England as the weather warmed. The D-backs took him in the third round, gave him an above-pick value $1 million bonus and then had him throw sparingly during his pro debut. He overcame a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018 to finish the season on a high note, and that success carried over into his age-20 campaign at Class A Kane County, with the right-hander compiling a 2.93 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 101/16 K/BB over 95 1/3 innings and 23 starts. Tabor’s advanced pitchability and polish at a young age is particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, he sits in the low 90s and touches a bit higher with a fastball that could gain a few more ticks as he adds strength to his projectable frame. He lost some feel for what was a plus changeup in 2019 as he worked to improve his breaking ball, and most scouts now view Tabor’s slider as his better secondary pitch. He has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career, averaging 1.6 walks-per-nine across his first three seasons, and showed more bat-missing ability in the Midwest League, posting a 26.8 percent strikeout rate with a 15 percent whiff rate. Refining his secondary pitches is a top priority in Tabor's development, and the D-backs believe his athleticism and clean arm action gives him a chance to do so. He shows more of a floor than a ceiling right now, though that could change with an uptick in velocity and better secondary stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt before his senior year led to a big uptick in stuff for Tabor, sending his Draft stock rising and scouts pouring into New England as the weather warmed. The D-backs took him in the third round, gave him an above-pick value $1 million bonus and then had him throw sparingly during his pro debut. After getting off to a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018, Tabor finished with a 1.74 ERA over his final 33 frames and then continued to pitch well in is first taste of full-season ball at Class A Kane County in 2019. Tabor has impressed with his stuff, pitchability and polish, the latter being particularly impressive given his cold-weather background. Working from an athletic and repeatable delivery, he'll touch 94-95 mph and sit in the low 90s with his fastball, and there's reason to believe there's more in the tank as he fills out his projectable frame. His changeup flashes plus, with the potential to get there long-term, and he also has feel for a slider that can be too slurvy. He threw strikes 70 percent of the time in the Northwest League in 2018, issuing 1.9 walks-per-nine, and should have at least average command in the future. Tabor understands how to change eye levels and keep hitters off-balance using his fastball-changeup pairing. Developing a better breaking ball, whether it's a slider or true curveball, is a top priority in Tabor's development, and the D-backs believe his athleticism and clean arm action gives him a chance to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt before his senior year led to a big uptick in stuff for Tabor, sending his Draft stock rising and scouts pouring into New England as the weather warmed. He ended up landing in the third round, where the D-backs gave him an above-pick value $1 million bonus. He threw sparingly during his summer debut, but stood out as the most exciting high school Draft prospect from the D-backs' crop of high schoolers selected. While Tabor has a ways to go as a prep pitcher from the Northeast, the D-backs were pleasantly surprised how polished and mature he was on the mound. He shows three plus pitches at times from an athletic and repeatable delivery. His fastball will touch 95-96 mph and sit in the low 90s and there's reason to believe there's more in the tank as he fills out his frame. He's already tightened up his slurvy breaking ball some into a slider that should be a very good weapon for him and he has feel for a solid changeup. He's around the strike zone and should have at least average command in the future. Showing a good sense of what he needs to do on the mound to improve, Tabor was advanced in his ability to change tempos and deliveries to keep hitters off-balance. The D-backs love his business-like approach to honing his craft and think it will serve him well as he begins his pro career in earnest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2017, Jimenez has some of the best all-around ability in the Red Sox system. He has batted .306 or better in each of his three pro seasons, including winning the Short-Season New York-Penn League batting title (.359) in his 2019 U.S. debut. But he's still raw in many phases of the game, so Boston declined to protect him on its 40-man roster last November. Jimenez has gained about 50 pounds since signing, giving him solid raw power, while retaining almost all of his speed, which still grades as double-plus. A natural right-handed hitter who began switch-hitting when he turned pro, he's still figuring out his identity at the plate. His strength is more notable than his bat speed, and while he makes a lot of contact with a flat stroke, he lacks selectivity and produces a lot of harmless grounders while showing little feel for pulling or launching pitches in the air. Jimenez also doesn’t make the most of his quickness on the bases, where he's not a prolific or particularly successful thief. His speed plays better in center field, where he has good instincts and plenty of range. His strong arm earns solid to well-above-average grades from evaluators and fits anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain $10,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2017, Jimenez began switch-hitting after turning pro. He won Boston's Latin program player of the year award in his first season and the short-season New York-Penn League batting title (.359) in his second. While the coronavirus pandemic limited his 2020 development to instructional league, he wowed the Red Sox by showing up with significant added muscle while still retaining his game-changing speed. Jimenez uses his plus-plus speed to turn routine grounders into singles and could be a prolific basestealer once he refines his technique. He now has at least solid raw power, though it's still unclear how much he'll be able to tap into it. He had a short, flat swing the last time he was seen in game action and he'll need to become more selective because his hand-eye coordination allows him to make almost too much contact for his own good. In addition to his offensive upside, Jimenez also ranks as the best defender among Boston farmhands. His combination of speed and instincts gives him more range than most center fielders. He also has a strong arm for his position, receiving well above-average grades from some evaluators.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Red Sox signed 71 players in their 2017 international class, including 49 for $10,000 or less who didn't count against their bonus pool. The best player in both groups is Jimenez, who inked for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic and began switch-hitting after turning pro. He earned Boston's Latin program player of the year award in his 2018 debut and won the short-season New York-Penn League batting title (.359) as an encore last summer. Jimenez has game-changing speed that earns top-of-the-scale grades from some evaluators. He uses it to turn routine grounders into hits, should be a dynamic basestealer once he improves his technique and covers plenty of ground in center field, where he also displays a plus arm. He has impressive feel for making contact from both sides of the plate, and has been more effective hitting left-handed despite being a natural right-hander. The biggest question with Jimenez is how much impact he'll make with his bat. He uses a short, flat swing to mostly slap ground balls to the opposite field and take advantage of his quickness. More physical than his listed 160 pounds, he does have the bat speed and strength to do some damage if he makes some adjustments, which he may have to do against better pitchers and defenses at higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Red Sox have high hopes for their 2017 international class, which included 66 signees and what looks like an absolute steal at $10,000 in Jimenez. Solely a right-handed hitter when he signed out of the Dominican Republic, he began switch-hitting after turning pro and fared better as a lefty (.350/.416/.478) than a righty (.204/.259/.204) while earning the organization's Latin program position player of the year award for his 2018 debut. He's both extremely raw and one of the best athletes in the system. Jimenez's game is built around plus-plus speed, though he's still in the early stages of figuring out how to use it. He has the quickness to be a prolific basestealer yet was caught 14 times in 30 attempts last year. He needs to improve his reads and jumps on the bases and in center field, where he can cover a lot of ground and shows average to solid arm strength. Jimenez has a slappy approach at the plate and is an extreme ground-ball hitter whose speed creates a lot of infield hits. He probably won't have much power, with 10 homers a year being a realistic ceiling, so he'll need to concentrate on getting on base. He already makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate but needs to draw more walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few Brewers prospects have ridden the roller coaster more than Gray in recent years. The 2018 second-rounder missed significant time with pneumonia and a hamstring strain over his first two seasons, both of which were spent in Rookie ball. After the missed pandemic year, he looked like he was finally coming into his own in 2021 with a 289/.407/.632 line and 12 homers in 51 games at Low-A. He hit a wall at High-A Wisconsin, hitting just .219 with a 28.2 percent strikeout rate, and looked gassed in a spell in the Arizona Fall League. When it’s working, Gray shows promise as a hitter who exhibits good raw power and puts the ball in the air often (48.0 percent of the time in 2021). He expands the zone too much at times, leading to the K issues, and that became even more of a concern last summer when it looked like he was pressing to recreate his Carolina success. The 21-year-old still ended up with a 20-20 season (20 homers, 23 steals) because of his above-average speed on top of the pop, and that speaks to his offensive ceiling if he makes enough contact to reach base. Gray played center primarily and mixed in some right field in 2021. The presence of Sal Frelick, Garrett Mitchell and even Joey Wiemer will likely move him to the corner full-time the closer he gets to American Family Field, and he has enough arm to work there. The Brewers hope a full offseason reset gets Gray back on track and helps him show just enough bat to get the rest of his tools in future Milwaukee lineups.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. He struggled to stay on the field early in his career and move forward with his development as a pro, with pneumonia and a hamstring strain limiting him to just 55 games across his first two seasons, both of which he spent in Rookie ball. Finally able to play regularly in 2021, Gray has taken off, first hitting .289/.407/.632 with 12 homers in 51 games at Low-A prior to a midseason promotion. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. A gifted athlete with a quick right-handed bat, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields and started to tap into that power more in 2021. The Brewers were most impressed by how he started to make the most of his pop potential and athleticism with an uppercut swing that results in lots of deep fly balls. Though that leads to a good amount of strikeouts, Gray takes his walks as well and now projects as much closer to an average hit tool. Gray’s defense was never in question. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high-school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National Showcase after his junior year. His accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired, though. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. Gray’s advancements in 2021 have made him an even more exciting prospect, and while his profile still comes with risk, his ceiling has jumped to that of a skilled everyday center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. But Gray has struggled to stay on the field and move forward with his development as a pro, with pneumonia and a hamstring strain limiting him to just 55 games across his first two seasons, both of which he spent in Rookie ball. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. A gifted athlete with a quick right-handed bat, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields but lacks feel to hit and is devoid of an approach. Those shortcomings fuel Gray’s swing-and-miss issues, and in turn scouts question whether he will ever make enough contact to unlock his potential at the plate. The Brewers reserve hope that Gray will be able to make strides at the plate as he gains much-needed on-field experience. Gray’s defense comes with fewer question marks. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National showcase after his junior year, though his accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. Gray got stronger during the offseason while training at the Brewers’ complex in Arizona. He still has impressive tools and is young enough to get back on track, though even club officials recognize that 2020 will be a crucial year for the once highly touted prep.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. He passed on a University of Mississippi commitment to sign for slot value ($1,113,500), and then began his pro career in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. With his lightning-fast bat and his physical strength, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields from the right side of the plate. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National showcase after his junior year, though his accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. That Gray has swing-and-miss concerns and has been inconsistent against quality pitchers leads some scouts to question whether he'll ever hit enough to get to his power and unlock his full potential. The guided instruction he'll receive in pro ball could go a long way on that front, though it also means he may need extra time to develop in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of La Romana, Dominican Republic, for $1.2 million in the 2018-’19 international signing period, De Castro finally had the opportunity to make his pro debut in ’21 in the Florida Complex League, hitting .238 with a .769 OPS. De Castro mixed in a handful of games at second base but primarily played shortstop, where he profiles as one of the highest-potential defenders in the system. De Castro makes some “wow” defensive plays on the infield, but can balance those out with fundamental errors at times, particularly when it comes to throwing. The club’s optimism lies in those errors smoothing out as he matures, because the upside is significant defensively and enough to carry De Castro to the upper levels of the Minor Leagues on its own. Offensively, there isn’t much power coming given his thin frame, so the focus going forward will be consistent contact and a strong approach. That will be tested well with a full season in ’22. It’s a matter of rounding out De Castro’s game from here, but the twitchy young shortstop still has plenty of development time ahead. In a system that’s been developing some stronger defenders of late, De Castro has the ability to be among the best, so it’s up to his offensive production to decide his long-term ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trained in the Dominican Republic by Angel Perez, a member of MLB's Trainer Partnership Program, De Castro received the top bonus in Toronto’s 2019-2020 international class, signing as a 16-year-old for $1.2 million on July 2. A twitchy defender with one of the better infield gloves in the system, De Castro comes with long-term upside. Scouts viewed De Castro as one of the stronger defenders in that international class, too, due to his natural defensive actions and strong throwing arm. You’ll hear the term “quick-twitch” with De Castro often, which is what makes him such a talented defender, and his baseball instincts and IQ only help the situation. Still listed at 6-foot, 150 pounds, De Castro’s physical development will be one of the most important factors in the coming years. An adjustment to the lower half of his swing has helped him drive the ball more consistently, but adding some muscle to his frame could bump that power tool without slowing him down too much in the field. De Castro is fully expected to stay at shortstop, but his development will require some patience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Doxakis’ numbers didn’t jump off the stat sheet as a freshman at Texas A&M, with a 5.44 ERA and 1.37 WHIP recorded between seven starts and 18 relief outings. But he moved into the Aggies’ rotation as a sophomore and quickly became one of the Southeastern Conference’s best starters the next two springs. His performance was good enough to inspire the Rays to select the lefty in the second round of the 2019 Draft, making him Texas A&M’s highest-drafted player in seven years. He had an excellent professional debut, posting a 1.93 ERA and 0.95 WHIP with nearly a strikeout per inning in the New York-Penn League, and likely would have moved up considerably if there had been a Minor League season in 2020. He’s not going to blow away anyone with his fastball velocity, typically sitting between 88-93 mph, but it plays up due to his command and the pitch’s arm side run. His breaking ball, a low-80s slider from which he can add/subtract velocity, makes him devastating against left-handed hitters and quite tough on right-handers as well because he can back-foot it against them. His changeup is the least reliable of his three offerings, although it’s shown flashes of becoming an average third pitch playing off his fastball if he can command it. He’s a confident pitcher, trusting his above-average control and command and attacking hitters on both sides of the plate. Some scouts look at Doxakis’ delivery and relatively limited arsenal and peg him as a reliever, a projection no doubt bolstered by him hitting 97 mph in that role as a freshman at Texas A&M. That gives him a high floor, even as someone who can turn over a lineup once, but he has the repertoire, control, frame and makeup and recent results to continue starting as he's done for all of 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 5 international prospect in 2019-20, Pena signed with the Royals for $3,897,500 shortly after the signing period started. But the Dominican native didn’t have his first full professional season stateside until 2021 because of the pandemic, although he was able to participate in the Royals’ instructional league against older competition in 2020. Pena struggled in 40 games in rookie ball, hitting just .161/.256/.314 with three home runs, but there were flashes of the dynamic player he can be. Pena’s bat is still his calling card despite the contact issues he faced in Arizona. Strong and physical, he possesses power with a slight uppercut swing that yields hard contact to all fields. The Royals are working on mechanical adjustments that will allow his rhythm and timing to be better, cutting down on the swing-and-miss tendency that saw him strike out more than a third of the time last year. Pena is an average runner and solid defender in center field, and the Royals will continue to let him play there unless he outgrows the position. His arm strength and offensive tools profile well in right field. Only 19 years old, Pena is no doubt still growing into his big, 6-foot-3 frame, and his youth and makeup give the Royals confidence he can bounce back after 2021. He has a long way to go, though, and his bat will have to speed up for him to reach his full potential. If the power doesn’t translate, Pena still has enough tools to be an off-the-bench type player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pena was MLB Pipeline’s No. 5 international prospect in the 2019-20 signing period and reminded scouts of a young Carlos Beltran in terms of skill set and potential. The Royals, the team that drafted Beltran back in 1995, gave Pena $3,897,500 to sign right after the signing period opened. The Dominican native has had a strange start to his career: He’s yet to play a professional season stateside because of the pandemic, but he participated in the Royals’ instructional league in both Kansas City and Arizona last fall, gaining valuable experience against older prospects. Pena’s bat and power are his best tools right now, but the other parts of his game are developing quickly. He has a sound approach with a slight uppercut swing and yields hard contact to all fields. He has some pop and has shown strength and quickness through the strike zone. Pena is an average runner with a solid-to-average arm and good defensive skills, so the Royals are going to let him play in center field for now. But he’s already added to his frame since he was signed and could outgrow the up-the-middle position and move to right field, where he has the offensive tools and arm to profile well. Pena had his moments last summer where he struggled against older pitching. But Royals officials were pleased to see that Pena is open to learning and making adjustments quickly, which could signal a quicker move through the Minors once he actually starts playing games. Despite gaining experiences last summer that someone his age usually doesn’t get, Pena’s still a young player and has a long way to go. But if it all clicks for him on the field, he has to potential to be the face of an organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts who saw Pena, who was MLB Pipeline's No. 5 international prospect for the 2019-20 signing period, were reminded of a young Carlos Beltran in terms of his skill set and potential. Perhaps that's why the Royals, the team that drafted Beltran back in 1995, gave the Dominican native $3,897,500 to sign right after the signing period opened on July 2. He received his first taste of stateside action during instructional league and impressed those who saw him with his athleticism, tools and advanced feel for the game. Pena's bat and power are his best tools at the moment, but the other parts of his game are not far behind. The left-handed hitter has a sound approach with a slight uppercut swing that yields hard contact to all fields. He has shown strength and quickness through the strike zone and the ball jumps off of his bat. He could end up having plus power and does not have a lot of swing and miss. An average runner with a solid-to-average arm and solid defensive skills, he runs well enough to at least be given a chance to stick in center field. He could outgrow the up-the-middle position and move to right field, where he has the offensive tools to profile well. Pena also gets high marks for his baseball IQ, solid instincts and plus makeup. If it all clicks for him on the field, he has the potential to be the face of an organization, much like the player he draws comps to was at one point in his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 65 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Puason signed with the A’s out of the Dominican Republic for $5.1 million in a 2019-20 international signing period that saw him and Jasson Dominguez rated as by far the top two prospects of the class. Confined to the alternate site in 2020 due to the pandemic and unable to play a Minor League game until 2021, the teenager was aggressively assigned to Low-A Stockton to begin the ‘21 campaign and worked through some early struggles with a solid end-of-season run to finish batting .215 in 91 games. There’s a lot to like about Puason’s offensive capabilities. Though there are some swing-and-miss issues, his smooth swing from both sides of the plate allows him to drive the ball to all fields, and there is some power that should develop as he grows into his 6-foot-3 frame. He also brings good speed on the base paths. The A’s believe Puason just needs to continue to play games in order to slow the game down. The expectations remain sky high, with comparisons to former All-Star shortstop Tony Fernandez. His strong defense and arm along with solid footwork on the left side of the infield should allow him to stick at shortstop for the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two top prospects received bonuses north of $5 million during the 2019-20 international signing period, Jasson Dominguez and Puason, who were ranked No. 1 and 2 on the Top 30 list. As soon as Puason was signed by the A’s for $5.1 million, he immediately flew to the United States for the instructional league and worked out at the A’s training facility in Mesa, Arizona. Yet to play a Minor League game, he was one of the youngest players to attend the A’s alternate site in San Jose, California last season. Puason’s long and wiry frame immediately evoked memories of former All-Star shortstop Tony Fernandez when the A’s were scouting him in the Dominican Republic. With a smooth swing from both sides that allows him to hit line drives all over the field, he should develop 15-homer type power as he grows into his 6-foot-3 frame. Puason can really pick it and throw it at shortstop. That, along with good speed and footwork, will keep him at the position as a solid defender. He will get a chance to put those tools to work once Minor League play resumes this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2019-20 international signing period opened last July, two top prospects got bonuses north of $5 million. One was Jasson Dominguez, MLB Pipeline’s top-rated international prospect, signed by the Yankees. The other was Puason, No. 2 on that top 30, who also received $5.1 million to sign with the A’s. He came to the United States for instructs and to work out at the A’s facility in Mesa, Ariz., and will make his official debut at some point in 2020. Puason is lean and wiry, with a frame that should add strength, and a body type that reminds some of former All-Star shortstop Tony Fernandez. He has a smooth stroke from both sides of the plate with the ability to barrel up the baseball consistently and spray line drives to all fields. As he matures and grows into his 6-foot-3 frame, there’s sure to be power to come. How much remains to be seen, but a floor of 15 homers annually seems more than reasonable given his long levers and some leverage to his swing. A plus runner, there’s no question about Puason’s ability to play shortstop. He can really pick it and throw it, with fluid actions, good footwork and plus range to go along with a very strong arm. He’s already displaying solid instincts as well and will get to show off his tools in earnest this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best Venezuelan prospect and one of the top all-around talents in the 2019 international class, Rodriguez signed for $2,667,500. The 2020 pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until last summer, when he homered four times in his first six games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League before tailing off and finishing with a .216/.326/.367 line and a 31 percent strikeout rate. He spent the offseason working out with J.D. Martinez and Miguel Cabrera, which the Dodgers hope will spark a rebound in 2022. When Rodriguez signed, he projected as a hit-over-power center fielder with a line-drive, all-fields approach. He has gotten stronger and more aggressive since turning pro, looking to crush homers to his pull side with a longer right-handed swing while chasing too many pitches out of the strike zone and giving away too many at-bats. He needs to regain some discipline, get back to barreling balls more consistently and just let his pop come naturally. Rodriguez is starting to slow a bit as he has added muscle, earning average to solid grades for his speed. He didn't stick out on the bases or in center field during his debut despite a reputation for a high baseball IQ that allows him to get the most out of his tools. If he does have to shift to a corner, his solid to plus arm would play in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Los Angeles has landed the best Venezuelan prospect in each of the last three international classes, including signing Rodriguez for $2,667,500 in 2019. He was advanced enough to make his U.S. debut at age 17 last summer, but the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the Minor League season. Instead, he participated in the Dodgers' Dominican instructional league program. More advanced than most teenage hitters, Rodriguez has a mature approach that produces line drives to all fields. He has a definite hit-over-power profile from the right side of the plate, though his bat speed and ability to barrel balls could translate into 20 or more homers per season. He's starting to add strength and show some feel for driving balls in the air. With solid speed and a high baseball IQ, Rodriguez can steal some bases and has a chance to remain in center field. It's possible that he could lose a step as he matures physically, which could push him to an outfield corner. If that happens, his offensive upside and solid to plus arm would fit well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top Venezuelan prospect and one of the best all-around talents on the 2019 international market, Rodriguez signed with the Dodgers for $2,667,500. That's the largest bonus they've ever paid to a true amateur internationally, surpassing the $2.5 million they gave fellow Venezuelan Diego Cartaya in 2018. Like Cartaya, he should be advanced enough to make his U.S. debut at age 17. An advanced hitter for his age, Rodriguez uses a patient approach to lace line drives to all fields from the right side of the plate. His pure hitting ability stands out more than his power, though club officials believe his pop could manifest itself sooner than expected. With his bat speed and ability to put the barrel on the ball, he could hit 20 or more homers on an annual basis once he matures physically. Rodriguez has solid speed and a high baseball IQ, making him a threat to steal bases and giving him a good chance to remain in center field. It's possible that he could shift to a corner if he loses some quickness as he adds strength, but his bat and solid to plus arm strength would profile well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers saw Cabrera as an advanced college hitter with the potential to move quickly through their system when they drafted him in the second round of the 2020 Draft and signed him for a $1,210,000 bonus. His first pro season was a reminder that even the best prospects lost valuable time in the pandemic-shortened 2020 college season. He hit .371 with 17 RBIs in as many games for Low-A West Michigan during a stretch from mid-May into June, batted just .182 in July and then drove in 20 runs in August to earn a promotion to Double-A Erie, where he batted .174 in 17 games. The full-season numbers showed a solid run producer who still has plenty of lessons to learn as a hitter. Cabrera turned pro with the reputation of a smooth left-handed swing and an ability to spray line drives all over the field. His pull and opposite-field percentages from 2021 back up the all-fields part, but the production didn’t follow. He had a surprisingly high ground-ball rate and low line-drive rate at West Michigan, and was caught in between on some pitches. Cabrera admittedly tried to do too much after Spencer Torkelson and Dillon Dingler were promoted from West Michigan to Erie, leaving Cabrera at the center of the lineup. He hit 48 points higher on the road than at home. Cabrera saw time at all three outfield positions at West Michigan, but profiles as a corner. The Tigers still believe in Cabrera’s big league future, and are likely to put him back in Erie to open the season. His best comp at this point might be former Tigers outfielder Andy Dirks, a solid complementary outfielder a decade ago before injuries shortened his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Detroit’s Tigers have had an affinity for LSU Tigers for at least the past decade, thanks in part to general manager Al Avila’s friendship with LSU head coach Paul Mainieri dating back to their days together at St. Thomas University in the 1980s. The link paid off again when the sweet-swinging Cabrera fell to Detroit’s competitive balance pick in the late stages of the second round, where the Tigers signed him for $1,210,000. He didn’t get any time that summer at the alternate training site but made an impression in their Florida instructional league. Cabrera might not put up gaudy power numbers, but his smooth left-handed swing and ability to hit around the field should translate well to Comerica Park. He credited growing up playing golf with helping his baseball swing, which might explain his ability to find natural lift. He had an advanced approach in college and quickly showed signs of adapting to the pro game during instructional ball. He added 10-15 pounds of muscle during baseball’s summer shutdown in 2020, which might help him maintain power and build arm strength. While not fast, Cabrera is a smart baserunner, having stolen 20 bases in 23 attempts in his college and summer ball career combined. The Tigers touted Cabrera as a hitter who could move relatively quickly and find a future as an everyday left fielder, but they left him out of their Summer Camp as well as big league Spring Training. He hurt his stock as well with a rough time at High-A West Michigan to start 2021, but given this is Cabrera's first taste of the pros, there remains the hope he can still claim that corner spot in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top Venezuelan pitching prospect in the 2019-20 international class, Medina signed with the Padres for $700,000 on July 2, 2019. After the pandemic cancelled the 2020 season, Medina spent some time in San Diego’s fall instructional camp and then made his professional debut in 2021, throwing a combined 33 2/3 innings in the Dominican Summer League and the Arizona Complex League. He’ll continue his professional climb with the Twins, who acquired him as the player to be named later in the deal that sent Taylor Rogers and Brent Rooker to the Padres. Medina is still growing into his 6-foot-1, 180-pound frame but already pitches with good velocity and should be able to add a bit more in the future. His fastball, which features good late life, sits in the mid-90s and touches the upper-90s on occasion. He also throws an above-average slider and shows good feel for a promising changeup. Medina repeats his delivery well and aggressively attacks hitters when he’s on the mound. He shows a good feel for all his pitches, but his consistency will need to improve. The right-hander issued 24 walks over 33 2/3 innings last season and although that’s a small sample size, it’s worth noting. That being said, Medina is still just 19 years old with plenty of ingredients to be high on. If he’s able to make the necessary adjustments to his command, he projects as a starter long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Medina was the top pitching prospect out of Venezuela in the 2019-20 international class, signing with the Padres for $700,000 on July 2. What was supposed to be Medina’s professional debut in 2020 was wiped out by the pandemic, though he did put forth an encouraging showing in San Diego’s fall instructional camp after the season. Medina is the prototypical starting-pitcher package, with a lean, athletic frame that should enable to him to add strength and velocity as he matures. He already features an explosive fastball as a teenager, with the ability to throw in the mid 90s with sink and late movement, and he could ultimately sit in the upper 90s once he’s grown into his projectable body. Medina has the makings of an above-average slider that he throws with power as well as feel for turning over a quality changeup. Medina repeats his delivery better than most teenage hurlers and should continue to improve in that department as he matures physically. He's aggressive on the mound and knows how to attack hitters, showing feel for his entire arsenal as well as an aptitude for making adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith already made a name for himself as an amateur as the Most Outstanding Pitcher at the 2016 Area Code Games but had a strong commitment to TCU that caused him to drop to the 38th round in 2017. He made six starts for the Horned Frogs as a freshman but missed all of 2019 due to Tommy John surgery and much of 2020 due to the pandemic. Pitching in his fourth collegiate season last year, he posted a 3.83 ERA with 101 strikeouts and 20 walks in 82 1/3 innings, prompting the Brewers to select him in the second round. Smith signed for below slot at $1 million. The first thing that stands out about the southpaw is his height at 6-foot-7. He puts that to good use by creating good extension and a tough angle on his 89-93 mph fastball. The heater, which can touch 95, also plays up because he commands the pitch well within the zone. His mid-80s changeup gives him another above-average offering because of its tough fade. A low-80s slider rounds out the package and was trending in the right direction before the Draft. Smith’s ability to pitch in the zone and avoid free passes differentiates him from other big hurlers, who typically thrive on throwing hard with little command. The lack of a true plus pitch won’t make him an ace, but the rest of the package makes him a potential back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a sign of what was to come, Holgate followed up a mundane freshman season at Arizona with a circuit-best 13 homers in the Northwoods League in the summer of 2019. He was off to a hot start before the 2020 shutdown, hit .351/.421/.576 with 11 homers as a junior last spring and mixed in a National Baseball Congress World Series win for the Santa Barbara Foresters in between. The Cardinals selected the slugger 70th overall last July and signed him for just under slot at $875,000. Holgate played 30 games with Low-A Palm Beach in his Draft year but managed just a .193/.279/.289 line and 35.7 percent K rate. The left-handed hitter’s power is what originally stood out to St. Louis, and that remained true in those early Minor League looks, where he maxed out with a 109.2 mph exit velocity. His plus raw power shows up more in batting practice, but it should be at least above-average on the pro side too. A longer swing, designed to make the most of that power, led to the swing-and-miss issues with Palm Beach, and it’s a bigger question now than it was on Draft Day if Holgate will be able to hit for a decent average. A career .314 mark in college provides some hope, and further adjustments to increase the contact rate after last year’s humbling could pay dividends. Holgate played his college position of right field in Low-A, but he projects better in left field due to a fringy arm. The former Wildcat will need to hit to be valuable in either corner outfield spot, and that starts with making more contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Elliott starred at Division II Lincoln Memorial University in Tennessee, posting a 2.23 ERA with 134 strikeouts and just 14 walks over 92 2/3 innings during his 2019 senior season. The Padres selected him in the 10th round that summer and inked him to a below-slot $5,000 bonus. The 6-foot-3 lefty posted a 1.77 ERA over 35 2/3 innings in his pro debut then broke out in 2021 as he worked his way up to Double-A. Pitching across two levels last season, Elliott racked up 87 strikeouts and issued just 19 walks over 70 2/3 innings Although Elliott’s velocity has ticked up since college, he remains a command-over-stuff type pitcher. His fastball sits in the low 90s, but plays up because his arm slot creates additional deception. A low-80s changeup, which features good downward action, is currently his best pitch, though there’s a chance his mid-70s slider claims that title in the future. None of Elliott’s pitches will overpower a hitter, but his delivery, coupled with his ability to locate to any corner of the zone helps his stuff play above its velocity. The development of Elliott’s slider may ultimately determine his ceiling. The southpaw has been a consistent performer during his time in pro ball and if the slider comes along, should be able to stick in the back of a rotation. If not, he could profile as an effective longman coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morris enjoyed some success in the 2018 Cape Cod League, where he hit .331, and that hit tool also showed itself in his final season at Virginia, where he handled ACC pitching with a .345 average. The Blue Jays selected Morris in the fifth round of the ’19 Draft, signing him to a slightly above-slot bonus of $397,500. Morris debuted in ’19 in Low-A, hitting .246 with a .730 OPS, but had more success when he returned to Vancouver as Toronto’s High-A affiliate in ’21. That season, Morris hit .285 with seven home runs and a .782 OPS over 103 games, playing across the infield. One of the most cerebral prospects in the system, Morris has an exceptional ability to recall past plate appearances and work through those for development. His hit tool has always been his calling card, but the Blue Jays are now expecting a little more power from Morris, with double-digit home runs the next step. Morris may be a below-average athlete on the field, but he has carved out a valuable resume with time at shortstop, second base and third base, a split that’s expected to continue. As long as he can continue to be reliable in those spots, there’s room for his bat to carry him through the system. Morris’ mental approach has helped him handle more advanced pitching at the upper levels, but he’ll need his offensive production to do most of the work. He’ll have plenty of opportunities in an organization looking to develop some lefty bats, and the utility role should give him plenty of pathways up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pérez might still be remembered best as a candidate for the first overall spot in the 2016 Draft. He tested positive for a performance-enhancing substance days before the process began, and MLB Pipeline’s No. 9 Draft prospect fell to the Cardinals at No. 23 overall instead. The Puerto Rico native hasn’t exactly enjoyed a strong offensive start to his career. A broken hand limited him in 2017, and he didn’t see his first full-season action until 2019 with Class A Peoria, where he hit just .269 with a .654 OPS in 118 games. Pérez added strength ahead of 2021 and enjoyed arguably his best offensive season yet at Double-A Springfield with a .265/.322/.339 line and a career-best four homers in 98 games. Pérez’s prospect stock remains in place because of his non-offensive tools. A near-plus-plus runner, he shows excellent range at the demanding position of shortstop and has the hands to handle most anything hit his way. A plus arm makes the defensive profile even better. Pérez has used his speed to swipe 20-plus bags each of his past two seasons, and his performance on the basepaths may be his best offensive asset. Otherwise, he can get too aggressive at the plate. So while his 14.9 percent swinging-strike rate isn’t overly high, he doesn’t quite drive balls adequately when he does make contact. Only 17 of his 86 hits went for extra bases in 2021, and his career full-season high for slugging percentage is a meager .339. Pérez hasn’t been added to the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible the past two years, but the glove and speed could get the 23-year-old a Major League look on their own merits, if only as a light-hitting bench option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not a whole lot has gone right for Perez in the last couple of years. Thought to be a potential top 10 pick in the 2016 Draft, he slid after a positive test for a performance-enhancer. The Cardinals took a chance and drafted him closer to the end of that first round, but while he did show some tools during his pro debut that summer, he struggled in 2017 and his summer ended with a broken hand in early August. That's the bad news. The good news is the shortstop had a productive offseason once his hand healed. That included playing for Team Puerto Rico, and manager Yadier Molina, in the Pan American U-23 Baseball Championship to earn a spot in next fall's World Cup. In addition to getting him more playing time, the Cardinals wanted to make sure he worked on getting more physical. Perez has solid bat-to-ball skills and drew some walks, even when struggling, but a serious lack of strength kept him from impacting the baseball. Some evaluators worry he won't be able to add the strength necessary to hit, but the Cardinals see strength in his hands and forearms and think his build will allow him to add good weight. There's no question about Perez's defense. He has plus speed and outstanding range as a result, to go along with above-average hands and a plus arm when he needs to. Still just 19, there's time yet, but he will have to start showing more at the plate to come close to reaching the potential of a big league regular people saw leading into the Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez's road to pro ball was tumultuous, to say the least. Leading up to the 2016 Draft, the Puerto Rican shortstop's name was popping up at the top of the first round. But news of a positive test for a performance-enhancing drug forced his stock to fall. The Cardinals nabbed him with the first of their three first-rounders, giving him full pick value to sign. During his pro debut, Perez showed all of the raw tools that had amateur scouts excited about his upside, all while dealing with the pre-Draft adversity with impressive maturity, though he didn't replicate that performance at the plate in 2017. For now, his defense is ahead of his bat, with no questions about his ability to stay at short long-term. He uses his outstanding speed well to cover a ton of ground and he has excellent hands and a strong arm to boot. He tends to try to do too much at times, something that he will harness as he gets more time under his belt. At the plate, he showed an ability to make hard contact at times, though he'll have to refine his approach and learn to recognize soft stuff better. He should grow into more power as he matures and his speed makes him a base-stealing threat. As time passes, Perez should be able to put his pre-Draft mistake more and more firmly in the rear-view mirror and show who he truly is. It could very well be that misstep allowed the Cardinals to acquire an elite-level player at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon joined the Dodgers organization for $350,000 as part of a 2015-16 international classic that included Yordan Alvarez, Yadier Alvarez and Yusniel Diaz. He put himself on the map with 13 homers and a 1.044 OPS over 52 games in the Dominican Summer League the following year but trailed off some due to low averages and high K rates in the seasons that followed. At age 23, Rincon looked like he was righting the ship in his second trip to Double-A in 2021 and was moved to the Mets last July in a trade for Billy McKinney. He finished with a .265/.334/.496 line and 22 homers between the two organizations, marking his third Minor League campaign with 20-plus dingers. As you might expect, power is what makes the 6-foot-3 right-handed slugger a notable prospect. Mets officials were quickly impressed by both his raw and in-game pop, and the latter plays so well because of Rincon’s ability to lift the ball, especially to his pull side. His 81 homers since 2017 (his first full season) are 16th-most in the Minor Leagues. Unfortunately, the power comes with whiff concerns; Rincon’s swinging strike rate of 17 percent was 17th-highest among 142 Double-A qualifiers, and it will only get worse at Triple-A or the Majors, barring changes. A below-average runner, Rincon is limited to the corner outfield spots. He has enough arm to play in right, and it was notable that the Mets moved him there after the trade, whereas the Dodgers featured him more in left. He doesn’t add much value defensively beyond the arm, and that places even more emphasis on the slugging ability. The 24-year-old will get to prove he can power his way to Queens with his first assignment to Triple-A in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yet another recipient of Los Angeles' largesse during the 2015-16 international signing period, Rincon turned pro for $350,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His bonus was an investment in his power potential, which was evident when he homered 13 times in 52 games while batting .328/.383/.661 between two Rookie leagues in his 2016 pro debut. He made his U.S. debut ahead of schedule in late July and went deep twice in the second game after his arrival. Already 6-foot-3 and 190 pounds when he turned pro, Rincon has impressive strength and loft in his right-handed swing. The Dodgers have faith in his ability to hit for average as well as for power, though he'll need to do tone down his extremely aggressive approach to make consistent contact against better pitching. After coming to the States, he drew two walks and struck out 30 times in 105 plate appearances. Rincon moves well for his size, though he may lose some of his presently average speed as he matures physically. He's raw defensively but could become an average right fielder with more experience. He has the solid arm strength desired at his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strotman underwent Tommy John surgery with the Rays back in June 2018 and returned to the mound in July 2019, but the shutdown made it impossible for him to get innings in 2020. Even though the former reliever at St. Mary's College of California earned a spot onto Tampa Bay's 40-man roster that fall and had a strong start to the 2021 season in Triple-A that caught the Twins’ eye enough for them to acquire him along with Joe Ryan in the Nelson Cruz deal, the lack of prior workload may have caught up to the right-hander as he posted a 7.33 ERA in 12 outings following the trade. Typically, Strotman's fastball sits around 95-96 mph and tops out at 99, but the Twins saw a noticeable drop in his velocity and command towards the end of the '21 season, leading them to believe the issues stemmed from the ramp-up in his workload. They're expecting the fastball to be at full strength in ‘22, and though it has good life and is complemented by three solid offspeed pitches, Strotman doesn't miss as many bats as his stuff might suggest. His newer cutter and slider have become more of a singular pitch, with him working to keep adding velocity to the pitch. Strotman has starter-caliber stuff, but he still needs to throw more strikes overall, which the Twins think is feasible considering his lack of extreme control issues in the past. There's a chance that he could maximize his potential more effectively in the bullpen, where the fastball-cutter/slider mix in particular could play up in short stints. Where he falls on that spectrum could depend on his ability to shoulder the workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever for most of his time at St. Mary’s College of California, Strotman moved into the rotation during his junior season and caught the Rays’ attention with his low-mileage arm and untapped upside as a starter. He went in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft, put together an outstanding professional debut and kept pitching well for Class A Bowling Green in 2018 until requiring Tommy John surgery that June. He returned on July 11, 2019, made up for some lost time in the Arizona Fall League then turned heads with a 2020 fall instructional league showing that catapulted him onto the Rays’ 40-man roster. He carried it forward to a successful year in Triple-A when he was sent, along with Joe Ryan, to the Twins in the Nelson Cruz deal. Strotman has a quick arm and plus velocity on his fastball, and that returned last year after coming back inconsistently during his late-2019 performance. He added a cutter while baseball was shut down last summer, and Rays officials believe that pitch is already his best breaking ball and a legitimate weapon for him. He also has an above-average slider, a loopy curveball and a below-average changeup to round out his starter’s arsenal. His fastball-cutter combination alone, especially with his plus command back in place two years after surgery, made him a legitimate risk to be selected in last year’s Rule 5 Draft had he not been protected. In 2017, Strotman posted a 4.67 strikeout-to-walk ratio. In instructs, he showed that level of command again. He has all the traits you’d want out of a starter: plus pitches, a deep repertoire, athleticism, a smooth delivery and plus command. The Rays kept developing him in that role, but the most important thing for the young right-hander in 2021 to keep gaining experience after all the development time he missed due to his surgery and the lost season in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An in-season move from St. Mary’s bullpen into the starting rotation during his junior year gave Strotman some late helium ahead of the 2017 Draft. Intrigued by his low-mileage right arm and untapped potential as a starter, the Rays made Strotman their fourth-round pick, and he rewarded them with a promising pro debut. He continued to pitch well at Class A Bowling Green early in 2018 before requiring Tommy John surgery that kept him out until the following July. He pitched in the Arizona Fall League after the season to recoup some of the innings he lost to injury, then turned in a standout performance during 2020 fall instructional camp that earned him a spot on Tampa Bay’s 40-man roster. Though the quick arm and plus velocity that Strotman showed before surgery wasn’t there in the AFL, it returned in earnest for him in 2020, with the right-hander’s fastball sitting comfortably in the mid-90s and occasionally touching higher. Rays officials really like the cutter Strotman added during the shutdown, with some already viewing it as an above-average pitch, and he continues to flash a plus slider when he’s at his best. Strotman masks his fringy changeup with fastball-like speed, and he can land his loopy, below-average curveball for a strike. He repeats his clean delivery well enough to project at least average control and command. Strotman has starter qualities in his athleticism, smooth delivery and increasingly deep arsenal, and the Rays intend to develop the right-hander in that role. For now, though, Strotman just needs to get experience after missing key development time in 2019-20.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite pitching to mixed results during his three years at St. Mary's, Strotman shot up teams' Draft boards in the spring of 2017 following a move from the bullpen to the rotation. Targeting his upside in the latter role, the Rays selected him in the fourth round in June and signed him for $367,500. The right-hander's pro debut only validated Tampa Bay's scouting efforts, as Strotman posted a 1.79 ERA and a 0.75 WHIP while holding hitters to a .168 average over 51 innings in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League. Advancing to Class A Bowling Green in 2018, Strotman got off to a strong start in the Midwest League before undergoing season-ending Tommy John surgery in June. When he's healthy, Strotman combines size and athleticism with a lightning-quick arm to generate a plus fastball that bumps 97-98 mph and sits at 93-95. His slider can be inconsistent but has the makings of at least an above-average pitch, while further strides in developing his changeup could give Strotman a third Major League-average offering at maturity. Meanwhile, Strotman's three-pitch mix plays up thanks to his advanced control and command and because he's adept at pitching down in the zone. Many expect Strotman, with his electric arm and promising arsenal, to serve as a valuable bullpen piece once he's fully developed. The Rays, however, will continue to deploy him as a starter, with the goal of offering him as many innings as possible so as to further his development. There is a chance that Strotman will be back before the end of the 2019 season, though a 2020 return might be more realistic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite pitching to mixed results during his three years at St. Mary's, Strotman shot up teams' Draft boards in the spring of 2017 following a move from the bullpen to the rotation. Targeting his upside in the latter role, the Rays selected him in the fourth round in June and signed him for $367,500. His slider can be inconsistent but has the makings of at least an above-average pitch, while further strides in developing his changeup could give Strotman a third Major League-average offering at maturity. Meanwhile, Strotman's three-pitch mix plays up thanks to his advanced control and command and because he's adept at pitching down in the zone. Many expect Strotman, with his electric arm and promising arsenal, to serve as a valuable bullpen piece once he's fully developed. The Rays, however, will continue to deploy him as a starter, with the goal of offering him as many innings as possible so as to further his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 60 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 Yurchak led NCAA Division I with a 41/12 BB/K ratio in 2017, his lone season at Binghamton after transferring from Wake Forest, prompting the White Sox to sign the redshirt sophomore for an over-slot $150,000 in the 12th round. The Dodgers acquired him in a November 2018 trade for Manny Banuelos that didn't appear to be very significant -- until last year. After going 4-for-42 in May, he batted .403 the rest of the way to lead the Minors in hitting (.365) and finish second in on-base percentage (.443). Thanks to his sweet left-handed swing, uncanny hand-eye coordination and fine command of the strike zone, Yurchak has posted a .321/.421/.466 line while advancing to Double-A in four pro seasons. While he's strong, he doesn't have much loft in his stroke and he doesn't produce high exit velocities. His hit-over-power approach might have him max out at 12-15 homers per season, which would make it difficult for him to profile as a regular at first base. First base and DH are the only realistic lineup options for Yurchak, who has well-below-average speed and athleticism. He's an adequate defender at best at first base, though he does have average arm strength. He has seen brief action at third base and left field as a pro but lacks the range for either position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yurchak posted an .880 OPS as a Wake Forest freshman in 2015, outperforming future White Sox second-rounder Gavin Sheets, but opted to transfer closer to home to Binghamton. After sitting out 2016, he was a Cape Cod League all-star that summer and led NCAA Division I with a 41/12 K/BB ratio last spring. Signed for an over-slot $150,000 as a 12th-round redshirt sophomore last June, he batted .345/.448/.520 in the Rookie-level Pioneer League during his pro debut and had other clubs ask about him in trade talks. An on-base machine, Yurchak has a pretty left-handed stroke and controls the strike zone exceptionally well. He's strong and could develop average or better power if he adds some loft to his swing, though for now he's content to hammer line drives from gap to gap. He's somewhat of a lefty version of Kevin Youkilis at the same stage of their careers, though the Greek God of Walks demonstrated more pop. Yurchak will really have to hit, because all of his value comes from his bat. He's a well below-average runner and athlete who moved to first base after committing eight errors in 12 pro games at third base. He does have solid arm strength and Chicago hopes he can develop into an adequate defender at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since signing with the Pirates for $350,000 in the 17th round of the 2017 Draft, Martin has been an on-again, off-again offensive player. He hit 11 homers in 39 games during his debut the summer after he signed, then struggled with a move to full-season ball in 2018. He smashed 35 homers across two levels of A ball in 2019 and the power continued to show up at the alternate site in 2020. There were 22 more long balls in Double-A a year ago, but with a regression in his approach, and the Pirates made the decision not to put him on the 40-man roster in the offseason. Outside of perhaps Oneil Cruz, no one has as much raw power in the organization as Martin does, and he’s shown the ability to get to it, recording tape-measure shots and high exit velocities as he’s moved up the ladder. There have been, and always will be, a lot of strikeouts in his game, but he had offset that in the past by drawing walks. In 2021, however, his walk rate dropped and his strikeout rate climbed to a career-high 34.3 percent. While Martin has worked hard on his defense, his power bat is going to be the thing that gets him to the big leagues. He’s no longer a liability at first, but he’s fringy. Having come from a rural area in Washington state, there should be some patience and the Pirates hope Martin’s desire to get better helps him make adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few people knew much about Martin when the Pirates gave him $350,000 to sign in the 17th round of the 2017 Draft. The Washington state high schooler gave an early return on the investment and put his name on the prospect map when he hit 11 homers in his 39-game Gulf Coast League debut that summer. A move to the full-season South Atlantic League in 2018 did not go well, but he turned things around in 2019, smashing 35 homers between two levels of A ball, power that continued to show up during his time at the club’s alternate training site in Altoona, Pa., in 2020. There’s no question about Martin’s raw power and whether it will play in any park he’s in. His average exit velocity during his breakout 2019 season was 91.5 mph, among the top averages in the game. There is considerable swing and miss to his game, with a strikeout rate of over 30 percent in his career, something he worked on addressing during his time at the alternate camp last summer. He also worked to put the ball in the air more consistently and cut down on his ground ball rate, and he exhibited the ability to damage any pitch, having added more man strength as he’s matured. Martin has also improved his overall conditioning while working very hard on his defense. He’s committed to not being a one-dimensional player and the Pirates feel he’ll be at least an average defender at first base, with the kind of left-handed swing that could deliver a lot of home runs at PNC Park.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates took an over-slot flier on Martin in the 17th round of the 2017 Draft, giving him $350,000 to keep him from heading to Gonzaga and hoping his raw power would play at the pro level. The early returns were good as he slugged .630 in his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League, but he struggled with an aggressive push to full-season ball in 2018. To his credit, he righted the ship and crushed 35 homers across two levels of A ball in 2019, tying for the South Atlantic League lead in homers with 23 even though he got promoted after just 82 games. Martin easily has the best power in the organization and is becoming one of the best power hitters in all of the Minors. He can crush the ball out to all fields and out of any ballpark, including in what’s usually a very pitching-friendly Florida State League, and there might be more to come given that he finished with more than 30 doubles in 2019 as well. The strikeouts are an issue, he whiffed in more than 30 percent of his plate appearances last year, but some of that came because he was so intent on working counts. A focus on figuring out how to do more damage early in the count so he doesn’t get to two strikes as much without sacrificing his on-base skills will be a key area of his offensive development. While Martin is never going to wow anyone with his glove, he has improved at first base and he works hard to become capable there. He’ll keep getting some work in the outfield, maybe even some in-game reps, to help with his athleticism, but it’s that power bat that’s going to push him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As teams get to the later rounds of the Draft, they rely heavily on the area scouts, who put in the work to really know players and finding value. The Pirates leaned on Pacific Northwest scout Max Kwan, who was on Martin's offensive upside from the get-go and knew what it would take to sign him. The Pirates gave Martin well above the $100,000 threshold in the 17th round to sign him away from his Gonzaga commitment and he promptly went out and led the Gulf Coast League in home runs, on-base percentage and slugging. Martin impressed immediately, and throughout his pro debut, with his professional at-bats. He has an advanced approach from the left side of the plate, particularly for a high schooler, drawing walks and not even giving in to left-handers on the mound. He has the chance to be at least an average hitter with above-average power if this continues, and was hitting balls over the center field wall in Pirate City during instructs. The son of a body builder, Martin is no stranger to the weight room and could approach plus power eventually. A well below-average runner, Martin played some outfield during his pro debut, but he is now a first baseman only with work to do to be adequate defensively. It will be his bat that carries him, however, and after struggling with an assignment in full-season ball, he righted the ship when he was sent down to the Appalachian League in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An all-state safety as a Utah high schooler, Corry tore the ACL in his knee playing football as a junior yet rebounded to earn a well over-slot $1 million bonus in the third round of the 2017 Draft. He blossomed into the Giants' best pitching prospect in 2019, when he won Low-A South Atlantic League pitcher of the year honors and ranked among the Minor League leaders in ERA (1.75, second), opponent average (.171, third), strikeouts (172, fourth) and strikeout rate (12.6 per nine innings, fifth). But after the pandemic layoff, he returned in 2021 and his mechanics fell apart, leading to 75 walks in 79 1/3 innings between High-A and the Arizona Fall League. There's nothing wrong with Corry's stuff, highlighted by an upper-70s downer curveball that he commands better than his fastball. His heater usually parks in the low 90s and tops out at 96 with some armside run but he really struggled to locate it last season. He can flash a plus changeup as well, with his low-80s cambio plummeting at the plate when at its best. Corry took off in the second half of 2019 when he found a better and more consistent tempo with his delivery, earning comparisons to a young Matt Moore. Last year, he was unable to repeat the mechanics that had worked so well for him. He now projects more as a curveball-heavy reliever than a three-pitch starter, but he's going to have to provide a lot more strikes before he can help the Giants, who declined to protect him on their 40-man roster last November.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An all-state safety as a Utah prepster, Corry tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his knee playing football as a junior but rebounded in 2017 to become the state's best high school prospect since Mark Pawelek was a Cubs first-rounder in 2005. Signed for a well-over-slot $1 million as a third-rounder, Corry broke out in the second half of 2019 and won low Class A South Atlantic League pitcher of the year honors after leading the circuit in ERA (1.76, second in the Minors), strikeouts (172, fourth), strikeout rate (12.6 per nine innings, fifth), whiff rate (34 percent, fifth) and opponent average (.171, third). After his 2020 development was limited to instructional league, his mechanics have gone haywire this season. Corry has three solid or better offerings, highlighted by an upper-70s curveball with downer action that he often commands better than his fastball. His heater usually operates in the low 90s and tops out at 96 mph with armside run, though he worked at 93-95 in shorter stints during instructional league. He made significant improvements with his changeup in 2019, which helped him do a better job of keeping right-handers in check. Corry finished strong in 2019 once he developed a better and more consistent tempo in his delivery, reducing his walk rate to 2.6 per nine innings in the second half from 6.2 earlier in his career. He has averaged nearly a walk per inning in 2021, however, though he's also missing more bats than ever. He elicits comparisons to a young Matt Moore, who like Corry repeated Rookie ball and needed time to learn to harness his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An all-state safety as a Utah high schooler, Corry tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his knee playing football as a junior, but he bounced back in 2017 to become the state's best prep prospect since the Cubs made Mark Pawelek a first-rounder in 2005. The Giants handled him carefully after paying him a well over-slot $1 million in the third round, having him repeat Rookie ball and delaying his full-season debut until 2019. He allowed a total of just 11 runs (nine earned) in his final 14 starts, winning South Atlantic League pitcher of the year honors after topping the low Class A circuit with a 1.76 ERA (second in the Minors), 172 strikeouts (fourth), 12.6 strikeouts per nine innings (fifth), a 34 percent whiff rate (fifth) and a .171 opponent average (third). Corry's best offering is an upper-70s curveball with downer break and he often commands it better than his fastball. His heater sits in the low 90s and peaks at 96 mph with armside run. His changeup showed significant improvement in 2019, allowing him to keep right-handers in check and look more like a starter than a two-pitch reliever. He has drawn comparisons to a young Matt Moore, who had trouble staying on top of his pitches early in his pro career, and Corry took off once he developed and maintained a better and more consistent tempo in his delivery. He cut his walk rate to 2.6 per nine innings during the second half of last season, down from 6.2 earlier in his career. He does throw with some effort, but if he can control and command his pitches like he did at the end of 2019, he could be a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star as a Utah high schooler, Corry was an all-state safety but also tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his knee playing football as a junior. He made a full recovery and signed for a well over-slot $1 million as a third-rounder in 2017, becoming the state's highest-drafted prepster since Cubs first-rounder Mark Pawelek in 2005. He has developed slowly, repeating Rookie ball and not making his full-season debut until 2019, but he started to take off when his control began to improve this June. Corry's best pitch is his curveball, which he commands better than his fastball and sits in the upper 70s with 12-to-6 break. His quick arm produces low-90s heaters that top out at 96 with running action. He has improved his changeup since turning pro, giving him the makings of an average third pitch. He elicits comparisons to a young Matt Moore, who also had trouble locating his pitches early in his pro career. Corry is athletic and started throwing more strikes once he developed a more consistent tempo with his delivery. He throws with effort and still has to prove he can repeat his mechanics over a full season, but he's young and San Francisco will give him plenty of time to develop as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Corry divided his time between two sports as a Utah high schooler, earning all-state honors as a safety in football but also tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in his knee on the gridiron in the fall of 2015. He still became the state's highest-drafted prepster since 2005 Cubs first-rounder Mark Pawelek, signing for a well over-slot $1 million in the third round last June. He's the type of raw mound prospect whom the Giants excel at polishing. Corry elicits some Matt Moore comparisons because he'll showcase a plus fastball and curveball on his best days. He currently pitches at 90-92 mph with nice running action on his fastball, and he already has touched 96 and should gain more consistent velocity as he gets stronger. He actually commands his upper-70s curve better than his heater but currently struggles to get ahead in the count to set up his breaker. Though his changeup is in its nascent stages, Corry maintains his arm speed when he throws it. Learning to locate his fastball is No. 1 on his to-do list, and while he has the athleticism to make it happen, he also has a lot of effort in his delivery. He could wind up as a reliever in the long run but San Francisco will give him plenty of time to make it as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's New Jersey state player of the year in 2018, Decker gave up a Maryland commitment to sign for an over-slot $1.25 million in the second round. Missed time has stunted his development since, as he broke his left wrist two games into his pro debut, lost the 2020 season to the pandemic and sat out seven weeks last summer with a hamstring injury. He put together the best two months of his career once he returned last July and will try to ride that momentum into 2022. Decker's carrying tool is his left-handed power, which he generates with his bat speed and strength. If he can make more consistent contact and launch balls in the air more regularly, he could produce 20 or more homers per season. He's willing to work counts and use the opposite field, but he swings and misses too frequently and will have to prove he can handle quality breaking balls at higher levels. Though Decker has average present speed, he projects as a fringy runner once he's physically developed. He's a decent athlete with average range and solid arm strength on the outfield corners. He spent most of his first three pro seasons in right field, recording nine assists in 78 games there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
