mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's New Jersey state player of the year in 2018, Decker signed for an over-slot $1.25 million in the second round. Because of a fractured left wrist that ended his debut after two games and the coronavirus pandemic that wiped out the 2020 Minor League season, he's already 21 but enters this year with just 174 pro at-bats and without having reached full-season ball. He used his downtime last summer to improve his conditioning and displayed some of the best power at Boston's instructional league camp. Decker generates plenty of raw pop with his bat speed and strength, and he taps into it by frequently turning on pitches and launching them in the air. He struck out in 30 percent of his plate appearances in 2019, reinforcing his need to improve his plate discipline and pitch recognition. His left-handed swing can get long and uphill, and he has yet to prove he can handle southpaws well enough to be more than a platoon player. Decker presently has average speed but likely will lose at least a half-step as he matures physically. He's a decent athlete with good instincts in right field. With his power potential and solid arm strength, he fits the classic profile in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's New Jersey state player of the year in 2018, Decker gave up a Maryland commitment to turn pro for a $1.25 million bonus in the second round. His debut lasted two games before he sustained a small fracture in his left wrist while taking a swing. Despite being one of the youngest and most inexperienced players in the short-season New York-Penn League last summer, he posted a .471 slugging percentage that would have ranked fifth if he hadn't fallen a few plate appearances short of qualifying. Decker's bat speed and strength generate plenty of raw power, and he already demonstrates the ability to tap into it by turning on pitches and lifting them. Though he struck out in 30 percent of his plate appearances in 2019, there are no glaring flaws with his left-handed swing or approach. He has some patience and utilizes the entire field, so he has a chance to be at least an average hitter to go with his pop. Decker offers decent athleticism in addition to his offensive potential. Presently an average runner, he'll probably have fringy speed once he's physically mature. He shows good instincts in the outfield and his solid arm strength adds to his right-field profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Decker had a memorable 2018 senior season at Seneca (N.J.) High, throwing six shutout innings to win the South Jersey Group 3 state title and capturing Gatorade state player of the year honors. Despite his heroics on the mound, teams were more interested in his potential at the plate. The Red Sox signed him away from a Maryland commitment for $1.25 million as a second-rounder, though his pro debut subsequently was delayed because he sustained a small fracture in his left wrist while taking a swing. Decker has the potential to produce solid batting averages with similar power, though he'll need some time to develop. He has a quick left-handed swing, employs a patient approach and uses the entire field. He focuses on making hard contact rather than worrying about home runs and should show more pop as he learns to turn on pitches more frequently. While he's a decent athlete, most of Decker's value will come from his bat. A center fielder in high school, he'll slide to a corner in pro ball. He has close to average speed and flashes solid arm strength, so he could wind up in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before he missed a month during his 2018 high school season with shoulder tightness, Hankins got mentioned as a possibility to become the first prep right-hander ever to get drafted No. 1 overall. Health and signability concerns allowed the Guardians to grab him at No. 35, where he signed for an over-slot $2,246,022. He hasn't pitched since 2019, however, because of the coronavirus shutdown followed by Tommy John surgery in May 2021. When healthy, Hankins shows off an electric fastball that sits at 92-95 mph and reaches 97 with so much run and sink that he can have trouble commanding it. He has nice feel for a changeup with similar action that plays as a plus pitch when it has enough velocity separation from his heater, though it does get too firm at times. He didn't demonstrate much aptitude for spinning the ball as an amateur but has made some progress as a pro, with his sharper low-80s slider showing more upside than his upper-70s curveball. Though he's 6-foot-6, Hankins does a good job of keeping his delivery in sync and throwing strikes. During his rehabilitation from elbow reconstruction, he has improved his conditioning, which should help expedite his comeback. He may not arrive in Cleveland as early as originally anticipated but still could become a mid-rotation starter, especially if he can upgrade his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hankins was discussed as potentially the first prep right-hander to get selected No. 1 overall in the Draft until he missed a month during his 2018 senior season with shoulder tightness. Questions about his health and signability allowed the Indians to grab him with their second of two first-rounders that June, and they signed him for an over-slot $2,246,022 as the 35th overall choice. He was healthy in his first three years as a pro, albeit while working just 63 official innings in large part because of the coroanvirus shutdown, but injured his elbow this spring and had Tommy John surgery in May. When healthy, Hankins has an electric fastball that sits at 92-95 mph and peaks at 97 with so much run and sink that it can be difficult to command at times. His best secondary pitch is a changeup with similar action that shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch but can get too firm. The key to his development will be coming up with the reliable breaking ball he lacked as an amateur, and his sharper slider shows more promise than his deeper curveball. With his athleticism and impressive body control for a 6-foot-6 youngster, Hankins should be able to provide plenty of strikes and already shows some feel for locating his fastball to both sides of the plate. Adding more strength will help and could increase his velocity as well. He will vary his tempo to throw off the timing of hitters and even uses a Johnny Cueto shimmy shake on occasion.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hankins was a candidate to become the first high school right-hander ever selected No. 1 overall, but he slid in the 2018 Draft after he missed a month with shoulder tightness. The Indians snapped him up with the second of their two first-round picks that June, signing him for an over-slot $2,246,022 as the 35th overall choice. He has had no health issues as a pro ball and reached low Class A at the end of his first full season. Hankins works at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with his fastball, and while he has some feel for throwing it to both sides of the plate, it features so much run and sink that it's sometimes difficult to command. He lacked a reliable breaking ball as an amateur but has made strides with a hard curveball with depth that was his best pitch at times in 2019. His changeup fades and sinks and shows flashes of being a plus pitch but can get too firm, and he'll also mix in an occasional slider. Athletic and possessing good body control for a lanky 6-foot-6 youngster, Hankins should be able to harness his arsenal and develop average control and command. He needs to get stronger and could add some more velocity once he does. He likes to vary his tempo to throw off hitters' timing and can use a Johnny Cuetoesque shimmy to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hankins entered 2018 with a chance to become the first high school right-hander selected No. 1 overall, but that ended when he missed a month during the spring with tightness in his shoulder. The Indians used their second of two first-round picks to grab him, signing him for an over-slot $2,246,022 as the 35th overall choice. Though Cleveland held him to three innings in his pro debut, his shoulder issue was determined to be muscular in nature and he's expected to have no restrictions in 2019. When fully healthy, Hankins had the best fastball in the 2018 Draft, operating at 92-96 mph and reaching 98 with electric life and the ability to spot it to both sides of the plate. His fading changeup has the potential to become a plus offering, though his breaking pitches still need work. His hard curveball has its moments and he also has begun using a slider, but both were fringy for much of his high school senior season. Hankins generates his premium fastball with little effort in his delivery, which bodes well for his future health and command. He'll vary his tempo to throw off hitters' timing, at times throwing in a Johnny Cueto-like shimmy. He must add strength to his lanky 6-foot-6 frame and could add velocity once he does.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick in 2018 after he won Big West Conference player of the year accolades at Cal Poly, McKenna slugged a feeble .303 in his full-season debut the following year. He used his pandemic layoff to add strength, hit the ball with more authority than ever in instructional league in 2020 and then got off to a .305/.390/.616 start. He injured his shoulder a week after his promotion to Double-A, missed a month and didn't hit nearly as well once he returned. More of a disciplined hitter who peppered the gaps in college, McKenna now is pulling the ball in the air with more authority. His bat speed and strength give him solid raw pop from the right side of the plate and he's doing a better job of tapping into it. His 34 percent strikeout rate last year leads to question about whether his power-seeking approach will work against more advanced pitchers, and Houston did leave him off its 40-man roster last November. A solid runner, McKenna can steal an occasional base and cover ground in the outfield. While he's not a burner, his quickness and instincts allow him to get the job done in center field. He has solid arm strength and threw out eight runners in 74 games last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the 2018 Draft's best college hitters on the West Coast, McKenna won Big West Conference player of the year honors last spring after batting .339/.424/.506 for Cal Poly. After signing for $430,000 as a fourth-rounder, he posted similar numbers while reaching low Class A in his pro debut. McKenna used a disciplined approach to drill line drives from gap to gap in college, then made a more concerted effort to drive the ball in his first taste of pro ball. His bat speed and strength give him solid raw power, which translated into more home runs when he added more loft to his right-handed stroke. He has solid speed and runs the bases well but isn't much of a basestealer. McKenna profiles better as a regular if he can stay in center field, where he played in college and most of his debut. His quickness and instincts allow him to cover ground, and his average arm will work on either corner if he has to move or serve as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knowles signed with the Angels for $850,000 back in July 2017 out of the Bahamas and it looked like a strong investment when he hit .311 with a .391 on-base percentage in his pro debut across two levels of Rookie ball in 2018. He didn’t perform as well in 2019 and really struggled offensively with a move to full-season ball for the first time in 2021. The fact that Knowles is a super high-energy player is a plus, but it’s also an obstacle. While he’s capable of making hard contact from both sides of the plate, he needs to learn to slow things down and rediscover his approach. Early on, he would draw walks and work counts, but that regressed in 2021, with his strikeout rate ticking up as he chased out of the zone too frequently. There isn’t much power in his profile, so he needs to get back to putting the ball in play and letting his plus speed wreak havoc. On the plus side, the Angels had encouraged Knowles to use that speed more aggressively on the basepaths and he responded by going 31-for-32 in stolen-base attempts last year. He’s a capable defender in center field, but showed that not only can he handle all three outfield spots, but he started getting reps at shortstop as well. If he can get back to more regular contact, he could be an athletic super-utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels handed out bonuses of six figures or more during the 2017-18 international signing period, led, of course, by the signing of Shohei Ohtani. Knowles, a toolsy outfielder from the Bahamas, got the third-highest bonus from the organization that period, $850,000, then made a strong debut in the United States in 2018. His 2019 wasn’t as solid, but he appeared to make some very good strides on both sides of the ball in instructional league play in 2020. While Knowles’ numbers dipped in 2019, he still did show off a good amount of tools to work with. He can make hard contact to all fields from both sides of the plate, and even in 2019, showed an ability to work counts and draw walks. Strong, but not big, he’s not likely ever to have more than fringy power, but should have the ability to drive the ball to the gaps and use his speed to his advantage. The Angels continue to encourage Knowles to use that plus speed more on the basepaths to become a threat to steal, something that improved at instructs. Knowles has the chance to be a very good defensive center fielder, one who could stay there long-term, and he’s shown the ability to play all three outfield spots well. He’s also gotten some time at second base, but it’ll be how much his bat advances that will determine if he can reach his ceiling as an everyday big leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has been a total of six players from the Bahamas to make it to the big leagues. That’s likely to change as Major League teams have been looking to the Caribbean nation for talent of late, producing bigger-name prospects like Jazz Chisholm and Lucius Fox. Knowles, who signed for $850,000 at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, isn’t as well-known yet, but has the tools to be part of the next wave of Bahamian big leaguers. As a 17-year old making his pro debut in the United States in 2018, Knowles set the expectations bar very high by putting up ridiculous numbers in two levels of rookie ball. Luck was on his side as he put up very inflated BABIP and that came down to earth with a return to the Pioneer League in 2019. Still one of the youngest players at his level, he did improve his approach beyond those numbers, cutting his strikeout rate and showing progress with his overall plate discipline. As the switch-hitter continues to refine that, he has the chance to be a solid hitter and there’s power to come, with most of it showing up now from the left side of the plate. A plus runner, Knowles is still learning how to steal a base. That speed helps him in the outfield and he’ll continue to get reps in all three spots, though he has the skills to play center full-time if needed. The Angels love his work ethic and his baseball IQ, providing confidence his performance will catch up to his tools as he plays all of 2020 at age 19.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Angels have been garnering a reputation of acquiring premium athletes in the early rounds of the Draft, they've also been busy bringing similar players via the international market. At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, they double-dipped in the Bahamas, signing a pair of outfielders: Trent Deveaux for $1.2 million and Knowles for $850,000. It's been Knowles who broke out of the gate during his pro debut in 2018, earning a promotion from the Arizona to the Pioneer League. Throughout his first summer of pro ball, Knowles showed a solid approach from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed. There's emerging power, though it only showed up from the left side during his debut. He's not afraid to draw walks and could be a plus hitter as he continues to refine his approach, perhaps eventually with average big league pop. Knowles has plus speed and loves to use it, though he'll have to learn the nuances of basestealing. The Angels exposed the teenager to all three outfield spots, and he should have the range to play center field and enough arm to man right. Some of that might depend on how he continues to develop as he hopes to join prospects like Jazz Chisholm of the D-backs and the Rays' Lucius Fox in putting Bahamanian baseball more firmly on the map.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson comes from a baseball family that includes a father (Marcel) who played three years in the Minors and two cousins (Jimmy Rollins, Tony Tarasco) who enjoyed lengthy big league careers. Signed for $1.35 million as a second-rounder in 2018, he was one of the youngest players in his Draft and still just 17 when the Marlins promoted him to Low-A for the final month of his pro debut. He lost all of 2019 following surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his right leg and all of 2020 to the pandemic shutdown, then started to take off last year once he moved from second base to center field. Johnson batted just .146/.214/.215 in Low-A during the first six weeks of last season, but looked like a more relaxed hitter after changing positions and batted .271/.349/.483 afterward (including some time in Rookie ball). With his stocky frame and penchant for hard contact, he has drawn some comparisons to Howie Kendrick. His bat speed and strength produce plus raw power, though his right-handed stroke can look stiff at times and he needs to broaden his approach rather than look to constantly lift balls to his pull side. A solid-to-plus runner, Johnson uses his speed well on the bases and in the outfield thanks to a quick first step and advanced instincts. He broke into pro ball as a shortstop before moving to second base at the outset of 2021, but he never seemed comfortable in the middle infield and committed 33 errors in 69 games. He looks far more natural in the outfield, with the chance to become a solid defender in center with arm strength to match.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2018 Draft, Johnson signed for $1.35 million in the second round and was still 17 when the Marlins promoted him to low Class A for the last month of his pro debut. He missed the entire 2019 season after having surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his right leg in March but returned for instructional league. He comes from a baseball family, with his father Marcel playing three years of pro ball and cousins Jimmy Rollins and Tony Tarasco reaching the big leagues. With his hitting ability and the way the ball jumps off his bat, Johnson earns some comparisons to Howie Kendrick. He has a quick right-handed swing that repeatedly produced exit velocities in the triple digits during his pro debut, and he has solid to plus raw power that could produce 20 homers per season once he gets stronger. He'll need to refine his aggressive approach to reach his offensive potential. An average runner, Johnson plays a bit faster than that on the bases and in the field thanks to his instincts and a quick first step. He has the arm strength for shortstop but could lose a step once he matures physically, which could prompt a move to third base. Some scouts think he may retain his athleticism but be better suited for center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson comes from a baseball family, as his father Marcel played three years of pro ball and he's a cousin of Jimmy Rollins and Tony Tarasco. He works out with Rollins, who helped prepare him for the mental challenges of pro ball after the Marlins signed him for $1.35 million in the second round last June. One of the youngest players in the Draft, Johnson was still just 17 when Miami promoted him to low Class A for the final month of his debut. He's expected to miss the 2019 season after having surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his right leg in late March. Bat speed and natural talent stand out with Johnson, who has the makings of being a 20-home-run player. He regularly produced exit velocities greater than 100 mph in his pro debut, though he also struck out in 28 percent of his at-bats and needs to hone his approach. He has average speed and the savvy to be a threat for double-digit steals. The question will be how long Johnson remains at shortstop. He has a quick first step and enough arm to make plays there now, but his sturdy frame may eventually dictate a move to second base or perhaps the hot corner. Some evaluators believe he has the athleticism to wind up in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The injuries have piled up for the 2018 27th overall pick. Biceps tendinitis as a high-school senior. Shoulder surgery in the fall of 2019. Shoulder issues before the 2020 shutdown. Tommy John surgery in the spring of 2021. In the nearly four years since he signed for $3 million, Denaburg has managed only 20 1/3 innings at pro ball, all of which came in the Gulf Coast League in 2019. The good news: he was back to throwing off a mound this spring and is still eyeing a return to play in the summer. If he was healthy and at his best, Denaburg could have been right up there with Cavalli, Henry and Rutledge for the top arms in the system. He could ramp up his fastball to the mid-90s, sitting a little below that, and showed a high-spin hammerlike curveball that also earned above-average grades. His changeup was expected to be the last pitch in his repertoire to come along as he gained experience. Perhaps the Tommy John surgery will be the last procedure needed to get Denaburg into a place of regular health. Even if that’s the case, he’ll need time to regain his stuff and show average control again. The 6-foot-4 right-hander is entering his age-22 season, so he’s far from over the hill as a prospect, but he can’t afford many more lost seasons if he’s going to fulfill his promise as a future Nationals starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Denaburg very much fit the Washington profile when the organization took him 27th overall in the 2018 Draft. At 6-foot-4, he had the size to dream on but slipped some due to biceps tendinitis that limited his high-school senior season. The Nationals signed him for $3 million, going well above the $2,472,700 slot to do so. The injury news hasn’t gotten much better since. Denaburg underwent shoulder surgery in the fall of 2019 after throwing only 20 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League and had some other shoulder issues in the spring before the pandemic shutdown. The Florida native worked with pitching and rehab coordinators during the summer and participated in instructional league before struggling with fatigue. Unfortunately, the injury woes continued this spring as Denaburg underwent Tommy John surgery. He will miss the entire 2021 season as a result. When healthy, the right-hander will get his fastball up to the mid-90s, though he’ll typically sit a little below that. The curveball, which comes in in the high-70s, earns points for its high spin rate and its hammer-like manner when it’s on. The changeup continues to need development, and that will only come with experience. Denaburg needed innings in 2021 but will have to wait until 2022 for those to come. There is hope that the Tommy John surgery is what was needed to get him over the healthy hill, and if his stuff returns to its pre-procedure levels, there is still the chance of a Major League starter in his profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Denaburg showed promise behind the plate as a catcher and also served as his high school football team’s kicker and punter before emerging as one of top prep pitching prospects in the country ahead of his senior year. But a bout of biceps tendinitis limited Denaburg's time on the mound that spring, and as a result many teams steered clear of the right-hander when the 2018 Draft finally arrived. The Nationals were not one of those teams, as they selected Denaburg with their first-round pick (No. 27 overall) and signed him for $3 million, more than $500,000 above his slot's recommended value. After pitching with diminished velocity and stuff while struggling to throw strikes in 2019 during an abbreviated pro debut in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, Denaburg underwent minor surgery in the fall to clean up his right shoulder. When healthy, Denaburg has the look of a future big league starter with his blend of athleticism, stuff and remaining projection. Though his velocity was down in 2019, Denaburg has shown the ability to sit 93-95 mph and bump 97 in the past, throwing his heater with good life down in the zone. His breaking ball is a high-spin-rate hammer, an above-average pitch that he throws in the upper 70s with depth and finish, and he also shows feel for developing a nascent changeup. Denaburg should have at least average control based on the merits of his sheer athleticism and clean arm action. Denaburg is in good shape physically after the offseason procedure and is expected to be ready in time for the start of the 2020 season. He’s fallen behind the development curve a bit due to injury, though it hasn’t impacted his promising future as a potential No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Denaburg intrigued scouts as an athletic catcher before emerging as one of top high school pitching prospects in the country ahead of his senior year. While biceps tendinitis limited Denaburg's time on the mound in the spring, the Nationals, long rumored to have interest in the Florida prep, took him with their first-round pick (No. 27 overall) and then signed him for $3 million, more than $500,000 above his slot's recommended value. The club cautiously chose not send him out for his pro debut, instead giving Denaburg extra rest until instructional league, where he drew rave reviews from those who saw him. An athletic righty with two plus pitches and plenty of room to fill out, Denaburg has the look of a future big league starter. He's been up to 97 mph in the past with his fastball and typically sits 93-95, throwing his heater with good life down in the zone. His breaking ball is a high-spin-rate hammer, a plus pitch that he throws in the upper 70s with depth and finish, and he also shows feel for developing a changeup with average-or-better potential. Denaburg should have at least average control based on the merits of his sheer athleticism and clean arm action. In addition to his two-way exploits on the diamond, Denaburg was also the kicker and punter on his high school's football team. Such a multi-sport, multi-position background underscores just how much upside Denaburg has left to unlock now that he's focused on pitching full time. If it all clicks, he could be a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thomas was an infielder who only pitched a little bit when he signed with Cleveland for $200,000 out of the Bahamas in the middle of the 2016-17 international signing period. His elite arm strength landed him on the mound after he signed and was what the Pirates were interested in when they acquired him in November 2018 in the Jordan Luplow deal. He took a big step forward in rookie ball in 2019, but the 2020 shutdown seemed to impact him adversely as a move to High-A in 2021 did not go so well. Even though Thomas didn’t throw quite as hard in 2021 as he has previously, there’s still plenty of fastball to work with. He’ll easily sit in the mid-90s and regularly touch the upper-90s and has hit triple digits in the past, with his four-seamer showing very good life up in the zone. He has not made much progress with his secondary stuff. He does show a solid slider that can miss bats, but it can lose its shape, and while he has a changeup, it hasn’t developed much. While he’s an athletic 6-foot-4 presence on the mound, Thomas has struggled to repeat his delivery and his walk rate jumped in 2021. He’s still more thrower than pitcher and was deemed so far away that he wasn’t protected on the 40-man roster last offseason. His best track at this point is probably as a reliever, though the Pirates might let him keep going out as a starter so he can work on his complete repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: What seemed like a minor trade at the time has provided the Pirates with one of their most exciting pitching prospects. An infielder in the Bahamas who was put on the mound because of his arm strength by the Indians after signing him for $200,000 in December 2016, Thomas spent the summers of 2017 and 2018 in the Dominican Summer League and Rookie-level Arizona Leagues before being sent to the Pirates, along with infielder Erik Gonzalez, in return for Jordan Luplow and Max Moroff. He dominated the Rookie-level Appalachian League in his first year with the Pirates. It’s hard not to like Thomas’ combination of size, arm strength and athleticism on the mound. Thomas has continued to add velocity as he’s filled out his 6-foot-4 frame, and he averaged 96 mph with his fastball in 2019 and reached triple digits, showing good life up in the zone. He will need to rely less on that fastball and trust his slider, which flashes above average and misses bats, but can get slurvy at times, and he will have to commit to throwing his changeup. Thomas took a nice step forward in terms of his command the last time he faced real competition, cutting his walk rate tremendously. He needs more time working on his craft to become a complete pitcher, one who has the chance to be a dynamic starter if his secondary pitches continue to improve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thomas was mostly known as an infielder in the Bahamas, but the Indians loved his arm strength and signed him for $200,000 in December 2016 and put him on the mound knowing he’d be a bit of a project. After two summers in rookie ball, Thomas was sent to the Pirates in the deal that brought Erik Gonzalez to Pittsburgh for Jordan Luplow and Max Moroff after the 2018 season. The big right-hander took a big step forward in his first year with his new organization in dominating the rookie-level Appalachian League. Very athletic at 6-foot-4, Thomas may look more like a power forward at this point than a pitcher, but he made huge strides in terms of his overall feel for pitching while his stuff continued to tick upwards. In 2018 with the Indians, Thomas maxed out at 96 mph with his fastball. In 2019, that was his average, and he topped 100 mph, with excellent life up in the zone. He commanded the pitch much better, cutting his walk rate considerably compared to his first two summers. He was, however, too fastball heavy and often was reluctant to throw his other pitches. He has a pretty good slider, one that misses bats in the zone, but it can blend in with his curve into a less-effective slurve and he threw it only 10 percent of the time. He has a changeup, but it doesn’t do much currently. Thomas’ priority in 2020 will be the use of his secondary pitches, especially that slider. It’s rare for a conversion guy to end up as a starter, but the Pirates don’t want to rule it out given the progress he’s made and will continue to let Thomas start so he can build up innings and work on all of his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily an infielder as an amateur in the Bahamas, Thomas signed with the Indians for $200,000 and focused on pitching for the first time. Very much a raw project, he threw just 58 total innings in two pro summers before he was sent to the Pirates along with Erik Gonzalez in return for Jordan Luplow and Max Moroff. At 6-foot-4, Thomas is an extremely athletic and projectable right-hander who has a long way to go before fulfilling his potential, considerable as it might be. His fastball in 2018 clocked in the 92-96 mph range with life up in the zone and it's much more control over command with it right now -- he's around the strike zone with it, but not putting it where he wants it at all times. His low-80s slider flashes plus with good biting action to it. He hasn't shown much of a changeup, showing one around 85-87 mph the few times he's thrown it, another area of focus as he moves forward. Thomas is the epitome of a long-range project, but the feel for his stuff and his athleticism give him a chance to eventually get there as a starting pitcher. He'd be just the second Bahamian hurler to reach the big leagues and the first player of any sort from the country to get there since Antoan Richardson played briefly with the Yankees in 2014.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres signed with Cleveland for $150,000 out of Colombia in July 2016 and was traded to St. Louis two years later in a three-player deal that sent Oscar Mercado the other way. A promising hitter in the domestic complex leagues in 2018, the right-handed slugger struggled out of the gate with a jump to Class A Peoria in 2019 and moved back down to Rookie-level Johnson City, where he hit .286/.391/.527 in 33 games to end his age-19 season. Following the canceled 2020 season, Torres was pushed to Peoria (then a High-A club), got off to a solid start and faded down the stretch to finish with a .238/.302/.366 line and six homers in 97 games. Standing in at a listed 6-foot-4, Torres shows the most promise as a potential power bat with good raw pop, bat speed and natural strength out of his large frame. Those same long levers have caused him some issues in trying to sync up an approach at the plate, and he struggled with chasing pitches outside of the zone in 2021, causing even lackluster power numbers. The Cardinals maintain that Torres’ discipline could improve with more exposure to full-season pitching, and the lost pandemic year could have interrupted that necessary experience. Torres has been primarily a right fielder for much of his pro career because of just average speed, and he has the arm to play out there. He picked up six outfield assists from right in 2021 and nine in total across all three spots on the grass. While Torres will still only be 22 for the entire 2022 season, his position as a corner outfielder raises the need for him to start hitting more regularly and turning that raw power into in-game performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres impressed with Colombia’s 15-and-under national team in the Pan-American Championships and signed with the Indians for $150,000 in 2016. However, his prospect stock started to elevate in 2018 with a strong performance in the Rookie-level Arizona League. The Cardinals noticed the impressive stateside debut and acquired Torres and Conner Capel that July in exchange for Oscar Mercado. Torres raked during a short stint in the Gulf Coast League to finish 2018 and was rewarded with an aggressive assignment to begin 2019, though he didn’t fare well initially and was bumped down a level, where he got back on track. Torres got off to a fast start with High-A Peoria in 2021 and showed impressive strides in several areas of his offensive game. Torres, listed at 6-foot-4, has a projectable frame and enticing tools across the board. Bat speed and natural strength help generate power to all fields, though he sometimes has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone. He does show the ability to manage an at-bat and there is confidence that better plate discipline will come with time. While he has played all three outfield positions in his career, he profiles best in right field long term. There’s still plenty of room for growth, but he has the look of a future right fielder. The outfielder has limited experience in full-season ball and will need time to develop on both offense and defense, but the potential is there for Torres to become a regular contributor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres endeared himself to Indians international scouts with a strong performance for Columbia's 15-and-under national team in the Pan-American Championships. He signed for $150,000 the following summer and established himself as a rising prospect in 2018, showing a blend of loud tools and production in the Rookie-level Arizona League. The Cardinals, who had shown interest in Torres as an amateur, took notice of his development and acquired him and Conner Capel that July in exchange for Oscar Mercado. He struggled in the face of an aggressive Opening Day assignment to Class A Peoria in 2019 but fared much better in the more age-appropriate Appalachian League after a June demotion. At 6-foot-4, Torres is a physical specimen with across-the-board tools who has already started to grow into his projectable frame. He generates plus raw power to all fields from the right side of the plate, combining bat speed and strength with a leveraged swing. He can expand the zone at times but has the foundation of a solid approach that gives scouts confidence in projecting him as a player who hits for both average and power. Torres’ athleticism and average speed has allowed for him to play all three outfield positions early in his career, but, long-term, he profiles best in right field, where his plus arm strength is a clean fit. Torres will need time to develop his game on both sides of the ball, but he fits the profile of a big league right fielder to a T with his promising right-handed bat and strong arm. There likely will be some growing pains in his development along the way, but the final product could be that of an above-average big leaguer who offers value in all facets of the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians signed Torres for $150,000 in July 2016, roughly one year after the club watched the young outfielder play for Columbia's 15-and-under national team in the Pan-American Championships. He showed promise the next year during his professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, then established himself as a bona fide prospect with a strong showing in the Arizona Rookie League. Torres' performance caught the attention of the Cardinals, who had scouted him as an amateur, and they acquired him and Conner Capel in July in exchange for Oscar Mercado. Bumped up to the Cardinals' Gulf Coast League affiliate after the trade, Torres slashed .397/.493/.683 over 17 games. Torres is a physical specimen who has already started to grow into his projectable frame and had his tools improve as a result. A 6-foot-4 right-handed hitter, he generates plus raw power to all fields through a combination of bat speed, physical strength and solid feel for the barrel. He has the foundation of a solid approach, leading scouts to peg him as someone who could hit for average and power. Torres has average speed and moves well in right field, where his plus arm strength is a clean fit. With his power-over-hit offensive profile and cannon arm, Torres looks every bit the part of a future big league right fielder. He's very young, and therefore will need time to develop, but the long-term product could be an impactful, above-average player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $300,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2017, Toribio ranked third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 10 homers in his pro debut and then posted an .887 OPS and led the Rookie-level Arizona League with 45 walks in 51 games. His first foray into full-season ball didn't go as well last year, as he batted just .229/.351/.356 with seven homers in 94 Low-A contests. He's still just 21, so he has plenty of time to rebound, but the Giants didn't protect him on their 40-man roster during the offseason. Toribio still has a quick left-handed swing, outstanding hand-eye coordination and a patient approach, so he's still equipped to hit for average and power. He continued to generate high exit velocities in 2021, but he also struck out at a career-worst 28 percent clip and produced a lot more harmless grounders than he had in the past. Not only does he need to improve his frequency and quality of contact, but he also needs to solve left-handers after going 4-for-42 with 22 strikeouts against them last year. While his plus arm strength fits at third base, Toribio is losing some quickness and athleticism as he gets bigger and thicker. The game speeds up on him at the hot corner, where he made 40 errors in 118 starts during his first three pro seasons. He's a below-average runner who likely is destined for first base, which will put more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best player in the Giants' 2017 international class, Toribio signed for $300,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He placed third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 10 homers in his pro debut, then encored with an .887 OPS and an Rookie-level Arizona League-leading 45 walks in 51 games in 2019. He spent 2020 at San Francisco's alternate site and instructional league program. One of the best pure hitters among Giants farmhands, Toribio produces some of the highest exit velocities as well. He makes hard contact with a vicious left-handed swing and uncanny hand-eye coordination. He's beginning to develop some power to the opposite field and could produce 20 or more homers per season if he starts turning on more pitches and adds more loft to his stroke. While Toribio has the requisite plus arm for third base, he'll have to work to stay there. He's a below-average runner who likely will have to move to first base if he loses any quickness. San Francisco believes he can stick at the hot corner and toyed with the idea of trying him at second base, but scouts outside the organization question his range and project him as a first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the international penalty box for the second straight year after paying Bahamian shortstop Lucius Fox $6 million in 2015, San Francisco went to its $300,000 max bonus for seven players in 2017, the best of whom is Toribio. The Dominican ranked third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 10 homers in his first season as a pro, then posted an .887 OPS in his U.S. debut last year. He easily led the Rookie-level Arizona League with 45 walks in 51 games before getting promoted for the short-season Northwest League playoffs. Toribio might be the best pure hitter in the system and his exit velocity ranks with the best as well. He has a vicious left-handed swing but makes consistent contact because he has such good feel for the barrel, and he already uses the entire field well for a youngster. After he pulled all 10 of his homers in 2018, all he hit his last year went to the opposite field, and he could have 20-25 homer power if he turns on more pitches and adds a bit of loft to his stroke. Presently a below-average runner, Toribio will have to watch his frame because losing a half-step likely would mean he'd have to move from third base. His plus arm fits at the hot corner, but scouts outside the organization question his range and think there's a good chance he'll have to move to first base. The Giants believe he can remain at third and once toyed with the idea of trying him at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Restricted to giving out no more than $300,000 in individual international bonuses in 2017, the Giants paid the maximum amount to seven different prospects. The best of that group is Toribio, a Dominican who ranked third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 10 homers in his 2018 pro debut. Despite that slugging display, Toribio's hitting ability and approach may be better than his power. He shows good feel for the barrel from the left side of the plate and walked in 19 percent of his plate appearances in the DSL. He has nice loft in his swing, drives the ball in the air and could have 20-homer pop once he adds more strength. Though Toribio is a below-average runner, San Francisco believes he'll be able to remain at third base and may give him a chance to show what he can do at second base. His strong arm fits at the hot corner and his soft hands are another asset. He still makes youthful errors, no surprise because he'll be 18 all season, but should develop into an average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Overworked as a high school pitcher in Taiwan, Liu took two years off from the mound and concentrated on playing shortstop at Culture University. He resumed pitched in 2019, hit 98 mph with his fastball and won MVP honors at the Asian Baseball Championship after leading Chinese Taipei to its first championship in eight years. The Red Sox signed him for $750,001 after previously scouting him as an infielder and getting to know him via his relationship with former Boston infielder Tzu-Wei Lin. Liu lacked training resources during the 2020 pandemic layoff and his velocity was down in instructional league that fall and inconsistent in his pro debut last summer. His four-seam fastball ranged from 92-96 mph at times and 90-94 at others, showing some promising carry up in the zone. He arrived in the United States with six pitches, and the Red Sox have had to simplify things by focusing on his heater, a mid-80s slider that he can land for strikes or use as a chase pitch and a deceptive low-90s changeup with fade. Liu also has a curveball, cutter and splitter in his arsenal if he needs another option. He's more athletic than physical, but he repeats his easy delivery and throws strikes. His size, repertoire and pitchability prompted comparisons to José Berrios in the past, but he'll have to prove he can maintain quality stuff over a full season to live up to that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Worn down from overuse as a high school pitcher in Taiwan, Liu took two years off from the mound while playing shortstop at Culture University. Once he resumed pitching in 2019, he reached 98 mph with his fastball in September and won MVP honors at the Asian Baseball Championship in October after leading Chinese Taipei to its first title in eight years. The Red Sox, who had scouted him as an infielder and knew him well via his relationship with former Boston infielder Tzu-Wei Lin, signed him for $750,001 in October. Liu lacked access to training resources during the pandemic layoff and his velocity was down in instructional league last fall, though he still showed feel for an intriguing mix of six pitches: a fastball, a curveball, a slider he can turn into a cutter, a splitter and a traditional changeup that fades. His four-seam heater sat at 90-92 mph and topped out at 94 last fall, down 3-4 mph from the previous year, but it has sat around 94 and hit 97 in his pro debut this summer. Boston has tried to simplify his mix by having him focus on his low-80s slider and changeup as his secondary offerings in 2021. Liu lacks the typical physicality of a starting pitcher, but the athleticism that made him a prospect as a switch-hitting shortstop and his clean delivery help his cause. He repeats his mechanics with ease and produces solid stuff without much effort. Though it remains to be seen how his repertoire will hold up over a full season, his size, pitches and feel have prompted comparisons to José Berrios.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A promising high school pitcher in Taiwan, Liu wore down from overuse and took a two-year break from the mound while playing shortstop at Culture University. He resumed pitching in 2019 and hit 98 mph with his fastball in September, then earned MVP honors at the Asian Baseball Championship in October while leading Chinese Taipei to its first title in eight years. The Red Sox, who had scouted him as an infielder and knew him well from his relationship with Tzu-Wei Lin, signed him for $750,001 in October. Liu operates at 92-96 mph with riding action on his four-seam fastball. He also can overpower hitters with a slider that sits at 86-88 mph and shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch. His mid-80s splitter has similar upside if less consistency, and some evaluators prefer it to his slider. Though he's somewhat small for a starting pitcher, Liu has a clean delivery and repeats it well. The athleticism that made him a prospect as a switch-hitting shortstop helps him produce quality stuff and strikes without much effort. Boston likes his feel for pitching and may have him work on a curveball to give him a softer option in his repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the Royals scouted Europe in 2017 and ’18, they could not ignore the contact skills of a young player in Honkbal Hoofdklasse, the Netherlands’ top professional level. That hitter was Darryl Collins, and he signed with the Royals at 16 years old for $97,500 on Aug. 26, 2018. A year later, Collins tore up Rookie ball with a .320 average, and his first taste of full-season ball came last season, when he posted a .705 OPS in 86 games for Low-A Columbia. Collins’ advanced bat-to-ball skills are what sticks out for the rare baseball prospect from the Netherlands. His knack for hitting and his hand-eye coordination are what the Royals noticed when they were scouting him and what still stands out now even as he’s added strength and faced tougher pitching in the States. Still filling out his wide-shouldered frame, Collins has shown power potential too, with the ability to pull the ball better now than in ’19 when his swing was more closed off. Collins’ bat has always been ahead of his defense, and his fringy arm strength profiles best in left field. Collins projects to be more of a contact hitter and on-base player with occasional power, but the focus for him is his defense. He makes up for his arm strength with accuracy and good reads, and the Royals hope to get his arm to at least average for him to be able to play in the big league outfield -- because the bat-to-ball skills certainly have a place in the Majors. The good news is that Collins has good makeup and is still young, so time is on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Eastlake High School in Southern California, the same program that produced former No. 1 overall pick Adrian Gonzalez, Cavaco played his way into the first round in 2019 with a big senior season. Since being taken No. 13 overall, the infielder has had some trouble gaining much traction offensively, missing a good chunk of his first full season in 2021 with a concussion. A return to Single-A Fort Myers in 2022 resulted in a bit more power, though he also showed there’s plenty of work to be done. The right-handed hitter continues to show glimpses of the raw tools that made him a first-rounder in the first place, and he’s still learning how to tap into them on a more consistent basis. He has plenty of raw power, and he did set a career high in home runs in 2022 as he worked to correct some mechanical issues with his swing -- including a swing path that is too uphill and a tendency to bail in his stride. While he has had a better bat path at times, he still needs to be more selective at the plate and cut down his swing-and-miss after whiffing in 34.8 percent of his plate appearances in 2022. A shortstop in high school who had some skills to stick there, Cavaco made the move to third in 2022, where his plus arm should work just fine. He doesn’t turn 22 until next June, so there’s time for him to figure things out, with more reps needed for him to find a better level of consistency on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eastlake High School in Southern California has had two first round picks in its history. The first was Adrian Gonzalez, the No. 1 overall selection in 2000. Cavaco became No. 2 when the Twins took him No. 13 overall in the 2019 Draft before he struggled during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League that summer. While the shutdown kept him from playing in 2020, the Twins were very happy with the work he put in on his own and how he performed during instructional league play last fall. During Cavaco’s brief debut in 2019, the infield struggled to make consistent contact, with a tendency to get too uphill the biggest contributor to all of the swing-and-miss. During his time at instructs, he worked to flatten his swing a little, stay in the zone more and make more contact, showing promising strides in that area. That should allow him to tap into his considerable raw power more consistently moving forward. Cavaco worked on his body and his conditioning during the shutdown, showing up to instructs much leaner and more athletic. That gives the plus runner a better chance to stick at shortstop, with enough arm to stay at the premium position. There is a chance he’ll outgrow the spot and he could easily handle a move to third, where he played for most of his high school career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heading into the fall of his senior year at Eastlake High School in Southern California, Cavaco was a relative unknown on the Draft scene. He started putting himself on the map with a very strong showing at the Angel Elite showcase that fall and kept it going throughout his senior season, making him one of the biggest pop-up prospects in the Class of 2019. The Twins liked what they saw and took him with the No. 13 pick last June, signing him for a bit below pick value. He struggled during his pro debut as a minor quad issue slowed him and he never quite got rolling as a result. While he scuffled in his first summer as a pro, the reasons Cavaco rose into first-round consideration are still very much there, namely his athleticism and his overall tool package. He has the chance to grow into some serious power, with easily plus raw pop now from the right side of the plate. He’s going to have to refine his approach at the plate and his mechanics as there is some swing and miss in his game. He’s also a plus runner who gets down the line in a hurry and that could translate to some stolen bases down the road. Cavaco’s athleticism also helps him on the other side of the ball. He had primarily been a third baseman, and a good one with great hands, footwork and a plus arm. Then he showed he could play shortstop and after sending him out at the premium position during his pro debut, the Twins will keep him there as he begins his pro career in earnest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Michigan recruited Brewer as a wide receiver until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, which led to him playing two years of baseball at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before joining the Wolverines on the diamond in 2019. He led Michigan to within a victory of a national championship, won Big Ten Conference player of the year honors and went in the third round of the Draft. He played just 81 games in his first three years as a pro because of a toe injury he sustained in college and recovery from left knee surgery that also would have cost him the 2020 season had it been played. One of the best all-around athletes in the system, Brewer has the potential for at least solid tools across the board but needs more at-bats against quality competition to refine his offensive game. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power, but he doesn't have the smoothest right-handed stroke and will have to make better swing decisions. He does show a willingness to take walks and knows how to make the most of his well above-average speed on the bases. Though he definitely has the speed for center field, Brewer's defense also requires more polish. His reads and routes can get better, though his quickness helps him recover. He has the solid arm strength for right field should he move to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brewer drew interest from Michigan as a wide receiver until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, which led him to spend two years playing baseball at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before joining the Wolverines on the diamond in 2019. The Big Ten Conference player of the year that spring, he led Michigan to a stunning runner-up finish at the College World Series and went in the third round of the Draft. A toe injury he sustained in college limited his pro debut to 16 games, and surgery on his left knee last spring prevented him from attending instructional league. The fastest player and one of the best all-around athletes among Astros prospects, Brewer could have solid tools across the board if he can add some polish at the plate. His quick right-handed swing and strength create plus raw power, but his less-than-smooth stroke and aggressive approach lead to swing-and-miss concerns. He was less refined than a typical player coming out of college and injuries severely restricted his development opportunities in his first year and a half as a pro. Brewer's well above-average speed contributes to the possibility that he becomes a 25-25 player and gives him a chance to play in center field. He played mostly right field and first base for the Wolverines because of team needs, but could be an asset in center if he improves his reads and routes. A rare bats-right, throws-left player, he has the solid arm and the offensive upside to profile in right field as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, Brewer drew interest from Big Ten Conference football programs such as Michigan and Wisconsin. He focused on baseball for two years at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before transferring to Michigan in 2019, when he led the Wolverines to a shocking runner-up finish at the College World Series and was named Big Ten player of the year. A turf toe injury sustained during the spring limited him to 16 games in his pro debut after he signed for $500,000 as a third-rounder. Brewer has some of the best all-around ability in the system with the potential for at least solid tools across the board. He combines plus speed and plus raw power, giving him at least 20-20 upside. A right-handed hitter, he doesn't have the smoothest stroke and comes with some swing-and-miss concerns, but he also has quality bat speed and strength that produce hard contact to all fields. A center fielder in junior college, Brewer played mostly right field and first base at Michigan because of team needs. If he can refine his reads and routes, he has the quickness to be an asset in center. His solid arm and his offensive ability fit the right field profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a big senior season at Missouri, where he finished with a .930 OPS, Harris still didn’t get a ton of attention from teams. The Braves took a low-risk chance by drafting him in the 32nd round, signing him for just $10,000. He initially took the opportunity and ran with it, hitting his way to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball and performing well in the Arizona Fall League. The shutdown hurt his momentum and he didn’t replicate his success in a full season in Double-A, posting a .671 OPS in 2021. Harris’ calling card during that first full season was his knack for barreling up the baseball. He employs a simple right-handed swing when he’s in sync that leads to hard, line drive contact to all fields. He has some extra-base authority, with a little home run pop to his pull side, but he’s definitely a hit-over-power kind of guy. An average runner with an average arm, Harris has played both outfield corners as a pro, with left being a better fit. It’s more likely he can carve out a career as a fourth or fifth outfielder if he can get back to the offensive consistency that was his hallmark in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harris didn’t have much to show for his first three years at Missouri except an uptick in power production as a junior. When he posted a .930 OPS as a senior, the Braves took a flier on him in the 32nd round and gave him $10,000. He hit his way across three levels, reaching Double-A, in his first full season of pro ball, and then performed well in the Arizona Fall League. He wasn’t able to build on that momentum when the 2020 season was shut down and he wasn’t a part of the action at the Braves’ alternate camp. More than anything, Harris’ feel for the barrel is what stands out. He has a simple right-handed swing that allows him to make consistent hard contact and send line drives to all fields. There’s extra-base thump in his bat as well, with home run power more to his pull side, and there could be more raw pop for him to tap into to all fields. Harris is an average runner and is probably best suited to be a left fielder if he’s going to be a regular at one position. He worked on his conditioning and his defense during the shutdown, which should help him maximize opportunities to get his bat into a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two nondescript years at Missouri, Harris’ power showed up as a junior, though his 12 homers that season in 2017 didn’t lead to anyone drafting him. A stronger senior year didn’t exactly put him on the map, but it was enough for his hometown team, the Braves, to take him in the 32nd round of the 2018 Draft and sign him for $10,000. Since that point, all he’s done is hit, reaching Double-A in his first full season and more than holding his own in the Arizona Fall League in 2019. Undersized and stocky, Harris is the type of over-achiever who maximizes his tools and uses the fact he was not recruited or drafted earlier to fuel his ascent through the Braves system. He’s shown that he can barrel up the baseball against any level of pitching, using a simple swing to spray balls all over the ballpark. He has plenty of extra-base power to all fields and even though most of his home runs came to his pull side in 2019, he can clear fences to the opposite field and might eventually reach average power overall. He’s probably an average runner when all is said and done and he’ll have to continue to watch his conditioning given his body type. Defensively, Harris is probably best suited for left field, but he played a capable right field during his time in the AFL. He might be a fourth outfielder, but seeing him hit his way into an everyday role would surprise no one.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. Kelly made his full-season debut with Class A Kane County and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and a .199 average against, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. Kelly was challenged with a bump up to Double-A in 2021, and after starting the year on the injured list, he struggled to find a rhythm in Amarillo. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly looks the part of a future big leaguer. In his first year in the system, he pitched with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggled to square up due to its angle and late life. His velocity dipped early in 2021, but after making some mechanical adjustments, it came back and even started to tick up to the mid-90s in the second half of the season. His two-plane slider is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering that registers in the low to mid-80s with hard bite and plays well off his fastball. The organization sees potentially three dominant pitches and Kelly has shown a willingness to mix in his split more, key to his possible future as a starting pitcher. Consistency was an issue for Kelly in 2021 as he struggled to throw strikes. The D-backs rave about his work ethic and he’s shown flashes of returning to form. After starting his career in the rotation, Kelly was shifted to the bullpen in 2021. The D-backs aren’t ruling out him developing into a starter, but at the moment, it looks as though Kelly’s future will come in a relief role, where he could play up his fastball/slider combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. Arizona seldom assigns high school pitchers right to Class A, but Kelly debuted with Kane County and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and .189 opponents’ average, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. Kelly was challenged with a bump up to Double-A in 2021 and after starting the year on the injured list, he struggled to find a rhythm in Amarillo. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly already looks the part of a future big leaguer. In his first year in the system, he pitched with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggled to square up due to its angle and late life. His velocity dipped early in 2021, but after making some mechanical adjustments, it started to come back in the second half of the season. His two-plane slider backed up a bit this season, but at its best, it is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering, registering in the low- to mid-80s with hard bite, and he knows how to use it in concert with his heater. The organization sees potentially three dominant pitches and Kelly has shown a willingness to mix in his split more which is a key if he wants to be a starting pitcher. Kelly made a big impression on the big league staff at the alternate training site in 2020, but consistency has been an issue in 2021. The D-backs rave about his work ethic and he’s shown signs of getting back to who he was in 2019 and ‘20. There are questions as to whether he’ll ultimately wind up in a rotation or a bullpen and his ability to consistently harness his stuff will go a long way toward answering those.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. He was deemed advanced enough to jump straight to Class A Kane County for his first full season -- an assignment Arizona seldom gives to its high school pitchers -- and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and .189 opponents’ average, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly already looks the part of a future big leaguer. He pitches in and out with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggle to square up due to its angle and late life. His two-plane slider is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering, registering in the low- to mid-80s with hard bite, and he knows how to use it in concert with his heater. Kelly’s tendency to fall in love with the pitch makes his sequencing too predictable at times, which is why club officials view the right-hander’s changeup development as a key for him to take the next step. While it is currently a distant third pitch, Kelly throws it with splitter-like action that plays nicely off of his fastball. Kelly's max-effort delivery raises questions about his control and command profile and has led some evaluators to peg him as a future bullpen piece. But the big right-hander has already simplified his mechanics and thrown more strikes than expected in pro ball, and the D-backs are quick to praise his determination and work ethic, qualities that could go a long way in helping him remain a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene starred at the 2019 Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad, propelling him to the Mets in the supplemental second round a year later. New York traded him to the Guardians along with Andrés Giménez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January 2021, so his pro debut came with his second organization. He has one of the higher ceilings among the system's outfielders but will require time to develop. Greene has some natural feel for hitting and makes consistent line-drive contact from the left side of the plate. He employed an extremely patient approach in his debut, drawing 35 walks in 43 games while repeatedly using the opposite field. He has enough bat speed and projectable strength to deliver 15-20 homers per season if he looks to turn on more pitches and launch them in the air. While Greene has plus speed, he's still learning how to get the most out of it as a basestealer and center fielder. He's smoothing out his reads and routes in center, where his quickness helps him recover from some of his mistakes. His fringy arm strength is playable in center field but precludes him from right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene's athleticism stood out on the prep showcase circuit in 2019, when he starred at the Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad. The Mets made him a supplemental second-round pick last June and signed him away from a Missouri commitment for $850,000. His only experience with the Mets came in instructional league before they traded him to the Indians along with Andrés Gimenez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January. Greene has the hand-eye coordination and line-drive-oriented left-handed stroke to hit for average. Scouts believe he relied more on natural ability than swing mechanics or approach as an amateur, giving him the opportunity to improve quickly as he gets more instruction in pro ball. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop 15-20 home run power, especially if he adds some more loft. With speed that earns plus and even some well-above-average grades from some evaluators, Greene is aggressive on the bases. His quickness helps him outrun some of his mistakes, but he needs to improve his reads and routes in center field. If he doesn't, his fringy arm strength will relegate him to left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring at San Jacinto Junior College in 2018, Soularie went on to Tennessee and was one of the best offensive players in the Southeastern Conference the following year. His shortened 2020 season wasn’t as explosive, but the Twins liked his tools enough to take him in the second round. They still haven’t really gotten a great look at him, as ankle and foot injuries limited him to just 34 games total in 2021. Soularie does have some skills from the right side of the plate when he’s healthy. He controls the strike zone very well and showed a propensity for drawing walks even in his brief pro debut last year. He’s capable of making a lot of contact with more of a line drive approach. Power did show up during his time at Tennessee, but he needs to get more physical in order for him to drive the ball with a wood bat in his hands. While Soularie doesn’t have blazing speed, he has good instincts on the basepaths and has shown he isn’t afraid to steal a base. He has pretty solid instincts, both in the outfield and at second base, with many thinking the latter is a better long-term option given his lack of arm strength. He could continue to get reps in both spots, with a full healthy season of reps needed to truly evaluate who he is as a prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soularie first truly appeared on the Draft map after he hit over .400 at San Jacinto Junior College in 2018. He moved on to Tennessee the following year and was among the Southeastern Conference leaders in average, on-base percentage and slugging. He wasn’t swinging the bat as well before the shutdown in '20, but the Twins had seen enough to take him in the second round, ahead of where projections had him. During his time at San Jac and then at Tennessee, Soularie has shown a very advanced approach at the plate, with a knack for barreling up the baseball. He’s geared more for line drives to all fields than power, though he tapped into his raw power as an amateur, hitting 16 homers in just over 250 at-bats with the Volunteers. His selectivity helps all of it play up, as he walked more than he struck out at Tennessee. Soularie doesn’t possess a lot of speed, but what he has, he uses well, and he likes to be aggressive on the basepaths. Defensively, he played center field at San Jac and mostly left at Tennessee, but while the Twins feel he has a good feel for the outfield, they plan to let him develop as a second baseman, where he worked out some in college. He’s shown good feel, hands and instincts, with the main concern being his below-average arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman at Arkansas, Martin finished with a .974 OPS and 13 homers. He hit 15 more during his 2019 sophomore season, though saw his strikeout rate tick up, a trend that continued during a rough 2020 that of course was shortened by the pandemic. He had shown first-round caliber tools, but went to the third round as teams were worried about his ability to hit, where the Phillies gave him $1.3 million to keep him from going back to school. The offensive woes continued in his first full season as he posted a .601 OPS while battling an ankle injury for most of the season. With his ankle repaired, the Phillies were hoping to get a real sense of who Martin is as a professional, though he once again struggled with the bat in 2022. At the very least, a return to health will let him use his close to top-of-the-scale speed more consistently, being a legitimate basestealing threat and covering a lot of ground defensively. There’s tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate, but he needs a swing overhaul and to tone down his swing and not sell out for power so he can cut down his tendency to swing and miss and chase pitches out of the zone. While Martin spent time on both sides of second base during his pro debut, the Phillies believe he has the tools to stick at shortstop long-term, with enough range and arm for the position. He’s played third in the past and has the speed to patrol the outfield if need be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A talented yet raw prospect from the Arkansas high school ranks in 2017, Martin jumped on the national stage quickly at the University of Arkansas, hitting 28 homers over his first two seasons with the Razorbacks. A premium athlete, Martin’s slow start in 2020, combined with concern about his hit tool, forced him to slide to the third round, where the Phillies went well over slot to keep him from going back to school in 2021. One of the fastest players in the Class of 2020, Martin got some 80 grades from scouts on the 20-80 scouting scale. He’s still learning to use his speed on the basepaths to be a true threat to steal, but when you combine it with his wiry strength and raw power, it’s easy to dream on a player who could be a 25-25 type threat in the future. To get to his power, he will have to cut down on his swing-and-miss, as he had a tendency to swing for the fences too often and get too uphill. At instructs, he worked on staying in the zone longer and swinging at strikes more consistently. Similarly, Martin can let things speed up a bit on the defensive end. But he has more than enough range and arm strength to play shortstop and the Phillies didn’t see anything that pointed to him needing to move from the premium position, though he played third in college and has the athleticism to handle center field if the need arises.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals selected Infante with the 71st overall selection in the 2020 Draft, using a compensation pick they acquired after losing Anthony Rendon in free agency, and signed the Miami commit to an above-slot $1 million bonus. While the club was impressed by his early skills coming out of that process, Washington kept Infante in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League for his first season, and it was clear he needed to overcome a learning curve in pro ball. The right-handed slugger hit just .215/.329/.364 with three homers and a 30.1 percent K rate over 37 games in his first taste of the Minors. Technically because of Infante’s lack of experience, everything said about him going into 2021 remains true. With decent bat speed, Infante has the look of a potential average hitter someday, and he projects to add some more power as he matures. But to get to his offensive ceiling, he will need to shorten his swing in hopes of barreling more balls in the zone. He still shows at least average athleticism for an infield prospect, and his move to third base this season at Single-A Fredericksburg had more to do with a deep list of low-level shortstops than it did Infante’s own defensive abilities. Infante was already old for the high-school segment of his Draft class, and he turned 21 in his second Minor League season. He has the power to fit a corner profile but will need to find a batter way to hit for average, if he’s going to meet the higher offensive threshold away from shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals received the 71st overall pick in the 2020 Draft as compensation for losing Anthony Rendon in free agency and grabbed Infante at that spot, signing him to a $1 million bonus (slightly above the $884,600 assigned to the slot).
