Infante is the sixth-highest pick ever out of Monsignor Edward Pace High School in Miami. Four of the five who went higher made the Majors. The fifth is top Red Sox prospect Jeter Downs. Like Downs, Infante is an infielder, albeit less of a lock to stick at short in the long run. The Nationals are going to give him plenty of opportunity to stay at the six, but with a plus arm and just average speed, a move over to third base could be in the cards down the line. After a brief look at last year’s instructs, Washington came away pleased with Infante’s bat path and average bat speed that is expected to develop well in time. That could lead to average power as he gets more exposure to the pro side. There were some pre-Draft questions about Infante’s hit tool due to contact concerns, but the pieces are there for it to be closer to average. Infante is a classic example of a player who can do many things well, if nothing quite at a plus level. The Nats were impressed by his baseball IQ coming right out of the Draft and think it will help him make the necessary adjustments to find a home on a Major League infield some day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a struggle for Miller to get development time on the field since the Reds took him with the 65th overall pick in the 2020 Draft and signed him away from his Wake Forest commitment for an above-slot bonus of $1.29 million. He’s had hernia surgery and ulcerative colitis, an intestine disorder, and he’s had to deal with COVID, reasons why he managed just seven plate appearances in 2021. The good news is the Reds are excited because he seems fully healthy for the first time since being drafted. If he is 100 percent, Miller has the chance to show off a solid all-around toolset at a premium position. He’s a left-handed hitter with a buggy whip of a swing and a solid approach. There’s strength and raw power to tap into and his line drives to all fields should turn into in-game power as he continues to create more leverage at the plate. Miller is athletic and runs well, especially for a catcher, even if he slows down a tick as he catches more. Miller has the tools to stick behind the plate, too. He has very good hands with good blocking and framing skills, and the Reds like his baseball IQ as well. He has plenty of arm strength with accuracy to come with more reps. There’s still big league regular backstop upside here, with him taking his first real step forward in that direction in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: J.W. Mitchell High School in Florida has had a pair of pitchers make it to the big leagues, Tyler Clippard and Jared Shuster, but before Miller was the Reds pick in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2020 Draft, it had never even had a position player selected. The third prep catcher to be taken in last year’s Draft, Jackson signed for a bit over slot, but wasn’t able to participate in instructional league play because of COVID. A left-handed hitting backstop, Miller could develop into a solid all-around catcher. He’s more of a gap hitter right now, one with a good approach and understanding of the zone who can send line drives to all fields. There is some present strength and he should be able to add more to his athletic frame, pointing to more power as he understands how to create more leverage in his swing. He might slow down with the wear and tear of catching, but he’s an average runner as of now who likes to run the bases. Miller’s athleticism should help him behind the plate, providing the agility for him to improve his blocking and overall receiving. He has an above-average arm as well, giving him every chance to become a big league regular, with an understanding that high school catchers can take a long time to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonnin began his career pitching out of the Arkansas bullpen, but wanted the chance to start, one he got when he transferred to Texas Tech for the 2019 season. He had mixed results in the Red Raiders’ rotation, but showed enough premium stuff for the Reds to take him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. He threw well across two levels of A-ball in his first full season, but managed to amass just 47 innings due to a broken rib suffered as part of his high-effort delivery. Shoulder issues limited him to just 25 IP in 2022. The right-hander has had that rib removed, but now has to get his shoulder healthy so he can go back to using his dominant two-pitch mix to miss bats. He struck out 13.6 per nine in 2021 relying on his fastball-slider combination. The heater touches 97 mph with impressive riding action as a result of that crossfire delivery. His slider is also a plus pitch that cuts across the plate. He does have a distinct curve he’s worked on and he’ll have to show he can use his seldom-used changeup in the future. While there are concerns about Bonnin’s ability to remain a starter because of his delivery, he tends to repeat it well and threw strikes fairly consistently last year. The Reds plan has been to let him continue to start, knowing he’ll have to show he can handle a full workload and command the baseball deep into outings in order to become a No. 4 type starter. If not, that fastball-slider combination could be very nasty in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way standout as a high schooler in Texas, Bonnin began his college career pitching out of Arkansas’ bullpen as a freshman. Seeking a chance to start, he transferred to Texas Tech and was a member of the Red Raiders’ rotation as a sophomore and in his shortened junior season, with mixed results. The Reds saw enough starter qualities to draft him in the third round of the 2020 Draft and signing for just below slot before sending him to get his feet wet in instructional league play. From a pure stuff standpoint, Bonnin does have what’s needed to start. His fastball touches 97 mph with riding action coming from his crossfire delivery. He couples that with a plus slider that cuts across the plate. While he showed a greater feel for that pitch at instructs, he also improved the depth of his curve, making it a more serviceable offering and his changeup can be average as well. Bonnin worked on his command and control at instructs and made strides on that front, focusing on his tendency to overthrow. There is effort in that delivery across his body, but he’s athletic enough to repeat it. It’s definitely control over command, but the Reds think both are projectable enough to be close to average, giving him a chance to start long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the fastest and most athletic high schoolers in the 2020 Draft, he also came with concerns about his physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), swing and strong commitment to UCLA. That enabled the Dodgers to take the local Southern California product with the 100th overall choice and sign him for a well-over-slot $1,622,500. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Low-A, where he hit .231/.323/.339 with a 30 percent strikeout rate and 12 steals in 76 games. Vogel's best tool is his plus-plus speed and he ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase. He's a potentially dynamic basestealer and could become a plus defender in center field once he refines his reads and routes. His plus arm is stronger than most in center. Vogel had an awkward load in his right-handed stroke when he turned pro, and Los Angeles is trying to help him smooth it out with some mechanical changes. He has good hand-eye coordination and can display electric bat speed at times, but he must get stronger so he can impact the ball more regularly. He did add 15 pounds this offseason, though he'll also need to develop a more patient approach to get going at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the better athletes in the 2020 Draft, he lasted until the third round because he lacked physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), missed a lot of the summer showcase circuit with a back injury and had a strong commitment to UCLA. The Dodgers pounced on the Southern California prep product with the 100th overall pick and signed him for a well over-slot $1,622,500. He was the youngest player (age 18) at their alternate site during the summer and performed well in instructional league. Vogel ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase and consistently displays plus-plus speed. He uses his quickness to create chaos on the bases and cover a lot of ground in center field, where his instincts could make him a plus defender. He also has a plus arm, stronger than most in center, and can play anywhere in the outfield. Vogel has both offensive upside and work to do at the plate. In addition to his quickness, which should help him get on base, he also can flash some electric bat speed and shows feel for recognizing pitches. He has an awkward load in his right-handed swing that can lead to swings and misses, however, so Los Angeles will try to smooth out his stroke and get him to drive the ball more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murray earned Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as a sophomore and junior in 2017 and ’18 at Kent State, going a combined 15-3 with 251 strikeouts over 170 2/3 innings across the two seasons. After going in the eighth round to the Blue Jays and signing a $169,600 bonus, Murray carried his success right into the Minor Leagues in short-season ball, posting a 1.75 ERA over 25 2/3 innings. In ’19, Murray established himself as a legitimate prospect with a 2.75 ERA over 137 1/3 innings, striking out 169 batters between Low-A, High-A and Double-A. He had a shot at impacting the MLB club in ’21, but elbow issues wiped out nearly his entire season. Those are now behind him entering ’22. The headliner with Murray is the “invisiball,” a fastball with an incredibly high spin rate that allows him to blow hitters away up in the zone despite sitting in the low-90s. Murray’s fastball had ticked up to the 92-93 mph range, but the right-hander could look more natural slightly below that, so his velocity is worth monitoring throughout ’22. A 12-6 curveball is Murray’s second-best weapon while his slider is close behind and the changeup is still developing. There’s certainly bullpen potential for Murray, with a multi-inning role appealing, but the Blue Jays will keep him as a traditional starter to open the ’22 season as he builds back up. Murray’s fastball is an MLB-ready pitch and he’s a proven producer at each level of the Minor Leagues, so even though he was left off the 40-man roster this past offseason, he’ll be a candidate to jump onto it if he’s pitching well at any point in ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After logging 39 innings as a true freshman in 2016, Murray garnered Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as both a sophomore and junior, going a combined 15-3 in 30 starts with 251 strikeouts in 170 2/3 innings between the two years. The Blue Jays selected Murray in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, signed him for $169,600 and watched him continue to dominate in his pro debut with the Vancouver Canadians. Murray split the ’19 season between three levels, posting a cumulative ERA of 2.75 over 137 1/3 innings with 169 strikeouts. He missed much of the first half of 2021 with an elbow sprain but avoided surgery and returned to the Minor League mound in August. Murray’s greatest tool is his fastball, which has an elite spin rate. This “invisiball” is an excellent weapon up in the zone and has taken another step forward with a recent velocity bump that sees Murray sitting in the 92-93 mph range. This isn’t typically the velocity that would blow hitters away, but the spin rate is what makes it special. A 12-6 curveball with good bite is Murray’s best secondary pitch. Murray will also feature an average slider while his changeup has shown encouraging development, and he's also working on a cutter that's becoming effective. One of the most unique evaluations in the Blue Jays’ system, Murray made great use of the shutdown in 2020 and will now have a shot to prove that his fastball can fool more advanced hitters in the upper Minors, too. A multi-inning relief role is possible, but the Blue Jays still see Murray as a starter, giving him multiple paths to the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hajjar was a solid pitching prospect while in high school in Massachusetts, but opted not to sign with the Brewers as a late-round choice in 2018 to honor his commitment to Michigan. He missed his freshman year after tearing his ACL playing pickup basketball, but came back and led the Wolverines rotation the next two years. While his stuff wasn’t super-sharp, he led the Big Ten in strikeouts in 2021 and landed in the second round of the Draft, where the Twins signed him to full slot. He was missing a lot of bats, albeit with a surprisingly high walk rate, in Single-A when he was part of the crop of prospects the Reds got from the Twins in return for Tyler Mahle at the Trade Deadline. The big lefty didn’t throw an official pitch for the Twins after a full workload at Michigan, but they were thrilled to see his stuff tick up in the short time they worked with Hajjar after he signed. While his fastball averaged around 90 mph in college in 2021, he was more around 93 mph, touching a bit higher, in bullpen sessions with the Twins, though he was averaging around 92 mph in the Florida State League this year. He can miss bats with all of his secondary offerings and he used his plus low-80s changeup with good tumble and his upper-70s curveball effectively last year. He’s been working to add velocity to his low-80s slider and to focus on adding lateral movement to it so it can be a better weapon against left-handed hitters. Hajjar’s overhand delivery creates deception, making him a tougher at-bat. He generally has a good feel for pitching, though he’s struggled with walks during his full-season debut, with a good chance to improve improve his command as he progresses, with perhaps more in the tank as he keeps adding strength to that 6-foot-5 frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most colleges recruited Barefoot as a pitcher, so he chose Campbell because it was the lone school that offered him a chance to hit. He missed his first season recovering from ankle surgery before starring as a redshirt sophomore in 2018, winning batting title in the Big South Conference (.364) and Cape Cod League (.379) as well as the Cape MVP award. He had an injury-marred pro debut after signing as a sixth-rounder in 2019, then saw his OPS decline from 1.017 in Low-A to .895 in High-A to .525 in Double-A during his first full pro season last year. A rare bats-right/throws-left player, Barefoot has a busy swing but makes it work thanks to his hand-eye coordination. Predominantly a contact hitter in college, he's now looking to launch balls in the air, which has resulted in inconsistent production and a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first two years as a pro. He was overmatched in his first taste of Double-A and will have to make better swing decisions in order to realize his 20-homer potential. Barefoot is deceptively athletic and can flash plus speed and arm strength. He's an aggressive baserunner who used his quickness to steal 21 bases in 25 attempts in 2021. He can play an average center field but fits better in right, where he's a solid defender and shows off an arm that was clocked up to 94 mph during his brief stints on the mound at Campbell.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Berryhill's college career took him from Georgia Southern to Walters State (Tenn.) CC to South Carolina before he signed with the Reds for $149,500 as a redshirt sophomore in 2019. After the Astros acquired him in exchange for Cionel Perez in January 2021, he won the organization's Minor League Player of the Year award by batting .295/.413/.562 with 15 homers in 73 games at three levels. An aspiring country singer, he performed the national anthem before games at Low-A Fayetteville and High-A Asheville last season. Berryhill started seeing the ball better last year once he started wearing contacts. His best tools is his plus raw power from the right side of the plate, and he started getting to it more consistently once he started making adjustments to close a hole at the top of his strike zone. He concentrates on launching balls to his pull side, which led to a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first full pro season, but he also draws a healthy number of walks. Surprisingly athletic for a 6-foot-1, 227-pound catcher, Berryhill has below-average speed and runs the bases well. Though he's relatively inexperienced behind the plate, he has soft hands and decent receiving skills, while his arm is fringy. He profiles as an offensive-minded backup who also can handle first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 45 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 A solid three-year career at Georgia Tech that saw him hit .355 or better in each season led to Guldberg’s selection by the A’s in the third round of the 2020 Draft. Injuries limited his first full season with the organization to just 48 games played in 2021, batting .259 with five home runs and 18 RBIs. Guldberg’s lean and wiry body makes him a fun player to watch. His pure hitting ability along with sneaky extra-base authority allows him to hit basically anywhere in the order. Good speed is also part of his game as he nabbed 11 stolen bases in 12 attempts last season. The soft tissue issues that Guldberg dealt with in college continue to creep up with the A’s, which is a bit of a concern. A favorite of many within the A’s system during the instructional league in terms of players to watch on a daily basis, getting healthy and staying on the field will be the biggest key to his progression.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a solid junior year as a starter at Stetson in 2017, Wilson was a late-round pick of the Rangers, but decided to return to college for his senior year. Moved into the closer role, he saved 20 games and became an intriguing money-saving senior sign option, one the Braves took in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft, signing Wilson for $80,000. He pitched well in the lower levels during his summer debut and in 2019, but jumped onto the prospect map with a stronger 2021, landing a spot on the 40-man roster. His momentum was stopped this spring when he needed Tommy John surgery, ending his 2022 season before it began. Wilson had success early in his pro career without much velocity or a true out pitch. He fine-tuned his delivery and that’s unlocked more mph, as he sat at 93 mph a year ago. But the biggest reason for Wilson’s success was him dusting off a seldom-used splitter and throwing it a lot in 2021. It became his go-to pitch, thrown with good depth and tumble, and was a big reason why he struck out 15.1 per nine for the season. He will also fold in a get-me-over curve to steal a strike on occasion. While he doesn’t have pinpoint command, Wilson throws enough strikes to be successful at the upper levels of the system. He might be a bit of a one-trick pitch reliever, but it’s a nasty enough of a pitch where the Braves think he could contribute to the big league bullpen once he returns to the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Collins starred at McKinney Boyd High School in Texas and looked like he might be headed to Oklahoma State for college ball. The Braves loved his speed and feel to hit enough to nab him in the eighth round of the 2021 Draft, signing him for an above-slot $447,500 and making him the first ever draftee from his school. Collins returned their faith in him by hitting .347/.424/.453 with 12 steals in 23 Florida Complex League games. The left-handed hitting outfielder’s calling card is his speed, which is nearly close to top of the scale. He’s a legitimate basestealing threat who registers very low times from home to first and uses his legs well to stretch singles to doubles and doubles to triples. He can make a lot of contact, but is content to spray the ball around the field. He’s not likely to ever be a big power guy, but added strength will help him impact the ball more consistently. Collins’ speed is also an asset in the outfield and while he’ll need to sharpen his reads and routes, he does have the chance to stick in center field. If he can keep getting on base and get strong enough to drive the ball a little, he could profile as an intriguing table-setting type in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After McCants signed for an over-slot $800,000 in the third round of the 2021 Draft, his older brother, T.J., could go in the same range as a sophomore-eligible at Mississippi in 2022. A Florida high school product, McCants is more advanced than his sibling was at the same stage of their careers. His struggles during his pro debut in Rookie ball indicate he'll need time to develop, but his athleticism and upside were evident. McCants has an efficient left-handed swing and repeats it well. He also has a disciplined approach and can beat out grounders with speed that grades as at least plus, so he should hit for average. He currently focuses on putting balls in play and uses the opposite field a lot, but once he packs some needed muscle on his projectable 6-foot-1 frame and learns to turn on pitches and drive them in the air, he could grow into 15-homer power. McCants still is learning how to maximize his quickness on the bases and in the field. He possesses shortstop actions and soft hands, but his average arm has led to him getting more action at second base in his first full pro season. The Marlins are loaded with young shortstop prospects, so he'll likely end up at second or in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Allen will be a hero at Mississippi State forever after leading the Bulldogs to their first College World Series championship in 2021, when he also won the Southeastern Conference batting title (.383) and player of the year award. One of the top hitters on the 2019 U.S. collegiate national team that included four of the first 14 picks in the 2020 Draft, he went unpicked in that reduced five-round event after breaking his hamate during the pandemic-shortened college season. Though he turned 23 a month before the 2021 Draft, he still drew a lot of interest as a gifted hitter who would come with a discount, and the Marlins grabbed him for a below-slot $247,500 in the fourth round. Though he looked tired after a long college season and his timing was off when he batted .189 in Low-A during his pro debut, Allen was one of the best pure hitters in his college class. Using a compact left-handed stroke and uncanny hand-eye coordination, he controls the strike zone and drills line drives from gap to gap. He has enough bat speed and strength to produce average power, but he struggled to lift balls in the air during his first taste of pro ball. After displaying fringy speed and athleticism earlier in his college career, Allen focused on improving those aspects of his game during his pandemic downtime. He now clocks solid run times on a consistent basis and has bolstered his range on the outfield corners, where he's an average defender with a fringy but accurate arm. He played first base in his first two seasons at Mississippi State and also saw brief action at third base with the Bulldogs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A defensive standout during his days at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Meyer was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 167 Draft prospect in the 2018 Draft and went right around that spot in the sixth round (170th overall). He struggled offensively in his first two trips to the Minors but started to show some offensive improvements in 2021, finishing with a .251/.337/.324 line and three homers in 62 games between Double-A and Triple-A. He wasn’t added to the 40-man roster when he first became Rule 5-eligible last November. It’s defense, defense and more defense when it comes to Meyer’s profile. He regularly shows good hands in his receiving behind the plate and moves well back there as well, which comes in handy with blocking. His arm strength is at least above-average, and it plays up even more because of his ability to record impressive pop times. It’s a strong defensive base for a catching prospect. Unfortunately, Meyer’s bat hurts his case to play a more prominent role. He makes contact at a decent rate (striking out 17.9 percent of the time in 2021) and takes his walks (9.3 percent), but that’s about where the positives end. Meyer has a history of putting the ball on the ground more than half the time and isn’t a threat to post a slugging percentage much above .350. That said, backstops with Meyer’s glovework will always get jobs as backups at the top level, and as he heads into his age-24 season, the former Mustang isn’t far off from helping the Mets in that way. They can’t allow him to carry a roster spot, however, until he can be slightly better offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peroza played out of Carlos Guillen’s academy in Venezuela before signing with the Mets for $280,000 on July 2, 2016. He moved stateside in his first Minor League season after a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, but it was a slow climb from there. Because of late development and the 2020 canceled season, the right-handed slugger didn’t see full-season ball until last year. It was at Low-A St. Lucie that he put up his best numbers yet -- .274/.404/.442, seven homers in 64 games. His numbers after a promotion to High-A Brooklyn were slightly stifled by an extreme pitchers' environment at Coney Island. It’s a classic power-first, corner-infielder profile. Peroza’s top exit velocity at Low-A was 110.6 mph, and he had two of the six hardest hit balls by a St. Lucie batter, despite his limited experience there. He shows natural strength from his 6-foot-1, 221-pound frame, and he plays into it with good lift at the plate. (Of his batted balls in St. Lucie, 42.3 percent were fly balls.) He showed promising patience with a 12.6 percent walk rate between the two levels, but that also led to him striking out in about a quarter of his plate appearances. That K rate could go up as he climbs toward Queens. Peroza’s above-average arm makes him a good fit for third base, though a lack of speed and range may move him to first, especially considering the Mets’ Minor League depth at the hot corner. His trajectory when it comes to getting the raw power to play in games will get him a chance to fight for a place in the New York infield hierarchy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies signed Azuaje out of Venezuela for $400,000 as part of an aggressive 2018-19 international signing period for the organization that saw them hand out bonuses of six figures or more to 15 players. He had a solid, if unspectacular, debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, missed 2020 because of the shutdown, then came to the United States and the Florida Complex League in 2021, where he swung the bat well, albeit in a 19-game sample. Small and stocky, Azuaje reminds some of former big league infielder Placido Polanco in terms of body type. He makes a ton of contact with a hit-over-power approach from the right side of the plate, showing the ability to send line drives to all fields. He’s had some home run pop show up, with five homers in 45 at-bats in the FCL, but he can get too overly aggressive at the plate and will have to keep refining his approach. When the Phillies first signed Azuaje, he was a plus runner with 6.5 speed. He’s physically matured and slowed down to be more of an average runner, though he’s worked to get in better shape. While he’s played three infield positions in his brief career, his best spot is second, the position he has the greatest chance to become an offensive-minded regular at.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals signed Luis García, Yasel Antuna and Israel Pineda -- one prospect graduate and two Top 30 stalwarts -- as part of their 2016-17 international class. Méndez, a $600,000 signing out of Venezuela, did not quite make the same noise on the professional scene during the early years of his career. That changed in 2021. The 5-foot-10 outfielder hit .287/.343/.440 with five homers, 36 total extra-base hits and 11 steals in 85 games at Low-A and High-A. His 111 wRC+ was third-best among Nats Minor League qualifiers. It’s the hit tool that drives Méndez’s rise to prospect prominence these days. He exhibits a repeatable swing from the left side, allowing him to display strong bat-to-ball skills. While he did strike out roughly a quarter of the time in 2021, Méndez does make decently hard contact when he strikes the ball, leading to an average hit projection. Double-digit homers might be a stretch with the power and launch angle playing more to gaps than over the fence. With above-average speed, Méndez is a threat to steal and can cover ground in the outfield. He played all three spots last year, but his below-average arm plays better in left or center. Nationals officials have drawn comparisons to Grégor Blanco, the 10-year Major Leaguer who was light on power but added speed and defensive value. That would be a positive outcome at its most extreme for Méndez, but it paints a picture of what type of player he could be if the 2021 gains continue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barley was known primarily for plus run tool when he signed with the Padres for $1 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2016. He was raw in every other aspect of the game, and that remains true nearly seven years later. The 6-foot infielder has yet to crack above Low-A ball, and it’s at that level that he spent the entire 2021 season. San Diego dealt Barley to Washington at the 2021 Trade Deadline in a move for Daniel Hudson, and while he managed only a .205/.312/.303 line in 33 games with Low-A Fredericksburg, he was still named the Nationals’ Minor League Baserunner of the Year with 12 steals in that timeframe. Barley uses a twitchy, uppercut swing designed to get the most of his above-average raw power. Sometimes, it leads to some impressive drives to left field. All too often, it leads to an unhealthy amount of strikeouts, specifically a K rate of 29.8 percent last season. The right-handed slugger did start to walk more in 2021, but it’s still going to take some significant improvements in his overall approach for him to become an average hitter. The speed continues to be dynamic; Barley ranked fifth in Low-A with 45 stolen bases in 2021. After their early looks, the Nationals believe their still relatively new prospect can stick at shortstop because of his range and strong arm, but developing defensive consistency will be key after Barley was error-prone in 2021. Perhaps the change of scenery is what will do Barley best, and Washington is ready to make him part of its rebuild movement. Considering Barley has been Rule 5-eligible and unprotected in each of the last two years, the clock is ticking for the 22-year-old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Ueckert logged a 6.17 ERA as a 23-year-old McNeese State senior in 2019, his arm strength intrigued the Cubs enough for them to sign him for $5,000 in the 27th round. He didn't get past Rookie ball in his pro debut and lost a year of development to the pandemic shutdown, so he began 2021 as an almost-25-year-old in High-A. He finished it in Double-A with a combined 1.45 ERA and 37 strikeouts in 31 innings between the two stops and turned himself into a legitimate prospect. Opponents batted just .129/.228/.238 against Ueckert, who took to some mechanical changes and came back from his layoff with dramatically improved stuff. His fastball gained 3-4 mph and now sits at 95-97 mph and reaches 99 with good carry in the zone. He backs it up with a short slider that often climbs into the low 90s and ties up both left-handers and right-handers. Ueckert has gotten stronger and has cleaned up his delivery since signing, which gave a boost to not only his stuff but also his control. He cut his walk rate from 5.7 per nine innings in two years at McNeese State to 4.6 in his debut to 3.5 last season. If he can build off his momentum from 2021, he could pitch in the big leagues this year and develop into a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson’s amateur career didn’t start out in any real noticeable way, not getting scouted or recruited out of his Tampa high school, then not playing every day at Northwest Florida State Junior College. It wasn’t until he erupted in his Atlantic Coast Conference debut following his transfer to North Carolina that he landed on scouts’ radars. A solid overall spring with the Tar Heels landed him with the Reds in the sixth round and he made his way to full-season ball during his pro debut. The right-handed hitting outfielder has athleticism to spare, which helps him on the basepaths and in the outfield. He’s an easily plus runner who should be a basestealing threat and has the skills to play center field for a very long time. He’s more athletic and fluid in games than he is in practice, and that translates to his work at the plate as well. While Thompson does have solid average raw power, the question is if he’ll hit enough to get to it. He’ll work counts, but he’ll also swing and miss quite a bit, making it tougher to project enough offensive upside for him to be a big league regular. He’s a bit of a tweener as a result, but could end up being a very good fourth outfielder who provides speed and excellent defense at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as an 18-year-old out of the Mexican League in July 2017, Castaneda didn’t get his first starting experience until the 2019 Arizona Fall League. He held his own as an inexperienced hurler in that prospect finishing school (1.99 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 29 strikeouts in 22 2/3 innings) and locked in the transition last year. Castaneda struck out 27.7 percent of the batters he faced for High-A Wisconsin, but he proved to be homer-prone, leading to a 5.20 ERA and a 5.07 FIP in 97 innings. Even after a late-season cameo at Triple-A Nashville, he was left off the 40-man roster last November when eligible for the Rule 5 Draft, and he was left off once again this November after another stint in the upper Minors. Castaneda doesn’t tower over batters at just 6-foot-1, but he can show decent velocity with a fastball at 92-94 mph. The heater can also feature decent arm-side run, and that can be a problem for his fellow righties. The splitter is far and away Castaneda’s standout pitch because of the way it divebombs below hitters’ hands with very little spin. He also sports a more traditional changeup, but it’s the split that shows the most promise. A below-average curveball is thrown for little more than show. The Mexico native is coming off his age-23 season, so he has some road ahead of him. He’s a likely two-pitch hurler at the top level, and that would point back to the bullpen. Castaneda might need to add more velocity to be effective there, or else hope the splitter on its own is good enough.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A .333 hitter over his two seasons as a leadoff man at Texas Tech, Holt inspired something in Brewers scouts because -- despite not being ranked among MLB Pipeline’s Top 200 in the 2019 Draft class -- he signed for $450,000 (the third-highest bonus given out by Milwaukee that year) as a seventh-rounder. After not being an instructional league standout in 2020, Holt certainly played to his strengths in his first full season last year, hitting .283/.403/.341 with 17 steals and a 52/68 K/BB ratio in 97 games at High-A and Double-A. In case that last stat didn’t make it clear, Holt hates to strike out. With two strikes, he will get wide in his left-handed hitting stance and choke up to spray the ball anywhere in play, bucking modern trends. As a result, he fanned only 11.8 percent of the time between Wisconsin and Biloxi last season for the best K rate among Milwaukee full-season qualifiers. Of course, Holt needs to be a big-time contact hitter because he showcases little raw power; only 18 of his 102 hits last season went for extra bases. A part-time outfielder in college, Holt split his time between second and third base in 2021. Despite good speed to help with range, he doesn’t quite have the hands to stick up the middle, meaning he might have to spend more time at the hot corner. He has the arm for the position, if not the traditional offensive profile associated with it. Whether it’s his speed or contact rate, Holt finds little ways to put his stamp on games, and it’s in those margins that he might carve out a Major League infield role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A teammate of fellow Cardinal Lars Nootbaar at USC, Lunn didn’t become a starter until his junior year in 2019, and he posted a 3.69 ERA with 79 strikeouts in 83 innings that spring. The Cardinals selected him in the 11th round and signed him for $125,000 -- the max they could without dipping into their bonus pool. Lunn’s full-season debut had to wait until 2021, and he spent it entirely with High-A Peoria, where he was a strike-throwing machine, especially late. He walked only five batters over his final 10 starts with the Chiefs and finished with a 3.96 ERA with 121 strikeouts and 20 walks over 120 1/3 frames. His 4.1 percent walk rate led Cardinals full-season qualifiers and was second among High-A starters. The 6-foot-3 right-hander won’t necessarily bowl anyone over with stuff. He throws around 90-92 mph with the fastball, though it features good ride at the top of the zone and he spots it well. A mid-70s, loopier curveball tunnels well off the heater, leaving some High-A hitters shaking their heads heading back to the dugout. He’ll throw the occasional low-80s slider as well to give another breaking-ball look, though it doesn’t pop the same way as the curve, and a mid-80s, though occasionally firm, changeup helped him keep pretty solid splits against righties and lefties. The strike-throwing ability is what makes Lunn pop, and it was certainly encouraging the way he grew into that skill as 2021 went on. It’s control over command, though, and he can get occasionally rocked if the stuff is too much in the zone, especially the fastball. The control will keep him in a starting role as he enters the upper Minors, but if the stuff is to truly tick up, a move back to the bullpen for the first time since 2018 might be in the cards down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $80,000 out of Mexico in the 2016-17 international period, Ruiz flew under the radar in a Padres class that also included Adrian Morejon, Michel Baez, Gabriel Arias and Tucupita Marcano. Ruiz put together a few average years in his introduction to pro ball, but broke out early in 2021 with a career-high 15 homers over 72 games for High-A Fort Wayne. He was promoted to Double-A, where he hit another six homers, but struggled over 35 games to end the season. Ruiz has a sound swing from the left side, though he’s yet to hit above .253 for a full-season club. He certainly takes his free passes with walk rates around 10 percent at every Minor League stop, and that helps the hit tool some. A slight leg kick and an improved fly-ball rate helped the pull-side power tick up in 2021, though he has a tendency to lose his approach and increase his strikeout rate when he starts trying to hit for too much power. Ruiz has played all three outfield positions, but profiles best in either center or right as he runs well and has an above-average arm. A lack of a true plus tool could limit Ruiz from being an everyday starting outfielder in the Majors, though his ability to play all three outfield spots could earn him a roster spot as a fourth outfielder, especially if he continues to make strides with the bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mets in 2016 out of Bonao, Dominican Republic, Espino debuted in the Dominican Summer League in ’17 and hit .267 with a .772 OPS over 64 games. He spent his next two summers in the GCL and Appalachian League, hitting .267 and .251 without much power to show for, then was selected by the Blue Jays in the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft prior to the ’21 season. With the Blue Jays, Espino took off, hitting .295 with eight home runs and an .859 OPS between Low-A and High-A in ’21, splitting his time between third base and left field. With some savvy scouting, the Blue Jays added a physically imposing 21-year-old who’s already shown more power potential than he ever did in the New York organization, where he hit just four home runs in his first three seasons. Espino is physically imposing at 6-foot-2 with an above-average arm, making the left side of the diamond a natural home for him. The consistency of Espino’s contact will be one of the most important factors to his development, but there are some enticing tools here if he can find some consistency. Espino remains a high-upside project for the Toronto player development staff, but it’s an accomplishment just to have him in the system as a Minor League Rule 5 pick. He’ll be tested by more advanced Double-A pitching this year and there’s still a very wide range of outcomes for Espino at this point, but he holds a valuable spot in an organization needing outfield prospect depth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dominguez was ancient by international standards when he signed with the Brewers at age 20 for $7,500 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2016. He had spent three seasons in Rookie ball when Milwaukee flipped him to the White Sox two years later along with outfield prospect Bryan Connell to acquire Xavier Cedeno in August 2018. He pitched at the upper three levels of Chicago's system in 2021, though he got shelled in two Triple-A starts in September and again during the Arizona Fall League. Though he's 6-foot-4, Dominguez utilizes a lower three-quarters arm slot that imparts good induced vertical break on a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 with late life. He throws two breaking balls, with his 82-85 mph slider that features more depth than sweep grading better than his 75-79 mph curveball. He can flash some average changeups with fade, but his cambio gets too firm and he has trouble landing it for strikes. After averaging 3.4 walks per nine innings in his first four pro seasons, Dominguez cut that rate to 2.2 in 2021. If his improved control is for real, he has a chance to become a back-of-the-rotation starter. If not, he's likely a fastball/slider middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending 2017 as Louisville's No. 2 starter behind fourth overall pick Brendan McKay, McClure went to the White Sox in the sixth round of the Draft. He lost most of his first full year as a pro to a knee injury that required surgery and displayed pedestrian stuff in his second, but he impressed with added velocity in instructional league following the cancelled 2020 season. He handled Double-A last year but got rocked in Triple-A, so Chicago opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster. McClure sat around 90 mph with his fastball in 2019 before jumping to 92-95 during instructs the next fall, and he maintained that velocity for most of last season. Though his heater has some armside run, it doesn't miss many bats. His most effective offering is a solid mid-80s slider/cutter with depth. McClure needs to find a secondary pitch that can counteract left-handers, but neither his upper-70s curveball nor his sinking mid-80s changeup was up to the task in 2021, when he seemed to lose faith in the latter. He also didn't throw as many strikes once he started getting knocked around in Triple-A, and he's starting to look more like a two-pitch reliever than a back-of-the-rotation starter. His fastball and slider could play up in shorter stints and he could provide some big league bullpen help in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Gonzalez didn't attract a lot of scouting attention as a Puerto Rican high schooler, the White Sox liked him enough to sign him for an over-slot $185,000 in the 12th round of the 2019 Draft. After looking overmatched in his pro debut that summer, he fared much better in his return to Rookie ball in 2021, more than doubling his OPS from .483 to .988. He struggled again following a promotion to Low-A, so his development is going to take time. Few White Sox prospects can match Gonzalez's combination of raw power and speed, both of which grade as plus. The right-handed hitter is still unrefined at the plate, focusing more on launching balls to his pull side rather than prioritizing hard contact. He won't make nearly enough of his bat speed and projectable strength unless he reduces his 37 percent strikeout rate from his first two pro seasons. While Gonzalez still is learning how to make the most of his quickness on the bases, it's more apparent in the outfielder. He exhibits solid range and an average arm in center field. He shifted to right field in Low-A in deference to speedster James Beard and is capable of handling all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 To date, the 2015-16 international amateur signing class is known mostly for producing stars like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Juan Soto, not to mention 2019 American League Rookie of the Year Yordan Alvarez and former No. 1 overall prospect Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Javier signed for more than any of those current big leaguers, getting $4 million from the Twins in July 2015. He’s had trouble staying on the field since, with a hamstring injury slowing him during his 2016 debut, a torn labrum costing him all of 2018 and a strained quad keeping him from making his full-season debut in 2019 until late May. He did pick up 300 at-bats, but had very little to show for it numbers-wise. Outside of a strong showing in the Appalachian League in 2017, all talk about Javier has been about potential and not production and he’s missed the reps needed to develop. He is capable of making loud contact and driving the ball. Some power did show up in 2019, especially to his pull side. He’s also shown an ability and willingness to draw walks, but he needs to work on pitch recognition and making more consistent contact, as his strikeout rate was close to 34 percent last year. When he’s been able to get out there, no one questions his ability to stay at shortstop for a very long time. He’s extremely comfortable at the premium position, with good hands, footwork, more than enough range and a very strong arm. The ingredients of an everyday shortstop at the big league level are still all there, but he needs to stay on the field for a full season to get moving in the right direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 There was obvious excitement when the Twins aggressively pursued Javier, one of the top prospects in the 2015-16 international class, and signed him for $4 million in July 2015. Since then, however, there have only been glimpses of what he can do. The talented infielder missed most of his first summer, in 2016, because of a hamstring injury, then re-set a high bar by being one of the best prospects in the Appalachian League in his United States debut in 2017. Momentum was halted when a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder kept him off the field for all of 2018. Because the injuries have limited his time on the field, Javier is a bit of a wild card. Once he can shake the rust off, there is confidence he'll once again show his considerable offensive upside. He makes consistent hard contact with a natural feel to hit and while as a young player without that many reps, he'll need to refine his approach. He does work counts and draw walks. As he fills out, his bat speed and potential plus hitting tool could lead to at least average power. Fortunately, Javier's injury wasn't to his throwing shoulder, so his plus arm should be just fine. Whether he outgrows the position remains to be seen. With a clean bill of health and no setbacks from his injury, Javier should be ready to show what he can do over the course of a long season. Getting at-bats and reps in the field is priority number one for now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Being ranked as one of the top international amateur prospects comes with certain expectations, and Javier was ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international list in 2015. Signing for a franchise-record $4 million dollars also raises the bar some. Javier's pro career started with a small roadblock, as a hamstring injury limited him to just nine games in the Dominican Summer League in 2016. He was one of the best prospects in the Rookie-level Appalachian League during his United States debut in 2017, starting to show what all the fuss was about. He wasn't able to repeat that performance in 2018 as a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder forced him to miss the 2018 season. When healthy, Javier has shown an outstanding feel to hit and an ability to make consistent hard contact to all fields. He is continuing to refine his approach at the plate, but he has drawn walks and there is confidence he'll cut his strikeout rate as he figures things out, to the point where some feel he could be a plus hitter in time. As he physically matures, he should be able to use his bat speed to tap into considerable raw power as well. While he still has some growing to do, he has all the skills needed to be a long-term shortstop. How that will work with Royce Lewis and Nick Gordon in front him remains to be seen, but for now, his focus will be on getting reps and staying healthy in the lower levels of the Twins' system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 After giving Javier, No. 12 on MLBPipeline.com's Top 30 International Prospects list in 2015, a franchise record $4 million bonus, the Twins were excited to see this talented infielder get his career started in the Dominican Summer League last year. A hamstring injury kept that from happening for the most part, as Javier appeared in just nine games, but he was able to make his United States debut in the Appalachian League in 2017. Now back to full speed, Javier can start showing off all of his considerable tools. He has shown the ability to make consistent hard contact with plus bat speed, and many think he could be an above-average hitter with more reps and perhaps even above-average power as he continues to add strength. He is more than athletic enough to stay at shortstop, perhaps even if he grows some more, and could follow in the footsteps of other big shortstops who stuck there. There's still a very long way for Javier to go before he lives up to his ceiling or the expectations that can come with a $4 million price tag. The first order of business is staying on the field. If that happens, the tools should take care of the rest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two-plus seasons have passed since Perez was the headline prospect in the Justin Verlander trade, instantly becoming Detroit’s top-rated prospect. He has thrown 27 innings over nine appearances since that deal thanks to injuries. A lat strain and shoulder inflammation shelved him for much of 2018, save for seven short midsummer appearances. After an impressive appearance in big league Spring Training, Perez suffered right shoulder tendinitis, a recurring issue that limited him to two rehab starts at Class A Advanced Lakeland in 2019. That he remains ranked speaks to the potential that earned him a $1 million signing bonus from the Astros out of Venezuela in 2014, just two years after converting from hitter to pitcher. For all the injuries, he has never needed surgery, keeping his valuable arm intact. Whenever Perez has been able to pitch, his potential has been evident. With a 6-foot-3 frame and fluid mechanics, he can overpower hitters with a 93-95 mph fastball or flummox them with a sharp curveball. His changeup could develop into a third pitch if given a full, healthy season to work on it. He also spent the offseason working on a slider. The lone silver lining to the injuries is that his time in the weight room has allowed his body to mature and fill out. The Tigers still viewed Perez as an important part of their future rotation a year ago. If he can develop into a Major Leaguer at this point, he might be a bonus. His durability concerns could move him to the bullpen, but the Tigers simply want to get him back on a mound at this point to see what he has. He still his age on his side, having just turned 22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez didn't become a full-time pitcher until he was 15 years old, after spending much of his amateur career as a third baseman, but he took quickly to the new role and received $1 million to sign with the Astros in 2014. He subsequently blossomed into one of the organization's better pitching prospects and had already reached Double-A at age 19 in '17 before being the marquee prospect sent to the Tigers in the Justin Verlander trade at the end of August. The high expectations for Perez's 2018 Tigers debut were quickly dashed by a lat strain that kept him out until late June, and he pitched only 19 1/3 innings upon returning before the club shut him down for the year in late July with right shoulder inflammation. Following the season, Perez was added to the Tigers' 40-man roster. Perez has four pitches at his disposal when he's healthy, all of which he can throw for strikes. He generally throws his lively fastball in the 92-94 mph range, but he can reach back for 95-96 mph when he needs to. Added velocity could come as he matures. He can really spin his curveball, a future plus offering, and he's taken to a relatively new slider as well. He throws his above-average changeup with solid fade. With an athletic and repeatable delivery, he should continue to command the ball well even if he adds velocity. Perez used his time on the shelf to add strength to his already strong frame, and he was able to resume throwing off flat ground with no ill effects in December. But right shoulder tendinitis sidelined Perez out of the gate in 2019, and while he returned to the mound for Lakeland in May, he was placed back on the disabled list with shoulder woes after just one start. The good news is that he's still young and has a relatively high floor as a mid-rotation-type starter, albeit one with major concerns about his long-term durability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A third baseman early in his amateur days, Perez didn't become a full-time pitcher until he was 15 years old. He took to it quickly, earning $1 million to sign with the Astros in 2014. The best term to describe the young right-hander has been precocious, as he has shown an advanced feel for pitching given his age. He reached Double-A at age 19 in 2017 before being the marquee prospect sent to the Tigers in the Justin Verlander trade at the end of August. Excitement for his Tigers debut in 2018 was dampened by a lat strain that kept him out until late June, then it became a lost season when he was shut down for the year in late July with right shoulder inflammation. Perez has four pitches at his disposal, all of which he can throw for strikes. He generally throws his lively fastball in the 92-94 mph range, but he can reach back for 95-96 mph when he needs to. Added velocity could come as he matures. He can really spin his curveball, a future plus offering, and he's taken to a relatively new slider as well. He throws his above-average changeup with solid fade. With an athletic and repeatable delivery, he should continue to command the ball well even if he adds velocity. The Verlander trade happened too late for Perez to make his Tigers debut in 2017, and the injury kept the Tigers from seeing the real Perez in 2018. He still has a relatively high floor as a mid-rotation-type starter and is just 20 years old for all of 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Perez attended Carlos Guillen's training academy in Venezuela, the former All-Star initially stationed him at third base. He became a full-time pitcher a year later at age 15, showing enough promise that the Astros signed him for $1 million in 2014. Very advanced for his age, he was the only 18-year-old to make 10 starts in the Class A Midwest League in 2016 and he reached Double-A in 2017 before being sent to the Tigers in the Justin Verlander trade at the end of August. Though he's just a teenager, Perez already demonstrates feel for four offerings. His most consistent pitch right now is his lively fastball, which sits at 92-94 mph, peaks at 96 and could add more velocity once he physically matures. His downer curveball projects as a future plus pitch, his fading changeup shows similar upside and his slider is developing nicely. The athleticism that made Perez a prospect as a corner infielder has translated into an easy delivery that he repeats well. He throws a lot of strikes and commands the bottom of the zone. He has the upside of a No. 3 starter and is on pace to reach the big leagues at a very young age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Brown pitched to mixed results during his three years at Kentucky while working as both a starter and reliever, Brewers scouts identified him as someone with untapped potential who could start in pro ball. Sure enough, Brown made steady progress in the role early in his career before breaking out in earnest in 2018 at Double-A Biloxi, where he garnered Most Outstanding Pitcher honors in the Southern League after he led the circuit in ERA (2.44) and ranked second in WHIP (1.06) and BAA (.210). All signs pointed to Brown contributing in the big leagues going into the 2019 season, but instead the right-hander regressed on all fronts in Triple-A, posting a 5.79 ERA and 1.73 WHIP over 116 2/3 innings. The Brewers chose to not add Brown to their 40-man roster after the season, and he went unselected in the Rule 5 Draft in December. The confidence Brown exhibited during his impressive 2018 campaign just wasn’t there in Triple-A, as he struggled to both get ahead of and put away hitters. Rather than attacking hitters as he had done in the past, Brown spent the year nibbling at the zone with non-competitive pitches as he tried to avoid getting hit hard. The Brewers even took Brown offline for part of July, hoping that a brief hiatus might help him right the ship, but he didn’t fare any better when he returned, with his strikeout and walk rates continuing to trend in the wrong direction. The good news is that Brown’s stuff was largely the same, as the right-hander sat 92-95 mph with his fastball, flashed plus with his curveball and mixed in his changeup effectively. He stayed healthy, too, accruing at least 110 innings for a third straight year, and generated ground balls at a 54.2 percent clip that was only slightly behind his 2018 mark (56.5 percent). The Brewers are optimistic about Brown’s chances of rebounding in 2020 and will continue to develop him as starter, knowing that they could try him in a full-time bullpen role if that doesn’t work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown pitched to uneven results during his three seasons at the University of Kentucky while working as both a starter and a reliever. Intrigued by his untapped potential, the Brewers made him their third-round pick in 2016, signing him for a shade over $400,000. After reaching Class A Wisconsin in his pro debut, Brown excelled in his return to the Midwest League in 2017 and received a late-season promotion to Class A Advanced Carolina, where he put a bow on his first full season with four solid outings. Moving up to Double-A in 2018, Brown broke out as he garnered honors as the Southern League's Most Outstanding Pitcher after he posted a circuit-best ERA (2.44) and finished second in WHIP (1.06) and BAA (.210). Brown confidently attacks hitters on both sides of the plate with a 92-95 mph fastball and holds his velocity deep into starts. He adeptly manipulates the pitch as dictated by the situation, as he'll either turn it over to create sinking action to induce weakly hit ground balls -- something he did at a 55.6-percent clip in 2018 -- or reach back for some extra velo to get whiffs with his four-seamer. His curveball is his best offering, a plus pitch, and he also has feel for a promising changeup that contrasts nicely against his heater. The Brewers have long been impressed with Brown's competitiveness on the mound and, more importantly, his ability to make adjustments and improve the deeper he worked into games. His delivery isn't the cleanest but also doesn't cost him control or command, so he should be able to remain a starter. If not, Brown's fastball-curveball combo and deceptive delivery could make him a late-inning weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs took a 38th-round flyer on Brown in the 2013 Draft, knowing that he likely would honor his commitment to the University of Kentucky. He did just that, but pitched to uneven results during his three seasons with the Wildcats while working as both a starter and a reliever. Intrigued by Brown's untapped potential, the Brewers made him their third-round pick in 2016, signing him for a shade over $400,000. After reaching Class A Wisconsin in his pro debut, Brown excelled in his return to the Midwest League in 2017 and received a late-season promotion to Class A Advanced Carolina, where he put a bow on his first full season with four solid outings. Brown has made strides as a professional in developing and locating his solid three-pitch mix. He pitches with a 92-95 mph fastball to both sides of the plate and did a better job holding that velocity deep into games in his first full season. He's adept at manipulating the pitch, too, as he'll turn it over to create sinking action at times while reaching back for extra velo with his four-seamer as dictated by the situation. His curveball, though currently underused, is a plus pitch, and he also has feel for a promising changeup that contrasts nicely against his heater. Brown's detractors believe that he'll end up in the bullpen on account of his high-effort delivery. The Brewers, however, believe he can stick as a starter, and they were impressed with his intensity on the mound and ability to improve the deeper he worked into games. Should that not happen, Brown's fastball-curveball combo and deceptive delivery could make him a late-inning weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lora offered the best raw power in the 2019 international class and the Rangers pulled off a trade to make sure they had the money to sign him. They shipped a pair of depth right-handers to the White Sox for injured Nate Jones last July, assuming $2.5 million in salary obligations while obtaining $1 million in bonus pool cash. They agreed to terms with Lora on a $3.9 million bonus in August and officially finalized the deal in September. More massive than his listed 6-foot-3 and 190 pounds, Lora is built like Joey Gallo and has the potential to do similar damage at the plate. He has uncanny bat speed and strength for a 17-year-old, producing elite exit velocities and huge right-handed power to all fields. His aggressive mentality does create some swing-and-miss concerns. Though he's huge for his age, Lora moves surprisingly well for his size. He has been clocked as fast as 6.7 seconds in the 60-yard dash and could have fringy to average speed once he's physically mature. He projects as an average defender on the outfield corners and may have enough arm strength to handle right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolf opened eyes when he hit 97 mph in his first appearance as a senior at St. Thomas High (Houston) in 2019, and he parlayed a strong spring into an above-slot $2.15 million bonus from the Mets as a second-rounder. He dazzled during his abbreviated pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he struck out 12 of the 33 batters he faced, and again in instructional league following the canceled 2020 Minor League season. The Indians acquired him as part of a four-player package in the January trade that sent Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco to New York. Adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and lowering his arm slot has helped Wolf’s stuff take off. Those changes increased the velocity and movement on his fastball, which ranged from 90-97 mph with armside run during the spring and averaged 94 mph during his pro debut. He has a second future plus pitch in a curveball that registers in the low 80s with 12-to-6 break when he stays on top of it. Wolf's changeup isn't as effective as his other two pitches, though he can flash some solid ones with fade and tumble that point toward it becoming at least average. Wolf’s athleticism, quick arm and clean delivery enable him to pitch to both sides of the plate and all four quadrants of the strike zone, and he earns high marks for his aptitude with regards to making adjustments. He has plenty of room still to add strength to his projectable frame and should continue to get better with those physical gains as well as his development on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been three players from the William Penn Charter School in Philadelphia to make it to the big leagues. Within the last two years, the school has churned out a pair of outfielders from the same family who hope to be the next to get there. Sammy Siani was taken in the Competitive Balance Round A in 2019, a year after his older brother Mike was the Reds’ fourth-round pick, then went and began his Pirates career in the Gulf Coast League. The Pirates scouting staff really liked Siani’s ability to barrel up the baseball on a consistent basis and believe he’s really going to hit at the next level. He has a good feel for and command of the strike zone with a smooth swing from the left side of the plate. He’s definitely hit over power right now and it will be interesting to see how his ability to impact the ball changes as he fills out physically, with some thinking there is power to come from his smallish frame. The Pirates liken Siani’s pure hitting ability to fellow Bucs prospect Cal Mitchell’s, noting that Siani has much more speed. He also has the ability to play center field, where he should get considerable time as his pro career progresses, while continuing to show he can handle all three outfield spots more than capably.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A fifth-round pick out of Oklahoma Baptist in 2014, Merryweather was on the cusp of the Major Leagues with Cleveland going into the ’18 season before needing Tommy John surgery. The Blue Jays acquired the right-hander mid-recovery after the season in the trade that sent Josh Donaldson to the Indians. Excited about the all-around impressive stuff Merryweather has in his tool box, Toronto didn’t get to see much of it last season, when his return was delayed after two rehab outings showed that he wasn’t yet ready. He reappeared in the Arizona Fall League, where his fastball velocity, changeup, slider and command impressed and helped him to eight strikeouts over six innings. Merryweather’s best weapon is his mid-to-high-90s fastball, with a changeup that is one of the best in the organization. The changeup is a weapon against left-handed hitters especially, with good arm speed and tailing action. His curveball flashes plus and his pure talent has team officials excited. He found success with his slider in the Fall League and the club hopes to see a lot more of it. Merryweather uses his height to get good angle and finish at the top of the zone. Throughout his pro career, Merryweather has shown good feel for the strike zone, consistently putting up decent strikeout numbers while limiting walks and hits. If he can stay healthy, he has a chance to slot into the back end of a big league rotation, with a move to the bullpen representing a nice fallback option for the right-hander.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Merryweather pitched at Skyline College for two years before transferring to Oklahoma Baptist, where he dominated as both a junior and senior while leading the program to a third-place finish in the 2014 NAIA World Series. A fifth-round pick by the Indians that June, Merryweather made slow but steady progress early in his career before breaking out in 2016 with an All-Star campaign in the Class A Advanced Carolina League that earned him a second-half promotion to Double-A Akron. He performed well in his return to Akron in 2017, but struggled over 16 starts in his first exposure at the Triple-A level. Impressed with his stuff and progress, Cleveland added Merryweather to its 40-man roster after the season. However, the right-hander will miss all of 2018 following his Tommy John surgery in mid-March. Merryweather pitches with a plus fastball that sits at 93-96 mph and at times touches higher, all while using his height to create downhill plane to the plate and generate ground-ball outs. He throws a pair of breaking balls in a curveball and a slider, though neither is particularly advanced and they bleed together at times. Merryweather's changeup is arguably his best secondary offering, flashing above average at times, but lacking in consistency overall. Though big and physical, Merryweather repeats his delivery well and has a long track record as a strike-thrower. He will, however, need to improve his fastball command as well as the quality of his strikes after International League hitters tagged him for 105 hits (12.5 H/9) and 13 home runs (1.5 HR/9) in 78 innings. Should Merryweather be unable to make the necessary adjustments to remain a starter, the right-hander's power arm could make him an effective late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 Merryweather's Draft stock steadily improved during his senior year at Oklahoma Baptist, where he posted a 1.07 ERA with a 0.85 WHIP and 11.8 strikeouts per nine while leading the program to a third-place finish in the 2014 NAIA World Series. The Indians made him their fifth-round pick that June. After two pedestrian seasons to begin his career, the right-hander broke out in 2016, earning All-Star honors in the Carolina League before a second-half promotion to Double-A. He's continued his ascent towards the Majors in 2017, posting strong numbers back in the Eastern League en route to a Triple-A promotion late in May. Big and physical, Merryweather generates a plus fastball that sits at 93-96 mph and at times touches higher, all the while working on a downhill plane that fuels his impressive ground-ball rate. He has a pair of promising secondary pitches in a curveball and a changeup, with the latter currently grading as the better offering. Meanwhile, Merryweather showed improved strike-throwing ability last season after working with the Indians to simplify his delivery. Merryweather was one the more improved players in the Indians' system since the start of 2016, and they believe he has the ingredients to start at the highest level. If not, the right-hander's power arm could make him an effective late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A top prospect in the 2015-16 international class, Matias stood out for his physical projection and loud tools, including huge raw power, as a Dominican amateur before signing with the Royals for $2.25 million in July. After offering a glimpse of that power during his first two seasons, Matias erupted to hit 31 home runs (and also strike out 131 times) in just 94 games Class A Lexington in 2018 before a freak thumb injury in August ended his season. He was struggling with the move to the Carolina League in 2019 when the injury bug hit again, this time a fractured hand on June 11 that wiped out the remainder of his season. Possessing as much raw power as just about anybody in Minor League baseball, Matias is capable of going deep to any part of any park and hits some of his farthest home runs to center and right-center field. But for Matias to apply his robust right-handed power at higher levels, he will first need to make consistent contact. That has been an issue in the pro ranks for Matias, who has fanned at a 38.4 percent clip in full-season ball and 36.4 percent of the time across four seasons. Pitch-recognition issues and a desire to swing early in the count cause Matias to chase too many pitches out of the zone with a swing that gets long when he tries to force contact. Defensively, Matias fits the profile of a big league right fielder to a T with massive power and plus-plus arm strength that is among the best in the organization. The good news is that even a fraction of improvement in Matias’ approach could help him get back on track, and he’s shown in the past that the power will play even as a .230-.240 hitter. While a healthy age-21 campaign in 2020 should help him with that, questions about his hitting ability and future role are likely to persist.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked in the top half of MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list as the 2015-16 international signing period opened, Matias, his tools and his projectable body received $2.25 million to sign that July. He immediately showed his prodigious power, along with a penchant for striking out, during his United States debut in '16. Both were on display in his '18 full-season debut as he hit 31 homers and struck out 131 times just 94 games. His season was cut short by a freakish thumb injury, but not before he showed off his pop with an opposite-field blast in the Futures Game. He was struggling with the move to the Carolina League in 2019 when the injury bug hit again, this time a fractured hand keeping him out of the lineup for over a month. Matias has as much raw power as just about anybody in Minor League baseball, with some evaluators saying putting an 80 on the 20-to-80 scouting scale on it would not be outlandish. The big question is whether he can make enough contact to continue to get to that power in games. When he's going well, Matias lays off breaking balls early in count, but he has a very high chase rate out of the strike zone early in at-bats. There's always going to be some swing and miss to his game, but even some modest improvement in his approach should allow him to be a middle-of-the-order run producer. Blessed with one of the strongest arms in the system, Matias has the chance to truly fit the right-field profile in the future. Moving to more pitching-friendly parks and facing more advanced pitching should provide a good challenge for the 20-year-old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Dominican with one of the best all-around toolsets available during the 2015-16 international signing period, Matias turned pro for $2,250,000. He led the Arizona League with eight homers in his 2016 pro debut as one of three 17-year-old regulars in the Rookie-level circuit. He continued to hit for power as one of the youngest players in his league (the Rookie-level Appalachian) last year and will make the jump to full-season ball at age 19 in 2018. Though Khalil Lee and Nick Pratto are more refined, Matias has the highest ceiling among Royals prospects as well as the most raw power and the strongest arm. With his electric bat speed, strength and leverage in his right-handed swing, he hits tape-measure home runs and can smack opposite-field blasts without squaring the ball up. He'll need to modify his approach and improve his pitch recognition after striking out in 34 percent of his plate appearances in his first two pro seasons. Matias has solid speed, but has yet to turn it loose much on the bases. After spending part of his debut in center field, he moved to right field in 2017 and has the tools to be an asset there, starting with a bazooka arm. With his combination of tools and physical presence, he draws comparisons to Yoenis Cespedes and Andre Dawson.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the toolsiest players available during the 2015-16 international period, Matias signed for $2.25 million out of the Dominican Republic. He spent most of his 2016 pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he was one of a handful of 17-year-old regulars and tied for the lead with eight homers. Though he also topped the AZL with 73 strikeouts, he cut his whiff rate and improved his batting average in each of his three months there. Matias might have the most raw power in the Royals' system. He's so strong and his right-handed swing is so quick and has so much leverage that he can crush 450-foot homers and even drive the ball out of the park to the opposite field without fully squaring it up. His approach is extremely aggressive and he'll need to improve his pitch recognition, though he shows some willingness to accept walks when pitchers won't challenge him. Already a physical presence at such a young age, Matias draws comparisons to Yoenis Cespedes and Andre Dawson from club officials. He's an average runner out of the batter's box but quicker underway, which gives him enough range to play center field for now. He's likely to wind up in right field, where his cannon arm will fit nicely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers viewed Estevez as an advanced hitter when they gave him $6 million and paid a $6 million penalty for exceeding their international bonus pool in November 2015. They started the Cuban defector in Class A at age 18 and he didn't take off until the final six weeks of 2018, when he finished the year as the Class A Advanced California League leader in runs (87) and doubles (43).
