He continued to swing a hot bat in Spring Training and the first month of last season, then lost six weeks to a hamstring injury and tailed off afterward. Estevez employs an open stance with a big leg kick, and he manages to barrel balls despite leaking out early. He has an efficient right-handed swing and recognizes pitches well, but his swing mechanics make it difficult to drive the ball to the opposite field, cutting into his power potential. He's at his best when he's patient and focuses on smoking balls to the gaps. Estevez's quick hands and instincts allowed him to survive two years primarily playing shortstop in high Class A, but he's not suited to do so in the big leagues. His fringy range and arm strength fit better at second base, where he spent most of his time in 2019. He doesn't have the defensive tools desired for a utility role, which puts more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Largely on the strength of what they considered an advanced bat, the Dodgers gave Estevez a $6 million bonus and paid a matching amount as a penalty for exceeding their international bonus pool in November 2015. They promoted him aggressively, starting the Cuban defector in low Class A at age 18 and promoting him to high Class A at 19, and he showed little consistency at the plate for most of his first three pro seasons. He seemed to turn a corner when he batted .340/.418/.547 in the final six weeks of 2018, finishing the year as the high Class A California League leader in runs (87) and doubles (43). Estevez has an unorthodox batting style in which his lower half tends to leak out while his shoulders remain square to the ball. During his late-season tear, he was more patient and hammered balls from gap to gap instead of trying to pull everything to left field. With his efficient right-handed stroke and advanced pitch-recognition skills, he could become a .275 hitter with 15 or more homers per year if he can maintain a disciplined approach. Estevez's quick hands and internal clock have helped him survive at shortstop, his primary position in two years in high Class A, but it will be a stretch for him to play there regularly in the Majors. His speed and arm are fringy and better suited for second base, where he can be an average defender. His lack of arm strength restricts his utility value, putting pressure on him to hit enough to become a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estevez has such an advanced bat that he debuted in Cuba's top league as a 16-year-old. After he defected and Major League Baseball expedited his free agency, the Dodgers signed him in November 2015 for a $6 million bonus and a matching penalty for exceeding their international allotment. Challenged with an assignment to low Class A at age 18 in his pro debut, he hit .293/.340/.458 in the second half of 2016 as the Midwest League's youngest regular but has yet to enjoy similar success in high class A this year. Estevez has one of the best right-handed swings among Dodgers farmhands and precocious feel for the barrel. He's still honing his pitch recognition and can get overly aggressive at times, shortcomings that much older pitchers have exploited in 2017. He has some raw power and the ability to translate it into production, which eventually could mean 12-15 homers per season. An offensive second baseman in the mold of Howie Kendrick, Estevez has fringy speed and arm strength. He has a good internal clock on the field and has shown the Dodgers a little more defensive ability than they expected. He has seen much more action at shortstop than at second base this year, but he's not suited for the left side of the infield and doesn't fit a utility profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Born in Mexico, Gonzalez attended high school in Arizona and played collegiately at New Mexico, where he was a two-way player who won 11 games on the mound in three seasons. He starred more as an outfielder, hitting .361./500/.598 with 14 steals and a school-record 58 walks as a junior in 2017, prompting the White Sox to draft him in the third round. After logging the second-best OPS (.866) in the system and ranking fourth in the Minors with 40 doubles in 2018, he hit the ball with much less authority in Double-A last season. Gonzalez is at his best when he uses his sweet left-handed swing to spray line drives all over the field. He became too concerned about hitting for power when he reached Double-A and got too aggressive and pull-happy, though he settled down in the second half. He needs to focus on getting on base and making use of his solid speed and instincts rather than worrying about home runs. Gonzalez has spent the majority of his pro career in center field while also receiving ample time in left and right. He's an average defender in center, where he profiles best offensively, and slightly better than that on the corners, where he doesn't project to provide enough offense to be a regular. His plus arm is an asset at all three positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Mexican-born Gonzalez attended high school in Arizona and became a two-way player at New Mexico, where he won 11 games in three seasons. He stood out more as an outfielder, batting .361/.500/.598 with 14 steals and a school-record 58 walks in 2017. A third-round pick that June, he posted an .866 OPS (second in the system to überprospect Eloy Jimenez) with 40 doubles (fourth in the Minors) in his first full pro season. Gonzalez has a natural left-handed stroke and laces line drives all over the field with his disciplined approach. He's more hitter than slugger, but he uses his lower half well and should provide double-digit home runs annually along with a healthy amount of doubles. He's an average runner whose instincts outshine his potential as a basestealer. Gonzalez has bounced between all three outfield positions in pro ball, seeing the majority of his time in center field. He projects as an average defender up the middle, where he profiles best offensively, and as a solid one on the corners. He ran his fastball into the low-90s in college and has more than enough arm strength for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed way back in 2010, Gonzalez spent his first three season in the Phillies' system while pitching to lackluster results. He continued to struggle after signing with the Orioles in 2013, mostly while working as a starter, but showed promise in a relief role during a truncated campaign in '16. He broke out the next year, his third straight in the Class A Carolina League, and then showed well in the Arizona Fall League while allowing five hits and zero earned runs over nine appearances. Gonzalez's velocity can fluctuate at times, but when he's at his best he'll sit around 92-93 mph with arm-side run and bump 94-95. His upper-80s slider and solid changeup fuels his ability to produce reverse splits, as right-handed hitters batted just .130 against Gonzalez in 2017 compared to lefties' .241 mark. He misses bats with all three pitches, helping him to compensate for fringy command. Gonzalez may be an older prospect with a limited track record and zero experience above the Class A Advanced level, but there's a lot to like in this late-bloomer's reliever profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bracho received the highest bonus in Cleveland's promising 2017 international class, signing for $1.5 million out of Venezuela. Ticketed to come to the United States for his pro debut at age 17 in 2018 before he broke his right arm, he also missed a month with an oblique injury in 2019, when he would have ranked sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League in slugging (.593) and OPS (1.009) if he had enough plate appearances to qualify. The youngest player (age 19) at the Indians' alternate training site last summer, he more than held his own against much more advanced pitchers. A switch-hitter, Bracho produces louder contact than would be expected from a player listed at 5-foot-11 and 175 pounds. He has a compact swing with plenty of bat speed and could produce 20 or more homers per season once he's fully developed. But after showing an advanced feel for the strike zone in his first taste of pro ball, he has been too aggressive following his jump to High-A this year and has been helpless against right-handers. The Indians planned on breaking Bracho into pro ball as a shortstop in 2018 but used him at second base during his debut a year later. Most international scouts thought he'd wind up at the keystone because he lacks true shortstop actions and possesses average arm strength and speed. His quick hands help him on the double-play pivot and even if he loses a half-step as he physically matures, he can become an average defender at second.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians added to their collection of infielders with promising bats when they signed Bracho out of Venezuela for $1.5 million, the largest bonus in their 2017 international class. He was ready to come to the United States for his pro debut at age 17 in 2018, but he broke his right arm in May and missed the entire season. He would have ranked sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League in slugging (.593) and OPS (1.009) last summer if he had enough plate appearances to qualify. Bracho displays a quick, compact swing and advanced feel for the barrel from both sides of the plate. He has a precocious command of the strike zone, drives the ball in the air from gap to gap and projects as a 20-homer threat once he's fully developed. He's an average runner who might lose a step once he's physically mature. Signed as a shortstop, Bracho would have played there in 2018 but spent all of last season at second base. Most international scouts thought he belonged there anyway, because his actions and average arm aren't up to shortstop standards. His fast hands should help him turn double plays at second base, where he can become an average defender if he can improve his footwork.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Indians continued their recent trend of collecting international players with advanced bats when they signed Bracho out of Venezuela for $1.5 million, the largest bonus in their 2017 class. He would have come to the United States for his debut at age 17 last summer, but he fractured his right arm in May and missed the entire Rookie-level Arizona League season. He's thriving while seeing his first pro action this summer in the AZL. A switch-hitter, Bracho has a quick, compact swing and exhibits precocious feel for the barrel from both sides of the plate. He makes repeated hard contact, already drives balls to the gaps and should have 20-homer power once he matures physically. Presently an above-average runner, he figures to slow down a bit as he gets stronger. Though Bracho would have broken into pro ball as a shortstop in 2018, most international scouts thought he was destined for second base and the Indians have deployed him there this summer. While his actions and average arm are substandard at short, his fast hands should be an asset when it comes to turning double plays at second. He could become a solid defender at second base if he can quicken his footwork.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 22 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for 2017-18, Bracho endeared himself to evaluators as a Venezuelan amateur with his projectable frame and overall potential as a switch-hitting shortstop. The Indians were among the teams intrigued by Bracho's upside, so much so that they signed him with a $1.5 million bonus, the largest of all their July 2 signees. Scouts like Bracho's balanced hitting approach at the plate, quick hands and short swing. He makes hard contact and has also shown the ability to hit for power, driving the ball with authority into the gaps from both sides of the plate. That will only improve as he adds strength to his projectable frame, leading many to project Bracho as at least an average hitter with similar power. On the other side of the ball, Bracho shows solid infield actions and a decent glove. There's still room for improvement with his footwork on defense, but there's no questioning his arm strength and accuracy. Because of his skill set, Bracho projects to be an average fielder and is likely best suited for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he originally signed with the Braves for $1 million in July 2016 for $1 million, Del Rosario was one of the dozen prospects declared a free agent by Major League Baseball as a result of Atlanta's international signing violations. Seeing an opportunity to land a promising young arm, the Royals swept in and signed the right-hander for $650,000. After he finished his first season in the organization on a high note, delivering six scoreless frames in a Class A Lexington playoff start, Del Rosario’s progress was delayed in 2019 by a nerve issue in his right elbow. He didn’t pitch at all during the regular season, but returned during fall instructional league to throw simulated games. Del Rosario had been brought along slowly by the Braves, as the club focused on building up the young right-hander’s workload, and that continued after he joined the Royals. Assigned to Lexington in June, he started to adapt to his new surroundings and gained an understanding of preparing between starts as the season progressed, going at least six innings in five of his six final regular season starts. The stuff was plenty good as well, with Del Rosario hitting 97 mph with his fastball and showing the potential for more velocity as he adds strength. His breaking ball is a bit of a hybrid between a curve and slider, but it's sharp and hard and misses bats. His changeup, though currently too firm, has the chance to be above-average when all is said and done. Del Rosario will pitch as a 20-year-old in 2020, so there’s still plenty of time for him to get back on track physically. While the Royals like his combination of fearlessness and stuff on the mound, they will proceed cautiously with Del Rosario’s development after the right-hander’s lost campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Braves in July 2016 for $1 million, Del Rosario quickly pitched his way to the United States during his 2017 debut. When he was one of the dozen prospects declared a free agent by Major League Baseball as a result of Atlanta's international signing violations, the Royals swept in and signed him for $650,000. After a bit of a slow start to his first season in the organization, Del Rosario finished strong, capping off the year with six shutout innings in a playoff start. That progress was slowed in 2019 as a nerve issue kept him off the mound for an extended period of time. It's taken some time for Del Rosario to build up to handling a starting pitcher's workload. The Braves had kept him to very tight pitch counts and he began his full-season debut in 2018 not ready to pitch deep into games every fifth day. He started to adapt to his new surroundings and gained an understanding of preparing between starts as the season progressed, going at least six innings in five of his six final regular season starts. His stuff was all there as well, with a live fastball coming from a fast arm that touches 97 mph and has the chance for more consistent velocity as he continues to add strength. His breaking ball is a bit of a hybrid between a curve and slider, but it's sharp and hard and misses bats. His changeup has the chance to be above-average when all is said and done and he's improved his command considerably. Because of his size and his fearlessness on the mound, some in the organization see a little Yordano Ventura in Del Rosario, though they obviously don't want to put that kind of pressure on him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves spent $27 million in bonuses and overage penalties on international players during the 2016-17 signing period, including a $1 million bonus for del Rosario. Atlanta considered him advanced enough to bring him to the United States last summer after just two appearances in his native Dominican Republic, and he proved up to the challenge. When he became one of 12 prospects declared a free agent after MLB found the Braves guilty of extensive violations of international signing rules, del Rosario signed with the Royals for $650,000 in December. Del Rosario owned an 89-94 mph fastball when he turned pro and saw it jump to 91-97 during his debut. His heater features promising life and could add more velocity as he gets stronger. His hard breaking ball with slider velocity and curveball break gives him a potential second plus pitch, though it presently lacks consistency. Del Rosario is working on a changeup that should become an average third offering. While he threw strikes in his introduction to pro ball, some scouts believe the effort and crossfire in his delivery will land him in the bullpen. The Royals think his athleticism will help him make it as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels signed the tall and projectable Aquino in December 2016 for $100,000, knowing that he’d be a bit of a project, both in terms of pitching development and strength and conditioning. He pitched sparingly in the Dominican Summer and Arizona Leagues during his pro debut in 2017, then he missed all of 2018 because of Tommy John surgery. He returned to the mound in June of 2019 and showed some good glimpses, though there’s clearly more work to do. Aquino’s velocity did come back to pre-surgery levels, with a heater up to 96 mph. He can still spin a very good breaking ball as well, and he shows feel for a changeup that could catch up in time with more reps. He’s added a good amount of strength to his 6-foot-6 frame, giving him the chance to maintain his velocity, and there might even be more in the tank. The one thing that did not come back was Aquino’s command, not unusual for a TJ surgery recipient. His walk rate wasn’t awful, but he wasn’t locating his stuff within the strike zone, leading to him getting hit more than he should given his stuff. A move to full-season ball will be a good test; he needs innings more than anything else given that he’s thrown just 66 heading into 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery is never thought of as a positive achievement, despite it becoming almost commonplace among young pitchers these days. But there might be a silver lining in having needed the surgery in 2018 for Aquino, the 6-foot-6 right-hander who got $100,000 to sign in Dec. 2016. Yes, he missed development time on the mound by being out for all of 2018, but the strength and conditioning that went along with rehabbing the injury could help him take a big step when he returns to the mound. Before Aquino went down with injury, he had already improved strength-wise enough to add velocity to his fastball. What was a 90-91 mph heater when he first signed was touching 96 mph at instructs in the fall of 2017 with excellent spin and riding life. He's filled out even more now, so dreaming about more velocity once he gets his feet under him isn't unrealistic. He can really spin his breaking ball, giving him the chance for a second plus pitch, and he'll continue to work on what could be a decent changeup. With his size, Aquino will have to work at repeating his delivery. He'll get a chance to do that as he puts his rehab in the rearview mirror and hopefully gets a full season of work in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If it seems like the Angels are collecting intriguing, young pitching prospects courtesy of their efforts on the international amateur market, looks are not deceiving. Aquino, a 6-foot-6 right-hander signed in December 2016, might have as much ceiling as any of them, though he also might have the furthest to go to get there, especially since offseason Tommy John surgery kept him from pitching during the 2018 season. The Angels compare Aquino's fastball-curve combination with that of Jose Soriano in terms of future impact and he used it to pitch his way from the Dominican Summer League to a brief taste of pro ball in the United States in the rookie-level Arizona League. When Aquino signed, he was 90-91 mph with his fastball, but thanks to some big strength gains, he was touching 96 mph and sitting 93-94 mph last fall at instructs, thrown with plus spin and riding life up in the zone. His curve already flashes plus with a very high spin rate, while his changeup will flash average, though it needs work. Aquino doesn't have as athletic a delivery as Soriano, and will need to continue to work to repeat it effectively. If he can get more consistent with his direction to the plate, his command should get better, as should his already impressive raw stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017-18 international signing period will always go down in Angels history as the time they brought Shohei Ohtani over from Japan. But five months before signing Ohtani, the Angels spent over $2 million on a pair of players from the Bahamas. D’Shawn Knowles got $850,000 while Deveaux got $1.25 million. The Angels knew it would take some time for Deveaux to sharpen his baseball tools and he understandably struggled in the United States during his pro debut in 2018. His return to the Rookie-level Arizona League in 2019 led to uneven results, but the outfielder played well enough to earn a late bump up to the Pioneer League. The Angels are thrilled with the progress Deveaux made in 2019, especially late in the year. The right-handed hitter started to get more rhythm in his swing, getting comfortable with his timing at the plate and his swing path. That resulted in him driving the ball better than he ever has in his brief career, with an ISO approaching .200 in the AZL to show for it. He’s still very raw and needs to cut down on his strikeouts to show more consistent impact with the bat, but there were enough glimpses to know it’s in there. An elite-level athlete with top-of-the-scale speed, Deveaux will continue to get better on the bases as he learns more about the craft. The same can be said for his outfield defense, which is plus at times but inconsistent. There’s still a lot of risk here, but it looks like perhaps he’s heading in the right direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Angels have been garnering a reputation of acquiring premium athletes in the early rounds of the Draft, they've also been busy bringing similar players via the international market. At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, they double-dipped in the Bahamas, signing a pair of outfielders: Trent Deveaux for $1.2 million and Knowles for $850,000. It's been Knowles who broke out of the gate during his pro debut in 2018, earning a promotion from the Arizona to the Pioneer League. Throughout his first summer of pro ball, Knowles showed a solid approach from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed. There's emerging power, though it only showed up from the left side during his debut. He's not afraid to draw walks and could be a plus hitter as he continues to refine his approach, perhaps eventually with average big league pop. Knowles has plus speed and loves to use it, though he'll have to learn the nuances of basestealing. The Angels exposed the teenager to all three outfield spots, and he should have the range to play center field and enough arm to man right. Some of that might depend on how he continues to develop as he hopes to join prospects like Jazz Chisholm of the D-backs and the Rays' Lucius Fox in putting Bahamanian baseball more firmly on the map.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Bahamas has become a bit of a hot spot in terms of amateur talent, with prospects like Lucius Fox, Jazz Chisholm and Kristian Robinson all fetching large bonuses to start their pro careers. The Angels hit the Bahamas hard at the start of the 2017 international signing period, signing Trent Deveaux for $1.2 million and getting Knowles for $850,000. Both have begun their careers officially in 2018 in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Knowles stands out with his above-average athleticism and the chance to have multiple tools on the field. The right-handed hitter has plus speed which should help him on both sides of the ball. He could eventually be a plus defender in center field with at least an above-average arm. He has a nice swing and solid approach at the plate, utilizing a line-drive path. There is some raw power to tap into, but he's likely to be more of a gap-to-gap type in the future. Everything about Knowles is projection. All he needs now is a ton of reps against good competition so he can catch up to the speed of the game at the pro level. Once he gets that experience under his belt, his ceiling is quite high.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers used early-round choices on West Orange High (Winter Garden, Fla.) infielders in back-to-back drafts, taking Kole Enright in 2016's third round and Seise in 2017's first. Since signing for $2 million as the 29th overall pick, Seise has displayed one of the higher ceilings in the system but played just 72 games in his first three seasons. He missed all of 2018 after having rotator-cuff surgery on his throwing shoulder, then played just 21 games last year when he hurt his left shoulder sliding into a base and required labrum surgery. His size, bat speed and increasing strength give Seise more raw power than most shortstops. He also possesses solid speed and the mentality to steal bases, giving him 20-20 upside. To realize his offensive potential, he'll have to keep his right-handed swing from getting too long and learn to control the strike zone, two issues that cropped up when he posted a 36 percent strikeout rate in his brief action last season. Seise's arm strength bounced back well from rotator-cuff surgery, so he's a definite shortstop. He has quick feet and soft hands, and he possesses a reliable internal clock on defense. With his tools, he's capable of playing almost anywhere on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers selected West Orange High (Winter Garden, Fla.) infielders in consecutive drafts, Kole Enright in the third round in 2016 and Seise in the first round in 2017. While Enright has struggled to get going offensively, Seise has exhibited some of the highest upside in the system since signing for $2 million as the 29th overall pick. But he missed all of 2018 after hurting his throwing shoulder and having rotator-cuff surgery, then played just 21 games this year before injuring his left shoulder sliding into a base and requiring season-ending labrum surgery. With Seise's size, bat speed and developing strength, he has more power than the typical shortstop. To get the most out of his power potential and hit for average, he'll have to improve his plate discipline and guard against his right-handed swing getting too long. He has the plus speed and aggressive mindset to steal bases. Assuming his arm bounces back, Seise has all the tools to remain at shortstop. He's quick, has soft hands and displayed plus arm strength in the past. He also has a good internal clock that helps him make plays, and his athleticism should give him the versatility to play almost anywhere on the diamond if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers went to West Orange High (Winter Garden, Fla.) for infielders in consecutive Drafts, taking Kole Enright in the third round in 2016 and Seise in the first round last year. The highest pick ever from a program that has produced a pair of big leaguers in Nolan Fontana and Mason Williams, he signed for a slightly under-slot $2 million as the 29th overall pick. Following a respectable pro debut, he injured his throwing shoulder in extended spring training and required rotator-cuff surgery that wiped out his entire 2018 season One of the best shortstops in a 2017 Draft notably thin at the position, Seise is well equipped to stick at the position if he recovers his health. He has the quickness, soft hands and strong arm for short, as well as keen instincts to go with his physical gifts. With his tools, he could play almost anywhere on the diamond if he didn't hit enough to be a regular. Offense shouldn't be a problem for Seise. His size, bat speed and developing strength give him more power than most shortstops, though he'll need to tighten his strike zone and guard against his right-handed stroke getting too long. He has the plus speed and aggressive nature to steal bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burrows, University of Alabama’s career saves leader, was the Mariners’ pick in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. He wasn’t with Seattle for long as he was sent to the Braves before the 2017 season as part of the trade that sent Mallex Smith to the Mariners for the first time. He reached Double-A in 2018 and pitched well in the Arizona Fall League, but shuttled between Double-A and Triple-A in 2019. He wasn’t protected on the 40-man roster this offseason, but wasn’t selected in the Rule 5 Draft. Though he hasn’t always been consistent, Burrows has shown enough glimpses of a strong fastball-slider combination to give faith he can be a big league bullpen piece in the near future. While his fastball sits typically in the low 90s, he throws it from a low three-quarters slot, making it tougher to pick up and hit. But his real bread-and-butter is his slider, which is particularly effective against left-handed hitters. Even with his up-and-down 2019 season, he missed plenty of bats (9.9 K/9). Burrows has struggled with his control for much of his professional career, as evidenced by his 4.0 BB/9 rate entering 2020, but he continues to be particularly nasty against left-handed hitters. At the very least, he has a future as a specialist, but there’s enough stuff there to get hitters from both sides of the plate out if he can refine his command just a little bit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 After three years pitching out of the University of Alabama bullpen, Burrows left as the school's career leader in saves with 30. Seeing him as a future left-handed big league reliever, the Mariners took him in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. He spent just one summer with Seattle as he was sent to the Braves in January 2017, along with Luiz Gohara in return for Mallex Smith and Shae Simmons. He reached Double-A in 2018, his second season in the organization, then capped things off in the Arizona Fall League. Burrows' calling card is his breaking ball, and it's a real weapon against left-handed hitters but nasty enough to miss right-handed bats as well. He throws it with deception with late, sharp break, and hitters don't see it. It's the main reason why he carries a 12.2 K/9 ratio into the 2019 season. His fastball sits in the low-90s coming from a low three-quarters slot, allowing it to play up beyond the velocity. Burrows' progress has been slowed a bit by a lack of consistency and command, though it's clear his two-pitch mix is plenty to get big league hitters out. At the very least, he's a left-handed specialist. At the top end, he's a seventh-inning type reliever, with an Eric O'Flaherty career path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Burrows took over the role of closer at the University of Alabama as a freshman and never let go of it. After three years, he held the career saves record for the school, which resulted in him being taken by the Mariners in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. After a summer of saving some more games in the Short Season Northwest League, Burrows was sent to the Braves along with Luiz Gohara in return for Mallex Smith and Shae Simmons. The lefty reliever didn't rack up saves in his first full season, but he did pitch very effectively in the South Atlantic League, striking out 12.4 per nine innings and keeping hitters to a .198 batting average against. He does it with a solid two-pitch mix, really all he needs to succeed in short relief. His fastball sits in the low-90s and touches 95 mph, but it plays up because it has plus movement and comes from a low three-quarters arm slot. His sweeping slider gets swings and misses from hitters on both sides of the plate. He has less than pinpoint command, but throws enough strikes to be effective. After Burrows spent the entire season at one level, look for him to start moving a little more quickly with his two plus pitches. While he's unlikely to close again, he does have the chance to be an effective lefty setup or middle man in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If there was a candidate for a pitching prospect in the Braves organization who needed a full 2020 season the most, it might’ve been De La Cruz. Signed for just $55,000 in June 2015, De La Cruz’s light really didn’t turn on until 2019, when he pitched his way across three levels of the system, with most of his time spent in Double-A, to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. Though he didn’t get the chance to build off of his breakout, he threw well enough at the Braves’ alternate training site to earn two separate callups to the big leagues in 2020, though he didn’t appear in a game. There’s no question about the right-hander’s pure stuff. De La Cruz will consistently hit 97-98 mph and he’s flirted with triple digits. His slider can be a nasty offering and is consistently an above-average pitch and he does have decent feel for his changeup, giving him an effective three-pitch mix, something that will have to continue to improve if he wants to continue starting, or at least face lefties in high-leverage situations. While his walk rate did improve in 2019, there are questions remaining about whether De La Cruz can harness his big stuff enough and find the strike zone consistently enough to land a spot in a rotation. He’s trending toward a future in the bullpen, where his fastball-slider combination could be downright filthy, though he’ll likely get the chance to pitch multiple innings in the short-term so he can keep working on all of his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The Braves handed out seven bonuses that were six figures or more in the 2014-15 international signing period, but De La Cruz wasn’t one of them. They inked the right-hander for just $55,000 close to the end of the period, in June 2015. It hasn’t been a rapid ascent, with De La Cruz not making it to full-season ball until his fourth summer of pro ball in 2018. It started to click for him in 2019, pitching across three levels of the Minors and spending most of the season in Double-A. He was rewarded with a spot on the 40-man roster after the season. De La Cruz has a really live arm and the chance to have a three-pitch mix that could allow him to stay in a rotation. He’ll sit in the mid-90s with his fastball, but shows regularly there’s more in there, touching 98-99 mph. His slider has improved and more consistently flashes above-average. He’s gained more feel for his changeup, with some thinking it will become an average third pitch for him. He’ll have to throw it more, especially now that he’s at the upper levels, with more reps leading to better usage of the offspeed offering. More than anything, De La Cruz needs more experience on the mound. The 2019 season was the first time he had topped 100 innings. He didn’t get hit hard in Double-A, but after making strides with his strike-throwing in A ball, his command backed up a bit against better hitters. Letting him start could allow him to refine those rough edges, with the Braves knowing his stuff would be nasty in shorter stints out of the pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The 2014-15 international signing period could end up being a very productive one for the Braves. The star of their crop of players is obviously Ronald Acuna Jr., but it also includes Izzy Wilson and De La Cruz on this Top 30 list. De La Cruz has been slow to advance, spending two summers in the Dominican Summer League and parts of two in the Gulf Coast League before finally getting the chance to move to full-season ball in 2018. The results have been up-and-down, but the Braves are still bullish on his stuff and the right-hander took a big step forward in 2019. De La Cruz has a live arm with a fastball up to 95-96 mph, a slider that flashes plus and misses bats and some feel for a changeup. What he hasn't shown to date is an ability to command his pitches or sequence them consistently. He falls in love with his fastball too much, thinking he can blow it by any hitter he faces. He needs to learn to trust his secondary stuff more, which in turn will help his fastball play up. That, plus dialing down his fastball a tick or two in order to achieve more consistent command, will help make him a more complete pitcher. De La Cruz has a long way to go in order to reach his ceiling. He surpassed the 100-innings plateau in a season for the first time in 2019 and needs those innings to take the next step in his development. He'll remain in a rotation, with no talk of moving him to a bullpen at this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 While the Braves have some exciting young arms getting ready to impact the big leagues, there's another wave coming from further down below. De La Cruz has the chance to be a part of that with exciting raw stuff, though he is still in the nascent stages of figuring out how to use it. The young right-hander, signed back in 2015, has moved slowly since signing, spending parts of two summers in the Dominican Summer League (2015-16) and two in the Gulf Coast League (2016-17). He has a power arm that is capable of firing fastballs up to 95-96 mph, though he is still learning how to consistently maintain that velocity. His slider has the chance to be at least average and can miss bats on occasion. He shows some feel for a changeup, but he'll need to work on making it a more usable weapon moving forward. Like with many young pitchers, command is an issue, but when he's down the zone, he's shown a propensity for generating ground-ball outs. At this point, De La Cruz doesn't always repeat his delivery, which leads to the control problems and fluctuating stuff. He's still very much a project, but one who could end up having starting pitcher potential down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pie checked in at No. 25 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2018-19 period before the Rays signed him for $1.385 million on July 2. As an amateur in the Dominican Republic, he endeared himself to scouts with his blend of athleticism, tools and physical projection. Evaluators look at Pie and see a prospect with lots of options and tons of upside. He moves well around the infield and impressed scouts with his smooth defensive actions and strong arm from shortstop. Whether he stays there long term will be determined by his physical development in the coming years, as Pie currently has considerable projection remaining in his 6-foot-4, 175-pound frame. Pie has already displayed above-average bat speed and projects to have above-average raw power in the future. He's an aggressive hitter and therefore still learning how to recognize pitches and manage the strike zone. He's a solid runner -- clocked in the 6.6- to 6.7-second range in the 60-yard run -- and shows good instincts on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox rated Bush as a fifth-round talent in the 2018 Draft, but his commitment to Mississippi State clouded his signability and they figured they had filled their quota of pricey prep third basemen when they picked Lency Delgado in the fourth round. When Bush kept sliding, Chicago determined it could close a deal for sixth-round money and signed him for $290,000 in the 33rd round. He opened his pro debut by going 19-for-43 (.442) in the Rookie-level Arizona League and finished it by posting a 1.518 OPS in the Rookie-level Pioneer League playoffs as Great Falls won the championship. Bush already is a physical presence as a teenager and has plenty of strength and bat speed in his right-handed swing. He has a disciplined approach, working counts and using the entire field, but he needs to add some loft to his stroke because too much of his hard contact last summer came in the form of ground balls. If he can make the necessary adjustments, he could become a .280 hitter with 20 or more homers per season. Mostly a shortstop in high school, Bush became a full-time third baseman after turning pro. He has enough arm strength for the hot corner but needs to clean up his footwork and the accuracy of his throws. Some scouts believe he's destined to wind up at an outfield corner, and he runs well enough to possibly develop into an average left or right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres parlayed a strong performance on the high school showcase circuit in 2017 into going 41st overall the following June, making him the second-highest New York prep arm taken in the last 25 Drafts (behind only 2016 No. 3 choice Ian Anderson). One of the youngest players in the 2018 Draft at 17 years and eight months, he proved more advanced than expected in his pro debut. He didn't pitch in another official game over the next two years, requiring Tommy John surgery in May 2019 and returning to the mound in instructional league last fall. Before he blew out his elbow, Torres displayed electric arm speed that generated fastballs that sat at 92-95 mph and topped out at 98 mph with riding action up in the zone. His low-80s slider also showed signs of becoming a plus pitch with power and high spin rates. He has a lot of work to do on a changeup that he didn't need much as an amateur, but it has some tumble and should become at least an average third offering. Torres isn't especially big for a starter, but he doesn't have much effort in his delivery and his athleticism helps him repeat it. While he pounded the strike zone in his brief debut, his command isn't as sharp as his control. He'll need to prove he can hold up when he takes a regular turn in the rotation, but the Indians believe his maturity and intelligence are two more assets that will help his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres burst into the scouting consciousness on the showcase circuit in 2017, working in the low 90s all summer before his high school senior season. He became the second-highest New York prep arm drafted last decade -- behind only 2016 No. 3 overall pick Ian Anderson -- when the Indians selected him 41st overall and signed him for a below-slot $1.35 million. One of the youngest players in the 2018 Draft, he excited Cleveland by proving more advanced than expected in his pro debut, but he blew out his elbow and had Tommy John surgery last May. Before he got hurt, Torres used electric arm speed to produce effortless fastballs that sat at 92-95 mph and peaked at 98 with riding action. His low-80s slider showed flashes of becoming a plus pitch with power and high spin rates. Many pitchers gain velocity after completing the grueling Tommy John rehab process, so he might throw harder once he returns. In addition to regaining his health, Torres needs to refine a changeup that he didn't have much use for as an amateur. His athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and provide consistent strikes, though his command isn't as sharp as his control. He's a bit undersized for a starter, so there were worries about his ability to handle a pro workload even before his elbow gave out, but his maturity and intelligence are two more assets that could help him remain in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres wasn't a big name at the start of the showcase circuit in 2017 but that changed when he repeatedly pitched in the low 90s all summer leading into his high school senior season. He continued to bring the heat last spring and worked his way into the supplemental first round, where he signed for a below-slot $1.35 million. He surprised the Indians by proving to be more advanced than they expected during his brief pro debut, especially considering he was one of the youngest players in the 2018 Draft. With a lightning-quick arm, Torres effortlessly works at 92-95 mph and touches 98 with riding life on his fastball. His low-80s slider has the makings of a plus pitch with power and high spin rates. He didn't need an offspeed pitch as an amateur but shows some feel for a changeup with a bit of fade. Torres' athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone, though his command isn't as sharp as his control. He's a bit undersized for a starter, so his ability to hold up under a pro workload was a concern even before he succumbed to Tommy John surgery in May. Club officials love his maturity and intelligence, two more assets that help his chances of remaining in the rotation once he returns to health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dallas Baptist University has churned out a ton of professional talent over the years, with Ben Zobrist clearly the most successful big league alum in school history, and even had two second-round picks in the 2020 Draft. But only one player, right-hander Vic Black, has been drafted earlier in the June Draft than Hannah, taken No. 50 overall by the A’s in the second round of the 2018 Draft. Since then, the talented outfielder has had to forward his address twice, going to the Reds at the 2019 Trade Deadline in the Tanner Roark deal, then heading to the Rockies along with Robert Stephenson in return for Jeff Hoffman and Case Williams last November. Hannah does have some offensive upside from the left side of the plate. There’s bat speed and the ability to make hard contact, with more gap-to-gap than over-the-fence pop. He’s shown an ability to work counts and take walks, though his approach wasn’t as solid during his first full year. While he’ll record plus run times, Hannah has yet to learn how to use that speed to steal bases. He has shown that his speed plays in the outfield, with a chance to play center field because of how much ground he can cover. He’s seen time at all three outfield spots as a pro, with perhaps a floor as a valuable fourth outfielder. But with a fringy arm, Hannah's best chance at an everyday spot would likely be in center or left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick of the A’s in 2018 after three years as a starter for Dallas Baptist, the Reds acquired Hannah on July 31, 2019, in the trade that sent veteran pitcher Tanner Roark to Oakland. Hannah, the earliest-drafted hitter in his school’s history, was having a decent first full pro season in the California League before the trade and then scuffled at the plate over his 18 games for Daytona in the Florida State League. He was on the move again in late November, when the Reds sent him and Robert Stephenson to the Rockies for Jeff Hoffman and 2020 draftee Case Williams. Hannah has an intriguing offensive profile and the Reds were attracted by his bat and a belief he can be a strong gap-to-gap left-handed hitter. He has good bat speed, makes hard contact and has solid strength. His approach is advanced and allows him to get on base effectively. A plus runner, he needs to get more out of his speed to become a base stealing threat. That speed serves Hannah reasonably well in center field as he can cover a lot of ground and defend well. His arm is below average. He could wind up playing all three outfield spots at some point as he moves up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Dallas Baptist, Hannah improved each year in college and as he turned in a huge junior season, his name was popping up in 2018 first-round conversations. The A's were very happy he lasted until the second round, the earliest the Patriots have had a hitter selected, and signed him for an above-pick value bonus of $1.8 million. He was able to show off some of his tools in the short-season New York-Penn League during his pro debut, but a foot injury shelved him for the summer in mid-July. He was having a solid full-season debut in the California League when he was sent to the Reds at the Trade Deadline for right-hander Tanner Roark. While he isn't the tallest guy in the world, he's strong and athletic and has a strong track record of consistent hard contact from the left side of the plate. He has an advanced approach, managing the strike zone well and finding the barrel while being very quick to the ball. His bat speed and strength point to some over-the-fence pop and plenty of extra-base power. He's shown he can handle wood just fine, both in a scorching hot stretch to end his Cape Cod season in 2017 and during his brief pro debut. A plus runner, Hannah is an efficient baserunner with the potential to steal bases and cover a ton of ground in center field. He's a capable defender, albeit one with a fringy arm. He could start to move quickly given his all-around skillset, with a potential future as a No. 2 type hitter in a big league lineup awaiting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard spent four years on Texas Christian’s pitching staff, the last two as a full-time member of the rotation. A strong final season led to the A’s picking him in the eighth round of the 2017 Draft as a money-saving senior sign, giving the 6-foot-9 right-hander $40,000 to join the organization. He’s proven to be a durable pitchability starter thus far, reaching Triple-A in 2019, his second full pro season. Despite his size, Howard isn’t a pure stuff or power pitcher, though he does throw everything from a very good downward angle. His fastball is typically in the 89-92 mph range and he attacks the strike zone well with it. His cutter/slider is really one pitch that Howard manipulates, adding and subtracting from it when he wants to create two different offerings. He does fold in a fringe-average curve and has an OK changeup as part of his repertoire. There’s very little margin for error for Howard since he doesn’t have put-away stuff, and while he’s generally been a strike-thrower, he’ll need to improve his ability to pitch up and down in the zone as well as his pitch sequencing to succeed as a starter. Some feel the bullpen might be a better place for him, where his fastball might tick up and he can become a two-pitch, fastball-cutter type in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's might have hit the senior sign jackpot in the 2017 Draft. One round after getting Parker Dunshee in the seventh round, they were able to get Howard, a four-year member of TCU's pitching staff, in the eighth for just $40,000. Like Dunshee, he pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season and finished fourth in the organization in ERA and third in strikeouts. Howard and Dunshee have similarities beyond beyond being shrewd senior signs. Both right-handers use a bevy of largely average offerings and the ability to command them to succeed. While Howard doesn't miss quite as many bats as his rotation-mate, he does have a healthy strikeout rate and gets more ground-ball outs thanks in part to the good sink on his 89-92 mph fastball that plays as average due to its movement. His best secondary pitch is an 89 mph cutter that misses bats and gets more weak contact on the ground. Howard can morph his cutter into a slightly slower slider that flashes plus, and he mixes in an effective curve and changeup as well. Howard uses his 6-foot-9 frame extremely well with outstanding extension to create uncomfortable at-bats, a big reason why he has a high pop-up rate in addition to his ground-ball tendencies. A's fans could see he and Dunshee fill the back end of the big league rotation soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez set the amateur scouting world abuzz when he was hitting the upper-90s with his fastball early in his junior season at Texas A&M-Corpus Christi. He wasn’t that electric or as dominant as he was in those first couple of outings all spring, but he showed enough to become the highest-drafted player in school history when the Angels took him in the third round of the 2018 Draft. Sent up to the Class A Advanced California League for his pro debut in 2019, his performance didn’t match the expectations. Part of Hernandez’s issues with Inland Empire stem from the fact his stuff backed up. The upper-90s fastball did not materialize and he tended to sit in the low-90s and couldn’t always maintain his velocity throughout a start. He does have a legitimate four-pitch mix, but it’s now largely average to a tick above across the board. His curve and slider sometimes run into each other, though he still has a feel to spin and he can mix in a solid changeup, but he lacks a true out pitch. In addition to the regression of his stuff, Hernandez’s command, which deserted him in college at times, remained an issue, leading to a 5.7/9 walk rate. He did turn things around with a strong Arizona Fall League campaign as he learned a bit more about what it takes to compete and pitched with a bit of a chip on his shoulder. He’ll need to show that fire on a consistent basis as he moves to the upper levels of the Angels system as a stater.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to the 2018 Draft, the earliest a player from Texas A&M-Corpus Christi had been drafted was the ninth round. Hernandez's path to easily beating that hasn't necessarily been straight. He was academically ineligible as a sophomore, but then came out and showed very good stuff early in the spring. While he wasn't as dominant all year, it was still enough for the Angels to take him in the third round and he went straight to the Class A Advanced California League for his full-season debut. Hernandez was up to 98 mph at times during his junior season, sitting more in the 92-95 mph range, throwing the pitch with good sink and showing he could maintain his velocity through starts. He has good feel for his secondary stuff and can throw a distinct curve and slider, though they sometimes blur together into a power slurve. He can really spin it and his breaking stuff does flash plus and he has solid tumbling changeup. Though he has swing-and-miss stuff, Hernandez didn't dominate in college as much as one would think, as he has trouble commanding his pitches both within and outside the strike zone. With a funky delivery, he might best be suited for the bullpen, but he was given a chance to start at the start of his pro career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tampa's Plant High has produced 12 big leaguers, including Hall of Famer Wade Boggs, Pete Alonso and Kyle Tucker, and three first-round choices, most recently the 13th overall pick in the 2018 Draft in Scott. Signed for $4,083,220, he hit just .240/.310/.342 in his first two pro seasons while getting promoted aggressively and advancing to high Class A at age 19. Scott has some of the best all-around tools in the system and has drawn comparisons to Bradley Zimmer. He possesses a balanced left-handed stroke, some feel for hitting and well above-average speed, but he gets too aggressive at the plate for his own good. He's stronger than most speedsters and owns solid raw power that he won't fully tap into until he starts driving more balls in the air, though he did make some progress in that regard in 2019. Scott's quickness and aggressiveness on the bases make him a threat to steal, giving him the upside of a 20-20 player. With his speed and plus arm strength, he's a quality defender in center field and easily capable of handling all three outfield spots. He drew some scouting attention as a pitcher in high school, when he ran his fastball up to 93 mph and showed feel for spinning a curveball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 13th overall pick in the 2018 Draft, Scott became the third first-rounder from Tampa's Plant High, whose 11 big league alumni include Hall of Famer Wade Boggs, Pete Alonso and Kyle Tucker. Signed for $4,038,220, Scott batted .240/.310/.342 in his two pro seasons while getting pushed aggressively and reaching high Class A as a 19-year-old at the end of 2019. He's a quality athlete with some of the best all-around tools in the system and projection remaining in his 6-foot-4 frame. Scott elicits comparisons to Bradley Zimmer and is just scratching the surface of his offensive potential. His balanced left-handed swing, feel for hitting and well-above-average speed give him the ingredients to hit for average once he refines his plate discipline. He has solid raw power that he won't fully tap into until he hits more balls in the air, though he did a better job of driving the ball to all fields in 2019. Scott's funky running style belies his quickness, which couples with his aggressive mentality to make him a basestealing threat. His speed also plays well in center and his strong arm fits anywhere in the outfield. He drew some scouting interest as a pitcher in high school, running his fastball up to 93 mph and showing some feel to spin a curveball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest standout from Plant High (Tampa), which produced Hall of Famer Wade Boggs and nine other big leaguers, Scott was the first outfielder taken in the first round by the Marlins since Christian Yelich in 2010. Club officials see some parallels between Yelich and Scott, who signed for $4,038,200 as the 13th overall pick in the 2018 Draft. Though he didn't post big numbers in his pro debut, Miami felt he was advanced enough to push to low Class A for the final month of the season. Scott has the makings of a five-tool player and also draws comparisons to Bradley Zimmer. The Marlins felt Scott's left-handed swing was pretty polished for a high school hitter, though they would like to see him turn on more pitches and tap into his solid raw power after he used more of an opposite-field approach in his debut. He has a lofty offensive ceiling but will have to make more contact to reach it. Scott has a funky running style yet has well above-average speed. He can go get the ball in center field and use his quickness to chase down balls from gap to gap. He also has a plus arm that delivered fastballs up to 93 mph and decent curveballs when he pitched in high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With his big body and power potential, Valdez was one of the more physically advanced players in the the 2018-19 international class. Targeting exactly that type of prospect, the Mets inked the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder for $1.45 million on July 2. Making his pro debut in 2019, Valdez garnered honors as the Mets Dominican Summer League player of the year after slugging .432 with 23 extra-base hits and 36 RBIs in 57 games. He finished the year with a brief but impressive showing in the Gulf Coast League. Listed at 6-foot-3, 212 pounds, Valdez is already a physical specimen and still has plenty of room left to grow into his frame. His bat is his carrying tool, with tremendous raw power that already shows up in games at times. Swing-and-miss issues stemming from an aggressive, pull-heavy approach gives evaluators pause in projecting Valdez as anything more than a below-average hitter, though all agree that the power is for real. He’s a good athlete but a below-average runner and may lose a step as he begins to grow into his body. Valdez has prototypical right-field tools with his power potential and strong arm, but he is going to need many years in the Minors to develop his game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 28 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2018-19 signing period, Valdez, with his big body and power potential, was viewed by scouts as one of the more physically advanced players in his class. Targeting exactly that type of prospect, the Mets inked the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder for $1.45 million on July 2. Listed at 6-foot-3, 212 pounds, Valdez is already a physical specimen and still has plenty of room left to grow into his frame. His bat is his carrying tool, with tremendous raw power that already shows up in games at times. In the past, he's been overly aggressive and pull-happy, leading to some swing-and-miss issues, but scouts were pleased with how he improved his overall approach this past year. He's solid athletically, earning at least average grades as a runner, and the Mets view him as a pure center fielder that should stay up the middle. Earning high praise for his makeup, scouts like the way Valdez competes and his joy for the game. That should help him deal with the long road ahead through the Mets' Minor League system, with enough offensive potential to carry him to Citi Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cate worked primarily as a starter in all three of his years at UConn, and he left the program as the all-time leader in strikeouts with 270 in 210 2/3 innings, ahead of Major Leaguers Anthony Kay (263) and Matt Barnes (247). Despite his size at 6-foot and past Tommy John surgery from high school, the Nationals liked his breaking stuff enough to take him in the second round in 2018. He rewarded that confidence as the organization’s 2019 Minor League Pitcher of the Year, with a 3.07 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 139 K’s in 143 2/3 innings across two Class A levels. He was an alternate-site participant in 2020. Any discussion of Cate has to start with the curveball. It’s a true plus pitch with a hammer-like drop, and he commands it well for a pitch with that much movement. The velocity on his fastball typically averaged around 89 mph but can touch a few ticks higher, making it an average offering. The changeup developed enough at the alternate site that it’s a good third option at this point. Cate uses that three-pitch mix to get ground balls at an impressive rate – a valuable skill in the age of the launch angle – and he throws plenty of strikes, having walked only 5.5 percent of his batters faced in 2019. Cate’s size and lack of plus velocity do not scream dominant starter who must stick in the rotation, but his stuff is such that he could be able to face batters multiple times in a single outing at the top level. Even if he can’t stick as a back-end starter, a multi-inning reliever role isn’t out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year member of UConn’s starting rotation as well as a reliever for USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team, Cate didn’t fit into a neat box as a potential first-round pick due to his undersized frame and his previous Tommy John surgery as a prep. The Nationals saw plenty of value in Cate’s outstanding curveball and track record as a starter and took him in the second round, and he rewarded the organization by turning in an impressive first full season in which he led qualified Nationals Minor League pitchers in strikeouts (139), starts (26) and ranked second in ERA (3.07) and WHIP (1.14). Cate’s curveball, a 12-to-6 downer with tilt, is a true plus pitch and the best among Nats prospects. He throws it in every count and commands it well to generate a decent number of whiffs and even more ground-ball contact. His 58.3 percent ground-ball rate in 2019 was the 10th-best mark in the Minors and led all Nationals farmhands. Cate’s velocity fluctuated in his first full season, with the southpaw’s fastball averaging 89 mph, but he’s capable of touching 92 mph and knows how to pitch to both sides of the plate. His changeup is a potentially average pitch that he’ll need to develop to be successful against right-handed hitters at higher levels. The Nationals hope that Cate can add more velocity to his fastball through physical development and were encouraged by the strength gains he made in his first true offseason. He profiles as a high-floor back-end starter in the big leagues, perhaps even a No. 4 if the fastball velocity and changeup take a step forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cate was a reliever for USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team but otherwise spent his college career in UConn's rotation, spending two years as the program's Friday night ace. His Draft appeal was tied to his future in that role, so naturally there was concern when forearm tightness forced him to miss several starts as a junior. He still earned a second-round selection that June, and then reached Class A Hagerstown in his pro debut after signing for slot value. Cate might have had the best breaking ball in his Draft class, a 12-to-6 hammer that is widely viewed as at least a plus pitch. Cate will throw it whenever he wants in the count and can command it very well in the strike zone. He throws it from the same plane as his fastball, giving hitters little chance to pick it up. That, in turn, allows his 90-93 mph fastball to be more effective. It has more run than sink, with average life overall, and Cate can throw it to both sides of the plate consistently. His changeup is a little firm and a distant third pitch, but he shows enough feel for it to be a future average offering. Cate isn't the biggest guy in the world at 6 feet, and concern about overuse during his time at UConn certainly wasn't assuaged with his 2018 injury. The Nationals expect to see a better, more physical version of him moving forward, and the hope is that he can move quickly through the Minors en route to a spot at the back of Washington's big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roederer drew Andrew Bentinendi comparisons as a California high school senior in 2018, but also injured his non-throwing shoulder and had a UCLA commitment, so he was available to Chicago at the 77th overall pick. Signed for an over-slot $1.2 million, he endured a rough first full pro season because low Class A pitchers quickly exploited his aggressiveness by throwing him changeups. He made some progress in the final six weeks but has barely played since then, because the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the 2020 Minor League season and he injured his throwing elbow this May, requiring Tommy John surgery. The key for Roederer will be to understand who he is as a hitter. With a smooth left-handed swing, bat speed and the ability to work counts, he could hit .280-.300 with 20-25 homers on an annual basis. He won't reach that potential, however, unless he stops worrying about launching balls to his pull side, develops a gap-to-gap approach and does a better job recognizing offspeed pitches. Roederer is an asset on the bases with solid speed, good instincts and an aggressive nature. The Cubs believe his high baseball IQ gives him the chance to remain in center field, though he'll have to shift to a corner if he loses any quickness as he adds muscle. His arm strength graded as fringy before his elbow reconstruction and is better suited for left field than right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Though Roederer elicited comparisons to Andrew Benintendi as a California high school senior in 2018, he lasted 77 picks because he injured his non-throwing shoulder and had a strong commitment to UCLA. Signed for an over-slot $1.2 million, he received a rude awakening during his first full pro season, when Class A pitchers exploited his aggressiveness with a steady diet of changeups. He struggled for most of the first four months before rallying to hit .252/.374/.395 in the final six weeks. Roederer has the raw tools to hit .280-.300 with 20-25 homers per season if he can adapt his approach. He has a quick, smooth left-handed swing that produces impressive exit velocities and he isn't afraid to work deep counts. He got too concerned with pulling and lifting pitches in 2019, however, and needs to do a better job of using the whole field and letting his power come naturally. Roederer currently possesses solid speed and will steal and take extra bases when given the opportunity. The Cubs believe his defensive instincts give him a good chance to stick in center field, though he may have to move to a corner if he loses any quickness as he gets stronger. His fringy arm would fit better in left field than in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Roederer drew comparisons to Andrew Benintendi but not the commensurate amount of Draft buzz as a California high school senior in 2018. An injury to his non-throwing shoulder and a strong commitment to UCLA clouded his status a bit and dropped him to the 77th overall pick, where he signed for an over-slot $1.2 million. He has one of the highest offensive ceilings of any position player in the system. Roederer added noticeable strength in 2018 and could become a .300 hitter with 25-homer power if everything comes together for him. He has advanced bat-to-ball skills and a quick left-handed swing that produces impressive exit velocities, though he has been overly aggressive during his first full pro season. He's presently a solid runner with the savvy to steal a few bases. Some scouts wonder if Roederer will lose a half-step as he continues to mature physically, which could prompt a move from center field. The Cubs like his defensive instincts and his chances to remain in center. His arm may fit better in left field than in right if he has to shift to a corner, though he'd still fit the offensive profile at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bello became the first Hawaiian high school position player to be drafted in the top five rounds since 2013 when the Brewers took him with the No. 73 overall pick in ‘18. Viewed as a well-rounded prep player who could move through the Minors relatively quickly, Bello has struggled to gain traction in pro ball while standing out more for his defense than bat. Assigned to the Pioneer League in 2019, he showed some power potential that was mitigated by below-average hitting ability, while a concussion limited him to just 50 games. Though he currently lacks the bat speed and swing path needed to consistently impact the ball, Bello can show some sneaky raw pop from the right side of the plate when’s on time. Adding strength should help bring out some of the extra-base potential in Bello's swing, but his game power likely will always be below-average. An above-average runner, Bello can steal bases and cover a lot of ground in center field, where he profiles as at least an above-average defender with a plus arm. Bello’s ability to remain in center field is crucial to his long-term profile, because it is unlikely he will ever do enough damage at the plate to profile at an outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With his selection by the Brewers with the No. 73 overall pick in the 2018 Draft, Bello became the first Hawaiian high school positional player to be taken in the top five rounds since 2013. He signed for $550,000, forgoing his commitment to St. Mary's, then made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Bello makes consistent contact with a simple swing that enables him to use the whole field and leads scouts to project him as an average hitter. Adding strength should help bring out some of the extra-base potential in Bello's swing, but his game power likely will always be below-average. He has the kind of speed to steal bases and cover a lot of ground in the outfield, with the chance to be an above-average defender eventually, and a plus arm to boot. Bello's bat and above-average speed could one day have him hitting atop a lineup. Being able to stay in center field adds value to his overall profile, as Bello lacks the power potential expected from corner outfielders at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the more projectable prep right-handers in the 2019 Draft, Williams intrigued the Dodgers, but the Blue Jays beat them to him in the second round and signed him for an over-slot $1,547,500. Los Angeles got him a year later as the first of two players to be named (outfielder Ryan Noda was the other) in an August deal for Ross Stripling. He logged 16 innings in his 2019 pro debut and spent time at the Dodgers' alternate site and instructional league last year. Williams deals at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96 mph with his fastball while using his 6-foot-6 frame and high three-quarters delivery to create a downhill plane that's tough on hitters. Scouts prefer his upper-70s downer curveball over his harder slider, though he made progress with the latter during instructs. He's also gaining confidence in his changeup, which features some tumble and fade. Williams' velocity was up a bit in instructional league and could continue to grow as he matures physically. He has good body control for a pitcher so young and tall, which should help him repeat his delivery, throw strikes and stay healthy. The Dodgers have been working with him to quicken his tempo and make better use of his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more projectable high school right-handers in the 2019 Draft, Williams passed on a Vanderbilt scholarship to sign with the Blue Jays for $1,547,500 in the second round. He posted a 1.13 ERA with 19 strikeouts in 16 Rookie-ball innings last summer, but his full-season debut was delayed until 2021 after the coronavirus shut down the Minors. The Dodgers acquired him as the first of two players to be named in the August trade that sent Ross Stripling to Toronto. Williams presently sits in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph with his fastball, which plays up because he uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create steep plane and angle. He throws two different breaking balls, with scouts preferring his curveball to his slider because of its spin and his high-three-quarters arm slot. He shows some feel for a changeup that should become an average offering as he uses it more. Williams has more body control than most pitchers his size and age, which bodes well for his ability to repeat his delivery, throw strikes and stay healthy. He'll need time to refine his craft, but if his stuff improves as he gets stronger, he could become a No. 3 or 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had Packard on an aggressive track after drafting the reigning American Athletic Conference Player of the Year out of East Carolina in the fifth round in 2019. He tore up Midwest League hitting that summer at Class A West Michigan, then had a brief stint of High-A play. The cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season cost him a chance to build upon that momentum and potentially work his way toward the upper levels. Packard has a bat-first profile with a pure, polished left-handed swing and a disciplined approach that keeps him from wandering outside the strike zone. His big frame allows him to produce power without too much vulnerability to strikeouts. His extra-base power beyond home runs is more from exit velocity than his slow foot speed. He has worked on his instincts in left field but has limited range and athleticism, leading some to wonder whether he could eventually shift to first base. The Tigers have found few productive hitters beyond early Draft picks in recent years, but Packard has the skill set and work ethic to potentially contribute at the big league level. His upside will be almost entirely determined by his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The American Athletic Conference Player of the Year as a sophomore at East Carolina, Packard had the potential to become a first-day MLB Draft pick in 2019 before back issues hampered him as a junior. The Tigers selected him in the fifth round and pushed him aggressively, sending him to Class A West Michigan after he overmatched Short-Season pitching in Connecticut. He responded by tearing up the Midwest League for just over a month, posing an .898 OPS for the Whitecaps before finishing the season at Class A Advanced Lakeland. Packard is a pure hitter with the polish of someone who looks like he has been playing pro ball for a few years. He has raw power to various parts of the field without relying on an all-or-nothing approach, and enough discipline not to chase pitches well outside his zone. His extra bases are based more on power than speed, which he lacks. He’s an adequate defender in left field with limited range, but his value is almost purely offensive. The Tigers have struggled to find Major League hitters in the Draft beyond the first couple rounds, but Packard could end up a value pick if he can stay healthy and continue to learn how to approach advanced pitching. The Tigers could move him up aggressively if he handles the Florida State League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had a run of college infielders in the 2019 Draft led by Quintana, a converted shortstop turned third baseman at the University of Arizona, who slugged his way into becoming one of the more productive hitters in the Pac-12 Conference. His 77 RBIs as a junior ranked fifth among NCAA Division I hitters in 2019 to go with a .342 average, 15 home runs and a .626 slugging percentage. After signing for $1.58 million in the second round, Quintana had an encouraging first week as a pro at Class A West Michigan before slumping to a .155 average and 36 strikeouts in July. Once the offensive struggles followed him into the infield, the Tigers pushed him to Short-Season Connecticut to regain his bearings as the season ended. Quintana generates a surprising amount of power for his size. It also leaves him susceptible to all-or-nothing outcomes, which seemed to amass around him in his introduction to pro ball. After hitting his first home run in his fifth pro game, he went 17-for-98 (.173) with 38 strikeouts over his next 106 plate appearances, including an 0-for-12, nine-strikeout stretch over three games in late July. Ironically, both of his home runs at West Michigan and Connecticut came in games in which he didn’t strike out.
