Defensively, his quick first step and sure hands made him a plus defender in college, with arm strength when needed. The Tigers drafted Quintana early hoping for an eventual quality two-way player for the hot corner. If he’s going to make it, he’ll have to learn to separate the two sides of his game and keep his defense out of slumps. He’ll approach the 2020 season with a fresh start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After being limited by injury to just nine games as a Florida freshman, McConnell rebounded in 2019 as a Draft-eligible sophomore to hit .332/.385/.576 with 15 home runs. His performance in college baseball’s best conference (Southeastern) and the fact that McConnell was a highly regarded prep prospect prompted the Royals to draft him in the second round and offer him first-round money ($2,222,500) to sign. A quick stop in the Rookie-level Arizona League to begin his pro debut was followed by a promotion to the Pioneer League, where McConnell produced uneven numbers (.667 OPS, 39.1% K%) before suffering a concussion in late August that kept him off the field during fall instructional league. McConnell's offensive profile stands out the most. The 6-foot-3 infielder has a knack for barreling up the baseball from the right side of the plate, with power that has begun to emerge in concert with his physical gains. He will need to refine his approach and trim some of the swing-and-miss from his game to reach his ceiling, but club officials believe he has the physical tools and remaining projection needed to become an average hitter with at least average power. He is a good athlete and plus runner but is unlikely to steal many bases as a pro due to a lack of explosiveness. The jury is out on whether he can stick at shortstop, and a 16-error pro debut didn’t help to sway opinions in his favor. Some scouts believe he’ll eventually move over to second base, while those who think his actions and hands are what's holding him back believe he'd be best off in center field, where his athleticism would play well. The Royals sent him out as a shortstop and will likely give him every opportunity to stick there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler in Virginia, Stallings showed polish on the mound but not enough stuff to really register on the Draft radar, so he went to the University of Tennessee. He was pretty much the same pitcher with the Volunteers, but this time with three years of solid track record in the Southeastern Conference on his resume. That led to the Angels taking him in the fifth round of the 2019 Draft, though after not pitching that summer after a heavy college workload and the 2020 shutdown, he never threw an official pitch for the Angels before he was traded to the Orioles in the José Iglesias deal in early December. None of Stallings' offerings jump off the page, but he has a legitimate four-pitch mix. His fastball will top out at 93 mph and more often comes in at 88-91 mph, but he commands the pitch very well and throws it with a ton of sink. His changeup, which has similar movement, plays off it nicely and he sells it well. His curve got better during his junior year and he also has a slider/cutter at his disposal. Stallings’ stuff plays up because he tunnels his pitches effectively and can throw all four of them for strikes. He rarely hurts himself with walks, allowing just 1.3 per nine innings at Tennessee. That gives him a chance to fit into the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ball’s home run power started showing up during his sophomore season at North Iowa Community College in 2018 and he brought the pop with him when he transferred to Dallas Baptist. His 18 homers last spring made the Braves take a chance in the 24th round and go above pick value to sign him for $197,500. He rewarded the organization’s faith by hitting 17 more homers and finishing with a 1.023 OPS while reaching full-season ball in his pro debut. The Braves think they might have a steal in Ball, who has the chance to hit for average and power. The left-handed hitter has tremendous hand-eye coordination at the plate and a good idea of the strike zone, which helps him tap into his ridiculous raw power. The ball doesn’t typically carry in either Danville or Rome, his home parks during his debut, and he made them seem small. He makes consistent hard contact and generally kept his strikeouts low, though the K rate did go up a bit when he made it to the South Atlantic League. He’s not going to scare anyone on the bases, but he’s more athletic than you might think, given his 6-foot-6 frame, and runs decently underway. Ball is limited to first base and he has work to do there, with some stiff actions defensively. He has good hands and some arm strength, though he’s working to improve his throwing mechanics so he can get to average there. It’s his power bat, though, that has the Braves excited and thinking they have a Day 3 Draft steal on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Venezuelan amateur, Cornielly endeared himself to scouts with his clean, athletic delivery and advanced feel for pitching. The Mets signed him for $25,000 at the outset of the 2017-18 international period, and he responded with a strong professional debut the next year in the Dominican Summer League. The right-hander didn’t fare as well last season in his return to the DSL, though he did perform better after a midseason jump over to the Rookie Gulf Coast League, where the 19-year-old impressed club officials with his endurance and aptitude on the mound. With a projectable frame and an innate ability for flooding the zone with strikes, Cornielly has a solid foundation as a starting pitcher. He doesn’t overpower hitters with his stuff, sitting in the low 90s with an above-average changeup and a fringy breaking ball, but he knows how to mix his pitches and commands his fastball better than most hurlers his age. He threw 84 percent of his pitches for strikes and posted a 52/9 K/BB ratio over 46 innings in 2019, all while inducing whiffs at an impressive 23-percent clip. Cornielly’s curveball is his least-advanced pitch, though club officials are optimistic that it will improve as he adds strength and refines his arm action. Cornielly is unique in the sense that he stands out more for his floor than ceiling even though he’s just 19 and has a projectable frame. Adding a bit more velocity could improve the effectiveness of his fastball-changeup combo, but even if he doesn’t, Cornielly still has enough starter qualities to profile to succeed at the back end of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 by the Nationals at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, Yean first provided a glimpse of return on that investment when he made his United States debut in 2019 and pitched his way from the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League to the short-season New York-Penn League. He created a lot of buzz at the Nationals’ instructional league program last fall, and the Pirates clearly noticed, acquiring the young right-hander in the deal that sent Josh Bell to Washington. His first year with his new organization, and his first taste of full-season ball, were uneven as he struggled with command in 2021. Yean has added a lot of strength since signing, which has led to some serious upticks in velocity. His fastball now touches 97 mph on a regular basis and will often sit in the mid-90s with life and good angle. He features both a power sinker and a four-seamer up in the zone. His upper-80s slider with depth might be a plus out pitch in time, and he’s shown good feel for his changeup, a pitch that’s come along nicely of late. While he’s gotten stronger and thrown harder, Yean has shown good athleticism on the mound and an ability to repeat his delivery, though he lost feel for the strike zone for much of 2021. He still has every chance to grow into a pitcher with average control of three above-average or better pitches eventually, a profile which could make him a future starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals gave out six-figure bonuses to 16 different players at the outset of the 2017-18 international period including Yean, whom they signed out of the Dominican Republic for $100,000 on July 2. He pitched to mixed results during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the next year but jumped onto the prospect radar in 2019, thanks to an eye-opening age-18 campaign that saw his stuff improve across the board and concluded with a late-season promotion to Class A Short Season Auburn. He was one of the more talked-about prospects during Washington’s fall instructional league two years in a row, impressing in the fall of 2020 before being sent to the Pirates in the Josh Bell deal. Yean’s improved velocity can be attributed to his recent physical gains, as he’s quickly grown into his projectable frame without it detracting from his athleticism and clean delivery. His explosive fastball touches 97 mph regularly and parks in the low- to mid-90s with late life and angle, setting up an a slider up to 88 mphr with depth that projects as at least an above-average pitch. A promising changeup gives Yean another potential weapon, and club officials are pleased with his progress in developing the pitch. With his stuff, size and delivery, Yean looks every bit the part of a future big league starter. While conditioning will be a major focus in the young right-hander’s development going forward, it looks like he has the requisite athleticism to make it all work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendoza was a highly regarded prospect in the 2016 Draft, but a strong commitment to Florida State led to him being taken by the Tigers in the 36th round. Three years later, after batting .298 with 31 homers and 124 RBIs in 160 games with the Seminoles, he became the Nationals’ third-round pick and signed for above slot value. A successful pro debut at Class A Hagerstown came next, with Mendoza flashing his power potential while making a smooth transition as a first baseman. As a 6-foot-5, 230-pound left-handed hitter, it is easy to dream on Mendoza’s potential at the plate. He gets good leverage in his swing and knows how to impact the baseball, showing plus raw power that should improve as he adds strength. He is still figuring out how to get to that power consistently, though, with swing-and-miss issues and a passive approach currently holding him back. Though he does work his share of walks, the Nationals would like to see him be more aggressive early in the count, viewing it as key for unlocking both his hitting ability and power. Mendoza’s defense at the hot corner with the Seminoles drew mixed reviews from scouts, with most of the concerns stemming from his size and actions. The Nationals immediately moved him to first base in pro ball and have been pleased with the early results, noting that his feet and hands both work well there. They may still offer him reps at third base, where his above-average arm fits well, but their hopeful that Mendoza’s bat will flourish now that he no longer has to focus on improving defensively at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dyson was viewed as potential first-round pick going into his junior year at Florida before some early struggles cost him a spot in the Gators’ rotation. His stuff was impressive even when he struggled, though, and he pitched with more velocity while working in shorter bursts in relief. The Nationals saw untapped potential and value in Dyson as a potential starter and went nearly $150,000 over slot value to sign him after selecting him in the fifth round. He rewarded the organization with a strong debut, posting a 1.14 ERA over eight starts at Class A Short Season Auburn. Dyson’s plus fastball carried over into pro ball as the Nationals hoped it would, with the right-hander sitting in the mid-90s and locating it well in the New York-Penn League. Dyson’s heater jumps on hitters due to his clean arm action and easy delivery, though it can be hittable when he misses his spot due to a lack of movement. Dyson’s slider lacks depth but should be an average pitch once developed, and he’ll need to make similar gains with a changeup that currently is below average. Though the Nationals think Dyson can remain a starter and were encouraged by his strong pro, club officials also acknowledge that the 6-foot-3 righty has some major hurdles to clear in his development. If that doesn’t work, Dyson has the type of stuff that could play up in shorter bursts in relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the best high school catcher in a lean 2019 crop, Hearn figured to go in the top three rounds based on talent. Worries about the strength of his commitment to Mississippi State dropped him to the sixth round, though he was still the first prep backstop selected. He signed for $950,000, the equivalent of second-round money, then struck out 36 times in 80 at-bats while hitting .163 in his debut. Hearn offers plenty of bat speed and strength from the left side of the plate. Instead of letting his plus raw power to all fields translate into home runs naturally, he got too aggressive and pull-oriented in his introduction to pro ball, resulting in too many whiffs and rolled-over grounders to the right side of the infield. If he can settle down, he could develop into a decent hitter with 20 or more homers per season. Hearn runs like a typical catcher but moves well enough behind the plate. He had concentration lapses as an amateur but appeared more focused in his debut and should become an average to solid receiver. He has a plus arm with a quick release, and he has recorded 1.9-second pop times to second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs not only corralled 2019's best high school catching prospect in Ethan Hearn, but also snagged the top international catching prospect in Quintero. A Venezuelan, he signed for $2.9 million, the largest bonus Chicago ever has given an international amateur. The previous record was $2.8 million in 2013 for Eloy Jimenez, one of the game's premier young sluggers (albeit now with the White Sox). Quintero has a lofty offensive ceiling as well. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power from the left side of the plate, and he already shows some ability to knock the ball out of the park to the opposite field. More than just a slugger, he has good feel for hitting and could offer production similar to that of Willson Contreras if he reaches his potential. Quintero has solid-to-plus arm strength with a quick transfer, and he also exhibits strong leadership skills. In order to remain behind the plate, he'll need to clean up his receiving, but he's also 17 years old and time is on his side. His below-average speed makes him faster than most catchers, though he could slow down as he fills out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top pitcher in Louisville's 2016 recruiting class, McAvene succumbed to Tommy John surgery in April of his freshman year and returned to the mound 12 months later. He became the Cardinals' closer in 2019 and boosted his Draft stock when his velocity surged during the team's postseason run to the College World Series. Though he hadn't started a game since 2017, the Cubs immediately moved him to the rotation after signing him in the third round. After spending most of his junior season operating at 93-96 mph with riding life on his four-seam fastball, McAvene started hitting 98s and 99s in the NCAA tournament and kept doing so in short starts during his pro debut. His breaking ball shows signs of becoming a plus pitch, combining slider velocity with curveball depth. Now that he's a starter, one of his primary focuses will be to develop his nascent changeup. McAvene has a strong, durable 6-foot-3 frame and is throwing more strikes as he puts elbow reconstruction further behind him. Chicago believes he's equipped to stay in the rotation and plans to develop him alongside 2019 fourth-rounder Chris Clarke, another college closer turned starter. Should he return to the bullpen, McAvene could move quickly and eventually claim a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Malone turned a strong senior season at IMG Academy in Florida into becoming the No. 33 overall pick of the 2019 Draft and signing with the D-backs for a full-slot $2.2 million bonus. He had barely begun his pro career -- a total of eight Rookie-level innings after signing -- when he was sent to the Pirates in the January 2020 Starling Marte deal. He was at his new organization’s alternate training site during the season but didn’t actually pitch. The Pirates will get to see Malone’s four-pitch mix for real in 2021. Athletic and projectable, the right-hander has shown the ability to get his fastball up to 96-97 mph regularly while maintaining his velocity deep into his starts. He throws both a slider and a curve, the former a plus put-away pitch and ahead of his 11-to-5 curve, though he worked during 2020 to improve that breaking ball. He’s had some feel for his changeup but will need to keep working on his arm action to sell it well. Malone has a repeatable delivery that leads most to believe he’ll have at least average command as he develops. The ingredients might still be raw, especially after a year of not pitching competitively, but they are all there for Malone to become a big league starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft class, Malone was the epitome of the projectable, athletic, high-ceilinged right-handers some teams covet. A move from North Carolina to IMG Academy helped his stock, as did a dominant outing at USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational. He went No. 33 overall to the D-backs and then pitched sparingly during his pro debut. His time with Arizona was short-lived as the Pirates acquired him along with shortstop Liover Peguero in the trade for Starling Marte. Malone now brings his potential four-pitch mix to the Pirates organization. He’s always had arm strength, with a fastball he could run up to 96 mph and he started showing a better ability to consistently maintain that velocity deeper into his outings during his senior year. He has two different breaking pitches, with his slider now a plus out pitch and a better weapon than his average 11-to-5 curve. He hasn’t always maintained his arm slot for that pitch and while he has feel for a changeup, he’ll need to keep working on maintaining his arm speed to sell it well. With an athletic delivery and easy arm action, it’s easy to see Malone having solid command in the future, and he made strides in that regard at IMG Academy. He’s far away, but all of the ingredients to become a big league starter are there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Locey teamed with Jake Fromm to help Houston County High (Warner Robins, Ga.) win the Georgia state 5-A baseball championship as a senior in 2016. Both headed to the University of Georgia, where Fromm starred at quarterback while Locey emerged as a key starter on a Bulldogs team that won a school-record 21 Southeastern Conference games in 2019. While there's debate as to whether he winds up as a starter or reliever in the long run, there's no question that his arm was among the best in college baseball's top conference. That arm was part of the package the Rockies acquired as part of the return for Nolan Arenado in early February. A big right-hander who works from a high-three-quarters slot to create angle to the plate, Locey operates at 94-96 mph and can touch 98 mph with his fastball, He maintains his velocity throughout his starts and figures to hit 100 mph if he works shorter stints out of the bullpen. His low-80s slider can be sharp and a solid pitch when he commands it, and he also shows promising shape on a curveball that's a work in progress. As a power pitcher, Locey didn’t have much need for a changeup in college. Locey is strong and physical, though to remain a starter he'll have to do a better job of repeating his delivery and commanding his pitches. If he does become a reliever, he has late-inning potential and perhaps a chance to become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green pitched out of the bullpen during his first three years Southeastern Louisiana before sliding into the starting rotation as a senior in 2018 and showing improved pitchability and control in the new role. The D-backs saw untapped potential in Green as a starter and made him their 14th-round pick in June, signing the right-hander for just $5,000. He impressed during his pro debut that summer, earning All-Star honors as a reliever in the Pioneer League, then opened his first full season as a starter in the Class A Advanced California League. He dominated the hitter-friendly league, going 9-1 with 1 .73 ERA over his first 14 starts to earn a Double-A promotion in July. Green’s calling card is a low- to mid-90s bowling-ball sinker that helps him induce ground balls at an elite rate. After posting a near 68-percent ground-all rate in his pro debut, he led all Minor League hurlers (120 IP min.) in that department in 2019 by inducing grounders at a 67.2-percent clip. Green’s downer curveball is consistently an average or better pitch, and he also throws a slider that has cutter action. A mid-80s changeup gives the right-hander a third usable pitch, though it is behind both of his breaking balls. He issued 1.7 walks-per-nine in 2019, exhibiting above-average control and command. Beyond the effectiveness of his stuff, Green stands out for his stamina and durability. He worked at least five innings in all 22 starts in 2019, averaging better than 5 2/3 innings per turn. Though he did struggle a bit in Double-A (4.28 ERA, .318 BAA) as he attempted to mix his pitches more, the D-backs believe it was a valuable learning experience that will aid him going forward. Green has all the ingredients to become a big league starter, perhaps even a No. 4 if he can trade some of those grounders for a few more strikeouts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top relief prospects in the 2019 Draft, Wallace set a Connecticut record with 16 saves while posting a 0.64 ERA with 68 strikeouts in 42 innings. He continued to dominate after signing with the Rockies as a third-round pick, leading the Short Season Northwest League with 12 saves while recording a 1.29 ERA. The Red Sox acquired him this September as the player to be named in the Kevin Pillar trade. Wallace aggressively goes after hitters with a hard two-pitch mix. He couples a 93-95 mph fastball that tops out at 97 with a nasty 82-85 mph slider that can be a well above-average offering at times. He creates good deception with his slider, throwing it on the same plane as his fastball with sweep and depth. Wallace's delivery features some effort, though it's not too violent and adds to his deception without preventing him from throwing strikes. He has a resilient arm and the mentality to handle high-leverage situations. Though he won't make his full-season debut until 2021, he could move quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Mann played at Louisville, scouts regarded him as a fine college player but didn't see a standout tool or think he fit the profile at second base. The Dodgers selected him in 2018's fifth round because they thought they could unlock some improvements, and he went from a .680 OPS in his pro debut to ranking seventh in the high Class A California League with 19 homers in 2019 despite missing a month with a sprained right knee. He got his 2020 development time at Los Angeles' alternate site. Mann hit just 15 homers in three years of college but looks like a different hitter these days after the Dodgers got him to use his legs more, add some loft to his right-handed stroke and seek out more pitches to attack. After focusing on making contact and reaching base at Louisville, he now looks to launch balls and shows at least average power to all fields. Though he has changed his identity at the plate, he still has maintained some discipline. Mann has transformed himself in the field as well, though his long-term defensive home is still uncertain. While he's still a fringy runner, he has quickened his footwork and strengthened his arm. He has sure hands but his actions are a bit stiff for second base, so he may fit better at third base, where his average arm might be a tick short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The consensus on Mann when he played at Louisville was that he was a good college player but lacked an above-average tool and didn't fit the second-base profile. The Dodgers drafted him in the fifth round in 2018 because they thought he could improve with some adjustments, but he posted a .680 OPS in his pro debut. He looked like a different player last season, when he placed seventh in the Class A Advanced California League with 19 homers despite missing a month with a sprained right knee. After his initial foray into pro ball, Mann got stronger and adopted a more aggressive approach, using his legs more and adding loft to his right-handed swing. While he focused on making contact and getting on base in college, he's now looking to launch balls and displaying at least average power to all fields. He has changed his offensive identity while still maintaining some plate discipline. Mann has transformed himself defensively as well. He still has fringy speed but he has quickened his footwork and strengthened his arm. He has sure hands at second base but his actions are a little stiff for the middle infield, so he could wind up at third base after seeing extensive action there in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lake Travis High (Austin, Texas) had two premium prospects last spring in Brett Baty, the 12th overall pick by the Mets, and Lewis, who went in the second round -- just like his father Jimmy did with the Astros in 1991. The younger Lewis missed the state playoffs with what was believed to be a lat strain but was diagnosed as a partially torn labrum in his shoulder during a pre-signing physical. The Dodgers still signed him for an above-slot $1,097,500 and put his debut on hold. Lewis already demonstrates the ability to carry a low-90s fastball deep into games while topping out at 95 mph, and he should add velocity as he adds strength to his lanky 6-foot-6 frame. He could have a pair of plus pitches if he can develop more consistency with his upper-70s downer curveball. He has some feel for a changeup but didn't have much need for it as an amateur. Lewis's athleticism and strength should help him throw strikes and pile up innings. He has a fairly simple delivery for a tall youngster, using his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. He also intrigued scouts with his hitting ability and power potential, and he might have played both ways had he gone to Louisiana State rather than turning pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big, athletic, wiry and full of potential, Mena has drawn comparisons to a young Franchy Cordero or Gregory Polanco. That combination of tools and ceiling earned Mena a $2.2 million bonus from the Padres at the outset of the 2019-20 international signing period. The Cubs bought into his upside when they acquired him, three other prospects and Zach Davies in exchange for Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini in December. Mena covers the strike zone well and hits everything hard from the left side of the plate. He has a knack for barreling up balls and has the potential for future average power, though his hitting ability stands out more than his pop. He projects to hit second or third in the lineup but could eventually be a leadoff hitter because of his hit tool and his plus-plus speed, which makes him a basestealing threat. Mena is already viewed as an above-average defender who has a talent for reading and picking up balls off the bat. He gets good jumps and takes great angles and routes, utilizing his plus-plus speed, and his arm strength has above-average potential. He's also been praised for his makeup and baseball IQ. Mena, based on his remaining physical projection, could end up at 6-foot-4 and 225 pounds if he continues to develop at a normal pace.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2009, the Giants used a fifth-round pick on a college first baseman whose hitting ability and plate discipline stood out more than his power, finding a long-term starter in Brandon Belt. They see similar traits in Wyatt, who replaced two-way star Brandon McKay (the No. 4 overall pick in 2017) at first base at Louisville and ranked third in NCAA Division I in walks in each of his two seasons as a starter, including a school-record 72 in 2019. Signed for a well-below-slot $997,500 in the second round last June, he reached low Class A in his pro debut. Wyatt has a sound left-handed swing, good feel for hitting and an extremely patient approach that borders on passive at times. His strength gives him at least solid raw power and 20-homer potential, but he won't tap into it unless he attacks more pitches and drives them in the air more often. After he produced a lot of rolled-over, weak ground-ball contact in his debut, San Francisco is trying to help him become more aggressive while still maintaining his discipline. Wyatt is a better athlete than his well-below-average speed might suggest. He moves well enough at first base, displaying soft hands and decent arm strength. Some evaluators who scouted him as an amateur thought he might be able to handle playing some left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carraway first piqued Dallas Baptist's interest as a center fielder and threw in the mid-80s as a Texas high school senior in 2017, so he wasn't a high-priority recruit and didn't attract interest from pro clubs. His velocity began to climb as a freshman but he was so raw that he made just two appearances and retired only one of the seven batters he faced. He made a huge leap forward as a sophomore, averaging 15.6 strikeouts per nine innings as the Patriots' closer and becoming the first player in school history to make the U.S. collegiate national team. The favorite to be the first reliever drafted in 2020, Carraway has a pair of overpowering pitches in his fastball and curveball. His heater sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with riding action, while his downer curve usually parks in the upper 70s. His pitches play up because they have high spin rates and he gets good extension in his delivery, and both can grade as well above average when at their best. As a 6-footer who lacks physicality and features a lot of effort in his high three-quarters delivery, Carraway is strictly a reliever. His control and command have improved in college but still need to get better if he's going to hold down a high-leverage role in the big leagues. He should be one of the first players from the 2020 Draft to reach the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wright State's Sean Murphy has developed into one of baseball's top catching prospects since signing with the Athletics in the third round three years ago. The Raiders have two more position players who should go on day two of the 2019 Draft, with most scouts preferring Gray ahead of outfielder Peyton Burdick. Gray features plenty of strength in his 6-foot-3, 205-pound frame and has upped his power production as a junior. His bat speed is more ordinary, so he'll need to show he can do damage with wood bats after a so-so showing in the Cape Cod League last summer. A left-handed hitter, he's exhibiting more plate discipline than he has in the past. Gray moves well for a big man and makes the most of his below-average speed on the bases. He covers more than enough ground at third base and will be able to remain there as a pro. His soft hands and strong arm add to a solid defensive package.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown already has overcome more adversity than most players will face, losing his mother to cancer when he was 13, blowing out his elbow and having Tommy John surgery as a high school sophomore, and fathering a daughter born with Down syndrome and life-threatening heart defects when he was a Vanderbilt freshman. His toughness translates to the mound, where he set a school record with 17 saves in 2019, including three in Omaha as the Commodores won their second national championship. He wasn't as sharp in the shortened 2020 season but still should be one of the first relievers drafted. Brown usually attacks hitters with a 91-94 mph fastball with running action that misses bats up in the strike zone, topping out at 96, and an 83-86 mph slider. Both pitches were more solid than plus this spring but have shown better in the past. He also mixes in a mid-70s curveball with more depth than power to give batters a different look, and he can throw them off balance with a decent low-80s changeup. As with his stuff, Brown's control and command were a tick down this year but he usually pounds the zone. With his four pitches, strike-throwing ability and a strong 6-foot-4 build, some scouts think he has the ingredients to start and could get the opportunity to do so in pro ball. Other evaluators believe his delivery and mentality are better suited for late-inning relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez showed plenty of upside when the Padres signed the Dominican outfielder for $300,000 at the start of the 2017-18 international period. Despite slashing just .176/.354/.270 with 80 strikeouts in 61 games in his first pro season in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, his knack for squaring up the ball impressed the club. Playing in the Rookie-level Arizona League in 2019 at age 17, Perez showed vast improvement as he hit .268/.349/.512 and tied for second-most in the league with 11 homers. That impressive bat enticed the A’s enough to nab him as the player to be named later in the 2020 deal that sent Jorge Mateo to the Padres. Perez could develop into a strong power bat given his physical frame. Like most young players, he’s still working through some swing-and-miss issues. That said, Perez does make a lot of quality contact with his quick bat and lofty swing. He has played mostly right field since 2019 and is destined for a corner outfield spot due to below-average speed. Perez's slightly above-average arm probably makes left field a better fit for the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman, Powell took over as UCLA’s closer and held on to the job until the 2020 season was ended prematurely. He racked up 26 saves, second in school history behind only David Berg, and was quickly becoming one of the best relief pitching options in the Draft class this spring, with a 20/2 K/BB ratio while allowing just three hits and no runs over 9 1/3 innings in eight appearances. Powell isn’t one of those college relievers you wonder about whether he could start at the next level. The nation’s Stopper of the Year as a sophomore, the 6-foot right-hander is bullpen only, but the type who could move quickly. He typically sits in the low 90s with his fastball and is regularly up to 96 mph. It’s his slider, though, that’s the real separator. It’s a filthy out pitch that gets a ton of swings and misses, a plus pitch for sure. Powell does have a changeup, but it’s that electric fastball-slider combination that has peaked scouts’ interest. With a loud delivery, he’s had trouble with command, but was finding the strike zone more consistently this spring and throws enough strikes to profile well in the back of a bullpen, a role he relishes, with the makeup to close games at the next level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 One of 15 players signed by the Padres for at least $300,000 during the 2017-18 international period, Santana quickly emerged as San Diego's most promising prospect from the class. A natural shortstop who also projects well at the plate, he garnered Dominican Summer League All-Star honors during his pro debut and then broke out offensively in the 2019 Rookie-level Arizona League, slashing .346/.429/.494 at age 18. The Cubs grabbed him and three other prospects along with Zach Davies in a December trade that cost them Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini. Santana’s selectively aggressive approach is advanced for a player his age, and he has already shown that he can do damage on pitches in the zone. He has a solid foundation for development, possessing a blend of bat speed, patience and feel for the barrel, with remaining physical projection that points toward future power gains. Santana has proven difficult to strike out early in his career, showing a penchant for quality opposite-field contact. Defensively, Santana looks like a future big league shortstop: he’s twitchy and athletic, with smooth actions, plus arm strength and plenty of range, and he already plays the position with confidence. Those qualities all give Santana realistic floor value in the big leagues, and there’s everyday-shortstop upside in the profile should his hitting ability and power both reach fruition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts flock to the Excellence Tournament in Puerto Rico every year to get the chance to see the top talent the island has to offer prior to the Draft. Contreras, a middle infielder with some present hitting skills, was the only player to hit homer in this year's event. Big and strong, Contreras has more present strength than some of his fellow Puerto Rican infielders in the class. When he keeps his swing under control, he can drive the ball. He has serious raw power, especially to the pull side, but has the tendency to lose his mechanics and get out of control trying to show off that power. A solid runner when underway, there is some question over whether he has the range to stick at shortstop, though most teams would send him out at the spot and see if he can stick there. He has a plus arm and good enough hands for the position. If Contreras does slow down as he matures, he still has a future on the dirt, perhaps as an offensive second baseman. Some scouts think he'll hit enough to profile at third base, reminding some of an Asdrubal Cabrera type. He'll head to San Jacinto Junior College if the Draft doesn't work out for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the delayed 2020-21 international signing period began in the middle of January 2021, the Reds jumped in and handed out two seven-figure bonuses. Ariel Almonte got $1.85 million while Valdez topped him with a $1.9 million bonus, signing at the start of the period on Jan. 15 and perhaps giving the Reds two-thirds of their future outfield. That bonus is the largest the Reds have given to an international amateur free agent not from Cuba since 2008. The 6-foot-2 Valdez is chock full of tools, starting with his at-least plus speed. That should allow him to be a threat on the bases and to cover a lot of ground in center field, where he should be able to stay long-term. He also has a strong arm, which could eventually be plus, an asset in center and one that would work just fine in right should a move be necessary down the line. A right-handed hitter, Valdez has showed off some bat speed and the ability to drive the ball. There’s raw power to tap into, and he’s showed it off in batting practice, but there’s work to be done in terms of pitch recognition and consistent contact. He might be a bit of a project, but he could eventually turn into a dynamic up-the-middle player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A position player at Junipero Serra (Calif.) HS, Garcia headed to Division III Chapman as an infielder. He appeared in just 24 games as a freshman then moved to the mound as a sophomore. He found immediate success in the bullpen, winning nine games and saving 12 more to help the Panthers win a national title, earning College World Series Most Outstanding Player honors in the process. After pitching well out of the pen on the Cape last summer, Garcia moved into the rotation at the start of his junior year and created a lot of early buzz in the process. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has shown glimpses of three pitches that have the chance to be above average. He came out of the gate this spring throwing much harder than in the past, showcasing a fastball consistently up to 97 mph. He backs it up with a mid-80s slider and an 86-88 mph cutter, though he hasn’t shown much of a changeup in the past. Garcia’s command has been spotty at times, but he’s generally around the strike zone, and given his athletic delivery and arm action, there’s some confidence he’ll improve on this front in the future. He doesn’t have a ton of track record against good competition – the stint on the Cape helped a bit – or as a starter, but he’s a relatively fresher arm with perhaps more projection than most college pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two years after producing a first-round outfielder in Jordyn Adams, Green Hope High (Cary, N.C.) has another early-round prospect in Norris. While Adams didn't break out until the National High School Invitational during his senior year, Norris has been famous on the showcase circuit for a while. He has the pitches and physicality to go in the first round but won't because he hasn't been able to harness them. Norris' powerful 6-foot-4 frame already produces fastballs that sit at 90-94 mph and peak at 96 with some late life. When he's on, both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider grade as at least plus offerings. He's in the early stages of developing a changeup with some sink. More strong than athletic, Norris has difficulty keeping his delivery in sync and staying online to the plate. He has 107 walks in 141 career innings at Green Hope and his command is shakier than his control. He might not go high enough in the Draft to divert him from a North Carolina commitment and his long-term role could be as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pardinho signed with the Blue Jays out of Brazil for $1.4 million as a 16-year-old in 2017 and immediately became one of the more unique arms in the systems, but injuries have held the right-hander back through his early years of development. Now 20, the right-hander is coming off Tommy John surgery and is expected to make his return to the mound in 2021. Pardinho last pitched in ’19, when he posted a 2.41 ERA over 33 2/3 innings with Class A Lansing. He returned for two Florida Coast League rehab starts this July but suffered a setback that has slowed his comeback attempt. When healthy, Pardinho has a feel for pitching well beyond his years, and he improved his physique over the past year while recovering from surgery. After reaching the mid-90s with his fastball in the lower levels, Pardinho’s velocity had dipped a bit prior to the surgery, so those radar readings and his ability to sustain them will be a key factor in his return. Pardinho pairs that live fastball with a plus curveball, a useful slider and a changeup that has potential. With a repeatable delivery that generates plenty of drive from his strong lower body, Pardinho has all of the building blocks to remain a starter. Although undersized at 5-foot-10, that hasn’t held Pardinho back and he could fully revive his prospect stock with a strong return to the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After impressing through his first two professional seasons – and through multiple injury woes – the young right-hander is slated to miss at least all of 2020 after undergoing Tommy John surgery in February. At almost four years younger than the average age in the Midwest League in ’19, the Brazilian who signed with Toronto for $1.4 million as a 16-year-old in 2017 posted a 2.41 ERA over seven starts and 33 2/3 innings with 13 walks and 30 strikeouts. He’d been sidelined in the first half with elbow issues before being shut down in August with a lower back injury and won’t see game action again until 2021. Pardinho’s stuff and feel for pitching are well advanced for his age, and while his velocity increased in his first year of pro ball, giving him a low 90s fastball with late life that reached the mid-90s, it was down last season. He pairs the heater with a plus curveball, his best secondary pitch, and while he added a slider in 2018 that had the makings of becoming at least average, he stayed away from it last season. He also has a promising changeup, a relatively new pitch for the young hurler. What might be most impressive about Pardinho is his ability to execute his pitches as part of an overall game plan. His arm action and delivery are clean and repeatable, and he effectively compensates for being somewhat undersized by getting good extension over his front side. While development gains remain, all the ingredients are there for Pardinho to develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pardinho ranked as MLB Pipeline's No. 5 prospect for the 2017-18 international period after an impressive amateur career in Brazil before signing with Toronto for $1.4 million. The Blue Jays deemed him advanced enough to make the jump straight to the Rookie-level Appalachian League for his pro debut, and Pardinho, just 17, rewarded the club's confidence by posting a 2.88 ERA over 50 innings and finishing third in the circuit in strikeouts (64). Pardinho's stuff and feel for pitching is exceptional for his age. His velocity has ticked up since signing, giving him a low 90s fastball with late life that can touch 96 mph. He pairs his heater with a plus curveball, his best secondary pitch, and he added a slider in 2018 that already has the makings of becoming at least average. The same can be said about Pardinho's promising changeup, also a relatively new pitch for him. Perhaps what's most impressive about Pardinho is his ability execute his pitches as part of an overall game plan. His arm action and delivery are clean and repeatable, and he effectively compensates for being somewhat undersized by getting good extension over his front side. He still has quite a bit of development remaining, but all the ingredients are there for Pardinho to develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A shortstop in Venezuela before changing positions and becoming the top catching prospect in the 2016 international class, Garcia signed for $800,000. He struggled with the physical demands of his new position and pro ball in his first two seasons before he began hitting the ball with more authority and earned short-season Northwest League all-star accolades at age 19 in 2019. Though he has yet to make his full-season debut, the Rangers protected him on their 40-man roster in November. Garcia has soft hands and has become a solid to plus receiver as he has added some much-needed strength. With a strong arm and a quick release, he erased 35 percent of basestealers during his first three years as a pro. He's quicker and more athletic than a typical catcher, and he has remarkably advanced defensive instincts for someone who didn't move behind the plate until 2015. Garcia has put on 30 pounds since turning pro and made some swing changes in 2018 to unlock his bat speed, improving the likelihood that he provides enough offense to become a regular catcher rather than a defensive-minded backup. A switch-hitter with a compact stroke, he has started launching balls in the air more often and could become a 12-15 homer threat. He has been more productive hitting left-handed but club officials think his swing is better from the right side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia grew up playing shortstop in Venezuela before moving behind the plate and becoming the best catching prospect in the 2016 international class. Signed for $800,000, he initially struggled to handle the rigors of his position and pro ball. He began hitting the ball with more authority while continuing to provide quality defense in 2019, earning all-star recognition in the short-season Northwest League at age 19. Quicker and more athletic than most catchers, Garcia has advanced defensive instincts, especially considering he first donned the tools of ignorance in 2015. He has soft hands and has developed into a solid receiver as he has gotten stronger. He also has a strong arm with a quick release that has helped him throw out 35 percent of basestealers in his first three seasons. After making some swing changes in 2018 to unlock his bat speed and adding some much-needed muscle, Garcia now looks more like an everyday catcher and less like a defensive-minded backup. A switch-hitter with a short stroke designed for line-drive contract, he has started driving the ball in the air more frequently and should provide at least 12-15 homers per season. Though he has been more productive hitting left-handed, the Rangers believe his swing is better from the right side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 A former shortstop who moved behind the plate and became the best catcher in the 2016 international class, Garcia signed out of Venezuela for $800,000. More lean and twitchy than physical, he initially struggled with the rigors of catching and pro ball. He did a better job of adapting when he made his U.S. debut in 2018, finishing on a .426/.491/.617 tear in August that has the Rangers optimistic about his offensive future. Garcia's defense has been as good as advertised. He's quicker and more athletic than most catchers and has advanced instincts for someone who first donned the tools of ignorance in 2015. He should become at least a solid receiver and thrower as he gets stronger, and he erased 37 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. Garcia made some swing changes last summer to help unlock his quick hands and Texas believes he has a chance to become an above-average hitter. His short swing is geared for line-drive contact rather than driving the ball, and he may never provide more than gap power. A switch-hitter, he'll have to make further adjustments against left-handers after batting just .152/.287/.177 against them in two years of Rookie ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former shortstop who blossomed into the best catcher on the 2016-17 international market, Garcia signed out of Venezuela for $800,000. Despite adding 25 pounds in the year before joining the Rangers, he's still not very strong and struggled with the rigors of catching and pro ball during his 2017 debut. He batted just .215/.321/.280 as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, though his defense was as good as advertised. Garcia is currently less advanced than Jose Trevino, who's seven years older than him, but eventually could surpass Trevino as the best defender among Texas' deep group of catching prospects. He's quicker and more athletic than most backstops, has soft hands and projects as at least a solid receiver and thrower once he matures physically. He possesses advanced instincts for someone who began catching in 2015. A switch-hitter, Garcia was helpless against left-handers in his debut and won't do any damage until he adds some much-needed muscle. He's equipped to make line-drive contact with his compact swing but may never have more than gap power. He's presently a fringy runner but will lose a step as he fills out and spends more time behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best catcher on the 2016-17 international market, Garcia signed for a relative bargain at $800,000. A former shortstop, he added 25 pounds in the year before he turned pro. He has a similar build and offensive profile to fellow Venezuelan Tomas Telis, another infielder-turned-backstop whom the Rangers sent to the Marlins in a 2015 trade for Sam Dyson, though Garcia has a higher defensive ceiling. More athletic than most catchers, Garcia has quick feet, soft hands and improving arm strength. He projects to become at least solid at receiving and throwing as he develops physically. He's agile and has advanced instincts for someone who moved behind the plate in 2015. A switch-hitter with a short stroke, Garcia uses a contact approach and focuses on hitting line drives from gap to gap. While he has room on his 5-foot-11 frame to continue adding strength, he's unlikely to grow into more than gap power. He has fringy speed, which makes him a better runner than most catchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former multi-sport star from the Rhode Island high school ranks, Reed showed off his raw tools and athleticism in spurts during three years at the University of Florida. The Padres liked his very high ceiling enough to take him in the second round of the 2016 Draft. Following a rough first full season, Reed broke out in 2018, played in the Futures Game and advanced to Double-A. His struggles there carried over to his 2019 season back in the Texas League and he wasn’t protected from, nor was he selected in, the Rule 5 Draft. He was then sent to the A’s as the player to be named later for Jurickson Profar. The A’s are hoping a change of scenery, some new instructors and new ideas might be just what is needed to unlock Reed’s treasure trove of raw tools more consistently. The switch-hitter can make loud contact and drive the ball from both sides of the plate, though his right-handed swing is a bit better. He had changed his swing path to be shorter to the ball with more extension, leading to his breakout to start 2018, but his strikeout rate soared once he got to Double-A. Reed’s speed is close to top of the scale and he’s a major basestealing threat, swiping 51 bags in 2018. It also helps him cover a ton of ground in the outfield, where he’s a plus defender in center and has an arm that works really well in the corners. He still has 20-20 potential if he can refine his approach enough to make more contact with his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best all-around athletes in the 2016 Draft class, the Padres selected Reed with the 48th overall pick and signed him for slightly over $1 million. After struggling in his first full season, Reed went to the Australian Baseball League and rediscovered his swing. It led to a breakout 2018. Reed reached base consistently, and he wreaked havoc on the bases, swiping 51 bags between Lake Elsinore and Double-A San Antonio. Reed earned his Double-A promotion after playing in the All-Star Futures Game at Nationals Park, but his transition to the level didn't go smoothly and he continued to struggle with the bat in a return to the level in 2019. Left off the 40-man roster, he was sent to the A's as the player to be named later in the Jurickson Profar deal after the Rule 5 Draft in December. A switch-hitter, Reed has the potential to hit for both average and power, though he's historically been better form the right side. Before the 2018 season, he made an adjustment, allowing him to be shorter to the ball with more extension after contact. But he'll need to continue to cut down on the strikeouts. If he can add more contact to his game, he has plus-plus speed -- which translates on both sides of the ball. Reed has a tall, athletic build that gives him the potential to do a lot of things well on the baseball field, but he still has gains to make as a hitter. If he can get back to a more refined approach and better swing mechanics, he has the tools to be an impact player. But questions linger as to whether his game, particularly his hitting, will translate at higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selected in the fifth round of the 2011 Draft out of Leander (Texas) High, Reed made a steady climb through the Minor Leagues before breaking out between Double-A Biloxi and Triple-A Colorado Springs in 2015. The Brewers rewarded the athletic outfielder with a September callup, and he returned to the big leagues again late last year, albeit after an uneven campaign back at Triple-A Colorado Springs. Reed's contact skills and advanced plate discipline are his strengths, and he's piled up walks -- his 74 walks paced the Pacific Coast League in 2016 -- while getting on base at a high clip throughout his career. There is some swing-and-miss to his game, however, and his strikeout rate has steadily increased in the upper Minors. He has a short, compact swing from the right side that yields lines drives and consistent gap power, and some evaluators believe he'll eventually show some over-the-fence pop. An above-average runner, Reed has good instincts on the bases and has proven to be a legitimate base-stealing threat, swiping at least 20 bags in each of the last four years. Reed is fast enough to play center field and has the necessary arm strength for right, but his lack of power portends to a career as a fourth outfielder. Meanwhile, the Brewers' ongoing stockpiling of toolsy center fielders doesn't bode well for Reed's chances of achieving an everyday role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 The sixth overall pick in the 2017 Draft by the A’s out of North Davidson High School in North Carolina, Beck positioned himself as a top-10 pick following a strong pre-Draft workout that continued his positive trend that started with an impressive senior season. Progressing nicely through the Minors in 2018, he remained stuck in the Class A Advanced California League in 2019. Beck did not receive an invite to the club’s alternate training site last year. Beck has struggled to live up to the high expectations that were placed on him. His combination of a strikeout rate over 34 percent in 2019 and inconsistent power in games at the pro level has hindered him at the High-A level. But the A’s still believe they have a good player in Beck, it’s just a matter of figuring it all out. He does have premium bat speed and worked hard on calming down in the box with the confidence that if he can make more contact, the power will naturally come. Although it doesn’t necessarily show up in the stolen base numbers, Beck has very good speed. It helps him play strong defense in center field, a spot where he has also shown a solid arm. He’s still young, and there are still some tools he’s working to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Beck missed the summer showcase circuit before his senior year of high school because of a torn ACL, keeping scouts from compiling reports of the outfielder against top competition. A strong senior season in North Carolina, along with what was a ridiculous pre-Draft workout, led the A’s to roll the dice on his athleticism and considerable tools with the sixth overall selection in the 2017 Draft. He did a nice job advancing to full-season ball for his first full season in 2018 but didn’t take a comparable step forward with a move to the California League in 2019. Overall, Beck hasn’t lived up to the expectations usually put on a top 10 Draft pick. After chasing power too much during his debut, he became a better hitter in his first full season. His swing and miss skyrocketed in 2019, though, with a strikeout rate over 34 percent and he hasn’t been able to get to his considerable raw power consistently at all in games at the pro level. He struggles recognizing breaking stuff and his struggles seemed to get in his head at times. He has premium bat speed and his rotation and acceleration are elite and he worked on calming down in the box during instructs with the confidence that if he can make more contact, the power will naturally come. Beck runs very well, and while that hasn’t translated to stolen bases, it does help him play a very good center field. He has an above-average arm that would work well in an outfield corner if he slows down enough to necessitate a move. But more than anything, he needs to refine his approach and start turning his tools into production at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 When the high school season began back in 2017, Beck was a bit of an unknown quantity because he had missed the previous summer after tearing his left ACL and meniscus that May. A big senior season in North Carolina sent him soaring up Draft boards and the A's were even more confident his tools would play after a pre-Draft workout, so they nabbed him with the No. 6 overall pick and gave him a franchise-record $5,303,000 to sign. His pro debut that summer was uneven, at best, but he turned in a solid full-season debut in 2018 as a Midwest League All-Star. Beck's tools are undeniable, though he is still learning to use them consistently on the field. While he hit close to .300 in 2018 and led his league in hits, he still needs to refine his overall approach to see more pitches and work counts more effectively. He does have the bat speed that should allow him to continue to hit for average, while that improved approach should allow him to tap into his very good raw power more than he's been able to so far in his brief pro career. With excellent speed and athleticism, Beck has the skills to play center field, the only spot he's manned so far as a pro, while he has the arm strength to profile in right field should he slow down as he matures. His power will have to show up for him to profile well there, but there's plenty of time for that, and all facets of his game, to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A torn anterior cruciate ligament and meniscus in his left knee cost Beck, a high school junior at the time, exposure on the 2016 showcase circuit. But he shot up Draft boards upon returning last spring, when he displayed some of the best all-around tools available in the 2017 Draft while hitting .590 with 12 home runs in 28 games. Beck continued to impress during a pre-Draft workout for the A's at the Coliseum, so much so that they gave him a franchise-record $5,303,000 bonus after selecting him sixth overall. Though the results were mixed during Beck's pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League, he did make strides during the second half, posting an .823 OPS with 10 extra-base hits over his final 22 games after producing a .468 OPS in the first half. Beck is loaded with loud, promising tools. He generates well-above-average bat speed from the right side of the plate, albeit with a swing that currently has some holes and overall inconsistencies. That should improve as Beck gains pro experience, however, and it could make him an average hitter in time. Beck's plus raw power likely will be his calling card and could translate to 25-plus-homer seasons during his prime. Beyond his offensive tools, Beck also possesses the plus speed and athleticism needed to play center field, where he spent his entire pro debut, though some evaluators peg him as a future right fielder on account of his remaining physical projection and plus arm strength. It may take Beck some time to learn to harness his tools and refine his game, but the final product could be that of a run-producing, everyday outfielder who also adds value with his baserunning and defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Going on four years since he signed to an above-slot bonus of $2,352,000 in 2017 after the Brewers took him with the No. 34 pick, Lutz opened 2021 as an enigma. His baseball card numbers are solid if not eye-opening, including a .742 OPS with 13 homers as a 19-year-old at Low-A in 2018, and 13 more homers en route to a .754 OPS at Class A Advanced in 2019. It’s how Lutz got to those numbers that give the Brewers optimism. He has been traditionally an extreme slow starter who came around after April turned to May, the weather began to warm and Lutz locked in his timing. He took his lumps against older pitchers at the Brewers’ alternate site in 2020, especially early in the summer, and was invited to his first big league Spring Training in 2021. Athletic and strong, Lutz could have four average or better tools when all is said and done -- perhaps five if his bat comes around. His right-handed power is his calling card and he can get to it during games, though he remains pull-heavy. He has some of the biggest power in the entire system, and there is even more to access if Lutz learns to cover the outer half of the plate and cleans up some mechanical issues in his swing. On pitches over the inner half of home plate, he does consistent damage. The Brewers have experimented with moving Lutz around the batter’s box and laud his relatively advanced approach to hitting from a young age. He is also a hard worker who tends to be tough on himself during those moments of struggle. Lutz gets the most out of his average speed, running the bases well and showing better-than-expected range in center field. Most scouts continue to peg him as a future right fielder on account of his strong, accurate arm. He has been challenged at Double-A in 2021, flirting with the Mendoza line for much of the summer, and that has dinged his profile. A fractured hand suffered on a hit-by-pitch didn’t help matters either. At just 22 years old, time remains on Lutz’s side to get back on track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed to an above-slot bonus of $2,352,000 in 2017 after the Brewers took him with the No. 34 pick, Lutz offered a glimpse of his offensive ceiling during his first two full seasons, overcoming a slow start each year to finish with nearly identical numbers. After posting a .742 OPS with 13 homers as a 19-year-old at Class A Wisconsin in 2018, Lutz moved up to the Class A Advanced Carolina last season and hit another 13 homers en route to a .754 OPS. Athletic and strong, Lutz could have four average or better tools when all is said and done -- perhaps five if his bat comes around. His right-handed power is his calling card and he can get to it during games, though, right now, it plays almost exclusively to his pull-side. He stands to add even more pop as he adds strength to his impressive frame and learns to leverage the ball more consistently. A lack of plate coverage on the outer-half on top of some mechanical issues in his swing mitigates Lutz’s natural hitting ability and results in too much swing-and-miss. The Brewers believe he’ll benefit from moving closer to the plate and are quick to note that Lutz already employs an advanced approach for his age. Lutz gets the most out of his average speed, running the bases well and showing better-than-expected range in center field. His jumps and routes require more work, however, and he has had some issues with reading the ball off the bat early in his career. Most scouts peg him as a future right fielder on account of his strong, accurate arm, and the Brewers believe he’ll have the requisite impact potential at the plate needed to profile there at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Lutz for $2,352,000, going $368,400 above to help lure him away from a Texas commitment after they drafted him with the No. 34 overall pick. He was a standout during his pro debut in the Pioneer League, slashing .311/.398/.957 with nine home runs, and continued to show a blend of hitting ability and power in his first full season, coming on strong after a slow start in the cold-weather Midwest League. Athletic and strong, Lutz has a real chance of developing at least average tools across the board. His right-handed power is his calling card, and he tapped into it promisingly at Class A Wisconsin, totaling 49 extra-base hits including 13 home runs. He stands to add even more pop as he adds strength needed to his impressive frame and learns to leverage the ball more consistently. He should hit for some average, too, as Lutz recognizes pitches well and uses the whole field better than most players his age. An average runner, Lutz gets the most out of his speed, running the bases well and showing better-than-expected range in center field, where he spent much of his pro debut. He'll need to improve his jumps and routes to stay there, as he at times struggled with reading the ball off the bat in 2018. Most scouts peg him as a future right fielder on account of his strong, accurate arm, and he should make enough of an impact at the plate to fulfill that profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lutz parlayed a strong showing at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October and a fine senior season into a Day 1 selection by the Brewers, who then lured him away from a Texas commitment with a $2,352,000 bonus, $368,400 above recommend slot value. He proved worthy of such an investment during an impressive pro debut that saw him reach the Rookie-level Pioneer League while slashing .311/.398/.559 with nine home runs at two stops. Lutz is an impressive athlete who shows the makings of five average-or-better tools. The right-handed power he showed during his debut, a product of his bat speed and strength, is Lutz's calling card. He stands to add even more pop by modifying his crouched stance and creating more leverage through the zone using his 6-foot-3, 210-pound frame. More than just a slugger, Lutz also shows natural hitting ability, recognizes pitches well and uses the whole field better than most players his age. An average runner, Lutz gets the most out of his speed, running the bases well and showing better-than-expected range in center field, where he spent much of his pro debut. While there's a non-zero chance of him sticking up the middle, most scouts peg him as a future right fielder on account of his strong, accurate arm. The sky is seemingly the limit for Lutz, and he has both the tools and accompanying skills to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years before the Yankees drafted him in 2018's third round, signing him away from a Vanderbilt commitment with an above-slot $997,500 bonus. His demanding pregame routine often left him worn out during his lackluster pro debut, but he paced himself better and ranked eighth in steals (10) and ninth in extra-base hits (24) in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019. Known for putting on impressive batting-practice displays on the prep showcase circuit, Green generates well-above-average raw power from the right side of the plate with his bat speed and strength. He did a better job of driving the ball in the air during his second pro season after his pull-happy approach led to a slew of rolled-over grounders in his debut. While he has some patience at the plate, he lapses into swinging for the fences and will need to make more consistent contact. Green shows average speed out of the batter's box, is quicker once he gets going and runs the bases aggressively. After spending most of his first pro season in center field, he played much of his second on the corners. He fits best in right field and has the arm for the position, having reached 93 mph with his fastball and backing it up with a hard curveball while pitching in high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years and consistently put on impressive shows in batting practice on the showcase circuit. A third-round pick in 2018, he leveraged a commitment to Vanderbilt into an above-slot $997,500 bonus. Adhering to a rigorous pregame routine often left him worn out during a lackluster pro debut, but he adapted and ranked eighth in steals (10) and ninth in extra-base hits (24) in the Rookie-level Appalachian League last summer. Green's bat speed and strength combine to give him well above-average raw power from the right side of the plate. He did a better job of tapping into his pop in his second pro season, driving the ball more consistently in the air after his aggressive nature led to too many rolled-over grounders in his debut. He shows some patience at the plate but still swings and misses too much when he gets caught hunting home runs. An average runner out of the batter's box, Green is quicker underway and looks to steal and take extra bases. He spent most of his first pro season in center field but much of last year on the corners, projecting best as a right fielder. He has the strong arm for the position, reaching 93 mph with his fastball and flashing a hard curveball as a prep pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years while also earning a reputation for putting on some of the best batting-practice displays on the showcase circuit. His commitment to Vanderbilt gave him added leverage in the 2018 Draft, with the Yankees paying him an above-slot $997,500 bonus in the third round. He fits the classic right-field profile but may take a while to develop after striking out at a 37 percent rate in his debut. Green has obvious bat speed and strength that create above-average raw power from the right side of the plate. He has a decent understanding of the strike zone but can lapse into selling out for home runs instead of letting them come naturally. When he did make contact in his first taste of pro ball, much of it came on rolled-over grounders to the left side of the infield. More than a one-dimensional slugger, Green shows average speed out of the batter's box and is a solid runner once underway. Though he began his pro career in center field, his quickness and arm strength fit best in right. As a pitcher in high school, he reached 93 mph with his fastball and flashed a hard curveball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians rated Sanquintin as one of the five best prospects on the 2018 international market and paid him accordingly, signing him for $1.25 million out of the Dominican Republic. Compared to Cleveland's other top signing from last summer, Venezuelan shortstop Gabriel Rodriguez, he's a little less polished as a hitter but might have a bit more raw power. Sanquintin is stronger and more physical than the typical teenaged middle infielder, and he has impressive bat speed from both sides of the plate. He's aggressive and his power plays to all fields, though he may need to temper his approach somewhat to succeed against pro pitching. An average runner, he won't be a huge factor on the bases. Sanquintin possesses the quickness, hands and arm to play shortstop, though that could change if he loses a step as he matures physically. His bat and defensive tools would profile well at third base, his most likely destination. The Indians also may try him at second base and some scouts project him as a right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rijo was a modest signing by the Yankees, getting $50,000 back in July 2015 to begin his pro career. He's moved incrementally, from the Dominican Summer League in 2016 to two levels of rookie ball in 2017-18. He had made one start in the short-season New York-Penn League in late July when he was included in the package sent to the Twins in return for big league veteran Lance Lynn. A control-over-stuff right-hander, Rijo fills up the strike zone with his three-pitch mix. His fastball typically sits in the 91-92 mph range, but can reach back for 95 mph every once in a while. He throws his average curveball in the mid-70s and mixes in what will be an average changeup. He has a good feel for the pitch, but there isn't enough separation velocity-wise between it and his fastball. Pitching to contact, Rijo is efficient on the mound and can pitch deep into games as a result. Once a bit overweight, Rijo has gotten into better shape and maintains his conditioning well. He gets high marks for his makeup and intangibles, which could help him reach his ceiling as a back-end big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels have come to be known as an organization that covets premium athletes. Top prospects in the system like Jo Adell and Jordyn Adams prove that point. Holmes, who was known as William English when the Angels drafted him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft out of the Detroit high school ranks and signed him for $700,000, belongs in the conversation of best athletes with the Angels. A legitimate two-way player, Holmes did some exciting things both on the mound and at the plate across two levels of rookie ball in his second pro summer in 2019. Holmes continues to add strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and is a physical specimen. As a hitter, he had very competitive at-bats in the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues last year, showing patience at the plate and the ability to make hard contact and drive the ball. On the mound, he was even more impressive. While his control is still below average, the Angels aren’t overly concerned because of his age and lack of experience. He showed he could overpower hitters with a potential three-pitch mix. During the regular season, he averaged 93 mph with his fastball and touched 97. He was up to 98 mph at instructs and his strength gains could mean more consistent velocity is on its way. His changeup took a big step forward and flashed plus and he can mix in a fringe average curve. Holmes is on this list more because of his arm than his bat, but the Angels plan to let him continue to do both in 2020. He’ll develop as a starting pitcher for now and hit between his pitching routines. His development might take a bit longer as a result, but the wait could very well be worth it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
