mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017 Cape Cod League MVP, Jenista's strong summer likely helped his stock avoid falling too much after an uneven junior season at Wichita State, as he landed in the second round with the Braves. He did make it to Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in his first full year of pro ball, but didn’t swing the bat very well and didn’t get any official reps in 2020. The power showed up a bit more in 2021, though he wasn't added to the Braves' 40-man roster in the offseason. There is some juice in Jenista’s left-handed bat, but there are questions as to whether he’ll be able to get to it at the highest level. The power has shown up at times, including hitting 19 homers in a tough hitters' park in 2021. But while he does draw some walks, the swing-and-miss is a real concern, as he has struck out in more than 32 percent of his plate appearances in his first two full seasons of pro ball. Jenista runs well enough for his size and has the athleticism and arm strength needed to play right field well. He saw time at first base in the AFL to close out 2019 and continued to do so in 2021. In the end, though, it will be Jenista’s ability to unlock his offensive potential that will determine his future value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jenista won the Cape Cod League MVP the summer before his junior year at Wichita State, putting him on somewhat equal footing at the time with teammate Alec Bohm. Bohm went on to have a huge junior year while Jenista was more inconsistent, leading Bohm to be taken No. 3 overall in the 2018 Draft and Jenista sliding into the second round. While he split the year between the Class A Advanced Florida State League and Double-A Southern League, he didn’t swing the bat well, a trend that continued during his time in the Arizona Fall League. Big, strong and athletic, Jenista still has some offensive tools to work with; he just hasn’t figured out how to implement them successfully on a consistent basis. The more he struggled, the more he tried to change his setup at the plate, which rarely works. He did come to the Braves’ hitting camp during the offseason and left it feeling more comfortable than he had all year. There’s definite raw power in his 6-foot-3 frame, but the left-handed hitter had typically been using more of a line-drive, flat bat path. Jenista is fine in an outfield corner with an above-average arm, but he also saw considerable time at first base in the AFL, partially because that’s where he could find at-bats and partially to add to his versatility. If he can get his bat back on track in 2020, he still has the chance to be an everyday hitter in a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Wichita State, Jenista formed a formidable 1-2 punch with Alec Bohm in the Shockers lineup. Bohm went No. 3 overall in the 2018 Draft, but because Jenista wasn't able to carry over his Cape Cod League MVP performance and turned in a bit of an uneven junior season, he ended up being available for the Braves to select in the second round. He did hit his way up to the Class A Advanced Florida State League in his pro debut. Big and physical at 6-foot-4, Jenista is surprisingly athletic and shows more tools than you might think upon first glance. In college and during most of his pro debut, Jenista showed the ability to consistently barrel up the baseball with a largely line-drive-oriented approach and swing path, while limiting strikeouts and drawing some walks. There's a lot of raw power in his left-handed swing that he hasn't always tapped into, and it could be plus when all is said and done if he can hit enough to get to it. Jenista played first and right field at Wichita State and showed he could do a capable job in center field in the Cape. He'll likely stick at an outfield corner, where he played during his debut, as a pro, but there is pressure on that power bat to progress.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It is somewhat unbelievable to think that Newton is entering only his age-22 season, given the way the clock has already ticked on his professional career. Signed for $50,000 out of the Netherlands in July 2015, Newton spent two seasons playing in the Dominican Summer League before jumping stateside with Rookie Advanced Kingsport in 2018. The switch-hitter truly popped onto the prospect radar at that stop with burgeoning power, a .408 on-base percentage and an .857 OPS. The bat came back down, however, at Class A Columbia where he hit just .209 and struck out in 32.9 percent of his plate appearances. As such, Newton wasn’t added to the 40-man when he was first eligible, and he was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft last fall as well. He went unselected on both occasions. Any chance to prove his worth in 2021 was ended early when Newton injured his left shoulder while diving for a ball at Low-A St. Lucie in mid-June. He is expected to miss the rest of the season. Despite that inability to crack the roster, Newton retains some prospect stature because of his fielding capabilities on the infield. Even at 6-foot-4, he isn’t too tall for shortstop given that he covers adequate ground and shows good hands. His above-average arm also helps his case at the six, and it helped him move around the infield in 2019 when Ronny Mauricio and Mark Vientos both needed time at short. The bat will be an issue. Newton shows good bat speed, and his power will show up in the cage. But his inability to manage the strike zone and recognize pitches brings down the entire profile. The glove and power give the Mets hope that Newton won’t be lost in the shuffle as he works more into his 20s. A utility infielder role in the Majors is a possibility, but there will have to be more contact from both sides to make even that a likelihood.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing his first two pro seasons in the Dominican Summer League, Newton, whom the Mets signed out of the Netherlands for $50,000 in July 2015, offered a glimpse of his potential in ’17, hitting for both average and power while also getting on base at a high clip in the Rookie-level Appalachian League. But the switch-hitting infielder was unable to build upon that performance in his first full season, with an increase in whiffs resulting in an across-the-board drop-off in production. Newton finished the season with the South Atlantic League’s 10th-worst average (.209) and sixth-worst OPS (.613), and the Mets opted not to add him to their 40-man roster in November. While Newton went unselected in the Rule 5 Draft, he also was one of the more interesting names available. A switch-hitter with an ultra-projectable 6-foot-4 frame, Newton already shows power potential and will develop even more as he gets stronger. Many evaluators wonder if Newton will ever make enough contact to reach his power ceiling due to the inconsistent swing mechanics and free-swinging approach that fueled his 32.9 percent strikeout rate in 2019. Club officials would like to see Newton shorten his left-handed stroke, do a better job controlling the zone and make better overall swing decisions. Newton played mostly second base at Columbia in deference to Ronny Mauricio and Mark Vientos, though he did log 29 games at shortstop and another 27 at third base. The Mets believe he has the hands, footwork and plus arm strength to stick at shortstop, where he played primarily in 2018, and they plan to offer him more reps at the position in 2020. Newton’s future as an everyday player is tied directly to his development at the plate, though he might still be able to provide value as a power-hitting utility infielder even if his bat doesn’t come to fruition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Netherlands for $50,000 back in July 2015, Newton spent his first two pro seasons in the Dominican Summer League, faring much better in his return to the level in '17. That success prompted the Mets to challenge Newton with an assignment to the Rookie-level Appalachian League for his United States debut, and he responded by hitting for both average and power against advanced pitching, all while reaching base more than 40 percent of the time. An athletic, 6-foot-4 switch-hitter, Newton has shown a very advanced approach at the plate for a prospect his age, drawing a ton of walks and keeping his strikeout rate relatively low. With his mix of bat speed and strength, Newton has the physical tools needed to develop an above-average bat, though some evaluators do question his overall feel to hit, because his swing mechanics are inconsistent. He has plus raw power that he's already starting to get to, and given Newton's size, it's easy to dream on more as he matures. Defensively, Newton has shown the hands, footwork and instincts -- not to mention the plus arm strength -- to potentially stay at shortstop, though the Mets played him more at second base in 2019, while also giving him reps at the hot corner. Regardless of where he ends up on the defensive spectrum, Newton should have the power-over-hit offensive profile and necessary defensive skills to be an impactful regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gilliam threw to current Reds backstop Tyler Stephenson as his high-school catcher before moving on to Clemson in 2016. He became a full-time reliever as a sophomore and was the Tigers' closer in his junior season, finishing with 11 saves, a 1.41 ERA and 54 strikeouts in 38 1/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft and signed the right-hander for $550,000, well above the $379,400 assigned to the slot. He climbed three levels in his first full season the following year but saw some a stumble at Triple-A that the Mets chalked up to his quick ascent more than anything. At 5-foot-10, Gilliam doesn’t fit the stereotypical look of a dominant reliever, but the stuff matches the profile. The fastball comes in comfortably at the mid-90s with good spin. The curveball features good sharpness in the upper 70s and is a swing-and-miss power pitch of its own. He started throwing a more horizontal breaking ball in a slider/cutter this past spring. The changeup is little more than a show-me pitch at this stage, and it’s unlikely he’ll need it to be much more, given the other stuff. Control has been an issue for him in both the college and pro ranks. The right-hander has a tendency to speed up and get out of his delivery when he goes too high-effort, leading to walks or just missed command. Gilliam was off to a rough start in 2021 at Double-A Binghamton but showed signs of a turnaround in June and July before things fell off a cliff again. He went on the injured list on July 24 for an elbow issue that required ulnar nerve relocation surgery, the same procedure Jacob deGrom underwent in late 2016. Because it’s not Tommy John, there is hope that Gilliam can return next spring and get back to what has made him such a promising relief prospect. He’ll be entering his age-26 season then, so the clock is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gilliam showed a low-90s fastball as a teammate of Reds first-round pick Tyler Stephenson at Kennesaw Mountain High (Kennesaw, Ga.) in 2015, but his smaller build and commitment to Clemson left him undrafted. He served as a mid-week starter for part of his freshman year before finding his niche as the Tigers' closer the next two years. That late-inning potential earned Gilliam a fifth-round selection by the Mets in '18, and he rewarded the Mets for their pick by reaching Triple-A in his first full season. Gilliam may be an undersized right-hander, but he has a super quick arm that produces a plus fastball at 94-96 mph. His curveball gives him a second plus pitch, registering in the upper 70s with a big shape and hard downer action. Capable of inducing whiffs with both pitches, Gilliam leads all Mets Minor Leaguers (50 IP min.) with a 35.1 percent strikeout rate since the start of 2018. While a high-tempo delivery gives Gilliam some funk and deception, it also hinders his ability to throw strikes consistently. As a result, the right-hander has issued 5.0 walks-per-nine in the pro ranks after averaging 4.7 BB/9 in three years at Clemson. That Gilliam is a good athlete reduces some of the durability concerns that his size creates, and it should also allow him to make gains in terms of harnessing his stuff. With more consistency, Gilliam could carve out a role as a seventh- or eighth-inning reliever at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gilliam showed a low-90s fastball as a teammate of Reds first-round pick Tyler Stephenson at Kennesaw Mountain High (Kennesaw, Ga.) in 2015, but his diminutive build and commitment to Clemson left him undrafted. He served as a mid-week starter for part of his freshman year before finding his niche as the Tigers' closer the next two years. That late-inning potential earned Gilliam a fifth-round selection by the Mets in '18, and he excelled as Short-Season Class A Brooklyn's closer in his pro debut, saving five games and averaging better than 16 strikeouts per nine across 17 appearances. Gilliam may be undersized, listed at 5-foot-10, but he has a super quick arm that produces a plus fastball at 96-97 mph. His curveball gives him a second plus pitch, registering in the upper 70s with downer action. He can induce whiffs with both pitches, and did so at a 17-percent clip in his pro debut while striking out nearly 42 percent of the hitters he faced. Gilliam works with a high-tempo delivery that adds some funk and deception, but also makes it difficult for him to control his offerings at times. He averaged 4.7 walks per nine in college, followed by 6.8 in the New York-Penn League. That Gilliam is a good athlete reduces some of the durability concerns that his size creates, and it should also allow him to make gains in terms of harnessing his stuff. If he can learn to do that, Gilliam could rise quickly through the Minors en route to a late-inning role in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schaller flashed a low-90s fastball as an Indiana high schooler in 2016, but he went undrafted because he battled injuries during his senior year and was strongly committed to Vanderbilt. He missed all of his first year with the Commodores following Tommy John surgery and worked just 24 2/3 innings during the regular season in 2018, albeit while hitting 98 mph with his fastball as a rare Draft-eligible redshirt freshman. Intrigued by Schaller’s untapped potential and low-mileage arm, the Nationals made him their third-round pick that June and have developed him as a starter in pro ball. Schaller was sidelined with an oblique injury for most of the first half and didn’t take the mound for Class A Hagerstown until late June. When he finally did, the big-bodied right-hander flashed impressive stuff, sitting 93-95 mph with his fastball and complementing it with a high-spin breaking ball and a changeup that flashed above-average at times. Schaller needs to develop his secondary offerings and refine his control, and the Nationals believe starting offers the best platform for those improvements. He likely will end up in the bullpen as a hard-throwing reliever – a role in which he’s sat 95-98 mph in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best position player to come out of Loyola Marymount to date has to be Angels infielder David Fletcher, a sixth-round pick back in 2015. Three years later, it was Decolati’s turn to represent the Lions in the sixth round when the Rockies took him. After a very successful debut in 2018, a broken hand kept him out until June '19, and he wasn't able to match his production from the summer prior. Decolati might have been one of the players in the Rockies system to suffer the most from the shutdown as he needs reps to turn his athleticism into consistent performance. He was rusty during instructional league play, though it started to come together by the end of the fall. The right-handed hitter can make loud contact and has plenty of raw power, but his overly aggressive approach was exposed in 2019 and led to a high strikeout rate. With plus speed, Decolati can steal a base and cover a lot of ground in the outfield. He’s shown he can handle center field and his above-average arm works well from right field. He might settle in as a fourth outfielder type, but more than anything, he just needs to go out and play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A toolsy outfielder from Loyola Marymount, Decolati excited scouts with a strong Cape Cod League performance in the summer of 2017. His struggles as a junior worked out to the Rockies’ advantage, as they were able to get him in the sixth round of the 2018 Draft then watched him finish among the Pioneer League leaders in a host of offensive categories during his pro debut. His first full season didn’t go exactly as planned, as a broken right hand suffered near the end of Spring Training kept him off the field until June. Decolati might be the best athlete in the Rockies' system, with strength and speed to spare. He’s capable of making hard contact from the right side of the plate, the type of hitter who creates a different sound off the bat. There’s plenty of raw power to tap into and he’s learning how to let it play for him while using the whole field. He has a tendency to be overaggressive which leads to higher strikeout totals. With more reps, he should begin to understand his impact zones better and stop chasing pitches as much. Decolati’s athleticism allows him to be a threat on the bases and really plays in the outfield, where he has excellent instincts with good makeup speed. He can play center field and has the kind of arm strength that fits in right as well. Give him a mulligan for 2019, with the real Decolati more likely to show up in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over the course of his three years playing for Loyola Marymount, Decolati intrigued scouts by showing flashes of five playable tools. He really stood out in the Cape Cod League in 2017, but when he didn't carry over that performance to his junior year, he ended up being available for the Rockies in the sixth round of the 2018 Draft, where he signed for full pick value. He looked much more like the Cape Cod version of himself during his pro debut, finishing in the top 10 in a host of categories and earning an All-Star nod in the rookie-level Pioneer League. Primarily a shortstop in college, the Rockies immediately moved him to the outfield and liked what they saw there. He played most of the summer in right field, and has the arm for the spot, but he could have the speed and instincts to be a solid average defender in center field. That speed also helps him on the bases, and he broke out of the gate with 17 steals in his pro debut. Everything else went well for him during his debut, from managing the strike zone and drawing walks to toning down his overly aggressive approach in order to use all fields to hit for average and power. If you saw Decolati on the right day, you might put above-average grades on him across the board. The Rockies love Decolati's makeup and natural leadership ability. If he can show that his summer debut is for real, he could move up this list, and the Rockies' ladder, in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres’ fabled 2016-17 international spending spree is bearing fruit across the system, and they used the entirety of that window to haul in top-tier prospects. Case in point: Osvaldo Hernandez. The Friars inked the then-18-year-old to a $2.5 million contract out of Cuba in March 2017, three months before the window closed. Hernandez pitched at three different levels during his debut season, but his breakout came in ’18 at Class A Fort Wayne where he posted a 1.81 ERA, which would’ve led the Midwest League with a few more innings to qualify. Injuries prevented Hernandez from building upon that performance much in 2019, though he did pitch well in the California League during the second half before losing all of ’20 to the pandemic. Hernandez fits the mold of a crafty and deceptive southpaw, even if he doesn’t boast big-time velocity. His fastball sits in the low 90s but can reach the mid 90s. He’s got a put-away curveball, and he pairs it with a serviceable slider and changeup. What stands out most about Hernandez is his savvy on the mound. He constantly changes speeds and varies his delivery, and he routinely induces weak contact from opposing hitters. Hernandez is athletic, and he boasts an easy, smooth delivery. There’s no one trait that jumps off the page, but his creativity and pitchability could make him a solid middle-to-back-of-the-rotation starter in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivera declined to sign with the Giants as a 32nd-rounder after his freshman season at Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC, then became the second-highest drafted player in school history (Craig Kimbrel, third round, 2008) when San Francisco landed him in the fourth round for an above-slot $800,000 a year later. With their college connection and his ability to spin a nasty breaking ball that could make him a closer, Rivera has some parallels to Kimbrel. He worked just 94 innings in his first three years as a pro -- he was worn down in his debut, had a lower back strain in 2019 and the cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season restricted him to instructional league -- and missed the first three months of this season with shoulder issues. Rivera's curveball is a legitimate hammer with power in the low 80s, high spin rates and true 12-6 break. His fastball gives him a second plus pitch that touches 97 mph with electric cutting action, though he tends to command it better when he works around 92-93. He also flashes a solid changeup but lacks consistency with his third offering. While he has the upside of a No. 3 starter, Rivera has a long ways to go to get there. He has to prove he can stay healthy, refine his changeup and harness his fastball and curveball to throw more strikes. His stuff could be even nastier if he moves to the bullpen and just airs out his two main weapons in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because he attended Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC and can spin a nasty breaking ball that might make him a closer, Rivera has drawn comparisons to the greatest player in school history, Craig Kimbrel. He turned down the Giants as a 32nd-rounder after his freshman season in 2017, then became the second-highest Lion drafted after (behind Kimbrel) when San Francisco signed him for an above-slot $800,000 in the fourth round a year later. He was worn down in his pro debut and missed time in 2019 with a lower back strain but has shown electric stuff when 100 percent. Rivera owns the best curveball in the system, a true hammer in the low-80s with high spin rates and 12-6 break. His fastball can reach 97 mph with dynamic cutting action, though he commands it better when he works around 92-93 mph. He can flash a solid changeup though it's very much a work in progress. Rivera offers the upside of a No. 3 starter, but to get there he'll have to prove he can stay healthy and do a better job of locating his pitches. His fastball and curveball move so much that he has difficulty finding the strike zone at times. If he can't stick in the rotation, his stuff could become even filthier if he just airs it out in short relief stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Craig Kimbrel spurned the Braves as a 33rd-rounder in 2007 to return to Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC for his sophomore season, then went 30 rounds higher to the same club the following June. Rivera took a similar path, turning down the Giants as a 32nd-rounder in 2017 to return to the Lions and then becoming the second-highest pick in the program's history when San Francisco redrafted him in the fourth round last June. Signed for a well over-slot $800,000 in the fourth round, he was tired and didn't have his best stuff in his pro debut. When he's fully rested, Rivera has a legitimate out pitch in a low-80s curveball with sharp break. He's also capable of reaching 96 mph with his fastball, though he's most effective when he operates in the low 90s with sink. He began using his changeup more as a sophomore, showing the potential to become a solid third pitch. Rivera has a smoother delivery when he paces himself as a starter but features more effort and some head whack when he reaches back for maximum velocity. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter if he can get more consistent with his control and changeup. Some scouts who saw him as an amateur liked him more as a late-inning reliever who could focus on his curve and fastball, with one even comparing him to Kimbrel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best pitcher ever at Navy, Song led NCAA Division I in strikeouts per nine innings (15.4, the sixth-highest rate in D-I history) in 2019 and finished his career with school records for career wins (32), innings (334 1/3) and whiffs (428). He became the highest pick in Navy history when the Red Sox took him in the fourth round, and he would have gone much higher and signed for more than $100,000 if not for his two-year military commitment. He dominated in his brief pro debut and with Team USA at the Premier 12 tournament that November, then reported to flight school in June 2020 and hasn't petitioned for an early release, which he could have in May 2021. Song has first-round stuff, starting with a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-96 mph and reaches 99 with late riding action. His mid-80s slider grades as his best secondary pitch and can be a legitimate wipeout offering at its best. He gets good depth on an upper-70s curveball that shows flashes of being a plus pitch and surprised the Red Sox with the quality of his fading changeup during his debut. Song uses his 6-foot-4 frame and high three-quarters slot to create downhill plane on his pitches. He doesn't feature much effort in his delivery and throws strikes, though some evaluators quibble with his arm action and whether he'll ever have better than average command. He has as much upside as any Boston pitching prospect, but it's unclear when he might return and how much his long layoff will affect him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Song led NCAA Division I in strikeout rate (15.4 per nine innings, sixth-best in D-I history) and finished third in strikeouts (161, a Navy record) last spring, capping a career in which he set school marks for career wins (32), innings (334 1/3) and whiffs (428). The best college senior in the 2019 Draft, he became the highest pick in Navy history when he went in the fourth round, and he would have gone earlier and received more than $100,000 had it not been for his two-year military commitment. Opponents batted just .145 against him between his pro debut and five scoreless relief outings with Team USA at the Premier 12 tournament in November. Song could have gone in the first round on stuff alone, as he has a quality four-pitch mix that begins with a four-seam fastball that parks at 93-96 mph and tops out at 99 with some late riding action. He has three solid secondary offerings, led by a mid-80s slider that can be a legitimate wipeout pitch at times. He surprised the Red Sox a bit with the quality of his changeup in his debut while not using his curveball as much as he had in college. Employing a high three-quarters delivery with little effort, Song creates downhill plane and throws strikes. Secretary of Defense Mark Esper signed a memo in November that potentially allows for athletes from military academies to postpone their service to pursue a professional sports career, though the Navy decided not to apply that policy retroactively to Song. Unless something changes, he won't rejoin the Red Sox until after the 2021 season and it's unclear how the long layoff will affect him, but his upside could make him well worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cannon significantly improved from season to season at Arizona and finished second in the Pacific-12 Conference batting race behind No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman with a .397/.478/.651 line as a junior in 2019. Boston's top pick (second round) that June, he signed for $1.3 million and hit just .200/.284/.324 in his pro debut. He didn't get a chance to rebound in 2020, when the pandemic limited his development to instructional league. For Cannon to become a big league regular, he'll have to get back to what made him a star with the Wildcats, which was controlling the strike zone with a line-drive, all-fields approach. After walking more than he struck out in college, he whiffed in one-third of his plate appearances in his first month as a pro before making better contact afterward. He doesn't possess more than average raw power, but his hitting ability should allow him to make the most of it and produce 12-15 homers per year. Cannon's bat is his only potential above-average tool. He shows fringy speed out of the batter's box and is a little faster underway, but most scouts don't think he has the quickness or arm strength to play shortstop at the upper levels. He has reliable hands and his average arm is a better fit at second base, where he looked much more comfortable during his first taste of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cannon improved throughout his college career at Arizona, leading NCAA Division I with 29 doubles and finishing second in the Pac-12 Conference batting race (behind No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman) at .397 last spring. The Red Sox's top pick (second round) in June, he signed for $1.3 million as the 43rd overall choice. Known for his bat and polished approach, he surprisingly hit just .200/.284/.324 in his pro debut. After walking more than he struck out during his college career, Cannon whiffed in one-third of his plate appearances in his first month as a pro before making better contact afterward. He usually drills repeated line drives from the right side of the plate while controlling the strike zone. While he doesn't have more than average raw power, his hitting ability allows him to get to most of it. Cannon posts fringy run times out of the batter's box and is a little faster underway, though probably not quick enough to play shortstop at upper levels. He has reliable hands but his arm is just average and another reason he'll probably wind up at second base. Compared to Brian Dozier by some scouts, he looked much more comfortable at second during his debut

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Politi redshirted in his first year at Seton Hall and went 6-7 with a 5.04 ERA in the next three seasons. Despite his modest success and fastball velocity, the Red Sox liked his pitch data enough to draft him in the 15th round and sign him for $25,000 in 2018. He acquitted himself well as a multi-inning reliever in high Class A during his first full pro season, then posted a 1.27 ERA in five late-season starts that left Boston rethinking his long-term role. Politi has added 2-3 mph to his fastball in pro ball and now deals at 92-95 mph and reaches 97. His four-seamer features some of the highest fastball spin rates in the system, creating armside run that eats up right-handers. His second-best offering is an upper-80s slider, and he also has made progress with a curveball while continuing to try to refine his changeup. While Politi had success in the rotation last summer, his long-term future likely will be in the bullpen. There's a lot going on in his max-effort delivery, making it difficult to repeat and thus to command his pitches. He projects as a long reliever who may not need much more than another year in the Minors before he's ready for an audition in Boston.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high school outfielder from Mississippi who was the fastest player in the 2019 Draft, Beard inevitably drew comparisons to Billy Hamilton. He had almost no history facing quality pitching, so scouts weren't sure what to make of his bat, but his speed and athleticism landed him in the fourth round with a below-slot $350,000 bonus. His first taste of pro ball was a challenge, as he struck out in 39 percent of his plate appearances in Rookie ball. On the showcase circuit during the summer of 2018, Beard ran a 6.21-second 60-yard dash at a Prospect Development Pipeline event and created havoc on the bases at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He's so fast that he can beat out routine grounders, and once he improves his jumps, he could become a dynamic basestealer. If he gets more aggressive, he could become a plus defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable. Beard needs to gain a better understanding of his right-handed swing, improve his pitch recognition and plate discipline and figure out how pitchers are attacking him. Though he mostly hit soft grounders when he made contact in his debut, he has the bat speed, strong hands and ability to backspin the ball to be more than just a slap hitter. Though he'll require plenty of development time, he has the upside of an average hitter with double-digit homers and league-leading stolen base totals.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for just $35,000 out of Panama, Bailey has provided the most positive early returns from the White Sox 2018-19 international class. He batted .324/.477/.454 in his 2019 pro debut, leading the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in on-base percentage and placing fourth with 52 walks. Beyond those stats, he's a 6-foot-4, 215-pounder with solid raw power and surprising athleticism. Very patient for his age without being too passive, Bailey has a relatively compact right-handed swing for his size and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Content to make line-drive contact for now, he shows some home run power to his pull side and could have all-fields pop as he gets stronger and drives more balls in the air. As he matures physically, he likely will lose a step and become more of an average runner. Though he's athletic for his size and played all three outfield positions in his debut, Bailey spent most of his time in left field. With average speed and fringy arm strength, that likely will be his long-term position. In addition to his tools, club officials also praise his intelligence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyes ranked 23rd on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list, having impressed scouts with his physicality and power potential, before the Tigers signed him in July 2018. He hit .331 with seven homers, 48 RBIs and an .887 OPS in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 before his stateside debut in 2020 was canceled due to the COVID shutdown of the Minor League season. He spent the summer adding strength to his frame and reported to the Tigers’ Florida instructional league in good shape. Reyes moves well at shortstop and on the bases for a relatively big player, though any further growth could bump him over to third. He combines an advanced approach with plus bat speed to barrel pitches in the zone, which should translate to more power as he continues to physically mature. He has reliable hands and a strong arm at short. While he runs well, Reyes is likely to lose a step with physical maturation. Beyond the physical tools, Reyes shows competitiveness and intensity in the field. He opened his 2021 season in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout in the International Prospect League, Reyes impressed scouts with his physicality and power potential while performing well in games. It earned him a ranking as MLB Pipeline's No. 23 international prospect for the 2018-19 international period as well as a $1.45 million bonus from the Tigers, who signed the Dominican infielder on July 2. He made his professional debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019. Physically advanced for his age, Reyes is stocky for his position, which could move him from shortstop to third base as he advances while boosting his home run power. He has an advanced approach at the plate and already shows feel for finding the barrel, with plus bat speed and some natural leverage to his swing that could make him at least an average hitter. While he runs well, Reyes is likely to lose a step with physical maturation. On defense, Reyes shows good hands and a good arm, which he’ll need to stick in the infield. He’s a competitor who has been praised for his intensity on the field and how he really enjoys playing the game. He’ll make his stateside debut in 2020 in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tigers general manager Al Avila and LSU head coach Paul Mainieri worked together three decades ago at St. Thomas University in Miami. When Hess had an up-and-down junior season, bouncing between the rotation and bullpen, Detroit saw him fall down draft boards and selected him in the seventh round of the 2019 MLB Draft, believing he could be a solid reliever. After dominating NY-Penn League hitters, his midsummer jump to Class A West Michigan flashed the potential the Tigers believed they could tap, including 22 strikeouts over 21 innings. The combination of Hess’ 6-foot-6 frame and a projectable power fastball tantalized scouts, even if the statistics didn’t back it up. Though Hess started for most of his collegiate career, he was more effective out of bullpen, including a dominant freshman season. His fastball plays more solidly into the mid-90s in shorter stints, pairing with a slider that works in the low to mid-80s with darting movement. He has a changeup but neither needs nor uses it much in relief stints. While his tall frame creates leverage, command has been a challenge throughout his career, including 11 walks at West Michigan. Like former University of Miami closer Bryan Garcia a few years earlier, the Tigers drafted Hess hoping his college experience would allow him to move quickly through the system and reach Detroit sooner than expected. Garcia moved from West Michigan to Triple-A Toledo in his first full pro season; the Tigers would love to see Hess do the same, giving them a middle relief or setup option in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals took a chance on Haake in the sixth round of the 2018 Draft after the right-hander’s up-and-down college career, which included three different colleges in as many years. Haake responded by being one of biggest surprises of the class when he posted a 2.85 ERA over 18 starts in Class A in 2019. His only 2020 action came during the Royals’ fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Haake dominates with a plus fastball that sits in the mid-90s. It’s a deceptive pitch thanks to his 6-foot-4 frame and features a ton of movement. His changeup plays well off that deception, and the pitch comes in with splitter action. The fastball-changeup combo helps Haake get whiffs from hitters on both sides of the plate and he rounds out his arsenal with an average slider that can flash plus. Haake sometimes struggles with repeating his delivery, and that has led to control issues that he needs to shore up to be successful. Haake missed two months with shoulder issues in 2019 and missed another six weeks with an injury for High-A Quad Cities during the 2021 season. The Royals had hopes he could have made Double-A at least by now, so it’s an open question how much Haake’s health will further hold him back in 2022 and beyond. The stuff, which Kansas City is not concerned about, could work in a relief setting, especially if he squeezes out even more velocity in short spurts. That might be the best role for the right-hander to get him going for good.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Haake pitched for three different colleges in as many years. He put up underwhelming numbers as an Arkansas State freshman in 2016 and again at Kentucky two years later, with an impressive season at John A. Logan Junior College sandwiched between. The Royals took a chance on his power repertoire in the sixth round in 2018, and Haake has responded by being one of the biggest surprises of the class, though some minor shoulder soreness did shelve him for a time during an otherwise impressive first full season at Class A Lexington. The 6-foot-4 right-hander can dominate with a plus fastball that sits comfortably in the mid 90s and routinely touches 97 mph with late life. An above-average changeup that plays nicely off his fastball and with splitter action is Haake’s go-to secondary pitch, and together they help him pile up whiffs against hitters on both sides of the plate. He posted the best swinging-strike rate (16.1 percent) and second-highest strikeout rate (28.6) among Royals farmhands (70 IP min.) in 2019. Club officials are intrigued by Haake’s breaking ball, which can occasionally flash plus, though they haven’t yet pushed it in his development. Haake seemed ticketed for a bullpen role when he began his career, and his shoulder injury in early 2019 did little to change that belief. But the right-hander’s improved command of his fastball-changeup combo that he showed once healthy last year has left club officials increasingly optimistic about Haake’s chance to be starter, especially with his size and remaining projection. If that doesn’t work out, the Royals have zero doubt that Haake has the stuff and natural bat-missing ability needed to be a bullpen force at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The 2019 Draft class was deep in terms of college shortstops and the spring began with Holland looking like he could be one of the first ones taken, especially after a very strong Cape Cod League showing the summer prior. But the Auburn product struggled during his junior year, allowing him to slide to the fifth round, where the Twins were able to sign him for $575,000. He continued to scuffle with the bat during his pro debut in the rookie-level Appalachian League. Holland is an impressive athlete with speed and plenty of raw power. His biggest problem is that he hasn’t incorporated his athleticism into his swing. He seemed uncomfortable and unnatural at the plate during his pro debut using a setup some felt was too spread out. He spent the offseason hitting with fellow Twins prospect Brent Rooker in the hopes of finding some rhythm and timing from the right side of the plate. Getting the bat going would allow Holland to become an intriguing all-around player. He plays good defense at short, with a strong arm and his plus speed helping him with enough range. He continued to work on his swing at the Twins’ minicamp and if he can take that into his first full season of pro ball, he could shoot up this list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivera was already well past 19 years old when the Astros signed him in October 2016 for just $10,000 and he didn't break out as a prospect until his 2019 full-season debut, when he struck out 11.3 per nine innings in low Class A. His only development in 2020 came in instructional league, after which Houston opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster because he was 23 and had yet to advance to the upper levels. The Angels selected him in the Rule 5 draft in December but returned him to the Astros in March, and he has barely pitched this year while dealing with persistent shoulder soreness. Rivera has one of the better fastballs in system after its velocity shot up from 89-93 mph in his 2018 U.S. debut to 94-98 and touching 100 a year later. His changeup is his best secondary offering, showing signs of becoming a solid weapon with splitter action. His slider has similar velocity but lacks consistency. The Astros have used Rivera in a hybrid role and most scouts think he's destined to become a multi-inning reliever. He features a lot of effort in his delivery and has a long arm action that compromise his control and command and ability to maintain his stuff over longer stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have excelled at finding older pitchers on the international market and helping them find more velocity. Another example is Rivera, who was 19 years and seven months old when he signed for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in October 2016. His fastball made a huge jump in 2019 while he averaged 11.3 strikeouts per nine innings in his full-season debut. The Angels rolled the dice on that velocity by taking him in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Rivera's four-seam fastball sat at 89-93 mph during his U.S. debut in 2018 before rising to 94-98 and topping out at 100 last year. His secondary pitches have been slower to develop, though his mid-80s changeup with splitter action shows some glimpses of becoming at least a solid offering. His slider has similar velocity and stands out more for its power than its bite. Rivera is yet another pitching prospect who had been developed by the Astros as a hybrid starter but is likely to end up as a multi-inning reliever. His effortful delivery and long arm action are better suited for shorter stints and compromise his ability to control and command his pitches. That’s probably his best chance at sticking on the Angels’ big league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers intended to sign Torres for $7,500 out of the Dominican Republic in August 2015 until an age discrepancy killed the deal and landed him on MLB's ineligible list for a year. When he finally turned pro with the Astros for $150,000 in April 2018, he was already 22 years and eight months old, but he made up for lost time by dominating in his U.S. debut in 2019. He also pitched well in the Arizona Fall League that offseason and in Summer Camp and at Houston's alternate site in 2020, though his year ended when he was shut down with a sore elbow in August and he had arthroscopic surgery in July 2021 to remove bone chips from the joint. Torres operates at 94-98 mph and tops out at 100 with high spin rates on his four-seam fastball, showing the ability to keep that velocity for five or six innings per start. If hitters try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with a mid-80s slider that peaks at 90 mph. As a contrast to his pair of power pitches, he'll use a changeup that shows some signs of becoming an average third offering. Torres entered his age-25 season with just 135 2/3 innings of pro experience and little track record of throwing strikes. He's not physical and has trouble repeating his delivery, so he may not develop the command required to be a starter. Given his age and lack of finesse, it may be best to just let him try to overpower hitters as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers tried to sign Torres for $7,500 out of the Dominican Republic in August 2015, but an age discrepancy scuttled that deal and landed him on the ineligible list for a year. He didn't sign a pro contract until the Astros gave him $150,000 in April 2018 at the relatively ancient age of 22 years and eight months. He dominated in his U.S. debut last year, going 12-0 with a 1.71 ERA, .175 opponent average and 107 strikeouts in 94 2/3 innings between two Class A levels, and also impressed in the Arizona Fall League. Torres not only works at 94-98 and peaks at 100 mph with a high-spin four-seam fastball, but he also maintains that velocity for five or six innings at a time. He also can overpower hitters with a mid-80s slider that tops out at 90 mph. To contrast his hard stuff, he'll mix in a changeup that shows flashes of becoming an average offering. While there's no question that Torres has the pure stuff to pitch in the big leagues, he must learn to harness it first. He lacks physicality and has trouble repeating his delivery and locating his pitches. He's already 24, so Houston could expedite his development in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1.8 million last July, Lorenzo received the largest bonus the Astros have given an international amateur position player since they paid since-traded Gilberto Celestino $2.25 million in 2015. Though he had one of the more advanced bats among middle infielders in the 2019 international crop, he'll likely make his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2020 and come to the United States at age 18 the next summer. A switch-hitter, Lorenzo has a compact swing from both sides that is built for hitting line drives to all fields. While he's a hit-over-power guy, his bat speed and feel for the barrel could produce 12-15 homers per season once he matures physically. He manages the strike zone better than most youngsters. Lorenzo will flash plus speed on occasion but is more of a solid runner who could slow down as he fills out. Scouts aren't completely sold that he'll stay at shortstop, though his instincts and strong, accurate arm give him a good chance. He's capable of playing second and third base, and his bat could profile at both spots if he develops more power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a pitcher in his first two seasons at Gonzaga, Jones didn't become a full-time starter at first base until he was a senior in 2016, when he set a school record and placed second in NCAA Division I with 27 doubles. Signed for $2,500 in the 19th round that June, he didn't start to realize his power potential until he slammed 18 homers in Double-A in 2018. He encored with 22 more last year while enhancing his versatility in Triple-A. Though Jones has plenty of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-7 frame, he only began tapping into his power once he did a better job of staying back on pitches and stopped diving so much at the plate. He's driving the ball in the air more often and to all fields. While his size results in a naturally long right-handed swing, he does a good job of making contact and draws walks with a patient approach. Part of a Washington state 4-A basketball championship team at Kentwood High -- where his baseball teammates included future big leaguers Reese McGuire and Austin Voth -- Jones is athletic for his size. He's a below-average runner but not a baseclogger, and he's a quality defender with a strong arm at first base. He also can provide adequate defense on the outfield corners and looked fine in his initial exposure to third base in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A closer at Cal State Fullerton, Conine had more saves (25) than walks (19) in three college seasons. The Astros made him a tandem starter almost immediately after drafting him in the 11th round in 2018, and they have been pleased with the results. He posted the best K/BB ratio (4.6) and second-best ERA (2.20) in the system last year while advancing to Double-A in his first full pro season. Conine is throwing harder as a pro starter than he did as a college reliever, though his fastball still has average velocity (90-96 mph) with ordinary life. The key to his success has been the development of his changeup as a legitimate weapon with deception, fade and two-plane depth. He also has good feel for spinning two distinct breaking balls, an upper-70s downer curveball and a tighter slider in the low 80s. Conine thrives as a finesse right-hander because he can locate his pitches where he wants. He can't throw his fastball by hitters but can command it to both sides of the plate, and the depth on his offerings creates weak ground-ball contact. Efficient and durable, he could fit toward the back of a rotation or in a multi-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lopez lacked physicality as a skinny 5-foot-11 right-hander in Venezuela, but the Astros liked his arm speed and polish enough to sign him for $300,000 in 2017. He made an impressive U.S. debut in 2019, compiling a 1.41 ERA, .140 opponent average and 61 strikeouts in 51 innings between Rookie and short-season ball. Other teams already have started asking about him in trade talks. Lopez's most impressive trait is his ability to spin the ball, resulting in a downer curveball in the upper 70s and a tight slider in the low 80s. He already works at 92-95 mph with his four-seam fastball, though he has less projection remaining than a typical teenager. He also shows some feel for a fading changeup. Though he has four pitches and doesn't feature much effort in his delivery, he faces an uphill battle to remain a starter. His size and long arm action make it more likely he winds up in the bullpen. He's still young, so for now Houston will keep feeding him innings so he can work on refining his repertoire and improving his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Eierman’s impressive sophomore season at Missouri State, which included 23 home runs and 17 stolen bases, he struggled a bit the following year, which led to him dropping to the second round to the A’s in the 2018 Draft. He flashed some tools at Class A Advanced Stockton with 13 homers and 11 stolen bases, though strikeouts were an issue as he struck out in 32 percent of his plate appearances. Eierman’s power generated from his right-handed swing is often negated by his inconsistency in making contact. He has tinkered with his stance, but his timing sometimes remains off. However, Eierman did show progress in his pitch recognition during the instructional league, something the A’s hope can help him regain some confidence. Oakland believes part of Eierman’s struggles in recent years has been the result of putting too much pressure on himself. He’s worked hard to become a plus defender as a shortstop and should be able to stick at the position. Eierman will look for a bounce-back year in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eierman had a huge sophomore season at Missouri State, with 23 homers and 17 steals, to excite scouts for the potential to draft him the following June in 2018. The infielder struggled in his junior year, dropping into the second round of the Draft, and he’s been chasing those sophomore numbers since. Sent to the Class A Advanced California League for his first full season, Eierman struck out in 32 percent of his plate appearances. There’s definite power in Eierman’s right-handed swing, but he’s struggled to make contact to get to it with any consistency. As the strikeouts mounted, he fiddled with his stance, changed his approach, but could never get his timing down. The A’s held him out of games at instructs, instead retooling his swing from start to finish, with some results by the end of camp. He had more balance and more leverage while keeping his barrel in the zone longer. His mental approach, worrying about striking out, was as much of a culprit as his inability to pick up spin. One of the big positives for Eierman was that he actually exceeded expectations defensively. The jury was out whether he could stick at shortstop as a bigger-bodied infielder, but he showed off an easily plus arm and at least an above-average defensive skill set. With the slate wiped clean and the work he put in with his swing, the A’s are hopeful he can have a bounce-back season in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Romero spent four seasons pitching in Cuba, mostly as a reliever, before he left in the hopes of landing a job in the United States. The A’s signed him for $350,000 in February 2017, and once they could get him to the United States that season, he pitched his way up to the California League. He closed for that Stockton team to start 2019 and earned a bump up to Double-A, then leapt to Triple-A in 2019, where he was considered for a callup to bolster the big league bullpen in September. The A’s opted not to recall Romero because they felt he was lacking in some of the intangibles, like holding runners on and fielding his position, that would get exposed at the highest level. Stuff-wise, there’s no question he’s just about ready to get big league hitters out. He can miss bats with both his fastball and his breaking ball. He’ll throw his heater up to 98 mph and is consistently in the 95-98 mph range. He complements it with a breaking ball he calls a slider, but is a bit more slurvy, thrown 86-89 mph with more tilt than a typical slider. Romero has the right mentality for the back end of a bullpen, going right after hitters without any fear. While he did improve his strike-throwing as 2019 went on, he can get out of whack with his delivery, leading to a spike in his walk rate. He’s worked on the little things that held him back and should contribute to the big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur in Cuba, Martinez hit over .400 in the island country’s 18U national league in 2016 to win the batting title and trailed only current White Sox outfielder Luis Robert in slugging percentage. Martinez joined the Angels in August 2017 for $250,000 and reached full-season ball in his first year in the United States, hitting over .300 across two levels. More power showed up with a move to High A in 2019. Though he wasn’t added to the 40-man roster after the 2020 season, no one took him in the Rule 5 Draft. Martinez is the kind of prospect whose whole is greater than the sum of his parts. He doesn’t have a plus tool, but instead can do a lot of things well, the type of player you like the more you see of him. He has a smooth left-handed swing with a solid overall approach, making a lot of contact and drawing some walks along the way. There might be a bit more power to come beyond what started showing up in 2019, but he’s more a contact-first kind of hitter. Still just 23 for all of the 2021 season, Martinez runs well enough, though he’s not really a basestealing threat. He can play all three outfield spots well and while he may never win a Gold Glove, he has very clean and efficient routes. Any surprising offensive gains could make Martinez a big league regular, but it’s looking like he has a pretty high floor as a fourth outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez was one of the best hitters in Cuba’s 18-and-Under National League in 2016, trailing perhaps only Luis Robert. Robert would go on to sign a huge deal with the White Sox in May 2017, while Martinez would join the Angels for $250,000 just a few months later. Making his pro debut in the Pioneer League in 2018, he quickly hit his way to full-season ball. While he missed about six weeks due to injury early in 2019, he had a solid, albeit unspectacular season up a level in the California League. Solid, yet unspectacular might be the best way to describe the 22-year-old outfielder. He’s not flashy and doesn’t have a plus tool, like his former countryman Robert, but he can do a little bit of everything well. He has a solid approach from the plate, drawing a fair amount of walks and not striking out a ton. He’s always had solid raw power and he tapped into it a bit more in 2019, though he’s probably more hit over power. An average runner, Martinez doesn’t have elite range, but he has proven more and more capable of playing an above-average defense in center field thanks to his solid instincts. He’ll continue to see time in all three spots, with a career as a fourth outfielder a likely ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels clearly have a thing for two-way players. We all know about Shohei Ohtani, and Jared Walsh got to the big leagues in 2019. In 2018, they drafted William Holmes and are letting him both hit and pitch as a pro. They took Rivera from the Puerto Rico high school ranks in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, giving him an above-slot $597,500 bonus to sign him away from his Florida International commitment. He only hit during his pro debut in the Rookie-Level Arizona League, but the plan is to let him follow in Holmes’ footsteps. Rivera has some serious raw power to tap into from the left side of the plate, but there’s question about whether he’ll make enough contact to get to it consistently. There are some swing-and-miss issues -- he struck out in more than 37 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut -- and he’ll have to refine his approach. But Angels hitting instructors like his swing and think that will come with experience. On the mound, Rivera has been up to 95-96 mph with his fastball, sitting more in the low 90s, with plenty of room to add strength and consistent velocity. He’s shown both feel for spinning his breaking ball and for a changeup, but he’ll need to work on improving his secondary stuff along with his command of all his offerings. Like with his swing, Angels instructors like the biomechanics of Rivera’s delivery, leaving it a bit of a tossup which area he might have the better chance with if he had to choose one to pursue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Arol Vera and Adrian Placencia received seven-figure bonuses as shortstops at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Bonilla wasn’t too far behind. The Dominican received $600,000 to sign and was the one of the three to get his professional career officially started, performing well over 20 games in the Dominican Summer League. Bonilla has the chance to really hit. It was a small sample size in the DSL, but he showed off an advanced approach at the plate, limiting strikeouts and drawing walks. There’s extra-base authority for the right-handed hitter now, more to his pull side, and there’s a chance he could eventually be an above average hitter with at least average power. Not known for his speed, Bonilla does have a plus arm and will get the chance to play shortstop for the immediate future. He did get some time at third base during his debut, and given the potential of him being a bit thicker-framed as he matures, the hot corner could end up being his long-term defensive home. That might put more pressure on his bat, but it looks like he might have the tools to profile well at the infield corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Expectations for a college senior reliever taken in the 23rd round of the Draft are understandably low, so Delaplane flew under the radar after coming out of Eastern Michigan. While he spent his first full season in the Midwest League, his 15.1 K/9 ratio certainly opened some eyes. When he reached and dominated Double-A in 2019, then did the same in the Arizona Fall League, it seemed fairly clear that he had the stuff to be a successful big league reliever. Delaplane goes after hitters with a nasty two-pitch mix. His fastball typically sits in the 94-96 mph range with outstanding life when he's healthy, and he does an excellent job of throwing it by hitters up in the zone. His slider has become an absolutely nasty out pitch, one that had the second highest swing-and-miss rates for a slider of anyone in baseball. It’s a hard, short downer breaking ball that was up to 87 mph in the AFL. The right-handed reliever throws everything from the same arm slot, with hitters clearly never seeing the breaking ball coming out of his hand, which led to his high strikeout rates wherever he’s been, including an astounding 16.9 per nine rate in the AFL. His command has been an issue at times but it improved in Double-A and the Fall League, adding confidence he’ll be able to pitch late in games at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at the University of Georgia, Elliott pitched as a reliver and a swingman. He got a chance to be a part of the Bulldogs’ rotation as a junior and had a breakthrough season, establishing himself as the best midweek starter in the nation. The Mariners were hunting college pitching in the 2019 Draft and made Elliott the fifth of five college arms they took to kick things off, signing him for a below-slot $400,000 and sending him out for a solid pro debut in the short-season Northwest League. Elliott was a lean 6-foot-1, 170 pounds when he began his college career, but was up to 200 lbs by the time he began his pro career, allowing his stuff to play up. He throws his fastball in the 89-94 mph range and showed he can maintain that velocity deep into starts. He does a nice job mixing in three secondary offerings. His changeup is the best of the lot, an above-average offspeed pitch, and he makes good use of his average slider and even his fringy curve. Command has been an issue for Elliott at times, though he did much better in the strike-throwing department as a starter during his junior year. If he can continue that, with his repertoire, he has the chance to eventually develop into a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last catcher from the Southern Indiana to make it to the big leagues was Kevin Brown, a Rangers second-round pick who spent parts of seven seasons in the Majors as a backup. His son Logan followed in his footsteps to USI, starting for the Division II school for two years and eventually being taken in the 35th round by the Braves in 2018. The defensive-minded backstop was a South Atlantic League All-Star and earned a promotion up to the Florida State League in his first full season of pro ball. While Brown hit well in Rome, it’s still his defense that stands out. He has excellent catch and throw skills, throwing out 40 percent of potential basestealers in 2019. He also receives very well and gets high marks for his game-calling, working with pitchers and leadership behind the plate. The left-handed hitter makes a ton of contact, though he doesn’t walk a ton, and hasn’t shown much ability to impact the baseball. The Braves think there’s more bat to come, which would help him develop into a very good glove-first backup catcher at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A high school lefty from Georgia, Lindow’s uptick in velocity as a senior likely helped him go from sure-fire Alabama-Birmingham student to a fifth-round pick in the 2017 Draft, signing for $500,000, a bit over slot. His feel for pitching has been very effective at the lower levels of the Minors, with Lindow winning Phillies Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors after pitching across two levels of Class-A ball in 2019. He didn’t pitch at the alternate training site or instructs in 2020. Lindow’s stuff is largely average, at best, across the board, starting with a fastball that touches 92 mph. The velocity might be a bit below-average, but the spin rate up in the zone allows it to play up. He throws his above-average changeup with good deception and fade and he has a pair of breaking balls, with a curve that hits the mid-70s a touch ahead of his low-80s slider that has cutter action to it. All four of the 6-foot-3 southpaw’s pitches play up because he’s an extreme strike-thrower who really knows how to read swings and hitters’ tendencies. He has a bulldog mentality on the mound and goes right after those hitters’ weaknesses, giving him the chance to pitch in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 In 2018, control-and-command lefty David Parkinson was the Phillies’ Minor League pitcher of the year. A year later it was Lindow’s turn to be the pitchability southpaw to earn the award. Drafted out of the Georgia high school ranks in the fifth round of the 2017 Draft and signed for an above-slot $500,000 carved up hitters across two levels of A ball during his full-season debut to put himself more on the map. The 6-foot-3 left-hander has a legitimate four-pitch mix that he can all throw for strikes. While his fastball tops out at 92 mph right now, it plays up because of his plus command of it as well as its spin rate above barrels up in the strike zone. His changeup is his best pitch and he sells it with excellent arm action. He’s still working on two distinct breaking balls, a curve and a slider with cutter-like action to it. A bulldog on the mound, Lindow goes right after hitters and never hurts himself with walks, giving up just 1.8 BB/9 in 2019, and he missed a lot of bats (9.7 K/9) thanks to his command, his ability to mix his pitches and the deception in his delivery. His ceiling is a bit limited, but he’s looking like he could be a workhorse No. 4 or 5 type starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing Christopher Morel for $800,000 in 2015, the Cubs added his younger brother and fellow Dominican shortstop Rafael for $850,000 in 2018. They're two of the toolsier players in the system, with Rafael smaller and sturdier than his sibling. He broke into pro ball with an .821 OPS, 25 extra-base hits and 23 steals in 60 games in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Morel has a sound right-handed swing, manages the strike zone well and makes consistent hard contact. He shows the aptitude to turn on pitches and drive them in the air, displaying solid raw power that already is starting to translate into games. He has the plus speed and the instincts to be a basestealing threat. When Morel was an amateur, scouts were split on whether he'd be better off playing shortstop or center field. The Cubs don't think he'll have any problem staying on the dirt with his athletic actions, quickness and strong arm. Should he wind up in a utility role, he has the tools to play almost anywhere on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 For the first time since 2016, the Reds were allowed to spend more than $300,000 on a player on the international market. So they were thrilled when they were able to ink Triana out of Cuba for $1.3 million on July 2, 2019, the first day international players could sign with teams. He did not go to an affiliate but the 20-year-old spent the rest of the summer working out at the organization’s complex in the Dominican Republic. A big kid at 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds, Triana has big raw power and a handsy swing. Although still very projectable, he has good hitting tools that scouts can dream on, leaving most to believe he’ll hit enough for that raw pop to show up in games consistently. Considered below average defensively, Triana could develop into a serviceable fielder that won’t be a liability. With his size, first base could wind up being the best fit. But he was taken because he can hit for power and if he does that, the Reds will find a spot for Triana.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Kahle first got to the University of Washington in 2017 after playing his high school ball in Southern California, he got to learn under the wing of Joey Morgan, who ended up being a third-round pick of the Tigers that June. Kahle took over as the Huskies' everyday backstop the following year, then led the team in all three triple-slash categories (.339/.506/.532) during a breakout junior campaign before signing with Milwaukee as a fourth-round pick in 2019. Kahle's uptick in production during his sophomore and junior years has the Brewers believing that he'll at least hit for average in pro ball. He's shown the ability to catch up to good fastballs with solid bat speed and recognizes breaking stuff well. He has an advanced approach and takes his share of walks, giving him strong on-base skills on the top of the natural hitting ability. While Kahle’s power plays mostly to the gaps, he does stay inside the ball well and shows some ability to turn on pitches for some over-the-fence pop. Short and stocky, Kahle is a below-average runner and doesn't have that much agility behind the plate. But he has improved his receiving and blocks well, and while his arm strength is fringy, it's accurate. Whether Kahle can unlock all of his hitting ability will likely determine his ultimate role. If he can make the necessary offensive gains, Kahle has the chance to play a long time, with a floor as a very good backup and the chance to be a solid regular if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2018-19 international class, Parra was also one of its more physically advanced prospects, showing a promising mix of strength and hitting ability as a Venezuelan amateur. The Brewers signed him for $210,000 on Aug. 30, 2018, Parra’s 16th birthday, and he rewarded the organization by having a successful 2019 pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he was nearly two years younger than the circuit’s average player. Listed at 6-foot-2, 184 pounds, Parra has present strength and plenty of room still to grow into his projectable frame. He has impressive natural hitting ability for a young player, with an impactful right-handed swing that already yields hard contact as well as raw power. Parra’s swing can get long at times, resulting in some and miss, though the Brewers think that will be less of an issue once the teenager adds strength and has more experience under his belt. He split time between second and third base in his pro debut but profiles better at the latter position, where his plus arm and below-average speed are fits. Parra offered an early glimpse of his offensive potential when he went 5-for-5 with two home runs, two doubles and five RBIs in his third game as a professional. He improved as the season unfolded, batting .329/.451/.573 with 19 RBIs in July, and finished the year with 23 extra-base hits and a .770 OPS in 65 games. The Brewers are understandably excited about the 17-year-old’s bat and view him as someone who could one day hit in the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dillard led all national high school players with 16 homers as a senior in 2016 -- finishing one ahead of Kyle Muller, who signed with the Braves for $2.5 million as a pitcher -- but went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Mississippi and lacked an obvious position. He continued to hit for power in the Southeastern Conference, and after compiling a .286/.419/.505 line with 31 homers in three years with the Rebels, he became the Brewers’ fifth-round pick in the 2019 Draft. In 2020, Milwaukee pushed Dillard’s defensive development by assigning him to its alternate training site, where he caught a mix of top pitching prospects and more established Major Leaguers. A switch-hitter who earned Kyle Schwarber comparisons for his blend of power and patience at Mississippi, Dillard generates impressive raw pop by combining bat speed and strength with a lofty swing. The Brewers think Dillard also will hit for average because of an advanced feel for the strike zone, with club officials citing the gains he made in his approach and contact rate throughout college as reasons to be optimistic. Though his speed is below average, Dillard is surprisingly aggressive on the bases and picks his spots to steal. The 2020 season was supposed to give the Brewers a gauge on whether Dillard could stick at catcher so as to maximize his offensive value. Dillard saw brief time behind the plate this summer but has played primarily at first base. He did hit enough at High-A to earn a midseason promotion to Double-A, but there will now be even more emphasis on his bat since it looks like he’ll be sticking to the cold corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dillard led all national high school players with 16 homers as a senior in 2016 -- finishing one ahead of Kyle Muller, who signed with the Braves for $2.5 million as a pitcher -- but went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Mississippi and lacked an obvious position. He continued to hit for power in the Southeastern Conference, and after compiling a .286/.419/.505 line with 31 homers in three years with the Rebels, he became the Brewers’ fifth-round pick in the 2019 Draft. A switch-hitter who earned Kyle Schwarber comparisons for his blend of power and patience at Mississippi, Dillard generates impressive raw pop by combining bat speed and strength with a lofty swing. The Brewers think that Dillard will also hit for average, with club officials citing the gains he made in his approach and contact rate throughout college as reasons to be optimistic. Though his speed is below average, Dillard is surprisingly aggressive on the bases and picks his spots to steal. The jury is still out as to where Dillard profiles best on the diamond. For now, however, the Brewers intend on trying him out behind the plate so as to maximize his offensive value. He saw brief action as a catcher at Mississippi but played the position almost exclusively in high school. Ideally, Dillard will catch two or three games a week in 2020, and when he’s not behind the dish he’ll likely line up at first base or at a corner-outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates spread out their international bonus pool money during the 2018-19 signing period, handing out a total of 17 six-figure bonuses. Mojica’s $390,000 bonus was the fifth-largest of the group, but he made the most noise in his professional debut in the Domincan Summer League, finishing second in the league with an 1.048 OPS while not turning 17 until August. Mojica is strong and big-bodied -- think Vladimir Guerrero Jr. as a physical comparison -- with the chance to hit for both average and power. He has impressive bat-to-ball skills with a ton of impact, regularly registering exit velocities over 100 mph. He also walked more than he struck out and ended up with 23 extra-base hits in 55 games. He earned those because he’s a well below-average runner, one who’s going to have to maintain his conditioning. That’s even more important in terms of his ultimate defensive home. He has decent hands and a plus arm and moves well for his size right now, but he could easily end up having to move across the diamond to first. The Pirates feel the bat has a chance to be special, one that could profile just fine at first if he continues swinging it like he did in his pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his high school career in New York, Fletcher transferred to Maine and reclassified into the 2019 Draft, where the Cardinals selected him 58th overall.
