The second-round selection secured Fletcher’s status as the highest position player ever selected out of a Maine high school. (The Tigers’ eighth-round selection of Kurt Hall in 1977 previously held the record.) The Cardinals signed him for an above-slot bonus, which led Fletcher to forgo his Vanderbilt commitment and join the professional ranks, where he hit .244 with four homers over two levels of Rookie ball (43 games) in 2019 and then repeated the level in 2021. Fletcher’s raw tools are exciting, though they don’t always show up in games. He struck out in roughly 44 percent of his plate appearances in his professional debut, prompting the Cardinals to work with Fletcher on eliminating his big leg kick. While he needs to improve his contact rate, Fletcher does hit the ball hard and has plus power when he connects. Fletcher participated in St. Louis’ alternate training site during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic, which provided him with valuable reps against advanced pitchers. There’s 20-20 potential if everything goes well, but the tools haven’t translated to on-field production so far. A good athlete with plus speed, Fletcher has the tools -- including an arm that used to fire 93-mph fastballs from the mound -- to play center field, but needs to improve upon his reads and jumps to stay there long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fletcher spent his first two years of high school at a New York prep school, then transferred back home to Maine and reclassified as a senior for the 2019 Draft. One of the premier athletes in his class, he became the highest position player ever drafted out of a Pine Tree State high school when the Cardinals took him in the second round, surpassing Tigers 1977 eighth-rounder Kurt Hall. He signed for above-slot value, forgoing what was thought to be a strong Vanderbilt commitment, then flashed loud tools across a pair of Rookie levels in his pro debut. Fletcher offers a tantalizing combination of plus raw power, speed and arm strength. He also has run his fastball up to 93 mph and flashed a hard slider on the mound. He's a potential 20-20 center fielder if everything comes together, but he's also going to require a lot of time and patience with his development. Fletcher makes loud contact when he connects at the plate, but there are questions about his hitting ability and how well his raw power will translate into production. He has a big leg kick that he'll need to tone down and may have to rework his right-handed swing after striking out more than 43 percent of the time in his pro debut. He must refine his reads and jumps to get the most out of his speed on the bases and in center field, where he could be an above-average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55| Field: 55 | Overall: 40 With baseball bloodlines as the son of former big league infielder Benji Gil, who won the World Series with the Angels in 2002, Mateo Gil endeared himself to scouts with his advanced feel and overall knowledge of the game as an amateur. But a strong commitment to Texas Christian coupled with the fact that Gil lacked prototypical early-round tools led some to question whether he would be drafted high enough to sign. The Cardinals ended up taking Gil in the third round, then lured him away from his college commitment with an above-slot bonus of $900,000. It already looks like money well spent after Gil’s impressive age-18 campaign in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, but it’ll now be the Rockies who benefit after they acquired him in the package for Nolan Arenado in February. Gil is solid in all facets of the game. He's a natural at shortstop, possessing smooth actions and excellent hands that enable him to make all the plays, as well as a quick first step and advanced instincts that give him range in all directions. The low-to-mid-90s fastball that helped Gil excel as his high school team's closer is also an asset for him as a shortstop, and he earns high marks for his throwing accuracy as well as his strong internal clock. He runs well but will never be much of a threat on the basepaths. The Cardinals saw untapped potential in Gil's right-handed bat when they drafted him, and he's already made significant gains as a hitter early in his career, showing sneaky power potential and a knack for barreling the baseball. And while the progress that Gil makes at the plate going forward will ultimately dictate his role and ceiling, his defense and contact skills give him a solid floor and could one day help him contribute in the big leagues in some capacity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed Espinal for $200,000 at the beginning of the 2018-19 international period after being impressed with his premium athleticism and raw ability as a Dominican amateur. After he showed advanced baseball skills in the DSL, where he hit .358/.412/.460 over 47 games, the D-backs brought him stateside to finish the season in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he continued to perform. Espinal began 2021 in Rookie ball once again, but worked his way up Low-A Visalia in July. Espinal’s top-flight athleticism and plus speed are on full display in center field, where he covers a lot of ground and projects as a plus defender. As he continues to develop physically, the D-backs think he will begin hitting for more power. As it is, he shows a really good feel for the strike zone, especially for someone so young. Espinal reminds some D-backs officials of what Geraldo Perdomo looked like at a similar age. It will take a while for Espinal to mature and refine his skills, but given those skills and his tools, there's plenty to dream on.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by Arizona for $200,000 at the beginning of the 2018-19 international period, Espinal stood out for his premium athleticism and raw ability as a Dominican amateur. But he surprised the Diamondbacks by showing surprisingly advanced baseball skills last summer during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, and after Espinal hit .358/.412/.460 over 47 games, they brought the recently turned 17-year-old stateside to finish the season in the Rookie Arizona League, where he continued to perform. Espinal’s top-flight athleticism and plus speed are on full display in center field, where he aggressively runs down everything hit his way, projecting as a plus defender. Club officials think the teenager also will be a physical player who hits for average as well as some power from the left side of the plate. He does a good job controlling the zone and shows feel for the barrel with a clean left-handed swing. Espinal doesn’t hit the ball particularly hard right now, though that should change as he adds strength to his ultra-athletic and projectable frame. The D-backs have been successful in developing young international players of the same ilk as Espinal. His potential and ceiling are still coming into view, but the package of athleticism, tools and skills give plenty to dream on.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz received the second-highest bonus the Rockies gave out in the 2017-18 international signing period, behind Ezequiel Tovar, getting $750,000 to sign right when the period opened on July 2. The first Cuban player ever signed by the Rockies, Diaz spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League and one in the rookie-level Pioneer League hitting for average (.317 career average entering 2021) and stealing a lot of bases (104 in 126 games). The right-handed hitting infielder is a gamer who plays hard and at a high speed at all times. Outside of his speed, his tools don’t jump off the page, but he’s the kind of player who helps a team win games. He has a knack for contact and while he has a very aggressive approach, he doesn’t strike out much, though his K rate did go up a bit while his walk rate dropped with his move to the United States in 2019. He has added some strength, but will need more to impact the ball consistently, with a ceiling likely as a gap-to-gap doubles hitter rather than one who clears fences often. If Diaz is going to be a big league regular at one position, it’s likely going to be at second base, though he can handle shortstop as well. He likely profiles best as a super-utility guy who finds ways to help his team win from a number of positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies signed Diaz out of Cuba for $750,000 in July 2017 and he immediately started showing it might be a very wise investment with his bat and legs. He spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League hitting over .300 and swiping a total of 84 bases, then came to the United States and did more of the same in the Pioneer League. Diaz isn’t the type of player who’ll wow scouts in batting practice, but who grows on you the more you see him in games. He’s very aggressive at the plate with an innate ability to make contact and doesn’t strike out much. He’s drawn walks in the past, but not as much in the Pioneer League. He’s still growing and he’s had some strength gains, so he might develop some power in the future, though it’s likely to be more of the gap-to-gap doubles variety. A plus runner, he’s already shown he’s an efficient basestealer and he plays the game with passion and energy at all times. With an above-average arm, Diaz can play some shortstop, but profiles better at second base if he’s going to settle into one spot long-term. He might mix in some third as the Rockies make a habit of moving their infielders around during development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At nearly 22, Jimenez was ancient by international standards when he signed with the Blue Jays out of the Dominican Republic in 2015. He didn't do much to distinguish himself until the second half of 2019, when he logged a 1.87 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 33 2/3 innings in his first taste of Double-A. When Toronto opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, the Giants nabbed him in the Rule 5 Draft a month later. He was sent back to the Blue Jays last August and was once again left unprotected, leading to the A’s taking him in the 2020 edtion of the Rule 5. Jimenez can overpower hitters with his fastball, which parks at 94-96 mph, peaks at 98 and features above-average spin rates and riding life. He also misses bats with a low-80s slider with two-plane break. He uses a changeup with similar velocity to keep left-handers in check. Jimenez uses his 6-foot-3 frame and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill angle on his pitches. Though he has three effective pitches and throws strikes, he has been a full-time reliever since 2018 and he should remain in that role. The A’s must keep him on their active big league roster throughout 2021 and can't send him to the Minors without placing him on waivers and offering him back to the Jays for half of his $100,000 draft price.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Nova Scotia high schooler, Sanford drew no scouting or recruiting interest and his only college offer was to play volleyball at Dalhousie University in his home province. He walked on at McCook (Neb.) CC, where he hit 23 homers in two years with wood bats, then transferred to Western Kentucky in 2019 and won the first regular-season triple crown in Conference USA history. After he went undrafted the previous three years, the Yankees made him a third-round pick. One of the best power prospects in the 2019 Draft, Sanford creates well-above-average raw pop with plenty of bat speed, strength and leverage in his 6-foot-2, 215-pound frame. Some scouts worry about the deep load in his left-handed swing and his tendency to get off balance at the plate, though New York believes his hand-eye coordination and quick stroke can make it work. He struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances while batting .238/.289/.411 in his pro debut at short-season Staten Island, so he has adjustments to make. In addition to his big power, Sanford features plus speed and can flash even faster running times, though he's not much of a basestealer. A first baseman in junior college, he made a nice transition to right field at Western Kentucky. The Yankees deployed him in center field to see how his quickness played there during his first pro summer, and his fringy arm strength likely will land him in left field if he shifts back to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The maternal grandson of former Orioles outfielder and 1965 AL Rookie of the Year Curt Blefary, Servideo played sparingly as a Mississippi freshman in 2018, then spent most of 2019 shuttling between right field and center field for the Rebels before posting the worst batting line (.149/.228/.277) in the Cape Cod League. He looked like a different player as a junior, starting on Opening Day by singling, doubling and walking against Louisville left-hander Reid Detmers, the eventual No.10 overall pick. Servideo emerged as one of college baseball's better shortstops, slashing .390/.575/.695 in the shortened season. That showed the Orioles enough to take him in the third round and give him a slightly above-slot $950,000 bonus to sign. Servideo’s plus speed and selective approach allowed him to play a table-setting role in college, where he drew 24 walks in 17 games during his junior year and then routinely created havoc on the bases. He’ll need to add strength and cut down his left-handed swing to remain at the top of the order at the next level, where it’ll be necessary to make more consistent contact. He's not big and won't be a slugger, but he displayed more pop as a junior, homering five times after going deep just four times in 100 previous contests. While there are mixed opinions on how much impact Servideo will have at the plate, there are no questions about his ability to play shortstop. He’s a flashy defender, with smooth hands, quick feet and enough arm strength to profile at the position long-term. His athleticism and strong instincts up the middle should give him time to grow into more of an offensive threat. If he doesn't hit enough to be a regular, he'd be capable of playing anywhere in the infield and outfield as a utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Daniels' loud tools stood out much more than his performance in his first two years in college, when he batted .176 with a 38-percent strikeout rate at Tennessee and .168 with a 44-percent whiff rate in the wood-bat Cape Cod League. He did an about-face to hit .357/.478/.750 with 13 extra-base hits in 17 games as a junior in 2020, though scouts still weren't completely sure what to make of him because the shortened season ended before he could prove himself in Southeastern Conference play. He became one of the highest-ceilinged players in the Houston system after signing for $400,000 as a fourth-rounder. Daniels wowed the Astros during instructional league, where he generated impressive exit velocities and displayed the best speed among position players in camp. The ball makes a different sound coming off his bat and he has well above-average raw power, but he still has to show he can erase a history of swinging through hittable fastballs and struggling against breaking balls and changeups. He spent the fall trying to simplify his right-handed swing, starting his hands higher to shorten his first move and elevate more balls. With speed that draws well above-average grades from some evaluators, Daniels could be at least at 20-20 player if he figures things out at the plate. Though he spent much of his final season in college at DH, he has the quickness to stick in center field as a pro if he improves his reads and routes. He has average arm strength and can play all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansen was primarily a reliever at Oklahoma, leading the Sooners with nine saves in 2018 before signing with the Astros as an eighth-rounder. Houston incorporated him into its tandem-starter program during his first full pro season, with impressive results. He fashioned a 33 2/3-inning scoreless streak early in '19 and finished with a 2.11 ERA with a .159 opponents' average and 128 strikeouts in 94 innings between two Class A stops. Despite his relative inexperience as a starter, Hansen has enough pitches for the role. He has a quick arm that produces fastballs that park at 92-95 mph and top out at 97 with some running life. His best secondary offering is a sweeping low-80s slider, and both his upper-70s downer curveball and his changeup show flashes of becoming solid options. While Hansen has improved his fastball velocity and the quality of his secondary pitches since turning pro, he still may be destined for the bullpen. His control and command are shaky and his walk rate has risen as he has climbed through the Minors, increasing to 5.5 per nine innings once he reached high Class A. He lacks physicality and there's some effort in his delivery, so he's probably best served by working shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round pick out of a Virginia high school in 2017, Perry spent most of his first two pro seasons in Rookie ball before breaking out in the New York-Penn League in 2019. He finished second in the short-season circuit in homers and won MVP honors at the New York-Penn all-star game, where he went deep in his lone at-bat. He was slated to finally make his full-season debut in 2020 before the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League season. Perry stands out with his strength and plus raw power, most of which comes to his pull side. He has a short left-handed stroke with natural loft and enjoyed more success once he realized he didn't need to sell out for home runs. He still needs to make more consistent contact, but he's willing to work counts and draw walks. While Perry shared time behind the plate in the New York-Penn League, that was in deference to 2019 first-rounder Korey Lee, and the Astros believe he can stick at catcher. He has improved as a receiver since turning pro and does a nice job of framing pitches, though he can look a bit stiff at times. He has average arm strength, a quick transfer and makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brady went from his high school in southern New Jersey to East Carolina University, but after not seeing much mound time as a freshman in 2016, he returned to the Garden State and Mercer Community College. A standout season there in 2017 landed him in the seventh round with the Angels. Some arm issues slowed him early on in his career -- he amassed just 144 2/3 innings over his first two-plus seasons, but he’s healthy now and would have been ready to go for a full 2020 season had it transpired. The 6-foot-1 right-hander has a three-pitch mix and an idea of what to do with it, giving him some starting pitcher qualities. His fastball sits in the 92-93 mph range, and he can reach back for 95 mph on occasion. Depending on who sees him and how he’s throwing it, Brady has either a hard curve or a slider, and a decent slurvy breaking ball that he has a good feel to spin while adding to and subtracting from it. He’ll mix in a changeup that flashes average as well. Despite not having wow stuff, Brady has done a nice job of missing bats while filling up the strike zone fairly consistently. The lack of an out pitch or premium velocity kept him off the radar enough to not be selected in the 2020 Rule 5 Draft, even though he was left unprotected. After a solid showing at instructs this fall, the Angels are intrigued to see what Brady can do in a full healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter at California Baptist University, Rinehart pitched well in relief in the Cape Cod League and continued to impress out of the bullpen in his professional debut. After the Mariners grabbed the right-hander in the 16th-round of the 2019 Draft, he pitched his way to full-season ball, where he posted a 3.52 ERA over 10 appearances. Listed at 6-foot-3, 185 pounds, Rinehart showed up to Spring Training in exceptional shape and appeared ready to put together a breakout campaign. Of course, COVID-19 shut down the 2020 Minor League season so Rinehart didn’t get a chance to compete against other organizations, but he did impress at Seattle’s alternate site. The right-hander throws his fastball in the 94-96 mph range and complements it with a trio of secondary offerings. Rinehart has plus control of a changeup that he throws in the upper 70s, a stark separation from his fastball, and also throws both a sweeping slider and a downer curveball that is used as an out pitch early in counts. Rinehart has thrown strikes as a pro, but the improved velocity and usage of the zone has helped him miss more bats. While the Mariners plan to let him start for now, he needs to continue to refine his breaking stuff to remain in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, the Phillies handed out a $2.5 million bonus to shortstop Luis Garcia. Six months later, and at the other end of the bonus spectrum, they inked Martinez for $10,000. Martinez put up pedestrian numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and while he pitched sparingly in his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2019, he created some buzz with his size, stuff and upside potential. The 6-foot-2 left-hander is lanky and loose and has a legitimate three-pitch mix at his disposal. He can throw his fastball in the 91-96 mph range, throwing it with good late life. His slider has the chance to be a true out pitch, and he has surprisingly good feel for his changeup at a young age, selling it well with good arm speed. Martinez has shown the ability to throw strikes with a clean, easy and relatively effortless delivery that also provides some deception, with an idea of how to mix his pitches. It’s been a very small sample size of performance thus far, but scouts are excited to see what he can do with more time on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed a pair of promising 16-year-old Dominican outfielders at the outset of the 2018-19 international period, signing Marte and Jeremy De La Rosa for $300,000 apiece -- the maximum amount allowed without incurring a penalty -- on July 2. Though both players flashed a collection of intriguing tools during the pro debuts in the 2019 Dominican Summer League, it was Marte who led the team in home runs (tied, 5), slugging (.448) and total bases (94) at age 17, and he was one of Washington’s most impressive prospects during fall instructional camp in 2020. Marte possesses a blend of athleticism and physicality that has already earned him comparisons to an NFL running back. His projectable frame is ideal for adding more strength, and club officials do not expect those physical gains to detract from the plus speed that also enables Marte to play a quality center field. The Nationals believe he has a chance to remain at the position long-term, but his strong arm would more than suffice if he’s forced to move to an outfield corner. Marte’s development as a hitter will be key in unlocking his overall potential. He can do damage from the right side of the plate, combining strength and bat speed into an explosive swing, and Marte already showcases plus raw power to his pull side that should begin to play to all fields more consistently as he gains experience. Marte’s approach and pitch selection will both require considerable refinement (as is the case with most teenage hitters), but the raw ingredients are all there for him to become an impact talent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed two of the top infield prospects in the 2016-17 international class with seven-figure bonuses, signing Yasel Antuna ($3.9 million bonus) and Luis Garcia ($1.3 million) as part of a larger haul. They added another promising infielder the following year in Pena, inking the undersized switch-hitter for $150,000. The Dominican native has done nothing but hit since entering Washington’s system and batted .359/.455/.481 over 37 Rookie-level Gulf Coast League games in 2019, making his stateside debut at age 18. Pena’s ability to repeat his swing and barrel the ball from both sides of the plate already ranks among the best in the organization and could help him develop into an above-average hitter in the big leagues. He has a small frame and will never much in the way of home-run power, he does have the bat speed and strength needed to turn around good velocity and is comfortable hitting to all fields. A solid-to-plus runner, Pena’s quickness and speed help him on both sides of the ball. Though he’s seen time at shortstop, second and third base early in his career, Pena’s best long-term fit might be at the keystone based on his size and offensive profile. If it all clicks, he could develop into a scrappy, top-of-the-order catalyst type who wears out pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star out of the high school ranks in Ohio who played wide receiver at football powerhouse St. Edward outside of Cleveland, Wainwright could have headed to college on the gridiron but committed to Ohio State for baseball. Wainwright wasn’t as strong on the Draft radar because an injury (fractured tibia) had interfered with much of his summer showcase work before his senior year. The team he was supposed to play for at East Coast Pro Showcase was run by Reds scouts, and the relationship they forged with the young outfielder, not to mention a return to health that fall and before the shutdown this spring, gave the Reds confidence to take Wainwright in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft and sign him for full pick value. After signing, Wainwright stood out with his all-around tools and work ethic in his introduction to the club at instructs. He’s strong with an athletic frame, and while it might take some time for his tools to sharpen given his dual-sport focus and living in a cold-weather state, there are some serious skills that show up now. He has excellent bat speed and solid raw power, though he’ll need some reps to learn to catch up to premium velocity and recognize breaking stuff. While he’s not a burner, Wainwright does run well and provides a solid arm to go along with strong defense. He’s a center fielder now and could be given the chance to stay up the middle, though some evaluators feel he’ll outgrow the position and end up in a corner spot, where he could eventually develop into a prototypical athletic run-producing right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star at Teurlings Catholic High (Lafayette, La.), Cantrelle led his school’s baseball team to the state 4-A championships as a junior and senior and drew college football interest as a quarterback. After turning down the Yankees as a 40th-rounder in 2017, he became an immediate starter at Louisiana-Lafayette and was one of just six NCAA Division I players to total as many as 25 extra-base hits and 25 steals in 2019. That and a strong Cape Cod League performance put him in position to go in the top two rounds, but he batted just .148 during the shortened 2020 season and dropped to the Brewers in the fifth round and signed for $300,000. After picking up summer at-bats in the City of Champions Cup, a pop-up league in Joliet, Ill., Brewers coaches first saw Cantrelle in person during the fall instructional league. He sparked some comparisons to Scooter Gennett, with less power than Gennett at the moment and better defensive skills, with a similar ability to square up the baseball foul line to foul line. Second base is probably Cantrelle’s best position, but he has the quickness, solid arm and baseball IQ to play above-average there. He was primarily at the keystone with High-A Wisconsin in 2021 prior to an August promotion to Double-A Biloxi. Despite his pre-Draft slump, Cantrelle has the potential to hit near the top of a batting order. A switch-hitter who impacts the ball with more authority from the left side, he posted a .315 average with wood bats on the Cape, has a knack for getting on base and possesses plus speed and savvy on the bases. He has some sneaky pop with 15-homer upside, but he's better off when he worries less about power and more about making consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of six players drafted out of Florida’s IMG Academy in 2019, Romeri went off the board in the 12th round, but signed for an above-slot $200,00, forgoing a commitment to Villanova. The outfielder showed flashes of power in his professional debut, finishing tied for third in the Rookie Gulf Coast League with six homers over 41 games. He also drove in 20 runs and slashed .246/.346/.464. Romeri has a decent all-around game, but the power is his carrying tool. He shows a good feel for the barrel and has consistently posted strong exit velocities as well. With a projectable 6-foot-3, 195-pound frame, the Cardinals believe he will be able to tap into more power as he matures. The power is impressive, but Romeri is still learning his swing and there’s room for improvement in his approach as he can get too pull happy and overly aggressive at times. He’s presently an average runner, but may lose a step as he fills out. A good athlete, Romeri profiles well in either corner outfield spot and takes good routes defensively. His arm, which touched 92 mph with his fastball in high school, is strong enough to handle right field. He could develop into a solid fourth outfielder, or perhaps an everyday player if his hit tools improves. The Cardinals have been pleased with his work ethic and the strides he’s made in the short time he’s been in the organization and view him as someone who has the potential to be a fast riser.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prater was part of a loaded weekend rotation for an Oklahoma squad that also featured 2020 first-round pick Cade Cavalli (Nationals) and fourth-rounder Dane Acker (A’s). However, Prater had the best ERA (3.42) of the bunch and struck out 33 in his 23 2/3 innings before the coronavirus pandemic halted the 2020 season and the Cardinals selected him with the 93rd overall pick (third round) that June. In a more complete sample size, the lefty was named to the 2019 All-Big 12 Second Team and led Sooners’ starters that year with 97 strikeouts and a 3.26 ERA in 80 innings. While there’s still room for growth, Prater did show an ability to miss bats in his professional debut, racking up 83 strikeouts over his first 52 1/3 innings in Low-A. A deceptive, crossfire delivery helps Prater’s stuff play up and makes him hard to hit. He throws his fastball with armside run in the low 90s and sits around 80 mph with his slider. He also throws a changeup around 80 mph that flashes plus, but isn’t always consistent. The development of that pitch, as well as his overall command, will likely go a long way into determining his future role. The Cardinals are giving Prater an opportunity to start as he begins his professional career and he’ll be able to remain there if he’s able to improve upon his control. His delivery features some effort, which may push Prater into a reliever role. He profiles well as a middle reliever and may ultimately wind up in the bullpen, depending on how he develops that third pitch. If he is able to put everything together, his ceiling is likely that of a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing both ways but struggling on the mound as a North Carolina State freshman, Mendoza focused on his bat and his play at third and put together a strong sophomore campaign that he furthered with standout summer in the Cape Cod League. While an inconsistent junior campaign caused him to last until the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, he did rebound to win the New York-Penn League batting title (.370) in his pro debut and then spent most of his first full season in Double-A before reaching Triple-A in the next. Mendoza was a standout at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020. Mendoza has a knack for barreling the baseball from the right side of the plate with a line-drive swing that he controls well. He hits the ball to all fields, showing some extra-base pop but well-below-average over-the-fence power. Mendoza does have some strength, though, and he flashed sneaky power in his first full season. He’s a good athlete and fringy runner who earns high marks for his baserunning. Mendoza is an easy plus defender at third base and has the hands, footwork and arm strength needed to play anywhere on the infield. That includes shortstop, a position the Cardinals deployed him at more consistently with encouraging results in 2020. He also has seen time as a first baseman. Mendoza doesn’t have the power to fit the typical corner-infield offensive profile in the big leagues, but he does hit well enough to serve as a utility infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a sophomore at UConn in 2018, Feole collected the second-most strikeouts in school history. When he followed that up with 11 shutout innings for USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team, he looked poised to be one of the more intriguing college lefties in the 2019 Draft class. But a forearm issue slowed him early as his velocity dipped, hurting his stock considerably, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in July after the Padres took him in the 11th round. After completing his rehab process, Feole appeared physically stronger and operated with better stuff when he returned to mound in San Diego’s fall instructional camp. At his best, Feole leans heavily on his fastball-curve combination. The former will sit in the low 90s and was touching higher during instructional league, while the breaking ball serves as his out pitch, flashing plus at times. Feole has a third-pitch changeup that is below average. An unorthodox delivery that includes a head snap makes it difficult for Feole to find the strike zone consistently and portends a full-time move to the bullpen, where his two-pitch repertoire could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts had a tough time getting an accurate read on Frechette, who sold out for power too often on the high school showcase circuit before coming down with mononucleosis during his 2019 senior season. He won the Giants over with an impressive pre-Draft workout at Oracle Park, sending multiple balls into McCovey Cove and drilling one off the top of the right-field foul pole. After signing for a well over-slot $797,500 in the fifth round, he batted .290/.364/.366 in Rookie ball. Frechette has the ingredients to hit for both average and power if he doesn't try to do too much at the plate. When he came back from mono, he used a shorter, smoother left-handed stroke and showed the ability to barrel balls consistently. His bat speed combines with the leverage and projectable strength in his 6-foot-3 frame to create considerable raw pop, though he needs to learn to let it come naturally. Frechette displays fringy speed out of the batter's box and is an average runner once he gets going. He moves well around the bag at first base and has decent arm strength. San Francisco plans on trying him in left field, though its outfield depth at the lower levels may make that difficult.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Missouri Valley Conference freshman and defensive player of the year in 2018, Glowenke finished fourth in the league in batting (.328) last spring and then hit .296 in the Cape Cod League. One of the better hitters among this year's college shortstops, he missed the first weekend of his junior year recovering from offseason elbow surgery and didn't play in the field before the season ended. He could go in the first five rounds and is a righty-hitting version of the only Dallas Baptist infielder ever to do so (Ryan Goins, fourth round, 2009), albeit with less arm strength. Glowenke's lone better-than-average tool is his bat, as he makes line-drive contact with ease. He controls the strike zone well and enhances his on-base ability by getting hit by more than his share of pitches. He can provide some doubles and perhaps 10-12 homers per season at the next level, but he didn't drive the ball with wood bats on the Cape. Glowenke's below-average speed almost certainly will push him to second base in pro ball. He's a sure-handed defender at shortstop, but he lacks the range to stay there. His average arm may be enough to get by at third base in a utility role, though neither it nor his power fits the profile to play regularly at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year after signing Bryce Bush for $290,000 in the 33rd round of the 2018 Draft, the White Sox used an over-slot bonus and late pick to snag another high school third baseman from the Midwest, nabbing Gladney for $225,000 in the 16th round. Gladney stayed on Bush's path by hitting for power in the Rookie-level Arizona League during his pro debut, going deep eight times in 50 games. His 2020 development was restricted to instructional league after the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League schedule. Gladney's carrying tool is his plus raw power, which he creates with bat speed, projectable strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame. He already has a feel for driving the ball in the air with his right-handed stroke and exhibits pop to all fields. He comes with serious swing-and-miss concerns, however, posting a 37 percent strikeout rate in his debut because his approach and pitch-recognition skills are rudimentary. Though Gladney moves well for his size and can flash average speed, he figures to lose a step as he matures physically. The White Sox had him focus on improving his footwork and the consistency of his arm stroke during instructs and think he can become an average third baseman. While he has solid arm strength and decent hands, scouts outside the organization question his range and reliability at the hot corner and project him as a left fielder or first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chatham was an outfielder who flashed a mid-90s fastball as a reliever at American Heritage High (Plantation, Fla.), which has produced four big leaguers and five first-round picks, including 2018 Red Sox choice Triston Casas. Chatham went to Florida Atlantic, where he moved to shortstop and blossomed into the highest pick in school history (51st overall) as well as the Conference USA player and defensive player of the year in 2016. Persistent hamstring injuries limited him to seven games during his first full pro season, but he stayed healthy in 2018 and finished second in the Class A Advanced Carolina League batting race at .315. Chatham's most valuable attribute is his ability to make consistent line-drive contact. He hinted at average raw power as an amateur that has yet to translate to home run production as a pro, though Boston hopes he can unlock more pop if he adds some strength to his lanky frame and some loft to his relatively flat right-handed swing. He has average speed and is effective on the bases, albeit not much of a threat to steal. His instincts and quick first step allow Chatham to cover ground and get the job done at shortstop. He still has a strong arm and soft hands, and he should be able to play second or third base if needed. He has one of the higher floors among Red Sox position prospects and a decent upside as a reliable if unspectacular regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chatham led Florida Atlantic to its first-ever Conference USA regular-season title in 2016, winning accolades as the league's player and defensive player of the year while playing through a broken hamate in his right hand. The Red Sox made him the highest pick in Owls history, signing him for $1.1 million as the 51st overall choice, but haven't gotten to see much of him yet. The hamate injury hampered him during his pro debut, while repeated hamstring issues limited him to just seven games in 2017. Though he's just an average runner and taller than most shortstops at 6-foot-4, Chatham shouldn't have to move from shortstop. His instincts and quick first step improve his range, and his strong, accurate arm allows him to make all of the throws. If he winds up shifting to second base, he still should provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player. Chatham has a track record of making consistent line-drive contract from the right side of the plate, though he could use some more patience to draw more walks. His size gives him good leverage and more raw power than most shortstops, and he could produce 30 doubles and 12-15 homers annually. He won't steal many bases but is an effective runner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite playing with a right hand injury eventually diagnosed as a broken hamate bone, Chatham led Florida Atlantic to its first-ever Conference USA regular-season title in 2016, earning league player-of-the-year and defensive-player-of-the-year recognition along the way. The first college shortstop drafted in 2016 and the highest pick in school history, he went 51st overall and signed for $1.1 million. His hamate injury hampered him early in his debut but he hit .320 with four homers in his final two weeks, and then he missed most of the first three months of the 2017 season with repeated hamstring issues. Taller than most shortstops at 6-foot-4 and possessing just average speed, Chatham nevertheless should be able to stick at the position. His quick first step and his instincts enhance his range, and he has the strong, accurate arm to make any throw necessary. If he does have to move, he has enough bat to still profile as a regular at second base. Chatham has a track record of making consistent contact and could produce solid batting averages if he improves his patience at the plate. He has more raw power than the typical shortstop, thanks to the leverage in his right-handed swing, and should be good for double-digit home runs and plenty of doubles on an annual basis. He's not a threat to steal but runs the bases well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2016 second-rounder out of Santa Clara, White was the Broncos' highest selection since Randy Winn 21 years earlier and signed for a well below-slot $590,800. When former Dodgers vice president of baseball operations (now Braves GM) Alex Anthopoulos saw him in his first Spring Training the next year, he remarked that White's stuff looked worthy of a No. 1 overall pick. He has yet to stay healthy for a full season in pro ball, however, and got hammered while dealing with blister problems last year in Triple-A. White's stuff was sharp at the beginning of 2019, when he dominated in Double-A. His fastball ranged from 92-97 mph with natural cutting action, and he backed it up with a mid-80s slider with late bite and a high-spin curveball with downer break. But he had trouble adjusting to the big league balls used in Triple-A, where his heater sat more at 90-93 and his breaking pitches were more ordinary. White is working to refine a changeup to give him a pitch that runs away from left-handers, who slugged .507 against him last year. In order to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter, he needs to avoid nagging injuries and do a better job of repeating his delivery to maintain quality and command with his pitches. If he can't, he could be useful as a bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When former Dodgers vice president of baseball operations (now Braves GM) Alex Anthopoulos saw White during his first Spring Training as a pro, he remarked that White had the stuff worthy of a No. 1 overall pick. In actuality, he was a 2016 second-rounder out of Santa Clara, the Broncos' highest pick since Randy Winn in 1995, and he signed for a well-below-slot $590,800. White advanced to Double-A and continued to dazzle with his fastball and breaking pitches in 2017, though he wasn't as sharp last year after missing the first month with a sore arm. At his best, White features a 92-97 mph fastball with natural run and sink, an overpowering slider that climbs into the upper 80s with late bite and a hammer curveball. He spent the early part of 2018 working in the low 90s and with more ordinary sliders and curves, though his stuff picked back up later in the season. He also can morph his slider into a harder and equally nasty cutter and is working to refine a changeup to counteract left-handers. White sometimes battles his delivery and command but did a better job of repeating his mechanics and finding the strike zone during the second half of 2018. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter who can generate more than his share of swings and misses as well as ground-ball contact. He also could be a high-leverage reliever who could concentrate on attacking hitters with his fastball and breaking balls.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White had Tommy John surgery after graduating from high school in 2013 and served as a reliever at Santa Clara as a redshirt freshman two years later before surging up Draft boards after moving into the Broncos' rotation in 2016. The Dodgers selected him 65th overall, Santa Clara's highest pick since Randy Winn went in the same spot 21 years earlier, and signed him for a well below-slot $590,800. He advanced to Double-A in his first full pro season but his progress has been slowed in 2018 by a sore arm that sidelined him for the first month. When former Dodgers vice president of baseball operations (now Braves GM) Alex Anthopoulos saw him in Spring Training one day last year, he remarked that White had the type of stuff that would fit a No. 1 overall pick. His fastball sat around 90 mph at the start of 2016 but now operates at 92-97 mph and plays up with natural sink and run. That's not necessarily his best pitch because he also possesses a power slider with late bite that can reach 88 mph, and he also has the ability to morph it into an even harder and equally effective cutter. White also has a curveball that can be a true hammer at times, and after focusing on his breaking pitches in 2017, he'll work to refine his changeup this year. He also needs to sharpen his control and command, and he has the athleticism and sound delivery to do so. He generates a ton of swings and misses as well as weak contact, with 61 percent of the batters he faced in his first two pro seasons either striking out or grounding out against him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers took redshirt sophomores with consecutive early-round picks in the 2016 Draft, and second-rounder White outperformed supplemental first-rounder Jordan Sheffield in their debuts by posting a spotless ERA with 30 strikeouts in 22 innings. White had Tommy John surgery after graduating from high school in 2013 and saw his velocity and prospect stock soar after he moved into Santa Clara's rotation last spring. He went 65th overall, making him the highest Broncos pick since Randy Winn went in the same spot in 1995, and signed for a well below-slot $590,800. White opened 2016 with his fastball sitting around 90 mph but started hitting the mid-90s toward the end of the college season and worked at 92-96 in pro ball. His heater plays up because of its natural life, but his best pitch is an upper-80s cutter that can be unhittable. His downer curveball should be at least a solid offering, while his changeup is more of a work in progress. With his athleticism, sound delivery and strong build, White has the necessary ingredients to remain a starting pitcher. He has no trouble throwing strikes but still is refining his command, which continues to improve as he gets more innings and puts his elbow reconstruction further behind him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston gave seven-figure bonuses to three Venezuelans in 2017: catcher Daniel Flores ($3.1 million), who died of cancer four months later; and infielders Flores ($1.4 million) and Danny Diaz ($1.6 million), who quickly emerged as two of the best position prospects in a rebuilding farm system. Flores was advanced enough offensively and defensively to make his U.S. debut at age 17 last summer, though he missed six weeks after straining his left shoulder on a swing. One rival club told the Red Sox they considered him the best prospect in the organization. With a controlled but quick right-handed swing and an advanced approach for a teenager, Flores should hit for a high average. He controls the strike zone and employs the entire field, and his hitting ability and deceptive strength give him the chance to develop 20-homer power. While he's only an average runner and could lose a half-step as he matures physically, he has good instincts on the bases. Flores also shows nice savvy in the field, where he covers more ground at shortstop than his speed might suggest. He's a fluid defender with soft hands and the arm strength to make all the required throws at short. In the event he slows down and requires a shift to third base, he has the offensive potential to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of three Venezuelans to receive seven-figure signing bonuses from the Red Sox in 2017, Flores turned pro for $1.4 million. He's no relation to Daniel Flores, who died of cancer four months after signing for $3.1 million. His tools are fairly similar to those of C.J. Chatham's, Boston's top shortstop prospect, though Flores is much further away from the big leagues. Though Flores receives more praise for his instincts than his tools, he has the ability to contribute both offensively and defensively. He has good actions at shortstop, where his savvy allows him to cover more ground than his fringy speed would suggest. He has the arm strength for the position, though he needs to be mindful not to drop his arm slot and lose accuracy on his throws. With a nice right-handed swing and signs of an advanced approach, Flores should hit for average. He's not very physical but has some loft in his stroke and should develop some gap power once he gets stronger. He won't be a basestealer, but runs the bases well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Astros for $22,500 out of the Dominican Republic in June 2014, Guzman became part of two significant trades in the span of 13 months. Houston shipped him and right-hander Albert Abreu to the Yankees for Brian McCann in November 2016, and New York packaged him with Starlin Castro and shortstop Jose Devers to acquire Giancarlo Stanton from the Marlins in December 2017. He's one of the hardest-throwing starters in the Minors, but his control and command have backed up since he came to Miami. Guzman's electric arm speed produces riding fastballs that park at 95-98 mph and reach triple digits, and he shows the ability to maintain plus-plus velocity deep into starts. He has hit 103 mph but his radar-gun readings are more impressive than his ability to command his heater. He also can overpower hitters with a power slurve that combines slider velocity (mid-80s) with curveball depth, and there are times when his sinking changeup is his most reliable secondary pitch. Guzman has a short arm action and has trouble maintaining a rhythm with his delivery. Now 24 and in his sixth year as a pro, he averaged 5.2 walks per nine innings during his first two seasons in Miami's system. If he can develop more consistency and command, he has the pure stuff to become at least a No. 3 starter or perhaps a closer, but he needs to begin making more progress.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially signed by the Astros for $22,500 out of the Dominican Republic at the end of the 2013-14 international signing period, Guzman was traded to the Yankees along with right-hander Albert Abreu for Brian McCann in November 2016. Thirteen months later, New York shipped him along with Starlin Castro and shortstop Jose Devers to the Marlins for Giancarlo Stanton. Guzman pitched in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game during his first season with his third organization but also saw his control and command regress significantly. With a quick arm and little effort, Guzman sits at 95-98 mph with the ability to reach triple digits in the late innings. He has thrown as hard as 103 mph but his velocity is more impressive than his fastball command, and the latter will dictate how quickly he moves up the ladder. He also can miss bats with his power slider and a changeup that's improving as he uses it more. He's similar to fellow Marlins power righties Sandy Alcantara and Edward Cabrera, though scouts are less optimistic about Guzman's ability to harness his stuff. His walk rate jumped from 2.4 per nine innings in 2017 to 6.0 last year. Whether he can develop control, command and consistency will determine whether he becomes a frontline starter or winds up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman struggled early in his career, posting a combined 4.63 ERA during his first two seasons in Rookie ball after signing with Houston out of the Dominican Republic in 2014. His elite arm strength caught the attention of the Yankees, however, and they acquired him and Albert Abreu for Brian McCann in November 2016. Guzman was on the move again the following offseason, this time going to the Marlins with Jose Devers and Starlin Castro in the Giancarlo Stanton blockbuster. Guzman's lightning-quick arm and relatively easy delivery produces exceptional velocity in a fastball that sits 97-103 mph as a starter. He showed better control of the pitch in 2017 after improving his mechanics, but regressed as a strike-thrower in '18 while pitching in the Florida State League. Guzman's power slider is an above-average pitch and complements his heater nicely, and together they help him to rack up strikeouts. He also has changeup that's in its nascent stages. Guzman demonstrated the capacity to make adjustments during his time in the Yankees system, and he'll need to make even more in the coming years to reach his ceiling of a No. 3 starter or a dominant closer. Throwing strikes consistently is Guzman's biggest hurdle right now, but the power-armed righty could move quickly if it clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic by the Astros in 2014, Guzman compiled a 4.63 ERA in Rookie ball during his first two years as a pro. He can light up radar guns like few other pitches can, however. That captivated the Yankees enough to acquire him along with fellow right-hander Albert Abreu when they traded Brian McCann to Houston in November. He was on the move again the following offseason, this time going to the Marlins with Jose Devers and Starlin Castro in the Giancarlo Stanton blockbuster. With an extremely fast arm and without an excessive amount of effort in his delivery, Guzman can work with a 97-103 mph fastball as a starter. The downside is that he sometimes doesn't know where his heater is going, especially when he crosses into triple digits. He also throws a power slider that lacks consistency and a changeup in its nascent stages. Though Guzman's control and command require more refinement, they have improved significantly since he focused on his mechanics during extended spring training this year. That will give him a better chance of remaining a starter, and he'll be a potential closer if he winds up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It's not overly common to see a teenager already committing to a bullpen role, as teams tend to like to exhaust the possibility of a pitcher making it as a starter first. But Pinto, and undersized right-hander with a big arm, has done nothing but relieve and it seems to suit him. The Venzuelan product made his United States debut in 2016 and it was an effective one, missing a lot of bats along the way. He's pretty raw, but there's plenty of velocity coming from his right arm and he's shown the ability to spin a curveball, a pitch that eventually has the chance to be even better than average. He has shown some feel for a changeup, which might make some think about giving him a chance to start, though his stocky frame and command point to him sticking to relief work. Pinto is just getting started and learning how to pitch. Pro instruction as he approaches the full-season leagues will undoubtedly help him maximize his potential as a back-end short reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting .240 in his first three seasons at Southern California, Stubbs batted .346 with 20 steals as a senior in 2015, when he won the Johnny Bench Award as the top college catcher as well as Pacific-12 Conference defensive player of the year honors. An eighth-rounder that June, he reached Double-A in his first full season but stalled there in 2017. He rebounded last year in Triple-A to claim a spot on Houston's 40-man roster. Stubbs makes repeated contact with a simple left-handed swing and controls the strike zone better than any Astros product. He made a conscious effort to drive the ball more last year, though he's not very physical and his power will come more in the form of doubles than home runs. Extremely athletic for a catcher, he has average speed and knows what he's doing on the bases. Stubbs moves well behind the plate and shows solid receiving skills. He has arm strength to match and it plays up because of his quick transfer, enabling him to throw out 44 percent of basestealers in his first four years as a pro. His biggest drawback is that he's just 5-foot-10 and 175 pounds and wears down over the course of a season, making him more of a backup because he won't hold up as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stubbs hit .240 in his first three years at Southern California before batting .346 with 20 steals as a senior in 2015, winning the Johnny Bench Award as college baseball's top catcher and Pacific-12 Conference defensive player of the year honors. Signed for $100,000 as an eighth-rounder, he opened more eyes by hitting .304/.391/.469 while advancing to Double-A during his first full pro season. He started last year in similar fashion but slumped in May and never snapped out of it, finishing at .232/.328/.321. Stubbs is better than his 2017 numbers and has rebounded this season, but at 5-foot-10 and 175 pounds he's not equipped to handle a full season's workload behind the plate. He also looked worn down at the end of 2016 in the Arizona Fall League and will have to do a better job of managing his strength via nutrition and weightlifting. While he may not have the stamina to be a regular in the big leagues, he has the tools to be a quality backup. Using a simple left-handed swing, Stubbs makes consistent line-drive contact and excels at managing the strike zone. He's not geared for power but does have average speed and provides more value on the bases than a typical catcher. His athleticism pays off behind the plate, where he receives well and enhances his solid arm strength with a quick transfer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting .240 in his first three seasons at Southern California, Stubbs batted .346 with 20 steals as a senior, won the Johnny Bench Award as college baseball's best catcher and was named Pac-12 Conference defensive player of the year. He has continued to impress after signing for $100,000 as an eighth-rounder in 2015, batting .304/.391/.469 and reaching Double-A during his first full pro season. His 5-foot-10, 175-pound frame leads to a lot of questions about whether he'll be durable enough to be a big league starter, but that's the only real concern. His size also makes him the player he is, as he's much quicker and more athletic than the typical catcher. He receives and blocks well, and he enhances solid arm strength with fast footwork and impressive accuracy -- which allowed him to throw out 51 percent of basestealers in 2016. Stubbs excels at making contact at the plate and has walked (64) more than he has struck out (53) in his first two pro seasons. He uses a simple left-handed swing but can drive the ball on occasions and improved his slugging percentage at each of his first four Minor League stops, so he might be able to provide double-digit homers on an annual basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The epitome of the local kid done good, Bishop went to high school in California and was a 36th-round Draft pick of the Braves in 2012, then spent three solid years at the University of Washington. The local team, the Mariners, liked his profile in center field enough to take him in the third round of the 2015 Draft. Though a broken arm caused by a hit by pitch ended his season in late July 2018, the Texas League All-Star was added to the 40-man roster during the offseason. Bishop's calling card is still his play in center field, though he has made strides at the plate. He uses his outstanding speed to cover a lot of ground and is a premium defender up the middle, with a strong arm to boot. While his offensive game is still very much contact-oriented, Bishop has embraced changes to his swing, including the lowering of his hands and more of a leg kick to get more launch angle, and is impacting the ball more consistently. He's still controlling the strike zone well, drawing walks and limiting strikeouts, but he is driving the ball more and has a higher ISO in 2018 as evidence, with most of his home run juice coming to the pull side. The Mariners have talked to Bishop about reincorporating basestealing into his offensive game. He swiped 22 bases in 2017, but only five a year later. If his offense keeps ticking upward and he can be more aggressive on the basepaths, he has the chance to be an everyday catalyst in center field and at or near the top of a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-time member of the Pac-12 All-Defensive Team during his time at Washington, Bishop's abilities in center field have never been questioned. His hitting ability, on the other hand, drew mixed reviews from scouts leading up to the 2015 Draft. The Mariners, believing in his bat, selected him in the third round, and then watched him reach Double-A in his second full season. Returning to the level in 2018, Bishop was named a Texas League midseason All-Star before an errant pitch resulted in a broken arm and effectively ended his season in late July. Bishop impacts the baseball more consistently now after lowering his hands in his setup at the plate -- an adjustment that has been at heart of his uptick in production. He stands to improve upon those marks as he continues to clean up his swing, though it's unlikely that he'll ever offer much in the way of over-the-fence power. A well-above-average runner and defender, Bishop is graceful in center field with his great jumps and exceptional range. That speed also makes him a threat on the basepaths, though he still has gains to make with both his technique and feel for reading pitchers. Bishop's bat will need to continue to develop for him to reach his ceiling as a top-of-the-order center fielder. Even if it doesn't, Bishop has the contact skills and speed-defense combo to be a productive fourth outfielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-time member of the Pac-12 All-Defensive Team during his time at Washington, Bishop's abilities in center field have never been questioned. His hitting ability, on the other hand, drew mixed reviews from scouts leading up to the 2015 Draft. The Mariners, believing in his bat, took him in the third round of the Draft, and he rewarded them in his pro debut by finishing second in the Class A Short Season Northwest League with a .320 average. He made his full-season debut in '16, splitting the year between the Midwest and California Leagues, and then returned to the latter stop in 2017 to earn All-Star honors before moving up to Double-A in July. A well-above-average runner and defender, Bishop makes it look easy in center field with his great jumps and exceptional range. That speed also makes him a threat on the basepaths, though he does have gains to make with both his technique and feel for reading pitchers. Offensively, Bishop has good bat speed from the right side of the plate, and he's shorter to the ball now after working with the Mariners to clean up his swing last summer. He should add some strength as he matures, which should lead to more gap power, but he's never going to be a home-run threat. Whether Bishop can reach his ceiling as a top-of-the-order center fielder will depend on how much his bat develops moving forward. Even if it doesn't, he still has a chance to be a big leaguer based on the merits of his speed-defense combo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies gave Brito their second-highest bonus of the 2014-15 international signing period, giving the infielder $650,000 to sign in July 2014. Pushed aggressively to full-season ball in 2017, Brito struggled there and had to repeat the level a year ago. After a brutal April, Brito looked much more like the hitter the Phillies hoped they were signing, earning a promotion up to Clearwater in August. Brito hit .171 in April last year and spent much of the rest of 2018 digging his way out. The good news is he managed to do so, showing a hit tool that can be above-average and an ability to spray line drives to all fields from the left side of the plate. When he struggled, he got lungy at the plate and he needs to continue to work on being more patient and having more quality at-bats. He's never going to be a big power guy, but he is starting to add a little strength, which should allow him to have some extra-base authority. While perhaps just an average runner, Brito is an excellent athlete and has good baserunning instincts. His athleticism, range and hands all point to him being a very good defender at second base. If he can find some consistency with his offensive game, he has the chance to be a big league regular at the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $650,000 out of Venezuela as part of an exciting international class for the Phillies that included Arquimedes Gamboa, Brito put himself on the prospect map with a strong United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2016, showing off plus hitting skills. He lost himself a bit with the jump to full-season ball in 2017, but the Phillies are still bullish on his upside. Brito came out of the gate in his full-season debut doing what he had done so well previously, barreling up the baseball consistently and using the whole field to his advantage. Then he lost his approach and tried to do too much in a big ballpark, worrying too much about trying to drive the ball out. That led to a lot of 390-foot outs instead of spraying line drives everywhere. Brito needs to add strength, something he did work on during the offseason, but really needs to focus on being a plus hitter, with whatever power comes as a result serving as a bonus. An average runner, Brito has the potential to be an outstanding defender at second base. As long as he can get back to the realistic gameplan that works for him , he can get back on the road to being a solid everyday middle infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies have some very talented young pure hitters in their system. Behind Mickey Moniak and maybe Cornelius Randolph, the team's last two first-round Draft picks, Brito might be the best bet to hit his way to the big leagues. In his first two summers since signing out of Venezuela for $650,000 in July 2014, Brito showed an advanced approach at the plate, drawing more walks than strikeouts over his first 400 career at-bats, as well as an outstanding feel for barreling up the ball. He wasn't able to keep that trend going with his first taste of full-season ball in 2017. While he is capable of driving the ball, it's still going to be a while before the teenager grows into his strength, which will make him a bigger threat with the bat. Initially a shortstop, Brito has moved over to second base and has the chance to be an excellent defender on the right side of the infield. The Phillies are willing to be patient with Brito, knowing he is just getting started. But if someone told the player development staff that Robinson Cano looked like this when he was a teenager, they'd likely believe you. He has the chance to develop into the best pure hitting prospect in the system if he continues progressing as he has thus far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Read finally began to capitalize on his offensive potential during the second half of the 2016 season, and he broke out in earnest the following year by hitting .265 with a career-high 17 homers in his first Double-A campaign. He finished the season in the Major Leagues, collecting three hits in 11 at-bats, and was named the club's Bob Boone Award winner after the season on the merits of his leadership and professionalism. All of his progress came to a halt in 2018, however, as Read received a season-opening 80-game suspension after a positive offseason test for the steroid Boldenone, and he struggled at the plate between Double-A and Triple-A upon returning. Read has a mature approach and natural hitting ability, with a short right-handed swing that produces contact to all fields as well as above-average raw power. However, the game power Read showed in 2017 wasn't there last year, prompting some to speculate that his power potential may have been inflated by the performance-enhancing drug. But scouts still generally view him as a decent hitter who makes a lot of contact and understands the strike zone. Behind the plate, Read's above-average arm strength and solid catch-and-throw skills have helped him throw out 36.7 percent of attempted basestealers in his career through 2018. His defense could be above-average with further improvements, which, when combined with Read's hitting ability, portend to a backup role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals have long believed in Read's offensive potential, viewing him as someone who would hit for both average and power at a premium position. The Dominican catcher began to do so late in the 2016 season and then broke out in earnest in his first Double-A campaign, hitting .265 with a career-high 17 home runs. He finished the season in the Major Leagues, collecting three hits in 11 at-bats. But after all his progress, Read will miss the first 80 games of the 2018 season after testing positive for a performance-enhancing drug in February. Read has a mature approach, natural hitting ability and power potential. He knows how to control the strike zone to his advantage and shows good discipline, while his quick right-handed swing produces loud contact to all fields. Becoming comfortable turning on the ball and more aggressive firing his barrel has allowed Read to better tap into his above-average raw power, as he connected on some of the longest home runs in his career in 2017. Read's development behind the plate in the last two seasons has Nats club officials believing he can catch in the big leagues. His above-average arm strength and solid catch-and-throw skills helped him throw out 30.6 percent of attempted basestealers in the Eastern League, where he also made noticeable gains and both a blocker and receiver. Read will be limited in 2018 in the wake of his suspension, but he has requisite offensive and defensive tools to profile as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since reaching full-season ball for the first time in 2015, Read has had a tendency to begin each year slowly before turning the corner in the second half and finishing strong. That certainly was the case last season at Class A Advanced Potomac, as the Dominican native broke out to hit .272/.335/.465 after the All-Star break following a non-descript showing during the first half. Fearing he might be selected in the Rule 5 Draft, the Nationals added Read to their 40-man roster in November, and he rewarded them by earning All-Star honors in his first Double-A campaign Read stands out most for his mature approach and natural hitting ability. He knows how to control the strike zone to his advantage and shows good discipline, while his quick right-handed swing produces loud contact to all fields. He's still learning to tap into his above-average raw power, which he shows to all fields, and scouts believe he'll start to clear more fences as he moves up the ladder. Read was one of the Nationals' most improved prospects in 2016, and much of that had to do with the strides he made as a blocker and receiver. He has above-average arm strength and solid catch-and-throw skills, and the combination makes him effective at controlling the running game. While Read's overall defense requires further refinement, scouts are increasingly confident that he'll be able to remain behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a stellar U.S. collegiate national team outfield with Louisville's Corey Ray and Florida's Buddy Reed last summer, Banks led Team USA in hitting (.386) and on-base percentage (.491), leading some to project him as a mid-first-round pick. He wasn't the same after having a cyst removed from his lower back last fall, however, and didn't appear physically comfortable at the plate until late in his junior year at Texas A&M. Banks finished strong, garnering MVP honors in the Southeastern Conference tournament, and the Nationals gave him slightly above slot value as a fifth-round pick. The left-handed-hitting Banks employs a sleek swing and delivers line drives from gap to gap. He has above-average raw pop and drove the ball more often in 2015, but didn't look as fluid or powerful at the plate last year and did not homer during his 60-game pro debut. While Banks showed solid speed and arm strength with Team USA, those tools played closer to fringe-average in 2016. Banks profiles best in right field, where he's an average defender with solid-average arm strength, although he also saw time in center and right field after signing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds signed Rodriguez, a native of Cuba, with a $7 million bonus in 2016, they knew they had a player who was glove-first and didn't have much of a hitting resume. That has remained the case after two-plus years of Minor League baseball. It also puts the organization in a bit of a quandary. Can Alf-Rod's glove alone carry him to the big leagues? Offensively, Rodriguez hasn't shown much sign of progressing. That could partially be because of a hamate bone issue in 2018 that required two trips to the disabled list. But he also played in the instructional league and Arizona Fall League after the season and still didn't hit well. Plate discipline remains a stumbling block as he often swings and misses pitches out of the strike zones. A light hitter like Rodriguez needs to work counts and draw walks to get on base. The contrast couldn't be wider on the defensive side. His hands could be a 70 on the 20-to-80 scouting scale and he has good range and a plus arm to go with them, making it possible to make all the routine plays and many spectacular ones as well. Although his glove could play in the big leagues, the reality is that Rodriguez is a projectable utility player at best if he doesn't figure out how to hit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It looked like the Reds were going to sign Rodriguez, as they were attached to the Cuban shortstop almost from the minute he became eligible to be signed. It took a little longer than expected, but they finally got their man at the start of the 2016 signing period for a bonus of $7 million. During his full-season debut in the Florida State League, Rodriguez both lived up to his defensive reputation and down to concerns about his potential with the bat. He wasn't able to put those questions to rest as a hamate issue sent him to the disabled list on two different occasions in 2018. Rodriguez hadn't been overwhelmed in a pitching-friendly environment and he did hit .270 in the first half before running out of gas in 2017. More than anything, Rodriguez needs to refine his approach, learning the strike zone better and working counts more. He does have some raw power to tap into and he needs to try to do more damage rather than just playing for contact. On the other side of the ball, the Reds feel Rodriguez is one of the best defensive shortstops in the Minors. He has tremendous instincts and a strong arm, making all of the routine plays and then frequently making a play you don't expect he can. Those skills alone should get him to the big leagues, but he's going to have to hit a bit more to be an all-around regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds coveted Rodriguez, a talented Cuban shortstop, from the moment he was declared a free agent last January. It took until the start of the following signing period to sign him, and the Reds gave him $7 million to join the organization. He dipped his toes in the professional waters, shaking off the rust from a long layoff, in the Dominican Summer League, then spent his first full season in the Florida State League. There is no question that Rodriguez is a glove-first shortstop. His plus speed helps him have outstanding range, and he has a strong and accurate arm from anywhere on the field, leaving no doubt he will play the premium position for a long time to come. While there is consensus about his defensive abilities, the jury is split about his offensive potential. His speed should be an asset on the bases, and obviously the Reds think he is going to hit, while some evaluators outside the organization aren't so sure. Rodriguez has added strength and he worked with Barry Larkin during instructs last fall.
