His low-80s curve can be an absolute hammer with power and depth. There are no red flags with Staumont's delivery, yet he can't keep it together enough to throw strikes. The Royals moved him to the bullpen this year, though that hasn't helped him find the strikes zone with any more regularity. He also throws a changeup with splitter action, but he didn't use it enough as a starter and doesn't need it as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Staumont had the hardest fastball in the 2015 Draft, regularly reaching triple digits with little effort, which made him the highest pick ever (second round) from Azusa Pacific (Calif.). He has overpowered hitters in his two pro seasons, leading Rookie-level Pioneer League relievers in strikeout rate (14.6 per nine innings) during his pro debut, then topped the entire Minors in strikeout rate (12.2) and ranked second in whiffs (167) as a starter in his first full pro season. He also paced the Minors with 104 walks in 2016, and tied for the Arizona Fall League lead with 16 in 24 innings. Staumont's fastball is difficult to hit and difficult to control. He can maintain a 93-97 mph four-seam fastball and reach 99 as a starter, has been clocked as high as 102 as a reliever and has nice riding life. He also can run a two-seamer into the upper 90s with heavy sink but has even more trouble keeping that version in the strike zone. His low-80s curveball has power and depth, giving Staumont a second pitch that misses bats and can be difficult to harness, and he also mixes in a changeup with splitter action. There's nothing glaring with his delivery, though he struggles to keep it in sync. He has the highest ceiling among Royals pitching prospects, but he'll have to attain average command and improve his mound presence to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2016 Draft approached, scouts weren't sure what to make of Virginia high school senior Rizzo, a third baseman who looked like he could hit but who was hard to profile because of his 5-foot-9 frame and lack of a sure defensive home. Now, two-plus years after the Mariners went above pick value in the second round of that Draft to sign Rizzo for $1.75 million, he's still tough to figure out. Rizzo had a solid first full season, holding his own in the Midwest League as a teenager, earning a late bump up to the California League, where he caught fire and won the championship series MVP. It seemed to carry over to the first half of the 2018 season back with Modesto, but then he fell into bad habits and badly regressed. He often doesn't have a lot of balance or foundation in his swing, causing him to drift. He managed to cut his strikeout rate down, but he wasn't impacting the ball like he's capable of. The Mariners have worked with Rizzo on the timing of his swing along with where his lower half and hands are. Defensively, he's still a third baseman and will stay there, though he played a handful of games at second and first base last year. The Mariners would like Rizzo to get back to being the hitter he was at the Draft, one who made consistent hard contact with the ability to drive the ball. This is a big year for Rizzo, but he's still plenty young enough to head back in the right direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite batting .606 as a junior and then .392 as a senior at Oakton (Va.) High, Rizzo proved a divisive 2016 Draft prospect due to his lack of size as well as concerns surrounding his future position. The Mariners, however, were thrilled to find him still on the board in the second round, as they selected Rizzo with the No. 50 overall pick and then signed him for more than slot value at $1,750,000. Assigned to Class A Clinton for his first full season, Rizzo held his own in the Midwest League at age 19 before advancing to Class A Advanced Modesto late in the season. His bat came alive at the more advanced level, as Rizzo erupted to hit .421 in the postseason to garner honors as the California League Championship Series MVP. Rizzo shows feel to hit from the left side, with good bat speed and hand-eye coordination as well as a discernable eye. Club officials believe he'll develop into an above-average hitter with at least average power, though a penchant for swinging and missing has resulted in little pop early in his career. Whereas some scouts believe Rizzo can become an adequate third baseman, others feel he's destined for first base or left field, where his below-average speed and average arm strength would be less of an issue. Rizzo is thickly built and doesn't require much physical projection, so he will need to focus on conditioning and adding good strength to his 5-foot-9 frame in future seasons. Beyond Rizzo's physical tools, the Mariners rave about the makeup and baseball IQ, noting that it has already helped him to overcome adversity as a professional. He has many gains to make on both sides of the ball and is likely to move down the defensive spectrum, but the potential is there for him to develop into an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 It was with good reason that scouts viewed Rizzo as one of better prep hitters in the 2016 Draft. As a junior at Oakton (Va.) High, Rizzo batted a robust .606, and he followed that performance by posting a .392 mark last spring. While his lack of size as well as concerns about his future position may have turned off some teams, the Mariners were thrilled to find him still on the board in the second round and took him with the No. 50 overall pick. After signing for an above-slot bonus of $1,750,000, Rizzo showcased his promising bat with a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League and received an Opening Day assignment to Class A Clinton to begin 2017. Rizzo shows feel to hit from the left side, with good bat speed and hand-eye coordination as well as a discernable eye. Club officials believe he'll develop into an above-average hitter with at least average power, though a penchant for swinging and missing has been an issue early in his career. Whereas some scouts believe Rizzo can become an adequate third baseman, others feel he's destined for first base or left field, where his below-average speed and average arm strength would be less of an issue. Listed at 5-foot-9, Rizzo doesn't require much physical projection. Beyond Rizzo's physical tools, the Mariners rave about the makeup and baseball IQ, which helped him make a smooth transition into the professional ranks. He has many gains to make on both sides of the ball and is likely to move down the defensive spectrum, but the potential is there for him to develop into an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zavala missed a year with Tommy John surgery and didn't become a full-time catcher until his 2015 redshirt junior season at San Diego State. He hit 14 homers and threw out 46 percent of basestealers that spring, propelling him into the 12th round and to the White Sox. He led the system with 21 homers in 2017 and beat more highly touted catching prospect Zack Collins to Triple-A last year. His best tool is his plus raw power, and Zavala did a better job of tapping into it once he increased his launch angle in his right-handed swing in 2017. He did a better job of using the entire field last year, though most of his home runs still come to his pull side. He's definitely a power-over-hit guy who could stand to tighten up his plate discipline. Zavala's leadership and game-calling ability stand out more than his physical tools behind the plate. He has an average arm and similar receiving skills, though he struggles at times to handle premium velocity. He profiles more as a slugging backup than a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zavala didn't show he could handle starting catching duties until his fourth year at San Diego State, spending his freshman season as a part-time DH, missing all of 2013 following Tommy John surgery and returning as a left fielder. After hitting 14 homers and throwing out 46 percent of basestealers as a redshirt junior in 2015, he signed for $100,000 as a 12th-rounder. He led White Sox farmhands with 21 homers between two Class A stops in 2017 and continued to swing a hot bat in the Arizona Fall League. Quite similar offensively and defensively to Evan Skoug, Chicago's 2017 seventh-rounder, Zavala has a higher floor but a lower ceiling. He tripled his home run output from his first full pro season to his second after changing his load to increase his launch angle. Most of his right-handed power comes to his pull side, and he'll have to do a better job of using the whole field and managing the strike zone to hit for average at higher levels. Zavala projects more as an offensive-minded backup than a regular. He shows strong leadership skills, but his receiving and blocking are still works in progress. He has average arm strength that plays down a tick because he doesn't have the quickest release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A closer at South Carolina and for the U.S. collegiate national team, Johnson missed six weeks with a sore arm during his Draft year in 2017 but still went in the fifth round. Though a lat strain cost him the first half of 2019, he still advanced to Double-A while continuing to post dominant numbers. In his first three pro seasons, he compiled a 2.27 ERA with 169 strikeouts in 115 innings while holding opponents to a .197 average. Johnson depends heavily on his four-seam fastball, which operates at 92-96 mph and peaks at 98. While it's relatively straight, he's able to get it by hitters at the letters or create plane to work the bottom of the zone. He doesn't have a reliable second pitch, because his low-80s slider gets slurvy too often and his changeup lacks life. Scouts don't care for Johnson's delivery, which features some stab and wrist wrap in the back. It does provide some funkiness and deception without hampering his control, but it costs him feel for his secondary offerings and doesn't bode well for his long-term health. If his fastball continues to dodge bats at upper levels, he could make his big league debut in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After emerging as the closer for South Carolina and the U.S. collegiate national team as a sophomore, Johnson missed six weeks with a sore arm during his Draft year in 2017. He continued to excel when healthy, prompting the White Sox to take him in the fifth round, and he hasn't any problems since. He went 9-0 and converted 14 of his 15 save opportunities in his first full pro season, posting a 1.40 ERA with 89 strikeouts in 58 innings between two Class A stops. Johnson's success almost exclusively results from his fastball, which parks at 92-96 mph and tops out at 98. His heater doesn't feature a lot of life, but he can blow it by hitters at the letters or use his size to throw it down in the zone with plane. His low-80s slider has some bite at times but gets slurvy too often, and his changeup doesn't feature much action or deception. Scouts don't like the wrist wrap in the back of Johnson's delivery, which affects his feel for his secondary pitches and his command, if not his ability to throw strikes. He'll need to improve his slider and changeup because he can't handle more advanced hitters with just his fastball. Expected to move quickly in 2019, he instead missed the first 10 weeks of the season with a lat strain.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson pitched just 7 2/3 innings as a South Carolina freshman in 2015 before emerging as the closer for the Gamecocks and the U.S. collegiate national team as a sophomore. Though he missed six weeks with a sore arm last spring, he continued to excel in the late innings and earned a slightly over-slot $390,000 bonus as a White Sox fifth-rounder. He pitched well in his pro debut and converted both of his save opportunities in low Class A before tiring in the final two weeks. Johnson works off a fastball that ranges from 92-97 mph and tops out at 100, compensating for modest life by usually locating it well down in the strike zone. He backs up his heater with a low-80s slider that features nice bite at its best but also gets slurvy at times. He also has a fringy changeup that he may dust off more often after left-handers batted .341 against him in his first taste of pro ball. Some scouts who saw Johnson as an amateur thought he had the three-pitch mix and athleticism to make it as a starter, but Chicago plans to fast-track him as a reliever. How quickly he moves will depend on his control and command, which were less reliable in his debut than they were in college. He has closer upside but will need more consistency to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Warren spent his first two college seasons at Cincinnati, pitching somewhat sparingly in relief. He transferred to Division II Ashland University and started as a junior. The Mariners took a flier on him in the 23rd round of the 2015 Draft and let him spend most of his first full season as a starter. A move to the bullpen paid off, and he turned in a big California League campaign and was the talk of the Arizona Fall League following the 2017 season. His progress was stalled when a shoulder injury kept him out for most of 2018. The Mariners left him unprotected, but he wasn't taken in December's Rule 5 Draft. After spending all winter in Arizona, Warren appears healthy and ready to go, with the Mariners hopeful he can get back to the dominant reliever he was in the AFL. He was closing out games, coming in hitting 98-99 mph with his fastball and an absolutely filthy breaking ball. Analytics say his curve is the better pitch, though he also has a good slider with cutting action. Other than health, Warren's biggest obstacle is his command. He doesn't need pinpoint control, and he has thrown enough strikes at times in the past. Putting the shoulder issue behind him will be step one towards proving he can pitch at or near the end of games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 23rd-round pick in 2015 out of Division II Ashland, Warren began his career as a starter, earning mid-season All-Star honors with Class A Clinton before advancing to the Class A Advanced California League in his first full season. He returned to the Cal League in 2017, this time as full-time reliever, and promptly turned in a breakout campaign as part of a loaded Modesto bullpen and furthered that success in the Arizona Fall League. A candidate to move quickly in 2018, Warren instead has spent much of the season on the disabled list with a sore right shoulder. Warren's stuff has ticked up out of the bullpen, where he'll operate with a 94-98 mph fastball that previously sat in the low-90s as a starter. The pitch has late life, which enables him to pitch effectively up in the zone, and he complements it with a hard, late-breaking slider that serves as a swing-and-miss out pitch, and a less-consistent curveball. Warren's changeup was a pitch he had focused on developing as a starter, though that has become a bit of a moot point after his move to the bullpen. Warren's struggles in consistently repeating his high-effort delivery result in below-average control and too many free passes, some of which he's able to offset with his ability to induce whiffs. Both his stuff and feel require further refinement in the high Minors, but the overall profile is that of a seventh- or eighth-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not every successful international signing has to be a big-ticket expenditure. If the early returns are any indication, Diaz, who signed for $100,000 in September 2015 out of Venezuela, will be one of those bargain finds. He flashed big upside in 2017 over a full season in the Pioneer League, hitting .312/.357/.510 with seven homers in 57 games. His full-season debut didn't go as well, though, as Diaz struggled early before a groin injury in June wiped out his remaining season. He rebounded in 2019, showing an intriguing blend of power and speed at Class A Kane County before moving up to the California League in early July. Gains in strength led to an uptick in power, and the D-backs think Diaz has a lot more growing to do. With increased power comes increased responsibility to understand the strike zone. Diaz's strikeout and walk rates moved in the wrong direction in each of the past two years -- especially at Class A Kane County before his injury -- because he's developed an overly aggressive, swing-early approach that makes him susceptible to spin and sequence. With better selectivity and a more controllable approach, Diaz quickly could rediscover the hitting ability and power potential he showed in 2017. Diaz runs very well and can steal a base as well as cover ground in center field, where the D-backs think he could stay for a while. Even if he outgrows the position, he could have the offensive profile to be a regular as a tooled-up corner outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not every successful international signing has to be a big-ticket expenditure. If the early returns are any indication, Diaz, who signed for $100,000 in September 2015 out of Venezuela, will be one of those bargain finds. He hit his way out of the Dominican Summer League to make his United States debut in his first summer, then took another big step forward in the Rookie-level Pioneer League in 2017. Gains in strength led to an uptick in power, and the D-backs think Diaz has a lot more growing to do. With increased power comes increased responsibility to understand the strike zone. Diaz's strikeout rate went up in 2017 and he didn't draw as many walks as he was too aggressive, attacking early in the count at times. As he progresses, the right-handed hitter will have to learn to lay off the steady diet of breaking stuff he's sure to get from right-handed pitching. Better selectivity should lead to even more in-game power. Diaz runs very well and can steal a base as well as cover ground in center field, where the D-backs think he could stay for a while. Even if he outgrows the position and has to move to a corner, he could have the offensive profile to be a regular as a five-tool right fielder. The D-backs don't have to worry about that decision yet, instead focusing on getting Diaz at-bats and watching the return on the investment grow.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies handed out nine bonuses of at least six figures in the 2015-16 international signing period, none greater than the $2 million given to Montano to sign out of Venezuela. After two-plus summers playing in the Dominican Summer League, the outfielder made a solid United States debut in the rookie-level Pioneer League in 2018. Montano has always had tools and he's starting to grow into them. One of the biggest steps forward has been his ability to add man strength, with emotional maturity to match. He's an advanced hitter with an excellent left-handed swing, one who is getting more patient and using all fields better each year. He stuck to his gameplan well in 2018, handling offspeed stuff more consistently well and using the middle of the field better. As he continues to get stronger, the Rockies think he could have average power. He played a solid center field in Grand Junction a year ago and has a chance to stay there, though he's also seen time in right, with an arm that now plays average. While he's just getting started stateside, the Rockies feel Montano might be turning a corner physically and mentally. There's an up arrow next to his name, with a chance he could make a big step forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing well for the Venezuelan team at the World Youth Championships as a 15-year-old in 2014, Montano signed the next year for $2 million. Because the Rockies lack a complex-based affiliate, they had him spend the first two years of his pro career in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He made some nice adjustments during his second tour and will come to the United States in 2018. Montano employed an aggressive approach in his pro debut but displayed a more controlled left-handed swing in his second tour of the DSL. He's an advanced hitter for a teenager with the ability to recognize pitches and manage the strike zone. He uses the entire field and projects to hit for average with some gap power. Montano spent most of his debut in center field before seeing most of his action in right field last year. He's a solid runner with decent instincts but could slow down a step as he gets stronger. Because he has fringy arm strength, he ultimately could wind up in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 At 6-foot-5 and 204 pounds, Garcia was one of the most physically imposing players on the 2017 international market when he signed for $500,000 as a 16-year-old Dominican that July. His body and reputation grew in his first year in pro ball, as he added 25 pounds and topped the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League with 10 homers last summer. A switch-hitter, Garcia is more effective left-handed but his gargantuan raw power is obvious from either side of the plate. He has an extremely aggressive approach and a naturally long swing, which resulted in a 41 percent strikeout rate during his pro debut. While it's easy to dream on his bat speed and strength, he's going to have to make much more contact to deliver on his power potential. Though Garcia moves surprisingly well for his size, he already has lost a step since signing and could slow further if he continues to get bigger. He could become an average defender on either outfield corner if he works diligently on his defense and maintains his current athleticism. His arm earns average to solid grades from evaluators.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltman didn't become a full-time pitcher until his senior season in high school but took over as Texas Christian's closer as a freshman, eventually setting school records for saves in a season (17) and career (32). When the Red Sox made him a third-round pick in 2018 following a dominant spring, the consensus was that he'd be the first player from his Draft to reach the big leagues. He breezed through three levels in his pro debut but got knocked around in Double-A last year. When Feltman blew away hitters in college, he operated with a 95-99 mph fastball with running action and a wipeout slider in the mid-90s. In his first full pro season, his heater usually ranged from 93-97 and his slider featured less velocity and bite. When he lost feel for his slider early in the year, he turned to a slower, slurvy curveball, and he also can mix in a decent changeup. Feltman's control and command regressed significantly in the first half of 2019, and then he threw more strikes but got hit harder in the second half. He's small and falls into ruts where he struggles to repeat an effortful delivery that does provide some deception. He's still on the fast track to Boston but the likelihood that he'll become a closer has decreased.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltman didn't become a full-time pitcher until his senior season as a Texas high schooler, attracting little attention from scouts but earning a scholarship from Texas Christian. He became the Horned Frogs' closer as a freshman, set a program record with 17 saves as a sophomore and posted a 0.74 ERA and tied another school mark with his 32nd career save last spring. Signed for $559,600 as a third-round pick, he reached Class A Advanced in his pro debut but has stalled in Double-A during his first full season. Feltman has a devastating pair of pitches that could make him a closer in the Majors, though neither has been as sharp as usual in 2019. His fastball combines 95-99 mph velocity with running action and deception at its best, though it has sat more at 94-96 this year. The wipeout mid-80s slider he had in 2018 hasn't been as hard or featured as much bite in Double-A. In addition to blowing hitters away, Feltman can also throw them off balance with a decent changeup. Though he has three pitches, he's definitely a reliever because he's relatively small and there's effort in his delivery. After doing a nice job of locating his pitches where he wanted a year ago, he has battled his control and command this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Oregon State, Grenier won the Brooks Wallace Award as collegiate baseball’s best shortstop in 2018, when he helped the Beavers toward a College World Series crown. The Orioles snagged the Las Vegas product with the No. 37 overall pick that June, signed him for $1.8 million and hoped Grenier would adjust to pro pitching enough to keep up with his standout defensive skills. Two seasons in, Grenier’s strong glove, good range, solid arm and strong instincts still make him a plus defender at short. But the bat has been slow to come around, despite the pull side power and solid walk rate he showed in his second run at Class A Delmarva last season. Grenier coupled that, though, with a nearly 30 percent strikeout rate with the Shorebirds, then struck out 34 percent of the time following a promotion to Class A Advanced Frederick. There was some concern Grenier took those struggles with him into the field somewhat, as he uncharacteristically scuffled a bit defensively in 2019 as well. He is also a plus runner who draws praise for the energy he brings to the field. Grenier will always be a glove-first player, but if he can make more contact, he has a chance to fulfill his ceiling as an everyday shortstop in the Majors. If not, he still profiles as a valuable utility-type, someone whose athleticism and solid internal clock allows him to pick it at various points on the diamond. He could benefit from a big year at the plate about as much as any prospect in the Orioles’ system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of prep baseball powerhouse Bishop Gorman High School in Las Vegas, Grenier honored his commitment to Oregon State rather than sign with the Cardinals as their 21st-round pick in the 2015 Draft. He was a three-year starter for the Beavers and helped lead the program to a College World Series title in 2018, when he won the Brooks Wallace Award as college baseball's top shortstop. The Orioles made Grenier the No. 37 overall pick that June, signed him for $1.8 million and then sent him straight to Class A Delmarva for his professional debut. Grenier is a gifted defender at shortstop, with the range, actions and arm strength, as well as the soft hands and outstanding internal clock, needed to stay at the position long-term. There are questions about Grenier's bat, though, and he didn't assuage any concerns by hitting .216 with an elevated strikeout rate in his pro debut. That said, he does have bat speed and a little pop to his pull side, with solid understanding of the strike zone. The Orioles believe Grenier's emphasis on making contact early in the count instilled an element of panic in his swing, and they worked with him in during hitter mini camps in the fall on developing a better foundation to hit. At worst, Grenier has a career as a defensive-minded utilityman ahead of him, with the upside of being a glove-first regular at shortstop. The Orioles believe there's enough bat there for him to grow into the latter role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It can take years to evaluate who won a trade and sometimes it's the player who is the farthest away from the big leagues who creates the biggest tip in the scales. The Royals hope that's the case with Morel, one of the three prospects they got from the Nationals in the Kelvin Herrera trade. Signed in July 2017 for $100,000, the teenager had pitched just once in the Dominican Summer League before he was traded, then came to the United States and fared well in the rookie-level Arizona League while making his Royals organization debut. Strong and stocky, Morel stands out for his quick arm and what could eventually be consistent premium velocity. He dominated at times in the AZL with a fastball that was up to 94-96 mph at times and a slider, thrown 83-84 mph, that flashes plus at times. He shows a very advanced feel for his changeup, especially given his age. Morel's delivery can be a bit too upright and he's worked with the Royals to change that for long-term health. With a little recoil at times, he doesn't always allow himself to finish the way he should, another area of focus. Morel doesn't have much track record as of yet, but could start being recognized as the prize of this trade this season as he truly begins his pro career in earnest, spending nearly all of the 2019 season at age 18. It should shock no one if he makes a large leap up this list sooner rather than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feigl was set to start his college career at Mississippi in 2015, but needed Tommy John surgery, so he ended up redshirting. He pitched mostly in relief over the next two years, then returned for his redshirt junior season rather than sign with the Angels in the 35th round of the 2017 Draft. A move into the rotation raised his profile and he landed in the fifth round to the A’s in 2018, signing for a below slot $300,000 bonus. He spent his first full season in the Class A Advanced California League and made the All-Star team before fading in the second half. He followed that up with a very strong turn as a reliever in the Arizona Fall League. The 6-foot-4 Feigl has a decent three-pitch mix all coming from a funky and deceptive delivery. While he touched 95 mph at Ole Miss, he was more in the 90-92 mph range during his year in Stockton. He throws it with a very high spin rate and while he doesn’t strike out a ton of guys, he keeps the pitch down with sink, leading to a 55-percent groundball rate in 2019. His secondary stuff is average at best, with his slider ahead of his changeup. Feigl is big, strong and durable and showed an ability to consistently fill up the strike zone. That gives him a chance to advance as a back-end starter, but his high-spin stuff played up and missed more bats in shorter stints as a reliever in the AFL.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feigl had Tommy John surgery as a freshman at Mississippi, returning as a redshirt freshman in 2016 and pitching out of the bullpen. He pitched largely in relief in 2017, mixing in a few starts, and was drafted in the 35th round by the Angels. But Feigl opted to return to Ole Miss to pitch in the rotation for his junior season. He threw well enough to land in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft and while he didn't pitch much in his first summer, he did reach full-season ball, though he was too fatigued to throw at instructs. Big and strong, Feigl has an interesting three-pitch mix to work with, starting with a fastball that touched the mid-90s in his final college season, but sat more at 91-92 over the summer. It has a high spin rate and he can miss bats with it, though he also can keep it down in the zone with sink to elicit ground-ball outs. Both his slider and his changeup flash above-average at times, with his slider the more consistent of the two secondary offerings. Feigl has always been a strike-thrower, but didn't always command the ball well within the zone, leading to a higher hit rate in college than you'd expect given his stuff. That wasn't the case in his small sample size in pro ball, so the A's are intrigued to find out if he can continue that trend over 140-150 innings in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walsh had an up-and-down career as a two-way player at Georgia, serving at times as a lefty swingman and showing glimpses of offensive ability as a hitter. Taken with no expectations as a 39th-round senior sign, Walsh focused on his bat for much of his pro career. Playing mostly first base and a little outfield, he'd always hit well, then broke out across three levels and led the organization in RBIs and finished tied for the lead in home runs. At the same time, he started re-introducing pitching to his resume, showing some aptitude as a lefty reliever and making it to the big leagues in May as a two-way player. Walsh's raw power from the left side has always been intriguing and he started tapping into it consistently in 2018. There were plenty of strikeouts, but also a much higher walk rate, and that improved approach helped him get more pitches to drive. Defensively, he probably is a first baseman only, but it's the bat that gives him a chance to hit in the big leagues. It's hard to evaluate what kind of pitcher Walsh is. Without any real instruction or program, he was touching 93 mph with his fastball and could spin an occasional plus breaking ball. After Walsh's offseason with a dedicated throwing program, the Angels are anxious to see if he can be a two-way player at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While many international amateur free agent pitchers are signed because of big arms and the hope of premium velocity, Perez stood out for his advanced feel for pitching at his age, not to mention his left-handedness, and the Mariners gave him $300,000 to sign at the start of the 2017-18 signing period. He was as advertised during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2018. Just 18 for the 2019 season, Perez had a really good delivery and pitchability as he entered pro ball, but he lacked physicality. He's started to add strength, and his stuff is starting to tick upwards. His fastball usually sits in the 88-91 mph range, but he reaches back for 92-93 mph with ease. He throws a little across his body and the ball jumps out of his hand, with the ride on his fastball, thanks to high spin rates up in the zone, allowing the pitch to play above-average. He throws two distinct breaking balls, both are legitimate weapons, and he has some feel for his changeup as well. It's a small sample size, but Perez did fill up the strike zone during his debut in the DSL. Now he's coming to the United States to see how his feel for pitching will allow him to climb the Mariners' ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Riley transferred from Oklahoma State to John A. Logan Community College in Illinois after his freshman year and became one of the best junior college prospects in the 2018 Draft class. The Braves liked his arm strength and took him in the fifth round that June, going above slot to sign him for $450,000. After pitching sparingly in his summer debut, Riley struggled in his move to full-season ball in 2019. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is big, strong and has the kind of pure stuff that still gives him a chance to succeed. But given how much arm strength he has, it was surprising how he struggled to miss bats (6.3 K/9) during his first full season. He has a fastball that will touch 96-97 mph regularly and the ball comes out of his hand well, but he lacked a put-away pitch. His slider has the chance to be that swing-and-miss offering, and he worked on his breaking stuff during his time at instructs. His changeup remains behind his other two pitches. Riley also struggled to find the strike zone consistently, walking a whopping 7.1 per nine innings in 2019. He’s hitting the reset button in 2020 and the Braves were pleased that he stayed in Florida all offseason to work with a greater sense of urgency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Riley didn't see much mound time as a freshman at Oklahoma State, so he transferred to John A. Logan Community College back in his home state of Illinois. After a strong season in the rotation, Riley was considered to be one of the best JUCO players in the 2018 Draft class, landing in the fifth round and signing for an over-slot bonus of $450,000. Still more of a thrower than pitcher, Riley has two plus power pitches at his disposal. He'll touch 97 mph with his fastball, which has cutting action to it, and his mid-80s slider is a wipeout pitch that misses bats when he's at his best. His changeup is well behind the other two pitches, and he'll have to work on it for him to have a chance to start. With a maximum-effort delivery and super-quick arm, Riley's command will never be his forte, with future average control perhaps a dream at best. The Braves might let Riley start for now so he can get innings and work on his command and delivery. He likely profiles better as a one-inning short reliever that goes right after hitters with two plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at the University of Washington, Graffanino was a glove-first shortstop who didn't hit much in his first two years with the Huskies. The son of longtime big leaguer Tony Graffanino, AJ swung the bat better as a junior, but missed a chunk of the 2018 season with a hamstring injury. The Braves took him in the eighth round last June and went above pick value to sign him for $300,000. He responded with a strong pro debut, spent mostly in the full-season South Atlantic League, but could build off of that as he got hurt on opening day of 2019 and missed the rest of the season. When healthy, Graffanino's calling card is still his defense, and he has the same quick hands as his father, who used to play the infield in the big leagues for parts of 13 seasons. At times, Graffanino makes errors because he tries to speed up too much, something that will change once he trusts that his hands are plenty quick enough for the pro game. He has the range, footwork and arm to play shortstop long-term. He has the chance to be an average hitter with some sneaky pop and the ability to make consistent contact. He has an unorthodox setup at the plate, and he'll likely have to fix an issue with the load on his swing, but it's worked for him so far. After Graffanino got worn down by the end of the summer, he worked hard to add some strength to his frame to prepare him for the rigors of a full season before the injury bug hit. The Braves are eager to see how his baseball acumen and bloodlines help him along the way once he regains health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bourque pitched to mixed results as a swingman during his first two seasons at Michigan and didn't fare much better as a junior in 2014 after a move to the bullpen. His raw stuff continued to improve throughout his college career, though, and the Nationals took notice, eventually selecting Bourque in the 14th round that June. He struggled as a starter early in his pro career surrounding Tommy John surgery in 2015, but moved to the bullpen in 2018 and promptly took off in the new role, turning in a strong first half with Class A Advanced Potomac, then posting a 0.92 ERA over 15 appearances after a July promotion to Double-A. After the season, the Nationals added Bourque to their 40-man roster. A big and physical right-hander, Bourque will show two plus pitches in any given outing. He reaches 97-98 mph with his heater and throws it with late life that makes it difficult to lift for hitters on both sides of the plate. His breaking ball is equally dynamic, thrown in the upper 80s with sharp, downer action that helps him miss bats with ease. Pitching at two levels in 2018, Bourque averaged 12.9 strikeouts-per-nine, with a 16 percent swinging strike rate. Bourque's ability to induce whiffs with both pitches makes his below-average control (4.4 walks-per-nine in '18) a lesser issue, though there is some concern over whether hitters will continue to chase his stuff outside of the zone at higher levels. Given the Nationals' history of aggressively pushing their best relief prospects, Bourque could soon find himself in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals' 10th-round pick in the 2015 Draft, Guilbeau was a senior signed out of Alabama who received a $25,000 bonus. He operated mostly as a swingman early in his pro career and had a strong first full season, albeit as a 23-year-old in the Class A South Atlantic League. A move up to Class A Advanced Potomac the next year was met with struggles, and the Nationals shifted him to the bullpen full-time when he repeated the level in 2018. He took quickly to the new role, pitching increasingly well as the season progressed before an eye-opening performance in the Arizona Fall League. He pitched his way from Double- to Triple-A in 2019 when he was sent to the Mariners for Roenis Elias. After working in the low 90s during the regular season, Guilbeau's fastball was consistently 95-96 mph with improved late life in the Fall League. He has an above-average slider, thrown in the mid-80s with good depth, and also can mix in a fringy changeup. He has below-average control of all three pitches, though it stands to improve as he becomes more comfortable with his improved stuff out of the bullpen. Guilbeau dominated same-sided hitters in the Carolina League with his fastball-breaking ball combo, holding them to a .184 average without allowing an extra-base hit in 54 plate appearances. Such success highlights Guilbeau's potential as a left-handed specialist, though he'll first have to improve his control as he navigates the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic back in November 2014, it's taken some time for Bautista to translate his raw ability into production on the field. He spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League after signing and then made his United States debut in the rookie-level Arizona League in 2017. He might have started to figure some things out with a move to the Pioneer League in 2018, when he finished ninth in the rookie-level circuit in slugging percentage and OPS. A premium athlete, Bautista has long shown a feel to hit, posting batting averages over .300 for three summers running. He makes consistent contact, doesn't strike out much and even will draw some walks. The biggest difference in 2018 is that he started adding strength which helped him impact the ball more and tap into his raw power with some legitimate extra-base ability. A plus runner, Bautista's speed should allow him to steal bases and play center field for a long time. Reds player development people say Bautista reminds them a bit of Jose Siri at the same age, but with a bit more consistency to his game. If that continues as he approaches full-season leagues, he could make a huge jump up this list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has been a decent amount of pitching from Colombia to impact the big leagues in recent years, with Julio Teheran and Jose Quintana the biggest examples. While he is still very far away, the Pirates did give Florez $150,000 in July 2016 in the hopes he could eventually join his fellow countrymen at the highest level. The right-hander made his United States debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2018, and though he was slowed by an elbow tweak, he's gotten a clean bill of health this offseason. The Pirates love Florez's size and power stuff. He's already gained some velocity in his time in the organization, cranking his fastball up to 96 mph, and there's clearly more in the tank as he adds strength to his 6-foot-5 frame. He can also really spin his breaking ball, with a power curve that could eventually be better than average. His changeup remains a work in progress. There is also much work to be done in terms of his command if he wants to have any chance to start, though his strike-throwing improved from his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2017 and his move to the U.S. The Pirates will let him start for the time being, but seeing him approach triple digits coming out of the bullpen could be fun to watch eventually.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After struggling to throw strikes out of the bullpen as a Wake Forest freshman, Roberts started learning how to harness his stuff and became an all-conference closer in 2017, when he recorded eight saves while striking out 13.5 per nine. He moved into the rotation as a junior and blossomed, proving highly effective in the new role as he slashed his walk rate while leading the Atlantic Coast Conference in strikeouts (130). The Cardinals took Roberts with the No. 43 overall pick that June, signed him for full slot value and pushed him up to Class A Advanced Palm Beach's bullpen ahead of the Florida State League playoffs. After the season, Roberts was handed a 50-game suspension in December after a second positive test for a drug of abuse. When he returned from the ban in June, Roberts struggled to the tune of a 6.44 ERA and nearly issued as many walks (35) as strikeouts (36) over 65 2/3 frames at Palm Beach. Roberts' slider is a true plus pitch, one that many scouts regarded as the best college breaking ball in his Draft class. It's a mid-80s breaker that he throws with a nearly elite spin rate and devastating late break that elicits ugly swings from right-handed hitters. His fastball sits in the 90-95 mph range as a starter but touched 97 as a reliever in 2017. He flashes an average changeup with some fade that can play as an average pitch. Whether Roberts can remain a starter will depend largely on his control and command and whether his stuff will hold up over the course of a full season in a rotation. Though he struggled during the regular season, Roberts looked more like his college self in the Arizona Fall League. Tossing 14 2/3 innings across four starts, he posted a 3.07 ERA with 18 strikeouts and two walks. While the Cardinals are committed to developing Roberts as a starter, most evaluators think he’s destined for the bullpen. He certainly has the requisite two pitches to pitch in relief and could jump on the fast track to the big leagues in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After struggling to throw strikes out of the bullpen as a Wake Forest freshman, Roberts started learning how to harness his stuff and became an all-conference closer in 2017, when he recorded eight saves while striking out 13.5 per nine. He moved into the rotation as a junior and blossomed, proving highly effective in the new role as he slashed his walk rate while leading the Atlantic Coast Conference in strikeouts (130). The Cardinals took Roberts with the No. 43 overall pick that June, signed him for full slot value and pushed him up to Class A Advanced Palm Beach's bullpen ahead of the Florida State League playoffs. After the season, Roberts was handed a 50-game suspension in December after a second positive test for a drug of abuse. Roberts' calling card is his slider, a plus-plus pitch that many scouts regarded as the best college breaking ball in his Draft class. It's a mid-80s breaker with a high spin rate and so much break that some saw it as a power curve. As a starter, Roberts typically throws his fastball in the 90-95 mph range, but he sat in the mid-90s and touched 97 when he was relieving in 2017. He flashes an average changeup with some fade, a pitch he'll need more to succeed at the next level. Whether Roberts can remain a starter will depend largely on his control and command, which did improve in 2018, and whether his stuff will hold up over the course of a full season in a rotation. The Cards are committed to developing him in that role, where they believe he has untapped potential. However, many evaluators believe Roberts is destined for the bullpen and could jump on the fast track to the big leagues in the role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson burst onto the scene in June of his freshman season at Louisiana State, when he homered five times in 12 games to lead the Tigers to the College World Series final. Impressively consistent production defined his next two years in Baton Rouge, and after signability concerns dropped him to the Red Sox in the 40th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore, the Orioles grabbed Watson in the third round for slot value the following June. Watson wasn’t able to duplicate his career .311/.373/.484 collegiate slash line in his first taste of pro ball, hitting just .224/.295/.431 across 36 games between Class A Short Season Aberdeen and Class A Delmarva. A broken finger forced him to miss the Shorebirds’ playoff run. Watson flies. His toolset is anchored by his well above-average speed, which many consider plus-plus. His legs and instincts allow Watson to run down balls in the gaps and make him a threat on the bases, though he can get overaggressive there at times. While a fringy to average thrower, he possesses enough arm strength to stick in center field and potentially be an impact defender. It’s Watson’s offensive game that lends itself to fewer consensuses. An aggressive hitter with sneaky power who likes to attack early in counts, his approach initially translated to hard contact but few results in pro ball, and he had trouble making contact at both levels in 2019. Some believe that was due to an unorthodox swing that puts Watson in a deep hitting position, which he may benefit from refining as he develops. He may need to clean up some plate discipline issues to reach the Majors, where he has an everyday center fielder ceiling and a very good fourth outfielder floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Nationals for $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2011, Mercedes played three years in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before getting released and spending 2014 in a pair of independent circuits. After hooking up with the Orioles, he toiled for three years in their system before the White Sox grabbed him the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft at the 2017 Winter Meetings. He posted a 1.033 OPS in the final three months in Triple-A last season to finally claim a spot on a 40-man roster in November. Mercedes may be older than most prospects at age 27, but he has hit almost everywhere he has gone in pro ball and compiled a .302/.366/.491 line in his first eight seasons in the Minors. He makes consistent hard contact to all fields from the right side of the plate, generating most of his fringy to average power to the pull side. He controls the strike zone well, mashes left-handers and holds his own against righties. Mercedes also possesses a plus arm behind the plate and a long track record of erasing basestealers, including 44 percent in 2019. He's a very shaky receiver, however, which detracts from his ability to catch on a regular basis even though Chicago likes his framing metrics. His lack of speed limits his ability to play other positions, though he did get brief action at first and third base last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After saving international pool money in a vain attempt to land Shohei Ohtani in 2017, the Rangers spent their excess cash on six-figure bonuses for six different players, including $800,000 for Moss. A Bahamian, he would have had to wait until the 2018-19 signing period had he been born 12 days later. He scuffled in his 2018 pro debut but starred as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Arizona League last summer, hitting .429 in the playoffs to lead his club to the championship. Moss exhibits an innate feel for hitting from both sides of the plate, showing a quick swing, advanced understanding of the strike zone and a willingness to use the entire field. As he gets stronger, he should hit the ball with more authority and get to most of his average raw power. He possesses solid to plus speed and will bunt for hits and steal bases. Though Moss is quick and athletic, scouts are divided on whether he can stay in the infield. He has improved at second base but lacks smooth infield actions, and his averagish arm is a bet stretched at shortstop and third base, where he also has seen action. Texas plans on keeping him on the dirt but may expose him to center field in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates' first selection in the 2015 Draft, Newman came out of the University of Arizona known for his ability to make contact and hit for average. He's largely lived up to that billing, hitting .320 in his first full season of pro ball and then .302 in Triple-A in '18, after a bit of a down year, en route to making his big league debut, where he seemed overmatched in a small sample size. Newman has maintained the ability to consistently put the ball in play throughout his pro career, keeping his Minor League strikeout rates extremely low at every stop. He's also not drawn a ton of walks, but that's not as big of a concern if he can continue to swing at good pitches given that as a leadoff type hitter with no power, pitchers are likely to come right at him and working counts could put him behind easily. Newman will never be a power hitter, but being able to impact the ball with more authority and spray line drives to all fields -- he has extremely high ground ball rates -- will help him find a modicum of success in the big leagues. Newman runs well and is reliable at shortstop, his primary position, but his range and arm look better on the right side of second base. He's likely to yield the premium position to Cole Tucker when he's ready, and second base is crowded with Adam Frazier in Pittsburgh and Kevin Kramer waiting in the wings, so a career as a utility type might be his floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates took Newman in the first round of the 2015 Draft, it was largely because of a hit tool that allowed him to win two straight Cape Cod League batting titles and post a .370 average as a junior at Arizona. His bat-to-ball skills helped carry him all the way to Triple-A in 2017, with the fact that it comes in a middle infielder package only helping his value. Newman has put up very low strikeout rates wherever he's been, making consistent contact to all fields. His walk rate took a hit at the upper levels in 2017, though he still has a career .340 on-base percentage heading into the 2018 season. The high contact rate has come with almost no power and it doesn't appear likely that it will ever be a big part of his game. He's not a burner, but has enough speed to swipe a few bases and give him solid enough range to stay at shortstop. He had never played anywhere but short with the Pirates before 2018 and has been steady, if unspectacular, defensively there. He did start seeing time at second in Triple-A, given that Jordy Mercer is in his way in Pittsburgh. Newman will have to wait for a trade or for Mercer to leave via free agency to get a crack at the premium position in the big leagues, all while looking over his shoulder at Cole Tucker, unless he slides permanently to the right side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Newman parlayed back-to-back Cape Cod League batting titles -- the only player ever to pull off that feat -- and a .370 average as a junior at Arizona to move into first-round consideration in 2015. Despite being sidelined by a broken orbital bone during his first full season, he continued to hit as advertised and made it to Double-A. Newman found his groove using the same approach that served him so well in college: getting on base and making consistent contact. He draws walks and rarely strikes out. His contact-first philosophy does not lend itself to much power, but his offensive profile could fit very well as a No. 2 type hitter, though he hit predominantly from the leadoff spot in 2016. A solid runner, he should be able to steal a few bases. While some wondered about his ability to stay at shortstop, he played solid defense during his first full season, with decent range and enough arm to stay there. Newman jumped on the fast track by making it to Double-A in his full-season debut, and continued on it by getting bumped up to Triple-A in season 2. He should be ready to take over at short from Jordy Mercer when his contract is up after the 2018 season and likely could handle a move to second if they wanted to make room for him before that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stewart owned one of the best power bats in the entire 2015 Draft class and clubbed 15 home runs as a University of Tennessee junior before going to the Tigers with the No. 34 overall pick in June. His power has translated into the professional ranks like the Tigers hoped it would, as Stewart reached the Majors for the first time in September 2018 after hitting 93 home runs in 460 Minor League games. He homered twice in the big leagues during a multi-homer performance against the Royals that pushed his overall season total to 27. With his physical strength and quick bat, Stewart generates massive raw power that allows him to clear fences at all parts of the ballpark. There will always be some swing and miss to his game, but he did cut down his strikeout rate in 2017 and again in '18, all while improving upon his already solid walk rate. He has worked on his overall approach and tried to cut down on his swing to tap into his tremendous raw power more consistently, and he connected on at least 27 homers in each of his three full-season campaigns. Stewart is going to have to hit because he is a below-average defender in left field with a below-average arm. The Tigers love Stewart's work ethic and that he doesn't just spend all of his time in the cage working on his one carrying tool, instead putting in great effort to show he is capable enough to play the outfield regularly. The Tigers think he'll catch what he can get to and won't be a DH only. Either way, his power bat will be a welcomed addition to the Tigers' lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Stewart was coming out of the University of Tennessee in 2015, he had one of the best power bats in the entire Draft class. Since the Tigers took him 34th overall that June, he has more than lived up to that hype, hitting 58 homers over his first two full seasons of pro ball and carrying a career .508 slugging percentage into the 2018 season. Thanks to a very quick bat, Stewart can drive the ball out of the park, and for extra bases, to all fields. There will always be some swing and miss to his game, but he did cut down his strikeout rate a touch in 2017 and he does offset the whiffs by drawing a good amount of walks. He has worked on his overall approach and tried to cut down on his swing to allow him to tap into his tremendous raw power consistently. Stewart is going to have to hit because he is a below-average defender in left field with a below-average arm. The Tigers love Stewart's work ethic and that he doesn't just spend all of his time in the cage working on his one carrying tool, instead putting in great effort to show he is capable enough to play the outfield regularly. The Tigers think he'll catch what he can get to and won't be a DH only. Either way, his power bat is just about ready to contribute in Detroit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Tigers lost Max Scherzer to free agency prior to the 2015 season, they did get the 34th overall pick in that year's Draft as compensation. That turned out to be Stewart, who has shown that his power output at Tennessee was not an aberration, with big home run totals in each of his first two full seasons. Stewart has legitimate pop to all fields thanks to a very quick bat. While there is some swing and miss to his game, he has worked hard at shortening his swing and developing a better plan at the plate. He has shown some ability to draw walks, helping somewhat to offset the strikeout rate. His bat will have to be his carrying card because he is a below-average defender in left field. He has limited speed and a below-average arm, but the Tigers feel he'll eventually be adequate out there. The Tigers will live with fringy defense as Stewart continues to show he can punish the baseball at the upper levels of the system. If he continues to develop, he could be a left-handed-hitting middle-of-the-order run producer in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valdez first became eligible to turn pro in 2010 and was 21, ancient by international standards, when he signed for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015. He made up for lost time by rushing from Rookie ball to Class A Advanced during his U.S. debut the following summer, and he similarly jumped from Double-A to Houston last year. After a history of missing bats and generating groundouts in the Minors, he did the same in the Majors, with 34 strikeouts in 37 innings and a groundout/airout ratio of 3.4. Batters have difficulty making hard contact against Valdez because both of his primary pitches fall off the table when they get to the plate. He works at 91-94 mph and reaches 96 with heavy sink on his fastball, while his 78-82 mph curveball has so much spin, power and depth that it eats up left-handers and right-handers alike. He doesn't have as much success with his changeup and rarely used it in his introduction to the big leagues. Short and stocky, Valdez has some effort in his delivery but did a better job of throwing strikes in 2018 than he had in the past. He may never have more than fringy command, but when he misses he tends to do so down in or below the strike zone, so batters rarely make him pay. While a two-pitch guy who doesn't always locate his pitches where he wants doesn't exactly scream \"starter,\" the Astros think he can make it work and he did log a 2.59 ERA in five starts with them late last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valdez was 21, ancient by international standards, when he signed for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in March 2015. He has advanced quickly, rising from Rookie ball to high Class A in less than three months in 2016 and advancing to Double-A two months into last season. He has generated infrequent and weak contact, averaging 9.8 strikeouts per nine innings and a 2.6 groundout/airout ratio in his first three years as a pro. Valdez generates all those strikeouts and groundouts with three pitches that all tend to drop at the plate. His two-seam fastball usually sits at 91-96 mph with heavy life and his low-80s curveball has so much power and depth that it can overmatch both left-handers and right-handers. His changeup isn't as reliable but can be a solid third offering when he keeps it down in the strike zone. Though he has cleaned up his mechanics some since signing, Valdez is still short and stocky and has significant effort in his delivery. His control took a significant step backward in 2017 and he got hit hard for the first time when he didn't locate his pitches well in Double-A, increasing the chances that he'll eventually move to the bullpen. While the Astros haven't given up on him as a starter, he could turn into a dynamic reliever with a pair of well above-average pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively advanced age of 21 in March 2015, Valdez quickly has established himself as one of the top left-handers in the Astros system. He broke into pro ball as a reliever in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2015, then spent most of last year as a starter while earning three promotions that carried him from Rookie ball to Class A Advanced. Valdez's sinker and curveball both rank among the best among Houston farmhands. His two-seam fastball arrives at 91-96 with heavy life, helping him post a 3.6 groundout/flyout ratio in 2016. His curve has been so effective against lower-level hitters that he didn't surrender an extra-base hit to a lefty in his first two years as a pro. Valdez also shows promise with a changeup and provides a reasonable amount of strikes, so he'd seem to have the necessary ingredients to remain a starter. But he's small and stocky and features a high degree of effort, so the Astros may return him to the bullpen. If that happens, his stuff should play even better in shorter stints and he could advance rapidly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs ranked second behind only the Dodgers in international spending during the 2015-16 signing period, handing out $16.4 million in bonuses. The best player from that crop is Ademan, who landed a $2 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. His maturity has led Chicago to push him aggressively, and while he was able to handle low Class A at age 18 in 2017, he scuffled as the youngest regular in the high Class A Carolina League last year. Though he batted just .207/.291/.273 in 2018, Ademan still displayed an efficient left-handed swing and an advanced approach. He recognizes pitches well and uses the entire field, though his rough season demonstrated his need to add strength. He won't ever be a slugger but needs more muscle in order to reach his potential as an above-average hitter with some occasional pull power. Ademan's instincts allow him to play above his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has a good internal clock at shortstop, as well as the solid hands, range and arm to make plays there. His tools should allow him to play second base and third base if he needs to fill a utility role, though he should hit enough to be a regular if he gets the chance to catch his breath.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chicago invested heavily in the international market during the 2015-16 signing period, with Ademan receiving the third-largest bonus in its crop at $2 million. Extremely mature for his age, the Dominican made his full-season debut last August at 18 and didn't look out of place in the low Class A Midwest League. While he may not have as high a ceiling as former top Cubs infield prospects Javy Baez, Addison Russell and Gleyber Torres, he still offers plenty of upside and has a high floor. Despite his struggles in high Class A this year, Ademan is an advanced hitter who already recognizes pitches, uses the whole field and doesn't try to do too much. He makes repeated contact, drilling line drives to all fields while managing the strike zone well. Though he lacks size, he has a quick left-handed swing and some sneaky power that could translate into 12-15 homers annually once he adds some muscle. Ademan has average speed but plays quicker than that on the bases and in the field because of his instincts. He's still learning as a basestealer but already shows a propensity for making plays at shortstop. His hands, range and arm are all solid and should allow him to play a variety of positions if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect from the Cubs' spending spree during the 2015-16 international signing period, Ademan landed a $2 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He made his pro debut last summer in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, where he hit .254/.366/.316 with more walks (34) than strikeouts (28). He stood out by showing more polish than a typical 17-year-old. An advanced left-handed hitter with a mature approach, Ademan already recognizes pitches well and uses the whole field. He lacks size and strength but understands his limitations, focusing on stroking line drives and not worrying about driving the ball. With his hitting ability and bat speed, he could grow into double-digit home run power while providing high batting averages and on-base percentages. Ademan has solid speed and already shows some savvy on the bases. He has good instincts in the field as well and should be able to stay at shortstop. He's not the flashiest defender, but his feet, hands and arm all work well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros mine Oklahoma junior colleges better than any team and found a 34th-round steal at Western Oklahoma State JC in 2014 when they signed James for $15,000. He didn't do much in his first four pro seasons but took off in his fifth, leading the Minors in strikeout rate (13.5 per nine innings) and pitching so well in Houston that he claimed a spot on the postseason roster. He credits his surge to addressing his sleep apnea after the 2016 season, and the club also points to his improved conditioning. After working with a 92-94 mph fastball earlier in his pro career, James sat at 95-97 and reached triple digits as a starter in 2018, and he averaged 97 mph as a big league reliever. His heater has armside run to go with the premium velocity, and he can abuse hitters who try to sit on the fastball with a lively changeup that gives him a second plus-plus pitch when at its best. He can miss bats with his mid-80s slider as well, though it lacks the consistency of his other offerings and can get more sweepy than sharp. While James has the pure stuff to become a frontline starter, it remains to be seen whether he has the control and command to stay in a rotation for the long term. He struggles to repeat his delivery on a consistent basis, which hampers his ability to locate his pitches. At worst, his electric stuff should make him a late-inning bullpen weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick out of the University of Virginia in 2012, Kline was making steady progress through the Minors and had reached Double-A in 2015, only to suffer an early-season elbow injury for which he received a platelet-rich plasma injection. After his elbow continued to bother him that fall in instructional league, Kline underwent Tommy John surgery that cost him all of 2016, as well as a pair arthroscopic surgeries to address lodged tissue in the joint line in his right elbow that kept him off the mound again the following year. Finally healthy in '18, Kline made his return from a 59-month absence with a scoreless outing out of the bullpen at Class A Advanced Frederick on Minor League Opening Day. He only improved from there, earning a promotion to Double-A Bowie in May and then pitching to a 1.80 ERA with 15 saves and a sub-.200 opponent average in the Eastern League. With Kline's career back on track, the Orioles added him to their 40-man roster in November. Kline's electric fastball-slider pairing is ideal for a late-inning role. He showed the same velocity in 2018 as he did pre-injury, sitting in the mid-90s and bumping 97-98 mph, all while using his 6-foot-3 frame to create a downhill angle to the plate. Kline's slider registers in the mid-80s, flashes plus and is highly effective against right-handed hitters. He'll also mix in the occasional changeup, an average pitch for which he has good feel. Kline has long been a strike-thrower, but he will need to refine his command after his extended layoff. A starting pitcher before his injuries, Kline now has a bright future as a big league reliever. With his stuff and feel fully back, he enters 2019 on the cusp of the Major Leagues at age 27.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kline shined as both a closer and starter at the University of Virginia before the Orioles made him their second-round pick in 2012. He made steady progress early in his career and advanced to Double-A Bowie in 2015, only to leave his eighth start of the season with an elbow injury. Though he received a platelet-rich plasma injection and was able to get back on the mound in the fall, Kline's elbow discomfort returned and required Tommy John surgery that would cost him all of 2016. Kline will show impressive velocity when healthy. The right-hander's fastball reached 97 mph and sat in the low to mid 90s in 2015, and he knows how to use his 6-foot-3 frame to create a downhill angle to the plate. His slider is inconsistent but has the potential to become an average pitch, and he also has some feel for a fringy changeup. He's capable of throwing all three pitches for strikes, though he still has considerable gains to make with his command. Club officials were impressed with Kline's bullpens during mini-camp in January, and they plan to ease him back into action in 2017 after his lengthy layoff. Provided he can stay healthy, Kline shows the makings of becoming a big league pitcher with his size, strength and athleticism. Some evaluators believe he's destined for the bullpen, where his fastball-slider pairing could play up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stewart took home Atlantic Coast Conference Player of the Year honors as a Florida State sophomore in 2014 after he led the conference in all three triple-slash categories. He followed it up with a strong junior campaign, and the Orioles nabbed him with the first of their two first-round picks in June. After a sluggish start to his pro career, Stewart revamped his swing and began to put it all together in 2017, totaling 21 homers and 20 steals in Double-A. His production was less consistent last season in Triple-A, and he also missed some time with a hamstring injury, but the Orioles still gave him a look as a September callup, a challenge to which Stewart responded by hitting .250 with three homers in 17 games. The open, over-exaggerated crouch that Stewart employed at FSU has evolved into a more upright and closed-off stance as a pro. It's enabled him to make better use of his hands and wrists, helping him catch up to velocity and tap into some power, though, overall, his swing lacks versatility. Stewart's patient approach and strong on-base skills have long been strengths, and he offers value on the basepaths with his average speed. A good athlete despite his stocky build, he's a fringy defender at both outfielder corners, but profiles better in left field due to his below-average arm strength. After his first taste of the Majors last season, Stewart is positioned to see even more playing time in 2019 as the Orioles continue their rebuild. An everyday role might be a stretch, given Stewart's overall profile, but he contributes in enough facets of the game to serve as useful bench player or a platoon option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stewart was viewed as one of the better college hitters available in his Draft after he garnered Atlantic Coast Conference Player of the Year honors and paced the circuit in all three triple-slash categories in 2014 as a Florida State sophomore. The Orioles selected Stewart with their first of two picks in the first round the next year, only to see him struggle during much of his first two seasons before finishing 2016 on a positive note. A revamped swing helped Stewart to rebound in earnest in his first Double-A campaign, as he produced a .278 average with 21 homers and 20 steals over 126 Eastern League contests. After hitting from an open, over-exaggerated crouch in college and to begin his pro career, Stewart has worked to become more upright at the plate while also closing off in his stance. It's resulted in a more fluid swing that better incorporates his hands and wrists, thus allowing him to catch up to inner-half velocity and hit for power during games. Stewart's patient approach and strong on-base skills have long been strengths, and he continues to offer value on the basepaths with his average speed. While Stewart's speed and athleticism are better than his stocky build might suggest, he's already been relegated to left field on account of his fringy glove and below-average arm. Stewart contributes in enough facets of the game to serve as a fifth outfielder, and there's still a chance of him developing into a regular if his bat and power hold up at higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Named the 2014 Atlantic Coast Conference Player of the Year as a sophomore after leading the league in all three slash stats at .351/.472/.557, Stewart was viewed as one of the better college hitters in his Draft class. While he hasn't lived up to that billing in the professional ranks since the Orioles selected him with one of their two first-round picks in 2015, Stewart did show signs of life last season after a midseason promotion to Class A Advanced Frederick, and he continued to trend in the right direction in '17 in Double-A. Stewart is physically strong with a quick left-handed stroke, and his patient approach has long made him an on-base machine. The Orioles adjusted his setup to make him more upright and closed off at the plate, which has helped him catch up to inner-half velocity and begin to show power during games. An all-state running back in high school, Stewart has close to average speed and is a better athlete than his stocky build might suggest. He has good instincts as a runner and defender, though a below-average arm limits him to left field. After a discouraging start to his career, Stewart, thanks to his improvement at the plate, has a chance to develop into a reserve outfielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays drafted Whitley with the No. 13 overall pick in the 2015, making him the first player to ever be drafted out of Niskayuna (N.Y.) High. The rawness associated with such a distinction was obvious during his first two seasons, when Whitley appeared behind the talent curve at two lower levels before finishing 2016 on a high note. That success carried over into Whitley's full-season debut, when he made significant gains in all facets of the game as a member of Class A Bowling Green. He appeared poised for a breakout campaign in 2018, but instead suffered a torn right labrum during Spring Training which required surgery, effectively ending Whitley's season before it began. Whitley's speed is his best tool, grading as a legitimate plus. He let his tools play in the Midwest League in 2017 and saw his bat and power blossom as a result en route to a career-high 13 home runs. What's more, Whitley was able to start tapping into his power without detracting from his patient approach and feel to hit. Whitley's on-base skills fuel his ability to impact games with his speed, and he had swiped 21 bags in back-to-back years before losing all of 2018 to injury. Defensively, Whitley's athleticism and wheels give him a chance to remain in center field.
