He's now working on getting some separation so he can impact the ball, and he's learning to slash the ball to the left side so he can use his legs to help him more. The combination of approach and speed could make him an above-average hitter, albeit one with little power, in time. It's unclear what Merrell's long-term defensive home will be. He's unorthodox defensively at short, with a fringy arm, but he does have impressive range. He impressed in big league camp during 2018 Spring Training, playing on both sides of second base. He also played some outfield in college, though he's played shortstop almost exclusively as a pro. It could be that Merrell ends up fitting a super-utility role at the big league level, with his speed playing at a number of positions, though it's too early to rule out an every day gig at second base. Most importantly, he's making up for lost at-bats in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merrell's across-the-board improvements as a South Florida junior helped him stand out in a Draft class that was thin on impactful college bats. Impressed by Merrell's tools, most notably his plus-plus speed, and overall development on both sides of the ball, the A's selected him with the No. 33 overall pick in June, and then they saved money by signing him for less than slot value. Assigned to Class A Short Season Vermont for his pro debut, Merrell was hampered by minor shoulder and foot injuries, but still hit .320 with seven extra-base hits and 10 steals in 31 games. The only player in USF history to lead the club in hitting in three consecutive seasons, Merrell, a left-handed hitter, raked at a career-best .384 clip as a junior to finish his college career with a .353 average in 153 games. Perhaps more significant was the power uptick that produced seven homers and led scouts to believe he might be more than someone who hits for a high but empty average. Merrell's near top-of-the-scale speed -- he ran a 10.6-second 100-yard dash as a prep -- makes him a basestealing threat, one who knows his job is to get on base and wreak havoc. Merrell manned second base before making a full-time move to shortstop in 2017. His speed translates to above-average range at the position, though his other tools, such as his average arm strength, are merely modest fits. The A's will continue to deploy him there, but most scouts see a move in his future to either second base or center field, where his speed would truly be an asset. At the least, Merrell's speed, bat and versatility could make him a valuable bench piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez spent three years roaming the outfield at the University of North Carolina. Two of them were spent alongside Skye Bolt, who was an A's fourth-round Draft pick in 2015. Oakland went back to Chapel Hill in '16, taking Ramirez in the seventh round, and then watched him rejoin Bolt in the outfield and hit over .300 and reach Double-A in his first full season. A return to Midland for a full season in the Texas League wasn't quite as productive, but it did net him an All-Star nod. Ramirez is the kind of player whose whole is better than the sum of his parts. He's a professional hitter with an understanding of the strike zone from the left side of the plate. He'll draw walks and flash some power, but he's more about spraying the ball around the field and getting on base, with the chance to be an above-average hitter if he can cut down his strikeout rate a bit more. Ramirez won't wow you in the outfield, but he's a very good defender in all three spots and can even hold down center despite not being that fleet afoot. For Ramirez to be an every day player, it likely would be in left field, where there might be more pressure for power production. A career as a fourth outfielder is a more realistic outcome.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter during his time at the University of North Carolina, Ramirez showed improvement each year ahead of a breakout junior campaign that earned him a $300,000 bonus as the A's seventh-round pick in the 2016 Draft. Making the jump to Class A Advanced Stockton for his first full season, Ramirez garnered midseason All-Star honors in the California League before advancing to Double-A, where his bat and glove helped the RockHounds secure a Texas League title. Altogether, he finished first among A's farmhands in walks (73) and on-base percentage (.398), second in hits (148) and third in runs scored (tied-80) and batting average (.304). Ramirez's feel to hit and plate discipline have translated well in the professional ranks. He's adept at driving the ball to all fields from the left side of the plate and shows more power in the gaps than true over-the-fence pop despite totaling 11 homers in his full-season debut. A feel for controlling the strike zone leads to plenty of walks and fuels Ramirez's strong on-base skills, but he also leaves a lot of outcomes on the table with his penchant for striking out. On the other side of the ball, Ramirez is an average runner but an above-average defender at all three outfield spots -- a distinction that earned him a Minor League Gold Glove Award in 2017. That Ramirez handles both right- and left-handed pitching gives him a chance to be more than a platoon player or fourth outfielder, and he could enhance his profile even more by adding more power while reducing his strikeouts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Houser first reached the Major Leagues September 2015, roughly two months after the Brewers had acquired him as part of the trade that sent Carlos Gomez and Mike Fiers to Houston. He would make 13 starts at Double-A in 2016 before requiring Tommy John surgery, which knocked him out until July of the following year. Fully healthy in 2018, Houser bounced between Triple-A and the big leagues, struggling as a starter in the Minors but pitching well out of the Brewers' bullpen. A big and physical righty, Houser pitches with a 94-95 mph fastball that has good sinking action and nets him both whiffs and ground-ball outs. His 12-to-6 curveball in the low 80s previously earned plus grades, but it was more of an average pitch for him in 2018, generating more grounders than whiffs. His changeup, though still a bit on the firm side, has emerged as perhaps his better, more consistent secondary offering, registering in the mid-80s with some late tumble and fade. He's done a better job repeating his delivery post-Tommy John surgery, though he still has gains to make with both his control and command. Houser showed a more pitch-to-contact approach in 2018, employing a higher arm slot that led to an increase in ground balls but also a dropoff in whiffs and strikeouts. The Brewers will continue to develop Houser as a starter in the Minors, provided that's where he begins the season, but club officials acknowledge that the bullpen more than likely will be his long-term home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The difference between Lemons' stuff as a high school senior and his projection was wide enough that many teams expected him to honor his commitment to Mississippi. Willing to gamble on the Alabama prepster's upside, the Brewers grabbed Lemons with their second-round pick and signed him for $1.45 million. Since then the club has handled the ultra-thin right-hander with extreme caution, limiting his workload in each of his first two pro seasons. While Lemons' fastball touched the mid 90s in high school, he's pitched more in the 90-92 mph range as a pro. There should be more velocity on the way, as Lemons has plenty of room to grow into his projectable 6-foot-6 frame. His slider is his best secondary offering, with the potential to be at least average, and he can also mix in a curveball and changeup, both fringy. Like so many young pitchers, Lemons struggles to repeat his arm slot, making it difficult for him to stay on top of his breaking pitches and control his entire arsenal. He should gain better feel for his mechanics as he begins to fill out his slender frame. The Brewers are still getting a feel for Lemons, who has seen limited time on the mound despite never being officially diagnosed with an injury. He's very much a project and will likely require extra time to develop, but the long-term payoff could be worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lemons was well known within scouting circles entering his senior season at Vestavia Hills (Ala.) High, but the difference between his present stuff and his projection was wide enough that he was expected to continue his career at Mississippi rather than turn pro. The industry's perception of Lemons changed quickly when he showed better velocity in the spring, and he vaulted up teams' Draft boards as a result. In the end, it was the Brewers who secured the rights to the young right-hander's promising future, signing him for $1.45 million after selecting him in the second round. After topping out at 91 mph with his fastball on the summer showcase circuit, Lemons operated at 90-93 mph as a senior and touched 97, while also impressing scouts with his ability to create leverage to the plate using his 6-foot-6 frame. In terms of secondaries, Lemons' slider shows more potential than his curveball, and he'll flash a changeup as well. Lemons, like so many young pitchers, struggles to repeat his arm slot, making it difficult for him to stay on top of his breaking pitches and control his entire arsenal. He should gain better feel for his mechanics as he begins to fill in to his slender frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While a strong performance at the 2017 Boras Classic helped put Ward, who is the nephew of former NFL safety Mark Carrier, on the Draft radar, many teams expected that he would honor his commitment to Southern California because there was such a significant gap between his present ability and long-term projection as one of the youngest players in his class. The Brewers, however, took a gamble on him in the 12th round in June, then surprised many in the industry by signing him for $475,000. After performing well that summer during his pro debut, Ward made noticeable strides in the Pioneer League in 2018. Ward has plus speed and posts plus home-to-first run times from the left-handed batter's box. His speed also makes him a threat on the bases, and it gives him above-average range in the outfield. At the plate, Ward's left-handed swing yields hard contact and he'll flash power potential. Right now, however, the majority of his contact is on the ground, as his 69.9 percent ground-ball rate in 2018 was third-highest in the Minors among qualified hitters. Of course, that in turn highlights just how much Ward stands to improve in the coming years, with the final product being a player who hits for average and power. With enough arm and instincts, Ward has the chance to stay in center long-term, unless he fills out his 6-foot-5 frame too much, in which case he could fit a corner outfield profile. While opinions of Ward varied, there are some who feel he's the type of player who could continue to surpass projections.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former NFL safety Mark Carrier, Ward improved his Draft stock with a strong performance at the 2017 Boras Classic. That exposure, along with Ward's impressive physical tools and the fact that he was young for his class, prompted the Brewers to take a gamble on him in the 12th round in June. After signing for $475,000 and foregoing his commitment to Southern California, Ward made his professional debut in the Rookie Arizona League, slashing .276/.326/.325 over 32 games. Ward's best now tool is his speed which produces consistent plus run times from the left-handed batter's box. That speed also makes him a threat on the bases as well as covering ground in the outfield. He has some skills at the plate and makes hard contact when he stays behind the ball. There is a ton of left-handed raw power which shows up in batting practice, and the hope is that he'll eventually get to it in games. With enough arm and instincts, Ward has the chance to stay in center long-term, unless he fills out his 6-foot-5 frame too much, in which case he could fit a corner outfield profile from a power perspective just fine. While opinions of Ward varied, there are some who feel he's the type of player who could exceed projections.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ernesto endeared himself to international scouts with his across-the-board tools and his athletic projectable body and ranked as the No. 14 prospect on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 International Prospects for the 2017-18 signing period. Milwaukee made the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder its top priority, inking him with a $1.8 million bonus on July 2. He showed a high-risk/high-reward profile during his pro debut, hitting for power but also striking out at a high rate in the Dominican Summer League before heading stateside and finishing in the Arizona League. The switch-hitting Ernesto has an aggressive approach from both sides of the plate that he will need to tone down in order to make consistent contact at higher levels. He's a superior hitter as a left-handed hitter and slashed .282/.328/.491 from that side in his pro debut, compared to .150/.227/.150 as a righty. Scouts generally think he has a chance to hit for power, at least from the left side of the plate, as he develops physically. An average-or-better runner, Ernesto shows raw speed on the bases and could eventually become a basestealer. On defense, Ernesto has the speed and instincts to play center field, but like most prospects his age, he will have to work on improving his routes and angles to fly balls. The belief is that he has the potential to become an above-average defender, and there's hope that he will develop more arm strength once his body matures.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No. 14 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospect list for the 2017-18 signing period, Ernesto endeared himself to international scouts with his across-the-board tools and his athletic projectable body. Milwaukee made the 16-year-old outfielder its top priority and inked him with a $1.8 million bonus on July 2. The switch-hitting Ernesto has a good approach at the plate and likes to drive the ball into the gaps. He has a chance to hit for average and power from both sides of the plate as he develops physically, but he is considered a better left-handed hitter at the moment. Known as a speedy runner, the hope is that Ernesto will be able to use his raw speed on the bases and eventually become a basestealer. On defense, Ernesto has the speed and instincts to play center field, but like most prospects his age, he will have to work on improving his routes and angles to fly balls. The belief is that he has the potential to become an above-average defender, and there's hope that he will develop more arm strength once his body matures.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An infielder when he signed with the Cardinals in February 2014, Ynfante subsequently was moved to the outfield. His development has been slower than expected so far in the pro ranks, as he spent three summers in the Dominican Summer League before heading stateside for a brief United States debut in 2016. Ynfante offered a glimpse of his potential by slashing .299/.374/.491 with seven homers in 43 games in the Rookie-level Appalachian League, only to regress across the board last season with an assignment to the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League. When he first arrived in the States, Ynfante did show off some considerable tools, finishing in the top 10 in the Appy League in slugging percentage and OPS while also swiping 11 bases. Still maturing physically, Ynfante has shown that he is already capable of impacting the baseball, with most of his power coming to his pull side thus far. There is concern that Ynfante will not hit enough to tap into that power as he moves up, and his .213 average and 35 percent strikeout rate in 2018 won't inspire much confidence. However, the Cardinals feel he'll make the adjustments with his setup at the plate to improve his hit tool. Ynfante's plus speed will continue to make him a basestealing threat and give him enough range to play center field. He's an above-average defender and could very well stick up the middle long-term even though he's likely to see time at all three outfield spots going forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ynfante signed with the Cardinals back in February 2014 as an infielder, but was quickly moved to the outfield. That's the only fast transition Ynfante has made so far as his tools have taken a while to percolate, spending three summers in the Dominican Summer League before getting to the United States briefly in 2016 and making his full U.S. debut in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2017. He struggled in a move to the short-season New York-Penn League in 2018. When he first arrived in the States, Ynfante did show off some considerable tools, finishing in the top 10 in the Appy League in slugging percentage and OPS while also swiping 11 bases. Still maturing physically, Ynfante has shown that he is already capable of impacting the baseball, with most of his power coming to his pull side thus far. There is concern that Ynfante will hit enough to tap into that power as he moves up given a very high strikeout rate a summer ago, but the Cardinals feel he'll make the adjustments with his setup at the plate to improve his hit tool. Ynfante's plus speed will continue to make him a basestealing threat and give him enough range to play center field. The Cardinals have a number of athletic outfielders who can play center, so Ynfante will get exposed to all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lopez spent three years pitching professionally in Cuba before signing in 2015 for north of $8 million in a deal that cost the D-backs nearly as much in an overage penalty. The early returns suggested the money might go to waste, as a combination of struggles with performance to go along with off-the-field issues nearly forced the right-hander from the game. But Lopez turned the corner with a move to the bullpen in July 2017 -- a move prompted by the shoulder and blister issues that had wiped out his first half -- turning in a dominant stint in relief in the California League and following with a strong move up to Double-A and a trip to the Futures Game in 2018. Called up for the first time in September, Lopez gave up three earned runs without recording an out in his debut but was lights-out the rest of the way, tossing nine hitless frames over his next nine appearances. Lopez is flat-out nasty, boasting two dominant pitches that underscore his late-inning potential. He gets a ton of riding life on a fastball that averaged 97 mph and topped out at 99 during his 10 appearances in the big leagues. His slider is a true wipeout pitch, registering at 84-87 mph with two-plane action that enables him to miss bats with ease, and he also has a changeup that could become another swing-and-miss pitch if deployed more often. Since moving to the bullpen in 2017, Lopez has posted averages of 16.4 K/9 in Class A Advanced, 12.7 K/9 in Double-A and 11 K/BB in the Majors. Lopez saw mostly high-leverage work in his first big league audition, entering out of the D-backs' bullpen in the eighth inning in all but one outing. Prior to that, he had finished 35 of his 45 appearances in Double-A, saving 12 games while holding hitters to a .174 average. All the ingredients seem to be there for Lopez to become a big league closer, perhaps soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At one point in the not-too-distant past, it looked as if the millions the D-backs spent to sign Lopez would go to waste. He had received a bonus north of $8 million, and the team had to pay nearly as much in an overage penalty, but a combination of struggles with performance to go along with off-the-field issues nearly forced the right-hander from the game. It looks, however, like Lopez has put much of that, as well as shoulder and blister issues that kept him off the mound until July, behind him after an absolutely dominant stint in relief in the California League in 2017, a strong move up to Double-A and a trip to the Futures Game in 2018. When healthy -- and he has had some shoulder issues in the past -- Lopez has some nasty stuff well-suited for short relief. He throws his fastball regularly in the mid-to-upper 90s with some serious late life. His slider is a true wipeout pitch that greatly contributed to his insane 16.4 K/9 rate in Visalia last year. The fastball-slider combination was devastating to hitters particularly because he threw strikes at a better rate than he ever has. Lopez took a huge step forward in terms of maturity and understanding what it takes to be a professional pitcher here. If he can stay on the mound, he should be able to impact the D-backs bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kendall was one of the best high school athletes in the 2014 Draft, when he slid to the 30th round because of his strong commitment to Vanderbilt, and was the consensus best athlete in the 2017 crop. He entered that year as a candidate to go No. 1 overall but lasted 23 picks because of worries about his high price tag and swing-and-miss issues. The latter concern has intensified since he batted .225 with a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first two pro seasons after signing for $2,897,500. Kendall has all of the physical tools to be a star and has drawn comparisons to Jacoby Ellsbury in his prime, but it won't matter if he doesn't hit. Scouts aren't sold that he will because he doesn't recognize pitches particularly well and misses hittable offerings in the strike zone. The Dodgers overhauled his left-handed stroke during the offseason, widening his base and altering his bat path, and they're eager to see how well the changes work in 2019. With his bat speed, deceptive strength and plus-plus speed, Kendall could provide 20 homers and 40 steals in a season if he figures things out offensively. He's getting more aggressive and confident as a basestealer. He has the tools to become a Gold Glove center fielder with plus range and solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kendall could have gone in the top three rounds as a Wisconsin high schooler in 2014 if he weren't set on attending Vanderbilt, where he developed into a potential No. 1 overall pick for 2017. Though he was the best college athlete available, his college strikeout rate (24 percent) raised concerns about his hitting ability and enabled him to slide all the way to Los Angeles at No. 23. After signing for a slightly over-slot $2,897,500, he batted just .221 in low Class A while whiffing at a 27 percent clip. If Kendall hits, he'll be a star, and the Dodgers are encouraged by the adjustments he began to make to his setup and left-handed swing during instructional league. His tendency to miss hittable pitches at times and his so-so selectivity create questions about his pitch recognition. But he also has the bat speed and deceptive strength to hit 15-20 homers per season and the plus-plus speed to be a basestealing threat. Kendall can help a team win in multiple ways even if he doesn't hit for a high average. In addition to his speed and power, he also provides quality center-field defense and has a stronger arm than most players at the position. He has earned comparisons to a vintage Jacoby Ellsbury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Yankees failed to sign Shohei Ohtani after the 2017 season, they regrouped and spent their surplus international money on Venezuelan position players Raimfer Salinas ($1.85 million) and Cabello ($1.35 million) in December. Scouted and signed as a catcher, Cabello had atypical athleticism for the position and moved to center field before his 2018 pro debut. He showed enough in one week in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League for New York to decide he needed a tougher challenge and to bring him to the United States at age 17. Cabello has advanced discipline and bat-to-ball skills for a teenager. His bat speed and strength also give him plenty of raw power, which translated into him topping the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League with a .555 slugging percentage. He should develop even more pop as he adds more loft to his right-handed swing. Cabello's speed earns well-above-average grades from some evaluators, a major factor in the Yankees' decision to move him from behind the plate. He's still learning as a center fielder but should become at least an average defender once he improves his reads and routes. He has average arm strength and enough offensive ability to profile as a regular if he has to shift to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murray has been an intriguing talent since his high school days, but opted out of the Draft in 2015 so he could head to Texas A&M to play quarterback and the outfield. He transferred to Oklahoma, sitting out 2016, then backing up Heisman Trophy winner Baker Mayfield in 2017. He took a huge step forward on the baseball field as a redshirt sophomore in 2018 and the A's rolled the dice on his upside potential by taking him with the No. 9 overall pick in last June's Draft, signing him for just over $4.6 million and agreeing to let him return to Oklahoma to play football. After a huge season that brought the Sooners another Heisman Trophy, Murray decided to declare for the NFL Draft, putting his baseball career in jeopardy. The son of former A&M QB and Brewers Minor Leaguer Kevin Murray, not to mention the nephew of two-time first-rounder and former big leaguer Calvin Murray, Kyler Murray has raw tools aplenty to tap into. His improvements in 2018 stem from making more consistent contact, recognizing breaking stuff better and an overall more advanced approach. His outstanding speed makes him a basestealing threat and gives him the ability to cover a lot of ground in center field. There's enough bat speed and strength to project solid power in the future. He still needs to cut down the swing and miss and improve his reads and routes in the outfield, but it's all in there for him to be an impact, up-the-middle player. The A's will only get to see just how good he can become, of course, if he decides to dedicate himself to baseball. With first-round buzz surrounding him in the NFL Draft, there's a chance they won't get any return on their investment.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amid expectations that he'd lead Louisville's offense and go early in the 2018 Draft, Stowers tried to do too much and messed up his swing. After he settled down and was one of college baseball's hottest hitters down the stretch, the Mariners took him in the second round and signed him for $1.1 million. They traded him seven months later, shipping him to the Yankees for second-base prospect Shed Long in a three-team deal that sent Sonny Gray to the Reds. Stowers improved once he shortened his right-handed swing and focused on hitting line drives instead of trying to drive the ball. He has modest power, enough to produce maybe 15 homers on an annual basis, and his best offensive attributes are his on-base ability and solid speed. He has a very patient approach and the savvy to steal bases. Stowers will have a better chance of profiling as a regular if he can remain in center field. Scouts aren't totally sold he has the pure speed or instincts to stay up the middle, and he'll have to improve his reads and routes to do so. If he can't, his below-average arm will land him in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's 2018 Ohio state high school player of the year, Northcut was one of the best two-way prospects in last year's Draft. Though he had a low-90s fastball and a hard slider, teams valued his offensive potential even more. His bat might have landed him if the top three rounds if his commitment to Vanderbilt hadn't clouded his signability, and the Red Sox signed him for a well over-slot $565,000 after he slid to the 11th round. Northcut's bat speed, strength and the loft in his right-handed swing generate impressive raw power. After showing a polished approach as an amateur, he got overly aggressive and struck out in 29 percent of his plate appearances in his pro debut. He's most effective when he uses the whole field and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Though he's a bottom-of-the-scale runner, Northcut is a surprisingly effective defender at the hot corner. He has a better chance of becoming a solid third baseman than Boston's other young prospects at the position, Danny Diaz and Brandon Howlett. He has soft hands and a strong arm but will need to keep his thick frame in shape and improve his agility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Thornton's stuff took a downturn during his junior season at North Carolina, the Astros believed in his previous track record enough to take him in the fifth round of the 2015 Draft. He pitched well in his first two years as a pro, then struggled at the upper levels of the system in 2017. He has fared better and shown crisper stuff while repeating Triple-A this season. Thornton has added a couple ticks of velocity to his fastball in 2018, working at 93-95 mph and topping out at 97 with riding action. He has an interesting array of secondary pitches, including a curveball with some power and depth and an improved slider that he can turn into a true cutter. He needs to refine and trust his changeup more to find success against left-handers, however. Thornton has a funky delivery but it gives him deception and doesn't prevent him from filling the strike zone. With solid stuff and strike-throwing ability, he has the ingredients to become at least a No. 4 starter. But he often gets hit harder than he should, so his long-term role may be as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born and raised in the Bahamas, Young went to high school in Florida for several years before moving to Georgia for his senior campaign in 2016. That he was part of a program for international students at a Christian school likely caused him to fly under the radar during the spring, and it looked as though Young would go undrafted until the Blue Jays took him in the 39th round and signed him for $200,000. He rewarded the organization for its investment by turning in an eye-opening full-season debut in 2018. Spending the entire year in the Midwest League, Young produced a .285/.363/.445 line with 50 extra-base hits and 44 steals over 125 games at Class A Lansing. A switch-hitter with different profiles on each side of the plate, Young projects to hit for more average as a lefty. He'll demonstrate an advanced approach from that side, with a swing that produces line-drive contact across the entire field. His right-handed stroke is more power-oriented, but it also comes with natural swing-and-miss tendencies. He'll draw walks from both sides and generally gets on base at an above-average clip, while his above-average speed makes him a menace on the basepaths. Young's 44 steals tied him for third in the Midwest League, but he'll need to refine his technique and do a better job reading pitchers after being thrown out 13 times. Much of Young's future value is tied to his ability to stick in center field. He's a solid, if unspectacular defender up the middle, with good range and instincts, as well as arm strength that's among the best in the system and allows him to profile in right field. He saw near equal time at both spots last season, recording 15 outfield assists overall.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Danan Hughes is best known as a wide receiver who played six seasons in the NFL, but he also was the last Iowa position player selected in the first five rounds (third round to the Brewers in 1992). Thanks to an all-star summer in the Cape Cod League last year and a strong finish to his junior season, Neustrom could end that drought. He also led the Hawkeyes in hitting (.387) at the World University Games in August and has set career bests nearly across the board this spring. Neustrom's most attractive tool is his power potential, the product of strength, solid bat speed and loft in his left-handed swing. There are times when he focuses on using the opposite field, and others when he gets pull-happy and vulnerable on the other half. He makes consistent contact and draws his share of walks. While Neustrom is slow out of the box, he moves well for a 6-foot-3, 210-pounder and has at least average speed once he gets going. He plays right field for Iowa and possesses an average arm, though most scouts project him as a left fielder in pro ball. He needs to improve his reads and routes as a defender, and he has the work ethic to get the job done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It's certainly not uncommon to have the Cape Cod League batting champ rated highly for the next year's Draft. When that batting champion is almost certainly going to be drafted to pitch, that is a little more unusual. That was the dilemma with Dodson ahead of the 2018 Draft until the Rays, an organization one year removed from drafting two-way phenom Brendan McKay in the first round, selected him with the No. 71 overall pick and announced that he would both play the outfield and pitch in the professional ranks. He excelled on both sides of the ball during his pro debut in the New York-Penn League, converting skeptics of his two-way potential into believers. Dodson showed power stuff in an explosive 95-98 mph fastball and a wipeout slider that touched 91 mph while coming out of Hudson Valley's bullpen. The combo is already lethal on right-handed hitters, and he still has room to improve his control and command. When he's not on the mound, Dodson is an above-average defender in center field who hits for average from both sides of the plate and contributes on the basepaths with above-average wheels. The early returns from the start of Dodson's two-way career were all positive. He posted a 0.68 WHIP and averaged a strikeout-per-inning across 25 frames, holding hitters to a paltry .143 average. At the plate, he slashed .273/.344/.369 with 12 extra-base hits and eight steals. It will be interesting to see how well and for how long Dodson can continue that level of production in both roles, but even as just a reliever he offers the Rays plenty of value given his late-inning potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A teammate of Lucius Fox at American Heritage-Delray Beach High School in Florida, Frank went on to become a three-year starter at Florida Atlantic University and a member of USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team. He boosted his stock with a breakout sophomore campaign that saw him lead the Owls in a host of offensive categories while playing every inning of every game at shortstop. His success carried over to his junior season, while his profile as a college performer only boosted his stock as the Draft approached. The Rays ended up taking Frank in the second round and then saved money by signing him for under slot value. Sent to the New York-Penn League, Frank led the league with a .425 on-base percentage and ranked eighth with a .288 average. Scouts see a future solid, albeit unspectacular, everyday type big leaguer when they watch Frank, in a sort of Mark Ellis type of mold. He has a pro approach to hitting with a good gameplan at the plate, one that led to more walks (33) than strikeouts (28) in his pro debut. He sends line drives to all fields and has a little pop from the right side of the plate. Frank is an average runner who runs the bases well but isn't a threat to steal. Defensively, Frank has a strong arm and good hands that allow him to profile anywhere on the field. His best chance at becoming a regular is at either second or third base, though it's probably more like that Frank serves as a utility infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An 11th-round pick out of Tulane in 2015 by the Rays, Gibaut has seen his stuff get better in pro ball, enabling him to make a quick rise through the Minors. He has improved at every stop in his career and was at his best in 2018, when he led all Triple-A International League relievers in opponent average (.181) and finished third in strikeout rate (12.1 per nine innings). He missed the first two months of 2019 with a lat strain, made his big league debut in mid-July, then was designated for assignment and traded to the Rangers for a player to be named two weeks later. Gibaut attacks hitters with a mid-90s fastball that has tickled triple digits in the past. He throws a pair of quality secondary pitches in a power slider that can reach 90 mph with late diving action and a changeup that grades as well above-average at its best. His three-pitch mix makes him effective against lefties and righties alike, though his control and command leave something to be desired. Though the Rangers assigned Gibaut to Triple-A immediately after acquiring him, he quickly factored into their big league bullpen and could become a seventh-inning reliever if he can do a better job of locating his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 3 prospect on MLBPipeline.com's list of the top international prospects for the 2017-18 period, Marte signed with the Twins for $3 million in July 2017, only to have the deal voided when concerns about his vision arose during a physical. The Dominican native would sign again that December, this time inking an $820,000 pact with the Rays. Making his pro debut at age 17 in 2018, Marte posted a .281/.317/.314 line over 43 games in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League. Marte makes consistent hard contact from both sides of the plate, showing good bat speed and a solid hitting approach. He's a line-drive hitter right now, but with so much physical projection remaining, the hope is that he could eventually develop some pop as he grows and his body matures. He's a plus runner who can make an impact on the basepaths with his speed but will need to improve as a basestealer. One of the better defensive players in Tampa Bay's system, Marte has the hands, range and arm strength needed to remain at shortstop long-term. He has advanced feel for playing the position, and club officials are quick to praise his work ethic and capacity for making adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivera got just 19 at-bats at Miami as a freshman in 2014, then hit a combined .390 in one season at Chipola (Fla.) JC and two at NCAA Division II Tampa. He didn't get drafted until after his senior season, signing for $1,000 as a 28th-rounder in 2017. In his first full pro season, he was leading the low Class A South Atlantic League in hitting (.346) and on-base percentage (.395) when he got promoted in late June. Rivera has one of the best right-handed swings in the White Sox system, possesses nice feel for the barrel and makes consistent contact. Though his stroke is geared more for line drives, he has solid bat speed and enough strength for some pull-side power. He's so aggressive and puts the bat on the ball so easily that he rarely walks, so there's some concern that more advanced pitchers will exploit his impatience. A decent athlete, Rivera has a high baseball IQ that helps him get the most out of his tools. He's an average runner who will steal or take an extra base when the opportunity presents itself. His fringy arm and average range fit better at second base, where he played in the Arizona Fall League, than they do at shortstop, but he makes plays at the latter position because he reads balls well and has a good internal clock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers gave Swanson, a junior college standout in 2014, his first chance at pro ball by taking him in the eighth round of that year's Draft. After missing most of his first full season with a forearm strain, he started to show a little promise in 2016, then was sent to the Yankees in August as part of the Carlos Beltran deal. He really took off in his second season with New York, making it to Triple-A. The Mariners noticed his improvement and acquired him in the James Paxton trade last November. Swanson's combination of stuff, size and deception gives him the chance to remain a starter. Not only does his fastball sit in the low-90s and get to as high as 97 mph, the analytically inclined love his spin rate. That, combined with the deception in his delivery and his angle, often allows that fastball -- which he relies on heavy -- to play up better than plus. His slider and improved changeup give him two at least average secondary offerings. Not only does Swanson have a good strike-throwing resume, but again the analytics department was surprised to see he threw more quality strikes than initially thought. He's not far from being able to impact a big league staff in some capacity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias was the shortstop on a loaded Cuban 18-and-under national team in 2014, playing alongside Top 100 Prospects Michel Baez (Padres), Yusniel Diaz (Orioles), Julio Pablo Martinez (Rangers) and Luis Robert (White Sox). He debuted in Cuba's top national league at age 17 before defecting in 2015 and signing with the Rangers two years later for $700,000. He made a strong impression by topping the short-season Northwest League in batting (.366) and on-base percentage (.451) during his U.S. debut last summer. Though he was old for the NWL at age 21, Arias has advanced hitting skills. With a compact right-handed swing, nice feel for the barrel and a disciplined approach, he drills line drives to all fields. He's not a big home run threat but can drive the ball to the gaps and produce a healthy amount of doubles. A below-average runner, Arias lacks the range to play shortstop at the big league level. With his solid arm and reliable hands, he fits best at third base, where he saw the majority of his action in 2018. He projects as an average defender at the hot corner who also could fill in at second base on occasion.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sobotka racked up 19 saves at South Carolina Upstate as a freshman and sophomore, and many scouts viewed the 6-foot-7 right-hander as a potential first-rounder in 2014. A stress fracture kept him from taking the mound all season, but the Braves took a chance and drafted him in the fourth round that June. It was slow going at the outset, but things clicked in 2018 as he pitched his way from the Class A Advanced Florida State League all the way up to the big leagues. Sobotka has the power repertoire and the demeanor needed to pitch at or near the end of the games. He can crank his fastball up into the upper-90s now, touching triple-digits. He throws it up in the zone with elite spin, which leads to outstanding swing-and-miss rates. He complements his fastball with a solid slider that has good bite down in the zone. He has a changeup, but it's not something he needs as a one-inning short reliever. The only thing holding Sobotka back has been his command. It doesn't need to be pinpoint, but if he can locate his fastball consistently, he has the chance to close games in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canning has been a starter at Arizona State since the start of his freshman year and has improved his performance each season, hitting .269 as a freshman, then improving to .332 in his sophomore year. He’s saved his best for last as one of the better performers in Division I this spring. The 5-foot-11 left-handed hitter has put up the best numbers of his career as a junior, with teams that particularly covet college performers taking notice. Canning can really swing it with a line-drive approach and has extra-base ability, though it’s never likely to be major home run power. He does have some swing and miss in his game, though his walk rate has gone up this season to help offset it. While Canning has excellent speed, he has not been an efficient basestealer. After playing corner outfield spots his first two seasons, he’s showing he can play center field and should get the chance to play there at the next level. Canning gets respect from scouts as being a “baseball player,” one who can do the little things to help a team win. His performance in his junior season has set him up to come off the board in the top five rounds.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The youngest position player to appear in the U.S. Minors last season, Garcia didn't turn 17 until August. By then he already had established that he could hold his own against much older competition in the Rookie-level Arizona League. He's one of several prospects signed out of Mexico by the Cubs, who bought him from the Mexican League's Yucatan Lions for $500,000 in 2017. To call Garcia an advanced hitter for his age may not do him enough justice. A switch-hitter, he has a compact swing from both sides of the plate that produces easy line-drive contact to all fields. He needs to get stronger but may not have more than fringy power after he physically matures. In addition to his ability to put the bat on the ball, Garcia stands out for his instincts. He knows how to use his average speed on the bases and to get to balls in the middle infield. He has some experience at shortstop yet played solely at second in his pro debut, fitting better at the keystone with his average arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Curacao native, Clementina's career started in the Dodgers organization before he went to the Reds in a 2017 Trade Deadline deal that sent reliever Tony Cingrani to Los Angeles. An offense-first catcher, Clementina's last two seasons have seen him have hot starts and super cold finishes, though he did finish fifth in the Midwest League in home runs in 2018. In his first 45 games of 2018, Clementina batted .325 with a .997 OPS and nine home runs. Then he batted .221 with a .667 OPS -- and nine homers -- over his final 57 games. The Reds felt his large body composition -- he was listed at 6-feet tall and 250 pounds before the season -- was at the root of his second-half fades. During instructional league, the organization had him focus on non-baseball activities, namely conditioning, and both the club and player were rewarded as Clementina reported to 2019 camp having shed between 20-30 pounds. Scouts are still high on Clementina's offensive skills, especially with his 70 raw power, but the hope is that with a better body comes better defensive skills. He was already an adequate thrower and solid pitch framer but has lacked agility throughout his time in the Minors. He's an OK blocker but lacks lateral agility and ability. Except for his very slow running ability, all his other skills could potentially improve now that he's in good shape.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Injuries were a big part of Spillane's college resume at the University of Illinois. When he came out of high school, he was still coming back from Tommy John surgery and concussions kept him off the field in Champaign for much of his first two seasons. A healthy and robust junior season in 2018 saw Spillane lead Division I hitters in slugging percentage and OPS, while hitting 23 homers. He was named 2018 Big Ten Player of the Year and became the highest-drafted position player in program history when the Reds took him in the third round and signed him at below-slot value. In the Pioneer League, Spillane's plus raw power was on display. While he had a lengthy swing and 41 percent strikeout rate, he has some bat speed and there was a different sound and impact when he made contact with the baseball. His other offensive skills fall in the fringy-to-average range and he missed some time when he was banged up late in the season. Spillane does somewhat offset his high strikeout rate with an ability to draw walks, and he's expected to likely be a power-over-hit offensive player. A first baseman in college, Spillane is athletic and received more playing time in right field than first base during his first pro summer in the Reds organization. He could profile as an everyday right fielder if he hits enough and taps into his power consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acquired in the April 2018 trade that sent RHP Ariel Hernandez to the Dodgers' organization, Isabel is a questionable hitter but has 80 raw power that seems poised to go off the charts at times with booming home runs that would leave any stadium in the United States. He hit 35 home runs in 104 games for Daytona after the trade and his 36 total homers tied him for the Minor League lead. While there is no question about Isabel's ability to hit the ball out of the park, there are many worries about him making enough contact to use that power in games as he moves up the ladder. In 2018, Isabel also struck out 152 times or 36 percent of his at-bats. He has below average running ability and is below average as a defender. He does have an average arm and could be occasionally utilized in right field, where he played eight games for Daytona. Isabel could be a more athletic version of Chris Carter if he can refine his overall approach at the plate and harness his raw power. Otherwise, he's a likely one-trick pony who will hit the tape-measure homers and do little else, which would make it harder for him to reach the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Webb opened his senior season at Owasso (Okla.) High in 2014 with consecutive no-hitters then blew out his elbow in his third start and required Tommy John surgery. He spent 2015 rehabilitating his elbow and turned down the Indians as a 38th-round pick before enrolling at South Carolina. A rare Draft-eligible freshman, he led the Southeastern Conference with 128 strikeouts in 102 innings before going to the Brewers in the third round of the 2016 Draft. Webb's development accelerated in 2018, and the right-hander finished the year with a strong performance at Double-A Biloxi, striking out 10 batters and allowing one hit in his final regular-season start, then firing another six-inning, one-hit gem in the Southern League playoffs. He struggled to build on that progress in 2019, as a combination of control problems and diminished stuff led to a demotion from Biloxi back to Class A Advanced Carolina, and he ultimately landed on the injured list with tightness in the back of his shoulder in June. Webb's power stuff is headlined by a plus fastball-curveball combo. His heater currently sits in the mid-90s with riding life, and there's a chance he adds even more velocity as he continues to distance himself from the surgery. His curveball, meanwhile, is a 12-to-6 hammer that he throws with power in the mid- to upper-70s. Together, the two pitches give Webb the ability to induce ugly swings-and-misses, which he did at a near 15 percent clip in 2018, while averaging 9.5 strikeouts-per-nine. Webb's split-changeup gives him a third above-average-or-better pitch, one that at times can be almost as effective as his curveball. While Webb's dynamic arsenal and room for improvement give him a chance to remain a starter, most scouts project him as a reliever long-term because he doesn't have an athletic delivery, doesn't consistently throw strikes and his command is even more sporadic. He does create deception with his mechanics and does a good job attacking hitters north and south, using an aggressive nature that could work well in a high-leverage bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals took Poncedeleon in the ninth round of the 2014 Draft after his senior year at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, an NAIA school in Florida. He had already reached Triple-A in 2017 and was making his sixth career start at the level when he took a line drive off of his head and required emergency surgery to stop the bleeding in his brain. After a long layoff that included an extensive rehab process, Poncedeleon was cleared to return for Spring Training in 2018 and opened the season back in Triple-A. His success in the Pacific Coast League earned him his first callup to St. Louis at age 26 in July, and Poncedeleon tied a bow on his miraculous comeback story by tossing seven no-hit innings against the Reds in his big league debut. Poncedeleon's continued success throughout his career is a testimony to his stuff. He's consistently around the zone with a sinking fastball that touches the mid-90s and sits at 93-94 mph, while his above-average 90-91 mph cutter and average changeup are weapons for him against right- and left-handed hitters, respectively. He also has an upper-70s curveball at his disposal, but it's a below-average pitch, and he seldom threw it in the big leagues. After his tremendous debut in July, Poncedeleon went on to toss 33 innings for the Cardinals, posting a 2.73 ERA across 11 outings (four starts). While he's been a very capable starter in his career, Poncedeleon may offer the most value in the same type of swingman role he thrived in last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman signed with the D-backs for $1.85 million at the outset of last year's international period after he had ranked as the No. 19 prospect in his class. He impressed evaluators as a Dominican amateur with a combination of athleticism and overall tools that could help him stick in center field. Guzman has a pair of standout tools in his speed -- he was clocked at showcases in the 6.6- to 6.7-second range in the 60-yard run -- and arm strength that might have been the best among players in his class and is expected get even stronger as he develops. Projecting his impact at the plate will require more time, as Guzman won't make his pro debut until 2019, but he shows the signs of having the requisite athleticism and skills to develop a promising speed-power combo. Guzman is all projection right now, but he has the type of athletic body scouts covet, not to mention defensive abilities that could keep him on the field even when he struggles at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Francis family produced a pair of Draft picks in 2017, when the D-backs took Harrison in the fourth round out of the Florida prep ranks before the Brewers made his older brother, Bowden, their seventh-round pick. While Bowden has moved faster so far as a pro, Harrison has emerged as the better prospect since signing for $477,8000. After a brief pro debut, he impressed club officials with his steady improvement while pitching at a pair of Rookie-ball levels last summer. Francis has a nice foundation to develop as a starter. His three-pitch mix is headlined by a low-90s fastball with late movement that nets him whiffs as well as weak contact. He pulls the string on hitters with an excellent changeup that already earns above-average grades. Spinning a more consistent curveball will be a focal point for Francis moving forward, but club officials are encouraged by his progress to date. An aggressive delivery is the only thing that gives evaluators pause when projecting Francis as a long-term starter. But he repeats it well for the most part and should learn to do so more consistently as he adds strength to his solid frame. He may be a reliever or a No. 5 starter when all is done, but there's enough upside there for Francis to blow well past the relatively modest projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Humphreys was a talented two-way player as a high schooler in Mississippi, but Tommy John surgery kept him from pitching his senior year, though he took home state Gatorade Player of the Year honors anyway. The Nationals took him in the 36th round of the 2013 Draft, but he opted to honor his commitment to Mississippi State, where he was only a position player as a freshman and sophomore. He got back on the mound as a junior and saved seven games, enough for the Rockies to draft him as a pitcher in the seventh round of the 2016 Draft. He pitched his way to Double-A in 2018 and finished second in the organization with 26 saves. A shoulder injury in 2019 stopped his momentum as he missed most of the season. Humphreys misses a lot of bats with a deeper repertoire than most relievers. He can run his four-seam fastball up to 97-98 mph at times, but he uses his low-90s cutter as his primary fastball and it has solid average cut to it. He does a nice job at mixing in his low-80s slider and even has a changeup that can help him neutralize left-handed hitters. While his command wasn't quite as sharp in 2018, he should find the strike zone consistently enough to be effective. He's not far off from contributing to a big league bullpen, another power arm in the system who could be an effective setup man, if not more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Somewhat overlooked in a 2015-16 international class that cost the Dodgers $166.9 million, Valera turned pro for $50,000 out of Venezuela. He spent two years in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before making his U.S. debut last summer at age 18. He offers an interesting mix of tools for an infielder but is still very much a work in progress. Valera has a quick right-handed swing and a projectable 6-foot-1 frame, so he could develop 12-15 homer pop once he matures physically and turns on more pitches. His strikeout rate jumped from 20 percent in the DSL to 29 percent in his introduction to the United States, underscoring a need to hone his plate discipline. He does a nice job of using his solid speed to beat out infield hits and steal bases. With smooth actions and a strong arm, Valera has the makings of a solid shortstop. He also has seen action at third base and a bit of time at second base, and his tools should play anywhere in the infield. Whether he becomes a regular on the left side of the infield or a utilityman will depend on the development of his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-time first-rounder, Beede turned down the Blue Jays as the 21st overall pick out of high school in 2011 and signed with the Giants for $2,613,200 as the 14th overall choice shortly after helping Vanderbilt win the 2014 College World Series. He ranked as San Francisco's best prospect in 2017 and their top pitching prospect entering last year, then got knocked around in a couple of big league spot starts in April and went downhill from there. He pitched so poorly after returning to Triple-A that he moved to the bullpen in July in an attempt to simplify things. Beede has experimented with a number of pitches throughout his pro career, going more with a low-90s sinker at the lower levels before favoring a four-seamer that clocks at 94-97 mph. He never has shown consistent feel for spinning a breaking ball and plans on focusing on his curveball and scrapping his cutter/slider going forward. His fading changeup is his most reliable secondary offering and can be a well above average pitch at its best. Beede has the pure stuff to be a mid-rotation starter and outside of a groin injury that ended his 2017 season six weeks early, he has been durable throughout his pro career. But his control, consistency and confidence deteriorated so much last year that the Giants aren't really sure what to make of him or what role to use him in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of 20 players in baseball history taken in the first round of two Drafts, Beede went 21st overall to the Blue Jays in 2011 and 14th overall three years later, when he helped Vanderbilt win the 2014 College World Series. Signed for $2,613,200, he led the Double-A Eastern League with a 2.81 ERA in 2016, then got knocked around in Triple-A last year before a groin injury truncated his season in mid-July. He made his big league debut with a pair of starts this April, but pitched so poorly after returning to Triple-A that the Giants shifted him to the bullpen in June to simplify things. Beede's fastball velocity has fluctuated, in part depending on his usage of sinking two-seamers and harder four-seamers. He spent much of 2017 working at 90-93 mph after spending the previous year at 92-94 mph with a high of 97. The quality of his curveball and cutter vary as well, leaving his fading changeup as his best and most consistent secondary offering. Beede's control has slipped this year and his command is even less reliable, leaving him more hittable than he should be. Some club officials believe he'd be best served by simplifying his pitch mix and attacking hitters with his four-seamer, a true slider and his changeup. Reducing his arsenal could make it easier to refine his pitches and realize his upside as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beede spurned the Blue Jays as the 21st overall pick in 2011 before signing with the Giants for $2,613,200 as the 14th choice three years later, becoming one of just 20 players in Draft history to get popped in the first round more than once. Part of Vanderbilt's 2014 College World Series championship team, he advanced to Double-A two months into his first full pro season, but got pounded for a 5.23 ERA. He fared much better in his return to the level in 2016, leading the Eastern League in ERA (2.81) and finishing second in strikeouts (135 in 147 1/3 innings). Beede's fastball velocity dipped in 2015 as he adjusted to the long pro season and focused on his sinker and cutter. He added strength during the offseason before 2016 and bounced back to work at 92-94 mph and hit 97 last year, but has lost a couple of ticks in velocity while scuffling in Triple-A this season. His best secondary pitch is his fading changeup, which he sells with deceptive arm speed, and he employs both a curveball and the cutter. Inconsistent control and command undermined Beede while he was at Vanderbilt, but the Giants have helped him cut his walk rate from 4.7 per nine innings in college to 3.3 in his first three years as a pro. He's doing a better job of challenging hitters rather than nibbling at the plate, and he's also keeping the ball down in the strike zone. Despite his Triple-A struggles, he's still the best starting pitcher prospect in the upper levels of San Francisco's system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ockimey's impressive power display at Fenway Park before the 2014 Draft led the Red Sox to select him in the fifth round and lure him away from an Indiana commitment with an over-slot $450,000 bonus. He does have some of the best left-handed pop in the system and has slammed 52 homers in three years in full-season ball, but Boston chose not to protect him on its 40-man roster after the 2018 season. He scuffled in Triple-A and the Arizona Fall League, adding to concerns that he might be no more than a platoon player without a position. Ockimey's bat speed, strength and the loft in his stroke allow him to hit the ball out of any part of the ballpark. He's willing to take walks but his hefty strikeout rates (28 percent in his first five seasons, 31 percent in 2018) may hamper his ability to do damage against more advanced pitching. He especially struggles to make contact against better left-handers, and his platoon splits were pronounced last year: .273/.393/.531 versus right-handers, .186/.269/.295 versus southpaws. Limited athletically, Ockimey has to produce at the plate to have value. He works hard on his conditioning and defense, yet he's still a well below-average runner and shaky defender at first base. He doesn't move or throw well enough to play anywhere else and likely fits best at DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ockimey put on a show with his power during a Fenway Park workout in 2014, leading the Red Sox to pay him an over-slot $450,000 bonus as a fifth-rounder. He wasn't ready for full-season ball until his third year as a pro, but he displayed plenty of pop (32 homers) and patience (171 walks) in 2016-17 once he got there. He reached Double-A at age 21 last August and handled himself well there in the final month and again in 2018. With bat speed, strength and loft in his swing, Ockimey has the best raw power of any left-handed hitter in Boston's system. The question is whether he'll make enough contact to get the most out of it because he gets aggressive and lengthens his swing, resulting in a 28 percent strikeout rate though his first four seasons. He does manage deep counts and take walks, but more advanced pitchers aren't going to work around him as often if they can get him to chase. Ockimey has to hit because he's limited athletically. He has worked hard on his conditioning and defense, but he still has well below-average speed and will be adequate at best at first base. His only other option would be DH, which would put even more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ockimey's power display during a Fenway Park workout led the Red Sox to take him in the fifth round in 2014 and sign him for an over-slot $450,000. After scuffling in his first two pro seasons, he was Boston's most impressive hitter in instructional league following the 2015 season and led the low Class A South Atlantic League with 88 walks and ranked fourth with 18 homers last year. It was a tale of two halves, as Ockimey hit .297/.435/.531 before the All-Star break and .152/.291/.313 afterward. Ockimey's bat speed, strength and loft in his left-handed swing give him the ability to drive the ball out of the park to all fields. While his swing can get too long when he gets too aggressive, he showed signs of settling down in 2016. Ockimey stopped chasing as many pitches while drastically bettering his walk rate (18 percent, up from 11 percent in his first two years) and strikeout rate (26 percent, down from 32 percent in 2014-15). Almost all of Ockimey's value will come from his offensive production, because he's a well-below-average runner and athlete. That said, he has dedicated himself to losing weight and working diligently on his play at first base, where he could become an adequate defender. He also has improved his eyesight though the organization's vision program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Projected as a possible No. 1 overall pick in the 2016 Draft, Hansen pitched himself out of Oklahoma's rotation as his control disappeared and he fell to the White Sox in the second round with the 49th selection. After signing for $1.2 million and making some simple mechanical adjustments, he dominated in his first two pro seasons and led the Minors in strikeouts (191 in 141 1/3 innings) while reaching Double-A in his first full year. His 2018 was a disaster, however, as he missed the first two months with forearm soreness and wasn't the same pitcher when he returned. When he's right, Hansen has a 94-99 mph fastball with running action and downhill plane, as well as a pair of power breaking balls in a curveball with 12-to-6 break and a slider with late tilt. Last year, his mechanics deteriorated and he dipped into the upper-80s at times with his fastball while losing sharpness with his curve and slider. He still showed glimpses of an average changeup, though it's clearly his fourth pitch and requires more refinement. Hansen's walk rate more than tripled from 3.3 per nine innings in his first two years as a pro to 10.3 in 2018. Though Chicago has somewhat cleaned up his delivery, he still throws with effort and lacks the athleticism to keep all the moving parts in his 6-foot-7 frame in sync. The White Sox once had hopes that he could become a frontline starter, but most evaluators question whether he'll become more than a middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansen entered 2016 as a candidate to go No. 1 overall in the Draft, but his control deteriorated badly as he pitched himself out of Oklahoma's rotation and slipped all the way to the White Sox at pick 49 in the second round. Since signing for $1.2 million and making some simple mechanical adjustments, he has dominated in pro ball. He led the Minors with 191 strikeouts in 141 1/3 innings last year while finishing his first full season in Double-A but missed the first two months of 2018 with forearm soreness. Hansen's fastball sits at 94-97 mph early in games and tops out at 99, and its running life and the downhill plane he generates with his 6-foot-7 frame make it all the more difficult to hit. He owns a pair of power breaking balls, a curveball with 12-to-6 break and a slider with late tilt, and the curve has been more effective since he turned pro. He'll flash an average changeup at times, but it still needs more work. The concerns that dogged Hansen in the Draft still exist to some extent. There's effort in his delivery, which costs him not only control and command, but also some velocity in the late innings. He has cut his walk rate from 6.0 per nine innings in college to 3.3 in his first two years as a pro, though he had trouble finding the strike zone when he returned this summer and some evaluators still think he's destined for the bullpen rather than the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Based on early returns, Hansen could be the steal of the 2016 Draft. A candidate to go No. 1 overall heading into his junior season at Oklahoma, he was banished to the bullpen when his control fell apart. The White Sox still liked his pure stuff enough to take him in the second round and sign him for $1.2 million -- after which he recorded a 1.32 ERA, a .133 opponents' average and 81 strikeouts in 54 2/3 innings while reaching low Class A. When Hansen has his best stuff and can locate it in the strike zone, he looks like a frontline starter. His fastball sits at 94-97 mph and reaches 99 with running life, and he backs it up with a mid-80s slider with late tilt. His hard curveball is a solid third option, and he'll even flash at least an average changeup. However, Hansen doesn't always show that kind of arsenal and has little history of throwing strikes because his upper and lower halves get out of sync in his delivery and he doesn't stay online to the plate. Chicago kept things simple in his pro debut, having him focus on staying taller and getting the ball out of his glove more quickly, and the results were impressive. He does come with some health concerns because some scouts worry about his mechanics, and he missed the fall before his junior year with forearm tightness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A potential top-three-rounds talent in the 2014 Draft, Stephens blew out his elbow as a Rice junior and had Tommy John surgery instead. He signed for a below-slot $300,000 as a fifth-rounder in 2015 and has methodically worked his way through the system, reaching Triple-A last May. The White Sox added him to their 40-man roster after he recorded a 4.71 ERA in 21 starts at that level. Stephens has one pitch that grades better than average, a plus curveball that sits in the upper 70s with good depth. He's most successful when he uses his low-90s fastball to set up his curve, though he'll fall in love with his decent cutter at the expense of his bender. He has not had much success against left-handers and neither his cutter nor his fringy changeup have been able to solve that problem. Even before he scuffled in Triple-A, Stephens has been destined more for a middle-relief role than a rotation spot in the big leagues. In addition to the lack of a second quality pitch to pair with his curveball, his small stature and medical history (which includes forearm tendinitis in 2017) also present concerns. He throws strikes but needs to improve his command because he has little margin for error.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stephens injured his elbow three starts into his 2014 junior season at Rice, taking him from a possible third-round pick to Tommy John surgery. He rejoined the Owls rotation midway through the next spring and went in the fifth round of the 2015 Draft, signing for a below-slot $300,000. He topped the high Class A Carolina League in strikeouts (155) and strikeout rate (9.9 per nine innings) during his first full pro season, then missed the first two months of 2017 with forearm tendinitis and was effective but not as dominant in Double-A. Stephens has one plus pitch, an upper-70s curveball with good depth. He sets it up with a fastball a low-90s fastball that plays up a bit because he hides it and locates it well. He'll still looking for a way to get left-handers out consistently, as his fringy changeup and decent cutter don't get the job done consistently. Though Stephens has started throughout his first two full years as a pro, he's likely destined for the bullpen. He throws strikes but his small stature and medical history are concerns. His fastball has hit 96 mph in shorter stints, he could rely on his curveball even more heavily as a reliever and his competitiveness would serve him well in the late innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Projected as a possible third-round pick in 2014, Stephens blew out his elbow three starts into his junior season at Rice and had Tommy John surgery instead. He rejoined the Owls rotation midway through the following spring and pitched his way into the fifth round in 2015, signing for a below-slot $300,000. His first full pro season went well, as he made 27 healthy starts and led the Class A Advanced Carolina League in strikeouts (155) and strikeout rate (9.9 per nine innings). Stephens relies heavily on his lone plus pitch, an upper-70s curveball with good depth. His fastball operates in the low 90s and is effective because he hides it and commands it well. He has trouble against left-handers because his changeup is fringy, and he'll also mix in a decent cutter. Though he had a successful 2016 as a starter, Stephens may be better suited for the bullpen in the long run. Although he held up and maintained his stuff last year, his smaller stature and his medical history are concerns, and he did miss the first two months of 2017 with forearm tendinitis. His fastball has sat at 93-96 mph in shorter stints and his competitiveness would work well in a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson was inconsistent in three seasons at Texas-Arlington, yet his size and arm strength still enabled him to match 11-year big leaguer Mark Lowe as the highest-drafted pitcher in Mavericks history when he went in the fifth round in 2014. The White Sox intended on developing him as a starter but moved him to the bullpen in mid-2017 after he stalled in high Class A. He logged a 1.55 ERA during the 2018 regular season and continued to impress in the Arizona Fall League, yet went unclaimed in the Rule 5 Draft after Chicago left him off its 40-man roster. Thompson has more pitches than most relievers. He throws both low-90s two-seam fastballs with heavy sink and mid-90s four-seamers up in the zone. He also will mix spike curveballs with high-80s cutters, and he'll occasionally dust off a changeup he needed more when he was a starter. With the exception of Thompson's changeup, each of those pitches can grade as plus on a good day. His deep repertoire and his 6-foot-7 frame combine to keep hitters uncomfortable, though there still are times when his lack of reliable control and command get him in trouble. If he continues to progress like he did a year ago, he'll make his big league debut at some point in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson had only middling success in three years at Texas-Arlington, but his size and fastball enabled him to surpass big leaguer Mark Lowe as the highest-drafted pitcher in Mavericks history when the White Sox selected him 138th overall in 2014. More raw and projectable than most college pitchers, he has moved slowly in pro ball. He earned midseason All-Star honors in the low Class A South Atlantic League last year but got pasted for a 5.60 ERA following a July promotion to high Class A. He works in the low 90s and can reach 95 mph as a starter, and Thompson ran his fastball up to 97 in his brief appearance in the SAL all-star game. He has heavy sink and uses his 6-foot-7 frame to create downhill plane, so batters continually pound his fastball into the ground. He compiled a 1.9 groundout/flyout ratio in 2016, matching his previous career numbers. Thompson uses a spike curveball, which can have sharp break but also can be difficult to control. He's making strides with his changeup, control and command, and he'll have to continue to do so to advance as a starter. He could have late-inning value as a two-pitch reliever, possibly finding more velocity and consistency in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Baez signed back in 2011, he was the prototypical projectable teen-aged Dominican right-hander, one who it was easy to see could add weight, strength and stuff. He's done just that as he's moved methodically up the organizational ladder, making it to Double-A at the end of 2017 and reaching the Major Leagues for the first time in 2018. Baez's fastball has improved over time and now will sit in the 95-96 mph range and occasionally touch the upper-90s. His best secondary pitch is now his \"fosh\" changeup, a hybrid between a split-finger and straight change. It's at least Major League average and the bottom drops out of it when he throws it right. His slider has come and gone, with it looking like an average breaking ball one night, and a below-average one the next. The Tigers moved Baez to the bullpen in July while he was pitching in Double-A. His violent delivery and related control issues make him a cleaner fit as a reliever, and he was deployed in mostly low-leverage situations, often working multiple innings, after joining the Tigers as a September callup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
