They're hoping three is their lucky number again as they took Alemais in the same round of the 2016 Draft out of Tulane. There is no question Alemais will stick at the premium position defensively. He has very good hands and an arm that is at least above-average to go along with very good range. All of it plays up because he has outstanding instincts in the field. His ability to be an everyday player at the position will hinge on just how much he'll hit. He didn't produce during his pro debut, albeit in a small sample size, and he missed six weeks of his first full season with a thumb injury, but typically uses a contact-oriented approach with little to no power. He did sneak a few over the fence during instructs and while that will never be a big part of his game, having enough strength to drive the ball on occasion will help keep defenses honest. He's a good athlete with a tick above-average speed. The Pirates love Alemais' makeup, his energy and his intelligence on the field. That with his defensive skills could be enough to get him to the big leagues. If he can swing the bat at all, he could be a glove-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If it seems like Holmes has been a prospect forever, you're not wrong. Part of an aggressive Draft in 2011 that started with Gerrit Cole No. 1 overall and included way over-slot signings of Josh Bell and Tyler Glasnow, Holmes got $1.2 million in the ninth round. He missed all of 2014 and most of '15 following Tommy John surgery, finally making it to Pittsburgh for the first time in '18, though he struggled to find consistency there. There was some Jekyll and Hyde to Holmes in the big leagues in 2018, at times dominating and at times looking like an A ball pitcher. The stuff that allowed him to get to this level is still very much there. Hitters have never squared up his heavy, hard-sinking fastball that he could crank up to 96-97 mph in shorter relief stints, leading to a career 2.29 groundout-to-airout ratio in the Minors. None of his secondary pitches profile as true out pitches, but he does have solid changeup and a cutter with slider action, and can fold in an average curve at times. More than anything, Holmes needs to maintain an attack mentality in whatever role he has. If he falls behind, he gets in trouble and it often snowballs on him. He can get out of sync and then struggles to get back into a rhythm or make adjustments. He still might best be suited for the bullpen, but could get the chance to start if there's an organizational need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2011, the Pirates aggressively pursued some high-end high school arms in the middle rounds of the Draft. That effort netted them Tyler Glasnow, who is trying to establish himself as a big leaguer, in the fifth round, and Holmes, who signed for $1.2 million, in the ninth. Tommy John surgery forced Holmes to miss all of 2014 and most of 2015, though he did finally join Glasnow to make his big league debut in Pittsburgh in 2018. Throughout his career, Holmes has been an extreme groundball machine, with a 2.27 groundout-to-airout ratio that has gone up in his two full years since returning from elbow surgery. He gets all of that weak contact with his heavy power sinking fastball, thrown in the low 90s. He throws a solid changeup and will flash an average curveball at times, though he still doesn't command consistently. Holmes added a 90-91 mph cutter with slider action that was very effective against left-handed hitters in 2017 and allows his fastball to play up more, though he doesn't miss a ton of bats. There has been talk about moving Holmes to the bullpen, where that sinker-cutter combination could be extremely effective. For now, he'll likely keep starting as rotation depth so he can fill any kind of role once the need arises in Pittsburgh.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: By some measures, Holmes, who got $1.2 million to sign out of high school as a ninth rounder in the 2011 Draft, had a so-so first taste of Double-A. Considering it was his first full season back from Tommy John surgery in May 2014, however, it was a success, and the Pirates added him to the 40-man roster as a result. Holmes is all about his power sinking fastball. He'll throw it in the low 90s and hitters consistently beat it into the ground, proven by his 2.94 groundout-to-airout ratio in 2016. Both of his secondary pitches, a curve and a changeup, have the chance to be Major League average, and the breaking ball can miss bats at times, but he needs to land it in the strike zone more consistently. Holmes runs into trouble when he tries to be fine in and around the zone. He falls behind in the count when he doesn't need to, leading to him getting hit more, when all he needs to do is go after hitters early with his sinker and create weak contact early in counts. Officially out of rehab mode, Holmes' confidence could be skyrocketing with his addition to the 40-man roster. When he is efficient and challenges hitters, he has the look of an innings-eating, ground-ball machine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nikorak was raw with an enormously high ceiling when the Rockies took him from the Pennsylvania high school ranks at the end of the first round in the 2015 Draft. After a bit of a rocky debut in the Pioneer League, he went back there in 2016 and took a step forward. It looked like it was carrying over as he was throwing very well in Spring Training in 2017 when he tore the UCL in his elbow and needed Tommy John surgery. He returned to the mound in August 2018 to get a few Pioneer League innings in. Needing elbow surgery is never a good thing, but there can be benefits from it. For Nikorak, it gave him the chance to reset and focus on his delivery and now that he's healthy, he's ready to put the work he's done in being on time, in repeating his arm slot and in getting the ball down in the zone with his premium velocity. He was in the low-90s with his two-seamer, thrown with sink, while he was up to 97-98 mph with his four-seamer the Spring Training before he got hurt. His curve can be nasty, a low-80s hammer, and he has good feel for a changeup. As he gets more development time, his ability to repeat his delivery could get him to average control. The high ceiling is still there and he's added 25 pounds since he was drafted to help him try to reach that potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nikorak had as high a ceiling as any prep pitcher in 2015, though he was also inconsistent on the showcase circuit and during his senior season. It looked like a potential coup when Colorado landed him with the 23rd overall pick and a $2.3 million bonus, but he recorded a 6.70 ERA with 51 walks in 47 innings in two seasons of Rookie ball. The Rockies were encouraged by the progress he was making in Spring Training last year until he injured his elbow and required Tommy John surgery that cost him the entire 2017 season. Before he got hurt, Nikorak was throwing in the mid-90s with a simplified delivery. When he's at his best, he can throw two-seam fastballs in the low 90s with sink, four-seamers that reach 98 mph, spin a hammer curveball and even flash a plus changeup. During his first two pro seasons, however, he often worked with a fastball sitting around 90 mph and diminished secondary pitches. Nikorak has trouble keeping his delivery in sync and maintaining a consistent arm slot, leading him to pitch tentatively and lose the strike zone. He did make some improvements in 2016 and more last spring, and the Rockies thought he was on the verge of a breakthrough before his elbow gave out. Youth and the athleticism that made him an all-conference quarterback in high school are still on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nikorak had as high a ceiling as any prep pitcher in the 2015 Draft, though an inconsistent senior season mitigated his at-times spectacular showcase performance from the previous summer and dropped him to the 27th overall pick. After signing for $2.3 million, he walked 32 batters and recorded an 11.72 ERA in 17 2/3 innings at Rookie-level Grand Junction. He returned there last summer and while he wasn't as overmatched, he still struggled to find the strike zone and display the stuff that made him a first-rounder. When Nikorak can keep his delivery together, he can sit in the low 90s with sink on his two-seam fastball, reach 97 mph with his four-seamer, spin a hammer curveball in the low 80s and flash a plus changeup. But he has trouble repeating his mechanics and sometimes pitches tentatively, resulting in heaters sitting around 90 mph and diminished secondary stuff. If Nikorak can repeat his delivery, maintain a consistent arm slot and recapture the arsenal he has shown in the past, he still could become a frontline starter. The Rockies saw positive signs during instructional league and early in Spring Training, which offers hope that he'll figure it out, as do his youth and the athleticism that made him an all-conference quarterback in high school. But he injured his elbow and had Tommy John surgery in mid-April, so he won't be able to make any progress until he returns to the mound in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the first two-plus years of Mundell's pro career, it looked as if the Rockies had gotten a huge steal by taking him in the seventh round of the 2015 Draft out of Cal Poly as he used an advanced approach to hit his way to Double-A by the second half of 2017. A return to that level in 2018 didn't go as well and the Rockies did not protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, but he went unselected. Mundell's swing got out of whack in 2018 and it took him most of the year to get back on track. Even when he wasn't driving the ball like he had in the past, he was still managing the strike zone, limiting strikeouts and drawing walks and he still has a career .369 on-base percentage entering the 2019 season. When he's on time with his swing, he can hit to all fields, driving the gaps well, though most of his home run power has come to the pull side. There could be more over-the-fence pop as he gets more reps and gets back in a groove. A DH for most of his college career, Mundell has worked extremely hard at his defense. There's still work to do, but he should be an adequate defender at first base, where the hope is he'll prove once again he has the bat to profile at the infield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mundell mostly DHed and had an unremarkable three-year career at Cal Poly, yet the Rockies made him the first position player they selected (seventh round) in 2015. His first full pro season was a rousing success, as he set a modern Minor League record with 59 doubles and led the low Class A South Atlantic League in hits (168), extra-base hits (74), total bases (271) and RBIs (83). He continued to hit in 2017, albeit with a lot fewer doubles (28), while advancing to Double-A. Mundell focuses on managing the strike zone and making consistent contact. A right-handed hitter, he excels at driving balls to the opposite field and hit 13 of his 15 homers last year to the left side. He has the bat speed, strength and discipline to provide more power if he began turning on more pitches. Originally recruited as a catcher in college, Mundell has limited quickness and range but has worked hard to become an adequate defender at first base. He does have soft hands and is improving his instincts with experience. Club officials praise his leadership skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he had a modest career at Cal Poly and spent most of his three years with the Mustangs as a DH, the Rockies made Mundell the first college position player they selected (seventh round) in 2015. After a respectable pro debut, he exploded in 2016, setting a modern Minor League record with 59 doubles and leading the low Class A South Atlantic League in hits (168), extra-base hits (74), total bases (271) and RBI (83). He took advantage of the short right-field porch at Asheville's McCormick Field, batting .354/.425/.586 with 41 doubles in 67 home games. Mundell has plus raw power that hasn't fully translated into home run production because he focuses on making contact with a compact right-handed swing. He has a knack for driving the ball to the opposite-field gap, as evidenced by his doubles total. His combination of bat speed, strength and discipline gives him the potential to hit for average and power and could lead to another monster season in 2017 when he moves up to the launching pad at high Class A Lancaster. Originally recruited as a catcher by Cal Poly, Mundell has learned first base on the job in pro ball. He has limited speed and range, but he works hard, has soft hands and has improved his instincts. He also has made an immediate impression with his leadership skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading the Cape Cod League with eight homers the summer before, Shaw established himself as the best college power hitter in the 2015 Draft. He has lived up to his reputation since signing for $1.5 million as the 31st overall choice, topping the short-season Northwest League with 12 homers in his pro debut and the entire organization (Majors and Minors) with 24 blasts in 2017 and 25 last season. His first big league homer traveled 468 feet off Seung Hwan Oh in September. Shaw has plenty of strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-3 frame, giving him huge natural power to all fields. He could hit home runs without trying but sells out too much for power, letting his left-handed swing get too long and chasing pitches out of the strike zone. His whiff rate has jumped from 20 percent in Double-A to 32 percent in Triple-A to 37 percent in his first taste of the Majors, and he's unlikely to hit for much of an average unless he forces pitchers to challenge him more. Mostly a right fielder at Boston College, Shaw broke into pro ball as a first baseman and made himself into an average defender. With Brandon Belt ensconced there in San Francisco, the Giants shifted Shaw to left field in early 2017. His lack of speed limits his range but he does own solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best college power hitter available in the 2015 Draft, Shaw topped the Cape Cod League with eight homers the previous summer and hit 11 in 40 games as a Boston College junior despite breaking the hamate bone in his right hand. He has produced as advertised since signing for $1.4 million as the 31st overall pick, leading the short-season Northwest League with 12 homers in his pro debut and slamming a total of 45 homers in his first two full seasons while advancing to Triple-A. His 24 blasts last year were six more than anyone else hit in the organization in the Majors or Minors. Shaw's massive 6-foot-4 frame affords him plenty of strength and leverage, allowing him to hit the ball out of the park from foul pole to foul pole. Though he recognizes that his raw power means he doesn't have to swing for the fences, his left-handed swing can get long and he gets in trouble when he expands his strike zone. His whiff rate jumped to a career-worst 29 percent in Triple-A last year and he'll have to develop more patience to hit for average against advanced pitching. Primarily a right fielder in college, Shaw spent most of his first two pro seasons at first base and worked diligently to become an average defender there. He's blocked by Brandon Belt in San Francisco, however, so he shifted to left field last May. His lack of speed limits his range, though he does have solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shaw established himself as the best college power hitter available in the 2015 Draft, leading the Cape Cod League with eight homers the prior summer and then hitting 11 in 40 games as a junior despite breaking the hamate bone in his right hand. After signing for $1.4 million as the 31st overall pick, he paced the short-season Northwest League in homers (12) and slugging (.551) during his pro debut. He struggled when he reached Double-A in mid-2016, but he made adjustments and hit well there and in Triple-A this year. Shaw's big 6-foot-4 frame gives him a lot of strength and leverage, and he uses it to crush balls to all fields. His left-handed swing naturally gets long because of his size, so he probably won't hit for a high average, but he doesn't swing and miss excessively for a masher. He ran into trouble when he first got to Double-A when he expanded his strike zone, then showed more discipline in his return in 2017. While he has a strong arm, Shaw's lack of speed limits his defensive value. After spending most of his time at Boston College in right field, he spent his first two pro seasons in first base and worked hard to become an adequate defender. With Brandon Belt ensconced in San Francisco, the Giants have played Shaw mostly in left field this year, but he doesn't have much range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quinn ranked second in NCAA Division I in homers (21), RBIs (77) and total bases (165) at Samford in 2016, becoming the second-highest pick (third round) in Bulldogs history that June. He reached high Class A at the end of his strong pro debut but struggled mightily there in his first full season while dealing with hamate and shoulder injuries. He returned to the California League again in 2018 and reasserted himself as one of the better offensive prospects in the Giants system despite missing time with hamstring issues that have recurred this season. When Quinn tried to do too much while making up for lost time in 2017, he learned that he's at his best when he focused on making hard contact to all fields as opposed to trying to yank everything out of the park. The strength and leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame give him plenty of natural power that translated into more production last year, when he stopped chasing so many pitches off the plate. He runs well for his size but is a slightly below-average runner. Quinn fits the right-field profile with his solid power and arm strength. He shows average speed once he gets going and covers ground in the outfield, though not enough to fill in as a center fielder. Right field is spacious at Oracle Park, so he could wind up in left field when he gets to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quinn had a huge junior year at Samford in 2016, finishing second in NCAA Division I in homers (21), RBIs (77) and total bases (165) before the Giants made him the second-highest pick (third round) in school history. His OPS dropped from .998 in his pro debut to .661 in high Class A last year, when he was hampered by hamate and shoulder injuries. He has rebounded nicely in 2018 despite losing a month to a hamstring strain. Quinn doesn't have the smoothest right-handed swing but usually makes consistent hard contact to all fields. The strength and leverage in his 6-foot-3, 225-pound frame gives him power to all fields, and he's at his best when he doesn't worry about home runs. He fell into the trap of trying to do too much to make up for lost time in 2017 but has shown a more disciplined approach this year. Athletic for his size, Quinn has average speed out of the batter's box and is a step quicker once he hits his stride. He has solid arm strength and enough range for right field, though he'll likely be a better fit in left field at spacious AT&T Park.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts who trekked to see eventual Rockies first-rounder David Dahl in 2013 also got a look at his Oak Mountain High (Birmingham, Ala.) teammate Quinn, who turned down the Indians as a 12th-rounder to stay home and attend Samford. An immediate force for the Bulldogs, he finished second in NCAA Division I in homers (21), RBIs (77) and total bases (165) as a junior last year. The second-highest pick in school history, he went in the third round and led the short-season Northwest League in slugging (.571) and OPS (.993) during his pro debut. Quinn doesn't have the prettiest right-handed swing, but that doesn't stop him from making consistent hard contact. His considerable strength generates power to all fields, and his home run output could increase if he adopts more of a pull-oriented approach. More than just a slugger, he shows an aptitude for lashing line drives to the opposite field and has an eye for drawing walks. Though he carries more than the listed 190 pounds on his 6-foot-2 frame, Quinn is a good athlete for his size. He has average speed out of the batter's box and is even quicker once he gets going. His solid arm and decent range work in right field, though he eventually could wind up in left field at spacious AT&T Park.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he put himself on the prospect map by hitting 98 mph as a Southern Illinois freshman, Coonrod went just 8-17 in three years with the Salukis and lasted five rounds of the 2014 Draft. He progressed nicely in pro ball until stalling in Double-A in 2017, moving to the bullpen that August and blowing out his elbow after six relief appearances. After having Tommy John surgery, he returned to the mound last July and earned a spot on San Francisco's 40-man roster. Coonrod has gone from a 92-95 mph sinker as a starter to a 95-98 four-seam fastball as a reliever. His mid-80s slider/cutter can be a plus pitch at times but gets slurvy at others. He tried to develop a changeup when he worked out of the rotation but has abandoned it in his new role. Coonrod is more aggressive and does a better job of going after hitters as a reliever. The Giants once hoped he could become a mid-rotation starter but now see him as a possible late-inning bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coonrod caught the attention of scouts when he hit 98 mph as a freshman in Southern Illinois, but he went just 8-17 in three seasons with the Salukis and lasted five rounds in the 2014 Draft. He recorded a 2.82 ERA in his first two full seasons as a pro starter, but struggled in a return to Double-A last year and moved to the bullpen in August. He made just six relief appearances before blowing out his elbow and having Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for most of the 2018 season. After working at 92-95 mph with sink on his fastball as a starter, Coonrod flashed upper-90s heat in his brief foray as a reliever last year. His mid-80s slider/cutter should play as a plus pitch more consistently in shorter stints. He has made progress with a sinking changeup, though it may never be more than an average offering and he won't use it much coming out of the bullpen. Though the Giants have helped Coonrod calm down his delivery since college, his walk rate has risen at every level as he has climbed through the Minors. He still could project as a No. 4 starter if he could improve his changeup and his command, but banking on his pair of power pitches and his competitiveness as a reliever is more realistic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coonrod hit 98 mph as a freshman at Southern Illinois, but he went 8-17 in three seasons with the Salukis before San Francisco made him a fifth-round pick in 2014. He has enjoyed more consistent success as a pro and led the system with a 2.55 ERA while advancing to Double-A in 2016. The Giants asked him to pitch more to contact last year and he delivered, though his strikeout rate dropped to a career-low 6.0 per nine innings. Coonrod still can throw mid-90s four-seam fastballs by hitters up in the strike zone but he relies more on low-90s two-seamers with heavy sink. He also can miss bats with a slider that's a plus pitch in the mid-80s at its best. His sinking changeup continues to improve as he uses it more often, though it may never be more than an average offering. San Francisco has helped Coonrod tone down his delivery and improve his control, though his walk rate has risen at each level as he has moved through the Minors. He'll need to continue to refine his changeup and command to remain in the rotation. If he can't, his pair of power pitches and bulldog mentality give him the upside of a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia batted .368/.442/.626 at Florida International while winning Conference USA player of the year honors in 2014, but he hasn't approached those offensive numbers since the Giants took him in the second round that June. After setting career highs in most categories in 2017, he struggled in Double-A last season yet still earned his first big league callup. He homered four times in the final month with San Francisco but also struck out 31 times in 63 at-bats. Garcia has settled on a pull-heavy approach designed to get the most of out of his solid raw power, the product of his strength and the loft in his right-handed swing. He might hit 15-20 homers per year with regular playing time in the Majors, but his pop comes at a cost. He rolls over more soft grounders to the left side of the infield than he should and his aggressiveness means that he rarely walks. Somewhat rough behind the plate when he entered pro ball, Garcia has worked hard to improve defensively. He has turned himself into an average receiver while also getting quicker and more accurate with his throws. The Giants have Buster Posey in the big leagues and drafted Joey Bart No. 2 overall last June, so they've tried to add to Garcia's versatility by having him play first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick in 2014, when he won Conference USA player of the year honors while at Florida International, Garcia didn't have much offensive success above low Class A until last season. Despite missing two weeks with a concussion, he set career highs in most categories, including batting (.274), slugging (.485) and homers (17). But after hitting well in Double-A last August, he hasn't been able to replicate that success in 2018. Garcia is at his best when he shortens his right-handed swing, enabling him to pull pitches more consistently. His strength and the loft in his stroke could produce 15 or more homers per year with regular playing time at the big league level. He has gotten more aggressive as he has progressed through the Minors and will need to tighten his strike zone to succeed against more advanced pitching. Garcia has worked hard to get better defensively. He has made himself into an average receiver and also has enhanced his footwork and accuracy with his throws. Because San Francisco already has the game's best catcher in Buster Posey and spent the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 Draft on another backstop in Joey Bart, he may never be more than a backup and has begun playing first base to add to his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2014 Conference USA player of the year after hitting .368/.442/.626, Garcia went in the second round and signed for $1.1 million that June as a catcher with offensive potential. He didn't do much at the plate in his first three pro seasons -- fracturing bones in his face when he got hit by a knee while trying to break up a double play in 2016 didn't help -- but has started to drive the ball more consistently this year. Garcia's strength and the loft in his right-handed swing could translate into 15 homers per year at the big league level. He makes consistent contact but hasn't shown the same plate discipline he did at Florida International, so he may not hit for a high average. His offensive package profiles well enough to be a big league regular as a catcher, though he's hopelessly blocked in San Francisco by Buster Posey. Garcia's arm has gotten stronger and his release has gotten quicker since he has turned pro, and he recorded the best pop times (1.85 seconds) in the Arizona Fall League during the offseason. His receiving and blocking have improved as well. He has gotten some time at first base this year, enhancing his versatility if he winds up a backup to Posey.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Miller drew comparisons to fellow Georgia high schooler Brandon Phillips because they had similar offensive and defensive tools at the same stage of their careers. They went in the same area of the Draft, with Phillips an Expos second-rounder in 1999 and Miller signing for an over-slot $1.1 million as a Giants third-rounder in 2015. While Phillips immediately produced at the plate in pro ball, Miller struggled offensively until he repeated high Class A in 2018. Miller always had an efficient right-handed swing but didn't start making hard contact until he gained more muscle and experience. He has strong wrists and finished fifth in the California League with 51 extra-base hits last year after he started to turn on more pitches. His aggressive approach results in few walks, however, and may require an adjustment against more advanced pitchers. A solid runner, Miller can steal an occasional base. Like Phillips, he was drafted as a shortstop but wound up at second base. His below-average arm limited his effectiveness on the left side of the infield, but his quickness and soft hands make him an asset at the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller has earned Brandon Phillips comparisons because both were Georgia prep products with similar offensive and defensive profiles as amateurs. They went in the same range of the Draft, with Phillips an Expos second-rounder in 1999 and Miller a Giants third-rounder in 2015. Their paths diverge at that point, because while Phillips hit right away in pro ball, Miller batted .222/.277/.304 in his first two seasons. Signed for an over-slot $1.1 million, Miller still offers hope at the plate with his sound right-handed swing and strong wrists. He needs to get stronger, develop better rhythm at the plate and improve his pitch recognition so he can better cope with breaking balls and changeups. He has above-average speed and could reach double figures in homers and steals if he figures things out. Like Phillips, Miller broke into pro ball as a shortstop but was destined for second base. Though his below-average arm isn't suited for the left side of the infield, his quickness and hands could make him a solid defender at second. He needs to get more consistent after topping low Class A South Atlantic League second basemen with 20 errors last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams first made a name for himself on the mound by striking out 17 batters in a game at the 2007 Little League World Series. He projected as a possible first-rounder as both a prepster and collegian, but surgery to correct thoracic outlet syndrome before his senior high school season dropped him to the 33rd round (Padres) in 2013 and control woes undermined him at Oklahoma State. A seventh-rounder in 2016, he thrived at two Class A levels in his first full pro season but regressed terribly in Double-A last year. When Williams repeats his delivery and maintains his low-three-quarters arm slot, his fastball and curveball can grade as well above-average offerings. At his best, he can reach 96 mph with riding life on his fastball and snap off nasty low-80s breaking balls with power and depth. He didn't keep his mechanics together nearly as well in 2018 as he did the year before, resulting in a low-90s heater and a more benign curve. Williams' fading changeup also was less effective last season, when he also suffered from the control issues that plagued him as an amateur. The Giants were encouraged by the progress he made in six Arizona Fall League starts and plan on keeping him in the rotation. Simplifying things by moving him to the bullpen could give him crisper stuff in shorter stints, though he'll still have to throw more strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams first made baseball headlines by striking out 17 batters in a game at the 2007 Little League World Series and projected as a possible first-round choice out of high school and college. But thoracic outlet syndrome surgery before his prep senior season dropped him to the 33rd round (Padres) in 2013, and he battled his control so much that he worked just 73 1/3 innings in three years at Oklahoma State. After signing for an over-slot $250,000 in the seventh round in 2016, he made dramatic progress in his first full pro season. While Williams' fastball and curveball can be well above-average pitches at their best, his inability to repeat his mechanics detracts from their consistency and his ability to land him for strikes. He had more success in 2017 after he and the Giants worked diligently to help him maintain his low three-quarters release point. He spent most of the year pitching with a 92-96 mph fastball with riding life and a 79-83 mph curveball with power and depth. Williams also will flash at least a solid fading changeup with deceptive arm action. His ultimate success as a starter depends on his ability to stay on top of his pitches and continue to refine his changeup. If he can't find average control or command, his pure stuff alone should make him a valuable lefty reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams, who first made a name for himself by striking out 17 batters in a game at the 2007 Little League World Series, projected as a possible first-round pick out of high school and college but fell short each time. Thoracic outlet surgery before his senior season in high school dropped him to the Padres in the 33rd round in 2013, so he headed to Oklahoma. He showed spectacular stuff in two summers in the Cape Cod League but never threw strikes for the Sooners, working just 73 1/3 innings in three college seasons before signing for an over-slot $250,000 as a seventh-rounder last June. Williams displayed two well above-average pitches in the Cape, in the fall before his junior season at Oklahoma and again in instructional league following his first pro season. When he's going well, he has a 93-97 mph fastball with riding life and a hammer curveball in the upper 70s. But he has trouble keeping his mechanics together and trusting his stuff, so the quality of his heater and curve will vary. Though Williams can flash a decent changeup and broke into pro ball as a starter, he's likely destined for the bullpen. Whatever his role, he'll need to attack hitters more and maintain his low three-quarters arm slot so he doesn't get under his pitches and cause them to flatten out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castellanos has been one of the most consistent hitters in the Red Sox system since signing for $5,000 out of Venezuela in 2015. He hit .326 and led the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 23 doubles in his 2016 pro debut, then posted a .339 average and missed out on the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League batting title by .001 as an encore. His .302 average would have ranked second in the low Class A South Atlantic League last season if he hadn't been a few plate appearances short of qualifying, and he went on a .330 tear in the second half after recovering from a back injury that cost him six weeks. Castellanos makes contact with ease while concentrating on drilling line drives from gap to gap. He has good leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame and shows power in batting practice, though he has yet to do so often in games because his right-handed stroke is fairly flat. He'd fit the offensive profile at first base better if he worked deeper counts and drove the ball more often, as his pure hitting ability is obvious. Though Castellanos lacks speed, he's a decent athlete. He's a fringy defender at first base yet has enough range and arm strength that he also has seen action on both outfield corners during the last two seasons. In the end, however, it will be his bat that takes him to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After exceeding their international bonus pool in 2014-15, the Red Sox had spending limitations the next two periods, but came away with a possible steal for $5,000 in 2015. Castellanos, a Venezuelan, broke into pro ball by batting .326 and leading the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 23 doubles. He made his U.S. debut at age 19 last year, hitting .339 in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League (losing out on the batting title by .001) and getting promoted to Class A to help Greenville win the South Atlantic League title. Despite so-so numbers in Class A this year while he has been bothered by a lower back strain, Castellanos has some of the most intriguing offensive potential in the system. He has an advanced approach, focusing on making line-drive contact from gap to gap while posting an impressive 9 percent strikeout rate in his first two pro seasons. Big and physical, he shows home run power during batting practice and should start doing so in games as he continues to add strength. While most of his value will come from his offense, Castellanos has some defensive versatility. He lacks speed but has decent range and presents a good target at first base. He has average arm strength and saw action on both outfield corners during each of his first two seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $10,000 senior sign as a 14th-rounder in 2015, Poyner pitched on Florida staffs with future Red Sox Brian Johnson and Austin Maddox and five future first-rounders. He has breezed through the Minors with a 2.51 ERA and 5.0 K/BB ratio in his first four pro seasons and made Boston's Opening Day roster in 2018. He spent five separate stints with the eventual World Series champions, logging a 3.22 ERA and a 24/3 K/BB in 22 1/3 innings. Poyner's fastball is tough to grade on the 20-80 scouting scale because it has 40 velocity (ranging from 88-92 mph) with 70 command and 80 deception. Even if it doesn't excite radar guns, his heater plays as a plus pitch, as does his fading changeup. He'll dabble with both a curveball and cutter just to give hitters different looks but both are fringy, and he relies heavily on his main two pitches. Poyner isn't a lefty specialist because he doesn't have a quality breaking ball and actually has been slightly more effective against righties as a pro. He has no margin for error but commands his pitches well and is fearless on the mound. He performed well when the Red Sox trusted him with higher-leverage situations in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Relatively unheralded on stocked Florida pitching staffs that included future Red Sox Brian Johnson and Austin Maddox as well as five first-round arms, Poyner was a $10,000 senior sign as a 14th-rounder in 2015. Other than a rough patch in high Class A during the second half of his first full season, he has carved up pro hitters. He posted a 0.94 ERA after arriving in Double-A last June, lowering his career mark to 2.35 with 168 strikeouts in 149 2/3 innings. Poyner may get more swings and misses on fastballs below 90 mph than any pitcher in the Minors. He usually operates at 88-89 mph but his heater plays as a plus pitch because of exquisite command and a lot of deception. His changeup is also a weapon, and the combination of his two best offerings helped him hold right-handers to a .441 OPS and strike them out at a 35 percent clip last year. Poyner's hybrid breaking ball is closer to a slider than a curveball and doesn't distinguish itself with power or shape, so he's not quite as dominant against left-handers (.654 OPS, 35 percent strikeout rate). He doesn't have much margin for errors but rarely makes mistakes. He doesn't have much left to prove in the Minors and could become a newer version of Craig Breslow for Boston.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox picked Louisville closers in consecutive Drafts, taking Zack Burdi in the first round in 2016 and Henzman in the fourth round the following June. Henzman bounced back from Tommy John surgery as a high school junior in 2013 to star for the Cardinals, ranking third in NCAA Division I with 16 saves in 2017. Moved to the rotation early in his pro career, he compiled a 2.35 ERA in 27 games (22 starts) between two Class A stops in his first full pro season. Henzman thrives when he attacks the bottom of the strike zone with his two best pitches. His changeup has splitter action and helps him lock up left-handers, while his heavy low-90s fastball features plenty of running, sinking and cutting action. His heater tops out at 95 mph but is extremely difficult to lift, as evidenced by his 2.0 groundout/airout ratio in his first two years as a pro. Henzman's ability to come up with a reliable breaking ball will determine whether he ultimately becomes a starter or a multi-inning reliever. He has a fringy slider and has begun trying a curveball. He can't overpower hitters but has shown a knack for pounding the strike zone and generating weak contact early in counts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox took Louisville closers in successive drafts, selecting Zack Burdi in the first round in 2016 and Henzman in the fourth round last year. He overcame Tommy John surgery as a high school junior in 2013 and turned down the Mariners as a sophomore-eligible 31st-rounder in 2016 before ranking third in NCAA Division I with 16 saves last spring. After signing him for $450,000, Chicago shifted him to starting in August. Henzman has the three-pitch mix to make it in the rotation. When he keeps his heavy 90-95 mph fastball down in the zone, batters struggle to lift it, as evidenced by his 2.3 groundout/flyout ratio during his debut. His changeup has similar action, resembling a splitter and grading as a plus pitch at its best, while his cutter reaches the upper 80s. Henzman throws consistent strikes and has a strong build that should lend itself to durability. He started during two years of summer ball while in college, but he has yet to prove he can handle anything close to a full-season pro workload. If he doesn't make it as a starter, he could advance quickly as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The fastest player and one of the best athletes in the 2017 Draft, Holmes gave up a Mississippi State commitment to sign for $988,970 in the second round. Because he was a high schooler from the Northeast and didn't turn 18 until after he turned pro, the Indians knew his development would take time. But he has scuffled more than expected, batting .178 with a 36 percent strikeout rate in his first two pro seasons and missing most of 2018 with a hamstring injury. Holmes has legitimate top-of-the-scale speed that allows him to beat out routine grounders and wreak havoc on the bases. He's still learning to get the most out of his quickness as a basestealer, in part because his offensive and injury struggles have limited his attempts. He can track down balls from gap to gap in center field, and his fringy arm is playable there. Holmes showed some feel for the barrel as an amateur, so his inability to make contact early in his pro career has been surprising. Unlike a lot of elite speedsters, he's not a slappy hitter just trying to put the ball in play, as he has a quick right-handed stroke, at least average raw power and a willingness to drive the ball. He'll need to improve his pitch recognition and tone down his aggressiveness in order to get going offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Without a first-round pick in the 2017 Draft after their offseason signing of free agent Edwin Encarnacion, the Indians went for pure upside with their first-overall pick, selecting Holmes, arguably the class' fastest player, but also one of the rawest, in the second round. The 2016-17 Gatorade Player of the Year for New York, he signed for $988,970 and made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he showed impressive tools, but was largely overmatched in all facets of the game, especially at the plate. Holmes is a true top-of-the-scale runner, possessing elite, 80-grade speed. He had few opportunities to showcase those wheels during his pro debut, however, as Holmes struggled mightily at the plate to the tune of a .182/.220/.289 slash line and 36.1 strikeout rate. When he's right, Holmes will show bat speed, feel for the barrel and even some raw power to his pull side. Scouts believe he will impact the baseball more consistently once he's added strength to his lean frame. Holmes' speed makes him a basestealing threat and gives him range for days in center field, where he could develop into a plus defender. Whether Holmes reaches his lofty ceiling will depend on the development of his hit tool in the coming years. If it comes along enough, he could be the kind of dynamic leadoff hitter teams covet, but rarely find.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Haase was Michigan's best prep position player in 2011, the Indians still surprised a lot of clubs by giving him an over-slot $580,000 bonus in the seventh round to buy him away from an Ohio State commitment. He didn't catch regularly for his high school team and took several years to become an acceptable defender behind the plate. His stock began to rise when he won MVP honors in the Double-A Eastern League playoffs in 2016, and he totaled 47 homers in the upper Minors the next two years before making his big league debut last September. Haase has an all-or-nothing approach at the plate. He's going to swing and miss and he rarely walks, but the loft and strength in his right-handed swing give him tremendous power when he connects. Like most catchers, he offers little value on the bases. Haase has made himself into a decent receiver and scores well in Cleveland's framing metrics. He also has improved the quickness and accuracy of his throws, leading the Triple-A International League by throwing out 49 percent of basestealers in 2018. He doesn't project as a regular but could be useful as a slugging backup who's capable behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Haase landed an above-slot bonus from the Indians as a seventh-rounder in 2011, forgoing his commitment to Ohio State. He struggled to make progress early in his career, but finally advanced to Double-A Akron in his sixth professional season. Returning to Akron in 2017, Haase rewarded the Indians for their patience with a breakout campaign on both sides of the ball before finishing the season in Triple-A. After the season, the Indians rewarded him with a spot on their 40-man roster. Haase has long showed big right-handed power, but he didn't get to it consistently until 2017, when he connected on a career-high 27 homers and paced all Indians farmhands with a .578 slugging percentage after making several key adjustments to his swing. Strikeouts will always be a large part of Haase's game, but he does have some hitting ability as well as a solid approach that yielded a career-best walk rate in '17. Haase's defense, much like his bat, has steadily improved, though questions remain about whether he can catch regularly at the highest level. He's worked to clean up his footwork in recent years while also making gains as a blocker and receiver. He continues to show a strong arm, and it helped him throw out a career-high 37 percent of attempted basestealers in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians didn't spend big on the 2016 international market, with Gonzalez receiving the highest bonus they gave to a position player at $250,000. Like many of the young shortstops Cleveland has signed in recent years, he stands out with his polish at the plate and his instincts. Both were apparent while he batted .286/.381/.373 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons. Gonzalez has good feel for the barrel and making contact, using a compact right-handed swing to stroke line drives to all fields. He controls the strike zone well and has enough bat speed to develop at least 15-homer power once he gets stronger. He knows how to get the most out of his average speed on the bases. Gonzalez's offensive potential overshadows his defensive ability. His internal clock helps him make plays at shortstop, where he displays soft hands and a solid arm. He's capable of playing all over the infield, though his bat would profile at second base rather than third.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez made a name for himself with a strong showing in the Dominican Prospect League before signing with the Indians for $250,000 at the outset of the 2016 international period. Making his professional debut in '17, Gonzalez opened eyes in the Dominican Summer League by hitting .274 with a .371 on-base percentage and 13 steals in 56 games. Gonzalez stands out most for his hitting ability, as he features a compact right-handed swing with bat-to-ball skills that help him generate line-drive contact to all fields. He has pop to the gaps that could develop into some over-the-fence power as he grows into his projectable frame. Gonzalez's wheels aid him on the bases as well as at shortstop, where he profiles as a solid defender with strong instincts, giving hands and an above-average arm. He has the tools to remain at the position, though second base may represent a cleaner fit long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Campos was a key international signing of the Mariners in July 2016, getting a $575,000 bonus to join the organization, his stay there wasn't very long. After a very encouraging professional debut in the Dominican Summer League in '17, he was sent to the A's in the Ryon Healy deal that November. He came stateside for the first time to make his A's debut in '18 and struggled in the Rookie-level Arizona League. He didn't get the chance to improve upon that in 2019 as the UCL in his right elbow needed to be repaired. Campos is an athletic infielder who did keep his defensive profile intact upon his arrival. He's shown the ability to play multiple infield positions with excellent actions and an accurate arm. He might best be suited for second base long-term because he might not have the arm strength for shortstop (especially following elbow surgery), though he still may be given every opportunity to grow into the position as he develops in the lower levels of the A's system. His right-handed bat is still a work in progress. Campos showed an advanced approach in the DSL with the Mariners, drawing more walks than strikeouts, but his K rate spiked in his first go-round in the U.S. There's still a lot to like with Campos, who will be just 20 in 2020 when he returns healthy. Whether he can be an every day middle infielder or a utilityman will depend on how his offensive game progresses as he matures.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners made Campos one of their top international signings early in the 2016-17 period, inking the teenage shortstop out of Venezuela for $575,000 on July 4. He emerged as one of the organization's more promising middle-infield prospects in his first professional season, showing an advanced defensive skill set at shortstop as well a promising bat while playing in the Dominican Summer League. That performance put him on the A's radar, and they acquired him and reliever Emilio Pagan in November in exchange for Ryon Healy, further adding to the organization's glut of promising young shortstops. Evaluators believe Campos has the potential to stick at shortstop. He's an athletic and instinctual defender with good actions and the plus arm strength needed for the position. Campos' above-average speed translates on both sides of the ball, though he has gains to make as a baserunner. At the plate, the right-handed hitter is short to the ball and has good feel for the barrel, resulting in lots of line drives and some gap power, and he already has shown on-base skills -- he recorded more walks (41) than strikeouts (39) in his pro debut - thanks to an advanced approach. Campos has started to grow into his athletic frame since signing and should continue to tack on good strength. His defense-speed combination at an up-the-middle position gives him a possible floor as a big league reserve, though further progress at the plate could very well thrust him into the conversation as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's targeted middle infield talent in the 2016-17 international class, handing out seven-figure bonuses to Marcos Brito and Vargas in July of that summer. Both began their careers playing both shortstop and second in the Dominican Summer League in '17, though Vargas got to the United States ahead of his teammate. Both were together again in the Rookie-level Arizona League in '18. Vargas has outstanding actions defensively and can look very slick at shortstop. Like many young middle infielders, he'll make the spectacular play then boot the routine one, but he has the glove and arm to stay at the premium position despite fringy speed. Vargas' bat needs a lot more work and he hasn't developed much in terms of impacting the ball or pitch recognition, really struggling to pick up breaking stuff. There is some strength to hit the gaps and he did gain 10 pounds this offseason in an effort to become more physical. There are some encouraging tools to work with, but Vargas is still very far away. He hasn't shown much in the way of progress, but there is time for him to become a defensive-minded middle infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked 28th on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2016-17 period, Vargas was regarded by scouts as one of the better defensive shortstops from the Dominican Republic in his class. That present ability, along with his remaining projection, earned Vargas a $1.5 million bonus from the A's on July 2. He began his 2017 pro debut in the Dominican Summer League but received a quick stateside promotion to the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he proved raw but also held his own on both sides of the ball. Vargas is an average runner who stands out at shortstop for his smooth actions and strong arm, the combination of which could make him a plus defender at maturity. There's a chance he will outgrow the position, given his present strength and room for adding more, but he has the defensive tools needed to qualify anywhere on the infield. Offensively, Vargas pairs a quick bat and fluid swing from the right side of the plate to make solid contact to all fields. He swings hard and projects to hit for some power, though just how much will depend on how he develops physically in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2016-17 international amateur class, Brito got $1.1 million to sign with the A's in July 2016. He made his pro debut the following summer and came to the United States, following that up with a step up to the Short-Season New York-Penn League in 2018. While he hasn't wowed with performance, he has made slow and steady progress. It hasn't shown up on the stat line just yet, but Brito has the chance to hit from both sides of the plate, though he's a touch better swinging the bat left-handed. He's added some strength as he's matured and while he's never going to be a power guy, there should be the ability to impact the ball with some extra-base authority to all fields. Brito initially spent time bouncing between second and third, but it's looking more and more likely that second base is his long-term defensive home with an arm that's a little short for the left side of the infield. He could eventually be a plus defender, though right now he mixes in making the spectacular play with losing concentration and making needless errors on routine plays. Brito will play all of the 2019 season at age 19, so there's plenty of time for his production to catch up to his potential. If it all clicks, he eventually could be a solid every day second baseman in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 26 prospect on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 prospects for the 2016-17 international period, Brito showcased his all-around skills during three games at MLB's International Prospect Showcase in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, in February 2016. The A's liked what they saw from the switch-hitting shortstop and signed him for $1.1 million on July 2, and he made his U.S. debut the following year in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Brito has already made a name for himself as a quality hitting prospect, one who has a short, slight-upstroke swing through the hitting zone. He's shown impressive bat speed and the ability to make solid contact to all fields from both sides of the plate, though some scouts believe the teenager might be a better overall hitter from the left side. Brito has a short frame and a medium build with some physical projection, but he's unlikely to offer much in the way of power. In the field, Brito is a raw defender but has soft hands and clean actions. His average arm strength and speed raise questions pertaining to his ability to remain a shortstop, and he saw the bulk of his playing time at second base during his pro debut while logging the occasional start at shortstop and third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last outfielder from Brigham Young University to spend any time in the big leagues was Jaycob Brigman, who was up with the A's for 48 games in 2017. Lund, taken by the Angels in the 11th round of the 2016 Draft, hopes to be the next after reaching Double-A in his first full season, then spending the year there in 2018. Lund is the type who gets the complimentary label from evaluators as being a \"baseball player.\" At his best, he's a table-setting type who gets on base and uses his legs to help his team win. He still strikes out a bit too much, but he did draw walks in 2018 and can shoot line drives to all fields with a flat swing path, albeit without any real power. He's stolen 20 or more bases two years in a row and that should continue to be a big part of his game. He can handle all three outfield positions capably and is fine in center field, the spot he's played most frequently. Center field would be the only spot in the outfield Lund could play full-time. That spot is occupied at the moment in Los Angeles, which is fine because Lund profiles much better as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lund was a performer at Brigham Young University for three years, though did so mostly under the radar. The Angels feel fortunate to have gotten him in the 11th round of the 2016 Draft. The type of over-achiever who would have to prove himself at each level, Lund started to do so quickly in his first full season in 2017, beginning the year in the Class A Midwest League and finishing it up two levels in Double-A. If everything continues to click for Lund, he could be the type of hitter who helps set the table at the top of a lineup. He typically has a solid approach at the plate, making consistent line-drive contact and drawing walks to get on base. He lost sight of that philosophy once he got to Double-A (33 K's, three walks in 29 games) and his strikeout rate did go up with each promotion, so he'll have to make sure he stays true to himself as he advances, as there's no real power for him to rely on. He is a very good runner who knows how to steal a base. That speed also serves him well defensively, where he's shown he can handle all three outfield positions. That versatility should come in handy, as Lund's offensive profile looks more like one of a fourth outfielder in the future. He does have a high baseball IQ and plus makeup, so underselling him could be a mistake.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Angels drafted Swanda in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft and went over slot to sign him away from his Nebraska commitment for $625,000, they knew he would be more of a long-range project as a Midwest product who hadn't pitched a ton before jumping on the radar in his Draft year. The progress has been slow, as Swanda has compiled a grand total of just under 40 innings heading into the 2019 season. A former shortstop, Swanda is athletic on the mound with a sound and repeatable delivery. His fastball sits around the 90-91 mph range now with decent sink to it, and while there hasn't been the uptick in velocity some hoped to see, the right-hander continues to work on adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame, so it still could come. He's shown the ability to spin a solid breaking ball and his changeup continues to be a work in progress, though he's shown some feel for it. That althetic delivery should allow him to continue to keep throwing strikes as he progresses. While he hasn't taken the early step forward some might have liked to have seen from him, the Angels will be patient with Swanda. He'll be just 20 years old for all of the 2019 season, so there's time for him to develop into the starting pitcher many projected him to be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Swanda was primarily a shortstop for his high school team in Iowa who pitched only occasionally. The Angels liked his arm strength and athleticism enough to take him in the fourth round and give him an above-pick value deal of $625,000 to sign him away from heading to the University of Nebraska. The 6-foot-2 right-hander has a long way to go, but there are building blocks to like. Currently, he has largely average stuff across the board, but there's room for growth to go along with a solid delivery and a pretty good feel for pitching, especially considering his lack of experience. His fastball sits around 90 mph right now with a little bit of sink, he can spin a decent breaking ball and there's some feel for a changeup, though that's understandably inconsistent. With his athleticism and solid delivery, the Angels believe Swanda will get to Major League average control. As Swanda learns how to pitch and adds strength to his frame, all of his stuff could start ticking up as he progresses. Internally, the Angels see some Chris Rodriguez potential in Swanda, with similar upside as a future starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2016 Draft approached, members of the Mariners scouting staff went to a big Division II game to watch Brand Miller from Millersville University in Pennsylvania. Their eyes were opened when he was outdueled by Festa, a senior at East Stroudsburg. Seattle drafted both arms, getting Miller in the sixth round and signing Festa for a money-saving $10,000 in the seventh. Miller was traded to the Marlins in July 2017 and has yet to get out of A ball. Festa, meanwhile, transitioned to the bullpen and made his big league debut in 2018. Festa spent some time starting during his pro debut in the summer of 2016, but it was his full-time move to a relief role that allowed him to take off. The right-hander has missed bats at a 11.3 K/9 clip in the Minor Leagues thanks largely to his two above-average pitches in his fastball and slider. The heater sits at 92-95 mph, and his slider has good late break to it. Both played up in short relief, allowing him to lead the organization with 20 saves in 2018. He does have a curve and a changeup he mixes in to give hitters different looks. Festa and his slider were a bit of an unknown when he got to the big leagues and the key to his success will be how well he adjusts when Major League batters adjust to him. His stuff is a little short to close in the big leagues, but he's already exceeded expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Festa appeared in six games for Dominican College (N.Y) as a freshman before transferring to East Stroudsburg University (Pa.), where he showed steady improvement as a starter over the next three years en route to becoming Seattle's seventh-round pick as a senior in 2016. A full-time move to the bullpen led to a breakout first full season for Festa, as he showed impressive bat-missing ability, garnered All-Star honors in the Class A Advanced California League, and then capped his season with a successful turn in the Arizona Fall League. And while he began 2018 in extended spring training due to a hip/sciatic issue, Festa quickly made up for the lost time in Double-A upon returning and earned his first big league promotion in July. Festa's smooth delivery and short, clean arm action create late life on a fastball that will sit 92-95 mph while touching 96. He pairs his heater with a sharp, late-breaking slider in the mid- to upper-80s, and it's those two offerings that enabled him to pace all California League relievers with 13.1 strikeouts-per-nine innings. The right-hander also has a curveball and changeup, both slightly below-average pitches, at his disposal, and his entire arsenal does play up on account of his solid control and command. Festa's four-pitch mix and overall durability makes him a candidate to one day rejoin a starting rotation, should the Mariners ever choose to pursue that route. For now, however, it's Festa's knack for missing bats using largely his fastball-slider combo that is his ticket to a potential late-inning role in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nothing has come easily to Filia in the game of baseball. He missed two years at UCLA, one because of labrum surgery on his throwing shoulder and one because of a suspension for plagiarizing part of a paper for a class. By the time he was a 20th-round pick in the 2016 Draft, he was nearly 24 years old. He made up for lost time by hitting .326 in the California League in his first full season, then won both the batting title and the Stenson Sportsmanship Award in the Arizona Fall League that fall (after becoming the father of twins). He earned a 50-game suspension for a second positive test for a drug of abuse to start the 2018 season, got off to a red-hot start in Double-A, then was traded to the Red Sox in June to complete the Roenis Elias trade, only to be sent back because of a failed physical. With everything he's been through, Filia still knows how to have a quality at-bat. He's hit .319 in his pro career, entering 2019 with a lot more walks than strikeouts. While he doesn't have much over-the-fence power, he's shown he can impact the baseball and send line drives to all fields, which is still his calling card. He's adequate defensively in the outfield and was making a move to first base. Now he's likely to be asked to do both. Filia will have to keep hitting to get to the big leagues, but the good news is it looks like he has the skills do it. Whether he can do it in a part-time bench role will determine what kind of career he has, with a late-arriving Daniel Nava-type career a possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Filia emerged as UCLA's leading postseason hitter during the team's 2013 College World Series championship run, only to miss all of the next two seasons. He lost 2014 after injuring his right (throwing) shoulder and requiring labrum surgery, then he was suspended for all of '15 after he plagiarized part of a paper for a philosophy class. Filia returned to the Bruins in 2016 and then signed for $1,000 as a 20th-round pick at age 24, making him one of the oldest players in the 2016 Draft. After excelling in his first full season in the Class A Advanced California League and then again in the Arizona Fall League, Filia was suspended for the first 50 games of the 2018 season following his second positive test for a drug of abuse in January. The Red Sox acquired him in June as the player to be named in the trade that sent Roenis Elias to the Mariners in April, only to return him to Seattle several days later and instead settle for cash considerations to complete the trade. Filia has one of the more advanced approaches among Minor League hitters, with outstanding pitch and zone recognition, plus bat-to-ball skills and innate feel to hit from line to line. He led the Northwest League in hitting (.362) and on-base percentage (.450) and won the short-season circuit's MVP in his pro debut, and then ranked first in the California League in OBP (.407) and third in batting (.326) in his sophomore campaign. He encored with standout performance in the Arizona Fall League, where he saw time at both corner outfield positions as well as first base. Pure hitting ability and on-base skills -- he accrued 20 more walks than strikeouts in 2017 -- are Filia's calling cards to the Major Leagues, as he otherwise possesses average-at-best tools. But while it may be easy to peg him as a future fourth or fifth outfielder, there's something to be said about Filia's track record of surpassing expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best infield prospects available on the international market at the start of the 2017-18 signing period, Querecuto signed with the Mariners in July 2017 for $1.225 million. The son of former Minor League catcher Juan and younger brother of Juniel, who reached the big leagues with the Rays in 2016 and spent the 2018 season in the D-backs system, the younger Juan will bring his combination of skills and instincts to the United States for the first time in 2019. While his older brother is a 5-foot-8 utility type, Querecuto already stands 6-foot-2, with a lean and lanky frame. His glovework is currently ahead of his bat, partially because of his outstanding defensive skills and partially because of a lack of physicality at the plate. His hands, actions and plus arm all point to a future at shortstop, but a lack of speed and, as a result, range will mean he'll have to use his very high baseball IQ to stick at the premium position, something that is way too early to rule out. He does have a decent approach from the right side of the plate, with a willingness to draw walks. He will have to add strength in order to have any impact as a hitter. He has grown physically and mentally since signing, so the Mariners are hopeful there's more to unlock as he comes stateside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the son of Minor League catcher Juan Querecuto and younger brother of Juniel Querecuto, who reached the Majors with the Rays in 2016, the young Venezuelan shortstop has certainly grown up around the game. The No. 26 prospect on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2017-18 period, he signed for $1.225 million on July 2. Querecuto is a confident prospect with good plate discipline and good instincts on both sides of the ball. The teen has showed a mature approach, good bat speed and the ability to hit the ball to all fields. Scouts believe he'll add some power as he grows into his projectable frame, albeit mostly to the gaps rather than true over-the-fence pop. Defensively, Querecuto's plus arm strength is more than enough for him to remain at shortstop, where he stands out for his clean actions, soft hands and overall feel for the position. His remaining physical projection could ultimately force him to third base, a position he has the requisite tools for, though it also would place greater pressure on his offensive development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rumbelow spent three years as an impactful reliever at LSU, leading to a seventh-round selection in the 2013 Draft by the Yankees, who thought he could quickly provide bullpen support in the big leagues. Sure enough, he was in the big leagues in 2015, but then missed nearly all of 2016 following Tommy John surgery. He was designated for assignment, then re-signed by the Yankees, and he then went and pitched his way back onto the 40-man roster in 2017 before getting sent to the Mariners in a Minor League deal. His first year in the system was interrupted by injury, but he did make it back up to the big leagues last June. At his best, Rumbelow relies on his fastball-breaking ball combination. He's always been aggressive on the mound, dating back from his LSU days, and he's still learning how to do that at the highest level. His fastball will touch 96 mph thrown with good deception thanks to an unorthodox delivery. His breaking ball is an above-average power curve with good depth that misses bats. Rumbelow does have an above-average changeup, but he has had trouble getting to it enough for it to be effective. Some of that has been because of fastball command, especially when Rumbelow's been in the big leagues and hitters haven't chased his stuff out of the strike zone. If he can attack hitters within the zone as he has at times, he has the stuff to earn high leverage innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick out of Louisiana State in 2013, Rumbelow made his big league debut two years later, his first of four stints with the Yankees in 2015. He logged one inning back in Triple-A the following year before undergoing season-ending Tommy John surgery, and the Yankees designated him for assignment that November. Re-signed by New York to a Minor League deal before 2017, Rumbelow returned to the mound in June and pitched well enough across the Double- and Triple-A levels that the Yankees felt inclined to add him to their 40-man roster in November. It wasn't long thereafter that they dealt him to the Mariners in exchange for JP Sears and Juan Then. Rumbelow has three effective pitches, each of which grades as at least above-average. His best offering is his fastball, which sits at 92-94 mph, reaches 96 and plays up thanks to the deception created by his over-the-top release point and long arm action. He throws his curveball with power and depth in the low 80s, along with a changeup in the mid-80s that features splitter-like tumble. Rumbelow can miss bats with his entire arsenal and has thrown more strikes as a pro than was expected of him coming out of LSU. That the Mariners traded a pair of promising young arms for Rumbelow underscored their belief in him as an impactful big league reliever. After battling injuries and missing the first two months of the season, Rumbelow returned fully healthy in early June and earned his first callup with the Mariners two weeks later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of St. Maarten who moved to the Dominican Republic, Wilson has shown glimpses of tremendous tools ever since signing for $350,000 back in December 2014. He came to the United States to make his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League, reached full-season ball in 2017 and played across two levels of A ball in 2018. At times, Wilson will show all five tools. He'll show glimpses of using the whole field from the left side of the plate. But then he'll hit a home run or two, and he'll get pull happy, with his front side flying open and his swing mechanics getting out of whack. He has tremendous raw power, and it will be how his hit tool develops that determines how consistently he can tap into it. He runs well and can steal a base, and that speed allows him to cover ground in the outfield. He can play all three spots in the outfield capably, with right field the most logical spot for him to settle into should he find an every day role. At 21 years old for all of 2019, there is plenty of time for Wilson to figure things out. If he can buy into what he can do and refine his game plan at the plate, he could still turn into a dynamic big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in St. Maarten, Wilson moved to the Dominican Republic to train and caught the attention of Braves scouts before joining the organization for $350,000 in December 2014. He made his professional debut in the United States, in the Gulf Coast League in 2015, and has been making incremental progress in sharpening his considerable raw tools since, reaching full-season ball for the first time in 2017. Wilson was a shortstop as an amateur, but the Braves moved him to the outfield right after he signed and he took to it immediately, with the range and instincts to stay in center and enough arm to play right, seeing time in both spots so far. He's made strides in his overall approach at the plate and could eventually be close to an average power, which will help him tap into considerable raw power, especially as he continues to add strength. Wilson has worked to be more than the pure pull hitter he was when he started, learning to use the middle of the field. The in-game power he has displayed is still to the pull side, but he should be able to drive the ball to all fields in time. There is a lot of upside potential to unlock with Wilson, who will play all of the 2018 season at age 20. He could shoot up this list with another step in the right direction this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hill emerged as Texas A&M's No. 1 starter as a sophomore in 2016 after he had opened the year in the Aggies' bullpen, and he was one of the better Friday starters in the Southeastern Conference as a junior. He signed for $291,200 after the Nationals made him their fifth-round pick, then pitched his way up to full-season ball in his pro debut. Returning to Class A Hagerstown for his first full season, Hill was plagued by an oblique injury and logged just 50 innings in the South Atlantic League. Hill worked in the low 90s mph and topped out at 94 with the Aggies, and he more or less showed the same type of velocity at Hagerstown. He commands his fastball well and pairs it with a plus changeup that was considered to be one of the best in his Draft class. Together, the two pitches helped Hill record a 61 percent ground-ball rate that led all Nats full-season pitchers (50 IP min.). He also has feel for spinning an average curveball. Hill pitched with above-average control during college and in his pro debut but regressed in that department in 2018 while missing fewer bats. The Nationals are hopeful that he'll get back on track in 2019 with a clean bill of health, and they've long viewed him as someone who has the confidence and makeup needed to maximize his ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
