mlb_pipeline.text: After barely pitching as a freshman and opening 2016 in Texas A&M's bullpen, Hill took over as the Aggies' No. 1 starter by April. He would have gone in the top five rounds if signable, but ultimately slid to the Athletics in the 20th. Returning to College Station for his senior year, Hill was one of the best Friday starters in the Southeastern Conference before going to the Nationals in the fifth round and signing for slot value. After pitching at 91-93 mph and hitting 96 as a sophomore, Hill worked at 89-91 mph and topped out at 94 with the Aggies. He commands his fastball well, albeit with little movement, and it sets up a plus changeup that ranked among the best in his Draft class. He used a curveball more than a slider this year, and it gives him an average third pitch. Though Hill throws plenty of strikes and succeeded for two years in college baseball's best conference, there still are concerns about his long-term viability as a starter. He's a small right-hander who had Tommy John surgery as a high school sophomore. Club officials do rave about his confidence and makeup and believe he'll get the most out of his ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After taking a pair of high school pitchers at the top of their 2017 Draft, the Pirates went after prep bats with their next two selections in Calvin Mitchell and Uselton. While Mitchell has started to take off, Uselton has had trouble finding any traction. His debut summer ended after a serious hamstring injury, and he struggled to hit in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2018. The 2018 season was meant mostly for Uselton to get his professional legs under him, especially since he completely tore his hamstring the previous summer. It's unclear if there were some lingering effects, but he never could get his right-handed bat going. Uselton is believed to be more power over hit with some strength and leverage to his swing, and the Pirates still hope his power will start to show up the further removed from the injury he is. He'll need to get back to driving the ball to all fields. Uselton is also a former football player, and that athleticism was a plus for him as he entered pro ball. He played center field in high school, but played right in the Appy League in 2018. His arm works from the corner spot and if he can show the power potential he did as an amateur, he could profile well there offensively as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates went high school heavy at the top of the 2017 Draft, taking a prep player with each of their first four picks. Uselton, a former high school quarterback who focused on baseball after his sophomore year, was the fourth of that quartet to be taken. The Pirates only got to see him play two games in the Gulf Coast League during his pro debut with a hamstring injury ending his summer after just seven at-bats. Uselton did return to health in time to head to the organization's instructs in the Dominican Republic, where he was able to play for a couple of weeks before embarking on his offseason plan. The outfielder is more power over hit at this point, with some strength and leverage in his right-handed swing. In the past, he's had some mechanical issues with that swing, but he smoothed some of that during his senior year and showed he is capable of driving the ball to all fields. A solid athlete who runs fairly well, Uselton played center field in high school. He's likely to mostly play in an outfield corner as a pro, where his plus arm, not to mention his power profile, will play very well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It took Eusebio until his third summer of pro ball to reach the United States after signing out of the Dominican Republic for $100,000 in 2013, and he didn't reach full-season ball until July of season No. 4, though he was shut down before the season's end with an oblique injury. More patience has been needed as the talented left-hander needed Tommy John surgery after just three starts back in the South Atlantic League in 2018. When healthy, Eusebio stands out for his feel for pitching and was much more advanced than most young pitchers just coming to the U.S. His above-average fastball and curve combination have promise, with his heater topping out at 95-96 mph with good sink and his breaking ball showing power and depth at times. His changeup should be at least average in the future. He has a very good feel for changing speeds and eye levels for hitters and isn't afraid to come inside. Eusebio's rehab has gone well and he was progressing on schedule. The Rockies hope to see him pitching competitively with a full-season club by midseason, with plenty of time for him to reach his ceiling as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, Eusebio spent his first two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and began his next two in the short-season Northwest League. He made the jump to full-season ball last July, making eight starts before getting shut down with a strained oblique. He made just three starts in 2018 before going down with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. Prior to getting hurt, Eusebio showed signs of developing a plus fastball and curveball, though both offerings need more consistency. He worked at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 mph with good sink on his heater and his curveball featured power and depth. His changeup had its moments too, though it wasn't as effective as his top two pitches. Eusebio has a very compact delivery and is learning to repeat it efficiently. He should have at least average control but his command isn't yet as advanced, so he's more hittable than a lefty who can provide three solid pitches should be. If he can return to health and make the necessary refinements, he could be a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since getting drafted in the 10th round of the 2016 Draft and signing for full pick value out of UC-Riverside, Fernandez has shown he can do a little bit of everything well, particularly hit for power. That's come with a growing strikeout rate and in very hitting-friendly environments has some curious to see if it will work as he attacks the higher levels of the Rockies system. The power was showing up in his first taste of Double-A in 2019 when he was suspended for 50 games after testing positive for an amphetamine. There's no question Fernandez has some raw power from the left side of the plate, and he hit a career high 24 homers in 2018, albeit with some fairly dramatic home-road splits and most of his pop coming in Lancaster's bandbox of a ballpark. His strikeout rate has also crept up in each year of pro ball, though so has his walk rate, and he must cut down on his 34.5 percent strikeout rate from a year ago to have a chance as he advances. Fernandez runs well enough to steal an occasional base and cover ground in the outfield. He's seen almost all of his time defensively in the outfield corners, with enough arm for right. If he can learn to make enough contact, he could be a fourth outfielder type who provides left-handed pop off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fernandez showed off his pop by leading the Big West Conference with 112 total bases in 2016. That and his package of decent all-around tools got him drafted in the 10th round out of UC Riverside that June. He finished fifth in the low Class A South Atlantic League with 16 homers during his first full pro season despite missing a month with an oblique injury. He did much more damage at hitter-friendly Asheville (.913 OPS) than he did on the road (.717), however. Though Fernandez has enough raw power to hit at least 20 homers per season, he'll have to tone down his approach at the plate to get there. His left-handed swing is relatively sound but he's overly aggressive, resulting in a 29 percent strikeout rate last year. He has remained productive in 2018 at high Class A Lancaster, perhaps the best hitting environment in the Minors, but his all-out mentality may lead to struggles at higher levels. Fernandez possesses average speed out of the box, is a little quicker once he gets going and can steal an occasional base. He has enough arm strength to play right field, though he spent much of 2017 in left in deference to teammate Willie Abreu.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beaty increased his OPS in each of his four years at Belmont, batting .382/.469/.668 as a senior in 2015 and becoming the highest-drafted player in Bruins history when the Dodgers grabbed him in the 12th round. He broke out in 2017, winning the Texas League MVP award and leading the Double-A circuit in batting (.326) and OPS (.883). An intercostal strain and a torn thumb ligament ruined his encore, limiting him to just 34 games last year. With a disciplined approach and quality hand-eye coordination, Beaty makes repeated line-drive contact to all fields. He made some adjustments to his left-handed swing in mid-2017 that allowed him to drive the ball more often for some pull power, but he still stands out more for his hitting and on-base ability than as a home run threat. He has struggled against left-handers in the upper Minors, so he'll have to adapt or risk being tagged as a platoon player. A fringy runner with an average arm, Beaty has split most of his career between first base and third base. He's a decent defender at either corner and also has made brief appearances at second base, left field and right field as a pro. He also did some catching as an amateur and his versatility will come in handy as he tries to crack a Los Angeles roster with an overload of corner-infield options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-drafted position player in Belmont history, Beaty increased his OPS every year with the Bruins and batted .382/.469/.668 as a senior before signing for $60,000 as a 12th-rounder in 2015. He has steadily improved in his first three pro seasons as well, winning the 2017 Texas League MVP award after topping the Double-A circuit in batting (.326) and OPS (.883). An intercostal strain and a torn thumb ligament have prevented him from putting up much of an encore this year. Similar to fellow underappreciated Dodgers corner-infield prospect Edwin Rios, with more pure hitting ability but less power, Beaty makes consistent contact thanks to his disciplined approach and hand-eye coordination. He made some adjustments to his left-handed swing last summer so he could hit for more power, and 12 of his 15 homers came in the final three months. He handled lefties well in his first two pro seasons before slipping to a .651 OPS against them last year, and he'll have to improve to avoid being labeled as a platoon player. With fringy first-step quickness and an average arm, Beaty serves as a decent defender at either infield corner. He also has played second base and both outfielder corners in pro ball and did some catching as an amateur. Beating out Cody Bellinger or Justin Turner for a starting job in Los Angeles may be an impossible task, but his bat and versatility could make him a useful reserve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard spurned the Giants when they took him in the 31st round as a sophomore-eligible in 2015, opting to play for the U.S. collegiate national team and return to Missouri. San Francisco reeled him in the following June as a fifth-rounder and jumped him to high Class A for his first full season. He has one of the higher floors in the system and is in line to make his big league debut at some point in 2019. Already one of the best contact hitters among Giants farmhands, Howard improved his plate discipline in Double-A last season. He only has modest power, however, and may not make enough impact offensively to play every day in the Majors. He's an average runner with keen baserunning instincts. Howard also has a good internal clock and solid arm that help him make plays at shortstop despite fringy range there. A steady defender, he profiles better as a second baseman or utilityman. He also has seen action at third base in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants tried to sign Howard as a sophomore-eligible in 2015, but he turned them down as a 31st-rounder to play for the U.S. collegiate national team and return to Missouri. So they drafted him again the following June and nabbed him in the fifth round. He responded to a high Class A assignment in his first full pro season by batting .306 and has held his own in Double-A in 2018. While Howard makes contact more easily than most hitters in the system, he'll have to improve upon his modest power and on-base skills to profile as a regular. He may have some untapped strength that could translate into double-digit power if he does a better job of incorporating his legs into his right-handed swing. He has average speed but his instincts help him play quicker than that on the bases and in the field. Howard played solely at shortstop in his pro debut, split time between there and third base in the first two months of 2017, then returned exclusively to short. He has fringy range at shortstop but his solid arm helps him make plays. He profiles better at second base or as a utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees' trade for Luke Voit last July gave them not only a surprising slugger who hit 14 homers in the final two months of the season, but also international bonus pool money in exchange for shipping Giovanny Gallegos and Chasen Shreve to the Cardinals. They used most of that extra cash to sign Rodriguez for $600,000 the next day. He had overmatched Cuba's 15-and-under league and starred for its youth national teams before defecting. Somewhat reminiscent of former Yankees star Orlando Hernandez, Rodriguez has a seemingly endless combination of pitches and arm slots. He has an electric arm that produces 92-95 mph fastballs that top out at 97 with high spin rates that give him riding life up in the strike zone. His hard curveball is a bit more effective than his harder slider, with both displaying the potential to become plus pitches, and his changeup has splitter action and similar upside. Though Rodriguez varying his arm angle adds to his deception, New York probably will try to condense his pitch/slot options. Minor aches and pains have limited him in 2019. He doesn't have the cleanest arm action and there's effort in his delivery, yet he had no difficulty throwing strikes as an amateur. He has a lofty ceiling, as his chance to develop four plus offerings could make him a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Myatt helped Florence-Darlington (S.C.) Tech reach the Junior College World Series for the first time in 2017, touching 98 mph with his fastball but going undrafted because of signability concerns. He continued to light up radar guns as a sophomore and signed for a slightly over-slot $147,500 as an 11th-rounder last June. Though he got knocked around for a 5.40 ERA in his pro debut, he excited the Yankees with the progress he made with his secondary pitches. In junior college, Myatt relied heavily on his fastball, which parks in the mid-90s and peaks at 99 with some riding life. His 6-foot-7 frame gives him extension that adds deception and late finish to his heater. He also has power and some depth to his curveball, which has shown more consistency since he turned pro. Myatt's changeup has a bit of fade and also has started to improve as he has used it more often in pro ball. Though he's athletic, he's still learning to keep his mechanics in sync and has no track record of throwing strikes. New York sees him as a potential three-pitch starter but he could wind up as a flamethrowing reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maryland's top high school prospect in 2017, Cortijo impressed scouts with his speed and athleticism as an outfielder but they liked him more as a pitcher. He committed to Seminole State (Fla.) CC as a two-way player before signing with the Yankees for $125,000 in the 14th round. After relieving in his pro debut, he was the most effective starter at short-season Staten Island as a 19-year-old last summer. Cortijo has a quick arm that produces 91-95 mph fastballs with armside run. He has one of the better changeups in the system, getting some fade and good velocity separation from his heater. He'll need a better breaking ball than his presently slurvy slider when he faces more advanced hitters. Utilizing a fluid delivery, Cortijo has pounded the strike zone in his first two years as a pro. To remain a starter going forward, he'll need to improve his slider and prove his fastball will hold up under an increased workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Pirates fourth-round pick in 2011, Brewer pitched in just 11 games in his first four pro seasons and did little to distinguish himself before the Yankees claimed him in the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft at the 2016 Winter Meetings. The Red Sox tried to sign him as a Minor League free agent after the 2017 season but lost out to the Padres, who also rebuffed trade overtures from Boston last summer. Looking for low-cost bullpen options, the Sox finally landed him in a November trade for second-base prospect Esteban Quiroz. Brewer's signature pitch is described by different evaluators as a fastball with unusual cutting action or a cutter with unusual velocity. Whatever you want to call it, it sits at 92-94 mph and reaches 96 with tremendous natural life, missing bats and generating a lot groundouts. He relies on it heavily and also mixes in a low-80s curveball with power and depth that he can't always land for strikes. Brewer endeared himself to the Red Sox's analytic department with the movement on his pitches, high spin rates and pronounced groundout/airout rates (1.7 in his Minor League career). He throws strikes but battled his command in the big leagues with San Diego last year. If he can do a better job of locating his pitches, he could become a valuable member of Boston's 2019 bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A dominant Cape Cod League performance in 2016 set Schellenger up to go early in the 2017 Draft until biceps tendinitis sidelined him and sapped his stuff the next spring at Seton Hall. Boston bet a sixth-round pick and $175,000 bonus that he could bounce back, but he worked just three innings in his pro debut and 16 1/3 last year while dealing with back issues and a shoulder impingement. Healthy toward the end of the 2018 season and during instructional league, he excited the Red Sox with his fastball/slider combination. Schellenger's fastball sat around 90 mph at the end of his college career and his entry into pro ball, but it ranged from 93-97 mph with heavy sink late last year. His mid-80 slider was just as devastating, especially against right-handers. Multiple club officials likened him to the healthy version of Carson Smith. Schellenger still has a lot to prove. He has to show he can stay on the mound, maintain quality stuff throughout a full pro season and throw strikes consistently from a low three-quarters delivery with effort. If he can do that, he could accelerate quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baldwin was a catcher when he signed for $45,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, yet spent the majority of his first three pro seasons at third base. He moved back behind the plate full-time in 2017, when he finished second in the low Class A South Atlantic League in doubles (35) and slugging (.489), then homered twice in the playoffs to help Greenville win the championship. He broke his right thumb when hit by a pitch in Spring Training in 2018, setting the stage for a season in which he played just 53 games amid four trips to the disabled list, and has yet to play in 2019 after breaking his ankle on a slide during the spring. Baldwin is very much an offensive-minded catcher. He's strong and has solid raw power, with most of his home runs presently coming to his pull side. He makes consistent contact from the right side of the plate, though he could be more productive if he employed a more patient approach and did a better job of using the entire field. Because he caught just 187 games through his first five years as a pro, Baldwin is very much a work in progress defensively. He has solid arm strength and has improved the accuracy of his throws, erasing 45 percent of basestealers in 2018. The Red Sox believe he has the physical ability to get the job done as a receiver and blocker, but he still struggles in those aspects of the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Encarnacion, at age 18, was slightly older than the typical international prospect when the Braves inked him in May 2016. Making his United States debut the next year, Encarnacion impressed in both the Gulf Coast and Appalachian Leagues, putting him much more firmly on the prospect radar, and he made a nice transition to full-season ball in '18. His performance and progress caught the Orioles' attention, and the club acquired him along with Brett Cumberland, Evan Phillips and Bruce Zimmermann for Kevin Gausman at the Trade Deadline. A tall, lean and athletic player, Encarnacion oozes projection and upside. He's shown that he can impact the baseball to all fields from the right side, with impressive hand-eye coordination that allows him to find the barrel consistently. But after striking out nearly 28 percent of the time in 2018, with a sub-4 percent walk rate, he'll have to improve his plate discipline and pitch recognition to continue hitting for average. Progress on that front should also help him tap into his plus raw power, which is sure to show up even more as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. Encarnacion initially played some shortstop after signing, but he spent all of 2018 at third base. He's a raw and inconsistent defender at the hot corner right now, with arm strength and actions that give him a chance to stay there long-term. If that doesn't work out, a move down the defensive spectrum to first base is a possibility. While still very raw in all facets of the game, Encarnacion's upside is undeniable, and he has the type of dynamic tools to make it all work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the White Sox called Frare up last September, he joined Les Rohr (the No. 2 overall pick in 1965) as the only pitchers ever drafted out of a Montana high school to reach the big leagues. Signed for $100,000 by the Yankees as an 11th-rounder in 2012, he blew out his elbow and missed the next two seasons following Tommy John surgery. New York traded him to Chicago for $1.5 million in international bonus pool money last July. There's nothing subtle about Frare, who goes after hitters with a pair of power pitches. His four-seam fastball sits at 92-96 mph and peaks at 98 with riding life up in the strike zone. His slider/cutter also grades as a plus offering, arriving at 87-91 mph with some tilt. Left-handers managed just one extra-base hit in 90 at-bats against Frare in 2018, and he's also effective against right-handers. The key for him to finding a niche in the White Sox bullpen will be developing reliable control and command. He averaged 4.6 walks per nine innings in his first five years as a pro and got knocked around in the Majors when he fell behind in the count.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Cuba, Delgado moved to Florida as a child and wound up DHing for the U.S. national 18-and-under team that won a gold medal at the 2017 World Cup and featured a lineup with five future first-rounders and three other players who commanded seven-figure bonuses. He lasted until the sixth round in the 2018 Draft amid signability concerns but still landed a $900,000 bonus, the equivalent of late second-round money. He posted a .790 OPS and ranked third in the Rookie-level Arizona League with 30 walks during his pro debut. One of the more physical infielders in Cleveland's system, Delgado is a switch-hitter who has a chance to hit for average and power. He works counts well and has a track record of producing against top amateur competition. Though he slugged just .382 in his first taste of pro ball, he has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop into a 20-homer threat. Delgado bounced between shortstop, second base and third base during his debut, and his future defensive home remains in question. Though his instincts help him make plays at shortstop, his fringy speed and average arm won't hold up there in the long term. Second base may be his best bet, though he'd profile well at third base if he can strengthen his arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Woodrow improved in each of his three years at Creighton, earning Big East All-Conference honors as a junior. The Tigers took Woodrow in the 12th round that June, signing him for $150,000. He's done nothing but produce as a pro, using his blend of hitting ability, speed and defense to move quickly through the Tigers' system. He was a Midwest League All-Star in his first full season and played just five games at Class A Advanced Lakeland at the outset of 2018 before advancing to Double-A, where he was an Eastern League All-Star and produced a .317 average with 23 steals. After the season, Woodrow continued to boost his prospect stock with a strong turn in the Arizona Fall League. Woodrow has a good feel for what he's doing at the plate. His approach is geared toward hitting the ball back up the middle, and he does so often using a short left-handed swing. While Woodrow's contact is mostly of the ground-ball variety, it actually plays into his strength because he's a plus-plus runner with well-below-average power. Woodrow is a skilled bunter, with the ability to lay it down either line, and he's an aggressive, sometimes over-aggressive basestealer. He fared better against same-sided arms (.340 average) than righties (.301) in Double-A. Woodrow's wheels enable him to play center field, and he's seen significant time at all three outfield spots in full-season ball. That versatility, along with his speed and bat, give Woodrow a clear path to the Majors as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Deatherage hit just .218 as a junior after combining for a .307 average during his first two years at North Carolina State. The Pirates still took him in the 29th round that year, but Deatherage returned to college for his senior year. It proved a smart decision, as he set career highs in home runs (14) and steals (18) as a senior, leading to his selection by the Tigers in the 10th round. After signing for $10,000, Deatherage kicked off his pro debut with a three-homer game in the Gulf Coast League and finished the season at Class A Advanced Lakeland, ultimately slashing .326/.385/.504 with 19 steals across three levels. While he has good raw power to his pull side, Deatherage projects for below-average game power as he climbs the ladder and faces better pitching. He should hit for some average, though, and he adds value on both sides of the ball with his plus-plus speed. Those wheels give him a chance to stick in center, where he's an above-average defender with good instincts. Deatherage has made fans with his aggressive style of play and grinder mentality at every stage of his career. After a promising debut, he could move quickly as a future fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever for most of his college career at Mississippi State, Houston raised his profile a bit with some big starts down the stretch of his junior season. The Tigers, who have never shied away from arm strength, took him in the 11th round and immediately returned him to a relief role. After he pitched effectively across two levels of A ball during his first full season of pro ball, Houston excelled at Double-A and Triple-A in 2018, finishing the year on the cusp of the Major Leagues. Houston combines, size, power stuff and a funky delivery to get hitters out. The 6-foot-5 right-hander employs a jump in his delivery that reminds some of Carter Capps. It helps him create huge extension toward the plate, which in turn gives his fastball a higher effective velocity than 92-94 mph. He mixes in a slider that can be erratic, but helps him miss a ton of bats. He struck out 13-per-nine in 2018, bring his career average to 13.8 K/9. Houston has generated weak contact and struck out hitters in bunches in his pro career, but his lack of command (career 4.4 BB/9) makes it tougher to see him in a closing role. If he can find the strike zone more consistently, he does have the chance to pitch meaningful innings as a setup type reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pacific Northwest's top prep prospect in 2018, Schroeder signed for an over-slot $1.25 million as a second-round choice. He was the only high school pitcher selected by the Astros in the first 34 rounds last year, and he joins Lance McCullers Jr., Austin Nicely and Forrest Whitley as the only prep arms signed from the top 10 rounds in Jeff Luhnow's first seven Drafts as Houston GM. The Astros limited Schroeder to 18 innings in his debut, having him focus more on getting acclimated to their organization and to pro ball. Schroeder's fastball and curveball both have the potential to become plus pitches. He works at 91-95 mph and reaches 97 mph with heavy sink on his heater, and he shows advanced feel for spinning his mid-70s curve. He also flashes a sharp low-80s slider on occasion and has begun refining a changeup he rarely used as an amateur. As an amateur, Schroeder showed a sound delivery and repeated it well, which allowed him to locate his pitches better than most teenagers. But his control has fallen apart in 2019, leading to a lost season. His 6-foot-2 frame is fairly mature so he doesn't have much projection remaining, but his present stuff could make him a mid-rotation starter if he can rediscover the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Astros' franchise-record $19.3 million international spending spree in 2016, Carrasco signed for $480,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He made his U.S. debut last summer, ranking fifth in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League with 17 steals in just 38 games and batting .333 in the short-season New York-Penn League playoffs to help Tri-City win the championship. He's one of the smaller position players in the Houston system at 5-foot-9 and also one of the fastest, with his speed earning 65-70 grades on the 20-80 scouting scale. Carrasco could be a dangerous basestealer once he improves his reads and jumps, and he needs to do a better job of bunting for hits. A left-handed hitter, he has some patience at the plate but needs to improve the frequency and quality of his contact. He has some quickness to his swing that produces occasional power to the gaps, but getting on base is his primary offensive focus. While Carrasco still seeks consistency on defense, there's no question he has the tools to stick at shortstop. He has smooth actions, solid range, soft hands and a cannon arm that has been clocked at 100 mph on throws across the diamond. Houston believes his makeup will help him get the most out of his tools, and he has the highest upside of any middle infielder in the system with the exception of Freudis Nova.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adolph rebounded from multiple knee surgeries earlier in his career to lead the Mid-American Conference and set a Toledo record with 15 homers last spring. After signing with the Mets for $125,000 as a 12th-rounder, he led the short-season New York-Penn League in triples (12) and ranked third in OPS (.857). He came to the Astros in January along with second baseman Luis Santana and catcher Scott Manea in exchange for J.D. Davis and infielder Cody Bohanek. Adolph possesses two plus tools in his raw power and speed. A left-handed hitter, he has the strength to drive the ball out of the park to all fields but most of his home runs presently come to his pull side. He'll need to improve his plate discipline to hit for average against more advanced pitching. While teams worried about his medical history, Adolph has the upside of a 20-20 player who can stay in center field. He played center for the Rockets and all three outfield spots in his pro debut, showing the quickness to cover the gaps but also a need to refine his reads and routes. His average arm works anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because the A's went into the penalty during their international spending spree during the 2016-17 signing period, they were limited to a $300,000 maximum on individual bonuses in the 2017-18 period. That didn't stop them from aggressively pursuing talent, as they handed out 11 six-figure bonuses of $300,000 or less. They may have gotten a bargain when they were able to ink Blanco, a former Cuban star, for $200,000. When Blanco made his A's debut in the California League in 2018, it had been nearly two years since he had played competitively in Cuba. At the outset, it was all about his speed, an 80 on the 20-to-80 scouting scale, and defense. But he quickly shook the rust off and showed more offensive acumen than anticipated. There wasn't as much swing and miss as some expected to see and he often showed a solid approach at the plate, with some signs of potential extra-base ability. His physicality and speed could add up to an average hitter. There's no doubt Blanco's speed is his calling card. It allows him to be aggressive on the basepaths (22 steals in 82 games in his debut) and really go get the ball in the outfield. After his first season was cut short by a hamate injury, it will be interesting to see how quickly he can climb the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson-Williams showed enough glimpses of his athleticism translating into production in two years at Iowa Western Community College and then one season at South Carolina to get taken in the fifth round of the 2016 Draft by the Yankees. Things really didn't start clicking for the outfielder until 2018, when he put in a 20-20 season, mostly in the Florida State League, and earned a bump up to Double-A for the Eastern League playoffs. The Mariners had always liked his tools and acquired him in the package for James Paxton last November. DTW's power-speed combination has always been intriguing, but it's possible he tried to rely too much on his natural gifts in his first year-plus of pro ball. But he put in the work leading up to the offseason, which led to him producing 22 homers and 20 steals. He has serious raw pop from the left side of the plate, and he can drive the ball to all fields. If he can learn to control the strike zone a bit more consistently, he could make enough contact to have plus game power. Thompson-Williams has played all three outfield positions and has the skills to play center field on a regular basis. A career as a fourth outfielder might be in the offing, but a repeat of his 20-20 breakout could have evaluators projecting more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As every Draft goes on, area scouts will go to bat for guys in their region they really like. These \"gut feel\" types are often players who can be signed for below pick value. Such was the case with McGovern, who was coming off a strong senior season in Georgia during which he hit over .300 for the first time and bashed 18 home runs. He was John Wiedenbauer's gut feel guy. The Mariners took him in the ninth round of the 2018 Draft, signed him for $65,000, and he rewarded Wiedenbauer's faith by hitting 15 home runs in the full-season Midwest League in his debut. It should surprise no one to learn that McGovern's power is his calling card. It's legitimate plus raw power, and it was encouraging to see a solid approach employed to consistently get to it during his debut. Yes, there's swing and miss, but he also worked counts and drew walks. He's going to have to hit with power to advance because it's unclear where he'll play defensively. He's not a runner and he doesn't throw well, with left field or first base perhaps his best shots to find a home. He can work on his body to become a bit more athletic, but it's possible McGovern ends up as a DH when all is said and done. If he can go out and repeat what he did during his summer debut, how long before people start squinting and seeing a little Paul Goldschmidt, an unheralded eighth-rounder himself back in 2009?

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves went all-in during the 2016-17 international signing period, handing out several seven-figure bonuses and more six-figure ones after that. Most of those prospects were declared free agents by Major League Baseball in the wake of the organization's signing violations. Ramos, who got $250,000 to sign in July 2016, is one who got to stay and has made some nice strides, reaching full-season ball for the first time in 2018. A move up to the Class A Advanced Florida State League has produced uneven results, but he's still very young for his level. Ramos fits the profile a bat-first corner outfielder. It's very much power over hit, though he's worked on improving his swing, with hitting coordinator Mike Brumley helping him create a more consistent swing that has allowed him to get to his power more at imes, rather than having to cheat or guess to get to it. While Ramos will never thrill anyone with his defense, he has gotten better there as well. When he made his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League, he couldn't field at all. He's fringy now, with left field the only real option because of his below-average arm. That puts more pressure on Ramos's bat and he's going to have to continue to put up high ISO and SLG percentages to get to the big leagues. If he can keep getting to his power, he has the chance to be a right-handed power bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best player to come out of Aruba is Red Sox star Xander Bogaerts. Didder was born in the same town as Bogaerts, Oranjestad, and while he clearly can't match Bogaerts' tools, he does have the chance to join him in the big leagues. Signed back in April 2013 for $20,000, Didder has used his athleticism and versatility to get him up to Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in 2018. He was left unprotected in last December's Rule 5 Draft, but went unselected. Over the course of his Minor League career, Didder has played shortstop, second and all three outfield positions. He added third to his resume during his time in the AFL. And he can play all of them well, with at least above-average defense in the outfield and average glove work everywhere else to go along with a plus arm. Didder's speed helps him defensively and on the basepaths, and he's been in the top five in the system in stolen bases three years in a row. The only question with Didder is his bat. For someone with little to no power, he strikes out too much and doesn't have a great approach at the plate. That improved a bit in 2018, with the hopes he can hit just enough to be a super-utility and speed option off of a big league bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Dalton Pompey, Tristan has the offensive tools to have a more meaningful big league career than his sibling. He starred in his final two seasons at Kentucky, batting .350/.458/.548 with 17 homers and 19 steals in 116 games, though some scouts questioned his ability to hit with wood bats as well as his effort. Neither was an issue after the Marlins signed him for $645,000 in the third round last June, as he hit his way to Class A Advanced in his debut. A switch-hitter, Pompey has shown the ability to do damage from both sides of the plate. His hitting ability stands out a little more than his pop, and he has a quick swing, strong frame and patient approach. Though he has solid-to-plus speed once he gets going, he's not always that quick out of the batter's box and has had just middling success as a basestealer. Pompey's speed also doesn't play as well as hoped on defense. He played mostly on the corners for the Wildcats because his reads and routes leave a lot to be desired, and profiles best in left field with his fringy arm. Miami deployed him in center field for much of his pro debut and plans on introducing him to first base as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An unheralded 20th-round pick as an Alabama high schooler by the Phillies in 2015, Stewart finally broke out when he made his full-season debut in '18. After ranking second in the low Class A South Atlantic League in ERA (2.06) and WHIP (0.98), he went to the Marlins along with Jorge Alfaro and right-hander Sixto Sanchez in exchange for J.T. Realmuto in February. Miami reportedly considered Sanchez and Stewart the two best pitching prospects in Philadelphia's system. Stewart's fastball velocity has been down 2-3 mph in his first season in the Marlins system, as he has worked at 89-91 mph with plus movement. His low-three-quarters delivery creates a lot of sink and run on his heater, leading to a lot of weak contact -- his 2.4 groundout/flyout ratio ranked fifth in the Minors last year. He shows aptitude for throwing his slider and changeup for strikes, though neither projects as more than an average offering at this time. While Stewart significantly improved his command and control in 2018, he still didn't miss a ton of bats, and he hasn't located his pitches as well this year. Whether his sinker-heavy approach will remain as effective against more advanced hitters remains to be seen. If it does, he could blossom into a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Villines racked up 40 saves during his four years at Kansas and dominated for two summers on the Cape before signing with the Mets as a 10th-round pick in 2017. He's enjoyed similar success in the professional ranks so far and began to move quickly in 2018, ascending three levels to reach Double-A in his first full season. The Mets assigned him to Triple-A to open 2019, though early struggles in the International League led to a demotion back to Double-A Binghamton in June. Villines' fastball is below-average from a velocity standpoint, sitting mostly in the upper 80s, but he consistently gets it past hitters thanks to deception created by his low arm slot. Said slot gives his effective slider broad sweeping action, while his changeup drops off the table as it approaches the plate. The change is the better secondary offering, one that receives above-average grades from scouts, and was instrumental in him holding left-handed hitters to a .167/.254/.294 clip in 2018. He's an adept strike-thrower with all three pitches, demonstrating above-average control and command against hitters on both sides of the plate. But perhaps what's most intriguing about Villines is that he can induce whiffs with relative ease. Working 66 2/3 innings in his first full season, he struck out 37 percent of the hitters he faced while averaging 13 strikeouts-per-nine. Villines doesn't fit into a neat box as a big league reliever, but there's something to be said about his sustained dominance, and it would surprise no one in the organization if he continued his accelerated climb towards the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hanhold flew a bit under the radar as a bullpen piece and occasional starter as part of a loaded Florida Gators staff that featured future Draft prospects A.J. Puk, Alex Faedo, Dane Dunning, Logan Shore and Shaun Anderson. The Brewers liked his pure stuff enough to take him in the sixth round of the 2015 Draft, but they ended up sending him to the Mets as the player to be named later in the 2017 Neil Walker deal. After splitting much of '18 between Double-A and Triple-A, Hanhold had his contract purchased by the Mets and made his debut as a September callup, only to leave his third relief appearance with a strained left oblique muscle. Hanhold spent the first year-plus of his pro career giving starting a try, but it didn't really take, and a 2017 move to the bullpen suited him and allowed his power arsenal to play up. The big right-hander will now touch 98 mph with excellent life on his fastball, and he missed more bats than he had previously in his career during his first season in the Mets' system. He pairs a slider, which flashes plus and touches 91 mph, with his heater, giving him more than enough for him to hold down a short relief role. After getting a taste of the Majors last season, Hanhold should see even more work in 2019, especially if he can put the oblique issue behind him and miss bats like he did in '18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted out of Francis Parker High School in San Diego, Dowdy pitched at three different colleges over the next four years. He spent his freshman year working primarily as a reliever at Hawaii before transferring to Orange Coast College JC and performing well as a starter in 2013. He transferred again the following year, this time to the University of Houston, where, after redshirting for one season, he pitched well enough that the Tigers made him their 12th-round pick in the 2015 Draft. Dowdy has continued to bounce around in the pro ranks, as the Indians acquired him at the 2018 Trade Deadline in the Leonys Martin deal, only to have the Mets pluck Dowdy from their system in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft. Things seemed to click for Dowdy after he tweaked his delivery with Double-A Akron. Specifically, the right-hander pitched with consistent plus velocity, touching 98-99 mph with a fastball that averaged 96 mph in his final start of the season. It was a significant uptick in velocity for the right-hander, who previously had sat in the low 90s. Dowdy's curveball and changeup are considered to be above-average offerings, and he fills out his four-pitch mix with a fringy mid-80s slider. He has below-average control and command right now, with room for improvement as he learns to harness his upgraded stuff. Dowdy's experience pitching in a variety of roles, both as an amateur and pro, bodes well for his chances of sticking with the Mets. Additionally, the club views him as someone that can contribute now but also has projection remaining, the latter of which could provide the Mets with extra incentive to keep Dowdy on the 25-man roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 40th-round pick in the 2015 Draft out of Stony Brook, Zamora was moved from the rotation to bullpen upon entering Pittsburgh's season and had already experienced success at the Double-A level when the Mets acquired him for Josh Smoker in January '18. He made his Mets organizational debut several months later at Double-A Binghamton, where he earned Eastern League All-Star honors before his first big league callup in August. Though he has two pitches at his disposal, Zamora is largely a one-pitch reliever, throwing his slider about 79 percent of the time from a nearly sidearm slot. The extreme usage speaks to the pitch's effectiveness, as its high spin rate and hard downer action nets Zamora whiffs on both sides of the plate. His four-seam fastball averaged only 89 mph across his 16 appearances with the Mets, albeit with late sinking action. Zamora fared better against right-handed hitters (.157/.224/.243) than he did lefties (.240/.310/.404) in 2018. Those reverse splits highlight Zamora's potential as a situational reliever whose usage likely will be dictated by the situation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken by the Mets in the 14th round of the 2016 Draft, James is a physical right-hander who compensates for fringy stuff with late movement and advanced pitchability. It's why the organization felt comfortable turning to him when Double-A Binghamton needed a spot start in late May, and again with High Class A St. Lucie the following week. Those two outings aside, James spent his age-20 season in the New York-Penn League, posting a 2.01 ERA over 71 2/3 innings while making 13 starts. James' fastball sits at 89-91 mph with plus sinking action that helped him induce ground-ball contact at a 58 percent clip in 2018. His curveball is an above-average offering as well as a potential out-pitch for him, and he also demonstrates feel for throwing a fading changeup in the mid-80s. James already understands how to sequence his pitches and is consistently around the strike zone. Physically strong and durable, James completed at least five innings in 10 of his 15 starts in '18. The Mets have a track record of developing mid-to-late round high school pitchers that have average stuff but good feel for their craft. James certainly fits that description, and the organization believes he has the qualities needed to reach the big leagues as a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A prototypical projectable high school right-hander, Pipkin's stock initially rose with a big Area Code Games performance in the summer of 2017. An uneven senior season after that hurt, though he was pitching well as the Draft approached. The Phillies nabbed him in the ninth round and went way over pick value to sign him away from his California commitment for $800,000 and sent him out for his debut in the Gulf Coast League. Pipkin has the chance to have three average or better pitches when all is said and done. Tall and lean, the right-hander has a live and loose arm that currently throws a fastball anywhere in the 88-94 mph range. There's plenty of room for him to add strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, so dreaming on more consistent velocity is easy. He mostly threw his slider during his pro debut, and it shows flashes of a plus pitch, and the hope is he'll be able to mix in an average and distinct curveball, as well. He shows some feel for his changeup, but that is also a work in progress. With a free and easy delivery, Pipkin should be able to be a consistent strike-thrower as he gets more reps. It will take patience because he is so far away, but the chance to have a solid starting pitcher profile could be worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It was a pick that caused many to scratch their heads on Day 2 of the 2017 Draft. The Phillies selected Mezquita, a left-handed pitcher without a school from Hazelton, Pa. The organization was set to sign him as an international free agent from the Dominican Republic, but he was forced to enter the Draft because he had moved to Hazelton to go to high school. So Philadelphia took him in the eighth round instead, and watched him dominate in the Gulf Coast League. He wasn't bad when he moved up to the short-season New York-Penn League, but he was a bit more inconsistent. Mezquita was limited in 2018 somewhat by some minor injuries, so the hope is a fully healthy version of the left-hander will be ready to take on full-season ball in 2019. While he's not the biggest guy in the world, there is some arm strength and a feel for pitching that should help him along the way. His fastball will sit in the 91-92 mph range, but he can reach back for 94 mph on occasion. He can spin a breaking ball and has feel for his changeup with the chance to have three average or better offerings when all is said and done. He should be able to throw strikes, though his walk rate spiked a bit in 2018. The 21-year-old is still playing catch-up in terms of time on the mound, so getting a full season of innings will be important. There's still some upside here, with the ceiling of a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rated as the second-best pitcher on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International prospects list heading into the 2018-19 signing period, Castillo got $1.6 million from the Phillies to sign. Some international scouts thought he had the best arm in the class, and he'll make his official professional debut in 2019 at age 17. While Castillo isn't very tall, he's very physical and has the potential to have a solid three-pitch mix to use against hitters. It starts with his plus fastball, which he throws in the 92-95 mph range, though he's been up to 97 mph at times, throwing it with solid life. His slider should be an above-average breaking ball and while his changeup is behind, there is some projection to it and it flashes average. He has fringy-to-average command, though he can get in the habit of overthrowing, which leads to pitches up in the strike zone. There isn't much physical projection for this 6-foot super-competitive right-hander, but there is more to come as he truly learns how to pitch and control his emotions on the mound. He'll make his first step in that direction this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies handed out four six-figure or higher bonuses in the 2015-16 international signing period, starting with Jhailyn Ortiz and his $4 million bonus at the top. That July they also signed Silva, a projectable left-hander out of the Dominican Republic, for $100,000. He's moved incrementally, from the Dominican Summer League, to the Gulf Coast League to the New York-Penn League, over three summers of pro ball, performing well at all three stops. The word that comes up the most when evaluating Silva is \"projectable.\" He shows the makings of a three-pitch mix and the ability to throw them for strikes that gives hope he can remain a starting pitcher long-term. He typically sits in the low-90s with his fastball, touching a bit higher at times, and he should add some velocity as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. His fastball plays up because of its life and he backs it up with a slider and changeup that both need to be developed, though the former is ahead of the latter. He both missed bats and got weak contact on the ground consistently in 2018, though he'll need to refine his command. It's hard to know exactly what Silva, who will be 20 years old for all of 2019, will become. But there's enough upside potential to make the southpaw worth tracking as he attacks full-season ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnston boosted his Draft stock in the 2016 California Collegiate League, where he showcased the circuit's best arm and shut down the U.S. collegiate national team for six innings in a June start. He began his junior year as a starter before being asked to fill Texas' void at closer and cashing in on his first two save opportunities, but he subsequently lost command of the strike zone and returned to the rotation before going to the Nationals in the sixth round that June. He was used as a starter and reliever in his first full season, faring better in the latter role as he finished the year at Class A Advanced Potomac. Moved to the rotation full-time in 2019, Johnston took quickly to the new role and was pitching well back at Potomac before going to the Blue Jays for Daniel Hudson at the Trade Deadline. Johnston's fastball and slider both are viewed as plus pitches, giving him an ideal pairing for a long-term bullpen role. His heater registers in the low- to mid-90s, at times bumping higher, with arm-side run and late sinking action that nets him a lot of weakly-hit contact. His slider plays more like a cutter, sitting at 88-90 mph with darting action, and he also has a changeup that could become a serviceable pitch if he uses it more often. There is a lot of effort in Johnston's inconsistent overhand delivery, and it in turn impedes his ability to throw strikes. But with two big league-caliber pitches, Johnston has the raw ingredients to become an effective reliever at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Angels selected McGowin in the fifth round of the 2013 Draft as one of the seven straight pitchers the organization selected to start that Draft, the hope was that the Savannah State product could use his pitchability to make a beeline to the big leagues. A sore elbow shelved him for the second half of 2014, but once he shook the rust off, he started to show exactly that kind of polish before joining the Nationals in the December 2016 Danny Espinosa trade. McGowin struggled the following year in the upper Minors but regrouped in the Arizona Fall League, setting up a breakout 2018 campaign in which McGowin reached the Major Leagues for the first time at age 26. McGowin lacks dominant stuff but knows how to execute a solid three-pitch mix. His fastball sits at 90-92 mph with some sink on account of his three-quarter action. His slider started to snap back into shape during his AFL stint and serves as his go-to secondary pitch, featuring a well-above-average spin rate that gives it wipeout action and induces whiffs. McGowin also throws an average changeup and is consistently around the strike zone with his entire arsenal. McGowin's resurgence was largely tied to his improved mental approach on the mound, as he showed aggressiveness and confidence that he had struggled to channel in previous seasons. Because he has an out pitch in his slider and feel for a deep arsenal, McGowin has the chance to be a No. 5 starter, or a quality long reliever in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spurning the Dodgers as a 30th-rounder selected from a Louisiana high school in 2012, Giambrone spent two years each at Jones County (Miss.) JC and Delta State (Miss.). The NCAA Division II defensive player of the year in 2016, he also batted .386 as a senior before signing for $1,000 in the 25th round. His offensive ability, versatility and small-college background led multiple Cubs officials to compare him to David Bote. He's smaller and not quite as potent at the plate as Bote, but Giambrone makes hard contact to all fields from the right side of the plate. His aggressive approach and deceptive strength give him surprising power for someone who stands just 5-foot-8. His mindset isn't conducive to hitting for average, though he doesn't strike out excessively. Giambrone's full-tilt style of play helps him get the most out of his average speed on the basepaths. His defensive instincts also allow him to make more plays than expected from someone with ordinary arm strength and quickness. He has played all four infield positions and both outfield corners in pro ball, preparing him to become an offensive-minded utilityman in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mekkes redshirted when he arrived at Michigan State and worked just 12 innings in his first season on the mound, then led NCAA Division I in hit rate (4.1 per nine innings) and strikeout rate (15.2) as a sophomore in 2016. Since signing for $275,000 as a 10th-rounder that June, he has continued to put up crazy numbers in pro ball. He recorded a 1.16 ERA, .170 opponent average and 190 strikeouts in 147 innings while climbing to Triple-A during his first three seasons. Mekkes has uncommon size (6-foot-7, 250 pounds) and a delivery to match. He hides the ball behind his body and then launches himself at the plate, giving him great extension before he slings the ball from a low-three-quarters slot. His fastball has average velocity at 92-93 mph but top-of-the-scale deception, and the net effect is that it plays as a well-above-average pitch. Because his tricky fastball is his lone weapon, Mekkes is purely a reliever, though he can mix in a decent slider and changeup to give hitters different looks. While he has proven himself at every level but the Majors, he also has walked 4.5 batters per nine innings in full-season ball. He'll need to throw more strikes to succeed in the big leagues and should get that opportunity at some point in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs, who scout Mexico as heavily as any organization, paid $1.2 million to purchase Verdugo from the Mexican League's Mexico City Red Devils in 2017. His advanced instincts led Chicago to bring him to the United States for his pro debut as a 17-year-old. Though he batted just .193/.264/.295 in the Rookie-level Arizona League, he impressed observers with his play on both sides of the ball as well as his makeup. Despite below-average speed out of the batter's box, Verdugo has the athleticism and actions to stick at shortstop. His plus arm and quick hands are assets, and he possesses a precise internal clock that helps him make plays. He handled third base well last summer and theoretically could play second base if he wound up in a utility role. Verdugo prioritizes power at the plate and shows pop to all fields. His right-handed swing can get too long and his approach can get too aggressive, but he has enough pure hitting ability to make enough contact to become a 15-homer threat when he's physically mature. His profile earns comparisons to Starlin Castro, though Verdugo is unlikely to develop fast enough to make the All-Star Game at age 21.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two nondescript seasons at the plate, Weber batted .344/.415/.536 to lead Virginia in all three slash categories last spring and became the first Cavaliers second baseman ever to earn All-America honors. Chicago signed him for an above-slot $400,000 in the fifth round, then gave him more action at shortstop than at second in his pro debut. Weber added strength and began trying to drive the ball more often in 2018, making him more of an offensive threat. He still stands out more for his ability to make contact from the left side of the plate than his power, which could produce 12-15 homers on an annual basis. His uncharacteristic 26 percent strikeout rate in his first taste of pro ball may have been the result of fatigue because he fanned at just a 12 percent rate in college. Weber has fringy speed but plays faster than that on defense. With quick hands and a strong arm, he projects as a solid shortstop or a plus second baseman. He played briefly at third base in his debut and has the versatility needed for a utilityman, though the Cubs think he has a chance to hit enough to become a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Curacao in August 2015 as a bat-first infielder, Willems finally showed some of that ability in 2018 following two subpar years as a professional. After he batted .226 in the DSL in 2016 and .234 in the AZL in '17, things clicked once Willems reached the Appalachian League with Greeneville in '18. He spent most of the season there and batted .263/.300/.470 with eight homers in 55 games, then impressed during fall instructional league action. Willems has a good swing and can make the needed adjustments at the plate. He showed off more extra-base ability with his 13 doubles and four triples for Greeneville in 2018. He still needs to improve breaking ball recognition and refine his overall approach to improve his K/BB ratio moving forward so he can tap into that power more consistently. The Reds need to find a position for Willems, who has played mostly third and second base. He's been a little rigid at both positions and likely profiles as a platoon guy or bench player. If his bat continues to progress, he could have a shot at being an offensive-minded regular at second base in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a South Carolina junior in 2018, Hill flirted with no-hitters in back-to-back early-season starts against Charleston Southern and Clemson, striking out 14 in each outing. The performances sent his Draft stock soaring, though he wasn't nearly as dominant the rest of the way and missed time in March with shoulder tendinitis. After the Mets made him their fourth-round pick in June, Hill averaged 15.3 strikeouts-per-nine during his pro debut in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League. Hill was dealt to the Brewers in the Keon Broxton trade in January 2019. Hill's best pitch is his fastball, which sits around 91-93 mph and peaks at 95. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create good plane and extension, and has some crossfire in his delivery that imparts running life on his heater. His changeup has been more reliable than his slider this spring, with each showing signs of becoming a solid offering when at their best. Hill is more physical than athletic, and he sometimes struggles to keep his delivery together and locate his pitches where he wants. If he can do a better job of maintaining his velocity into the later innings, improving the consistency of his secondary offerings and commanding his stuff, he could be a No. 3 starter. If not, he might be more of a sixth- or seventh-inning reliever because he lacks an overpowering fastball or a dynamic second pitch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the entirety of his professional career with the Pirates, ever since signing back in May 2012, Reyes had flown under the radar. He spent two years in the Dominican Summer League before finally making his United States debut in 2014, moving one rung at a time after that and never having more than 400 at-bats in a year until the 2017 season. But a strong year in Triple-A in 2018 led to a September callup to Pittsburgh, where his energy on the field made many new fans. If the Pirates could bottle Reyes, they'd have the best energy drink on the market. He plays with infectious energy at all times, making him an exciting player to watch. Though he's just 5-foot-8, there is some impact from the right side of the plate thanks to very good bat speed in his buggy whip of a swing. While he can get streaky at times, he doesn't strike out much and he's shown he can handle any fastball, and any level, thanks to his quick hands. Reyes began his career as a shortstop, then started playing second base more frequently. Now he profiles as a guy meant to fill a super-utility role and he's shown he can be an average defender at three infield positions and all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The University of Akron has had five pitchers reach the big leagues, the most recent being Chris Bassitt, who saw time up with the A's in 2018. Brubaker's ascent up the Pirates' ladder since being a sixth-round pick in 2015 hasn't necessarily wowed anyone, but he's knocking on the door after reaching Triple-A and leading the organization in ERA in '18, earning him a spot on the 40-man roster. He seemed certain to be the next Zips hurler to make it to the highest level in 2019, but a forearm strain and elbow inflammation has kept him out of action for most of the season. Brubaker's two best pitches are his fastball and slider. He'll pitch in the 92-96 mph range with his heater, thrown with sink. His slider flashes plus and it's firm, around 88 mph. It has some dart-like life to it and sometimes looks more like a cutter, a pitch he gets a lot of weak contact on the ground with. He started mixing in a curveball to give hitters a different look and he also has a changeup, though that's too firm with not enough differential from his fastball. He can throw strikes with all of his offerings. With more of a ground-ball oriented approach to pitching, Brubaker has never missed a ton of bats. The one exception to that was when he pitched in relief in the Arizona Fall League in 2017. While he has the arsenal and durability to be a back-end starter, there are some who think he might have more long-term success as a two-pitch reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The international amateur market is often considered a long-term lottery ticket. Often they don't pan out, but sometimes that ticket gets turned into a star. The Pirates gave Pie $500,000 in the 2017-18 signing period to sign in the hopes that his offensive tools will allow him to approach that latter development. His pro debut in the Dominican Summer League was a strong first step in that direction. Pie's combination of athleticism and offensive potential give him the chance to be a dynamic outfielder if it all comes together. He's shown a solid approach at the plate, especially given his age, with a willingness to draw walks and manage his strikeout rate relatively well. His ground-ball rate was pretty low as well, and the 22 extra-base hits he collected might be the tip of the iceberg in terms of his ability to drive the ball. Pie runs well, though he has a lot to learn in terms of baserunning, and he saw time in all three outfield positions in the DSL. The Pirates are excited to see what Pie can do as he comes stateside for the first time. He might profile best as a fourth outfielder, but it's hard to know just yet how much potential there is to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite his lack of size and premium stuff, Gingery was having an outstanding collegiate career at Texas Tech, serving as the team's No. 2 starter during its College World Series run in 2016 and earning Big 12 Conference Pitcher of the Year honors the following season. After a strong turn with the U.S. national collegiate team last summer, there was excitement about his junior season, but it ended early when he blew out his elbow in February and needed Tommy John surgery. The Cardinals decided it was worth the risk to take Gingery and let him rehab with their staff, signing him in the fourth round for an above-pick-value bonus of $825,000. He suffered a setback while rehabbing during Spring Training that further delayed the start to his pro career. Gingery's velocity on his fastball is fringy, sitting at 88-92 mph and occasionally touching 94, but it plays up because it has good sink and he can command it to both sides of the plate. It's also helped by his best pitch, a plus fading changeup that was among the best in the 2018 Draft class. Gingery has an average curveball as well, one that he throws for strikes consistently. Gingery's ceiling is somewhat limited to that of a back-end starter. At the same time, he does have a fairly high floor as a pitchability lefty who can eat a lot of innings and is a plus competitor. Once healthy, Gingery will try to exceed the comps to Jason Vargas he elicited before getting hurt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kruczynski had a nondescript senior season at East Carolina in 2017 and signed with the Cardinals for just $3,000 after they had drafted him in the ninth round. He reached Double-A in his first full season, accruing 115 2/3 innings overall across two levels, then put himself on the prospect radar in the Arizona Fall League by posting three scoreless starts in six turns en route to a 1.99 ERA that was second among AFL starting pitchers. A 6-foot-5 left-hander, Kruczynski pitches with an 88-91 mph fastball that plays above its velocity because he gets such good extension towards the plate and knows how to effectively change hitters' eye levels. He has a trio of secondary pitches including an above-average changeup and average slider, and he can pound the zone with his entire four-pitch mix. That Kruczynski was successful against right- and left-handed hitters alike in 2018 only enhances his chances of reaching his ceiling as a No. 5 starter, and at the least, he should offer value at the highest level as a lefty specialist.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs had interest in Miroglio, a catcher at the University of San Francisco, in 2016, but a hand injury that cost him most of the year clouded things a bit. The Rays took a flier on him in the 16th round, but the backstop returned to San Francisco for another year. Arizona didn't miss on him in 2017, nabbing him in the 20th round. Miroglio was sent straight to the Class A Advanced California League for his full-season debut, where he turned in an All-Star performance to earn a promotion to Double-A in August and a trip to the Arizona Fall League. Defense will always be Miroglio's calling card. He is a very good receiver with outstanding leadership skills and feel for managing a game. His average arm plays up because he has a very quick release, and he's done a nice job controlling the running game as a pro, throwing out better than 34 percent of attempted basestealers through two seasons. Miroglio's development at the plate has been a pleasant surprise for the organization, as he's shown good feel for the strike zone and an ability to consistently barrel the baseball. It's a hit-over-power offensive profile, though he does have good pop to the gaps during games. While Miroglio shows all the ingredients to be a backup catcher in the big leagues, the start of his pro career has some inside the organization thinking he might develop into an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mercer underwent Tommy John surgery before his senior year of high school and unsurprisingly went undrafted that June. So he headed to the University of Oregon, where he pitched in relief as a freshman before joining the weekend rotation as a sophomore and then becoming the staff ace in 2018. While his performance was inconsistent, his stuff intrigued the D-backs enough that they made him their fifth-round pick. After signing for slot value, Mercer made all but one of his 13 starts in the Northwest League, racking up 37 strikeouts in 27 frames. He struck out eight batters over four one-hit innings in his final regular-season start, then struck out half of the batters he faced over four perfect frames in his only postseason start. Mercer stands out with his arm strength and power arsenal. His high-spin-rate fastball typically sits around 92-95 mph, but he can reach back for more, flashing a plus 97-mph heater at times, while maintaining his velocity throughout starts. Mercer's secondary stuff was better in his pro debut than during his junior year. His changeup is an above-average offering that plays nicely off his fastball, with late tumble and fading action, and his curveball can earn similar grades from evaluators, even flashing plus at times. While he does largely throw strikes, Mercer does need to refine his command within the zone. That, plus some effort in his delivery, has some scouts predicting a future in the bullpen, though the D-backs will give him every opportunity to prove himself as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Goddard entered his junior season looking like a top-two-rounds college pitcher, but his stock took a hit when he missed six weeks with a strained oblique. He was up-and-down after his return, but turned it up a notch near the end of his season at Kansas, and the D-backs saw enough to take him in the third round and give him $550,000 to sign, just a tick below pick value. He spent the bulk of his pro debut in the Class A Short Season Northwest League, where his stuff was down but he still performed well. Goddard has a power arsenal of three potential plus pitches when he's at his best. It starts with a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 97 mph and features some run and sink. Hitters have a difficult time laying off his low-80s slider, giving him a second swing-and-miss pitch, and there are times when his low-80s changeup is his most effective secondary offering, providing contrast to his lively fastball. Inconsistency plagued Goddard throughout his career and he's often struggled with command, which has led to him being more hittable than he should be given his stuff. The D-backs believe he'll throw more strikes as he learns to better repeat a delivery that currently involves some effort. Doing so will improve Goddard's chances of remaining a starter, though others believe his big league future will be out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A wrist injury kept Boswell from playing as a freshman at the University of Texas in 2014 and he largely struggled to get his bat going once he did return to play, though the Pirates drafted him in the 40th round of the 2016 Draft as a redshirt sophomore. His best season did come in 2017, following an MVP turn in the California Collegiate League, and the Rockies selected him in the 8th round of the 2017 Draft. He's hit since joining the organization, hitting for average and power during his debut in the Northwest League and then across two levels of A ball in his first full season. Though he's not the biggest guy in the world, Boswell has shown an ability to impact the baseball from the left side of the plate. He is capable of being short to the ball and barrels it up when he makes contact, but he will have to cut down his strikeout rate as he progresses. Boswell settled in defensively as a second baseman at Texas and that's where he played during his debut, but he split time between second and third, where his strong arm works well, during his first full season. Boswell hasn't played much shortstop, but he could probably play there in a pinch, which could come in handy for a future utility role. Perhaps because of his age, Boswell might be a bit underrated, but if his bat is this loud moving forward, he'll start getting a lot more love.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When hitters go off while playing in the California League, and in Lancaster in particular, there's always going to be a healthy dose of skepticism. But Ramos, a 16th-round pick out of College of the Canyons, a two-year school in California, kept on finding the seats after getting promoted to the Eastern League in 2018, making him a much more credible power-hitting prospect. Ramos finished the year with 32 homers, good for second in the organization, and 15 of those came in Double-A, which is much less hitting-friendly. He has the classic left-handed uppercut swing and easily has raw plus power. He's made some solid adjustments at the plate that allowed him to get to that power much more consistently in 2018, though he is still prone to the strikeout and gets pull-happy at times. He does draw some walks and has shown some aptitude to improving as an all-around hitter.
