Gettys fared much better in his return to Fort Wayne in 2016, however, earning mid-season All-Star honors in the Midwest League before advancing to Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in late June and finishing in the Arizona Fall League. Back in the California League in 2017, Gettys has struggled to build on his progress from the previous year despite flashing his usual loud tools. Gettys' swing is explosive and produces plus raw power that he began to show during games last season after making an adjustment in his swing. He continues to strike out at a disconcerting rate, a product of his subpar pitch recognition and strike-zone management, and he faces questions about the future utility of his hit tool. Plus speed allows Gettys to impact games on the basepaths as well as in center field, where he's a plus defender, with range for days and a cannon arm. With bat speed, foot speed, arm strength and defensive ability that all grade as well above average, Gettys has an undeniably impressive ceiling. That is of course is tied to his ability to hit and apply his power, but the speed and strong center-field defense alone could make him a valuable fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing one year at American Heritage (Plantation, Fla.) High and then moving back to the Dominican Republic, Almanzar ranked No. 4 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 prospects for the 2016-17 international period. While some teams even viewed Almanzar as his country's top prospect, it was the Padres, as part of their massive international spending spree that year, who ultimately landed him, signing Almanzar for $4 million on July 2. Though he struggled in his 2017 professional debut in the Class A Short Season Northwest League, Almanzar also played the entire summer at 17, making him one of the circuit's youngest players. Almanzar can hit to all fields and has a slightly uppercut swing that causes the ball to jump off his bat, leading scouts to believe that he'll hit eventually hit for average as well as for some power. He's athletic and toolsy, with good footwork and the ability to defend, and he also impresses scouts with his strong and accurate arm. Almanzar's thicker build has already led to reduced time at shortstop and more time at the hot corner, which many believe will be his final defensive home. Should he end up at third base, Almanzar will need to hit for both average and power to accommodate the position's traditional profile. It's early in his career, but Almanzar has shown enough offensive tools to believe that's a real possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Almanzar ranked No. 4 on MLB.com's list of the Top 30 international prospects, some teams viewed him as the Dominican Republic's top prospect in the 2016-17 international class. He became a part of the Padres' international spending spree last summer, signing for $4 million on July 2. Almanzar can hit to all fields and has a slightly uppercut swing that causes the ball to jump off his bat, leading scouts to believe that he'll eventually grow into at least average power. He's athletic and toolsy, with good footwork and the ability to defend, and he also impresses scouts with his strong and accurate arm. Almanzar's thicker build has raised doubt among evaluators about his ability to stick at shortstop long term, though there's little doubt that he has the tools and offensive potential to profile at third base. Almanzar has some experience playing in games and showcases in the United States, as he played one season at American Heritage (Plantation, Fla.) High at age 15 before moving back to the Dominican Republic. That experience has aided the teenager this season during his pro debut with Class A Short Season Tri-City.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gregorio helped the Giants win the Dominican Summer League championship in his 2010 pro debut and led the Arizona League with a 2.32 ERA the following year, but he has been frustratingly inconsistent since leaving Rookie ball. He was locating his fastball as well as he had in a while in Triple-A last year before his season ended in July with a suspension for testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. San Francisco designated him for assignment in February to make room for Tony Watson on the 40-man roster. As a starter, Gregorio operates at 92-95 mph with a fastball that plays up because his extra-long arms give him terrific extension and create a difficult angle when he keeps his mechanics in sync. His mid-80s slider gives him a solid second pitch, though he'll fall in love with it too much at times. He never has had great feel for his changeup and it regressed in 2017. Gregorio is 26 and has never demonstrated better than average control or fringy command, so it may be time to make him a reliever. In shorter stints, he might have a mid-90s fastball and a sharper slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gregorio may have posted the second-worst ERA (4.69) of his career in 2016, but his year didn't lack positives. He worked a career-high 134 1/3 innings, ranked third in the Triple-A Pacific Coast League in strikeouts (122) despite not arriving there until mid-May and would have placed second in whiff rate (10.2 per nine innings) if he hadn't fallen just short of enough innings to qualify. He continued to build on that progress in 2017 -- until he received a season-ending suspension on July 1 after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. Gregorio's fastball sits at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96, but it's much nastier than its velocity alone would indicate. He's 6-foot-7 and his long levers give him great extension and create a difficult plane and angle when he keeps his delivery in sync. His secondary pitches lack reliability, though his mid-80s slider is solid at times and his fringy changeup is improving. San Francisco still envisions Gregorio as a starter, and he'll need to refine his changeup, control and command to succeed in that role in the big leagues. He could make for a very dynamic reliever, giving hitters an unusual look while theoretically adding more velocity in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson flew under the radar at Cal State Northridge, missing most of his first two seasons with an elbow injury and subsequent Tommy John surgery and logging a 4.33 ERA as a redshirt sophomore in 2014. He created a stir in his first extended pro action the following year, flashing electric stuff while posting a 71/11 K/BB ratio across three levels. He hasn't been able to sustain that kind of success since, never getting into a rhythm in Double-A last season while losing a month to a hamstring injury. Johnson still can flash a three-pitch mix that seems to stamp him as a starter. At his best, he can sit at 92-96 mph with sink on his fastball, confound hitters with plus changeups that tumble and offer some curveballs with power and depth. But he doesn't show that kind of stuff consistently because he collapses on the backside of his delivery, flattening his pitches and leaving them up in the strike zone. While the Giants hold out hope that Johnson can improve his mechanics and become more consistent, they also declined to protect him on their 40-man roster after the 2017 season. He spent most of the season working with a 90-94 mph fastball while his control also regressed. If he doesn't start displaying more consistency, a bullpen move could be in his near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts had a difficult time seeing Johnson at Cal State Northridge, where he missed most of his first two years because of Tommy John surgery and went 3-6, 4.33 as a redshirt sophomore in 2014. The Giants liked his arm action and projectability, so they spent a 23rd-round pick and a $100,000 bonus on him that June. He spent 2016 in high Class A and tired in the second half while working 120 innings -- nearly as many as he pitched in the previous four years combined. Johnson's fastball parked at 93-96 mph and touched 98 while he was averaging an eye-opening 12.3 strikeout per nine innings during his first extended pro action in 2015. Last season, he fell into the bad habit of overstriding and getting under his pitches, which dropped his heater to 90-94 mph and also cost him some sink. He spent the offseason working to correct that flaw yet still is getting hit harder than hoped in Double-A. Johnson trusts his changeup, which can be a plus pitch when it tumbles at the plate, and sells it with deceptive arm speed. San Francisco had him shelve a hard slider that it believes contributed to his injuries, and he has come up with a curveball that has some power and depth. If he can straighten out his mechanics and improve his command, he could become a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A rare player who was drafted in the top 10 rounds three different times, Suarez declined to sign with the Blue Jays as a ninth-rounder out of high school in 2011 and the Nationals as a second-rounder as a redshirt sophomore at Miami in 2014. He has moved swiftly since signing for $1.1 million as a second-rounder in 2015, reaching Double-A a month into his first full pro season and leading Giants farmhands in wins (10), innings (155 2/3) and strikeouts (135) in 2017. Suarez doesn't have a true plus pitch but mixes four of them well and pounds the strike zone. His best offering is a slider that's rough on lefties and which he morphs into more of a cutter against righties. He can add and subtract from a fastball that usually parks around 89-93 mph with some run and sink, and he also utilizes an average curveball and changeup. Suarez operates without much margin for error but also doesn't beat himself with many mistakes. He keeps the ball down in the strike zone and avoids walks and home runs. Though he had labrum surgery in 2012, he has been durable ever since, contributing to his high-floor profile as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suarez turned down the Blue Jays as a ninth-rounder out of high school in 2011, missed most of his first year at Miami with a shoulder injury that necessitated labrum surgery and declined to sign with the Nationals as a second-rounder in 2014. He has made up for lost time since signing for $1.1 million as a repeat second-rounder in 2015, reaching Double-A a month into his first full pro season. Suarez masterfully mixes four pitches and locates them where he wants. His best is a slider that shows flashes of becoming a plus offering and is effective against both left-handers and right-handers. His 89-93 mph fastball can hit 95 and plays better than its average velocity because it features run and sink and he commands it well. His ability to spin a curveball and throw hitters off balance with a changeup give Suarez a pair of average pitches to round out his arsenal. He has little margin for error but doesn't make many mistakes, consistently pounding the bottom of the strike zone. He can throw too many strikes, so the Giants would like to see him try to get hitters to chase some pitches off the plate when he gets ahead in the count.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hinojosa spurned early-round interest from clubs in the 2012 Draft to attend Texas, where he never lived up to his hype outside of playing well at the 2014 College World Series. Signed for $200,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2015, he has been more impressive with wood bats as a pro than he was with metal bats in college. He has plateaued since reaching Double-A midway through his first full pro season and missed the first two months of 2018 after rupturing his left Achilles tendon last September and also getting hit with a 50-game suspension for a second positive test for a drug of abuse. Hinojosa has fared better in pro ball because he shortened his right-handed swing and stopped worrying about hitting home runs. He has a quick bat and makes contact more easily than any Giants farmhand, though that also cuts into his walk totals. He uses the entire field, has some gap power and can hit an occasional homer to his pull side. Though he's a well-below-average runner who lacks the quickness to play shortstop, Hinojosa manages to make plays there thanks to his solid arm and good internal clock. His substandard range won't fly at shortstop in the big leagues, however, so San Francisco began playing him at second and third base last year. There may not be enough impact in his bat to make him an everyday player but he could be a utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hinojosa turned down early-round overtures from clubs in the 2012 Draft so he could attend Texas, but outside of a strong performance at the 2014 College World Series, his Longhorns career was mostly a disappointment. He reversed course after signing for $200,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2015, hitting better with wood bats than he did with metal in college and reaching Double-A midway through his first full pro season. An offensive-minded shortstop, Hinojosa found more success in pro ball after he shortened his right-handed swing. He has a quick bat and controls the strike zone while using the entire field. He's at his best when he focuses on getting on base rather than hitting for power, though he can drive some doubles to the gaps and pull an occasional ball out the park. Hinojosa has the hands and arm to play the infield, as well as a good internal clock that helps him make plays. He has substandard range at shortstop because he's a well below-average runner, however, and fits better at second or third base. A likely utilityman in the future, he'll have to monitor his conditioning to maintain enough quickness for the middle infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moronta signed for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2010 and needed five years to reach full-season ball. He finally broke out as the high Class A California League's most dominant reliever in 2016 before progressing from Double-A to the big leagues last season. The Giants were impressed with his fearlessness after he joined them and struck out 11 of the 29 batters he faced. Moronta goes after hitters with two power pitches that are both well above average at their best. His fastball sits at 95-97 mph, can reach triple digits, appears even quicker because of deception in his delivery and features riding life. His slider usually operates at 82-84 mph, tops out at 87 and has late bite. The key for Moronta was realizing that he loses control and command when he worries about velocity and overthrows. There's still effort in his delivery, but he's doing a better job of repeating it and maintaining his release point. Though he won't ever locate his pitches with pinpoint precision, he still could blossom into a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Dominican Republic for $15,000 in 2010, Moronta didn't reach full-season ball until his fifth pro season and got shelled for a 5.73 ERA when he finally got to low Class A. He turned himself into a prospect last season, when he led high Class A California League relievers in opponent average (.195), strikeout rate (14.1 per nine innings) and holds (17). He also finished third in saves (14) despite not closing games before July. Moronta's live 95-97 mph fastball can reach triple digits and seems to get on hitters even quicker because of deception in his delivery. He backs up his heat with an improving slider that arrives in the mid-80s with late bite. He also can cross up hitters by mixing in a changeup every once in a while. Moronta expends effort in his delivery, which costs him some control and command. If he can throw more strikes and refine his slider into a plus pitch, he could develop into a closer at the big league level. He'll also need to watch his weight because he carries much more than the listed 175 pounds on his 6-foot frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants gave Beltre their highest bonus in their 2013-14 international class, signing him for $650,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His first two years in the United States were truncated by injuries, with hamstring issues limiting him to 14 games in 2015 and a broken forearm costing him two months in 2016. He finally stayed healthy last season, showing glimpses of talent and also inconsistency in low Class A, but started 2018 on the disabled list with a broken left tibia. Beltre's outstanding bat speed is what initially attracted San Francisco to him and gives him plus raw power from the right side of the plate. He could have 15-homer power if he continues to add strength and refine his approach at the plate. He did a better job of keeping his aggressiveness in check last year, improving his walk (up from 7 to 10 percent) and strikeout (down from 29 to 20 percent) rates compared to his introduction to low Class A in 2016. Beltre has shuffled all over the infield, playing mainly shortstop in his pro debut, shifting to second base in 2015 and third base in 2016, then returning to second last year. He still needs defensive polish and may fit best at the hot corner because his speed and quickness are just average. His strong arm works anywhere in the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beltre received the largest bonus San Francisco paid during the 2013-14 international signing period, getting $650,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He has yet to complete a fully healthy season, missing most of his 2015 U.S. debut with hamstring issues and losing more than two months last year when an errant pitch broke his left forearm. Beltre originally caught San Francisco's eye with his quick right-handed bat, and his outstanding bat speed gives him plus raw power. He could hit 15 homers per season if he adds strength and tones down his aggressive approach. He lacks polish at the plate, which is understandable considering he's 20 and totaled just 391 plate appearances in his first three pro seasons. Beltre has bounced among different positions, playing mostly shortstop in his pro debut, spending 2016 at third base and settling at second base this season. His strong arm would work anywhere in the infield, but he fits best at the hot corner because his speed and quickness are just average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Warmoth took over North Carolina's shortstop job a month into his freshman season and never relinquished it. After a solid summer offensively and defensively in the Cape Cod League, he continued to improve his game as a junior, emerging as the top college shortstop in the 2017 Draft class before going to the Blue Jays with the No. 22 overall pick and signing for $2,820,200. He made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League before advancing to Class A Short Season Vancouver, where he slashed .306/.356/.419 and helped lead the Canadians to a Northwest League title. Warmoth may not have a plus tool, but he also doesn't have any obvious holes in his game. He's an above-average hitter, one who controls the strike zone, handles good velocity and uses the entire field. He started to show some power toward the end of his sophomore season, and has enough raw pop to hit 12-15 homers per season in the big leagues if he can get to it with greater consistency. Warmoth is athletic and runs well, with instincts, footwork and quick hands that help him make all the plays at shortstop. That gives him a chance of sticking there long-term, though some believe he's better suited for second base on account of his modest range and average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bote walked on at Liberty in the fall of 2011 before deciding to transfer to Neosho County (Kan.) CC, where he batted .419 with 20 steals as a freshman and teamed with Matt Strahm to lead the Panthers to the 2012 Junior College World Series. After signing with the Cubs for $100,000 as an 18th-rounder that June, he didn't make much of an impression until he batted .337 in high Class A in 2016. He encored with a career-best 14 homers in Double-A last season and has continued to perform well in Triple-A and in his big league debut in 2018. His strength and bat speed combine to give Bote more power than most middle infielders and some of the highest exit velocities among Chicago farmhands. His home run surge came after he worked to add more loft to his right-handed stroke. His offensive game is steady if not spectacular, as he projects as a decent hitter who will draw a few walks and show average speed on the bases. Bote has enough athleticism, quickness and arm strength to play almost anywhere on the diamond. He has seen most of his action at second base, where he's an adequate defender, and also has logged time at third base, first base, shortstop, left field and right field while even pitching in five games. Originally projected as a utilityman, his offensive improvements could make him an everyday player, albeit probably not on the crowded Cubs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted after his junior year, Lucchesi became the highest-drafted player to ever come out of Southeast Missouri when the Padres selected him in the fourth round in 2016 following a senior campaign in which he went 10-5 with a 2.19 ERA and a Division I-leading 149 strikeouts. Signed for $100,000, Lucchesi has continued to dominate in the professional ranks. He finished his pro debut with Class A Fort Wayne before thriving across two levels, including Double-A, in his first full season, when he led all Padres farmhands in ERA (2.20) and ranked second in strikeouts (148). Lucchesi's stuff ticked up as a senior and has continued to improve as a professional. He uses his height effectively to create angle with a fastball that bumps 96 mph and sits 92-94 with late life that nets him whiffs inside the zone. His breaking ball gives him a second bat-missing offering, one thrown with top-to-bottom action, good pace and late bite, and he also has advanced feel for a changeup that offers deceptive contrast to the rest of his arsenal, with both secondaries receiving above-average grades from scouts. What's more, Lucchesi attacks hitters on both sides of the plate, showing present command of his entire arsenal. Lucchesi knows how to disrupt hitters' timing with his deceptive delivery, and he's athletic enough that scouts believe he'll continue to repeat it well enough to stick as a starter. He takes pride in having an excellent pick-off move and earns praise from club officials for his makeup and competitive demeanor on the mound. Once viewed as a likely reliever given his unique profile, Lucchesi now seems well on his way toward achieving his future as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Marlins for $40,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2009, German didn't reach full-season ball until 2014 but struck out Kris Bryant and Joey Gallo at the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game that summer. He came to the Yankees that December as part of a package for Martin Prado and David Phelps, then hurt his elbow and had Tommy John surgery, which sidelined him for all of 2015. He returned in 2016 and was back at full strength last year, when he made his big league debut in June. German averaged 94 mph as a Minor League starter and 96 mph as a Yankees reliever, featuring sink and run on his fastball and showing the ability to maintain his velocity into the late innings. His low-80s curveball improved in 2017, showing more consistent depth and neutralizing right-handers. He also can get swings and misses with his changeup. While German throws strikes, his command isn't as sharp as his control. He sometimes falls off in his delivery, elevating his pitches and making them more hittable, and his long arm action gives batters a good look at his pitches. He has had success as a starter in the Minors but may wind up as a reliever in the Majors because of his inconsistent command and lack of a track record of durability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 out of Mexico in 2011, Gallegos had Tommy John surgery before he made his pro debut. He got back on the mound in 2012 and didn't do much to distinguish himself until a strong winter in the Mexican Pacific League in 2014. He has progressed rapidly since and made his big league debut last year, when he served four different stints in New York. He had pitched in four big league games this year before being traded to the Cardinals. Gallegos has a quick arm, and his fastball has risen from 90-93 mph when he was a starter to 93-96 mph now that he's a reliever. His heater can get flat at the higher end of his velocity range, so he needs to be careful to keep it down in the zone. He has a second plus pitch in a low-80s curveball and does a nice job of manipulating its spin and shape. Gallegos also has a fringy changeup from his days in the rotation and occasionally will use it against left-handers. He has pounded the strike zone throughout his career and isn't afraid to challenge big leaguers. He has a higher floor than ceiling, looking like a good bet to become a seventh-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player in high school who could hit 94 mph as a left-handed pitcher, Cave became a full-time outfielder after signing for $800,000 (supplemental first-round money) as a sixth-rounder in 2011. He fractured his right kneecap in his first pro game and lost all of 2012 when it didn't heal properly, yet he recovered to advance to Triple-A by age 22 in 2015. Lost temporarily to the Reds as the No. 2 overall pick in the Rule 5 Draft, he had to begin 2016 and 2017 in Double-A because of the Yankees' wealth of outfield prospects but responded with two of his best seasons. The Twins acquired Cave in March for right-hander Luis Gil. Cave doesn't have a true plus tool, but also lacks a glaring weakness, a profile that might make it tough to take an everyday job but could make him a useful fourth outfielder. He has made consistently hard contact and shown the ability to work the entire field throughout his pro career. After hitting just 11 homers in his first three full seasons, he started incorporating his lower half better in his left-handed swing to generate power and went deep a career-high 20 times last season. Cave has the solid speed to provide occasional steals. His quickness and average arm allow him to play all three outfield positions, though he probably fits best in left field. He's an average defender in center field and solid on the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lane spent more time as an outfielder than on the mound in his first two college seasons at Campbell and Lower Columbia (Wash.) CC, then became more of a pitcher at Illinois-Chicago. After he won Horizon League reliever of the year honors in 2016, the Yankees made him a $10,000 senior sign as a 10th-rounder. His control and velocity improved dramatically in his first full pro season, when he logged a 1.52 ERA at two Class A stops to earn a non-roster invitation to Spring Training in 2018. In college, Lane operated with an 89-90 mph sinker and an effective slider. Now he's beating up hitters with a 92-97 mph and a high-spin breaker that looks more like a curveball with its depth. He also has a decent changeup that he can mix in for a different look. Lane also is doing a much better job of locating his pitches in pro ball, reducing his walk rate from 4.1 per nine innings at Illiniois-Chicago to 2.1 in his first two years as a pro. He pounds the bottom of the strike zone, missing bats and creating a lot of weak contact. As a multi-inning southpaw reliever who's effective against both left-handers and right-handers, he may not need much more time in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After displaying first-round potential on the high school showcase circuit in 2016, Brannen was hampered by a broken hamate bone in his right hand last spring. The Red Sox took him in the second round and lured him away from a Georgia Southern commitment with an over-slot $1.3 million bonus. He's the best athlete and fastest player in a system thinned by promotions and trades in recent years. Brannen has well-above-average speed and knows how to use it to reach base and create havoc once he does. He employs a compact left-handed swing geared to produce line drives and ground balls that he can beat out. He draws walks but can get too passive at times, and his inability to drive the ball in 2018 points to his need for increased strength. Brannen's quickness also plays well in center field. He could cover plenty of ground on speed alone, but he also has fine instincts and takes good routes. His average arm is better than most at his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson used a sinker/slider approach to great effect in 2017, leading NCAA Division I in victories while going 14-1 with a 1.96 ERA for a 56-6 Oregon State club that finished third at the College World Series. After the Red Sox signed the redshirt junior for a slightly below-slot $350,000 as a fourth-rounder, he told them that though the Beavers had him focus on two pitches, he also threw a curveball and splitter/changeup. He showed the makings of a possible mid-rotation starter during his pro debut but hasn't been as sharp during his first full season. Last summer, Thompson worked with a two-seam sinker at 92-94 mph, touched 98 with his four-seam fastball and flashed a plus slider and split/change. This year, his fastball velocity is down 2-3 mph and his secondary pitches haven't missed as many bats. With a deeper repertoire, Thompson has a better chance of remaining a starter. In college, several scouts projected him as a reliever because he lacks a smooth delivery and didn't have much success in his first three seasons at Oregon State (missing most of 2015 with a back injury). If his stuff doesn't trend back up, he may wind up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few college middle infielders in the 2017 Draft could match Netzer's track record of hitting. He won the Cal Ripken League batting title at .349 in the summer of 2015, hit .384 as a UNC Charlotte sophomore in 2016 and compiled a .351 average in three college seasons. His prowess at the plate made him a third-round pick, the fourth-highest in 49ers history, and earned him a slightly below-slot $475,000 bonus. He hit his way to Class A four weeks into his pro career. Netzer's bat speed and feel for the barrel allow him to make line-drive contact with ease. He walked almost as much as he struck out in college, though he expanded his strike zone in his introduction to pro ball. He has some raw power, though his left-handed swing is relatively flat and geared more for doubles than home runs. Netzer has average speed, but subpar arm strength, limiting his defensive options. He's an adequate second baseman whose only other position is left field, where he played as a college freshman. His bat-first profile at second base has drawn comparisons to Adam Kennedy and Tommy La Stella.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox grabbed two Florida two-way players in the 2012 Draft, Brian Johnson in the first round and Maddox in the third. The latter hit 17 homers as a Gators freshman but offers more upside on the mound. After he recorded a 5.05 ERA in his first four pro seasons, he added velocity in 2016 and made his big league debut last year, allowing one run in 17 1/3 innings to earn a spot on Boston's playoff roster. Maddox began the 2018 season on the Red Sox's disabled list with a shoulder strain. Maddox's four-seam fastball averaged 95 mph in his first taste of the Majors and usually ranges from 92-97 mph. He'll throw it up in the strike zone to set up his changeup, a mid-80s weapon with splitter action that also can be a plus pitch at times. He'll keep hitters off balance by mixing in an occasional mid-80s slider that shows some flashes of becoming an average offering. Maddox's control has slipped a bit as he has started throwing harder, and he has to be careful with his location because his reliance on four-seamers has made him a fly-ball pitcher. While he may not be a high-leverage reliever, he made a good first impression in Boston and could be a seventh-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Guerra was eligible for four straight Drafts from 2011-14 but went unselected as a California high school senior, JC of the Canyons (Calif.) freshman and sophomore and a Grand Canyon junior. He won the Western Athletic Conference batting title with a .373 average in 2014 and encored with a 24-game hitting streak in 2015, when the Red Sox made him a $5,000 senior sign in the 17th round. After not hitting much in his first two pro seasons and fracturing his lower leg in 2016, he batted .283/.361/.437 while advancing to Double-A last season. De la Guerra's instincts and inner drive stand out more than any of his tools, none of which grade better than average. However, he has a knack for making consistent line-drive contract and draws enough walks to post solid on-base percentages. He won't drive many balls over the fence but will lace his share of doubles to the gaps. A second baseman for much of his first two years as a pro, de la Guerra spent most of 2017 at shortstop. He enhanced his utility profile by proving capable at shortstop and also saw action at third base in the Arizona Fall League. He's a steady if unspectacular defender with reliable hands and average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jerez went in the second round of the 2011 Draft as an outfielder with a big league body and the potential for plus power, speed and arm strength. He batted just .221/.254/.275 in his first three pro seasons, however, so he switched to pitching in 2014. He advanced to Double-A a year after his mound debut, then saw his stuff and command regress in 2016 before righting himself last season. After losing velocity the year before, Jerez regained his 93-97 mph fastball, which features some sink. He also reclaimed the sharpness on his low-80s slider, giving him two pitches to attack left-handers, who posted just a .485 OPS against him last year. He has struggled against righties (.815 OPS in 2017) but hopes that scrapping a changeup for a promising splitter will help him going forward. Jerez also helped his cause by improving his strike-throwing last year. Whether he becomes a situational reliever or something more will depend on his ability to refine his splitter. After outrighting him off their 40-man roster following the 2016 season, the Red Sox added him back last November.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Given his fastball velocity and the success he has enjoyed early in his pro career, it's difficult to fathom why Martinez had to wait more than three years after he became eligible to land a pro contract. Even then, the Red Sox paid just $5,000 to sign him out of the Dominican Republic in January 2016. He recorded a 1.48 ERA in his first two pro seasons and helped low Class A Greenville win the South Atlantic League championship last September. Martinez worked with a 91-94 mph fastball when he broke into pro ball and boosted his velocity to 95-98 with some armside run during his first full pro season. He also can miss bats with a pair of secondary pitches. His mid-80s slider can be nasty albeit inconsistent, and his low-90s splitter is especially useful against left-handers. Though he has three quality pitches, Martinez will be a reliever. There's effort in his delivery, which also features a long arm action and a lot of moving parts. Though he has a lot going on with his mechanics, they add deception to his pitches and his athleticism helps him throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bishop was expected to serve as UC Irvine's Friday night starter until a preseason oblique suffered during a bullpen session prior to Opening Day wiped out his entire junior season. While the Orioles still took a flyer on him in the 26th round in June, it appeared that the two sides were unable to strike a deal prior to the July 7 signing deadline. It later was revealed, however, that Baltimore actually had submitted its $605,000 deal with Bishop nearly five minutes after the deadline had passed, and a corresponding investigation by Major League Baseball determined that the signing was valid because the parties agreed to a contract before the deadline. He spent most of his pro debut with Class A Short Season Aberdeen, pitching to a 0.78 ERA with 38 strikeouts in 35 innings, and continued to impress with Class A Delmarva in 2018. A 6-foot-4, 215-pound left-hander, Bishop can run his fastball up to 95 mph, albeit with little feel for where it's going. He features a pair of breaking balls in a curveball and slider, both of which currently grade as fringe-average but stand to improve with experience. The same can be said for his changeup, too. Bishop's feel for pitching leaves quite a bit to be desired, though he did make gains with both his control and command in his first full season. He has the raw components needed to stick as a starter at the next level, as well as the pure arm strength to become a late-inning reliever should that not work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round Draft pick in 2014 out of Tennessee Tech, Hess made steady progress early in his career while reaching Double-A in his first full season. Though he struggled the following year over a full season in the Eastern League, Hess rebounded in his return to the level in 2017, posting a 3.85 ERA and logging a career-high 154 1/3 innings, and the Orioles added him to their 40-man roster after the season. Hess attacks the zone from an over-the-top slot that helps him achieve downhill plane with a fastball that ranges from 89-95 mph and usually sits around 93. Both his slider and curveball are average offerings, with the former currently grading ahead of the latter, though he can get caught between them at times. He also has a serviceable changeup that plays against left-handed hitters and demonstrates average control of his four-pitch mix. Questions remain about whether Hess, with his high-effort delivery and lack of an out pitch, can remain a starter. It's long been thought that his stuff would play up in short bursts out of the bullpen, where his fastball-breaking ball pairing could make him a force against right-handed hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the D-backs in January 2011, Ramirez spent his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League as an infielder before making the transition to pitching full time the following year. He spent the next four seasons refining his craft in Rookie ball before joining the Yankees via the Minor League phase in the 2015 Rule 5 Draft. Ramirez broke out in his 2016 full-season debut, prompting the Yankees to add him to their 40-man roster in November, and then earned All-Star honors with Double-A Trenton in 2017 before heading to the Orioles in a Trade Deadline deal. After beginning the 2018 season with Triple-A Norfolk, Ramirez was called up for his Major League debut in June and quickly established himself as part of the Orioles' starting rotation. Operating from a high three-quarters slot, Ramirez will sit comfortably in the low-90s with his fastball while bumping 96. A plus changeup and an inconsistent slider comprise his secondary arsenal, and he's capable of generating whiffs against hitters on both sides of the plate with both. Ramirez has good feel for throwing strikes but below-average command. With an intriguing blend of stuff, pitchability and bat-missing ability, Ramirez has all the ingredients needed for him to stick as a big league starter. Should he be unable to do so, the right-hander should have no problem offering value as a long-reliever or swingman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sparks wasn't a big name in scouting circles leading up to the 2017 Draft, but he still intrigued enough with this tools and remaining projection to earn a selection in the fifth round by the Orioles. A two-way player at Seven Lakes (Texas) High, he signed for slot value, passing on a commitment to McLennan Community College, and then impressed club officials during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League and fall instructional league. Sparks shows a quick right-handed bat with present raw power from the right side of the plate, though there is some length to his swing that leads evaluators to question the future utility of his hit tool. He showed both swing-and-miss tendencies as well as on-base skills during his debut, recording 39 strikeouts and 33 walks in 42 games. Sparks has the speed and range needed to stick in center field, while the well above-average arm he showcased on the mound as a prep would also make him a clean fit in right. While Sparks' ceiling is tied to his potential as a hitter, his speed, defense and strong arm also suggest he'll have a solid floor. He will need time to refine his game in the Minors, but the Orioles have liked what they've seem from the toolsy outfielder so far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selected in the 10th round in 2013 following his senior year at Fresno State, Wynns made progress on both sides of the ball during his first two seasons before breaking out in earnest in '17 with a career-best performance across three levels including Triple-A. That across-the-board improvement prompted the Orioles to add Wynns to their 40-man roster after the season, and he rewarded the club by making his Major League debut in June 2018. Wynns is a strong defender behind the plate with above-average arm strength and advanced catch-and-throw skills that enabled him to throw out more than 38 percent of attempted basestealers in 2017. He also made strides with his blocking, and club officials speak highly of his feel for calling a game. No slouch with the bat, Wynns slashed .281/.377/.419 while establishing career highs in home runs (10), doubles (19) and walks (54). Wynns' breakout performance has thrust him into the Major League spotlight, portending a possible backup role for the 27-year-old catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Cubs in 2011, Araujo spent parts of his first four seasons in his native Dominican Summer League before finally heading stateside in '14. He impressed during his full-season debut two years later and then put it all together in 2017, earning mid-season All-Star honors in the Class A Advanced Carolina League before finishing in Double-A. That success followed Araujo to the Arizona Fall League, and the Orioles liked what they saw enough to take him in the December Rule 5 Draft. Big and physical, Araujo pitches with slightly above-average fastball velocity and pairs it with a plus curveball. Capable of missing bats with both offerings, his 11.6 strikeouts-per-nine innings with Myrtle Beach ranked third in the Carolina League and first among Cubs farmhands. Araujo also features a changeup, while his control of all three pitches helps his arsenal play up. Araujo has shown steady improvement in each season since making a full-time transition to the bullpen. Though he excelled at closing games in 2017, Araujo is more likely to assume a lesser late-inning role should he stick on the active roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles' system had its share of breakout performers in 2017, but Rifaela's was the most unexpected. After scuffling through his first two pro seasons, the Curacao native erupted to slug a Class A Advanced Carolina League-leading 24 homers while slashing .284/.358/.500 en route to circuit MVP honors. A stocky but physically strong player, Rifaela stands out most for his impressive left-handed power. He got to it more than ever in 2017 and also showed improved feel to hit despite striking out in 24.4 percent of his plate appearances with Frederick. Rifaela is a below-average runner but moves well enough to profile as an average defender at either corner outfield spot, even showing he can handle center field in a pinch. It's yet to be seen how Rifaela's game will translate at higher levels against more advanced arms, but there's enough thump in his left-handed bat to peg him as a potential big league contributor in some capacity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Rays for $10,000 out of Venezuela in June 2012, Chirinos has checked all the necessary boxes during his climb through the Minor Leagues despite little fanfare. That was especially true in 2017, when the Rays named Chirinos their Minor League pitcher of the year after he went 13-5 with a 2.73 ERA and a 0.97 WHIP in 168 1/3 innings between the Double- and Triple-A levels. Added to the 40-man roster after the season, Chirinos made his big league debut the following April and continued to pitch well while taking advantage of a depleted Rays' rotation. Chirinos lacks a plus offering but knows how to get the most out of his three-pitch mix. He'll operate at 92-94 mph with his fastball, imparting sinking action that nets him plenty of ground-ball outs, and he does a good job of keeping hitters off balance with a slider that has vastly improved in the last two years, as well as a changeup that he throws with late fading action. Plus control and command are Chirinos' greatest strengths, as he's consistently around the zone with his entire arsenal, seldom issues walks and knows how to induce weak contact early in counts. That allows his stuff to play up, and it gives him a chance to serve as a back-end starter in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Skoug could have gone in the first three rounds of the 2014 Draft if he hadn't been intent on attending Texas Christian, where he immediately became the Horned Frogs' cleanup hitter and led them to three College World Series in three years. In 2017, he overcame an early slump and 98 strikeouts (one short of the NCAA record) to share the Big 12 Conference player of the year award after leading the league with 20 homers and 71 RBI. He slid to the seventh round of the Draft, where the White Sox pounced on him with an over-slot $300,000 bonus. Skoug has impressive bat speed and strength that create plus raw power. He's at his best when he employs a compact left-handed swing, uses the entire field and lets his pop come naturally, but he fell into a rut at the beginning of his Draft year where his stroke got too long and he got too pull-happy while trying to do to much. He struck out in 38 percent of his plate appearances during his brief pro debut, and while fatigue played a part, he'll need to make adjustments to handle more advanced pitching. Though no one questions Skoug's leadership work ethic, there are concerns about his ability to stay behind the plate. He lacks athleticism and quickness, limiting his effectiveness as a receiver, and might wind up at first base. He compensates for fringy arm strength with a quick release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians selected Longo in the 14th round in 2016 out Ohio University, where he had posted a career .355 average over three seasons. He continued to show an advanced bat during his pro debut, but opened his first full season behind schedule due to a wrist injury. When he finally took the field in mid-May, Longo torched Class A Midwest League pitching at a .361/.431/.530 clip to earn a late promotion to Class A Advanced Lynchburg. Longo is a toolsy college product with remaining upside. Hitting from an open stance, he creates leverage to the ball and keeps his barrel in the zone for an extended period of time. It in turn allows him to effectively cover both sides of the plate and use the entire field, something he has always done well. Longo does have some pop in his bat, though it's mostly to the gaps right now. He's an above-average runner who gets out of the box well and finished fourth in the Indians' system with 20 steals in 2017 despite limited action. Longo's speed also plays well in right field, where he spent his entire full-season debut, and his above-average arm strength is a natural fit at the position. While his hit-over-power profile at a corner position might not hold up as well at higher levels, Longo's broad set of skills and solid tools give him a solid chance to consistently outperform projections.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When McMillan had some minor arm issues during his senior high school season in Florida, many thought he might go on to fulfill his commitment to the Florida Gators. The Tigers weren't deterred, however, liking his chances to be an all-around catcher enough to give him an above-pick value bonus of $1 million in the first round and sending him out for a solid pro debut in the Gulf Coast League. During his summer debut, McMillan showed a very strong hit tool, with a very advanced approach at the plate, especially given his age and experience. He made consistent contact and didn't strike out much, while drawing more walks than whiffs in the GCL. He will have to add some strength, with the hope of some power to come as he matures, even if he is more hit over power long-term. McMillan is a solid defender with good hands and receiving skills. The injury behind him, he should be able to get back to using his above-average arm more consistently. It can take a while for high school catchers to develop fully, given all of the responsibilities thrown at them behind the plate. McMillan's advanced feel to hit and his all-around defensive skills should help him shorten the learning curve as he begins his pro career in earnest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After losing his spot at Oregon, Morgan became a walk-on at the University of Washington and was forced to step right into the starting lineup as a freshman. Over his first two years, he was a glove-first backstop, but his Draft profile really jumped when his bat caught up to his defense as a junior, landing him in the third round. He was tired during his pro debut and the Tigers think they'll be getting a look at the real Joey Morgan in 2018. Morgan built a strong defensive reputation at Washington, showing good receiving and blocking skills and an above-average arm. It looked more like average during his summer pro debut, though he still threw out just over 30 percent of potential basestealers in the New York-Penn League. While he was a much better hitter in his junior season, it remains to be seen how the bat will play at this level. He makes consistent contact, but didn't show much in the way of the extra-base ability that raised his profile in college. Morgan will have to show how he can stand up to the rigors of a long season, while continuing to add strength and showing he can be an all-around catcher. If not, a future backup role seems extremely feasible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chipola Junior College won the JUCO World Series in 2017 with one of the most stacked rosters in recent junior college history. A total of 11 players from the program were drafted in 2017, led by Rivera, who went No. 57 overall, in the second round. He struggled out of the gate during his debut in the New York-Penn League, showing there's work to be done. Rivera has legitimate raw power, but the question is whether he'll be able to make the adjustments necessary to tap into it consistently. The mechanics of his swing led to him having trouble with balls on the inner part of the plate and a fair amount of swings and misses as a result. He'll have to smooth out those rough edges to become a serious offensive threat from the left side of the plate. Largely a first baseman at Chipola, the Tigers had the Puerto Rico native play a lot of right field during his debut. He'll continue to play both spots in 2018, likely more at first, but it's hard to walk away from his strong arm in an outfield corner. Regardless of his defensive home, it's going to be Rivera's bat that allows him to climb up the Tigers' ladder. How he adjusts in his first pro season should speak volumes about his future impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez was ranked No. 19 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International prospects list heading into the 2017 July 2 signing period. His overall tools, particularly at shortstop, stood out enough for the Tigers to give him $1 million to sign and he's starting his pro career in 2018. While player and organization are still getting to know each other, Gonzalez has already made an impression with his glove-work. He has very good actions and a strong arm to go along with outstanding hands, giving him the chance to be an above-average to plus defender when all is said and done. Some felt he might need to move to third in the future because of his age. It's going to take a long time to see if the investment in Gonzalez pays off for Detroit. But the teenager does have all the makings of a big league middle infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 4 starter on Howard (Texas) JC's 65-1 national champions in 2009, Smith transferred to Oklahoma and signed with the Padres for an above-slot $250,000 in the 14th round two years later. He advanced to San Diego by May 2013 but hurt his arm in Triple-A the following April and had Tommy John surgery four months after joining the Rays as part of the three-team Trea Turner trade in December 2014. He didn't appear in a regular-season game until June 2017, then pitched well enough in the Minors and the Arizona Fall League for the Mets to claim him in the Rule 5 Draft and immediately sell him to the Royals. Health is the only real issue with Smith. He has a 93-97 mph fastball with some life and Kansas City clocked him at 100 mph in the AFL. He also can miss bats with his solid changeup and a mid-70s curveball, though the latter isn't as consistent as his other two offerings. Smith has a history of throwing strikes, though his control wasn't as sharp in 2017, likely the result of his three-year layoff. He has the talent to compete for a spot in Kansas City's rotation, though his medical bet makes using him out of the bullpen a safer bet. Of the 18 players taken in the 2017 Rule 5 Draft, he should have the best chance of sticking with his new team.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-rounder as a Puerto Rican high schooler in 2015, Cancel passed on a commitment to Miami Dade JC and signed for $200,000. He spent two years in Rookie ball before moving to low Class A in 2017, when he ranked sixth in the South Atlantic League and first among its middle infielders with 46 extra-base hits. He has a chance to get the job done offensively and defensively and is the organization's top second-base prospect. Cancel is stronger than most second basemen and has the quick right-handed swing to catch up to good fastballs. He's built along the lines of Carlos Baerga and may have some more power he can tap into now that he's hitting more balls in the air. His biggest need at the plate is to add more discipline so he'll be able to handle more advanced pitching. Drafted as a shortstop, Cancel moved to second base two months into his pro debut. He has good hands and turns the double play well, though his fringy speed and average arm limit his ability to play other positions. He'll have to realize his offensive potential to make it as a regular and won't have a utility role as a fallback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Six years after signing for $13,000 out of Venezuela in 2010, Machado still hadn't reached full-season ball. Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of 2015 didn't help, but his 5-15, 4.91 record in five seasons in Rookie leagues didn't exactly scream success. His stock changed dramatically in 2017, however, which he began in high Class A and ended with two appearances in Kansas City. Machado sits at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with riding life on his four-seam fastball. His changeup shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch but also can get too firm at times and couldn't prevent left-handers from batting .300/.365/.525 against him last year. His mid-80s slider features more velocity than tilt and got hammered during his brief time in the big leagues, when he surrendered nine runs and got 11 outs. Machado's walk rate dropped from 4.7 per nine innings before he had his elbow reconstructed to 2.6 in the first two years afterward. While he's providing more strikes, his command lags behind his control and his delivery lacks deception, so he's fairly hittable. Though he fared well as a starter in Double-A last year, his inconsistencies and the fact that he never has pitched more than 77 innings in a season point to a likely future as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Steele intrigued scouts as a Georgia high schooler in 2015, but his Vanderbilt commitment and rough delivery left him undrafted. He pitched sparingly for the Commodores as a freshman before academic ineligibility prompted his transfer to Chipola (Fla.) JC for 2017. He won Most Valuable Pitcher honors at the Junior College World Series, helping the Indians capture their second national title and then signing for $826,500 as a supplemental second-round choice. Steele's 6-foot-5 frame and low three-quarters delivery allow him to make lefties uncomfortable and get in on the hands of righties. He throws sinking two-seam fastballs in the low 90s and running four-seamers that can reach 95, both of which play up because of the difficult angle his size and arm slot create. His sweeping slider and changeup show flashes of becoming solid secondary offerings but still lack consistency. Though he generally throws strikes, Steele will need to improve his command to remain a starter in pro ball. He missed a month during the spring with a blood clot and worked a combined 52 innings in two college seasons, so he'll need to establish he can hold up over a full pro season. If he's not durable enough to remain a starter, he could be an interesting bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Royals' international spending spree during the summer of 2015, Lara signed for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic. While he's still making the transition from thrower to pitcher, he has one of the quickest arms in the organization. After two seasons in Rookie ball, he made a successful jump to low Class A in 2018. Lara already has boosted his fastball from the low 90s when he signed to the mid-90s with a peak of 100 mph two years later, though his heater is fairly straight. He also has some power to a curveball that hovers around 80 mph and sometimes turns into more of a slider when he doesn't stay on top of it. He also has a circle changeup but needs to show more trust in it. Lara's control and command are very much works in progress. His small, lean frame and the funkiness of his arm action lead to questions about his durability and viability as a starter. Though Kansas City will continue to give him innings in the rotation for now, he could wind up as an upper-90s reliever in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chipola College not only won the Junior College World Series in 2017, it had a large chunk of its roster taken in the Draft that June. Bechtold was the third Indian taken, in the fifth round by the Twins, and he went out and had a very strong pro debut in the Appalachian League. Bechtold began his collegiate career at Maryland, but transferred to Chipola after redshirting his sophomore year and being told he would be a part-time player. He put up huge numbers with Chipola, but might have been dinged by some team's models that discount production at the junior college ranks. At least in his debut, Bechtold's approach translated quite nicely to the pro game, making consistent contact and drawing walks in an approach that's still hit over power. A solid athlete with very good range defensively, Bechtold has average speed and likes to run. His plus arm will work very well from the hot corner. It appears that Bechtold has an exciting package of tools to eventually develop into an everyday third baseman. That's starting with full-season ball and the end result could be one of the better steals of the 2017 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After dealing with Tommy John surgery and thoracic outlet syndrome while at the University of Texas, facing pro hitters late in games may seem like a walk in the park to Curtiss, the Twins' sixth-round pick in the 2014 Draft. After a strong first full season and showing in the Arizona Fall League in 2016, Curtiss pitched his way from Double-A to the big leagues and led the system in saves. He spent most of the 2018 season in Triple-A, though he did return to Minnesota, and was sent to the Angels in January in a Minor League deal. The Twins did give Curtiss the chance to start at the outset of his career, but it's clear the back end of the bullpen, where his fastball-slider combination plays up, is the place for him. He creates angle with his 6-foot-4 frame well, leading to weak contact off of his 94- to 98-mph fastball, though he also misses bats with it up in the zone. His slider has improved to the point of being a true out pitch with hard two-plane break. He's not a big command guy, and while he threw enough strikes previously in his career, his control regressed in 2018. Curtiss wasn't able to establish himself as a Major League reliever with the Twins. He gets a fresh start with the Angels and if he can rediscover the strike zone, he still has the chance to pitch in high-leverage situations in the back end of a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In recent drafts, the Angels had targeted young, athletic outfielders in the early rounds. Pearson, who was Louisiana's Gatorade state player of the year in 2017, fits that description and was taken in the third round, given an above-pick value bonus of $1 million to forego his LSU commitment. After struggling a bit in his pro debut, he was sent to the Twins for international bonus pool money, used to help bring Shohei Ohtani to Anaheim. The Twins liked Pearson in the Draft, but the Angels got to him first, so they're happy to have his athleticism and offensive potential in the fold. There's a power-speed mix to tap into, with 20-20 potential if everything clicks. A left-handed hitter, Pearson utilizes a simple approach with good bat speed and an ability to backspin the ball when he's locked in, pointing to hitting for average and power. He's a plus runner who should be able to steal some bases and cover ground in the outfield. While he played center field in high school, he played left during his pro debut, as his well below-average arm, which is still coming back from labrum surgery after his sophomore year of high school, might be better suited for that corner. Moving to the corner might put more pressure on him to produce offensively, but he has the potential to profile well there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Every spring, the Canadian Junior National Team heads to Florida to get work in, and be seen by scouts, before the weather turns warm north of the border. Countless prospects have raised their profile with strong showings on this trip and Leach was certainly one of them, raising his profile enough to land in the second round, where he signed with the Twins for $400,000 below pick value. There is quite a bit of upside potential to unlock with Leach. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has the perfect pitcher's build and the potential for a three-pitch mix to fit a starter's profile. He'll throw his fastball in the 92-94 mph range comfortably and he backs it up with an 81-84 mph breaking ball that has good slider action to it. He has enough feel for his changeup to believe it will be at least a Major League average offering in time. While there are some delivery issues for him to iron out, he's athletic enough to envision a repeatable delivery and solid average control. Leach is getting his pro career going in earnest in 2018. There could be more in the tank, not only as he fills out, but as he learns what it takes to pitch in a professional rotation. With some patience and his plus work ethic, he could be doing that eventually in Minnesota.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ferguson and Dodgers corner infielder Matt Beaty are battling to become the first Belmont position player to reach the big leagues after teaming up for four years in college. Both parlayed huge senior seasons into pro contracts in 2015, with Ferguson signing with the Astros for $1,000 as a 19th-rounder after hitting .395/.486/.682. He breezed through the Minors before struggling when he got to Triple-A last August. Houston executives rave about Ferguson's baseball IQ, which helps him play above his tools -- not that there are any glaring deficiencies with his tools. He makes consistent hard contact with a sound right-handed swing and a patient gameplan. Though he has a compact build, he has average power and could produce 12-15 homers per year if he tried to drive the ball more often. Ferguson has solid speed and uses it well on the bases and in center field. After getting relegated to the corners in his first two seasons while playing along higher-profile prospects, he showed that he could handle center in 2017. His average arm adds to his versatility, allowing him to man all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adcock parlayed three successful years at Michigan into getting drafted in 2016's fourth round, but he didn't make a very positive first or second impression on the Astros. He made just three starts in his pro debut before tearing the meniscus in his knee while fielding a bunt, then arrived at his first Spring Training well over his desired weight. He still made quick work of low Class A, earning a promotion a month into his first full season. Adcock has averaged more than a strikeout per inning in college and pro ball thanks mainly to his breaking pitches. He uses a big-breaking curveball in the mid-70s against left-handers and a sweeping slider in the low-80s, getting lots of swings and misses with both. He sets them up with a low-90s fastball that peaks at 94 mph and features some riding life. After averaging 7.1 walks per nine innings as a Wolverines junior, Adcock has improved his control as a pro by doing a better job of staying online to the plate. He'll need to further refine his control, command and changeup to make it as a No.4 starter. More likely, he'll move to the bullpen and rely even more heavily on his curveball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Naile returned from Tommy John surgery to pace Conference USA in strikeouts and innings in 2015, the same year that the A's took the Alabama-Birmingham hurler in the 20th round. Though he reached Triple-A while pitching at four levels last year in his first full professional season, Naile's shining moment came the next year in the Texas League finals, when he tossed six scoreless frames to lead Double-A Midland to its third straight title. Naile helped the RockHounds secure yet another title in 2017, though he also spent two months on the disabled list with an oblique injury. Naile relies heavily on his sinker, a low-90s offering that he consistently commands down in the zone and that has netted him twice as many ground-ball outs than air outs in his career. He can manipulate the pitch, too, at times imparting cutting action in order to keep hitters true. His slider is an average offering, thrown in the upper 70s, and he'll also mix in a firm changeup that grades as his least advanced offering. Naile's arsenal plays up thanks to his strike-throwing ability and bulldog mentality on the mound. Outside of the injury that sidelined him in 2017, Naile has proven plenty durable during his professional career. He also receives high praise for his defense -- he was a Minor League Gold Glove winner in 2016 -- and feel for controlling the running game. Naile will continue to be developed as a starter, but he also could reach the Majors quickly in a bullpen role, possibly as a long reliever, thanks to his excellent ground-ball tendencies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After beginning his college career as a swingman at Louisiana-Lafayette, Marks' transition to the rotation as a sophomore had mixed results. That prompted to a full-time move to the bullpen as in junior in 2017, a role in which Marks thrived. He struck out 100 batters and yielded just 29 hits in 59 1/3 innings to lead all Division I hurlers in both strikeouts-per-nine (15.17) and hits-per-nine (4.40). That overwhelming success earned him a 13th-round selection by the A's in June, and after signing for $110,000, Marks continued to miss bats with ease across two levels in his pro debut. Marks gets the most out of his two above-average pitches, missing bats inside and outside of the zone easily with each. He won't shy away from challenging hitters up in the zone with his low-90s fastball that he can also spot to both sides of the plate. His curveball is a hammer when it's on, registering in the low 80s with tight spin, and it serves as an ideal bat-missing complement to his fastball. Marks has a strong track record as a strike-thrower, but he'll need to improve his fastball command for continued success at higher levels. Though he started seven of his 13 games during his pro debut and has pitched almost exclusively in that role with Class A Beloit in 2018, Marks' future is likely in the bullpen. His fastball-curveball combo gives him upside as a high-leverage reliever, and with improved command of both pitches, he could hop on the fast track to the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sawyer turned down signing with the Twins as a 27th-rounder in 2015 to return for his senior year at the University of Minnesota. It proved to be a wise decision, as Sawyer drastically improved his Draft stock with a breakout performance in his first year as a full-time starter. Intrigued by his untapped potential in the role, the A's selected Sawyer in the ninth round and signed him for $45,000. Sawyer ranked among the A's system leaders with 140 strikeouts (third), nine wins (fourth), a 3.58 ERA (fifth) and 130 2/3 innings pitched (sixth) while pitching at three levels in his first full season, though Tommy John the following spring wiped out his entire 2018 campaign. After working out of the bullpen exclusively during his pro debut, Sawyer made the transition to starting in 2017 and passed all tests. A 6-foot-5 southpaw whose delivery is loaded with deception, Sawyer pitches with fringe-average velocity, usually sitting around 90 mph. A changeup and a curveball comprise his secondary arsenal, with the former grading as an above-average pitch and the latter needing further refinement. He throws a lot of strikes but needs to improve his command, especially when it comes to his fastball. Sawyer's effectiveness against same-sided hitters is his greatest strength, and he held them to a paltry .100/.202/.127 slash line in 125 plate appearances in his first full season. That said, he'll need to figure out a way to retire right-handed hitters to remain a starter after they slugged .446 with 17 home runs against him. Sawyer's future might not be as a starter, but there's enough there for him to carve out a bullpen role at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's viewed Trivino as a starter when they selected him in the 11th round of the 2013 Draft out of Division II Slippery Rock University. But he pitched to mixed results in the role during his first two seasons, and two years later the A's moved him to the bullpen full-time. Trivino has subsequently blossomed as a reliever, and done so while making a steady climb through the A's system. He pitched to a 3.30 ERA and averaged nearly a strikeout per inning in 2017 while making a career-high 48 appearances across the Double- and Triple-A levels. After the season, the A's added Trivino to their 40-man roster. Listed at 6-foot-5, 225 pounds, Trivino stands out on the mound for his physicality. The big right-hander's stuff is plenty good, too, as he'll run his fastball into the upper 90s while also showing good feel for a low-90s cutter and a quality breaking ball in the low 80s. Meanwhile, after making some key adjustments to his delivery, Trivino made strides as a strike-thrower in 2017 and walked one fewer batter per nine innings than he did the previous year. Trivino's combination of a high-effort delivery and downhill angle to the plate makes his stuff extremely difficult to lift, so much so that opposing hitters have tagged him for just two home runs in 178 1/3 career relief innings, none of which came in 2017. His breaking ball and control both require further improvement, but the raw ingredients are there for Trivino to serve as a late-inning weapon for the A's in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since being drafted out of Georgia Tech by the Twins in 2012, Bard has tantalized with good raw stuff, but injuries had not allowed him to get enough mound time to hone his craft. He missed the entire 2014 season, but he has stayed healthy since, allowing him to get all the way to Triple-A in 2017. The Twins rolled the dice and did not put him on the 40-man roster in the offseason, making it possible for the Angels to take him in the Rule 5 Draft. The right-hander got into eight big league games before being sent back to Minnesota in late April. A lot of things clicked for Bard, the younger brother of former big leaguer Daniel Bard, at the upper levels of the Minor Leagues in 2017 and he used his fastball-slider combination to miss more bats than he had any previous point in his career. From a pure velocity standpoint, Bard's 94-95 mph average fastball is a 60 on the 20-to-80 scouting scale, but it can play up because it has plus riding movement and spin. His slider is a potential plus pitch, a mid-80s power breaking ball. He missed bats during his Major League audition. Being able to stay on the mound, Bard's overall command has improved and certainly helped fuel his breakout in 2017. It's something he'll continue to work on refining as he works back in the Twins system to return to a big league bullpen in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were six players from Puerto Rico taken in the top 10 rounds of the 2017 Draft, starting with Giants first-rounder Heliot Ramos. The Angels think they have a real sleeper on their hands with Rivera, the first Puerto Rican taken after the 10th round, an athletic and extremely projectable left-hander they gave $450,000 to sign. Based solely on ceiling, the Angels feel Rivera could be higher on this list. While he entered the Draft as a bit of a soft-tosser, he's already added some velocity to his fastball, with every chance for it to become a plus pitch thrown with good sinking action. His changeup is currently his best secondary weapon and it could be an above-average offspeed pitch eventually, while his curve is a work in progress. One of the more athletic players in the system, Rivera has a strong and repeatable delivery and already has solid fastball command. With a strong foundation to build from with Rivera's athleticism and solid feel for pitching, there was hope he could take a huge step forward in 2018 as he continues to get stronger and refine his delivery. Struggles with command held him back. Still, the final product could be a No. 3 type starter, though it will take patience in the player development department for him to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ford garnered honors as both the Ivy League's hitter and pitcher of the year as a Princeton junior but ultimately went unselected in the 2013 Draft. He inked a deal with the Yankees shortly thereafter and made steady progress in subsequent years before missing much of 2016 due to wrist surgery. Ford would rebound in 2017, when he was named a Double-A Eastern League All-Star, established career highs in most offensive categories and excelled after a late-season promotion to Triple-A. Following the season, the Mariners selected Ford in the Rule 5 Draft's Major League phase. Ford has long stood out for his pure hitting ability, though it was his considerable uptick in power in 2017 -- his 20 home runs were tied for most among Yankees farmhands -- that helped thrust him into the Major League spotlight. Much of that power is to Ford's pull side, though he does have feel for using the entire field and has fared well against both right- and left-handed pitchers during his career. Ford's back-to-back seasons with a .400-plus OBP highlight his advanced approach and plate discipline, and he enters 2018 having accrued more walks than strikeouts in five professional seasons. As a Rule 5 Draft pick, Ford will need to stick on Seattle's 25-man roster for all of 2018 to avoid being offered back to New York. He has the bat to do so, but the overall profile as a first-base-only prospect in the American League who offers minimal value on the basepaths raises questions about his impact potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller amounted to little offensively during his first four pro seasons before revamping his swing and breaking out in 2017, when he was named as the organization's Ken Griffey Jr. Minor League Hitter of the Year. Opening the season back in the Double-A Texas League, Miller batted .326 to claim a share of the circuit's batting title while also ranking second in on-base percentage (.382) and stolen bases (30).
