While he didn't fare as well during his first Triple-A exposure after a July promotion, it didn't detract from a career-best year that saw Miller slash .307/.355/.393 with 43 steals and 85 runs across two levels. Miller's speed is his carrying tool, receiving plus-plus grades from scouts, and he's long showed that he knows how to use it on the basepaths. Since the start of the 2015 season, he's posted annual stolen-base totals of 50, 49 and 43, respectively. The left-handed hitter offers little power but uses the entire field well and makes a lot of contact, though at times it can be weak or forced. He continues to draw his share of walks despite an overly aggressive approach that resulted in a career-high strikeout total (102) and rate (18.2 percent) in 2017. Miller's wheels also aid him in the outfield, where he's an above-average defender with an average throwing arm that allows him to play all three spots. He profiles best as an extra outfielder who provides much of his value through his baserunning and defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was pure projection when the Mariners inked him for $350,000 at the outset of the 2013-14 international period. He spent the next three seasons playing in his native Dominican Summer League but showed improvement in each campaign before turning in a breakout 2017 campaign with Class A Short Season Everett at age 20. Rosario has impressed club officials with his above-average bat speed and overall feel to hit. He started to grow into his lean, athletic frame in 2017 and in turn saw his power blossom en route to career highs in both doubles and home runs. His swing can get too long at times, however, which leads to some swing-and-miss issues, but also highlights the left-handed hitter's room for improvement. Rosario's athleticism, speed and plus arm strength have netted him time at all three outfield spots, though he spent much of 2017 in center field. He'll need to improve his routes and jumps to remain there, as some evaluators already believe he's best suited for a corner spot long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick out of high school by the D-backs in 2012, Taylor spent parts of five seasons in the lower Minors before finally reaching the Double-A level in 2016 during an injury-plagued campaign. The Mariners selected Taylor from Arizona in the Minor League portion of the Rule 5 Draft in December and assigned him to Double-A, where he put together his best and most complete offensive season to date in the Texas League, earning All-Star honors for the first time in his professional career at age 23. Taylor has shown feel to hit throughout his time in the Minors. A switch-hitter, he has good bat speed, makes consistent contact and demonstrates good plate discipline as well as a knowledge of the strike zone. He's equally productive from both sides of the plate, a notion supported by his .286 and .270 averages last season as a right- and left-handed hitter, respectively. His uptick in the power department in 2017 was a major development, though he'll likely always offer more pop to the gaps than true over-the-fence thump. And while he may not be a burner, Taylor does have average speed and earns praise for his baserunning ability. Taylor is best suited for left field defensively on account of his below-average arm strength, though he does have experience at all three outfield positions. That versatility, along with his late-blooming bat, could help him carve out a role as fifth outfielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2015-16 international signing period opened on July 2, the Rangers landed a pair of center fielders. Leody Taveras quickly developed into the organization's top prospect after signing for $2.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. A Venezuelan who landed a $500,000 bonus, Aparicio wasn't ready for full-season ball at age 18 like Taveras was but stands out with the best instincts in the system. Aparicio plays way above his tools as a defender. He has fringy to average speed yet covers a lot of ground in center field because he reads balls well, has a quick first step and takes direct routes. Likewise, he keeps baserunners in check despite a fringy arm because he gets to balls quickly and makes accurate throws. Aparicio displays similar feel for hitting and running the bases. He makes repeated line-drive contact to all fields with his compact left-handed swing and a sound approach. While he's no slugger, he does have bat speed and should produce double-digit home run totals once he gets stronger.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After finding one of the game's best defensive catching prospects in Jose Trevino at Oral Roberts in 2014, the Rangers went back to the Golden Eagles for another backstop last June. The Johnny Bench Award winner as college baseball's top backstop in 2017, Whatley signed for $517,000 as a third-rounder. He hit better than expected in his pro debut while providing his usual strong work behind the plate. Whatley was arguably the best all-around defender among college catchers available in last year's Draft. He receives and blocks well, and he's tough on basestealers with his solid, accurate arm. He has more athleticism and speed than most players at his position, though he's still a below-average runner. Questions about Whatley's upside arose when he struggled with wood bats in the Cape Cod League in 2016 and slumped at the outset of last spring. He fared better when he stopped worrying about home runs and focused on sticking with his disciplined approach. He makes consistent contact, owns decent pop and will work counts to draw walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez had a mid-80s fastball when he first became eligible to sign out of Venezuela in 2008, and it took him an additional two years to add enough velocity to entice the Rangers to give him a pro contract. He spent his first two pro seasons and part of a third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, then blew out his elbow just when he was starting to gain some momentum in 2015. After missing all of 2016 while recovering from Tommy John surgery, he was spectacular last year, retiring 45 consecutive batters at one point in high Class A before jumping from Double-A to Texas in August. Strictly a reliever, Rodriguez works primarily with a four-seam fastball in the mid-90s and a solid slider in the mid-80s. While he was in the big leagues, his slider wasn't as sharp as it had been in the Minors. He'll occasionally use a low-80s curveball to give hitters a look at something with a little less power. Rodriguez has a clean delivery that has allowed him to fill the strike zone since he entered pro ball. It lacks deception, however, and he'll try to compensate by altering his leg kick or using a slide step. He opened 2018 on the big league disabled list with an elbow injury, but returned to the mound in May.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since his high school days, Seymour has intrigued with some raw tools, particularly his speed. It's why the Marlins drafted him in the seventh round of the 2014 Draft and signed the Bahamian-born hitter out of Miami-area high school powerhouse American Heritage for an above-pick value bonus of $400,000. It's why the Braves acquired him late in the 2016 season in the Hunter Cervenka trade. Seymour's speed is still very much his carrying tool, and it's top of the scale. He can flat-out fly, though he's still learning to use his speed effectively on the basepaths to be an efficient threat to steal and in the outfield. He is capable of making contact from both sides of the plate, albeit without power, but his approach has not improved over time. Seymour needs to cut down his strikeouts and get on base more frequently so he can use that plus tool to greater effect and allow the run-producers to do their job. A shortstop initially, Seymour has moved to the outfield full-time and is capable of manning all three spots, with a strong arm from his infield days. He'll continue to do that while focusing on his development as a table-setting type of speedster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lugbauer's power output ticked up when he was a junior at Michigan, and he finished with a dozen homers and a .518 slugging percentage. The fact that he does it from the left side of the plate, and perhaps has the chance to catch, made him an intriguing 11th-round pick by the Braves last June. He then slugged his way from the Appalachian League to the South Atlantic League during his pro debut, hitting another 13 balls out of the park. He couldn't quite replicate those results in his first full year, though he did reach double digits in home runs back in the SAL in 2018. It will be Lugbauer's bat that will allow him to continue to move up the Braves' ladder. The power is legitimate, with it perhaps coming more from strength than bat speed, but he did show in his debut that he can hit the ball out to both his pull side and the opposite field, going to left-center field with ease. With the power comes considerable swing and miss, but Lugbauer mitigates that, at times, with a willingness to take walks. While he played several positions at Michigan and saw time at first and third during his debut, Lugbauer committed himself to catching only for the time being. He has work to do on his receiving and he'll have to quicken his release to use his arm strength better, but the Braves like the strides he's made and the work he's put in to improving defensively, with the hopes of finding a power-hitting backup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee began his college career at Pearl River CC, playing two seasons there before transferring to Mississippi. A strong junior campaign with the Rebels netted him 12th-round selection by the Rays, and Lee rewarded the organization with a successful full-season debut with Class A Advance Charlotte in 2015. A move up to Double-A the following year proved a challenge for Lee but he bounced back to post a Southern League-best .309 average in 2017, and did so despite being traded to Miami in July. He continued to boost his stock in the Arizona Fall League, prompting the Marlins to add him to their 40-man roster, and then made his big league debut with the club in early 2018. His 2016 performance aside, Lee has a strong track record of hitting. He employs a compact left-handed swing that allows him to spray balls across the entire field and fuels his potential to hit for average. His patient approach results in some swing-and-miss but also plenty of walks and solid on-base skills. A plus runner, Lee is aggressive on the basepaths but needs to refine his basestealing technique. Lee's plus-plus speed translates better in center field, where he's a plus defender with good instincts and considerable range. His above-average arm strength is an asset there and allows him to profile at all three outfield spots. That versatility could make Lee a valuable fourth outfielder at the highest level, though an everyday role isn't yet out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 40th-round pick of the Giants in 2014, Mahan passed on launching his pro career in favor of attending Kentucky. He made strides in each of his three seasons there and was one of the top performers in the Southeastern Conference as a junior, showing improved hitting ability and power as well as second-base defense. Mahan's breakout campaign in college baseball's best league stood out in a thin crop of college hitters, and the Marlins were thrilled to find him still on the board in the third round. Mahan has a nice left-handed swing, shows good feel for the barrel and drives the ball across the entire field. After totaling six homers across his first two collegiate seasons, Mahan added some loft to his stroke and finally tapped into his raw power in 2017 to finish with 41 extra-base hits, including a team-high 15 home runs. An above-average runner, he moves well once underway but doesn't figure to be a stolen-base threat. Defensively, Mahan has looked comfortable at second base after previously struggling as a shortstop. He profiles as a passable defender there, one who can also play the outfield corners as well as first base. However, any future moves down the defensive spectrum will come with increased offensive demands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of Drury University (Springfield, Mo.), Richards spent two years pitching for the Gateway Grizzlies in the independent Frontier League before inking a deal with the Marlins in July 2016. He's since climbed quickly through the Minors, opening his first full professional campaign with Class A Advanced Jupiter, where he was a Florida State League All-Star, and reaching Double-A roughly a year after signing. He finished his first full professional season with 2.53 ERA and 158 strikeouts in 146 innings, earning Miami's Minor League pitcher of the year award. Richards may pitch with a tick below average velocity, usually sitting 90-92 mph, but his fastball plays up because he creates a good downhill angle to the plate with a deceptive delivery and locates it well. His changeup is above average, features good velocity separation and is effective against hitters on both sides of the plate. A fringy curveball gives Richards a third pitch that club officials say improved in his first full season. Richards gets the most out of his three-pitch mix because he's a consistent strike-thrower who has feel for changing speeds and keeping hitters off balance. And while his stuff may not be overpowering, it hasn't stopped the right-hander from piling up his share of whiffs early in his pro career. He profiles as a back-of-the-rotation starter or a long reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins have been successful in the past with their international signings, with outfielder Marcell Ozuna and right-hander Jose Urena representing recent examples. The club hopes Marinez can follow in their footsteps after they inked the teenage Dominican shortstop to a $1.2 million deal at the outset of the 2017-18 international signing period. Marinez is very athletic, and some viewed him as one of the best athletes on the market. While some scouts believe his physical development will eventually force him from shortstop to third base, there are others who believe he has the tools to stay in the middle of the diamond. What's more, the teenager has displayed soft hands, good body control and solid range to both sides. He has also shown plus arm strength and impressive actions on defense. A line-drive hitter with some natural loft to his swing, Marinez can spray the ball to all fields. He's still developing as a hitter but has already shown good bat speed and power potential. He destroys fastballs, and like most prospects his age, he's working on hitting secondary pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The move to Double-A is often the ultimate test for a prospect, with the general thinking being that if someone can succeed at that level, he can compete in the big leagues. If that's the case, Oswalt should be a big league starter soon after the 2012 seventh-round pick moved to the Eastern League in ERA and promptly led it in ERA and finished in the top 10 in a host of other pitching categories. While the San Diego native took a while to get going, making it to full-season ball in his fourth season, he's moved progressively since, using a solid four-pitch mix to get outs. Oswalt will throw his fastball in the 90-95 mph range and uses his 6-foot-5 frame well, throwing downhill and getting some sink on his heater to get groundball outs. His best pitch is his above-average curve, which has good depth and 12-to-6 shape to it, and he'll mix in a slider and a changeup to keep hitters guessing. Oswalt made a nice adjustment in getting his delivery more in line -- he had been cutting himself off -- and that has led to more consistent quality strikes. Oswalt's ceiling is somewhat limited to that of a back-end starter, but he's very close to reaching that and impacting a big league rotation. The Mets added him to the 40-man roster this offseason as a result.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brodey was a two-way prospect in high school, one some teams liked as a left-handed pitcher, who both pitched and hit in his first year at Stanford. He then focused on being an outfielder and while his junior season wasn't quite as strong as his All-Star turn in the Cape Cod League the summer prior, the Mets still saw enough to take him in the third round of the 2017 Draft and sign him for a slightly below pick value bonus of $500,000. He struggled in his first full season of pro ball, though he did finish with double digits in home runs and stolen bases. While Brodey doesn't possess any plus tools, he can do a number of things well. He had improved his approach and drew more walks during his junior season and showed some feel to hit along with decent strike zone awareness during his pro debut, though that regressed in 2018. He has good bat speed and considerable raw power to tap into, so the more he can work counts the better he will be at reaching that power. While he profiles more as a tweener, Brodey has mostly manned center field as a pro and has impressed the Mets with solid instincts and an average arm. He's likely not a full-time center fielder going forward, but knowing he can handle the position could serve him well as a future fourth outfielder. For him to be an everyday left fielder, he'll have to maximize his hit and power tools from the left side of the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rhame's college career in Oklahoma didn't start so well as a freshman, but he got straightened out with a move to Grayson Junior College. A starter there, he was selected by the Dodgers in the sixth round of the 2013 Draft and his arm strength was immediately moved to the bullpen. He pitched all year in Triple-A in 2017, then was dealt to the Mets in last August's Curtis Granderson deal and he made his big league debut for New York in September. Rhame has, and always will be, primarily about his fastball. It will sit 95-96 mph with plus riding life and he can reach back for upper-90s heat on occasion. That's his go-to pitch, but while his secondary stuff is fringy, at best, he does have two other offerings he uses. His slider will show glimpses of being a sharp breaking ball, but it's been inconsistent. His changeup is below-average, but it has shown improvement. He's generally been around the strike zone throughout his career. It's hard to define a future Major League role for a one-pitch reliever, even if it's a really good pitch. Continued development of his secondary stuff to help keep big league hitters from sitting on his fastball, certainly would help.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During a breakout performance in his first taste of full-season ball with the Nationals, Mills faced Lakewood, the Phillies' affiliate in the South Atlantic League, four times. He didn't give up a run until his third time around and overall finished with a 1.64 ERA and 28 strikeouts in 22 total innings. It's no wonder, then, the Phillies were glad to add him to their side in late July courtesy of the Howie Kendrick trade. His time in the Phillies' system was ultimately short-lived, however, as Mills was dealt to Miami for Justin Bour in August. Following the trade, the Marlins promoted him to Double-A. Mills has three solid weapons that he is just starting to figure out how to use regularly, not reaching full-season ball until his fourth summer as a pro, but finishing first in the Nats organization in wins and third in strikeouts despite not being there for the season's final month. He has a low-90s fastball with good life to it, an above-average curve and good feel for an average changeup, all coming from a fast arm and deceptive delivery. His improved ability to repeat his delivery greatly impacted his command and control. Mills has shown an ability to set up hitters really well, keeping them guessing and letting his mix of stuff play up more as a result. He has the ceiling of a back-end starter, but there could be more in the tank to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in August 2012, Reyes has pitched to mixed results in his five professionals seasons but continues to flash tantalizing stuff. That was especially true in 2017, when he ranked among the Class A Advanced Carolina League leaders with his 143 1/3 innings pitched (third) and 133 strikeouts (fifth), both far and away his career highs, while posting a 4.33 ERA and a 1.43 WHIP in 26 starts. Reyes' stuff arguably is the best among right-handed pitchers in Washington's system. Combining athleticism with a fast arm, Reyes pitches with a 92-94 mph sinking fastball that nets him both whiffs and ground balls. Club officials rave about his high-spin-rate curveball, a potential plus pitch, and Reyes impressed them with his changeup development in 2017. While Reyes' stuff may already be there, his control and command are not, with both grading as below average. Further experience and maturation should aid him on that front, giving Reyes a chance to serve as a Nos. 3 or 4 starter once fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals have been aggressive with Rodriguez since signing him in January 2012, believing that the ultra-projectable right-hander's performance would eventually catch up to his raw stuff. That finally occurred in 2017, as Rodriguez was in the midst of his best professional campaign and first in the Class A Advanced Carolina League when was he was hit with an 80-game ban in May after testing positive for a performance-enhancing substance. Luckily for the Nationals, Rodriguez's long layoff has had little impact on his performance in 2018. After pitching well early on in Double-A, Rodriguez made the jump directly to the Major Leagues in early June and logged 4 2/3 scoreless frames in long relief in his big league debut. A tall and physical righty with an electric arm, Rodriguez boasts an effortless plus-fastball that touches 97 mph and sits 93-95 with angle and sink. His above-average curveball is a hammer, standing out for its power as well as the late downer action that helps him miss bats. Better control should enable Rodriguez to generate even more whiffs, though he currently struggles to repeat his delivery and arm action. Rodriguez's PED suspension certainly hurt his progress, but the Nationals were still excited by the progress he had made up to that point. Throwing more strikes and developing a serviceable changeup would do wonders for Rodriguez's chances of starting games. A late-inning bullpen role is more realistic, as it would allow Rodriguez's electric fastball-curveball pairing to play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2010, Suero rewarded the Nationals for their patience with a breakout performance in his eighth professional season. Making 54 appearances between Double-A Harrisburg and Triple-A Syracuse, Suero recorded 20 saves, 10 at each level, while pitching to a 1.76 ERA and .209 opponents' average. It netted him honors as the Nationals' Minor League Pitcher of the Year, and they added him to the 40-man roster during the offseason. A raw thrower with little feel for the zone early in his career, Suero has since learned to harness and refine his stuff. He works with a 92-94 mph fastball that has natural cutting action and he locates to both sides of the plate, though it can get flat at times. He complements his heater with an above-average curveball and changeup that he made strides with in 2017. Suero's command leaves something to be desired even though his control has improved in each full-season campaign. The Nationals love Suero's fearlessness on the mound and cite him gaining confidence as a key to his recent progress. While the stuff might not be good enough for him to close games in the big leagues, Suero, with his strong track record against right-handed hitters, should have no trouble carving out a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of Washington's 2014-15 international class, Alastre has impressed the club with the quick progress he's made early in his career. After a rocky U.S. debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, Alastre was overmatched with an Opening Day assignment to Class A Short-Season Auburn in 2017. The right-hander fared much better back in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he showed improved feel for his promising stuff. Young and projectable, Alastre uses his height to leverage the baseball to the plate, working in the low-90s with his fastball and pairing it with an above-average curveball that features 12-to-6, downer shape. Club officials expect Alastre to add more velocity as he grows into his lean and athletic frame. The Nationals speak highly of Alastre's cerebral approach to pitching and expect his control and command to both improve as he gains experience and develops physically. He's poised to make gains on that front in 2018, in his age-20 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maples landed a $2.5 million deal as a 14th-rounder in 2011 -- still a Draft record for below the third round -- a product of his top-two-rounds talent and his complicated signability because he wanted to play two sports as a pitcher/kicker at North Carolina. He delivered discouraging returns on that investment in his first five pro seasons as he battled injuries and the strike zone. Then he suddenly reversed course in 2017, shooting from high Class A to Chicago while striking out 111 in 68 2/3 innings. Maples can choose from three overpowering pitches in his fastball, curveball and slider. His heater ranges from 94-100 mph with run and sink. He lost some feel for his curve while focusing on fastball command in his days as a starter, but it's back to the low 80s with downer break, and he has come up with a high-80s slider that's even more of a wipeout pitch. More than half the batters Maples faced last year failed to put the ball play, either striking out (37 percent) or reaching via a walk or hit batsman (16 percent). While he's athletic, he never has had a smooth delivery or has provided consistent strikes. His control has gotten worse in 2018 and his inability to locate his pitches has made him ineffective in brief trials with the Cubs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Cubs' 2013 international spending spree, Moreno has posted one of the system's best ground-ball rates since signing for $650,000 out of Colombia. But he also has had a difficult time remaining on the mound, blowing out his elbow and requiring Tommy John surgery after five pro games. He dazzled with a 1.88 ERA and 55/9 K/BB ratio in the lower levels of the system in his first full season back in 2016, but a sore shoulder limited him to 14 starts and diminished his performance in low Class A last year. When he's fully healthy, Moreno can generate groundout after groundout with the power sink and the downhill plane on his 92-96 mph fastball. His secondary pitches are more works in progress but show potential. He has feel for his changeup and while his curveball can get slurvy, he's doing better with it after also trying a slider. Moreno's health history and the effort in his delivery lead to questions about his ability to remain a starter. His walk rate more than tripled from 1.3 per nine innings in 2016 to 4.4 last year, which also doesn't help his cause. He needs innings to refine his repertoire and control, and missing the first two months of 2018 with more soreness means that he has yet to prove he can hold up over a full pro season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With the trades of superstar prospects Gleyber Torres and Eloy Jimenez, Galindo is the best position player remaining in the organization from the Cubs' $8.2 million international spending binge in 2013-14. He cost just $50,000 coming out of Venezuela but has developed into one of the better hitters in the system. He was thriving in his first taste of full-season ball in 2017 until he broke his leg in mid-June. Galindo has the potential to hit for both power and average. A right-handed hitter, he did a better job of making consistent contact last year. He has impressive strength and raw power, though he needs to curb his tendency to hit ground balls to realize his 20-homer potential. Despite his below-average speed, Galindo moves OK at third base and has the requisite strong arm for the position. Footwork issues and throwing inaccuracies led to 59 errors in his first 146 pro games at the hot corner, however. He could be destined for first base and may be able to handle left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round selection in 2013 out of Kent State, Williams had a very successful first full season of pro ball, finishing fourth in the organization in ERA, third in strikeouts and batting average against, as well as second in WHIP. He was unable to build on that success in 2015, when a strained flexor tendon shelved him for the entire season, while subsequent Tommy John surgery in the fall knocked him out for all of '16. Finally healthy in 2017, Williams got back on track at Double-A Biloxi to earn his first Major League callup in September. Williams might be undersized at 5-foot-11, but he's loaded with arm strength. Working out of the bullpen exclusively, Williams operates with a 95-98 mph fastball and pairs it with a plus slider in the mid- to upper-80s. The two-pitch combo fuels Williams' bat-missing ability and makes him a force against right-handed hitters, as they batted just .176 against him with a nearly 34 percent strikeout rate in 2017. Williams showed above-average control before his elbow injury, but he was less effective on that front when he returned last season. His feel for the zone should continue to return as he distances himself from surgery, while his power stuff points to a future role as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harrison turned down a chance to begin his pro career out of high school in 2014, when he opted to honor his commitment to Oregon State rather than sign with the Indians as a 25th-rounder. Known more for his hitting ability and power that produced a .904 OPS with 29 home runs in three seasons with the Beavers, Harrison intrigued teams in the 2017 Draft with his upside as a bat-first catcher. Hoping that his defense would develop, the Brewers drafted Harrison in the third round and signed him for pick value. He made a statement with his bat but struggled defensively during his pro debut in the Pioneer League, and then saw more time at first base with Class A Wisconsin in his first full season before going to the Nationals in the Gio Gonzalez deal at the Aug. 31 Waiver Trade Deadline. Harrison showed the ability to hit for average and power at times for the Beavers, reaching double digits in home runs as both a freshman and sophomore. He added nine more homers as a junior while showing a more refined approach at the plate that carried over into his pro career. Harrison's penchant for striking out, however, has plagued him in his first full season, leading some to question the future utility of his bat. Harrison caught a few times as a junior, but not enough for teams to have a real comfort level with how he looks back there. The Brewers gave him a chance behind the plate early in his career but moved him to first base in 2018 after Harrison struggled to throw out basestealers. Though he could still see some reps behind the plate, Harrison will need to slug his way up the ladder as a first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the second time in six Drafts, scouts flocked to see a left-hander at Mundelein (Ill.) High. Ryan Borucki landed late third-round money ($426,000) from the Blue Jays after dropping to the 15th round in 2012 because he needed Tommy John surgery. Murphy, the top prospect in the state of Illinois last spring, received a slightly larger bonus ($500,000) as the Brewers' fourth-round pick. Murphy usually operates at 88-91 mph and tops out at 93 with his fastball. He commands it well, generates some armside run and should have an above-average heater once his 6-foot-4 frame adds muscle. He does a good job of selling his fading changeup, which shows signs of becoming a plus pitch. Murphy exhibits much more feel for his changeup than his slurvy breaking ball. It's more of a soft curveball at this point, and he may be better off working with a harder slider in the future. More strong than athletic, he repeats his delivery and is expected to have at least average control once he's fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A third round pick out of Fresno State in 2014, Luplow, a former college outfield mate of the Yankees' Aaron Judge, had put in a pair of solid, but relatively nondescript full seasons in the lower levels of the Pirates system over his first two full years of pro ball. He surprised many when he moved to Double-A in 2017 and hit his way first to Triple-A and then to the big leagues, leading the organization in home runs and finishing second in batting average along the way. Luplow had always shown glimpses of power, but took a big step forward in turning his extra-base ability into over-the-fence pop in 2017. He can drive the ball to all fields and his continued improvements in terms of pitch recognition and plate discipline have made him a better all-around hitter. He'll have to trust that approach and his bat-to-ball skills to hit more consistently at the big league level. While he tried to play third for a season in 2015, he has settled into the outfield corners, where he has shown he is a capable defender. Luplow still looks like a fourth outfielder type when all is said and done. But he's ready for that role now and given that he's exceeded expectations in many ways, he could hit his way into more at-bats in Pittsburgh.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A supplemental first-round pick back in 2011, Crick was once the Giants' top prospect, a power right-hander with frontline starter potential. A few years later, he appeared on the brink of being another promising prospect lost to control problems when a full-time move to the bullpen sent him in the right direction in 2017. He made his big league debut with the Giants and then was sent to the Pirates in the offseason as part of the Andrew McCutchen trade. Crick still has the premium fastball that made him such a big prospect in the first place, sitting 94-97 mph and flirting with triple digits on occasion, especially in the shorter relief outings. He mixes in a heavy two-seamer with good sink and an above-average slider with excellent bite. He'll even mix in an occasional changeup. While he'll never be a command and control guy, he found the strike zone much more consistently with the move to the bullpen, with a career low 4.0 walks per nine in Triple-A in 2017. As long as Crick can continue to throw strikes with his fastball-slider combination like he did a year ago, he's ready for a full-time gig in Pittsburgh's big league bullpen. After seeming lost, a potential career as a setup man is within reach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Venezuela in 2012, Gonzalez has always shown intriguing arm strength, but has been slow to get moving through the Cardinals system. He spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League and one in the Gulf Coast League before hitting full-season ball in 2016. He has yet to pitch above A ball and has topped 100 innings just once, in 2016, though a strong finish to his 2017 season, including a handful of relief appearances, were enough to convince the Cardinals to protect him on the 40-man roster. Gonzalez will throw his fastball in the mid-90s and can reach back for more at times, especially in shorter stints, with average movement. His curveball is at least average, and flashes better than that, an effective breaking ball that he can use as an out pitch. He has a changeup, though it is below-average, as he learns how to change speeds effectively. He has a strong 6-foot-3 pitcher's frame that he is still learning to get in sync for a repeatable delivery. That leads to command issues, though he threw more strikes in Palm Beach in 2017. The Cardinals are hopeful the success he had down the stretch is a harbinger of things to come and a testament to the work Gonzalez has put in. There's a solid chance he ends up in a bullpen one day, but it looks like he's headed in the right direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sherriff has definitely defied the odds. The left-hander started out as a 28th-round Draft pick back in 2011 out of Glendale Community College. Devoloped initially as a starter, he moved to the bullpen in 2014 and started putting up numbers at the upper levels without much fanfare, earning Pacific Coast League All-Star honors in 2016 and '17. Ignored in the Rule 5 Draft, Sherriff finally got added to the roster and called up to the big leagues for the first time in August of last year. He landed on the disabled list in April with a broken toe, but did make it up to St. Louis twice before seeing his season end with Tommy John surgery in May. When Sherriff received his first callup to the big leagues, he largely did what he was supposed to do, keeping left-handed hitters to a .080 batting average over 25 at-bats. That should come as no surprise, given he'd kept lefties to averages under .200 in Triple-A the last two seasons. Sherriff comes at hitters with a funky arm angle that brings in fastballs up to 93-94 mph and thrown with a ton of sink that gets a lot of ground-ball outs. He complements that with a very good slider, which when coming from his lower arm slot, is death to lefties. This has the chance to be one of those outstanding player development stories of perseverance once he returns to health. As long as he keeps throwing his fastball-slider combination for strikes, and he has for most of his career, there's no reason to believe he can't be a big league reliever for many years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing out of Venezuela back in 2010, all Valera has done is hit. He's finished seven of his eight summers in the Cardinals system with a batting average over .300 and his .314 average in 2017 topped the system, leading to his first big league callup. Valera really knows how to hit and really knows the strike zone. That's led to a career average in the Minors of .303 to go along with a .359 on-base percentage heading into 2018. The switch-hitter has more walks than strikeouts in his career and has the confidence to have tough at-bats against any level of pitching. There isn't power to speak of, though he can find the gaps. An average runner, Valera has increased his positional versatility over time, showing he is capable at three infield positions as well as the outfield. He has good hands, solid range and outstanding instincts that allow all of his defensive tools to play up. That defensive flexibility will be crucial in order for Valera to get more big league time. He'll have to move around as a utility man to get at-bats, but few doubt he'll hit if given the chance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a strong junior season at Maryland that earned him Big Ten Pitcher of the Year honors in 2017, Shaffer entered pro ball as the D-backs' sixth-round pick with a reputation of being a good strike-thrower. Going out and walking just one batter in 24 innings in his pro debut certainly augmented his standing as a right-hander with plus control. Shaffer is going to have to command the baseball well in order to succeed with his largely average stuff. He will touch 94 mph with his fastball on occasion, but it's the sink to it coming from his 6-foot-5 frame that makes it play up and get ground ball outs. His slider is currently his best pitch, a breaking ball that is an above-average offering. His changeup is fringy, but improving, as it'ss a pitch he didn't throw much in college, but was a focal point during instructs. Throwing strikes obviously comes easily to Shaffer. Now he needs to learn how to consistently throw quality strikes, how to game plan and set up hitters. That will be key for him to reach his potential as a back-of-the-rotation starter, something that could happen fairly quickly given his advanced control and feel for pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramos jumped on the radar a bit in 2016 after scuffling during his U.S. debut the prior summer, finishing among the Pioneer League leaders in several offensive categories. He hit well in a step up to the Northwest League in 2017, albeit with less power, earning a promotion to the full-season Midwest League. Ramos has plus-plus raw power from the right side of the plate, but aside from the outburst with Missoula, it hasn't shown up in games consistently just yet. He was a better overall hitter in 2017, with fewer strikeouts, and the D-backs love the mechanics of his swing. The next step is for him to learn how to control his effort throughout his swing and be able to find that balance between being a solid hitter and tapping into that power. A below-average runner, Ramos is a fringy defender at third, though he does have a very strong arm. He's an average defender at first. Ramos will continue to see time at both infield corners moving forward, as much to make sure his bat is in the lineup as anything else. It's easy to dream of him fitting the infield corner profile from a run production standpoint, but it's going to take time for him to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCullough spent two years relieving for the University of North Carolina, but when he was dismissed from the school for a violation of team rules, he moved to Division II Lander and started there before landing in the fifth round of the 2014 Draft. Putting that adversity behind him, McCullough has been extremely hard to hit as a pro, though he has struggled to consistently find the strike zone. Left unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft last December, McCullough wasn't selected largely because of those command issues. There is absolutely no question about whether his pure stuff can get people out, as evidenced by his career 11.8 K/9 rate and .188 batting average against (14.1 and .158 in 2017 across two levels). His fastball is at least plus, typically in the upper 90s. Hitters don't see his slider and he misses a ton of bats with it. Coming off his best year as a pro, McCullough just needs to keep working on commanding his stuff more consistently. He never has to even have average control given how hard to hit he is. If he can find the strike zone semi-consistently, his fastball-slider combination is good enough to get big leaguers out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2016 Southern Conference pitcher of the year, Gaddis positioned himself as a potential second-rounder when he pitched well in the Cape Cod League and fall practice. His stuff regressed a bit last spring, though he still led the Southern Conference in wins (nine) and ERA (1.89) and became the highest pick in Furman history. After signing for a slightly below-slot $600,000 in the third round, Gaddis looked worn out in his pro debut. Gaddis has heavy sink on his fastball, which sat at 88-92 mph and topped out at 94 in 2017 after reaching 96 previously. He has great feel for his changeup, a plus pitch at times but merely average for much of last year. His curveball and cutter also weren't quite as sharp as usual but show the upside of solid offerings. Gaddis isn't very physical but projects as a starter because he repeats his delivery and pounds the strike zone, efficiently managing his pitching counts. He attacks hitters, even when his stuff is less than its best, and has a higher floor than most of Colorado's starting pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as a catcher out of Venezuela by the Angels in 2007, Diaz took a while to find success. He hit .157 in two seasons before moving to the mound, then didn't post a sub-5.00 ERA in full-season ball until 2014, when he rose from high Class A to Anaheim before going to the Rockies in a December deal for Josh Rutledge. He appeared to solidify his big league standing when he recorded a 2.37 ERA in 21 appearances with Colorado in 2015, but missed all of 2016 following Tommy John surgery and only briefly surfaced in the Majors last year. Diaz reclaimed his power stuff in 2017. His heavy fastball sits at 96-98 mph and can reach triple digits, eliciting a lot of swings and misses as well as weak ground balls. He gets similar results with his upper-80s slider, which can be nasty with late bite. Diaz does a better job of throwing strikes than he did while struggling early in his career, but he still has lapses where he overthrows. His command still needs more fine-tuning because his pair of power pitches get harder than they should. He might be a setup man if he can do a better job of locating his fastball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Spanberger homered just six times as a part-time player in his first two seasons at Arkansas, then went deep 10 times in his final 16 games last spring to finish his junior season with 20. After signing for $260,200 as a sixth-rounder, he kept mashing in pro ball. He homered in three of his first games at Rookie-level Grand Junction and ranked second in the Pioneer League with 19 homers, one behind teammate Casey Golden. Spanberger garners some comparisons to Chris Davis because he's a first baseman with big-time left-handed power and swing-and-miss concerns. His bat speed, strength and leverage give him massive raw power to all fields, and he doesn't get cheated with an aggressive approach. While he probably won't hit for a high average, he did make strides with using the entire field and made more consistent contact in 2017. A high school catcher who played some right field early in his college career, Spanberger has well below-average speed that limits him to first base as a pro. He can develop into an adequate defender but has a lot of work to do after committing 10 errors in 54 games during his debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rogers led Spartanburg Methodist (S.C.) to consecutive third-place finishes at the Junior College World Series before signing with the Rockies as a fourth-round pick in 2014. After posting the worst offensive numbers of his career when he got to the Class A Advanced level in 2016, he put up his best when he returned to that level last year, batting .319/.377/.488 with a Minor League-leading 70 steals. He's the premier basestealer in the Minors, swiping 166 bases in his three full pro seasons while succeeding at an 87 percent clip. Rogers wreaks havoc on the bases with his plus-plus speed. It also helps him cover ground in center field, though he played more in left field last season in deference to Yonathan Daza in Lancaster. His quickness also helps him compensate for a below-average arm by getting to balls quickly. Playing in Lancaster, perhaps the best hitting environment in the Minors, helped fuel Rogers' breakout as he batted .356/.418/.589 at home. The right-handed hitter also made a concerted effort to get stronger and hit the ball with more authority, and it showed. He won't ever be a power threat, so he needs to continue to enhance his plate discipline so he can get on base and run wild more often.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts saw plenty of Abreu when they were scouting Albert Almora (the sixth overall pick in the 2012 Draft) at Mater Academy Charter High (Hialeah Gardens, Fla.), and he had the tools to go in the top five rounds the following year. After he turned down the Reds as a 14th-rounder, he never quite put up big numbers in three years at Miami, though he did help the Hurricanes reach a pair of College World Series. A sixth-round selection in 2016, he hit 14 homers and stole 40 bases in low Class A during his first full pro season. Abreu's bat speed, strength and leverage create well above-average raw power from the left side of the plate, but he's not going to get to use all of it unless he improves as a hitter. He's overly aggressive, which leads to swing-and-misses and a lot of weak contact on pitches he'd be better off avoiding rather than putting in play. Whether he can make adjustments and provide more consistent pop remains to be seen. Abreu moves well for a 6-foot-4, 225-pounder but his 40 steals are as much a product of his instincts than his average speed. He has plus arm strength and showed it off by leading the South Atlantic League with 16 outfield assists in 2017. He gets the job done in right field and could fill in for short periods in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Dominican, Mendoza became eligible to sign in July 2013 but didn't find any takers until the Rockies gave him $80,000 in February 2016. He put himself on the prospect map with a spectacular U.S. debut in 2017, hitting .364/.412/.519 and ranking second in the Rookie-level Pioneer League in both batting and steals (25). Mendoza has a sound left-handed swing and a feel for making line-drive contact. He carries more than his listed 165 pounds and has some strength that could turn into double-digit home run power if he can learn to backspin the ball. He has plus speed and runs the bases aggressively. Mendoza spent his first two pro seasons at second base, but he lacked fluid actions and had a short arm action. He also topped Pioneer League second basemen with 21 errors in just 55 games in 2017, after which the Rockies moved him to the outfield for this season. With his quickness, he should be able to develop into at least an average defender in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at shortstop for Mississippi, Robinson helped the Rebels make the College World Series as a freshman in 2014 but didn't make much progress with the bat afterward. Posting the worst numbers of his college career during his Draft year dropped him to the sixth round in 2016. He has hit better than anticipated in pro ball and didn't look out of place in Double-A when a shortage of middle infielders necessitated his promotion there last June. In little more than a year, Robinson has established himself as the best defender among the system's infield prospects. He has nice actions, solid range to both sides, soft hands and the arm to make all of the throws. The Dodgers have given him extensive action at second base to enhance his versatility, and they've also played him briefly at third base and center field. Even with the good start to his pro career, Robinson still projects to hit at the bottom of a batting order. There's a lot going on in his right-handed swing and though he still manages to make consistent contact, he provides very little in the way of power or walks. He gets the most out of his solid speed on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A key reliever on Texas' 2014 College World Series team as a freshman, Cooper blew out his elbow that fall and missed all of 2015 following Tommy John surgery. He turned down the Nationals as a 34th-rounder after returning as a starter in 2016, then went 32 rounds earlier last year, when he was the Longhorns' ace. The Dodgers thought he showed first-round stuff early in the spring before he tired, and they opted to shut him down for the summer after signing him for a below-slot $867,500 as a redshirt junior. When he's at full strength, Cooper has a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96. His 6-foot-5 frame and overhand delivery create a steep downhill plane that results in swings and misses as well as groundouts. All of his secondary pitches are solid at their best, with his changeup showing more consistency than his curveball and cutter. Cooper's velocity decreased at the end of his last two college seasons, so he'll have to prove he can hold up over a full year as a pro. His clean delivery and arm action are well suited for starting, though his walk rate did rise in each of his three seasons at Texas. His curveball was his second-best pitch as a freshman but hasn't been as reliable since he got hurt and moved into the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Farmer made a cameo in the movie \"The Blind Side\" as a high school quarterback before focusing on baseball and starting at shortstop for four years at Georgia. He lacked the quickness to play shortstop in pro ball, however, so he converted to catcher as soon as he signed for $40,000 as a 2013 eighth-rounder. His steady improvement offensively and defensively paid off when he made his big league debut last July, delivering a game-winning pinch-hit double in the 11th inning against the Giants. Farmer's soft hands, strong arm and leadership skills all helped him make the move behind the plate. He focused on improving his agility after the 2016 season, and his receiving and blocking skills were better than ever last year. More versatile than most catchers, he also has gotten regular action at third base and made appearances at first and second base as well. While Farmer still projects more as a backup than a regular, he has gotten better with the bat as he has become more comfortable with catching. He makes consistent line-drive contact from the right side of the plate and has improved his discipline and power with experience. He even runs better than most catchers, though he still has below-average speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most expensive member of the Dodgers' 2014-15 international class, Cuadrado signed for $750,000 out of Venezuela. He played at three different levels of Rookie ball in his first three years as a pro and hit .335/.413/.523 in the hitter-friendly Pioneer League in 2017. He continued to rake in the playoffs, batting a team-high .526 to lead Ogden to the championship. Cuadrado's impressive size and strength give him plus raw power that doesn't play that way in games because he employs a flat right-handed stroke and hits too many balls on the ground. He strikes out too much for someone using a hit-over-power approach and would be better served by trying to drive more balls in the air. He does show a willingness to take walks and can use his average speed to steal an occasional base. Cuadrado has played all three outfield spots and profiles best in right field, where he played for much of last year. He has average range and plus arm strength but needs to improve his throwing accuracy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herb went 22-9 in four years at Coastal Carolina, three as a starter, before signing with the Mariners for $1,000 as a 29th-round senior in 2014. He didn't do much to distinguish himself in his first three pro seasons before successfully conquering Double-A in 2017, ranking 12th in the entire Minors in both innings (163 1/3) and groundout/flyout ratio (2.0). He came to the Giants in July as the player to be named in a trade for Chris Heston and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster in November. The sink on Herb's 89-93 mph two-seam fastball and the plane he creates with his 6-foot-3 frame generate a lot of ground balls. His secondary offerings all are average, with his slider perhaps the most consistently reliable. He keeps batters off balance by sequencing his pitches well. Herb did a better job of throwing quality strikes last season but has struggled to do so in 2018 while dealing with an oblique issue. He doesn't have a high ceiling but if he can build off the progress he made in 2017, he could be an innings eater at the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cave battled the strike zone in two years at Florida International before boosting his stock by leading the Cape Cod League with 10 saves and reaching 98 mph with his fastball during the summer of 2016. He decided to transfer to NCAA Division II power Tampa, where he continued to struggle to harness his power arsenal. That continued after the Giants signed him for $417,200 in the fourth round last June. Cave usually works with a 94-96 mph fastball that features armside run as a reliever and with a little less velocity when he starts. He also can miss bats with a pair of breaking balls, a low-80s curveball with good depth and an upper-80s slider/cutter, though he can't always land them in the strike zone. He also uses a changeup that might give him a decent offspeed pitch if he uses it more often. Though San Francisco drafted Cave with the idea of trying to develop him as a starter, club officials concede that his never-ending search for command means he'll likely be a reliever. He has cleaned up his delivery some since high school but it still contains a lot of effort and he has difficulty keeping it in sync. Coming out of the bullpen, he'd have late-inning upside if he could throw enough strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since batting .231 in his 2012 pro debut after signing out of the Dominican Republic, Gomez hit at least .305 in his next five years in the Minors. He didn't reach full-season ball until he was age 23 in 2016, but zoomed from low Class A at the beginning of that season to San Francisco last July. He played sparingly in his month with the Giants, though he did go 5-for-16 in the four full games he played. Gomez's simple swing from both sides of the plate and his tremendous hand-eye coordination make hitting a breeze. Besides his pure hitting ability, he also has the solid bat speed and strength to provide 15 homers per season. He's difficult to strike out but also to walk because he puts balls in play so easily. The drawback with Gomez is that he lacks a position because of his well-below-average speed and quickness. He debuted as a catcher, moved to third base three years later, shifted to second base in 2017 and also has seen action at first base and left field. He was too erratic at the hot corner and has substandard range at second, where the Giants will be happy if he can just make all of the routine plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Wolff continually showed promise as a power arm after joining the Rangers as a sixth-round senior sign out of New Mexico in 2013, he couldn't stay healthy. He missed all of 2015 after tearing his left Achilles tendon, the last three months of 2016 with a right forearm strain and the final month of 2017 with a torn flexor tendon in his right hand. Traded to the Giants with fellow righty prospect Israel Cruz for Matt Moore and $750,000 in international bonus pool funds last December, he missed the first 10 weeks of this season as well. Wolff's arm speed generates mid-90s fastballs with some armside run when he comes out of the bullpen, and he has been clocked as high as 100 mph. He still has a four-pitch repertoire from his days as a starter, with his slider his best secondary offering. He'll also mix in a curveball but rarely uses his changeup as a reliever. After Texas made Wolff a full-time reliever last year, he struck out 59 in 43 innings and was pushing for his first big league callup until he got hurt again in August. His control has regressed since he began dealing with the litany of injuries, but he could fill a seventh-inning role if he can provide consistent strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick from Minnesota in 2013, Snelten plateaued as a starter when he got to high Class A but began to take off once he moved to the bullpen in July 2016. He has shown more confidence as a reliever and ranked second among the system's full-season relievers with a 2.20 ERA in 2017. After he had similar success in the Arizona Fall League, San Francisco protected him on its 40-man roster. Snelten's best pitch is his changeup, which dives at the plate and works well against both left-handers and right-handers. He has added fastball velocity since working in shorter stints, now operating at 91-93 mph and peaking at 95 with run and sink. The movement on his fastball and changeup and the downhill plane he creates with his 6-foot-7 frame led to a 2.3 groundout/flyout ratio last year. Snelten has done a better job of maintaining his arm slot as a reliever, allowing him to do a better job of staying on top of his average slider. He has good feel for pitching and some funk in his delivery that adds to his deception. The Giants think he can be more than a lefty specialist, with one club official saying Snelten reminds him of Jeremy Affeldt, a key reliever on their three World Series championship clubs this decade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A four-sport athlete as an Iowa high schooler, Ziegler struggled to hit NCAA Division I pitching as a Northern Illinois freshman but batted .395 with 22 homers and 31 steals as a North Iowa Area CC sophomore in 2016. Though junior college offensive numbers don't necessarily have much predictive value, the Giants signed him for $100,000 as a 22nd-rounder because they believed in his speed and defense. He's still raw in all phases of the game, and losing nearly three months to an oblique strain while making his full-season debut this year didn't help his cause. Some evaluators have clocked Ziegler with top-of-the-scale run times and he builds his game around his well above-average speed. He can steal bases and chase down balls in center field on sheer quickness alone, though he needs to refine his reads and jumps on the bases and in the outfield. His solid arm strength enhances his defensive value. Ziegler needs to get on base more often to take advantage of his speed. He makes a decent amount of contact from the right side of the plate, but needs to add more strength and patience. His JUCO power doesn't translate to wood bats, though he does have some bat speed and can drive the ball to the gaps on occasion.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For much of his college career at Georgia Tech, Justus looked like a defense-only middle infielder. When he picked up the pace with the bat as a junior, his Draft stock shot up, landing in the fifth round of the 2016 Draft with the Angels. While he swung the bat well during his time in the Pioneer League in his summer debut, he's looked more like the all-glove, little-hit shortstop from his early time with the Yellow Jackets. Moved to the Class A Advanced California League to start his first full season, Justus really struggled out of the gate and was hitting .179 at the end of the first half. To his credit, he did make adjustments and hit .323 with an .800 OPS in July before tiring down the stretch. At his best, Justus works counts and gets on base and has worked to be more of a line-drive hitter, while added strength would allow him to find the gaps more consistently. He's still a solid runner who can really defend at shortstop, with excellent hands and a strong arm. Based on the adjustments he made and improvement he showed later in his first full season, Justus is getting the chance to check out the upper levels. Just how much his bat can improve will determine how far he can go as his glove carries him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Increased offensive output during his junior season at Georgia Tech turned Justus into an intriguing all-around shortstop prospect, and not just a defensive specialist. The Angels saw enough to nab him in the fifth round and he made it to full-season ball during his pro debut. While his bat did come to life at school, Justus' calling card will always be his glove. He might be the best defensive shortstop in the Angels' system, with tremendous hands, above-average arm strength and solid athleticism that allows him to make plays in every direction and throw from all angles. He does have some idea at the plate and doesn't chase too often, but he does need to improve his bat path and the mechanics of his swing so he can be more of a line-drive hitter. Adding physical strength will also help him be a bit more of an offensive weapon. Justus should be able to play for a long time because of his defensive acumen. How much his bat develops as his glove carries him up the ladder will determine just how prominent a role he has once he gets to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosa has quickly established himself as one of the more promising young hitters in Seattle's system after they signed him out of the Dominican Republic at the outset of the 2014-15 international period. Coming off of an eye-opening U.S. debut in which he batted .305, Rosa began his 2017 campaign by filling holes on several of the Mariners' full-season rosters, including both Double- and Triple-A. He spent the remainder of the season in the Class A Short Season Northwest League, finishing tied for the circuit lead with 26 extra-base hits, and then opened 2018 with Class A Clinton. The switch-hitting Rosa's bat is his calling card, and he's shown improved hitting ability with emerging power in each of his three seasons. Though undersized, he knows how to impact the baseball from both sides of the plate, and does so while exhibiting an advanced approach for a player his age. Rosa does most of his damage from the left-handed batter's box, and it's from that side that he batted .313/.385/.569 and hit five of his six home runs in 2017. While there could be some more power in his future, he projects more as a gap-to-gap guy at higher levels. Rosa saw time at shortstop early in his career but spent all of 2017 at second base, where he committed 15 errors and largely projects as a fringy defender with similar arm strength. Without the ability to offer value on the dirt, Rosa will be forced to hit his way to the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Jaskie only threw in the low 80s in high school, Michigan still valued him as a recruit because he was a projectable left-hander with a competitive streak. After pitching in middle relief as a freshman, he emerged as the Wolverines' best starter the last two seasons. His 119 strikeouts as a junior matched Michigan's single-season record (Jim Burton, 1970) and also ranked 17th among all NCAA Division I hurlers. That knack for missing bats earned Jaskie a selection in the fourth round by Seattle, and he made his pro debut with Class A Short Season Everett after signing for $245,600. Jaskie's standout pitch is a changeup that arrives in the low 80s and drops off the table as it approaches the plate. While he has gotten stronger, he won't overpower hitters with a fastball that tops out at 93 mph and usually settles in at 88-90. It plays above its velocity, however, because he commands it well and because his funky delivery leads to some awkward swings. Though his mechanics are unorthodox, Jaskie repeats them well and doesn't have any problem finding the strike zone. His biggest need is to improve his fringy slider, and he's committed to using it so he'll have a true three-pitch mix. His durable frame lends itself well to an innings-eating role at the back of a rotation or as a swingman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gillies bounced between the rotation and the bullpen during his first three years at Arizona State before carving out a role as a full-time reliever in 2015 and becoming a 10th-round pick of the Mariners in June. He split his first full season between the Midwest League, where he was a midseason All-Star, and the California League, and then spent all of '17 pitching out of the bullpen for Double-A Arkansas. Among Texas League relievers, Gillies ranked fifth in opponent average (.231) and 11th in appearances (39). Gillies represented Seattle in the Arizona Fall League and then began '18 back with Arkansas before advancing to Triple-A in May. A tall and physical right-hander, Gillies employs a clean delivery with short arm action on the backside that causes his 92-94 mph four-seam fastball to jump on opposing hitters. His slider represents a second average-or-better offering, registering at 82-83 mph with late, hard sweeping action. Gillies demonstrates confidence and feel for locating both pitches, especially the slider, though his current command profile leaves something to be desired. Gillies experienced a dip in his strikeout rate with the move up to the Texas League, but the right-hander still showed the ability to miss bats on both sides of the plate with his fastball-slider combo. That quality, as well as better fastball command, could lead to a seventh-inning role at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since joining the Pirates as an over-slot sign in 2011, Glasnow has moved steadily through the system, slowly evolving from pure thrower to more of a pitcher, all while missing a ton of bats, but also racking up the walks. That continued in 2016 while the tall right-hander made his big league debut, showing that his stuff will play, but that there is still work to be done. Still just 23 for nearly all of the 2017 season, Glasnow has the pure stuff and the body to be a frontline starter. He has a mid-to-upper-90s fastball that serves as an out pitch in and out of the zone at times, though he averaged about a 94 mph heater during his time with Pittsburgh last year. His breaking ball can also miss bats, but he continued to be inconsistent with it in terms of landing it for a strike. His changeup has improved, though it's still his third offering. While his delivery is clean, minor mechanical issues are common for pitchers his size, leading to command issues. There were times in the big leagues where it appeared that Glasnow was trying to be too fine and didn't trust his stuff. There will always be walks to contend with, but if he can go after Major League hitters like he did with opponents in the Minors, he should find more consistent success at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following in the footsteps of older brother Kyle, whom the Royals drafted fifth overall in 2012, Bradley became the second Zimmer to be selected in the first round in a two-year span when the Indians picked him 21st overall in 2014. He participated in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game as part of a breakout 2015 campaign but saw his numbers decline during the second half because he played the final two months of the season with a hairline fracture in his right foot. Fully healthy in 2016, Zimmer got back on track in Double-A and received a midseason promotion to Triple-A before wrapping up his year with an impressive campaign in the Arizona Fall League. Zimmer possesses average-or-better tools across the board, with his power-speed combination serving as his calling card. He drives the ball across the whole field with a clean and controlled stroke from the left side, and he gets to his raw power often enough to project for 20-plus home runs at maturity. Although his strikeout rate has spiked as he's climbed the ladder, Zimmer has maintained a patient approach and continues to coax plenty of walks while reaching base at a high clip. Zimmer's above-average speed plays up because of his strong instincts, as he's proved a stolen-base threat early in his career by tallying 82 steals across his first two full seasons. Defensively, Zimmer has improved his jumps and routes in center field and should be able to stick at the position. Zimmer has the hitting ability and on-base skills needed to become a dynamic top-of-the-order hitter, but it's his 20-20 potential that could make him one of the more valuable up-the-middle players in the game once he's fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates convinced Bell to forego his commitment to the University of Texas by giving him a record $5 million in the second round of the 2011 Draft, they envisioned a future run-producing. switch-hitting presence in the middle of their lineup. That future began in 2016 when Bell hit a pinch-hit grand slam in his second big league at-bat and was fairly productive in the season's closing months. Bell continued to show the ability to be a plus hitter, both in Triple-A and the big leagues. When facing a shift as a left-handed hitter, he was able to poke balls the other way to beat the shift with regularity. He draws walks and doesn't rack up a ton of strikeouts, all while his power continued to improve. Bell's work at first base, a position he started to play in 2015, continues to be a work in progress, and it was rough at times. The Pirates also moved him back to the outfield, playing right, to get his bat into the lineup. Bell is ready to be an everyday big leaguer, one who will continue to learn to drive the ball and be the run producer the Pirates initially envisioned, regardless of his long-term defensive home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Renfroe emerged as a viable first-round pick during the 2012 Cal Ripken League and then solidified his status the following spring at Mississippi State, leading to his selection as the 13th overall pick by San Diego. After finishing the 2015 season in Triple-A, Renfroe returned there last season to pace the Pacific Coast League in home runs (30) en route to the circuit's MVP award. That production carried over into his first taste of the big leagues in September, as he belted four homers in just 11 games to claim NL Player of the Week honors. Renfroe has little trouble applying his plus-plus raw power during games. His bat speed, physical strength and leveraged swing are all ideal for clearing fences, and he showed improved feel for driving the ball out of the park the other way in 2016. He's trimmed his strikeout rate, but will always have some swing-and-miss to his game due to his aggressive approach and at times a lengthy swing. The contact that Renfroe does make is consistently hard and loud, though, giving him the upside of an average hitter. Defensively, Renfroe's arm strength is nearly as impressive as his power and makes him a clean fit in right field, where he's notched 43 assists since 2014. He's athletic and moves well for his size, with average speed on the bases and range in the outfield. After his impressive showing in San Diego last September, Renfroe enters 2017 with an inside track toward a spot in the team's Opening Day outfield. Even if he struggles to hit for much of an average, Renfroe's power has him poised to serve as a key run-producer for the Padres for years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A leading candidate to go No. 1 overall in the 2014 Draft until he had Tommy John surgery that May, Hoffman still went ninth to the Blue Jays and signed for $3,080,000. His fastball reached 99 mph when he made his pro debut in May 2015, and two months later Toronto used him as the centerpiece prospect in a trade for Troy Tulowitzki. Hoffman joined the Rockies last August but uncharacteristically battled his command during his first stint in the Majors. When Hoffman is on top of his game, both his fastball and curveball can grade as well above-average pitches. His heater usually operates at 92-95 mph with some sinking and riding life, while his big-breaking curveball can lock up hitters. He uses a slider when he wants a harder breaking ball, and his changeup shows flashes of becoming a plus offering. With a repertoire that includes four solid-or-better pitches, Hoffman has the ingredients to become a No. 2 starter. He had a track record of not missing as many bats as would be expected given his stuff, and while he racked up more strikeouts in 2016, his control and command regressed. His time in Colorado taught him that he'll have to locate his pitches better to succeed against big leaguers, particularly at Coors Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the most physically imposing players in the game at 6-foot-7 and 275 pounds, Judge had college football offers to play tight end and has drawn body comps to NBA star Blake Griffin. Signed for $1.8 million as one of three Yankees first-round picks in the 2013 Draft, he reached New York at the end of his third pro season. He homered in his first at-bat but also struck out 42 times in 95 plate appearances. Judge generates massive raw power from the right side of the plate thanks to his impressive leverage and strength. He demonstrated an ability to work counts and use the center of the field in the lower Minors, but he has been more aggressive at the upper levels and pitchers have exploited that change in mindset. While he could deliver 25 or more homers per season, he won't hit for average unless he closes some holes in his swing and approach. A quality athlete for his size, Judge has average speed and plus arm strength. He has spent much of his pro career in right field and fits the profile at that position to a tee. The Yankees have drafted just one college position player in the first round who went on to become an All-Star -- Thurman Munson -- but Judge has the upside to become the second.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 55 Ever since leaving college basketball and dedicating himself to pitching full-time in 2014, Garrett has made steady progress on the mound. Now he's one of the best left-handed pitching prospects in the game and just about ready to impact a big league rotation. Garrett has an ever-improving three-pitch mix that he is continuing to learn to command better.
