His fastball will sit anywhere in the 91-96 mph range, and he backs it up with a slider that will flash plus at times. His changeup is his third pitch, but it's gotten better and should be a Major League average off-speed pitch for him. He uses his 6-foot-5 frame well, getting full extension and allowing his stuff to jump at hitters even more quickly. Quite physical, the former St. John's hoops player uses his athleticism on the mound well, leading many to believe his command will continue to improve. After reaching the highest level of the Minors in 2016, Garrett might be ready to contribute in the big leagues soon. He still hasn't reached his ceiling and could be a frontline starter when all is said and done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Often, pitching prospects coming out of college lose a little velocity when they switch to a five-day rotation instead of pitching weekly. It's been the opposite for Weaver, whose dip in velo as a Florida State junior contributed to him dropping to the end of the first round in 2014, only to see him regain a few ticks as a pro as he made it up to St. Louis in his second full season of pro ball. His ascent is all the more impressive given his delayed start to 2016 due to a non-throwing hand broken wrist. Despite his slight frame, Weaver will pump fastballs consistently up to 94 mph and can reach back for a few more miles per hour when needed. He basically throws two different heaters, one that sinks and one that cuts and he commands both extremely well. He complements the fastball with one of the best changeups among all pitching prospects, thrown with outstanding sink. His breaking stuff continues to be fringy and inconsistent, something that would help him find success in the big leagues. Weaver got away from what works for him a bit when he got to St. Louis last year, trying to be too fine rather than trusting his stuff. He got back to doing that in 2017 and is very close to reaching his ceiling as a mid-rotation type starter, though the Cardinals did bring him up to help out the bullpen during the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken in the middle of the first round of the 2014 Draft by the Angels, the highest-drafted player ever from Hartford, Newcomb spent one season with Los Angeles, pitching across three levels and in the Futures Game before being sent to the Braves in the Andrelton Simmons deal prior to 2016. He led the Double-A Southern League in strikeouts in his first season in Atlanta's organization. A big, strong power pitcher, Newcomb has seen his fastball touch the upper-90s and even triple digits in the past. He was mostly in the 93-97 mph range in 2016, reaching 99 mph on occasion, as he scaled back a bit and commanded his heater a bit better. His curve gives him a second plus pitch, one that elicits a good amount of swings and misses. His changeup is behind those two premium pitches, but it's good enough to be at least Major League average. Control has been Newcomb's biggest issue, but he made some good strides in that department in his first season with the Braves. There's still some upside here and if he continues to improve, especially with his ability to find the strike zone, he can at least be a rotation workhorse, if not more, in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fisher has tantalized scouts with his tools and frustrated them with his inconsistency since he was a Pennsylvania high schooler. A supplemental first-round pick in 2014 after helping Virginia reach the College World Series finals, he signed for $1,534,100. He delivered 43 homers and 59 steals while reaching Triple-A in his first two full pro seasons, but he also struck out 286 times in 252 games. No one in the Astros organization can match Fisher's combination of well above-average raw power and at least plus speed. He has a sweet left-handed stroke and plenty of bat speed, though he doesn't have strong feel for hitting and strikeouts will always be a part of his game. He has improved his plate discipline since turning pro and should draw a healthy amount of walks. Fisher's quickness plays much better on the bases than it does in the outfield. He should have the wheels to play center field, but he lacks instincts and is an iffy defender there. His below-average arm likely will relegate him to left field in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 45 | Overall: 55 Stephenson came out of the 2011 Draft as a projectable high school right-hander, one with plenty of velocity and pure stuff. He didn't exactly make a beeline to Cincinnati, spending parts of three seasons in Double-A, but he did get there in 2016. There, like throughout his career, his arch nemesis -- command -- led to some struggles. While Stephenson's high octane fastball has backed up a bit of late, he still brings three at least above-average pitches to the mound every fifth day. His average velocity is closer to the low-90s these days -- it averaged just over 93 mph in the big leagues last year -- as he's worked to control it more consistently, though he can still reach back for more. His low-80s power curve can still be an out pitch, though he actually threw his sinking changeup more frequently than his breaking ball when he was up in 2016. Overall, he missed fewer bats while his walk rate -- more than 4.5 per nine innings -- continues to be a concern. Comparisons to Homer Bailey continue to get made, both in terms of not wanting to rush Stephenson's development like what happened with Bailey, but also in terms of his early struggles. He'll be 24 for all of the 2017 season, with plenty of time to reach what is still a pretty high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for $500,000 in 2010, Candelario became part of a Cubs collection of position prospects that is unrivaled in recent memory. Many of those hitters fueled Chicago's drive to a 2016 World Series championship and others were used in trades that contributed to the title run. Candelario, meanwhile, was biding time in Triple-A, blocked at third by Kris Bryant and at first by Anthony Rizzo, when he was sent to the Tigers in the Justin Wilson trade at the Deadline. Candelario is a talented offensive player who could've started for several clubs at the start of 2017. A switch-hitter with a fluid stroke from both sides of the plate, he makes consistent hard contact and draws a healthy amount of walks. Most of his power has come in the form of doubles to this point, but he could develop into a 20-homer threat as he adds strength and experience. Though Candelario lacks speed and quickness, he has worked hard to become an average third baseman after there were questions earlier in his career as to whether he could stay there. His hands and arm play well at the hot corner, and his instincts help him make plays, though he has also seen action at first base. Freed from the Bryant-Rizzo roadblock, he'll now have to contend with Miguel Cabrera and Nick Castellanos.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the A's gave Chapman $1.75 million as the No. 25 overall Draft pick in 2014, they saw a toolsy-but-raw college player with untapped potential at the plate. After an uneventful pro debut, the Cal State Fullerton product paced Oakland's system with 23 home runs in his first full season -- despite playing in just 80 games -- and then finished third in the Minors with 36 in 2016 while reaching Triple-A for the first time. Though he was slowed by a wrist injury early in 2017, Chapman quickly made up for the lost time back in Triple-A en route to making his Major League debut in June. Chapman always possessed impressive raw power, but it wasn't until he entered pro ball and worked with the A's hitting coaches that he learned to consistently get to it during games. The power plays to all fields, too, thanks to his quick bat, leveraged swing and huge extension through point of contact, and it could make him a threat to hit 30-plus homers annually. But with that power comes quite a bit of swing-and-miss, and some scouts question his ability to hit for average at the highest level. Revered by scouts as a future Gold Glove award-winner at third base, Chapman makes it look easy with his excellent hands, smooth actions and plus range, as well as arm strength that's among the best in the Minor Leagues. Chapman's defense and power potential gives him the floor of a big league regular, though he could blow well past that projection with improved plate discipline and more contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round Draft pick in 2011 out of the California prep ranks, Faria was the co-Pitcher of the Year of the Florida State League in 2015 and led all Minor League pitchers in wins (17) while also ranking third in ERA (1.92) and sixth in strikeouts (159). The Rays added him to their 40-man roster after the season. Although he didn't fare as well in 2016, Faria still made progress up the Minor League ladder, pitching particularly well at Triple-A Durham after a mid-season promotion. After returning to Durham to begin 2017, Faria made his big league debut with Tampa Bay in June. Tall and athletic, Faria creates excellent plane toward the plate and works down in the zone with his fastball, sitting at 92-94 mph and bumping higher at times. His mid 80s changeup flashes plus and is thrown with fastball-like arm speed, making it a weapon against hitters on both sides of the plate. Faria's 12-to-6 curveball is below average, but he can throw it for a strike and mix it effectively, and the same goes for his short, low-80s slider. That Faria is athletic and repeats his delivery well leads scouts to believe that his control and command will continue to improve. Meanwhile, with Faria's success in the big leagues, there's little doubt that the right-hander can serve as a quality rotation piece at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams will keep close tabs on any hurler capable of hitting triple digits as a teenager. That's been the story in the career of Montas, who's been traded three times since signing with the Red Sox out of the Dominican Republic for $75,000 in 2009. He was sent to the White Sox in the Jake Peavy/Jose Iglesias deal in July 2013, then to Los Angeles in the swap that sent Todd Frazier from the Reds to Chicago in December '15, and, finally, to the A's as part of the Josh Reddick-Rich Hill deal at the Aug. 1 Trade Deadline in '16. A rib injury limited Montas to just 16 innings during the regular season, but he looked plenty healthy during an impressive stint in the Arizona Fall League, where his fastball sat in the upper-90s with late life and bumped 101 mph. He pairs his heater with a plus slider that he throws with power and depth at 88-90 mph, giving him two legitimate swing-and-miss offerings. Montas lacks consistency with a third pitch and will need to make progress in developing his changeup in order to turn over a lineup with frequency. Montas has struggled to stay healthy in the face of concerns about his size, but the arm action is clean, and he does a good job of repeating an athletic and surprisingly low-effort delivery. Though he throws enough strikes with his fastball-slider pairing to make an immediate impact out of the bullpen, the A's remain steadfast in their development of Montas as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There comes a point in time when you have to pay attention to a college hitter who keeps hitting at every level. After a tremendous first full season in 2015, Hoskins kept going with a move to Double-A in 2016, when the Sacramento State product finished second in the Minor Leagues in home runs to teammate Dylan Cozens and third in RBIs, and he kept hitting for power with the move to Triple-A in 2017. Hoskins provides an advanced approach at the plate with considerable raw power from the right side. An added leg kick has helped his timiing and allowed him to tap into that power more consistently. He draws a ton of walks and doesn't strike out a ton for a power hitter, helping him maintain a solid batting average. His home run numbers may have been helped a bit by the friendly confines of Reading in 2016, but he hit on the road and continued to find the seats in 2017. Hoskins is limited to first base defensively, but he is capable there. The Phillies have another right-handed first baseman blocking Hoskins' path to the big leagues in Tommy Joseph, so Hoskins can get more development time in the upper levels of the system, but his bat should be able to contribute soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 70 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 It's not often a prospect can claim to be untraded, but that's exactly what happened to Castillo in 2016. Originally signed by the Giants in 2011 and developed as a reliever, Castillo was traded to the Marlins following the 2014 season, who moved him into the rotation. Miami sent him to Padres in the Andrew Cashner deal, but when it turned out Colin Rea, another arm in the trade, had an elbow problem, Castillo was sent back to Miami. The Marlins re-traded him, this time to the Reds, in the Dan Straily trade in January. Castillo has the ingredients to be a very good starting pitcher. The fastball sits comfortably in the upper 90s, and he can maintain his velocity into starts thanks to a clean delivery. While some reports favor Castillo's slider, which is a bigger breaking ball that sometimes looks more like a curve, the Reds actually favor his changeup, which he'll throw at 85 mph in the zone to get a lot of weak contact from hitters trying to gear up for a triple-digit heater. Castillo has proven to be durable and a better strike-thrower than anticipated since moving into a starting role. If he can continue to refine his secondary stuff, he has top-of-the-rotation potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known as a big-game pitcher at South Carolina, Montgomery went 5-0 with a 0.93 ERA in five NCAA tournament starts and headlined the Gamecocks rotation as a sophomore and junior. Considered a finesse pitcher when New York drafted him in the fourth round of 2014, he started adding velocity toward the end of his first full pro season. In a system filled with superlative pitching performances in 2016, he led Yankees farmhands in wins (14), ranked second in ERA (2.13) and strikeouts (134 in 139 1/3 innings) and dominated in five Triple-A starts in August. Montgomery succeeded with an 88-92 mph fastball because he commands it to both sides of the plate and uses his 6-foot-6 frame to throw it on an extreme downhill plane. He has been even better now that he's working at 92-94, and he maintained his newfound velocity throughout last season. His fading changeup is his best secondary pitch, and he also can freeze hitters with the depth on his curve and mix in an upper-80s cutter. Unlike a lot of tall pitchers, Montgomery has never had difficulty repeating his mechanics. He pounds the bottom of the zone and generates plenty of strikeouts and groundouts. He may lack a true plus pitch and a ceiling as lofty as some of New York's more famous pitching prospects, but he has a high floor as a good bet to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees spent more than $17 million during the 2014-15 international signing period, handing out seven-figure bonuses to seven different position players. Garcia, who signed for $1.35 million out of Venezuela, has been the most impressive among that group to date. He had no problems transitioning to the United States at age 17 during his 2015 pro debut. While he was having a rough encore in the Appalachian League, he still was showing some ability to control the strike zone and use the entire field from both sides of the plate. Already strong for his age, he has the bat speed and projectable frame to perhaps grow into average power once he matures physically. Though some scouts questioned Garcia's long-term ability to remain at shortstop when he signed, New York has no such concerns. He has plus speed and arm strength, and his hands and feet work well on defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mancini has done nothing but surpass expectations since the Orioles drafted him in the eighth round of the 2013 Draft after his senior year at Notre Dame. He broke out in 2015, winning the Double-A Eastern League batting title (.359) as well as the organization's Player of the Year award after he paced the Minors in hits (182), ranked third in hitting (.341) and produced 21 home runs and 43 doubles. Mancini made a brief return to Bowie in 2016 before advancing to Triple-A and, ultimately, the Major Leagues in September, when he became the third player in history to homer in his first three starts. Mancini is an advanced right-handed hitter with above-average bat speed, excellent barrel control and a penchant for making hard contact. He works to drive the ball up the middle and to the opposite field, and he's strong enough to clear the fences to any part of the park. Being able to turn on the ball with consistency has helped Mancini tap into his plus raw power, and scouts believe he could hit 20 homers in the big leagues with regular playing time. Mancini's strikeout rate spiked in 2016, but he continues to earn praise for his overall strike-zone management. Mancini doesn't have much athleticism to his frame and is a below-average runner, but he's worked hard to become at least a passable defender at first base. Mancini fits the mold of a prototypical first baseman with his potential to hit for average and power, but the presence of Chris Davis means he'll likely be relegated to a bench or platoon role in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following in the footsteps of his older brother Conor, an All-American at Wichita State first-round (No. 37 overall) pick of the Giants in 2008, Casey received All-America honors as the Shockers' top hitter en route to becoming the 20th overall pick in the 2014 Draft. After a strong 2016 season in which he led Rays farmhands with 18 homers and an .866 OPS while reaching Triple-A, he slumped this year in his return to Durham. Tampa Bay traded him to the White Sox in July for Dan Jennings. A big, physical switch-hitter, Gillaspie's power is mostly strength-driven but a solid tool nonetheless. He shows it from both sides but does a majority of his damage from the left, the source of 14 of his home runs in 2016. His bat speed is only above average and there is some swing-and-miss to his game, but the overall swing is consistent, and he's long demonstrated an advanced feel for the zone with strong on-base skills. A well-below-average runner, Gillaspie is smooth enough around the bag to be a league-average defender at first base. With his strong on-base skills and power potential, Gillaspie shows the makings of becoming an everyday contributor at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 24 overall pick in a loaded 2011 Draft, Guerrieri started the '13 season at Class A Bowling Green and was set to pitch in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game before requiring Tommy John surgery in July. His rehab coincided with a 50-game suspension for a drug of abuse in 2015, though he did make up for the lost time with a dominant performance between Class A Advanced Charlotte and Double-A Montgomery. He continued to make strides in 2016 back in the Southern League, where he set career highs in starts (26) and innings pitched (146). Guerrieri hasn't shown the same velocity that made him a first-rounnder out of high school, but he still operates in the low 90s with his fastball, throwing it with late sinking action and run that enables him to pile up ground balls. His curveball is an above-average pitch with tight spin and good depth, and he's made major strides with his changeup since the start of 2015, giving him the potential for three average-or-better offerings. With good command of his four-pitch mix, Guerrieri shows the makings of becoming a back-of-the-rotation starter in the big leagues. However, scouts can't help but wonder whether he'd show more velocity in short bursts coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez saw time at every position (save for pitcher and catcher) early in his career before taking over at shortstop full time in 2013, after he was passed by Francisco Lindor on the organizational ladder. He reached Triple-A for the first time in 2015 and continued to build on that success last season in his return to Columbus before making his big league debut in July. Gonzalez has made strides offensively while ascending through the Indians' system, showing a better feel to hit as well as improved bat-to-ball skills. He generates good raw power with a combination of physical strength and bat speed, but has a barrel path that's more conducive to pounding the gaps than hitting home runs. Once a free swinger, Gonzalez whiffed less in '16, albeit with fewer walks. He's still learning how to utilize his slightly above-average speed on the basepaths, and was successful in just 12 of 22 stolen-base attempts in Triple-A. A gifted defender at shortstop, Gonzalez has the hands, actions and range needed to stay at the position, not to mention arguably the strongest arm in the Indians' system. Those tools also make him a capable defender elsewhere on the diamond, as he also logged two games in right field (including his first Major League start), five games at second base and two games at third base during his time in the big leagues. He's likely to serve in a utility role once again in 2017, though many scouts believe that he could be a solid everyday middle infielder if given the opportunity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz has proved to be one of the best and most disciplined hitters in the Indians' system since he defected from Cuba and signed for $300,000 in 2013. He broke out in '15, hitting .315 with an Eastern League-best 78 walks and .412 on-base percentage before finishing the year at Triple-A Columbus. A SiriusXM All-Stars Futures Game selection in 2016, Diaz was named International League Rookie of the Year after he paced the circuit in on-base percentage (.399), finished second in the batting race (.325) and ranked third in OPS (.860). He continued to rake during the offseason, hitting .371 over 40 games in the Venezuela Winter League, and he made his Major League debut early in the 2017 season. A disciplined right-handed hitter who never tries to do too much and knows how to control the zone, Diaz entered the 2017 with a .307 career average through three seasons, with more walks (198) than strikeouts (191). He lets the ball travel deep into the zone and makes good contact with a compact swing and flat path through the zone that produces line drives across the whole field, albeit with little over-the-fence power. Primarily a second baseman in Cuba, Diaz has since developed into an above-average defender at third base, where his range, soft hands and strong arm are all clean fits. He's seen quite a bit of time in the outfield since the beginning of 2016, on top of his usual work at the hot corner. That increased versatility has already helped Diaz crack the Indians' roster, and a growing number of scouts believe he can be an everyday player at either third base or an outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strahm pitched Neosho County (Kan.) to the Junior College World Series in 2012, when he led all national juco pitchers in strikeouts with 129 in 99 innings. His fastball sat around 90 mph, so he lasted until the 21st round, where he signed for $100,000. He lost all of 2013 and most of 2014 to Tommy John surgery and the rehab process, but he has progressed rapidly ever since and posted a 1.23 ERA in 21 relief appearances with Kansas City last year. Strahm's stuff and control seem to get better each year. His fastball sat at 93-95 mph and peaked at 97 mph when he came out of the bullpen with the Royals, featuring riding life that misses bats. His curveball has become harder and tighter, developing into a second plus pitch, and his changeup has some deception. Though he had continued success in the Minors as a starter and is equipped for that role, Kansas City must decide whether to get immediate use out of him as a reliever or further develop him in its Triple-A rotation. His fastball and curveball tend to tick down over longer stints, so he has a ceiling as either a mid-rotation starter or a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Curveball: 40 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 50 Mejia put a 50-game suspension in 2015 behind him with a strong 2016 in the Giants' system, earning a promotion from Double-A to Triple-A. Seven starts in, the Twins acquired him in the Eduardo Nunez deal at the Trade Deadline and he made his big league debut in late August, in a relief role. Long term, there is no question Mejia is a starting pitcher, one who is more about pitchability than he is pure stuff. He does have a good mix, albeit without a plus pitch, of four offerings, all of which he can throw for strikes. His fastball sits in the low 90s and can touch 95 mph and he throws it with some sink. His changeup is key to his success and it's an above-average offspeed offering that also has some tumble to it. He throws both a slider and curve, though he throws the former much more frequently and can land it in the strike zone with more consistency. Strong and durable, Mejia has all the makings of a workhorse starter in the big leagues. Without a plus pitch, his ceiling might be limited to the back end of a rotation, but he's very close to reaching that potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain signing for $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2011, Hernandez swiftly established himself as one of the best all-around athletes in the Astros' system. His prospect stock took a huge hit after he hit .219/.275/.362 in Double-A in '15, but he made adjustments the following year, batting .307/.377/.459 in the upper Minors and making his big league debut. He homered three times in his first nine starts for Houston before cooling off down the stretch. After he spent much of 2017 back in Triple-A, Hernandez was packaged with Nori Aoki in a Trade Deadline deal to the Blue Jays in exchange for Francisco Liriano. Hernandez sparked his turnaround by toning down an overly aggressive approach and improving his ability to recognize pitches. While he can make further improvements in both regards, he's doing a better job of making consistent contact (cutting his strikeout rate from 25 percent in '15 to 18 percent last year) and tapping into his solid raw power from the right side of the plate. He has started to wait for pitches to drive, and he draws a decent amount of walks rather than getting himself out with impatience. Hernandez has plus speed and knows how to use it on the bases, making him a potential 20-20 threat. His quickness doesn't play as well in the outfield, where his instincts remain somewhat raw. He's a competent center fielder and more of an asset in right field, where he has a strong arm and saw most of his action in 2016.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers first tried to sign Cotton as a non-drafted free agent out of Miami Dade JC in 2010 but didn't get him until two years later as a 20th-rounder out of East Carolina. After a quick rise through the Dodgers' system that saw him reach Triple-A in 2015, Cotton returned to the Pacific Coast League last season to pace the circuit in both WHIP (1.08) and strikeouts (155), only to be traded to the A's on Aug. 1 along with Grant Holmes and Frankie Montas in the deal for Josh Reddick and Rich Hill. His big league debut came the following month, making Cotton the second U.S. Virgin Island-born pitcher to reach the big leagues, following Al McBean. Cotton's fastball velocity has steadily improved as a pro and he now sits at 92-94 mph, touching 96. However, the pitch's lack of life, along with Cotton's short frame and tendency to work up in the zone, has made him homer-prone throughout his career, and he allowed a career-high 24 home runs in '16. Luckily, Cotton's changeup, an easy plus offering with superb tumbling action, is a true neutralizer that aids him against right- and left-handed hitters alike. While he mostly works off of those two main offerings, Cotton also has a curveball and a cutter/slider, both of which receive fringe-average grades from scouts. Despite being undersized with some effort in his delivery, Cotton is athletic enough to repeat his mechanics and consistently throw strikes, giving him the ceiling of a No. 3 or 4 starter. After his impressive performance as a September callup, Cotton could find himself in the big leagues for much of 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's landed Gossett in the second round of the 2014 Draft, targeting the accomplished college hurler after he had posted a 23-9 record with a 2.80 ERA and 285 strikeouts over three seasons at Clemson. He had an up-and-down introduction to full-season ball in 2015 before breaking out in '16, when he excelled at three levels including during a late-season audition at Triple-A Nashville. The 2017 season brought even more success for the right-hander, as got off to a strong start back with Nashville before earning his first big league call-up in June. Gossett has long shown a strong arm, with a fastball that sits in the low 90s, reaching 95-96 mph with good arm-side life and late sinking action. His curveball projects to be above average and is his best secondary offering, and he tightened up his upper-80s slider, a dominant offering in college, last season after losing feel for the pitch at the outset of his pro career. Gossett also has good feel for a changeup, giving him a weapon to help neutralize left-handed hitters. Gossett has made strides on all fronts since the start of 2016, generating more whiffs and inducing weaker contact, all while reducing his walk rate against advanced hitters. He's been a model of durability early in his career, too, and all signs point to him holding down a spot in the A's rotation in the years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinder has passed every test the A's have thrown his way since they drafted him 71st overall in 2013. The former Virginia Tech standout broke out in 2015, winning the Texas League MVP Award after he paced the circuit in RBIs (86) and total bases (232), ranked second in average (.317) and hit a career-high 15 home runs. Pinder didn't fare as well last season with the move up to Triple-A Nashville, though it didn't keep him from reaching the big leagues for the first time in August. Pinder has a knack for barreling the baseball, combining hand-eye coordination with bat speed as well as feel for finding the barrel. His level swing lends itself more to producing line drives than home runs, but there's enough juice in his bat to project double-digit homer power in the big leagues. A fringy runner, Pinder won't steal many bases but continues to be praised by scouts for his instincts and aptitude -- two qualities that bleed through in all facets of his game. Pinder primarily played third base in college but was moved to second base full-time the following year, only to be shifted back to shortstop in 2015. While his plus arm and clean actions are both fits on the left side of the infield, it's Pinder's ability to play multiple positions that could help him to carve out a regular role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 45 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 60 | Overall: 50 Moore dominated for three years in Oregon State's starting rotation, earning All-American honors twice before going to the Mariners in the Competitive Balance Round B of the 2015 Draft and signing for $800,000. He jumped on the fast track to the Majors in his first full season and was promoted to Double-A Jackson from Class A Advanced Bakersfield just two months into his first full season, after he had already bypassed the Class A level. The right-hander responded to the challenges by posting a system-best 2.65 ERA in 163 combined innings between the two levels and received the Jamie Moyer Minor League Pitcher of the Year Award as the organization's top hurler. He made his big league debut with Seattle in 2017 after a strong showing across the Double- and Triple-A levels. Moore has a preternatural feel for pitching, which in turn allows his entire arsenal to play up. The right-hander's fastball is merely average, registering at 89-92 mph, but features a high spin rate that nets him whiffs within the zone and sets up his above-average, fading changeup. He also will mix in a curveball and a slider, although neither breaking ball projects as an out pitch at the highest level. Throwing strikes has long been Moore's greatest strength, and he boasts the best control and command among Mariners pitching prospects. Club officials rave about Moore's intelligence, makeup and competitiveness on the mound. Though he doesn't have much of a ceiling, Moore's plus command of a four-pitch mix gives him No. 4-starter potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 75 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 50 Altavilla had an outstanding junior campaign at Mercyhurst University in 2014, earning Division II Pitcher of the Year honors and then going to the Mariners in the fifth round in June. His mixed results as a starter during first two pro seasons prompted the Mariners to shift Altavilla to the bullpen in 2016. The right-hander took off in the new role, posting a 1.91 ERA with 16 saves at Double-A Jackson en route to a big league callup in late August. He continued to dominate with the Mariners, allowing just one earned run in 15 appearances. After operating in the 93-94 mph range and touching 97 with his fastball as a starter, Altavilla was sitting in upper-90s and hit triple digits coming out of Seattle's bullpen. His plus slider is a true swing-and-miss offering, thrown at 90-92 mph with devastating biting action that makes it a weapon against right-handed hitters. His changeup is effective at times, with some splitter-like action, but is largely inconsistent and will be needed less as a reliever. Altavilla does a good job throwing strikes even though there's some effort in his delivery, although he can struggle at times against left-handed hitters. Altavilla's impressive showing in the big leagues last season has him primed for a greater bullpen role in 2017. He's likely to serve as a setup man to the similarly electric Edwin Diaz, but Altavilla, with his fastball-slider pairing, has the pure stuff to step in as closer if the need arises.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia cemented his status as one of Miami's top pitching prospects with a breakout full-season debut in 2014, five years after he signed out of the Dominican Republic as a 17-year-old, and he reached Double-A Jacksonville for the first time the following year. Garcia earned his first big league callup in May, but was unable to get into a game before being optioned back to Double-A. Less than two weeks later, Garcia landed on the disabled list with a triceps injury that ultimately cost him more than two months. He did, however, finish the year on a positive note in the Arizona Fall League. A 6-foot-3 left-hander, Garcia's clean delivery and quick arm generate easy velocity in the low-to-mid 90s. He regained feel for his curveball last season after regressing with the pitch in 2014, and he gives hitters a different look by mixing in a decent slider. Garcia's changeup emerged as his more reliable secondary offering last season as he learned to throw it with better arm speed and fading action to complement the movement on his heater. Garcia throws strikes with all four pitches, but he still has more control than command at this stage of his career. Scouts view him as a future No. 4 starter, and they expect him to miss more bats with improved fastball command and more consistent secondary offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 50 A command pitcher who relied on ground-ball outs for most of his Minor League career, Gsellman saw his stuff tick up in 2016. That allowed him to pitch his way from Double- to Triple-A, and he was an unexpected hero when he stepped into an injury-riddled big league rotation and pitched very well during the Mets' march to a National League Wild Card spot. For most of his career, Gsellman's fastball sat at 92-93 mph. He saw a small uptick last year, sitting closer to 93-94, but occasionally touching 97-98 mph. When he came up to the big leagues, there was another jump, perhaps because of adrenaline more than anything else, but it never came at the expense of his command or his sink. He missed more bats than he had previously, but he still elicited a ton of groundball outs, limiting damage because he keeps the ball in the park and doesn't give up a ton of walks. His changeup is his most effective secondary offering, and he also used his curve, which flashes above-average, and his slider effectively. Gsellman may never join the Noah Syndergaard or even Jacob deGrom ranks in terms of power pitchers, but his uptick in stuff, all while not losing his pitchability, all point to future success in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Player development can be a long process, and for every quick-to-the-big-leagues type, there are players like Nimmo, the 2011 first-round pick who has moved methodically up the Mets ladder. He put it all together in 2016, finishing third in the Minor Leagues in batting average and second in on-base percentage en route to earning his first callup to New York. Nimmo's standout tool is still his approach, and it's one he maintained during his time with the Mets. The Wyoming native is extremely patient at the plate, as evidenced by his .389 career OBP in the Minors. Because of that plate discipline, he should be able to continue to hit for average. How much power Nimmo has remains to be seen. He has raw pop, and he could tap into it more consistently if he learns to turn on pitches and drive them to the pull gap side. An average runner with decent defensive skills, Nimmo is adequate in center field, but his best chance at an everyday gig will likely be a corner spot. While many see Nimmo as a future fourth outfielder, the Mets still believe in his ability to be a regular. Despite the long process to reach New York, Nimmo will be just 24 for all of the 2017 season, with plenty of time to prove his organization right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Texas Rangers were flush with young hitting talent in their Minor League system in 2015, and Williams was one of the most promising of the bunch, showing vast improvement with his approach at the plate to tap into his tremendous natural ability. He was dealt at the Trade Deadline in the Cole Hamels deal, then had a disappointing first full season in the Phillies' organization in 2016. He turned it around in 2017 and made a strong contribution in the big leagues during his first callup. Few have questioned Williams' raw tools on the field, from his ability to drive the ball at the plate to his speed and defensive skills. Everything had gone in the wrong direction in 2016, especially with the bat. But while his walk rate was still low and strikeout rate high in 2017, he made enough hard contact to hit for average and power, continuing that trend in Philadelphia. There have been questions about Williams' effort in the past, but the Phillies felt it was a matter of handling adversity poorly, something he was better at this season. Williams has the skills to play all three outfield positions, though he mostly played the corners in the big leagues. Williams hit the reset button and got himself back on track and to Philadelphia. There's plenty of potential still for him to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Pivetta joined the Phillies in late 2015 via the Jonathan Papelbon trade, he didn't exactly put his best foot forward, getting knocked around in seven starts and having to deal with an oblique issue. He made amends during his first full season in the organization though, reaching Triple-A and finishing third in the system in strikeouts. With a stronger feel for how the Phillies do things, Pivetta was a much more consistent starter than he was when he first arrived, especially with his delivery. That allowed him to stay in the strike zone with regularity, something that had eluded him at the outset. His low-90s fastball -- sometimes touching 95 mph -- played up, especially since he throws it with such heavy sink. Pivetta has some power to his breaking ball, and while his slider and curve run together, he flashes a plus curveball at times. He'll show an average changeup as well, though it's more inconsistent. The key for the 6-foot-5 right-hander will be continued refinement of his command. If the member of Team Canada's World Baseball Classic staff can find the strike zone as regularly as he did in 2016, he has the chance to be a solid mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knapp's Phillies career hasn't exactly gone in a straight line since signing as a second-round pick out of Cal in 2013. He had Tommy John surgery the fall after he was drafted, then had a non-descript first full season in 2014. He had a huge breakout in 2015, perhaps aided by the hitting-friendly confines in Reading, then regressed a bit in his first taste of Triple-A in 2016. Even with his uneven performance a year ago, the Phillies believe Knapp is going to be a good hitter. His issues were largely approach related, with the switch-hitter not giving himself enough credit to control the zone like he did in 2015. That resulted in Knapp expanding his zone too much and getting himself out. When he can get back to controlling the zone and using the middle of the field, he can get back to being a better overall hitter, with perhaps a bit more power than he's shown. Knapp's defense has improved as he's worked hard at his craft, with the chance to be close to Major League average. He works well with pitchers and has learned to call a good game. The Phillies feel that pounding Knapp for the past two years on his defense has allowed him to improve tremendously, but may have impacted his bat a little in 2016. If he hits, he has the chance to be a regular. At worst, a long career as a solid backup awaits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 Before the rules for the Draft changed, a team could roll the dice more on a high school pitcher from the Northeast in the later rounds. The Reds did just that with Romano, a Connecticut native, in 2011, taking the big right-hander in the 23rd round and giving him $450,000 to sign. They knew it would take time for him to develop and their patience, and Romano's hard work, seem to be paying off as he took a big step forward in 2016 before continuing his progress en route to making his big league debut in 2017. Romano had struggled initially with the move to Double-A, but he put it all together in the second half, finishing with a 2.43 ERA after the Southern League All Star break. He's always had a good, sinking fastball thrown in the 93-98 mph range that creates weak contact on the ground consistently. He's really tightened up his breaking ball and commands it better to the point where it looks like it could be a plus pitch that will continue to miss bats, a hard curve that has some slider action to it. His changeup is still below-average, but he will mix it in. He has also become a much more consistent strike-thrower. The 23-year-old has worked very hard on his conditioning and has proven to be a very durable starting pitcher prospect. The Reds feel they have a underrated right-hander on their hands, one who reminds them of Josh Johnson.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates got a pair of left-handed pitchers from the Orioles in exchange for Travis Snider prior to the 2015 season, Stephen Tarpley and Brault. Tarpley has since been dealt to the Yankees in the Ivan Nova trade, but Brault pitched his way to Pittsburgh to make his Major League debut in 2016. His time at the highest level didn't go so well, but not because he lacks the weapons to succeed. Rather, he fell into a pattern of not trusting his stuff or his gameplan. The athletic lefty doesn't have plus stuff, so if he doesn't buy into mixing his pitches and his sequencing, as he did in the Minors, he's going to get hit. He can pitch off of his average fastball because he typically commands it well down in the zone with sink, creating weak contact on the ground. He now features just one breaking ball, a slider that continues to improve and flashes plus on occasion. His changeup has become a better weapon against right-handed hitters. When he second-guessed himself, particularly in the big leagues, Brault tried to be too fine and his walk rate shot up. Taking the lessons learned from 2016, he pitched very well in Triple-A in 2017, pointing him back toward a future as a reliable No. 4 starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals like to challenge college hitters they take in the Draft and send them straight to Double-A for their first full season. DeJong, a fourth-rounder out of Illinois State, responded by finishing second in the organization in home runs and third in RBIs. DeJong and fellow 2015 college draftee Harrison Bader, both sent to Double-A in 2016, are somewhat linked. But while Bader was red-hot out of the gate, DeJong started slowly and then came on, with an OPS more than 80 points higher in the second half. While he is aggressive at the plate, which does lead to high strikeout totals, he did cut that rate considerably as he made adjustments. With very good strength and bat speed, his power is legitimate. DeJong played third base for most of the season but saw some time at short at the end of the year. The Cardinals had him continue there during his Arizona Fall League stint, and he and most who saw him were pleasantly surprised at how comfortable he was there. St. Louis isn't sure if he's a long-term shortstop in the big leagues, but the club is going to have him play there primarily in 2017 while continuing to get some time at third and perhaps a little at second. The Cardinals haven't shied away from having offensive performers who can make steady plays field the premium position at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Freeland became the second-highest pick (eighth overall in 2014) from Evansville after establishing his bona fides as a strikeout pitcher, leading the Cape Cod League in whiffs (48) in 2013 and finishing second in NCAA Division I in K rate (11.6 per nine innings) in his Draft year. After signing for $2.3 million, he missed much of his first full pro season because of shoulder fatigue and surgery to remove bone chips from his elbow. He stayed healthy and advanced to Triple-A while working 162 innings in 2016, though his strikeout rate through three years as a pro is just 6.1 per nine. Freeland does have the stuff to miss more bats. His fastball operates in the low 90s and reaches 96, playing as a plus pitch because he hides and locates it well and it features heavy sink. His slider can be a wipeout pitch at its best, arriving in the low 80s on the same plane as his heater before darting at the plate, and sometimes it morphs into a mid-80s cutter. The Rockies say Freeland's strikeout rate has been depressed because they've had him focus on improving his changeup and getting early-contact outs. He commands the bottom of the strike zone and generates a lot of ground balls, which should help him succeed at Coors Field. The Colorado native should slot into the middle of his hometown team's rotation in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Illinois State coach and current Rays scout Jeff Stewart and brother of former Mets farmhand Luke Stewart, Brock began his college career with the Redbirds as an outfielder/third baseman. He served as a two-way player as a redshirt junior in 2014, pitching just 26 2/3 innings but intriguing the Dodgers enough that they took him in the sixth round. He took off last year, leading the Minors in WHIP (0.88) and ranking third in ERA (1.79) while jumping from high Class A to Los Angeles, where he won his final two starts. Stewart showed a strong arm as a position player and continues to do so on the mound, working at 92-95 mph and topping out at 97 with his fastball. He throws a two-seamer with sink and a four-seamer with riding life, commanding both of them very well. The rest of his arsenal has improved significantly as he has gained more pitching experience, with his tumbling changeup showing flashes of becoming a plus offering and his mid-80s slider/cutter serving as an effective third pitch. Stewart's control also has gotten better as he has focused on pitching, with his Minor League walk rate shrinking from 4.5 per nine innings in 2014 to 2.1 in 2015 to 1.4 in 2016. Though he surrendered four homers in his second big league start, he usually does a good job of keeping the ball down in the zone. If he can tighten his slider, he could become a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick out of high school in 2010, Toles turned down the Marlins to attend Tennessee, where his father Alvin starred at linebacker before becoming an NFL first-rounder and playing four seasons with the New Orleans Saints. Andrew got dismissed by the Volunteers after his freshman season and suspended as a sophomore at Chipola (Fla.) JC, yet his athleticism still led the Rays to make him a third-round pick in 2012. Tampa Bay suspended him for the latter half of 2014 and released him toward the end of Spring Training in 2015, when he sat out the entire season before signing with the Dodgers in September. In his first year with his new organization, he climbed from high Class A to the big leagues and capped it off by batting .462 in the National League Championship Series. Though Toles had performed well in the lower levels of the Rays system, he made more consistent contact and hit the ball with more authority in 2016. He has a quick left-handed swing and concentrates on hitting line drives to all fields. He does have some bat speed and strength, though his approach likely will limit him to 12-15 homers per season. Best known for his plus-plus speed in the past, Toles is more of a plus runner now and still has a lot to learn as a basestealer. He has the quickness to man center field, though his reads and routes need work and he's a better fit on the corners. With his raw speed and strong arm, he can play all three outfield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barnes entered Arizona State as a middle infielder -- the same position his uncle Mike Gallego played for 13 years in the big leagues -- and left as a catcher and a ninth-round pick by the Marlins in 2011. Sent to the Dodgers in the seven-player Dee Gordon trade in December 2014, Barnes has hit well in two Triple-A seasons since but has not gotten the opportunity to make much of an impact in Los Angeles. That should change in 2017, when he's slated to be the primary backup to Yasmani Grandal. While he's already 27, Barnes offers some intriguing upside as an everyday catcher. He's an accomplished hitter with a line-drive, up-the-middle approach and he manages the strike zone extremely well, producing high batting averages and on-base percentages. He also has some sneaky power from the right side of the plate and could reach double digits in homers given regular playing time. Barnes is more athletic than most catchers and somewhat underrated as a defender. He's agile behind the plate, receives well and has an average arm. He's also capable of playing second and third base, providing a unique utility profile if he's not a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lamet began his career late compared to most international prospects, signing with the Padres on his 22nd birthday in July 2014. He made the jump to full-season ball the next year and surged up the Minor League ladder in 2016, pitching at three levels and finishing the season in Triple-A El Paso's rotation. Lamet paced San Diego's system in wins (12) and strikeouts (158) in the process, also ranking second in ERA (3.00) and innings (150). Lamet's mid-90s fastball stands out for its late movement as much as its sheer velocity, and he's able to maintain it deep in games. His power slider is a true out pitch, thrown in the upper 80s with late diving action, and he showed capable of handling right-handed hitters last season with an improved changeup. Lamet has averaged 3.6 walks-per-nine and has obvious gains to make as a strike-thrower, though he does offset many of those free passes by inducing lots of whiffs as well as weak contact and by keeping the ball in the park. Lamet's ability to develop a third pitch and improve his control and command will determine whether he ultimately succeeds as a big league starter. The Padres are optimistic he will, because he's athletic and has little effort in his delivery, but should that not pan out, there's little doubt that he could become an impactful late-inning arm, possibly even a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 1 starter on Louisville's 2013 College World Series team ahead of third-rounders Dace Kime (Indians) and Jeff Thompson (Tigers), Green lasted until Detroit popped him in the 11th round. He made steady and unspectacular progress in the Tigers' system before joining the Yankees with Luis Cessa in a deal for Justin Wilson in December 2015. His velocity spiked after the trade and he made eight starts for New York -- including an 11-strikeout gem against the Blue Jays -- before spraining an elbow ligament in mid-September. Green's fastball sat at 90-94 mph with modest life when he was a Detroit farmhand, then show up to 93-95 and topped out at 97 last year. His 83-85 mph slider improved as well and there are days when it's his best pitch. He also can turn his slider into a solid 89-91 mph cutter and has a changeup that he uses only sparingly. Green uses his size to get good extension and downhill plane with his pitches. He fills the strike zone easily but needs to locate better, as evidenced by the 12 homers he surrendered in 45 2/3 big league innings last year. He projects as No. 4 starter or a possible late-inning reliever whose stuff would gain more power in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Yankees signed Finley for a well over-slot $950,000 as a third-round choice in 2015, they knew they were getting an advanced high school pitcher. He hailed from a Rancho Bernardo High (San Diego) program that has produced five big leaguers and five first-rounders in the last two decades, most notably Cole Hamels, and grew up around the game as the son of David Finley, who's now Dodgers vice president of amateur and international scouting. Drew's development has yet to take off because he only made six starts in 2016 before he was shut down with elbow fatigue. Finley had one of the best curveballs in the 2015 Draft, a true downer he throws with conviction, but it wasn't quite as sharp last year. His fastball ranges from 89-93 mph and is more effective than its velocity because it has sinking and tailing action, plus he hides and commands it well. His changeup is coming along nicely, showing signs of becoming a reliable offering. Finley has a chance to develop three solid or better pitches with command to match. Thus far as a pro, he has been an extreme flyball pitcher with close to average stuff. That has made him vulnerable to homers, a problem that could be exacerbated when he gets to Yankee Stadium.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holder went to Grossmont (Calif.) JC with the intention of playing both baseball and basketball before deciding to focus on the diamond. That decision paid off as he blossomed into a 2015 first-round pick after a year at Grossmont and two at San Diego. Known primarily for his defense, he raised his OPS from .527 in his pro debut to .669 in his first full season. The athleticism that made Holder a star as a shooting guard in high school also makes him arguably the best defensive player in the Minor Leagues. The best shortstop to come out of college baseball in years, he displays outstanding actions, quickness, range, hands and footwork. He has solid arm strength and is as consistent in the field as he is brilliant. While Holder likely will bat at the bottom of a batting order, he encouraged the Yankees with the changes he was able to implement with low Class A Charleston hitting coach Greg Colbrunn in 2016. He improved his load and took better swings from the left side of the plate. He has ordinary bat speed, however, and rarely drives the ball or draws walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holder set a Southeastern Conference record with 21 saves while helping Mississippi State reach the College World Series finals in 2013, and he recorded a 1.59 ERA while striking out 12.7 batters per nine innings during three years with the Bulldogs. Though he never started a game in college, New York used him in the rotation during his first two pro seasons after making him a sixth-round pick in 2014. Returned to the bullpen last year, he put up silly numbers (1.65 ERA, .160 opponent average, 101/7 K/BB ratio in 65 1/3 innings) at three Minor League stops and joined the Yankees in September. Holder can miss bats with three different pitches. His running fastball zoomed from 89-92 mph when he started to 93-97 when he worked shorter outings last year, and his high-80s cutter and tight mid-70s curveball also are weapons. The distinctive shapes and velocities of those offerings make the combination tough to deal with. He also has a changeup from his days as a starter but rarely uses it. There's some effort in Holder's delivery and he's more thick than athletic, yet he always has thrown a lot of strikes. He took that to another level in 2016, though his control wasn't as pinpoint in eight appearances with New York. If he'll attack big league hitters, he should find a role with the Yankees this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way star at Florida who drew pro interest with his left-handed power potential, Johnson became a full-time pitcher after signing for $1,575,000 as the 31st overall choice in the 2012 Draft. He cruised through the Minors with a 2.32 ERA in his first four pro seasons and made his big league debut in July 2015, but little has gone right for him since. He was shut down shortly afterward with nerve irritation in his elbow amid a downturn in his stuff, which regressed further in 2016, when he missed six weeks to deal with anxiety issues. In 2014, Johnson had a plus curveball, an 88-94 mph fastball with life and premium command and a solid sinking changeup. Last year, his curve wasn't as sharp, his heater ranged from 86-90 mph and his changeup wasn't as deceptive. He also throws a cutter, though its main purpose is just to give batters a different look. Johnson regained his feel for pitching when he returned to Triple-A last July. He can add and subtract from his pitches and locate them down in the strike zone, so he doesn't have to overpower hitters to success. Boston hopes that having a full offseason of work for the first time in three years will help him reclaim his former stuff and upside as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cosart went undrafted as a Texas high school outfielder in 2012 and couldn't get on the field as a Duke freshman the following spring. He transferred to Seminole State (Fla.) CC because he wanted to pitch and immediately attracted scouts when he showed arm strength similar to that of his older brother Jarred, who's now with the Padres. The second juco player drafted (third round) in 2014, Cosart dominated Class A hitters when he became a full-time reliever last year but has seen his control disintegrate in 2017. After operating with an 88-92 mph fastball in his two seasons as a pro starter, Cosart recaptured the velocity he flashed at Seminole State when he moved to the bullpen. He now works at 94-97 mph and can hit 99 with some natural cutting action. He has scrapped an ineffective changeup in favor of a splitter that shows potential and is better than his soft curveball. There's a lot of effort in Cosart's delivery, which hampers his control but does bolster his deception. He'll always be much more about power than finesse, but he'll have to find the strike zone much more consistently to realize his upside of a set-up man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox drafted Martin as a sidearming reliever out of Texas A&M in the 35th round in 2012, but he turned them down and then raised his arm angle to high three-quarters and hit 95 mph as a starter in a college summer circuit. When he struggled in the Aggies rotation as a senior the following spring, he returned to a low slot and the bullpen before signing for $10,000 as a ninth-rounder. The Red Sox had him use the higher angle again and deployed him as a reliever, and he made his big league debut in July after averaging more than a strikeout per inning at each of the three highest levels in the system. Atypical for a reliever, Martin features a changeup as his best pitch. Despite their platoon advantage, lefties find him harder to hit because he has such good feel for his circle changeup with fade. He sets it up with a 91-95 mph sinker and uses his 6-foot-7 frame and arm slot to create downhill plane on his heater. Still working to come up with a breaking ball, Martin has a mostly ineffective slider/cutter. He throws strikes but his command isn't as sharp as his control, so he can be hittable at times. Those limitations restrict his ceiling to seventh-inning reliever as opposed to a higher-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible for the Draft every year from 2011-14, Taylor went unpicked each time. Yet he soared to Double-A in less than a year after turning pro in 2015 as a $10,000 senior sign out of South Alabama. After averaging 13.1 strikeouts per nine innings in two years, he recorded a 10.2 whiff rate in his first two seasons as a pro. Taylor misses bats without lighting up radar guns. His four-seam fastball has respectable velocity, sitting in the low 90s and topping out at 95, but hitters don't catch up to it because it has a high spin rate that gives it riding life and creates the illusion that it rises through the strike zone. He changes eye levels by pairing his heater with a changeup that tumbles at the plate. Taylor also uses a short slider to keep hitters off balance. He commands his fastball well and throws strikes with all of his offerings. He made Boston's Opening Day roster in 2017 and has shuttled between Fenway Park and Triple-A throughout the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed at the relatively advanced age of 20 out of Venezuela by the Giants in 2012, Ysla led the low Class A South Atlantic League with a 2.45 ERA in his introduction to full-season ball two years later. When he got pounded in high Class A in 2015, San Francisco turned him into a reliever before dealing him to the Red Sox for Alejandro de Aza in August. Boston added him to its 40-man roster in November following an up-and-down season in Double-A. Ysla throws harder than any of the Red Sox' lefty bullpen prospects. He operates at 93-96 mph and tops out at 98 with his fastball, which has some natural cutting action. His long-term success depends on his ability to come up with a consistent second pitch, because his slider and changeup lack consistency and aren't more than average pitches at this point. Because he's a smaller guy who works with a lot of effort from a low arm slot, Ysla never was going to last long as a starter. His delivery makes it tough to pick up his pitches but also to land them in the strike zone, limiting his effectiveness. He'll need to transition from thrower to pitcher before he's ready to help in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A month before the Red Sox spent $63 million in bonuses and tax penalties to land Yoan Moncada, who became the centerpiece in the Chris Sale trade, they signed Cedrola for a bargain $35,000 out of Venezuela in February 2015. After working out for clubs as a shortstop, he moved to center field and was named the organization's Latin American program player of the year in his first taste of pro ball. His U.S. debut in 2016 also went well, as he led the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in hits (62) and doubles (14). Cedrola has a chance to have four solid or better tools, with his well above-average speed (which projects as plus once he's physically mature) standing out the most. While he's still refining his skills as a basestealer, his quickness already plays well in center field, where he shows advanced instincts. The solid arm strength he showed at shortstop is an asset in center and also will allow him to play either corner. Cedrola has uncanny bat-to-ball skills for a teenager and could develop into a high-average hitter. While he makes easy contact, he could use more patience to improve his on-base ability and maximize the use of his speed. That will be important because he's not very physical and won't ever be a power hitter, though he can sting some balls into the gaps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Washington's combination of power and speed electrified scouts who attended the Cape Cod League's Fenway Park workout day in the summer of 2014. But he also compiled a 28 percent strikeout rate in three years at Longwood, so he dropped to the 23rd round of the 2015 Draft. Signed for $100,000, he has some of the best raw power in the Red Sox system. With his prodigious strength and the loft in his right-handed swing, Washington generates easy raw power and can hit tape-measure shots to his pull side. How often he'll be able to tap into that pop remains a question because he sometimes struggles to catch up to premium velocity, struggles to identify breaking balls and chases pitches out of the strike zone too often. He won't hit for a high batting average, but if he improves his approach, he could hit deliver 20-plus homers per season and draw walks from pitchers forced to respect his power. Though Washington showed plus speed at the Cape workout, he's more of an average runner now. His quickness plays better on the bases than in the outfield, where he doesn't read balls well off the bat. He's best suited for left field with his so-so range and below-average arm, but he does make accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A four-year starter at Florida, Tobias helped the Gators reach the College World Series in 2012 and '15. The leading hitter (.355) on the latter CWS club, which may produce as many as seven position players drafted in the top three rounds, Tobias signed with the Phillies for $10,000 as a 10th-round senior. He batted .301/.362/.439 in his first two pro seasons, reaching high Class A, before Philadelphia traded him for Clay Buchholz in December. Tobias' strong suit is his ability to make consistent line-drive contact. A switch-hitter who's more effective from his natural right side, he can drive some balls to the gaps and has occasional home run power to his pull side. While he doesn't strike out excessively, he would benefit from a more patient approach to bolster his walk totals. Primarily a third baseman in college, Tobias has played mostly second base as a pro. An average runner with arm strength to match, he doesn't quite have the quickness desired at the keystone and is a fringy defender there. He also has seen action in left field and profiles best as a bat-first utility guy who earns raves for his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick in consecutive Drafts, Stankiewicz spurned the Mets in 2012 when they offered him a below-slot bonus. After a year at Seminole State (Okla.) JC, he agreed to a $1.1 million bonus with the Red Sox that got discounted to $915,000 after a physical revealed he had been born without a right pectoral muscle. His lack of an effective breaking ball resulted in modest success as a pro until he improved his slider late in 2016. Stankiewicz has spent most of his pro career relying heavily on a fastball that sat at 91-93 mph and peaked at 95, commanding it well in part because it lacked life. His velocity ticked up in the second half of last season, and he kept hitters off his heater with a harder, sharper slider in the mid-80s. He also has a curveball and changeup, but both are fringy offerings. Stankiewicz repeats his delivery well and throws strikes, but must pound the bottom of the zone because he lacks a plus pitch that misses bats consistently. He's durable and profiles as an innings eater at the back of a rotation. Boston hopes that his strong finish last year -- he had a 3.15 ERA and 33/7 K/BB ratio in his final six starts, including a complete-game one-hitter -- is a sign that he could become more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harris shot up Draft boards in 2015 as the ace for a Missouri State program that won a school-record 49 games and contended for a trip to Omaha. He was viewed by some as a potential Top-15 pick but ultimately fell to back end of the first round, where the Blue Jays picked him 29th overall and signed him for $1,944,800. He had an understandably uneven pro debut after a lengthy college season but was able to make developmental strides in his full-season debut, finishing the year in the Class A Advanced Florida State League. Unfortunately for Harris, that success hasn't followed him with the move up to Double-A in 2017. A tall, athletic right-hander, Harris uses his height to create a favorable plane toward the plate, and he did a better job of repeating his delivery in 2016 after the Blue Jays toned down his leg kick. He sits in the low 90s and can reach back for more with his fastball, throwing the pitch with sinking action and late, arm-side life. His lanky frame leaves room to add some strength, and some scouts believe he'll continue to add velocity as he develops physically. His power slider plays more like a cutter, thrown in the upper-80s with good tilt, and both his curveball and changeup have average potential. He throws strikes with his entire arsenal and can pitch to both sides of the plate with his heater, although Harris' overall control and command require further refinement. Harris wore down physically during his professional debut but showed better durability and stamina in 2016 after he added strength during the offseason. He lacks a plus offering but mixes his pitches well, giving Harris a higher floor than ceiling. While he's taken a step back this year in Double-A, Harris, with improvements to his secondary pitches and command, could still develop into a No. 4 or 5 starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 Ynoa's feel for pitching was on full display during his full-season debut in 2013 for the Mets, when he was pitcher of the year in the South Atlantic League after going 15-4 with a 2.72 ERA and 16 walks in more than 135 innings. He's made steady progress since then, albeit with lesser results, reaching Double-A in 2015 and then advancing to Triple-A in last season en route to his big league debut in August. The Orioles acquired Ynoa in February in exchange for cash considerations. Ynoa has long been among the best control artists in the Minor Leagues and entered his first season with the Orioles sporting a career 1.5 BB/9 ratio in more than 795 innings. It helps his average stuff play up, as he'll mix his two- and four-seam fastballs -- the latter registering in the low-90s -- with a pair of breaking balls and a changeup. While he knows how to change speeds and will throw all of his pitches at any point in the count, Ynoa's tendency to nibble at the corners rather than attack hitters has led to harder contact and fewer strikeouts as he's climbed the ladder, while a lack of a put-away pitch makes him particularly vulnerable versus left-handed hitters. After being passed in the Mets' system by the likes of Noah Syndergaard, Jacob deGrom, Steven Matz and Robert Gsellman, Ynoa has been used in a long-relief role with the Orioles. He'll need to improve his breaking pitches and figure out how to neutralize lefties to be an effective starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dietz took a huge step forward last spring, first by adding strength to his already physical frame, and then with a breakout sophomore campaign during which he went 12-1 and posted a 1.22 ERA in 13 starts with 117 strikeouts in 103 innings, ranking among the national junior college leaders in wins, ERA and whiffs. Viewed by scouts as the top junior college prospect in the 2016 Draft, Dietz became the second-highest drafted player in John A. Logan (Ill.) CC history when the Orioles selected him in the second round. A big, physical right-hander with a three-quarters delivery, Dietz pitches at 91-94 mph with his fastball but can reach back for more, all the while using his size to create good angle to the plate. His slider has gotten harder and sharper, showing flashes of becoming an above-average pitch, and he'll also mix in a curveball and changeup, though neither pitch is particularly advanced. Dietz was a solid strike-thrower in college but has had trouble pounding the zone consistently since entering the professional ranks. He possesses the requisite size and durability but will need to improve the command of his fastball, as well as the consistency of his secondary pitches, to make it as a big league starter. If he can't, he has promise as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bridwell was a three-sport standout in high school before going to the Orioles in the ninth round of the 2010 Draft. He advanced to Double-A for the first time in 2015, his fifth professional season, and was having arguably his most consistent season before landing on the disabled list with elbow tendinitis in August. Injuries continued to plague Bridwell in 2016, as he missed more than a month of action during the middle of the season as the result of a left rib injury. The Orioles shifted him from the rotation to the bullpen upon his return, and it was in relief that Bridwell made his big league debut in August. He had made two relief outings in 2017 when he was sent to the Angels in mid-April. Bridwell uses his athletic, 6-foot-4 frame to create a steep angle to the plate with his fastball, which has been as high as 94-96 mph but typically sits in the low 90s with good sink. His changeup is a plus pitch and gives Bridwell a weapon against left-handed hitters. He also throws a slider, with the latter slightly ahead of the former. The biggest challenge for Bridwell has been commanding his fastball. When he can throw the pitch for strikes, and complement it with that changeup, he has the potential to dominate. After struggling as a starter for much of his pro career, it looked like Bridwell may have found his calling in the bullpen, but the trade to the Angels gave him another shot and he was taking advantage of it in the big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles signed Peralta for $325,000 back in September 2013 after he had impressed club officials during an event in his native Dominican Republic. He showed promise during his stateside debut in the Gulf Coast League and continued to make progress last year in his full-season debut, only to regress this season as a member of Class A Advanced Frederick's starting rotation. Peralta can run his fastball up to 98 mph and typically sits in the low 90s, though his velocity did fluctuate at times in 2016. His changeup is his best secondary pitch and receives solid-average grades from evaluators, who note that the right-hander throws the pitch with confidence. Peralta's breaking ball and control are both well below average and will be focal points in his development in 2017. The Orioles have helped Peralta simplify his delivery in the past year, but scouts still question whether his wiry frame will be able to handle the rigors of a full regular-season workload. If he's unable to stick in the rotation, Peralta's power arm and changeup could make him an effective late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walker broke out in 2014, hitting 26 home runs en route to making his Major League debut with the Orioles, two years after being taken in the fourth round of the 2012 Draft out of South Carolina, where he had helped guide the Gamecocks to back-to-back national titles (2010-11). While he did return to the big leagues briefly in 2015, he's stalled out a bit since then. He's also been on the move quite a bit as the 2017 season approached, being claimed off of waivers by the Braves, Reds and, most recently, D-backs.
