Coming out of college, Walker profiled as a light-hitting first baseman with an advanced approach and good on-base skills. The Orioles helped him unlock his raw power in 2014 and he's produced at least 18 homers in three straight seasons, but with that improved power has come a pull-happy approach and a penchant for whiffing. Despite being a passable defender at first base, he was blocked with the Orioles by both Chris Davis and Trey Mancini, so Walker started seeing time in left field in 2016, and he spent nearly all of the regular season at the position. With more contact and fewer strikeouts, Walker could find a role coming off the bench at both corner spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles lost their top two picks in the 2014 Draft as compensation for free-agent signings, making Gonzalez their top selection in the third round. He was part of three Florida state championship teams at Archbishop McCarthy High School, the same school that produced big leaguers Alex Avila and Nick Castellanos. After an inconsistent full-season debut with Class A Delmarva in which he wore down late and finished the year on the disabled list, Gonzalez earned All-Star honors in his second tour of the South Atlantic League as he ranked third in the circuit in both ERA (2.50) and innings pitched (147 2/3). Gonzalez's velocity ticked up in his second full season as he bumped 93-94 mph while sitting comfortably in the low 90s. He struggles to maintain his velocity deep into games, however, and at times will pitch in the upper 80s. The 6-foot-3 left-hander creates a good downhill angle to the plate that gives his heater late life and makes him difficult to lift. Gonzalez's secondary offerings show promise but currently lag behind his fastball. He can flash a plus with his changeup, throwing it with good arm speed and late fading action, and gets good depth to his curveball. Gonzalez struggled with his command in 2015, when he walked 5.0 batters per nine innings, but he improved that number to 3.5 last season and should continue to make strides as he becomes more comfortable repeating his delivery. If all comes together for the left-hander, he could develop into a quality back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros took Garcia with the No. 4 pick in the 2014 Rule 5 Draft and then flipped him to the Orioles, whom he had impressed with his arm strength during instructional league a few months prior. He made the Orioles' Opening Day roster as a reliever that year but struggled to stay healthy, with a bout of right shoulder tendinitis in May resulting in a stint on the 60-day DL. He returned to Double-A Bowie in 2016 and spent the entire season in the rotation, albeit with underwhelming results. Garcia showed mid-to-upper-90s velocity coming out of the bullpen but works more in the 92-94 mph range as a starter. His slider has the chance to be at least Major League average, and he's also capable of mixing in a changeup. However, Garcia's below-average control, especially with his fastball, continues to hold him back, as it limits the effectiveness of his secondary pitches as well as his overall bat-missing potential. The Orioles deployed Garcia as a starter so that he could develop his slider and changeup in advance of the right-hander's eventual return to the Orioles' bullpen. While he lacks a late-inning profile, Garcia's two quality pitches and ability to work multiple innings could make him a valuable big league reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles' signing of Ortega flew under the radar, as they inked the Dominican shortstop for just $60,000 in October 2014. He's since impressed club officials with his athleticism, tools and advanced feel for the game at a young age, and he fared well on both sides of the ball last season in the Rookie Gulf Coast League before finishing the year with Class A Short Season Aberdeen. Ortega's defense currently is well ahead of his hitting, but evaluators expect the latter to catch up as he continues adding strength to his athletic and projectable frame. There's little doubt he'll be able to remain at shortstop, where he shows good range and speed as well as an above-average arm. At the plate, the right-handed hitter makes consistent contact but offers little in the way of power. Set to play all of 2017 at age 20, Ortega, who has yet to reach full-season ball, is slightly behind the developmental curve and requires considerable projection. But the Orioles like Ortega's chances of becoming a big league shortstop and believe he's poised to make strides in the coming year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in October 2010, Tavarez made a slow but steady climb through Boston's system before breaking out in 2016, when he finished second in the Eastern League batting race with a .335 average at Double-A Portland. Impressed by his development, the Orioles selected Tavarez in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Though undersized and lacking in terms of physical projection, Tavarez is an excellent athlete who has long stood out for his above-average speed and ability to play both outfield corners. He has good bat speed and a short stroke from the left side of the plate, with an approach that has continued to improve as he's climbed the ladder. And while he doesn't offer much in the way of over-the-fence pop, Tavarez's combination of gap power and speed yields plenty of extra-base hits. With his solid collection of tools, Tavarez shows the makings of becoming a fourth outfielder at the highest level, a role that the Orioles hope he can fill for them in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles knew that Gassaway would need time to develop when they took him in the 16th round of the 2013 Draft out of the Georgia prep ranks. He finally rewarded the organization's patience without a breakout performance in 2016, when he hit a robust .340/.384/.535 with seven home runs in 55 games, and he further rewarded the organization this season by reaching Double-A. A big, physical right-handed hitter, Gassaway began to tap into his plus raw power last season after connecting on just two home runs in his first 126 pro games. He has the strength and bat speed needed to drive the ball out of the park to all fields, and club officials believe he'll develop even more power as he continues to refine his approach and develops physically. Defensively, Gassaway's below-average speed and arm strength limit him to left field. Club officials rave about Gassaway's work ethic and desire to learn, not to mention his promising offensive tools. That combination could make Gassaway an everyday left fielder at maturity, though expectations should remain tempered until he completes a year in full-season ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays were willing to blow past their bonus pool and incur a heavy tax to sign Rondon, who some scouts considered the top player in the 2014 international signing class, for $2.95 million on his 16th birthday in July. After striking out at a 34.8 percent clip and ranking last among qualified hitters in average (.166) during his pro debut in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, Rondon played up to his prospect pedigree last season in the Rookie-level Appalachian League, showing vastly improved hitting ability and power, though he struggled to build on that momentum during his full-season debut in 2017. A right-handed hitter, Rondon has good bat speed and makes hard contact, with plus raw power to his pull side that scouts expect will eventually translate to the whole field. After playing shortstop to begin his career, Rondon has since moved to third base, where he profiles a solid defender with giving hands and a strong arm. He's a below-average runner and stands to lose another step with physical maturation. Club officials were encouraged by Rondon's performance in 2016, noting his overall physical and mental progress, and they expect the youngster to continue making strides as he become more acclimated to pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schultz has shown a combination of swing-and-miss stuff and below-average command since joining the Rays in 2013 as a 14th-round Draft pick. The right-hander led the Southern League in strikeouts (168) and walks (90) in 2015, but trimmed his walk rate by over a batter-per-inning the next year in Triple-A, all the while maintaining an impressive strikeout rate. Officially moved to the bullpen ahead of the 2017 season, Schultz spent the first three months on the disabled list after suffering a groin injury in his season debut. He returned to the mound late in July 2017 and performed well back in Triple-A. Schultz has power stuff that misses bats consistently, a notion supported by his 11.6 strikeouts-per-nine in 40 career appearances at the Triple-A level. The right-hander will reach 98-99 mph with his fastball but usually sits in the mid 90s with considerable arm-side run, maintaining his velocity deep into starts. He pairs his heater with a power breaking ball that piles up whiffs with its depth and bite, and he also throws a fading changeup. After issuing 6.0 walks-per-nine in 2015, Schultz has trimmed his walk rate in each of the past two seasons, though he still falls behind in the count too often. Schultz has all the ingredients to serve as a late-inning force out of the bullpen, a role that allows him to better utilize his two plus pitches without having worry about throwing strikes or working deep into games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stanek was viewed as a future first-rounder during much of his career at Arkansas until a subpar junior season and concerns about a hip injury caused him to fall to the Rays at the end of the first round. He underwent hip surgery after signing, which kept him from throwing a professional pitch for nearly a year after he was drafted. He made a successful return in 2015 and took off the next year, pitching in the SiriusXM All-Stars Futures Game and reaching Triple-A for the first time. After returning to the International League in 2017, Stanek made his big league debut for the Rays in May. Stanek is capable of hitting triple digits out of the bullpen, just as he did in the 2016 SiriusXM Futures Game, and sits in the upper 90s. Stanek's slider gives him a second above-average offering, and he also has changeup that he'll need to develop more in order to be successful against left-handed hitters. That Stanek's control and command are both lacking portends more of a setup role than closing duties at the highest level, although he has the stuff needed to close games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez has done nothing but impress the Rays since signing for $600,000 out of Venezuela in 2012. His loud tools were on display last year in the Class A Midwest League, where Rodriguez showed improve hitting ability and power while dazzling with his defense behind the plate. He boosted his stock even more during the offseason in the Australian Baseball League, hitting a robust .442/.494/.753 with six home runs in 19 games for the Brisbane Bandits. Rodriguez shows the makings of an impact defensive catcher. His athleticism and agility translate to strong blocking skills, and evaluators raved about his progress as a receiver and framer in 2016. His plus arm strength enabled him to throw out a whopping 56 percent of attempted basestealers in his full-season debut, highlighting his ability to control the running game. Rodriguez requires more work offensively and will need to simplify his swing, but there's enough juice in his right-handed bat to forecast at least average power at maturity. While the Rays are working to develop several young catchers, it can be argued that Rodriguez has the highest ceiling of the group. His electric defense should at least lead to a career as a backup in the Major Leagues, but it will be up to Rodriguez's bat to unlock his everyday potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gadea pushed back his signing as a international free agent by a year with the goal of improving his prospect stock by moving to the mound from third base. The decision proved wise, and the Mariners signed the right-hander for $42,000 in November 2012. He was brought along slowly to begin his career before dominating in his first full-season exposure in 2016, when he posted a 2.15 ERA and a 72-to-11 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 50 1/3 innings at Class A Clinton. Intrigued by his combination of size and stuff at a young age, the Rays selected Gadea with the fourth pick in December's Rule 5 Draft. Gadea is both strong and athletic, with considerable room left to grow into his projectable frame. He uses his height to pound the bottom of the strike zone with a fastball that sits 91-94 mph and touches 95, and he pairs it with an above-average changeup that he throws with convincing arm speed. He also exhibits feel for mixing a curveball to keep hitters off balance, although the pitch his least-advanced offering. Gadea's athleticism and smooth delivery give him above-average control at a young age, especially in regards to his fastball, and scouts believe his command could receive a similar grade once he's fully developed. As a Rule 5 pick, Gadea will need to spend the entire season on the active roster to remain in the Rays' system. The club believes he's capable of doing so -- despite having never pitched above the Class A level -- and intend to use him out of the bullpen before resuming his development as a starter in the Minors in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Betts appeared poised to become a first-round pick in 2015 in a Draft class that lacked both impact talent and depth behind the plate. However, elbow concerns caused the Wilson (Calif.) High graduate to fall to the second round, where the Rays signed him above slot value for $1,482,500. After Tommy John surgery wiped out his pro debut, Betts, at age 19, made his long awaited pro debut last season while appearing in 27 of his 39 games behind the plate. Betts makes hard contact from the left side of the plate thanks to a smooth and controlled swing that has little wasted movement. He's physically strong and gets good use of his lower half to generate plus raw power, though he struggled to apply it and finished last season with zero home runs. Betts' arm strength returned last season and he threw without issue from behind the plate, though he'll need to shorten his arm stroke and clean up his transfer skills to be more effective at controlling the running game. He's fallen behind the developmental curve as a result of Tommy John surgery, but the Rays believe Betts' tools will allow him to make up for the lost time and, ultimately, reach his ceiling as a bat-first, everyday backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of the Arkansas prep ranks, Wood spent a year at Howard (Texas) JC before going to the Rays in the 29th round of the 2013 Draft. Though he was initially developed as a reliever, Wood made a smooth transition to starting in 2015 and the continued to impress in the role during the Arizona Fall League. He built on that success last season in the Florida State League before moving up to Double-A Montgomery in late May. A broken thumb suffered on a comebacker cost him a month at the level, but, overall, Wood fared well during his time in the Southern League. Though he's an undersized right-hander, Wood's lightning-quick arm generates a fastball that sits 92-95 mph and reaches 97 mph, and he does a good job of locating it to both sides of the plate. He supports his heater with a sharp curveball that has late, 12-to-6 biting action that helps him miss bats. He'll also mix in a decent cutter as well a changeup that could serve as a third average-or-better offering for him with improved feel. Wood's four-pitch mix, track record of being difficult to barrel while missing bats and solid control profile highlight his upside as a starter, but concerns about his durability and a lack of a true third pitch may ultimately force him back into a bullpen role. Should that happen, Wood has the stuff to emerge as an effective setup man for the Rays in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harris comes from strong baseball bloodlines, as his father, also named Greg Harris, pitched parts of the 15 seasons in the Major Leagues. The Dodgers drafted him in the 17th round out of the California prep ranks in 2013, and Harris impressed the following year by making a successful jump to Class A Great Lakes for his first full season. Acquired by the Rays that offseason in the Joel Peralta trade, the right-hander made strides last year back at Class A Advanced Charlotte to earn a late-season spot start in Triple-A. Harris saw his velocity tick up in 2016, sitting at 92-95 mph with his running fastball while reaching 97-98, and it made his above-average changeup all the more effective. He also showed better feel for his upper-80s cutter and curveball, with scouts preferring the former to the latter. But while his stuff has improved, Harris remains inconsistent as a strike-thrower because he struggles to repeat his delivery and locate his fastball. Harris' progress as a starter has the Rays encouraged about his prospects of sticking in that role, but there are many evaluators who believe the right-hander will wind up in the bullpen on account of his two above-average-or-better pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fisher ranked 15th in NCAA Division I baseball with a .389 batting average as a sophomore in 2014 then missed all of the next season following surgery to repair a torn labrum in his throwing shoulder. He continued to rake when he returned in 2016, leading D-I in on-base percentage (.558) and coming in second in hitting (.424) while setting Southeastern Louisiana single-season records and career marks in both (.375, .483) as well. After he signed for a slightly below-slot $485,000 in the fourth round, he batted .342/.436/.487 in the Rookie-level Pioneer League. Some scouts rated Fisher as the best pure hitter in the 2016 college crop. He has a smooth left-handed swing, recognizes pitches easily and manages the strike zone well. Though he employs a line-drive, all-fields approach, his hitting ability, bat speed and strength could translate into average power. A catcher before he hurt his shoulder, Fisher played left field in his pro debut. He's a decent athlete for his size but has below-average speed and arm strength, so he's likely to wind up at first base, where he played as a redshirt junior for the Lions. Chicago tried him at third base during instructional league, but his tools don't fit there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes and biggest enigmas in the 2013 Draft, Engel dropped to the 19th round after batting .265 with two homers in three seasons at Louisville. Since signing for $100,000, he has been one of the best athletes and biggest enigmas in the system. He looked like he might have started to figure things out when he won MVP honors in the Arizona Fall League and led the developmental circuit in all three slash stats at .403/.536/.642 in 2015, but he encored by batting .259/.344/.406 at the top three levels of the White Sox system. After showing a smoother right-handed swing and better rhythm in the AFL, Engel had a busier stroke and worse timing last season. He's equipped with bat speed and strength, he doesn't tap into his raw power because he strikes out too much and hits too many balls on the ground. A top-of-the-scale runner, he's a prolific and success basestealer who would be more of a weapon if he could get on base more often. Now 25 and entering his fifth pro season, Engel is running out of time to show he can produce enough offense to be an everyday player. At the very least, he has the tools to become a speed-and-defense fourth outfielder. He has the speed to chase down balls in both gaps from center field and enough arm strength to handle any of the three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the bonus-pool system came into play, the White Sox usually adhered to slot recommendations from the Commissioner's Office. Since the new rules began in 2013, they've picked their spots to spend more lavishly, such as when they paid Michalczewski $500,000 as a seventh-rounder that June. He handled a series of aggressive assignments well until posting career-worst .226/.314/.363 numbers last year in Double-A, where at 21 he was three years younger than the typical position player in the Southern League. A switch-hitter, he has a better swing and is more productive from right side. His bat speed, strength and loft in his stroke creates above-average raw power that he doesn't get to consistently because his swing can get loopy. He'll have to prove he can make enough quality contact against good pitching to become a big league regular. A good athlete for his size, Michalczewski hauled in a 66-yard touchdown pass as a tight end to help win the Oklahoma 6-A football championship game in 2012. A high school shortstop, he has below-average speed but has worked to develop range to both sides at the hot corner. He has a solid arm and led Southern League third basemen with a .951 fielding percentage last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez signed for $900,000 out of the Dominican Republic, getting the largest bonus in the White Sox's 2014-15 international class. More advanced than most of Chicago's international bonus babies, he made his U.S. debut at age 17 in 2015 but played in just 21 games because of hamstring issues. He stayed healthy and topped the Rookie-level Arizona League with 62 hits when he returned there last summer. Though Nunez is still raw offensively, the tools are there to hit for some average and power from the right side of the plate. He already shows a propensity for using the opposite field and has enough strength and bat speed for 12-15 homers per year once he starts turning and lifting pitches more frequently. He's in the process of figuring out pitch recognition and plate discipline. Most scouts thoughts Nunez would lack the quickness and range for shortstop once he's physically mature, and the White Sox moved him to third base in 2017. He's presently an average runner with nice hands and a strong arm, but he led AZL shortstops with 30 errors in 41 games last year. His bat will profile at the hot corner if it develops like Chicago expects it will.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the White Sox charged Marco Paddy with rebuilding their international program following a bonus-skimming scandal, his first six-figure signing was Martinez for $250,000 out of Venezuela in December 2011. He hurt his elbow shortly after turning pro and had Tommy John surgery that delayed his pro debut until 2014. He led the low Class A South Atlantic League in 2015 but sliced his ERA from 5.38 to 3.81 and finished third with 141 strikeouts in 137 innings when he returned there last year. As a tall, lanky right-hander with a loose arm, Martinez elicited comparisons to former All-Star Ramon Martinez (no relation) when he signed. His low-90s fastball tops out at 95 mph, with the sink and angle on his heater creating swings and misses as well as groundouts. While his secondary pitches lack consistency, his slider displays some bite and he improved the arm speed on his fading changeup last year Martinez still is learning to repeat his delivery and command his pitches. He did a better job in the second half of 2016, when he recorded a 2.79 ERA and limited opponents to a .202 average in his final 14 starts. If he can build on that progress, he could factor into the back of Chicago's rotation in a couple of years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for a mere $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, Diaz created a stir when his fastball reached 102 mph during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League the following year. He struggled when he jumped to the United States and low Class A in 2016, though he finished by not allowing a run in his final 16 appearances while striking out 31 in 23 2/3 innings. The White Sox scouted the Red Sox system heavily last summer and noted that he got better every time they went back to see him, so they made sure to acquire him as the fourth prospect in the Chris Sale trade at the Winter Meetings. Diaz's fastball usually sits at 95-98 mph and continues to peak in the triple digits. His heater has some late life to go with its impressive velocity, and it elicits swings and misses in the strike zone -- when he finds the strike zone. He also has a pair of intriguing if inconsistent power secondary pitches in a short slider and a splitter that both range from 88-93 mph. Diaz still is learning to harness his stuff. He has a lot of effort in his delivery, which hinders his ability to repeat his three-quarters arm slot. While there's a big gap between his floor and his ceiling, he does have the upside of a high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Peter reached 96 mph with his fastball as a two-way player at Creighton, his elbow often bothered him after he pitched and he preferred playing every day. A White Sox seventh-rounder in 2014, he reached Triple-A midway through his second full season and batted .291/.351/.506 there in the second half of 2017. The Dodgers acquired him in January as part of a six-player, three-team deal that also brought them Scott Alexander from the Royals. In a White Sox system with a lot of high-risk/high-reward bats, Peter stood out for his ability to make consistent line-drive contact at the plate. He did adjust his approach last season, hitting a career-best 13 homers but also striking out a career-high 124 times. He can use his average speed to swipe an occasional base. The versatile Peter has played every position except for pitcher and catcher as a pro. He's fundamentally sound and possesses solid arm strength, though his elbow sometimes bothers him when he has to make longer throws. He profiles best at second base and is most likely to serve as a utility man in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: May is on the verge of giving his family its third big leaguer, following his grandfather Lee and great-uncle Carlos, both of whom were All-Stars. Jacob's tools are similar to those of his father Lee Jr., a 1986 Mets first-round choice who reached Triple-A. May advanced to that level in 2016 but had a rough year while battling an oblique injury. Though the White Sox had hopes that May would develop into a starting center fielder, he now looks like more of a fourth outfielder because he has done little damage against upper-level pitching. A switch-hitter whose game centers around his double-plus speed, he focuses on contact over power and hit just five homers in his first full three seasons after going deep eight times in 66 games during his 2013 pro debut. His plate discipline has deteriorated as he has risen through the Minors, with his on-base percentage sinking to a career-low .309 last year. May does provide some usefulness with his baserunning and basestealing ability and his center-field defense. He has improved his reads and routes since turning pro, making himself into a solid defender. His below-average arm is playable in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prepared to sign with the Brewers as the 14th overall pick in 2010 until a post-Draft physical revealed he had diabetes, Covey opted to stay home and attend the University of San Diego. He had mixed results in three years with the Toreros and in four years in the Athletics' system after Oakland made him a fourth-rounder in 2013. He lost most of the 2016 season to an oblique strain but pitched well in the Arizona Fall League, prompting the White Sox to pluck him in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Covey showcased a 93-96 mph fastball in high school but now sits at 89-93 mph and tops out at 95 with heavy sink. His most reliable offering is a changeup with splitter action. He utilizes both a curveball and a slider, both of which usually play as average pitches. Covey lacks an out pitch, so he must throw strikes and keep the ball down in the zone to succeed. He doesn't offer a lot of upside as a starter but has a high floor as one who could eat innings in the back of a rotation. Rule 5 mandates that Chicago keep him on its active big league roster throughout 2017, or else it will have to put him on waivers and offer him back to the A's for half of his $100,000 Draft price.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cooper spent two years at Bellevue (Wash.) CC before transferring to Hawaii, where he posted a 2.29 ERA in two seasons. Since signing for $5,000 as a 16th-rounder in 2014, he has continued to produce. He dominated as a reliever in his first two pro seasons, pitched well as a starter in high Class A to begin 2016 and thrived back in the bullpen in Double-A. The White Sox will continue to develop Cooper as a starter after he led their farmhands in strikeout rate (10.8 per nine innings) last year while working a career-high 118 2/3 innings. His fastball has improved from 86-90 mph in college to 88-93 mph in pro ball, and it plays up because he commands it well and creates steep downhill plane with his over-the-top delivery. His high arm slot also adds depth to his curveball, his best pitch. Cooper also employs a slider and changeup that give him two additional average offerings. His success is built on pounding the strike zone and keeping batters off balance by throwing any of his pitches in any count. He already has exceeded expectations and could make it as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A freshman set-up man on Kent State's 2012 College World Series team, Clark became the Golden Flashes' closer as a sophomore and a weekend starter as a junior. He has enjoyed success in the rotation as well as the bullpen in pro ball, though he pitched exclusively in relief last year. He's almost impossible to go deep against, having surrendered one homer in 151 1/3 college innings and two in 194 frames through three pro seasons. Clark sits in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph with his fastball, which features heavy sink and nifty downhill plane. He consistently gets groundouts and also has averaged nearly a strikeout per inning by pairing his sinker with a solid slider. He has improved his changeup, but it's still a fringy offering and he doesn't use it as much in a bullpen role. Clark struggled with his control in 2015 but found the strike zone again last year, halving his walk rate from 3.8 to 1.9 per nine innings. Though he showed some upside as a potential No. 4 starter, the White Sox seem committed to making him a reliever. He gets outs against both left-handers and right-handers, so he can be more than just a specialist.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hillman transferred to Olympia (Fla.) High ahead of his sophomore year and became teammates with Twins 2014 first-rounder Nick Gordon. Gordon's father Tom, a former All-Star closer, became his legal guardian at that time, and he's since played an integral role in the young left-hander's development on the mound. The Indians selected Hillman in the second round of the 2015 Draft, making him the fourth Olympia product in as many years to be drafted within the top 60 picks. While the results haven't been there to begin his career, Hillman has made strides with Class A Lake County in 2017 as the season has progressed. Much like his senior year, Hillman sat 89-92 mph with his fastball but wore down physically as the season progressed, pitching more in the upper 80s late in the year. His changeup continues to be his best secondary pitch and has a chance to be above average once developed, while his curveball, which has good shape and depth, projects as at least an average offering. Hillman's quick arm and clean mechanics make him a natural strike thrower, though he'll need to pitch down in the zone more consistently to be effective at higher levels. Hillman's lean, athletic frame leaves room for physical projection, and he'll need to add considerable strength, as well as improve his durability, to stick as a starter. He may not have a high ceiling like some of the Tribe's other young arms, but Hillman has all the ingredients to become a dependable back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Plutko was overshadowed by 2011 first-rounders Gerrit Cole and Trevor Bauer as a freshman at UCLA, but he emerged as the Bruins ace the following year before leading them to a College World Series championship in 2013. An 11th-round pick that June, Plutko made strides in his second pro season in 2015, finishing at Double-A Akron, and continued to climb through the system en route to his big league debut last September. Plutko's plus control and feel for sequencing are his greatest strengths. The right-hander is adept at painting both sides of the plate with his fastball, which sits around 90-91 mph, but can reach 94. His changeup is his best secondary offering, receiving a plus grade from scouts, and he knows how to keep hitters off balance with both his slider and curveball, with the former currently ahead of the latter. Plutko has been nothing but durable as a pro. After logging a career-high 166 innings in 2015, he ranked second in Cleveland's system in innings pitched (161 2/3) last season, going at least five innings in 25 of his 28 starts. That stamina, as well as his ability to pound the zone with four pitches, could make Plutko a back-end starter in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mejia has quickly made a name for himself with his elite, 80-grade speed since signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2013. He stole 72 bases in his pro debut and followed it up with 40 steals in his U.S. debut, and then finished second in the New York-Penn League last season with 29, also hitting .322 and earning All-Star honors. Unsurprisingly, Mejia's game is built on his outstanding speed. The switch-hitter makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate, with an approach that's geared towards hitting the ball on the ground and getting on base. Once there, Mejia has proven successful 78 percent of the time, while accruing 140 steals in his first three seasons. Mejia's impressive wheels also translate in center field, where he shows the makings of becoming a plus defender with exceptional range. Mejia has a high ceiling as a potential top-of-the-order hitter who can stick in center. That said, his elite speed alone could make him a big league contributor in some capacity, even if it's just as a pinch-runner or a late-inning defensive replacement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted as an advanced lefty out of Wake Forest in 2012, Cooney has been just that, reaching the upper levels of the Cardinals' system quickly. He made his Major League debut in early 2015, stepping into the rotation in July and filling in more than capably. The thought was he'd fill a similar role in 2016, but a bone spur in his left shoulder, which required subsequent surgery, sidelined him for the entire season. In November, Cooney was claimed off waivers by the Indians. Cooney stands out for his overall feel and above-average command of four pitches. His fastball sits at 90-92 mph, a tick above average for a lefty, and he's adept at changing hitters' eye levels with the pitch. His changeup is above average at times and could be consistently so in the future, while his curveball gives him at least a third Major League average offering. He'll mix in a slider as well. As his 1.8 BB/9 ratio throughout his Minor League career attests, Cooney is always around the plate. Cooney continues to be limited as a result of his injured shoulder, and that's likely to carry over into Spring Training. If he can get back to full strength, the southpaw has the potential to provide rotation insurance or serve as a versatile bullpen piece for the Indians.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians went well above slot to secure Armstrong, signing him for $325,000 as an 18th-round pick in 2011. A reliever from the outset of his pro career, he made a steady climb through the Minors en route to his big league debut in August 2015. The right-hander dominated at Triple-A Columbus last season, earning All-Star honors in the International League, and he fared well across 10 stints in the Major Leagues. Armstrong has ideal stuff for a late-inning bullpen role. His fastball typically sits between 93-96 mph but has been up to 98. His slider has fastball velocity at 89-92 mph, thrown with tight spin and late, short slicing action that helps him miss bats, and he'll mix in a curveball sparingly to give hitters a different look. The right-hander has some crossfire to his delivery, which gives him natural deception but also hinders his control. Control and command issues aside, Armstrong's knack for generating whiffs with his fastball-slider pairing highlights his late-inning potential in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 15th-round Draft pick in 2012 out of George Washington (N.Y.) High, Rodriguez broke out in his second full season in '14, hitting 22 home runs to tie for the Midwest League lead. He moved up to Class A Advanced Lynchburg the next year and paced the Carolina League with 17 home runs, though he struggled after receiving a late-season promotion to Double-A. In his return to Akron last season, Rodriguez connected on a career-high 26 home runs, good for third in the Eastern League. A physically strong right-handed hitter, Rodriguez has big raw power that has produced at least 20 homers in three consecutive seasons. Though his power comes with quite a bit of swing-and-miss, Rodriguez has shown a consistent approach at every level, and he paced the Eastern League with 75 walks in 2016. Meanwhile, the Indians are impressed with his progress as a hitter, and praise his improved feel for driving the ball the other way. Rodriguez's size and poor speed limit him to first base, where he is a passable defender. It won't be easy for him to fulfill the right-handed-hitting first baseman profile in the big leagues, though there's little doubt that he has the power to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Big West Conference player of the year as a redshirt sophomore, Calica was unable to build on that success the next year. The Indians still took him in the 11th round in June, and Calica immediately rewarded the organization by hitting .382/.474/.556 with 15 steals over 50 games between Class A Short Season Mahoning Valley and Class A Lake County in his pro debut. An advanced left-handed hitter, Calica has simple, repeatable swing that allows him to make consistently hard contact and spray the ball from line to line. He showed improved gap power upon turning pro, tallying 19 extra-base hits between the two levels, though he likely will never offer much in the way of over-the-fence pop. Calica also stands out for a mature approach that netted him the second-best on-base percentage as a junior, as well as 24 hit-by-pitches. An above-average runner, Calica's wheels play up on the basepaths due to his instincts and because he knows how to read pitchers and picks his spots to run. He's capable of playing center field, but saw more time in left during his pro debut. Regardless of his position, it will be Calica's bat that gets him to the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miniard was viewed as a development project when the Indians drafted him in the eighth round out of the Kentucky prep ranks in 2014. As expected, the big right-hander scuffled to begin his career before making strides last year, when, at age 20, he turned in a breakout performance between the New York-Penn and Midwest Leagues. Miniard uses his height (6-foot-7) to his advantage by creating excellent downhill plane to the plate that makes his mid-90s fastball difficult to lift. The pitch also stands out for its natural cutting action, helping him evade barrels and generate plenty of weak contact, especially on the ground. His power curveball projects to be average, while his nascent changeup will need to be developed in the coming years. As is common with young hurlers who have long levers, Miniard struggles to harness his body during his delivery, in turn giving him below-average control. The Indians believe that will improve as he continues grow into his large frame, though it may take time for Miniard to put it all together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 For years, Jones has been known as a toolsy, yet raw, player, from his high school days through his career at LSU and even during his pro career. The Tigers liked his upside enough to acquire him from the Pirates in 2015 for Joakim Soria, then saw him miss 50 games in 2016 for a positive \"drug of abuse\" test. The season ended on a much better note, with his big league debut and a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. After largely playing shortstop with the Pirates and initially some third with the Tigers, it looks like Jones has found a home in center field, where his athleticism really plays well. While he still needs more reps -- that was the main focus for him in the AFL -- it's looking like he could be an above-average defender out there. He has a strong arm and runs well, covering a lot of ground and showing the ability to steal bases. There is no question he has power, both the gaps and over the fence, but there's long been an issue with his strikeout rate and his inability to draw walks. Jones is just about ready to impact the big league club on a regular basis. How much he can refine his approach will go a long way towards defining his future role, with a ceiling of a Mike Cameron-type regular in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 30 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 In many other organizations, Machado would be preparing to take over as the everyday shortstop, a defensive wizard who has improved enough physically and with the bat to be a big league regular. With the Major League personnel in place in Detroit, however, Machado's role is more up in the air. There is no question Machado could play shortstop in the big leagues, and he's been called upon to do so in short stints over the past couple of seasons. He has terrific hands and more than enough range and arm to play the premium position long-term. He can seamlessly move over to the right side of the infield and play an outstanding defensive second base if needed. While his glove will always be ahead of his bat, he's added enough strength and refine his approach enough where he's no longer an automatic out. There's no power to speak of, but his line-drive approach does have some results. He runs well enough to steal some bases as well. With Jose Iglesias at short and Ian Kinsler at second, Machado's ticket to the big leagues will have to be as a utility guy for the time being. But the Tigers would feel more than comfortable having him step in on either side of second base full-time should the need arise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 70 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After a stellar career at Vanderbilt that included closing out the school's 2014 College World Series championship, Ravenelle's pro success after the Tigers took him in the fourth round of the 2014 Draft was initially interrupted by injury. However, pitching across two levels in 2016, reaching Double-A, and throwing in the Arizona Fall League for a second straight season could have him on the path to helping the big league bullpen soon. Ravenelle can hit triple digits with his fastball on a regular basis, but that's not where he's at his best. He tends to give hitters a very good view of his arm slot when he's throwing that hard, leading to him being hit more than he should. When he's sitting 95-96 mph, his fastball has a lot of sink and he'll miss bats and get ground-ball outs. He complements the fastball with a slider that can be nasty at times. He can get too rotational when he overthrows and will then fly out of the strike zone. Command has been an issue for him, even as he climbed to Double-A in 2016. Ravenelle simply has to learn to trust his stuff to have long-term success. Once he realizes he doesn't have to throw 100 mph all the time to get hitters out, his power arsenal should be more than enough to succeed against big league hitters late in ballgames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Curveball: 40 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Sometimes it can take a while for a player to find a home. Jaye was originally drafted by the Blue Jays back in 2010 and has made stops with the White Sox and Rangers - though he never pitched an inning for Texas - before landing with the Tigers just prior to the 2016 season. He reached Triple-A for the first time in his first year with Detroit, topping the system in strikeouts and finishing in the top five in both WHIP and batting average against. Jaye will use four pitches to find ways of getting hitters out. He has good life on his low-90s fastball and generates a good amount of groundball outs. He'll use a curveball on occasion to get over for strike one, but it's his slider, which can be plus at times, that is his true out pitch. It's better than his changeup, which also is a Major League average weapon for the right-hander. He's around the strike zone and cut his walk rate down considerably in 2016. Jaye topped 160 innings in three different Minor League seasons, pointing to the potential to be a workhorse at the back end of a big league rotation. It may not be that high of a ceiling, but he's just about ready to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Ziomek hadn't moved as quickly as some might have expected as a lefty out of Vanderbilt with a good feel for pitching, he was making slow and steady progress up the organizational ladder. Some shoulder discomfort combined with tingling in his fingers in 2016 were tell-tale signs something wasn't right and it turned out he had thoracic outlet syndrome and had surgery last June to try and address it. When healthy -- and reports were that he was and heading in the right direction for 2017 -- Ziomek combines pitchability with solid stuff across the board. He does a nice job commanding his sinking fastball down in the zone, getting groundball outs. His curve, while inconsistent, showed signs of being a very good breaking ball and his changeup was above-average at times. He'd mix in his slider against left-handed hitters mostly. There are have been some marquee names -- most recently Matt Harvey - to be diagnosed with TOS, and the jury is still out about recovery success. If Ziiomek can return to health -- the Tigers will have to play a wait and see game as he gets back out there -- he does have some weapons to work with.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith had an inconsistent career at Dallas Baptist, but the Tigers, who originally drafted him, don't shy away from plus arm strength when they see it. It's come slowly, with injuries slowing him down some, but the right-hander has proven to be an effective relief prospect in his first year-plus as a pro. In late April, Smith was dealt to the Rays as the PTBNL, completing the January trade that had sent Mikie Mahtook to Detroit. He was on the move again in July as the return sent to the Mets from the Rays for Lucas Duda. Smith is largely a fastball/breaking ball short reliever. His heater will sit comfortably in the 92-95 mph range, and he can reach back for more, all from a clean and easy delivery. He'll show an above-average curveball at times with really good snap to it, but not consistently. Smith doesn't throw his changeup enough, and he'll need to improve his feel for the pitch and use it more in the future, though he did make strides as a strike-thrower in his second full season. That he dealt with some minor arm issues early in his career ended talk about perhaps seeing how Smith would fare in a rotation. He has all the ingredients to be an effective short reliever, with a ceiling of a future setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Catchers who show they can catch have the chance to play the game for a long time. On the player development side, patience will always be exhibited to let a backstop's offensive game catch up to his defense, knowing it can take a while. Perez is living proof, moving very slowly in the early stages of his career. Perez's catch and throw skills will always be his calling card. He has a plus arm that shuts down the running game. He has good feet and moves well as he continue to work on blocking and other parts of his receiving. Perez swung the bat better than he had previously in 2016 as he worked to improve his overall approach. That didn't extend to 2017 and he'll need to keep improving his pitch recognition as he advances. There's no real power right now, but he's strong and shows the ability to drive the ball. Perez's defense should be able to carry him up the ladder. He doesn't have to hit much to be a serviceable backup, but the Tigers aren't giving up hope the bat will develop enough for him to be glove-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed back in 2012 as a 16-year-old from Australia, the Tigers took it slowly with Shepherd, letting him start off with a couple of seasons at home in the Australian Baseball League. When he hit over .300 and slugged close to .500 during his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2014, his prospect stock soared. He's moved across two full-season levels the last two years, but hasn't found the same modicum of success. Shepherd hit under .200 in the Florida State League in 2016, though he did show some over-the-fence power. He's always had some swing and miss to his game, to go along with a healthy walk rate. And while he still did pick up free passes, his strikeout rate spiked. As the strikeouts piled up, it snowballed some and he was slow to make adjustments. The Tigers sill believe in his offensive potential, that he will figure it out and develop into the kind of bat that profiles well at third. He's athletic with a good arm and should be able to defend the hot corner for the long term. Shepherd is just 21 for all of the 2017 season, so there's no reason not to give him a mulligan and let him try to get moving in the right direction again. He will have to show he can make adjustments at the plate in order to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even since his days at the University of Virgnia, Lewicki has shown the aptitude to get hitters out, but staying healthy has always been an issue. He had Tommy John surgery at Virginia in 2013. The right-hander missed two months of his first full pro season with a pectoral muscle injury. The 2016 season saw more of the same, with Lewicki getting shelved for six weeks. A healthy 2017 at the upper levels, however, set him up for his first big league callup last September. Lewicki has shown feel for four pitches at times, all of which he can throw for strikes. His fastball might typically sit around 92 mph, but he gets it up to 95 mph with regularity, throwing it with good sink. His slider will flash above-average and he'll also show an average changeup at times, albeit inconsistently, while mixing in a curveball as well. He doesn't miss a ton of bats, but he also doesn't hurt himself that much with walks. Lewicki had worked some in relief at Virginia, and while he has largely started throughout his Minor League career, he pitched out of the bullpen for Detrot last September (with one start mixed in) and served the same role when he was summoned from Triple-A in 2018. His fastball-slider combination could continue to play up should he stay in a relief gig long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The Tigers like to draft arm strength. Dallas Baptist University has developed a well-earned reputation as having a pitching staff typically filled with hard throwers. It only stands to reason, then, that the Tigers would look there for talent in the Draft, taking Drew Smith in 2015 and Voelker a year before that. Voelker was making progress up the organizational ladder until he was hit with a 50-game suspension for testing positive for an amphetamine in May. Voelker isn't big and physical, but he's shown that his stuff could play in the back end of a bullpen. He goes right after hitters with a fastball-slider combination. There isn't much angle because of his size, but he does throw it in the mid-90s with regularity and can get a little more on occasion. His slider is a Major League-average breaking ball with good late life and he's even working on a changeup. He's missed a ton of bats wherever he has pitched, though he did get hit a bit more when he first made the move to the upper levels in 2016. Voelker has served as a closer at various stops in the Minor Leagues and he does have the right mentality for such a role. He's probably a touch shy stuff-wise to do the job in the big leagues, but it's clear he won't shy away from the bright lights in whatever role he's given, though he'll first have to get past the inevitable reputation of a positive drug test.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After barely being able to find any innings as a freshman at Texas A&M, Ecker earned the closer's role as a sophomore and proceeded to save 16 games of the next two years. A completely dominant junior season landed him in the fifth round, where the Tigers gave him full pick value to sign. Ecker is the kind of college reliever who could move quickly though the system. While he's a reliever only, he does have a three-pitch mix he uses effectively. He'll throw his fastball in the mid-90s with good life and he's not afraid to pitch inside with it. His best secondary offering is his changeup, which has splitter action to it and is thrown with good deception. His slider can be nasty at times, but it also can morph into a bit of a hybrid breaking ball at times. He's a bit undersized and can have a long arm action at times, but hitters have never been successful in picking his stuff up. A combination of that kind of stuff with excellent strike-throwing ability often means a quick path to the big leagues. Whether he can close at that level remains to be seen, but the Tigers could get a rapid return on their Draft investment.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: From the start of Alcantara's career with the Angels, there has always been the thought that perhaps he'd be best suited for the bullpen based on his power stuff and command issues. He finally made that move late in the 2016 season, making some strides in adjusting to the role. He was continuing to adjust in the Arizona Fall League when the Tigers acquired him in return for Cameron Maybin. Alcantara's raw stuff certainly works in shorter stints. He'll sit 95-96 mph and touch 98-99 with heavy sink. His power slider is a plus 91- to 92-mph breaking ball at times. He has a below-average changeup, and while he may not need it as much now, the Tigers do preach having one for right-handed relievers to throw to left-handed hitters. Alcantara struggles to find the strike zone consistently and that continued even in the shorter relief stints, though he was very tough to hit. Alcantara gets to settle in to his new organization and his new role in 2017. He doesn't have to be pinpoint with his control, but if he can throw a few more strikes, his stuff should get him to the big leagues, perhaps as a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his junior season at Tennessee, it seemed Simcox wanted to return for his senior year. The Tigers, who took him in the 14th round, went way above the $100,000 pick value to sign him for $600,000 and keep him from doing so. Paired with college teammate -- and first-rounder -- Christin Stewart, Simcox helped West Michigan win the Midwest League title in his first summer then moved up to Lakeland with Stewart in 2016. Simcox will have to play catch-up now, as Stewart got promoted to Double-A last season. Unlike his teammate, Simcox does not have one plus carrying tool. He does have excellent contact skills, with a line-drive approach. He'll have to use all fields to be successful as there's not much power there and upping his on-base skills would be a good idea -- he expanded out of the strike zone too much in 2016. Simcox is a solid defender who can stay at short despite having just average speed. He has good footwork, and his angles to the ball have improved. Simcox will reunite with Stewart in 2017. For him to keep up, some added strength would help along with a more refined approach at the plate to show he can perhaps be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers liked Pinero in 2015 when he was a Draft-eligible sophomore at Virginia, taking him in the 36th round. A year later, the Tigers nabbed him a lot earlier, in the ninth, and he had a solid pro debut. Pinero's best offensive skill is his plate discipline. He has an advanced approach at the plate and recognizes pitches very well. He can use all fields and while he is not a power guy, tightening up his swing might help him drive the ball, as he can currently get a bit long, making it easier for him to be tied up on inside pitches. At 6-foot-5, he doesn't look like he should be able to play shortstop, but he has surprisingly good actions at the position, with good hands and enough arm. Pinero will be given the chance to play his way off of shortstop. His bat doesn't really profile well anywhere else as an everyday player, so a future as a utility man seems to be the most likely result.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals spent $14 million on bonuses in the 2011 Draft, the last one unaffected by bonus-pool limitations, and shelled out $675,000 to land Junis in the 29th round. Because he signed late that summer and spent two years in different Rookie leagues, he didn't reach full-season ball until 2014. Since then, he has improved steadily and developed into one of Kansas City's most reliable starting pitching prospects. As he has added strength and polished his delivery, Junis has gone from sitting in the high 80s with his sinker to operating at 92-94 mph and topping out at 96. His curveball also has added some power and developed into a solid second offering. His changeup lacks consistency but does feature some fade and sink and might become an average third pitch. As a high schooler, Junis averaged 19 points per game in basketball as a senior and displayed intriguing power potential as a third baseman. That athleticism enables him to repeat his delivery with ease, and he has repeatedly pounded the strike zone in pro ball. He was more aggressive and added more plane to his pitches in 2016, enhancing his chances of becoming a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arguably the best pitcher available in the 2012 Draft, Zimmer rarely has been healthy since signing for $3 million as the No. 5 overall pick. The Royals expected him to reach the big leagues within two years, but elbow, biceps, lat and shoulder injuries restricted him to 222 1/3 innings in his first five pro seasons. He worked just 5 2/3 in 2016 before undergoing thoracic outlet surgery that left Kansas City guardedly optimistic about his future. Before he got hurt, Zimmer could showcase frontline-starter stuff with a 92-97 mph fastball that reached triple digits, a hammer curveball and flashes of a solid slider and changeup. In 2017, he has pitched more at 91-94 mph with his heater and his breaking pitches have yet to regain their former power as well. He opened the year as a starter but came down with shoulder soreness after three outings, and he headed to the bullpen after spending another two months on the disabled list. Originally recruited by the University of San Francisco as a third baseman, Zimmer is a fine athlete who has no trouble repeating his mechanics and delivering strikes. If he has to remain a reliever, he could offer closer upside if he regains his former stuff. His younger brother Bradley was also a first-round pick (2014, Indians) and made his big league debut in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of former Royal and longtime utility infielder Emilio Bonifacio, Jorge signed for $135,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2009. He hit more for average than power early in his pro career, then swung for the fences and struggled to make quality contact while in Double-A in 2014 and 2015. He finally found a happy medium in 2016, when he set full-season bests with 19 homers and an .812 OPS in Triple-A. Scouts are split on whether Bonifacio has the bat to profile as a regular on an outfield corner. Those who believe in him think that now that he has toned down what had been a pull-happy approach, he has enough bat speed, strength and hitting ability to bat .270 with as many as 20 homers per year. Others question how well his right-handed swing will play against big league pitchers and think he might not produce enough power. Bonifacio has lost some speed as he has matured physically, but he's not a baseclogger and has decent range. His best pure tool is his strong arm, which helped him finish second in the Pacific Coast League with 17 outfield assists last year. He needs to play more under control, however, after leading PCL outfielders with eight errors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals had two first-round picks in 2015 and spent them both on Indianapolis prep right-handers, Ashe Russell at No. 21 and Watson at No. 33. Signed for $1,825,200, Watson looked so good in his first Spring Training that Kansas City thought he'd have no trouble handling an assignment to low Class A at age 19 in 2016. Hitters have lit him up the last two seasons instead -- although he's still faring better than Russell, who suddenly lost the ability to throw strikes in 2016 and took a leave of absence from baseball this June. Watson still can show the arm strength that helped make him a first-rounder, ranging from 91-95 mph with life on his fastball. Though he showed the potential for a plus slider in high school, it has regressed since the Royals had him curtail its use to focus on his other secondary pitches. He has an average curveball and some feel for a comparable changeup. Watson has had trouble missing bats and has lost some confidence. His high three-quarters arm slot wavers at times, costing him life and command and leaving him vulnerable to walks and home runs. His struggles this year have been compounded by shoulder issues that sidelined him for nearly two months.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davila impressed scouts with his polish on the showcase circuit during the summer of 2014, but his mid-80s fastballs detracted from his Draft stock. He added about 5 mph while allowing just one earned run in 64 1/3 innings as a senior the next spring, leading the Royals to pay him a well-over-slot $746,000 bonus in the fourth round. They had Davila focus on getting stronger and delayed his pro debut until '16, when he finished second in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in wins (seven) and third in ERA (2.77). Davila has gained 10 pounds since signing and now works with an 87-91 mph fastball that features late sink. He isn't afraid to work inside against right-handers, setting up a fading changeup that has become his most reliable secondary pitch. He has feel for spinning a curveball, though his needs more power to go with its depth. Though he's an advanced pitcher for his age, Davila lacks physicality and got knocked around by low Class A hitters in his introduction to full-season ball in 2017. Once he matures physically, he could have a solid three-pitch repertoire and control and command to match. Kansas City will manage his innings carefully while he continues to add strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duenez was Kansas City's top international amateur signing in 2012, when his hitting ability merited a $425,000 bonus. A third baseman in Venezuela, he moved to first base as a pro and batted .273 with just two home runs in his first three seasons. Duenez broke out in 2016 by hitting .284 with 13 homers and 100 RBIs between three levels, and he slammed three more homers in the Double-A Texas League playoffs. Duenez incorporated more leverage in his left-handed swing during instructional league in 2015, and it paid off with more power last year. He's still much more hitter than slugger, focusing on making contact with a compact stroke and using the entire field. Duenez may not quite fit the power profile at first base, but he could deliver 15 homers per season if he continues to improve his pitch selection. More athletic than most first basemen, Duenez has fringy speed and won't be a big league basestealer, but he managed to parlay his instincts into 26 steals in 30 attempts in 2016. He gets the job done and has some arm strength at first base, though he still must improve his defensive consistency. Duenez moves and throws well enough that he has seen action in left field in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Gasparini signed for $1.3 million out of Italy in 2013, he eclipsed the European bonus record of $800,000 set by Germany's Max Kepler four years earlier. Though he has some of the best tools in the system, his first taste of full-season ball last year produced a .196/.256/.293 line with 48 errors -- 10 more than any other Minor Leaguer. He has had more success in 2017 while repeating low Class A and moving from shortstop to the outfield. Given his background and youth, the Royals knew Gasparini would need a lot of time to develop, and they are willing to give it to him because of the potential payoff. A switch-hitter with good bat speed from both sides, he shows better-than-average raw power during batting practice, but he's still extremely raw at the plate in terms of his approach, plate discipline and pitch recognition. Gasparini's most usable tool at this point is his plus speed, though he's still figuring out how to steal bases. His quickness and arm strength are suited for shortstop, but he lacks soft hands and committed 98 errors in 181 games there in his first three pro seasons. He transitioned to center field during instructional league and can become an asset there once he gains more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A full-time starter at Rend Lake (Ill.) CC and Western Kentucky, Edwards became a reliever when he turned pro as a 19th-rounder in 2013. He finished each of his first three years as a pro in high Class A before dominating Double-A and earning a promotion to Triple-A a month into last season. Edwards' velocity skyrocketed in '16 and so did his strikeout rate, jumping to 10.9 per nine innings after he previously averaged 6.5. After ranging from 91-96 mph with his fastball in '2015, Edwards operated at 94-97 and hit 102 with sinking and tailing action last year. His slider improved as well, climbing into the upper 80s and touching 92, though it's still more notable for its power than its break. Edwards destroys right-handers with those two pitches, but he is still looking for a way to solve left-handers, who aren't fooled by his ineffective changeup. Edwards' extra-large frame and the effort in his delivery give him some deception, but they also hamper his control and command. Once he begins finding the strike zone with more consistency, he'll be ready to help the Royals.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Area scout Justin Lehr found two possible big leaguers at Sam Houston State in the 2014 Draft, signing first baseman Ryan O'Hearn in the eighth round and Toups in the 15th. Toups topped the Rookie-level Pioneer League with a .453 on-base percentage in his pro debut and continues to deliver quality at-bats as consistently as any Royals farmhand. He hit his way to Double-A two months into his second full season and surprisingly hit four homers in eight Texas League playoff games. A gamer who plays above his tools, Toups has feel for the barrel and understands that his primary role is to get on base. He has surprising strength for someone generously listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, but he lets his power come naturally instead of trying to do too much. Toups' strikeout rate did spike to 24 percent once he got to Double-A, so he'll have to make adjustments to handle more advanced pitching. After missing the entire 2013 college season following surgery on his left knee, Toups has regained his average speed and shows good instincts on the bases. A shortstop for the Bearkats and in his pro debut, he now sees most of his action at second base. That's a better fit for Toups' average arm and quickness, and he's a sure-handed defender at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLBPipeline's top-rated high school pitcher in the 2015 Draft, Russell went 21st overall, the earliest the Royals had taken a prep arm since grabbing Zack Greinke with the sixth choice in 2002. Signed for $2,190,200, he was ticketed for low Class A in 2016, but he worked just two innings in Rookie ball as his mechanics and control completely fell apart. When his situation didn't improve this year, he took a leave of absence from baseball in June. As an amateur, Russell used a quick arm and a low three-quarters delivery to generate nasty life on a pair of plus pitches. He sat at 92-95 mph and reached 97 with running action on his fastball and worked in the low 80s with a slider that featured hard bite when he stayed on top of it. Russell's velocity dropped precipitously last year as he battled to find the strike zone. Some scouts thought Russell was destined for the bullpen because his delivery features effort and is long in back, leading to questions about his durability and command. If he can recapture the stuff he had in high school, he'll still need to refine a changeup to be an effective starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $850,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, Aracena draws comparisons to former All-Star Rafael Furcal because of his size (generously listed at 5-foot-8) and style of play. He came straight to the United States for his pro debut in 2015 and spent last year as the third-youngest regular (age 18) in the Rookie-level Pioneer League. A switch-hitter with a naturally compact stroke, Aracena has had little trouble making consistent contact against more advanced pitchers. He could use more patience to enhance his ability to get on base, where his plus speed makes him a threat to steal. Aracena also has some sneaky power, but he needs to get stronger to hold up over the course of a full pro season. Aracena's biggest need is to settle down defensively after committing a Pioneer League-high 38 errors in just 61 games, the result of concentration lapses more than any glaring flaw. With a well-above-average arm, solid range and good instincts, he should be able to stay at shortstop provided he improves his consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Joining the Twins following the 2015 season, Palka had a strong first season in the organization, especially in the power department. He led the system in both home runs and RBIs while reaching Triple-A, and his left-handed power bat is just about ready to help out in Minnesota, thought that was delayed because of a fractured finger in 2017. Palka has the chance to be a solid overall hitter, but he gives up at-bats too often because he tries to sell out for power too frequently. That leads to high strikeout totals and the inability to string consistent at-bats together. He is always a threat thanks to his well above-average power and plus bat speed, with the ability to turn around any fastball. The Georgia Tech product played right field almost exclusively in 2016 and while he doesn't have great speed, he's fine in the outfield corner and has the skills to play first base as well. As a power-only guy, Palka could profile well on the long end of a platoon at first, right field and DH. If he can elevate his hit skills with better on-base ability, he could become a power-first everyday player. He'll need to find more consistency in his at-bats to succeed in Minnesota, but he's on the verge of getting the chance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 40 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 Relievers with low arm slots who don't necessarily light up radar guns can often be underrated and underappreciated. That might be the case for Hildenberger, who has proven to be very difficult to hit wherever he's been and slung his way up to the big leagues in 2017. Outside of a minor forearm issue that shut him down in August, Hildenberger tore through two levels of the Minors in 2016 and finished with an ERA under 1.00. He has enough fastball to be successful, in the low 90s, and he throws it with a ton of sink to be a ground-ball machine. He also can go to a more high-3/4 slot for move velocity when he needs to. He mixes in a good changeup and a slider as well and is an extreme strike-thrower, with a K/BB ratio of over 9.00 in his career. He might not blow you away with stuff, but he can really pitch and has plus mound presence to spare. He's the type who will keep sneaking up on people until he's an established, and very effective, big league setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After Reed came out of the University of Oregon and dominated both in his pro debut and in the Arizona Fall League in 2014, he looked poised to get to Minnesota in a hurry. His trip was delayed when he scuffled with a move to Double-A in 2015, though he righted the ship with a bounce-back 2016 season that saw him reach Triple-A for the first time. However, his progress was slowed by a shoulder strain that forced him out for the first two months of the 2017 season. With renewed confidence and a more streamlined delivery that was consistently online, Reed had better results. His velocity ticked upward, sitting consistently in the 94-96 mph range and thrown with good movement to get ground-ball outs. His slider also improved and he continues to refine it. He actually has shown glimpses of a decent changeup, but he doesn't use it enough. His command got better, thanks to his online delivery. He can still get under the ball at times with too much of a low-3/4 slot, which impacts both his command and the quality of his pitches. Hard-throwing right-handed relievers are becoming a depth position for the Twins farm system and Reed once again looks like he belongs in the group that will help out in Minnesota soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 While the Twins have a fair share of hard-throwing right-handed relievers in their system -- just look up and down this list for proof -- they're not afraid of left-handed power arms, either. Melotakis, drafted back in 2012 as a college reliever but initially developed as a starter, was settling back into a bullpen role when he needed Tommy John surgery and missed all of 2015. He had an encouraging first year back, capped off by a very strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. The key is that Melotakis made it through 2016 healthy, save for one DL stint due to fatigue, as his workload was carefully monitored. The stuff came back, with a fastball that topped out at 96-97 mph and sat at 94 mph to go along with a power curve in the mid-80s. He does have a changeup he worked on when he was starting, but he didn't throw it much last year. His command is a work in progress, but that should improve the further removed from the surgery he gets. The kid gloves will come off now, with Melotakis getting the chance to show how he responds to things like pitching on consecutive nights or multiple innings in one outing. How his stuff holds up then might determine how quickly he gets his first callup to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 When the Twins signed Wells out of Australia in Nov. 2014, he was a scrawny 5-foot-8 lefty who tipped the scales at about 165 pounds. The southpaw with an excellent feel for pitching is now 5-foot-11 and around 180 pounds, and that physical maturity has translated to his performance on the mound, though he spent time on the disabled list in 2017 with a forearm strain. Held back in Extended Spring Training until last June to monitor his workload, Wells' strong performance at age 19 in the Midwest League was one of the pleasant surprises in the Twins' system and enabled him to jump up to the Florida State League in 2017. He has average stuff across the board, starting with a fastball that now sits 90-91 mph. His changeup is a tick above average and his breaking ball should give him a third Major League average offering.
