All of it plays up because of his outstanding command and an understanding of how to mix his pitches to keep hitters off-balance. Wells isn't going to blow anyone away with his stuff, but there are plenty of lefties in the big leagues who fit a similar profile. Just 20 for all of 2017, his feel for pitching could let him move a little more quickly, with the end result being a back-end starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the most fundamentally sound shortstops available during the 2014-15 international signing period, Sierra landed a $1 million bonus out of Venezuela. He made his U.S. debut midway through his first pro season, then homered eight times in the first two weeks of the Rookie-level Appalachian League schedule last summer. He got too power-conscious afterward and tailed off, particularly after making the jump to the Short Season New York-Penn League, where he was the circuit's youngest regular at age 18. Sierra has started to mature physically and has gotten significantly stronger since turning pro, though he projects more as a 15-homer guy than the slugger he looked like last summer. That's still plenty of power for a legitimate shortstop, and he needs to realize he's at his best when he focuses on hitting line drives to all fields. He'll always be an aggressive hitter but will need to make more contact at higher levels. Though he has just average speed, Sierra covers more than enough ground at shortstop because he has keen instincts and a quick first step. A reliable defender with soft hands and an accurate arm, he also has seen action at second base. A utility role could be a fallback, but he has the tools to profile as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Astros' franchise-record $8.9 million spending spree during the 2016-17 international signing period, Sierra received a $1.5 million bonus in July. Before he left Cuba, he reached the island's top league at age 18 and had limited success there in three seasons as a part-time player. He batted .316/.465/.506 in his pro debut, though the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League wasn't much of a test for a 22-year-old. Sierra offers intriguing offensive potential for a shortstop. He has bat speed and has gotten stronger since defecting, which could result in 15-homer power if he improves the leverage in his right-handed swing. He's aggressive at the plate but shows a willingness to use the entire field. Houston is confident that Sierra will stay at shortstop despite average speed. His actions and quick first step give him range to both sides. He also played second and third base in Cuba, and he has the soft hands and solid arm to do so if needed in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodgers became the best strike-thrower in the Houston system as soon as he signed as a third-round pick in 2012, but he had trouble missing bats and recorded a 4.69 ERA in his first three years in full-season ball. He was a different pitcher in 2016, thanks to an improved slider that Luke Gregerson taught him during Spring Training. Rodgers led the Triple-A Pacific Coast League in ERA (2.86), made his Major league debut in September and won pitcher of the year awards from the Astros and the PCL. Rodgers' slider went from a decent pitch in 2015 to his best offering in 2016. It sits in the low 80s and he has tremendous feel for it, showing the ability to back-door it for strikes or morph it into a cutter to keep left-handers at bay. The threat of his slider keeps hitters from teeing off on the rest of his repertoire: an 89- to 93-mph fastball he commands well, an average changeup and a slow curveball. In order to succeed, Rodgers still has to locate his pitches with precision, a lesson that was reinforced when big leaguers hit .385 against him in the final month. While he lacks a high ceiling, he's a tough competitor capable of helping Houston as a back-of-the-rotation starter or middle reliever. But that won't happen in 2017 after he had Tommy John surgery in May.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hoyt's backstory seems almost too incredible to be true. His baseball career appeared over when he went undrafted after posting an 18.82 ERA as a 23-year-old senior at Centenary in 2010. While working as a deckhand on a sailboat in San Diego the following year, he tried out and made an independent league team managed by Jose Canseco. That franchise folded, and Hoyt pitched in two independent league circuits and the Mexican League before the Braves signed him for $500 in November 2012. They sent him to the Astros in the Evan Gattis trade in January 2015, and he finally made it to the big leagues last August at age 29. A rare reliever with three distinct plus offerings, Hoyt led the Triple-A Pacific Coast League with 29 saves last year while inducing strikeouts or groundouts from 69 percent of the batters he faced. His mid-90s fastball features running life, his mid-80s slider can be a wipeout pitch and his upper-80s splitter is almost impossible to lift. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame and high three-quarters delivery to leverage his pitches down in the strike zone. Hoyt battled his control early in his career but has done a better job of providing strikes in the last two seasons. He wasn't as sharp in his first taste of the Majors as he had been in Triple-A, in part because he didn't attack hitters as much and got away from using his splitter. But there's no question that he has the pure stuff to be a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A full-time infielder as a sophomore at Howard (Texas) JC in 2012, McCurry transferred to Oklahoma State and set Cowboys records for single-season (19) and career (29) saves, eclipsing Jordy Mercer in the latter category. A $1,000 senior sign by the Athletics in the 22nd round of the 2014 Draft, he came to the Astros in the Jed Lowrie trade in November 2015. He advanced to Triple-A last June and began to push for a bullpen job in Houston, but he'll miss the first 50 games in 2017 because of an offseason suspension for testing positive for a stimulant. Though he's undersized and lacks a true plus pitch, McCurry recorded a 2.18 ERA, 11.0 strikeouts per nine innings and a .205 opponents' average during his first three pro seasons. His pitchability, deception and competitiveness are more impressive than his stuff. He generates swings and misses as well as ground-ball contact, and he breaks more than his share of bats. McCurry has two separate game plans on the mound. He's more effective against left-handers, neutralizing their platoon advantage by using a high three-quarters arm slot to deliver low-90s four-seam fastballs with riding life and solid curveballs with good depth. Against righties, he drops down sidearm and relies on sinking changeups (his best offering) and sweeping sliders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With a strong summer in the Cape Cod League and tools that fit the center-field profile, Wrenn looked poised to go in the top three rounds of the 2016 Draft. His junior year didn't go as planned, however, because a ball tipped off his glove and broke three bones in his face just before the start of the season and his offensive numbers took a downturn. After the Astros snapped him up in the sixth round, he hit 12 homers and stole 15 bases in 71 games but slumped after a promotion to Class A. Wrenn's most notable tool is his speed, which gets double-plus grades from some scouts. He steals bases with a high success rate, though he should take more opportunities to run. He covers plenty of ground in center field, where he shows a playable arm. Wrenn is still figuring out his identity at the plate. He could parlay his speed into a table-setting role atop a lineup yet also has more pop than Houston expected, especially to his pull side. He gets caught in between focusing on reaching base and trying to drive the ball, leading to some swing-and-miss issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maxwell led NCAA Division III with 15 homers and a .918 slugging percentage in 2012, when the Athletics made him the highest-drafted D-III player in nearly a decade by taking him 62nd overall. Maxwell struggled to match that level of production early in his pro career, but finally turned the corner last season in Triple-A en route to his big league debut in July and a solid 33-game showing with the A's. It took parts of six seasons for Maxwell to tap into his raw power, but he finally did it in 2016, hitting 11 home runs between Triple-A and the Majors after totaling just 14 during the previous five years. He continues to demonstrate an advanced approach and works deep counts, with a focus on driving the ball from gap to gap from the left side of the plate. He has made significant strides defensively in the Minor Leagues, especially with his blocking and framing, while his strong arm enabled him to post a career-high 39 percent caught-stealing rate in Triple-A. Maxwell proved a more than capable backup in 2016, and he stands to serve a similar role for the A's moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A sixth-round pick by the Indians in 2012, Wendle put himself on the A's radar by winning the Tribe's Minor League Player of the Year award in his first full professional season. Wendle reached Double-A the following year, and Oakland acquired him that offseason for Brandon Moss. He repeated the Triple-A level in 2016 with impressive results, leading the Pacific Coast League and ranking fourth in the Minors in hits (167), and then batted .260 in 28 games with the A's after debuting in late August. Wendle's 2017 campaign began ominously, with a strained right shoulder sidelining him for the first month of the season, though he returned to the field fully healthy in late April. Wendle stands out most for his natural hitting ability from the left side of the plate. He uses the whole field to hit, squaring up balls with a compact swing that produces a lot of line-drive contact, and can hold his own against same-side pitching. Wendle's average raw power plays to the gaps and makes him a consistent source of extra-base hits, including the occasional home run. He made strides defensively last season in the PCL, ranking first among second basemen in fielding percentage (.986) and total chances (565), and club officials are increasingly optimistic about his chances of becoming an average defender in the big leagues. Wendle's shoulder injury hurt his chances of making the A's Opening Day roster and forced him to begin the season in Triple-A, where he has little left to prove. With other younger and more impactful players such as Franklin Barreto ahead of him on the organizational depth chart, Wendle gives the A's quality depth at a shallow position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Szynski threw a perfect game as sophomore at Penn High (Mishawaka, Ind.) and then won five playoff games to lead the Kingsmen to the state 4-A title as a junior in 2015. He boosted his stock with a succession of strong performances on the showcase circuit during the summer and fall, and he continued to impress scouts throughout his senior season. The A's went well over slot to land Szynski in the fourth round, giving him $1 million to forego his commitment to Indiana, and he showed promise in his pro debut despite poor results. A projectable right-hander, Szynski generates 90-93 mph fastballs and bumps 95 thanks a combination of arm speed and present strength. His high-three-quarters arm slot enables him to spin a tight curveball, a potentially above-average offering, and he also shows some aptitude for throwing a changeup. Szynski's around the zone with all three pitches, and both his control and command should only improve once he's able to repeat his delivery with greater consistency. With a strong, durable frame and feel for three average-or-better offerings, Szynski has a solid foundation for development as a starting pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's proceeded cautiously with Alcantara when he returned from Tommy John surgery in June 2015, temporarily banning his use of a slider while limiting his workload. They loosened the reigns in 2016 and the right-hander surged through the system, beginning in Double-A and making a brief stop in Triple-A en route to five starts with the A's as a September callup, albeit with mixed results. Alcantara sat mostly 92-95 mph with his fastball and quickly regained feel for his slider in his first full season removed from surgery. His changeup has above-average potential and complements his fastball well, and he'll also mix in a show-me curveball. Throwing strikes has never been a problem for Alcantara, who's issued just 1.9 walks-per-nine in seven Minor League seasons, but he continues to induce fewer whiffs than his stuff suggests he should. Big league hitters exploited Alcantara's below-average fastball command, connecting on nine home runs in 22 innings while batting .333 against the right-hander. Improvement in that department would make Alcantara's secondary pitches more effective in theory, though with limited bat-missing ability, he's unlikely to serve as anything more than a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brugman and Jacob Hannemann comprised two-thirds of a talented Brighman Young outfield in 2013. While Hannemann was a higher Draft pick that June, going to the Cubs in the third round, it's been Brugman who's had the better career since signing as a 17th-rounder. He continued to climb the ladder in 2016, ranking second in the A's farm system in hits (155), extra-base hits (tied, 52) and total bases (238) while reaching Triple-A for the first time. After being added to the A's 40-man roster last November, Brugman began his 2017 season back in the Pacific Coast League before moving up to Major Leagues in June. Brugman is a mature left-handed hitter who has a knack for staying inside the ball and using the entire field. His surprising raw power shows to his pull side and has produced double-digit home runs in two of the past three years, although it's unlikely to translate to anything more than below-average pop at the highest level. Brugman isn't much of a basestealer despite having average speed, but it does give him sufficient range in center field, and he logged a career-high 103 games there in 2016 while continuing to see time at both outfield corners. Brugman's left-handed bat and his ability to play all three outfield positions is his greatest strength, and the combination gives him the potential to serve as a fourth outfielder in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blackburn was the first of four high school pitchers taken by the Cubs in the first five rounds of the 2012 Draft, going in the supplemental first round and signing for $911,700. After an up-and-down full-season debut in 2014, he found more success in the Florida State League the following year before making even greater strides at Double-A Tennessee in 2016. Blackburn's time with the Cubs came to an end in July when he was dealt to the Mariners, who then traded him to the A's for Danny Valencia in November. After getting off to a strong start in his first Triple-A campaign, Blackburn, at age 23, was called up to make his Major League debut on July 1. Blackburn knows how to induce ground balls with his 90-94 mph sinker, throwing it with steep downhill plane to both sides of the plate and backing it up with a sharp curveball that flashes plus. His changeup has its moments but is below average overall and limits his effectiveness against left-handed hitters. Blackburn has the athleticism to repeat his delivery and throw strikes, and he continues to pound the zone even when his pitches aren't at their best. Blackburn answered questions about his durability in 2016 by logging a career-high 143 innings on the heels of a 2015 campaign that saw him make two trips to the disabled list. A healthy 2017 campaign has led to even more progress for the right-hander, who profiles as a No. 5 starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An eighth-round pick out of Furman who got just $12,000 to sign, Smith has already exceeded expectations by pitching all year in Triple-A in 2016. He might have beat projections even further with big league innings, but a mild flexor strain at the end of the season may have derailed hopes for a September callup, and his 2017 season was derailed with a shoulder injury that kept him out for an extended period. On the surface, Smith struggled a bit in his first full season in the Pacific Coast League, a circuit less than pitcher-friendly. But the Angels were pleased overall with his progress, and the southpaw did post both a higher strikeout rate and lower walk rate than he did the year prior. Smith has success largely with average stuff across the board. His fastball will touch 90-91 mph, but it plays up because of his command and his ability to mix in his secondary pitches effectively. His changeup is his best, his one above-average pitch that serves as his top out pitch. His slider has improved and is now his better breaking ball, but he'll still mix in a big, loopy curve as well. Smith does have a limited ceiling because of his lack of plus stuff, but he's just about ready to reach it. He could fill a spot in the back end of the rotation or as a long reliever, if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star in junior college, Middleton, a former shooting guard, struggled as a starting pitcher in the Angels system ever since joining it out of the 2013 Draft. The Angels finally pulled the plug and moved him to the bullpen in 2016 and it all clicked faster than anyone could have imagined, with Middleton pitching across three levels, finishing the year in Triple-A. Whenever a pitcher shortens up into a relief role, the hope is he'll pick up a few ticks in velocity. That happened, and then some, for Middleton, who now sports a heater thrown consistently in the 95-99 mph range with plus plus life. His slider also improved and is now an above-average out pitch as well. While his changeup is below-average, it can serve as a weapon against left-handed hitters. His command improved dramatically as well, thanks to some mechanical changes to his delivery and a better understanding of that it takes to fill the role of a short reliever. The Angels give Middleton a ton of credit for buying into the move as he both physically and mentally matures on the mound. He has the right mentality for the bullpen and the swing and miss stuff to pitch meaningful innings late in games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels know all the history Meyer brings with him, from the injuries to his inability to find the strike zone consistently. They were nonetheless thrilled to get add his arm strength to the system when they acquired him from the Twins for Hector Santiago at the non-waiver Trade Deadline last July. Meyer still has the huge stuff that made him a first-round pick out of Kentucky back in 2011, but he's yet to consistently harness it. He has plus velocity and a high spin rate on his fastball, cranking it up to the upper-90s with extreme ride and sink. His hard breaking ball can miss a ton of bats and his changeup continues to be viable weapon. Over the years, Meyer has struggled with walks and the missed development time because of injuries -- he threw just 64 1/3 innings in 2016 because of shoulder issues -- hasn't helped. The Twins tried him in relief, with some moderate success, but the Angels see him as a starter and he did throw more strikes during his time in their Minor League system. After an offseason working with their staff, the Angels feel, at age 27, Meyer might just be ready to put it together in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It hasn't been an easy path for Campos, both in terms of being injured and changing teams. Traded from the Mariners to the Yankees in January 2012, he missed the 2014 season after needing Tommy John surgery. He finally got comfortable in 2016, pitching his way up to Triple-A before he was traded to the D-Backs in the Tyler Clippard deal. He made his big league debut then fractured his right ulnar, leading to Arizona waiving him. The Angels, always on the lookout for pitching depth, took a chance and claimed him. Injuries have followed him to Los Angeles, as a nerve issue in his forearm shelved him in April followed by surgery to remove a bone spur from his elbow in June. The stuff is legit when healthy, with a plus fastball in the mid-90s that has outstanding action to it, thrown with good deception and extension. He can miss bats with both his curve and changeup, both of which are at least Major League average. He throws strikes with all three offerings. After pitching for five minor league teams and briefly for one big league team in 2016, Campos simply needs to stay away from the disabled list. He'll try to make a fresh start in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pounders spent three seasons in the Pirates system after being drafted in the second round of the 2009 Draft, pitching mostly in relief. When he was dealt to the Royals in December 2011, Kansas City moved him into a starting role and he reached Double-A. The momentum stopped when he missed nearly all of 2014 because of Tommy John surgery and most of 2015 with a lat issue. Back in relief in 2016, he reached the big leagues, then was dealt to the Angels for a minor leaguer following the season. The Angels plan to stretch Pounders back into a starting role, feeling comfortable that he is healthy and that his four-pitch mix works coming out of a rotation. His fastball has picked up a tick or two since he's returned, sitting in the 92-93 mph range with the ability to reach back for more, particularly in shorter stints. His slider will flash above-average, he misses bats and gets weak contact with it. He will mix in a usable curveball and changeup. The Angels like that Pounders is big league ready and has shown the versatility to pitch in a number of roles. Seeing him in Los Angeles either as a back-end starter or reliever is extremely possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The Brewers drafted Haniger with the No. 38 overall pick out of Cal Poly in 2012, targeting his natural hitting ability and strong tools. But injuries delayed his progress up ladder, and the Brewers dealt him to Arizona in the Gerardo Parra trade in July 2014. Haniger blossomed in the D-backs' system and reached the big leagues for the first time in 2016 en route to the organization's Minor League Player of the Year Award. However, his time in the desert came to an end in November, when he was traded to the Mariners as part of the deal for Taijuan Walker and Ketel Marte. Haniger generates hard contact to all fields from the right side of the plate through a combination of physical strength, plus bat speed and a sound swing. He tapped into his above-average raw power more consistently last season, setting a career high with 30 home runs between the Minor and Major Leagues after adding a more pronounced leg kick to his swing. He has a good approach, recognizes pitches well and isn't afraid to take a walk. Haniger's athleticism and average speed make him a capable defender at all three outfield positions, and he has the plus arm strength needed for right field at the highest level. Although he has the floor of a productive fourth outfielder, there are many who believe that Haniger's newfound power will thrust him into an everyday role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 40 | Overall: 45 Peterson appeared on the fast track to the Major Leagues after Seattle made him the No. 12 overall pick in 2013. The University of New Mexico product slugged his way to Double-A in his first full season, when he led all Mariners Minor Leaguers in home runs (31) and RBIs (111). He stalled back at that level in '15, however, and then suffered a season-ending Achilles injury shortly after the Mariners tried to jump-start his bat with a promotion to Triple-A. He got back on track last year in his third tour of the Southern League and hit for more power after a promotion to Triple-A, only to have his season end abruptly due to a fractured finger on his left hand in August. He returned to Triple-A fully healthy in 2017. Peterson's right-handed swing is compact and straight to the ball when he's right, with bat speed and loft that produce above-average power. After a pull-heavy approach led to a regression in Peterson's hitting ability and approach in '15, he made a concerted effort to better control the strike zone last season and showed better feel to hit as well as improved power to the opposite field. Peterson's strong arm was his only stand-out tool at third base, where he was a below-average defender with limited range and sub-par hands. He's since moved to first base, where his defensive shortcomings are less of a concern.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 70 | Slider: 60 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Zych's dominant junior season as Louisville's closer led to his selection by the Cubs in the fourth round, and he signed for $400,000. He reached Double-A the following year in his first full season as a pro, only to stall out in the Southern League over the next two seasons. The Mariners acquired Zych for all of $1 in April 2015, and he made his big league debut that September. He was expected to be a key part of the Mariners' bullpen last season until right shoulder tendinitis forced him to the 60-day disabled list early in May. Zych's two-pitch attack is ideal for a late-inning bullpen role. The right-hander complements his 96-97 mph heater with a sharp, late-breaking slider in the mid-80s, and he's capable of missing bats with both offerings. Zych's shoulder injury impacted his strike-throwing ability last season, though, when healthy, he has average control. Zych returned from the disabled list in late August to made two appearances out of the bullpen, but lingering discomfort in his shoulder prompted the Mariners to shut him down for the remainder of '16. He underwent surgery for the injury during the offseason, and the Mariners expect the right-hander to be fully healthy for the start of the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 The younger brother of former big leaguer Mat Gamel, Ben signed for $500,000 as a 10th-round pick in 2010 and showed promise in the lower Minors before stalling in Double-A in 2013-14. He got back on track in Triple-A the following year, garnering All-Star honors as well as the circuit's Rookie of the Year Award. Gamel made his big league debut with the Yankees last May but spent most of year back in Triple-A, where he was named International League MVP. In August, the Yankees traded Gamel to the Mariners for right-handed prospects Jio Orozco and Juan De Paula. Gamel started to hit upper-level pitching with more authority once he stopped worrying about hitting for power and focusing on what he does best, using his quick left-handed bat to spray line drives from line to line. He worked with Yankees Minor League hitting coordinator James Rowson to improve his load at the plate and hit a career-best 10 homers in 2015, matching his career total from his first five pro seasons. Gamel has played right field primarily in the big leagues but profiles better in center, where his speed, quickness and instincts translate to above-average defense. He has enough arm strength to play anywhere in the outfield, making him an ideal fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 An elbow injury suffered during his junior year at Oklahoma kept Overton from becoming a first-round Draft pick in 2013. While he didn't fall far, ultimately going to the A's in the second round, Overton required Tommy John surgery after signing and didn't return to action until June 2014. Finally healthy, the left-hander surged up the Minor League ladder en route to his first big league callup in June 2016. Overton struggled mightily during his stint the Majors, however, and the Mariners acquired him in January after Oakland had designated him for assignment. Overton boasted a mid-90s fastball before undergoing surgery, but he now pitches with fringe velocity, sitting at 87-90 mph but locating it well. A fading changeup remains his best secondary weapon, and he keeps hitters off balance by adding and subtracting with his curveball. Overton's control helps his average stuff play up, and he'll show the ability to locate his three-pitch mix in a given start. Overton surrendered just six homers in 125 2/3 Triple-A innings last season but proved highly susceptible to the long ball during his brief time with the A's, where he gave up a whopping 12 homers in 24 1/3 innings and posted an 11.47 ERA. While he still has a chance to serve as a No. 5 starter, Overton's ineffectiveness against right-handed hitters portends a career in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cape Cod League All-Star in 2015, Miller continued to improve his Draft stock the next year while helping Millersville advance to the Division II Championship Tournament. One of 10 finalists for the Brett Tomko Award, presented annually to the nation's top Division II hurler, Miller became the highest Draft pick in Marauder history when the Mariners selected him in the sixth round. Though he would garner Midwest League All-Star honors in his full-season debut, Miller's time with the Mariners came to an end in July when he was traded to Miami, along with Brayan Hernandez, Pablo Lopez and Lukas Schiraldi, in the deal for David Phelps. Miller sits in the low 90s with his fastball, touching 93 mph, but it plays up, thanks to a high spin rate, and because he locates it to all quadrants of the zone. His slider is a plus offering, thrown with short, late biting action that misses bats, and he also shows feel for mixing in a curveball and a changeup, though both are currently fringy. Miller's strike-throwing ability is another strength. He walked just 13 batters in 107 2/3 innings as a junior, and then posted a 51-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 56 innings during his pro debut in the Northwest League. Miller has a clean arm action and repeats his delivery with ease, but a general lack of movement on his pitches has led some to project him in a long-relief role. The Mariners were more optimistic, believing that Miller can develop into a solid back-of-the-rotation starter, and he certainly looked the part this season during his time in the Midwest League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Andrade shined as an amateur playing for Venezuela's national team before Seattle signed him for more than $1 million during the 2013 international period. After two seasons in the Dominican and Venezuelan Summer Leagues, Andrade traveled stateside last season to slash .341/.396/.549 over 26 games in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Andrade stands out for his pure hitting ability, with excellent bat-to-ball skills and hand-eye coordination that produce line drives from gap to gap. His aggressive approach will need to be toned down as he moves up the ladder, though that should happen as he gains experience. With the present pop in his right-handed bat and physical projection remaining, Andrade could develop enough in-game power to reach double-digit home runs in his prime. An outfielder as an amateur, Andrade shifted to the dirt after signing and has since seen time at multiple positions. He primarily played second base in 2016, where his athleticism, range and arm are all clean fits, though he's returned to the outfield on a full-time basis in '17.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 30 | Run: 60 | Arm: 40 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Powell received a 50-game suspension after testing positive for amphetamines in 2014, and the A's traded him to the Rays that offseason in the Ben Zobrist deal. He was on the move once again in November 2015, this time going to Mariners in a six-player deal that sent big leaguers Brad Miller, Logan Morrison and Danny Farquhar to Tampa Bay. Assigned to Triple-A Tacoma to begin 2016, Powell received another suspension in June, this time for 80 games, after he tested positive for a performance-enhancing substance. With a patient approach and a feel for working the count, Powell has long shown strong on-base skills, posting a .387 OBP in 358 Minor League games. He doesn't hit for much power, save for some doubles and triples, but the bat-to-ball skills are advanced and yield hard contact across the entire field. He has above-average speed and defensive chops in center field -- and played there exclusively last season in Triple-A -- and he's proved capable at all three outfield positions during his career. Powell has five games remaining on his suspension and won't begin the 2017 season on time as a result. His character issues aside, Powell still has a good chance of reaching the Major Leagues, where he's likely to serve as a fourth or fifth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 A 13th-round pick in 2012 out of San Diego who signed for $100,000, Pazos was a September callup and earned a spot on the Yankees' Wild Card roster in '15, prompting the team's managing general partner Hal Steinbrenner to deem him untouchable in trade talks that offseason. But his struggles across three stints in the Majors, as well his two-plus months spent on the Triple-A disabled list with an undisclosed injury, caused the Yankees to change their tone following the 2016 season, when they dealt Pazos to Seattle for right-hander Zack Littell. Pazos operates in the mid 90s and bumps 98 mph with his fastball, which he pairs with an above-average slider in the low 80s. The two pitches make him highly effective against left-handed hitters, whom he's limited to a .184 average since the start of 2015. Pazos has an unorthodox delivery that adds life and deception to his pitches, though throwing strikes consistently remains a challenge for the left-hander. Pazos missed time in 2013 and '15 with shoulder issues, but if he can stay healthy and improve his control, he stands to help bolster the Mariners' bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 30 | Arm: 55 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 The Mariners had high hopes for Marlette when they gave him $650,000 as a fifth-round pick in 2011. He reached Double-A for the first time at age 21 in '14, only to regress in the Southern League and receive a demotion back to Class A Advanced Bakersfield the next year. But Marlette's arrow started to point up again in 2016, as he fared much better in his return to California League and continued to hit after a late-season promotion Double-A. Despite his offensive struggles, Marlette has a sound approach and handles the bat well, showing good bat speed and power potential from the right side of the plate. His defense continues to be a work in progress, though Marlette does have a solid arm and a quick release, which has allowed him to throw out would-be basestealers at a respectable rate in his Minor League career, and he has made strides with his blocking. While his framing and overall receiving skills require further refinement, there's been no talk of moving him from behind the plate. Marlette fits the profile of a backup who can help a team offensively, with the upside of a bat-first regular if he can improve behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Fry earned the Mariners' Minor League Relief Pitcher of the Year award in 2015, two years after they had taken him in the 17th round out of St. Clair County (Mich.) CC. His control backed up in 2016 with a move up to Triple-A, but the left-hander still put together a strong overall campaign and was dominant down the stretch, allowing one earned run over his final 12 appearances. The Mariners added Fry to their 40-man roster in November to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, only to designate him for assignment and then trade him to the Orioles in April. Fry pitches mostly at 90-91 mph and tops out at 93 with his fastball, which he throws with good sinking action and excellent arm-side run. He can generate whiffs with his above-average, mid-80s slider, and also with a firm-by-design changeup that has late tumble and some cutting action. Fry is consistently around the zone and induces weak contact, mostly of the ground-ball variety, with all three pitches, and he allowed just eight extra-base hits last season in the hitter-friendly Pacific Coast League. Fry's effectiveness against right-handed hitters as well as his ability to log multiple innings give him a chance to be more than just a LOOGY in the big leagues. He should make his debut at some point in 2017, but not before making gains with his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 70 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Sadzeck turned down the Pirates as a 45th-round pick out of high school in 2010, then created buzz by pitching in the mid 90s during the fall at Howard (Texas) JC. Signed for $350,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2011, he led the low Class A South Atlantic League with a 2.25 ERA two years later but missed all of 2014 following Tommy John surgery. After the Rangers eased him back in during '15, he ranked second in the Double-A Texas League in strikeouts (133) and third in strikeout rate (8.5 per nine innings) last year. Sadzeck's best pitch is his fastball, which sits in the mid 90s with heavy sink. His mid-80s slider gives him a solid second offering when he stays on top of it. His changeup lags behind the rest of his arsenal because it gets too firm and he had trouble locating it for strikes. The key for Sadzeck is maintaining a direct line to the plate, because when he doesn't, his pitches lose their sharpness and wander up in the strike zone. He has decent control but his command isn't as fine, so some scouts think he'll be better suited for the bullpen. His fastball sat at 97-99 mph and repeatedly reached triple digits when he was a reliever in the Arizona Fall League in 2015.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Ibanez was the youngest player (age 19) on Cuba's 2013 World Baseball Classic squad and one of the best young hitters in the island's top league before he defected in 2014. Signed for $1.6 million in July 2015, he made his pro debut in 2016 after a two-year layoff and hit his way to Double-A. The Rangers continued to accelerate his development by sending him to the Arizona Fall League in the offseason. A bat-first infielder, Ibanez has a compact right-handed stroke that produces line drive after line drive. He doesn't try to do too much, focusing on using the middle of the field while controlling the strike zone. He has a knack for barreling the ball but most of his power comes to gaps in the form of doubles rather than home runs. While Ibanez won the Cuban equivalent of a Gold Glove as an 18-year-old in 2011, he has fringy speed and average arm strength. He's a decent defender at second base and also has seen action at third base, though he doesn't have the power to profile at the hot corner. Stuck behind a logjam of middle infielders in Texas, he has drawn comparisons to Howie Kendrick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 40 | Run: 70 | Arm: 40 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 One of the fastest players in the 2015 Draft, Jenkins hailed from the same West Columbus High (Cerro Gordo, N.C.) program that spawned speedsters Otis and Donell Nixon. Signed for an above-slot $2 million as a second-round choice, Jenkins led the low Class A South Atlantic League and ranked third in the Minors with 51 steals in his first full pro season. But he also scuffled at the plate, hitting .220/.277/.327 with a strikeout rate of 28 percent. Jenkins obviously needs to do a better job of using his well above-average speed at the plate by making more contact. Amateur scouts liked his feel for hitting and he makes an effort to utilize the entire field, but he struggles to handle offspeed pitches. He has some deceptive pull power and could reach double figures in home runs once he makes some adjustments to his approach. Jenkins does a good job of using his quickness. He succeeded on 81 percent of his steal attempts in his first two pro seasons and covers a lot of ground in center field. His arm is below average but isn't a liability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 45 | Arm: 70 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Beras controversially signed with the Rangers for $4.5 million in February 2012 after submitting an older birthdate than he had previously, a move some teams believe was designed to circumvent upcoming bonus restrictions in a new Collective Bargaining Agreement. When MLB couldn't determine his true birthdate, it allowed the deal to stand but suspended him until July 2013. Though his bat has been slow to develop, he started to realize some of his considerable power potential with a career-high 22 homers in Class A Advanced last year. Beras has two well above-average tools in his raw power and his arm, with some evaluators putting top-of-the-scale 80 grades on his arm. He has impressive bat speed and his 6-foot-6 frame gives him terrific leverage, but his long arms also mean he has a long right-handed swing. He has yet to display much consistency at the plate because his aggressive, pull-happy approach has resulted in a 28 percent strikeout rate through his first four seasons. Though Beras moves well for a big man, he has below-average speed that limits his effectiveness on the bases and in the outfield corners. He has a lot of work to do defensively, as his jumps, routes and throwing accuracy all need improvement. Most of his value will come from his bat, and Texas hopes his eight homers last August are a sign that he's about to take off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 70 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 The Rangers led the industry by spending $8.4 million during the 2013-14 international signing period, including $1.35 million to land Yrizarri from the Dominican Republic. He has more power potential and a huskier build than most shortstops -- as did his uncle, former big leaguer Deivi Cruz. Texas pushed him aggressively, getting him to high Class A at age 20, before trading him to the White Sox in July for international bonus pool money. With his sound right-handed stroke and his bat speed, Yrizarri makes a lot of hard contact. He could hit in the neighborhood of .260 with 15 homers if he can add some strength and tone down his approach. He seemingly swings at and tries to pull every pitch he sees, and his nine walks last year were the second-fewest among batting qualifiers in all full-season leagues. Yrizarri is still learning how to use his solid speed on the bases after getting caught in 45 percent of his steal attempts in his first three years as a pro. He has started to settle down defensively and should be able to remain at shortstop with his good range and cannon arm. He also has seen action at second and third base and definitely has the tools to provide utility value if he can't make it as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 30 | Run: 45 | Arm: 55 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 The most advanced player in the Rangers' $8.4 million crop from the 2013-14 international signing period, De Leon has advanced quickly since turning pro for $550,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He made his debut in Double-A as a 17-year-old emergency fill-in in May 2014 and became the youngest player in Arizona Fall League history that fall when he replaced an injured Jurickson Profar. Annually one of the youngest regulars in his circuit, he spent 2016 in Advanced Class A as a 19-year-old and helped High Desert win the California League championship. Uncannily polished on defense for his age, De Leon led Cal League shortstops with a .964 fielding percentage last year. His outstanding instincts help him play faster than his fringy speed, he has quick hands and he makes strong, accurate throws. He also has played some second base and has the tools and versatility to play anywhere but catcher and center field. While De Leon has a modest offensive ceiling, he's one of the best contact hitters in the Texas system. A switch-hitter, he employs a short, easy stroke from both sides of the plate and uses the entire field. He has added some muscle but must continue to get stronger, and his career-high nine homers last year were more a product of High Desert's ballpark than an indication of developing power potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Miffed when Coastal Carolina rescinded its scholarship offer when he had a lackluster junior season and subsequent summer, Enright worked to get stronger and improve his mental approach. He led West Orange High (Winter Garden) to its first Florida class 9-A semifinal appearance and boosted himself into the third round of the Draft in 2016. Signed for an over-slot $675,000, he finished sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League batting race (.313). A switch-hitter who makes line-drive contact from both sides, Enright has a mature approach and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. He doubled 13 times in his 42-game pro debut and could have average or better power once he adds needed muscle to his 6-foot-1 frame. He's an average runner with good instincts but won't steal many bases. Enright has a strong arm spent the majority of his first pro summer at third base while also getting time at shortstop and second base. He focused on second base during instructional league and will see most of his action there in 2017. He projects as an average defender at second and potentially as a solid glove at the hot corner, and he also has the tools to man the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 45 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 A Las Vegas high school contemporary of Kris Bryant and Bryce Harper, Robinson eschewed a Nebraska commitment to turn pro as a fourth-rounder in 2010. His career appeared to be stalling when he hit .190/.273/.366 in Double-A in 2014, but he rebounded to hit 41 homers in the next two seasons. The most versatile player in the Rangers system, he enhanced his value by adding center field to his résumé last summer and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster last November. A .245 hitter in his first seven pro seasons, Robinson won't ever hit for a high average because he has a long left-handed swing and strikes out too frequently. He has outstanding secondary skills, however, with his bat speed producing power and his patience allowing him to lead Texas farmhands in walks three times in the last five years. He can look helpless against left-handers but batted .271/.368/.525 against righties in 2016 and has the upside of a platoon player. Robinson plays above his average speed because he's aggressive on the bases and has good instincts on defense. He played all four infield and all three outfield positions last season and impressed with his ability to go get the ball in center field. His best position is third base and he could make for a valuable, offensive-minded utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 20 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Nicholas took a long and circuitous path to the big leagues. He went from a backup first baseman at Gonzaga in 2008 to a catcher on Scottsdale (Ariz.) CC's Division II Junior College World Series runners-up in 2009 to a catcher/third baseman at Missouri in 2010. After signing as a sixth-rounder, he primarily played first base in his first three full pro seasons before returning behind the plate and finally making it to Texas last April. Though he's 28 and unlikely to be an everyday player in the big leagues, Nicholas has the ingredients to be a useful reserve. He offers good offensive upside for a catcher as a left-handed hitter with average power, and he homered off Dellin Betances and R.A. Dickey during his brief stay with the Rangers. He tightened his strike zone and did a better job of dealing with southpaws in 2016. Nicholas has worked hard to become an average receiver. He has fringy arm strength but isn't a liability against the running game. He also can play first base, albeit with limited range, but his well below-average speed otherwise restricts his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 The Rangers signed Dominican right-hander Angelo Leclerc in June 2010 and his younger brother Jose six months later. Angelo isn't much of a prospect and went to the Red Sox in the Triple-A phase of the 2015 Rule 5 Draft. Jose has some of the best pure stuff in the organization and reached the big leagues last July, recording a 1.80 ERA in 12 relief appearances. Leclerc's most effective pitch during his first stint in the Majors was his changeup. He has one version with unusual cutting action that hitters can't help chase out of the zone, as well as a more traditional changeup with fade that he can throw for strikes. His cut changeup plays well off his fastball, which runs from 92-98 mph with running life. Leclerc also can flash a plus curveball but has trouble locating his hard downer and didn't use it much with the Rangers. While he's fairly unhittable and misses a lot of bats, his value is limited because he never has thrown consistent strikes. He issued 13 free passes in his 15 innings with Texas and had a career walk rate of 5.1 per nine innings through six pro seasons, so it's hard to trust him in crucial late-inning situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 When the Rangers were in the process of signing Jurickson Profar for $1.55 million in 2009, they got to know his younger brother and wound up inking Juremi three years later for $150,000. He lacks the brilliant tools that made Jurickson the best prospect in baseball at one point, but Jeremi has the same instincts and game awareness, allowing him to get the most out of his physical ability. He was part of three championship clubs in his first four pro seasons, winning titles in the Rookie-level Dominican (2013), Class A South Atlantic (2015) and Advanced Class A California (2016) leagues. Profar has a sound right-handed swing and a knack for putting the bat on the ball. He employs a line-drive, all-fields approach and has some power to his pull side. He doesn't work deep counts and almost makes too much contact, because it cuts into his walk totals and on-base percentage. A fringy runner with average arm strength, Profar has seen action at all four infield positions as a pro and even caught one game when he was in Rookie ball. He has sure hands and finds a way to make plays. His best defensive position is probably third base, though he's more likely to become a utility player than a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 45 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Then-Rangers area scout Chris Kemp (now the Padres' international scouting director) found two big league relievers in the South Carolina high school ranks in 2011, signing Faulkner for $125,000 in the 14th round and since-traded C.J. Edwards for $50,000 in the 48th. Faulkner spent most of his early pro career as a starter before moving to the bullpen in July 2015. He made it to Texas two months later and pitched well in 11 appearances, but he got hit hard in two early-season stints with the Rangers in 2016. When Faulkner had big league success two years ago, he worked at 92-94 mph and hit 97 with a fastball that featured riding life and deception. Last season, he lost a couple of mph and fooled fewer hitters. His average changeup with splitter action didn't keep right-handers from teeing off on him and his slider lacked bite. Faulkner's crossfire delivery can make life difficult on left-handers, though he sometimes struggles to keep his mechanics in sync. If he can regain his lost velocity and throw more strikes, he can help a Rangers club looking for lefty relievers while Jake Diekman is sidelined until at least the All-Star break.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For his first two years at Louisville, Harrington pitched largely out of the bullpen. The left-hander moved to the rotation as a junior and was named the Atlantic Coast Conference's pitcher of the year. His performance moved him into the third round where the Braves grabbed him. He pitched sparingly in his pro debut after the long college season but is ready to attack pro ball as a starter. Harrington is definitely pitchability and command over pure stuff. He'll throw his fastball in the 86- to 92-mph range. It plays up because of its sink and because he locates it so well at the bottom of the strike zone. He has a decent three-quarters breaking ball and a changeup, both of which can grade out as Major League average. There is a ton of deception to his delivery, and he pounds the zone with quality strikes, keeping hitters from squaring up his pitches. Harrington's stuff does play up a tick if he's coming out of the bullpen, but his command, deception and competitiveness all point to him having a future as a back-of-the-rotation starter. If it doesn't work, he could move very quickly as a middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson was drafted by the Rangers out of the Florida high school ranks in 2010 then worked over the next four-plus years trying to develop as a starting pitcher. Command issues led to a move to the bullpen in 2015, and while strike-throwing was still an issue, he was much more effective in shorter stints. That led to his big league debut in 2015 and a little more Major League time in 2016, but he was then sent to the Braves in exchange for Brady Feigl and Tyrell Jenkins last December. Jackson's fastball, which was already good in a starting role, kicked up a tick or two in relief stints, sitting in the 95- to 97-mph range with a lot of life. He works mostly with his fastball and his power overhand curveball. He does have a fringy changeup that he will mix in from time to time. While his delivery has improved, there is still a lot of effort to it. It adds deception but makes it harder for him to find the strike zone consistently. If Jackson can command the baseball better, both in walking fewer hitters and in keeping the ball down in the zone, he has the pure stuff to close games. Even a moderate improvement could mean a long career as a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Morris was a surprise callup to the big leagues with the Mets in 2015, he became the second pitcher from the U.S. Virgin Islands to pitch at the highest level. That was just a one-game visit, but he pitched his way from Double-A to the big leagues again in 2017 with the Braves, who acquired him in June 2016 via the Kelly Johnson deal. Morris misses a ton of bats with his fastball-changeup combination. While he'll sit in the 92- to 93-mph range with his fastball, he can get 95-96 mph whenever he needs to and throws it with good life. His bread and butter is that changeup, thrown in the mid-70s with the same arm speed, generating a lot of swings-and-misses. He will mix in a below-average slider to keep hitters honest, but it's really those two offerings, thrown with a ton of deception, that's led Morris to hold hitters to a miniscule batting average against. Improvements with his breaking ball have helped, and he's thrown more strikes this year, though his overall control could stand to improve as well. He has the ceiling of a setup man in the big leagues in the near future. Seeing him in a seventh-inning gig is also a possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davidson was taken at the end of the first round of the 2014 Draft because of his left-handed swing and his potential to profile well in a corner outfield spot. He hasn't quite produced the way some may have hoped. The skills that made him a coveted Draft pick are still there, however, and he's plenty young enough to figure things out. Davidson has a smooth swing and a ton of raw power to tap into, but there has been too much swing-and-miss to his game for him to reach it consistently. One thing holding him back is that he tends to be too patient at the plate. He draws a ton of walks but gets too passive, a contributing factor to his very high strikeout totals. If he can learn to be aggressive on pitches he likes earlier in counts, both his average and his power output will improve. Davidson started his pro career in left field but now mans right and has worked hard to become an adequate defender there despite below-average speed. His arm works just fine for the position. Having a young hitter with good strike zone knowledge is never a bad thing, but in Davidson's case, it's clearly held him back. Even if his development is slowed down so he can get things sorted out, he has plenty of time to get thing to click offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had four Draft picks over the first two rounds of the 2015 Draft. The quartet of picks turned out to be a San Clemente High School sandwich, with Kolby Allard going in the first round and his battery mate, Herbert, being the last of the four chosen. While Allard has moved quickly, Herbert was slowed by a torn meniscus during his pro debut, then struggled to hit in the South Atlantic League in 2016. Known as a glove-first backstop, Herbert tore his meniscus during his pro debut in 2015 then struggled to hit during his first full season in the South Atlantic League, though he fared a bit better in his return to the level in 2016. There is no question about Herbert's catch-and-throw skills. He's very agile, blocks well, has great hands and a strong arm that plays up even more because of his quick release and accuracy. He's taken quickly to things like game-calling, having done some of it in high school, and has excellent leadership skills and an ability to work well with pitchers. Herbert has struggled to hit, but he has strong hands and raw power at the plate but needs to continue to refine his approach and plate discipline to get to it. Herbert doesn't have to hit a ton to move up the ladder and he's shown he works well with the young arms in the Braves system. He will have to get the bat going a little in order to catch up with them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It wasn't more than a year after the Marlins made Steckenrider their eighth-round pick in the 2012 Draft that the Tennessee product underwent Tommy John surgery, which cost him the next 18 months. A shift from the rotation to the bullpen during the 2015 season helped Steckenrider get his career back on track and he built on that success in '16, reaching Triple-A for the first time before a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. A tall and physical right-hander, Steckenrider relies heavily on a 95-98 mph fastball that has a high spin rate, as well as late running action that helps him miss bats inside the zone. He can also generate whiffs with his slider, a hard downer thrown in the mid-80s, and mixes in the occasional changeup. However, it's his fastball-slider pairing that's led scouts to project Steckenrider as a potential late-inning asset. After his breakthrough campaign and impressive performance in the AFL, Steckenrider, now several years removed from elbow surgery, should compete for a spot in Miami's big league bullpen in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A shortstop at Georgia Tech who also pitched out of the bullpen, Miami selected Esch in the 11th round of the 2011 Draft and then made him a starter. After being eased along early in his career, the right-hander broke out and reached Double-A in 2015, prompting the Marlins to add him to their 40-man roster following the season. Esch built on that success last season en route to his big league debut at age 26 in late August. The tall and athletic righty's fastball operates at 91-94 mph, and he demonstrates feel for pitching to both sides of the plate. Esch supports his heater with a low- to mid-80s slider and a fading changeup, both of which flash above-average potential, and he also mixes in a curveball that is below average but has good shape and depth. After getting a taste of the big leagues late last season, Esch should compete for a spot in the Marlins' starting rotation in 2017, though he's unlikely to serve as anything more than a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Named Mr. Baseball in the state of Kentucky in 2010, Riddle went on to have a solid three-year career at the University of Kentucky before going to the Marlins in the 13th round of the 2013 Draft. Since then, he's advanced through Miami's system at a steady pace, as Riddle earned postseason All-Star honors back in the Southern League in 2016 and finished the year in Triple-A. Riddle is an aggressive hitter with a short left-handed swing that helps him make consistent contact and limits his swing-and-miss. He offers little home-run power but has a knack for pounding the gaps, and he did so more consistently in 2016. Riddle isn't a basestealer despite possessing average speed, though he does receive high marks for his baserunning instincts. A second baseman in college who played mostly third base to begin his pro career, Riddle moved to shortstop full time in 2015 and impressed with his average defense and overall feel for the position. He continued to make strides at short last season, committing just six errors in 84 games, while also seeing some time at the keystone. He has the hands, range and arm strength to play anywhere on the infield, and that versatility should help him carve out a utility role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Guaimaro, along with several Venezuelan amateurs in 2015, only to have those players declared free agents after Major League Baseball ruled the team had evaded the set limitations pertaining to international bonus pool spending. In July 2016, Guaimaro signed with the Marlins. With present strength to his athletic frame, Guaimaro draws physical comparisons to Marlon Byrd from club officials. He has plus bat speed and impacts the baseball from the right side of the plate, all the while showing the ability to recognize spin and work counts at a young age. He's an above-average runner and plays a strong center field, though further physical development likely will force him to right field, where his plus arm would be a fit. The Marlins have high hopes for Guaimaro, who will be 18 for the entire 2017 season. He'll require considerable time to develop in the Minors, but the final product could be that of an everyday corner outfielder who can hit for average and power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A workhorse during his senior season at Missouri State, Perez logged 91 1/3 innings while making a program-record 36 relief appearances. The right-hander struck out 112 hitters in that span and did not record a loss, finishing the year with a perfect 8-0 record and a streak of 22 2/3 consecutive scoreless innings for the Bears. Targeting Perez's untapped potential as a starter as well as his potential discount as a senior, the Marlins made him their fifth-round pick in the 2016 Draft and and signed him for just $20,000. A tall, physical right-hander, Perez's velocity steadily improved during his four years at Missouri State, and he was up to 95 mph as a senior. He's adept at pounding the bottom of the strike zone with the pitch, and complements it with a power slider and changeup, with the former currently ahead of the latter. All of Perez's pitches play up due to his deceptive delivery and because he hides the ball well. Given his ability to eat innings but also pitch in high-leverage situations, Perez could turn out to be a valuable signing for the Marlins. He'll be given a chance to start next year in his first full season, though he stands to reach the Major Leagues faster in a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guerrero was a tall, skinny 170-pounder with well below-average velocity when he signed with the Padres out of Colombia in 2009. He's added more than forty pounds to his lanky frame since then, and he now boasts a fastball that can hit triple digits. The right-hander made his big league debut with the Padres in May 2016 but was back pitching in Double-A when the Marlins acquired him along with Andrew Cashner in July. Guerrero generates easy velocity, sitting in the high 90s on a regular basis and touching 100 mph. While his heater doesn't feature much life, its sheer velocity and his ability to use his 6-foot-8 frame to create downhill plane makes him difficult to square up. His low-80s slider is a legitimate out pitch and will flash plus, though, overall, it lacks consistency. The only thing keeping Guerrero from becoming an impact reliever in the big leagues is his below-average strike-throwing ability. He's made strides in that regard at times in his career, only to regress. If he can learn to harness his big body and gangly limbs during his delivery, he could be a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A broken right wrist in 2013 enabled Morales to repeat his senior year of high school, and the Marlins made him their 12th-round pick the following year. He emerged as the organization's top catching prospect in 2016, showing his trademark defensive skills and improved feel to hit over 60 games in the Class A South Atlantic League. He advanced to the Florida State League in 2017 and was playing well before he received an 80-game suspension in June after testing positive for the performance-enhancing substance Stanozolol. Morales' defense is his calling card to the big leagues, as there's little he can't do behind the plate. His combination of strength and agility makes him an adept blocker, with receiving and framing skills that earn praise from pitchers and coaches. His plus arm helps him control the running game, evidenced by his 33-percent caught-stealing rate last season -- a mark he stands to improve by improving his footwork. At the plate, Morales projects to hit for more average than power at the present, although scouts believe the latter will develop given his bat speed, physical strength and sound approach. Unsurprisingly, the backstop is a well below-average runner. A right wrist sprain sidelined Morales for the final month last season and kept him from participating in fall instructional league, and he was dinged up once again early in '17 before joining Jupiter. Even with the suspension, the Marlins remain high on Morales' upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not viewed as much of a prospect out of high school back in 2013, Reed pitched a year at Navarro (Texas) JC -- after going undrafted -- before transferring to Oklahoma State, where he would develop into a key bullpen piece for the Cowboys over the next three years. Believing that Reed's size, durability and deep arsenal were underutilized as a reliever, the Marlins drafted him in the sixth round last June with the intention of making him a starter. Reed's velocity was inconsistent as a junior because he was overworked, but then he showed a better fastball after signing, sitting 94-95 mph and hitting 97 mph in short bursts during his pro debut. Reed's curveball, a fairly recent addition to his arsenal, and slider both show average potential, and at times he'll mix in a changeup that currently grades as well below average. He does a good job pounding the zone, and uses his height to create plane to the plate. A big, physical right-hander, Reed should be able to handle the rigors of a full season as a starter. With feel for a four-pitch mix and a knack for throwing strikes, he has the makings of a back-end starter. That said, he stands to reach the big leagues faster in a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lilek entered his Draft year in 2015 as a potential first-round pick, but an uneven season removed him from Friday night duties at Arizona State. He did perform better near the end of the season, leading to his selection in the second round by the Marlins. Lilek pitched well during his pro debut, but was limited to just seven appearances and 16 innings in 2016 as he dealt with left biceps tendinitis and general fatigue. When he's healthy, Lilek sits at 90-93 mph and bumps 94 with his fastball. His breaking ball also grades out as at least a Major League offering, one thrown with downward tilt that induces whiffs from both sides of the plate. Lilek's changeup gives him a third potentially average offering, and he throws everything from the same deceptive arm slot. Lilek is a consistent strike-thrower, but his command will need to improve. Lilek spent the fall rehabbing in the Marlins' fall instructional league, setting the stage for his return to game action in 2017. He has a chance to move quickly through the Minors, although the left-hander's health will always be a concern.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Marlins in 2010, Beltre was beset by injuries early in his career before undergoing Tommy John surgery and missing all of the 2015 season. Fully healthy in 2016, the right-hander broke out with a dominant campaign, recording 10.4 strikeouts per nine innings and a .178 opponents' average between the South Atlantic and Florida State leagues. Beltre's power arm produces an upper-90s fastball that can flirt with triple digits, and he also utilizes a slider that will flash above average with late, short slicing action. His control leaves much to be desired, but there's reason to believe it will improve as Beltre continues to distance himself from elbow surgery. Beltre went unselected in the 2016 Rule 5 Draft after the Marlins opted not to add him to their 40-man roster during the offseason. Though he's yet to pitch at the Double-A level, the right-hander has the type of power stuff to move quickly in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more athletic prep prospects available in the 2014 Draft, Twine signed with the Marlins for $1,316,000 as a second-round pick out of Falls City (Texas) High, where he had starred as the school's quarterback and won a gold medal in long jump and two relays in the state championships. Though he's struggled to translate his athleticism and tools into baseball skills early in his career, Twine did make strides on both sides of the ball last season in his second tour of the South Atlantic League. Twine makes hard contact from the right side of the plate through a combination of strength and bat speed that leads scouts to believe he'll eventually tap into his above-average raw power. He made strides in cleaning up his approach last season, showing a desire to go the other way more often while not expanding his zone, but still whiffed quite a bit. Twine's double-plus speed is his greatest asset and should make him a base-stealing threat once he learns to read pitches and refines his stealing technique. While Twine made progress as a shortstop in 2015, he also committed 29 errors. The Marlins decided to move him to second base that fall, and Twine thrived at the position in 2016, showing plus range and actions as well as a more accurate arm en route to committing just seven errors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Norwood is best remembered for hitting the game-winning home run that propelled Vanderbilt to its first-ever College World Series title in 2014. He went undrafted in June but performed well during the summer in the Cape Cod League before signing with the Marlins for $275,000. He's since made a steady climb through the Marlins' system, highlighted by an All-Star campaign in the Double-A Southern League in 2017. Norwood generates big pull-side raw power with his strong core and quick bat. He sells out for it too often, though, pulling off the ball with a long swing that limits his use of the opposite field and results in too many strikeouts. Norwood also has issues recognizing spin, but there's little doubt he can turn around a good fastball. An above-average runner, Norwood's speed translates better in the outfield than on the basepaths. He's capable of playing center field in a pinch but profiles better at an outfield corner. Norwood's right-handed power could make him an option off the bench in the big leagues, but he'll first need to show he can make adjustments against upper-level pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $130,000 out of Venezuela in 2007, Telis underwent Tommy John surgery in 2010 and then stalled out for several years in the mid-Minors before finally making his big league debut in '14. He returned to the Major Leagues the following year and appeared in six games before heading to the Marlins as part of the Sam Dyson trade. Telis turned in his best offensive campaign to date last season in the Pacific Coast League, and then reached the Major Leagues for the third time in as many years in September. Telis stands out for his consistent bat, which has produced a .311 average at the Triple-A level over parts of four seasons. He's a switch-hitter who makes a lot of line-drive contact from both sides of the plate and uses the whole field. Telis has below-average power and has tallied double-digit home runs just once in his pro career. The Rangers moved Telis behind the plate from shortstop at the outset of his career, and he's since developed into an average defender. His athleticism shows up in blocking ability, while his average arm strength plays up thanks to his clean footwork and quick release. Telis will have to make even greater strides at the plate to profile as an everyday catcher in the big leagues, but he has the defensive chops and the contact skills to serve as a quality backup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jacome cracked UC Santa Barbara's rotation as a true freshman and showed steady improvement before breaking out in the 2014 Cape Cod League. That success continued into his junior season, and the Marlins made him a fifth-round Draft pick in June. Assigned to Class A Greensboro for his first full season, the big left-hander made just four starts before left biceps tendinitis landed him on the disabled list for more than two months. Jacome stands out more for his pitchability and command than his pure stuff, although there's nothing wrong with the latter. He knows how to change eye levels with an 88-92 mph fastball and uses his smooth but deceptive delivery to his advantage. Jacome's best pitch is an above-average changeup that he throws with convincing arm speed from the same slot as his heater, and he also shows the makings of having an average slider, giving him three Major League-caliber offerings. Jacome has the ingredients needed to become a workhorse No. 5 starter, though he may be a better fit as a long-relief option or swingman because he lacks a plus pitch. The Marlins like how he processes the game and competes on the mound, qualities they believe could make him successful in either role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cespedes signed for $725,000 out of the Dominican Republic on August 24, 2013, his 16th birthday, because he was too young when the international signing period began on July 2. After debuting in the Dominican Summer League in 2014, his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League the following season was rather ordinary from a production standpoint. He used his considerable tools more consistently and finished sixth in the Appalachian League in hitting in 2016. He reached full-season ball ahead of schedule in May 2017, only to land on the disabled list for six weeks shortly after joining Columbia. While working his way back from injury in late July, Cespedes was dealt to the Marlins with Merandy Gonzalez in exchange for A.J. Ramos. Cespedes has the chance to be a five-tool player. With a loose, whippy bat, Cespedes started showing that he can drive the ball, especially to the pull side. He's shown some occasional power, with more to come as he matures physically. He's played a good amount of center field thus far in his career, and while he could play there, it seems more likely that his home will be in a corner, where his above-average arm would play well -- although there might be more pressure for the power to show up. All teams look for athletes who can grow with experience, and Cespedes looks like he could be that type of player.
