He has a long way to go, but if it all clicks, he could have a future as an everyday right fielder who does everything well at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It's the kind of story tailor-made for a Disney movie. Smoker, a former supplemental first-round pick of the Nationals, has his career derailed by injuries. He eventually pitches a year of independent ball in 2014 then gets signed off of a workout with the Mets in 2015. His velocity returned as a reliever, and he pitched his way to the big leagues in 2016. Smoker has a huge fastball that touches 98 mph and averaged over 95 mph during his time in New York last year. He likes to elevate it and blow it by hitters. The left-hander has an average slider the Mets would love to see him use more. He actually will throw both a splitter and a changeup with tumbling action, but there's been talk about paring the repertoire down, although it's hard to mess with what's worked since he joined the Mets -- he's missed a ton of bats and gotten a lot of groundball outs at all levels. Smoker did give up four home runs in just 15 1/3 big league innings a year ago, a sign that he was too amped up and left his stuff up in the zone more than usual. Given the chance to settle in, Smoker could prove to be a very valuable left-handed setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known as a glove-first shortstop coming out of the Florida high school ranks in the 2014 Draft, the Mets started Ramos off slowly, first in the Gulf Coast League and then up to the Appalachian League. After swinging the bat better than expected there, they jumped him to full-season ball in 2016, which may have been too aggressive of a move. Ramos didn't fare any better this year in his second crack at the South Atlantic League, prompting the Mets to deal him to Baltimore in July in exchange for international signing bonus slots. Playing in over 100 games for the first time can be an arduous task, and Ramos did struggle with focus, leading to an inconsistent approach. He does have the tools to hit -- he raised his walk rate from his time in the Appy League and doesn't strike out a ton -- and he can even drive the ball on occasion, though power is not going to be a part of his game. But he had difficulty finding a consistent swing path, hampering his production. Ramos has the speed to steal a base, and that should be a bigger part of his game. He definitely has the tools to stay at shortstop, with good hands and instincts and a solid arm. Ramos showed a renewed focus during instructional league play last fall, and played well as a result. Though he's struggled to build on that momentum in 2017, the Orioles are hopeful Ramos' game will flourish following a change of scenery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Phoenix native who stayed home to go to Arizona State, Woodmansee was the Sun Devils' starting shortstop for more than two years. A fifth-round pick after a good junior season, he started out well in the New York-Penn League during his pro debut but faded down the stretch. Woodmansee does have some offensive upside coming from his tall and lanky frame. He does get pull-happy at times -- his approach definitely suffered as he tired late in his first summer as a pro -- but he has the chance to be an average hitter if he uses the whole field consistently. Refinement of his approach could lead to more power in the future as well. With good hands and a strong arm, Woodmansee showed average defense at shortstop at times, though a lack of quickness could eventually mean a move from the premium position. He would be an above-average defender at third, but it remains to be seen if his bat will profile there. The Mets think they might have an intriguing piece moving forward, especially if he can stick at shortstop. The hope is he can shake off the uneven pro debut and turn in a strong first full season, much like 2015 draftee David Thompson did.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia's full-season debut in 2015 had the Mets very excited to see what would come next as a power-hitting third baseman of the future. That future got clouded by an 80-game suspension following a positive test for performance-enhancing drugs, though he returned to the South Atlantic League in the second half of the 2016 season. When Garcia is going right, he shows an ability to drive the ball to all fields, banging balls off of the left-center-field wall on occasion. For a player with good raw power, Garcia does not strike out a ton, though he could stand to refine his approach to draw more walks and work more favorable hitters' counts. A below-average defender at third, Garcia did see some time at first base in 2016, and that could be his eventual home. Because of the positive test, Garcia will likely have to prove himself one level at a time to show that his early success wasn't artificial. A strong 2017 season could help erase some of the doubt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An undrafted free agent after a senior season at Troy University in Alabama, Rivera is an easy guy to root for. He has had to prove himself at every single level, hitting his way rung-by-rung up the organizational ladder and going virtually unnoticed. Then he won the Pacific Coast League batting title in 2016, and the native of the Bronx became a bit of a folk hero in Queens by continuing to swing the bat well during a big league playoff race. Rivera has hit close to, or over, .300 at every stop he's made during his professional career. And even though he was 27 when he made it to the big leagues, he showed his incredible contact skills work at the highest level. While he doesn't draw a ton of walks, he almost never strikes out. There's not a ton of power, but he hits line drives and finds holes. With fringy speed, he's not a basestealer and it limits his range somewhat. He has shown he is capable enough to fill in at second and at third and continues to work to improve his versatility. Rivera will likely never be an everyday presence in a big league lineup, but the bat will play, and his positional flexibility should help him continue to defy the odds and find a spot on a 25-man roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2011, Garcia was doing exactly what organizations want to see from pitching prospects: Getting better with age and more experience as he moved up the ladder. After having no problems handling the Florida State League in 2016 and finishing things off with a playoff win in Double-A Reading, he was set to start the year back in Reading, but an 80-game suspension levied at the start of the 2017 season for a performance-enhancing drug put some of that progress in question. Garcia is more or less a three-pitch guy who relies on mixing his pitches well, though he has seen an uptick in the velocity of his fastball. He was up to 95 mph consistently at the end of last summer. He can spin a good curveball and he'll even mix in an occasional slider. His changeup looks like it could give him another Major League average pitch. Garcia's secondary pitches have improved enough that it keeps hitters honest and allows him to get swings and misses on his fastball. Garcia exudes confidence on the mound and stays around the strike zone. His mix is better than any one of his pitches, and he was looking like a future mid-rotation starter, though he'll have to prove himself all over again following his suspension.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Appel was taken No. 1 overall by the Astros after a stellar senior season at Stanford, most felt that at the very least he'd make a beeline to the big leagues. After two-plus uneven seasons in Houston's system, he was sent to the Phillies as part of the Ken Giles trade. His first year with his new team was equally frustrating, as surgery to remove bone spurs from his elbow ended his season after just eight starts. Appel remains an enigmatic pitching prospect. When healthy, the pure stuff still grades out pretty well. He'll show a 70 fastball at times, but it doesn't play that way consistently because it flattens out and is too hittable. That was particularly true out of the stretch, when he would lose any angle on his fastball. He still has an solid slider and he'll flash an average changeup. The Phillies feel with his stuff he should be making hitters more uncomfortable, perhaps by using a two-seamer more and by coming inside with more frequency. The injury kept Appel from putting his best foot forward with his new organization and the hope is he can do so with a healthy 2017. He has starter's stuff, but at some point one has to wonder if the fastball-slider combination would do better coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lively's first full professional season saw him start the All-Star Game for the California League before moving up to Double-A Pensacola for the second half. After his breakout year, the Reds traded him to the Phillies in exchange for Marlon Byrd. None of Lively's pitches jump off the page, but he does have four of them that he can throw for strikes. His fastball can touch 93-94 mph, and his slider has the potential to be an above-average pitch, as well. Lively mixes in his curve and changeup well to keep hitters guessing. All of his stuff plays up because of the deception his unusual delivery creates, making it tough for hitters to pick up the ball. When he was a member of the Reds system, Lively was often compared to Tony Cingrani for his stuff and deception. It didn't take long for Cingrani to get to the big leagues, and Lively could be on a similar track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canelo enjoyed a breakout season in 2015, hitting over .300, making the South Atlantic League All-Star team and earning a promotion while showing off his defensive chops at shortstop. A return to the Florida State League in 2016 did not go as well, leaving his prospect stock somewhat in flux. There is no question Canelo can defend. While he'll still make careless errors at times, he is built to play the premium position with plus range, outstanding hands and a strong arm. Consistency will come as he continues to mature. His plus speed should allow him to be more of a basestealing threat, another skill he'll have to refine as he moves up the ladder. Just how good a player Canelo can be depends on how his bat develops. He has the ingredients to hit, and added strength prior to the 2015 season allowed him to barrel up balls with more authority, although he regressed some in the FSL in that regard. Canelo has plenty of time to get his offensive game back on track and won't turn 23 until September. His glove should carry him up the ladder and make him a utility man at the least. If he gets his bat going, he still could become a defensive-oriented regular at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since being a highly touted prospect coming from the Dominican amateur ranks, Pujols has carried with him a tremendous amount of offensive potential. While there are still some serious holes to address, his leading the South Atlantic League in home runs in 2016, in his full-season debut, was a very nice step in the right direction. Pujols has as much raw power as anyone in Phillies system, including slugger Jhailyn Ortiz. Proof of that came with that power output in Lakewood, which is not exactly friendly for power hitters. And it's not just pull power for Pujols, who exhibited the ability to drive the ball out in right- and left-center. He needs to vastly improve his strikeout rate -- 32.6 percent in 2016 -- but the Phillies did see progress with his two-strike approach. He's improved his outfield play and has a very strong arm that works well from a corner spot. Just 21 years old for all of the 2017 season, Pujols is as confident as he's ever been in his Phillies career after having sustained success for the first time. The Phillies believe he could be primed for a big year this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals selected Glover in the eighth round of the 2015 Draft out of Oklahoma State on the heels of a dominant junior campaign. He made his big league debut a little more than a year later, earning a callup after excelling at three Minor League levels, and quickly emerged as a key bullpen piece for the Nationals before wearing down in September. A physically imposing right-hander with a power arm, Glover has all the ingredients needed to become a late-inning force. He sits in the mid-to-upper 90s with his fastball and can dial it up to triple digits, while his plus slider, thrown with power at 88-90 mph, is an out pitch capable of missing bats. He also employs a changeup and a curveball, but both lag well behind his other two other offerings and will never be a major part of his arsenal. Glover is a fierce competitor with excellent mound presence, and the Nationals love how he pounds the zone and fearlessly attacks opposing hitters. That mentality, along with the high-octane stuff, could help Glover develop into a big league closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Voth ranked third in strikeouts in the Pac-12 Conference in 2013 at the University of Washington before going to the Nationals in the fifth round that June. He continued to pile up K's early in his pro career, leading the Nationals' system in strikeouts for three straight years (2014-16) while reaching Triple-A Syracuse, though a regression of both his stuff and command in '17 led to a demotion back to Double-A in July. He pitched better in his return to Syracuse early in 2018 and earned his first Major League callup in late April. Voth sits at 89-92 mph with his fastball but can run it as high as 93-94 mph. He can impart cutting action on the pitch, and his velocity plays up because he hides the ball well. Voth's slider and changeup give him a pair of Major League-caliber secondary offerings, and club officials were particularly impressed with his development of the latter during the 2016 Arizona Fall League. Pitching with above-average control and command was long viewed as one of Voth's strengths, though he now has much left to prove in that department after struggling in 2017, when he shied away from attacking hitters in the strike zone and spent much of the season nibbling at the corners so as to avoid yielding hard contact. The Nationals are optimistic that Voth will eventually right the ship, and they still view him as a potential back-end starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals gave Cole an above-slot bonus of $2 million as a fourth-round pick in 2010, only to ship him to the Athletics as part of the Gio Gonzalez trade after the 2011 season. He returned to Washington the following year in a three-team deal for Mike Morse and made a steady climb through the Minors en route to his big league debut in April 2015. He saw even more time in the Majors last season, logging eight starts for the Nationals. Cole sits in the low 90s with his fastball, with a clean arm action and a simple, repeatable delivery that enables him to pitch to both sides of the plate. His above-average changeup is his best secondary offering and plays nicely off his fastball, although it doesn't aid his effectiveness against left-handed hitters. He has good feel for his slider and will mix in a curveball, and club officials were pleased with his improved ability to throw both breaking balls for strikes in 2016. Cole has average control and doesn't issue many walks, but his lack of a plus pitch as well as reliance on location makes him susceptible to hard contact and limits his bat-missing potential. Cole's four-pitch mix and ability to eat innings gives him a solid floor as a back-end starter, but much like Austin Voth, Cole will need something to go his way to crack the Nationals' rotation in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abreu enjoyed a breakout full-season debut at Class A Hagerstown in 2015, three years after he had signed with the Nationals out of the Dominican Republic. While he has yet to repeat that type of performance, Abreu has still made steady climb through the Minors en route to a Double-A assignment in 2017. Abreu has a quick right-handed bat and good strength to his frame, which he proved by winning the Nationals' strength and conditioning competition during instructional league in 2015. His approach has regressed against Eastern League pitching this season, as he's produced less hard contact with strikeout and walk rates that continue to trend in the wrong direction. Abreu's average speed has yet to translate on the basepaths, and he'll likely to lose a step as he continues to tack on strength. He saw time at both middle-infield positions in 2015 but has manned shortstop exclusively since the start of the 2016 season. He has the quickness, range and arm strength for the position, but like many young shortstops, lacks consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for $7,500 in 2014, Baez struggled in his first full season, beginning the year at Class A Hagerstown before receiving demotions to the New York-Penn and Gulf Coast Leagues. He made some strides in improving his control and missed more bats back with Hagerstown in 2016, only to regress the following year with the move up to the Class A Advanced Carolina League. Baez has big-time arm strength, usually working in the low-to-mid 90s and at times flirting with triple digits, but his velocity isn't consistent because he struggles to repeat his delivery. His curveball has the makings of an above-average pitch, one thrown in the high 70s with decent depth and shape, although his varying release point compromises the pitch's effectiveness. Baez's changeup is a work in progress, and he'll need to develop it thoroughly to remain a starter. Baez's inconsistent mechanics and lack of a third pitch make him to difficult to project as a starter long term, though, at age 22, he still has time on his side. At the worst, the right-hander's impressive arm strength and potential for two average-or-better pitches should allow him to carve out a late-inning bullpen role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Goodwin received a $3 million bonus as a 2011 supplemental first-rounder (No. 34 overall) and impressed in his professional debut the following year, finishing in Double-A. He wasn't able to repeat that success over the next three seasons and appeared to have stalled out in the upper Minors, but he managed to resuscitate his career in 2016 and reached the Majors for the first time in early August. Goodwin showed more of the blend of tools and polish last year that he did at the onset of his career. He has a patient approach, knows how to get on base and, at his best, uses the whole field to hit. His power also has returned, as Goodwin connected on 14 home runs last season after combining for 12 during his two previous years. He creates good bat speed and has improved against left-handed pitching, although there's still a fair amount of swing-and-miss in his game. Defensively, Goodwin's speed, arm strength and instincts make him a solid defender capable of playing all three outfield spots, which he did upon joining the Nationals. He should continue to serve as a fourth outfielder moving forward after getting his first taste of the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted out of high school, Upshaw spent the 2016 season at Pensacola (Fla.) JC, where he showed dynamic athleticism and tools but produced uneven results. The Nationals still made him their 11th round pick that June, and he signed for $400,000. Much like they did with 2015 second-rounder Blake Perkins, the Nationals drafted Upshaw with the intention of making him a switch-hitter. He's impressed the club with his aptitude in learning to hit from the left side, but, overall, he's a bit of a project at the plate. Upshaw's elite speed is a weapon, both in center field and on the basepaths, but he needs to improve his basestealing technique. Upshaw also has a well above-average arm, especially for center field. Team officials rave about Upshaw's athleticism, speed and promising hitting ability, and the belief is that he'll eventually develop the necessary baseball skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez played briefly in Cuba's top league as a teenager before defecting in November 2014 and getting declared a free agent by Major League Baseball six months later. The Giants thought they had a deal done with him for $2.5 million, but before it was finalized, the Cubs swooped in and landed him for a $3 million bonus and matching overage tax penalty. His tools were evident during his 2016 pro debut in low Class A, and so was his rust after a two-year layoff. Though Martinez has a quick right-handed stroke and feel for the barrel, there are mixed reports on his hitting ability. He got too pull-happy at times last season and while he doesn't swing and miss excessively, his consistency of hard contact needs to improve. Chicago believes he'll make adjustments and start to tap into his loft power to his pull side. Martinez's best tool is his arm strength, which earns plus-plus grades from some scouts. His arm and his solid speed allow him to play all three outfield positions, though he's still honing his jumps and routes. His quickness enhances his offensive game as well, as he can bunt for hits and steal some bases but needs to be more aggressive in doing so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Young has an impeccable track record at the plate. He ranked second in NCAA Division I with 105 hits while batting .401 as a sophomore in 2013, and he hit .373 in three years at Mercer before signing for $75,000 as a 14th-rounder in 2014. He won the Class A Carolina League batting title (.321) in his first full year as a pro, ranked second in the Double-A Southern League (.303) in 2016 and batted .351 in the Dominican Winter League during the offseason. Young makes line-drive contact with ease, thanks to his fabulous hand-eye coordination, simple right-handed swing and quality approach. He uses the entire field and walks nearly as much as he strikes out. He offers little power and won't be a stolen base threat with his average speed, though he is aggressive on the bases. A third baseman in college, Young has played all four infield spots and both outfield corners as a pro. His sure hands make him a reliable defender at any spot, though his fringy arm is stretched as a shortstop and third baseman. While he's actually older than Chicago's star double-play tandem of Javy Baez and Addison Russell, Young could help the Cubs as a sweet-swinging utilityman in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While several of the Cubs' best young lefty pitching prospects regressed last year, Paulino took a significant step in the other direction and claimed a spot on Chicago's 40-man roster. He spent his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball and began 2016 by repeating the short-season Northwest League, which he was leading in ERA (0.51), opponent average (.156) and K/BB ratio (12.3) before earning his first promotion to full-season ball. He recorded five quality starts in eight low Class A outings, including South Bend's lone playoff win. Paulino's best pitch is a fastball that operates at 90-92 mph and can reach as high as 96, though it's more notable for its groundout-inducing sink than its velocity. He's still refining his secondary pitches and is making progress with both of them. His slider shows the potential to become a solid complement to his sinker, and his changeup has the makings of an average offering. Paulino sliced his walk rate from 3.0 per nine innings in his first four pro seasons to 1.6 last year. He did a better job of challenging hitters and understanding how to sequence his pitches. He carries more than the listed 165 pounds on his 6-foot-2 frame and should be durable enough to remain a starter if he can build on the progress he made in 2016.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Cubs blew past their international bonus pool and spent $8.2 million in 2013-14 -- and landing elite prospects Eloy Jimenez and Gleyber Torres in the process -- baseball rules prohibited them from spending more than $250,000 on an individual player in the next signing period. They still found an intriguing hitter in Sepulveda, whom they purchased from the Mexico City Red Devils in December 2014. He had no trouble making the jump to low Class A at age 19 last year, batting .310 while playing steady defense at second base, though shoulder soreness has hampered him in 2017. Sepulveda's hands work at the plate and in the field as well as those of any Cubs prospect. With his hand-eye coordination and easy left-handed swing, he repeatedly strokes line drives from gap to gap. He's not physical and won't hit for a lot of power, though he does have some sneaky pop to his pull side. Sepulveda profiles best at second base, where he has exceptional polish for a teenager. He has enough arm strength for third base, where Chicago plans on giving him some exposure in 2017, and could make for an intriguing catcher. The one aspect of his game that needs refinement is his baserunning, as he has fringy speed and got caught on 11 of his 15 steal attempts a year ago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in New York but raised in the Dominican Republic, Rosario turned pro in 2008 and spent most of his first four years in Rookie ball. He didn't make it to full-season ball to stay until 2014, then missed the following season after Tommy John surgery. He came back better than ever in 2016, rising from high Class A to Triple-A after re-signing with the organization as a Minor League free agent and claiming a spot on the 40-man roster in November. Rosario isn't very physical but has a very quick arm, and he's throwing harder than ever since having his elbow reconstructed. He sits at 96-98 mph and can reach back for 100 and keeps his heater down in the strike zone, generating lots of swings and misses as well as groundouts. His breaking ball has curveball depth and slider power, consistently arriving in the mid 80s. Rosario can flash an average changeup from his days as a starter, though the Cubs made him a full-time reliever last year and will keep him in the bullpen. He has some effort in his delivery, so it's unlikely he'd maintain the same kind of stuff in the rotation. He also lacks the necessary control and command, though he did a better job of throwing strikes in 2016.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pena ranked second in the Double-A Southern League in strikeouts (140) and strikeout rate (9.7 per nine innings) in 2015, yet the Cubs opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster. After he snuck through the Rule 5 Draft without getting picked, they made him a full-time reliever last year. He missed even more bats as his stuff played up in shorter stints, and he whiffed 13 in nine innings after finally making it to Chicago in his eighth pro season. Pena works primarily with a four-seam fastball and a slider. His heater parks at 93-95 mph and reaches 97, and he can throw it by hitters up in the zone. Hitters had trouble solving his low-80s slider during his brief big league stint. He doesn't use it much as a reliever, but Pena also has a decent changeup that he can throw for strikes. He could help the Cubs in middle relief this year, though he'll need to improve his command to earn a higher-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter throughout his career since signing for $1.1 million as a second-rounder in 2013, Zastryzny got summoned to Chicago as a reliever last August. He posted a 1.13 ERA and 17 strikeouts in 16 innings and earned a spot on the National League Championship Series roster, though he was left out of the World Series to make room for Kyle Schwarber. The key to his success in 2016 was coming up with a cutter that kept hitters from sitting on his fastball. Zastryzny lacks a plus pitch, and while his fastball and changeup can be solid offerings, they also lack consistency. He throws both two- and four-seam fastballs, ranging from 87-95 mph and sitting around 90. In the big leagues, he mostly abandoned his changeup in favor of his cutter, which generates groundouts, and his curveball, which lacks depth but had surprising success in a small sample size. Zastryzny's crossfire delivery gives him deception and is tough on left-handers, but it also hurts his control and command. He could wind up as a back-of-the-rotation starter or a middle reliever, filling whatever role the Cubs need a lefty in just like Travis Wood did for five seasons before departing as a free agent. A lat strain cost him most of May and June this year, however.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first pitcher drafted by the Theo Epstein/Jed Hoyer regime for Chicago, Johnson signed for $1,196,000 as a supplemental first-rounder out of Missouri State in 2012. A member of the Top 100 Prospects list in 2014, he would have led the Double-A Southern League in ERA that year (2.55) and the next (2.08) if hamstring and lat injuries hadn't kept him a few innings shy of qualifying. He had the worst season of his career in 2016, getting rocked for a 6.14 ERA in Triple-A and missing more time after getting hit by a comebacker and with lat and blister problems. The Cubs moved Johnson to the bullpen last July and may make the move permanent after he recorded a 3.22 ERA with 35 strikeouts in 22 1/3 innings. Working in relief allowed him to concentrate on his two best pitches, a 92-94 mph fastball that can reach 96 and a curveball that can be a true hammer but also gets slurvy. As a starter, he'd mix in a decent changeup and a mid-80s cutter. Johnson has a long history of injuries, many of which aren't arm-related, dating back to high school. He also has spotty control and command that have gotten worse since he reached Double-A in 2014. He has the stuff and mentality to thrive in the bullpen, though he'll have to locate his pitches better before he can help the Cubs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hannemann put his baseball career on hold after the Royals made him a 48th-round pick out of high school in 2010, taking two years off to serve a Mormon mission and redshirting for a year as a Brigham Young defensive back. After emerging as one of the best college athletes available in the Draft when he returned to the diamond in 2013, he signed for $1 million as a third-round pick. Slow to develop as a pro, he repeated Double-A in 2016 and missed the final two months with a thumb injury. Though he has yet to produce consistently at the plate, Hannemann still offers an enticing combination of speed and raw left-handed power. Some club officials believe he's the best defensive outfielder in the entire organization, as his well-above-average quickness translates into tremendous range in center field. He has worked hard on his defense, upgrading his instincts and arm strength since turning pro. Hannemann's speed also plays well on the bases, as he succeeded on 83 percent of his steal attempts in his first four pro seasons and ranked seventh in the Minors with 26 steals when he got hurt last July. He still has to prove he can deliver at the plate, where he tries to do too much and doesn't get on base or tap into his strength as much as he should. While he'll be 26 this season and won't live up to the Johnny Damon and Jacoby Ellsbury comparisons he used to generate, he did set career bests in homers (10) and strikeout rate (17 percent) in 2016 and could be a useful fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round senior sign for $10,000 out of East Carolina in 2014, Williams saved Chicago money against its signing pool and helped it find room for seven-figure bonuses for high school arms Dylan Cease, Carson Sands and Justin Steele. He was spectacular in his first full pro season, transitioning from reliever to starter and winning organization Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors after leading the system with 14 wins and a 2.16 ERA while reaching Double-A. The Cubs expected him to make the jump to Wrigley Field at some point in 2016, but he was shut down with shoulder soreness in mid-May. Williams' fastball sits in the upper 80s and tops out at 92 mph, yet it's a legitimate plus pitch because of his sink and command. He doesn't miss a lot of bats but repeatedly yields easy ground balls because his sinker dives sharply when it arrives at the plate. It's the main reason he posted a 1.6 groundout/airout ratio and a 1.4 walk rate per nine innings during his first three pro seasons. While Williams lacks an average secondary pitch, he mixes in a curveball, slider and changeup and can throw them all for strikes. Chicago thinks his sinker and his mental toughness could make him a back-of-the-rotation starter. If not, he could help as a middle reliever who could eat innings and get groundouts when necessary.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After losing their top two picks in the 2016 Draft for signing free agents Jason Heyward and John Lackey, the Cubs focused on college arms with 16 of their first 18 selections. The best pure stuff in that group belongs to Clark, a fifth-rounder who signed for an above-slot $450,000. He had a chance to go in the first round after he worked in the mid 90s while dominating his first three starts at Duke last spring, but he pitched his way out of the rotation by midseason after his velocity and command slipped. Clark's fastball operates at 92-96 mph and can reach 99 mph, featuring nice run and sink when he doesn't overthrow. He also can overpower hitters with an 83-86 mph slider when he stays on top of it. He generates his power with a lot of effort in his delivery, however, making it difficult to maintain the velocity, quality and command of his pitches. Clark's changeup isn't as effective as his other offerings and scouts don't like his arm action, so there's a good chance he eventually winds up in the bullpen. If he can build on the consistency he showed in his brief debut, he could become a high-leverage reliever. Chicago will use him as a starter for at least the short term so he can get innings to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Higgins played mostly second and third base at Old Dominion and continued to do so in his 2015 pro debut after signing for $110,000 as a 12th-rounder. He also had caught a bit in college and the Cubs drafted him with the idea of moving him behind the plate, which they did in instructional league that fall. His build, athleticism and background as an infielder prompted one club official to compare him to Brad Ausmus. While Higgins has substandard quickness for a pro infielder, he has better athleticism and agility than most catchers. His average arm strength plays up because he has a clean, quick throwing stroke and good accuracy. He's still learning the intricacies of his new position, but he has soft hands and should develop into an average-or-better receiver. He's also getting some time at first base to enhance his versatility. Higgins controls the strike zone better than most Cubs prospects, walking (72) nearly as much as he struck out (75) and recording a .389 on-base percentage in his first full pro season. He focuses on getting on base and serving line drives from gap to gap with his inside-out, right-handed swing. He has some doubles power and displays good instincts on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morrison had a spectacular career at Texas Christian, going 37-12 with a 1.85 ERA in four seasons and helping the Horned Frogs reach the College World Series in 2014 and '15. A $30,000 senior sign in the eighth round of the 2015 Draft, he has enjoyed similar success early in his pro career. He posted a 0.81 ERA in his pro debut and led Cubs farmhands in wins (12) and ERA (2.11) while reaching high Class A in his first full season. A classic crafty right-hander, Morrison messes with hitters' timing by varying his pitches, location and arm angle. His fastball has below-average velocity at 85-88 mph, but he gets a lot of easy outs with it because he sinks and commands it so well. His solid changeup grades out as his best pitch and also features quality sink, while his sweeping slider neutralizes right-handers and his slow curveball can be effective. Morrison pounds the bottom of the strike zone and rarely makes mistakes. He's especially tough on right-handers with his low three-quarters and side-arm slots, creating good angle on his pitches. If he can continue to keep lefties at bay as he rises through the Minors, he could be a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The move to Double-A has derailed the progress of more than one prospect over the years. There were high hopes Travieso was ready for the jump after a solid 2015 season, albeit interrupted by a broken forearm, and a strong Arizona Fall League campaign. Instead the 2012 first-rounder saw his stuff back up and he had an overall disappointing first experience in the Southern League. Travieso got away from what had worked for him in the past, which was trusting his power stuff and filling the strike zone with it. At his best, the right-hander relies largely on his four-seam fastball, which he had been able to get up to 97 mph in the past but largely had it in the low 90s in 2016, and a slider that he's been able to miss bats with in the past. His changeup has improved, but it's still behind the other two pitches. In Pensacola, Travieso's walk rate skyrocketed as he was too fine, perhaps giving the higher-level hitters too much credit. The 2017 season will be all about Travieso re-establishing who he is and going out and proving he can handle the jump. The Reds expect to see a pitcher with a chip on his shoulder, one who still has the chance to develop into a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 For six years, Brice tried to find a way to harness his excellent stuff as a starting pitcher in the Marlins organization. In 2016, he moved to the bullpen, with a very positive effect, reaching the big leagues for the first time. He was one of three prospects the Reds got in January in return for Dan Straily. Brice is ready to get a full-time shot at a big league relief gig. His heavy fastball plays up in shorter stints, thrown in the low-to-mid-90s from a lower slot, and his power slider has emerged as an above-average breaking ball. He does have a changeup, though it's below-average, and while it would come in handy to keep left-handed hitters honest, it's not as essential as when he was developing as a starter. He's always been at his best when he comes right at hitters, and he found that attack mentality consistently when he changed roles. As a result, he found the strike zone with more regularity while still missing bats. Brice has the look of a future seventh-inning type reliever. His past as a starter could help him be a multi-inning guy out of the pen, but without having to worry about turning the lineup over a few times in an outing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 75 | Curveball: 60 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Hernandez toiled for five summers in the Giants system but couldn't get out of rookie ball because of an inability to throw strikes. The D-backs signed him out of indy ball, and while the strike zone still wasn't his friend, the Reds rolled very low-risk dice by taking him in the Minor League phase of the 2015 Rule 5 Draft. He pitched across two levels of full-season Class A ball, got added to the 40-man roster at the end of the 2016 season and made his big league debut in 2017. Earlier in his career, Hernandez had some serious difficulty with direction to the plate, contributing to his wildness. That has been addressed with some success, and while he still walks too many, he is able to more frequently attack the zone with his two plus pitches. Even if he's more control over command and getting too much of the plate, he's still successful because of how good his raw stuff is. He'll throw his fastball in the 95-100 mph range, and according to the data the Reds collect, he has one of the best curveballs in the system. Hernandez came back from his 2016 success with a breakout year in 2017 that saw him get big league innings. He has the stuff to pitch in the back of a bullpen, with an ultimate role somewhat dependent on how consistently he can throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Elizalde spent parts of four seasons playing in the Mexican League until the Reds signed him in May 2013. Since that time, the unassuming left-handed hitter has swung his way to the upper levels of the system and played on Team Mexico in the World Baseball Classic Qualifier in March 2016. Elizalde is, simply put, a professional hitter. He understands how to take an at-bat with an advanced contact-oriented approach. There aren't many moving parts to his swing, with a low maintenance setup that allows him to get to any fastball. He's a solid outfielder, mostly in right these days, and he has seen some time at first base in the past. He tends to perform well in the Mexican Winter League every year. More than likely, Elizalde profiles as an extra outfielder type at the highest level. Because his swing is so simple, he is the type who could thrive coming off the bench and being ready to swing the bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A smart and steady middle infielder from Curacao, Daal was not added to the 40-man roster this offseason and was thus left unprotected from last December's Rule 5 Draft. Largely because of a labrum tear in his shoulder that required surgery, he was not selected, and the Reds are happy to have him stay in the fold. Daal is an outstanding athlete, a plus runner whose speed helps him on the basepaths and defensively. He's gotten steadily better at the plate with a simple line-drive approach. He's gotten stronger over the last couple of years; it won't lead to power but should help him compete as he continues to move up the ladder. He's a steady defender with good hands and, at least before the shoulder surgery, had solid arm strength. Daal is expected to make a full recovery, though his 2017 season is going to get off to a delayed start. If he returns and takes another step forward, a spot on the 40-man roster this time around could be his for the taking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Lara for $3.1 million in July 2014, blowing well past their designated bonus pool to land the Dominican shortstop and incurring a penalty tax in the process. So far he's stood out for his defense more than the hitting ability that had originally attracted Milwaukee, although the Brewers remain confident that the teenager's bat will catch up. Lara combines strength and bat speed to generate plus raw power from the right side of the plate, but he's struggled to apply it in games because his swing too often gets long and stiff. The Brewers continue to work with Lara to better isolate and use his hands, which they believe are key to unlocking his offensive potential. Defensively, Lara has surpassed expectations with his glove, range and arm strength at shortstop, though club officials do acknowledge that Lara likely will end up at third base given his current size and remaining physical projection. Lara may not be as advanced as first thought and will need years to refine his game in the Minors, but the foundation is there for him to develop into a big leaguer provided the bat comes around.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pennington was on course to become one of the first high school pitchers drafted from the Northeast in 2014 before he blew out his elbow that April. Though he needed Tommy John surgery, the Red Sox drafted him in the 29th round and signed him away from his St. John's commitment for $90,000. He's been eased into action since returning but impressed in short stints in the New York-Penn League in 2016, prompting the Brewers to acquire him along with three other players for right-hander Tyler Thornburg in December. After offseason surgery to remove bone chips in his elbow, Pennington made his 2017 and Brewers debut late in June. Pennington worked in the low 90s in high school but now operates at 94-98 mph, giving him one of the best fastballs in Milwaukee's system. His movement and command with his heater don't stand out as much as its velocity, however. He shows aptitude for spinning an upper-70s curveball with good depth that could develop into a plus second pitch. Whether Pennington winds up as a starter or reliever remains to be seen. His changeup and control are still works in progress, and his lack of size and a less-than-clean delivery could point him to the bullpen. He'll remain in the rotation for now to give him some much-needed innings, but he could make for a high-leverage power reliever in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Nigeria, Orimoloye moved to Canada when he was 10 months old and went on to have a decorated amateur career. An uneven senior campaign enabled the Brewers to land the toolsy outfielder in the fourth round of the 2015 Draft, and he signed for $450,000. Those tools were on display during Orimoloye's professional debut, though he struggled to apply them consistently last season in the Rookie-level Pioneer League. Orimoloye is a physical specimen with three legit plus tools in his raw power, speed and arm strength. That strength, along with his bat speed and leveraged swing, gives him power to all fields, and club officials believe his feel to hit will improve with experience. He's still very raw defensively, but he has all the prototypical right-field tools. Orimoloye's rawness isn't surprising given his background and previous competition, and it also highlights his considerable room for improvement. He's years away from making an impact, but it's easy to dream on Orimoloye becoming an impact bat in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever as a Virginia freshman in 2013, Kirby emerged as the Cavaliers' ace the following year and pitched the program to a runner-up finish in the College World Series. Though he began the 2015 season as the top college lefty in the Draft class and ultimately led Virginia to a CWS title, a drop in velocity and command issues, as well as a lat strain that shelved Kirby in April, raised some red flags ahead of the Draft. The Brewers signed him at the deadline for under pick value, but Kirby logged just 13 innings at Class A Wisconsin before requiring Tommy John surgery that would sideline him for all of 2016. When healthy, Kirby's fastball will reach 94 mph and sit in the low 90s, but the pitch tends to play up because of its life and angle and his ability to locate it to both sides of the plate. His slider is a plus pitch, thrown with good depth and tilt and late downer action, and he also has a quality changeup. Kirby spent last year rehabbing with Taylor Williams, another Brewers Tommy John victim, and both hurlers are expected to be fully healthy for the start of the season. Though his progress has been delayed, the future is still very bright for Kirby, whose track record, arm strength and stuff point to him becoming a mid-to-back-end starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Regarded by some as the best prep player in Arizona last spring, McClanahan performed well for evaluators throughout his senior season, but concerns about his signability made him a wild card headed into the Draft. The Brewers made a calculated gamble by selecting McClanahan in the 11th round, and they lured him away from an Arizona State commitment with a $1.2 million bonus, which is generally second-round money. A 6-foot-5 left-handed hitter, McClanahan has present strength to his frame with plenty of room to grow. His hitting ability requires projection, but the Brewers like that he already has some feel to hit with good barrel control. He showed game power during his senior year -- and homered in his first professional at-bat in the Rookie-level Arizona League -- and scouts believe he'll produce above-average pop once he's grown into his frame. A good athlete who also played football, McClanahan has a solid arm at third, though most see a move either to first base or left field in his future. Regardless of McClanahan's long-term position, it's his offensive upside that has the Brewers excited.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz jumped on the true prospect radar with a breakout season in 2014 when he got the opportunity to be a regular behind the plate with Double-A Altoona and reached Triple-A for the first time. This is his third straight year in the Pirates' Top 15, but he has yet to break through to the big leagues, save for six at-bats. Injuries were the culprit in 2016, as an elbow injury kept him out until midseason and then an infected cut forced him off the field at the end. The injury bug even followed Diaz to winter ball as an oblique strain made him shut it down early in Venezuela. When he's healthy, he's one of the best defensive backstops in the Minor Leagues, with plus hands, good blocking and game-calling skills and an absolute cannon for an arm. He's long showed the ability to make consistent contact without striking out much and he's gotten better at controlling at-bats, with some gap power. Diaz used his time rehabbing well, taking on a leadership role and mentoring players while in Bradenton. The Pirates hope he has learned some lessons about taking care of his body and he did report early in the spring in good shape. He might profile best as a backup, one who will wait for his chance for a full-time crack at a big league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered \"old\" as an international signee, Garcia joined the Pirates at age 20, but has responded to being challenged with new roles and levels. Initially pitching out of the bullpen during his 2015 full-season debut, he moved into the rotation and posted one of the best ERAs in the Minor Leagues. He finished third in the organization in strikeouts and fifth in the Florida State League in ERA in 2016, though he pitched at times with a shoulder issue that required minor offseason surgery. The move to Double-A in 2017 proved to be a tough task and Garcia moved back to a relief role in July. Garcia succeeds when he commands his stuff down in the zone. Garcia's has backed up a bit, but can still touch the mid-90s with sink. He backs it up with a hard slider that can give him an out pitch at times. His changeup is below-average, something not as crucial out of the bullpen. Garcia had improved his delivery, making it more repeatable and allowing him to work through lineups and stay in the strike zone, though his walk rate spiked in 2017. Originally a shortstop who didn't garner much interest, Garcia is athletic and doesn't have a ton of mileage on his arm. It remains to be seen if the move back to the pen will be beneficial.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: This is Hanson's sixth year on the Pirates' list, ranking as high as No. 3 when his tools and up-the-middle potential landed him in the Top 100 overall list. Those days seem like the ancient past as Hanson is out of options and trying to stick in the big leagues as a super-utility type. Hanson still has some considerable offensive skills. He's hit for average and with some extra-base pop, looking like the type who not only would hit a dozen homers annually, but would also stretch doubles into triples with his speed. The speed plays on the basepaths, as he finished second in the organization in stolen bases in 2016. He hasn't always maintained his approach at the plate or completely embraced a role of being that on-base table-setting type. Initially a shortstop, Hanson played more second base than anywhere else the last two years. He saw time at third and the outfield as well to try to add to his potential versatility. Now it's up to Hanson to own his new identity. His effort level hasn't always been present at all times, but the stakes are higher now that he is out of options. Even after all this time, he's still just 24 years old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Things didn't go so well for the Pirates down the stretch in 2016, with slim postseason hopes slipping away as the second half of the season unfolded. Perhaps the biggest highlight was when Williams, who was acquired as unofficial compensation from the Marlins when they hired pitching guru Jim Benedict away, picked up his first Major League win with his father, who had been battling lymphoma, in attendance. Williams has the chance to contribute more than just one emotional moment. Pitching with largely average stuff, Williams' command, feel for pitching and competitiveness allows it to play up. Velocity-wise, his fastball might be Major League average, but its sink makes it above-average and generates a lot of groundball outs. He used to try to throw two breaking balls, but they ran together, so he's focused on his slider, which is a tighter pitch. He has a fringy changeup but mixes it in well. Williams attacks the zone and follows his gameplan well, going right after hitters and eliciting early contact. His ceiling might be that of a No. 4 type starter, but he's just about ready to fill that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Striving to become the first Lithuanian-born-and-raised player to reach the big leagues, Neverauskas took a big step forward in 2016, his first full season as a reliever. The right-hander reached the highest level of the Minors and pitched in the Futures Game. The only negative was a suspension levied by the organization following a bar fight when he was in Triple-A, which ended any chance of a September callup. The Pirates were pleased with how he responded after the incident, including taking on a leadership role at instructs with younger players, and they added Neverauskas to the 40-man roster in the offseason because his fastball-slider-cutter combination certainly would've garnered some interest in the Rule 5 Draft. Now in shorter stints, he'll throw his fastball in the 95-98 mph range while mixing in those effective sliders and cutters, both Major League average pitches. He goes right after hitters, missing bats and inducing weak contact on the ground. Nevarauskus put the end-of-season incident behind him and received his first big league callup in 2017. He has the chance to impact the big league bullpen full-time soon, with a ceiling of a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Plate discipline and the ability to get on base have obviously become important to all Major League organizations, something that is preached to all prospects. Sometimes, a prospect can be too patient. That's what happened to Moroff in Triple-A in 2016, though he still was called upon to make his Major League debut at the end of July. Moroff has always drawn a lot of walks since the Pirates gave him $300,000 to sign in the 16th round of the 2012 Draft, with 90 of them in 2016 alone. But there's a fine line between patience and passiveness and Moroff sometimes leans toward the latter, working counts too deep because of a lack of aggressiveness. As a result, he puts up high strikeout rates as well. He's working on attacking more at the plate, so if he sees a pitch early in the count he likes, he doesn't let it go. Originally a shortstop, Moroff had settled in at second, but is now moving around the diamond more and will get reps at second, third and back at shortstop, where he hasn't gotten much time in deference to the superior defender Gift Ngoepe. If Moroff can be selectively aggressive while not abandoning his on-base skills, he has enough offensive ability from both sides of the plate, including some extra-base pop, to go along with enough defensive dexterity to be a valuable utilityman in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2013, the Pirates drafted Cody Dickson in the fourth round of the Draft out of Sam Houston State. They went back to that campus a year later in the sixth round to get Eppler, who after being slowed by injuries initially went out and had a solid first full season of pro ball. Eppler has the chance to have an above-average fastball-slider combination coming from a big, physical 6-foot-6 frame. He'll now touch the mid-90s with regularity and he's tightened up his breaking ball into a slider that should be at least Major League average. He has the ingredients for a solid changeup as well and if it all comes together, he could have a three-pitch mix ideal for starting. Eppler certainly looks the part and is a very good strike-thrower. The one thing holding Eppler back from fitting the starting profile is durability. An elbow issue delayed his start in 2015, so he'll have to show he can handle a full season's workload. If that's a question, his fastball-slider could play up coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes slow and steady can win the race. Osuna signed with the Pirates back in December 2009. It's been a gradual climb since then, including parts or all of three seasons in the Florida State League. But the first baseman/corner outfielder reached Triple-A in 2016 and was added to the 40-man roster in the offseason, finally seeing the big league light at the end of the tunnel. Osuna has the tools to impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. He goes up ready to hit, but doesn't chase pitches out of the zone too frequently, Occasionally, in RBI situations, he'll try to do too much and will expand, but more often than not, he's an average hitter with at least average power, which has started showing up in games more frequently. He's not overly athletic, but is a capable defensive first baseman and while his range is limited, he can handle an outfield corner, with a strong arm that works well from out there. Osuna will continue to get looks at those corners -- first, right and left field -- as he tries to stay as versatile as possible. His first opportunity in the big leagues will likely come as a bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates liked Barnes' offensive potential enough to take him early in the 2012 Draft at No. 45 overall. But a series of leg injuries has seldom allowed him to develop or show what he could do. He finally stayed healthy in 2016, topping 100 games, and putting up numbers for the first time in his career. That was particularly true in the second half, when the Texas Tech product put up a .367/.440/.627 line. He finished sixth in the Eastern League with his .306 average for the year, as getting the daily reps allowed him to refine his approach and use his bat speed more consistently. His 44 extra-base hits show there is pop in his bat and that his legs still allow him to take extra bases. A center fielder when he first entered pro ball, he mostly sees time in the corners with speed that is closer to average now. Barnes found a good routine that works for him to help him keep his body intact and healthy. It's obviously a crowded outfield in Pittsburgh, but for right now it's just encouraging that Barnes is headed in that direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alvarez jumped onto the prospect radar with a breakout move to full-season ball in 2016 that saw him lead the organization with his .323 average and 36 stolen bases, though he took a step backward in '17, struggling with a move to Double-A before hitting the disabled list with a sprained ankle in May. He had returned and finished the season on a stronger note when he was sent to the Phillies in return for Juan Nicasio. Alvarez had hit for a high average every year since repeating the Gulf Coast League in 2014, using a short, level swing from the left side of the plate to make consistent, hard contact, though his approach did not serve him well initially with the double-jump to the Texas League. He has the chance to grow into more power, but he might be more of a line-drive, doubles-type hitter because of his approach. Alvarez is an above-average runner with excellent instincts that allow him to be a threat on the bases. He has a very strong arm, but he needs to work on his footwork and hands to be a more effective defender at second. The Cardinals added Alvarez to the 40-man roster last offseason, thinking he might be their future second baseman. Now with the Phils, he's blocked by the likes of Scott Kingery, but he has plenty of time to show what he can do in his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It might seem like a lifetime ago, but it was 2014 when Gonzales zipped to the big leagues less than a year after getting drafted, and he ended up pitching very meaningful innings out of the bullpen in that year's postseason. He had some shoulder soreness impact him in 2015, then came the elbow trouble that required Tommy John surgery and wiped out his 2016 season. But a return to health has Gonzales back on track this season, as he pitched well enough in Triple-A to earn a brief callup with St. Louis in June. The Mariners took notice of the left-hander's progress and acquired him in July in exchange for Tyler O'Neill. All signs point to the 25-year-old getting back to the athletic lefty with plus pitchability he was before he got hurt. Gonzales pitches with an average fastball that plays up because of his command, and because of his plus changeup, he can throw in any count to any hitter. His curve is his third pitch, but it has the potential to be Major League average as well. No longer blocked by the Cardinals' starting pitching depth, Gonzales should be given every chance in Seattle to show he can once again be a reliable mid- to back-of-the-rotation starter. It's in that role where he stands to offer the most value, though a gig as a long reliever is also a possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gant has been on the move quite a bit in the last couple of years. Originally a late-round Draft pick of the Mets, he was dealt to the Braves at the Trade Deadline in 2015. A big spring vaulted Gant onto Atlanta's Opening Day roster a year ago and he was about to make a move from the bullpen into the rotation when an oblique injury knocked him out of action, though he did return to the big leagues. He landed with the Cardinals in December as part of the Jaime Garcia deal. Gant has never been a big stuff guy, but rather has succeeded thanks to his feel for pitching. His fastball might be average, though the velocity has trended up a bit over time, but he can move it to all quadrants of the strike zone. Gant's changeup sinks as well, and both offerings generate weak contact on the ground. His curve is a third average offering that has some good break to it. Gant uses a very unorthodox windup that seems to work for him. Gant doesn't have much projection left, but he does provide some versatility. He could step in and be a solid back-end starter or fit into a bullpen, depending on organizational need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams was a two-way standout playing high school ball in Florida and had a pretty light pitching resume when the Cardinals took him in the second round of the 2014 Draft. Other arms from that class have moved more rapidly, from college right-hander Luke Weaver reaching the big leagues to high schooler Jack Flaherty making it to Class A Advanced. Williams' progress has been much slower, though he did reach full-season ball in 2016, a sign that things are moving in the right direction. Things started trending up for Williams in the Short-Season New York-Penn League last year for the small but athletic right-hander, and his bump to the Midwest League was a tip of the cap that he was ready to take another step. His velocity is ticking upwards as he matures, with a fastball that will sit in the low 90s, and touches higher, with some good tail to it. Williams' breaking ball keeps getting better, and if he can command it, it might be an above-average pitch for him. His changeup gives him a third viable weapon. The more time on the mound Williams gets, the better he keeps getting. It's easy to lose track of prospects who make such incremental progress, but at age 21, there's plenty of time for him to figure it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Denton, a Tennessee high school product signed away from going to Vanderbilt by the Cardinals in the second round of the 2015 Draft, really struggled during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League. He learned from adversity, and he had a strong second summer in the Appalachian League. A jump up to full-season ball in 2017 didn't go well, but Denton righted the ship a bit when he went down to the Class A Short-Season New York-Penn League. Denton was drafted largely because of his potential with the bat. He can drive the ball to all fields when he stays up the middle with his approach and there is raw power, though he has yet to tap into it. Denton broke into pro ball as a third baseman, but he has made the move to the outfield. He's played both corners, with a strong enough arm to profile in right if needed. Perhaps pushed too aggressively to start the year, Denton might be a one-level-per-year player, but his work ethic and makeup should allow him to see it through.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There are pitchers who perform well despite not having great stuff. Then there are those who are stuff-over-performance guys, where the results don't quite measure up to how the pitches grade out. Ellis fits into that latter category, and he's now been traded twice because of that intriguing stuff. The Angels sent him to the Braves in the Andrelton Simmons deal. A year later, Ellis was moved to the Cardinals as part of the return for Jaime Garcia. Even with the mixed results, Ellis reached Triple-A at age 23 with Atlanta in 2013 and St. Louis still sees potential in his his three-pitch mix. His fastball sits in the low 90s and plays up because it has a lot of life to it. Ellis backs that up with a cutter-like slider that can miss bats. He has a usuable changeup, but it's behind the other two offerings. Part of the reason Ellis' lively stuff hasn't led to success is his trouble with finding the strike zone. The right-hander walked 5.4 per nine innings last season. Ellis is plenty young enough to figure it out, and the Cards have had success in helping pitchers reach their potential. Shortening him up and putting him in the bullpen is an option, where he could focus on his fastball-cutter combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high school catcher, Martinez won two National High School Invitational titles at Mater Dei and played twice on the U.S. National 18-and-under team. He had a rather pedestrian career at USC following that, though a hot finish as a junior moved him to the fourth round. Martinez certainly got off on the right foot in his pro career, finishing second in the Short-Season New York-Penn League in batting average and third in OPS. Martinez isn't the type who jumps out at you with incredible tools -- he's average at best across the board -- but he maximizes what he has with tremendous makeup and intangibles. He possesses the kind of leadership skills teams love to have behind the plate, and he was able to transition to the pro game having called pitches a bit while at USC. Martinez doesn't have a plus arm, but it's accurate and he threw out 46 percent of would-be basestealers during his pro debut. At the plate, he doesn't have a ton of power, but he can hold his own and drive the ball. Martinez has outstanding plate discipline, walking twice as much as he struck out last summer. Martinez may not dazzle those who watch him for one game, but he's definitely the type that grows on you. Scouting director Randy Flores' ties to USC -- he pitched there as a collegian -- may have uncovered a future big league catcher, even if he is just a solid backup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor became the highest-drafted player from the University of British Columbia since Jeff Francis (2002) when the D-backs selected him in the fourth round in 2016. He was eased into pro ball via a bullpen role with Hillsboro in the short-season Northwest League before shifting to the rotation in 2017, when he made 13 starts for Class A Kane County but failed to take the mound after July 13 due to a right shoulder impingement. Following the season, the D-backs sent Curtis to Tampa Bay in exchange for reliever Brad Boxberger. For now, the plan is to let the 6-foot-6 Taylor work out of a rotation so he can work on all of his pitches, particularly the development of his below-average changeup. His other two offerings could end up as plus pitches, especially in shorter relief stints. He'll throw his fastball in the 94-95 mph range and can reach back to touch the upper 90s with heavy sink. He combines it with an upper-80s slider that can be nasty at times. He threw a lot of strikes, missed bats and generated groundball outs during his pro debut. Some feel with his arm action, he's better suited for the bullpen, and his sinker-slider combination would certainly play up. That might be his long-term future, but for now he'll work on developing as a complete pitcher in a starting role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Koch was a reliever at Louisville when the Mets drafted him in the third round of the 2012 Draft. Getting mound time as both a starter and out of the bullpen, he was making his way up their organizational ladder slowly when he was dealt to the D-backs late in 2015 in the Addison Reed trade. He made his brief, but effective, Major League debut last season. Koch might be the best strike-thrower in the D-backs system, filling the zone with four pitches. None of them are above average, but his ability to throw them to all four corners of the strike zone allow all of them to play up. His fastball is average, but he throws it with a ton of sink to get groundball outs. His slider is the better of his two breaking balls -- he tends to go with a fastball-slider combination when pitching in relief -- but he'll mix in his curve and occasionally his below-average changeup as well. The D-backs love Koch's competitive nature and that he pitched in the big leagues like he belonged. They think he can start as a No. 4 or 5 starter, but also like his versatility and know he can handle any role given to him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially drafted out of high school by the Nationals in the 14th round of the 2015 Draft, Lemieux opted not to sign. But instead of heading to Florida Atlantic, he went to Palm Beach State, a two-year junior college. That meant he was eligible for the Draft a year later, and the D-backs nabbed him in the sixth round. He struck out more than a batter per inning at two stops during his summer debut. The big lefty has the chance to have a good three-pitch mix when all is said and done. He has good life on his low-90s fastball and can command it to both sides of the plate, impressing the D-backs with his willingness to pitch inside effectively. He can spin a good breaking ball and has feel for his developing changeup. With a good delivery and mound presence, there might be more in the tank as he physically matures. Lemieux's pro debut last summer had the D-backs encouraged, though he struggled to replicate the results during his full season debut in 2017 There's some ceiling here, with the potential for the southpaw to develop into a solid mid-to-back-of-the-rotation piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A known quantity heading into the 2016 Draft as a San Jacinto Junior College catcher, January helped his stock out late by going off offensively during the JUCO World Series, landing in the eighth round. He continued to show power in his pro debut, hitting 10 homers in the Pioneer League. His pop from the left side of the plate is his best offensive tool and he was able to get to it fairly consistently with Missoula, even hitting four long balls in August as he tired out a bit. There is some swing and miss to his game, striking out in 34 percent of his at-bats during his pro debut. January broke his thumb during his San Jac season, so he didn't get to catch down the stretch, but he played regularly behind the plate with Missoula and is eager to show he can stick there. He does have a strong arm, but the rest of his defensive game needs refinement. If he can remain a catcher, January could be, at the very least, a lefty power-hitting backup. He might be athletic enough to handle an outfield corner or a move to first, where his bat could profile well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The early-round Draft picks may get more of the attention, but starting pitching help can come from anywhere. Take Donatella, for example. The former Friday night starter for UC San Diego was a 15th round pick but put himself very much on the radar by pitching across two levels of Class A ball and topping the system in WHIP and wins while finishing third in batting average against and fourth in ERA. Donatella uses his 6-foot-6 frame well to throw his heavy sinking fastball, which touches 94 mph, downhill. He keeps it down in the zone consistently and gets ground balls early in counts. He combines it with a solid average slider he throws in the mid-80s, and while his changeup is his third pitch, it's a usable offering. He is a big-time strike-thrower who doesn't miss a ton of bats but also rarely hurts himself with walks. A lack of a plus pitch does limit his ceiling somewhat. But there is nothing that says he doesn't have what it takes to be a back-end starter. It will be interesting to see how he takes his early success with him to the upper levels of the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas originally signed with the Cardinals back in 2008, but save for a handful of at-bats in 2014, he couldn't make it out of Class A ball. He was playing in the independent Atlantic League when the D-backs signed him in 2015. The following year, after finishing sixth in the Venezuelan Winter League batting race, he hit his way to Triple-A and earned a spot on the D-backs' 40-man roster. Since joining the organization, Vargas has done nothing but perform on both sides of the ball. He controls at-bats incredibly well, walking more than he struck out while making consistent hard contact. He's not a burner, but he's a very good baserunner, one who stole 21 bases in 22 attempts in 2016. He's capable of playing above-average defense at multiple positions. He's played mostly the middle infield but can handle third and has even seen time in the outfield in the past. Vargas is proof positive that talent can come from just about anywhere. He's gone from out of affiliated baseball to knocking on the big league door in less than two years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mark was a pop-up Draft prospect in 2015 as a closer at Concordia who set the NAIA single-season saves record. The D-backs took him in the sixth round of that June's Draft and decided to try to let him develop as a starter. He didn't take to it as much as hoped, so now he's back in the bullpen. While he is a bit of an undersized right-hander, his clean delivery and potential for a three-pitch mix made the organization think Mark could work out of a rotation. His stuff backed up in the role, but the year spent trying it out will certainly make him a better pitcher. In shorter stints, his fastball touched 94-95 mph consistently, and he complemented it with a slider that flashed plus at times when he landed it for strikes. He incorporates a good splitter as well, and while he doesn't have pinpoint command, he throws more than enough strikes, especially coming out of the bullpen. After throwing over 100 innings in his year as a starter, Mark has a better feel for his pitches and understanding of his delivery. His stuff isn't strong enough to close like he did in college, but he could have a future as a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $1,000 senior sign as a 21st-rounder out of Bethune-Cookman in 2012, Gonzalez made gradual progress in the lower levels until he repeated high Class A in 2015. When he got pounded for a 6.45 ERA and missed half the season with an oblique injury, his future looked bleak. But he stayed healthy in 2016, rebounding in Double-A and performing well in the Arizona Fall League to earn a spot on the Rockies' 40-man roster and Puerto Rico's designated pitcher pool for the World Baseball Classic. Gonzalez's 93-98 mph fastball has a combination of natural cutting action and some sink, helping him post an outstanding 2.5 groundout/airout ratio through his first five pro seasons. He found more success last year when he improved his ability to control how much his heater cuts. He gets good depth on his curveball and also employs a decent changeup to keep left-handers honest.
