The life on Gonzalez's fastball can make it difficult to command, though it moves so much that it can be tough to hit even when he leaves it over the plate. He won't be able to immediately build on the progress he made in 2016, however, because he injured his elbow in Spring Training and had Tommy John surgery that will sideline him until 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: French turned down the Tigers as a 19th-rounder in 2014 to return for his senior year at Texas, where he compiled a 2.60 ERA in four seasons as a starter. A $100,000 senior sign as a fifth-rounder in 2015, he posted a 36/2 K/BB ratio in his pro debut and set the stage for a terrific first full pro season. He needed just four starts to earn a promotion to high Class A, where he paced the California League in ERA (2.85), WHIP (1.04), walk rate (1.5 per nine innings) and groundout/flyout ratio (1.9), and topped the Minors with 177 2/3 total innings. He relies mostly on his two-seam fastball, which he can spot on either side of the plate with late, heavy sink. It usually arrives at 89-92 mph, though French has picked up some velocity in pro ball and is touching 94 more frequently than he did with the Longhorns. He doesn't miss a lot of bats but resolves a lot of at-bats with early-count groundouts. French maintains his arm speed while throwing his changeup, which also features sink and shows flashes of becoming a solid pitch. He also works in an average slider that he throws for strikes. He doesn't have a huge ceiling, but his efficiency gives him a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year in 2013, Musgrave beat out Rockies No. 3 overall pick Jon Gray among others after missing the previous season recovering from Tommy John surgery. He turned down the Phillies in the 33rd round to return for his redshirt junior season in 2014, when the Rockies made him an eighth-rounder. Put on the fast track because of his age (22 when he signed) and strike-throwing ability, he reached Triple-A Albuquerque a month into his second full pro season. Musgrave's best offering unquestionably is his changeup, a plus offering at times that tumbles at the plate. His fastball sits around 90 mph but he makes it work thanks to command and deception. He never has had much of a breaking ball and his slider remains fringy. He may have just one pitch that qualifies as even average, but that doesn't stop Musgrave from challenging hitters and pounding the strike zone. He has little margin for error, a point that was driven home when he gave up 17 homers in 19 starts at hitter-friendly Albuquerque. He's on the verge of reaching Colorado as a No. 5 starter or middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The MVP of the 2015 College World Series, Sborz led Virginia to its first national championship by pitching 13 scoreless innings in relief and earning three victories and a save. A starter as a sophomore with the Cavaliers, he returned to the rotation in his first full pro season after the Dodgers made him a supplemental second-round pick. He added the 2016 California League pitcher of the year award to his trophy case, and he would have led the high Class A circuit in ERA (2.66), WHIP (1.03) and opponent average (.207) if an August promotion hadn't left him a few innings shy of qualifying. As a starter, Sborz operates with a low-90s fastball and a mid-80s slider. Neither pitch is truly overpowering, but their late life and the deception in his arm action elicit a lot of bad swings. He has made some progress with a hard curveball that sometimes outshines his slider, but his curveball still lags well behind the rest of his repertoire. Most scouts believe Sborz will wind up back in the bullpen, though his move to relief in Double-A last August was made solely to cap his innings in his first full year. He has gotten more consistent with the front side of his delivery and has improved his control since leaving college, but there's still a lot of effort in his delivery. Whatever his role, he appears destined for a longer big league career than his older brother Jay, who pitched one game for the 2010 Tigers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $40,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, Mieses spent two years in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and was ticketed for the Rookie-level Pioneer League when he came to the United States in '15. Instead, he forced his way to low Class A in late April and earned a promotion to high Class A in June. He returned to the California League last year and won the home run crown with 28 as a 20-year-old. Mieses' quick right-handed bat and strength give him some of the best raw power in the Dodgers' system. He's very aggressive at the plate, however, seemingly trying to pull and lift every pitch out of the park. A streaky hitter, he homered 13 times in 19 games last July and August but also is prone to extended droughts where he struggles to make contact. Mieses uses his average speed well as a baserunner yet isn't much of a threat to steal. He has good instincts in center field and projects as an average defender. He plays all three outfield positions and fits best in right thanks to a plus arm that allowed him to record 14 assists last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sopko declined to sign with the Padres as a 14th-round choice from a Montana high school in 2012, opting instead to pitch at Gonzaga. A seventh-rounder three years later, he's a pitchability right-hander who reached Double-A at the end of his first full pro season in 2016. He won more games last year (13) than he did in three college seasons (12). Though Sopko's fastball doesn't light up radar guns at 88-92 mph with a peak of 94, it plays better than its velocity and ranks as his best pitch because it's deceptive and appears to rise at the plate. He uses two different breaking balls, with his low-80s slider a little more reliable than his high-70s curveball. He needs to improve his changeup to develop a weapon against left-handers. With nothing better than an average offering, Sopko must rely on mixing pitches, speeds and locations to keep hitters off balance. Double-A hitters tagged him for a 4.94 ERA and 15 extra-base hits in his six late-season starts, so he'll return there in 2017. If he can solve upper-level hitters, he could serve the Dodgers as a spot starter or middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Red Sox for $60,000 in 2013 after they drafted him in the 11th round out of NCAA Division II Nova Southeastern, Asuaje topped the Class A South Atlantic League in slugging (.542) and OPS (.933) in his first full pro season. That success did not translate to Double-A the next year, and the Red Sox traded him, along with Manuel Margot, Javier Guerra and Logan Allen, to the Padres during the offseason in exchange for Craig Kimbrel. Asuaje would get back on track in his first year with the Padres, however, as he was selected to the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game at PetCo Park, claimed the Pacific Coast League's Rookie of the Year award and made his big league debut in September. Asuaje stands out for his pure hitting ability from the left side. He produces line drives from line to line thanks to a combination of hand-eye coordination and advanced bat-to-ball skills, and he possesses more pop than his size suggests, with the potential to achieve double-digit home runs. Despite being an average runner with good instincts, Asuaje is limited to second base defensively on account of his fringy arm strength and range. To go along with his primary work at the keystone, Asuaje has also seen time at third base and left field. If he's unable to take over at second base in San Diego, Asuaje's bat could help him carve out a utility role in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Angels out of Venezuela in 2011, Rondon spent three years in Rookie ball before making the jump to the Class A Advanced level for his full-season debut in '14. The Padres acquired him at the Trade Deadline in a prospect package for Huston Street, and Rondon advanced to Double-A the next year, only to have his campaign cut short due to fractured right elbow. Fully healthy in 2016, Rondon was named a Texas League Mid-Season All-Star en route to his Major League debut in late July. Rondon stands out for his floor more than his ceiling, as he's a well-rounded player who projects to have three average-or-better tools. A right-handed hitter, he makes consistent contact, albeit with minimal power, with a flat path through the zone and barrel control that allows him to spray the ball from line to line. While he doesn't strike out much, Rondon can be aggressive to a fault at times and needs to develop more selectivity and learn to work counts in his favor. Rondon's above-average speed shows at shortstop, and he has the necessary range, footwork and arm strength to remain there long term. But despite having all of the defensive tools to be a big league shortstop, he will need to unlock his offensive potential to become an impactful regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays' pursuit of Rodriguez during the 2013-14 international period led the club to acquire additional international pool money, which they used to sign the then-16-year-old for $330,000 in January 2014. His rawness showed during his pro debut in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, but he made strides in his second tour of the GCL in 2015 and was continuing to climb the ladder when the Blue Jays dealt him to San Diego for Melvin Upton Jr. ahead of the 2016 Trade Deadline. Rodriguez saw an uptick in velocity in 2015 as he continued to get stronger and grow into his projectable frame. He showed the ability to bump 94 mph with his fastball as an amateur and has continued to sit in the low 90s with good sinking action as a pro. His slider and changeup are below-average pitches for him, though both should improve as he gains better feel for pitching. Learning how to repeat his delivery will be key for Rodriguez, who struggles to keep his body and lightning-quick arm in sync. The right-hander's arm strength offers plenty to dream on, but he'll have to check many developmental boxes before being deemed ready for the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blach's ability to fill the strike zone and pile up innings made him a fifth-round pick in 2012, and he has continued to display those traits in pro ball. He led the Triple-A Pacific Coast League in innings in each of the last two years (165 1/3 in 2015, 162 2/3 in 2016) as well as with 14 victories in 2016. Called up in September, he beat Clayton Kershaw with eight shutout innings on Oct. 1 to clinch at least a Wild Card tie for the Giants. Blach's already impressive pitchability got even better when he repeated the hitter-friendly PCL, and his stuff ticked up a little as well. His fastball now sits at 90-92 mph with sink on his two-seamer and cutting action on his four-seamer, and his curveball got a little sharper. His solid changeup remains his best offering, and his slider gives him a second fringy breaking pitch. With his fairly ordinary stuff, Blach has to do the little things to win -- and he does. He keeps the ball down in the strike zone to generate groundouts and avoid homers, controls the running game, fields his position well and hits better than most pitchers. He lacks a high ceiling but could be an effective innings-eater at the back of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Okert breezed through his first three years as a pro and dominated in the Arizona Fall League after the 2014 season, he seemed poised to help the Giants. Instead he spent all of 2015 getting knocked around in Triple-A while having trouble maintaining his arm slot. He got back on track last year and had three stints in San Francisco, where he posted a 3.21 ERA in 16 appearances. Okert beats up left-handers by throwing fastballs and sliders with a low arm angle and a crossfire delivery. His heater sits at 91-94 and can reach 97 mph but takes a back seat to his sharp slider, a true plus pitch. While the Giants see him as more than just a specialist, he's still looking for a pitch that can truly neutralize righties, and his cutter has replaced his changeup as his best option. Though Okert won't ever have pinpoint control, he cut his walk rate to 2.2 per nine innings in 2016 after averaging 3.6 previously. If he continues to throw strikes, he should serve as San Francisco's No. 2 bullpen lefty this year. If he can reclaim the little bit of velocity he has lost in the last couple of years, he could develop into a set-up man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible to sign out of the Dominican Republic as a 16-year-old in July 2010, he had to wait until September 2013 to find a deal. His fastball had improved to the mid-90s, so he was able to command a $350,000 bonus, and has continued to add velocity. He hit 102 mph while recording a 0.88 ERA in high Class A during the first half of the 2016 season. Martinez's heater sat in the upper 90s with some sink and cut when he was dominating, though it started to dip when he got knocked around to the tune of a 6.65 ERA in Double-A and fell to the low 90s during a brief Arizona Fall League stint. The Giants thought it was a matter of Martinez wearing down while pitching more innings than he ever had before, but shoulder issues have limited him in 2017. Improving the consistency of his delivery, which can get violent when he tries to light up the radar gun, should help him hold up better in the future. Martinez's second pitch is an upper-80s slider more notable for its velocity than its bite, and it ranges from a plus offering to a hittable slurve. He has problems providing strikes when he overthrows, which causes him to drop his elbow and lose his arm slot. He has closer upside but needs to add considerable polish to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Notre Dame's career leader in ERA (1.71) and saves (30), Slania was expected to move quickly as a reliever after turning pro as a fifth-rounder in 2013. That didn't happen, and when he posted a 5.32 ERA in Double-A during the first two months of last season, the Giants decided to shake things up by putting him in the rotation. After he went 8-4 with a 2.42 ERA in 16 starts at three levels, including two strong outings in Triple-A, San Francisco added him to its 40-man roster in November. One of the reasons the Giants changed Slania's role is that he has a deep repertoire and they wanted him to learn how to use it better. He doesn't have a plus pitch but does own three potential solid offerings: a low-90s fastball that peaks at 95 mph with armside run, a low-80s slider with depth and a mid-80s splitter. He also has a decent changeup and a slow curveball at his disposal. Slania did a better job of pitching inside and changing speeds as a starter, and San Francisco will continue to deploy him as one. He has a huge physical presence at 6-foot-5 and 275 pounds, though he works with a shorter arm action and stride than would be expected for his size. His delivery gives him deception and doesn't prevent him from finding the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: North Texas area scouts had two big-bodies college right-handers with nearly identical names to follow in 2015. Texas Tech's Corey Taylor topped NCAA Division I with a 0.31 ERA before the Mets took him in the seventh round, while Cory Taylor was one of five arms selected off a hard-throwing Dallas Baptist staff. An eighth-rounder, he thrived in low Class A and reached Double-A in his first full pro season. Taylor lives off his sinker, which usually arrives at 91-94 mph and was clocked as high as 97 in college. Hitters usually beat it into the ground, which is why he posted a 1.7 groundout/airout ratio and allowed just five homers in 152 innings during his first two pro seasons. He complements it with a decent slider but must improve his changeup to combat left-handers, who batted .301 against him last year. Taylor has a better floor than ceiling and projects as a back-of-the-rotation starter of middle reliever. If he continues to pound the strike zone and elicit groundballs, he could move quickly. He'll need to keep his 6-foot-2, 255-pound frame in shape.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With a fastball that hit 96 mph and a wipeout slider, Stratton earned Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year honors and worked his way into the first round in 2012. He rarely has shown the same stuff since signing for $1.85 million, however, lowering his ceiling from No. 2 starter to back-of-the-rotation option. He made his big league debut last May as a middle reliever. Stratton has a trio of average pitches and must mix them well to succeed. His fastball sits at 90-92 mph and touches 95 with a bit of sink, his short slider arrives at 82-85 mph and his changeup improved last season. His fringy curveball grades as his worst pitch, yet it was his most effective during his short time in San Francisco. Though he doesn't have the stuff that made him a first-rounder, Stratton compensates by moving his pitches around the strike zone. He has become more willing to challenge hitters and posted the best walk rate (2.9 per nine innings) of his career in 2016. He'll be on call in Triple-A again this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson served as Cal Poly's closer as a sophomore but had control issues and pitched sparingly in his Draft year in 2013. He impressed the Giants enough during the NCAA playoffs that they selected him in the third round and turned him into starter. Moved back to the bullpen last May in Double-A, he recorded a 2.30 ERA as a reliever and claimed a spot on San Francisco's 40-man roster. While Johnson had decent success as a starter, his lack of quality secondary pitches makes him better suited for relief work. His fastball sits at 94-96 mph and can climb to 98 with heavy sink, allowing him to miss bats and generate groundouts. His slurvy breaking ball looked more like a curve and had its moments in 2016, and he also has a fringy changeup. After working exclusively out of the stretch in college, Johnson has incorporated a windup in pro ball. He hasn't had any more problems throwing strikes but lacks fine command, so he can be fairly hittable. He'll need to prove he can stay healthy after missing a month each with forearm and shoulder issues last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After finding four big leaguers out of Oregon State in Tyler Graham, Joe Paterson, Andrew Susac and Josh Osich, San Francisco went back to the Beavers for Davis, their 2014 third-rounder. He has some of the best raw power in the system but had trouble tapping into it as a pro in his first two seasons, when he hit a combined .235/.308/.381. He broke out with 26 homers in 2016, including 18 in 63 games following a promotion to high Class A. Davis has the bat speed and strength to naturally generate power to all fields from the right side of the plate. He runs into trouble when he gets pull-conscious and chases pitches out of the zone, but he settled down and had more success last year. While he strikes out too much to hit for a high average, he will draw a few walks. Davis' power will have to carry him because he doesn't offer much on the bases or in the outfield. He's a well below-average runner and a subpar defender in the right field, where an arm that hit 97 mph when he pitched as a college reliever plays closer to average. The Giants tried him at third base during instructional league last fall.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best two-way prospect and the No. 7 overall pick in the 2013 Draft, Ball offered upside as both an athletic, power-hitting outfielder and a potential frontline starter. Most teams preferred him on the mound, the Red Sox among them after signing him for $2.75 million. He has been an enigma as a pro, however, posting a 4.45 ERA and 6.0 strikeouts per nine innings in his first four years as a pro. As a high school senior, Ball had a 91-94 mph fastball that figured to heat up more as he matured physically, as well as an advanced changeup and a promising curveball. Though he has gotten stronger, his stuff has regressed. He usually works with a 91-92 mph fastball and has had so much trouble refining a breaking ball that he may have to stick with a cutter. Ball's changeup remains impressive for both its fade and deception, but it seems unlikely that he's going to reach his once-lofty ceiling. Though he's still athletic, he doesn't delivery consistent strikes and often gets hit hard when he finds the zone. He got pounded as a reliever in the Arizona Fall League after the 2016 season, and his average fastball and mediocre breaking stuff don't make him a great matchup option out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years as a starter at Broward (Fla.) JC, Scott worked just 14 innings in two seasons as a reliever at Florida State, so it was no surprise he went undrafted after graduating in 2011. The Red Sox noticed him while he was stringing together 11 shutout innings on an independent league team managed by Jose Canseco, and they signed him that August. He spent the next five years making the climb from Rookie ball to the big leagues, where he made seven scoreless appearances last September. There's no point in using a radar gun to gauge Scott, who averages 87 mph and only rarely hits 90 mph with his fastball, but his deception is off the charts. He varies his arm angle while mixing a running fastball, sweeping slider and tumbling changeup. He shuts down left-handed hitters and holds his own against right-handers, though he can been vulnerable to home runs (15 in 2015-16) against the latter. Scott has little margin for error, but he knows it and thrives on the edge. He goes after hitters and won't beat himself with walks. He's already exceeded expectations and scouting reports, and he could fill a specialist role for Boston in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Means began his college career at Fort Scott CC (Kan.) before transferring to West Virginia, where he excelled for two seasons in the Mountaineers' rotation before the Orioles made him their 11th-round Draft pick in 2014. The durable left-hander dominated last season back at Class A Advanced Frederick to earn a late-May promotion to Double-A Bowie, where he opened the 2017 season. A 6-foot-3 lefty, Means uses his height to create downhill plane toward the plate, giving him a propensity for generating groundball outs with a 88-92 mph heater. His curveball, which flashes above average, has good pace and shape, and he's adept at throwing it for strikes. Means' changeup has the potential to be a Major League average offering as well, while his advanced control allows him to get the most out of his three-pitch mix. Means is never going to miss many bats, but he knows how to get outs and rarely hurts himself with walks. All in all, Means has the makings of a future back-end starter who could also serve as a solid lefty reliever capable of working multiple frames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two full years with the Tigers since coming out of Rice in 2013, Kubitza pitched out of a rotation with mixed results. Season one in the Midwest League was a success, while a double-jump to Double-A the following year did not go well. A move to the bullpen may help Kubitza find his way again, even if the early results don't necessarily show it. Kubitza's average fastball has some serious sink to it, making him an extreme ground-ball pitcher who had a 2.77 groundout-to-flyout ratio entering 2017. Kubitza struggles commanding his fastball and that did continue even in the bullpen, though there's hope it will improve. He throws a slider and a changeup, both inconsistent, as his sinker is really his go-to pitch. Freed from having to worry about turning a lineup over and facing hitters repeatedly, the hope is Kubitza will be able to relax and get in a groove as a full-time reliever, the kind who is called upon with runners on base to get a big inning-ending ground ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gallagher's father Glenn and his brother Austin were both third-round picks, and Cam surpassed them both by going in the second round in 2011. When he signed for an above-slot $750,000 bonus, his offensive potential outshone his defensive prowess. Six years later, the exact opposite is true, as Gallagher's catching ability was the reason the Royals added him to the 40-man roster last November. Though Gallagher is big for a catcher at 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds, he moves well behind the plate. He receives and blocks well, and he's a skilled pitch-framer. Gallagher's solid arm strength and impressive accuracy helped him lead the Double-A Texas League by throwing out 48 percent of basestealers last year. A .234/.314/.339 hitter through his first six pro seasons, Gallagher doesn't produce enough to be more than a backup. He has ordinary bat speed and doesn't do much beyond putting the ball in play consistently. Gallagher offers modest power and no speed on the basepaths.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De Los Santos began his career as a starter with the Rangers, but after a few years and little progress, he moved into the bullpen and started taking off. The Nationals noticed and acquired him following the 2014 season in the Ross Detwiler deal and the right-hander made his big league debut the following season. The Reds claimed him when the Nats put him on waivers last July and gave him a little more big league time. When Cincinnati placed him on waivers this offseason, the Angels pounced. While De Los Santos has had some inconsistent performances at the upper levels, he shows flashes of plus stuff in the strike zone, thrown with a very quick arm. He'll generate weak contact on his live fastball that reaches 95 mph with some deception. He has a big breaking curve ball that misses bats and a decent slider. He does have a changeup, but he rarely uses it. De Los Santos has gotten a taste of the highest level in each of the last two years, giving him a sense of what's needed to succeed at the level. He gives the Angels some depth and at just 24, he still has time to figure out how to get back there full-time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morales spent seven summers in the Mariners organization without too much progress. Four of those were in the Venezuelan Summer League and one in the rookie-level Arizona League. He finally reached full-season ball as a reliever in 2015, then got a chance to start in the California League a year ago and finished seventh in the circuit in strikeouts. When he became a Minor League free agent, the Angels made him an early target. The right-hander has missed bats wherever he's gone, striking out more than 10 batters per nine innings without the luxury of an above-average pitch. His upper-80s fastball plays up because he has outstanding extension and very good spin. He gets swings and misses on his curveball and changeup as well and will occasionally mix in a slider. He throws them all with a lot of deception and hitters simply don't pick up the ball well. Even with his slow path over the first several years of his career, Morales is still only 24 years old. His ceiling is undoubtedly limited given the lack of a true out pitch, but it was certainly a low-risk move to see if he can build on the step forward he took in 2016.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A high school draftee of the Orioles in 2012, Grendell couldn't get to full-season ball and was released following the 2015 season. Angels scouts had some good reports on the left-hander and rolled the dice, signing him to a Minor League deal. Pitching entirely in relief, Grendell pitched across three levels, reaching Double-A and putting himself on the prospect map. He earned his first invite to big league camp this spring, but spent the first two and a half months of the 2017 season on the disabled list. Grendell has always missed bats and induced a swing-and-miss rate about 60 percent higher than league average in 2016. He does it with a low-to-mid-90s fastball and a good breaking ball. He has a changeup, one he didn't use much in A ball, but started to employ effectively at times when he was in Double-A. Control continues to be an issue, something he'll have to refine to continue to have success at the upper levels. Grendell, who is hearing impaired and hopes to inspire others by reaching the big leagues, has the raw stuff to help a bullpen there. All he needs is more healthy reps at the upper levels and an ability to find the strike zone more consistently to reach his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport athlete at LSU -- he was the football team's back-up quarterback -- Foster didn't play a ton of baseball until his senior season, collecting just 61 at-bats as a junior, but over 200 in his final year before getting selected in the fifth round of the 2015 Draft by the Angels. He had a solid first full year, earning a promotion in July. His progress was slowed in his second season however, as he landed on the disabled list in mid-May. The 2016 season, when Foster picked up 427 at-bats, was the most baseball the athletic outfielder had ever played in his life. So while he's 24 years old, his experience on the diamond doesn't match his age. He has a pretty solid approach at the plate and has some gap power, with potentially more to come. A plus runner, his stolen-base numbers should also improve, and he made good progress on his reads and routes in the outfield. Foster's baseball skills are still raw, and his time on the DL in 2017 doesn't help, but the tools are all there. The more reps he gets, the more those tools will become refined, and the more they will show up in his everyday performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels obviously believe in Garcia's upside. They wouldn't have given him $565,000 to sign in July 2014 otherwise. But the talented shortstop hasn't been able to take any steps forward as a series of injuries has kept him from important development time. The most recent malady was a fractured cheekbone suffered when he fouled a bunt off his face, limiting him to just 14 Rookie-level Arizona League games in 2016. The adversity has helped Garcia mature, a small silver lining, and he has also grown physically. He looks like a big league shortstop now, with outstanding defensive actions and a strong arm. He has a good swing from both sides of the plate, but hasn't made any progress offensively, largely due to all of the missed time on the field. Still a teenager, Garcia has time to figure things out and get his career moving in the right direction. He's yet to amass a full season's worth of at-bats in his three years in the organization, so staying healthy and putting in a full year will be a good first step.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout at Louisiana-Lafayette, Adams has been an organizational favorite since being taken in the 10th round of the 2014 Draft because of his makeup and hustle on the field. He also hit well enough to advance, reaching Double-A in his second full season, though the leap proved to be a difficult one for him. Adams does have some offensive skills, showing the ability to make hard contact with some extra-base pop at times. There's always been some swing and miss to his game, but he did a fair job at drawing walks early on. He lost his approach in Double-A, with his strikeout rate going up and his walk rate dropping following his promotion. A solid average runner, Adams is capable of playing center, but is better suited for an outfield corner position. Adams will need to show he can adjust the more difficult pitching he'll face in the upper levels of the system. He certainly won't be outworked and could eventually make his way to the big leagues as a fourth or fifth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Billy Eppler spent 11 years with the Yankees before becoming the general manager of the Angels, so he had a long history with Banuelos, who once upon a time was an elite-level prospect in that organization. Since that time, he missed nearly two seasons dealing with Tommy John surgery and rehab, got traded to the Braves, made his big league debut, then saw his 2016 season derailed by more elbow soreness. When Atlanta released him, Eppler scooped him up. The Angels felt it was a low-risk move with the chance of a pretty high reward. Banuelos came to the Angels' complex in Arizona over the fall and invested himself in a program with the strength and conditioning staff. That's enabled him to get back to 100 percent healthy, where perhaps he can utilize his four-pitch mix effectively once again. All of his pitches are average, with the exception of his changeup, but he can mix his pitches well and the relatively new cutter gives him one more weapon. Banuelos will get stretched out and get a chance to start once again. Despite all of his setbacks, he'll still only be 26 years old for the 2017 season, with plenty of time to impact a big league pitching staff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hinshaw had a lot of early momentum going in his career as a senior sign who had a solid first full season in 2014, backed it up with a 2015 season that saw him reach Double-A and capped it off with a strong Arizona Fall League performance. But injuries derailed his return to that level in 2016 and his offense regressed against Texas League pitching. When Hinshaw was swinging the bat well, he was using the middle of the field and showed some capacity to drive the ball. He wasn't able to do that consistently in 2016 and his extra-base pop seemed to vanish to an extent. With good speed, Hinshaw is aggressive on the bases and covers a lot of ground in the outfield. He's played more center field than anywhere else, but is capable of manning all three outfield spots defensively. The Illinois State product is still on the depth chart, though he's fallen behind some others in the system. The key is for him to stay healthy after 79 games in 2015 and just 62 the season after that, so he can get the reps at the plate he needs.
